an2.5:1.11.verse: “Gladly would we let the flesh & blood in our bodies dry up, leaving just the skin, tendons, & bones, but if we have not attained what can be reached through manly firmness, manly persistence, manly striving, there will be no relaxing our persistence.”’

an2.5:1.12.verse: That’s how you should train yourselves.”

an2.9:1.1.verse: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world.

an2.9:1.4.verse: If these two bright qualities did not guard the world, there would be no recognition of ‘mother’ here, no recognition of ‘mother’s sister,’ ‘uncle’s wife,’ ‘teacher’s wife,’ or ‘wives of those who deserve respect.’

an2.9:1.5.verse: The world would be immersed in promiscuity, like rams with goats, roosters with pigs, or dogs with jackals.

an2.9:1.6.verse: But because these two bright qualities guard the world, there is recognition of ‘mother,’ ‘mother’s sister,’ ‘uncle’s wife,’ ‘teacher’s wife,’ & ‘wives of those who deserve respect.’”

an2.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an2.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an2.1:2.3.verse: The fault apparent in this life, and the fault to do with lives to come.

an2.1:2.4.verse: What is the fault apparent in this life?

an2.1:2.5.verse: It’s when someone sees that kings have arrested a bandit, a criminal, and subjected them to various punishments—

an2.1:2.6.verse: whipping, caning, and clubbing; cutting off hands or feet, or both; cutting off ears or nose, or both; the ‘porridge pot’, the ‘shell-shave’, the ‘Rāhu’s mouth’, the ‘garland of fire’, the ‘burning hand’, the ‘bulrush twist’, the ‘bark dress’, the ‘antelope’, the ‘meat hook’, the ‘coins’, the ‘caustic pickle’, the ‘twisting bar’, the ‘straw mat’; being splashed with hot oil, being fed to the hounds, being impaled alive, and being beheaded.

an2.1:3.2.verse: ‘If I were to commit the kinds of bad deeds for which the kings arrested that bandit, that criminal,

an2.1:3.4.verse: the rulers would arrest me and subject me to the same punishments.’

an2.1:3.6.verse: Afraid of the fault apparent in this life, they do not steal the belongings of others.

an2.1:3.7.verse: This is called the fault apparent in this life.

an2.1:4.1.verse: What is the fault to do with lives to come?

an2.1:4.3.verse: ‘Bad conduct of body, speech, or mind has a bad, painful result in the next life.

an2.1:4.5.verse: then, when my body breaks up, after death, won’t I be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell?’

an2.1:4.6.verse: Afraid of the fault to do with lives to come, they give up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develop good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, keeping themselves pure.

an2.1:4.7.verse: This is called the fault to do with lives to come.

an2.1:4.9.verse: So you should train like this:

an2.1:4.10.verse: ‘We will fear the fault apparent in this life, and we will fear the fault to do with lives to come. We will fear faults, seeing the danger in faults.’

an2.1:4.12.verse: If you fear faults, seeing the danger in faults, you can expect to be freed from all faults.”

an2.2:1.1.verse: “These two endeavors are challenging in the world.

an2.2:1.3.verse: The endeavor of laypeople staying in a home to provide robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. And the endeavor of those gone forth from the lay life to homelessness to let go of all attachments.

an2.2:1.4.verse: These are the two endeavors that are challenging in the world.

an2.2:2.1.verse: The better of these two endeavors is the effort to let go of all attachments.

an2.2:2.2.verse: So you should train like this:

an2.2:2.3.verse: ‘We shall endeavor to let go of all attachments.’

an2.3:1.3.verse: It’s when someone has done bad things and not done good things, by way of body, speech, and mind.

an2.3:1.6.verse: Thinking, ‘I’ve done bad things by way of body, speech, and mind’, they’re mortified. Thinking, ‘I haven’t done good things by way of body, speech, and mind’, they’re mortified.

an2.3:1.9.verse: These are the two things that are mortifying.”

an2.4:1.1.verse: “These two things, mendicants, are not mortifying.

an2.4:1.3.verse: It’s when someone has done good things and not done bad things, by way of body, speech, and mind.

an2.4:1.6.verse: Thinking, ‘I’ve done good things by way of body, speech, and mind’, they’re not mortified. Thinking, ‘I haven’t done bad things by way of body, speech, and mind’, they’re not mortified.

an2.4:1.9.verse: These are the two things that are not mortifying.”

an2.5:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I have learned these two things for myself—

an2.5:1.2.verse: to never be content with skillful qualities, and to never stop trying.

an2.5:1.4.verse: ‘Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.’

an2.5:1.5.verse: It was by diligence that I achieved awakening, and by diligence that I achieved the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

an2.5:1.6.verse: If you too never stop trying, thinking:

an2.5:1.7.verse: ‘Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.’

an2.5:1.8.verse: You will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

an2.5:1.9.verse: So you should train like this:

an2.5:1.11.verse: “Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.”’

an2.6:1.3.verse: Seeing things that tighten the fetters as gratifying, and seeing things that tighten the fetters as boring.

an2.6:1.4.verse: When you keep seeing things that tighten the fetters as gratifying, you don’t give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an2.6:1.5.verse: When these are not given up, you’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

an2.6:1.6.verse: You’re not freed from suffering, I say.

an2.6:2.1.verse: When you keep seeing things that tighten the fetters as boring, you give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an2.6:2.2.verse: When these are given up, you’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

an2.6:2.3.verse: You’re freed from suffering, I say.

an2.7:1.4.verse: These are the two things that are dark.”

an2.8:1.4.verse: These are the two things that are bright.”

an2.9:1.1.verse: “These two bright things, mendicants, protect the world.

an2.9:1.4.verse: If these two bright things did not protect the world, there would be no recognition of the status of mother, aunts, or wives and partners of tutors and respected people.

an2.9:1.5.verse: The world would become dissolute, like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and hounds and jackals.

an2.9:1.6.verse: But because the two bright things protect the world, there is recognition of the status of mother, aunts, and wives and partners of tutors and respected people.”

an2.10:1.1.verse: “There are, mendicants, these two entries to the rainy season.

an2.10:1.4.verse: These are the two entries to the rainy season.”

an2.18:1.1.verse: Then Ven. Ānanda went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him,

an2.18:1.2.verse: “I say categorically, Ānanda, that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct should not be done.”

an2.18:1.3.verse: “Given that the Blessed One has declared, lord, that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct should not be done, what drawbacks can one expect when doing what should not be done?”

an2.18:1.4.verse: “Given that I have declared, Ānanda, that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct should not be done, these are the drawbacks one can expect when doing what should not be done:

an2.18:1.6.verse: observant people, on close examination, criticize one;

an2.18:1.7.verse: one’s bad reputation gets spread about;

an2.18:1.9.verse: and—on the break-up of the body, after death—one reappears in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.

an2.18:1.10.verse: Given that I have declared, Ānanda, that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct should not be done, these are the drawbacks one can expect when doing what should not be done.

an2.18:2.1.verse: “I say categorically, Ānanda, that good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, & good mental conduct should be done.”

an2.18:2.2.verse: “Given that the Blessed One has declared, lord, that good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, & good mental conduct should be done, what rewards can one expect when doing what should be done?”

an2.18:2.3.verse: “Given that I have declared, Ānanda, that good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, & good mental conduct should be done, these are the rewards one can expect when doing what should be done:

an2.18:2.5.verse: observant people, on close examination, praise one;

an2.18:2.6.verse: one’s good reputation gets spread about;

an2.18:2.8.verse: and—on the break-up of the body, after death—one reappears in a good destination, a heavenly world.

an2.18:2.9.verse: Given that I have declared, Ānanda, that good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, & good mental conduct should be done, these are the rewards one can expect when doing what should be done.”

an2.19:1.2.verse: It is possible to abandon what is unskillful.

an2.19:1.3.verse: If it were not possible to abandon what is unskillful, I would not say to you,

an2.19:1.5.verse: But because it is possible to abandon what is unskillful, I say to you,

an2.19:1.7.verse: If this abandoning of what is unskillful were conducive to harm and pain, I would not say to you,

an2.19:1.9.verse: But because this abandoning of what is unskillful is conducive to benefit and pleasure, I say to you,

an2.19:2.2.verse: It is possible to develop what is skillful.

an2.19:2.3.verse: If it were not possible to develop what is skillful, I would not say to you,

an2.19:2.5.verse: But because it is possible to develop what is skillful, I say to you,

an2.19:2.7.verse: If this development of what is skillful were conducive to harm and pain, I would not say to you,

an2.19:2.9.verse: But because this development of what is skillful is conducive to benefit and pleasure, I say to you,

an2.11:1.3.verse: The power of reflection and the power of development.

an2.11:1.4.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of reflection?

an2.11:1.6.verse: ‘Bad conduct of body, speech, or mind has a bad, painful result in both this life and the next.’

an2.11:1.7.verse: Reflecting like this, they give up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develop good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, keeping themselves pure.

an2.11:1.8.verse: This is called the power of reflection.

an2.11:2.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of development?

an2.11:2.2.verse: In this context, the power of development is the power of the trainees.

an2.11:2.3.verse: For when you rely on the power of a trainee, you give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an2.11:2.4.verse: Then you don’t do anything unskillful, or practice anything bad.

an2.11:2.5.verse: This is called the power of development.

an2.12:1.3.verse: The power of reflection and the power of development.

an2.12:1.4.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of reflection?

an2.12:1.6.verse: ‘Bad conduct of body, speech, or mind has a bad, painful result in both this life and the next.’

an2.12:1.7.verse: Reflecting like this, they give up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develop good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, keeping themselves pure.

an2.12:1.8.verse: This is called the power of reflection.

an2.12:2.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of development?

an2.12:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

an2.12:2.8.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

an2.12:2.9.verse: This is called the power of development.

an2.13:1.3.verse: The power of reflection and the power of development.

an2.13:1.4.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of reflection?

an2.13:1.6.verse: ‘Bad conduct of body, speech, or mind has a bad, painful result in both this life and the next.’

an2.13:1.7.verse: Reflecting like this, they give up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develop good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, keeping themselves pure.

an2.13:1.8.verse: This is called the power of reflection.

an2.13:2.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the power of development?

an2.13:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an2.13:2.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an2.13:2.4.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

an2.13:2.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an2.13:2.6.verse: This is called the power of development.

an2.14:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the Realized One has two ways of teaching the Dhamma.

an2.14:1.4.verse: These are the Realized One’s two ways of teaching the Dhamma.”

an2.15:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, in a disciplinary issue, if neither the offending mendicant nor the accusing mendicant carefully checks themselves, you can expect that issue

an2.15:1.2.verse: will lead to lasting acrimony and enmity, and the mendicants won’t live comfortably.

an2.15:1.3.verse: But in a disciplinary issue, if both the offending mendicant and the accusing mendicant carefully check themselves, you can expect that issue

an2.15:1.4.verse: won’t lead to lasting acrimony and enmity, and the mendicants will live comfortably.

an2.15:2.1.verse: And how, mendicants, does an offending mendicant carefully check themselves?

an2.15:2.3.verse: ‘I have committed a certain unskillful offense with the body.

an2.15:2.4.verse: That mendicant saw me do this.

an2.15:2.5.verse: If I hadn’t committed that offense, they wouldn’t have seen me.

an2.15:2.6.verse: But since I did commit that offense, they did see me.

an2.15:2.7.verse: When they saw me, they were upset,

an2.15:2.8.verse: and they voiced their unhappiness to me.

an2.15:2.11.verse: So the mistake is mine alone, like someone who owes customs duty on their goods.’

an2.15:2.12.verse: That’s how, mendicants, an offending mendicant carefully checks themselves.

an2.15:3.1.verse: And how, mendicants, does an accusing mendicant carefully check themselves?

an2.15:3.3.verse: ‘This mendicant has committed a certain unskillful offense with the body.

an2.15:3.5.verse: If they hadn’t committed that offense, I wouldn’t have seen them.

an2.15:3.6.verse: But since they did commit that offense, I did see them.

an2.15:3.7.verse: When I saw them, I was upset,

an2.15:3.8.verse: and I voiced my unhappiness to them.

an2.15:3.11.verse: So the mistake is mine alone, like someone who owes customs duty on their goods.’

an2.15:3.12.verse: That’s how, mendicants, an accusing mendicant carefully checks themselves.

an2.15:4.1.verse: In a disciplinary issue, if neither the offending mendicant nor the accusing mendicant carefully checks themselves, you can expect that issue will lead to lasting acrimony and enmity, and the mendicants won’t live comfortably.

an2.15:4.2.verse: But in a disciplinary issue, if both the offending mendicant and the accusing mendicant carefully checks themselves, you can expect that issue won’t lead to lasting acrimony and enmity, and the mendicants will live comfortably.”

an2.16:1.1.verse: Then a certain brahmin went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

an2.16:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an2.16:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell?”

an2.16:1.4.verse: “Unprincipled and immoral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.”

an2.16:2.1.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”

an2.16:2.2.verse: “Principled and moral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

an2.16:3.2.verse: As if he was righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an2.16:3.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an2.16:3.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an2.17:1.1.verse: Then the brahmin Jānussoṇi went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an2.17:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an2.17:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell?”

an2.17:1.4.verse: “What they’ve done and what they’ve not done.

an2.17:1.5.verse: That’s why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.”

an2.17:1.6.verse: “But what is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”

an2.17:1.7.verse: “What they’ve done and what they’ve not done.

an2.17:1.8.verse: That’s why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

an2.17:1.9.verse: “I don’t understand the meaning of what the worthy Gotama has said in brief, without explaining the details.

an2.17:1.10.verse: Worthy Gotama, please teach me this matter in detail so I can understand the meaning.”

an2.17:1.11.verse: “Well then, brahmin, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an2.17:2.1.verse: “Firstly, brahmin, someone has done bad things and not done good things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an2.17:2.4.verse: So what they’ve done and what they’ve not done is why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an2.17:2.5.verse: Furthermore, brahmin, someone has done good things and not done bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an2.17:2.8.verse: So what they’ve done and what they’ve not done is why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

an2.17:3.1.verse: “Excellent, worthy Gotama! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an2.18:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

an2.18:1.2.verse: “Ānanda, I absolutely say that you should not do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.”

an2.18:1.3.verse: “But, sir, if someone does these things that should not be done, what drawbacks should they expect?”

an2.18:1.6.verse: After examination, sensible people criticize them.

an2.18:1.8.verse: They feel lost when they die.

an2.18:1.9.verse: And when their body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an2.18:1.10.verse: These are the drawbacks they should expect.”

an2.18:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, I absolutely say that you should do good things by way of body, speech, and mind.”

an2.18:2.2.verse: “But, sir, if someone does these things that should be done, what benefits should they expect?”

an2.18:2.5.verse: After examination, sensible people praise them.

an2.18:2.7.verse: They don’t feel lost when they die.

an2.18:2.8.verse: And when the body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an2.18:2.9.verse: These are the benefits they should expect.”

an2.19:1.2.verse: It is possible to give up the unskillful.

an2.19:1.3.verse: If it wasn’t possible, I wouldn’t say:

an2.19:1.5.verse: But it is possible, and so I say:

an2.19:1.7.verse: And if giving up the unskillful led to harm and suffering, I would not say:

an2.19:1.9.verse: But giving up the unskillful leads to welfare and happiness, so I say:

an2.19:2.2.verse: It is possible to develop the skillful.

an2.19:2.3.verse: If it wasn’t possible, I wouldn’t say:

an2.19:2.5.verse: But it is possible, and so I say:

an2.19:2.7.verse: If developing the skillful led to harm and suffering I wouldn’t say:

an2.19:2.9.verse: But developing the skillful leads to welfare and happiness, so I say:

an2.20:1.1.verse: “These two things, mendicants, lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching.

an2.20:1.3.verse: The words and phrases are misplaced, and the meaning is misinterpreted.

an2.20:1.4.verse: When the words and phrases are misplaced, the meaning is misinterpreted.

an2.20:1.5.verse: These two things lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching.

an2.20:2.1.verse: These two things lead to the continuation, persistence, and enduring of the true teaching.

an2.20:2.3.verse: The words and phrases are well organized, and the meaning is correctly interpreted.

an2.20:2.4.verse: When the words and phrases are well organized, the meaning is correctly interpreted.

an2.20:2.5.verse: These two things lead to the continuation, persistence, and enduring of the true teaching.”

an2.21:1.3.verse: The one who doesn’t see his transgression as a transgression, and the one who doesn’t rightfully pardon another who has confessed his transgression.

an2.21:2.3.verse: The one who sees his transgression as a transgression, and the one who rightfully pardons another who has confessed his transgression.

an2.23:1.3.verse: He who explains what was not said or spoken by the Tathāgata as said or spoken by the Tathāgata. And he who explains what was said or spoken by the Tathāgata as not said or spoken by the Tathāgata.

an2.23:1.4.verse: These are the two who slander the Tathāgata.”

an2.24:1.3.verse: He who explains a discourse whose meaning needs to be inferred as one whose meaning has already been fully drawn out. And he who explains a discourse whose meaning has already been fully drawn out as one whose meaning needs to be inferred.

an2.24:1.4.verse: These are the two who slander the Tathāgata.”

an2.31:1.0.verse: 29–30. A Share in Clear Knowing & Release

an2.31:1.1.verse: “These two qualities have a share in clear knowing.

an2.31:1.4.verse: “When tranquility is developed, what purpose does it serve?

an2.31:1.6.verse: And when the mind is developed, what purpose does it serve?

an2.31:1.8.verse: “When insight is developed, what purpose does it serve?

an2.31:1.10.verse: And when discernment is developed, what purpose does it serve?

an2.31:1.12.verse: “Defiled by passion, the mind is not released. Defiled by ignorance, discernment does not develop.

an2.31:1.13.verse: Thus from the fading of passion is there awareness-release. From the fading of ignorance is there discernment-release.”

an2.21:1.3.verse: One who doesn’t recognize when they’ve made a mistake. And one who doesn’t properly accept the confession of someone who’s made a mistake.

an2.21:2.1.verse: There are two who are astute.

an2.21:2.3.verse: One who recognizes when they’ve made a mistake. And one who properly accepts the confession of someone who’s made a mistake.

an2.21:2.4.verse: These are the two who are astute.”

an2.22:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.22:1.3.verse: One who is hateful and hides it, and one whose faith is mistaken.

an2.22:1.4.verse: These two misrepresent the Realized One.”

an2.23:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.23:1.3.verse: One who explains what was not spoken by the Realized One as spoken by him. And one who explains what was spoken by the Realized One as not spoken by him.

an2.23:1.4.verse: These two misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.23:2.1.verse: These two don’t misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.23:2.3.verse: One who explains what was not spoken by the Realized One as not spoken by him. And one who explains what was spoken by the Realized One as spoken by him.

an2.23:2.4.verse: These two don’t misrepresent the Realized One.”

an2.24:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.24:1.3.verse: One who explains a discourse in need of interpretation as a discourse whose meaning is explicit. And one who explains a discourse whose meaning is explicit as a discourse in need of interpretation.

an2.24:1.4.verse: These two misrepresent the Realized One.”

an2.25:1.1.verse: “These two don’t misrepresent the Realized One.

an2.25:1.3.verse: One who explains a discourse in need of interpretation as a discourse in need of interpretation. And one who explains a discourse whose meaning is explicit as a discourse whose meaning is explicit.

an2.25:1.4.verse: These two don’t misrepresent the Realized One.”

an2.26:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, one who is underhand can expect one of two destinies:

an2.26:2.1.verse: One who is aboveboard can expect one of two destinies:

an2.26:2.2.verse: as a god or a human.”

an2.27:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, one who has wrong view can expect one of two destinies:

an2.28:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, one who has right view can expect one of two destinies:

an2.28:1.2.verse: as a god or a human.”

an2.29:1.1.verse: “There are two places waiting to receive an unethical person:

an2.29:2.1.verse: There are two places waiting to receive an ethical person:

an2.29:2.2.verse: the realms of gods and humans.”

an2.30:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I see two reasons to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

an2.30:1.3.verse: Seeing happiness for oneself in this life, and having sympathy for future generations.

an2.30:1.4.verse: I see two reasons to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.”

an2.31:1.1.verse: “These two things play a part in realization.

an2.31:1.4.verse: What is the benefit of developing serenity?

an2.31:1.6.verse: What is the benefit of developing the mind?

an2.31:1.8.verse: What is the benefit of developing discernment?

an2.31:1.10.verse: What is the benefit of developing wisdom?

an2.31:1.12.verse: The mind corrupted by greed is not free; and wisdom corrupted by ignorance does not grow.

an2.31:1.13.verse: In this way, freedom of heart comes from the fading away of greed, while freedom by wisdom comes from the fading away of ignorance.”

an2.32:1.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you the level of a person of no integrity and the level of a person of integrity.

an2.32:1.2.verse: Listen & pay close attention. I will speak.”

an2.32:1.3.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monks responded to him.

an2.32:2.1.verse: “Now what is the level of a person of no integrity?

an2.32:2.2.verse: A person of no integrity is ungrateful & unthankful.

an2.32:2.3.verse: This ingratitude, this lack of thankfulness, is advocated by rude people.

an2.32:2.4.verse: It is entirely on the level of people of no integrity.

an2.32:2.5.verse: A person of integrity is grateful & thankful.

an2.32:2.6.verse: This gratitude, this thankfulness, is advocated by civil people.

an2.32:2.7.verse: It is entirely on the level of people of integrity.”

an2.33:1.1.verse: “I tell you, monks, there are two people who are not easy to repay.

an2.33:1.4.verse: Even if you were to carry your mother on one shoulder & your father on the other shoulder for 100 years, and were to look after them by anointing, massaging, bathing, & rubbing their limbs,

an2.33:1.5.verse: and they were to defecate & urinate right there [on your shoulders], you would not in that way pay or repay your parents.

an2.33:1.6.verse: If you were to establish your mother & father in absolute sovereignty over this great earth, abounding in the seven treasures, you would not in that way pay or repay your parents.

an2.33:1.8.verse: Mother & father do much for their children. They care for them, they nourish them, they introduce them to this world.

an2.33:1.9.verse: But anyone who rouses his unbelieving mother & father, settles & establishes them in conviction; rouses his unvirtuous mother & father, settles & establishes them in virtue; rouses his stingy mother & father, settles & establishes them in generosity; rouses his foolish mother & father, settles & establishes them in discernment: To this extent one pays & repays one’s mother & father.“

an2.36:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an2.36:1.3.verse: And on that occasion Ven. Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother.

an2.36:1.6.verse: “Yes, friend,” the monks responded to him.

an2.36:1.8.verse: “Friends, I will teach you the person fettered outside & the person fettered inside.

an2.36:1.9.verse: Listen to that & pay careful attention. I will speak.”

an2.36:1.10.verse: “As you say, friend,” the monks responded to him.

an2.36:2.1.verse: “And which, friends, is the person fettered inside?

an2.36:2.2.verse: There is the case where a monk is virtuous. He dwells restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in his behavior & sphere of activity. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.

an2.36:2.3.verse: He—with the breakup of the body, after death—reappears in a certain deva-host.

an2.36:2.4.verse: Falling from there, he is a returner, one who returns to this state of being.

an2.36:2.5.verse: This is called a person fettered inside, a returner, one who returns to this state of being.

an2.36:3.1.verse: “And which is the person fettered outside?

an2.36:3.2.verse: There is the case where a monk is virtuous. He dwells restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in his behavior & sphere of activity. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.

an2.36:3.3.verse: He enters & remains in a certain peaceful awareness release.

an2.36:3.4.verse: He—with the breakup of the body, after death—reappears in a certain deva-host.

an2.36:3.5.verse: Falling from there, he is a non-returner, one who doesn’t return to this state of being.

an2.36:3.6.verse: This is called a person fettered outside, a non-returner, one who doesn’t return to this state of being.

an2.36:4.1.verse: “Then again, a monk is virtuous. He dwells restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in his behavior & sphere of activity. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.

an2.36:4.2.verse: He is one who practices for disenchantment, for dispassion, for & the cessation of sensuality.

an2.36:4.3.verse: He is one who practices for disenchantment, for dispassion, for & the cessation of becoming.

an2.36:4.4.verse: He is one who practices for the ending of craving.

an2.36:4.5.verse: He is one who practices for the ending of greed.

an2.36:4.6.verse: He—with the breakup of the body, after death—reappears in a certain deva-host.

an2.36:4.7.verse: Falling from there, he is a non-returner, one who doesn’t return to this state of being.

an2.36:4.8.verse: This is called a person fettered outside, a non-returner, one who doesn’t return to this state of being.”

an2.36:5.1.verse: Then many Like-minded Devas went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side. As they were standing there, they said to him,

an2.36:5.2.verse: “Lord, Ven. Sāriputta, in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, is teaching the monks about the person fettered inside & the person fettered outside.

an2.36:5.4.verse: It would be good, lord, if the Blessed One went to Ven. Sāriputta, out of sympathy.”

an2.36:5.5.verse: The Blessed One acquiesced with silence.

an2.36:5.6.verse: Then—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—the Blessed One disappeared from Jeta’s Grove and re-appeared in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, right in front of Ven. Sāriputta.

an2.36:5.7.verse: He sat down on a seat laid out.

an2.36:5.8.verse: Ven. Sāriputta, bowing down to the Blessed One, sat to one side.

an2.36:5.9.verse: As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him,

an2.36:6.1.verse: “Just now, Sāriputta, many Like-minded Devas went to me and, on arrival, having bowed down to me, stood to one side. As they were standing there, they said to me,

an2.36:6.2.verse: ‘Lord, Ven. Sāriputta, in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, is teaching the monks about the person fettered inside & the person fettered outside.

an2.36:6.4.verse: It would be good, lord, if the Blessed One went to Ven. Sāriputta, out of sympathy.’

an2.36:6.5.verse: “Those devas, Sāriputta— whether there are ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty—can stand on an area the size of a hole pierced by the point of an awl and not disturb one another.

an2.36:6.6.verse: And if the thought should occur to you,

an2.36:6.7.verse: ‘Surely it was there [in their heaven] that those devas developed such a mind-state that—whether there are ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty—they can stand on an area the size of a hole pierced by the point of an awl and not disturb one another,’

an2.36:6.8.verse: it shouldn’t be seen that way.

an2.36:6.9.verse: It was right here that they developed such a mind-state that—whether there are ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty—they can stand on an area the size of a hole pierced by the point of an awl and not disturb one another.

an2.36:6.11.verse: ‘We will be peaceful in our faculties & peaceful in our hearts.’

an2.36:6.12.verse: That’s how you should train yourselves.

an2.36:6.13.verse: When you are peaceful in your faculties & peaceful in your hearts, peaceful will be your bodily actions, peaceful your verbal actions, peaceful your mental actions.

an2.36:6.14.verse: [Thinking,] ‘We will render only peaceful service to our fellows in the holy life’:

an2.36:6.15.verse: That’s how you should train yourselves.

an2.36:6.16.verse: “The wanderers of other sects are lost, Sāriputta, in that they don’t get to hear this Dhamma sequence.”

an2.37:1.2.verse: On one occasion Ven. Mahā Kaccāna was staying at Varaṇā on the shore of Kaddama (Muddy) Lake.

an2.37:1.3.verse: Then Ārāmadaṇḍa the brahman went to Ven. Mahā Kaccāna and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him.

an2.37:1.4.verse: After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to Ven. Mahā Kaccāna,

an2.37:1.5.verse: “What is the cause, Master Kaccāna, what is the reason, why noble warriors dispute with noble warriors, brahmans dispute with brahmans, and householders dispute with householders?”

an2.37:1.6.verse: “Brahman, it’s with relishing, possession, greed, bondage, & entrenchment in passion for sensuality as a cause that noble warriors dispute with noble warriors, brahmans dispute with brahmans, and householders dispute with householders.”

an2.37:2.1.verse: “And what is the cause, Master Kaccāna, what is the reason, why contemplatives dispute with contemplatives?”

an2.37:2.2.verse: “Brahman, it’s with relishing, possession, greed, bondage, & entrenchment in passion for views as a cause that contemplatives dispute with contemplatives.”

an2.37:3.1.verse: “And is there anyone in the world, Master Kaccāna, who has overcome both this relishing… entrenchment in passion for sensuality, and… this relishing… entrenchment in passion for views?”

an2.37:3.2.verse: “There is, brahman, someone in the world who has overcome both this relishing… entrenchment in passion for sensuality, and… this relishing… entrenchment in passion for views.”

an2.37:4.1.verse: “And who in the world, Master Kaccāna, has overcome both this relishing… entrenchment in passion for sensuality, and… this relishing… entrenchment in passion for views?”

an2.37:4.2.verse: “There is, brahman, in the eastern countryside, a city named Sāvatthī.

an2.37:4.3.verse: There the Blessed One—the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One—is now dwelling.

an2.37:4.4.verse: That Blessed One has overcome this relishing… entrenchment in passion for sensuality, and… this relishing… entrenchment in passion for views.”

an2.37:5.1.verse: When this was said, Ārāmadaṇḍa the brahman—getting up from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, lowering his right knee to the ground, and raising his hands palm-to-palm over the heart—exclaimed three times:

an2.37:6.1.verse: “Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One!

an2.37:7.1.verse: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One!

an2.37:8.1.verse: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One!

an2.37:9.1.verse: For that Blessed One is one who has overcome both this relishing, possession, greed, bondage, & entrenchment in passion for sensuality, and this relishing, possession, greed, bondage, & entrenchment in passion for views!

an2.37:10.2.verse: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Kaccāna—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

an2.37:10.3.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, & to the Saṅgha of monks.

an2.37:10.4.verse: May Master Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for life.”

an2.38:1.1.verse: On one occasion Ven. Mahā Kaccāna was staying near Madhura in the Gundā Forest.

an2.38:1.2.verse: Then Kaṇḍarāyana the brahman went to Ven. Mahā Kaccāna and on arrival exchanged courteous greetings with him. After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to Ven. Mahā Kaccāna,

an2.38:1.3.verse: “I have heard it said, Master Kaccāna, that, ‘Kaccāna the contemplative does not raise his hands in respect to aged, venerable brahmans—advanced in years, come to the last stage of life—nor does he rise up to greet them, nor does he offer them a seat.’

an2.38:1.4.verse: Insofar as you don’t raise your hands in respect to aged, venerable brahmans—advanced in years, come to the last stage of life—

an2.38:1.5.verse: nor rise up to greet them, nor offer them a seat,

an2.38:1.6.verse: that is simply not right, Master Kaccāna.”

an2.38:2.1.verse: “Brahman, the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—has declared the level of one who is venerable and the level of one who is a youngster.

an2.38:2.2.verse: Even if one is venerable—80, 90, 100 years old—yet if one partakes of sensuality, lives in the midst of sensuality, burns with sensual fever, is chewed up by sensual thoughts, and is eager in the search for sensuality,

an2.38:2.3.verse: then one is reckoned simply as a young fool, not an elder.

an2.38:2.4.verse: But if one is a youngster, youthful—a black-haired young person endowed with the blessings of youth in the first stage of life—

an2.38:2.5.verse: yet does not partake of sensuality, does not live in the midst of sensuality, does not burn with sensual fever, is not chewed up by sensual thoughts, and is not eager in the search for sensuality,

an2.38:2.6.verse: then one is reckoned as a wise elder.”

an2.38:3.1.verse: When this was said, Kaṇḍarāyana the brahman rose up from his seat, arranged his cloak over one shoulder, and bowed down at the feet of the monks who were youngsters, (saying,)

an2.38:3.2.verse: “You, sirs, are the venerable ones, standing on the level of those who are venerable.

an2.38:3.3.verse: We are the youngsters, standing on the level of those who are youngsters.

an2.38:4.1.verse: “Magnificent, Master Kaccāna! Magnificent! Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Kaccāna—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, & to the Saṅgha of monks. May Master Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for life.”

an2.32:0.2.verse: The Chapter on the Peaceful Mind

an2.32:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the level of the untrue person and the level of the true person.

an2.32:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an2.32:2.1.verse: “What is the level of the untrue person?

an2.32:2.2.verse: The untrue person is ungrateful and thankless,

an2.32:2.3.verse: for the wicked only know how to be ungrateful and thankless.

an2.32:2.4.verse: It is totally the level of an untrue person to be ungrateful and thankless.

an2.32:2.5.verse: The true person is grateful and thankful,

an2.32:2.6.verse: for the virtuous only know how to be grateful and thankful.

an2.32:2.7.verse: It is totally the level of a true person to be grateful and thankful.”

an2.33:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I say that these two individuals cannot easily be repaid.

an2.33:1.4.verse: You would not have done enough to repay your mother and father even if you were to carry your mother around on one shoulder and your father on the other, and if you lived like this for a hundred years, and if you were to anoint, massage, bathe, and rub them;

an2.33:1.5.verse: and even if they were to defecate and urinate right there.

an2.33:1.6.verse: Even if you were to establish your mother and father as supreme monarchs of this great earth, abounding in the seven treasures, you would still not have done enough to repay them.

an2.33:1.8.verse: Parents are very helpful to their children: they raise them, nurture them, and show them the world.

an2.33:1.9.verse: But you have done enough, more than enough, to repay them if you encourage, settle, and ground unfaithful parents in faith, unethical parents in ethical conduct, stingy parents in generosity, or ignorant parents in wisdom.”

an2.34:1.1.verse: Then a certain brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

an2.34:1.2.verse: “What does the worthy Gotama teach? What does he explain?”

an2.34:1.4.verse: “But in what way does the worthy Gotama teach action and inaction?”

an2.34:2.1.verse: “I teach inaction regarding bad bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an2.34:2.2.verse: I teach action regarding good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and the many kinds of skillful things.

an2.34:2.3.verse: This is the kind of action and inaction that I teach.”

an2.34:3.1.verse: “Excellent, worthy Gotama! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an2.35:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an2.35:1.2.verse: “How many in the world are worthy of a religious donation? And where should a gift be given?”

an2.35:1.3.verse: “Householder, there are two in the world who are worthy of a religious donation:

an2.35:1.5.verse: These two in the world are worthy of a religious donation, and that’s where you should give a gift.”

an2.35:2.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an2.35:2.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

an2.35:3.1.verse: “In this world, the trainee and the adept,

an2.35:3.2.verse: are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods.

an2.35:3.5.verse: This is the field for sponsors of sacrifice—

an2.35:3.6.verse: what’s given here is very fruitful.”

an2.36:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an2.36:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

an2.36:1.8.verse: “I will teach you about an individual fettered internally and one fettered externally.

an2.36:1.9.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an2.36:2.2.verse: It’s a mendicant who is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an2.36:2.3.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an2.36:2.4.verse: When they pass away from there, they’re a returner, who comes back to this place.

an2.36:2.5.verse: This is called an individual who is fettered internally, a returner, who comes back to this place.

an2.36:3.1.verse: Who is an individual fettered externally?

an2.36:3.2.verse: It’s a mendicant who is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an2.36:3.3.verse: They enter and remain in a certain peaceful state of freed mind.

an2.36:3.4.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an2.36:3.5.verse: When they pass away from there, they’re a non-returner, not coming back to this place.

an2.36:3.6.verse: This is called an individual who is fettered externally, a non-returner, who does not come back to this place.

an2.36:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is ethical … they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an2.36:4.2.verse: They simply practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding sensual pleasures.

an2.36:4.3.verse: They simply practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding future lives.

an2.36:4.4.verse: They practice for the ending of craving.

an2.36:4.5.verse: They practice for the ending of greed.

an2.36:4.6.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an2.36:4.7.verse: When they pass away from there, they are non-returners, not coming back to this place.

an2.36:4.8.verse: This is called an individual who is fettered externally, a non-returner, who does not come back to this place.”

an2.36:5.1.verse: Then several peaceful-minded deities went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to the Buddha,

an2.36:5.2.verse: “Sir, Venerable Sāriputta is in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, where he is teaching the mendicants about an individual with internal fetters and one with external fetters.

an2.36:5.4.verse: Sir, please go to Venerable Sāriputta out of sympathy.”

an2.36:5.6.verse: Then the Buddha, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from Jeta’s Grove and reappeared in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, in front of Sāriputta.

an2.36:5.7.verse: He sat down on the seat spread out.

an2.36:5.8.verse: Sāriputta bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side.

an2.36:6.1.verse: “Just now, Sāriputta, several peaceful-minded deities came up to me, bowed, and stood to one side. Those deities said to me:

an2.36:6.2.verse: ‘Sir, Venerable Sāriputta is in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, where he is teaching the mendicants about an individual with internal fetters and one with external fetters.

an2.36:6.4.verse: Sir, please go to Venerable Sāriputta out of sympathy.’

an2.36:6.5.verse: Those deities, though they number ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty, can stand on the point of a needle without bumping up against each other.

an2.36:6.7.verse: ‘Surely those deities, since so many of them can stand on the point of a needle without bumping up against each other, must have developed their minds in that place.’

an2.36:6.8.verse: But you should not see it like this.

an2.36:6.9.verse: It was right here that those deities developed their minds.

an2.36:6.10.verse: So you should train like this:

an2.36:6.11.verse: ‘We shall have peaceful faculties and peaceful minds.’

an2.36:6.13.verse: When your faculties and mind are peaceful, your acts of body, speech, and mind will be peaceful, thinking:

an2.36:6.14.verse: ‘We shall present the gift of peace to our spiritual companions.’

an2.36:6.16.verse: Those wanderers of other religions, Sāriputta, who have not heard this exposition of the teaching are lost.”

an2.37:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying at Varaṇā, on the bank of the Kaddama Lake.

an2.37:1.3.verse: Then the brahmin Ārāmadaṇḍa went up to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

an2.37:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Mahākaccāna:

an2.37:1.5.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Kaccāna, what is the reason why aristocrats fight with aristocrats, brahmins fight with brahmins, and householders fight with householders?”

an2.37:1.6.verse: “It is because of their insistence on sensual desire, their shackles, avarice, and attachment, that aristocrats fight with aristocrats, brahmins fight with brahmins, and householders fight with householders.”

an2.37:2.1.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Kaccāna, what is the reason why ascetics fight with ascetics?”

an2.37:2.2.verse: “It is because of their insistence on views, their shackles, avarice, and attachment, that ascetics fight with ascetics.”

an2.37:3.1.verse: “Worthy Kaccāna, is there anyone in the world who has gone beyond the insistence on sensual desire and the insistence on views?”

an2.37:4.1.verse: “Who in the world has gone beyond the insistence on sensual desire and the insistence on views?”

an2.37:4.2.verse: “In the eastern lands there is a city named Sāvatthī.

an2.37:4.3.verse: There the Blessed One is now staying, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an2.37:4.4.verse: He, brahmin, has gone beyond the insistence on sensual desire and the insistence on views.”

an2.37:5.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Ārāmadaṇḍa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:

an2.37:6.1.verse: “Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

an2.37:7.1.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

an2.37:8.1.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

an2.37:9.1.verse: He who has gone beyond the insistence on sensual desire and the insistence on views.

an2.37:10.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Kaccāna has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an2.37:10.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an2.37:10.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an2.38:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying near Madhurā in the Nut Grass Grove.

an2.38:1.2.verse: Then the brahmin Kandarāyana went up to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him … He sat down to one side and said to Mahākaccāna:

an2.38:1.3.verse: “I have heard, worthy Kaccāna, that the ascetic Kaccāna doesn’t bow to old brahmins, the elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.

an2.38:1.4.verse: And this is indeed the case,

an2.38:1.5.verse: for the ascetic Kaccāna does not bow to old brahmins, elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.

an2.38:1.6.verse: This is not appropriate, worthy Kaccāna.”

an2.38:2.1.verse: “There is the stage of an elder and the stage of youth as explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an2.38:2.2.verse: If an elder, though eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, still dwells in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, consumed by thoughts of them, burning with fever for them, and eagerly seeking more,

an2.38:2.3.verse: they are reckoned as a child, not a senior.

an2.38:2.4.verse: If a youth, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life,

an2.38:2.5.verse: does not dwell in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, consumed by thoughts of them, burning with fever for them, and eagerly seeking more,

an2.38:2.6.verse: they are reckoned as astute, a senior.”

an2.38:3.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Kandarāyana got up from his seat, placed his robe over one shoulder, and bowed with his head to the feet of the young mendicants, saying,

an2.38:3.2.verse: “The good fellows are elders, at the stage of the elder;

an2.38:3.3.verse: we are youths, at the stage of youth.

an2.38:4.1.verse: Excellent, worthy Kaccāna! … From this day forth, may the worthy Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an2.39:1.1.verse: “At a time when bandits are strong, kings are weak.

an2.39:1.2.verse: Then the king is not at ease when going out or coming back or when touring the provinces.

an2.39:1.3.verse: The brahmins and householders, likewise, are not at ease when going out or coming back, or when inspecting their external business activities.

an2.39:1.4.verse: In the same way, at a time when bad mendicants are strong, good-hearted mendicants are weak.

an2.39:1.5.verse: Then the good-hearted mendicants continually adhere to silence in the midst of the Saṅgha, or they stay in the borderlands.

an2.39:1.6.verse: This is for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

an2.39:2.1.verse: At a time when kings are strong, bandits are weak.

an2.39:2.2.verse: Then the king is at ease when going out or coming back or when inspecting the provinces.

an2.39:2.3.verse: The brahmins and householders, likewise, are at ease when going out or coming back, or when inspecting their external business activities.

an2.39:2.4.verse: In the same way, at a time when good-hearted mendicants are strong, bad mendicants are weak.

an2.39:2.5.verse: Then the bad mendicants continually adhere to silence in the midst of the Saṅgha, or they leave for some place or other.

an2.39:2.6.verse: This is for the welfare and happiness of the people, for the people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.”

an2.40:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I don’t praise wrong practice for these two, for laypeople and renunciates.

an2.40:1.2.verse: Because of wrong practice, neither laypeople nor renunciates succeed in completing the system of the skillful teaching.

an2.40:2.1.verse: I praise right practice for these two, for laypeople and renunciates.

an2.40:2.2.verse: Because of right practice, both laypeople and renunciates succeed in completing the system of the skillful teaching.”

an2.41:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, by memorizing the discourses incorrectly, taking only a semblance of the phrasing, some mendicants shut out the meaning and the teaching. They act for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

an2.41:1.2.verse: They brim with much wickedness and make the true teaching disappear.

an2.41:2.1.verse: But by memorizing the discourses well, not taking only a semblance of the phrasing, some mendicants conform to the meaning and the teaching. They act for the welfare and happiness of the people, for the people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

an2.41:2.2.verse: They brim with much merit and make the true teaching continue.”

an2.47:1.3.verse: The assembly trained in bombast and not in cross-questioning, and the assembly trained in cross-questioning and not in bombast.

an2.47:1.4.verse: “And which is the assembly trained in bombast and not in cross-questioning?

an2.47:1.5.verse: There is the case where in any assembly when the discourses of the Tathāgata—deep, deep in their meaning, transcendent, connected with emptiness—are recited, the monks don’t listen, don’t lend ear, don’t set their hearts on knowing them, don’t regard them as worth grasping or mastering.

an2.47:1.6.verse: But when discourses that are literary works—the works of poets, artful in sound, artful in expression, the work of outsiders, words of disciples—are recited, they listen, they lend ear, they set their hearts on knowing them, they regard them as worth grasping & mastering. Yet when they have mastered that Dhamma, they don’t cross-question one another about it, don’t dissect:

an2.47:1.7.verse: ‘How is this? What is the meaning of this?’

an2.47:1.8.verse: They don’t make open what isn’t open, don’t make plain what isn’t plain, don’t dispel doubt on its various doubtful points.

an2.47:1.9.verse: This is called an assembly trained in bombast, not in cross-questioning.

an2.47:2.1.verse: “And which is the assembly trained in cross-questioning and not in bombast?

an2.47:2.2.verse: “There is the case where in any assembly when discourses that are literary works—the works of poets, artful in sound, artful in rhetoric, the work of outsiders, words of disciples—are recited, the monks don’t listen, don’t lend ear, don’t set their hearts on knowing them; don’t regard them as worth grasping or mastering.

an2.47:2.3.verse: But when the discourses of the Tathāgata—deep, deep in their meaning, transcendent, connected with emptiness—are recited, they listen, they lend ear, they set their hearts on knowing them, they regard them as worth grasping & mastering.

an2.47:2.4.verse: And when they have mastered that Dhamma, they cross-question one another about it and dissect it:

an2.47:2.5.verse: ‘How is this? What is the meaning of this?’

an2.47:2.6.verse: They make open what isn’t open, make plain what isn’t plain, dispel doubt on its various doubtful points.

an2.47:2.7.verse: This is called an assembly trained in cross-questioning and not in bombast.”

an2.47:2.8.verse: These, monks, are the two assemblies.

an2.47:2.9.verse: Of these two assemblies, this is supreme: the assembly trained in cross-questioning and not in bombast.”

an2.42:1.3.verse: A shallow assembly and a deep assembly.

an2.42:1.4.verse: And what is a shallow assembly?

an2.42:1.5.verse: An assembly where the mendicants are haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, loose-tongued, unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties.

an2.42:1.6.verse: This is called a shallow assembly.

an2.42:2.1.verse: And what is a deep assembly?

an2.42:2.2.verse: An assembly where the mendicants are not haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, or loose-tongued, but have established mindfulness, situational awareness, immersion, unified minds, and restrained faculties.

an2.42:2.3.verse: This is called a deep assembly.

an2.42:2.5.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the deep assembly.”

an2.43:1.3.verse: A divided assembly and a harmonious assembly.

an2.43:1.4.verse: And what is a divided assembly?

an2.43:1.5.verse: An assembly where the mendicants fight, quarrel, and dispute, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

an2.43:1.6.verse: This is called a divided assembly.

an2.43:2.1.verse: And what is a harmonious assembly?

an2.43:2.2.verse: An assembly where the mendicants live in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.

an2.43:2.3.verse: This is called a harmonious assembly.

an2.43:2.5.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the harmonious assembly.”

an2.44:1.3.verse: An assembly of the worst and an assembly of the best.

an2.44:1.4.verse: And what is an assembly of the worst?

an2.44:1.5.verse: An assembly where the senior mendicants are indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion, not rousing energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an2.44:1.6.verse: Those who come after follow their example.

an2.44:1.7.verse: They too become indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion, not rousing energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an2.44:1.8.verse: This is called an assembly of the worst.

an2.44:2.1.verse: And what is an assembly of the best?

an2.44:2.2.verse: An assembly where the senior mendicants are not indulgent or slack, nor are they backsliders; instead, they take the lead in seclusion, rousing energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an2.44:2.3.verse: Those who come after follow their example.

an2.44:2.4.verse: They too are not indulgent or slack, nor are they backsliders; instead, they take the lead in seclusion, rousing energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an2.44:2.5.verse: This is called an assembly of the best.

an2.44:2.7.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the assembly of the best.”

an2.45:1.3.verse: An ignoble assembly and a noble assembly.

an2.45:1.4.verse: And what is an ignoble assembly?

an2.45:1.5.verse: An assembly where the mendicants don’t truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an2.45:1.6.verse: This is called an ignoble assembly.

an2.45:2.1.verse: And what is a noble assembly?

an2.45:2.2.verse: An assembly where the mendicants truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an2.45:2.3.verse: This is called a noble assembly.

an2.45:2.5.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the noble assembly.”

an2.46:1.3.verse: An assembly of the dregs and an assembly of the cream.

an2.46:1.4.verse: And what is an assembly of the dregs?

an2.46:1.5.verse: An assembly where the mendicants make decisions prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice.

an2.46:1.6.verse: This is called an assembly of the dregs.

an2.46:2.1.verse: And what is an assembly of the cream?

an2.46:2.2.verse: An assembly where the mendicants make decisions unprejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice.

an2.46:2.3.verse: This is called an assembly of the cream.

an2.46:2.5.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the assembly of the cream.”

an2.47:1.3.verse: An assembly educated in fancy talk, not in questioning, and an assembly educated in questioning, not in fancy talk.

an2.47:1.4.verse: And what is an assembly educated in fancy talk, not in questioning?

an2.47:1.5.verse: It is an assembly where, when discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited the mendicants do not want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand, nor do they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

an2.47:1.6.verse: But when discourses composed by poets—poetry, with fancy words and phrases, composed by outsiders or spoken by disciples—are being recited the mendicants do want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand, and they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing. But when they’ve memorized those teachings they don’t question or examine each other, saying:

an2.47:1.7.verse: ‘Why does it say this? What does that mean?’

an2.47:1.8.verse: So they don’t reveal what is hidden or clarify what is unclear, or dispel doubt regarding the many doubtful matters.

an2.47:1.9.verse: This is called an assembly educated in fancy talk, not in questioning.

an2.47:2.1.verse: And what is an assembly educated in questioning, not in fancy talk?

an2.47:2.2.verse: It is an assembly where, when discourses composed by poets—poetry, with fancy words and phrases, composed by outsiders or spoken by disciples—are being recited the mendicants do not want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand, nor do they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

an2.47:2.3.verse: But when discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited the mendicants do want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand, and they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

an2.47:2.4.verse: And when they’ve memorized those teachings they question and examine each other, saying:

an2.47:2.5.verse: ‘Why does it say this? What does that mean?’

an2.47:2.6.verse: So they reveal what is hidden, clarify what is unclear, and dispel doubt regarding the many doubtful matters.

an2.47:2.7.verse: This is called an assembly educated in questioning, not in fancy talk.

an2.47:2.9.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the assembly educated in questioning, not in fancy talk.”

an2.48:1.3.verse: An assembly that values things of the flesh, not the true teaching, and an assembly that values the true teaching, not things of the flesh.

an2.48:1.4.verse: And what is an assembly that values things of the flesh, not the true teaching?

an2.48:1.5.verse: It is an assembly where the mendicants praise each other in front of the white-clothed laypeople, saying:

an2.48:1.6.verse: ‘The mendicant so-and-so is freed both ways; so-and-so is freed by wisdom; so-and-so is a direct witness; so-and-so is attained to view; so-and-so is freed by faith; so-and-so is a follower of teachings; so-and-so is a follower by faith; so-and-so is ethical, of good character; so-and-so is unethical, of bad character.’

an2.48:1.8.verse: And when they get these things, they use them tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

an2.48:1.9.verse: This is called an assembly that values things of the flesh, not the true teaching.

an2.48:2.1.verse: And what is an assembly that values the true teaching, not things of the flesh?

an2.48:2.2.verse: It is an assembly where the mendicants don’t praise each other in front of the white-clothed laypeople, saying:

an2.48:2.3.verse: ‘The mendicant so-and-so is freed both ways; so-and-so is freed by wisdom; so-and-so is a direct witness; so-and-so is attained to view; so-and-so is freed by faith; so-and-so is a follower of teachings; so-and-so is a follower by faith; so-and-so is ethical, of good character; so-and-so is unethical, of bad character.’

an2.48:2.5.verse: And when they get these things, they use them untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

an2.48:2.6.verse: This is called an assembly that values the true teaching, not things of the flesh.

an2.48:2.8.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the assembly that values the true teaching, not things of the flesh.”

an2.49:1.3.verse: An unjust assembly and a just assembly.

an2.49:1.4.verse: And what is an unjust assembly?

an2.49:1.5.verse: An assembly where legal acts against the teaching proceed, while legal acts following the teaching don’t proceed. Legal acts against the training proceed, while legal acts following the training don’t proceed. Legal acts against the teaching are explained, while legal acts following the teaching aren’t explained. Legal acts against the training are explained, while legal acts following the training aren’t explained.

an2.49:1.6.verse: This is called an unjust assembly.

an2.49:2.1.verse: And what is a just assembly?

an2.49:2.2.verse: An assembly where legal acts following the teaching proceed, while legal acts against the teaching don’t proceed. Legal acts following the training proceed, while legal acts against the training don’t proceed. Legal acts following the teaching are explained, while legal acts against the teaching aren’t explained. Legal acts in line with the training are explained, while legal acts following training aren’t explained.

an2.49:2.3.verse: This is called a just assembly.

an2.49:2.5.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the just assembly.”

an2.50:1.3.verse: An unprincipled assembly and a principled assembly …

an2.50:1.4.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the principled assembly.”

an2.51:1.3.verse: An assembly with unprincipled speech, and an assembly with principled speech.

an2.51:1.4.verse: And what is an assembly with unprincipled speech?

an2.51:1.5.verse: It is an assembly where the mendicants take up disciplinary issues, whether legitimate or not.

an2.51:1.6.verse: But they don’t persuade each other or allow themselves to be persuaded, nor do they convince each other or allow themselves to be convinced.

an2.51:1.7.verse: Unable to persuade or convince each other, they can’t let go of their opinions. They obstinately stick to that disciplinary issue, insisting that:

an2.51:1.8.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

an2.51:1.9.verse: This is called an assembly with unprincipled speech.

an2.51:2.1.verse: And what is an assembly with principled speech?

an2.51:2.2.verse: It is an assembly where the mendicants take up disciplinary issues, whether legitimate or not.

an2.51:2.3.verse: Then they persuade each other or allow themselves to be persuaded, and they convince each other or allow themselves to be convinced.

an2.51:2.4.verse: Since they are able to persuade and convince each other, they let go of their opinions. They don’t obstinately stick to that disciplinary issue or insist that:

an2.51:2.5.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

an2.51:2.6.verse: This is called an assembly with principled speech.

an2.51:2.8.verse: The better of these two assemblies is the assembly with principled speech.”

an2.62:1.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you the communal living of the bad & the communal living of the good.

an2.62:1.2.verse: Listen to that & pay careful attention. I will speak.”

an2.62:1.3.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monks responded to the Blessed One.

an2.62:2.1.verse: “And how is there the communal living of the bad? And how do the bad live together?

an2.62:2.2.verse: “There is the case where the thought occurs to an elder monk,

an2.62:2.3.verse: ‘I should not correct an elder monk, nor should I correct a monk of middling standing,

an2.62:2.4.verse: nor should I correct a newcoming monk.

an2.62:2.5.verse: ‘If an elder monk were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends.

an2.62:2.6.verse: ‘If a monk of middle standing were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends. ‘If a newcoming monk were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends.’

an2.62:2.7.verse: “The thought occurs to a monk of middle standing… “The thought occurs to a newcoming monk,

an2.62:2.8.verse: ‘I should not correct an elder monk, nor should I correct a monk of middling standing,

an2.62:2.9.verse: nor should I correct a newcoming monk.

an2.62:2.10.verse: ‘If an elder monk were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends.

an2.62:2.11.verse: ‘If a monk of middle standing were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends. ‘If a newcoming monk were to correct me, he would correct me unsympathetic for my welfare, and not sympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “No,” and that would annoy him. Even seeing (my offense), I wouldn’t make amends.’

an2.62:2.12.verse: “This, monks, is how there is the communal living of the bad, and this is how the bad live together.

an2.62:3.1.verse: “And how is there the communal living of the good? And how do the good live together?

an2.62:3.2.verse: “There is the case where the thought occurs to an elder monk,

an2.62:3.3.verse: ‘I should correct an elder monk, I should correct a monk of middling standing,

an2.62:3.4.verse: and I should correct a newcoming monk.

an2.62:3.5.verse: ‘If an elder monk were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends.

an2.62:3.6.verse: ‘If a monk of middle standing were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends. ‘If a newcoming monk were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends.’

an2.62:3.7.verse: “The thought occurs to a monk of middle standing… “The thought occurs to a newcoming monk,

an2.62:3.8.verse: ‘I should correct an elder monk, I should correct a monk of middling standing,

an2.62:3.9.verse: and I should correct a newcoming monk.

an2.62:3.10.verse: ‘If an elder monk were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends.

an2.62:3.11.verse: ‘If a monk of middle standing were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends. ‘If a newcoming monk were to correct me, he would correct me sympathetic for my welfare, and not unsympathetic for my welfare. I would say, “Good,” and that would not annoy him. Seeing (my offense), I would make amends.’

an2.62:3.12.verse: “This, monks, is how there is the communal living of the good, and this is how the good live together.”

an2.52:1.1.verse: “These two individuals, mendicants, arise in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, for the people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

an2.52:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha; and the wheel-turning monarch.

an2.52:1.4.verse: These are the two individuals who arise in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, for the people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.”

an2.53:1.1.verse: “These two individuals, mendicants, arise in the world who are incredible human beings.

an2.53:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha; and the wheel-turning monarch.

an2.53:1.4.verse: These are the two individuals who arise in the world who are incredible human beings.”

an2.54:1.1.verse: “There are two individuals, mendicants, whose death is regretted by many people.

an2.54:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha; and the wheel-turning monarch.

an2.54:1.4.verse: These are the two individuals, mendicants, whose death is regretted by many people.”

an2.55:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two are worthy of a monument.

an2.55:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha; and the wheel-turning monarch.

an2.55:1.4.verse: These are the two who are worthy of a monument.”

an2.56:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are two kinds of Buddhas.

an2.56:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha; and an independent Buddha.

an2.56:1.4.verse: These are the two kinds of Buddhas.”

an2.57:1.1.verse: “These two, mendicants, are not startled by a crack of thunder.

an2.57:1.3.verse: A mendicant who has ended defilements; and a thoroughbred elephant.

an2.57:1.4.verse: These are the two who are not startled by a crack of thunder.”

an2.58:1.1.verse: “These two, mendicants, are not startled by a crack of thunder.

an2.58:1.3.verse: A mendicant who has ended defilements; and a thoroughbred horse.

an2.58:1.4.verse: These are the two who are not startled by a crack of thunder.”

an2.59:1.1.verse: “These two, mendicants, are not startled by a crack of thunder.

an2.59:1.3.verse: A mendicant who has ended defilements; and a lion, king of beasts.

an2.59:1.4.verse: These are the two who are not startled by a crack of thunder.”

an2.60:1.1.verse: “Mystery men see two reasons not to use regular speech.

an2.60:1.3.verse: Thinking: ‘May we not lie, and may we not misrepresent others with falsehoods.’

an2.60:1.4.verse: Mystery men see these two reasons not to use regular speech.”

an2.61:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, ladies die without getting enough of two things.

an2.61:1.4.verse: Ladies die without getting enough of these two things.”

an2.62:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you about living with bad people and living with good people.

an2.62:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an2.62:2.1.verse: “What is it like living with bad people? How do bad people live together?

an2.62:2.2.verse: It’s when a senior mendicant thinks:

an2.62:2.3.verse: ‘No mendicant, whether senior, middle, or junior, should admonish me;

an2.62:2.4.verse: and I shouldn’t admonish any mendicant, whether senior, middle, or junior.

an2.62:2.5.verse: If a mendicant—whether senior, middle, or junior—were to admonish me, they wouldn’t be sympathetic, and I’d bother them by saying “No!” And anyway I wouldn’t deal with it even if I saw what I did wrong.’
