an3.36:1.1.verse: “There are, mendicants, these three messengers of the gods.

an3.36:1.3.verse: Firstly, someone does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.36:1.4.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an3.36:1.5.verse: The wardens of hell take them by the arms and present them to King Yama, saying,

an3.36:1.6.verse: ‘Your Majesty, this person did not pay due respect to their mother and father, ascetics and brahmins, or honor the elders in the family.

an3.36:2.1.verse: King Yama pursues, presses, and grills them about the first messenger of the gods:

an3.36:2.2.verse: ‘My man, did you not see the first messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’

an3.36:3.2.verse: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings an elderly woman or a man—eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old—bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as they walk, ailing, past their prime, with teeth broken, hair grey and scanty or bald, skin wrinkled, and limbs blotchy?’

an3.36:4.2.verse: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

an3.36:4.3.verse: “I, too, am liable to grow old. I’m not exempt from old age. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’

an3.36:5.2.verse: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.36:5.3.verse: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

an3.36:5.4.verse: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

an3.36:5.5.verse: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

an3.36:6.1.verse: King Yama grills them about the second messenger of the gods:

an3.36:6.2.verse: ‘My man, did you not see the second messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’

an3.36:6.6.verse: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, sick, suffering, gravely ill, collapsed in their own urine and feces, being picked up by some and put down by others?’

an3.36:7.2.verse: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

an3.36:7.3.verse: “I, too, am liable to become sick. I’m not exempt from sickness. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’

an3.36:8.2.verse: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.36:8.3.verse: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

an3.36:8.4.verse: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

an3.36:8.5.verse: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

an3.36:9.1.verse: King Yama grills them about the third messenger of the gods:

an3.36:9.2.verse: ‘My man, did you not see the third messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’

an3.36:10.2.verse: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering?’

an3.36:11.2.verse: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

an3.36:11.3.verse: “I, too, am liable to die. I’m not exempt from death. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’

an3.36:12.2.verse: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.36:12.3.verse: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

an3.36:12.4.verse: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

an3.36:12.5.verse: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

an3.36:13.1.verse: After grilling them about the third messenger of the gods, King Yama falls silent.

an3.36:13.2.verse: The wardens of hell punish them with the five-fold crucifixion.

an3.36:13.3.verse: They drive red-hot stakes through the hands and feet, and another in the middle of the chest.

an3.36:13.4.verse: And there they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.

an3.36:14.1.verse: The wardens of hell throw them down and hack them with axes. …

an3.36:15.1.verse: They hang them upside-down and hack them with hatchets. …

an3.36:15.2.verse: They harness them to a chariot, and drive them back and forth across burning ground, blazing and glowing. …

an3.36:15.3.verse: They make them climb up and down a big mountain of burning coals, blazing and glowing. …

an3.36:15.4.verse: The wardens of hell turn them upside down and throw them in a red-hot copper pot, burning, blazing, and glowing.

an3.36:15.5.verse: There they’re seared in boiling scum, and they’re swept up and down and round and round.

an3.36:15.6.verse: And there they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.

an3.36:15.7.verse: The wardens of hell toss them into the Great Hell.

an3.36:16.1.verse: ‘Four are its corners, four its doors,

an3.36:17.1.verse: The ground is even made of iron,

an3.36:18.1.verse: Once upon a time, King Yama thought,

an3.36:18.2.verse: ‘Those who do such bad deeds in the world receive these many different punishments.

an3.36:18.3.verse: Oh, I hope I may be reborn as a human being! And that a Realized One—a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha—arises in the world! And that I may pay homage to the Buddha!

an3.36:18.4.verse: Let that Buddha teach me Dhamma, so that I may understand his teaching!’

an3.36:18.5.verse: Now, I don’t say this because I’ve heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin. I only say it because I’ve known, seen, and realized it for myself.

an3.36:19.1.verse: When warned by the gods’ messengers,

an3.36:19.2.verse: those sons of Manu who are negligent

an3.36:19.4.verse: when they go to that wretched place.

an3.36:20.1.verse: When warned by the gods’ messengers,

an3.36:20.2.verse: the good and true persons here

an3.36:20.4.verse: the teaching of the Noble One.

an3.36:21.2.verse: the origin of birth and death,

an3.36:21.4.verse: with the ending of birth and death.

an3.36:22.1.verse: Happy, they’ve come to a safe place,

an3.36:22.3.verse: They’ve gone beyond all enmities and fears,

an3.37:1.1.verse: “On the eighth day of the fortnight, mendicants, the ministers and councillors of the four great kings wander about the world, thinking:

an3.37:1.2.verse: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents, ascetics and brahmins, honoring the elders in their families, observing and keeping vigil on the sabbath, and making merit.’

an3.37:1.3.verse: And on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, the sons of the four great kings wander about the world, thinking:

an3.37:1.4.verse: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

an3.37:1.5.verse: And on the fifteenth day sabbath, the four great kings themselves wander about the world, thinking:

an3.37:1.6.verse: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

an3.37:2.1.verse: If only a few humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit,

an3.37:2.2.verse: the four great kings address the gods of the thirty-three, seated together in the Hall of Clear Right:

an3.37:2.3.verse: ‘Only a few humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

an3.37:2.4.verse: Then the gods of the thirty-three are disappointed, thinking,

an3.37:2.5.verse: ‘The heavenly hosts will dwindle, while the titan hosts will swell!’

an3.37:3.1.verse: But if many humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit,

an3.37:3.2.verse: the four great kings address the gods of the thirty-three, seated together in the Hall of Clear Right:

an3.37:3.3.verse: ‘Many humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

an3.37:3.4.verse: Then the gods of the thirty-three are pleased, thinking,

an3.37:3.5.verse: ‘The heavenly hosts will swell, while the titan hosts will dwindle!’

an3.37:4.1.verse: Once upon a time, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:

an3.37:5.4.verse: on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,

an3.37:5.5.verse: and the eighth day of the fortnight,

an3.37:5.6.verse: as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

an3.37:6.1.verse: But that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, lord of gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken.

an3.37:6.3.verse: Because Sakka, lord of gods, is not free of greed, hate, and delusion.

an3.37:7.1.verse: But for a mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—it is appropriate to say:

an3.37:8.4.verse: on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,

an3.37:8.5.verse: and the eighth day of the fortnight,

an3.37:8.6.verse: as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

an3.37:9.2.verse: Because that mendicant is free of greed, hate, and delusion.”

an3.38:1.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:

an3.38:2.4.verse: on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,

an3.38:2.5.verse: and the eighth day of the fortnight,

an3.38:2.6.verse: as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

an3.38:3.1.verse: But that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, lord of gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken.

an3.38:3.3.verse: Because Sakka, lord of gods, is not exempt from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. He is not exempt from suffering, I say.

an3.38:4.1.verse: But for a mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—it is appropriate to say:

an3.38:5.4.verse: on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,

an3.38:5.5.verse: and the eighth day of the fortnight,

an3.38:5.6.verse: as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

an3.38:6.2.verse: Because that mendicant is exempt from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. He is exempt from suffering, I say.”

an3.39:1.1.verse: “Monks, I lived in refinement, utmost refinement, total refinement.

an3.39:1.2.verse: My father even had lotus ponds made in our palace:

an3.39:1.3.verse: one where red lotuses bloomed, one where white lotuses bloomed, one where blue lotuses bloomed, all for my sake.

an3.39:1.4.verse: I used no sandalwood that was not from Vārāṇasī. My turban was from Vārāṇasī, as were my tunic, my lower garments, & my outer cloak.

an3.39:1.5.verse: A white sunshade was held over me day & night

an3.39:1.6.verse: to protect me from cold, heat, dust, dirt, & dew.

an3.39:2.1.verse: “I had three palaces: one for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season.

an3.39:2.2.verse: During the four months of the rainy season I was entertained in the rainy-season palace by minstrels without a single man among them, and I did not once come down from the palace.

an3.39:2.3.verse: Whereas the servants, workers, & retainers in other people’s homes are fed meals of lentil soup & broken rice, in my father’s home the servants, workers, & retainers were fed wheat, rice, & meat.

an3.39:3.1.verse: “Even though I was endowed with such fortune, such total refinement, the thought occurred to me:

an3.39:3.2.verse: ‘When an untaught, run-of-the-mill person, himself subject to aging, not beyond aging, sees another who is aged, he is repelled, ashamed, & disgusted, oblivious to himself that he too is subject to aging, not beyond aging.

an3.39:3.3.verse: If I—who am subject to aging, not beyond aging—were to be repelled, ashamed, & disgusted on seeing another person who is aged, that would not be fitting for me.’

an3.39:3.4.verse: As I noticed this, the (typical) young person’s intoxication with youth entirely dropped away.

an3.39:4.1.verse: “Even though I was endowed with such fortune, such total refinement, the thought occurred to me: ‘When an untaught, run-of-the-mill person, himself subject to illness, not beyond illness, sees another who is ill, he is repelled, ashamed, & disgusted, oblivious to himself that he too is subject to illness, not beyond illness.

an3.39:4.2.verse: And if I—who am subject to illness, not beyond illness—were to be repelled, ashamed, & disgusted on seeing another person who is ill, that would not be fitting for me.’

an3.39:4.3.verse: As I noticed this, the healthy person’s intoxication with health entirely dropped away.

an3.39:5.1.verse: “Even though I was endowed with such fortune, such total refinement, the thought occurred to me: ‘When an untaught, run-of-the-mill person, himself subject to death, not beyond death, sees another who is dead, he is repelled, ashamed, & disgusted, oblivious to himself that he too is subject to death, not beyond death.

an3.39:5.2.verse: And if I—who am subject to death, not beyond death—were to be repelled, ashamed, & disgusted on seeing another person who is dead, that would not be fitting for me.’

an3.39:5.3.verse: As I noticed this, the living person’s intoxication with life entirely dropped away.

an3.39:6.1.verse: “Monks, there are these three forms of intoxication.

an3.39:6.3.verse: Intoxication with youth, intoxication with health, intoxication with life.

an3.39:6.4.verse: “Drunk with the intoxication of youth, an uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person engages in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct.

an3.39:6.5.verse: Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct, he—on the break-up of the body, after death—reappears in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower realms, in hell.

an3.39:6.6.verse: “Drunk with the intoxication of health, an uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person engages in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct. Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct, he—on the break-up of the body, after death—reappears in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower realms, in hell.

an3.39:6.7.verse: “Drunk with the intoxication of life, an uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person engages in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct.

an3.39:6.8.verse: Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, & mental misconduct, he—on the break-up of the body, after death—reappears in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower realms, in hell.

an3.39:7.1.verse: “Drunk with the intoxication of youth, a monk leaves the training and returns to the lower life.

an3.39:7.2.verse: Drunk with the intoxication of health, a monk leaves the training and returns to the lower life.

an3.39:7.3.verse: Drunk with the intoxication of life, a monk leaves the training and returns to the lower life.”

an3.39:8.4.verse: are repelled by those who suffer from that to which they are subject.

an3.39:9.1.verse: And if I were to be repelled

an3.39:9.2.verse: by beings subject to these things,

an3.39:9.3.verse: it would not be fitting for me,

an3.39:12.2.verse: I could partake of sensual pleasures.

an3.39:1.1.verse: “My lifestyle was delicate, mendicants, most delicate, extremely delicate.

an3.39:1.2.verse: In my father’s home, lotus ponds were made just for me.

an3.39:1.3.verse: In some, blue water lilies blossomed, while in others, there were pink or white lotuses, just for my benefit.

an3.39:1.4.verse: I only used sandalwood from Kāsi, and my turbans, jackets, sarongs, and upper robes also came from Kāsi.

an3.39:1.5.verse: And a white parasol was held over me night and day, with the thought:

an3.39:1.6.verse: ‘Don’t let cold, heat, grass, dust, or damp bother him.’

an3.39:2.1.verse: I had three stilt longhouses—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.

an3.39:2.2.verse: I stayed in a stilt longhouse without coming downstairs for the four months of the rainy season, where I was entertained by musicians—none of them men.

an3.39:2.3.verse: While the bondservants, workers, and staff in other houses are given sour gruel with false black pepper to eat, in my father’s home they are given fine rice with meat.

an3.39:3.1.verse: Amid such prosperity and such a delicate lifestyle, I thought:

an3.39:3.2.verse: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to grow old, not being exempt from old age—sees someone else who is old, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

an3.39:3.3.verse: But since I, too, am liable to grow old, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is old.’

an3.39:3.4.verse: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of youth.

an3.39:4.1.verse: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to get sick, not being exempt from sickness—sees someone else who is sick, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

an3.39:4.2.verse: But since I, too, am liable to get sick, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is sick.’

an3.39:4.3.verse: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of health.

an3.39:5.1.verse: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to die, not being exempt from death—sees someone else who is dead, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

an3.39:5.2.verse: But since I, too, am liable to die, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is dead.’

an3.39:5.3.verse: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of life.

an3.39:6.3.verse: The vanity of youth, of health, and of life.

an3.39:6.4.verse: Intoxicated with the vanity of youth, an unlearned ordinary person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.39:6.5.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an3.39:6.6.verse: Intoxicated with the vanity of health …

an3.39:6.7.verse: Intoxicated with the vanity of life, an unlearned ordinary person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.39:6.8.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an3.39:7.1.verse: Intoxicated with the vanity of youth, health, or life, a mendicant resigns the training and returns to a lesser life.

an3.39:8.2.verse: and so are old age and death.

an3.39:8.3.verse: Though this is how their nature is,

an3.39:9.1.verse: If I were to be disgusted

an3.39:9.2.verse: with creatures whose nature is such,

an3.39:9.3.verse: it would not be appropriate for me,

an3.39:9.4.verse: since my life is just the same.

an3.39:10.2.verse: I understood the truth without attachments.

an3.39:12.4.verse: I’m committed to the spiritual life.”

an3.40:1.3.verse: The self as a governing principle, the cosmos as a governing principle, and the Dhamma as a governing principle.

an3.40:1.4.verse: “And what is the self as a governing principle?

an3.40:1.5.verse: There is the case where a monk, having gone to a wilderness, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, reflects on this:

an3.40:1.6.verse: ‘It is not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:1.7.verse: It is not for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of this or that state of (future) becoming that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:1.8.verse: Simply that I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress,

an3.40:1.9.verse: (and I hope,) “Perhaps the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!”

an3.40:1.10.verse: Now, if I were to seek the same sort of sensual pleasures that I abandoned in going forth from home into homelessness—or a worse sort—that would not be fitting for me.’

an3.40:1.12.verse: ‘My persistence will be aroused & not lax; my mindfulness established & not confused; my body calm & not aroused; my mind centered & unified.’

an3.40:1.13.verse: Having made himself his governing principle, he abandons what is unskillful, develops what is skillful, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is unblameworthy, and looks after himself in a pure way.

an3.40:1.14.verse: This is called the self as a governing principle.

an3.40:2.1.verse: “And what is the cosmos as a governing principle?

an3.40:2.2.verse: There is the case where a monk, having gone to a wilderness, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, reflects on this:

an3.40:2.3.verse: ‘It’s not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:2.4.verse: It’s not for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of this or that state of (future) becoming that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:2.5.verse: Simply that I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress,

an3.40:2.6.verse: (and I hope,) “Perhaps the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!”

an3.40:2.7.verse: Now if I, having gone forth, were to think thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill will, or thoughts of harmfulness: Great is the community of this cosmos,

an3.40:2.8.verse: and in the great community of this cosmos there are contemplatives & brahmans endowed with psychic power, clairvoyant, skilled (in reading) the minds of others.

an3.40:2.9.verse: They can see even from afar. Even up close, they are invisible. With their awareness they know the minds of others.

an3.40:2.10.verse: They would know this of me:

an3.40:2.11.verse: “Look, my friends, at this clansman who—though he has in good faith gone forth from the home life into homelessness—remains overcome with evil, unskillful mental qualities.”

an3.40:2.12.verse: There are also devas endowed with psychic power, clairvoyant, skilled (in reading) the minds of others.

an3.40:2.13.verse: They can see even from afar. Even up close, they are invisible. With their awareness they know the minds of others.

an3.40:2.14.verse: They would know this of me:

an3.40:2.15.verse: “Look, my friends, at this clansman who—though he has in good faith gone forth from the home life into homelessness—remains overcome with evil, unskillful mental qualities.”’

an3.40:2.17.verse: ‘My persistence will be aroused & not lax; my mindfulness established & not confused; my body calm & not aroused; my mind centered & unified.’

an3.40:2.18.verse: Having made the cosmos his governing principle, he abandons what is unskillful, develops what is skillful, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is unblameworthy, and looks after himself in a pure way.

an3.40:2.19.verse: This is called the cosmos as a governing principle.

an3.40:3.1.verse: “And what is the Dhamma as a governing principle?

an3.40:3.2.verse: There is the case where a monk, having gone to a wilderness, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, reflects on this:

an3.40:3.3.verse: ‘It’s not for the sake of robes that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:3.4.verse: It’s not for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of this or that state of (future) becoming that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

an3.40:3.5.verse: Simply that I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress,

an3.40:3.6.verse: (and I hope,) “Perhaps the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!”

an3.40:3.7.verse: Now, the Dhamma is well taught by the Blessed One, to be seen here & now, timeless, inviting verification, pertinent, to be experienced by the observant for themselves.

an3.40:3.8.verse: There are companions in the holy life who dwell knowing & seeing it.

an3.40:3.9.verse: If I—having gone forth in this well-taught Dhamma & Vinaya—were to remain lazy & heedless, that would not be fitting for me.’

an3.40:3.11.verse: ‘My persistence will be aroused & not lax; my mindfulness established & not confused; my body calm & not aroused; my mind centered & unified.’

an3.40:3.12.verse: Having made the Dhamma his governing principle, he abandons what is unskillful, develops what is skillful, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is unblameworthy, and looks after himself in a pure way.

an3.40:3.13.verse: This is called the Dhamma as a governing principle.

an3.40:4.1.verse: There is in the cosmos no secret

an3.40:4.2.verse: place for one who has done an evil deed.

an3.40:4.3.verse: Your own self knows, my good man,

an3.40:4.4.verse: whether you are true or false.

an3.40:6.1.verse: The devas & Tathāgatas see the fool

an3.40:6.2.verse: who goes about off-pitch in the cosmos.

an3.40:6.3.verse: Thus you should go about self-governed,

an3.40:6.4.verse: mindful; governed by the cosmos, masterful, absorbed in jhāna;

an3.40:6.5.verse: governed by the Dhamma, acting in line with the Dhamma.

an3.40:6.6.verse: The sage who makes an effort in truth doesn’t fall back.

an3.40:7.1.verse: Whoever through striving—overpowering Māra, conquering the Ender—

an3.40:7.2.verse: touches the stopping of birth, is Such,

an3.40:7.3.verse: a knower of the cosmos, wise,

an3.40:7.4.verse: a sage unfashioned with regard to all things.”

an3.40:1.1.verse: “There are, mendicants, these three things to put in charge.

an3.40:1.3.verse: Putting oneself, the world, or the teaching in charge.

an3.40:1.4.verse: And what, mendicants, is putting oneself in charge?

an3.40:1.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an3.40:1.6.verse: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

an3.40:1.7.verse: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

an3.40:1.8.verse: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

an3.40:1.9.verse: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

an3.40:1.10.verse: But it would not be appropriate for me to seek sensual pleasures like those I abandoned when I went forth, or even worse.’

an3.40:1.12.verse: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

an3.40:1.13.verse: Putting themselves in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.

an3.40:1.14.verse: This is called putting oneself in charge.

an3.40:2.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is putting the world in charge?

an3.40:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an3.40:2.3.verse: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

an3.40:2.4.verse: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

an3.40:2.5.verse: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

an3.40:2.6.verse: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

an3.40:2.7.verse: And now, since I’ve now gone forth, I might have sensual, malicious, or cruel thoughts. But the population of the world is large,

an3.40:2.8.verse: and there are ascetics and brahmins who have psychic power—they’re clairvoyant, and can read the minds of others.

an3.40:2.9.verse: They see far without being seen, even by those close; and they understand the minds of others.

an3.40:2.11.verse: “Look at this gentleman; he’s gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, but he’s living mixed up with bad, unskillful qualities.”

an3.40:2.12.verse: And there are deities, too, who have psychic power—they’re clairvoyant, and can read the minds of others.

an3.40:2.13.verse: They see far without being seen, even by those close; and they understand the minds of others.

an3.40:2.15.verse: “Look at this gentleman; he’s gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, but he’s living mixed up with bad, unskillful qualities.”’

an3.40:2.17.verse: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

an3.40:2.18.verse: Putting the world in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.

an3.40:2.19.verse: This is called putting the world in charge.

an3.40:3.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is putting the teaching in charge?

an3.40:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an3.40:3.3.verse: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

an3.40:3.4.verse: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

an3.40:3.5.verse: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

an3.40:3.6.verse: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

an3.40:3.7.verse: The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.40:3.8.verse: I have spiritual companions who live knowing and seeing.

an3.40:3.9.verse: Now that I’ve gone forth in this well explained teaching and training, it would not be appropriate for me to live lazy and heedless.’

an3.40:3.11.verse: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

an3.40:3.12.verse: Putting the teaching in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.

an3.40:3.13.verse: This is called putting the teaching in charge.

an3.40:3.14.verse: These are the three things to put in charge.

an3.40:4.1.verse: There’s no privacy in the world,

an3.40:4.2.verse: for someone who does bad deeds.

an3.40:4.4.verse: whether you’ve lied or told the truth.

an3.40:5.1.verse: When you witness your good self,

an3.40:6.1.verse: The gods and the Realized One see

an3.40:6.2.verse: the fool who lives unjustly in the world.

an3.40:6.3.verse: So with yourself in charge, live mindfully;

an3.40:6.4.verse: with the world in charge, be alert and practice absorption;

an3.40:6.5.verse: with the teaching in charge, live in line with that teaching:

an3.40:6.6.verse: a sage who tries for the truth doesn’t deteriorate.

an3.40:7.2.verse: one who strives reaches the end of rebirth.

an3.40:7.4.verse: that sage is determined by nothing at all.”

an3.41:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when three things are present, a faithful gentleman brims with much merit.

an3.41:1.4.verse: when a gift to give is present,

an3.41:1.5.verse: and when those worthy of a religious donation are present.

an3.41:1.6.verse: When these three things are present, a faithful gentleman brims with much merit.”

an3.42:1.1.verse: “In these three instances, monks, one can be recognized as a person of conviction & confidence.

an3.42:1.3.verse: One wants to see virtuous people. One wants to hear the True Dhamma. One’s awareness cleansed of the stain of stinginess, one lives at home, freely generous, openhanded, delighting in being magnanimous, responsive to requests, delighting in the distribution of alms.

an3.42:1.4.verse: In these three instances, monks, one can be recognized as a person of conviction & confidence.”

an3.42:2.1.verse: One who wants to see virtuous ones,

an3.42:2.2.verse: & wants to hear the True Dhamma

an3.42:1.1.verse: “There are three grounds, mendicants, by which a person with faith and confidence can be known.

an3.42:1.3.verse: They like to see ethical people. They like to hear the true teaching. And they live at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.

an3.42:1.4.verse: These are the three grounds by which a person with faith and confidence can be known.

an3.42:2.1.verse: They like to see ethical people;

an3.42:2.2.verse: they want to hear the true teaching;

an3.42:2.3.verse: they’ve driven out the stain of stinginess:

an3.42:2.4.verse: that’s who’s called an individual of faith.”

an3.43:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, taking three reasons into consideration provides quite enough motivation to teach Dhamma to another.

an3.43:1.3.verse: When the teacher understands the meaning and the teaching.

an3.43:1.4.verse: When the audience understands the meaning and the teaching.

an3.43:1.5.verse: When both the teacher and the audience understand the meaning and the teaching.

an3.43:1.6.verse: Taking these three reasons into consideration provides quite enough motivation to teach Dhamma to another.”

an3.44:1.3.verse: When the teacher understands the meaning and the teaching.

an3.44:1.4.verse: When the audience understands the meaning and the teaching.

an3.44:1.5.verse: When both the teacher and the audience understand the meaning and the teaching.

an3.44:1.6.verse: These are the three situations in which conversation flows.”

an3.45:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these three things are recommended by astute true persons.

an3.45:1.5.verse: and taking care of your mother and father.

an3.45:1.6.verse: These are the three things recommended by astute true persons.

an3.45:3.1.verse: These are the things recommended by the good,

an3.45:3.4.verse: will enjoy a world of grace.”

an3.46:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when ethical renunciates are supported by a town or village,

an3.46:1.2.verse: the people there brim with much merit in three ways.

an3.46:1.4.verse: By way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.46:1.5.verse: When ethical renunciates are supported by a town or village,

an3.46:1.6.verse: the people there brim with much merit in these three ways.”

an3.47:1.1.verse: “Monks, these three are fabricated characteristics of what is fabricated.

an3.47:1.3.verse: Arising is discernable, passing away is discernable, alteration [literally: otherness] while staying is discernable.

an3.47:1.4.verse: “These are three fabricated characteristics of what is fabricated.”

an3.47:2.1.verse: “Now these three are unfabricated characteristics of what is unfabricated.

an3.47:2.3.verse: No arising is discernable, no passing away is discernable, no alteration while staying is discernable.

an3.47:2.4.verse: “These are three unfabricated characteristics of what is unfabricated.”

an3.47:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the conditioned has these three characteristics.

an3.47:1.3.verse: Arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

an3.47:1.4.verse: These are the three characteristics of the conditioned.”

an3.47:2.3.verse: No arising is evident, no vanishing is evident, and no change while persisting is evident.

an3.47:2.4.verse: These are the three characteristics of the unconditioned.”

an3.48:1.1.verse: “Monks, the great Sal trees that live in dependence on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, prosper in terms of three kinds of prosperity.

an3.48:1.3.verse: They prosper in terms of branches, leaves, & foliage. They prosper in terms of bark & shoots. They prosper in terms of softwood and heartwood.

an3.48:1.4.verse: The great Sal trees that grow in dependence on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, prosper in terms of these three kinds of prosperity.

an3.48:2.1.verse: “In the same way, the descendants who live in dependence on a clansman of conviction prosper in terms of three kinds of prosperity.

an3.48:2.3.verse: They prosper in terms of conviction. They prosper in terms of virtue. They prosper in terms of discernment.

an3.48:2.4.verse: The descendants who live in dependence on a clansman of conviction prosper in terms of these three kinds of prosperity.

an3.48:3.2.verse: in the wilderness, in a mighty grove,

an3.48:3.4.verse: lords of the forest, great trees—

an3.48:4.2.verse: those who here live dependent on

an3.48:5.1.verse: Seeing the virtue of that virtuous one,

an3.48:6.1.verse: Having, here in this world, followed the Dhamma,

an3.48:6.2.verse: the path to a good destination,

an3.48:6.3.verse: they delight in the world of the devas,

an3.48:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, great sal trees grow in three ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

an3.48:1.3.verse: The branches, leaves, and foliage; the bark and shoots; and the softwood and heartwood.

an3.48:1.4.verse: Great sal trees grow in these three ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

an3.48:2.1.verse: In the same way, a family grows in three ways supported by a family head with faith.

an3.48:2.4.verse: A family grows in these three ways supported by a family head with faith.

an3.48:3.2.verse: in the wilds, the formidable forest,

an3.48:3.4.verse: to become lord of the forest.

an3.48:4.1.verse: So too, when the family head

an3.48:4.6.verse: and those dependent for their livelihood.

an3.48:5.1.verse: Seeing the ethical conduct of the virtuous,

an3.48:6.2.verse: the path that goes to a good place,

an3.48:6.3.verse: they delight in the heavenly realm,

an3.48:6.4.verse: enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”

an3.49:1.1.verse: “In three instances, monks, ardency should be exercised.

an3.49:1.3.verse: “Ardency should be exercised for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unskillful qualities. “Ardency should be exercised for the arising of unarisen skillful qualities. “Ardency should be exercised for enduring bodily feelings that have arisen and are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, displeasing, & menacing to life.

an3.49:2.1.verse: “When one exercises ardency for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unskillful qualities, when one exercises ardency for the arising of unarisen skillful qualities, and when one exercises ardency for enduring bodily feelings that have arisen and are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, displeasing, & menacing to life,

an3.49:2.2.verse: then one is said to be a monk who is ardent, adept, & mindful for the right ending of suffering & stress.”

an3.49:1.1.verse: “In three situations, mendicants, you should be keen.

an3.49:1.3.verse: You should be keen to prevent bad, unskillful qualities from arising. You should be keen to give rise to skillful qualities. And you should be keen to endure physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, life-threatening.

an3.49:1.4.verse: In these three situations, you should be keen.

an3.49:2.1.verse: It’s a mendicant who is keen to prevent bad, unskillful qualities from arising. They’re keen to give rise to skillful qualities. And they’re keen to endure physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, life-threatening.

an3.49:2.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who is keen, alert, and mindful so as to rightly make an end of suffering.”

an3.50:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a master thief with three factors breaks into houses, plunders wealth, steals from isolated buildings, and commits highway robbery.

an3.50:1.3.verse: A master thief relies on uneven ground, on thick cover, and on the powerful.

an3.50:1.4.verse: And how does a master thief rely on uneven ground?

an3.50:1.5.verse: It’s when a master thief relies on inaccessible riverlands or rugged mountains.

an3.50:1.6.verse: That’s how a master thief relies on uneven ground.

an3.50:2.1.verse: And how does a master thief rely on thick cover?

an3.50:2.2.verse: It’s when a master thief relies on thick grass, thick trees, a blind spot, or a large forest grove.

an3.50:2.3.verse: That’s how a master thief relies on thick cover.

an3.50:3.1.verse: And how does a master thief rely on the powerful?

an3.50:3.2.verse: It’s when a master thief relies on rulers or their chief ministers.

an3.50:3.4.verse: ‘If anyone accuses me of anything, these rulers or their chief ministers will speak in my defense in the case.’

an3.50:3.6.verse: That’s how a master thief relies on the powerful.

an3.50:3.7.verse: A master thief with these three factors breaks into houses, plunders wealth, steals from isolated buildings, and commits highway robbery.

an3.50:4.1.verse: In the same way, when a bad mendicant has three factors, they keep themselves broken and damaged. They deserve to be blamed and criticized by sensible people, and they brim with much wickedness.

an3.50:4.3.verse: A bad mendicant relies on uneven ground, on thick cover, and on the powerful.

an3.50:5.1.verse: And how does a bad mendicant rely on uneven ground?

an3.50:5.2.verse: It’s when a bad mendicant has unethical conduct by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.50:5.3.verse: That’s how a bad mendicant relies on uneven ground.

an3.50:6.1.verse: And how does a bad mendicant rely on thick cover?

an3.50:6.2.verse: It’s when a bad mendicant has wrong view, he’s attached to an extremist view.

an3.50:6.3.verse: That’s how a bad mendicant relies on thick cover.

an3.50:7.1.verse: And how does a bad mendicant rely on the powerful?

an3.50:7.2.verse: It’s when a bad mendicant relies on rulers or their chief ministers.

an3.50:7.4.verse: ‘If anyone accuses me of anything, these rulers or their chief ministers will speak in my defense in the case.’

an3.50:7.6.verse: That’s how a bad mendicant relies on the powerful.

an3.50:7.7.verse: When a bad mendicant has these three qualities, they keep themselves broken and damaged. They deserve to be blamed and criticized by sensible people, and they brim with much wickedness.”

an3.51:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then two brahmans—feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old—went to the Blessed One. On arrival, they exchanged courteous greetings with him

an3.51:1.2.verse: and, after an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to him:

an3.51:1.3.verse: “Master Gotama, we are brahmans—feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old.

an3.51:1.4.verse: And we have done no admirable deeds, no skillful deeds, no deeds that allay our fears.

an3.51:1.5.verse: Teach us, Master Gotama. Instruct us, Master Gotama, for our long-term benefit & happiness.”

an3.51:2.1.verse: “Indeed, brahmans, you are feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old.

an3.51:2.2.verse: And you have done no admirable deeds, no skillful deeds, no deeds that allay your fears.

an3.51:2.3.verse: This world is swept away by aging, by illness, by death.

an3.51:2.4.verse: With the world thus swept away by aging, illness, & death, any restraint of body, speech, & intellect practiced here will be one’s shelter, cave, island, & refuge after death in the world beyond.”

an3.51:3.1.verse: It’s swept along: life, its next-to-nothing span.

an3.51:3.2.verse: For one swept on by aging no shelters exist.

an3.51:3.3.verse: Keeping sight of this danger in death,

an3.51:4.3.verse: when you make merit while still alive:

an3.51:4.4.verse: That will be for your bliss after death.”

an3.51:1.1.verse: Then two old brahmins—elderly and senior, who were advanced in years and had reached the final stage of life, a hundred and twenty years old—went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an3.51:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:

an3.51:1.3.verse: “We brahmins, worthy Gotama, are old, elderly and senior, we’re advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; we’re a hundred and twenty years old.

an3.51:1.4.verse: And we haven’t done what is good and skillful, nor have we made a shelter from fear.

an3.51:1.5.verse: Advise us, worthy Gotama, instruct us! It will be for our lasting welfare and happiness.”

an3.51:2.1.verse: “Indeed, brahmins, you’re old, elderly and senior.

an3.51:2.2.verse: And you haven’t done what is good and skillful, nor have you made a shelter from fear.

an3.51:2.3.verse: This world is led onward by old age, sickness, and death.

an3.51:2.4.verse: But restraint here by way of body, speech, and mind is the shelter, asylum, island, refuge, and final haven for the departed.

an3.51:3.1.verse: This life, so very short, is led onward.

an3.51:3.2.verse: One led on to old age has no shelter.

an3.51:3.4.verse: do good deeds that bring you joy.

an3.51:4.4.verse: as the good deeds done while living.”

an3.52:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then two brahmans—feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old—went to the Blessed One. On arrival, they exchanged courteous greetings with him and, after an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to him:

an3.52:1.2.verse: “Master Gotama, we are brahmans—feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old.

an3.52:1.3.verse: And we have done no admirable deeds, no skillful deeds, no deeds that allay our fears.

an3.52:1.4.verse: Teach us, Master Gotama. Instruct us, Master Gotama, for our long-term benefit & happiness.”

an3.52:2.1.verse: “Indeed, brahmans, you are feeble old men, aged, advanced in years, having come to the last stage of life, 120 years old.

an3.52:2.2.verse: And you have done no admirable deeds, no skillful deeds, no deeds that allay your fears.

an3.52:2.3.verse: This world is on fire with aging, illness, & death.

an3.52:2.4.verse: With the world thus on fire with aging, illness, & death, any restraint of body, speech, & intellect practiced here will be one’s shelter, cave, island, & refuge after death in the world beyond.”

an3.52:3.3.verse: is the one that will be of use,

an3.52:3.4.verse: not the one left there to burn.

an3.52:4.1.verse: So when the world is on fire

an3.52:4.3.verse: you should salvage (your wealth) by giving:

an3.52:5.3.verse: when you make merit while still alive:

an3.52:5.4.verse: That will be for your bliss after death.”

an3.52:1.1.verse: Then two old brahmins—elderly and senior, who were advanced in years and had reached the final stage of life, a hundred and twenty years old—went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an3.52:1.2.verse: “We brahmins, worthy Gotama, are old, elderly and senior, we’re advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; we’re a hundred and twenty years old.

an3.52:1.3.verse: And we haven’t done what is good and skillful, nor have we made a shelter from fear.

an3.52:1.4.verse: Advise us, worthy Gotama, instruct us! It will be for our lasting welfare and happiness.”

an3.52:2.1.verse: “Indeed, brahmins, you’re old, elderly and senior.

an3.52:2.2.verse: And you haven’t done what is good and skillful, nor have you made a shelter from fear.

an3.52:2.3.verse: This world is burning with old age, sickness, and death.

an3.52:2.4.verse: But restraint here by way of body, speech, and mind is the shelter, asylum, island, refuge, and final haven for the departed.

an3.52:3.1.verse: When your house is on fire,

an3.52:4.1.verse: And as the world is on fire

an3.52:5.4.verse: as the good deeds done while living.”

an3.53:1.1.verse: Then a brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. Seated to one side he said to the Buddha:

an3.53:1.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, they speak of ‘a teaching apparent in the present life’.

an3.53:1.3.verse: In what way is the teaching apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves?”

an3.53:2.1.verse: “A greedy person, overcome and overwhelmed by greed, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:2.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:2.7.verse: This is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.53:3.1.verse: A hateful person, overcome by hate, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:3.2.verse: When hate has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:3.3.verse: This, too, is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.53:4.1.verse: A deluded person, overcome by delusion, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:4.2.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.53:4.3.verse: This, too, is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.”

an3.53:5.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an3.53:5.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an3.53:5.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.54:1.1.verse: Then a brahmin wanderer went up to the Buddha … Seated to one side he said to the Buddha:

an3.54:1.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, they speak of ‘a teaching apparent in the present life’.

an3.54:1.3.verse: In what way is the teaching apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves?”

an3.54:2.1.verse: “A greedy person, overcome by greed, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.54:2.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.54:3.1.verse: A greedy person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.54:3.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.54:4.1.verse: A greedy person doesn’t truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.54:4.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.54:4.3.verse: This is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.54:5.2.verse: A deluded person, overcome by delusion, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.54:5.3.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.54:6.1.verse: A deluded person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.54:6.2.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.54:7.1.verse: A deluded person doesn’t truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.54:7.2.verse: When delusion has been given up, they truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.54:7.3.verse: This, too, is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.”

an3.54:8.2.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.55:1.1.verse: Then the brahmin Jānussoṇi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an3.55:1.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, they say that ‘extinguishment is apparent in the present life’.

an3.55:1.3.verse: In what way is extinguishment apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves?”

an3.55:2.1.verse: “A greedy person, overcome by greed, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.55:2.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.55:2.3.verse: This is how extinguishment is apparent in the present life.

an3.55:3.2.verse: A deluded person, overcome by delusion, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.55:3.3.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.55:3.4.verse: This, too, is how extinguishment is apparent in the present life.

an3.55:4.1.verse: When you experience the ending of greed, hate, and delusion without remainder,

an3.55:4.2.verse: that’s how extinguishment is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.”

an3.55:5.2.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.56:1.1.verse: Then a certain well-to-do brahmin went up to the Buddha, and seated to one side he said to him:

an3.56:1.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, I have heard that brahmins of the past who were elderly and senior, the tutors of tutors, said:

an3.56:1.3.verse: ‘In the old days this world was so full of humans you’d think they were squashed together. The villages, towns, and capital cities were no more than a chicken’s flight apart.’

an3.56:1.4.verse: What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why these days human numbers have dwindled, a decline in population is evident, and whole villages, towns, cities, and countries have disappeared?”

an3.56:2.1.verse: “These days, brahmin, humans just love illicit desire. They’re overcome by immoral greed, and mired in wrong religious teachings.

an3.56:2.2.verse: Taking up sharp knives, they murder each other. And so many people perish.

an3.56:2.3.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why these days human numbers have dwindled.

an3.56:3.1.verse: Furthermore, because these days humans just love illicit desire …

an3.56:3.2.verse: the heavens don’t provide enough rain,

an3.56:3.3.verse: so there’s famine, a bad harvest, with crops blighted and turned to straw.

an3.56:3.5.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why these days human numbers have dwindled.

an3.56:4.1.verse: Furthermore, because these days humans just love illicit desire …

an3.56:4.2.verse: native spirits let vicious monsters loose. And so many humans perish.

an3.56:4.3.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why these days human numbers have dwindled.”

an3.56:5.2.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.57:1.1.verse: Then Vacchagotta the wanderer went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him.

an3.57:1.2.verse: After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One:

an3.57:1.3.verse: “Master Gotama, I have heard that ‘Gotama the contemplative says this:

an3.57:1.4.verse: “Only to me should a gift be given, and not to others.

an3.57:1.5.verse: Only to my disciples should a gift be given, and not to others.

an3.57:1.6.verse: Only what is given to me bears great fruit, and not what is given to others.

an3.57:1.7.verse: Only what is given to my disciples bears great fruit, and not what is given to the disciples of others.”’

an3.57:1.13.verse: Are they reporting the Master Gotama’s actual words, are they not misrepresenting him with what is unfactual, are they answering in line with the Dhamma, so that no one whose thinking is in line with the Dhamma will have grounds for criticizing them?

an3.57:1.14.verse: For we don’t want to misrepresent the Master Gotama.”

an3.57:2.3.verse: “Only to me should a gift be given.…

an3.57:2.4.verse: Only what is given to my disciples bears great fruit, and not what is given to the disciples of others,”

an3.57:2.5.verse: is not reporting my actual words, is misrepresenting me with what is unfactual & untrue.

an3.57:2.6.verse: “Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates three obstructions, three impediments.

an3.57:2.8.verse: He creates an obstruction to the merit of the giver, an obstruction to the recipient’s gains, and prior to that he undermines and harms his own self.

an3.57:2.9.verse: Whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates these three obstructions, these three impediments.

an3.57:3.2.verse: even if a person throws the rinsings of a bowl or a cup into a village pool or pond,

an3.57:3.3.verse: thinking, ‘May whatever animals live here feed on this,’ that would be a source of merit,

an3.57:3.4.verse: to say nothing of what is given to human beings.

an3.57:3.5.verse: But I do say that what is given to a virtuous person is of great fruit, and not so much what is given to an unvirtuous person. And the virtuous person has abandoned five factors and is endowed with five.

an3.57:4.2.verse: He has abandoned sensual desire… ill will… sloth & drowsiness… restlessness & anxiety… uncertainty.

an3.57:4.3.verse: These are the five factors he has abandoned.

an3.57:5.1.verse: And with which five is he endowed?

an3.57:5.2.verse: He is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training… the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training… the aggregate of discernment of one beyond training… the aggregate of release of one beyond training… the aggregate of knowledge & vision of release of one beyond training.

an3.57:5.3.verse: These are the five factors with which he is endowed.

an3.57:5.4.verse: “I tell you: What is given to one who has abandoned these five factors and is endowed with these five, bears great fruit.

an3.57:8.2.verse: wherever one is born among human beings—

an3.57:9.1.verse: if one is tame, with good practices,

an3.57:12.4.verse: and don’t come near the good.

an3.57:13.1.verse: While those who do come near the good

an3.57:13.3.verse: whose conviction in the One Well-Gone

an3.57:14.1.verse: They go to the world of the devas

an3.57:14.2.verse: or are reborn here in good family.

an3.57:1.1.verse: Then the wanderer Vacchagotta went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an3.57:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an3.57:1.3.verse: “I have heard, worthy Gotama, that the ascetic Gotama says this:

an3.57:1.4.verse: ‘Gifts should only be given to me, not to others.

an3.57:1.5.verse: Gifts should only be given to my disciples, not to the disciples of others.

an3.57:1.6.verse: Only what is given to me is very fruitful, not what is given to others.

an3.57:1.7.verse: Only what is given to my disciples is very fruitful, not what is given to the disciples of others.’

an3.57:1.13.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the worthy Gotama has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?

an3.57:1.14.verse: For we don’t want to misrepresent the worthy Gotama.”

an3.57:2.5.verse: do not repeat what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue.

an3.57:2.6.verse: Anyone who prevents another from giving makes an obstacle and a roadblock for three individuals.

an3.57:2.8.verse: The giver is obstructed from making merit. The receiver is obstructed from getting what is offered. And they’ve already broken and damaged themselves.

an3.57:2.9.verse: Anyone who prevents another from giving makes an obstacle and a roadblock for these three individuals.

an3.57:3.1.verse: Vaccha, this is what I say:

an3.57:3.2.verse: ‘You even make merit by tipping out dish-washing water in a cesspool or a sump with living creatures in it, thinking,

an3.57:3.4.verse: How much more then for human beings!

an3.57:3.5.verse: However, I also say that a gift to an ethical person is more fruitful than one to an unethical person. They’ve given up five factors, and possess five factors.

an3.57:4.1.verse: What are the five factors they’ve given up?

an3.57:4.2.verse: Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

an3.57:4.3.verse: These are the five factors they’ve given up.

an3.57:5.1.verse: What are the five factors they possess?

an3.57:5.2.verse: The entire spectrum of an adept’s ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and knowledge and vision of freedom.

an3.57:5.3.verse: These are the five factors they possess.

an3.57:5.4.verse: I say that a gift to anyone who has given up these five factors and possesses these five factors is very fruitful.

an3.57:6.1.verse: Cows may be black or white,

an3.57:7.1.verse: But when one is born among them,

an3.57:7.5.verse: they yoke the load just to him,

an3.57:9.3.verse: Firm in principle, accomplished in ethical conduct,

an3.57:10.1.verse: they’ve given up birth and death.

an3.57:10.4.verse: they’ve completed the task and are free of defilements.

an3.57:12.3.verse: give their gifts to those outside,

an3.57:12.4.verse: and don’t attend the peaceful ones.

an3.57:13.1.verse: But those who do attend the peaceful ones—

an3.57:13.3.verse: and whose faith in the Holy One

an3.57:14.1.verse: they go to the realm of the gods,

an3.57:14.2.verse: or are born here in a good family.

an3.58:1.1.verse: Then Tikaṇṇa the brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an3.58:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, in front of the Buddha, Tikaṇṇa praised the brahmins who were proficient in the three Vedas,

an3.58:1.3.verse: “Such are the brahmins, masters of the three Vedic knowledges! Thus are the brahmins, masters of the three Vedic knowledges!”

an3.58:2.1.verse: “But brahmin, how do the brahmins describe a brahmin who is master of the three Vedic knowledges?”

an3.58:2.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, it’s when a brahmin is well born on both his mother’s and father’s side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation. He recites and remembers the hymns, and has mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. He knows them word-by-word, and their grammar. He is well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man.

an3.58:2.3.verse: That’s how the brahmins describe a brahmin who is master of the three Vedic knowledges.”

an3.58:3.1.verse: “Brahmin, a master of three knowledges according to the brahmins is quite different from a master of the three knowledges in the training of the Noble One.”

an3.58:3.2.verse: “But worthy Gotama, how is one a master of the three knowledges in the training of the Noble One?

an3.58:3.3.verse: Worthy Gotama, please teach me this.”

an3.58:3.4.verse: “Well then, brahmin, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an3.58:4.1.verse: “Brahmin, it’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an3.58:4.2.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an3.58:4.3.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

an3.58:4.4.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an3.58:5.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

an3.58:5.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

an3.58:5.3.verse: This is the first knowledge that they attain.

an3.58:5.4.verse: Ignorance is banished and knowledge has arisen; darkness is banished and light has arisen, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an3.58:6.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

an3.58:6.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an3.58:6.3.verse: This is the second knowledge that they attain.

an3.58:6.4.verse: Ignorance is banished and knowledge has arisen; darkness is banished and light has arisen, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an3.58:7.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

an3.58:7.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an3.58:7.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

an3.58:7.4.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an3.58:7.5.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

an3.58:7.6.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

an3.58:7.7.verse: This is the third knowledge that they attain.

an3.58:7.8.verse: Ignorance is banished and knowledge has arisen; darkness is banished, and light has arisen, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an3.58:8.1.verse: For someone whose ethical conduct doesn’t waver,

an3.58:9.1.verse: That attentive one dispels the darkness,

an3.58:9.2.verse: master of the three knowledges, conqueror of death.

an3.58:9.3.verse: For the welfare of gods and humans,

an3.58:9.4.verse: he has given up everything, they say.

an3.58:11.1.verse: One who knows their past lives,

an3.58:11.2.verse: sees heaven and places of loss,

an3.58:11.3.verse: and has attained the ending of rebirth,

an3.58:12.1.verse: it’s because of these three knowledges

an3.58:12.2.verse: that a brahmin is a master of the three knowledges.

an3.58:12.3.verse: That’s who I call a three-knowledge master,

an3.58:12.4.verse: and not the other who repeats what they are told.

an3.58:13.1.verse: This, brahmin, is a master of the three knowledges in the training of the Noble One.”

an3.58:13.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, a master of three knowledges according to the brahmins is quite different from a master of the three knowledges in the training of the Noble One.

an3.58:13.3.verse: And, worthy Gotama, a master of three knowledges according to the brahmins is not worth a sixteenth part of a master of the three knowledges in the training of the Noble One.

an3.58:14.2.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.59:1.1.verse: Then the brahmin Jānussoṇi went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. Seated to one side he said to the Buddha:

an3.59:1.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, whoever has a sacrifice, an offering of food for ancestors, a dish of milk-rice prepared for an auspicious ceremony, or a gift to give, should give it to the brahmins who have mastered the three Vedic knowledges.”

an3.59:1.3.verse: “But brahmin, how do the brahmins describe a brahmin who is proficient in the three Vedic knowledges?”

an3.60:1.1.verse: Then the brahman Saṅgārava went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him.

an3.60:1.2.verse: After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to the Blessed One:

an3.60:1.4.verse: perform sacrifices and get others to perform sacrifices.

an3.60:1.5.verse: And whoever performs a sacrifice, whoever gets others to perform a sacrifice, they have all practiced a practice of merit—the business of a sacrifice—(that benefits) countless beings.

an3.60:1.6.verse: But whoever, leaving his family, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and tames his single self, brings his single self into tune, brings his single self to unbinding: his practice of merit—this business of going forth—is one (that benefits) only one being.”

an3.60:2.1.verse: “Very well then, brahman, in that case I will cross-question you. Answer as you see fit.

an3.60:2.3.verse: There is the case where a Tathāgata appears in the world, a worthy one, rightly-self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, Well-Gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed.

an3.60:2.5.verse: ‘Here! This is the path, this is the practice which, having practiced, I make known the unexcelled gaining of a footing in the holy life,1 having directly known & realized it for myself.

an3.60:2.6.verse: Come! You, too, practice in such a way that you will remain in the unexcelled gaining of a footing in the holy life, having directly known & realized it for yourselves.’

an3.60:2.7.verse: Thus the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice, for authenticity [tathattā].2 And there are countless hundreds of them, countless thousands of them, countless hundreds of thousands of them.

an3.60:3.2.verse: is this practice of merit—this business of going-forth—one that benefits countless beings, or only one being?”

an3.60:3.3.verse: “This being the case, Master Gotama, this practice of merit—this business of going-forth—is one that benefits countless beings.”

an3.60:4.1.verse: When this was said, Ven. Ānanda said to the brahman Saṅgārava,

an3.60:4.2.verse: “Of these two practices, brahman, which appeals to you as the less complicated, the less violent, the more fruitful, & the more rewarding?”

an3.60:4.3.verse: When this was said, the brahman Saṅgārava said to Ven. Ānanda,

an3.60:4.4.verse: “Just as with Master Gotama & Master Ānanda,

an3.60:4.5.verse: I worship them, I praise them (both).”

an3.60:5.1.verse: A second time, Ven. Ānanda said to him,

an3.60:5.3.verse: whom you worship and whom you praise.

an3.60:5.5.verse: ‘Of these two practices, brahman, which appeals to you as the less complicated, the less violent, the more fruitful, & the more rewarding?’”

an3.60:5.6.verse: A second time, the brahman Saṅgārava said to Ven. Ānanda,

an3.60:5.7.verse: “Just as with Master Gotama & Master Ānanda,

an3.60:5.8.verse: I worship them, I praise them (both).”

an3.60:6.1.verse: A third time, Ven. Ānanda said to him,

an3.60:6.3.verse: whom you worship and whom you praise.

an3.60:6.5.verse: ‘Of these two practices, brahman, which appeals to you as the less complicated, the less violent, the more fruitful, & the more rewarding?’”

an3.60:6.6.verse: A third time, the brahman Saṅgārava said to Ven. Ānanda,

an3.60:6.7.verse: “Just as with Master Gotama & Master Ānanda,

an3.60:6.8.verse: I worship them, I praise them (both).”

an3.60:7.1.verse: Then the thought occurred to the Blessed One,

an3.60:7.2.verse: “Being asked a legitimate question by Ānanda up to the third time, the brahman Saṅgārava evades it and does not reply to it.

an3.60:7.3.verse: Suppose I were to get him out (of this dilemma).”

an3.60:7.4.verse: So the Blessed One said to the brahman Saṅgārava,

an3.60:7.5.verse: “Brahman, what was the topic of conversation that arose today when the royal court sat gathered in the royal palace?”

an3.60:7.6.verse: “Master Gotama, this was the topic of conversation that arose today when the royal court sat gathered in the royal palace:

an3.60:7.7.verse: ‘In the past, there were fewer monks but more who, endowed with superior human attainments, displayed the miracle of psychic power.

an3.60:7.8.verse: Now there are more monks but fewer who, endowed with superior human attainments, display the miracle of psychic power.’

an3.60:7.9.verse: This, Master Gotama, was the topic of conversation that arose today when the royal court sat gathered in the royal palace.”

an3.60:8.3.verse: The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of telepathy, & the miracle of instruction.

an3.60:8.4.verse: “And what is the miracle of psychic power?

an3.60:8.5.verse: There is the case where a certain person wields manifold psychic powers. Having been one he becomes many; having been many he becomes one. He appears. He vanishes. He goes unimpeded through walls, ramparts, & mountains as if through space. He dives in and out of the earth as if it were water. He walks on water without sinking as if it were dry land. Sitting cross-legged he flies through the air like a winged bird. With his hand he touches and strokes even the sun & moon, so mighty & powerful. He exercises influence with his body even as far as the Brahmā worlds.

an3.60:8.6.verse: This is called the miracle of psychic power.

an3.60:9.1.verse: “And what is the miracle of telepathy?

an3.60:9.2.verse: There is the case where a certain person reads (another person’ thoughts) by means of a sign [vision], (saying,)

an3.60:9.3.verse: ‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’

an3.60:9.4.verse: And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.

an3.60:10.1.verse: Then there is the case where a certain person reads (another person’s thoughts), not by means of a sign or vision, but by hearing the voice of human beings, non-human beings, or devas, (saying,)

an3.60:10.2.verse: ‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’

an3.60:10.3.verse: And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.

an3.60:11.1.verse: Then there is the case where a certain person reads (another person’s thoughts), not by means of a sign or vision; not by hearing the voice of human beings, non-human beings, or devas; but by hearing the sound of the directed thought & evaluation of a person thinking directed thoughts and evaluating, (saying,)

an3.60:11.2.verse: ‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’

an3.60:11.3.verse: And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.

an3.60:12.1.verse: Then there is the case where a certain person reads (another person’s thoughts), not by means of a sign or vision; not by hearing the voice of human beings, non-human beings, or devas; not by hearing the sound of the directed thought & evaluation of a person thinking directed thoughts and evaluating; but by encompassing with his own awareness the awareness of one who has attained a concentration devoid of directed thought & evaluation, he discerns,

an3.60:12.2.verse: ‘Given the way the mental fabrications of this venerable person are inclined, the directed thoughts of his mind will immediately think about this.’

an3.60:12.3.verse: And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.

an3.60:12.4.verse: “This, brahman, is the miracle of telepathy.

an3.60:13.1.verse: “And what is the miracle of instruction?

an3.60:13.2.verse: There is the case where a certain person gives instruction in this way:
