an3.60:13.3.verse: ‘Direct your thought in this way, don’t direct it in that. Attend to things in this way, don’t attend to them in that. Let go of this, enter and remain in that.’

an3.60:13.4.verse: This is called the miracle of instruction.

an3.60:13.6.verse: “Now, brahman, of these three miracles, which one appeals to you as the highest & most sublime?”

an3.60:14.1.verse: “Master Gotama, of these three miracles, the miracle of psychic power where a certain person wields manifold psychic powers…

an3.60:14.2.verse: (and) exercises influence with his body even as far as the Brahmā worlds:

an3.60:14.3.verse: That is a miracle experienced only by him who does it; it belongs only to him who does it.

an3.60:14.4.verse: It seems to me to be of the nature of an illusion.

an3.60:15.1.verse: “As for the miracle where a certain person by means of a sign or vision…

an3.60:15.2.verse: ‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’

an3.60:15.3.verse: by hearing the voice of human beings, non-human beings, or devas…

an3.60:15.4.verse: by hearing the sound of the directed thought & evaluation of a person thinking directed thoughts and evaluating, (saying,)

an3.60:15.5.verse: (or) who by encompassing with his own awareness the awareness of one who has attained a concentration devoid of directed thought & evaluation, he discerns,

an3.60:15.6.verse: ‘Given the way the mental fabrications of this venerable person are inclined, the directed thoughts of his mind will immediately think about this.’ And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise:

an3.60:15.7.verse: That is a miracle experienced only by him who does it; it belongs only to him who does it.

an3.60:15.8.verse: It seems to me to be of the nature of an illusion.

an3.60:16.1.verse: “As for the miracle where a certain person gives instruction in this way:

an3.60:16.2.verse: ‘Direct your thought in this way, don’t direct it in that. Attend to things in this way, don’t attend to them in that. Let go of this, enter and remain in that’:

an3.60:16.3.verse: this is the miracle that, of the three, appeals to me as the highest & most sublime.

an3.60:17.2.verse: how well this has been said by Master Gotama. And we hold that Master Gotama is endowed with these three marvels:

an3.60:17.3.verse: Master Gotama wields manifold psychic powers… (and) exercises influence with his body even as far as the Brahmā worlds. …

an3.60:17.4.verse: By encompassing with his own awareness the awareness of one who has attained a concentration devoid of directed thought & evaluation, Master Gotama discerns,

an3.60:17.5.verse: ‘Given the way the mental fabrications of this venerable person are inclined, the directed thoughts of his mind will immediately think about this.’

an3.60:17.6.verse: Master Gotama gives instruction in this way:

an3.60:17.7.verse: ‘Direct your thought in this way, don’t direct it in that. Attend to things in this way, don’t attend to them in that. Let go of this, enter and remain in that.’”

an3.60:18.1.verse: “Well, brahman, you are certainly being rude & presumptuous in making this statement,

an3.60:18.2.verse: but still I will respond to you.

an3.60:18.3.verse: Yes, I wield manifold psychic powers… (and) exercise influence with my body even as far as the Brahmā worlds; …

an3.60:18.4.verse: by encompassing with my own awareness the awareness of one who has attained a concentration devoid of directed thought & evaluation, I discern,

an3.60:18.5.verse: ‘Given the way the mental fabrications of this venerable person are inclined, the directed thoughts of his mind will immediately think about this.’

an3.60:18.6.verse: I give instruction in this way:

an3.60:18.7.verse: ‘Direct your thought in this way, don’t direct it in that. Attend to things in this way, don’t attend to them in that. Let go of this, enter and remain in that.’”

an3.60:19.1.verse: “Aside from Master Gotama, is there another monk who is endowed with these three miracles?”

an3.60:19.2.verse: “Brahman, there are not only one hundred other monks… two… three… four… five hundred other monks: The monks who are endowed with these three miracles are many more than that.”

an3.60:19.3.verse: “And, Master Gotama, where do those monks now live?”

an3.60:19.4.verse: “In this very same Saṅgha of monks.”

an3.60:20.2.verse: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

an3.60:20.3.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, & to the Saṅgha of monks.

an3.60:20.4.verse: May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for life.”

an3.60:1.1.verse: Then Saṅgārava the brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an3.60:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an3.60:1.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, we who are called brahmins

an3.60:1.4.verse: make sacrifices and encourage others to make sacrifices.

an3.60:1.5.verse: Now, worthy Gotama, both of these people—the one who sacrifices and the one who encourages others to sacrifice—are doing good for many people on account of that sacrifice.

an3.60:1.6.verse: But, worthy Gotama, when someone has gone forth from the lay life to homelessness, they tame, calm, and extinguish themselves alone. That being so, they are doing good for just one person on account of that going forth.”

an3.60:2.1.verse: “Well then, brahmin, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

an3.60:2.3.verse: A Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

an3.60:2.5.verse: ‘Come, this is the path, this is the practice. Practicing like this, I realized the supreme objective of the spiritual life with my own insight, and I make it known.

an3.60:2.6.verse: Please, all of you, practice like this, and you too will realize the supreme objective of the spiritual life, and will live having realized it with your own insight.’

an3.60:2.7.verse: So the Teacher teaches Dhamma, and others practice accordingly, in their hundreds and thousands, and hundreds of thousands.

an3.60:3.2.verse: This being so, are they doing good for just one person or for many people on account of going forth?”

an3.60:3.3.verse: “This being so, worthy Gotama, they are doing good for many people on account of going forth.”

an3.60:4.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to Saṅgārava,

an3.60:4.2.verse: “Brahmin, which of these two practices do you believe has fewer obligations and undertakings, yet is more fruitful and beneficial?”

an3.60:4.4.verse: “Those such as the worthies Gotama and Ānanda

an3.60:4.5.verse: are honored and praised by me!”

an3.60:5.1.verse: For a second time, Ānanda said to Saṅgārava,

an3.60:5.5.verse: which of these two practices do you believe has fewer obligations and undertakings, yet is more fruitful and beneficial?”

an3.60:5.6.verse: For a second time Saṅgārava said to Ānanda,

an3.60:5.7.verse: “Those such as the worthies Gotama and Ānanda

an3.60:5.8.verse: are honored and praised by me!”

an3.60:6.1.verse: For a third time, Ānanda said to Saṅgārava,

an3.60:6.5.verse: which of these two practices do you believe has fewer obligations and undertakings, yet is more fruitful and beneficial?”

an3.60:6.6.verse: For a third time Saṅgārava said to Ānanda,

an3.60:6.7.verse: “Those such as the worthies Gotama and Ānanda

an3.60:6.8.verse: are honored and praised by me!”

an3.60:7.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

an3.60:7.2.verse: “Though Ānanda asked him a sensible question three times, Saṅgārava falters without answering.

an3.60:7.3.verse: Why don’t I give him a way out?”

an3.60:7.4.verse: So the Buddha said to Saṅgārava,

an3.60:7.5.verse: “Brahmin, what came up in the conversation among the king’s retinue today, sitting together in the royal compound?”

an3.60:7.7.verse: ‘Formerly, it seems, there were fewer mendicants, but more of them displayed superhuman demonstrations of psychic power;

an3.60:7.8.verse: while these days, there are more mendicants, but fewer display superhuman demonstrations of psychic power.’

an3.60:7.9.verse: This is what came up in the conversation among the king’s retinue today, while sitting together in the royal compound.”

an3.60:8.1.verse: “Brahmin, there are three kinds of demonstration.

an3.60:8.3.verse: A demonstration of psychic power, a demonstration of revealing, and a demonstration of instruction.

an3.60:8.4.verse: And what is the demonstration of psychic power?

an3.60:8.5.verse: It’s when someone wields the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. They control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

an3.60:8.6.verse: This is called the demonstration of psychic power.

an3.60:9.1.verse: And what is the demonstration of revealing?

an3.60:9.2.verse: In one case, someone reveals by means of a sign:

an3.60:9.3.verse: ‘This is what you’re thinking, such is your thought, and thus is your state of mind.’

an3.60:9.4.verse: And even if they reveal this many times, it turns out exactly so, not otherwise.

an3.60:10.1.verse: In another case, someone reveals after hearing it from humans or non-humans or deities:

an3.60:10.2.verse: ‘This is what you’re thinking, such is your thought, and thus is your state of mind.’

an3.60:10.3.verse: And even if they reveal this many times, it turns out exactly so, not otherwise.

an3.60:11.1.verse: In another case, someone reveals by hearing the sound of thought spreading as someone thinks and considers:

an3.60:11.2.verse: ‘This is what you’re thinking, such is your thought, and thus is your state of mind.’

an3.60:11.3.verse: And even if they reveal this many times, it turns out exactly so, not otherwise.

an3.60:12.1.verse: In another case, someone comprehends the mind of one who has attained the immersion that’s free of placing the mind and keeping it connected. They understand:

an3.60:12.2.verse: ‘Judging by the way this worthy’s intentions are directed, immediately after this mind state, they’ll think this thought.’

an3.60:12.3.verse: And even if they reveal this many times, it turns out exactly so, not otherwise.

an3.60:12.4.verse: This is called the demonstration of revealing.

an3.60:13.1.verse: And what is a demonstration of instruction?

an3.60:13.2.verse: It’s when someone instructs others like this:

an3.60:13.3.verse: ‘Think like this, not like that. Focus your mind like this, not like that. Give up this, and live having achieved that.’

an3.60:13.4.verse: This is called a demonstration of instruction.

an3.60:13.5.verse: These are the three kinds of demonstration.

an3.60:13.6.verse: Of these three kinds of demonstration, which do you consider to be the finest?”

an3.60:14.1.verse: “Regarding this, worthy Gotama, a demonstration of psychic power

an3.60:14.3.verse: is experienced only by the one who performs it, occurring only to them.

an3.60:14.4.verse: This seems to me like an illusion.

an3.60:15.1.verse: And the demonstration where someone reveals something by means of a sign,

an3.60:15.3.verse: or after hearing it from humans, non-humans, or deities,

an3.60:15.4.verse: or by hearing the sound of thought spreading as someone thinks and considers,

an3.60:15.5.verse: or by comprehending the mind of another,

an3.60:15.7.verse: is also experienced only by the one who performs it, occurring only to them.

an3.60:15.8.verse: This also seems to me like an illusion.

an3.60:16.1.verse: But as to the demonstration where someone instructs others:

an3.60:16.2.verse: ‘Think like this, not like that. Focus your mind like this, not like that. Give up this, and live having achieved that.’

an3.60:16.3.verse: I prefer this demonstration, worthy Gotama. It’s the finest of the three kinds of demonstration.

an3.60:17.1.verse: It’s incredible, worthy Gotama, it’s amazing,

an3.60:17.2.verse: how well this was said by the worthy Gotama. We regard the worthy Gotama as someone who possesses these three kinds of demonstration.

an3.60:17.3.verse: For the worthy Gotama wields the many kinds of psychic power … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.

an3.60:17.4.verse: And Worthy Gotama comprehends the mind of another who has attained the immersion that is free of placing the mind and keeping it connected. He understands:

an3.60:17.5.verse: ‘Judging by the way this worthy’s intentions are directed, immediately after this mind state they’ll think this thought.’

an3.60:17.6.verse: And the worthy Gotama instructs others like this:

an3.60:17.7.verse: ‘Think like this, not like that. Focus your mind like this, not like that. Give up this, and live having achieved that.’”

an3.60:18.1.verse: “Your words are clearly invasive and intrusive, brahmin.

an3.60:18.3.verse: For I do wield the many kinds of psychic power … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.

an3.60:18.4.verse: And I do comprehend the mind of another individual who has attained the immersion that is free of placing the mind and keeping it connected. I understand:

an3.60:18.5.verse: ‘Judging by the way this worthy’s intentions are directed, immediately after this mind state they’ll think this thought.’

an3.60:18.6.verse: And I do instruct others like this:

an3.60:18.7.verse: ‘Think like this, not like that. Focus your mind like this, not like that. Give up this, and live having achieved that.’”

an3.60:19.1.verse: “But worthy Gotama, is there even one other mendicant who possesses these three kinds of demonstration, apart from the worthy Gotama?”

an3.60:19.2.verse: “There’s not just one hundred mendicants, brahmin, who possess these three kinds of demonstration, nor two, three, four, or five hundred, but many more than that.”

an3.60:19.3.verse: “But where are these mendicants now staying?”

an3.60:19.4.verse: “Right here, brahmin, in this Saṅgha of mendicants.”

an3.60:20.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an3.60:20.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an3.60:20.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.61:1.1.verse: “Monks, there are these three sectarian guilds that—when cross-examined, pressed for reasons, & rebuked by wise people—even though they may explain otherwise, remain stuck in (a doctrine of) inaction.

an3.61:1.3.verse: “There are contemplatives & brahmans who hold this teaching, hold this view:

an3.61:1.4.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful—is all caused by what was done in the past.’

an3.61:1.5.verse: There are contemplatives & brahmans who hold this teaching, hold this view:

an3.61:1.6.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful—is all caused by a supreme being’s act of creation.’

an3.61:1.7.verse: There are contemplatives & brahmans who hold this teaching, hold this view:

an3.61:1.8.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful—is all without cause & without condition.’

an3.61:2.1.verse: “Having approached the contemplatives & brahmans who hold that…

an3.61:2.2.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences… is all caused by what was done in the past,’ I said to them:

an3.61:2.3.verse: ‘Is it true that you hold that… whatever a person experiences… is all caused by what was done in the past?’

an3.61:2.5.verse: Thus asked by me, they admitted, ‘Yes.’

an3.61:2.7.verse: ‘Then in that case, a person is a killer of living beings because of what was done in the past. A person is a thief… uncelibate… a liar… a divisive speaker… a harsh speaker… an idle chatterer… greedy… malicious… a holder of wrong views because of what was done in the past.’

an3.61:3.1.verse: When one falls back on what was done in the past as being essential, monks, there is no desire, no effort (at the thought), ‘This should be done. This shouldn’t be done.’

an3.61:3.2.verse: When one can’t pin down as a truth or reality what should & shouldn’t be done, one dwells bewildered & unprotected. One cannot righteously refer to oneself as a contemplative.

an3.61:3.3.verse: This was my first righteous refutation of those contemplatives & brahmans who hold to such teachings, such views.

an3.61:4.1.verse: “Having approached the contemplatives & brahmans who hold that…

an3.61:4.2.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences… is all caused by a supreme being’s act of creation,’ I said to them:

an3.61:4.3.verse: ‘Is it true that you hold that… whatever a person experiences… is all caused by a supreme being’s act of creation?’

an3.61:4.5.verse: Thus asked by me, they admitted, ‘Yes.’

an3.61:4.7.verse: ‘Then in that case, a person is a killer of living beings because of a supreme being’s act of creation. A person is a thief… uncelibate… a liar… a divisive speaker… a harsh speaker… an idle chatterer… greedy… malicious… a holder of wrong views because of a supreme being’s act of creation.’

an3.61:5.1.verse: When one falls back on a supreme being’s act of creation as being essential, monks, there is no desire, no effort (at the thought), ‘This should be done. This shouldn’t be done.’

an3.61:5.2.verse: When one can’t pin down as a truth or reality what should & shouldn’t be done, one dwells bewildered & unprotected. One cannot righteously refer to oneself as a contemplative.

an3.61:5.3.verse: This was my second righteous refutation of those contemplatives & brahmans who hold to such teachings, such views.

an3.61:6.1.verse: “Having approached the contemplatives & brahmans who hold that…

an3.61:6.2.verse: ‘Whatever a person experiences… is all without cause, without condition,’ I said to them:

an3.61:6.3.verse: ‘Is it true that you hold that… whatever a person experiences… is all without cause, without condition?’

an3.61:6.5.verse: Thus asked by me, they admitted, ‘Yes.’

an3.61:6.7.verse: ‘Then in that case, a person is a killer of living beings without cause, without condition. A person is a thief… uncelibate… a liar… a divisive speaker… a harsh speaker… an idle chatterer… greedy… malicious… a holder of wrong views without cause, without condition.’

an3.61:7.1.verse: When one falls back on lack of cause and lack of condition as being essential, monks, there is no desire, no effort (at the thought), ‘This should be done. This shouldn’t be done.’

an3.61:7.2.verse: When one can’t pin down as a truth or reality what should & shouldn’t be done, one dwells bewildered & unprotected. One cannot righteously refer to oneself as a contemplative.

an3.61:7.3.verse: This was my third righteous refutation of those contemplatives & brahmans who hold to such teachings, such views.

an3.61:8.1.verse: “These are the three sectarian guilds that—when cross-examined, pressed for reasons, & rebuked by wise people—even though they may explain otherwise, remain stuck in inaction.

an3.61:9.1.verse: “But this Dhamma taught by me is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans.

an3.61:9.2.verse: And which Dhamma taught by me is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans?

an3.61:9.3.verse: ‘There are these six properties’ is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans.

an3.61:9.4.verse: ‘There are these six media of sensory contact’ is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans.

an3.61:9.5.verse: ‘There are these eighteen explorations for the intellect’ is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans.

an3.61:9.6.verse: ‘There are these four noble truths’ is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans.

an3.61:10.1.verse: “‘“There are these six properties” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:10.3.verse: And in reference to what was it said?

an3.61:10.5.verse: earth-property, liquid-property, fire-property, wind-property, space-property, consciousness-property.

an3.61:10.6.verse: ‘“There are these six properties” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:10.7.verse: Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said.

an3.61:11.1.verse: “‘“There are these six media of sensory contact” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:11.3.verse: And in reference to what was it said?

an3.61:11.4.verse: These are the six media of sensory contact:

an3.61:11.5.verse: the eye as a medium of sensory contact, the ear as a medium of sensory contact, the nose as a medium of sensory contact, the tongue as a medium of sensory contact, the body as a medium of sensory contact, the intellect as a medium of sensory contact.

an3.61:11.6.verse: ‘“There are these six media of sensory contact” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:11.7.verse: Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said.

an3.61:12.1.verse: “‘“There are these eighteen explorations for the intellect” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:12.3.verse: And in reference to what was it said?

an3.61:12.4.verse: Seeing a form via the eye, one explores a form that can act as the basis for happiness, one explores a form that can act as the basis for unhappiness, one explores a form that can act as the basis for equanimity.

an3.61:12.5.verse: Hearing a sound via the ear…

an3.61:12.6.verse: Smelling an aroma via the nose…

an3.61:12.7.verse: Tasting a flavor via the tongue…

an3.61:12.8.verse: Touching a tactile sensation via the body…

an3.61:12.9.verse: Cognizing an idea via the intellect, one explores an idea that can act as the basis for happiness, one explores an idea that can act as the basis for unhappiness, one explores an idea that can act as the basis for equanimity.

an3.61:12.10.verse: ‘“There are these eighteen explorations for the intellect” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:12.11.verse: Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said.

an3.61:13.1.verse: “‘“There are these four noble truths” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:13.3.verse: And in reference to what was it said?

an3.61:13.4.verse: Sustained by/clinging to the six properties, there is an alighting of an embryo.

an3.61:13.5.verse: There being an alighting, there is name-&-form. From name-&-form as a requisite condition come the six sense media. From the six sense media as a requisite condition comes contact. From contact as a requisite condition comes feeling.

an3.61:13.6.verse: To one experiencing feeling I declare, ‘This is stress.’ I declare, ‘This is the origination of stress.’ I declare, ‘This is the cessation of stress.’ I declare, ‘This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of stress.’

an3.61:14.1.verse: “And what is the noble truth of stress?

an3.61:14.2.verse: Birth is stress, aging is stress, death is stress; sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, & despair are stress; association with what is not loved is stress, separation from what is loved is stress, not getting what is wanted is stress. In short, the five clinging-aggregates are stress.

an3.61:14.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of stress.

an3.61:15.1.verse: “And what is the noble truth of the origination of stress?

an3.61:15.2.verse: From ignorance as a requisite condition come fabrications.

an3.61:15.3.verse: From fabrications as a requisite condition comes consciousness.

an3.61:15.4.verse: From consciousness as a requisite condition comes name-&-form.

an3.61:15.5.verse: From name-&-form as a requisite condition come the six sense media.

an3.61:15.6.verse: From the six sense media as a requisite condition comes contact.

an3.61:15.7.verse: From contact as a requisite condition comes feeling.

an3.61:15.8.verse: From feeling as a requisite condition comes craving.

an3.61:15.9.verse: From craving as a requisite condition comes clinging/sustenance.

an3.61:15.10.verse: From clinging/sustenance as a requisite condition comes becoming.

an3.61:15.11.verse: From becoming as a requisite condition comes birth.

an3.61:15.12.verse: From birth as a requisite condition, then old age & death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, & despair come into play.

an3.61:15.13.verse: Such is the origination of this entire mass of stress & suffering.

an3.61:15.14.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origination of stress.

an3.61:16.1.verse: “And what is the noble truth of the cessation of stress?

an3.61:16.2.verse: From the remainderless fading & cessation of that very ignorance comes the cessation of fabrications.

an3.61:16.3.verse: From the cessation of fabrications comes the cessation of consciousness.

an3.61:16.4.verse: From the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-&-form.

an3.61:16.5.verse: From the cessation of name-&-form comes the cessation of the six sense media.

an3.61:16.6.verse: From the cessation of the six sense media comes the cessation of contact.

an3.61:16.7.verse: From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.

an3.61:16.8.verse: From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.

an3.61:16.9.verse: From the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging/sustenance.

an3.61:16.10.verse: From the cessation of clinging/sustenance comes the cessation of becoming.

an3.61:16.11.verse: From the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth.

an3.61:16.12.verse: From the cessation of birth, then old age & death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, & despair all cease.

an3.61:16.13.verse: Such is the cessation of this entire mass of stress & suffering.

an3.61:16.14.verse: “This is called the noble truth of the cessation of stress.

an3.61:17.1.verse: “And what is the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of stress?

an3.61:17.3.verse: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

an3.61:17.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of stress.

an3.61:17.5.verse: “‘“There are these four noble truths” is a Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, undefiled, blameless, not faulted by knowledgeable contemplatives & brahmans’:

an3.61:17.6.verse: Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said.”

an3.61:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these three sectarian tenets—as pursued, pressed, and grilled by the astute—when taken to their conclusion, end with inaction.

an3.61:1.3.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

an3.61:1.4.verse: ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of past deeds.’

an3.61:1.5.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

an3.61:1.6.verse: ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of God Almighty’s creation.’

an3.61:1.7.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

an3.61:1.8.verse: ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—has no cause or reason.’

an3.61:2.1.verse: Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that

an3.61:2.2.verse: everything an individual person experiences is because of past deeds, and I said to them:

an3.61:2.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

an3.61:2.7.verse: ‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of past deeds.’

an3.61:3.1.verse: Those who believe that past deeds are the most important thing have no enthusiasm or effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.

an3.61:3.2.verse: Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.

an3.61:3.3.verse: This is my first legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.

an3.61:4.1.verse: Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that

an3.61:4.2.verse: everything that an individual person experiences is because of God Almighty’s creation, and I said to them:

an3.61:4.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

an3.61:4.7.verse: ‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of God Almighty’s creation.’

an3.61:5.1.verse: Those who believe that God Almighty’s creative power is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.

an3.61:5.2.verse: Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.

an3.61:5.3.verse: This is my second legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.

an3.61:6.1.verse: Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that

an3.61:6.2.verse: everything that an individual person experiences has no cause or reason, and I said to them:

an3.61:6.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

an3.61:6.7.verse: ‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all without cause or reason.’

an3.61:7.1.verse: Those who believe that the absence of cause or reason is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.

an3.61:7.2.verse: Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.

an3.61:7.3.verse: This is my third legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.

an3.61:8.1.verse: These are the three sectarian tenets—as pursued, pressed, and grilled by the astute—which, when taken to their conclusion, end with inaction.

an3.61:9.1.verse: But the Dhamma that I’ve taught is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.

an3.61:9.2.verse: What is the Dhamma that I’ve taught?

an3.61:9.3.verse: ‘These are the six elements’: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …

an3.61:9.4.verse: ‘These are the six fields of contact’: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …

an3.61:9.5.verse: ‘These are the eighteen mental preoccupations’: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …

an3.61:9.6.verse: ‘These are the four noble truths’: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught that is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and is not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.

an3.61:10.1.verse: ‘“These are the six elements”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:10.3.verse: but why did I say it?

an3.61:10.5.verse: the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.

an3.61:10.6.verse: ‘“These are the six elements”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:10.7.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an3.61:11.1.verse: ‘“These are the six fields of contact”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:11.3.verse: but why did I say it?

an3.61:11.4.verse: There are these six fields of contact:

an3.61:11.5.verse: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind contact.

an3.61:11.6.verse: ‘“These are the six fields of contact”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:11.7.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an3.61:12.1.verse: ‘“These are the eighteen mental preoccupations”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:12.3.verse: but why did I say it?

an3.61:12.4.verse: Seeing a sight with their eyes, one is preoccupied with a sight that’s a basis for happiness or sadness or equanimity.

an3.61:12.5.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an3.61:12.6.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an3.61:12.7.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an3.61:12.8.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an3.61:12.9.verse: Becoming conscious of an idea with their mind, one is preoccupied with an idea that’s a basis for happiness or sadness or equanimity.

an3.61:12.10.verse: ‘“These are the eighteen mental preoccupations”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:12.11.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an3.61:13.1.verse: ‘“These are the four noble truths”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught …’

an3.61:13.3.verse: but why did I say it?

an3.61:13.4.verse: Supported by the six elements, an embryo is conceived.

an3.61:13.5.verse: When it is conceived, there are name and form. Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields. The six sense fields are requirements for contact. Contact is a requirement for feeling.

an3.61:13.6.verse: It’s for one who feels that I declare: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an3.61:14.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

an3.61:14.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

an3.61:14.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

an3.61:15.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

an3.61:15.2.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

an3.61:15.3.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

an3.61:15.4.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

an3.61:15.5.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

an3.61:15.6.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

an3.61:15.7.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

an3.61:15.8.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

an3.61:15.9.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

an3.61:15.10.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

an3.61:15.11.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

an3.61:15.12.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

an3.61:15.13.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

an3.61:15.14.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

an3.61:16.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

an3.61:16.2.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease.

an3.61:16.4.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

an3.61:16.5.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

an3.61:16.6.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

an3.61:16.10.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

an3.61:16.11.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

an3.61:16.12.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

an3.61:16.13.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

an3.61:16.14.verse: This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

an3.61:17.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

an3.61:17.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

an3.61:17.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an3.61:17.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

an3.61:17.5.verse: ‘“These are the four noble truths”: this is the Dhamma I’ve taught that is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and is not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.’

an3.61:17.6.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

an3.62:1.1.verse: “Monks, uneducated run-of-the-mill people describe three things as mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:1.3.verse: “There comes a time when a great fire-conflagration breaks out.

an3.62:1.4.verse: When a great fire-conflagration breaks out, it burns villages, towns, & cities.

an3.62:1.5.verse: When it is burning villages, towns, & cities, a mother there can’t get to her child, and the child can’t get to its mother.

an3.62:1.6.verse: This is the first thing that uneducated run-of-the-mill people describe as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:2.1.verse: “Then again there comes a time when a great cloud arises.

an3.62:2.2.verse: When a great cloud arises, a great flood of water is produced.

an3.62:2.3.verse: When a great flood of water is produced, it floods villages, towns, & cities.

an3.62:2.4.verse: When it is flooding villages, towns, & cities, a mother there can’t get to her child, and the child can’t get to its mother.

an3.62:2.5.verse: This is the second thing that uneducated run-of-the-mill people describe as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:3.1.verse: “Then again there comes a time when there is danger and an invasion of savage tribes. Taking power, they surround the countryside.

an3.62:3.2.verse: When this happens, a mother there can’t get to her child, and the child can’t get to its mother.

an3.62:3.3.verse: This is the third thing that uneducated run-of-the-mill people describe as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:3.4.verse: “These are the three things that uneducated run-of-the-mill people describe as mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:4.1.verse: “But there are these three things that are mother-&-child-uniting dangers, yet run-of-the-mill people describe them as mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:4.3.verse: “There comes a time when a great fire-conflagration breaks out.

an3.62:4.4.verse: When a great fire-conflagration breaks out, it burns villages, towns, & cities.

an3.62:4.5.verse: When it is burning villages, towns, & cities, there are times when it so happens that a mother can get to her child, and the child can get to its mother.

an3.62:4.6.verse: This is the first thing that is a mother-&-child-uniting danger, yet run-of-the-mill people describe it as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:5.1.verse: “Then again there comes a time when a great cloud arises.

an3.62:5.2.verse: When a great cloud arises, a great flood of water is produced.

an3.62:5.3.verse: When a great flood of water is produced, it floods villages, towns, & cities.

an3.62:5.4.verse: When it is flooding villages, towns, & cities, there are times when it so happens that a mother can get to her child, and the child can get to its mother.

an3.62:5.5.verse: This is the second thing that is a mother-&-child-uniting danger, yet run-of-the-mill people describe it as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:6.1.verse: “Then again there comes a time when there is danger and an invasion of savage tribes. Taking power, they surround the countryside.

an3.62:6.2.verse: When this happens, there are times when it so happens that a mother can get to her child, and the child can get to its mother.

an3.62:6.3.verse: This is the third thing that is a mother-&-child-uniting danger, yet run-of-the-mill people describe it as a mother-&-child-separating danger.

an3.62:6.4.verse: “These are the three things that are mother-&-child-uniting dangers, yet run-of-the-mill people describe them as mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:7.1.verse: “There are these three things that are (genuine) mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:7.3.verse: The danger of aging, the danger of illness, the danger of death.

an3.62:7.4.verse: “A mother can’t get (her wish) with regard to her child who is aging,

an3.62:7.5.verse: ‘I am aging, but may my child not age.’

an3.62:7.6.verse: A child can’t get (its wish) with regard to its mother who is aging,

an3.62:7.7.verse: ‘I am aging, but may my mother not age.’

an3.62:8.1.verse: “A mother can’t get (her wish) with regard to her child who is growing ill,

an3.62:8.2.verse: ‘I am growing ill, but may my child not grow ill.’

an3.62:8.3.verse: A child can’t get (its wish) with regard to its mother who is growing ill,

an3.62:8.4.verse: ‘I am growing ill, but may my mother not grow ill.’

an3.62:9.1.verse: “A mother can’t get (her wish) with regard to her child who is dying,

an3.62:9.2.verse: ‘I am dying, but may my child not die.’

an3.62:9.3.verse: A child can’t get (its wish) with regard to its mother who is dying,

an3.62:9.4.verse: ‘I am dying, but may my mother not die.’

an3.62:9.5.verse: “These are the three things that are (genuine) mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:10.1.verse: “There is a path, there is a practice, that leads to the abandoning and overcoming of these three mother-&-child-uniting dangers and these three mother-&-child-separating dangers.

an3.62:10.2.verse: “And which is that path, which is that practice…?

an3.62:10.3.verse: Just this very noble eightfold path, i.e.,

an3.62:10.4.verse: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

an3.62:10.5.verse: This is the path, this the practice, that leads to the abandoning and overcoming of these three mother-&-child-uniting dangers and these three mother-&-child-separating dangers.”

an3.62:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of three perils that tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:1.3.verse: There comes a time when a great fire flares up,

an3.62:1.4.verse: and it burns villages, towns, and cities.

an3.62:1.5.verse: When this happens, a mother can’t find her child, and a child can’t find their mother.

an3.62:1.6.verse: This is the first peril that tears mothers and children apart.

an3.62:2.1.verse: Furthermore, there comes a time when a great storm gathers,

an3.62:2.2.verse: and it unleashes a mighty flood

an3.62:2.3.verse: that sweeps away villages, towns, and cities.

an3.62:2.4.verse: When this happens, a mother can’t find her child, and a child can’t find their mother.

an3.62:2.5.verse: This is the second peril that tears mothers and children apart.

an3.62:3.1.verse: Furthermore, there comes a time of peril due to turmoil in the wilds, so the countryfolk mount their vehicles and flee everywhere.

an3.62:3.2.verse: When this happens, a mother can’t find her child, and a child can’t find their mother.

an3.62:3.3.verse: This is the third peril that tears mothers and children apart.

an3.62:3.4.verse: These are the three perils an unlearned ordinary person speaks of that tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:4.1.verse: Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of three perils that don’t tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:4.3.verse: There comes a time when a great fire flares up,

an3.62:4.4.verse: and it burns villages, towns, and cities.

an3.62:4.5.verse: When this happens, sometimes a mother can find her child, and a child can find their mother.

an3.62:4.6.verse: This is the first peril that doesn’t tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:5.1.verse: Furthermore, there comes a time when a great storm gathers,

an3.62:5.2.verse: and it unleashes a mighty flood

an3.62:5.3.verse: that sweeps away villages, towns, and cities.

an3.62:5.4.verse: When this happens, sometimes a mother can find her child, and a child can find their mother.

an3.62:5.5.verse: This is the second peril that doesn’t tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:6.1.verse: Furthermore, there comes a time of peril due to turmoil in the wilds, so the countryfolk mount their vehicles and flee everywhere.

an3.62:6.2.verse: When this happens, sometimes a mother can find her child, and a child can find their mother.

an3.62:6.3.verse: This is the third peril that doesn’t tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:6.4.verse: These are the three perils an unlearned ordinary person speaks of that don’t tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:7.1.verse: There are three perils that tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:7.3.verse: The perils of old age, sickness, and death.

an3.62:7.4.verse: When a child is growing old, a mother doesn’t get her wish:

an3.62:7.5.verse: ‘Let me grow old, may my child not grow old!’

an3.62:7.6.verse: When a mother is growing old, a child doesn’t get their wish:

an3.62:7.7.verse: ‘Let me grow old, may my mother not grow old!’

an3.62:8.1.verse: When a child is sick, a mother doesn’t get her wish:

an3.62:8.2.verse: ‘Let me be sick, may my child not be sick!’

an3.62:8.3.verse: When a mother is sick, a child doesn’t get their wish:

an3.62:8.4.verse: ‘Let me be sick, may my mother not be sick!’

an3.62:9.1.verse: When a child is dying, a mother doesn’t get her wish:

an3.62:9.2.verse: ‘Let me die, may my child not die!’

an3.62:9.3.verse: When a mother is dying, a child doesn’t get their wish:

an3.62:9.4.verse: ‘Let me die, may my mother not die!’

an3.62:9.5.verse: These are the three perils that tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:10.1.verse: There is a path and a practice that leads to giving up and going beyond the three perils that don’t tear mothers and children apart, and the three perils that do tear mothers and children apart.

an3.62:10.2.verse: What is that path and practice?

an3.62:10.3.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

an3.62:10.4.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an3.62:10.5.verse: This is the path, this is the practice that leads to giving up and going beyond the three perils that don’t tear mothers and children apart, and the three perils that do tear mothers and children apart.”

an3.63:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One, on a wandering tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks, arrived at Venāgapura, a brahman town of the Kosalans.

an3.63:1.2.verse: The brahman householders of Venāgapura heard it said,

an3.63:1.3.verse: “Gotama the contemplative—the son of the Sakyans, having gone forth from the Sakyan clan—has arrived at Venāgapura.

an3.63:1.4.verse: And of that Master Gotama this fine reputation has spread:

an3.63:1.5.verse: ‘He is indeed a Blessed One, worthy & rightly self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, Well-Gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed.

an3.63:1.6.verse: He makes known—having realized it through direct knowledge—this world with its devas, Māras, & Brahmās, this generation with its contemplatives & brahmans, its rulers & commonfolk;

an3.63:1.7.verse: he explains the Dhamma admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, admirable in the end; he expounds the holy life both in its particulars & in its essence, entirely perfect, surpassingly pure.

an3.63:1.8.verse: It is good to see such a worthy one.’”

an3.63:2.1.verse: So the brahman householders of Venāgapura went to the Blessed One. On arrival, some of them bowed down to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Some of them exchanged courteous greetings with him and, after an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, sat to one side. Some of them sat to one side having saluted him with their hands palm-to-palm over their hearts. Some of them sat to one side having announced their name & clan. Some of them sat to one side in silence. As they were sitting there, the brahman Vaccagotta of Venāgapura said to the Blessed One,

an3.63:3.2.verse: How clear Master Gotama’s faculties are; how pure his complexion, & bright!

an3.63:3.3.verse: “Just as a yellow jujube fruit in the autumn is pure & bright,

an3.63:3.4.verse: in the same way, clear are Master Gotama’s faculties, pure his complexion, & bright!

an3.63:3.5.verse: “Just as a palmyra fruit, freshly removed from its stalk, is pure & bright,

an3.63:3.6.verse: in the same way, clear are Master Gotama’s faculties, pure his complexion, & bright!

an3.63:3.7.verse: “Just as an ornament of gold from the Jambū River—well-crafted by a skilled goldsmith, very skillfully wrought & placed on a red brocade—shines, glows, & radiates,

an3.63:3.8.verse: in the same way, clear are Master Gotama’s faculties, pure his complexion, & bright!

an3.63:3.9.verse: “Whatever high or luxurious beds there are—

an3.63:3.10.verse: a dais, a throne, a long-haired coverlet, a decorated coverlet, a white spread made of animal hair, a wool coverlet with floral designs, a blanket of cotton batting, a wool coverlet decorated with animals, a wool covering with fleece on both sides, a wool covering with fleece on one side, a silken sheet decorated with jewels, fringed with silver or gold, a dancer’s carpet, an elephant-back rug, a horse-back rug, a chariot rug, a spread of black antelope skins, a sheet of kadali-deer hide, a bed with a canopy above, a bed with red cushions at either end: Surely Master Gotama obtains them at will, without trouble, without difficulty!”

an3.63:4.1.verse: “But, brahman, those high or luxurious beds—

an3.63:4.2.verse: a dais, a throne… a bed with red cushions at either end—

an3.63:4.3.verse: are rarely obtained by one gone forth, and even if obtained, are not allowable.

an3.63:5.1.verse: “However, there are these three high & luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without trouble, without difficulty.

an3.63:5.3.verse: The divine high & luxurious bed, the Brahmā high & luxurious bed, the noble high & luxurious bed.

an3.63:5.4.verse: These are the three high & luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without trouble, without difficulty.”

an3.63:6.1.verse: “But which, Master Gotama, is the divine high & luxurious bed that Master Gotama now obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty?”

an3.63:6.2.verse: “There is the case, brahman, where I dwell in dependence on a village or town. Early in the morning, having adjusted my under robe and carrying my bowl & robes, I enter that village or town for alms.

an3.63:6.3.verse: After my meal, returning from my alms round, I go right into the forest.

an3.63:6.4.verse: Gathering the grass & leaves there into a pile, I sit down cross-legged with my body erect, establishing mindfulness to the fore.

an3.63:6.5.verse: “Quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter & remain in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

an3.63:6.6.verse: With the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, I enter & remain in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

an3.63:6.7.verse: With the fading of rapture, I remain in equanimity, mindful & alert, and sense pleasure with the body. I enter & remain in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’

an3.63:6.8.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation & distress—I enter & remain in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain.”

an3.63:6.9.verse: “If, brahman, having become like this, I am walking back & forth, my walking back & forth on that occasion is divine.

an3.63:6.10.verse: If, having become like this, I am standing, my standing on that occasion is divine.

an3.63:6.11.verse: If, having become like this, I am sitting, my sitting on that occasion is divine.

an3.63:6.12.verse: If, having become like this, I am lying down, this, on that occasion, is my divine high & luxurious bed.”

an3.63:7.2.verse: Who else aside from Master Gotama could obtain at will, without trouble, without difficulty, such a divine high & luxurious bed?

an3.63:8.1.verse: “But which, Master Gotama, is the Brahmā high & luxurious bed that Master Gotama now obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty?”

an3.63:8.2.verse: “There is the case, brahman, where I dwell in dependence on a village or town. Early in the morning, having adjusted my under robe and carrying my bowl & robes, I enter that village or town for alms.

an3.63:8.3.verse: After my meal, returning from my alms round, I go right into the forest.

an3.63:8.4.verse: Gathering the grass & leaves there into a pile, I sit down cross-legged with my body erect, establishing mindfulness to the fore.

an3.63:8.5.verse: “I dwell pervading the first direction [the east] with an awareness imbued with goodwill, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, I dwell pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with goodwill—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

an3.63:8.6.verse: I dwell pervading the first direction with an awareness imbued with compassion…

an3.63:8.8.verse: equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, I dwell pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with equanimity—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

an3.63:8.9.verse: “If, brahman, having become like this, I am walking back & forth, my walking back & forth on that occasion is Brahmā-like.

an3.63:8.10.verse: If, having become like this, I am standing, my standing on that occasion is Brahmā-like.

an3.63:8.11.verse: If, having become like this, I am sitting, my sitting on that occasion is Brahmā-like.

an3.63:8.12.verse: If, having become like this, I am lying down, this, on that occasion, is my Brahmā high & luxurious bed.”

an3.63:9.2.verse: Who else aside from Master Gotama could obtain at will, without trouble, without difficulty, such a Brahmā high & luxurious bed?

an3.63:10.1.verse: “But which, Master Gotama, is the noble high & luxurious bed that Master Gotama now obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty?”

an3.63:10.2.verse: “There is the case, brahman, where I dwell in dependence on a village or town. Early in the morning, having adjusted my under robe and carrying my bowl & robes, I enter that village or town for alms.

an3.63:10.3.verse: After my meal, returning from my alms round, I go right into the forest.

an3.63:10.4.verse: Gathering the grass & leaves there into a pile, I sit down cross-legged with my body erect, establishing mindfulness to the fore.

an3.63:10.6.verse: ‘Passion has been abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.63:10.7.verse: Aversion has been abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.63:10.8.verse: Delusion has been abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.63:10.9.verse: “If, brahman, having become like this, I am walking back & forth, my walking back & forth on that occasion is noble.

an3.63:10.10.verse: If, having become like this, I am standing, my standing on that occasion is noble.

an3.63:10.11.verse: If, having become like this, I am sitting, my sitting on that occasion is noble.

an3.63:10.12.verse: If, having become like this, I am lying down, this, on that occasion, is my noble high & luxurious bed.”

an3.63:11.2.verse: Who else aside from Master Gotama could obtain at will, without trouble, without difficulty, such a noble high & luxurious bed?

an3.63:12.2.verse: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

an3.63:12.3.verse: We go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.

an3.63:12.4.verse: May Master Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone to him for refuge, from this day forward, for life.”

an3.63:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Venāgapura.

an3.63:1.2.verse: The brahmins and householders of Venāgapura heard:

an3.63:1.3.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Venāgapura.

an3.63:1.5.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an3.63:1.6.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

an3.63:1.7.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

an3.63:1.8.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

an3.63:2.1.verse: Then the brahmins and householders of Venāgapura went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. Then the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said to the Buddha:

an3.63:3.2.verse: how your faculties are so very clear, and the complexion of your skin is pure and bright.

an3.63:3.3.verse: It’s like a golden brown jujube in the autumn,

an3.63:3.5.verse: or a ripe palmyra fruit freshly plucked from the stalk,

an3.63:3.7.verse: or a pendant of Black Plum River gold, fashioned by a deft smith, well-wrought in the forge, and placed on a cream rug where it shines and glows and dazzles.

an3.63:3.8.verse: In the same way, your faculties are so very clear, and the complexion of your skin is pure and bright.

an3.63:3.9.verse: Surely the worthy Gotama gets when he wants, without trouble or difficulty, various kinds of high and luxurious bedding, such as:

an3.63:3.10.verse: sofas, couches, woolen covers—shag-piled, colorful, white, embroidered with flowers, quilted, embroidered with animals, double or single fringed—and silk covers studded with gems, as well as silken sheets, wollen carpets, rugs for elephants, horses, or chariots, black antelope hides and woven rugs, and spreads of fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends.”

an3.63:4.1.verse: “Brahmin, these various kinds of high and luxurious bedding

an3.63:4.3.verse: are hard for renunciates to find. And even if they do get them, they’re not allowed.

an3.63:5.1.verse: There are, brahmin, these three high and luxurious beds that I get these days when I want, without trouble or difficulty.

an3.63:5.3.verse: The heavenly high and luxurious bed, the divine high and luxurious bed, and the noble high and luxurious bed.

an3.63:5.4.verse: These are the three high and luxurious beds that I get these days when I want, without trouble or difficulty.”

an3.63:6.1.verse: “But what, worthy Gotama, is the heavenly high and luxurious bed?”

an3.63:6.2.verse: “Brahmin, when I am living supported by a village or town, I robe up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.

an3.63:6.3.verse: After the meal, on my return from almsround, I enter within a forest.

an3.63:6.4.verse: I gather up some grass or leaves into a pile and sit down cross-legged, setting my body straight, and bringing mindfulness to the present.

an3.63:6.5.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an3.63:6.6.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, I enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an3.63:6.7.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, I enter and remain in the third absorption, where I meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

an3.63:6.8.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an3.63:6.9.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I walk, at that time my walking is heavenly.

an3.63:6.10.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I stand, at that time my standing is heavenly.

an3.63:6.11.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I sit, at that time my sitting is heavenly.

an3.63:6.12.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I lie down, at that time my lying is heavenly.

an3.63:6.13.verse: This is the heavenly high and luxurious bed that I get these days when I want, without trouble or difficulty.”

an3.63:7.2.verse: Who but the worthy Gotama could get such a heavenly high and luxurious bed when he wants, without trouble or difficulty?

an3.63:8.1.verse: But what, worthy Gotama, is the divine high and luxurious bed?”

an3.63:8.2.verse: “Brahmin, when I am living supported by a village or town, I robe up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.

an3.63:8.3.verse: After the meal, on my return from almsround, I enter within a forest.

an3.63:8.4.verse: I gather up some grass or leaves into a pile and sit down cross-legged, setting my body straight, and bringing mindfulness to the present.

an3.63:8.5.verse: I meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, I spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.63:8.6.verse: I meditate spreading a heart full of compassion to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, I spread a heart full of compassion to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.63:8.7.verse: I meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, I spread a heart full of rejoicing to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.63:8.8.verse: I meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, I spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.63:8.9.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I walk, at that time my walking is divine.

an3.63:8.12.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I lie down, at that time my lying is divine.

an3.63:8.13.verse: This is the divine high and luxurious bed that I get these days when I want, without trouble or difficulty.”

an3.63:9.2.verse: Who but the worthy Gotama could get such a divine high and luxurious bed when he wants, without trouble or difficulty?

an3.63:10.1.verse: But what, worthy Gotama, is the noble high and luxurious bed?”

an3.63:10.2.verse: “Brahmin, when I am living supported by a village or town, I robe up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.

an3.63:10.3.verse: After the meal, on my return from almsround, I enter within a forest.

an3.63:10.4.verse: I gather up some grass or leaves into a pile and sit down cross-legged, setting my body straight, and bringing mindfulness to the present.

an3.63:10.6.verse: ‘I’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they’re unable to arise in the future.’

an3.63:10.9.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I walk, at that time my walking is noble.

an3.63:10.12.verse: When I’m practicing like this, if I lie down, at that time my lying is noble.

an3.63:10.13.verse: This is the noble high and luxurious bed that I get these days when I want, without trouble or difficulty.”

an3.63:11.2.verse: Who but the worthy Gotama could get such a noble high and luxurious bed when he wants, without trouble or difficulty?

an3.63:12.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an3.63:12.3.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an3.63:12.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

an3.64:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an3.64:1.3.verse: Now at that time a wanderer named Sarabha had recently left this teaching and training.

an3.64:1.4.verse: He was telling a crowd in Rājagaha,

an3.64:1.5.verse: “I learned the teaching of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan,

an3.64:1.6.verse: then I left their teaching and training.”

an3.64:1.7.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Rājagaha for alms.

an3.64:1.8.verse: They heard what Sarabha was saying.

an3.64:2.1.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an3.64:2.2.verse: “The wanderer named Sarabha has recently left this teaching and training.

an3.64:2.3.verse: He was telling a crowd in Rājagaha:

an3.64:2.4.verse: ‘I learned the teaching of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan,

an3.64:2.5.verse: then I left their teaching and training.’

an3.64:2.6.verse: Worthy sir, please go to the wanderers’ monastery on the bank of the Serpentine River to see Sarabha the wanderer out of sympathy.”

an3.64:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the wanderers’ monastery on the bank of the Serpentine River to visit Sarabha the wanderer. He sat down on the seat spread out and said to the wanderer Sarabha,

an3.64:3.2.verse: “Is it really true, Sarabha, that you’ve been saying:

an3.64:3.3.verse: ‘I learned the teaching of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan,

an3.64:3.4.verse: then I left their teaching and training.’”

an3.64:3.5.verse: When he said this, Sarabha kept silent.

an3.64:4.1.verse: For a second time, the Buddha said to Sarabha,

an3.64:4.2.verse: “Tell me, Sarabha, what exactly have you learned of the teachings of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan?

an3.64:4.3.verse: If you’ve not learned it fully, I’ll fill you in.

an3.64:4.4.verse: But if you have learned it fully, I’ll agree.”

an3.64:4.5.verse: For a second time, Sarabha kept silent.

an3.64:5.1.verse: For a third time, the Buddha said to Sarabha,

an3.64:5.2.verse: “Sarabha, the teachings of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan are clear to me. What exactly have you learned of the teachings of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan?

an3.64:5.3.verse: If you’ve not learned it fully, I’ll fill you in.

an3.64:5.4.verse: But if you have learned it fully, I’ll agree.”

an3.64:5.5.verse: For a third time, Sarabha kept silent.

an3.64:6.1.verse: Then those wanderers said to Sarabha,

an3.64:6.2.verse: “The ascetic Gotama has offered to tell you anything you ask for.

an3.64:6.3.verse: Speak, reverend Sarabha, what exactly have you learned of the teachings of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan?

an3.64:6.4.verse: If you’ve not learned it fully, he’ll fill you in.

an3.64:6.5.verse: But if you have learned it fully, he’ll agree.”

an3.64:6.6.verse: When this was said, Sarabha sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

an3.64:7.1.verse: Knowing this, the Buddha said to the wanderers:

an3.64:8.2.verse: ‘You claim to be a fully awakened Buddha, but you don’t understand these things.’ Then I’d carefully pursue, press, and grill them on that point.

an3.64:8.3.verse: When grilled by me, they would, without a doubt, fall into one of these three categories. They’d dodge the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. They’d display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. Or they’d sit silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say, like Sarabha.

an3.64:9.1.verse: Wanderers, someone might say to me:

an3.64:9.2.verse: ‘You claim to have ended all defilements, but you still have these defilements.’ Then I’d carefully pursue, press, and grill them on that point.

an3.64:9.3.verse: When grilled by me, they would, without a doubt, fall into one of these three categories. They’d dodge the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. They’d display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. Or they’d sit silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say, like Sarabha.

an3.64:10.1.verse: Wanderers, someone might say to me:

an3.64:10.2.verse: ‘Regardless of your goal in teaching the Dhamma, it does not deliver one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.’ Then I’d carefully pursue, press, and grill them on that point.

an3.64:10.3.verse: When grilled by me, they would, without a doubt, fall into one of these three categories. They’d dodge the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. They’d display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. Or they’d sit silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say, like Sarabha.”

an3.64:10.4.verse: Then the Buddha, having roared his lion’s roar three times in the monastery for the wanderers on the bank of the Serpentine River, rose into the air and flew away.

an3.64:11.1.verse: Soon after the Buddha left, those wanderers beset Sarabha on all sides with sneering and jeering.

an3.64:11.2.verse: “Reverend Sarabha, you’re just like an old jackal in the formidable wilderness who thinks, ‘I’ll roar a lion’s roar!’ but they still only manage to squeal and yelp like a jackal.

an3.64:11.3.verse: In the same way, when the ascetic Gotama wasn’t here you said ‘I’ll roar a lion’s roar!’ but you only managed to squeal and yelp like a jackal.

an3.64:11.4.verse: You’re just like a marsh hen who thinks, ‘I’ll cry like a cuckoo!’ but they still only manage to cry like a marsh hen.

an3.64:11.5.verse: In the same way, when the ascetic Gotama wasn’t here you said ‘I’ll cry like a cuckoo!’ but you still only managed to cry like a marsh hen.

an3.64:11.6.verse: You’re just like a bull that thinks to bellow only when the cowstall is empty.

an3.64:11.7.verse: In the same way, you only thought to bellow when the ascetic Gotama wasn’t here.”

an3.64:11.8.verse: That’s how those wanderers beset Sarabha on all sides with sneering and jeering.

an3.65:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One, on a wandering tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks, arrived at Kesaputta, a town of the Kālāmas.

an3.65:1.3.verse: The Kālāmas of Kesaputta heard it said,

an3.65:1.4.verse: “Gotama the contemplative—the son of the Sakyans, having gone forth from the Sakyan clan—has arrived at Kesaputta.

an3.65:1.5.verse: And of that Master Gotama this fine reputation has spread:

an3.65:1.6.verse: ‘He is indeed a Blessed One, worthy & rightly self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, Well-Gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed. He makes known—having realized it through direct knowledge—this world with its devas, Māras, & Brahmās, this generation with its contemplatives & brahmans, its royalty & commonfolk; he explains the Dhamma admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, admirable in the end; he expounds the holy life both in its particulars & in its essence, entirely perfect, surpassingly pure.

an3.65:1.7.verse: It is good to see such a worthy one.’”

an3.65:2.1.verse: So the Kālāmas of Kesaputta went to the Blessed One. On arrival, some of them bowed down to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Some of them exchanged courteous greetings with him and, after an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, sat to one side. Some of them sat to one side having saluted him with their hands palm-to-palm over their hearts. Some of them sat to one side having announced their name & clan. Some of them sat to one side in silence. As they were sitting there, the Kālāmas of Kesaputta said to the Blessed One,

an3.65:3.1.verse: “Lord, there are some contemplatives & brahmans who come to Kesaputta.

an3.65:3.2.verse: They expound & glorify their own doctrines, but as for the doctrines of others, they deprecate them, disparage them, show contempt for them, & pull them to pieces.

an3.65:3.3.verse: And then other contemplatives & brahmans come to Kesaputta.

an3.65:3.4.verse: They expound & glorify their own doctrines, but as for the doctrines of others, they deprecate them, disparage them, show contempt for them, & pull them to pieces.

an3.65:3.5.verse: They leave us absolutely uncertain & in doubt:

an3.65:3.6.verse: Which of these venerable contemplatives & brahmans are speaking the truth, and which ones are lying?”

an3.65:3.7.verse: “Of course you are uncertain, Kālāmas. Of course you are in doubt.

an3.65:3.8.verse: When there are reasons for doubt, uncertainty is born.

an3.65:4.1.verse: So in this case, Kālāmas, don’t go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by scripture, by logical conjecture, by inference, by analogies, by agreement through pondering views, by probability, or by the thought, ‘This contemplative is our teacher.’

an3.65:4.2.verse: When you know for yourselves that,

an3.65:4.3.verse: ‘These qualities are unskillful; these qualities are blameworthy; these qualities are criticized by the observant; these qualities, when adopted & carried out, lead to harm & to suffering’—then you should abandon them.

an3.65:5.2.verse: When greed arises in a person, does it arise for welfare or for harm?”

an3.65:7.1.verse: “And this greedy person, overcome by greed, his mind possessed by greed, kills living beings, takes what is not given, goes after another person’s wife, tells lies, and induces others to do likewise, all of which is for long-term harm & suffering.”

an3.65:9.2.verse: When aversion arises in a person, does it arise for welfare or for harm?”

an3.65:11.1.verse: “And this aversive person, overcome by aversion, his mind possessed by aversion, kills living beings, takes what is not given, goes after another person’s wife, tells lies, and induces others to do likewise, all of which is for long-term harm & suffering.”

an3.65:13.2.verse: When delusion arises in a person, does it arise for welfare or for harm?”

an3.65:15.1.verse: “And this deluded person, overcome by delusion, his mind possessed by delusion, kills living beings, takes what is not given, goes after another person’s wife, tells lies, and induces others to do likewise, all of which is for long-term harm & suffering.”

an3.65:17.1.verse: “So what do you think, Kālāmas: Are these qualities skillful or unskillful?”
