an3.65:42.1.verse: “Now, Kālāmas, one who is a disciple of the noble ones—thus devoid of greed, devoid of ill will, undeluded, alert, & resolute—keeps pervading the first direction [the east]—as well as the second direction, the third, & the fourth—with an awareness imbued with goodwill. Thus he keeps pervading above, below, & all around, everywhere & in every respect the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with goodwill: abundant, expansive, immeasurable, free from hostility, free from ill will.

an3.65:42.2.verse: “He keeps pervading the first direction—as well as the second direction, the third, & the fourth—with an awareness imbued with compassion. Thus he keeps pervading above, below, & all around, everywhere & in every respect the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with compassion: abundant, expansive, immeasurable, free from hostility, free from ill will.

an3.65:42.3.verse: “He keeps pervading the first direction—as well as the second direction, the third, & the fourth—with an awareness imbued with empathetic joy. Thus he keeps pervading above, below, & all around, everywhere & in every respect the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with empathetic joy: abundant, expansive, immeasurable, free from hostility, free from ill will.

an3.65:42.4.verse: “He keeps pervading the first direction—as well as the second direction, the third, & the fourth—with an awareness imbued with equanimity. Thus he keeps pervading above, below, & all around, everywhere & in every respect the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with equanimity: abundant, expansive, immeasurable, free from hostility, free from ill will.

an3.65:43.1.verse: “Now, Kālāmas, one who is a disciple of the noble ones—his mind thus free from hostility, free from ill will, undefiled, & pure—

an3.65:43.2.verse: acquires four assurances in the here & now:

an3.65:43.3.verse: ‘If there is a world after death, if there is the fruit & result of actions rightly & wrongly done, then this is the basis by which, with the break-up of the body, after death, I will reappear in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ This is the first assurance he acquires.

an3.65:44.1.verse: ‘But if there is no world after death, if there is no fruit & result of actions rightly & wrongly done, then here in the present life I look after myself with ease—free from hostility, free from ill will, free from trouble.’ This is the second assurance he acquires.

an3.65:45.1.verse: ‘If evil is done through acting, still I have willed no evil for anyone.

an3.65:45.2.verse: Having done no evil action, from where will suffering touch me?’ This is the third assurance he acquires.

an3.65:46.1.verse: ‘But if no evil is done through acting, then I can assume myself pure in both respects.’ This is the fourth assurance he acquires.

an3.65:47.1.verse: “One who is a disciple of the noble ones—his mind thus free from hostility, free from ill will, undefiled, & pure—

an3.65:47.2.verse: acquires these four assurances in the here & now.”

an3.65:48.1.verse: “So it is, Blessed One. So it is, O One Well-Gone.

an3.65:48.2.verse: One who is a disciple of the noble ones—his mind thus free from hostility, free from ill will, undefiled, & pure—

an3.65:48.3.verse: acquires four assurances in the here & now:

an3.65:53.1.verse: “Magnificent, lord! Magnificent! Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has the Blessed One—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

an3.65:53.2.verse: We go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.

an3.65:53.3.verse: May the Blessed One remember us as lay followers who have gone to him for refuge, from this day forward, for life.”

an3.65:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a town of the Kālāmas named Kesamutta.

an3.65:1.4.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Kesamutta.

an3.65:1.6.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha …’

an3.65:1.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

an3.65:2.1.verse: Then the Kālāmas went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. Seated to one side the Kālāmas said to the Buddha:

an3.65:3.1.verse: “There are, sir, some ascetics and brahmins who come to Kesamutta.

an3.65:3.2.verse: They explain and promote only their own doctrine, while they attack, badmouth, disparage, and smear the doctrines of others.

an3.65:3.3.verse: Then some other ascetics and brahmins come to Kesamutta.

an3.65:3.4.verse: They too explain and promote only their own doctrine, while they attack, badmouth, disparage, and smear the doctrines of others.

an3.65:3.5.verse: So, sir, we’re doubting and uncertain:

an3.65:3.6.verse: ‘I wonder who of these respected ascetics and brahmins speaks the truth, and who speaks falsehood?’”

an3.65:3.7.verse: “It is enough, Kālāmas, for you to be doubting and uncertain.

an3.65:3.8.verse: Doubt has come up in you about an uncertain matter.

an3.65:4.1.verse: Please, Kālāmas, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think ‘The ascetic is our respected teacher.’

an3.65:4.2.verse: But when you know for yourselves:

an3.65:4.3.verse: ‘These things are unskillful, blameworthy, criticized by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering’, then you should give them up.

an3.65:5.2.verse: Does greed come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an3.65:7.1.verse: “A greedy individual, overcome by greed, kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.65:9.2.verse: Does hate come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an3.65:11.1.verse: “A hateful individual, overcome by hate, kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.65:13.2.verse: Does delusion come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an3.65:15.1.verse: “A deluded individual, overcome by delusion, kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.65:17.1.verse: “What do you think, Kālāmas, are these things skillful or unskillful?”

an3.65:23.1.verse: “When you undertake them, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?

an3.65:23.2.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an3.65:24.1.verse: “When you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering.

an3.65:42.1.verse: Then that noble disciple is rid of desire, rid of ill will, unconfused, aware, and mindful. They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.65:42.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of compassion to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.65:42.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of rejoicing to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.65:42.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.65:43.1.verse: When that noble disciple has a mind that’s free of enmity and ill will, uncorrupted and purified,

an3.65:43.2.verse: they’ve won four consolations in this very life.

an3.65:43.3.verse: ‘If it turns out there is another world, and good and bad deeds have a result, then—when the body breaks up, after death—I’ll be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ This is the first consolation they’ve won.

an3.65:44.1.verse: ‘If it turns out there is no other world, and good and bad deeds don’t have a result, then in this very life I’ll keep myself free of enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy.’ This is the second consolation they’ve won.

an3.65:45.1.verse: ‘If it turns out that bad things happen to people who do bad things, then since I have no bad intentions,

an3.65:45.2.verse: and since I’m not doing anything bad, how can suffering touch me?’ This is the third consolation they’ve won.

an3.65:46.1.verse: ‘If it turns out that bad things don’t happen to people who do bad things, then I still see myself pure on both sides.’ This is the fourth consolation they’ve won.

an3.65:47.1.verse: When that noble disciple has a mind that’s free of enmity and ill will, uncorrupted and purified,

an3.65:47.2.verse: they’ve won these four consolations in this very life.”

an3.65:48.1.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

an3.65:48.2.verse: When that noble disciple has a mind that’s free of enmity and ill will, uncorrupted and purified,

an3.65:48.3.verse: they’ve won these four consolations in this very life. …

an3.65:53.2.verse: We go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an3.65:53.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

an3.66:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Nandaka was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

an3.66:1.3.verse: Then Sāḷha, Migāra’s grandson, and Rohaṇa, Pekhuṇiya’s grandson went up to Venerable Nandaka, bowed, and sat down to one side. Then Venerable Nandaka said to Sāḷha:

an3.66:2.1.verse: “Please, Sāḷha and friend, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think ‘The ascetic is our respected teacher.’

an3.66:2.2.verse: But when you know for yourselves: ‘These things are unskillful, blameworthy, criticized by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering’, then you should give them up.

an3.66:5.1.verse: “‘Covetousness’ is what I mean by this.

an3.66:5.2.verse: A person who is greedy and covetous kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.66:9.1.verse: “‘Malice’ is what I mean by this.

an3.66:9.2.verse: A hateful and malicious person kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.66:13.1.verse: “‘Ignorance’ is what I mean by this.

an3.66:13.2.verse: A person who is deluded and ignorant kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an3.66:15.1.verse: “What do you think, Sāḷha, are these things skillful or unskillful?”

an3.66:21.1.verse: “When you undertake them, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?

an3.66:21.2.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an3.66:22.1.verse: “When you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering.

an3.66:31.2.verse: A loving and kind-hearted person doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit adultery, lie, or encourage others to do the same. Is that for their lasting welfare and happiness?”

an3.66:46.1.verse: Then that noble disciple is rid of desire, rid of ill will, unconfused, aware, and mindful. They meditate spreading a heart full of love …

an3.66:46.4.verse: equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an3.66:46.6.verse: ‘There is this, there is what is worse than this, there is what is better than this, and there is an escape beyond the scope of perception.’

an3.66:46.7.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an3.66:46.8.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

an3.66:46.9.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

an3.66:47.2.verse: ‘Formerly there was greed, which was unskillful. Now there is none, so that’s skillful.

an3.66:47.3.verse: Formerly there was hate, which was unskillful. Now there is none, so that’s skillful.

an3.66:47.4.verse: Formerly there was delusion, which was unskillful. Now there is none, so that’s skillful.’

an3.66:47.5.verse: So they live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.”

an3.67:1.1.verse: “Monks, there are these three topics for discussion.

an3.67:1.3.verse: “One may talk about the past, saying,

an3.67:1.5.verse: One may talk about the future, saying,

an3.67:1.6.verse: ‘Thus it will be in the future.’

an3.67:1.7.verse: Or one may talk about now in the present, saying,

an3.67:1.8.verse: ‘Thus it is now in the present.’

an3.67:2.1.verse: “Monks, it’s through his way of participating in a discussion that a person can be known as fit to talk with or unfit to talk with.

an3.67:2.2.verse: If a person, when asked a question, doesn’t give a categorical answer to a question deserving a categorical answer, doesn’t give an analytical (qualified) answer to a question deserving an analytical answer, doesn’t give a counter-question to a question deserving a counter-question, doesn’t put aside a question deserving to be put aside, then—that being the case—he is a person unfit to talk with.

an3.67:2.3.verse: But if a person, when asked a question, gives a categorical answer to a question deserving a categorical answer, gives an analytical answer to a question deserving an analytical answer, gives a counter-question to a question deserving a counter-question, and puts aside a question deserving to be put aside, then—that being the case—he is a person fit to talk with.

an3.67:3.1.verse: “Monks, it’s through his way of participating in a discussion that a person can be known as fit to talk with or unfit to talk with.

an3.67:3.2.verse: If a person, when asked a question, doesn’t stand by what is possible and impossible, doesn’t stand by agreed-upon assumptions, doesn’t stand by teachings known to be true,1 doesn’t stand by standard procedure, then—that being the case—he is a person unfit to talk with.

an3.67:3.3.verse: But if a person, when asked a question, stands by what is possible and impossible, stands by agreed-upon assumptions, stands by teachings known to be true, stands by standard procedure, then—that being the case—he is a person fit to talk with.

an3.67:4.1.verse: “Monks, it’s through his way of participating in a discussion that a person can be known as fit to talk with or unfit to talk with.

an3.67:4.2.verse: If a person, when asked a question, wanders from one thing to another, pulls the discussion off the topic, shows anger & aversion and sulks, then—that being the case—he is a person unfit to talk with.

an3.67:4.3.verse: But if a person, when asked a question, doesn’t wander from one thing to another, doesn’t pull the discussion off the topic, doesn’t show anger or aversion or sulk, then—that being the case—he is a person fit to talk with.

an3.67:5.1.verse: “Monks, it’s through his way of participating in a discussion that a person can be known as fit to talk with or unfit to talk with.

an3.67:5.2.verse: If a person, when asked a question, puts down (the questioner), crushes him, ridicules him, grasps at his little mistakes, then—that being the case—he is a person unfit to talk with.

an3.67:5.3.verse: But if a person, when asked a question, doesn’t put down (the questioner), doesn’t crush him, doesn’t ridicule him, doesn’t grasp at his little mistakes, then—that being the case—he is a person fit to talk with.

an3.67:6.1.verse: “Monks, it’s through his way of participating in a discussion that a person can be known as drawing near or not drawing near.

an3.67:6.2.verse: One who lends ear draws near; one who doesn’t lend ear doesn’t draw near.

an3.67:6.3.verse: Drawing near, one clearly knows one quality, comprehends one quality, abandons one quality, and realizes one quality.2

an3.67:6.4.verse: Clearly knowing one quality, comprehending one quality, abandoning one quality, and realizing one quality, one touches right release.

an3.67:6.5.verse: For that’s the purpose of discussion,

an3.67:6.7.verse: that’s the purpose of drawing near,

an3.67:6.8.verse: that’s the purpose of lending ear: i.e., the liberation of the mind through lack of clinging/sustenance.

an3.67:7.3.verse: following what’s not the noble ones’ way,

an3.67:7.4.verse: seeking to expose each other’s faults,

an3.67:8.1.verse: delight in each other’s misspoken word,

an3.67:9.1.verse: If wise people, knowing the right time,

an3.67:9.4.verse: following the ways of the noble ones:

an3.67:10.1.verse: That’s what the enlightened ones speak,

an3.67:10.3.verse: with a mind not boiling over,

an3.67:11.3.verse: They would delight in what’s well-said

an3.67:12.1.verse: They don’t study to find fault,

an3.67:13.2.verse: for the purpose of (inspiring) clear confidence, counsel that’s true:

an3.67:13.3.verse: That’s how noble ones give counsel.

an3.67:1.1.verse: “There are, mendicants, these three topics of discussion.

an3.67:1.4.verse: ‘That is how it was in the past.’

an3.67:1.6.verse: ‘That is how it will be in the future.’

an3.67:1.7.verse: Or you might discuss the present:

an3.67:1.8.verse: ‘This is how it is at present.’

an3.67:2.1.verse: You can know whether or not an individual is competent to hold a discussion by seeing how they take part in a discussion.

an3.67:2.2.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if it needs to be answered categorically and they don’t answer it categorically; or if it needs analysis and they answer without analyzing it; or if it needs a counter-question and they answer without a counter-question; or if it should be set aside and they don’t set it aside, then that individual is not competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:2.3.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if it needs to be answered categorically and they answer it categorically; or if it needs analysis and they answer after analyzing it; or if it needs a counter-question and they answer with a counter-question; or if it should be set aside and they set it aside, then that individual is competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:3.1.verse: You can know whether or not an individual is competent to hold a discussion by seeing how they take part in a discussion.

an3.67:3.2.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they’re not consistent about what their position is and what it isn’t; about what they propose; about speaking from what they know; and about the appropriate procedure, then that individual is not competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:3.3.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they are consistent about what their position is and what it isn’t; about what they propose; about speaking from what they know; and about the appropriate procedure, then that individual is competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:4.1.verse: You can know whether or not an individual is competent to hold a discussion by seeing how they take part in a discussion.

an3.67:4.2.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they dodge the issue; distract the discussion with irrelevant points; or display annoyance, hate, and bitterness, then that individual is not competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:4.3.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they don’t dodge the issue; distract the discussion with irrelevant points; or display annoyance, hate, and bitterness, then that individual is competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:5.1.verse: You can know whether or not an individual is competent to hold a discussion by seeing how they take part in a discussion.

an3.67:5.2.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they intimidate, crush, mock, or seize on trivial mistakes, then that individual is not competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:5.3.verse: When an individual is asked a question, if they don’t intimidate, crush, mock, or seize on trivial mistakes, then that individual is competent to hold a discussion.

an3.67:6.1.verse: You can know whether or not an individual has what’s required by seeing how they take part in a discussion.

an3.67:6.2.verse: If they actively listen they have what’s required; if they don’t actively listen they don’t have what’s required.

an3.67:6.3.verse: Someone who has what’s required directly knows one thing, completely understands one thing, gives up one thing, and realizes one thing—

an3.67:6.4.verse: and then they experience complete freedom.

an3.67:6.5.verse: This is the purpose of discussion,

an3.67:6.8.verse: and listening well, that is, the liberation of the mind by not grasping.

an3.67:7.4.verse: they look for flaws in each other.

an3.67:8.1.verse: They rejoice together when their opponent

an3.67:8.2.verse: speaks poorly and makes a mistake,

an3.67:8.4.verse: but the noble ones don’t discuss like this.

an3.67:9.1.verse: If an astute person wants to hold a discussion

an3.67:9.2.verse: connected with the teaching and its meaning—

an3.67:9.3.verse: the kind of discussion that noble ones hold—

an3.67:9.4.verse: then that attentive one should start the discussion,

an3.67:10.1.verse: knowing when the time is right,

an3.67:11.1.verse: or with a mind full of jealousy,

an3.67:11.2.verse: they’d speak from what they rightly know.

an3.67:11.3.verse: They agree with what was well spoken,

an3.67:11.4.verse: without criticizing what was poorly said.

an3.67:12.1.verse: They’d not persist in finding faults,

an3.67:12.3.verse: neither intimidating nor crushing the other,

an3.67:13.2.verse: for the sake of knowledge and clarity.

an3.67:13.3.verse: That’s how the noble ones consult,

an3.68:1.1.verse: “Monks, if you are asked by wanderers of other sects,

an3.68:1.6.verse: Now what is the difference, what the distinction, what the distinguishing factor among these three qualities?’

an3.68:1.7.verse: —when thus asked, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?”

an3.68:1.8.verse: “For us, lord, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root, their guide, & their arbitrator. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would explicate the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”

an3.68:1.9.verse: “In that case, monks, listen & pay close attention. I will speak.”

an3.68:1.10.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monks responded to him.

an3.68:2.1.verse: “Monks, if you are asked by wanderers of other sects,

an3.68:2.6.verse: Now what is the difference, what the distinction, what the distinguishing factor among these three qualities?’

an3.68:2.7.verse: —when thus asked, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way,

an3.68:2.8.verse: ‘Friends, passion carries little blame and is slow to fade. Aversion carries great blame and is quick to fade. Delusion carries great blame and is slow to fade.

an3.68:3.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen passion arises, or arisen passion tends to growth & abundance?’

an3.68:3.2.verse: ‘The theme of the attractive,’ it should be said.

an3.68:3.3.verse: ‘For one who attends inappropriately to the theme of the attractive, unarisen passion arises and arisen passion tends to growth & abundance.

an3.68:4.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen aversion arises, or arisen aversion tends to growth & abundance?’

an3.68:4.2.verse: ‘The theme of irritation,’ it should be said.

an3.68:4.3.verse: ‘For one who attends inappropriately to the theme of irritation, unarisen aversion arises and arisen aversion tends to growth & abundance.

an3.68:5.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen delusion arises, or arisen delusion tends to growth & abundance?’

an3.68:5.3.verse: ‘For one who attends inappropriately, unarisen delusion arises and arisen delusion tends to growth & abundance.

an3.68:6.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen passion does not arise, or arisen passion is abandoned?’

an3.68:6.2.verse: ‘The theme of the unattractive’ it should be said.

an3.68:6.3.verse: ‘For one who attends appropriately to the theme of the unattractive, unarisen passion does not arise and arisen passion is abandoned.

an3.68:7.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen aversion does not arise, or arisen aversion is abandoned?’

an3.68:7.2.verse: ‘Goodwill as an awareness-release,’ it should be said.

an3.68:7.3.verse: ‘For one who attends appropriately to goodwill as an awareness-release, unarisen aversion does not arise and arisen aversion is abandoned.

an3.68:8.1.verse: “(Then if they ask,) ‘But what, friends, is the reason, what the cause, why unarisen delusion does not arise, or arisen delusion is abandoned?’

an3.68:8.3.verse: ‘For one who attends appropriately, unarisen delusion does not arise and arisen delusion is abandoned.

an3.68:8.4.verse: This is the reason, this the cause, why unarisen delusion does not arise and arisen delusion is abandoned.’”

an3.68:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an3.68:1.8.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

an3.68:1.9.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an3.68:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an3.68:2.8.verse: ‘Greed, reverends, is mildly blameworthy, but slow to fade away. Hate is very blameworthy, but quick to fade away. Delusion is very blameworthy, and slow to fade away.’

an3.68:3.1.verse: And if they ask: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why greed arises, and once arisen it increases and grows?’

an3.68:3.2.verse: You should say: ‘The feature of beauty.

an3.68:3.3.verse: When you apply the mind irrationally to the feature of beauty, greed arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.

an3.68:3.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why greed arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.’

an3.68:4.1.verse: And if they ask: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why hate arises, and once arisen it increases and grows?’

an3.68:4.2.verse: You should say: ‘The feature of aversion.

an3.68:4.3.verse: When you apply the mind irrationally to the feature of aversion, hate arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.

an3.68:4.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why hate arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.’

an3.68:5.1.verse: And if they ask: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why delusion arises, and once arisen it increases and grows?’

an3.68:5.2.verse: You should say: ‘Irrational application of mind.

an3.68:5.3.verse: When you apply the mind irrationally, delusion arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.

an3.68:5.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why delusion arises, and once arisen it increases and grows.’

an3.68:6.1.verse: And if they ask, ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why greed doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up?’

an3.68:6.2.verse: You should say: ‘The feature of ugliness.

an3.68:6.3.verse: When you apply the mind rationally on the ugly feature of things, greed doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.

an3.68:6.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why greed doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.’

an3.68:7.1.verse: And if they ask, ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why hate doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up?’

an3.68:7.2.verse: You should say: ‘The heart’s release by love.

an3.68:7.3.verse: When you apply the mind rationally on the heart’s release by love, hate doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.

an3.68:7.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why hate doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.’

an3.68:8.1.verse: And if they ask, ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why delusion doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up?’

an3.68:8.2.verse: You should say: ‘Rational application of mind.

an3.68:8.3.verse: When you apply the mind rationally, delusion doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.

an3.68:8.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why delusion doesn’t arise, or if it’s already arisen it’s given up.’”

an3.69:1.1.verse: “Monks, there are these three roots of what is unskillful.

an3.69:1.3.verse: Greed is a root of what is unskillful, aversion is a root of what is unskillful, delusion is a root of what is unskillful.

an3.69:2.2.verse: Whatever a greedy person fabricates by means of body, speech, or intellect, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:2.3.verse: Whatever suffering a greedy person—his mind overcome with greed, his mind consumed—wrongly inflicts on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power,’ that too is unskillful.

an3.69:2.4.verse: Thus it is that many evil, unskillful qualities/events—born of greed, caused by greed, originated through greed, conditioned by greed—come into play.

an3.69:3.2.verse: Whatever an aversive person fabricates by means of body, speech, or intellect, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:3.3.verse: Whatever suffering an aversive person—his mind overcome with aversion, his mind consumed—wrongly inflicts on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power,’ that too is unskillful.

an3.69:3.4.verse: Thus it is that many evil, unskillful qualities—born of aversion, caused by aversion, originated through aversion, conditioned by aversion—come into play.

an3.69:4.2.verse: Whatever a deluded person fabricates by means of body, speech, or intellect, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:4.3.verse: Whatever suffering a deluded person—his mind overcome with delusion, his mind consumed—wrongly inflicts on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power,’ that too is unskillful.

an3.69:4.4.verse: Thus it is that many evil, unskillful qualities—born of delusion, caused by delusion, originated through delusion, conditioned by delusion—come into play.

an3.69:4.5.verse: “And a person like this is called one who speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is unfactual, speaks what is irrelevant, speaks contrary to the Dhamma, speaks contrary to the Vinaya.

an3.69:5.2.verse: Because of having wrongly inflicted suffering on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power.’

an3.69:5.3.verse: When told what is factual, he denies it and doesn’t acknowledge it.

an3.69:5.4.verse: When told what is unfactual, he doesn’t make an ardent effort to untangle it (to see), ‘This is unfactual. This is baseless.’

an3.69:5.5.verse: That’s why a person like this is called one who speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is unfactual, speaks what is irrelevant, speaks contrary to the Dhamma, speaks contrary to the Vinaya.

an3.69:6.1.verse: “A person like this—his mind overcome with evil, unskillful qualities born of greed… born of aversion… born of delusion, his mind consumed—

an3.69:6.2.verse: dwells in suffering right in the here & now—feeling threatened, turbulent, feverish—and at the break-up of the body, after death, can expect a bad destination.

an3.69:7.4.verse: “Just as a Sal tree, a birch, or an aspen, when smothered & surrounded by three parasitic vines, falls into misfortune, falls into disaster, falls into misfortune & disaster, in the same way, a person like this—his mind overcome with evil, unskillful qualities born of greed… born of aversion… born of delusion, his mind consumed—

an3.69:7.5.verse: dwells in suffering right in the here & now—feeling threatened, turbulent, feverish—

an3.69:7.6.verse: and at the break-up of the body, after death, can expect a bad destination.

an3.69:8.4.verse: “These are the three roots of what is unskillful.

an3.69:9.1.verse: “Now, there are these three roots of what is skillful.

an3.69:9.3.verse: Lack of greed is a root of what is skillful, lack of aversion is a root of what is skillful, lack of delusion is a root of what is skillful.

an3.69:10.2.verse: Whatever an ungreedy person fabricates by means of body, speech, or intellect, that too is skillful.

an3.69:10.3.verse: Whatever suffering an ungreedy person—his mind not overcome with greed, his mind not consumed—does not wrongly inflict on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power,’ that too is skillful.

an3.69:10.4.verse: Thus it is that many skillful qualities—born of lack of greed, caused by lack of greed, originated through lack of greed, conditioned by lack of greed—come into play.

an3.69:12.2.verse: Whatever an undeluded person fabricates by means of body, speech, or intellect, that too is skillful.

an3.69:12.3.verse: Whatever suffering an undeluded person—his mind not overcome with delusion, his mind not consumed—does not wrongly inflict on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power,’ that too is skillful.

an3.69:12.4.verse: Thus it is that many skillful qualities—born of lack of delusion, caused by lack of delusion, originated through lack of delusion, conditioned by lack of delusion—come into play.

an3.69:12.5.verse: “And a person like this is called one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is relevant, speaks in line with the Dhamma, speaks in line with the Vinaya.

an3.69:13.2.verse: Because of not having wrongly inflicted suffering on another person through beating or imprisonment or confiscation or placing blame or banishment, (with the thought,) ‘I have power. I want power.’

an3.69:13.3.verse: When told what is factual, he acknowledges it and does not deny it.

an3.69:13.4.verse: When told what is unfactual, he makes an ardent effort to untangle it (to see),

an3.69:13.6.verse: That’s why a person like this is called one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is relevant, speaks in line with the Dhamma, speaks in line with the Vinaya.

an3.69:14.1.verse: “In a person like this, evil, unskillful qualities born of greed… born of aversion… born of delusion have been abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.69:14.2.verse: He dwells in ease right in the here & now—feeling unthreatened, placid, unfeverish—

an3.69:14.3.verse: and is unbound right in the here & now.

an3.69:15.5.verse: “Just as if there were a Sal tree, a birch, or an aspen, smothered & surrounded by three parasitic vines.

an3.69:15.6.verse: A man would come along, carrying a spade & a basket.

an3.69:15.7.verse: He would cut the vines at the root and, having cut them at the root, would dig around them. Having dug around them, he would pull them out, even down to the rootlets.

an3.69:15.8.verse: He would cut the stalks of the vines. Having cut them, he would slice them into splinters. Having sliced them into splinters, he would pound them into bits. Having pounded them into bits, he would dry them in the wind & sun. Having dried them in the wind & sun, he would burn them in a fire. Having burned them in a fire, he would reduce them to powdered ash. Having reduced them to powdered ash, he would winnow them before a high wind or let them be washed away in a swift-flowing stream.

an3.69:15.9.verse: In that way the parasitic vines would have their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.69:15.10.verse: “In the same way, in a person like this, evil, unskillful qualities born of greed… born of aversion… born of delusion have been abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

an3.69:15.11.verse: He dwells in ease right in the here & now—feeling unthreatened, placid, unfeverish—

an3.69:15.12.verse: and is unbound right in the here & now.

an3.69:16.5.verse: “These are the three roots of what is skillful.”

an3.69:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these three unskillful roots.

an3.69:2.1.verse: Greed is a root of the unskillful.

an3.69:2.2.verse: When a greedy person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:2.3.verse: When a greedy person, overcome by greed, causes another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:2.4.verse: And so these many bad, unskillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by greed.

an3.69:3.1.verse: Hate is a root of the unskillful.

an3.69:3.2.verse: When a hateful person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:3.3.verse: When a hateful person, overcome by hate, causes another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:3.4.verse: And so these many bad, unskillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by hate.

an3.69:4.1.verse: Delusion is a root of the unskillful.

an3.69:4.2.verse: When a deluded person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:4.3.verse: When a deluded person, overcome by delusion, causes another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is unskillful.

an3.69:4.4.verse: And so these many bad, unskillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by delusion.

an3.69:4.5.verse: Such an individual is said to have speech that’s ill-timed, false, meaningless, not in line with the teaching and training.

an3.69:5.2.verse: This individual causes another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’.

an3.69:5.3.verse: So when someone makes a valid criticism, they’re scornful and admit nothing.

an3.69:5.4.verse: When someone makes a baseless criticism, they make no effort to explain, ‘This is why that’s untrue, this is why that’s false.’

an3.69:5.5.verse: That’s why such an individual is said to have speech that’s ill-timed, false, meaningless, not in line with the teaching and training.

an3.69:6.1.verse: Such an individual—overcome with bad, unskillful qualities born of greed, hate, and delusion—suffers in this very life, with distress, anguish, and fever.

an3.69:6.2.verse: And when the body breaks up, after death, they can expect to be reborn in a bad place.

an3.69:7.4.verse: Suppose a sal, axlewood, or sandan tree was choked and enveloped by three camel’s foot creepers. It would fall to ruin and disaster.

an3.69:7.5.verse: In the same way, such an individual—overcome with bad, unskillful qualities born of greed, hate, and delusion—suffers in this very life, with distress, anguish, and fever.

an3.69:7.6.verse: And when the body breaks up, after death, they can expect to be reborn in a bad place.

an3.69:8.4.verse: These are the three unskillful roots.

an3.69:9.1.verse: There are these three skillful roots.

an3.69:10.1.verse: Contentment is a root of the skillful.

an3.69:10.2.verse: When a contented person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is skillful.

an3.69:10.3.verse: When a contented person, not overcome by greed, doesn’t cause another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is skillful.

an3.69:10.4.verse: And so these many skillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by contentment.

an3.69:11.1.verse: Love is a root of the skillful.

an3.69:11.2.verse: When a loving person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is skillful.

an3.69:11.3.verse: When a loving person, not overcome by hate, doesn’t cause another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is skillful.

an3.69:11.4.verse: And so these many skillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by love.

an3.69:12.1.verse: Understanding is a root of the skillful.

an3.69:12.2.verse: When an understanding person chooses to act by way of body, speech, or mind, that too is skillful.

an3.69:12.3.verse: When an understanding person, not overcome by delusion, doesn’t cause another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’, that too is skillful.

an3.69:12.4.verse: And so these many skillful things are produced in them, born, sourced, originated, and conditioned by understanding.

an3.69:12.5.verse: Such an individual is said to have speech that’s well-timed, true, meaningful, in line with the teaching and training.

an3.69:13.2.verse: This individual doesn’t cause another to suffer under a false pretext—by execution or imprisonment or confiscation or condemnation or banishment—thinking ‘I’m powerful, I want power’.

an3.69:13.3.verse: So when someone makes a valid criticism, they admit it and aren’t scornful.

an3.69:13.4.verse: When someone makes a baseless criticism, they make an effort to explain,

an3.69:13.5.verse: ‘This is why that’s untrue, this is why that’s false.’

an3.69:13.6.verse: That’s why such an individual is said to have speech that’s well-timed, true, meaningful, in line with the teaching and training.

an3.69:14.1.verse: For such an individual, bad unskillful qualities born of greed, hate, and delusion are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an3.69:14.2.verse: In this very life they’re happy, free of distress, anguish, and fever,

an3.69:14.3.verse: and they’re also extinguished in this very life.

an3.69:15.5.verse: Suppose a sal, axlewood, or sandan tree was choked and enveloped by three camel’s foot creepers.

an3.69:15.6.verse: Then along comes a person with a spade and basket.

an3.69:15.7.verse: They’d cut the creeper out by the roots, dig them up, and pull them out, down to the fibers and stems.

an3.69:15.8.verse: Then they’d split the creeper apart, cut up the parts, and chop it into splinters. They’d dry the splinters in the wind and sun, burn them with fire, and reduce them to ashes. Then they’d whisk away the ashes in a strong wind, or glide them down a swift stream.

an3.69:15.9.verse: So those camel’s foot creepers would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and obliterated, unable to arise in the future.

an3.69:15.10.verse: In the same way, for such an individual, bad unskillful qualities born of greed, hate, and delusion are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an3.69:15.11.verse: In this very life they’re happy, free of  distress, anguish, and fever,

an3.69:15.12.verse: and they’re also extinguished in this very life.

an3.69:16.5.verse: These are the three skillful roots.”

an3.70:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

an3.70:1.3.verse: Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to her,

an3.70:1.4.verse: “So, Visākhā, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

an3.70:2.3.verse: The sabbath of the cowherds, the sabbath of the Jains, and the sabbath of the noble ones.

an3.70:2.4.verse: And what is the sabbath of the cowherds?

an3.70:2.5.verse: It’s just like a cowherd who, in the late afternoon, takes the cows back to their owners. They reflect:

an3.70:2.6.verse: ‘Today the cows grazed in this spot and that, and they drank in this spot and that.

an3.70:2.7.verse: Tomorrow the cows will graze in this spot and that, and drink in this spot and that.’

an3.70:2.8.verse: In the same way, someone keeping the sabbath reflects:

an3.70:2.9.verse: ‘Today I ate this and that, and had a meal of this and that.

an3.70:2.10.verse: Tomorrow I’ll eat this and that, and have a meal of this and that.’

an3.70:2.11.verse: And so they spend their day with a mind full of covetousness.

an3.70:2.12.verse: That’s the sabbath of the cowherds.

an3.70:2.13.verse: When the cowherd’s sabbath is observed like this it’s not very fruitful or beneficial or brilliant or bountiful.

an3.70:3.1.verse: And what is the sabbath of the Jains?

an3.70:3.2.verse: There’s a kind of ascetic belonging to a group called the Jains.

an3.70:3.4.verse: ‘Please, my man, don’t hurt any living creatures more than a hundred leagues away to the east.

an3.70:3.5.verse: Don’t hurt any living creatures more than a hundred leagues away to the west.

an3.70:3.6.verse: Don’t hurt any living creatures more than a hundred leagues away to the north.

an3.70:3.7.verse: Don’t hurt any living creatures more than a hundred leagues away to the south.’

an3.70:3.8.verse: So they encourage kindness and sympathy for some creatures and not others.

an3.70:3.9.verse: On the sabbath, they encourage their disciple:

an3.70:3.10.verse: ‘Please, my man, take off all your clothes and say:

an3.70:3.11.verse: “I don’t belong to anyone anywhere! And nothing belongs to me anywhere!”’

an3.70:3.12.verse: But their mother and father still know,

an3.70:3.20.verse: Bondservants, workers, and staff still know:

an3.70:3.23.verse: ‘These are my bondservants, workers, and staff.’

an3.70:3.24.verse: So, at a time when they should be encouraged to speak the truth, the Jains encourage them to lie.

an3.70:3.26.verse: When the night has passed they use their possessions once more, though they’ve not been given back to them.

an3.70:3.28.verse: That’s the sabbath of the Jains.

an3.70:3.29.verse: When the Jain’s sabbath is observed like this it’s not very fruitful or beneficial or brilliant or bountiful.

an3.70:4.1.verse: And what is the sabbath of the noble ones?

an3.70:4.2.verse: A corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:4.3.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:4.4.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the Realized One:

an3.70:4.5.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an3.70:4.6.verse: As they recollect the Realized One, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up. It’s just like cleaning a dirty head by exertion.

an3.70:5.1.verse: And how is a dirty head cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:5.2.verse: With cleansing paste, clay, and water, and by applying the appropriate effort.

an3.70:5.3.verse: In the same way, a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:6.1.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the Realized One:

an3.70:6.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an3.70:6.4.verse: As they recollect the Realized One, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.

an3.70:6.6.verse: ‘A noble disciple who observes the sabbath of the divinity, living together with the divinity. And because they think of the divinity their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.’

an3.70:6.7.verse: That’s how a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:7.1.verse: A corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:7.2.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:7.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the teaching:

an3.70:7.4.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

an3.70:7.5.verse: As they recollect the teaching, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up. It’s just like cleaning a dirty body by exertion.

an3.70:8.1.verse: And how is a dirty body cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:8.2.verse: With cleanser and powder, water, and by applying the appropriate effort.

an3.70:8.3.verse: That’s how a dirty body is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:8.4.verse: In the same way, a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:9.1.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:9.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the teaching:

an3.70:9.3.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

an3.70:9.4.verse: As they recollect the teaching, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.

an3.70:9.5.verse: This is called: ‘A noble disciple who observes the sabbath of Dhamma, living together with Dhamma. And because they think of the Dhamma their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.’

an3.70:9.6.verse: That’s how a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:10.1.verse: A corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:10.2.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:10.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha:

an3.70:10.4.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

an3.70:10.5.verse: As they recollect the Saṅgha, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up. It’s just like cleaning a dirty cloth by exertion.

an3.70:11.1.verse: And how is a dirty cloth cleaned by applying effort?

an3.70:11.2.verse: With salt, lye, cow dung, and water, and by applying the appropriate effort.

an3.70:11.3.verse: That’s how a dirty cloth is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:11.4.verse: In the same way, a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:12.1.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:12.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha:

an3.70:12.3.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, and worthy of veneration with cupped palms. It is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

an3.70:12.4.verse: As they recollect the Saṅgha, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.

an3.70:12.5.verse: This is called: ‘A noble disciple who observes the sabbath of the Saṅgha, living together with the Saṅgha. And because they think of the Saṅgha their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.’

an3.70:12.6.verse: That’s how a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:13.1.verse: A corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:13.2.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:13.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects their own ethical precepts, which are intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

an3.70:13.4.verse: As they recollect their ethical conduct, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up. It’s just like cleaning a dirty mirror by exertion.

an3.70:14.1.verse: And how is a dirty mirror cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:14.2.verse: With oil, ash, a rolled-up cloth, and by applying the appropriate effort.

an3.70:14.3.verse: That’s how a dirty mirror is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:14.4.verse: In the same way, a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:15.1.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:15.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects their own ethical precepts, which are intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

an3.70:15.3.verse: As they recollect their ethical conduct, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.

an3.70:15.4.verse: This is called: ‘A noble disciple who observes the sabbath of ethical conduct, living together with ethics. And because they think of their ethical conduct their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.’

an3.70:15.5.verse: That’s how a corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:16.1.verse: A corrupt mind is cleaned by exertion.

an3.70:16.2.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:16.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the deities:

an3.70:16.4.verse: ‘There are the gods of the four great kings, the gods of the thirty-three, the gods of Yama, the joyful gods, the gods who love to create, the gods who control what is created by others, the gods of the Divinity’s host, and gods even higher than these.

an3.70:16.5.verse: When those deities passed away from here, they were reborn there because of their faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom. I, too, have the same kind of faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.’

an3.70:16.10.verse: As they recollect the faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both themselves and those deities, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up. It’s just like cleansing corrupt native gold by exertion.

an3.70:17.1.verse: And how is corrupt native gold cleansed by applying effort?

an3.70:17.2.verse: With a furnace, flux, a blowpipe, and tongs, and by applying the appropriate effort.

an3.70:17.3.verse: That’s how corrupt native gold is cleansed by exertion.

an3.70:17.4.verse: In the same way, a corrupt mind is cleaned by applying effort.

an3.70:18.1.verse: And how is a corrupt mind cleaned by exertion?

an3.70:18.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple recollects the deities:

an3.70:18.3.verse: ‘There are the gods of the four great kings, the gods of the thirty-three, the gods of Yama, the joyful gods, the gods who love to imagine, the gods who control what is imagined by others, the gods of the Divinity’s host, and gods even higher than these.

an3.70:18.4.verse: When those deities passed away from here, they were reborn there because of their faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom. I, too, have the same kind of faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.’

an3.70:18.9.verse: As they recollect the faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both themselves and those deities, their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.

an3.70:18.10.verse: This is called: ‘A noble disciple who observes the sabbath of the deities, living together with the deities. And because they think of the deities their mind becomes clear, joy arises, and mental corruptions are given up.’

an3.70:18.11.verse: That’s how a corrupt mind is cleaned by applying effort.

an3.70:19.2.verse: ‘As long as they live, the perfected ones give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They are scrupulous and kind, and live full of sympathy for all living beings.

an3.70:19.3.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. I’ll be scrupulous and kind, and live full of sympathy for all living beings.

an3.70:19.4.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:20.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

an3.70:20.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up stealing. I’ll take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. I’ll keep myself clean by not thieving.

an3.70:20.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:21.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

an3.70:21.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up unchastity. I will be chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

an3.70:21.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:22.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

an3.70:22.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up lying. I’ll speak the truth and stick to the truth. I’ll be honest and dependable, and won’t trick the world with my words.

an3.70:22.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:23.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones give up intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an3.70:23.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an3.70:23.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:24.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and from food at the wrong time.

an3.70:24.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

an3.70:24.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:25.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music; and attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

an3.70:25.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music; and attiring and adorning myself with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

an3.70:25.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.

an3.70:26.1.verse: As long as they live, the perfected ones give up high and luxurious beds. They sleep in a low place, either a cot or a grass mat.

an3.70:26.2.verse: I, too, for this day and night will give up high and luxurious beds. I’ll sleep in a low place, either a cot or a grass mat.

an3.70:26.3.verse: I will observe the sabbath by doing as the perfected ones do in this respect.’

an3.70:27.1.verse: That’s the sabbath of the noble ones.

an3.70:27.2.verse: When the sabbath of the noble ones is observed like this it’s very fruitful and beneficial and brilliant and bountiful.

an3.70:28.2.verse: Suppose you were to rule as sovereign lord over these sixteen great countries—Aṅga, Magadha, Kāsi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Cetī, Vaccha, Kuru, Pañcāla, Maccha, Sūrasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhāra, and Kamboja—full of the seven treasures.

an3.70:28.3.verse: This wouldn’t be worth a sixteenth part of the sabbath with its eight factors.

an3.70:28.5.verse: Because human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.

an3.70:29.1.verse: Fifty years in the human realm is one day and night for the gods of the four great kings.

an3.70:29.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:29.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:29.4.verse: The lifespan of the gods of the four great kings is five hundred of these heavenly years.

an3.70:29.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the gods of the four great kings.

an3.70:29.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:29.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:30.1.verse: A hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the gods of the thirty-three.

an3.70:30.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:30.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:30.4.verse: The lifespan of the gods of the thirty-three is a thousand of these heavenly years.

an3.70:30.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

an3.70:30.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:30.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:31.1.verse: Two hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the gods of Yama.

an3.70:31.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:31.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:31.4.verse: The lifespan of the gods of Yama is two thousand of these heavenly years.

an3.70:31.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the gods of Yama.

an3.70:31.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:31.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:32.1.verse: Four hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the joyful gods.

an3.70:32.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:32.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:32.4.verse: The lifespan of the joyful gods is four thousand of these heavenly years.

an3.70:32.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the joyful gods.

an3.70:32.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:32.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:33.1.verse: Eight hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the gods who love to create.

an3.70:33.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:33.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:33.4.verse: The lifespan of the gods who love to create is eight thousand of these heavenly years.

an3.70:33.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the gods who love to create.

an3.70:33.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:33.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:34.1.verse: Sixteen hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the gods who control what is created by others.

an3.70:34.2.verse: Thirty such days make up a month.

an3.70:34.3.verse: Twelve such months make up a year.

an3.70:34.4.verse: The lifespan of the gods who control what is created by others is sixteen thousand of these heavenly years.

an3.70:34.5.verse: It’s possible that some woman or man who has observed the eight-factored sabbath will—when their body breaks up, after death—be reborn in the company of the gods who control what is created by others.

an3.70:34.6.verse: This is what I was referring to when I said:

an3.70:34.7.verse: ‘Human kingship is a poor thing compared to the happiness of the gods.’

an3.70:35.1.verse: You shouldn’t kill living creatures, or steal,

an3.70:35.4.verse: and don’t eat at night, the wrong time.

an3.70:36.1.verse: Not wearing garlands or applying fragrance,

an3.70:36.2.verse: you should sleep on a low bed, or a mat on the ground.

an3.70:36.3.verse: This is the eight-factored sabbath, they say,

an3.70:36.4.verse: revealed by the Buddha, who has gone to suffering’s end.

an3.70:37.1.verse: The moon and sun are both fair to see,

an3.70:37.2.verse: radiating as far as they revolve.

an3.70:37.3.verse: Those dispellers of darkness, travelers in midair,

an3.70:37.4.verse: shine in the firmament, dazzling the quarters.

an3.70:38.1.verse: All of the wealth that’s found in this realm—

an3.70:39.1.verse: they’re not worth a sixteenth part

an3.70:39.2.verse: of the sabbath with its eight factors,

an3.70:39.3.verse: as starlight cannot rival the moon.

an3.70:40.1.verse: So an ethical woman or man,

an3.70:40.2.verse: who has observed the eight-factored sabbath,

an3.70:40.3.verse: having made merit whose outcome is happiness,

an3.70:40.4.verse: blameless, they go to a heavenly place.”

an3.71:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an3.71:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Channa went up to Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.

an3.71:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda:

an3.71:1.4.verse: “Reverend Ānanda, do you advocate giving up greed, hate, and delusion?”

an3.71:2.1.verse: “But what drawbacks have you seen, Reverend Ānanda, that you advocate giving up greed, hate, and delusion?”

an3.71:3.1.verse: “A greedy person, overcome by greed, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.71:3.2.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.71:3.3.verse: A greedy person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.71:3.4.verse: When greed has been given up, they don’t do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.71:3.5.verse: A greedy person doesn’t truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.71:3.6.verse: When greed has been given up, they truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.71:3.7.verse: Greed is a destroyer of sight, vision, and knowledge. It blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment.

an3.71:4.1.verse: A hateful person, overcome by hate, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. …

an3.71:4.2.verse: A deluded person, overcome by delusion, intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.71:4.3.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both. They don’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an3.71:4.4.verse: A deluded person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.71:4.5.verse: When delusion has been given up, they don’t do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

an3.71:4.6.verse: A deluded person doesn’t truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.71:4.7.verse: When delusion has been given up, they truly understand what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both.

an3.71:4.8.verse: Delusion is a destroyer of sight, vision, and knowledge; it blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment.

an3.71:4.9.verse: This is the drawback we’ve seen in greed, hate, and delusion, and this is why we advocate giving them up.”

an3.71:5.1.verse: “But, reverend, is there a path and a practice for giving up that greed, hate, and delusion?”

an3.71:5.2.verse: “There is, reverend, a path and a practice for giving up that greed, hate, and delusion.”

an3.71:5.4.verse: “It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

an3.71:5.5.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an3.71:5.6.verse: This is the path, this is the practice for giving up that greed, hate, and delusion.”

an3.71:5.7.verse: “This is a fine path, a fine practice, for giving up that greed, hate, and delusion.

an3.71:5.8.verse: Just this much is enough for diligence.”

an3.72:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

an3.72:1.2.verse: Then a householder who was a disciple of the Ājīvaka ascetics went up to Venerable Ānanda, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to Ānanda:

an3.72:2.1.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, whose teaching is well explained?

an3.72:2.2.verse: Who in the world is practicing well?

an3.72:2.3.verse: Who in the world has done well?”

an3.72:2.4.verse: “Well then, householder, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

an3.72:2.6.verse: Is the teaching of those who teach for giving up greed, hate, and delusion well explained or not?

an3.72:2.7.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an3.72:2.8.verse: “The teaching of those who teach for giving up greed, hate, and delusion is well explained.

an3.72:3.2.verse: Are those who practice for giving up greed, hate, and delusion practicing well or not?

an3.72:3.3.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an3.72:3.4.verse: “Those who practice for giving up greed, hate, and delusion are practicing well.

an3.72:4.2.verse: Have those who’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion—so they’re cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future—done well in the world, or not?

an3.72:4.3.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an3.72:4.4.verse: “Those who’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion have done well in the world.

an3.72:5.2.verse: ‘The teaching of those who teach for giving up greed, hate, and delusion is well explained.’

an3.72:5.4.verse: ‘Those who practice for giving up greed, hate, and delusion are practicing well.’

an3.72:5.6.verse: ‘Those who’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion have done well in the world.’”

an3.72:6.2.verse: There’s no acclaiming your own teaching or disrespecting someone else’s,

an3.72:6.3.verse: just teaching what’s relevant in that context. The goal is spoken of, but the self is not involved.

an3.72:6.4.verse: You, sir, teach Dhamma for giving up greed, hate, and delusion.

an3.72:6.6.verse: You, sir, practice for giving up greed, hate, and delusion.

an3.72:6.7.verse: You in the world are practicing well.

an3.72:6.8.verse: You’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion.

an3.72:6.9.verse: You in the world have done well.

an3.72:7.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, Master Ānanda has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an3.72:7.3.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an3.72:7.4.verse: From this day forth, may Master Ānanda remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an3.73:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

an3.73:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha had recently recovered from an illness.

an3.73:1.4.verse: Then Mahānāma the Sakyan went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an3.73:1.5.verse: “For a long time, sir, I have understood your teaching like this:

an3.73:1.6.verse: ‘Knowledge is for those with immersion, not those without immersion.’

an3.73:1.7.verse: But, sir, does immersion come first, then knowledge?

an3.73:1.8.verse: Or does knowledge come first, then immersion?”

an3.73:1.10.verse: “The Buddha has recently recovered from an illness,

an3.73:1.11.verse: and this Mahānāma asks him a question that’s too deep.

an3.73:1.12.verse: Why don’t I take him off to one side and teach him the Dhamma?”

an3.73:2.1.verse: Then Ānanda took Mahānāma by the arm, led him off to one side, and said to him,

an3.73:2.2.verse: “Mahānāma, the Buddha has spoken of the ethics, immersion, and wisdom of a trainee; and the ethics, immersion, and wisdom of an adept.

an3.73:2.3.verse: What is the ethics of a trainee?

an3.73:2.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an3.73:2.5.verse: This is called the ethics of a trainee.

an3.73:3.1.verse: And what is the immersion of a trainee?

an3.73:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption … second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an3.73:3.3.verse: This is called the immersion of a trainee.

an3.73:4.1.verse: And what is the wisdom of a trainee?

an3.73:4.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an3.73:4.3.verse: This is called the wisdom of a trainee.

an3.73:5.1.verse: Then a noble disciple—accomplished in ethics, immersion, and wisdom—realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an3.73:5.2.verse: In this way the Buddha has spoken of the ethics, immersion, and wisdom of both a trainee and an adept.”

an3.74:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an3.74:1.2.verse: Then the Licchavis Abhaya and Paṇḍitakumāra went up to Venerable Ānanda, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an3.74:1.3.verse: “Sir, the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to know and see everything without exception, thus:

an3.74:1.4.verse: ‘Knowledge and vision are constantly and continually present to me, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.’

an3.74:1.5.verse: He advocates the elimination of past deeds by fervent mortification, and breaking the bridge by not doing any new deeds.

an3.74:1.6.verse: So with the ending of deeds, suffering ends; with the ending of suffering, feeling ends; and with the ending of feeling, all suffering will have been worn away.

an3.74:1.7.verse: This is how to go beyond suffering by means of this purification by wearing away in the present life.

an3.74:1.8.verse: What, sir, does the Buddha say about this?”

an3.74:2.1.verse: “Abhaya, these three kinds of purification by wearing away have been rightly explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

an3.74:2.3.verse: It’s when, Abhaya, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an3.74:2.4.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an3.74:2.5.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.74:3.1.verse: Then a mendicant accomplished in ethics, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption … second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an3.74:3.2.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an3.74:3.3.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.74:4.1.verse: Then a mendicant accomplished in immersion realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an3.74:4.2.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an3.74:4.3.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an3.74:4.4.verse: These are the three kinds of purification by wearing away that have been rightly explained by the Buddha … in order to realize extinguishment.”

an3.74:5.1.verse: When he said this, Paṇḍitakumāra said to Abhaya,

an3.74:5.2.verse: “Dear Abhaya, is there anything in what Ānanda has said so well that you would disagree with?”

an3.74:5.3.verse: “How could I not agree with what was said so well by Ānanda?

an3.74:5.4.verse: If anyone didn’t agree with him, their head would explode!”

an3.75:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an3.75:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, those who you have sympathy for, and those worth listening to—friends and colleagues, relatives and family—should be encouraged, supported, and established in three things.
