an4.10:1.3.verse: The yokes of sensual pleasures, future lives, views, and ignorance.

an4.10:1.4.verse: And what is the yoke of sensual pleasures?

an4.10:1.5.verse: It’s when you don’t truly understand sensual pleasures’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:1.6.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for sensual pleasures linger on inside.

an4.10:1.7.verse: This is called the yoke of sensual pleasures.

an4.10:1.8.verse: Such is the yoke of sensual pleasures.

an4.10:2.1.verse: And what is the yoke of future lives?

an4.10:2.2.verse: It’s when you don’t truly understand future lives’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:2.3.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for continued existence linger on inside.

an4.10:2.4.verse: This is called the yoke of future lives.

an4.10:2.5.verse: Such are the yokes of sensual pleasures and future lives.

an4.10:3.1.verse: And what is the yoke of views?

an4.10:3.2.verse: It’s when you don’t truly understand views’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:3.3.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for views linger on inside.

an4.10:3.4.verse: This is called the yoke of views.

an4.10:3.5.verse: Such are the yokes of sensual pleasures, future lives, and views.

an4.10:4.1.verse: And what is the yoke of ignorance?

an4.10:4.2.verse: It’s when you don’t truly understand the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape,

an4.10:4.3.verse: so ignorance and unknowing of the six fields of contact linger on inside.

an4.10:4.4.verse: This is called the yoke of ignorance.

an4.10:4.5.verse: Such are the yokes of sensual pleasures, future lives, views, and ignorance.

an4.10:4.6.verse: These are bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death. That’s why someone yoked to them is called: ‘one who has not found sanctuary from the yoke’.

an4.10:5.1.verse: There are these four kinds of unyoking.

an4.10:5.3.verse: Unyoking from sensual pleasures, future lives, views, and ignorance.

an4.10:5.4.verse: And what is unyoking from sensual pleasures?

an4.10:5.5.verse: It’s when you truly understand sensual pleasures’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:5.6.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for sensual pleasures don’t linger on inside.

an4.10:5.7.verse: This is called unyoking from sensual pleasures.

an4.10:5.8.verse: Such is unyoking from sensual pleasures.

an4.10:6.1.verse: And what is unyoking from future lives?

an4.10:6.2.verse: It’s when you truly understand future lives’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:6.3.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for continued existence don’t linger on inside.

an4.10:6.4.verse: This is called unyoking from future lives.

an4.10:6.5.verse: Such is unyoking from sensual pleasures and future lives.

an4.10:7.1.verse: And what is unyoking from views?

an4.10:7.2.verse: It’s when you truly understand views’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

an4.10:7.3.verse: So greed, relishing, affection, infatuation, thirst, passion, attachment, and craving for views don’t linger on inside.

an4.10:7.4.verse: This is called unyoking from views.

an4.10:7.5.verse: Such is unyoking from sensual pleasures, future lives, and views.

an4.10:8.1.verse: And what is unyoking from ignorance?

an4.10:8.2.verse: It’s when you truly understand the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape,

an4.10:8.3.verse: so ignorance and unknowing of the six fields of contact don’t linger on inside.

an4.10:8.4.verse: This is called unyoking from ignorance.

an4.10:8.5.verse: Such is unyoking from sensual pleasures, future lives, views, and ignorance.

an4.10:8.6.verse: These are bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death. That’s why someone unyoked from them is called: ‘one who has found sanctuary from the yoke’.

an4.10:8.7.verse: These are the four kinds of unyoking.

an4.12:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.

an4.12:1.2.verse: When you’ve done this, what more is there to do?

an4.13:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four right efforts.

an4.13:1.3.verse: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

an4.13:1.4.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up.

an4.13:1.5.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

an4.13:1.6.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

an4.13:1.7.verse: These are the four right efforts.

an4.13:2.1.verse: By rightly striving, they’ve crushed Māra’s sovereignty;

an4.13:2.2.verse: unattached, they’ve gone beyond  the peril of birth and death.

an4.13:2.3.verse: Contented and unstirred, they’ve vanquished Māra with his legions;

an4.13:2.4.verse: now they’ve gone beyond all Namuci’s forces, they’re happy.”

an4.14:1.3.verse: The efforts to restrain, to give up, to develop, and to preserve.

an4.14:1.4.verse: And what, mendicants, is the effort to restrain?

an4.14:1.5.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.14:1.6.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

an4.14:1.7.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

an4.14:1.8.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

an4.14:1.9.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

an4.14:1.10.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

an4.14:1.11.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.14:1.12.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

an4.14:1.13.verse: This is called the effort to restrain.

an4.14:2.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the effort to give up?

an4.14:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t tolerate a sensual,

an4.14:2.5.verse: They don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

an4.14:2.6.verse: This is called the effort to give up.

an4.14:3.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the effort to develop?

an4.14:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

an4.14:3.8.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

an4.14:3.9.verse: This is called the effort to develop.

an4.14:4.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the effort to preserve?

an4.14:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant preserves a meditation subject that’s a fine basis of immersion: the perception of a skeleton, a worm-infested corpse, a livid corpse, a split open corpse, or a bloated corpse.

an4.14:4.3.verse: This is called the effort to preserve.

an4.21:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an4.21:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an4.21:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, this one time, when I was first awakened, I was staying in Uruvelā at the goatherd’s banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

an4.21:2.2.verse: As I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

an4.21:2.3.verse: ‘One without respect and reverence lives in suffering.

an4.21:2.4.verse: What ascetic or brahmin should I honor and respect and rely on?’

an4.21:3.2.verse: ‘I would honor and respect and rely on another ascetic or brahmin so as to complete the entire spectrum of ethics, if it were incomplete.

an4.21:3.3.verse: But I don’t see any other ascetic or brahmin in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who is more accomplished than myself in ethics, who I should honor and respect and rely on.

an4.21:4.1.verse: I would honor and respect and rely on another ascetic or brahmin so as to complete the entire spectrum of immersion, if it were incomplete.

an4.21:4.2.verse: But I don’t see any other ascetic or brahmin … who is more accomplished than myself in immersion …

an4.21:5.1.verse: I would honor and respect and rely on another ascetic or brahmin so as to complete the entire spectrum of wisdom, if it were incomplete.

an4.21:5.2.verse: But I don’t see any other ascetic or brahmin in this world … who is more accomplished than myself in wisdom …

an4.21:6.1.verse: I would honor and respect and rely on another ascetic or brahmin so as to complete the entire spectrum of freedom, if it were incomplete.

an4.21:6.2.verse: But I don’t see any other ascetic or brahmin in this world … who is more accomplished than myself in freedom …’

an4.21:7.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I honor and respect and rely on the same teaching to which I was awakened?’

an4.21:8.1.verse: And then the divinity Sahampati, knowing my train of thought, vanished from the realm of divinity and appeared in front of me, as easily as a strong man would extend or contract his arm.

an4.21:8.2.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his cupped palms toward me, and said:

an4.21:8.3.verse: ‘That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

an4.21:8.4.verse: All the perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas who lived in the past honored and respected and relied on this same teaching.

an4.21:8.5.verse: All the perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas who will live in the future will honor and respect and rely on this same teaching.

an4.21:8.6.verse: May the Blessed One, who is the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha at present, also honor and respect and rely on this same teaching.’

an4.21:8.7.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

an4.21:8.8.verse: Then he went on to say:

an4.21:9.4.verse: destroyer of the sorrows of many—

an4.21:10.2.verse: they did live, they do live,

an4.21:10.4.verse: This is the nature of the Buddhas.

an4.21:11.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.’

an4.21:12.1.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

an4.21:12.2.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right side, before vanishing right there.

an4.21:12.3.verse: Then, knowing the request of the Divinity and what was suitable for myself, I honored and respected and relied on the same teaching to which I was awakened.

an4.21:12.4.verse: And since the Saṅgha has also achieved greatness, I also respect the Saṅgha.”

an4.22:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, this one time, when I was first awakened, I was staying in Uruvelā at the goatherd’s banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

an4.22:1.2.verse: Then several old brahmins—elderly and senior, who were advanced in years and had reached the final stage of life—came up to me, and exchanged greetings with me.

an4.22:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side, and said to me:

an4.22:1.5.verse: “The ascetic Gotama does not bow to old brahmins, elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.”

an4.22:1.6.verse: And this is indeed the case,

an4.22:1.7.verse: for the worthy Gotama does not bow to old brahmins, elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.

an4.22:1.8.verse: This is not appropriate, worthy Gotama.’

an4.22:2.2.verse: ‘These venerables don’t know what a senior is, or what qualities make you a senior.’

an4.22:2.3.verse: Mendicants, suppose you’re eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old.

an4.22:2.4.verse: But your speech is untimely, false, meaningless, and against the teaching or training. You say things at the wrong time which are worthless, unreasonable, rambling, and unbeneficial.

an4.22:2.5.verse: Then you’ll be reckoned a ‘childish senior’.

an4.22:3.1.verse: Now suppose you’re a youth, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life.

an4.22:3.2.verse: But your speech is timely, true, meaningful, and in line with the teaching and training. You say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

an4.22:3.3.verse: Then you’ll be reckoned an ‘astute senior’.

an4.22:4.1.verse: There are these four qualities that make a senior.

an4.22:4.3.verse: A mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an4.22:4.4.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an4.22:4.5.verse: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

an4.22:4.6.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an4.22:4.7.verse: These are the four qualities that make a senior.

an4.22:5.1.verse: The creature with a restless mind

an4.22:5.4.verse: and they don’t like the true teaching.

an4.22:5.5.verse: They’re far from seniority, with their bad views

an4.22:5.6.verse: and their lack of regard for others.

an4.22:6.2.verse: learned and eloquent, that attentive one

an4.22:7.3.verse: they’ve given up birth and death,

an4.22:7.4.verse: and have completed the spiritual journey.

an4.22:8.1.verse: That’s who I call a senior,

an4.22:8.3.verse: With the ending of defilements, a mendicant

an4.23:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the world has been understood by the Realized One;

an4.23:1.2.verse: and he is detached from the world.

an4.23:1.3.verse: The origin of the world has been understood by the Realized One;

an4.23:1.4.verse: and he has given up the origin of the world.

an4.23:1.5.verse: The cessation of the world has been understood by the Realized One;

an4.23:1.6.verse: and he has realized the cessation of the world.

an4.23:1.7.verse: The practice that leads to the cessation of the world has been understood by the Realized One;

an4.23:1.8.verse: and he has developed the practice that leads to the cessation of the world.

an4.23:2.1.verse: In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind, all that has been understood by the Realized One.

an4.23:2.2.verse: That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.

an4.23:3.1.verse: From the night when the Realized One awakens to the supreme perfect awakening until the night he becomes fully extinguished—in the element of extinguishment with no residue—everything he speaks, says, and expresses is real, not otherwise.

an4.23:3.2.verse: That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.

an4.23:4.1.verse: The Realized One does as he says, and says as he does.

an4.23:4.3.verse: that’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.

an4.23:5.1.verse: In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—the Realized One is the vanquisher, the unvanquished, the universal seer, the wielder of power.

an4.23:5.2.verse: That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.

an4.23:6.1.verse: Directly knowing the whole world as it is,

an4.23:6.3.verse: he is detached from the whole world,

an4.23:7.1.verse: That attentive one is the vanquisher of all

an4.23:7.2.verse: who is released from all ties.

an4.23:7.4.verse: extinguishment, fearing nothing from any quarter.

an4.23:8.1.verse: He is the Buddha, with defilements ended,

an4.23:8.3.verse: He has attained the end of all deeds,

an4.23:8.4.verse: freed with the ending of attachments.

an4.23:9.1.verse: That Blessed One is the Buddha,

an4.23:9.3.verse: in all the world with its gods,

an4.23:10.1.verse: And so those gods and humans,

an4.23:10.2.verse: who have gone to the Buddha for refuge,

an4.23:11.1.verse: ‘Tamed, he is the best of tamers,

an4.23:11.2.verse: peaceful, he is the seer among the peaceful,

an4.23:11.3.verse: liberated, he is the foremost of liberators,

an4.23:11.4.verse: crossed over, he is the most excellent of guides across.’

an4.23:12.3.verse: In the world with its gods,

an4.24:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāketa in Kāḷaka’s monastery.

an4.24:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an4.24:2.1.verse: “In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind: that I know.

an4.24:3.1.verse: In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind: that I have insight into.

an4.24:3.2.verse: That has been known by a Realized One, but a Realized One is not subject to it.

an4.24:4.1.verse: If I were to say that ‘I do not know … the world with its gods’, I would be lying.

an4.24:5.1.verse: If I were to say that ‘I both know and do not know … the world with its gods’, that would be just the same.

an4.24:6.1.verse: If I were to say that ‘I neither know nor do not know … the world with its gods’, that would be my fault.

an4.24:7.1.verse: So a Realized One sees what is to be seen, but does not conceive what is seen, does not conceive what is unseen, does not conceive what is to be seen, and does not conceive a seer.

an4.24:7.2.verse: He hears what is to be heard, but does not conceive what is heard, does not conceive what is unheard, does not conceive what is to be heard, and does not conceive a hearer.

an4.24:7.3.verse: He thinks what is to be thought, but does not conceive what is thought, does not conceive what is not thought, does not conceive what is to be thought, and does not conceive a thinker.

an4.24:7.4.verse: He knows what is to be known, but does not conceive what is known, does not conceive what is unknown, does not conceive what is to be known, and does not conceive a knower.

an4.24:7.5.verse: Since a Realized One is unaffected in the midst of things that ought be seen, heard, thought, and known, he is the unaffected one.

an4.24:7.6.verse: And I say that there is no better or finer poise than this.

an4.24:8.1.verse: Such a one does not take anything

an4.24:8.2.verse: seen, heard, or thought to be ultimately true or false.

an4.24:8.3.verse: But others get attached, thinking it’s the truth,

an4.24:9.2.verse: to which people are attached and cling,

an4.24:9.3.verse: saying, ‘I know, I see, that’s how it is’,

an4.24:9.4.verse: the Realized Ones have no attachments.”

an4.25:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, this spiritual life is not lived for the sake of fawning or flattering people, nor for the benefit of possessions, honor, or popularity, nor for the benefit of winning debates, nor thinking, ‘So let people know about me!’

an4.25:1.2.verse: This spiritual life is lived for the sake of restraint, giving up, fading away, and cessation.

an4.25:2.1.verse: The Buddha taught the spiritual life

an4.25:2.3.verse: but for the sake of restraint and giving up,

an4.25:2.4.verse: and because its objective is extinguishment.

an4.25:2.5.verse: This is the path followed by the big-hearted,

an4.25:3.2.verse: as it was taught by the Buddha,

an4.26:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, those mendicants who are deceivers and flatterers, pompous and fake, insolent, and scattered: those mendicants are no followers of mine.

an4.26:1.2.verse: They’ve left this teaching and training, and they don’t achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an4.26:1.3.verse: But those mendicants who are genuine, not flatterers, attentive, amenable, and serene: those mendicants are followers of mine.

an4.26:1.4.verse: They haven’t left this teaching and training, and they achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an4.26:2.1.verse: Those who are deceivers and flatterers, pompous and fake,

an4.26:2.3.verse: these don’t grow in the teaching

an4.26:2.4.verse: that was taught by the perfected Buddha.

an4.26:3.1.verse: But those who are genuine, not flatterers, attentive,

an4.26:3.3.verse: these do grow in the teaching

an4.26:3.4.verse: that was taught by the perfected Buddha.”

an4.27:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four trifles are easy to find and are blameless.

an4.27:1.5.verse: Lodgings at the root of a tree …

an4.27:1.7.verse: These four trifles are easy to find and are blameless.

an4.27:1.8.verse: When a mendicant is content with trifles that are easy to find, they have one of the factors of the ascetic life, I say.

an4.27:2.1.verse: When you’re content with what’s blameless,

an4.27:3.1.verse: These qualities are said to be

an4.27:3.3.verse: They’re mastered by one who trains,

an4.28:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four noble customs are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now, nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.28:1.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is content with any kind of robe, and praises such contentment. They don’t employ improper solicitation for the sake of a robe. They don’t worry if they don’t get a robe. And if they do get a robe, they use it untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawback, and understanding the escape.

an4.28:1.4.verse: But they don’t glorify themselves or put others down on account of their contentment.

an4.28:1.5.verse: A mendicant who is deft, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primordial noble custom.

an4.28:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of almsfood …

an4.28:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of lodgings …

an4.28:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant enjoys meditation and loves to meditate. They enjoy giving up and love to give up.

an4.28:4.2.verse: But they don’t glorify themselves or put down others on account of their love for meditation and giving up.

an4.28:4.3.verse: A mendicant who is deft, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primordial noble custom.

an4.28:4.4.verse: These four noble customs are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.28:5.1.verse: When a mendicant possesses these four noble customs, if they live in the east they prevail over discontent, and discontent doesn’t prevail over them.

an4.28:5.2.verse: If they live in the west …

an4.28:5.4.verse: the south, they prevail over discontent, and discontent doesn’t prevail over them.

an4.28:5.6.verse: Because the attentive prevail over desire and discontent.

an4.28:6.1.verse: Discontent cannot prevail over the attentive;

an4.28:6.2.verse: the attentive are not prevailed over by discontent.

an4.28:6.3.verse: The attentive can prevail over discontent,

an4.28:6.4.verse: for the attentive are those who prevail over discontent.

an4.28:7.1.verse: Who can hold back the dispeller,

an4.28:7.3.verse: Like a pendant of Black Plum River gold,

an4.28:7.4.verse: who is worthy to criticize them?

an4.28:7.6.verse: and by the Divinity, too, they’re praised.”

an4.29:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four footprints of the Dhamma are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.29:1.3.verse: Contentment, good will, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an4.29:4.2.verse: These four footprints of the Dhamma are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.29:5.2.verse: and a heart of good will,

an4.30:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an4.30:1.2.verse: Now at that time several very well-known wanderers were residing in their monastery on the bank of the Serpentine River. They included Annabhāra, Varadhara, Sakuludāyī, and other very well-known wanderers.

an4.30:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the wanderer’s monastery on the bank of the Serpentine River. He sat down on the seat spread out and said to the wanderers:

an4.30:2.1.verse: “Wanderers, these four footprints of the Dhamma are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.30:2.4.verse: Good will … Right mindfulness … Right immersion …

an4.30:2.5.verse: These four footprints of the Dhamma are primordial, long-standing, customary, and traditional. They are uncorrupted, as they have been since the beginning. They’re not being corrupted now nor will they be. Sensible ascetics and brahmins don’t look down on them.

an4.30:3.2.verse: ‘I’ll deny this Dhamma footprint of contentment, and describe a true ascetic or brahmin who covets sensual pleasures with acute lust.’ Then I’d say to them:

an4.30:3.3.verse: ‘Let them come, speak, and discuss. We’ll see how powerful they are.’

an4.30:3.4.verse: It is quite impossible to deny this Dhamma footprint of contentment, and point out a true ascetic or brahmin who covets sensual pleasures with acute lust.

an4.30:4.2.verse: ‘I’ll deny this Dhamma footprint of good will, and describe a true ascetic or brahmin who has ill will and malicious intent.’ Then I’d say to them:

an4.30:4.3.verse: ‘Let them come, speak, and discuss. We’ll see how powerful they are.’

an4.30:4.4.verse: It is quite impossible to deny this Dhamma footprint of good will, and point out a true ascetic or brahmin who has ill will and malicious intent.

an4.30:5.2.verse: ‘I’ll deny this Dhamma footprint of right mindfulness, and describe a true ascetic or brahmin who is unmindful, with no situational awareness.’ Then I’d say to them:

an4.30:5.3.verse: ‘Let them come, speak, and discuss. We’ll see how powerful they are.’

an4.30:5.4.verse: It is quite impossible to deny this Dhamma footprint of right mindfulness, and point out a true ascetic or brahmin who is unmindful, with no situational awareness.

an4.30:6.2.verse: ‘I’ll deny this Dhamma footprint of right immersion, and describe a true ascetic or brahmin who is scattered, with straying mind.’ Then I’d say to them:

an4.30:6.3.verse: ‘Let them come, speak, and discuss. We’ll see how powerful they are.’

an4.30:6.4.verse: It is quite impossible to deny this Dhamma footprint of right immersion, and point out a true ascetic or brahmin who is scattered, with straying mind.

an4.30:7.1.verse: If anyone imagines they can criticize and reject these four footprints of the Dhamma, they deserve rebuttal and criticism on four legitimate grounds in this very life.

an4.30:7.3.verse: If you reject the Dhamma footprint of contentment, then you must honor and praise those ascetics and brahmins who covet sensual pleasures with acute lust.

an4.30:7.4.verse: If you reject the Dhamma footprint of good will, you must honor and praise those ascetics and brahmins who have ill will and malicious intent.

an4.30:7.5.verse: If you reject the Dhamma footprint of right mindfulness, then you must honor and praise those ascetics and brahmins who are unmindful, with no situational awareness.

an4.30:7.6.verse: If you reject the Dhamma footprint of right immersion, you must honor and praise those ascetics and brahmins who are scattered, with straying minds.

an4.30:8.1.verse: If anyone imagines they can criticize and reject these four footprints of the Dhamma, they deserve rebuttal and criticism on four legitimate grounds in this very life.

an4.30:8.2.verse: Even those who were loud and bold advocates of the doctrines of no-cause, inaction, and nihilism didn’t imagine that these four footprints of the Dhamma should be criticized or rejected.

an4.30:8.4.verse: For fear of being blamed, provoked, and faulted.

an4.30:9.1.verse: One who has good will, ever mindful,

an4.31:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four situations. When these situations come about, any god or human who takes advantage of them will soon acquire great and abundant wealth.

an4.31:1.3.verse: Living in a suitable region, relying on true persons, being rightly resolved in oneself, and past merit.

an4.31:1.4.verse: These are the four situations. When these situations come about, any god or human who takes advantage of them will soon acquire great and abundant wealth.

an4.31:2.1.verse: When a man lives in a suitable region,

an4.31:2.4.verse: and having merit from the past,

an4.32:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of being inclusive.

an4.32:1.3.verse: Giving, kindly words, taking care, and equality.

an4.32:1.4.verse: These are the four ways of being inclusive.

an4.32:2.3.verse: and treating equally in worldly conditions,

an4.32:2.4.verse: as they deserve in each case.

an4.32:2.5.verse: These ways of being inclusive in the world

an4.32:2.6.verse: are like a moving chariot’s linchpin.

an4.32:3.1.verse: If there were no such ways of being inclusive,

an4.32:3.4.verse: for what they’ve done for their children.

an4.32:4.1.verse: But since these ways of being inclusive do exist,

an4.32:4.2.verse: the astute do regard them well,

an4.33:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, toward evening the lion, king of beasts, emerges from his den,

an4.33:1.4.verse: and roars his lion’s roar three times.

an4.33:1.5.verse: Then he sets out on the hunt.

an4.33:1.6.verse: And the animals who hear the roar of the lion, king of beasts, are typically filled with fear, awe, and terror.

an4.33:1.7.verse: They return to their lairs, be they in a hole, the water, or a wood; and the birds take to the air.

an4.33:1.8.verse: Even the royal elephants, bound with strong harnesses in the villages, towns, and capital cities, break apart their bonds, and urinate and defecate in terror as they flee here and there.

an4.33:1.9.verse: That’s how powerful is the lion, king of beasts, over animals, how illustrious and mighty.

an4.33:2.1.verse: In the same way, when a Realized One arises in the world—perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed—he teaches the Dhamma:

an4.33:2.2.verse: ‘Such is substantial reality, such is the origin of substantial reality, such is the cessation of substantial reality, such is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.’

an4.33:2.3.verse: Now, there are gods who are long-lived, beautiful, and very happy, lasting long in their divine palaces. When they hear this teaching by the Realized One, they’re typically filled with fear, awe, and terror.

an4.33:2.4.verse: ‘Oh no! It turns out we’re impermanent, though we thought we were permanent!

an4.33:2.5.verse: It turns out we don’t last, though we thought we were everlasting!

an4.33:2.6.verse: It turns out we’re transient, though we thought we were eternal!

an4.33:2.7.verse: It turns out that we’re impermanent, not lasting, transient, and included within substantial reality.’

an4.33:2.8.verse: That’s how powerful is the Realized One in the world with its gods, how illustrious and mighty.

an4.33:3.2.verse: in all the world with its gods,

an4.33:3.3.verse: rolls forth the Wheel of Dhamma

an4.33:4.4.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

an4.33:5.3.verse: are afraid and full of terror,

an4.33:5.4.verse: like the other beasts when they hear a lion.

an4.33:6.3.verse: So they say when they hear the word

an4.33:6.4.verse: of the perfected one, free and unaffected.”

an4.34:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four kinds of confidence are the best.

an4.34:1.3.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is said to be the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception or with neither perception nor non-perception.

an4.34:1.4.verse: Those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the best.

an4.34:1.5.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an4.34:2.1.verse: The noble eightfold path is said to be the best of all conditioned things.

an4.34:2.2.verse: Those who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in the best.

an4.34:2.3.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an4.34:3.1.verse: Fading away is said to be the best of all things whether conditioned or unconditioned. That is, the quelling of vanity, the removing of thirst, the uprooting of clinging, the breaking of the round, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

an4.34:3.2.verse: Those who have confidence in the teaching of fading away have confidence in the best.

an4.34:3.3.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an4.34:4.1.verse: The Saṅgha of the Realized One’s disciples is said to be the best of all communities and groups. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an4.34:4.2.verse: Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the best.

an4.34:4.3.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an4.34:4.4.verse: These are the four best kinds of confidence.

an4.34:5.1.verse: For those who, knowing the best teaching,

an4.34:5.2.verse: base their confidence on the best—

an4.34:5.3.verse: confident in the best Awakened One,

an4.34:5.4.verse: supremely worthy of a religious donation;

an4.34:6.2.verse: the bliss of fading and stilling;

an4.34:8.1.verse: An intelligent person gives to the best,

an4.34:8.3.verse: When they become a god or human,

an4.34:8.4.verse: they rejoice at reaching the best.”

an4.35:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

an4.35:1.2.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, a chief minister of Magadha, went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an4.35:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an4.35:2.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, when someone has four qualities we describe him as a great man with great wisdom.

an4.35:2.3.verse: They are very learned in diverse fields of learning.

an4.35:2.4.verse: They understand the meaning of diverse statements, saying: ‘This is what that statement means; that is what this statement means.’

an4.35:2.5.verse: They are mindful, able to remember and recollect what was said and done long ago.

an4.35:2.6.verse: They are deft and tireless in household duties, understanding how to go about things in order to complete and organize the work.

an4.35:2.7.verse: When someone possesses these four qualities we describe him as a great man with great wisdom.

an4.35:2.8.verse: If the worthy Gotama agrees with me, please say so.

an4.35:2.9.verse: If he disagrees, please say so.”

an4.35:3.1.verse: “Brahmin, I neither agree nor disagree with you,

an4.35:3.2.verse: but when someone has four qualities I describe him as a great man with great wisdom.

an4.35:3.4.verse: It’s when someone practices for the welfare and happiness of the people.

an4.35:3.5.verse: They’ve established many people in the noble system, that is, the principles of goodness and skillfulness.

an4.35:3.6.verse: They think what they want to think, and don’t think what they don’t want to think.

an4.35:3.7.verse: They consider what they want to consider, and don’t consider what they don’t want to consider.

an4.35:3.8.verse: Thus they have achieved mental mastery of the paths of thought.

an4.35:3.9.verse: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

an4.35:3.10.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an4.35:3.11.verse: Brahmin, I neither agree nor disagree with you,

an4.35:3.12.verse: but when someone possesses these four qualities I describe him as a great man with great wisdom.”

an4.35:4.2.verse: How well said this was by the worthy Gotama!

an4.35:4.3.verse: And we will remember the worthy Gotama as someone who possesses these four qualities.

an4.35:4.4.verse: For the worthy Gotama practices for the welfare and happiness of the people …

an4.35:4.7.verse: The worthy Gotama has achieved mental mastery of the paths of thought.

an4.35:4.8.verse: The worthy Gotama gets the four absorptions … when he wants, without trouble or difficulty.

an4.35:4.9.verse: The worthy Gotama has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. He lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

an4.35:5.1.verse: “Your words are clearly invasive and intrusive, brahmin.

an4.35:5.3.verse: For I do practice for the welfare and happiness of the people …

an4.35:5.6.verse: I have achieved mental mastery of the paths of thought.

an4.35:5.7.verse: I do get the four absorptions … when I want, without trouble or difficulty.

an4.35:5.8.verse: I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an4.35:6.1.verse: He discovered release from the snare of death

an4.35:6.3.verse: and explained the system of the teaching

an4.35:6.4.verse: for the welfare of gods and humans.

an4.35:6.5.verse: When they see him or hear him,

an4.35:7.1.verse: He is skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,

an4.35:7.2.verse: he has completed the task and is free of defilements.

an4.35:7.3.verse: The Buddha, bearing his final body,

an4.35:7.4.verse: is called ‘a great man, of great wisdom’.”

an4.36:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā,

an4.36:1.3.verse: Doṇa saw that the Buddha’s footprints had thousand-spoked wheels, with rims and hubs, complete in every detail.

an4.36:1.6.verse: Surely these couldn’t be the footprints of a human being?”

an4.36:1.7.verse: The Buddha had left the road and sat at the root of a tree cross-legged, setting his body straight, and bringing mindfulness to the present.

an4.36:1.8.verse: Then Doṇa, following the Buddha’s footprints, saw him sitting at the tree root—impressive and inspiring, with peaceful faculties and heart, attained to the highest self-control and serenity, like an elephant with tamed, guarded, and controlled faculties.

an4.36:1.9.verse: He went up to the Buddha and said to him:

an4.36:2.2.verse: “I will not be a god, brahmin.”

an4.36:3.1.verse: “When asked whether you might be a god, centaur, spirit, or human,

an4.36:3.2.verse: you answer that you will not be any of these.

an4.36:3.9.verse: So what then might you be?”

an4.36:4.1.verse: “Brahmin, if I had not given up defilements I might have become a god … a centaur … a spirit … or a human. But I have given up those defilements, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so they are unable to arise in the future.

an4.36:4.3.verse: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Though it sprouted and grew in the water, it would rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to it.

an4.36:4.4.verse: In the same way, though I was born and grew up in the world, I live having mastered the world, unsullied by the world.

an4.36:4.5.verse: Remember me, brahmin, as a Buddha.

an4.36:5.1.verse: I could have been reborn as a god,

an4.36:5.2.verse: or as a centaur flying through the sky.

an4.36:5.3.verse: I could have become a spirit,

an4.36:5.6.verse: they’re blown away and mown down.

an4.36:6.2.verse: to which water does not cling,

an4.36:6.3.verse: the world doesn’t cling to me,

an4.36:6.4.verse: and so, brahmin, I am a Buddha.”

an4.37:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who possesses four qualities can’t decline, and has drawn near to extinguishment.

an4.37:1.3.verse: A mendicant is accomplished in ethics, guards the sense doors, eats in moderation, and is dedicated to wakefulness.

an4.37:2.1.verse: And how is a mendicant accomplished in ethics?

an4.37:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an4.37:2.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is accomplished in ethics.

an4.37:3.1.verse: And how does a mendicant guard the sense doors?

an4.37:3.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.37:3.3.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

an4.37:3.4.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an4.37:3.5.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an4.37:3.6.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an4.37:3.7.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an4.37:3.8.verse: Knowing an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.37:3.9.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

an4.37:3.10.verse: That’s how a mendicant guards the sense doors.

an4.37:4.1.verse: And how does a mendicant eat in moderation?

an4.37:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant reflects rationally on the food that they eat:

an4.37:4.3.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

an4.37:4.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant eats in moderation.

an4.37:5.1.verse: And how is a mendicant dedicated to wakefulness?

an4.37:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant practices walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying their mind from obstacles.

an4.37:5.3.verse: In the first watch of the night, they continue to practice walking and sitting meditation.

an4.37:5.4.verse: In the middle watch, they lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

an4.37:5.5.verse: In the last watch, they get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying their mind from obstacles.

an4.37:5.6.verse: This is how a mendicant is dedicated to wakefulness.

an4.37:5.7.verse: A mendicant who possesses these four qualities can’t decline, and has drawn near to extinguishment.

an4.37:7.1.verse: a mendicant lives like this, with keen energy,

an4.37:7.4.verse: for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.

an4.37:8.4.verse: and has drawn near to extinguishment.”

an4.38:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth, has totally given up searching, has stilled the physical process, and is said to be ‘withdrawn’.

an4.38:1.2.verse: And how has a mendicant cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth?

an4.38:1.3.verse: Different ascetics and brahmins have different idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth. For example:

an4.38:1.4.verse: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

an4.38:1.5.verse: A mendicant has cast out, cast aside, thrown out, discarded, let go of, given up, and relinquished all these.

an4.38:1.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth.

an4.38:2.1.verse: And how has a mendicant totally given up searching?

an4.38:2.2.verse: It’s when they’ve given up searching for sensual pleasures, for continued existence, and for a spiritual path.

an4.38:2.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has totally given up searching.

an4.38:3.1.verse: And how has a mendicant stilled the physical process?

an4.38:3.2.verse: It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an4.38:3.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has stilled the physical process.

an4.38:4.1.verse: And how is a mendicant withdrawn?

an4.38:4.2.verse: It’s when they’ve given up the conceit ‘I am’, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

an4.38:4.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is withdrawn.

an4.38:4.4.verse: A mendicant has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth, has totally given up searching, has stilled the physical process, and is said to be ‘withdrawn’.

an4.38:5.1.verse: The search for sensual pleasures, for continued existence,

an4.38:5.2.verse: and the search for a spiritual path;

an4.38:5.3.verse: the holding tight to the thought, ‘this is the truth’,

an4.38:5.4.verse: and the mass of grounds for views—

an4.38:6.1.verse: for one detached from all lusts,

an4.38:6.2.verse: freed by the ending of craving,

an4.38:6.4.verse: and those grounds for views eradicated.

an4.38:7.1.verse: That mendicant is peaceful and mindful,

an4.38:7.3.verse: And when they’re awakened by comprehending conceit,

an4.39:1.1.verse: Then Ujjaya the brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an4.39:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an4.39:1.5.verse: Nor do I criticize all sacrifices.

an4.39:1.6.verse: Take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are slaughtered.

an4.39:1.7.verse: I don’t praise that kind of violent sacrifice.

an4.39:1.9.verse: Because neither perfected ones nor those who are on the path to perfection will attend such a violent sacrifice.

an4.39:2.1.verse: But take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are not slaughtered.

an4.39:2.2.verse: I do praise that kind of non-violent sacrifice; for example, a regular gift as a propitious sacrifice.

an4.39:2.4.verse: Because perfected ones and those who are on the path to perfection will attend such a non-violent sacrifice.

an4.39:3.2.verse: the sacrifices of the ‘casting of the yoke-pin’,

an4.39:3.4.verse: these grand, violent sacrifices yield no great fruit.

an4.39:4.1.verse: The great sages of right comportment

an4.39:5.1.verse: But the great sages of right comportment

an4.39:5.5.verse: and various creatures are not killed.

an4.39:6.1.verse: An intelligent person should sacrifice like this,

an4.39:6.2.verse: for this sacrifice is very fruitful.

an4.39:6.3.verse: For a sponsor of sacrifices like this,

an4.39:6.5.verse: Such a sacrifice is truly abundant,

an4.39:6.6.verse: and even the deities are pleased.”

an4.40:1.1.verse: Then Udāyī the brahmin went up to the Buddha, … and asked him,

an4.40:1.4.verse: Nor do I criticize all sacrifices.

an4.40:1.5.verse: Take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are slaughtered.

an4.40:1.6.verse: I don’t praise that kind of violent sacrifice.

an4.40:2.1.verse: But take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are not slaughtered.

an4.40:2.2.verse: I do praise that kind of non-violent sacrifice; for example, a regular gift as a propitious sacrifice.

an4.40:3.2.verse: a sacrifice that’s allowable and timely,

an4.40:4.1.verse: The Buddhas—who have cast off the world’s veil,

an4.40:4.4.verse: as they are expert in sacrifice.

an4.40:5.1.verse: When you’ve prepared a suitable offering,

an4.40:5.2.verse: whether as sacrifice or for ancestors,

an4.40:5.4.verse: in the fertile field of spiritual practitioners.

an4.40:6.1.verse: When it’s well-gotten, well-offered, and well-sacrificed,

an4.40:6.2.verse: to those worthy of a religious donation,

an4.40:6.4.verse: and even the deities are pleased.

an4.40:7.2.verse: sacrifices like this, with a mind of letting go,

an4.41:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of developing immersion further.

an4.41:1.3.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life.

an4.41:1.4.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision.

an4.41:1.5.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness.

an4.41:1.6.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements.

an4.41:2.1.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life?

an4.41:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption … second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an4.41:2.3.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life.

an4.41:3.1.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision?

an4.41:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant applies their mind to the perception of light, focusing on the perception of day:

an4.41:3.3.verse: as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.

an4.41:3.4.verse: And so, with an open and unenveloped heart, they develop a mind that’s full of radiance.

an4.41:3.5.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision.

an4.41:4.1.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness?

an4.41:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an4.41:4.3.verse: They know perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away. They know thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an4.41:4.4.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness.

an4.41:5.1.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements?

an4.41:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

an4.41:5.3.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

an4.41:5.4.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

an4.41:5.5.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

an4.41:5.6.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

an4.41:5.7.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

an4.41:5.8.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements.

an4.41:5.9.verse: These are the four ways of developing immersion further.

an4.41:5.10.verse: And it was in this connection that I said in ‘The Way to the Far Shore’, in ‘The Questions of Puṇṇaka’:

an4.41:6.1.verse: ‘Having appraised the world high and low,

an4.41:6.2.verse: there is nothing in the world that disturbs them.

an4.41:6.3.verse: Peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, with no need for hope,

an4.41:6.4.verse: they’ve crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.’”

an4.42:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of answering questions.

an4.42:1.3.verse: There is a question that should be answered categorically.

an4.42:1.4.verse: There is a question that should be answered analytically.

an4.42:1.5.verse: There is a question that should be answered with a counter-question.

an4.42:1.6.verse: There is a question that should be set aside.

an4.42:1.7.verse: These are the four ways of answering questions.

an4.42:2.4.verse: while a fourth is set aside.

an4.42:3.1.verse: That sort of mendicant, who knows each of these,

an4.42:3.4.verse: in the four kinds of questions.

an4.42:4.4.verse: what the meaning is and what it isn’t.

an4.42:5.1.verse: Shunning what is not the meaning,

an4.42:5.2.verse: an astute person grasps the meaning.

an4.42:5.3.verse: An attentive one, comprehending the meaning,

an4.43:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four individuals are found in the world.

an4.43:1.3.verse: People who value anger, or denigration, or material things, or honor rather than the true teaching.

an4.43:1.4.verse: These are the four individuals found in the world.

an4.43:2.1.verse: These four individuals are found in the world.

an4.43:2.3.verse: People who value the true teaching rather than anger, or denigration, or material things, or honor.

an4.43:2.4.verse: These are the four individuals found in the world.

an4.43:3.1.verse: Mendicants who value anger and denigration,

an4.43:3.4.verse: that was taught by the perfected Buddha.

an4.43:4.1.verse: But those who value the true teaching,

an4.43:4.2.verse: who have lived it, and are living it now,

an4.43:4.3.verse: these do grow in the teaching

an4.43:4.4.verse: that was taught by the perfected Buddha.”

an4.44:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four things oppose the true teaching.

an4.44:1.3.verse: Valuing anger, denigration, material things, and honor rather than the true teaching.

an4.44:1.4.verse: These are the four things that oppose the true teaching.

an4.44:2.1.verse: These four things are the true teaching.

an4.44:2.3.verse: Valuing the true teaching rather than anger, denigration, material things, and honor.

an4.44:2.4.verse: These are the four things that are the true teaching.

an4.44:3.1.verse: A mendicant who values anger and denigration,

an4.44:3.3.verse: doesn’t grow in the true teaching,

an4.44:3.4.verse: like a rotten seed in a good field.

an4.44:4.1.verse: But those who value the true teaching,

an4.44:4.2.verse: who have lived it, and are living it now,

an4.44:4.3.verse: these do grow in the teaching,

an4.45:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an4.45:1.2.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious godling Rohitassa, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him:

an4.45:2.1.verse: “Sir, is it possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn?”

an4.45:2.2.verse: “Reverend, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.”

an4.45:3.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha.

an4.45:4.1.verse: Once upon a time, I was a seer named Rohitassa, son of the benefactors. I was a sky-walker with psychic powers.

an4.45:4.2.verse: I was as fast as a light arrow easily shot across the shadow of a palm tree by a well-trained expert archer with a strong bow.

an4.45:4.3.verse: My stride was such that it could span from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.

an4.45:4.4.verse: Having such speed and stride, this wish came to me:

an4.45:4.5.verse: ‘I will reach the end of the world by traveling.’

an4.45:4.6.verse: I traveled for my whole lifespan of a hundred years—pausing only to eat and drink, go to the toilet, and sleep to dispel weariness—and I passed away along the way, never reaching the end of the world.

an4.45:5.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha.”

an4.45:6.1.verse: “Reverend, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.

an4.45:6.2.verse: But I also say there’s no making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world.

an4.45:6.3.verse: For it is in this fathom-long carcass with its perception and mind that I describe the world, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

an4.45:7.1.verse: The end of the world can never

an4.45:7.3.verse: But without reaching the end of the world,

an4.45:8.1.verse: So an intelligent person, understanding the world,

an4.45:8.2.verse: has completed the spiritual journey and gone to the end of the world.

an4.45:8.3.verse: Assuaged, knowing the end of the world,

an4.45:8.4.verse: they do not hope for this world or the next.”

an4.46:1.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an4.46:1.2.verse: “Tonight, the glorious godling Rohitassa, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, came to me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me:

an4.46:1.3.verse: ‘Sir, is it possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn?’ …”

an4.47:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four things are very far apart.

an4.47:1.5.verse: The near and the far shore of the ocean. …

an4.47:1.7.verse: Where the dazzling sun rises and where it sets. …

an4.47:1.9.verse: The teaching of the virtuous and the teaching of the wicked. …

an4.47:1.11.verse: These are the four things very far apart.

an4.47:2.1.verse: The firmament is far from the earth;

an4.47:2.2.verse: they say the other shore of the ocean is far;

an4.47:2.3.verse: and where the dazzling sun rises is far

an4.47:2.5.verse: But even further apart than that, they say,

an4.47:2.6.verse: is the teaching of the virtuous from the wicked.

an4.47:3.1.verse: The company of the virtuous is reliable;

an4.47:3.2.verse: as long as it remains, it stays the same.

an4.47:3.3.verse: But the company of the wicked is fickle,

an4.47:3.4.verse: and so the teaching of the virtuous is far from the wicked.”

an4.48:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an4.48:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son, was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk. His words were polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.

an4.48:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,

an4.48:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, who was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk?”

an4.48:2.2.verse: “Sir, it was Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son.”

an4.48:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Visākha,

an4.48:3.3.verse: It’s good that you educate, encourage, fire up, and inspire the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk, with words that are polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.

an4.48:4.1.verse: Though an astute person is mixed up with fools,

an4.48:4.2.verse: they don’t know unless he speaks.

an4.48:4.3.verse: But when he speaks they know,

an4.48:4.4.verse: he’s teaching the state free of death.

an4.48:5.1.verse: He should speak and illustrate the teaching,

an4.48:5.2.verse: holding up the banner of the seers.

an4.48:5.3.verse: Words well spoken are the seers’ banner,

an4.48:5.4.verse: for the teaching is the banner of the seers.”

an4.49:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four perversions of perception, thought, and view.

an4.49:1.7.verse: These are the four perversions of perception, thought, and view.

an4.49:2.1.verse: There are these four corrections of perception, thought, and view.

an4.49:2.7.verse: These are the four corrections of perception, thought, and view.

an4.49:3.5.verse: sentient beings are ruined by wrong view,

an4.49:4.1.verse: Yoked by Māra’s yoke, these people

an4.49:4.2.verse: find no sanctuary from the yoke.

an4.49:5.4.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

an4.49:6.1.verse: When a wise person hears them,

an4.50:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four corruptions obscure the sun and moon, so they don’t glow and shine and dazzle.

an4.50:4.1.verse: An eclipse of Rāhu, lord of titans …

an4.50:4.2.verse: These are four corruptions that obscure the sun and moon, so they don’t glow and shine and dazzle.

an4.50:5.1.verse: In the same way, these four things corrupt ascetics and brahmins, so they don’t glow and shine and dazzle.

an4.50:5.3.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who drink beer and wine, not refraining from drinking beer and wine.

an4.50:5.4.verse: This is the first thing that corrupts ascetics and brahmins …

an4.50:6.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have sex, not refraining from sex.

an4.50:6.2.verse: This is the second thing that corrupts ascetics and brahmins …

an4.50:7.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who accept gold and currency, not refraining from receiving gold and currency.

an4.50:7.2.verse: This is the third thing that corrupts ascetics and brahmins …

an4.50:8.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who make a living the wrong way, not refraining from wrong livelihood.

an4.50:8.2.verse: This is the fourth thing that corrupts ascetics and brahmins …

an4.50:8.3.verse: These are four things that corrupt ascetics and brahmins, so they don’t glow and shine and dazzle.

an4.50:9.2.verse: are plagued by greed and hate;

an4.50:10.6.verse: make a living the wrong way.

an4.50:11.2.verse: by the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun.

an4.50:12.2.verse: bondservants of craving, full of attachments,

an4.50:12.3.verse: swell the horrors of the charnel ground,

an4.51:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an4.51:1.4.verse: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while using a robe, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

an4.51:2.1.verse: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while eating almsfood, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

an4.51:3.1.verse: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while using lodgings, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

an4.51:4.1.verse: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while using medicines and supplies for the sick, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

an4.51:4.2.verse: These are the four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an4.51:5.1.verse: When a noble disciple has these four kinds of overflowing merit and goodness, it’s not easy to grasp how much merit they have by saying that this is the extent of their overflowing merit … that leads to happiness. It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

an4.51:6.1.verse: It’s like trying to grasp how much water is in the ocean. It’s not easy to say how many gallons, how many hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands of gallons there are. It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water.

an4.51:6.2.verse: In the same way, when a noble disciple has these four kinds of overflowing merit it’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

an4.51:7.1.verse: Hosts of people use the rivers,

an4.51:7.2.verse: and though the rivers are many,

an4.51:7.3.verse: all reach the great deep, the boundless ocean,

an4.51:7.4.verse: the cruel sea that’s home to precious gems.

an4.51:8.1.verse: In the same way, when a person gives food, drink, and clothes;

an4.51:8.2.verse: and they’re a giver of beds, seats, and mats—

an4.51:8.3.verse: the streams of merit reach that astute person,

an4.51:8.4.verse: as the rivers bring their waters to the sea.”

an4.52:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an4.52:1.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha:

an4.52:1.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an4.52:1.5.verse: This is the first kind of overflowing merit …

an4.52:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the teaching:

an4.52:2.2.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

an4.52:2.3.verse: This is the second kind of overflowing merit …

an4.52:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

an4.52:3.2.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

an4.52:3.3.verse: This is the third kind of overflowing merit …

an4.52:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a noble disciple’s ethical conduct is loved by the noble ones, unbroken, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

an4.52:4.2.verse: This is the fourth kind of overflowing merit …

an4.52:4.3.verse: These are the four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an4.52:5.1.verse: Whoever has faith in the Realized One,

an4.52:5.4.verse: praised and loved by the noble ones;

an4.52:6.1.verse: who has confidence in the Saṅgha,

an4.52:6.4.verse: their life is not in vain.

an4.52:7.1.verse: So let the wise devote themselves

an4.52:7.3.verse: confidence, and insight into the teaching,

an4.52:7.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”

an4.53:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā,

an4.53:1.2.verse: as were several householders, both women and men.

an4.53:1.3.verse: The Buddha left the road and sat at the root of a tree,

an4.53:1.5.verse: They went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

an4.53:2.1.verse: “Householders, there are four ways of living together.

an4.53:2.3.verse: A male zombie living with a female zombie;

an4.53:2.4.verse: a male zombie living with a goddess;

an4.53:2.5.verse: a god living with a female zombie;

an4.53:2.6.verse: a god living with a goddess.

an4.53:3.1.verse: And how does a male zombie live with a female zombie?

an4.53:3.2.verse: It’s when the husband kills living creatures, steals, commits sexual misconduct, lies, and consumes intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. He’s unethical, of bad character, living at home with his heart full of the stain of stinginess, abusing and insulting ascetics and brahmins.

an4.53:3.3.verse: And the wife is also … unethical, of bad character …

an4.53:3.4.verse: That’s how a male zombie lives with a female zombie.

an4.53:4.1.verse: And how does a male zombie live with a goddess?

an4.53:4.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is unethical, of bad character …

an4.53:4.3.verse: But the wife doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants. She’s ethical, of good character, living at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, not abusing and insulting ascetics and brahmins.

an4.53:4.4.verse: That’s how a male zombie lives with a goddess.

an4.53:5.1.verse: And how does a god live with a female zombie?

an4.53:5.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is ethical, of good character …

an4.53:5.3.verse: But the wife … is unethical, of bad character …

an4.53:5.4.verse: That’s how a god lives with a female zombie.

an4.53:6.1.verse: And how does a god live with a goddess?

an4.53:6.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is ethical, of good character …

an4.53:6.3.verse: And the wife is also … ethical, of good character …

an4.53:6.4.verse: That’s how a god lives with a goddess.

an4.53:6.5.verse: These are the four ways of living together.

an4.53:8.6.verse: with a zombie for a husband.

an4.53:9.6.verse: with a god for a husband.

an4.53:10.1.verse: When both are faithful and bountiful,

an4.53:10.4.verse: say nice things to each other.

an4.53:11.4.verse: when both are equal in ethics.

an4.53:12.2.verse: both equal in precepts and observances,

an4.53:12.3.verse: they delight in the heavenly realm,

an4.53:12.4.verse: enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”

an4.54:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are four ways of living together.

an4.54:1.3.verse: A male zombie living with a female zombie;

an4.54:1.4.verse: a male zombie living with a goddess;

an4.54:1.5.verse: a god living with a female zombie;

an4.54:1.6.verse: a god living with a goddess.

an4.54:2.1.verse: And how does a male zombie live with a female zombie?

an4.54:2.2.verse: It’s when the husband kills living creatures, steals, commits sexual misconduct; he uses speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; and he’s covetous, malicious, and has wrong view. He’s unethical, of bad character, living at home with his heart full of the stain of stinginess, abusing and insulting ascetics and brahmins.

an4.54:2.3.verse: And the wife is also … unethical, of bad character …

an4.54:2.4.verse: That’s how a male zombie lives with a female zombie.

an4.54:3.1.verse: And how does a male zombie live with a goddess?

an4.54:3.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is unethical, of bad character …

an4.54:3.3.verse: But the wife doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, or commit sexual misconduct. She doesn’t use speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical. And she’s contented, kind-hearted, with right view. She’s ethical, of good character, living at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, not abusing and insulting ascetics and brahmins.

an4.54:3.4.verse: That’s how a male zombie lives with a goddess.

an4.54:4.1.verse: And how does a god live with a female zombie?

an4.54:4.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is ethical, of good character …

an4.54:4.3.verse: But the wife … is unethical, of bad character …

an4.54:4.4.verse: That’s how a god lives with a female zombie.

an4.54:5.1.verse: And how does a god live with a goddess?

an4.54:5.2.verse: It’s when the husband … is ethical, of good character …

an4.54:5.3.verse: And the wife is also … ethical, of good character …

an4.54:5.4.verse: That’s how a god lives with a goddess.

an4.54:5.5.verse: These are the four ways of living together.” …

an4.55:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

an4.55:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Nakula’s father, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an4.55:1.4.verse: Then the householder Nakula’s father and the housewife Nakula’s mother went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Nakula’s father said to the Buddha,

an4.55:2.1.verse: “Sir, ever since we were both young, and Nakula’s mother was given to me in marriage, I can’t recall betraying her even in thought, still less in deed.

an4.55:2.2.verse: We want to see each other in both this life and the next.”

an4.55:2.3.verse: Then Nakula’s mother said to the Buddha,

an4.55:2.4.verse: “Sir, ever since we were both young, and I was given in marriage to Nakula’s father, I can’t recall betraying him even in thought, still less in deed.

an4.55:2.5.verse: We want to see each other in both this life and the next.”

an4.55:3.1.verse: “Householders, if wife and husband want to see each other in both this life and the next, they should be equals in faith, ethics, generosity, and wisdom.

an4.55:4.1.verse: When both are faithful and bountiful,

an4.55:4.4.verse: say nice things to each other.

an4.55:5.4.verse: when both are equal in ethics.

an4.55:6.2.verse: both equal in precepts and observances,

an4.55:6.3.verse: they delight in the heavenly realm,

an4.55:6.4.verse: enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”

an4.56:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wife and husband want to see each other in both this life and the next, they should be equals in faith, ethics, generosity, and wisdom. …”

an4.57:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Koliyans, where they have a town named Pajjanika.

an4.57:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of Suppavāsā the Koliyan, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an4.57:1.3.verse: Then Suppavāsā served and satisfied the Buddha with her own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

an4.57:1.4.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, she sat down to one side.

an4.57:2.1.verse: “Suppavāsā, when a noble disciple gives food, she gives the recipients four things.

an4.57:2.3.verse: Long life, beauty, happiness, and strength.

an4.57:2.4.verse: Giving long life, she has long life as a god or human.

an4.57:2.5.verse: Giving beauty, she has beauty as a god or human.

an4.57:2.6.verse: Giving happiness, she has happiness as a god or human.

an4.57:2.7.verse: Giving strength, she has strength as a god or human.

an4.57:2.8.verse: When a noble disciple gives food, she gives the recipients these four things.

an4.57:3.2.verse: pure, fine, and full of flavor,

an4.57:3.4.verse: who have good conduct, and are big-hearted—

an4.57:3.5.verse: joins merit to merit. It’s very fruitful,

an4.57:3.6.verse: and is praised by those who know the world.

an4.57:4.2.verse: live in the world full of inspiration.

an4.57:4.3.verse: They’ve driven out the stain of stinginess, root and all,

an4.57:4.4.verse: blameless, they go to a heavenly place.”

an4.58:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an4.58:2.1.verse: “Householder, when a noble disciple gives food, they give the recipients four things.

an4.58:2.3.verse: Long life, beauty, happiness, and strength.

an4.58:2.4.verse: Giving long life, they have long life as a god or human. …

an4.58:2.6.verse: When a noble disciple gives food, they give the recipients these four things.

an4.58:3.1.verse: Carefully giving food at the right time,

an4.58:3.2.verse: to those who are disciplined, eating only what others give,

an4.58:3.3.verse: you provide them with four things:

an4.58:3.4.verse: long life, beauty, happiness, and strength.

an4.58:4.1.verse: A person who gives long life, beauty,

an4.59:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a donor gives food, they give the recipients four things.

an4.59:1.3.verse: Long life, beauty, happiness, and strength. …”

an4.60:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an4.60:2.1.verse: “Householder, when a noble disciple does four things they are practicing appropriately for a layperson, which brings fame and leads to heaven.

an4.60:2.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple serves the mendicant Saṅgha with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an4.60:2.4.verse: When a noble disciple does these four things they are practicing appropriately for a layperson, which brings fame and leads to heaven.

an4.60:3.1.verse: Those who are astute practice the way

an4.60:3.3.verse: They provide those who are ethical

an4.60:4.5.verse: They pass on to a place in heaven,

an4.61:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an4.61:2.1.verse: “Householder, these four things, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable are hard to get in the world.

an4.61:2.3.verse: The first thing is the wish: ‘May wealth come to me by legitimate means!’

an4.61:3.1.verse: The second thing, having got wealth by legitimate means, is the wish: ‘May fame come to me, together with my family and mentors.’
