an4.184:7.2.verse: It’s someone who is rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

an4.184:7.5.verse: ‘The sensual pleasures that I love so much will leave me, and I’ll leave them.’

an4.184:7.6.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.184:7.7.verse: This is someone who’s not frightened of death.

an4.184:8.1.verse: Furthermore, it’s someone who is rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for the body.

an4.184:8.4.verse: ‘This body that I love so much will leave me, and I’ll leave it.’

an4.184:8.5.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.184:8.6.verse: This, too, is someone who’s not frightened of death.

an4.184:9.1.verse: Furthermore, it’s someone who hasn’t done bad things, violence and sin, but has done good and skillful deeds that keep them safe.

an4.184:9.4.verse: ‘Well, I haven’t done bad things, violence and sin.

an4.184:9.5.verse: And I have done good and skillful deeds that keep me safe.

an4.184:9.6.verse: When I depart, I’ll go to the place where people who’ve done such things go.’

an4.184:9.7.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.184:9.8.verse: This, too, is someone who’s not frightened of death.

an4.184:10.1.verse: Furthermore, it’s someone who’s not doubtful, uncertain, or undecided about the true teaching.

an4.184:10.4.verse: ‘I’m not doubtful, uncertain, or undecided about the true teaching.’

an4.184:10.5.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.184:10.6.verse: This, too, is someone who’s not frightened of death.

an4.184:10.7.verse: These are the four individuals liable to death who are not frightened and terrified of death.”

an4.184:11.1.verse: “Excellent, worthy Gotama! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an4.185:1.1.verse: Once the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an4.185:1.2.verse: Now at that time several very well-known wanderers were residing in their monastery on the bank of the Serpentine River. They included Annabhāra, Varadhara, Sakuludāyī, and other very well-known wanderers.

an4.185:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the monastery for the wanderers on the bank of the Serpentine River.

an4.185:2.1.verse: Now at that time this discussion came up while those wanderers of other religions were sitting together,

an4.185:2.2.verse: “The truths of the brahmins are like this; the truths of the brahmins are like that.”

an4.185:2.3.verse: Then the Buddha went up to those wanderers, sat down on the seat spread out, and said to them,

an4.185:3.1.verse: “Wanderers, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

an4.185:3.2.verse: “Well, worthy Gotama, this discussion came up among us while we were sitting together:

an4.185:3.3.verse: ‘The truths of the brahmins are like this; the truths of the brahmins are like that.’”

an4.185:4.1.verse: “Wanderers, I declare these four truths of the brahmins, having realized them with my own insight.

an4.185:4.5.verse: In speaking like this, a brahmin speaks the truth, not lies.

an4.185:4.6.verse: But they don’t think of themselves as an ‘ascetic’ or ‘brahmin’ because of that. Nor do they think ‘I’m better’ or ‘I’m equal’ or ‘I’m worse’.

an4.185:4.7.verse: Rather, they simply practice out of kindness and sympathy for living creatures, having had insight into the truth of that.

an4.185:5.2.verse: ‘All sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and perishable.’

an4.185:5.3.verse: Saying this, a brahmin speaks the truth, not lies.

an4.185:5.4.verse: But they don’t think of themselves as an ‘ascetic’ or ‘brahmin’ because of that. Nor do they think ‘I’m better’ or ‘I’m equal’ or ‘I’m worse’.

an4.185:5.5.verse: Rather, they simply practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding sensual pleasures, having had insight into the truth of that.

an4.185:6.2.verse: ‘All states of existence are impermanent, suffering, and perishable.’ … They simply practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding future lives, having had insight into the truth of that.

an4.185:7.2.verse: ‘I don’t belong to anyone anywhere. And nothing belongs to me anywhere.’

an4.185:7.3.verse: In speaking like this, a brahmin speaks the truth, not lies.

an4.185:7.4.verse: But they don’t think of themselves as an ‘ascetic’ or ‘brahmin’ because of that. Nor do they think ‘I’m better’ or ‘I’m equal’ or ‘I’m worse’.

an4.185:7.5.verse: Rather, they simply practice the path of nothingness, having had insight into the truth of that.

an4.185:7.6.verse: These are the four truths of the brahmins that I declare, having realized them with my own insight.”

an4.186:1.1.verse: Then one of the mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an4.186:1.2.verse: “Sir, what leads the world on? What drags it around? What arises and takes control?”

an4.186:2.2.verse: Your approach and eloquence are excellent, and it’s a good question.

an4.186:2.4.verse: ‘What leads the world on? What drags it around? What arises and takes control?’”

an4.186:2.6.verse: “Mendicant, the mind leads the world on. The mind drags it around. When the mind arises, it takes control.”

an4.186:3.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

an4.186:3.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘a learned memorizer of the teaching’.

an4.186:3.3.verse: How is a learned memorizer of the teaching defined?”

an4.186:4.2.verse: Your approach and eloquence are excellent, and it’s a good question. …

an4.186:4.8.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

an4.186:4.9.verse: But if anyone understands the meaning and the text of even a four-line verse, and if they practice in line with that teaching, they’re qualified to be called a ‘learned memorizer of the teaching’.”

an4.186:5.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

an4.186:5.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘a learned person with penetrating wisdom’.

an4.186:5.3.verse: How is a learned person with penetrating wisdom defined?”

an4.186:6.2.verse: Your approach and eloquence are excellent, and it’s a good question. …

an4.186:6.7.verse: Take a mendicant who has heard: ‘This is suffering.’ They see what it means with penetrating wisdom.

an4.186:6.8.verse: They’ve heard: ‘This is the origin of suffering’ …

an4.186:6.10.verse: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ They see what it means with penetrating wisdom.

an4.186:6.11.verse: That’s how an individual is learned, with penetrating wisdom.”

an4.186:7.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

an4.186:7.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘an astute person with great wisdom’.

an4.186:7.3.verse: How is an astute person with great wisdom defined?”

an4.186:8.2.verse: Your approach and eloquence are excellent, and it’s a good question. …

an4.186:8.7.verse: An astute person with great wisdom is one who has no intention to hurt themselves, or to hurt others, or to hurt both. When they think, they only think of the benefit for themselves, for others, for both, and for the whole world.

an4.186:8.8.verse: That’s how an individual is astute, with great wisdom.”

an4.187:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

an4.187:1.2.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, a chief minister of Magadha, went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an4.187:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an4.187:2.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, could an untrue person know of an untrue person:

an4.187:2.2.verse: ‘This worthy one is an untrue person’?”

an4.187:2.5.verse: “Could an untrue person know of a true person:

an4.187:2.6.verse: ‘This worthy one is a true person’?”

an4.187:2.7.verse: “That too is impossible, it can’t happen.”

an4.187:2.9.verse: “Worthy Gotama, could a true person know of a true person:

an4.187:2.10.verse: ‘This worthy one is a true person’?”

an4.187:2.13.verse: “Could a true person know of an untrue person:

an4.187:2.14.verse: ‘This worthy one is an untrue person’?”

an4.187:3.2.verse: how well said this was by the worthy Gotama:

an4.187:3.3.verse: ‘It’s impossible, it can’t happen, that an untrue person could know …

an4.187:3.7.verse: But it is possible that a true person could know …’

an4.187:4.1.verse: Once, members of the brahmin Todeyya’s assembly were going on complaining about others:

an4.187:4.2.verse: ‘This King Eḷeyya is a fool to be so devoted to the ascetic Rāmaputta. He even shows him the utmost deference by bowing down to him, rising up for him, greeting him with cupped palms, and observing proper etiquette for him.

an4.187:4.3.verse: And these king’s men are fools too—

an4.187:4.4.verse: Yamaka, Moggalla, Ugga, Nāvindakī, Gandhabba, and Aggivessa—for they show the same kind of deference to Rāmaputta.’

an4.187:4.5.verse: Then the brahmin Todeyya reasoned with them like this:

an4.187:4.7.verse: When it comes to the various duties and speeches, isn’t King Eḷeyya astute, even better than the experts?’

an4.187:5.1.verse: ‘It’s because the ascetic Rāmaputta is even more astute and expert than King Eḷeyya that the king is so devoted to him. That’s why he even shows Rāmaputta the utmost deference by bowing down to him, rising up for him, greeting him with cupped palms, and observing proper etiquette for him.

an4.187:6.3.verse: When it comes to the various duties and speeches, aren’t the king’s men—Yamaka, Moggalla, Ugga, Nāvindakī, Gandhabba, and Aggivessa—astute, even better than the experts?’

an4.187:7.1.verse: ‘It’s because Rāmaputta is even more astute and expert than the king’s men that they have such devotion to him. …

an4.187:7.2.verse: It’s because Rāmaputta is even more astute and expert than King Eḷeyya that the king is so devoted to him. That’s why he even shows Rāmaputta the utmost deference by bowing down to him, rising up for him, greeting him with cupped palms, and observing proper etiquette for him.’

an4.187:8.1.verse: It’s incredible, worthy Gotama, it’s amazing,

an4.187:8.2.verse: how well said this was by the worthy Gotama:

an4.187:8.3.verse: ‘It’s impossible, it can’t happen, that an untrue person could know …

an4.187:8.7.verse: But it is possible that a true person could know …’

an4.187:8.11.verse: Well, now, worthy Gotama, I must go.

an4.187:8.12.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

an4.187:9.1.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, rose from his seat and left.

an4.188:1.1.verse: Once the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an4.188:1.2.verse: Then Upaka the son of Maṇḍikā went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an4.188:2.1.verse: “Sir, this is my doctrine and view:

an4.188:2.2.verse: ‘Whoever goes on complaining about others without giving any reasons

an4.188:2.4.verse: “Upaka, if someone goes on complaining about others without giving a reason, they’re reprehensible and at fault.

an4.188:2.5.verse: But that’s what you do, so you’re reprehensible and at fault!”

an4.188:2.6.verse: “Sir, like a fish caught in a big trap just as it rises,

an4.188:2.7.verse: so the Buddha caught me in a big trap of words just as I rose up.”

an4.188:3.2.verse: And for that there are limitless words, phrasings, and teachings of the Realized One:

an4.188:3.3.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that this is unskillful.’

an4.188:3.4.verse: I’ve declared: ‘The unskillful should be given up.’

an4.188:3.5.verse: And for that there are limitless words, phrasings, and teachings of the Realized One:

an4.188:3.6.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that the unskillful should be given up.’

an4.188:4.2.verse: And for that there are limitless words, phrasings, and teachings of the Realized One:

an4.188:4.3.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that this is skillful.’

an4.188:4.4.verse: I’ve declared: ‘The skillful should be developed.’

an4.188:4.5.verse: And for that there are limitless words, phrasings, and teachings of the Realized One:

an4.188:4.6.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that the skillful should be developed.’”

an4.188:5.1.verse: And then Upaka son of Maṇḍikā approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went up to King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha. He told the King of all they had discussed.

an4.188:5.2.verse: But Ajātasattu became angry and upset, and said to Upaka,

an4.188:5.3.verse: “How rude of this salt-maker’s boy! How scurrilous and impudent of him to imagine he could attack the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

an4.188:5.4.verse: Get out, Upaka, go away! Don’t let me see you again.”

an4.189:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four things should be realized.

an4.189:1.3.verse: There are things to be realized with direct meditative experience.

an4.189:1.4.verse: There are things to be realized with recollection.

an4.189:1.5.verse: There are things to be realized with vision.

an4.189:1.6.verse: There are things to be realized with wisdom.

an4.189:1.7.verse: What things are to be realized with direct meditative experience?

an4.189:2.1.verse: What things are to be realized with recollection?

an4.189:3.1.verse: What things are to be realized with vision?

an4.189:3.2.verse: The passing away and rebirth of sentient beings.

an4.189:4.1.verse: What things are to be realized with wisdom?

an4.189:4.3.verse: These are the four things to be realized.”

an4.190:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

an4.190:1.2.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath, and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

an4.190:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them:

an4.190:2.1.verse: “This assembly has no chaff, monks, it is free of chaff, pure, and consolidated in the core.

an4.190:2.2.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly!

an4.190:2.3.verse: An assembly such as this is rarely seen in the world.

an4.190:2.4.verse: An assembly such as this is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an4.190:2.5.verse: For an assembly such as this, giving little becomes much, while giving much becomes even more.

an4.190:2.6.verse: An assembly such as this is worth traveling many leagues to see, even if you have to carry your own provisions in a knapsack.

an4.190:3.1.verse: There are mendicants staying in this Saṅgha who have attained to the gods.

an4.190:3.2.verse: There are mendicants staying in this Saṅgha who have attained to divinity.

an4.190:3.3.verse: There are mendicants staying in this Saṅgha who have attained to the imperturbable.

an4.190:3.4.verse: There are mendicants staying in this Saṅgha who have attained to nobility.

an4.190:4.1.verse: And how has a mendicant attained to the gods?

an4.190:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption …

an4.190:4.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption …

an4.190:4.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant has attained to the gods.

an4.190:5.1.verse: And how has a mendicant attained to divinity?

an4.190:5.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an4.190:5.3.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of compassion …

an4.190:5.5.verse: equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an4.190:5.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant has attained to divinity.

an4.190:6.1.verse: And how has a mendicant attained to the imperturbable?

an4.190:6.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

an4.190:6.3.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, he enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

an4.190:6.4.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, he enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

an4.190:6.5.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, he enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

an4.190:6.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant has attained to the imperturbable.

an4.190:7.1.verse: And how has a mendicant attained to nobility?

an4.190:7.2.verse: It’s when they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an4.190:7.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has attained to nobility.”

an4.191:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you can expect four benefits when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.

an4.191:1.3.verse: Take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching—

an4.191:1.4.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

an4.191:1.5.verse: They’ve followed those teachings by ear, consolidated them by voice, examined them by the mind, and well penetrated them theoretically.

an4.191:1.6.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an4.191:1.7.verse: Being happy there, passages of the teaching come back to them.

an4.191:1.9.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:1.10.verse: This is the first benefit you can expect when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.

an4.191:2.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching—

an4.191:2.2.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

an4.191:2.3.verse: They’ve followed those teachings by ear, consolidated them by voice, examined them by the mind, and well penetrated them theoretically.

an4.191:2.4.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an4.191:2.5.verse: Though they’re happy there, passages of the teaching don’t come back to them.

an4.191:2.6.verse: However, a mendicant with psychic powers, who has achieved mastery of the mind, teaches Dhamma to the assembly of gods.

an4.191:2.8.verse: ‘I used to lead the spiritual life in this same teaching and training.’

an4.191:2.10.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:2.11.verse: Suppose a person was skilled in the sound of drums.

an4.191:2.12.verse: While traveling along a road they hear the sound of drums.

an4.191:2.13.verse: They wouldn’t have any doubts or uncertainties about whether

an4.191:2.14.verse: that was the sound of drums or not.

an4.191:2.15.verse: They’d just conclude, ‘That’s the sound of drums.’

an4.191:2.16.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching …

an4.191:2.19.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods. …

an4.191:2.25.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:2.26.verse: This is the second benefit you can expect when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.

an4.191:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching—

an4.191:3.2.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

an4.191:3.3.verse: They’ve followed those teachings by ear, consolidated them by voice, examined them by the mind, and well penetrated them theoretically.

an4.191:3.4.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an4.191:3.5.verse: But passages of the teaching don’t come back to them when they’re happy, nor does a mendicant with psychic powers … teach Dhamma to the assembly of gods.

an4.191:3.6.verse: However, a godling teaches Dhamma to the assembly of gods.

an4.191:3.8.verse: ‘I used to lead the spiritual life in this same teaching and training.’

an4.191:3.10.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:3.11.verse: Suppose a person was skilled in the sound of horns.

an4.191:3.12.verse: While traveling along a road they hear the sound of horns.

an4.191:3.13.verse: They wouldn’t have any doubt about whether

an4.191:3.14.verse: that was the sound of horns or not.

an4.191:3.15.verse: They’d just conclude, ‘That’s the sound of horns.’

an4.191:3.16.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching …

an4.191:3.19.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods. …

an4.191:3.25.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:3.26.verse: This is the third benefit you can expect when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.

an4.191:4.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching—

an4.191:4.2.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

an4.191:4.3.verse: They’ve followed those teachings by ear, consolidated them by voice, examined them by the mind, and well penetrated them theoretically.

an4.191:4.4.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods.

an4.191:4.5.verse: But passages of the teaching don’t come back to them when they’re happy, and neither a mendicant with psychic powers … nor a godling teaches Dhamma to the assembly of gods.

an4.191:4.6.verse: But a being who has been reborn spontaneously reminds another such being:

an4.191:4.7.verse: ‘Do you remember, good fellow? Do you remember where we used to lead the spiritual life?’

an4.191:4.11.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:4.12.verse: Suppose there were two friends who had played together in the sand.

an4.191:4.13.verse: Some time or other they’d meet.

an4.191:4.14.verse: And one friend would say to the other:

an4.191:4.15.verse: ‘Do you remember this, my dear? Do you remember that, my dear?’

an4.191:4.18.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who memorizes the teaching …

an4.191:4.21.verse: But they die unmindful and are reborn in one of the orders of gods. …

an4.191:4.28.verse: but then that being quickly reaches distinction.

an4.191:4.29.verse: This is the fourth benefit you can expect when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.

an4.191:4.30.verse: You can expect these four benefits when the teachings have been followed by ear, consolidated by voice, examined by the mind, and well penetrated theoretically.”

an4.192:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four things can be known in four situations.

an4.192:1.3.verse: You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

an4.192:1.4.verse: You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …

an4.192:1.5.verse: You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …

an4.192:1.6.verse: You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

an4.192:2.1.verse: ‘You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.’

an4.192:2.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an4.192:2.3.verse: Take an individual who’s living with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:2.4.verse: ‘For a long time this venerable’s deeds have been broken, tainted, spotty, and marred. Their deeds and behavior are inconsistent.

an4.192:2.5.verse: This venerable is unethical, not ethical.’

an4.192:3.1.verse: Take another individual who’s living with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:3.2.verse: ‘For a long time this venerable’s deeds have been intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred. Their deeds and behavior are consistent.

an4.192:3.3.verse: This venerable is ethical, not unethical.’

an4.192:3.4.verse: That’s why I said that you can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not a short time; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

an4.192:4.1.verse: ‘You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …’

an4.192:4.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an4.192:4.3.verse: Take an individual who has dealings with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:4.4.verse: ‘This venerable deals with one person in one way. Then they deal with two, three, or many people each in different ways.

an4.192:4.5.verse: They’re not consistent from one deal to the next.

an4.192:4.6.verse: This venerable’s dealings are impure, not pure.’

an4.192:5.1.verse: Take another individual who has dealings with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:5.2.verse: ‘This venerable deals with one person in one way. Then they deal with two, three, or many people each in the same way.

an4.192:5.3.verse: They’re consistent from one deal to the next.

an4.192:5.4.verse: This venerable’s dealings are pure, not impure.’

an4.192:5.5.verse: That’s why I said that you can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …

an4.192:6.1.verse: ‘You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …’

an4.192:6.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an4.192:6.3.verse: Take someone who experiences loss of family, wealth, or health. But they don’t reflect:

an4.192:6.4.verse: ‘Worldly life is like that. Incarnation is like that. That’s why the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions:

an4.192:6.5.verse: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.’

an4.192:6.6.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.192:7.1.verse: Take someone else who experiences loss of family, wealth, or health. But they reflect:

an4.192:7.2.verse: ‘Worldly life is like that. Incarnation is like that. That’s why the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around the eight worldly conditions:

an4.192:7.3.verse: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.’

an4.192:7.4.verse: They don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an4.192:7.5.verse: That’s why I said that you can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …

an4.192:8.1.verse: ‘You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.’

an4.192:8.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an4.192:8.3.verse: Take an individual who is discussing with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:8.4.verse: ‘Judging by this venerable’s approach, by what they’re getting at, and by how they discuss a question, they’re witless, not wise.

an4.192:8.6.verse: This venerable does not bring up a deep and meaningful saying that is peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

an4.192:8.7.verse: When this venerable speaks on Dhamma they’re not able to explain the meaning, either briefly or in detail. They can’t teach it, assert it, establish it, clarify it, analyze it, or reveal it.

an4.192:8.8.verse: This venerable is witless, not wise.’

an4.192:9.1.verse: Suppose a person with clear eyes was standing on the bank of a lake. They’d see a little fish rising,

an4.192:9.3.verse: ‘Judging by this fish’s approach, by the ripples it makes, and by its force, it’s a little fish, not a big one.’

an4.192:9.4.verse: In the same way, an individual who is discussing with someone else would come to know:

an4.192:9.5.verse: ‘Judging by this venerable’s approach, by what they’re getting at, and by how they discuss a question, they’re witless, not wise. …’

an4.192:10.1.verse: Take another individual who is discussing with someone else. They come to know:

an4.192:10.2.verse: ‘Judging by this venerable’s approach, by what they’re getting at, and by how they discuss a question, they’re wise, not witless.

an4.192:10.4.verse: This venerable brings up a deep and meaningful saying that is peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

an4.192:10.5.verse: When this venerable speaks on Dhamma they’re able to explain the meaning, either briefly or in detail. They teach it, assert it, establish it, clarify it, analyze it, and reveal it.

an4.192:10.6.verse: This venerable is wise, not witless.’

an4.192:11.1.verse: Suppose a man with clear eyes was standing on the bank of a lake. He’d see a big fish rising,

an4.192:11.3.verse: ‘Judging by this fish’s approach, by the ripples it makes, and by its force, it’s a big fish, not a little one.’

an4.192:11.4.verse: In the same way, an individual who is discussing with someone else would come to know:

an4.192:11.5.verse: ‘Judging by this venerable’s approach, by what they’re getting at, and by how they articulate a question, they’re wise, not witless. …’

an4.192:12.1.verse: That’s why I said that you can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

an4.192:12.2.verse: These are the four things that can be known in four situations.”

an4.193:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an4.193:1.2.verse: Then Bhaddiya the Licchavi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an4.193:2.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is deceitful. He knows a conversion trick, and uses it to convert the disciples of those of other religions.’

an4.193:2.4.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the Buddha has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

an4.193:3.1.verse: “Please, Bhaddiya, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think ‘The ascetic is our respected teacher.’

an4.193:3.2.verse: But when you know for yourselves:

an4.193:3.3.verse: ‘These things are unskillful, blameworthy, criticized by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering’, then you should give them up.

an4.193:4.2.verse: Does greed come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an4.193:4.4.verse: “A greedy individual, overcome by greed, kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an4.193:5.2.verse: Does hate … or delusion … or aggression come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an4.193:5.4.verse: “An aggressive individual kills living creatures, steals, commits adultery, lies, and encourages others to do the same. Is that for their lasting harm and suffering?”

an4.193:6.1.verse: “What do you think, Bhaddiya, are these things skillful or unskillful?”

an4.193:6.7.verse: “When you undertake them, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?

an4.193:6.8.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an4.193:6.9.verse: “When you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering.

an4.193:7.2.verse: ‘Please, Bhaddiya, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think “The ascetic is our respected teacher.”

an4.193:7.3.verse: But when you know for yourselves:

an4.193:7.4.verse: “These things are unskillful, blameworthy, criticized by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to harm and suffering”, then you should give them up.’

an4.193:7.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an4.193:8.1.verse: Please, Bhaddiya, don’t rely on oral transmission …

an4.193:8.2.verse: But when you know for yourselves:

an4.193:8.3.verse: ‘These things are skillful, blameless, praised by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to welfare and happiness’, then you should acquire them and keep them.

an4.193:9.2.verse: Does contentment … love … understanding … benevolence come up in a person for their welfare or harm?”

an4.193:10.3.verse: “An individual who is benevolent—not overcome by aggression—doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit adultery, lie, or encourage others to do the same. Is that for their lasting welfare and happiness?”

an4.193:11.1.verse: “What do you think, Bhaddiya, are these things skillful or unskillful?”

an4.193:11.7.verse: “When you undertake them, do they lead to welfare and happiness, or not?

an4.193:11.8.verse: Or how do you see this?”

an4.193:11.9.verse: “When you undertake them, they lead to welfare and happiness.

an4.193:12.2.verse: ‘Please, Bhaddiya, don’t go by oral transmission, don’t go by lineage, don’t go by testament, don’t go by canonical authority, don’t rely on logic, don’t rely on inference, don’t go by reasoned train of thought, don’t go by the acceptance of a view after deliberation, don’t go by the appearance of competence, and don’t think “The ascetic is our respected teacher.”

an4.193:12.3.verse: But when you know for yourselves:

an4.193:12.4.verse: “These things are skillful, blameless, praised by sensible people, and when you undertake them, they lead to welfare and happiness”, then you should acquire them and keep them.’

an4.193:12.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an4.193:13.1.verse: The good and true persons in the world encourage their disciples:

an4.193:13.2.verse: ‘Please, my man, live rid of greed.

an4.193:13.3.verse: Then you won’t act out of greed by way of body, speech, or mind.

an4.193:13.4.verse: Live rid of hate … delusion … aggression.

an4.193:13.5.verse: Then you won’t act out of hate … delusion … aggression by way of body, speech, or mind.”

an4.193:14.1.verse: When he said this, Bhaddiya the Licchavi said to the Buddha,

an4.193:14.2.verse: “Excellent, sir! … From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an4.193:15.1.verse: “Well, Bhaddiya, did I say to you:

an4.193:15.3.verse: and I will be your teacher’?”

an4.193:15.5.verse: “Though I state and assert this, certain ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with the incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim:

an4.193:15.6.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is deceitful. He knows a conversion trick, and uses it to convert the disciples of those of other religions.’”

an4.193:15.9.verse: If my loved ones—relatives and kin—were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

an4.193:15.10.verse: If all the aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

an4.193:16.1.verse: “That’s so true, Bhaddiya! That’s so true, Bhaddiya!

an4.193:16.2.verse: If all the aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

an4.193:16.4.verse: If the whole world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—were to be converted by this, for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

an4.193:16.5.verse: If these great sal trees were to be converted by this, for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness—if they were sentient.

an4.193:16.6.verse: How much more then a human being!”

an4.194:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying in the land of the Koliyans, where they have a town named Sāpūga.

an4.194:1.2.verse: Then several Koliyans from Sāpūga went up to Ānanda, bowed, and sat down to one side. Then Venerable Ānanda said to them:

an4.194:2.1.verse: “Byagghapajjas, these four factors of trying to be pure have been rightly explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

an4.194:2.3.verse: The factors of trying to be pure in ethics, mind, view, and freedom.

an4.194:3.1.verse: And what is the factor of trying to be pure in ethics?

an4.194:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an4.194:3.3.verse: This is called purity of ethics.

an4.194:3.4.verse: They think: ‘I will fulfill such purity of ethics, or, if it’s already fulfilled, I’ll support it in every situation by wisdom.’ Their enthusiasm for that—their effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness—is called the factor of trying to be pure in ethics.

an4.194:4.1.verse: And what is the factor of trying to be pure in mind?

an4.194:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption … second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an4.194:4.3.verse: This is called purity of mind.

an4.194:4.4.verse: They think: ‘I will fulfill such purity of mind, or, if it’s already fulfilled, I’ll support it in every situation by wisdom.’ Their enthusiasm for that—their effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness—is called the factor of trying to be pure in mind.

an4.194:5.1.verse: And what is the factor of trying to be pure in view?

an4.194:5.2.verse: Take a mendicant who truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an4.194:5.3.verse: This is called purity of view.

an4.194:5.4.verse: They think: ‘I will fulfill such purity of view, or, if it’s already fulfilled, I’ll support it in every situation by wisdom.’ Their enthusiasm for that—their effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness—is called the factor of trying to be pure in view.

an4.194:6.1.verse: And what is the factor of trying to be pure in freedom?

an4.194:6.2.verse: That noble disciple—who has these factors of trying to be pure in ethics, mind, and view—detaches their mind from things that arouse greed, and frees their mind from things that it should be freed from.

an4.194:6.3.verse: Doing so, they experience perfect freedom.

an4.194:6.4.verse: This is called purity of freedom.

an4.194:6.5.verse: They think: ‘I will fulfill such purity of freedom, or, if it’s already fulfilled, I’ll support it in every situation by wisdom.’ Their enthusiasm for that—their effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness—is called the factor of trying to be pure in freedom.

an4.194:7.1.verse: These four factors of trying to be pure have been rightly explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.”

an4.195:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

an4.195:1.2.verse: Then Vappa of the Sakyans, a disciple of the Jains, went up to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, bowed, and sat down to one side. Mahāmoggallāna said to him:

an4.195:2.1.verse: “Vappa, take an individual who, due to the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, is restrained in body, speech, and mind.

an4.195:2.2.verse: Do you see any reason why defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life?”

an4.195:2.3.verse: “Sir, I do see such a case.

an4.195:2.4.verse: Take someone who did bad deeds in a past life. But the result of that has not yet ripened.

an4.195:2.5.verse: For this reason defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life.”

an4.195:2.6.verse: But this conversation between Mahāmoggallāna and Vappa was left unfinished.

an4.195:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out, and said to Mahāmoggallāna,

an4.195:4.1.verse: “Moggallāna, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

an4.195:4.2.verse: Moggallāna repeated the entire conversation to the Buddha, and concluded:

an4.195:4.9.verse: “This was my conversation with Vappa that was unfinished when the Buddha arrived.”

an4.195:5.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Vappa,

an4.195:5.2.verse: “Vappa, we can discuss this. But only if you grant what should be granted, and reject what should be rejected. And if you ask me the meaning of anything you don’t understand, saying:

an4.195:5.3.verse: ‘Sir, why is this? What’s the meaning of that?’”

an4.195:5.4.verse: “Sir, let us discuss this. I will do as you say.”

an4.195:6.2.verse: There are distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of instigating bodily activity. These don’t occur in someone who refrains from such bodily activity.

an4.195:6.3.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little. This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an4.195:6.4.verse: Do you see any reason why defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life?”

an4.195:7.2.verse: There are distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of instigating verbal activity. These don’t occur in someone who refrains from such verbal activity.

an4.195:7.3.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an4.195:7.4.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an4.195:7.5.verse: Do you see any reason why defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life?”

an4.195:8.2.verse: There are distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of instigating mental activity. These don’t occur in someone who refrains from such mental activity.

an4.195:8.3.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an4.195:8.4.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an4.195:8.5.verse: Do you see any reason why defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life?”

an4.195:9.2.verse: There are distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of ignorance. These don’t occur when ignorance fades away and knowledge arises.

an4.195:9.3.verse: They don’t perform any new deeds, and old deeds are eliminated by experiencing their results little by little.

an4.195:9.4.verse: This wearing away is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

an4.195:9.5.verse: Do you see any reason why defilements giving rise to painful feelings would defile that person in the next life?”

an4.195:10.1.verse: “A mendicant whose mind is rightly freed like this has achieved six consistent responses.

an4.195:10.2.verse: Seeing a sight with their eyes, they’re neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an4.195:10.3.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an4.195:10.4.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an4.195:10.5.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an4.195:10.6.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an4.195:10.7.verse: Knowing an idea with their mind, they’re neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an4.195:10.8.verse: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

an4.195:10.9.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’

an4.195:11.1.verse: Suppose there was a shadow cast by a post.

an4.195:11.2.verse: Then along comes a person with a spade and basket.

an4.195:11.3.verse: They cut down the post at its base,

an4.195:11.5.verse: and pull it out by its roots, right down to the fibers and stems.

an4.195:11.9.verse: Next they dry the splinters in the wind and sun,

an4.195:11.12.verse: Then they whisk away the ashes in a strong wind, or glide them down a swift stream.

an4.195:11.13.verse: And so the shadow cast by the post is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an4.195:12.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant whose mind is rightly freed like this has achieved six consistent responses.

an4.195:12.2.verse: Seeing a sight with their eyes, they’re neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an4.195:12.3.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an4.195:12.4.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an4.195:12.5.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an4.195:12.6.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an4.195:12.7.verse: Knowing an idea with their mind, they’re neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an4.195:12.8.verse: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

an4.195:12.9.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’”

an4.195:13.1.verse: When he said this, Vappa the Sakyan, the disciple of the Jains, said to the Buddha:

an4.195:13.2.verse: “Sir, suppose there was a man who raised commercial horses for profit.

an4.195:13.3.verse: But he never made any profit, and instead just got weary and frustrated.

an4.195:13.4.verse: In the same way, I paid homage to those Jain fools for profit.

an4.195:13.5.verse: But I never made any profit, and instead just got weary and frustrated.

an4.195:13.6.verse: From this day forth, any confidence I had in those Jain fools I whisk away as in a strong wind, or glide away as down a swift stream.

an4.195:13.7.verse: Excellent, sir! … From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an4.196:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an4.196:1.2.verse: Then Sāḷha and Abhaya the Licchavis went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an4.196:2.1.verse: “There are, sir, some ascetics and brahmins who advocate crossing the flood by means of two things:

an4.196:2.2.verse: purification of ethics, and mortification in disgust of sin.

an4.196:2.3.verse: What does the Buddha say about this?”

an4.196:3.1.verse: “Sāḷha, purification of ethics is one of the factors of the ascetic life, I say.

an4.196:3.2.verse: But those ascetics and brahmins who teach fervent mortification in disgust of sin—regarding it as essential and sticking to it—are incapable of crossing the flood.

an4.196:3.3.verse: And those ascetics and brahmins whose livelihood and behavior by way of body, speech, and mind, is not pure are also incapable of knowing and seeing, of supreme awakening.

an4.196:4.1.verse: Suppose a man who wanted to cross a river took a sharp axe into a wood.

an4.196:4.2.verse: There he’d see a large green sal tree, straight and young and grown unskewed.

an4.196:4.3.verse: He’d cut it down at the base,

an4.196:4.5.verse: and completely strip off the branches and foliage.

an4.196:4.6.verse: Then he’d trim it with axes and

an4.196:4.9.verse: and sand it with a rock.

an4.196:4.10.verse: Finally, he’d launch out on the river.

an4.196:5.2.verse: Is that man capable of crossing the river?”

an4.196:5.5.verse: Because that green sal tree is well worked on the outside, but inside it’s still not cleared out.

an4.196:5.6.verse: I’d expect that green sal tree to sink, and the man to come to ruin.”

an4.196:6.1.verse: “In the same way, Sāḷha, those ascetics and brahmins who teach fervent mortification in disgust of sin—regarding it as essential and sticking to it—are incapable of crossing the flood.

an4.196:6.2.verse: And those ascetics and brahmins whose livelihood and behavior by way of body, speech, and mind is not pure are also incapable of knowing and seeing, of supreme awakening.

an4.196:7.1.verse: But those ascetics and brahmins who don’t teach mortification in disgust of sin—not regarding it as essential or sticking to it—are capable of crossing the flood.

an4.196:7.2.verse: And those ascetics and brahmins whose behavior by way of body, speech, and mind is pure are also capable of knowing and seeing, of supreme awakening.

an4.196:8.1.verse: Suppose a man who wanted to cross a river took a sharp axe into a wood.

an4.196:8.2.verse: There he’d see a large green sal tree, straight and young and grown unskewed.

an4.196:8.3.verse: He’d cut it down at the base,

an4.196:8.5.verse: and completely strip off the branches and foliage.

an4.196:8.6.verse: Then he’d trim it with axes and

an4.196:8.8.verse: Then he’d take a chisel and completely clear it out inside.

an4.196:8.11.verse: and make it into a boat.

an4.196:8.12.verse: Finally he’d fix it with oars and rudder,

an4.196:8.13.verse: and launch out on the river.

an4.196:9.2.verse: Is that man capable of crossing the river?”

an4.196:9.5.verse: Because that green sal tree is well worked on the outside, cleared out on the inside, made into a boat, and fixed with oars and rudder.

an4.196:9.7.verse: that boat to not sink, and the man to safely make it to the far shore.”

an4.196:10.1.verse: “In the same way, Sāḷha, those ascetics and brahmins who don’t teach fervent mortification in disgust of sin—not regarding it as essential or sticking to it—are capable of crossing the flood.

an4.196:10.2.verse: And those ascetics and brahmins whose behavior by way of body, speech, and mind is pure are also capable of knowing and seeing, of supreme awakening.

an4.196:10.3.verse: Suppose there was a warrior who knew lots of fancy archery tricks.

an4.196:10.4.verse: It is only with these three factors that he becomes worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, and is reckoned a factor of kingship.

an4.196:10.6.verse: He’s a long-distance shooter, a marksman, and one who shatters large objects.

an4.196:11.1.verse: Just as a warrior is a long-distance shooter,

an4.196:11.2.verse: a noble disciple has right immersion.

an4.196:11.3.verse: A noble disciple with right immersion truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

an4.196:11.4.verse: They truly see any kind of feeling …

an4.196:11.7.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

an4.196:12.1.verse: Just as a warrior is a marksman,

an4.196:12.2.verse: a noble disciple has right view.

an4.196:12.3.verse: A noble disciple with right view truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an4.196:13.1.verse: Just as a warrior shatters large objects,

an4.196:13.2.verse: a noble disciple has right freedom.

an4.196:13.3.verse: A noble disciple with right freedom shatters the great mass of ignorance.”

an4.197:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an4.197:1.2.verse: Then Queen Mallikā went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an4.197:2.1.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why in this life some ladies are ugly, unattractive, and bad-looking;

an4.197:2.2.verse: and poor, with few assets and possessions; and insignificant?

an4.197:3.1.verse: And why are some ladies ugly, unattractive, and bad-looking;

an4.197:3.2.verse: but rich, affluent, wealthy, and illustrious?

an4.197:4.1.verse: And why are some ladies attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty;

an4.197:4.2.verse: but poor, with few assets and possessions; and insignificant?

an4.197:5.1.verse: And why are some ladies attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty; and rich, affluent, wealthy, and illustrious?”

an4.197:6.1.verse: “Take a lady who is irritable and bad-tempered.

an4.197:6.2.verse: Even when criticized a little bit she loses her temper, becoming annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, and displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

an4.197:6.3.verse: She doesn’t give to ascetics or brahmins such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting.

an4.197:6.5.verse: envying, resenting, and begrudging the possessions, honor, respect, reverence, homage, and veneration given to others.

an4.197:6.6.verse: If she comes back to this place after passing away, wherever she is reborn she’s ugly, unattractive, and bad-looking;

an4.197:6.7.verse: and poor, with few assets and possessions; and insignificant.

an4.197:7.1.verse: Take another lady who is irritable and bad-tempered. …

an4.197:7.3.verse: But she does give to ascetics or brahmins …

an4.197:7.6.verse: If she comes back to this place after passing away, wherever she is reborn she’s ugly, unattractive, and bad-looking;

an4.197:7.7.verse: but rich, affluent, wealthy, and illustrious.

an4.197:8.1.verse: Take another lady who isn’t irritable and bad-tempered. …

an4.197:8.3.verse: But she doesn’t give to ascetics or brahmins …

an4.197:8.6.verse: If she comes back to this place after passing away, wherever she is reborn she’s attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty;

an4.197:8.7.verse: but poor, with few assets and possessions; and insignificant.

an4.197:9.1.verse: Take another lady who isn’t irritable and bad-tempered. …

an4.197:9.3.verse: She gives to ascetics and brahmins …

an4.197:9.6.verse: If she comes back to this place after passing away, wherever she is reborn she’s attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty;

an4.197:9.7.verse: and rich, affluent, wealthy, and illustrious.

an4.197:10.1.verse: This is why some ladies are ugly …

an4.197:11.1.verse: When this was said, Queen Mallikā said to the Buddha:

an4.197:11.2.verse: “Sir, in another life I must have been irritable and bad-tempered.

an4.197:11.3.verse: Even when lightly criticized I must have lost my temper, becoming annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, and displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

an4.197:11.4.verse: For now I am ugly, unattractive, and bad-looking.

an4.197:12.1.verse: In another life I must have given to ascetics or brahmins such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting. For now I am rich, affluent, and wealthy.

an4.197:13.1.verse: In another life, I must not have been jealous, envying, resenting, and begrudging the possessions, honor, respect, reverence, homage, and veneration given to others. For now I am illustrious.

an4.197:13.2.verse: In this royal court I command maidens of the aristocrats, brahmins, and householders.

an4.197:13.3.verse: So, sir, from this day forth I will not be irritable and bad-tempered.

an4.197:13.4.verse: Even when heavily criticized I won’t lose my temper, become annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, or display annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

an4.197:13.5.verse: I will give to ascetics or brahmins such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting.

an4.197:13.6.verse: I will not be jealous, envying, resenting, and begrudging the possessions, honor, respect, reverence, homage, and veneration given to others.

an4.197:13.7.verse: Excellent, sir! … From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an4.198:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four individuals are found in the world.

an4.198:1.3.verse: One individual mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves.

an4.198:1.4.verse: One individual mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others.

an4.198:1.5.verse: One individual mortifies themselves and others, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves and others.

an4.198:1.6.verse: One individual neither mortifies themselves nor others, pursuing the practice of not mortifying themselves or others.

an4.198:1.7.verse: They live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.

an4.198:2.1.verse: And how does one individual mortify themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves?

an4.198:2.2.verse: It’s when someone goes naked, ignoring conventions. They lick their hands, and don’t come or wait when called. They don’t consent to food brought to them, or food prepared on their behalf, or an invitation for a meal.

an4.198:2.3.verse: They don’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or who lives with a man; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. They accept no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drink no fermented gruel.

an4.198:2.4.verse: They go to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls.

an4.198:2.5.verse: They feed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

an4.198:2.6.verse: They eat once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. They live pursuing the practice of eating food at set intervals.

an4.198:3.1.verse: They eat herbs, millet, wild rice, poor rice, water lettuce, rice bran, scum from boiling rice, sesame flour, grass, or cow dung. They survive on forest roots and fruits, or eating fallen fruit.

an4.198:4.1.verse: They wear robes of sunn hemp, mixed hemp, corpse-wrapping cloth, rags, lodh tree bark, antelope hide (whole or in strips), kusa grass, bark, wood-chips, human hair, horse-tail hair, or owls’ wings.

an4.198:4.2.verse: They tear out hair and beard, pursuing this practice.

an4.198:4.3.verse: They constantly stand, turning down seats.

an4.198:4.4.verse: They squat, committed to the endeavor of squatting.

an4.198:4.5.verse: They lie on a mat of thorns, making a mat of thorns their bed.

an4.198:4.6.verse: They’re devoted to ritual bathing three times a day, including at dusk.

an4.198:4.7.verse: And so they live pursuing these various ways of mortifying and tormenting the body.

an4.198:4.8.verse: That’s how one individual mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves.

an4.198:5.1.verse: And how does one individual mortify others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others?

an4.198:5.2.verse: It’s when an individual is a slaughterer of sheep, pigs, poultry, or deer, a hunter or fisher, a bandit, an executioner, a butcher of cattle, a jailer, or has some other cruel livelihood.

an4.198:5.3.verse: That’s how one individual mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others.

an4.198:6.1.verse: And how does one individual mortify themselves and others, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves and others?

an4.198:6.2.verse: It’s when an individual is an anointed aristocratic king or a well-to-do brahmin.

an4.198:6.3.verse: He has a new ceremonial hall built to the east of the citadel. He shaves off his hair and beard, dresses in a rough antelope hide, and smears his body with ghee and oil. Scratching his back with antlers, he enters the hall with his chief queen and the brahmin high priest.

an4.198:6.4.verse: There he lies on the bare ground strewn with grass.

an4.198:6.5.verse: The king feeds on the milk from one teat of a cow that has a calf of the same color. The chief queen feeds on the milk from the second teat. The brahmin high priest feeds on the milk from the third teat. The milk from the fourth teat is served to the sacred flame. The calf feeds on the leftovers.

an4.198:6.7.verse: ‘Slaughter this many bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats, rams, and horses for the sacrifice! Fell this many trees and reap this much grass for the sacrificial equipment!’

an4.198:6.8.verse: His bondservants, servants, and workers do their jobs under threat of punishment and danger, weeping, with tearful faces.

an4.198:6.9.verse: That’s how one individual mortifies themselves and others, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves and others.

an4.198:7.1.verse: And how does one individual neither mortify themselves nor others, pursuing the practice of not mortifying themselves or others,

an4.198:7.2.verse: living without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine?

an4.198:7.3.verse: It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

an4.198:7.4.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

an4.198:7.5.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

an4.198:7.6.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

an4.198:7.7.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One

an4.198:7.9.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

an4.198:7.10.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

an4.198:7.11.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

an4.198:7.12.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

an4.198:8.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

an4.198:8.2.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

an4.198:8.3.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

an4.198:8.4.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

an4.198:8.5.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

an4.198:8.6.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, likable, and agreeable to the people.

an4.198:8.7.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

an4.198:9.1.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

an4.198:9.2.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

an4.198:9.3.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

an4.198:9.4.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

an4.198:9.5.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

an4.198:9.6.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

an4.198:9.15.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

an4.198:9.19.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

an4.198:10.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

an4.198:10.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

an4.198:10.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

an4.198:10.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

an4.198:11.1.verse: Seeing a sight with the eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.198:11.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

an4.198:11.3.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an4.198:11.4.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an4.198:11.5.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an4.198:11.6.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an4.198:11.7.verse: Knowing an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

an4.198:11.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

an4.198:11.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

an4.198:12.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

an4.198:13.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

an4.198:13.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

an4.198:13.3.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

an4.198:13.4.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

an4.198:13.5.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

an4.198:13.6.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

an4.198:13.7.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

an4.198:13.8.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

an4.198:13.9.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

an4.198:13.10.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption … second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an4.198:14.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives …

an4.198:14.2.verse: knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings …

an4.198:14.3.verse: knowledge of the ending of defilements.

an4.198:14.4.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an4.198:14.5.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

an4.198:15.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an4.198:15.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

an4.198:15.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

an4.198:15.4.verse: That’s how one individual neither mortifies themselves nor others, pursuing the practice of not mortifying themselves or others,

an4.198:15.5.verse: living without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.

an4.198:15.6.verse: These are the four individuals found in the world.”

an4.199:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you about craving—the weaver, the migrant, the creeping, the clinging. This world is choked by it, enveloped by it. It makes the world tangled like yarn, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, not escaping the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.

an4.199:1.3.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an4.199:2.2.verse: There are eighteen currents of craving that derive from the interior, and eighteen that derive from the exterior.

an4.199:3.1.verse: What are the eighteen currents of craving that derive from the interior?

an4.199:3.2.verse: When there is the concept ‘I am’, there are the concepts ‘I am such’, ‘I am thus’, ‘I am otherwise’; ‘I am fleeting’, ‘I am lasting’; ‘mine’, ‘such is mine’, ‘thus is mine’, ‘otherwise is mine’; ‘also mine’, ‘such is also mine’, ‘thus is also mine’, ‘otherwise is also mine’; ‘I will be’, ‘I will be such’, ‘I will be thus’, ‘I will be otherwise’.

an4.199:3.3.verse: These are the eighteen currents of craving that derive from the interior.

an4.199:4.1.verse: What are the eighteen currents of craving that derive from the exterior?

an4.199:4.2.verse: When there is the concept ‘I am because of this’, there are the concepts ‘I am such because of this’, ‘I am thus because of this’, ‘I am otherwise because of this’; ‘I am fleeting because of this’, ‘I am lasting because of this’; ‘mine because of this’, ‘such is mine because of this’, ‘thus is mine because of this’, ‘otherwise is mine because of this’; ‘also mine because of this’, ‘such is also mine because of this’, ‘thus is also mine because of this’, ‘otherwise is also mine because of this’; ‘I will be because of this’, ‘I will be such because of this’, ‘I will be thus because of this’, ‘I will be otherwise because of this’.

an4.199:4.3.verse: These are the eighteen currents of craving that derive from the exterior.

an4.199:5.1.verse: So there are eighteen currents of craving that derive from the interior, and eighteen that derive from the exterior.

an4.199:5.2.verse: These are called the thirty-six currents of craving.

an4.199:5.3.verse: Each of these pertain to the past, future, and present,

an4.199:5.4.verse: making one hundred and eight currents of craving.

an4.199:6.1.verse: This is that craving—the weaver, the migrant, the creeping, the clinging. This world is choked by it, enveloped by it. It makes the world tangled like yarn, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, not escaping the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.”

an4.200:1.5.verse: fondness is born of hate, and

an4.200:2.1.verse: And how is fondness born of fondness?

an4.200:2.2.verse: It’s when someone likes, loves, and cares for an individual.

an4.200:2.3.verse: Others treat them with liking, love, and care.

an4.200:2.5.verse: ‘These others like the individual I like.’

an4.200:2.6.verse: And so fondness for them springs up.

an4.200:2.7.verse: That’s how fondness is born of fondness.

an4.200:3.1.verse: And how is hate born of fondness?

an4.200:3.2.verse: It’s when someone likes, loves, and cares for an individual.

an4.200:3.3.verse: Others treat them with disliking, loathing, and detestation.

an4.200:3.5.verse: ‘These others dislike the individual I like.’

an4.200:3.6.verse: And so hate for them springs up.

an4.200:3.7.verse: That’s how hate is born of fondness.

an4.200:4.1.verse: And how is fondness born of hate?

an4.200:4.2.verse: It’s when someone dislikes, loathes, and detests an individual.

an4.200:4.3.verse: Others treat them with disliking, loathing, and detestation.

an4.200:4.5.verse: ‘These others dislike the individual I dislike.’

an4.200:4.6.verse: And so fondness for them springs up.

an4.200:4.7.verse: That’s how fondness is born of hate.

an4.200:5.1.verse: And how is hate born of hate?

an4.200:5.2.verse: It’s when someone dislikes, loathes, and detests an individual.

an4.200:5.3.verse: Others treat them with liking, love, and care.

an4.200:5.5.verse: ‘These others like the individual I dislike.’

an4.200:5.6.verse: And so hate for them springs up.

an4.200:5.7.verse: That’s how hate is born of hate.

an4.200:5.8.verse: These are the four things that are born.

an4.200:6.1.verse: A time comes when a mendicant … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an4.200:6.2.verse: At that time they have no fondness born of fondness, hate born of fondness, fondness born of hate, or hate born of hate.

an4.200:7.1.verse: A time comes when a mendicant … enters and remains in the second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.

an4.200:7.2.verse: At that time they have no fondness born of fondness, hate born of fondness, fondness born of hate, or hate born of hate.

an4.200:8.1.verse: A time comes when a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an4.200:8.2.verse: At that time any fondness born of fondness, hate born of fondness, fondness born of hate, or hate born of hate is given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an4.200:8.3.verse: This is called a mendicant who doesn’t draw close or push back or fume or ignite or burn up.

an4.200:9.1.verse: And how does a mendicant draw close?

an4.200:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant regards form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

an4.200:9.3.verse: They regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

an4.200:9.4.verse: They regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

an4.200:9.5.verse: They regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

an4.200:9.6.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

an4.200:9.7.verse: That’s how a mendicant draws close.

an4.200:10.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not draw close?

an4.200:10.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

an4.200:10.3.verse: They don’t regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

an4.200:10.4.verse: They don’t regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

an4.200:10.5.verse: They don’t regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

an4.200:10.6.verse: They don’t regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

an4.200:10.7.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t draw close.
