an5.26:4.5.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.

an5.26:4.6.verse: When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss.

an5.26:4.7.verse: And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

an5.26:4.8.verse: This is the third opportunity for freedom. …

an5.26:5.1.verse: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor … the mendicant teaches Dhamma … nor does the mendicant rehearse the teaching.

an5.26:5.2.verse: But the mendicant thinks about and considers the teaching in their heart, examining it with the mind as they learned and memorized it.

an5.26:5.3.verse: In whatever way that mendicant thinks about and considers the teaching in their heart, examining it with the mind as they learned and memorized it, they always feel inspired by the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma.

an5.26:5.6.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.

an5.26:5.7.verse: When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss.

an5.26:5.8.verse: And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

an5.26:5.9.verse: This is the fourth opportunity for freedom. …

an5.26:6.1.verse: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor … the mendicant teaches Dhamma … nor does the mendicant rehearse the teaching … or think about it.

an5.26:6.2.verse: But a meditation subject as a basis of immersion is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom.

an5.26:6.3.verse: In whatever way a mendicant’s meditation subject as a basis of immersion is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom, they always feel inspired by the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma.

an5.26:6.6.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.

an5.26:6.7.verse: When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss.

an5.26:6.8.verse: And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

an5.26:6.9.verse: This is the fifth opportunity for freedom. …

an5.26:7.1.verse: These are the five opportunities for freedom. If a mendicant stays diligent, keen, and resolute at these times, their mind is freed, their defilements are ended, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.”

an5.27:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, develop limitless immersion, alert and mindful.

an5.27:1.2.verse: When you develop limitless immersion, alert and mindful, five knowledges arise for you personally.

an5.27:1.4.verse: ‘This immersion is blissful now, and results in bliss in the future.’ …

an5.27:1.5.verse: ‘This immersion is noble and not of the flesh.’ …

an5.27:1.6.verse: ‘This immersion is not cultivated by reprobates.’ …

an5.27:1.7.verse: ‘This immersion is peaceful and sublime and tranquil and unified, not held in place by forceful suppression.’ …

an5.27:1.8.verse: ‘I mindfully enter into and emerge from this immersion.’ …

an5.27:2.1.verse: Develop limitless immersion, alert and mindful.

an5.27:2.2.verse: When you develop limitless immersion, alert and mindful, these five knowledges arise for you personally.”

an5.28:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you how to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an5.28:2.1.verse: “And how do you develop noble right immersion with five factors?

an5.28:2.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an5.28:2.3.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

an5.28:2.4.verse: It’s like when a deft bathroom attendant or their apprentice pours bath powder into a bronze dish, sprinkling it little by little with water. They knead it until the ball of bath powder is soaked and saturated with moisture, spread through inside and out; yet no moisture oozes out.

an5.28:2.5.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

an5.28:2.6.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

an5.28:2.7.verse: This is the first way to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:3.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an5.28:3.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

an5.28:3.3.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

an5.28:3.4.verse: It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time.

an5.28:3.5.verse: But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.

an5.28:3.6.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

an5.28:3.7.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

an5.28:3.8.verse: This is the second way to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:4.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption. They meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

an5.28:4.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture.

an5.28:4.3.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

an5.28:4.4.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater.

an5.28:4.5.verse: From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water.

an5.28:4.6.verse: There’s no part of them that’s not spread through with cool water.

an5.28:4.7.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture.

an5.28:4.8.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

an5.28:4.9.verse: This is the third way to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:5.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption. It is without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an5.28:5.2.verse: They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind.

an5.28:5.3.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

an5.28:5.4.verse: It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth.

an5.28:5.5.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.

an5.28:5.6.verse: In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind.

an5.28:5.7.verse: There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

an5.28:5.8.verse: This is the fourth way to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:6.1.verse: Furthermore, the meditation that is a basis for reviewing is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom by a mendicant.

an5.28:6.2.verse: It’s like when someone views someone else. Someone standing might view someone sitting, or someone sitting might view someone lying down.

an5.28:6.3.verse: In the same way, the meditation that is a basis for reviewing is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom by a mendicant.

an5.28:6.4.verse: This is the fifth way to develop noble right immersion with five factors.

an5.28:7.1.verse: When the noble right immersion with five factors is developed and cultivated in this way, a mendicant extends the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:8.1.verse: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

an5.28:8.2.verse: If a strong man was to tip it any which way, would water pour out?”

an5.28:8.4.verse: “In the same way, when noble right immersion with five factors is developed and cultivated in this way, a mendicant extends the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:9.1.verse: Suppose there was a square, walled lotus pond on level ground, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

an5.28:9.2.verse: If a strong man was to open the wall on any side, would water pour out?”

an5.28:9.4.verse: “In the same way, when noble right immersion with five factors is developed and cultivated in this way, a mendicant extends the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:10.1.verse: Suppose a chariot stood harnessed to thoroughbreds at a level crossroads, with a goad ready.

an5.28:10.2.verse: A deft horse trainer, a master charioteer, might mount the chariot, taking the reins in his right hand and goad in the left. He’d drive out and back wherever he wishes, whenever he wishes.

an5.28:10.3.verse: In the same way, when noble right immersion with five factors is developed and cultivated in this way,

an5.28:10.4.verse: a mendicant extends the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:11.1.verse: If you wish: ‘May I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.’

an5.28:11.2.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:12.1.verse: If you wish: ‘With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, may I hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.’

an5.28:12.2.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:13.1.verse: If you wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my mind.

an5.28:13.2.verse: May I understand mind with greed as “mind with greed”,

an5.28:13.3.verse: and mind without greed as “mind without greed”;

an5.28:13.4.verse: mind with hate as “mind with hate”,

an5.28:13.5.verse: and mind without hate as “mind without hate”;

an5.28:13.6.verse: mind with delusion as “mind with delusion”,

an5.28:13.7.verse: and mind without delusion as “mind without delusion”;

an5.28:13.12.verse: mind that is not supreme as “mind that is not supreme”,

an5.28:13.13.verse: and mind that is supreme as “mind that is supreme”;

an5.28:13.14.verse: mind immersed in samādhi as “mind immersed in samādhi”,

an5.28:13.15.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as “mind not immersed in samādhi”;

an5.28:13.18.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:14.1.verse: If you wish: ‘May I recollect many kinds of past lives, with features and details.’

an5.28:14.2.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:15.1.verse: If you wish: ‘With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, may I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn according to their deeds.’

an5.28:15.2.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.

an5.28:16.1.verse: If you wish: ‘May I realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

an5.28:16.2.verse: You’re capable of realizing it, since each and every one is within range.”

an5.29:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are five benefits of walking meditation.

an5.29:1.3.verse: You get fit for traveling, fit for striving in meditation, and healthy. What’s eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested. And immersion gained while walking lasts long.

an5.29:1.4.verse: These are the five benefits of walking meditation.”

an5.30:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Icchānaṅgala.

an5.30:1.3.verse: He stayed in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

an5.30:1.4.verse: The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:

an5.30:1.5.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Icchānaṅgala. He is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

an5.30:1.7.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an5.30:1.8.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

an5.30:1.9.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

an5.30:1.10.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

an5.30:1.11.verse: Then, when the night had passed, they took abundant fresh and cooked foods and went to the forest near Icchānaṅgala, where they stood outside the gates making a colossal racket.

an5.30:2.1.verse: Now, at that time Venerable Nāgita was the Buddha’s attendant.

an5.30:2.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to Nāgita,

an5.30:2.3.verse: “Nāgita, who’s making that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

an5.30:2.4.verse: “Sir, it’s these brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala. They’ve brought many fresh and cooked foods, and they’re standing outside the gates wanting to offer it specially to the Buddha and the mendicant Saṅgha.”

an5.30:2.5.verse: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

an5.30:2.6.verse: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an5.30:2.7.verse: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.”

an5.30:3.1.verse: “Sir, may the Blessed One please relent now! May the Holy One relent!

an5.30:3.2.verse: Now is the time for the Buddha to relent.

an5.30:3.3.verse: Wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.

an5.30:3.4.verse: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily and the water flows downhill.

an5.30:3.5.verse: In the same way, wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.

an5.30:3.7.verse: Because of the Buddha’s ethics and wisdom.”

an5.30:4.1.verse: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

an5.30:4.2.verse: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an5.30:4.3.verse: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.

an5.30:4.4.verse: What you eat, drink, chew, and taste ends up as excrement and urine.

an5.30:4.6.verse: When loved ones decay and perish, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.

an5.30:4.8.verse: When you pursue meditation on the feature of ugliness, revulsion at the feature of beauty becomes stabilized.

an5.30:4.10.verse: When you meditate observing impermanence in the six fields of contact, revulsion at contact becomes stabilized.

an5.30:4.12.verse: When you meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates, revulsion at grasping becomes stabilized.

an5.31:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.31:1.2.verse: Then Princess Sumanā, escorted by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal maidens, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an5.31:2.1.verse: “Sir, suppose there were two disciples equal in faith, ethics, and wisdom.

an5.31:2.2.verse: One is a giver, one is not.

an5.31:2.3.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an5.31:2.4.verse: When they have become gods, would there be any distinction or difference between them?”

an5.31:3.1.verse: “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

an5.31:3.2.verse: “As a god, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects:

an5.31:3.3.verse: heavenly lifespan, beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty.

an5.31:3.4.verse: As a god, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

an5.31:4.1.verse: “But sir, if they pass away from there and come back to this place as human beings, would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”

an5.31:4.2.verse: “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

an5.31:4.3.verse: “As a human being, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects:

an5.31:4.4.verse: human lifespan, beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty.

an5.31:4.5.verse: As a human being, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

an5.31:5.1.verse: “But sir, if they both go forth from the lay life to homelessness, would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”

an5.31:5.2.verse: “There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

an5.31:5.3.verse: “As a renunciate, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects.

an5.31:5.4.verse: They usually use only what they’ve been invited to accept—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—rarely using them without invitation.

an5.31:5.5.verse: When living with other spiritual practitioners, they usually find themselves treated agreeably by them by way of body, speech, and mind, and rarely disagreeably. And they are usually presented with agreeable things by them, rarely with disagreeable ones.

an5.31:5.6.verse: As a renunciate, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

an5.31:6.1.verse: “But sir, if they both attain perfection, as perfected ones would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”

an5.31:6.2.verse: “In that case, I say there is no difference between the freedom of one and the freedom of the other.”

an5.31:7.2.verse: This is quite enough to justify giving gifts and making merit.

an5.31:7.3.verse: For merit is helpful for those who have become gods, human beings, and renunciates.”

an5.31:7.5.verse: It’s quite enough to justify giving gifts and making merit.

an5.31:7.6.verse: For merit is helpful for those who have become gods, human beings, and renunciates.”

an5.31:8.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an5.31:8.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

an5.31:9.2.verse: journeying across the dimension of space;

an5.31:11.2.verse: its hundred peaks wreathed in lightning,

an5.31:11.3.verse: pours down over the rich earth,

an5.31:12.1.verse: Even so, an astute person accomplished in vision,

an5.31:12.2.verse: a disciple of the fully awakened Buddha,

an5.31:13.4.verse: they depart to rejoice in heaven.”

an5.32:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

an5.32:1.2.verse: Then Princess Cundī, escorted by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal maidens, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an5.32:2.1.verse: “Sir, my brother, Prince Cunda, says this:

an5.32:2.2.verse: ‘Take a woman or man who goes for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. Only then do they get reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when their body breaks up, after death.’

an5.32:2.3.verse: And so I ask the Buddha:

an5.32:2.4.verse: Sir, what kind of teacher should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

an5.32:2.5.verse: Sir, what kind of teaching should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

an5.32:2.6.verse: Sir, what kind of Saṅgha should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

an5.32:2.7.verse: Sir, what kind of ethics should you fulfill so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?”

an5.32:3.1.verse: “Cundī, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is said to be the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception or with neither perception nor non-perception.

an5.32:3.2.verse: Those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the best.

an5.32:3.3.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an5.32:4.1.verse: The noble eightfold path is said to be the best of all conditioned things.

an5.32:4.2.verse: Those who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in the best. Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an5.32:5.1.verse: Fading away is said to be the best of all things whether conditioned or unconditioned.

an5.32:5.2.verse: That is, the quelling of vanity, the removing of thirst, the uprooting of clinging, the breaking of the round, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

an5.32:5.3.verse: Those who have confidence in the teaching of fading away have confidence in the best.

an5.32:5.4.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an5.32:6.1.verse: The Saṅgha of the Realized One’s disciples is said to be the best of all communities and groups.

an5.32:6.2.verse: It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an5.32:6.3.verse: Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the best.

an5.32:6.4.verse: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

an5.32:7.1.verse: The ethical conduct loved by the noble ones is said to be the best of all ethics.

an5.32:7.2.verse: It is intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

an5.32:7.3.verse: Those who fulfill the ethics loved by the noble ones fulfill the best.

an5.32:7.4.verse: Fulfilling the best, the result is the best.

an5.32:8.1.verse: For those who, knowing the best teaching,

an5.32:8.2.verse: base their confidence on the best—

an5.32:8.3.verse: confident in the best Awakened One,

an5.32:8.4.verse: supremely worthy of a religious donation;

an5.32:9.2.verse: the bliss of fading and stilling;

an5.32:11.1.verse: An intelligent person gives to the best,

an5.32:11.3.verse: When they become a god or human,

an5.32:11.4.verse: they rejoice at reaching the best.”

an5.33:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Bhaddiya in Jātiyā Wood.

an5.33:1.2.verse: Then Uggaha, Meṇḍaka’s grandson, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an5.33:2.1.verse: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with three other monks, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

an5.33:2.3.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Uggaha rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an5.33:3.1.verse: Then when the night had passed, the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Uggaha’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an5.33:3.2.verse: Then Uggaha served and satisfied the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

an5.33:3.3.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Uggaha sat down to one side,

an5.33:3.5.verse: “Sir, these girls of mine will be going to their husbands’ families.

an5.33:3.7.verse: and instruct them. It will be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

an5.33:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to those girls:

an5.33:4.2.verse: “So, girls, you should train like this:

an5.33:4.3.verse: ‘Our parents will give us to a husband wanting what’s best, out of kindness and sympathy. We will get up before him and go to bed after him, and be obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.’

an5.33:5.1.verse: So, girls, you should train like this:

an5.33:5.2.verse: ‘Those our husband respects—mother and father, ascetics and brahmins—we will honor, respect, revere, and venerate, and serve with a seat and a drink when they come as guests.’

an5.33:6.1.verse: So, girls, you should train like this:

an5.33:6.2.verse: ‘We will be deft and tireless in doing domestic duties for our husband, such as knitting and sewing. We will have an understanding of how to go about things in order to complete and organize the work.’

an5.33:7.1.verse: So, girls, you should train like this:

an5.33:7.2.verse: ‘We will know what work our husband’s domestic bondservants, servants, and workers have completed, and what they’ve left incomplete. We will know who is sick, and who is fit or unwell. We will distribute to each a fair portion of fresh and cooked foods.’

an5.33:8.1.verse: So, girls, you should train like this:

an5.33:8.2.verse: ‘We will ensure that any income our husbands earn is guarded and protected, whether money, grain, silver, or gold. We will not overspend, steal, waste, or lose it.’

an5.33:8.4.verse: When they possess these five qualities, ladies—when their body breaks up, after death—are reborn in company with the Gods of the Agreeable Host.

an5.33:9.1.verse: She’d never look down on her husband,

an5.33:9.2.verse: who’s always eager to work hard,

an5.33:10.1.verse: And a good woman never scolds her husband

an5.33:11.1.verse: She gets up early, works tirelessly,

an5.33:12.1.verse: A lady who fulfills these duties

an5.34:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an5.34:1.2.verse: Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and asked him,

an5.34:1.3.verse: “Sir, can you point out a fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life?”

an5.34:2.2.verse: “A giver, a donor is dear and beloved to many people.

an5.34:2.3.verse: This is a fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

an5.34:3.1.verse: Furthermore, good and true persons associate with a giver.

an5.34:3.2.verse: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

an5.34:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a giver gains a good reputation.

an5.34:4.2.verse: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

an5.34:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a giver enters any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

an5.34:5.2.verse: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

an5.34:6.1.verse: Furthermore, when a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an5.34:6.2.verse: This is a fruit of giving to do with lives to come.”

an5.34:7.1.verse: When he said this, General Sīha said to the Buddha,

an5.34:7.2.verse: “When it comes to those four fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha, for I know them too.

an5.34:7.3.verse: I’m a giver, a donor, and am dear and beloved to many people.

an5.34:7.4.verse: I’m a giver, and good and true persons associate with me.

an5.34:7.5.verse: I’m a giver, and I have this good reputation: ‘General Sīha gives, serves, and attends on the Saṅgha.’

an5.34:7.6.verse: I’m a giver, and I enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

an5.34:7.7.verse: When it comes to these four fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha, for I know them too.

an5.34:7.9.verse: ‘When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ I don’t know this, so I have to rely on faith in the Buddha.”

an5.34:7.10.verse: “That’s so true, Sīha! That’s so true!

an5.34:7.11.verse: When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an5.34:8.1.verse: Giving, you’re loved and befriended by many people.

an5.34:8.2.verse: You get a good reputation, and your fame grows.

an5.34:8.3.verse: A generous man enters an assembly

an5.34:9.1.verse: So an astute person, seeking happiness, would give gifts,

an5.34:9.2.verse: having driven out the stain of stinginess.

an5.34:9.3.verse: They live long in the Third Heaven,

an5.34:9.4.verse: enjoying the company of the gods.

an5.34:10.1.verse: Having taken the opportunity to do good, when they pass from here

an5.34:10.2.verse: they wander self-radiant in the Garden of Delight.

an5.34:10.3.verse: There they delight, rejoice, and enjoy themselves,

an5.34:10.4.verse: provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

an5.34:10.5.verse: Having practiced the word of the unattached, the unaffected,

an5.34:10.6.verse: disciples of the Holy One rejoice in heaven.”

an5.35:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are five benefits of giving.

an5.35:1.3.verse: A giver, a donor is dear and beloved by many people.

an5.35:1.4.verse: Good and true persons associate with them.

an5.35:1.6.verse: They don’t neglect a layperson’s duties.

an5.35:1.7.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an5.35:1.8.verse: These are the five benefits of giving.

an5.35:2.2.verse: and follows the way of the good.

an5.35:3.4.verse: the undefiled one is fully extinguished.”

an5.36:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five timely gifts.

an5.36:1.4.verse: A gift to someone setting out on a journey.

an5.36:1.5.verse: A gift to someone who is sick.

an5.36:1.6.verse: A gift at a time of famine.

an5.36:1.7.verse: Presenting the freshly harvested grains and fruits first to those who are ethical.

an5.36:1.8.verse: These are the five timely gifts.

an5.36:2.1.verse: The wise give at the right time,

an5.36:2.2.verse: being bountiful and rid of stinginess.

an5.36:2.3.verse: A religious donation at the right time

an5.36:2.4.verse: to the noble ones, upright and unaffected,

an5.36:3.1.verse: given with a clear and confident mind,

an5.36:3.5.verse: don’t miss out on the offering;

an5.36:3.6.verse: they too have a share in the merit.

an5.36:4.1.verse: So you should give without holding back,

an5.36:4.2.verse: where a gift is very fruitful.

an5.36:4.3.verse: The good deeds of sentient beings

an5.36:4.4.verse: support them in the next world.”

an5.37:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a giver gives food, they give the recipients five things.

an5.37:1.3.verse: Long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and eloquence.

an5.37:1.4.verse: Giving long life, they have long life as a god or human.

an5.37:1.5.verse: Giving beauty, they have beauty as a god or human.

an5.37:1.6.verse: Giving happiness, they have happiness as a god or human.

an5.37:1.7.verse: Giving strength, they have strength as a god or human.

an5.37:1.8.verse: Giving eloquence, they are eloquent as a god or human.

an5.37:1.9.verse: When a giver gives food, they give the recipients five things.

an5.37:2.1.verse: Being attentive, one is a giver of life, strength,

an5.38:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a faithful gentleman gets five benefits.

an5.38:1.3.verse: The true persons in the world show sympathy first to the faithful, not so much to the unfaithful.

an5.38:1.4.verse: They first approach the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

an5.38:1.5.verse: They first receive alms from the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

an5.38:1.6.verse: They first teach Dhamma to the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

an5.38:1.7.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, the faithful are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

an5.38:1.8.verse: A faithful gentleman gets these five benefits.

an5.38:2.1.verse: Suppose there was a great banyan tree at a level crossroads. It would become a refuge for birds from all around.

an5.38:2.2.verse: In the same way, a faithful gentleman becomes a refuge for many people—monks, nuns, laywomen, and laymen.

an5.38:3.1.verse: With its branches, leaves, and fruit,

an5.38:3.2.verse: a great tree with its strong trunk,

an5.38:4.3.verse: Those that need shade go in the shade,

an5.38:4.4.verse: those that need fruit enjoy the fruit.

an5.38:6.1.verse: Those free of greed, freed of hate,

an5.38:6.3.verse: fields of merit for the world,

an5.38:7.4.verse: the undefiled one is fully extinguished.”

an5.39:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, parents see five reasons to wish for the birth of a child in the family.

an5.39:1.3.verse: Since we looked after them, they’ll look after us.

an5.39:1.4.verse: They’ll do their duty for us.

an5.39:1.6.verse: They’ll take care of the inheritance.

an5.39:1.7.verse: Or else when we have passed away they’ll give an offering on our behalf.

an5.39:1.8.verse: Parents see these five reasons to wish for the birth of a child in the family.

an5.39:2.2.verse: astute people wish for a child.

an5.39:2.3.verse: Since we looked after them, they’ll look after us.

an5.39:2.4.verse: They’ll do their duty for us.

an5.39:3.2.verse: They’ll take care of the inheritance.

an5.39:3.3.verse: Or else when we have passed away

an5.39:3.4.verse: they’ll give an offering on our behalf.

an5.39:4.2.verse: astute people wish for a child.

an5.39:5.4.verse: as their parents did for them in the past.

an5.39:6.1.verse: Following their advice, looking after those who raised them,

an5.39:6.2.verse: the family customs are not lost.

an5.40:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, great sal trees grow in five ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

an5.40:1.8.verse: Great sal trees grow in these five ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

an5.40:1.9.verse: In the same way, a family grows in five ways supported by a family head with faith.

an5.40:1.16.verse: A family grows in these five ways supported by a family head with faith.

an5.40:2.2.verse: in the wilds, the formidable forest,

an5.40:2.4.verse: to become lord of the forest.

an5.40:3.1.verse: So too, when the family head

an5.40:3.6.verse: and those dependent for their livelihood.

an5.40:4.1.verse: Seeing the ethical conduct of the virtuous,

an5.40:5.2.verse: the path that goes to a good place,

an5.40:5.3.verse: they delight in the heavenly realm,

an5.40:5.4.verse: enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”

an5.41:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.41:1.2.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an5.41:1.3.verse: “Householder, there are these five reasons to get rich.

an5.41:1.5.verse: Firstly, with his legitimate wealth—earned by his efforts and initiative, built up with his own hands, gathered by the sweat of the brow—a noble disciple makes himself happy and pleased, keeping himself properly happy.

an5.41:1.6.verse: He makes his mother and father happy …

an5.41:1.7.verse: He makes his children, partners, bondservants, workers, and staff happy …

an5.41:1.8.verse: This is the first reason to get rich.

an5.41:2.1.verse: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he makes his friends and colleagues happy …

an5.41:2.2.verse: This is the second reason to get rich.

an5.41:3.1.verse: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he protects himself against losses from such things as fire, water, kings, bandits, or unloved heirs.

an5.41:3.4.verse: This is the third reason to get rich.

an5.41:4.1.verse: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he makes five spirit-offerings:

an5.41:4.2.verse: to relatives, guests, ancestors, king, and deities.

an5.41:4.3.verse: This is the fourth reason to get rich.

an5.41:5.1.verse: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he establishes an uplifting religious donation for ascetics and brahmins—those who refrain from intoxication and negligence, are settled in patience and gentleness, and who tame, calm, and extinguish themselves—that’s conducive to heaven, ripens in happiness, and leads to heaven.

an5.41:5.2.verse: This is the fifth reason to get rich.

an5.41:5.3.verse: These are the five reasons to get rich.

an5.41:6.1.verse: Now if the riches a noble disciple gets for these five reasons run out, he thinks:

an5.41:6.2.verse: ‘So, the riches I have obtained for these reasons are running out.’

an5.41:6.3.verse: And so he has no regrets.

an5.41:6.4.verse: But if the riches a noble disciple gets for these five reasons increase, he thinks:

an5.41:6.5.verse: ‘So, the riches I have obtained for these reasons are increasing.’

an5.41:6.6.verse: And so he has no regrets in both cases.

an5.41:7.1.verse: ‘I’ve enjoyed my wealth, supporting those who depend on me;

an5.41:7.5.verse: I have looked after the ethical and

an5.41:8.4.verse: I don’t regret what I’ve done.’

an5.41:9.1.verse: A mortal man who recollects this

an5.41:9.2.verse: stands firm in the teaching of the noble ones.

an5.41:9.3.verse: They’re praised in this life by the astute,

an5.41:9.4.verse: and they depart to rejoice in heaven.”

an5.42:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a true person is born in a family for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people.

an5.42:1.2.verse: For the benefit, welfare, and happiness of mother and father;

an5.42:2.1.verse: It’s like a great rain cloud, which nourishes all the crops for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people.

an5.42:2.2.verse: In the same way, a true person is born in a family for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people. …

an5.42:3.1.verse: The gods protect one who is guarded by principle,

an5.42:3.2.verse: who uses their wealth for the welfare of the many.

an5.42:3.3.verse: One who is learned, with precepts and observances intact,

an5.42:3.4.verse: and steady in principle, doesn’t lose their reputation.

an5.42:4.1.verse: Firm in principle, accomplished in ethical conduct,

an5.42:4.3.verse: like a pendant of Black Plum River gold,

an5.42:4.4.verse: who is worthy to criticize them?

an5.42:4.6.verse: and by the Divinity, too, they’re praised.”

an5.43:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an5.43:2.1.verse: “Householder, these five things, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable are hard to get in the world.

an5.43:2.8.verse: These are the five things, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable, but hard to get in the world.

an5.43:3.1.verse: And I say that these five things are not got by supplication or wishing for them.

an5.43:3.2.verse: If they were, who would lack them?

an5.43:4.1.verse: A noble disciple who wants to live long ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

an5.43:4.2.verse: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to long life.

an5.43:4.3.verse: For by practicing that way they gain long life

an5.43:4.4.verse: as a god or a human being.

an5.43:5.1.verse: A noble disciple who wants to be beautiful ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

an5.43:5.2.verse: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to beauty.

an5.43:5.3.verse: For by practicing that way they gain beauty

an5.43:5.4.verse: as a god or a human being.

an5.43:6.1.verse: A noble disciple who wants to be happy ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

an5.43:6.2.verse: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to happiness.

an5.43:6.3.verse: For by practicing that way they gain happiness

an5.43:6.4.verse: as a god or a human being.

an5.43:7.1.verse: A noble disciple who wants to be famous ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

an5.43:7.2.verse: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to fame.

an5.43:7.3.verse: For by practicing that way they gain fame

an5.43:7.4.verse: as a god or a human being.

an5.43:8.1.verse: A noble disciple who wants to go to heaven ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

an5.43:8.2.verse: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to heaven.

an5.43:8.3.verse: For by practicing that way they gain heaven,

an5.43:8.4.verse: they are one who gains the heavens.

an5.43:9.1.verse: For one who desires lofty delights

an5.43:9.3.verse: long life, beauty, fame and reputation,

an5.43:11.3.verse: An attentive one, comprehending the meaning,

an5.44:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an5.44:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Ugga of Vesālī, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an5.44:1.3.verse: Then Ugga went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an5.44:2.1.verse: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

an5.44:2.2.verse: ‘The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.’

an5.44:2.3.verse: My sal flower porridge is agreeable:

an5.44:2.4.verse: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:2.5.verse: So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

an5.44:3.1.verse: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

an5.44:3.2.verse: ‘The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.’

an5.44:3.3.verse: My pork with jujube is agreeable:

an5.44:3.4.verse: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:3.5.verse: So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

an5.44:4.3.verse: “… My fried vegetable stalks are agreeable:

an5.44:4.4.verse: may the Buddha please accept them from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:4.5.verse: So the Buddha accepted them out of sympathy.

an5.44:5.3.verse: “… My boiled fine rice with the dark grains picked out, served with many soups and sauces is agreeable:

an5.44:5.4.verse: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:5.5.verse: So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

an5.44:6.3.verse: “… My cloths imported from Kāsi are agreeable:

an5.44:6.4.verse: may the Buddha please accept them from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:6.5.verse: So the Buddha accepted them out of sympathy.

an5.44:7.3.verse: “… My couch spread with woolen covers—shag-piled or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends is agreeable.

an5.44:7.5.verse: this is not proper for the Buddha.

an5.44:7.6.verse: However, this plank of sandalwood is worth over a thousand dollars.

an5.44:7.7.verse: May the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”

an5.44:7.8.verse: So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

an5.44:7.9.verse: And then the Buddha rejoiced with Ugga with these verses of appreciation:

an5.44:8.1.verse: “The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable,

an5.44:8.3.verse: food and drink, and various requisites

an5.44:9.1.verse: Knowing the perfected ones to be like a field

an5.44:9.2.verse: for what’s given, offered and not held back,

an5.44:9.3.verse: a true person gives what’s hard to give:

an5.44:9.4.verse: the giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.”

an5.44:10.1.verse: And then the Buddha, having rejoiced with Ugga with these verses of appreciation, rose from his seat and left.

an5.44:11.1.verse: Then after some time Ugga passed away,

an5.44:11.2.verse: and was reborn in a host of mind-made gods.

an5.44:11.3.verse: At that time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.44:11.4.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious godling Ugga, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to him,

an5.44:11.5.verse: “Ugga, I trust it is all you wished?”

an5.44:11.6.verse: “Sir, it is indeed just as I wished.”

an5.44:11.7.verse: Then the Buddha addressed Ugga in verse:

an5.44:12.1.verse: “The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable,

an5.44:12.2.verse: the giver of the foremost gets the foremost,

an5.44:12.3.verse: the giver of the excellent gets the excellent,

an5.44:12.4.verse: the giver of the best gets the best.

an5.44:13.1.verse: A person who gives the foremost,

an5.45:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an5.45:2.2.verse: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while using a robe …

an5.45:4.1.verse: medicines and supplies for the sick, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

an5.45:4.2.verse: These are the five kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness, and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness, and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

an5.45:5.1.verse: When a noble disciple has these five kinds of overflowing merit and goodness, it’s not easy to grasp how much merit they have by saying that

an5.45:5.2.verse: this is the extent of their overflowing merit … that leads to happiness.

an5.45:5.3.verse: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

an5.45:6.1.verse: It’s like trying to grasp how much water is in the ocean. It’s not easy to say:

an5.45:6.2.verse: ‘This is how many gallons, how many hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands of gallons there are.’

an5.45:6.3.verse: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water.

an5.45:6.4.verse: In the same way, when a noble disciple has these five kinds of overflowing merit and goodness, it’s not easy to grasp how much merit they have:

an5.45:6.5.verse: ‘This is how much this overflowing merit … leads to happiness.’

an5.45:6.6.verse: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

an5.45:7.1.verse: Hosts of people use the rivers,

an5.45:7.2.verse: and though the rivers are many,

an5.45:7.3.verse: all reach the great deep, the boundless ocean,

an5.45:7.4.verse: the cruel sea that’s home to precious gems.

an5.45:8.1.verse: So too, when a person gives food, drink, and clothes;

an5.45:8.2.verse: and they’re a giver of beds, seats, and mats—

an5.45:8.3.verse: the streams of merit reach that astute person,

an5.45:8.4.verse: as the rivers bring their waters to the sea.”

an5.46:1.3.verse: Accomplishment in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an5.47:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five kinds of wealth.

an5.47:1.3.verse: The wealth of faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an5.47:2.1.verse: And what is the wealth of faith?

an5.47:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

an5.47:2.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an5.47:2.4.verse: This is called the wealth of faith.

an5.47:3.1.verse: And what is the wealth of ethics?

an5.47:3.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an5.47:3.3.verse: This is called the wealth of ethics.

an5.47:4.1.verse: And what is the wealth of learning?

an5.47:4.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s totally full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an5.47:4.3.verse: This is called the wealth of learning.

an5.47:5.1.verse: And what is the wealth of generosity?

an5.47:5.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple lives at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.

an5.47:5.3.verse: This is called the wealth of generosity.

an5.47:6.1.verse: And what is the wealth of wisdom?

an5.47:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an5.47:6.3.verse: This is called the wealth of wisdom.

an5.47:6.4.verse: These are the five kinds of wealth.

an5.47:7.1.verse: Whoever has faith in the Realized One,

an5.47:7.4.verse: praised and loved by the noble ones;

an5.47:8.1.verse: who has confidence in the Saṅgha,

an5.47:8.4.verse: their life is not in vain.

an5.47:9.1.verse: So let the wise devote themselves

an5.47:9.3.verse: confidence, and insight into the teaching,

an5.47:9.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”

an5.48:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

an5.48:1.3.verse: That someone liable to old age should not grow old.

an5.48:1.4.verse: That someone liable to sickness should not get sick. … That someone liable to death should not die. … That someone liable to ending should not end. … That someone liable to perishing should not perish. …

an5.48:2.1.verse: An unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to old age who grows old.

an5.48:2.2.verse: But they don’t reflect on old age:

an5.48:2.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to old age who grows old. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to old age who grows old.

an5.48:2.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.48:2.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.48:2.7.verse: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

an5.48:3.1.verse: Furthermore, an unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to sickness … death … ending … perishing.

an5.48:3.2.verse: But they don’t reflect on perishing:

an5.48:3.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to perishing who perishes. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to perishing who perishes.

an5.48:3.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to perishing perishes, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.48:3.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.48:3.7.verse: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

an5.48:4.2.verse: So they reflect on old age:

an5.48:4.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.48:4.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.48:4.7.verse: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.

an5.48:4.8.verse: Sorrowless, free of thorns, that noble disciple only extinguishes themselves.

My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.48:5.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.48:5.7.verse: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.

an5.48:7.2.verse: doesn’t do even a little bit of good.

an5.48:7.3.verse: When they know that you’re sad,

an5.48:8.1.verse: When an astute person doesn’t waver in the face of adversity,

an5.48:8.2.verse: as they’re able to evaluate what’s beneficial,

an5.48:8.4.verse: seeing that their normal expression doesn’t change.

an5.48:9.3.verse: if by means of any such things you benefit,

an5.48:9.4.verse: then by all means keep doing them.

an5.48:10.1.verse: But if you understand that ‘this good thing

an5.48:10.2.verse: can’t be had by me or by anyone else’,

an5.48:10.3.verse: you should accept it without sorrowing, thinking:

an5.48:10.4.verse: ‘The deed is powerful. What can I do now?’”

an5.49:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.49:1.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

an5.49:2.2.verse: Then a man went up to the king and whispered in his ear,

an5.49:2.3.verse: “Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has passed away.”

an5.49:2.4.verse: When this was said, King Pasenadi was miserable and sad. He sat with his shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

an5.49:3.1.verse: Knowing this, the Buddha said to him,

an5.49:3.2.verse: “Great king, there are five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

an5.49:3.4.verse: That someone liable to old age should not grow old. … Sorrowing and lamenting doesn’t do even a little bit of good … ‘The deed is powerful. What can I do now?’”

an5.50:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Nārada was staying near Pāṭaliputta, in the Chicken Monastery.

an5.50:1.2.verse: Now at that time King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā had just passed away.

an5.50:1.3.verse: And since that time, the king did not bathe, anoint himself, eat his meals, or apply himself to his work.

an5.50:1.4.verse: Day and night he brooded over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

an5.50:1.5.verse: Then King Muṇḍa addressed Piyaka, the keeper of the treasury,

an5.50:1.6.verse: “So, my good Piyaka, please place Queen Bhaddā’s corpse in an iron casket filled with oil. Then close it up with another casket, so that we can view Queen Bhaddā’s body even longer.”

an5.50:1.7.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka, and he did as the king instructed.

an5.50:2.2.verse: “King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā has passed away.

an5.50:2.3.verse: Since then the king does not bathe, anoint himself, eat his meals, or apply himself to his work.

an5.50:2.4.verse: Day and night he broods over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

an5.50:2.5.verse: Now, what ascetic or brahmin might the king pay homage to, whose teaching could help the king give up sorrow’s arrow?”

an5.50:3.2.verse: “This Venerable Nārada is staying in the Chicken Monastery at Pāṭaliputta.

an5.50:3.4.verse: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

an5.50:3.5.verse: What if King Muṇḍa was to pay homage to Venerable Nārada? Hopefully when he hears Nārada’s teaching, the king could give up sorrow’s arrow.”

an5.50:4.1.verse: Then Piyaka went to the king and said to him,

an5.50:4.2.verse: “Your Majesty, this Venerable Nārada is staying in the Chicken Monastery at Pāṭaliputta.

an5.50:4.4.verse: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

an5.50:4.5.verse: What if Your Majesty was to pay homage to Venerable Nārada? Hopefully when you hear Nārada’s teaching, you could give up sorrow’s arrow.”

an5.50:4.6.verse: “Well then, my good Piyaka, let Nārada know.

an5.50:4.7.verse: For how on earth could one such as I presume to visit an ascetic or brahmin in my realm without letting them know beforehand?”

an5.50:4.8.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka. He went to Nārada, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an5.50:5.1.verse: “Sir, King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā has passed away.

an5.50:5.2.verse: And since she passed away, the king has not bathed, anointed himself, eaten his meals, or got his business done.

an5.50:5.3.verse: Day and night he broods over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

an5.50:5.4.verse: Sir, please teach the king so that, when he hears your teaching, he can give up sorrow’s arrow.”

an5.50:5.5.verse: “Please, Piyaka, let the king come at his convenience.”

an5.50:6.1.verse: Then Piyaka rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled Venerable Nārada, keeping him on his right, before going to the king and saying,

an5.50:6.2.verse: “Your Majesty, the request for an audience with Venerable Nārada has been granted.

an5.50:6.3.verse: Please, Your Majesty, go at your convenience.”

an5.50:6.4.verse: “Well then, my good Piyaka, harness the finest chariots.”

an5.50:6.5.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka. He did so, then told the king:

an5.50:6.6.verse: “Your Majesty, the finest chariots are harnessed.

an5.50:6.7.verse: Please, Your Majesty, go at your convenience.”

an5.50:7.1.verse: Then King Muṇḍa mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out in full royal pomp to see Venerable Nārada at the Chicken Monastery.

an5.50:7.2.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and entered the monastery on foot.

an5.50:7.3.verse: Then the king went up to Nārada, bowed, and sat down to one side. Then Nārada said to him:

an5.50:8.1.verse: “Great king, there are five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

an5.50:8.3.verse: That someone liable to old age should not grow old. …

an5.50:8.4.verse: That someone liable to sickness should not get sick. … That someone liable to death should not die. … That someone liable to ending should not end. … That someone liable to perishing should not perish. …

an5.50:9.1.verse: An unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to old age who grows old.

an5.50:9.2.verse: But they don’t reflect on old age:

an5.50:9.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to old age who grows old. For all sentient beings have someone liable to old age who grows old, as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn.

an5.50:9.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.50:9.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.50:9.7.verse: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

an5.50:10.1.verse: Furthermore, an unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to sickness … death … ending … perishing.

an5.50:10.2.verse: But they don’t reflect on perishing:

an5.50:10.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to perishing who perishes. For all sentient beings have someone liable to perishing who perishes, as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn.

an5.50:10.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to perishing perishes, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.50:10.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.50:10.7.verse: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

an5.50:11.1.verse: A learned noble disciple has someone liable to old age who grows old.

an5.50:11.2.verse: So they reflect on old age:

an5.50:11.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to old age who grows old. For all sentient beings have someone liable to old age who grows old, as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn.

an5.50:11.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.50:11.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.50:11.7.verse: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.

an5.50:11.8.verse: Sorrowless, free of thorns, that noble disciple only extinguishes themselves.

an5.50:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a learned noble disciple has someone liable to sickness … death … ending … perishing.

an5.50:12.3.verse: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to perishing who perishes. For all sentient beings have someone liable to perishing who perishes, as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn.

an5.50:12.4.verse: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to perishing perishes, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

an5.50:12.5.verse: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

an5.50:12.7.verse: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.

an5.50:12.8.verse: Sorrowless, free of thorns, that noble disciple only extinguishes themselves.

an5.50:13.1.verse: These are the five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

an5.50:14.2.verse: doesn’t do even a little bit of good.

an5.50:14.3.verse: When they know that you’re sad,

an5.50:15.1.verse: When an astute person doesn’t waver in the face of adversity,

an5.50:15.2.verse: as they’re able to evaluate what’s beneficial,

an5.50:15.4.verse: seeing that their normal expression doesn’t change.

an5.50:16.3.verse: if by means of any such things you benefit,

an5.50:16.4.verse: then by all means keep doing them.

an5.50:17.1.verse: But if you understand that ‘this good thing

an5.50:17.2.verse: can’t be had by me or by anyone else’,

an5.50:17.3.verse: you should accept it without sorrowing, thinking:

an5.50:17.4.verse: ‘The deed is powerful. What can I do now?’”

an5.50:18.1.verse: When he said this, King Muṇḍa said to Venerable Nārada,

an5.50:18.2.verse: “Sir, what is the name of this exposition of the teaching?”

an5.50:18.3.verse: “Great king, this exposition of the teaching is named ‘Pulling Out Sorrow’s Arrow’.”

an5.50:18.4.verse: “Indeed, sir, this is the pulling out of sorrow’s arrow!

an5.50:18.5.verse: Hearing this exposition of the teaching, I’ve given up sorrow’s arrow.”

an5.50:19.1.verse: Then King Muṇḍa addressed Piyaka, the keeper of the treasury,

an5.50:19.2.verse: “Well then, my good Piyaka, cremate Queen Bhaddā’s corpse and build a monument.

an5.50:19.3.verse: From this day forth, I will bathe, anoint myself, eat my meals, and apply myself to my work.”

an5.51:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.51:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an5.51:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom.

an5.51:2.8.verse: These are the five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom.

an5.51:3.1.verse: Take a mendicant who has feeble and weak wisdom, not having given up these five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom. It is quite impossible that they would know what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both; or that they would realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

an5.51:3.2.verse: Suppose there was a mountain river that flowed swiftly, going far, carrying all before it.

an5.51:3.3.verse: But then a man would open channels on both sides,

an5.51:3.4.verse: so the mid-river current would be dispersed, displaced, and separated. The river would no longer flow swiftly, going far, carrying all before it.

an5.51:3.5.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who has feeble and weak wisdom, not having given up these five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom. It is not possible that they would know what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both; or that they would realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

an5.51:4.1.verse: Take a mendicant who has powerful wisdom, having given up these five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom. It’s quite possible that they would know what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both; or that they would realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

an5.51:4.2.verse: Suppose there was a mountain river that flowed swiftly, going far, carrying all before it.

an5.51:4.3.verse: But then a man would close up the channels on both sides,

an5.51:4.4.verse: so the mid-river current would not be dispersed, displaced, and separated. The river would keep flowing swiftly for a long way, carrying all before it.

an5.51:4.5.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who has powerful wisdom, having given up these five obstacles and hindrances, parasites of the mind that weaken wisdom. It’s quite possible that they would know what’s for their own good, the good of another, or the good of both; or that they would realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.”

an5.52:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, rightly speaking, you’d call the five hindrances a ‘heap of the unskillful’.

an5.52:1.2.verse: For these five hindrances are entirely a heap of the unskillful.

an5.52:1.4.verse: The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

an5.52:1.5.verse: Rightly speaking, you’d call these five hindrances a ‘heap of the unskillful’.

an5.52:1.6.verse: For these five hindrances are entirely a heap of the unskillful.”

an5.53:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five factors that support meditation.

an5.53:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

an5.53:1.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an5.53:1.5.verse: They are rarely ill or unwell.

an5.53:1.6.verse: Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

an5.53:1.8.verse: They reveal themselves honestly to the Teacher or sensible spiritual companions.

an5.53:1.9.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an5.53:1.10.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an5.53:1.11.verse: These are the five factors that support meditation.”

an5.54:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are five times that are not good for meditation.

an5.54:1.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is old, overcome with old age.

an5.54:1.4.verse: This is the first time that’s not good for meditation.

an5.54:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is sick, overcome by sickness.

an5.54:2.2.verse: This is the second time that’s not good for meditation.

an5.54:3.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s a famine, a bad harvest, so it’s hard to get almsfood, and not easy to keep going by collecting alms.

an5.54:3.2.verse: This is the third time that’s not good for meditation.

an5.54:4.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s peril due to turmoil in the wilds, so the countryfolk mount their vehicles and flee everywhere.

an5.54:4.2.verse: This is the fourth time that’s not good for meditation.

an5.54:5.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s a schism in the Saṅgha.

an5.54:5.2.verse: When the Saṅgha is split, they abuse, insult, block, and forsake each other.

an5.54:5.3.verse: This doesn’t inspire confidence in those without it, and it causes some with confidence to change their minds.

an5.54:5.4.verse: This is the fifth time that’s not good for meditation.

an5.54:5.5.verse: These are the five times that are not good for meditation.

an5.54:6.1.verse: There are five times that are good for meditation.

an5.54:6.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is a youth, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life.

an5.54:6.4.verse: This is the first time that’s good for meditation.

an5.54:7.1.verse: Furthermore, they are rarely ill or unwell. Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

an5.54:7.2.verse: This is the second time that’s good for meditation.

an5.54:8.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s plenty of food, a good harvest, so it’s easy to get almsfood, and easy to keep going by collecting alms.

an5.54:8.2.verse: This is the third time that’s good for meditation.

an5.54:9.1.verse: Furthermore, people live in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.

an5.54:9.2.verse: This is the fourth time that’s good for meditation.

an5.54:10.1.verse: Furthermore, the Saṅgha lives comfortably, in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, with one recitation.

an5.54:10.2.verse: When the Saṅgha is in harmony, they don’t abuse, insult, block, or forsake each other.

an5.54:10.3.verse: This inspires confidence in those without it, and increases confidence in those who have it.

an5.54:10.4.verse: This is the fifth time that’s good for meditation.

an5.54:10.5.verse: These are the five times that are good for meditation.”

an5.55:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an5.55:1.2.verse: Now, at that time a mother and son had both entered the rainy season residence at Sāvatthī,

an5.55:1.3.verse: as a monk and a nun.

an5.55:1.4.verse: They wanted to see each other often.

an5.55:1.5.verse: The mother wanted to see her son often,

an5.55:1.7.verse: Seeing each other often, they became close.

an5.55:1.8.verse: Being so close, they became intimate.

an5.55:1.9.verse: And being intimate, lust overcame them.

an5.55:1.10.verse: With their minds swamped by lust, without resigning the training and declaring their inability to continue, they had sex.

an5.55:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

an5.55:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, how could that futile man imagine that

an5.55:3.2.verse: a mother cannot lust for her son, or that a son cannot lust for his mother?

an5.55:3.3.verse: Compared to the sight of a woman, I do not see a single sight that is so arousing, sensuous, intoxicating, captivating, and infatuating, and such an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

an5.55:3.4.verse: Sentient beings are lustful, greedy, tied, infatuated, and attached to the sight of a woman.

an5.55:3.5.verse: They sorrow for a long time under the sway of a woman’s sight.

an5.55:4.1.verse: Compared to the sound … smell … taste … touch of a woman, I do not see a single touch that is so arousing, sensuous, intoxicating, captivating, and infatuating, and such an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

an5.55:4.2.verse: Sentient beings are lustful, greedy, tied, infatuated, and attached to the touch of a woman.

an5.55:4.3.verse: They sorrow for a long time under the sway of a woman’s touch.

an5.55:5.1.verse: When a woman walks, she occupies a man’s mind.

an5.55:5.2.verse: When a woman stands … sits … lies down … laughs … speaks … sings … cries … is injured, she occupies a man’s mind. Even when a woman is dead, she occupies a man’s mind.

an5.55:5.3.verse: For if anyone should be rightly called ‘an all-round snare of Māra’, it’s ladies.

an5.55:6.1.verse: You might chat with someone who has knife in hand.

an5.55:6.2.verse: You might even chat with a goblin.

an5.55:6.3.verse: You might sit close by a viper,

an5.55:6.4.verse: whose bite would take your life.

an5.55:6.6.verse: one on one with a lady.

an5.55:7.2.verse: with a glance and a smile.

an5.55:7.5.verse: It’s not good to sit with such a person,

an5.55:7.6.verse: even if she’s injured or dead.

an5.55:8.1.verse: These five kinds of sensual stimulation

an5.55:8.2.verse: are apparent in a woman’s body:

an5.55:9.1.verse: Those swept away by the flood of sensual pleasures,

an5.55:9.4.verse: time and destination, and life after life.

an5.55:10.1.verse: But those who fully understand sensual pleasures

an5.55:10.2.verse: live fearing nothing from any quarter.

an5.55:10.3.verse: They are those in the world who’ve crossed over,

an5.55:10.4.verse: having reached the ending of defilements.”

an5.56:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to his own mentor, and said,

an5.56:1.2.verse: “Now, sir, my body feels like it’s drugged. I’m disorientated, the teachings don’t spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and have doubts about the teachings.”

an5.56:2.1.verse: Then that mendicant took his protégé to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an5.56:2.3.verse: ‘Now, sir, my body feels like it’s drugged. I’m disorientated, the teachings don’t spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and have doubts about the teachings.’”

an5.56:3.1.verse: “That’s how it is, mendicant, when your sense doors are unguarded, you eat too much, you’re not dedicated to wakefulness, you’re unable to discern skillful qualities, and you don’t pursue the development of the qualities on the side of awakening in the evening and toward dawn. Your body feels like it’s drugged. You’re disorientated, the teachings don’t spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill your mind. You lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and have doubts about the teachings.

an5.56:3.2.verse: So you should train like this:

an5.56:3.3.verse: ‘I will guard my sense doors, eat in moderation, be dedicated to wakefulness, discern skillful qualities, and pursue the development of the qualities on the side of awakening in the evening and toward dawn.’

an5.56:4.1.verse: When that mendicant had been given this advice by the Buddha, he rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an5.56:4.2.verse: Then that mendicant, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

an5.56:4.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

an5.56:4.4.verse: And that mendicant became one of the perfected.

an5.56:5.1.verse: When that mendicant had attained perfection, he went up to his own mentor, and said,

an5.56:5.2.verse: “Now, sir, my body doesn’t feel like it’s drugged. I’m not disorientated, the teachings spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness don’t fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life satisfied, and have no doubts about the teachings.”

an5.56:5.3.verse: Then that mendicant took his protégé to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an5.56:5.5.verse: ‘Now, sir, my body doesn’t feel like it’s drugged. I’m not disorientated, the teachings spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness don’t fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life satisfied, and have no doubts about the teachings.’”

an5.56:6.1.verse: “That’s how it is, mendicant, when your sense doors are guarded, you’re moderate in eating, you’re dedicated to wakefulness, you’re able to discern skillful qualities, and you pursue the development of the qualities on the side of awakening in the evening and toward dawn. Your body doesn’t feel like it’s drugged. You’re not disorientated, the teachings spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness don’t fill your mind. You lead the spiritual life satisfied, and have no doubts about the teachings.

an5.56:6.2.verse: So you should train like this:

an5.56:6.3.verse: ‘We will guard our sense doors, eat in moderation, be dedicated to wakefulness, discern skillful qualities, and pursue the development of the qualities on the side of awakening in the evening and toward dawn.’

an5.57:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a woman or a man, a layperson or a renunciate should often review these five subjects.

an5.57:1.3.verse: ‘I am liable to grow old, I am not exempt from old age.’ A woman or a man, a layperson or a renunciate should often review this.

an5.57:1.4.verse: ‘I am liable to get sick, I am not exempt from sickness.’ …

an5.57:1.5.verse: ‘I am liable to die, I am not exempt from death.’ …

an5.57:1.6.verse: ‘I must be parted and separated from all I hold dear and beloved.’ …
