an6.77:2.4.verse: After giving up these six qualities you can realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.”

an6.78:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant has six things they’re full of joy and happiness in this very life, and they have laid the groundwork for ending the defilements.

an6.78:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant enjoys the teaching, meditation, giving up, seclusion, kindness, and non-proliferation.

an6.78:1.4.verse: When a mendicant possesses these six things they’re full of joy and happiness in this very life, and they have laid the groundwork for ending the defilements.”

an6.79:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who has six qualities is unable to acquire more skillful qualities or to increase the skillful qualities they’ve already acquired.

an6.79:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is not skilled in progress, skilled in regress, or skilled in means. They don’t generate enthusiasm to achieve skillful qualities not yet achieved. They don’t protect skillful qualities they have achieved. And they don’t try to persist in the task.

an6.79:1.4.verse: A mendicant who possesses these six qualities is unable to acquire more skillful qualities or to increase the skillful qualities they’ve already acquired.

an6.79:2.1.verse: A mendicant who has six qualities is able to acquire more skillful qualities or to increase the skillful qualities they’ve already acquired.

an6.79:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is skilled in progress, skilled in regress, and skilled in means. They generate enthusiasm to achieve skillful qualities not yet achieved. They protect skillful qualities they have achieved. And they try to persist in the task.

an6.79:2.4.verse: A mendicant who possesses these six qualities is able to acquire more skillful qualities or to increase the skillful qualities they’ve already acquired.”

an6.80:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with six qualities soon acquires great and abundant good qualities.

an6.80:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is full of light, full of practice, full of inspiration, and full of eagerness. They don’t slack off when it comes to developing skillful qualities. They reach further.

an6.80:1.4.verse: A mendicant who possesses these six qualities soon acquires great and abundant good qualities.”

an6.81:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, someone with six qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.

an6.81:1.3.verse: They kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, and lie. And they have corrupt wishes and wrong view.

an6.81:1.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.

an6.81:2.1.verse: Someone with six qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.

an6.81:2.3.verse: They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, or lie. And they have few desires and right view.

an6.81:2.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.”

an6.82:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, someone with six qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.

an6.82:1.3.verse: They kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, and lie. And they’re greedy and rude.

an6.82:1.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.

an6.82:2.1.verse: Someone with six qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.

an6.82:2.3.verse: They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, or lie. And they’re not greedy or rude.

an6.82:2.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.”

an6.83:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with six qualities can’t realize the best thing, perfection.

an6.83:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is faithless, shameless, imprudent, lazy, and witless. And they’re concerned with their body and their life.

an6.83:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can’t realize the best thing, perfection.

an6.83:2.1.verse: A mendicant with six qualities can realize the best thing, perfection.

an6.83:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is faithful, conscientious, prudent, energetic, and wise. And they have no concern for their body and their life.

an6.83:2.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can realize the best thing, perfection.”

an6.84:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with six qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an6.84:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant has many desires—they’re frustrated and not content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. And they’re faithless, unethical, unmindful, and witless.

an6.84:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an6.84:2.1.verse: A mendicant with six qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an6.84:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t have many desires—they’re not frustrated but content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. And they’re faithful, ethical, mindful, and wise.

an6.84:2.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.”

an6.85:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with six qualities can’t realize supreme coolness.

an6.85:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t keep their mind in check when they should. They don’t exert their mind when they should. They don’t encourage the mind when they should. They don’t watch over the mind with equanimity when they should. They have inferior convictions. They delight in substantial reality.

an6.85:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can’t realize supreme coolness.

an6.85:2.1.verse: A mendicant with six qualities can realize supreme coolness.

an6.85:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant keeps their mind in check when they should. They exert their mind when they should. They encourage the mind when they should. They watch over the mind with equanimity when they should. They have excellent convictions. They delight in extinguishment.

an6.85:2.4.verse: A mendicant with these six qualities can realize supreme coolness.”

an6.86:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, someone with six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.86:1.3.verse: They’re obstructed by deeds, defilements, or results. And they’re faithless, unenthusiastic, and witless.

an6.86:1.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities, even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.86:2.1.verse: Someone with six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.

an6.86:2.3.verse: They’re not obstructed by deeds, defilements, or results. And they’re faithful, enthusiastic, and wise.

an6.86:2.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.”

an6.87:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, someone with six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.87:1.3.verse: They murder their mother or father or a perfected one. They maliciously shed the blood of a Realized One. They cause a schism in the Saṅgha. They’re witless, dull, and idiotic.

an6.87:1.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities, even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.87:2.1.verse: Someone with six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.

an6.87:2.3.verse: They don’t murder their mother or father or a perfected one. They don’t maliciously shed the blood of a Realized One. They don’t cause a schism in the Saṅgha. They’re wise, bright, and clever.

an6.87:2.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.”

an6.88:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, someone with six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.88:1.3.verse: When the teaching and practice proclaimed by the Realized One is being taught they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They learn the incorrect meaning and neglect the correct meaning. They accept views that contradict the teaching.

an6.88:1.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is unable to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities, even when listening to the true teaching.

an6.88:2.1.verse: Someone with six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.

an6.88:2.3.verse: When the teaching and practice proclaimed by the Realized One is being taught they want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand. They learn the correct meaning and neglect the incorrect meaning. They accept views that conform with the teaching.

an6.88:2.4.verse: Someone with these six qualities is able to step into the sure path with regard to skillful qualities when listening to the true teaching.”

an6.89:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, without giving up six things you can’t become accomplished in view.

an6.89:1.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, and forms of greed, hate, and delusion that lead to rebirth in places of loss.

an6.89:1.4.verse: Without giving up these six things you can’t become accomplished in view.

an6.89:2.1.verse: After giving up six things you can become accomplished in view.

an6.89:2.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, and forms of greed, hate, and delusion that lead to rebirth in places of loss.

an6.89:2.4.verse: After giving up these six things you can become accomplished in view.”

an6.90:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an individual accomplished in view has given up these six things.

an6.90:1.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, and forms of greed, hate, and delusion that lead to rebirth in places of loss.

an6.90:1.4.verse: An individual accomplished in view has given up these six things.”

an6.91:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an individual accomplished in view can’t give rise to six things.

an6.91:1.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, and forms of greed, hate, and delusion that lead to rebirth in places of loss.

an6.91:1.4.verse: An individual accomplished in view can’t give rise to these six things.”

an6.92:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these six things can’t be done.

an6.92:1.3.verse: An individual accomplished in view can’t live disrespectful and irreverent toward the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, or the training. They can’t establish their belief on unreliable grounds. And they can’t generate an eighth rebirth.

an6.92:1.4.verse: These are the six things that can’t be done.”

an6.93:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these six things can’t be done.

an6.93:1.3.verse: An individual accomplished in view can’t take conditions to be permanent. They cannot take conditions to be happiness. They cannot take anything to be the self. They can’t do deeds with fixed result in the next life. They can’t fall back on purification through boisterous, superstitious rites. They can’t seek outside of the Buddhist community for those worthy of religious donations.

an6.93:1.4.verse: These are the six things that can’t be done.”

an6.94:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these six things can’t be done.

an6.94:1.3.verse: An individual accomplished in view can’t murder their mother or father or a perfected one. They can’t maliciously shed the blood of the Realized One. They can’t cause a schism in the Saṅgha. They can’t dedicate themselves to another teacher.

an6.94:1.4.verse: These are the six things that can’t be done.”

an6.95:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these six things can’t be done.

an6.95:1.3.verse: An individual accomplished in view can’t fall back on the idea that pleasure and pain are made by oneself, or that they’re made by another, or that they’re made by both. Nor can they fall back on the idea that pleasure and pain arise anomalously, not made by oneself, by another, or by both.

an6.95:1.5.verse: It is because an individual accomplished in view has clearly seen causes and the phenomena that arise from causes.

an6.95:1.6.verse: These are the six things that can’t be done.”

an6.96:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the appearance of six things is rare in the world.

an6.96:1.3.verse: A Realized One, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. A teacher of the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One. Rebirth in a civilized region. Unimpaired sense faculties. Being bright and clever. Enthusiasm for skillful qualities.

an6.96:1.4.verse: The appearance of these six things is rare in the world.”

an6.97:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these are the six benefits of realizing the fruit of stream-entry.

an6.97:1.3.verse: You’re bound for the true teaching. You’re not liable to decline. You suffer only for a limited period. You have distinct knowledge. You’ve clearly seen causes and the phenomena that arise from causes.

an6.97:1.4.verse: These are the six benefits of realizing the fruit of stream-entry.”

an6.98:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is quite impossible for a mendicant who regards any condition as permanent to accept views that conform with the teaching.

an6.98:1.2.verse: Without accepting views that conform with the teaching, it’s impossible to step into the sure path.

an6.98:1.3.verse: Without stepping into the sure path, it’s impossible to realize the fruit of stream-entry, once-return, non-return, or perfection.

an6.98:2.1.verse: It’s quite possible for a mendicant who regards all conditions as impermanent to accept views that conform with the teaching.

an6.98:2.2.verse: Having accepted views that conform with the teaching, it’s possible to step into the sure path.

an6.98:2.3.verse: Having stepped into the sure path, it’s possible to realize the fruit of stream-entry, once-return, non-return, or perfection.”

an6.99:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is quite impossible for a mendicant who regards any condition as pleasurable to accept views that agree with the teaching. …

an6.99:1.2.verse: It’s quite possible for a mendicant who regards all conditions as suffering to accept views that agree with the teaching. …”

an6.100:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is quite impossible for a mendicant who regards any thing as self to accept views that agree with the teaching. …

an6.100:1.2.verse: It’s quite possible for a mendicant who regards all things as not-self to accept views that agree with the teaching. …”

an6.101:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is quite impossible for a mendicant who regards extinguishment as suffering to accept views that conform with the teaching. …

an6.101:2.1.verse: It’s quite possible for a mendicant who regards extinguishment as pleasurable to accept views that conform with the teaching. …”

an6.102:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, seeing six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of impermanence in all conditions without qualification.

an6.102:1.3.verse: ‘All conditions will appear to me as transient.’ ‘My mind will not delight anywhere in the world.’ ‘My mind will rise above the whole world.’ ‘My heart will incline to extinguishment.’ ‘My fetters will be given up.’ ‘I will achieve the ultimate goal of the ascetic life.’

an6.102:1.4.verse: Seeing these six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of impermanence in all conditions without qualification.”

an6.103:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, seeing six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of suffering in all conditions without qualification.

an6.103:1.3.verse: ‘Perception of disillusionment will be established in me for all conditions, like a killer with a drawn sword.’

an6.103:1.4.verse: ‘My mind will rise above the whole world.’ ‘I will see extinguishment as peaceful.’ ‘My underlying tendencies will be uprooted.’ ‘I will fulfill my duty.’ ‘I will have served my Teacher with love.’

an6.103:1.5.verse: Seeing these six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of suffering in all conditions without qualification.”

an6.104:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, seeing six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of not-self in all things without qualification.

an6.104:1.3.verse: ‘I will not be determined by anything in the world.’ ‘My I-making will stop.’ ‘My mine-making will stop.’ ‘I will have distinct knowledge.’ ‘I will clearly see causes and the phenomena that arise from causes.’

an6.104:1.4.verse: Seeing these six benefits is quite enough to establish the perception of not-self in all things without qualification.”

an6.105:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you should give up these three states of existence. And you should train in three trainings.

an6.105:1.2.verse: What are the three states of existence you should give up?

an6.105:1.3.verse: Existence in the sensual realm, the realm of luminous form, and the formless realm.

an6.105:1.4.verse: These are the three states of existence you should give up.

an6.105:1.5.verse: What are the three trainings you should train in?

an6.105:1.6.verse: The training in the higher ethics, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom.

an6.105:1.7.verse: These are the three trainings you should train in.

an6.105:1.8.verse: When a mendicant has given up these three states of existence and has trained in these three trainings

an6.105:1.9.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.”

an6.106:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you should give up these three cravings and three conceits.

an6.106:1.2.verse: What three cravings should you give up?

an6.106:1.3.verse: Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

an6.106:1.4.verse: These are the three cravings you should give up.

an6.106:1.5.verse: What three conceits should you give up?

an6.106:1.6.verse: Conceit, inferiority complex, and superiority complex.

an6.106:1.7.verse: These are the three conceits you should give up.

an6.106:1.8.verse: When a mendicant has given up these three cravings and these three conceits

an6.106:1.9.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.”

an6.107:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.107:1.7.verse: You should develop the perception of ugliness to give up greed, love to give up hate, and wisdom to give up delusion.

an6.107:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.108:1.3.verse: Bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind.

an6.108:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.108:1.7.verse: You should develop good bodily conduct to give up bad bodily conduct, good verbal conduct to give up bad verbal conduct, and good mental conduct to give up bad mental conduct.

an6.108:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.109:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.109:1.7.verse: You should develop thoughts of renunciation to give up sensual thoughts, thoughts of good will to give up malicious thoughts, and thoughts of harmlessness to give up cruel thoughts.

an6.109:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.110:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.110:1.7.verse: You should develop perceptions of renunciation to give up sensual perceptions, perceptions of good will to give up malicious perceptions, and perceptions of harmlessness to give up cruel perceptions.

an6.110:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.111:1.3.verse: The elements of sensuality, malice, and cruelty.

an6.111:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.111:1.7.verse: You should develop the element of renunciation to give up the element of sensuality, the element of good will to give up the element of malice, and the element of harmlessness to give up the element of cruelty.

an6.111:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.112:1.3.verse: The view that things are gratifying, the theory of self, and wrong view.

an6.112:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.112:1.7.verse: You should develop the perception of impermanence to give up the view that things are gratifying; the perception of not-self to give up the theory of self; and right view to give up wrong view.

an6.112:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.113:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.113:1.7.verse: You should develop rejoicing to give up discontent, harmlessness to give up cruelty, and principled conduct to give up unprincipled conduct.

an6.113:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.114:1.3.verse: Lack of contentment, lack of situational awareness, and having many wishes.

an6.114:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.114:1.7.verse: You should develop contentment to give up lack of contentment, situational awareness to give up lack of situational awareness, and having few wishes to give up having many wishes.

an6.114:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.115:1.3.verse: Being hard to admonish, bad friendship, and a scattered mind.

an6.115:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.115:1.7.verse: You should develop being easy to admonish to give up being hard to admonish, good friendship to give up bad friendship, and mindfulness of breathing to give up a scattered mind.

an6.115:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.116:1.3.verse: Restlessness, lack of restraint, and negligence.

an6.116:1.5.verse: To give up these three things you should develop three things.

an6.116:1.7.verse: You should develop serenity to give up restlessness, restraint to give up lack of restraint, and diligence to give up negligence.

an6.116:1.8.verse: These are the three things you should develop to give up those three things.”

an6.117:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, without giving up these six qualities you can’t meditate observing an aspect of the body.

an6.117:1.3.verse: Relishing work, talk, sleep, and company, not guarding the sense doors, and eating too much.

an6.117:1.4.verse: Without giving up these six qualities you can’t meditate observing an aspect of the body.

an6.117:2.1.verse: But after giving up these six qualities you can meditate observing an aspect of the body.

an6.117:2.3.verse: Relishing work, talk, sleep, and company, not guarding the sense doors, and eating too much.

an6.117:2.4.verse: After giving up these six qualities you can meditate observing an aspect of the body.”

an6.118:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, without giving up six things you can’t meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

an6.118:1.14.verse: Relishing work, talk, sleep, and company, not guarding the sense doors, and eating too much.

an6.118:1.15.verse: After giving up these six qualities you can meditate observing an aspect of principles internally and externally.”

an6.119:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, having six qualities the householder Tapussa is certain about the Realized One, sees freedom from death  and lives having realized freedom from death.

an6.119:1.3.verse: Experiential confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and noble ethics, knowledge, and freedom.

an6.119:1.4.verse: Having these six qualities the householder Tapussa is certain about the Realized One, sees freedom from death and lives having realized freedom from death.”

an6.120-139:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, having six qualities the householders Bhallika …

an6.120-139:1.20.verse: and Sāragga are certain about the Realized One, see freedom from death and live having realized freedom from death.

an6.120-139:1.22.verse: Experiential confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and noble ethics, knowledge, and freedom.

an6.120-139:1.23.verse: Having these six qualities the lay follower Sāragga is certain about the Realized One, sees freedom from death and lives having realized freedom from death.”

an6.140:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, six things should be developed.

an6.140:1.3.verse: The unsurpassable seeing, listening, acquisition, training, service, and recollection.

an6.140:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these six things should be developed.”

an6.141:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, six things should be developed.

an6.141:1.3.verse: The recollection of the Buddha, the teaching, the Saṅgha, ethics, generosity, and the deities.

an6.141:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these six things should be developed.”

an6.142:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, six things should be developed.

an6.142:1.3.verse: The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of giving up, the perception of fading away, and the perception of cessation.

an6.142:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these six things should be developed.”

an6.143-169:1.9.verse: letting go of greed these six things should be developed.”

an6.170-649:1.25.verse: For the letting go of negligence

an6.170-649:1.26.verse: these six things should be developed.”

an6.170-649:1.27.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an6.170-649:1.28.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

an6.170-649:1.30.verse: The Book of the Sixes is finished.

an7.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an7.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an7.1:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is disliked and disapproved by their spiritual companions, not respected or admired.

an7.1:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant desires material things, honor, and status. They lack conscience and prudence. They have corrupt wishes and wrong view.

an7.1:2.4.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities is disliked and disapproved by their spiritual companions, not respected or admired.

an7.1:3.1.verse: A mendicant with seven qualities is liked and approved by their spiritual companions, respected and admired.

an7.1:3.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t desire material things, honor, and status. They have conscience and prudence. They have few desires and right view.

an7.1:3.4.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities is liked and approved by their spiritual companions, respected and admired.”

an7.2:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is disliked and disapproved by their spiritual companions, not respected or admired.

an7.2:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant desires material things, honor, and status. They lack conscience and prudence. They’re jealous and stingy.

an7.2:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities is disliked and disapproved by their spiritual companions, not respected or admired.

an7.2:2.1.verse: A mendicant with seven qualities is liked and approved by their spiritual companions, respected and admired.

an7.2:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t desire material things, honor, and status. They have conscience and prudence. They’re not jealous or stingy.

an7.2:2.4.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities is liked and approved by their spiritual companions, respected and admired.”

an7.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. …

an7.3:1.5.verse: The powers of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom.

an7.3:2.1.verse: The powers are faith and energy,

an7.3:2.4.verse: and wisdom as the seventh power.

an7.3:3.1.verse: They should examine the teaching rationally,

an7.3:3.4.verse: is like a lamp going out.”

an7.4:1.3.verse: The powers of faith, energy, conscience, prudence, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom.

an7.4:2.1.verse: And what is the power of faith?

an7.4:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

an7.4:2.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an7.4:2.4.verse: This is called the power of faith.

an7.4:3.1.verse: And what is the power of energy?

an7.4:3.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an7.4:3.3.verse: This is called the power of energy.

an7.4:4.1.verse: And what is the power of conscience?

an7.4:4.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has a conscience. They’re conscientious about bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and conscientious about acquiring any bad, unskillful qualities.

an7.4:4.3.verse: This is called the power of conscience.

an7.4:5.1.verse: And what is the power of prudence?

an7.4:5.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is prudent. They’re prudent when it comes to bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and prudent when it comes to the acquiring of any bad, unskillful qualities.

an7.4:5.3.verse: This is called the power of prudence.

an7.4:6.1.verse: And what is the power of mindfulness?

an7.4:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is mindful. They have utmost mindfulness and alertness, and can remember and recall what was said and done long ago.

an7.4:6.3.verse: This is called the power of mindfulness.

an7.4:7.1.verse: And what is the power of immersion?

an7.4:7.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. …

an7.4:7.4.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an7.4:7.5.verse: This is called the power of immersion.

an7.4:8.1.verse: And what is the power of wisdom?

an7.4:8.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an7.4:8.3.verse: This is called the power of wisdom.

an7.4:10.1.verse: The powers are faith and energy,

an7.4:10.4.verse: and wisdom as the seventh power.

an7.4:11.1.verse: They should examine the teaching rationally,

an7.4:11.4.verse: is like a lamp going out.”

an7.5:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven kinds of wealth.

an7.5:1.3.verse: The wealth of faith, ethics, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an7.5:1.4.verse: These are the seven kinds of wealth.

an7.5:2.1.verse: Faith and ethical conduct are kinds of wealth,

an7.5:2.4.verse: and wisdom is the seventh kind of wealth.

an7.5:3.4.verse: their life is not in vain.

an7.5:4.1.verse: So let the wise devote themselves

an7.5:4.3.verse: confidence, and insight into the teaching,

an7.5:4.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”

an7.6:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven kinds of wealth.

an7.6:1.3.verse: The wealth of faith, ethics, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an7.6:2.1.verse: And what is the wealth of faith?

an7.6:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening …

an7.6:2.4.verse: This is called the wealth of faith.

an7.6:3.1.verse: And what is the wealth of ethical conduct?

an7.6:3.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an7.6:3.3.verse: This is called the wealth of ethical conduct.

an7.6:4.1.verse: And what is the wealth of conscience?

an7.6:4.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has a conscience. They’re conscientious about bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and conscientious about having any bad, unskillful qualities.

an7.6:4.3.verse: This is called the wealth of conscience.

an7.6:5.1.verse: And what is the wealth of prudence?

an7.6:5.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is prudent. They’re prudent when it comes to bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and prudent when it comes to the acquiring of any bad, unskillful qualities.

an7.6:5.3.verse: This is called the wealth of prudence.

an7.6:6.1.verse: And what is the wealth of learning?

an7.6:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an7.6:6.3.verse: This is called the wealth of learning.

an7.6:7.1.verse: And what is the wealth of generosity?

an7.6:7.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple lives at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.

an7.6:7.3.verse: This is called the wealth of generosity.

an7.6:8.1.verse: And what is the wealth of wisdom?

an7.6:8.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an7.6:8.3.verse: This is called the wealth of wisdom.

an7.6:9.1.verse: These are the seven kinds of wealth.

an7.6:10.1.verse: Faith and ethical conduct are kinds of wealth,

an7.6:10.4.verse: and wisdom is the seventh kind of wealth.

an7.6:11.4.verse: their life is not in vain.

an7.6:12.1.verse: So let the wise devote themselves

an7.6:12.3.verse: confidence, and insight into the teaching,

an7.6:12.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”

an7.7:1.1.verse: Then Ugga the government chief minister went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an7.7:2.2.verse: Migāra of Rohaṇa is so rich, so very wealthy.”

an7.7:2.4.verse: “He has a hundred thousand gold coins, not to mention the silver coins!”

an7.7:2.5.verse: “Well, Ugga, that is wealth, I can’t deny it.

an7.7:2.6.verse: But fire, water, rulers, thieves, and unloved heirs all take a share of that wealth.

an7.7:2.7.verse: There are these seven kinds of wealth that they can’t take a share of.

an7.7:2.9.verse: The wealth of faith, ethics, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an7.7:2.10.verse: There are these seven kinds of wealth that fire, water, rulers, thieves, and unloved heirs can’t take a share of.

an7.7:3.1.verse: Faith and ethical conduct are kinds of wealth,

an7.7:3.4.verse: and wisdom is the seventh kind of wealth.

an7.7:4.3.verse: they’re really rich in the world,

an7.7:5.1.verse: So let the wise devote themselves

an7.7:5.3.verse: confidence, and insight into the teaching,

an7.7:5.4.verse: remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”

an7.8:1.3.verse: The fetters of attraction, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, desire for continued existence, and ignorance.

an7.9:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the spiritual life is lived to give up and cut out these seven fetters.

an7.9:1.3.verse: The fetters of attraction, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an7.9:1.9.verse: The spiritual life is lived to give up and cut out these seven fetters.

an7.9:1.10.verse: When a mendicant has given up the fetters of attraction, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance—cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future—

an7.9:1.17.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.”

an7.10:1.3.verse: The fetters of attraction, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, jealousy, and stinginess.

an7.11:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven underlying tendencies.

an7.11:1.3.verse: The underlying tendencies of sensual desire, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, desire for continued existence, and ignorance.

an7.11:1.4.verse: These are the seven underlying tendencies.”

an7.12:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the spiritual life is lived to give up and cut out these seven underlying tendencies.

an7.12:1.3.verse: The underlying tendencies of sensual desire, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an7.12:1.9.verse: The spiritual life is lived to give up and cut out these seven underlying tendencies.

an7.12:2.1.verse: When a mendicant has given up the underlying tendencies of sensual desire, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, desire to be reborn, and ignorance—cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future—

an7.12:2.8.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.”

an7.13:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, visiting a family with seven factors is not worthwhile, or if you’ve already arrived, sitting down is not worthwhile.

an7.13:1.3.verse: They don’t politely rise, bow, or offer a seat. They hide what they have. Even when they have much they give little. Even when they have fine things they give coarse things. They give carelessly, not carefully.

an7.13:1.4.verse: Visiting a family with these seven factors is not worthwhile, or if you’ve already arrived, sitting down is not worthwhile.

an7.13:2.1.verse: Visiting a family with seven factors is worthwhile, or if you’ve already arrived, sitting down is worthwhile.

an7.13:2.3.verse: They politely rise, bow, and offer a seat. They don’t hide what they have. When they have much they give much. When they have refined things they give refined things. They give carefully, not carelessly.

an7.13:2.4.verse: Visiting a family with these seven factors is worthwhile, or if you’ve already arrived, sitting down is worthwhile.”

an7.14:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these seven individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

an7.14:1.3.verse: The one freed both ways, the one freed by wisdom, the direct witness, the one attained to view, the one freed by faith, the follower of teachings, and the follower by faith.

an7.14:1.4.verse: These are the seven individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an7.15:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these seven individuals found in the world are like those in water.

an7.15:1.3.verse: One individual sinks under once and stays under.

an7.15:1.4.verse: One individual rises up then sinks under.

an7.15:1.5.verse: One individual rises up then stays put.

an7.15:1.6.verse: One individual rises up then sees and discerns.

an7.15:1.7.verse: One individual rises up then crosses over.

an7.15:1.8.verse: One individual rises up then finds a foothold.

an7.15:1.9.verse: One individual has risen up, crossed over, and gone to the far shore, a brahmin who stands on solid ground.

an7.15:2.1.verse: And what kind of individual sinks under once and stays under?

an7.15:2.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who has absolutely dark, unskillful qualities.

an7.15:2.3.verse: This kind of individual sinks under once and stays under.

an7.15:3.1.verse: And what kind of individual rises up then sinks under?

an7.15:3.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:3.6.verse: However their faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom don’t last or grow, but dwindle away.

an7.15:3.10.verse: This kind of individual rises up then sinks under.

an7.15:4.1.verse: And what kind of individual rises up then stays put?

an7.15:4.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:4.6.verse: And their faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom lasts, neither dwindling nor growing.

an7.15:4.11.verse: This kind of individual rises up then stays put.

an7.15:5.1.verse: And what kind of individual rises up then sees and discerns?

an7.15:5.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:5.6.verse: With the ending of three fetters they’re a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

an7.15:5.7.verse: This kind of individual rises up then sees and discerns.

an7.15:6.1.verse: And what kind of individual rises up then crosses over?

an7.15:6.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:6.6.verse: With the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, they’re a once-returner. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

an7.15:6.7.verse: This kind of individual rises up then crosses over.

an7.15:7.1.verse: And what kind of individual rises up then finds a foothold?

an7.15:7.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:7.6.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re reborn spontaneously. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

an7.15:7.7.verse: This kind of individual rises up then finds a foothold.

an7.15:8.1.verse: And what kind of individual has risen up, crossed over, and gone to the far shore, a brahmin who stands on solid ground?

an7.15:8.2.verse: It’s the kind of individual who, rising up, thinks: ‘It’s good to have faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom regarding skillful qualities.’

an7.15:8.6.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an7.15:8.7.verse: This kind of individual has risen up, crossed over, and gone to the far shore, a brahmin who stands on solid ground.

an7.15:9.1.verse: These seven individuals found in the world are like those in water.”

an7.16:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these seven individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

an7.16:1.3.verse: First, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in all conditions. They perceive impermanence and experience impermanence. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom.

an7.16:1.4.verse: They’ve realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an7.16:2.1.verse: Next, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in all conditions.

an7.16:2.2.verse: Their defilements and their life come to an end at exactly the same time.

an7.16:3.1.verse: Next, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in all conditions.

an7.16:3.2.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished between one life and the next. …

an7.16:3.3.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing. …

an7.16:3.4.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort. …

an7.16:3.5.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort. …

an7.16:3.6.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

an7.16:3.8.verse: These are the seven individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an7.17:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these seven individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

an7.17:1.3.verse: First, take an individual who meditates observing suffering in all conditions. They perceive suffering and experience suffering. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom. …”

an7.18:1.1.verse: “First, take an individual who meditates observing not-self in all things. They perceive not-self and experience not-self. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom. …”

an7.19:1.1.verse: “One meditates observing the happiness in extinguishment. They perceive happiness and experience happiness. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom.

an7.19:1.2.verse: They’ve realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an7.19:1.3.verse: This is the first individual worthy of offerings.

an7.19:2.1.verse: Next, take an individual who meditates observing the happiness in extinguishment. They perceive happiness and experience happiness. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom.

an7.19:2.2.verse: Their defilements and their life come to an end at exactly the same time.

an7.19:3.1.verse: Next, take an individual who meditates observing the happiness in extinguishment. They perceive happiness and experience happiness. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom.

an7.19:3.2.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished between one life and the next. …

an7.19:3.3.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing. …

an7.19:3.4.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort. …

an7.19:3.5.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort. …

an7.19:3.6.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

an7.19:3.8.verse: These are the seven individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an7.20:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven qualifications for graduation.

an7.20:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant has a keen enthusiasm to undertake the training …

an7.20:1.9.verse: to penetrate theoretically. And they don’t lose these desires in the future.

an7.20:1.10.verse: These are the seven qualifications for graduation.”

an7.21:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Sārandada Shrine.

an7.21:1.3.verse: Then several Licchavis went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and the Buddha said to these Licchavis:

an7.21:1.4.verse: “Licchavis, I will teach you these seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.21:1.5.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an7.21:2.1.verse: “And what are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.21:2.2.verse: As long as the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings,

an7.21:2.3.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:3.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony,

an7.21:3.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:4.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the ancient Vajjian principles as they have been decreed,

an7.21:4.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:5.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate Vajjian elders, and think them worth listening to,

an7.21:5.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:6.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis don’t forcibly abduct the women or girls of the clans and make them live with them,

an7.21:6.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:7.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines, whether inner or outer, not neglecting the proper spirit-offerings that were given and made in the past,

an7.21:7.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:8.1.verse: As long as the Vajjis organize proper protection, shelter, and security for perfected ones, so that

an7.21:8.2.verse: more perfected ones might come to the realm and those already here may live in comfort,

an7.21:8.3.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.21:9.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the Vajjis, and as long as the Vajjis are seen following them,

an7.21:9.2.verse: they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.22:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an7.22:1.3.verse: Now at that time King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, wanted to invade the Vajjis.

an7.22:1.5.verse: “I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!”

an7.22:2.1.verse: And then King Ajātasattu addressed Vassakāra the brahmin, a chief minister of Magadha,

an7.22:2.2.verse: “Please, brahmin, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

an7.22:2.5.verse: ‘Sir, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, wants to invade the Vajjis.

an7.22:2.7.verse: “I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!”’

an7.22:2.8.verse: Remember well how the Buddha answers and tell it to me.

an7.22:2.9.verse: For Realized Ones say nothing that is not so.”

an7.22:3.1.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” Vassakāra replied. He went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

an7.22:3.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an7.22:3.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, King Ajātasattu bows with his head to your feet. He asks if you are healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

an7.22:3.4.verse: King Ajātasattu wants to invade the Vajjis.

an7.22:3.6.verse: ‘I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!’”

an7.22:4.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him.

an7.22:4.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to him:

an7.22:4.3.verse: “Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings?”

an7.22:4.5.verse: “As long as the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:5.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony?”

an7.22:5.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:6.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the ancient Vajjian principles as they have been decreed?”

an7.22:6.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the ancient Vajjian principles as they have been decreed, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:7.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate Vajjian elders, and think them worth listening to?”

an7.22:7.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate Vajjian elders, and think them worth listening to, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:8.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis don’t forcibly abduct the women or girls of the clans and make them live with them?”

an7.22:8.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis don’t forcibly abduct the women or girls of the clans and make them live with them, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:9.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines, whether inner or outer, not neglecting the proper spirit-offerings that were given and made in the past?”

an7.22:9.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines, whether inner or outer, not neglecting the proper spirit-offerings that were given and made in the past, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:10.1.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis organize proper protection, shelter, and security for perfected ones, so that more perfected ones might come to the realm and those already here may live in comfort?”

an7.22:10.3.verse: “As long as the Vajjis organize proper protection, shelter, and security for perfected ones, so that more perfected ones might come to the realm and those already here may live in comfort, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.22:11.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Vassakāra:

an7.22:11.2.verse: “Brahmin, this one time I was staying near Vesālī at the Sārandada Shrine.

an7.22:11.3.verse: There I taught the Vajjis these principles that prevent decline.

an7.22:11.4.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the Vajjis, and as long as the Vajjis are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.22:12.1.verse: When the Buddha had spoken, Vassakāra said to him: “Worthy Gotama, if the Vajjis follow even a single one of these principles they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.22:12.2.verse: How much more so all seven!

an7.22:12.3.verse: King Ajātasattu cannot defeat the Vajjis in war, unless by bribery or by sowing dissension.

an7.22:12.4.verse: Well, now, worthy Gotama, I must go. I have many duties, and much to do.”

an7.22:12.6.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, rose from his seat and left.

an7.23:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an7.23:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an7.23:1.4.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you these seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.23:1.5.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an7.23:2.1.verse: “What are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.23:2.2.verse: As long as the mendicants meet frequently and have many meetings, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:3.1.verse: As long as the mendicants meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:4.1.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the training rules as they have been decreed, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:5.1.verse: As long as the mendicants honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the senior mendicants—of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha—and think them worth listening to, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:6.1.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t fall under the sway of arisen craving for future lives, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:7.1.verse: As long as the mendicants take care to live in wilderness lodgings, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:8.1.verse: As long as the mendicants individually establish mindfulness, so that more good-hearted spiritual companions might come, and those that have already come may live comfortably, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.23:9.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.24:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.24:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well …

an7.24:1.3.verse: And what are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.24:2.1.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t relish work, loving it and liking to relish it, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.24:3.1.verse: As long as they don’t enjoy talk …

an7.24:3.4.verse: they don’t have corrupt wishes, falling under the sway of corrupt wishes …

an7.24:3.5.verse: they don’t have bad friends, companions, and associates …

an7.24:3.6.verse: they don’t stop half-way after achieving some trifling distinction, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.24:4.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.25:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.25:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well …

an7.25:1.3.verse: And what are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.25:1.4.verse: As long as the mendicants are faithful …

an7.25:2.6.verse: wise, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.25:3.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.26:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.26:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well …

an7.26:1.3.verse: And what are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.26:1.4.verse: As long as the mendicants develop the awakening factor of mindfulness …

an7.26:2.6.verse: equanimity, they can expect growth, not decline.

an7.26:3.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.27:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.

an7.27:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well …

an7.27:1.3.verse: And what are the seven principles that prevent decline?

an7.27:1.4.verse: As long as the mendicants develop the perception of impermanence …

an7.27:3.1.verse: they can expect growth, not decline. As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

an7.28:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an7.28:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an7.28:1.4.verse: “These seven things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an7.28:1.6.verse: They relish work, talk, sleep, and company. They don’t guard the sense doors and they eat too much. And when there is Saṅgha business to be carried out, they don’t reflect:

an7.28:1.7.verse: ‘There are senior mendicants in the Saṅgha of long standing, long gone forth, responsible. They’ll be known for taking care of this.’ So they get involved in that.

an7.28:1.8.verse: These seven things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an7.28:2.1.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an7.28:2.3.verse: They don’t relish work, talk, sleep, and company. They guard the sense doors and don’t eat too much. And when there is Saṅgha business to be carried out, they reflect:

an7.28:2.4.verse: ‘There are senior mendicants in the Saṅgha of long standing, long gone forth, responsible. They’ll be known for taking care of this.’ So they don’t get involved in that.

an7.28:2.5.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.”

an7.29:1.1.verse: “These seven things lead to the decline of a lay follower.

an7.29:1.3.verse: They miss out on seeing the mendicants.

an7.29:1.4.verse: They neglect listening to the true teaching.

an7.29:1.5.verse: They don’t train in higher ethical conduct.

an7.29:1.6.verse: They’re very suspicious about mendicants, whether senior, junior, or middle.

an7.29:1.7.verse: They listen to the teaching with a hostile, fault-finding mind.

an7.29:1.8.verse: They seek outside of the Buddhist community for those worthy of religious donations.

an7.29:1.10.verse: These seven things lead to the decline of a lay follower.

an7.29:2.1.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a lay follower.

an7.29:2.3.verse: They don’t miss out on seeing the mendicants.

an7.29:2.4.verse: They don’t neglect listening to the true teaching.

an7.29:2.5.verse: They train in higher ethical conduct.

an7.29:2.6.verse: They’re very confident about mendicants, whether senior, junior, or middle.

an7.29:2.7.verse: They don’t listen to the teaching with a hostile, fault-finding mind.

an7.29:2.8.verse: They don’t seek outside of the Buddhist community for those worthy of religious donations.

an7.29:2.9.verse: And they serve the Buddhist community first.

an7.29:2.10.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a lay follower.”

an7.29:2.11.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an7.29:2.12.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

an7.29:3.1.verse: “A lay follower misses out on seeing

an7.29:3.3.verse: and listening to the teachings of the Noble One.

an7.29:3.4.verse: They don’t train in higher ethical conduct,

an7.29:4.3.verse: They want to listen to the true teaching

an7.29:5.1.verse: They seek outside the Buddhist community

an7.29:5.2.verse: for someone else worthy of religious donations,

an7.29:6.1.verse: These seven principles leading to decline

an7.29:6.3.verse: A lay follower who practices them

an7.29:6.4.verse: falls away from the true teaching.

an7.29:7.1.verse: A lay follower doesn’t miss out on seeing

an7.29:7.3.verse: and listening to the teachings of the Noble One.

an7.29:7.4.verse: They train in higher ethical conduct,

an7.29:8.3.verse: They want to listen to the true teaching

an7.29:9.1.verse: They don’t seek outside the Buddhist community

an7.29:9.2.verse: for someone else worthy of religious donations,

an7.29:10.1.verse: These seven principles that prevent decline

an7.29:10.3.verse: A lay follower who practices them

an7.29:10.4.verse: doesn’t fall away from the true teaching.”

an7.30:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven failures for a lay follower …

an7.30:1.2.verse: There are these seven accomplishments for a lay follower …”

an7.31:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these seven downfalls for a lay follower …

an7.31:1.2.verse: There are these seven successes for a lay follower.

an7.31:1.4.verse: They don’t miss out on seeing the mendicants.

an7.31:1.5.verse: They don’t neglect listening to the true teaching.

an7.31:1.6.verse: They train in higher ethical conduct.

an7.31:1.7.verse: They’re very confident about mendicants, whether senior, junior, or middle.

an7.31:1.8.verse: They don’t listen to the teaching with a hostile, fault-finding mind.

an7.31:1.9.verse: They don’t seek outside of the Buddhist community for those worthy of religious donations.

an7.31:1.10.verse: And they serve the Buddhist community first.

an7.31:1.11.verse: These are the seven successes for a lay follower.

an7.31:2.1.verse: A lay follower misses out on seeing

an7.31:2.3.verse: and listening to the teachings of the Noble One.

an7.31:2.4.verse: They don’t train in higher ethical conduct,

an7.31:3.3.verse: They want to listen to the true teaching

an7.31:4.1.verse: They seek outside the Buddhist community

an7.31:4.2.verse: for someone else worthy of religious donations,

an7.31:5.1.verse: These seven principles leading to decline

an7.31:5.3.verse: A lay follower who practices these

an7.31:5.4.verse: falls away from the true teaching.

an7.31:6.1.verse: A lay follower doesn’t miss out on seeing

an7.31:6.3.verse: and listening to the teachings of the Noble One.

an7.31:6.4.verse: They train in higher ethical conduct,

an7.31:7.3.verse: They want to listen to the true teaching

an7.31:8.1.verse: They don’t seek outside the Buddhist community

an7.31:8.2.verse: for someone else worthy of religious donations,

an7.31:9.1.verse: These seven principles that prevent decline

an7.31:9.3.verse: A lay follower who practices them

an7.31:9.4.verse: doesn’t fall away from the true teaching.”

an7.32:1.1.verse: Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him:

an7.32:2.1.verse: “Sir, these seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.

an7.32:2.3.verse: Respect for the Teacher, for the teaching, for the Saṅgha, for the training, for immersion, for diligence, and for hospitality.

an7.32:2.4.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.”

an7.32:2.5.verse: That is what that deity said,

an7.32:2.7.verse: Then that deity, knowing that the Teacher concurred, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

an7.32:3.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened, adding:

an7.32:4.1.verse: “Respect for the Teacher and the teaching,

an7.32:4.2.verse: and keen respect for the Saṅgha;

an7.32:4.4.verse: and keen respect for the training.

an7.32:5.4.verse: and has drawn near to extinguishment.”

an7.33:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, tonight, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, came to me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me:

an7.33:1.2.verse: ‘Sir, these seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.

an7.33:1.4.verse: Respect for the Teacher, for the teaching, for the Saṅgha, for the training, for immersion, for conscience, and for prudence.

an7.33:1.5.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.’

an7.33:1.6.verse: That is what that deity said.

an7.33:1.7.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right side, before vanishing right there.

an7.33:2.1.verse: One respectful of the Teacher and the teaching,

an7.33:3.3.verse: it is impossible for them to decline;

an7.33:3.4.verse: they have drawn near to extinguishment.”

an7.34:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, tonight a deity … said to me:

an7.34:1.2.verse: ‘Sir, these seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.

an7.34:1.4.verse: Respect for the Teacher, for the teaching, for the Saṅgha, for the training, for immersion; being easy to admonish, and good friendship.

an7.34:1.5.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.’

an7.34:1.6.verse: That is what that deity said.

an7.34:1.7.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right side, before vanishing right there.

an7.34:2.1.verse: Respect for the Teacher and the teaching,

an7.34:2.2.verse: and keen respect for the Saṅgha;

an7.34:2.4.verse: and keen respect for the training.

an7.34:3.1.verse: One with good friends, easy to admonish,

an7.34:3.4.verse: and has drawn near to extinguishment.”

an7.35:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, tonight a deity … said to me:

an7.35:1.2.verse: ‘Sir, these seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.

an7.35:1.4.verse: Respect for the Teacher, for the teaching, for the Saṅgha, for the training, for immersion; being easy to admonish, and good friendship.

an7.35:1.5.verse: These seven things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant.’

an7.35:1.6.verse: That is what that deity said.

an7.35:1.7.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right side, before vanishing right there.”

an7.35:2.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Sāriputta said to the Buddha:

an7.35:2.2.verse: “Sir, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.

an7.35:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant personally respects the Teacher and praises such respect.

an7.35:2.4.verse: And they encourage other mendicants who lack such respect to respect the Teacher.

an7.35:2.5.verse: And they praise other mendicants who respect the Teacher at the right time, truthfully and correctly.

an7.35:2.10.verse: They are personally easy to admonish …

an7.35:2.11.verse: They personally have good friends, and praise such friendship.

an7.35:2.12.verse: And they encourage other mendicants who lack good friends to develop good friendship.

an7.35:2.13.verse: And they praise other mendicants who have good friends at the right time, truthfully and correctly.

an7.35:2.14.verse: That’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

an7.35:3.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of what I’ve said in brief like this.

an7.35:3.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant personally respects the Teacher …

an7.35:3.4.verse: And they encourage other mendicants who lack such respect to respect the Teacher.

an7.35:3.5.verse: And they praise other mendicants who respect the Teacher at the right time, truthfully and correctly.

an7.35:3.10.verse: They are personally easy to admonish …

an7.35:3.11.verse: They personally have good friends, and praise such friendship.

an7.35:3.12.verse: And they encourage other mendicants who lack good friends to develop good friendship.

an7.35:3.13.verse: And they praise other mendicants who have good friends at the right time, truthfully and correctly.

an7.35:3.14.verse: This is how to see the detailed meaning of what I said in brief.”

an7.36:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you should associate with a friend who has seven factors.

an7.36:1.3.verse: They give what is hard to give. They do what is hard to do. They endure what is hard to endure. They reveal their secrets to you. They keep your secrets. They don’t abandon you in times of trouble. They don’t look down on you in times of loss.

an7.36:1.4.verse: You should associate with a friend who has these seven factors.

an7.36:2.1.verse: A friend gives what is hard to give,

an7.36:2.2.verse: and does what’s hard to do.

an7.36:2.3.verse: They put up with your harsh words,

an7.36:2.4.verse: and with things hard to endure.

an7.36:3.2.verse: and keep your secrets for you.

an7.36:3.3.verse: They don’t abandon you in times of trouble,

an7.36:3.4.verse: or look down on you in times of loss.

an7.36:4.2.verse: these things are found is your friend.

an7.36:4.3.verse: If you want to have a friend,

an7.36:4.4.verse: you should keep company with that sort.”

an7.37:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a friend has seven qualities you should associate with, accompany, and attend them, even if they drive you away.

an7.37:1.3.verse: They’re liked, agreeable, respected, and admired. They admonish you and they accept admonishment. They speak on deep matters. And they don’t urge you to do bad things.

an7.37:1.4.verse: When a friend has these seven qualities you should associate with, accompany, and attend them, even if they drive you away.

an7.37:2.4.verse: and doesn’t urge you to do bad.

an7.37:3.2.verse: these things are found is your friend.

an7.37:3.3.verse: If you want to have a friend,

an7.37:3.5.verse: then even if they chase you away,

an7.37:3.6.verse: you should keep company with that sort.”

an7.38:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities will soon realize the four kinds of textual analysis and live having achieved them with their own insight.

an7.38:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is mental sluggishness’.

an7.38:1.4.verse: They truly understand internally constricted mind as ‘internally constricted mind’.

an7.38:1.5.verse: They truly understand externally scattered mind as ‘externally scattered mind’.

an7.38:1.6.verse: They know feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an7.38:1.7.verse: They know perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an7.38:1.8.verse: They know thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an7.38:1.9.verse: The patterns of qualities—suitable or unsuitable, inferior or superior, or those with a portion of dark or bright—are properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom.

an7.38:1.10.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities will soon realize the four kinds of textual analysis and live having achieved them with their own insight.”

an7.39:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, having seven qualities, Sāriputta realized the four kinds of textual analysis and lives having achieved them with his own insight.

an7.39:1.3.verse: It’s when Sāriputta truly understood: ‘This is mental sluggishness’.

an7.39:1.4.verse: He truly understood internally constricted mind as ‘internally constricted mind’.

an7.39:1.5.verse: He truly understood externally scattered mind as ‘externally scattered mind’.

an7.39:1.6.verse: He knew feelings, perceptions, and thoughts as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

an7.39:1.9.verse: The patterns of qualities—suitable or unsuitable, inferior or superior, or those with a portion of dark or bright—were properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom.

an7.39:1.10.verse: Having these seven qualities, Sāriputta realized the four kinds of textual analysis and lives having achieved them with his own insight.”

an7.40:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities masters their mind and is not mastered by it.

an7.40:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is skilled at immersion, skilled in entering immersion, skilled in remaining in immersion, skilled in emerging from immersion, skilled in positivity for immersion, skilled in the territory of immersion, and skilled in projecting the mind purified by immersion.

an7.40:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these seven qualities masters their mind and is not mastered by it.”

an7.41:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, having seven qualities Sāriputta has mastered his mind and is not mastered by it.

an7.41:1.3.verse: Sāriputta is skilled at immersion, skilled in entering immersion, skilled in remaining in immersion, skilled in emerging from immersion, skilled in positivity for immersion, skilled in the territory of immersion, and skilled in projecting the mind purified by immersion.

an7.41:1.4.verse: Having these seven qualities Sāriputta has mastered his mind and is not mastered by it.”

an7.42:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

an7.42:1.3.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.

an7.42:1.4.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an7.42:1.5.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

an7.42:1.6.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

an7.42:1.7.verse: Now at that time while those wanderers of other religions were sitting together this discussion came up among them,

an7.42:1.8.verse: “Reverends, anyone who lives the full and pure spiritual life for twelve years is qualified to be called a ‘graduate mendicant’.”

an7.42:2.1.verse: Sāriputta neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.

an7.42:2.2.verse: He rose from his seat, thinking,

an7.42:2.3.verse: “I will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

an7.42:2.4.verse: Then Sāriputta wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding:

an7.42:3.12.verse: “Sir, in this teaching and training can we describe a mendicant as a ‘graduate’ solely because they have completed a certain number of years?”

an7.42:4.2.verse: I make known these seven qualifications for graduation after realizing them with my own insight.

an7.42:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has a keen enthusiasm to undertake the training … to examine the teachings … to get rid of desires … for retreat … to rouse up energy … for mindfulness and alertness … to penetrate theoretically. And they don’t lose these desires in the future.

an7.42:5.3.verse: These are the seven qualifications for graduation that I make known after realizing them with my own insight.

an7.42:5.4.verse: A mendicant who has these seven qualifications for graduation is qualified to be called a ‘graduate mendicant’. This is so whether they have lived the full and pure spiritual life for twelve years,

an7.43:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

an7.43:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

an7.43:1.5.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Kosambī.

an7.43:1.6.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an7.43:1.7.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

an7.43:1.8.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

an7.43:2.1.verse: Now at that time while those wanderers of other religions were sitting together this discussion came up among them,

an7.43:2.2.verse: “Reverends, anyone who lives the full and pure spiritual life for twelve years is qualified to be called a ‘graduate mendicant’.”

an7.43:3.1.verse: Ānanda neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.

an7.43:3.2.verse: He rose from his seat, thinking,

an7.43:3.3.verse: “I will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

an7.43:3.4.verse: Then Ānanda wandered for alms in Kosambī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding:

an7.43:5.6.verse: “Sir, in this teaching and training can we describe a mendicant as a ‘graduate’ solely because they have completed a certain number of years?”

an7.43:6.2.verse: These are the seven qualifications for graduation that I make known after realizing them with my own insight.

an7.43:7.2.verse: It’s when someone is faithful, conscientious, prudent, learned, energetic, mindful, and wise.
