an8.7:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

an8.7:1.2.verse: There the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about Devadatta:

an8.7:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, it’s good for a mendicant to check their own failings from time to time.

an8.7:1.4.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check the failings of others from time to time.

an8.7:1.5.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check their own successes from time to time.

an8.7:1.6.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check the successes of others from time to time.

an8.7:1.7.verse: Overcome and overwhelmed by eight things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.7:2.9.verse: bad friendship, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.7:2.10.verse: Overcome and overwhelmed by these eight things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.7:3.1.verse: It’s good for a mendicant, whenever they encounter it, to overcome gain …

an8.7:4.1.verse: What advantage does a mendicant gain by overcoming these eight things?

an8.7:5.1.verse: The distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without overcoming these eight things do not arise when they have overcome them.

an8.7:5.9.verse: This is the advantage that a mendicant gains by overcoming these eight things.

an8.7:6.1.verse: So, mendicants, you should train like this:

an8.7:6.2.verse: ‘Whenever we encounter it, we will overcome gain …

an8.8:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Uttara was staying on the Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisa region near Dhavajālikā.

an8.8:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, it’s good for a mendicant to check their own failings from time to time.

an8.8:1.4.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check the failings of others from time to time.

an8.8:1.5.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check their own successes from time to time.

an8.8:1.6.verse: It’s good for a mendicant to check the successes of others from time to time.”

an8.8:2.1.verse: Now at that time the great king Vessavaṇa was on his way from the north to the south on some business.

an8.8:2.2.verse: He heard Venerable Uttara teaching this to the mendicants on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain.

an8.8:3.1.verse: Then Vessavaṇa vanished from Saṅkheyyaka Mountain and appeared among the gods of the thirty-three, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm.

an8.8:3.2.verse: Then he went up to Sakka, lord of gods, and said to him:

an8.8:3.3.verse: “Please good fellow, you should know this.

an8.8:3.4.verse: Venerable Uttara is teaching the mendicants on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in this way:

an8.8:3.5.verse: ‘It’s good for a mendicant from time to time to check their own failings. …

an8.8:4.1.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, Sakka vanished from the gods of the thirty-three and reappeared on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in front of Venerable Uttara.

an8.8:4.2.verse: Then Sakka went up to Venerable Uttara, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him:

an8.8:5.1.verse: “Is it really true, sir, that you teach the mendicants in this way:

an8.8:5.2.verse: ‘It’s good for a mendicant from time to time to check their own failings …

an8.8:5.7.verse: “Sir, did this teaching come to you from your own inspiration, or was it spoken by the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

an8.8:5.8.verse: “Well then, lord of gods, I shall give you a simile.

an8.8:5.9.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

an8.8:6.1.verse: Suppose there was a large heap of grain not far from a town or village.

an8.8:6.2.verse: And a large crowd were to take away grain

an8.8:6.3.verse: with carrying poles, baskets, hip sacks, or their cupped hands.

an8.8:6.4.verse: If someone were to go to that crowd and ask them

an8.8:6.5.verse: where they got the grain from, how should that crowd rightly reply?”

an8.8:6.6.verse: “Sir, they should reply that they took it from the large heap of grain.”

an8.8:6.7.verse: “In the same way, lord of gods, whatever is well spoken is spoken by the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an8.8:6.8.verse: Both myself and others rely completely on that when we speak.”

an8.8:7.2.verse: How well this was said by Venerable Uttara!

an8.8:7.3.verse: ‘Whatever is well spoken is spoken by the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an8.8:7.4.verse: Both myself and others rely completely on that when we speak.’

an8.8:7.5.verse: At one time, Honorable Uttara, the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

an8.8:7.6.verse: There the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about Devadatta:

an8.8:8.1.verse: ‘Mendicants, it’s good for a mendicant from time to time to check their own failings …

an8.8:8.5.verse: Overcome and overwhelmed by eight things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.8:8.14.verse: bad friendship, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.8:8.15.verse: Overcome and overwhelmed by these eight things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.

an8.8:9.1.verse: It’s good for a mendicant, whenever they encounter it, to overcome gain …

an8.8:10.1.verse: What advantage does a mendicant gain by overcoming these eight things?

an8.8:11.1.verse: The distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without overcoming these eight things do not arise when they have overcome them.

an8.8:11.9.verse: This is the advantage that a mendicant gains by overcoming these eight things.

an8.8:12.1.verse: So you should train like this:

an8.8:12.2.verse: “Whenever we encounter it, we will overcome gain …

an8.8:13.1.verse: Honorable Uttara, this exposition of the teaching is not established anywhere in the four assemblies—

an8.8:13.4.verse: Sir, learn this exposition of the teaching!

an8.8:13.5.verse: Memorize this exposition of the teaching!

an8.8:13.6.verse: Remember this exposition of the teaching!

an8.8:13.7.verse: Sir, this exposition of the teaching is beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life.”

an8.9:1.5.verse: How could he live the full and pure spiritual life unless he guards the sense doors, eats in moderation, is dedicated to wakefulness, and has mindfulness and situational awareness?

an8.9:1.6.verse: This is how Nanda guards the sense doors.

an8.9:1.7.verse: If he has to look to the east, he wholeheartedly concentrates before looking, thinking:

an8.9:1.8.verse: ‘When I look to the east, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

an8.9:1.9.verse: In this way he’s aware of the situation.

an8.9:2.1.verse: If he has to look to the west …

an8.9:2.6.verse: If he has to survey the intermediate directions, he wholeheartedly concentrates before looking, thinking:

an8.9:2.7.verse: ‘When I survey the intermediate directions, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

an8.9:2.8.verse: In this way he’s aware of the situation.

an8.9:2.9.verse: This is how Nanda guards the sense doors.

an8.9:3.1.verse: This is how Nanda eats in moderation.

an8.9:3.2.verse: Nanda reflects rationally on the food he eats:

an8.9:3.3.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

an8.9:3.4.verse: This is how Nanda eats in moderation.

an8.9:4.1.verse: This is how Nanda is committed to wakefulness.

an8.9:4.2.verse: Nanda practices walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying his mind from obstacles.

an8.9:4.3.verse: In the first watch of the night, he continues to practice walking and sitting meditation.

an8.9:4.4.verse: In the middle watch, he lies down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

an8.9:4.5.verse: In the last watch, he gets up and continues to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying his mind from obstacles.

an8.9:4.6.verse: This is how Nanda is committed to wakefulness.

an8.9:5.1.verse: This is how Nanda has mindfulness and situational awareness.

an8.9:5.2.verse: Nanda knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an8.9:5.3.verse: He knows perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an8.9:5.4.verse: He knows thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

an8.9:5.5.verse: This is how Nanda has mindfulness and situational awareness.

an8.9:6.1.verse: How could Nanda live the full and pure spiritual life unless he guards the sense doors, eats in moderation, is dedicated to wakefulness, and has mindfulness and situational awareness?”

an8.10:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.

an8.10:1.2.verse: Now at that time the mendicants accused a mendicant of an offense.

an8.10:1.3.verse: The accused mendicant dodged the issue, distracted the discussion with irrelevant points, and displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

an8.10:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

an8.10:2.4.verse: This individual should be shown the door.

an8.10:2.5.verse: Why should you be vexed by an outsider?

an8.10:2.6.verse: Take a case where a certain individual looks just the same as other good-natured mendicants when going out and coming back, when looking ahead and aside, when bending and extending the limbs, and when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes.

an8.10:2.7.verse: That is, so long as the mendicants don’t notice his offense.

an8.10:2.8.verse: But when the mendicants notice the offense, they know that he’s

an8.10:2.9.verse: a corrupt ascetic, just useless trash.

an8.10:2.10.verse: When they realize this they send him away.

an8.10:2.12.verse: So that he doesn’t corrupt good-natured mendicants.

an8.10:3.1.verse: Suppose in a growing field of barley some bad barley appeared, just useless trash.

an8.10:3.2.verse: Its roots, stem, and leaves would look just the same as the healthy barley.

an8.10:3.5.verse: That is, so long as the head doesn’t appear.

an8.10:3.6.verse: But when the head appears, they know that it’s

an8.10:3.8.verse: When they realize this they pull it up by the roots and throw it outside the field.

an8.10:3.10.verse: So that it doesn’t spoil the good barley.

an8.10:4.1.verse: In the same way, take a case where a certain individual looks just the same as other good-natured mendicants when going out and coming back, when looking ahead and aside, when bending and extending the limbs, and when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes.

an8.10:4.2.verse: That is, so long as the mendicants don’t notice his offense.

an8.10:4.3.verse: But when the mendicants notice the offense, they know that he’s

an8.10:4.4.verse: a corrupt ascetic, just useless trash.

an8.10:4.5.verse: When they realize this they send him away.

an8.10:4.7.verse: So that he doesn’t corrupt good-natured mendicants.

an8.10:5.1.verse: Suppose that a large heap of grain is being winnowed. The grains that are firm and solid form a heap on one side. And the grains that are flimsy and insubstantial are blown over to the other side.

an8.10:5.2.verse: The owners take a broom and sweep them even further away.

an8.10:5.4.verse: So that it doesn’t spoil the good grain.

an8.10:5.5.verse: In the same way, take a case where a certain individual looks just the same as other good-natured mendicants when going out and coming back, when looking ahead and aside, when bending and extending the limbs, and when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes.

an8.10:5.6.verse: That is, so long as the mendicants don’t notice his offense.

an8.10:5.7.verse: But when the mendicants notice the offense, they know that he’s

an8.10:5.8.verse: a corrupt ascetic, just useless trash.

an8.10:5.9.verse: When they realize this they send him away.

an8.10:5.11.verse: So that he doesn’t corrupt good-natured mendicants.

an8.10:6.1.verse: Suppose a man needs an irrigation gutter for a well. He’d take a sharp axe and enter the wood,

an8.10:6.2.verse: where he’d knock various trees with the axe. The trees that were firm and solid made a cracking sound.

an8.10:6.3.verse: But the trees that were rotten inside, decomposing and decayed, made a thud.

an8.10:6.4.verse: He’d cut down such a tree at the root, lop off the crown, and thoroughly clear out the insides. Then he’d use it as an irrigation gutter for the well.

an8.10:6.5.verse: In the same way, take a case where a certain individual looks just the same as other good-natured mendicants when going out and coming back, when looking ahead and aside, when bending and extending the limbs, and when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes.

an8.10:6.6.verse: That is, so long as the mendicants don’t notice his offense.

an8.10:6.7.verse: But when the mendicants notice the offense, they know that he’s

an8.10:6.8.verse: a corrupt ascetic, just useless trash.

an8.10:6.9.verse: When they realize this they send him away.

an8.10:6.11.verse: So that he doesn’t corrupt good-natured mendicants.

an8.10:8.1.verse: They speak to people with a voice

an8.10:8.2.verse: so smooth, just like an ascetic.

an8.10:8.3.verse: But they act in secret, with their bad views

an8.10:8.4.verse: and their lack of regard for others.

an8.10:9.1.verse: You should recognize them for what they are:

an8.10:10.4.verse: they’re not ascetics, they just think they are.

an8.10:11.1.verse: When you’ve thrown out those of corrupt wishes,

an8.10:11.6.verse: you’ll make an end of suffering.”

an8.11:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in Verañjā at the root of a neem tree dedicated to Naḷeru.

an8.11:1.3.verse: Then the brahmin Verañja went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an8.11:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an8.11:2.2.verse: the ascetic Gotama doesn’t bow to old brahmins, the elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.

an8.11:2.3.verse: And this is indeed the case,

an8.11:2.4.verse: for the worthy Gotama does not bow to old brahmins, elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise in their presence or offer them a seat.

an8.11:2.5.verse: This is not appropriate, worthy Gotama.”

an8.11:2.6.verse: “Brahmin, I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—for whom I should bow down or rise up or offer a seat.

an8.11:2.7.verse: If the Realized One bowed down or rose up or offered a seat to anyone, their head would explode!”

an8.11:3.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say

an8.11:3.4.verse: For the Realized One has given up taste for sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:3.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I lack taste.

an8.11:3.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:4.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say

an8.11:4.4.verse: For the Realized One has given up delight in sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:4.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m indelicate.

an8.11:4.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:5.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama is a teacher of inaction.”

an8.11:5.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:5.4.verse: For I teach inaction regarding bad bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.11:5.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m a teacher of inaction.

an8.11:5.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:6.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama is a teacher of annihilationism.”

an8.11:6.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:6.4.verse: For I teach the annihilation of greed, hate, and delusion, and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.11:6.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m a teacher of annihilationism.

an8.11:6.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:7.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:7.4.verse: For I’m disgusted by bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and by attainment of the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.11:7.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m disgusted.

an8.11:7.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:8.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:8.4.verse: For I teach the extermination of greed, hate, and delusion, and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.11:8.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m an exterminator.

an8.11:8.6.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:9.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:9.4.verse: For I say that bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind should be mortified.

an8.11:9.5.verse: I say that a mortifier is someone who has given up unskillful qualities that should be mortified. They’ve cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:9.6.verse: The Realized One is someone who has given up unskillful qualities that should be mortified. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:9.7.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m a mortifier.

an8.11:9.8.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.”

an8.11:10.2.verse: “There is, brahmin, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.11:10.4.verse: I say that a gutless person is someone who has given up future wombs and regeneration into a new state of existence. They’ve cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:10.5.verse: The Realized One has given up future wombs and regeneration into a new state of existence. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.11:10.6.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I am gutless.

an8.11:10.7.verse: But that’s not what you’re talking about.

an8.11:11.1.verse: Suppose, brahmin, there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs.

an8.11:11.2.verse: And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

an8.11:11.3.verse: Now, the chick that is first to break out of the eggshell with its claws and beak and hatch safely: should that be called the eldest or the youngest?”

an8.11:11.4.verse: “Worthy Gotama, that should be called the eldest. For it is the eldest among them.”

an8.11:12.1.verse: “In the same way, in this population lost in ignorance, swaddled in their shells, I alone have broken open the egg of ignorance and realized the supreme perfect awakening.

an8.11:12.2.verse: So, brahmin, I am the eldest and the first in the world.

an8.11:13.1.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and lucid, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind was immersed and unified in samādhi.

an8.11:13.2.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an8.11:13.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an8.11:13.4.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, I entered and remained in the third absorption, where I meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

an8.11:13.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an8.11:14.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives.

an8.11:14.2.verse: I recollected many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. I remembered: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so I recollected my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

an8.11:15.1.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

an8.11:15.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an8.11:15.3.verse: This was my first breaking out, like a chick breaking out of the eggshell.

an8.11:16.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

an8.11:16.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an8.11:17.1.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night.

an8.11:17.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an8.11:17.3.verse: This was my second breaking out, like a chick breaking out of the eggshell.

an8.11:18.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

an8.11:18.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

an8.11:18.3.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

an8.11:18.4.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

an8.11:18.5.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

an8.11:18.6.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.’

an8.11:19.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night.

an8.11:19.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

an8.11:19.3.verse: This was my third breaking out, like a chick breaking out of the eggshell.”

an8.11:20.1.verse: When he said this, the brahmin Verañja said to the Buddha:

an8.11:20.2.verse: “The worthy Gotama is the eldest! The worthy Gotama is the best!

an8.11:20.4.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

an8.11:20.5.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an8.11:20.6.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an8.12:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an8.12:1.2.verse: Now at that time several very prominent Licchavis were sitting together at the town hall, praising the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha in many ways.

an8.12:2.1.verse: Now at that time General Sīha, a disciple of the Jains, was sitting in that assembly.

an8.12:2.3.verse: “That Blessed One must without a doubt be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. For several very prominent Licchavis are praising the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha in many ways.

an8.12:2.4.verse: Why don’t I go to see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!”

an8.12:2.5.verse: Then General Sīha went to the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan and said to him,

an8.12:2.6.verse: “Sir, I’d like to go to see the ascetic Gotama.”

an8.12:3.1.verse: “But Sīha, you believe in the doctrine of action. Why should you go to see the ascetic Gotama, who teaches a doctrine of inaction?

an8.12:3.2.verse: For the ascetic Gotama believes in a doctrine of inaction, he teaches inaction, and he guides his disciples in that way.”

an8.12:3.3.verse: Then Sīha’s determination to go and see the Buddha died down.

an8.12:4.1.verse: For a second time, several prominent Licchavis were sitting together at the town hall, praising the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha in many ways.

an8.12:4.2.verse: And for a second time Sīha thought:

an8.12:4.4.verse: “Why don’t I go to see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!”

an8.12:4.5.verse: Then General Sīha went to the Jain Ñātika …

an8.12:5.3.verse: Then for a second time Sīha’s determination to go and see the Buddha died down.

an8.12:6.1.verse: For a third time, several prominent Licchavis were sitting together at the town hall, praising the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha in many ways.

an8.12:6.2.verse: And for a third time Sīha thought,

an8.12:6.3.verse: “That Blessed One must without a doubt be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. For several very prominent Licchavis are praising the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha in many ways.

an8.12:6.4.verse: What can these Jains do to me, whether I take leave of them or not?

an8.12:6.5.verse: Why don’t I, without taking leave of them, go to see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!”

an8.12:7.1.verse: Then Sīha, with around five hundred chariots, set out from Vesālī in the middle of the day to see the Buddha.

an8.12:7.2.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and went by foot.

an8.12:7.3.verse: Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an8.12:8.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama believes in a doctrine of inaction, he teaches inaction, and he guides his disciples in that way.’

an8.12:8.3.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the Buddha has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?

an8.12:8.4.verse: For we don’t want to misrepresent the Blessed One.”

an8.12:9.1.verse: “There is, Sīha, a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:9.2.verse: I believe in inaction, I teach inaction, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:10.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:10.2.verse: I believe in action, I teach action, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:11.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:11.2.verse: I believe in annihilationism, I teach annihilation, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:12.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:12.2.verse: I’m disgusted, I teach disgust, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:13.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:13.2.verse: I’m an exterminator, I teach extermination, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:14.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:14.2.verse: I’m a mortifier, I teach mortification, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:15.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:15.2.verse: I’m gutless, I teach gutlessness, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:16.1.verse: And there is a sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:16.2.verse: I’m ambitious, I teach ambition, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:17.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:17.2.verse: I believe in inaction, I teach inaction, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:17.3.verse: I teach inaction regarding bad bodily, verbal, and mental conduct,

an8.12:17.4.verse: and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.12:17.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I teach inaction.

an8.12:18.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:18.2.verse: I believe in action, I teach action, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:18.3.verse: I teach action regarding good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct,

an8.12:18.4.verse: and the many kinds of skillful things.

an8.12:18.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I teach action.

an8.12:19.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:19.2.verse: I believe in annihilationism, I teach annihilation, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:19.3.verse: I teach the annihilation of greed, hate, and delusion,

an8.12:19.4.verse: and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.12:19.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I teach annihilationism.

an8.12:20.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:20.2.verse: I’m disgusted, I teach disgust, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:20.3.verse: I’m disgusted by bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind,

an8.12:20.4.verse: and by attainment of the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.12:20.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m disgusted.

an8.12:21.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:21.2.verse: I’m an exterminator, I teach extermination, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:21.3.verse: I teach the extermination of greed, hate, and delusion,

an8.12:21.4.verse: and the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.12:21.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m an exterminator.

an8.12:22.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:22.2.verse: I’m a mortifier, I teach mortification, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:22.3.verse: I say that bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind should be mortified.

an8.12:22.4.verse: I say that a mortifier is someone who has given up unskillful qualities that should be mortified. They’ve cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.12:22.5.verse: The Realized One is someone who has given up unskillful qualities that should be mortified. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.12:22.6.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m a mortifier.

an8.12:23.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:23.2.verse: I’m gutless, I teach gutlessness, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:23.3.verse: I say that a gutless person is someone who has given up future wombs and rebirth into a new state of existence. They’ve cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.12:23.4.verse: The Realized One has given up future wombs and regeneration into a new state of existence. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so that they’re unable to arise in the future.

an8.12:23.5.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m gutless.

an8.12:24.1.verse: And what’s the sense in which you could rightly say that

an8.12:24.2.verse: I’m ambitious, I teach ambition, and I guide my disciples in that way?

an8.12:24.3.verse: I’m ambitious to offer solace, the highest solace, I teach solace, and I guide my disciples in that way.

an8.12:24.4.verse: In this sense you could rightly say that I’m ambitious.”

an8.12:25.1.verse: When he said this, General Sīha said to the Buddha,

an8.12:25.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an8.12:26.1.verse: “Sīha, you should act after careful consideration. It’s good for well-known people such as yourself to act after careful consideration.”

an8.12:26.2.verse: “Now I’m even more delighted and satisfied with the Buddha, since he tells me to act after careful consideration.

an8.12:26.3.verse: For if the followers of other religions were to gain me as a disciple, they’d carry a banner all over Vesālī, saying:

an8.12:26.5.verse: And yet the Buddha tells me to act after careful consideration.

an8.12:26.6.verse: For a second time, I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an8.12:26.7.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an8.12:27.1.verse: “For a long time now, Sīha, your family has been a well-spring of support for the Jain ascetics. You should consider giving to them when they come.”

an8.12:27.2.verse: “Now I’m even more delighted and satisfied with the Buddha, since he tells me to

an8.12:27.3.verse: consider giving to the Jain ascetics when they come.

an8.12:27.6.verse: ‘Gifts should only be given to me, and to my disciples.

an8.12:27.7.verse: Only what is given to me is very fruitful, not what is given to others.

an8.12:27.8.verse: Only what is given to my disciples is very fruitful, not what is given to the disciples of others.’

an8.12:27.9.verse: Yet the Buddha encourages me to give to the Jain ascetics.

an8.12:27.10.verse: Well, sir, we’ll know the proper time for that.

an8.12:27.11.verse: For a third time, I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

an8.12:27.12.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

an8.12:28.1.verse: Then the Buddha taught Sīha step by step, with

an8.12:28.2.verse: a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

an8.12:28.3.verse: And when the Buddha knew that Sīha’s mind was ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

an8.12:28.4.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

an8.12:28.5.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

an8.12:28.6.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in General Sīha:

an8.12:28.7.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

an8.12:29.1.verse: Then Sīha saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. He went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. He said to the Buddha,

an8.12:29.2.verse: “Sir, would the Buddha together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

an8.12:29.4.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Sīha rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an8.12:30.1.verse: Then Sīha addressed a certain man,

an8.12:30.2.verse: “My man, please find out if there is any meat ready for sale.”

an8.12:30.3.verse: And when the night had passed General Sīha had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own home. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

an8.12:30.4.verse: “Sir, it’s time. The meal is ready.”

an8.12:31.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Sīha’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.

an8.12:31.2.verse: Now at that time many Jain ascetics in Vesālī went from street to street and from square to square, calling out with raised arms:

an8.12:31.3.verse: “Today General Sīha has slaughtered a fat calf for the ascetic Gotama’s meal.

an8.12:31.4.verse: The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared specially for him: this is a deed he caused.”

an8.12:32.1.verse: Then a certain person went up to Sīha and whispered in his ear,

an8.12:32.3.verse: Many Jain ascetics in Vesālī are going from street to street and square to square, calling out with raised arms:

an8.12:32.4.verse: ‘Today General Sīha has slaughtered a fat calf for the ascetic Gotama’s meal.

an8.12:32.5.verse: The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared specially for him: this is a deed he caused.’”

an8.12:32.6.verse: “Enough, master. For a long time those venerables have wanted to discredit the Buddha, his teaching, and his Saṅgha.

an8.12:32.7.verse: They’ll never stop misrepresenting the Buddha with their incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claims.

an8.12:32.8.verse: We would never deliberately take the life of a living creature, not even for life’s sake.”

an8.12:33.1.verse: Then Sīha served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

an8.12:33.2.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Sīha sat down to one side.

an8.12:33.3.verse: Then the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk, after which he rose from his seat and left.

an8.13:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a fine royal thoroughbred with eight factors is worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, and reckoned a factor of kingship.

an8.13:1.3.verse: It’s when a fine royal thoroughbred is well born on both

an8.13:1.4.verse: the mother’s and the father’s sides.

an8.13:1.5.verse: He’s bred in the region fine thoroughbreds come from.

an8.13:1.8.verse: he eats carefully, without making a mess.

an8.13:1.9.verse: He’s disgusted by sitting or lying down in excrement or urine.

an8.13:1.10.verse: He’s gentle and pleasant to live with, and he doesn’t upset the other horses.

an8.13:1.11.verse: He openly shows his tricks, bluffs, ruses, and feints to his trainer,

an8.13:1.12.verse: so the trainer can try to subdue them.

an8.13:1.14.verse: ‘Whether or not the other horses carry their loads, I’ll carry mine.’

an8.13:1.15.verse: He always walks in a straight path.

an8.13:1.16.verse: He’s strong, and stays strong even until death.

an8.13:1.17.verse: A fine royal thoroughbred with these eight factors is worthy of a king. …

an8.13:2.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant with eight qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an8.13:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an8.13:2.7.verse: They’re disgusted with bad conduct by way of body, speech, or mind,

an8.13:2.8.verse: and by attainment of the many kinds of unskillful things.

an8.13:2.9.verse: They’re gentle and pleasant to live with, and they don’t upset the other mendicants.

an8.13:2.10.verse: They openly show their tricks, bluffs, ruses, and feints to their sensible spiritual companions,

an8.13:2.11.verse: so they can try to subdue them.

an8.13:2.13.verse: ‘Whether or not the other mendicants do their training, I’ll do mine.’

an8.13:2.14.verse: They always walk in a straight path.

an8.13:2.15.verse: And here the straight path is

an8.13:2.16.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an8.13:2.18.verse: ‘Gladly, let my skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the blood and flesh waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.’

an8.13:2.19.verse: A mendicant with these eight qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of veneration with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an8.14:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you about eight wild colts and eight defects in horses, and about eight wild people and eight defects in people.

an8.14:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an8.14:2.1.verse: “And what, mendicants, are the eight wild colts and eight defects in horses?

an8.14:2.2.verse: Firstly, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts back right up and spin the chariot behind them.

an8.14:2.3.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:2.4.verse: This is the first defect of a horse.

an8.14:3.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts jump back, wreck the hub, and break the triple rod.

an8.14:3.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:3.3.verse: This is the second defect of a horse.

an8.14:4.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts shake the draft-pole off their thigh and trample it.

an8.14:4.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:4.3.verse: This is the third defect of a horse.

an8.14:5.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts take a wrong turn, sending the chariot off track.

an8.14:5.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:5.3.verse: This is the fourth defect of a horse.

an8.14:6.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts rear up and strike out with their fore-legs.

an8.14:6.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:6.3.verse: This is the fifth defect of a horse.

an8.14:7.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts ignore the trainer and the goad, spit out the bit, and go wherever they want.

an8.14:7.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:7.3.verse: This is the sixth defect of a horse.

an8.14:8.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts don’t step forward or turn back but stand right there still as a post.

an8.14:8.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:8.3.verse: This is the seventh defect of a horse.

an8.14:9.1.verse: Furthermore, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, some wild colts tuck in their fore-legs and hind-legs, and sit right down on their four legs.

an8.14:9.2.verse: Some wild colts are like that.

an8.14:9.3.verse: This is the eighth defect of a horse.

an8.14:9.4.verse: These are the eight wild colts and the eight defects in horses.

an8.14:10.1.verse: And what are the eight wild people and eight defects in people?

an8.14:10.2.verse: Firstly, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:10.3.verse: But the accused mendicant evades it by saying they don’t remember.

an8.14:10.4.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, back right up and spin the chariot behind them.

an8.14:10.6.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:10.7.verse: This is the first defect of a person.

an8.14:11.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:11.2.verse: But the accused mendicant objects to the accuser:

an8.14:11.3.verse: ‘What has an incompetent fool like you got to say?

an8.14:11.4.verse: How on earth could you imagine you’ve got something worth saying!’

an8.14:11.5.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, jump back, wreck the hub, and break the triple rod.

an8.14:11.7.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:11.8.verse: This is the second defect of a person.

an8.14:12.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:12.2.verse: But the accused mendicant retorts to the accuser:

an8.14:12.3.verse: ‘Well, you’ve fallen into an offense named such-and-such. You should deal with that first.’

an8.14:12.4.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, shake the draft-pole off their thigh and trample it.

an8.14:12.6.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:12.7.verse: This is the third defect of a person.

an8.14:13.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:13.2.verse: But the accused mendicant dodges the issue, distracts the discussion with irrelevant points, and displays annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

an8.14:13.3.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, take a wrong turn, sending the chariot off track.

an8.14:13.5.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:13.6.verse: This is the fourth defect of a person.

an8.14:14.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:14.2.verse: But the accused mendicant gesticulates while speaking in the middle of the Saṅgha.

an8.14:14.3.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, rear up and strike out with their fore-legs.

an8.14:14.5.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:14.6.verse: This is the fifth defect of a person.

an8.14:15.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:15.2.verse: But the accused mendicant ignores the Saṅgha and the accusation and, though still guilty of the offense, they go wherever they want.

an8.14:15.3.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, ignore the trainer and the goad, spit out the bit, and go wherever they want.

an8.14:15.5.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:15.6.verse: This is the sixth defect of a person.

an8.14:16.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:16.2.verse: But the accused mendicant neither confesses to the offense nor denies it, but frustrates the Saṅgha by staying silent.

an8.14:16.3.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, don’t step forward or turn back but stand right there still as a post.

an8.14:16.5.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:16.6.verse: This is the seventh defect of a person.

an8.14:17.1.verse: Furthermore, the mendicants accuse a mendicant of an offense.

an8.14:17.2.verse: But the accused mendicant says this:

an8.14:17.3.verse: ‘Why are you venerables making so much of an issue over me? Now I’ll resign the training and return to a lesser life.’

an8.14:17.4.verse: When they have resigned the training, they say:

an8.14:17.6.verse: I say that this individual is comparable to the wild colts who, when the trainer says ‘giddyup!’ and spurs and goads them on, tuck in their fore-legs and hind-legs, and sit right down on their four legs.

an8.14:17.8.verse: Some wild people are like that.

an8.14:17.9.verse: This is the eighth defect of a person.

an8.14:17.10.verse: These are the eight wild people and eight defects in people.”

an8.15:1.3.verse: Not rehearsing is the stain of hymns.

an8.15:1.4.verse: Neglect is the stain of houses.

an8.15:1.5.verse: Laziness is the stain of beauty.

an8.15:1.9.verse: Bad, unskillful qualities are a stain in this world and the next.

an8.15:1.10.verse: Worse than any of these is ignorance, the worst stain of all.

an8.15:2.1.verse: Not rehearsing is the stain of hymns.

an8.15:2.2.verse: The stain of houses is neglect.

an8.15:2.3.verse: Laziness is the stain of beauty.

an8.15:3.4.verse: in this world and the next.

an8.15:3.5.verse: But a worse stain than these

an8.15:3.6.verse: is ignorance, the worst stain of all.”

an8.16:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with eight qualities is worthy of going on a mission.

an8.16:1.3.verse: It’s a mendicant who learns and educates others. They memorize and remember. They understand and help others understand. They’re skilled at knowing what’s on topic and what isn’t. And they don’t cause quarrels.

an8.16:1.4.verse: A mendicant with these eight qualities is worthy of going on a mission.

an8.19:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in Verañjā at the root of a neem tree dedicated to Naḷeru.

an8.19:1.2.verse: Then Pahārāda, lord of titans, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to him,

an8.19:2.1.verse: “Well, Pahārāda, do the titans love the ocean?”

an8.19:2.3.verse: “But seeing what incredible and amazing things do the titans love the ocean?”

an8.19:2.4.verse: “Sir, seeing eight incredible and amazing things the titans love the ocean.

an8.19:2.6.verse: The ocean gradually slants, slopes, and inclines, with no abrupt precipice.

an8.19:2.8.verse: This is the first thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:3.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean is consistent and doesn’t overflow its boundaries.

an8.19:3.3.verse: This is the second thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:4.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean doesn’t accommodate a carcass, but quickly carries it to the shore and strands it on the beach.

an8.19:4.3.verse: This is the third thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:5.1.verse: Furthermore, when they reach the ocean, all the great rivers—that is,

an8.19:5.2.verse: the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—lose their names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘the ocean’.

an8.19:5.4.verse: This is the fourth thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:6.1.verse: Furthermore, for all the world’s streams that reach it, and the showers that fall from the sky, the ocean never empties or fills up.

an8.19:6.3.verse: This is the fifth thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:7.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean has just one taste, the taste of salt.

an8.19:7.3.verse: This is the sixth thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:8.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean is full of many kinds of treasures, such as pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, native gold, rubies, and emeralds.

an8.19:8.3.verse: This is the seventh thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:9.1.verse: Furthermore, many great beings live in the ocean, such as leviathans, leviathan-gulpers, leviathan-gulper-gulpers, titans, dragons, and centaurs. In the ocean there are life-forms a hundred leagues long, or even two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred leagues long.

an8.19:9.3.verse: This is the eighth thing the titans love about the ocean.

an8.19:9.4.verse: Seeing these eight incredible and amazing things the titans love the ocean.

an8.19:10.1.verse: Well, sir, do the mendicants love this teaching and training?”

an8.19:10.3.verse: “But seeing how many incredible and amazing things do the mendicants love this teaching and training?”

an8.19:10.4.verse: “Seeing eight incredible and amazing things, Pahārāda, the mendicants love this teaching and training.

an8.19:10.6.verse: The ocean gradually slants, slopes, and inclines, with no abrupt precipice.

an8.19:10.7.verse: In the same way in this teaching and training the penetration to enlightenment comes from gradual training, progress, and practice, not abruptly.

an8.19:10.9.verse: This is the first thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:11.1.verse: The ocean is consistent and doesn’t overflow its boundaries.

an8.19:11.2.verse: In the same way, when a training rule is laid down for my disciples they wouldn’t break it even for the sake of their own life.

an8.19:11.4.verse: This is the second thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:12.1.verse: The ocean doesn’t accommodate a carcass, but quickly carries it to the shore and strands it on the beach.

an8.19:13.1.verse: In the same way, the Saṅgha doesn’t accommodate an individual who is unethical, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved. But they quickly gather and expel them. Even if they are sitting in the middle of the Saṅgha, they’re far from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from them.

an8.19:13.3.verse: This is the third thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:14.1.verse: When they reach the ocean, all the great rivers—that is, the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—lose their names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘the ocean’.

an8.19:14.2.verse: In the same way, when they go forth from the lay life to homelessness, all four classes—aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials—lose their former names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘ascetics who follow the Sakyan’.

an8.19:14.4.verse: This is the fourth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:15.1.verse: For all the world’s streams that reach it, and the showers that fall from the sky, the ocean never empties or fills up.

an8.19:15.2.verse: In the same way, though several mendicants become fully extinguished in the element of extinguishment with no residue, the element of extinguishment never empties or fills up.

an8.19:15.4.verse: This is the fifth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:16.1.verse: The ocean has just one taste, the taste of salt.

an8.19:16.2.verse: In the same way, this teaching and training has one taste, the taste of freedom.

an8.19:16.4.verse: This is the sixth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:17.1.verse: The ocean is full of many kinds of treasures, such as pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, native gold, rubies, and emeralds.

an8.19:17.2.verse: In the same way, this teaching and training is full of many kinds of treasures, such as the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

an8.19:17.4.verse: This is the seventh thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:18.1.verse: Many great beings live in the ocean, such as leviathans, leviathan-gulpers, leviathan-gulper-gulpers, titans, dragons, and centaurs. In the ocean there are life-forms a hundred leagues long, or even two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred leagues long.

an8.19:18.2.verse: In the same way, great beings live in this teaching and training, and these are those beings. The stream-enterer and the one practicing to realize the fruit of stream-entry. The once-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of once-return. The non-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of non-return. The perfected one, and the one practicing for perfection.

an8.19:18.4.verse: This is the eighth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

an8.19:19.1.verse: Seeing these eight incredible and amazing things, Pahārāda, the mendicants love this teaching and training.”

an8.20:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

an8.20:1.2.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath, and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

an8.20:1.3.verse: And then, as the night was getting late, in the first watch of the night, Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

an8.20:1.4.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the first watch of the night, and the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting long.

an8.20:1.5.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

an8.20:2.1.verse: But when he said this, the Buddha kept silent.

an8.20:2.2.verse: For a second time, as the night was getting late, in the middle watch of the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

an8.20:2.3.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the middle watch of the night, and the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting long.

an8.20:2.4.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

an8.20:2.5.verse: But for a second time the Buddha kept silent.

an8.20:2.6.verse: For a third time, as the night was getting late, in the last watch of the night, as dawn stirred, bringing joy to the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

an8.20:2.7.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the last watch of the night and dawn stirs, bringing joy to the night.

an8.20:2.8.verse: And the Saṅgha has been sitting long.

an8.20:2.9.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

an8.20:3.4.verse: Then he focused on encompassing the minds of everyone in the Saṅgha.

an8.20:3.5.verse: He saw that unethical individual, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved, sitting in the middle of the Saṅgha.

an8.20:3.6.verse: When he saw him he rose from his seat, went up to him and said,

an8.20:3.7.verse: “Get up, reverend. The Buddha has seen you.

an8.20:3.8.verse: You can’t live in communion with the monks.”

an8.20:4.1.verse: But when he said this, that individual kept silent.

an8.20:4.7.verse: he asked that monk to leave.

an8.20:4.9.verse: But for a third time that individual kept silent.

an8.20:5.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna took that individual by the arm, ejected him out the gate, and bolted the door. Then he went up to the Buddha, and said to him,

an8.20:5.4.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

an8.20:5.6.verse: how that futile man waited to be taken by the arm!”

an8.20:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the monks:

an8.20:6.2.verse: “Now, monks, you should perform the sabbath and recite the monastic code.

an8.20:6.3.verse: From this day forth, I will not perform the sabbath or recite the monastic code.

an8.20:6.4.verse: It’s impossible, monks, it can’t happen that a Realized One could recite the monastic code in an impure assembly.

an8.21:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an8.21:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an8.21:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, you should remember the householder Ugga of Vesālī as someone who has eight amazing and incredible qualities.”

an8.21:1.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an8.21:1.5.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

an8.21:2.1.verse: Then a certain mendicant robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Ugga of Vesālī, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an8.21:2.2.verse: Then Ugga of Vesālī went up to that mendicant, bowed, and sat down to one side. The mendicant said to him:

an8.21:3.1.verse: “Householder, the Buddha declared that you have eight amazing and incredible qualities.

an8.21:3.2.verse: What are the eight qualities that he spoke of?”

an8.21:3.4.verse: what eight amazing and incredible qualities the Buddha was referring to.

an8.21:3.5.verse: But these eight amazing and incredible qualities are found in me.

an8.21:3.6.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an8.21:3.9.verse: “Sir, when I first saw the Buddha off in the distance,

an8.21:3.10.verse: my heart was inspired as soon as I saw him.

an8.21:3.11.verse: This is the first incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:4.1.verse: With confident heart I paid homage to the Buddha.

an8.21:4.2.verse: The Buddha taught me step by step,

an8.21:4.3.verse: with a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

an8.21:4.4.verse: And when he knew that my mind was ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

an8.21:4.5.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

an8.21:4.6.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

an8.21:4.7.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in me:

an8.21:4.8.verse: ‘Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.’

an8.21:4.9.verse: I saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. I went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions.

an8.21:4.10.verse: Right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, his teaching, and the Saṅgha. And I undertook the five training rules with chastity as the fifth.

an8.21:4.11.verse: This is the second incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:5.2.verse: And I went to them and said:

an8.21:5.3.verse: ‘Sisters, I’ve undertaken the five training rules with chastity as fifth.

an8.21:5.4.verse: If you wish, you may stay here, enjoy my wealth, and do good deeds. Or you can return to your own families.

an8.21:5.5.verse: Or would you prefer if I gave you to another man?’

an8.21:5.6.verse: When I said this, my eldest wife said to me:

an8.21:5.7.verse: ‘Master, please give me to a man named so-and-so.’

an8.21:5.8.verse: Then I summoned that man. Taking my wife with my left hand and a ceremonial vase with my right, I presented her to that man with the pouring of water.

an8.21:5.9.verse: But I can’t recall getting upset while giving away my teenage wife.

an8.21:5.10.verse: This is the third incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:6.1.verse: And though my family has wealth,

an8.21:6.2.verse: it’s shared without reserve with ethical people of good character.

an8.21:6.3.verse: This is the fourth incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:7.1.verse: When I pay homage to a mendicant,

an8.21:7.2.verse: I do so carefully, not carelessly.

an8.21:7.3.verse: This is the fifth incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:8.1.verse: If that venerable teaches me the Dhamma,

an8.21:8.3.verse: But if they don’t teach me the Dhamma, I teach them.

an8.21:8.4.verse: This is the sixth incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:9.1.verse: It’s not unusual for deities to come to me and announce:

an8.21:9.2.verse: ‘Householder, the Buddha’s teaching is well explained!’

an8.21:9.3.verse: When they say this I say to them:

an8.21:9.4.verse: ‘The Buddha’s teaching is well explained, regardless of whether or not you deities say so!’

an8.21:9.5.verse: But I don’t recall getting too excited by the fact that

an8.21:9.6.verse: the deities come to me, and I have a conversation with them.

an8.21:9.7.verse: This is the seventh incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:10.1.verse: Of the five lower fetters taught by the Buddha, I don’t see any that I haven’t given up.

an8.21:10.2.verse: This is the eighth incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.21:11.1.verse: These eight amazing and incredible qualities are found in me.

an8.21:11.3.verse: what eight amazing and incredible qualities the Buddha was referring to.”

an8.21:12.1.verse: Then that mendicant, after taking almsfood in Ugga of Vesālī’s home, rose from his seat and left.

an8.21:12.2.verse: Then after the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

an8.21:12.3.verse: He informed the Buddha of all he had discussed with the householder Ugga of Vesālī. The Buddha said:

an8.21:13.2.verse: When I declared that the householder Ugga of Vesālī was someone who has eight amazing and incredible qualities, I was referring to the same eight qualities that he rightly explained to you.

an8.21:13.3.verse: You should remember the householder Ugga of Vesālī as someone who possesses these eight amazing and incredible qualities.”

an8.22:7.6.verse: This is the fifth incredible and amazing quality found in me.

an8.22:10.2.verse: ‘The householder Uggata of Elephant Village is bound by no fetter that might return him to this world.’

an8.22:10.3.verse: This is the eighth incredible and amazing quality found in me.
