an8.79:1.1.verse: “These eight things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an8.79:1.3.verse: They relish work, talk, sleep, and company. They don’t guard the sense doors and they eat too much. They relish closeness and proliferation.

an8.79:1.4.verse: These eight things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an8.79:2.1.verse: These eight things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.

an8.79:2.3.verse: They don’t relish work, talk, sleep and company. They guard the sense doors, and they don’t eat too much. They don’t relish closeness and proliferation.

an8.79:2.4.verse: These eight things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.”

an8.80:0.3.verse: Grounds for Laziness and Arousing Energy

an8.80:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are eight grounds for laziness.

an8.80:1.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has some work to do.

an8.80:1.5.verse: ‘I have some work to do. But while doing it my body will get tired. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:1.6.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:1.7.verse: This is the first ground for laziness.

an8.80:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has done some work.

an8.80:2.3.verse: ‘I’ve done some work. But while working my body got tired. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:2.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:2.5.verse: This is the second ground for laziness.

an8.80:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has to go on a journey.

an8.80:3.3.verse: ‘I have to go on a journey. But while walking my body will get tired. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:3.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:3.5.verse: This is the third ground for laziness.

an8.80:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has gone on a journey.

an8.80:4.3.verse: ‘I’ve gone on a journey. But while walking my body got tired. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:4.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:4.5.verse: This is the fourth ground for laziness.

an8.80:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has wandered for alms, but they didn’t get to fill up on as much food as they like, coarse or fine.

an8.80:5.3.verse: ‘I’ve wandered for alms, but I didn’t get to fill up on as much food as I like, coarse or fine. My body is tired and unfit for work. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:5.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for achieving the unachieved, attaining the unattained, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:5.5.verse: This is the fifth ground for laziness.

an8.80:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has wandered for alms, and they got to fill up on as much food as they like, coarse or fine.

an8.80:6.3.verse: ‘I’ve wandered for alms, and I got to fill up on as much food as I like, coarse or fine. My body is heavy, unfit for work, like I’ve just eaten a load of beans. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:6.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for achieving the unachieved, attaining the unattained, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:6.5.verse: This is the sixth ground for laziness.

an8.80:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant feels a little sick.

an8.80:7.3.verse: ‘I feel a little sick. Lying down would be good for me. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:7.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for achieving the unachieved, attaining the unattained, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:7.5.verse: This is the seventh ground for laziness.

an8.80:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has recently recovered from illness.

an8.80:8.3.verse: ‘I’ve recently recovered from illness. My body is weak and unfit for work. I’d better have a lie down.’

an8.80:8.4.verse: They lie down, and don’t rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:8.5.verse: This is the eighth ground for laziness.

an8.80:8.6.verse: These are the eight grounds for laziness.

an8.80:9.1.verse: There are eight grounds for arousing energy.

an8.80:9.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has some work to do.

an8.80:9.5.verse: ‘I have some work to do. While working it’s not easy to focus on the instructions of the Buddhas. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.’

an8.80:9.6.verse: They rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:9.7.verse: This is the first ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has done some work.

an8.80:10.3.verse: ‘I’ve done some work. While I was working I wasn’t able to focus on the instructions of the Buddhas. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.’

an8.80:10.5.verse: This is the second ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has to go on a journey.

an8.80:11.3.verse: ‘I have to go on a journey. While walking it’s not easy to focus on the instructions of the Buddhas. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy …’ …

an8.80:11.4.verse: This is the third ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has gone on a journey.

an8.80:12.3.verse: ‘I’ve gone on a journey. While I was walking I wasn’t able to focus on the instructions of the Buddhas. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy …’ …

an8.80:12.4.verse: This is the fourth ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has wandered for alms, but they didn’t get to fill up on as much food as they like, coarse or fine.

an8.80:13.3.verse: ‘I’ve wandered for alms, but I didn’t get to fill up on as much food as I like, rough or fine. My body is light and fit for work. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy …’ …

an8.80:13.4.verse: This is the fifth ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has wandered for alms, and they got to fill up on as much food as they like, coarse or fine.

an8.80:14.3.verse: ‘I’ve wandered for alms, and I got to fill up on as much food as I like, coarse or fine. My body is strong and fit for work. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy …’ …

an8.80:14.4.verse: This is the sixth ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant feels a little sick.

an8.80:15.3.verse: ‘I feel a little sick. It’s possible this illness will worsen. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy …’ …

an8.80:15.4.verse: This is the seventh ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:16.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has recently recovered from illness.

an8.80:16.3.verse: ‘I’ve recently recovered from illness. It’s possible the illness will come back. I’d better preemptively rouse up energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.’

an8.80:16.4.verse: They rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an8.80:16.5.verse: This is the eighth ground for arousing energy.

an8.80:17.1.verse: These are the eight grounds for arousing energy.”

an8.81:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when there is no mindfulness and situational awareness, one who lacks mindfulness and situational awareness has destroyed a vital condition for conscience and prudence.

an8.81:1.2.verse: When there is no conscience and prudence, one who lacks conscience and prudence has destroyed a vital condition for sense restraint.

an8.81:1.3.verse: When there is no sense restraint, one who lacks sense restraint has destroyed a vital condition for ethical conduct.

an8.81:1.4.verse: When there is no ethical conduct, one who lacks ethics has destroyed a vital condition for right immersion.

an8.81:1.5.verse: When there is no right immersion, one who lacks right immersion has destroyed a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an8.81:1.6.verse: When there is no true knowledge and vision, one who lacks true knowledge and vision has destroyed a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an8.81:1.7.verse: When there is no disillusionment and dispassion, one who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an8.81:1.8.verse: Suppose there was a tree that lacked branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would not grow to fullness.

an8.81:1.9.verse: In the same way, when there is no mindfulness and situational awareness, one who lacks mindfulness and situational awareness has destroyed a vital condition for conscience and prudence.

an8.81:1.10.verse: When there is no conscience and prudence …

an8.81:1.11.verse: One who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an8.81:2.1.verse: When there is mindfulness and situational awareness, one who has fulfilled mindfulness and situational awareness has fulfilled a vital condition for conscience and prudence.

an8.81:2.2.verse: When there is conscience and prudence, one who has fulfilled conscience and prudence has fulfilled a vital condition for sense restraint.

an8.81:2.3.verse: When there is sense restraint, one who has fulfilled sense restraint has fulfilled a vital condition for ethical conduct.

an8.81:2.4.verse: When there is ethical conduct, one who has fulfilled ethical conduct has fulfilled a vital condition for right immersion.

an8.81:2.5.verse: When there is right immersion, one who has fulfilled right immersion has fulfilled a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an8.81:2.6.verse: When there is true knowledge and vision, one who has fulfilled true knowledge and vision has fulfilled a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an8.81:2.7.verse: When there is disillusionment and dispassion, one who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an8.81:2.8.verse: Suppose there was a tree that was complete with branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would grow to fullness.

an8.81:2.9.verse: In the same way, when there is mindfulness and situational awareness, one who has fulfilled mindfulness and situational awareness has fulfilled a vital condition for conscience and prudence.

an8.81:2.10.verse: When there is conscience and prudence …

an8.81:2.11.verse: One who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.”

an8.82:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Puṇṇiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an8.82:1.2.verse: “Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why sometimes the Realized One feels inspired to teach, and other times not?”

an8.82:1.3.verse: “Puṇṇiya, when a mendicant has faith but doesn’t approach,

an8.82:1.4.verse: the Realized One doesn’t feel inspired to teach.

an8.82:1.5.verse: But when a mendicant has faith and approaches,

an8.82:1.6.verse: the Realized One feels inspired to teach.

an8.82:1.7.verse: When a mendicant has faith and approaches, but doesn’t pay homage …

an8.82:1.8.verse: they pay homage, but don’t ask questions …

an8.82:1.9.verse: they ask questions, but don’t actively listen to the teaching …

an8.82:1.10.verse: they actively listen to the teaching, but don’t remember the teaching they’ve heard …

an8.82:1.11.verse: they remember the teaching they’ve heard, but don’t examine the meaning of the teachings they’ve remembered …

an8.82:1.12.verse: they examine the meaning of the teachings they’ve remembered, but, not having understood the meaning and the teaching, they don’t practice in line with the principle of the teaching.

an8.82:1.13.verse: The Realized One doesn’t feel inspired to teach.

an8.82:2.1.verse: But when a mendicant has faith, approaches, pays homage, asks questions, actively listens to the teachings, remembers the teachings, examines the meaning, and practices in line with the principle of the teaching,

an8.82:2.2.verse: the Realized One feels inspired to teach.

an8.82:2.3.verse: When someone possesses these eight qualities, the Realized One feels totally inspired to teach.”

an8.83:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an8.83:1.2.verse: ‘Reverends, all things have what as their root? What produces them? What is their origin? What is their meeting place? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their overseer? What is their core?’ How would you answer them?”

an8.83:1.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

an8.83:2.1.verse: “Well then, mendicants, I will teach it.

an8.83:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an8.83:2.5.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an8.83:2.6.verse: ‘Reverends, all things have what as their root? What produces them? What is their origin? What is their meeting place? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their overseer? What is their core?’

an8.83:2.8.verse: ‘Reverends, all things are rooted in desire. They are produced by application of mind. Contact is their origin. Feeling is their meeting place. Immersion is their chief. Mindfulness is their ruler. Wisdom is their overseer. Freedom is their core.’

an8.83:2.9.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.”

an8.84:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a master thief with eight factors is soon executed, and doesn’t have long to live.

an8.84:1.3.verse: He attacks unprovoked. He steals everything without exception. He kills a woman. He rapes a girl. He robs a monk. He robs the royal treasury. He works close to home. He’s not skilled at hiding his booty.

an8.84:1.4.verse: A master thief with these eight factors is soon executed, and doesn’t have long to live.

an8.84:2.1.verse: A master thief with eight factors is not soon executed, and lives long.

an8.84:2.3.verse: He doesn’t attack unprovoked. He doesn’t steal everything without exception. He doesn’t kill a woman. He doesn’t rape a girl. He doesn’t rob a monk. He doesn’t rob the royal treasury. He doesn’t work close to home. He’s skilled at hiding his booty.

an8.84:2.4.verse: A master thief with these eight factors is not soon executed, and lives long.”

an8.85:1.1.verse: “‘Ascetic’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an8.85:1.8.verse: and ‘Freed’ are terms for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an8.85:2.1.verse: The supreme should be attained by an ascetic,

an8.85:2.2.verse: a brahmin who has lived the life;

an8.85:2.3.verse: it should be attained by a knowledge master,

an8.85:3.1.verse: The supreme should be attained by the unstained,

an8.85:3.3.verse: it should be attained by a knower,

an8.85:4.2.verse: Released, I release others from their chains.

an8.85:4.3.verse: I am a giant completely tamed,

an8.86:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Icchānaṅgala.

an8.86:1.2.verse: He stayed in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

an8.86:1.3.verse: The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:

an8.86:1.4.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Icchānaṅgala. He is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

an8.86:1.6.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ …

an8.86:1.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

an8.86:2.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, they took abundant fresh and cooked foods and went to the forest near Icchānaṅgala, where they stood outside the gates making a colossal racket.

an8.86:2.2.verse: Now, at that time Venerable Nāgita was the Buddha’s attendant.

an8.86:2.3.verse: Then the Buddha said to Nāgita,

an8.86:2.4.verse: “Nāgita, who’s making that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

an8.86:2.5.verse: “Sir, it’s these brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala. They’ve brought abundant fresh and cooked foods, and they’re standing outside the gates wanting to offer it specially to the Buddha and the mendicant Saṅgha.”

an8.86:2.6.verse: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

an8.86:2.7.verse: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:2.8.verse: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.”

an8.86:3.1.verse: “Sir, may the Blessed One please relent now! May the Holy One relent!

an8.86:3.2.verse: Now is the time for the Buddha to relent.

an8.86:3.3.verse: Wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.

an8.86:3.4.verse: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily and the water flows downhill.

an8.86:3.5.verse: In the same way, wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.

an8.86:3.7.verse: Because of the Buddha’s ethics and wisdom.”

an8.86:4.1.verse: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

an8.86:4.2.verse: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:4.3.verse: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.

an8.86:5.1.verse: Even some of the deities can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:5.2.verse: When you all come together to enjoy each other’s company, I think:

an8.86:5.3.verse: ‘These venerables mustn’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:5.4.verse: That must be because they come together to enjoy each other’s company.’

an8.86:6.1.verse: Take mendicants I see poking each other with their fingers, giggling and playing together.

an8.86:6.3.verse: ‘These venerables mustn’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:6.4.verse: That must be because they’re poking each other with their fingers, giggling and playing together.’

an8.86:7.1.verse: Take mendicants I see eat as much as they like until their bellies are full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing.

an8.86:7.3.verse: ‘These venerables mustn’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

an8.86:7.4.verse: That must be because they eat as much as they like until their bellies are full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing.’

an8.86:8.1.verse: Take a mendicant living within a village who I see sitting immersed in samādhi.

an8.86:8.3.verse: ‘Now a monastery worker, a novice, or a fellow practitioner will make this venerable fall from immersion.’

an8.86:8.4.verse: So I’m not pleased that that mendicant is living within a village.

an8.86:9.1.verse: Take a mendicant in the wilderness who I see sitting nodding in meditation.

an8.86:9.3.verse: ‘Now this venerable, having dispelled that sleepiness and weariness, will focus just on the unified perception of wilderness.’

an8.86:9.4.verse: So I’m pleased that that mendicant is living in the wilderness.

an8.86:10.1.verse: Take a mendicant in the wilderness who I see sitting without being immersed in samādhi.

an8.86:10.3.verse: ‘Now if this venerable’s mind is not immersed in samādhi they will immerse it; or if it is immersed in samādhi, they will preserve it.’

an8.86:10.4.verse: So I’m pleased that that mendicant is living in the wilderness.

an8.86:11.1.verse: Take a mendicant in the wilderness who I see sitting immersed in samādhi.

an8.86:11.3.verse: ‘Now this venerable will free the unfreed mind or preserve the freed mind.’

an8.86:11.4.verse: So I’m pleased that that mendicant is living in the wilderness.

an8.86:12.1.verse: Take a mendicant who I see living within a village receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an8.86:12.2.verse: Enjoying possessions, honor, and popularity they neglect retreat, and they neglect remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

an8.86:12.3.verse: They come down to villages, towns, and capital cities and make their home there.

an8.86:12.4.verse: So I’m not pleased that that mendicant is living within a village.

an8.86:13.1.verse: Take a mendicant who I see in the wilderness receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an8.86:13.2.verse: Fending off possessions, honor, and popularity they don’t neglect retreat, and they don’t neglect remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

an8.86:13.3.verse: So I’m pleased that that mendicant is living in the wilderness.

an8.86:14.1.verse: Nāgita, when I’m walking along a road and I don’t see anyone ahead or behind I feel relaxed, even if I need to urinate or defecate.”

an8.87:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the Saṅgha may, if it wishes, turn the bowl upside down for a lay follower on eight grounds.

an8.87:1.3.verse: They try to prevent the mendicants from getting material things. They try to harm mendicants. They try to drive mendicants from a monastery. They insult and abuse mendicants. They divide mendicants against each other. They criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha.

an8.87:1.4.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, turn the bowl upside down for a lay follower on these eight grounds.

an8.87:2.1.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, turn the bowl upright for a lay follower on eight grounds.

an8.87:2.3.verse: They don’t try to prevent the mendicants from getting material things. They don’t try to harm mendicants. They don’t try to drive mendicants from a monastery. They don’t insult and abuse mendicants. They don’t divide mendicants against each other. They don’t criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha.

an8.87:2.4.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, turn the bowl upright for a lay follower on these eight grounds.”

an8.88:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the lay followers may, if they wish, make a proclamation of no confidence in a mendicant who has eight qualities.

an8.88:1.3.verse: They try to prevent laypeople from getting material things. They try to harm laypeople. They insult and abuse laypeople. They divide lay people against each other. They criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They’re seen at an inappropriate place for collecting alms.

an8.88:1.4.verse: The lay followers may, if they wish, make a proclamation of no confidence in a mendicant who possesses these eight qualities.

an8.88:2.1.verse: The lay followers may, if they wish, make a proclamation of confidence in a mendicant who has eight qualities.

an8.88:2.3.verse: They don’t try to prevent laypeople from getting material things. They don’t try to harm laypeople. They don’t insult and abuse laypeople. They don’t divide laypeople against each other. They don’t criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They’re not seen at an inappropriate place for collecting alms.

an8.88:2.4.verse: The lay followers may, if they wish, make a proclamation of confidence in a mendicant who possesses these eight qualities.”

an8.89:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the Saṅgha may, if it wishes, perform an act requiring that a mendicant who has eight qualities should pursue reconciliation.

an8.89:1.3.verse: They try to prevent laypeople from getting material things. They try to harm laypeople. They insult and abuse lay people. They divide laypeople against each other. They criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They don’t keep a legitimate promise made to a layperson.

an8.89:1.4.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, perform an act requiring that a mendicant who has eight qualities should pursue reconciliation.

an8.89:2.1.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, revoke the act requiring that a mendicant who has eight qualities should pursue reconciliation.

an8.89:2.3.verse: They don’t try to prevent the laypeople from getting material things. They don’t try to harm laypeople. They don’t insult and abuse laypeople. They don’t divide laypeople against each other. They don’t criticize the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They keep a legitimate promise made to a layperson.

an8.89:2.4.verse: The Saṅgha may, if it wishes, revoke the act requiring that a mendicant who has eight qualities should pursue reconciliation.”

an8.90:0.3.verse: Proper Behavior in a Case of Aggravated Misconduct

an8.90:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who has been convicted of aggravated misconduct must behave themselves properly in eight respects.

an8.90:1.2.verse: They must not perform an ordination, give dependence, or be attended by a novice. They must not consent to being appointed as adviser for nuns, and if they are appointed they should not give such advice. They must not consent to any Saṅgha appointment. They must not be put in a position of seniority. They must not resolve others from any offense similar to that which they have transgressed.

an8.90:1.3.verse: A mendicant who has been convicted of aggravated misconduct must behave themselves properly in these eight respects.”

an8.91-117:0.3.verse: Untitled Discourses With Various Laywomen on the Sabbath

an8.91-117:1.1.verse: And then the lay woman Bojjhā … Sirīmā … Padumā … Sutanā … Manujā … Uttarā … Muttā … Khemā … Somā … Rucī … Cundī … Bimbī … Sumanā … Mallikā … Tissā … Tissamātā … Soṇā … Soṇā’s mother … Kāṇā … Kāṇamātā … Uttarā, Nanda’s mother … Visākhā, Migāra’s mother … the lay woman Khujjuttarā … the lay woman Sāmāvatī … Suppavāsā the Koliyan … the lay woman Suppiyā … the housewife Nakula’s mother …

an8.118:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, eight things should be developed.

an8.118:1.3.verse: Right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

an8.118:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these eight things should be developed.”

an8.119:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, eight things should be developed.

an8.119:1.3.verse: Perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, limited, both pretty and ugly.

an8.119:1.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an8.119:1.5.verse: Perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, limitless, both pretty and ugly. …

an8.119:1.6.verse: Not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, limited, both pretty and ugly. …

an8.119:1.7.verse: Not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, limitless, both pretty and ugly. …

an8.119:1.8.verse: Not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, blue, with blue color and blue appearance. …

an8.119:1.11.verse: Not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally, white, with white color and white appearance.

an8.119:1.12.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an8.119:1.13.verse: For insight into greed, these eight things should be developed.”

an8.120:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, eight things should be developed.

an8.120:1.3.verse: Having physical form, they see forms … not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally … they’re focused only on beauty … going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space … going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness … going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness … going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception … going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, they enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling …

an8.120:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these eight things should be developed.”

an9.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an9.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an9.1:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an9.1:2.2.verse: ‘Reverends, what is the vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening?’ How would you answer them?”

an9.1:2.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. … The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

an9.1:3.1.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an9.1:4.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an9.1:4.2.verse: ‘Reverends, what is the vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening?’ You should answer them:

an9.1:5.1.verse: ‘It’s when a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.

an9.1:5.2.verse: This is the first vital condition for the development of the awakening factors.

an9.1:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an9.1:6.2.verse: This is the second vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening.

an9.1:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant gets to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart, when they want, without trouble or difficulty. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

an9.1:7.2.verse: This is the third vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening.

an9.1:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an9.1:8.2.verse: This is the fourth vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening.

an9.1:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an9.1:9.2.verse: This is the fifth vital condition for the development of the qualities on the same side as awakening.’

an9.1:10.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.1:11.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.1:11.2.verse: take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart …

an9.1:12.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.1:13.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.1:14.1.verse: But then, a mendicant grounded on these five things should develop four further things.

an9.1:14.2.verse: They should develop the perception of ugliness to give up greed, love to give up hate, mindfulness of breathing to cut off thinking, and perception of impermanence to uproot the conceit ‘I am’.

an9.1:14.3.verse: When you perceive impermanence, the perception of not-self becomes stabilized.

an9.1:14.4.verse: Perceiving not-self, you uproot the conceit ‘I am’ and attain extinguishment in this very life.”

an9.2:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an9.2:1.3.verse: How is a mendicant who is supported defined?”

an9.2:1.4.verse: “Mendicant, if a mendicant supported by faith gives up the unskillful and develops the skillful, the unskillful is actually given up by them.

an9.2:1.5.verse: If a mendicant supported by conscience …

an9.2:1.6.verse: If a mendicant supported by prudence …

an9.2:1.7.verse: If a mendicant supported by energy …

an9.2:1.8.verse: If a mendicant supported by wisdom gives up the unskillful and develops the skillful, the unskillful is actually given up by them.

an9.2:1.9.verse: What’s been given up is completely given up when it has been given up by seeing with noble wisdom.

an9.2:2.1.verse: But then, a mendicant grounded on these five things should rely on four things.

an9.2:2.3.verse: After appraisal, a mendicant uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.

an9.2:2.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant is supported.”

an9.3:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Cālikā, on the Cālikā mountain.

an9.3:1.2.verse: Now, at that time Venerable Meghiya was the Buddha’s attendant.

an9.3:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

an9.3:1.4.verse: “Sir, I’d like to enter Jantu village for alms.”

an9.3:2.1.verse: Then Meghiya robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Jantu village for alms.

an9.3:2.2.verse: After the meal, on his return from almsround in Jantu village, he went to the shore of Kimikālā River.

an9.3:2.3.verse: As he was going for a walk along the shore of the river he saw a lovely and delightful mango grove.

an9.3:2.4.verse: Seeing this, it occurred to him,

an9.3:2.5.verse: “Oh, this mango grove is lovely and delightful! This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.

an9.3:2.6.verse: If the Buddha allows me, I’ll come back to this mango grove to meditate.”

an9.3:3.1.verse: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding,

an9.3:4.8.verse: “If the Buddha allows me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

an9.3:4.9.verse: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

an9.3:5.1.verse: For a second time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

an9.3:5.2.verse: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

an9.3:5.4.verse: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

an9.3:5.5.verse: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

an9.3:6.1.verse: For a third time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

an9.3:6.2.verse: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

an9.3:6.4.verse: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

an9.3:6.5.verse: “Meghiya, since you speak of striving in meditation, what can I say?

an9.3:6.6.verse: Please, Meghiya, go at your convenience.”

an9.3:7.1.verse: Then Meghiya got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went to that mango grove, and, having plunged deep into it, sat at the root of a certain tree for the day’s meditation.

an9.3:7.2.verse: But while Meghiya was meditating in that mango grove he was beset mostly by three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts, namely,

an9.3:7.6.verse: I’ve gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness,

an9.3:7.7.verse: but I’m still harassed by these three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts:

an9.3:8.1.verse: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

an9.3:10.1.verse: “Meghiya, when the heart’s release is not ripe, five things help it ripen.

an9.3:10.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.

an9.3:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an9.3:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant gets to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart, when they want, without trouble or difficulty. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

an9.3:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an9.3:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an9.3:14.2.verse: This is the fifth thing that, when the heart’s release is not ripe, helps it ripen.

an9.3:15.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.3:16.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to

an9.3:16.2.verse: take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart …

an9.3:17.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be energetic …

an9.3:18.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be wise …

an9.3:19.1.verse: But then, a mendicant grounded on these five things should develop four further things.

an9.3:19.2.verse: They should develop the perception of ugliness to give up greed, love to give up hate, mindfulness of breathing to cut off thinking, and perception of impermanence to uproot the conceit ‘I am’.

an9.3:19.3.verse: When you perceive impermanence, the perception of not-self becomes stabilized.

an9.3:19.4.verse: Perceiving not-self, you uproot the conceit ‘I am’ and attain extinguishment in this very life.”

an9.4:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an9.4:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Nandaka was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk.

an9.4:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He stood outside the door waiting for the talk to end.

an9.4:1.4.verse: When he knew the talk had ended he cleared his throat and knocked on the door-panel.

an9.4:1.5.verse: The mendicants opened the door for the Buddha,

an9.4:2.1.verse: and he entered the assembly hall, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an9.4:2.3.verse: “Nandaka, that was a long exposition of the teaching you gave to the mendicants.

an9.4:2.4.verse: My back was aching while I stood outside the door waiting for the talk to end.”

an9.4:3.1.verse: When he said this, Nandaka felt embarrassed and said to the Buddha,

an9.4:3.2.verse: “Sir, we didn’t know that the Buddha was standing outside the door.

an9.4:3.3.verse: If we’d known, I wouldn’t have said so much.”

an9.4:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing that Nandaka was embarrassed, said to him,

an9.4:4.3.verse: It’s appropriate for gentlemen like you, who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, to sit together for a Dhamma talk.

an9.4:4.4.verse: When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

an9.4:4.5.verse: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.

an9.4:4.6.verse: Nandaka, a mendicant is faithful but not ethical.

an9.4:4.7.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an9.4:4.9.verse: ‘How can I become faithful and ethical?’

an9.4:4.10.verse: When a mendicant is faithful and ethical, they’re complete in that respect.

an9.4:5.1.verse: A mendicant is faithful and ethical, but does not get internal serenity of heart.

an9.4:5.2.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an9.4:5.4.verse: ‘How can I become faithful and ethical and get internal serenity of heart?’

an9.4:5.5.verse: When a mendicant is faithful and ethical and gets internal serenity of heart, they’re complete in that respect.

an9.4:6.1.verse: A mendicant is faithful, ethical, and gets internal serenity of heart, but they don’t get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles.

an9.4:6.2.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect.

an9.4:6.3.verse: Suppose, Nandaka, there was a four-footed animal

an9.4:6.5.verse: It would be incomplete in that respect.

an9.4:6.6.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is faithful, ethical, and gets internal serenity of heart, but they don’t get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles.

an9.4:6.7.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an9.4:6.9.verse: ‘How can I become faithful and ethical and get internal serenity of heart and get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles?’

an9.4:7.1.verse: When a mendicant is faithful and ethical and gets internal serenity of heart and gets the higher wisdom of discernment of principles, they’re complete in that respect.”

an9.4:7.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an9.4:7.3.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

an9.4:8.1.verse: Then, not long after the Buddha left, Venerable Nandaka said to the mendicants,

an9.4:8.2.verse: “Just now, reverends, the Buddha revealed a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure in four statements, before getting up from his seat and entering his dwelling:

an9.4:8.3.verse: ‘Nandaka, a mendicant is faithful but not ethical.

an9.4:8.4.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an9.4:8.6.verse: “How can I become faithful and ethical?”

an9.4:8.7.verse: When a mendicant is faithful and ethical, they’re complete in that respect.

an9.4:8.8.verse: A mendicant is faithful and ethical, but does not get internal serenity of heart. …

an9.4:8.9.verse: They get internal serenity of heart, but they don’t get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles.

an9.4:8.10.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect.

an9.4:8.11.verse: Suppose, Nandaka, there was a four-footed animal that was lame and disabled.

an9.4:8.12.verse: It would be incomplete in that respect.

an9.4:8.13.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is faithful, ethical, and gets internal serenity of heart, but they don’t get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles.

an9.4:8.14.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an9.4:8.16.verse: “How can I become faithful and ethical and get internal serenity of heart and get the higher wisdom of discernment of principles?”

an9.4:8.17.verse: When a mendicant is faithful and ethical and gets internal serenity of heart and gets the higher wisdom of discernment of principles,

an9.4:9.1.verse: Reverends, there are these five benefits of listening to the teachings at the right time and discussing the teachings at the right time.

an9.4:9.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant teaches Dhamma to the mendicants that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

an9.4:9.4.verse: Whenever they do this, they become liked and approved by the Teacher, respected and admired.

an9.4:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant teaches the mendicants the Dhamma …

an9.4:10.2.verse: Whenever they do this, they feel inspired by the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma.

an9.4:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant teaches the mendicants the Dhamma …

an9.4:11.2.verse: Whenever they do this, they see the meaning of a deep saying in that Dhamma with penetrating wisdom.

an9.4:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant teaches the mendicants the Dhamma …

an9.4:12.2.verse: Whenever they do this, their spiritual companions esteem them more highly, thinking,

an9.4:12.3.verse: ‘For sure this venerable has attained or will attain.’

an9.4:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant teaches the mendicants the Dhamma …

an9.4:13.2.verse: Whenever they do this, there may be trainee mendicants present, who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke. Hearing that teaching, they rouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

an9.4:13.3.verse: There may be perfected mendicants present, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment. Hearing that teaching, they simply live happily in this life.

an9.4:13.5.verse: These are the five benefits of listening to the teachings at the right time and discussing the teachings at the right time.”

an9.5:1.3.verse: The powers of wisdom, energy, blamelessness, and inclusiveness.

an9.5:1.4.verse: And what is the power of wisdom?

an9.5:1.5.verse: One has clearly seen and clearly contemplated with wisdom those qualities that are skillful and considered to be skillful; those that are unskillful … blameworthy … blameless … dark … bright … to be cultivated … not to be cultivated … not worthy of the noble ones … worthy of the noble ones and considered to be worthy of the noble ones.

an9.5:1.6.verse: This is called the power of wisdom.

an9.5:2.1.verse: And what is the power of energy?

an9.5:2.2.verse: One generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives to give up those qualities that are unskillful and considered to be unskillful; those that are blameworthy … dark … not to be cultivated … not worthy of the noble ones and considered to be not worthy of the noble ones.

an9.5:2.3.verse: One generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives to gain those qualities that are skillful and considered to be skillful; those that are blameless … bright … to be cultivated … worthy of the noble ones and considered to be worthy of the noble ones.

an9.5:2.4.verse: This is called the power of energy.

an9.5:3.1.verse: And what is the power of blamelessness?

an9.5:3.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has blameless conduct by way of body, speech, and mind.

an9.5:3.3.verse: This is called the power of blamelessness.

an9.5:4.1.verse: And what is the power of inclusiveness?

an9.5:4.2.verse: There are these four ways of being inclusive.

an9.5:4.3.verse: Giving, kindly words, taking care, and equality.

an9.5:4.4.verse: The best of gifts is the gift of the teaching.

an9.5:4.5.verse: The best sort of kindly speech is to teach the Dhamma again and again to someone who is engaged and who actively listens.

an9.5:4.6.verse: The best way of taking care is to encourage, settle, and ground the unfaithful in faith, the unethical in ethics, the stingy in generosity, and the ignorant in wisdom.

an9.5:4.7.verse: The best kind of equality is the equality of a stream-enterer with another stream-enterer, a once-returner with another once-returner, a non-returner with another non-returner, and a perfected one with another perfected one.

an9.5:4.8.verse: This is called the power of inclusiveness.

an9.5:5.1.verse: A noble disciple who has these four powers has got past five fears.

an9.5:5.3.verse: Fear regarding livelihood, disrepute, feeling insecure in an assembly, death, and bad rebirth.

an9.5:5.6.verse: Why would I be afraid of that?

an9.5:5.8.verse: the powers of wisdom, energy, blamelessness, and inclusiveness.

an9.5:5.9.verse: A witless person might fear for their livelihood.

an9.5:5.10.verse: A lazy person might fear for their livelihood.

an9.5:5.11.verse: Someone who does blameworthy things by way of body, speech, and mind might fear for their livelihood.

an9.5:5.12.verse: Someone who does not include others might fear for their livelihood.

an9.5:5.13.verse: I have no fear of disrepute …

an9.5:5.14.verse: I have no fear about feeling insecure in an assembly …

an9.5:5.15.verse: I have no fear of death …

an9.5:5.16.verse: I have no fear of a bad rebirth.

an9.5:5.17.verse: Why would I be afraid of that?

an9.5:5.19.verse: the powers of wisdom, energy, blamelessness, and inclusiveness.

an9.5:5.20.verse: A witless person might be afraid of a bad rebirth.

an9.5:5.21.verse: A lazy person might be afraid of a bad rebirth.

an9.5:5.22.verse: Someone who does blameworthy things by way of body, speech, and mind might be afraid of a bad rebirth.

an9.5:5.23.verse: Someone who does not include others might be afraid of a bad rebirth.’

an9.5:5.24.verse: A noble disciple who has these four powers has got past these five fears.”

an9.6:2.1.verse: “Reverends, you should distinguish two two kinds of individual:

an9.6:2.2.verse: those you should associate with, and those you shouldn’t associate with.

an9.6:2.3.verse: You should distinguish two kinds of robes:

an9.6:2.4.verse: those you should wear, and those you shouldn’t wear.

an9.6:2.5.verse: You should distinguish two kinds of almsfood:

an9.6:2.6.verse: that which you should eat, and that which you shouldn’t eat.

an9.6:2.7.verse: You should distinguish two kinds of lodging:

an9.6:2.8.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.

an9.6:2.9.verse: You should distinguish two kinds of village or town:

an9.6:2.10.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.

an9.6:2.11.verse: You should distinguish two kinds of country:

an9.6:2.12.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.

an9.6:3.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two two kinds of individual:

an9.6:3.2.verse: those you should associate with, and those you shouldn’t associate with.’

an9.6:3.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:3.4.verse: Well, should you know of an individual:

an9.6:3.5.verse: ‘When I associate with this individual, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.

an9.6:3.6.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by.

an9.6:3.7.verse: And the goal of the ascetic life for which I went forth from the lay life to homelessness is not being fully developed.’ In this case you should leave that individual at that very time of the day or night, without asking. You shouldn’t follow them.

an9.6:4.1.verse: Whereas, should you know of an individual:

an9.6:4.2.verse: ‘When I associate with this individual, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.

an9.6:4.3.verse: But the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are easy to come by.

an9.6:4.4.verse: However, the goal of the ascetic life for which I went forth from the lay life to homelessness is not being fully developed.’ In this case you should leave that individual after reflecting, without asking. You shouldn’t follow them.

an9.6:5.1.verse: Well, should you know of an individual:

an9.6:5.2.verse: ‘When I associate with this individual, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.

an9.6:5.3.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by.

an9.6:5.4.verse: But the goal of the ascetic life for which I went forth from the lay life to homelessness is being fully developed.’ In this case you should follow that individual after appraisal. You shouldn’t leave them.

an9.6:6.1.verse: Whereas, should you know of an individual:

an9.6:6.2.verse: ‘When I associate with this individual, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.

an9.6:6.3.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are easy to come by.

an9.6:6.4.verse: And the goal of the ascetic life for which I went forth from the lay life to homelessness is being fully developed.’ In this case you should follow that individual. You shouldn’t leave them, even if they send you away.

an9.6:6.5.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of individual:

an9.6:6.6.verse: those you should associate with, and those you shouldn’t associate with.’

an9.6:6.7.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an9.6:7.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of robes:

an9.6:7.2.verse: those you should wear, and those you shouldn’t wear.’

an9.6:7.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:7.4.verse: Well, should you know of a robe:

an9.6:7.5.verse: ‘When I wear this robe, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not wear that kind of robe.

an9.6:7.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of a robe:

an9.6:7.7.verse: ‘When I wear this robe, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should wear that kind of robe.

an9.6:7.8.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of robes:

an9.6:7.9.verse: those you should wear, and those you shouldn’t wear.’

an9.6:7.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an9.6:8.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of almsfood:

an9.6:8.2.verse: that which you should eat, and that which you shouldn’t eat.’

an9.6:8.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:8.4.verse: Well, should you know of almsfood:

an9.6:8.5.verse: ‘When I eat this almsfood, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not eat that kind of almsfood.

an9.6:8.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of almsfood:

an9.6:8.7.verse: ‘When I eat this almsfood, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should eat that kind of almsfood.

an9.6:8.8.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of almsfood:

an9.6:8.9.verse: that which you should eat, and that which you shouldn’t eat.’

an9.6:8.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an9.6:9.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of lodging:

an9.6:9.2.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:9.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:9.4.verse: Well, should you know of a lodging:

an9.6:9.5.verse: ‘When I frequent this lodging, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not frequent that kind of lodging.

an9.6:9.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of a lodging:

an9.6:9.7.verse: ‘When I frequent this lodging, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should frequent that kind of lodging.

an9.6:9.8.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of lodging:

an9.6:9.9.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:9.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an9.6:10.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of village or town:

an9.6:10.2.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:10.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:10.4.verse: Well, should you know of a village or town:

an9.6:10.5.verse: ‘When I frequent this village or town, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not frequent that kind of village or town.

an9.6:10.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of a village or town:

an9.6:10.7.verse: ‘When I frequent this village or town, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should frequent that kind of village or town.

an9.6:10.8.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of village or town:

an9.6:10.9.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:10.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an9.6:11.1.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of country:

an9.6:11.2.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:11.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an9.6:11.4.verse: Well, should you know of a country:

an9.6:11.5.verse: ‘When I frequent this country, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not frequent that kind of country.

an9.6:11.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of a country:

an9.6:11.7.verse: ‘When I frequent this country, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should frequent that kind of country.

an9.6:11.8.verse: ‘You should distinguish two kinds of country:

an9.6:11.9.verse: those you should frequent, and those you shouldn’t frequent.’

an9.6:11.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

an9.7:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an9.7:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Sutavā went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an9.7:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an9.7:2.1.verse: “Sir, this one time the Buddha was staying right here in Rājagaha, the Mountainfold.

an9.7:2.2.verse: There I heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

an9.7:2.3.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in five respects.

an9.7:2.4.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a lay person.’

an9.7:2.5.verse: I trust I properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that from the Buddha?”

an9.7:3.1.verse: “Indeed, Sutavā, you properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that.

an9.7:3.2.verse: In the past, as today, I say this:

an9.7:3.3.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in nine respects.

an9.7:3.4.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a lay person. And they can’t make decisions prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, or cowardice.’

an9.7:3.5.verse: In the past, as today, I say this:

an9.7:3.6.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in these nine respects.’”

an9.8:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

an9.8:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Sajjha went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an9.8:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

an9.8:2.1.verse: “Sir, this one time the Buddha was staying right here in Rājagaha, the Mountainfold.

an9.8:2.2.verse: There I heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

an9.8:2.3.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in five respects.

an9.8:2.4.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a lay person.’

an9.8:2.5.verse: I trust I properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that from the Buddha?”

an9.8:3.1.verse: “Indeed, Sajjha, you properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that.

an9.8:3.2.verse: In the past, as today, I say this:

an9.8:3.3.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in nine respects.

an9.8:3.4.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a lay person. And they can’t abandon the Buddha, the teaching, the Saṅgha, or the training.’

an9.8:3.5.verse: In the past, as today, I say this:

an9.8:3.6.verse: ‘A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in these nine respects.’”

an9.9:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these nine individuals are found in the world.

an9.9:1.3.verse: The perfected one and the one practicing for perfection. The non-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of non-return. The once-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of once-return. The stream-enterer and the one practicing to realize the fruit of stream-entry. And the ordinary person.

an9.9:1.4.verse: These are the nine individuals found in the world.”

an9.10:0.3.verse: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods

an9.10:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these nine individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

an9.10:1.3.verse: The perfected one and the one practicing for perfection. The non-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of non-return. The once-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of once-return. The stream-enterer and the one practicing to realize the fruit of stream-entry. And a lamb of the flock.

an9.10:1.4.verse: These are the nine individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an9.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an9.11:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an9.11:1.3.verse: “Sir, I have completed the rainy season residence at Sāvatthī.

an9.11:1.4.verse: I wish to leave to wander the countryside.”

an9.11:1.6.verse: Then Sāriputta rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an9.11:1.7.verse: And then, not long after Sāriputta had left, a certain monk said to the Buddha,

an9.11:1.8.verse: “Sir, Venerable Sāriputta attacked me and left without saying sorry.”

an9.11:1.9.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

an9.11:1.10.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell Sāriputta that

an9.11:1.12.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Sāriputta and said to him,

an9.11:2.1.verse: Now at that time the venerables Mahāmoggallāna and Ānanda, taking a latchkey, went from dwelling to dwelling, saying:

an9.11:2.3.verse: Now Venerable Sāriputta will roar his lion’s roar in the presence of the Buddha!”

an9.11:2.4.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an9.11:2.5.verse: “Sāriputta, one of your spiritual companions has made this complaint:

an9.11:2.6.verse: ‘Venerable Sāriputta attacked me and left without saying sorry.’”

an9.11:3.1.verse: “Sir, someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:4.1.verse: Suppose they were to toss both clean and unclean things on the earth, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The earth isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.

an9.11:4.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like the earth, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:4.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:5.1.verse: Suppose they were to wash both clean and unclean things in water, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The water isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.

an9.11:5.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like water, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:5.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:6.1.verse: Suppose a fire were to burn both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The fire isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.

an9.11:6.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like fire, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:6.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:7.1.verse: Suppose the wind was to blow on both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The wind isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.

an9.11:7.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like the wind, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:7.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:8.1.verse: Suppose a rag was to wipe up both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The rag isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.

an9.11:8.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like a rag, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:8.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:9.1.verse: Suppose a boy or girl of a corpse-worker tribe, holding a pot and clad in rags, were to enter a town or village. They’d enter with a humble mind.

an9.11:9.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like a boy or girl of a corpse-worker tribe, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:9.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:10.1.verse: Suppose there was a bull with his horns cut, gentle, well tamed and well trained. He’d wander from street to street and square to square without hurting anyone with his feet or horns.

an9.11:10.2.verse: In the same way, I live with a heart like a bull with horns cut, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

an9.11:10.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:11.1.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and had bathed their head. If the carcass of a snake or a dog or a human were hung around their neck, they’d be horrified, repelled, and disgusted.

an9.11:11.2.verse: In the same way, I’m horrified, repelled, and disgusted by this rotting body.

an9.11:11.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.

an9.11:12.1.verse: Suppose someone was to carry around a bowl of fat that was leaking and oozing from holes and cracks.

an9.11:12.2.verse: In the same way, I carry around this body that’s leaking and oozing from holes and cracks.

an9.11:12.3.verse: Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.”

an9.11:13.1.verse: Then that monk rose from his seat, placed his robe over one shoulder, bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet, and said,

an9.11:13.2.verse: “I made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me to speak ill of Venerable Sāriputta with an incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim.

an9.11:13.3.verse: Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

an9.11:13.4.verse: “Indeed, monk, you made a mistake. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of you to act in that way.

an9.11:13.5.verse: But since you have recognized your mistake for what it is, and have dealt with it properly, I accept it.

an9.11:13.6.verse: For it is growth in the training of the Noble One to recognize a mistake for what it is, deal with it properly, and commit to restraint in the future.”

an9.11:14.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Sāriputta,

an9.11:14.2.verse: “Sāriputta, forgive that futile man before his head explodes into seven pieces right here.”

an9.11:14.3.verse: “I will pardon that venerable if he asks me:

an9.11:14.4.verse: ‘May the venerable please pardon me too.’”

an9.12:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an9.12:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

an9.12:1.4.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.

an9.12:1.5.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an9.12:1.6.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

an9.12:1.7.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

an9.12:2.1.verse: Now at that time while those wanderers of other religions were sitting together this discussion came up among them:

an9.12:2.2.verse: “Reverends, no one who dies with residue is exempt from hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. They’re not exempt from places of loss, bad places, the underworld.”

an9.12:2.3.verse: Sāriputta neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.

an9.12:2.4.verse: He rose from his seat, thinking,

an9.12:2.5.verse: “I will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

an9.12:2.6.verse: Then Sāriputta wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

an9.12:4.1.verse: “Sāriputta, these foolish, incompetent wanderers following other religions: who are they to know whether someone has residue or not?

an9.12:5.1.verse: There are these nine individuals who, dying with residue, are exempt from hell, the animal realm, and the ghost realm. They’re exempt from places of loss, bad places, the underworld.

an9.12:5.3.verse: There’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics and immersion, but has limited wisdom.

an9.12:5.4.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished between one life and the next.

an9.12:6.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics and immersion, but has limited wisdom.

an9.12:6.2.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing. This is the second individual …

an9.12:6.3.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort.

an9.12:6.5.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort.

an9.12:6.7.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

an9.12:7.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics, but has limited immersion and wisdom.

an9.12:7.2.verse: With the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, they’re a once-returner. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

an9.12:8.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics, but has limited immersion and wisdom.

an9.12:8.2.verse: With the ending of three fetters, they’re a one-seeder. They will be reborn just one time in a human existence, then make an end of suffering.

an9.12:9.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics, but has limited immersion and wisdom.

an9.12:9.2.verse: With the ending of three fetters, they go from family to family. They will transmigrate between two or three families and then make an end of suffering.

an9.12:10.1.verse: Furthermore, there’s an individual who has fulfilled ethics, but has limited immersion and wisdom.

an9.12:10.2.verse: With the ending of three fetters, they have at most seven rebirths. They will transmigrate at most seven times among gods and humans and then make an end of suffering.

an9.12:11.1.verse: These foolish, incompetent wanderers following other religions: who are they to know whether someone has residue or not?

an9.12:11.2.verse: These are the nine individuals who, dying with residue, are exempt from hell, the animal realm, and the ghost realm. They’re exempt from places of loss, bad places, the underworld.

an9.12:11.3.verse: Up until now, Sāriputta, I have not felt the need to give this exposition of the teaching to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

an9.12:11.5.verse: For I didn’t want those who heard it to introduce negligence.

an9.12:11.6.verse: However, I have spoken it in order to answer your question.”

an9.13:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita went up to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

an9.13:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

an9.13:1.3.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced in this life be experienced by me in lives to come’?”

an9.13:2.1.verse: “Then is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced in lives to come be experienced by me in this life’?”

an9.13:3.1.verse: “Is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced as pleasant be experienced by me as painful’?”

an9.13:4.1.verse: “Then is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced as painful be experienced by me as pleasant’?”

an9.13:5.1.verse: “Is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced when ripe be experienced by me when unripe’?”

an9.13:6.1.verse: “Then is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced when unripe be experienced by me when ripe’?”

an9.13:7.1.verse: “Is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced a lot be experienced by me a little’?”

an9.13:8.1.verse: “Then is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced a little be experienced by me a lot’?”

an9.13:9.1.verse: “Is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds to be experienced by me be not experienced’?”

an9.13:10.1.verse: “Then is the spiritual life led under the Buddha for this goal: ‘May deeds not to be experienced be experienced’?”

an9.13:11.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, when you were asked whether the spiritual life was lived under the Buddha so that deeds to be experienced in this life are experienced in lives to come, you said, ‘Certainly not’.

an9.13:12.1.verse: When you were asked whether the spiritual life was lived under the Buddha so that deeds to be experienced in lives to come are experienced in this life …

an9.13:13.1.verse: deeds to be experienced as pleasant are experienced as painful …

an9.13:14.1.verse: deeds to be experienced as painful are experienced as pleasant …

an9.13:15.1.verse: deeds to be experienced when ripe are experienced when unripe …

an9.13:16.1.verse: deeds to be experienced when unripe are experienced when ripe …

an9.13:17.1.verse: deeds to be experienced a lot are experienced a little …

an9.13:18.1.verse: deeds to be experienced a little are experienced a lot …

an9.13:19.1.verse: deeds to be experienced are not experienced …

an9.13:20.1.verse: When you were asked whether the spiritual life was lived under the Buddha so that deeds not to be experienced are experienced, you said, ‘Certainly not.’

an9.13:20.2.verse: Then what exactly is the goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha?”

an9.13:21.1.verse: “Reverend, the spiritual life is lived under the Buddha to know, see, attain, realize, and comprehend that which is unknown, unseen, unattained, unrealized, and uncomprehended.”

an9.13:21.2.verse: “But what is the unknown, unseen, unattained, unrealized, and uncomprehended?”

an9.13:21.5.verse: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ …

an9.13:21.6.verse: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ …

an9.13:21.8.verse: This is the unknown, unseen, unattained, unrealized, and uncomprehended.

an9.13:21.9.verse: The spiritual life is lived under the Buddha to know, see, attain, realize, and comprehend this.”

an9.14:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Samiddhi went up to Venerable Sāriputta, bowed, and sat to one side. Venerable Sāriputta said to him:

an9.14:2.1.verse: “Samiddhi, based on what do thoughts arise in a person?”

an9.14:11.1.verse: “Samiddhi, when you were asked what is the basis on which thoughts arise in a person, you answered ‘name and form’.

an9.14:11.9.verse: what is their objective, you answered ‘freedom from death’.

an9.14:11.11.verse: It’s good that you answered each question. But don’t get conceited because of that.”

an9.15:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose there was a boil that was many years old.

an9.15:1.2.verse: And that boil had nine orifices that were continually open wounds.

an9.15:1.4.verse: would be filthy, stinking, and disgusting.

an9.15:1.6.verse: would be filthy, stinking, and disgusting.

an9.15:2.1.verse: ‘Boil’ is a term for this body made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

an9.15:2.2.verse: And that boil has nine orifices that are continually open wounds.

an9.15:2.7.verse: So, mendicants, have no illusion about this body.”

an9.16:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are very fruitful and beneficial. Their objective and culmination is freedom from death.
