an9.39:7.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

an9.39:8.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. …

an9.39:8.2.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness. …

an9.39:8.3.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. …

an9.39:8.4.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, they enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.39:8.5.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see. And they’ve crossed over clinging to the world.”

an9.40:0.3.verse: The Simile of the Bull Elephant in the Forest

an9.40:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a wild bull elephant is engrossed in the pasture, but other elephants—males, females, younglings, or cubs—got there first and trampled the grass, the wild bull elephant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted by that.

an9.40:1.2.verse: When the wild bull elephant is engrossed in the pasture, but other elephants—males, females, younglings, or cubs—eat the broken branches that he has dragged down, the wild bull elephant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted by that.

an9.40:1.3.verse: When a wild bull elephant has plunged into the pool, but other elephants—males, females, younglings, or cubs—got there first and stirred up the water with their trunks, the wild bull elephant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted by that.

an9.40:1.4.verse: When a wild bull elephant has come out of the pool and the female elephants bump into him, the wild bull elephant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted by that.

an9.40:2.1.verse: At that time the wild bull elephant thinks:

an9.40:2.2.verse: ‘These days I live crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs.

an9.40:2.3.verse: I eat the grass they’ve trampled, and they eat the broken branches I’ve dragged down. I drink muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bump into me.

an9.40:2.4.verse: Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the herd?’

an9.40:2.5.verse: After some time he lives alone, withdrawn from the herd, and he eats untrampled grass, and other elephants don’t eat the broken branches he has dragged down. He doesn’t drink muddy water, and the female elephants don’t bump into him after his bath.

an9.40:3.1.verse: At that time the wild bull elephant thinks:

an9.40:3.2.verse: ‘Formerly I lived crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I ate the grass they’d trampled, and they ate the broken branches I’d dragged down. I drank muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bumped into me. Now I live alone, and I’m free of all these things.’ He breaks off a branch and scratches his body, happily relieving his itches.

an9.40:4.1.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant lives crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and by monastics of other religions and their disciples, they think:

an9.40:4.2.verse: ‘These days I live crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples.

an9.40:4.3.verse: Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the group?’

an9.40:4.4.verse: They frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

an9.40:4.5.verse: Gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, they sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

an9.40:5.1.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

an9.40:5.2.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

an9.40:5.3.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

an9.40:5.4.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

an9.40:5.5.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

an9.40:5.6.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

an9.40:5.7.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an9.40:5.9.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption …

an9.40:6.1.verse: Going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

an9.40:6.3.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness. …

an9.40:6.4.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness. …

an9.40:6.5.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. …

an9.40:6.6.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.41:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Mallas, near the Mallian town named Uruvelakappa.

an9.41:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Uruvelakappa for alms.

an9.41:1.3.verse: Then, after the meal, on his return from almsround, he addressed Venerable Ānanda,

an9.41:1.4.verse: “Ānanda, you stay right here, while I plunge deep into the Great Wood for the day’s meditation.”

an9.41:1.6.verse: Then the Buddha plunged deep into the Great Wood and sat at the root of a tree for the day’s meditation.

an9.41:2.1.verse: The householder Tapussa went up to Venerable Ānanda, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an9.41:3.1.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, we are laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures. We like sensual pleasures, we love them and take joy in them.

an9.41:3.2.verse: But renunciation seems like an abyss.

an9.41:3.3.verse: I have heard that in this teaching and training there are very young mendicants whose minds leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in renunciation. They see it as peaceful.

an9.41:3.4.verse: Renunciation is the dividing line between the multitude and the mendicants in this teaching and training.”

an9.41:4.1.verse: “Householder, we should see the Buddha about this matter.

an9.41:4.2.verse: Come, let’s go to the Buddha and inform him about this.

an9.41:4.3.verse: As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”

an9.41:5.2.verse: Then Ānanda together with Tapussa went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Ānanda told him what had happened.

an9.41:7.1.verse: “That’s so true, Ānanda! That’s so true!

an9.41:7.2.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too thought,

an9.41:7.4.verse: But my mind did not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in renunciation. I didn’t see it as peaceful.

an9.41:7.6.verse: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in renunciation? Why don’t I see it as peaceful?’

an9.41:7.8.verse: ‘I haven’t seen the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, and so I haven’t cultivated that. I haven’t realized the benefits of renunciation, and so I haven’t developed that.

an9.41:7.9.verse: That’s why my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in renunciation. And it’s why I don’t see it as peaceful.’

an9.41:7.11.verse: ‘Suppose that, seeing the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, I were to cultivate that. And suppose that, realizing the benefits of renunciation, I were to develop that.

an9.41:7.12.verse: It’s possible that my mind would leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in renunciation. And I would see it as peaceful.’

an9.41:7.13.verse: And so, after some time, I saw the drawbacks of sensual pleasures and cultivated that, and I realized the benefits of renunciation and developed that.

an9.41:7.14.verse: Then my mind leapt forth, gained confidence, settled down, and became decided in renunciation. I saw it as peaceful.

an9.41:7.15.verse: And so, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

an9.41:7.16.verse: While I was in that meditation, perception and focus accompanied by sensual pleasures beset me, and that was an affliction for me.

an9.41:7.17.verse: Suppose a happy person were to experience pain; that would be an affliction for them.

an9.41:7.18.verse: In the same way, when perception and focus accompanied by sensual pleasures beset me, that was an affliction for me.

an9.41:8.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled … enter and remain in the second absorption?’

an9.41:8.3.verse: But my mind did not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in not placing the mind. I didn’t see it as peaceful.

an9.41:8.5.verse: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in not placing the mind? Why don’t I see it as peaceful?’

an9.41:8.7.verse: ‘I haven’t seen the drawbacks of placing the mind, and so I haven’t cultivated that. I haven’t realized the benefits of not placing the mind, and so I haven’t developed that.

an9.41:8.8.verse: That’s why my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in not placing the mind. And it’s why I don’t see it as peaceful.’

an9.41:8.10.verse: ‘Suppose that, seeing the drawbacks of placing the mind, I were to cultivate that. And suppose that, realizing the benefits of not placing the mind, I were to develop that. an9.41:8.11.verse: And so, after some time, I saw the drawbacks of placing the mind and cultivated that, and I realized the benefits of not placing the mind and developed that.

an9.41:8.12.verse: Then my mind did leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in not placing the mind. I saw it as peaceful.

an9.41:9.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I, with the fading away of rapture, enter and remain in the third absorption, where I will meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, “Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss”?’

an9.41:9.3.verse: But my mind did not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in freedom from rapture. I didn’t see it as peaceful.

an9.41:9.5.verse: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided in freedom from rapture? Why don’t I see it as peaceful?’

an9.41:9.7.verse: ‘I haven’t seen the drawbacks of rapture, and so I haven’t cultivated that. I haven’t realized the benefits of freedom from rapture, and so I haven’t developed that.

an9.41:16.1.verse: As long as I hadn’t entered into and withdrawn from these nine progressive meditative attainments in both forward and reverse order, I didn’t announce my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

an9.41:16.2.verse: But when I had entered into and withdrawn from these nine progressive meditative attainments in both forward and reverse order, I announced my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

an9.41:16.3.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

an9.41:16.4.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

an9.42:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

an9.42:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Udāyī went up to Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.

an9.42:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda,

an9.42:1.4.verse: “Reverend, this was said by the godling Pañcālacaṇḍa:

an9.42:2.2.verse: was discovered by the Buddha of vast intelligence,

an9.42:2.4.verse: the sage, the solitary boss bull.’

an9.42:3.1.verse: But what is confinement, and what is the opening amid confinement that the Buddha spoke of?”

an9.42:3.2.verse: “Reverend, these five kinds of sensual stimulation are called ‘confinement’ by the Buddha.

an9.42:3.4.verse: Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an9.42:3.8.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an9.42:3.9.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation that are called ‘confinement’ by the Buddha.

an9.42:4.1.verse: Now, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.42:4.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:4.5.verse: Whatever placing of the mind and keeping it connected has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:5.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled … enters and remains in the second absorption.

an9.42:5.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:5.5.verse: Whatever rapture has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:6.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, with the fading away of rapture … enters and remains in the third absorption.

an9.42:6.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of creating an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:6.5.verse: Whatever bliss with equanimity has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:7.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, giving up pleasure and pain … enters and remains in the fourth absorption.

an9.42:7.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:7.5.verse: Whatever perception of form has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:8.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

an9.42:8.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:8.5.verse: Whatever perception of the dimension of infinite space has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

an9.42:9.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:9.5.verse: Whatever perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

an9.42:10.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:10.5.verse: Whatever perception of the dimension of nothingness has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:11.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

an9.42:11.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a qualified sense.

an9.42:11.5.verse: Whatever perception of neither perception nor non-perception has not ceased is the confinement there.

an9.42:12.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.42:12.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of an opening amid confinement in a definitive sense.”

an9.43:1.2.verse: What is the direct witness that the Buddha spoke of?”

an9.43:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.43:2.2.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way.

an9.43:2.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the direct witness in a qualified sense.

an9.43:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, enters and remains in the second absorption …

an9.43:3.4.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way.

an9.43:3.5.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the direct witness in a qualified sense.

an9.43:4.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

an9.43:4.2.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way.

an9.43:4.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the direct witness in a qualified sense. Furthermore, take a mendicant who enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness … the dimension of nothingness … the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception …

an9.43:5.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.43:5.2.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way.

an9.43:5.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the direct witness in a definitive sense.”

an9.44:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of one ‘freed by wisdom’.

an9.44:1.2.verse: What is the one freed by wisdom that the Buddha spoke of?”

an9.44:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.44:2.2.verse: And they understand that with wisdom.

an9.44:2.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the one freed by wisdom in a qualified sense. …

an9.44:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.44:3.2.verse: And they understand that with wisdom.

an9.44:3.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the one freed by wisdom in a definitive sense.”

an9.45:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of one ‘freed both ways’.

an9.45:1.2.verse: What is the one freed both ways that the Buddha spoke of?”

an9.45:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.45:2.2.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way. And they understand that with wisdom.

an9.45:2.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the one freed both ways in a qualified sense. …

an9.45:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.45:3.2.verse: They meditate directly experiencing that dimension in every way. And they understand that with wisdom.

an9.45:3.3.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the one freed both ways in a definitive sense.”

an9.46:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘a teaching apparent in the present life’.

an9.46:1.2.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of a teaching apparent in the present life?”

an9.46:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.46:2.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the teaching apparent in the present life in a qualified sense. …

an9.46:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.46:3.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of the teaching apparent in the present life in a definitive sense.”

an9.47:0.3.verse: Extinguishment is Apparent in the Present Life

an9.47:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they say that ‘extinguishment is apparent in the present life’.

an9.47:1.2.verse: In what way did the Buddha say extinguishment is apparent in the present life?”

an9.47:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.47:2.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha said that extinguishment is apparent in the present life in a qualified sense. …

an9.47:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.47:3.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha said that extinguishment is apparent in the present life in a definitive sense.”

an9.50:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘extinguishment in a certain respect’. …”

an9.51:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘extinguishment in this life’.

an9.51:1.2.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of extinguishment in this life?”

an9.51:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.51:2.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of extinguishment in this life in a qualified sense. …

an9.51:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.51:3.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of extinguishment in this life in a definitive sense.”

an9.52:1.2.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of a safe place?”

an9.52:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.52:2.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of a safe place in a qualified sense. …

an9.52:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.52:3.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of a safe place in a definitive sense.”

an9.53:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘reaching a safe place’. …”

an9.55:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘reaching freedom from death’. …”

an9.56:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘a place without fear’. …”

an9.57:1.1.verse: “Reverend, they speak of ‘reaching a place without fear’. …”

an9.61:1.2.verse: What is the progressive cessation that the Buddha spoke of?”

an9.61:2.1.verse: “First, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and remains in the first absorption.

an9.61:2.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of progressive cessation in a qualified sense. …

an9.61:3.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

an9.61:3.2.verse: To this extent the Buddha spoke of progressive cessation in a definitive sense.”

an9.62:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, without giving up nine things you can’t realize perfection.

an9.62:1.3.verse: Greed, hate, delusion, anger, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, and stinginess.

an9.62:1.4.verse: Without giving up these nine things you can’t realize perfection.

an9.62:2.1.verse: After giving up nine things you can realize perfection.

an9.62:2.3.verse: Greed, hate, delusion, anger, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, and stinginess.

an9.62:2.4.verse: After giving up these nine things you can realize the fruit of perfection.”

an9.63:0.3.verse: Weaknesses in Training and Mindfulness Meditation

an9.63:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.63:1.3.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an9.63:1.4.verse: These are the five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.63:2.1.verse: To give up these five weaknesses in your training you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

an9.63:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.63:2.4.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

an9.63:2.5.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind …

an9.63:2.6.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.63:2.7.verse: To give up those five weaknesses in your training you should develop these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

an9.64:1.3.verse: Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

an9.64:2.1.verse: To give up these five hindrances you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

an9.64:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.64:2.4.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

an9.64:2.5.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind …

an9.64:2.6.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.64:2.7.verse: To give up those five hindrances you should develop these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

an9.65:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

an9.65:1.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an9.65:1.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an9.65:1.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

an9.65:2.1.verse: To give up these five kinds of sensual stimulation you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.66:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five grasping aggregates.

an9.66:1.3.verse: The grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

an9.66:1.4.verse: These are the five grasping aggregates.

an9.66:2.1.verse: To give up these five grasping aggregates you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.67:1.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.

an9.67:1.4.verse: These are the five lower fetters.

an9.67:2.1.verse: To give up these five lower fetters you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.68:1.3.verse: Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humanity, and the gods.

an9.68:2.1.verse: To give up these five destinations you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.69:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five kinds of stinginess.

an9.69:1.3.verse: Stinginess with dwellings, families, material things, praise, and the teaching.

an9.69:1.4.verse: These are the five kinds of stinginess.

an9.69:2.1.verse: To give up these five kinds of stinginess you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.70:1.3.verse: Desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, desire for rebirth in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

an9.70:1.4.verse: These are the five higher fetters.

an9.70:2.1.verse: To give up these five higher fetters you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.71:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are five kinds of hard-heartedness.

an9.71:1.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has doubts about the Teacher. They’re uncertain, undecided, and lacking confidence.

an9.71:1.4.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an9.71:1.5.verse: This is the first kind of hard-heartedness.

an9.71:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has doubts about the teaching …

an9.71:2.4.verse: A mendicant is angry and upset with their spiritual companions, resentful and closed off.

an9.71:2.5.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an9.71:2.6.verse: This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness.

an9.71:3.1.verse: To give up these five kinds of hard-heartedness you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …”

an9.72:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five shackles of the heart.

an9.72:1.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant isn’t free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

an9.72:1.4.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an9.72:1.5.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart.

an9.72:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t free of greed for the body …

an9.72:2.2.verse: They’re not free of greed for form …

an9.72:2.3.verse: They eat as much as they like until their belly is full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

an9.72:2.4.verse: They lead the spiritual life wishing to be reborn in one of the orders of gods: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

an9.72:2.5.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an9.72:2.6.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart.

an9.72:2.7.verse: These are the five shackles of the heart.

an9.72:3.1.verse: To give up these five shackles of the heart you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

an9.72:3.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.72:3.4.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

an9.72:3.5.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind …

an9.72:3.6.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

an9.72:3.7.verse: To give up these five shackles of the heart you should develop these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

an9.73:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.73:1.3.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an9.73:1.4.verse: These are the five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.73:2.1.verse: To give up these five weaknesses in your training you should develop the four right efforts.

an9.73:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

an9.73:2.4.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up.

an9.73:2.5.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

an9.73:2.6.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

an9.73:2.7.verse: To give up these five weaknesses in your training you should develop these four right efforts.”

an9.82:2.6.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

an9.82:2.7.verse: To give up these five shackles of the hearts you should develop these four right efforts.”

an9.83:0.3.verse: Weaknesses in Training and the Bases of Psychic Power

an9.83:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.83:1.3.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

an9.83:1.4.verse: These are the five weaknesses when you’re training.

an9.83:2.1.verse: To give up these five weaknesses in your training you should develop the four bases of psychic power.

an9.83:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort.

an9.83:2.4.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy, and active effort.

an9.83:2.5.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to mental development, and active effort.

an9.83:2.6.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to inquiry, and active effort.

an9.83:2.7.verse: To give up these five weaknesses in your training you should develop these four bases of psychic power.”

an9.93:1.1.verse: “For insight into greed, nine things should be developed.

an9.93:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these nine things should be developed.”

an9.94:1.4.verse: For insight into greed, these nine things should be developed.”

an9.95-112:1.10.verse: these nine things should be developed.”

an10.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.1:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.1:2.1.verse: “Sir, what is the goal and benefit of skillful ethics?”

an10.1:2.2.verse: “Ānanda, having no regrets is the goal and benefit of skillful ethics.”

an10.1:3.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of having no regrets?”

an10.1:3.2.verse: “Joy is the goal and benefit of having no regrets.”

an10.1:4.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of joy?”

an10.1:5.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of rapture?”

an10.1:6.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of tranquility?”

an10.1:7.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of bliss?”

an10.1:8.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of immersion?”

an10.1:9.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of truly knowing and seeing?”

an10.1:10.1.verse: “But what is the goal and benefit of disillusionment and dispassion?”

an10.1:10.2.verse: “Knowledge and vision of freedom is the goal and benefit of disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.1:11.1.verse: So, Ānanda, the goal and benefit of skillful ethics is not having regrets.

an10.1:11.2.verse: Joy is the goal and benefit of not having regrets.

an10.1:11.3.verse: Rapture is the goal and benefit of joy.

an10.1:11.4.verse: Tranquility is the goal and benefit of rapture.

an10.1:11.5.verse: Bliss is the goal and benefit of tranquility.

an10.1:11.6.verse: Immersion is the goal and benefit of bliss.

an10.1:11.7.verse: Truly knowing and seeing is the goal and benefit of immersion.

an10.1:11.8.verse: Disillusionment and dispassion is the goal and benefit of truly knowing and seeing.

an10.1:11.9.verse: Knowledge and vision of freedom is the goal and benefit of disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.1:11.10.verse: So, Ānanda, skillful ethics progressively lead up to the highest.”

an10.2:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an ethical person, who has fulfilled ethical conduct, need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.3.verse: It’s only natural that an ethical person has no regrets.

an10.2:1.4.verse: When you have no regrets you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.6.verse: It’s only natural that joy springs up when you have no regrets.

an10.2:1.7.verse: When you feel joy you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.9.verse: It’s only natural that rapture arises when you’re joyful.

an10.2:1.10.verse: When your mind is full of rapture you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.12.verse: It’s only natural that your body becomes tranquil when your mind is full of rapture.

an10.2:1.13.verse: When your body is tranquil you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.15.verse: It’s only natural to feel bliss when your body is tranquil.

an10.2:1.16.verse: When you feel bliss you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.17.verse: ‘May my mind be immersed in samādhi!’

an10.2:1.18.verse: It’s only natural for the mind to be immersed in samādhi when you feel bliss.

an10.2:1.19.verse: When your mind is immersed in samādhi you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.21.verse: It’s only natural to truly know and see when your mind is immersed in samādhi.

an10.2:1.22.verse: When you truly know and see you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.24.verse: It’s only natural to become disillusioned and dispassionate when you truly know and see.

an10.2:1.25.verse: When you’re disillusioned and dispassionate you need not make a wish:

an10.2:1.26.verse: ‘May I realize the knowledge and vision of freedom!’

an10.2:1.27.verse: It’s only natural to realize the knowledge and vision of freedom when you’re disillusioned and dispassionate.

an10.2:2.1.verse: And so, mendicants, the knowledge and vision of freedom is the goal and benefit of disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.2:2.2.verse: Disillusionment and dispassion is the goal and benefit of truly knowing and seeing.

an10.2:2.3.verse: Truly knowing and seeing is the goal and benefit of immersion.

an10.2:2.4.verse: Immersion is the goal and benefit of bliss.

an10.2:2.5.verse: Bliss is the goal and benefit of tranquility.

an10.2:2.6.verse: Tranquility is the goal and benefit of rapture.

an10.2:2.7.verse: Rapture is the goal and benefit of joy.

an10.2:2.8.verse: Joy is the goal and benefit of not having regrets.

an10.2:2.9.verse: Not having regrets is the goal and benefit of skillful ethics.

an10.2:2.10.verse: And so, mendicants, good qualities flow on and fill up from one to the other, for going from the near shore to the far shore.”

an10.3:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an unethical person, who lacks ethics, has destroyed a vital condition for having no regrets.

an10.3:1.2.verse: When there are regrets, one who has regrets has destroyed a vital condition for joy.

an10.3:1.3.verse: When there is no joy, one who lacks joy has destroyed a vital condition for rapture.

an10.3:1.4.verse: When there is no rapture, one who lacks rapture has destroyed a vital condition for tranquility.

an10.3:1.5.verse: When there is no tranquility, one who lacks tranquility has destroyed a vital condition for bliss.

an10.3:1.6.verse: When there is no bliss, one who lacks bliss has destroyed a vital condition for right immersion.

an10.3:1.7.verse: When there is no right immersion, one who lacks right immersion has destroyed a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an10.3:1.8.verse: When there is no true knowledge and vision, one who lacks true knowledge and vision has destroyed a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.3:1.9.verse: When there is no disillusionment and dispassion, one who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.3:1.10.verse: Suppose there was a tree that lacked branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would not grow to fullness.

an10.3:1.11.verse: In the same way, an unethical person, who lacks ethics, has destroyed a vital condition for having no regrets.

an10.3:1.12.verse: When there are regrets, one who has regrets has destroyed a vital condition for joy. …

an10.3:1.13.verse: One who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.3:2.1.verse: An ethical person, who has fulfilled ethics, has fulfilled a vital condition for not having regrets.

an10.3:2.2.verse: When there are no regrets, one who has no regrets has fulfilled a vital condition for joy.

an10.3:2.3.verse: When there is joy, one who has fulfilled joy has fulfilled a vital condition for rapture.

an10.3:2.4.verse: When there is rapture, one who has fulfilled rapture has fulfilled a vital condition for tranquility.

an10.3:2.5.verse: When there is tranquility, one who has fulfilled tranquility has fulfilled a vital condition for bliss.

an10.3:2.6.verse: When there is bliss, one who has fulfilled bliss has fulfilled a vital condition for right immersion.

an10.3:2.7.verse: When there is right immersion, one who has fulfilled right immersion has fulfilled a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an10.3:2.8.verse: When there is true knowledge and vision, one who has fulfilled true knowledge and vision has fulfilled a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.3:2.9.verse: When there is disillusionment and dispassion, one who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.3:2.10.verse: Suppose there was a tree that was complete with branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would grow to fullness.

an10.3:2.11.verse: In the same way, an ethical person, who has fulfilled ethics, has fulfilled a vital condition for not having regrets.

an10.3:2.12.verse: When there are no regrets, one who has no regrets has fulfilled a vital condition for joy. …

an10.3:2.13.verse: One who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.”

an10.4:1.3.verse: When there are regrets, one who has regrets has destroyed a vital condition for joy. …

an10.4:1.4.verse: One who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.4:1.8.verse: One who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.4:2.2.verse: When there are no regrets, one who has no regrets has fulfilled a vital condition for joy. …

an10.4:2.7.verse: One who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.”

an10.5:1.1.verse: There Venerable Ānanda addressed the mendicants …

an10.5:1.2.verse: “Reverends, an unethical person, who lacks ethics, has destroyed a vital condition for having no regrets.

an10.5:1.3.verse: When there are regrets, one who has regrets has destroyed a vital condition for joy.

an10.5:1.4.verse: When there is no joy, one who lacks joy has destroyed a vital condition for rapture.

an10.5:1.5.verse: When there is no rapture, one who lacks rapture has destroyed a vital condition for tranquility.

an10.5:1.6.verse: When there is no tranquility, one who lacks tranquility has destroyed a vital condition for bliss.

an10.5:1.7.verse: When there is no bliss, one who lacks bliss has destroyed a vital condition for right immersion.

an10.5:1.8.verse: When there is no right immersion, one who lacks right immersion has destroyed a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an10.5:1.9.verse: When there is no true knowledge and vision, one who lacks true knowledge and vision has destroyed a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.5:1.10.verse: When there is no disillusionment and dispassion, one who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.5:1.11.verse: Suppose there was a tree that lacked branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would not grow to fullness.

an10.5:1.12.verse: In the same way, an unethical person, who lacks ethics, has destroyed a vital condition for having no regrets.

an10.5:1.14.verse: One who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.5:2.1.verse: An ethical person, who has fulfilled ethics, has fulfilled a vital condition for not having regrets.

an10.5:2.2.verse: When there are no regrets, one who has no regrets has fulfilled a vital condition for joy.

an10.5:2.3.verse: When there is joy, one who has fulfilled joy has fulfilled a vital condition for rapture.

an10.5:2.4.verse: When there is rapture, one who has fulfilled rapture has fulfilled a vital condition for tranquility.

an10.5:2.5.verse: When there is tranquility, one who has fulfilled tranquility has fulfilled a vital condition for bliss.

an10.5:2.6.verse: When there is bliss, one who has fulfilled bliss has fulfilled a vital condition for right immersion.

an10.5:2.7.verse: When there is right immersion, one who has fulfilled right immersion has fulfilled a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

an10.5:2.8.verse: When there is true knowledge and vision, one who has fulfilled true knowledge and vision has fulfilled a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

an10.5:2.9.verse: When there is disillusionment and dispassion, one who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.5:2.10.verse: Suppose there was a tree that was complete with branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would grow to fullness.

an10.5:2.11.verse: In the same way, an ethical person, who has fulfilled ethics, has fulfilled a vital condition for not having regrets.

an10.5:2.12.verse: When there are no regrets, one who has no regrets has fulfilled a vital condition for joy. …

an10.5:2.13.verse: One who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.”

an10.6:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.6:1.2.verse: “Could it be, sir, that a mendicant might gain a state of immersion like this? They wouldn’t perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, or air in air. And they wouldn’t perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, or the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. And they wouldn’t perceive this world in this world, or the other world in the other world. And yet they would still perceive.”

an10.6:1.3.verse: “It could be, Ānanda, that a mendicant might gain a state of immersion like this. They wouldn’t perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, or air in air. And they wouldn’t perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, or the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. And they wouldn’t perceive this world in this world, or the other world in the other world. And yet they would still perceive.”

an10.6:3.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.’

an10.6:3.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant might gain a state of immersion like this. They wouldn’t perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, or air in air. And they wouldn’t perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, or the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. And they wouldn’t perceive this world in this world, or the other world in the other world. And yet they would still perceive.”

an10.7:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

an10.7:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

an10.7:2.1.verse: “Could it be, reverend Sāriputta, that a mendicant might gain a state of immersion like this? They wouldn’t perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, or air in air. And they wouldn’t perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, or the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. And they wouldn’t perceive this world in this world, or the other world in the other world. And yet they would still perceive.”

an10.7:4.2.verse: “Reverend Ānanda, this one time I was staying right here at Sāvatthī in the Dark Forest.

an10.7:4.3.verse: There I gained a state of immersion like this. I didn’t perceive earth in earth, water in water, fire in fire, or air in air. And I didn’t perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, or the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. And I didn’t perceive this world in this world, or the other world in the other world. And yet I still perceived.”

an10.7:5.1.verse: “But at that time what did Reverend Sāriputta perceive?”

an10.7:5.2.verse: “One perception arose in me and another perception ceased: ‘The cessation of continued existence is extinguishment. The cessation of continued existence is extinguishment.’

an10.7:5.3.verse: Suppose there was a burning pile of twigs. One flame would arise and another would cease.

an10.7:5.4.verse: In the same way, one perception arose in me and another perception ceased: ‘The cessation of continued existence is extinguishment. The cessation of continued existence is extinguishment.’

an10.7:5.5.verse: At that time I perceived that the cessation of continued existence is extinguishment.”

an10.8:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant is faithful but not ethical.

an10.8:1.2.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an10.8:1.4.verse: ‘How can I become faithful and ethical?’

an10.8:1.5.verse: When the mendicant is faithful and ethical, they’re complete in that respect.

an10.8:2.1.verse: A mendicant is faithful and ethical, but not learned. …

an10.8:2.4.verse: they don’t teach Dhamma to the assembly with assurance …

an10.8:2.5.verse: they’re not an expert in the monastic law …

an10.8:2.6.verse: they don’t stay in the wilderness, in remote lodgings …

an10.8:2.7.verse: they don’t get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty …

an10.8:2.8.verse: they don’t realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.8:2.9.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an10.8:2.11.verse: ‘How can I become faithful, ethical, and learned, a Dhamma speaker, one who frequents assemblies, one who teaches Dhamma to the assembly with assurance, an expert in the training, one who lives in the wilderness, in remote lodgings, one who gets the four absorptions when they want, and one who lives having realized the ending of defilements?’

an10.8:3.1.verse: When they’re faithful, ethical, and learned, a Dhamma speaker, one who frequents assemblies, one who teaches Dhamma to the assembly with assurance, an expert in the training, one who lives in the wilderness, in remote lodgings, one who gets the four absorptions when they want, and one who lives having realized the ending of defilements,

an10.8:3.3.verse: A mendicant who possesses these ten qualities is impressive all around, and is complete in every respect.”

an10.10:1.1.verse: “A mendicant is faithful, but not ethical.

an10.10:1.2.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an10.10:1.4.verse: ‘How can I become faithful and ethical?’

an10.10:1.5.verse: When the mendicant is faithful and ethical, they’re complete in that respect.

an10.10:2.1.verse: A mendicant is faithful and ethical, but not learned …

an10.10:2.4.verse: they don’t teach Dhamma to the assembly with assurance …

an10.10:2.7.verse: they don’t, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, see sentient beings passing away and being reborn …

an10.10:2.8.verse: they don’t realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.10:2.9.verse: So they’re incomplete in that respect,

an10.10:3.1.verse: When they are faithful, ethical, and learned, a Dhamma speaker, one who frequents assemblies, one who teaches Dhamma to the assembly with assurance, an expert in the training, one who recollects their many kinds of past lives, one who with clairvoyance that surpasses the human sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn, and one who lives having realized the ending of defilements,

an10.10:3.3.verse: A mendicant who possesses these ten qualities is impressive all around, and is complete in every respect.”

an10.11:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with five factors, using and frequenting lodgings with five factors, will soon realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they will live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.11:2.1.verse: And how does a mendicant have five factors?

an10.11:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

an10.11:2.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an10.11:2.4.verse: They are rarely ill or unwell. Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

an10.11:2.5.verse: They’re not devious or deceitful. They reveal themselves honestly to the Teacher or sensible spiritual companions.

an10.11:2.6.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an10.11:2.7.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an10.11:2.8.verse: That’s how a mendicant has five factors.

an10.11:3.1.verse: And how does a lodging have five factors?

an10.11:3.2.verse: It’s when a lodging is neither too far nor too near, but convenient for coming and going.

an10.11:3.3.verse: It’s not bothered by people by day, and at night it’s quiet and still.

an10.11:3.4.verse: There’s little disturbance from flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles.

an10.11:3.5.verse: While staying in that lodging the necessities of life—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are easy to come by.

an10.11:3.6.verse: And in that lodging there are several senior mendicants who are very learned, inheritors of the heritage, who have memorized the teachings, the monastic law, and the outlines.

an10.11:3.7.verse: From time to time they go up to those mendicants and ask them questions:

an10.11:3.8.verse: ‘Why, sir, does it say this? What does that mean?’

an10.11:3.9.verse: Those venerables reveal what is hidden, clarify what is unclear, and dispel doubt regarding the many doubtful matters.

an10.11:3.10.verse: That’s how a lodging has five factors.

an10.11:3.11.verse: A mendicant with five factors, using and frequenting lodgings with five factors, will soon realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they will live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

an10.12:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, in this teaching and training a mendicant who has given up five factors and possesses five factors is called consummate, accomplished, a supreme person.

an10.12:1.2.verse: And how has a mendicant given up five factors?

an10.12:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

an10.12:1.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant has given up five factors.

an10.12:2.1.verse: And how does a mendicant have five factors?

an10.12:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has the entire spectrum of an adept’s ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.12:2.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has five factors.

an10.12:3.1.verse: In this teaching and training a mendicant who has given up five factors and possesses five factors is called consummate, accomplished, a supreme person.

an10.12:4.4.verse: are not found in a mendicant at all.

an10.13:1.3.verse: The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters.

an10.13:1.4.verse: What are the five lower fetters?

an10.13:1.5.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.

an10.13:1.6.verse: These are the five lower fetters.

an10.13:2.1.verse: What are the five higher fetters?

an10.13:2.2.verse: Desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, desire for rebirth in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

an10.13:2.3.verse: These are the five higher fetters.

an10.14:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a monk or nun who has not given up five kinds of hard-heartedness and has not severed five shackles of the heart can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.14:2.1.verse: What are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up?

an10.14:2.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has doubts about the Teacher. They’re uncertain, undecided, and lacking confidence.

an10.14:2.3.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:2.4.verse: This is the first kind of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

an10.14:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has doubts about the teaching …

an10.14:3.4.verse: A mendicant is angry and upset with their spiritual companions, resentful and closed off.

an10.14:3.5.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:3.6.verse: This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

an10.14:3.7.verse: These are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

an10.14:4.1.verse: What are the five shackles of the heart they haven’t severed?

an10.14:4.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant isn’t free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

an10.14:4.3.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:4.4.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart they haven’t severed.

an10.14:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t free of greed for the body …

an10.14:5.2.verse: They’re not free of greed for form …

an10.14:5.3.verse: They eat as much as they like until their belly is full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

an10.14:5.4.verse: They lead the spiritual life wishing to be reborn in one of the orders of gods: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

an10.14:5.5.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:5.6.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart they haven’t severed.

an10.14:5.7.verse: These are the five shackles of the heart they haven’t severed.

an10.14:6.1.verse: A monk or nun who has not given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and has not severed these five shackles of the heart can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.14:7.1.verse: It’s like the moon in the waning fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only decline.

an10.14:7.2.verse: In the same way, a monk or nun who has not given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and has not severed these five shackles of the heart can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.14:8.1.verse: A monk or nun who has given up five kinds of hard-heartedness and has severed five shackles of the heart can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.14:9.1.verse: What are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they’ve given up?

an10.14:9.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has no doubts about the Teacher. They’re not uncertain, undecided, or lacking confidence.

an10.14:9.3.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:9.4.verse: This is the first kind of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

an10.14:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has no doubts about the teaching …

an10.14:10.4.verse: A mendicant is not angry and upset with their spiritual companions, not resentful or closed off.

an10.14:10.5.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:10.6.verse: This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

an10.14:10.7.verse: These are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

an10.14:11.1.verse: What are the five shackles of the heart they’ve severed?

an10.14:11.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

an10.14:11.3.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:11.4.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart they’ve severed.

an10.14:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is rid of greed for the body …

an10.14:12.2.verse: They’re rid of greed for form …

an10.14:12.3.verse: They don’t eat as much as they like until their belly is full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

an10.14:12.4.verse: They don’t lead the spiritual life wishing to be reborn in one of the orders of gods: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

an10.14:12.5.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

an10.14:12.6.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart they’ve severed.

an10.14:12.7.verse: These are the five shackles of the heart they’ve severed.

an10.14:13.1.verse: A monk or nun who has given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and has severed these five shackles of the heart can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.14:14.1.verse: It’s like the moon in the waxing fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only grow.

an10.14:14.2.verse: In the same way, a monk or nun who has given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and has severed these five shackles of the heart can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.”

an10.15:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is said to be the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception or with neither perception nor non-perception.

an10.15:1.2.verse: In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is said to be the best of them.

an10.15:2.1.verse: The footprints of all creatures that walk can fit inside an elephant’s footprint, so an elephant’s footprint is said to be the biggest of them all.

an10.15:2.2.verse: In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is said to be the best of them.

an10.15:3.1.verse: The rafters of a bungalow all lean to the peak, slope to the peak, and meet at the peak, so the peak is said to be the topmost of them all.

an10.15:3.2.verse: In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is said to be the best of them.

an10.15:4.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant root, spikenard is said to be the best.

an10.15:5.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant heartwood, red sandalwood is said to be the best.

an10.15:6.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant flower, jasmine is said to be the best.

an10.15:7.1.verse: All lesser kings are vassals of a wheel-turning monarch, so the wheel-turning monarch is said to be the foremost of them all.

an10.15:8.1.verse: The radiance of all the stars is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance, so the moon’s radiance is said to be the best of them all.

an10.15:9.1.verse: In the autumn the heavens are sunny and cloudless. And as the sun is rising to the firmament, having dispelled all the darkness of space, it shines and glows and dazzles.

an10.15:10.1.verse: All the great rivers—that is, the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—flow, slant, slope, and incline toward the ocean, and the ocean is said to be the greatest of them.

an10.15:10.2.verse: In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and meet at diligence, and diligence is said to be the best of them.”

an10.16:0.3.verse: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods

an10.16:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these ten individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

an10.16:1.3.verse: A Realized One, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha; an independent Buddha; one freed both ways; one freed by wisdom; a direct witness; one attained to view; one freed by faith; a follower by faith; a follower of teachings; a lamb of the flock.

an10.16:1.4.verse: These are the ten individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an10.17:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you should live with a protector, not without one.

an10.17:1.2.verse: Living without a protector is suffering.

an10.17:1.3.verse: There are ten qualities that serve as protector.

an10.17:1.5.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.17:1.7.verse: This is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.17:2.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.

an10.17:3.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They’re patient, and take instruction respectfully.

an10.17:4.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is deft and tireless in a diverse spectrum of duties for their spiritual companions, understanding how to go about things in order to complete and organize the work.

an10.17:5.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant loves the teachings and is a delight to converse with, being full of joy in the teaching and training.

an10.17:6.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

an10.17:7.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an10.17:8.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is mindful. They have utmost mindfulness and alertness, and can remember and recall what was said and done long ago.

an10.17:9.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an10.17:10.3.verse: This too is a quality that serves as protector.

an10.17:11.1.verse: You should live with a protector, not without one.

an10.17:11.2.verse: Living without a protector is suffering.

an10.17:11.3.verse: These are the ten qualities that serve as protector.”

an10.19:1.1.verse: “There are these ten abodes of the noble ones in which the noble ones of the past, present, and future abide.

an10.19:1.3.verse: A mendicant has given up five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth, has totally given up searching, has unsullied intentions, has stilled the physical process, and is well freed in mind and well freed by wisdom.

an10.19:1.4.verse: These are the ten abodes of the noble ones in which the noble ones of the past, present, and future abide.”

an10.20:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.

an10.20:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an10.20:2.1.verse: “There are these ten abodes of the noble ones in which the noble ones of the past, present, and future abide.

an10.20:2.3.verse: A mendicant has given up five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth, has totally given up searching, has unsullied intentions, has stilled the physical process, and is well freed in mind and well freed by wisdom.

an10.20:3.1.verse: And how has a mendicant given up five factors?

an10.20:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

an10.20:3.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has given up five factors.

an10.20:4.1.verse: And how does a mendicant possess six factors?

an10.20:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, seeing a sight with their eyes, is neither happy nor sad. They remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an10.20:4.3.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

an10.20:4.4.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

an10.20:4.5.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

an10.20:4.6.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

an10.20:4.7.verse: Knowing an idea with their mind, they’re neither happy nor sad. They remain equanimous, mindful and aware.

an10.20:4.8.verse: That’s how a mendicant possesses six factors.

an10.20:5.1.verse: And how does a mendicant have a single guard?

an10.20:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant’s heart is guarded by mindfulness.

an10.20:5.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has a single guard.

an10.20:6.1.verse: And how does a mendicant have four supports?

an10.20:6.2.verse: After appraisal, a mendicant uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.

an10.20:6.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has four supports.

an10.20:7.1.verse: And how has a mendicant cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth?

an10.20:7.2.verse: Different ascetics and brahmins have different idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth. For example:

an10.20:7.3.verse: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

an10.20:7.4.verse: A mendicant has cast out, cast aside, thrown out, discarded, let go of, given up, and relinquished all these.

an10.20:7.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant has cast aside idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth.

an10.20:8.1.verse: And how has a mendicant totally given up searching?

an10.20:8.2.verse: It’s when they’ve given up searching for sensual pleasures, for continued existence, and for a spiritual life.

an10.20:8.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has totally given up searching.

an10.20:9.1.verse: And how does a mendicant have unsullied intentions?

an10.20:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up intentions of sensuality, malice, and cruelty.

an10.20:9.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has unsullied intentions.

an10.20:10.1.verse: And how has a mendicant stilled the physical process?

an10.20:10.2.verse: It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

an10.20:10.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has stilled the physical process.

an10.20:11.1.verse: And how is a mendicant well freed in mind?

an10.20:11.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant’s mind is freed from greed, hate, and delusion.

an10.20:11.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is well freed in mind.

an10.20:12.1.verse: And how is a mendicant well freed by wisdom?

an10.20:12.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands: ‘I’ve given up greed, hate, and delusion, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they’re unable to arise in the future.’

an10.20:12.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant’s mind is well freed by wisdom.

an10.20:13.1.verse: Mendicants, whether in the past, future, or present, all noble ones abide in these same ten abodes of the noble ones.

an10.20:13.4.verse: These are the ten abodes of the noble ones in which the noble ones of the past, present, and future abide.”

an10.21:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, toward evening the lion, king of beasts, emerges from his den,

an10.21:1.4.verse: and roars his lion’s roar three times.

an10.21:1.5.verse: Then he sets out on the hunt.

an10.21:1.7.verse: ‘May I not injure any little creatures on unclear ground.’

an10.21:2.1.verse: ‘Lion’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

an10.21:2.2.verse: When the Realized One teaches Dhamma to an assembly, this is his lion’s roar.

an10.21:3.1.verse: The Realized One possesses ten powers of a Realized One. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

an10.21:3.3.verse: Firstly, the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.

an10.21:3.4.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. Relying on this he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

an10.21:4.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the result of deeds undertaken in the past, future, and present in terms of grounds and causes.

an10.21:4.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:5.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands where all paths of practice lead.

an10.21:5.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:6.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the world with its many and diverse elements.

an10.21:6.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:7.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the diverse convictions of sentient beings.

an10.21:7.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:8.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the faculties of other sentient beings and other individuals after encompassing them with his mind.

an10.21:8.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:9.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands corruption, cleansing, and emergence regarding the absorptions, liberations, immersions, and attainments.

an10.21:9.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:10.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One recollects many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. He remembers: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food.
