This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his many past lives, with features and details.

an10.21:10.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:11.1.verse: Furthermore, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Realized One sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, he sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an10.21:11.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:12.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.21:12.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.21:13.1.verse: These are the ten powers of a Realized One that the Realized One possesses. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.”

an10.22:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an10.22:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, I claim to be self-assured regarding the teachings that lead to realizing by insight the various different hypotheses.

an10.22:2.2.verse: So I am able to teach the Dhamma in appropriate ways to different people. Practicing accordingly, when something exists they’ll know it exists. When it doesn’t exist they’ll know it doesn’t exist. When something is inferior they’ll know it’s inferior. When it’s superior they’ll know it’s superior. When something is not supreme they’ll know it’s not supreme. When it is supreme they’ll know it’s supreme.

an10.22:2.3.verse: And they will know or see or realize it in whatever way it should be known or seen or realized. This is possible.

an10.22:2.4.verse: But this is the unsurpassable knowledge, that is: truly knowing each and every case.

an10.22:2.5.verse: And Ānanda, I say that there is no other knowledge better or finer than this.

an10.22:3.1.verse: The Realized One possesses ten powers of a Realized One. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

an10.22:3.3.verse: Firstly, the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible, and the impossible as impossible.

an10.22:3.4.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. Relying on this he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

an10.22:4.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the result of deeds undertaken in the past, future, and present in terms of grounds and causes.

an10.22:4.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:5.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands where all paths of practice lead.

an10.22:5.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:6.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the world with its many and diverse elements.

an10.22:6.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:7.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the diverse convictions of sentient beings.

an10.22:7.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:8.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the faculties of other sentient beings and other individuals after encompassing them with his mind.

an10.22:8.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:9.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands corruption, cleansing, and emergence regarding the absorptions, liberations, immersions, and attainments.

an10.22:9.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:10.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One recollects many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

an10.22:10.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:11.1.verse: Furthermore, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Realized One sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an10.22:11.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:12.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.22:12.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

an10.22:13.1.verse: These are the ten powers of a Realized One that the Realized One possesses. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.”

an10.23:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are things that should be given up by the body, not by speech.

an10.23:1.2.verse: There are things that should be given up by speech, not by the body.

an10.23:1.3.verse: There are things that should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom.

an10.23:2.1.verse: And what are the things that should be given up by the body, not by speech?

an10.23:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has committed a certain unskillful offense by way of body.

an10.23:2.3.verse: After examination, sensible spiritual companions say this to them:

an10.23:2.4.verse: ‘Venerable, you’ve committed a certain unskillful offense by way of body.

an10.23:2.5.verse: Please give up that bad bodily conduct and develop good bodily conduct.’

an10.23:2.6.verse: When spoken to by their sensible spiritual companions they give up that bad bodily conduct and develop good bodily conduct.

an10.23:2.7.verse: These are the things that should be given up by the body, not by speech.

an10.23:3.1.verse: And what are the things that should be given up by speech, not by the body?

an10.23:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has committed a certain unskillful offense by way of speech.

an10.23:3.3.verse: After examination, sensible spiritual companions say this to them:

an10.23:3.4.verse: ‘Venerable, you’ve committed a certain unskillful offense by way of speech.

an10.23:3.5.verse: Please give up that bad verbal conduct and develop good verbal conduct.’

an10.23:3.6.verse: When spoken to by their sensible spiritual companions they give up that bad verbal conduct and develop good verbal conduct.

an10.23:3.7.verse: These are the things that should be given up by speech, not by the body.

an10.23:4.1.verse: And what are the things that should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom?

an10.23:4.9.verse: and stinginess are things that should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom.

an10.23:5.1.verse: Nasty jealousy should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom.

an10.23:5.3.verse: It’s when a householder or their child is prospering in money, grain, silver, or gold.

an10.23:5.4.verse: And a bondservant or dependent thinks:

an10.23:5.5.verse: ‘Oh, may that householder or their child not prosper in money, grain, silver, or gold!’

an10.23:5.6.verse: Or an ascetic or brahmin receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an10.23:5.7.verse: And some other ascetic or brahmin thinks:

an10.23:5.8.verse: ‘Oh, may that venerable not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.’

an10.23:6.1.verse: Corrupt wishes should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom.

an10.23:6.3.verse: It’s when a faithless person wishes to be known as faithful.

an10.23:6.4.verse: An unethical person wishes to be known as ethical.

an10.23:6.5.verse: An unlearned person wishes to be known as learned.

an10.23:6.6.verse: A lover of company wishes to be known as secluded.

an10.23:6.7.verse: A lazy person wishes to be known as energetic.

an10.23:6.8.verse: An unmindful person wishes to be known as mindful.

an10.23:6.9.verse: A person without immersion wishes to be known as having immersion.

an10.23:6.10.verse: A witless person wishes to be known as wise.

an10.23:6.11.verse: Someone who has not ended the defilements wishes to be known as having ended the defilements.

an10.23:6.13.verse: Corrupt wishes should be given up neither by the body, nor by speech, but by seeing again and again with wisdom.

an10.23:7.1.verse: Suppose that greed masters that mendicant and keeps going.

an10.23:7.10.verse: or corrupt wishes master them and keep going.

an10.23:7.12.verse: ‘This venerable does not have the understanding that would eliminate greed, so greed masters them and keeps going.

an10.23:7.13.verse: They don’t have the understanding that would eliminate hate …

an10.23:7.21.verse: or corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes master them and keep going.’

an10.23:8.1.verse: Suppose that greed does not master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.23:8.10.verse: or corrupt wishes don’t master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.23:8.12.verse: ‘This venerable has the understanding that eliminates greed, so greed doesn’t master them and keep going.

an10.23:8.13.verse: They have the understanding that eliminates hate …

an10.23:8.21.verse: and corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes don’t master them and keep going.’”

an10.24:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was staying in the land of the Cetīs at Sahajāti.

an10.24:2.1.verse: “Reverends, a mendicant who makes a declaration of knowledge says:

an10.24:2.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching.’

an10.24:2.3.verse: Suppose that greed masters that mendicant and keeps going.

an10.24:2.12.verse: or corrupt wishes master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:2.13.verse: ‘This venerable does not have the understanding that would eliminate greed, so greed masters them and keeps going.

an10.24:2.14.verse: They don’t have the understanding that would eliminate hate …

an10.24:2.22.verse: or corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes master them and keep going.’

an10.24:3.1.verse: A mendicant who makes a declaration of development says:

an10.24:3.2.verse: ‘I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:3.3.verse: Suppose that greed masters that mendicant and keeps going.

an10.24:3.12.verse: or corrupt wishes master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:3.13.verse: ‘This venerable does not have the understanding that would eliminate greed, so greed masters them and keeps going.

an10.24:3.14.verse: They don’t have the understanding that would eliminate hate …

an10.24:3.22.verse: or corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes master them and keep going.’

an10.24:4.1.verse: A mendicant who makes a declaration of both knowledge and development says:

an10.24:4.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching. And I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:4.3.verse: Suppose that greed masters that mendicant and keeps going.

an10.24:4.12.verse: or corrupt wishes master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:4.13.verse: ‘This venerable does not have the understanding that would eliminate greed, so greed masters them and keeps going.

an10.24:4.14.verse: They don’t have the understanding that would eliminate hate …

an10.24:4.22.verse: or corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes master them and keep going.’

an10.24:5.1.verse: Suppose a poor, needy, and penniless person was to declare themselves to be rich, affluent, and wealthy.

an10.24:5.2.verse: But when it came time to make a payment they weren’t able to come up with any money, grain, silver, or gold.

an10.24:5.4.verse: ‘This person declares themselves to be rich, affluent, and wealthy, but they are in fact poor, penniless, and needy.’

an10.24:5.6.verse: Because when it came time to make a payment they weren’t able to come up with any money, grain, silver, or gold.

an10.24:6.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant who makes a declaration of knowledge and development says:

an10.24:6.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching. And I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:6.3.verse: Suppose that greed masters that mendicant and keeps going.

an10.24:6.12.verse: or corrupt wishes master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:6.13.verse: ‘This venerable does not have the understanding that would eliminate greed, so greed masters them and keeps going.

an10.24:6.14.verse: They don’t have the understanding that would eliminate hate …

an10.24:6.22.verse: or corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes master them and keep going.’

an10.24:7.1.verse: A mendicant who makes a declaration of knowledge says:

an10.24:7.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching.’

an10.24:7.3.verse: Suppose that greed does not master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.24:7.12.verse: or corrupt wishes don’t master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:7.13.verse: ‘This venerable has the understanding that eliminates greed, so greed doesn’t master them and keep going.

an10.24:7.14.verse: They have the understanding that eliminates hate …

an10.24:7.22.verse: and corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes don’t master them and keep going.’

an10.24:8.1.verse: A mendicant who makes a declaration of development says:

an10.24:8.2.verse: ‘I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:8.3.verse: Suppose that greed does not master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.24:8.12.verse: or corrupt wishes don’t master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:8.13.verse: ‘This venerable has the understanding that eliminates greed, so greed doesn’t master them and keep going.

an10.24:8.14.verse: They have the understanding that eliminates hate …

an10.24:8.22.verse: and corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes don’t master them and keep going.’

an10.24:9.1.verse: A mendicant who makes a declaration of both knowledge and development says:

an10.24:9.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching. And I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:9.3.verse: Suppose that greed does not master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.24:9.12.verse: or corrupt wishes don’t master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:9.13.verse: ‘This venerable has the understanding that eliminates greed, so greed doesn’t master them and keep going.

an10.24:9.14.verse: They have the understanding that eliminates hate …

an10.24:9.22.verse: and corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes don’t master them and keep going.’

an10.24:10.1.verse: Suppose a rich, affluent, and wealthy person was to declare themselves to be rich, affluent, and wealthy.

an10.24:10.2.verse: And whenever it came time to make a payment they were able to come up with the money, grain, silver, or gold.

an10.24:10.4.verse: ‘This person declares themselves to be rich, affluent, and wealthy, and they are in fact rich, affluent, and wealthy.’

an10.24:10.6.verse: Because when it came time to make a payment they were able to come up with the money, grain, silver, or gold.

an10.24:11.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant who makes a declaration of knowledge and development says:

an10.24:11.2.verse: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching. And I am developed in physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.’

an10.24:11.3.verse: Suppose that greed does not master that mendicant and keep going.

an10.24:11.12.verse: or corrupt wishes don’t master that mendicant and keep going. You should know of them:

an10.24:11.13.verse: ‘This venerable has the understanding that eliminates greed, so greed doesn’t master them and keep going.

an10.24:11.14.verse: They have the understanding that eliminates hate …

an10.24:11.22.verse: and corrupt wishes, so corrupt wishes don’t master them and keep going.’”

an10.25:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these ten universal dimensions of meditation.

an10.25:1.3.verse: Someone perceives the meditation on universal earth above, below, across, undivided and limitless.

an10.25:1.4.verse: They perceive the meditation on universal water …

an10.25:1.12.verse: They perceive the meditation on universal consciousness above, below, across, undivided and limitless.

an10.25:1.13.verse: These are the ten universal dimensions of meditation.”

an10.26:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis near Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain.

an10.26:1.2.verse: Then the laywoman Kāḷī of Kurughara went up to Venerable Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an10.26:1.3.verse: “Sir, this was said by the Buddha in ‘The Maidens’ Questions’:

an10.26:2.1.verse: ‘I’ve reached the goal, peace of heart.

an10.26:2.2.verse: Having conquered the army of the likable and pleasant,

an10.26:2.3.verse: alone, practicing absorption, I awakened to bliss.

an10.26:2.4.verse: That’s why I don’t get too close to people,

an10.26:2.5.verse: and no one gets too close to me.’

an10.26:3.1.verse: How should we see the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement?”

an10.26:4.1.verse: “Sister, some ascetics and brahmins regard the attainment of the meditation on universal earth to be the ultimate. Thinking ‘this is the goal’, they are reborn.

an10.26:4.2.verse: The Buddha directly knew the extent to which the attainment of the meditation on universal earth was the ultimate.

an10.26:4.3.verse: Directly knowing this he saw the beginning, the drawback, and the escape. And he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

an10.26:4.4.verse: Because he saw the beginning, the drawback, and the escape, and he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, he knew that he had reached the goal, peace of heart.

an10.26:5.1.verse: Some ascetics and brahmins regard the attainment of the meditation on universal water to be the ultimate. Thinking ‘this is the goal’, they are reborn. …

an10.26:5.2.verse: Some ascetics and brahmins regard the attainment of the meditation on universal fire …

an10.26:5.9.verse: universal consciousness to be the ultimate. Thinking ‘this is the goal’, they are reborn.

an10.26:5.10.verse: The Buddha directly knew the extent to which the attainment of the meditation on universal consciousness was the ultimate.

an10.26:5.11.verse: Directly knowing this he saw the beginning, the drawback, and the escape. And he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

an10.26:5.12.verse: Because he saw the beginning, the drawback, and the escape, and he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, he knew that he had reached the goal, peace of heart.

an10.26:5.13.verse: So, sister, that’s how to understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha said in brief in ‘The Maidens’ Questions’:

an10.26:6.1.verse: ‘I’ve reached the goal, peace of heart.

an10.26:6.2.verse: Having conquered the army of the likable and pleasant,

an10.26:6.3.verse: alone, practicing absorption, I awakened to bliss.

an10.26:6.4.verse: That’s why I don’t get too close to people,

an10.26:6.5.verse: and no one gets too close to me.’”

an10.27:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.27:1.2.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

an10.27:1.4.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.

an10.27:1.5.verse: Why don’t we visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an10.27:2.1.verse: Then they went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

an10.27:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. The wanderers said to them:

an10.27:3.1.verse: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples like this:

an10.27:3.2.verse: ‘Please, mendicants, directly know all things. Meditate having directly known all things.’

an10.27:3.4.verse: ‘Please, reverends, directly know all things. Live having directly known all things.’

an10.27:3.5.verse: What, then, is the difference between the ascetic Gotama’s teaching and instruction and ours?”

an10.27:4.1.verse: Those mendicants neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.

an10.27:4.2.verse: They rose from their seats, thinking,

an10.27:4.3.verse: “We will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

an10.27:5.1.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

an10.27:9.1.verse: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other religions say this, you should say to them:

an10.27:9.2.verse: ‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer. Two … Three … Four … Five … Six … Seven … Eight … Nine … Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.27:9.3.verse: Questioned like this, the wanderers of other religions would be stumped, and, in addition, would get frustrated.

an10.27:9.5.verse: Because they’re out of their element.

an10.27:9.6.verse: I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could provide a satisfying answer to these questions except the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.

an10.27:10.1.verse: ‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.27:10.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an10.27:10.3.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding one thing, seeing its limits and fully comprehending its meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.27:10.5.verse: ‘All sentient beings are sustained by food.’

an10.27:10.6.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding this one thing, seeing its limits and fully comprehending its meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.27:10.7.verse: ‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.27:10.8.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an10.27:18.5.verse: The nine abodes of sentient beings. …

an10.27:19.1.verse: ‘Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.27:19.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an10.27:19.3.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding ten things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.27:19.5.verse: The ten ways of performing unskillful deeds.

an10.27:19.6.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding these ten things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.27:19.7.verse: ‘Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.27:19.8.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

an10.28:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kajaṅgalā in a bamboo grove.

an10.28:1.2.verse: Then several lay followers of Kajaṅgalā went to the nun Kajaṅgalikā, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to her:

an10.28:2.1.verse: “Ma’am, this was said by the Buddha in ‘The Great Questions’:

an10.28:2.2.verse: ‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer. Two … Three … Four … Five … Six … Seven … Eight … Nine … Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’

an10.28:2.3.verse: How should we see the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement?”

an10.28:3.1.verse: “Respectable sirs, I haven’t heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha or from esteemed mendicants.

an10.28:3.2.verse: But as to how it seems to me,

an10.28:3.3.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an10.28:4.1.verse: “‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer.’ That’s what the Buddha said,

an10.28:4.2.verse: but why did he say it?

an10.28:4.3.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding one thing, seeing its limits and fully comprehending its meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:4.5.verse: ‘All sentient beings are sustained by food.’

an10.28:4.6.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding this one thing, seeing its limits and fully comprehending its meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:4.7.verse: ‘One thing: question, summary recital, and answer.’ That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

an10.28:6.3.verse: With a mind well developed in four things—seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning—a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:6.5.verse: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation. …

an10.28:6.6.verse: With a mind well developed in these four things—seeing their limits and fully fathoming their meaning—a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life. …

an10.28:8.3.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding nine things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:8.5.verse: The nine abodes of sentient beings.

an10.28:8.6.verse: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding these nine things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:9.1.verse: ‘Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’ That’s what the Buddha said,

an10.28:9.2.verse: but why did he say it?

an10.28:9.3.verse: Becoming well developed in ten things—seeing their limits and fully fathoming their meaning—a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:9.5.verse: The ten ways of performing skillful deeds.

an10.28:9.6.verse: With a mind well developed in these ten things—seeing their limits and fully fathoming their meaning—a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.

an10.28:9.7.verse: ‘Ten things: question, summary recital, and answer.’ That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

an10.28:10.1.verse: That’s how I understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha said in brief in ‘The Great Questions’.

an10.28:10.4.verse: If you wish, you may go to the Buddha and ask him about this.

an10.28:10.5.verse: You should remember it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

an10.28:10.6.verse: “Yes, ma’am,” replied those lay followers, approving and agreeing with what the nun Kajaṅgalikā said. Then they rose from their seats, bowed, and respectfully circled her, keeping her on their right. Then they went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

an10.28:10.7.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

an10.28:11.2.verse: The nun Kajaṅgalikā is astute, she has great wisdom.

an10.28:11.3.verse: If you came to me and asked this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way as the nun Kajaṅgalikā.

an10.28:11.4.verse: That is what it means, and that’s how you should remember it.”

an10.29:1.1.verse: “As far as Kāsi and Kosala extend, and as far as the dominion of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, King Pasenadi is said to be the foremost.

an10.29:1.2.verse: But even King Pasenadi decays and perishes.

an10.29:1.3.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:1.4.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:2.1.verse: A galaxy extends a thousand times as far as the moon and sun revolve and the dazzling ones light up the quarters.

an10.29:2.2.verse: In that galaxy there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sinerus king of mountains, a thousand Black Plum Tree Lands, a thousand lands west of Godāvarī, a thousand lands north of Kuru, a thousand lands east of Videha, four thousand oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand realms of the gods of the four great kings, a thousand realms of the gods of the thirty-three, of the gods of Yama, of the joyful gods, of the gods who love to create, of the gods who control what is created by others, and a thousand realms of divinity.

an10.29:2.3.verse: As far as the galaxy extends, the Great Divinity is said to be the foremost.

an10.29:2.4.verse: But even the Great Divinity decays and perishes.

an10.29:2.5.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:2.6.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:3.1.verse: There comes a time when this cosmos contracts.

an10.29:3.2.verse: As it contracts, most sentient beings migrate to the realm of sublime luminosity.

an10.29:3.3.verse: There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-radiant, wandering in midair, steadily glorious, and they remain like that for a very long time.

an10.29:3.4.verse: When the cosmos is contracting, the gods of sublime luminosity are said to be the foremost.

an10.29:3.5.verse: But even the gods of sublime luminosity decay and perish.

an10.29:3.6.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:3.7.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:4.1.verse: There are these ten universal dimensions of meditation.

an10.29:4.3.verse: Someone perceives the meditation on universal earth above, below, across, undivided and limitless.

an10.29:4.4.verse: They perceive the meditation on universal water …

an10.29:4.12.verse: They perceive the meditation on universal consciousness above, below, across, undivided and limitless.

an10.29:4.13.verse: These are the ten universal dimensions of meditation.

an10.29:5.1.verse: The best of these ten universal dimensions of meditation is when someone perceives the meditation on universal consciousness above, below, across, undivided and limitless.

an10.29:5.2.verse: Some sentient beings perceive like this.

an10.29:5.3.verse: But even the sentient beings who perceive like this decay and perish.

an10.29:5.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:5.5.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:6.1.verse: There are these eight dimensions of mastery.

an10.29:6.3.verse: Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limited, both pretty and ugly.

an10.29:6.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:6.5.verse: This is the first dimension of mastery.

an10.29:7.1.verse: Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limitless, both pretty and ugly.

an10.29:7.2.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:7.3.verse: This is the second dimension of mastery.

an10.29:8.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limited, both pretty and ugly.

an10.29:8.2.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:8.3.verse: This is the third dimension of mastery.

an10.29:9.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, limitless, both pretty and ugly.

an10.29:9.2.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:9.3.verse: This is the fourth dimension of mastery.

an10.29:10.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, blue, with blue color and blue appearance.

an10.29:10.2.verse: They’re like a flax flower that’s blue, with blue color and blue appearance. Or a cloth from Varanasi that’s smoothed on both sides, blue, with blue color and blue appearance.

an10.29:10.3.verse: In the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, blue, with blue color and blue appearance.

an10.29:10.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:10.5.verse: This is the fifth dimension of mastery.

an10.29:11.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, yellow, with yellow color and yellow appearance.

an10.29:11.2.verse: They’re like a champak flower that’s yellow, with yellow color and yellow appearance. Or a cloth from Varanasi that’s smoothed on both sides, yellow, with yellow color and yellow appearance.

an10.29:11.3.verse: In the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, yellow, with yellow color and yellow appearance.

an10.29:11.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:11.5.verse: This is the sixth dimension of mastery.

an10.29:12.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, red, with red color and red appearance.

an10.29:12.2.verse: They’re like a scarlet mallow flower that’s red, with red color and red appearance. Or a cloth from Varanasi that’s smoothed on both sides, red, with red color and red appearance.

an10.29:12.3.verse: In the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, red, with red color and red appearance.

an10.29:12.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:12.5.verse: This is the seventh dimension of mastery.

an10.29:13.1.verse: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, white, with white color and white appearance.

an10.29:13.2.verse: They’re like the morning star that’s white, with white color and white appearance. Or a cloth from Varanasi that’s smoothed on both sides, white, with white color and white appearance.

an10.29:13.3.verse: In the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally, white, with white color and white appearance.

an10.29:13.4.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:13.5.verse: This is the eighth dimension of mastery.

an10.29:13.6.verse: These are the eight dimensions of mastery.

an10.29:14.1.verse: The best of these dimensions of mastery is when someone, not perceiving form internally, sees forms externally, white, with white color and white appearance.

an10.29:14.2.verse: Mastering them, they perceive: ‘I know and see.’

an10.29:14.3.verse: Some sentient beings perceive like this.

an10.29:14.4.verse: But even the sentient beings who perceive like this decay and perish.

an10.29:14.5.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:14.6.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:15.1.verse: There are four ways of practice.

an10.29:15.5.verse: pleasant practice with slow insight, and

an10.29:15.7.verse: These are the four ways of practice.

an10.29:16.1.verse: The best of these four ways of practice is the pleasant practice with swift insight.

an10.29:16.2.verse: Some sentient beings practice like this.

an10.29:16.3.verse: But even the sentient beings who practice like this decay and perish.

an10.29:16.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:16.5.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:17.6.verse: One individual, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, perceives the dimension of nothingness.

an10.29:18.1.verse: The best of these four perceptions is when someone, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, perceives the dimension of nothingness.

an10.29:18.2.verse: Some sentient beings perceive like this.

an10.29:18.3.verse: But even the sentient beings who perceive like this decay and perish.

an10.29:18.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:18.5.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:19.1.verse: This is the best of the convictions of outsiders, that is: ‘I might not be, and it might not be mine. I will not be, and it will not be mine.’

an10.29:19.2.verse: When someone has such a view, you can expect

an10.29:19.3.verse: that they will not be attracted to continued existence,

an10.29:19.4.verse: and they will not be repulsed by the cessation of continued existence.

an10.29:19.5.verse: Some sentient beings have such a view.

an10.29:19.6.verse: But even the sentient beings who have views like this decay and perish.

an10.29:19.7.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:19.8.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:20.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who advocate the ultimate purity of the spirit.

an10.29:20.2.verse: This is the best of the advocates of the ultimate purity of the spirit, that is, when someone, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

an10.29:20.3.verse: They teach Dhamma in order to directly know and realize this.

an10.29:20.4.verse: Some sentient beings have such a doctrine.

an10.29:20.5.verse: But even the sentient beings who have such a doctrine decay and perish.

an10.29:20.6.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it.

an10.29:20.7.verse: Their desire fades away even for the foremost, let alone the inferior.

an10.29:21.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who advocate ultimate extinguishment in this very life.

an10.29:21.2.verse: This is the best of those who advocate extinguishment in this very life, that is, liberation by not grasping after truly understanding the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape of the six fields of contact.

an10.29:21.3.verse: Though I state and assert this, certain ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with the incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim:

an10.29:21.4.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama doesn’t advocate the complete understanding of sensual pleasures, forms, or feelings.’

an10.29:21.5.verse: But I do advocate the complete understanding of sensual pleasures, forms, and feelings. And I advocate complete extinguishment with no fuel for grasping in this very life, wishless, quenched, and cooled.”

an10.30:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.30:1.2.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala returned from combat after winning a battle and succeeding in his strategy.

an10.30:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the monastery.

an10.30:1.4.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and entered the monastery on foot.

an10.30:1.5.verse: At that time several mendicants were walking mindfully in the open air.

an10.30:1.6.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to them and said,

an10.30:1.7.verse: “Sirs, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?

an10.30:1.8.verse: For I want to see the Buddha.”

an10.30:1.9.verse: “Great king, that’s his dwelling, with the door closed. Approach it quietly, without hurrying; go onto the porch, clear your throat, and knock on the door-panel. The Buddha will open the door.”

an10.30:2.1.verse: So the king approached the Buddha’s dwelling, cleared his throat and knocked on the door-panel, and the Buddha opened the door.

an10.30:2.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi entered the Buddha’s dwelling. He bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet, caressing them and covering them with kisses, and pronounced his name:

an10.30:2.3.verse: “Sir, I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!

an10.30:2.4.verse: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!”

an10.30:3.1.verse: “But, Great King, for what reason do you act with such utmost deference for this body, conveying your manifest love?”

an10.30:3.2.verse: “Sir, it’s because of my gratitude and thanks for the Buddha that I act with such utmost deference, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:4.1.verse: The Buddha is practicing for the welfare and happiness of the people. He has established many people in the noble system, that is, the principles of goodness and skillfulness.

an10.30:4.2.verse: This is a reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:5.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha is ethical, possessing ethical conduct that is mature, noble, and skillful.

an10.30:5.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:6.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha lives in the wilderness, frequenting remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

an10.30:6.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:7.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an10.30:7.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:8.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an10.30:8.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:9.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha gets to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart, when he wants, without trouble or difficulty. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.30:9.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:10.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha gets the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when he wants, without trouble or difficulty.

an10.30:10.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:11.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha recollects many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. He remembers: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so he recollects his many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

an10.30:11.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:12.1.verse: Furthermore, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an10.30:12.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:13.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.30:13.2.verse: This is another reason that I act with such utmost deference for the Buddha, conveying my manifest love.

an10.30:14.1.verse: Well, now, sir, I must go.

an10.30:14.2.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

an10.30:14.3.verse: “Please, Great King, go at your convenience.”

an10.30:14.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an10.31:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Upāli went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.31:1.2.verse: “Sir, for how many reasons did the Realized One lay down training rules for his disciples and recite the monastic code?”

an10.31:2.1.verse: “Upāli, the Realized One laid down training rules for his disciples and recited the monastic code for ten reasons.

an10.31:2.3.verse: For the well-being of the Saṅgha and for the comfort of the Saṅgha. For keeping difficult individuals in check and for the comfort of good-hearted mendicants. For restraining defilements that affect this life and protecting against defilements that affect lives to come. For inspiring confidence in those without it, and increasing confidence in those who have it. For the continuation of the true teaching and the support of the training.

an10.31:2.4.verse: The Realized One laid down training rules for his disciples and recited the monastic code for these ten reasons.”

an10.32:0.3.verse: Suspending the Recitation of the Monastic Code

an10.32:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many grounds are there to suspend the recitation of the monastic code?”

an10.32:1.2.verse: “Upāli, there are ten grounds to suspend the recitation of the monastic code.

an10.32:1.4.verse: A mendicant who has committed an expulsion offense is sitting in the assembly. A discussion about whether someone has committed an expulsion offense is unfinished. Someone who is not fully ordained is sitting in the assembly. A discussion about whether someone is fully ordained or not is unfinished. Someone who has resigned the training is sitting in the assembly. A discussion about whether someone has resigned the training or not is unfinished. A eunuch is sitting in the assembly. A discussion about whether someone is a eunuch is unfinished. A raper of nuns is sitting in the assembly. A discussion about whether or not someone is a raper of nuns is unfinished.

an10.32:1.5.verse: These are the ten grounds to suspend the recitation of the monastic code.”

an10.33:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many qualities should a mendicant have to be deemed a judge?”

an10.33:1.2.verse: “Upāli, a mendicant should have ten qualities to be deemed a judge.

an10.33:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.33:1.5.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.33:1.6.verse: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

an10.33:1.7.verse: They’re firm and unfaltering in the training.

an10.33:1.8.verse: When there are opposing parties, they’re able to persuade, advocate, and convince them, make them see the other side and trust each other.

an10.33:1.9.verse: They’re skilled in the instigation and settlement of disciplinary issues.

an10.33:1.10.verse: They know what a disciplinary issue is.

an10.33:1.11.verse: They know how a disciplinary issue originates.

an10.33:1.12.verse: They know how a disciplinary issue ceases.

an10.33:1.13.verse: They know the practical way leading to the cessation of a disciplinary issue.

an10.33:1.14.verse: A mendicant should possess these ten qualities to be deemed a judge.”

an10.34:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many qualities should a mendicant have to give ordination?”

an10.34:1.2.verse: “Upāli, a mendicant should have ten qualities to give ordination.

an10.34:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.34:1.5.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.34:1.6.verse: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

an10.34:1.7.verse: They’re able to care for the sick or get someone else to do so.

an10.34:1.8.verse: They’re able to settle dissatisfaction or get someone else to do so.

an10.34:1.9.verse: They’re able to dispel remorse when it has come up.

an10.34:1.10.verse: They’re able to rationally dissuade someone from misconceptions that come up.

an10.34:1.11.verse: They’re able to encourage someone in the higher ethics,

an10.34:1.14.verse: A mendicant should possess these ten qualities to give ordination.”

an10.35:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many qualities should a mendicant have to give dependence?”

an10.35:1.2.verse: “Upāli, a mendicant should have ten qualities to give dependence.

an10.35:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical …

an10.35:1.6.verse: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

an10.35:1.7.verse: They’re able to care for the sick or get someone else to do so.

an10.35:1.8.verse: They’re able to settle dissatisfaction or get someone else to do so.

an10.35:1.9.verse: They’re able to dispel remorse when it has come up.

an10.35:1.10.verse: They’re able to rationally dissuade someone from misconceptions that come up.

an10.35:1.11.verse: They’re able to encourage someone in the higher ethics,

an10.35:1.14.verse: A mendicant should possess these ten qualities to give dependence.”

an10.36:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many qualities should a mendicant have to be attended on by a novice?”

an10.36:1.2.verse: “Upāli, a mendicant should have ten qualities to be attended on by a novice.

an10.36:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical …

an10.36:1.6.verse: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

an10.36:1.7.verse: They’re able to care for the sick or get someone else to do so.

an10.36:1.8.verse: They’re able to settle dissatisfaction or get someone else to do so.

an10.36:1.9.verse: They’re able to dispel remorse when it has come up.

an10.36:1.10.verse: They’re able to rationally dissuade someone from misconceptions that come up.

an10.36:1.11.verse: They’re able to encourage someone in the higher ethics,

an10.36:1.14.verse: A mendicant should possess these ten qualities to be attended on by a novice.”

an10.37:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘schism in the Saṅgha’.

an10.37:1.2.verse: How is schism in the Saṅgha defined?”

an10.37:1.3.verse: “Upāli, it’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as the teaching, and what is the teaching as not the teaching. They explain what is not the training as the training, and what is the training as not the training. They explain what was not spoken and stated by the Realized One as spoken and stated by the Realized One, and what was spoken and stated by the Realized One as not spoken and stated by the Realized One. They explain what was not practiced by the Realized One as practiced by the Realized One, and what was practiced by the Realized One as not practiced by the Realized One. They explain what was not prescribed by the Realized One as prescribed by the Realized One, and what was prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.37:1.4.verse: On these ten grounds they split off and go their own way. They perform legal acts autonomously and recite the monastic code autonomously.

an10.37:1.5.verse: That is how schism in the Saṅgha is defined.”

an10.38:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘harmony in the Saṅgha’.

an10.38:1.2.verse: How is harmony in the Saṅgha defined?”

an10.38:1.3.verse: “Upāli, it’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as not the teaching, and what is the teaching as the teaching. They explain what is not the training as not the training, and what is the training as the training. They explain what was not spoken and stated by the Realized One as not spoken and stated by the Realized One, and what was spoken and stated by the Realized One as spoken and stated by the Realized One. They explain what was not practiced by the Realized One as not practiced by the Realized One, and what was practiced by the Realized One as practiced by the Realized One. They explain what was not prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One, and what was prescribed by the Realized One as prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.38:1.4.verse: On these ten grounds they don’t split off and go their own way. They don’t perform legal acts autonomously or recite the monastic code autonomously.

an10.38:1.5.verse: That is how harmony in the Saṅgha is defined.”

an10.39:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.39:1.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘schism in the Saṅgha’.

an10.39:1.3.verse: How is schism in the Saṅgha defined?”

an10.39:1.4.verse: “Ānanda, it’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as the teaching …

an10.39:1.5.verse: and what was prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.39:1.6.verse: On these ten grounds they split off and go their own way. They perform legal acts autonomously and recite the monastic code autonomously.

an10.39:1.7.verse: That is how schism in the Saṅgha is defined.”

an10.39:2.1.verse: “But sir, what does someone who has split a harmonious Saṅgha brim with?”

an10.39:2.2.verse: “They brim with sin that lasts for an eon.”

an10.39:2.3.verse: “But sir, what is the sin that lasts for an eon?”

an10.39:2.4.verse: “They burn in hell for an eon, Ānanda.

an10.39:3.1.verse: A schismatic remains for the eon

an10.39:3.2.verse: in a place of loss, in hell.

an10.39:3.3.verse: Taking a stand against the teaching,

an10.39:3.4.verse: favoring factions, they ruin their sanctuary.

an10.39:3.5.verse: After causing schism in a harmonious Saṅgha,

an10.39:3.6.verse: they burn in hell for an eon.”

an10.40:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘harmony in the Saṅgha’.

an10.40:1.2.verse: How is harmony in the Saṅgha defined?”

an10.40:1.3.verse: “Ānanda, it’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as not the teaching, and what is the teaching as the teaching. They explain what is not the training as not the training, and what is the training as the training. They explain what was not spoken and stated by the Realized One as not spoken and stated by the Realized One, and what was spoken and stated by the Realized One as spoken and stated by the Realized One. They explain what was not practiced by the Realized One as not practiced by the Realized One, and what was practiced by the Realized One as practiced by the Realized One. They explain what was not prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One, and what was prescribed by the Realized One as prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.40:1.4.verse: On these ten grounds they don’t split off and go their own way. They don’t perform legal acts autonomously or recite the monastic code autonomously.

an10.40:1.5.verse: That is how harmony in the Saṅgha is defined.”

an10.40:2.1.verse: “But sir, what does someone who has forged harmony in a schismatic Saṅgha brim with?”

an10.40:2.4.verse: “They rejoice in heaven for an eon, Ānanda.

an10.40:3.1.verse: A Saṅgha in harmony is happy,

an10.40:3.2.verse: as is support for those in harmony.

an10.40:3.3.verse: Taking a stand on the teaching,

an10.40:3.4.verse: favoring harmony, they ruin no sanctuary.

an10.40:3.5.verse: After forging harmony in the Saṅgha,

an10.40:3.6.verse: they rejoice in heaven for an eon.”

an10.41:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Upāli went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.41:1.2.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason, why fights, quarrels, arguments, and disputes arise in the Saṅgha, and the mendicants don’t live happily?”

an10.41:1.3.verse: “Upāli, it’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as the teaching, and what is the teaching as not the teaching. They explain what is not the training as the training, and what is the training as not the training. They explain what was not spoken and stated by the Realized One as spoken and stated by the Realized One, and what was spoken and stated by the Realized One as not spoken and stated by the Realized One. They explain what was not practiced by the Realized One as practiced by the Realized One, and what was practiced by the Realized One as not practiced by the Realized One. They explain what was not prescribed by the Realized One as prescribed by the Realized One, and what was prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.41:1.4.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why fights, quarrels, arguments, and disputes arise in the Saṅgha, and the mendicants don’t live happily.”

an10.42:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many roots of dispute are there?”

an10.42:1.2.verse: “Upāli, there are ten roots of dispute.

an10.42:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant explains what is not the teaching as the teaching, and what is the teaching as not the teaching. They explain what is not the training as the training, and what is the training as not the training. They explain what was not spoken and stated by the Realized One as spoken and stated by the Realized One, and what was spoken and stated by the Realized One as not spoken and stated by the Realized One. They explain what was not practiced by the Realized One as practiced by the Realized One, and what was practiced by the Realized One as not practiced by the Realized One. They explain what was not prescribed by the Realized One as prescribed by the Realized One, and what was prescribed by the Realized One as not prescribed by the Realized One.

an10.42:1.5.verse: These are the ten roots of dispute.”

an10.43:1.1.verse: “Sir, how many roots of dispute are there?”

an10.43:1.2.verse: “Upāli, there are ten roots of disputes.

an10.43:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant explains what is not an offense as an offense, and what is an offense as not an offense. They explain a light offense as a heavy offense, and a heavy offense as a light offense. They explain a grave offense as a minor offense, and a minor offense as a grave offense. They explain a curable offense as an incurable offense, and an incurable offense as a curable offense. They explain an offense requiring amends as an offense not requiring amends, and an offense not requiring amends as an offense requiring amends.

an10.43:1.5.verse: These are the ten roots of dispute.”

an10.44:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kusinārā in the Forest of Offerings.

an10.44:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an10.44:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who wants to accuse another should first check five things in themselves and establish five things in themselves.

an10.44:2.2.verse: What five things should they check in themselves?

an10.44:2.3.verse: A mendicant who wants to accuse another should check this:

an10.44:2.4.verse: ‘Is my bodily behavior pure? Do I have pure bodily behavior that is impeccable and irreproachable?

an10.44:2.5.verse: Is this thing found in me or not?’

an10.44:2.6.verse: If it’s not, there’ll be some who say:

an10.44:2.7.verse: ‘Come on, venerable, train your own bodily behavior first.’

an10.44:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant who wants to accuse another should check this:

an10.44:3.2.verse: ‘Is my verbal behavior pure? Do I have pure verbal behavior that is impeccable and irreproachable?

an10.44:3.3.verse: Is this thing found in me or not?’

an10.44:3.4.verse: If it’s not, there will be people who say:

an10.44:3.5.verse: ‘Come on, venerable, train your own verbal behavior first.’

an10.44:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant who wants to accuse another should check this:

an10.44:4.2.verse: ‘Is my heart established in love for my spiritual companions, without resentment?

an10.44:4.3.verse: Is this thing found in me or not?’

an10.44:4.4.verse: If it’s not, there will be people who say:

an10.44:4.5.verse: ‘Come on, venerable, establish your heart in love for your spiritual companions first.’

an10.44:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant who wants to accuse another should check this:

an10.44:5.2.verse: ‘Am I very learned, remembering and keeping what I’ve learned? These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. Am I very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically?

an10.44:5.3.verse: Is this thing found in me or not?’

an10.44:5.4.verse: If it’s not, there will be people who say:

an10.44:5.5.verse: ‘Come on, venerable, memorize the scriptures first.’

an10.44:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant who wants to accuse another should check this:

an10.44:6.2.verse: ‘Have both monastic codes been passed down to me in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, and well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material?

an10.44:6.3.verse: Is this thing found in me or not?’

an10.44:6.4.verse: If it’s not, and if they are unable to respond when asked “Venerable, where was this spoken by the Buddha?” there will be people who say:

an10.44:6.6.verse: ‘Come on, venerable, train in the monastic code first.’

an10.44:6.7.verse: These are the five things they should check in themselves.

an10.44:7.1.verse: What five things should they establish in themselves?

an10.44:7.2.verse: ‘I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time.

an10.44:7.3.verse: I will speak truthfully, not falsely.

an10.44:7.4.verse: I will speak gently, not harshly.

an10.44:7.5.verse: I will speak beneficially, not harmfully.

an10.44:7.6.verse: I will speak lovingly, not from secret hate.’

an10.44:7.7.verse: These are the five things they should establish in themselves.

an10.44:7.8.verse: A mendicant who wants to accuse another should first check these five things in themselves and establish these five things in themselves.”

an10.45:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are ten drawbacks to entering a royal compound.

an10.45:1.3.verse: Firstly, a king is sitting with his chief queen

an10.45:1.5.verse: When the queen sees the monk she smiles, or when the monk sees the queen he smiles.

an10.45:1.7.verse: ‘They’ve done it for sure, or they will do it.’

an10.45:1.8.verse: This is the first drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a king has many duties, and much to do. He has sex with one of the women but doesn’t remember.

an10.45:2.4.verse: ‘No-one else has entered here, except that monk.

an10.45:2.5.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:2.6.verse: This is the second drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a gem is lost somewhere in the royal compound.

an10.45:3.3.verse: ‘No-one else has entered here, except that monk.

an10.45:3.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:3.5.verse: This is the third drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:4.1.verse: Furthermore, secret deliberations in the royal compound are leaked outside.

an10.45:4.3.verse: ‘No-one else has entered here, except that monk.

an10.45:4.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:4.5.verse: This is the fourth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:5.1.verse: Furthermore, in a royal compound, a father longs for their son, or a son longs for his father.

an10.45:5.3.verse: ‘No-one else has entered here, except that monk.

an10.45:5.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:5.5.verse: This is the fifth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:6.1.verse: Furthermore, the king promotes someone to a higher position.

an10.45:6.2.verse: Those who are upset by this think:

an10.45:6.3.verse: ‘The king is close to that monk.

an10.45:6.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:6.5.verse: This is the sixth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:7.1.verse: Furthermore, the king demotes someone to a lower position.

an10.45:7.2.verse: Those who are upset by this think:

an10.45:7.3.verse: ‘The king is close to that monk.

an10.45:7.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:7.5.verse: This is the seventh drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:8.1.verse: Furthermore, the king dispatches the army at the wrong time.

an10.45:8.2.verse: Those who are upset by this think:

an10.45:8.3.verse: ‘The king is close to that monk.

an10.45:8.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:8.5.verse: This is the eighth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:9.1.verse: Furthermore, the king dispatches the army at the right time, but orders it to turn back while still on the road.

an10.45:9.2.verse: Those who are upset by this think:

an10.45:9.3.verse: ‘The king is close to that monk.

an10.45:9.4.verse: Could this be the monk’s doing?’

an10.45:9.5.verse: This is the ninth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:10.1.verse: Furthermore, in the royal compound there is a trampling of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as arousing sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches that do not befit a monk.

an10.45:10.2.verse: This is the tenth drawback of entering a royal compound.

an10.45:10.3.verse: These are the ten drawbacks of entering a royal compound.”

an10.46:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

an10.46:1.2.verse: Then on the sabbath several Sakyan lay followers went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

an10.46:1.3.verse: “Sakyans, do you observe the sabbath with its eight factors?”

an10.46:1.4.verse: “Sir, sometimes we do, sometimes we don’t.”

an10.46:1.5.verse: “That’s your loss, Sakyans, it’s your misfortune. In this life with its fear of sorrow and death, you sometimes keep the sabbath and you sometimes don’t.

an10.46:2.2.verse: Take a man who earns half a dollar for an honest day’s work.

an10.46:2.3.verse: Is this enough to call him a deft and industrious man?”

an10.46:3.2.verse: Take a man who earns a dollar for an honest day’s work.

an10.46:3.3.verse: Is this enough to call him a deft and industrious man?”

an10.46:4.2.verse: Take a man who, for an honest day’s work, earns two dollars …

an10.46:4.16.verse: Is this enough to call him a deft and industrious man?”

an10.46:5.2.verse: Suppose that man earned a hundred or a thousand dollars every day and saved it all up. If he lived for a hundred years, would he not accumulate a large mass of wealth?”

an10.46:6.2.verse: Would that man, on account of that wealth, experience absolute happiness for a single day or night, or even half a day or night?”

an10.46:6.5.verse: “Because sensual pleasures, sir, are impermanent, hollow, false, and deceptive.”

an10.46:7.1.verse: “But take one of my disciples who lives diligent, keen, and resolute for ten years, practicing in line with my instructions. They can experience absolute happiness for a hundred years, ten thousand years, or a hundred thousand years.

an10.46:7.2.verse: And they could become a once-returner or a non-returner, or, as a sure bet, a stream-enterer.

an10.46:8.1.verse: take one of my disciples who lives diligent, keen, and resolute for nine years …

an10.46:12.9.verse: Let alone two days, take one of my disciples who lives diligent, keen, and resolute for one day, practicing in line with my instructions. They can experience absolute happiness for a hundred years, ten thousand years, or a hundred thousand years. And they could become a once-returner or a non-returner, or, as a sure bet, a stream-enterer.

an10.46:12.10.verse: It’s your loss, Sakyans, it’s your misfortune. In this life with its fear of sorrow and death, you sometimes keep the sabbath and you sometimes don’t.”

an10.46:12.11.verse: “Well, sir, from this day forth we will observe the sabbath with its eight factors.”

an10.47:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

an10.47:1.2.verse: Then Mahāli the Licchavi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.47:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason for doing bad deeds, for performing bad deeds?”

an10.47:1.4.verse: “Greed is a cause, Mahāli, greed is a reason for doing bad deeds, for performing bad deeds.

an10.47:1.5.verse: Hate is a cause of bad deeds …

an10.47:1.6.verse: Delusion is a cause of bad deeds …

an10.47:1.7.verse: Irrational application of mind is the cause of bad deeds …

an10.47:1.8.verse: A wrongly directed mind is a cause of bad deeds …

an10.47:1.9.verse: This is the cause, Mahāli, this is the reason for doing bad deeds, for performing bad deeds.”

an10.47:2.1.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason for doing good deeds, for performing good deeds?”

an10.47:2.2.verse: “Contentment is a cause, Mahāli, contentment is a reason for doing good deeds, for performing good deeds.

an10.47:2.3.verse: Love is a cause of good deeds …

an10.47:2.4.verse: Understanding is a cause of good deeds …

an10.47:2.5.verse: Rational application of mind is the cause of good deeds …

an10.47:2.6.verse: A rightly directed mind is a cause of good deeds …

an10.47:2.7.verse: This is the cause, Mahāli, this is the reason for doing good deeds, for performing good deeds.

an10.47:2.8.verse: If these ten things were not found in the world, we wouldn’t see either unprincipled and immoral conduct, or principled and moral conduct.

an10.47:2.9.verse: But since these ten things are found in the world, we see both unprincipled and immoral conduct, and principled and moral conduct.”

an10.48:1.1.verse: “There are these ten things, monks, that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on.

an10.48:2.1.verse: “I have become one who has no (distinctive) appearance”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:3.1.verse: “I am bound to others for my livelihood”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:4.1.verse: “I should comport myself differently”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:5.1.verse: “Can I myself find no fault with my virtue?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:6.1.verse: “Will my wise companions in the spiritual life, after testing me, find no fault with my virtue?”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:7.1.verse: “There is alteration in, and separation from, all that is dear and appealing to me”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:8.1.verse: “It is actions that I own, it is actions that I am heir to, it is actions that I am born from, actions are my kinsfolk, actions are my refuge -

an10.48:9.1.verse: whatever actions I perform, whether good or bad, to that I will be the heir”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:10.1.verse: “In what way do the nights and days pass for me?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:11.1.verse: “Do I delight in empty places?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:12.1.verse: “Has a state beyond (ordinary) human beings - the distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and seeing - been attained by me? ° Will I at the end, when questioned by my companions in the spiritual life, not be embarrassed?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

an10.48:13.1.verse: These are the ten things, monks, that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on.”

an10.48:0.3.verse: Ten Regular Reflections for a Renunciate

an10.48:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, one who has gone forth should often review these ten things.

an10.48:2.1.verse: One who has gone forth should often review this: ‘I have secured freedom from class.’

an10.48:3.1.verse: ‘My livelihood is tied up with others.’

an10.48:5.1.verse: ‘I hope there’s no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct?’

an10.48:6.1.verse: ‘I hope that, after examination, sensible spiritual companions don’t reproach any aspect of my ethics?’

an10.48:7.1.verse: ‘I must be parted and separated from all I hold dear and beloved.’

an10.48:8.1.verse: ‘I am the owner of my deeds and heir to my deeds. Deeds are my womb, my relative, and my refuge.

an10.48:9.1.verse: I shall be the heir of whatever deeds I do, whether good or bad.’

an10.48:10.1.verse: ‘As the days and nights pass by, what sort of person am I becoming?’

an10.48:11.1.verse: ‘Do I love to stay in empty huts?’

an10.48:12.1.verse: ‘Do I have any superhuman distinctions in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, so that when my spiritual companions question me on my deathbed I will not be embarrassed?’

an10.48:13.1.verse: One who has gone forth should often review these ten things.”

an10.49:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these ten things exist because of the body.

an10.49:1.3.verse: Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, feces, urine, restraint of body, speech, and livelihood, and the will to live that leads to future lives.

an10.49:1.4.verse: These ten things exist because of the body.”

an10.50:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.50:1.2.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall. They were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, wounding each other with barbed words.

an10.50:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,

an10.50:2.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

an10.50:3.1.verse: “Sir, after the meal, on return from almsround, we sat together in the assembly hall, fighting, quarreling, and disputing, wounding each other with barbed words.”

an10.50:3.2.verse: “Mendicants, this is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness.

an10.50:4.1.verse: There are ten warm-hearted qualities that make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without dispute.

an10.50:4.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.50:4.5.verse: this warm-hearted quality makes for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without dispute.

an10.50:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically. …

an10.50:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates. …

an10.50:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They’re patient, and take instruction respectfully. …

an10.50:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is deft and tireless in a diverse spectrum of duties for their spiritual companions, understanding how to go about things in order to complete and organize the work. …

an10.50:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant loves the teachings and is a delight to converse with, being full of joy in the teaching and training. …

an10.50:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities. …

an10.50:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. …

an10.50:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is mindful. They have utmost mindfulness and alertness, and can remember and recall what was said and done long ago. …

an10.50:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

an10.50:13.3.verse: this warm-hearted quality makes for fondness and respect, helping the Saṅgha to live in harmony and unity, without quarreling.

an10.50:14.1.verse: These ten warm-hearted qualities make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without dispute.”

an10.51:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.51:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
