an10.51:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, if a mendicant isn’t skilled in encompassing another’s mind, then they should train themselves: ‘I will be skilled in encompassing my own mind.’

an10.51:3.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in encompassing their own mind?

an10.51:3.2.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

an10.51:3.3.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for:

an10.51:3.5.verse: In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities.

an10.51:3.6.verse: ‘Am I often covetous or not? Am I often malicious or not? Am I often overcome with dullness and drowsiness or not? Am I often restless or not? Am I often doubtful or not? Am I often irritable or not? Am I often corrupted in mind or not? Am I often disturbed in body or not? Am I often energetic or not? Am I often immersed in samādhi or not?’

an10.51:4.1.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.51:4.2.verse: ‘I am often covetous, malicious, overcome with dullness and drowsiness, restless, doubtful, irritable, corrupted in mind, disturbed in body, lazy, and not immersed in samādhi.’ In order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.51:4.3.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.51:4.4.verse: In the same way, in order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, that mendicant should apply extraordinary enthusiasm …

an10.51:5.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.51:5.2.verse: ‘I am often content, kind-hearted, rid of dullness and drowsiness, calm, confident, loving, pure in mind, undisturbed in body, energetic, and immersed in samādhi.’ Grounded on those skillful qualities, they should practice meditation further to end the defilements.”

an10.52:2.1.verse: “Reverends, if a mendicant isn’t skilled in encompassing another’s mind, then they should train themselves: ‘I will be skilled in encompassing my own mind.’

an10.52:3.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in encompassing their own mind?

an10.52:3.2.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

an10.52:3.3.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for:

an10.52:4.1.verse: In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities.

an10.52:4.2.verse: ‘Am I often covetous or not? Am I often malicious or not? Am I often overcome with dullness and drowsiness or not? Am I often restless or not? Am I often doubtful or not? Am I often irritable or not? Am I often corrupted in mind or not? Am I often disturbed in body or not? Am I often energetic or not? Am I often immersed in samādhi or not?’

an10.52:5.1.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.52:5.2.verse: ‘I am often covetous, malicious, overcome with dullness and drowsiness, restless, doubtful, irritable, defiled in mind, disturbed in body, lazy, and not immersed in samādhi.’ In order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.52:5.3.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.52:5.4.verse: In the same way, in order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, that mendicant should apply extraordinary enthusiasm …

an10.52:6.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.52:6.2.verse: ‘I am often content, kind-hearted, rid of dullness and drowsiness, calm, confident, loving, pure in mind, undisturbed in body, energetic, and immersed in samādhi.’ Grounded on those skillful qualities, they should practice meditation further to end the defilements.”

an10.53:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I don’t praise stagnation in skillful qualities, let alone decline.

an10.53:1.2.verse: I praise growth in skillful qualities, not stagnation or decline.

an10.53:2.1.verse: And how is there decline in skillful qualities, not stagnation or growth?

an10.53:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has a certain degree of faith, ethics, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence. Those qualities neither stagnate nor grow in them.

an10.53:2.3.verse: I call this decline in skillful qualities, not stagnation or growth.

an10.53:2.4.verse: This is how there’s decline in skillful qualities, not stagnation or growth.

an10.53:3.1.verse: And how is there stagnation in skillful qualities, not decline or growth?

an10.53:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has a certain degree of faith, ethics, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence. Those qualities neither decline nor grow in them.

an10.53:3.3.verse: I call this stagnation in skillful qualities, not decline or growth.

an10.53:3.4.verse: This is how there’s stagnation in skillful qualities, not decline or growth.

an10.53:4.1.verse: And how is there growth in skillful qualities, not stagnation or decline?

an10.53:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has a certain degree of faith, ethics, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence. Those qualities neither stagnate nor decline in them.

an10.53:4.3.verse: I call this growth in skillful qualities, not stagnation or decline.

an10.53:4.4.verse: This is how there’s growth in skillful qualities, not stagnation or decline.

an10.53:5.1.verse: If a mendicant isn’t skilled in encompassing another’s mind, then they should train themselves: ‘I will be skilled in encompassing my own mind.’

an10.53:6.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in encompassing their own mind?

an10.53:6.2.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

an10.53:6.3.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for:

an10.53:6.5.verse: In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities.

an10.53:6.6.verse: ‘Am I often covetous or not? Am I often malicious or not? Am I often overcome with dullness and drowsiness or not? Am I often restless or not? Am I often doubtful or not? Am I often irritable or not? Am I often corrupted in mind or not? Am I often disturbed in body or not? Am I often energetic or not? Am I often immersed in samādhi or not?’

an10.53:7.1.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.53:7.2.verse: ‘I am often covetous, malicious, overcome with dullness and drowsiness, restless, doubtful, irritable, corrupted in mind, disturbed in body, lazy, and not immersed in samādhi.’ In order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.53:7.3.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.53:7.5.verse: In the same way, in order to give up those bad, unskillful qualities, that mendicant should apply extraordinary enthusiasm …

an10.53:8.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.53:8.2.verse: ‘I am often content, kind-hearted, rid of dullness and drowsiness, calm, confident, loving, pure in mind, undisturbed in body, energetic, and immersed in samādhi.’ Grounded on those skillful qualities, they should practice meditation further to end the defilements.”

an10.54:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if a mendicant isn’t skilled in encompassing another’s mind, then they should train themselves: ‘I will be skilled in encompassing my own mind.’

an10.54:2.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in encompassing their own mind?

an10.54:2.2.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

an10.54:2.3.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for:

an10.54:2.5.verse: In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities.

an10.54:2.6.verse: ‘Do I have internal serenity of heart or not? Do I have the higher wisdom of discernment of principles or not?’

an10.54:3.1.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.54:3.2.verse: ‘I have serenity but not discernment.’ Grounded on serenity, they should practice meditation to get discernment.

an10.54:3.3.verse: After some time they have both serenity and discernment.

an10.54:4.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.54:4.2.verse: ‘I have discernment but not serenity.’ Grounded on discernment, they should practice meditation to get serenity.

an10.54:4.3.verse: After some time they have both serenity and discernment.

an10.54:5.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.54:5.2.verse: ‘I have neither serenity nor discernment.’ In order to get those skillful qualities, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.54:5.3.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.54:5.5.verse: In the same way, in order to get those skillful qualities, that mendicant should apply extraordinary enthusiasm …

an10.54:5.6.verse: After some time they have both serenity and discernment.

an10.54:6.1.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

an10.54:6.2.verse: ‘I have both serenity and discernment.’ Grounded on those skillful qualities, they should practice meditation further to end the defilements.

an10.54:8.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of robes:

an10.54:8.2.verse: those you should wear, and those you shouldn’t wear.’

an10.54:8.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

an10.54:8.4.verse: Well, should you know of a robe:

an10.54:8.5.verse: ‘When I wear this robe, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not wear that kind of robe.

an10.54:8.6.verse: Whereas, should you know of a robe:

an10.54:8.7.verse: ‘When I wear this robe, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should wear that kind of robe.

an10.54:8.8.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of robes:

an10.54:8.9.verse: those you should wear, and those you shouldn’t wear.’

an10.54:8.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

an10.55:2.1.verse: “Reverends, they speak of an individual liable to decline,

an10.55:2.2.verse: and one not liable to decline.

an10.55:2.3.verse: But how did the Buddha define an individual liable to decline, and one not liable to decline?”

an10.55:2.4.verse: “Reverend, we would travel a long way to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta.

an10.55:2.5.verse: May Venerable Sāriputta himself please clarify the meaning of this.

an10.55:2.6.verse: The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

an10.55:3.1.verse: “Then listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an10.55:4.1.verse: “How did the Buddha define an individual liable to decline?

an10.55:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t get to hear a teaching they haven’t heard before. They forget those teachings they have heard. They don’t keep exercising the teachings with which they are already familiar. And they don’t come to understand what they haven’t understood before.

an10.55:4.3.verse: That’s how the Buddha defined an individual liable to decline.

an10.55:5.1.verse: And how did the Buddha define an individual not liable to decline?

an10.55:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant gets to hear a teaching they haven’t heard before. They remember those teachings they have heard. They keep exercising the teachings with which they are already familiar. And they come to understand what they haven’t understood before.

an10.55:5.3.verse: That’s how the Buddha defined an individual not liable to decline.

an10.55:6.1.verse: If a mendicant isn’t skilled in encompassing another’s mind, then they should train themselves: ‘I will be skilled in encompassing my own mind.’

an10.55:7.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in encompassing their own mind?

an10.55:7.2.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

an10.55:7.3.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for:

an10.55:7.5.verse: In the same way, checking is very helpful for a mendicant’s skillful qualities.

an10.55:7.6.verse: ‘Is contentment often found in me or not? Is good will often found in me or not? Is freedom from dullness and drowsiness often found in me or not? Is calm often found in me or not? Is confidence often found in me or not? Is love often found in me or not? Is purity of mind often found in me or not? Is internal joy with the teaching found in me or not? Is internal serenity of heart found in me or not? Is the higher wisdom of discernment of principles found in me or not?’

an10.55:8.1.verse: Suppose a mendicant, while checking, doesn’t see any of these skillful qualities in themselves. In order to get them they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.55:8.2.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.55:8.4.verse: In the same way, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm to get those skillful qualities …

an10.55:9.1.verse: Suppose a mendicant, while checking, sees some of these skillful qualities in themselves, but doesn’t see others. Grounded on the skillful qualities they see, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness in order to get the skillful qualities they don’t see.

an10.55:9.2.verse: Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, you’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness.

an10.55:9.4.verse: In the same way, grounded on the skillful qualities they see, they should apply extraordinary enthusiasm to get those skillful qualities they don’t see.

an10.55:10.1.verse: But suppose a mendicant, while checking, sees all of these skillful qualities in themselves. Grounded on all these skillful qualities they should practice meditation further to end the defilements.”

an10.56:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are very fruitful and beneficial. They have freedom from death as their objective and culmination.

an10.56:1.3.verse: The perceptions of ugliness, death, repulsiveness of food, dissatisfaction with the whole world, impermanence, suffering in impermanence, and not-self in suffering, giving up, fading away, and cessation.

an10.56:1.4.verse: These ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are very fruitful and beneficial. They have freedom from death as their objective and culmination.”

an10.57:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are very fruitful and beneficial. They have freedom from death as their objective and culmination.

an10.57:1.3.verse: The perceptions of impermanence, not-self, death, repulsiveness of food, dissatisfaction with the whole world, a skeleton, a worm-infested corpse, a livid corpse, a split open corpse, and a bloated corpse.

an10.57:1.4.verse: These ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are very fruitful and beneficial. They have freedom from death as their objective and culmination.”

an10.58:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an10.58:1.2.verse: ‘Reverends, all things have what as their root? What produces them? What is their origin? What is their meeting place? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their overseer? What is their core? What is their objective? What is their culmination?’ How would you answer them?”

an10.58:1.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

an10.58:2.1.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

an10.58:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other religions were to ask:

an10.58:3.2.verse: ‘Reverends, all things have what as their root? What produces them? What is their origin? What is their meeting place? What is their chief? What is their ruler? What is their overseer? What is their core? What is their objective? What is their culmination?’

an10.58:3.4.verse: ‘Reverends, all things are rooted in desire. They are produced by application of mind. Contact is their origin. Feeling is their meeting place. Immersion is their chief. Mindfulness is their ruler. Wisdom is their overseer. Freedom is their core. Their objective is freedom from death. And extinguishment is their culmination.’

an10.58:3.5.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.”

an10.59:1.2.verse: ‘Our minds will be consolidated as they were when we went forth, and arisen bad unskillful qualities will not occupy our minds.

an10.59:1.3.verse: Our minds will be consolidated in the perceptions of impermanence, not-self, ugliness, and drawbacks. Knowing what is fair and unfair in the world, our minds will be consolidated in that perception. Knowing  existence and nonexistence in the world, our minds will be consolidated in that perception. Knowing the origin and disappearance of the world, our minds will be consolidated in that perception. Our minds will be consolidated in the perceptions of giving up, fading away, and cessation.’

an10.59:2.1.verse: When your minds are consolidated in these ten perceptions, you can expect one of two results:

an10.59:2.2.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.”

an10.60:1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

an10.60:1.2.verse: Then at that time venerable Girimānanda was afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

an10.60:1.3.verse: Then venerable Ānanda approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, he sat down on one side. While sitting on one side venerable Ānanda said this to the Fortunate One:

an10.60:2.1.verse: “Reverend Sir, venerable Girimānanda is afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

an10.60:2.2.verse: Please, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One approach venerable Girimānanda, taking pity on him.”

an10.60:2.3.verse: “If you, Ānanda, having approached the monk Girimānanda, were to recite the ten perceptions, then it is possible that having heard the ten perceptions, the monk Girimānanda’s affliction would immediately abate.

an10.60:3.2.verse: The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of giving up, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of impermanence in all processes, mindfulness while breathing.

an10.60:4.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence?

an10.60:4.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

an10.60:4.3.verse: form is impermanent, feelings are impermanent, perceptions are impermanent, (mental) processes are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.

an10.60:4.4.verse: Thus in regard to these five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment he dwells contemplating impermanence.

an10.60:4.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of impermanence.

an10.60:5.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self?

an10.60:5.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

an10.60:5.3.verse: the eye is not self - forms are not self, the ear is not self - sounds are not self, the nose is not self - smells are not self, the tongue is not self - tastes are not self, the body is not self - tangibles are not self, the mind is not self - thoughts are not self.

an10.60:5.4.verse: Thus in regard to these six internal and external sense spheres he dwells contemplating non-self.

an10.60:5.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-self.

an10.60:6.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of the unattractive?

an10.60:6.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk (in regard to) this body - from the sole of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head down, bounded by the skin, and filled with manifold impurities - reflects (thus):

an10.60:6.3.verse: There are in this body: hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spit, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.

an10.60:6.4.verse: Thus in regard to this body he dwells contemplating what is unattractive.

an10.60:6.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of the unattractive.

an10.60:7.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger?

an10.60:7.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

an10.60:7.3.verse: This body has many sufferings, many dangers, thus, in connection with this body, various afflictions arise, like this:

an10.60:7.4.verse: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease (i.e diseases affecting the sense spheres), head-disease, ear-disease, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, pyrexia, fever, stomach-ache, fainting, diarrhoea, gripes, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scab, chickenpox, scabies, haemorrhage, diabetes, piles, cancer, ulcers, afflictions arising from excess bile, afflictions arising from excess phlegm, afflictions arising from excess wind, afflictions arising from a conflict of humours, afflictions born of a change of season, afflictions born of not being careful, afflictions from being attacked, afflictions born as a result of (previous unwholesome) actions, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, stool, urine.

an10.60:7.5.verse: Thus, in regard to this body, he dwells contemplating danger.

an10.60:7.6.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.

an10.60:8.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of giving up?

an10.60:8.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk does not consent to thoughts of sense desire that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to thoughts of ill-will that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to thoughts of violence that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to any bad, unwholesome, thoughts that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent.

an10.60:8.3.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of giving up.

an10.60:9.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of dispassion?

an10.60:9.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

an10.60:9.3.verse: This is peaceful, this is excellent, that is to say: the calming of all processes, the letting go of all bases for cleaving, the end of craving, dispassion, Nibbāna.

an10.60:9.4.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of dispassion.

an10.60:10.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation?

an10.60:10.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

an10.60:10.3.verse: This is peaceful, this is excellent, that is to say: the calming of all processes, the letting go of all bases for cleaving, the end of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.

an10.60:10.4.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of cessation.

an10.60:11.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world?

an10.60:11.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk in regard to whatever in the world are selfish means and attachments, or mental determinations, settled beliefs, and tendencies, giving these up, not being attached, he abstains (from them).

an10.60:11.3.verse: This, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world.

an10.60:12.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence in all processes?

an10.60:12.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk in regard to all processes is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.

an10.60:12.3.verse: This, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence in all processes.

an10.60:13.1.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is mindfulness while breathing?

an10.60:13.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down. After folding his legs crosswise, setting his body straight, and establishing mindfulness at the front,

an10.60:13.3.verse: mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.

an10.60:13.4.verse: While breathing in long, he knows “I am breathing in long”, while breathing out long, he knows “I am breathing out long”,

an10.60:13.5.verse: while breathing in short, he knows “I am breathing in short”, while breathing out short, he knows “I am breathing out short”,

an10.60:13.6.verse: he trains like this: experiencing the whole body I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the whole body I will breathe out,

an10.60:13.7.verse: he trains like this: making the bodily process calm I will breathe in, he trains like this: making the bodily process calm I will breathe out.

an10.60:13.8.verse: He trains like this: experiencing joy I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing happiness I will breathe out,

an10.60:13.9.verse: he trains like this: experiencing pleasure I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing pleasure I will breathe out,

an10.60:13.10.verse: he trains like this: experiencing the mental process I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the mental process I will breathe out,

an10.60:13.11.verse: he trains like this: making the mental process calm I will breathe in, he trains like this: making the mental process calm I will breathe out.

an10.60:13.12.verse: He trains like this: experiencing the mind I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the mind I will breathe out,

an10.60:13.19.verse: he trains like this: contemplating letting go I will breathe in, he trains like this: contemplating letting go I will breathe out.

an10.60:13.20.verse: This, Ānanda, is mindfulness while breathing.

an10.60:14.1.verse: If you, Ānanda, having approached the monk Girimānanda, were to recite these ten percpetions, then it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, the monk Girimānanda’s affliction would immediately abate.”

an10.60:15.1.verse: Then venerable Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions from the Fortunate One, approached venerable Girimānanda, and after approaching he recited these ten perceptions to venerable Girimānanda.

an10.60:15.2.verse: Then, having heard these ten perceptions, venerable Girimānanda’s affliction immediately abated,

an10.60:15.3.verse: and venerable Girimānanda recovered from that affliction, and by that venerable Girimānanda’s affliction was brought to an end.

an10.60:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.60:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

an10.60:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.60:2.1.verse: “Sir, Venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

an10.60:2.2.verse: Sir, please go to Venerable Girimānanda out of sympathy.”

an10.60:2.3.verse: “Ānanda, if you were to recite to the mendicant Girimānanda these ten perceptions, it’s possible that after hearing them his illness will die down on the spot.

an10.60:3.2.verse: The perceptions of impermanence, not-self, ugliness, drawbacks, giving up, fading away, cessation, dissatisfaction with the whole world, impermanence of all conditions, and mindfulness of breathing.

an10.60:4.1.verse: And what is the perception of impermanence?

an10.60:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an10.60:4.3.verse: ‘Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.’

an10.60:4.4.verse: And so they meditate observing impermanence in the five grasping aggregates.

an10.60:4.5.verse: This is called the perception of impermanence.

an10.60:5.1.verse: And what is the perception of not-self?

an10.60:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an10.60:5.3.verse: ‘The eye and sights, ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and tastes, body and touches, and mind and ideas are not-self.’

an10.60:5.4.verse: And so they meditate observing not-self in the six interior and exterior sense fields.

an10.60:5.5.verse: This is called the perception of not-self.

an10.60:6.1.verse: And what is the perception of ugliness?

an10.60:6.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant examines their own body up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

an10.60:6.3.verse: ‘In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

an10.60:6.4.verse: And so they meditate observing ugliness in this body.

an10.60:6.5.verse: This is called the perception of ugliness.

an10.60:7.1.verse: And what is the perception of drawbacks?

an10.60:7.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an10.60:7.3.verse: ‘This body has much suffering and many drawbacks. For this body is beset with many kinds of affliction, such as the following.

an10.60:7.4.verse: Diseases of the eye, inner ear, nose, tongue, body, head, outer ear, mouth, teeth, and lips. Cough, asthma, catarrh, inflammation, fever, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, gastric pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, herpes, itch, scabs, smallpox, scabies, hemorrhage, diabetes, piles, pimples, and ulcers. Afflictions stemming from disorders of bile, phlegm, wind, or their conjunction. Afflictions caused by change in weather, by not taking care of yourself, by exertion, or as the result of past deeds. Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.’

an10.60:7.5.verse: And so they meditate observing drawbacks in this body.

an10.60:7.6.verse: This is called the perception of drawbacks.

an10.60:8.1.verse: And what is the perception of giving up?

an10.60:8.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t tolerate a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen, and they don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

an10.60:8.3.verse: This is called the perception of giving up.

an10.60:9.1.verse: And what is the perception of fading away?

an10.60:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an10.60:9.3.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, extinguishment.’

an10.60:9.4.verse: This is called the perception of fading away.

an10.60:10.1.verse: And what is the perception of cessation?

an10.60:10.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

an10.60:10.3.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, cessation, extinguishment.’

an10.60:10.4.verse: This is called the perception of cessation.

an10.60:11.1.verse: And what is the perception of dissatisfaction with the whole world?

an10.60:11.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant lives giving up and not grasping on to the attraction and grasping to the world, the mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies.

an10.60:11.3.verse: This is called the perception of dissatisfaction with the whole world.

an10.60:12.1.verse: And what is the perception of the impermanence of all conditions?

an10.60:12.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted with all conditions.

an10.60:12.3.verse: This is called the perception of the impermanence of all conditions.

an10.60:13.1.verse: And what is mindfulness of breathing?

an10.60:13.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

an10.60:13.3.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

an10.60:13.4.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

an10.60:13.5.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

an10.60:13.6.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

an10.60:13.7.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

an10.60:13.8.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’

an10.60:13.9.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’

an10.60:13.10.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mental process.’

an10.60:13.11.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

an10.60:13.12.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

an10.60:13.13.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out gladdening the mind.’

an10.60:13.14.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out immersing the mind in samādhi.’

an10.60:13.15.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in freeing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out freeing the mind.’

an10.60:13.16.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing impermanence.’

an10.60:13.17.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing fading away.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing fading away.’

an10.60:13.18.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing cessation.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing cessation.’

an10.60:13.19.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

an10.60:13.20.verse: This is called mindfulness of breathing.

an10.60:14.1.verse: If you were to recite to the mendicant Girimānanda these ten perceptions, it’s possible that after hearing them his illness will die down on the spot.”

an10.60:15.1.verse: Then Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions from the Buddha himself, went to Girimānanda and recited them.

an10.60:15.2.verse: Then after Girimānanda heard these ten perceptions his illness died down on the spot.

an10.60:15.3.verse: And that’s how he recovered from that illness.

an10.61:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is said that no prior point of ignorance is found, before which there was no ignorance, and afterwards it came to be.

an10.61:1.2.verse: And yet it is evident that there is a specific condition for ignorance.

an10.61:2.1.verse: I say that ignorance is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.2.verse: And what is the fuel for ignorance?

an10.61:2.4.verse: I say that the five hindrances are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:2.5.verse: And what is the fuel for the five hindrances?

an10.61:2.6.verse: You should say: ‘The three kinds of misconduct.’

an10.61:2.7.verse: I say that the three kinds of misconduct are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:2.8.verse: And what is the fuel for the three kinds of misconduct?

an10.61:2.9.verse: You should say: ‘Lack of sense restraint.’

an10.61:2.10.verse: I say that lack of sense restraint is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.11.verse: And what is the fuel for lack of sense restraint?

an10.61:2.12.verse: You should say: ‘Lack of mindfulness and situational awareness.’

an10.61:2.13.verse: I say that lack of mindfulness and situational awareness is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.14.verse: And what is the fuel for lack of mindfulness and situational awareness?

an10.61:2.15.verse: You should say: ‘Irrational application of mind.’

an10.61:2.16.verse: I say that irrational application of mind is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.17.verse: And what is the fuel for irrational application of mind?

an10.61:2.19.verse: I say that lack of faith is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.20.verse: And what is the fuel for lack of faith?

an10.61:2.21.verse: You should say: ‘Listening to an untrue teaching.’

an10.61:2.22.verse: I say that listening to an untrue teaching is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:2.23.verse: And what is the fuel for listening to an untrue teaching?

an10.61:2.24.verse: You should say: ‘Associating with untrue persons.’

an10.61:3.1.verse: In this way, when the factor of associating with untrue persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of listening to an untrue teaching. When the factor of listening to an untrue teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of lack of faith … irrational application of mind … lack of mindfulness and situational awareness … lack of sense restraint … the three kinds of misconduct … the five hindrances. When the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance.

an10.61:3.2.verse: That’s the fuel for ignorance, and that’s how it’s fulfilled.

an10.61:4.1.verse: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily on a mountain top, and the water flows downhill to fill the hollows, crevices, and creeks. As they become full, they fill up the pools. The pools fill up the lakes, the lakes fill up the streams, and the streams fill up the rivers. And as the rivers become full, they fill up the ocean.

an10.61:4.2.verse: That’s the fuel for the ocean, and that’s how it’s filled up.

an10.61:5.1.verse: In the same way, when the factor of associating with untrue persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of listening to an untrue teaching. When the factor of listening to an untrue teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of lack of faith … irrational application of mind … lack of mindfulness and situational awareness … lack of sense restraint … the three kinds of misconduct … the five hindrances. When the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance.

an10.61:5.2.verse: That’s the fuel for ignorance, and that’s how it’s fulfilled.

an10.61:6.1.verse: I say that knowledge and freedom are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:6.2.verse: And what is the fuel for knowledge and freedom?

an10.61:6.3.verse: You should say: ‘The seven awakening factors.’

an10.61:6.4.verse: I say that the seven awakening factors are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:6.5.verse: And what is the fuel for the seven awakening factors?

an10.61:6.6.verse: You should say: ‘The four kinds of mindfulness meditation.’

an10.61:6.7.verse: I say that the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:6.8.verse: And what is the fuel for the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?

an10.61:6.9.verse: You should say: ‘The three kinds of good conduct.’

an10.61:6.10.verse: I say that the three kinds of good conduct are fueled by something, they’re not unfueled.

an10.61:6.11.verse: And what is the fuel for the three kinds of good conduct?

an10.61:6.13.verse: I say that sense restraint is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:6.14.verse: And what is the fuel for sense restraint?

an10.61:6.15.verse: You should say: ‘Mindfulness and situational awareness.’

an10.61:6.16.verse: I say that mindfulness and situational awareness is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:6.17.verse: And what is the fuel for mindfulness and situational awareness?

an10.61:6.18.verse: You should say: ‘Rational application of mind.’

an10.61:6.19.verse: I say that rational application of mind is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:6.20.verse: And what is the fuel for rational application of mind?

an10.61:6.22.verse: I say that faith is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:6.23.verse: And what is the fuel for faith?

an10.61:6.24.verse: You should say: ‘Listening to the true teaching.’

an10.61:6.25.verse: I say that listening to the true teaching is fueled by something, it’s not unfueled.

an10.61:6.26.verse: And what is the fuel for listening to the true teaching?

an10.61:6.27.verse: You should say: ‘Associating with true persons.’

an10.61:7.1.verse: In this way, when the factor of associating with true persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of listening to the true teaching. When the factor of listening to the true teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of faith … rational application of mind … mindfulness and situational awareness … sense restraint … the three kinds of good conduct … the four kinds of mindfulness meditation … the seven awakening factors. When the seven awakening factors are fulfilled, they fulfill knowledge and freedom.

an10.61:7.2.verse: That’s the fuel for knowledge and freedom, and that’s how it’s fulfilled.

an10.61:8.1.verse: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily on a mountain top, and the water flows downhill to fill the hollows, crevices, and creeks. As they become full, they fill up the pools. The pools fill up the lakes, the lakes fill up the streams, and the streams fill up the rivers. And as the rivers become full, they fill up the ocean.

an10.61:8.2.verse: That’s the fuel for the ocean, and that’s how it’s filled up.

an10.61:9.1.verse: In the same way, when the factor of associating with true persons is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of listening to the true teaching. When the factor of listening to the true teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills the factor of faith … rational application of mind … mindfulness and situational awareness … sense restraint … the three kinds of good conduct … the four kinds of mindfulness meditation … the seven awakening factors. When the seven awakening factors are fulfilled, they fulfill knowledge and freedom.

an10.61:9.2.verse: That’s the fuel for knowledge and freedom, and that’s how it’s fulfilled.”

an10.63:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, all those who have come to a conclusion about me are accomplished in view.

an10.63:1.2.verse: Of those who are accomplished in view, five conclude their path in this realm, and five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.

an10.63:1.3.verse: Which five conclude their path in this realm?

an10.63:1.4.verse: The one who has seven rebirths at most, the one who goes from family to family, the one-seeder, the once returner, and the one who is perfected in this very life.

an10.63:1.5.verse: These five conclude their path in this realm.

an10.63:1.6.verse: Which five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind?

an10.63:1.7.verse: The one who is extinguished between one life and the next, the one who is extinguished upon landing, the one who is extinguished without extra effort, the one who is extinguished with extra effort, and the one who heads upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

an10.63:1.8.verse: These five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.

an10.63:1.9.verse: All those who have come to a conclusion about me are accomplished in view.

an10.63:1.10.verse: Of those who are accomplished in view, these five conclude their path in this realm, and these five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.”

an10.64:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, all those who have experiential confidence in me have entered the stream.

an10.64:1.2.verse: Of those who have entered the stream, five conclude their path in this realm, and five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.

an10.64:1.3.verse: Which five conclude their path in this realm?

an10.64:1.4.verse: The one who has seven rebirths at most, the one who goes from family to family, the one-seeder, the once returner, and the one who is perfected in this very life.

an10.64:1.5.verse: These five conclude their path in this realm.

an10.64:1.6.verse: Which five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind?

an10.64:1.7.verse: The one who is extinguished between one life and the next, the one who is extinguished upon landing, the one who is extinguished without extra effort, the one who is extinguished with extra effort, and the one who heads upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

an10.64:1.8.verse: These five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.

an10.64:1.9.verse: All those who have experiential confidence in me have entered the stream.

an10.64:1.10.verse: Of those who have entered the stream, these five conclude their path in this realm, and these five conclude their path after leaving this realm behind.”

an10.65:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the land of the Magadhans near the little village of Nālaka.

an10.65:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni went up to Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.

an10.65:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, Sāmaṇḍakāni sat down to one side, and said to Sāriputta:

an10.65:2.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, what is happiness and what is suffering?”

an10.65:2.2.verse: “Rebirth is suffering, reverend, no rebirth is happiness.

an10.65:2.3.verse: When there is rebirth, you can expect this kind of suffering.

an10.65:2.4.verse: Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination. Contact with fire, clubs, and knives. And relatives and friends get together and annoy you.

an10.65:2.5.verse: When there is rebirth, this is the kind of suffering you can expect.

an10.65:2.6.verse: When there is no rebirth, you can expect this kind of happiness.

an10.65:2.7.verse: No cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, or urination. No contact with fire, clubs, or knives. And relatives and friends don’t get together and annoy you.

an10.65:2.8.verse: When there is no rebirth, this is the kind of happiness you can expect.”

an10.66:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the land of the Magadhans near the little village of Nālaka.

an10.66:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni went up to Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.

an10.66:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, Sāmaṇḍakāni sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

an10.66:2.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, in this teaching and training, what is happiness and what is suffering?”

an10.66:2.2.verse: “Reverend, in this teaching and training dissatisfaction is suffering and satisfaction is happiness.

an10.66:2.3.verse: When you’re dissatisfied, you can expect this kind of suffering.

an10.66:2.4.verse: You find no happiness or pleasure while walking …

an10.66:2.10.verse: at the root of a tree …

an10.66:2.14.verse: When you’re dissatisfied, this is the kind of suffering you can expect.

an10.66:3.1.verse: When you’re satisfied, you can expect this kind of happiness.

an10.66:3.2.verse: You find happiness or pleasure while walking …

an10.66:3.8.verse: at the root of a tree …

an10.66:3.12.verse: When you’re satisfied, this is the kind of happiness you can expect.”

an10.67:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of monks when he arrived at a town of the Kosalans named Naḷakapāna.

an10.67:1.2.verse: There the Buddha stayed near Naḷakapāna in the grove of flame-of-the-forest trees.

an10.67:1.3.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath, and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

an10.67:1.4.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the monks with a Dhamma talk. Then he looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed Venerable Sāriputta:

an10.67:2.1.verse: “Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of monks is rid of dullness and drowsiness.

an10.67:2.2.verse: Give them some Dhamma talk as you feel inspired.

an10.67:3.1.verse: And then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

an10.67:4.1.verse: “Reverends, whoever has no faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:4.4.verse: can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:4.5.verse: It’s like the moon in the waning fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only decline.

an10.67:4.6.verse: In the same way, whoever has no faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:4.9.verse: can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:5.1.verse: A faithless individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.2.verse: An individual with no conscience is in decline.

an10.67:5.3.verse: An imprudent individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.4.verse: A lazy individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.5.verse: A witless individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.6.verse: An irritable individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.7.verse: An acrimonious individual is in decline.

an10.67:5.8.verse: An individual with corrupt wishes is in decline.

an10.67:5.9.verse: An individual with bad friends is in decline.

an10.67:5.10.verse: An individual with wrong view is in decline.

an10.67:6.1.verse: Whoever has faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:6.3.verse: can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:6.4.verse: It’s like the moon in the waxing fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only grow.

an10.67:6.5.verse: In the same way, whoever has faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:6.8.verse: can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:7.2.verse: An individual with a conscience doesn’t decline.

an10.67:7.8.verse: An individual with few desires doesn’t decline.

an10.67:7.9.verse: An individual with good friends doesn’t decline.

an10.67:7.10.verse: An individual with right view doesn’t decline.”

an10.67:8.1.verse: Then the Buddha got up and said to Venerable Sāriputta:

an10.67:8.3.verse: Whoever has no faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:8.6.verse: can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:8.7.verse: It’s like the moon in the waning fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only decline.

an10.67:8.8.verse: In the same way, whoever has no faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:8.9.verse: can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:9.1.verse: A faithless individual is in decline.

an10.67:9.10.verse: An individual with wrong view is in decline.

an10.67:10.1.verse: Whoever has faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:10.4.verse: can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:10.5.verse: It’s like the moon in the waxing fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only grow.

an10.67:10.6.verse: In the same way, whoever has faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom when it comes to skillful qualities

an10.67:10.9.verse: can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.67:11.10.verse: An individual with right view doesn’t decline.”

an10.68:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha stayed near Naḷakapāna in the grove of flame-of-the-forest trees.

an10.68:1.2.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath, and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

an10.68:1.3.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the monks with a Dhamma talk. Then he looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed Venerable Sāriputta,

an10.68:2.1.verse: “Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of monks is rid of dullness and drowsiness.

an10.68:2.2.verse: Give them some Dhamma talk as you feel inspired.

an10.68:3.1.verse: And then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

an10.68:4.9.verse: and is negligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:4.10.verse: It’s like the moon in the waning fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only decline.

an10.68:4.11.verse: In the same way, whoever has no faith, conscience,

an10.68:4.19.verse: and is negligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:5.9.verse: and is diligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:5.10.verse: It’s like the moon in the waxing fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only grow.

an10.68:5.11.verse: In the same way, whoever has faith, conscience, prudence, energy, and wisdom; who wants to listen, memorizes the teachings, examines their meaning, and practices accordingly,

an10.68:5.12.verse: and is diligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.”

an10.68:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha got up and said to Venerable Sāriputta:

an10.68:6.11.verse: and is negligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:6.12.verse: It’s like the moon in the waning fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only decline.

an10.68:6.13.verse: In the same way, whoever has no faith …

an10.68:6.14.verse: and is negligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:7.9.verse: and is diligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.

an10.68:7.10.verse: It’s like the moon in the waxing fortnight. Whether by day or by night, its beauty, roundness, luminosity, and diameter and circumference only grow.

an10.68:7.11.verse: In the same way, whoever has faith …

an10.68:7.12.verse: and is diligent when it comes to skillful qualities can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.”

an10.69:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.69:1.2.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall. They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as

an10.69:1.3.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

an10.69:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall, where he sat down on the seat spread out

an10.69:2.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

an10.69:3.1.verse: And they told him what had happened.

an10.69:3.3.verse: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to engage in these kinds of low talk.

an10.69:4.1.verse: There are, mendicants, these ten topics of discussion.

an10.69:4.3.verse: Talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.69:4.4.verse: These are the ten topics of discussion.

an10.69:5.1.verse: Mendicants, if you bring up these topics of conversation again and again then your glory could surpass even the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful, let alone the wanderers of other religions.”

an10.70:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.70:1.2.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall.

an10.70:1.3.verse: They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that state of existence.

an10.70:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are ten grounds for praise.

an10.70:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant personally has few wishes, and speaks to the mendicants on having few wishes.

an10.70:2.4.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:3.1.verse: A mendicant personally is content, and speaks to the mendicants on contentment.

an10.70:3.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:4.1.verse: A mendicant personally is secluded, and speaks to the mendicants on seclusion.

an10.70:4.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:5.1.verse: A mendicant personally doesn’t mix closely with others, and speaks to the mendicants on not mixing closely with others.

an10.70:5.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:6.1.verse: A mendicant personally is energetic, and speaks to the mendicants on rousing energy.

an10.70:6.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:7.1.verse: A mendicant personally is accomplished in ethics, and speaks to the mendicants on being accomplished in ethics.

an10.70:7.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:8.1.verse: A mendicant personally is accomplished in immersion, and speaks to the mendicants on being accomplished in immersion.

an10.70:8.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:9.1.verse: A mendicant personally is accomplished in wisdom, and speaks to the mendicants on being accomplished in wisdom.

an10.70:9.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:10.1.verse: A mendicant personally is accomplished in freedom, and speaks to the mendicants on being accomplished in freedom.

an10.70:10.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:11.1.verse: A mendicant personally is accomplished in the knowledge and vision of freedom, and speaks to the mendicants on being accomplished in the knowledge and vision of freedom.

an10.70:11.2.verse: This is a ground for praise.

an10.70:12.1.verse: These are the ten grounds for praise.”

an10.71:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.71:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

an10.71:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.

an10.71:3.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I be liked and approved by my spiritual companions, respected and admired.’ So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

an10.71:4.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.’ So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

an10.71:5.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May the services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick I enjoy be very fruitful and beneficial for them.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:6.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘When deceased family and relatives who have passed away recollect me with a confident mind, may this be very fruitful and beneficial for them.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:7.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I be content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:8.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I endure cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. May I endure the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles. May I endure rude and unwelcome criticism. And may I put up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:9.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I prevail over desire and discontent, and may desire and discontent not prevail over me. May I live having mastered desire and discontent whenever they have arisen.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:10.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I prevail over fear and dread, and may fear and dread not prevail over me. May I live having mastered fear and dread whenever they arise.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:11.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when I want, without trouble or difficulty.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

an10.71:12.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’ So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

an10.71:13.1.verse: ‘Live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.’

an10.71:13.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

an10.72:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof, together with several well-known senior disciples.

an10.72:1.2.verse: They included the venerables Cāla, Upacāla, Kakkaṭa, Kaṭimbha, Kaṭa, Kaṭissaṅga,

an10.72:2.1.verse: Now at that time several well-known Licchavis plunged deep into the Great Wood to see the Buddha. Driving a succession of fine carriages, they made a colossal racket.

an10.72:2.3.verse: “These several well-known Licchavis have plunged deep into the Great Wood to see the Buddha. Driving a succession of fine carriages, they’re making a colossal racket.

an10.72:2.4.verse: But the Buddha has said that sound is a thorn to absorption.

an10.72:2.5.verse: Let’s go to the Gosiṅga Sal Wood.

an10.72:2.6.verse: There we can meditate comfortably, free of noise and crowds.”

an10.72:2.7.verse: Then those venerables went to the Gosiṅga Sal Wood,

an10.72:2.8.verse: where they meditated comfortably, free of noise and crowds.

an10.72:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

an10.72:3.2.verse: “Mendicants, where are Cāla, Upacāla, Kakkaṭa, Kaṭimbha, Kaṭa, and Kaṭissaṅga?

an10.72:3.3.verse: Where have these senior disciples gone?”

an10.72:4.1.verse: And the mendicants told him what had happened.

an10.72:5.1.verse: “Good, good, mendicants! It’s just as those great disciples have so rightly explained. I have said that sound is a thorn to absorption.

an10.72:6.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these ten thorns.

an10.72:6.3.verse: Relishing company is a thorn for someone who loves seclusion. Focusing on the feature of beauty is a thorn for someone pursuing the meditation on the feature of ugliness. Seeing shows is a thorn to someone restraining the senses. Lingering in the neighborhood of females is a thorn to chastity. Sound is a thorn to the first absorption. Placing the mind and keeping it connected are a thorn to the second absorption. Rapture is a thorn to the third absorption. Breathing is a thorn to the fourth absorption. Perception and feeling are a thorn to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Greed, hate, and delusion are thorns.

an10.72:7.3.verse: Mendicants, live free of thorns and rid of thorns!

an10.72:7.4.verse: The perfected ones live free of thorns,

an10.73:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things are rare in the world.

an10.73:1.12.verse: and heaven are likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.

an10.73:2.1.verse: Ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.

an10.73:2.2.verse: Sloth and lack of initiative are a roadblock for wealth. Lack of adornment and decoration are a roadblock for beauty. Unsuitable activity is a roadblock for health. Bad friendship is a roadblock for ethical conduct. Lack of sense restraint is a roadblock for the spiritual life. Dishonesty is a roadblock for friends. Not rehearsing is a roadblock for learning. Not wanting to listen and ask questions are roadblocks for wisdom. Lack of commitment and reviewing are roadblocks for good qualities. Wrong practice hinders heaven.

an10.73:2.3.verse: These ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.

an10.73:3.1.verse: Ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.

an10.73:3.2.verse: Application and initiative nourish wealth. Adornment and decoration nourish beauty. Suitable activity nourishes health. Good friendship nourishes ethical conduct. Sense restraint nourishes the spiritual life. Honesty nourishes friends. Rehearsing nourishes learning. Eagerness to listen and ask questions nourishes wisdom. Commitment and reviewing nourish good qualities. Right practice nourishes heaven.

an10.73:3.3.verse: These ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.”

an10.74:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a noble disciple who grows in ten ways grows nobly, taking on what is essential and excellent in this life.

an10.74:1.3.verse: He grows in fields and lands, money and grain, wives and children, in bondservants, workers, and staff, and in livestock. And he grows in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

an10.74:1.4.verse: A noble disciple who grows in ten ways grows nobly, taking on what is essential and excellent in this life.

an10.74:2.1.verse: Someone who grows in money and grain,

an10.74:2.4.verse: by relatives and friends, and even by royals.

an10.74:3.1.verse: When someone grows in faith and ethics,

an10.74:3.2.verse: wisdom, and both generosity and learning—

an10.74:3.3.verse: a good man such as he sees clearly,

an10.74:3.4.verse: and in this very life he grows in both ways.”

an10.75:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.75:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the laywoman Migasālā, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

an10.75:1.3.verse: Then the laywoman Migasālā went up to Ānanda, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.75:2.1.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, how on earth are we supposed to understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, when the chaste and the unchaste are both reborn in exactly the same place in the next life?

an10.75:2.2.verse: My father Purāṇa was chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

an10.75:2.3.verse: When he passed away the Buddha declared that, since he was a once-returner, he was reborn in the host of joyful gods.

an10.75:2.4.verse: But my uncle Isidatta was not chaste; he lived content with his wife.

an10.75:2.5.verse: When he passed away the Buddha declared that, since he too was a once-returner, he was reborn in the host of joyful gods.

an10.75:3.1.verse: How on earth are we supposed to understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, when the chaste and the unchaste are both reborn in exactly the same place in the next life?”

an10.75:3.2.verse: “You’re right, sister, but that’s how the Buddha declared it.”

an10.75:4.1.verse: Then Ānanda, after receiving almsfood at Migasālā’s home, rose from his seat and left.

an10.75:4.2.verse: Then after the meal, on his return from almsround, Ānanda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

an10.75:8.1.verse: “Ānanda, who is this laywoman Migasālā, a foolish incompetent aunty, with an aunty’s wit? And who is it that knows how to assess individual persons?

an10.75:9.1.verse: These ten individuals are found in the world.

an10.75:9.3.verse: Take a certain individual who is unethical.

an10.75:9.4.verse: And they don’t truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where that unethical conduct ceases without remainder.

an10.75:9.5.verse: And they’ve not listened or learned or penetrated theoretically or found even temporary freedom.

an10.75:9.6.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they depart for a lower place, not a higher.

an10.75:9.7.verse: They’re going to a lower place, not a higher.

an10.75:11.3.verse: This will be for their lasting harm and suffering.

an10.75:12.2.verse: but truly understands the freedom of heart …

an10.75:12.3.verse: and has listened and learned and penetrated theoretically and found at least temporary freedom

an10.75:26.1.verse: Who is this laywoman Migasālā, a foolish incompetent aunty, with an aunty’s wit? And who is it that knows how to assess individual persons?

an10.75:26.2.verse: These ten individuals are found in the world.

an10.75:27.1.verse: If Isidatta had achieved Purāṇa’s level of ethical conduct, Purāṇa could not have even known Isidatta’s destination.

an10.75:27.2.verse: And if Purāṇa had achieved Isidatta’s level of wisdom, Isidatta could not have even known Purāṇa’s destination.

an10.75:27.3.verse: So both individuals were lacking in one respect.”

an10.76:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if three things were not found, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha would not arise in the world, and the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One would not shine in the world.

an10.76:1.4.verse: If these three things were not found, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha would not arise in the world, and the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One would not shine in the world.

an10.76:1.5.verse: But since these three things are found, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha arises in the world, and the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One shines in the world.

an10.76:2.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up rebirth, old age, and death.

an10.76:2.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up rebirth, old age, and death.

an10.76:3.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an10.76:3.3.verse: Substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

an10.76:3.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an10.76:4.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

an10.76:4.3.verse: Irrational application of mind, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness.

an10.76:4.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

an10.76:5.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up irrational application of mind, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness.

an10.76:5.3.verse: Unmindfulness, lack of situational awareness, and scattered mind.

an10.76:5.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up irrational application of mind, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness.

an10.76:6.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up unmindfulness, lack of situational awareness, and scattered mind.

an10.76:6.3.verse: Not wanting to see the noble ones, not wanting to hear the teaching of the noble ones, and a fault-finding mind.

an10.76:6.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up unmindfulness, lack of situational awareness, and scattered mind.

an10.76:7.3.verse: Restlessness, lack of restraint, and unethical conduct.

an10.76:7.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up not wanting to see the noble ones, not wanting to hear the teaching of the noble ones, and a fault-finding mind.

an10.76:8.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up restlessness, lack of restraint, and unethical conduct.

an10.76:9.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up faithlessness, uncharitableness, and laziness.

an10.76:9.3.verse: Disregard, being hard to admonish, and having bad friends.

an10.76:9.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up faithlessness, uncharitableness, and laziness.

an10.76:10.1.verse: Without giving up three things you can’t give up disregard, being hard to admonish, and having bad friends.

an10.76:10.3.verse: Lack of conscience, imprudence, and negligence.

an10.76:10.4.verse: Without giving up these three things you can’t give up disregard, being hard to admonish, and having bad friends.

an10.76:11.1.verse: Mendicants, someone who lacks conscience and prudence is negligent.

an10.76:11.2.verse: When you’re negligent you can’t give up disregard, being hard to admonish, and having bad friends.

an10.76:11.3.verse: When you’ve got bad friends you can’t give up faithlessness, uncharitableness, and laziness.

an10.76:11.4.verse: When you’re lazy you can’t give up restlessness, lack of restraint, and unethical conduct.

an10.76:11.5.verse: When you’re unethical you can’t give up not wanting to see the noble ones, not wanting to hear the teaching of the noble ones, and a fault-finding mind.

an10.76:11.6.verse: When you’ve got a fault-finding mind you can’t give up unmindfulness, lack of situational awareness, and a scattered mind.

an10.76:11.7.verse: When your mind is scattered you can’t give up irrational application of mind, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness.

an10.76:11.8.verse: When your mind is sluggish you can’t give up substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

an10.76:11.9.verse: When you have doubts you can’t give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an10.76:11.10.verse: Without giving up greed, hate, and delusion you can’t give up rebirth, old age, and death.

an10.76:12.1.verse: After giving up three things you can give up rebirth, old age, and death.

an10.76:12.4.verse: After giving up these three things you can give up rebirth, old age, and death.

an10.76:21.1.verse: Mendicants, someone who has conscience and prudence is diligent.

an10.76:21.2.verse: When you’re diligent you can give up disregard, being hard to admonish, and having bad friends.

an10.76:21.3.verse: When you’ve got good friends you can give up faithlessness, uncharitableness, and laziness.

an10.76:21.4.verse: When you’re energetic you can give up restlessness, lack of restraint, and unethical conduct.

an10.76:21.5.verse: When you’re ethical you can give up not wanting to see the noble ones, not wanting to hear the teaching of the noble ones, and a fault-finding mind.

an10.76:21.6.verse: When you don’t have a fault-finding mind you can give up unmindfulness, lack of situational awareness, and a scattered mind.
