an10.76:21.7.verse: When your mind isn’t scattered you can give up irrational application of mind, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness.

an10.76:21.8.verse: When your mind isn’t sluggish you can give up substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

an10.76:21.9.verse: When you have no doubts you can give up greed, hate, and delusion.

an10.76:21.10.verse: After giving up greed, hate, and delusion you can give up rebirth, old age, and death.”

an10.77:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a crow possesses ten bad qualities.

an10.77:1.3.verse: They’re rude and impudent, gluttonous and voracious, cruel and pitiless, weak and raucous, unmindful and acquisitive.

an10.77:1.4.verse: A crow possesses these ten bad qualities.

an10.77:1.5.verse: In the same way, a bad mendicant possesses these ten bad qualities.

an10.77:1.7.verse: They’re rude and impudent, gluttonous and voracious, cruel and pitiless, weak and raucous, unmindful and acquisitive.

an10.77:1.8.verse: A bad mendicant possesses these ten bad qualities.”

an10.78:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, Jain ascetics possess ten bad qualities.

an10.78:1.8.verse: They glorify themselves and put others down.

an10.78:1.9.verse: They’re attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go.

an10.78:1.13.verse: Jain ascetics possess these ten bad qualities.”

an10.79:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are ten grounds for resentment.

an10.79:1.3.verse: Thinking: ‘They did wrong to me,’ you harbor resentment.

an10.79:1.4.verse: Thinking: ‘They are doing wrong to me’ …

an10.79:1.6.verse: ‘They did wrong by someone I love’ …

an10.79:1.7.verse: ‘They are doing wrong by someone I love’ …

an10.79:1.8.verse: ‘They will do wrong by someone I love’ …

an10.79:1.11.verse: Thinking: ‘They will help someone I dislike,’ you harbor resentment.

an10.79:1.12.verse: You get angry for no reason.

an10.79:1.13.verse: These are the ten grounds for resentment.”

an10.80:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these ten ways to get rid of resentment.

an10.80:1.3.verse: Thinking: ‘They harmed me, but what can I possibly do?’ you get rid of resentment.

an10.80:1.8.verse: ‘They will harm someone I love …’ … They helped someone I dislike …’ …

an10.80:1.10.verse: Thinking: ‘They will help someone I dislike, but what can I possibly do?’ you get rid of resentment.

an10.80:1.11.verse: And you don’t get angry for no reason.

an10.80:1.12.verse: These are the ten ways of getting rid of resentment.”

an10.81:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.

an10.81:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Bāhuna went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.81:1.3.verse: “Sir, how many things has the Realized One escaped from, so that he lives detached, liberated, with mind free of boundaries?”

an10.81:2.1.verse: “Bāhuna, the Realized One has escaped from ten things, so that he lives detached, liberated, with mind free of boundaries.

an10.81:2.13.verse: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Though it sprouted and grew in the water, it would rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to it.

an10.81:2.14.verse: In the same way, the Realized One has escaped from ten things, so that he lives detached, liberated, with mind free of boundaries.”

an10.82:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an10.82:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, it is quite impossible for a faithless mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an10.82:3.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant who is unethical …

an10.82:11.1.verse: of wrong view to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an10.82:12.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant with these ten qualities to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an10.82:13.1.verse: It is quite possible for a faithful mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an10.82:14.1.verse: It is quite possible for a mendicant who is ethical …

an10.82:22.1.verse: of right view to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

an10.82:23.1.verse: It is quite possible for a mendicant with these ten qualities to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.”

an10.83:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Puṇṇiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

an10.83:1.2.verse: “Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why sometimes the Realized One feels inspired to teach, and other times not?”

an10.83:2.1.verse: “Puṇṇiya, when a mendicant has faith but doesn’t approach, the Realized One doesn’t feel inspired to teach.

an10.83:2.2.verse: But when a mendicant has faith and approaches, the Realized One feels inspired to teach.

an10.83:3.1.verse: When a mendicant has faith and approaches, but doesn’t pay homage …

an10.83:3.2.verse: they pay homage, but don’t ask questions …

an10.83:3.3.verse: they ask questions, but don’t actively listen to the teaching …

an10.83:3.4.verse: they actively listen to the teaching, but don’t remember the teaching they’ve heard …

an10.83:3.5.verse: they remember the teaching they’ve heard, but don’t examine the meaning of the teachings they’ve remembered …

an10.83:3.6.verse: they examine the meaning of the teachings they’ve remembered, but, not having understood the meaning and the teaching, they don’t practice in line with the principle of the teaching …

an10.83:3.7.verse: they practice in line with the teaching, but they’re not a good speaker and do not enunciate well. Their voice is not polished, clear, articulate, and doesn’t express the meaning …

an10.83:3.8.verse: They’re a good speaker who enunciates well, but they don’t educate, encourage, fire up, and inspire their spiritual companions. The Realized One doesn’t feel inspired to teach.

an10.83:4.1.verse: But when a mendicant has faith, approaches, pays homage, asks questions, actively listens to the teachings, remembers the teachings, examines the meaning, practices in line with the principle of the teaching, has a good voice, and encourages their spiritual companions,

an10.83:4.2.verse: the Realized One feels inspired to teach.

an10.83:4.3.verse: When someone possesses these ten qualities, the Realized One feels totally inspired to teach.”

an10.84:1.1.verse: There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the mendicants:

an10.84:2.2.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’

an10.84:2.3.verse: They’re pursued, pressed, and grilled by the Realized One, or by one of his disciples who is a meditator skilled in attainments, in the minds of others, and in encompassing another’s mind.

an10.84:2.4.verse: Grilled in this way they get stuck or lose their way. They fall to ruin and disaster.

an10.84:3.1.verse: The Realized One or one of his disciples encompasses their mind and investigates:

an10.84:3.2.verse: ‘Why does this venerable declare enlightenment, saying:

an10.84:3.3.verse: “I understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place’”?’

an10.84:5.2.verse: and often lives with a heart full of anger.

an10.84:5.3.verse: But being full of anger means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

an10.84:13.2.verse: and often lives with a heart full of desire.

an10.84:13.3.verse: But being full of desire means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

an10.84:14.1.verse: When there is still more to be done, this venerable stopped half-way after achieving some trifling distinction.

an10.84:14.2.verse: But stopping half-way means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.’

an10.84:15.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training without giving up these ten qualities.

an10.84:15.2.verse: It is quite possible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training after giving up these ten qualities.”

an10.85:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was staying in the land of the Cetīs at Sahajāti.

an10.85:2.1.verse: “Take a mendicant who boasts and brags about their achievements:

an10.85:2.2.verse: ‘I enter and emerge from the first absorption, the second absorption, the third absorption, and the fourth absorption. And I enter and emerge from the dimensions of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither perception nor non-perception. And I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.’

an10.85:3.1.verse: They’re pursued, pressed, and grilled by the Realized One, or by one of his disciples who has the absorptions, and is skilled in attainments, in the minds of others, and in encompassing another’s mind.

an10.85:3.2.verse: Grilled in this way they get stuck or lose their way. They fall to ruin and disaster.

an10.85:4.1.verse: The Realized One or one of his disciples encompasses their mind and investigates:

an10.85:4.2.verse: ‘Why does this venerable boast and brag about their achievements, saying,

an10.85:4.3.verse: “I enter and emerge from the first absorption …

an10.85:4.4.verse: and the cessation of perception and feeling.”’

an10.85:6.1.verse: ‘For a long time this venerable’s deeds have been broken, tainted, spotty, and marred. Their deeds and behavior are inconsistent.

an10.85:6.3.verse: and unethical conduct means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

an10.85:7.2.verse: and lack of faith means decline …

an10.85:8.1.verse: This venerable is unlearned and unpracticed,

an10.85:8.2.verse: and lack of learning means decline …

an10.85:9.1.verse: This venerable is hard to admonish,

an10.85:9.2.verse: and being hard to admonish means decline …

an10.85:15.2.verse: and lack of wisdom means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.’

an10.85:16.1.verse: Suppose one friend was to say to another:

an10.85:16.2.verse: ‘My dear, when you need money for some payment, just ask me and I’ll give it.’

an10.85:16.3.verse: Then when some payment falls due, that friend says to their friend: ‘I need some money, my dear. Give me some.’

an10.85:16.5.verse: ‘Well then, my dear, dig here.’ So they dig there, but don’t find anything.

an10.85:16.7.verse: ‘You lied to me, my dear, you spoke hollow words when you told me to dig here.’

an10.85:16.9.verse: ‘My dear, I didn’t lie or speak hollow words. Well then, dig here.’

an10.85:16.10.verse: So they dig there as well, but don’t find anything.

an10.85:16.12.verse: ‘You lied to me, my dear, you spoke hollow words when you said dig here.’

an10.85:16.14.verse: ‘My dear, I didn’t lie or speak hollow words. Well then, dig here.’

an10.85:16.15.verse: So they dig there as well, but don’t find anything.

an10.85:16.17.verse: ‘You lied to me, my dear, you spoke hollow words when you said dig here.’

an10.85:16.19.verse: ‘My dear, I didn’t lie or speak hollow words. But I had gone mad, I was out of my mind.’

an10.85:17.1.verse: In the same way, take a mendicant who boasts and brags about their achievements:

an10.85:17.2.verse: ‘I enter and emerge from the first absorption … and the cessation of perception and feeling.’

an10.85:18.1.verse: They’re pursued, pressed, and grilled by the Realized One, or by one of his disciples …

an10.85:18.2.verse: Grilled in this way they get stuck or lose their way. They fall to ruin and disaster.

an10.85:19.1.verse: The Realized One or one of his disciples encompasses their mind and investigates:

an10.85:19.2.verse: ‘Why does this venerable boast and brag about their achievements, saying,

an10.85:19.3.verse: “I enter and emerge from the first absorption …

an10.85:19.4.verse: and the cessation of perception and feeling.”’

an10.85:21.1.verse: ‘For a long time this venerable’s deeds have been broken, tainted, spotty, and marred. Their deeds and behavior are inconsistent.

an10.85:21.3.verse: and unethical conduct means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

an10.85:30.2.verse: and lack of wisdom means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.’

an10.85:31.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training without giving up these ten qualities.

an10.85:31.2.verse: It is quite possible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training after giving up these ten qualities.”

an10.86:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

an10.86:2.2.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’

an10.86:2.3.verse: They’re pursued, pressed, and grilled by the Realized One, or by one of his disciples who has the absorptions, and is skilled in attainments, in the minds of others, and in encompassing another’s mind.

an10.86:2.4.verse: Grilled in this way they get stuck or lose their way. They fall to ruin and disaster.

an10.86:3.1.verse: The Realized One or one of his disciples encompasses their mind and investigates:

an10.86:3.2.verse: ‘Why does this venerable declare enlightenment, saying,

an10.86:3.3.verse: “I understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place’”?’

an10.86:5.1.verse: ‘This venerable overestimates themselves and takes that to be the truth. They perceive that they’ve attained what they haven’t attained, done what they haven’t done, and achieved what they haven’t achieved.

an10.86:5.2.verse: And they declare enlightenment out of overestimation:

an10.86:5.3.verse: “I understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”’

an10.86:6.1.verse: The Realized One or one of his disciples encompasses their mind and investigates:

an10.86:6.2.verse: ‘Why does this venerable overestimate themselves and take that to be the truth? Why do they perceive that they’ve attained what they haven’t attained, done what they haven’t done, and achieved what they haven’t achieved?

an10.86:6.3.verse: And why do they declare enlightenment out of overestimation:

an10.86:6.4.verse: “I understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”’

an10.86:8.1.verse: ‘This venerable is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.86:8.2.verse: Therefore this venerable overestimates themselves and takes that to be the truth. …’

an10.86:10.2.verse: and often lives with a heart full of covetousness.

an10.86:10.3.verse: But being full of covetousness means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.

an10.86:15.1.verse: This venerable relishes work. They love it and like to relish it …

an10.86:19.1.verse: When there is still more to be done, this venerable stopped half-way after achieving some trifling distinction.

an10.86:19.2.verse: But stopping half-way means decline in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One.’

an10.86:20.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training without giving up these ten qualities.

an10.86:20.2.verse: It is quite possible for a mendicant to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training after giving up these ten qualities.”

an10.87:1.1.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants concerning the mendicant Kalandaka:

an10.87:2.1.verse: “Firstly, a mendicant raises disciplinary issues and doesn’t praise the settling of disciplinary issues.

an10.87:2.2.verse: This quality doesn’t conduce to fondness, respect, esteem, harmony, and unity.

an10.87:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant doesn’t want to train, and doesn’t praise taking up the training. …

an10.87:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has corrupt wishes, and doesn’t praise getting rid of wishes. …

an10.87:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is irritable, and doesn’t praise getting rid of anger. …

an10.87:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant denigrates others, and doesn’t praise getting rid of denigration. …

an10.87:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is devious, and doesn’t praise getting rid of deviousness. …

an10.87:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is deceitful, and doesn’t praise getting rid of deceitfulness. …

an10.87:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant doesn’t pay attention to the teachings, and doesn’t praise attending to the teachings. …

an10.87:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is not in retreat, and doesn’t praise retreat. …

an10.87:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is inhospitable to their spiritual companions, and doesn’t praise hospitality.

an10.87:11.2.verse: This quality doesn’t conduce to fondness, respect, esteem, harmony, and unity.

an10.87:12.1.verse: Even though a mendicant such as this might wish:

an10.87:12.2.verse: ‘If only my spiritual companions would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!’ Still they don’t honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them.

an10.87:12.4.verse: Because their sensible spiritual companions see that they haven’t given up those bad unskillful qualities.

an10.87:13.1.verse: Suppose a wild colt was to wish:

an10.87:13.2.verse: ‘If only the humans would put me in a thoroughbred’s place, feed me a thoroughbred’s food, and give me a thoroughbred’s grooming.’ Still the humans wouldn’t put them in a thoroughbred’s place, feed them a thoroughbred’s food, or give them a thoroughbred’s grooming.

an10.87:13.4.verse: Because sensible humans see that they haven’t given up their tricks, bluffs, ruses, and feints.

an10.87:13.5.verse: In the same way, even though a mendicant such as this might wish:

an10.87:13.6.verse: ‘If only my spiritual companions would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!’ Still they don’t honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them.

an10.87:13.8.verse: Because their sensible spiritual companions see that they haven’t given up those bad unskillful qualities.

an10.87:14.1.verse: Next, a mendicant doesn’t raise disciplinary issues and praises the settling of disciplinary issues.

an10.87:14.2.verse: This quality conduces to fondness, respect, esteem, harmony, and unity.

an10.87:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant wants to train, and praises taking up the training. …

an10.87:16.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has few desires, and praises getting rid of desires. …

an10.87:17.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is not irritable, and praises getting rid of anger. …

an10.87:18.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant doesn’t denigrate others, and praises getting rid of denigration. …

an10.87:19.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t devious, and praises getting rid of deviousness. …

an10.87:20.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t deceitful, and praises getting rid of deceitfulness. …

an10.87:21.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant pays attention to the teachings, and praises attending to the teachings. …

an10.87:22.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is in retreat, and praises retreat. …

an10.87:23.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is hospitable to their spiritual companions, and praises hospitality.

an10.87:23.2.verse: This quality conduces to fondness, respect, esteem, harmony, and unity.

an10.87:24.1.verse: Even though a mendicant such as this might never wish:

an10.87:24.2.verse: ‘If only my spiritual companions would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!’ Still they honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them.

an10.87:24.4.verse: Because their sensible spiritual companions see that they’ve given up those bad unskillful qualities.

an10.87:25.1.verse: Suppose a fine thoroughbred never wished:

an10.87:25.2.verse: ‘If only the humans would put me in a thoroughbred’s place, feed me a thoroughbred’s food, and give me a thoroughbred’s grooming.’ Still the humans would put them in a thoroughbred’s place, feed them a thoroughbred’s food, and give them a thoroughbred’s grooming.

an10.87:25.4.verse: Because sensible humans see that they’ve given up their tricks, bluffs, ruses, and feints.

an10.87:26.1.verse: In the same way, even though a mendicant such as this might never wish:

an10.87:26.2.verse: ‘If only my spiritual companions would honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me!’ Still they honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them.

an10.87:26.4.verse: Because their sensible spiritual companions see that they’ve given up those bad unskillful qualities.”

an10.88:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, any mendicant who abuses and insults their spiritual companions, denouncing the noble ones, will, without a doubt, fall into one or other of these ten disasters.

an10.88:1.3.verse: They don’t achieve the unachieved. What they have achieved falls away. They don’t refine their good qualities. They overestimate their good qualities. Or they lead the spiritual life dissatisfied. Or they commit a corrupt offense. Or they contract a severe illness. Or they go mad and lose their mind. They feel lost when they die. And when their body breaks up, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

an10.88:1.4.verse: Any mendicant who abuses and insults their spiritual companions, denouncing the noble ones, will, without a doubt, fall into one or other of these ten disasters.”

an10.89:1.1.verse: Then the mendicant Kokālika went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an10.89:1.2.verse: “Sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They’ve fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.”

an10.89:1.3.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika! Don’t say that, Kokālika!

an10.89:1.4.verse: Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

an10.89:2.1.verse: For a second time Kokālika said to the Buddha,

an10.89:2.2.verse: “Despite my faith and trust in the Buddha, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They’ve fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.”

an10.89:2.3.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika! Don’t say that, Kokālika!

an10.89:2.4.verse: Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

an10.89:3.1.verse: For a third time Kokālika said to the Buddha,

an10.89:3.2.verse: “Despite my faith and trust in the Buddha, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They’ve fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.”

an10.89:3.3.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika! Don’t say that, Kokālika!

an10.89:3.4.verse: Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

an10.89:4.1.verse: Then Kokālika rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an10.89:4.2.verse: Not long after he left his body erupted with boils the size of mustard seeds.

an10.89:4.3.verse: The boils grew to the size of mung beans, then chickpeas, then jujube seeds, then jujubes, then myrobalans, then unripe wood-apples, then ripe wood-apples. Finally they burst open, and pus and blood oozed out.

an10.89:4.4.verse: He just laid down on banana leaves like a poisoned fish.

an10.89:5.1.verse: Then Tudu the independent divinity went to Kokālika, and standing in the air he said to him,

an10.89:5.2.verse: “Kokālika, have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

an10.89:5.6.verse: “Didn’t the Buddha declare you a non-returner? So what then are you doing back here?

an10.89:5.7.verse: See how far you have strayed!”

an10.89:6.1.verse: Then Tudu addressed Kokālika in verse:

an10.89:7.2.verse: with an axe in their mouth.

an10.89:7.3.verse: A fool cuts themselves with it

an10.89:8.1.verse: When you praise someone worthy of criticism,

an10.89:8.2.verse: or criticize someone worthy of praise,

an10.89:8.3.verse: you choose a losing hand with your own mouth:

an10.89:8.4.verse: you’ll never find happiness that way.

an10.89:9.1.verse: A losing hand at dice is a trivial thing,

an10.89:9.2.verse: if all you lose is your money

an10.89:9.3.verse: and all you own, even yourself.

an10.89:9.5.verse: is to hate the holy ones.

an10.89:10.1.verse: For a hundred thousand times a hundred million

an10.89:10.2.verse: times five hundred and thirty-six times a thousand times ten million years

an10.89:10.3.verse: a slanderer of noble ones goes to hell,

an10.89:10.4.verse: having aimed bad words and thoughts at them.”

an10.89:11.1.verse: Then the mendicant Kokālika died of that illness.

an10.89:11.2.verse: He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

an10.89:12.1.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious divinity Sahampati, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

an10.89:12.2.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Kokālika has passed away.

an10.89:12.3.verse: He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

an10.89:12.4.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

an10.89:12.5.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

an10.89:13.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened.

an10.89:14.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

an10.89:14.2.verse: “Sir, how long is the lifespan in the Pink Lotus hell?”

an10.89:14.5.verse: how many years, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of years it lasts.”

an10.89:15.1.verse: “But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”

an10.89:15.3.verse: “Suppose there was a Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed. And at the end of every hundred years someone would remove a single seed from it.

an10.89:15.4.verse: By this means the Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed would run out faster than a single lifetime in the Abbuda hell.

an10.89:15.5.verse: Now, twenty lifetimes in the Abbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Nirabbuda hell.

an10.89:15.6.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Nirabbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Ababa hell.

an10.89:15.7.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Ababa hell equal one lifetime in the Aṭaṭa hell.

an10.89:15.8.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Aṭaṭa hell equal one lifetime in the Ahaha hell.

an10.89:15.9.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Ahaha hell equal one lifetime in the Yellow Lotus hell.

an10.89:15.10.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Yellow Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Fragrant Water Lily hell.

an10.89:15.11.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Fragrant Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the Blue Water Lily hell.

an10.89:15.12.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Blue Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the White Lotus hell.

an10.89:15.13.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the White Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Pink Lotus hell.

an10.89:15.14.verse: The mendicant Kokālika has been reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

an10.89:15.15.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

an10.89:15.16.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

an10.89:16.2.verse: with an axe in their mouth.

an10.89:16.3.verse: A fool cuts themselves with it

an10.89:17.1.verse: When you praise someone worthy of criticism,

an10.89:17.2.verse: or criticize someone worthy of praise,

an10.89:17.3.verse: you choose a losing hand with your own mouth:

an10.89:17.4.verse: you’ll never find happiness that way.

an10.89:18.1.verse: A losing hand at dice is a trivial thing,

an10.89:18.2.verse: if all you lose is your money

an10.89:18.3.verse: and all you own, even yourself.

an10.89:18.5.verse: is to hate the holy ones.

an10.89:19.1.verse: For a hundred thousand times a hundred million,

an10.89:19.2.verse: times five hundred and thirty-six times a thousand times ten million years

an10.89:19.3.verse: a slanderer of noble ones goes to hell,

an10.89:19.4.verse: having aimed bad words and thoughts at them.”

an10.90:0.3.verse: The Powers of One Who has Ended Defilements

an10.90:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an10.90:1.2.verse: “Sāriputta, how many powers does a mendicant who has ended the defilements have that qualify them to claim:

an10.90:2.1.verse: “Sir, a mendicant who has ended the defilements has ten powers that qualify them to claim:

an10.90:2.4.verse: Firstly, a mendicant with defilements ended has clearly seen with right wisdom all conditions as truly impermanent.

an10.90:2.5.verse: This is a power that a mendicant who has ended the defilements relies on to claim:

an10.90:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant with defilements ended has clearly seen with right wisdom that sensual pleasures are truly like a pit of glowing coals.

an10.90:3.2.verse: This is a power that a mendicant who has ended the defilements relies on to claim:

an10.90:4.1.verse: Furthermore, the mind of a mendicant with defilements ended slants, slopes, and inclines to seclusion. They’re withdrawn, loving renunciation, and have totally eliminated defiling influences.

an10.90:4.2.verse: This is a power that a mendicant who has ended the defilements relies on to claim:

an10.90:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant with defilements ended has well developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

an10.90:5.2.verse: This is a power that a mendicant who has ended the defilements relies on to claim:

an10.90:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant with defilements ended has well developed the four right efforts. …

an10.90:6.2.verse: the four bases of psychic power …

an10.90:6.7.verse: This is a power that a mendicant who has ended the defilements relies on to claim:

an10.90:7.1.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements possesses these ten powers that qualify them to claim:

an10.91:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.91:1.2.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Buddha said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:

an10.91:2.1.verse: “These ten pleasure seekers are found in the world.

an10.91:2.3.verse: First, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means.

an10.91:2.4.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit.

an10.91:3.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means.

an10.91:3.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, but don’t share it and make merit.

an10.91:4.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means.

an10.91:4.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

an10.91:5.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

an10.91:5.2.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit.

an10.91:6.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

an10.91:6.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, but don’t share it and make merit.

an10.91:7.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

an10.91:7.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

an10.91:8.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

an10.91:8.2.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit.

an10.91:9.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

an10.91:9.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, but don’t share it and make merit.

an10.91:10.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

an10.91:10.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

an10.91:10.3.verse: But they enjoy that wealth tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

an10.91:11.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

an10.91:11.2.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

an10.91:11.3.verse: And they enjoy that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

an10.91:12.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit. They may be criticized on three grounds.

an10.91:12.2.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

an10.91:12.3.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for criticism.

an10.91:12.4.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the third ground for criticism.

an10.91:12.5.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on these three grounds.

an10.91:13.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, but doesn’t share it and make merit. They may be criticized on two grounds, and praised on one.

an10.91:13.2.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

an10.91:13.3.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the one ground for praise.

an10.91:13.4.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the second ground for criticism.

an10.91:13.5.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on these two grounds, and praised on this one.

an10.91:14.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit. They may be criticized on one ground, and praised on two.

an10.91:14.2.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the one ground for criticism.

an10.91:14.3.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:14.4.verse: They share it and make merit. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:14.5.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on this one ground, and praised on these two.

an10.91:15.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit. They may be praised on one ground, and criticized on three.

an10.91:15.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the one ground for praise.

an10.91:15.3.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

an10.91:15.4.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for criticism.

an10.91:15.5.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the third ground for criticism.

an10.91:15.6.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on this one ground, and criticized on these three.

an10.91:16.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, but doesn’t share it and make merit. They may be praised on two grounds, and criticized on two.

an10.91:16.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:16.3.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

an10.91:16.4.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:16.5.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the second ground for criticism.

an10.91:16.6.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these two grounds, and criticized on these two.

an10.91:17.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit. They may be praised on three grounds, and criticized on one.

an10.91:17.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:17.3.verse: They seek for wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the one ground for criticism.

an10.91:17.4.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:17.5.verse: They share it and make merit. This is the third ground for praise.

an10.91:17.6.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these three grounds, and criticized on this one.

an10.91:18.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, nor share it and make merit. They may be praised on one ground and criticized on two.

an10.91:18.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the one ground for praise.

an10.91:18.3.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased. This is the first ground for criticism.

an10.91:18.4.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the second ground for criticism.

an10.91:18.5.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on this one ground, and criticized on these two.

an10.91:19.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, but doesn’t share it and make merit. They may be praised on two grounds and criticized on one.

an10.91:19.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:19.3.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:19.4.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the one ground for criticism.

an10.91:19.5.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these two grounds, and criticized on this one.

an10.91:20.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit. But they enjoy that wealth tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape. They may be praised on three grounds and criticized on one.

an10.91:20.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:20.3.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:20.4.verse: They share it and make merit. This is the third ground for praise.

an10.91:20.5.verse: They enjoy that wealth tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape. This is the one ground for criticism.

an10.91:20.6.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these three grounds, and criticized on this one.

an10.91:21.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit. And they enjoy that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape. They may be praised on four grounds.

an10.91:21.2.verse: They seek for wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

an10.91:21.3.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

an10.91:21.4.verse: They share it and make merit. This is the third ground for praise.

an10.91:21.5.verse: They enjoy that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape. This is the fourth ground for praise.

an10.91:21.6.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these four grounds.

an10.91:22.1.verse: These are the ten pleasure seekers found in the world.

an10.91:22.2.verse: The pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit, and who uses that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape is the foremost, best, chief, highest, and finest of the ten.

an10.91:22.3.verse: From a cow comes milk, from milk comes curds, from curds come butter, from butter comes ghee, and from ghee comes cream of ghee. And the cream of ghee is said to be the best of these.

an10.91:23.1.verse: In the same way, the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means, who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit, and who uses that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape is the foremost, best, chief, highest, and finest of the ten.”

an10.92:1.1.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

an10.92:2.1.verse: “Householder, when a noble disciple has quelled five fears and enmities, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and has clearly seen and penetrated the noble system with wisdom, they may, if they wish, declare of themselves:

an10.92:2.2.verse: ‘I’ve finished with rebirth in hell, the animal realm, and the ghost realm. I’ve finished with all places of loss, bad places, the underworld. I am a stream-enterer! I’m not liable to be reborn in the underworld, and am assured, destined for awakening.’

an10.92:3.1.verse: What are the five fears and enmities they have quelled?

an10.92:3.2.verse: Anyone who kills living creatures brims with fear and enmity both in this life and in lives to come, and experiences mental pain and sadness. Anyone who refrains from killing living creatures does not brim with fear and enmity either in this life or in lives to come, and doesn’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an10.92:3.3.verse: So that fear and enmity is quelled for anyone who refrains from killing living creatures.

an10.92:4.4.verse: Anyone who consumes beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants brims with fear and enmity both in this life and in lives to come, and experiences mental pain and sadness. Anyone who refrains from beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants does not brim with fear and enmity either in this life or in lives to come, and doesn’t experience mental pain and sadness.

an10.92:4.5.verse: So that fear and enmity is quelled for anyone who refrains from beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants.

an10.92:4.6.verse: These are the five fears and enmities they have quelled.

an10.92:5.1.verse: What are the four factors of stream-entry that they possess?

an10.92:5.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha:

an10.92:5.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

an10.92:5.4.verse: They have experiential confidence in the teaching:

an10.92:5.5.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

an10.92:5.6.verse: They have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

an10.92:5.7.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

an10.92:5.8.verse: And a noble disciple’s ethical conduct is loved by the noble ones, unbroken, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

an10.92:5.9.verse: These are the four factors of stream-entry that they possess.

an10.92:6.1.verse: And what is the noble system that they have clearly seen and penetrated with wisdom?

an10.92:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple reflects:

an10.92:6.3.verse: ‘So, when this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

an10.92:6.4.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

an10.92:6.5.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

an10.92:6.6.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

an10.92:6.7.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

an10.92:6.8.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

an10.92:6.9.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

an10.92:6.10.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

an10.92:6.11.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

an10.92:6.12.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

an10.92:6.13.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

an10.92:6.14.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

an10.92:6.15.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

an10.92:6.16.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

an10.92:6.17.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease. When choices cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease. When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases. When contact ceases, feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

an10.92:6.18.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’

an10.92:6.19.verse: This is the noble system that they have clearly seen and penetrated with wisdom.

an10.92:7.1.verse: When a noble disciple has quelled five fears and enmities, possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and has clearly seen and penetrated the noble system with wisdom, they may, if they wish, declare of themselves:

an10.92:7.2.verse: ‘I’ve finished with rebirth in hell, the animal realm, and the ghost realm. I’ve finished with all places of loss, bad places, the underworld. I am a stream-enterer! I’m not liable to be reborn in the underworld, and am assured, destined for awakening.’”

an10.93:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

an10.93:1.2.verse: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika left Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Buddha.

an10.93:1.4.verse: “It’s the wrong time to see the Buddha,

an10.93:1.6.verse: And it’s the wrong time to see the esteemed mendicants,

an10.93:1.8.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an10.93:2.1.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions.

an10.93:2.2.verse: Now at that time, the wanderers of other religions had come together, making an uproar, a colossal racket as they sat and talked about all kinds of low topics.

an10.93:2.3.verse: They saw Anāthapiṇḍika coming off in the distance,

an10.93:2.5.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

an10.93:2.6.verse: The householder Anāthapiṇḍika, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming into our monastery.

an10.93:2.7.verse: He is included among the white-clothed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama, who is residing in Sāvatthī.

an10.93:2.8.verse: Such venerables like the quiet, are educated to be quiet, and praise the quiet.

an10.93:2.9.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

an10.93:3.1.verse: Then those wanderers of other religions fell silent.

an10.93:3.2.verse: Then Anāthapiṇḍika went up to them, and exchanged greetings with those wanderers.

an10.93:3.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The wanderers said to him,

an10.93:3.4.verse: “Tell us, householder, what is the view of the ascetic Gotama?”

an10.93:3.5.verse: “Sirs, I don’t know all his views.”

an10.93:4.1.verse: “Well then, since it seems you don’t know all the views of the ascetic Gotama,

an10.93:4.2.verse: tell us, what are the views of the mendicants?”

an10.93:4.3.verse: “Sirs, I don’t know all the mendicants’ views.”

an10.93:5.1.verse: “Well then, since it seems you don’t know all the views of the ascetic Gotama or of the mendicants,

an10.93:5.2.verse: tell us, householder, what is your view?”

an10.93:5.3.verse: “Sirs, it’s not hard for me to explain what my views are.

an10.93:5.4.verse: But please, let the venerables explain their own convictions first. Afterwards it won’t be hard for me to explain my views.”

an10.93:6.1.verse: When he said this, one of the wanderers said to him,

an10.93:6.2.verse: “The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:7.2.verse: “The cosmos is not eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:8.4.verse: “The soul and the body are one and the same …” …

an10.93:8.5.verse: “The soul is one thing, the body another …” …

an10.93:8.6.verse: “A realized one still exists after death …” …

an10.93:8.7.verse: “A realized one no longer exists after death …” …

an10.93:8.8.verse: “A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death …” …

an10.93:8.9.verse: “A Realized One neither still exists nor no longer exists after death. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:9.1.verse: When this was said, Anāthapiṇḍika said this,

an10.93:9.2.verse: “Sirs, regarding the venerable who said this:

an10.93:9.3.verse: ‘The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:9.5.verse: This view of his has either arisen from his own irrational application of mind, or is conditioned by what someone else says.

an10.93:9.6.verse: But that view is created, conditioned, chosen, dependently originated.

an10.93:9.7.verse: Whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:9.9.verse: What he clings to and holds to is just suffering.

an10.93:10.1.verse: Regarding the venerable who said this:

an10.93:10.2.verse: ‘The cosmos is not eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:10.4.verse: This view of his has either arisen from his own irrational application of mind, or is conditioned by what someone else says.

an10.93:10.5.verse: But that view is created, conditioned, chosen, dependently originated.

an10.93:10.6.verse: Whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:10.8.verse: What he clings to and holds to is just suffering.

an10.93:11.1.verse: Regarding the venerable who said this:

an10.93:11.4.verse: ‘The soul and the body are one and the same …’ …

an10.93:11.5.verse: ‘The soul is one thing, the body another …’ …

an10.93:11.6.verse: ‘A realized one still exists after death …’ …

an10.93:11.7.verse: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.93:11.8.verse: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.93:11.9.verse: ‘A Realized One neither still exists nor no longer exists after death. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.

an10.93:11.11.verse: This view of his has either arisen from his own irrational application of mind, or is conditioned by what someone else says.

an10.93:11.12.verse: But that view is created, conditioned, chosen, dependently originated.

an10.93:11.13.verse: Whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:11.15.verse: What he clings to and holds to is just suffering.”

an10.93:12.1.verse: When he said this the wanderers said to him,

an10.93:12.2.verse: “Householder, we’ve each explained our own convictions.

an10.93:12.3.verse: Tell us, householder, what is your view?”

an10.93:12.4.verse: “Sirs, whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:12.6.verse: And what’s suffering is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.

an10.93:13.1.verse: “Householder, whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:13.3.verse: What you cling to and hold to is just suffering.”

an10.93:14.1.verse: “Sirs, whatever is created, conditioned, chosen, and dependently originated is impermanent.

an10.93:14.3.verse: And I’ve truly seen clearly with right wisdom that what’s suffering is not mine, I am not this, it’s not my self.

an10.93:14.4.verse: And I truly understand the escape beyond that.”

an10.93:15.1.verse: When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

an10.93:15.2.verse: Seeing this, Anāthapiṇḍika rose from his seat. He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

an10.93:15.4.verse: That’s how you should legitimately and completely refute those futile men from time to time.”

an10.93:16.1.verse: Then the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with a Dhamma talk,

an10.93:16.2.verse: after which Anāthapiṇḍika got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an10.93:17.1.verse: Then, not long after Anāthapiṇḍika had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an10.93:17.2.verse: “Mendicants, even a mendicant who has ordained for a hundred years in this teaching and training would legitimately and completely refute those wanderers of other religions just as the householder Anāthapiṇḍika did.”

an10.94:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.

an10.94:1.2.verse: Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita left Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Buddha.

an10.94:1.4.verse: “It’s the wrong time to see the Buddha,

an10.94:1.6.verse: And it’s the wrong time to see the esteemed mendicants,

an10.94:1.8.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

an10.94:2.1.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions.

an10.94:2.2.verse: Now at that time, the wanderers of other religions had come together, making an uproar, a colossal racket as they sat and talked about all kinds of low topics.

an10.94:3.1.verse: They saw Vajjiyamāhita coming off in the distance, and stopped each other, saying,

an10.94:3.2.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

an10.94:3.3.verse: The householder Vajjiyamāhita, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming into our monastery.

an10.94:3.4.verse: He is included among the white-clothed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama, who is residing near Campā.

an10.94:3.5.verse: Such venerables like the quiet, are educated to be quiet, and praise the quiet.

an10.94:3.6.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

an10.94:4.1.verse: Then those wanderers of other religions fell silent.

an10.94:4.2.verse: Then Vajjiyamāhita went up to them, and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

an10.94:4.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The wanderers said to him:

an10.94:4.4.verse: “Is it really true, householder? Does the ascetic Gotama criticize all forms of mortification? Does he categorically condemn and denounce those fervent mortifiers who live rough?”

an10.94:4.5.verse: “No, sirs, the Buddha does not criticize all forms of mortification. Nor does he categorically condemn and denounce those fervent mortifiers who live rough.

an10.94:4.6.verse: The Buddha criticizes where it is due, and praises where it is due.

an10.94:4.7.verse: In doing so he is one who speaks after analyzing the question,

an10.94:4.8.verse: and is not one-sided on this point.”

an10.94:5.1.verse: When he said this, one of the wanderers said to him,

an10.94:5.2.verse: “Hold on, householder! That ascetic Gotama who you praise is an exterminator who refrains from making statements.”

an10.94:5.3.verse: “On this point, also, I reasonably respond to the venerables.

an10.94:5.4.verse: The Buddha has stated ‘This is skillful’ and

an10.94:5.6.verse: So when it comes to what is skillful and unskillful the Buddha makes a statement.

an10.94:5.7.verse: He is not an exterminator who refrains from making statements.”

an10.94:6.1.verse: When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

an10.94:6.2.verse: Seeing this, Vajjiyamāhita rose from his seat. He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

an10.94:6.3.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

an10.94:7.2.verse: That’s how you should legitimately and completely refute those futile men from time to time.

an10.94:7.3.verse: Householder, I don’t say that all mortifications should be undergone.

an10.94:7.4.verse: But I don’t say that no mortifications should be undergone.

an10.94:7.5.verse: I don’t say that all observances should be undertaken.

an10.94:7.6.verse: But I don’t say that no observances should be undertaken.

an10.94:7.7.verse: I don’t say that all efforts should be tried.

an10.94:7.8.verse: But I don’t say that no efforts should be tried.

an10.94:7.9.verse: I don’t say that everything should be given up.

an10.94:7.10.verse: But I don’t say that nothing should be given up.

an10.94:7.11.verse: I don’t say that you should be liberated with all kinds of freedom.

an10.94:7.12.verse: But I don’t say that you should not be liberated with any kind of freedom.

an10.94:8.1.verse: When undergoing certain mortifications, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t undergo those mortifications.

an10.94:8.2.verse: When undergoing certain mortifications, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should undergo those mortifications.

an10.94:9.1.verse: When undertaking certain observances, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t undertake those observances.

an10.94:9.2.verse: When undertaking certain observances, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should undertake those observances.

an10.94:10.1.verse: When trying certain efforts, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t try those efforts.

an10.94:10.2.verse: When trying certain efforts, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should try those efforts.

an10.94:11.1.verse: When giving up certain things, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t give up those things.

an10.94:11.2.verse: When giving up certain things, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should give up those things.

an10.94:12.1.verse: When being liberated with certain kinds of freedom, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. I say that you shouldn’t be liberated with those kinds of freedom.

an10.94:12.2.verse: When being liberated with certain kinds of freedom, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. I say that you should be liberated with those kinds of freedom.”

an10.94:13.1.verse: After Vajjiyamāhita had been educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired with a Dhamma talk by the Buddha, he got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

an10.94:14.1.verse: Then, not long after Vajjiyamāhita had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

an10.94:14.2.verse: “Mendicants, even a mendicant who for a long time has had little dust in their eye in this teaching and training would legitimately and completely refute those wanderers of other religions just as the householder Vajjiyamāhita did.”

an10.95:1.1.verse: Then the wanderer Uttiya went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

an10.95:1.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

an10.95:1.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, is this right: ‘The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.95:1.4.verse: “This has not been declared by me, Uttiya.”

an10.95:2.1.verse: “Then is this right: ‘The cosmos is not eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.95:2.2.verse: “This has not been declared by me, Uttiya.”

an10.95:3.1.verse: “Then is this right: ‘The cosmos is finite …’ …

an10.95:3.3.verse: ‘The soul and the body are one and the same …’ …

an10.95:3.4.verse: ‘The soul is one thing, the body another …’ …

an10.95:3.5.verse: ‘A realized one still exists after death …’ …

an10.95:3.6.verse: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.95:3.7.verse: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.95:3.8.verse: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.95:3.9.verse: “This has not been declared by me, Uttiya.”

an10.95:4.1.verse: “When asked about all these points, worthy Gotama says that they have not been declared by him.

an10.95:6.11.verse: So what then has been declared by Worthy Gotama?”

an10.95:7.1.verse: “Uttiya, I teach my disciples from my own insight in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to end the cycle of suffering, and to realize extinguishment.”

an10.95:8.1.verse: “But when the worthy Gotama teaches in this way, is the whole world saved, or half, or a third?”

an10.95:8.2.verse: But when he said this, the Buddha kept silent.

an10.95:9.2.verse: “The wanderer Uttiya must not get the harmful misconception:

an10.95:9.3.verse: ‘When the ascetic Gotama was asked this all-important question he falters without answering. He just can’t do it!’

an10.95:9.4.verse: That would be for his lasting harm and suffering.”

an10.95:10.1.verse: Then Ānanda said to the wanderer Uttiya,

an10.95:10.2.verse: “Well then, Reverend Uttiya, I shall give you a simile.

an10.95:10.3.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

an10.95:10.4.verse: Suppose there was a king’s frontier citadel with fortified embankments, ramparts, and arches, and a single gate.

an10.95:10.5.verse: And it has a gatekeeper who is astute, competent, and intelligent. He keeps strangers out and lets known people in.

an10.95:10.6.verse: As he walks around the patrol path, he doesn’t see a hole or cleft in the wall, not even one big enough for a cat to slip out.

an10.95:10.7.verse: He doesn’t know how many creatures enter or leave the citadel.

an10.95:10.8.verse: But he does know that whatever sizable creatures enter or leave the citadel, all of them do so via this gate.

an10.95:11.1.verse: In the same way, it’s not the Realized One’s concern whether the whole world is saved by this, or half, or a third.

an10.95:11.2.verse: But the Realized One knows that whoever is saved from the world—whether in the past, the future, or the present—all have given up the five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom. They have firmly established their mind in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. And they have truly developed the seven awakening factors.

an10.95:11.3.verse: That’s how they’re saved from the world, in the past, future, or present.

an10.95:11.4.verse: Uttiya, you were just asking the Buddha the same question as before in a different way.

an10.96:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Monastery.

an10.96:1.2.verse: Then Ānanda rose at the crack of dawn and went to the hot springs to bathe.

an10.96:1.3.verse: When he had bathed and emerged from the water he stood in one robe drying his limbs.

an10.96:1.4.verse: The wanderer Kokanada also rose at the crack of dawn and went to the hot springs to bathe.

an10.96:2.1.verse: He saw Ānanda coming off in the distance

an10.96:3.2.verse: “Of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan.”

an10.96:4.1.verse: “I’d like to ask the venerable about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

an10.96:4.2.verse: “Ask, reverend. When I’ve heard it I’ll know.”

an10.96:5.1.verse: “Is this your view: ‘The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.96:6.1.verse: “Then is this your view: ‘The cosmos is not eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.96:7.1.verse: “Then is this your view: ‘The cosmos is finite …’ …

an10.96:7.3.verse: ‘The soul and the body are one and the same …’ …

an10.96:7.4.verse: ‘The soul is one thing, the body another …’ …

an10.96:7.5.verse: ‘A realized one still exists after death …’ …

an10.96:7.6.verse: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.96:7.7.verse: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.96:7.8.verse: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death. This is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

an10.96:8.1.verse: “Then, sir, do you neither know nor see?”

an10.96:9.1.verse: “When asked about all these points, you say that’s not your view.

an10.96:12.1.verse: Yet when asked whether you neither know nor see,

an10.96:12.4.verse: How then should we see the meaning of this statement?”

an10.96:13.1.verse: “‘The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile:’ that’s a misconception.

an10.96:13.2.verse: ‘The cosmos is not eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile:’ that’s a misconception.

an10.96:13.5.verse: ‘The soul and the body are one and the same …’ …

an10.96:13.6.verse: ‘The soul is one thing, the body another …’ …

an10.96:13.7.verse: ‘A realized one still exists after death …’ …

an10.96:13.8.verse: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.96:13.9.verse: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death …’ …

an10.96:13.10.verse: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death. This is the only truth, anything else is futile:’ that’s a misconception.

an10.96:14.1.verse: I know and see the scope of convictions, the scope of grounds for views, fixation on views, obsession with views, the origin of views, and the uprooting of views.

an10.96:14.2.verse: Knowing and seeing thus, why should I say:

an10.96:15.1.verse: “What is the venerable’s name? And how are you known among your spiritual companions?”

an10.96:15.3.verse: And that’s how I’m known among my spiritual companions.”

an10.96:15.4.verse: “Goodness! I had no idea I was consulting such a great tutor as

an10.96:15.7.verse: you were, I wouldn’t have said so much.

an10.96:15.8.verse: May Venerable Ānanda please forgive me.”

an10.97:0.3.verse: Worthy of Offerings Dedicated to the Gods

an10.97:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant with ten qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of veneration with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

an10.97:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.97:3.1.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.97:4.1.verse: They have good friends, companions, and associates.

an10.97:5.1.verse: They have right view, possessing right perspective.

an10.97:6.1.verse: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. They control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

an10.97:7.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.

an10.97:8.1.verse: They understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind.

an10.97:8.2.verse: They understand mind with greed as ‘mind with greed’,

an10.97:8.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed’.

an10.97:8.17.verse: They understand unfreed mind as ‘unfreed mind’.

an10.97:9.1.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ Thus they recollect their many past lives, with features and details.

an10.97:10.1.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

an10.97:11.1.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.97:12.1.verse: A mendicant with these ten qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of veneration with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.”

an10.98:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a senior mendicant with ten qualities lives comfortably in whatever region they live.

an10.98:1.3.verse: They are long standing and have long gone forth.

an10.98:1.4.verse: They’re ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

an10.98:1.5.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reinforcing them by recitation, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

an10.98:1.6.verse: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

an10.98:1.7.verse: They’re skilled in the instigation and settlement of disciplinary issues.

an10.98:1.8.verse: They love the teachings and are a delight to converse with, being full of joy in the teaching and training.

an10.98:1.9.verse: They’re content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

an10.98:1.10.verse: They look impressive when going out and coming back, and are well restrained when sitting in an inhabited area.

an10.98:1.11.verse: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

an10.98:1.12.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

an10.98:1.13.verse: A senior mendicant with these ten qualities lives comfortably in whatever region they live.”

an10.99:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Upāli went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

an10.99:1.2.verse: “Sir, I wish to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.”

an10.99:2.1.verse: “Upāli, remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest are challenging.

an10.99:2.2.verse: It’s hard to maintain seclusion and hard to find joy in it.

an10.99:2.3.verse: Staying alone, the forests seem to rob the mind of a mendicant who isn’t immersed in samādhi.

an10.99:2.5.verse: ‘Though I don’t have immersion, I’m going to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.’ You can expect that

an10.99:2.6.verse: they’ll sink down or float away.

an10.99:3.1.verse: Suppose there was a large lake,

an10.99:3.2.verse: and along comes a bull elephant that’s three or three and a half meters tall.

an10.99:3.4.verse: ‘Why don’t I plunge into this lake and play around while washing my ears and back?

an10.99:3.5.verse: When I’ve bathed and drunk, I’ll emerge from the water and go wherever I want.’

an10.99:3.6.verse: And that’s just what he does.

an10.99:3.9.verse: Because his large incarnation finds a footing in the depths.

an10.99:4.1.verse: Then along comes a rabbit or a cat.

an10.99:4.3.verse: ‘What difference is there between me and a bull elephant?

an10.99:4.4.verse: Why don’t I plunge into this lake and play around while washing my ears and back?

an10.99:4.5.verse: When I’ve bathed and drunk, I’ll emerge from the water and go wherever I want.’

an10.99:4.6.verse: They jump into the lake rashly, without thinking.

an10.99:4.8.verse: they’ll sink down or float away.

an10.99:4.10.verse: Because their little incarnation finds no footing in the depths.

an10.99:4.12.verse: ‘Though I don’t have immersion, I’m going to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.’ You can expect that

an10.99:4.13.verse: they’ll sink down or float away.

an10.99:5.1.verse: Suppose there was a little baby boy playing in his own urine and feces.

an10.99:5.3.verse: Isn’t that a totally foolish game?”

an10.99:6.1.verse: “After some time that boy grows up and his faculties mature.

an10.99:6.2.verse: He accordingly plays childish games such as toy plows, tip-cat, somersaults, pinwheels, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows.

an10.99:6.4.verse: Aren’t such games better than what he did before?”

an10.99:7.1.verse: “After some time that boy grows up and his faculties mature further.

an10.99:7.2.verse: He accordingly amuses himself, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

an10.99:7.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an10.99:7.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

an10.99:7.9.verse: Aren’t such games better than what he did before?”

an10.99:8.1.verse: “Now in this regard, Upāli, a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

an10.99:8.2.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

an10.99:8.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

an10.99:9.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

an10.99:9.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One

an10.99:9.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

an10.99:9.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

an10.99:9.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

an10.99:10.1.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

an10.99:11.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

an10.99:12.1.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

an10.99:13.1.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

an10.99:14.1.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

an10.99:15.1.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

an10.99:16.1.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.
