dn10:2.36.2.verse: In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

dn10:2.37.1.verse: This is that spectrum of noble wisdom that the Buddha praised.

dn10:2.37.2.verse: And there is nothing more to be done.”

dn10:2.37.4.verse: This spectrum of noble wisdom is complete, not lacking anything!

dn10:2.37.5.verse: Such a complete spectrum of wisdom cannot be seen among the other ascetics and brahmins.

dn10:2.37.6.verse: And there is nothing more to be done.

dn10:2.37.8.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Ānanda has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn10:2.37.9.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

dn10:2.37.10.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Ānanda remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

dn11:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

dn11:1.3.verse: Then the householder Kevaḍḍha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn11:1.4.verse: “Sir, this Nāḷandā is successful and prosperous, populous and full of people.

dn11:1.5.verse: Please direct a mendicant to perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power.

dn11:1.6.verse: Then Nāḷandā will become even more devoted to the Buddha!”

dn11:1.7.verse: When he said this, the Buddha said,

dn11:1.8.verse: “Kevaḍḍha, I do not teach Dhamma to the mendicants like this:

dn11:1.9.verse: ‘Come now, mendicants, perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power for the white-clothed laypeople.’”

dn11:2.1.verse: For a second time, Kevaḍḍha made the same request,

dn11:2.2.verse: “Sir, I am not teaching you the Dhamma,

dn11:2.4.verse: ‘Sir, this Nāḷandā is successful and prosperous, populous and full of people.

dn11:2.5.verse: Please direct a mendicant to perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power.

dn11:2.6.verse: Then Nāḷandā will become even more devoted to the Buddha!’”

dn11:2.7.verse: But for a second time, the Buddha gave the same answer.

dn11:3.1.verse: For a third time, Kevaḍḍha made the same request,

dn11:3.6.verse: at which the Buddha said the following.

dn11:3.8.verse: “Kevaḍḍha, there are three kinds of demonstration, which I declare having realized them with my own insight.

dn11:3.10.verse: The demonstration of psychic power, the demonstration of revealing, and the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:4.1.verse: And what is the demonstration of psychic power?

dn11:4.2.verse: It’s a mendicant who wields the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.

dn11:4.3.verse: Someone with faith and confidence sees that mendicant performing those superhuman feats.

dn11:4.4.verse: They tell someone else who lacks faith and confidence:

dn11:4.5.verse: ‘Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The ascetic has such psychic power and might!

dn11:4.6.verse: I saw him myself, performing all these superhuman feats!’

dn11:5.1.verse: But the one lacking faith and confidence would say to them:

dn11:5.3.verse: Using that a mendicant can perform such superhuman feats.’

dn11:5.5.verse: Wouldn’t someone lacking faith speak like that?”

dn11:5.7.verse: “Seeing this drawback in psychic power, I’m horrified, repelled, and disgusted by demonstrations of psychic power.

dn11:6.1.verse: And what is the demonstration of revealing?

dn11:6.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant reveals the mind, mentality, thoughts, and reflections of other beings and individuals:

dn11:6.3.verse: ‘This is what you’re thinking, such is your thought, and thus is your state of mind.’

dn11:6.4.verse: Someone with faith and confidence sees that mendicant revealing another individual’s thoughts.

dn11:6.6.verse: They tell someone else who lacks faith and confidence:

dn11:6.7.verse: ‘Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The ascetic has such psychic power and might!

dn11:6.8.verse: I saw him myself, revealing the thoughts of another individual!’

dn11:7.1.verse: But the one lacking faith and confidence would say to them:

dn11:7.3.verse: Using that a mendicant can reveal another individual’s thoughts.’

dn11:7.6.verse: Wouldn’t someone lacking faith speak like that?”

dn11:7.8.verse: “Seeing this drawback in revealing, I’m horrified, repelled, and disgusted by demonstrations of revealing.

dn11:8.1.verse: And what is the demonstration of instruction?

dn11:8.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant instructs others like this:

dn11:8.3.verse: ‘Think like this, not like that. Focus your mind like this, not like that. Give up this, and live having achieved that.’

dn11:8.4.verse: This is called the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:9-66.1.verse: Furthermore, a Realized One arises in the world …

dn11:9-66.2.verse: That’s how a mendicant is accomplished in ethics. …

dn11:9-66.3.verse: They enter and remain in the first absorption …

dn11:9-66.4.verse: This is called the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:9-66.5.verse: They enter and remain in the second absorption …

dn11:9-66.8.verse: This too is called the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:9-66.9.verse: They project and extend the mind toward knowledge and vision …

dn11:9-66.10.verse: This too is called the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:9-66.11.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

dn11:9-66.12.verse: This too is called the demonstration of instruction.

dn11:67.1.verse: These, Kevaḍḍha, are the three kinds of demonstration, which I declare having realized them with my own insight.

dn11:67.2.0.verse: 4. On the Mendicant in Search of the Cessation of Being

dn11:67.3.verse: Once upon a time, Kevaḍḍha, a mendicant in this very Saṅgha had the following thought,

dn11:67.4.verse: ‘Where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?’

dn11:68.1.verse: Then that mendicant attained a state of immersion such that a path to the gods appeared.

dn11:68.2.verse: Then he approached the gods of the four great kings and said,

dn11:68.3.verse: ‘Respectable sirs, where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?’

dn11:68.4.verse: When he said this, those gods said to him,

dn11:68.5.verse: ‘Mendicant, we too do not know this.

dn11:68.7.verse: But the four great kings are our superiors.

dn11:69.1.verse: Then he approached the four great kings and asked the same question.

dn11:69.3.verse: But they also said to him,

dn11:69.4.verse: ‘Mendicant, we too do not know this.

dn11:69.6.verse: But the gods of the thirty-three …

dn11:76.1.verse: the gods who love to create …

dn11:77.2.verse: the gods who control the creation of others …

dn11:79.6.verse: the gods of the Divinity’s host are our superiors.

dn11:80.1.verse: Then that mendicant attained a state of immersion such that a path to divinity appeared.

dn11:80.2.verse: Then he approached the gods of the Divinity’s host and said,

dn11:80.3.verse: ‘Respectable sirs, where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?’

dn11:80.4.verse: But they also said to him,

dn11:80.5.verse: ‘Mendicant, we too do not know this.

dn11:80.7.verse: But there is the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born. He is our superior.

dn11:80.10.verse: ‘But respectable sirs, where is that divinity now?’

dn11:80.11.verse: ‘We also don’t know where he is or what way he lies.

dn11:80.12.verse: But by the signs that are seen—light arising and radiance appearing—we know that divinity will appear. For this is the harbinger for the appearance of the Divinity, namely light arising and radiance appearing.’

dn11:81.1.verse: Not long afterwards, the Great Divinity appeared.

dn11:81.2.verse: Then that mendicant approached the Great Divinity and said to him,

dn11:81.3.verse: ‘Respectable sir, where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?’

dn11:81.4.verse: The Great Divinity said to him,

dn11:81.5.verse: ‘I am the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.’

dn11:82.1.verse: For a second time, that mendicant said to the Great Divinity,

dn11:82.2.verse: ‘Respectable sir, I am not asking you whether you are

dn11:82.3.verse: the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.

dn11:82.5.verse: where these four principal states cease without remainder.’

dn11:82.6.verse: For a second time, the Great Divinity said to him,

dn11:82.7.verse: ‘I am the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.’

dn11:83.1.verse: For a third time, that mendicant said to the Great Divinity,

dn11:83.2.verse: ‘Respectable sir, I am not asking you whether you are

dn11:83.3.verse: the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.

dn11:83.5.verse: where these four principal states cease without remainder.’

dn11:83.6.verse: Then the Great Divinity took that mendicant by the arm, led him off to one side, and said to him,

dn11:83.7.verse: ‘Mendicant, these gods think that there is nothing at all that I don’t know and see and understand and realize.

dn11:83.8.verse: That’s why I didn’t answer in front of them.

dn11:83.9.verse: But I too do not know where these four principal states cease with no residue left behind.

dn11:83.10.verse: Therefore, mendicant, the misdeed is yours alone, the mistake is yours alone, in that you passed over the Buddha and searched elsewhere for an answer to this question.

dn11:83.11.verse: Mendicant, go to the Buddha and ask him this question. You should remember it in line with his answer.’

dn11:84.1.verse: Then that mendicant, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of me.

dn11:84.2.verse: Then he bowed, sat down to one side, and said to me,

dn11:84.3.verse: ‘Sir, where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?’

dn11:85.0.verse: 4.1. The Simile of the Land-Spotting Bird

dn11:85.1.verse: When he said this, I said to him:

dn11:85.2.verse: ‘Once upon a time, mendicant, some sea-merchants set sail for the ocean deeps, taking with them a land-spotting bird.

dn11:85.3.verse: When their ship was out of sight of land, they released the bird.

dn11:85.4.verse: It flew right away to the east, the west, the north, the south, upwards, and in-between.

dn11:85.5.verse: If it saw land on any side, it went there and stayed.

dn11:85.6.verse: But if it saw no land on any side it returned to the ship.

dn11:85.7.verse: In the same way, after failing to get an answer to this question even after searching as far as the realm of divinity, you’ve returned to me.

dn11:85.8.verse: Mendicant, this is not how the question should be asked:

dn11:85.9.verse: “Sir, where do these four principal states cease without remainder, namely, the elements of earth, water, fire, and air?”

dn11:85.10.verse: This is how the question should be asked:

dn11:85.12.verse: fire and air have no footing;

dn11:85.14.verse: tiny and huge, beautiful and ugly?

dn11:85.17.verse: And the answer to that is:

dn11:85.21.verse: fire and air have no footing;

dn11:85.23.verse: tiny and huge, beautiful and ugly.

dn11:85.25.verse: cease with no residue left behind—

dn11:85.28.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn11:85.29.verse: Satisfied, the householder Kevaḍḍha approved what the Buddha said.

dn12:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants when he arrived at Sālavatikā.

dn12:1.3.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Lohicca was living in Sālavatikā. It was a crown property given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, teeming with living creatures, full of hay, wood, water, and grain, a royal park endowed to a brahmin.

dn12:2.1.verse: Now at that time Lohicca had the following harmful misconception:

dn12:2.2.verse: “Should an ascetic or brahmin achieve some skillful quality, they ought not inform anyone else. For what can one person do for another?

dn12:2.3.verse: Suppose someone cut off an old bond, only to create another new bond.

dn12:2.4.verse: That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one person do for another?”

dn12:3.2.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Sālavatikā, together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants.

dn12:3.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

dn12:3.5.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

dn12:3.6.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

dn12:3.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

dn12:4.1.verse: Then Lohicca addressed his barber Rosika,

dn12:4.2.verse: “Here, dear Rosika, go to the ascetic Gotama and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

dn12:4.4.verse: And then ask him whether he,

dn12:4.5.verse: together with the mendicant Saṅgha, would please accept tomorrow’s meal from the brahmin Lohicca.”

dn12:5.1.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” Rosika replied. He did as he was asked, and

dn12:6.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Rosika rose from his seat, went to Lohicca, and said to him,

dn12:7.1.verse: And when the night had passed Lohicca had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own home. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

dn12:7.2.verse: “Here, dear Rosika, go to the ascetic Gotama and announce the time, saying:

dn12:7.3.verse: ‘It’s time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready.’”

dn12:7.4.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” Rosika replied. He did as he was asked.

dn12:7.7.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Sālavatikā together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.

dn12:8.1.verse: Now, Rosika was following behind the Buddha,

dn12:8.2.verse: and told him of Lohicca’s views, adding,

dn12:8.9.verse: “Sir, please dissuade him from that harmful misconception.”

dn12:8.10.verse: “Hopefully that’ll happen, Rosika, hopefully that’ll happen.”

dn12:9.1.verse: Then the Buddha approached Lohicca’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

dn12:9.2.verse: Then Lohicca served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

dn12:9.4.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Lohicca took a low seat and sat to one side.

dn12:9.6.verse: “Is it really true, Lohicca, that you have such a harmful misconception:

dn12:9.7.verse: ‘Should an ascetic or brahmin achieve some skillful quality, they ought not inform anyone else. For what can one person do for another?

dn12:9.8.verse: Suppose someone cut off an old bond, only to create another new bond.

dn12:9.9.verse: That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one person do for another?’”

dn12:10.6.verse: He alone should enjoy the revenues produced in Sālavatikā and not share them with anyone else.’

dn12:10.7.verse: Would the one who spoke like that make it difficult for those whose living depends on you or not?”

dn12:10.9.verse: “But is someone who creates difficulties for others acting kindly or unkindly?”

dn12:10.11.verse: “But does an unkind person have love in their heart or hostility?”

dn12:10.13.verse: “And when the heart is full of hostility, is there right view or wrong view?”

dn12:10.15.verse: “An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say:

dn12:11.2.verse: Does King Pasenadi reign over Kāsi and Kosala?”

dn12:11.5.verse: ‘King Pasenadi reigns over Kāsi and Kosala.

dn12:11.6.verse: He alone should enjoy the revenues produced in Kāsi and Kosala and not share them with anyone else.’

dn12:11.7.verse: Would the one who spoke like that make it difficult for yourself and others whose living depends on King Pasenadi or not?”

dn12:11.9.verse: “But is someone who creates difficulties for others acting kindly or unkindly?”

dn12:11.11.verse: “But does an unkind person have love in their heart or hostility?”

dn12:11.13.verse: “And when the heart is full of hostility, is there right view or wrong view?”

dn12:11.15.verse: “An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say:

dn12:12.1.verse: So it seems, Lohicca, that should someone say such a thing either of Lohicca or of King Pasenadi,

dn12:13.3.verse: In the same way, suppose someone were to say:

dn12:13.4.verse: ‘Should an ascetic or brahmin achieve some skillful quality, they ought not inform anyone else. For what can one person do for another?

dn12:13.5.verse: Suppose someone cut off an old bond, only to create another new bond.

dn12:13.6.verse: That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one person do for another?’

dn12:13.7.verse: Now, there are gentlemen who, relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, achieve a high distinction such as the following: they realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-return, the fruit of non-return, or perfection. And in addition, there are those who ripen the seeds for rebirth in a heavenly state. The person who spoke like that makes it difficult for them. They’re acting unkindly, their heart is full of hostility, and they have wrong view.

dn12:13.8.verse: An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say:

dn12:16.0.verse: 2. Three Teachers Who Deserve to Be Reprimanded

dn12:16.1.verse: Lohicca, there are three kinds of teachers in the world who deserve to be reprimanded.

dn12:16.2.verse: When someone reprimands such teachers, the reprimand is true, correct, legitimate, and blameless.

dn12:16.4.verse: Firstly, take a teacher who has not reached the goal of the ascetic life for which they went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn12:16.6.verse: ‘This is for your welfare. This is for your happiness.’

dn12:16.7.verse: But their disciples don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:16.8.verse: That teacher deserves to be reprimanded:

dn12:16.9.verse: ‘Venerable, you haven’t reached the goal of the ascetic life; and when you teach disciples

dn12:16.11.verse: they proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:16.12.verse: It’s like a man who makes advances on a woman though she pulls away, or embraces her though she turns her back.

dn12:16.13.verse: That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one do for another?’

dn12:16.15.verse: This is the first kind of teacher who deserves to be reprimanded.

dn12:17.1.verse: Furthermore, take a teacher who has not reached the goal of the ascetic life for which they went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn12:17.3.verse: ‘This is for your welfare. This is for your happiness.’

dn12:17.4.verse: Their disciples do want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand. They don’t proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:17.5.verse: That teacher deserves to be reprimanded:

dn12:17.6.verse: ‘Venerable, you haven’t reached the goal of the ascetic life; and when you teach disciples

dn12:17.8.verse: they don’t proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:17.9.verse: It’s like someone who abandons their own field and presumes to weed someone else’s field. That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one do for another?’

dn12:17.10.verse: This is the second kind of teacher who deserves to be reprimanded.

dn12:18.1.verse: Furthermore, take a teacher who has reached the goal of the ascetic life for which they went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn12:18.3.verse: ‘This is for your welfare. This is for your happiness.’

dn12:18.4.verse: But their disciples don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:18.5.verse: That teacher deserves to be reprimanded:

dn12:18.6.verse: ‘Venerable, you have reached the goal of the ascetic life; yet when you teach disciples

dn12:18.9.verse: they proceed having turned away from the teacher’s instruction.

dn12:18.10.verse: Suppose someone cut off an old bond, only to create another new bond.

dn12:18.11.verse: That’s the consequence of such a wicked, greedy deed, I say. For what can one person do for another?’

dn12:18.12.verse: This is the third kind of teacher who deserves to be reprimanded.

dn12:18.14.verse: These are the three kinds of teachers in the world who deserve to be reprimanded.

dn12:18.15.verse: When someone reprimands such teachers, the reprimand is true, correct, legitimate, and blameless.”

dn12:19.0.verse: 3. A Teacher Who Does Not Deserve to Be Reprimanded

dn12:19.1.verse: When he had spoken, Lohicca said to the Buddha,

dn12:19.2.verse: “But worthy Gotama, is there a teacher in the world who does not deserve to be reprimanded?”

dn12:20-55.1.verse: “It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha …

dn12:20-55.2.verse: That’s how a mendicant is accomplished in ethics. …

dn12:20-55.3.verse: They enter and remain in the first absorption …

dn12:20-55.4.verse: A teacher under whom a disciple achieves such a high distinction is one who does not deserve to be reprimanded.

dn12:20-55.5.verse: When someone reprimands such a teacher, the reprimand is false, baseless, illegitimate, and blameworthy.

dn12:56-62.2.verse: They enter and remain in the second absorption …

dn12:56-62.5.verse: A teacher under whom a disciple achieves such a high distinction is one who does not deserve to be reprimanded. …

dn12:63-77.2.verse: They project and extend the mind toward knowledge and vision …

dn12:63-77.3.verse: A teacher under whom a disciple achieves such a high distinction is one who does not deserve to be reprimanded. …

dn12:63-77.5.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

dn12:63-77.6.verse: A teacher under whom a disciple achieves such a high distinction is one who does not deserve to be reprimanded. When someone reprimands such a teacher, the reprimand is false, baseless, illegitimate, and blameworthy.”

dn12:78.1.verse: When he had spoken, Lohicca said to the Buddha:

dn12:78.2.verse: “Suppose, Worthy Gotama, a person was falling over a cliff, and another person were to grab them by the hair, pull them up, and place them on solid ground.

dn12:78.3.verse: In the same way, when I was falling off a cliff Worthy Gotama pulled me up and placed me on solid ground.

dn12:78.5.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the Teaching clear in many ways.

dn12:78.6.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

dn12:78.7.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

dn13:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Manasākaṭa.

dn13:1.3.verse: He stayed in a mango grove on a bank of the Aciravatī River to the north of Manasākaṭa.

dn13:2.1.verse: Now at that time several very well-known well-to-do brahmins were residing in Manasākaṭa. They included

dn13:2.2.verse: the brahmins Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jānussoṇi, Todeyya, and others.

dn13:3.1.verse: Then as the students Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were going for a walk they began a discussion regarding what is the path and what is not the path.

dn13:4.2.verse: “This is the only straight path, the direct route that delivers one who applies it to the company of Divinity; namely, that explained by the brahmin Pokkharasāti.”

dn13:5.2.verse: “This is the only straight path, the direct route that delivers one who applies it to the company of Divinity; namely, that explained by the brahmin Tārukkha.”

dn13:6.1.verse: But neither was able to persuade the other.

dn13:7.2.verse: “Bhāradvāja, the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—is staying in a mango grove on a bank of the Aciravatī River to the north of Manasākaṭa.

dn13:7.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

dn13:7.5.verse: Come, let’s go to see him and ask him about this matter.

dn13:7.6.verse: As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”

dn13:8.0.verse: 1. What is the Path and What is Not the Path

dn13:8.1.verse: So they went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

dn13:8.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and Vāseṭṭha told him of their conversation, adding:

dn13:8.8.verse: “In this matter we have a dispute, a disagreement, a difference of opinion.”

dn13:9.1.verse: “So, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that you say that

dn13:9.2.verse: the straight path is that explained by Pokkharasāti,

dn13:9.4.verse: the straight path is that explained by Tārukkha.

dn13:9.5.verse: But what exactly is your disagreement about?”

dn13:10.1.verse: “About what is the path and what is not the path, worthy Gotama.

dn13:10.2.verse: Even though brahmins describe different paths—the Adhvaryu brahmins, the Taittirīya brahmins, the Chāndogya brahmins, the Cāndrāyaṇa brahmins, and the Bahvṛca brahmins—all of them still lead someone who practices them to the company of Divinity.

dn13:10.3.verse: It’s like a village or town that has many different roads nearby, yet all of them meet at that village.

dn13:10.4.verse: In the same way, even though brahmins describe different paths—the Adhvaryu brahmins, the Taittirīya brahmins, the Chāndogya brahmins, the Cāndrāyaṇa brahmins, and the Bahvṛca brahmins—all of them still lead someone who practices them to the company of Divinity.”

dn13:12.1.verse: “Well, of the brahmins who are proficient in the three Vedas, Vāseṭṭha, is there even a single one who has seen the Divinity with their own eyes?”

dn13:12.3.verse: “Well, has even a single one of their tutors seen the Divinity with their own eyes?”

dn13:12.5.verse: “Well, has even a single one of their tutors’ tutors seen the Divinity with their own eyes?”

dn13:12.7.verse: “Well, has anyone back to the seventh generation of tutors seen the Divinity with their own eyes?”

dn13:13.1.verse: “Well, what of the ancient seers of the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, namely Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu? They were the authors and propagators of the hymns. Their hymnal was sung and propagated and compiled in ancient times; and these days, brahmins continue to sing and chant it, chanting what was chanted and teaching what was taught.

dn13:13.3.verse: ‘We know and see where the Divinity is or what way he lies’?”

dn13:14.1.verse: “So it seems that none of those brahmins have seen the Divinity with their own eyes,

dn13:14.5.verse: and not even the ancient seers

dn13:14.6.verse: claimed to know where he is.

dn13:14.7.verse: Yet the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas say:

dn13:14.8.verse: ‘We teach the path to the company of that which we neither know nor see.

dn13:14.9.verse: This is the only straight path, the direct route that delivers one who applies it to the company of Divinity.’

dn13:14.11.verse: This being so, doesn’t their statement turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:15.1.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha. For it is impossible that they should teach the path to that which they neither know nor see.

dn13:15.2.verse: Suppose there was a queue of blind men, each holding the one in front: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

dn13:15.3.verse: In the same way, it seems to me that the brahmins’ statement turns out to be comparable to a queue of blind men: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

dn13:15.4.verse: Their statement turns out to be a joke—mere words, vacuous and hollow.

dn13:16.2.verse: Do the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas see the sun and moon just as other folk do? And do they supplicate and entreat them, following their course from where they rise to where they set with cupped palms held in worship?”

dn13:17.2.verse: Though this is so, are the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas able to teach the path to the company of the sun and moon, saying:

dn13:17.3.verse: ‘This is the only straight path, the direct route that delivers one who applies it to the company of the sun and moon’?”

dn13:18.1.verse: “So it seems that even though the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas see the sun and moon, they are not able to teach the path to the company of the sun and moon.

dn13:18.3.verse: But it seems that even though they have not seen the Divinity with their own eyes,

dn13:18.10.verse: to teach the path to the company of that which they neither know nor see.

dn13:18.12.verse: This being so, doesn’t their statement turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:18.14.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha. For it is impossible that they should teach the path to that which they neither know nor see.

dn13:19.0.verse: 2.1. The Simile of the Finest Lady in the Land

dn13:19.1.verse: Suppose a man were to say,

dn13:19.2.verse: ‘Whoever the finest lady in the land is, it is her that I want, her that I desire!’

dn13:19.4.verse: ‘My man, that finest lady in the land who you desire—do you know whether

dn13:19.5.verse: she’s an aristocrat, a brahmin, a peasant, or a menial?’

dn13:19.8.verse: ‘My friend, that finest lady in the land who you desire—do you know her name or clan? Whether she’s tall or short or medium? Whether her skin is black, brown, or dingy? Whether she comes from such-and-such village, town, or city?’

dn13:19.11.verse: ‘My man, do you desire someone who you’ve never even known or seen?’

dn13:19.14.verse: This being so, doesn’t that man’s statement turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:20.7.verse: doesn’t the statement of those brahmins turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:20.9.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha. For it is impossible that they should teach the path to that which they neither know nor see.

dn13:21.1.verse: Suppose a man was to build a ladder at the crossroads for climbing up to a stilt longhouse.

dn13:21.3.verse: ‘My man, that stilt longhouse for which you’re building a ladder—do you know whether it’s to the north, south, east, or west? Or whether it’s tall or short or medium?’

dn13:22.2.verse: ‘My man, are you building a ladder for a longhouse that you’ve never even known or seen?’

dn13:22.5.verse: This being so, doesn’t that man’s statement turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:22.12.verse: doesn’t the statement of those brahmins turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

dn13:23.1.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha. For it is impossible that they should teach the path to that which they neither know nor see.

dn13:24.0.verse: 2.3. The Simile of the Aciravatī River

dn13:24.1.verse: Suppose the Aciravatī River was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

dn13:24.2.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to cross over to the far shore.

dn13:24.3.verse: Standing on the near shore, they’d call out to the far shore,

dn13:24.4.verse: ‘Come here, far shore! Come here, far shore!’

dn13:24.6.verse: Would the far shore of the Aciravatī River come over to the near shore because of that man’s call, request, desire, or expectation?”

dn13:25.1.verse: “In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas proceed having given up those things that make one a true brahmin, and having undertaken those things that make one not a true brahmin. Yet they say:

dn13:25.2.verse: ‘We call upon Indra! We call upon Soma! We call upon Varuṇa! We call upon Īsāna! We call upon the Progenitor! We call upon the Divinity! We call upon Mahiddhi! We call upon Yama!’

dn13:25.3.verse: So long as they proceed in this way it’s impossible that they will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity.

dn13:26.1.verse: Suppose the Aciravatī River was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

dn13:26.2.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to cross over to the far shore.

dn13:26.3.verse: But while still on the near shore, their arms are tied tightly behind their back with a strong chain.

dn13:26.5.verse: Could that person cross over to the far shore?”

dn13:27.1.verse: “In the same way, the five kinds of sensual stimulation are called ‘chains’ and ‘fetters’ in the training of the Noble One.

dn13:27.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

dn13:27.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

dn13:27.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation that are called ‘chains’ and ‘fetters’ in the training of the Noble One.

dn13:27.9.verse: The brahmins proficient in the three Vedas enjoy these five kinds of sensual stimulation tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

dn13:28.1.verse: So long as they enjoy them it’s impossible that they will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity.

dn13:29.1.verse: Suppose the Aciravatī River was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

dn13:29.2.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to cross over to the far shore.

dn13:29.3.verse: But they’d lie down wrapped in cloth from head to foot.

dn13:29.5.verse: Could that person cross over to the far shore?”

dn13:30.1.verse: “In the same way, the five hindrances are called ‘obstacles’ and ‘hindrances’ and ‘encasings’ and ‘shrouds’ in the training of the Noble One.

dn13:30.3.verse: The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

dn13:30.4.verse: These five hindrances are called ‘obstacles’ and ‘hindrances’ and ‘encasings’ and ‘shrouds’ in the training of the Noble One.

dn13:30.5.verse: The brahmins proficient in the three Vedas are obstructed, hindered, swathed, and enveloped by these five hindrances.

dn13:30.6.verse: So long as they are so obstructed it’s impossible that they will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity.

dn13:31.2.verse: Have you heard that the brahmins who are elderly and senior, the tutors of tutors, say whether the Divinity is encumbered with possessions or not?”

dn13:31.4.verse: “Is his heart full of enmity or not?”

dn13:31.6.verse: “Is his heart full of ill will or not?”

dn13:32.2.verse: Are the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas encumbered with possessions or not?”

dn13:32.4.verse: “Are their hearts full of enmity or not?”

dn13:32.6.verse: “Are their hearts full of ill will or not?”

dn13:33.1.verse: “So it seems that the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas are encumbered with possessions, but the Divinity is not.

dn13:33.2.verse: But would brahmins who are encumbered with possessions join together and converge with the Divinity, who isn’t encumbered with possessions?”

dn13:34.1.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha! It’s impossible that the brahmins who are encumbered with possessions will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity, who isn’t encumbered with possessions.

dn13:35.1.verse: And it seems that the brahmins have enmity,

dn13:35.4.verse: and do not wield power, while the Divinity has no enmity, ill will, or corruption, and who does wield power. But would brahmins who are opposite to the Divinity in all these things join together and converge with him?”

dn13:36.1.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha! It’s impossible that brahmins who are opposite to the Divinity in all these things will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity.

dn13:36.2.verse: Now in this regard, Vāseṭṭha, those brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, having dived in, sink down. Having sunk down, they undergo drowning, imagining they are crossing to the dry shore.

dn13:36.3.verse: That’s why the three Vedas of the brahmins are called a ‘salted land’ and a ‘barren land’ and a ‘disaster’.”

dn13:37.1.verse: When he said this, Vāseṭṭha said to the Buddha,

dn13:37.2.verse: “I have heard, worthy Gotama, that you know the path to company with Divinity.”

dn13:37.4.verse: Is the village of Manasākaṭa nearby?”

dn13:37.7.verse: Suppose a person was born and raised in Manasākaṭa.

dn13:37.8.verse: And as soon as they left the town some people asked them for the road to Manasākaṭa.

dn13:37.9.verse: Would they be slow or hesitant to answer?”

dn13:37.12.verse: Because they were born and raised in Manasākaṭa. They’re well acquainted with all the roads to the village.”

dn13:38.1.verse: “Still, it’s possible they might be slow or hesitant to answer. But the Realized One is never slow or hesitant when questioned about the realm of divinity or the practice that leads to the realm of divinity.

dn13:38.2.verse: I understand the Divinity, the realm of divinity, and the practice that leads to the realm of divinity, practicing in accordance with which one is reborn in the realm of divinity.”

dn13:39.1.verse: When he said this, Vāseṭṭha said to the Buddha,

dn13:39.2.verse: “I have heard, worthy Gotama, that you teach the path to company with Divinity.

dn13:39.3.verse: Please teach us that path and elevate this generation of brahmins.”

dn13:39.4.verse: “Well then, Vāseṭṭha, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

dn13:40-75.0.verse: 4. Teaching the Path to the Divinity

dn13:40-75.2.verse: “It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha …

dn13:40-75.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is accomplished in ethics. …

dn13:40-75.4.verse: Seeing that the hindrances have been given up in them, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed.

dn13:76.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn13:77.1.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

dn13:77.2.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by love has been developed like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

dn13:77.3.verse: This is a path to company with Divinity.

dn13:78.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of compassion …

dn13:78.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

dn13:78.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn13:79.1.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

dn13:79.2.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by equanimity has been developed and cultivated like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

dn13:79.3.verse: This too is a path to company with Divinity.

dn13:80.2.verse: When a mendicant meditates like this, are they encumbered with possessions or not?”

dn13:80.4.verse: “Is their heart full of enmity or not?”

dn13:80.6.verse: “Is their heart full of ill will or not?”

dn13:81.1.verse: “So it seems that that mendicant is not encumbered with possessions, and neither is the Divinity.

dn13:81.2.verse: Would a mendicant who is not encumbered with possessions join together and converge with the Divinity, who isn’t encumbered with possessions?”

dn13:81.4.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha! It’s quite possible that a mendicant who is not encumbered with possessions will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity, who isn’t encumbered with possessions.

dn13:81.5.verse: And it seems that that mendicant has no enmity,

dn13:81.8.verse: and does wield power, while the Divinity is the same in all these things. Would a mendicant who is the same as the Divinity in all things join together and converge with him?”

dn13:81.10.verse: “Good, Vāseṭṭha! It’s quite possible that that mendicant will, when the body breaks up, after death, be reborn in the company of Divinity.”

dn13:82.1.verse: When he had spoken, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to him,

dn13:82.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn13:82.4.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

dn13:82.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

dn14:0.2.verse: The Great Discourse on Traces Left Behind

dn14:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, in the hut by the kareri tree.

dn14:1.1.3.verse: Then after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the pavilion by the kareri tree and this Dhamma talk on the subject of past lives came up among them,

dn14:1.1.4.verse: “So it was in a past life; such it was in a past life.”

dn14:1.2.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard that discussion among the mendicants.

dn14:1.2.2.verse: So he got up from his seat and went to the pavilion, where he sat on the seat spread out and addressed the mendicants:

dn14:1.2.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

dn14:1.2.4.verse: The mendicants told him what had happened, adding,

dn14:1.2.7.verse: “This is the conversation that was unfinished when the Buddha arrived.”

dn14:1.3.1.verse: “Would you like to hear a Dhamma talk on the subject of past lives?”

dn14:1.3.2.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

dn14:1.3.3.verse: Let the Buddha give a Dhamma talk on the subject of past lives. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

dn14:1.3.4.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

dn14:1.4.1.verse: “Ninety-one eons ago, the Buddha Vipassī arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.4.2.verse: Thirty-one eons ago, the Buddha Sikhī arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.4.3.verse: In the same thirty-first eon, the Buddha Vessabhū arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.4.4.verse: In the present fortunate eon, the Buddhas Kakusandha,

dn14:1.4.6.verse: and Kassapa arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.4.7.verse: And in the present fortunate eon, I have arisen in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.5.3.verse: and Vessabhū were born as aristocrats into aristocrat families.

dn14:1.5.6.verse: and Kassapa were born as brahmins into brahmin families.

dn14:1.5.7.verse: I was born as an aristocrat into an aristocrat family.

dn14:1.6.1.verse: Koṇḍañña was the clan of Vipassī,

dn14:1.6.4.verse: Kassapa was the clan of Kakusandha,

dn14:1.7.1.verse: For Vipassī, the lifespan was 80,000 years.

dn14:1.7.2.verse: For Sikhī, the lifespan was 70,000 years.

dn14:1.7.3.verse: For Vessabhū, the lifespan was 60,000 years.

dn14:1.7.4.verse: For Kakusandha, the lifespan was 40,000 years.

dn14:1.7.5.verse: For Koṇāgamana, the lifespan was 30,000 years.

dn14:1.7.6.verse: For Kassapa, the lifespan was 20,000 years.

dn14:1.7.7.verse: For me at this time the lifespan is short, brief, and fleeting. A long life is a hundred years or a little more.

dn14:1.8.1.verse: Vipassī was awakened at the root of a patala tree.

dn14:1.8.2.verse: Sikhī was awakened at the root of a white-mango tree.

dn14:1.8.3.verse: Vessabhū was awakened at the root of a sal tree.

dn14:1.8.4.verse: Kakusandha was awakened at the root of a lebbeck tree.

dn14:1.8.5.verse: Koṇāgamana was awakened at the root of a cluster fig tree.

dn14:1.8.6.verse: Kassapa was awakened at the root of a banyan tree.

dn14:1.8.7.verse: I was awakened at the root of a peepal tree.

dn14:1.9.1.verse: Vipassī had a fine pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa.

dn14:1.9.2.verse: Sikhī had a fine pair of chief disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava.

dn14:1.9.3.verse: Vessabhū had a fine pair of chief disciples named Soṇa and Uttara.

dn14:1.9.4.verse: Kakusandha had a fine pair of chief disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva.

dn14:1.9.5.verse: Koṇāgamana had a fine pair of chief disciples named Bhiyyosa and Uttara.

dn14:1.9.6.verse: Kassapa had a fine pair of chief disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.

dn14:1.9.7.verse: I have a fine pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

dn14:1.10.1.verse: Vipassī had three gatherings of disciples—one of 6,800,000, one of 100,000, and one of 80,000—all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.2.verse: Sikhī had three gatherings of disciples—one of 100,000, one of 80,000, and one of 70,000—all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.3.verse: Vessabhū had three gatherings of disciples—one of 80,000, one of 70,000, and one of 60,000—all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.4.verse: Kakusandha had one gathering of disciples—40,000 mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.5.verse: Koṇāgamana had one gathering of disciples—30,000 mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.6.verse: Kassapa had one gathering of disciples—20,000 mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.10.7.verse: I have had one gathering of disciples—1,250 mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.11.1.verse: Vipassī had as chief attendant a mendicant named Asoka.

dn14:1.11.2.verse: Sikhī had as chief attendant a mendicant named Khemaṅkara.

dn14:1.11.3.verse: Vessabhū had as chief attendant a mendicant named Upasanta.

dn14:1.11.4.verse: Kakusandha had as chief attendant a mendicant named Buddhija.

dn14:1.11.5.verse: Koṇāgamana had as chief attendant a mendicant named Sotthija.

dn14:1.11.6.verse: Kassapa had as chief attendant a mendicant named Sabbamitta.

dn14:1.11.7.verse: I have as chief attendant a mendicant named Ānanda.

dn14:1.12.2.verse: his birth mother was Queen Bandhumatī,

dn14:1.12.3.verse: and their capital city was named Bandhumatī.

dn14:1.12.5.verse: his birth mother was Queen Pabhāvatī,

dn14:1.12.6.verse: and their capital city was named Aruṇavatī.

dn14:1.12.8.verse: his birth mother was Queen Vassavatī,

dn14:1.12.9.verse: and their capital city was named Anoma.

dn14:1.12.10.verse: Kakusandha’s father was the brahmin Aggidatta,

dn14:1.12.11.verse: and his birth mother was the brahmin lady Visākhā.

dn14:1.12.12.verse: At that time the king was Khema,

dn14:1.12.13.verse: whose capital city was named Khemavatī.

dn14:1.12.14.verse: Koṇāgamana’s father was the brahmin Yaññadatta,

dn14:1.12.15.verse: and his birth mother was the brahmin lady Uttarā.

dn14:1.12.16.verse: At that time the king was Sobha,

dn14:1.12.17.verse: whose capital city was named Sobhavatī.

dn14:1.12.18.verse: Kassapa’s father was the brahmin Brahmadatta,

dn14:1.12.19.verse: and his birth mother was the brahmin lady Dhanavatī.

dn14:1.12.20.verse: At that time the king was Kikī,

dn14:1.12.21.verse: whose capital city was named Varanasi.

dn14:1.12.22.verse: In this life, my father was King Suddhodana,

dn14:1.12.23.verse: my birth mother was Queen Māyā,

dn14:1.12.24.verse: and our capital city was Kapilavatthu.”

dn14:1.12.25.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn14:1.12.26.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

dn14:1.13.1.verse: Soon after the Buddha left, those mendicants discussed among themselves:

dn14:1.13.2.verse: “It’s incredible, reverends, it’s amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

dn14:1.13.3.verse: For he is able to recollect the birth, names, clans, lifespan, chief disciples, and gatherings of disciples of the Buddhas of the past who have become fully quenched, cut off proliferation, cut off the course, finished off the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering:

dn14:1.13.4.verse: ‘Such is the birth, names, clans, conduct, teachings, wisdom, meditation, and freedom of those Blessed Ones.’

dn14:1.13.5.verse: Is it because the Realized One has clearly penetrated the principle of the teachings that he can recollect all these things?

dn14:1.13.7.verse: But this conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

dn14:1.14.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the pavilion by the kareri tree, where he sat down on the seat spread out

dn14:1.14.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

dn14:1.14.4.verse: The mendicants told him what had happened, adding,

dn14:1.14.13.verse: “This was our conversation that was unfinished when the Buddha arrived.”

dn14:1.15.1.verse: “It is because the Realized One has clearly penetrated the principle of the teachings that he can recollect all these things.

dn14:1.15.3.verse: And the deities also told me.

dn14:1.15.5.verse: Would you like to hear a further Dhamma talk on the subject of past lives?”

dn14:1.15.6.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

dn14:1.15.7.verse: Let the Buddha give a further Dhamma talk on the subject of past lives. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

dn14:1.15.8.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

dn14:1.16.1.verse: “Ninety-one eons ago, the Buddha Vipassī arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:1.16.2.verse: He was born as an aristocrat into an aristocrat family.

dn14:1.16.5.verse: He was awakened at the root of a patala tree.

dn14:1.16.6.verse: He had a fine pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa.

dn14:1.16.7.verse: He had three gatherings of disciples—

dn14:1.16.8.verse: one of 6,800,000, one of 100,000, and one of 80,000—

dn14:1.16.9.verse: all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:1.16.10.verse: He had as chief attendant a mendicant named Asoka.

dn14:1.16.12.verse: his birth mother was Queen Bandhumatī,

dn14:1.16.13.verse: and their capital city was named Bandhumatī.

dn14:1.17.0.verse: 2. What’s Normal For One Intent on Awakening

dn14:1.17.1.verse: When Vipassī, the being intent on awakening, passed away from the host of joyful gods, he was conceived in his mother’s womb, mindful and aware.

dn14:1.17.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.17.3.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening passes away from the host of joyful gods, he is conceived in his mother’s womb.

dn14:1.17.4.verse: And then—in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.17.5.verse: Even in the boundless gloom of interstellar space—so utterly dark that even the luminosity of the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful, makes no impression—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.17.6.verse: And the sentient beings reborn there recognize each other by that light: ‘So, it seems other sentient beings have been reborn here!’

dn14:1.17.7.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shakes and rocks and trembles. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.17.8.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.17.9.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, four godlings approach to guard the four quarters, so that no human or non-human or anyone at all shall harm the being intent on awakening or his mother.

dn14:1.17.10.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.18.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she becomes naturally ethical. She refrains from killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants.

dn14:1.18.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.19.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she no longer thinks of men in a sexual way, and she cannot be violated by a man of lustful intent.

dn14:1.19.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.20.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she obtains the five kinds of sensual stimulation and amuses herself, supplied and provided with them.

dn14:1.20.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.21.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, no afflictions beset her. She’s happy and free of bodily fatigue. And she sees the being intent on awakening in her womb, whole in his major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.

dn14:1.21.2.verse: Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities. And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.

dn14:1.21.3.verse: And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it: ‘This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities. And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.’

dn14:1.21.4.verse: In the same way, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, no afflictions beset her. She’s happy and free of bodily fatigue. And she sees the being intent on awakening in her womb, whole in his major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.

dn14:1.21.5.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.22.1.verse: It’s normal that, seven days after the being intent on awakening is born, his mother passes away and is reborn in the host of joyful gods.

dn14:1.22.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.23.1.verse: It’s normal that, while other women carry the infant in the womb for nine or ten months before giving birth, not so the mother of the being intent on awakening. She gives birth after exactly ten months.

dn14:1.23.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.24.1.verse: It’s normal that, while other women give birth while sitting or lying down, not so the mother of the being intent on awakening. She only gives birth standing up.

dn14:1.24.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.25.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, gods receive him first, then humans.

dn14:1.25.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.26.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, before he reaches the ground, four godlings receive him and place him before his mother, saying: ‘Rejoice, O Queen! An illustrious son is born to you.’

dn14:1.26.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.27.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges already clean, unsoiled by waters, mucus, blood, or any other kind of impurity, pure and clean.

dn14:1.27.2.verse: Suppose a jewel-treasure was placed on a cloth from Kāsi. The jewel would not soil the cloth, nor would the cloth soil the jewel.

dn14:1.27.4.verse: Because of the cleanliness of them both.

dn14:1.27.5.verse: In the same way, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges already clean, unsoiled by waters, mucus, blood, or any other kind of impurity, pure and clean.

dn14:1.27.6.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.28.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, two showers of water appear from the sky, one cool, one warm, for bathing the being intent on awakening and his mother.

dn14:1.28.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.29.1.verse: It’s normal that, as soon as he’s born, the being intent on awakening stands firm with his own feet on the ground. Facing north, he takes seven strides with a white parasol held above him, surveys all quarters, and makes this dramatic proclamation: ‘I am the foremost in the world! I am the eldest in the world! I am the first in the world! This is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’

dn14:1.29.2.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.30.1.verse: It’s normal that, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, then—in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.30.2.verse: Even in the boundless gloom of interstellar space—so utterly dark that even the luminosity of the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful, makes no impression—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.30.3.verse: And the sentient beings reborn there recognize each other by that light: ‘So, it seems other sentient beings have been reborn here!’

dn14:1.30.4.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shakes and rocks and trembles. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn14:1.30.5.verse: This is normal in such a case.

dn14:1.31.0.verse: 3. The Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

dn14:1.31.1.verse: When Prince Vipassī was born, they announced it to King Bandhumā,

dn14:1.31.2.verse: ‘Your Majesty, your son is born! Let Your Majesty examine him!’

dn14:1.31.3.verse: When the king had examined the prince, he had the brahmin soothsayers summoned and said to them,

dn14:1.31.5.verse: When they had examined him they said to the king,

dn14:1.31.6.verse: ‘Rejoice, O King! An illustrious son is born to you. You are fortunate, so very fortunate, to have a son such as this born in this family!

dn14:1.31.7.verse: For the prince possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man. A great man who possesses these has only two possible destinies, no other.

dn14:1.31.8.verse: If he stays at home he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king. His dominion extends to all four sides, he achieves stability in the country, and he possesses the seven treasures.

dn14:1.31.9.verse: He has the following seven treasures:

dn14:1.31.10.verse: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure.

dn14:1.31.11.verse: He has over a thousand sons who are valiant and heroic, crushing the armies of his enemies.

dn14:1.31.12.verse: After conquering this land girt by sea, he reigns by principle, without rod or sword.

dn14:1.31.13.verse: But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, who has cast off the veil from the world.

dn14:1.32.1.verse: And what are the marks which he possesses?

dn14:1.32.8.verse: On the soles of his feet there are thousand-spoked wheels, with rims and hubs, complete in every detail.

dn14:1.32.11.verse: His hands and feet are soft and tender.

dn14:1.32.12.verse: He has serried hands and feet.

dn14:1.32.13.verse: The tops of his feet are arched.

dn14:1.32.14.verse: His calves are like those of an antelope.

dn14:1.32.15.verse: When standing upright and not bending over, the palms of both hands touch the knees.

dn14:1.32.16.verse: His private parts are sheathed in a foreskin.

dn14:1.32.17.verse: He is golden colored; his skin shines like lustrous gold.

dn14:1.32.18.verse: He has delicate skin, so delicate that dust and dirt don’t stick to his body.

dn14:1.32.19.verse: His hairs grow one per pore.

dn14:1.32.20.verse: His hairs stand up; they’re blue-black and curl clockwise.

dn14:1.32.21.verse: His body is tall and straight-limbed.

dn14:1.32.22.verse: He has bulging muscles in seven places.

dn14:1.32.23.verse: His chest is like that of a lion.

dn14:1.32.24.verse: He is filled out between the shoulders.

dn14:1.32.25.verse: He has the proportional circumference of a banyan tree: the span of his arms equals the height of his body.

dn14:1.32.28.verse: His jaw is like that of a lion.

dn14:1.32.34.verse: He has the voice of the Divinity, like a cuckoo’s call.

dn14:1.32.36.verse: He has eyelashes like a cow’s.

dn14:1.32.37.verse: Between his eyebrows there grows a tuft, soft and white like cotton-wool.

dn14:1.32.38.verse: The crown of his head is like a turban.

dn14:1.33.1.verse: These are the thirty-two marks of a great man that the prince has. A great man who possesses these has only two possible destinies, no other.

dn14:1.33.2.verse: If he stays at home he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch.

dn14:1.33.7.verse: But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, who has cast off the veil from the world.’

dn14:1.33.8.0.verse: 4. How He Came to be Known as Vipassī

dn14:1.33.9.verse: Then King Bandhumā had the brahmin soothsayers dressed in unworn clothes and satisfied all their needs.

dn14:1.34.1.verse: Then the king appointed nursemaids for Prince Vipassī.

dn14:1.34.2.verse: Some suckled him, some bathed him, some held him, and some carried him on their hip.

dn14:1.34.3.verse: From when he was born, a white parasol was held over him night and day, with the thought,

dn14:1.34.4.verse: ‘Don’t let cold, heat, grass, dust, or damp bother him.’

dn14:1.34.5.verse: He was dear and beloved by many people,

dn14:1.34.6.verse: like a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus.

dn14:1.34.8.verse: He was always passed from hip to hip.

dn14:1.35.1.verse: From when he was born, his voice was charming, graceful, sweet, and endearing.

dn14:1.35.2.verse: It was as sweet as the song of a cuckoo-bird found in the Himalayas.

dn14:1.36.1.verse: From when he was born, Prince Vipassī had the power of clairvoyance which manifested as a result of past deeds, by which he could see for a league all around both by day and by night.

dn14:1.37.1.verse: And he was unblinkingly watchful, like the gods of the thirty-three.

dn14:1.37.2.verse: And because it was said that he was unblinkingly watchful, he came to be known as ‘Vipassī’.

dn14:1.37.3.verse: Then while King Bandhumā was sitting in court, he’d sit Prince Vipassī in his lap and explain the case to him.

dn14:1.37.4.verse: And sitting there in his father’s lap, Vipassī would thoroughly consider the case and draw a conclusion using a logical system.

dn14:1.37.5.verse: So this was all the more reason for him to be known as ‘Vipassī’.

dn14:1.38.1.verse: Then King Bandhumā had three stilt longhouses built for him—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season,

dn14:1.38.2.verse: and provided him with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

dn14:1.38.3.verse: Prince Vipassī stayed in a stilt longhouse without coming downstairs for the four months of the rainy season, where he was entertained by musicians—none of them men.

dn14:2.1.1.verse: Then, after many years, many hundred years, many thousand years had passed, Prince Vipassī addressed his charioteer,

dn14:2.1.2.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, harness the finest chariots. We will go to a park and see the scenery.’

dn14:2.1.3.verse: ‘Yes, sir,’ replied the charioteer. He harnessed the chariots and informed the prince,

dn14:2.1.4.verse: ‘Your Majesty, the finest chariots are harnessed.

dn14:2.1.6.verse: Then Prince Vipassī mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out for the park.

dn14:2.2.1.verse: Along the way he saw an elderly man, bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as he walked, ailing, past his prime.

dn14:2.2.3.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, what has that man done?

dn14:2.2.4.verse: For his hair and his body are unlike those of other men.’

dn14:2.2.5.verse: ‘That, Your Majesty, is called an old man.’

dn14:2.2.6.verse: ‘But why is he called an old man?’

dn14:2.2.7.verse: ‘He’s called an old man because now he has not long to live.’

dn14:2.2.8.verse: ‘But my dear charioteer, am I liable to grow old? Am I not exempt from old age?’

dn14:2.2.9.verse: ‘Everyone is liable to grow old, Your Majesty, including you. No one is exempt from old age.’

dn14:2.2.10.verse: ‘Well then, my dear charioteer, that’s enough of the park for today. Let’s return to the royal compound.’

dn14:2.2.11.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer and did so.

dn14:2.2.12.verse: Back at the royal compound, the prince brooded, miserable and sad:

dn14:2.2.13.verse: ‘Curse this thing called rebirth, since old age will come to anyone who’s born.’

dn14:2.3.1.verse: Then King Bandhumā summoned the charioteer and said,

dn14:2.3.2.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, I hope the prince enjoyed himself at the park? I hope he was happy there?’

dn14:2.3.3.verse: ‘No, Your Majesty, the prince didn’t enjoy himself at the park.’

dn14:2.3.4.verse: ‘But what did he see on the way to the park?’

dn14:2.3.5.verse: And the charioteer told the king about seeing the old man and the prince’s reaction.

dn14:2.4.2.verse: ‘Prince Vipassī must not renounce the throne. He must not go forth from the lay life to homelessness. And the words of the brahmin soothsayers must not come true.’

dn14:2.4.3.verse: To this end he provided the prince with even more of the five kinds of sensual stimulation,

dn14:2.4.5.verse: with which the prince amused himself.

dn14:2.5.1.verse: Then, after many thousand years had passed, Prince Vipassī had his charioteer drive him to the park once more.

dn14:2.6.1.verse: Along the way he saw a man who was sick, suffering, gravely ill, collapsed in his own urine and feces, being picked up by some and put down by others.

dn14:2.6.3.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, what has that man done?

dn14:2.6.4.verse: For his eyes and his voice are unlike those of other men.’

dn14:2.6.5.verse: ‘That, Your Majesty, is called a sick man.’

dn14:2.6.6.verse: ‘But why is he called a sick man?’

dn14:2.6.7.verse: ‘He’s called a sick man; hopefully he will recover from that illness.’

dn14:2.6.8.verse: ‘But my dear charioteer, am I liable to fall sick? Am I not exempt from sickness?’

dn14:2.6.9.verse: ‘Everyone is liable to fall sick, Your Majesty, including you. No one is exempt from sickness.’

dn14:2.6.10.verse: ‘Well then, my dear charioteer, that’s enough of the park for today. Let’s return to the royal compound.’

dn14:2.6.11.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer and did so.

dn14:2.6.12.verse: Back at the royal compound, the prince brooded, miserable and sad:

dn14:2.6.13.verse: ‘Curse this thing called rebirth, since old age and sickness will come to anyone who’s born.’

dn14:2.7.1.verse: Then King Bandhumā summoned the charioteer and said,

dn14:2.7.2.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, I hope the prince enjoyed himself at the park? I hope he was happy there?’

dn14:2.7.3.verse: ‘No, Your Majesty, the prince didn’t enjoy himself at the park.’

dn14:2.7.4.verse: ‘But what did he see on the way to the park?’

dn14:2.7.5.verse: And the charioteer told the king about seeing the sick man and the prince’s reaction.

dn14:2.8.2.verse: ‘Prince Vipassī must not renounce the throne. He must not go forth from the lay life to homelessness. And the words of the brahmin soothsayers must not come true.’

dn14:2.8.3.verse: To this end he provided the prince with even more of the five kinds of sensual stimulation,

dn14:2.9.1.verse: with which the prince amused himself.

dn14:2.9.2.verse: Then, after many thousand years had passed, Prince Vipassī had his charioteer drive him to the park once more.

dn14:2.10.1.verse: Along the way he saw a large crowd gathered making a bier out of garments of different colors.

dn14:2.10.3.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, why is that crowd making a bier?’

dn14:2.10.4.verse: ‘That, Your Majesty, is for someone who’s departed.’

dn14:2.10.5.verse: ‘Well then, drive the chariot up to the departed.’

dn14:2.10.6.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer, and did so.

dn14:2.10.7.verse: When the prince saw the corpse of the departed, he addressed the charioteer,

dn14:2.10.9.verse: ‘He’s called departed because now his mother and father, his relatives and kin shall see him no more, and he shall never again see them.’

dn14:2.10.10.verse: ‘But my dear charioteer, am I liable to die? Am I not exempt from death?

dn14:2.10.11.verse: Will the king and queen and my other relatives and kin see me no more?

dn14:2.10.12.verse: And shall I never again see them?’

dn14:2.10.13.verse: ‘Everyone is liable to die, Your Majesty, including you. No one is exempt from death.

dn14:2.10.14.verse: The king and queen and your other relatives and kin shall see you no more,

dn14:2.10.15.verse: and you shall never again see them.’

dn14:2.10.16.verse: ‘Well then, my dear charioteer, that’s enough of the park for today. Let’s return to the royal compound.’

dn14:2.10.17.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer and did so.

dn14:2.10.18.verse: Back at the royal compound, the prince brooded, miserable and sad:

dn14:2.10.19.verse: ‘Curse this thing called rebirth, since old age, sickness, and death will come to anyone who’s born.’

dn14:2.11.1.verse: Then King Bandhumā summoned the charioteer and said,

dn14:2.11.2.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, I hope the prince enjoyed himself at the park? I hope he was happy there?’

dn14:2.11.3.verse: ‘No, Your Majesty, the prince didn’t enjoy himself at the park.’

dn14:2.11.4.verse: ‘But what did he see on the way to the park?’

dn14:2.11.5.verse: And the charioteer told the king about seeing the dead man and the prince’s reaction.

dn14:2.12.2.verse: ‘Prince Vipassī must not renounce the throne. He must not go forth from the lay life to homelessness. And the words of the brahmin soothsayers must not come true.’

dn14:2.12.3.verse: To this end he provided the prince with even more of the five kinds of sensual stimulation,

dn14:2.13.1.verse: with which the prince amused himself.

dn14:2.13.2.verse: Then, after many thousand years had passed, Prince Vipassī had his charioteer drive him to the park once more.

dn14:2.14.1.verse: Along the way he saw a man, a renunciate with shaven head, wearing an ocher robe.

dn14:2.14.3.verse: ‘My dear charioteer, what has that man done?

dn14:2.14.4.verse: For his head and his clothes are unlike those of other men.’

dn14:2.14.5.verse: ‘That, Your Majesty, is called a renunciate.’

dn14:2.14.6.verse: ‘But why is he called a renunciate?’

dn14:2.14.7.verse: ‘He is called a renunciate because he celebrates principled and fair conduct, skillful actions, good deeds, harmlessness, and sympathy for living creatures.’

dn14:2.14.8.verse: ‘Then I celebrate the one called a renunciate, who celebrates principled and fair conduct, skillful actions, good deeds, harmlessness, and sympathy for living creatures!

dn14:2.14.9.verse: Well then, drive the chariot up to that renunciate.’

dn14:2.14.10.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer, and did so.

dn14:2.14.11.verse: Then Prince Vipassī said to that renunciate,

dn14:2.14.13.verse: For your head and your clothes are unlike those of other men.’

dn14:2.14.14.verse: ‘Your Majesty, I am what is called a renunciate.’

dn14:2.14.15.verse: ‘But why are you called a renunciate?’

dn14:2.14.16.verse: ‘I am called a renunciate because I celebrate principled and fair conduct, skillful actions, good deeds, harmlessness, and sympathy for living creatures.’

dn14:2.14.17.verse: ‘Then I celebrate the one called a renunciate, who celebrates principled and fair conduct, skillful actions, good deeds, harmlessness, and sympathy for living creatures!’

dn14:2.15.1.verse: Then the prince addressed the charioteer,

dn14:2.15.2.verse: ‘Well then, my dear charioteer, take the chariot and return to the royal compound.

dn14:2.15.3.verse: I shall shave off my hair and beard right here, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

dn14:2.15.4.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the charioteer and did so.

dn14:2.15.5.verse: Then Prince Vipassī shaved off his hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn14:2.16.1.verse: A large crowd of 84,000 people in the capital of Bandhumatī heard

dn14:2.16.4.verse: ‘This must be no ordinary teaching and training, no ordinary going forth in which Prince Vipassī has gone forth.

dn14:2.16.5.verse: If even the prince goes forth, why don’t we do the same?’

dn14:2.16.6.verse: Then that great crowd of 84,000 people shaved off their hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and followed the one intent on awakening, Vipassī, by going forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn14:2.16.7.verse: Escorted by that assembly, Vipassī wandered on tour among the villages, towns, and capital cities.

dn14:2.17.1.verse: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

dn14:2.17.2.verse: ‘It’s not appropriate for me to live in a crowd. Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the group?’

dn14:2.17.3.verse: After some time he withdrew from the group to live alone. The 84,000 went one way, but Vipassī went another.

dn14:2.18.1.verse: Then as Vipassī, the one intent on awakening, was in private retreat in his dwelling, this thought came to his mind,

dn14:2.18.2.verse: ‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble. It’s born, grows old, dies, passes away, and is reborn, yet it doesn’t understand how to escape from this suffering, from old age and death.

dn14:2.18.3.verse: Oh, when will an escape be found from this suffering, from old age and death?’

dn14:2.18.5.verse: ‘When what exists is there old age and death? What is a requirement for old age and death?’

dn14:2.18.6.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.7.verse: ‘When rebirth exists there’s old age and death. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death.’

dn14:2.18.9.verse: ‘When what exists is there rebirth? What is a requirement for rebirth?’

dn14:2.18.10.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.11.verse: ‘When continued existence exists there’s rebirth. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.’

dn14:2.18.13.verse: ‘When what exists is there continued existence? What is a requirement for continued existence?’

dn14:2.18.14.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.15.verse: ‘When grasping exists there’s continued existence. Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.’

dn14:2.18.17.verse: ‘When what exists is there grasping? What is a requirement for grasping?’

dn14:2.18.18.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.19.verse: ‘When craving exists there’s grasping. Craving is a requirement for grasping.’

dn14:2.18.21.verse: ‘When what exists is there craving? What is a requirement for craving?’

dn14:2.18.22.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.23.verse: ‘When feeling exists there’s craving. Feeling is a requirement for craving.’

dn14:2.18.25.verse: ‘When what exists is there feeling? What is a requirement for feeling?’

dn14:2.18.26.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.27.verse: ‘When contact exists there’s feeling. Contact is a requirement for feeling.’

dn14:2.18.29.verse: ‘When what exists is there contact? What is a requirement for contact?’

dn14:2.18.30.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.31.verse: ‘When the six sense fields exist there’s contact. The six sense fields are requirements for contact.’

dn14:2.18.33.verse: ‘When what exists are there the six sense fields? What is a requirement for the six sense fields?’

dn14:2.18.34.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.35.verse: ‘When name and form exist there are the six sense fields. Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.’

dn14:2.18.37.verse: ‘When what exists are there name and form? What is a requirement for name and form?’

dn14:2.18.38.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.39.verse: ‘When consciousness exists there are name and form. Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.’

dn14:2.18.41.verse: ‘When what exists is there consciousness? What is a requirement for consciousness?’
