dn14:2.18.42.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.18.43.verse: ‘When name and form exist there’s consciousness. Name and form are requirements for consciousness.’

dn14:2.19.2.verse: ‘This consciousness turns back from name and form, and doesn’t go beyond that.’

dn14:2.19.3.verse: This is the extent to which one may be reborn, grow old, die, pass away, or reappear. That is:

dn14:2.19.4.verse: Name and form are requirements for consciousness. Consciousness is a requirement for name and form. Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields. The six sense fields are requirements for contact. Contact is a requirement for feeling. Feeling is a requirement for craving. Craving is a requirement for grasping. Grasping is a requirement for continued existence. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

dn14:2.19.5.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’

dn14:2.19.6.verse: ‘Origination, origination.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in Vipassī, the one intent on awakening, regarding teachings not learned before from another.

dn14:2.20.2.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no old age and death? When what ceases do old age and death cease?’

dn14:2.20.3.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.4.verse: ‘When rebirth doesn’t exist there’s no old age and death. When rebirth ceases, old age and death cease.’

dn14:2.20.6.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no rebirth? When what ceases does rebirth cease?’

dn14:2.20.7.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.8.verse: ‘When continued existence doesn’t exist there’s no rebirth. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.’

dn14:2.20.10.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no continued existence? When what ceases does continued existence cease?’

dn14:2.20.11.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.12.verse: ‘When grasping doesn’t exist there’s no continued existence. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.’

dn14:2.20.14.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no grasping? When what ceases does grasping cease?’

dn14:2.20.15.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.16.verse: ‘When craving doesn’t exist there’s no grasping. When craving ceases, grasping ceases.’

dn14:2.20.18.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no craving? When what ceases does craving cease?’

dn14:2.20.19.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.20.verse: ‘When feeling doesn’t exist there’s no craving. When feeling ceases, craving ceases.’

dn14:2.20.22.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no feeling? When what ceases does feeling cease?’

dn14:2.20.23.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.24.verse: ‘When contact doesn’t exist there’s no feeling. When contact ceases, feeling ceases.’

dn14:2.20.26.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no contact? When what ceases does contact cease?’

dn14:2.20.27.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.28.verse: ‘When the six sense fields don’t exist there’s no contact. When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.’

dn14:2.20.30.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist are there no six sense fields? When what ceases do the six sense fields cease?’

dn14:2.20.31.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.32.verse: ‘When name and form don’t exist there are no six sense fields. When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.’

dn14:2.20.34.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist are there no name and form? When what ceases do name and form cease?’

dn14:2.20.35.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.36.verse: ‘When consciousness doesn’t exist there are no name and form. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.’

dn14:2.20.38.verse: ‘When what doesn’t exist is there no consciousness? When what ceases does consciousness cease?’

dn14:2.20.39.verse: Then, through rational application of mind, Vipassī penetrated with wisdom,

dn14:2.20.40.verse: ‘When name and form don’t exist there’s no consciousness. When name and form cease, consciousness ceases.’

dn14:2.21.2.verse: ‘I have discovered the path to awakening. That is:

dn14:2.21.3.verse: When name and form cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease. When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases. When contact ceases, feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

dn14:2.21.4.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’

dn14:2.21.5.verse: ‘Cessation, cessation.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in Vipassī, the one intent on awakening, regarding teachings not learned before from another.

dn14:2.22.1.verse: After some time he meditated observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

dn14:2.22.2.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

dn14:2.22.3.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

dn14:2.22.4.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

dn14:2.22.5.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

dn14:2.22.6.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

dn14:2.22.7.verse: Meditating like this his mind was soon freed from defilements by not grasping.

dn14:3.1.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha,

dn14:3.1.4.verse: ‘This principle I have discovered is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

dn14:3.1.5.verse: But people like clinging, they love it and enjoy it.

dn14:3.1.6.verse: It’s hard for them to see this topic; that is, specific conditionality, dependent origination.

dn14:3.1.7.verse: It’s also hard for them to see this topic; that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

dn14:3.1.8.verse: And if I were to teach this principle, others might not understand me, which would be wearying and troublesome for me.’

dn14:3.2.1.verse: And then these verses, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to him:

dn14:3.2.3.verse: there’s no need to reveal it now!

dn14:3.2.4.verse: Those mired in greed and hate

dn14:3.2.6.verse: It goes against the stream, subtle,

dn14:3.2.8.verse: Those besotted by greed cannot see,

dn14:3.2.9.verse: for they’re cloaked in a mass of darkness.’

dn14:3.2.10.verse: So, as the Buddha Vipassī reflected like this, his mind inclined to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.

dn14:3.2.11.verse: Then, knowing the Buddha Vipassī’s train of thought, it occurred to a certain Great Divinity,

dn14:3.2.12.verse: ‘Oh lord! The world will be lost, the world will perish! For the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, inclines to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.’

dn14:3.2.13.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha Vipassī.

dn14:3.3.1.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha Vipassī, and said,

dn14:3.3.2.verse: ‘Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach the Dhamma!

dn14:3.3.3.verse: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching.

dn14:3.3.4.verse: There will be those who understand the teaching!’

dn14:3.4.1.verse: When he said this, the Buddha Vipassī said to him,

dn14:3.4.9.verse: “If I were to teach this principle, others might not understand me, which would be wearying and troublesome for me.”

dn14:3.4.19.verse: So, as I reflected like this, my mind inclined to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.’

dn14:3.5.2.verse: For a third time that Great Divinity begged the Buddha to teach.

dn14:3.6.1.verse: Then, understanding the Divinity’s invitation, the Buddha Vipassī surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, out of his compassion for sentient beings.

dn14:3.6.2.verse: And he saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes; with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach. And some of them lived seeing the danger in the fault to do with the next world, while others did not.

dn14:3.6.3.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. Some of them sprout and grow in the water reaching the water’s surface. And some of them sprout and grow in the water but rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to them.

dn14:3.6.4.verse: In the same way, the Buddha Vipassī saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes.

dn14:3.7.1.verse: Then that Great Divinity, knowing the Buddha Vipassī’s train of thought, addressed him in verse:

dn14:3.7.3.verse: you can see the people all around.

dn14:3.7.4.verse: In just the same way, All-seer, so intelligent,

dn14:3.7.5.verse: having ascended the Temple of Truth,

dn14:3.7.6.verse: rid of sorrow, look upon the people

dn14:3.7.7.verse: swamped with sorrow, overcome by rebirth and old age.

dn14:3.7.8.verse: Rise, hero! Victor in battle, caravan leader,

dn14:3.7.9.verse: wander the world free of debt.

dn14:3.7.10.verse: Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma!

dn14:3.7.11.verse: There will be those who understand!’

dn14:3.7.12.verse: Then the Buddha Vipassī addressed that Great Divinity in verse:

dn14:3.7.13.verse: ‘Flung open are the doors to freedom from death!

dn14:3.7.14.verse: Let those with ears to hear commit to faith.

dn14:3.7.15.verse: Thinking it would be troublesome, Divinity, I did not teach

dn14:3.7.16.verse: the sophisticated, sublime Dhamma among mankind.’

dn14:3.7.17.verse: Then the Great Divinity, knowing that his request for the Buddha Vipassī to teach the Dhamma had been granted, bowed and respectfully circled him, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

dn14:3.8.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha,

dn14:3.8.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

dn14:3.8.3.verse: Who will quickly understand this teaching?’

dn14:3.8.5.verse: ‘That Khaṇḍa, the king’s son, and Tissa, the high priest’s son, are astute, competent, intelligent, and have long had little dust in their eyes.

dn14:3.8.6.verse: Why don’t I teach them first of all? They will quickly understand this teaching.’

dn14:3.9.1.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the tree of awakening and reappeared near the capital city of Bandhumatī, in the deer park named Sanctuary.

dn14:3.9.2.verse: Then the Buddha Vipassī addressed the park keeper,

dn14:3.9.3.verse: ‘My dear park keeper, please enter the city and say this to the king’s son Khaṇḍa and the high priest’s son Tissa:

dn14:3.9.4.verse: “Sirs, the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, has arrived at Bandhumatī and is staying in the deer park named Sanctuary. He wishes to see you.”’

dn14:3.9.5.verse: ‘Yes, sir,’ replied the park keeper, and did as he was asked.

dn14:3.10.1.verse: Then the king’s son Khaṇḍa and the high priest’s son Tissa had the finest carriages harnessed. Then they mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out from Bandhumatī for the Sanctuary.

dn14:3.10.2.verse: They went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and approached the Buddha Vipassī on foot. They bowed and sat down to one side.

dn14:3.11.1.verse: The Buddha Vipassī taught them step by step, with

dn14:3.11.2.verse: a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

dn14:3.11.3.verse: And when he knew that their minds were ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

dn14:3.11.4.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

dn14:3.11.5.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

dn14:3.11.6.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in the king’s son Khaṇḍa and the high priest’s son Tissa:

dn14:3.11.7.verse: ‘Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.’

dn14:3.12.1.verse: They saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. They went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. They said to the Buddha Vipassī,

dn14:3.12.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn14:3.12.4.verse: We go for refuge to the Blessed One and to the teaching.

dn14:3.12.5.verse: Sir, may we receive the going forth and ordination in the Buddha’s presence?’

dn14:3.13.1.verse: And they received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha Vipassī’s presence.

dn14:3.13.2.verse: Then the Buddha Vipassī educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired them with a Dhamma talk.

dn14:3.13.3.verse: He revealed the drawbacks of conditioned phenomena, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of extinguishment.

dn14:3.13.4.verse: Being taught like this their minds were soon freed from defilements by not grasping.

dn14:3.14.0.verse: 14. The Going Forth of the Large Crowd

dn14:3.14.1.verse: A large crowd of 84,000 people in the capital of Bandhumatī heard

dn14:3.14.2.verse: that the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, had arrived at Bandhumatī and was staying in the deer park named Sanctuary.

dn14:3.14.3.verse: And they heard that the king’s son Khaṇḍa and the high priest’s son Tissa had shaved off their hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and gone forth from the lay life to homelessness in the Buddha’s presence.

dn14:3.14.5.verse: ‘This must be no ordinary teaching and training, no ordinary going forth in which the king’s son Khaṇḍa and the high priest’s son Tissa have gone forth.

dn14:3.14.6.verse: If even they go forth, why don’t we do the same?’

dn14:3.14.7.verse: Then those 84,000 people left Bandhumatī for the deer park named Sanctuary, where they approached the Buddha Vipassī, bowed and sat down to one side.

dn14:3.15.1.verse: The Buddha Vipassī taught them step by step, with

dn14:3.15.2.verse: a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

dn14:3.15.3.verse: And when he knew that their minds were ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

dn14:3.15.4.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

dn14:3.15.5.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

dn14:3.15.6.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in those 84,000 people:

dn14:3.15.7.verse: ‘Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.’

dn14:3.16.1.verse: They saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. They went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. They said to the Buddha Vipassī,

dn14:3.16.3.verse: And just like Khaṇḍa and Tissa they asked for and received ordination. Then the Buddha taught them further.

dn14:3.17.4.verse: Being taught like this their minds were soon freed from defilements by not grasping.

dn14:3.18.0.verse: 15. The 84,000 Who Had Gone Forth Previously

dn14:3.18.1.verse: The 84,000 people who had gone forth previously also heard:

dn14:3.18.2.verse: ‘It seems the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, has arrived at Bandhumatī and is staying in the deer park named Sanctuary. And he is teaching the Dhamma!’

dn14:3.18.3.verse: Then they too went to the Buddha Vipassī, realized the Dhamma, went forth, and became freed from defilements.

dn14:3.22.1.verse: Now at that time a large Saṅgha of 6,800,000 mendicants were residing at Bandhumatī.

dn14:3.22.2.verse: As the Buddha Vipassī was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

dn14:3.22.3.verse: ‘The Saṅgha residing at Bandhumatī now is large. What if I was to urge them:

dn14:3.22.4.verse: “Wander forth, mendicants, for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

dn14:3.22.5.verse: Let not two go by one road.

dn14:3.22.6.verse: Teach the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

dn14:3.22.7.verse: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching.

dn14:3.22.8.verse: There will be those who understand the teaching!

dn14:3.22.9.verse: But when six years have passed, you must all come to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.”’

dn14:3.23.1.verse: Then a certain Great Divinity, knowing the Buddha Vipassī’s train of thought, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha Vipassī.

dn14:3.23.2.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha Vipassī, and said,

dn14:3.23.3.verse: ‘That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

dn14:3.23.4.verse: The Saṅgha residing at Bandhumatī now is large. Please urge them to wander, as you thought.

dn14:3.23.9.verse: And sir, I’ll make sure that when six years have passed the mendicants will return to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’

dn14:3.23.10.verse: That is what that Great Divinity said.

dn14:3.23.11.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha Vipassī, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

dn14:3.24.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha Vipassī came out of retreat and addressed the mendicants, telling them all that had happened. Then he said,

dn14:3.26.1.verse: ‘Wander forth, mendicants, for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

dn14:3.26.2.verse: Let not two go by one road.

dn14:3.26.3.verse: Teach the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

dn14:3.26.4.verse: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching.

dn14:3.26.5.verse: There will be those who understand the teaching!

dn14:3.26.6.verse: But when six years have passed, you must all come to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’

dn14:3.26.7.verse: Then most of the mendicants left to wander the country that very day.

dn14:3.27.1.verse: Now at that time there were 84,000 monasteries in the Black Plum Tree Land.

dn14:3.27.2.verse: And when the first year came to an end the deities raised the cry:

dn14:3.27.3.verse: ‘Good fellows, the first year has ended.

dn14:3.27.5.verse: When five years have passed, you must all go to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’

dn14:3.27.9.verse: the fifth year came to an end, the deities raised the cry:

dn14:3.27.10.verse: ‘Good fellows, the fifth year has ended.

dn14:3.27.12.verse: When one year has passed, you must all go to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’

dn14:3.27.13.verse: And when the sixth year came to an end the deities raised the cry:

dn14:3.27.14.verse: ‘Good fellows, the sixth year has ended.

dn14:3.27.15.verse: Now is the time that you must go to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’

dn14:3.27.16.verse: Then that very day the mendicants went to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code. Some went by their own psychic power, and some by the psychic power of the deities.

dn14:3.28.1.verse: And there the Blessed One Vipassī, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, recited the monastic code thus:

dn14:3.28.3.verse: Extinguishment is the ultimate, say the Buddhas.

dn14:3.28.5.verse: nor does an ascetic hurt another.

dn14:3.28.9.verse: this is the instruction of the Buddhas.

dn14:3.28.10.verse: Not speaking ill nor doing harm;

dn14:3.28.15.verse: this is the instruction of the Buddhas.’

dn14:3.29.1.verse: This one time, mendicants, I was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Forest at the root of a magnificent sal tree.

dn14:3.29.2.verse: As I was in private retreat this thought came to mind,

dn14:3.29.3.verse: ‘It’s not easy to find an abode of sentient beings where I haven’t previously abided in all this long time, except the gods of the pure abodes.

dn14:3.29.4.verse: Why don’t I go to see them?’

dn14:3.29.5.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, I vanished from the Subhaga Forest and reappeared with the gods of Aviha.

dn14:3.29.6.verse: In that order of gods, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of deities approached me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me,

dn14:3.29.7.verse: ‘Ninety-one eons ago, good fellow, the Buddha Vipassī arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:3.29.8.verse: He was born as an aristocrat into an aristocrat family.

dn14:3.29.11.verse: He was awakened at the root of a patala tree.

dn14:3.29.12.verse: He had a fine pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa.

dn14:3.29.13.verse: He had three gatherings of disciples—one of 6,800,000, one of 100,000, and one of 80,000—all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:3.29.14.verse: He had as chief attendant a mendicant named Asoka.

dn14:3.29.16.verse: his birth mother was Queen Bandhumatī,

dn14:3.29.17.verse: and their capital city was named Bandhumatī.

dn14:3.29.18.verse: And such was his renunciation, such his going forth, such his striving, such his awakening, and such his rolling forth of the Wheel of Dhamma.

dn14:3.29.19.verse: And good fellow, after leading the spiritual life under that Buddha Vipassī we lost our desire for sensual pleasures and were reborn here.’

dn14:3.29.20.verse: And other deities came and similarly recounted the details of the Buddhas Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa.

dn14:3.30.1.verse: In that order of gods, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of deities approached me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me,

dn14:3.30.2.verse: ‘In the present fortunate eon, good fellow, you have arisen in the world, perfected and fully awakened.

dn14:3.30.3.verse: You were born as an aristocrat into an aristocrat family.

dn14:3.30.5.verse: For you the lifespan is short, brief, and fleeting. A long life is a hundred years or a little more.

dn14:3.30.6.verse: You were awakened at the root of a peepal tree.

dn14:3.30.7.verse: You have a fine pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

dn14:3.30.8.verse: You have had one gathering of disciples—1,250 mendicants who had ended their defilements.

dn14:3.30.9.verse: You have as chief attendant a mendicant named Ānanda.

dn14:3.30.11.verse: your birth mother was Queen Māyā,

dn14:3.30.12.verse: and your capital city was Kapilavatthu.

dn14:3.30.13.verse: And such was your renunciation, such your going forth, such your striving, such your awakening, and such your rolling forth of the Wheel of Dhamma.

dn14:3.30.14.verse: And good fellow, after leading the spiritual life under you we lost our desire for sensual pleasures and were reborn here.’

dn14:3.31.1.verse: Then together with the gods of Aviha I went to see the gods of Atappa …

dn14:3.31.3.verse: and the fair seeing gods. Then together with all these gods I went to see the gods of Akaniṭṭha, where we had a similar conversation.

dn14:3.33.1.verse: And that is how the Realized One is able to recollect the birth, names, clans, lifespan, chief disciples, and gatherings of disciples of the Buddhas of the past who have become fully quenched, cut off proliferation, cut off the course, finished off the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering. It is both because I have clearly penetrated the principle of the teachings,

dn14:3.33.3.verse: and also because the deities told me.”

dn14:3.33.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn14:3.33.6.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

dn15:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.

dn15:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn15:1.5.verse: in that this dependent origination is deep and appears deep, yet to me it seems as plain as can be.”

dn15:1.6.verse: “Don’t say that, Ānanda, don’t say that!

dn15:1.7.verse: This dependent origination is deep and appears deep.

dn15:1.8.verse: It is because of not understanding and not penetrating this teaching that this population has become tangled like string, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, and it doesn’t escape the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.

dn15:2.1.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for old age and death?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.2.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for old age and death?’ you should answer, ‘Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death.’

dn15:2.3.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for rebirth?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.4.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for rebirth?’ you should answer, ‘Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.’

dn15:2.5.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for continued existence?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.6.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for continued existence?’ you should answer, ‘Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.’

dn15:2.7.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for grasping?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.8.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for grasping?’ you should answer, ‘Craving is a requirement for grasping.’

dn15:2.9.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for craving?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.10.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for craving?’ you should answer, ‘Feeling is a requirement for craving.’

dn15:2.11.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for feeling?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.12.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for feeling?’ you should answer, ‘Contact is a requirement for feeling.’

dn15:2.13.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for contact?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.14.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for contact?’ you should answer, ‘Name and form are requirements for contact.’

dn15:2.15.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for name and form?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.16.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for name and form?’ you should answer, ‘Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.’

dn15:2.17.verse: When asked, ‘Is there a specific condition for consciousness?’ you should answer, ‘There is.’

dn15:2.18.verse: If they say, ‘What is a requirement for consciousness?’ you should answer, ‘Name and form are requirements for consciousness.’

dn15:3.1.verse: So: name and form are requirements for consciousness. Consciousness is a requirement for name and form. Name and form are requirements for contact. Contact is a requirement for feeling. Feeling is a requirement for craving. Craving is a requirement for grasping. Grasping is a requirement for continued existence. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

dn15:3.2.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

dn15:4.1.verse: ‘Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:4.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no rebirth for anyone anywhere.

dn15:4.3.verse: That is, there were no rebirth of sentient beings into their various realms—of gods, centaurs, spirits, creatures, humans, quadrupeds, birds, or reptiles, each into their own realm. When there’s no rebirth at all, with the cessation of rebirth, would old age and death still be found?”

dn15:4.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of old age and death, namely rebirth.

dn15:5.1.verse: ‘Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:5.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no continued existence for anyone anywhere.

dn15:5.3.verse: That is, continued existence in the sensual realm, the realm of luminous form, or the formless realm. When there’s no continued existence at all, with the cessation of continued existence, would rebirth still be found?”

dn15:5.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of rebirth, namely continued existence.

dn15:6.1.verse: ‘Grasping is a requirement for continued existence’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:6.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no grasping for anyone anywhere.

dn15:6.3.verse: That is, grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self. When there’s no grasping at all, with the cessation of grasping, would continued existence still be found?”

dn15:6.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of continued existence, namely grasping.

dn15:7.1.verse: ‘Craving is a requirement for grasping’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:7.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no craving for anyone anywhere.

dn15:7.3.verse: That is, craving for sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas. When there’s no craving at all, with the cessation of craving, would grasping still be found?”

dn15:7.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of grasping, namely craving.

dn15:8.1.verse: ‘Feeling is a requirement for craving’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:8.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no feeling for anyone anywhere.

dn15:8.3.verse: That is, feeling born of contact through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. When there’s no feeling at all, with the cessation of feeling, would craving still be found?”

dn15:8.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of craving, namely feeling.

dn15:9.1.verse: So it is, Ānanda, that feeling gives rise to craving. Craving gives rise to searching. Searching gives rise to gaining material things. Gaining material things gives rise to evaluation. Evaluation gives rise to desire and lust. Desire and lust gives rise to attachment. Attachment gives rise to ownership. Ownership gives rise to stinginess. Stinginess gives rise to safeguarding.

dn15:9.2.verse: Owing to safeguarding, many bad, unskillful things come to be: taking up the rod and the sword, quarrels, arguments, and disputes, accusations, backbiting, and lies.

dn15:10.1.verse: ‘Owing to safeguarding, many bad, unskillful things come to be: taking up the rod and the sword, quarrels, arguments, and disputes, accusations, backbiting, and lies’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:10.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no safeguarding for anyone anywhere. When there’s no safeguarding at all, with the cessation of safeguarding, would those many bad, unskillful things still come to be?”

dn15:10.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason for the origination of those many bad, unskillful things, namely safeguarding.

dn15:11.1.verse: ‘Stinginess gives rise to safeguarding’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:11.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no stinginess for anyone anywhere. When there’s no stinginess at all, with the cessation of stinginess, would safeguarding still be found?”

dn15:11.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of safeguarding, namely stinginess.

dn15:12.1.verse: ‘Ownership gives rise to stinginess’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:12.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no ownership for anyone anywhere. When there’s no ownership at all, with the cessation of ownership, would stinginess still be found?”

dn15:12.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of stinginess, namely ownership.

dn15:13.1.verse: ‘Attachment gives rise to ownership’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:13.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no attachment for anyone anywhere. When there’s no attachment at all, with the cessation of attachment, would ownership still be found?”

dn15:13.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of ownership, namely attachment.

dn15:14.1.verse: ‘Desire and lust gives rise to attachment’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:14.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no desire and lust for anyone anywhere. When there’s no desire and lust at all, with the cessation of desire and lust, would attachment still be found?”

dn15:14.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of attachment, namely desire and lust.

dn15:15.1.verse: Evaluation gives rise to desire and lust’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:15.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no evaluation for anyone anywhere. When there’s no evaluation at all, with the cessation of evaluation, would desire and lust still be found?”

dn15:15.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of desire and lust, namely evaluation.

dn15:16.1.verse: ‘Gaining material things gives rise to evaluation’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:16.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no gaining of material things for anyone anywhere. When there’s no gaining of material things at all, with the cessation of gaining material things, would evaluation still be found?”

dn15:16.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of evaluation, namely the gaining of material things.

dn15:17.1.verse: ‘Searching gives rise to gaining material things’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:17.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no searching for anyone anywhere. When there’s no searching at all, with the cessation of searching, would the gaining of material things still be found?”

dn15:17.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of gaining material things, namely searching.

dn15:18.1.verse: ‘Craving gives rise to searching’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:18.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no craving for anyone anywhere.

dn15:18.3.verse: That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence. When there’s no craving at all, with the cessation of craving, would searching still be found?”

dn15:18.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of searching, namely craving.

dn15:18.6.verse: And so, Ānanda, these two things meet at the two aspects of feeling.

dn15:19.1.verse: ‘Contact is a requirement for feeling’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:19.2.verse: Suppose there were totally and utterly no contact for anyone anywhere.

dn15:19.3.verse: That is, contact through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. When there’s no contact at all, with the cessation of contact, would feeling still be found?”

dn15:19.5.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of feeling, namely contact.

dn15:20.1.verse: ‘Name and form are requirements for contact’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:20.2.verse: Suppose there were none of the features, attributes, signs, and details by which the set of mental phenomena known as name is found. Would labeling contact still be found in the set of physical phenomena?”

dn15:20.4.verse: “Suppose there were none of the features, attributes, signs, and details by which the set of physical phenomena known as form is found. Would impingement contact still be found in the set of mental phenomena?”

dn15:20.6.verse: “Suppose there were none of the features, attributes, signs, and details by which the set of phenomena known as name and the set of phenomena known as form are found. Would either labeling contact or impingement contact still be found?”

dn15:20.8.verse: “Suppose there were none of the features, attributes, signs, and details by which name and form are found. Would contact still be found?”

dn15:20.10.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of contact, namely name and form.

dn15:21.1.verse: ‘Consciousness is a requirement for name and form’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:21.2.verse: If consciousness were not conceived in the mother’s womb, would name and form coagulate there?”

dn15:21.4.verse: “If consciousness, after being conceived in the mother’s womb, were to be miscarried, would name and form be born into this place?”

dn15:21.6.verse: “If the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off, would name and form achieve growth, increase, and maturity?”

dn15:21.8.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of name and form, namely consciousness.

dn15:22.1.verse: ‘Name and form are requirements for consciousness’—that’s what I said. And this is a way to understand how this is so.

dn15:22.2.verse: If consciousness were not established in name and form, would the coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future—be found?”

dn15:22.4.verse: “That’s why this is the cause, source, origin, and reason of consciousness, namely name and form.

dn15:22.5.verse: This is the extent to which one may be reborn, grow old, die, pass away, or reappear.

dn15:22.6.verse: This is how far the scope of labeling, definition, and description extends; how far the sphere of wisdom extends; how far the cycle of rebirths spins so that this state of being may be found; namely, name and form together with consciousness.

dn15:23.1.verse: How do those who describe the self describe it?

dn15:23.2.verse: They describe it as formed and limited:

dn15:23.4.verse: Or they describe it as formed and infinite:

dn15:23.6.verse: Or they describe it as formless and limited:

dn15:23.8.verse: Or they describe it as formless and infinite:

dn15:24.1.verse: Now, take those who describe the self as formed and limited.

dn15:24.2.verse: They describe the self in the present as formed and limited; or they describe it as sure to be in some other place formed and limited; or else they think: ‘Though it is not like that, I will ensure it is provided with what it needs to become like that.’

dn15:24.3.verse: This being so, it’s appropriate to say that a theory of self as formed and limited underlies them.

dn15:24.4.verse: Now, take those who describe the self as formed and infinite …

dn15:24.11.verse: They describe the self as formless and infinite in the present; or as sure to become formless and infinite in some other place; or else they think: ‘Though it is not like that, I will ensure it is provided with what it needs to become like that.’

dn15:24.12.verse: This being so, it’s appropriate to say that a theory of self as formless and infinite underlies them.

dn15:24.13.verse: That’s how those who describe the self describe it.

dn15:25.1.verse: How do those who don’t describe the self not describe it?

dn15:25.2.verse: They don’t describe it as formed and limited …

dn15:26.1.verse: Now, take those who don’t describe the self as formed and limited …

dn15:26.11.verse: They don’t describe the self in the present as formless and infinite; or as sure to become in some other place formless and infinite; and they don’t think: ‘Though it is not like that, I will ensure it is provided with what it needs to become like that.’

dn15:26.12.verse: This being so, it’s appropriate to say that a theory of self as formless and infinite doesn’t underlie them.

dn15:26.13.verse: That’s how those who don’t describe the self don’t describe it.

dn15:27.1.verse: How do those who regard the self regard it?

dn15:27.4.verse: Or they regard it like this: ‘Feeling is definitely not my self. My self does not experience feeling.’

dn15:27.5.verse: Or they regard it like this: ‘Feeling is definitely not my self. But it’s not that my self does not experience feeling. My self feels, for my self is liable to feel.’

dn15:28.1.verse: Now, as to those who say:

dn15:28.3.verse: You should say this to them:

dn15:28.6.verse: Which one of these do you regard as self?’

dn15:28.7.verse: Ānanda, at a time when you feel a pleasant feeling, you don’t feel a painful or neutral feeling;

dn15:28.8.verse: you only feel a pleasant feeling.

dn15:28.9.verse: At a time when you feel a painful feeling, you don’t feel a pleasant or neutral feeling;

dn15:28.10.verse: you only feel a painful feeling.

dn15:28.11.verse: At a time when you feel a neutral feeling, you don’t feel a pleasant or painful feeling;

dn15:28.12.verse: you only feel a neutral feeling.

dn15:29.1.verse: Pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neutral feelings are all impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

dn15:29.4.verse: When feeling a pleasant feeling they think: ‘This is my self.’

dn15:29.5.verse: When their pleasant feeling ceases they think: ‘My self has expired.’

dn15:29.6.verse: When feeling a painful feeling they think: ‘This is my self.’

dn15:29.7.verse: When their painful feeling ceases they think: ‘My self has expired.’

dn15:29.8.verse: When feeling a neutral feeling they think: ‘This is my self.’

dn15:29.9.verse: When their neutral feeling ceases they think: ‘My self has expired.’

dn15:29.10.verse: So those who say ‘feeling is my self’ regard as self that which is evidently impermanent, mixed with pleasure and pain, and liable to rise and fall.

dn15:29.11.verse: That’s why it’s not acceptable to regard feeling as my self.

dn15:30.1.verse: Now, as to those who say:

dn15:30.2.verse: ‘Feeling is definitely not my self. My self does not experience feeling.’ You should say this to them,

dn15:30.3.verse: ‘But reverend, where there is nothing felt at all, would the thought “I am” occur there?’”

dn15:30.5.verse: “That’s why it’s not acceptable to regard self as that which does not experience feeling.

dn15:31.1.verse: Now, as to those who say:

dn15:31.2.verse: ‘Feeling is definitely not my self. But it’s not that my self does not experience feeling. My self feels, for my self is liable to feel.’

dn15:31.3.verse: You should say this to them,

dn15:31.4.verse: ‘Suppose feelings were to totally and utterly cease without remainder.

dn15:31.5.verse: When there’s no feeling at all, with the cessation of feeling, would the thought “I am this” occur there?’”

dn15:31.7.verse: “That’s why it’s not acceptable to regard self as that which is liable to feel.

dn15:32.1.verse: When a mendicant does not regard feeling as self; does not regard self as not experiencing feeling; and does not regard it thus: ‘my self feels, for my self is liable to feel’—

dn15:32.2.verse: not regarding in this way, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

dn15:32.3.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

dn15:32.4.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

dn15:32.5.verse: It wouldn’t be appropriate to say that a mendicant whose mind is freed like this holds the following views:

dn15:32.6.verse: ‘A realized one still exists after death’;

dn15:32.7.verse: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death’;

dn15:32.8.verse: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death’;

dn15:32.9.verse: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death’.

dn15:32.11.verse: A mendicant is freed by directly knowing this: how far labeling and the scope of labeling extend; how far definition and the scope of definition extend; how far description and the scope of description extend; how far wisdom and the sphere of wisdom extend; how far the cycle of rebirths and its continuation extend. It wouldn’t be appropriate to say that a mendicant freed by directly knowing this holds the view: ‘There is no such thing as knowing and seeing.’

dn15:33.1.verse: Ānanda, there are seven planes of consciousness and two dimensions.

dn15:33.3.verse: There are sentient beings that are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings, some gods, and some beings in the underworld.

dn15:33.4.verse: This is the first plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.5.verse: There are sentient beings that are diverse in body and unified in perception, such as the gods reborn in the Divinity’s host through the first absorption.

dn15:33.6.verse: This is the second plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.7.verse: There are sentient beings that are unified in body and diverse in perception, such as the gods of sublime luminosity.

dn15:33.8.verse: This is the third plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.9.verse: There are sentient beings that are unified in body and unified in perception, such as the gods of universal beauty.

dn15:33.10.verse: This is the fourth plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.11.verse: There are sentient beings that have gone totally beyond perceptions of form. With the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they have been reborn in the dimension of infinite space.

dn15:33.12.verse: This is the fifth plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.13.verse: There are sentient beings that have gone totally beyond the dimension of infinite space. Aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they have been reborn in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

dn15:33.14.verse: This is the sixth plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.15.verse: There are sentient beings that have gone totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness. Aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they have been reborn in the dimension of nothingness.

dn15:33.16.verse: This is the seventh plane of consciousness.

dn15:33.17.verse: Then there is the dimension of non-percipient beings, and secondly, the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

dn15:34.1.verse: Now, regarding these seven planes of consciousness and two dimensions,

dn15:34.2.verse: is it appropriate for someone who understands them—and their origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape—to take pleasure in them?”

dn15:34.10.verse: “When a mendicant, having truly understood the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape regarding these seven planes of consciousness and these two dimensions, is freed by not grasping, they’re called a mendicant who is freed by wisdom.

dn15:35.1.verse: Ānanda, there are these eight liberations.

dn15:35.3.verse: Having physical form, they see forms.

dn15:35.5.verse: Not perceiving form internally, they see forms externally.

dn15:35.9.verse: Going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

dn15:35.11.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

dn15:35.13.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.

dn15:35.15.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

dn15:35.17.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, they enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling.

dn15:36.1.verse: When a mendicant enters into and withdraws from these eight liberations—in forward order, in reverse order, and in forward and reverse order—wherever they wish, whenever they wish, and for as long as they wish;

dn15:36.2.verse: and when they realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements, they’re called a mendicant who is freed both ways.

dn15:36.3.verse: And, Ānanda, there is no other freedom both ways that is better or finer than this.”

dn15:36.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn15:36.5.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

dn16:0.2.verse: The Great Discourse on the Buddha’s Extinguishment

dn16:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

dn16:1.1.3.verse: Now at that time King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, wanted to invade the Vajjis.

dn16:1.1.5.verse: “I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!”

dn16:1.2.1.verse: And then King Ajātasattu addressed Vassakāra the brahmin, a chief minister of Magadha,

dn16:1.2.2.verse: “Please, brahmin, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

dn16:1.2.5.verse: ‘Sir, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, wants to invade the Vajjis.

dn16:1.2.7.verse: “I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!”’

dn16:1.2.8.verse: Remember well how the Buddha answers and tell it to me.

dn16:1.2.9.verse: For Realized Ones say nothing that is not so.”

dn16:1.3.1.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” Vassakāra replied. He had the finest carriages harnessed. Then he mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out from Rājagaha for the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

dn16:1.3.2.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and approached the Buddha on foot, and exchanged greetings with him.

dn16:1.3.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

dn16:1.3.4.verse: “Worthy Gotama, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, bows with his head to your feet. He asks if you are healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

dn16:1.3.5.verse: Worthy Gotama, King Ajātasattu wants to invade the Vajjis.

dn16:1.3.7.verse: ‘I shall wipe out these Vajjis, so mighty and powerful! I shall destroy them, and lay ruin and devastation upon them!’”

dn16:1.4.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him.

dn16:1.4.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to him,

dn16:1.4.3.verse: “Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings?”

dn16:1.4.5.verse: “As long as the Vajjis meet frequently and have many meetings, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.6.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony?”

dn16:1.4.8.verse: “As long as the Vajjis meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.9.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the ancient Vajjian principles as they have been decreed?”

dn16:1.4.11.verse: “As long as the Vajjis don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the ancient Vajjian principles as they have been decreed, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.12.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate Vajjian elders, and think them worth listening to?”

dn16:1.4.14.verse: “As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate Vajjian elders, and think them worth listening to, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.15.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis don’t forcibly abduct the women or girls of the clans and make them live with them?”

dn16:1.4.17.verse: “As long as the Vajjis don’t forcibly abduct the women or girls of the clans and make them live with them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.18.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines, whether inner or outer, not neglecting the proper spirit-offerings that were given and made in the past?”

dn16:1.4.20.verse: “As long as the Vajjis honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian shrines, whether inner or outer, not neglecting the proper spirit-offerings that were given and made in the past, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.4.21.verse: Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjis organize proper protection, shelter, and security for perfected ones, so that more perfected ones might come to the realm and those already here may live in comfort?”

dn16:1.4.23.verse: “As long as the Vajjis organize proper protection, shelter, and security for perfected ones, so that more perfected ones might come to the realm and those already here may live in comfort, they can expect growth, not decline.”

dn16:1.5.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Vassakāra,

dn16:1.5.2.verse: “Brahmin, this one time I was staying near Vesālī at the Sārandada Shrine.

dn16:1.5.3.verse: There I taught the Vajjis these seven principles that prevent decline.

dn16:1.5.4.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the Vajjis, and as long as the Vajjis are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

dn16:1.5.5.verse: When the Buddha had spoken, Vassakāra said to him,

dn16:1.5.6.verse: “Worthy Gotama, if the Vajjis follow even a single one of these principles they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.5.7.verse: How much more so all seven!

dn16:1.5.8.verse: King Ajātasattu cannot defeat the Vajjis in war, unless by bribery or by sowing dissension.

dn16:1.5.9.verse: Well, now, worthy Gotama, I must go. I have many duties, and much to do.”

dn16:1.5.11.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, rose from his seat and left.

dn16:1.6.0.verse: 3. Principles That Prevent Decline Among the Mendicants

dn16:1.6.1.verse: Soon after he had left, the Buddha said to Ānanda,

dn16:1.6.2.verse: “Go, Ānanda, gather all the mendicants staying in the vicinity of Rājagaha together in the assembly hall.”

dn16:1.6.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. He did what the Buddha asked. Then he went back, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

dn16:1.6.4.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Saṅgha has assembled. Please, sir, go at your convenience.”

dn16:1.6.5.verse: Then the Buddha went to the assembly hall, where he sat down on the seat spread out

dn16:1.6.7.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you these seven principles that prevent decline.

dn16:1.6.8.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

dn16:1.6.11.verse: “As long as the mendicants meet frequently and have many meetings, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.12.verse: As long as the mendicants meet in harmony, leave in harmony, and carry on their business in harmony, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.13.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t make new decrees or abolish existing decrees, but proceed having undertaken the training rules as they have been decreed, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.14.verse: As long as the mendicants honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the senior mendicants—of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha—and think them worth listening to, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.15.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t fall under the sway of arisen craving for future lives, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.16.verse: As long as the mendicants take care to live in wilderness lodgings, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.17.verse: As long as the mendicants individually establish mindfulness, so that more good-hearted spiritual companions might come, and those that have already come may live comfortably, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.6.18.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.7.1.verse: I will teach you seven more principles that prevent decline. …

dn16:1.7.4.verse: As long as the mendicants don’t relish work, loving it and liking to relish it, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.7.5.verse: As long as they don’t relish talk …

dn16:1.7.8.verse: they don’t have corrupt wishes, falling under the sway of corrupt wishes …

dn16:1.7.9.verse: they don’t have bad friends, companions, and associates …

dn16:1.7.10.verse: they don’t stop half-way after achieving some trifling distinction, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.8.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.8.2.verse: I will teach you seven more principles that prevent decline. …

dn16:1.8.3.verse: As long as the mendicants are faithful …

dn16:1.8.9.verse: wise, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.8.10.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.8.11.verse: I will teach you seven more principles that prevent decline. …

dn16:1.9.1.verse: As long as the mendicants develop the awakening factors of mindfulness …

dn16:1.9.7.verse: equanimity, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.10.1.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.10.2.verse: I will teach you seven more principles that prevent decline. …

dn16:1.10.5.verse: As long as the mendicants develop the perceptions of impermanence …

dn16:1.10.11.verse: cessation, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.10.12.verse: As long as these seven principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.11.1.verse: I will teach you six principles that prevent decline. …

dn16:1.11.4.verse: As long as the mendicants consistently treat their spiritual companions with bodily kindness …

dn16:1.11.6.verse: and mental kindness both in public and in private, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.11.7.verse: As long as the mendicants share without reservation any material things they have gained by legitimate means, even the food placed in the alms-bowl, using them in common with their ethical spiritual companions, they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.11.8.verse: As long as the mendicants live according to the precepts shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private—such precepts as are intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion—they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.11.9.verse: As long as the mendicants live according to the view shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private—the view that is noble and emancipating, and delivers one who applies it to the complete end of suffering—they can expect growth, not decline.

dn16:1.11.10.verse: As long as these six principles that prevent decline last among the mendicants, and as long as the mendicants are seen following them, they can expect growth, not decline.”

dn16:1.12.1.verse: And while staying there at the Vulture’s Peak the Buddha often gave this Dhamma talk to the mendicants:

dn16:1.12.2.verse: “Such is ethics, such is immersion, such is wisdom.

dn16:1.12.3.verse: When immersion is imbued with ethics it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.12.4.verse: When wisdom is imbued with immersion it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.12.5.verse: When the mind is imbued with wisdom it is rightly freed from the defilements, namely,

dn16:1.12.6.verse: the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.”

dn16:1.13.1.verse: When the Buddha had stayed in Rājagaha as long as he pleased, he addressed Venerable Ānanda,

dn16:1.13.4.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants arrived at Ambalaṭṭhikā,

dn16:1.14.1.verse: where he stayed in the royal rest-house.

dn16:1.14.2.verse: And while staying there, too, he often gave this Dhamma talk to the mendicants:

dn16:1.14.3.verse: “Such is ethics, such is immersion, such is wisdom.

dn16:1.14.4.verse: When immersion is imbued with ethics it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.14.5.verse: When wisdom is imbued with immersion it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.14.6.verse: When the mind is imbued with wisdom it is rightly freed from the defilements, namely,

dn16:1.14.7.verse: the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.”

dn16:1.15.1.verse: When the Buddha had stayed in Ambalaṭṭhikā as long as he pleased, he addressed Venerable Ānanda,

dn16:1.15.4.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants arrived at Nāḷandā,

dn16:1.15.5.verse: where he stayed in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

dn16:1.16.1.verse: Then Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn16:1.16.2.verse: “Sir, I have such confidence in the Buddha that

dn16:1.16.3.verse: I believe there’s no other ascetic or brahmin—whether past, future, or present—whose direct knowledge is superior to the Buddha when it comes to awakening.”

dn16:1.16.4.verse: “That’s a grand and bold statement, Sāriputta. You’ve roared a definitive, categorical lion’s roar, saying:

dn16:1.16.5.verse: ‘I have such confidence in the Buddha that

dn16:1.16.6.verse: I believe there’s no other ascetic or brahmin—whether past, future, or present—whose direct knowledge is superior to the Buddha when it comes to awakening.’

dn16:1.16.7.verse: What about all the perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas who lived in the past? Have you encompassed their minds to know that

dn16:1.16.8.verse: those Buddhas had such ethics, or such qualities, or such wisdom, or such meditation, or such freedom?”

dn16:1.16.10.verse: “And what about all the perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas who will live in the future? Have you encompassed their minds to know that

dn16:1.16.11.verse: those Buddhas will have such ethics, or such qualities, or such wisdom, or such meditation, or such freedom?”

dn16:1.16.13.verse: “And what about me, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha at present? Have you encompassed my mind to know that

dn16:1.16.14.verse: I have such ethics, or such qualities, or such wisdom, or such meditation, or such freedom?”

dn16:1.16.16.verse: “In that case, Sāriputta, given that you don’t encompass the minds of Buddhas past, future, or present,

dn16:1.16.17.verse: what then are you doing, making such a grand and bold statement, roaring such a definitive, categorical lion’s roar?”

dn16:1.17.1.verse: “Sir, though I don’t encompass the minds of Buddhas past, future, and present,

dn16:1.17.2.verse: still I understand this by inference from the teaching.

dn16:1.17.3.verse: Suppose there was a king’s frontier citadel with fortified embankments, ramparts, and arches, and a single gate.

dn16:1.17.4.verse: And it has a gatekeeper who is astute, competent, and intelligent. He keeps strangers out and lets known people in.

dn16:1.17.5.verse: As he walks around the patrol path, he doesn’t see a hole or cleft in the wall, not even one big enough for a cat to slip out.

dn16:1.17.7.verse: ‘Whatever sizable creatures enter or leave the citadel, all of them do so via this gate.’

dn16:1.17.8.verse: In the same way, I understand this by inference from the teaching:

dn16:1.17.9.verse: ‘All the perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas—whether past, future, or present—give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom. Their mind is firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. They correctly develop the seven awakening factors. And they awaken to the supreme perfect awakening.’”

dn16:1.18.1.verse: And while staying at Nāḷandā, too, the Buddha often gave this Dhamma talk to the mendicants:

dn16:1.18.2.verse: “Such is ethics, such is immersion, such is wisdom.

dn16:1.18.3.verse: When immersion is imbued with ethics it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.18.4.verse: When wisdom is imbued with immersion it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:1.18.5.verse: When the mind is imbued with wisdom it is rightly freed from the defilements, namely,

dn16:1.18.6.verse: the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.”

dn16:1.19.1.verse: When the Buddha had stayed in Nāḷandā as long as he pleased, he addressed Venerable Ānanda,

dn16:1.19.2.verse: “Come, Ānanda, let’s go to Pāṭali Village.”

dn16:1.19.4.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants arrived at Pāṭali Village.

dn16:1.20.1.verse: The lay followers of Pāṭali Village heard that he had arrived.

dn16:1.20.2.verse: So they went to see him, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn16:1.20.3.verse: “Sir, please consent to come to our guest house.”

dn16:1.21.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the lay followers of Pāṭali Village rose from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. Then they went to the guest house, where they spread carpets all over, prepared seats, set up a water jar, and placed an oil lamp. Then they went back to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and told him of their preparations, saying:

dn16:1.22.1.verse: In the morning, the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the guest house together with the Saṅgha of mendicants. Having washed his feet, he entered the guest house and sat against the central column facing east.

dn16:1.22.2.verse: The Saṅgha of mendicants also washed their feet, entered the guest house, and sat against the west wall facing east, with the Buddha right in front of them.

dn16:1.22.3.verse: The lay followers of Pāṭali Village also washed their feet, entered the guest house, and sat against the east wall facing west, with the Buddha right in front of them.

dn16:1.23.2.verse: “Householders, there are these five drawbacks for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics.

dn16:1.23.4.verse: Firstly, an unethical person loses great wealth on account of negligence.

dn16:1.23.5.verse: This is the first drawback for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics.

dn16:1.23.6.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person gets a bad reputation.

dn16:1.23.8.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person enters any kind of assembly unconfident and embarrassed, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

dn16:1.23.10.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person feels lost when they die.

dn16:1.23.12.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

dn16:1.23.14.verse: These are the five drawbacks for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics.

dn16:1.24.1.verse: There are these five benefits for an ethical person because of their accomplishment in ethics.

dn16:1.24.3.verse: Firstly, an ethical person gains great wealth on account of diligence.

dn16:1.24.5.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person gets a good reputation.

dn16:1.24.7.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person enters any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

dn16:1.24.9.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person dies not feeling lost.

dn16:1.24.11.verse: Furthermore, when an ethical person’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn16:1.24.13.verse: These are the five benefits for an ethical person because of their accomplishment in ethics.”

dn16:1.25.1.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the lay followers of Pāṭali Village with a Dhamma talk. Then he sent them off,

dn16:1.25.2.verse: “The night is getting late, householders. Please go at your convenience.”

dn16:1.25.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the lay followers of Pāṭali Village. They got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before leaving.

dn16:1.25.4.verse: Soon after they left the Buddha entered a private cubicle.

dn16:1.26.1.verse: Now at that time the Magadhan chief ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra were building a citadel at Pāṭali Village to keep the Vajjis out.

dn16:1.26.2.verse: At that time thousands of deities were taking possession of building sites in Pāṭali Village.

dn16:1.26.3.verse: Illustrious rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by illustrious deities.

dn16:1.27.1.verse: Middling rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by middling deities.

dn16:1.27.2.verse: Lesser rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by lesser deities.

dn16:1.27.3.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha saw those deities taking possession of building sites in Pāṭali Village.

dn16:1.27.4.verse: The Buddha rose at the crack of dawn and addressed Ānanda,

dn16:1.27.5.verse: “Ānanda, who is building a citadel at Pāṭali Village?”

dn16:1.27.6.verse: “Sir, the Magadhan ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra are building a citadel to keep the Vajjis out.”

dn16:1.28.1.verse: “It’s as if they were building the citadel in consultation with the gods of the thirty-three.

dn16:1.28.3.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw those deities taking possession of building sites.

dn16:1.28.4.verse: Illustrious rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by illustrious deities.

dn16:1.28.5.verse: Middling rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by middling deities.

dn16:1.28.6.verse: Lesser rulers or royal ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by lesser deities.

dn16:1.28.7.verse: As far as the civilized region extends, as far as the trading zone extends, this will be the chief city: the Pāṭaliputta trade center.

dn16:1.28.8.verse: But Pāṭaliputta will face three threats:

dn16:1.29.1.verse: Then the Magadhan ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra approached the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

dn16:1.29.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they stood to one side and said,

dn16:1.29.3.verse: “Would the worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept today’s meal from me?”

dn16:1.30.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, they went to their own guest house, where they had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared. Then they had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

dn16:1.30.2.verse: “It’s time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready.”

dn16:1.30.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to their guest house together with the mendicant Saṅgha, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

dn16:1.30.4.verse: Then Sunidha and Vassakāra served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with their own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

dn16:1.30.5.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Sunidha and Vassakāra took a low seat and sat to one side.

dn16:1.31.1.verse: The Buddha expressed his appreciation with these verses:

dn16:1.31.2.verse: “In the place he makes his dwelling,

dn16:1.31.10.verse: After that they have sympathy for him,

dn16:1.31.11.verse: like a mother the child at her breast.

dn16:1.31.12.verse: A man beloved of the deities

dn16:1.31.14.verse: When the Buddha had expressed his appreciation to Sunidha and Vassakāra with these verses, he rose from his seat and left.

dn16:1.32.1.verse: Sunidha and Vassakāra followed behind the Buddha, thinking,

dn16:1.32.2.verse: “The gate through which the ascetic Gotama exits today shall be named the Gotama Gate.

dn16:1.32.3.verse: The ford at which he crosses the Ganges River shall be named the Gotama Ford.”

dn16:1.32.4.verse: Then the gate through which the Buddha exited was named the Gotama Gate.

dn16:1.32.5.verse: Then the Buddha came to the Ganges River.

dn16:1.33.1.verse: Now at that time the Ganges was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

dn16:1.33.2.verse: Wanting to cross from the near to the far shore, some people were seeking a boat, some a dinghy, while some were tying up a raft.

dn16:1.33.3.verse: But, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, the Buddha, together with the mendicant Saṅgha, vanished from the near shore and landed on the far shore.

dn16:1.34.1.verse: He saw all those humans wanting to cross over.

dn16:1.34.2.verse: Knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

dn16:1.34.3.verse: “Those who cross a deluge or stream

dn16:1.34.4.verse: have built a bridge and left the marshes behind.

dn16:1.34.5.verse: While some people are still tying a raft,

dn16:2.1.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

dn16:2.1.2.verse: “Come, Ānanda, let’s go to the village of Koṭi.”

dn16:2.1.4.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants arrived at the village of Koṭi,

dn16:2.2.2.verse: “Mendicants, due to not understanding and not penetrating four noble truths, both you and I have wandered and transmigrated for such a very long time.

dn16:2.2.7.verse: and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

dn16:2.2.8.verse: These noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path have been understood and comprehended. Craving for continued existence has been cut off; the leash to existence is ended; now there’ll be no more future lives.”

dn16:2.3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn16:2.3.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn16:2.3.5.verse: we have transmigrated for a long time

dn16:2.3.6.verse: from one rebirth to the next.

dn16:2.3.7.verse: But now that these truths have been seen,

dn16:2.3.8.verse: the leash to existence is eradicated.

dn16:2.3.9.verse: The root of suffering is cut off,

dn16:2.3.10.verse: now there’ll be no more future lives.”

dn16:2.4.1.verse: And while staying at the village of Koṭi, too, the Buddha often gave this Dhamma talk to the mendicants:

dn16:2.4.2.verse: “Such is ethics, such is immersion, such is wisdom.

dn16:2.4.3.verse: When immersion is imbued with ethics it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:2.4.4.verse: When wisdom is imbued with immersion it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

dn16:2.4.5.verse: When the mind is imbued with wisdom it is rightly freed from the defilements, namely,

dn16:2.4.6.verse: the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.”

dn16:2.5.1.verse: When the Buddha had stayed in the village of Koṭi as long as he pleased, he said to Ānanda,

dn16:2.5.2.verse: “Come, Ānanda, let’s go to the land of the Ñātikas.”

dn16:2.5.4.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants arrived in the land of the Ñātikas,

dn16:2.5.5.verse: where he stayed in the brick house at Ñātika.

dn16:2.6.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn16:2.6.2.verse: “Sir, the monk named Sāḷha has passed away in Ñātika. Where has he been reborn in his next life?

dn16:2.6.5.verse: and the laywoman named Sujātā have passed away in Ñātika. Where have they been reborn in the next life?

dn16:2.6.13.verse: Subhadda have passed away in Ñātika. Where have they been reborn in the next life?”

dn16:2.7.1.verse: “Ānanda, the monk Sāḷha had realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

dn16:2.7.2.verse: The nun Nandā had ended the five lower fetters. She’s been reborn spontaneously, and will be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.

dn16:2.7.3.verse: The layman Sudatta had ended three fetters, and weakened greed, hate, and delusion. He’s a once-returner; he will come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

dn16:2.7.4.verse: The laywoman Sujātā had ended three fetters. She’s a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

dn16:2.7.12.verse: and Subhadda had ended the five lower fetters. They’ve been reborn spontaneously, and will be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.

dn16:2.7.13.verse: Over fifty laymen in Ñātika have passed away having ended the five lower fetters. They’ve been reborn spontaneously, and will be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.

dn16:2.7.14.verse: More than ninety laymen in Ñātika have passed away having ended three fetters, and weakened greed, hate, and delusion. They’re once-returners, who will come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.
