dn17:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying between a pair of sal trees in the sal forest of the Mallas at Upavattana near Kusinārā at the time of his full extinguishment.

dn17:1.2.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn17:1.2.2.verse: “Sir, please don’t be fully extinguished in this little hamlet, this jungle hamlet, this branch hamlet.

dn17:1.2.3.verse: There are other great cities such as

dn17:1.2.4.verse: Campā, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Varanasi.

dn17:1.2.5.verse: Let the Buddha be fully extinguished there.

dn17:1.2.6.verse: There are many well-to-do aristocrats, brahmins, and householders there who are devoted to the Buddha. They will perform the rites of venerating the Realized One’s corpse.”

dn17:1.3.1.verse: “Don’t say that, Ānanda! Don’t say that

dn17:1.3.2.verse: this is a little hamlet, a jungle hamlet, a branch hamlet.

dn17:1.3.4.verse: Once upon a time, there was a king named Mahāsudassana whose dominion extended to all four sides, and who achieved stability in the country.

dn17:1.3.5.verse: His capital was this Kusinārā, which at the time was named Kusāvatī.

dn17:1.3.6.verse: It stretched for twelve leagues from east to west, and seven leagues from north to south.

dn17:1.3.7.verse: The royal capital of Kusāvatī was successful and prosperous, populous and full of people, with plenty of food.

dn17:1.3.8.verse: It was just like Āḷakamandā, the royal capital of the gods, which is successful and prosperous, populous and full of spirits, with plenty of food.

dn17:1.3.10.verse: Kusāvatī was never free of ten sounds by day or night, namely:

dn17:1.3.11.verse: the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, drums, clay drums, arched harps, singing, horns, gongs, and handbells; and the cry, ‘Eat, drink, be merry!’ as the tenth.

dn17:1.4.1.verse: Kusāvatī was encircled by seven ramparts:

dn17:1.4.2.verse: one made of gold, one made of silver, one made of beryl, one made of crystal, one made of ruby, one made of emerald, and one made of all precious things.

dn17:1.5.2.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.5.3.verse: At each gate there were seven pillars, three fathoms deep and four fathoms high,

dn17:1.5.4.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, ruby, emerald, and all precious things.

dn17:1.6.1.verse: It was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees,

dn17:1.6.2.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, ruby, emerald, and all precious things.

dn17:1.6.3.verse: The golden palms had trunks of gold, and leaves and fruits of silver.

dn17:1.6.4.verse: The silver palms had trunks of silver, and leaves and fruits of gold.

dn17:1.6.5.verse: The beryl palms had trunks of beryl, and leaves and fruits of crystal.

dn17:1.6.6.verse: The crystal palms had trunks of crystal, and leaves and fruits of beryl.

dn17:1.6.7.verse: The ruby palms had trunks of ruby, and leaves and fruits of emerald.

dn17:1.6.8.verse: The emerald palms had trunks of emerald, and leaves and fruits of ruby.

dn17:1.6.9.verse: The palms of all precious things had trunks of all precious things, and leaves and fruits of all precious things.

dn17:1.6.10.verse: When those rows of palm trees were blown by the wind they sounded graceful, tantalizing, sensuous, lovely, and intoxicating,

dn17:1.6.11.verse: like a quintet made up of skilled musicians who had practiced well and kept excellent rhythm.

dn17:1.6.13.verse: And any addicts, carousers, or drunkards in Kusāvatī at that time were entertained by that sound.

dn17:1.7.1.verse: King Mahāsudassana possessed seven treasures and four blessings.

dn17:1.7.3.verse: On a fifteenth day sabbath, King Mahāsudassana had bathed his head and gone upstairs in the royal longhouse to observe the sabbath.

dn17:1.7.4.verse: And the heavenly wheel-treasure appeared to him, with a thousand spokes, with rim and hub, complete in every detail.

dn17:1.7.6.verse: ‘I have heard that when the heavenly wheel-treasure appears to a king in this way, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.

dn17:1.7.7.verse: Am I then a wheel-turning monarch?’

dn17:1.8.1.verse: Then King Mahāsudassana, rising from his seat and arranging his robe over one shoulder, took a ceremonial vase in his left hand and besprinkled the wheel-treasure with his right hand, saying:

dn17:1.8.2.verse: ‘Roll forth, O wheel-treasure! Triumph, O wheel-treasure!’

dn17:1.8.3.verse: Then the wheel-treasure rolled toward the east. And the king followed it together with his army of four divisions. In whatever place the wheel-treasure stood still, there the king came to stay together with his army.

dn17:1.9.1.verse: And any opposing rulers of the eastern quarter came to him and said,

dn17:1.9.2.verse: ‘Come, Great King! Welcome, Great King! We are yours, Great King, instruct us.’

dn17:1.9.4.verse: ‘Do not kill living creatures. Do not steal. Do not commit sexual misconduct. Do not lie. Do not drink liquor. Maintain the current level of taxation.’

dn17:1.9.5.verse: And so the opposing rulers of the eastern quarter became his vassals.

dn17:1.10.1.verse: Then the wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged again, rolled toward the south. …

dn17:1.10.2.verse: Having plunged into the southern ocean and emerged again, it rolled toward the west. …

dn17:1.10.3.verse: Having plunged into the western ocean and emerged again, it rolled toward the north, followed by the king together with his army of four divisions.

dn17:1.10.4.verse: In whatever place the wheel-treasure stood still, there the king came to stay together with his army.

dn17:1.10.5.verse: And any opposing rulers of the northern quarter came to him and said,

dn17:1.10.6.verse: ‘Come, Great King! Welcome, Great King! We are yours, Great King, instruct us.’

dn17:1.10.8.verse: ‘Do not kill living creatures. Do not steal. Do not commit sexual misconduct. Do not lie. Do not drink liquor. Maintain the current level of taxation.’

dn17:1.10.9.verse: And so the opposing rulers of the northern quarter became his vassals.

dn17:1.11.1.verse: And then the wheel-treasure, having triumphed over this land surrounded by ocean, returned to the royal capital. There it stood still by the gate to the royal compound at the High Court as if fixed to an axle, illuminating the royal compound.

dn17:1.11.2.verse: Such is the wheel-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.12.1.verse: Next, the elephant-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.12.2.verse: It was an all-white sky-walker with psychic power, touching the ground in seven places, a king of elephants named Sabbath.

dn17:1.12.3.verse: Seeing him, the king was impressed,

dn17:1.12.4.verse: ‘This would truly be a fine elephant vehicle, if he would submit to taming.’

dn17:1.12.5.verse: Then the elephant-treasure submitted to taming, as if he was a fine thoroughbred elephant that had been tamed for a long time.

dn17:1.12.6.verse: Once it so happened that King Mahāsudassana, testing that same elephant-treasure, mounted him in the morning and traversed the land surrounded by ocean before returning to the royal capital in time for breakfast.

dn17:1.12.7.verse: Such is the elephant-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.13.1.verse: Next, the horse-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.13.2.verse: It was an all-white sky-walker with psychic power, with head of black and mane like woven reeds, a royal steed named Thundercloud.

dn17:1.13.3.verse: Seeing him, the king was impressed,

dn17:1.13.4.verse: ‘This would truly be a fine horse vehicle, if he would submit to taming.’

dn17:1.13.5.verse: Then the horse-treasure submitted to taming, as if he was a fine thoroughbred horse that had been tamed for a long time.

dn17:1.13.6.verse: Once it so happened that King Mahāsudassana, testing that same horse-treasure, mounted him in the morning and traversed the land surrounded by ocean before returning to the royal capital in time for breakfast.

dn17:1.13.7.verse: Such is the horse-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.14.1.verse: Next, the jewel-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.14.2.verse: It was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.

dn17:1.14.3.verse: And the radiance of that jewel spread all-round for a league.

dn17:1.14.4.verse: Once it so happened that King Mahāsudassana, testing that same jewel-treasure, mobilized his army of four divisions and, with the jewel hoisted on his banner, set out in the dark of the night.

dn17:1.14.5.verse: Then the villagers around them set off to work, thinking that it was day.

dn17:1.14.6.verse: Such is the jewel-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.15.1.verse: Next, the woman-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.15.2.verse: She was attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. She was neither too tall nor too short; neither too thin nor too fat; neither too dark nor too light. She outdid human beauty without reaching heavenly beauty.

dn17:1.15.3.verse: And her touch was like a tuft of cotton-wool or kapok.

dn17:1.15.4.verse: When it was cool her limbs were warm, and when it was warm her limbs were cool.

dn17:1.15.5.verse: The fragrance of sandal floated from her body, and lotus from her mouth.

dn17:1.15.6.verse: She got up before the king and went to bed after him, and was obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.

dn17:1.15.7.verse: The woman-treasure did not betray the wheel-turning monarch even in thought, still less in deed.

dn17:1.15.8.verse: Such is the woman-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.16.1.verse: Next, the householder-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.16.2.verse: The power of clairvoyance manifested in him as a result of past deeds, by which he sees treasure troves, both owned and ownerless.

dn17:1.16.3.verse: He approached the king and said,

dn17:1.16.4.verse: ‘Relax, Your Majesty. I will take care of the treasury.’

dn17:1.16.5.verse: Once it so happened that the wheel-turning monarch, testing that same householder-treasure, boarded a boat and sailed to the middle of the Ganges River. Then he said to the householder-treasure,

dn17:1.16.6.verse: ‘Householder, I need gold, both coined and uncoined.’

dn17:1.16.7.verse: ‘Well then, Great King, draw the boat up to one shore.’

dn17:1.16.8.verse: ‘It’s right here, householder, that I need gold, both coined and uncoined.’

dn17:1.16.9.verse: Then that householder-treasure, immersing both hands in the water, pulled up a pot full of gold, both coined and uncoined, and said to the king,

dn17:1.16.10.verse: ‘Is this sufficient, Great King? Has enough been done, Great King, enough offered?’

dn17:1.16.12.verse: ‘That is sufficient, householder. Enough has been done, enough offered.’

dn17:1.16.13.verse: Such is the householder-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.18.1.verse: Next, the commander-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.18.2.verse: He is astute, competent, intelligent, and capable regarding who should be ushered in to the king’s presence, who should be ushered out, and who should be kept by his side.

dn17:1.18.3.verse: He approached the king and said,

dn17:1.18.4.verse: ‘Relax, Your Majesty. I shall issue instructions.’

dn17:1.18.5.verse: Such is the commander-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.18.6.verse: These are the seven treasures possessed by King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.18.9.verse: And what are the four blessings?

dn17:1.18.10.verse: He was attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty, more so than other humans.

dn17:1.19.1.verse: Furthermore, he was long-lived, more so than other humans.

dn17:1.20.1.verse: Furthermore, he was rarely ill or unwell, and his stomach digested well, being neither too hot nor too cold, more so than other humans.

dn17:1.21.1.verse: Furthermore, he was as dear and beloved to the brahmins and householders

dn17:1.21.2.verse: as a father is to his children.

dn17:1.21.4.verse: And the brahmins and householders were as dear to the king

dn17:1.21.5.verse: as children are to their father.

dn17:1.21.7.verse: Once it so happened that King Mahāsudassana went with his army of four divisions to visit a park.

dn17:1.21.8.verse: Then the brahmins and householders went up to him and said,

dn17:1.21.9.verse: ‘Slow down, Your Majesty, so we may see you longer!’

dn17:1.21.10.verse: And the king addressed his charioteer,

dn17:1.21.11.verse: ‘Drive slowly, charioteer, so I can see the brahmins and householders longer!’

dn17:1.21.13.verse: These are the four blessings possessed by King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.22.0.verse: 4. Lotus Ponds in the Palace of Principle

dn17:1.22.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I have lotus ponds built between the palms, at intervals of a hundred bow lengths?’

dn17:1.22.4.verse: The lotus ponds were lined with tiles of four colors,

dn17:1.22.5.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.22.6.verse: And four flights of stairs of four colors descended into each lotus pond,

dn17:1.22.7.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.22.8.verse: The golden stairs had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.22.9.verse: The silver stairs had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.22.10.verse: The beryl stairs had posts of beryl, and banisters and finials of crystal.

dn17:1.22.11.verse: The crystal stairs had posts of crystal, and banisters and finials of beryl.

dn17:1.22.12.verse: Those lotus ponds were surrounded by two balustrades, made of gold and silver.

dn17:1.22.13.verse: The golden balustrades had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.22.14.verse: The silver balustrades had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.23.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I plant flowers in the lotus ponds such as blue water lilies, and lotuses of pink, yellow, and white, blooming all year round, and accessible to the public?’

dn17:1.23.5.verse: ‘Why don’t I appoint bath attendants to help bathe the people who come to bathe in the lotus ponds?’

dn17:1.23.8.verse: ‘Why don’t I set up charities on the banks of the lotus ponds,

dn17:1.23.9.verse: so that those in need of food, drink, clothes, vehicles, beds, women, coined gold, or uncoined gold can get what they need?’

dn17:1.24.1.verse: Then the brahmins and householders came to the king bringing abundant wealth and said,

dn17:1.24.2.verse: ‘Your Majesty, this abundant wealth is specially for you alone; may Your Majesty accept it!’

dn17:1.24.3.verse: ‘There’s enough raised for me through regular taxes. Let this be for you; and here, take even more!’

dn17:1.24.4.verse: When the king turned them down, they withdrew to one side to think up a plan,

dn17:1.24.5.verse: ‘It wouldn’t be proper for us to take this abundant wealth back to our own homes.

dn17:1.24.6.verse: Why don’t we build a home for King Mahāsudassana?’

dn17:1.24.7.verse: They went up to the king and said,

dn17:1.24.8.verse: ‘We shall have a home built for you, Your Majesty!’

dn17:1.25.1.verse: And then Sakka, lord of gods, knowing the king’s train of thought, addressed the godling Vissakamma,

dn17:1.25.2.verse: ‘Come, dear Vissakamma, build a palace named Principle as a home for King Mahāsudassana.’

dn17:1.25.3.verse: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Vissakamma. Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the gods of the thirty-three and appeared in front of King Mahāsudassana.

dn17:1.25.5.verse: ‘I shall build a palace named Principle as a home for you, Your Majesty.’

dn17:1.25.7.verse: And so that’s what Vissakamma did.

dn17:1.25.8.verse: The Palace of Principle stretched for a league from east to west, and half a league from north to south.

dn17:1.25.9.verse: It was lined with tiles of four colors, three fathoms high,

dn17:1.25.10.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.26.1.verse: It had 84,000 pillars of four colors,

dn17:1.26.2.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.26.3.verse: It was covered with panels of four colors,

dn17:1.26.4.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.26.5.verse: It had twenty-four staircases of four colors,

dn17:1.26.6.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.26.7.verse: The golden stairs had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.26.8.verse: The silver stairs had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.26.9.verse: The beryl stairs had posts of beryl, and banisters and finials of crystal.

dn17:1.26.10.verse: The crystal stairs had posts of crystal, and banisters and finials of beryl.

dn17:1.26.11.verse: It had 84,000 chambers of four colors,

dn17:1.26.12.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.26.13.verse: In each chamber a couch was spread: in the golden chamber a couch of silver; in the silver chamber a couch of gold; in the beryl chamber a couch of ivory; in the crystal chamber a couch of hardwood.

dn17:1.26.14.verse: At the door of the golden chamber stood a palm tree of silver, with trunk of silver, and leaves and fruits of gold.

dn17:1.26.15.verse: At the door of the silver chamber stood a palm tree of gold, with trunk of gold, and leaves and fruits of silver.

dn17:1.26.16.verse: At the door of the beryl chamber stood a palm tree of crystal, with trunk of crystal, and leaves and fruits of beryl.

dn17:1.26.17.verse: At the door of the crystal chamber stood a palm tree of beryl, with trunk of beryl, and leaves and fruits of crystal.

dn17:1.27.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I build a grove of golden palm trees at the door to the Chamber of the Grand Tower, where I can sit for the day?’

dn17:1.28.1.verse: The Palace of Principle was surrounded by two balustrades, made of gold and silver.

dn17:1.28.2.verse: The golden balustrades had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.28.3.verse: The silver balustrades had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.29.1.verse: The Palace of Principle was surrounded by two nets of bells,

dn17:1.29.3.verse: The golden net had bells of silver, and the silver net had bells of gold.

dn17:1.29.4.verse: When those nets of bells were blown by the wind they sounded graceful, tantalizing, sensuous, lovely, and intoxicating,

dn17:1.29.5.verse: like a quintet made up of skilled musicians who had practiced well and kept excellent rhythm.

dn17:1.29.7.verse: And any addicts, carousers, or drunkards in Kusāvatī at that time were entertained by that sound.

dn17:1.29.8.verse: When it was finished, the palace was hard to look at, dazzling to the eyes.

dn17:1.29.9.verse: It was like how in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the heavens are sunny and cloudless, as the sun is rising to the firmament, it is hard to look at, dazzling to the eyes.

dn17:1.30.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I build a lotus pond named Principle in front of the palace?’

dn17:1.30.4.verse: The Lotus Pond of Principle stretched for a league from east to west, and half a league from north to south.

dn17:1.30.5.verse: It was lined with tiles of four colors,

dn17:1.30.6.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.31.1.verse: It had twenty-four staircases of four colors,

dn17:1.31.2.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.

dn17:1.31.3.verse: The golden stairs had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.31.4.verse: The silver stairs had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.31.5.verse: The beryl stairs had posts of beryl, and banisters and finials of crystal.

dn17:1.31.6.verse: The crystal stairs had posts of crystal, and banisters and finials of beryl.

dn17:1.31.7.verse: It was surrounded by two balustrades, made of gold and silver.

dn17:1.31.8.verse: The golden balustrades had posts of gold, and banisters and finials of silver.

dn17:1.31.9.verse: The silver balustrades had posts of silver, and banisters and finials of gold.

dn17:1.32.1.verse: It was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees,

dn17:1.32.2.verse: made of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, ruby, emerald, and all precious things.

dn17:1.32.3.verse: The golden palms had trunks of gold, and leaves and fruits of silver.

dn17:1.32.4.verse: The silver palms had trunks of silver, and leaves and fruits of gold.

dn17:1.32.5.verse: The beryl palms had trunks of beryl, and leaves and fruits of crystal.

dn17:1.32.6.verse: The crystal palms had trunks of crystal, and leaves and fruits of beryl.

dn17:1.32.7.verse: The ruby palms had trunks of ruby, and leaves and fruits of emerald.

dn17:1.32.8.verse: The emerald palms had trunks of emerald, and leaves and fruits of ruby.

dn17:1.32.9.verse: The palms of all precious things had trunks of all precious things, and leaves and fruits of all precious things.

dn17:1.32.10.verse: When those rows of palm trees were blown by the wind they sounded graceful, tantalizing, sensuous, lovely, and intoxicating,

dn17:1.32.11.verse: like a quintet made up of skilled musicians who had practiced well and kept excellent rhythm.

dn17:1.32.13.verse: And any addicts, carousers, or drunkards in Kusāvatī at that time were entertained by that sound.

dn17:1.33.1.verse: When the palace and its lotus pond were finished, King Mahāsudassana served those who were deemed true ascetics and brahmins with all they desired. Then he ascended the Palace of Principle.

dn17:2.1.2.verse: ‘Of what deed of mine is this the fruit and result, that I am now so mighty and powerful?’

dn17:2.1.4.verse: ‘It is the fruit and result of three kinds of deeds:

dn17:2.2.1.verse: Then he went to the Chamber of the Grand Tower, stood at the door, and expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

dn17:2.2.2.verse: ‘Stop here, sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts—

dn17:2.3.1.verse: Then he entered the Chamber of the Grand Tower and sat on the golden couch. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn17:2.3.2.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, he entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn17:2.3.3.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, he entered and remained in the third absorption, where he meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

dn17:2.3.4.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, he entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

dn17:2.4.1.verse: Then King Mahāsudassana left the Chamber of the Grand Tower and entered the golden chamber, where he sat on the golden couch.

dn17:2.4.2.verse: He meditated spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way he spread a heart full of love above, below, across, everywhere, all around, to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn17:2.4.3.verse: He meditated spreading a heart full of compassion …

dn17:2.4.4.verse: He meditated spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

dn17:2.4.5.verse: He meditated spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, he spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn17:2.5.1.verse: King Mahāsudassana had 84,000 cities, with the royal capital of Kusāvatī the foremost.

dn17:2.5.2.verse: He had 84,000 palaces, with the Palace of Principle the foremost.

dn17:2.5.3.verse: He had 84,000 chambers, with the Chamber of the Grand Tower the foremost.

dn17:2.5.4.verse: He had 84,000 couches made of gold, silver, ivory, and hardwood. They were spread with woollen covers—shag-piled, pure white, or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends.

dn17:2.5.5.verse: He had 84,000 bull elephants with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the royal bull elephant named Sabbath foremost.

dn17:2.5.6.verse: He had 84,000 horses with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the royal steed named Thundercloud foremost.

dn17:2.5.7.verse: He had 84,000 chariots upholstered with the hide of lions, tigers, and leopards, and cream rugs, with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the chariot named Triumph foremost.

dn17:2.5.8.verse: He had 84,000 jewels, with the jewel-treasure foremost.

dn17:2.5.9.verse: He had 84,000 women, with Queen Subhaddā foremost.

dn17:2.5.10.verse: He had 84,000 householders, with the householder-treasure foremost.

dn17:2.5.11.verse: He had 84,000 aristocrat vassals, with the commander-treasure foremost.

dn17:2.5.12.verse: He had 84,000 milk-cows with silken halter and bronze pails.

dn17:2.5.13.verse: He had 8,400,000,000 cloths of delicate linen, cotton, silk, and wool.

dn17:2.5.14.verse: He had 84,000 servings of food, which were presented to him as offerings at daybreak and dusk.

dn17:2.6.1.verse: Now at that time his 84,000 royal elephants came to attend on him at daybreak and dusk.

dn17:2.6.3.verse: ‘What if instead half of the elephants took turns to attend on me at the end of each century?’

dn17:2.6.4.verse: He instructed the commander-treasure to do this, and so it was done.

dn17:2.7.1.verse: Then, after many years, many hundred years, many thousand years had passed, Queen Subhaddā thought,

dn17:2.7.2.verse: ‘It is long since I have seen the king. Why don’t I go to see him?’

dn17:2.7.3.verse: So the queen addressed the ladies of the harem,

dn17:2.7.4.verse: ‘Come, bathe your heads and dress in yellow.

dn17:2.7.5.verse: It is long since we saw the king, and we shall go to see him.’

dn17:2.7.6.verse: ‘Yes, ma’am,’ replied the ladies of the harem. They did as she asked and returned to the queen.

dn17:2.8.1.verse: Then the queen addressed the commander-treasure,

dn17:2.8.2.verse: ‘Dear commander-treasure, please ready the army of four divisions. It is long since we saw the king, and we shall go to see him.’

dn17:2.8.3.verse: ‘Yes, my queen,’ he replied, and did as he was asked. He informed the queen,

dn17:2.8.4.verse: ‘My queen, the army of four divisions is ready,

dn17:2.8.6.verse: Then Queen Subhaddā together with the ladies of the harem went with the army to the Palace of Principle. She ascended the palace and went to the Chamber of the Grand Tower,

dn17:2.8.7.verse: where she stood leaning against a door-post.

dn17:2.8.9.verse: ‘What’s that, it sounds like a big crowd!’ Coming out of the chamber he saw Queen Subhaddā leaning against a door-post and said to her,

dn17:2.8.10.verse: ‘Please stay there, my queen, don’t enter in here.’

dn17:2.9.1.verse: Then he addressed a certain man,

dn17:2.9.2.verse: ‘Come, my man, bring the golden couch from the Chamber of the Grand Tower and set it up in the golden palm grove.’

dn17:2.9.3.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ that man replied, and did as he was asked.

dn17:2.9.4.verse: The king laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware.

dn17:2.10.2.verse: ‘The king’s faculties are so very clear, and the complexion of his skin is pure and bright. Let him not pass away!’ She said to him,

dn17:2.10.3.verse: ‘Your Majesty, you have 84,000 cities, with the royal capital of Kusāvatī foremost.

dn17:2.10.4.verse: Arouse desire for these! Take an interest in life!’

dn17:2.10.5.verse: And she likewise urged the king to live on by taking an interest in all his possessions as described above.

dn17:2.11.1.verse: When the queen had spoken, the king said to her,

dn17:2.11.2.verse: ‘For a long time, my queen, you have spoken to me with words that are welcome, desirable, agreeable, and pleasant.

dn17:2.11.3.verse: And yet in my final hour, your words are unwelcome, undesirable, disagreeable, and unpleasant!’

dn17:2.11.4.verse: ‘So how then, Your Majesty, am I to speak to you?’

dn17:2.11.6.verse: “Your Majesty, we must be parted and separated from all we hold dear and beloved. Don’t pass away with concerns. Such concern is suffering, and it’s criticized.

dn17:2.11.7.verse: Your Majesty, you have 84,000 cities, with the royal capital of Kusāvatī foremost.

dn17:2.11.8.verse: Give up desire for these! Take no interest in life!”’

dn17:2.11.9.verse: And so on for all the king’s possessions.

dn17:2.12.1.verse: When the king had spoken, Queen Subhaddā cried and burst out in tears.

dn17:2.12.2.verse: Wiping away her tears, the queen said to the king:

dn17:2.12.3.verse: ‘Your Majesty, we must be parted and separated from all we hold dear and beloved. Don’t pass away with concerns. Such concern is suffering, and it’s criticized.

dn17:2.12.4.verse: Your Majesty, you have 84,000 cities, with the royal capital of Kusāvatī foremost.

dn17:2.12.5.verse: Give up desire for these! Take no interest in life!’

dn17:2.12.6.verse: And she continued, listing all the king’s possessions.

dn17:2.13.0.verse: 8. Rebirth in the Realm of Divinity

dn17:2.13.1.verse: Not long after that, King Mahāsudassana passed away.

dn17:2.13.2.verse: And the feeling he had close to death was like a householder or their child falling asleep after eating a satisfying meal.

dn17:2.13.3.verse: When he passed away King Mahāsudassana was reborn in a good place, a realm of divinity.

dn17:2.13.4.verse: Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana played children’s games for 84,000 years.

dn17:2.13.5.verse: He ruled as viceroy for 84,000 years.

dn17:2.13.6.verse: He ruled as king for 84,000 years.

dn17:2.13.7.verse: He led the spiritual life as a layman in the Palace of Principle for 84,000 years.

dn17:2.13.8.verse: And having developed the four divine meditations, when his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in a good place, a realm of divinity.

dn17:2.14.2.verse: ‘Surely King Mahāsudassana must have been someone else at that time?’

dn17:2.14.3.verse: But you should not see it like that. I myself was King Mahāsudassana at that time.

dn17:2.14.4.verse: Mine were the 84,000 cities, with the royal capital of Kusāvatī foremost. And mine were all the other possessions.

dn17:2.15.1.verse: Of those 84,000 cities, I only stayed in one, the capital Kusāvatī.

dn17:2.15.2.verse: Of those 84,000 palaces, I only dwelt in one, the Palace of Principle.

dn17:2.15.3.verse: Of those 84,000 chambers, I only dwelt in the Chamber of the Grand Tower.

dn17:2.15.4.verse: Of those 84,000 couches, I only used one, made of gold or silver or ivory or heartwood.

dn17:2.15.5.verse: Of those 84,000 bull elephants, I only rode one, the royal bull elephant named Sabbath.

dn17:2.15.6.verse: Of those 84,000 horses, I only rode one, the royal horse named Thundercloud.

dn17:2.15.7.verse: Of those 84,000 chariots, I only rode one, the chariot named Triumph.

dn17:2.15.8.verse: Of those 84,000 women, I was only served by one, an aristocrat maiden or a coquette.

dn17:2.15.9.verse: Of those 8,400,000,000 cloths, I only wore one pair, made of delicate linen, cotton, silk, or wool.

dn17:2.15.10.verse: Of those 84,000 servings of food, I only had one, eating at most a cup of rice with suitable sauce.

dn17:2.16.1.verse: See, Ānanda! All those conditioned phenomena have passed, ceased, and perished.

dn17:2.16.5.verse: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.

dn17:2.17.1.verse: Six times, Ānanda, I recall having laid down my body at this place. And the seventh time was as a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king, at which time my dominion extended to all four sides, I achieved stability in the country, and I possessed the seven treasures.

dn17:2.17.2.verse: But Ānanda, I do not see any place in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans where the Realized One would lay down his body for the eighth time.”

dn17:2.17.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn17:2.17.4.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn17:2.17.6.verse: their nature is to rise and fall;

dn18:1.0.verse: 1. Declaring the Rebirths of People From Ñātika and Elsewhere

dn18:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying at Ñātika in the brick house.

dn18:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was explaining the rebirths of devotees all over the nations; the Kāsis and Kosalans, Vajjis and Mallas, Cetīs and Vacchas, Kurus and Pañcālas, Macchas and Sūrasenas:

dn18:1.4.verse: “This one was reborn here, while that one was reborn there.

dn18:1.5.verse: Over fifty devotees in Ñātika have passed away having ended the five lower fetters. They’ve been reborn spontaneously, and will be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.

dn18:1.6.verse: More than ninety devotees in Ñātika have passed away having ended three fetters, and weakened greed, hate, and delusion. They’re once-returners, who will come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

dn18:1.7.verse: More than five hundred devotees in Ñātika have passed away having ended three fetters. They’re stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

dn18:2.1.verse: When the devotees of Ñātika heard about the Buddha’s

dn18:2.7.verse: answers to those questions, they became uplifted and overjoyed, full of rapture and happiness.

dn18:3.1.verse: Venerable Ānanda heard of the Buddha’s statements and the Ñātikans’ happiness.

dn18:4.2.verse: “But there were also Magadhan devotees—many, and of long standing too—who have passed away.

dn18:4.3.verse: You’d think that Aṅga and Magadha were empty of devotees who have passed away!

dn18:4.4.verse: But they too had confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and had fulfilled their ethics.

dn18:4.5.verse: The Buddha hasn’t declared their passing.

dn18:4.6.verse: It would be good to do so, for many people would gain confidence, and so be reborn in a good place.

dn18:4.7.verse: That King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was a just and principled king who benefited the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country.

dn18:4.9.verse: ‘That just and principled king, who made us so happy, has passed away. Life was good under his dominion.’

dn18:4.10.verse: He too had confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and had fulfilled his ethics.

dn18:4.12.verse: ‘Until his dying day, King Bimbisāra sang the Buddha’s praises!’

dn18:4.13.verse: The Buddha hasn’t declared his passing.

dn18:4.14.verse: It would be good to do so, for many people would gain confidence, and so be reborn in a good place.

dn18:4.15.verse: Besides, the Buddha was awakened in Magadha;

dn18:4.16.verse: so why hasn’t he declared the rebirth of the Magadhan devotees?

dn18:4.17.verse: If he fails to do so, they will be disheartened.”

dn18:5.1.verse: After pondering the fate of the Magadhan devotees alone in private, Ānanda rose at the crack of dawn and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and told the Buddha of his concerns, finishing by saying,

dn18:6.9.verse: “Why hasn’t the Buddha declared the rebirth of the Magadhan devotees? If he fails to do so, they will be disheartened.”

dn18:6.10.verse: Then Ānanda, after making this suggestion regarding the Magadhan devotees, rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

dn18:7.1.verse: Soon after Ānanda had left, the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Ñātika for alms.

dn18:7.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Ñātika. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he washed his feet and entered the brick house. He paid attention, applied the mind, and concentrated wholeheartedly on the fate of Magadhan devotees, and sat down on the seat spread out, thinking,

dn18:7.3.verse: “I shall know their destiny, where they are reborn in the next life.”

dn18:7.4.verse: And he saw where they had been reborn.

dn18:7.6.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat. Emerging from the brick house, he sat down on the seat spread out in the shade of the porch.

dn18:8.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn18:8.2.verse: “Sir, you look so serene; your face seems to shine owing to the clarity of your faculties.

dn18:8.3.verse: Have you been abiding in a peaceful meditation today, sir?”

dn18:9.1.verse: The Buddha then recounted what had happened since speaking to Ānanda, revealing that he had seen the destiny of the Magadhan devotees. He continued:

dn18:9.5.verse: “Then, Ānanda, an invisible spirit called out:

dn18:9.8.verse: Ānanda, do you recall having previously heard such a name as Janavasabha?”

dn18:9.9.verse: “No, worthy sir. But when I heard the word, I got goosebumps!

dn18:9.11.verse: ‘This must be no ordinary spirit to bear such an exalted name as Janavasabha.’”

dn18:10.1.verse: “After making himself heard while invisible, Ānanda, an exceptionally beautiful spirit appeared in front of me.

dn18:10.2.verse: And for a second time he called out:

dn18:10.5.verse: This is the seventh time I am reborn in the company of the Great King Vessavaṇa. When I pass away from here, I can become a king of men.

dn18:10.6.verse: Seven from here, seven from there—

dn18:10.10.verse: For a long time I’ve known that I won’t be reborn in the underworld, but that I still hope to become a once-returner.’

dn18:10.11.verse: ‘It’s incredible and amazing that you, the venerable spirit Janavasabha, should say:

dn18:10.12.verse: “For a long time I’ve been aware that I won’t be reborn in the underworld” and also “But I still hope to become a once-returner.” But from what source do you know that you’ve achieved such a high distinction?’

dn18:11.1.verse: ‘None other than the Blessed One’s instruction! None other than the Holy One’s instruction!

dn18:11.2.verse: From the day I had absolute devotion to the Buddha I have known that I won’t be reborn in the underworld, but that I still hope to become a once-returner.

dn18:11.3.verse: Just now, sir, I had been sent out by the great king Vessavaṇa to the great king Virūḷhaka’s presence on some business, and on the way I saw the Buddha giving his attention to the fate of the Magadhan devotees.

dn18:11.5.verse: But it comes as no surprise that I have heard and learned the fate of the Magadhan devotees in the presence of the great king Vessavaṇa as he was speaking to his assembly.

dn18:11.8.verse: “I shall see the Buddha and inform him of this.”

dn18:11.9.verse: These are the two reasons I’ve come to see the Buddha.

dn18:12.1.verse: Sir, it was more than a few days ago—on the fifteenth day sabbath on the full moon day at the entry to the rainy season—when all the gods of the thirty-three were sitting together in the Hall of Clear Right.

dn18:12.2.verse: A large assembly of gods was sitting all around, and the four great kings were seated at the four quarters.

dn18:12.3.verse: The Great King Dhataraṭṭha was seated to the east, facing west, in front of his gods.

dn18:12.4.verse: The Great King Virūḷhaka was seated to the south, facing north, in front of his gods.

dn18:12.5.verse: The Great King Virūpakkha was seated to the west, facing east, in front of his gods.

dn18:12.6.verse: The Great King Vessavaṇa was seated to the north, facing south, in front of his gods.

dn18:12.7.verse: When the gods of the thirty-three have a gathering like this, that is how they are seated.

dn18:12.9.verse: Sir, those gods who had been recently reborn in the company of the thirty-three after leading the spiritual life under the Buddha outshone the other gods in beauty and glory.

dn18:12.10.verse: The gods of the thirty-three became uplifted and overjoyed at that, full of rapture and happiness, saying,

dn18:12.11.verse: “The heavenly hosts swell, while the titan hosts dwindle!”

dn18:13.1.verse: Seeing the joy of those gods, Sakka, lord of gods, celebrated with these verses:

dn18:13.5.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching;

dn18:13.8.verse: who have come here after leading

dn18:13.9.verse: the spiritual life under the Buddha!

dn18:13.13.verse: of he whose wisdom is vast.

dn18:13.17.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching.”

dn18:13.18.verse: The gods of the thirty-three became even more uplifted and overjoyed at that, saying:

dn18:13.19.verse: “The heavenly hosts swell, while the titan hosts dwindle!”

dn18:14.1.verse: Then the gods of the thirty-three, having considered and deliberated on the matter for which they were seated together in the Hall of Clear Right, advised and instructed the four great kings on the subject.

dn18:14.2.verse: Each one, having been advised, stood at his own seat without leaving.

dn18:14.6.verse: they stood by their own seats.

dn18:15.1.verse: Then in the northern quarter a magnificent light arose and radiance appeared, surpassing the glory of the gods.

dn18:15.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three,

dn18:15.3.verse: “As indicated by the signs—light arising and radiance appearing—The Divinity will appear. For this is the harbinger for the appearance of the Divinity, namely light arising and radiance appearing.”

dn18:15.6.verse: For this is the sign of the Divinity:

dn18:16.1.verse: Then the gods of the thirty-three sat in their own seats, saying,

dn18:16.2.verse: “We shall find out what has caused that light, and only when we have realized it shall we go to it.”

dn18:16.3.verse: And the four great kings did likewise.

dn18:16.5.verse: Hearing that, the gods of the thirty-three agreed in unison,

dn18:16.6.verse: “We shall find out what has caused that light, and only when we have realized it shall we go to it.”

dn18:17.1.verse: When the divinity Sanaṅkumāra appears to the gods of the thirty-three, he does so after manifesting a solid incarnation.

dn18:17.2.verse: For a Divinity’s normal appearance is imperceptible in the visual range of the gods of the thirty-three.

dn18:17.3.verse: When the divinity Sanaṅkumāra appears to the gods of the thirty-three, he outshines the other gods in beauty and glory,

dn18:17.4.verse: as a golden statue outshines the human form.

dn18:17.6.verse: When the divinity Sanaṅkumāra appears to the gods of the thirty-three, not a single god in that assembly greets him by bowing down or rising up or inviting him to a seat.

dn18:17.7.verse: They all sit silently on their couches with their cupped palms raised, thinking,

dn18:17.8.verse: “Now the divinity Sanaṅkumāra will sit on the couch of whatever god he chooses.”

dn18:17.9.verse: And the god on whose couch the Divinity sits is overjoyed and brimming with happiness,

dn18:18.1.verse: like a king on the day of his coronation.

dn18:18.3.verse: Then the divinity Sanaṅkumāra manifested a solid incarnation, taking on the appearance of the youth Pañcasikha, and appeared to the gods of the thirty-three.

dn18:18.4.verse: Rising into the air, he sat cross-legged in the sky,

dn18:18.5.verse: like a strong man might sit cross-legged on a well-appointed couch or on level ground.

dn18:18.6.verse: Seeing the joy of those gods, the divinity Sanaṅkumāra celebrated with these verses:

dn18:18.10.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching;

dn18:18.13.verse: who have come here after leading

dn18:18.14.verse: the spiritual life under the Buddha!

dn18:18.18.verse: of he whose wisdom is vast.

dn18:18.22.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching!”

dn18:19.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke.

dn18:19.2.verse: And while he was speaking on that topic, his voice had eight qualities: it was clear, comprehensible, charming, audible, lucid, undistorted, deep, and resonant.

dn18:19.3.verse: He makes sure his voice is intelligible as far as the assembly goes, but the sound doesn’t extend outside the assembly.

dn18:19.4.verse: When someone has a voice like this, they’re said to have the voice of the Divinity.

dn18:20.1.verse: Then the divinity Sanaṅkumāra, having manifested thirty-three life-forms, sat down on the couches of each of the gods of the thirty-three and addressed them,

dn18:20.2.verse: “What do the good gods of the thirty-three think? How the Buddha has acted for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans!

dn18:20.3.verse: For consider those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and have fulfilled their ethics. When their bodies break up, after death, some are reborn in the company of the gods who control what is created by others, some with the gods who love to create, some with the joyful gods, some with the gods of Yama, some with the gods of the thirty-three, and some with the gods of the four great kings.

dn18:20.4.verse: And at the very least they swell the hosts of the centaurs.”

dn18:21.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke.

dn18:21.2.verse: And hearing the sound of the Divinity speaking on that topic, the gods fancied,

dn18:21.3.verse: “The one sitting on my couch is the only one speaking.”

dn18:21.10.verse: that the one on their seat

dn18:21.11.verse: is the only one to speak.

dn18:22.1.verse: Next the divinity Sanaṅkumāra merged into one corporeal form. Then he sat on the couch of Sakka, lord of gods, and addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

dn18:22.2.0.verse: 6. Developing the Bases of Psychic Power

dn18:22.3.verse: “What do the good gods of the thirty-three think? How well described by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha—are the four bases of psychic power! They are taught for the amplification, burgeoning, and transformation of psychic power.

dn18:22.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort.

dn18:22.6.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy, and active effort.

dn18:22.7.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to mental development, and active effort.

dn18:22.8.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to inquiry, and active effort.

dn18:22.9.verse: These are the four bases of psychic power taught by the Buddha for the amplification, burgeoning, and transformation of psychic power.

dn18:22.10.verse: All the ascetics and brahmins in the past,

dn18:22.12.verse: or present who wield the many kinds of psychic power do so by developing and cultivating these four bases of psychic power.

dn18:22.13.verse: Gentlemen, do you see such psychic might and power in me?”

dn18:22.15.verse: “I too became so mighty and powerful by developing and cultivating these four bases of psychic power.”

dn18:23.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke.

dn18:23.2.verse: And having spoken about that, he addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

dn18:23.4.verse: “What do the good gods of the thirty-three think? How well understood by the Buddha are the three opportunities for achieving happiness!

dn18:23.6.verse: First, take someone who lives mixed up with sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

dn18:23.7.verse: After some time they hear the teaching of the noble ones, rationally apply the mind to how it applies to them, and practice in line with the teaching.

dn18:23.8.verse: They live aloof from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

dn18:23.9.verse: That gives rise to pleasure, and more than pleasure, happiness,

dn18:23.10.verse: like the joy that’s born from gladness.

dn18:23.12.verse: This is the first opportunity for achieving happiness.

dn18:24.1.verse: Next, take someone whose coarse physical, verbal, and mental processes have not died down.

dn18:24.2.verse: After some time they hear the teaching of the noble ones, rationally apply the mind to how it applies to them, and practice in line with the teaching.

dn18:24.3.verse: Their coarse physical, verbal, and mental processes die down.

dn18:24.4.verse: That gives rise to pleasure, and more than pleasure, happiness,

dn18:24.5.verse: like the joy that’s born from gladness.

dn18:24.7.verse: This is the second opportunity for achieving happiness.

dn18:25.1.verse: Next, take someone who doesn’t truly understand what is skillful and what is unskillful,

dn18:25.2.verse: what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, and what has a portion of dark or bright.

dn18:25.3.verse: After some time they hear the teaching of the noble ones, rationally apply the mind to how it applies to them, and practice in line with the teaching.

dn18:25.4.verse: They truly understand what is skillful and what is unskillful, and so on.

dn18:25.6.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises.

dn18:25.7.verse: That gives rise to pleasure, and more than pleasure, happiness,

dn18:25.8.verse: like the joy that’s born from gladness.

dn18:25.10.verse: This is the third opportunity for achieving happiness.

dn18:25.11.verse: These are the three opportunities for achieving happiness that have been understood by the Buddha.”

dn18:26.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke.

dn18:26.2.verse: And having spoken about that, he addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

dn18:26.4.verse: “What do the good gods of the thirty-three think? How well described by the Buddha are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation! They are taught for achieving what is skillful.

dn18:26.6.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body internally—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn18:26.7.verse: As they meditate in this way, they become rightly immersed in that, and rightly serene.

dn18:26.8.verse: Then they give rise to knowledge and vision of other people’s bodies externally.

dn18:26.9.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings internally …

dn18:26.10.verse: Then they give rise to knowledge and vision of other people’s feelings externally.

dn18:26.11.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind internally …

dn18:26.12.verse: Then they give rise to knowledge and vision of other people’s minds externally.

dn18:26.13.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles internally—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn18:26.14.verse: As they meditate in this way, they become rightly immersed in that, and rightly serene.

dn18:26.15.verse: Then they give rise to knowledge and vision of other people’s principles externally.

dn18:26.16.verse: These are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation taught by the Buddha for achieving what is skillful.”

dn18:27.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke.

dn18:27.2.verse: And having spoken about that, he addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

dn18:27.4.verse: “What do the good gods of the thirty-three think? How well described by the Buddha are the seven prerequisites of immersion for the development and fulfillment of right immersion!

dn18:27.6.verse: Right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.

dn18:27.7.verse: Unification of mind with these seven factors as prerequisites is called noble right immersion ‘with its vital conditions’ and also ‘with its prerequisites’.

dn18:27.8.verse: Right view produces right purpose. Right purpose produces right speech. Right speech produces right action. Right action produces right livelihood. Right livelihood produces right effort. Right effort produces right mindfulness. Right mindfulness produces right immersion. Right immersion produces right knowledge. Right knowledge produces right freedom.

dn18:27.9.verse: If anything should be rightly described as

dn18:27.10.verse: ‘a teaching that’s well explained by the Buddha, apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves; and the doors to freedom from death are flung open,’ it’s this.

dn18:27.11.verse: For the teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves—and the doors to freedom from death are flung open.

dn18:27.12.verse: Whoever has experiential confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and has the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones; and whoever is spontaneously reborn, and is trained in the teaching; more than 2,400,000 such Magadhan devotees have passed away having ended three fetters. They’re stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

dn18:27.13.verse: And there are once-returners here, too.

dn18:27.14.verse: And as for the rest of folk,

dn18:27.15.verse: who I think have shared in merit—

dn18:28.1.verse: That is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke. And while he was speaking on that topic, this thought came to the great king Vessavaṇa,

dn18:28.2.verse: “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! That there should be such a magnificent Teacher, and such a magnificent exposition of the teaching! And that such achievements of high distinction should be made known!”

dn18:28.3.verse: And then the divinity Sanaṅkumāra, knowing the great king Vessavaṇa’s train of thought, said to him,

dn18:28.4.verse: “What does Great King Vessavaṇa think? In the past, too, there was such a magnificent Teacher, and such a magnificent exposition of the teaching! And such achievements of high distinction were made known!

dn18:28.5.verse: In the future, too, there will be such a magnificent Teacher, and such a magnificent exposition of the teaching! And such achievements of high distinction will be made known!”

dn18:29.1.verse: That, sir, is the topic on which the divinity Sanaṅkumāra spoke to the gods of the thirty-three. And the great king Vessavaṇa, having heard and learned it in the presence of the Divinity as he was speaking on that topic, informed his own assembly.’”

dn18:29.2.verse: And the spirit Janavasabha, having heard and learned it in the presence of the great king Vessavaṇa as he was speaking on that topic to his own assembly, informed the Buddha.

dn18:29.3.verse: And the Buddha, having heard and learned it in the presence of the spirit Janavasabha, and also from his own direct knowledge, informed Venerable Ānanda. And Venerable Ānanda, having heard and learned it in the presence of the Buddha, informed the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

dn18:29.4.verse: And that’s how this spiritual life has become successful and prosperous, extensive, popular, widespread, and fully revealed among gods and humans.

dn19:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

dn19:1.3.verse: Then, late at night, the centaur Pañcasikha, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

dn19:1.4.verse: “Sir, I would tell you of what I heard and learned directly from the gods of the thirty-three.”

dn19:2.1.verse: “Sir, it was more than a few days ago—on the fifteenth day sabbath on the full moon day at the invitation to admonish held at the end of the rainy season—when all the gods of the thirty-three were sitting together in the Hall of Clear Right.

dn19:2.2.verse: A large assembly of gods was sitting all around, and the four great kings were seated at the four quarters.

dn19:2.3.verse: The Great King Dhataraṭṭha was seated to the east, facing west, in front of his gods.

dn19:2.4.verse: The Great King Virūḷhaka was seated to the south, facing north, in front of his gods.

dn19:2.5.verse: The Great King Virūpakkha was seated to the west, facing east, in front of his gods.

dn19:2.6.verse: The Great King Vessavaṇa was seated to the north, facing south, in front of his gods.

dn19:2.7.verse: When the gods of the thirty-three have a gathering like this, that is how they are seated.

dn19:3.1.verse: Sir, those gods who had been recently reborn in the company of the thirty-three after leading the spiritual life under the Buddha outshine the other gods in beauty and glory.

dn19:3.2.verse: The gods of the thirty-three became uplifted and overjoyed at that, full of rapture and happiness, saying,

dn19:3.3.verse: ‘The heavenly hosts swell, while the titan hosts dwindle!’

dn19:3.4.verse: Seeing the joy of those gods, Sakka, lord of gods, celebrated with these verses:

dn19:3.8.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching;

dn19:3.11.verse: who have come here after leading

dn19:3.12.verse: the spiritual life under the Buddha!

dn19:3.16.verse: of he whose wisdom is vast.

dn19:3.20.verse: and the clear rightness of the teaching!’

dn19:3.21.verse: The gods of the thirty-three became even more uplifted and overjoyed at that, full of rapture and happiness, saying,

dn19:3.22.verse: ‘The heavenly hosts swell, while the titan hosts dwindle!’

dn19:4.1.verse: Seeing the joy of those gods, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed them,

dn19:4.2.verse: ‘Gentlemen, would you like to hear eight genuine praises of the Buddha?’

dn19:4.4.verse: Then Sakka proffered these eight genuine praises of the Buddha:

dn19:5.1.verse: ‘What do the good gods of the thirty-three think?

dn19:5.2.verse: How the Buddha has acted for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans!

dn19:5.3.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who has such sympathy for the world, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:6.1.verse: Also, the Buddha has explained the teaching well—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

dn19:6.2.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who explains such a relevant teaching, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:7.1.verse: Also, the Buddha has well described what is skillful and what is unskillful,

dn19:7.2.verse: what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, and what has a portion of dark or bright.

dn19:7.3.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who so clearly describes all these things, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:8.1.verse: Also, the Buddha has well described the practice that leads to extinguishment for his disciples. And extinguishment converges with the practice,

dn19:8.2.verse: as the waters of the Ganges join together and converge with the waters of the Yamunā.

dn19:8.4.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who so clearly describes the practice that leads to extinguishment for his disciples, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:9.1.verse: Also, possessions and popularity have accrued to the Buddha, so much that you’d think it would thrill even the aristocrats. But he takes his food free of vanity.

dn19:9.2.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who takes their food so free of vanity, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:10.1.verse: Also, the Buddha has gained companions, both trainees who are practicing, and those with defilements ended who have completed their journey.

dn19:10.2.verse: The Buddha is committed to the joy of solitude, but doesn’t send them away.

dn19:10.3.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, so committed to the joy of solitude, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:11.1.verse: Also, the Buddha does as he says, and says as he does, thus: he does as he says, and says as he does.

dn19:11.2.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who so practices in line with the teaching, apart from the Buddha.

dn19:12.1.verse: Also, the Buddha has gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision. He has achieved all he wished for regarding the fundamental goal of the spiritual life.

dn19:12.2.verse: I don’t see any Teacher, past or present, who has achieved these things, apart from the Buddha.’

dn19:29.1.verse: Once upon a time, there was a king named Disampati.

dn19:29.2.verse: He had a brahmin high priest named the Steward.

dn19:29.3.verse: Disampati’s son was the prince named Reṇu,

dn19:29.4.verse: while the Steward’s son was the student named Jotipāla.

dn19:29.5.verse: There were Reṇu the prince, Jotipāla the student, and six other aristocrats; these eight became friends.

dn19:29.6.verse: In due course the brahmin Steward passed away.

dn19:29.7.verse: At his passing, King Disampati lamented,

dn19:29.8.verse: “At a time when I have relinquished all my duties to the brahmin Steward and amuse myself, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation, he passes away!”

dn19:29.9.verse: When he said this, Prince Reṇu said to him,

dn19:29.10.verse: “Your Majesty, don’t lament too much at the Steward’s passing.

dn19:29.11.verse: He has a son named Jotipāla, who is even more astute and expert than his father.

dn19:29.12.verse: He should manage the affairs that were managed by his father.”

dn19:30.0.verse: 6. The Story of the Great Steward

dn19:30.1.verse: So King Disampati addressed one of his men,

dn19:30.2.verse: “Please, my man, go to the student Jotipāla, and say to him,

dn19:30.3.verse: ‘Best wishes, Jotipāla! You are summoned by King Disampati; he wants to see you.’”

dn19:30.4.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied that man, and did as he was asked.

dn19:30.6.verse: Then Jotipāla went to the king and exchanged greetings with him.

dn19:30.7.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and the king said to him,

dn19:30.8.verse: “May you, Jotipāla, manage my affairs—please don’t turn me down!

dn19:30.9.verse: I shall appoint you to your father’s position, and anoint you as Steward.”

dn19:31.1.verse: So the king anointed him as Steward and appointed him to his father’s position.

dn19:31.2.verse: After his appointment, the Steward Jotipāla managed both the affairs that his father had managed, and other affairs that his father had not managed.

dn19:31.3.verse: He organized both the works that his father had organized, and other works that his father had not organized.

dn19:31.4.verse: When people noticed this they said,

dn19:31.5.verse: “The brahmin is indeed a Steward, a Great Steward!”

dn19:31.6.verse: And that’s how the student Jotipāla came to be known as the Great Steward.

dn19:59.1.verse: And the Great Steward meditated spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. dn19:59.2.verse: He meditated spreading a heart full of compassion …

dn19:59.4.verse: equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, he spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn19:59.5.verse: And he taught his disciples the path to rebirth in the company of Divinity.

dn19:60.1.verse: Those of his disciples who completely understood the Great Steward’s instructions,

dn19:60.2.verse: at the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in the realm of divinity.

dn19:60.3.verse: Of those disciples who only partly understood the Great Steward’s instructions, some were reborn in the company of the gods who control what is created by others,

dn19:60.4.verse: while some were reborn in the company of the gods who love to create,

dn19:60.7.verse: or the gods of the thirty-three,

dn19:60.8.verse: or the gods of the four great kings.

dn19:60.9.verse: And at the very least they swelled the hosts of the centaurs.

dn19:60.10.verse: And so the going forth of all those gentlemen was not in vain, was not barren, but was fruitful and fertile.’

dn19:60.11.verse: Do you remember this, Blessed One?”

dn19:61.2.verse: I myself was the brahmin Great Steward at that time.

dn19:61.3.verse: And I taught those disciples the path to rebirth in the company of Divinity.

dn19:61.4.verse: But that spiritual path of mine doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the realm of divinity.

dn19:61.5.verse: But this spiritual path does lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

dn19:61.6.verse: And what is the spiritual path that leads to extinguishment?

dn19:61.7.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

dn19:61.8.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

dn19:61.9.verse: This is the spiritual path that leads to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

dn19:62.1.verse: Those of my disciples who completely understand my instructions realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

dn19:62.2.verse: Of those disciples who only partly understand my instructions, some, with the ending of the five lower fetters, become reborn spontaneously. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

dn19:62.3.verse: Some, with the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, become once-returners. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

dn19:62.4.verse: And some, with the ending of three fetters, become stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

dn19:62.5.verse: And so the going forth of all those gentlemen was not in vain, was not barren, but was fruitful and fertile.”

dn19:62.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn19:62.7.verse: Delighted, the centaur Pañcasikha approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

dn20:1.3.verse: and almost all of the gods from the ten world-elements had assembled to see the Fortunate One and the Saṅgha of monks.

dn20:2.1.verse: Then this occurred to four gods from among the hosts in the Pure Abodes:

dn20:2.2.verse: “The Fortunate One is dwelling amongst the Sakyans in the Great Wood near Kapilavatthu with a great Saṅgha of moṅks consisting of five hundred monks, all of them Worthy Ones,

dn20:2.3.verse: and almost all of the gods from the ten world elements have assembled to see the Fortunate One and the Saṅgha of monks.

dn20:2.4.verse: Well now, we too could approach the Fortunate One, and after approaching the Fortunate One we could recite a verse each in his presence.”

dn20:3.1.verse: Then those gods, just as a strong man might stretch out a bent arm, or bend in an outstretched arm, in the same way disappeared from among the gods of the Pure Abodes and appeared in front of the Fortunate One.

dn20:3.2.verse: Then those gods after worshipping the Fortunate One, stood on one side.

dn20:3.3.verse: While standing on one side one of the gods recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

dn20:3.4.verse: “There is a great convention in the wood,

dn20:3.5.verse: and a host of gods have come,

dn20:3.6.verse: we have come to this Dhamma convention

dn20:3.7.verse: to see the Saṅgha, who are undefeated.”

dn20:3.8.verse: Then another god recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

dn20:3.9.verse: “In this place the monks are concentrated,

dn20:3.10.verse: they have straightened out their minds by themselves,

dn20:3.11.verse: like a charioteer who has taken the reins,

dn20:3.12.verse: the wise protect their sense faculties.”

dn20:3.13.verse: Then another god recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

dn20:3.14.verse: “Having cut off the hindrance and obstacle,

dn20:3.15.verse: and dug up the locking post, they are unmoved,

dn20:3.17.verse: young nāgas, well-tamed by the Visionary.”

dn20:3.19.verse: “Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge

dn20:3.20.verse: will not go to the lower worlds.

dn20:3.21.verse: After giving up the human body

dn20:3.22.verse: they will fill up the ranks of the gods.”
