dn21:1.1.6.verse: Seeing that the Buddha was at Indra’s hill cave,

dn21:1.1.7.verse: he addressed the gods of the thirty-three,

dn21:1.1.8.verse: “Good fellows, the Buddha is staying in the land of the Magadhans at Indra’s hill cave.

dn21:1.1.9.verse: What if we were to go and see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

dn21:1.2.1.verse: Then Sakka addressed the centaur Pañcasikha,

dn21:1.2.2.verse: “Dear Pañcasikha, the Buddha is staying in the land of the Magadhans at Indra’s hill cave.

dn21:1.2.3.verse: What if we were to go and see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

dn21:1.2.4.verse: “Yes, lord,” replied the centaur Pañcasikha. Taking his arched harp made from the pale timber of wood-apple, he went as Sakka’s attendant.

dn21:1.2.5.verse: Then Sakka went at the head of a retinue consisting of the gods of the thirty-three and the godling centaur Pañcasikha.

dn21:1.2.6.verse: As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the heaven of the gods of the thirty-three and landed on Mount Vediyaka north of Ambasaṇḍā.

dn21:1.3.1.verse: Now at that time a dazzling light appeared over Mount Vediyaka and Ambasaṇḍā, as happens through the glory of the gods.

dn21:1.3.2.verse: People in the villages round about, terrified, shocked, and awestruck, said,

dn21:1.3.3.verse: “Mount Vediyaka must be on fire today, blazing and burning!

dn21:1.3.4.verse: Oh why has such a dazzling light appeared over Mount Vediyaka and Ambasaṇḍā?”

dn21:1.4.1.verse: Then Sakka addressed the centaur Pañcasikha,

dn21:1.4.2.verse: “My dear Pañcasikha, it is hard for one like me to get near the Realized Ones while they are on retreat practicing absorption, enjoying absorption.

dn21:1.4.3.verse: But if you were to charm the Buddha first, then I could go to see him.”

dn21:1.4.4.verse: “Yes, lord,” replied the centaur Pañcasikha. Taking his arched harp made from the pale timber of wood-apple, he went to Indra’s hill cave. When he had drawn near, he stood to one side, thinking,

dn21:1.4.5.verse: “This is neither too far nor too near; and he’ll hear my voice.”

dn21:1.4.8.verse: Standing to one side, Pañcasikha played his arched harp, and sang these verses on the Buddha, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the perfected ones, and sensual love.

dn21:1.5.2.verse: I pay homage to your father Timbaru,

dn21:1.5.3.verse: through whom was born a lady so fine,

dn21:1.5.4.verse: to fill me with a joy I never knew.

dn21:1.5.5.verse: As sweet as a breeze to one who’s sweating,

dn21:1.5.6.verse: or when thirsty, a sweet and cooling drink,

dn21:1.5.7.verse: so dear are you, Aṅgīrasi, to me—

dn21:1.5.8.verse: just like the teaching is to all the saints!

dn21:1.5.9.verse: Like a cure when you’re struck by fever dire,

dn21:1.5.10.verse: or food to ease the hunger pain,

dn21:1.5.11.verse: come on, Bhaddā, please put out my fire,

dn21:1.5.12.verse: quench me like water on a flame.

dn21:1.5.13.verse: As elephants burning in the heat of summer,

dn21:1.5.14.verse: sink down in a lotus pond to rest,

dn21:1.5.15.verse: so cool, full of petals and of pollen—

dn21:1.5.16.verse: that’s how I would plunge into your breast.

dn21:1.5.17.verse: Like elephants bursting bonds in rutting season,

dn21:1.5.18.verse: beating off the pricks of lance and pikes—

dn21:1.5.19.verse: I just don’t understand what is the reason

dn21:1.5.20.verse: I’m so crazy for your shapely thighs!

dn21:1.5.21.verse: For you, my heart is full of passion,

dn21:1.5.22.verse: I’m in a besotted state of mind.

dn21:1.5.23.verse: There is no going back, I’m just not able,

dn21:1.5.24.verse: I’m like a fish that’s hooked up on the line.

dn21:1.5.25.verse: Come on, my Bhaddā, hold me, fair of thighs!

dn21:1.5.26.verse: Embrace me, maid of captivating eyes!

dn21:1.5.27.verse: Take me in your arms, my lovely lady,

dn21:1.5.28.verse: that’s all I’d ever want or could desire.

dn21:1.5.29.verse: Ah, then my desire was such a small thing,

dn21:1.5.30.verse: my sweet, with your curling wavy hair;

dn21:1.5.31.verse: now, like to arahants an offering,

dn21:1.5.32.verse: it’s grown so very much from there.

dn21:1.5.33.verse: Whatever the merit I have forged

dn21:1.5.34.verse: by giving to such perfected beings—

dn21:1.5.37.verse: Whatever the merit I have forged

dn21:1.5.41.verse: As the Sakyan, absorbed, did meditate

dn21:1.5.42.verse: at one, alert, and mindful too,

dn21:1.5.43.verse: the sage seeking the state free of death—

dn21:1.5.44.verse: so I, oh my Sunshine, seek for you!

dn21:1.5.45.verse: And just like the sage would delight,

dn21:1.5.46.verse: once he had awakened to the truth,

dn21:1.5.47.verse: so I would delight, my fine lady,

dn21:1.5.48.verse: were I to become one with you.

dn21:1.5.49.verse: If Sakka were to grant me one wish,

dn21:1.5.50.verse: as Lord of the Thirty and Three,

dn21:1.5.51.verse: my Bhaddā, you’re all I would wish for,

dn21:1.5.52.verse: so strong is the love in me.

dn21:1.5.53.verse: Like a freshly blossoming sal tree

dn21:1.5.54.verse: is your father, my lady so wise.

dn21:1.5.55.verse: I pay homage to he, bowing humbly,

dn21:1.5.56.verse: whose daughter is of such a kind.”

dn21:1.6.1.verse: When Pañcasikha had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

dn21:1.6.2.verse: “Pañcasikha, the sound of your strings blends well with the sound of your singing,

dn21:1.6.3.verse: so that neither overpowers the other.

dn21:1.6.4.verse: But when did you compose these verses on the Buddha, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the perfected ones, and sensual love?”

dn21:1.6.5.verse: “This one time, sir, when you were first awakened, you were staying in Uruvelā at the goatherd’s banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

dn21:1.6.6.verse: And at that time I was in love with Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, who they call ‘Darling Sunshine’, the daughter of the centaur king Timbaru.

dn21:1.6.8.verse: It was the one named Sikhaṇḍī, the son of Mātali the chariot handler, who she loved.

dn21:1.6.9.verse: Since I couldn’t win that sister by any means,

dn21:1.6.10.verse: I took my arched harp to Timbaru’s home, where I played those verses.

dn21:1.7.10.verse: When I finished, Suriyavaccasā said to me,

dn21:1.7.11.verse: ‘Good fellow, I have not personally seen the Buddha. But I did hear about him when I went to dance for the gods of the thirty-three in the Hall of Clear Right.

dn21:1.7.12.verse: Since you extol the Buddha, let us meet up today.’

dn21:1.7.13.verse: And that’s when I met up with that sister.

dn21:1.7.14.verse: But we have not met since.”

dn21:1.8.1.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, thought,

dn21:1.8.2.verse: “Pañcasikha is exchanging pleasantries with the Buddha.”

dn21:1.8.4.verse: “My dear Pañcasikha, please bow to the Buddha for me, saying:

dn21:1.8.5.verse: ‘Sir, Sakka, lord of gods, with his ministers and retinue, bows with his head at your feet.’”

dn21:1.8.6.verse: “Yes, lord,” replied Pañcasikha. He bowed to the Buddha and said,

dn21:1.8.7.verse: “Sir, Sakka, lord of gods, with his ministers and retinue, bows with his head at your feet.”

dn21:1.8.8.verse: “So may Sakka with his ministers and retinue be happy, Pañcasikha,” said the Buddha,

dn21:1.8.9.verse: “for all want to be happy—whether gods, humans, titans, dragons, centaurs, or any of the other diverse creatures there may be.”

dn21:1.8.10.verse: For that is how the Realized Ones salute such illustrious spirits.

dn21:1.8.11.verse: And being saluted by the Buddha, Sakka entered Indra’s hill cave, bowed to the Buddha, and stood to one side.

dn21:1.8.12.verse: And the gods of the thirty-three did likewise,

dn21:1.9.1.verse: And at that time the uneven places were evened out, the cramped places were opened up, the darkness vanished in the cave and light appeared, as happens through the glory of the gods.

dn21:1.9.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to Sakka,

dn21:1.9.3.verse: “It’s incredible and amazing that you, the venerable Kosiya, who has so many duties and so much to do, should come here.”

dn21:1.9.4.verse: “For a long time I’ve wanted to come and see the Buddha, but I wasn’t able, being prevented by my many duties and responsibilities for the gods of the thirty-three.

dn21:1.9.5.verse: This one time, sir, the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the salaḷa tree hut.

dn21:1.9.6.verse: Then I went to Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

dn21:1.10.1.verse: But at that time the Buddha was sitting immersed in some kind of meditation. And a divine maiden of Great King Vessavaṇa named Bhūjati was attending on the Buddha, standing there paying homage to him with cupped palms.

dn21:1.10.3.verse: ‘Sister, please bow to the Buddha for me, saying:

dn21:1.10.4.verse: “Sir, Sakka, lord of gods, with his ministers and retinue, bows with his head at your feet.”’

dn21:1.10.5.verse: When I said this, she said to me,

dn21:1.10.6.verse: ‘It’s the wrong time to see the Buddha,

dn21:1.10.8.verse: ‘Well then, sister, please convey my message when the Buddha emerges from that immersion.’

dn21:1.10.10.verse: I hope that sister bowed to you?

dn21:1.10.11.verse: Do you remember what she said?”

dn21:1.10.12.verse: “She did bow, lord of gods, and I remember what she said.

dn21:1.10.13.verse: I also remember that it was the sound of your chariot wheels that pulled me out of that immersion.”

dn21:1.11.1.verse: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the gods who were reborn in the host of the thirty-three before me:

dn21:1.11.2.verse: ‘When a Realized One arises in the world, perfected and fully awakened, the heavenly hosts swell, while the titan hosts dwindle.’

dn21:1.11.3.verse: And I have seen this with my own eyes.

dn21:1.11.5.verse: Right here in Kapilavatthu there was a Sakyan lady named Gopikā who had confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and had fulfilled her ethics.

dn21:1.11.6.verse: Losing her attachment to femininity, she developed masculinity. When her body broke up, after death, she was reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn21:1.11.7.verse: In the company of the gods of the thirty-three she became one of my sons.

dn21:1.11.10.verse: Meanwhile three others, mendicants who had led the spiritual life under the Buddha, were reborn in the inferior centaur realm.

dn21:1.11.11.verse: There they amused themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation, and became my servants and attendants.

dn21:1.11.13.verse: ‘Where on earth were you at, good fellows, when you heard the Buddha’s teaching!

dn21:1.11.14.verse: For while I was still a woman I had confidence in the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and had fulfilled my ethics. I lost my attachment to femininity and developed masculinity. When my body broke up, after death, I was reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm. In the company of the gods of the thirty-three I became one of Sakka’s sons.

dn21:1.11.17.verse: But you, having led the spiritual life under the Buddha, were reborn in the inferior centaur realm.

dn21:1.11.18.verse: It is a sad sight indeed to see fellow practitioners reborn in the inferior centaur realm.’

dn21:1.11.19.verse: When scolded by Gopaka, two of those gods regained their memory right away. They went to the host of the priests of Divinity, but one god remained attached to sensual pleasures.

dn21:1.12.1.verse: ‘“I was a laywoman disciple of the Clear-eyed One,

dn21:1.12.3.verse: I was devoted to the Buddha and the teaching,

dn21:1.12.4.verse: and I faithfully served the Saṅgha.

dn21:1.12.5.verse: Because of the clear rightness of the Buddha’s teaching,

dn21:1.12.6.verse: I’m now a mighty, dazzling son of Sakka,

dn21:1.12.8.verse: And here they know me as Gopaka.

dn21:1.12.9.verse: Then I saw some mendicants who I’d seen before,

dn21:1.12.10.verse: dwelling in the host of centaurs.

dn21:1.12.12.verse: when I used to be a human.

dn21:1.12.13.verse: I served them with food and drink,

dn21:1.12.14.verse: and clasped their feet in my own home.

dn21:1.12.15.verse: Where on earth were these good fellows at

dn21:1.12.16.verse: when they learned the Buddha’s teachings?

dn21:1.12.17.verse: For each must know for themselves the teaching

dn21:1.12.18.verse: so well-taught, realized by the Clear-eyed One.

dn21:1.12.19.verse: I was one who followed you,

dn21:1.12.20.verse: having heard the fine words of the noble ones.

dn21:1.12.21.verse: I’m now a mighty, dazzling son of Sakka,

dn21:1.12.23.verse: But you followed the best of men,

dn21:1.12.24.verse: and led the supreme spiritual life,

dn21:1.12.25.verse: but still you’re born in this lesser realm,

dn21:1.12.27.verse: It’s a sad sight I see, good fellows,

dn21:1.12.28.verse: fellow practitioners in a lesser realm.

dn21:1.12.29.verse: Reborn in the host of centaurs,

dn21:1.12.30.verse: only to wait upon the gods.

dn21:1.12.31.verse: Meanwhile, I dwelt in a house—

dn21:1.12.33.verse: Having been a woman now I’m a male god,

dn21:1.12.35.verse: Scolded by that disciple of Gotama,

dn21:1.12.36.verse: comprehending Gopaka, they were struck with urgency.

dn21:1.12.38.verse: we won’t serve others any more!”

dn21:1.12.39.verse: Two of them roused up energy,

dn21:1.12.42.verse: seeing the drawbacks in sensual pleasures.

dn21:1.12.43.verse: The fetters and bonds of sensual pleasures—

dn21:1.12.44.verse: the ties of the Wicked One so hard to break—

dn21:1.12.45.verse: they burst them like a bull elephant his ropes,

dn21:1.12.46.verse: and passed right over the thirty-three.

dn21:1.12.47.verse: The gods with Indra and the Progenitor

dn21:1.12.48.verse: were all gathered in the Hall of Clear Right.

dn21:1.12.49.verse: As they sat there, they passed over them,

dn21:1.12.51.verse: Seeing them, Vāsava was struck with urgency;

dn21:1.12.52.verse: the master of gods in the midst of the group said,

dn21:1.12.53.verse: “These were born in the lesser centaur realm,

dn21:1.12.54.verse: but now they pass us by!”

dn21:1.12.55.verse: Heeding the speech of one so moved,

dn21:1.12.57.verse: “There is a Buddha, a lord of men, in the world.

dn21:1.12.58.verse: Known as the Sakyan Sage, he’s mastered the senses.

dn21:1.12.59.verse: Those sons of his lost their memory;

dn21:1.12.60.verse: but when scolded by me they gained it back.

dn21:1.12.61.verse: Of the three, there is one who remains

dn21:1.12.62.verse: dwelling in the host of centaurs.

dn21:1.12.63.verse: But two, recollecting the path to awakening,

dn21:1.12.65.verse: Such is the explanation of the teaching here:

dn21:1.12.66.verse: not a single disciple doubts that.

dn21:1.12.67.verse: We venerate the Buddha, the victor, lord of men,

dn21:1.12.68.verse: who has crossed the flood and cut off doubt.

dn21:1.12.69.verse: They attained distinction to the extent

dn21:1.12.72.verse: in the host of the priests of Divinity.”’

dn21:1.12.73.verse: We have come here, dear sir,

dn21:1.12.75.verse: If the Buddha would give me a chance,

dn21:1.12.76.verse: I would ask a question, dear sir.”

dn21:1.13.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

dn21:1.13.2.verse: “For a long time now this spirit has led a pure life. Any question he asks me will be beneficial, not unbeneficial.

dn21:1.13.3.verse: And he will quickly understand any answer I give to his question.”

dn21:1.13.4.verse: So the Buddha addressed Sakka in verse:

dn21:1.13.9.verse: The first recitation section is complete.

dn21:2.1.1.verse: Having been granted an opportunity by the Buddha, Sakka asked the first question.

dn21:2.1.2.verse: “Good fellow, what fetters bind the gods, humans, titans, dragons, centaurs—and any of the other diverse creatures—

dn21:2.1.3.verse: so that, though they wish to be free of enmity, violence, hostility, and hate, they still have enmity, violence, hostility, and hate?”

dn21:2.1.4.verse: Such was Sakka’s question to the Buddha.

dn21:2.1.6.verse: “Lord of gods, the fetters of jealousy and stinginess bind the gods, humans, titans, dragons, centaurs—and any of the other diverse creatures—

dn21:2.1.7.verse: so that, though they wish to be free of enmity, violence, hostility, and hate, they still have enmity, violence, hostility, and hate.”

dn21:2.1.8.verse: Such was the Buddha’s answer to Sakka.

dn21:2.1.9.verse: Delighted, Sakka approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, saying,

dn21:2.1.10.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

dn21:2.1.11.verse: Hearing the Buddha’s answer, I’ve gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision.”

dn21:2.2.1.verse: And then, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, Sakka asked another question:

dn21:2.2.2.verse: “But good fellow, what is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of jealousy and stinginess?

dn21:2.2.3.verse: When what exists is there jealousy and stinginess?

dn21:2.2.4.verse: When what doesn’t exist is there no jealousy and stinginess?”

dn21:2.2.5.verse: “The liked and the disliked, lord of gods, are the source of jealousy and stinginess.

dn21:2.2.6.verse: When the liked and the disliked exist there is jealousy and stinginess.

dn21:2.2.7.verse: When the liked and the disliked don’t exist there is no jealousy and stinginess.”

dn21:2.2.8.verse: “But good fellow, what is the source of what is liked and disliked?”

dn21:2.2.11.verse: “Desire is the source of what is liked and disliked.”

dn21:2.2.14.verse: “But what is the source of desire?”

dn21:2.2.20.verse: “But what is the source of thought?”

dn21:2.2.23.verse: “Judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions are the source of thoughts.”

dn21:2.3.1.verse: “But how does a mendicant fittingly practice for the cessation of judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions?”

dn21:2.3.3.verse: “Lord of gods, there are two kinds of happiness, I say:

dn21:2.3.4.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.3.5.verse: There are two kinds of sadness, I say:

dn21:2.3.6.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.3.7.verse: There are two kinds of equanimity, I say:

dn21:2.3.8.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.3.9.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of happiness?

dn21:2.3.10.verse: Well, should you know of a happiness:

dn21:2.3.11.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of happiness, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not cultivate that kind of happiness.

dn21:2.3.12.verse: Whereas, should you know of a happiness:

dn21:2.3.13.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of happiness, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should cultivate that kind of happiness.

dn21:2.3.14.verse: And that which is free of placing the mind and keeping it connected is better than that which still involves placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn21:2.3.15.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of happiness.

dn21:2.3.17.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of sadness?

dn21:2.3.18.verse: Well, should you know of a sadness:

dn21:2.3.19.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of sadness, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not cultivate that kind of sadness.

dn21:2.3.20.verse: Whereas, should you know of a sadness:

dn21:2.3.21.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of sadness, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should cultivate that kind of sadness.

dn21:2.3.22.verse: And that which is free of placing the mind and keeping it connected is better than that which still involves placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn21:2.3.23.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of sadness.

dn21:2.3.25.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of equanimity?

dn21:2.3.26.verse: Well, should you know of an equanimity:

dn21:2.3.27.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of equanimity, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not cultivate that kind of equanimity.

dn21:2.3.28.verse: Whereas, should you know of an equanimity:

dn21:2.3.29.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of equanimity, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should cultivate that kind of equanimity.

dn21:2.3.30.verse: And that which is free of placing the mind and keeping it connected is better than that which still involves placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn21:2.3.31.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of equanimity.

dn21:2.3.33.verse: That’s how a mendicant fittingly practices for the cessation of judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions.”

dn21:2.3.34.verse: Such was the Buddha’s answer to Sakka.

dn21:2.3.35.verse: Delighted, Sakka approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, saying,

dn21:2.3.36.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

dn21:2.3.37.verse: Hearing the Buddha’s answer, I’ve gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision.”

dn21:2.4.1.verse: And then Sakka asked another question:

dn21:2.4.2.verse: “But good fellow, how does a mendicant practice for restraint in the monastic code?”

dn21:2.4.3.verse: “Lord of gods, I say that there are two kinds of bodily behavior:

dn21:2.4.4.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.4.5.verse: I say that there are two kinds of verbal behavior:

dn21:2.4.6.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.4.7.verse: There are two kinds of search, I say:

dn21:2.4.8.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.4.9.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of bodily behavior?

dn21:2.4.10.verse: Well, should you know of a bodily behavior:

dn21:2.4.11.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of bodily behavior, unskillful qualities grow, and skillful qualities decline.’ You should not cultivate that kind of bodily conduct.

dn21:2.4.12.verse: Whereas, should you know of a bodily behavior:

dn21:2.4.13.verse: ‘When I cultivate this kind of bodily behavior, unskillful qualities decline, and skillful qualities grow.’ You should cultivate that kind of bodily conduct.

dn21:2.4.14.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of bodily behavior.

dn21:2.4.17.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of verbal behavior?

dn21:2.4.19.verse: Well, should you know of a kind of verbal behavior that it causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline, you should not cultivate it.

dn21:2.4.20.verse: Whereas, should you know of a kind of verbal behavior that it causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow, you should cultivate it.

dn21:2.4.21.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of verbal behavior.

dn21:2.4.24.verse: Why did I say that there are two kinds of search?

dn21:2.4.26.verse: Well, should you know of a kind of search that it causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline, you should not cultivate it.

dn21:2.4.27.verse: Whereas, should you know of a kind of search that it causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow, you should cultivate it.

dn21:2.4.28.verse: That’s why I said there are two kinds of search.

dn21:2.4.31.verse: That’s how a mendicant practices for restraint in the monastic code.”

dn21:2.4.32.verse: Such was the Buddha’s answer to Sakka.

dn21:2.4.33.verse: Delighted, Sakka approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, saying,

dn21:2.4.34.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

dn21:2.4.35.verse: Hearing the Buddha’s answer, I’ve gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision.”

dn21:2.5.1.verse: And then Sakka asked another question:

dn21:2.5.2.verse: “But good fellow, how does a mendicant practice for restraint of the sense faculties?”

dn21:2.5.3.verse: “Lord of gods, I say that there are two kinds of sight known by the eye:

dn21:2.5.4.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

dn21:2.5.5.verse: There are two kinds of sound known by the ear …

dn21:2.5.14.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.”

dn21:2.5.15.verse: When the Buddha said this, Sakka said to him:

dn21:2.5.16.verse: “Sir, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement:

dn21:2.5.17.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of sight known by the eye which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

dn21:2.5.18.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of sight known by the eye which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

dn21:2.5.19.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of sound,

dn21:2.5.23.verse: or idea known by the mind which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

dn21:2.5.24.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of idea known by the mind which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

dn21:2.5.25.verse: Sir, that’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.

dn21:2.5.26.verse: Hearing the Buddha’s answer, I’ve gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision.”

dn21:2.6.1.verse: And then Sakka asked another question:

dn21:2.6.2.verse: “Good fellow, do all ascetics and brahmins have a single doctrine, ethics, desire, and attachment?”

dn21:2.6.3.verse: “No, lord of gods, they do not.”

dn21:2.6.5.verse: “The world has many and diverse elements.

dn21:2.6.6.verse: Whatever element sentient beings insist on in this world of many and diverse elements, they obstinately stick to it, insisting that:

dn21:2.6.7.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

dn21:2.6.8.verse: That’s why not all ascetics and brahmins have a single doctrine, ethics, desire, and attachment.”

dn21:2.6.9.verse: “Good fellow, have all ascetics and brahmins reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal?”

dn21:2.6.10.verse: “No, lord of gods, they have not.”

dn21:2.6.12.verse: “Those mendicants who are freed through the ending of craving have reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal.

dn21:2.6.13.verse: That’s why not all ascetics and brahmins have reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal.”

dn21:2.6.14.verse: Such was the Buddha’s answer to Sakka.

dn21:2.6.15.verse: Delighted, Sakka approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, saying,

dn21:2.6.16.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

dn21:2.6.17.verse: Hearing the Buddha’s answer, I’ve gone beyond doubt and got rid of indecision.”

dn21:2.6.18.verse: And then Sakka, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, said to him,

dn21:2.7.1.verse: “Turbulence, sir, is a disease, a boil, a dart. Turbulence drags a person to be regenerated in one state of existence or another.

dn21:2.7.2.verse: That’s why a person finds themselves in states high and low.

dn21:2.7.3.verse: Elsewhere, among other ascetics and brahmins, I wasn’t even given a chance to ask these questions that the Buddha has answered.

dn21:2.7.4.verse: The dart of doubt and indecision has lain within me for a long time, but the Buddha has plucked it out.”

dn21:2.7.5.verse: “Lord of gods, do you recall having asked this question of other ascetics and brahmins?”

dn21:2.7.7.verse: “If you wouldn’t mind, lord of gods, tell me how they answered.”

dn21:2.7.8.verse: “It’s no trouble when someone such as the Blessed One is sitting here.”

dn21:2.7.10.verse: “Sir, I approached those who I imagined were ascetics and brahmins living in the wilderness, in remote lodgings. But they were stumped by my question, and they even questioned me in return:

dn21:2.7.13.verse: ‘Good fellow, I am Sakka, lord of gods.’

dn21:2.7.14.verse: So they asked me another question:

dn21:2.7.15.verse: ‘But lord of gods, what deed brought you to this position?’

dn21:2.7.16.verse: So I taught them the Dhamma as I had learned and memorized it.

dn21:2.7.17.verse: And they were pleased with just that much:

dn21:2.7.18.verse: ‘We have seen Sakka, lord of gods! And he answered our questions!’

dn21:2.7.19.verse: Invariably, they become my disciples, I don’t become theirs.

dn21:2.7.20.verse: But sir, I am the Buddha’s disciple, a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

dn21:2.7.22.verse: “Lord of gods, do you recall ever feeling such joy and happiness before?”

dn21:2.7.25.verse: “Once upon a time, sir, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

dn21:2.7.26.verse: In that battle the gods won and the titans lost.

dn21:2.7.27.verse: It occurred to me as victor,

dn21:2.7.28.verse: ‘Now the gods shall enjoy both the nectar of the gods and the nectar of the titans.’

dn21:2.7.29.verse: But sir, that joy and happiness is in the sphere of the rod and the sword. It doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

dn21:2.7.30.verse: But the joy and happiness I feel listening to the Buddha’s teaching is not in the sphere of the rod and the sword. It does lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.”

dn21:2.8.1.verse: “But lord of gods, what reason do you see for speaking of such joy and happiness?”

dn21:2.8.2.verse: “I see six reasons to speak of such joy and happiness, sir.

dn21:2.8.5.verse: I have gained an extended life:

dn21:2.8.8.verse: When I fall from the heavenly host,

dn21:2.8.10.verse: I shall consciously go to a new womb,

dn21:2.8.14.verse: of the one of unclouded wisdom,

dn21:2.8.20.verse: I shall live as one who understands,

dn21:2.8.21.verse: and my end shall come right there.

dn21:2.8.23.verse: When I fall from the human realm,

dn21:2.8.25.verse: I shall become a god again,

dn21:2.8.28.verse: They are the finest of gods,

dn21:2.8.30.verse: So long as my final life goes on,

dn21:2.8.33.verse: Seeing these six reasons I speak of such joy and happiness.

dn21:2.9.3.verse: I wandered for such a long time,

dn21:2.9.4.verse: in search of the Realized One.

dn21:2.9.8.verse: so I went to sit near them.

dn21:2.9.11.verse: But they were stumped by such questions

dn21:2.9.13.verse: And when they found out that I

dn21:2.9.14.verse: was Sakka, come from the gods,

dn21:2.9.16.verse: the deed that brought me to this state.

dn21:2.9.18.verse: as I had learned it among men.

dn21:2.9.19.verse: They were delighted with that, saying:

dn21:2.9.21.verse: Now since I’ve seen the Buddha,

dn21:2.9.24.verse: I pay homage to the awakened one.

dn21:2.9.25.verse: Destroyer of the dart of craving,

dn21:2.9.27.verse: I bow to the great hero,

dn21:2.9.28.verse: the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun.

dn21:2.9.29.verse: In the same way that divinity ought be revered

dn21:2.9.32.verse: come, let us revere you ourselves!

dn21:2.9.35.verse: In the world with its gods,

dn21:2.10.1.verse: Then Sakka addressed the centaur Pañcasikha,

dn21:2.10.2.verse: “Dear Pañcasikha, you were very helpful to me, since you first charmed the Buddha,

dn21:2.10.3.verse: after which I went to see him.

dn21:2.10.4.verse: I shall appoint you to your father’s position—you shall be king of the centaurs. And I give you Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, for she loves you very much.”

dn21:2.10.5.verse: Then Sakka, touching the ground with his hand, expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:

dn21:2.10.6.verse: “Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

dn21:2.10.7.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

dn21:2.10.8.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!”

dn21:2.10.9.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Sakka, lord of gods:

dn21:2.10.10.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

dn21:2.10.12.verse: Such were the questions Sakka was invited to ask, and which were answered by the Buddha.

dn21:2.10.13.verse: And that’s why the name of this discussion is “Sakka’s Questions”.

dn22:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation

dn22:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.

dn22:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

dn22:1.7.verse: “Mendicants, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

dn22:1.9.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:1.10.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:1.11.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:1.12.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:2.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the body?

dn22:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

dn22:2.3.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

dn22:2.4.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

dn22:2.5.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

dn22:2.6.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

dn22:2.7.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

dn22:2.8.verse: It’s like a deft lathe-turner or lathe-turner’s apprentice. When drawing a long pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a long pull,’ and when drawing a short pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a short pull.’

dn22:2.11.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:2.12.verse: With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:2.13.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:2.14.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:3.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant is walking they know: ‘I am walking.’ When standing they know: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting they know: ‘I am sitting.’ And when lying down they know: ‘I am lying down.’

dn22:3.2.verse: Whatever posture their body is in, they know it.

dn22:3.3.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:3.4.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the body, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:3.5.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:3.6.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant acts with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

dn22:4.2.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

dn22:4.3.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

dn22:5.2.verse: ‘In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

dn22:5.3.verse: It’s as if there were a bag with openings at both ends, filled with various kinds of grains, such as fine rice, wheat, mung beans, peas, sesame, and ordinary rice. And a person with clear eyes were to open it and examine the contents: ‘These grains are fine rice, these are wheat, these are mung beans, these are peas, these are sesame, and these are ordinary rice.’

dn22:5.6.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

dn22:5.7.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, whatever its placement or posture, according to the elements:

dn22:6.2.verse: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

dn22:6.3.verse: It’s as if a deft butcher or butcher’s apprentice were to kill a cow and sit down at the crossroads with the meat cut into chops.

dn22:6.6.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

dn22:6.7.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:7.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose a mendicant were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground. And it had been dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering.

dn22:7.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

dn22:7.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

dn22:7.4.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

dn22:7.5.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:8.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, herons, hounds, tigers, leopards, jackals, and many kinds of little creatures.

dn22:8.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

dn22:8.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

dn22:8.4.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

dn22:8.5.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:9.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

dn22:9.2.verse: A skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, and held together by sinews …

dn22:9.3.verse: A skeleton rid of flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

dn22:9.4.verse: Bones rid of sinews scattered in every direction. Here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here an arm-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth, here the skull. …

dn22:10.1.verse: White bones, the color of shells …

dn22:10.2.verse: Decrepit bones, heaped in a pile …

dn22:10.3.verse: Bones rotted and crumbled to powder.

dn22:10.4.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

dn22:10.5.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

dn22:10.6.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:10.7.verse: With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:10.8.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:10.9.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

dn22:11.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of feelings?

dn22:11.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant who feels a pleasant feeling knows: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling.’

dn22:11.3.verse: When they feel a painful feeling, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling.’

dn22:11.4.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling.’

dn22:11.5.verse: When they feel a pleasant feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling of the flesh.’

dn22:11.6.verse: When they feel a pleasant feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling not of the flesh.’

dn22:11.7.verse: When they feel a painful feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling of the flesh.’

dn22:11.8.verse: When they feel a painful feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling not of the flesh.’

dn22:11.9.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling of the flesh.’

dn22:11.10.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling not of the flesh.’

dn22:11.11.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:11.12.verse: With respect to feelings, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:11.13.verse: Or mindfulness is established that feelings exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:11.14.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of feelings.

dn22:12.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the mind?

dn22:12.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands mind with greed as ‘mind with greed,’

dn22:12.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed.’

dn22:12.4.verse: They understand mind with hate as ‘mind with hate,’

dn22:12.5.verse: and mind without hate as ‘mind without hate.’

dn22:12.6.verse: They understand mind with delusion as ‘mind with delusion,’

dn22:12.7.verse: and mind without delusion as ‘mind without delusion.’

dn22:12.8.verse: They know constricted mind as ‘constricted mind,’

dn22:12.10.verse: They know expansive mind as ‘expansive mind,’

dn22:12.12.verse: They know mind that is not supreme as ‘mind that is not supreme,’

dn22:12.13.verse: and mind that is supreme as ‘mind that is supreme.’

dn22:12.14.verse: They know mind immersed in samādhi as ‘mind immersed in samādhi,’

dn22:12.15.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as ‘mind not immersed in samādhi.’

dn22:12.16.verse: They know freed mind as ‘freed mind,’

dn22:12.18.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:12.19.verse: With respect to the mind, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:12.20.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the mind exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:12.21.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the mind.

dn22:13.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles?

dn22:13.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances.

dn22:13.3.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances?

dn22:13.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant who has sensual desire in them understands: ‘I have sensual desire in me.’ When they don’t have sensual desire in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have sensual desire in me.’ They understand how sensual desire arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

dn22:13.5.verse: When they have ill will in them, they understand: ‘I have ill will in me.’ When they don’t have ill will in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have ill will in me.’ They understand how ill will arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

dn22:13.6.verse: When they have dullness and drowsiness in them, they understand: ‘I have dullness and drowsiness in me.’ When they don’t have dullness and drowsiness in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have dullness and drowsiness in me.’ They understand how dullness and drowsiness arise; how, when they’ve already arisen, they’re given up; and how, once they’re given up, they don’t arise again in the future.

dn22:13.7.verse: When they have restlessness and remorse in them, they understand: ‘I have restlessness and remorse in me.’ When they don’t have restlessness and remorse in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have restlessness and remorse in me.’ They understand how restlessness and remorse arise; how, when they’ve already arisen, they’re given up; and how, once they’re given up, they don’t arise again in the future.

dn22:13.8.verse: When they have doubt in them, they understand: ‘I have doubt in me.’ When they don’t have doubt in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have doubt in me.’ They understand how doubt arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

dn22:13.9.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:13.10.verse: They meditate observing the principles as liable to originate, as liable to fall, and as liable to both originate and vanish.

dn22:13.11.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:13.12.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances.

dn22:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates.

dn22:14.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates?

dn22:14.4.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

dn22:14.5.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

dn22:14.6.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

dn22:14.7.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

dn22:14.8.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

dn22:14.9.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally …

dn22:14.12.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates.

dn22:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields.

dn22:15.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields?

dn22:15.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands the eye, sights, and the fetter that arises dependent on both of these. They understand how the fetter that has not arisen comes to arise; how the arisen fetter comes to be abandoned; and how the abandoned fetter comes to not rise again in the future.

dn22:15.4.verse: They understand the ear, sounds, and the fetter …

dn22:15.5.verse: They understand the nose, smells, and the fetter …

dn22:15.6.verse: They understand the tongue, tastes, and the fetter …

dn22:15.7.verse: They understand the body, touches, and the fetter …

dn22:15.8.verse: They understand the mind, ideas, and the fetter that arises dependent on both of these. They understand how the fetter that has not arisen comes to arise; how the arisen fetter comes to be abandoned; and how the abandoned fetter comes to not rise again in the future.

dn22:15.9.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally …

dn22:15.12.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields.

dn22:16.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors.

dn22:16.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors?

dn22:16.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant who has the awakening factor of mindfulness in them understands: ‘I have the awakening factor of mindfulness in me.’ When they don’t have the awakening factor of mindfulness in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have the awakening factor of mindfulness in me.’ They understand how the awakening factor of mindfulness that has not arisen comes to arise; and how the awakening factor of mindfulness that has arisen becomes fully developed.

dn22:16.4.verse: When they have the awakening factor of investigation of principles …

dn22:16.9.verse: equanimity in them, they understand: ‘I have the awakening factor of equanimity in me.’ When they don’t have the awakening factor of equanimity in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have the awakening factor of equanimity in me.’ They understand how the awakening factor of equanimity that has not arisen comes to arise; and how the awakening factor of equanimity that has arisen becomes fully developed.

dn22:16.10.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:16.11.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the principles, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:16.12.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:16.13.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors.

dn22:17.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths.

dn22:17.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths?

dn22:17.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

dn22:17.4.verse: The first recitation section is complete.

dn22:18.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

dn22:18.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

dn22:18.4.verse: The rebirth, inception, conception, regeneration, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense fields of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

dn22:18.7.verse: The old age, decrepitude, broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkly skin, diminished vitality, and failing faculties of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

dn22:18.10.verse: The passing away, passing on, disintegration, demise, mortality, death, decease, breaking up of the aggregates, laying to rest of the corpse, and cutting off of the life faculty of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

dn22:18.13.verse: The sorrow, sorrowing, state of sorrow, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

dn22:18.16.verse: The wail, lament, wailing, lamenting, state of wailing and lamentation in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

dn22:18.19.verse: Physical pain, physical unpleasantness, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from physical contact.

dn22:18.22.verse: Mental pain, mental displeasure, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from mind contact.

dn22:18.25.verse: The stress, distress, state of stress and distress in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

dn22:18.27.verse: And what is meant by ‘being coupled with the disliked is suffering’?

dn22:18.28.verse: There are sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas, which are unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable. And there are those who want to harm, injure, disturb, and threaten you. The coming together with these, the joining, inclusion, mixing with them:

dn22:18.29.verse: this is what is meant by ‘being coupled with the disliked is suffering’.

dn22:18.30.verse: And what is meant by ‘separation from the liked is suffering’?

dn22:18.31.verse: There are sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable. And there are those who want to help, benefit, comfort, and protect you: mother and father, brother and sister, friends and colleagues, relatives and kin. The division from these, the disconnection, segregation, and parting from them:

dn22:18.32.verse: this is what is meant by ‘separation from the liked is suffering’.

dn22:18.33.verse: And what is meant by ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’?

dn22:18.34.verse: In sentient beings who are liable to be reborn, such a wish arises:

dn22:18.35.verse: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to be reborn! If only rebirth would not come to us!’

dn22:18.36.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

dn22:18.37.verse: This is what is meant by ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

dn22:18.38.verse: In sentient beings who are liable to grow old …

dn22:18.45.verse: experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, such a wish arises: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress! If only sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress would not come to us!’

dn22:18.46.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

dn22:18.47.verse: This is what is meant by ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

dn22:18.48.verse: And what is meant by ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’?

dn22:18.49.verse: They are the grasping aggregates that consist of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

dn22:18.50.verse: This is what is meant by ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’.

dn22:18.51.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

dn22:19.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

dn22:19.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

dn22:19.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

dn22:19.4.verse: But where does that craving arise and where does it settle?

dn22:19.5.verse: Whatever in the world seems nice and pleasant, it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.6.verse: And what in the world seems nice and pleasant?

dn22:19.7.verse: The eye in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.12.verse: mind in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.18.verse: ideas in the world seem nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.24.verse: mind consciousness in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.30.verse: mind contact in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.36.verse: feeling born of mind contact in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.42.verse: perception of ideas in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.48.verse: intention regarding ideas in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.54.verse: craving for ideas in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.60.verse: thoughts about ideas in the world seem nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.66.verse: considerations regarding ideas in the world seem nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving arises and settles.

dn22:19.67.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

dn22:20.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

dn22:20.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving with no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

dn22:20.4.verse: Whatever in the world seems nice and pleasant, it is there that craving is given up and ceases.

dn22:20.5.verse: And what in the world seems nice and pleasant?

dn22:20.6.verse: The eye in the world seems nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving is given up and ceases. …

dn22:20.65.verse: Considerations regarding ideas in the world seem nice and pleasant, and it is there that craving is given up and ceases.

dn22:20.66.verse: This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

dn22:21.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

dn22:21.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

dn22:21.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

dn22:21.5.verse: Knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

dn22:21.8.verse: Purposes of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness.

dn22:21.11.verse: Refraining from lying, backbiting, harsh speech, and talking nonsense.

dn22:21.14.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

dn22:21.17.verse: It’s when a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and earns a living by right livelihood.

dn22:21.20.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

dn22:21.21.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up.

dn22:21.22.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

dn22:21.23.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

dn22:21.26.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:21.27.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:21.28.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:21.29.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

dn22:21.32.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn22:21.33.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn22:21.34.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

dn22:21.35.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

dn22:21.37.verse: This is called the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

dn22:21.38.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

dn22:21.39.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the principles, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

dn22:21.40.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

dn22:21.41.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths.

dn22:22.1.verse: Anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for seven years can expect one of two results:

dn22:22.2.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.

dn22:22.4.verse: anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for six years …

dn22:22.22.verse: anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for seven days can expect one of two results:

dn22:22.23.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.

dn22:22.24.verse: ‘The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.’

dn22:22.25.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

dn22:22.26.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn22:22.27.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

dn23:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Kassapa the Prince was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants when he arrived at a Kosalan citadel named Setavyā.

dn23:1.3.verse: He stayed in the rosewood grove to the north of Setavyā.

dn23:1.4.verse: Now at that time the chieftain Pāyāsi was living in Setavyā. It was a crown property given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, teeming with living creatures, full of hay, wood, water, and grain, a royal park endowed to a brahmin.

dn23:2.1.verse: Now at that time Pāyāsi had the following harmful misconception:

dn23:2.2.verse: “There is no afterlife. No beings are reborn spontaneously. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”

dn23:2.3.verse: The brahmins and householders of Setavyā heard,

dn23:2.4.verse: “It seems the ascetic Kassapa the Prince—a disciple of the ascetic Gotama—is staying in the rosewood grove to the north of Setavyā.

dn23:2.6.verse: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

dn23:2.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

dn23:2.8.verse: Then, exiting Setavyā, they formed into companies and headed north to the grove.

dn23:3.1.verse: Now at that time the chieftain Pāyāsi had retired to the upper floor of his stilt longhouse for his midday nap.

dn23:3.2.verse: He saw the brahmins and householders heading north toward the grove,

dn23:3.4.verse: “My butler, why are the brahmins and householders heading north toward the grove?”

dn23:3.5.verse: “The ascetic Kassapa the Prince—a disciple of the ascetic Gotama—is staying in the rosewood grove to the north of Setavyā.

dn23:3.7.verse: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

dn23:3.8.verse: They’re going to see that Kassapa the Prince.”

dn23:3.9.verse: “Well then, go to the brahmins and householders and say to them:

dn23:3.11.verse: you to wait, as he will also go to see the ascetic Kassapa the Prince.’

dn23:3.12.verse: Before Kassapa the Prince persuades those foolish and incompetent brahmins and householders that

dn23:3.13.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds—

dn23:3.14.verse: for none of these things are true!”

dn23:3.15.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” replied the butler, and did as he was asked.

dn23:4.1.verse: Then Pāyāsi escorted by the brahmins and householders, went up to Kassapa the Prince, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

dn23:4.2.verse: Before sitting down to one side, some of the brahmins and householders of Setavyā bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward Kassapa the Prince, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

dn23:5.1.verse: Seated to one side, the chieftain Pāyāsi said to Venerable Kassapa the Prince,

dn23:5.2.verse: “Worthy Kassapa, this is my doctrine and view:

dn23:5.3.verse: ‘There is no afterlife. No beings are reborn spontaneously. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

dn23:5.4.verse: “Chieftain, may I never see or hear of anyone holding such a doctrine or view!

dn23:5.5.verse: For how on earth can anyone say such a thing?

dn23:5.7.0.verse: 2.1. The Simile of the Moon and Sun

dn23:5.8.verse: Well then, chieftain, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

dn23:5.10.verse: Are the moon and sun in this world or the other world? Are they gods or humans?”

dn23:5.11.verse: “They are in the other world, worthy Kassapa, and they are gods, not humans.”

dn23:5.12.verse: “By this method it ought to be proven that

dn23:5.13.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”

dn23:6.1.verse: “Even though the worthy Kassapa says this, still I think that

dn23:6.2.verse: there is no afterlife, no beings are reborn spontaneously, and there’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”

dn23:6.3.verse: “Is there a method by which you can prove what you say?”

dn23:6.8.verse: “Well, I have friends and colleagues, relatives and kin who kill living creatures, steal, and commit sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, with wrong view.

dn23:6.9.verse: Some time later they become sick, suffering, gravely ill.

dn23:6.11.verse: they will not recover from their illness, I go to them and say,

dn23:6.12.verse: ‘Worthy sir, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

dn23:6.13.verse: “Those who kill living creatures, steal, and commit sexual misconduct; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; and are covetous, malicious, and have wrong view—when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.”

dn23:6.15.verse: If what those ascetics and brahmins say is true, when your body breaks up, after death, you’ll be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

dn23:6.16.verse: If that happens, worthy sir, come and tell me that

dn23:6.17.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds.

dn23:6.18.verse: I trust you and believe you. Anything you see will be just as if I’ve seen it for myself.’

dn23:6.19.verse: They agree to this. But they don’t come back to tell me, nor do they send a messenger.

dn23:6.20.verse: This is the method by which I prove that

dn23:6.21.verse: there is no afterlife, no beings are reborn spontaneously, and there’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”

dn23:7.3.verse: Suppose they were to arrest a bandit, a criminal and present him to you, saying,

dn23:7.4.verse: ‘Sir, this is a bandit, a criminal.

dn23:7.7.verse: ‘Well then, my men, tie this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope. Shave his head and march him from street to street and square to square to the beating of a harsh drum. Then take him out the south gate and there, at the place of execution to the south of the city, chop off his head.’

dn23:7.8.verse: Saying, ‘Good,’ they’d do as they were told, sitting him down at the place of execution.

dn23:7.9.verse: Could that bandit get the executioners to wait, saying,

dn23:7.10.verse: ‘Please, good executioners! I have friends and colleagues, relatives and kin in such-and-such village or town. Wait until I’ve visited them, then I’ll come back’? Or would they just chop off his head as he prattled on?”

dn23:7.14.verse: “So even a human bandit couldn’t get his human executioners to stay his execution.

dn23:7.16.verse: What then of your friends and colleagues, relatives and kin who are reborn in a lower realm after doing bad things? Could they get the wardens of hell to wait, saying,

dn23:7.17.verse: ‘Please, good wardens of hell! Wait until I’ve gone to the chieftain Pāyāsi to tell him that

dn23:7.18.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds’?

dn23:7.19.verse: By this method, too, it ought to be proven that

dn23:7.20.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”

dn23:11.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

dn23:11.2.verse: A hundred human years are equivalent to one day and night for the gods of the thirty-three. Thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year. The gods of the thirty-three have a lifespan of a thousand such years.

dn23:11.3.verse: Now, as to your friends who are reborn in the company of the gods of the thirty-three after doing good things.

dn23:11.5.verse: ‘First I’ll amuse myself for two or three days, supplied and provided with the five kinds of heavenly sensual stimulation. Then I’ll go back to Pāyāsi and tell him that

dn23:11.19.verse: There’s no such thing as blue,

dn23:13.0.verse: 2.6. The Simile of the Pregnant Woman

dn23:13.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I shall give you a simile.

dn23:13.2.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

dn23:13.3.verse: Once upon a time, a certain brahmin had two wives.

dn23:13.4.verse: One had a son ten or twelve years of age, while the other was pregnant and about to give birth.

dn23:13.6.verse: So the youth said to his mother’s co-wife,

dn23:13.7.verse: ‘Madam, all the money, grain, silver, and gold is mine,

dn23:13.9.verse: Transfer to me my father’s inheritance.’

dn23:13.11.verse: ‘Wait, my dear, until I give birth.

dn23:13.12.verse: If it’s a boy, one portion shall be his.

dn23:13.13.verse: If it’s a girl, she will be your reward.’

dn23:13.22.verse: and a third time, the youth insisted that the entire inheritance must be his.

dn23:13.26.verse: So the brahmin lady took a knife, went to her bedroom, and sliced open her belly, thinking,

dn23:13.27.verse: ‘Until I give birth—whether it’s a boy or a girl!’

dn23:13.28.verse: She destroyed her own life and that of the fetus, as well as any wealth.

dn23:13.29.verse: Being foolish and incompetent, she sought an inheritance irrationally and fell to ruin and disaster. In the same way, chieftain, being foolish and incompetent, you’re seeking the other world irrationally and will fall to ruin and disaster,

dn23:13.31.verse: Good ascetics and brahmins don’t force what is unripe to ripen;

dn23:13.32.verse: rather, they wait for it to ripen.

dn23:13.33.verse: For the life of astute ascetics and brahmins is beneficial.

dn23:13.34.verse: So long as they remain, good ascetics and brahmins brim with merit, and act for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

dn23:13.35.verse: By this method, too, it ought to be proven that

dn23:14.10.verse: ‘Well then, worthy sir, place this man in a pot while he’s still alive. Close up the mouth, bind it up with damp leather, and seal it with a thick coat of damp clay. Then lift it up on a stove and light the fire.’

dn23:14.11.verse: They agree, and do what I ask.

dn23:14.12.verse: When we know that that man has passed away, we lift down the pot and break it open, uncover the mouth, and slowly peek inside, thinking,

dn23:14.14.verse: But we don’t see his soul escaping.

dn23:14.15.verse: This is how I prove that

dn23:15.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

dn23:15.2.verse: Do you recall ever having a midday nap and seeing delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds in a dream?”

dn23:15.4.verse: “At that time were you guarded by hunchbacks, dwarves, coquettes, and maidens?”

dn23:15.6.verse: “But did they see your soul entering or leaving?”

dn23:15.8.verse: “So if they couldn’t even see your soul entering or leaving while you were still alive,

dn23:15.9.verse: how could you see the soul of a dead man?

dn23:15.10.verse: By this method, too, it ought to be proven that

dn23:15.11.verse: there is an afterlife, there are beings reborn spontaneously, and there is a fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”
