dn23:16.6.verse: “Suppose they were to arrest a bandit, a criminal and present him to me, saying,

dn23:16.7.verse: ‘Sir, this is a bandit, a criminal.

dn23:16.10.verse: ‘Well then, worthy sir, weigh this man with scales while he’s still alive. Then strangle him with a bowstring, and when he’s dead, weigh him again.’

dn23:16.11.verse: They agree, and do what I ask.

dn23:16.12.verse: So long as they are alive, they’re lighter, softer, more flexible.

dn23:16.13.verse: But when they die they become heavier, stiffer, less flexible.

dn23:16.14.verse: This is how I prove that

dn23:17.0.verse: 2.8. The Simile of the Hot Iron Ball

dn23:17.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I shall give you a simile.

dn23:17.2.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

dn23:17.3.verse: Suppose a person was to heat an iron ball all day until it was burning, blazing, and glowing, and then they weigh it with scales.

dn23:17.4.verse: After some time, when it had cooled and become quenched, they’d weigh it again.

dn23:17.5.verse: When would that iron ball be lighter, softer, and more workable—when it’s burning or when it’s cool?”

dn23:17.6.verse: “So long as the iron ball is full of heat and air—burning, blazing, and glowing—it’s lighter, softer, and more workable.

dn23:17.7.verse: But when it lacks heat and air—cooled and quenched—it’s heavier, stiffer, and less workable.”

dn23:17.8.verse: “In the same way, so long as this body is full of life and warmth and consciousness it’s lighter, softer, and more flexible.

dn23:17.9.verse: But when it lacks life and warmth and consciousness it’s heavier, stiffer, and less flexible.

dn23:17.10.verse: By this method, too, it ought to be proven that

dn23:18.1.verse: “Even though the worthy Kassapa says this, still I think that

dn23:18.6.verse: “Suppose they were to arrest a bandit, a criminal and present him to me, saying,

dn23:18.7.verse: ‘Sir, this is a bandit, a criminal.

dn23:18.10.verse: ‘Well then, worthy sir, take this man’s life without damaging his outer skin, inner skin, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow. Hopefully we’ll see his soul escaping.’

dn23:18.11.verse: They agree, and do what I ask.

dn23:18.12.verse: When he’s nearly dead, I tell them to

dn23:18.13.verse: lay him on his back in hope of seeing his soul escape.

dn23:18.15.verse: But we don’t see his soul escaping.

dn23:18.18.verse: to lay him on his side,

dn23:18.19.verse: to lay him on the other side;

dn23:18.26.verse: and to give him a good shaking in hope of seeing his soul escape.

dn23:18.28.verse: But we don’t see his soul escaping.

dn23:18.29.verse: For him the eye itself is present, and so are those sights. Yet he does not experience that sense-field.

dn23:18.30.verse: The ear itself is present, and so are those sounds. Yet he does not experience that sense-field.

dn23:18.31.verse: The nose itself is present, and so are those smells. Yet he does not experience that sense-field.

dn23:18.32.verse: The tongue itself is present, and so are those tastes. Yet he does not experience that sense-field.

dn23:18.33.verse: The body itself is present, and so are those touches. Yet he does not experience that sense-field.

dn23:18.34.verse: This is how I prove that

dn23:19.0.verse: 2.9. The Simile of the Horn Blower

dn23:19.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I shall give you a simile.

dn23:19.2.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

dn23:19.3.verse: Once upon a time, a certain horn blower took his horn and traveled to a borderland,

dn23:19.4.verse: where he went to a certain village. Standing in the middle of the village, he sounded his horn three times, then placed it on the ground and sat down to one side.

dn23:19.5.verse: Then the people of the borderland thought,

dn23:19.6.verse: ‘Oh my, what is making this sound, so arousing, sensuous, intoxicating, infatuating, and captivating?’

dn23:19.7.verse: They gathered around the horn blower and said,

dn23:19.8.verse: ‘Oh my, what is making this sound, so arousing, sensuous, intoxicating, infatuating, and captivating?’

dn23:19.9.verse: ‘The sound is made by this, which is called a horn.’

dn23:19.10.verse: They laid that horn on its back, saying,

dn23:19.12.verse: But still the horn made no sound.

dn23:19.13.verse: Then they lay the horn bent over, they lay it on its side, they lay it on its other side; they stood it upright, they stood it upside down; they struck it with fists, stones, rods, and swords; and they gave it a good shake, saying,

dn23:19.15.verse: But still the horn made no sound.

dn23:19.17.verse: ‘How foolish are these borderland folk! For how on earth can they seek the sound of a horn so irrationally?’

dn23:19.18.verse: And as they looked on, he picked up the horn, sounded it three times, and took it away with him.

dn23:19.19.verse: Then the people of the borderland thought,

dn23:19.20.verse: ‘So, it seems, when what is called a horn is accompanied by a person, effort, and wind, it makes a sound. But when these things are absent it makes no sound.’

dn23:19.21.verse: In the same way, so long as this body is full of life and warmth and consciousness it walks back and forth, stands, sits, and lies down. It sees sights with the eye, hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, encounters touches with the body, and knows ideas with the mind.

dn23:19.22.verse: But when it lacks life and warmth and consciousness it does none of these things.

dn23:19.23.verse: By this method, too, it ought to be proven that

dn23:20.1.verse: “Even though the worthy Kassapa says this, still I think that

dn23:20.6.verse: “Suppose they were to arrest a bandit, a criminal and present him to me, saying,

dn23:20.7.verse: ‘Sir, this is a bandit, a criminal.

dn23:20.10.verse: ‘Well then, worthy sir, cut open this man’s outer skin. Hopefully we might see his soul.’

dn23:20.11.verse: They cut open his outer skin,

dn23:20.14.verse: ‘Well then, worthy sir, cut open his inner skin, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow. Hopefully we’ll see his soul.’

dn23:20.15.verse: They do so, but we see no soul.

dn23:20.16.verse: This is how I prove that

dn23:21.0.verse: 2.10. The Simile of the Fire-Worshiping Matted-Hair Ascetic

dn23:21.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I shall give you a simile.

dn23:21.2.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

dn23:21.3.verse: Once upon a time, a certain fire-worshiping matted-hair ascetic settled in a leaf hut in a wilderness region.

dn23:21.4.verse: Then a caravan came out from a certain country.

dn23:21.5.verse: It stayed for one night not far from that ascetic’s hermitage, and then moved on.

dn23:21.7.verse: ‘Why don’t I go to that caravan’s campsite? Hopefully I’ll find something useful there.’

dn23:21.8.verse: So he went, and he saw a little baby boy abandoned there.

dn23:21.9.verse: When he saw this he thought,

dn23:21.10.verse: ‘It’s not proper for me to look on while a human being dies.

dn23:21.11.verse: Why don’t I bring this boy back to my hermitage, nurse him, provide for him, and raise him?’

dn23:21.13.verse: When the boy was ten or twelve years old, the ascetic had some business come up in the country.

dn23:21.14.verse: So he said to the boy,

dn23:21.15.verse: ‘My dear, I wish to go to the country.

dn23:21.18.verse: But if you should extinguish it, here is the hatchet, the firewood, and the bundle of drill-sticks. Light the fire and serve it.’

dn23:21.19.verse: And having instructed the boy, the ascetic went to the country.

dn23:21.20.verse: But the boy was so engrossed in his play, the fire went out.

dn23:21.22.verse: ‘My father told me to serve the sacred flame.

dn23:21.26.verse: Why don’t I light it again and serve it?’

dn23:21.27.verse: So he chopped the bundle of drill-sticks with the hatchet, thinking,

dn23:21.29.verse: But he still got no fire.

dn23:21.30.verse: He split the bundle of drill-sticks into two, three, four, five, ten, or a hundred parts. He chopped them into splinters, pounded them in a mortar, and swept them away in a strong wind, thinking,

dn23:21.32.verse: But he still got no fire.

dn23:21.33.verse: Then the matted-hair ascetic, having concluded his business in the country, returned to his own hermitage, and said to the boy,

dn23:21.34.verse: ‘I trust, my dear, that the fire didn’t go out?’

dn23:21.35.verse: And the boy told him what had happened.

dn23:21.48.verse: ‘How foolish is this boy, how incompetent! For how on earth can he seek a fire so irrationally?’

dn23:21.49.verse: So while the boy looked on, he took a bundle of fire-sticks, lit the fire, and said,

dn23:21.50.verse: ‘Dear boy, this is how to light a fire.

dn23:21.51.verse: Not the foolish and incompetent way you sought it so irrationally.’

dn23:21.52.verse: In the same way, chieftain, being foolish and incompetent, you seek the other world irrationally.

dn23:21.53.verse: Let go of this harmful misconception, chieftain, let go of it!

dn23:21.54.verse: Don’t create lasting harm and suffering for yourself!”

dn23:22.1.verse: “Even though the worthy Kassapa says this, still I’m not able to let go of that harmful misconception.

dn23:22.2.verse: King Pasenadi of Kosala knows my views, and so do foreign kings.

dn23:22.5.verse: If I let go of this harmful misconception, there will be some who say to me,

dn23:22.6.verse: ‘How foolish is the chieftain Pāyāsi, how incompetent, that he should hold on to a mistake!’

dn23:22.7.verse: I shall carry on with this view out of anger, contempt, and spite!”

dn23:25.4.verse: There he saw a large pile of dry dung abandoned.

dn23:25.6.verse: ‘This pile of dry dung can serve as food for my pigs.

dn23:25.7.verse: Why don’t I carry it off?’

dn23:25.9.verse: While on his way a large storm out of season poured down.

dn23:25.10.verse: Smeared with leaking, oozing dung down to his fingernails, he kept on carrying the load of dung.

dn23:25.11.verse: When people saw him they said,

dn23:25.12.verse: ‘Have you gone mad, lad? Have you lost your mind? For how on earth can you, smeared with leaking, oozing dung down to your fingernails, keep on carrying that load of dung?’

dn23:25.13.verse: ‘You’re the mad ones, lads! You’re the ones who’ve lost your minds! For this will serve as food for my pigs.’

dn23:25.14.verse: In the same way, chieftain, you seem like the dung carrier in the simile.

dn23:25.15.verse: Let go of this harmful misconception, chieftain, let go of it!

dn23:29.0.verse: 2.14. The Simile of the Man Who Carried Hemp

dn23:29.1.verse: “Well then, chieftain, I shall give you a simile.

dn23:29.2.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

dn23:29.3.verse: Once upon a time, the inhabitants of a certain country emigrated.

dn23:29.4.verse: Then one friend said to another,

dn23:29.5.verse: ‘Come, dear, let’s go to that country. Hopefully we’ll get some riches there!’

dn23:29.7.verse: They went to that country, and to a certain deserted village. There they saw a pile of abandoned sunn hemp. Seeing it, one friend said to the other,

dn23:29.8.verse: ‘This is a pile of abandoned sunn hemp. Well then, dear, you make up a load of hemp, and I’ll make one too. Let’s both take a load of hemp and go on.’

dn23:29.9.verse: ‘Yes, dear,’ he said. Carrying their loads of hemp they went to another deserted village.

dn23:29.10.verse: There they saw much sunn hemp thread abandoned. Seeing it, one friend said to the other,

dn23:29.11.verse: ‘This pile of abandoned sunn hemp thread is just what we wanted the hemp for!

dn23:29.12.verse: Well then, dear, let’s abandon our loads of hemp, and both take a load of hemp thread and go on.’

dn23:29.13.verse: ‘I’ve already carried this load of hemp a long way, and it’s well tied up. It’s good enough for me, you understand.’

dn23:29.14.verse: So one friend abandoned their load of hemp and picked up a load of hemp thread.

dn23:29.15.verse: They went to another deserted village.

dn23:29.16.verse: There they saw much sunn hemp cloth abandoned. Seeing it, one friend said to the other,

dn23:29.17.verse: ‘This pile of abandoned sunn hemp cloth is just what we wanted the hemp and hemp thread for!

dn23:29.18.verse: Well then, dear, let’s abandon our loads, and both take a load of hemp cloth and go on.’

dn23:29.19.verse: ‘I’ve already carried this load of hemp a long way, and it’s well tied up. It’s good enough for me, you understand.’

dn23:29.20.verse: So one friend abandoned their load of hemp thread and picked up a load of hemp cloth.

dn23:29.21.verse: They went to another deserted village.

dn23:29.22.verse: There they saw a pile of flax, and by turn,

dn23:29.33.verse: and gold abandoned. Seeing it, one friend said to the other,

dn23:29.34.verse: ‘This pile of gold is just what we wanted all those other things for!

dn23:29.35.verse: Well then, dear, let’s abandon our loads, and both take a load of gold and go on.’

dn23:29.36.verse: ‘I’ve already carried this load of hemp a long way, and it’s well tied up. It’s good enough for me, you understand.’

dn23:29.37.verse: So one friend abandoned their load of silver and picked up a load of gold.

dn23:29.38.verse: Then they returned to their own village.

dn23:29.39.verse: When one friend returned with a load of sunn hemp, they didn’t please their parents, their partners and children, or their friends and colleagues. And they got no pleasure and happiness on that account.

dn23:29.40.verse: But when the other friend returned with a load of gold, they pleased their parents, their partners and children, and their friends and colleagues. And they got much pleasure and happiness on that account.

dn23:29.41.verse: In the same way, chieftain, you seem like the hemp-carrier in the simile.

dn23:29.42.verse: Let go of this harmful misconception, chieftain, let go of it!

dn23:29.43.verse: Don’t create lasting harm and suffering for yourself!”

dn23:30.1.verse: “I was delighted and satisfied with your very first simile, worthy Kassapa!

dn23:30.2.verse: Nevertheless, I wanted to hear your various solutions to the problem, so I thought I’d oppose you in this way.

dn23:30.4.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Kassapa has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn23:30.5.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

dn23:30.6.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Kassapa remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.

dn23:30.7.verse: Worthy Kassapa, I wish to perform a great sacrifice. Please instruct me so it will be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

dn23:31.1.verse: “Chieftain, take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are slaughtered. And the recipients have wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion. That kind of sacrifice is not very fruitful or beneficial or brilliant or bountiful.

dn23:31.2.verse: Suppose a farmer was to enter a wood taking seed and plough.

dn23:31.3.verse: And on that barren field, that barren ground, with uncleared stumps he sowed seeds that were broken, spoiled, weather-damaged, infertile, and ill kept.

dn23:31.4.verse: And the heavens don’t provide enough rain when needed.

dn23:31.5.verse: Would those seeds grow, increase, and mature, and would the farmer get abundant fruit?”

dn23:31.7.verse: “In the same way, chieftain, take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are slaughtered. And the recipients have wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion. That kind of sacrifice is not very fruitful or beneficial or brilliant or bountiful.

dn23:31.8.verse: But take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are not slaughtered. And the recipients have right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion. That kind of sacrifice is very fruitful and beneficial and brilliant and bountiful.

dn23:31.9.verse: Suppose a farmer was to enter a wood taking seed and plough.

dn23:31.10.verse: And on that fertile field, that fertile ground, with well-cleared stumps he sowed seeds that were intact, unspoiled, not weather-damaged, fertile, and well kept.

dn23:31.11.verse: And the heavens provide plenty of rain when needed.

dn23:31.12.verse: Would those seeds grow, increase, and mature, and would the farmer get abundant fruit?”

dn23:31.14.verse: “In the same way, chieftain, take the kind of sacrifice where cattle, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and various kinds of creatures are not slaughtered. And the recipients have right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion. That kind of sacrifice is very fruitful and beneficial and brilliant and bountiful.”

dn23:32.1.verse: Then the chieftain Pāyāsi set up an offering for ascetics and brahmins, for paupers, vagrants, supplicants, and beggars.

dn23:32.2.verse: At that offering such food as sour gruel with false black pepper was given, and rough clothes with knotted fringes.

dn23:32.3.verse: Now, it was a student named Uttara who organized that offering.

dn23:32.4.verse: When the offering was over he referred to it like this,

dn23:32.5.verse: “Through this offering may I be together with the chieftain Pāyāsi in this world, but not in the next.”

dn23:32.9.verse: so he summoned Uttara and said,

dn23:32.10.verse: “Is it really true, dear Uttara, that you referred to the offering in this way?”

dn23:32.15.verse: Don’t we who seek merit expect some result from the offering?”

dn23:32.16.verse: “At your offering such food as sour gruel with false black pepper was given, which you wouldn’t even want to touch with your foot, much less eat. And also rough clothes with knotted fringes, which you also wouldn’t want to touch with your foot, much less wear.

dn23:32.17.verse: Worthy sir, you’re dear and beloved to me. But how can I reconcile one so dear with something so disagreeable?”

dn23:32.18.verse: “Well then, dear Uttara, set up an offering with the same kind of food that I eat,

dn23:32.19.verse: and the same kind of clothes that I wear.”

dn23:32.20.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” replied Uttara, and did so.

dn23:32.22.verse: So the chieftain Pāyāsi gave gifts carelessly, thoughtlessly, not with his own hands, giving the dregs. When his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in company with the gods of the four great kings, in an empty palace of sirisa wood.

dn23:32.23.verse: But the student Uttara who organized the offering gave gifts carefully, thoughtfully, with his own hands, not giving the dregs. When his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in company with the gods of the thirty-three.

dn23:33.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Gavampati would often go to that empty sirisa palace for the day’s meditation.

dn23:33.2.verse: Then the godling Pāyāsi went up to him, bowed, and stood to one side. Gavampati said to him,

dn23:33.6.verse: there is no afterlife, no beings are reborn spontaneously, and there’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds?”

dn23:33.7.verse: “It’s true, sir, I did have such a view.

dn23:33.9.verse: But Master Kassapa the Prince dissuaded me from that harmful misconception.”

dn23:33.10.verse: “But the student named Uttara who organized that offering for you—where has he been reborn?”

dn23:33.11.verse: “Sir, Uttara gave gifts carefully, thoughtfully, with his own hands, not giving the dregs. When his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in company with the gods of the thirty-three.

dn23:33.12.verse: But I gave gifts carelessly, thoughtlessly, not with my own hands, giving the dregs. When my body broke up, after death, I was reborn in company with the gods of the four great kings, in an empty sirisa palace.

dn23:33.13.verse: So, sir, when you’ve returned to the human realm, please announce this:

dn23:33.14.verse: ‘Give gifts carefully, thoughtfully, with your own hands, not giving the dregs.

dn23:33.15.verse: The chieftain Pāyāsi gave gifts carelessly, thoughtlessly, not with his own hands, giving the dregs. When his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in company with the gods of the four great kings, in an empty palace of sirisa.

dn23:33.16.verse: But the student Uttara who organized the offering gave gifts carefully, thoughtfully, with his own hands, not giving the dregs. When his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in company with the gods of the thirty-three.’”

dn23:34.1.verse: So when Venerable Gavampati returned to the human realm he made that announcement.

dn24:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Mallas, near the Mallian town named Anupiya.

dn24:1.1.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Anupiya for alms.

dn24:1.1.5.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Anupiya.

dn24:1.1.6.verse: Why don’t I go to visit the wanderer of the Bhaggava clan in his monastery?”

dn24:1.2.2.verse: Then the wanderer of the Bhaggava clan said to the Buddha,

dn24:1.2.4.verse: Welcome to the Blessed One, sir!

dn24:1.2.5.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

dn24:1.2.6.verse: Please, sir, sit down, here, a seat is ready.”

dn24:1.2.7.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

dn24:1.2.8.verse: while the wanderer of the Bhaggava clan took a low seat, sat to one side,

dn24:1.2.10.verse: “Sir, a few days ago Sunakkhatta the Licchavi came to me and said:

dn24:1.2.11.verse: ‘Now, Bhaggava, I have disavowed the Buddha.

dn24:1.2.12.verse: Now I no longer live dedicated to him.’

dn24:1.2.13.verse: Sir, is what Sunakkhatta said true?”

dn24:1.3.1.verse: A few days ago Sunakkhatta the Licchavi came to me, bowed, sat down to one side, and said:

dn24:1.3.3.verse: Now I shall no longer live dedicated to you.’

dn24:1.3.4.verse: When Sunakkhatta said this, I said to him,

dn24:1.3.5.verse: ‘But Sunakkhatta, did I ever say to you:

dn24:1.3.8.verse: ‘Or did you ever say to me:

dn24:1.3.9.verse: “Sir, I shall live dedicated to the Buddha”?’

dn24:1.3.11.verse: ‘So it seems that I did not ask you to

dn24:1.3.13.verse: nor did you say you would

dn24:1.3.15.verse: In that case, you futile man, who are you and what do you disavow?

dn24:1.3.16.verse: See how far you have strayed!’

dn24:1.4.1.verse: ‘But sir, the Buddha never performs any superhuman demonstrations of psychic power for me.’

dn24:1.4.2.verse: ‘But Sunakkhatta, did I ever say to you:

dn24:1.4.3.verse: “Come, live dedicated to me and I will perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power for you”?’

dn24:1.4.5.verse: ‘Or did you ever say to me:

dn24:1.4.6.verse: “Sir, I shall live dedicated to the Buddha, and the Buddha will perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power for me”?’

dn24:1.4.8.verse: ‘So it seems that I did not ask this of you, and you did not require it of me.

dn24:1.4.12.verse: In that case, you futile man, who are you and what do you disavow?

dn24:1.4.14.verse: Whether or not there is a demonstration of psychic power, and regardless of the goal for which I taught the Dhamma, does it deliver one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering?’

dn24:1.4.16.verse: ‘So it seems that whether or not there is a demonstration of psychic power, and regardless of the goal for which I taught the Dhamma, it delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.

dn24:1.4.17.verse: In that case, what is the point of superhuman demonstrations of psychic power?

dn24:1.4.18.verse: See how far you have strayed, you silly man!’

dn24:1.5.1.verse: ‘But sir, the Buddha never describes the origin of the world to me.’

dn24:1.5.2.verse: ‘But Sunakkhatta, did I ever say to you:

dn24:1.5.3.verse: “Come, live dedicated to me and I will describe the origin of the world to you”?’

dn24:1.5.5.verse: ‘Or did you ever say to me:

dn24:1.5.6.verse: “Sir, I shall live dedicated to the Buddha, and the Buddha will describe the origin of the world to me”?’

dn24:1.5.8.verse: ‘So it seems that I did not ask this of you, and you did not require it of me.

dn24:1.5.12.verse: In that case, you futile man, who are you and what do you disavow?

dn24:1.5.14.verse: Whether or not the origin of the world is described, and regardless of the goal for which I taught the Dhamma, does it deliver one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering?’

dn24:1.5.16.verse: ‘So it seems that whether or not the origin of the world is described, and regardless of the goal for which I taught the Dhamma, it delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.

dn24:1.5.17.verse: In that case, what is the point of describing the origin of the world?

dn24:1.5.18.verse: See how far you have strayed, you silly man!

dn24:1.6.1.verse: In many ways, Sunakkhatta, you have praised me like this in the Vajjian capital:

dn24:1.6.2.verse: “That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.”

dn24:1.6.4.verse: In many ways you have praised the teaching like this in the Vajjian capital:

dn24:1.6.5.verse: “The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.”

dn24:1.6.7.verse: In many ways you have praised the Saṅgha like this in the Vajjian capital:

dn24:1.6.8.verse: “The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.”

dn24:1.6.10.verse: I declare this to you, Sunakkhatta, I announce this to you!

dn24:1.6.11.verse: There will be some who say to you that Sunakkhatta was unable to lead the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama. That’s why he resigned the training and returned to a lesser life.

dn24:1.6.13.verse: Though I spoke to Sunakkhatta like this, he still left this teaching and training, like someone on the highway to hell.

dn24:1.7.1.verse: Bhaggava, this one time I was staying in the land of the Kurus where they have a town named Uttarakā.

dn24:1.7.2.verse: Then I robed up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, entered Uttarakā for alms with Sunakkhatta the Licchavi as my second monk.

dn24:1.7.3.verse: Now at that time a naked ascetic who was an aristocrat of Kuru had taken a vow to behave like a dog. When food is tossed on the ground, he gets down on all fours, eating and devouring it just with his mouth.

dn24:1.7.7.verse: Then, knowing Sunakkhatta’s train of thought, I said to him,

dn24:1.7.8.verse: ‘Don’t you claim to be an ascetic who follows the Sakyan, you silly man?’

dn24:1.7.9.verse: ‘But why does the Buddha say this to me?’

dn24:1.7.11.verse: ‘When you saw that naked ascetic of Kuru, didn’t you think,

dn24:1.7.14.verse: But sir, are you jealous of the perfected ones?’

dn24:1.7.15.verse: ‘I’m not jealous of the perfected ones, you silly man.

dn24:1.7.16.verse: Rather, you should give up this harmful misconception that has arisen in you.

dn24:1.7.17.verse: Don’t create lasting harm and suffering for yourself!

dn24:1.7.18.verse: That naked ascetic the aristocrat of Kuru, who you imagine to be a holy man, will die of flatulence in seven days.

dn24:1.7.19.verse: And when he dies, he’ll be reborn in the very lowest rank of titans, named the Kālakañjas.

dn24:1.7.20.verse: And they’ll throw him in the charnel ground on a clump of vetiver.

dn24:1.7.21.verse: If you wish, Sunakkhatta, go to the aristocrat of Kuru and ask him

dn24:1.7.22.verse: whether he knows his own destiny.

dn24:1.7.23.verse: It’s possible that he will answer:

dn24:1.7.24.verse: “Reverend Sunakkhatta, I know my own destiny.

dn24:1.7.25.verse: I’ve been reborn in the very lowest rank of titans, named the Kālakañjas.”’

dn24:1.8.1.verse: So, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta went to see the aristocrat of Kuru and said to him,

dn24:1.8.2.verse: ‘Reverend aristocrat of Kuru, the ascetic Gotama has declared

dn24:1.8.3.verse: that you will die of flatulence in seven days.

dn24:1.8.4.verse: And when you die, you’ll be reborn in the very lowest rank of titans, named the Kālakañjas.

dn24:1.8.5.verse: And when you die, they’ll throw you in the charnel ground on a clump of vetiver.

dn24:1.8.6.verse: But by eating just a little food and drinking just a little water,

dn24:1.8.7.verse: you’ll prove what the ascetic Gotama says to be false.’

dn24:1.8.8.verse: Then Sunakkhatta counted up the days until the seventh day, as happens when you have no faith in the Realized One.

dn24:1.8.9.verse: But on the seventh day, the naked ascetic who was an aristocrat of Kuru died of flatulence.

dn24:1.8.10.verse: And when he passed away, he was reborn in the very lowest rank of titans, named the Kālakañjas.

dn24:1.8.11.verse: And when he passed away, they threw him in the charnel ground on a clump of vetiver.

dn24:1.9.1.verse: Sunakkhatta the Licchavi heard about this.

dn24:1.9.3.verse: So he went to see the aristocrat of Kuru in the charnel ground on the clump of vetiver. There he struck him with his fist three times,

dn24:1.9.4.verse: ‘Reverend aristocrat of Kuru, do you know your destiny?’

dn24:1.9.5.verse: Then the aristocrat of Kuru got up, rubbing his back with his hands, and said,

dn24:1.9.6.verse: ‘Reverend Sunakkhatta, I know my own destiny.

dn24:1.9.7.verse: I’ve been reborn in the very lowest rank of titans, named the Kālakañjas.’ After speaking, he fell flat right there.

dn24:1.10.1.verse: Then Sunakkhatta came to me, bowed, and sat down to one side. I said to him,

dn24:1.10.3.verse: Did the prediction I made about the aristocrat of Kuru turn out to be correct, or not?’

dn24:1.10.6.verse: If that is so, has a superhuman demonstration of psychic power been performed or not?’

dn24:1.10.7.verse: ‘Clearly, sir, a superhuman demonstration of psychic power has been performed.’

dn24:1.10.8.verse: ‘Though I performed such a superhuman demonstration of psychic power you say this:

dn24:1.10.9.verse: “But sir, the Buddha never performs any superhuman demonstrations of psychic power for me.”

dn24:1.10.10.verse: See how far you have strayed!’

dn24:1.10.11.verse: Though I spoke to Sunakkhatta like this, he still left this teaching and training, like someone on the highway to hell.

dn24:1.11.1.verse: This one time, Bhaggava, I was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

dn24:1.11.2.verse: Now at that time the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka was residing in Vesālī. And in the Vajjian capital he had reached the peak of material things and fame.

dn24:1.11.3.verse: He had undertaken these seven vows.

dn24:1.11.4.verse: ‘As long as I live, I will be a naked ascetic, not wearing clothes. As long as I live, I will be chaste, not having sex. As long as I live, I will consume only meat and beer, not eating rice and porridge.

dn24:1.11.5.verse: And I will not go past the following shrines near Vesālī: the Udena Shrine to the east, the Gotamaka to the south, the Seven Maidens to the west, and the Many Sons to the north.’

dn24:1.11.6.verse: And it was due to undertaking these seven vows that he had reached the peak of material things and fame.

dn24:1.12.1.verse: So, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta went to see Kaḷāramaṭṭaka and asked him a question.

dn24:1.12.3.verse: he displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

dn24:1.12.5.verse: ‘I’ve offended the holy man, the perfected one, the ascetic.

dn24:1.12.6.verse: I mustn’t create lasting harm and suffering for myself!’

dn24:1.13.1.verse: Then Sunakkhatta came to me, bowed, and sat down to one side. I said to him,

dn24:1.13.2.verse: ‘Don’t you claim to be an ascetic who follows the Sakyan, you silly man?’

dn24:1.13.3.verse: ‘But why does the Buddha say this to me?’

dn24:1.13.5.verse: ‘Didn’t you go to see the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka and ask him a question?

dn24:1.13.7.verse: he displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

dn24:1.13.9.verse: “I’ve offended the holy man, the perfected one, the ascetic.

dn24:1.13.10.verse: I mustn’t create lasting harm and suffering for myself!”’

dn24:1.13.12.verse: But sir, are you jealous of perfected ones?’

dn24:1.13.13.verse: ‘I’m not jealous of the perfected ones, you silly man.

dn24:1.13.14.verse: Rather, you should give up this harmful misconception that has arisen in you.

dn24:1.13.15.verse: Don’t create lasting harm and suffering for yourself!

dn24:1.13.16.verse: That naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka, who you imagine to be a true holy man,

dn24:1.13.17.verse: will shortly be clothed, living with a partner, eating rice and porridge, having gone past all the shrines near Vesālī. And he will die after losing all his fame.’

dn24:1.14.3.verse: He came to me, bowed, and sat down to one side. I said to him,

dn24:1.14.5.verse: Did the declaration I made about Kaḷāramaṭṭaka turn out to be correct, or not?’

dn24:1.14.8.verse: If that is so, has a superhuman demonstration of psychic power been performed or not?’

dn24:1.14.9.verse: ‘Clearly, sir, a superhuman demonstration of psychic power has been performed.’

dn24:1.14.10.verse: ‘Though I perform such a superhuman demonstration of psychic power you say this:

dn24:1.14.11.verse: “But sir, the Buddha never performs any superhuman demonstrations of psychic power for me.”

dn24:1.14.12.verse: See how far you have strayed!’

dn24:1.14.13.verse: Though I spoke to Sunakkhatta like this, he still left this teaching and training, like someone on the highway to hell.

dn24:1.15.1.verse: This one time, Bhaggava, I was staying right there near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

dn24:1.15.2.verse: Now at that time the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta was residing in Vesālī. And in the Vajjian capital he had reached the peak of material things and fame.

dn24:1.15.3.verse: He was telling a crowd in Vesālī:

dn24:1.15.4.verse: ‘Both the ascetic Gotama and I speak from knowledge.

dn24:1.15.5.verse: One who speaks from knowledge ought to display a superhuman demonstration of psychic power to another who speaks from knowledge.

dn24:1.15.6.verse: If the ascetic Gotama meets me half-way,

dn24:1.15.7.verse: there we should both perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power.

dn24:1.15.8.verse: If he performs one demonstration of psychic power, I’ll perform two.

dn24:1.15.9.verse: If he performs two, I’ll perform four.

dn24:1.15.10.verse: If he performs four, I’ll perform eight.

dn24:1.15.11.verse: However many demonstrations of psychic power the ascetic Gotama performs, I’ll perform double.’

dn24:1.16.1.verse: Then Sunakkhatta came to me, bowed, sat down to one side, and told me of all this.

dn24:1.16.13.verse: ‘Sunakkhatta, the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta is not capable of meeting me face to face, unless he gives up that statement and that intention, and lets go of that view.

dn24:1.16.15.verse: meet me face to face without giving up those things, his head may explode.’

dn24:1.17.1.verse: ‘Careful what you say, Blessed One! Careful what you say, Holy One!’

dn24:1.17.2.verse: ‘But why do you say this to me, Sunakkhatta?’

dn24:1.17.4.verse: ‘Sir, the Buddha has categorically asserted that

dn24:1.17.5.verse: Pāṭikaputta is not capable of meeting the Buddha face to face, otherwise

dn24:1.17.8.verse: But Pāṭikaputta might meet the Buddha face to face in disguise, proving the Buddha wrong.’

dn24:1.18.1.verse: ‘Sunakkhatta, would the Realized One make an ambiguous statement?’

dn24:1.18.2.verse: ‘But sir, did you make that statement after encompassing Pāṭikaputta’s mind with your mind?

dn24:1.18.6.verse: Or did deities tell you about it?’

dn24:1.18.18.verse: For Ajita the Licchavi general has recently passed away and been reborn in the host of the thirty-three.

dn24:1.18.19.verse: He came and told me this,

dn24:1.18.20.verse: “The naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta is shameless, sir,

dn24:1.18.22.verse: For he has declared of me in the Vajjian capital:

dn24:1.18.23.verse: ‘Ajita the Licchavi general has been reborn in the Great Hell.’

dn24:1.18.25.verse: I have been reborn in the host of the thirty-three.

dn24:1.18.26.verse: The naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta is shameless, sir,

dn24:1.18.28.verse: Pāṭikaputta is not capable of meeting the Buddha face to face, otherwise

dn24:1.18.31.verse: Thus I both made that statement after encompassing Pāṭikaputta’s mind with my mind,

dn24:1.18.34.verse: and deities told me about it.

dn24:1.18.38.verse: So Sunakkhatta, I’ll wander for alms in Vesālī. After the meal, on my return from almsround, I’ll go to Pāṭikaputta’s monastery for the day’s meditation.

dn24:1.18.39.verse: Now you may tell him, if you so wish.’

dn24:1.19.1.verse: Then, Bhaggava, I robed up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.

dn24:1.19.2.verse: After the meal, on my return from almsround, I went to Pāṭikaputta’s monastery for the day’s meditation.

dn24:1.19.3.verse: Then Sunakkhatta rushed into Vesālī to see the very well-known Licchavis and said to them,

dn24:1.19.4.verse: ‘Respectable sirs, after his almsround, the Buddha has gone to Pāṭikaputta’s monastery for the day’s meditation.

dn24:1.19.5.verse: Come forth, good sirs, come forth! There will be a superhuman demonstration of psychic power by the holy ascetics!’

dn24:1.19.6.verse: So the very well-known Licchavis thought,

dn24:1.19.7.verse: ‘It seems there will be a superhuman demonstration of psychic power by the holy ascetics!

dn24:1.19.9.verse: Then he went to see the very well-known well-to-do brahmins, rich householders, and ascetics and brahmins who follow various other religions, and said the same thing.

dn24:1.19.13.verse: ‘It seems there will be a superhuman demonstration of psychic power by the holy ascetics!

dn24:1.19.15.verse: Then all those very well-known people went to Pāṭikaputta’s monastery.

dn24:1.19.16.verse: That assembly was large, Bhaggava; there were many hundreds, many thousands of them.

dn24:1.20.2.verse: ‘It seems that very well-known Licchavis, well-to-do brahmins, rich householders, and ascetics and brahmins who follow various other religions have come forth.

dn24:1.20.3.verse: And the ascetic Gotama is sitting in my monastery for the day’s meditation.’

dn24:1.20.4.verse: When he heard that, he became frightened, scared, his hair standing on end.

dn24:1.20.5.verse: In fear he went to the Pale-Moon Ebony Trunk monastery for the wanderers.

dn24:1.20.9.verse: ‘Come, my man, go to see Pāṭikaputta at the Pale-Moon Ebony Trunk Monastery and say to him,

dn24:1.20.10.verse: “Come forth, Reverend Pāṭikaputta! All these very well-known people have come forth, and the ascetic Gotama is sitting in your monastery for the day’s meditation.

dn24:1.20.11.verse: For you stated this in the assembly at Vesālī:

dn24:1.20.12.verse: ‘Both the ascetic Gotama and I speak from knowledge.

dn24:1.20.13.verse: One who speaks from knowledge ought to display a superhuman demonstration of psychic power to another who speaks from knowledge.

dn24:1.20.14.verse: If the ascetic Gotama meets me half-way,

dn24:1.20.15.verse: there we should both perform a superhuman demonstration of psychic power.

dn24:1.20.16.verse: If he performs one demonstration of psychic power, I’ll perform two.

dn24:1.20.17.verse: If he performs two, I’ll perform four.

dn24:1.20.18.verse: If he performs four, I’ll perform eight.

dn24:1.20.19.verse: However many demonstrations of psychic power the ascetic Gotama performs, I’ll perform double.’

dn24:1.20.21.verse: The ascetic Gotama has come the first half, and is sitting in your monastery.”’

dn24:2.13.1.verse: Then, Bhaggava, I educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired that assembly with a Dhamma talk. I released that assembly from the great bondage, and lifted 84,000 beings from the great swamp. Next I entered upon the fire element, rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees, and created a flame another seven palm trees high, blazing and smoking. Finally I landed at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

dn24:2.13.2.verse: Then Sunakkhatta came to me, bowed, and sat down to one side. I said to him,

dn24:2.13.4.verse: Did the declaration I made about Pāṭikaputta turn out to be correct, or not?’

dn24:2.13.7.verse: If that is so, has a superhuman demonstration of psychic power been performed or not?’

dn24:2.13.8.verse: ‘Clearly, sir, a superhuman demonstration of psychic power has been performed.’

dn24:2.13.9.verse: ‘Though I perform such a superhuman demonstration of psychic power you say this:

dn24:2.13.10.verse: “But sir, the Buddha never performs any superhuman demonstrations of psychic power for me.”

dn24:2.13.11.verse: See how far you have strayed!’

dn24:2.13.12.verse: Though I spoke to Sunakkhatta like this, he still left this teaching and training, like someone on the highway to hell.

dn24:2.14.0.verse: 6. On Describing the Origin of the World

dn24:2.14.1.verse: Bhaggava, I understand the origin of the world.

dn24:2.14.2.verse: I understand this, and what goes beyond it. Yet since I do not misapprehend that understanding, I have realized quenching within myself. Directly knowing this, the Realized One does not come to ruin.

dn24:2.14.3.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who describe the origin of the world in their denomination as created by the God Almighty, by the Divinity.

dn24:2.14.4.verse: I go up to them and say,

dn24:2.14.5.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

dn24:2.14.8.verse: ‘But how do you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about as created by the God Almighty, by the Divinity?’

dn24:2.14.9.verse: But they are stumped by my question, and they even question me in return.

dn24:2.14.11.verse: ‘There comes a time when, reverends, after a very long period has passed, this cosmos contracts.

dn24:2.14.12.verse: As the cosmos contracts, sentient beings are mostly headed for the realm of sublime luminosity.

dn24:2.14.13.verse: There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-radiant, wandering in midair, steadily glorious, and they remain like that for a very long time.

dn24:2.15.1.verse: There comes a time when, after a very long period has passed, this cosmos expands.

dn24:2.15.2.verse: As it expands an empty mansion of divinity appears.

dn24:2.15.3.verse: Then a certain sentient being—due to the running out of their life-span or merit—passes away from that host of luminous deities and is reborn in that empty mansion of divinity.

dn24:2.15.4.verse: There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-radiant, wandering in midair, steadily glorious, and they remain like that for a very long time.

dn24:2.16.1.verse: But after staying there all alone for a long time, they become dissatisfied and anxious,

dn24:2.16.2.verse: “Oh, if only other beings would come to this place.”

dn24:2.16.3.verse: Then other sentient beings—due to the running out of their life-span or merit—pass away from that host of luminous deities and are reborn in that mansion of divinity in company with that being.

dn24:2.16.4.verse: There they too are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-radiant, wandering in midair, steadily glorious, and they remain like that for a very long time.

dn24:2.17.1.verse: Now, the being who was reborn there first thinks,

dn24:2.17.2.verse: “I am the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power,  God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born. And these beings were created by me.

dn24:2.17.5.verse: ‘Oh, if only other beings would come to this place.’

dn24:2.17.6.verse: Such was my heart’s wish, and then these creatures came to this place.”

dn24:2.17.7.verse: And the beings who were reborn there later also think,

dn24:2.17.8.verse: “This must be the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.

dn24:2.17.9.verse: And we were created by him.

dn24:2.17.11.verse: Because we see that he was reborn here first, and we arrived later.”

dn24:2.17.12.verse: And the being who was reborn first is more long-lived, beautiful, and illustrious than those who arrived later.

dn24:2.17.14.verse: It’s possible that one of those beings passes away from that host and is reborn in this place.

dn24:2.17.15.verse: Having done so, they go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn24:2.17.16.verse: By dint of keen, resolute, committed, and diligent effort, and right application of mind, they experience an immersion of the heart of such a kind that they recollect that past life, but no further.

dn24:2.17.18.verse: “He who is the Divinity—the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born—by he we were created. He is permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, remaining the same for all eternity.

dn24:2.17.19.verse: We who were created by that divinity are impermanent, not lasting, short-lived, liable to pass away, and have come to this place.”

dn24:2.17.20.verse: Is this how you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about as created by the God Almighty, by the Divinity?’

dn24:2.17.22.verse: ‘That is what we have heard, Reverend Gotama, just as you say.’

dn24:2.17.23.verse: Bhaggava, I understand the origin of the world.

dn24:2.17.24.verse: I understand this, and what goes beyond it. Yet since I do not misapprehend that understanding, I have realized quenching within myself. Directly knowing this, the Realized One does not come to ruin.

dn24:2.18.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who describe the origin of the world in their denomination as due to those depraved by play.

dn24:2.18.2.verse: I go up to them and say,

dn24:2.18.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

dn24:2.18.6.verse: ‘But how do you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about due to those depraved by play?’

dn24:2.18.7.verse: But they are stumped by my question, and they even question me in return.

dn24:2.18.9.verse: ‘Reverends, there are gods named “depraved by play”. They spend too much time laughing, playing, and making merry. And in doing so, they lose their mindfulness, and they pass away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.18.10.verse: It’s possible that one of those beings passes away from that host and is reborn in this place.

dn24:2.18.11.verse: Having done so, they go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn24:2.18.12.verse: By dint of keen, resolute, committed, and diligent effort, and right application of mind, they experience an immersion of the heart of such a kind that they recollect that past life, but no further.

dn24:2.18.14.verse: “The gods not depraved by play don’t spend too much time laughing, playing, and making merry. So they don’t lose their mindfulness, and don’t pass away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.18.15.verse: They are permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, remaining the same for all eternity.

dn24:2.18.16.verse: But we who were depraved by play spent too much time laughing, playing, and making merry. In doing so, we lost our mindfulness, and passed away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.18.17.verse: We are impermanent, not lasting, short-lived, liable to pass away, and have come to this place.”

dn24:2.18.18.verse: Is this how you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about due to those depraved by play?’

dn24:2.18.20.verse: ‘That is what we have heard, Reverend Gotama, just as you say.’

dn24:2.18.21.verse: Bhaggava, I understand the origin of the world.

dn24:2.18.22.verse: Directly knowing this, the Realized One does not come to ruin.

dn24:2.19.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who describe the origin of the world in their denomination as due to those who are malevolent.

dn24:2.19.2.verse: I go up to them and say,

dn24:2.19.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

dn24:2.19.6.verse: ‘But how do you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about due to those who are malevolent?’

dn24:2.19.7.verse: But they are stumped by my question, and they even question me in return.

dn24:2.19.9.verse: ‘Reverends, there are gods named “malevolent”. They spend too much time gazing at each other, so they grow angry with each other, and their bodies and minds get tired. They pass away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.19.10.verse: It’s possible that one of those beings passes away from that host and is reborn in this place.

dn24:2.19.11.verse: Having done so, they go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn24:2.19.12.verse: By dint of keen, resolute, committed, and diligent effort, and right application of mind, they experience an immersion of the heart of such a kind that they recollect that past life, but no further.

dn24:2.19.14.verse: “The gods who are not malevolent don’t spend too much time gazing at each other, so they don’t grow angry with each other, their bodies and minds don’t get tired, and they don’t pass away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.19.15.verse: They are permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, remaining the same for all eternity.

dn24:2.19.16.verse: But we who were malevolent spent too much time gazing at each other, so our minds grew angry with each other, our bodies and minds got tired, and we passed away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.19.17.verse: We are impermanent, not lasting, short-lived, liable to pass away, and have come to this place.”

dn24:2.19.18.verse: Is this how you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about due to those who are malevolent?’

dn24:2.19.20.verse: ‘That is what we have heard, Reverend Gotama, just as you say.’

dn24:2.19.21.verse: Bhaggava, I understand the origin of the world.

dn24:2.19.22.verse: Directly knowing this, the Realized One does not come to ruin.

dn24:2.20.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who describe the origin of the world in their denomination as having arisen as an anomaly.

dn24:2.20.2.verse: I go up to them and say,

dn24:2.20.3.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

dn24:2.20.6.verse: ‘But how do you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about anomalously?’

dn24:2.20.7.verse: But they are stumped by my question, and they even question me in return.

dn24:2.20.10.verse: When perception arises they pass away from that host of gods.

dn24:2.20.11.verse: It’s possible that one of those beings passes away from that host and is reborn in this place.

dn24:2.20.12.verse: Having done so, they go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

dn24:2.20.13.verse: By dint of keen, resolute, committed, and diligent effort, and right application of mind, they experience an immersion of the heart of such a kind that they recollect the arising of perception, but no further.

dn24:2.20.15.verse: “The self and the cosmos arose anomalously.

dn24:2.20.17.verse: Because formerly I didn’t exist, whereas now, having not existed, I’ve transformed into the state of existing.”

dn24:2.20.18.verse: Is this how you describe in your denomination that the origin of the world came about anomalously?’

dn24:2.20.20.verse: ‘That is what we have heard, Reverend Gotama, just as you say.’

dn24:2.20.21.verse: I understand this, and what goes beyond it. Yet since I do not misapprehend that understanding, I have realized quenching within myself. Directly knowing this, the Realized One does not come to ruin.

dn24:2.21.1.verse: Though I state and assert this, certain ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with the incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim:

dn24:2.21.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has a distorted perspective, and so have his monks.

dn24:2.21.4.verse: “When one enters and remains in the liberation of the beautiful, at that time one only perceives what is ugly.”’

dn24:2.21.8.verse: ‘When one enters and remains in the liberation of the beautiful, at that time one only perceives what is beautiful.’”

dn24:2.21.9.verse: “They are the ones with a distorted perspective, sir, who regard the Buddha and the mendicants in this way.

dn24:2.21.10.verse: Sir, I am quite confident that the Buddha is capable of teaching me so that I can enter and remain in the liberation on the beautiful.”

dn24:2.21.11.verse: “It’s hard for you to enter and remain in the liberation on the beautiful, since you have a different view, creed, and belief, and another discipline and denomination.

dn24:2.21.12.verse: Come on, Bhaggava, carefully preserve the confidence that you have in me.”

dn24:2.21.13.verse: “If it’s hard for me to enter and remain in the liberation on the beautiful, since I have a different view, creed, and belief, and another discipline and denomination.

dn24:2.21.14.verse: I shall carefully preserve the confidence that I have in the Buddha.”

dn24:2.21.15.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn24:2.21.16.verse: Satisfied, the wanderer of the Bhaggava clan approved what the Buddha said.

dn25:0.2.verse: The Lion’s Roar at the Monastery of Lady Udumbarikā

dn25:1.0.verse: 1. The Story of the Wanderer Nigrodha

dn25:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

dn25:1.3.verse: Now at that time the wanderer Nigrodha was residing in the lady Udumbarikā’s monastery for wanderers, together with a large assembly of three thousand wanderers.

dn25:1.4.verse: Then the householder Sandhāna left Rājagaha in the middle of the day to see the Buddha.

dn25:1.6.verse: “It’s the wrong time to see the Buddha,

dn25:1.8.verse: And it’s the wrong time to see the esteemed mendicants,

dn25:1.10.verse: Why don’t I visit the wanderer Nigrodha at the lady Udumbarikā’s monastery for wanderers?”

dn25:1.11.verse: So he went to the monastery for the wanderers.

dn25:2.1.verse: Now at that time, Nigrodha was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers making an uproar, a colossal racket. They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as

dn25:2.2.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

dn25:3.1.verse: Nigrodha saw Sandhāna coming off in the distance,

dn25:3.3.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

dn25:3.4.verse: The householder Sandhāna, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming.

dn25:3.5.verse: He is included among the white-clothed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama, who is residing near Rājagaha.

dn25:3.6.verse: Such venerables like the quiet, are educated to be quiet, and praise the quiet.

dn25:3.7.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

dn25:4.1.verse: Then Sandhāna went up to the wanderer Nigrodha, and exchanged greetings with him.

dn25:4.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Nigrodha,

dn25:4.3.verse: “The way the wanderers make an uproar as they sit together and talk about all kinds of low topics is one thing.

dn25:4.5.verse: It’s quite different to the way the Buddha frequents remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest that are quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat.”

dn25:5.1.verse: When Sandhāna said this, Nigrodha said to him,

dn25:5.2.verse: “Surely, householder, you should know better! With whom does the ascetic Gotama converse? With whom does he engage in discussion? With whom does he achieve lucidity of wisdom?

dn25:5.3.verse: Staying in empty huts has destroyed the ascetic Gotama’s wisdom. Not frequenting assemblies, he is unable to hold a discussion.

dn25:5.4.verse: He just lurks on the periphery.

dn25:5.5.verse: He’s just like a one-eyed cow, circling around and lurking on the periphery.

dn25:5.10.verse: Go on, householder! Were the ascetic Gotama to come to this assembly, I’d sink him with just one question! I’d tie him up like a hollow pot!”

dn25:6.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard this discussion between the householder Sandhāna and the wanderer Nigrodha.

dn25:6.2.verse: Then the Buddha descended from Vulture’s Peak Mountain and went to the peacocks’ feeding ground on the bank of the Sumāgadhā, where he walked mindfully in the open air.

dn25:6.5.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound. Here, the ascetic Gotama is walking mindfully on the bank of the Sumāgadhā.

dn25:6.6.verse: The venerable likes quiet and praises quiet.

dn25:6.7.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.

dn25:6.8.verse: If he comes, I’ll ask him this question:

dn25:6.9.verse: ‘Sir, what teaching do you use to guide your disciples, through which they claim solace in the fundamental goal of the spiritual life?’”

dn25:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha went up to the wanderer Nigrodha,

dn25:7.3.verse: “Let the Blessed One come, sir! Welcome to the Blessed One, sir!

dn25:7.4.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

dn25:7.5.verse: Please, sir, sit down, here, a seat is ready.”

dn25:7.6.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

dn25:7.7.verse: while Nigrodha took a low seat and sat to one side.

dn25:7.9.verse: “Nigrodha, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

dn25:7.11.verse: “Well, sir, I saw you walking mindfully and said:

dn25:7.12.verse: ‘If the ascetic Gotama comes, I’ll ask him this question:

dn25:7.13.verse: “Sir, what teaching do you use to guide your disciples, through which they claim solace in the fundamental goal of the spiritual life?”’

dn25:7.14.verse: This is the conversation that was unfinished when the Buddha arrived.”

dn25:7.15.verse: “It’s hard for you to understand this, Nigrodha, since you have a different view, creed, and belief, and another discipline and denomination.

dn25:7.16.verse: Please ask me a question about the higher disgust of sin in your own denomination:

dn25:7.17.verse: ‘How are the conditions for the fervent mortification in disgust of sin completed, and how are they incomplete?’”

dn25:7.18.verse: When he said this, those wanderers made an uproar,

dn25:7.19.verse: “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The ascetic Gotama has such power and might! For he sets aside his own doctrine and invites discussion on the doctrine of others!”

dn25:8.1.verse: Then Nigrodha, having quieted those wanderers, said to the Buddha,

dn25:8.2.verse: “Sir, we teach fervent mortification in disgust of sin, regarding it as essential and sticking to it.

dn25:8.3.verse: How are the conditions for the fervent mortification in disgust of sin completed, and how are they incomplete?”

dn25:8.4.verse: “Nigrodha, it’s when a mortifier goes naked, ignoring conventions. They lick their hands, and don’t come or wait when called. They don’t consent to food brought to them, or food prepared on their behalf, or an invitation for a meal.

dn25:8.5.verse: They don’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breast-feeding, or who lives with a man; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. They accept no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drink no fermented gruel.

dn25:8.6.verse: They go to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls. They feed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

dn25:8.7.verse: They eat once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. They live committed to the practice of eating food at set intervals.

dn25:8.8.verse: They eat herbs, millet, wild rice, poor rice, water lettuce, rice bran, scum from boiling rice, sesame flour, grass, or cow dung. They survive on forest roots and fruits, or eating fallen fruit.

dn25:8.9.verse: They wear robes of sunn hemp, mixed hemp, corpse-wrapping cloth, rags, lodh tree bark, antelope hide (whole or in strips), kusa grass, bark, wood-chips, human hair, horse-tail hair, or owls’ wings.

dn25:8.10.verse: They tear out their hair and beard, committed to this practice.

dn25:8.11.verse: They constantly stand, turning down seats.

dn25:8.12.verse: They squat, committed to the endeavor of squatting.

dn25:8.13.verse: They lie on a mat of thorns, making a mat of thorns their bed.

dn25:8.14.verse: They make their bed on a plank, or the bare ground.

dn25:8.15.verse: They lie only on one side.

dn25:8.17.verse: They stay in the open air.

dn25:8.18.verse: They sleep wherever they lay their mat.

dn25:8.19.verse: They eat unnatural things, committed to the practice of eating unnatural foods.

dn25:8.20.verse: They don’t drink, committed to the practice of not drinking liquids.

dn25:8.21.verse: They’re devoted to ritual bathing three times a day, including at dusk.

dn25:8.23.verse: If this is so, is the fervent mortification in disgust of sin complete, or incomplete?”

dn25:8.24.verse: “Clearly, sir, if that is so the fervent mortification in disgust of sin is complete, not incomplete.”

dn25:8.25.verse: “But even such a completed mortification has many defects, I say.”

dn25:9.1.verse: “But how does the Buddha say that even such a completed mortification has many defects?”

dn25:9.2.verse: “Firstly, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for.

dn25:9.4.verse: This is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:9.5.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

dn25:9.7.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:9.8.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They become indulgent and infatuated and fall into negligence on account of that.

dn25:9.10.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They generate possessions, honor, and popularity through that mortification. They’re happy with that, as they’ve got all they wished for.

dn25:10.3.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:10.4.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They generate possessions, honor, and popularity through that mortification. They glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

dn25:10.6.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:10.7.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They generate possessions, honor, and popularity through that mortification. They become indulgent and infatuated and fall into negligence on account of that.

dn25:10.9.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:10.10.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier becomes fussy about food, saying,

dn25:10.11.verse: ‘This is acceptable to me, this is not acceptable to me.’

dn25:10.12.verse: What is not acceptable they give up in expectation.

dn25:10.13.verse: But what is acceptable they eat tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

dn25:10.14.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:10.15.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification out of longing for possessions, honor, and popularity, thinking,

dn25:10.16.verse: ‘Kings, royal ministers, aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and sectarians will honor me!’

dn25:10.17.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier rebukes a certain ascetic or brahmin,

dn25:11.2.verse: ‘What is it with this one living in abundance, devouring everything—

dn25:11.3.verse: plants propagated from roots, trunks, cuttings, or joints; and those from regular seeds as the fifth. According to this ascetic’s doctrine, the crown of the tooth is forked lightning!’

dn25:11.4.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:11.5.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier sees a certain ascetic or brahmin being honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.

dn25:11.7.verse: ‘This one, who lives in abundance, is honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.

dn25:11.8.verse: But I, a fervent mortifier who lives rough, am not honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.’ Thus they give rise to jealousy and stinginess regarding families.

dn25:11.9.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:11.10.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier sits meditation only when people can see them.

dn25:11.11.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:11.12.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier sneaks about among families, thinking,

dn25:11.13.verse: ‘This is part of my mortification; this is part of my mortification.’

dn25:11.14.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:11.15.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier sometimes behaves in an underhand manner.

dn25:11.16.verse: When asked whether something is acceptable to them, they say it is, even though it isn’t.

dn25:11.17.verse: Or they say it isn’t, even though it is.

dn25:11.18.verse: Thus they tell a deliberate lie.

dn25:11.19.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier disagrees with the way that the Realized One or their disciple teaches Dhamma, even when they make a valid point.

dn25:12.2.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:12.3.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier is irritable and acrimonious …

dn25:12.10.verse: they have corrupt wishes, falling under the sway of corrupt wishes …

dn25:12.11.verse: they have wrong view, being attached to an extremist view …

dn25:12.12.verse: they’re attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go.

dn25:12.14.verse: This too is a defect in that mortifier.

dn25:12.16.verse: Are such mortifications defective or not?”

dn25:12.18.verse: It’s possible that a mortifier might have all of these defects,

dn25:12.19.verse: let alone one or other of them.”

dn25:13.1.verse: “Firstly, Nigrodha, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. But they’re not happy with that, as they still haven’t got all they wished for.

dn25:13.3.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:13.4.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They don’t glorify themselves or put others down on account of that.

dn25:13.5.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:13.8.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier undertakes a practice of mortification. They generate possessions, honor, and popularity through that mortification. They’re not happy with that, as they still haven’t got all they wished for …

dn25:13.10.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of possessions, honor, and popularity …

dn25:13.12.verse: They don’t become indulgent because of it …

dn25:13.13.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:13.14.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier doesn’t become fussy about food, saying,

dn25:13.15.verse: ‘This is acceptable to me, this is not acceptable to me.’

dn25:13.16.verse: What is not acceptable they give up without concern.

dn25:13.17.verse: But what is acceptable they eat without being tied, infatuated, attached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

dn25:13.18.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:13.19.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier doesn’t undertake a practice of mortification out of longing for possessions, honor, and popularity …

dn25:13.20.verse: ‘Kings, royal ministers, aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and sectarians will honor me!’

dn25:13.21.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:13.22.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier doesn’t rebuke a certain ascetic or brahmin,

dn25:13.23.verse: ‘What is it with this one living in abundance, devouring everything—

dn25:13.24.verse: plants propagated from roots, trunks, cuttings, or joints; and those from regular seeds as the fifth. According to this ascetic’s doctrine, the crown of the tooth is like forked lightning!’

dn25:13.25.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier sees a certain ascetic or brahmin being honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.

dn25:14.3.verse: ‘This one, who lives in abundance, is honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.

dn25:14.4.verse: But I, a fervent mortifier who lives rough, am not honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated among good families.’ Thus they don’t give rise to jealousy and stinginess regarding families.

dn25:14.5.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:14.6.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier doesn’t sit meditation only when people can see them.

dn25:14.7.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:14.8.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier doesn’t sneak about among families, thinking,

dn25:14.9.verse: ‘This is part of my mortification; this is part of my mortification.’

dn25:14.10.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:14.11.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier never behaves in an underhand manner.

dn25:14.12.verse: When asked whether something is acceptable to them, they say it isn’t when it isn’t.

dn25:14.14.verse: Or they say it is when it is.

dn25:14.16.verse: Thus they don’t tell a deliberate lie.

dn25:14.17.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier agrees with the way that the Realized One or their disciple teaches Dhamma when they make a valid point.

dn25:15.2.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:15.3.verse: Furthermore, a mortifier is not irritable and acrimonious …

dn25:15.11.verse: they’re not attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go.

dn25:15.13.verse: So they’re pure on that point.

dn25:15.15.verse: If this is so, is the fervent mortification in disgust of sin purified or not?”

dn25:15.16.verse: “Clearly, sir, it is purified. It has reached the peak and the pith.”

dn25:15.17.verse: “No, Nigrodha, at this point the fervent mortification in disgust of sin has not yet reached the peak and the pith.

dn25:15.18.verse: Rather, it has only reached the shoots.”

dn25:16.1.verse: “But at what point, sir, does the fervent mortification in disgust of sin reach the peak and the pith?

dn25:16.2.verse: Please help me reach the peak and the pith!”

dn25:16.3.verse: “Nigrodha, take a mortifier who is restrained in the fourfold constraint.

dn25:16.4.verse: And how is a mortifier restrained in the fourfold constraint?

dn25:16.5.verse: It’s when a mortifier doesn’t kill living creatures, doesn’t get others to kill, and doesn’t approve of killing.

dn25:16.6.verse: They don’t steal, get others to steal, or approve of stealing.

dn25:16.7.verse: They don’t lie, get others to lie, or approve of lying.

dn25:16.8.verse: They don’t expect rewards from their practice, they don’t lead others to expect rewards, and they don’t approve of expecting rewards.

dn25:16.9.verse: That’s how a mortifier is restrained in the fourfold constraint.

dn25:16.10.verse: When a mortifier is restrained in the fourfold constraint, that is their mortification.

dn25:16.11.verse: They step forward, not falling back.

dn25:16.12.verse: They frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

dn25:16.13.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

dn25:16.14.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

dn25:16.15.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

dn25:16.16.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

dn25:16.17.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

dn25:16.18.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

dn25:17.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

dn25:17.2.verse: Then they meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn25:17.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

dn25:17.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

dn25:17.5.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn25:17.7.verse: If this is so, is the fervent mortification in disgust of sin purified or not?”

dn25:17.8.verse: “Clearly, sir, it is purified. It has reached the peak and the pith.”

dn25:17.9.verse: “No, Nigrodha, at this point the fervent mortification in disgust of sin has not yet reached the peak and the pith.

dn25:17.10.verse: Rather, it has only reached the bark.”

dn25:18.1.verse: “But at what point, sir, does the fervent mortification in disgust of sin reach the peak and the pith?

dn25:18.2.verse: Please help me reach the peak and the pith!”

dn25:18.3.verse: “Nigrodha, take a mortifier who is restrained in the fourfold constraint.

dn25:18.8.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

dn25:18.9.verse: Then they meditate spreading a heart full of love …

dn25:18.13.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

dn25:18.15.verse: If this is so, is the fervent mortification in disgust of sin purified or not?”

dn25:18.16.verse: “Clearly, sir, it is purified. It has reached the peak and the pith.”

dn25:18.17.verse: “No, Nigrodha, at this point the fervent mortification in disgust of sin has not yet reached the peak and the pith.

dn25:18.18.verse: Rather, it has only reached the softwood.”

dn25:19.1.verse: “But at what point, sir, does the fervent mortification in disgust of sin reach the peak and the pith?

dn25:19.2.verse: Please help me reach the peak and the pith!”

dn25:19.3.verse: “Nigrodha, take a mortifier who is restrained in the fourfold constraint.

dn25:19.8.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

dn25:19.9.verse: Then they meditate spreading a heart full of love …

dn25:19.11.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

dn25:19.12.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

dn25:19.14.verse: If this is so, is the fervent mortification in disgust of sin purified or not?”

dn25:19.15.verse: “Clearly, sir, it is purified. It has reached the peak and the pith.”

dn25:19.16.verse: “Nigrodha, at this point the fervent mortification in disgust of sin has reached the peak and the pith.

dn25:19.17.verse: Nigrodha, remember you said this to me:

dn25:19.18.verse: ‘Sir, what teaching do you use to guide your disciples, through which they claim solace in the fundamental goal of the spiritual life?’

dn25:19.19.verse: Well, there is something better and finer than this. That’s what I use to guide my disciples, through which they claim solace in the fundamental goal of the spiritual life.”

dn25:19.20.verse: When he said this, those wanderers made an uproar,

dn25:19.21.verse: “In that case, we’re lost, and so is our denomination! We don’t know anything better or finer than that!”

dn25:20.2.verse: “Obviously, now these wanderers want to listen to what the Buddha says. They’re actively listening and trying to understand!”

dn25:20.3.verse: So he said to the wanderer Nigrodha,

dn25:20.4.verse: “Honorable Nigrodha, remember you said this to me:
