dn30:2.17.6.verse: He has many close adherents among the monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, titans, dragons, and centaurs.

dn30:2.17.7.verse: That’s what he obtains as Buddha.”

dn30:2.18.2.verse: “In past lives he was true to his promise,

dn30:2.18.3.verse: with no forked tongue, he shunned lies.

dn30:2.18.4.verse: He never broke his word to anyone,

dn30:2.18.5.verse: but spoke what was true, real, and factual.

dn30:2.18.6.verse: A tuft so very white like cotton-wool

dn30:2.18.8.verse: And never two, but only one,

dn30:2.18.9.verse: hair grew in each of his pores.

dn30:2.18.11.verse: and expert in signs gathered and prophesied:

dn30:2.18.12.verse: ‘One like this, with tuft and hair so prominent,

dn30:2.18.13.verse: will have many as his close adherents.

dn30:2.18.14.verse: Even as householder many people will follow him,

dn30:2.18.15.verse: due to the power of deeds in the past.

dn30:2.18.16.verse: But once gone forth, owning nothing,

dn30:2.18.17.verse: as Buddha the people will follow him.’”

dn30:2.19.1.verse: “Mendicants, in some past lives the Realized One was reborn as a human being.

dn30:2.19.2.verse: He refrained from backbiting. He didn’t repeat in one place what he heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, he reconciled those who were divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

dn30:2.19.3.verse: Due to performing those deeds he was reborn in a heavenly realm.

dn30:2.19.4.verse: When he came back to this place he obtained these two marks:

dn30:2.19.5.verse: he has forty teeth, and his teeth have no gaps.

dn30:2.20.1.verse: Possessing these marks, if he stays at home he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.

dn30:2.20.2.verse: And what does he obtain as king?

dn30:2.20.3.verse: His retinue cannot be divided. This includes brahmins and householders, people of town and country, treasurers and chief ministers, military officers, guardsmen, ministers, councillors, rulers, tax beneficiaries, and princes.

dn30:2.20.4.verse: That’s what he obtains as king.

dn30:2.20.5.verse: And what does he obtain as Buddha?

dn30:2.20.6.verse: His retinue cannot be divided. This includes monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, titans, dragons, and centaurs.

dn30:2.20.7.verse: That’s what he obtains as Buddha.”

dn30:2.21.2.verse: “He spoke no divisive words splitting the united,

dn30:2.21.5.verse: sowing division in those who are united.

dn30:2.21.6.verse: He spoke kind words to foster harmony,

dn30:2.21.8.verse: He cast aside quarrels among the people,

dn30:2.21.10.verse: In good rebirths he enjoyed the fruit

dn30:2.21.12.verse: Here his teeth are gapless, close-set,

dn30:2.21.13.verse: forty standing prominent in his mouth.

dn30:2.21.14.verse: If he becomes an aristocrat, ruler of the land,

dn30:2.21.16.verse: And as an ascetic, stainless, immaculate,

dn30:2.21.17.verse: his assembly will follow him, unshakable.”

dn30:2.22.0.verse: 28–29. A Large Tongue and the Voice of the Divinity

dn30:2.22.1.verse: “Mendicants, in some past lives the Realized One was reborn as a human being.

dn30:2.22.2.verse: He refrained from harsh speech. He spoke in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

dn30:2.22.3.verse: Due to performing those deeds he was reborn in a heavenly realm.

dn30:2.22.4.verse: When he came back to this place he obtained these two marks:

dn30:2.22.5.verse: he has a large tongue, and the voice of the Divinity, like a cuckoo’s call.

dn30:2.23.1.verse: Possessing these marks, if he stays at home he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.

dn30:2.23.2.verse: And what does he obtain as king?

dn30:2.23.3.verse: He has a compelling voice. His words are compelling to brahmins and householders, people of town and country, treasurers and chief ministers, military officers, guardsmen, ministers, councillors, rulers, tax beneficiaries, and princes.

dn30:2.23.4.verse: That’s what he obtains as king.

dn30:2.23.5.verse: And what does he obtain as Buddha?

dn30:2.23.6.verse: He has a compelling voice. His words are compelling to monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, titans, dragons, and centaurs.

dn30:2.23.7.verse: That’s what he obtains as Buddha.”

dn30:2.24.2.verse: “He never spoke a loud harsh word,

dn30:2.24.4.verse: causing harm, rude, crushing the people.

dn30:2.24.5.verse: His speech was sweet, helpful, and courteous.

dn30:2.24.6.verse: He uttered words dear to the mind,

dn30:2.24.7.verse: going to the heart, pleasing to the ear.

dn30:2.24.8.verse: He enjoyed the fruit of his good verbal conduct,

dn30:2.24.9.verse: experiencing the fruit of good deeds in heaven.

dn30:2.24.11.verse: on his return to here he acquired the voice of the Divinity.

dn30:2.24.12.verse: His tongue was long and wide,

dn30:2.24.14.verse: Even as householder his speech brings prosperity.

dn30:2.24.15.verse: But if that man goes forth,

dn30:2.24.17.verse: they’ll be compelled by his fair words.”

dn30:2.25.1.verse: “Mendicants, in some past lives the Realized One was reborn as a human being.

dn30:2.25.2.verse: He refrained from talking nonsense. His words were timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. He said things at the right time which were valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

dn30:2.25.3.verse: Due to performing those deeds he was reborn in a heavenly realm.

dn30:2.25.4.verse: When he came back to this place he obtained this mark:

dn30:2.25.5.verse: his jaw is like that of a lion.

dn30:2.26.1.verse: Possessing this mark, if he stays at home he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.

dn30:2.26.2.verse: And what does he obtain as king?

dn30:2.26.3.verse: He can’t be destroyed by any human foe or enemy.

dn30:2.26.4.verse: That’s what he obtains as king.

dn30:2.26.5.verse: And what does he obtain as Buddha?

dn30:2.26.6.verse: He can’t be destroyed by any foe or enemy whether internal or external; nor by greed, hate, or delusion; nor by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

dn30:2.26.7.verse: That’s what he obtains as Buddha.”

dn30:2.27.3.verse: his way of speaking was never loose.

dn30:2.27.4.verse: He cast aside what was unbeneficial,

dn30:2.27.5.verse: and spoke for the welfare and happiness of the people.

dn30:2.27.6.verse: So doing he passed from here to be reborn in heaven,

dn30:2.27.7.verse: where he enjoyed the fruit of deeds well done.

dn30:2.27.8.verse: Passing away, on his return to here,

dn30:2.27.9.verse: he gained a jaw like the finest of beasts.

dn30:2.27.10.verse: He became a king so very hard to defeat,

dn30:2.27.11.verse: a mighty lord and ruler of mankind.

dn30:2.27.12.verse: He was equal to the best in the city of the Third Heaven,

dn30:2.27.13.verse: like Indra, the finest of gods.

dn30:2.27.14.verse: One such as that is not easily beaten by centaurs,

dn30:2.27.16.verse: If he becomes of that sort,

dn30:2.27.17.verse: he illuminates the quarters and in-between.”

dn30:2.28.1.verse: “Mendicants, in some past lives the Realized One was reborn as a human being.

dn30:2.28.2.verse: He gave up wrong livelihood and earned a living by right livelihood. He refrained from falsifying weights, metals, or measures; bribery, fraud, cheating, and duplicity; mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

dn30:2.28.3.verse: Due to performing, accumulating, heaping up, and amassing those deeds, when his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn30:2.28.4.verse: There he surpassed the other gods in ten respects: heavenly lifespan, beauty, happiness, glory, sovereignty, sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches.

dn30:2.28.5.verse: When he came back to this place he obtained these two marks: his teeth are even and perfectly white.

dn30:2.29.1.verse: Possessing these marks, if he stays at home he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king. His dominion extends to all four sides, he achieves stability in the country, and he possesses the seven treasures.

dn30:2.29.2.verse: He has the following seven treasures:

dn30:2.29.3.verse: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure.

dn30:2.29.4.verse: He has over a thousand sons who are valiant and heroic, crushing the armies of his enemies.

dn30:2.29.5.verse: After conquering this land girt by sea—free of harassment by bandits, successful and prosperous, safe, blessed, free of pests—he reigns by principle, without rod or sword.

dn30:2.29.6.verse: And what does he obtain as king?

dn30:2.29.7.verse: His retinue is pure. This includes brahmins and householders, people of town and country, treasurers and chief ministers, military officers, guardsmen, ministers, councillors, rulers, tax beneficiaries, and princes.

dn30:2.29.8.verse: That’s what he obtains as king.

dn30:2.30.1.verse: But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, who has cast off the world’s veil.

dn30:2.30.2.verse: And what does he obtain as Buddha?

dn30:2.30.3.verse: His retinue is pure. This includes monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, titans, dragons, and centaurs.

dn30:2.30.4.verse: That’s what he obtains as Buddha.”

dn30:2.31.3.verse: a way of life that’s fair, pure, and just.

dn30:2.31.4.verse: He cast aside what was unbeneficial,

dn30:2.31.5.verse: and lived for the welfare and happiness of the people.

dn30:2.31.6.verse: Having done what’s praised by the clever, the wise, and the good,

dn30:2.31.7.verse: that man experienced the fruit in heaven.

dn30:2.31.8.verse: Equal to the best in the Third Heaven,

dn30:2.31.9.verse: he enjoyed himself with pleasure and play.

dn30:2.31.10.verse: From there he passed back to a human life.

dn30:2.31.11.verse: With the remaining ripening of the fruit of good deeds,

dn30:2.31.12.verse: he obtained teeth that are even,

dn30:2.31.14.verse: Many soothsayers regarded as wise men

dn30:2.31.16.verse: ‘With twice-born teeth so even, so white, so clean and bright

dn30:2.31.17.verse: his retinue will be so pure.

dn30:2.31.18.verse: As king, his people will also be pure,

dn30:2.31.19.verse: when he rules having conquered this earth so broad.

dn30:2.31.21.verse: but will live for the welfare and happiness of the people.

dn30:2.31.22.verse: But if he goes forth he’ll be an ascetic free of ill,

dn30:2.31.23.verse: his passions quelled, the veil cast off.

dn30:2.31.25.verse: he sees this world and the next.

dn30:2.31.26.verse: Those who do his bidding, both lay and renunciate,

dn30:2.31.27.verse: shake off wickedness, impure and blameworthy.

dn30:2.31.28.verse: He’s surrounded by pure people, who cast aside

dn30:2.31.30.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn30:2.31.31.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

dn31:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

dn31:1.3.verse: Now at that time the householder’s son Sigālaka rose early and left Rājagaha. With his clothes and hair all wet, he raised his cupped palms to revere the various quarters—

dn31:1.4.verse: east, south, west, north, below, and above.

dn31:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

dn31:2.2.verse: He saw Sigālaka revering the various quarters

dn31:2.5.verse: “Householder’s son, why are you revering the various quarters in this way?”

dn31:2.7.verse: “Sir, on his deathbed my father said to me:

dn31:2.9.verse: Honoring, respecting, and venerating my father’s words, I rose early and left Rājagaha and, with my clothes and hair all wet, raised my cupped palms to revere the various quarters—

dn31:2.10.verse: east, south, west, north, below, and above.”

dn31:2.12.verse: “Householder’s son, that’s not how the six directions should be revered in the training of the Noble One.”

dn31:2.13.verse: “But sir, how should the six directions be revered in the training of the Noble One?

dn31:2.15.verse: “Well then, householder’s son, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

dn31:3.1.verse: “Householder’s son, a noble disciple gives up four corrupt deeds, doesn’t do bad deeds on four grounds, and avoids six drains on wealth. When they’ve left these fourteen bad things behind they have the six directions covered.

dn31:3.2.verse: They’re practicing to win in both worlds, and they succeed in this world and the next.

dn31:3.3.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn31:3.5.verse: What four corrupt deeds have they given up?

dn31:3.6.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying: these are corrupt deeds.

dn31:3.7.verse: These are the four corrupt deeds they’ve given up.”

dn31:3.8.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:3.9.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:4.4.verse: astute people don’t praise these things.”

dn31:5.1.verse: “On what four grounds do they not do bad deeds?

dn31:5.2.verse: One does bad deeds prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice.

dn31:5.3.verse: When a noble disciple is not prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice,

dn31:5.4.verse: they don’t do bad deeds on these four grounds.”

dn31:5.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:5.6.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:6.2.verse: out of favoritism, hostility, cowardice, or stupidity,

dn31:6.4.verse: like the moon in the waning fortnight.

dn31:6.5.verse: If you don’t act against the teaching

dn31:6.6.verse: out of favoritism, hostility, cowardice, and stupidity,

dn31:6.8.verse: like the moon in the waxing fortnight.”

dn31:7.1.verse: “What six drains on wealth do they avoid?

dn31:7.2.verse: Habitually engaging in the following things is a drain on wealth: beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants; roaming the street markets at night; frequenting festivals; gambling; bad friends; laziness.

dn31:8.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of habitually consuming intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

dn31:8.2.verse: Immediate loss of wealth, promotion of quarrels, susceptibility to illness, disrepute, indecent exposure; and weakened wisdom is the sixth thing.

dn31:8.3.verse: These are the six drawbacks of habitually consuming intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

dn31:9.0.verse: 6. Six Drawbacks of Roaming the Street Markets at Night

dn31:9.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of roaming the street markets at night.

dn31:9.2.verse: Yourself, your partners and children, and your property are all left unguarded. You’re suspected of bad deeds. Untrue rumors spread about you. You’re at the forefront of many things that entail suffering.

dn31:9.3.verse: These are the six drawbacks of roaming the street markets at night.

dn31:10.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of frequenting festivals.

dn31:10.2.verse: You’re always thinking: ‘Where’s the dancing? Where’s the singing? Where’s the music? Where are the stories? Where’s the applause? Where are the kettledrums?’

dn31:10.3.verse: These are the six drawbacks of frequenting festivals.

dn31:11.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of habitually gambling.

dn31:11.2.verse: Victory breeds enmity. The loser mourns their money. There is immediate loss of wealth. A gambler’s word carries no weight in public assembly. Friends and colleagues treat them with contempt. And no one wants to marry a gambler, for they think:

dn31:11.3.verse: ‘This individual is a gambler—they’re not able to support a partner.’

dn31:11.4.verse: These are the six drawbacks of habitually gambling.

dn31:12.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of bad friends.

dn31:12.2.verse: You become friends and companions with those who are addicts, carousers, drunkards, frauds, swindlers, and thugs.

dn31:12.3.verse: These are the six drawbacks of bad friends.

dn31:13.1.verse: There are these six drawbacks of habitual laziness.

dn31:13.2.verse: You don’t get your work done because you think: ‘It’s too cold! It’s too hot. It’s too late! It’s too early! I’m too hungry! I’m too full!’

dn31:13.3.verse: By dwelling on so many excuses for not working, you don’t make any more money, and the money you already have runs out.

dn31:13.4.verse: These are the six drawbacks of habitual laziness.”

dn31:13.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:13.6.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:14.2.verse: some call you their dear, dear friend;

dn31:14.3.verse: but a friend in times of need

dn31:14.8.verse: these six grounds ruin a person.

dn31:14.12.verse: in both this world and the next.

dn31:14.13.verse: Dice, women, toddy, song and dance;

dn31:14.14.verse: sleeping by day and roaming at night;

dn31:14.16.verse: these six grounds ruin a person.

dn31:14.17.verse: They play dice and drink beer,

dn31:14.18.verse: and consort with women loved by others.

dn31:14.19.verse: Associating with the worse, not the better,

dn31:14.20.verse: they diminish like the waning moon.

dn31:14.21.verse: One who is broke and destitute due to toddy,

dn31:14.25.verse: When you’re in the habit of sleeping late,

dn31:14.26.verse: seeing night as time to rise,

dn31:14.28.verse: you can’t keep up the household life.

dn31:14.31.verse: When the young neglect their work like this,

dn31:14.33.verse: But one who considers heat and cold

dn31:14.34.verse: as no more than blades of grass—

dn31:14.35.verse: he does his duties as a man,

dn31:15.1.verse: “Householder’s son, you should recognize these four enemies disguised as friends:

dn31:15.2.verse: the taker, the talker, the flatterer, the spender.

dn31:16.1.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s all take on four grounds.

dn31:16.3.verse: Giving little, they expect a lot.

dn31:16.4.verse: They do their duty out of fear.

dn31:16.5.verse: They associate for their own advantage.

dn31:16.6.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s all take on these four grounds.

dn31:17.1.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s all talk on four grounds.

dn31:17.2.verse: They’re hospitable in the past. They’re hospitable in the future. They’re full of meaningless pleasantries. When something needs doing in the present they point to their own misfortune.

dn31:17.3.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s all talk on these four grounds.

dn31:18.1.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s a flatterer on four grounds.

dn31:18.2.verse: They support you equally in doing bad and doing good. They praise you to your face, and put you down behind your back.

dn31:18.3.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s a flatterer on these four grounds.

dn31:19.1.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s a spender on four grounds.

dn31:19.2.verse: They accompany you when drinking, roaming the street markets at night, frequenting festivals, and gambling.

dn31:19.3.verse: You can recognize a fake friend who’s a spender on these four grounds.”

dn31:19.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:19.5.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:20.4.verse: and one’s a comrade who spends.

dn31:20.6.verse: these four enemies for what they are

dn31:20.7.verse: and keeps them at a distance,

dn31:20.8.verse: as they’d shun a risky road.”

dn31:21.1.verse: “Householder’s son, you should recognize these four good-hearted friends:

dn31:21.2.verse: the helper, the friend in good times and bad, the counselor, and the one who’s sympathetic.

dn31:22.1.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s a helper on four grounds.

dn31:22.2.verse: They guard you when you’re negligent. They guard your property when you’re negligent. They keep you safe in times of danger. When something needs doing, they provide you with twice the money you need.

dn31:22.3.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s a helper on these four grounds.

dn31:23.1.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s the same in good times and bad on four grounds.

dn31:23.2.verse: They tell you secrets. They keep your secrets. They don’t abandon you in times of trouble. They’d even give their life for your welfare.

dn31:23.3.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s the same in good times and bad on these four grounds.

dn31:24.1.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s a counselor on four grounds.

dn31:24.2.verse: They keep you from doing bad. They support you in doing good. They teach you what you do not know. They explain the path to heaven.

dn31:24.3.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s a counselor on these four grounds.

dn31:25.1.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s sympathetic on four grounds.

dn31:25.2.verse: They don’t delight in your misfortune. They delight in your good fortune. They keep others from criticizing you. They encourage praise of you.

dn31:25.3.verse: You can recognize a good-hearted friend who’s sympathetic on these four grounds.”

dn31:25.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:25.5.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:26.2.verse: one the same in both pleasure and pain,

dn31:26.6.verse: these four friends for what they are

dn31:26.8.verse: like a mother the child at her breast.

dn31:26.11.verse: They pick up riches as bees

dn31:26.13.verse: And their riches proceed to grow,

dn31:26.14.verse: like a termite mound piling up.

dn31:26.16.verse: a householder does enough for their family.

dn31:26.17.verse: And they’d hold on to friends

dn31:26.18.verse: by dividing their wealth in four.

dn31:26.21.verse: And the fourth should be kept

dn31:27.1.verse: “And how, householder’s son, does a noble disciple cover the six directions?

dn31:27.2.verse: These six directions should be recognized:

dn31:27.3.verse: parents as the east, tutors as the south, partner and children as the west, friends and colleagues as the north, bondservants and workers as beneath, and ascetics and brahmins as above.

dn31:28.1.verse: A child should serve their parents as the eastern quarter in five ways, thinking:

dn31:28.2.verse: ‘I will support those who supported me. I’ll do my duty for them. I’ll maintain the family lineage. I’ll take care of the inheritance. When they have passed away, I’ll make an offering on their behalf.’

dn31:28.3.verse: Parents served by the children in these five ways show sympathy to them in five ways.

dn31:28.4.verse: They keep them from doing bad. They support them in doing good. They train them in a profession. They connect them with a suitable partner. They transfer the inheritance in due time.

dn31:28.5.verse: Parents served by their children in these five ways show sympathy to them in these five ways.

dn31:28.6.verse: And that’s how the eastern quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.

dn31:29.1.verse: A pupil should serve their tutor as the southern quarter in five ways:

dn31:29.2.verse: by rising for them, by serving them, by listening well, by looking after them, and by carefully learning their profession.

dn31:29.3.verse: Tutors served by their pupils in these five ways show sympathy to them in five ways.

dn31:29.4.verse: They make sure they’re well educated and well drilled in memorization. They clearly explain all the knowledge of the profession. They introduce them to their friends and colleagues. They provide protection in every region.

dn31:29.5.verse: Tutors served by their pupils in these five ways show sympathy to them in these five ways.

dn31:29.6.verse: And that’s how the southern quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.

dn31:30.1.verse: A husband should serve his wife as the western quarter in five ways:

dn31:30.2.verse: by treating her with honor, by not looking down on her, by not being unfaithful, by relinquishing authority to her, and by presenting her with adornments.

dn31:30.3.verse: A wife served by her husband in these five ways shows sympathy to him in five ways.

dn31:30.4.verse: She’s well-organized in her work. She manages the domestic help. She’s not unfaithful. She preserves his earnings. She’s deft and tireless in all her duties.

dn31:30.5.verse: A wife served by her husband in these five ways shows sympathy to him in these five ways.

dn31:30.6.verse: And that’s how the western quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.

dn31:31.1.verse: A gentleman should serve his friends and colleagues as the northern quarter in five ways:

dn31:31.2.verse: giving, kindly words, taking care, equality, and not using tricky words.

dn31:31.3.verse: Friends and colleagues served by a gentleman in these five ways show sympathy to him in five ways.

dn31:31.4.verse: They guard him when they’re negligent. They guard his property when they’re negligent. They keep him safe in times of danger. They don’t abandon him in times of trouble. They honor his descendants.

dn31:31.5.verse: Friends and colleagues served by a gentleman in these five ways show sympathy to him in these five ways.

dn31:31.6.verse: And that’s how the northern quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.

dn31:32.1.verse: A master should serve their bondservants and workers as the lower quarter in five ways:

dn31:32.2.verse: by organizing work according to ability, by paying food and wages, by nursing them when sick, by sharing special treats, and by giving time off work.

dn31:32.3.verse: Bondservants and workers served by a master in these five ways show sympathy to him in five ways.

dn31:32.4.verse: They get up first, and go to bed last. They don’t steal. They do their work well. And they promote a good reputation.

dn31:32.5.verse: Bondservants and workers served by a master in these five ways show sympathy to him in these five ways.

dn31:32.6.verse: And that’s how the lower quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.

dn31:33.1.verse: A gentleman should serve ascetics and brahmins as the upper quarter in five ways:

dn31:33.2.verse: by loving deeds of body, speech, and mind, by not turning them away at the gate, and by providing them with material needs.

dn31:33.3.verse: Ascetics and brahmins served by a gentleman in these five ways show sympathy to him in six ways.

dn31:33.4.verse: They keep him from doing bad. They support him in doing good. They think of him with kindly thoughts. They teach him what he does not know. They clarify what he’s already learned. They explain the path to heaven.

dn31:33.5.verse: Ascetics and brahmins served by a gentleman in these five ways show sympathy to him in these six ways.

dn31:33.6.verse: And that’s how the upper quarter is covered, kept safe and free of peril.”

dn31:33.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn31:33.8.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

dn31:34.8.verse: a householder does enough for their family.

dn31:34.11.verse: the placid in manner and the amenable:

dn31:34.12.verse: they’re the kind who win glory.

dn31:34.15.verse: those consistent in conduct, the intelligent:

dn31:34.16.verse: they’re the kind who win glory.

dn31:34.17.verse: The inclusive, the makers of friends,

dn31:34.18.verse: the bountiful, those rid of stinginess,

dn31:34.19.verse: those who lead, train, and persuade:

dn31:34.20.verse: they’re the kind who win glory.

dn31:34.23.verse: and treating equally in worldly conditions,

dn31:34.24.verse: as they deserve in each case;

dn31:34.25.verse: these ways of being inclusive in the world

dn31:34.26.verse: are like a moving chariot’s linchpin.

dn31:34.27.verse: If there were no such ways of being inclusive,

dn31:34.30.verse: for what they’ve done for their children.

dn31:34.31.verse: But since these ways of being inclusive do exist,

dn31:34.32.verse: the astute do regard them well,

dn31:35.1.verse: When this was said, Sigālaka the householder’s son said to the Buddha,

dn31:35.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn31:35.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

dn31:35.5.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

dn32:1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha on the Vultures’ Peak mountain.

dn32:1.3.verse: Then the Four Great Kings, with a great army of yakkhas, with a great army of gandhabbas, with a great army of kumbhaṇḍas, with a great army of nāgas, having set up a protection over the four quarters, having set serried troops at the four directions, having set up a barricade at the four directions, at the end of the night, having lit up the whole of Vultures’ Peak with their surpassing beauty, approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, they sat down on one side.

dn32:1.4.verse: Then of those yakkhas, some, after worshipping the Fortunate One, sat down on one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Fortunate One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down on one side. Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to the Fortunate One, sat down on one side. Some, after announcing their name and family, sat down on one side. Some, while keeping silent, sat down on one side.

dn32:2.1.verse: Then, while sitting on one side, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to the Fortunate One:

dn32:2.2.verse: “There are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.3.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.4.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.5.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.6.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.7.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One.

dn32:2.8.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas are not pleased with the Fortunate One.

dn32:2.9.verse: What is the reason for that?

dn32:2.10.verse: Because, reverend Sir, the Fortunate One preaches the Dhamma of refraining from killing living creatures, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from taking what has not been given, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from sexual misconduct, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from false speech, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from liquor, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

dn32:2.11.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas do not refrain from killing living creatures, do not refrain from taking what has not been given, do not refrain from sexual misconduct, do not refrain from false speech, do not refrain from liquors, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

dn32:2.12.verse: To them that is neither dear nor appealing.

dn32:2.13.verse: There are, reverend Sir, disciples of the Fortunate One in the wilderness, who are practising in remote jungle dwelling places, where there is little sound, little noise, which have a lonely atmosphere, lying hidden away from men, which are suitable for seclusion.

dn32:2.14.verse: And there are high ranking yakkhas settled there who are not pleased with the word of the Fortunate One,

dn32:2.15.verse: To please then, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One learn this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.”

dn32:2.16.verse: The Fortunate One by keeping silent gave consent.

dn32:3.1.verse: Then the Great King Vessavaṇa having understood the Fortunate One’s consent on that occasion recited this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection:

dn32:3.5.verse: who has pity on all beings,

dn32:3.13.verse: who is free in every respect.

dn32:3.15.verse: the glorious son of the Sakyans,

dn32:3.17.verse: which is the dispelling of all suffering.

dn32:3.18.verse: Those who are emancipated in the world,

dn32:3.19.verse: who have insight (into things) as they are,

dn32:3.20.verse: those people free from malicious speech,

dn32:3.21.verse: who are great and fully mature,

dn32:3.23.verse: who is of benefit to gods and men,

dn32:3.24.verse: who has understanding and good conduct,

dn32:3.25.verse: who is great and fully mature.

dn32:4.1.verse: From where the sun comes up,

dn32:4.2.verse: the son of Aditi, the great circle,

dn32:4.3.verse: while that one is coming up,

dn32:4.4.verse: the darkness of night comes to an end,

dn32:4.5.verse: and after the sun has come up,

dn32:8.1.verse: This, dear Sir, is the “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.

dn32:8.2.verse: Whoever, dear Sir - be they monk or nun or layman or laywoman - learns this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection well, and will master it in its entirety,

dn32:8.3.verse: then if a non-human being - be they male yakkha or female yakkha or yakkha boy or yakkha girl or yakkha minister or yakkha councillor or yakkha messenger or male gandhabba or female gandhabba or gandhabba boy or gandhabba girl or gandhabba minister or gandhabba councillor or gandhabba messenger or male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍa or kumbhaṇḍa boy or kumbhaṇḍa girl or kumbhaṇḍa minister or kumbhaṇḍa councillor or kumbhaṇḍa messenger or male nāga or female nāga or nāga boy or nāga girl or nāga minister or nāga councillor or nāga messenger - with a wicked mind come near while they are going, or stand near while they are standing, or sit near while they are sitting, or lie near while they are lying,

dn32:8.4.verse: then that non-human being, dear Sir, would not receive in my villages and towns, honour or respect.

dn32:8.5.verse: That non-human being, dear Sir, would not receive in my royal city Ālakamandā, ground or dwelling.

dn32:8.6.verse: That non-human being, dear Sir, would not be able to go to the gathering of the yakkhas.

dn32:8.7.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would not give or take him in marriage.

dn32:8.8.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would abuse him with very personal abuse.

dn32:8.9.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would drop an empty bowl over his head.

dn32:8.10.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would split his head into seven pieces.

dn32:9.1.verse: There are non-human beings, dear Sir, who are fierce, cruel, and violent, they do not take notice of the Great Kings, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ men, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ mens’ men,

dn32:9.2.verse: and those non-human beings, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the Great Kings.

dn32:9.3.verse: Just as, dear Sir, there are thieves in the king of Magadha’s realm,

dn32:9.4.verse: who do not take notice of the king of Magadha, who do not take notice of the king of Magadha’s men, who do not take notice of the king of Magadha’s mens’ men,

dn32:9.5.verse: and those great thieves, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the king of Magadha.

dn32:9.6.verse: Even so, dear Sir, there are non-human beings who are fierce, cruel, and violent, they do not take notice of the Great Kings, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ men, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ mens’ men,

dn32:9.7.verse: and those non-human beings, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the Great Kings.

dn32:9.8.verse: Now, dear Sir, whatever non-human beings - be they male yakkha or female yakkha or yakkha boy or yakkha girl or yakkha minister or yakkha councillor or yakkha messenger or male gandhabba or female gandhabba or gandhabba boy or gandhabba girl or gandhabba minister or gandhabba councillor or gandhabba messenger or male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍa or kumbhaṇḍa boy or kumbhaṇḍa girl or kumbhaṇḍa minister or kumbhaṇḍa councillor or kumbhaṇḍa messenger or male nāga or female nāga or nāga boy or nāga girl or nāga minister or nāga councillor or nāga messenger - with a wicked mind should come near a monk or a nun or a layman or a laywoman while they are going, or stand near while they are standing, or sit near while they are sitting, or lie near while they are lying,

dn32:9.9.verse: then to these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, great generals, one should call out, one should shout out, one should cry out:

dn32:9.10.verse: “This yakkha has seized me, this yakkha has grabbed me, this yakkha annoys me, this yakkha harasses me, this yakkha hurts me, this yakkha injures me, this yakkha will not release me.”

dn32:11.2.verse: And now, dear Sir, we shall go, as we have many duties, and there is much which ought to be done.”

dn32:11.5.verse: ° Then some yakkhas rose from their seats and after worshipping and circumambulating the Fortunate One, vanished right there. ° Some exchanged greetings with the Fortunate One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, vanished right there. ° Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to the Fortunate One, vanished right there. Some, after announcing their name and family vanished right there. And some, while keeping silent, vanished right there.

dn32:12.1.verse: Then the Fortunate One when that night had passed addressed the monks, saying:

dn32:12.2.verse: “This night, monks, the Four Great Kings, with a great army of yakkhas, with a great army of gandhabbas, with a great army of kumbhaṇḍas, with a great army of nāgas, having set up a protection over the four quarters, having set serried troops at the four directions, having set up a barricade at the four directions, at the end of the night, having lit up the whole of Vultures’ Peak with their surpassing beauty, approached me, and after approaching and worshipping me, they sat down on one side.

dn32:12.3.verse: Then of those yakkhas, monks, some, after worshipping me, sat down on one side. Some exchanged greetings with me, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down on one side. Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to me, sat down on one side. Some, after announcing their name and family, sat down on one side. Some, while keeping silent, sat down on one side.

dn32:12.4.verse: Then, while sitting on one side, monks, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to me:

dn32:12.6.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas are not pleased with the Fortunate One.

dn32:12.7.verse: What is the reason for that?

dn32:12.10.verse: To them that is neither dear nor appealing.

dn32:12.11.verse: There are, reverend Sir, disciples of the Fortunate One in the wilderness, who are practising in remote jungle dwelling places, where there is little sound, little noise, which have a lonely atmosphere, lying hidden away from men, which are suitable for seclusion.

dn32:12.12.verse: And there are high ranking yakkhas settled there who are not pleased with the word of the Fortunate One, To please then, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One learn this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.”

dn32:12.13.verse: And I, monks, by keeping silent, gave consent.

dn32:12.14.verse: Then the Great King Vessavaṇa, monks, having understood my consent on that occasion recited this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection:

dn32:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

dn32:1.3.verse: Then, late at night, the four great kings—with large armies of spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—set guards, troops, and wards at the four quarters and then, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak with their beauty, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

dn32:1.4.verse: Before sitting down to one side, some spirits bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

dn32:2.13.verse: Sir, there are disciples of the Buddha who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest that are quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat.

dn32:2.14.verse: There dwell high spirits who have no confidence in the Buddha’s dispensation.

dn32:2.15.verse: To give them confidence, may the Buddha please learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”

dn32:8.1.verse: This, good fellow, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

dn32:8.2.verse: The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen should learn this Āṭānāṭiya protection well and completely memorize it.

dn32:8.3.verse: If anyone who does so is approached while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down by any non-human being with malicious intent—including males, females, boys, girls, chief ministers, councillors, and servants among the spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—

dn32:8.4.verse: that non-human will receive no homage or respect in any village or town.

dn32:8.5.verse: And they will receive no ground or dwelling in my capital of Ālakamandā.

dn32:8.6.verse: Nor will they get to go to the conference of the spirits.

dn32:8.7.verse: In addition, the non-humans would not give or take them in marriage.

dn32:8.8.verse: They’d heap personal abuse on them,

dn32:8.9.verse: drop an empty bowl on their head,

dn32:8.10.verse: and even split their head into seven pieces!

dn32:9.1.verse: For there are, good fellow, non-humans who are fierce, cruel, and violent. They don’t obey the Great Kings or their men or their men’s men.

dn32:9.2.verse: They’re said to be rebelling against the Great Kings.

dn32:9.3.verse: They’re just like the bandits in the king of Magadha’s realm

dn32:9.4.verse: who don’t obey the king, his men, or his men’s men,

dn32:9.5.verse: and are said to be rebelling against the king.

dn32:9.8.verse: If any non-human being with malicious intent—including males, females, boys, girls, ministers, councillors, and servants among the spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—approaches a monk, nun, layman, or laywoman while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,

dn32:9.9.verse: one ought to yell, cry, and scream to the spirits, great spirits, generals, great generals:

dn32:9.10.verse: ‘This spirit’s got me! This spirit’s entered me! This spirit’s annoying me! This spirit’s harassing me! This spirit’s hurting me! This spirit’s harming me! This spirit won’t let me go!’

dn32:10.1.verse: To what spirits, great spirits, generals, great generals?

dn32:10.9.verse: and the kings Nala and Janesabha,

dn32:11.1.verse: This, good fellow, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

dn32:11.2.verse: Well, now, good fellow, I must go. I have many duties, and much to do.”

dn32:11.3.verse: “Please, Great Kings, go at your convenience.”

dn32:11.4.verse: Then the four great kings got up from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, before vanishing right there.

dn32:11.5.verse: And before the other spirits present vanished, some bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

dn32:11.6.verse: The first recitation section is complete.

dn32:12.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened, repeating all the verses spoken. Then he added:

dn32:13.4.verse: The Āṭānāṭiya protection is beneficial, and is for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”

dn32:13.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

dn32:13.6.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

dn33:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Mallas together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants when he arrived at a Mallian town named Pāvā.

dn33:1.1.3.verse: There he stayed in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.

dn33:1.2.1.verse: Now at that time a new town hall named Ubbhaṭaka had recently been constructed for the Mallas of Pāvā. It had not yet been occupied by an ascetic or brahmin or any human at all.

dn33:1.2.2.verse: The Mallas of Pāvā also heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in Cunda’s mango grove.

dn33:1.2.3.verse: Then they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

dn33:1.2.4.verse: “Sir, a new town hall named Ubbhaṭaka has recently been constructed for the Mallas of Pāvā. It has not yet been occupied by an ascetic or brahmin or any human at all.

dn33:1.2.5.verse: May the Buddha be the first to use it, and only then will the Mallas of Pāvā use it.

dn33:1.2.6.verse: That would be for the lasting welfare and happiness of the Mallas of Pāvā.”

dn33:1.3.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the Mallas got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. Then they went to the new town hall, where they spread carpets all over, prepared seats, set up a water jar, and placed an oil lamp. Then they went back to the Buddha,

dn33:1.3.3.verse: and told him of their preparations, saying,

dn33:1.4.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the new town hall together with the Saṅgha of mendicants. Having washed his feet, he entered the town hall and sat against the central column facing east.

dn33:1.4.2.verse: The Saṅgha of mendicants also washed their feet, entered the town hall, and sat against the west wall facing east, with the Buddha right in front of them.

dn33:1.4.3.verse: The Mallas of Pāvā also washed their feet, entered the town hall, and sat against the east wall facing west, with the Buddha right in front of them.

dn33:1.4.4.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the Mallas with a Dhamma talk. Then he sent them off,

dn33:1.4.7.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the Mallas. They got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before leaving.

dn33:1.5.1.verse: Soon after they left, the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of mendicants, who were so very silent. He addressed Venerable Sāriputta,

dn33:1.5.2.verse: “Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of mendicants is rid of dullness and drowsiness.

dn33:1.5.3.verse: Give them some Dhamma talk as you feel inspired.

dn33:1.5.7.verse: And then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

dn33:1.6.1.verse: Now at that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan had recently passed away at Pāvā.

dn33:1.6.2.verse: With his passing the Jain ascetics split, dividing into two factions, fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words:

dn33:1.6.3.verse: “You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. I stay on topic, you don’t. You said last what you should have said first. You said first what you should have said last. What you’ve thought so much about has been disproved. Your doctrine is refuted. Go on, save your doctrine! You’re trapped; get yourself out of this—if you can!”

dn33:1.6.4.verse: You’d think there was nothing but slaughter going on among the Jain ascetics.

dn33:1.6.5.verse: And the Jain Ñātika’s white-clothed lay disciples were disillusioned, dismayed, and disappointed in the Jain ascetics. They were equally disappointed with a teaching and training so poorly explained and poorly propounded, not emancipating, not leading to peace, proclaimed by someone who is not a fully awakened Buddha, with broken monument and without a refuge.

dn33:1.7.1.verse: Then Sāriputta told the mendicants about these things. He went on to say,

dn33:1.7.4.verse: “That’s what happens, reverends, when a teaching and training is poorly explained and poorly propounded, not emancipating, not leading to peace, proclaimed by someone who is not a fully awakened Buddha.

dn33:1.7.5.verse: But this teaching is well explained and well propounded to us by the Blessed One, emancipating, leading to peace, proclaimed by someone who is a fully awakened Buddha.

dn33:1.7.6.verse: You should all recite this in concert, without disputing, so that this spiritual path may last for a long time. That would be for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

dn33:1.11.10.verse: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

dn33:1.11.12.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

dn33:1.11.13.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

dn33:1.11.15.verse: A mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort.

dn33:1.11.16.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to mental development, and active effort.

dn33:1.11.17.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy, and active effort.

dn33:1.11.18.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to inquiry, and active effort.

dn33:1.11.20.verse: A mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn33:1.11.21.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

dn33:1.11.22.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

dn33:1.11.23.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

dn33:1.11.24.verse: Four ways of developing immersion further:

dn33:1.11.25.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life.

dn33:1.11.26.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision.

dn33:1.11.27.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness.

dn33:1.11.28.verse: There is a way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements.

dn33:1.11.29.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life?

dn33:1.11.30.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption …

dn33:1.11.33.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to blissful meditation in this life.

dn33:1.11.34.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision?

dn33:1.11.35.verse: A mendicant applies their mind to the perception of light, focusing on the perception of day regardless of whether it’s night or day.

dn33:1.11.36.verse: And so, with an open and unenveloped heart, they develop a mind that’s full of radiance.

dn33:1.11.37.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to gaining knowledge and vision.

dn33:1.11.38.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness?

dn33:1.11.39.verse: A mendicant knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

dn33:1.11.40.verse: They know perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

dn33:1.11.41.verse: They know thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

dn33:1.11.42.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to mindfulness and awareness.

dn33:1.11.43.verse: And what is the way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements?

dn33:1.11.44.verse: A mendicant meditates observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

dn33:1.11.45.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

dn33:1.11.49.verse: consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

dn33:1.11.50.verse: This is the way of developing immersion further that leads to the ending of defilements.

dn33:1.11.52.verse: A mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn33:1.11.53.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

dn33:1.11.55.verse: equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

dn33:1.11.57.verse: A mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

dn33:1.11.58.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

dn33:1.11.59.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.

dn33:1.11.60.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

dn33:1.11.62.verse: After appraisal, a mendicant uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.

dn33:1.11.64.verse: A mendicant is content with any kind of robe, and praises such contentment. They don’t employ improper solicitation for the sake of a robe. They don’t worry if they don’t get a robe. And if they do get a robe, they use it untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawback, and understanding the escape. And on account of that they don’t glorify themselves or put others down.

dn33:1.11.65.verse: A mendicant who is deft, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primordial noble custom.

dn33:1.11.66.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of almsfood …

dn33:1.11.68.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of lodgings …

dn33:1.11.70.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant enjoys giving up and loves to give up. They enjoy meditation and love to meditate. But they don’t glorify themselves or put down others on account of their love for giving up and meditation.

dn33:1.11.71.verse: A mendicant who is deft, tireless, aware, and mindful in this is said to stand in the ancient, primordial noble custom.

dn33:1.11.73.verse: The efforts to restrain, to give up, to develop, and to preserve.

dn33:1.11.74.verse: And what is the effort to restrain?

dn33:1.11.75.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

dn33:1.11.76.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

dn33:1.11.77.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

dn33:1.11.78.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

dn33:1.11.79.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

dn33:1.11.80.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

dn33:1.11.81.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

dn33:1.11.82.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

dn33:1.11.83.verse: This is called the effort to restrain.

dn33:1.11.84.verse: And what is the effort to give up?

dn33:1.11.85.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t tolerate a sensual,

dn33:1.11.87.verse: or cruel thought that’s arisen, but gives it up, dispels it, eliminates it, and obliterates it.

dn33:1.11.88.verse: They don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

dn33:1.11.89.verse: This is called the effort to give up.

dn33:1.11.90.verse: And what is the effort to develop?

dn33:1.11.91.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

dn33:1.11.97.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

dn33:1.11.98.verse: This is called the effort to develop.

dn33:1.11.99.verse: And what is the effort to preserve?

dn33:1.11.100.verse: It’s when a mendicant preserves a meditation subject that’s a fine basis of immersion: the perception of a skeleton, a worm-infested corpse, a livid corpse, a split open corpse, or a bloated corpse.

dn33:1.11.101.verse: This is called the effort to preserve.

dn33:1.11.103.verse: knowledge of the teaching, inferential knowledge, knowledge of encompassing, and conventional knowledge.

dn33:1.11.105.verse: knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

dn33:1.11.107.verse: associating with true persons, listening to the true teaching, rational application of mind, and practicing in line with the teaching.

dn33:1.11.109.verse: A noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha:

dn33:1.11.110.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

dn33:1.11.111.verse: They have experiential confidence in the teaching:

dn33:1.11.112.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

dn33:1.11.113.verse: They have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

dn33:1.11.114.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

dn33:1.11.115.verse: And a noble disciple’s ethical conduct is loved by the noble ones, unbroken, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

dn33:1.11.116.verse: Four fruits of the ascetic life:

dn33:1.11.121.verse: edible food, whether solid or subtle; contact is the second, mental intention the third, and consciousness the fourth.

dn33:1.11.123.verse: As long as consciousness continues, it gets involved with form, supported by form, established on form. And with a sprinkle of relishing, it grows, increases, and matures.

dn33:1.11.124.verse: Or consciousness gets involved with feeling …

dn33:1.11.125.verse: Or consciousness gets involved with perception …

dn33:1.11.126.verse: Or as long as consciousness continues, it gets involved with choices, supported by choices, established on choices. And with a sprinkle of relishing, it grows, increases, and matures.

dn33:1.11.128.verse: making decisions prejudiced by favoritism, hostility, stupidity, and cowardice.

dn33:1.11.129.verse: Four things that give rise to craving:

dn33:1.11.130.verse: Craving arises in a mendicant for the sake of robes,

dn33:1.11.133.verse: or rebirth in this or that state.

dn33:1.11.135.verse: painful practice with slow insight, painful practice with swift insight, pleasant practice with slow insight, and pleasant practice with swift insight.

dn33:1.11.137.verse: impatient practice, patient practice, taming practice, and calming practice.

dn33:1.11.139.verse: contentment, good will, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

dn33:1.11.140.verse: Four ways of taking up practices:

dn33:1.11.141.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.

dn33:1.11.142.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure.

dn33:1.11.143.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain.

dn33:1.11.144.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.

dn33:1.11.150.verse: the foundations of wisdom, truth, generosity, and peace.

dn33:1.11.152.verse: There is a question that should be answered categorically. There is a question that should be answered analytically. There is a question that should be answered with a counter-question. There is a question that should be set aside.

dn33:1.11.154.verse: There are deeds that are dark with dark result.

dn33:1.11.155.verse: There are deeds that are bright with bright result.

dn33:1.11.156.verse: There are deeds that are dark and bright with dark and bright result.

dn33:1.11.157.verse: There are neither dark nor bright deeds with neither dark nor bright results, which lead to the ending of deeds.

dn33:1.11.159.verse: Past lives are to be realized with recollection.

dn33:1.11.160.verse: The passing away and rebirth of sentient beings is to be realized with vision.

dn33:1.11.161.verse: The eight liberations are to be realized with direct meditative experience.

dn33:1.11.162.verse: The ending of defilements is to be realized with wisdom.

dn33:1.11.164.verse: the floods of sensuality, desire for rebirth, views, and ignorance.

dn33:1.11.166.verse: the yokes of sensuality, desire for rebirth, views, and ignorance.

dn33:1.11.168.verse: unyoking from the yokes of sensuality, desire for rebirth, views, and ignorance.

dn33:1.11.170.verse: the personal ties to covetousness, ill will, misapprehension of precepts and observances, and the insistence that this is the only truth.

dn33:1.11.172.verse: grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

dn33:1.11.174.verse: reproduction for creatures born from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, or spontaneously.

dn33:1.11.176.verse: Someone is unaware when conceived in their mother’s womb, unaware as they remain there, and unaware as they emerge. This is the first kind of conception.

dn33:1.11.177.verse: Furthermore, someone is aware when conceived in their mother’s womb, but unaware as they remain there, and unaware as they emerge. This is the second kind of conception.

dn33:1.11.178.verse: Furthermore, someone is aware when conceived in their mother’s womb, aware as they remain there, but unaware as they emerge. This is the third kind of conception.

dn33:1.11.179.verse: Furthermore, someone is aware when conceived in their mother’s womb, aware as they remain there, and aware as they emerge. This is the fourth kind of conception.

dn33:1.11.181.verse: There is an incarnation where only one’s own intention is effective, not that of others.

dn33:1.11.182.verse: There is an incarnation where only the intention of others is effective, not one’s own.

dn33:1.11.183.verse: There is an incarnation where both one’s own and others’ intentions are effective.

dn33:1.11.184.verse: There is an incarnation where neither one’s own nor others’ intentions are effective.

dn33:1.11.185.verse: Four ways of purifying a religious donation:

dn33:1.11.186.verse: There’s a religious donation that’s purified by the giver, not the recipient.

dn33:1.11.187.verse: There’s a religious donation that’s purified by the recipient, not the giver.

dn33:1.11.188.verse: There’s a religious donation that’s purified by neither the giver nor the recipient.

dn33:1.11.189.verse: There’s a religious donation that’s purified by both the giver and the recipient.

dn33:1.11.191.verse: giving, kindly words, taking care, and equality.

dn33:1.11.193.verse: speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical.

dn33:1.11.195.verse: refraining from speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical.

dn33:1.11.197.verse: saying you’ve seen, heard, thought, or known something, but you haven’t.

dn33:1.11.199.verse: saying you haven’t seen, heard, thought, or known something, and you haven’t.

dn33:1.11.201.verse: saying you haven’t seen, heard, thought, or known something, and you have.

dn33:1.11.203.verse: saying you’ve seen, heard, thought, or known something, and you have.

dn33:1.11.205.verse: One individual mortifies themselves, committed to the practice of mortifying themselves.

dn33:1.11.206.verse: One individual mortifies others, committed to the practice of mortifying others.

dn33:1.11.207.verse: One individual mortifies themselves and others, committed to the practice of mortifying themselves and others.

dn33:1.11.208.verse: One individual doesn’t mortify either themselves or others, committed to the practice of not mortifying themselves or others.

dn33:1.11.209.verse: They live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.

dn33:1.11.211.verse: One individual practices to benefit themselves, but not others.

dn33:1.11.212.verse: One individual practices to benefit others, but not themselves.

dn33:1.11.213.verse: One individual practices to benefit neither themselves nor others.

dn33:1.11.214.verse: One individual practices to benefit both themselves and others.

dn33:1.11.216.verse: the dark bound for darkness, the dark bound for light, the light bound for darkness, and the light bound for light.

dn33:1.11.218.verse: the confirmed ascetic, the white lotus ascetic, the pink lotus ascetic, and the delicate ascetic of ascetics.

dn33:1.11.219.verse: These are the teachings grouped by four that have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

dn33:1.11.220.verse: You should all recite these in concert.

dn33:1.11.221.verse: The first recitation section is complete.

dn33:2.1.1.verse: There are teachings grouped by five that have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

dn33:2.1.2.verse: You should all recite these in concert.

dn33:2.1.3.verse: What are the teachings grouped by five?

dn33:2.1.5.verse: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

dn33:2.1.7.verse: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

dn33:2.1.9.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

dn33:2.1.13.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

dn33:2.1.15.verse: hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humanity, and the gods.

dn33:2.1.17.verse: stinginess with dwellings, families, material things, praise, and the teachings.

dn33:2.1.19.verse: sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

dn33:2.1.21.verse: substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.

dn33:2.1.23.verse: desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, desire for rebirth in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

dn33:2.1.25.verse: refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

dn33:2.1.26.verse: Five things that can’t be done:

dn33:2.1.27.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a layperson.

dn33:2.1.29.verse: loss of relatives, wealth, health, ethics, and view.

dn33:2.1.30.verse: It is not because of loss of relatives, wealth, or health that sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

dn33:2.1.31.verse: It is because of loss of ethics or view that sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

dn33:2.1.33.verse: endowment with relatives, wealth, health, ethics, and view.

dn33:2.1.34.verse: It is not because of endowment with family, wealth, or health that sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn33:2.1.35.verse: It is because of endowment with ethics or view that sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn33:2.1.36.verse: Five drawbacks for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics:

dn33:2.1.37.verse: Firstly, an unethical person loses great wealth on account of negligence.

dn33:2.1.39.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person gets a bad reputation.

dn33:2.1.41.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person enters any kind of assembly unconfident and embarrassed, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

dn33:2.1.43.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person feels lost when they die.

dn33:2.1.45.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

dn33:2.1.47.verse: Five benefits for an ethical person because of their accomplishment in ethics:

dn33:2.1.48.verse: Firstly, an ethical person gains great wealth on account of diligence.

dn33:2.1.50.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person gets a good reputation.

dn33:2.1.52.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person enters any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

dn33:2.1.54.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person dies not feeling lost.

dn33:2.1.56.verse: Furthermore, when an ethical person’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

dn33:2.1.58.verse: A mendicant who wants to accuse another should first establish five things in themselves:

dn33:2.1.59.verse: I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time.

dn33:2.1.60.verse: I will speak truthfully, not falsely.

dn33:2.1.61.verse: I will speak gently, not harshly.

dn33:2.1.62.verse: I will speak beneficially, not harmfully.

dn33:2.1.63.verse: I will speak lovingly, not from secret hate.

dn33:2.1.64.verse: A mendicant who wants to accuse another should first establish these five things in themselves.

dn33:2.1.66.verse: A mendicant has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

dn33:2.1.67.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

dn33:2.1.68.verse: They are rarely ill or unwell. Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

dn33:2.1.69.verse: They’re not devious or deceitful. They reveal themselves honestly to the Teacher or sensible spiritual companions.

dn33:2.1.70.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

dn33:2.1.71.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

dn33:2.1.73.verse: Aviha, Atappa, the gods fair to see, the fair seeing gods, and Akaniṭṭha.

dn33:2.1.75.verse: one who is extinguished between one life and the next, one who is extinguished upon landing, one who is extinguished without extra effort, one who is extinguished with extra effort, and one who heads upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

dn33:2.1.77.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has doubts about the Teacher. They’re uncertain, undecided, and lacking confidence.

dn33:2.1.78.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving. This is the first kind of hard-heartedness.

dn33:2.1.79.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has doubts about the teaching …

dn33:2.1.82.verse: A mendicant is angry and upset with their spiritual companions, resentful and closed off.

dn33:2.1.83.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving. This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness.

dn33:2.1.85.verse: Firstly, a mendicant isn’t free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

dn33:2.1.87.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

dn33:2.1.88.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart.

dn33:2.1.89.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t free of greed for the body …

dn33:2.1.90.verse: They’re not free of greed for form …

dn33:2.1.91.verse: They eat as much as they like until their bellies are full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

dn33:2.1.92.verse: They lead the spiritual life hoping to be reborn in one of the orders of gods, thinking: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

dn33:2.1.93.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

dn33:2.1.94.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart.

dn33:2.1.96.verse: eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

dn33:2.1.98.verse: pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity.

dn33:2.1.100.verse: faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom.

dn33:2.1.102.verse: Take a case where a mendicant focuses on sensual pleasures, but on that their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.

dn33:2.1.103.verse: But when they focus on renunciation, on that their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

dn33:2.1.104.verse: Their mind is in a good state, well developed, well risen, well freed, and well detached from sensual pleasures.

dn33:2.1.105.verse: They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of sensual pleasures, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.

dn33:2.1.106.verse: This is how the escape from sensual pleasures is explained.

dn33:2.1.107.verse: Take another case where a mendicant focuses on ill will, but their mind does not leap forth …

dn33:2.1.108.verse: But when they focus on good will, their mind leaps forth …

dn33:2.1.109.verse: Their mind is in a good state … well detached from ill will.

dn33:2.1.110.verse: They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of ill will, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.

dn33:2.1.111.verse: This is how the escape from ill will is explained.

dn33:2.1.112.verse: Take another case where a mendicant focuses on harming, but their mind does not leap forth …

dn33:2.1.113.verse: But when they focus on compassion, their mind leaps forth …

dn33:2.1.114.verse: Their mind is in a good state … well detached from harming.

dn33:2.1.115.verse: They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of harming, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.

dn33:2.1.116.verse: This is how the escape from harming is explained.

dn33:2.1.117.verse: Take another case where a mendicant focuses on form, but their mind does not leap forth …

dn33:2.1.118.verse: But when they focus on the formless, their mind leaps forth …

dn33:2.1.119.verse: Their mind is in a good state … well detached from forms.

dn33:2.1.120.verse: They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of form, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.

dn33:2.1.121.verse: This is how the escape from forms is explained.

dn33:2.1.122.verse: Take a case where a mendicant focuses on substantial reality, but their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.

dn33:2.1.123.verse: But when they focus on the cessation of substantial reality, their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

dn33:2.1.124.verse: Their mind is in a good state, well developed, well risen, well freed, and well detached from substantial reality.

dn33:2.1.125.verse: They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of substantial reality, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.

dn33:2.1.126.verse: This is how the escape from substantial reality is explained.

dn33:2.1.128.verse: Firstly, the Teacher or a respected spiritual companion teaches Dhamma to a mendicant.

dn33:2.1.129.verse: That mendicant feels inspired by the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma, no matter how the Teacher or a respected spiritual companion teaches it.

dn33:2.1.130.verse: Feeling inspired, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed.

dn33:2.1.131.verse: This is the first opportunity for freedom.

dn33:2.1.132.verse: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a respected spiritual companion teaches Dhamma to a mendicant. But the mendicant teaches Dhamma in detail to others as they learned and memorized it. …

dn33:2.1.133.verse: Or the mendicant rehearses the teaching in detail as they learned and memorized it. …

dn33:2.1.134.verse: Or the mendicant thinks about and considers the teaching in their heart, examining it with the mind as they learned and memorized it. …

dn33:2.1.135.verse: Or a meditation subject as a basis of immersion is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom.

dn33:2.1.136.verse: That mendicant feels inspired by the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma, no matter how a meditation subject as a basis of immersion is properly grasped, focused on, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom.
