He had a penetrating intellect, was heir to the tradition, having penetrated the analytical knowledges, he was expert in the nine scriptural divisions of the Teacher’s dispensation knowing them all by heart; he had attained to the perfections, and was skilled in the penetration into the essence of Dhamma in the Conqueror’s words; he was of inexhaustible and varied eloquence, a brilliant speaker, of beautiful speech, difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, unsurpassable, difficult to obstruct, difficult to turn back, imperturbable like the ocean, immovable like the king of mountains, conqueror in debate, dispeller of darkness, bearer of light, a great orator, confounder of opposing sectarians, trampler of other doctrines, honoured, respected, esteemed, venerated, revered by bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen, laywomen, kings, and king’s ministers, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and requisites of medicine for the sick. He was attained to the highest gain and fame, demonstrating to the elders who are wise and endowed with attention the jewel of the nine-fold Conqueror’s dispensation, instructing in the way of Dhamma, bearing the light of Dhamma, raising up the pillar of Dhamma, performing the sacrifice of Dhamma, lifting high the banner of Dhamma, raising up the standard of Dhamma, blowing the conch of Dhamma, beating the drum of Dhamma, roaring the lion’s roar, thundering the thunder of Indra, with the great cloud of the nectar of Dhamma filled with the water of compassion, enveloped in the net of the lightning of excellent knowledge and sweet utterance, scorching the entire world. Wandering on tour through villages, towns, and royal capitals, gradually he arrived at Sāgala city.

mil2:65.2.verse: There the Venerable Nāgasena was living in Saṅkheyya hermitage together with eighty thousand bhikkhus.

mil2:67.1.verse: Those bhikkhus versed in the threefold Tipiṭaka,

mil2:67.2.verse: and also those of the five collections;

mil2:67.3.verse: And those of the four collections as well,

mil2:68.2.verse: skilled in distinguishing the path from the wrong path;

mil2:70.4.verse: like a maned lion on a mountain.”

mil2:71.1.verse: Then Devamantiya said to King Milinda:

mil2:71.3.verse: There is, your majesty, an elder named Nāgasena—learned, skilled, intelligent, disciplined, confident, of great learning, eloquent in speech, of excellent wit, who has reached perfection in the analytical knowledges of meaning, doctrine, language, and eloquence. He is now residing at the Saṅkheyya hermitage. Go, your majesty, and ask the Venerable Nāgasena questions. He is able to converse with you and dispel your doubts.”

mil2:71.4.verse: Then King Milinda, upon suddenly hearing the word “Nāgasena,” experienced fear, astonishment, and a bristling of his hair.

mil2:71.5.verse: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya:

mil2:71.6.verse: “Is the bhikkhu Nāgasena really able to converse with me?”

mil2:71.7.verse: “He is able, your majesty, even to converse with Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Pajāpati, Suyāma, Santusita, the world-protectors, and even with the great Brahmā, the progentor of all—how much more so with a mere human being!”

mil2:72.1.verse: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya:

mil2:72.2.verse: “Well then, Devamantiya, send a messenger to the venerable one.”

mil2:72.3.verse: “Yes, lord,” said Devamantiya, and he sent a messenger to the Venerable Nāgasena saying: “The king Milinda, venerable sir, desires to see you.”

mil2:73.1.verse: Then King Milinda, surrounded by about five hundred Bactrian Greeks, mounted an excellent chariot and with a great army approached the Saṅkheyya hermitage where the Venerable Nāgasena was.

mil2:73.2.verse: At that time, the Venerable Nāgasena was seated in the circular pavilion together with eighty thousand bhikkhus.

mil2:73.3.verse: King Milinda saw the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena from afar, and having seen it, he said to Devamantiya:

mil2:73.5.verse: “It is the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena, your majesty.”

mil2:74.1.verse: Then King Milinda, seeing the assembly of the Venerable Nāgasena from afar, experienced fear, astonishment, and a bristling of his hair.

mil2:74.2.verse: Then King Milinda felt like an elephant surrounded by rhinoceroses, like a serpent surrounded by eagles, like a little jackal surrounded by pythons, like a bear surrounded by buffaloes, like a frog pursued by a serpent, like a deer pursued by a leopard, like a snake encountering a snake-charmer, like a mouse encountering a cat, like a demon encountering an exorcist, like the moon seized by Rāhu, like a snake caught in a basket, like a bird entered into a cage, like a fish entered into a net, like a man entered into a forest of wild beasts, like a yakkha who has offended Vessavaṇa, like a deva whose life-span is exhausted—frightened, agitated, terrified, alarmed, with hair standing on end, dejected, dismayed, with confused mind and disturbed heart. Thinking “May this retinue not despise me,” he established mindfulness and said to Devamantiya:

mil2:74.3.verse: “Do not, Devamantiya, point out the Venerable Nāgasena to me—I will recognize Nāgasena without being told.”

mil2:75.1.verse: Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgasena was more junior than the forty thousand bhikkhus in front of him and more senior than the forty thousand bhikkhus behind him.

mil2:76.1.verse: Then King Milinda, surveying the entire assembly of bhikkhus—front, back, and middle—saw the Venerable Nāgasena from afar, seated in the middle of the assembly of monks like a maned lion, free from fear and dread, free from hair-raising terror, free from timidity and trembling. Having seen him, he recognized him by his appearance alone, thinking “This one here must be Nāgasena.”

mil2:77.1.verse: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya:

mil2:77.2.verse: “This one, Devamantiya, is the Venerable Nāgasena.”

mil2:77.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, this is Nāgasena. You have recognized Nāgasena well, your majesty.”

mil2:77.4.verse: Then the king was pleased, thinking “Nāgasena was recognized by me without being pointed out.”

mil2:77.5.verse: But then, upon seeing the Venerable Nāgasena, King Milinda experienced fear, astonishment, and a bristling of his hair.

mil2:80.4.verse: as the dread I feel today.

mil2:81.4.verse: for my mind is not settled.’”

mil3.1.1:1.1.verse: Then, King Milinda approached Venerable Nāgasena, exchanged cordial and polite greetings with him, and sat down at one side.

mil3.1.1:1.2.verse: Venerable Nāgasena, by returning polite greetings back, gladdened King Milinda’s heart.

mil3.1.1:2.1.verse: Then, King Milinda said to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.1:2.2.verse: “How is the reverend one known, what is your name, venerable sir?”

mil3.1.1:2.3.verse: “I am called Nāgasena, your majesty, my holy life companions address me as Nāgasena. Though parents make such names as Nāgasena, or Sūrasena, or Vīrasena, or Sīhasena, your majesty, Nāgasena is only a concept, a designation, a label, an appellation, a mere name; no person actually obtains here.”

mil3.1.1:3.2.verse: “May the venerable five hundred Bactrian Greeks and the eighty thousand bhikkhus hear me. This Nāgasena said,

mil3.1.1:3.3.verse: ‘no person obtains here’; is it proper to approve that?”

mil3.1.1:3.4.verse: Then, King Milinda said this to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.1:3.5.verse: “If, Venerable Nāgasena, no person obtains, who therefore gives you robes, alms food, lodgings and medicinal requisites? Who enjoys the use of them? Who guards their ethical behaviour? Who engages in meditation? Who attains the path and fruit of nibbāna? Who kills a living being? Who takes what is not given? Who commits wrong conduct in sensual pleasures? Who speaks falsely? Who drinks intoxicants? Who commits any of the five deeds that bear fruit without delay? Therefore, there is nothing wholesome, nothing unwholesome. There is no doer of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, nor anyone who makes another do wholesome or unwholesome deeds. There is no fruit or result of good or bad deeds. If, Venerable Nāgasena, there was someone who caused you to die, there is no killing of living beings for that person. Venerable Nāgasena, there is no teacher, no preceptor, and no ordination for you.

mil3.1.1:3.6.verse: You say ‘my holy life companions address me as Nāgasena.’ But who here is Nāgasena?

mil3.1.1:3.7.verse: Is it, venerable sir, that the hairs of the head are Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.1:3.9.verse: “Are the hairs of the body Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.1:3.40.verse: the brain in the head Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.1:3.52.verse: “Then, venerable sir, are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness combined Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.1:3.54.verse: “Then, venerable sir, is something other than form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness combined Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.1:3.56.verse: “Though, venerable sir, I am asking you repeatedly, I do not see Nāgasena.

mil3.1.1:3.59.verse: “Then, who here is Nāgasena? You speak a falsehood, venerable sir, there is no Nāgasena.”

mil3.1.1:4.1.verse: Then, Venerable Nāgasena said this to King Milinda,

mil3.1.1:4.2.verse: “You are, your majesty, a delicate noble, exceedingly delicate. For one going on foot at midday, on the scorching ground, the hot sand, the rough, sharp pebbles and gravel, the feet are sore, the body is tired, the mind is upset, and body consciousness arises accompanied by suffering. Did you come on foot or rather in a vehicle?”

mil3.1.1:4.3.verse: “I did not come on foot, venerable sir, I came in a chariot.”

mil3.1.1:4.4.verse: “If, your majesty, you came in a chariot, tell me about a chariot. Is the carriage pole the chariot?”

mil3.1.1:4.10.verse: “Is the body of the chariot the chariot?”

mil3.1.1:4.20.verse: “Then, your majesty, are the carriage pole, axle, wheels, body of the chariot, flag-staff, yoke, reins, and goad the chariot?”

mil3.1.1:4.22.verse: “Then, your majesty, is something apart from the carriage pole, axle, wheels, body of the chariot, flag-staff, yoke, reins, and goad the chariot?”

mil3.1.1:4.24.verse: “Though, your majesty, I am asking you repeatedly, I do not see a chariot.

mil3.1.1:4.25.verse: Is a chariot only the sound ‘chariot’?”

mil3.1.1:4.27.verse: “Then, what here is a chariot? You speak a falsehood, your majesty, there is no chariot. You are, your majesty, a mighty king of all Jambudīpa, who then do you fear that you speak a falsehood. May the venerable five hundred Bactrian Greeks and the eighty thousand bhikkhus hear me. This King Milinda said,

mil3.1.1:4.28.verse: ‘I came by chariot’. But, on being told, ‘if, your majesty, you came by chariot, declare to me a chariot,’ he is unable to produce a chariot. Is it proper to approve that?”

mil3.1.1:5.1.verse: When this was said, the five hundred Bactrian Greeks applauded the Venerable Nāgasena and said to King Milinda,

mil3.1.1:5.2.verse: “Now then, your majesty, speak if you can!”

mil3.1.1:6.1.verse: Then King Milinda said this to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.1:6.2.verse: “I do not speak falsely, venerable sir, because of the carriage pole, the axle, the wheels, the body of the chariot, the flag-staff, there exists a ‘chariot’, as a concept, a designation, a label, an appellation, a mere name.”

mil3.1.1:7.1.verse: “Good, your majesty, you know a chariot.

mil3.1.1:7.2.verse: In the same way, your majesty, because of the head hairs, the body hairs, … brain in the head, and because of form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness, there exists ‘Nāgasena’, as a concept, a designation, a label, an appellation, a mere name, however in the absolute sense there obtains no person here.

mil3.1.1:7.3.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by Sister Vajirā in the presence of the Blessed One:

mil3.1.1:8.1.verse: ‘Just as, by the coexistence of the various parts,

mil3.1.1:8.3.verse: So, by the existence of the aggregates,

mil3.1.1:8.4.verse: there is a “being” is agreed upon.’”

mil3.1.1:9.1.verse: “Wonderful, Venerable Nāgasena! Marvelous, Venerable Nāgasena! Your answers to the questions asked are very brilliant! If the Buddha were here, he would applaud them. Excellent, excellent, Venerable Nāgasena! Your answers to the questions asked are very brilliant!”

mil3.1.2:1.1.verse: “How many rains do you have, Venerable Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.2:1.3.verse: “What are these seven, venerable sir, are you the seven, or is the reckoning seven?”

mil3.1.2:2.1.verse: Then, at that time, the shadow of the king adorned with all his ornaments, all decked up and prepared, appeared on the ground and is seen in a vessel of water.

mil3.1.2:2.2.verse: Then Venerable Nāgasena said this to King Milinda,

mil3.1.2:2.3.verse: “This shadow appears on the ground and in the vessel of water. Are you the king, your majesty, or is the shadow the king?”

mil3.1.2:2.4.verse: “I am the king, Venerable Nāgasena, this shadow is not the king. The shadow comes into existence dependent on me.”

mil3.1.2:2.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, seven is the reckoning of rains. I am not the seven, but dependent on me seven comes into existence, similarly to your shadow, your majesty.”

mil3.1.2:2.6.verse: “Wonderful, Venerable Nāgasena! Marvelous, Venerable Nāgasena! Your answers to the questions asked are very brilliant!”

mil3.1.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, will you converse with me?”

mil3.1.3:1.3.verse: “If, your majesty, you will converse in the speech of wise people, I will converse, however, I will not do so if you converse like a king.”

mil3.1.3:1.4.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, do wise people converse?”

mil3.1.3:1.5.verse: “In a conversation among wise people, your majesty, both a summing up and an unravelling are made, a refutation and a redress are made, an assertion and a counter-assertion are made, and wise people do not become angry because of that. That is the way, your majesty, wise people converse.”

mil3.1.3:1.6.verse: “Then how, venerable sir, do kings converse?”

mil3.1.3:1.7.verse: “In a conversation, your majesty, kings assert some point of view, and for the one who disputes that view, they order punishment, saying ‘Punish that person.’ That is the way, your majesty, kings converse.”

mil3.1.3:1.8.verse: “I will converse, venerable sir, in the speech of wise people, not in the speech of kings. May the venerable one converse freely just like he does with a bhikkhu, a novice, a lay supporter, or with a monastery attendant. May the venerable one converse freely and not be afraid.”

mil3.1.3:1.9.verse: The elder approved, saying “It is well, your majesty.”

mil3.1.3:2.4.verse: “You have been asked by me, venerable sir.”

mil3.1.3:2.6.verse: “Then, what has been answered by you, venerable sir?”

mil3.1.3:2.7.verse: “Then, what has been asked by you, your majesty?”

mil3.1.4:1.1.verse: Then, it occurred to King Milinda,

mil3.1.4:1.2.verse: “This wise bhikkhu is very competent to converse with me. There will be many matters to be asked, but there will be so many unasked and then the sun will set. Why don’t I converse with him in the inner palace tomorrow?”

mil3.1.4:2.1.verse: Then the king said to Devamantiya,

mil3.1.4:2.2.verse: “Well then, Devamantiya, announce this to the venerable one, ‘There will be conversation with the king in the inner palace tomorrow morning’.”

mil3.1.4:2.3.verse: After he said this, King Milinda rose from his seat, having received permission from the elder Nāgasena, mounted his chariot, and left, repeating to himself, “Nāgasena, Nāgasena!”

mil3.1.4:3.1.verse: Then Devamantiya said to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.4:3.3.verse: ‘There will be conversation with the king in the inner palace tomorrow morning’.”

mil3.1.4:3.4.verse: The elder approved, saying “It is well.”

mil3.1.4:3.5.verse: Then, in the early morning, Devamantiya, Anantakāya, Maṅkura, and Sabbadinna approached King Milinda, and said to him,

mil3.1.4:3.8.verse: “With how many bhikkhus may he come?”

mil3.1.4:3.9.verse: “He may come with as many bhikkhus as he likes.”

mil3.1.4:4.2.verse: “May he come with ten bhikkhus, your majesty?”

mil3.1.4:4.3.verse: For a second time, the king said,

mil3.1.4:4.4.verse: “He may come with as many bhikkhus as he likes.”

mil3.1.4:4.5.verse: For a second time, Sabbadinna said,

mil3.1.4:4.6.verse: “May he come with ten bhikkhus, your majesty?”

mil3.1.4:4.7.verse: For a third time, the king said,

mil3.1.4:4.8.verse: “He may come with as many bhikkhus as he likes.”

mil3.1.4:4.9.verse: For a third time, Sabbadinna said,

mil3.1.4:4.10.verse: “May he come with ten bhikkhus, your majesty?”

mil3.1.4:4.11.verse: “All this hospitality has been prepared. I say, ‘He may come with as many bhikkhus as he likes.’

mil3.1.4:4.12.verse: I say this and Sabbadinna says otherwise! Are we not competent to give food to the bhikkhus?”

mil3.1.4:4.13.verse: When this was said, Sabbadinna was ashamed.

mil3.1.4:5.1.verse: Then, Devamantiya, Anantakāya, and Maṅkura, approached Venerable Nāgasena, and said to him,

mil3.1.4:5.3.verse: ‘You may come with as many bhikkhus as you like.’”

mil3.1.4:5.4.verse: Then, in the morning, Venerable Nāgasena arose, got dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāgala with eighty thousand bhikkhus.

mil3.1.4:6.1.verse: Now, Anantakāya walking alongside Venerable Nāgasena said to him,

mil3.1.4:6.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, that which you call ‘Nāgasena’, what here is Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.4:6.4.verse: “Who do you think here is Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.4:6.5.verse: “The breath within, the life force, which goes in and comes out, that I consider ‘Nāgasena’.”

mil3.1.4:6.6.verse: “When, then, the breath goes out and does not come in, or it comes in and doesn’t go out, would that man live?”

mil3.1.4:6.8.verse: “Then, when those conch blowers sound the conch, does their breath re-enter?”

mil3.1.4:6.10.verse: “Then when those bamboo flute blowers sound the flute, does their breath re-enter?”

mil3.1.4:6.12.verse: “Then, when those horn blowers sound the horn, does their breath re-enter?”

mil3.1.4:6.14.verse: “Why, then, do they not die because of that?”

mil3.1.4:6.15.verse: “I am not competent to converse with you, a debater of the doctrine. It would be good, venerable sir, if you told me the meaning.”

mil3.1.4:6.16.verse: “It is not the life force, in-breathing and out-breathing are just bodily activities.” The elder gave a talk on Abhidhamma.

mil3.1.4:6.17.verse: Then, Anantakāya announced that he was a lay follower.

mil3.1.5:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Nāgasena approached King Milinda’s dwelling, and on arriving sat on the seat prepared.

mil3.1.5:1.2.verse: King Milinda then served and satisfied with his own hands Venerable Nāgasena and his assembly with delicious hard and soft foods, presented to each bhikkhu a pair of cloths, and to Venerable Nāgasena a set of three robes. He said to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.5:1.3.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, sit here with ten bhikkhus and let the rest of them go.”

mil3.1.5:2.1.verse: Then King Milinda, having seen that Venerable Nāgasena had eaten, and had withdrawn his hand from his bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down on one side. Seated there, King Milinda said to Venerable Nāgasena,

mil3.1.5:2.2.verse: “What is the conversation to be about, Venerable Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.5:2.3.verse: “We need a goal, your majesty. Let the conversation be about the goal.”

mil3.1.5:3.2.verse: “What use for you, Venerable Nāgasena, is your going forth? What is the ultimate goal for you?”

mil3.1.5:3.4.verse: “How then, your majesty, would this suffering cease, and other suffering not arise?

mil3.1.5:3.5.verse: This, your majesty, is the purpose of our going forth, and our ultimate goal is final nibbāna without any clinging.”

mil3.1.5:4.1.verse: “Do all go forth for this goal, Venerable Nāgasena?”

mil3.1.5:4.2.verse: “Certainly not, your majesty, some go forth through fear of kings, some go forth through fear of thieves, some go forth oppressed by debts, and others go forth for the sake of livelihood. But those who go forth the right way, go forth for such a goal.”

mil3.1.5:5.1.verse: “Did you go forth for this goal, venerable sir?”

mil3.1.5:5.2.verse: “I went forth, your majesty, when I was a child and I did not know that I was going forth for this goal. Then, it occurred to me, ‘These recluses, Sakyan sons, are wise and they will train me. Now, I have been trained by them, and I know and see that the going forth is for that goal.’”

mil3.1.6:1.2.verse: “Is there anyone who has died, Venerable Nāgasena, who is not reconnected?”

mil3.1.6:1.4.verse: “There are some who reconnect and some who don’t reconnect.”

mil3.1.6:1.6.verse: “One with defilements reconnects and one without defilements doesn’t reconnect.”

mil3.1.6:1.8.verse: “If, your majesty, I am with clinging I will reconnect, and if I am without clinging I will not.”

mil3.1.7:1.2.verse: “Is it not, Venerable Nāgasena, that the one who does not reconnect does not do so because of careful attention?”

mil3.1.7:1.3.verse: “It is because of careful attention, your majesty, and because of wisdom and other wholesome mental states.”

mil3.1.7:1.4.verse: “Is careful attention, venerable sir, the same as wisdom?”

mil3.1.7:1.5.verse: “Certainly not, your majesty, careful attention is one thing, wisdom is another. Goats, rams, bulls, buffalos, camels, and donkeys also have careful attention, but they do not have wisdom.”

mil3.1.8:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of attention, and what is the distinguishing characteristic of wisdom?”

mil3.1.8:1.3.verse: “Examination is the distinguishing characteristic of attention, and severing is the distinguishing characteristic of wisdom.”

mil3.1.8:2.1.verse: “How does attention have the distinguishing characteristic of examination? And how does wisdom have the distinguishing characteristic of severing?

mil3.1.8:2.3.verse: “Do you know barley reapers, your majesty?”

mil3.1.8:2.5.verse: “How, your majesty, do barley reapers reap barley?”

mil3.1.8:2.6.verse: “Venerable sir, they take a sheaf of barley in the left hand, and take a sickle in the right hand, and they cut with the sickle.”

mil3.1.8:3.1.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a barley reaper takes a sheaf of barley in the left hand, takes a sickle in the right hand, and cuts the barley,

mil3.1.8:3.2.verse: in the same way, your majesty, does the spiritual aspirant take hold of the mind with attention, and cut off the defilements with wisdom. Indeed thus, your majesty, examination is the distinguishing characteristic of attention, and severing is the distinguishing characteristic of wisdom.”

mil3.1.8:5.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Attention Question eighth

mil3.1.9:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, that which you called ‘and other wholesome mental states’, what are these wholesome mental states?”

mil3.1.9:1.3.verse: “Virtue, your majesty, faith, energy, mindfulness, and concentration; these are those wholesome mental states.”

mil3.1.9:1.4.verse: “What, venerable sir, is the distinguishing characteristic of virtue?”

mil3.1.9:1.5.verse: “Virtue, your majesty, has the distinguishing characteristic of being the ground for all wholesome mental states.  Virtue is the ground for the faculties, the powers, the enlightenment factors, the path factors, the establishments of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, meditation, emancipation, concentration, and the attainments. A spiritual aspirant, your majesty, dependent on virtue, grounded in virtue, develops the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. None of these wholesome mental states decrease.”

mil3.1.9:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, whatever seeds and plants attain to growth, development, and abundance, do so in dependence on the earth, and grounded by the earth.

mil3.1.9:2.3.verse: In the same way, a spiritual aspirant, your majesty, dependent on virtue, grounded in virtue, develops the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.”

mil3.1.9:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, whatever actions are to be done with strength, all of these are done in dependence on the earth, and grounded by the earth.

mil3.1.9:3.3.verse: In the same way, a spiritual aspirant, your majesty, dependent on virtue, grounded in virtue, develops the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.”

mil3.1.9:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a city architect, desiring to build a city, would first clear a site for the city, remove the trees and stumps, make the ground even, and there at a future time, divide it up into streets and four-way crossroads, and build the city.

mil3.1.9:4.3.verse: In the same way, a spiritual aspirant, your majesty, dependent on virtue, grounded in virtue, develops the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.”

mil3.1.9:5.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, an acrobat, desiring to display their craft, would dig the earth, remove the gravel and stones, make the ground even, and thus display their craft on soft earth.

mil3.1.9:5.3.verse: In the same way, a spiritual aspirant, your majesty, dependent on virtue, grounded in virtue, develops the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

mil3.1.9:5.4.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.1.9:7.1.verse: This is the support, as the earth is for living beings.

mil3.1.9:7.2.verse: And this is the root for growth in wholesome qualities.

mil3.1.9:7.3.verse: It is the starting point for all the Conqueror’s teachings.

mil3.1.9:7.4.verse: This collection of virtue is supremely binding.’”

mil3.1.9:9.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Virtue Question ninth

mil3.1.10:0.3.verse: 10. Calming as a Distinguishing Characteristic of Faith Question

mil3.1.10:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of faith?”

mil3.1.10:1.3.verse: “Faith, your majesty, has calming as a distinguishing characteristic, and also aspiration.”

mil3.1.10:1.4.verse: “How, venerable sir, is calming a distinguishing characteristic of faith?”

mil3.1.10:1.5.verse: “Faith arising suppresses the hindrances, and thus there is a clear, bright, clean mind free of the hindrances.

mil3.1.10:1.6.verse: That’s how, your majesty, calming is a distinguishing characteristic of faith.”

mil3.1.10:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a wheel-turning king going on a long journey might cross a small body of water, and that water disturbed by the elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, would become stirred up, turbid, and muddy;

mil3.1.10:2.3.verse: and after crossing, the king would command his men, ‘Bring me water, I will drink,’ and the king would possess a water-clearing gem.

mil3.1.10:2.4.verse: The men having given their assent to the wheel-turning king, saying ‘Yes, lord’, would place that water-clearing gem in the water, and after it is placed in that water, the various water plants, slime, and leaves  would disappear, the mud would settle, and the water would become clear, bright, and clean.

mil3.1.10:2.5.verse: Then they would bring the water to the wheel-turning king, saying, ‘Drink the water, lord.’

mil3.1.10:3.1.verse: Just like the water, your majesty, so the mind is to be understood; just like the men, so the spiritual aspirant is to be understood; just like the various water plants, slime, and leaves  and the mud, so the defilements are to be understood;

mil3.1.10:3.2.verse: just like the water-clearing gem, so faith is to be understood. Just like after the water-clearing gem is placed in the water, the various water plants, slime, and leaves would disappear, and the mud would settle, and the water would become clear, bright, and clean;

mil3.1.10:3.3.verse: in the same way, your majesty, faith arising suppresses the hindrances and the unobstructed mind is clear, bright, and clean.

mil3.1.10:3.4.verse: And in this way, your majesty, calming is a distinguishing characteristic of faith.”

mil3.1.10:5.1.verse: Calming as a Distinguishing Characteristic of Faith Question tenth

mil3.1.11:0.3.verse: 11. Aspiration as a Distinguishing Characteristic of Faith Question

mil3.1.11:1.1.verse: “How, venerable sir, is aspiration a distinguishing characteristic of faith?”

mil3.1.11:1.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a spiritual aspirant, having seen the liberated mind of others, aspires to the fruit of stream entry, or to the fruit of once-returning, or to the fruit of non-returning, or to the fruit of arahantship, and practices for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, and for the realisation of the unrealised.

mil3.1.11:1.3.verse: Thus, your majesty, is aspiration a distinguishing characteristic of faith.”

mil3.1.11:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a great cloud might pour down rain on the top of a mountain, and that water flowing down according to the slope, having filled the gullies, clefts, and rivulets on the mountain, would fill the river which would proceed along overflowing both banks. And then a great crowd of people having gone to that river, not knowing how shallow or deep it is, would stand frightened and spread out on the bank, and then a certain man might come, and considering his own power and strength, would bind tightly his loincloth and cross over. The great crowd of people having seen him cross would cross over also.

mil3.1.11:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, a spiritual aspirant, having seen the liberated mind of others, aspires to the fruit of stream entry, or to the fruit of once-returning, or to the fruit of non-returning, or to the fruit of arahantship, and practices for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, and for the realisation of the unrealised.

mil3.1.11:2.4.verse: In the same way, your majesty, is aspiration a distinguishing characteristic of faith.

mil3.1.11:2.5.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:

mil3.1.11:5.1.verse: Aspiration as a Distinguishing Characteristic of Faith Question eleventh

mil3.1.12:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of exertion?”

mil3.1.12:1.3.verse: “Exertion, your majesty, has supporting as a distinguishing characteristic, and no wholesome mental states supported by exertion decline.”

mil3.1.12:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a man, when his house is falling down, might support it with additional wood, so that, being thus supported, that house would not fall down.

mil3.1.12:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, exertion has supporting as a distinguishing characteristic, and no wholesome mental states supported by exertion decline.”

mil3.1.12:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a large army might destroy a small army, then the king would recall another and send for them in order to give additional strength to his own small army, and with that, the small army would destroy the large army.

mil3.1.12:3.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, exertion has supporting as a distinguishing characteristic, and no wholesome mental states supported by exertion decline.

mil3.1.12:3.4.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.1.12:3.5.verse: ‘A noble disciple endowed with exertion abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome;

mil3.1.12:3.6.verse: Abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless,

mil3.1.12:5.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Exertion Question twelfth

mil3.1.13:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of mindfulness?”

mil3.1.13:1.3.verse: “Mindfulness, your majesty, has not wavering as a distinguishing characteristic, and also taking up.”

mil3.1.13:1.4.verse: “How, venerable sir, does mindfulness have not wavering as a distinguishing characteristic?”

mil3.1.13:1.5.verse: “Mindfulness arising, your majesty, does not waver concerning things that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and light, or evenly mixed, thinking ‘these are the four establishments of mindfulness, these the four right strivings, these the four bases for psychic power, these the five faculties, these the five powers, these the seven factors of enlightenment, this the noble eightfold path, this serenity, this insight, this knowledge, this liberation’.

mil3.1.13:1.6.verse: Then, the spiritual aspirant engages in the things that should be engaged in, and does not engage in the things that should not be engaged in;

mil3.1.13:1.7.verse: associates with things that should be associated with, and does not associate with things that should not be associated with.

mil3.1.13:1.8.verse: Thus, your majesty, does mindfulness have not wavering as a distinguishing characteristic.”

mil3.1.13:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a wheel-turning king’s storekeeper reminds that king by night and day of his fame, saying, ‘So many elephants are yours, sire, so many horses, so many chariots, so many foot-soldiers, so much gold, so many gold objects, so much wealth, let his majesty remember it’, and he does not waver concerning the king’s wealth.

mil3.1.13:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, mindfulness arising does not waver concerning things that are wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and light, or evenly mixed, thinking ‘these are the four establishments of mindfulness, these the four right strivings, these the four bases for psychic power, these the five faculties, these the five powers, these the seven factors of enlightenment, this the noble eightfold path, this serenity, this insight, this knowledge, this liberation’.

mil3.1.13:2.4.verse: Then, the spiritual aspirant engages in the things that should be engaged in, and does not engage in the things that should not be engaged in;

mil3.1.13:2.5.verse: associates with things that should be associated with, and does not associate with things that should not be associated with.

mil3.1.13:2.6.verse: Thus, your majesty, does mindfulness have not wavering as a distinguishing characteristic.”

mil3.1.13:3.1.verse: “How, venerable sir, does mindfulness have taking up as a distinguishing characteristic?”

mil3.1.13:3.2.verse: “Mindfulness arising, your majesty, examines the courses of mental states that are beneficial or non-beneficial, thinking ‘these mental states are beneficial, these are non-beneficial;

mil3.1.13:3.3.verse: these mental states are supportive, these are not supportive.’

mil3.1.13:3.4.verse: Then, the spiritual aspirant dispels non-beneficial mental states and takes up beneficial mental states;

mil3.1.13:3.5.verse: dispels non-supportive mental states and takes up supportive ones.

mil3.1.13:3.6.verse: Thus, your majesty, does mindfulness have taking up as a distinguishing characteristic.”

mil3.1.13:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a wheel-turning king’s treasured adviser knows what is beneficial and non-beneficial for the king, thinking ‘these are beneficial for the king, these are non-beneficial;

mil3.1.13:4.3.verse: these are supportive, these are not supportive.’

mil3.1.13:4.4.verse: Then, he dispels the non-beneficial and takes up the beneficial;

mil3.1.13:4.5.verse: dispels the non-supportive and takes up the supportive.

mil3.1.13:4.6.verse: In the same way, your majesty, mindfulness arising examines mental states that are beneficial or non-beneficial, thinking ‘these mental states are beneficial, these are non-beneficial;

mil3.1.13:4.7.verse: these mental states are supportive, these are not supportive.’

mil3.1.13:4.8.verse: Then, the spiritual aspirant dispels non-beneficial mental states and takes up beneficial mental states;

mil3.1.13:4.9.verse: dispels non-supportive mental states and takes up supportive ones.

mil3.1.13:4.10.verse: Thus, your majesty, does mindfulness have taking up as a distinguishing characteristic.

mil3.1.13:4.11.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.1.13:4.12.verse: ‘I say, bhikkhus, that mindfulness is always useful.’”

mil3.1.13:6.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Mindfulness Question thirteenth

mil3.1.14:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of concentration?”

mil3.1.14:1.3.verse: “Concentration, your majesty, has being the foremost as a distinguishing characteristic, whatever wholesome mental states there are all these have concentration as the foremost, they lean towards concentration, slope towards concentration, and incline towards concentration.”

mil3.1.14:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, whatever rafters there are in a house with a ridge pole, all the rafters go to that ridge pole, lean towards it, converge at it, and it is considered to be the chief of them.

mil3.1.14:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, whatever wholesome mental states there are all these have concentration as the foremost, they lean towards concentration, slope towards concentration, and incline towards concentration.”

mil3.1.14:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, whatever king with his four-factored army would go down into battle, all the army – the elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers – would have him as the foremost, lean towards him, slope towards him, and incline towards him, and would gather around him.

mil3.1.14:3.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, whatever wholesome mental states there are all these have concentration as the foremost, they lean towards concentration, slope towards concentration, and incline towards concentration.

mil3.1.14:3.4.verse: Thus, your majesty, concentration has being the foremost as a distinguishing characteristic.

mil3.1.14:3.5.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.1.14:3.6.verse: ‘Develop concentration, bhikkhus. A concentrated bhikkhu knows things as they really are.’”

mil3.1.15:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of wisdom?”

mil3.1.15:1.4.verse: severing is a distinguishing characteristic of wisdom, and also illuminating is a distinguishing characteristic of wisdom.”

mil3.1.15:1.5.verse: “How, venerable sir, is illuminating a distinguishing characteristic of wisdom.”

mil3.1.15:1.6.verse: “Wisdom arising, your majesty, dispels the darkness of ignorance, generates the radiance of true knowledge, displays the light of understanding, and makes evident the noble truths.

mil3.1.15:1.7.verse: Then, a spiritual practitioner sees with right wisdom what is ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not self’.”

mil3.1.15:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a person might bring a lamp into a dark house, and this lamp brought in dispels the darkness, generates radiance, displays light, and makes evident forms.

mil3.1.15:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, wisdom arising dispels the darkness of ignorance, generates the radiance of true knowledge, displays the light of understanding, and makes evident the noble truths.

mil3.1.15:2.4.verse: Then, a spiritual practitioner sees with right wisdom what is ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not self’.

mil3.1.15:2.5.verse: Thus, your majesty, is illuminating a distinguishing characteristic of wisdom.”

mil3.1.15:4.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Wisdom Question fifteenth

mil3.1.16:0.3.verse: 16. Production of One Result from Various Mental States Question

mil3.1.16:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, do these mental states, though being diverse, produce the one result?”

mil3.1.16:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, these mental states, though being diverse, do produce the one result; they kill the defilements.”

mil3.1.16:2.1.verse: “How is it, venerable sir, these mental states, though being diverse, produce the one result, and kill the defilements?

mil3.1.16:2.3.verse: “Just as, your majesty, an army is diverse, and its elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers produce the one result; they conquer an opposing army in battle,

mil3.1.16:2.4.verse: in the same way, your majesty, these mental states, though being diverse, produce the one result; they kill the defilements.”

mil3.1.16:4.1.verse: Production of One Result from Various Mental States Question sixteenth

mil3.2.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the one who arises the same or otherwise?”

mil3.2.1:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you were a child, young and tender and lying on your back, were you the same as you are now that you are grown?”

mil3.2.1:2.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir. That child, young and tender and lying on his back was one thing, and I now grown am another.”

mil3.2.1:2.4.verse: “That being so, your majesty, there would be no notion of mother, nor of father, nor of teacher, nor of a craftsperson, nor of a virtuous person, nor of a wise person.

mil3.2.1:2.5.verse: Can it be, your majesty, that the mother of the embryo is different from the mother at the next foetal stage, which is different from the mother of following foetal stages, that the mother of a child is different from the mother of the grown person, that one who trains in a craft is different from the one who is trained, that the one who commits an evil deed is different from the one whose hands and feet are cut off?”

mil3.2.1:2.7.verse: And what would you say if somebody said this to be so?”

mil3.2.1:2.9.verse: “It was just I, your majesty, who was a child, young and tender and lying on my back, and now it is just I who has grown, and all these states are held together dependent on just this body.”

mil3.2.1:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person might light a lamp, might it stay lit all night?”

mil3.2.1:3.3.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, it might stay lit all night.”

mil3.2.1:3.4.verse: “Is it so, your majesty, that the flame in the first watch of the night is the same as that in the middle watch?”

mil3.2.1:3.6.verse: “Is the flame in the middle watch of the night the same as that in the last watch?”

mil3.2.1:3.8.verse: “Is it then so, your majesty, that the lamp in the first watch of the night is different from that in the middle watch, which is different from that in the last watch?”

mil3.2.1:3.9.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir. It was burning all through the night dependent on just itself.”

mil3.2.1:3.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, a continuity of states runs on; as one arises, another ceases. It runs on like there was no before and no after. Consequently, it is neither the same nor the other and the last consciousness is comprised of the first consciousness.”

mil3.2.1:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, milk some time after being milked from a cow would turn to curds, and from curds into butter, and from butter to ghee, would someone who might say, ‘That milk is those curds, those curds is that butter, that butter is that ghee,’ be speaking rightly?”

mil3.2.1:4.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, they come into being because of it.”

mil3.2.1:4.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, a continuity of states runs on; as one arises, another ceases. It runs on like there was no before and no after. Consequently, it is neither the same nor the other and the last consciousness is comprised of the first consciousness.”

mil3.2.2:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does someone who does not reconnect know ‘I will not reconnect’?”

mil3.2.2:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, someone who does not reconnect knows ‘I will not reconnect’.”

mil3.2.2:1.5.verse: “From the cessation, your majesty, of the cause and condition for reconnecting one knows ‘I will not reconnect’.”

mil3.2.2:2.2.verse: “Just like, your majesty, a householder farmer, having ploughed and sown might fill his grain house.

mil3.2.2:2.3.verse: But then, after some time, he would not plough and sow, and would use up the grain he had stored, or dispose of it, or deal with it according to conditions, would that householder farmer know, your majesty, ‘I will not fill my grain house’?”

mil3.2.2:2.6.verse: “From the cessation of that cause and condition for filling the grain house one knows ‘I will not fill my grain house’.”

mil3.2.2:2.7.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, from the cessation of the cause and condition for reconnecting one knows ‘I will not reconnect’.”

mil3.2.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, would wisdom also have arisen?”

mil3.2.3:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, wisdom also has arisen.”

mil3.2.3:1.4.verse: “What, venerable sir, is knowledge the same as wisdom?”

mil3.2.3:1.5.verse: “Yes, your majesty, knowledge is the same as wisdom.”

mil3.2.3:1.6.verse: “Then, venerable sir, for one in whom knowledge has arisen which is the same as wisdom, would he be confused or would he not be confused?”

mil3.2.3:1.7.verse: “He would be confused in some instances, your majesty, and would not be confused in other instances.”

mil3.2.3:1.8.verse: “When, venerable sir, would he be confused?”

mil3.2.3:1.9.verse: “He would be confused, your majesty, concerning those aspects of a craft that he did not know before, or those directions in which he has not gone before, or those names and designations he has not heard before.”

mil3.2.3:1.10.verse: “When, venerable sir, would he not be confused?”

mil3.2.3:1.11.verse: “He would not be confused, your majesty, concerning that which he has discerned by wisdom, that is, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self.”

mil3.2.3:1.12.verse: “Then where, venerable sir, does his confusion go?”

mil3.2.3:1.13.verse: “Confusion ceases, your majesty, at that very moment when knowledge arises.”

mil3.2.3:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person might bring in a lamp to a dark house, then the darkness ceases, and light appears.

mil3.2.3:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, at the moment when knowledge arises, right there confusion ceases.”

mil3.2.3:3.1.verse: “Then where, venerable sir, does wisdom go?”

mil3.2.3:3.2.verse: “Wisdom, your majesty, ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.”

mil3.2.3:4.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what you have just said, ‘Wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease,’ please make an analogy for that.”

mil3.2.3:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person, wishing to send a letter at night, would summon a scribe and light a lamp, and have the letter written. Then, when the letter is written, he would extinguish the lamp. And when the lamp is extinguished the letter would not be destroyed.

mil3.2.3:4.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.”

mil3.2.3:5.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, people in the eastern districts might set up five water pots in each house so as to extinguish any burning, and when a house is on fire, they would throw these five pots of water on top of the house, then the fire would be extinguished. Would it occur to these people, your majesty, ‘We must make use of these pots again’?”

mil3.2.3:5.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, those pots have done their job, what further need would there be for them?”

mil3.2.3:5.4.verse: “As, your majesty, are the five pots of water, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen.

mil3.2.3:5.5.verse: As those people, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen.

mil3.2.3:5.6.verse: As the fire, so the defilements are to be seen.

mil3.2.3:5.7.verse: As the fire is extinguished by the five pots of water, so the defilements are extinguished by the five faculties, and those extinguished defilements do not arise again.

mil3.2.3:5.8.verse: In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.”

mil3.2.3:6.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a doctor, having taken the five root medicines and approached a sick person, might crush the five root medicines and get the sick person to drink them, and the sickness would disappear. Would it occur to that doctor, your majesty, ‘I will make use of the five root medicines again’?”

mil3.2.3:6.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, those five root medicines have done their job, what further need would there be for them?”

mil3.2.3:6.4.verse: “As, your majesty, are the five root medicines, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen. As the doctor, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen.

mil3.2.3:6.5.verse: As the disease, so the defilements are to be seen.

mil3.2.3:6.6.verse: As the sick person, so the common person is to be seen.

mil3.2.3:6.7.verse: As the disease of the sick person is expelled by the five root medicines such that when the disease is expelled the sick person becomes well, so the defilements are expelled by the five faculties, and those expelled defilements do not arise again.

mil3.2.3:6.8.verse: In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.”

mil3.2.3:7.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a warrior, skilled in battle, having taken five arrows and entered into battle in order to defeat an opposing army, and gone into battle he might let fly those five arrows, and the opposing army is destroyed by them. Would it occur to that warrior, skilled in battle, your majesty, ‘I will make use of these five arrows again’?”

mil3.2.3:7.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, those five arrows have done their job, what further need would there be for them?”

mil3.2.3:7.4.verse: “As, your majesty, are the five arrows, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen.

mil3.2.3:7.5.verse: As the warrior, skilled in battle, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen.

mil3.2.3:7.6.verse: As the opposing army, so the defilements are to be seen.

mil3.2.3:7.7.verse: As the opposing army is destroyed by the five arrows, so the defilements are destroyed by the five faculties, and those destroyed defilements do not arise again.

mil3.2.3:7.8.verse: In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.”

mil3.2.4:0.3.verse: 4. Question on the Feelings of an Individual Reconnecting

mil3.2.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who does not reconnect feel a painful feeling?”

mil3.2.4:1.4.verse: “He feels some, and he does not feel others.”

mil3.2.4:1.5.verse: “Which does he feel, and which does he not feel?”

mil3.2.4:1.6.verse: “He feels bodily feelings, your majesty, and he does not feel mental feelings.”

mil3.2.4:1.7.verse: “How, venerable sir, does he feel bodily feelings, and how does he not feel mental feelings?”

mil3.2.4:1.8.verse: “There is no ceasing of that cause and condition for the arising of a painful bodily feeling, and thus he feels a painful bodily feeling. There is ceasing of that cause and condition for the arising of a painful mental feeling, and thus he does not feel a painful mental feeling.

mil3.2.4:1.9.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.2.4:1.10.verse: ‘He only feels one feeling, the bodily one, not the mental.’”

mil3.2.4:2.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, why does one who feels a painful feeling not experience final nibbāna?”

mil3.2.4:2.2.verse: “For an arahant, your majesty, there is no delight nor repugnance, and arahants do not destroy what is unripe. The wise ones wait for full maturing.

mil3.2.4:2.3.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the elder Sāriputta, the general of the Dhamma:

mil3.2.4:3.2.verse: nor do I delight in living.

mil3.2.4:3.3.verse: But I wait for the right time,

mil3.2.4:3.4.verse: as a servant waits for his wages.

mil3.2.4:4.2.verse: nor do I delight in living.

mil3.2.4:4.3.verse: But I wait for the right time,

mil3.2.4:6.1.verse: Question on the Feelings of an Individual Reconnecting fourth

mil3.2.5:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is pleasant feeling wholesome or unwholesome or indeterminate?”

mil3.2.5:1.3.verse: “It could be wholesome, your majesty, or it could be unwholesome, or it could be indeterminate.”

mil3.2.5:1.4.verse: “If, venerable sir, wholesome feelings are not painful, and if painful feelings are not wholesome, then there does not arise a wholesome feeling which is painful.”

mil3.2.5:1.5.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, if one might place a hot iron ball in a man’s hand and place a snowball in his other hand, would both hurt him?”

mil3.2.5:1.6.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, they would both hurt him.”

mil3.2.5:1.7.verse: “Well, your majesty, are they both hot?”

mil3.2.5:1.9.verse: “What then, your majesty, are they both cold?”

mil3.2.5:1.11.verse: “Know your own refutation. If something hot hurts, and they are not both hot, it is not because of that the suffering arises.

mil3.2.5:1.12.verse: And, if something cold hurts, and they are not both cold, it is not because of that the suffering arises.

mil3.2.5:1.13.verse: So, how is it, your majesty, that both hurt, and they are not both hot, and they are not both cold?

mil3.2.5:1.14.verse: And, how is it that with one hot and the other cold, they both hurt, and it is not because of that the suffering arises?”

mil3.2.5:1.15.verse: “I am not competent to converse with you, a debater of the doctrine. It would be good, venerable sir, if you told me the meaning.”

mil3.2.5:1.16.verse: Then the elder instructed King Milinda with a talk connected with Abhidhamma.

mil3.2.5:2.1.verse: “There are, your majesty, these six joys dependent on the householder life, these six joys dependent on renunciation, these six sorrows dependent on the householder life, these six sorrows dependent on renunciation, these six neutral feelings dependent on the householder life, these six neutral feelings dependent on renunciation. Thus, there are these six sets of six. There are then thirty-six types of feeling in the past, thirty-six types of feeling in the future, and thirty-six types of feeling in the present. So, assembling them and bringing them all together, there are one hundred and eight types of feeling.”

mil3.2.6:0.3.verse: 6. Question on the Identity or Difference of Name-and-Form

mil3.2.6:1.6.verse: “This very name-and-form, your majesty, does not reconnect. With this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects.”

mil3.2.6:1.7.verse: “If, venerable sir, this very name-and-form does not reconnect, is it not then that it would be freed from evil actions?”

mil3.2.6:1.9.verse: “If it would not reconnect, then it would be freed from evil actions.

mil3.2.6:1.10.verse: But because, your majesty, it does reconnect, it therefore is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s mangos, and the mango owner might grab that person and point him out to the king, saying ‘My mangos have been stolen by this man.’ And he might say ‘Lord, I did not steal this person’s mangos. Those mangos I took are not the same as those that this person planted; I do not deserve punishment.’

mil3.2.6:2.3.verse: Would that man, your majesty, deserve punishment?”

mil3.2.6:2.4.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.”

mil3.2.6:2.6.verse: “Whatever he might say, venerable sir, while not disavowing the earlier mangos, he would be deserving of punishment due to the later mangos.”

mil3.2.6:2.7.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s rice, …

mil3.2.6:3.4.verse: Just as, your majesty, some person or other might light a fire during the wintertime, and warm himself, and might leave without having extinguished it, and that fire might burn another person’s field. And the owner of the field might grab that person and point him out to the king, saying ‘My field has been burned by this man.’

mil3.2.6:3.5.verse: And he might say ‘Lord, I did not set fire to this person’s field. The fire I did not extinguish was not the same as the fire that burned this person’s field; I do not deserve punishment.’

mil3.2.6:3.6.verse: Would that man, your majesty, deserve punishment?”

mil3.2.6:3.7.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.”

mil3.2.6:3.9.verse: “Whatever he might say, venerable sir, while not disavowing the earlier fire, he would be deserving of punishment by means of the later fire.”

mil3.2.6:3.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having taken a lamp and ascended to the top of a mansion, might use it, and the burning lamp might set fire to the roof thatch, and the burning thatch might set fire to the house, and the burning house might set fire to the village, and the villagers, having seized that man, might say, ‘Why, sir, did you set fire to the village?’ And he might say ‘I did not, friend, set fire to the village. The fire in the lamp whose light I enjoyed was not the same as the fire that burned the village.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing, whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?”

mil3.2.6:4.5.verse: “Since, whatever he might say, this fire was produced just from that one.”

mil3.2.6:4.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:5.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having contracted for a young girl in marriage and having paid the bride price, might leave.

mil3.2.6:5.3.verse: Then, after some time, she would reach full marriageable age, then another man, having paid the bride price would lead her away in marriage. The former man would come and say, ‘Why, sir, have you led away my wife?’

mil3.2.6:5.4.verse: And he might say ‘I have not led away your wife. The young girl for whom you have contracted and paid the bride price is not the same as the young woman who has attained marriageable age and been contracted for and paid for by me.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing,

mil3.2.6:5.5.verse: whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?”

mil3.2.6:5.6.verse: “That of the former man, venerable sir.”

mil3.2.6:5.8.verse: “Since, whatever he might say, this grown woman was produced just from that one.”

mil3.2.6:5.9.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:6.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having bought a pot of milk from the hand of a cowherd, might put it in his care and leave, saying, ‘I will come back for it tomorrow,’ and that milk would become curds.

mil3.2.6:6.3.verse: Then, he might come back and say ‘Give me my pot of milk.’

mil3.2.6:6.4.verse: And the cowherd would show him the curds.

mil3.2.6:6.5.verse: The other would then say, ‘I did not buy curds from you, give me my pot of milk.’

mil3.2.6:6.6.verse: Then, that one would say, ‘Without you knowing it, the milk has become curds.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing, whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?”

mil3.2.6:6.9.verse: “Since, whatever he might say, this one was produced just from that one.”

mil3.2.6:6.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.2.6:8.1.verse: Question on the Identity or Difference of Name-and-Form sixth

mil3.2.7:0.3.verse: 7. Question on the Elder’s Reconnection or Non-Reconnection

mil3.2.7:1.3.verse: “Enough, your majesty, why are you asking this? Have I not declared to you previously, ‘If, your majesty, I am with clinging I will reconnect, and if I am without clinging I will not reconnect’?”

mil3.2.7:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a service for the king,

mil3.2.7:2.3.verse: and the king, satisfied, would repay that service. And that person, because of that service, would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and might announce to the populace, ‘The king does not do anything for me.’

mil3.2.7:2.4.verse: Would that man, your majesty, be acting rightly?”

mil3.2.7:2.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, why are you asking this? Have I not declared to you previously, ‘If I am with clinging I will reconnect, and if I am without clinging I will not reconnect’?”

mil3.2.7:4.1.verse: Question on the Elder’s Reconnection or Non-Reconnection seventh

mil3.2.8:0.3.verse: 8. Question on the Reconnection of Name-and-form

mil3.2.8:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, you talked then of name-and-form. What in there is name, and what is form?”

mil3.2.8:1.3.verse: “Whatever in there, your majesty, is gross, that is form. Whatever in there are subtle mental states that are mental factors in the mind, that is name.”

mil3.2.8:1.4.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, why doesn’t just name alone reconnect, nor form alone?”

mil3.2.8:1.5.verse: “These things, your majesty, are mutually dependent and they only arise together.”

mil3.2.8:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, there could not be just a yolk nor just an egg-shell, since the yoke and the egg-shell are both mutually dependent and they only arise together.

mil3.2.8:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, if there were no name there would be no form, and what name there is and what form there is, these are both mutually dependent and they only arise together.

mil3.2.8:2.4.verse: Thus, there is this long extent of transmigration time.”

mil3.2.8:4.1.verse: Question on the Reconnection of Name-and-form eighth

mil3.2.9:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, you talked then of a long extent of transmigration time. What is this thing called transmigration time?”

mil3.2.9:1.3.verse: “The past, your majesty, is transmigration time, the future is transmigration time, the present is transmigration time.”

mil3.2.9:1.4.verse: “But, venerable sir, does all transmigration time exist?”

mil3.2.9:1.5.verse: “Some transmigration time exists, your majesty, and some does not.”

mil3.2.9:1.6.verse: “What then, venerable sir, exists and what does not?”

mil3.2.9:1.7.verse: “Those mental formations, your majesty, that are past, gone, ceased, and changed, that transmigration time does not exist. Those mental formations that have reached fruition, or have the nature to be liable for fruition, or those that give reconnection elsewhere, that transmigration time does exist.

mil3.2.9:1.8.verse: Those beings that have died and arisen elsewhere, that transmigration time does exist.

mil3.2.9:1.9.verse: Those beings that have died and not arisen elsewhere, that transmigration time does not exist.

mil3.2.9:1.10.verse: And those beings that have attained final nibbāna, that transmigration time does not exist because of the attainment of nibbāna.”

mil3.3.1:0.3.verse: 1. Question on the Root of Time

mil3.3.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the root of transmigration time in the past, what is the root of transmigration time in the future, what is the root of transmigration time in the present?”

mil3.3.1:1.3.verse: “The root of transmigration time in the past, your majesty, and of transmigration time in the future, and of transmigration time in the present is ignorance.

mil3.3.1:1.4.verse: From the condition of ignorance there are fabrications, from the condition of fabrications there is consciousness, from the condition of consciousness there is name-and-form, from the condition of name-and-form there are the six sense bases, from the condition of the six sense bases there is contact, from the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is becoming, from the condition of becoming there is birth, from the condition of birth there is old age and death; sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair arise.

mil3.3.1:1.5.verse: Thus, no earliest point of this whole mass of suffering of transmigration time can be discerned.”

mil3.3.1:3.1.verse: Question on the Root of Time first

mil3.3.2:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ please give me an analogy for that.”

mil3.3.2:1.3.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a man might put a small seed in the ground, then it having produced a sprout and having gradually undergone increase, growth, and full maturity, it would ripen into fruit.

mil3.3.2:1.4.verse: Then again having taken from that a seed and cultivated it, then it having produced a sprout and having gradually undergone increase, growth, and full maturity, it would ripen into fruit.

mil3.3.2:1.5.verse: Is there thus an end to this continuity?”

mil3.3.2:1.7.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.”

mil3.3.2:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, an egg might be produced from a hen, a hen from that egg, and an egg from that hen, and so on.

mil3.3.2:2.3.verse: Is there thus an end to this continuity?”

mil3.3.2:2.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.”

mil3.3.2:3.2.verse: The elder drew a circle on the ground and said to King Milinda,

mil3.3.2:3.3.verse: “Is there an end to this circle?”

mil3.3.2:3.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, these cycles spoken of by the Blessed One, ‘Dependent on the eye and form, eye consciousness arises, and the meeting of the three is contact. From the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is kamma, and again the eye is born from kamma.’

mil3.3.2:3.6.verse: Is there thus an end to this continuity?”

mil3.3.2:4.2.verse: Dependent on the mind and thought, mind consciousness arises, and the meeting of the three is contact. From the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is kamma, and again the mind is born from kamma.’

mil3.3.2:4.3.verse: Is there thus an end to this continuity?”

mil3.3.2:4.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.”

mil3.3.2:6.1.verse: Question on the Earliest Point second

mil3.3.3:0.3.verse: Question on the Discernment of an End Point

mil3.3.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ what is this earliest point?”

mil3.3.3:1.3.verse: “That which is time in the past, your majesty, is the earliest point.”

mil3.3.3:1.4.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ is it that all earliest points cannot be discerned?”

mil3.3.3:1.5.verse: “Some can be discerned, your majesty, and some cannot be.”

mil3.3.3:1.6.verse: “What can be discerned, venerable sir, and what cannot?”

mil3.3.3:1.7.verse: “That earliest point cannot be discerned, your majesty, where earlier than this no ignorance was existing at all, by any means, or in any way. That which having not existed arose, and having existed disappeared again, that earliest point can be discerned.”

mil3.3.3:2.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, that which having not existed arose, and having existed disappeared again would it not, having been cut off at both ends, be entirely destroyed?”

mil3.3.3:2.2.verse: “If, your majesty, having been cut off at both ends, it was entirely destroyed, is it possible, being cut off at both ends, to grow?”

mil3.3.3:2.3.verse: “Yes, it is possible for it to grow.

mil3.3.3:2.4.verse: I am not asking that, venerable sir; is it possible for it to grow from that end?”

mil3.3.3:2.5.verse: “Yes, it is possible for it to grow.”

mil3.3.3:3.2.verse: The elder made him an analogy of a tree, “The aggregates are the seeds of this whole mass of suffering.”

mil3.3.3:5.1.verse: Question on the Discernment of an End Point third

mil3.3.4:0.3.verse: 4. Question on the Production of Fabrications

mil3.3.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, are there any fabrications which are produced?”

mil3.3.4:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, there are fabrications which are produced.”

mil3.3.4:1.5.verse: “When there is the eye and forms, your majesty, there is eye consciousness. When there is eye consciousness, there is eye contact. When there is eye contact, there is feeling. When there is feeling, there is craving. When there is craving, there is becoming. When there is becoming, there is birth. When there is birth, there is old age and death, and sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair come to be. Thus, there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.

mil3.3.4:1.6.verse: When there is no eye and forms, your majesty, there is no eye consciousness. When there is no eye consciousness, there is no eye contact. When there is no eye contact, there is no feeling. When there is no feeling, there is no craving. When there is no craving, there is no becoming. When there is no becoming, there is no birth. When there is no birth, there is no old age and death, and there is no sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair. Thus, there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

mil3.3.4:3.1.verse: Question on the Production of Fabrications fourth

mil3.3.5:0.3.verse: 5. Question on the Production and Development of Fabrications

mil3.3.5:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, are there any fabrications which are produced without development?”

mil3.3.5:1.3.verse: “Your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, was this house that you are sitting in produced without development?”

mil3.3.5:2.3.verse: “There is nothing here, venerable sir, produced without development; it is produced only with development. These pieces of wood were in the forest, and this clay was in the ground, and thus this house was produced by the appropriate effort of women and men.”

mil3.3.5:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:3.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, whatever seeds and plants thrown on the ground gradually attain to growth, development, and maturity, and would give flowers and fruit, no trees would be produced without development, and trees would only be produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:3.3.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:4.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a potter might take clay from the ground and make various bowls, those bowls are not produced without development, and bowls would only be produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:4.3.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:5.2.verse: “Just as if, your majesty, there were no sound-board for a lute, no parchment, no belly, no arm, no neck, no strings, no plectrum, and no suitable effort from a person, would sound be produced?”

mil3.3.5:5.4.verse: “But if, your majesty, there were a sound-board for a lute, parchment, a belly, an arm, a neck, strings, a plectrum, and suitable effort from a person, would sound be produced?”

mil3.3.5:5.5.verse: “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.5:5.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:6.2.verse: “Just as if, your majesty, there were no lower piece of wood, no twirling stick, no string for the twirling stick, no upper piece of wood, no bark, and no suitable effort from a person, would fire be produced?”

mil3.3.5:6.4.verse: “But if, your majesty, there were a lower piece of wood, a twirling stick, string for the twirling stick, an upper piece of wood, bark, and suitable effort from a person, would fire be produced?”

mil3.3.5:6.5.verse: “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.5:6.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:7.2.verse: “Just as if, your majesty, there were no crystal glass, no heat, and no cow-dung, would fire be produced?”

mil3.3.5:7.4.verse: “But if, your majesty, there were a crystal glass, heat, and cow-dung, would fire be produced?”

mil3.3.5:7.5.verse: “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.5:7.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:8.2.verse: “Just as if, your majesty, there were no mirror, no light, and no face, would an image be produced?”

mil3.3.5:8.4.verse: “But if, your majesty, there were a mirror, light, and a face, would an image be produced?”

mil3.3.5:8.5.verse: “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.5:8.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.”

mil3.3.5:10.1.verse: Question on the Production and Development of Fabrications fifth

mil3.3.6:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is an experiencer to be found?”

mil3.3.6:1.3.verse: “But what then is this thing called an experiencer?”

mil3.3.6:1.4.verse: “That soul within, venerable sir, that sees a form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear, smells an odour with the nose, tastes a flavour with the tongue, touches a tangible with the body, and knows a thought with the mind, just as we, seated here in the palace, might look out of whichever window we wish to look out of – whether that be the east, the west, the north, or the south window.

mil3.3.6:1.5.verse: Even so, venerable sir, this soul within looks out of whatever door it wishes to look out of.”

mil3.3.6:2.2.verse: “I will talk to you, your majesty, about the five doors. Listen to this and pay careful attention. If the soul within sees form with the eye, just as we, sitting here in the palace can see material form through whatever window we wish to look through, whether through the east, the west, the north, or the south window, could a material form be seen by this soul within by means of the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind?

mil3.3.6:2.3.verse: And could a sound be heard by means of the eye, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind?

mil3.3.6:2.4.verse: And could an odour be smelled by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind?

mil3.3.6:2.5.verse: And could a flavour be tasted by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the body, or by the mind?

mil3.3.6:2.6.verse: And could a tangible be felt by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the mind?

mil3.3.6:2.7.verse: And could a thought be known by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body?”

mil3.3.6:3.1.verse: “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as, your majesty, when these grilled windows are removed, we seated here in the palace, looking outward, see form more clearly through great space, would the soul within see form more clearly through great space when the doors of the eyes have been removed? ... when the ears have been removed? ... when the nose has been removed? ... when the tongue has been removed? And would it feel a tangible more clearly when the body has been removed?”

mil3.3.6:4.1.verse: “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as if, your majesty, this Dinna were to depart and stand in the entrance way outside the door, would you know ‘this Dinna has departed and is standing in the entrance way outside the door’?”

mil3.3.6:4.3.verse: “And then, just as if, your majesty, this Dinna were to come back inside and stand in front of you, would you know ‘this Dinna has come back inside and is standing in front of me’?”

mil3.3.6:4.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, when a flavour is placed on the tongue, would the soul within know whether its essence were sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, or sweet?”

mil3.3.6:4.7.verse: “And when it has gone from your tongue into your inside would it know whether its essence were sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, or sweet?”

mil3.3.6:5.1.verse: “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as if, your majesty, some person or other might fetch a hundred pots of honey, fill a large trough with this honey, cover the mouth of a man, and throw him into the trough of honey, would that man know whether the honey were sweet or not?”

mil3.3.6:5.4.verse: “Because, venerable sir, the honey has not entered his mouth.”

mil3.3.6:6.1.verse: “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter.”

mil3.3.6:6.2.verse: “I am not competent to converse with you, a debater of the doctrine.

mil3.3.6:6.3.verse: It would be good, venerable sir, if you told me the meaning.”

mil3.3.6:7.1.verse: The elder instructed King Milinda with a talk connected with Abhidhamma.

mil3.3.6:7.2.verse: “Here, your majesty, dependent on the eye and form, eye consciousness arises, and from the coming together of that there is contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life faculty, and attention. Thus, these things are produced from conditions, and no experiencer is found here. Dependent on the ear and sounds …

mil3.3.6:7.3.verse: dependent on the mind and thoughts, mind consciousness arises, and from the coming together of that there is contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life faculty, and attention. Thus, these things are produced from conditions, and no experiencer is found here.”

mil3.3.7:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does mind consciousness arise where eye consciousness arises?”

mil3.3.7:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises.”

mil3.3.7:2.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does eye consciousness arise first, then mind consciousness after, or does mind consciousness arise first, then eye consciousness after?”

mil3.3.7:2.2.verse: “Eye consciousness arises first, your majesty, then mind consciousness arises after.”
