mil3.3.7:3.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does eye consciousness instruct mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ or does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’?”

mil3.3.7:3.2.verse: “Certainly not, your majesty, there is no conversation between them.”

mil3.3.7:4.1.verse: “Then, how is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?”

mil3.3.7:4.2.verse: “It is because of inclination, your majesty, and because of door, of habit, and of practice.”

mil3.3.7:5.1.verse: “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of inclination mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?

mil3.3.7:5.3.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when it is raining what way would the water go?”

mil3.3.7:5.4.verse: “It would go according to the inclination, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.7:5.5.verse: “And if it would continue to rain for some time, what way would that water go?”

mil3.3.7:5.6.verse: “It would go in the same direction as the earlier water, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.7:6.1.verse: “Does the earlier water, your majesty, instruct the later water, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later water instruct the earlier water ‘where you will go, there I will go’?”

mil3.3.7:6.2.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of the inclination.”

mil3.3.7:6.3.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, because of the inclination eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of the inclination.”

mil3.3.7:7.1.verse: “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of door mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?

mil3.3.7:7.3.verse: “What do you think, your majesty? There might be a king’s border town with strong ramparts, an arched gateway, and only one door, and there, if a man were wishing to depart, how would he do so?”

mil3.3.7:7.4.verse: “He would depart through the door, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.7:7.5.verse: “Then, if there was another man wishing to depart, how would he do so?”

mil3.3.7:7.6.verse: “He would depart in the same way as the first man, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.7:8.1.verse: “Does the first man, your majesty, instruct the later man, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later man instruct the first man ‘where you will go, there I will go’?”

mil3.3.7:8.2.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of the door.”

mil3.3.7:8.3.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, because of the door eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of the door.”

mil3.3.7:9.1.verse: “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of habit mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?

mil3.3.7:9.3.verse: “What do you think, your majesty? If one cart goes first, then which way would a second cart go?”

mil3.3.7:9.4.verse: “It would go in the same way as the first cart, venerable sir.”

mil3.3.7:10.1.verse: “Does the first cart, your majesty, instruct the later cart, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later cart instruct the first cart ‘where you will go, there I will go’?”

mil3.3.7:10.2.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of habit.”

mil3.3.7:10.3.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, because of habit eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of habit.”

mil3.3.7:11.1.verse: “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of practice mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?

mil3.3.7:11.3.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a beginner might be clumsy in the arts of hand reckoning, calculation, mental reckoning, and writing, but then, after some time, with careful working and practice, he would become skilful.

mil3.3.7:11.4.verse: In the same way, your majesty, because of practice eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of practice.”

mil3.3.7:12.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does mind consciousness arise where ear consciousness arises? ...

mil3.3.7:12.2.verse: where nose consciousness arises … where tongue consciousness arises … where body consciousness arises?”

mil3.3.7:12.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, mind consciousness arises where body consciousness arises.”

mil3.3.7:13.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does body consciousness arise first, then mind consciousness after, or does mind consciousness arise first, then body consciousness after?”

mil3.3.7:13.2.verse: “Body consciousness arises first, your majesty, then mind consciousness arises after.”

mil3.3.7:14.2.verse: there is no conversation between them, they arise because of practice.”

mil3.3.7:16.1.verse: Question on Eye Consciousness, Etc. seventh

mil3.3.8:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, do contact and also feeling arise where mind consciousness arises?”

mil3.3.8:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, where mind consciousness arises, there too contact, feeling, perception, intention, applied thought, and examination arise, and all mental states that arise there are led by contact.”

mil3.3.8:2.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of contact?”

mil3.3.8:2.2.verse: “Touching, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of contact.”

mil3.3.8:3.2.verse: “Suppose, your majesty, that two rams were fighting. One of these rams is to be seen as the eye,

mil3.3.8:3.3.verse: the other ram is to be seen as form,

mil3.3.8:3.4.verse: and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.”

mil3.3.8:4.2.verse: “Suppose, your majesty, that two hands were clapped together. One of these hands is to be seen as the eye,

mil3.3.8:4.3.verse: the other hand is to be seen as form,

mil3.3.8:4.4.verse: and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.”

mil3.3.8:5.2.verse: “Suppose, your majesty, that two cymbals were clanged together. One of these cymbals is to be seen as the eye,

mil3.3.8:5.3.verse: the other cymbal is to be seen as form,

mil3.3.8:5.4.verse: and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.”

mil3.3.8:7.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Contact Question eighth

mil3.3.9:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of feeling?”

mil3.3.9:1.2.verse: “Being felt and experiencing, your majesty, are the distinguishing characteristics of feeling.”

mil3.3.9:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a service for the king, and the king, satisfied, would repay that service. And that person, because of that service, would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and it might occur to him ‘previously I performed a service for the king and he, satisfied, repaid me for that service, and for that reason I experience such and such feelings.’

mil3.3.9:3.1.verse: Or just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a good deed and at the beak up of the body after dying, might be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, and there would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of divine sensual pleasure, and it might occur to him ‘previously I performed a good deed, and for that reason I experience such and such feelings.’

mil3.3.9:3.2.verse: In the same way, your majesty, being felt and experiencing are the distinguishing characteristics of feeling.”

mil3.3.9:5.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Feeling Question ninth

mil3.3.10:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of perception?”

mil3.3.10:1.2.verse: “Perceiving, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of perception.

mil3.3.10:1.4.verse: One perceives blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.

mil3.3.10:1.5.verse: Thus, your majesty, perceiving is the distinguishing characteristic of perception.”

mil3.3.10:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a king’s storekeeper, having entered the warehouse and seen the forms of the king’s goods there, perceives blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.

mil3.3.10:2.3.verse: Thus, your majesty, perceiving is the distinguishing characteristic of perception.”

mil3.3.10:4.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Perception Question tenth

mil3.3.11:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of intention?”

mil3.3.11:1.2.verse: “Willing and arranging, your majesty, are the distinguishing characteristics of intention.”

mil3.3.11:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might prepare a poison and drink it himself and get others to drink it, then he himself would become afflicted and others would become afflicted.

mil3.3.11:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, some person here, through intention, would will an unwholesome action and on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a bad destination, a state of suffering, a hell realm.

mil3.3.11:2.4.verse: And those who followed him, on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a bad destination, a state of suffering, a hell realm.

mil3.3.11:3.1.verse: Or just as, your majesty, some person or other might prepare a mixture of ghee, butter, oil, honey and molasses and drink it himself and get others to drink it, then he himself would become happy and others would become happy.

mil3.3.11:3.2.verse: In the same way, your majesty, some person here, through intention, would will a wholesome action and on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly realm.

mil3.3.11:3.3.verse: And those who followed him, on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly realm.

mil3.3.11:3.4.verse: So too, your majesty, willing and arranging are the distinguishing characteristics of intention.”

mil3.3.11:5.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Intention Question eleventh

mil3.3.12:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?”

mil3.3.12:1.2.verse: “Knowing, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?”

mil3.3.12:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a town guardian sitting in the middle of the crossroads of the town would see a man coming from the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, and the northern direction.

mil3.3.12:2.3.verse: In the same way, your majesty, a person knows with consciousness whatever form he sees with his eyes,

mil3.3.12:2.4.verse: he knows with consciousness whatever sound he hears with his ears,

mil3.3.12:2.5.verse: he knows with consciousness whatever odour he smells with his nose,

mil3.3.12:2.6.verse: he knows with consciousness whatever flavour he tastes with his tongue,

mil3.3.12:2.7.verse: he knows with consciousness whatever tangible he touches with his body, and he knows with consciousness whatever thought he knows with his mind.

mil3.3.12:2.8.verse: So too, your majesty, knowing is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?”

mil3.3.12:4.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Consciousness Question twelfth

mil3.3.13:0.3.verse: 13. Distinguishing Characteristic of Applied Thought Question

mil3.3.13:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought?”

mil3.3.13:1.2.verse: “Mental fixing, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought.”

mil3.3.13:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a carpenter fixes a superbly crafted piece of wood into a join,

mil3.3.13:2.3.verse: in the same way mental fixing is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought.”

mil3.3.13:4.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Applied Thought Question thirteenth

mil3.3.14:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of examination?”

mil3.3.14:1.2.verse: “Continuity, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of examination.”

mil3.3.14:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, a bronze bowl which has been struck resounds afterwards, and lingers on, applied thought is to be seen as striking,

mil3.3.14:2.3.verse: examination is to be seen as resounding.”

mil3.3.14:4.1.verse: Distinguishing Characteristic of Examination Question fourteenth

mil3.4.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible, having repeatedly analysed these mental states that are of the nature to arise together, to declare a difference between them, saying ‘this is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is intention, this is consciousness, this is applied thought, this is examination’?”

mil3.4.1:1.3.verse: “No, your majesty, it is not possible to do that.”

mil3.4.1:2.2.verse: “Just as if, your majesty, a king’s cook might prepare a soup or sauce and put in it curds, salt, ginger, cumin, hot pepper, and various other things, and the king might say ‘bring me a taste of curds, a taste of salt, a taste of ginger, a taste of cumin, a taste of hot pepper, or a taste of all the other things put in.’

mil3.4.1:2.3.verse: Is it possible, your majesty, having repeatedly analysed these tastes that are of the nature to arise together to bring forward an acidic flavour, a salty flavour, a bitter flavour, a sharp flavour, or a pungent flavour, or a sweet flavour?”

mil3.4.1:2.4.verse: “It is certainly not possible, venerable sir, to do that.”

mil3.4.1:2.5.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, it is not possible, having repeatedly analysed these mental states that are of the nature to arise together, to declare a difference between them, saying ‘this is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is intention, this is consciousness, this is applied thought, this is examination’?”

mil3.4.1:4.1.verse: Question on Analysing Contact, Etc. first

mil3.4.2:1.2.verse: “Is salt, your majesty, cognizable by the eye?”

mil3.4.2:1.3.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, it is cognizable by the eye.”

mil3.4.2:1.5.verse: “Is it then, venerable sir, cognizable by the tongue?”

mil3.4.2:1.6.verse: “Yes, your majesty, it is cognizable by the tongue.”

mil3.4.2:1.7.verse: “Then, venerable sir, is all salt cognizable by the tongue?”

mil3.4.2:1.8.verse: “Yes, your majesty, all salt is cognizable by the tongue.”

mil3.4.2:2.1.verse: “If, venerable sir, all salt is cognizable by the tongue, why then do oxen bring it by the cartload, shouldn’t just salt be brought?”

mil3.4.2:2.2.verse: “It is not possible to bring just salt, your majesty, since these things arise together with a diversity in their range, and as well, salt has heaviness.

mil3.4.2:2.3.verse: Is it possible to weigh salt on scales?”

mil3.4.2:2.5.verse: “It is not possible, your majesty, to weigh salt on scales. One weighs the heaviness on scales.”

mil3.4.3:0.3.verse: 3. Question on the Five Sense Bases Produced from Kamma

mil3.4.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, are these five sense bases produced from different kamma or from just one kamma?”

mil3.4.3:1.3.verse: “They are produced from different kamma, your majesty, not from just one kamma.”

mil3.4.3:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, if one were to sow different seeds in this field, would a diversity of fruits be produced from this diversity of seeds?”

mil3.4.3:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, these five sense bases are produced from different kamma, and not from just one kamma.”

mil3.4.3:4.1.verse: Question on the Five Sense Bases Produced from Kamma third

mil3.4.4:0.3.verse: 4. Question on the Workings of Different Kamma

mil3.4.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, why is it that not all people are the same? Some people are short-lived, others long-lived, some have much affliction and others little affliction, some are ugly and others beautiful, some have little power and others great power, some have little wealth and others great wealth, some come from an inferior clan and others from a superior clan, some are foolish and others are wise.”

mil3.4.4:2.2.verse: “Why then, your majesty, is it that not all trees are the same? Some are acidic, some are salty, some are bitter, some are pungent, some are astringent, and some are sweet?”

mil3.4.4:2.3.verse: “I think, venerable sir, that it is because of the difference in seeds.”

mil3.4.4:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, it is because of the difference in kamma that not all people are the same. Some people are short-lived, others long-lived, some have much affliction and others little affliction, some are ugly and others beautiful, some have little power and others great power, some have little wealth and others great wealth, some come from an inferior clan and others from a superior clan, some are foolish and others are wise.

mil3.4.4:2.5.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.4.4:2.6.verse: ‘Young man, beings are the owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma, born from their kamma, bound to their kamma, and protected by their kamma. Kamma divides beings into inferior and superior.’”

mil3.4.4:4.1.verse: Question on the Workings of Different Kamma fourth

mil3.4.5:0.3.verse: 5. Question on the Reason for Effort

mil3.4.5:1.3.verse: that, so that this suffering would cease and another suffering would not arise,

mil3.4.5:1.4.verse: that was the goal of your going forth.

mil3.4.5:1.5.verse: Is it just because of previous effort? Should not one make an effort at the current time?”

mil3.4.5:1.7.verse: “Effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.”

mil3.4.5:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you become thirsty, would you then have a well or a dam dug and say ‘I will drink water’?”

mil3.4.5:2.4.verse: “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.”

mil3.4.5:3.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you become hungry, would you then have a field ploughed, plant rice, and have the grain brought in, and say ‘I will eat rice’?”

mil3.4.5:3.4.verse: “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.”

mil3.4.5:4.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you are faced with a battle, would you then have a moat dug, a rampart, a gateway, and a watchtower constructed, and then train in the use of elephants, horses, chariots, bows and swords?”

mil3.4.5:4.4.verse: “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.

mil3.4.5:4.5.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.4.5:5.2.verse: what one knows is for one’s benefit;

mil3.4.5:5.3.verse: Not having thoughts like a wagon driver,

mil3.4.5:6.1.verse: As a wagon driver who has abandoned

mil3.4.5:6.4.verse: just broods with his axle broken,

mil3.4.5:7.3.verse: The lazy one coming face-to-face with death,

mil3.4.5:7.4.verse: just broods with his axle broken.’”

mil3.4.5:9.1.verse: Question on the Reason for Effort fifth

mil3.4.6:0.3.verse: 6. Question on the Nature of Heat in the Fires of Hell

mil3.4.6:1.3.verse: that the heat of hell has a far greater intensity than that of a normal fire, and that a small stone placed in a normal fire cooking all day would not be dissolved, whereas a stone the size of a gabled house placed in the fire of hell would be dissolved in a moment. I do not believe this assertion. And then you say that those various beings who have arisen in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved. That assertion too I do not believe.”

mil3.4.6:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, do those female sharks, crocodiles, turtles, pea-hens, and pigeons eat hard stones and gravel?”

mil3.4.6:2.4.verse: “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:2.6.verse: “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:2.9.verse: “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.”

mil3.4.6:2.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved.

mil3.4.6:2.11.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.4.6:2.12.verse: ‘One does not complete one’s time until there is an end to one’s evil kamma.’”

mil3.4.6:3.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, do female lions, tigers, panthers, and dogs eat hard bones and flesh?”

mil3.4.6:3.4.verse: “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:3.6.verse: “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:3.9.verse: “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.”

mil3.4.6:3.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved.”

mil3.4.6:4.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, do those delicate Bactrian Greek women, noble women, brahmin women, and householder women eat hard cakes and meat?”

mil3.4.6:4.4.verse: “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:4.6.verse: “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?”

mil3.4.6:4.9.verse: “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.”

mil3.4.6:4.10.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved.

mil3.4.6:4.11.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.4.6:4.12.verse: ‘One does not complete one’s time until there is an end to one’s evil kamma.’”

mil3.4.6:6.1.verse: Question on the Nature of Heat in the Fires of Hell sixth

mil3.4.7:0.3.verse: 7. Question on the Bearing Up of the Earth

mil3.4.7:1.3.verse: this great earth is established on water, water is established on air, and air is established on space. I do not believe this assertion.”

mil3.4.7:1.4.verse: The elder took some water in a water vessel and explained to King Milinda,

mil3.4.7:1.5.verse: “Just as, your majesty, this water is supported by the air, so too is that water supported by air.”

mil3.4.7:3.1.verse: Question on the Bearing Up of the Earth seventh

mil3.4.8:1.5.verse: “All those foolish ordinary people, your majesty, who delight in the internal and external sense bases, welcome them, remain clinging to them, and are carried away by that stream, are not free from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair, they are not free from suffering, I say.

mil3.4.8:1.6.verse: A well-taught noble disciple, your majesty, does not delight in the internal and external sense bases, nor welcome them, nor remain clinging to them. The one, not delighting in them, not welcoming them, not remaining clinging to them, is free from craving. From the cessation of craving, there is cessation of birth. From the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cease, and thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. In this way, your majesty, cessation is nibbāna.”

mil3.4.8:3.1.verse: Question on Cessation and Nibbāna eighth

mil3.4.9:0.3.verse: 9. Question on the Attaining of Nibbāna

mil3.4.9:1.3.verse: “Not everyone, your majesty, attains nibbāna. Whoever, practicing rightly, directly knows those things which should be directly known, completely comprehends those things that should be completely comprehended, abandons those things that should be abandoned, develops those things that should be developed, personally realises those things that should be personally realised, that one attains nibbāna.”

mil3.4.9:3.1.verse: Question on the Attaining of Nibbāna ninth

mil3.4.10:0.3.verse: 10. Question on Knowing the Happiness of Nibbāna

mil3.4.10:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who does not attain nibbāna know the happiness of nibbāna?”

mil3.4.10:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, one who does not attain nibbāna knows the happiness of nibbāna.”

mil3.4.10:1.4.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, not attaining it does one know the happiness of nibbāna?”

mil3.4.10:1.5.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, would those who haven’t had their hands and feet cut off know the suffering of having one’s hands and feet cut off?”

mil3.4.10:1.8.verse: “Having heard, venerable sir, the sounds of lamentation of those who have had their hands and feet cut off, they would know the suffering of having one’s hands and feet cut off.”

mil3.4.10:1.9.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, having heard the sound of one who has seen nibbāna, one knows the happiness of nibbāna.”

mil3.4.10:3.1.verse: Question on Knowing the Happiness of Nibbāna tenth

mil3.5.1:0.3.verse: 1. Question on the Existence or Non-existence of the Buddha

mil3.5.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, have you seen the Buddha?”

mil3.5.1:1.4.verse: “Then, have your teachers seen the Buddha?”

mil3.5.1:1.6.verse: “Therefore, Venerable Nāgasena, there is no Buddha.”

mil3.5.1:1.7.verse: “Well then, your majesty, have you seen the River Ūhā in the Himalayas?”

mil3.5.1:1.9.verse: “Then has your father seen the River Ūhā?”

mil3.5.1:1.11.verse: “Because of this, your majesty, there is no River Ūhā.”

mil3.5.1:1.12.verse: “There is, venerable sir. Even though the River Ūhā has not been seen by me nor by my father, there is a River Ūhā.”

mil3.5.1:1.13.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, even though the Blessed One has not been seen by me nor by my teachers, there is a Blessed One.”

mil3.5.1:3.1.verse: Question on the Existence or Non-existence of the Buddha first

mil3.5.2:0.3.verse: 2. Question on the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha

mil3.5.2:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, the Blessed One is unsurpassed.”

mil3.5.2:1.4.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, do you know the Buddha is unsurpassed if you haven’t seen him before?”

mil3.5.2:1.5.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, would those who have not seen the great ocean before know that this great ocean is huge, deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, such that as these five great rivers that flow into it constantly and continually, that is

mil3.5.2:1.6.verse: the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī, neither the depletion nor filling up of it is discerned?”

mil3.5.2:1.8.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, when I think of the great disciples who have attained final nibbāna, I know the Blessed One is unsurpassed.”

mil3.5.2:3.1.verse: Question on the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha second

mil3.5.3:0.3.verse: 3. Question on Knowing the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha

mil3.5.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to know that the Buddha is unsurpassed?”

mil3.5.3:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, it is possible to know that the Blessed One is unsurpassed.”

mil3.5.3:1.4.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to know that the Buddha is unsurpassed?”

mil3.5.3:1.5.verse: “In the past, your majesty, an elder named Tissa was a teacher of writing and many years have passed since he passed away. How is it that he is still known?”

mil3.5.3:1.7.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Blessed One, for the Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One.”

mil3.5.3:3.1.verse: Question on Knowing the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha third

mil3.5.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, have you seen the Dhamma?”

mil3.5.4:1.3.verse: “Throughout their lives, your majesty, disciples should proceed with the Buddha as their guide, the Buddha as the one showing the way.”

mil3.5.4:3.1.verse: Question on Seeing the Dhamma fourth

mil3.5.5:0.3.verse: 5. Question on Reconnecting and Not Transmigrating

mil3.5.5:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it so that one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects?”

mil3.5.5:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.”

mil3.5.5:1.4.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is it that one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects? Please give me an analogy.”

mil3.5.5:1.5.verse: “Just as, your majesty, if a person kindled one lamp from another would that lamp have transmigrated from the other lamp?”

mil3.5.5:1.7.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.”

mil3.5.5:2.2.verse: “Do you remember, your majesty, learning some verse from your teacher of verses?”

mil3.5.5:2.4.verse: “Then, your majesty, has that verse transmigrated from the teacher?”

mil3.5.5:2.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.”

mil3.5.5:4.1.verse: Question on Reconnecting and Not Transmigrating fifth

mil3.5.6:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is an experiencer to be found?”

mil3.5.6:1.4.verse: “According to ultimate reality, an experiencer is not to be found.”

mil3.5.7:0.3.verse: 7. Question on Transmigrating to Another Body

mil3.5.7:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is there any being at all that transmigrates from this body to another body?”

mil3.5.7:1.4.verse: “If, venerable sir, there is no transmigrating from this body to another body, is it not then that one would be freed from evil actions?”

mil3.5.7:1.5.verse: “Yes, your majesty, if it would not reconnect, then one would be freed from evil actions. But because, your majesty, it does reconnect, one therefore is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.5.7:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s mangos, would that man deserve punishment?”

mil3.5.7:2.3.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.”

mil3.5.7:2.4.verse: “But, your majesty, those mangos that were taken are not the same as those that were planted, why would he deserve punishment?”

mil3.5.7:2.5.verse: “Those mangos, venerable sir, arose dependent on the others, therefore he would deserve punishment.”

mil3.5.7:2.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.”

mil3.5.7:4.1.verse: Question on Transmigrating to Another Body seventh

mil3.5.8:0.3.verse: 8. Question on the Existence of the Fruits of Actions

mil3.5.8:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, for a wholesome or unwholesome action done by this name-and-form, where do those actions remain?”

mil3.5.8:1.3.verse: “Those actions would follow one, your majesty, like a shadow that never leaves.”

mil3.5.8:1.4.verse: “Is it then possible, venerable sir, to point to those actions and say they remain here or there?”

mil3.5.8:1.5.verse: “It is not possible, your majesty, to point to those actions and say they remain here or there.”

mil3.5.8:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, for those trees where the fruit has not yet arisen, is it possible to point to those fruits and say those fruits remain here or there?”

mil3.5.8:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, as long as the continuity of life is not cut off, it is not possible to point to those actions and say they remain here or there.”

mil3.5.8:4.1.verse: Question on the Existence of the Fruits of Actions eighth

mil3.5.9:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who re-arises know, ‘I will re-arise’?”

mil3.5.9:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, one who re-arises knows, ‘I will re-arise’.”

mil3.5.9:2.2.verse: “Just as, your majesty, when a householder farmer plants seeds in the ground and it rains well, does he know that grain will grow?”

mil3.5.9:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, one who re-arises knows, ‘I will re-arise’.”

mil3.5.10:0.3.verse: 10. Question on Pointing Out the Buddha

mil3.5.10:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, the Blessed One exists.”

mil3.5.10:1.4.verse: “Is it then possible, venerable sir, to point to the Buddha as being either here or there?”

mil3.5.10:1.5.verse: “The Blessed One has passed away, your majesty, in the element of nibbāna without residue remaining, so it is not possible to point to the Blessed One as being either here or there.”

mil3.5.10:2.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when the flame of a great burning mass of fire has been extinguished, is it possible to point to that flame and say it remains here or there?”

mil3.5.10:2.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, for that flame has ceased and gone beyond description.”

mil3.5.10:2.4.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, the Blessed One has passed away in the element of nibbāna without residue remaining, so it is not possible to point to the Blessed One as being either here or there. However, your majesty, it is possible to point out the Blessed One through the body of Dhamma,

mil3.5.10:2.5.verse: for this Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One.”

mil3.5.10:4.1.verse: Question on Pointing Out the Buddha tenth

mil3.6.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the body dear to recluses?”

mil3.6.1:1.3.verse: “No, your majesty, the body is not dear to recluses.”

mil3.6.1:1.4.verse: “Then, venerable sir, why do you cherish and treasure it?”

mil3.6.1:1.5.verse: “But, your majesty, when you have gone into battle have you been struck by arrows from time to time?”

mil3.6.1:1.7.verse: “And would the wound, your majesty, be anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage?”

mil3.6.1:1.8.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, the wound would be.”

mil3.6.1:1.9.verse: “And was the wound dear to you, your majesty, that it was anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage?”

mil3.6.1:1.10.verse: “No, venerable sir, the wound was not dear to me, it was for the healing of the flesh that it was anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage.”

mil3.6.1:1.11.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, the body is not dear to recluses, but recluses look after the body without attachment for the maintenance of the holy life.

mil3.6.1:1.12.verse: And moreover, your majesty, the body is said by the Blessed One to be like a wound, and therefore recluses look after the body as they would a wound without attachment.

mil3.6.1:1.13.verse: And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One:

mil3.6.1:2.2.verse: the great wound with nine openings

mil3.6.1:4.1.verse: Love of the Body Question first

mil3.6.2:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the Buddha all-knowing and all-seeing?”

mil3.6.2:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, the Buddha is all-knowing and all-seeing.”

mil3.6.2:1.4.verse: “Then why, Venerable Nāgasena, did he proclaim the training steps for his disciples gradually?”

mil3.6.2:1.5.verse: “But, your majesty, is there some doctor who knows all the medicines on this earth?”

mil3.6.2:1.7.verse: “And would that doctor, your majesty, administer medicine to a sick person at the time of being ill or when not ill?”

mil3.6.2:1.8.verse: “He would administer medicine to a sick person, venerable sir, at the time of being ill and not when not ill.”

mil3.6.2:1.9.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, the Blessed One who is all-knowing and all-seeing did not proclaim a training rule to his disciples at the wrong time, but when the time was right he proclaimed a training rule to his disciples, which is not to be transgressed all life long.”

mil3.6.3:0.3.verse: 3. Characteristics of a Great Person Question

mil3.6.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person and distinguished with the eighty secondary features, with radiant complexion, skin like gold, and a halo that extends for one fathom?”

mil3.6.3:2.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, were his mother and father endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person … and a halo that extends for one fathom?”

mil3.6.3:3.1.verse: “That being so, venerable sir, is it not then that the Buddha arose endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person … and a halo that extends for one fathom? But surely a child is like their mother or those on their mother’s side or like their father or those on their father’s side.”

mil3.6.3:3.3.verse: “But is there, your majesty, any lotus with a hundred leaves?”

mil3.6.3:3.5.verse: “And where then is the origin for that?”

mil3.6.3:3.6.verse: “It is born from mud and it thrives in water.”

mil3.6.3:3.7.verse: “Then, your majesty, is the lotus like the mud in colour, smell, or taste?”

mil3.6.3:3.9.verse: “Or is it like the water in smell or taste?”

mil3.6.3:3.11.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, the Buddha was endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person and distinguished with the eighty secondary features, with radiant complexion, skin like gold, and a halo that extends for one fathom, and his parents were not.”

mil3.6.3:5.1.verse: Characteristics of a Great Person Question third

mil3.6.4:0.3.verse: 4. Celibacy of the Blessed One Question

mil3.6.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha a Brahma-farer (celibate)?”

mil3.6.4:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, the Buddha was celibate.”

mil3.6.4:1.4.verse: “Well then, Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha a student of Brahmā?”

mil3.6.4:1.5.verse: “But, your majesty, do you have a chief elephant?”

mil3.6.4:1.7.verse: “And does this elephant, your majesty, roar the ‘Heron’s roar’ from time to time?”

mil3.6.4:1.9.verse: “Well then, your majesty, is this elephant a student of the heron?”

mil3.6.4:1.11.verse: “Was Brahmā, your majesty, one with intelligence or without?”

mil3.6.4:1.13.verse: “Well then, your majesty, Brahmā was a student of the Blessed One.”

mil3.6.4:3.1.verse: Celibacy of the Blessed One Question fourth

mil3.6.5:0.3.verse: 5. Higher Ordination of the Blessed One Question

mil3.6.5:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the higher ordination good?”

mil3.6.5:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, the higher ordination is good.”

mil3.6.5:1.4.verse: “But, Venerable Nāgasena, did the Buddha receive the higher ordination or not?”

mil3.6.5:1.5.verse: “The Blessed One, your majesty, reached the highest attainment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with omniscience. There was no giving of ordination to the Blessed One by others, in the way that the Blessed One proclaimed a training rule to his disciples, which is not to be transgressed all life long.”

mil3.6.5:3.1.verse: Higher Ordination of the Blessed One Question fifth

mil3.6.6:0.3.verse: 6. Question on Tears Being a Medicine or Not

mil3.6.6:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, those who weep on the death of a mother, and those who weep with affection for the Dhamma, for whom of these two weeping are the tears a medicine, and for whom are the tears not a medicine?”

mil3.6.6:1.3.verse: “The tears of one, your majesty, are hot and stained with lust, anger, and delusion, and the tears of the other are cool and unstained with rapture and joy.

mil3.6.6:1.4.verse: That which is cool, your majesty, is a medicine; that which is hot is not a medicine.”

mil3.6.6:3.1.verse: Question on Tears Being a Medicine or Not sixth

mil3.6.7:0.3.verse: 7. Question on the Difference Between Being With Attachment and Without Attachment

mil3.6.7:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the difference between being with attachment and being without attachment?”

mil3.6.7:1.3.verse: “One is sticky, your majesty, and the other is not sticky.”

mil3.6.7:1.4.verse: “What is the meaning, venerable sir, of ‘sticky’ and ‘not sticky’?”

mil3.6.7:1.5.verse: “One is desirable, your majesty, and the other is not desirable.”

mil3.6.7:1.6.verse: “As I see it, venerable sir, both the one with attachment and the one without attachment wish for beautiful hard and soft food, and neither wishes for something bad.”

mil3.6.7:1.7.verse: “One who is not without attachment, your majesty, eats their food and experiences both the taste and the attachment to the taste. But the one who is without attachment eats their food and experiences just the taste and not the attachment to the taste.”

mil3.6.7:3.1.verse: Question on the Difference Between Being With Attachment and Without Attachment seventh

mil3.6.8:0.3.verse: 8. Question on the Establishment of Wisdom

mil3.6.8:1.4.verse: “Then, Venerable Nāgasena, is there no wisdom?”

mil3.6.8:1.5.verse: “Where does the wind reside, your majesty?”

mil3.6.8:1.7.verse: “Then, your majesty, is there no wind?”

mil3.6.8:3.1.verse: Question on the Establishment of Wisdom eighth

mil3.6.9:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, as to which you said ‘cyclic existence’. What is this cyclic existence?”

mil3.6.9:1.3.verse: “Your majesty, that which is born here dies here, and having died here, it arises elsewhere. Then, having been born there it dies there, and having died there, it arises elsewhere. Thus, your majesty, this is cyclic existence.”

mil3.6.9:1.5.verse: “Just as, your majesty, some person may eat a ripe mango and plant the seed. Then, when it has grown up as a mature mango tree, it would give fruit. And then that man might eat a ripe mango from it and plant the seed and, when it has grown up as a mature mango tree, it too would give fruit. And thus, no end to these mango trees can be discerned.

mil3.6.9:1.6.verse: In the same way, your majesty, that which is born here dies here, and having died here, it arises elsewhere. Then, having been born there it dies there, and having died there, it arises elsewhere. Thus, your majesty, this is cyclic existence.”

mil3.6.10:0.3.verse: 10. Question on Remembrance of What was Done Long Ago

mil3.6.10:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, how does one remember what was done long ago in the past?”

mil3.6.10:1.4.verse: “Is it not, Venerable Nāgasena, that one remembers with one’s mind and not with mindfulness?”

mil3.6.10:1.5.verse: “Do you not know personally, your majesty, about some task you have done and have forgotten?”

mil3.6.10:1.7.verse: “Then were you, your majesty, on that occasion without a mind?”

mil3.6.10:1.8.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, on that occasion there was no mindfulness.”

mil3.6.10:1.9.verse: “So, why do you say, your majesty, that

mil3.6.10:1.10.verse: one remembers with one’s mind and not with mindfulness?”

mil3.6.10:3.1.verse: Question on Remembrance of What was Done Long Ago tenth

mil3.6.11:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, does all mindfulness arise through knowing directly or does it come with outside help?”

mil3.6.11:1.3.verse: “By knowing directly, your majesty, and with outside help.”

mil3.6.11:1.4.verse: “If thus, Venerable Nāgasena, all mindfulness is from directly knowing, there is none with outside help.”

mil3.6.11:1.5.verse: “If there were no mindfulness with outside help, your majesty, then artisans would have no need for practice, or craftsmanship, or schooling, and teachers would be useless, but since there is mindfulness with outside help, the opposite is true.”

mil3.7.1:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, in how many ways does mindfulness arise?”

mil3.7.1:1.3.verse: “Your majesty, mindfulness arises in seventeen ways.”

mil3.7.1:1.5.verse: “Mindfulness arises, your majesty, through knowing directly, with outside help, from consciousness of a substantiality, from consciousness of welfare, from consciousness of misfortune, from a common sign, from an uncommon sign, from understanding due to speech, from a distinguishing characteristic, from remembering, from reckoning, from calculation, from bearing in mind, from mental development, from recording in books, from association of ideas, and from experience.

mil3.7.1:2.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise through knowing directly?

mil3.7.1:2.2.verse: Just as, your majesty, Venerable Ānanda or the female lay follower Khujjuttarā or those others who remember past births remember a past birth, thus does mindfulness arise through knowing directly.

mil3.7.1:3.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise with outside help?

mil3.7.1:3.2.verse: If others urge one who is naturally muddled in mindfulness so that he remembers, thus does mindfulness arise with outside help.

mil3.7.1:4.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from consciousness of a substantiality?

mil3.7.1:4.2.verse: When there is a consecration into sovereignty or the attainment of the fruit of stream entry, thus does mindfulness arise from consciousness of a substantiality.

mil3.7.1:5.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from consciousness of welfare?

mil3.7.1:5.2.verse: One remembers when one was happy, ‘There was happiness because of that.’ Thus, does mindfulness arise from consciousness of welfare.

mil3.7.1:6.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from consciousness of misfortune?

mil3.7.1:6.2.verse: One remembers when one was suffering, ‘There was suffering because of that.’ Thus, does mindfulness arise from consciousness of misfortune.

mil3.7.1:7.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from a common sign?

mil3.7.1:7.2.verse: Having seen a person similar to oneself one remembers his mother, father, brother, or sister, and having seen a camel, an ox, or a donkey, one remembers a camel, an ox, or a donkey. Thus, does mindfulness arise from a common sign.

mil3.7.1:8.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from an uncommon sign?

mil3.7.1:8.2.verse: When one remembers that such is the colour of a certain thing, such the sound, such the smell, such the taste, such the touch, thus does mindfulness arise from an uncommon sign.

mil3.7.1:9.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from understanding due to speech?

mil3.7.1:9.2.verse: If others remind one who is naturally muddled in mindfulness so that he remembers, thus does mindfulness arise from understanding due to speech.

mil3.7.1:10.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from a distinguishing characteristic?

mil3.7.1:10.2.verse: One who knows an ox based on a conventional factor, remembers it by its distinguishing characteristic. Thus, does mindfulness arise from a distinguishing characteristic.

mil3.7.1:11.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from remembering?

mil3.7.1:11.2.verse: If one causes someone who is usually muddled in mindfulness to remember by repeatedly saying, ‘Remember, sir! Remember, sir!’ thus does mindfulness arise from remembering.

mil3.7.1:12.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from reckoning?

mil3.7.1:12.2.verse: From being trained in writing, one knows, ‘This letter is to be made immediately after that letter.’ Thus, does mindfulness arise from reckoning.

mil3.7.1:13.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from calculation?

mil3.7.1:13.2.verse: From being trained in calculation, accountants calculate even very large sums. Thus, does mindfulness arise from calculation.

mil3.7.1:14.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from bearing in mind?

mil3.7.1:14.2.verse: From being trained in bearing in mind, those who bear in mind can remember even a large amount. Thus, does mindfulness arise from from bearing in mind.

mil3.7.1:15.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from mental development?

mil3.7.1:15.2.verse: Here, a bhikkhu recalls his various past lives, that is,

mil3.7.1:15.4.verse: such that he remembers them with all their aspects and features. Thus, does mindfulness arise from mental development.

mil3.7.1:16.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from recording in books?

mil3.7.1:16.2.verse: A king’s minister when not remembering an administrative rule might have a book brought to him, and then would remember by means of that book. Thus, does mindfulness arise from from recording in books.

mil3.7.1:17.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from association of ideas?

mil3.7.1:17.2.verse: When one remembers after seeing goods laid aside, thus does mindfulness arise from association of ideas.

mil3.7.1:18.1.verse: How does mindfulness arise from experience?

mil3.7.1:18.2.verse: From what was seen one remembers material form, from what was heard one remembers sound, from what was smelled one remembers odour, from what was tasted one remembers flavour, from what was touched one remembers tangibles, from what was cognised one remembers thought. Thus, does mindfulness arise from experience.

mil3.7.1:18.3.verse: In these seventeen ways, your majesty, mindfulness arises.”

mil3.7.2:0.3.verse: 2. Question on Obtaining Mindfulness on a Quality of the Buddha

mil3.7.2:1.3.verse: ‘One could do evil for a hundred years, but at the time of death might obtain a single mindful moment on a quality of the Buddha, and thus arise in the realm of the devas,’ I don’t believe this. And then you said, ‘One might arise in a hell realm by killing one person,’ this too I don’t believe.”

mil3.7.2:2.1.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, could even a small stone float on the water without a boat?”

mil3.7.2:2.3.verse: “But, your majesty, could even a load of a hundred stones loaded onto a boat float on the water?”

mil3.7.2:2.5.verse: “Your majesty, skilled deeds should be considered as like a boat.”

mil3.7.2:4.1.verse: Question on Obtaining Mindfulness on a Quality of the Buddha second

mil3.7.3:0.3.verse: 3. Question on Striving for the Abandonment of Suffering

mil3.7.3:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, are you striving for the abandonment of past suffering?”

mil3.7.3:1.4.verse: “Then, venerable sir, are you striving for the abandonment of future suffering?”

mil3.7.3:1.6.verse: “Then, venerable sir, are you striving for the abandonment of present suffering?”

mil3.7.3:1.8.verse: “If you are not striving for the abandonment of past suffering, nor for the abandonment of future suffering, nor for the abandonment of present suffering, then what are you striving for?”

mil3.7.3:1.10.verse: “Your majesty, I am striving so that this suffering would cease and that no other suffering would arise.”

mil3.7.3:2.1.verse: “Is there now, Venerable Nāgasena, future suffering for you?”

mil3.7.3:2.3.verse: “Indeed, Venerable Nāgasena, you are very wise that you strive for abandoning future suffering that is not existing.”

mil3.7.3:2.4.verse: “Are there, your majesty, any opposing kings, that are adversaries, that have risen up against you?”

mil3.7.3:2.6.verse: “Is it then, your majesty, that you had a moat dug, a rampart put up, and a gateway and watchtower constructed?”

mil3.7.3:2.7.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, these were prepared previously.”

mil3.7.3:2.8.verse: “Is it then, your majesty, that you would train in elephant warfare, in horse warfare, in chariot warfare, in archery, and in swordsmanship?”

mil3.7.3:2.9.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, I had trained in these previously.”

mil3.7.3:2.11.verse: “In order to prevent future perils, venerable sir.”

mil3.7.3:2.12.verse: “Is there a future peril now, your majesty?”

mil3.7.3:2.14.verse: “Indeed, your majesty, you are very wise that you would prepare for the prevention of a future peril that is not existing.”

mil3.7.3:3.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you might become thirsty is it then that you would have a well, a pond, or a reservoir dug, thinking, ‘I will drink water’?”

mil3.7.3:3.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, this has been arranged for previously.”

mil3.7.3:3.5.verse: “It has been arranged, venerable sir, in order to prevent future thirst.”

mil3.7.3:3.6.verse: “Is there a future thirst now, your majesty?”

mil3.7.3:3.8.verse: “Indeed, your majesty, you are very wise that you would prepare for the prevention of a future thirst that is not existing.”

mil3.7.3:4.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, when you might become hungry is it then that you would have a field ploughed, and rice sowed, thinking, ‘I will eat food’?”

mil3.7.3:4.3.verse: “Certainly not, venerable sir, this has been arranged for previously.”

mil3.7.3:4.5.verse: “In order, venerable sir, to prevent future hunger.”

mil3.7.3:4.6.verse: “Is there a future hunger now, your majesty?”

mil3.7.3:4.8.verse: “Indeed, your majesty, you are very wise that you would prepare for the prevention of a future hunger that is not existing.”

mil3.7.3:6.1.verse: Question on Striving for the Abandonment of Suffering third

mil3.7.4:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, how far away is it from here to the Brahma world?”

mil3.7.4:1.3.verse: “So far, your majesty, that if a rock the size of a peaked-roof building had fallen from there, and falling at the speed of eighty-four thousand yojanas per day, it would take four months to land on the earth.”

mil3.7.4:2.2.verse: ‘Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his stretched arm,

mil3.7.4:2.3.verse: in the same way a bhikkhu with psychic powers who has attained mastery over his mind could disappear from Jambudīpa and appear in the Brahma world.’ This I do not believe that one might go so quickly over so many hundreds of yojanas.”

mil3.7.4:3.2.verse: “Where then, your majesty, is the place of your birth?”

mil3.7.4:3.3.verse: “There is, venerable sir, an island called Alasanda, there I was born.”

mil3.7.4:3.4.verse: “How far away, your majesty, is Alasanda from here?”

mil3.7.4:3.6.verse: “Do you not know, your majesty, of some business that you have completed there and now remember?”

mil3.7.4:3.8.verse: “Indeed, so quickly you have gone about two hundred yojanas, your majesty!”

mil3.7.4:5.1.verse: Question on the Brahma World fourth

mil3.7.5:0.3.verse: 5. Question on Arising in Two Places Taking the Same Time

mil3.7.5:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, for one who having passed away is reborn in the Brahma world, and for one who having passed away is reborn in Kashmir, which one takes the longer time, and which the shorter?”

mil3.7.5:2.2.verse: “Where then, your majesty, is your town of birth?”

mil3.7.5:2.3.verse: “There is a place called Kalasigāma, there I was born.”

mil3.7.5:2.4.verse: “How far away, your majesty, is Kalasigāma from here?”

mil3.7.5:2.6.verse: “How far away, your majesty, is Kashmir from here?”

mil3.7.5:2.8.verse: “Go on then, your majesty, think about Kalasigāma.”

mil3.7.5:2.9.verse: “I have thought about it, venerable sir.”

mil3.7.5:2.10.verse: “Go on then, your majesty, think about Kashmir.”

mil3.7.5:2.11.verse: “I have thought about it, venerable sir.”

mil3.7.5:2.12.verse: “Which thinking took a long time, your majesty, and which a short time?”

mil3.7.5:2.14.verse: “Just so, your majesty, for one who having passed away is reborn in the Brahma world, and for one who having passed away is reborn in Kashmir, they happen in the same time.”

mil3.7.5:3.2.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, if two birds fly in the sky and one sits in a high tree, and the other in a low tree, if these happen at the same time, the shadow of which one would settle on the ground first, and which one later?”

mil3.7.5:3.4.verse: “Just so, your majesty, for one who having passed away is reborn in the Brahma world, and for one who having passed away is reborn in Kashmir, they happen in the same time.”

mil3.7.5:5.1.verse: Question on Arising in Two Places Taking the Same Time fifth

mil3.7.6:0.3.verse: 6. Question on the Factors for Awakening

mil3.7.6:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, how many factors for awakening are there?”

mil3.7.6:1.3.verse: “There are seven factors for awakening, your majesty.”

mil3.7.6:1.4.verse: “By how many of these seven factors for awakening, venerable sir, does one awaken?”

mil3.7.6:1.5.verse: “One awakens by one of these, your majesty, the awakening factor of discrimination of states.”

mil3.7.6:1.6.verse: “Then, venerable sir, why is it that one speaks of seven factors?”

mil3.7.6:1.7.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, if a sword is placed in its sheath and not grasped in the hand is it able to cut what is to be cut?”

mil3.7.6:1.9.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, without the investigation of states awakening factor, one cannot awaken by the other six factors.”

mil3.7.6:3.1.verse: Question on the Factors for Awakening sixth

mil3.7.7:0.3.verse: 7. Question on the Increase or Decrease of Merit and Demerit

mil3.7.7:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, which of the two is greater, merit or demerit?”

mil3.7.7:1.3.verse: “Merit is greater, your majesty, demerit is small.”

mil3.7.7:1.5.verse: “For one doing demerit, your majesty, there is the regret, ‘I have committed an evil deed’, and therefore demerit does not increase.

mil3.7.7:1.6.verse: But for one doing merit, your majesty, there is no regret; and for one without regret gladness arises; for one who is glad joy arises; for one with a joyous mind the body calms down; one with a calmed body experiences happiness; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; and one who is concentrated knows things as they really are. For this reason, merit increases.

mil3.7.7:1.7.verse: Even if a man with his hands and feet cut off gives just a handful of lotuses to the Blessed One, he will not go to a hell realm for ninety-one aeons.

mil3.7.7:1.8.verse: For this reason, your majesty, merit is greater and demerit is small.”

mil3.7.7:3.1.verse: Question on the Increase or Decrease of Merit and Demerit seventh

mil3.7.8:0.3.verse: 8. Question on Doing Evil Knowingly or Unknowingly

mil3.7.8:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, for whom is the greater demerit, one who knowingly does evil, or one who does evil unknowingly?”

mil3.7.8:1.3.verse: The elder replied: “Indeed, your majesty, for him who does evil unknowingly is the greater demerit.”

mil3.7.8:1.4.verse: “In that case, Venerable Nāgasena, that one who is our prince or king’s chief minister who unknowingly does evil, we should doubly punish him?”

mil3.7.8:1.5.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, who would get burned more, one who knowingly picks up a hot iron ball, ablaze and glowing, or one who unknowingly picks it up?”

mil3.7.8:1.6.verse: “Indeed, venerable sir, he who unknowingly picks it up would get burned more.”

mil3.7.8:1.7.verse: “Indeed, your majesty, in the same way the greater demerit is for him who does evil unknowingly.”

mil3.7.8:3.1.verse: Question on Doing Evil Knowingly or Unknowingly eighth

mil3.7.9:0.3.verse: 9. Question on Travelling to Uttarakuru and Other Places

mil3.7.9:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is there anybody who, with this mortal body, could go to Uttarakuru or to the Brahma world or to another continent?”

mil3.7.9:1.3.verse: “There is, your majesty, someone who could, with this body composed of the four great elements, go to Uttarakuru or to the Brahma world or to another continent.”

mil3.7.9:2.1.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, could one, with this body composed of the four great elements, go to Uttarakuru or to the Brahma world or to another continent?”

mil3.7.9:2.2.verse: “Your majesty, have you had the direct experience of jumping a hand span or a cubit on this earth?”

mil3.7.9:2.3.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, I have had that direct experience, in fact I jump even eight cubits.”

mil3.7.9:2.4.verse: “How, your majesty, do you jump even eight cubits?”

mil3.7.9:2.5.verse: “Venerable sir, I generate the thought ‘I will land here,’ and with that thought my body is buoyant.”

mil3.7.9:2.6.verse: “In the same way, your majesty, a bhikkhu with psychic power and who has achieved mastery over his own mind, having entrusted his body to his mind, travels in the sky by means of this mind mastery.”

mil3.7.9:4.1.verse: Question on Travelling to Uttarakuru and Other Places ninth

mil3.7.10:1.3.verse: ‘There are long bones extending one hundred yojanas.’ Since there is no tree extending that far, how then could there be long bones extending one hundred yojanas?”

mil3.7.10:2.1.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, have you heard that in the great ocean there are fish extending for five hundred yojanas?”

mil3.7.10:2.2.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, I have heard so.”

mil3.7.10:2.3.verse: “Is it not, your majesty, that the long bones of such a fish would extend for a hundred yojanas?”

mil3.7.11:0.3.verse: 11. Question on the Cessation of In and Out Breathing

mil3.7.11:1.3.verse: ‘It is possible to cease in and out breathing’?”

mil3.7.11:1.4.verse: “Yes, your majesty, it is possible to cease in and out breathing.”

mil3.7.11:1.5.verse: “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to cease in and out breathing?”

mil3.7.11:1.6.verse: “What do you think, your majesty, have you heard before of someone snoring?”

mil3.7.11:1.7.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, I have heard of it.”

mil3.7.11:1.8.verse: “Would that sound be stopped, your majesty, if the body were bent?”

mil3.7.11:1.10.verse: “Since, your majesty, that sound would be stopped if the body were bent by someone undeveloped in body, virtue, mind, and wisdom, why could not the breathing in and the breathing out be ceased for someone developed in body, virtue, mind, and wisdom, and who has attained the fourth jhāna?”

mil3.7.11:3.1.verse: Question on the Cessation of In and Out Breathing eleventh

mil3.7.12:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, it is called ‘the sea, the sea’. Why is the water called the sea?”

mil3.7.12:1.4.verse: “Just as much as there is water, your majesty, so much there is salt.

mil3.7.12:1.5.verse: Just as much as there is salt, so much there is water.

mil3.7.13:0.3.verse: 13. Question on the One Taste of the Sea

mil3.7.13:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, why does the sea have just one taste, the taste of salt?”

mil3.7.13:1.3.verse: “The sea has just one taste, the taste of salt, your majesty, because it has been around a long time.”

mil3.7.13:3.1.verse: Question on the One Taste of the Sea thirteenth

mil3.7.14:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to cut through the subtlest of all things?”

mil3.7.14:1.3.verse: “Yes, your majesty, it is possible to cut through the subtlest of all things.”

mil3.7.14:1.4.verse: “Then what, venerable sir, is the subtlest of all things?”

mil3.7.14:1.5.verse: “The Dhamma, your majesty, is the subtlest of all things. But not all qualities are subtle, your majesty, subtle or coarse is a designation for a quality.

mil3.7.14:1.6.verse: Whatever is to be cut through, all that is cut through by wisdom. There is nothing else other than wisdom for cutting through.”

mil3.7.15:0.3.verse: 15. Question on the Distinction of Consciousness

mil3.7.15:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, when it is said ‘consciousness’ or ‘wisdom’ or ‘the life principle in a being’, are these things distinct from each other in actuality, or only in name?”

mil3.7.15:1.3.verse: “Discrimination, your majesty, is a distinguishing characteristic of consciousness, discernment is a distinguishing characteristic of wisdom, and the life principle in a being cannot be found.”

mil3.7.15:1.4.verse: “If the life principle in a being cannot be found, then how is it that one sees a form with the eyes, hears a sound with the ears, smells an odour with the nose, tastes a flavour with the tongue, touches a tangible with the body, and knows a thought with the mind?”

mil3.7.15:1.6.verse: “If the life principle sees form with the eyes, … and knows thought with the mind, then when the doors of the eyes are destroyed would not the life principle see form more clearly out there before it in the great space? When the ears, the nose, the tongue and the body are all destroyed, would it not hear a sound, smell an odour, taste a flavour, touch a tangible more clearly in the great space?”

mil3.7.15:1.8.verse: “Well then, your majesty, the life principle in a being cannot be found.”

mil3.7.15:3.1.verse: Question on the Distinction of Consciousness fifteenth

mil3.7.16:0.3.verse: 16. The Question on the Difficulty of Distinguishing Formless Dhammas

mil3.7.16:1.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, did the Blessed One accomplish something difficult?”

mil3.7.16:1.4.verse: “The Blessed One accomplished something difficult, your majesty.”

mil3.7.16:1.5.verse: “But what difficult thing, Venerable Nāgasena, did the Blessed One accomplish?”

mil3.7.16:1.6.verse: “The Blessed One accomplished something difficult, your majesty, in that he explained the distinction of these formless mental dhammas that occur with a single object, declaring: ‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.’”

mil3.7.16:2.2.verse: “Suppose, your majesty, some man were to go out onto the great ocean in a boat, take up water in the hollow of his hand, taste it with his tongue—would that man be able to know: ‘This is water from the Ganges, this is water from the Yamunā, this is water from the Aciravatī, this is water from the Sarabhū, this is water from the Mahī’?”

mil3.7.16:2.3.verse: “It would be difficult to know, venerable sir.”

mil3.7.16:2.4.verse: “More difficult than that, your majesty, is what the Blessed One accomplished in explaining the distinction of these formless phenomena that occur with a single object, declaring: ‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.’”

mil3.7.16:2.5.verse: “Very good, venerable sir,” said the king in approval.

mil3.7.16:3.1.verse: The Question on the Difficulty of Distinguishing Formless Dhammas sixteenth

mil3.7.16:4.1.verse: Analysis of Formless Dhammas Chapter seventh

mil3.8:0.2.verse: 8. The Asking and Answering of Milinda’s Questions

mil3.8:1.2.verse: “Do you know, your majesty, what time it is now?”

mil3.8:1.3.verse: “Yes, venerable sir, I know. ‘The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch is proceeding, the torches are lit, and the four banners have been commanded to go from the treasury bearing royal gifts.’”

mil3.8:2.1.verse: The Bactrian Greeks said this: “You are clever, your majesty, the elder is wise.”

mil3.8:2.2.verse: “Yes, friends, the elder is wise. If there were a teacher such as he and a pupil such as myself, before long a wise person would understand the Dhamma.”

mil3.8:2.3.verse: Pleased with his answering of questions, the king covered the elder Nāgasena with a blanket worth a hundred thousand (kahāpaṇas) saying: “Venerable Nāgasena, from today I establish for you a meal for eight hundred, and I invite you with whatever is allowable in the inner palace.”

mil3.8:2.5.verse: “I know, Venerable Nāgasena, that you are living, but still protect yourself and protect me too.”

mil3.8:2.6.verse: “How do you protect yourself? ‘Nāgasena pleased King Milinda but received nothing’—lest such reproach should come, thus protect yourself.

mil3.8:2.7.verse: How should you protect me? ‘King Milinda was pleased but showed no sign of his pleasure’—lest such reproach should come, thus protect me.”

mil3.8:2.9.verse: “Just as, venerable sir, a lion, the king of beasts, even when placed in a golden cage, remains outward-facing;

mil3.8:2.10.verse: even so, venerable sir, though I dwell in a house, I remain outward-facing.

mil3.8:2.11.verse: If I, venerable sir, were to go forth from the household life into homelessness, I would not live long, so many are my enemies.”

mil3.8:3.1.verse: Then the Venerable Nāgasena, having answered King Milinda’s question, rose from his seat and went to the monastery.

mil3.8:3.2.verse: Not long after the Venerable Nāgasena had departed, this occurred to King Milinda:

mil3.8:3.3.verse: “What did I ask? What did the Venerable Nāgasena answer?”

mil3.8:3.4.verse: Then this occurred to King Milinda:

mil3.8:3.5.verse: “Everything was well asked by me, everything was well answered by the Venerable Nāgasena.”

mil3.8:3.6.verse: And to the Venerable Nāgasena, having reached the monastery, this occurred:

mil3.8:3.7.verse: “What did King Milinda ask? What did I answer?”

mil3.8:3.8.verse: Then this occurred to the Venerable Nāgasena:

mil3.8:3.9.verse: “Everything was well asked by King Milinda, everything was well answered by me.”

mil3.8:4.1.verse: Then the Venerable Nāgasena, when that night had passed, in the morning having dressed and taking his bowl and robe, approached King Milinda’s dwelling, and then sat down on the seat prepared.

mil3.8:4.2.verse: Then King Milinda, paid respects to the Venerable Nāgasena, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, King Milinda said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:

mil3.8:5.1.verse: “May the venerable one not think thus: ‘Nāgasena was asked a question by me,’ and with that very joy pass the rest of that night—it should not be seen thus by you.

mil3.8:5.2.verse: For me, venerable sir, during the rest of that night, this occurred:

mil3.8:5.3.verse: ‘What did I ask? What was answered by the venerable one?’—‘Everything was well asked by me, everything was well answered by the venerable one.’”

mil3.8:6.2.verse: “May it not occur to your majesty thus: ‘King Milinda’s question was answered by me,’ and with that very joy pass the rest of that night—it should not be seen thus by you.

mil3.8:6.3.verse: For me, your majesty, during the rest of that night, this occurred:

mil3.8:6.4.verse: ‘What was asked by King Milinda? What did I answer?’—‘Everything was well asked by King Milinda, everything was well answered by me.’” Thus these great beings mutually rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken words.

mil3.8:7.1.verse: The Asking and Answering of Milinda’s Questions completed

mil4.1:0.4.verse: 1. The Eight Places for Discussion to be Avoided

mil4.1:1.3.verse: Milinda, to break through to knowledge,

mil4.1:2.3.verse: Having become one of penetrating intellect,

mil4.1:2.4.verse: he too became a master of the Tipiṭaka.

mil4.1:3.2.verse: having gone into seclusion in the night watch;

mil4.1:3.4.verse: hard to unravel, with their refutations.

mil4.1:4.4.verse: in the dispensation of the King of Dhamma.

mil4.1:5.1.verse: Not understanding the meaning of these,

mil4.1:5.2.verse: the dilemmas spoken about by the Conqueror;

mil4.1:5.4.verse: there will be argument about them.

mil4.1:6.1.verse: Come, having confidence in the speaker,

mil4.1:6.2.verse: I shall have the dilemmas cut through;

mil4.1:6.3.verse: By the path pointed out by him,

mil4.1:6.4.verse: people will explain accordingly in the future.”

mil4.1:7.1.verse: Then King Milinda, when the night had brightened, and dawn had arisen, having washed his head, raising his joined palms to his head, having recollected the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present, undertook eight observance practices: “From now for the next seven days, having undertaken the eight qualities, asceticism is to be practiced by me. Having practiced asceticism, and having pleased the teacher, I shall ask about the dilemmas.”

mil4.1:7.2.verse: Then King Milinda, removed his ordinary pair of garments, took off his ornaments, dressed in ochre robes, wrapped a head covering on his shaved-head, and having entered the state of a sage, undertook the eight qualities: “During these seven days, royal affairs should not be administered by me, thoughts connected with lust should not be aroused, thoughts connected with anger should not be aroused, thoughts connected with delusion should not be aroused, conduct towards slaves, workers, and servants should be with humility, bodily and verbal conduct should be guarded, the six sense bases should be completely guarded, the mind should be directed to the development of loving-kindness.”

mil4.1:7.3.verse: Having undertaken these eight qualities, and having established his mind in these very eight qualities, not going outside for seven days, and on the eighth day, when the night had brightened, having taken the morning meal early, with downcast eyes, measured in speech, with well-composed deportment and undistracted mind, joyful, uplifted, and serene, he approached the elder Nāgasena and bowed his head to the elder’s feet. Standing to one side, he said this:

mil4.1:8.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, I have a certain matter to discuss with you and I wish it to be in private, in an empty place, in seclusion, in the forest, endowed with the eight qualities, fitting for an ascetic.

mil4.1:8.2.verse: There, that question should be asked. Nothing there should be kept hidden or secret from me. I am worthy to hear secrets when we have gone into proper discussion. That matter should also be examined with similes. Like what? Just as, Venerable Nāgasena, the great earth is worthy of a deposit (of treasure) when a deposit is made.

mil4.1:8.3.verse: Even so, Venerable Nāgasena, I am worthy to hear secrets when we have gone into proper discussion.”

mil4.1:9.1.verse: Having entered a secluded place with his teacher, he said this:

mil4.1:9.2.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, here a person desiring to take counsel should avoid eight places. A wise person does not discuss matters in those places; for even if discussed, the matter comes to naught and does not succeed.

mil4.1:9.4.verse: Uneven ground should be avoided, a dangerous place should be avoided, an excessively windy place should be avoided, a concealed place should be avoided, a deva-shrine should be avoided, a road should be avoided, a battlefield should be avoided, a water-crossing should be avoided.

mil4.1:9.5.verse: These eight places should be avoided.”

mil4.1:10.2.verse: “What is the fault in uneven ground, in a dangerous place, in excessive wind, in a concealed place, in a deva-shrine, on a road, in a battlefield, at a water-crossing?”

mil4.1:10.3.verse: “On uneven ground, Venerable Nāgasena, a matter discussed scatters, breaks apart, flows away, does not succeed; in a dangerous place the mind becomes frightened; being frightened, one does not properly consider the matter; in excessive wind the sound is unclear; in a concealed place eavesdroppers stand by; in a deva-shrine a matter discussed becomes grave; on a road a matter discussed becomes trivial; in a battlefield it becomes fickle; at a water-crossing it becomes public.

mil4.1:11.1.verse: ‘Uneven ground, a dangerous place, excessive wind,

mil4.1:11.2.verse: A concealed place, a shrine to devas;

mil4.1:11.3.verse: A road, a battlefield, and a water-crossing.

mil4.1:12.1.verse: The Eight Places for Discussion to be Avoided

mil4.2:0.4.verse: 2. The Eight Persons Who Destroy Counsel

mil4.2:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, these eight persons, when taking counsel, ruin the matter discussed.

mil4.2:1.3.verse: One who behaves with lust, one who behaves with anger, one who behaves with delusion, one who behaves with conceit, a greedy person, a lazy person, a single-minded person, and a fool.

mil4.2:1.4.verse: These eight persons ruin the matter discussed.”

mil4.2:2.3.verse: “One behaving with lust, Venerable Nāgasena, ruins the matter discussed through the power of lust; one behaving with anger ruins the matter discussed through the power of anger; one behaving with delusion ruins the matter discussed through the power of delusion; one behaving with conceit ruins the matter discussed through the power of conceit; a greedy person ruins the matter discussed through the power of greed; a lazy person ruins the matter discussed through laziness; a single-minded person ruins the matter discussed through single-mindedness; a fool ruins the matter discussed through foolishness.

mil4.2:3.1.verse: ‘One full of lust, one angry, and one deluded,

mil4.2:3.2.verse: One conceited, greedy, and likewise lazy;

mil4.2:3.4.verse: These are destroyers of the matter.’”

mil4.2:4.1.verse: The Eight Persons Who Destroy Counsel

mil4.3:0.4.verse: 3. Nine Kinds of People Who Can’t Keep Secrets

mil4.3:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, there are these nine types of people who disclose and do not keep secret counsel.

mil4.3:1.3.verse: A person characterized by lust, a person characterized by anger, a person characterized by delusion, a fearful person, a person attached to sensual things, a woman, a drunkard, a eunuch, and a child.”

mil4.3:2.3.verse: “A person characterized by lust, Venerable Nāgasena, discloses and does not keep secret counsel, on account of lust; a person characterized by anger, venerable sir, discloses and does not keep secret counsel on account of anger; a deluded person discloses and does not keep secret counsel on account of delusion; a fearful person discloses and does not keep secret counsel on account of fear; a person attached to sensual things discloses and does not keep secret counsel for the sake of material pleasures; a woman discloses and does not keep secret counsel due to changeableness; a drunkard discloses and does not keep secret counsel because of addiction to drink; a eunuch discloses and does not keep secret counsel due to uncertainty; and a child discloses and does not keep secret counsel due to fickleness.

mil4.3:3.1.verse: ‘An infatuated person, a malicious one, a deluded one,

mil4.3:3.3.verse: A woman, a drunkard, a eunuch,

mil4.3:4.1.verse: These nine types of people in the world,

mil4.3:4.3.verse: From these counsel that is hidden

mil4.3:5.1.verse: Nine Kinds of People Who Can’t Keep Secrets

mil4.4:0.4.verse: 4. The Eight Causes for the Attainment of Wisdom

mil4.4:1.1.verse: “Venerable Nāgasena, through eight causes wisdom matures and reaches full development.

mil4.4:1.3.verse: Through the maturation of age, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through the maturation of fame, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through questioning, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through association with the learned, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through wise attention, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through discussion, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through association with friends, wisdom matures and reaches full development; through dwelling in a suitable location, wisdom matures and reaches full development.

mil4.4:2.2.verse: Through dwelling with the learned, through wise attention;

mil4.4:2.4.verse: And through dwelling in a suitable place.

mil4.4:3.2.verse: Are causes for the clarification of wisdom;

mil4.4:3.3.verse: For those in whom these are present,

mil4.4:4.1.verse: The Eight Causes for the Attainment of Wisdom
