snp3.9:37.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:38.2.verse: the end of suffering in this life;

snp3.9:38.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:39.2.verse: expert in the path and what is not the path;

snp3.9:39.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:40.3.verse: a migrant with no bastion, few in wishes:

snp3.9:40.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:41.3.verse: not killing or making others kill:

snp3.9:41.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:42.1.verse: Not fighting among those who fight,

snp3.9:42.2.verse: quenched among those who have taken up arms,

snp3.9:42.3.verse: not grasping among those who grasp:

snp3.9:42.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:43.3.verse: like a mustard seed off the point of a pin:

snp3.9:43.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:44.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:45.1.verse: They don’t steal anything in the world,

snp3.9:45.3.verse: tiny or huge, beautiful or ugly:

snp3.9:45.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:46.2.verse: for this world or the next;

snp3.9:46.3.verse: with no need for hope, detached:

snp3.9:46.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:47.2.verse: knowledge has freed them of indecision,

snp3.9:47.3.verse: they’ve arrived at the objective, freedom from death:

snp3.9:47.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:48.2.verse: to both good and bad deeds;

snp3.9:48.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:49.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:50.1.verse: They’ve got past this grueling swamp

snp3.9:50.3.verse: Meditating in stillness, free of indecision,

snp3.9:50.4.verse: they have crossed over to the far shore.

snp3.9:50.6.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:51.2.verse: and have gone forth from lay life;

snp3.9:51.3.verse: they’ve ended rebirth in the sensual realm:

snp3.9:51.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:52.2.verse: and have gone forth from lay life;

snp3.9:52.3.verse: they’ve ended craving to be reborn:

snp3.9:52.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:53.1.verse: They’ve thrown off the human yoke,

snp3.9:53.2.verse: and slipped out of the heavenly yoke;

snp3.9:53.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:54.2.verse: they’re cooled and free of attachments;

snp3.9:54.3.verse: a hero, master of the whole world:

snp3.9:54.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:55.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:56.3.verse: the perfected ones with defilements ended:

snp3.9:56.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:57.1.verse: They have nothing before or after,

snp3.9:57.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:58.1.verse: Captain of the herd, excellent hero,

snp3.9:58.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:59.1.verse: They who know their past lives,

snp3.9:59.2.verse: see heaven and places of loss,

snp3.9:59.3.verse: and have attained the ending of rebirth,

snp3.9:59.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.

snp3.9:60.1.verse: For name and clan are formulated

snp3.9:60.2.verse: as mere convention in the world.

snp3.9:61.2.verse: has prejudiced those who don’t understand.

snp3.9:61.4.verse: that one is a brahmin by birth.

snp3.9:62.1.verse: You’re not a brahmin by birth,

snp3.9:62.3.verse: You’re a brahmin by your deeds,

snp3.9:63.1.verse: You’re a farmer by your deeds,

snp3.9:63.3.verse: you’re a trader by your deeds,

snp3.9:64.1.verse: you’re a bandit by your deeds,

snp3.9:64.3.verse: you’re a sacrificer by your deeds,

snp3.9:65.4.verse: they’re expert in deeds and their results.

snp3.9:66.3.verse: sentient beings are bound by deeds,

snp3.9:68.4.verse: as the Divinity and Sakka to the wise.”

snp3.9:69.1.verse: When he had spoken, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to him,

snp3.10:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

snp3.10:1.3.verse: Then the monk Kokālika1 went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, bowed down to him and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One,

snp3.10:1.4.verse: “Lord, Sāriputta & Moggallāna have evil desires. They have fallen under the sway of evil desires.”

snp3.10:2.1.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One said to him,

snp3.10:2.2.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika. Don’t say that, Kolālika.

snp3.10:2.3.verse: Make your mind confident in Sāriputta & Moggallāna.

snp3.10:3.2.verse: A third time, the monk Kokālika said to the Blessed One,

snp3.10:3.3.verse: “Even though the lord Blessed One2 inspires conviction and faith in me, Sāriputta & Moggallāna have evil desires. They have fallen under the sway of evil desires.”

snp3.10:3.4.verse: A third time, the Blessed One said to him,

snp3.10:3.5.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika. Don’t say that, Kolālika.

snp3.10:3.6.verse: Make your mind confident in Sāriputta & Moggallāna.

snp3.10:4.1.verse: Then the monk Kokālika, getting up from his seat, bowed down to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, keeping him to his right, and departed.

snp3.10:4.2.verse: Then not long after he had departed, Kokālika’s whole body became covered with boils the size of mustard seeds.

snp3.10:4.3.verse: From the size of mustard seeds, they became the size of green gram. From the size of green gram, they became the size of black beans. From the size of black beans, they became the size of jujube pits. From the size of jujube pits, they became the size of jujube fruits. From the size of jujube fruits, they became the size of myrobalans. From the size of myrobalans, they became the size of unripe vilva fruits. From the size of unripe vilva fruits, they became the size of small jackfruits. When they were the size of small jackfruits, they burst. Blood and pus flowed out.

snp3.10:4.4.verse: Then the monk Kokālika died of that disease

snp3.10:4.5.verse: and, having died, he reappeared in the Paduma hell for engendering hatred in his heart against Sāriputta & Moggallāna.

snp3.10:5.1.verse: Then Brahmā Sahampati,3 in the far extreme of the night, his extreme radiance lighting up the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, went to the Blessed One. On arrival, having bowed down to him, he stood to one side. As he was standing there, he said to the Blessed One,

snp3.10:5.3.verse: and, having died, has reappeared in the Paduma hell for engendering hatred in his heart against Sāriputta & Moggallāna.”

snp3.10:5.4.verse: That is what Brahmā Sahampati said.

snp3.10:5.5.verse: Having said that, having bowed down, he circumambulated the Blessed One, keeping him to his right, and disappeared right there.

snp3.10:6.1.verse: Then when the night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the monks,

snp3.10:6.2.verse: “Monks, last night Brahmā Sahampati, in the far extreme of the night, his extreme radiance lighting up the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, came to me. On arrival, having bowed down to me, he stood to one side. As he was standing there, he said to me, ‘Lord, the monk Kokālika has died and, having died, has reappeared in the Paduma hell for engendering hatred in his heart against Sāriputta & Moggallāna.’

snp3.10:6.3.verse: That is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said that, having bowed down, he circumambulated me, keeping me to his right, and disappeared right there.”

snp3.10:7.1.verse: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One,

snp3.10:7.2.verse: “Lord, how long is the measure of the lifespan in the Paduma hell?”

snp3.10:7.3.verse: “Long, monk, is the measure of the lifespan in the Paduma hell.

snp3.10:7.4.verse: It’s not easy to calculate ‘this many years’ or ‘this many hundreds of years’ or ‘this many thousands of years’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands of years.’”

snp3.10:7.5.verse: “But, lord, can a simile be made?”

snp3.10:7.6.verse: “It can, monk,” said the Blessed One.

snp3.10:8.1.verse: “Suppose that there were a twenty-measure Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds. From that, a man would remove a sesame seed every hundred years.4

snp3.10:8.2.verse: That twenty-measure Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds would come to an end in this manner more quickly than a single Abbuda [Swelling] hell.

snp3.10:8.3.verse: Like twenty Abbuda hells is one Nirabbuda [Free from Swelling] hell.

snp3.10:8.4.verse: Like twenty Nirabbuda hells is one Ababa [Alas!] hell.

snp3.10:8.5.verse: Like twenty Ababa hells is one Aṭaṭa hell.

snp3.10:8.6.verse: Like twenty Aṭaṭa hells is one Ahaha hell.

snp3.10:8.7.verse: Like twenty Ahaha hells is one Kumuda [White Water Lily] hell.

snp3.10:8.8.verse: Like twenty Kumuda hells is one Sogandhika [Fragrant White Water Lily] hell.

snp3.10:8.9.verse: Like twenty Sogandhika hells is one Uppalaka [Blue Lotus] hell.

snp3.10:8.10.verse: Like twenty Uppalaka hells is one Puṇḍarīka [White Lotus] hell.

snp3.10:8.11.verse: Like twenty Puṇḍarīka hells is one Paduma [Red Lotus] hell.5

snp3.10:8.12.verse: The monk Kokālika has reappeared in the Paduma hell, for engendering hatred in his heart against Sāriputta & Moggallāna.”

snp3.10:8.13.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

snp3.10:8.14.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

snp3.10:9.2.verse: an axe is born in his mouth,

snp3.10:9.4.verse: the fool saying a bad statement.

snp3.10:10.4.verse: and in that wickedness finds no ease.

snp3.10:11.1.verse: Next to nothing is the bad throw

snp3.10:11.2.verse: when one loses money at dice.

snp3.10:11.3.verse: But great is the bad throw

snp3.10:12.3.verse: one who maligns noble ones, goes to hell,

snp3.10:12.4.verse: directing his words & heart toward evil.7

snp3.10:13.1.verse: He goes to hell, the one who asserts what didn’t take place,

snp3.10:13.2.verse: as does the one who, having done, says, ‘I didn’t.’

snp3.10:13.4.verse: after death, in the place beyond.8

snp3.10:14.3.verse: The evil comes right back to the fool

snp3.10:14.4.verse: like fine dust thrown against the wind.9

snp3.10:15.1.verse: One devoted to the strings of greed

snp3.10:16.1.verse: You with your hard road of a mouth, untrue, ignoble,

snp3.10:16.2.verse: destroyer          of progress, evil, doer          of wrong,

snp3.10:16.4.verse: Don’t speak a lot here. You are headed to hell.

snp3.10:17.1.verse: You scatter dust to your harm.

snp3.10:17.2.verse: You, an offender, malign the good,

snp3.10:17.3.verse: and, having engaged in many sorts of bad conduct

snp3.10:17.4.verse: are going for a long time to the pit.

snp3.10:18.1.verse: For no one’s action is annihilated.

snp3.10:18.2.verse: Surely its owner gets it back.

snp3.10:18.3.verse: An offender, the fool, sees suffering for himself

snp3.10:19.1.verse: He goes to the place set with iron spikes,

snp3.10:19.3.verse: where the food, as is fitting,

snp3.10:19.4.verse: resembles a ball of heated iron.

snp3.10:20.1.verse: When they [the hell-wardens] speak, they don’t speak lovingly.

snp3.10:20.2.verse: They [the hell beings] can’t run away. They’re not going to shelter.

snp3.10:20.3.verse: They lie on ashes strewn about.

snp3.10:20.4.verse: They enter a blazing mass of fire.

snp3.10:21.2.verse: they [the hell-wardens] strike them with hammers made of iron.

snp3.10:21.3.verse: Truly, they go to a blind darkness

snp3.10:21.4.verse: that spreads out like a fog.

snp3.10:22.1.verse: Then they enter a copper pot,

snp3.10:22.3.verse: in which they cook for a long, long time,

snp3.10:22.4.verse: bobbing up & down in a mass of fire.

snp3.10:23.1.verse: Then in a mixture of pus & blood,

snp3.10:23.3.verse: In whatever direction he leans to rest

snp3.10:24.1.verse: In an ooze where worms live,

snp3.10:24.3.verse: and there is no shore to which he can go,

snp3.10:24.4.verse: for the cooking pots all          around are all          the same.

snp3.10:25.1.verse: Then they enter the sharp sword-leaf forest

snp3.10:25.2.verse: where their limbs are cut off.

snp3.10:25.3.verse: Seizing them by the tongue with a hook,

snp3.10:25.4.verse: they [the hell-wardens] strike them, dragging them back & forth.

snp3.10:26.1.verse: Then they come to the Vettaraṇin,10 hard to cross,

snp3.10:26.3.verse: and there they fall in, the fools,

snp3.10:27.3.verse: jackals, & flocks of ravens chew on them.

snp3.10:28.1.verse: How hard, indeed, is this way of life there

snp3.10:28.2.verse: that offending people come to see.11

snp3.10:28.3.verse: So, for the remainder of life here,

snp3.10:28.4.verse: a person, heedful, should do his duty.

snp3.10:29.3.verse: have been calculated by those who know as five times ten thousand crores,12

snp3.10:29.4.verse: plus twelve times one hundred more.

snp3.10:30.1.verse: The length of the hells of suffering described here

snp3.10:30.2.verse: is how long [the hell-beings] will have to dwell there.

snp3.10:30.3.verse: So when in the company of those who are pure, admirable, excellent,

snp3.10:30.4.verse: one should constantly guard one’s words & heart.”

snp3.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

snp3.10:1.3.verse: Then the mendicant Kokālika went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

snp3.10:1.4.verse: “Sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They’ve fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.”

snp3.10:2.1.verse: When this was said, the Buddha said to Kokālika,

snp3.10:2.2.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika! Don’t say that, Kokālika!

snp3.10:2.3.verse: Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

snp3.10:3.2.verse: For a third time Kokālika said to the Buddha,

snp3.10:3.3.verse: “Despite my faith and trust in the Buddha, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They’ve fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.”

snp3.10:3.4.verse: For a third time, the Buddha said to Kokālika,

snp3.10:3.5.verse: “Don’t say that, Kokālika! Don’t say that, Kokālika!

snp3.10:3.6.verse: Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna,

snp3.10:4.1.verse: Then Kokālika rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

snp3.10:4.2.verse: Not long after he left his body erupted with boils the size of mustard seeds.

snp3.10:4.3.verse: The boils grew to the size of mung beans, then chickpeas, then jujube seeds, then jujubes, then myrobalans, then unripe wood-apples, then ripe wood-apples. Finally they burst open, and pus and blood oozed out.

snp3.10:4.4.verse: Then the mendicant Kokālika died of that illness.

snp3.10:4.5.verse: He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

snp3.10:5.1.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious divinity Sahampati, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

snp3.10:5.2.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Kokālika has passed away.

snp3.10:5.3.verse: He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

snp3.10:5.4.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

snp3.10:5.5.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

snp3.10:6.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened.

snp3.10:7.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

snp3.10:7.2.verse: “Sir, how long is the lifespan in the Pink Lotus hell?”

snp3.10:7.4.verse: It’s not easy to calculate how many years, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of years it lasts.”

snp3.10:7.5.verse: “But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”

snp3.10:8.1.verse: “Suppose there was a Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed. And at the end of every hundred years someone would remove a single seed from it.

snp3.10:8.2.verse: By this means the Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed would run out faster than a single lifetime in the Abbuda hell.

snp3.10:8.3.verse: Now, twenty lifetimes in the Abbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Nirabbuda hell.

snp3.10:8.4.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Nirabbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Ababa hell.

snp3.10:8.5.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Ababa hell equal one lifetime in the Aṭaṭa hell.

snp3.10:8.6.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Aṭaṭa hell equal one lifetime in the Ahaha hell.

snp3.10:8.7.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Ahaha hell equal one lifetime in the Yellow Lotus hell.

snp3.10:8.8.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Yellow Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Fragrant Water Lily hell.

snp3.10:8.9.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Fragrant Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the Blue Water Lily hell.

snp3.10:8.10.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the Blue Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the White Lotus hell.

snp3.10:8.11.verse: Twenty lifetimes in the White Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Pink Lotus hell.

snp3.10:8.12.verse: The mendicant Kokālika has been reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

snp3.10:8.13.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

snp3.10:8.14.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

snp3.10:9.2.verse: with an axe in their mouth.

snp3.10:9.3.verse: A fool cuts themselves with it

snp3.10:10.1.verse: When you praise someone worthy of criticism,

snp3.10:10.2.verse: or criticize someone worthy of praise,

snp3.10:10.3.verse: you choose a losing hand with your own mouth:

snp3.10:10.4.verse: you’ll never find happiness that way.

snp3.10:11.1.verse: A losing hand at dice is a trivial thing,

snp3.10:11.2.verse: if all you lose is your money

snp3.10:11.3.verse: and all you own, even yourself.

snp3.10:11.5.verse: is to hate the holy ones.

snp3.10:12.1.verse: For a hundred thousand times a hundred million,

snp3.10:12.2.verse: times five hundred and thirty-six times a thousand times ten million years

snp3.10:12.3.verse: a slanderer of noble ones goes to hell,

snp3.10:12.4.verse: having aimed bad words and thoughts at them.

snp3.10:13.2.verse: as does one who denies what they did.

snp3.10:13.3.verse: Both are equal in the hereafter,

snp3.10:14.1.verse: Whoever wrongs a man who has done no wrong,

snp3.10:14.2.verse: a pure man who has not a blemish,

snp3.10:14.3.verse: the evil backfires on the fool,

snp3.10:15.1.verse: One addicted to the way of greed,

snp3.10:16.4.verse: quiet now, for you are bound for hell.

snp3.10:17.1.verse: You stir up dust, causing harm,

snp3.10:17.2.verse: when you, sinner, malign the good.

snp3.10:17.4.verse: you’ll go to the pit for a long time.

snp3.10:18.1.verse: For no one’s deeds are ever lost,

snp3.10:18.3.verse: In the next life that stupid sinner

snp3.10:19.1.verse: They approach the place of impalement,

snp3.10:19.2.verse: with its iron spikes, sharp blades, and iron stakes.

snp3.10:19.3.verse: Then there is the food, which appropriately,

snp3.10:19.4.verse: is like a red-hot iron ball.

snp3.10:20.1.verse: For the speakers speak not sweetly,

snp3.10:20.2.verse: they don’t hurry there, or find shelter.

snp3.10:20.3.verse: They lie upon a spread of coals,

snp3.10:20.4.verse: they enter a blazing mass of fire.

snp3.10:21.2.verse: they strike them there with iron hammers.

snp3.10:21.4.verse: which spreads about them like a fog.

snp3.10:22.1.verse: Next they enter a copper pot,

snp3.10:22.3.verse: There they roast for a long time,

snp3.10:22.4.verse: writhing in the masses of fire.

snp3.10:23.2.verse: in a mixture of pus and blood.

snp3.10:23.4.verse: everything they touch there hurts them.

snp3.10:24.3.verse: There’s not even a shore to go to,

snp3.10:24.4.verse: for all around are the same kind of pots.

snp3.10:25.2.verse: so sharp they cut their body to pieces.

snp3.10:25.3.verse: Having grabbed the tongue with a hook,

snp3.10:25.4.verse: they stab it, slashing back and forth.

snp3.10:26.1.verse: Then they approach the impassable Vetaraṇī River,

snp3.10:26.2.verse: with its sharp blades, its razor blades.

snp3.10:26.4.verse: the wicked who have done wicked deeds.

snp3.10:27.1.verse: There dogs all brown and spotted,

snp3.10:27.2.verse: and raven flocks, and greedy jackals

snp3.10:27.4.verse: while hawks and crows attack them.

snp3.10:28.1.verse: Hard, alas, is the life here

snp3.10:28.3.verse: That’s why for the rest of this life

snp3.10:28.4.verse: a person ought do their duty without fail.

snp3.10:29.1.verse: Experts have counted the loads of sesame

snp3.10:29.2.verse: as compared to the Pink Lotus hell.

snp3.10:29.3.verse: For there are five times ten thousand times ten million,

snp3.10:29.4.verse: plus another twelve hundred times ten million years—

snp3.10:30.1.verse: as painful as life is said to be in hell,

snp3.10:30.2.verse: that’s how long one must dwell there.

snp3.10:30.3.verse: That’s why, for those who are pure, well-behaved, full of good qualities,

snp3.10:30.4.verse: one should always guard one’s speech and mind.”

snp3.11:1.1.verse: The Group of Thirty, born of delight, joyful,

snp3.11:1.2.verse: Sakka1 the king, and devas dressed in pure white;

snp3.11:1.4.verse: Asita the seer saw, in his mid-day meditation.

snp3.11:2.1.verse: & on seeing the devas so joyful & happy,

snp3.11:2.2.verse: having paid his respects, he said:

snp3.11:2.3.verse: “Why is the deva community so wildly elated?

snp3.11:2.4.verse: Why are they holding up banners & waving them around?

snp3.11:3.1.verse: Even after the war with the Asuras

snp3.11:3.2.verse: —when victory was the devas’, the Asuras defeated—

snp3.11:3.3.verse: even then there was nothing hair-raising like this.

snp3.11:3.4.verse: Seeing what marvel are the devas so joyful?

snp3.11:4.1.verse: They whistle, they sing, play music,

snp3.11:4.3.verse: So I ask you, who live on Mount Meru’s summit.

snp3.11:4.4.verse: Please dispel my doubt quickly, dear sirs.”

snp3.11:5.2.verse: has been born for welfare & happiness in the human world,

snp3.11:5.3.verse: in a town in the Sakyan countryside, Lumbini.

snp3.11:5.4.verse: That’s why we’re contented, so wildly elated.

snp3.11:6.1.verse: He, the highest of all beings, the ultimate person,

snp3.11:6.2.verse: a bull among men, highest of all people,

snp3.11:6.3.verse: will set turning the Wheel [of Dhamma] in the forest named after the seers,

snp3.11:6.4.verse: like a strong, roaring lion, the conqueror of beasts.”

snp3.11:7.2.verse: Asita quickly descended [from heaven] and went to Suddhodana’s dwelling.

snp3.11:7.3.verse: There, taking a seat, he said to the Sakyans:

snp3.11:7.4.verse: “Where is the prince? I, too, want to see him.”

snp3.11:8.1.verse: Then the prince, like gold aglow,

snp3.11:8.2.verse: burnished by a most skillful smith in the mouth of the furnace,

snp3.11:8.3.verse: blazing with glory, flawless in color,

snp3.11:8.4.verse: the Sakyans showed their son to the seer named Asita.

snp3.11:9.1.verse: On seeing the prince blazing like flame,

snp3.11:9.2.verse: pure like the bull of the stars going across the sky

snp3.11:9.3.verse: —the burning sun, released from the clouds of autumn—

snp3.11:9.4.verse: he was exultant, filled with abundant rapture.

snp3.11:10.1.verse: A many-spoked sunshade of a thousand circles,

snp3.11:10.2.verse: the devas held in the sky.

snp3.11:10.4.verse: but those holding the whisks & the sunshade couldn’t be seen.

snp3.11:11.1.verse: The coiled-haired seer named Dark Splendor, seeing

snp3.11:11.2.verse: the boy, like an ornament of gold on the red woolen blanket,

snp3.11:11.3.verse: a white sunshade held over his head,

snp3.11:11.4.verse: received him, joyful in mind & pleased.

snp3.11:12.1.verse: And on receiving the bull of the Sakyans,

snp3.11:12.2.verse: longingly, the master of mantras & signs

snp3.11:12.4.verse: “This one is unsurpassed, the highest of the biped race.”

snp3.11:13.1.verse: Then, foreseeing his own imminent departure,

snp3.11:13.3.verse: On seeing him weeping, the Sakyans asked:

snp3.11:13.4.verse: “But surely there will be no danger for the prince?”

snp3.11:14.1.verse: On seeing the Sakyans’ concern he replied,

snp3.11:14.2.verse: “I foresee for the prince no harm.

snp3.11:14.3.verse: Nor will there be any danger for him.

snp3.11:14.4.verse: This one’s not insignificant: Be assured.

snp3.11:15.1.verse: This prince will touch the ultimate self-awakening.

snp3.11:15.2.verse: He, seeing the utmost purity, will set rolling the Wheel of Dhamma

snp3.11:15.3.verse: through sympathy for the welfare of many.

snp3.11:15.4.verse: His holy life will spread far & wide.

snp3.11:16.1.verse: But as for me, my life here has no long remainder.

snp3.11:16.2.verse: My death will take place before then.

snp3.11:16.3.verse: I won’t get to hear the Dhamma of this one with the peerless role.

snp3.11:16.4.verse: That’s why I’m stricken, afflicted, & pained.”

snp3.11:17.1.verse: He, having brought the Sakyans abundant rapture,

snp3.11:17.2.verse: the follower of the holy life left the inner chamber and,

snp3.11:17.3.verse: out of sympathy for his nephew,

snp3.11:17.4.verse: urged him on toward the Dhamma of the one with the peerless role:

snp3.11:18.1.verse: “When you hear from another the word, ‘Awakened One,’

snp3.11:18.2.verse: or ‘Attaining self-awakening, he lays open the path of the Dhamma,’

snp3.11:18.3.verse: go there and, asking him yourself,

snp3.11:18.4.verse: follow the holy life under that Blessed One.”

snp3.11:19.1.verse: Instructed by the one whose mind was set on his benefit, Such,

snp3.11:19.2.verse: seeing in the future the utmost purity,

snp3.11:19.3.verse: Nālaka, who had laid up a store of merit,

snp3.11:19.4.verse: awaited the Victor expectantly, guarding his senses.

snp3.11:20.1.verse: On hearing word of the Victor’s turning of the foremost wheel,

snp3.11:20.2.verse: he went, he saw the bull among seers. Confident,

snp3.11:20.3.verse: he asked the foremost sage about the utmost sagacity,

snp3.11:20.4.verse: now that Asita’s forecast had come to pass.

snp3.11:21.4.verse: you who have gone to the beyond of all dhammas.

snp3.11:22.1.verse: I’m intent on the homeless life;

snp3.11:23.1.verse: “I’ll teach you a sagacity          hard to do,

snp3.11:24.2.verse: for in a village there’s praise & abuse.

snp3.11:24.3.verse: Ward off any flaw in the heart.

snp3.11:25.1.verse: High & low things will come up

snp3.11:27.2.verse: As are these, so am I.’

snp3.11:27.4.verse: neither kill nor get others to kill.

snp3.11:29.1.verse: Stomach not full, moderate in food,

snp3.11:29.4.verse: One without hunger is one who’s unbound.

snp3.11:30.1.verse: Having gone on his almsround, the sage

snp3.11:30.2.verse: should then go to the forest,

snp3.11:30.3.verse: approaching the root of a tree,

snp3.11:31.1.verse: The enlightened one, intent on jhāna,

snp3.11:31.2.verse: should find delight in the forest,

snp3.11:31.3.verse: should practice jhāna at the foot of a tree,

snp3.11:32.1.verse: Then, at the end of the night,

snp3.11:32.2.verse: he should go to the village,

snp3.11:33.1.verse: Having gone to the village, the sage should not go

snp3.11:33.4.verse: he shouldn’t utter a scheming word.

snp3.11:34.2.verse: I got nothing. That, too, is good.’

snp3.11:34.3.verse: Being such with regard to both,

snp3.11:34.4.verse: he returns to the very same tree.

snp3.11:35.1.verse: Wandering with his bowl in hand

snp3.11:35.3.verse: he shouldn’t despise a piddling gift

snp3.11:36.3.verse: They don’t go twice to the further shore.

snp3.11:37.1.verse: In one who has no attachment—

snp3.11:37.2.verse: the monk who has cut the stream,4

snp3.11:37.3.verse: abandoning what is & isn’t a duty—

snp3.11:39.3.verse: Be free of raw stench,5 independent,

snp3.11:39.4.verse: having the holy life as your aim.

snp3.11:41.1.verse: On hearing the fame of the enlightened

snp3.11:41.4.verse: my disciple should foster all the more.

snp3.11:42.3.verse: Those in small channels flow noisily,

snp3.11:43.3.verse: The fool is like a half-empty pot;

snp3.11:43.4.verse: one who is wise, a full lake.6

snp3.11:44.1.verse: A contemplative who speaks a great deal

snp3.11:44.4.verse: knowing, he speaks a great deal.

snp3.11:45.1.verse: But he who, knowing, is restrained,

snp3.11:45.2.verse: knowing, doesn’t speak a great deal:

snp3.11:45.3.verse: He is a sage worthy of sagehood.

snp3.11:45.4.verse: He is a sage, his sagehood attained.”

snp3.11:1.1.verse: The seer Asita in his daily meditation

snp3.11:1.2.verse: saw the bright-clad gods of the host of Thirty

snp3.11:1.3.verse: and their lord Sakka joyfully celebrating,

snp3.11:2.2.verse: he paid respects and said this there:

snp3.11:2.3.verse: “Why is the community of gods in such excellent spirits?

snp3.11:2.4.verse: Why take up streamers and whirl them about?

snp3.11:3.1.verse: Even in the war with the titans,

snp3.11:3.2.verse: when gods were victorious and titans defeated,

snp3.11:3.4.verse: What marvel have the celestials seen that they so rejoice?

snp3.11:4.1.verse: Shouting and singing and playing music,

snp3.11:4.2.verse: they clap their hands and dance.

snp3.11:4.3.verse: I ask you, dwellers on Mount Meru’s peak,

snp3.11:4.4.verse: quickly dispel my doubt, good fellows!”

snp3.11:5.1.verse: “The being intent on awakening, a peerless gem,

snp3.11:5.2.verse: has been born in the human realm for the sake of welfare and happiness,

snp3.11:5.3.verse: in Lumbinī, a village in the Sakyan land.

snp3.11:5.4.verse: That’s why we’re so happy, in such excellent spirits.

snp3.11:6.1.verse: He is supreme among all beings, the peak individual,

snp3.11:6.2.verse: captain of men, supreme among all creatures.

snp3.11:6.3.verse: He will roll forth the wheel in the grove of the seers,

snp3.11:6.4.verse: roaring like a mighty lion, lord of beasts.”

snp3.11:7.2.verse: and right away approached Suddhodana’s home.

snp3.11:7.3.verse: Seated there he said this to the Sakyans,

snp3.11:7.4.verse: “Where is the boy? I too wish to see him!”

snp3.11:8.1.verse: Then the Sakyans showed their son to the one named Asita—

snp3.11:8.2.verse: the boy shone like burning gold

snp3.11:8.4.verse: dazzling with glory, of peerless beauty.

snp3.11:9.1.verse: The boy beamed like crested flame,

snp3.11:9.2.verse: pure as the moon, lord of stars traversing the sky,

snp3.11:9.3.verse: blazing like the sun free of stormclouds after the rains;

snp3.11:9.4.verse: seeing him, he was joyful, brimming with happiness.

snp3.11:10.1.verse: The celestials held up a parasol in the sky,

snp3.11:10.4.verse: but none could see who held the chowries or the parasols.

snp3.11:11.1.verse: When the matted hair seer named “Dark Splendor”

snp3.11:11.2.verse: had seen the boy like a gold ingot on a cream rug

snp3.11:11.3.verse: with a white parasol held over his head,

snp3.11:11.4.verse: he received him, elated and happy.

snp3.11:12.2.verse: the seeker, master of marks and hymns,

snp3.11:12.3.verse: lifted up his voice with confident heart:

snp3.11:12.4.verse: “He is supreme, the best of men!”

snp3.11:13.1.verse: But then, remembering he would depart this world,

snp3.11:13.2.verse: his spirits fell and his tears flowed.

snp3.11:13.3.verse: Seeing the weeping seer, the Sakyans said,

snp3.11:13.4.verse: “Surely there will be no threat to the boy?”

snp3.11:14.1.verse: Seeing the crestfallen Sakyans, the seer said,

snp3.11:14.2.verse: “I do not forsee harm befall the boy,

snp3.11:14.3.verse: and there will be no threat to him,

snp3.11:14.4.verse: not in the least; set your minds at ease.

snp3.11:15.1.verse: This boy shall reach the highest awakening.

snp3.11:15.2.verse: As one of perfectly purified vision, compassionate for the welfare of the many,

snp3.11:15.3.verse: he shall roll forth the wheel of the teaching;

snp3.11:15.4.verse: his spiritual path will become widespread.

snp3.11:16.1.verse: But I have not long left in this life,

snp3.11:16.3.verse: I will never hear the teaching of the one who bore the unequaled burden.

snp3.11:16.4.verse: That’s why I’m so upset and distraught—it’s a disaster for me!”

snp3.11:17.1.verse: Having brought abundant happiness to the Sakyans,

snp3.11:17.2.verse: the spiritual seeker left the royal compound.

snp3.11:17.3.verse: He had a nephew; and out of sympathy

snp3.11:17.4.verse: he encouraged him in the teaching of the one who bore the unequaled burden.

snp3.11:18.1.verse: “When you hear the voice of another saying ‘Buddha’—

snp3.11:18.2.verse: one who has attained awakening and who reveals the foremost teaching—

snp3.11:18.3.verse: go there and ask about his breakthrough;

snp3.11:18.4.verse: lead the spiritual life under that Blessed One.”

snp3.11:19.1.verse: Now, that Nālaka had a store of accumulated merit;

snp3.11:19.2.verse: so when instructed by one of such kindly intent,

snp3.11:19.3.verse: with perfectly purified vision of the future,

snp3.11:19.4.verse: he waited anticipating the Victor, guarding his senses.

snp3.11:20.1.verse: When he heard of the Victor rolling forth the excellent wheel he went to him,

snp3.11:20.2.verse: and seeing the boss seer, he became confident.

snp3.11:20.3.verse: The time of Asita’s instruction had arrived;

snp3.11:20.4.verse: so he asked the excellent sage about the highest sagacity.

snp3.11:21.2.verse: have turned out to be true.

snp3.11:21.4.verse: who has gone beyond all things:

snp3.11:22.1.verse: For one who has entered the homeless life,

snp3.11:22.3.verse: when questioned, O sage, please tell me

snp3.11:23.4.verse: Come, I shall tell you all about it.

snp3.11:24.1.verse: In the village, keep the same attitude

snp3.11:24.2.verse: no matter if reviled or praised.

snp3.11:25.2.verse: like tongues of fire in a forest.

snp3.11:25.3.verse: Women try to seduce a sage—

snp3.11:26.2.verse: having left behind sensual pleasures high and low,

snp3.11:26.4.verse: to living creatures firm or frail.

snp3.11:27.2.verse: as are they, so am I’—

snp3.11:27.4.verse: neither kill nor incite to kill.

snp3.11:28.2.verse: for what ordinary people are attached to,

snp3.11:28.3.verse: one whose eye is clear would set out to practice,

snp3.11:29.1.verse: With empty stomach, taking limited food,

snp3.11:30.2.verse: they’d take themselves into the forest;

snp3.11:30.3.verse: and nearing the foot of a tree,

snp3.11:30.4.verse: the sage would take their seat.

snp3.11:31.1.verse: That attentive one intent on absorption,

snp3.11:31.3.verse: They’d practice absorption at the foot of a tree,

snp3.11:32.1.verse: Then, at the end of the night,

snp3.11:32.2.verse: they’d take themselves into a village.

snp3.11:32.4.verse: nor offerings brought from the village.

snp3.11:33.1.verse: A sage who has come to a village

snp3.11:33.2.verse: would not walk hastily among the families.

snp3.11:33.3.verse: They’d not discuss their search for food,

snp3.11:34.4.verse: they return right to the tree.

snp3.11:35.2.verse: not dumb, but thought to be dumb,

snp3.11:35.3.verse: they wouldn’t scorn a tiny gift,

snp3.11:35.4.verse: nor look down upon the giver.

snp3.11:36.1.verse: For the practice has many aspects,

snp3.11:36.3.verse: They do not go to the far shore twice,

snp3.11:36.4.verse: nor having gone once do they fall away.

snp3.11:37.1.verse: When a mendicant has no creeping,

snp3.11:37.2.verse: and has cut the stream of craving,

snp3.11:37.3.verse: and given up all the various duties,

snp3.11:37.4.verse: no fever is found in them.

snp3.11:38.1.verse: I shall school you in sagacity.

snp3.11:38.2.verse: Practice as if you were licking a razor’s edge.

snp3.11:38.3.verse: With tongue pressed against the roof of your mouth,

snp3.11:39.3.verse: Be free of putrefaction and unattached,

snp3.11:40.5.verse: you’ll light up the ten directions.

snp3.11:41.1.verse: Having heard the words of the attentive,

snp3.11:41.2.verse: the meditators who’ve given up sensual desires,

snp3.11:41.3.verse: a follower of mine would develop

snp3.11:41.4.verse: conscience and faith all the more.

snp3.11:42.1.verse: Understand this by the way streams move

snp3.11:42.3.verse: the little creeks flow on resounding,

snp3.11:42.4.verse: while silent flow the great rivers.

snp3.11:43.2.verse: what is full is at peace.

snp3.11:43.3.verse: The fool is like a half-full pot;

snp3.11:43.4.verse: the wise like a brimfull lake.

snp3.11:45.1.verse: But one who, knowing, is self-controlled,

snp3.11:45.3.verse: that sage is worthy of sagacity,

snp3.12:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother.

snp3.12:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion—the uposatha day of the fifteenth, a perfect full-moon night—the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

snp3.12:1.4.verse: Surveying the silent Saṅgha of monks, he addressed them:

snp3.12:2.1.verse: “Monks, if there are any who ask, ‘Your listening to teachings that are skillful, noble, leading onward, going to self-awakening is a prerequisite for what?’ they should be told,

snp3.12:2.2.verse: ‘For the sake of knowing qualities of dualities as they actually are.’

snp3.12:2.3.verse: Which duality are you speaking about?

snp3.12:3.1.verse: ‘This is stress. This is the origination of stress’: This is one contemplation.

snp3.12:3.2.verse: ‘This is the cessation of stress. This is the path of practice leading to the cessation of stress’: This is a second contemplation.

snp3.12:3.3.verse: For a monk rightly contemplating this duality in this way—heedful, ardent, & resolute—one of two fruits can be expected:

snp3.12:3.4.verse: either gnosis right here-&-now, or—if there be any remnant of clinging-sustenance—non-return.”

snp3.12:4.1.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

snp3.12:4.2.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

snp3.12:5.6.verse: the way to the stilling of stress:

snp3.12:7.6.verse: the way to the stilling of stress:

snp3.12:8.4.verse: they aren’t headed to birth & aging.1

snp3.12:9.1.verse: Now, if there are any who ask, ‘Would there be the right contemplation of dualities in yet another way?’

snp3.12:9.4.verse: ‘Whatever stress comes into play is all from acquisition2 as a requisite condition’: This is one contemplation.

snp3.12:9.5.verse: ‘From the remainderless fading & cessation of that very acquisition, there is no coming into play of stress’: This is a second contemplation.

snp3.12:9.6.verse: For a monk rightly contemplating this duality in this way—heedful, ardent, & resolute—one of two fruits can be expected: either gnosis right here-&-now, or—if there be any remnant of clinging-sustenance—non-return. That is what the Blessed One said.

snp3.12:9.7.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

snp3.12:10.2.verse: the many forms of stress come into being in the world.

snp3.12:10.5.verse: Therefore, discerning, you shouldn’t create acquisitions

snp3.12:10.6.verse: as you stay focused on the birth & origin of stress.

snp3.12:11.1.verse: Now, if there are any who ask, ‘Would there be the right contemplation of dualities in yet another way?’

snp3.12:11.4.verse: ‘Whatever stress comes into play is all from ignorance as a requisite condition’: This is one contemplation.

snp3.12:11.5.verse: ‘From the remainderless fading & cessation of that very ignorance, there is no coming into play of stress’: This is a second contemplation.

snp3.12:11.6.verse: For a monk rightly contemplating this duality in this way—heedful, ardent, & resolute—one of two fruits can be expected: either gnosis right here-&-now, or—if there be any remnant of clinging-sustenance—non-return. That is what the Blessed One said.

snp3.12:11.7.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

snp3.12:12.4.verse: or anywhere else, that destination is simply through ignorance.

snp3.12:13.1.verse: This ignorance is a great delusion

snp3.12:13.2.verse: whereby they have wandered-on a long, long time.

snp3.12:13.3.verse: While beings immersed in clear knowing

snp3.12:14.1.verse: Now, if there are any who ask, ‘Would there be the right contemplation of dualities in yet another way?’ they should be told, ‘There would.’

snp3.12:14.3.verse: ‘Whatever stress comes into play is all from fabrication as a requisite condition’: This is one contemplation.

snp3.12:14.4.verse: ‘From the remainderless fading & cessation of that very fabrication, there is no coming into play of stress’: This is a second contemplation.

snp3.12:14.5.verse: For a monk rightly contemplating this duality in this way—heedful, ardent, & resolute—one of two fruits can be expected: either gnosis right here-&-now, or—if there be any remnant of clinging-sustenance—non-return. That is what the Blessed One said.

snp3.12:14.6.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

snp3.12:15.2.verse: is all from fabrication as a requisite condition.

snp3.12:15.4.verse: there is no stress coming into play.

snp3.12:16.2.verse: that stress comes from fabrication as a requisite condition—

snp3.12:16.3.verse: with the tranquilizing of all fabrication,

snp3.12:16.5.verse: That’s how there is the ending of stress.

snp3.12:16.6.verse: Knowing this as it actually is,

snp3.12:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

snp3.12:1.3.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

snp3.12:1.4.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them:

snp3.12:2.1.verse: “Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: ‘There are skillful teachings that are noble, emancipating, and lead to awakening. What is the real reason for listening to such teachings?’ You should answer:

snp3.12:2.2.verse: ‘Only so as to truly know the pairs of teachings.’

snp3.12:2.3.verse: And what pairs do they speak of?

snp3.12:3.1.verse: ‘This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering’: this is the first contemplation.

snp3.12:3.2.verse: ‘This is the cessation of suffering; this is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’: this is the second contemplation.

snp3.12:3.3.verse: When a mendicant meditates rightly contemplating a pair of teachings in this way—diligent, keen, and resolute—they can expect one of two results:

snp3.12:3.4.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.”

snp3.12:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

snp3.12:4.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

snp3.12:5.1.verse: “There are those who don’t understand suffering

snp3.12:5.5.verse: And they do not know the path

snp3.12:5.6.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

snp3.12:6.2.verse: as well as the release by wisdom.

snp3.12:6.4.verse: they continue to be reborn and grow old.

snp3.12:7.1.verse: But there are those who understand suffering

snp3.12:7.4.verse: ceases with no residue left behind.

snp3.12:7.6.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

snp3.12:8.1.verse: They’re endowed with the heart’s release,

snp3.12:8.2.verse: as well as the release by wisdom.

snp3.12:8.4.verse: they don’t continue to be reborn and grow old.”

snp3.12:9.1.verse: “Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: ‘Could there be another way to contemplate the pairs?’

snp3.12:9.4.verse: ‘All the suffering that originates is caused by attachment’: this is one contemplation.

snp3.12:9.5.verse: ‘When attachment has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering’: this is the second contemplation.

snp3.12:9.6.verse: When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return.”
