thig16.1:32.1.verse: As she spoke thus to her father,

thig16.1:32.2.verse: Anīkaratta, to whom she was betrothed,

thig16.1:32.4.verse: at the time appointed for the marriage.

thig16.1:33.1.verse: Then Sumedhā took up a knife,

thig16.1:33.2.verse: and cut off her hair, so black, thick, and soft.

thig16.1:34.1.verse: And as she entered it there,

thig16.1:34.4.verse: well developed the perception of impermanence.

thig16.1:35.3.verse: His limbs adorned with gems and honey-yellow gold,

thig16.1:35.4.verse: he begged Sumedhā with cupped palms:

thig16.1:36.1.verse: “As a royal there is command, wealth, authority,

thig16.1:36.3.verse: Enjoy sensual pleasures while you’re still young!

thig16.1:36.4.verse: Sensual pleasures are hard to find in the world!

thig16.1:38.1.verse: Sumedhā, having no use for sensual pleasures,

thig16.1:38.2.verse: and having done away with delusion, spoke right back:

thig16.1:38.4.verse: See the danger in sensual pleasures!

thig16.1:40.1.verse: Were the seven jewels to rain from the sky

thig16.1:40.3.verse: there would be no sating of sensual pleasures:

thig16.1:41.1.verse: Like a butcher’s knife and chopping board,

thig16.1:41.2.verse: sensual pleasures are like a cobra’s head.

thig16.1:42.1.verse: Sensual pleasures are impermanent and unstable,

thig16.1:42.2.verse: they’re full of suffering, a terrible poison;

thig16.1:42.4.verse: the root of gloom, their fruit is pain.

thig16.1:43.1.verse: Sensual pleasures are like fruits of a tree,

thig16.1:43.3.verse: they trick you like a dream;

thig16.1:43.4.verse: sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods.

thig16.1:44.1.verse: Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears;

thig16.1:44.2.verse: a disease, a boil, gloom and trouble.

thig16.1:44.3.verse: Like a pit of glowing coals,

thig16.1:44.4.verse: the root of gloom, fear and slaughter.

thig16.1:45.1.verse: Thus sensual pleasures have been explained

thig16.1:45.2.verse: to be obstructions, so full of suffering.

thig16.1:45.4.verse: I have no trust in any state of life.

thig16.1:46.1.verse: What can someone else do for me

thig16.1:46.2.verse: when their own head is burning?

thig16.1:46.3.verse: When stalked by old age and death,

thig16.1:46.4.verse: you should strive to destroy them.”

thig16.1:47.2.verse: and saw her parents with Anīkaratta,

thig16.1:48.2.verse: crying again and again at that with no known beginning—

thig16.1:48.4.verse: the killing of a brother or of themselves.

thig16.1:49.1.verse: Remember the ocean of tears, of milk, of blood—

thig16.1:50.2.verse: compared with tears, milk, and blood.

thig16.1:50.3.verse: Remember bones piled up high as Mount Vepulla

thig16.1:50.4.verse: in the course of a single eon.

thig16.1:51.2.verse: is compared to this broad Black Plum Tree Land;

thig16.1:51.3.verse: if divided into lumps the size of jujube seeds,

thig16.1:51.4.verse: they’d still be fewer than his mother’s mothers.

thig16.1:52.1.verse: Remember the grass, sticks, and leaves,

thig16.1:52.2.verse: compare that with no known beginning:

thig16.1:52.3.verse: if split into chips four inches in size,

thig16.1:52.4.verse: they’d still be fewer than his father’s fathers.

thig16.1:53.1.verse: Remember the one-eyed turtle and the yoke with a hole

thig16.1:53.2.verse: blown in the ocean from east to west—

thig16.1:53.3.verse: sticking the head in the hole

thig16.1:53.4.verse: is a metaphor for gaining a human birth.

thig16.1:54.1.verse: Remember the form of this unlucky body,

thig16.1:54.2.verse: insubstantial as a lump of foam.

thig16.1:54.4.verse: remember the hells so full of distress.

thig16.1:55.1.verse: Remember those swelling the charnel grounds

thig16.1:55.2.verse: again and again in life after life.

thig16.1:56.1.verse: When freedom from death is there to be found,

thig16.1:56.2.verse: why would you drink the five bitter poisons?

thig16.1:56.4.verse: are so much more bitter than them.

thig16.1:57.1.verse: When freedom from death is there to be found,

thig16.1:57.2.verse: why would you burn for sensual pleasures?

thig16.1:58.1.verse: When there is freedom from enmity,

thig16.1:58.2.verse: why would you want your enemy, sensual pleasures?

thig16.1:58.3.verse: Many enemies take a share of your sensual pleasures:

thig16.1:58.4.verse: kings, fire, robbers, flood, and unloved heirs.

thig16.1:59.1.verse: When liberation is there to be found,

thig16.1:59.2.verse: what good are sensual pleasures that kill and bind?

thig16.1:59.3.verse: For though unwilling, when sensual pleasures are there,

thig16.1:59.4.verse: they are subject to the pain of killing and binding.

thig16.1:60.2.verse: burns one who grasps it without letting go,

thig16.1:60.3.verse: sensual pleasures are like a grass torch,

thig16.1:60.4.verse: burning those who do not let go.

thig16.1:61.2.verse: for the trivial joys of sensual pleasure.

thig16.1:61.4.verse: like a catfish on a hook.

thig16.1:62.1.verse: Deliberately control yourself among sensual pleasures!

thig16.1:62.2.verse: You’re like a hound fixed to a chain:

thig16.1:62.3.verse: sensual pleasures will surely devour you

thig16.1:62.4.verse: as hungry corpse-workers would a hound.

thig16.1:63.4.verse: relinquish sensual pleasures, they don’t last!

thig16.1:64.1.verse: When the unaging is there to be found,

thig16.1:64.2.verse: what good are sensual pleasures in which is old age?

thig16.1:64.4.verse: are bonded to death and sickness.

thig16.1:65.1.verse: This is freedom from old age, freedom from death!

thig16.1:65.2.verse: This is freedom from old age and death, the sorrowless state!

thig16.1:66.1.verse: This freedom from death has been realized by many;

thig16.1:66.2.verse: even today it can be obtained

thig16.1:66.3.verse: by those who rationally apply themselves;

thig16.1:66.4.verse: but it’s impossible if you don’t try.”

thig16.1:67.4.verse: Sumedhā cast her hair on the ground.

thig16.1:68.2.verse: raised his cupped palms to her father and begged:

thig16.1:68.3.verse: “Let go of Sumedhā, so that she may go forth!

thig16.1:68.4.verse: She will see the truth of liberation.”

thig16.1:69.1.verse: Released by her mother and father,

thig16.1:69.2.verse: she went forth, afraid of grief and fear.

thig16.1:69.3.verse: While still a trainee nun she realized the six direct knowledges,

thig16.1:71.1.verse: “In the time of the Buddha Koṇāgamana,

thig16.1:71.2.verse: we three friends gave the gift

thig16.1:72.2.verse: a thousand times, ten thousand times,

thig16.1:72.3.verse: we were reborn among the gods,

thig16.1:73.1.verse: We were mighty among the gods,

thig16.1:73.3.verse: I was queen to a king with the seven treasures—

thig16.1:73.4.verse: I was the treasure of a wife.

thig16.1:74.1.verse: That was the cause, that the origin, that the root,

thig16.1:74.2.verse: that was the acceptance of the dispensation;

thig16.1:74.3.verse: that first meeting culminated in extinguishment

thig16.1:74.4.verse: for one delighting in the teaching.

thig16.1:75.1.verse: So say those who have faith in the words

thig16.1:75.2.verse: of the one unrivaled in wisdom.

thig16.1:75.3.verse: They’re disillusioned with any state of life,

thig16.1:75.4.verse: and being disillusioned they become dispassionate.”

thig16.1:76.1.verse: That is how these verses were recited by the senior nun Sumedhā.

thig16.1:77.5.verse: The Verses of the Senior Nuns are finished.

ud1.1:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the tree of awakening on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud1.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud1.1:1.4.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion. In the first part of the night, he carefully applied the mind to dependent origination, going with the grain:

ud1.1:2.1.verse: “So, when this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises. That is:

ud1.1:2.2.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

ud1.1:2.3.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

ud1.1:2.4.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

ud1.1:2.5.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

ud1.1:2.6.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

ud1.1:2.7.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

ud1.1:2.8.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

ud1.1:2.9.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

ud1.1:2.10.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

ud1.1:2.11.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

ud1.1:2.12.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

ud1.1:2.13.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.”

ud1.1:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.1:4.4.verse: since he understands each thing and its cause.”

ud1.2:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the tree of awakening on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud1.2:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud1.2:1.4.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion. In the second part of the night, he carefully applied the mind to dependent origination, going against the grain:

ud1.2:2.1.verse: “So, when this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

ud1.2:2.4.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

ud1.2:2.5.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

ud1.2:2.6.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

ud1.2:2.10.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

ud1.2:2.11.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

ud1.2:2.12.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

ud1.2:2.13.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”

ud1.2:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.2:4.4.verse: since he’s known the end of conditions.”

ud1.3:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the tree of awakening on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud1.3:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud1.3:1.4.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion. In the last watch, he carefully applied the mind to dependent origination, going both with and against the grain:

ud1.3:2.1.verse: “So, when this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

ud1.3:2.2.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

ud1.3:2.3.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

ud1.3:2.4.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

ud1.3:2.5.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

ud1.3:2.6.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

ud1.3:2.7.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

ud1.3:2.8.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

ud1.3:2.9.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

ud1.3:2.10.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

ud1.3:2.11.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

ud1.3:2.12.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

ud1.3:2.13.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

ud1.3:2.14.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

ud1.3:3.1.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease.

ud1.3:3.3.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

ud1.3:3.4.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

ud1.3:3.5.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

ud1.3:3.9.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

ud1.3:3.10.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

ud1.3:3.11.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

ud1.3:3.12.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”

ud1.3:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.3:5.4.verse: as the sun lights up the sky.”

ud1.4:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the goatherd’s banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud1.4:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud1.4:1.4.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion.

ud1.4:2.1.verse: Then a certain brahmin, one of those who murmured the mystic syllable huṁ, huṁ, went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

ud1.4:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side and said,

ud1.4:2.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, how do you define a brahmin? And what are the things that make one a brahmin?”

ud1.4:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.4:4.1.verse: “Any brahmin who has banished bad qualities—

ud1.4:4.2.verse: not murmuring the mystic syllable huṁ, unstained, self-controlled,

ud1.4:4.3.verse: a complete knowledge master who has completed the spiritual journey—

ud1.4:4.4.verse: they may legitimately proclaim the divine doctrine;

ud1.4:4.5.verse: who have no pretensions about anything in the world.”

ud1.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud1.5:1.3.verse: Now at that time a number of senior monks approached the Buddha—the venerables Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāna, Mahākoṭṭhita, Mahākappina, Mahācunda, Anuruddha, Revata, and Nanda.

ud1.5:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw them coming off in the distance,

ud1.5:2.5.verse: When he said this, a certain mendicant who was brahmin by birth asked the Buddha,

ud1.5:2.6.verse: “Sir, how do you define a brahmin? And what are the things that make one a brahmin?”

ud1.5:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.5:4.4.verse: they are the world’s true brahmins.”

ud1.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud1.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali cave, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

ud1.6:1.4.verse: Then after some time he recovered from that illness.

ud1.6:2.1.verse: Now at that time five hundred deities were ready and eager for the chance to offer alms to Mahākassapa.

ud1.6:2.2.verse: But Mahākasspa turned down those deities. In the morning, he robed up, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.

ud1.6:2.3.verse: He went to the street markets of the poor, the destitute, and the embroiderers.

ud1.6:2.4.verse: The Buddha saw him wandering for alms in the street markets of the poor, the destitute, and the embroiderers.

ud1.6:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.6:4.3.verse: with defilements ended and flaws purged:

ud1.6:4.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.”

ud1.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in Pāvā at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine, the haunt of the native spirit Ajakalāpaka.

ud1.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was meditating in the open during the dark of night, while a gentle rain drizzled down.

ud1.7:1.4.verse: Then Ajakalāpaka, wanting to make the Buddha feel fear, terror, and goosebumps, approached him, and while not far away yelled three times, “Havoc and heck!” Then he added,

ud1.7:1.5.verse: “Now that’s a goblin for you, ascetic!”

ud1.7:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud1.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Saṅgāmaji had arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

ud1.8:1.6.verse: and went to the Jetavana, taking their boy.

ud1.8:2.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Saṅgāmaji was sitting at the root of a tree for the day’s meditation.

ud1.8:2.2.verse: Then his former wife went up to him and said,

ud1.8:2.4.verse: When she said this, Saṅgāmaji kept silent.

ud1.8:3.1.verse: For a second time she said,

ud1.8:3.3.verse: For a second time, Saṅgāmaji kept silent.

ud1.8:4.1.verse: For a third time she said,

ud1.8:4.3.verse: For a third time, Saṅgāmaji kept silent.

ud1.8:5.1.verse: Then she put down the boy in front of Saṅgāmaji, saying,

ud1.8:5.2.verse: “This is your child, ascetic. Please raise him.”

ud1.8:6.1.verse: But Saṅgāmaji neither looked at the boy nor spoke to him.

ud1.8:6.2.verse: Then his former wife went a little distance away. Looking back, she saw Saṅgāmaji ignoring the boy, and thought,

ud1.8:6.3.verse: “This ascetic doesn’t even want his child.”

ud1.8:6.4.verse: She returned to pick up the boy, then left.

ud1.8:6.5.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha saw how Saṅgāmaji’s former wife went back for the child.

ud1.8:7.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.8:8.1.verse: “When she came he was not glad,

ud1.8:8.2.verse: when she left he did not grieve.

ud1.8:8.3.verse: Victorious in battle, freed from chains,

ud1.8:8.4.verse: that’s who I declare a brahmin.”

ud1.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Gayā on Gayā Head.

ud1.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time—during the cold spell when the snow falls in the January winter—many matted hair ascetics plunged in and out of the Gayā river. Plunging and showering, they served the sacred flame, thinking:

ud1.9:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw them plunging in and out.

ud1.9:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.9:4.2.verse: no matter how many people bathe there.

ud1.9:4.3.verse: One who has truth and principle,

ud1.9:4.4.verse: they are pure, they are brahmins.”

ud1.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud1.10:1.3.verse: Now at that time Bāhiya of the Bark Cloth was residing by Suppāraka on the ocean shore, where he was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud1.10:1.4.verse: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

ud1.10:1.5.verse: “I am one of those in the world who are perfected or on the path to perfection.”

ud1.10:2.1.verse: Then a deity who was a former relative of Bāhiya, having sympathy and wanting what’s best for him, approached him and said:

ud1.10:2.2.verse: “Bāhiya, you’re not a perfected one, nor on the path to perfection.

ud1.10:2.3.verse: You don’t have the practice by which you might become a perfected one or one on the path to perfection.”

ud1.10:3.1.verse: “So who then are those in the world who are perfected or on the path to perfection?”

ud1.10:3.2.verse: “In the northern lands there is a city named Sāvatthī.

ud1.10:3.3.verse: There that Blessed One is now staying, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

ud1.10:3.4.verse: He is a perfected one and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of perfection.”

ud1.10:4.1.verse: Impelled by that deity, Bāhiya left Suppāraka right away.

ud1.10:4.2.verse: Sojourning no more than a single night in any place, he made his way to Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery in the Jeta Grove at Sāvatthī.

ud1.10:4.3.verse: At that time several mendicants were walking mindfully in the open air.

ud1.10:4.5.verse: “Sirs, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?

ud1.10:4.6.verse: For I want to see him.”

ud1.10:4.7.verse: “He has entered an inhabited area for almsfood, Bāhiya.”

ud1.10:5.1.verse: Then Bāhiya rushed out of the Jeta Grove and entered Sāvatthī, where he saw the Buddha walking for alms. He was impressive and inspiring, with peaceful faculties and heart, attained to the highest self-control and serenity, like an elephant with tamed, guarded, and controlled faculties.

ud1.10:5.2.verse: Bāhiya went up to the Buddha, bowed down with his head to the Buddha’s feet, and said,

ud1.10:5.3.verse: “Sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach me the Dhamma!

ud1.10:5.4.verse: That would be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

ud1.10:5.6.verse: “It’s not the time, Bāhiya, so long as I have entered an inhabited area for almsfood.”

ud1.10:6.1.verse: For a second time, Bāhiya said,

ud1.10:6.2.verse: “But you never know, sir, when life is at risk, either the Buddha’s or my own.

ud1.10:6.3.verse: Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach me the Dhamma!

ud1.10:6.4.verse: That would be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

ud1.10:6.5.verse: For a second time, the Buddha said,

ud1.10:6.6.verse: “It’s not the time, Bāhiya, so long as I have entered an inhabited area for almsfood.”

ud1.10:7.1.verse: For a third time, Bāhiya said,

ud1.10:7.2.verse: “But you never know, sir, when life is at risk, either the Buddha’s or my own.

ud1.10:7.3.verse: Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach me the Dhamma!

ud1.10:7.4.verse: That would be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

ud1.10:8.1.verse: “In that case, Bāhiya, you should train like this:

ud1.10:8.2.verse: ‘In the seen will be merely the seen; in the heard will be merely the heard; in the thought will be merely the thought; in the known will be merely the known.’

ud1.10:8.4.verse: When you have trained in this way,

ud1.10:8.9.verse: you won’t be in this life or the next or between the two.

ud1.10:8.10.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

ud1.10:9.1.verse: Then, due to this brief Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, Bāhiya’s mind was right away freed from defilements by not grasping.

ud1.10:10.1.verse: And when the Buddha had given Bāhiya this brief advice he left.

ud1.10:10.2.verse: But soon after the Buddha had left, a cow with a baby calf charged at Bāhiya and took his life.

ud1.10:11.1.verse: Then the Buddha wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he exited the city together with several mendicants and saw that Bāhiya had passed away.

ud1.10:11.3.verse: “Mendicants, pick up Bāhiya’s corpse. Having lifted it onto a cot and carried it, cremate it and build a monument.

ud1.10:11.4.verse: Mendicants, one of your spiritual companions has passed away.”

ud1.10:12.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied those mendicants. They did as the Buddha asked, then returned to the Buddha

ud1.10:12.3.verse: “Sir, Bāhiya’s corpse has been cremated and a monument built for him.

ud1.10:12.4.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

ud1.10:12.5.verse: “Mendicants, Bāhiya was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

ud1.10:12.6.verse: Bāhiya of the Bark Cloth has become fully quenched.”

ud1.10:13.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud1.10:14.2.verse: fire and air have no footing—

ud1.10:14.4.verse: nor does the sun shed its light;

ud1.10:15.1.verse: And when a sage, a brahmin, finds understanding

ud1.10:15.4.verse: from pleasure and pain they are released.”

ud1.10:16.1.verse: This too is a heartfelt saying that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.

ud2.1:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the Mucalinda tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud2.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud2.1:2.1.verse: Just then a large storm blew up out of season, bringing seven days of precipitation, with cold winds and overcast skies.

ud2.1:2.2.verse: Mucalinda, the dragon king, came out from his abode, encircled the Buddha’s body with seven coils and spread his large hood over his head, thinking,

ud2.1:2.3.verse: “May the Buddha not be hot or cold, nor be bothered by flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, or reptiles.”

ud2.1:3.1.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion.

ud2.1:3.2.verse: When he knew the heavens were clear and cloudless, Mucalinda unwrapped his coils from the Buddha’s body. Hiding his own form, he manifested in the form of a brahmin youth. He stood in front of the Buddha, venerating him with cupped palms.

ud2.1:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.1:5.2.verse: who see the teaching they have learned.

ud2.1:5.3.verse: Kindness for the world is happiness

ud2.1:5.4.verse: for one who’d not harm a living creature.

ud2.1:6.1.verse: Dispassion for the world is happiness

ud2.1:6.2.verse: for one who has gone beyond sensual pleasures.

ud2.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.2:1.3.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall and this discussion came up among them:

ud2.2:1.4.verse: “Which of these two kings has greater wealth, riches, treasury, dominion, vehicles, forces, might, and power: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha or King Pasenadi of Kosala?”

ud2.2:1.5.verse: At that point the conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

ud2.2:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat, went to the assembly hall, sat down on the seat spread out,

ud2.2:2.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

ud2.2:3.1.verse: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about when the Buddha arrived. The Buddha said,

ud2.2:4.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to talk about such things.

ud2.2:4.2.verse: When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

ud2.2:4.3.verse: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.”

ud2.2:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.2:6.3.verse: is worth even a sixteenth part

ud2.2:6.4.verse: of the happiness of craving’s end.”

ud2.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.3:1.3.verse: Now at that time, between Sāvatthī and the Jeta Grove, several boys were hitting a snake with a stick.

ud2.3:1.4.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud2.3:1.5.verse: He saw the boys hitting the snake.

ud2.3:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.3:3.2.verse: so if you harm them with a stick

ud2.3:3.3.verse: in search of your own happiness,

ud2.3:3.4.verse: after death you’ll find no happiness.

ud2.3:4.2.verse: so if you don’t harm them with a stick

ud2.3:4.3.verse: in search of your own happiness,

ud2.3:4.4.verse: after death you will find happiness.”

ud2.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud2.4:1.4.verse: And the mendicant Saṅgha was also honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud2.4:1.5.verse: But the wanderers who followed other religions were not honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they didn’t receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud2.4:1.6.verse: Then those wanderers who followed other religions, unable to bear the esteem of the mendicant Saṅgha, abused, attacked, harassed, and troubled the mendicants in the village and the wilderness.

ud2.4:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

ud2.4:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.4:4.1.verse: “When struck by pleasure and pain in the village or wilderness,

ud2.4:4.2.verse: regard it not as self or alien.

ud2.4:4.4.verse: how would contacts strike one free of attachment?”

ud2.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.5:1.3.verse: Now at that time a certain lay follower from Icchānaṅgalaka arrived at Sāvatthī on some business.

ud2.5:1.4.verse: Having concluded his business in Sāvatthī he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud2.5:1.5.verse: The Buddha said this to him:

ud2.5:1.6.verse: “It’s been a long time, lay follower, since you took the opportunity to come here.”

ud2.5:2.1.verse: “For a long time I’ve wanted to come and see the Buddha, but I wasn’t able, being prevented by my many duties and responsibilities.”

ud2.5:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.5:4.1.verse: “One who has nothing is happy indeed,

ud2.5:4.2.verse: a learned person who has appraised the teaching.

ud2.5:4.3.verse: See how troubled are those with attachments,

ud2.5:4.4.verse: a person bound tight to people.”

ud2.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time a certain wanderer had a young brahmin wife who was pregnant and about to give birth.

ud2.6:1.5.verse: “Go, brahmin, bring oil for my delivery.”

ud2.6:2.2.verse: “But where, my dear, can I get oil?”

ud2.6:2.3.verse: For a second time, she said,

ud2.6:2.4.verse: “Go, brahmin, bring oil for my delivery.”

ud2.6:2.5.verse: For a second time, the wanderer said,

ud2.6:2.6.verse: “But where, my dear, can I get oil?”

ud2.6:2.7.verse: For a third time, she said,

ud2.6:2.8.verse: “Go, brahmin, bring oil for my delivery.”

ud2.6:3.1.verse: Now at that time ghee and oil were being given away to any ascetic or brahmin at the storehouse of King Pasenadi of Kosala. But it was only to drink there, not to take away.

ud2.6:4.3.verse: “Why don’t I go to the king’s storehouse, drink as much oil as I can, then come home and throw it up so it can be used for the delivery?”

ud2.6:5.1.verse: Then he did just that. But when he got home he was unable to either bring it up or pass it out.

ud2.6:5.2.verse: He rolled to and fro, suffering painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings.

ud2.6:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud2.6:6.2.verse: He saw the wanderer in agony.

ud2.6:7.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.6:8.1.verse: “Oh! How happy are those with nothing!

ud2.6:8.2.verse: Hence knowledge masters are people with nothing.

ud2.6:8.3.verse: See how troubled are those with attachments,

ud2.6:8.4.verse: a person bound tight to people.”

ud2.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud2.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time a certain lay follower’s dear and beloved only child passed away.

ud2.7:2.1.verse: Then in the middle of the day several lay followers with wet clothes and hair went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

ud2.7:2.2.verse: “Why, lay followers, have you come here in the middle of the day with wet clothes and hair?”

ud2.7:3.2.verse: “Sir, my dear and beloved only child has passed away.

ud2.7:3.3.verse: That’s why we came here in the middle of the day with wet clothes and hair.”

ud2.7:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.7:5.1.verse: “Hosts of gods and most human beings are bound

ud2.7:5.2.verse: to what seems dear and pleasant.

ud2.7:5.4.verse: they fall under the sway of the King of Death.

ud2.7:6.1.verse: The diligent, who day and night

ud2.7:6.3.verse: dig out the root of gloom—

ud2.7:6.4.verse: Death’s bait so hard to escape.”

ud2.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kuṇḍiyā in the Kuṇḍadhāna Grove.

ud2.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time Suppavāsā the Koliyan had been pregnant for seven years, and in obstructed labor for seven days.

ud2.8:1.4.verse: While suffering painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings, three thoughts helped her endure:

ud2.8:1.5.verse: “Oh! The Blessed One is indeed a fully awakened Buddha, who teaches the Dhamma for giving up suffering such as this.

ud2.8:1.6.verse: Oh! The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is indeed practicing well, who practice for giving up suffering such as this.

ud2.8:1.7.verse: Oh! Extinguishment is so very blissful, where such suffering as this is not found.”

ud2.8:2.2.verse: “Please, master, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

ud2.8:2.5.verse: ‘Suppavāsā the Koliyan has been pregnant for seven years, and in obstructed labor for seven days.

ud2.8:2.6.verse: While suffering painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings, three thoughts help her endure:

ud2.8:2.7.verse: “Oh! The Blessed One is indeed a fully awakened Buddha, who teaches the Dhamma for giving up suffering such as this.

ud2.8:2.8.verse: Oh! The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is indeed practicing well, who practice for giving up suffering such as this.

ud2.8:2.9.verse: Oh! Extinguishment is so very blissful, where such suffering as this is not found.”’”

ud2.8:3.1.verse: “Excellent idea,” he replied. He went to the Buddha and told him of his wife’s struggles. The Buddha said:

ud2.8:4.1.verse: “May Suppavāsā the Koliyan be happy and healthy! May she give birth to a healthy child!”

ud2.8:4.2.verse: As soon as he spoke, Suppavāsā, happy and healthy, gave birth to a healthy child.

ud2.8:5.1.verse: Saying “Yes, sir,” the Koliyan gentleman approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he returned to his own house.

ud2.8:5.2.verse: He saw that his wife, happy and healthy, had given birth to a healthy child,

ud2.8:5.4.verse: “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might! For as soon as he spoke, Suppavāsā, happy and healthy, gave birth to a healthy child.”

ud2.8:5.5.verse: He became uplifted and overjoyed, full of rapture and happiness.

ud2.8:6.2.verse: “Please, master, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet.

ud2.8:6.5.verse: ‘Suppavāsā the Koliyan, who was pregnant for seven years, and in obstructed labor for seven days,

ud2.8:6.6.verse: is now happy and healthy and has given birth to a healthy child.

ud2.8:6.7.verse: She invites the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha to a meal for seven days.

ud2.8:6.8.verse: Sir, would the Buddha please accept seven meals from Suppavāsā?’”

ud2.8:7.1.verse: “Excellent idea,” he replied. He went to the Buddha, told him the good news, and conveyed his wife’s invitation.

ud2.8:9.1.verse: Now at that time a certain lay follower had already invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for the meal on the following day.

ud2.8:9.2.verse: That lay follower was Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s supporter.

ud2.8:9.3.verse: Then the Buddha addressed Venerable Mahāmoggallāna,

ud2.8:9.4.verse: “Please, Moggallāna, go to that lay follower and say to him,

ud2.8:9.5.verse: ‘Suppavāsā the Koliyan, who was pregnant for seven years, and in obstructed labor for seven days,

ud2.8:9.6.verse: is now happy and healthy and has given birth to a healthy child.

ud2.8:9.7.verse: She invites the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha to a meal for seven days.

ud2.8:9.8.verse: Let Suppavāsā make seven meals, afterwards you can make yours.’

ud2.8:10.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Mahāmoggallāna. He went to that lay follower and conveyed the Buddha’s request.

ud2.8:11.1.verse: “If, sir, Master Mahāmoggallāna can guarantee me three things—

ud2.8:11.3.verse: then let Suppavāsā make seven meals, afterwards I shall make mine.”

ud2.8:11.6.verse: But as for faith, you alone are the guarantor.”

ud2.8:12.1.verse: “If, sir Master Mahāmoggallāna can guarantee me two things—

ud2.8:12.3.verse: then let Suppavāsā make seven meals, afterwards I shall make mine.”

ud2.8:13.1.verse: Having persuaded that lay follower, Mahāmoggallāna went to the Buddha and said,

ud2.8:13.3.verse: Let Suppavāsā make seven meals, afterwards he shall make his.”

ud2.8:14.1.verse: For seven days Suppavāsā served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with her own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

ud2.8:14.2.verse: And she made her little boy bow to the Buddha and the mendicant Saṅgha.

ud2.8:15.1.verse: Then Sāriputta said to the boy,

ud2.8:15.2.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, little boy, I hope you’re all right. I hope you are not in pain.”

ud2.8:15.3.verse: “How could I be keeping well? How could I be getting by?

ud2.8:15.4.verse: For seven years I lived in a pot of blood.”

ud2.8:16.2.verse: “My child is conversing with the General of the Dhamma!” was uplifted and overjoyed, full of rapture and happiness.

ud2.8:16.3.verse: Knowing this, the Buddha said to her,

ud2.8:16.4.verse: “Would you like to have another child like this?”

ud2.8:16.5.verse: “Sir, I would like to have seven more children like this!”

ud2.8:17.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.8:18.2.verse: the disliked in the guise of the liked,

ud2.8:18.3.verse: suffering in the guise of happiness,

ud2.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

ud2.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time Visākhā was caught up in some business with King Pasenadi.

ud2.9:1.4.verse: But the king’s settlement did not meet her expectations.

ud2.9:2.1.verse: Then, in the middle of the day, she went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.

ud2.9:2.3.verse: “So, Visākhā, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

ud2.9:2.4.verse: “Sir, I am caught up in some business with King Pasenadi.

ud2.9:2.5.verse: But the king’s settlement did not meet my expectations.”

ud2.9:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.9:4.2.verse: all under one’s own authority is pleasing;

ud2.9:4.3.verse: what’s shared is stressful for both parties,

ud2.9:4.4.verse: for yokes are hard to escape.”

ud2.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Anupiya in a mango grove.

ud2.10:1.3.verse: Now at that time, Venerable Bhaddiya son of Kāḷīgodhā, even in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, frequently expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.10:2.4.verse: “Without a doubt, Venerable Bhaddiya leads the spiritual life dissatisfied.

ud2.10:2.5.verse: It’s when recalling the pleasures of royalty he formerly enjoyed as a layperson that, even in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, he frequently expresses this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.10:3.1.verse: Then those mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud2.10:4.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

ud2.10:4.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Bhaddiya that

ud2.10:5.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Bhaddiya and said to him,

ud2.10:5.3.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Bhaddiya replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

ud2.10:6.1.verse: “Is it really true, Bhaddiya, that even in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, you frequently express this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.10:7.3.verse: “Formerly, as a layperson ruling the land, my guard was well organized within and without the royal compound, within and without the city, and within and without the country.

ud2.10:7.4.verse: But although I was guarded and defended in this way, I remained fearful, scared, suspicious, and nervous.

ud2.10:7.5.verse: But these days, even when alone in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, I’m not fearful, scared, suspicious, or nervous. I live relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, my heart free as a wild deer.

ud2.10:7.6.verse: It is for this reason that, even in the wilderness, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, I frequently expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.10:8.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud2.10:9.2.verse: passed beyond any kind of existence;

ud2.10:9.3.verse: happy, free from fear and sorrow—

ud2.10:9.4.verse: even the gods can’t see them.”

ud3.1:0.2.verse: Born of the Fruits of Deeds

ud3.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.1:1.3.verse: Now, at that time a certain mendicant was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight. As a result of past deeds, he suffered painful, sharp, severe, and acute feelings, which he endured unbothered, with mindfulness and awareness.

ud3.1:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating and enduring that pain.

ud3.1:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.1:4.1.verse: “A mendicant who has left all deeds behind,

ud3.1:4.2.verse: shaking off the dust of past deeds,

ud3.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.2:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Nanda, the Buddha’s brother and maternal cousin, informed several mendicants:

ud3.2:1.5.verse: I am unable to keep up the spiritual life. I shall resign the training and return to a lesser life.”

ud3.2:2.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud3.2:3.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

ud3.2:3.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Nanda that

ud3.2:3.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Nanda and said to him,

ud3.2:4.1.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Nanda replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

ud3.2:5.1.verse: “Is it really true, Nanda, that you informed several mendicants that

ud3.2:5.2.verse: you are unable to keep up the spiritual life; that you shall resign the training and return to a lesser life?”

ud3.2:6.1.verse: “But why are you so dissatisfied with the spiritual life?”

ud3.2:6.2.verse: “As I left my house, sir, the finest lady of the Sakyan land, her hair half-combed, glanced at me and said,

ud3.2:6.4.verse: Recalling that, I am dissatisfied and shall resign the training.”

ud3.2:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha took Nanda by the arm and, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from Jeta’s Grove and reappeared among the gods of the thirty-three.

ud3.2:8.1.verse: Now at that time five hundred dove-footed nymphs had come to attend to Sakka, the lord of gods.

ud3.2:8.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to Nanda,

ud3.2:8.3.verse: “Nanda, do you see these five hundred dove-footed nymphs?”

ud3.2:9.1.verse: “What do you think, Nanda? Who is more attractive, good-looking, and lovely—the finest lady of the Sakyan land, or these five hundred dove-footed nymphs?”

ud3.2:9.2.verse: “Compared to these five hundred dove-footed nymphs, the finest lady of the Sakyan land is like a deformed monkey with its ears and nose cut off.

ud3.2:9.3.verse: She doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, she’s not worth a fraction.

ud3.2:9.4.verse: These five hundred dove-footed nymphs are far more attractive, good-looking, and lovely.”

ud3.2:10.2.verse: I guarantee you five hundred dove-footed nymphs.”

ud3.2:10.3.verse: “If, sir, you guarantee me five hundred dove-footed nymphs, I shall happily lead the spiritual life under the Buddha.”

ud3.2:11.1.verse: Then the Buddha took Nanda by the arm and, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the gods of the thirty-three and reappeared at Jeta’s Grove.

ud3.2:12.2.verse: “It seems Venerable Nanda—who is both the Buddha’s half-brother and maternal cousin—leads the spiritual life for the sake of nymphs.

ud3.2:12.3.verse: And it seems that the Buddha guaranteed him five hundred dove-footed nymphs.”

ud3.2:13.1.verse: Monks who were his friends accused him of being a hireling and a lackey,

ud3.2:13.2.verse: “It seems Nanda is a hireling, it seems he is a lackey: he leads the spiritual life for the sake of nymphs.

ud3.2:13.3.verse: And it seems that the Buddha guaranteed him five hundred dove-footed nymphs.”

ud3.2:14.1.verse: Then Nanda—embarrassed, ashamed, and disgusted at being called a hireling and a lackey—living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

ud3.2:14.2.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

ud3.2:14.3.verse: Venerable Nanda became one of the perfected.

ud3.2:15.1.verse: Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him:

ud3.2:15.2.verse: “Sir, Venerable Nanda—who is both the Buddha’s half-brother and maternal cousin—has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. He lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

ud3.2:15.3.verse: And the knowledge also came to the Buddha:

ud3.2:15.4.verse: “Nanda has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. He lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

ud3.2:16.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, Nanda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

ud3.2:16.2.verse: “Worthy sir, you guaranteed me five hundred dove-footed nymphs. I release you from that promise.”

ud3.2:16.3.verse: “Nanda, I encompassed your mind and knew that

ud3.2:16.4.verse: you had realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom.

ud3.2:16.5.verse: And deities also told me about this.

ud3.2:16.7.verse: As soon as your mind was freed from defilements by not grasping, I was released from that promise.”

ud3.2:17.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.2:18.1.verse: “The mendicant who has crossed over the bog,

ud3.2:18.2.verse: who has crushed the thorn of sensuality,

ud3.2:18.3.verse: who has reached the end of delusion,

ud3.2:18.4.verse: trembles not at pleasure and pain.”

ud3.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.3:1.3.verse: Now at that time five hundred mendicants headed by Yasoja arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

ud3.3:1.4.verse: At that, those visiting mendicants, while exchanging pleasantries with the resident mendicants, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, made a colossal racket.

ud3.3:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud3.3:2.2.verse: “Ānanda, who’s making that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

ud3.3:2.3.verse: “Sir, those five hundred mendicants headed by Yasoja have arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

ud3.3:2.4.verse: It’s those visiting mendicants who, while exchanging pleasantries with the resident mendicants, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, made a colossal racket.”

ud3.3:2.5.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, in my name tell those mendicants that

ud3.3:3.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” Ānanda replied. He went to those mendicants and said,

ud3.3:3.3.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants. Then they rose from their seats and went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them,

ud3.3:4.1.verse: “Mendicants, what’s with that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

ud3.3:4.2.verse: When he said this, Venerable Yasoja said to the Buddha,

ud3.3:4.3.verse: “Sir, these five hundred mendicants have arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

ud3.3:4.4.verse: It’s these visiting mendicants who, while exchanging pleasantries with the resident mendicants, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, made a colossal racket.”

ud3.3:4.5.verse: “Go away, mendicants, I dismiss you. You are not to stay in my presence.”

ud3.3:5.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied those mendicants. They got up from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. They set their lodgings in order and left, taking their bowls and robes.

ud3.3:5.2.verse: Traveling stage by stage in the land of the Vajjis, they arrived at the Vaggumudā River. They built leaf huts near the riverbank and there they entered the rainy season.

ud3.3:6.1.verse: Then Venerable Yasoja, having entered the rainy season, addressed the mendicants:

ud3.3:6.2.verse: “Out of sympathy, reverends, the Buddha dismissed us, wanting what’s best for us.

ud3.3:6.3.verse: Come, let us live in such a way that the Buddha would be pleased with us.”

ud3.3:6.5.verse: Then those mendicants, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, all realized the three knowledges in that same rainy season.

ud3.3:7.1.verse: When the Buddha had stayed in Sāvatthī as long as he pleased, he set out for Vesālī.

ud3.3:7.2.verse: Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Vesālī,

ud3.3:7.3.verse: where he stayed in the hall with the peaked roof.

ud3.3:8.1.verse: Then, having applied his mind to comprehending the minds of the mendicants staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River, the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud3.3:8.2.verse: “A light, it appears to me, has arisen in this quarter, Ānanda; a brightness has arisen.

ud3.3:8.3.verse: I’m not put off at the thought of going to where the mendicants are staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River.

ud3.3:8.4.verse: Send a message to those mendicants:

ud3.3:8.5.verse: ‘Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.’”

ud3.3:9.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” Ānanda replied. He went to one of the mendicants and said,

ud3.3:9.2.verse: “Please, Reverend, go to the mendicants staying on the bank of the Vaggumudā River and say to them,

ud3.3:9.3.verse: ‘Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.’”

ud3.3:10.2.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof, and reappeared in front of those mendicants on the bank of the Vaggumudā River.

ud3.3:10.3.verse: Then he said to those mendicants,

ud3.3:10.4.verse: “Venerables, the Teacher summons you. He wants to see you.”

ud3.3:11.1.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants. They set their lodgings in order and took their bowls and robes.

ud3.3:11.2.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, they vanished from the bank of the Vaggumudā River, and reappeared in the presence of the Buddha in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

ud3.3:11.3.verse: But at that time the Buddha was sitting immersed in imperturbable meditation.

ud3.3:11.5.verse: “What kind of meditation is the Buddha practicing right now?”

ud3.3:11.8.verse: They all sat in imperturbable meditation.

ud3.3:12.1.verse: And then, as the night was getting late, in the first watch of the night, Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud3.3:12.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the first watch of the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.

ud3.3:12.3.verse: Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”

ud3.3:13.1.verse: For a second time, as the night was getting late, in the middle watch of the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud3.3:13.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the second watch of the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.

ud3.3:13.5.verse: Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”

ud3.3:13.6.verse: But for a second time the Buddha kept silent.

ud3.3:14.1.verse: For a third time, as the night was getting late, in the last watch of the night, as dawn stirred, bringing joy to the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud3.3:14.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the last watch of the night; dawn stirs, bringing joy to the night, and the visiting mendicants have been sitting long.

ud3.3:14.7.verse: Sir, please greet the visiting mendicants.”

ud3.3:15.1.verse: Then the Buddha emerged from that immersion and addressed Ānanda,

ud3.3:15.2.verse: “If you’d known, Ānanda, you wouldn’t have said so much.

ud3.3:15.3.verse: Both I and these five hundred mendicants have been sitting in imperturbable meditation.”

ud3.3:16.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.3:17.1.verse: “A mendicant who has beaten the thorn of sensuality—

ud3.3:17.4.verse: trembles not at pleasure and pain.”

ud3.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, his body set straight, and mindfulness brought to the present.

ud3.4:1.4.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud3.4:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.4:3.4.verse: a monk, like a mountain, doesn’t tremble.”

ud3.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.5:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight and mindfulness of the body well-established in himself.

ud3.5:1.4.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud3.5:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.5:3.2.verse: restrained in the six fields of contact,

ud3.5:3.3.verse: a mendicant always immersed in samādhi

ud3.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud3.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Pilindavaccha addressed the mendicants as “lowlifes”.

ud3.6:1.4.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

ud3.6:1.5.verse: “Sir, Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’.”

ud3.6:2.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

ud3.6:2.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Pilindavaccha that

ud3.6:2.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Pilindavaccha and said to him,

ud3.6:3.1.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Pilindavaccha replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

ud3.6:3.2.verse: “Is it really true, Vaccha, that you addressed the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’?”

ud3.6:4.1.verse: Then, having applied his mind to Pilindavaccha’s past lives, the Buddha said to the mendicants,

ud3.6:4.2.verse: “Mendicants, don’t complain about the mendicant Vaccha.

ud3.6:4.3.verse: He doesn’t address the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’ out of hate.

ud3.6:4.4.verse: For five hundred lives without interruption he was reborn in a brahmin family.

ud3.6:4.5.verse: For a long time, he has addressed people as ‘lowlife’.

ud3.6:4.6.verse: That’s why he addresses the mendicants as ‘lowlifes’.”

ud3.6:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.6:6.1.verse: “In whom dwells no deceit or conceit,

ud3.6:6.2.verse: rid of greed, unselfish, with no need for hope,

ud3.6:6.4.verse: they are a brahmin, an ascetic, a mendicant.”

ud3.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud3.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali cave. Having entered a certain state of immersion, he sat cross-legged for seven days without moving.

ud3.7:1.4.verse: When seven days had passed, Mahākassapa emerged from that state of immersion.

ud3.7:2.1.verse: Now at that time five hundred deities were ready and eager for the chance to offer alms to Mahākassapa.

ud3.7:2.2.verse: But Mahākasspa turned down those deities. In the morning, he robed up, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.

ud3.7:2.3.verse: Now at that time Sakka, lord of gods, wished to give alms to Mahākassapa.

ud3.7:3.2.verse: Having manifested in the appearance of an embroiderer, he wove the thread. The titan maiden Sujā spun it onto the spindle.

ud3.7:3.3.verse: Then, as Mahākassapa wandered indiscriminately for almsfood in Rājagaha, he approached Sakka’s house.

ud3.7:3.4.verse: Seeing Mahākassapa coming off in the distance,

ud3.7:3.5.verse: Sakka came out of his house, greeted him, and took the bowl from his hand. He re-entered the house and filled the bowl with rice from the pot.

ud3.7:3.6.verse: That almsfood had many tasty soups and sauces.

ud3.7:3.8.verse: “Now, what being is this who has such psychic power?”

ud3.7:3.11.verse: Knowing this, he said to Sakka,

ud3.7:3.13.verse: don’t do such a thing again.”

ud3.7:3.14.verse: “But Honorable Kassapa, we too need merit!

ud3.7:3.15.verse: We too ought to make merit.”

ud3.7:4.1.verse: Then Sakka bowed and respectfully circled Mahākassapa, keeping him on his right. Then he rose into the air and, sitting cross-legged in midair, expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:

ud3.7:4.2.verse: “Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!

ud3.7:4.3.verse: Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!

ud3.7:4.4.verse: Oh the gift, the best gift is well established in Kassapa!”

ud3.7:4.5.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard Sakka express this heartfelt sentiment while sitting in the sky.

ud3.7:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.7:6.3.verse: the unaffected one is envied by even the gods,

ud3.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the pavilion by the kareri tree and this discussion came up among them:

ud3.8:2.1.verse: “Reverends, when a mendicant who eats only almsfood is wandering for alms, from time to time they get to see pleasing sights, hear pleasing sounds, smell pleasing odors, taste pleasing flavors, and encounter pleasing touches.

ud3.8:2.2.verse: They wander for alms being honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed.

ud3.8:2.3.verse: Come, we too should eat only almsfood.

ud3.8:2.4.verse: From time to time we too will get to see pleasing sights, hear pleasing sounds, smell pleasing odors, taste pleasing flavors, and encounter pleasing touches.

ud3.8:2.5.verse: We too shall wander for alms being honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed.”

ud3.8:2.6.verse: At that point the conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

ud3.8:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the pavilion by the kareri tree, where he sat down on the seat spread out

ud3.8:3.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

ud3.8:4.1.verse: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about. The Buddha said,

ud3.8:6.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to talk about such things.

ud3.8:6.2.verse: When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

ud3.8:6.3.verse: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.”

ud3.8:7.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.8:8.3.verse: the unaffected one is envied by even the gods,

ud3.8:8.4.verse: but not if they’re after popularity and reputation.”

ud3.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud3.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the pavilion and this discussion came up among them:

ud3.9:2.2.verse: elephant-craft is the best of crafts.

ud3.9:2.3.verse: Others said that the best craft is

ud3.9:2.25.verse: At that point the conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

ud3.9:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,

ud3.9:3.3.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

ud3.9:4.1.verse: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about when the Buddha arrived. The Buddha said,

ud3.9:6.1.verse: “Mendicants, it is not appropriate for you gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness to talk about such things.

ud3.9:6.2.verse: When you’re sitting together you should do one of two things:

ud3.9:6.3.verse: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.”

ud3.9:7.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.9:8.1.verse: “Living without a craft, light, wanting what is best,

ud3.9:8.3.verse: a migrant with no bastion, unselfish, with no need for hope,

ud3.9:8.4.verse: having given up conceit, wandering alone: that is a mendicant.”

ud3.10:1.2.verse: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the root of the tree of awakening on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

ud3.10:1.3.verse: There the Buddha sat cross-legged for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of freedom.

ud3.10:2.1.verse: When seven days had passed, the Buddha emerged from that state of immersion and surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.

ud3.10:2.2.verse: He saw sentient beings tormented with many torments, and burning with many fevers

ud3.10:2.3.verse: born of greed, hate, and delusion.

ud3.10:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud3.10:4.2.verse: overcome by contact, speaks of disease as the self.

ud3.10:4.4.verse: it turns out to be something else.

ud3.10:5.1.verse: The world is attached to continued existence, overcome by continued existence,

ud3.10:5.2.verse: taking pleasure only in continued existence, yet it becomes something else.

ud3.10:5.3.verse: What it enjoys, that is the fear;

ud3.10:5.4.verse: what it fears, that is the suffering.

ud3.10:5.5.verse: But this spiritual life is led

ud3.10:5.6.verse: in order to give up continued existence.

ud3.10:6.1.verse: Of the ascetics and brahmins who say that through continued existence one is freed from continued existence, none are themselves freed from continued existence, I say.

ud3.10:6.2.verse: Of the ascetics and brahmins who say that through nonexistence one escapes from existence, none have themselves escaped from existence, I say.

ud3.10:7.1.verse: For this suffering originates dependent on all attachment. With the ending of all grasping there is no origination of suffering.

ud3.10:7.3.verse: Mired in many ways by ignorance, beings in love with being are not released from continued existence.

ud3.10:7.4.verse: Whatever states of continued existence there are—everywhere, all over—all are impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

ud3.10:8.1.verse: One who sees truly like this,

ud3.10:8.3.verse: gives up craving for continued existence,

ud3.10:8.4.verse: while not looking forward to nonexistence.

ud3.10:8.5.verse: Extinguishment comes from the ending of all cravings;

ud3.10:8.6.verse: fading away and cessation no residue left behind.

ud3.10:9.2.verse: for that mendicant extinguished by not grasping.

ud3.10:9.3.verse: Victorious in battle, such a one has defeated Māra;

ud3.10:9.4.verse: they’ve gone beyond all states of existence.”

ud4.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Cālikā, on the Cālikā mountain.

ud4.1:1.3.verse: Now, at that time Venerable Meghiya was the Buddha’s attendant.

ud4.1:1.4.verse: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

ud4.1:1.5.verse: “Sir, I’d like to enter Jantu village for alms.”

ud4.1:2.1.verse: Then Meghiya robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Jantu village for alms.

ud4.1:2.2.verse: After the meal, on his return from almsround in Jantu village, he went to the shore of Kimikālā River.

ud4.1:2.3.verse: As he was going for a walk along the shore of the river he saw a lovely and delightful mango grove.

ud4.1:2.4.verse: Seeing this, it occurred to him,

ud4.1:2.5.verse: “Oh, this mango grove is lovely and delightful! This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.

ud4.1:2.6.verse: If the Buddha allows me, I’ll come back to this mango grove to meditate.”

ud4.1:3.1.verse: Then Venerable Meghiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding,

ud4.1:4.8.verse: “If the Buddha allows me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

ud4.1:5.1.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

ud4.1:5.2.verse: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

ud4.1:6.1.verse: For a second time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

ud4.1:6.2.verse: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

ud4.1:6.4.verse: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

ud4.1:6.5.verse: For a second time the Buddha said,

ud4.1:6.6.verse: “We’re alone, Meghiya. Wait until another mendicant comes.”

ud4.1:7.1.verse: For a third time Meghiya said to the Buddha,

ud4.1:7.2.verse: “Sir, the Buddha has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

ud4.1:7.4.verse: If you allow me, I’ll go back to that mango grove to meditate.”

ud4.1:7.5.verse: “Meghiya, since you speak of striving in meditation, what can I say?

ud4.1:7.6.verse: Please, Meghiya, go at your convenience.”

ud4.1:8.1.verse: Then Meghiya got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went to that mango grove, and, having plunged deep into it, sat at the root of a certain tree for the day’s meditation.

ud4.1:8.2.verse: But while Meghiya was meditating in that mango grove he was beset mostly by three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts, namely,

ud4.1:9.3.verse: I’ve gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness,

ud4.1:9.4.verse: but I’m still harassed by these three kinds of bad, unskillful thoughts:

ud4.1:10.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Meghiya came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and told the Buddha what had happened.

ud4.1:11.1.verse: “Meghiya, when the heart’s release is not ripe, five things help it ripen.

ud4.1:12.1.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.

ud4.1:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

ud4.1:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant gets to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart and leads solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment when they want, without trouble or difficulty. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

ud4.1:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

ud4.1:16.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

ud4.1:16.2.verse: This is the fifth thing that, when the heart’s release is not ripe, helps it ripen.

ud4.1:16.3.verse: These are the five things that, when the heart’s release is not ripe, help it ripen.

ud4.1:17.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be ethical …

ud4.1:18.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart …

ud4.1:19.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be energetic …

ud4.1:20.1.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to be wise …

ud4.1:21.1.verse: But then, a mendicant grounded on these five things should develop four further things.

ud4.1:21.2.verse: They should develop the perception of ugliness to give up greed, love to give up hate, mindfulness of breathing to cut off thinking, and perception of impermanence to uproot the conceit ‘I am’.

ud4.1:21.3.verse: When you perceive impermanence, the perception of not-self becomes stabilized.

ud4.1:21.4.verse: Perceiving not-self, you uproot the conceit ‘I am’ and attain extinguishment in this very life.”

ud4.1:22.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.1:23.2.verse: arise, springing up in the mind.

ud4.1:23.4.verse: one with mind astray runs from one thing to the next.

ud4.1:24.2.verse: that arise, springing up in the mind,

ud4.1:24.3.verse: an awakened one—keen, restrained, and mindful—

ud4.1:24.4.verse: has given them up without remainder.”

ud4.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the sal forest of the Mallas at Upavattana near Kusinārā.

ud4.2:1.3.verse: Now at that time several mendicants were staying not far from the Buddha in a wilderness hut. They were haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, loose-tongued, unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties.

ud4.2:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw those mendicants staying nearby.

ud4.2:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.2:5.1.verse: That’s why you should guard the mind,

ud4.2:5.3.verse: and right view at the fore.

ud4.2:5.5.verse: a mendicant who has overcome dullness and drowsiness

ud4.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

ud4.3:1.3.verse: And then the Buddha left the road, went to the root of a certain tree, and sat down on the seat spread out.

ud4.3:2.1.verse: Then a certain cowherd went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud4.3:2.2.verse: The Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk.

ud4.3:3.1.verse: Then the cowherd said to the Buddha,

ud4.3:3.2.verse: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with the mendicant Saṅgha, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

ud4.3:3.4.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the cowherd rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

ud4.3:4.1.verse: And when the night had passed the cowherd had plenty of thick milk-rice prepared in his own home, with fresh ghee. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

ud4.3:4.2.verse: “Sir, it’s time. The meal is ready.”

ud4.3:5.1.verse: The Buddha robed up, took his bowl and robe and, together with the Saṅgha of monks, went to the house of that cowherd, where he sat down on the prepared seat in the dining hall.

ud4.3:5.2.verse: Then the cowherd served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with a thick milk-rice and fresh ghee.

ud4.3:5.3.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, the cowherd took a low seat and sat to one side.

ud4.3:5.4.verse: The Buddha then educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a teaching, after which he got up and left.

ud4.3:5.5.verse: But soon after the Buddha had left, the cowherd was killed by a certain man in the gap between village perimeters.

ud4.3:6.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

ud4.3:7.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.3:8.3.verse: than a hater to the hated,

ud4.3:8.4.verse: or an enemy to their foe.”

ud4.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud4.4:1.3.verse: At that time the venerables Sāriputta and Moggallāna were staying near the pigeons’ alcove.

ud4.4:1.4.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting outdoors in the moonlight, his head freshly shaven, having entered a certain state of immersion.

ud4.4:2.1.verse: Now at that time two native spirits who were friends were on their way from the north to the south on some business.

ud4.4:2.3.verse: One of the spirits said to the other,

ud4.4:2.4.verse: “I feel inspired, my dear, to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

ud4.4:2.6.verse: “Enough, my dear, don’t hit the ascetic!

ud4.4:2.7.verse: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

ud4.4:3.1.verse: For a second time the first spirit said to the other,

ud4.4:3.2.verse: “I feel inspired to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

ud4.4:3.3.verse: For a second time, the other spirit replied,

ud4.4:3.5.verse: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

ud4.4:3.6.verse: For a third time the first spirit said to the other,

ud4.4:3.7.verse: “I feel inspired to give this ascetic a blow on the head!”

ud4.4:3.8.verse: For a third time, the other spirit replied,

ud4.4:3.10.verse: That is an eminent ascetic, powerful and mighty!”

ud4.4:4.1.verse: Ignoring his friend, the first spirit struck Sāriputta.

ud4.4:4.2.verse: The blow was so strong it would have felled a bull elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall, or split apart a great mountain peak.

ud4.4:4.3.verse: But then the spirit, crying out, “I burn, I burn!” fell into the Great Hell right there.

ud4.4:5.1.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, Venerable Moggallāna saw that spirit striking Venerable Sāriputta.

ud4.4:5.3.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, reverend, I hope you’re all right. I hope you are not in pain.”

ud4.4:5.5.verse: but my head does hurt a little.”

ud4.4:6.2.verse: How mighty and powerful is Venerable Sāriputta!

ud4.4:6.3.verse: Just now, a native spirit struck you on the head.

ud4.4:6.4.verse: The blow was so strong it would have felled a bull elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall, or split apart a great mountain peak.

ud4.4:6.5.verse: Yet you say, ‘I am keeping well, Reverend Moggallāna;

ud4.4:6.6.verse: but my head does hurt a little.’”

ud4.4:7.2.verse: How mighty and powerful is Venerable Moggallāna, in that he can even see a native spirit!

ud4.4:7.3.verse: Whereas I can’t even see a mud-goblin right now.”

ud4.4:8.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard that discussion between those two spiritual giants.

ud4.4:9.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.4:10.1.verse: “One whose mind is like a rock,

ud4.4:10.3.verse: free of desire for desirable things,

ud4.4:10.4.verse: not getting annoyed when things are annoying:

ud4.4:10.5.verse: from where will suffering strike one

ud4.4:10.6.verse: whose mind is developed like this?”

ud4.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

ud4.5:1.3.verse: Now at that time Buddha lived crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples.

ud4.5:1.4.verse: Crowded, he lived in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:1.6.verse: “These days I live crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples.

ud4.5:1.7.verse: Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:1.8.verse: Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the group?”

ud4.5:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

ud4.5:2.2.verse: After the meal, on his return from almsround, he set his lodgings in order himself. Taking his bowl and robe, without informing his supporters or taking leave of the mendicant Saṅgha, he set out to go wandering alone toward Pārileyyaka, with no companion.

ud4.5:2.4.verse: he stayed in a protected forest grove, at the foot of a sacred sal tree.

ud4.5:3.1.verse: A certain bull elephant was also living crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. He ate the grass they’d trampled, and they ate the broken branches he dragged down. He drank muddy water, and after his bath the female elephants bumped into him.

ud4.5:3.2.verse: Crowded, he lived in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:3.4.verse: “These days I live crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I eat the grass they’ve trampled, and they eat the broken branches I’ve dragged down. I drink muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bump into me. Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:3.5.verse: Why don’t I live alone, withdrawn from the herd?”

ud4.5:4.1.verse: So he left the herd and went to Pārileyyaka, where he approached the Buddha in the protected forest grove at the foot of a sacred sal tree.

ud4.5:4.2.verse: There he attended on the Buddha, clearing the vegetation from the place where the Buddha stayed, and using his trunk to set out water for drinking and washing.
