ud4.5:5.1.verse: Then as the Buddha was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

ud4.5:5.2.verse: “Formerly I lived crowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples. Crowded, I live in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:5.3.verse: But now I live uncrowded by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by rulers and their chief ministers, and monastics of other religions and their disciples. Being uncrowded, I live in happiness and comfort.”

ud4.5:6.1.verse: And to the bull elephant also this thought came to mind,

ud4.5:6.2.verse: “Formerly I lived crowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I ate the grass they’d trampled, and they ate the broken branches I’d dragged down. I drank muddy water, and after my bath the female elephants bumped into me. Crowded, I lived in suffering and discomfort.

ud4.5:6.3.verse: But now I live uncrowded by other males, females, younglings, and cubs. I eat untrampled grass, and other elephants don’t eat the broken branches I have dragged down. I don’t drink muddy water, and the female elephants don’t bump into me after my bath. Being uncrowded, I live in happiness and comfort.”

ud4.5:7.1.verse: Then, understanding his own seclusion and knowing that elephant’s train of thought, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.5:8.3.verse: agrees heart to heart with the spiritual giant,

ud4.5:8.4.verse: since each finds joy in the woods alone.”

ud4.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud4.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight. He was one who lived in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and owned just three robes. He was of few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, and energetic, an advocate of austerities, dedicated to the higher mind.

ud4.6:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud4.6:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.6:4.6.verse: this is the instruction of the Buddhas.”

ud4.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud4.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight. He was of few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, energetic, dedicated to the higher mind.

ud4.7:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud4.7:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.7:4.2.verse: training in the ways of sagacity:

ud4.7:4.3.verse: there are no sorrows for the unaffected,

ud4.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud4.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud4.8:1.4.verse: And the mendicant Saṅgha was also honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud4.8:1.5.verse: But the wanderers who followed other religions were not honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they didn’t receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud4.8:2.1.verse: Then those wanderers who followed other religions, unable to bear the esteem of the mendicant Saṅgha, approached the female wanderer Sundarī and said,

ud4.8:2.2.verse: “Sister, are you able to do something for the welfare of your kin?”

ud4.8:2.5.verse: I’d even give my life for the welfare of my kin.”

ud4.8:3.1.verse: “Well then, sister, frequently visit Jeta’s Grove.”

ud4.8:3.2.verse: “Yes, masters,” she replied, and did as they asked.

ud4.8:4.2.verse: that Sundarī had been clearly seen by many people frequently visiting Jeta’s Grove,

ud4.8:4.3.verse: they killed her and dumped her in the ditch around Jeta’s Grove. Then they went to see King Pasenadi of Kosala and said to him,

ud4.8:4.4.verse: “Great king, we cannot find the female wanderer Sundarī.”

ud4.8:4.5.verse: “But where do you suspect she is?”

ud4.8:5.1.verse: So the wanderers searched Jeta’s Grove. They pulled her body up from the ditch where they had dumped it, and lifted it on a bier. Having entered Sāvatthī, they went from street to street and from square to square, complaining to people:

ud4.8:6.1.verse: “See the deed of the ascetics who follow the Sakyan!

ud4.8:6.2.verse: Shameless are these ascetics who follow the Sakyan, immoral and wicked. They are liars and unchaste.

ud4.8:6.3.verse: Sure, they claim to be of principled and moral conduct, to be chaste, truthful, ethical, and of good character.

ud4.8:6.4.verse: But they have no asceticism, no spirituality.

ud4.8:6.5.verse: Asceticism and spirituality are lost to them!

ud4.8:6.6.verse: Where is their asceticism, where their spirituality?

ud4.8:6.7.verse: They have abandoned asceticism and spirituality!

ud4.8:6.8.verse: How on earth can a man, having done a man’s business, kill a woman!”

ud4.8:7.1.verse: Then at that time when the people of Sāvatthī saw the mendicants they abused and insulted them with rude, harsh words:

ud4.8:8.1.verse: “Shameless are these ascetics who follow the Sakyan, immoral, wicked. They are liars and unchaste.

ud4.8:8.2.verse: Sure, they claim to be of principled and moral conduct, to be chaste, truthful, ethical, and of good character.

ud4.8:8.3.verse: But they have no asceticism, no spirituality.

ud4.8:8.4.verse: Asceticism and spirituality are lost to them!

ud4.8:8.5.verse: Where is their asceticism, where their spirituality?

ud4.8:8.6.verse: They have abandoned asceticism and spirituality!

ud4.8:8.7.verse: How on earth can a man, having done a man’s business, kill a woman!”

ud4.8:9.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud4.8:9.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud4.8:11.1.verse: “That rumor, mendicants, won’t last long. It will only be seven days, then it will vanish.

ud4.8:11.2.verse: So you may respond to those critics with this verse:

ud4.8:12.2.verse: as does one who denies what they did.

ud4.8:12.3.verse: Both are equal in the hereafter,

ud4.8:13.1.verse: The mendicants memorized that verse in the Buddha’s presence, then used it to respond to those critics.

ud4.8:15.2.verse: “These ascetics who follow the Sakyan didn’t do it, it was not done by them, they swear it.”

ud4.8:15.3.verse: That rumor didn’t last long. It was seven days, then it vanished.

ud4.8:16.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

ud4.8:17.2.verse: How well said this was by the Buddha:

ud4.8:17.3.verse: ‘That rumor, mendicants, won’t last long. It will only be seven days, then it will vanish.’

ud4.8:18.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.8:19.1.verse: “People out of control stab with words,

ud4.8:19.2.verse: like they stab a tusker in battle with darts.

ud4.8:19.3.verse: When they hear a harsh word spoken,

ud4.8:19.4.verse: a mendicant should endure with no anger in heart.”

ud4.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud4.9:1.3.verse: Then as Venerable Upasena son of Vaṅgantā was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:

ud4.9:1.5.verse: My Teacher is the Blessed One, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

ud4.9:1.6.verse: Well explained is the teaching and training in which I have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness.

ud4.9:1.7.verse: My spiritual companions are ethical and of good character.

ud4.9:1.9.verse: My mind is unified and serene.

ud4.9:1.10.verse: I am a perfected one who has ended the defilements.

ud4.9:1.11.verse: I am of great might and power.

ud4.9:1.12.verse: My life has been good, and my death will be good.”

ud4.9:2.1.verse: Then, knowing that Venerable Upasena’s train of thought, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.9:3.1.verse: “One who has no guilt in life,

ud4.9:3.3.verse: that attentive one who has seen the truth,

ud4.9:4.1.verse: For the mendicant with peaceful mind,

ud4.9:4.2.verse: who has cut off craving for continued existence,

ud4.9:4.4.verse: there’ll be no more future lives for them.”

ud4.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud4.10:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight, reviewing his own peacefulness.

ud4.10:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud4.10:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud4.10:4.1.verse: “With mind at peace, so full of peace,

ud4.10:4.2.verse: for a mendicant who has cut the cord,

ud5.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala was upstairs in the royal longhouse together with Queen Mallikā.

ud5.1:1.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi addressed Queen Mallikā,

ud5.1:1.5.verse: “Mallikā, is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

ud5.1:2.2.verse: But is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

ud5.1:2.3.verse: “For me also, Mallikā, there’s no one.”

ud5.1:3.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala came downstairs from the stilt longhouse, went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

ud5.1:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.1:6.1.verse: “Having explored every quarter with the mind,

ud5.1:6.2.verse: one finds no one dearer than oneself.

ud5.1:6.3.verse: Likewise for others, each holds themselves dear;

ud5.1:6.4.verse: so one who desires self-knowledge would harm no other.”

ud5.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.2:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

ud5.2:1.5.verse: How short-lived was the Blessed One’s mother! For seven days after the Blessed One was born, his mother passed away and was reborn in the host of joyful gods.”

ud5.2:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Ānanda! For the mothers of beings intent of awakening are short-lived.

ud5.2:2.2.verse: Seven days after the beings intent on awakening are born, their mothers pass away and are reborn in the host of joyful gods.”

ud5.2:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.2:4.2.verse: all depart, leaving the body behind.

ud5.2:4.3.verse: The skillful, understanding that all is lost,

ud5.2:4.4.verse: would keenly practice the spiritual life.”

ud5.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud5.3:1.3.verse: At that time in Rājagaha there was a leper called Suppabuddha.

ud5.3:1.4.verse: He was a poor person, destitute, and pitiful.

ud5.3:1.5.verse: Now, at that time the Buddha was teaching Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.

ud5.3:2.1.verse: Suppabuddha saw the crowd seated off in the distance

ud5.3:2.3.verse: “Surely some fresh and cooked foods will be distributed there.

ud5.3:2.4.verse: Why don’t I approach the crowd?

ud5.3:2.5.verse: Hopefully I’ll get something to eat.”

ud5.3:3.2.verse: where he saw the Buddha teaching Dhamma, surrounded by a large assembly.

ud5.3:3.3.verse: When he saw this he thought,

ud5.3:3.5.verse: The ascetic Gotama is teaching Dhamma in an assembly.

ud5.3:3.6.verse: Why don’t I also listen to the teaching?”

ud5.3:3.7.verse: Right there he sat down to one side, thinking,

ud5.3:3.8.verse: “I also will listen to the teaching.”

ud5.3:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha focused on encompassing the minds of everyone in the assembly, thinking,

ud5.3:4.2.verse: “Who here is capable of understanding the teaching?”

ud5.3:4.3.verse: He saw Suppabuddha sitting in the assembly,

ud5.3:4.5.verse: “He is capable of understanding the teaching.”

ud5.3:4.6.verse: He gave a step by step talk especially for Suppabuddha

ud5.3:4.7.verse: on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

ud5.3:4.8.verse: When the Buddha knew that Suppabuddha’s mind was ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

ud5.3:4.9.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

ud5.3:4.10.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

ud5.3:4.11.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Suppabuddha:

ud5.3:4.12.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

ud5.3:5.1.verse: Then Suppabuddha saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. He went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. He rose from his seat and went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said:

ud5.3:6.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

ud5.3:6.3.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

ud5.3:6.4.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

ud5.3:7.1.verse: After Suppabuddha had been educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired with a Dhamma talk by the Buddha, he got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

ud5.3:7.2.verse: But soon after Suppabuddha had left, a cow with a baby calf charged at him and took his life.

ud5.3:8.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said,

ud5.3:8.3.verse: “The leper named Suppabuddha, after being educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired with a Dhamma talk by the Buddha, has passed away.

ud5.3:8.4.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

ud5.3:9.1.verse: “Mendicants, Suppabuddha was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

ud5.3:9.2.verse: With the ending of three fetters, Suppabuddha is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

ud5.3:10.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

ud5.3:10.2.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why Suppabuddha became a leper,

ud5.3:10.3.verse: a poor person, destitute, and pitiful?”

ud5.3:11.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Suppabuddha used to be a financier’s son right here in Rājagaha.

ud5.3:11.2.verse: On his way to visit a park, he saw Tagarasikhī, an independent Buddha, entering the city for alms.

ud5.3:11.3.verse: When he saw this he thought,

ud5.3:11.4.verse: “Who is this leper wandering about with his leper’s robe?”

ud5.3:11.5.verse: Before leaving, he spat on the ground and turned his left side to Tagarasikhī.

ud5.3:11.6.verse: As a result of that deed he burned in hell for many years, for many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of years.

ud5.3:11.7.verse: And as a residual result of that same deed, he became a leper right here in Rājagaha, a poor person, destitute and pitiful.

ud5.3:11.8.verse: But owing to faith in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, he undertook ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

ud5.3:11.9.verse: After undertaking these things, when his body broke up, after death, he was reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

ud5.3:11.10.verse: There he outshines the other gods in beauty and glory.”

ud5.3:12.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.3:13.1.verse: “As a clear-eyed man would avoid rough paths,

ud5.3:13.2.verse: so long as strength is found;

ud5.3:13.3.verse: an astute person in the living world,

ud5.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time, between Sāvatthī and the Jeta Grove, several boys were tormenting some fish.

ud5.4:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud5.4:2.2.verse: He saw the boys tormenting the fish.

ud5.4:2.3.verse: He went to them and said,

ud5.4:2.4.verse: “Boys, do you fear pain? Do you dislike pain?”

ud5.4:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.4:5.1.verse: If you should do a bad deed,

ud5.4:5.3.verse: you won’t be freed from suffering,

ud5.4:5.4.verse: though you fly away and flee.”

ud5.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

ud5.5:1.3.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath, and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

ud5.5:2.1.verse: And then, as the night was getting late, in the first watch of the night, Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud5.5:2.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the first watch of the night, and the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting long.

ud5.5:2.3.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

ud5.5:2.4.verse: But when he said this, the Buddha kept silent.

ud5.5:3.1.verse: For a second time, as the night was getting late, in the middle watch of the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud5.5:3.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the middle watch of the night, and the Saṅgha of monks has been sitting long.

ud5.5:3.3.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

ud5.5:3.4.verse: But for a second time the Buddha kept silent.

ud5.5:4.1.verse: For a third time, as the night was getting late, in the last watch of the night, as dawn stirred, bringing joy to the night, Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha and said,

ud5.5:4.2.verse: “Sir, the night is getting late. It is the last watch of the night and dawn stirs, bringing joy to the night.

ud5.5:4.3.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

ud5.5:5.4.verse: Then he focused on encompassing the minds of everyone in the Saṅgha.

ud5.5:5.5.verse: He saw that unethical individual, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved, sitting in the middle of the Saṅgha.

ud5.5:5.6.verse: When he saw him he rose from his seat, went up to him and said,

ud5.5:5.7.verse: “Get up, reverend. The Buddha has seen you.

ud5.5:5.8.verse: You can’t live in communion with the monks.”

ud5.5:5.9.verse: But when he said this, that individual kept silent.

ud5.5:6.1.verse: For a second time and a third time,

ud5.5:6.2.verse: he asked that monk to leave.

ud5.5:6.5.verse: But for a third time that individual kept silent.

ud5.5:7.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna took that individual by the arm, ejected him out the gate, and bolted the door. Then he went up to the Buddha, and said to him,

ud5.5:7.4.verse: Please, sir, may the Buddha recite the monastic code to the monks.”

ud5.5:7.6.verse: how that futile man waited to be taken by the arm!”

ud5.5:8.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the monks,

ud5.5:8.2.verse: “From this day forth, monks, I will not perform the sabbath or recite the monastic code.

ud5.5:8.3.verse: Now you should perform the sabbath and recite the monastic code.

ud5.5:8.4.verse: It’s impossible, monks, it can’t happen that a Realized One could recite the monastic code in an impure assembly.

ud5.5:9.1.verse: Seeing these eight incredible and amazing things the titans love the ocean.

ud5.5:10.1.verse: The ocean gradually slants, slopes, and inclines, with no abrupt precipice.

ud5.5:10.3.verse: This is the first thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:11.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean is consistent and doesn’t overflow its boundaries.

ud5.5:11.3.verse: This is the second thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:12.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean doesn’t accommodate a carcass, but quickly carries it to the shore and strands it on the beach.

ud5.5:12.3.verse: This is the third thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:13.1.verse: Furthermore, when they reach the ocean, all the great rivers—that is, the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—lose their names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘the ocean’.

ud5.5:13.3.verse: This is the fourth thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:14.1.verse: Furthermore, for all the world’s streams that reach it, and the showers that fall from the sky, the ocean never empties or fills up.

ud5.5:14.3.verse: This is the fifth thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:15.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean has just one taste, the taste of salt.

ud5.5:15.3.verse: This is the sixth thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:16.1.verse: Furthermore, the ocean is full of many kinds of treasures, such as pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, native gold, rubies, and emeralds.

ud5.5:16.3.verse: This is the seventh thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:17.1.verse: Furthermore, many great beings live in the ocean, such as leviathans, leviathan-gulpers, leviathan-gulper-gulpers, titans, dragons, and centaurs. In the ocean there are life-forms a hundred leagues long, or even two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred leagues long.

ud5.5:17.3.verse: This is the eighth thing the titans love about the ocean.

ud5.5:17.4.verse: Seeing these eight incredible and amazing things the titans love the ocean.

ud5.5:18.1.verse: In the same way, seeing eight incredible and amazing things, monks, the mendicants love this teaching and training.

ud5.5:19.1.verse: The ocean gradually slants, slopes, and inclines, with no abrupt precipice.

ud5.5:19.2.verse: In the same way in this teaching and training the penetration to enlightenment comes from gradual training, progress, and practice, not abruptly.

ud5.5:19.4.verse: This is the first thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:20.1.verse: The ocean is consistent and doesn’t overflow its boundaries.

ud5.5:20.2.verse: In the same way, when a training rule is laid down for my disciples they wouldn’t break it even for the sake of their own life.

ud5.5:20.4.verse: This is the second thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:21.1.verse: The ocean doesn’t accommodate a carcass, but quickly carries it to the shore and strands it on the beach.

ud5.5:21.2.verse: In the same way, the Saṅgha doesn’t accommodate an individual who is unethical, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved. But they quickly gather and expel them. Even if such an individual is sitting in the middle of the Saṅgha, they’re far from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from them.

ud5.5:21.4.verse: This is the third thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:22.1.verse: Furthermore, when they reach the ocean, all the great rivers—that is, the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—lose their names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘the ocean’.

ud5.5:22.2.verse: In the same way, when they go forth from the lay life to homelessness, all four classes—aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials—lose their former names and clans and are simply reckoned as ‘ascetics who follow the Sakyan’.

ud5.5:22.4.verse: This is the fourth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:23.1.verse: For all the world’s streams that reach it, and the showers that fall from the sky, the ocean never empties or fills up.

ud5.5:23.2.verse: In the same way, though several mendicants become fully extinguished in the element of extinguishment with no residue, the element of extinguishment never empties or fills up.

ud5.5:23.4.verse: This is the fifth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:24.1.verse: The ocean has just one taste, the taste of salt.

ud5.5:24.2.verse: In the same way, this teaching and training has one taste, the taste of freedom.

ud5.5:24.4.verse: This is the sixth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:25.1.verse: The ocean is full of many kinds of treasures, such as pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, native gold, rubies, and emeralds.

ud5.5:25.2.verse: In the same way, this teaching and training is full of many kinds of treasures, such as the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

ud5.5:25.4.verse: This is the seventh thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:26.1.verse: Many great beings live in the ocean, such as leviathans, leviathan-gulpers, leviathan-gulper-gulpers, titans, dragons, and centaurs. In the ocean there are life-forms a hundred leagues long, or even two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred leagues long.

ud5.5:26.2.verse: In the same way, great beings live in this teaching and training, and these are those beings. The stream-enterer and the one practicing to realize the fruit of stream-entry. The once-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of once-return. The non-returner and the one practicing to realize the fruit of non-return. The perfected one, and the one practicing for perfection.

ud5.5:26.4.verse: This is the eighth thing the mendicants love about this teaching and training.

ud5.5:26.5.verse: Seeing these eight incredible and amazing things, the mendicants love this teaching and training.”

ud5.5:27.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.5:28.1.verse: “The rain saturates things that are covered up;

ud5.5:28.2.verse: it doesn’t saturate things that are open.

ud5.5:28.3.verse: Therefore you should open up a covered thing,

ud5.5:28.4.verse: so the rain will not saturate it.”

ud5.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis near Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain.

ud5.6:1.4.verse: And the layman Soṇa of the Sharp Ears was Mahākaccāna’s attendant.

ud5.6:2.1.verse: Then as Soṇa was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

ud5.6:2.2.verse: “As I understand Master Mahākaccāna’s teachings, it’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

ud5.6:2.3.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from lay life to homelessness?”

ud5.6:3.1.verse: Then Soṇa went up to Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what he was thinking. Then he said,

ud5.6:4.4.verse: “May Master Mahākaccāna please give me the going forth!”

ud5.6:5.1.verse: When this was said, Mahākaccāna said to him,

ud5.6:5.2.verse: “It’s hard to lead the spiritual life as long as you live, eating in one part of the day and sleeping alone.

ud5.6:5.3.verse: Come now, Soṇa, while remaining a layperson just as you are, devote yourself to the instructions of the Buddhas, leading the spiritual life at suitable times, eating in one part of the day and sleeping alone.”

ud5.6:5.4.verse: Then Soṇa’s aspiration to go forth died down.

ud5.6:6.1.verse: For a second time, while in private retreat the thought came to Soṇa that he should go forth, but the outcome was the same.

ud5.6:7.1.verse: For a third time, as Soṇa was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

ud5.6:7.2.verse: “As I understand Master Mahākaccāna’s teachings, it’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

ud5.6:7.3.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from lay life to homelessness?”

ud5.6:7.4.verse: For a third time, Soṇa went up to Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what he was thinking. Then he said,

ud5.6:8.4.verse: “May Master Mahākaccāna please give me the going forth!”

ud5.6:9.1.verse: Then Mahākaccāna gave Soṇa the going forth.

ud5.6:9.2.verse: Now at that time the southern region, including Avanti, was short of monks.

ud5.6:9.3.verse: It took three years and much struggle and difficulty before Venerable Mahākaccāna was able to assemble from here and there a Saṅgha consisting of ten monks and give Venerable Soṇa the full ordination.

ud5.6:10.1.verse: Then as Venerable Soṇa was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

ud5.6:10.2.verse: “I have not personally seen the Buddha. I have only heard reports that

ud5.6:10.3.verse: that Blessed One is like this or like that.

ud5.6:10.4.verse: If my mentor allows, I should go to see that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.”

ud5.6:11.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Soṇa came out of retreat, went up to Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what he was thinking. Then Mahākaccāna said,

ud5.6:13.2.verse: Go to see the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

ud5.6:13.3.verse: You will see that Blessed One who is impressive and inspiring, with peaceful faculties and heart, attained to the highest self-control and serenity, like an elephant with tamed, guarded, and controlled faculties.

ud5.6:13.4.verse: On seeing him, in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably, saying,

ud5.6:13.5.verse: ‘Sir, my mentor Venerable Mahākaccāna bows with his head to your feet. He asks if you are healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.’”

ud5.6:14.1.verse: Saying, “Yes, sir,” Soṇa welcomed and agreed with Mahākaccāna’s words. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled Mahākaccāna, keeping him on his right. Then he set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, set out for Sāvatthī.

ud5.6:14.2.verse: Eventually he came to Sāvatthī and Jeta’s Grove. He went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud5.6:14.4.verse: “Sir, my mentor Venerable Mahākaccāna bows with his head to your feet. He asks if you are healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.”

ud5.6:15.1.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, mendicant, I hope you’re all right. And I hope you have arrived from your journey unwearied, having had no trouble getting almsfood.”

ud5.6:15.2.verse: “I’m keeping well, Blessed One, I’m all right. And I have arrived from my journey unwearied, having had no trouble getting almsfood.”

ud5.6:16.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud5.6:16.5.verse: to prepare lodgings for a specific mendicant, he wishes to stay in the same dwelling with that mendicant. The Buddha wishes to stay together with Venerable Soṇa.”

ud5.6:16.6.verse: He prepared lodgings for Soṇa in the same dwelling where the Buddha was staying.

ud5.6:17.1.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night sitting meditation in the open. Then he got up from his seat, washed his feet, and entered the dwelling.

ud5.6:17.3.verse: Then the Buddha rose at the crack of dawn and addressed Soṇa,

ud5.6:17.4.verse: “Speak some Dhamma, mendicant, as you feel inspired.”

ud5.6:18.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Soṇa. He intoned all sixteen discourses in the Chapter of the Eights.

ud5.6:18.2.verse: When Soṇa finished his intoning, the Buddha applauded, saying,

ud5.6:18.3.verse: “Good, good, mendicant! You have learned the sixteen discourses of the Chapter of the Eights well, you have applied the mind and remembered it well. You are a good speaker, with a polished, clear, and articulate voice that expresses the meaning.

ud5.6:18.4.verse: How many rains have you been ordained, mendicant?”

ud5.6:18.6.verse: “But why did it take you so long to make it?”

ud5.6:18.7.verse: “Sir, I have long seen the drawbacks of sensual pleasures,

ud5.6:18.8.verse: yet living in a house is cramped, with many duties and much to do.”

ud5.6:19.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.6:20.2.verse: I understood the truth without attachments.

ud5.6:20.3.verse: The Noble One does not delight in evil,

ud5.6:20.4.verse: the Pure One does not delight in evil.”

ud5.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Revata the Doubter was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight, reviewing his own purification by traversing doubt.

ud5.7:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud5.7:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.7:4.1.verse: “Any doubts about this life or the next,

ud5.7:4.2.verse: about one’s own experiences or those of another:

ud5.7:4.3.verse: those who meditate give them all up,

ud5.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud5.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

ud5.8:2.1.verse: Devadatta saw him wandering for alms,

ud5.8:2.2.verse: so he went up to him and said,

ud5.8:2.3.verse: “From this day forth, Reverend Ānanda, I shall perform the sabbath and legal proceedings of the Saṅgha apart from the Buddha and the Saṅgha of mendicants.”

ud5.8:3.1.verse: Then Ānanda wandered for alms in Rājagaha. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

ud5.8:3.2.verse: and told him what had just happened, adding:

ud5.8:4.5.verse: “Today, sir, Devadatta will split the Saṅgha. He will perform the sabbath and legal proceedings of the Saṅgha.”

ud5.8:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.8:6.1.verse: “It’s easy for the good to do good,

ud5.8:6.2.verse: but for the bad, doing good is hard.

ud5.8:6.3.verse: For the bad, it’s easy to do bad,

ud5.8:6.4.verse: but for the noble ones, doing bad is hard.”

ud5.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

ud5.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time several young students were passing by not far from the Buddha in a teasing manner.

ud5.9:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.9:3.2.verse: they talk, their words out of bounds.

ud5.9:3.3.verse: They blab at will, their mouths agape,

ud5.9:3.4.verse: and no one knows what leads them on.”

ud5.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud5.10:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, his body set straight, and mindfulness brought to the present.

ud5.10:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud5.10:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud5.10:4.3.verse: a mendicant focusing on this mindfulness

ud5.10:4.5.verse: And when they have done so,

ud5.10:4.6.verse: they vanish from the King of Death.”

ud6.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

ud6.1:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.

ud6.1:1.4.verse: Then, after the meal, on his return from almsround, he addressed Venerable Ānanda:

ud6.1:1.6.verse: Let’s go to the Cāpāla Shrine for the day’s meditation.”

ud6.1:2.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. Taking his sitting cloth he followed behind the Buddha.

ud6.1:2.2.verse: Then the Buddha went up to the Cāpāla Shrine, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

ud6.1:2.3.verse: When he was seated he said to Venerable Ānanda:

ud6.1:3.1.verse: “Ānanda, Vesālī is lovely. And the Udena, Gotamaka, Seven Maidens, Many Sons, Sārandada, and Cāpāla Shrines are all lovely.

ud6.1:3.2.verse: Whoever has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power—made them a vehicle and a basis, kept them up, consolidated them, and properly implemented them—may, if they wish, live for the proper lifespan or what’s left of it.

ud6.1:3.3.verse: The Realized One has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power, made them a vehicle and a basis, kept them up, consolidated them, and properly implemented them. If he wished, the Realized One could live for the proper lifespan or what’s left of it.”

ud6.1:4.1.verse: But Ānanda didn’t get it, even though the Buddha dropped such an obvious hint, such a clear sign.

ud6.1:4.3.verse: “Sir, may the Blessed One please remain for the proper lifespan! May the Holy One please remain for the proper lifespan! That would be for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.” For his mind was as if possessed by Māra.

ud6.1:4.5.verse: For a third time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:

ud6.1:5.1.verse: “Ānanda, Vesālī is lovely. And the Udena, Gotamaka, Seven Maidens, Many Sons, Sārandada, and Cāpāla Shrines are all lovely.

ud6.1:5.2.verse: Whoever has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power—made them a vehicle and a basis, kept them up, consolidated them, and properly implemented them—may, if they wish, live for the proper lifespan or what’s left of it.

ud6.1:5.3.verse: The Realized One has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power, made them a vehicle and a basis, kept them up, consolidated them, and properly implemented them. If he wished, the Realized One could live for the proper lifespan or what’s left of it.”

ud6.1:6.1.verse: But Ānanda didn’t get it, even though the Buddha dropped such an obvious hint, such a clear sign.

ud6.1:6.3.verse: “Sir, may the Blessed One please remain for the proper lifespan! May the Holy One please remain for the proper lifespan! That would be for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.” For his mind was as if possessed by Māra.

ud6.1:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud6.1:7.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before sitting at the root of a tree close by.

ud6.1:8.1.verse: And then, not long after Ānanda had left, Māra the Wicked went up to the Buddha, stood to one side, and said to him:

ud6.1:9.1.verse: “May the Blessed One now be fully extinguished! May the Holy One now be fully extinguished! Now is the time for the full extinguishment of the Buddha.

ud6.1:9.2.verse: Sir, you once made this statement:

ud6.1:9.3.verse: ‘Wicked One, I shall not be fully extinguished until I have monk disciples who are competent, educated, assured, learned, have memorized the teachings, and practice in line with the principle of the teaching. Not until they practice properly, living in line with the teaching. Not until they’ve learned their own denomination, and explain, teach, assert, establish, disclose, analyze, and make it clear. Not until they can legitimately and completely refute the doctrines of others that come up, and teach with a demonstrable basis.’

ud6.1:9.4.verse: Today you do have such monk disciples.

ud6.1:9.5.verse: May the Blessed One now be fully extinguished! May the Holy One now be fully extinguished! Now is the time for the full extinguishment of the Buddha.

ud6.1:10.1.verse: Sir, you once made this statement:

ud6.1:10.2.verse: ‘Wicked One, I shall not be fully extinguished until I have nun disciples who are competent, educated, self-assured, learned …’ …

ud6.1:10.3.verse: Today you do have such nun disciples.

ud6.1:11.2.verse: ‘Wicked One, I shall not be fully extinguished until I have layman disciples who are competent, educated, self-assured, learned …’

ud6.1:11.3.verse: Today you do have such layman disciples.

ud6.1:12.2.verse: ‘Wicked One, I shall not be fully extinguished until I have laywoman disciples who are competent, educated, self-assured, learned …’

ud6.1:12.3.verse: Today you do have such laywoman disciples.

ud6.1:12.4.verse: May the Blessed One now be fully extinguished! May the Holy One now be fully extinguished! Now is the time for the full extinguishment of the Buddha.

ud6.1:13.1.verse: Sir, you once made this statement:

ud6.1:13.2.verse: ‘I shall not be fully extinguished until my spiritual path is successful and prosperous, extensive, popular, widespread, and fully revealed among gods and humans.’

ud6.1:13.3.verse: Today your spiritual path is successful and prosperous, extensive, popular, widespread, and fully revealed among gods and humans.

ud6.1:13.4.verse: May the Blessed One now be fully extinguished! May the Holy One now be fully extinguished! Now is the time for the full extinguishment of the Buddha.”

ud6.1:14.1.verse: When this was said, the Buddha said to Māra,

ud6.1:14.2.verse: “Relax, Wicked One. The full extinguishment of the Realized One will be soon.

ud6.1:14.3.verse: Three months from now the Realized One will be fully extinguished.”

ud6.1:15.1.verse: So at the Cāpāla Shrine the Buddha, mindful and aware, surrendered the life force.

ud6.1:15.2.verse: When he did so there was a great earthquake, awe-inspiring and hair-raising, and thunder cracked the sky.

ud6.1:16.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.1:17.1.verse: “Comparing the incomparable with the creation of prolonged life,

ud6.1:17.2.verse: the sage surrendered the life force.

ud6.1:17.4.verse: he shattered self-creation like a suit of armor.”

ud6.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

ud6.2:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and sat outside the gate.

ud6.2:1.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud6.2:2.1.verse: Now at that time seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain ascetics, seven naked ascetics, seven one-cloth ascetics, and seven wanderers passed by not far from the Buddha. Their armpits and bodies were hairy, and their nails were long; and they carried their pack with shoulder-poles.

ud6.2:3.1.verse: King Pasenadi saw them passing by.

ud6.2:3.2.verse: He got up from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his joined palms toward those various ascetics, and pronounced his name three times:

ud6.2:3.3.verse: “Sirs, I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!

ud6.2:3.4.verse: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!

ud6.2:3.5.verse: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!”

ud6.2:4.1.verse: Then, not long after those ascetics had left, King Pasenadi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

ud6.2:4.2.verse: “Sir, these are among those in the world who are perfected or who are on the path to perfection!”

ud6.2:5.1.verse: “Great king, as a layman enjoying sensual pleasures, living at home with your children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency, it’s hard for you to know who is perfected or on the path to perfection.

ud6.2:6.1.verse: You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

ud6.2:6.2.verse: You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …

ud6.2:6.3.verse: You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …

ud6.2:6.4.verse: You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.”

ud6.2:7.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha. …

ud6.2:8.1.verse: Sir, these are my spies, my undercover agents returning after spying on the country.

ud6.2:8.2.verse: I shall later make use of what they first spied out.

ud6.2:8.3.verse: Now—when they have rinsed off the dust and dirt, and are nicely bathed and anointed, with hair and beard dressed, and dressed in white—they will amuse themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.”

ud6.2:9.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.2:10.4.verse: and don’t use the teaching to make money.”

ud6.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.3:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was sitting reviewing his own giving up of many bad, unskillful qualities, and the many skillful qualities he had fully developed.

ud6.3:2.1.verse: Then, knowing the many bad, unskillful qualities that he had given up and the many skillful qualities he had fully developed, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.3:3.2.verse: what before was not then was.

ud6.3:3.3.verse: It never was, nor will it be,

ud6.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time several ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers who followed various other religions were residing in Sāvatthī, holding different views, beliefs, and opinions, relying on different views.

ud6.4:2.1.verse: There were some ascetics and brahmins who had this doctrine and view:

ud6.4:2.2.verse: “The cosmos is eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

ud6.4:3.1.verse: Others held views such as the following, each regarding their own view as true and others as silly.

ud6.4:6.2.verse: “The soul and the body are one and the same.”

ud6.4:7.2.verse: “The soul is one thing, the body another.”

ud6.4:8.2.verse: “A realized one still exists after death.”

ud6.4:9.2.verse: “A realized one no longer exists after death.”

ud6.4:10.2.verse: “A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death.”

ud6.4:11.2.verse: “A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death.”

ud6.4:12.1.verse: They were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words:

ud6.4:12.2.verse: “Such is Truth, such is not Truth!

ud6.4:12.3.verse: Such is not Truth, such is Truth!”

ud6.4:13.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud6.4:13.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening. The Buddha said:

ud6.4:16.1.verse: “The wanderers of other religions are blind and sightless.

ud6.4:16.2.verse: They don’t understand what is beneficial or what is not beneficial, nor what is the truth and what is not the truth.

ud6.4:16.3.verse: That’s why they are fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

ud6.4:17.1.verse: Once upon a time, mendicants, right here in Sāvatthī there was a certain king.

ud6.4:17.2.verse: Then the king addressed a man,

ud6.4:17.3.verse: ‘Please, my man, gather all those blind from birth throughout Sāvatthī and bring them together in one place.’

ud6.4:17.4.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ that man replied. He did as the king asked, then said to him,

ud6.4:17.5.verse: ‘Your Majesty, the blind people throughout Sāvatthī have been gathered.’

ud6.4:17.6.verse: ‘Well then, lad, show them an elephant.’

ud6.4:17.7.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ that man replied. He did as the king asked.

ud6.4:18.1.verse: To some of the blind people he showed the elephant’s head, saying,

ud6.4:18.3.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s ear, saying,

ud6.4:18.5.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s tusk, saying,

ud6.4:18.7.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s trunk, saying,

ud6.4:18.9.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s flank, saying,

ud6.4:18.11.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s leg, saying,

ud6.4:18.13.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s thigh, saying,

ud6.4:18.15.verse: To some of them he showed the elephant’s tail, saying,

ud6.4:18.17.verse: To some of them he showed the tip of the elephant’s tail, saying,

ud6.4:19.1.verse: Then he approached the king and said,

ud6.4:19.2.verse: ‘Your Majesty, the blind people have been shown the elephant.

ud6.4:20.1.verse: Then the king went up to the blind people and said,

ud6.4:20.3.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty, we have been shown the elephant.’

ud6.4:20.4.verse: ‘Then tell us, what kind of thing is an elephant?’

ud6.4:21.1.verse: The blind people who had been shown the elephant’s head said,

ud6.4:21.2.verse: ‘Your Majesty, an elephant is like a pot.’

ud6.4:22.1.verse: Those who had been shown the ear said,

ud6.4:22.2.verse: ‘An elephant is like a winnowing fan.’

ud6.4:23.1.verse: Those who had been shown the tusk said,

ud6.4:24.1.verse: Those who had been shown the trunk said,

ud6.4:25.1.verse: Those who had been shown the flank said,

ud6.4:26.1.verse: Those who had been shown the leg said,

ud6.4:27.1.verse: Those who had been shown the thigh said,

ud6.4:28.1.verse: Those who had been shown the tail said,

ud6.4:29.1.verse: Those who had been shown the tip of the tail said,

ud6.4:30.1.verse: Saying, ‘Such is an elephant, not such!

ud6.4:30.2.verse: Such is not an elephant, such is!’ they punched each other with their fists.

ud6.4:30.3.verse: At that, the king was pleased.

ud6.4:31.1.verse: In the same way, mendicants, the wanderers of other religions are blind and sightless.

ud6.4:31.2.verse: They don’t understand what is beneficial or what is not beneficial, nor what is the truth and what is not the truth.

ud6.4:31.3.verse: That’s why they are fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

ud6.4:31.5.verse: Such is not Truth, such is!’”

ud6.4:32.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.4:33.4.verse: the folk who see just one part.”

ud6.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.5:1.3.verse: Now at that time several ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers who followed various other religions were residing in Sāvatthī, holding different views, beliefs, and opinions, relying on different views.

ud6.5:2.1.verse: There were some ascetics and brahmins who had this doctrine and view:

ud6.5:2.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

ud6.5:3.1.verse: Others held views such as the following, each regarding their own view as true and others as silly.

ud6.5:3.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are not eternal.”

ud6.5:4.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are both eternal and not eternal.”

ud6.5:5.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are neither eternal nor not eternal.”

ud6.5:6.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by oneself.”

ud6.5:7.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by another.”

ud6.5:8.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by both oneself and another.”

ud6.5:9.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos have arisen anomalously, not made by oneself or another.”

ud6.5:10.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:11.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:12.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are both eternal and not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:13.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are neither eternal nor not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:14.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by oneself, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:15.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:16.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by both oneself and another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:17.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain have arisen anomalously, not made by oneself or another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.5:18.1.verse: They were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words:

ud6.5:18.2.verse: “Such is Truth, such is not Truth!

ud6.5:18.3.verse: Such is not Truth, such is Truth!”

ud6.5:19.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud6.5:19.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud6.5:23.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time several ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers who followed various other religions were residing in Sāvatthī, holding different views, beliefs, and opinions, relying on different views.

ud6.6:2.1.verse: There were some ascetics and brahmins who had this doctrine and view:

ud6.6:2.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

ud6.6:3.1.verse: Others held views such as the following, each regarding their own view as true and others as silly.

ud6.6:3.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are not eternal.”

ud6.6:4.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are both eternal and not eternal.”

ud6.6:5.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are neither eternal nor not eternal.”

ud6.6:6.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by oneself.”

ud6.6:7.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by another.”

ud6.6:8.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos are made by both oneself and another.”

ud6.6:9.2.verse: “The self and the cosmos have arisen anomalously, not made by oneself or another.”

ud6.6:10.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:11.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:12.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are both eternal and not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:13.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are neither eternal nor not eternal, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:14.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by oneself, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:15.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:16.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain are made by both oneself and another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:17.2.verse: “Pleasure and pain have arisen anomalously, not made by oneself or another, and the self and the cosmos.”

ud6.6:18.1.verse: They were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words:

ud6.6:18.2.verse: “Such is Truth, such is not Truth!

ud6.6:18.3.verse: Such is not Truth, such is Truth!”

ud6.6:19.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud6.6:19.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud6.6:23.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.6:24.2.verse: which is tied up with the other-maker.

ud6.6:24.3.verse: There are some who do not realize this,

ud6.6:24.4.verse: they do not see the dart.

ud6.6:25.1.verse: But when they see this dart,

ud6.6:25.2.verse: they do not think, ‘I make it’,

ud6.6:26.1.verse: These folk are caught up in conceit,

ud6.6:26.2.verse: tied by conceit, shackled by conceit.

ud6.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Subhūti was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight, having attained the immersion free of placing the mind.

ud6.7:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud6.7:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.7:4.1.verse: “In whom mental vibrations are cleared away,

ud6.7:4.4.verse: having overcome the four yokes, they never return.”

ud6.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud6.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time two gangs were both hopelessly in love with a certain courtesan.

ud6.8:1.4.verse: Fighting, quarreling, and disputing, they attacked each other with fists, stones, rods, and swords,

ud6.8:1.5.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

ud6.8:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Rājagaha for alms.

ud6.8:2.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud6.8:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.8:5.1.verse: “What has been attained and what is to be attained are both strewn over with dust for that one training while still sick.

ud6.8:5.2.verse: Those for whom the training is the essence, or precepts and observances, chastity, and service as the essence: this is one extreme.

ud6.8:5.4.verse: ‘There’s nothing wrong with sensual pleasures’: this is the second extreme.

ud6.8:5.5.verse: Thus these two extremes swell the charnel grounds, while the charnel grounds swell wrong view.

ud6.8:5.6.verse: Not realizing these two extremes, some get stuck and some overreach.

ud6.8:5.7.verse: For those who realize these things, who were not found there, who did not conceive by that, there is no cycle of rebirths to be found.”

ud6.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was meditating in the open during the dark of night, while oil lamps were burning.

ud6.9:2.1.verse: And many moths were falling down and crashing down into the lamps, coming to grief and ruin.

ud6.9:2.2.verse: The Buddha saw the moths coming to grief.

ud6.9:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.9:4.3.verse: Like moths falling in the flame,

ud6.9:4.4.verse: some have become fixed in what is seen or heard.”

ud6.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud6.10:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

ud6.10:2.1.verse: “Sir, so long as the Realized Ones, the perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas do not arise in the world, the wanderers of other religions are honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud6.10:2.2.verse: But when the Realized Ones do arise in the world, the wanderers of other religions are no longer honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they do not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud6.10:2.3.verse: Now only the Buddha is honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.”

ud6.10:3.1.verse: “That’s so true, Ānanda. So long as the Realized Ones do not arise in the world, the wanderers of other religions are honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And they receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

ud6.10:3.2.verse: But when the Realized Ones do arise in the world, the wanderers of other religions are no longer honored in this way.

ud6.10:3.3.verse: Now only the Realized One is honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed. And he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. And so does the mendicant Saṅgha.”

ud6.10:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud6.10:5.2.verse: as the beacon of the sun does not rise.

ud6.10:5.3.verse: But when the dazzling sun has come up,

ud6.10:5.4.verse: that light is erased and shines no more.

ud6.10:6.1.verse: So too the sophists shine bright

ud6.10:6.2.verse: so long as the Buddhas don’t arise in the world.

ud6.10:6.3.verse: The sophists are not purified, nor are their disciples.

ud6.10:6.4.verse: Having bad views, they are not freed from suffering.”

ud7.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf in many ways with a Dhamma talk.

ud7.1:2.1.verse: Then after being taught like this Bhaddiya’s mind was freed from defilements by not grasping.

ud7.1:3.1.verse: The Buddha saw what had happened.

ud7.1:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.1:5.3.verse: Freed like this, he has crossed the flood

ud7.1:5.4.verse: not crossed before, so as to not be reborn.”

ud7.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.2:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf in even more ways with a Dhamma talk, thinking that he was still a trainee.

ud7.2:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw what was happening.

ud7.2:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.2:4.1.verse: “They’ve cut the cycle, gone to the wishless;

ud7.2:4.2.verse: the streams are dried, they flow no more.

ud7.2:4.3.verse: Cut, the cycle no longer spins.

ud7.2:4.4.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

ud7.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.3:1.3.verse: Now at that time most of the people in Sāvatthī overly clung to sensual pleasures. Lustful, greedy, tied, infatuated, they lived completely addicted to sensual pleasures.

ud7.3:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud7.3:2.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

ud7.3:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.3:4.1.verse: “Clinging to sensual pleasures, to the chains of the senses,

ud7.3:4.2.verse: blind to the faults of the fetters,

ud7.3:4.3.verse: clinging to the chain of the fetters,

ud7.3:4.4.verse: they’ll never cross the flood so vast.”

ud7.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time most of the people in Sāvatthī clung to sensual pleasures. Lustful, greedy, tied, infatuated, attached, and blinded, they lived completely addicted to sensual pleasures.

ud7.4:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

ud7.4:2.2.verse: He saw how attached the humans were.

ud7.4:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.4:4.1.verse: “Blinded by sensual pleasures, wrapped in a net,

ud7.4:4.2.verse: they are smothered over by craving;

ud7.4:4.3.verse: bound by the kinsman of the negligent,

ud7.4:4.4.verse: like a fish caught in a funnel-net trap.

ud7.4:4.5.verse: They chase old age and death,

ud7.4:4.6.verse: like a suckling calf its mother.”

ud7.5:0.2.verse: Another Discourse with Bhaddiya the Dwarf

ud7.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.5:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf, closely following several mendicants, approached the Buddha.

ud7.5:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw Venerable Bhaddiya coming off in the distance—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and despised by most of the mendicants.

ud7.5:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you see this monk coming—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and despised by most of the mendicants?”

ud7.5:4.1.verse: “That mendicant is very mighty and powerful. It’s not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained.

ud7.5:4.2.verse: And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

ud7.5:5.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.6:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Koṇḍañña Who Understood was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight, reviewing the freedom through the ending of craving.

ud7.6:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud7.6:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.6:4.1.verse: “There is no root or ground or leaves for them,

ud7.6:4.2.verse: so where would creepers sprout from?

ud7.6:4.3.verse: That attentive one is released from bonds:

ud7.6:4.4.verse: who is worthy to criticize them?

ud7.6:4.6.verse: and by the Divinity, too, they’re praised.”

ud7.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was sitting reviewing his own giving up of the judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions.

ud7.7:2.1.verse: Then, understanding his own giving up of the judgments driven by the proliferation of perceptions, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.7:3.1.verse: “There is no proliferation remaining in those

ud7.7:3.2.verse: who have passed beyond the halter and cross-bar.

ud7.7:3.3.verse: The sage who lives without craving

ud7.7:3.4.verse: is never scorned by the world with its gods.”

ud7.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud7.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākaccāna was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, with his body straight and mindfulness of the body well-established internally on the present.

ud7.8:2.1.verse: The Buddha saw him meditating there.

ud7.8:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.8:4.2.verse: be established in the body, constant:

ud7.8:4.3.verse: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine,

ud7.8:4.4.verse: It will not be, and it will not be mine.’

ud7.8:4.5.verse: Meditating stage by stage on that,

ud7.8:4.6.verse: in time they’d cross over clinging.”

ud7.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Mallas together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a brahmin town of the Mallas named Thūṇa.

ud7.9:1.3.verse: The brahmins and householders of Thūṇa heard:

ud7.9:1.4.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—while wandering in the land of the Mallas has arrived at Thūṇa, together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.”

ud7.9:1.5.verse: They filled the well with grass and hay right to the top, thinking,

ud7.9:1.6.verse: “Don’t let these shavelings, these fake ascetics drink the water.”

ud7.9:2.1.verse: And then the Buddha left the road, went to the root of a tree, and sat down on the seat spread out.

ud7.9:2.2.verse: When he was seated he said to Venerable Ānanda:

ud7.9:2.3.verse: “Go on then, Ānanda, fetch me some water from that well.”

ud7.9:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

ud7.9:3.2.verse: “Just now, sir, the brahmins and householders of Thūṇa filled the well with grass and hay right to the top, thinking,

ud7.9:3.3.verse: ‘Don’t let these shavelings, these fake ascetics drink the water.’”

ud7.9:4.2.verse: For a third time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:

ud7.9:4.3.verse: “Go on then, Ānanda, fetch me some water from that well.”

ud7.9:4.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. Taking his bowl he went to the well.

ud7.9:4.5.verse: As he approached the well, all the grass and hay erupted out of the well-mouth. The water stood transparent, unclouded, and clear right up to the top, seeming to overflow.

ud7.9:5.2.verse: “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

ud7.9:5.3.verse: For when I approached this well, all the grass and hay erupted out of the well-mouth. The water stood transparent, unclouded, and clear right up to the top, seeming to overflow.”

ud7.9:5.4.verse: Gathering a bowl of drinking water he went back to the Buddha, and said to him,

ud7.9:5.5.verse: “It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

ud7.9:5.6.verse: For when I approached that well, all the grass and hay erupted out of the well-mouth. The water stood transparent, unclouded, and clear right up to the top, seeming to overflow.

ud7.9:5.7.verse: Drink the water, Blessed One! Drink the water, Holy One!”

ud7.9:6.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.9:7.2.verse: if water is there all the time?

ud7.9:7.3.verse: Having cut off craving at the root,

ud7.9:7.4.verse: who would go out on a quest?”

ud7.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

ud7.10:1.3.verse: Now at that time, while King Udena was visiting a park, his royal compound burned down. Five hundred women died, with Queen Sāmāvatī at their head.

ud7.10:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Kosambī for alms.

ud7.10:2.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him had happened. They asked the Buddha,

ud7.10:2.5.verse: “Sir, where have those laywomen been reborn in the next life?”

ud7.10:3.1.verse: “Among those laywomen there were stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners.

ud7.10:3.2.verse: None of those laywomen died without some fruit of the practice.”

ud7.10:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud7.10:5.1.verse: “The world is caught up in delusion,

ud7.10:5.2.verse: but is looked on as making sense.

ud7.10:5.3.verse: The fool caught up in attachment

ud7.10:5.6.verse: but for one who sees, there is nothing.”

ud8.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud8.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants with a Dhamma talk about extinguishment.

ud8.1:1.4.verse: And those mendicants were paying attention, applying the mind, concentrating wholeheartedly, and actively listening.

ud8.1:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.1:3.1.verse: “There is, mendicants, that dimension where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind; no dimension of infinite space, no dimension of infinite consciousness, no dimension of nothingness, no dimension of neither perception nor non-perception; no this world, no other world, no moon or sun.

ud8.1:3.2.verse: There, mendicants, I say there is no coming or going or remaining or passing away or reappearing.

ud8.1:3.3.verse: It is not established, does not proceed, and has no support.

ud8.1:3.4.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

ud8.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud8.2:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants with a Dhamma talk about extinguishment.

ud8.2:1.4.verse: And those mendicants were paying attention, applying the mind, concentrating wholeheartedly, and actively listening.

ud8.2:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.2:3.1.verse: “It’s hard to see what they call the ‘uninclined’,

ud8.2:3.2.verse: for the truth is not easy to see.

ud8.2:3.3.verse: For one who has penetrated craving,

ud8.2:3.4.verse: who knows and sees, there is nothing.”

ud8.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud8.3:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants with a Dhamma talk about extinguishment.

ud8.3:1.4.verse: And those mendicants were paying attention, applying the mind, concentrating wholeheartedly, and actively listening.

ud8.3:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.3:3.1.verse: “There is, mendicants, freedom from rebirth, freedom from what has been produced, made, and conditioned.

ud8.3:3.2.verse: If there were no freedom from rebirth, freedom from what has been produced, made, and conditioned, then you would find no escape here from rebirth, from what has been produced, made, and conditioned.

ud8.3:3.3.verse: But since there is freedom from rebirth, freedom from what has been produced, made, and conditioned, an escape is found from rebirth, from what has been produced, made, and conditioned.”

ud8.4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud8.4:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants with a Dhamma talk about extinguishment.

ud8.4:1.4.verse: And those mendicants were paying attention, applying the mind, concentrating wholeheartedly, and actively listening.

ud8.4:2.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.4:3.1.verse: “For the dependent there is quivering. For the independent there’s no quivering.

ud8.4:3.2.verse: When there’s no quivering there is tranquility.

ud8.4:3.3.verse: When there is tranquility there’s no inclination.

ud8.4:3.4.verse: When there’s no inclination, there’s no coming and going.

ud8.4:3.5.verse: When there’s no coming and going, there’s no passing away and reappearing.

ud8.4:3.6.verse: When there’s no passing away and reappearing there’s no this life or the next or between the two.

ud8.4:3.7.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

ud8.5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Mallas together with a large Saṅgha when he arrived at Pāvā.

ud8.5:1.3.verse: There he stayed in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.

ud8.5:2.1.verse: Cunda heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in his mango grove.

ud8.5:2.2.verse: Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud8.5:2.3.verse: The Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk.

ud8.5:2.4.verse: Then Cunda said to the Buddha,

ud8.5:2.5.verse: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with the mendicant Saṅgha, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

ud8.5:3.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Cunda rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

ud8.5:3.2.verse: And when the night had passed Cunda had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own home, and plenty of pork on the turn. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

ud8.5:3.3.verse: “Sir, it’s time. The meal is ready.”

ud8.5:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of Cunda together with the mendicant Saṅgha, where he sat down on the seat spread out

ud8.5:4.3.verse: “Cunda, please serve me with the pork on the turn that you’ve prepared.

ud8.5:4.4.verse: And serve the mendicant Saṅgha with the other foods.”

ud8.5:4.5.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Cunda, and did as he was asked.

ud8.5:5.2.verse: “Cunda, any pork on the turn that’s left over, you should bury it in a pit.

ud8.5:5.3.verse: I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could properly digest it except the Realized One.”

ud8.5:5.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Cunda. He did as he was asked, then came back to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

ud8.5:5.5.verse: Then the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk, after which he rose from his seat and left.

ud8.5:6.1.verse: After the Buddha had eaten Cunda’s meal, he fell severely ill with bloody dysentery, struck by dreadful pains, close to death.

ud8.5:6.2.verse: But he endured unbothered, with mindfulness and situational awareness.

ud8.5:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud8.5:8.2.verse: the meal of Cunda the smith,

ud8.5:8.3.verse: the attentive one fell severely ill,

ud8.5:9.1.verse: A severe sickness struck the Teacher

ud8.5:9.2.verse: who had eaten the pork on the turn.

ud8.5:9.3.verse: While still purging the Buddha said:

ud8.5:9.4.verse: “I’ll go to the citadel of Kusinārā.”

ud8.5:10.1.verse: Then the Buddha left the road and went to the root of a certain tree, where he addressed Ānanda,

ud8.5:10.2.verse: “Go on then, Ānanda, fold my outer robe in four and spread it out for me. I am tired and will sit down.”

ud8.5:10.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda, and did as he was asked.

ud8.5:10.4.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

ud8.5:10.6.verse: “Go on then, Ānanda, fetch me some water. I am thirsty and will drink.”
