ud8.5:11.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

ud8.5:11.2.verse: “Sir, just now around five hundred carts have passed by. The shallow water has been churned up by their wheels, and it flows cloudy and murky.

ud8.5:11.3.verse: The Kakutthā River is not far away, with clear, sweet, cool water, clean, with smooth banks, delightful.

ud8.5:11.4.verse: There the Buddha can drink and cool his limbs.”

ud8.5:12.2.verse: For a third time, the Buddha said to Ānanda,

ud8.5:12.3.verse: “Go on then, Ānanda, fetch me some water. I am thirsty and will drink.”

ud8.5:12.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. Taking his bowl he went to the river.

ud8.5:12.5.verse: Now, though the shallow water in that river had been churned up by wheels, and flowed cloudy and murky, when Ānanda approached it flowed transparent, clear, and unclouded.

ud8.5:13.2.verse: “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

ud8.5:13.3.verse: For though the shallow water in that river had been churned up by wheels, and flowed cloudy and murky, when I approached it flowed transparent, clear, and unclouded.”

ud8.5:13.4.verse: Gathering a bowl of drinking water he went back to the Buddha, and said to him,

ud8.5:13.5.verse: “It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

ud8.5:13.6.verse: For though the shallow water in that river had been churned up by wheels, and flowed cloudy and murky, when I approached it flowed transparent, clear, and unclouded.

ud8.5:13.7.verse: Drink the water, Blessed One! Drink the water, Holy One!”

ud8.5:14.1.verse: So the Buddha drank the water.

ud8.5:14.2.verse: Then the Buddha together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants went to the Kakutthā River. He plunged into the river and bathed and drank.

ud8.5:14.3.verse: And when he had emerged, he went to the mango grove, where he addressed Venerable Cundaka,

ud8.5:14.4.verse: “Go on then, Cundaka, fold my outer robe in four and spread it out for me. I am tired and will lie down.”

ud8.5:15.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Cundaka, and did as he was asked.

ud8.5:15.2.verse: And then the Buddha laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

ud8.5:15.3.verse: But Cundaka sat down right there in front of the Buddha.

ud8.5:16.2.verse: whose water was transparent, sweet, and clear,

ud8.5:16.3.verse: the Teacher, being tired, plunged in,

ud8.5:16.4.verse: the Realized One, without compare in the world.

ud8.5:17.1.verse: And after bathing and drinking the Teacher emerged.

ud8.5:17.2.verse: Before the group of mendicants, in the middle, the Buddha,

ud8.5:17.3.verse: the Teacher who rolled forth the present dispensation,

ud8.5:17.4.verse: the great seer went to the mango grove.

ud8.5:17.5.verse: He addressed the mendicant named Cundaka:

ud8.5:17.6.verse: “Spread out my folded robe so I can lie down.”

ud8.5:18.2.verse: who quickly spread the folded robe.

ud8.5:18.3.verse: The Teacher lay down so tired,

ud8.5:18.4.verse: while Cunda sat there before him.

ud8.5:19.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

ud8.5:19.2.verse: “Now it may happen, Ānanda, that others may give rise to some regret for Cunda the smith:

ud8.5:19.3.verse: ‘It’s your loss, respectable Cunda, it’s your misfortune, in that the Realized One was fully quenched after eating his last almsmeal from you.’

ud8.5:19.4.verse: You should dispel remorse in Cunda the smith like this:

ud8.5:20.1.verse: ‘You’re fortunate, respectable Cunda, you’re so very fortunate,

ud8.5:20.2.verse: in that the Realized One was fully quenched after eating his last almsmeal from you.

ud8.5:20.3.verse: I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha.

ud8.5:20.4.verse: There are two almsmeal offerings that have identical fruit and result, and are more fruitful and beneficial than other almsmeal offerings.

ud8.5:20.6.verse: The almsmeal after eating which a Realized One awakens to the supreme perfect awakening; and the almsmeal after eating which he becomes fully extinguished in the element of extinguishment with no residue.

ud8.5:20.7.verse: These two almsmeal offerings have identical fruit and result, and are more fruitful and beneficial than other almsmeal offerings.

ud8.5:21.1.verse: You’ve accumulated a deed that leads to long life, beauty, happiness, glory, heaven, and sovereignty.’

ud8.5:21.2.verse: You should dispel remorse in Cunda the smith like this.”

ud8.5:22.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.5:23.2.verse: enmity doesn’t build up when you have self-control.

ud8.5:23.3.verse: A skillful person gives up bad things—

ud8.5:23.4.verse: with the end of greed, hate, and delusion, they’re quenched.”

ud8.6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Magadhans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at the village of Pāṭali.

ud8.6:1.3.verse: The lay followers of Pāṭali Village heard that he had arrived.

ud8.6:1.5.verse: So they went to see him, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

ud8.6:1.7.verse: “Sir, please consent to come to our guest house.”

ud8.6:2.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the lay followers of Pāṭali Village rose from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. Then they went to the guest house, where they spread carpets all over, prepared seats, set up a water jar, and placed an oil lamp. Then they went back to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and told him of their preparations, saying:

ud8.6:3.1.verse: In the morning, the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the guest house together with the Saṅgha of mendicants. Having washed his feet, he entered the guest house and sat against the central column facing east.

ud8.6:3.2.verse: The Saṅgha of mendicants also washed their feet, entered the guest house, and sat against the west wall facing east, with the Buddha right in front of them.

ud8.6:3.3.verse: The lay followers of Pāṭali Village also washed their feet, entered the guest house, and sat against the east wall facing west, with the Buddha right in front of them.

ud8.6:4.1.verse: “Householders, there are these five drawbacks for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics.

ud8.6:4.3.verse: Firstly, an unethical person loses great wealth on account of negligence.

ud8.6:5.1.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person gets a bad reputation.

ud8.6:6.1.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person enters any kind of assembly unconfident and embarrassed, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

ud8.6:7.1.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person feels lost when they die.

ud8.6:8.1.verse: Furthermore, an unethical person, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

ud8.6:8.3.verse: These are the five drawbacks for an unethical person because of their failure in ethics.

ud8.6:9.1.verse: There are these five benefits for an ethical person because of their accomplishment in ethics.

ud8.6:9.3.verse: Firstly, an ethical person gains great wealth on account of diligence.

ud8.6:10.1.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person gets a good reputation.

ud8.6:11.1.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person enters any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

ud8.6:12.1.verse: Furthermore, an ethical person dies not feeling lost.

ud8.6:13.1.verse: Furthermore, when an ethical person’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

ud8.6:13.3.verse: These are the five benefits for an ethical person because of their accomplishment in ethics.”

ud8.6:14.1.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the lay followers of Pāṭali Village with a Dhamma talk. Then he sent them off,

ud8.6:14.2.verse: “The night is getting late, householders. Please go at your convenience.”

ud8.6:14.3.verse: And then the lay followers of Pāṭali Village approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. They got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before leaving.

ud8.6:14.4.verse: Soon after they left the Buddha entered a private cubicle.

ud8.6:15.1.verse: Now at that time the Magadhan ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra were building a citadel at Pāṭali Village to keep the Vajjis out.

ud8.6:15.2.verse: At that time thousands of deities were taking possession of building sites in Pāṭali Village.

ud8.6:15.3.verse: Illustrious rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by illustrious deities.

ud8.6:15.4.verse: Middling rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by middling deities.

ud8.6:15.5.verse: Lesser rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by lesser deities.

ud8.6:16.1.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha saw those deities taking possession of building sites in Pāṭali Village,

ud8.6:16.2.verse: and the people building houses in accord with the station of the deities.

ud8.6:16.5.verse: The Buddha rose at the crack of dawn and addressed Ānanda,

ud8.6:17.1.verse: “Ānanda, who is building a citadel at Pāṭali Village?”

ud8.6:17.2.verse: “Sir, the Magadhan chief ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra are building a citadel to keep the Vajjis out.”

ud8.6:17.3.verse: “It’s as if they were building the citadel in consultation with the gods of the thirty-three.

ud8.6:17.5.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw those deities taking possession of building sites.

ud8.6:17.6.verse: Illustrious rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by illustrious deities.

ud8.6:17.7.verse: Middling rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by middling deities.

ud8.6:17.8.verse: Lesser rulers or royal chief ministers inclined to build houses at sites possessed by lesser deities.

ud8.6:17.9.verse: As far as the civilized region extends, as far as the trading zone extends, this will be the chief city: the Pāṭaliputta trade center.

ud8.6:17.10.verse: But Pāṭaliputta will face three threats:

ud8.6:18.1.verse: Then the Magadhan ministers Sunidha and Vassakāra approached the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

ud8.6:18.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they stood to one side and said,

ud8.6:18.4.verse: “Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept today’s meal from me?”

ud8.6:19.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, they went to their own guest house, where they had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared. Then they had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

ud8.6:19.2.verse: “It’s time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready.”

ud8.6:20.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to their guest house together with the mendicant Saṅgha, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

ud8.6:20.2.verse: Then Sunidha and Vassakāra served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with their own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

ud8.6:21.1.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Sunidha and Vassakāra took a low seat and sat to one side.

ud8.6:21.2.verse: The Buddha expressed his appreciation with these verses:

ud8.6:22.1.verse: “In the place he makes his dwelling,

ud8.6:24.1.verse: After that they have sympathy for him,

ud8.6:24.2.verse: like a mother for the child at her breast.

ud8.6:24.3.verse: A man beloved of the deities

ud8.6:25.1.verse: When the Buddha had expressed his appreciation to Sunidha and Vassakāra with these verses, he rose from his seat and left.

ud8.6:26.1.verse: Sunidha and Vassakāra followed behind the Buddha, thinking,

ud8.6:26.2.verse: “The gate through which the ascetic Gotama exits today shall be named the Gotama Gate.

ud8.6:26.3.verse: The ford at which he crosses the Ganges River shall be named the Gotama Ford.”

ud8.6:27.1.verse: Then the gate through which the Buddha exited was named the Gotama Gate.

ud8.6:27.2.verse: Then the Buddha came to the Ganges River.

ud8.6:27.3.verse: Now at that time the Ganges was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

ud8.6:27.4.verse: Wanting to cross from the near to the far shore, some people were seeking a boat, some a dinghy, while some were tying up a raft.

ud8.6:27.5.verse: But, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, the Buddha, together with the mendicant Saṅgha, vanished from the near shore and landed on the far shore.

ud8.6:28.1.verse: He saw all those humans wanting to cross over.

ud8.6:29.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.6:30.1.verse: “Those who cross a deluge or stream

ud8.6:30.2.verse: have built a bridge and left the marshes behind.

ud8.6:30.3.verse: While some people are still tying a raft,

ud8.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was traveling along a road in the Kosalan lands with Venerable Nāgasamāla as his second monk.

ud8.7:1.3.verse: Nāgasamāla saw a fork in the road

ud8.7:1.7.verse: But when he said this the Buddha responded,

ud8.7:2.2.verse: For a third time Nāgasamāla said to the Buddha,

ud8.7:2.5.verse: And for a third time the Buddha responded,

ud8.7:2.8.verse: Then Nāgasamāla put the Buddha’s bowl and robes down on the ground right there and left, saying,

ud8.7:2.9.verse: “Sir, here are your bowl and robes.”

ud8.7:3.1.verse: Then as Nāgasamāla was going down that road, he was set upon by bandits who struck him with fists and feet, broke his bowl, and tore up his outer robe.

ud8.7:3.2.verse: Then Nāgasamāla—with his bowl broken and his outer robe torn—went to the Buddha and told him what had happened.

ud8.7:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.7:5.2.verse: the knowledge master mixes with foolish folk.

ud8.7:5.3.verse: Knowing this, they give up wickedness,

ud8.7:5.4.verse: like a milk-drinking heron the water.”

ud8.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

ud8.8:1.3.verse: Now at that time the dear and beloved granddaughter of Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, had just passed away.

ud8.8:1.4.verse: Then, in the middle of the day, Visākhā with wet clothes and hair went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.

ud8.8:2.1.verse: “So, Visākhā, where are you coming from in the middle of the day with wet clothes and hair?”

ud8.8:2.2.verse: “Sir, my beloved granddaughter has just passed away.

ud8.8:2.3.verse: That’s why I came here in the middle of the day with wet clothes and hair.”

ud8.8:2.4.verse: “Visākhā, would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in the whole of Sāvatthī?”

ud8.8:3.1.verse: “But Visākhā, how many people pass away each day in Sāvatthī?”

ud8.8:3.2.verse: “Every day, sir, there are ten people passing away in Sāvatthī.

ud8.8:3.11.verse: or at least one person who passes away every day in Sāvatthī.

ud8.8:3.12.verse: Sāvatthī is never without someone passing away.”

ud8.8:4.1.verse: “What do you think, Visākhā? Would there ever be a time when your clothes and hair were not wet?”

ud8.8:4.3.verse: Enough, sir, with so many children and grandchildren.”

ud8.8:5.1.verse: “Those who have a hundred loved ones, Visākhā, have a hundred sufferings.

ud8.8:5.2.verse: Those who have ninety loved ones,

ud8.8:5.19.verse: or one loved one have one suffering.

ud8.8:5.20.verse: Those who have no loved ones have no suffering. They are free of sorrow, stains, and anguish I say.”

ud8.8:6.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.8:7.2.verse: and the countless forms of suffering in the world

ud8.8:7.3.verse: occur because of those that we love;

ud8.8:7.4.verse: without loved ones they do not occur.

ud8.8:8.1.verse: That’s why those who have no loved ones at all in the world

ud8.8:8.2.verse: are happy and free of grief.

ud8.8:8.3.verse: So aspiring to the sorrowless and stainless,

ud8.8:8.4.verse: have no loved ones in the world at all.”

ud8.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

ud8.9:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Dabba the Mallian went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

ud8.9:1.5.verse: “Holy One, it is the time for my full extinguishment.”

ud8.9:1.6.verse: “Please, Dabba, do as you see fit.”

ud8.9:2.1.verse: Then Dabba rose from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he rose into the air and, sitting cross-legged in midair, entered and withdrew from the fire element before becoming fully extinguished.

ud8.9:3.1.verse: Then when he was fully quenched while sitting cross-legged in midair, his body burning and combusting left neither ashes nor soot to be found.

ud8.9:3.2.verse: It’s like when ghee or oil blaze and burn, and neither ashes nor soot are found.

ud8.9:4.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.9:5.1.verse: “The body is broken up, perception has ceased,

ud8.9:5.4.verse: and consciousness come to an end.”

ud8.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

ud8.10:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

ud8.10:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, when Dabba the Mallian rose into the air and, sitting cross-legged in midair, entered and withdrew from the fire element before becoming fully quenched, his body burning and combusting left neither ashes nor soot to be found.

ud8.10:2.2.verse: It’s like when ghee or oil blaze and burn, and neither ashes nor soot are found.

ud8.10:2.3.verse: In the same way, when Dabba the Mallian rose into the air and, sitting cross-legged in midair, entered and withdrew from the fire element before becoming fully quenched, his body burning and combusting left neither ashes nor soot to be found.”

ud8.10:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

ud8.10:4.1.verse: “Just as the glow of iron struck

ud8.10:4.2.verse: by a hammer in the fire of Jātaveda

ud8.10:5.1.verse: in the same way, for the rightly released,

ud8.10:5.2.verse: who have crossed the flood of sensual bonds,

ud8.10:5.3.verse: there is no destination to describe—

mn1:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā, in the shade of a royal Sal tree in the Very Blessed Forest.

mn1:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn1:2.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you the sequence of the root of all phenomena [or: the root sequence of all phenomena].

mn1:2.2.verse: Listen & pay close attention. I will speak.”

mn1:2.3.verse: “As you say, lord,” they responded to him.

mn1:3.1.verse: “There is the case, monks, where an uninstructed run-of-the-mill person—who has no regard for noble ones, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma; who has no regard for people of integrity, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma—

mn1:3.3.verse: Perceiving earth as earth, he supposes (things) about earth, he supposes (things) in earth, he supposes (things) coming out of earth, he supposes earth as ‘mine,’ he delights in earth.

mn1:3.5.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:4.2.verse: Perceiving water as water, he supposes (things) about water, he supposes (things) in water, he supposes (things) coming out of water, he supposes water as ‘mine,’ he delights in water.

mn1:4.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:5.2.verse: Perceiving fire as fire, he supposes (things) about fire, he supposes (things) in fire, he supposes (things) coming out of fire, he supposes fire as ‘mine,’ he delights in fire.

mn1:5.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:6.2.verse: Perceiving wind as wind, he supposes (things) about wind, he supposes (things) in wind, he supposes (things) coming out of wind, he supposes wind as ‘mine,’ he delights in wind.

mn1:6.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:7.2.verse: Perceiving beings as beings, he supposes (things) about beings, he supposes (things) in beings, he supposes (things) coming out of beings, he supposes beings as ‘mine,’ he delights in beings.

mn1:8.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:9.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:26.4.verse: Because he has not comprehended it, I tell you.

mn1:27.1.verse: A monk who is a trainee—yearning for the unexcelled relief from bondage, his aspirations as yet unfulfilled—directly knows earth as earth.

mn1:27.2.verse: Directly knowing earth as earth, let him not suppose things about earth, let him not suppose things in earth, let him not suppose things coming out of earth, let him not suppose earth as ‘mine,’ let him not delight in earth.

mn1:27.4.verse: So that he may comprehend it, I tell you.

mn1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Forest at the root of a magnificent sal tree.

mn1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn1:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the explanation of the root of all things.

mn1:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your minds well, I will speak.”

mn1:3.1.verse: “Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn1:3.3.verse: Having perceived earth as earth, they conceive it to be earth, they conceive it in earth, they conceive it as earth, they conceive that ‘earth is mine’, they approve earth.

mn1:3.5.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:4.2.verse: Having perceived water as water, they conceive it to be water …

mn1:4.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:5.2.verse: Having perceived fire as fire, they conceive it to be fire …

mn1:5.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:6.2.verse: Having perceived air as air, they conceive it to be air …

mn1:6.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:7.2.verse: Having perceived creatures as creatures, they conceive them to be creatures …

mn1:7.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:8.2.verse: Having perceived gods as gods, they conceive them to be gods …

mn1:8.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:9.1.verse: They perceive the Progenitor as the Progenitor.

mn1:9.2.verse: Having perceived the Progenitor as the Progenitor, they conceive him to be the Progenitor …

mn1:9.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:10.1.verse: They perceive the Divinity as the Divinity.

mn1:10.2.verse: Having perceived the Divinity as the Divinity, they conceive him to be the Divinity …

mn1:10.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:11.1.verse: They perceive those of sublime luminosity as those of sublime luminosity.

mn1:11.2.verse: Having perceived those of sublime luminosity as those of sublime luminosity, they conceive them to be those of sublime luminosity …

mn1:11.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:12.1.verse: They perceive those of universal beauty as those of universal beauty.

mn1:12.2.verse: But then they conceive them to be those of universal beauty …

mn1:12.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:13.1.verse: They perceive those of abundant fruit as those of abundant fruit.

mn1:13.2.verse: Having perceived those of abundant fruit as those of abundant fruit, they conceive them to be those of abundant fruit …

mn1:13.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:14.1.verse: They perceive the Vanquisher as the Vanquisher.

mn1:14.2.verse: Having perceived the Vanquisher as the Vanquisher, they conceive him to be the Vanquisher …

mn1:14.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:15.1.verse: They perceive the dimension of infinite space as the dimension of infinite space.

mn1:15.2.verse: Having perceived the dimension of infinite space as the dimension of infinite space, they conceive it to be the dimension of infinite space …

mn1:15.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:16.1.verse: They perceive the dimension of infinite consciousness as the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn1:16.2.verse: Having perceived the dimension of infinite consciousness as the dimension of infinite consciousness, they conceive it to be the dimension of infinite consciousness …

mn1:16.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:17.1.verse: They perceive the dimension of nothingness as the dimension of nothingness.

mn1:17.2.verse: Having perceived the dimension of nothingness as the dimension of nothingness, they conceive it to be the dimension of nothingness …

mn1:17.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:18.1.verse: They perceive the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception as the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn1:18.2.verse: Having perceived the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception as the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, they conceive it to be the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception …

mn1:18.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:19.1.verse: They perceive the seen as the seen.

mn1:19.2.verse: Having perceived the seen as the seen, they conceive it to be the seen …

mn1:19.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:20.1.verse: They perceive the heard as the heard.

mn1:20.2.verse: Having perceived the heard as the heard, they conceive it to be the heard …

mn1:20.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:21.1.verse: They perceive the thought as the thought.

mn1:21.2.verse: Having perceived the thought as the thought, they conceive it to be the thought …

mn1:21.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:22.1.verse: They perceive the known as the known.

mn1:22.2.verse: Having perceived the known as the known, they conceive it to be the known …

mn1:22.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:23.2.verse: Having perceived oneness as oneness, they conceive it to be oneness …

mn1:23.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:24.2.verse: Having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive it to be diversity …

mn1:24.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:25.2.verse: Having perceived all as all, they conceive it to be all …

mn1:25.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:26.2.verse: Having perceived extinguishment as extinguishment, they conceive it to be extinguishment, they conceive it in extinguishment, they conceive it as extinguishment, they conceive that ‘extinguishment is mine’, they approve extinguishment.

mn1:26.4.verse: Because they haven’t completely understood it, I say.

mn1:27.1.verse: A mendicant who is a trainee, who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire, but lives aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, directly knows earth as earth.

mn1:27.2.verse: Having directly known earth as earth, let them not conceive it to be earth, let them not conceive it in earth, let them not conceive it as earth, let them not conceive that ‘earth is mine’, let them not approve earth.

mn1:27.4.verse: So that they may completely understand it, I say.

mn1:50.1.verse: They directly know extinguishment as extinguishment.

mn1:50.2.verse: Having directly known extinguishment as extinguishment, let them not conceive it to be extinguishment, let them not conceive it in extinguishment, let them not conceive it as extinguishment, let them not conceive that ‘extinguishment is mine’, let them not approve extinguishment.

mn1:51.1.verse: A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—directly knows earth as earth.

mn1:51.4.verse: Because they have completely understood it, I say.

mn2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park.

mn2:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the monks:

mn2:1.5.verse: “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.

mn2:2.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you how to control every vice.

mn2:2.2.verse: Listen to this and carefully apply your mind to it; I will speak.”

mn2:2.3.verse: “Yes, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Buddha.

mn2:3.1.verse: “Monks, I say that the elimination of vices is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.

mn2:3.2.verse: For one who knows and sees what?

mn2:3.3.verse: Application of mind based on an understanding of causality, and application of mind not based on an understanding of causality.

mn2:3.4.verse: Monks, when one applies one’s mind without an understanding of causality, one develops new vices, and one’s old vices grow stronger.

mn2:3.5.verse: Monks, when one applies one’s mind based on an understanding of causality, one does not develop new vices, and one’s old vices are abandoned.

mn2:4.1.verse: Monks, there are vices to be abandoned by seeing, vices to be abandoned by self-control, vices to be abandoned by using, vices to be abandoned by enduring, vices to be abandoned by avoiding, vices to be abandoned by removing, and vices to be abandoned by cultivating.

mn2:5.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Seeing

mn2:5.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by seeing?

mn2:5.2.verse: In this case, monks, an uneducated commoner—one who does not see noble people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who does not see good people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people—

mn2:5.3.verse: does not understand what the mind should not be applied to and what the mind should be applied to.

mn2:5.4.verse: Since they do not understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do not apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

mn2:6.1.verse: And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they apply their mind to?

mn2:6.2.verse: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger;

mn2:6.3.verse: or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger;

mn2:6.4.verse: or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger;

mn2:6.5.verse: this is what the mind should not be applied to that they apply their mind to.

mn2:6.6.verse: And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they do not apply their mind to?

mn2:6.7.verse: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned;

mn2:6.8.verse: or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned;

mn2:6.9.verse: or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned;

mn2:6.10.verse: this is what the mind should be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.

mn2:7.1.verse: So when they apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do not apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they develop new vices and their old vices grow stronger.

mn2:7.2.verse: This is how they apply their mind without an understanding of causality:

mn2:7.3.verse: they think, ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having done what, what did I become in the past?’

mn2:7.4.verse: ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having done what, what will I become in the future?’

mn2:7.5.verse: Or they are confused about the present:

mn2:7.6.verse: ‘Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go from here?’

mn2:8.1.verse: When one applies one’s mind in this way, one of six beliefs arises:

mn2:8.2.verse: The belief ‘I have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.

mn2:8.3.verse: Or the belief ‘I do not have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.

mn2:8.4.verse: Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.

mn2:8.5.verse: Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive what is not the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.

mn2:8.6.verse: Or the belief ‘Using what is not the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.

mn2:8.8.verse: ‘This is my soul; it speaks, it feels, it experiences the results of good and evil actions; and this soul of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and will remain like this for eternity.’

mn2:8.9.verse: Monks, this is called settling on a belief, becoming entangled in a belief, becoming disturbed by a belief, becoming agitated by a belief, becoming shackled by a belief.

mn2:8.10.verse: Shackled by a belief, monks, the uneducated commoner is not freed from birth, decrepitude, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and anguish;

mn2:8.11.verse: they are not freed from suffering, I say.

mn2:9.1.verse: Monks, an educated disciple of the noble ones—

mn2:9.2.verse: one who sees noble people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who sees good people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people—

mn2:9.3.verse: understands what the mind the should be applied to and what the mind should not be applied to.

mn2:9.4.verse: Since they understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they do not apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

mn2:10.1.verse: And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to?

mn2:10.2.verse: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger;

mn2:10.3.verse: or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger;

mn2:10.4.verse: or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger;

mn2:10.5.verse: this is what the mind should not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.

mn2:10.6.verse: And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they apply their mind to?

mn2:10.7.verse: Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned;

mn2:10.8.verse: or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned;

mn2:10.9.verse: or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned;

mn2:10.10.verse: this is what the mind should be applied to that they apply their mind to.

mn2:10.11.verse: So when they do not apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they do not develop new vices and their old vices are abandoned.

mn2:11.1.verse: They apply their mind based on an understanding of causality in this way: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the cause suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path of practice which leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn2:11.2.verse: Applying the mind based on an understanding of causality in this way, three shackles are abandoned:

mn2:11.3.verse: belief in self-existence, skepticism, and misapprehension of habitual practices.

mn2:11.4.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by seeing.

mn2:12.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Self-Control

mn2:12.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by self-control?

mn2:12.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sight.

mn2:12.3.verse: Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of sight, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of sight, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:12.4.verse: Contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sound…

mn2:12.9.verse: Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:12.10.verse: Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:12.11.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by self-control.

mn2:13.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Using

mn2:13.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by using?

mn2:13.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk uses their robe

mn2:13.3.verse: just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; and to cover the genitals.

mn2:14.1.verse: Contemplating causality, a monk uses almsfood

mn2:14.2.verse: not for entertainment, not for intoxication, not for beauty, not for decoration; but just for the sustenance and health of their body, and to support the spiritual life; thinking, ‘In this way, I will remove old feelings and I will not produce new feelings, so that I will be blameless and comfortable.’

mn2:15.1.verse: Contemplating causality, a monk uses their dwelling

mn2:15.2.verse: just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; protection from weather; and to enjoy personal retreat.

mn2:16.1.verse: Contemplating causality, a monk uses medicines and medicinal supplies

mn2:16.2.verse: just for the purpose of preventing affliction and to be free from illness.

mn2:17.1.verse: Because, monks, when one does not practice proper use, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices proper use, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:17.2.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by using.

mn2:18.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Enduring

mn2:18.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by enduring?

mn2:18.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk endures cold and heat; hunger and thirst; contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; improper and unwelcome statements; physical sensations that are painful, sharp, harsh, severe, uncomfortable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.

mn2:18.3.verse: Because, monks, when one does not endure, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one endures, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:18.4.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by enduring.

mn2:19.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Avoiding

mn2:19.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by avoiding?

mn2:19.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild ox, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, a thorn-bush, a pit, a precipice, a swamp, a sewer;

mn2:19.3.verse: contemplating causality, a monk avoids sitting in improper places, going to improper places, or associating with evil friends, since such behavior might give one’s discerning spiritual companions cause for suspicion.

mn2:19.4.verse: Because, monks, when one does not avoid such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one avoids such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:19.5.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by avoiding.

mn2:20.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Removing

mn2:20.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by removing?

mn2:20.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk does not tolerate a sensual thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate an aversive thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate a malicious thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate any harmful, unwholesome qualities that are present, but instead abandons them, removes them, terminates them, and annihilates them.

mn2:20.3.verse: Because, monks, when one does not remove such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one removes such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:20.4.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by removing.

mn2:21.0.verse: Vices to be Abandoned by Cultivating

mn2:21.1.verse: Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by cultivating?

mn2:21.2.verse: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment;

mn2:21.3.verse: contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the investigation factor of awakening…

mn2:21.8.verse: the equanimity factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment;

mn2:21.9.verse: Because, monks, when one does not cultivate such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one cultivates such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

mn2:21.10.verse: Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by cultivating.

mn2:22.1.verse: Monks, when a monk has abandoned by seeing the vices to be abandoned by seeing, has abandoned by self-control the vices to be abandoned by self-control, has abandoned by using the vices to be abandoned by using, has abandoned by enduring the vices to be abandoned by enduring, has abandoned by avoiding the vices to be abandoned by avoiding, has abandoned by removing the vices to be abandoned by removing, and has abandoned by cultivating the vices to be abandoned by cultivating,

mn2:22.2.verse: that monk is called a monk who has controlled every vice, cut off craving, opened the shackles, and through a correct comprehension of conceit has put an end to suffering.”

mn2:22.3.verse: This is what the Buddha said.

mn2:22.4.verse: Satisfied, those monks rejoiced in the Buddha’s statement.

mn2:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn2:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn2:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, I shall expound to you a discourse on the restraint of all the taints (āsava),

mn2:2.2.verse: listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn2:3.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus. I say that there is an exhaustion of taints in one who knows and sees, not in one who does not know and see.

mn2:3.4.verse: ‘When a man attends unwisely both unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.

mn2:3.5.verse: When he attends wisely, both unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.

mn2:5.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by seeing?

mn2:5.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, an untaught ordinary man, who has no regard for Noble Ones, and is inconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it, who has no regard for True Men and is inconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it,

mn2:5.3.verse: does not understand what dhammas are fit for attention, or what dhammas are unfit for attention.

mn2:5.4.verse: Since that is so, he does not attend to dhammas fit for attention and he attends to dhammas unfit for attention.

mn2:6.1.verse: ‘What dhammas unfit for attention does he attend to?

mn2:6.2.verse: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them with his attention, the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance arise in him, or the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance increase in him.

mn2:6.5.verse: These are the dhammas unfit for attention to which he attends.

mn2:6.6.verse: And what dhammas fit for attention does not attend to?

mn2:6.7.verse: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them with his attention, the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, do not arise in him, and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.

mn2:6.8.verse: the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, do not arise in him, and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.

mn2:6.10.verse: These are the dhammas fit for attention to which he does not attend.

mn2:7.1.verse: By attending to dhammas unfit for attention and by not attending to dhammas fit for attention, both unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.

mn2:7.3.verse: Was I in past time? Was I not in past time? What was I in past time? How was I in past time? Having been what, what was I in past time?

mn2:7.4.verse: Shall I be in future time? Shall I not be in future time? What shall I be in future time? How shall I be in future time? Having been what, what shall I be in future time?”

mn2:7.5.verse: Or else he is doubtful in himself about presently existing time thus: “

mn2:7.6.verse: Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Whence will this being have come? Whither will it be bound?”’

mn2:8.1.verse: ‘When he attends unwisely in this way, one of six kinds of view arises in him:

mn2:8.2.verse: The view self exists for me arises in him as true and established,

mn2:8.3.verse: or the view no self exists for me arises in him as true and established,

mn2:8.4.verse: or the view I perceive self with self arises in him as true and established,

mn2:8.5.verse: or the view I perceive not-self with self arises in him as true and established,

mn2:8.6.verse: or the view I perceive self with not-self arises in him as true and established,

mn2:8.7.verse: or else he has some such view as

mn2:8.8.verse: It is this my self that speaks and feels, and that experiences here or there the ripening of good and bad actions; but this my self is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and it will endure as long as eternity.

mn2:8.9.verse: “This type of view is called the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views.

mn2:8.10.verse: No untaught ordinary man bound by the fetter of views is freed by birth, ageing and death, by sorrows and lamentations, by pains, griefs and despairs;

mn2:8.11.verse: he is not freed from suffering, I say.

mn2:9.2.verse: ‘The well-taught disciple of Noble Ones, who has regard for Noble Ones, and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it, who has regard for True Men and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it,

mn2:9.3.verse: understands what dhammas are fit for attention and what dhammas are unfit for attention.

mn2:9.4.verse: Since that is so, he does not attend to dhammas unfit for attention. He attends to dhammas fit for attention.

mn2:10.1.verse: ‘What dhammas unfit for attention does he not attend to?

mn2:10.2.verse: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, arise in him, or the arisen taints of sensual pleasure, being and ignorance increase in him.

mn2:10.5.verse: These are the dhammas unfit for attention that he does not attend to.

mn2:10.6.verse: ‘And what dhammas fit for attention does he attend to?

mn2:10.7.verse: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them the unarisen taints of sensual desire,

mn2:10.9.verse: and ignorance, do not arise in him and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.

mn2:10.10.verse: These are the dhammas fit for attention that he attends to.

mn2:10.11.verse: ‘By not attending to dhammas unfit for attention and by attending to dhammas fit for attention both unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.

mn2:11.1.verse: ‘This is how he attends wisely: this is suffering, and this is the origin of suffering and this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

mn2:11.2.verse: ‘When he attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned in him:

mn2:11.3.verse: the embodiment-view, uncertainty, and adherence to rites and rituals.

mn2:11.4.verse: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by seeing.

mn2:12.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by restraining?

mn2:12.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely abides with the eye faculty restrained.

mn2:12.3.verse: While taints and fever of defilement might arise in a bhikkhu who abode with the eye faculty unrestrained, there are no taints or fever of defilement in him when he abides with the eye faculty restrained.

mn2:12.4.verse: ‘Reflecting wisely he abides with the ear faculty restrained …

mn2:12.8.verse: ‘Reflecting wisely he abides with the mind faculty restrained …

mn2:12.9.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in him when he abides with the mind faculty restrained.

mn2:12.10.verse: ‘While taints and fever of difilement might arise in one who abode unrestrained, there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abides restrained.

mn2:12.11.verse: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by restraining.

mn2:13.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by using?

mn2:13.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely uses a robe

mn2:13.3.verse: only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, flics, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of concealing what disturbs conscience.

mn2:14.2.verse: neither for amusement nor for intoxication (of vanity), nor for smartening, nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the life divine (considering:) “Thus shall I terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and blameless, shall live in comfort and health.”

mn2:15.1.verse: ‘Reflecting wisely he uses a resting place

mn2:15.2.verse: only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, only for the purpose of warding off the perils of climate for enjoying retreat.

mn2:16.1.verse: ‘Reflecting wisely he uses the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick,

mn2:17.1.verse: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not use (the requisites thus), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who uses (them thus).

mn2:17.2.verse: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by using.

mn2:18.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by enduring?

mn2:18.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely bears cold, heat, hunger, thirst and contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, he endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing and menacing to life.

mn2:18.3.verse: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not endure, there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who endures.

mn2:18.4.verse: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by enduring.

mn2:19.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by avoiding?

mn2:19.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely avoids a savage elephant, a savage horse, a savage bull, a savage dog, a snake, a stump, a bramble (patch), a chasm, a cliff, a cess-pit, a sewer;

mn2:19.3.verse: reflecting wisely he avoids sitting on unsuitable seats, wandering to unsuitable resorts, frequenting bad friends, such that wise companions in the life divine might believe to be evidence of evil-doing.

mn2:19.4.verse: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not avoid (these things), there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who avoids (them).

mn2:19.5.verse: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by avoiding.

mn2:20.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by removing?

mn2:20.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely does not endure an arisen thought affected by sensual desire … by ill-will … by cruelty; he abandons it, removes it, does away with and annihilates it. He does not endure arisen, evil, unprofitable dhammas; he abandons them, removes them, does away with and annihilates them.

mn2:20.3.verse: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not remove (these thoughts), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who removes (them).

mn2:20.4.verse: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by removing.

mn2:21.1.verse: ‘What taints can be abandoned by developing?

mn2:21.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely develops the mindfulness enlightenment-factor which has seclusion, passionlessness and cessation for its support and changes to relinquishment.

mn2:21.3.verse: ‘He develops the investigation of Dhamma enlightenment-factor

mn2:21.8.verse: ‘ … the equanimity enlightenment-factor, which has seclusion, passionlessness and cessation for its support and changes to relinquishment.

mn2:21.9.verse: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not develop (them), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who develops (them).

mn2:21.10.verse: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by developing.

mn2:22.1.verse: ‘As soon as a bhikkhu’s taints that can be abandoned by seeing (insight) have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by restraining have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by using have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by enduring have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by avoiding have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by removing have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by developing have been so abandoned—

mn2:22.2.verse: then he is called a bhikkhu who dwells restrained with the restraint of all the taints: he has severed craving, flung off the fetters, and has made an end of suffering with the complete penetration of conceit.’

mn2:22.3.verse: That was what the Blessed One said.

mn2:22.4.verse: The bhikkhus where satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn2:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn2:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the explanation of the restraint of all defilements.

mn2:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn2:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see.

mn2:3.2.verse: For one who knows and sees what?

mn2:3.3.verse: Rational application of mind and irrational application of mind.

mn2:3.4.verse: When you apply the mind irrationally, defilements arise, and once arisen they grow.

mn2:3.5.verse: When you apply the mind rationally, defilements don’t arise, and those that have already arisen are given up.

mn2:4.1.verse: Some defilements should be given up by seeing, some by restraint, some by using, some by enduring, some by avoiding, some by dispelling, and some by developing.

mn2:5.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by seeing?

mn2:5.2.verse: Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn2:5.3.verse: They don’t understand to which things they should apply the mind and to which things they should not apply the mind.

mn2:5.4.verse: So they apply the mind to things they shouldn’t and don’t apply the mind to things they should.

mn2:6.1.verse: And what are the things to which they apply the mind but should not?

mn2:6.2.verse: They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, give rise to unarisen defilements and make arisen defilements grow: the defilements of sensual desire,

mn2:6.5.verse: These are the things to which they apply the mind but should not.

mn2:6.6.verse: And what are the things to which they do not apply the mind but should?

mn2:6.7.verse: They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, do not give rise to unarisen defilements and give up arisen defilements: the defilements of sensual desire,

mn2:6.10.verse: These are the things to which they do not apply the mind but should.

mn2:7.1.verse: Because of applying the mind to what they should not and not applying the mind to what they should, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements grow.

mn2:7.2.verse: This is how they apply the mind irrationally:

mn2:7.3.verse: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? After being what, what did I become in the past?

mn2:7.4.verse: Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? After being what, what will I become in the future?’

mn2:7.5.verse: Or they are undecided about the present thus:

mn2:7.6.verse: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This sentient being—where did it come from? And where will it go?’

mn2:8.1.verse: When they apply the mind irrationally in this way, one of the following six views arises in them and is taken as a genuine fact.

mn2:8.3.verse: The view: ‘My self does not survive.’

mn2:8.4.verse: The view: ‘I perceive the self with the self.’

mn2:8.5.verse: The view: ‘I perceive what is not-self with the self.’

mn2:8.6.verse: The view: ‘I perceive the self with what is not-self.’

mn2:8.7.verse: Or they have such a view:

mn2:8.8.verse: ‘This self of mine is he, the one who speaks, the one who knows, who experiences the results of good and bad deeds in all the different realms. This self is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’

mn2:8.9.verse: This is called a misconception, the thicket of views, the desert of views, the twist of views, the dodge of views, the fetter of views.

mn2:8.10.verse: An unlearned ordinary person who is fettered by views is not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn2:8.11.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

mn2:9.2.verse: But take a learned noble disciple who has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn2:9.3.verse: They understand to which things they should apply the mind and to which things they should not apply the mind.

mn2:9.4.verse: So they apply the mind to things they should and don’t apply the mind to things they shouldn’t.

mn2:10.1.verse: And what are the things to which they don’t apply the mind and should not?

mn2:10.2.verse: They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, give rise to unarisen defilements and make arisen defilements grow: the defilements of sensual desire,

mn2:10.5.verse: These are the things to which they don’t apply the mind and should not.

mn2:10.6.verse: And what are the things to which they do apply the mind and should?

mn2:10.7.verse: They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, do not give rise to unarisen defilements and give up arisen defilements: the defilements of sensual desire,

mn2:10.10.verse: These are the things to which they do apply the mind and should.

mn2:10.11.verse: Because of not applying the mind to what they should not and applying the mind to what they should, unarisen defilements don’t arise and arisen defilements are given up.

mn2:11.1.verse: They rationally apply the mind: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn2:11.2.verse: And as they do so, they give up three fetters:

mn2:11.3.verse: substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances.

mn2:11.4.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by seeing.

mn2:12.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by restraint?

mn2:12.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, lives restraining the eye faculty.

mn2:12.3.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint of the eye faculty do not arise when there is such restraint.

mn2:12.4.verse: Reflecting rationally, they live restraining the ear faculty …

mn2:12.9.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint of the mind faculty do not arise when there is such restraint.

mn2:12.10.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint do not arise when there is such restraint.

mn2:12.11.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by restraint.

mn2:13.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by using?

mn2:13.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, makes use of robes:

mn2:13.3.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; and for covering up the private parts.’

mn2:14.1.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of almsfood:

mn2:14.2.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

mn2:15.1.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of lodgings:

mn2:15.2.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; to shelter from harsh weather and to enjoy retreat.’

mn2:16.1.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of medicines and supplies for the sick:

mn2:16.2.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off the pains of illness and to promote good health.’

mn2:17.1.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without using these things do not arise when they are used.

mn2:17.2.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by using.

mn2:18.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by enduring?

mn2:18.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. They endure the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles. They endure rude and unwelcome criticism. And they put up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.

mn2:18.3.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without enduring these things do not arise when they are endured.

mn2:18.4.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by enduring.

mn2:19.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by avoiding?

mn2:19.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild ox, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, thorny ground, a pit, a cliff, a swamp, and a sewer.

mn2:19.3.verse: Reflecting rationally, they avoid sitting on inappropriate seats, walking in inappropriate neighborhoods, and mixing with bad friends—whatever sensible spiritual companions would believe to be a bad setting.

mn2:19.4.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without avoiding these things do not arise when they are avoided.

mn2:19.5.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by avoiding.

mn2:20.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by dispelling?

mn2:20.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, doesn’t tolerate a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen, but gives it up, dispels it, eliminates it, and obliterates it. They don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

mn2:20.3.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without dispelling these things do not arise when they are dispelled.

mn2:20.4.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by dispelling.

mn2:21.1.verse: And what are the defilements that should be given up by developing?

mn2:21.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

mn2:21.8.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

mn2:21.9.verse: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without developing these things do not arise when they are developed.

mn2:21.10.verse: These are called the defilements that should be given up by developing.

mn2:22.1.verse: Now, take a mendicant who, by seeing, has given up the defilements that should be given up by seeing. By restraint, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by restraint. By using, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by using. By enduring, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by enduring. By avoiding, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by avoiding. By dispelling, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by dispelling. By developing, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by developing.

mn2:22.2.verse: They’re called a mendicant who lives having restrained all defilements, who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.”

mn2:22.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn2:22.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn3:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn3:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn3:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.

mn3:2.2.verse: Out of pity for you I have thought:

mn3:2.3.verse: “How shall my disciples be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things?”

mn3:2.4.verse: If you are my heirs in material things, not my heirs in Dhamma, it will be a reproach to you:

mn3:2.5.verse: “The Master’s disciples live as his heirs in material things, not as his heirs in Dhamma”,

mn3:2.6.verse: and it will be a reproach to me that

mn3:2.7.verse: “The Master’s disciples live as his heirs in material things, not as his heirs in Dhamma”.

mn3:2.8.verse: If you are my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things, it will be no reproach to you that

mn3:2.9.verse: “The Master’s disciples live as his heirs in Dhamma, not as his heirs in material things”,

mn3:2.10.verse: and it will be no reproach to me that

mn3:2.11.verse: “The Master’s disciples live as his heirs in Dhamma, not as his heirs in material things”.

mn3:2.12.verse: Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.

mn3:2.13.verse: Out of pity for you I have thought:

mn3:2.14.verse: “How shall my disciples be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things?”

mn3:3.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, suppose that I had eaten, refused more, had my fill, finished, had enough, had what I needed,

mn3:3.2.verse: and some alms-food was left over to be thrown away.

mn3:3.3.verse: Then two bhikkhus arrived hungry and weak,

mn3:3.5.verse: “Bhikkhus, I have eaten, refused more … had what I needed,

mn3:3.6.verse: but there is this alms-food of mine left over to be thrown away;

mn3:3.7.verse: eat if you like; if you do not then I shall throw it now where there is no greenery or drop into water where there is no life”;

mn3:3.9.verse: “The Blessed One has eaten, refused more … had what he needed,

mn3:3.10.verse: but there is this alms-food of the Blessed One left over to be thrown away;

mn3:3.11.verse: if we do not eat it the Blessed One will throw it away …

mn3:3.12.verse: but this has been said by the Blessed One:

mn3:3.13.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things’:

mn3:3.14.verse: now this alms-food is one of the material things;

mn3:3.15.verse: suppose that instead of eating this alms-food I pass the night and day hungry and weak?”

mn3:3.16.verse: and instead of eating that alms-food he passed that night and day hungry and weak;

mn3:3.18.verse: “The Blessed One has eaten … had what he needed,

mn3:3.19.verse: but there is this alms-food of the Blessed One’s left over to be thrown away …

mn3:3.21.verse: Suppose that I eat this alms-food and pass the night and day neither hungry nor weak?”

mn3:3.22.verse: And after eating that alms-food he passed the night and day not hungry and weak.

mn3:3.23.verse: Now although that bhikkhu by eating that alms-food passed the night and day neither hungry nor weak, yet the first bhikkhu is more to be respected and commended by me.

mn3:3.25.verse: Because that will for long conduce to his fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, easy support and arousal of energy.

mn3:3.26.verse: Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things.

mn3:3.27.verse: Out of pity for you I have thought:

mn3:3.28.verse: “How shall my disciples be my heirs in Dhamma, not my heirs in material things?”’

mn3:4.1.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn3:4.2.verse: Having said that, he rose from his seat and went into his dwelling.

mn3:4.3.verse: Soon after he had gone, the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn3:5.1.verse: ‘Friends, in what way do disciples of a Master who lives secluded not train in seclusion? And in what way do disciples of a Master who lives secluded train in seclusion?’

mn3:5.2.verse: ‘Indeed, friend, we would come from far away to learn from the venerable Sāriputta the meaning of this pronouncement.

mn3:5.3.verse: It would be good if the meaning of this pronouncement would occur to the venerable Sāriputta;

mn3:5.4.verse: having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it.’

mn3:5.5.verse: ‘Then, listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn3:6.1.verse: ‘Friends, in what way do disciples of a Master who lives secluded not train in seclusion?

mn3:6.2.verse: Here, friends, disciples of a Master who lives secluded do not train in seclusion,

mn3:6.3.verse: they do not abandon what the Master tells them to abandon,

mn3:6.4.verse: they are busy and careless, forward in erring, giving up seclusion.

mn3:6.5.verse: In this the elder bhikkhus are to be blamed for three reasons.

mn3:6.6.verse: ‘As disciples of a Master who lives secluded they do not train in seclusion’:

mn3:6.7.verse: they are to be blamed for this first reason.

mn3:6.8.verse: ‘They do not abandon what the Master tells them to abandon’:

mn3:6.9.verse: they are to be blamed for this second reason.

mn3:6.10.verse: ‘They are busy, careless, forward in erring, giving up seclusion’:

mn3:6.11.verse: they are to be blamed for this third reason.

mn3:6.12.verse: The elder bhikkhus are to be blamed for these three reasons.

mn3:6.13.verse: In this the middle bhikkhus are to be blamed for three reasons …

mn3:6.14.verse: In this the new bhikkhus are to be blamed for three reasons.

mn3:6.15.verse: ‘As disciples of a Master who lives secluded they do not train in seclusion’:

mn3:6.16.verse: they are to be blamed for this first reason.

mn3:6.17.verse: ‘They do not abandon what the Master tells them to abandon’:

mn3:6.18.verse: they are to be blamed for this second reason.

mn3:6.19.verse: ‘They are busy, careless, forward in erring, giving up seclusion’:

mn3:6.20.verse: they are to be blamed for this third reason.

mn3:6.21.verse: The new bhikkhus are to be blamed for these three reasons.

mn3:6.22.verse: It is in this way that disciples of a Master who lives secluded do not train in seclusion.

mn3:7.1.verse: ‘In what way do disciples of a Master who lives secluded train in seclusion?

mn3:7.2.verse: Here, disciples of a Master who lives secluded train in seclusion;

mn3:7.3.verse: they abandon what the Master tells them to abandon;

mn3:7.4.verse: they are not busy and not careless, they give up erring and are forward in seclusion.

mn3:7.5.verse: In this the elder bhikkhus are to be commended for three reasons.

mn3:7.6.verse: ‘As disciples of a Master who lives secluded they train in seclusion’:

mn3:7.7.verse: they are to be commended for this first reason.

mn3:7.8.verse: ‘They abandon what the Master tells them to abandon’:

mn3:7.9.verse: they are to be commended for this second reason.

mn3:7.10.verse: ‘They are not busy and not careless; they give up erring and are forward in seclusion’:

mn3:7.11.verse: they are to be commended for this third reason.

mn3:7.12.verse: The elder bhikkhus are to be commended for these three reasons.

mn3:7.13.verse: In this the middle bhikkhus are to be commended for three reasons …

mn3:7.14.verse: In this the new bhikkhus are to be commended for three reasons.

mn3:7.15.verse: ‘As disciples of a Master who lives secluded they train in seclusion’:

mn3:7.16.verse: they are to be commended for this first reason.

mn3:7.17.verse: ‘They abandon what the Master tells them to abandon’:

mn3:7.18.verse: they are to be commended for this second reason.

mn3:7.19.verse: ‘They are not busy and not careless; they give up erring and are forward in seclusion’:

mn3:7.20.verse: they are to be commended for this third reason.

mn3:7.21.verse: The new bhikkhus are to be commended for these three reasons.

mn3:7.22.verse: It is in this way that the disciples of a Master who lives secluded train in seclusion.

mn3:8.1.verse: ‘Friends, the evil herein is greed and it is hate.

mn3:8.2.verse: There is a Middle Way for the abandoning of greed and hate, giving vision, giving knowledge, that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

mn3:8.3.verse: And what is that Middle Way?

mn3:8.4.verse: It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn3:8.5.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

mn3:8.6.verse: This is the Middle Way giving vision, giving knowledge, that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

mn3:9-15.1.verse: ‘Friends, the evil herein is anger and it is revenge …

mn3:9-15.2.verse: the evil herein is contempt and it is domineering,

mn3:9-15.3.verse: the evil herein is envy and it is avarice,

mn3:9-15.4.verse: the evil herein is deceit and it is fraud,

mn3:9-15.5.verse: the evil herein is obduracy and it is presumption,

mn3:9-15.6.verse: the evil herein is conceit and it is pride (haughtiness),

mn3:9-15.7.verse: the evil herein is vanity and it is negligence.

mn3:9-15.8.verse: There is a Middle Way for the abandoning of vanity and negligence, giving vision, giving knowledge, that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

mn3:9-15.9.verse: And what is that Middle Way?

mn3:9-15.10.verse: It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn3:9-15.11.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

mn3:9-15.12.verse: This is the Middle Way giving vision, giving knowledge, that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.’”

mn3:9-15.13.verse: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

mn3:9-15.14.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words.

mn3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn3:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn3:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, be my heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.

mn3:2.2.verse: Out of sympathy for you, I think,

mn3:2.3.verse: ‘How can my disciples become heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh?’

mn3:2.4.verse: If you become heirs in things of the flesh, not in the teaching, that will make you liable to the accusation:

mn3:2.5.verse: ‘The Teacher’s disciples live as heirs in things of the flesh, not in the teaching.’

mn3:2.6.verse: And it will make me liable to the accusation:

mn3:2.7.verse: ‘The Teacher’s disciples live as heirs in things of the flesh, not in the teaching.’

mn3:2.8.verse: If you become heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh, that will make you not liable to the accusation:

mn3:2.9.verse: ‘The Teacher’s disciples live as heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.’

mn3:2.10.verse: And it will make me not liable to the accusation:

mn3:2.11.verse: ‘The Teacher’s disciples live as heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.’

mn3:2.12.verse: So, mendicants, be my heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.

mn3:2.13.verse: Out of sympathy for you, I think,

mn3:2.14.verse: ‘How can my disciples become heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh?’

mn3:3.1.verse: Suppose that I had eaten and refused more food, being replete, and having had as much as I needed.

mn3:3.2.verse: And there was some extra almsfood that was going to be thrown away.

mn3:3.3.verse: Then two mendicants were to come who were weak with hunger.

mn3:3.5.verse: ‘Mendicants, I have eaten and refused more food, being replete, and having had as much as I need.

mn3:3.6.verse: And there is this extra almsfood that’s going to be thrown away.

mn3:3.7.verse: Eat it if you like. Otherwise I’ll throw it out where there is little that grows, or drop it into water that has no living creatures.’

mn3:3.8.verse: Then one of those mendicants thought,

mn3:3.9.verse: ‘The Buddha has eaten and refused more food.
