mn3:3.10.verse: And he has some extra almsfood that’s going to be thrown away.

mn3:3.11.verse: If we don’t eat it he’ll throw it away.

mn3:3.12.verse: But the Buddha has also said:

mn3:3.13.verse: “Be my heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.”

mn3:3.14.verse: And almsfood is one of the things of the flesh.

mn3:3.15.verse: Instead of eating this almsfood, why don’t I spend this day and night weak with hunger?’

mn3:3.17.verse: Then the second of those mendicants thought,

mn3:3.18.verse: ‘The Buddha has eaten and refused more food.

mn3:3.19.verse: And he has some extra almsfood that’s going to be thrown away.

mn3:3.20.verse: If we don’t eat it he’ll throw it away.

mn3:3.21.verse: Why don’t I eat this almsfood, then spend the day and night having dispelled my hunger and weakness?’

mn3:3.23.verse: Even though that mendicant, after eating the almsfood, spent the day and night having dispelled hunger and weakness, it is the former mendicant who is more worthy of respect and praise.

mn3:3.25.verse: Because for a long time that will conduce to that mendicant being of few wishes, content, self-effacing, unburdensome, and energetic.

mn3:3.26.verse: So, mendicants, be my heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.

mn3:3.27.verse: Out of sympathy for you, I think,

mn3:3.28.verse: ‘How can my disciples become heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh?’”

mn3:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn3:4.2.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

mn3:4.3.verse: Then, not long after the Buddha left, Venerable Sāriputta said to the mendicants,

mn3:5.1.verse: “Reverends, how do the disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion not train in seclusion? And how do they train in seclusion?”

mn3:5.2.verse: “Reverend, we would travel a long way to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta.

mn3:5.3.verse: May Venerable Sāriputta himself please clarify the meaning of this.

mn3:5.4.verse: The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn3:5.5.verse: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn3:6.1.verse: “Reverends, how do the disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion not train in seclusion?

mn3:6.2.verse: The disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion do not train in seclusion.

mn3:6.3.verse: They don’t give up what the Teacher tells them to give up.

mn3:6.4.verse: They’re indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion.

mn3:6.5.verse: In this case, the senior mendicants should be criticized on three grounds.

mn3:6.6.verse: ‘The disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion do not train in seclusion.’

mn3:6.8.verse: ‘They don’t give up what the Teacher tells them to give up.’

mn3:6.10.verse: ‘They’re indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion.’

mn3:6.12.verse: The senior mendicants should be criticized on these three grounds.

mn3:6.13.verse: In this case, the middle mendicants

mn3:6.14.verse: and the junior mendicants should be criticized on the same three grounds.

mn3:6.22.verse: This is how the disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion do not train in seclusion.

mn3:7.1.verse: And how do the disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion train in seclusion?

mn3:7.2.verse: The disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion train in seclusion.

mn3:7.3.verse: They give up what the Teacher tells them to give up.

mn3:7.4.verse: They’re not indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion.

mn3:7.5.verse: In this case, the senior mendicants should be praised on three grounds.

mn3:7.6.verse: ‘The disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion train in seclusion.’

mn3:7.8.verse: ‘They give up what the Teacher tells them to give up.’

mn3:7.10.verse: ‘They’re not indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion.’

mn3:7.12.verse: The senior mendicants should be praised on these three grounds.

mn3:7.13.verse: In this case, the middle mendicants

mn3:7.14.verse: and the junior mendicants should be praised on the same three grounds.

mn3:7.22.verse: This is how the disciples of a Teacher who lives in seclusion train in seclusion.

mn3:8.1.verse: The bad thing here is greed and hate.

mn3:8.2.verse: There is a middle way of practice for giving up greed and hate. It gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn3:8.3.verse: And what is that middle way of practice?

mn3:8.4.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn3:8.5.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

mn3:8.6.verse: This is that middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn3:9-15.1.verse: The bad thing here is anger and acrimony. …

mn3:9-15.8.verse: There is a middle way of practice for giving up vanity and negligence. It gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn3:9-15.9.verse: And what is that middle way of practice?

mn3:9-15.10.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn3:9-15.11.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

mn3:9-15.12.verse: This is that middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.”

mn3:9-15.13.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

mn3:9-15.14.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Sāriputta said.

mn4:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn4:2.1.verse: Then Jānussoṇi of the divine caste went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,

mn4:2.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn4:2.3.verse: ‘Master Gotama, when clansmen have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in Master Gotama, do they have Master Gotama for their leader, their helper and their guide?

mn4:2.4.verse: And do these people follow the implications of Master Gotama’s view?’

mn4:2.5.verse: ‘That is so, divine, that is so.

mn4:2.6.verse: When clansmen have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in me, they have me for their leader, their helper and their guide.

mn4:2.7.verse: And these people do follow the implications of my view.’

mn4:2.8.verse: ‘But Master Gotama, remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest are hard to endure, seclusion is hard to achieve and it is hard to enjoy isolation.

mn4:2.9.verse: One would think the jungles must rob a bhikkhu of his mind, if he has no concentration.’

mn4:2.10.verse: ‘That is so, divine, that is so.

mn4:2.11.verse: Remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest are hard to endure, seclusion is hard to achieve and it is hard to enjoy isolation.

mn4:2.12.verse: One would think the jungles must rob a bhikkhu of his mind, if he has no concentration.’

mn4:3.1.verse: ‘Before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I too (considered) thus:

mn4:3.2.verse: “Remote jungle-thicket resting places are hard to endure …

mn4:3.3.verse: the jungles must rob a bhikkhu of his mind, if he has no concentration.”

mn4:4.2.verse: “Whenever monks or divines resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest unpurified in bodily conduct, then owing to the defect in their unpurified bodily conduct these worthy monks and divines evoke unprofitable fear and dread.

mn4:4.3.verse: But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest unpurified in bodily conduct.

mn4:4.4.verse: I am purified in bodily conduct.

mn4:4.5.verse: I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places, as it were, one of the Noble Ones, with bodily conduct purified.”

mn4:4.6.verse: Seeing in myself this purity of bodily conduct, I found great solace dwelling in the forest.

mn4:5.2.verse: “Whenever monks or divines … unpurified in verbal conduct … evoke unprofitable fear and dread. But I … am purified in verbal conduct …” I found great solace dwelling in the forest.

mn4:5.3.verse: ‘I (considered) thus: “Whenever monks or divines … unpurified in mental conduct … evoke great fear and dread. I am purified in mental conduct …”

mn4:8.2.verse: “… covetous and keenly affected by lust for sensual desires …

mn4:9.4.verse: I have a mind of loving-kindness …”

mn4:10.4.verse: I am without lethargy and drowsiness …”

mn4:13.2.verse: ‘ “… given to self-praise and disparagement of others …

mn4:13.4.verse: I am not given to self-praise and disparagement of others …”

mn4:14.4.verse: I am not subject to alarm and terror …”

mn4:15.2.verse: “… desirous of gain, honour and renown …

mn4:19.2.verse: “Whenever monks or divines resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest devoid of understanding and drivelling, then owing to the defect of their being devoid of understanding and drivelling, these worthy monks and divines evoke unprofitable fear and dread.

mn4:19.3.verse: But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest devoid of understanding and drivelling.

mn4:19.5.verse: I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest, as it were, one of the Noble ones perfect in understanding.”

mn4:19.6.verse: Seeing in myself this perfection of understanding, I found great solace in dwelling in the forest.

mn4:20.2.verse: “There are the specially holy nights of the (half-moon of the) Fourteenth, the (half-moon of the) Fifteenth, and the Quarter-moon of the Eighth.

mn4:20.4.verse: Now what if I dwell on such nights as these in such awe-inspiring, horrifying abodes such as orchard shrines, woodland shrines, and tree shrines. Perhaps I too might encounter that fear and dread?”

mn4:20.5.verse: ‘And later, on such specially holy nights as the (half-moon of the) Fourteenth, the (half-moon of the) Fifteenth, and the quarter-moon of the Eighth,

mn4:20.7.verse: I dwelt in such awe-inspiring, horrifying abodes such as orchard shrines, woodland shrines and tree shrines.

mn4:20.8.verse: And while I dwelt there, a wild animal would come up to me, or a peacock would knock off a branch, or the wind would rustle the leaves.

mn4:20.10.verse: “What now if this is the fear and dread coming?”

mn4:20.12.verse: “Why do I dwell always expecting fear and dread?

mn4:20.13.verse: What if I subdue that fear and dread while keeping the posture that I am in when it finds me?’

mn4:20.14.verse: ‘While I walked, the fear and dread came upon me.

mn4:20.15.verse: I neither stood nor sat nor lay down till I had subdued that fear and dread.

mn4:20.16.verse: While I stood, the fear and dread came upon me.

mn4:20.17.verse: I neither walked nor sat nor lay down till I had subdued that fear and dread.

mn4:20.18.verse: While I sat, the fear and dread came upon me.

mn4:20.19.verse: I neither walked nor stood nor lay down till I had subdued that fear and dread.

mn4:20.20.verse: While I lay down, the fear and dread came upon me.

mn4:20.21.verse: I neither walked nor stood nor sat till I had subdued that fear and dread.

mn4:21.1.verse: There are monks and divines who perceive day when it is night and perceive night when it is day.

mn4:21.2.verse: I say that on their part that is a deluded man’s abiding.

mn4:21.3.verse: Now I perceive night when it is night and perceive day when it is day.

mn4:21.4.verse: Rightly speaking, were it to be said of someone:

mn4:21.5.verse: “A being not subject to delusion has appeared in the world for the welfare and happiness of many, out of pity for the world, for the benefit, welfare and happiness of gods and men”,

mn4:21.6.verse: it is of me indeed that rightly speaking it should be said thus.

mn4:22-26.1.verse: Tireless energy was aroused in me and unforgetting mindfulness established, my body was tranquil and untroubled, my mind was concentrated and unified.

mn4:22-26.2.verse: Quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, I entered upon and abode in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial and sustained application with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of seclusion.

mn4:22-26.3.verse: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, I entered upon and abode in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn4:22-26.4.verse: With the fading as well of happiness I abode in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, I entered upon and abode in the third jhāna, on which account Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”

mn4:22-26.5.verse: With the abandoning of (bodily) pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of (mental) joy and grief, I entered upon and abode in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn4:27.1.verse: When the concentrated mind was thus quite purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed, I inclined the mind to knowledge of the recollection of past life. I recollected my manifold past life.

mn4:27.2.verse: that is to say, one birth, two births … five births, ten births … fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (world) contraction, many aeons of (world) expansion, many aeons of (world) contraction and expansion: “There I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I appeared elsewhere; and there too I was so-named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared here. Thus with details and particulars I recollected my manifold past life.

mn4:28.1.verse: This was the first True Knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night.

mn4:28.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and true Knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as (happens) in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn4:29.1.verse: When the concentrated mind was thus quite purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to imperturbability, I directed, I inclined the mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn4:29.2.verse: With the heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; I understood how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings, who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; I understood how beings pass on according to their kammas.

mn4:30.1.verse: This was the second True Knowledge attained by me in the second watch of the night.

mn4:30.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and True Knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose as (happens) in one who abides diligent ardent and self-controlled.

mn4:31.1.verse: When the concentrated mind was thus purified and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to unperturbability, I directed, I inclined the mind to knowledge of exhaustion of taints.

mn4:31.2.verse: I had direct knowledge thus: “This is suffering”; I had direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of suffering”; I had direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of suffering”; I had direct knowledge thus: “The is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”

mn4:31.3.verse: I had direct knowledge thus: “These are taints”; I had direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of taints”; I had direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of taints”; I had direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of taints.”

mn4:32.1.verse: When I knew and saw thus, the mind was liberated from the taints of sensual desire, from the taints of being and from the taints of ignorance.

mn4:32.2.verse: When liberated there came the knowledge: “It is liberated”.

mn4:32.3.verse: I had direct knowledge thus: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what can be done is done, there is no more of this in the beyond.”

mn4:33.1.verse: ‘This was the third True Knowledge attained by me in the third watch of the night.

mn4:33.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and True Knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose as (happens) in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn4:34.1.verse: ‘Now, divine, it might be that you (think) thus:

mn4:34.2.verse: “Perhaps the monk Gotama is not free from lust, hate and delusion even today, which is why he still resorts to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest.”

mn4:34.3.verse: But you should not think thus.

mn4:34.4.verse: It is because I see two benefits that I still resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest:

mn4:34.5.verse: I see a pleasant abiding for myself here and now, and I have pity on the future generations.’

mn4:35.1.verse: ‘Indeed it is because Master Gotama is an Arahant and Fully Enlightened that he has pity on future generations.

mn4:35.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.

mn4:35.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn4:35.5.verse: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn4:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn4:2.1.verse: Then the brahmin Jānussoṇi went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn4:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn4:2.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, those gentlemen who, out of faith in you, have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness have you to lead the way, help them out, and give them encouragement.

mn4:2.4.verse: And those people follow the worthy Gotama’s example.”

mn4:2.5.verse: “That’s so true, brahmin! Everything you say is true, brahmin!”

mn4:2.8.verse: “But worthy Gotama, remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest are challenging. It’s hard to maintain seclusion and hard to find joy in solitude.

mn4:2.9.verse: The forests seem to rob the mind of a mendicant who isn’t immersed in samādhi.”

mn4:2.10.verse: “That’s so true, brahmin! Everything you say is true, brahmin!

mn4:3.1.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too thought,

mn4:3.2.verse: ‘Remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest are challenging. It’s hard to maintain seclusion and hard to find joy in solitude.

mn4:3.3.verse: The forests seem to rob the mind of a mendicant who isn’t immersed in samādhi.’

mn4:4.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins with unpurified conduct of body, speech, and mind who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest. Those ascetics and brahmins summon unskillful fear and dread because of these defects in their conduct.

mn4:4.3.verse: But I don’t frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest with unpurified conduct of body, speech, and mind.

mn4:4.5.verse: I am one of those noble ones who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest with purified conduct of body, speech, and mind.’

mn4:4.6.verse: Seeing this purity of conduct in myself I felt even more unruffled about staying in the forest.

mn4:5.4.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins with unpurified livelihood who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest. Those ascetics and brahmins summon unskillful fear and dread because of these defects in their livelihood.

mn4:6.1.verse: But I don’t frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest with unpurified livelihood.

mn4:7.1.verse: I am one of those noble ones who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest with purified livelihood.’

mn4:7.2.verse: Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself I felt even more unruffled about staying in the forest.

mn4:8.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins full of desire for sensual pleasures, with acute lust …

mn4:8.4.verse: I am not full of desire …’

mn4:9.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins full of ill will, with malicious intentions …

mn4:9.4.verse: I have a heart full of love …’

mn4:10.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins overcome with dullness and drowsiness …

mn4:10.4.verse: I am rid of dullness and drowsiness …’

mn4:11.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are restless, with minds unsettled …

mn4:12.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are doubting and uncertain …

mn4:13.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who glorify themselves and put others down …

mn4:13.4.verse: I don’t glorify myself and put others down …’

mn4:14.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are cowardly and craven …

mn4:15.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who enjoy possessions, honor, and popularity …

mn4:16.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are lazy and lack energy …

mn4:17.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are unmindful and lack situational awareness …

mn4:18.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who lack immersion, with straying minds …

mn4:19.2.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are witless and idiotic who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest. Those ascetics and brahmins summon unskillful fear and dread because of the defects of witlessness and stupidity.

mn4:19.3.verse: But I don’t frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest witless and idiotic.

mn4:19.5.verse: I am one of those noble ones who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest accomplished in wisdom.’

mn4:19.6.verse: Seeing this accomplishment of wisdom in myself I felt even more unruffled about staying in the forest.

mn4:20.2.verse: ‘There are certain nights that are recognized as specially portentous:

mn4:20.3.verse: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight.

mn4:20.4.verse: On such nights, why don’t I stay in awe-inspiring and hair-raising shrines in parks, forests, and trees? In such lodgings, hopefully I might see that fear and dread.’

mn4:20.5.verse: Some time later, that’s what I did.

mn4:20.8.verse: As I was staying there a deer came by, or a peacock snapped a twig, or the wind rustled the leaves.

mn4:20.10.verse: ‘Is this that fear and dread coming?’

mn4:20.12.verse: ‘Why do I always meditate expecting that fear to come?

mn4:20.13.verse: Why don’t I get rid of that fear and dread just as it comes, while remaining just as I am?’

mn4:20.14.verse: Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was walking.

mn4:20.15.verse: I didn’t stand still or sit down or lie down until I had got rid of that fear and dread while walking.

mn4:20.16.verse: Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was standing.

mn4:20.17.verse: I didn’t walk or sit down or lie down until I had got rid of that fear and dread while standing.

mn4:20.18.verse: Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was sitting.

mn4:20.19.verse: I didn’t lie down or stand still or walk until I had got rid of that fear and dread while sitting.

mn4:20.20.verse: Then that fear and dread came upon me as I was lying down.

mn4:20.21.verse: I didn’t sit up or stand still or walk until I had got rid of that fear and dread while lying down.

mn4:21.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who perceive that it’s day when in fact it’s night, or perceive that it’s night when in fact it’s day.

mn4:21.2.verse: This meditation of theirs is delusional, I say.

mn4:21.3.verse: I perceive that it’s night when in fact it is night, and perceive that it’s day when in fact it is day.

mn4:21.4.verse: And if there’s anyone of whom it may be rightly said that

mn4:21.5.verse: a being not liable to delusion has arisen in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, it’s of me that this should be said.

mn4:22-26.1.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and lucid, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind was immersed and unified in samādhi.

mn4:22-26.2.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn4:22-26.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn4:22-26.4.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, I entered and remained in the third absorption, where I meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn4:22-26.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn4:27.1.verse: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives. I recollected many kinds of past lives.

mn4:27.2.verse: That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. I remembered: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so I recollected my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn4:28.1.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

mn4:28.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn4:29.1.verse: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn4:29.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn4:30.1.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night.

mn4:30.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn4:31.1.verse: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn4:31.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn4:31.3.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn4:32.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn4:32.2.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

mn4:32.3.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn4:33.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the final watch of the night.

mn4:33.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn4:34.2.verse: ‘Perhaps the ascetic Gotama is not free of greed, hate, and delusion even today, and that is why he still frequents remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.’

mn4:34.3.verse: But you should not see it like this.

mn4:34.4.verse: I see two reasons to frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

mn4:34.5.verse: I see happiness for myself in this life, and I have sympathy for future generations.”

mn4:35.1.verse: “Indeed, worthy Gotama has sympathy for future generations, since he is a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn4:35.2.verse: Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent, worthy Gotama!

mn4:35.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn4:35.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn4:35.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn5:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn5:1.3.verse: There Ven. Sāriputta addressed the monks:

mn5:1.5.verse: “Yes, friend,” the monks responded to him.

mn5:2.1.verse: “There are these four individuals to be found existing in the world.

mn5:2.3.verse: There is the case where a certain individual, being blemished, does not discern as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish.’

mn5:2.4.verse: Then there is the case where a certain individual, being blemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish.’

mn5:2.5.verse: Then there is the case where a certain individual, being unblemished, does not discern as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish.’

mn5:2.6.verse: Then there is the case where a certain individual, being unblemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish.’

mn5:2.7.verse: With regard to that, the individual who, being blemished, doesn’t discern as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish’ is called the inferior man of the two individuals who are blemished.

mn5:2.8.verse: The individual who, being blemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish’ is called the superior man of the two individuals who are blemished.

mn5:2.9.verse: Then again, the individual who, being unblemished, doesn’t discern as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish’ is called the inferior man of the two individuals who are unblemished.

mn5:2.10.verse: The individual who, being unblemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish’ is called the superior man of the two individuals who are unblemished.”

mn5:3.1.verse: When this was said, Ven. Mahā Moggallāna said to Ven. Sāriputta,

mn5:3.2.verse: “Friend, what is the reason, what is the cause, that of the two individuals who are blemished, one is called the inferior man and one is called the superior man?

mn5:3.3.verse: And what is the reason, what is the cause, that of the two individuals who are unblemished, one is called the inferior man and one is called the superior man?”

mn5:4.1.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “With regard to that, my friend, when an individual, being blemished, doesn’t discern that ‘I have an inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will not generate desire, endeavor, or arouse persistence for the abandoning of that blemish.

mn5:4.2.verse: He will die with passion, with aversion, with delusion—blemished & with a mind defiled.

mn5:4.3.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths all covered with dust & dirt,

mn5:4.4.verse: that the owners would neither use nor clean, but would throw away in a dusty place:

mn5:4.5.verse: Wouldn’t that bronze bowl eventually become even more dirty & defiled with time?”

mn5:4.7.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “In the same way, friend, when an individual, being blemished, doesn’t discern as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will not generate desire, endeavor, or arouse persistence for the abandoning of that blemish.

mn5:4.8.verse: He will die with passion, with aversion, with delusion—blemished & with a mind defiled.

mn5:5.1.verse: “Then again, when an individual, being blemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will generate desire, endeavor, & arouse persistence for the abandoning of that blemish.

mn5:5.2.verse: He will die without passion, without aversion, without delusion—unblemished & with a mind undefiled.

mn5:5.3.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths all covered with dust & dirt,

mn5:5.4.verse: that the owners would both use & clean, and would not throw away in a dusty place:

mn5:5.5.verse: Wouldn’t that bronze bowl eventually become clean & pure with time?”

mn5:5.7.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “In the same way, friend, when an individual, being blemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have an inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will generate desire, endeavor, & arouse persistence for the abandoning of that blemish.

mn5:5.8.verse: He will die without passion, without aversion, without delusion—unblemished & with a mind undefiled.

mn5:6.1.verse: “Then again, when an individual, being unblemished, doesn’t discern as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will attend to the theme of beauty. As he attends to the theme of beauty, passion will assault his mind.

mn5:6.2.verse: He will die with passion, with aversion, with delusion—blemished & with a mind defiled.

mn5:6.3.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths clean & pure,

mn5:6.4.verse: that the owners would neither use nor clean, but would throw away in a dusty place.

mn5:6.5.verse: Wouldn’t that bronze bowl eventually become dirty & defiled with time?”

mn5:6.7.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “In the same way, when an individual, being unblemished, doesn’t discern as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will attend to the theme of beauty. As he attends to the theme of beauty, passion will assault his mind.

mn5:6.8.verse: He will die with passion, with aversion, with delusion—blemished & with a mind defiled.

mn5:7.1.verse: “Then again, when an individual, being unblemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will not attend to the theme of beauty. As he doesn’t attend to the theme of beauty, passion won’t assault his mind.

mn5:7.2.verse: He will die without passion, without aversion, without delusion—unblemished & with a mind undefiled.

mn5:7.3.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths clean & pure,

mn5:7.4.verse: that the owners would both use & clean, and would not throw away in a dusty place:

mn5:7.5.verse: Wouldn’t that bronze bowl eventually become even more clean & pure with time?”

mn5:7.7.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “In the same way, friend, when an individual, being unblemished, discerns as it has come to be that ‘I have no inner blemish,’ it can be expected of him that he will not attend to the theme of beauty. As he doesn’t attend to the theme of beauty, passion won’t assault his mind.

mn5:7.8.verse: He will die without passion, without aversion, without delusion—unblemished & with a mind undefiled.

mn5:8.1.verse: “This, friend Moggallāna, is the reason, this is the cause why, of the two individuals who are blemished, one is called the inferior man and one is called the superior man.

mn5:8.2.verse: This is the reason, this is the cause why, of the two individuals who are unblemished, one is called the inferior man and one is called the superior man.”

mn5:9.3.verse: [Ven. Sāriputta:] “The influences of evil, unskillful wishes: That’s what ‘blemish’ stands for.

mn5:10.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:10.2.verse: ‘O, should I have fallen into an offense, may the monks not know about me, that I have fallen into an offense.’

mn5:10.3.verse: But it’s possible that the monks would know about that monk

mn5:10.4.verse: that he had fallen into an offense.

mn5:10.5.verse: (Thinking,) ‘The monks know about me that I have fallen into an offense,’

mn5:11.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:11.2.verse: ‘O, should I have fallen into an offense, may the monks accuse me in private, and not in the middle of the Saṅgha.’

mn5:11.3.verse: But it’s possible that the monks would accuse him in the middle of the Saṅgha, not in private.

mn5:11.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s in the middle of the Saṅgha that the monks accuse me, and not in private,’

mn5:12.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:12.2.verse: ‘O, should I have fallen into an offense, may a friend accuse me, and not an enemy.’

mn5:12.3.verse: But it’s possible that an enemy would accuse him, and not a friend.

mn5:12.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘An enemy accuses me, and not a friend,’

mn5:13.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:13.2.verse: ‘O, may the Teacher instruct the monks, cross-questioning just me again & again, and not cross-questioning another monk again & again.’

mn5:13.3.verse: But it’s possible that the Teacher would instruct the monks, cross-questioning another monk again & again, and not cross-questioning that monk again & again.

mn5:13.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘The Teacher instructs the monks, cross-questioning another monk again & again, and not cross-questioning me again & again,’

mn5:14.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:14.2.verse: ‘O, may the monks enter the village for alms following just me, and not following another monk.’

mn5:14.3.verse: But it’s possible that the monks would enter the village for alms following another monk, and not following that monk.

mn5:14.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s following another monk, and not me, that the monks enter the village for alms,’

mn5:15.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:15.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone receive the foremost meals, the foremost seat, the foremost water, the foremost alms, and not another monk.’

mn5:15.3.verse: But it’s possible that another monk would receive the foremost meals, the foremost seat, the foremost water, the foremost alms.

mn5:15.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who receives the foremost meals, the foremost seat, the foremost water, the foremost alms, and not me,’

mn5:16.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:16.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone give the blessing in the dining hall after the meal, and not another monk.’

mn5:16.3.verse: But it’s possible that another monk would give the blessing in the dining hall after the meal.

mn5:16.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who gives the blessing in the dining hall after the meal, and not me,’

mn5:17.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:17.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone, and not another monk, teach the Dhamma to monks who have come to the monastery.’

mn5:17.3.verse: But it’s possible that another monk would teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery, and not that monk.

mn5:17.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who teaches the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery, and not me,’

mn5:18-20.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:18-20.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone, and not another monk, teach the Dhamma to nuns…

mn5:18-20.4.verse: women lay followers who have come to the monastery.’

mn5:18-20.5.verse: But it’s possible that another monk would teach the Dhamma to the women lay followers who have come to the monastery, and not that monk.

mn5:18-20.6.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who teaches the Dhamma to the women lay followers who have come to the monastery, and not me,’

mn5:21.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:21.2.verse: ‘O, may the monks pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to me alone, and not to another monk.’

mn5:21.3.verse: But it’s possible that the monks would pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to another monk, and not to that monk.

mn5:21.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk that the monks pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to, and not me,’

mn5:22-24.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:22-24.4.verse: women lay followers pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to me alone, and not to another monk.’

mn5:22-24.5.verse: But it’s possible that the women lay followers would pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to another monk, and not to that monk.

mn5:22-24.6.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk that the women lay followers pay honor, respect, reverence, & veneration to, and not me,’

mn5:25.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:25.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone, and not another monk, be the one who receives exquisite robes.’

mn5:25.3.verse: But it’s possible that another monk, and not that monk, is the one who receives exquisite robes.

mn5:25.4.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who receives exquisite robes, and not me,’

mn5:26-27.1.verse: “It’s possible, friend, that there’s the case where this sort of wish might arise in a certain monk:

mn5:26-27.2.verse: ‘O, may I alone, and not another monk, be the one who receives exquisite alms…

mn5:26-27.4.verse: exquisite medicinal requisites for curing the ill.’

mn5:26-27.5.verse: But it’s possible that another monk, and not that monk, is the one who receives exquisite medicinal requisites for curing the ill.

mn5:26-27.6.verse: (Thinking,) ‘It’s another monk who receives exquisite medicinal requisites for curing the ill, and not me,’

mn5:28.1.verse: This, friend, is what these influences of evil, unskillful wishes stand for: ‘blemish.’

mn5:29.1.verse: “Now friend, if these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be unabandoned in any monk, then even though he’s a wilderness dweller, a dweller in isolated lodgings, an alms-goer, a house-to-house alms-goer, a refuse-rag wearer, a wearer of coarse robes, still his companions in the holy life don’t pay him honor, respect, reverence, or veneration.

mn5:29.3.verse: Because these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be unabandoned in him.

mn5:29.4.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths clean & pure, into which the owners would arrange the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human being

mn5:29.5.verse: and—covering it with another bronze bowl—would carry back into the market:

mn5:29.6.verse: A person, seeing them, would say,

mn5:29.7.verse: ‘Well, what’s this, being carried around as if it were so splendid?’

mn5:29.8.verse: He, raising & opening the lid, would look in.

mn5:29.9.verse: As soon as he saw, he would be inspired with displeasure, with loathing, with disgust,

mn5:29.10.verse: so that even if he were hungry, he would not want to eat—to say nothing of if he were full.

mn5:29.11.verse: “In the same way, if these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be unabandoned in any monk, then even though he’s a wilderness dweller, a dweller in isolated lodgings, an alms-goer, a house-to-house alms-goer, a refuse-rag wearer, a wearer of coarse robes, still his companions in the holy life don’t pay him honor, respect, reverence, or veneration.

mn5:29.13.verse: Because these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be unabandoned in him.

mn5:30.1.verse: “But, friend, if these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be abandoned in any monk, then even though he’s a village dweller, a receiver of meal invitations, a wearer of robes given by lay people, still his companions in the holy life pay him honor, respect, reverence, or veneration.

mn5:30.3.verse: Because these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be abandoned in him.

mn5:30.4.verse: “Just like a bronze bowl brought back from a shop or a family of smiths clean & pure, into which the owners would arrange boiled white rice with various sauces and curries

mn5:30.5.verse: and—covering it with another bronze bowl—would carry back into the market:

mn5:30.6.verse: A person, seeing them, would say,

mn5:30.7.verse: ‘Well, what’s this, being carried around as if it were so splendid?’

mn5:30.8.verse: He, raising & opening the lid, would look in.

mn5:30.9.verse: As soon as he saw, he would be inspired with enticement, with non-loathing, & with non-disgust,

mn5:30.10.verse: so that even if he were full, he would want to eat—to say nothing of if he were hungry.

mn5:30.11.verse: “In the same way, if these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be abandoned in any monk, then even though he’s a village dweller, a receiver of meal invitations, a wearer of robes given by lay people, still his companions in the holy life pay him honor, respect, reverence, or veneration.

mn5:30.13.verse: Because these influences of evil, unskillful wishes are seen or heard to be abandoned in him.”

mn5:31.1.verse: When this was said, Ven. Moggallāna said to Ven. Sāriputta,

mn5:31.2.verse: “A simile occurs to me, friend Sāriputta.”

mn5:31.3.verse: “Let it occur to you, friend Moggallāna.”

mn5:31.4.verse: “On one occasion I was staying near Rājagaha, at the Hill Fort.

mn5:31.5.verse: Then, early in the morning, I adjusted my lower robe and—taking my bowl & outer robe—went into Rājagaha for alms.

mn5:31.6.verse: And on that occasion Samīti the cartwright was planing the rim of a chariot wheel,

mn5:31.7.verse: and the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, a former cartwright, was standing by.

mn5:31.8.verse: Then this line of thinking arose in the awareness of Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the former cartwright:

mn5:31.9.verse: ‘O, may Samīti the cartwright plane away this bend, this twist, this fault in this rim, so that this rim would be clean—its bends, twists, and faults removed—standing in heartwood.’

mn5:31.10.verse: And just as the line of thinking occurred to Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the former cartwright, in just the same way did Samīti the cartwright plane away that bend, that twist, that fault in the rim.

mn5:31.11.verse: So Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the former cartwright, gratified, uttered words of gratification:

mn5:31.12.verse: ‘He planes, knowing my heart with his heart, as it were!’

mn5:32.1.verse: “In the same way, any individuals without conviction, who—for the sake of a livelihood and not out of conviction—have gone forth from the home life into homelessness; who are fraudulent, deceitful, wily, restless, rowdy, flighty, talkative, of loose words; who leave their faculties unguarded; who know no moderation in food, are undevoted to wakefulness, unconcerned with the qualities of a contemplative, with no respect for the training; who are luxurious, lethargic, foremost in falling back; who shirk the duties of solitude; who are lazy, lowly in their persistence, of muddled mindfulness, unalert, unconcentrated, their minds scattered, undiscerning, drivelers: Ven. Sāriputta, with this Dhamma discourse, planes away their (faults), knowing my heart with his heart, as it were!

mn5:32.2.verse: “But as for those sons of good families who, out of conviction, have gone forth from the home life into homelessness; who are unfraudulent, undeceitful, not wily, not restless, not rowdy, not flighty, not talkative or of loose words; who guard their faculties, know moderation in food, are devoted to wakefulness, are concerned with the qualities of a contemplative, have fierce respect for the training; who are not luxurious, not lethargic, not foremost in falling back; who observe the duties of solitude; who are not lazy; who are aroused in their effort, of unmuddled mindfulness, alert, concentrated, their minds unified, discerning, not drivelers: They, hearing this Dhamma discourse from Ven. Sāriputta, drink it up & devour it, as it were, both by word & by mind:

mn5:32.3.verse: ‘How good it is that, having made his companions in the holy life rise up from what’s unskillful, he establishes them in what’s skillful!’

mn5:33.1.verse: “Just as a young & youthful woman or man—fond of adornment, with head bathed—on receiving a garland of blue lotuses, jasmine, or camellias, would take it with both hands and place it on top of his or her head;

mn5:33.2.verse: in the same way, those sons of good families who, out of conviction, have gone forth from the home life into homelessness; who are unfraudulent, undeceitful, not wily, not restless, not rowdy, not flighty, not talkative or of loose words; who guard their faculties, know moderation in food, are devoted to wakefulness, are concerned with the qualities of a contemplative, have fierce respect for the training; who are not luxurious, not lethargic, not foremost in falling back; who observe the duties of solitude; who are not lazy; who are aroused in their effort, of unmuddled mindfulness, alert, concentrated, their minds unified, discerning, not drivelers: They, hearing this Dhamma discourse from Ven. Sāriputta, drink it up & devour it, as it were, both by word & by mind:

mn5:33.3.verse: ‘How good it is that, having made his companions in the holy life rise up from what’s unskillful, he establishes them in what’s skillful!’”

mn5:33.4.verse: Thus did those two great beings [nāgas] rejoice in each other’s well-spoken words.

mn5:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn5:2.1.verse: “Reverends, these four individuals are found in the world.

mn5:2.3.verse: One individual with a blemish doesn’t truly understand: ‘There is a blemish in me.’

mn5:2.4.verse: But another individual with a blemish does truly understand: ‘There is a blemish in me.’

mn5:2.5.verse: One individual without a blemish doesn’t truly understand: ‘There is no blemish in me.’

mn5:2.6.verse: But another individual without a blemish does truly understand: ‘There is no blemish in me.’

mn5:2.7.verse: In this case, of the two individuals with a blemish, the one who doesn’t understand is said to be worse,

mn5:2.8.verse: while the one who does understand is better.

mn5:2.9.verse: And of the two individuals without a blemish, the one who doesn’t understand is said to be worse,

mn5:2.10.verse: while the one who does understand is better.”

mn5:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to him:

mn5:3.2.verse: “What is the cause, Reverend Sāriputta, what is the reason why, of the two individuals with a blemish, one is said to be worse and one better?

mn5:3.3.verse: And what is the cause, what is the reason why, of the two individuals without a blemish, one is said to be worse and one better?”

mn5:4.1.verse: “Reverends, take the case of the individual who has a blemish and does not understand it. You can expect that they won’t generate enthusiasm, make an effort, or rouse up energy to give up that blemish.

mn5:4.2.verse: And they will die with greed, hate, and delusion, blemished, with a corrupted mind.

mn5:4.3.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy enveloped with dirt or stains.

mn5:4.4.verse: And the owners neither used it or had it cleaned, but kept it in a dirty place.

mn5:4.5.verse: Over time, wouldn’t that bronze cup get even dirtier and more stained?”

mn5:4.7.verse: “In the same way, take the case of the individual who has a blemish and does not understand it. You can expect that …

mn5:4.8.verse: they will die with a corrupted mind.

mn5:5.1.verse: Take the case of the individual who has a blemish and does understand it. You can expect that they will generate enthusiasm, make an effort, and rouse up energy to give up that blemish.

mn5:5.2.verse: And they will die without greed, hate, and delusion, unblemished, with an uncorrupted mind.

mn5:5.3.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy enveloped with dirt or stains.

mn5:5.4.verse: But the owners used it and had it cleaned, and didn’t keep it in a dirty place.

mn5:5.5.verse: Over time, wouldn’t that bronze cup get cleaner and brighter?”

mn5:5.7.verse: “In the same way, take the case of the individual who has a blemish and does understand it. You can expect that …

mn5:5.8.verse: they will die with an uncorrupted mind.

mn5:6.1.verse: Take the case of the individual who doesn’t have a blemish but does not understand it. You can expect that they will focus on the feature of beauty, and because of that, lust will infect their mind.

mn5:6.2.verse: And they will die with greed, hate, and delusion, blemished, with a corrupted mind.

mn5:6.3.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy clean and bright.

mn5:6.4.verse: And the owners neither used it or had it cleaned, but kept it in a dirty place.

mn5:6.5.verse: Over time, wouldn’t that bronze cup get dirtier and more stained?”

mn5:6.7.verse: “In the same way, take the case of the individual who has no blemish and does not understand it. You can expect that …

mn5:6.8.verse: they will die with a corrupted mind.

mn5:7.1.verse: Take the case of the individual who doesn’t have a blemish and does understand it. You can expect that they won’t focus on the feature of beauty, and because of that, lust won’t infect their mind.

mn5:7.2.verse: And they will die without greed, hate, and delusion, unblemished, with an uncorrupted mind.

mn5:7.3.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy clean and bright.

mn5:7.4.verse: And the owners used it and had it cleaned, and didn’t keep it in a dirty place.

mn5:7.5.verse: Over time, wouldn’t that bronze cup get cleaner and brighter?”

mn5:7.7.verse: “In the same way, take the case of the individual who doesn’t have a blemish and does understand it. You can expect that …

mn5:7.8.verse: they will die with an uncorrupted mind.

mn5:8.1.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why, of the two individuals with a blemish, one is said to be worse and one better.

mn5:8.2.verse: And this is the cause, this is the reason why, of the two individuals without a blemish, one is said to be worse and one better.”

mn5:9.2.verse: But what is ‘blemish’ a term for?”

mn5:9.3.verse: “Reverend, ‘blemish’ is a term for the spheres of bad, unskillful wishes.

mn5:10.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:10.2.verse: ‘If I commit an offense, I hope the mendicants don’t find out!’

mn5:10.3.verse: But it’s possible that the mendicants do find out that that mendicant

mn5:10.5.verse: Thinking, ‘The mendicants have found out about my offense,’

mn5:10.7.verse: And that anger and that bitterness

mn5:11.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:11.2.verse: ‘If I commit an offense, I hope the mendicants accuse me in private, not in the middle of the Saṅgha.’

mn5:11.3.verse: But it’s possible that the mendicants do accuse that mendicant in the middle of the Saṅgha …

mn5:12.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:12.2.verse: ‘If I commit an offense, I hope I’m accused by a peer, not by someone who is not a peer.’

mn5:12.3.verse: But it’s possible that someone who is not a peer accuses that mendicant …

mn5:13.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:13.2.verse: ‘Oh, I hope the Teacher will teach the mendicants by repeatedly questioning me alone, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:13.3.verse: But it’s possible that the Teacher will teach the mendicants by repeatedly questioning some other mendicant …

mn5:14.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:14.2.verse: ‘Oh, I hope the mendicants will enter the village for the meal putting me at the very front, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:14.3.verse: But it’s possible that the mendicants will enter the village for the meal putting some other mendicant at the very front …

mn5:15.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:15.2.verse: ‘Oh, I hope that I alone get the best seat, the best drink, and the best almsfood in the refectory, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:15.3.verse: But it’s possible that some other mendicant gets the best seat, the best drink, and the best almsfood in the refectory …

mn5:16.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:16.2.verse: ‘I hope that I alone give the verses of appreciation after eating in the refectory, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:16.3.verse: But it’s possible that some other mendicant gives the verses of appreciation after eating in the refectory …

mn5:17.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:17.2.verse: ‘Oh, I hope that I might teach the Dhamma to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen in the monastery, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:18-20.5.verse: But it’s possible that some other mendicant teaches the Dhamma …

mn5:21.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:21.2.verse: ‘Oh, I hope that the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen will honor, respect, revere, and venerate me alone, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:22-24.5.verse: But it’s possible that some other mendicant is honored, respected, revered, and venerated …

mn5:25.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant might wish:

mn5:25.2.verse: ‘I hope I get the nicest robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, not some other mendicant.’

mn5:25.3.verse: But it’s possible that some other mendicant gets the nicest robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick …

mn5:26-27.6.verse: Thinking, ‘Some other mendicant has got the nicest robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick’,

mn5:26-27.8.verse: And that anger and that bitterness

mn5:28.1.verse: ‘Blemish’ is a term for these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes.

mn5:29.1.verse: Suppose these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be not given up by a mendicant. Even though they dwell in the wilderness, in remote lodgings, eat only almsfood, wander indiscriminately for almsfood, wear rag robes, and wear shabby robes, their spiritual companions don’t honor, respect, revere, and venerate them.

mn5:29.3.verse: It’s because these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be not given up by that venerable.

mn5:29.4.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy clean and bright.

mn5:29.5.verse: The owners were to prepare it with the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human, cover it with a bronze lid, and parade it through the market-place.

mn5:29.6.verse: When people saw it they’d say:

mn5:29.7.verse: ‘Oh my, what is it that you’re carrying like a precious treasure?’

mn5:29.8.verse: So they’d open up the lid for people to look inside.

mn5:29.9.verse: But as soon as they saw it they were filled with loathing, revulsion, and disgust.

mn5:29.10.verse: Not even those who were hungry wanted to eat it, let alone those who were replete.

mn5:29.11.verse: In the same way, when these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be not given up by a mendicant … their spiritual companions don’t honor, respect, revere, and venerate them.

mn5:29.13.verse: It’s because these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be not given up by that venerable.

mn5:30.1.verse: Suppose these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be given up by a mendicant. Even though they dwell within a village, accept invitations to a meal, and wear robes offered by householders, their spiritual companions honor, respect, revere, and venerate them.

mn5:30.3.verse: It’s because these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be given up by that venerable.

mn5:30.4.verse: Suppose a bronze cup was brought from a shop or smithy clean and bright.

mn5:30.5.verse: The owners were to prepare it with boiled fine rice with the dark grains picked out and served with many soups and sauces, cover it with a bronze lid, and parade it through the market-place.

mn5:30.6.verse: When people saw it they’d say:

mn5:30.7.verse: ‘Oh my, what is it that you’re carrying like a precious treasure?’

mn5:30.8.verse: So they’d open up the lid for people to look inside.

mn5:30.9.verse: And as soon as they saw it they were filled with liking, attraction, and relish.

mn5:30.10.verse: Even those who were replete wanted to eat it, let alone those who were hungry.

mn5:30.11.verse: In the same way, when these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be given up by a mendicant … their spiritual companions honor, respect, revere, and venerate them.

mn5:30.13.verse: It’s because these spheres of bad, unskillful wishes are seen and heard to be given up by that venerable.”

mn5:31.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to him,

mn5:31.3.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said Sāriputta.

mn5:31.4.verse: “Reverend, this one time I was staying right here in Rājagaha, the Mountainfold.

mn5:31.5.verse: Then I robed up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

mn5:31.6.verse: Now at that time Samīti of the wainwrights was planing the rim of a chariot wheel.

mn5:31.7.verse: The Ājīvaka ascetic Paṇḍuputta, who was formerly of the wainwrights, was standing by,

mn5:31.8.verse: and this thought came to his mind:

mn5:31.9.verse: ‘Oh, I hope Samīti the wainwright planes out the crooks, bends, and flaws in this rim. Then the rim will be rid of crooks, bends, and flaws, pure, and consolidated in the core.’

mn5:31.10.verse: And Samīti planed out the flaws in the rim just as Paṇḍuputta thought.

mn5:31.12.verse: ‘He planes like he knows my heart with his heart!’

mn5:32.1.verse: In the same way, there are those faithless individuals who went forth from the lay life to homelessness not out of faith but to earn a livelihood. They’re devious, deceitful, and sneaky. They’re haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, and loose-tongued. They do not guard their sense doors or eat in moderation, and they are not dedicated to wakefulness. They don’t care about the ascetic life, and don’t keenly respect the training. They’re indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion, lazy, and lacking energy. They’re unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds, witless and idiotic. Venerable Sāriputta planes their faults with this exposition of the teaching as if he knows my heart with his heart!

mn5:32.2.verse: But there are those gentlemen who went forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith. They’re not devious, deceitful, and sneaky. They’re not haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, and loose-tongued. They guard their sense doors and eat in moderation, and they are dedicated to wakefulness. They care about the ascetic life, and keenly respect the training. They’re not indulgent or slack, nor are they leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion. They’re energetic and determined. They’re mindful, with situational awareness, immersion, and unified minds; wise and clever. Hearing this exposition of the teaching from Venerable Sāriputta, they drink it up and devour it, as it were. And in speech and thought they say:

mn5:32.3.verse: ‘It’s good, sir, that he draws his spiritual companions away from the unskillful and establishes them in the skillful.’

mn5:33.1.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and had bathed their head. Presented with a garland of lotuses, jasmine, or liana flowers, they would take them in both hands and place them on the crown of the head.

mn5:33.2.verse: In the same way, those gentlemen who went forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith … say:

mn5:33.3.verse: ‘It’s good, sir, that he draws his spiritual companions away from the unskillful and establishes them in the skillful.’”

mn5:33.4.verse: And so these two spiritual giants agreed with each other’s fine words.

mn6:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn6:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn6:2.1.verse: “Monks, dwell consummate in virtue, consummate in terms of the Pāṭimokkha. Dwell restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in your behavior & sphere of activity. Train yourselves, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.

mn6:3.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I be dear & pleasing to my companions in the holy life, respected by & inspiring to them,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:4.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I be someone who receives robes, alms food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for curing the sick,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:5.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘Whatever I use or consume in terms of robes, alms food, lodgings, & medical requisites for curing the sick, may that be of great fruit, of great benefit to those who provided them,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:6.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘When my kinsmen & relatives who have died & passed away recollect me with brightened minds, may it be of great fruit, of great benefit,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:7.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I overcome displeasure & delight, and not be overcome by displeasure & delight. May I dwell conquering again & again any displeasure & delight that has arisen,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:8.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I overcome fear & dread, and not be overcome by fear & dread. May I dwell conquering again & again any fear & dread that have arisen,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:9.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I attain—whenever I want, without strain, without difficulty—the four jhānas that are heightened mental states, pleasant abidings in the here & now,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:10.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I dwell touching with the body those liberations that are peaceful, formless, transcending forms,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:11.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I—with the ending of (the first) three fetters—be a stream-winner, certain, never again destined for the lower realms, headed for self-awakening,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:12.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I—with the ending of (the first) three fetters, and with the attenuation of passion, aversion, & delusion—be a once-returner, who, on returning only once more to this world, would make an ending to stress,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:13.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I—with the ending of the five lower fetters, be one who is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, destined never again to return from that world,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:14.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I wield manifold supranormal powers. Having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one. May I appear & vanish. May I go unimpeded through walls, ramparts, & mountains as if through space. May I dive in & out of the earth as if it were water. May I walk on water without sinking as if it were dry land. Sitting cross-legged, may I fly through the air like a winged bird. With my hand may I touch & stroke even the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. May I influence with my body even as far as the Brahmā worlds,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:15.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I hear—by means of the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human—both kinds of sounds: divine and human, whether near or far,’ then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:16.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I know the awareness of other beings, other individuals, having encompassed it with my own awareness.

mn6:16.2.verse: May I discern a mind with passion as “a mind with passion,”

mn6:16.3.verse: and a mind without passion as “a mind without passion.”

mn6:16.4.verse: May I discern a mind with aversion as “a mind with aversion,”

mn6:16.5.verse: and a mind without aversion as “a mind without aversion.”

mn6:16.6.verse: May I discern a mind with delusion as “a mind with delusion,”

mn6:16.7.verse: and a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion.”

mn6:16.8.verse: May I discern a restricted mind as “a restricted mind,”

mn6:16.9.verse: and a scattered mind as “a scattered mind.”

mn6:16.10.verse: May I discern an enlarged mind as “an enlarged mind,”

mn6:16.11.verse: and an unenlarged mind as “an unenlarged mind.”

mn6:16.12.verse: May I discern an excelled mind [one that is not at the most excellent level] as “an excelled mind,”

mn6:16.13.verse: and an unexcelled mind as “an unexcelled mind.”

mn6:16.14.verse: May I discern a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind,”

mn6:16.15.verse: and an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind.”

mn6:16.16.verse: May I discern a released mind as “a released mind,”

mn6:16.17.verse: and an unreleased mind as “an unreleased mind,”’

mn6:16.18.verse: Then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:17.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I recollect my manifold past lives, i.e., one birth, two births, three births, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, one hundred, one thousand, one hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction & expansion, (recollecting,) ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure & pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from that state, I re-arose there. There too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure & pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from that state, I re-arose here.’ Thus may I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes & details,’

mn6:17.2.verse: Then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:18.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I see—by means of the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human—beings passing away and re-appearing, and may I discern how they are inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate in accordance with their kamma: ‘These beings—who were endowed with bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views and undertook actions under the influence of wrong views—with the break-up of the body, after death, have re-appeared in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. But these beings—who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views and undertook actions under the influence of right views—with the break-up of the body, after death, have re-appeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus—by means of the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human—may I see beings passing away and re-appearing, and may I discern how they are inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate in accordance with their kamma,’

mn6:18.2.verse: Then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:19.1.verse: “If a monk would wish, ‘May I—with the ending of effluents—remain in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for myself right in the here & now,’

mn6:19.2.verse: Then he should be one who brings the precepts to perfection, who is committed to inner tranquility of awareness, who doesn’t neglect jhāna, who is endowed with insight, and who frequents empty dwellings.

mn6:20.1.verse: “‘Monks, dwell consummate in virtue, consummate in terms of the Pāṭimokkha. Dwell restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in your behavior & sphere of activity. Train yourselves, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.’

mn6:20.2.verse: Thus was it said. And in reference to this was it said.”

mn6:20.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn6:20.4.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn6:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn6:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn6:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.

mn6:3.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I be liked and approved by my spiritual companions, respected and admired.’ So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

mn6:4.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.’ So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

mn6:5.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May the services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick I enjoy be very fruitful and beneficial for them.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:6.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘When deceased family and relatives who have passed away recollect me with a confident mind, may this be very fruitful and beneficial for them.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …
