mn6:7.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I prevail over desire and discontent, and may desire and discontent not prevail over me. May I live having mastered desire and discontent whenever they arose.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:8.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I prevail over fear and dread, and may fear and dread not prevail over me. May I live having mastered fear and dread whenever they arose.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:9.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when I want, without trouble or difficulty.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:10.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I have direct meditative experience of the peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:11.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I, with the ending of three fetters, become a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:12.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I, with the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, become a once-returner, coming back to this world once only, then making an end of suffering.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:13.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I, with the ending of the five lower fetters, be reborn spontaneously and become extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:14.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:15.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, may I hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.’ So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:16.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my mind.

mn6:16.2.verse: May I understand mind with greed as “mind with greed”,

mn6:16.3.verse: and mind without greed as “mind without greed”;

mn6:16.4.verse: mind with hate as “mind with hate”,

mn6:16.5.verse: and mind without hate as “mind without hate”;

mn6:16.6.verse: mind with delusion as “mind with delusion”,

mn6:16.7.verse: and mind without delusion as “mind without delusion”;

mn6:16.12.verse: mind that is not supreme as “mind that is not supreme”,

mn6:16.13.verse: and mind that is supreme as “mind that is supreme”;

mn6:16.14.verse: mind immersed in samādhi as “mind immersed in samādhi”,

mn6:16.15.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as “mind not immersed in samādhi”;

mn6:16.18.verse: So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:17.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. May I remember: “There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.” May I thus recollect my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.’

mn6:17.2.verse: So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:18.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, may I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place—and understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: “These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.” And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, may I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. And may I understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.’

mn6:18.2.verse: So let them fulfill their precepts …

mn6:19.1.verse: A mendicant might wish: ‘May I realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

mn6:19.2.verse: So let them fulfill their precepts, be committed to inner serenity of the heart, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and frequent empty huts.

mn6:20.1.verse: ‘Mendicants, live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.’

mn6:20.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

mn6:20.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn6:20.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn7:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn7:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn7:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were defiled and stained,

mn7:2.2.verse: and a dyer dipped it in some dye or other, whether blue or yellow or red or pink, it would look ill-dyed and impure in colour.

mn7:2.4.verse: Because of the impurity of the cloth;

mn7:2.5.verse: so too, when mind is defiled, an unhappy destination may be expected.

mn7:2.6.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were pure and bright,

mn7:2.7.verse: and a dyer dipped it in some dye or other, whether blue or yellow or red or pink, it would look well-dyed and pure in colour.

mn7:2.9.verse: Because of the purity of the cloth;

mn7:2.10.verse: so too, when mind is undefiled, a happy destination may be expected.

mn7:3.1.verse: ‘What are the imperfections that defile mind?

mn7:3.2.verse: Covetousness and unrighteous greed is an imperfection that defile mind. Ill-will … Anger … Revenge … Contempt … Domineering … Envy … Avarice … Deceit … Fraud … Obduracy … Presumption … Conceit … Pride (haughtiness) … Vanity … Negligence … is an imperfection that defile mind.

mn7:4.1.verse: ‘When a bhikkhu knows that covetousness and unrighteous greed is an imperfection that defile mind, he abandons it.

mn7:4.30.verse: negligence are imperfections that defile mind,

mn7:5.1.verse: ‘As soon as it is known that covetousness and unrighteous greed is an imperfection that defiles mind, it is abandoned in him;

mn7:5.2.verse: as soon as it is known that ill-will

mn7:5.31.verse: negligence are imperfections that defile mind, they are abandoned in him.

mn7:5.32.verse: ‘Thereupon, he becomes possessed of perfect confidence in the Buddha thus:

mn7:5.33.verse:
“That Blessed One is such since he is Arahant, fully enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds,’

incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.”

mn7:6.1.verse: ‘And he becomes possessed of confidence in the Dhamma thus:

mn7:6.2.verse: “The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, (it has effect) visible here and now, not (after a lapse) of time; it invites inspection, is onward-leading, and experienceable by the wise each for himself.”

mn7:7.1.verse: ‘And he becomes possessed of perfect confidence in the Sangha thus:

mn7:7.2.verse: “The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way, has entered on the straight way, has entered on the true way, has entered on the proper way, that is to say, the four Pairs of Men, the Eight (types of) Persons; this Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is fit for gifts, fit for hospitality, fit for offerings, and fit for reverential salutation, as the incomparable field of merit for the world.”

mn7:8.1.verse:
‘And whatever (from among those imperfections) has, according to the limitation (set by whichever of the first three paths he has attained), been given up, has been (for ever) dropped, let go, abandoned, relinquished.

‘He (considers) thus: “I am possessed of perfect confidence in the Buddha” and he gains experience of meanings, he gains experience of dhammas, and so he finds gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn7:8.2.verse: ‘When he is glad, happiness is born in him; being happy in mind, his body becomes tranquillized; when his body is tranquil, he feels pleasure; feeling pleasure, his mind becomes concentrated.

mn7:9.1.verse: ‘He (considers) thus: “I am possessed of perfect confidence in the Dhamma” and he gains experience of meanings, he gains experience of dhammas, and so he finds gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn7:10.1.verse: ‘He (considers) thus: “I am possessed of perfect confidence in the Sangha” and he gains experience of meanings, he gains experience of dhammas, and so he finds gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn7:10.2.verse: ‘When he is glad … his mind becomes concentrated.

mn7:11.1.verse: ‘He (considers) thus: “And whatever has, according to limitation, been given up, it has been dropped, let go, abandoned, relinquished, and he gains experience of meanings, he gains experience of dhammas, and so he finds gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn7:11.2.verse: ‘When he is glad … his mind becomes concentrated.

mn7:12.1.verse: ‘If a bhikkhu of such virtue, such dhammas and such understanding eats alms-food consisting of rice with the dark grains picked out accompanied by many sauces and curries, even that will be no obstacle for him.

mn7:12.2.verse: ‘Just as a cloth that is defiled and stained becomes pure and bright with the help of clear water, or just as gold becomes pure and bright with the help of a furnace,

mn7:12.3.verse: so too, if a bhikkhu of such virtue … eats alms-food … that will be no obstacle for him.

mn7:13.1.verse: ‘He abides with his heart endued with loving-kindness extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with his heart abundant with loving-kindness, exalted, measureless, without hostility or ill-will extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn7:14.1.verse: ‘He abides with his heart endued with compassion … over the all-encompassing world.

mn7:15.1.verse: ‘He abides with his heart endued with gladness … over the all-encompassing world.

mn7:16.1.verse: ‘He abides with his heart endued with equanimity … over the all-encompassing world.

mn7:17.1.verse: ‘(Of that) he understands thus: “There is this (pure state of Divine Abiding), there is the inferior (state of defilements abandoned), there is the superior (goal of the Arahant Path yet to be attained), and there is the escape (which is Nibbāna) from this (whole) field of perception.”

mn7:18.1.verse: ‘When he knows and sees in this way, the mind becomes liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, and liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn7:18.2.verse: When liberated, there is knowledge: “It is liberated”.

mn7:18.3.verse: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what can be done is done, there is no more of this in the beyond.”

mn7:19.1.verse: Now on that occasion Sundavika Bhāradvāja of the divine caste had seated himself not far from the Blessed One.

mn7:19.2.verse: Then he said to the Blessed One:

mn7:19.3.verse: ‘But does Master Gotama go to the Bahukā River to bathe?’

mn7:19.5.verse: What can the Bahukā River do?’

mn7:19.6.verse: ‘Master Gotama, the Bahukā River is held by many to give liberation; it is held by many to give merit, and many wash away in the Bahukā River the evil kammas they have done.’

mn7:20.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed Sundarika Bhāradvāja of the divine caste in stanzas:

mn7:20.7.verse: Yet will not wash black kamma white.

mn7:20.8.verse: What can Sundarikā bring to pass?

mn7:20.9.verse: What the Payāga? What the Bahukā?

mn7:20.11.verse: A man that has done brutal acts and cruel.

mn7:20.12.verse: One pure in heart has evermore

mn7:20.13.verse: The Feast of Spring, the Holy Day;

mn7:20.14.verse: One fair in act, one pure in heart

mn7:20.16.verse: ’Tis here, divine, that thou shouldst come to bathe,

mn7:20.17.verse: To make thyself safe refuge for all beings.

mn7:20.18.verse: And if thou speakest no untruth,

mn7:20.19.verse: Nor workest harm for living beings,

mn7:20.20.verse: Nor takest what is offered not,

mn7:20.21.verse: With faith and with no avarice,

mn7:20.22.verse: To Gayā gone what wouldst thou do?

mn7:20.23.verse: Let any well thy Gayā be.

mn7:21.1.verse: When this was said, Sundarika Bhāradvāja of the divine caste said:

mn7:21.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who is lost, holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyesight to see forms.

mn7:21.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn7:21.5.verse: I would receive the Going-forth under Master Gotama, I would receive the Full Admission.’

mn7:22.1.verse: And Sundarika Bhāradvāja of the divine caste received the Going-forth under the Blessed One, and he received the Full Admission.

mn7:22.2.verse: And not long after his Full Admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, the venerable Bhāradvāja, by realization himself with direct knowledge here and now, entered upon and abode in that supreme goal of the life divine, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn7:22.3.verse: He had direct knowledge thus: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what is to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn7:22.4.verse: And the venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the Arahants.

mn7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn7:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn7:2.1.verse: “Suppose, mendicants, there was a cloth that was dirty and soiled.

mn7:2.2.verse: No matter what dye the dyer applied—whether blue or yellow or red or magenta—it would look poorly dyed and impure in color.

mn7:2.4.verse: Because of the impurity of the cloth.

mn7:2.5.verse: In the same way, when the mind is corrupt, a bad destiny is to be expected.

mn7:2.6.verse: Suppose there was a cloth that was pure and clean.

mn7:2.7.verse: No matter what dye the dyer applied—whether blue or yellow or red or magenta—it would look well dyed and pure in color.

mn7:2.9.verse: Because of the purity of the cloth.

mn7:2.10.verse: In the same way, when the mind isn’t corrupt, a good destiny is to be expected.

mn7:3.1.verse: And what are the corruptions of the mind?

mn7:3.2.verse: Covetousness and immoral greed, ill will, anger, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, deviousness, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, vanity, and negligence are corruptions of the mind.

mn7:4.1.verse: A mendicant who understands that covetousness and immoral greed are corruptions of the mind gives them up.

mn7:4.2.verse: A mendicant who understands that ill will …

mn7:4.30.verse: negligence is a corruption of the mind gives it up.

mn7:5.1.verse: When they have understood these corruptions of the mind

mn7:5.2.verse: for what they are, and have given them up,

mn7:5.32.verse: they have experiential confidence in the Buddha:

mn7:5.33.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn7:6.1.verse: They have experiential confidence in the teaching:

mn7:6.2.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

mn7:7.1.verse: They have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

mn7:7.2.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

mn7:8.1.verse: When a mendicant has discarded, eliminated, released, given up, and relinquished to this extent, thinking, ‘I have experiential confidence in the Buddha …

mn7:10.1.verse: the Saṅgha,’ they find inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and find joy connected with the teaching.

mn7:11.1.verse: Thinking: ‘I have discarded, eliminated, released, given up, and relinquished to this extent,’ they find inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and find joy connected with the teaching.

mn7:11.2.verse: When they’re joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. And when they’re blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn7:12.1.verse: When a mendicant of such ethics, such qualities, and such wisdom eats boiled fine rice with the dark grains picked out and served with many soups and sauces, that is no obstacle for them.

mn7:12.2.verse: Compare with cloth that is dirty and soiled; it can be made pure and clean by pure water. Or native gold, which can be made pure and bright by a forge.

mn7:12.3.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant of such ethics, such qualities, and such wisdom eats boiled fine rice with the dark grains picked out and served with many soups and sauces, that is no obstacle for them.

mn7:13.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn7:14.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of compassion to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn7:15.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of rejoicing to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn7:16.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn7:17.1.verse: They understand: ‘There is this, there is what is worse than this, there is what is better than this, and there is an escape beyond the scope of perception.’

mn7:18.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn7:18.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn7:18.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn7:18.5.verse: a mendicant who is bathed with the inner bathing.”

mn7:19.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā was sitting not far from the Buddha.

mn7:19.3.verse: “But does Worthy Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe?”

mn7:19.4.verse: “Brahmin, why go to the Bāhukā River?

mn7:19.5.verse: What can the Bāhukā River do?”

mn7:19.6.verse: “Many people deem that the Bāhukā River leads to a heavenly world and bestows merit. And many people rinse off their bad deeds in the Bāhukā River.”

mn7:20.1.verse: Then the Buddha addressed Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā in verse:

mn7:20.3.verse: at Gayā and the Sundarikā too,

mn7:20.6.verse: a fool can constantly plunge into them

mn7:20.7.verse: but it won’t purify their dark deeds.

mn7:20.9.verse: What the Payāga or the Bāhukā?

mn7:20.10.verse: They can’t cleanse a cruel person, a sinner

mn7:20.12.verse: For the pure in heart it’s always

mn7:20.13.verse: the spring festival or the sabbath.

mn7:20.14.verse: For the pure in heart and clean of deed,

mn7:20.15.verse: their vows will always be fulfilled.

mn7:20.16.verse: It’s here alone that you should bathe, brahmin,

mn7:20.17.verse: making yourself a sanctuary for all creatures.

mn7:20.18.verse: And if you speak no lies,

mn7:20.21.verse: and you’re faithful and not stingy:

mn7:20.22.verse: what’s the point of going to Gayā?

mn7:20.23.verse: For any well may be your Gayā!”

mn7:21.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā said to the Buddha,

mn7:21.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn7:21.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn7:21.5.verse: May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama’s presence?”

mn7:22.1.verse: And the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

mn7:22.2.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Bhāradvāja, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn7:22.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn7:22.4.verse: And Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the perfected.

mn8:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn8:2.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Mahā Cunda rose from meditation, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn8:3.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, (there are) these various views that arise in the world

mn8:3.2.verse: associated either with self-doctrines or with world-doctrines:

mn8:3.3.verse: (now) does the abandoning and relinquishing of such views come about in a bhikkhu who is giving attention only to the beginning?’

mn8:3.4.verse: ‘There are, Cunda, these various views that arise in the world

mn8:3.5.verse: associated either with self-doctrine or with world-doctrine:

mn8:3.6.verse: (Now) whatever (the basis) those views arise on, whatever they underlie, whatever they are exercised on, when a man sees (that basis) as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not myself”, then in that way comes about in him the abandoning of such views, and likewise the relinquishment of them.

mn8:4.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn8:4.4.verse: But it is not these (attainments) that are called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline:

mn8:4.5.verse: these are called “a pleasant abiding here and now” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:5.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that with the stilling of initial and sustained application, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn8:5.4.verse: But it is not these (attainments) that are called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline:

mn8:5.5.verse: these are called “a pleasant abiding here and now” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:6.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that with the fading as well of happiness some bhikkhu abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna on account of which Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful”.

mn8:6.4.verse: But it is not these (attainments) that are called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline:

mn8:6.5.verse: these are called “a pleasant abiding here and now” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:7.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn8:7.4.verse: But it is not these (attainments) that are called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline:

mn8:7.5.verse: these are called “a pleasant abiding here and now” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:8.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that with complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of difference, (aware that) “space is infinite”, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consiting of the infinity of space.

mn8:8.4.verse: But it is not these attainments that are called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline:

mn8:8.5.verse: these are called “quiet abidings” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:9.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of space, (aware that) “consciousness is infinite”, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness.

mn8:9.5.verse: “quiet abidings” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:10.1.verse: ‘It is possible here that by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness, (aware that) “there is nothing”, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.

mn8:10.5.verse: these are called “quiet abidings” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:11.1.verse: ‘It it possible here that by completely surmounting the base consisting of nothingness, some bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn8:11.4.verse: But these (attainments) are not called “effacement” in the Noble One’s discipline;

mn8:11.5.verse: these are called “quiet abidings” in the Noble One’s discipline.

mn8:12.1.verse: ‘Now, Cunda, here is where effacement can be effected:

mn8:12.2.verse: ‘1. Others will be cruel; we shall not be cruel here: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:12.3.verse: ‘2. Others will kill living beings; we shall abstain from killing living beings here: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:12.4.verse: ‘3. Others will take what is not given; we shall abstain from taking what is not given here: effacement …

mn8:12.5.verse: ‘4. Others will not live the life divine; we shall live the life divine here: effacement …

mn8:12.6.verse: ‘5. Others will speak falsehood; we shall abstain from flase speech here: effacement …

mn8:12.7.verse: ‘6. Others will speak maliciously; we shall abstain from malicious speech here: effacement …

mn8:12.8.verse: ‘7. Others will speak harshly; we shall abstain from harsh speech here: effacement …

mn8:12.9.verse: ‘8. Others will gossip; we shall abstain from gossip here: effacement …

mn8:12.10.verse: ‘9. Others will be covetous; we shall be uncovetous here: effacement …

mn8:12.11.verse: ‘10. Others will have a mind of ill-will; we shall have no mind of ill-will here: effacement …

mn8:12.12.verse: ‘11. Others will have wrong view; we shall have right views here: effacement …

mn8:12.13.verse: ‘12. Others will have wrong intention; we shall have right intention here: effacement …

mn8:12.14.verse: ‘13. Others will have wrong speech; we shall have right speech here: effacement …

mn8:12.15.verse: ‘14. Others will have wrong action; we shall have right action here: effacement …

mn8:12.16.verse: ‘15. Others will have wrong livelihood; we shall have right livelihood here: effacement …

mn8:12.17.verse: ‘16. Others will have wrong effort; we shall have right effort here: effacement …

mn8:12.18.verse: ‘17. Others will have wrong mindfulness; we shall have right mindfulness here: effacement …

mn8:12.19.verse: ‘18. Others will have wrong concentration; we shall have right concentration here: effacement …

mn8:12.20.verse: ‘19. Others will have wrong knowledge; we shall have right knowledge here: effacement …

mn8:12.21.verse: ‘20. Others will have wrong deliverance; we shall have right deliverance here: effacement …

mn8:12.22.verse: ‘21. Others will be obsessed by sleepiness and drowsiness; we shall be free from sleepiness and drowsiness here: effacement …

mn8:12.23.verse: ‘22. Others will be agitated, we shall not be agitated here: effacement …

mn8:12.24.verse: ‘23. Others will be uncertain; we shall get beyond uncertainty here: effacement …

mn8:12.25.verse: ‘24. Others will be angry; we shall not be angry here: effacement …

mn8:12.26.verse: ‘25. Others will be inimical; we shall be without enmity here: effacement …

mn8:12.27.verse: ‘26. Others will be contemptuous; we shall not be contemptuous here: effacement …

mn8:12.28.verse: ‘27. Others will be domineering; we shall not be domineering here: effacement …

mn8:12.29.verse: ‘28. Others will be envious; we shall not be envious here: effacement …

mn8:12.30.verse: ‘29. Others will be avaricious; we shall not be avaricious here: effacement …

mn8:12.31.verse: ‘30. Others will be fraudulent; we shall not be fraudulent here: effacement …

mn8:12.32.verse: ‘31. Others will be deceitful; we shall not be deceitful here: effacement …

mn8:12.33.verse: ‘32. Others will be obdurate; we shall not be obdurate here: effacement …

mn8:12.34.verse: ‘33. Others will be haughty; we shall not be haughty here: effacement …

mn8:12.35.verse: ‘34. Others will be difficult to admonish; we shall be easy to admonish here: effacement …

mn8:12.36.verse: ‘35. Others will have bad friends; we shall have good friends here: effacement …

mn8:12.37.verse: ‘36. Others will be negligent; we shall be diligent here: effacement …

mn8:12.38.verse: ‘37. Others will be faithless; we shall be faithful here: effacement …

mn8:12.39.verse: ‘38. Others will be conscienceless; we shall be conscience-minded here: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:12.40.verse: ‘39. Others will be shameless; we shall have shame here: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:12.41.verse: ‘40. Others will be of little learning; we shall be of great learning here: effacement …

mn8:12.42.verse: ‘41. Others will be idle; we shall have aroused energy here: effacement …

mn8:12.43.verse: ‘42. Others will be unmindful; we shall have established mindfulness here: effacement …

mn8:12.44.verse: ‘43. Others will have poor understanding; we shall possess understanding here: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:12.45.verse: ‘44. Others will misapprehend according to their individual views, hold on (to them) tenaciously and relinquish (them) with difficulty; we shall not misapprehend according to individual views, shall not hold on tenaciously, and shall relinquish with ease: effacement can be effected thus.

mn8:13.1.verse: ‘Cunda, I say that even the arising of mind in profitable dhammas is of great importance, so what should be said of bodily and verbal operations consequent thereupon? Therefore, Cunda:

mn8:13.2.verse: ‘1. Mind should be aroused thus: Others will be cruel; we shall not be cruel here.

mn8:13.3.verse: ‘2. Mind should be aroused thus: Others will kill living beings; we shall not kill living beings here. ‘3-43 … ’

mn8:13.4.verse: ‘44. Mind should be aroused thus: Others will misapprehend according to individual views, hold on (to them) tenaciously and relinquish (them) with difficulty; we shall not misapprehend according to individual views, shall not hold on tenaciously, and shall relinquish with ease.

mn8:14.1.verse: ‘Cunda, suppose there were an uneven path and another even path by which to avoid it;

mn8:14.2.verse: and suppose there were an uneven ford and another even ford by which to avoid it, so too:

mn8:14.3.verse: ‘1. A person given to cruelty has non-cruelty by which to avoid it. ‘2. One given to killing living beings has abstention from killing living beings by which to avoid it. ‘3. One given to taking what is not given has abstention from taking what is not given by which to avoid it. ‘4. One given to what is not the life divine has the life divine by which to avoid it. ‘5. One given to false speech has abstention from false speech by which to avoid it. ‘6. One given to malicious speech has abstention from malicious speech by which to avoid it. ‘7. One given to harsh speech has abstention from harsh speech by which to avoid it. ‘8. One given to gossip has abstention from gossip by which to avoid it. ‘9. One given to covetousness has uncovetousness by which to avoid it. ‘10. One given to a mind of ill-will has non-ill-will by which to avoid it.

mn8:14.4.verse: ‘11. One given to wrong view has right view by which to avoid it. ‘12. One given to wrong intention has right intention by which to avoid it. ‘13. One given to wrong speech has right speech by which to avoid it. ‘14. One given to wrong action has right action by which to avoid it. ‘15. One given to wrong livelihood has right livelihood by which to avoid it. ‘16. One given to wrong effort has right effort by which to avoid it. ‘17. One given to wrong mindfulness has right mindfulness by which to avoid it. ‘18. One given to wrong concentration has right concentration by which to avoid it. ‘19. One given to wrong knowledge has right knowledge by which to avoid it. ‘20. One given to wrong deliverance has right deliverance by which to avoid it.

mn8:14.5.verse: ‘21. One obsessed by sluggishness and drowsiness has freedom from sluggishness ane drowsiness by which to avoid it. ‘22. One given to distraction has non-distraction by which to avoid it. ‘23. One given to uncertainty has the state of having got beyond uncertainty by which to avoid it. ‘24. One given to anger has non-anger by which to avoidit. ‘25. One given to enmity has non-enmity by which to avoid it. ‘26. One given to contempt has non-contempt by which to avoid it. ‘27. One given to domineering has non-domineering by which to avoid it. ‘28. One given to envy has non-envy by which to avoid it. ‘29. One given to avarice has non-avarice by which to avoid it. ‘30. One given to fraud has non-fraud by which to avoid it. ‘31. One given to deceit has non-deceit by which to avoid it. ‘32. One given to obduracy has non-obduracy by which to avoid it. ‘33. One given to haughtiness has non-haughtiness by which to avoid it. ‘34. One given to difficulty of admonishment has ease of admonishment by which to avoid it ‘35. One given to making bad friends has making good friends by which to avoid it. ‘36. One given to negligence has diligence by which to avoid it. ‘37. One given to faithlessness has faith by which to avoid it. ‘38. One given to lack of conscience has conscience by which to avoid it. ‘39. One given to shamelessness has shame by which to avoidit. ‘40. One given to little learning has great learning by which to avoid it. ‘41. One given to idleness has aroused energy by which to avoid it. ‘42. One given to forgetfulness has establishment of mindfulness by which to avoid it. ‘43. One given to lack of understanding has perfection of understanding by which to avoid it. ‘44. One given to misapprehension according to individual views, to holding on (to them) tenaciously, and to difficulty in relinquishing them, has not misapprehending according to individual views, not holding on tenaciously, and ease in relinquishment, by which to avoid it.

mn8:15.1.verse: ‘Cunda, just as no matter what unprofitable dhammas there are, they all lead to a lower state; and just as, no matter what profitable dhammas there are, they all lead to a higher state, so too:

mn8:15.2.verse: ‘1. A person given to cruelty has non-cruelty as a higher state. ‘2. One given to killing living beings has abstention from killing living beings as a higher state. ‘3-43 ...

mn8:15.3.verse: ‘44. One given to misapprehension according to individual views, to holding on (to them) tenaciously, and to difficulty in relinquishing (them), has not misapprehending according to individual views, not holding on tenaciously, and ease in relinquishing, as a higher state.

mn8:16.1.verse: ‘Cunda, that one who is himself floundering in a slough should pull out another who is floundering in the slough is not possible;

mn8:16.2.verse: that one who is not himself floundering in a slough should pull out another who is floundering in the slough is possible;

mn8:16.3.verse: that one who is himself untamed, undisciplined, and unattained to Nibbāna, should tame another, discipline him, and lead him to Nibbāna, is not possible;

mn8:16.4.verse: that one who is himself tamed, disciplined and attained to Nibbāna should tame another, discipline him and lead him to Nibbāna, is possible. So too:

mn8:16.5.verse: ‘1. A person given to cruelty has non-cruelty by which to attain Nibbāna. ‘2. One given to killing living beings by which to attain Nibbāna.

mn8:16.47.verse: ‘44. One given to misapprehension according to individual views, to holding on (to them) tenaciously, and to difficulty in relinquishing (them), has, not misapprehending according to individual views, not holding on tenaciously, ease in relinquishing, by which to attain Nibbāna.

mn8:17.1.verse: ‘So, Cunda, the way of effacement has been shown by me, the way of arising of mind has been shown by me, the way of avoidance has been shown by me, the way of the higher state has been shown by me, and the way of Nibbāna has been shown by me.

mn8:17.2.verse: ‘What should be done for his disciples out of pity by a Master who seeks their welfare and has pity (on them), that I have done for you, Cunda.

mn8:17.3.verse: There are these roots of trees, these empty huts. Develop jhāna, Cunda, do not delay, lest you later regret it. This is our message for you.’

mn8:17.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn8:17.5.verse: The venerable Mahā Cunda was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn8:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahācunda came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:

mn8:3.1.verse: “Sir, there are many different views that arise in the world

mn8:3.2.verse: connected with theories of self or with theories of the cosmos.

mn8:3.3.verse: How does a mendicant who is focusing on the starting point give up and let go of these views?”

mn8:3.4.verse: “Cunda, there are many different views that arise in the world

mn8:3.5.verse: connected with theories of self or with theories of the cosmos.

mn8:3.6.verse: A mendicant gives up and lets go of these views by truly seeing with right wisdom where they arise, where they settle in, and where they operate as: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn8:4.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, might enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn8:4.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:4.5.verse: they’re called ‘blissful meditations in this life’.

mn8:5.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, might enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn8:5.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:5.5.verse: they’re called ‘blissful meditations in this life’.

mn8:6.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, with the fading away of rapture, might enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn8:6.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:6.5.verse: they’re called ‘blissful meditations in this life’.

mn8:7.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, might enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn8:7.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:7.5.verse: they’re called ‘blissful meditations in this life’.

mn8:8.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, might enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

mn8:8.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:9.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, might enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn8:9.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:10.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, might enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.

mn8:10.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:11.1.verse: It’s possible that some mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, might enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn8:11.4.verse: But in the training of the Noble One these are not called ‘self-effacement’;

mn8:12.1.verse: Now in this regard, Cunda, you should work on self-effacement in each of the following ways.

mn8:12.2.verse: ‘Others will be cruel, but here we will not be cruel.’

mn8:12.3.verse: ‘Others will kill living creatures, but here we will not kill living creatures.’

mn8:12.4.verse: ‘Others will steal, but here we will not steal.’

mn8:12.5.verse: ‘Others will be unchaste, but here we will not be unchaste.’

mn8:12.6.verse: ‘Others will lie, but here we will not lie.’

mn8:12.7.verse: ‘Others will backbite, but here we will not backbite.’

mn8:12.8.verse: ‘Others will speak harshly, but here we will not speak harshly.’

mn8:12.9.verse: ‘Others will talk nonsense, but here we will not talk nonsense.’

mn8:12.10.verse: ‘Others will be covetous, but here we will not be covetous.’

mn8:12.11.verse: ‘Others will have ill will, but here we will not have ill will.’

mn8:12.12.verse: ‘Others will have wrong view, but here we will have right view.’

mn8:12.13.verse: ‘Others will have wrong purpose, but here we will have right purpose.’

mn8:12.14.verse: ‘Others will have wrong speech, but here we will have right speech.’

mn8:12.15.verse: ‘Others will have wrong action, but here we will have right action.’

mn8:12.16.verse: ‘Others will have wrong livelihood, but here we will have right livelihood.’

mn8:12.17.verse: ‘Others will have wrong effort, but here we will have right effort.’

mn8:12.18.verse: ‘Others will have wrong mindfulness, but here we will have right mindfulness.’

mn8:12.19.verse: ‘Others will have wrong immersion, but here we will have right immersion.’

mn8:12.20.verse: ‘Others will have wrong knowledge, but here we will have right knowledge.’

mn8:12.21.verse: ‘Others will have wrong freedom, but here we will have right freedom.’

mn8:12.22.verse: ‘Others will be overcome with dullness and drowsiness, but here we will be rid of dullness and drowsiness.’

mn8:12.23.verse: ‘Others will be restless, but here we will not be restless.’

mn8:12.24.verse: ‘Others will have doubts, but here we will have gone beyond doubt.’

mn8:12.25.verse: ‘Others will be irritable, but here we will be without anger.’

mn8:12.26.verse: ‘Others will be acrimonious, but here we will be without acrimony.’

mn8:12.27.verse: ‘Others will be offensive, but here we will be inoffensive.’

mn8:12.28.verse: ‘Others will be contemptuous, but here we will be without contempt.’

mn8:12.29.verse: ‘Others will be jealous, but here we will be without jealousy.’

mn8:12.30.verse: ‘Others will be stingy, but here we will be without stinginess.’

mn8:12.31.verse: ‘Others will be devious, but here we will not be devious.’

mn8:12.32.verse: ‘Others will be deceitful, but here we will not be deceitful.’

mn8:12.33.verse: ‘Others will be pompous, but here we will not be pompous.’

mn8:12.34.verse: ‘Others will be arrogant, but here we will not be arrogant.’

mn8:12.35.verse: ‘Others will be hard to admonish, but here we will not be hard to admonish.’

mn8:12.36.verse: ‘Others will have bad friends, but here we will have good friends.’

mn8:12.37.verse: ‘Others will be negligent, but here we will be diligent.’

mn8:12.38.verse: ‘Others will be faithless, but here we will have faith.’

mn8:12.39.verse: ‘Others will be conscienceless, but here we will have a sense of conscience.’

mn8:12.40.verse: ‘Others will be imprudent, but here we will be prudent.’

mn8:12.41.verse: ‘Others will be unlearned, but here we will be well learned.’

mn8:12.42.verse: ‘Others will be lazy, but here we will be energetic.’

mn8:12.43.verse: ‘Others will be unmindful, but here we will be mindful.’

mn8:12.44.verse: ‘Others will be witless, but here we will be accomplished in wisdom.’

mn8:12.45.verse: ‘Others will be attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go, but here we will not be attached to our own views, not holding them tight, but will let them go easily.’

mn8:13.1.verse: Cunda, I say that even giving rise to the thought of skillful qualities is very helpful, let alone following that path in body and speech.

mn8:13.2.verse: That’s why you should give rise to the following thoughts. ‘Others will be cruel, but here we will not be cruel.’

mn8:13.3.verse: ‘Others will kill living creatures, but here we will not kill living creatures.’ …

mn8:13.4.verse: ‘Others will be attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go, but here we will not be attached to our own views, not holding them tight, but will let them go easily.’

mn8:14.1.verse: Cunda, suppose there was a rough path and another smooth path to get around it.

mn8:14.2.verse: Or suppose there was a rough ford and another smooth ford to get around it.

mn8:14.3.verse: In the same way, a cruel individual bypasses it by not being cruel. An individual who kills bypasses it by not killing. …

mn8:14.5.verse: An individual who is attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go, gets around it by not being attached to their own views, not holding them tight, but letting them go easily.

mn8:15.1.verse: Cunda, all unskillful qualities lead downwards, while all skillful qualities lead upwards.

mn8:15.2.verse: In the same way, a cruel individual is led upwards by not being cruel. An individual who kills is led upwards by not killing …

mn8:15.3.verse: An individual who is attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go, is led upwards by not being attached to their own views, not holding them tight, but letting them go easily.

mn8:16.1.verse: If you’re sinking in the mud yourself, Cunda, it is quite impossible for you to pull out someone else who is sinking in the mud.

mn8:16.2.verse: But if you’re not sinking in the mud yourself, it is quite possible for you to pull out someone else who is sinking in the mud.

mn8:16.3.verse: If you’re not tamed, trained, and quenched yourself, it is quite impossible for you to help tame, train, and extinguish someone else.

mn8:16.4.verse: But if you are tamed, trained, and quenched yourself, it is quite possible for you to help tame, train, and extinguish someone else.

mn8:16.5.verse: In the same way, a cruel individual extinguishes it by not being cruel. An individual who kills extinguishes it by not killing. …

mn8:16.47.verse: An individual who is attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go, extinguishes it by not being attached to their own views, not holding them tight, but letting them go easily.

mn8:17.1.verse: So, Cunda, I’ve taught the expositions by way of self-effacement, arising of thought, bypassing, going up, and extinguishing.

mn8:17.2.verse: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

mn8:17.3.verse: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, Cunda! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction.”

mn8:17.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn8:17.5.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Mahācunda approved what the Buddha said.

mn8:17.8.verse: “Effacement” is the name of this discourse,

mn8:17.9.verse: which is deep as the ocean.

mn9:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn9:1.3.verse: There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn9:2.1.verse: ‘“A man of right view” is said, friends.

mn9:2.2.verse: In what way is a noble disciple a man of right view, his view rectified, having perfect [confidence in the Dhamma, this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:2.3.verse: ‘Indeed, friend, we would come from far away to learn from the venerable Sāriputta the meaning of this pronouncement.

mn9:2.4.verse: It would be good if the meaning of this pronouncement would occur to the venerable Sāriputta.

mn9:2.5.verse: Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it.’

mn9:2.6.verse: ‘Then, friends, listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn9:3.1.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands the unprofitable, the root of the unprofitable, the profitable, and the root of the profitable,

mn9:3.2.verse: in that way he is a man of right view, his view rectified, having perfect confidence in the Dhamma, this being the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:4.1.verse: ‘And what is the unprofitable, the root of the unprofitable; what is the profitable, the root of the profitable?

mn9:4.2.verse: ‘Killing beings is unprofitable. Taking what is not given is unprofitable. Misconduct in sexual desires is unprofitable. False speech is unprofitable. Malicious speech is unprofitable. Harsh speech is unprofitable. Gossip is unprofitable. Covetousness is unprofitable. Ill-will is unprofitable. Wrong view is unprofitable.

mn9:4.3.verse: This is what is called unprofitable.

mn9:5.1.verse: ‘And what is the root of the unprofitable?

mn9:5.2.verse: Greed is a root of the unprofitable. Hate is a root of the unprofitable. Delusion is a root of the unprofitable.

mn9:5.3.verse: This is what is called the root of the unprofitable.

mn9:6.2.verse: Abstention from killing living beings is profitable. Abstention from taking what is not given is profitable. Abstention from misconduct in sexual desires is profitable. Abstention from false speech is profitable. Abstention from malicious speech is profitable. Abstention from harsh speech is profitable. Abstention from gossip is profitable. Abstention from covetousness is profitable. Abstention from ill-will is profitable. Abstention from wrong view is profitable.

mn9:6.3.verse: This is what is called profitable.

mn9:7.1.verse: ‘And what is the root of the profitable?

mn9:7.2.verse: Non-greed is a root of the profitable. Non-hate is a root of the profitable. Non-delusion is a root of the profitable.

mn9:7.3.verse: This is what is called the root of the profitable.

mn9:8.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood the unprofitable, the root of the unprofitable, the profitable and the root of the profitable he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, he abolishes the underlying tendency to resistance, extirpates the underlying tendency to the view and conceit “I am”, and by abandoning ignorance and arousing True Knowledge he here and now makes an end of suffering.

mn9:8.2.verse: In that way a noble disciple is a man of right view, his view is rectified, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.’

mn9:9.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:9.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view, his view rectified, having perfect confidence in the Dhamma, this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:10.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands nutriment, the arising of nutriment, the cessation of nutriment, and the way leading to the cessation of nutriment,

mn9:10.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view, his view is rectified, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:11.1.verse: ‘And what is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment?

mn9:11.2.verse: ‘There are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance and support of beings that already exist and for those seeking renewal of being.

mn9:11.4.verse: They are, physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle, contact as the second, volition about (the state of) the mind as the third and consciousness as the fourth.

mn9:11.5.verse: With the arising of craving there is the arising of nutriment. With the cessation of craving there is the cessation of nutriment. The way leading to the cessation of nutriment is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:11.6.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

mn9:12.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood nutriment … he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to greed … makes an end of suffering.

mn9:12.2.verse: In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.’

mn9:13.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:13.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:14.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering and the the way leading to the cessation of suffering,

mn9:14.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view, his view is rectified, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:15.1.verse: ‘And what is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering?

mn9:15.2.verse: ‘Birth is suffering, ageing is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair are suffering, not to get what one wants is suffering, in short, the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering.

mn9:15.3.verse: This is what is called suffering.

mn9:16.1.verse: ‘And what is the origin of suffering?

mn9:16.2.verse: It is craving which produces renewed being, is accompanied by delight and lust, delights in this and that, that is to say,

mn9:16.3.verse: craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being.

mn9:16.4.verse: This is what is called the origin of suffering.

mn9:17.1.verse: ‘And what is the cessation of suffering?

mn9:17.2.verse: It is the remainderless fading and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting of that same craving.

mn9:17.3.verse: This is what is called the cessation of suffering.

mn9:18.1.verse: ‘And what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering?

mn9:18.2.verse: It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:19.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …

mn9:19.2.verse: he is one of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.’

mn9:20.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:20.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith he has come to?’

mn9:21.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands ageing and death, the origin of ageing and death, the cessation of ageing and death, and the way leading to the cessation of ageing and death,

mn9:21.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:22.1.verse: ‘But what is ageing and death, what is the origin of ageing and death, what is the cessation of ageing and death, what is the way leading to the cessation of ageing and death?

mn9:22.2.verse: ‘In the various orders of beings, the ageing of beings, their old age, brokenness (of teeth), grayness (of hair), wrinkles, decline of life, and weakness of faculties—

mn9:22.3.verse: that is what is called ageing.

mn9:22.5.verse: ‘In the various orders of beings, the decease, the deceasing, passing-away, dissolution, disappearance, dying, completion of time, dissolution of aggregates—

mn9:22.6.verse: that is what is called death.

mn9:22.9.verse: With the arising of birth there is the arising of ageing-and-death. With the cessation of birth there is the cessation of ageing-and-death. The way leading to the cessation of ageing-and-death is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:23.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:24.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:24.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view, so that his view is rectified … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:25.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands birth, the origin of birth, the way leading to the cessation of birth,

mn9:25.3.verse: in that way he is one of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:26.1.verse: ‘And what is birth, what is the origin of birth, what is the cessation of birth, what is the way leading to the cessation of birth?

mn9:26.2.verse: ‘In the various orders of beings, the birth of beings, their coming to birth, precipitation (in the womb), generation, manifestation of aggregates, obtaining the bases for contact,

mn9:26.4.verse: With the arising of being there is the arising of birth. With the cessation of being there is the cessation of birth. The way leading to the cessation of birth is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:27.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:28.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:28.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:29.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands being, the origin of being, the cessation of being, the way leading to the cessation of being,

mn9:29.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:30.1.verse: ‘And what is being, what is the origin of being, what is the cessation of being, what is the way leading to the cessation of being?

mn9:30.2.verse: ‘There are these three kinds of being:

mn9:30.3.verse: sensual desire being, (subtle) form being and formless being.

mn9:30.4.verse: With the arising of clinging there is the arising of being. With the cessation of clinging there is the cessation of being. The way leading to the cessation of being is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:31.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:32.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question.

mn9:32.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:33.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands clinging, the origin of clinging, the way leading to the cessation of clinging,

mn9:33.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:34.1.verse: ‘And what is clinging, what is the origin of clinging, what is the cessation of clinging, what is the way leading to the cessation of clinging?

mn9:34.2.verse: ‘There are these four kinds of clinging:

mn9:34.3.verse: sensual desire clinging, (false) view clinging, rite and ritual clinging, and self-theory clinging.

mn9:34.4.verse: With the arising of craving there is the arising of clinging. With the cessation of craving there is the cessation of clinging. The way leading to the cessation of clinging is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:35.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:36.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:36.2.verse: ‘But, [friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view, his view rectified … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:37.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands craving, the origin of craving, the cessation of craving and the way leading to the cessation of craving,

mn9:37.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:38.1.verse: ‘And what is craving, what is the cessation of craving, what is the way leading to the cessation of craving?

mn9:38.2.verse: ‘There are these six classes of craving:

mn9:38.3.verse: craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odours, craving for flavours, craving for tangibles, craving for dhammas.

mn9:38.4.verse: With the arising of feeling there is the arising of craving. With the cessation of feeling there is the cessation of craving. The way leading to the cessation of craving is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:39.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:40.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:40.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:41.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands feeling, the origin of feeling, the cessation of feeling, and the way leading to the cessation of feeling,

mn9:41.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:42.1.verse: ‘And what is feeling, what is the origin of feeling, what is the cessation of feeling, what is the way leading to the cessation of feeling?

mn9:42.2.verse: ‘There are these six classes of feeling:

mn9:42.3.verse: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, feeling born of mind contact.

mn9:42.4.verse: With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling. With cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling. The way leading to the cessation of feeling is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:43.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:44.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question.

mn9:44.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:45.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands contact, the origin of contact, the cessation of contact, and the way leading to the cessation of contact,

mn9:45.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:46.1.verse: ‘And what is contact, what is the origin of contact, what is the cessation of contact, what is the way leading to the cessation of contact?

mn9:46.2.verse: ‘There are these six classes of contact:

mn9:46.3.verse: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-contact.

mn9:46.4.verse: With the arising of the sixfold base there is the arising of contact. With the cessation of the sixfold base there is the cessation of contact. The way leading to the cessation of contact is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:47.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:48.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:48.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith which he has come to?’

mn9:49.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands the sixfold base, the origin of the sixfold base, the cessation of the sixfold base, and the way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base,

mn9:49.3.verse: he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:50.1.verse: ‘And what is the sixfold base, what is the origin of the sixfold base, what is the cessation of the sixfold base, what is the way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base?

mn9:50.3.verse: the eye-base, the-ear base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, the mind-base.

mn9:50.4.verse: With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of the sixfold base. With the cessation of name and-form there is the cessation of the sixfold base. The way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:51.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:52.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:52.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith which he has come to?’

mn9:53.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands name-and-form, the origin of name-and-form, the cessation of name-and-form, and the way leading to the cessation of name-and-form,

mn9:53.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:54.1.verse: ‘And what is name-and-form, what is the origin of name-and-form, what is the cessation of name-and-form, what is the way leading to the cessation of name-and-form?

mn9:54.3.verse: these are what is called name.

mn9:54.4.verse: ‘The four great primary elements and the form derived from the four great primary elements,

mn9:54.5.verse: these are what is called form.

mn9:54.8.verse: With the arising of consciousness there is the arising of name-and-form. With the cessation of consciousness there is the cessation of name-and-form. The way leading to the cessation of name-and-form is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:55.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:56.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:56.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view … this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:57.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands consciousness, the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the way leading to the cessation of consciousness,

mn9:57.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view … and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:58.1.verse: ‘And what is consciousness, what is the origin of consciousness, what is the cessation of consciousness, what is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness?

mn9:58.2.verse: ‘There are these six classes of consciousness:

mn9:58.3.verse: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness.

mn9:58.4.verse: With the arising of formations there is the arising of consciousness. With the cessation of formations there is the cessation of consciousness. The way leading to the cessation of consciousness is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:59.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:60.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:60.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view ... this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:61.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands formations, the arising of formations, the cessation of formations, and the way leading to the cessation of formations,

mn9:61.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view ... and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:62.1.verse: ‘And what are formations, what is the origin of formations, what is the cessation of formations, what is the way leading to the cessation of formations?

mn9:62.2.verse: ‘There are these three kinds of formations:

mn9:62.3.verse: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, the mental formation.

mn9:62.4.verse: With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of formations. With the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of formations. The way leading to the cessation of formations is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:63.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood ...’

mn9:64.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:64.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view ... this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:65.1.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands ignorance, the origin of ignorance, the cessation of ignorance, and the way leading to the cessation of ignorance,

mn9:65.2.verse: in that way he is a man of right view ... and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.

mn9:65.3.verse: ‘And what is ignorance, what is the origin of ignorance, what is the cessation of ignorance, what is the way leading to the cessation of ignorance?

mn9:65.4.verse: ‘Unknowing about suffering, about the origin of suffering, about the cessation of suffering, about the way leading to the cessation of suffering,

mn9:66.1.verse: With the arising of taints there is the arising of ignorance. With the cessation of taints there is the cessation of ignorance. The way leading to the cessation of ignorance is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:67.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood …’

mn9:68.1.verse: Saying, ‘Good, friend,’ the bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question:

mn9:68.2.verse: ‘But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is a man of right view, his view is rectified, having perfect confidence in the Dhamma, this being the true object of faith that he has come to?’

mn9:69.2.verse: ‘As soon as a noble disciple understands the taints, the origin of taints, the cessation of taints, and the way leading to the cessation of taints,

mn9:69.3.verse: in that way he is a man of right view, his view is rectified, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.’

mn9:70.1.verse: ‘And what are the taints, what is the origin of taints, what is the cessation of taints, what is the way leading to the cessation of taints?

mn9:70.3.verse: the taint of sensual desires, the taint of being, and the taint of ignorance.

mn9:70.4.verse: With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of taints. With the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of taints. The way leading to the cessation of taints is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn9:70.5.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.’

mn9:71.1.verse: ‘After a noble disciple has thus understood the taints, the origin of taints, the cessation of taints, and the way leading to the cessation of taints, he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, he abolishes the underlying tendency to resistance, extirpates the underlying tendency to the view and conceit “I am”, and by abandoning ignorance and arousing True Knowledge he here and now makes an end of suffering.

mn9:71.2.verse: In that way too a noble disciple is a man of right view, his view is rectified, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and this is the true object of faith that he has come to.’

mn9:71.3.verse: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

mn9:71.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words.

mn9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn9:2.1.verse: “Reverends, they speak of this thing called ‘right view’.

mn9:2.2.verse: How do you define a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching?”

mn9:2.3.verse: “Reverend, we would travel a long way to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta.

mn9:2.4.verse: May Venerable Sāriputta himself please clarify the meaning of this.

mn9:2.5.verse: The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn9:2.6.verse: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn9:3.1.verse: “A noble disciple understands the unskillful and its root, and the skillful and its root.

mn9:3.2.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.

mn9:4.1.verse: But what is the unskillful and what is its root? And what is the skillful and what is its root?

mn9:4.2.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct; speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical; covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.

mn9:5.1.verse: And what is the root of the unskillful?

mn9:5.3.verse: This is called the root of the unskillful.

mn9:6.2.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct; refraining from speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical; contentment, good will, and right view.

mn9:7.1.verse: And what is the root of the skillful?

mn9:7.3.verse: This is called the root of the skillful.

mn9:8.1.verse: A noble disciple understands in this way the unskillful and its root, and the skillful and its root. They’ve completely given up the underlying tendency to greed, dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, and eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’. They’ve given up ignorance and given rise to knowledge, and make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn9:8.2.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.”

mn9:9.1.verse: Saying “Good, reverend,” those mendicants approved and agreed with what Sāriputta said. Then they asked another question:

mn9:9.2.verse: “But reverend, might there be another way to describe a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching?”

mn9:10.2.verse: A noble disciple understands fuel, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

mn9:10.3.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.

mn9:11.1.verse: But what is fuel? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:11.2.verse: These four fuels maintain sentient beings that have been born and help those about to be born.

mn9:11.4.verse: Edible food, whether solid or subtle; contact is the second, mental intention the third, and consciousness the fourth.

mn9:11.5.verse: Fuel originates from craving. Fuel ceases when craving ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of fuel is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn9:11.6.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.
