mn9:12.1.verse: A noble disciple understands in this way fuel, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. They’ve completely given up the underlying tendency to greed, dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, and eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’. They’ve given up ignorance and given rise to knowledge, and make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn9:12.2.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.”

mn9:13.1.verse: Saying “Good, reverend,” those mendicants … asked another question:

mn9:13.2.verse: “But reverend, might there be another way to describe a noble disciple who … has come to the true teaching?”

mn9:14.2.verse: A noble disciple understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

mn9:14.3.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who … has come to the true teaching.

mn9:15.1.verse: But what is suffering? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:15.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

mn9:16.1.verse: And what is the origin of suffering?

mn9:16.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

mn9:16.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

mn9:16.4.verse: This is called the origin of suffering.

mn9:17.1.verse: And what is the cessation of suffering?

mn9:17.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving with no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

mn9:17.3.verse: This is called the cessation of suffering.

mn9:18.1.verse: And what is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

mn9:18.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn9:18.4.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

mn9:19.1.verse: A noble disciple understands in this way suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. They’ve completely given up the underlying tendency to greed, dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, and eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’. They’ve given up ignorance and given rise to knowledge, and make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn9:19.2.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.”

mn9:20.1.verse: Saying “Good, reverend,” those mendicants … asked another question:

mn9:20.2.verse: “But reverend, might there be another way to describe a noble disciple who … has come to the true teaching?”

mn9:21.2.verse: A noble disciple understands old age and death, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation …

mn9:22.1.verse: But what are old age and death? What is their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation?

mn9:22.2.verse: The old age, decrepitude, broken teeth, gray hair, wrinkly skin, diminished vitality, and failing faculties of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn9:22.5.verse: The passing away, perishing, disintegration, demise, mortality, death, decease, breaking up of the aggregates, laying to rest of the corpse, and cutting off of the life faculty of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn9:22.7.verse: Such is old age, and such is death.

mn9:22.8.verse: This is called old age and death.

mn9:22.9.verse: Old age and death originate from rebirth. Old age and death cease when rebirth ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of old age and death is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:24.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:25.2.verse: A noble disciple understands rebirth, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:26.1.verse: But what is rebirth? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:26.2.verse: The rebirth, inception, conception, regeneration, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense fields of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn9:26.4.verse: Rebirth originates from continued existence. Rebirth ceases when continued existence ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of rebirth is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:28.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:29.2.verse: A noble disciple understands continued existence, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

mn9:30.1.verse: But what is continued existence? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:30.2.verse: There are these three states of continued existence.

mn9:30.3.verse: Existence in the sensual realm, the realm of luminous form, and the formless realm.

mn9:30.4.verse: Continued existence originates from grasping. Continued existence ceases when grasping ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of continued existence is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:32.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:33.2.verse: A noble disciple understands grasping, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:34.1.verse: But what is grasping? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:34.2.verse: There are these four kinds of grasping.

mn9:34.3.verse: Grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

mn9:34.4.verse: Grasping originates from craving. Grasping ceases when craving ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of grasping is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:36.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:37.2.verse: A noble disciple understands craving, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:38.1.verse: But what is craving? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:38.2.verse: There are these six classes of craving.

mn9:38.3.verse: Craving for sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

mn9:38.4.verse: Craving originates from feeling. Craving ceases when feeling ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of craving is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:40.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:41.2.verse: A noble disciple understands feeling, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:42.1.verse: But what is feeling? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:42.2.verse: There are these six classes of feeling.

mn9:42.3.verse: Feeling born of contact through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

mn9:42.4.verse: Feeling originates from contact. Feeling ceases when contact ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of feeling is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:44.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:45.2.verse: A noble disciple understands contact, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:46.1.verse: But what is contact? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:46.2.verse: There are these six classes of contact.

mn9:46.3.verse: Contact through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

mn9:46.4.verse: Contact originates from the six sense fields. Contact ceases when the six sense fields cease. The practice that leads to the cessation of contact is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:48.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:49.2.verse: A noble disciple understands the six sense fields, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation …

mn9:50.1.verse: But what are the six sense fields? What is their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation?

mn9:50.2.verse: There are these six sense fields.

mn9:50.3.verse: The sense fields of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

mn9:50.4.verse: The six sense fields originate from name and form. The six sense fields cease when name and form cease. The practice that leads to the cessation of the six sense fields is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:52.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:53.2.verse: A noble disciple understands name and form, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation …

mn9:54.1.verse: But what are name and form? What is their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation?

mn9:54.2.verse: Feeling, perception, intention, contact, and application of mind—

mn9:54.4.verse: The four principal states, and form derived from the four principal states—

mn9:54.6.verse: Such is name and such is form.

mn9:54.7.verse: This is called name and form.

mn9:54.8.verse: Name and form originate from consciousness. Name and form cease when consciousness ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of name and form is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:56.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:57.2.verse: A noble disciple understands consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:58.1.verse: But what is consciousness? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:58.2.verse: There are these six classes of consciousness.

mn9:58.3.verse: Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness.

mn9:58.4.verse: Consciousness originates from choices. Consciousness ceases when choices cease. The practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:60.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:61.2.verse: A noble disciple understands choices, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation …

mn9:62.1.verse: But what are choices? What is their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation?

mn9:62.2.verse: There are these three kinds of choice.

mn9:62.3.verse: Choices by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn9:62.4.verse: Choices originate from ignorance. Choices cease when ignorance ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of choices is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:64.2.verse: “Might there be another way to describe a noble disciple?”

mn9:65.1.verse: A noble disciple understands ignorance, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation …

mn9:65.3.verse: But what is ignorance? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:65.4.verse: Not knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

mn9:66.1.verse: Ignorance originates from defilement. Ignorance ceases when defilement ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of ignorance is simply this noble eightfold path …”

mn9:68.1.verse: Saying “Good, reverend,” those mendicants approved and agreed with what Sāriputta said. Then they asked another question:

mn9:68.2.verse: “But reverend, might there be another way to describe a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching?”

mn9:69.2.verse: A noble disciple understands defilement, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

mn9:69.3.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.

mn9:70.1.verse: But what is defilement? What is its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation?

mn9:70.3.verse: The defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn9:70.4.verse: Defilement originates from ignorance. Defilement ceases when ignorance ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of defilement is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn9:70.5.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

mn9:71.1.verse: A noble disciple understands in this way defilement, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. They’ve completely given up the underlying tendency to greed, dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, and eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’. They’ve given up ignorance and given rise to knowledge, and make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn9:71.2.verse: When they’ve done this, they’re defined as a noble disciple who has right view, whose view is correct, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to the true teaching.”

mn9:71.3.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

mn9:71.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Sāriputta said.

mn10:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kuru country. There is town of theirs called Kammāssadamma,

mn10:1.3.verse: and there he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn10:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this path, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, is a path that goes in one way only: to the purification of beings, to the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, to the disappearance of pain and grief, to the attainment of the true way, to the realization of Nibbāna.

mn10:3.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides contemplating a body as a body fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn10:3.3.verse: He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn10:3.4.verse: He abides contemplating mind as mind, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn10:3.5.verse: He abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn10:4.1.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplationg the body as a body?

mn10:4.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, established mindfulness (on the breath) in front of him,

mn10:4.3.verse: always mindful he breaths in, mindful he breathes out.

mn10:4.4.verse: ‘Breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”.

mn10:4.5.verse: Breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”.

mn10:4.6.verse: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”.

mn10:4.7.verse: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the body process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.

mn10:4.8.verse: ‘Just as skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn understands: “I make a long turn”; or when making a short turn understands: “I make a short turn”;

mn10:4.9.verse: so too, breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”: …

mn10:4.11.verse: he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.

mn10:5.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body in himself and externally.

mn10:5.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:5.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a body” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:5.4.verse: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.

mn10:6.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu, when walking, understands: “I walk”; when standing, understands: “I stand”; when sitting, understands: “I sit”; when lying down, understands: “I am lying down”;

mn10:6.2.verse: or however his body is disposed he understands accordingly.

mn10:7.1.verse: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally.

mn10:7.2.verse: ‘… contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:7.3.verse: ‘… mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:7.4.verse: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.

mn10:8.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu is one who acts in full awareness when moving to and fro, who acts in full awareness when looking at and away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when feeding, drinking, chewing and supping, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent.

mn10:9.1.verse: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:9.2.verse: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.

mn10:10.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth, thus:

mn10:10.2.verse: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine.”’

mn10:10.3.verse: ‘Just as though there were a bag with an opening at both (ends) full of many sorts of grain such as hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet and white rice, and a man with (clear) eyes had opened it and were reviewing it thus: “This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice”,

mn10:10.4.verse: so too, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth …

mn10:11.1.verse: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplatng … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:12.1.verse: ‘Again, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body (consisting of) elements, thus:

mn10:12.2.verse: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”

mn10:12.3.verse: ‘Just as though a skilled butcher or his apprentice had a killed a cow and were seated at the four crossroads with it cut up into pieces:

mn10:12.4.verse: so too, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body … and the air element.

mn10:12.5.verse: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”

mn10:13.1.verse: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplating … arising factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:14.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing matter,

mn10:14.3.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”

mn10:15.1.verse: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:16.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, kites, vultures, dogs, jackals, and the multitudinous kinds of worms,

mn10:16.3.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”

mn10:17.1.verse: ‘... contemplating ... in himself ... not clinging to anything in the world.’

mn10:18.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood held together with sinews, thus: “This body too is of such a nature...”’

mn10:19.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood and held together with sinews, ...’

mn10:20.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton without flesh and blood held together with sinews ...’

mn10:24.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, bones without sinews scattered in all directions, here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a back-bone, there a rib-bone, there a breast-bone, there an arm-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull ...’

mn10:25.1.verse: ‘... contemplating ... in himself ... not clinging to anything in the world.’

mn10:26-28.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, bones bleached white, the colour of shells ...’

mn10:29.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown in a charnel ground, bones heaped up, more than a year old ...

mn10:30.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown in a charnel ground, bones rotted and crumbled to dust,

mn10:30.3.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”

mn10:31.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself and externally.

mn10:31.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:31.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a body” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:31.4.verse: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.

mn10:32.1.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating feelings as feelings?

mn10:32.2.verse: ‘Here, when feeling a pleasant feeling, a bhikkhu undertsands: “I feel a pleasant feeling”;

mn10:32.3.verse: when feeling a painful feeling, he understands: “I feel a painful feeling”;

mn10:32.4.verse: when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”.

mn10:32.5.verse: When feeling a materialistic pleasant feeling he understands: “I feel a materialistic pleasant feeling”;

mn10:32.6.verse: when feeling an unmaterialistic pleasant feeling,, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic pleasant feeling”;

mn10:32.7.verse: when feeling a materialistic painful feeling, he understands: “I feel a materialistic painful feeling;

mn10:32.8.verse: when feeling an unmaterialistic painful feeling, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic painful feeling”;

mn10:32.9.verse: when feeling a materialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel a materialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”;

mn10:32.10.verse: when feeling an unmaterialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”.

mn10:33.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating feelings as feelings in himself, or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings externally, or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings in himself and externally.

mn10:33.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in feeling its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in feeling its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in feeling its arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:33.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is feeling” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:33.4.verse: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating feelings as feelings.

mn10:34.1.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating mind as mind?

mn10:34.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands mind affected by lust as affected by lust,

mn10:34.3.verse: and mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust.

mn10:34.4.verse: He under-stands mind affected by hate as affected by hate,

mn10:34.5.verse: and mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate.

mn10:34.6.verse: He understands mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion,

mn10:34.7.verse: and mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion.

mn10:34.8.verse: He understands contracted mind as contracted,

mn10:34.10.verse: He understands exalted mind as exalted,

mn10:34.12.verse: He understands surpassed mind as surpassed,

mn10:34.14.verse: He understands concentrated mind as concentrated,

mn10:34.16.verse: He understands liberated mind as liberated

mn10:35.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating mind as mind in himself, or he abides contemplating mind as mind externally, or he abides contemplating mind as mind in himself and externally.

mn10:35.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the mind its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the mind its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the mind its arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:35.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a mind” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:35.4.verse: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the mind as mind.

mn10:36.1.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas?

mn10:36.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances.

mn10:36.3.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances?

mn10:36.4.verse: ‘Here, there being desire for sensual pleasures in him, a bhikkhu understands: “There is desire for sensual pleasures in me”, or there being no desire for sensual pleasures in him, he understands: “There is no desire for sensual pleasures in me”, and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen desire for sensual pleasures, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen desire for sensual pleasures, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned desire for sensual pleasures.

mn10:36.8.verse: ‘There being uncertainty in him … the future non-arising of abandoned uncertainty.

mn10:37.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas externally, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself and externally.

mn10:37.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising and vanishing factors

mn10:37.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there are dhammas” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:37.4.verse: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances.

mn10:38.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn10:38.2.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five aggregates affected by clinging?

mn10:38.4.verse: “Such is form, such its origin, such its disappearance;

mn10:38.5.verse: such is feeling, such its origin, such its disappearance;

mn10:38.6.verse: such is perception, such its origin, such its disappearance;

mn10:38.7.verse: such is formations, such their origin, such their disappearance;

mn10:38.8.verse: such is consciousness, such its origin, such its disappearance”.

mn10:39.1.verse: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …

mn10:39.2.verse: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …

mn10:39.3.verse: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:40.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the six in-oneself/external bases.

mn10:40.2.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the six in-oneself/external bases?

mn10:40.3.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands the eye, he understands forms, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent on both; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

mn10:40.4.verse: ‘He understands the ear, he understands sounds …

mn10:40.5.verse: ‘He understands the nose, he understands odours …

mn10:40.6.verse: ‘He understands the tongue, he understands flavours …

mn10:40.7.verse: ‘He understands the body, he understands tangibles …

mn10:40.8.verse: ‘He understands the mind, he understands dhammas, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent on both, he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

mn10:41.1.verse: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …

mn10:41.2.verse: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …

mn10:41.3.verse: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:42.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the seven enlightenment factors.

mn10:42.2.verse: ‘And how he does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the seven enlightenment factors?

mn10:42.3.verse: ‘Here, there being the mindfulness enlightenment factor in him, a bhikkhu understands: “There is the mindfulness enlightenment factor in me”, there being no mindfulness enlightenment factor in him, he understands: “There is no mindfulness enlightenment factor in me”; and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, and he understands how the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor comes to be developed and perfected.

mn10:42.4.verse: ‘There being the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor in him …

mn10:42.5.verse: ‘There being the energy enlightenment factor in him …

mn10:42.6.verse: ‘There being the happiness factor in him …

mn10:42.7.verse: ‘There being the tranquillity enlightenment factor in him …

mn10:42.8.verse: ‘There being the concentration enlightenment factor in him …

mn10:42.9.verse: ‘There being the equanimity enlightenment factor in him … he understands: “There is the equanimity enlightenment factor in me”, there being no equanimity enlightenment factor in him, he understands: “There is no equanimity enlightenment factor in me”, and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor, and he understands how the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor comes to be developed and perfected.

mn10:43.1.verse: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …

mn10:43.2.verse: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …

mn10:43.3.verse: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:44.1.verse: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths.

mn10:44.2.verse: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths?

mn10:44.3.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands as it actually is that: “Such is suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the origin of suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.

mn10:45.1.verse: ‘In this way he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas externally, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself and externally.

mn10:45.2.verse: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their vanishing factors or he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising and vanishing factors.

mn10:45.3.verse: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there are dhammas” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

mn10:45.4.verse: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths.

mn10:46.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, were anyone to develop these four foundations of mindfulness for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected for him:

mn10:46.2.verse: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return.

mn10:46.4.verse: were anyone to develop these four foundations for six years …

mn10:46.5.verse: ‘Let alone six years … for five years …

mn10:46.6.verse: ‘Let alone five years … for four years …

mn10:46.7.verse: ‘Let alone four years … for three years …

mn10:46.8.verse: ‘Let alone three years … for two years …

mn10:46.9.verse: ‘Let alone two years … for one year …

mn10:46.15.verse: ‘Let alone six months … for five months …

mn10:46.16.verse: ‘Let alone five months … for four months …

mn10:46.17.verse: ‘Let alone four months … for three months …

mn10:46.18.verse: ‘Let alone three months … for two months …

mn10:46.19.verse: ‘Let alone two months … for one month …

mn10:46.20.verse: ‘Let alone one month … for half a month …

mn10:46.22.verse: were anyone to develop these four foundations of mindfulness for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him:

mn10:46.23.verse: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return.

mn10:47.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, this path, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, is a path that he goes in one way only: to the purification of beings, to the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, to the disappearance of pain and grief, to the attainment of the true way, to the realization of Nibbāna.”’

mn10:47.2.verse: So it was in reference to this that it was said:

mn10:47.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn10:47.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.

mn10:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn10:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

mn10:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn10:3.3.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn10:3.4.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn10:3.5.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn10:4.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the body?

mn10:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

mn10:4.3.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

mn10:4.4.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

mn10:4.5.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

mn10:4.6.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

mn10:4.7.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

mn10:4.8.verse: It’s like a deft lathe-turner or lathe-turner’s apprentice. When drawing a long pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a long pull,’ and when drawing a short pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a short pull.’

mn10:5.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:5.2.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the body, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:5.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:5.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:6.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant is walking they know: ‘I am walking.’ When standing they know: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting they know: ‘I am sitting.’ And when lying down they know: ‘I am lying down.’

mn10:6.2.verse: Whatever posture their body is in, they know it.

mn10:7.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:7.2.verse: With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:7.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:7.4.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant acts with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn10:9.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

mn10:9.2.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

mn10:10.2.verse: ‘In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

mn10:10.3.verse: It’s as if there were a bag with openings at both ends, filled with various kinds of grains, such as fine rice, wheat, mung beans, peas, sesame, and ordinary rice. And a person with clear eyes were to open it and examine the contents: ‘These grains are fine rice, these are wheat, these are mung beans, these are peas, these are sesame, and these are ordinary rice.’

mn10:11.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

mn10:11.2.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:12.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, whatever its placement or posture, according to the elements:

mn10:12.2.verse: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

mn10:12.3.verse: It’s as if a deft butcher or butcher’s apprentice were to kill a cow and sit down at the crossroads with the meat cut into chops.

mn10:13.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

mn10:13.2.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:14.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose a mendicant were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground. And it had been dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering.

mn10:14.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn10:14.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn10:15.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

mn10:15.2.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:16.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, herons, hounds, tigers, leopards, jackals, and many kinds of little creatures.

mn10:16.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn10:16.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn10:17.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally …

mn10:17.2.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:18-23.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

mn10:18-23.2.verse: A skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, and held together by sinews …

mn10:18-23.3.verse: A skeleton rid of flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

mn10:24.1.verse: Bones rid of sinews scattered in every direction. Here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here an arm-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth, here the skull. …

mn10:26-28.1.verse: White bones, the color of shells …

mn10:29.1.verse: Decrepit bones, heaped in a pile …

mn10:30.1.verse: Bones rotted and crumbled to powder.

mn10:30.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn10:30.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn10:31.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:31.2.verse: With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:31.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:31.4.verse: That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

mn10:32.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of feelings?

mn10:32.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant who feels a pleasant feeling knows: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling.’

mn10:32.3.verse: When they feel a painful feeling, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling.’

mn10:32.4.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling.’

mn10:32.5.verse: When they feel a pleasant feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling of the flesh.’

mn10:32.6.verse: When they feel a pleasant feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling not of the flesh.’

mn10:32.7.verse: When they feel a painful feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling of the flesh.’

mn10:32.8.verse: When they feel a painful feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling not of the flesh.’

mn10:32.9.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling of the flesh.’

mn10:32.10.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling not of the flesh, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling not of the flesh.’

mn10:33.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:33.2.verse: With respect to feelings, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:33.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that feelings exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:33.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of feelings.

mn10:34.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the mind?

mn10:34.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands mind with greed as ‘mind with greed,’

mn10:34.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed.’

mn10:34.4.verse: They understand mind with hate as ‘mind with hate,’

mn10:34.5.verse: and mind without hate as ‘mind without hate.’

mn10:34.6.verse: They understand mind with delusion as ‘mind with delusion,’

mn10:34.7.verse: and mind without delusion as ‘mind without delusion.’

mn10:34.8.verse: They know constricted mind as ‘constricted mind,’

mn10:34.10.verse: They know expansive mind as ‘expansive mind,’

mn10:34.12.verse: They know mind that is not supreme as ‘mind that is not supreme,’

mn10:34.13.verse: and mind that is supreme as ‘mind that is supreme.’

mn10:34.14.verse: They know mind immersed in samādhi as ‘mind immersed in samādhi,’

mn10:34.15.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as ‘mind not immersed in samādhi.’

mn10:34.16.verse: They know freed mind as ‘freed mind,’

mn10:35.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:35.2.verse: With respect to the mind, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:35.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that the mind exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:35.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the mind.

mn10:36.1.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles?

mn10:36.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances.

mn10:36.3.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances?

mn10:36.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant who has sensual desire in them understands: ‘I have sensual desire in me.’ When they don’t have sensual desire in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have sensual desire in me.’ They understand how sensual desire arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

mn10:36.5.verse: When they have ill will in them, they understand: ‘I have ill will in me.’ When they don’t have ill will in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have ill will in me.’ They understand how ill will arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

mn10:36.6.verse: When they have dullness and drowsiness in them, they understand: ‘I have dullness and drowsiness in me.’ When they don’t have dullness and drowsiness in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have dullness and drowsiness in me.’ They understand how dullness and drowsiness arise; how, when they’ve already arisen, they’re given up; and how, once they’re given up, they don’t arise again in the future.

mn10:36.7.verse: When they have restlessness and remorse in them, they understand: ‘I have restlessness and remorse in me.’ When they don’t have restlessness and remorse in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have restlessness and remorse in me.’ They understand how restlessness and remorse arise; how, when they’ve already arisen, they’re given up; and how, once they’re given up, they don’t arise again in the future.

mn10:36.8.verse: When they have doubt in them, they understand: ‘I have doubt in me.’ When they don’t have doubt in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have doubt in me.’ They understand how doubt arises; how, when it’s already arisen, it’s given up; and how, once it’s given up, it doesn’t arise again in the future.

mn10:37.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:37.2.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the principles, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:37.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:37.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five hindrances.

mn10:38.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates.

mn10:38.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates?

mn10:38.4.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

mn10:38.5.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

mn10:38.6.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

mn10:38.7.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

mn10:38.8.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

mn10:39.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally …

mn10:39.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the five grasping aggregates.

mn10:40.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields.

mn10:40.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields?

mn10:40.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands the eye, sights, and the fetter that arises dependent on both of these. They understand how the fetter that has not arisen comes to arise; how the arisen fetter comes to be abandoned; and how the abandoned fetter comes to not rise again in the future.

mn10:40.4.verse: They understand the ear, sounds, and the fetter …

mn10:40.5.verse: They understand the nose, smells, and the fetter …

mn10:40.6.verse: They understand the tongue, tastes, and the fetter …

mn10:40.7.verse: They understand the body, touches, and the fetter …

mn10:40.8.verse: They understand the mind, ideas, and the fetter that arises dependent on both of these. They understand how the fetter that has not arisen comes to arise; how the arisen fetter comes to be abandoned; and how the abandoned fetter comes to not rise again in the future.

mn10:41.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally …

mn10:41.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the six interior and exterior sense fields.

mn10:42.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors.

mn10:42.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors?

mn10:42.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant who has the awakening factor of mindfulness in them understands: ‘I have the awakening factor of mindfulness in me.’ When they don’t have the awakening factor of mindfulness in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have the awakening factor of mindfulness in me.’ They understand how the awakening factor of mindfulness that has not arisen comes to arise; and how the awakening factor of mindfulness that has arisen becomes fully developed.

mn10:42.4.verse: When they have the awakening factor of investigation of principles …

mn10:42.9.verse: equanimity in them, they understand: ‘I have the awakening factor of equanimity in me.’ When they don’t have the awakening factor of equanimity in them, they understand: ‘I don’t have the awakening factor of equanimity in me.’ They understand how the awakening factor of equanimity that has not arisen comes to arise; and how the awakening factor of equanimity that has arisen becomes fully developed.

mn10:43.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:43.2.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the principles, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:43.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:43.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the seven awakening factors.

mn10:44.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths.

mn10:44.2.verse: And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths?

mn10:44.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn10:45.1.verse: And so they meditate observing an aspect of principles internally, externally, and both internally and externally.

mn10:45.2.verse: They meditate observing, with respect to the principles, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.

mn10:45.3.verse: Or mindfulness is established that principles exist, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.

mn10:45.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles with respect to the four noble truths.

mn10:46.1.verse: Anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for seven years can expect one of two results:

mn10:46.2.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.

mn10:46.4.verse: anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for six years …

mn10:46.22.verse: anyone who develops these four kinds of mindfulness meditation in this way for seven days can expect one of two results:

mn10:46.23.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.

mn10:47.1.verse: ‘The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.’

mn10:47.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

mn10:47.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn10:47.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn11:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn11:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn11:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, only here is there a monk, only here a second monk, only here a third monk, only here a fourth monk.

mn11:2.2.verse: The doctrines of others are devoid of monks:

mn11:2.3.verse: that is how you should rightly roar your lion’s roar.

mn11:3.1.verse: ‘It is possible that wanderers of other sects here might ask:

mn11:3.2.verse: “But what is the venerable ones’ (source of) comfort and strength that you venerable ones say thus?”

mn11:3.5.verse: Wanderers of other sects who ask thus may be answered in this way:

mn11:3.6.verse: “Friends, four dhammas have been declared to us by the Blessed One who knows and sees, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, on seeing which in ourselves we say thus:

mn11:3.7.verse: ‘Only here is there a monk, only here a second monk, only here a third monk, only here a fourth monk.

mn11:3.8.verse: The doctrines of others are devoid of monks.’

mn11:3.10.verse: We have confidence in the Master, we have confidence in the Dhamma, we have perfected the virtues,

mn11:3.11.verse: and those who share the Dhamma are dear to us

mn11:3.12.verse: whether they are laymen or gone forth and they are loved by us.

mn11:3.13.verse: These are the four dhammas declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, an Arahant and Fully Enlightened, on seeing which in ourselves we say as we do.”

mn11:4.1.verse: ‘It is possible that wanderers of other sects might say thus:

mn11:4.2.verse: “Friends, we too have confidence in the Master, that is, our Master; we too have confidence in the Dhamma, that is, our Dhamma; we too have perfected the virtues, that is, our virtues;

mn11:4.3.verse: and those who share Dhamma are dear to us too

mn11:4.4.verse: whether they are laymen or gone forth and they are loved by us.

mn11:4.5.verse: what is the distinction here, friends, what is the variance, what is the difference, between you and us?’’

mn11:5.1.verse: Wanderers of other sects who ask thus may be answered in this way:

mn11:5.2.verse: “How then, friends, is the goal? One or many?’’

mn11:5.3.verse: Answering rightly, the wanderers of other sects would answer thus:

mn11:5.4.verse: “Friends, the goal is one, not many.”-

mn11:5.5.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one affected by lust or free from lust?’’

mn11:5.6.verse: Answering rightly, the wanderers from other sects would answer thus:

mn11:5.7.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one free from lust, not affected by lust.”-

mn11:5.8.verse: ”But, friends is that goal for one affected by hate or free from hate?’’

mn11:5.10.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one free from hate, not affected by hate.”-

mn11:5.11.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one affected by delusion or free from delusion?’’

mn11:5.13.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one free from delusion, not affected by delusion.”-

mn11:5.14.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one affected by craving or free from craving?’’

mn11:5.16.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one free from craving, not affected by craving.”-

mn11:5.17.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one affected by clinging, or free from clinging?’’

mn11:5.19.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one free from clinging, not affected by clinging.”-

mn11:5.20.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one who has vision or for one without vision?’’

mn11:5.22.verse: “Friends, that goal is for one with vision, not for one without vision.”-

mn11:5.23.verse: ”But, friends, is that goal for one who favours and opposes, or for one who does not favour and oppose?’’

mn11:5.25.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one who does not favour and oppose, not for one who favours and opposes.”-

mn11:5.26.verse: ”But, friend, is that goal for one who delights in diversification or for one who has no delight in diversification?’’

mn11:5.28.verse: “Friends, the goal is for one who has no delight in diversification, not for one who delights in diversification.”

mn11:6.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of views:

mn11:6.2.verse: the view of being and the view of non-being.

mn11:6.3.verse: Any monks or divines who rely on the view of being, adopt the view of being and accept the view of being, are opposed to the view of non-being.

mn11:6.4.verse: Any monks or divines who rely on the view of non-being, adopt the view of non-being and accept the view of non-being, are opposed to the view of being.

mn11:7.1.verse: Any monks or divines who do not understand as they actually are the origin and the disappearance and the gratification and the danger and the escape in (the case of) these two kinds of views, are affected by lust, affected by hate, affected by delusion, affected by craving, affected by clinging, without vision, given over to favouring and opposing, and who delight in diversification, enjoy diversification;

mn11:7.2.verse: they are not liberated from birth, ageing and death, from sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair,

mn11:7.3.verse: they are not liberated from suffering, I say.

mn11:8.1.verse: Any monks or divines who understand as they actually are the origin and the disappearance, and the gratification and the danger and the escape in (the case of) these two kinds of views, are without lust, without hate, without delusion, without craving, without clinging, with vision, not given over to favouring and opposing, and who have no delight in diversification, no enjoyment in diversification;

mn11:8.2.verse: they are liberated from birth, ageing and death, from sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair,

mn11:8.3.verse: they are liberated from suffering, I say.

mn11:9.1.verse: Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds clinging:

mn11:9.3.verse: clinging to sensual desires, clinging to wrong views, clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:10.1.verse: When certain monks and divines claim to propound the full knowledge of all kinds of clinging,

mn11:10.2.verse: they do not completely describe full knowledge of all kinds of clinging.

mn11:10.3.verse: They describe full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires without describing clinging to (wrong) views, clinging to rites and rituals, or clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:10.5.verse: Those good monks and divines do not understand these three instances (of clinging) as they actually are.

mn11:10.6.verse: Consequently while these good monks and divines claim to propound full knowledge of all kinds of clinging,

mn11:10.8.verse: they describe (only) full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires without describing clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:11.1.verse: When certain monks and divines claim to propound the full knowledge of all kinds of clinging,

mn11:11.3.verse: they describe full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires and clinging to views, without describing clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a self-doctrine

mn11:11.5.verse: … they do not understand two instances …

mn11:11.8.verse: They describe full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires and clinging to views, without describing clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:12.1.verse: When certain monks and divines claim to propound the full knowledge of all kinds of clinging,

mn11:12.3.verse: they describe full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires, clinging to views and clinging to rites and rituals, without describing clinging to a self-doctrine

mn11:12.5.verse: they do not understand one instance

mn11:12.8.verse: They describe full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires and clinging to views and clinging to rites and rituals without describing clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:13.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, in such a Dhamma and Discipline as that it is plain that confidence in the Master is not rightly directed,

mn11:13.2.verse: it is plain that confidence in the Dhamma is not rightly directed,

mn11:13.3.verse: that perfecting of the virtues is not rightly directed,

mn11:13.4.verse: and that the dearness and love among those who share the Dhamma are not rightly directed.

mn11:13.6.verse: Because that is how it is when the Dhamma and the Discipline is ill-expounded, ill-proclaimed, leading nowhere, unconducive to peace and proclaimed by one not fully enlightened.

mn11:14.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata, an Arahant and Fully Enlightened One, claims to propound full knowledge of all kinds of clinging, he completely describes all kinds of clinging:

mn11:14.2.verse: he describes full knowledge of clinging to sensual desires and clinging to (wrong) view and clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a self-doctrine.

mn11:15.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, in such a Dhamma and Discipline as that it is plain that confidence in the Master is rightly directed,

mn11:15.2.verse: that confidence in the Dhamma is rightly directed,

mn11:15.3.verse: that perfecting of virtues is rightly directed,

mn11:15.4.verse: and that dearness and love among those who share the Dhamma are rightly directed.

mn11:15.6.verse: Because that is how it is when the Dhamma and the Discipline is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading onward, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one fully enlightened.

mn11:16.1.verse: ‘Now these four kind of clinging have what as their source, what as their origin, from what are they born, by what are they produced?

mn11:16.2.verse: ‘These four kinds of clinging have craving as their source, craving as their origin, they are born from craving, and produced by craving.

mn11:16.4.verse: ‘Craving has feeling as its source... produced by feeling.

mn11:16.6.verse: ‘Feeling has contact as its source... produced by contact.

mn11:16.8.verse: ‘Contact has the sixfold base as its source... produced by the sixfold base.

mn11:16.9.verse: ‘The sixfold base has what as its source...?

mn11:16.10.verse: ‘The sixfold base has name-and-form as its source... produced by name-and-form.

mn11:16.12.verse: ‘Name-and-form has consciousness as its source... produced by consciousness.

mn11:16.14.verse: ‘Consciousness has formations as its source... produced by formations.

mn11:16.16.verse: ‘Formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, they are born from ignorance, and produced by ignorance.

mn11:17.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, as soon as ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen in a bhikkhu, then with the fading of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge he no longer clings to sensual desires (as fuel for) clinging, or to (wrong) views (as fuel for) clinging, or to rites and rituals (as fuel for) clinging, or to a self-doctrine (as fuel for) clinging.

mn11:17.2.verse: When he does not cling, he has no anguish. When he has no anguish, he attains Nibbāna for himself:

mn11:17.3.verse: Birth is is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what can be done is done, there is no more of this in the beyond.’

mn11:17.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn11:17.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn11:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar

mn11:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn11:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn11:2.1.verse: “‘Only here is there a true ascetic, here a second ascetic, here a third ascetic, and here a fourth ascetic.

mn11:2.2.verse: Other sects are empty of ascetics.’

mn11:2.3.verse: This, mendicants, is how you should rightly roar your lion’s roar.

mn11:3.1.verse: It’s possible that wanderers of other religions might say:

mn11:3.2.verse: ‘But what is the source of the venerables’ certainty and forcefulness that they say this?’

mn11:3.6.verse: ‘There are four things explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. Seeing these things in ourselves we say that:

mn11:3.7.verse: “Only here is there a true ascetic, here a second ascetic, here a third ascetic, and here a fourth ascetic.

mn11:3.8.verse: Other sects are empty of ascetics.”

mn11:3.10.verse: We have confidence in the Teacher, we have confidence in the teaching, and we have fulfilled the precepts.

mn11:3.11.verse: And we have love and affection for those who share our path,

mn11:4.1.verse: It’s possible that wanderers of other religions might say:

mn11:4.2.verse: ‘We too have confidence in the Teacher—our Teacher; we have confidence in the teaching—our teaching; and we have fulfilled the precepts—our precepts.

mn11:4.3.verse: And we have love and affection for those who share our path,

mn11:4.5.verse: What, then, is the difference between you and us?’

mn11:5.2.verse: ‘Well, reverends, is the goal one or many?’

mn11:5.3.verse: Answering rightly, the wanderers would say:

mn11:5.4.verse: ‘The goal is one, reverends, not many.’

mn11:5.5.verse: ‘But is that goal for the greedy or for those free of greed?’

mn11:5.6.verse: Answering rightly, the wanderers would say:

mn11:5.7.verse: ‘That goal is for those free of greed, not for the greedy.’

mn11:5.8.verse: ‘Is it for the hateful or those free of hate?’

mn11:5.11.verse: ‘Is it for the delusional or those free of delusion?’

mn11:5.14.verse: ‘Is it for those who crave or those rid of craving?’

mn11:5.17.verse: ‘Is it for those who have fuel for grasping or those who do not?’

mn11:5.19.verse: ‘It’s for those who do not have fuel for grasping.’

mn11:5.20.verse: ‘Is it for the knowledgeable or the ignorant?’

mn11:5.23.verse: ‘Is it for those who favor and oppose or for those who don’t favor and oppose?’

mn11:5.25.verse: ‘It’s for those who don’t favor and oppose.’

mn11:5.26.verse: ‘But is that goal for those who enjoy proliferation or for those who enjoy non-proliferation?’

mn11:5.27.verse: Answering rightly, the wanderers would say:

mn11:5.28.verse: ‘It’s for those who enjoy non-proliferation, not for those who enjoy proliferation.’

mn11:6.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these two views:

mn11:6.2.verse: views favoring existence and views favoring nonexistence.

mn11:6.3.verse: Any ascetics or brahmins who resort to, draw near to, and cling to a view favoring existence will oppose a view favoring nonexistence.

mn11:6.4.verse: Any ascetics or brahmins who resort to, draw near to, and cling to a view favoring nonexistence will oppose a view favoring existence.

mn11:7.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand these two views’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape. They’re greedy, hateful, delusional, craving, grasping, and ignorant. They favor and oppose, and they enjoy proliferation.

mn11:7.2.verse: They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn11:7.3.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

mn11:8.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand these two views’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape. They’re rid of greed, hate, delusion, craving, grasping, and ignorance. They don’t favor and oppose, and they enjoy non-proliferation.

mn11:8.2.verse: They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn11:8.3.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.

mn11:9.1.verse: There are these four kinds of grasping.

mn11:9.3.verse: Grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

mn11:10.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping.

mn11:10.2.verse: But they don’t correctly describe the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping.

mn11:10.3.verse: They describe the complete understanding of grasping at sensual pleasures, but not views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

mn11:10.5.verse: Because those gentlemen don’t truly understand these three things.

mn11:10.6.verse: That’s why they claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping,

mn11:11.1.verse: There are some other ascetics and brahmins who claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping,

mn11:11.3.verse: They describe the complete understanding of grasping at sensual pleasures and views, but not precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

mn11:11.5.verse: Because those gentlemen don’t truly understand these two things.

mn11:11.6.verse: That’s why they claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping,

mn11:12.1.verse: There are some other ascetics and brahmins who claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping,

mn11:12.3.verse: They describe the complete understanding of grasping at sensual pleasures, views, and precepts and observances, but not theories of a self.

mn11:12.5.verse: Because those gentlemen don’t truly understand this one thing.

mn11:12.6.verse: That’s why they claim to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping,

mn11:13.1.verse: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is said to be not rightly placed.

mn11:13.4.verse: and love and affection for those sharing the same path are said to be not rightly placed.

mn11:13.6.verse: It’s because that teaching and training is poorly explained and poorly propounded, not emancipating, not leading to peace, proclaimed by someone who is not a fully awakened Buddha.

mn11:14.1.verse: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha claims to propound the complete understanding of all kinds of grasping.

mn11:14.2.verse: He describes the complete understanding of grasping at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, and theories of a self.

mn11:15.1.verse: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is said to be rightly placed.

mn11:15.4.verse: and love and affection for those sharing the same path are said to be rightly placed.

mn11:15.6.verse: It’s because that teaching and training is well explained and well propounded, emancipating, leading to peace, proclaimed by a fully awakened Buddha.

mn11:16.1.verse: What is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of these four kinds of grasping?

mn11:16.3.verse: And what is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of craving?

mn11:16.5.verse: And what is the source of feeling?

mn11:16.7.verse: And what is the source of contact?

mn11:16.9.verse: And what is the source of the six sense fields?

mn11:16.11.verse: And what is the source of name and form?

mn11:16.13.verse: And what is the source of consciousness?

mn11:16.15.verse: And what is the source of choices?

mn11:17.1.verse: When that mendicant has given up ignorance and given rise to knowledge, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge they don’t grasp at sensual pleasures, views, precepts and observances, or theories of a self.

mn11:17.2.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

mn11:17.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

mn11:17.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn11:17.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn12:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the grove outside the city to the west.

mn12:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis had recently forsaken this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn12:2.2.verse: He was making this statement before the Vesālī Assembly:

mn12:2.3.verse: ‘The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state (dhamma).

mn12:2.4.verse: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by human thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him,

mn12:2.5.verse: and whoever is taught that Dhamma for his benefit, it (only) leads rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him when he practises it, (but not to anything else).’

mn12:3.1.verse: Then, it being morning, the venerable Sāriputta dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe he went into Vesālī for alms.

mn12:3.2.verse: Then he heard of (what) Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, was saying.

mn12:3.6.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Vesālī and had returned from his alms-round, after his meal, he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he told the Blessed One what had taken place.

mn12:4.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, the misguided man Sunakkhatta is angry,

mn12:4.2.verse: and his words are spoken out of anger.

mn12:4.3.verse: Thinking to condemn the Tathāgata, he actually commends the Tathāgata;

mn12:4.4.verse: for it is a commendation of the Tathāgata to say of him

mn12:4.5.verse: “and whoever is taught the Dhamma for his benefit, it (only) leads rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him who practises it (but not to anything else)”.’

mn12:5.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, this misguided man Sunakkhatta will never infer of me according to Dhamma that:

mn12:5.2.verse: “That Blessed One is such since he is Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, Enlightened, Blessed.”

mn12:6.1.verse: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:

mn12:6.2.verse: “That Blessed One is such that he enjoys the various kinds of (supernormal) success; having been one he becomes many, having been many he becomes one: he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain, as through space; he dives in and out of earth as though it were water; he goes on unbroken water as though it were earth; seated cross-legged he travels in space like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the world of Divinity (Brahmā).”

mn12:7.1.verse: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:
