mn12:7.2.verse: “That Blessed One is such that with the heavenly ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the heavenly and the human, those that are far as well as near.”

mn12:8.1.verse: ‘And he will never infer of me according to Dhamma:

mn12:8.2.verse: “That Blessed One is such that he encompasses with his mind the minds of other beings, other persons.

mn12:8.3.verse: He understands the mind affected by lust as affected by lust

mn12:8.4.verse: and the mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust;

mn12:8.5.verse: he understands the mind affected by hate as affected by hate

mn12:8.6.verse: and the mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate;

mn12:8.7.verse: he understands the mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion

mn12:8.8.verse: and the mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion;

mn12:8.9.verse: he understands the contracted mind as contracted

mn12:8.10.verse: and the distracted mind as distracted;

mn12:8.11.verse: he understands the exalted mind as exalted

mn12:8.12.verse: and the unexalted mind as unexalted;

mn12:8.13.verse: he understands the surpassed mind as surpassed

mn12:8.14.verse: and the unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed;

mn12:8.15.verse: he understands the concentrated mind as concentrated

mn12:8.16.verse: and the unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated;

mn12:8.17.verse: he understands the liberated mind as liberated

mn12:8.18.verse: and the unliberated mind as unliberated.”

mn12:9.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, a Tathāgata has these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar before the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.

mn12:10.1.verse: (1) ‘Here a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.

mn12:10.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power that a Tathāgata has by virtue of which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar before the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.

mn12:11.1.verse: (2) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the ripening of kammas undertaken, past, future and present, with possiblities and with causes.

mn12:11.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:12.1.verse: (3) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, whither all ways lead.

mn12:12.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:13.1.verse: (4) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the world with its many and differing elements.

mn12:13.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:14.1.verse: (5) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is how beings have different inclinations.

mn12:14.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:15.1.verse: (6) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the disposition of the faculties of other beings, other persons.

mn12:15.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:16.1.verse: (7) ‘Again, a Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the defilement of, the cleansing of and the emergence from the jhānas, liberations, concentrations and attainments.

mn12:16.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:17.1.verse: (8) ‘Again, a Tathāgata recollects his manifold past life, that is to say, one birth, two births … five births, ten births … fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (universal) contraction, many aeons of (universal) expansion, many aeons of (universal) contraction and expansion: There I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named... such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared here. Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.

mn12:17.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:18.1.verse: (9) ‘Again, a Tathāgata, with the heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved: understands how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of the Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas, have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of the Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas, have, on the dissolution of the body after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight … he sees beings passing away and reappearing … He understands how beings pass on according to their kammas.

mn12:18.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power …

mn12:19.1.verse: (10) ‘Again, a Tathāgata, by realization himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of the heart and deliverance by understanding that are taintless, with (final) exhaustion of taints.

mn12:19.2.verse: And that is a Tathāgata’s power that a Tathāgata has, by virtue of which he claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.

mn12:20.1.verse: ‘A Tathāgata has these ten Tathāgata’s Powers, possessing which he claims the herd-leader’s place …

mn12:21.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus, say:

mn12:21.2.verse: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state.

mn12:21.3.verse: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,

mn12:21.4.verse: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).

mn12:21.5.verse: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say, that

mn12:21.6.verse: unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, then as (sure as if he had been) carried off (and) put (there) so he (will find himself) in hell.

mn12:22.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, there are four kinds of intrepidity, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.

mn12:23.1.verse: ‘Here I can see no reason why any monk or divine or god or māra or divinity at all in the world could, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me thus: “While you claim discovery of full enlightenment, you are not enlightened in these dhammas.”

mn12:23.2.verse: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.

mn12:24.1.verse: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “While you claim to have exhausted the taints, these taints are unexhausted in you.”

mn12:24.2.verse: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in … intrepidity.

mn12:25.1.verse: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “Those dhammas which are said by you to be obstructive are not in fact obstructive to one who practises them.”

mn12:25.2.verse: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in … intrepidity.

mn12:26.1.verse: ‘I can see no reason why any monk … could … accuse me thus: “Whoever is taught the Dhamma by you for his benefit, it does not lead rightly to the exhaustion of suffering in him when he practises it.”

mn12:26.2.verse: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.

mn12:27.1.verse: ‘These are the four kinds of intrepidity possessing which a Tathāgata claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies and sets the Divine Wheel rolling forward.

mn12:28.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …

mn12:28.2.verse: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state. The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,

mn12:28.3.verse: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).

mn12:28.4.verse: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say,

mn12:28.5.verse: that unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind and unless he recants that view, then as (sure as if he had been) carried off (and) put (there) so he (will find himself) in hell.

mn12:29.3.verse: A warrior-nobles’ assembly, a divines’ assembly, a householders’ assembly, a monks’ assembly, an assembly of gods of the Four Kings, an assembly of gods of the Thirty-three, a Māra’s assembly, a Divinities’ assembly.

mn12:29.5.verse: Possessing these four kinds of intrepidity, a Tathāgata approaches and goes into these eight kinds of assembly.

mn12:29.6.verse: ‘I have had direct knowledge, as a visitor, of many hundred warrior-noble caste assemblies.

mn12:29.7.verse: And formerly, I had sat with them there and talked and held converse with them.

mn12:29.8.verse: I see no reason why fear or timidity should come upon me there.

mn12:29.9.verse: And seeing no reason for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity.

mn12:30.1.verse: ‘I have had direct knowledge, as a visitor, of many hundred divine-caste assemblies ...

mn12:30.4.verse: ‘... assemblies of gods of the Four Kings ...

mn12:30.5.verse: ‘... assemblies of gods of the Thirty-Three ...

mn12:30.10.verse: I abide in safety, fearlessness and intrepidity. (These are the eight kinds of assemblies).

mn12:31.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …

mn12:31.3.verse: unless he abandons that assertion … carried off (and) put … in hell.

mn12:32.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of generation.

mn12:32.3.verse: Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, spontaneous generation.

mn12:33.2.verse: There are beings born by breaking out of the shell of an egg;

mn12:33.5.verse: There are those beings born by breaking out from the caul;

mn12:33.8.verse: There are those beings born in a rotten fish, in a rotten corpse, or in rotten dough, or in a cesspit or in a sewer;

mn12:33.11.verse: There are gods and denizens of hell and certain human beings and certain denizens of the states of deprivation, of spontaneous generation;

mn12:33.13.verse: ‘These are the four kinds of generation.

mn12:34.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone knowing and seeing me thus …

mn12:34.3.verse: unless he abandons that assertion … carried off (and) put … in hell.

mn12:35.3.verse: Hell, the animal womb, the realm of ghosts, human beings and gods.

mn12:36.1.verse: (1) ‘I understand hell; and the path and the way leading to hell,

mn12:36.2.verse: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell; that too I understand.

mn12:36.3.verse: (2) ‘I understand the animal womb; and the path and the way leading to the animal womb,

mn12:36.4.verse: where he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in the animal womb; that too I understand.

mn12:36.5.verse: (3) ‘I understand the realm of ghosts; and the path and way leading to the realm of ghosts,

mn12:36.6.verse: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in the realm of ghosts; that too I understand.

mn12:36.7.verse: (4) ‘I understand human beings; and the path and the way leading to the human world,

mn12:36.8.verse: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear among human beings; that too I understand.

mn12:36.9.verse: (5) ‘I understand the gods; and the path and the way leading to the world of gods,

mn12:36.10.verse: whereon he who has entered will, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world; that too I understand.

mn12:36.11.verse: (6) ‘I understand Nibbāna; and the path and the way leading to Nibbāna,

mn12:36.12.verse: whereon he who has entered will, by realization himself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and deliverance of understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints; that too I understand.

mn12:37.1.verse: (1) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:

mn12:37.2.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell.”

mn12:37.3.verse: And then later on with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell and is experiencing unremitting, painful, racking, piercing feelings.

mn12:37.4.verse: ‘Suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height full of glowing coals without flame or smoke;

mn12:37.5.verse: and then a man, scorched and exhausted by the hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to the same charcoal pit;

mn12:37.6.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:37.7.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same charcoal pit”;

mn12:37.8.verse: and then later on he sees that he has fallen into that charcoal pit and is experiencing unremitting painful, racking, piercing feelings;

mn12:37.9.verse: so too, by encompassing mind with mind ...

mn12:38.1.verse: (2) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:

mn12:38.2.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the animal womb.”

mn12:38.3.verse: And then later on, with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the animal womb and is experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings.

mn12:38.4.verse: ‘Suppose there were a cesspit more than a man’s height deep, full of filth;

mn12:38.5.verse: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same cesspit;

mn12:38.6.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:38.7.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same cesspit”;

mn12:38.8.verse: and then later on he sees that he has fallen into the cesspit and is experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings;

mn12:38.9.verse: so too, by encompassing mind with mind …

mn12:39.1.verse: (3) ‘By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:

mn12:39.2.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the realm of ghosts.

mn12:39.3.verse: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared in the realm of ghosts and is experiencing much painful feeling.

mn12:39.4.verse: ‘Suppose there were a tree growing on uneven ground with scanty foliage casting a dappled shade;

mn12:39.5.verse: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same tree;

mn12:39.6.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:39.7.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same tree”;

mn12:39.8.verse: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade of that tree experiencing much painful feeling;

mn12:39.9.verse: so too by encompassing mind with mind …

mn12:40.1.verse: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear among human beings.”

mn12:40.3.verse: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared among human beings and is experiencing much pleasant feeling.

mn12:40.4.verse: Suppose there were a tree growing on even ground with thick foliage casting a deep shade;

mn12:40.5.verse: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same tree;

mn12:40.6.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:40.7.verse: “This person so behaves … that he will come to this same tree”;

mn12:40.8.verse: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade of that tree experiencing much pleasant feeling;

mn12:40.9.verse: so too, encompassing mind with mind …

mn12:41.1.verse: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: “This person so behaves …

mn12:41.2.verse: that … after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.”

mn12:41.3.verse: And then later on … I see that … he has reappeared in a happy destination, in the heavenly world and is experiencing unremitting pleasant feelings.

mn12:41.4.verse: Suppose there were a mansion, and in it an upper chamber plastered within and without, shut off, secured by bars, and with shuttered windows,

mn12:41.5.verse: and in it a couch spread with rugs and blankets and sheets, with a deerskin coverlet, and with a canopy as well as crimson pillow for both (head and feet);

mn12:41.6.verse: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same mansion;

mn12:41.7.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:41.8.verse: “This person so behaves … that he will come to this same mansion;

mn12:41.9.verse: and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in that upper chamber in that mansion experiencing unremitting pleasant feelings,

mn12:41.10.verse: so too, by encompassing mind with mind …

mn12:42.1.verse: By encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus:

mn12:42.2.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such that, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the heart’s deliverance and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints.”

mn12:42.3.verse: And then later on I see that by realization for himself with direct knowledge he here and now enters upon and abides in the heart’s deliverance and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free, with exhaustion of taints, and is experiencing unremitting pleasant feeling.

mn12:42.4.verse: ‘Suppose there were a pond with clean, agreeable, cool water, transparent, with smooth banks and delightful,

mn12:42.6.verse: and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed towards that same pond;

mn12:42.7.verse: then a man with (good) eyes on seeing him would say:

mn12:42.8.verse: “This person so behaves, his deportment is such, the path he has taken is such, that he will come to this same pond;

mn12:42.9.verse: and then later on he sees that he has gone down to the pond and bathed and drunk and relieved all his distress, fatigue and fever and has come out again and is sitting or lying in the wood experiencing unremitting pleasant feelings;

mn12:42.10.verse: so too, by encompassing mind with mind …

mn12:42.13.verse: ‘These are the five kinds of destination

mn12:43.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, should anyone, knowing and seeing me thus say:

mn12:43.2.verse: “The monk Gotama has no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision (that is) higher than the human state.

mn12:43.3.verse: The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma (merely) hammered out by thought, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him”,

mn12:43.4.verse: then unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind, and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).

mn12:43.5.verse: Just as a bhikkhu perfected in virtue, concentration and understanding would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it (will) happen in this case, I say,

mn12:43.6.verse: that unless he abandons that assertion and that (state of) mind, and unless he recants that view, he (will find himself) in hell (sure as if he had been) carried off (and put there).

mn12:44.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, I have had direct knowledge of (what is called) the four-factored life divine as one who has lived it.

mn12:44.2.verse: I have practised the extreme of asceticism, of coarseness, of scrupulousness, and of seclusion.

mn12:45.1.verse: ‘Such was my asceticism here that I went naked, rejecting conventions, licking my hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; I did not accept a thing brought or a thing specially made or an invitation;

mn12:45.2.verse: I received nothing from out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman was lying with a man, from where food was advertised to be distributed, from where a dog was waiting, from where flies were buzzing; I accepted no fish or meat, I drank no liquor, wine or besotting drink.

mn12:45.3.verse: I kept to one house, to one morsel; I kept to two houses, to two morsels … I kept to seven houses, to seven morsels.

mn12:45.4.verse: I lived on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day;

mn12:45.5.verse: I took food once a day, once each two days, … once each seven days; and so on, up to once each fortnight. I dwelt pursuing the practice of taking food at stated intervals.

mn12:45.6.verse: I was an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-parings, or moss, or ricebran, or rinsings, or sesamum flour, or grass, or cowdung. I lived on forest roots and on fruits as a feeder on windfalls.

mn12:45.7.verse: I clothed myself in hemp, in hemp mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood (shavings) fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings.

mn12:45.8.verse: I was one who pulled out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of pulling out hair and beard.

mn12:45.9.verse: I was one who stood continuously, rejecting seats.

mn12:45.10.verse: I was one who squatted continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position.

mn12:45.11.verse: I was one who used a mattress of spikes; I made a mattress of spikes my bed.

mn12:45.12.verse: I dwelt pursuing the practice of bathing in water for the third time by nightfall.

mn12:46.3.verse: just as the bole of a plane tree, accumulating over the years, cakes and flakes off, so too, the dust and dirt, accumlating over the years, caked on my body and flaked off.

mn12:46.5.verse: “Oh, let me rub this dust and dirt off with my hand, or let another rub this dust and dirt off with his hand”—

mn12:46.6.verse: it never occurred to me thus.

mn12:47.2.verse: I was always mindful in stepping forwards and stepping backwards: So much so that I was full of pity for even a drop of water, thus:

mn12:47.3.verse: “Let me not hurt the tiny breathing things in the crevices of the ground”.

mn12:48.2.verse: I would go away into some forest and dwell there.

mn12:48.3.verse: And when I saw a cowherd or a shepherd or someone gathering grass or sticks, or a woodsman, I would flee from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock—

mn12:48.5.verse: So that they should not see me or I see them.

mn12:48.6.verse: Just as a forest-bred deer on seeing human beings flees from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock,

mn12:49.1.verse: I would go on all fours to the byres when the cattle had gone out and the cowherds had left them, and I would feed on the young sucking-calves’ dung.

mn12:49.2.verse: As long as my own excrement and urine lasted, I fed on my own excrement and urine.

mn12:49.3.verse: Such was my great distortion in feeding.

mn12:50.1.verse: I would go off to some awe-inspiring grove and dwell there—

mn12:50.3.verse: normally it would make a man’s hair stand up if he were not free from lust.

mn12:50.4.verse: I would dwell by night in the open and by day in the grove when those cold wintry nights came during the Eight-days Interval of Frost.

mn12:50.5.verse: I would dwell by day in the open and by night in the grove in the last month of the hot season.

mn12:50.6.verse: And there came to me spontaneously this stanza never heard before:

mn12:50.7.verse: > Chilled by night and scorched by day,

mn12:50.9.verse: > Naked, no fire to sit beside,

mn12:50.10.verse: > The hermit yet pursues his quest.

mn12:51.1.verse: ‘I would make my bed in a charnel ground with the bones of the dead for a pillow.

mn12:51.2.verse: And cowherd boys came up and spat on me, made water on me, threw dirt at me, and poked sticks into my ears.

mn12:51.3.verse: Yet I never knew the arising of an evil mind (thoughts) about them.

mn12:51.4.verse: Such was my abiding in equanimity.

mn12:52.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn12:52.5.verse: and they eat kola-fruits, and they eat kola-fruit powder, and they drink kola-fruit water,

mn12:52.6.verse: and they make many kinds of kola-fruit concoctions.

mn12:52.7.verse: Now I have had direct knowledge of eating a single kola-fruit a day.

mn12:52.8.verse: But, Sāriputta, you may think that

mn12:52.9.verse: the kola-fruit was bigger at that time,

mn12:52.10.verse: yet you should not regard it so:

mn12:52.11.verse: the kola-fuit was then at most the same size as now.

mn12:52.12.verse: Through feeding on a single kola-fruit a day, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.

mn12:52.13.verse: Because of eating so little my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems.

mn12:52.14.verse: Because of eating so little my backside became like a camel’s hoof.

mn12:52.15.verse: Because of eating so little the projections on my spine stood out like corded beads.

mn12:52.16.verse: Because of eating so little my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn.

mn12:52.17.verse: Because of eating so little the gleam of my eyes sunk far down in their sockets looked like the gleam of water sunk far down in a deep well.

mn12:52.18.verse: Because of eating so little my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun.

mn12:52.19.verse: Because of eating so little, if I touched by belly skin, I encountered my backbone too; if I touched my backbone, I encountered my bell-skin too.

mn12:52.20.verse: Because of eating so little, if I made water or evacuated my bowels, I fell over on my face there.

mn12:52.21.verse: Because of eating so little, if I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.

mn12:53-55.1.verse: ‘There are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn12:53-55.7.verse: And they eat rice, and they eat rice powder, and they drink rice water,

mn12:53-55.8.verse: and they make various kinds of rice concoctions.

mn12:53-55.9.verse: Now I have had direct knowledge of eating a single rice grain a day.

mn12:53-55.10.verse: But, Sāriputta, you may think that

mn12:53-55.11.verse: the rice grain was bigger at that time;

mn12:53-55.12.verse: yet you should not regard it so:

mn12:53-55.13.verse: the rice grain was at most the same size as now.

mn12:53-55.14.verse: Through feeding on a single rice grain a day my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.

mn12:53-55.23.verse: the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.’

mn12:56.1.verse: ‘Yet, Sāriputta, by such deportment, by such practice, by such performance of difficult feats, I attained no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision higher than the human state (dhamma).

mn12:56.3.verse: Because I did not attain this Noble Understanding, which, on being attained, being Noble and an outlet, rightly leads to the exhaustion of suffering in him who practise it.’

mn12:57.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn12:57.2.verse: “Purification comes about through (the process of) a round of rebirths (itself).”

mn12:57.3.verse: But it is impossible to find the round of rebirths that I have not already gone the round of in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes:

mn12:57.4.verse: and had I gone the round as a god in the Pure Abodes, I should never have returned to this world.

mn12:58.1.verse: ‘There are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn12:58.2.verse: “Purification comes through (some particular kind of) rebirth.”

mn12:58.3.verse: But it is impossible to find the kind of rebirth that I have not been reborn in already in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes: …

mn12:59.3.verse: But it is impossible to find the kind of abode that I have not dwelt in … except for the Pure Abodes… .

mn12:60.3.verse: But it is impossible to find the kind of sacrifice that has not already been offered up by me in this long journey, either as a head-anointed warrior-noble king or as a divine with great property.

mn12:61.3.verse: But it is impossible to find the kind of fire that has not already been worshipped by me in this long journey, either as a head-anointed warrior-noble king or as a divine of great property.

mn12:62.1.verse: ‘Sāriputta, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn12:62.2.verse: “As long as this good man is still young, a black-haired boy endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first phase of life, so long is he perfect in his lucid understanding.

mn12:62.3.verse: But when this good man is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage, being eighty, ninety or a hundred years old, then the lucidity of his understanding is lost.”

mn12:62.4.verse: But it should not be regarded so.

mn12:62.5.verse: I am now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage: my years have turned eighty.

mn12:62.6.verse: Now suppose that I had four disciples with a hundred years’ life, a hundred years’ span, perfect in mindfulness, attentiveness, memory and lucidity of understanding—

mn12:62.7.verse: just as a well-equipped archer, trained, practised and tested, could easily shoot a light arrow arrow across a palm’s shadow:

mn12:62.8.verse: suppose they were even to that extent perfect in mindfulness, attentiveness, memory and lucidity of understanding—

mn12:62.9.verse: and suppose that they continuously asked about the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and that I answered when asked and that they remembered each answer of mine and never asked a subsidiary question or paused except to eat, drink, chew, taste, make water, evacuate the bowels and rest in order to remove sleepiness and tiredness:

mn12:62.10.verse: still the Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dhamma, his explanations of factors of the Dhamma, and his replies to questions, would be unexhausted.

mn12:62.11.verse: But meanwhile those four disciples of mine with their hundred-years’ life, their hundred-years’ span, would have died at the end of those hundred years.

mn12:62.12.verse: Sāriputta, even if you have to carry me about on a bed, still there will be no change in the lucidity of the Tathāgata’s understanding.

mn12:63.1.verse: ‘Rightly speaking, were it to be said of someone.

mn12:63.2.verse: “A being not subject to delusion has appeared in the world for the welfare and happiness of many, out of pity for the world, for the benefit, welfare and happiness of gods and men”, it is of me indeed that rightly speaking it should be said.’

mn12:64.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Blessed One fanning him.

mn12:64.2.verse: Then he said to the Blessed One:

mn12:64.3.verse: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous!

mn12:64.4.verse: As I listened to this discourse the hairs of my body stood up.

mn12:64.5.verse: Venerable sir, what is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?”

mn12:64.6.verse: ‘As to that, Nāgasamāla, you may remember this discourse on the Dhamma as the Hair-raising Discourse.’

mn12:64.7.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn12:64.8.verse: The venerable Nāgasamāla was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn12:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on the Lion’s Roar

mn12:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying outside the city of Vesālī in a woodland grove west of the town.

mn12:2.1.verse: Now at that time Sunakkhatta the Licchavi had recently left this teaching and training.

mn12:2.2.verse: He was telling a crowd in Vesālī:

mn12:2.3.verse: “The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn12:2.4.verse: He teaches what he’s worked out by logic, following a line of inquiry, expressing his own perspective.

mn12:2.5.verse: Regardless of his goal in teaching the Dhamma, it delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.”

mn12:3.1.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.

mn12:3.2.verse: He heard what Sunakkhatta was saying.

mn12:3.6.verse: Then he wandered for alms in Vesālī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

mn12:4.1.verse: “Sāriputta, Sunakkhatta, that futile man, is angry.

mn12:4.2.verse: His words are spoken out of anger.

mn12:4.3.verse: Thinking he criticizes the Realized One, in fact he just praises him.

mn12:4.4.verse: For it is praise of the Realized One to say:

mn12:4.5.verse: ‘Regardless of his goal in teaching the Dhamma, it delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.’

mn12:5.1.verse: But there’s no way Sunakkhatta will infer about me from the teaching:

mn12:5.2.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn12:6.1.verse: And there’s no way Sunakkhatta will infer about me from the teaching:

mn12:6.2.verse: ‘That Blessed One wields the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying himself and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.’

mn12:7.1.verse: And there’s no way Sunakkhatta will infer about me from the teaching:

mn12:7.2.verse: ‘That Blessed One, with clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, hears both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.’

mn12:8.1.verse: And there’s no way Sunakkhatta will infer about me from the teaching:

mn12:8.2.verse: ‘That Blessed One understands the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with his own mind.

mn12:8.3.verse: He understands mind with greed as “mind with greed,”

mn12:8.4.verse: and mind without greed as “mind without greed.”

mn12:9.1.verse: There are these ten powers of a Realized One that the Realized One possesses. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:10.1.verse: Firstly, the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible, and the impossible as impossible.

mn12:10.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. Relying on this he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:11.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the result of deeds undertaken in the past, future, and present in terms of grounds and causes.

mn12:11.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:12.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands where all paths of practice lead.

mn12:12.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:13.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the world with its many and diverse elements.

mn12:13.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:14.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the diverse convictions of sentient beings.

mn12:14.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:15.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands the faculties of other sentient beings and other individuals after encompassing them with his mind.

mn12:15.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:16.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One truly understands corruption, cleansing, and emergence regarding the absorptions, liberations, immersions, and attainments.

mn12:16.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:17.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One recollects many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. He remembers: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so he recollects his many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn12:17.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:18.1.verse: Furthermore, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, the Realized One sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, he sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. He understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn12:18.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. …

mn12:19.1.verse: Furthermore, the Realized One has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with his own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn12:19.2.verse: Since he truly understands this, this is a power of the Realized One. Relying on this he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:20.1.verse: A Realized One possesses these ten powers of a Realized One. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:21.1.verse: When I know and see in this way, suppose someone were to say this:

mn12:21.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn12:21.3.verse: He teaches what he’s worked out by logic, following a line of inquiry, expressing his own perspective.’

mn12:21.4.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:21.5.verse: Just as a mendicant accomplished in ethics, immersion, and wisdom would reach enlightenment in this very life, such is the consequence, I say.

mn12:21.6.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:22.1.verse: Sāriputta, a Realized One has four kinds of self-assurance. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:23.1.verse: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying: ‘You claim to be a fully awakened Buddha, but you don’t understand these things.’

mn12:23.2.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:24.1.verse: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying: ‘You claim to have ended all defilements, but you still have these defilements.’

mn12:24.2.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:25.1.verse: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying: ‘The acts that you say are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them.’

mn12:25.2.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:26.1.verse: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying: ‘Regardless of your goal in teaching the Dhamma, it does not deliver one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.’

mn12:26.2.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:27.1.verse: A Realized One possesses these four kinds of self-assurance. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

mn12:28.1.verse: When I know and see in this way, suppose someone were to say this:

mn12:28.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones …’

mn12:28.3.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:29.1.verse: Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies.

mn12:29.3.verse: The assemblies of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and ascetics. An assembly of the gods of the four great kings. An assembly of the gods of the thirty-three. An assembly of Māras. An assembly of divinities.

mn12:29.5.verse: Possessing these four kinds of self-assurance, the Realized One approaches and enters right into these eight assemblies.

mn12:29.6.verse: I recall having approached an assembly of hundreds of aristocrats.

mn12:29.7.verse: There I used to sit with them, converse, and engage in discussion.

mn12:29.8.verse: But I don’t see any reason to feel afraid or insecure.

mn12:29.9.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:30.1.verse: I recall having approached an assembly of hundreds of brahmins …

mn12:30.4.verse: the gods of the four great kings …

mn12:30.8.verse: There too I used to sit with them, converse, and engage in discussion.

mn12:30.9.verse: But I don’t see any reason to feel afraid or insecure.

mn12:30.10.verse: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

mn12:31.1.verse: When I know and see in this way, suppose someone were to say this:

mn12:31.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones …’

mn12:31.3.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:32.1.verse: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of reproduction.

mn12:32.3.verse: Reproduction for creatures born from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, or spontaneously.

mn12:33.1.verse: And what is reproduction from an egg?

mn12:33.2.verse: There are beings who are born by breaking out of an eggshell.

mn12:33.3.verse: This is called reproduction from an egg.

mn12:33.4.verse: And what is reproduction from a womb?

mn12:33.5.verse: There are beings who are born by breaking out of the amniotic sac.

mn12:33.6.verse: This is called reproduction from a womb.

mn12:33.7.verse: And what is reproduction from moisture?

mn12:33.8.verse: There are beings who are born in a rotten fish, a rotten carcass, rotten porridge, a cesspool, or a sump.

mn12:33.9.verse: This is called reproduction from moisture.

mn12:33.11.verse: Gods, hell-beings, certain humans, and certain beings in the lower realms.

mn12:33.13.verse: These are the four kinds of reproduction.

mn12:34.1.verse: When I know and see in this way, suppose someone were to say this:

mn12:34.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones …’

mn12:34.3.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:35.3.verse: Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humanity, and the gods.

mn12:36.1.verse: I understand hell, and the path and practice that leads to hell.

mn12:36.2.verse: And I understand how someone practicing that way, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn12:36.9.verse: gods, and the path and practice that leads to the world of the gods.

mn12:36.10.verse: And I understand how someone practicing that way, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn12:36.11.verse: And I understand extinguishment, and the path and practice that leads to extinguishment.

mn12:36.12.verse: And I understand how someone practicing that way realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn12:37.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:37.2.verse: ‘This individual is practicing in such a way and is riding upon such a path that when their body breaks up, after death, they will be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.’

mn12:37.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed been reborn in hell, where they experience absolutely painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn12:37.4.verse: Suppose there was a pit of glowing coals deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals that neither flamed nor smoked.

mn12:37.5.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same pit of coals.

mn12:37.6.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:37.7.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very pit of coals.’

mn12:37.8.verse: Some time later they see that they have indeed fallen into that pit of coals, where they experience absolutely painful feelings, sharp and severe. …

mn12:38.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:38.2.verse: ‘This individual … will be reborn in the animal realm.’

mn12:38.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed been reborn in the animal realm, where they suffer painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn12:38.4.verse: Suppose there was a sewer deeper than a man’s height, full to the brim with feces.

mn12:38.5.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same sewer.

mn12:38.6.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:38.7.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very sewer.’

mn12:38.8.verse: Some time later they see that they have indeed fallen into that sewer, where they suffer painful feelings, sharp and severe. …

mn12:39.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:39.2.verse: ‘This individual … will be reborn in the ghost realm.’

mn12:39.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed been reborn in the ghost realm, where they experience mostly painful feelings.

mn12:39.4.verse: Suppose there was a tree growing on rugged ground, with thin foliage casting dappled shade.

mn12:39.5.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same tree.

mn12:39.6.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:39.7.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very tree.’

mn12:39.8.verse: Some time later they see them sitting or lying under that tree, where they experience mostly painful feelings. …

mn12:40.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:40.2.verse: ‘This individual … will be reborn among human beings.’

mn12:40.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed been reborn among human beings, where they experience mostly pleasant feelings.

mn12:40.4.verse: Suppose there was a tree growing on smooth ground, with abundant foliage casting dense shade.

mn12:40.5.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same tree.

mn12:40.6.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:40.7.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very tree.’

mn12:40.8.verse: Some time later they see them sitting or lying under that tree, where they experience mostly pleasant feelings. …

mn12:41.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:41.2.verse: ‘This individual … will be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’

mn12:41.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed been reborn in a heavenly realm, where they experience feelings of absolute happiness.

mn12:41.4.verse: Suppose there was a stilt longhouse with a peaked roof, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with door fastened and window shuttered.

mn12:41.5.verse: And it had a couch spread with woolen covers—shag-piled, pure white, or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends.

mn12:41.6.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same stilt longhouse.

mn12:41.7.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:41.8.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very stilt longhouse.’

mn12:41.9.verse: Some time later they see them sitting or lying in that stilt longhouse, where they experience feelings of absolute happiness. …

mn12:42.1.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

mn12:42.2.verse: ‘This individual is practicing in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

mn12:42.3.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight  in this very life due to the ending of defilements, experiencing feelings of absolute happiness.

mn12:42.4.verse: Suppose there was a lotus pond with clear, sweet, cool water, clean, with smooth banks, delightful.

mn12:42.5.verse: Nearby was a dense forest grove.

mn12:42.6.verse: Then along comes a person struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. And they have set out on a path that meets with that same lotus pond.

mn12:42.7.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say:

mn12:42.8.verse: ‘This person is proceeding in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will arrive at that very lotus pond.’

mn12:42.9.verse: Some time later they would see that person after they had plunged into that lotus pond, bathed and drunk. When all their stress, weariness, and heat exhaustion had faded away, they emerged and sat or lay down in that woodland thicket, where they experienced feelings of absolute happiness.

mn12:42.10.verse: In the same way, when I’ve comprehended the mind of an individual, I understand:

mn12:42.11.verse: ‘This individual is practicing in such a way and is riding upon such a path that they will realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

mn12:42.12.verse: Some time later I see that they have indeed realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements, experiencing feelings of absolute happiness.

mn12:43.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn12:43.3.verse: He teaches what he’s worked out by logic, following a line of inquiry, expressing his own perspective.’

mn12:43.4.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

mn12:43.5.verse: Just as a mendicant accomplished in ethics, immersion, and wisdom would reach enlightenment in this very life, such is the consequence, I say.

mn12:44.1.verse: Sāriputta, I recall having practiced a spiritual path consisting of four factors.

mn12:44.2.verse: I used to be a fervent mortifier, the ultimate fervent mortifier. I used to live rough, the ultimate rough-liver. I used to live in disgust of sin, the ultimate one living in disgust of sin. I used to be secluded, in ultimate seclusion.

mn12:45.1.verse: And this is what my fervent mortification was like. I went naked, ignoring conventions. I licked my hands, and didn’t come or stop when asked. I didn’t consent to food brought to me, or food prepared specially for me, or an invitation for a meal.

mn12:45.2.verse: I didn’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or who lives with a man; or where food for distribution is advertised; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. I accepted no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drank no fermented gruel.

mn12:45.3.verse: I went to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls.

mn12:45.4.verse: I fed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

mn12:45.5.verse: I ate once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. I lived committed to the practice of eating food at set intervals.

mn12:45.6.verse: I ate herbs, millet, wild rice, poor rice, water lettuce, rice bran, scum from boiling rice, sesame flour, grass, or cow dung. I survived on forest roots and fruits, or eating fallen fruit.

mn12:45.7.verse: I wore robes of sunn hemp, mixed hemp, corpse-wrapping cloth, rags, lodh tree bark, antelope hide (whole or in strips), kusa grass, bark, wood-chips, human hair, horse-tail hair, or owls’ wings.

mn12:45.8.verse: I tore out hair and beard, committed to this practice.

mn12:45.9.verse: I constantly stood, turning down seats.

mn12:45.10.verse: I squatted, committed to the endeavor of squatting.

mn12:45.11.verse: I lay on a mat of thorns, making a mat of thorns my bed.

mn12:45.12.verse: I was devoted to ritual bathing three times a day, including at dusk.

mn12:45.13.verse: And so I lived committed to practicing these various ways of mortifying and tormenting the body.

mn12:45.14.verse: Such was my practice of fervent mortification.

mn12:46.1.verse: And this is what my rough living was like.

mn12:46.2.verse: The dust and dirt built up on my body over many years until it started flaking off.

mn12:46.3.verse: It’s like the trunk of a pale-moon ebony tree, which builds up bark over many years until it starts flaking off.

mn12:46.4.verse: But it didn’t occur to me:

mn12:46.5.verse: ‘Oh, this dust and dirt must be rubbed off by my hand or another’s.’

mn12:47.1.verse: And this is what my living in disgust of sin was like.

mn12:47.2.verse: I’d step forward or back ever so mindfully, so I was full of pity regarding even a drop of water, thinking:

mn12:47.3.verse: ‘May I not injure any little creatures on unclear ground.’

mn12:47.4.verse: Such was my living in disgust of sin.

mn12:48.1.verse: And this is what my seclusion was like.

mn12:48.2.verse: I would plunge deep into a wilderness region and stay there.

mn12:48.3.verse: When I saw a cowherd or a shepherd, or someone gathering grass or sticks, or a lumberjack, I’d flee from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from valley to valley, from uplands to uplands.

mn12:48.5.verse: So that I wouldn’t see them, nor they me.

mn12:48.6.verse: I fled like a wild deer seeing a human being.

mn12:48.10.verse: Such was my practice of seclusion.

mn12:49.1.verse: I would go on all fours into the cow-pens after the cattle had left and eat the dung of the young suckling calves.

mn12:49.2.verse: As long as my own urine and excrement lasted, I would even eat that.

mn12:49.3.verse: Such was my eating of most unnatural things.

mn12:50.1.verse: I would plunge deep into an awe-inspiring forest grove and stay there.

mn12:50.3.verse: normally it would make your hair stand on end if you weren’t free of greed.

mn12:50.4.verse: And on days such as the cold spell when the snow falls in the January winter, I stayed in the open by night and in the forest by day.

mn12:50.5.verse: But in the last month of summer I’d stay in the open by day and in the forest by night.

mn12:50.6.verse: And then these verses, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me:

mn12:50.9.verse: nude, no fire to sit beside,

mn12:50.10.verse: the sage still pursues his quest.’

mn12:51.1.verse: I would make my bed in a charnel ground, with the bones of the dead for a pillow.

mn12:51.2.verse: Then village louts would come up to me. They’d spit and piss on me, throw mud on me, even poke twigs in my ears.

mn12:51.3.verse: But I don’t recall ever having a bad thought about them.

mn12:51.4.verse: Such was my abiding in equanimity.

mn12:52.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:52.5.verse: So they eat jujubes and jujube powder, and drink jujube juice.

mn12:52.6.verse: And they enjoy many jujube concoctions.

mn12:52.7.verse: I recall eating just a single jujube.

mn12:52.9.verse: at that time the jujubes must have been very big.

mn12:52.10.verse: But you should not see it like this.

mn12:52.11.verse: The jujubes then were at most the same size as today.

mn12:52.12.verse: Eating so very little, my body became severely emaciated.

mn12:52.13.verse: Due to eating so little, my major and minor limbs became like the joints of an eighty-year-old or a dying man,

mn12:52.14.verse: my bottom became like a camel’s hoof,

mn12:52.15.verse: my vertebrae stuck out like beads on a string,

mn12:52.16.verse: and my ribs were as gaunt as the broken-down rafters on an old barn.

mn12:52.17.verse: Due to eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets, like the gleam of water sunk deep down a well.

mn12:52.18.verse: Due to eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter-gourd in the wind and sun.

mn12:52.19.verse: Due to eating so little, the skin of my belly stuck to my backbone, so that when I tried to rub the skin of my belly I grabbed my backbone, and when I tried to rub my backbone I rubbed the skin of my belly.

mn12:52.20.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to urinate or defecate I fell face down right there.

mn12:52.21.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell out.

mn12:53-55.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:53-55.23.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell out.

mn12:56.1.verse: But Sāriputta, I did not achieve any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones by that conduct, that practice, that grueling work.

mn12:56.3.verse: Because I didn’t achieve that noble wisdom that’s noble and emancipating, and which delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.

mn12:57.3.verse: But it’s not easy to find a realm that I haven’t previously transmigrated to in all this long time, except the gods of the pure abodes.

mn12:57.4.verse: For if I had transmigrated to the gods of the pure abodes I would not have returned to this realm again.

mn12:58.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:58.3.verse: But it’s not easy to find any rebirth that I haven’t previously been reborn in …

mn12:59.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:59.3.verse: But it’s not easy to find an abode where I haven’t previously abided …

mn12:60.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:60.3.verse: But it’s not easy to find a sacrifice that I haven’t previously offered in all this long time, when I was an anointed aristocratic king or a well-to-do brahmin.

mn12:61.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:61.2.verse: ‘Purity comes from serving the sacred flame.’

mn12:61.3.verse: But it’s not easy to find a fire that I haven’t previously served in all this long time, when I was an anointed aristocratic king or a well-to-do brahmin.

mn12:62.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn12:62.2.verse: ‘So long as this gentleman is youthful, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life he will be endowed with perfect lucidity of wisdom.

mn12:62.3.verse: But when he’s old, elderly, and senior, advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life—eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old—he will lose his lucidity of wisdom.’

mn12:62.4.verse: But you should not see it like this.

mn12:62.5.verse: For now I am old, elderly, and senior, I’m advanced in years, and have reached the final stage of life. I am eighty years old.

mn12:62.6.verse: Suppose I had four disciples with a lifespan of a hundred years. And they each were perfect in memory, rememberance, retention, and perfect lucidity of wisdom.

mn12:62.7.verse: Imagine how easily a well-trained expert archer with a strong bow would shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree.

mn12:62.8.verse: That’s how extraordinary they were in memory, rememberance, retention, and perfect lucidity of wisdom.

mn12:62.9.verse: They’d bring up questions about the four kinds of mindfulness meditation again and again, and I would answer each question. They’d remember the answers and not ask the same question twice.

mn12:62.10.verse: And they’d pause only to eat and drink, go to the toilet, and sleep to dispel weariness. But the Realized One would not run out of Dhamma teachings, words and phrases of the teachings, or spontaneous answers.

mn12:62.11.verse: And at the end of a hundred years my four disciples would pass away.

mn12:62.12.verse: Even if you have to carry me around on a stretcher, there will never be any deterioration in the Realized One’s lucidity of wisdom.

mn12:63.1.verse: And if there’s anyone of whom it may be rightly said that

mn12:63.2.verse: a being not liable to delusion has arisen in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, it’s of me that this should be said.”

mn12:64.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Buddha fanning him.

mn12:64.2.verse: Then he said to the Buddha:

mn12:64.4.verse: While I was listening to this exposition of the teaching my hair stood up!

mn12:64.5.verse: What is the name of this exposition of the teaching?”

mn12:64.6.verse: “Well then, Nāgasamāla, you may remember this exposition of the teaching as ‘The Hair-raising Discourse’.”

mn12:64.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn12:64.8.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Nāgasamāla approved what the Buddha said.

mn13:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn13:2.1.verse: Then, it being morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, and taking their bowls and (outer) robes, they went into Sāvatthi for alms.

mn13:2.3.verse: ‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthi;

mn13:2.4.verse: suppose we went to the Other Sectarian Wanderers’ Park? ’

mn13:2.5.verse: So they went to the Other Sectarian Wanderers’ Park, and they exchanged greetings with the Other Sectarian Wanderers,

mn13:2.6.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, the Wanderers said to them:

mn13:3.1.verse: ‘Friends, the Monk Gotama makes known full-knowledge of sensual desires, and so too do we;

mn13:3.2.verse: the Monk Gotama makes known full-knowledge of form, and so too do we;

mn13:3.3.verse: the Monk Gotama makes known full-knowledge of feelings, and so too do we.

mn13:3.4.verse: What then is the distinction here, what is the variance, what is the difference between the Monk Gotama’s teaching of the Dhamma and ours,

mn13:4.1.verse: Then without agreeing or disagreeing with these words,

mn13:4.2.verse: the bhikkhus got up from their seats and went away,

mn13:4.3.verse: (thinking:) ‘We shall come to know the meaning of these words in the Blessed One’s presence.’

mn13:5.1.verse: When they had wandered for alms in Sāvatthi and had returned from their alms-round after the meal, they went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, they told him what had taken place.

mn13:6.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who say thus should be questioned thus:

mn13:6.2.verse: “But, friends, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape, in the case of sensual desire?

mn13:6.3.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape, in the case of form?

mn13:6.4.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape, in the case of feelings?”

mn13:6.5.verse: Being questioned thus wanderers of other sects will fail to account for the matter, and what is more, they will get into difficulties.

mn13:6.7.verse: Because it is not their province.

mn13:6.8.verse: Bhikkhus, I see no one in the world with its gods, its Māras and Divinities, in this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, who could satisfy the mind a reply to these questions, unless it were a Tathāgata or a Tathāgata’s disciple, or else one who has learnt it from that (source).

mn13:7.1.verse: (i) ‘And what is gratification in the case of sensual desires?

mn13:7.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual desires.

mn13:7.4.verse: Forms cognizable through the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative, of lust.

mn13:7.8.verse: Tangibles cognizable through the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likable, connected with sensual desires, and provocative of lust.

mn13:7.9.verse: These are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn13:7.10.verse: ‘Now the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on those five cords of sensual desire are the gratification in the case of sensual desires.

mn13:8.1.verse: (ii) ‘And what is the danger in the case of sensual desires?

mn13:8.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, on account of the calling by which a clansman makes a living,

mn13:8.3.verse: whether checking or accounting or calculating or ploughing or trading or cattle farming or archery or as a king’s man, or whatever the calling may be,

mn13:8.4.verse: he has to face cold, he has to face heat, he is harassed by mosquitoes and flies, wind and sun and creeping things, risking death by hunger and thirst.

mn13:8.5.verse: ‘Now this danger in the case of sensual desires, (this) mass of suffering visible here and now, has sensual desires for its reason, sensual desires for its source, sensual desires for its cause, the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn13:9.1.verse: ‘If no property comes to the clansman while he works and strives and makes efforts thus,

mn13:9.2.verse: he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast he weeps till he is distraught,

mn13:9.3.verse: (crying:) “My work is vain, my work is fruitless!”’

mn13:9.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual deisres … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn13:10.1.verse: ‘If property comes to the clansman while he works and strives and makes efforts thus,

mn13:10.2.verse: he experiences pain and grief in protecting it:

mn13:10.3.verse: “How shall neither kings nor thieves make off with my property nor fire burn it nor water sweep it away nor hateful heirs make off with it?”

mn13:10.4.verse: And as he guards and protects his property, kings or thieves make off with it or fire burns it or water sweeps it away or hateful heirs make off with it.

mn13:10.5.verse: And he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast he weeps till he is distraught, (crying):

mn13:10.6.verse: “What I had I have no more.”

mn13:10.7.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn13:11.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason, sensual desires for the source, sensual desires for the cause, the reason being simply sensual desires, kings quarrel with kings, warrior-nobles with warrior-nobles, divines with divines, householders with householders, mother with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, brother with sister, friend with friend.

mn13:11.2.verse: And here in their quarrels, brawls and disputes they attack each other with fists or with clods or with sticks or with knives,

mn13:11.3.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn13:11.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn13:12.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) take swords and shields and buckle on bows and quivers, and they charge into battle massed in double array with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing;

mn13:12.2.verse: and there they are wounded by arrows and spears, and their heads are cut off by swords,

mn13:12.3.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn13:12.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn13:13.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) take swords, and shields and buckle on bows and quivers, and they charge slippery bastions, with arrows and spears flying, and swords flashing;

mn13:13.2.verse: and there they are wounded by arrows and spears and splashed with boiling liquids and crushed under heavy weights, and their heads are cut off by swords,

mn13:13.3.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn13:13.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn13:14.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) break in and steal, turn bandit, rob highways, seduce others’ wives;

mn13:14.2.verse: so that when they are caught, kings have many kinds of torture inflicted on them.

mn13:14.3.verse: They have them flogged with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with clubs, they have their hands cut off, their feet cut off, their hands and feet cut off, their ears cut off, their noses cut off, their ears and noses cut off, they have them subjected to the “porridge-pot”, to the “polished-shell shave”, to the “eclipse’s mouth”, to the “fiery wreath”, to the “fiery hand”, to the “blades of grass”, to the “bark dress”, to the “antelope”, to the “meat-hooks”, to the “coins”, to the “lye-pickling”, to the “pivotting-pin”, to the “rolled-up palliasse”, and they have them splashed with boiling oil, and they have them thrown to dogs to devour, and they have them impaled alive on stakes, and they have their heads cut off with swords—

mn13:14.4.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn13:14.5.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn13:15.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason, sensual desires for the source, sensual desires for the cause, the reason being simply sensual desires, (men) indulge in misconduct of body, speech and mind:

mn13:15.2.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn13:15.3.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires, this mass of suffering in life to come, has sensual desires for its reason, sensual desires for its source, sensual desires for its cause, the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn13:16.1.verse: (iii) ‘And what is escape in the case of sensual desires?

mn13:16.2.verse: It is the removal of lustful desire, the abandonment of lustful desire, for sensual pleasures. ‘This is the escape in the case of sensual desires.

mn13:17.1.verse: ‘That those monks and divines who do not understand, as it actually is, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger and the escape as escape, in the case of sensual desires, can either themselves fully know sensual desires or instruct so that another can fully know sensual desires—that is not possible.

mn13:17.2.verse: ‘That those monks and divines who understand, as it actually is, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger and the escape as escape, in the case of sensual desires, can either themselves fully know sensual desires or instruct so that another can fully know sensual desires—that is possible.

mn13:18.1.verse: (i) ‘And what is the gratification in the case of form?

mn13:18.2.verse: ‘Suppose there were a girl of warrior-noble caste or divine caste or householder stock, in her fifteenth or sixteenth year, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair: is her beauty and loveliness then at its height?’

mn13:18.4.verse: ‘Now the pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on that beauty and loveliness are

mn13:18.5.verse: the gratification in the case of form.

mn13:19.1.verse: (ii) ‘And what is the danger in the case of form?

mn13:19.2.verse: ‘Later on one might see that same woman here at eighty, ninety or a hundred years, aged, as crooked as a roof, doubled up, tottering with the aid of sticks, frail, her youth gone, her teeth broken, grey-haired, scanty-haired, bald, wrinkled, with limbs all blotchy:

mn13:19.3.verse: how do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn13:19.4.verse: has her former beauty and loveliness vanished and the danger become evident ?’

mn13:19.6.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this is the danger in the case of form.

mn13:20.1.verse: ‘Again, one might see that same woman afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, lying fouled in her own excrement and urine, lifted up by some and set down by others.

mn13:20.2.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn13:20.3.verse: has the former beauty and loveliness vanished and the danger become evident ?’

mn13:20.5.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this too is the danger in the case of form.

mn13:21.1.verse: ‘Again, one might see that same woman as a corpse thrown on the charnel ground,

mn13:21.2.verse: one-day dead, two-days dead, three-days dead, bloated, livid and oozing with matter.

mn13:21.3.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn13:21.4.verse: has the former beauty and loveliness vanished and the danger become evident?’

mn13:21.6.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this too is the danger in the case of form.

mn13:22.1.verse: ‘Again, one might see that same woman as a corpse thrown on a charnel ground,

mn13:22.2.verse: devoured by crows, kites, vultures, dogs, jackals and various kinds of worms.

mn13:22.5.verse: … the danger in the case of form.

mn13:23-28.2.verse:
‘… a skeleton with flesh and blood held together by sinews …

‘… a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood and held together by sinews …

‘… a skeleton without flesh or blood held together by sinews …

‘… bones without sinews, scattered in all directions,

mn13:23-28.3.verse: here a hand-bone there a foot-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there the back-bone, there the skull …

mn13:29.1.verse: Again, one might see that same woman as a corpse thrown on a charnel ground:

mn13:29.2.verse: bones bleached white, the colour of shells … bones heaped up, more than a year old … bones rotted and crumbled to dust.

mn13:29.3.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn13:29.4.verse: has the former beauty and loveliness vanished and the danger become evident?’

mn13:29.6.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this too is the danger in the case of form.’

mn13:30.1.verse: (iii) ‘And what is escape in the case of form?

mn13:30.2.verse: It is the removal of lustful desire, the abandonment of lustful desire, for form.’ ‘This is the escape in the case of form.’
