mn13:31.1.verse: ‘That those monks and divines who do not understand, as it actually is, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger and the escape as escape, in the case of form, can either themselves fully know or instruct so that another can fully know form—that is not possible.’

mn13:32.1.verse: (i) ‘And what is the gratification in the case of feelings?

mn13:32.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn13:32.3.verse: ‘On such an occasion he does not choose for his own affliction, or for another’s affliction, or for the affliction of both.

mn13:32.4.verse: On that occasion he feels only feeling that is free from affliction.

mn13:32.5.verse: Gratification in the case of feeling in its highest aspect is freedom from affliction, I say.

mn13:33-35.1.verse: ‘Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial application and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration. ‘On such an occasion … freedom from affliction, I say.

mn13:33-35.2.verse: ‘With the fading as well of happiness a bhikkhu abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, feeling pleasure with his body he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”’ ‘On such an occasion … freedom from affliction, I say.

mn13:33-35.3.verse: ‘With the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. ‘On such an occasion he does not choose for his own affliction, or for another’s affliction, or for the affliction of both.

mn13:33-35.4.verse: On that occasion he feels only feeling that is free from affliction.

mn13:33-35.5.verse: Gratification in the case of feeling in its highest aspect is freedom from affliction, I say.

mn13:36.1.verse: (ii) ‘And what is the danger in the case of feelings?

mn13:36.2.verse: ‘Feelings are impermanent, painful, and inseparable from changefulness. ‘This is the danger in the case of feelings.

mn13:37.1.verse: (iii) ‘And what is the escape in the case of feelings?

mn13:37.2.verse: ‘It is the remove of lustful desire, the abandonment of lustful desire, for feelings. ‘This is the escape in the case of feelings.

mn13:38.1.verse: ‘That those monks and divines who do not understand, as it actually is, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, in the case of feelings, can either themselves fully know feelings or instruct so that another can fully know feelings—that is not possible.

mn13:38.2.verse: ‘That these monks and divines who understand, as it actually is, the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger and the escape as escape, in the case of feelings, can either themselves fully know feelings or instruct so that another can fully know feelings—that is possible.’

mn13:38.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn13:38.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn13:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on the Mass of Suffering

mn13:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn13:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

mn13:2.3.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.

mn13:2.4.verse: Why don’t we visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

mn13:2.5.verse: Then they went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

mn13:2.6.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. The wanderers said to them:

mn13:3.1.verse: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama advocates the complete understanding of sensual pleasures, and so do we.

mn13:3.2.verse: The ascetic Gotama advocates the complete understanding of forms, and so do we.

mn13:3.3.verse: The ascetic Gotama advocates the complete understanding of feelings, and so do we.

mn13:3.4.verse: What, then, is the difference between the ascetic Gotama’s teaching and instruction and ours?”

mn13:4.1.verse: Those mendicants neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.

mn13:4.2.verse: They rose from their seats, thinking,

mn13:4.3.verse: “We will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

mn13:5.1.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. The Buddha said:

mn13:6.1.verse: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other religions say this, you should say to them:

mn13:6.2.verse: ‘But reverends, what’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to sensual pleasures?

mn13:6.3.verse: What’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to forms?

mn13:6.4.verse: What’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to feelings?’

mn13:6.5.verse: Questioned like this, the wanderers of other religions would be stumped, and, in addition, would get frustrated.

mn13:6.7.verse: Because they’re out of their element.

mn13:6.8.verse: I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could provide a satisfying answer to these questions except the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.

mn13:7.1.verse: And what is the gratification of sensual pleasures?

mn13:7.2.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn13:7.4.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn13:7.8.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn13:7.9.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn13:7.10.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation: this is the gratification of sensual pleasures.

mn13:8.1.verse: And what is the drawback of sensual pleasures?

mn13:8.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman earns a living by means such as

mn13:8.3.verse: arithmetic, accounting, calculating, farming, trade, raising cattle, archery, government service, or one of the professions.

mn13:8.4.verse: But they must face cold and heat, being hurt by the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and risking death from hunger and thirst.

mn13:8.5.verse: This is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:9.1.verse: That gentleman might try hard, strive, and make an effort, but fail to accrue riches.

mn13:9.2.verse: If this happens, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion, saying:

mn13:9.3.verse: ‘Oh, my hard work is wasted. My efforts are fruitless!’

mn13:9.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:10.1.verse: That gentleman might try hard, strive, and make an effort, and succeed in accruing riches.

mn13:10.2.verse: But they experience pain and sadness when they try to protect it, thinking:

mn13:10.3.verse: ‘How can I prevent my wealth from being taken by rulers or bandits, consumed by fire, swept away by flood, or taken by unloved heirs?’

mn13:10.4.verse: And even though they protect it and ward it, rulers or bandits take it, or fire consumes it, or flood sweeps it away, or unloved heirs take it.

mn13:10.5.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion:

mn13:10.7.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:11.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures kings fight with kings, aristocrats fight with aristocrats, brahmins fight with brahmins, and householders fight with householders. A mother fights with her child, child with mother, father with child, and child with father. Brother fights with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, and friend fights with friend.

mn13:11.2.verse: Once they’ve started quarreling, arguing, and disputing, they attack each other with fists, stones, rods, and swords,

mn13:11.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn13:11.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:12.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they don their sword and shield, fasten their bow and arrows, and plunge into a battle massed on both sides, with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing.

mn13:12.2.verse: There they are struck with arrows and spears, and their heads are chopped off,

mn13:12.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn13:12.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:13.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they don their sword and shield, fasten their bow and arrows, and charge wetly plastered bastions, with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing.

mn13:13.2.verse: There they are struck with arrows and spears, splashed with dung, crushed by a superior force, and their heads are chopped off,

mn13:13.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn13:13.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:14.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they break into houses, plunder wealth, steal from isolated buildings, commit highway robbery, and commit adultery.

mn13:14.2.verse: The rulers would arrest them and subject them to various punishments—

mn13:14.3.verse: whipping, caning, and clubbing; cutting off hands or feet, or both; cutting off ears or nose, or both; the ‘porridge pot’, the ‘shell-shave’, the ‘Rāhu’s mouth’, the ‘garland of fire’, the ‘burning hand’, the ‘bulrush twist’, the ‘bark dress’, the ‘antelope’, the ‘meat hook’, the ‘coins’, the ‘caustic pickle’, the ‘twisting bar’, the ‘straw mat’; being splashed with hot oil, being fed to the hounds, being impaled alive, and being beheaded.

mn13:14.4.verse: These result in death and deadly pain.

mn13:14.5.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:15.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures, they conduct themselves badly by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn13:15.2.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn13:15.3.verse: This is a drawback of sensual pleasures to do with lives to come, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn13:16.1.verse: And what is the escape from sensual pleasures?

mn13:16.2.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for sensual pleasures: this is the escape from sensual pleasures.

mn13:17.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand sensual pleasures’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It’s impossible for them to completely understand sensual pleasures themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand sensual pleasures.

mn13:17.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand sensual pleasures’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It is possible for them to completely understand sensual pleasures themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand sensual pleasures.

mn13:18.1.verse: And what is the gratification of forms?

mn13:18.2.verse: Suppose there was a girl of the brahmins, aristocrats, or householders in her fifteenth or sixteenth year, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair. Is she not at the height of her beauty and prettiness?”

mn13:18.4.verse: “The pleasure and happiness that arise from this beauty and prettiness

mn13:19.1.verse: And what is the drawback of forms?

mn13:19.2.verse: Suppose that some time later you were to see that same sister—eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old—bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as they walk, ailing, past their prime, with teeth broken, hair grey and scanty or bald, skin wrinkled, and limbs blotchy.

mn13:19.4.verse: Has not that former beauty vanished and the drawback become clear?”

mn13:20.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose that you were to see that same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, collapsed in her own urine and feces, being picked up by some and put down by others.

mn13:20.3.verse: Has not that former beauty vanished and the drawback become clear?”

mn13:20.5.verse: “This too is the drawback of forms.

mn13:21.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose that you were to see that same sister as a corpse discarded in a charnel ground. And it had been dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering.

mn13:21.4.verse: Has not that former beauty vanished and the drawback become clear?”

mn13:21.6.verse: “This too is the drawback of forms.

mn13:22.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose that you were to see that same sister as a corpse discarded in a charnel ground. And it was being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, herons, hounds, tigers, leopards, jackals, and many kinds of little creatures …

mn13:23-28.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose that you were to see that same sister as a corpse discarded in a charnel ground.

mn13:23-28.2.verse: And it had been reduced to a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews … A skeleton rid of flesh but smeared with blood, and held together by sinews … A skeleton rid of flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

mn13:23-28.3.verse: Bones rid of sinews scattered in every direction. Here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here an arm-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth, here the skull. …

mn13:29.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose that you were to see that same sister as a corpse discarded in a charnel ground.

mn13:29.2.verse: And it had been reduced to white bones, the color of shells … Decrepit bones, heaped in a pile … Bones rotted and crumbled to powder.

mn13:29.4.verse: Has not that former beauty vanished and the drawback become clear?”

mn13:29.6.verse: “This too is the drawback of forms.

mn13:30.1.verse: And what is the escape from forms?

mn13:30.2.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for forms: this is the escape from forms.

mn13:31.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand forms’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It’s impossible for them to completely understand forms themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand forms.

mn13:31.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand forms’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It is possible for them to completely understand forms themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand forms.

mn13:32.1.verse: And what is the gratification of feelings?

mn13:32.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn13:32.3.verse: At that time a mendicant doesn’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, or hurt both;

mn13:32.4.verse: they feel only feelings that are not hurtful.

mn13:32.5.verse: Freedom from being hurt is the ultimate gratification of feelings, I say.

mn13:33-35.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn13:33-35.3.verse: fourth absorption. At that time a mendicant doesn’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, or hurt both;

mn13:33-35.4.verse: they feel only feelings that are not hurtful.

mn13:33-35.5.verse: Freedom from being hurt is the ultimate gratification of feelings, I say.

mn13:36.1.verse: And what is the drawback of feelings?

mn13:36.2.verse: That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is their drawback.

mn13:37.1.verse: And what is the escape from feelings?

mn13:37.2.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for feelings: this is the escape from feelings.

mn13:38.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand feelings’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It’s impossible for them to completely understand feelings themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand feelings.

mn13:38.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand feelings’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are. It is possible for them to completely understand feelings themselves, or to instruct another so that, practicing accordingly, they will completely understand feelings.”

mn13:38.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn13:38.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn14:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Sakyan country at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park.

mn14:2.1.verse: Then Mahānāma the Sakyan went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so he said:

mn14:2.2.verse: “Venerable Sir, I have long known the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus:

mn14:2.3.verse: “Greed is an imperfection of mind, hate is an imperfection of mind, delusion is an imperfection of mind.”

mn14:2.4.verse: Yet while I know the Dhamma as taught by the Blessed One thus,

mn14:2.6.verse: at times ideas (dhammas) of greed invade my mind and remain, ideas of hate invade my mind and remain, ideas of delusion invade my mind and remain:

mn14:2.8.verse: what dhamma is still unabandoned by me in myself owing to which at times these ideas (dhammas) invade my mind and remain.’

mn14:3.1.verse: ‘Mahānāma, there is still a dhamma unabandoned in you, owing to which at times ideas (dhamma) of greed … of hate … of delusion invade your mind and remain;

mn14:3.2.verse: for were that dhamma already abandoned by you in yourself you would not be living the house life, you would not be enjoying sensual desires.

mn14:3.3.verse: It is because there is still that dhamma unabandoned by you in yourself that you are living the house life and enjoying sensual desires.

mn14:4.1.verse: ‘If, though a Noble Disciple has clearly seen, as it actually is, with right understanding how sensual desires provide little gratification and much suffering and despair, and how great is the danger in them,

mn14:4.2.verse: then for as long as he still does not attain to the happiness and pleasure that are quite apart from sensual desires, apart from unprofitable dhammas, or to something more peaceful even than that,

mn14:4.3.verse: he is still not averse to sensual desires.

mn14:4.4.verse: ‘But when a noble disciple has clearly seen, as it actually is, with right understanding how sensual desires provide little gratification and much suffering and despair and how great is the danger in them, then when he attains to the happiness and pleasure that are quite apart from sensual desires, apart from unprofitable dhammas, or to something more peaceful even than that,

mn14:4.5.verse: he is no more unaverse to sensual desires.

mn14:5.1.verse: ‘Before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta,

mn14:5.2.verse: when I too saw clearly as it actually is, with right understanding, how sensual desires provide little gratification and much suffering and despair, and how great is the danger in them,

mn14:5.3.verse: then for as long as I still did not attain to the happiness and pleasure that are quite apart from sensual desires, apart from unprofitable dhammas, or to something more peaceful even than that,

mn14:5.4.verse: I recognized that I was still not averse to sensual desires.

mn14:5.5.verse: ‘But when I clearly saw, as it actually is, with right understanding, how sensual desires provide little gratification and much suffering and despair, and how great is the danger in them, then when I attained to the happiness and pleasure that are quite apart from sensual desire, apart from unprofitable dhammas, or to something more peaceful even than that,

mn14:5.6.verse: I recognized that I was no more unaverse to sensual desires.

mn14:6.1.verse: (i) ‘And what is the gratification in the case of sensual desires?

mn14:6.2.verse: Mahānāma, there are ... these five cords of sensual desires.

mn14:6.4.verse: Forms cognizable through the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn14:6.8.verse: Tangibles cognizable through the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn14:6.9.verse: These are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn14:6.10.verse: ‘Now the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on those five cords of sensual desire

mn14:6.11.verse: are the gratification in the case of sensual desires.

mn14:7.1.verse: (ii) ‘And what is the danger in the case of sensual desires?

mn14:7.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, on account of the calling by which a clansman makes a living,

mn14:7.3.verse: whether checking or accounting or calculating or ploughing or trading or cattle farming or archery or as a king’s man, or whatever the calling may be,

mn14:7.4.verse: he has to face cold, he has to face heat, he is harassed by mosquitoes and flies, wind and sun and creeping things, risking death by hunger and thirst.

mn14:7.5.verse: ‘Now this danger in the case of sensual desires, (this) mass of suffering visible here and now, has sensual desires for its reason, sensual desires for its source, sensual desires for its cause, the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn14:8.1.verse: ‘If no property comes to the clansman while he works and strives and makes efforts thus,

mn14:8.2.verse: he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast he weeps till he is distraught, (crying:) “My work is vain, my work is fruitless!”

mn14:8.3.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn14:9.1.verse: ‘If property comes to the clansman while he works and strives and makes efforts thus,

mn14:9.2.verse: he experiences pain and grief in protecting it:

mn14:9.3.verse: “How shall neither kings nor thieves make off with my property nor fire burn it nor water sweep it away nor hateful heirs make off with it?”

mn14:9.4.verse: And as he guards and protects his property, kings or thieves make off with it or fire burns it or water sweeps it away or hateful heirs make off with it.

mn14:9.5.verse: And he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast he weeps till he is distraught, (crying:)

mn14:9.6.verse: “What I had I have no more.”

mn14:9.7.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn14:10.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason, sensual desires for the source, sensual desires for the cause, the reason being simply sensual desires, kings quarrel with kings, warrior-nobles with warrior-nobles, divines with divines, householders with householders, mother with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, brother with sister, friend with friend.

mn14:10.2.verse: And here in their quarrels, brawls and disputes they attack each other with fists or with clods or with sticks or with knives,

mn14:10.3.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn14:10.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn14:11.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) take swords and shields and buckle on bows and quivers, and they charge into battle massed in double array with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing;

mn14:11.2.verse: and there they are wounded by arrows and spears, and their heads are cut off by swords,

mn14:11.3.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn14:11.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn14:12.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) take swords and shields and buckle on bows and quivers, and they charge slippery bastions, with arrows and spears flying, and swords flashing;

mn14:12.2.verse: and there they are wounded by arrows and spears and splashed with boiling liquids and crushed under heavy weights, and their heads are cut off by swords,

mn14:12.3.verse: wherby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn14:12.4.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn14:13.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason … (men) break in and steal, turn bandit, rob highways, seduce others’ wives;

mn14:13.2.verse: so that when they are caught, kings have many kinds of torture inflicted on them.

mn14:13.3.verse: They have them flogged with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with clubs, they have their hands cut off, their feet cut off, their hands and feet cut off, their ears cut off, their noses cut off, their ears and noses cut off, they have them subjected to the “porridge-pot”, to the “polished-shell shave”, to the “eclipse’s mouth”, to the “fiery wreath”, to the “fiery hand”, to the “blades of grass”, to the “bark dress”, to the “antelope”, to the “meat-hooks”, to the “coins”, to the “lye-pickling”, to the “pivotting-pin”, to the “rolled-up palliasse”, and they have them splashed with boiling oil, and they have them thrown to dogs to devour, and they have them impaled alive on stakes, and they have their heads cut off with swords,

mn14:13.4.verse: whereby they incur death or deadly suffering.

mn14:13.5.verse: ‘Now this danger too in the case of sensual desires … the reason is simply sensual desires.

mn14:14.1.verse: ‘Again, with sensual desires for the reason, sensual desires for the source, sensual desires for the cause, the reason being simply sensual desires, (men) indulge in misconduct of body, speech and mind:

mn14:14.2.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn14:14.3.verse: Now this danger in the case of sensual desires, this mass of suffering in lives to come, has sensual desires for its reason, sensual desires for its source, sensual desires for its course, the reason being simply sensual desires.

mn14:15.1.verse: ‘Now, Mahānāma, on one occasion I was living at Rājagaha on the Vulture Peak Rock.

mn14:15.2.verse: On that occasion a number of Niganthas (Jains) living on the Black Rock on the slopes of the Anchorets’ Gullet (Isigili) were practising continuous standing, rejecting seats, and experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving.

mn14:16.1.verse: ‘Then when it was evening, I rose from meditation, and went to the Niganthas there. I asked them:

mn14:16.2.verse: “Friends, why do you practise continuous standing, rejecting seats, and experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving?”

mn14:17.2.verse: “Friend, the Nigantha Nātaputta, the Omniscient All-seer, claims to have complete knowledge and vision thus:

mn14:17.3.verse: ‘Whether I am walking or standing or sleeping or waking, my knowledge and vision are continuously, unceasingly maintained.’

mn14:17.5.verse: ‘Niganthas, you have done evil kammas in the past; exhaust them with piercing mortification.

mn14:17.6.verse: And when you are here and now restrained in body, speech and mind, that is doing no evil kammas for the future.

mn14:17.7.verse: So by annihilating with penance past evil kammas, and by doing no fresh evil knmmas, there will be no consequence in the future.

mn14:17.8.verse: With no consequence in the future there is exhaustion of kammas. With exhaustion of kammas there is exhaustion of suffering. With exhaustion of suffering there is exhaustion of feeling. With the exhaustion of feeling all suffering will be used up.’

mn14:17.9.verse: This is our preference and to our liking, and we are satisfied with it.”

mn14:18.1.verse: ‘When this was said, I told them:

mn14:18.3.verse: that you were (existed) in the past, and that it is not that your were (existed) not? ” ’

mn14:18.6.verse: that you did evil kammas in that past and did not abstain from them? ” ’

mn14:18.12.verse: that so much suffering has already been used up or that so much suffering has still to be used up or that when so much suffering has been used up all suffering will have been used up?’ “

mn14:18.15.verse: what the abandoning of unprofitable dhammas is and the cultivation of profitable dhammas here and now?’ “

mn14:19.1.verse: “ ‘So, friends, it seems that you do not know

mn14:19.2.verse: that you were in the past and that it is not that you were not;

mn14:19.3.verse: or that you did evil kammas in the past and did not abstain from them;

mn14:19.4.verse: or that you did such and such evil kammas;

mn14:19.5.verse: or that so much suffering has already been used up; or that when so much suffering has been used up, all suffering will have been used up;

mn14:19.7.verse: or what the abandoning of unprofitable dhammas is and the cultivation of profitable dhammas here and now.

mn14:19.8.verse: That being so, those who are murderers, bloody-handed evil-doers in the world go into homelessness as Niganthas when they are reborn among human beings?’ “

mn14:20.1.verse: “ ‘Friend Gotama, pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain.

mn14:20.2.verse: For were pleasure to be gained through pleasure, then Seniya Bimbisāra king of Madagha would gain pleasure, since he abides in greater pleasure than the venerable Gotama does.’ “

mn14:20.3.verse: “ ‘Surely the venerable Niganthas have uttered those words rashly and without reflection.

mn14:20.6.verse: Rather it is I who ought to be asked:

mn14:20.7.verse: ‘Who abides in greater pleasure, Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha, or the venerable Gotama?’ ‘ “

mn14:20.8.verse: “ ‘Surely, friend Gotama, we uttered those words rashly and without reflection.

mn14:20.10.verse: But let that be. Now we ask the venerable Gotama:

mn14:20.11.verse: ‘Who abides in greater pleasure, Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or the venerable Gotama?’ ‘ “

mn14:21.1.verse: “ ‘Then, friends, I shall ask you a question in return. Answer it as you like.

mn14:21.2.verse: How do you conceive this, friends,

mn14:21.3.verse: can Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha abide without moving this body or uttering a word for seven days experiencing unremitting pleasure?’ “

mn14:21.6.verse: can Seniya Bimbisāra … without moving his body … six days …

mn14:21.13.verse: “ ‘Friends, I can abide without moving my body or uttering a word for one day …

mn14:21.20.verse: “ ‘How do you conceive this, friends, that being so, who dwells in greater pleasure, Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha, or I?’ ”

mn14:21.21.verse: “ ‘That being so, the venerable Gotama abides is greater pleasure than Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha does.’ ”

mn14:21.22.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn14:21.23.verse: Mahānāma the Sakyan was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn14:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering

mn14:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

mn14:2.1.verse: Then Mahānāma the Sakyan went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn14:2.2.verse: “For a long time, sir, I have understood your teaching like this:

mn14:2.3.verse: ‘Greed, hate, and delusion are corruptions of the mind.’

mn14:2.6.verse: Despite understanding this, sometimes my mind is occupied by thoughts of greed, hate, and delusion.

mn14:2.8.verse: I wonder what qualities remain in me that I have such thoughts?”

mn14:3.1.verse: “Mahānāma, there is a quality that remains in you that makes you have such thoughts.

mn14:3.2.verse: For if you had given up that quality you would not still be living at home and enjoying sensual pleasures.

mn14:3.3.verse: But because you haven’t given up that quality you are still living at home and enjoying sensual pleasures.

mn14:4.1.verse: Sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn14:4.2.verse: So, Mahānāma, even though a noble disciple has clearly seen this with right wisdom, as long as they do not achieve the rapture and bliss that are apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that,

mn14:4.3.verse: they can return to sensual pleasures.

mn14:4.4.verse: But when they do achieve that rapture and bliss, or something more peaceful than that,

mn14:4.5.verse: they do not return to sensual pleasures.

mn14:5.1.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too clearly saw with right wisdom that:

mn14:5.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.’

mn14:5.3.verse: But so long as I didn’t achieve the rapture and bliss that are apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that,

mn14:5.4.verse: I didn’t announce that I would not return to sensual pleasures.

mn14:5.5.verse: But when I did achieve that rapture and bliss, or something more peaceful than that,

mn14:5.6.verse: I announced that I would not return to sensual pleasures.

mn14:6.1.verse: And what is the gratification of sensual pleasures?

mn14:6.2.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn14:6.4.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn14:6.8.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn14:6.9.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn14:6.10.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation: this is the gratification of sensual pleasures.

mn14:7.1.verse: And what is the drawback of sensual pleasures?

mn14:7.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman earns a living by means such as

mn14:7.3.verse: arithmetic, accounting, calculating, farming, trade, raising cattle, archery, government service, or one of the professions.

mn14:7.4.verse: But they must face cold and heat, being hurt by the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and risking death from hunger and thirst.

mn14:7.5.verse: This is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:8.1.verse: That gentleman might try hard, strive, and make an effort, but fail to accrue riches.

mn14:8.2.verse: If this happens, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion, saying: ‘Oh, my hard work is wasted. My efforts are fruitless!’

mn14:8.3.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:9.1.verse: That gentleman might try hard, strive, and make an effort, and succeed in accruing riches.

mn14:9.2.verse: But they experience pain and sadness when they try to protect it, thinking:

mn14:9.3.verse: ‘How can I prevent my wealth from being taken by rulers or bandits, consumed by fire, swept away by flood, or taken by unloved heirs?’

mn14:9.4.verse: And even though they protect it and ward it, rulers or bandits take it, or fire consumes it, or flood sweeps it away, or unloved heirs take it.

mn14:9.5.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion:

mn14:9.7.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:10.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures kings fight with kings, aristocrats fight with aristocrats, brahmins fight with brahmins, and householders fight with householders. A mother fights with her child, child with mother, father with child, and child with father. Brother fights with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, and friend fights with friend.

mn14:10.2.verse: Once they’ve started quarreling, arguing, and disputing, they attack each other with fists, stones, rods, and swords,

mn14:10.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn14:10.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:11.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they don their sword and shield, fasten their bow and arrows, and plunge into a battle massed on both sides, with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing.

mn14:11.2.verse: There they are struck with arrows and spears, and their heads are chopped off,

mn14:11.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn14:11.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:12.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they don their sword and shield, fasten their bow and arrows, and charge wetly plastered bastions, with arrows and spears flying and swords flashing.

mn14:12.2.verse: There they are struck with arrows and spears, splashed with dung, crushed by a superior force, and their heads are chopped off,

mn14:12.3.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

mn14:12.4.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:13.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures they break into houses, plunder wealth, steal from isolated buildings, commit highway robbery, and commit adultery.

mn14:13.2.verse: The rulers would arrest them and subject them to various punishments—

mn14:13.3.verse: whipping, caning, and clubbing; cutting off hands or feet, or both; cutting off ears or nose, or both; the ‘porridge pot’, the ‘shell-shave’, the ‘Rāhu’s mouth’, the ‘garland of fire’, the ‘burning hand’, the ‘bulrush twist’, the ‘bark dress’, the ‘antelope’, the ‘meat hook’, the ‘coins’, the ‘caustic pickle’, the ‘twisting bar’, the ‘straw mat’; being splashed with hot oil, being fed to the hounds, being impaled alive, and being beheaded.

mn14:13.4.verse: These result in death and deadly pain.

mn14:13.5.verse: This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in the present life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:14.1.verse: Furthermore, for the sake of sensual pleasures, they conduct themselves badly by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn14:14.2.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn14:14.3.verse: This is a drawback of sensual pleasures to do with lives to come, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures.

mn14:15.1.verse: Mahānāma, this one time I was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

mn14:15.2.verse: Now at that time several Jain ascetics on the slopes of Isigili at the Black Rock were constantly standing, turning down seats. And they felt painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion.

mn14:16.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, I came out of retreat and went to the Black Rock to visit those Jain ascetics. I said to them,

mn14:16.2.verse: ‘Reverends, why are you constantly standing, turning down seats, so that you suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion?’

mn14:17.1.verse: When I said this, those Jain ascetics said to me,

mn14:17.2.verse: ‘Reverend, the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to know and see everything without exception, thus:

mn14:17.3.verse: “Knowledge and vision are constantly and continually present to me, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.”

mn14:17.5.verse: “O Jain ascetics, you have done bad deeds in a past life. Wear them away with these severe and grueling austerities.

mn14:17.6.verse: And when in the present you are restrained in body, speech, and mind, you’re not doing any bad deeds for the future.

mn14:17.7.verse: So, due to eliminating past deeds by fervent mortification, and not doing any new deeds, there’s nothing to come up in the future.

mn14:17.8.verse: With no future consequence, deeds end. With the ending of deeds, suffering ends. With the ending of suffering, feeling ends. And with the ending of feeling, all suffering will have been worn away.”

mn14:17.9.verse: We endorse and accept this, and we are satisfied with it.’

mn14:18.1.verse: When they said this, I said to them,

mn14:18.3.verse: for sure that you existed in the past, and it is not the case that you did not exist?’

mn14:18.6.verse: for sure that you did bad deeds in the past?’

mn14:18.9.verse: that you did bad deeds of this type or that?’

mn14:18.12.verse: that so much suffering has already been worn away? Or that so much suffering still remains to be worn away? Or that when so much suffering is worn away all suffering will have been worn away?’

mn14:18.15.verse: about giving up unskillful qualities in this very life and embracing skillful qualities?’

mn14:19.1.verse: ‘So it seems that you don’t know any of these things.

mn14:19.8.verse: That being so, when those in the world who are violent and bloody-handed and of cruel livelihood are reborn among humans they go forth as Jain ascetics.’

mn14:20.1.verse: ‘Reverend Gotama, pleasure is not gained through pleasure; pleasure is gained through pain.

mn14:20.2.verse: For if pleasure were to be gained through pleasure, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would gain pleasure, since he lives in greater pleasure than Venerable Gotama.’

mn14:20.3.verse: ‘Clearly the venerables have spoken rashly, without reflection.

mn14:20.6.verse: Rather, I’m the one who should be asked about

mn14:20.7.verse: who lives in greater pleasure, King Bimbisāra or Venerable Gotama?’

mn14:20.8.verse: ‘Clearly we spoke rashly and without reflection.

mn14:20.10.verse: But let that be. Now we ask Venerable Gotama:

mn14:20.11.verse: “Who lives in greater pleasure, King Bimbisāra or Venerable Gotama?”’

mn14:21.1.verse: ‘Well then, reverends, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn14:21.3.verse: Is King Bimbisāra capable of experiencing absolute happiness for seven days and nights without moving his body or speaking?’

mn14:21.6.verse: Is King Bimbisāra capable of experiencing absolute happiness for six days …

mn14:21.13.verse: ‘But I am capable of experiencing absolute happiness for one day and night without moving my body or speaking.

mn14:21.14.verse: I am capable of experiencing perfect happiness for two days …

mn14:21.20.verse: What do you think, reverends? This being so, who lives in greater pleasure, King Bimbisāra or I?’

mn14:21.21.verse: ‘This being so, Venerable Gotama lives in greater pleasure than King Bimbisāra.’”

mn14:21.22.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn14:21.23.verse: Satisfied, Mahānāma the Sakyan approved what the Buddha said.

mn15:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

mn15:1.3.verse: There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the mendicants:

mn15:2.2.verse: other mendicants to admonish them. But they’re hard to admonish, having qualities that make them hard to admonish. They’re impatient, and don’t take instruction respectfully. So their spiritual companions don’t think it’s worth advising and instructing them, and that individual doesn’t gain their trust.

mn15:3.1.verse: And what are the qualities that make them hard to admonish?

mn15:3.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has corrupt wishes, having fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes.

mn15:3.4.verse: This is a quality that makes them difficult to admonish.

mn15:3.5.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant glorifies themselves and puts others down. …

mn15:3.11.verse: They’re irritable, and acrimonious due to anger …

mn15:3.14.verse: They’re irritable, and stubborn due to anger …

mn15:3.17.verse: They’re irritable, and blurt out words bordering on anger …

mn15:3.20.verse: When accused, they object to the accuser …

mn15:3.23.verse: When accused, they rebuke the accuser …

mn15:3.26.verse: When accused, they retort to the accuser …

mn15:3.29.verse: When accused, they dodge the issue, distract the discussion with irrelevant points, and display annoyance, hate, and bitterness …

mn15:3.32.verse: When accused, they are unable to account for the evidence …

mn15:3.47.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go.

mn15:3.49.verse: This too is a quality that makes them difficult to admonish.

mn15:3.50.verse: These are the qualities that make them hard to admonish.

mn15:4.2.verse: other mendicants to admonish them. But they’re easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They’re accepting, and take instruction respectfully. So their spiritual companions think it’s worth advising and instructing them, and that individual gains their trust.

mn15:5.1.verse: And what are the qualities that make them easy to admonish?

mn15:5.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant doesn’t have corrupt wishes …

mn15:5.47.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t attached to their own views, not holding them tight, but letting them go easily.

mn15:5.50.verse: These are the qualities that make them easy to admonish.

mn15:6.1.verse: In such a case, a mendicant should measure themselves like this.

mn15:6.2.verse: ‘This individual has corrupt wishes, having fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes. And I don’t like or approve of this individual.

mn15:6.3.verse: And if I were to fall under the sway of corrupt wishes, others wouldn’t like or approve of me.’

mn15:6.4.verse: A mendicant who knows this should give rise to the thought: ‘I will not fall under the sway of corrupt wishes.’ …

mn15:6.47.verse: ‘This individual is attached to their own views, holding them tight and refusing to let go. And I don’t like or approve of this individual.

mn15:6.48.verse: And if I were to be attached to my own views, holding them tight and refusing to let go, others wouldn’t like or approve of me.’

mn15:6.49.verse: A mendicant who knows this should give rise to the thought: ‘I will not be attached to my own views, holding them tight, but will let them go easily.’

mn15:7.1.verse: In such a case, a mendicant should check themselves like this:

mn15:7.2.verse: ‘Do I have corrupt wishes? Have I fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes?’

mn15:7.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn15:7.4.verse: they have fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes. Then they should make an effort to give up those bad, unskillful qualities.

mn15:7.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn15:7.6.verse: they haven’t fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes. Then they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities. …

mn15:7.89.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn15:7.90.verse: they are attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go. Then they should make an effort to give up those bad, unskillful qualities.

mn15:7.91.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn15:7.92.verse: they’re not attached to their own views, holding them tight, but let them go easily. Then they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn15:8.1.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant sees that they haven’t given up all these bad, unskillful qualities. Then they should make an effort to give them all up.

mn15:8.2.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant sees that they have given up all these bad, unskillful qualities. Then they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn15:8.3.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they see any dirt or blemish there, they’d try to remove it.

mn15:8.4.verse: But if they don’t see any dirt or blemish there, they’re happy, thinking:

mn15:8.6.verse: In the same way, suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant sees that they haven’t given up all these bad, unskillful qualities. Then they should make an effort to give them all up.

mn15:8.7.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant sees that they have given up all these bad, unskillful qualities. Then they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.”

mn15:8.8.verse: That is what Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said.

mn15:8.9.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Mahāmoggallāna said.

mn16:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn16:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn16:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant has not given up five kinds of hard-heartedness and severed five shackles of the heart, it’s not possible for them to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

mn16:3.1.verse: What are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up?

mn16:3.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has doubts about the Teacher. They’re uncertain, undecided, and lacking confidence.

mn16:3.3.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:3.4.verse: This is the first kind of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

mn16:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has doubts about the teaching …

mn16:4.2.verse: This is the second kind of hard-heartedness.

mn16:5.1.verse: They have doubts about the Saṅgha …

mn16:5.2.verse: This is the third kind of hard-heartedness.

mn16:6.1.verse: They have doubts about the training …

mn16:6.3.verse: This is the fourth kind of hard-heartedness.

mn16:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is angry and upset with their spiritual companions, resentful and closed off.

mn16:7.2.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:7.3.verse: This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

mn16:7.4.verse: These are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they haven’t given up.

mn16:8.1.verse: What are the five shackles of the heart they haven’t severed?

mn16:8.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant isn’t free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

mn16:8.3.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:8.4.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart they haven’t severed.

mn16:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t free of greed for the body …

mn16:9.2.verse: This is the second shackle of the heart.

mn16:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant isn’t free of greed for form …

mn16:10.2.verse: This is the third shackle of the heart.

mn16:11.1.verse: They eat as much as they like until their belly is full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

mn16:11.3.verse: This is the fourth heart shackle.

mn16:12.1.verse: They lead the spiritual life hoping to be reborn in one of the orders of gods, thinking: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

mn16:12.2.verse: This being so, their mind doesn’t incline toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:12.3.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart they haven’t severed.

mn16:12.4.verse: These are the five shackles of the heart they haven’t severed.

mn16:13.1.verse: When a mendicant has not given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and severed these five shackles of the heart, it’s not possible for them to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

mn16:14.1.verse: When a mendicant has given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and severed these five shackles of the heart, it is possible for them to achieve growth, improvement, and maturity in this teaching and training.

mn16:15.1.verse: What are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they’ve given up?

mn16:15.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant has no doubts about the Teacher. They’re not uncertain, undecided, or lacking confidence.

mn16:15.3.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:15.4.verse: This is the first kind of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

mn16:16.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant has no doubts about the teaching …

mn16:17.1.verse: They have no doubts about the Saṅgha …

mn16:18.1.verse: They have no doubts about the training …

mn16:19.1.verse: They’re not angry and upset with their spiritual companions, not resentful or closed off.

mn16:19.2.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:19.3.verse: This is the fifth kind of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

mn16:19.4.verse: These are the five kinds of hard-heartedness they’ve given up.

mn16:20.1.verse: What are the five shackles of the heart they’ve severed?

mn16:20.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

mn16:20.3.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:20.4.verse: This is the first shackle of the heart they’ve severed.

mn16:21.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is rid of greed for the body …

mn16:22.1.verse: They’re rid of greed for form …

mn16:23.1.verse: They don’t eat as much as they like until their belly is full, then indulge in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing …

mn16:24.1.verse: They don’t lead the spiritual life hoping to be reborn in one of the orders of gods, thinking: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’

mn16:24.2.verse: This being so, their mind inclines toward keenness, commitment, persistence, and striving.

mn16:24.3.verse: This is the fifth shackle of the heart they’ve severed.

mn16:24.4.verse: These are the five shackles of the heart they’ve severed.

mn16:25.1.verse: When a mendicant has given up these five kinds of hard-heartedness and severed these five shackles of the heart, it is possible for them to achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

mn16:26.1.verse: They develop the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort …

mn16:26.2.verse: the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy, and active effort …

mn16:26.3.verse: the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to mental development, and active effort …

mn16:26.4.verse: the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to inquiry, and active effort. And the fifth is sheer vigor.

mn16:27.1.verse: A mendicant who possesses these fifteen factors, including vigor, is capable of breaking out, becoming awakened, and reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn16:27.2.verse: Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs.

mn16:27.3.verse: And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

mn16:27.4.verse: Even if that chicken doesn’t wish:

mn16:27.5.verse: ‘If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!’

mn16:27.6.verse: Still they can break out and hatch safely.

mn16:27.7.verse: In the same way, a mendicant who possesses these fifteen factors, including vigor, is capable of breaking out, becoming awakened, and reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.”

mn16:27.8.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn16:27.9.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn17:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Savatthi, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn17:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn17:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, I shall expound to you a discourse on jungle thickets.

mn17:2.2.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn17:2.3.verse: ‘Even so, venerable sir’, the bhikkhus replied.

mn17:3.1.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives in some jungle thicket.

mn17:3.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness does not become established, his unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated, his unexhausted taints do not come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is not attained;

mn17:3.3.verse: and also the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are hard to come by.

mn17:3.4.verse: The bhikkhu should take count of this.

mn17:3.7.verse: He should depart from that jungle thicket that very night or that very day; he should not continue living there.

mn17:4.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives in some jungle thicket.

mn17:4.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness does not become established, his unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated, his unexhausted taints do not come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is not attained;

mn17:4.3.verse: yet the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are easy to come by.

mn17:4.4.verse: The bhikkhu should take count of this, but he should reflect thus:

mn17:4.7.verse: “I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medcine as cure for the sick;

mn17:4.8.verse: but yet I make no progress here.”

mn17:4.9.verse: He should depart from that jungle thicket after weighing the matter; he should not continue living there.

mn17:5.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives in some jungle thicket.

mn17:5.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness becomes established, his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is attained;

mn17:5.3.verse: yet the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are hard to come by. The bhikkhu should take count of this, but should reflect thus:

mn17:5.7.verse: “I did not go forth from home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, alms-food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick;

mn17:5.8.verse: but yet I make progress here.”

mn17:5.9.verse: He should continue living in that jungle thicket after weighing the matter; he should not depart.

mn17:6.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives in some jungle thicket.

mn17:6.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness becomes established, his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is attained;

mn17:6.3.verse: and also the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are easy to come by.

mn17:6.4.verse: The bhikkhu should take count of this.

mn17:6.7.verse: He should continue living in that jungle thicket as long as life lasts; he should not depart.

mn17:7-10.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives in a certain village …

mn17:23.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives with a certain person …

mn17:23.7.verse: He should depart from that person that very night or that very day without asking; he should not continue following him.

mn17:24.1.verse: Here a bhikkhu lives with a certain person …

mn17:24.6.verse: yet the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are easy to come by.

mn17:24.7.verse: “I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medcine as cure for the sick;

mn17:24.8.verse: but yet I make no progress here.”

mn17:24.9.verse: He should depart from that person, after weighing the matter, without asking; he should not go on following him.

mn17:25.1.verse: Here a bhikkhu lives with a certain person …

mn17:25.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness becomes established, his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is attained;

mn17:25.3.verse: yet the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are hard to come by.

mn17:25.4.verse: The bhikkhu should take count of this, but should reflect thus: “

mn17:25.7.verse: I did not go forth from home life into homelessness for the sake of robes, alms-food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick;

mn17:25.8.verse: but yet I make progress here.”

mn17:25.9.verse: He should continue following that person after weighing the matter; he should not depart from him.

mn17:26.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu lives with a certain person …

mn17:26.2.verse: While living there his unestablished mindfulness becomes established, his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, his unexhausted taints come to exhaustion, the unattained supreme surcease of bondage is attained;

mn17:26.3.verse: and also the requisites for the life of one gone forth that should be available—robes, alms-food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick—are easy to come by.

mn17:26.7.verse: He should continue following that person as long as life lasts; he should not depart from him even if told to go.’

mn17:26.8.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn17:26.9.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn17:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn17:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn17:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you an exposition about jungle thickets.

mn17:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn17:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, take the case of a mendicant who lives close by a jungle thicket.

mn17:3.2.verse: As they do so, their mindfulness does not become established, their mind does not become immersed in samādhi, their defilements do not come to an end, and they do not arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn17:3.3.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by.

mn17:3.5.verse: ‘While living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness does not become established, my mind does not become immersed in samādhi, my defilements do not come to an end, and I do not arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn17:3.6.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by.’

mn17:3.7.verse: That mendicant should leave that jungle thicket that very time of night or day; they should not stay there.

mn17:4.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives close by a jungle thicket.

mn17:4.2.verse: Their mindfulness does not become established …

mn17:4.3.verse: But the necessities of life are easy to come by.

mn17:4.5.verse: ‘While living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness does not become established …

mn17:4.6.verse: But the necessities of life are easy to come by.

mn17:4.7.verse: But I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe, almsfood, lodgings, or medicines and supplies for the sick.

mn17:4.8.verse: Moreover, while living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness does not become established …’

mn17:4.9.verse: That mendicant should, after appraisal, leave that jungle thicket; they should not stay there.

mn17:5.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives close by a jungle thicket.

mn17:5.2.verse: As they do so, their mindfulness becomes established, their mind becomes immersed in samādhi, their defilements come to an end, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn17:5.3.verse: But the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by. That mendicant should reflect:

mn17:5.5.verse: ‘While living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness becomes established …

mn17:5.6.verse: But the necessities of life are hard to come by.

mn17:5.7.verse: But I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe, almsfood, lodgings, or medicines and supplies for the sick.

mn17:5.8.verse: Moreover, while living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness becomes established …’

mn17:5.9.verse: That mendicant should, after appraisal, stay in that jungle thicket; they should not leave.

mn17:6.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives close by a jungle thicket.

mn17:6.3.verse: And the necessities of life are easy to come by.

mn17:6.5.verse: ‘While living close by this jungle thicket, my mindfulness becomes established …

mn17:6.6.verse: And the necessities of life are easy to come by.’

mn17:6.7.verse: That mendicant should stay in that jungle thicket for the rest of their life; they should not leave.

mn17:7-10.1.verse: Take the case of a mendicant who lives supported by a village …

mn17:23.2.verse: As they do so, their mindfulness does not become established, their mind does not become immersed in samādhi, their defilements do not come to an end, and they do not arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn17:23.3.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are hard to come by.

mn17:23.5.verse: ‘… my mindfulness does not become established …

mn17:23.6.verse: And the necessities of life are hard to come by.’

mn17:23.7.verse: That mendicant should leave that individual at any time of the day or night, without taking leave; they should not follow them. …

mn17:24.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives supported by an individual.

mn17:24.2.verse: Their mindfulness does not become established …

mn17:24.3.verse: But the necessities of life are easy to come by.

mn17:24.5.verse: ‘… my mindfulness does not become established …

mn17:24.6.verse: But the necessities of life are easy to come by.’ …

mn17:24.9.verse: That mendicant should, after appraisal, leave that individual having taken leave; they should not follow them. …

mn17:25.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives supported by an individual.

mn17:25.3.verse: But the necessities of life are hard to come by.

mn17:25.6.verse: But the necessities of life are hard to come by.’ …

mn17:25.9.verse: That mendicant should, after appraisal, follow that individual; they should not leave.

mn17:26.1.verse: Take another case of a mendicant who lives supported by an individual.

mn17:26.2.verse: As they do so, their mindfulness becomes established, their mind becomes immersed in samādhi, their defilements come to an end, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn17:26.3.verse: And the necessities of life that a renunciate requires—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—are easy to come by.

mn17:26.5.verse: ‘While living supported by this individual, my mindfulness becomes established …

mn17:26.6.verse: And the necessities of life are easy to come by.’

mn17:26.7.verse: That mendicant should follow that individual for the rest of their life; they should not leave them, even if driven away.”

mn17:26.8.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn17:26.9.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn18:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Sakka country at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park.

mn18:2.1.verse: Then it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Kapilavatthu for alms.

mn18:2.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu and had returned from his almsround after the meal, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s abiding

mn18:2.3.verse: and went into the Great Wood and sat down at the root of a bilva sapling.

mn18:3.1.verse: ‘Stick-in-hand’ (Daṇḍapāṇi) the Sakyan also went to the Great Wood, walking and wandering for exercise,

mn18:3.2.verse: and when he had gone into the Great Wood, he went to the bilva sapling where the Blessed One was and exchanged greetings with him.

mn18:3.3.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side leaning on his stick. When he had done so, he asked the Blessed One:

mn18:3.4.verse: ‘What does the monk tell, what does he preach?’

mn18:4.1.verse: ‘Friend, as one who tells that whereby he quarrels with no one in the world with its gods, its Māras and its Divinities, in this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, and who tells that whereby perceptions no more underlie that divine one when he abides dissociated from sensual desires, undoubting, shorn of worry, rid of craving for any kind of being—

mn18:4.2.verse: so do I tell, friend, so do I preach.’

mn18:5.1.verse: When this was said, ‘Stick-in-hand’ the Sakyan shook his head, wagged his tongue and raised his eyebrows till his forehead was puckered in three lines. Then he departed, leaning on his stick.

mn18:6.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation, and he went to Nigrodha’s Park where he sat down on a seat prepared (for him),

mn18:6.2.verse: when he had done so, he told the bhikkhus what had taken place.

mn18:6.14.verse: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:

mn18:7.1.verse: ‘But, venerable sir, what is it that the Blessed One tells whereby he has no quarrel with any one in the world with its gods, its Māras and its Divinities, in this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men?

mn18:7.2.verse: And, venerable sir, how is it that perceptions no more underlie that divine one when he abides dissociated from sensual desires, undoubting, shorn of worry, rid of craving for any kind of being?’

mn18:8.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, as to that with which as their source the evaluation of diversifying perceptions besets a man:

mn18:8.2.verse: if there is (found to be) nothing there to delight in, affirm or to accept,

mn18:8.3.verse: this is the end of underlying tendencies to lust, resistance, views, uncertainty, conceit, lust for being and ignorance; this is the end of resorting to sticks, resorting to weapons, quarrels, brawls, disputes, recrimination, malice and speech;

mn18:8.4.verse: here unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.’

mn18:9.2.verse: Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling.

mn18:10.1.verse: Then soon after the Blessed One had gone, the bhikkhus (considered):

mn18:10.2.verse: ‘Now, friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without the detailed meaning,

mn18:10.3.verse: that is that is to say: “Bhikkhus, as to that with which as their source...

mn18:10.7.verse: Now who will expound this in detail?’

mn18:10.9.verse: ‘The venerable Mahā-Kaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Blessed One and by companions in the the life divine.

mn18:10.10.verse: He is capable of doing that.

mn18:10.11.verse: Suppose we went to him and asked him the meaning of this?’

mn18:11.1.verse: Then they went to the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna and exchanged greetings with him,

mn18:11.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, they told him what had taken place, and they added: ‘Let the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna expound it to us.’

mn18:12.1.verse: ‘Friends; it is as though a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, conceived that heartwood should be sought among the branches and leaves of a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, after passing over the root and the trunk.

mn18:12.2.verse: And so it is with you, venerable sirs, that you conceive that we should be asked about the meaning of this, after passing the Blessed One by when you were face-to-face with the Master.

mn18:12.3.verse: For, Knowing, the Blessed One knows; Seeing, he sees; he is the Eye, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Divine; the Tathāgata is the Sayer, the Proclaimer, the Elucidator of Meaning, the Giver of the Deathless.

mn18:12.4.verse: That was the time when you should have asked the Blessed One the meaning.

mn18:12.5.verse: As he told you so you should have remembered it.’

mn18:13.1.verse: ‘Surely, friend Kaccāna, Knowing, the Blessed One knows; Seeing, he sees; (surely) he is the Eye, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Divine; (surely) the Tathāgata is the Sayer, the Proclaimer, the Elucidator of Meaning, the Giver of the Deathless.

mn18:13.2.verse: (Surely) that was the time when we should have asked the Blessed One the meaning;

mn18:13.3.verse: and as he told us so we should have remembered it.

mn18:13.4.verse: Yet the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Blessed One and by companions in the life divine.

mn18:13.5.verse: The venerable Mahā-Kaccāna is capable of expounding the detailed meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One without expounding the detailed meaning.

mn18:13.6.verse: Let the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna expound (it) without finding it troublesome.’

mn18:14.1.verse: ‘Then listen, friends, and heed well what I shall say.’

mn18:15.1.verse: ‘Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, that is to say:

mn18:15.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, as to that with which as their source the evaluation of diversifying perceptions besets a man:

mn18:15.3.verse: if there is (found to be) nothing there to delight in, to affirm or to accept, this is the end of underlying tendencies to lust, resistance, views, uncertainty, conceit, lust for being, and ignorance;

mn18:15.4.verse: this is the end of the use of sticks, the use of weapons, quarrels, brawls, disputes, recrimination, malice and false speech; here evil, unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder”, I understand the detailed meaning of it to be as follows:

mn18:16.1.verse: ‘Dependent on eye and forms, eye consciousness arises. The coincidence of these three is contact. With contact as condition there is feeling. What a man feels that he perceives. What he perceives that he thinks about. What he thinks about that he diversifies. With what he has diversified as the source the evaluation of diversifying perceptions beset a man with respect to past, future and present forms cognizable by the eye.

mn18:16.2.verse: ‘Dependent on ear and sounds... with respect to past, future and present sounds cognizable by the ear.

mn18:16.3.verse: ‘Dependent on nose and odours... with respect to past, future and present odours cognizable by the nose.

mn18:16.4.verse: ‘Dependent on tongue and flavours... with respect to past, future and present flavours cognizable by the tongue.

mn18:16.5.verse: ‘Dependent on body and tangibles... with respect to past, future and present tangibles cognizable by the body.

mn18:16.6.verse: ‘Dependent on mind and dhammas, mind consciousness arises. The coincidence of these three is contact. With contact as condition there is feeling. What a man feels that he perceives. What he perceives that he thinks about. What he thinks about that he diversifies. With what he has diversified as the source the evaluation of diversifying perceptions beset a man with respect to past, future and present dhammas cognizable by the mind.

mn18:17.1.verse: ‘When there is eye and there is form and there is eye consciousness, it is possible that one will recognize that manifestation of contact.

mn18:17.2.verse: When there is the manifestation of contact, it is possible the one will recognize the manifestation of feeling.

mn18:17.3.verse: When there is the manifestation of feeling, it is possible that one will recognize the manifestation of perception.

mn18:17.4.verse: When there is the manifestation of perception, it is possible that one will recognize the manifestation of thinking.

mn18:17.5.verse: When there is the manifestation of thinking, it is possible that one will recognize the manifestation of being beset by evaluation of diversifying perceptions.

mn18:17.6.verse: ‘When there is ear and there is sound and there is ear consciousness …

mn18:17.7.verse: ‘When there is nose and there is odour and there is nose consciousness …

mn18:17.8.verse: ‘When there is tongue and there is flavour and there is tongue consciousness …

mn18:17.9.verse: ‘When there is body and there is tangible and there is body consciousness …

mn18:17.10.verse: ‘When there is mind and there is dhamma and there is mind consciousness …

mn18:17.14.verse: it is possible that one will recognize the manifestation of being beset by evaluation of diversifying perceptions.’

mn18:18.1.verse: ‘When there is no eye and there is no form and there is no eye consciousness, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of contact.

mn18:18.2.verse: When there is no manifestation of contact, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of feeling.

mn18:18.3.verse: When there is no manifestation of feeling, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of perception.

mn18:18.4.verse: When there is no manifestation of perception, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of thinking.

mn18:18.5.verse: When there is no manifestation of thinking, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of being beset by evaluation of diversifying perceptions.

mn18:18.10.verse: ‘When there is no mind and there is no dhamma and there is no mind consciousness, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of contact.

mn18:18.11.verse: When there is no manifestation of contact, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of feeling.
