mn18:18.12.verse: When there is no manifestation of feeling, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of perception.

mn18:18.13.verse: When there is no manifestation of perception, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of thinking.

mn18:18.14.verse: When there is no manifestation of thinking, it is impossible that one will recognize the manifestation of being beset by evaluation of diversifying perceptions.

mn18:19.1.verse: ‘Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, that is to say:

mn18:19.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, as to that with which as their source … (para. 8) … cease without remainder”,

mn18:19.3.verse: I understand the detailed meaning of it to be thus.

mn18:19.4.verse: Now, friends, if you wish, go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this.

mn18:19.5.verse: As the Blessed One tells you so should you remember it.’

mn18:20.1.verse: Then the bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighting in the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna’s words, they rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, they told him all that had taken place after the Blessed One had left, and they added:

mn18:20.16.verse: ‘Then, venerable sir, we went to the venerable Mahā-Kaccāna and asked him about the meaning.

mn18:20.17.verse: Venerable sir, the meaning has been expounded to us with these reasons, these phrases and these syllables.’

mn18:21.1.verse: ‘Mahā-Kaccāna is wise, bhikkhus, Mahā-Kaccāna has great understanding.

mn18:21.2.verse: Had you asked me the meaning of this, I should have given you the same answer as Mahā-Kaccāna has given you.

mn18:21.3.verse: Such is the meaning and so should you remember it.’

mn18:22.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

mn18:22.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, just as if a man exhausted by hunger and weakness came by a sweet morsel, he would, in the course of eating it, find a sweet, unadulterated flavour,

mn18:22.3.verse: so too, venerable sir, any able-minded bhikkhu would, in the course of scrutinizing with understanding the meaning of this discourse on the Dhamma, find satisfaction and confidence of heart.

mn18:22.4.verse: Venerable sir, what is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?’

mn18:22.5.verse: ‘As to that, Ānanda, you may remember this discourse on the Dhamma as “The Sweet-Morsel Discourse”.’

mn18:22.6.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn18:22.7.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn18:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

mn18:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms.

mn18:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s meditation,

mn18:2.3.verse: plunged deep into it, and sat at the root of a young wood-apple tree to meditate.

mn18:3.1.verse: Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan, while going for a walk,

mn18:3.2.verse: plunged deep into the Great Wood. He approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn18:3.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side leaning on his staff, and said to the Buddha,

mn18:3.4.verse: “What is the ascetic’s doctrine? What does he assert?”

mn18:4.1.verse: “Respectable sir, my doctrine is such that one does not argue with anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans. And it is such that perceptions do not underlie the brahmin who lives detached from sensual pleasures, without indecision, stripped of worry, and rid of craving for rebirth in this or that state.

mn18:4.2.verse: That is my doctrine, and that is what I assert.”

mn18:5.1.verse: When he had spoken, Daṇḍapāṇi shook his head, waggled his tongue, raised his eyebrows until his brow puckered in three furrows, and left leaning on his staff.

mn18:6.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the Banyan Tree Monastery, sat down on the seat spread out,

mn18:6.2.verse: and told the mendicants what had happened.

mn18:6.14.verse: When he had spoken, one of the mendicants said to him,

mn18:7.1.verse: “But sir, asserting what doctrine does the Buddha not argue with anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans?

mn18:7.2.verse: And how is it that perceptions do not underlie the Buddha, the brahmin who lives detached from sensual pleasures, without indecision, stripped of worry, and rid of craving for rebirth in this or that state?”

mn18:8.1.verse: “Mendicant, judgments driven by proliferating perceptions beset a person.

mn18:8.2.verse: If they don’t find anything worth approving, welcoming, or getting attached to in the source from which these arise,

mn18:8.3.verse: just this is the end of the underlying tendencies to desire, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, the desire for continued existence, and ignorance. This is the end of taking up the rod and the sword, the end of quarrels, arguments, and disputes, of accusations, backbiting, and lies.

mn18:8.4.verse: This is where these bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.”

mn18:9.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn18:9.2.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

mn18:10.1.verse: Soon after the Buddha left, those mendicants considered,

mn18:10.2.verse: “The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail.

mn18:10.7.verse: Who can explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha?”

mn18:10.9.verse: “This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

mn18:10.10.verse: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

mn18:10.11.verse: Let’s go to him, and ask him about this matter.”

mn18:11.1.verse: Then those mendicants went to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn18:11.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. They told him what had happened, and said:

mn18:12.1.verse: “Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But he’d pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves.

mn18:12.2.verse: Such is the consequence for the venerables. Though you were face to face with the Buddha, you bypassed him, imagining that you should ask me about this matter.

mn18:12.3.verse: For he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

mn18:12.4.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

mn18:12.5.verse: You should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

mn18:13.1.verse: “Certainly he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

mn18:13.2.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

mn18:13.3.verse: We should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.

mn18:13.4.verse: Still, Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

mn18:13.5.verse: You are capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

mn18:13.6.verse: Please explain this, if it’s no trouble.”

mn18:14.1.verse: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn18:15.1.verse: “Reverends, the Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:

mn18:15.2.verse: ‘Judgments driven by proliferating perceptions beset a person.

mn18:15.3.verse: If they don’t find anything worth approving, welcoming, or getting attached to in the source from which these arise,

mn18:15.4.verse: just this is the end of the underlying tendencies to desire, repulsion, views, doubt, conceit, the desire to be reborn, and ignorance. This is the end of taking up the rod and the sword, the end of quarrels, arguments, and disputes, of accusations, backbiting, and lies. This is where these bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.’ This is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.

mn18:16.1.verse: Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a requirement for feeling. What you feel, you perceive. What you perceive, you think about. What you think about, you proliferate. What you proliferate is the source from which judgments driven by proliferating perceptions beset a person. This occurs with respect to sights known by the eye in the past, future, and present.

mn18:16.2.verse: Ear consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds. …

mn18:16.3.verse: Nose consciousness arises dependent on the nose and smells. …

mn18:16.4.verse: Tongue consciousness arises dependent on the tongue and tastes. …

mn18:16.5.verse: Body consciousness arises dependent on the body and touches. …

mn18:16.6.verse: Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and ideas. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a requirement for feeling. What you feel, you perceive. What you perceive, you think about. What you think about, you proliferate. What you proliferate is the source from which judgments driven by proliferating perceptions beset a person. This occurs with respect to ideas known by the mind in the past, future, and present.

mn18:17.1.verse: Where there is the eye, sights, and eye consciousness, it will be possible to discover evidence of contact.

mn18:17.2.verse: Where there is evidence of contact, it will be possible to discover evidence of feeling.

mn18:17.3.verse: Where there is evidence of feeling, it will be possible to discover evidence of perception.

mn18:17.4.verse: Where there is evidence of perception, it will be possible to discover evidence of thought.

mn18:17.5.verse: Where there is evidence of thought, it will be possible to discover evidence of being beset by judgments driven by proliferating perceptions.

mn18:17.10.verse: mind, ideas, and mind consciousness, it will be possible to discover evidence of contact.

mn18:17.11.verse: Where there is evidence of contact, it will be possible to discover evidence of feeling.

mn18:17.12.verse: Where there is evidence of feeling, it will be possible to discover evidence of perception.

mn18:17.13.verse: Where there is evidence of perception, it will be possible to discover evidence of thinking.

mn18:17.14.verse: Where there is evidence of thinking, it will be possible to discover evidence of being beset by judgments driven by proliferating perceptions.

mn18:18.1.verse: Where there is no eye, no sights, and no eye consciousness, it will not be possible to discover evidence of contact.

mn18:18.2.verse: Where there is no evidence of contact, it will not be possible to discover evidence of feeling.

mn18:18.3.verse: Where there is no evidence of feeling, it will not be possible to discover evidence of perception.

mn18:18.4.verse: Where there is no evidence of perception, it will not be possible to discover evidence of thinking.

mn18:18.5.verse: Where there is no evidence of thinking, it will not be possible to discover evidence of being beset by judgments driven by proliferating perceptions.

mn18:18.10.verse: no mind, no ideas, and no mind consciousness, it will not be possible to discover evidence of contact.

mn18:18.11.verse: Where there is no evidence of contact, it will not be possible to discover evidence of feeling.

mn18:18.12.verse: Where there is no evidence of feeling, it will not be possible to discover evidence of perception.

mn18:18.13.verse: Where there is no evidence of perception, it will not be possible to discover evidence of thinking.

mn18:18.14.verse: Where there is no evidence of thinking, it will not be possible to discover evidence of being beset by judgments driven by proliferating perceptions.

mn18:19.1.verse: This is how I understand the detailed meaning of that brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

mn18:19.4.verse: If you wish, you may go to the Buddha and ask him about this.

mn18:19.5.verse: You should remember it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

mn18:20.1.verse: Then those mendicants, approving and agreeing with what Mahākaccāna said, rose from their seats and went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding:

mn18:20.17.verse: “Mahākaccāna clearly explained the meaning to us in this manner, with these words and phrases.”

mn18:21.1.verse: “Mahākaccāna is astute, mendicants, he has great wisdom.

mn18:21.2.verse: If you came to me and asked this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way as Mahākaccāna.

mn18:21.3.verse: That is what it means, and that’s how you should remember it.”

mn18:22.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

mn18:22.2.verse: “Sir, suppose a person who was weak with hunger was to obtain a honey-cake. Wherever they taste it, they would enjoy a sweet, delectable flavor.

mn18:22.3.verse: In the same way, wherever a sincere, proficient mendicant might examine with wisdom the meaning of this exposition of the teaching they would only gain joy and clarity.

mn18:22.4.verse: Sir, what is the name of this exposition of the teaching?”

mn18:22.5.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, you may remember this exposition of the teaching as ‘The Honey-Cake Discourse’.”

mn18:22.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn18:22.7.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn19:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn19:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn19:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta, it occurred to me:

mn19:2.2.verse: “Suppose that I divide my thinking into two classes?”

mn19:2.3.verse: Then I set on one side thinking with sensual desires, thinking with ill-will, and thinking with cruelty,

mn19:2.5.verse: and I set on the other side thinking with renunciation, thinking with non-ill-will, and thinking with non-cruelty.

mn19:3.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, thinking with sensual desire arose in me.

mn19:3.3.verse: “There is this thinking with sensual desire arisen in me.

mn19:3.4.verse: And that leads to my own affliction, to others’ affliction and to the affliction of both; it obstructs understanding, promotes annoyance, and leads away from Nibbāna.”

mn19:3.5.verse: When I considered: “This leads to my own affliction”, it subsided in me;

mn19:3.6.verse: when I considered: “This leads to others’ affliction”, it subsided in me;

mn19:3.7.verse: when I considered: “This leads to the affliction of both”, it subsided in me;

mn19:3.8.verse: when I considered: “This obstructs understanding, promotes annoyance and leads away from Nibbāna”, it subsided in me.

mn19:3.9.verse: Whenever thinking with sensual desire arose in me, I abandoned it, removed it, did away with it.

mn19:4-5.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, thinking with ill-will arose in me … I abandoned it, removed it, did away with it.

mn19:4-5.2.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, thinking with cruelty arose in me … I abandoned it, removed it, did away with it.

mn19:6.1.verse: ‘In whatever way a bhikkhu keeps thinking and pondering, that will effect the inclination of his mind accordingly.

mn19:6.2.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with sensual desire and pondering with sensual desire, he has abandoned thinking with renunciation to cultivate thinking with sensual desire, and then his mind is inclined to thinking with sensual desire.

mn19:6.3.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with ill-will … his mind his mind is inclined to thinking with ill-will.

mn19:6.4.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with cruelty … his mind is inclined to thinking with cruelty.

mn19:7.1.verse: ‘Just as, in the last month of the Rains, in the autumn season when the crops thicken, a herdsman would guard his cows

mn19:7.2.verse: (constantly) tapping and poking them on this side and that with a stick to check and curb them.

mn19:7.4.verse: Because he foresees the flogging or imprisonment or loss or blame that could befall (him if he let them stray into the crops),

mn19:7.5.verse: so too, I foresaw in unprofitable dhammas a danger of degradation and defilement, and in profitable dhammas a blessing in renunciation, which blessing is on the side of cleansing.

mn19:8.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent and self-controlled thinking with renunciation arose in me.

mn19:8.3.verse: “There is this thinking with renunciation arisen in me.

mn19:8.4.verse: And that does not lead to my own affliction, or to others’ affliction or to the affliction of both, it aids understanding, does not promote annoyance and leads to Nibbāna.

mn19:8.5.verse: If I think with that and ponder with that even for a night,

mn19:8.7.verse: even for a night and day, I foresee nothing to fear from it:

mn19:8.8.verse: only that with the continuous thinking and pondering I might tire my body,

mn19:8.9.verse: and a tired body harries the mind,

mn19:8.10.verse: and a harried mind is far from concentration.”

mn19:8.11.verse: (Accordingly), I settled mind in myself, quieted it, brought it to singleness and concentrated it.

mn19:8.13.verse: So that my mind should not be harried.

mn19:9-10.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent ardent and self-controlled, thinking with non-ill-will arose in me … my mind should not be harried.

mn19:9-10.2.verse: ‘As I dwelt thus, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, thinking with non-cruelty arose in me … my mind should not be harried.

mn19:11.1.verse: ‘In whatever way a bhikkhu keeps thinking and pondering, that will affect the inclination of his mind accordingly.

mn19:11.2.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with renunciation and pondering with renunciation, he has abandoned thinking with sensual desire to cultivate thinking with renunciation, and then his mind is inclined to thinking with renunciation.

mn19:11.3.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with non-ill-will … his mind is inclined to thinking with non-ill-will.

mn19:11.4.verse: ‘If he keeps thinking with non-cruelty … his mind is inclined to thinking with non-cruelty.

mn19:12.1.verse: ‘Just as in the last month of the Heat, when all the crops have been brought inside the villages, a herdsman would guard his cows while staying at the root of a tree out in the open since he needs only to be mindful that

mn19:12.3.verse: so too there was need for me only to be mindful that

mn19:13.1.verse: 11-22. ‘Tireless energy was aroused in me (as in Sutta 4, para. 22-33) as (happens) in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn19:25.1.verse: ‘Suppose that in a wooded range there was a great low-lying marsh,

mn19:25.2.verse: near which a big herd of deer lived,

mn19:25.3.verse: and then a man appeared seeking what was not their good, their welfare, their surcease of bondage,

mn19:25.4.verse: and he closed the safe and good path that led to their happiness and opened a false path, and he put out a decoy and set up a dummy,

mn19:25.5.verse: so that later on the big herd of deer might come to loss, ruin and calamity;

mn19:25.6.verse: but suppose some man came seeking their good, their welfare, their surcease of bondage,

mn19:25.7.verse: and he reopened the safe and good path that led to their happiness and closed the false path, and he harried away the decoy and destroyed the dummy,

mn19:25.8.verse: so that later on the big herd of deer might come to growth, increase and fulfilment.

mn19:26.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, I have given you this simile in order to intimate a meaning.

mn19:26.2.verse: Now the meaning here is this:

mn19:26.3.verse: The great low-lying marsh stands for sensual desires;

mn19:26.4.verse: the big herd of deer stands for beings,

mn19:26.5.verse: the man who sought what was not their good, their happiness and their surcease of bondage stands for Māra the Evil One;

mn19:26.6.verse: the false path stands for the wrong Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn19:26.7.verse: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration,

mn19:26.8.verse: the decoy stands for delight and lust,

mn19:26.10.verse: the man seeking their good, their happiness and their surcease of bondage stands for the Tathāgata, Arahant and Full Enlightened,

mn19:26.11.verse: the safe and good path that led to their happiness stands for the Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say,

mn19:26.12.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

mn19:26.13.verse: ‘So, bhikkhus, the safe and good path that leads to happiness has been reopened by me, the wrong path has been closed, the decoy harried away, and the dummy destroyed.’

mn19:27.1.verse: ‘What should be done for his disciples out of pity by a Master who seeks their welfare and has pity (on them), that I have done for you.

mn19:27.2.verse: There these roots of trees, these empty huts. Develop meditation, bhikkhus, do not delay lest you later regret it. This is our message to you.’

mn19:27.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn19:27.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn19:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn19:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn19:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

mn19:2.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I meditate by continually dividing my thoughts into two classes?’

mn19:2.3.verse: So I assigned sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts

mn19:2.5.verse: And I assigned thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness

mn19:3.1.verse: Then, as I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a sensual thought arose.

mn19:3.3.verse: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me.

mn19:3.4.verse: It leads to hurting myself, hurting others, and hurting both. It blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment.’

mn19:3.5.verse: When I reflected that it leads to hurting myself, it went away.

mn19:3.6.verse: When I reflected that it leads to hurting others, it went away.

mn19:3.7.verse: When I reflected that it leads to hurting both, it went away.

mn19:3.8.verse: When I reflected that it blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment, it went away.

mn19:3.9.verse: So I gave up, dispelled, and eliminated any sensual thoughts that arose.

mn19:4-5.1.verse: Then, as I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a malicious thought arose …

mn19:4-5.4.verse: ‘This cruel thought has arisen in me.

mn19:4-5.5.verse: It leads to hurting myself, hurting others, and hurting both. It blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment.’

mn19:4-5.6.verse: When I reflected that it leads to hurting myself …

mn19:4-5.9.verse: When I reflected that it blocks wisdom, it’s on the side of distress, and it doesn’t lead to extinguishment, it went away.

mn19:4-5.10.verse: So I gave up, dispelled, and eliminated any cruel thoughts that arose.

mn19:6.1.verse: Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes their heart’s inclination.

mn19:6.2.verse: If they often think about and consider sensual thoughts, they’ve given up the thought of renunciation to cultivate sensual thought. Their mind inclines to sensual thoughts.

mn19:6.3.verse: If they often think about and consider malicious thoughts … their mind inclines to malicious thoughts.

mn19:6.4.verse: If they often think about and consider cruel thoughts … their mind inclines to cruel thoughts.

mn19:7.1.verse: Suppose it’s the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the crops grow closely together, and a cowherd must take care of the cattle.

mn19:7.2.verse: He’d tap and poke them with his staff on this side and that to keep them in check.

mn19:7.4.verse: For he sees that if they wander into the crops he could be executed, imprisoned, fined, or condemned.

mn19:7.5.verse: In the same way, I saw that unskillful qualities have the drawbacks of sordidness and corruption, and that skillful qualities have the benefit and cleansing power of renunciation.

mn19:8.1.verse: Then, as I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a thought of renunciation arose.

mn19:8.3.verse: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me.

mn19:8.4.verse: It doesn’t lead to hurting myself, hurting others, or hurting both. It nourishes wisdom, it’s on the side of freedom from distress, and it leads to extinguishment.’

mn19:8.5.verse: If I were to keep on thinking and considering this all night …

mn19:8.7.verse: all night and day, I see no danger that would come from that.

mn19:8.8.verse: Still, thinking and considering for too long would tire my body.

mn19:8.9.verse: And when the body is tired, the mind is stressed.

mn19:8.10.verse: And when the mind is stressed, it’s far from immersion.

mn19:8.11.verse: So I stilled, settled, unified, and immersed my mind internally.

mn19:8.13.verse: So that my mind would not be stressed.

mn19:9-10.1.verse: Then, as I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a thought of good will arose …

mn19:9-10.4.verse: ‘This thought of harmlessness has arisen in me.

mn19:9-10.5.verse: It doesn’t lead to hurting myself, hurting others, or hurting both. It nourishes wisdom, it’s on the side of freedom from distress, and it leads to extinguishment.’

mn19:9-10.6.verse: If I were to keep on thinking and considering this all night …

mn19:9-10.8.verse: all night and day, I see no danger that would come from that.

mn19:9-10.9.verse: Still, thinking and considering for too long would tire my body.

mn19:9-10.10.verse: And when the body is tired, the mind is stressed.

mn19:9-10.11.verse: And when the mind is stressed, it’s far from immersion.

mn19:9-10.12.verse: So I stilled, settled, unified, and immersed my mind internally.

mn19:9-10.14.verse: So that my mind would not be stressed.

mn19:11.1.verse: Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes their heart’s inclination.

mn19:11.2.verse: If they often think about and consider thoughts of renunciation, they’ve given up sensual thought to cultivate the thought of renunciation. Their mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation.

mn19:11.3.verse: If they often think about and consider thoughts of good will … their mind inclines to thoughts of good will.

mn19:11.4.verse: If they often think about and consider thoughts of harmlessness … their mind inclines to thoughts of harmlessness.

mn19:12.1.verse: Suppose it’s the last month of summer, when all the crops have been gathered within a village, and a cowherd must take care of the cattle. While at the root of a tree or in the open he need only be mindful that

mn19:12.3.verse: In the same way I needed only to be mindful that

mn19:13.1.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and lucid, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind was immersed and unified in samādhi.

mn19:14.1.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn19:15.1.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn19:16.1.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, I entered and remained in the third absorption, where I meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn19:17.1.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn19:18.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives.

mn19:18.2.verse: I recollected many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn19:19.1.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

mn19:19.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn19:20.1.verse: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this, I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn19:20.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn19:21.1.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night.

mn19:21.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn19:22.1.verse: When my mind had become immersed in samādhi like this, I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn19:22.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn19:23.1.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn19:23.2.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn19:23.3.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.’

mn19:24.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night.

mn19:24.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn19:25.1.verse: Suppose that in a forested wilderness there was an expanse of low-lying marshes,

mn19:25.2.verse: and a large herd of deer lived nearby.

mn19:25.3.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten them.

mn19:25.4.verse: They close off the safe, secure path that leads to happiness, and open the wrong path. There they plant domesticated male and female deer as decoys

mn19:25.5.verse: so that, in due course, that herd of deer would fall to ruin and disaster.

mn19:25.6.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to help keep the herd of deer safe.

mn19:25.7.verse: They open up the safe, secure path that leads to happiness, and close off the wrong path. They get rid of the decoys

mn19:25.8.verse: so that, in due course, that herd of deer would grow, increase, and mature.

mn19:26.1.verse: I’ve made up this simile to make a point.

mn19:26.2.verse: And this is what it means.

mn19:26.3.verse: ‘An expanse of low-lying marshes’ is a term for sensual pleasures.

mn19:26.4.verse: ‘A large herd of deer’ is a term for sentient beings.

mn19:26.5.verse: ‘A person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten them’ is a term for Māra the Wicked.

mn19:26.6.verse: ‘The wrong path’ is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is,

mn19:26.7.verse: wrong view, wrong purpose, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion.

mn19:26.8.verse: ‘A domesticated male deer’ is a term for greed and relishing.

mn19:26.9.verse: ‘A domesticated female deer’ is a term for ignorance.

mn19:26.10.verse: ‘A person who wants to help keep the herd of deer safe’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn19:26.11.verse: ‘The safe, secure path that leads to happiness’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is:

mn19:26.12.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

mn19:26.13.verse: So, mendicants, I have opened up the safe, secure path to happiness and closed off the wrong path. And I have got rid of the male and female decoys.

mn19:27.1.verse: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

mn19:27.2.verse: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

mn19:27.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn19:27.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn20:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park.

mn20:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the monks:

mn20:1.5.verse: “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.

mn20:2.1.verse: “Monks, a monk who is committed to developing a heightened mind should regularly direct their mind in five ways.

mn20:3.1.verse: In this case, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk should redirect their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome.

mn20:3.2.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:3.3.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:3.4.verse: Monks, just as a skillful carpenter or apprentice carpenter could replace a coarse peg with a fine peg,

mn20:3.5.verse: in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk should redirect their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome.

mn20:3.6.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:3.7.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:4.1.verse: Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts:

mn20:4.2.verse: ‘These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts result in suffering.’

mn20:4.3.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:4.4.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:4.5.verse: Monks, just as a young and well-adorned woman or man would be irritated, ashamed, and disgusted if the corpse of a snake, dog, or human was draped around their neck,

mn20:4.6.verse: in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they redirect their mind, then they should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts:

mn20:4.7.verse: ‘These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts result in suffering.’

mn20:4.8.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:4.9.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:5.1.verse: Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should not pay any attention to those thoughts.

mn20:5.2.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:5.3.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:5.4.verse: Monks, just as a person with eyes who did not want to see something in their field of view

mn20:5.5.verse: could close their eyes or look away,

mn20:5.6.verse: in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they examine the drawbacks of those thoughts, then by doing this those thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:5.7.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:6.1.verse: Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should direct the mind to stilling the production of those thoughts.

mn20:6.2.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:6.3.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:6.4.verse: Monks, just as a person who was moving quickly

mn20:6.21.verse: Monks, in this way that person gradually replaces coarse postures with more subtle ones.

mn20:6.22.verse: in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they pay no attention to those thoughts, then by doing this those thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:6.23.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:7.1.verse: Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them,

mn20:7.2.verse: then that monk should clench their teeth, press their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppress, overpower, and immobilize the mind.

mn20:7.3.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:7.4.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:7.5.verse: Monks, just as a strong person could grab a weaker person by the head, neck, or shoulders and suppress, overpower, and immobilize them,

mn20:7.6.verse: in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they still the production of those thoughts,

mn20:7.7.verse: then that monk should clench their teeth, press their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppress, overpower, and immobilize the mind.

mn20:7.8.verse: When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:7.9.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.1.verse: Monks, when evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk redirects their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome, and those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:8.2.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.3.verse: When one also examines the drawbacks of those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:8.4.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.5.verse: When one also does not pay any attention to those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:8.6.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.7.verse: When one also stills the production of those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:8.8.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.9.verse: When one clenches their teeth, presses their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppresses, overpowers, and immobilize the minds, then those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.

mn20:8.10.verse: Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

mn20:8.11.verse: Monks, this is called a monk that is in control of all the avenues of thought.

mn20:8.12.verse: One will think whatever one wishes to think, and one will not think whatever one wishes to not think.

mn20:8.13.verse: Craving will be cut off, the shackles will be opened, and through a correct comprehension of conceit suffering will be put to an end.”

mn20:8.14.verse: This is what the Buddha said.

mn20:8.15.verse: Satisfied, those monks rejoiced in the Buddha’s statement.

mn20:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Savatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapindika’s Park.

mn20:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn20:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is pursuing the Higher Mind, five signs can be given attention by him from time to time.

mn20:3.1.verse: (i) ‘When, owing to some sign to which he is giving attention there arise in him evil, unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion, then some sign other than that sign and connected with what is profitable should be given attention by him.

mn20:3.2.verse: When he gives attention to some sign other than that sign and connected with what is profitable, then any evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion, are abandoned in him and subside.

mn20:3.3.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:3.4.verse: ‘Just as a skilled joiner or his apprentice might knock out, remove and extract a coarse peg by means of a fine one,

mn20:3.5.verse: so too, when, owing to some sign ...

mn20:3.7.verse: his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:4.1.verse: (ii) ‘If, while he is giving attention to some sign other than that sign [first mentioned] and connected with what is profitable, there still arise in him evil, unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion, then the danger in those thoughts should be scrutinized by him thus:

mn20:4.2.verse: “These thoughts are such that they are unprofitable, that they are reprehensible, that they result in suffering.”

mn20:4.3.verse: When he scrutinizes the danger in those thoughts then any evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion are abandoned in him and subside.

mn20:4.4.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:4.5.verse: ‘Just as a woman—or a man—young, youthful and fond of ornaments would be horrified, humiliated and disgusted if a snake’s or a dog’s or a human being’s carcase, were hung round her neck,

mn20:4.6.verse: so too, if, while he is giving attention …

mn20:4.9.verse: his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:5.1.verse: (iii) ‘If, when he is scrutinizing the danger in those thoughts, there still arise in him evil, unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion, then forgetting of those thoughts and non-attention to them should be tried.

mn20:5.2.verse: When he tries forgetting those thoughts and non-attention to them then any evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion are abandoned in him and subside.

mn20:5.3.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:5.4.verse: ‘Just as a man with [good] eyes who did not want to see forms that had come within [the eyes’] range,

mn20:5.5.verse: would either shut his eyes or look away,

mn20:5.6.verse: so too, if, when he scrutinizes … his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:6.1.verse: (iv) ‘If, when he tries forgetting those thoughts and non-attention to them, there still arise in him evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion, then settling of thought-formations should be given attention by him with respect to these thoughts.

mn20:6.2.verse: When he gives attention to settling thought-formations with respect to those thoughts any evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion are abandoned in him and subside.

mn20:6.3.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:6.21.verse: for by doing so he would substitute for each grosser mode of deportment one that was subtler;

mn20:6.22.verse: so too, if when he tries forgetting … his mind is settled in himself quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:7.1.verse: (v) ‘If, while he is giving attention to settling of thought-formations with respect to those thoughts, there still arise in him evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion,

mn20:7.2.verse: then with his teeth clenched and his tongue pressed against the roof of his mouth he should beat down, constrain and crush mind with mind.

mn20:7.3.verse: When with his teeth clenched and his tongue pressed against the roof of his mouth, he beats down, constrains and crushes mind with mind, then any evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate and with delusion are abandoned in him and subside.

mn20:7.4.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:7.5.verse: ‘Just as a strong man might seize a weaker one by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain and crush him,

mn20:7.6.verse: so too, if, while he is giving attention to settling …

mn20:7.9.verse: With the abandoning of them his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn20:8.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, as soon as, after evil unprofitable thoughts connected with desire, with hate, and with delusion have arisen in a bhikkhu owing to some sign to which sign he was giving attention, any [such] evil unprofitable thoughts are abandoned in him and subside, when he gives attention to a sign other than that and connected with what is profitable,

mn20:8.2.verse: and so his mind is settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated—

mn20:8.3.verse: and [as soon as] any [further] evil unprofitable thoughts ... are abandoned in him and subside when he scrutinizes the danger in those thoughts,

mn20:8.4.verse: and so with the abandoning of them his mind is settled, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated—

mn20:8.5.verse: and [as soon as] any [further] evil unprofitable thoughts ... are abandoned in him and subside when he tries forgetting these thoughts and non-attention to them,

mn20:8.6.verse: and so his mind is settled, brought to singleness and concentrated—

mn20:8.7.verse: and [as soon as] any [further] evil unprofitable thoughts ... are abandoned in him and subside when he gives attention to the settling of thought-formations with respect to those thoughts,

mn20:8.8.verse: and so with the abandoning of them his mind is settled, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated—

mn20:8.9.verse: and [as soon as] any [further] evil unprofitable thoughts ... are abandoned in him and subside when, with his teeth clenched and his tongue pressed against the roof of his mouth, he beats down, constrains and crushes mind with mind,

mn20:8.10.verse: and so with the abandoning of them his mind is settled, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated,

mn20:8.11.verse: then that bhikkhu is called a master of the courses of thought processes,

mn20:8.12.verse: he will think the thoughts that he wishes, and he will not think the thoughts that he does not wish.

mn20:8.13.verse: He has severed craving, flung off the fetters, and rightly made an end of suffering with the penetration of conceit.’

mn20:8.14.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn20:8.15.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn20:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn20:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn20:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant committed to the higher mind should focus on five subjects from time to time.

mn20:3.1.verse: Take a mendicant who is focusing on some subject that gives rise to bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion. That mendicant should focus on some other subject connected with the skillful.

mn20:3.2.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:3.3.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:3.4.verse: It’s like a deft mason or their apprentice who’d knock out or extract a large peg with a finer peg.

mn20:3.5.verse: In the same way, a mendicant … should focus on some other basis of meditation connected with the skillful …

mn20:4.1.verse: Now, suppose that mendicant is focusing on some other subject connected with the skillful, but bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion keep coming up. They should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts:

mn20:4.2.verse: ‘So these thoughts are unskillful, they’re blameworthy, and they result in suffering.’

mn20:4.3.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:4.4.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:4.5.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments. If the carcass of a snake or a dog or a human were hung around their neck, they’d be horrified, repelled, and disgusted.

mn20:4.6.verse: In the same way, a mendicant … should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts …

mn20:5.1.verse: Now, suppose that mendicant is examining the drawbacks of those thoughts, but bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion keep coming up. They should try to forget and ignore them.

mn20:5.2.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:5.3.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:5.4.verse: Suppose there was a person with clear eyes, and some undesirable sights came into their range of vision.

mn20:5.5.verse: They’d just close their eyes or look away.

mn20:5.6.verse: In the same way, a mendicant … those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end …

mn20:6.1.verse: Now, suppose that mendicant is ignoring and forgetting about those thoughts, but bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion keep coming up. They should focus on stopping the formation of those thoughts.

mn20:6.2.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:6.3.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:6.4.verse: Suppose there was a person walking quickly.

mn20:6.21.verse: And so that person would shun successively coarser postures and adopt more subtle ones.

mn20:6.22.verse: In the same way, a mendicant … those thoughts are given up and come to an end …

mn20:7.1.verse: Now, suppose that mendicant is focusing on stopping the formation of those thoughts, but bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion keep coming up.

mn20:7.2.verse: With teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, they should squeeze, squash, and crush mind with mind.

mn20:7.3.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:7.4.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:7.5.verse: It’s like a strong man who grabs a weaker man by the head or throat or shoulder and squeezes, squashes, and crushes them.

mn20:7.6.verse: In the same way, a mendicant …

mn20:7.7.verse: with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, should squeeze, squash, and crush mind with mind.

mn20:7.8.verse: As they do so, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:7.9.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:8.1.verse: Now, take the mendicant who is focusing on some subject that gives rise to bad, unskillful thoughts connected with desire, hate, and delusion. They focus on some other subject connected with the skillful …

mn20:8.3.verse: They examine the drawbacks of those thoughts …

mn20:8.5.verse: They try to forget and ignore about those thoughts …

mn20:8.7.verse: They focus on stopping the formation of those thoughts …

mn20:8.9.verse: With teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of the mouth, they squeeze, squash, and crush mind with mind. When they succeed in each of these things, those bad thoughts are given up and come to an end.

mn20:8.10.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn20:8.11.verse: This is called a mendicant who is a master of the ways of thought.

mn20:8.12.verse: They will think what they want to think, and they won’t think what they don’t want to think.

mn20:8.13.verse: They’ve cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit have made an end of suffering.”

mn20:8.14.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn20:8.15.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn21:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn21:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Moliya Phagguna was associating over much with the bhikkhunis.

mn21:2.2.verse: He was associating so much with bhikkhunis that

mn21:2.3.verse: if any bhikkhu in his presence spoke dispraise of those bhikkhunis, he would be angry and displeased and would rebuke him,

mn21:2.4.verse: and if any bhikkhu in those bhikkhunis’ presence spoke dispraise of the venerable Moliya Phagguna, they would be angry and displeased and would rebuke him,

mn21:2.5.verse: so much was the venerable Moliya Phagguna associating with bhikkhunis.

mn21:3.1.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he recounted what was taking place.

mn21:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu thus:

mn21:4.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, tell the bhikkhu Moliya Phagguna in my name that

mn21:4.4.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the bhikkhu replied and he went to the venerable Moliya Phagguna and told him:

mn21:4.6.verse: ‘Yes, friend,’ he replied, and he went to the Blessed One and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One asked him:

mn21:5.1.verse: ‘Phagguna, is it true, as it seems, that you are associating over much with bhikkhunis,

mn21:5.2.verse: that you are associating so much with bhikkhunis that

mn21:5.3.verse: if any bhikkhu in your presence speaks dispraise of those bhikkhunis, you are angry and displeased and rebuke him,

mn21:5.4.verse: and that if any bhikkhu in those bhikkhunis’ presence speaks dispraise of you, they are angry and displeased and rebuke him,

mn21:5.5.verse: so much are you associating, it seems, with bhikkhunis?’

mn21:5.7.verse: ‘Phagguna, are you not a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness?’

mn21:6.1.verse: ‘Phagguna, it is not proper for you, as a clansman gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness to associate over much with bhikkhunis.

mn21:6.2.verse: Therefore if anyone in your presence speaks dispraise of those bhikkhunis you should abandon any wish and any thoughts based on the home life.

mn21:6.3.verse: And herein you should train thus:

mn21:6.4.verse: “My mind will be unaffected, and I shall utter no bad words, and I shall abide compassionate for welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness and no inner hate”;

mn21:6.6.verse: ‘Therefore, if anyone in your presence gives those bhikkhunis a blow with his hand or a blow with a clod or a blow with a stick or a blow with a knife, you should abandon any wish and any thoughts based on the home life …

mn21:6.10.verse: ‘Therefore, if anyone in your presence speaks dispraise, you should abandon …

mn21:6.13.verse: ‘Therefore if anyone should give you a blow with the hand … with a clod … a stick … a knife, you should abandon any wish and any thoughts based on the home life.

mn21:6.14.verse: And herein you should train thus: “My mind will be unaffected, and I shall utter no bad words, and I shall abide compassionate for welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness and no inner hate”;

mn21:7.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn21:7.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there was an occasion when the bhikkhus satisfied my mind.

mn21:7.4.verse: “Bhikkhus, I eat food at a single sitting.

mn21:7.5.verse: By doing so I perceive little affliction, little ailment, and also lightness, strength and a comfortable abiding”.

mn21:7.8.verse: And I had no need to keep on instructing those bhikkhus:

mn21:7.9.verse: I had only to arouse mindfulness in them.

mn21:7.10.verse: ‘Suppose there were a chariot on even ground at the four crossroads, harnessed to thoroughbreds, waiting with whips lying ready,

mn21:7.11.verse: so that a skilled trainer, driver of horses to be tamed, might mount, and, taking the reins in his hand, drive out and back by any road in any way he liked,

mn21:7.12.verse: so too I had no need …

mn21:7.13.verse: I had only to arouse mindfulness in them.

mn21:7.14.verse: ‘Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon what is unprofitable and devote yourselves to what is profitable,

mn21:7.15.verse: for that is how you will come to growth, increase and fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn21:8.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a big sala-tree grove near a village or town,

mn21:8.2.verse: and it was choked with castor-oil weeds,

mn21:8.3.verse: and some man appeared, seeking its benefit, its surcease of bondage,

mn21:8.4.verse: and he cut down and threw out the crooked saplings that robbed the sap, and he cleaned up the interior of the grove,

mn21:8.5.verse: and he tended the straight well-formed saplings,

mn21:8.6.verse: so that the sāla-tree grove later on came to growth, increase and fulfilment;

mn21:8.7.verse: so too, bhikkhus, abandon what is unprofitable …

mn21:8.8.verse: fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn21:9.1.verse: ‘Formerly, bhikkhus, in this same Sāvatthi there was a housewife called Vedehikā.

mn21:9.2.verse: And the good name of Mistress Vedehikā had spread thus:

mn21:9.3.verse: “Mistress Vedehikā is kind, Mistress Videhikā is gentle, Mistress Vedehikā is demure”.

mn21:9.4.verse: ‘Now Mistress Vedehikā had a maid called Kālī, who was clever, nimble and neat in her work.

mn21:9.6.verse: “My lady’s good name has spread thus:

mn21:9.7.verse: ‘Mistress Vedehikā is kind, Mistress Vedehikā is gentle, Mistress Vedehikā is demure’.

mn21:9.8.verse: How is it, now, while she does not show anger, is it nevertheless actually present in herself, or is it absent?

mn21:9.9.verse: Or else is it just because my work is neat that my lady shows no anger though it is actually present in herself?

mn21:9.11.verse: ‘So the maid Kālī got up when it was day.

mn21:9.15.verse: ‘“What is the matter that you get up when it is day?”’

mn21:9.17.verse: ‘“Nothing is the matter, you wicked girl, yet you get up when it is day!” and she was angry and displeased, and she scowled.

mn21:9.19.verse: “The fact is that while my lady does not show anger, it is actually present in herself, not absent;

mn21:9.20.verse: and it is just because my work is neat that my lady shows no anger though it is actually present in herself, not absent.

mn21:9.21.verse: Suppose I test my lady a little more?”’

mn21:9.22.verse: ‘So the maid Kālī got up when it was later in the day.

mn21:9.26.verse: ‘“What is the matter that you get up when it is day?”’

mn21:9.28.verse: ‘“Nothing is the matter, you wicked girl, yet you get up when it is day!” and she was angry and displeased, and she spoke words of displeasure.

mn21:9.30.verse: “The fact is that while my lady does not show anger, it is actually present in herself, not absent;

mn21:9.31.verse: and it is just because my work is neat that my lady shows no anger though it is actually present in herself, not absent.

mn21:9.32.verse: Suppose I test my lady a little more?”’

mn21:9.33.verse: ‘So the maid Kālī got up when it was still later in the day.

mn21:9.37.verse: “‘What is the matter that you get up when it is day?”’

mn21:9.39.verse: “‘Nothing is the matter, you wicked girl, yet you get up later in the day!” and she was angry and displeased, and she took a rolling-pin and gave her a blow and broke her head.

mn21:9.40.verse: ‘Then the maid Kālī, with blood running from her broken head, denounced (her mistress) to the neighbours:

mn21:9.42.verse: See, ladies, the Gentle One’s work! See, ladies, the Demure One’s work!

mn21:9.43.verse: See how angry and displeased she was with her only maid for getting up when it was day, and how she took a rolling-pin and gave her a blow on the head!”’

mn21:9.44.verse: ‘Then later on the bad name of Mistress Vedehikā spread thus:

mn21:9.45.verse: “Mistress Vedehikā is rough, Mistress Vedehikā is violent, Mistress Vedehikā is merciless.”’

mn21:10.1.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, some bhikkhu is quite kind, quite gentle, quite demure, so long as no disagreeable words touch him.

mn21:10.2.verse: But it is as soon as disagreeable words touch him that a bhikkhu needs to appear kind and gentle and demure.

mn21:10.3.verse: I do not call a bhikkhu easy to correct, who is only easy to correct by reason of the robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, that he gets.

mn21:10.5.verse: Because that bhikkhu is not easy to correct when he gets no robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.

mn21:10.6.verse: But when a bhikkhu is easy to correct since he honours, respects and reveres only the Dhamma, him I call easy to correct.

mn21:10.7.verse: Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train thus: “We shall be easy to correct, honouring, respecting and revering only the Dhamma”;

mn21:11.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech that others may use when they address you:

mn21:11.2.verse: their speech may be timely or untimely,

mn21:11.5.verse: connected with good or with harm,

mn21:11.6.verse: accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness or by inner hate.

mn21:11.7.verse: ‘When others address you, their speech may be timely or untimely;

mn21:11.8.verse: when others address you, their speech may be true or untrue;

mn21:11.9.verse: when others address you, their speech may be gentle or harsh;

mn21:11.10.verse: when others address you, their speech may be connected with good or with harm;

mn21:11.11.verse: when others address you, their speech may be accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness or by inner hate.

mn21:11.12.verse: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:

mn21:11.13.verse: “Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no bad words and we shall abide compassionate for welfare with a mind of loving-kindness and no inner hate.

mn21:11.14.verse: We shall abide with a mind of loving-kindness extending to that person, and we shall abide with an abundant, exalted, measureless mind of loving-kindness, without hostility or ill-will, extending over the all-encompassing world (universe) as its supporting object.”

mn21:11.15.verse: That is how you should train.

mn21:12.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose a man came with a hoe and a basket

mn21:12.3.verse: “I shall make this Great Earth to be without earth”

mn21:12.4.verse: and he dug here and there, and strewed here and there, and spat here and there, and made water here and there, saying:

mn21:12.6.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn21:12.7.verse: would that man make this Great Earth to be without earth?’

mn21:12.10.verse: Because this Great Earth is deep and immense:

mn21:12.11.verse: it cannot possibly be made to be without earth thus.

mn21:12.12.verse: Eventually the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn21:13.1.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech that others may use when they address you:

mn21:13.2.verse: their speech may be timely or untimely,

mn21:13.5.verse: connected with good or with harm,

mn21:13.6.verse: accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness or by inner hate.

mn21:13.7.verse: When others address you, their speech may be timely or untimely;

mn21:13.8.verse: when others address you, their speech may be true or untrue;

mn21:13.9.verse: when others address you, their speech may be gentle or harsh;

mn21:13.10.verse: when others address you, their speech may be connected with good or with harm;

mn21:13.11.verse: when others address you, their speech may be accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness or by inner hate.

mn21:13.12.verse: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:

mn21:13.13.verse: “Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no bad words and we shall abide compassionate for welfare with a mind of loving-kindness and no inner hate.

mn21:13.14.verse: We shall abide with a mind of loving-kindness extending to that person, and we shall abide with an abundant, exalted, measureless mind of loving-kindness like the earth, without hostility or ill-will, extending over the all-encompassing world (universe) as its supporting object.”

mn21:13.15.verse: That is how you should train.

mn21:14.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose a man came with (crimson-) lake or turmeric or indigo or carmine

mn21:14.3.verse: “I shall draw pictures, I shall make pictures appear, on this empty space”.

mn21:14.4.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn21:14.5.verse: would that man draw pictures, would he make pictures appear, on that empty space?’

mn21:14.8.verse: Because that empty space is formless and invisible;

mn21:14.9.verse: he cannot possibly draw pictures, make pictures appear there thus.

mn21:14.10.verse: Eventually the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn21:15.1.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech … inner hate.

mn21:16.1.verse: ‘Suppose bhikkhus, a man came with a burning grass-torch

mn21:16.3.verse: “I shall warm up, I shall heat up, the River Ganges with this burning grass-torch”.

mn21:16.4.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn21:16.5.verse: would that man warm up, would he heat up, the River Ganges with the burning grass-torch?’

mn21:16.8.verse: Because the River Ganges is deep and immense;

mn21:16.9.verse: it cannot possibly be warmed up, heated up, with a burning grass-torch.

mn21:16.10.verse: Eventually the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn21:17.1.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech … inner hate.

mn21:18.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose there were a cat (-skin) bag that was rubbed, well-rubbed, thoroughly well-rubbed, soft, silky, rid of rustling, rid of crackling,

mn21:18.2.verse: and a man came with a stick or a potsherd

mn21:18.4.verse: “There is this cat (-skin) bag that is rubbed … and rid of crackling: I shall make it rustle, I shall make it crackle”.

mn21:18.5.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn21:18.6.verse: would that man make it rustle or make it crackle with the stick or the potsherd?’

mn21:18.9.verse: Because that cat (-skin) bag, being rubbed … rid of crackling,

mn21:18.10.verse: cannot possibly be made to rustle or made to crackle with the stick or the potsherd.

mn21:18.11.verse: Eventually that man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn21:19.1.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech … inner hate.

mn21:20.1.verse: ‘Even were bandits savagely to sever you limb from limb with a two-handed saw, he who entertained hate in his heart on that account would not be one who carried out my teaching.

mn21:20.2.verse: Now this is how you should train herein:

mn21:20.3.verse: “Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no bad words, and we shall abide compassionate for welfare with a mind of loving-kindness and no inner hate.

mn21:20.4.verse: We shall abide with a mind of loving-kindness extending to that person, and we shall abide with an abundant, exalted, mind of loving-kindness, without hostility or ill-will, extending over the all-encompassing world as its supporting object.”

mn21:20.5.verse: That is how you should train yourselves.

mn21:21.1.verse: ‘And, bhikkhus, you should keep this instruction of the Simile of the Saw constantly in mind.

mn21:21.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, do you see the course of speech, trivial or gross, that you could not endure?’

mn21:21.4.verse: ‘Therefore, bhikkhus, you should keep this instruction of the Simile of the Saw constantly in mind.

mn21:21.5.verse: That will be long for your welfare and happiness.’

mn21:21.6.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn21:21.7.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn21:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn21:2.1.verse: Now at that time, Venerable Phagguna of the Top-Knot was spending too long mixing closely with some nuns.

mn21:2.3.verse: if any mendicant criticized those nuns in his presence, Phagguna of the Top-Knot got angry and upset, and even instigated disciplinary proceedings.

mn21:2.4.verse: And if any mendicant criticized Phagguna of the Top-Knot in their presence, those nuns got angry and upset, and even instigated disciplinary proceedings.

mn21:2.5.verse: That’s how close Phagguna of the Top-Knot was with those nuns.

mn21:3.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was going on.

mn21:4.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

mn21:4.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Phagguna of the Top-Knot that

mn21:4.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Phagguna of the Top-Knot and said to him,

mn21:4.6.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Phagguna replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

mn21:5.1.verse: “Is it really true, Phagguna, that you’ve been spending too long mixing closely with some nuns?

mn21:5.3.verse: if any mendicant criticizes those nuns in your presence, you get angry and upset, and even instigate disciplinary proceedings?

mn21:5.4.verse: And if any mendicant criticizes you in those nuns’ presence, they get angry and upset, and even instigate disciplinary proceedings?

mn21:5.5.verse: Is that how close you’ve become with those nuns?”

mn21:5.7.verse: “Phagguna, are you not a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness?”

mn21:6.1.verse: “As such, it’s not appropriate for you to mix so closely with those nuns.

mn21:6.2.verse: So if anyone criticizes those nuns in your presence, you should give up any desires or thoughts of domestic life.

mn21:6.3.verse: If that happens, you should train like this:

mn21:6.4.verse: ‘My mind will not degenerate. I will blurt out no bad words. I will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.’

mn21:6.6.verse: So even if someone strikes those nuns with fists, stones, rods, and swords in your presence, you should give up any desires or thoughts of domestic life.

mn21:6.7.verse: If that happens, you should train like this:

mn21:6.8.verse: ‘My mind will not degenerate. I will blurt out no bad words. I will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.’

mn21:6.10.verse: So if anyone criticizes you in your presence, you should give up any desires or thoughts of domestic life.

mn21:6.11.verse: If that happens, you should train like this: ‘My mind will not degenerate. I will blurt out no bad words. I will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.’

mn21:6.13.verse: So Phagguna, even if someone strikes you with fists, stones, rods, and swords, you should give up any desires or thoughts of domestic life.

mn21:6.14.verse: If that happens, you should train like this: ‘My mind will not degenerate. I will blurt out no bad words. I will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.’

mn21:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

mn21:7.2.verse: “Mendicants, I used to be satisfied with the mendicants.

mn21:7.4.verse: ‘I eat my food in one sitting per day.

mn21:7.5.verse: Doing so, I find that I’m healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

mn21:7.6.verse: You too should eat your food in one sitting per day.

mn21:7.7.verse: Doing so, you’ll find that you’re healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.’

mn21:7.8.verse: I didn’t have to keep on instructing those mendicants;

mn21:7.9.verse: I just had to prompt their mindfulness.

mn21:7.10.verse: Suppose a chariot stood harnessed to thoroughbreds at a level crossroads, with a goad ready.

mn21:7.11.verse: A deft horse trainer, a master charioteer, might mount the chariot, taking the reins in his right hand and goad in the left. He’d drive out and back wherever he wishes, whenever he wishes.

mn21:7.12.verse: In the same way, I didn’t have to keep on instructing those mendicants;

mn21:7.13.verse: I just had to prompt their mindfulness.

mn21:7.14.verse: So, mendicants, you too should give up what’s unskillful and devote yourselves to skillful qualities.

mn21:7.15.verse: In this way you’ll achieve growth, improvement, and maturity in this teaching and training.

mn21:8.1.verse: Suppose that not far from a town or village there was a large grove of sal trees

mn21:8.2.verse: that was choked with castor-oil weeds.

mn21:8.3.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to help protect and nurture that grove.

mn21:8.4.verse: They’d cut down the crooked sal saplings that were robbing the sap, and throw them out. They’d clean up the interior of the grove,

mn21:8.5.verse: and properly care for the straight, well-formed sal saplings.

mn21:8.6.verse: In this way, in due course, that sal grove would grow, increase, and mature.

mn21:8.7.verse: In the same way, mendicants, you too should give up what’s unskillful and devote yourselves to skillful qualities.

mn21:8.8.verse: In this way you’ll achieve growth, improvement, and maturity in this teaching and training.

mn21:9.1.verse: Once upon a time, mendicants, right here in Sāvatthī there was a housewife named Vedehikā.

mn21:9.3.verse: ‘The housewife Vedehikā is gentle, placid, and calm.’

mn21:9.4.verse: Now, Vedehikā had a bonded maid named Kāḷī who was deft, tireless, and well-organized in her work.

mn21:9.6.verse: ‘My mistress has a good reputation as being

mn21:9.8.verse: But does she actually have anger in her and just not show it? Or does she have no anger?

mn21:9.9.verse: Or is it just because my work is well-organized that she doesn’t show anger, even though she still has it inside?

mn21:9.10.verse: Why don’t I test my mistress?’

mn21:9.11.verse: So Kāḷī got up during the day.

mn21:9.15.verse: ‘You’re getting up in the day—what’s up with you, wench?’

mn21:9.17.verse: ‘Oh, so nothing’s up, you naughty maid, but you get up in the day!’ Angry and upset, she scowled.

mn21:9.19.verse: ‘My mistress actually has anger in her and just doesn’t show it; it’s not that she has no anger.

mn21:9.20.verse: It’s just because my work is well-organized that she doesn’t show anger, even though she still has it inside.

mn21:9.21.verse: Why don’t I test my mistress further?’

mn21:9.22.verse: So Kāḷī got up later in the day.

mn21:9.26.verse: ‘You’re getting up later in the day—what’s up with you, wench?’

mn21:9.28.verse: ‘Oh, so nothing’s up, you naughty maid, but you get up later in the day!’ Angry and upset, she blurted out angry words.

mn21:9.30.verse: ‘My mistress actually has anger in her and just doesn’t show it; it’s not that she has no anger.

mn21:9.31.verse: It’s just because my work is well-organized that she doesn’t show anger, even though she still has it inside.

mn21:9.32.verse: Why don’t I test my mistress further?’

mn21:9.33.verse: So Kāḷī got up even later in the day.

mn21:9.37.verse: ‘You’re getting up even later in the day—what’s up with you, wench?’

mn21:9.39.verse: ‘Oh, so nothing’s up, you naughty maid, but you get up even later in the day!’ Angry and upset, she grabbed a door-pin and hit Kāḷī on the head, cracking it open.

mn21:9.40.verse: Then Kāḷī, with blood pouring from her cracked skull, denounced her mistress to the neighbors,

mn21:9.41.verse: ‘See, ladies, what the gentle one did!

mn21:9.42.verse: See what the placid one did! See what the calm one did!

mn21:9.43.verse: How on earth can she grab a door-pin and hit her only maid on the head, cracking it open, just for getting up late?’

mn21:9.44.verse: Then after some time the housewife Vedehikā got this bad reputation:

mn21:9.45.verse: ‘The housewife Vedehikā is fierce, ill-tempered, and not calm at all.’

mn21:10.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant may be the gentlest of the gentle, the most placid of the placid, the calmest of the calm, so long as they don’t encounter any disagreeable criticism.

mn21:10.2.verse: But it’s when they encounter disagreeable criticism that you’ll know whether they’re really gentle, placid, and calm.

mn21:10.3.verse: I don’t say that a mendicant is easy to admonish if they make themselves easy to admonish only for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

mn21:10.5.verse: Because when they don’t get robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, they’re no longer easy to admonish.

mn21:10.6.verse: But when a mendicant is easy to admonish purely because they honor, respect, revere, worship, and venerate the teaching, then I say that they’re easy to admonish.

mn21:10.7.verse: So, mendicants, you should train yourselves: ‘We will be easy to admonish purely because we honor, respect, revere, worship, and venerate the teaching.’

mn21:11.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these five ways in which others might criticize you.

mn21:11.2.verse: Their speech may be timely or untimely,

mn21:11.6.verse: from a heart of love or from secret hate.
