mn21:11.7.verse: When others criticize you, they may do so in any of these ways.

mn21:11.12.verse: If that happens, you should train like this:

mn21:11.13.verse: ‘Our minds will not degenerate. We will blurt out no bad words. We will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.

mn21:11.14.verse: We will meditate spreading a heart of love to that individual. And with them as a basis, we will meditate spreading a heart full of love to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.’

mn21:12.1.verse: Suppose a person was to come along carrying a spade and basket

mn21:12.3.verse: ‘I shall make this great earth be without earth!’

mn21:12.4.verse: And they’d dig all over, scatter all over, spit all over, and urinate all over, saying,

mn21:12.7.verse: Could that person make this great earth be without earth?”

mn21:12.10.verse: Because this great earth is deep and limitless.

mn21:12.11.verse: It’s not easy to make it be without earth.

mn21:12.12.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn21:13.2.verse: Their speech may be timely or untimely,

mn21:13.6.verse: from a heart of love or from secret hate.

mn21:13.7.verse: When others criticize you, they may do so in any of these ways.

mn21:13.12.verse: If that happens, you should train like this:

mn21:13.14.verse: We will meditate spreading a heart of love to that individual. And with them as a basis, we will meditate spreading a heart like the earth to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.’

mn21:14.1.verse: Suppose a person was to come along with dye such as red lac, turmeric, indigo, or rose madder,

mn21:14.3.verse: ‘I shall draw pictures in space, making pictures appear there.’

mn21:14.5.verse: Could that person draw pictures in space?”

mn21:14.8.verse: Because space has no form or appearance.

mn21:14.9.verse: It’s not easy to draw pictures there.

mn21:14.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn21:15.1.verse: “In the same way, if others criticize you in any of these five ways … you should train like this:

mn21:15.2.verse: ‘… We will meditate spreading a heart of love to that person. And with them as a basis, we will meditate spreading a heart like space to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.’

mn21:16.1.verse: Suppose a person was to come along carrying a blazing grass torch,

mn21:16.3.verse: ‘I shall burn and scorch the Ganges River with this blazing grass torch.’

mn21:16.5.verse: Could that person burn and scorch the Ganges River with a blazing grass torch?”

mn21:16.8.verse: Because the Ganges River is deep and limitless.

mn21:16.9.verse: It’s not easy to burn and scorch it with a blazing grass torch.

mn21:16.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn21:17.1.verse: “In the same way, if others criticize you in any of these five ways … you should train like this:

mn21:17.2.verse: ‘… We will meditate spreading a heart of love to that individual. And with them as a basis, we will meditate spreading a heart like the Ganges to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.’

mn21:18.1.verse: Suppose there was a catskin bag that was rubbed, well-rubbed, very well-rubbed, soft, silky, rid of rustling and crackling.

mn21:18.2.verse: Then a person comes along carrying a stick or a stone,

mn21:18.4.verse: ‘I shall make this soft catskin bag rustle and crackle with this stick or stone.’

mn21:18.6.verse: Could that person make that soft catskin bag rustle and crackle with that stick or stone?”

mn21:18.9.verse: Because that catskin bag is rubbed, well-rubbed, very well-rubbed, soft, silky, rid of rustling and crackling.

mn21:18.10.verse: It’s not easy to make it rustle or crackle with a stick or stone.

mn21:18.11.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn21:19.2.verse: Their speech may be timely or untimely,

mn21:19.6.verse: from a heart of love or from secret hate.

mn21:19.7.verse: When others criticize you, they may do so in any of these ways.

mn21:20.1.verse: Even if low-down bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handed saw, anyone who had a malevolent thought on that account would not be following my instructions.

mn21:20.2.verse: If that happens, you should train like this:

mn21:20.3.verse: ‘Our minds will not degenerate. We will blurt out no bad words. We will remain full of sympathy, with a heart of love and no secret hate.

mn21:20.4.verse: We will meditate spreading a heart of love to that individual. And with them as a basis, we will meditate spreading a heart full of love to everyone in the world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.’

mn21:21.1.verse: If you frequently reflect on this advice on the simile of the saw,

mn21:21.2.verse: do you see any criticism, large or small, that you could not endure?”

mn21:21.4.verse: “So, mendicants, you should frequently reflect on this advice on the simile of the saw.

mn21:21.5.verse: This will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn21:21.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn21:21.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn22:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn22:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion this evil viewpoint had arisen in the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers:

mn22:2.2.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in, are not genuine obstructions.”

mn22:2.3.verse: A large number of monks heard,

mn22:2.4.verse: “They say that this evil viewpoint has arisen in the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers:

mn22:2.5.verse: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in, are not genuine obstructions.’”

mn22:3.1.verse: So they went to the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers and on arrival said to him,

mn22:3.2.verse: “Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that this evil viewpoint has arisen in you—

mn22:3.3.verse: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in, are not genuine obstructions’?”

mn22:3.4.verse: “Yes, indeed, friends. I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, and those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions.”

mn22:3.5.verse: Then those monks, desiring to pry the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers away from that evil viewpoint, quizzed him back and forth and rebuked him, saying,

mn22:3.6.verse: “Don’t say that, friend Ariṭṭha. Don’t slander the Blessed One, for it is not good to slander the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that.

mn22:3.7.verse: In many ways, friend, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.

mn22:3.8.verse: The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:3.9.verse: The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a chain of bones: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:3.10.verse: The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a lump of flesh…

mn22:3.16.verse: a butcher’s ax and chopping block…

mn22:3.18.verse: a snake’s head: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.”

mn22:3.19.verse: And yet even though he was quizzed back & forth and rebuked by those monks, the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers, through stubbornness and attachment to that very same evil viewpoint, continued to insist,

mn22:3.20.verse: “Yes, indeed, friends. I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, and those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions.”

mn22:3.21.verse: So when the monks were unable to pry the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers away from that evil viewpoint, they went to the Blessed One and on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, they told him what had happened.

mn22:5.1.verse: So the Blessed One told a certain monk,

mn22:5.2.verse: “Come, monk. In my name, call the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers, saying,

mn22:5.4.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monk responded and, having gone to the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers, on arrival he said,

mn22:5.6.verse: “As you say, my friend,” the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers responded. Then he went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him,

mn22:5.7.verse: “Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that this evil viewpoint has arisen in you—

mn22:5.8.verse: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in, are not genuine obstructions’?”

mn22:5.9.verse: “Yes, indeed, lord. I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, and those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions.”

mn22:6.1.verse: “Worthless man, from whom have you understood that Dhamma taught by me in such a way?

mn22:6.2.verse: Worthless man, haven’t I in many ways described obstructive acts? And when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.

mn22:6.3.verse: I have said that sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:6.4.verse: I have compared sensual pleasures to a chain of bones: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:6.5.verse: I have compared sensual pleasures to a lump of flesh…

mn22:6.11.verse: a butcher’s ax and chopping block…

mn22:6.13.verse: a snake’s head: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:6.14.verse: But you, worthless man, through your own wrong grasp (of the Dhamma), have both slandered us as well as injuring yourself and accumulating much demerit for yourself,

mn22:6.15.verse: for that will lead to your long-term harm & suffering.”

mn22:7.1.verse: Then the Blessed One said to the monks,

mn22:7.3.verse: Is this monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers even warm in this Dhamma & Vinaya?”

mn22:7.6.verse: When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers sat silent, abashed, his shoulders drooping, his head down, brooding, at a loss for words.

mn22:7.7.verse: Then the Blessed One, seeing that the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers was sitting silent, abashed, his shoulders drooping, his head down, brooding, at a loss for words, said to him,

mn22:7.8.verse: “Worthless man, you will be recognized for your own evil viewpoint.

mn22:7.9.verse: I will cross-examine the monks on this matter.”

mn22:8.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks,

mn22:8.2.verse: “Monks, do you, too, understand the Dhamma as taught by me in the same way that the monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers does when, through his own wrong grasp, he both slanders us as well as injuring himself and accumulating much demerit for himself?”

mn22:8.4.verse: for in many ways the Blessed One has described obstructive acts to us as obstructive,

mn22:8.5.verse: and indulged in they are genuine obstructions.

mn22:8.6.verse: The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:8.7.verse: The Blessed One has compared sensual pleasures to a chain of bones, a lump of flesh, a grass torch, a pit of glowing embers, a dream, borrowed goods, the fruits of a tree, a butcher’s ax and chopping block, swords and spears,

mn22:8.8.verse: and a snake’s head: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.”

mn22:8.9.verse: “It’s good, monks, that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way,

mn22:8.10.verse: for in many ways I have described obstructive acts to you, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.

mn22:8.11.verse: I have said that sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:8.12.verse: I have compared sensual pleasures to a chain of bones, a lump of flesh, a grass torch, a pit of glowing embers, a dream, borrowed goods, the fruits of a tree, a butcher’s ax and chopping block, swords and spears,

mn22:8.13.verse: and a snake’s head: of much stress, much despair, & greater drawbacks.

mn22:8.14.verse: But this monk Ariṭṭha Formerly-of-the-Vulture-Killers, through his own wrong grasp (of the Dhamma), has both slandered us as well as injuring himself and accumulating much demerit for himself,

mn22:8.15.verse: and that will lead to this worthless man’s long-term harm & suffering.

mn22:9.1.verse: For a person to indulge in sensual pleasures without sensual passion, without sensual perception, without sensual thinking: That isn’t possible.

mn22:10.1.verse: “Monks, there is the case where some worthless men study the Dhamma:

mn22:10.2.verse: dialogues, narratives of mixed prose and verse, explanations, verses, spontaneous exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing events, question & answer sessions [the earliest classifications of the Buddha’s teachings].

mn22:10.3.verse: Having studied the Dhamma, they don’t ascertain the meaning [or: the purpose] of those Dhammas with their discernment.

mn22:10.4.verse: Not having ascertained the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment, they don’t come to an agreement through pondering.

mn22:10.5.verse: They study the Dhamma both for attacking others and for defending themselves in debate.

mn22:10.6.verse: They don’t reach the goal for which (people) study the Dhamma.

mn22:10.7.verse: Their wrong grasp of those Dhammas will lead to their long-term harm & suffering.

mn22:10.9.verse: Because of the wrong-graspedness of the Dhammas.

mn22:10.10.verse: “Suppose there were a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake.

mn22:10.11.verse: He would see a large water-snake

mn22:10.12.verse: and grasp it by the coils or by the tail.

mn22:10.13.verse: The water-snake, turning around, would bite him on the hand, on the arm, or on one of his limbs,

mn22:10.14.verse: and from that cause he would suffer death or death-like suffering.

mn22:10.16.verse: Because of the wrong-graspedness of the water-snake.

mn22:10.17.verse: In the same way, there is the case where some worthless men study the Dhamma.…

mn22:10.18.verse: dialogues, narratives of mixed prose and verse, explanations, verses, spontaneous exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing events, question & answer sessions.

mn22:10.19.verse: Having studied the Dhamma, they don’t ascertain the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment.

mn22:10.20.verse: Not having ascertained the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment, they don’t come to an agreement through pondering.

mn22:10.21.verse: They study the Dhamma both for attacking others and for defending themselves in debate.

mn22:10.22.verse: They don’t reach the goal for which (people) study the Dhamma.

mn22:10.23.verse: Their wrong grasp of those Dhammas will lead to their long-term harm & suffering.

mn22:10.25.verse: Because of the wrong-graspedness of the Dhammas.

mn22:11.1.verse: “But then there is the case where some clansmen study the Dhamma.…

mn22:11.2.verse: dialogues, narratives of mixed prose and verse, explanations, verses, spontaneous exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing events, question & answer sessions.

mn22:11.3.verse: Having studied the Dhamma, they ascertain the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment.

mn22:11.4.verse: Having ascertained the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment, they come to an agreement through pondering.

mn22:11.5.verse: They don’t study the Dhamma either for attacking others or for defending themselves in debate.

mn22:11.6.verse: They reach the goal for which people study the Dhamma.

mn22:11.7.verse: Their right grasp of those Dhammas will lead to their long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:11.9.verse: Because of the right-graspedness of the Dhammas.

mn22:11.10.verse: “Suppose there were a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake.

mn22:11.11.verse: He would see a large water-snake

mn22:11.12.verse: and pin it down firmly with a cleft stick.

mn22:11.13.verse: Having pinned it down firmly with a forked stick, he would grasp it firmly by the neck.

mn22:11.14.verse: Then no matter how much the water-snake might wrap its coils around his hand, his arm, or any of his limbs, he would not from that cause suffer death or death-like suffering.

mn22:11.16.verse: Because of the right-graspedness of the water-snake.

mn22:11.17.verse: In the same way, there is the case where some clansmen study the Dhamma.…

mn22:11.18.verse: dialogues, narratives of mixed prose and verse, explanations, verses, spontaneous exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing events, question & answer sessions.

mn22:11.19.verse: Having studied the Dhamma, they ascertain the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment.

mn22:11.20.verse: Having ascertained the meaning of those Dhammas with their discernment, they come to an agreement through pondering.

mn22:11.21.verse: They don’t study the Dhamma either for attacking others or for defending themselves in debate.

mn22:11.22.verse: They reach the goal for which people study the Dhamma.

mn22:11.23.verse: Their right grasp of those Dhammas will lead to their long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:11.25.verse: Because of the right-graspedness of the Dhammas.

mn22:12.1.verse: “Therefore, monks, when you understand the meaning of my statements, that is how you should remember them.

mn22:12.2.verse: But when you don’t understand the meaning of my statements, then right there you should ask me or the experienced monks.

mn22:13.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding onto.

mn22:13.2.verse: Listen & pay close attention. I will speak.”

mn22:13.3.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monks responded to the Blessed One.

mn22:13.5.verse: “Suppose a man were traveling along a path.

mn22:13.6.verse: He would see a great expanse of water, with the near shore dubious & risky, the further shore secure & free from risk,

mn22:13.7.verse: but with neither a ferryboat nor a bridge going from this shore to the other.

mn22:13.8.verse: The thought would occur to him,

mn22:13.9.verse: ‘Here is this great expanse of water, with the near shore dubious & risky, the further shore secure & free from risk,

mn22:13.10.verse: but with neither a ferryboat nor a bridge going from this shore to the other.

mn22:13.11.verse: What if I were to gather grass, twigs, branches, & leaves and, having bound them together to make a raft, were to cross over to safety on the other shore in dependence on the raft, making an effort with my hands & feet?’

mn22:13.12.verse: Then the man, having gathered grass, twigs, branches, & leaves, having bound them together to make a raft, would cross over to safety on the other shore in dependence on the raft, making an effort with his hands & feet.

mn22:13.13.verse: Having crossed over to the further shore, he might think,

mn22:13.14.verse: ‘How useful this raft has been to me!

mn22:13.15.verse: For it was in dependence on this raft that, making an effort with my hands & feet, I have crossed over to safety on the further shore.

mn22:13.16.verse: Why don’t I, having hoisted it on my head or carrying it on my back, go wherever I like?’

mn22:13.18.verse: Would the man, in doing that, be doing what should be done with the raft?”

mn22:13.20.verse: “And what should the man do in order to be doing what should be done with the raft?

mn22:13.21.verse: There is the case where the man, having crossed over, would think,

mn22:13.22.verse: ‘How useful this raft has been to me!

mn22:13.23.verse: For it was in dependence on this raft that, making an effort with my hands & feet, I have crossed over to safety on the further shore.

mn22:13.24.verse: Why don’t I, having dragged it on dry land or sinking it in the water, go wherever I like?’

mn22:13.25.verse: In doing this, he would be doing what should be done with the raft.

mn22:13.26.verse: In the same way, monks, I have taught the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding onto.

mn22:14.1.verse: Understanding the Dhamma as taught compared to a raft, you should let go even of Dhammas, to say nothing of non-Dhammas.

mn22:15.3.verse: There is the case where an uninstructed run-of-the-mill person—who has no regard for noble ones, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma; who has no regard for people of integrity, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma—

mn22:15.4.verse: assumes about form: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:15.5.verse: He assumes about feeling: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:15.6.verse: He assumes about perception: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:15.7.verse: He assumes about fabrications: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:15.8.verse: He assumes about what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, pondered by the intellect: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:15.10.verse: ‘This cosmos is the self. After death this I will be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I will stay just like that for an eternity’:

mn22:15.11.verse: ‘This is me, this is my self, this is what I am.’

mn22:16.1.verse: “Then there is the case where a well-instructed disciple of the noble ones—who has regard for noble ones, is well-versed & disciplined in their Dhamma; who has regard for people of integrity, is well-versed & disciplined in their Dhamma

mn22:16.2.verse: assumes about form: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:16.3.verse: He assumes about feeling: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:16.4.verse: He assumes about perception: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:16.5.verse: He assumes about fabrications: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:16.6.verse: He assumes about what is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, pondered by the intellect: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:16.8.verse: ‘This cosmos is the self. After death this I will be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I will stay just like that for an eternity’:

mn22:16.9.verse: ‘This is not me, this is not my self, this is not what I am.’

mn22:17.1.verse: “Seeing thus, he is not agitated over what is not present.”

mn22:18.1.verse: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One,

mn22:18.2.verse: “Lord, might there be agitation over what is externally not present?”

mn22:18.3.verse: “There might, monk,” the Blessed One said.

mn22:18.4.verse: “There is the case where someone thinks,

mn22:18.5.verse: ‘O, it was mine! O, what was mine is not!

mn22:18.6.verse: O, may it be mine! O, I don’t obtain it!’

mn22:18.7.verse: He grieves & is tormented, weeps, beats his breast, & grows delirious.

mn22:18.8.verse: It’s thus that there is agitation over what is externally not present.”

mn22:19.1.verse: “But, lord, might there be non-agitation over what is externally not present?”

mn22:19.2.verse: “There might, monk,” the Blessed One said.

mn22:19.3.verse: “There is the case where someone doesn’t think,

mn22:19.4.verse: ‘O, it was mine! O, what was mine is not!

mn22:19.5.verse: O, may it be mine! O, I don’t obtain it!’

mn22:19.6.verse: He doesn’t grieve, isn’t tormented, doesn’t weep, beat his breast, or grow delirious.

mn22:19.7.verse: It’s thus that there is non-agitation over what is externally not present.”

mn22:20.1.verse: “But, lord, might there be agitation over what is internally not present?”

mn22:20.2.verse: “There might, monk,” the Blessed One said.

mn22:20.3.verse: “There is the case where someone has this view:

mn22:20.4.verse: ‘This cosmos is the self. After death this I will be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I will stay just like that for an eternity.’

mn22:20.5.verse: He hears a Tathāgata or a Tathāgata’s disciple teaching the Dhamma for the elimination of all view-positions, determinations, biases, inclinations, & obsessions; for the pacification of all fabrications; for the relinquishing of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.

mn22:20.7.verse: ‘So it might be that I will be annihilated! So it might be that I will perish! So it might be that I will not exist!’

mn22:20.8.verse: He grieves & is tormented, weeps, beats his breast, & grows delirious.

mn22:20.9.verse: It’s thus that there is agitation over what is internally not present.”

mn22:21.1.verse: “But, lord, might there be non-agitation over what is internally not present?”

mn22:21.2.verse: “There might, monk,” the Blessed One said.

mn22:21.3.verse: “There is the case where someone doesn’t have this view:

mn22:21.4.verse: ‘This cosmos is the self. After death this I will be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I will stay just like that for an eternity.’

mn22:21.5.verse: He hears a Tathāgata or a Tathāgata’s disciple teaching the Dhamma for the elimination of all view-positions, determinations, biases, inclinations, & obsessions; for the pacification of all fabrications; for the relinquishing of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.

mn22:21.6.verse: The thought doesn’t occur to him,

mn22:21.7.verse: ‘So it might be that I will be annihilated! So it might be that I will perish! So it might be that I will not exist!’

mn22:21.8.verse: He doesn’t grieve, isn’t tormented, doesn’t weep, beat his breast, or grow delirious.

mn22:21.9.verse: It’s thus that there is non-agitation over what is internally not present.”

mn22:22.1.verse: “Monks, you would do well to possess that possession, the possession of which would be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change, that would stay just like that for an eternity.

mn22:22.2.verse: But do you see that possession, the possession of which would be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change, that would stay just like that for an eternity?”

mn22:22.5.verse: I, too, do not envision a possession, the possession of which would be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change, that would stay just like that for an eternity.

mn22:23.1.verse: “Monks, you would do well to cling to that clinging to a doctrine of self, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair.

mn22:23.2.verse: But do you see a clinging to a doctrine of self, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair?”

mn22:23.5.verse: I, too, do not envision a clinging to a doctrine of self, clinging to which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair.

mn22:24.1.verse: “Monks, you would do well to depend on a view-dependency [diṭṭhi-nissaya], depending on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair.

mn22:24.2.verse: But do you see a view-dependency, depending on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair?”

mn22:24.5.verse: I, too, do not envision a view-dependency, depending on which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, & despair.

mn22:25.1.verse: “Monks, where there is a self, would there be (the thought,) ‘belonging to my self’?”

mn22:25.3.verse: “Or, monks, where there is what belongs to self, would there be (the thought,) ‘my self’?”

mn22:25.5.verse: “Monks, where a self or what belongs to self are not pinned down as a truth or reality, then the view-position—

mn22:25.6.verse: ‘This cosmos is the self. After death this I will be constant, permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I will stay just like that for an eternity’—

mn22:25.7.verse: Isn’t it utterly & completely a fool’s teaching?”

mn22:25.8.verse: “What else could it be, lord? It’s utterly & completely a fool’s teaching.”

mn22:26.4.verse: “And is that which is inconstant easeful or stressful?”

mn22:26.6.verse: “And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant, stressful, subject to change as:

mn22:26.7.verse: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?”

mn22:26.15.verse: “And is that which is inconstant easeful or stressful?”

mn22:26.17.verse: “And is it fitting to regard what is inconstant, stressful, subject to change as:

mn22:26.18.verse: ‘This is mine. This is my self. This is what I am’?”

mn22:27.1.verse: “Thus, monks, any form whatsoever that is past, future, or present; internal or external; blatant or subtle; common or sublime; far or near: Every form is to be seen as it has come to be with right discernment as: ‘This is not mine. This is not my self. This is not what I am.’

mn22:27.5.verse: “Any consciousness whatsoever that is past, future, or present; internal or external; blatant or subtle; common or sublime; far or near: Every consciousness is to be seen as it has come to be with right discernment as: ‘This is not mine. This is not my self. This is not what I am.’

mn22:28.1.verse: “Seeing thus, the instructed disciple of the noble ones grows disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with fabrications, disenchanted with consciousness.

mn22:29.1.verse: Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is released. With release, there is the knowledge, ‘Released.’

mn22:29.2.verse: He discerns that ‘Birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, the task done. There is nothing further for this world.’

mn22:30.1.verse: “This, monks, is called a monk whose cross-bar is thrown off, whose moat is filled in, whose pillar is pulled out, whose bolt is withdrawn, a noble one with banner lowered, burden placed down, unfettered.

mn22:31.1.verse: “And how is a monk one whose cross-bar is thrown off?

mn22:31.2.verse: There is the case where a monk’s ignorance is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn22:31.3.verse: This is how a monk is one whose cross-bar is thrown off.

mn22:32.1.verse: “And how is a monk one whose moat is filled in?

mn22:32.2.verse: There is the case where a monk’s wandering-on to birth, leading on to further-becoming, is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn22:32.3.verse: This is how a monk is one whose moat is filled in.

mn22:33.1.verse: “And how is a monk one whose pillar is pulled out?

mn22:33.2.verse: There is the case where a monk’s craving is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn22:33.3.verse: This is how a monk is one whose pillar is pulled out.

mn22:34.1.verse: “And how is a monk one whose bolt is withdrawn?

mn22:34.2.verse: There is the case where a monk’s five lower fetters are abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn22:34.3.verse: This is how a monk is one whose bolt is withdrawn.

mn22:35.1.verse: “And how is a monk a noble one with banner lowered, burden placed down, unfettered?

mn22:35.2.verse: There is the case where a monk’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn22:35.3.verse: This is how a monk is a noble one with banner lowered, burden placed down, unfettered.

mn22:36.1.verse: “And when the devas, together with Indra, the Brahmās, & Pajāpati, search for the monk whose mind is thus released, they cannot find that

mn22:36.2.verse: ‘The consciousness of the one truly gone [tathāgata] is dependent on this.’

mn22:36.4.verse: The one truly gone is untraceable even in the here & now.

mn22:37.1.verse: “Speaking in this way, teaching in this way, I have been erroneously, vainly, falsely, unfactually slandered by some contemplatives & brahmans (who say),

mn22:37.2.verse: ‘Gotama the contemplative is one who misleads. He declares the annihilation, destruction, extermination of the existing being.’

mn22:37.3.verse: But as I am not that, as I do not say that, so I have been erroneously, vainly, falsely, unfactually slandered by those venerable contemplatives & brahmans (who say),

mn22:37.4.verse: ‘Gotama the contemplative is one who misleads. He declares the annihilation, destruction, extermination of the existing being.’

mn22:37.5.verse: “Both formerly and now, monks, I declare only stress and the cessation of stress.

mn22:37.6.verse: And if others insult, abuse, taunt, bother, & harass the Tathāgata for that, he feels no hatred, no resentment, no dissatisfaction of heart because of that.

mn22:38.1.verse: And if others honor, respect, revere, & venerate the Tathāgata for that, he feels no joy, no happiness, no elation of heart because of that.

mn22:38.2.verse: And if others honor, respect, revere, & venerate the Tathāgata for that, he thinks,

mn22:38.3.verse: ‘They do me such service at this that has already been comprehended.’

mn22:39.1.verse: “Therefore, monks, if others insult, abuse, taunt, bother, & harass you as well, you should feel no hatred, no resentment, no dissatisfaction of heart because of that.

mn22:39.2.verse: And if others honor, respect, revere, & venerate you as well, you should feel no joy, no gladness, no elation of heart because of that.

mn22:39.3.verse: And if others honor, respect, revere, & venerate you, you should think,

mn22:39.4.verse: ‘They do us such service at this that has already been comprehended.’

mn22:40.1.verse: “Therefore, monks, whatever isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:40.2.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.2.verse: Form isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.3.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.4.verse: Feeling isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.5.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.6.verse: Perception isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.7.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.8.verse: Fabrications aren’t yours: Let go of them.

mn22:41.9.verse: Your letting go of them will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.10.verse: Consciousness isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.11.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.13.verse: If a person were to gather or burn or do as he likes with the grass, twigs, branches & leaves here in Jeta’s Grove,

mn22:41.14.verse: would the thought occur to you,

mn22:41.15.verse: ‘It’s us that this person is gathering, burning, or doing with as he likes’?”

mn22:41.18.verse: Because those things are not our self, nor do they belong to our self.”

mn22:41.19.verse: “Even so, monks, whatever isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.20.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.22.verse: Form isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.23.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:41.27.verse: Consciousness isn’t yours: Let go of it.

mn22:41.28.verse: Your letting go of it will be for your long-term welfare & happiness.

mn22:42.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:42.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—there is for those monks who are arahants—whose effluents are ended, who have reached fulfillment, done the task, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, totally destroyed the fetter of becoming, and who are released through right gnosis—no (future) cycle for manifestation. This is how the Dhamma well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:43.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:43.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—those monks who have abandoned the five lower fetters are all due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This is how the Dhamma well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:44.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:44.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—those monks who have abandoned (the first) three fetters, with the attenuation of passion, aversion, & delusion, are all once-returners who, on returning only one more time to this world, will make an ending to stress. This is how the Dhamma well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:45.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:45.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—those monks who have abandoned (the first) three fetters, are all stream-winners, certain, never again destined for the lower realms, headed for self-awakening. This is how the Dhamma well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:46.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:46.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—those monks who are Dhamma-followers and conviction-followers are all headed for self-awakening. This is how the Dhamma well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:47.1.verse: “The Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me is clear, open, evident, stripped of rags.

mn22:47.2.verse: In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me—clear, open, evident, stripped of rags—those monks who have a (sufficient) measure of conviction in me, a (sufficient) measure of love for me, are all headed for heaven.”

mn22:47.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn22:47.4.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn22:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn22:2.1.verse: Now at that time a mendicant named Ariṭṭha, who had previously been a vulture trapper, had the following harmful misconception:

mn22:2.2.verse: “As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the acts that he says are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them.”

mn22:3.1.verse: They went up to Ariṭṭha and said to him,

mn22:3.2.verse: “Is it really true, Reverend Ariṭṭha, that you have such a harmful misconception:

mn22:3.3.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the acts that he says are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them’?”

mn22:3.4.verse: “Indeed, reverends. As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the acts that he says are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them.”

mn22:3.5.verse: Then, wishing to dissuade Ariṭṭha from his view, the mendicants pursued, pressed, and grilled him,

mn22:3.6.verse: “Don’t say that, Ariṭṭha! Don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for misrepresentation of the Buddha is not good. And the Buddha would not say that.

mn22:3.7.verse: In many ways the Buddha has said that obstructive acts are obstructive, and that they really do obstruct the one who performs them.

mn22:3.8.verse: The Buddha says that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn22:3.9.verse: With the similes of a skeleton …

mn22:3.16.verse: a butcher’s knife and chopping board …

mn22:3.18.verse: a cobra’s head, the Buddha says that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.”

mn22:3.19.verse: But even though the mendicants pursued, pressed, and grilled him in this way, Ariṭṭha obstinately stuck to his misconception and insisted on it.

mn22:3.21.verse: When they weren’t able to dissuade Ariṭṭha from his view, the mendicants went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

mn22:5.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

mn22:5.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, that

mn22:5.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Ariṭṭha and said to him,

mn22:5.6.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Ariṭṭha replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn22:5.7.verse: “Is it really true, Ariṭṭha, that you have such a harmful misconception:

mn22:5.8.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the acts that he says are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them’?”

mn22:5.9.verse: “Indeed, sir. As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the acts that he says are obstructions are not really obstructions for the one who performs them.”

mn22:6.1.verse: “Futile man, who on earth have you ever known me to teach in that way?

mn22:6.2.verse: Haven’t I said in many ways that obstructive acts are obstructive, and that they really do obstruct the one who performs them?

mn22:6.3.verse: I’ve said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn22:6.4.verse: With the similes of a skeleton …

mn22:6.11.verse: a butcher’s knife and chopping board …

mn22:6.13.verse: a cobra’s head, I’ve said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn22:6.14.verse: But still you misrepresent me by your wrong grasp, harm yourself, and brim with much wickedness.

mn22:6.15.verse: This will be for your lasting harm and suffering.”

mn22:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn22:7.3.verse: Has this mendicant Ariṭṭha kindled even a spark of ardor in this teaching and training?”

mn22:7.6.verse: When this was said, Ariṭṭha sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

mn22:7.8.verse: “Futile man, you will be known by your own harmful misconception.

mn22:7.9.verse: I’ll question the mendicants about this.”

mn22:8.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn22:8.2.verse: “Mendicants, do you understand my teaching as Ariṭṭha does, when he misrepresents me by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and brims with much wickedness?”

mn22:8.4.verse: For in many ways the Buddha has told us that obstructive acts are obstructive, and that they really do obstruct the one who performs them.

mn22:8.6.verse: The Buddha has said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn22:8.7.verse: With the similes of a skeleton …

mn22:8.8.verse: a cobra’s head, the Buddha has said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.”

mn22:8.9.verse: “Good, good, mendicants! It’s good that you understand my teaching like this.

mn22:8.10.verse: For in many ways I have said that obstructive acts are obstructive …

mn22:8.13.verse: I’ve said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.

mn22:8.14.verse: But still this Ariṭṭha misrepresents me by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and brims with much wickedness.

mn22:8.15.verse: This will be for his lasting harm and suffering.

mn22:9.1.verse: Truly, mendicants, it is quite impossible to perform sensual acts without sensual desires, sensual perceptions, and sensual thoughts.

mn22:10.1.verse: Take a futile person who memorizes the teaching—

mn22:10.2.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

mn22:10.3.verse: But they don’t examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom,

mn22:10.4.verse: and so don’t come to an acceptance of them after deliberation.

mn22:10.5.verse: They memorize the teaching for the sake of finding fault and winning debates.

mn22:10.6.verse: They don’t realize the goal for which they memorized them.

mn22:10.7.verse: Because they’re wrongly grasped, those teachings lead to their lasting harm and suffering.

mn22:10.9.verse: Because of their wrong grasp of the teachings.

mn22:10.10.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of a cobra. And while wandering in search of a cobra

mn22:10.12.verse: and grasp it by the coil or the tail.

mn22:10.13.verse: But that cobra would twist back and bite them on the hand or the arm or other major or minor limb,

mn22:10.14.verse: resulting in death or deadly pain.

mn22:10.16.verse: Because of their wrong grasp of the cobra.

mn22:10.17.verse: In the same way, a futile person memorizes the teaching …

mn22:10.23.verse: and those teachings lead to their lasting harm and suffering.

mn22:10.25.verse: Because of their wrong grasp of the teachings.

mn22:11.1.verse: Now, take a gentleman who memorizes the teaching—

mn22:11.2.verse: statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.

mn22:11.3.verse: And once he’s memorized them, he examines their meaning with wisdom,

mn22:11.4.verse: and comes to an acceptance of them after deliberation.

mn22:11.5.verse: He doesn’t memorize the teaching for the sake of finding fault and winning debates.

mn22:11.6.verse: He realizes the goal for which he memorized them.

mn22:11.7.verse: Because they’re correctly grasped, those teachings lead to his lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:11.9.verse: Because of his correct grasp of the teachings.

mn22:11.10.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of a cobra. And while wandering in search of a cobra

mn22:11.12.verse: and hold it down carefully with a cleft stick.

mn22:11.13.verse: Only then would they correctly grasp it by the neck.

mn22:11.14.verse: And even though that cobra might wrap its coils around that person’s hand or arm or some other major or minor limb, that wouldn’t result in death or deadly pain.

mn22:11.16.verse: Because of their correct grasp of the cobra.

mn22:11.17.verse: In the same way, a gentleman memorizes the teaching …

mn22:11.23.verse: and those teachings lead to his lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:11.25.verse: Because of his correct grasp of the teachings.

mn22:12.1.verse: So, mendicants, when you understand what I’ve said, you should remember it accordingly.

mn22:12.2.verse: But if I’ve said anything that you don’t understand, you should ask me about it, or some competent mendicants.

mn22:13.1.verse: Mendicants, I will teach you a simile of the teaching as a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on.

mn22:13.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn22:13.5.verse: “Suppose there was a person traveling along the road.

mn22:13.6.verse: They’d see a large deluge, whose near shore was dubious and perilous, while the far shore was a sanctuary free of peril.

mn22:13.7.verse: But there was no ferryboat or bridge for crossing over.

mn22:13.11.verse: ‘Why don’t I gather grass, sticks, branches, and leaves and make a raft? Riding on the raft, and paddling with my hands and feet, I can safely reach the far shore.’

mn22:13.12.verse: And so they’d do exactly that.

mn22:13.13.verse: And when they’d crossed over to the far shore, they’d think,

mn22:13.14.verse: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me.

mn22:13.15.verse: Riding on the raft, and paddling with my hands and feet, I have safely crossed over to the far shore.

mn22:13.16.verse: Why don’t I hoist it on my head or pick it up on my shoulder and go wherever I want?’

mn22:13.18.verse: Would that person be doing what should be done with that raft?”

mn22:13.20.verse: “And what, mendicants, should that person do with the raft?

mn22:13.21.verse: When they’d crossed over they should think,

mn22:13.22.verse: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me. …

mn22:13.24.verse: Why don’t I beach it on dry land or set it adrift on the water and go wherever I want?’

mn22:13.25.verse: That’s what that person should do with the raft.

mn22:13.26.verse: In the same way, I have taught a simile of the teaching as a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on.

mn22:14.1.verse: By understanding the simile of the raft, you will even give up the teachings, let alone what is not the teachings.

mn22:15.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these six grounds for views.

mn22:15.3.verse: Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn22:15.4.verse: They regard form as: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

mn22:15.8.verse: whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind as: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

mn22:15.9.verse: And as for this ground for views:

mn22:15.10.verse: ‘The cosmos and the self are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’

mn22:15.11.verse: They regard this also as: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

mn22:16.1.verse: But a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn22:16.2.verse: They regard form like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn22:16.6.verse: whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn22:16.7.verse: And the same for this ground for views:

mn22:16.8.verse: ‘The cosmos and the self are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’

mn22:16.9.verse: They also regard like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn22:17.1.verse: Seeing in this way they’re not anxious about what doesn’t exist.”

mn22:18.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

mn22:18.2.verse: “Sir, can there be anxiety about what doesn’t exist externally?”

mn22:18.5.verse: ‘Oh, it once was mine but is mine no more.

mn22:18.6.verse: Oh, it could be mine but I do not get it.’

mn22:18.7.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn22:18.8.verse: That’s how there is anxiety about what doesn’t exist externally.”

mn22:19.1.verse: “But can there be no anxiety about what doesn’t exist externally?”

mn22:19.4.verse: ‘Oh, it once was mine but is mine no more.

mn22:19.5.verse: Oh, it could be mine but I do not get it.’

mn22:19.6.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn22:19.7.verse: That’s how there is no anxiety about what doesn’t exist externally.”

mn22:20.1.verse: “But can there be anxiety about what doesn’t exist internally?”

mn22:20.3.verse: “It’s when someone has such a view:

mn22:20.4.verse: ‘The cosmos and the self are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’

mn22:20.5.verse: They hear the Realized One or their disciple teaching Dhamma for the uprooting of all grounds, fixations, obsessions, insistences, and underlying tendencies regarding views; for the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

mn22:20.7.verse: ‘Whoa, I’m going to be annihilated and destroyed! I won’t even exist any more!’

mn22:20.8.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn22:20.9.verse: That’s how there is anxiety about what doesn’t exist internally.”

mn22:21.1.verse: “But can there be no anxiety about what doesn’t exist internally?”

mn22:21.3.verse: “It’s when someone doesn’t have such a view:

mn22:21.4.verse: ‘The cosmos and the self are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’

mn22:21.5.verse: They hear the Realized One or their disciple teaching Dhamma for the uprooting of all grounds, fixations, obsessions, insistences, and underlying tendencies regarding views; for the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

mn22:21.7.verse: ‘Whoa, I’m going to be annihilated and destroyed! I won’t even exist any more!’

mn22:21.8.verse: They don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn22:21.9.verse: That’s how there is no anxiety about what doesn’t exist internally.

mn22:22.1.verse: Mendicants, it would make sense to be possessive about something that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

mn22:22.2.verse: But do you see any such possession?”

mn22:22.5.verse: I also can’t see any such possession.

mn22:23.1.verse: It would make sense to grasp at a theory of self that didn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn22:23.2.verse: But do you see any such theory of self?”

mn22:23.5.verse: I also can’t see any such theory of self.

mn22:24.1.verse: It would make sense to rely on a view that didn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn22:24.2.verse: But do you see any such view to rely on?”

mn22:24.5.verse: I also can’t see any such view to rely on.

mn22:25.1.verse: Mendicants, were a self to exist, would there be the thought, ‘Belonging to my self’?”

mn22:25.3.verse: “Were what belongs to a self to exist, would there be the thought, ‘My self’?”

mn22:25.5.verse: “But since a self and what belongs to a self are not found as a genuine fact, is not the following a totally foolish teaching:

mn22:25.6.verse: ‘The cosmos and the self are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever’?”

mn22:25.8.verse: “How could it not, sir? It’s a totally foolish teaching.”

mn22:26.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn22:26.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn22:26.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn22:26.15.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn22:26.17.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn22:26.18.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn22:27.1.verse: “So, mendicants, you should truly see any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn22:27.2.verse: You should truly see any kind of feeling …

mn22:27.5.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn22:28.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn22:29.1.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn22:29.2.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn22:30.1.verse: Such a mendicant is one who is called ‘one who has lifted the cross-bar’, ‘one who has filled in the moat’, ‘one who has pulled up the pillar’, ‘one who is unimpeded’, and also ‘a noble one with banner lowered and burden dropped, detached’.

mn22:31.1.verse: And how has a mendicant raised the cross-bar?

mn22:31.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn22:31.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has lifted the cross-bar.

mn22:32.1.verse: And how has a mendicant filled in the moat?

mn22:32.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up transmigrating through births in future lives, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn22:32.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has filled in the moat.

mn22:33.1.verse: And how has a mendicant pulled up the pillar?

mn22:33.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn22:33.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant has pulled up the pillar.

mn22:34.1.verse: And how is a mendicant unimpeded?

mn22:34.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up the five lower fetters, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they’re unable to arise in the future.

mn22:34.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is unimpeded.

mn22:35.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a noble one with with banner lowered and burden dropped, detached?

mn22:35.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up the conceit ‘I am’, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn22:35.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a noble one with banner lowered and burden dropped, detached.

mn22:36.1.verse: When a mendicant’s mind was freed like this, the gods together with Indra, the Divinity, and the Progenitor, search as they may, will not discover:

mn22:36.2.verse: ‘This is the basis of that realized one’s consciousness.’

mn22:36.4.verse: Because even in this very life that realized one is not found, I say.

mn22:37.1.verse: Though I state and assert this, certain ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with the incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim:

mn22:37.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an exterminator. He advocates the annihilation, eradication, and nonexistence of an existing being.’

mn22:37.3.verse: They misrepresent me as what I am not, and saying what I do not say.

mn22:37.5.verse: In the past, as today, what I describe is suffering and the cessation of suffering.

mn22:37.6.verse: This being so, if others abuse, attack, harass, and trouble the Realized One, he doesn’t get resentful, bitter, and emotionally exasperated.

mn22:38.1.verse: Or if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate him, he doesn’t get thrilled, elated, and emotionally excited.

mn22:38.2.verse: If they praise him, he just thinks,

mn22:38.3.verse: ‘They do such things for me regarding what in the past was completely understood.’

mn22:39.1.verse: So, mendicants, if others abuse, attack, harass, and trouble you, don’t make yourselves resentful, bitter, and emotionally exasperated.

mn22:39.2.verse: Or if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate you, don’t make yourselves thrilled, elated, and emotionally excited.

mn22:39.3.verse: If they praise you, just think,

mn22:39.4.verse: ‘They do such things for us regarding what in the past was completely understood.’

mn22:40.1.verse: So, mendicants, give up what isn’t yours.

mn22:40.2.verse: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:41.2.verse: Form isn’t yours: give it up.

mn22:41.3.verse: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:41.10.verse: consciousness isn’t yours: give it up.

mn22:41.11.verse: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:41.13.verse: Suppose a person was to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do what they want with them.

mn22:41.15.verse: ‘This person is carrying us off, burning us, or doing what they want with us’?”

mn22:41.18.verse: Because  to us that’s neither self nor belonging to self.”

mn22:41.19.verse: “In the same way, mendicants, give up what isn’t yours.

mn22:41.20.verse: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:41.27.verse: consciousness isn’t yours: give it up.

mn22:41.28.verse: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn22:42.1.verse: The teaching well-explained thus by me is clarified, revealed, illuminated, and stripped of patchwork.

mn22:42.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, for those mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment, there is no cycle of rebirths to be found. …

mn22:43.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, those mendicants who have given up the five lower fetters are all reborn spontaneously. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world. …

mn22:44.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, those mendicants who, having given up three fetters, and weakened greed, hate, and delusion, are all once-returners. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering. …

mn22:45.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, those mendicants who have ended three fetters are all stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening. …

mn22:46.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, those mendicants who are followers of teachings or followers by faith are all are assured, destined for awakening.

mn22:47.1.verse: The teaching well-explained thus by me is clarified, revealed, illuminated, and stripped of patchwork.

mn22:47.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, those who have a degree of faith and love for me are all bound for heaven.”

mn22:47.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn22:47.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn23:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn23:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Kassapa the Prince was staying in the Dark Forest.

mn23:1.4.verse: Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Dark Forest, went up to Kassapa the Prince, stood to one side, and said:

mn23:2.1.verse: “Monk, monk! This termite mound fumes by night and flames by day.

mn23:2.3.verse: ‘Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.4.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a sticking point:

mn23:2.8.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.9.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a bullfrog:

mn23:2.13.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.14.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a forked path:

mn23:2.18.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.19.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a filter of ash:

mn23:2.23.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.24.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a tortoise:

mn23:2.28.verse: Dig, clever one, having taken up the sword!’

mn23:2.29.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a butcher’s knife and chopping board:

mn23:2.30.verse: ‘A butcher’s knife and chopping board, sir!’

mn23:2.32.verse: ‘Throw out the butcher’s knife and chopping board!

mn23:2.33.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.34.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a scrap of meat:

mn23:2.38.verse: Dig, clever one, having picked up the sword!’

mn23:2.39.verse: Picking up the sword and digging, the clever one saw a king cobra:

mn23:2.42.verse: ‘Leave the king cobra! Do not disturb the cobra! Worship the cobra!’

mn23:2.43.verse: Mendicant, go to the Buddha and ask him about this riddle. You should remember it in line with his answer.

mn23:2.44.verse: I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could provide a satisfying answer to this riddle except the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.”

mn23:2.45.verse: That is what that deity said

mn23:3.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, Kassapa the Prince went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. Then he asked:

mn23:3.10.verse: “Sir, what is the termite mound? What is the fuming by night and flaming by day? Who is the brahmin, and who the clever one? What are the sword, the digging, the sticking point, the bullfrog, the forked path, the filter of ash, the tortoise, the butcher’s knife and chopping board, and the scrap of meat? And what is the king cobra?”

mn23:4.1.verse: “Mendicant, ‘termite mound’ is a term for this body made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

mn23:4.2.verse: Thinking and considering all night about what you did during the day—

mn23:4.3.verse: this is the fuming at night.

mn23:4.4.verse: The work you apply yourself to during the day by body, speech, and mind after thinking about it all night—

mn23:4.5.verse: this is the flaming by day.

mn23:4.6.verse: ‘Brahmin’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn23:4.7.verse: ‘Clever one’ is a term for the trainee mendicant.

mn23:4.8.verse: ‘Sword’ is a term for noble wisdom.

mn23:4.9.verse: ‘Digging’ is a term for rousing energy.

mn23:4.10.verse: ‘Sticking point’ is a term for ignorance.

mn23:4.11.verse: ‘Throw out the sticking point’ means ‘give up ignorance,

mn23:4.12.verse: dig, clever one, having picked up the sword.’

mn23:4.13.verse: ‘Bullfrog’ is a term for anger and distress.

mn23:4.14.verse: ‘Throw out the bullfrog’ means ‘give up anger and distress’ …

mn23:4.16.verse: ‘A forked path’ is a term for doubt.

mn23:4.17.verse: ‘Throw out the forked path’ means ‘give up doubt’ …

mn23:4.19.verse: ‘A filter of ash’ is a term for the five hindrances, that is:

mn23:4.20.verse: the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

mn23:4.21.verse: ‘Throw out the filter of ash’ means ‘give up the five hindrances’ …

mn23:4.23.verse: ‘Tortoise’ is a term for the five grasping aggregates, that is:

mn23:4.24.verse: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn23:4.25.verse: ‘Throw out the tortoise’ means ‘give up the five grasping aggregates’ …

mn23:4.27.verse: ‘Butcher’s knife and chopping board’ is a term for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn23:4.28.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn23:4.32.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn23:4.33.verse: ‘Throw out the butcher’s knife and chopping board’ means ‘give up the five kinds of sensual stimulation’ …

mn23:4.35.verse: ‘Scrap of meat’ is a term for greed and relishing.

mn23:4.36.verse: ‘Throw out the scrap of meat’ means ‘give up greed and relishing’ …

mn23:4.38.verse: ‘King cobra’ is a term for a mendicant who has ended the defilements.

mn23:4.39.verse: This is the meaning of: ‘Leave the king cobra! Do not disturb the cobra! Worship the cobra!’”

mn23:4.40.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn23:4.41.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Kassapa the Prince approved what the Buddha said.

mn24:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn24:2.1.verse: Then a number of bhikkhus from (the Blessed One’s) native land who had spent the Rains there, went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, the Blessed One asked them:

mn24:2.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, who is there in (my) native land that is esteemed by the bhikkhus of (my) native land, his companions in the life divine, in this way:

mn24:2.3.verse: with few wishes himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on fewness of wishes; content himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on contentment; secluded himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on seclusion; aloof from society himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on aloofness from society; energetic himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on energy; perfect in virtue himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on perfection of virtue; perfect in concentration himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on perfection of concentration; perfect in understanding himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on perfection of understanding; perfect in deliverance himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on perfection of deliverance; perfect in the knowing and seeing of deliverance himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on perfection in knowing and seeing deliverance; who advises, informs, instructs, urges, rouses and encourages his companions in the life divine?’

mn24:2.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the venerable Mantāniputta called Punna is esteemed in the native land by bhikkhus of the native land, his companions in the life divine, in this way:

mn24:2.5.verse: with few wishes himself, he talks to the bhikkhus on fewness of wishes … rouses and encourages his companions in the life divine.’

mn24:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Sāriputta was seated near the Blessed One.

mn24:3.2.verse: Then it occurred to the venerable Sāriputta:

mn24:3.3.verse: ‘It is gain for the venerable Punna Mantāniputta, it is great gain for him

mn24:3.4.verse: that wise companions in the life divine praise him point by point in the Master’s presence.

mn24:3.5.verse: Now suppose that sometime or other, we were to meet the venerable Punna Mantāniputta and have some conversation with him?’

mn24:4.1.verse: Then, when the Blessed One had stayed at Rājagaha as long as he chose, he set out to go by stages to Sāvatthi.

mn24:4.2.verse: Wandering by stages, he at length arrived at Sāvatthi.

mn24:4.3.verse: There he lived in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn24:4.4.verse: The venerable Punna Mantāniputta heard: ‘The Blessed One, it seems, has arrived at Sāvatthi and is living in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.’

mn24:5.1.verse: Then the venerable Punna Mantāniputta set his resting-place in order and taking his outer robe and bowl set out to go by stages to Sāvatthi.

mn24:5.2.verse: Wandering by stages, he at length arrived at Sāvatthi (and he went) to Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park, to (see) the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.

mn24:5.3.verse: When he had done so, the Blessed One instructed, roused and encouraged him with talk on the Dhamma.

mn24:5.4.verse: Then satisfied and delighting in the Blessed One’s words, the venerable Punna Mantāniputta rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he went to the Blind Mens’ Grove for the day’s abiding.

mn24:6.1.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu went to the venerable Sāriputta and said to him:

mn24:6.2.verse: ‘Friend Sāriputta, the bhikkhu Punna Mantāniputta of whom you have always spoken highly has just been instructed, urged, roused and encouraged by the Blessed One with talk on the Dhamma and being satisfied and delighting in the Blessed One’s words, he has now risen from his seat, and after paying homage to him, keeping him on his right, he is going to the Blind Mens’ Grove for the day’s abiding.’

mn24:7.1.verse: Then the venerable Sāriputta quickly picked up a mat and followed close behind the venerable Punna Mantāniputta, keeping his head in sight.

mn24:7.2.verse: Then the venerable Punna Mantāniputta went in to the Blind Mens’ Grove and sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a tree.

mn24:7.3.verse: And the venerable Sāriputta went into the Blind Mens’ Grove and sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a tree.

mn24:8.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Sāriputta rose from meditation, and went to the venerable Punna Mantāniputta and exchanged greetings with him,

mn24:8.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the venerable Punna Mantāniputta:

mn24:9.1.verse: ‘Is the life divine lived under the Blessed One, friend?’

mn24:9.3.verse: ‘But, friend, is it for the goal of purification of virtue that the life divine is lived under the Blessed One?’

mn24:9.5.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification of mind?’

mn24:9.7.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification of view?’

mn24:9.9.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification by overcoming doubt?’

mn24:9.11.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path?’

mn24:9.13.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification by knowledge and vision of the way?’

mn24:9.15.verse: ‘Then is it for the goal of purification by knowledge and vision?’

mn24:10.1.verse: ‘Friend, when asked: “But, friend is it for the goal of purification of virtue that the life divine is lived under the Blessed One”, you replied: “No, friend”,

mn24:10.2.verse: and when asked: “Then is it for the goal of purification of mind

mn24:10.5.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the Path

mn24:10.6.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision of the Way

mn24:10.7.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision” you replied: “No, friend”.

mn24:10.8.verse: For what goal, then, is the life divine lived under the Blessed One?’

mn24:10.9.verse: ‘Friend, it is for the goal of Nibbāna through not clinging that the life divine is lived under the Blessed One.’

mn24:11.1.verse: ‘But, friend, is the purification of virtue Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.3.verse: ‘Then is the purification of mind Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.5.verse: ‘Then is the purification of view Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.7.verse: ‘Then is the purification by overcoming doubt Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.9.verse: ‘Then is the purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the Path Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.11.verse: ‘Then is the purification by knowledge and vision of the Way Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.13.verse: ‘Then is the purification by knowledge and vision Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:11.15.verse: ‘Then is it apart from these dhammas that there is Nibbāna through not clinging?’

mn24:12.1.verse: ‘When asked: “But, friend, is the purification of virtue Nibbāna through not clinging?” you replied: “No, friend”,

mn24:12.2.verse: and when asked: “Then is the purification of mind

mn24:12.5.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the Path

mn24:12.6.verse: … the purification by knowledge and vision of the Way

mn24:12.7.verse: … the purification by knowledge and vision Nibbāna through not clinging?” you replied: “No, friend”.

mn24:12.8.verse: And when asked: “Is it apart from these dhammas that there is Nibbāna through not clinging?” you replied: “No, friend”.

mn24:12.9.verse: But how should the meaning of these statements be regarded?’

mn24:13.1.verse: ‘Friend, if the Blessed One had described purification of virtue as Nibbāna through not clinging, he would have described what is still accompanied by clinging as Nibbāna through not clinging.

mn24:13.2.verse: If the Blessed One had described purification of mind

mn24:13.5.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the Path

mn24:13.6.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision of the Way

mn24:13.7.verse: … purification by knowledge and vision as Nibbāna through not clinging, he would have described what is still accompanied by clinging as Nibbāna through not clinging.

mn24:13.8.verse: And if what is without these dhammas were Nibbāna through not clinging, then an ordinary man would have reached Nibbāna,

mn24:13.9.verse: for an ordinary man is without these dhammas.’

mn24:14.1.verse: ‘As to that, friend, I shall give you a simile,

mn24:14.2.verse: for some wise men understand by means of a simile the meaning of what is said first.

mn24:14.3.verse: Suppose the King Pasenadi of Kosala while living at Sāvatthi had some urgent business to settle at Sāketa,

mn24:14.4.verse: and that between Sāvatthi and Sāketa seven relay coaches were kept ready for him;

mn24:14.5.verse: and then King Pasenadi of Kosala came out of the inner palace door in Sāvatthi and mounted the first relay coach; and by means of the first relay coach he arrived at the second relay coach; then he dismounted from the first coach and mounted the second coach;

mn24:14.6.verse: and by means of the second coach he arrived at the third coach …

mn24:14.7.verse: by means of the third coach he arrived at the fourth coach …

mn24:14.8.verse: by means of the fourth coach he arrived at the fifth coach …

mn24:14.9.verse: by means of the fifth coach he arrived at the sixth coach …

mn24:14.10.verse: by means of the sixth coach he arrived at the seventh coach,

mn24:14.11.verse: and by means of the seventh coach he arrived at the inner palace door in Sāketa.

mn24:14.12.verse: Then, when he had come to the inner palace door, his friends and acquaintances, his relatives and kin, asked him:

mn24:14.13.verse: “Sire, did you come from Sāvatthi by means of this coach to the inner palace door in Sāketa?”—

mn24:14.14.verse: how then should King Pasenadi of Kosala answer in order to answer correctly?”

mn24:14.15.verse: ‘In order to answer correctly, friend, he should answer thus:

mn24:14.16.verse: “Here while living at Sāvatthi I had some urgent business to settle at Sāketa.

mn24:14.17.verse: And between Sāvatthi and Sāketa seven relay coaches are kept ready for me.

mn24:14.18.verse: Then I came out of the inner palace door in Sāvatthi and mounted the first relay coach

mn24:14.19.verse: and by means of the first relay coach I arrived at the second …

mn24:14.20.verse: and by means of the second coach I arrived at the third …

mn24:14.21.verse: and by means of the third coach I arrived at the fourth …

mn24:14.22.verse: and by means of the fourth coach I arrived at the fifth …

mn24:14.23.verse: and by means of the fifth coach I arrived at the sixth …

mn24:14.24.verse: and by means of the sixth coach I arrived at the seventh —

mn24:14.25.verse: and by means of the seventh relay coach I arrived at the inner palace door in Sāketa.”

mn24:14.26.verse: In order to answer correctly he should answer thus.’
