mn26:13.4.verse: Why don’t I seek that which is free of rebirth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, extinguishment?’

mn26:14.1.verse: Some time later, while still with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life—though my mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn26:15.1.verse: Once I had gone forth I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn26:15.2.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn26:15.5.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn26:15.7.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn26:15.9.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn26:15.10.verse: Surely he meditates knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn26:15.11.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn26:15.12.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, to what extent do you say you’ve realized this teaching with your own insight?’

mn26:15.13.verse: When I said this, he declared the dimension of nothingness.

mn26:15.15.verse: ‘It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith,

mn26:15.19.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn26:15.20.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma says he has realized with his own insight?’

mn26:15.21.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn26:15.22.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn26:15.23.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, is it up to this point that you realized this teaching with your own insight, and declare having achieved it?’

mn26:15.25.verse: ‘I too, reverend, have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn26:15.26.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn26:15.27.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn26:15.28.verse: So the teaching that I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn26:15.29.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it.

mn26:15.30.verse: So the teaching that I know, you know, and the teaching that you know, I know.

mn26:15.31.verse: I am like you and you are like me.

mn26:15.32.verse: Come now, reverend! We should both lead this community together.’

mn26:15.33.verse: And that is how my tutor Āḷāra Kālāma placed me, his pupil, on the same position as him, and honored me with high praise.

mn26:15.35.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of nothingness.’

mn26:15.36.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn26:16.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn26:16.2.verse: ‘Reverend, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn26:16.5.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn26:16.7.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn26:16.9.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Rāma declared: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn26:16.10.verse: Surely he meditated knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn26:16.11.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn26:16.12.verse: ‘Reverend, to what extent did Rāma say he’d realized this teaching with his own insight?’

mn26:16.13.verse: When I said this, Uddaka son of Rāma declared the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn26:16.15.verse: ‘It’s not just Rāma who had faith,

mn26:16.19.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn26:16.20.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Rāma said he had realized with his own insight?’

mn26:16.21.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn26:16.22.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn26:16.23.verse: ‘Reverend, had Rāma realized this teaching with his own insight up to this point, and declared having achieved it?’

mn26:16.25.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn26:16.26.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn26:16.27.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn26:16.28.verse: So the teaching that Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn26:16.29.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it.

mn26:16.30.verse: So the teaching that Rāma directly knew, you know, and the teaching you know, Rāma directly knew.

mn26:16.31.verse: Rāma was like you and you are like Rāma.

mn26:16.32.verse: Come now, reverend! You should lead this community.’

mn26:16.33.verse: And that is how my spiritual companion Uddaka son of Rāma placed me in the position of a tutor and honored me with high praise.

mn26:16.35.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn26:16.36.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn26:17.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. Traveling stage by stage in the Magadhan lands, I arrived at the town of Senā in Uruvelā.

mn26:17.2.verse: There I saw a delightful park, a lovely grove with a flowing river that was clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby was a village to resort to for alms.

mn26:17.4.verse: ‘This park is truly delightful, a lovely grove with a flowing river that’s clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby there’s a village to resort to for alms.

mn26:17.5.verse: This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.’

mn26:17.6.verse: So I sat down right there, thinking,

mn26:18.1.verse: And so, being myself liable to be reborn, understanding the drawbacks in being liable to be reborn, I sought that which is free of rebirth, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, extinguishment—and I found it. Being myself liable to grow old, fall sick, die, sorrow, and become corrupted, understanding the drawbacks in these things, I sought that which is free of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, extinguishment—and I found it.

mn26:18.2.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

mn26:18.3.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’

mn26:19.2.verse: ‘This principle I have discovered is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

mn26:19.3.verse: But people like clinging, they love it and enjoy it.

mn26:19.4.verse: It’s hard for them to see this topic; that is, specific conditionality, dependent origination.

mn26:19.5.verse: It’s also hard for them to see this topic; that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

mn26:19.6.verse: And if I were to teach this principle, others might not understand me, which would be wearying and troublesome for me.’

mn26:19.7.verse: And then these verses, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me:

mn26:19.9.verse: there’s no need to reveal it now!

mn26:19.10.verse: Those mired in greed and hate

mn26:19.12.verse: It goes against the stream, subtle,

mn26:19.14.verse: Those besotted by greed cannot see,

mn26:19.15.verse: for they’re cloaked in a mass of darkness.’

mn26:19.16.verse: So, as I reflected like this, my mind inclined to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.

mn26:20.1.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing my train of thought, thought,

mn26:20.2.verse: ‘Oh lord! The world will be lost, the world will perish! For the mind of the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, inclines to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.’

mn26:20.3.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, the divinity Sahampati vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of me.

mn26:20.4.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward me, and said,

mn26:20.5.verse: ‘Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach the Dhamma!

mn26:20.6.verse: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching.

mn26:20.7.verse: There will be those who understand the teaching!’

mn26:20.8.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

mn26:20.9.verse: Then he went on to say:

mn26:20.10.verse: ‘Among the Magadhans there appeared in the past

mn26:20.11.verse: an impure teaching thought up by the stained.

mn26:20.12.verse: Fling open the door to freedom from death!

mn26:20.13.verse: Let them hear the teaching the immaculate one discovered.

mn26:20.14.verse: Standing high on a rocky mountain,

mn26:20.15.verse: you can see the people all around.

mn26:20.16.verse: In just the same way, All-seer, so intelligent,

mn26:20.17.verse: having ascended the Temple of Truth,

mn26:20.18.verse: rid of sorrow, look upon the people

mn26:20.19.verse: swamped with sorrow, overcome by rebirth and old age.

mn26:20.20.verse: Rise, hero! Victor in battle, caravan leader,

mn26:20.21.verse: wander the world free of debt.

mn26:20.22.verse: Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma!

mn26:20.23.verse: There will be those who understand!’

mn26:21.1.verse: Then, understanding the Divinity’s invitation, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, because of my compassion for sentient beings.

mn26:21.2.verse: And I saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes; with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach. And some of them lived seeing the danger in the fault to do with the next world, while others did not.

mn26:21.3.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. Some of them sprout and grow in the water reaching the water’s surface. And some of them sprout and grow in the water but rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to them.

mn26:21.4.verse: In the same way, I saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes.

mn26:21.5.verse: Then I replied in verse to the divinity Sahampati:

mn26:21.6.verse: ‘Flung open are the doors to freedom from death!

mn26:21.7.verse: Let those with ears to hear commit to faith.

mn26:21.8.verse: Thinking it would be troublesome, Divinity, I did not teach

mn26:21.9.verse: the sophisticated, sublime Dhamma among mankind.’

mn26:21.10.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing that his request for me to teach the Dhamma had been granted, bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right, before vanishing right there.

mn26:22.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn26:22.3.verse: Who will quickly understand this teaching?’

mn26:22.5.verse: ‘That Āḷāra Kālāma is astute, competent, intelligent, and has long had little dust in his eyes.

mn26:22.6.verse: Why don’t I teach him first of all?

mn26:22.8.verse: But a deity came to me and said,

mn26:22.9.verse: ‘Sir, Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’

mn26:22.10.verse: And knowledge and vision arose in me,

mn26:22.11.verse: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’

mn26:22.13.verse: ‘This is a great loss for Āḷāra Kālāma.

mn26:22.14.verse: If he had heard the teaching, he would have understood it quickly.’

mn26:23.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn26:23.3.verse: Who will quickly understand this teaching?’

mn26:23.5.verse: ‘That Uddaka son of Rāma is astute, competent, intelligent, and has long had little dust in his eyes.

mn26:23.6.verse: Why don’t I teach him first of all?

mn26:23.8.verse: But a deity came to me and said,

mn26:23.9.verse: ‘Sir, Uddaka son of Rāma passed away just last night.’

mn26:23.10.verse: And knowledge and vision arose in me,

mn26:23.11.verse: ‘Uddaka son of Rāma passed away just last night.’

mn26:23.13.verse: ‘This is a great loss for Uddaka.

mn26:23.14.verse: If he had heard the teaching, he would have understood it quickly.’

mn26:24.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn26:24.3.verse: Who will quickly understand this teaching?’

mn26:24.5.verse: ‘The group of five mendicants were very helpful to me. They looked after me during my time of resolute striving.

mn26:24.6.verse: Why don’t I teach them first of all?’

mn26:24.8.verse: ‘Where are the group of five mendicants staying these days?’

mn26:24.9.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman I saw that the group of five mendicants were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

mn26:24.10.verse: So, when I had stayed in Uruvelā as long as I pleased, I set out for Varanasi.

mn26:25.1.verse: While I was traveling along the road between Gayā and Bodhgaya, the Ājīvaka ascetic Upaka saw me

mn26:25.3.verse: ‘Reverend, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

mn26:25.4.verse: In whose name have you gone forth, reverend? Who is your Teacher? Whose teaching do you believe in?’

mn26:25.5.verse: I replied to Upaka in verse:

mn26:25.6.verse: ‘I am the vanquisher of all, the knower of all,

mn26:25.7.verse: unsullied in the midst of all things.

mn26:25.8.verse: I’ve given up all, freed through the ending of craving.

mn26:25.9.verse: Since I know for myself, whose follower should I be?

mn26:25.11.verse: There is no one like me.

mn26:25.12.verse: In the world with its gods,

mn26:25.14.verse: For in this world, I am the perfected one;

mn26:25.18.verse: I am going to the city of Kāsi

mn26:25.19.verse: to roll forth the Wheel of Dhamma.

mn26:25.20.verse: In this world that is so blind,

mn26:25.21.verse: I’ll beat the drum of freedom from death!’

mn26:25.22.verse: ‘According to what you claim, reverend, you ought to be the Infinite Victor.’

mn26:25.23.verse: ‘The victors are those who, like me,

mn26:25.24.verse: have reached the ending of defilements.

mn26:25.25.verse: I have conquered bad qualities, Upaka—

mn26:25.27.verse: When I had spoken, Upaka said: ‘If you say so, reverend.’ Shaking his head, he took a wrong turn and left.

mn26:26.1.verse: Traveling stage by stage, I arrived at Varanasi, and went to see the group of five mendicants in the deer park at Isipatana.

mn26:26.2.verse: The group of five mendicants saw me coming off in the distance

mn26:26.4.verse: ‘Here comes the ascetic Gotama. He’s so indulgent; he strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.

mn26:26.5.verse: We shouldn’t bow to him or rise for him or receive his bowl and robe.

mn26:26.6.verse: But we can set out a seat; he can sit if he likes.’

mn26:26.7.verse: Yet as I drew closer, the group of five mendicants were unable to stop themselves per their own agreement.

mn26:26.8.verse: Some came out to greet me and receive my bowl and robe, some spread out a seat, while others set out water for washing my feet.

mn26:26.9.verse: But they still addressed me by name and as ‘reverend’.

mn26:27.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, don’t address me by name and as “reverend”.

mn26:27.3.verse: The Realized One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn26:27.4.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn26:27.5.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn26:27.7.verse: ‘Reverend Gotama, even by that conduct, that practice, that grueling work you did not achieve any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How could you have achieved such a state now that you’ve become indulgent, strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence?’

mn26:27.9.verse: ‘The Realized One has not become indulgent, strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.

mn26:27.10.verse: The Realized One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn26:27.11.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn26:27.12.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life.’

mn26:27.13.verse: But for a second time they said to me,

mn26:27.15.verse: So for a second time I said to them,

mn26:27.16.verse: ‘The Realized One has not become indulgent …’

mn26:27.18.verse: But for a third time they said to me,

mn26:27.19.verse: ‘Reverend Gotama, even by that conduct, that practice, that grueling work you did not achieve any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How could you have achieved such a state now that you’ve become indulgent, strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence?’

mn26:28.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, have you ever known me to speak like this before?’

mn26:28.4.verse: ‘The Realized One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn26:28.5.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn26:28.6.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn26:29.1.verse: I was able to persuade the group of five mendicants.

mn26:29.2.verse: Then sometimes I advised two mendicants, while the other three went for alms.

mn26:29.3.verse: Then those three would feed all six of us with what they brought back.

mn26:29.4.verse: Sometimes I advised three mendicants, while the other two went for alms.

mn26:29.5.verse: Then those two would feed all six of us with what they brought back.

mn26:30.1.verse: As the group of five mendicants were being advised and instructed by me like this, being themselves liable to be reborn, understanding the drawbacks in being liable to be reborn, they sought that which is free of rebirth, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, extinguishment—and they found it. Being themselves liable to grow old, fall sick, die, sorrow, and become corrupted, understanding the drawbacks in these things, they sought that which is free of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and corruption, the supreme sanctuary from the yoke, extinguishment—and they found it.

mn26:30.2.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in them:

mn26:30.3.verse: ‘Our freedom is unshakable; this is our last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’

mn26:31.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn26:31.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn26:31.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn26:31.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn26:32.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who enjoy these five kinds of sensual stimulation tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape. You should understand that they

mn26:32.2.verse: have met with calamity and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

mn26:32.3.verse: Suppose a deer in the wilderness was lying caught on a pile of snares.

mn26:32.5.verse: has met with calamity and disaster, and the hunter can do with them what he wants.

mn26:32.6.verse: And when the hunter comes, it cannot flee where it wants.

mn26:32.7.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who enjoy these five kinds of sensual stimulation tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape. You should understand that they

mn26:32.8.verse: have met with calamity and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

mn26:33.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who enjoy these five kinds of sensual stimulation without being tied, infatuated, or attached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape. You should understand that they

mn26:33.2.verse: haven’t met with calamity and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do what he wants with them.

mn26:33.3.verse: Suppose a deer in the wilderness was lying on a pile of snares without being caught.

mn26:33.5.verse: hasn’t met with calamity and disaster, and the hunter cannot do what he wants with them.

mn26:33.6.verse: And when the hunter comes, it can flee where it wants.

mn26:33.7.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who enjoy these five kinds of sensual stimulation without being tied, infatuated, or attached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape. You should understand that they

mn26:33.8.verse: haven’t met with calamity and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do what he wants with them.

mn26:34.1.verse: Suppose there was a wild deer wandering in the forest that walked, stood, sat, and laid down in confidence.

mn26:34.3.verse: Because it’s out of the hunter’s range.

mn26:34.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn26:34.5.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

mn26:35.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn26:35.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:36.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn26:36.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:37.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn26:37.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:38.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

mn26:38.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:39.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn26:39.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:40.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn26:40.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:41.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn26:41.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra …

mn26:42.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

mn26:42.2.verse: This is called a mendicant who has blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see.

mn26:42.3.verse: They’ve crossed over clinging to the world. And they walk, stand, sit, and lie down in confidence.

mn26:42.5.verse: Because they’re out of the Wicked One’s range.”

mn26:42.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn26:42.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn27:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn27:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion Jānussoni of the divine caste drove in broad day through Sāvatthī in a chariot drawn by mares, all in white.

mn27:2.2.verse: He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming.

mn27:2.3.verse: When he saw him, he asked him:

mn27:2.4.verse: ‘Now where is Master Vacchāyana coming from in broad day?’

mn27:2.5.verse: ‘Sir, I am coming from the monk Gotama’s presence.’

mn27:2.6.verse: ‘How does Master Vacchāyana conceive the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding? He is wise, is he not?’

mn27:2.7.verse: ‘Sir, who am I to know the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding.

mn27:2.8.verse: One would surely have to be his equal to know the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding.’

mn27:2.9.verse: ‘Master Vacchāyana praises the monk Gotama with high praise indeed.’

mn27:2.10.verse: ‘Sir, who am I to praise the monk Gotama,

mn27:2.11.verse: the monk Gotama is praised by the praised—as best among gods and men.’

mn27:2.12.verse: ‘What value does Master Vacchāyana see that he has such confidence in the monk Gotama?’

mn27:3.1.verse: ‘Sir, suppose a wise elephant-woodsman went into an elephant wood,

mn27:3.2.verse: and he saw in the elephant wood a big elephant’s footprint long in extent and broad across,

mn27:3.4.verse: “It is a bull elephant and a big one.”

mn27:3.5.verse: So too, as soon as I saw four footprints in the monk Gotama, I concluded:

mn27:3.6.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”

mn27:4.2.verse: ‘Sir, I have seen here certain warrior-noble caste scholars that were clever and knew others’ theories as a hairsplitter (marksman knows archery): one would fancy they must go about demolishing views with the understanding that they have.

mn27:4.4.verse: “The monk Gotama will visit such a village or town.”

mn27:4.6.verse: “We shall approach the monk Gotama and ask him this question.

mn27:4.7.verse: If he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong;

mn27:4.8.verse: and if he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so again we shall prove his theory wrong.”

mn27:4.10.verse: “The monk Gotama has come to visit such and such a village or town.”

mn27:4.11.verse: They go to the monk Gotama.

mn27:4.12.verse: The monk Gotama instructs, urges, rouses and encourages them with a talk on the Dhamma.

mn27:4.13.verse: After that they do not so much as ask him the question, so how should they prove his theory wrong?

mn27:4.14.verse: In actual fact they become his disciples.

mn27:4.15.verse: When I saw this first footprint in the monk Gotama, I concluded:

mn27:4.16.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way.”

mn27:5.1.verse: ‘Again, I have seen certain divine caste scholars that were clever … this second footprint … the Sangha has entered on the good way.”

mn27:6.1.verse: ‘Again, I have seen certain householder scholars that were clever … this third footprint …

mn27:6.2.verse: the Sangha has entered on the good way.”

mn27:7.1.verse: ‘Again, I have seen certain monk scholars that were clever and knew others’ theories as a hair-splitter (marksman knows archery): one would fancy they must go about demolishing views with the understanding that they have.

mn27:7.3.verse: “The monk Gotama will visit such and such a village or town.”

mn27:7.5.verse: “If he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong,

mn27:7.6.verse: and if he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so again we shall prove his theory wrong.”

mn27:7.7.verse: They hear: “The monk Gotama has come to visit such and such a village or town.”

mn27:7.8.verse: They go to the monk Gotama.

mn27:7.9.verse: The monk Gotama instructs, urges, rouses and encourages them with talk on the Dhamma.

mn27:7.10.verse: They do not so much as ask him the question, so how should they prove his theory wrong?

mn27:7.11.verse: In actual fact they ask the monk Gotama to allow them to go forth from the home life into homelessness,

mn27:7.12.verse: and he gives them the Going-forth.

mn27:7.13.verse: Not long after they have gone forth in this way, dwelling alone and withdrawn, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, by realization themselves, with direct knowledge they here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the life divine for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn27:7.15.verse: “We were very nearly lost, we were very nearly undone,

mn27:7.16.verse: for formerly we claimed that we were monks though we were not, we claimed that we were divines though we were not, we claimed that we were Arahants though we were not,

mn27:7.17.verse: but now we are monks, now we are divines, now we are Arahants.”

mn27:7.18.verse: When I saw this fourth footprint in the monk Gotama, I concluded:

mn27:7.19.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way.”

mn27:7.20.verse: ‘As soon as I saw these four footprints in the monk Gotama I concluded:

mn27:7.21.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way.” ‘

mn27:8.1.verse: When this was said, Jānussoni of the divine caste got down from his chariot drawn by mares, all in white, and arranging his robes on one shoulder, he raised his hands palms together towards where the Blessed One was, and uttered this exclamation three times:

mn27:8.2.verse: ‘Honour to the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened!

mn27:8.3.verse: Honour to the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened!

mn27:8.4.verse: Honour to the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened!

mn27:8.5.verse: Now suppose that, sometime or other, we were to meet Master Gotama and have some conversation with him?’

mn27:9.1.verse: Then Jānussoni of the divine caste went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,

mn27:9.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

mn27:9.3.verse: When he had done so, he related to the Blessed One all his conversation with the wanderer Pilotikā.

mn27:9.4.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One told him:

mn27:9.5.verse: ‘At this point, divine, the simile of the elephant’s footprint has not yet been completed in detail.

mn27:9.6.verse: So listen then how it is completed in detail

mn27:9.7.verse: and attend carefully to what I shall say.’

mn27:9.8.verse: ‘Yes, sir,’ Jannussoni of the divine caste replied.

mn27:10.1.verse: ‘Divine, suppose an elephant woodsman went into an elephant wood,

mn27:10.2.verse: and he saw in the elephant wood a big elephant’s footprint long in extent and broad across:

mn27:10.3.verse: a wise elephant woodsman would not yet conclude

mn27:10.4.verse: “It is a bull elephant and a big one.”

mn27:10.6.verse: In an elephant wood there are small cow elephants that leave a big footprint. It might be the footprint of one of those.

mn27:10.8.verse: As he does so, he sees in the elephant wood a big elephant’s footprint long in extent and broad across and something used high up:

mn27:10.9.verse: a wise elephant woodsman would not yet conclude

mn27:10.10.verse: “It is a bull elephant and a big one.”

mn27:10.12.verse: In an elephant wood there are tall cow elephants with prominent teeth that leave a big footprint. It might be the footprint of one of those.

mn27:10.14.verse: As he does so, he sees in the elephant wood an elephant’s footprint long in extent and broad across and something used high up and marks made by tusks:

mn27:10.15.verse: a wise elephant woodsman would not yet conclude

mn27:10.16.verse: “It is a bull elephant and a big one.”

mn27:10.18.verse: In an elephant wood there are tall cow elephants with tusks that have a big footprint. It might be the footprint of one of those.

mn27:10.20.verse: As he does so, he sees in the elephant wood an elephant’s footprint long in extent and broad across and something used high up and marks made by tusks and broken-off branches.

mn27:10.21.verse: And he sees the bull elephant at the root of a tree or in the open, walking about or standing, sitting or lying down.

mn27:11.1.verse: ‘So too, divine, here a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahat and Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.

mn27:11.2.verse: ‘He declares this world with its gods, its Māras and its (Brahmā) Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings, and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn27:11.3.verse: ‘He teaches Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end, with (the right) meaning and phrasing, and he announces a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn27:12.1.verse: ‘A householder or householder’s son or one born in some clan hears that Dhamma.

mn27:12.2.verse: On hearing the Dhamma he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.

mn27:12.3.verse: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:

mn27:12.4.verse: “House life is crowded and dirty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn27:12.5.verse: It is not possible, living in a household, to lead a life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.

mn27:12.6.verse: Suppose I shaved off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”

mn27:12.7.verse: ‘And on another occasion, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large fortune, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large circle of relatives, he shaves off hair and beard, puts on the yellow cloth, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn27:13.1.verse: ‘Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.

mn27:13.2.verse: ‘Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given, taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.

mn27:13.3.verse: ‘Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart abstaining from vulgar lechery.

mn27:13.4.verse: ‘Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trustworthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.

mn27:13.5.verse: ‘Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.

mn27:13.6.verse: ‘Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.

mn27:13.7.verse: ‘Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.

mn27:13.8.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.

mn27:13.9.verse: ‘He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.

mn27:13.10.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.

mn27:13.11.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.

mn27:13.12.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.

mn27:13.13.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.

mn27:13.14.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.

mn27:13.15.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.

mn27:13.16.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.

mn27:13.17.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondswomen and bondsmen.

mn27:13.18.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.

mn27:13.19.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.

mn27:13.20.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses and mares.

mn27:13.21.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.

mn27:13.22.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.

mn27:13.23.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.

mn27:13.24.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.

mn27:13.25.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.

mn27:13.26.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.

mn27:14.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn27:14.2.verse: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,

mn27:14.3.verse: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn27:14.4.verse: ‘Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn27:15.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who, on seeing a visible form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features

mn27:15.2.verse: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn27:15.3.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn27:15.4.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn27:15.5.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn27:15.6.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn27:15.7.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind he apprehends no signs and features

mn27:15.8.verse: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn27:15.9.verse: ‘Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn27:16.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who acts in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, robes and bowl, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, waking up, talking and keeping silent.

mn27:17.1.verse: ‘Possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,

mn27:17.2.verse: he resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn27:18.1.verse: ‘On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.

mn27:18.2.verse: ‘Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies mind from covetousness.

mn27:18.3.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.

mn27:18.4.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.

mn27:18.5.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself, he purifies mind from agitation and worry.

mn27:18.6.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas, he purifies mind from uncertainty.

mn27:19.1.verse: ‘Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn27:19.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of seclusion.

mn27:19.3.verse: ‘This is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata,

mn27:19.4.verse: but a noble disciple does not yet conclude:

mn27:19.5.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”’

mn27:20.1.verse: ‘Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.’

mn27:20.2.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata …’

mn27:20.3.verse: the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”’

mn27:21.1.verse: ‘Again, with the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna on account of which Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”’

mn27:21.2.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata …’

mn27:21.3.verse: the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”’

mn27:22.1.verse: ‘Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’

mn27:22.2.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata,

mn27:22.3.verse: but a noble disciple does not yet conclude:

mn27:22.4.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”’

mn27:23.1.verse: ‘When the concentrated mind is thus purified and bright, unblemished, rid of defilement and become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of recollection of past life …

mn27:23.2.verse: (as in Sutta 4, para. 27)… thus with its aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.’

mn27:23.3.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata,

mn27:23.4.verse: but a noble disciple does not yet conclude:

mn27:23.5.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”’

mn27:24.1.verse: ‘When concentrated mind is thus purified … and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings …

mn27:24.2.verse: (as in Sutta 4, para. 29)… thus with heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees … how beings pass on according to their kammas.’

mn27:24.3.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata,

mn27:24.4.verse: but a noble disciple does not yet conclude:

mn27:24.5.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”

mn27:25.1.verse: ‘When concentrated mind is thus purified … and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn27:25.2.verse: He understands as it actually is: “This is suffering” … (complete as in Sutta 4, para. 31) …

mn27:25.3.verse: He understands as it actually is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of taints.”

mn27:25.4.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata,

mn27:25.5.verse: but a noble disciple has not already concluded, but rather is in the act of concluding:

mn27:25.6.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”

mn27:26.1.verse: ‘Knowing thus, seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance.

mn27:26.2.verse: When liberated, there is the knowledge “It is liberated”.

mn27:26.3.verse: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what can be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”

mn27:26.4.verse: ‘This also is called a footprint of a Tathāgata, something used by a Tathāgata, something marked by a Tathāgata.

mn27:26.5.verse: It is at this point that a noble disciple has concluded:

mn27:26.6.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered upon the good way.”

mn27:26.7.verse: ‘It is at this point, divine, that the simile of the elephant’s footprint has been completed in detail.’

mn27:27.1.verse: When this was said, Jāņussoni of the divine caste said:

mn27:27.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.

mn27:27.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn27:27.5.verse: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn27:0.2.verse: The Shorter Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint

mn27:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn27:2.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Jānussoṇi drove out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares.

mn27:2.2.verse: He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming off in the distance,

mn27:2.4.verse: “So, worthy Vacchāyana, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

mn27:2.5.verse: “Just now, worthy sir, I’ve come from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.”

mn27:2.6.verse: “What do you think of the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? Do you think he’s astute?”

mn27:2.7.verse: “Worthy sir, who am I to judge the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom?

mn27:2.8.verse: You’d really have to be on the same level to judge his lucidity of wisdom.”

mn27:2.9.verse: “Worthy Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with high praise indeed.”

mn27:2.10.verse: “Who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama?

mn27:2.11.verse: He is praised by the praised as the first among gods and humans.”

mn27:2.12.verse: “But for what reason are you so devoted to the ascetic Gotama?”

mn27:3.1.verse: “Suppose that a skilled bull elephant tracker were to enter a bull elephant wood.

mn27:3.2.verse: There he’d see a large elephant’s footprint, long and broad.

mn27:3.3.verse: He would come to the conclusion,

mn27:3.4.verse: ‘This must be a big bull elephant.’

mn27:3.5.verse: In the same way, because I saw four footprints of the ascetic Gotama I came to the conclusion,

mn27:3.6.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:4.2.verse: Firstly, I see some astute aristocrats who are subtle, accomplished in the doctrines of others, hair-splitters. You’d think they live to demolish convictions with their intellect.

mn27:4.4.verse: ‘So, worthy sir, that ascetic Gotama will come down to such-and-such village or town.’

mn27:4.6.verse: ‘We’ll approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question.

mn27:4.7.verse: If he answers like this, we’ll refute him like that;

mn27:4.8.verse: and if he answers like that, we’ll refute him like this.’

mn27:4.12.verse: The ascetic Gotama educates, encourages, fires up, and inspires them with a Dhamma talk.

mn27:4.13.verse: They don’t even get around to asking their question to the ascetic Gotama, so how could they refute his answer?

mn27:4.15.verse: When I saw this first footprint of the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion,

mn27:4.16.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:5.1.verse: Furthermore, I see some astute brahmins …

mn27:7.1.verse: Furthermore, I see some astute ascetics who are subtle, accomplished in the doctrines of others, hair-splitters. …

mn27:7.10.verse: They don’t even get around to asking their question to the ascetic Gotama, so how could they refute his answer?

mn27:7.11.verse: Invariably, they ask the ascetic Gotama for the chance to go forth.

mn27:7.12.verse: And he gives them the going-forth.

mn27:7.13.verse: Soon after going forth, living withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, they realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn27:7.15.verse: ‘We were almost lost! We almost perished!

mn27:7.16.verse: For we used to claim that we were ascetics, brahmins, and perfected ones, but we were none of these things.

mn27:7.17.verse: But now we really are ascetics, brahmins, and perfected ones!’

mn27:7.18.verse: When I saw this fourth footprint of the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion,

mn27:7.19.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:7.20.verse: It’s because I saw these four footprints of the ascetic Gotama that I came to the conclusion,

mn27:7.21.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’”

mn27:8.1.verse: When he had spoken, Jānussoṇi got down from his chariot, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:

mn27:8.2.verse: “Homage to that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

mn27:8.3.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

mn27:8.4.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

mn27:8.5.verse: Hopefully, some time or other I’ll get to meet the worthy Gotama, and we can have a discussion.”

mn27:9.1.verse: Then the brahmin Jānussoṇi went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn27:9.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side,

mn27:9.3.verse: and informed the Buddha of all he had discussed with the wanderer Pilotika.

mn27:9.4.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

mn27:9.5.verse: “Brahmin, the simile of the elephant’s footprint is not yet completed in detail.

mn27:9.6.verse: As to how it is completed in detail,

mn27:9.7.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn27:10.1.verse: “Suppose a bull elephant tracker were to enter a bull elephant wood.

mn27:10.2.verse: There they’d see a large elephant’s footprint, long and broad.

mn27:10.3.verse: A skilled bull elephant tracker does not yet come to the conclusion,

mn27:10.4.verse: ‘This must be a big bull elephant.’

mn27:10.6.verse: Because in an elephant wood there are dwarf cow elephants with big footprints, and this footprint might be one of theirs.

mn27:10.8.verse: They keep following the track until they see a big footprint, long and broad, and traces high up.

mn27:10.9.verse: A skilled bull elephant tracker does not yet come to the conclusion,

mn27:10.10.verse: ‘This must be a big bull elephant.’

mn27:10.12.verse: Because in an elephant wood there are tall lofty cow elephants with big footprints, and this footprint might be one of theirs.

mn27:10.14.verse: They keep following the track until they see a big footprint, long and broad, and traces and tusk-marks high up.

mn27:10.15.verse: A skilled bull elephant tracker does not yet come to the conclusion,

mn27:10.16.verse: ‘This must be a big bull elephant.’

mn27:10.18.verse: Because in an elephant wood there are tall matriarch cow elephants with big footprints, and this footprint might be one of theirs.

mn27:10.20.verse: They keep following the track until they see a big footprint, long and broad, and traces, tusk-marks, and broken branches high up.

mn27:10.21.verse: And they see that bull elephant walking, standing, sitting, or lying down at the root of a tree or in the open.

mn27:10.22.verse: Then they’d come to the conclusion,

mn27:11.1.verse: In the same way, brahmin, a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn27:11.2.verse: He realizes with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn27:11.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely complete and pure.

mn27:12.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

mn27:12.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One,

mn27:12.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn27:12.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn27:12.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn27:12.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn27:13.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn27:13.2.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

mn27:13.3.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn27:13.4.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

mn27:13.5.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn27:13.6.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, likable, and agreeable to the people.

mn27:13.7.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn27:13.8.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

mn27:13.9.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and at the wrong time.

mn27:13.10.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn27:13.11.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn27:13.12.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

mn27:13.13.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

mn27:13.22.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

mn27:13.26.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn27:14.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn27:14.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn27:14.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn27:14.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

mn27:15.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn27:15.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn27:15.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn27:15.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn27:15.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn27:15.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn27:15.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn27:15.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn27:15.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

mn27:16.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn27:17.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn27:17.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn27:18.1.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn27:18.2.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn27:18.3.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn27:18.4.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn27:18.5.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn27:18.6.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn27:19.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn27:19.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn27:19.3.verse: This, brahmin, is that which is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ and also ‘a trace of the Realized One’ and also ‘a mark of the Realized One’.

mn27:19.4.verse: But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion,

mn27:19.5.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:20.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn27:20.2.verse: This too is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ …

mn27:21.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn27:21.2.verse: This too is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ …

mn27:22.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn27:22.2.verse: This too is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ …

mn27:23.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn27:23.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. … They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn27:23.3.verse: This too is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ …

mn27:24.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn27:24.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human, they understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn27:24.3.verse: This too is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ …

mn27:25.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn27:25.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn27:25.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn27:25.4.verse: This, brahmin, is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ and also ‘a trace of the Realized One’ and also ‘a mark of the Realized One’.

mn27:25.5.verse: At this point a noble disciple has not yet come to a conclusion, but they are coming to the conclusion,

mn27:25.6.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:26.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn27:26.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn27:26.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn27:26.4.verse: This, brahmin, is what is called ‘a footprint of the Realized One’ and also ‘a trace of the Realized One’ and also ‘a mark of the Realized One’.

mn27:26.5.verse: At this point a noble disciple has come to the conclusion,

mn27:26.6.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn27:26.7.verse: And it is at this point that the simile of the elephant’s footprint has been completed in detail.”

mn27:27.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmin Jānussoṇi said to the Buddha,

mn27:27.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn27:27.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn27:27.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn28:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn28:1.3.verse: There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn28:2.1.verse: ‘Friends, just as the footprint of any living being that walks can be placed within an elephant’s footprint, and so the elephant’s footprint is declared the chief of them because of its great size,

mn28:2.2.verse: so too, whatever profitable dhammas there are can all be included in the Four Noble Truths.

mn28:2.4.verse: In the Noble Truth of Suffering, in the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, in the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and in the Noble Truth of the Way leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

mn28:3.1.verse: ‘And what is the Noble Truth of Suffering?

mn28:3.2.verse: Birth is suffering, ageing is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair are suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in short the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering.

mn28:3.3.verse: ‘And what are the five aggregates affected by clinging?

mn28:3.4.verse: They are: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn28:4.1.verse: ‘And what is the form aggregate affected by clinging?

mn28:4.2.verse: It is the four great primary elements and any form derived from them.

mn28:5.1.verse: ‘And what are the four great primary elements?

mn28:5.2.verse: They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element and the air element.

mn28:6.2.verse: The earth element can be either in oneself or external.

mn28:6.3.verse: ‘What is the earth element in oneself?

mn28:6.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified and clung-to, that is to say,

mn28:6.5.verse: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lights, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, that is solid, solidified and clung-to:

mn28:6.6.verse: this is called earth element in oneself.

mn28:6.7.verse: ‘Now earth element in oneself and external earth element are simply earth element.

mn28:6.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn28:6.9.verse: When a man sees it with right understanding as it actually is thus, he becomes dispassionate towards the earth element, and he fades lust for the earth element out of his mind.

mn28:7.1.verse: ‘Now there is the occasion when the external earth element is disturbed

mn28:7.2.verse: and then the external earth element vanishes.

mn28:7.3.verse: ‘For even this external earth element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,

mn28:7.4.verse: so what of this body, which is clung to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.

mn28:8.1.verse: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus,) if others abuse and scold, curse and threaten a bhikkhu, he understands thus:

mn28:8.2.verse: “This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me.

mn28:8.6.verse: Then he sees that contact is impermanent, that feeling is impermanent, that perception is impermanent, that formations are impermanent, and that consciousness is impermanent.

mn28:8.7.verse: And his mind, which has already made an element (constituent of the form aggregate) its objective support, enters into that (new objective support now contemplated) and acquires confidence, steadiness and decision.

mn28:9.1.verse: ‘Now if others attack that bhikkhu with unwished-for, undesired and disagreeable

mn28:9.2.verse: contact of fists, clods, sticks or knives,

mn28:9.4.verse: “This body is a thing such that contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives takes place in it.

mn28:9.5.verse: But this has been said by the Blessed One in his discourse on the Simile of the Saw:

mn28:9.6.verse: “Even if bandits savagely severed limb from limb with a two-handled saw, he who entertained hate in his heart on that account would not be one who carried out my teaching.”

mn28:9.7.verse: So tireless energy shall be aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness established, my body shall be tranquil and unexcited, my mind shall be concentrated and unified.

mn28:9.8.verse: And now let contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives take place in this body; for this is just how the Buddha’s message is put into effect.’

mn28:10.1.verse: ‘If, when he thus recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,

mn28:10.2.verse: then he arouses a sense of urgency thus:

mn28:10.3.verse: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,

mn28:10.4.verse: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”

mn28:10.5.verse: Just as when a daughter-in-law sees her father-in-law, she has a sense of urgency,

mn28:10.8.verse: ‘But if when a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity becomes established in him with what is profitable as its support, then he is satisfied.

mn28:10.9.verse: And at that point, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhus.

mn28:11.2.verse: The water element can be either in oneself or external.

mn28:11.3.verse: ‘What is the water element in oneself?

mn28:11.4.verse: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn28:11.5.verse: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to:

mn28:11.6.verse: this is called water element in oneself.

mn28:11.7.verse: ‘Now water element in oneself and external water element are simply water element.

mn28:11.8.verse: That should be seen with right understanding as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this not I, this is not my self.”

mn28:11.9.verse: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the water element, he fades lust for the water element out of his mind.

mn28:12.1.verse: ‘Now there is an occasion when the water element is disturbed.

mn28:12.2.verse: It carries away village, town, city, district and country.

mn28:12.3.verse: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean sink down a hundred leagues, two hundred leagues … seven hundred leagues.

mn28:12.4.verse: There is an occasion when the water in the great ocean stands seven palm trees deep, six palm trees deep … two palm trees deep, only a palm tree deep.

mn28:12.5.verse: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean stand seven fathoms deep, six … only a fathom deep.

mn28:12.6.verse: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean stand half fathom deep, only waist deep, only knee deep, only ankle deep.

mn28:12.7.verse: There is an occasion when the waters in the great ocean are not enough to wet even the joint of a finger.

mn28:12.8.verse: ‘For even this external water element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,

mn28:13.1.verse: so what of this body which is clung to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.

mn28:14.1.verse: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus), if others abuse … (repeat paras. 11-14) …

mn28:15.1.verse: much has been done by that bhikkhu.

mn28:16.2.verse: The fire element can either be in oneself or external.

mn28:16.3.verse: ‘And what is the fire element in oneself?

mn28:16.4.verse: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn28:16.5.verse: that whereby one is warmed, ages, and is consumed, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to:

mn28:16.6.verse: this is called fire element in oneself.

mn28:16.7.verse: ‘Now fire element in oneself and external fire element are simply fire element.

mn28:16.8.verse: That should be seen with right understanding as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn28:16.9.verse: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the fire element, he fades lust for the fire element out of his mind.

mn28:17.1.verse: ‘There is an occasion when the external fire element is disturbed.

mn28:17.2.verse: It burns up village, town, city, district and country.

mn28:17.3.verse: It only goes out when it comes to green grass, or to a road, or to a rock, or to water or a fair open space, for want of fuel.

mn28:17.4.verse: There is an occasion when they seek to make a fire even with fowls’ claws and hide-parings.

mn28:17.5.verse: ‘For even this external fire element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,

mn28:17.6.verse: so what of this body, which is clung-to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.’

mn28:18-20.1.verse: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus) if others abuse (repeat paras. 11-14) …

mn28:18-20.2.verse: much has been done by that bhikkhu.

mn28:21.2.verse: The air element can either be in oneself or external.

mn28:21.3.verse: ‘What is the air element in oneself?

mn28:21.4.verse: ‘Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn28:21.5.verse: up-going winds (forces), down-going winds (forces), winds (forces) in the belly, winds (forces) in the bowels, winds (forces) that pervade all the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to:

mn28:21.6.verse: this is called air element in oneself.

mn28:21.7.verse: ‘Now air element in oneself and external air element are simply air element.

mn28:21.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not myself.”

mn28:21.9.verse: When a man sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, he becomes dispassionate towards the air element, he fades lust for the air element out of his mind.

mn28:22.1.verse: ‘There is an occasion when the external air element is disturbed.

mn28:22.2.verse: It sweeps away village, town, city, district and country.

mn28:22.3.verse: There is an occasion in the last month of the hot season when they seek wind by means of a fan or bellows and even the strands of straw in the drip-fringe of the thatch do not stir.

mn28:22.4.verse: ‘For even this external air element, great as it is, is describable as impermanent, as subject to destruction, as subject to disappearance, as subject to change,

mn28:22.5.verse: so what of this body, which is clung-to and lasts but a while? There can be no (considering) that as “I” or “mine” or “am”.

mn28:23.1.verse: ‘So then, (having seen this element as it actually is, thus,) if others abuse and scold, curse and threaten a bhikkhu,

mn28:23.2.verse: he understands thus: “This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me.

mn28:23.6.verse: Then he sees that contact is impermanent, that feeling is impermanent, that perception is impermanent, that formations are impermanent, and that consciousness is impermanent.

mn28:23.7.verse: And his mind, which has already made an element its objective support, enters into that (new objective support now contemplated) and acquires confidence, steadiness and decision.

mn28:24.1.verse: ‘Now if others attack that bhikkhu with unwished-for, undesired and disagreeable contact of fists, clods, sticks or knives,
