mn28:24.2.verse: he understands thus: “This body is a thing such that contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives takes place in it.

mn28:24.3.verse: But this has been said by the Blessed One in his discourse on the Simile of the Saw: “Even if bandits savagely severed limb from limb with a two-handled saw, he who entertained hate in his heart on that account would not be one who carried out my teaching.”

mn28:24.4.verse: So tireless energy shall be aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness established, my body shall be tranquil and unexcited, my mind shall be concentrated and unified.

mn28:24.5.verse: And now let contact with fists, clods, sticks and knives take place in this body; for this is just how the Buddha’s message is put into effect.’

mn28:25.1.verse: ‘If, when he thus recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,

mn28:25.2.verse: then he arouses a sense of urgency thus:

mn28:25.3.verse: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,

mn28:25.4.verse: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”

mn28:25.5.verse: Just as when a daughter-in-law sees her father-in-law, she has a sense of urgency,

mn28:25.6.verse: so too, if a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, and equanimity does not persist in him with the profitable as its support,

mn28:25.7.verse: he arouses a sense of urgency thus:

mn28:25.8.verse: “It is loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,

mn28:25.9.verse: that when I recollect the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity does not persist in me with the profitable as its support.”

mn28:25.10.verse: ‘But if when a bhikkhu recollects the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha thus, equanimity becomes established in him with what is profitable as its support, then he is satisfied.

mn28:25.11.verse: And at that point, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.

mn28:26.1.verse: ‘Just as when a space is enclosed by timber and creepers, grass and clay, there comes to be the term “house”,

mn28:26.2.verse: so too, when a space is enclosed by bones and sinews, flesh and skin, there comes to be the term “form”.

mn28:27.1.verse: ‘If the eye in oneself were intact but no external forms came to its threshold (of consciousness) and there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, then there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:27.2.verse: If the eye in oneself were intact and external forms came to its threshold but there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:27.3.verse: But it is owing to the fact that the eye in oneself is intact and that external forms come to its threshold, and that there is the appropriate (conscious) engagement, that there is manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:28.1.verse: ‘Whatever form of what has come to be thus, is included in the form aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever feeling of what has come to be thus, is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever perception of what has come to be thus, is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever formations of what has come to be thus, are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever consciousness of what has come to be thus, is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn28:28.3.verse: “This, it seems, is how there comes to be inclusion, gathering, amassing into these five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn28:28.4.verse: Now this has been said by the Blessed One:

mn28:28.5.verse: “He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma:

mn28:28.6.verse: he who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.”

mn28:28.7.verse: And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen.

mn28:28.8.verse: The wish for reliance on, approval or acceptance of, these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering.

mn28:28.9.verse: The removal of wishing and lust, the abandoning of wishing and lust for them is the cessation of suffering.”

mn28:28.10.verse: And at this point too, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.

mn28:29-30.1.verse: ‘If the ear in oneself were intact but no external sounds came to its threshold …

mn28:31-32.1.verse: If the nose in oneself were intact but no external smells came to its threshold …

mn28:33-34.1.verse: If the tongue in oneself were intact but no external flavours came to its threshold …

mn28:35-36.1.verse: If the body in oneself were intact but no external tangibles came to its threshold …

mn28:37.1.verse: ‘If the mind in oneself were intact but no external dhammas came to its threshold … and there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, then there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:38.1.verse: If the mind in oneself were intact and external dhammas came to its threshold but there were no appropriate (conscious) engagement, there would be no manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:38.2.verse: But it is owing to the fact that the mind in oneself is intact and that external dhammas come to its threshold, and that there is the appropriate (conscious) engagement, that there is manifestation of the appropriate class of consciousness.

mn28:38.3.verse: Whatever form of what has come to be thus, is included in the form aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever feeling of what has come to be thus, is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever perception of what has come to be thus, is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever formations of what has come to be thus, are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging. Whatever consciousness of what has come to be thus, is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn28:38.5.verse: “This, it seems, is how there comes to be inclusion, gathering, amassing into these five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn28:38.6.verse: Now this has been said by the Blessed One:

mn28:38.7.verse: “He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma:

mn28:38.8.verse: he who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.”

mn28:38.9.verse: And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen.

mn28:38.10.verse: The wish for reliance on, approval or acceptance of, these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering.

mn28:38.11.verse: The removal of wishing and lust, the abandoning of wishing and lust for them is the cessation of suffering.”

mn28:38.12.verse: And at this point too, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.’

mn28:38.13.verse: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

mn28:38.14.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in his words.

mn28:0.2.verse: The Longer Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint

mn28:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn28:2.1.verse: “The footprints of all creatures that walk can fit inside an elephant’s footprint, so an elephant’s footprint is said to be the biggest of them all.

mn28:2.2.verse: In the same way, all skillful qualities are included in the four noble truths.

mn28:2.4.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

mn28:3.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

mn28:3.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

mn28:3.3.verse: And what are the five grasping aggregates?

mn28:3.4.verse: They are as follows: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn28:4.1.verse: And what is the grasping aggregate of form?

mn28:4.2.verse: The four principal states, and form derived from the four principal states.

mn28:5.1.verse: And what are the four principal states?

mn28:5.2.verse: The elements of earth, water, fire, and air.

mn28:6.1.verse: And what is the earth element?

mn28:6.2.verse: The earth element may be interior or exterior.

mn28:6.3.verse: And what is the interior earth element?

mn28:6.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s hard, solid, and appropriated. This includes:

mn28:6.5.verse: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces; or anything else internal, personal, that’s hard, solid, and appropriated.

mn28:6.6.verse: This is called the interior earth element.

mn28:6.7.verse: The interior earth element and the exterior earth element are just the earth element.

mn28:6.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn28:6.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the earth element, detaching the mind from the earth element.

mn28:7.1.verse: There comes a time when the exterior water element flares up.

mn28:7.2.verse: At that time the exterior earth element vanishes.

mn28:7.3.verse: So for all its great age, the earth element will be revealed as impermanent, liable to end, vanish, and perish.

mn28:7.4.verse: What then of this ephemeral body appropriated by craving? Rather than ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’, they consider it to be none of these things.

mn28:8.1.verse: If others abuse, attack, harass, and trouble that mendicant, they understand:

mn28:8.2.verse: ‘This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me.

mn28:8.6.verse: They see that contact, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.

mn28:8.7.verse: Based on that element alone, their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

mn28:9.1.verse: Others might treat that mendicant with disliking, loathing, and detestation,

mn28:9.2.verse: striking them with fists, stones, sticks, and swords.

mn28:9.4.verse: ‘This body is such that fists, stones, sticks, and swords strike it.

mn28:9.5.verse: But the Buddha has said in the Advice on the Simile of the Saw:

mn28:9.6.verse: “Even if low-down bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handed saw, anyone who had a malevolent thought on that account would not be following my instructions.”

mn28:9.7.verse: My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness established and lucid, my body tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind immersed and unified in samādhi.

mn28:9.8.verse: Gladly now, let fists, stones, sticks, and swords strike this body! For this is how the instructions of the Buddhas are followed.’

mn28:10.1.verse: While recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful may not become stabilized in them.

mn28:10.2.verse: In that case they stir up a sense of urgency:

mn28:10.4.verse: that while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does not become stabilized in me.’

mn28:10.5.verse: They’re like a daughter-in-law who stirs up a sense of urgency when they see their father-in-law.

mn28:10.8.verse: But if, while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does become stabilized in them, they’re happy with that.

mn28:10.9.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.

mn28:11.1.verse: And what is the water element?

mn28:11.2.verse: The water element may be interior or exterior.

mn28:11.3.verse: And what is the interior water element?

mn28:11.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s water, watery, and appropriated. This includes:

mn28:11.5.verse: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine; or anything else internal, personal, that’s water, watery, and appropriated.

mn28:11.6.verse: This is called the interior water element.

mn28:11.7.verse: The interior water element and the exterior water element are just the water element.

mn28:11.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn28:11.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the water element, detaching the mind from the water element.

mn28:12.1.verse: There comes a time when the exterior water element flares up.

mn28:12.2.verse: It sweeps away villages, towns, cities, countries, and regions.

mn28:12.3.verse: There comes a time when the water in the ocean sinks down a hundred leagues, or two, three, four, five, six, up to seven hundred leagues.

mn28:12.4.verse: There comes a time when the water in the ocean stands just seven palm trees deep, or six, five, four, three, two, or even just one palm tree deep.

mn28:12.5.verse: There comes a time when the water in the ocean stands just seven fathoms deep, or six, five, four, three, two, or even just one fathom deep.

mn28:12.6.verse: There comes a time when the water in the ocean stands just half a fathom deep, or waist deep, or knee deep, or even just ankle deep.

mn28:12.7.verse: There comes a time when there’s not even enough water left in the great ocean to wet the tip of the toe.

mn28:12.8.verse: So for all its great age, the water element will be revealed as impermanent, liable to end, vanish, and perish.

mn28:13.1.verse: What then of this ephemeral body appropriated by craving? Rather than ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’, they consider it to be none of these things. …

mn28:14.1.verse: If, while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does become stabilized in them, they’re happy with that.

mn28:15.1.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.

mn28:16.1.verse: And what is the fire element?

mn28:16.2.verse: The fire element may be interior or exterior.

mn28:16.3.verse: And what is the interior fire element?

mn28:16.4.verse: Anything internal, pertaining to an individual that’s fire, fiery, and appropriated. This includes:

mn28:16.5.verse: that which warms, that which ages, that which heats you up when feverish, that which properly digests food and drink; or anything else internal, personal, that’s fire, fiery, and appropriated.

mn28:16.6.verse: This is called the interior fire element.

mn28:16.7.verse: The interior fire element and the exterior fire element are just the fire element.

mn28:16.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn28:16.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the fire element, detaching the mind from the fire element.

mn28:17.1.verse: There comes a time when the exterior fire element flares up.

mn28:17.2.verse: It burns up villages, towns, cities, countries, and regions until

mn28:17.3.verse: it reaches a green field, a roadside, a cliff’s edge, a body of water, or cleared parkland, where it’s extinguished due to not being fed.

mn28:17.4.verse: There comes a time when they go looking for a fire, taking just a chicken feather or a scrap of sinew as kindling.

mn28:17.5.verse: So for all its great age, the fire element will be revealed as impermanent, liable to end, vanish, and perish.

mn28:17.6.verse: What then of this ephemeral body appropriated by craving? Rather than ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’, they consider it to be none of these things. …

mn28:18-20.1.verse: If, while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does become stabilized in them, they’re happy with that.

mn28:18-20.2.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.

mn28:21.1.verse: And what is the air element?

mn28:21.2.verse: The air element may be interior or exterior.

mn28:21.3.verse: And what is the interior air element?

mn28:21.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s air, airy, and appropriated. This includes:

mn28:21.5.verse: winds that go up or down, winds in the belly or the bowels, winds that flow through the limbs, in-breaths and out-breaths; or anything else internal, personal, that’s air, airy, and appropriated.

mn28:21.6.verse: This is called the interior air element.

mn28:21.7.verse: The interior air element and the exterior air element are just the air element.

mn28:21.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn28:21.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the air element, detaching the mind from the air element.

mn28:22.1.verse: There comes a time when the exterior air element flares up.

mn28:22.2.verse: It sweeps away villages, towns, cities, countries, and regions.

mn28:22.3.verse: There comes a time, in the last month of summer, when they look for wind by using a palm-leaf or fan, and even the grasses in the drip-fringe of a thatch roof don’t stir.

mn28:22.4.verse: So for all its great age, the air element will be revealed as impermanent, liable to end, vanish, and perish.

mn28:22.5.verse: What then of this ephemeral body appropriated by craving? Rather than ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’, they consider it to be none of these things.

mn28:23.1.verse: If others abuse, attack, harass, and trouble that mendicant, they understand:

mn28:23.2.verse: ‘This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me.

mn28:23.6.verse: They see that contact, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.

mn28:23.7.verse: Based on that element alone, their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

mn28:24.1.verse: Others might treat that mendicant with disliking, loathing, and detestation, striking them with fists, stones, sticks, and swords.

mn28:24.2.verse: They understand: ‘This body is such that fists, stones, sticks, and swords strike it.

mn28:24.3.verse: But the Buddha has said in the Advice on the Simile of the Saw: “Even if low-down bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handed saw, anyone who had a thought of hate on that account would not be following my instructions.”

mn28:24.4.verse: My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness established and lucid, my body tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind immersed and unified in samādhi.

mn28:24.5.verse: Gladly now, let fists, stones, sticks, and swords strike this body! For this is how the instructions of the Buddhas are followed.’

mn28:25.1.verse: While recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful may not become stabilized in them.

mn28:25.2.verse: In that case they stir up a sense of urgency:

mn28:25.4.verse: that while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does not become stabilized in me.’

mn28:25.5.verse: They’re like a daughter-in-law who stirs up a sense of urgency when they see their father-in-law.

mn28:25.10.verse: But if, while recollecting the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the skillful does become stabilized in them, they’re happy with that.

mn28:25.11.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.

mn28:26.1.verse: When a space is enclosed by sticks, creepers, grass, and mud it becomes known as a ‘building’.

mn28:26.2.verse: In the same way, when a space is enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin it becomes known as a ‘form’.

mn28:27.1.verse: Reverends, though the interior eye is intact, so long as exterior sights don’t come into range and there’s no corresponding engagement, there’s no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:27.2.verse: Though the interior eye is intact and exterior sights come into range, so long as there’s no corresponding engagement, there’s no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:27.3.verse: But when the interior eye is intact and exterior sights come into range and there is corresponding engagement, there is the manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:28.1.verse: The form produced in this way is included in the grasping aggregate of form. The feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness produced in this way are each included in the corresponding grasping aggregate.

mn28:28.3.verse: ‘So this is how there comes to be inclusion, gathering together, and assimilation into these five grasping aggregates.

mn28:28.5.verse: “One who sees dependent origination sees the teaching.

mn28:28.6.verse: One who sees the teaching sees dependent origination.”

mn28:28.7.verse: And these five grasping aggregates are indeed dependently originated.

mn28:28.8.verse: The desire, clinging, attraction, and attachment for these five grasping aggregates is the origin of suffering.

mn28:28.9.verse: Giving up and getting rid of desire and greed for these five grasping aggregates is the cessation of suffering.’

mn28:28.10.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.

mn28:37.1.verse: mind is intact internally, so long as exterior ideas don’t come into range and there’s no corresponding engagement, there’s no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:38.1.verse: Though the mind is intact internally and exterior ideas come into range, so long as there’s no corresponding engagement, there’s no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:38.2.verse: But when the mind is intact internally and exterior ideas come into range and there is corresponding engagement, there is the manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.

mn28:38.3.verse: The form produced in this way is included in the grasping aggregate of form. The feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness produced in this way are each included in the corresponding grasping aggregate.

mn28:38.5.verse: ‘So this is how there comes to be inclusion, gathering together, and assimilation into these five grasping aggregates.

mn28:38.6.verse: But the Buddha has also said:

mn28:38.7.verse: “One who sees dependent origination sees the teaching.

mn28:38.8.verse: One who sees the teaching sees dependent origination.”

mn28:38.9.verse: And these five grasping aggregates are indeed dependently originated.

mn28:38.10.verse: The desire, clinging, attraction, and attachment for these five grasping aggregates is the origin of suffering.

mn28:38.11.verse: Giving up and getting rid of desire and greed for these five grasping aggregates is the cessation of suffering.’

mn28:38.12.verse: At this point, much has been done by that mendicant.”

mn28:38.13.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

mn28:38.14.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Sāriputta said.

mn29:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture Peak mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

mn29:1.3.verse: Referring to Devadatta, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

mn29:2.1.verse: “Monks, there is the case where a certain son of good family, out of conviction, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn29:2.2.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, by aging-&-death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs, beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn29:2.3.verse: Perhaps the end of this entire mass of stress might be discerned!’

mn29:2.4.verse: Having thus gone forth, he encounters gain, offerings, & fame.

mn29:2.5.verse: He is gratified with that gain, offerings, & fame, his resolve fulfilled.

mn29:2.6.verse: Because of that gain, offerings, & fame he exalts himself and disparages others:

mn29:2.7.verse: ‘I am a person with gain, offerings, & fame, but these other monks are unknown & of little influence.’

mn29:2.8.verse: He is intoxicated with that gain, offerings, & fame, heedless about it, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering & stress.

mn29:2.9.verse: “Just as if a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood—passing over the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, passing over the outer bark—cutting away the twigs & leaves, were to go off carrying them, thinking, ‘heartwood.’

mn29:2.10.verse: A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say,

mn29:2.11.verse: ‘Ah, how this good man didn’t know heartwood, didn’t know sapwood, didn’t know inner bark, didn’t know outer bark, didn’t know twigs & leaves!

mn29:2.12.verse: That’s why he, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood—passing over the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, passing over the outer bark—cutting away the twigs & leaves, went off carrying them, thinking, “heartwood.”

mn29:2.13.verse: Whatever heartwood-business he had with heartwood, his purpose won’t be served.’

mn29:2.14.verse: “In the same way, monks, there is the case where a certain son of good family, out of conviction, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn29:2.15.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, by aging-&-death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs, beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn29:2.20.verse: He is intoxicated with that gain, offerings, & fame, heedless about it, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering & stress.

mn29:2.21.verse: This, monks, is called a monk who grasps the twigs & leaves of the holy life,

mn29:2.22.verse: and with that he falls short.

mn29:6.17.verse: And it is impossible, monks, there is no opportunity, for that monk to fall from that non-occasional release.

mn29:6.18.verse: “Just as if a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, cutting away just the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, were to go off carrying it, knowing, ‘heartwood.’

mn29:6.19.verse: A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say,

mn29:6.20.verse: ‘Ah, how this good man did know heartwood, did know sapwood, did know inner bark, did know outer bark, did know twigs & leaves!

mn29:6.21.verse: That’s why he, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, cutting away just the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, were to go off carrying it, knowing, “heartwood.”

mn29:6.22.verse: Whatever heartwood-business he had with heartwood, his purpose will be served.’

mn29:6.23.verse: “In the same way, monks, there is the case where a certain son of good family, out of conviction, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn29:6.24.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, by aging-&-death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs, beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn29:6.25.verse: Perhaps the end of this entire mass of stress might be discerned!’

mn29:6.26.verse: Having thus gone forth, he encounters gain, offerings, & fame.

mn29:6.27.verse: He is not gratified with that gain, offerings, & fame, his resolve not fulfilled.

mn29:6.28.verse: Because of that gain, offerings, & fame he does not exalt himself or disparage others.

mn29:6.29.verse: He is not intoxicated with that gain, offerings, & fame, not heedless about it, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he achieves consummation in virtue.

mn29:6.30.verse: He is gratified with that consummation in virtue, but his resolve is not fulfilled.

mn29:6.31.verse: Because of that consummation in virtue he does not exalt himself or disparage others.

mn29:6.32.verse: He is not intoxicated with that consummation in virtue, not heedless about it, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he achieves consummation in concentration.

mn29:6.33.verse: He is gratified with that consummation in concentration, but his resolve is not fulfilled.

mn29:6.34.verse: Because of that consummation in concentration he does not exalt himself or disparage others.

mn29:6.35.verse: He is not intoxicated with that consummation in concentration, not heedless about it, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he achieves knowledge & vision.

mn29:6.36.verse: He is gratified with that knowledge & vision, but his resolve is not fulfilled.

mn29:6.37.verse: Because of that knowledge & vision he does not exalt himself or disparage others.

mn29:6.38.verse: He is not intoxicated with that knowledge & vision, not heedless about it, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he achieves a non-occasional liberation.

mn29:6.39.verse: It is impossible, monks, there is no opportunity, for that monk to fall from that non-occasional release.

mn29:7.1.verse: “Monks, this holy life doesn’t have as its reward gain, offerings, & fame, doesn’t have as its reward consummation of virtue, doesn’t have as its reward consummation of concentration, doesn’t have as its reward knowledge & vision,

mn29:7.3.verse: That is the purpose of this holy life, that is its heartwood, that its final end.”

mn29:7.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn29:7.5.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn29:0.2.verse: The Longer Simile of the Heartwood

mn29:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

mn29:1.3.verse: There the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about Devadatta:

mn29:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, take the case of a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking,

mn29:2.2.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn29:2.3.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn29:2.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn29:2.5.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn29:2.6.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down because of that:

mn29:2.7.verse: ‘I’m the one with possessions, honor, and popularity. These other mendicants are obscure and insignificant.’

mn29:2.8.verse: And so they become indulgent and fall into negligence on account of those possessions, honor, and popularity. And being negligent they live in suffering.

mn29:2.9.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But, passing over the heartwood, softwood, bark, and shoots, he’d cut off the branches and leaves and leave imagining they were heartwood.

mn29:2.10.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say,

mn29:2.11.verse: ‘This gentleman doesn’t know what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn29:2.12.verse: That’s why he passed them over, cut off the branches and leaves, and left imagining they were heartwood.

mn29:2.13.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he won’t succeed.’ …

mn29:2.21.verse: This is called a mendicant who has grabbed the branches and leaves of the spiritual life

mn29:3.1.verse: Next, take a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn29:3.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn29:3.5.verse: They’re not happy with that, and haven’t got all they wished for.

mn29:3.6.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn29:3.7.verse: Nor do they become indulgent and fall into negligence on account of those possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn29:3.8.verse: Being diligent, they achieve accomplishment in ethics.

mn29:3.9.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn29:3.10.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that:

mn29:3.11.verse: ‘I’m the one who is ethical, of good character. These other mendicants are unethical, of bad character.’

mn29:3.12.verse: And so they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding their accomplishment in ethics. And being negligent they live in suffering.

mn29:3.13.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But, passing over the heartwood, softwood, and bark, he’d cut off the shoots and leave imagining they were heartwood.

mn29:3.14.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say,

mn29:3.15.verse: ‘This gentleman doesn’t know what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn29:3.16.verse: That’s why he passed them over, cut off the shoots, and left imagining they were heartwood.

mn29:3.17.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he won’t succeed.’ …

mn29:4.13.verse: This is called a mendicant who has grabbed the shoots of the spiritual life

mn29:4.15.verse: Next, take a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn29:4.18.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity. …

mn29:4.25.verse: Being diligent, they achieve accomplishment in immersion.

mn29:4.26.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn29:4.27.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that:

mn29:4.28.verse: ‘I’m the one with immersion and unified mind. These other mendicants lack immersion, they have straying minds.’

mn29:4.29.verse: And so they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding that accomplishment in immersion. And being negligent they live in suffering.

mn29:4.30.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But, passing over the heartwood and softwood, he’d cut off the bark and leave imagining it was heartwood.

mn29:4.31.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say: ‘This gentleman doesn’t know what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn29:4.32.verse: That’s why he passed them over, cut off the bark, and left imagining it was heartwood.

mn29:4.33.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he won’t succeed.’ …

mn29:4.48.verse: This is called a mendicant who has grabbed the bark of the spiritual life

mn29:5.1.verse: Next, take a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn29:5.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity. …

mn29:5.14.verse: Being diligent, they achieve knowledge and vision.

mn29:5.15.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn29:5.16.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that,

mn29:5.17.verse: ‘I’m the one who meditates knowing and seeing.

mn29:5.18.verse: These other mendicants meditate without knowing and seeing.’

mn29:5.19.verse: And so they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding that knowledge and vision. And being negligent they live in suffering.

mn29:5.20.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But, passing over the heartwood, he’d cut out the softwood and leave imagining it was heartwood.

mn29:5.21.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say,

mn29:5.22.verse: ‘This gentleman doesn’t know what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn29:5.23.verse: That’s why he passed them over, cut out the softwood, and left imagining it was heartwood.

mn29:5.24.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he won’t succeed.’ …

mn29:5.42.verse: This is called a mendicant who has grabbed the softwood of the spiritual life

mn29:6.1.verse: Next, take a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking,

mn29:6.2.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn29:6.3.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn29:6.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn29:6.5.verse: They’re not happy with that, and haven’t got all they wished for.

mn29:6.6.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn29:6.7.verse: Nor do they become indulgent and fall into negligence on account of those possessions, honor, and popularity. Being diligent, they achieve accomplishment in ethics.

mn29:6.8.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn29:6.9.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn29:6.10.verse: Nor do they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding that accomplishment in ethics. Being diligent, they achieve accomplishment in immersion.

mn29:6.11.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn29:6.12.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn29:6.13.verse: Nor do they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding that accomplishment in immersion. Being diligent, they achieve knowledge and vision.

mn29:6.14.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn29:6.15.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn29:6.16.verse: Nor do they become indulgent and fall into negligence regarding that knowledge and vision. Being diligent, they achieve irreversible freedom.

mn29:6.17.verse: And it’s impossible for that mendicant to fall away from that irreversible freedom.

mn29:6.18.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. He’d cut out just the heartwood and leave knowing it was heartwood.

mn29:6.19.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say,

mn29:6.20.verse: ‘This gentleman knows what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, and branches and leaves are.

mn29:6.21.verse: That’s why he cut out just the heartwood and left knowing it was heartwood.

mn29:6.22.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he will succeed.’ …

mn29:6.39.verse: It’s impossible for that mendicant to fall away from that irreversible freedom.

mn29:7.1.verse: And so, mendicants, this spiritual life is not lived for the sake of possessions, honor, and popularity, or for accomplishment in ethics, or for accomplishment in immersion, or for knowledge and vision.

mn29:7.2.verse: It is this unshakable freedom of heart

mn29:7.3.verse: that is the goal of the spiritual life, the core and the final end.”

mn29:7.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn29:7.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn30:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn30:2.1.verse: Then Pingalakoccha of the divine caste went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,

mn30:2.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:

mn30:2.3.verse: ‘Master Gotama, there are these ascetics and divines, each with his order, with his group, leading a group, each a known and famous philosopher and reckoned by many as a saint—

mn30:2.4.verse: I mean Purāṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalin, Pakudha Kaccayana, Sañjaya Belatthiputta, and the Nigaṇṭha (Jain) Nātaputta—

mn30:2.5.verse: have they all had direct knowledge as they claim, or have none of them had direct knowledge, or have some of them had direct knowledge and some not?’

mn30:2.7.verse: whether they have all had direct knowledge as they claim, or none of them … or some of them … and some not, let that be.

mn30:2.8.verse: I shall teach you the Dhamma, divine.

mn30:2.9.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn30:2.10.verse: ‘Even so, sir,’ Pingalakoccha of the divine caste replied.

mn30:3.1.verse: ‘Suppose a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood and its sapwood and its inner bark and its outer bark, he cut its twigs and leaves and took them away thinking they were heartwood;

mn30:3.2.verse: then a man with good sight, seeing him might observe his actions and say:

mn30:3.5.verse: “So whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.”

mn30:8.1.verse: ‘So too, brahman, here some clansman out of faith goes forth from the home life into homelessness, (considering:)

mn30:8.2.verse: “I am a victim of birth, ageing and death, of sorrows and lamentations, pains, griefs and despairs. I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering.

mn30:8.3.verse: Surely the ending of this whole mass of suffering can be known?”

mn30:8.4.verse: When he has gone forth thus, he acquires great gain, honour and renown.

mn30:8.5.verse: He is pleased with that and his intention is fulfilled.

mn30:8.6.verse: On that account he lauds himself and disparages others thus: “

mn30:8.7.verse: “I have gain, I have renown, but these other bhikkhus are unknown, of no account.”

mn30:8.8.verse: So he arouses no desire to act, he makes no effort, for the realization of other _dhammas_ higher than that gain, honour and renown and superior to it.

mn30:8.9.verse: ‘I say that this person is like a man needing heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood (who comes to) a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood and its sapwood and its inner bark and its outer bark he cuts its twigs and leaves and takes them away thinking they are heartwood;

mn30:8.10.verse: and so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.

mn30:12.10.verse: He does not, on that account, laud himself and disparage others.

mn30:12.11.verse: He arouses desire to act, and he makes effort, for the realization of dhammas higher than that perfection of virtue and superior to that. He does not hang back and slack.

mn30:12.14.verse: He does not, on that account, laud himself and disparage others.

mn30:13.1.verse: ‘Here, divine, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of seclusion.

mn30:13.2.verse: ‘This can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:14.1.verse: ‘Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna which has self-confidence and singleness of mind and is without initial application and without sustained application with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn30:14.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:15.1.verse: Again, with the fading as well as happiness he abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on which account Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”

mn30:15.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:16.1.verse: Again, with the abandoning of (bodily) pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of (mental) joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn30:16.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:17.1.verse: Again, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of difference, (aware that) “space is infinite”, he enters on and abides in the base consisting of infinite space.

mn30:17.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:18.1.verse: Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of infinite space, (aware that) “consciousness is infinite” he enters upon and abides in the base consisting of infinite consciousness.

mn30:18.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:19.1.verse: Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of infinite consciousness, (aware that) “there is nothing”, he enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.

mn30:19.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:20.1.verse: Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of nothingness, he enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn30:20.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:21.1.verse: Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. And his taints are exhausted by his seeing with understanding.

mn30:21.2.verse: This too can be a dhamma higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:21.3.verse: These are the dhammas that are higher than that knowledge and vision and superior to it.

mn30:22.1.verse: I say that this person is like a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, (who comes to) a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and cutting its heartwood, he takes it away, knowing that it is heartwood;

mn30:22.2.verse: and so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood, his purpose will be served.

mn30:22.3.verse: ‘I say that's what this person is like.

mn30:23.1.verse: ‘So this life divine does not have gain, honour and renown for its advantage, or perfection of virtue for its advantage, or perfection of concentration for its advantage, or knowledge and vision for its advantage.

mn30:23.2.verse: But it is this unassailable deliverance of the mind

mn30:23.3.verse: that is the goal of this life divine, its heartwood and its end.’

mn30:24.1.verse: When this was said, Pingalakoccha of the divine caste said to the Blessed One:

mn30:24.3.verse: from today let Master Gotama accept me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn30:0.2.verse: The Shorter Simile of the Heartwood

mn30:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn30:2.1.verse: Then the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn30:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn30:2.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, there are those ascetics and brahmins who lead an order and a community, and tutor a community. They’re well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people.

mn30:2.4.verse: Namely: Pūraṇa Kassapa, the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, Ajita of the hair blanket, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan.

mn30:2.5.verse: According to their own claims, did all of them have direct knowledge, or none of them, or only some?”

mn30:2.7.verse: ‘According to their own claims, did all of them have direct knowledge, or none of them, or only some?’

mn30:2.8.verse: I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn30:2.9.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn30:3.1.verse: “Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But, passing over the heartwood, softwood, bark, and shoots, he’d cut off the branches and leaves and leave imagining they were heartwood.

mn30:3.2.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say:

mn30:3.3.verse: ‘This gentleman doesn’t know what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn30:3.4.verse: That’s why he passed them over, cut off the branches and leaves, and left imagining they were heartwood.

mn30:3.5.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he won’t succeed.’

mn30:4.1.verse: Suppose there was another person in need of heartwood … he’d cut off the shoots and leave imagining they were heartwood …

mn30:5.1.verse: Suppose there was another person in need of heartwood … he’d cut off the bark and leave imagining it was heartwood …

mn30:6.1.verse: Suppose there was another person in need of heartwood … he’d cut out the softwood and leave imagining it was heartwood …

mn30:7.1.verse: Suppose there was another person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. He’d cut out just the heartwood and leave knowing it was heartwood.

mn30:7.2.verse: If a person with clear eyes saw him they’d say:

mn30:7.3.verse: ‘This gentleman knows what heartwood, softwood, bark, shoots, or branches and leaves are.

mn30:7.4.verse: That’s why he cut out just the heartwood and left knowing it was heartwood.

mn30:7.5.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he will succeed.’

mn30:8.1.verse: In the same way, take a certain individual who goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn30:8.2.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn30:8.3.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn30:8.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn30:8.5.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn30:8.6.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that:

mn30:8.7.verse: ‘I’m the one with possessions, honor, and popularity. These other mendicants are obscure and insignificant.’

mn30:8.8.verse: They become lazy and slack on account of their possessions, honor, and popularity, not generating enthusiasm or trying to realize those things that are better and finer. …

mn30:8.11.verse: They’re like the individual who mistakes branches and leaves for heartwood, I say.

mn30:9.1.verse: Next, take an individual who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn30:9.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn30:9.5.verse: They’re not happy with that, and haven’t got all they wished for.

mn30:9.6.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn30:9.7.verse: They don’t become lazy and slack regarding their possessions, honor, and popularity, but generate enthusiasm and try to realize those things that are better and finer.

mn30:9.9.verse: They’re happy with that, and they’ve got all they wished for.

mn30:9.10.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that:

mn30:9.11.verse: ‘I’m the one who is ethical, of good character. These other mendicants are unethical, of bad character.’

mn30:9.12.verse: They become lazy and slack regarding their accomplishment in ethics, not generating enthusiasm or trying to realize those things that are better and finer. …

mn30:9.15.verse: They’re like the individual who mistakes shoots for heartwood, I say.

mn30:10.1.verse: Next, take an individual who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn30:10.16.verse: They become lazy and slack regarding their accomplishment in immersion, not generating enthusiasm or trying to realize those things that are better and finer. …

mn30:10.19.verse: They’re like the individual who mistakes bark for heartwood, I say.

mn30:11.1.verse: Next, take an individual who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness …

mn30:11.20.verse: They become lazy and slack regarding their knowledge and vision, not generating enthusiasm or trying to realize those things that are better and finer. …

mn30:11.23.verse: They’re like the individual who mistakes softwood for heartwood, I say.

mn30:12.1.verse: Next, take an individual who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn30:12.2.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn30:12.3.verse: Hopefully I can find an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn30:12.4.verse: When they’ve gone forth they generate possessions, honor, and popularity.

mn30:12.5.verse: They’re not happy with that, and haven’t got all they wished for.

mn30:12.6.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn30:12.7.verse: They don’t become lazy and slack on account of their possessions, honor, and popularity, but generate enthusiasm and try to realize those things that are better and finer.

mn30:12.9.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn30:12.10.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn30:12.11.verse: They don’t become lazy and slack regarding their accomplishment in ethics, but generate enthusiasm and try to realize those things that are better and finer.

mn30:12.13.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn30:12.14.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn30:12.15.verse: They don’t become lazy and slack regarding their accomplishment in immersion, but generate enthusiasm and try to realize those things that are better and finer.

mn30:12.17.verse: They’re happy with that, but they haven’t got all they wished for.

mn30:12.18.verse: They don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn30:12.19.verse: They don’t become lazy and slack regarding their knowledge and vision, but generate enthusiasm and try to realize those things that are better and finer.

mn30:12.20.verse: And what are those things that are better and finer than knowledge and vision?

mn30:13.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn30:13.2.verse: This is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:14.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn30:14.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:15.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn30:15.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:16.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn30:16.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:17.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

mn30:17.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:18.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn30:18.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:19.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn30:19.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:20.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn30:20.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:21.1.verse: Furthermore, take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

mn30:21.2.verse: This too is something better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:21.3.verse: These are the things that are better and finer than knowledge and vision.

mn30:22.1.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. He’d cut out just the heartwood and leave knowing it was heartwood.

mn30:22.2.verse: Whatever he needs to make from heartwood, he will succeed.

mn30:22.3.verse: That’s what this individual is like, I say.

mn30:23.1.verse: And so, brahmin, this spiritual life is not lived for the sake of possessions, honor, and popularity, or for accomplishment in ethics, or for accomplishment in immersion, or for knowledge and vision.

mn30:23.2.verse: It is this unshakable freedom of heart

mn30:23.3.verse: that is the goal of the spiritual life, the core and the final end.”

mn30:24.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said to the Buddha,

mn30:24.3.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn31:1.2.verse: One one occasion the Blessed One was living at Nādika in the Giñjaka House.

mn31:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila were living at the Park of the Gosinga (Cow’s Horn) Sāla-tree Wood.

mn31:3.1.verse: When it was evening the Blessed One rose from meditation and went to the Park of the Gosinga Sāla-tree Wood.

mn31:3.2.verse: The park-keeper saw the Blessed One coming.

mn31:3.4.verse: ‘Do not come into this park, monk.

mn31:3.5.verse: There are three clansmen here seeking their own good.

mn31:4.1.verse: The venerable Anuruddha heard the park-keeper speaking to the Blessed One.

mn31:4.3.verse: ‘Friend park-keeper, do not keep the Blessed One out.

mn31:4.4.verse: It is our Master, the Blessed One, who has come.’

mn31:4.5.verse: The venerable Anuruddha went to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila and said:

mn31:4.6.verse: ‘Come out, venerable sirs, come out: our Master has come.’

mn31:5.1.verse: Then all three went to meet the Blessed One.

mn31:5.2.verse: One took his bowl and outer robe, one prepared a seat, and one placed water for washing the feet.

mn31:5.3.verse: The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared,

mn31:5.4.verse: and having done so, he washed his feet.

mn31:5.5.verse: Then they paid homage to him and sat down at one side.

mn31:5.6.verse: When they had done so, the Blessed One said to them:

mn31:5.7.verse: ‘I hope that you are all keeping well, Anuruddha, that you all are comfortable, and that you have no trouble on account of alms-food.’

mn31:5.8.verse: ‘We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are comfortable, and we have no trouble on account of alms-food.’

mn31:6.1.verse: ‘I hope that you all live in concord and agreement, Anuruddha, as undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.’

mn31:6.3.verse: ‘But, Anuruddha, how do you live thus?’

mn31:7.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, as to that, I think thus:

mn31:7.2.verse: “It is gain for me, it is great gain for me

mn31:7.3.verse: that I am living with such companions in the life divine.”

mn31:7.4.verse: I maintain bodily, verbal and mental acts of living-kindness towards these venerable ones in public and in private.

mn31:7.8.verse: “Why should I not set aside what I am minded to do and do only what they are minded to do?”

mn31:7.10.verse: We are different in body, venerable sir, but only one in mind, I think.’

mn31:7.11.verse: The venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila each spoke likewise. They added:

mn31:7.23.verse: ‘That is how we live in concord, venerable sir, as friendly and undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.’

mn31:8.2.verse: I hope that you all dwell diligent, ardent and self-controlled.’

mn31:9.2.verse: ‘But, Anuruddha, how do you dwell thus?’

mn31:9.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, as to that, whichever of us returns first from the village with alms-food prepares the seats, sets outs the water [for drinking and for washing and puts the refuse bucket in its place.

mn31:9.4.verse: Whichever of us returns last eats any food left over, if he wishes; otherwise he throws it away where there is no greenery or drops it into water where there is no life.

mn31:9.5.verse: He puts away the seats and the water for drinking and for washing. He puts away the refuse bucket after washing it, and he sweeps out the refectory.

mn31:9.6.verse: Whoever notices that the pots of drinking water or washing water or water for the privy are low or empty sees to them.

mn31:9.7.verse: If they are too heavy for him, he calls someone else by a sign of the hand and they move it by joining hands. We do not speak for that purpose.

mn31:9.8.verse: But every five days we sit out the night together in talk on the Dhamma.

mn31:9.9.verse: That is how we dwell diligent, ardent and self-controlled.’

mn31:10.2.verse: but while dwelling diligent, ardent and self-controlled in this way, have you attained as a comfortable abiding any distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma?’

mn31:10.4.verse: Here whenever we want, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, we enter upon and abide in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn31:10.5.verse: Venerable sir, this is a distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma, which we have attained as a comfortable abiding while dwelling diligent, ardent and self-controlled.’

mn31:11-13.2.verse: But is there any other distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma, which you have attained as a comfortable abiding by surmounting that abiding, by tranquillizing that abiding?’

mn31:11-13.4.verse: Here whenever we want, with the stilling of initial application … the second jhāna … self-controlled.’

mn31:14.4.verse: Here whenever we want, with the fading as well of happiness … the third jhāna … self-controlled.’

mn31:15.4.verse: Here whenever we want, with the abandoning of (bodily) pleasure and pain … the fourth jhāna … self-controlled.’

mn31:16.4.verse: Here whenever we want, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form … base consisting of infinite space …’

mn31:18.2.verse: But is there any other distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma, which you have attained as a comfortable abiding by surmounting that abiding, by tranquillizing that abiding?’

mn31:18.4.verse: Here whenever we want, by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception we enter upon and abide in the cessation of perception and feeling. And our taints are exhausted by our seeing with understanding.

mn31:18.5.verse: Venerable sir, that is a distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma, which we have attained as a comfortable abiding by surmounting that (former) abiding, by tranquillizing that (former) abiding.’

mn31:18.8.verse: There is no comfortable abiding higher or more sublime than that.’

mn31:19.1.verse: Then when the Blessed One had instructed, urged, roused and encouraged the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila with a talk on the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and departed.

mn31:20.1.verse: Now when they had accompanied the Blessed One a little on his way and turned back again, the venerable Nandiya asked the venerable Anuruddha and the venerable Kimbila:

mn31:20.2.verse: ‘Have we ever announced to the venerable Anuruddha

mn31:20.3.verse: our obtaining such and such abidings and attainments that he proclaims them in the Blessed One’s presence up to the exhaustion of taints?’

mn31:20.4.verse: ‘The venerable ones have never announced to me

mn31:20.5.verse: their obtaining of such and such abidings and attainments. Yet by encompassing the venerable ones’ minds with my mind it is known to me

mn31:20.6.verse: that they have obtained such and such abidings and attainments.

mn31:20.7.verse: Besides deities have told me this fact (saying:)

mn31:20.8.verse: “These venerable ones have obtained such and such abidings and attainments.”

mn31:20.9.verse: Then I declared it when directly questioned by the Blessed One.’

mn31:21.1.verse: Then the spirit Digha the Sorcerer went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he stood at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn31:21.2.verse: ‘It is gain for the Vajjians, venerable sir, it is great gain for the Vajjians,

mn31:21.3.verse: where the Tathāgata dwells, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, and these three clansmen,

mn31:21.4.verse: the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila!’

mn31:21.5.verse: And on hearing the voice of the spirit Digha the Sorcerer, the Earth gods responded:

mn31:21.9.verse: And on hearing the voice of the Earth gods, the gods of the Four Kings responded: ‘It is gain …

mn31:21.11.verse: … The gods who have Gone to Bliss …

mn31:21.13.verse: … The gods who delight in Creating …

mn31:21.14.verse: And on hearing the voice of the gods who delight in Creating, the gods who wield Power over Others’ Creations responded: ‘It is gain …’

mn31:21.15.verse: And on hearing the voice of the gods who wield Power over Others’ Creations, the gods of the Retinue of the Divinity (Brahmā) responded:

mn31:21.16.verse: ‘It is gain for the Vajjians, it is great gain for the Vajjians,

mn31:21.17.verse: where the Tathāgata dwells, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, and these three clansmen,

mn31:21.18.verse: the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila!’

mn31:22.1.verse: ‘So it is, Digha, so it is.

mn31:22.2.verse: And if the clan from which those three clansmen went forth from the home life into homelessness should remember them with confident heart, that would be long for the welfare and happiness of that clan.

mn31:22.3.verse: And if the retainers of the clan from which those three clansmen went forth …

mn31:22.7.verse: And if the country from which those three clansmen went forth from the home life into homelessness should remember them with confident heart, that would be long for the welfare and happiness of that country.

mn31:22.8.verse: If all of the warrior-noble caste …

mn31:22.11.verse: If all the artisan caste should remember them with confident heart, that would be long for the welfare and happiness of the artisan caste.

mn31:22.12.verse: If the world with its gods, its Māras and its divinity (Brahmā), this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, should remember them with confident heart, that would be long for the welfare and happiness of the world.

mn31:22.13.verse: See, Digha, how far these three clansmen are practising the way of welfare and happiness of the many out of pity for the world, for the benefit, welfare and happiness of gods and men!’

mn31:22.14.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn31:22.15.verse: The spirit Digha the Sorcerer was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn31:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying at Ñātika in the brick house.

mn31:2.1.verse: Now at that time the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila were staying in the sal forest park at Gosiṅga.

mn31:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to that park.

mn31:3.2.verse: The park keeper saw the Buddha coming off in the distance

mn31:3.5.verse: There are three gentlemen staying here whose nature is to desire self-knowledge.

mn31:4.1.verse: Anuruddha heard the park keeper conversing with the Buddha,

mn31:4.3.verse: “Don’t keep the Buddha out, good park keeper!

mn31:4.4.verse: Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”

mn31:4.5.verse: Then Anuruddha went to Nandiya and Kimbila, and said to them,

mn31:4.6.verse: “Come forth, venerables, come forth! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived!”

mn31:5.1.verse: Then Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila came out to greet the Buddha.

mn31:5.2.verse: One received his bowl and robe, one spread out a seat, and one set out water for washing his feet.

mn31:5.3.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

mn31:5.5.verse: Those venerables bowed and sat down to one side.

mn31:5.7.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Anuruddha and friends, I hope you’re all right. And I hope you’re having no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn31:5.8.verse: “We’re keeping well, Blessed One, we’re getting by. And we have no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn31:6.1.verse: “I hope you’re living in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes?”

mn31:6.2.verse: “Indeed, sir, we live in harmony as you say.”

mn31:6.3.verse: “But how do you live this way?”

mn31:7.3.verse: to live together with spiritual companions such as these.’

mn31:7.4.verse: I consistently treat these venerables with kindness by way of body, speech, and mind, both in public and in private.

mn31:7.8.verse: ‘Why don’t I set aside my own ideas and just go along with these venerables’ ideas?’

mn31:7.10.verse: Though we’re different in body, sir, we’re one in mind, it seems to me.”

mn31:7.11.verse: And the venerables Nandiya and Kimbila spoke likewise, and they added:

mn31:7.23.verse: “That’s how we live in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.”

mn31:8.2.verse: But I hope you’re living diligently, keen, and resolute?”

mn31:9.2.verse: “But how do you live this way?”

mn31:9.3.verse: “In this case, sir, whoever returns first from almsround prepares the seats, and puts out the drinking water and the rubbish bin.

mn31:9.4.verse: If there’s remainder, whoever returns last eats it if they like. Otherwise they throw it out where there is little that grows, or drop it into water that has no living creatures.

mn31:9.5.verse: Then they put away the seats, drinking water, and rubbish bin, and sweep the refectory.

mn31:9.6.verse: If someone sees that the pot of water for washing, drinking, or the toilet is empty they set it up.

mn31:9.7.verse: If he can’t do it, he summons another with a wave of the hand, and they set it up by lending each other a hand to lift. But we don’t break into speech for that reason.

mn31:9.8.verse: And every five days we sit together for the whole night and discuss the teachings.

mn31:9.9.verse: That’s how we live diligently, keen, and resolute.”

mn31:10.2.verse: But as you live diligently like this, have you achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation?”

mn31:10.4.verse: Whenever we want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, we enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn31:10.5.verse: This is a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation, that we have achieved while living diligent, keen, and resolute.”

mn31:11-13.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:11-13.4.verse: Whenever we want, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, we enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn31:11-13.5.verse: This is another superhuman distinction that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.”

mn31:14.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:14.4.verse: Whenever we want, with the fading away of rapture, we enter and remain in the third absorption, where we meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn31:14.5.verse: This is another superhuman distinction that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.”

mn31:15.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:15.4.verse: Whenever we want, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, we enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn31:15.5.verse: This is another superhuman distinction that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.”

mn31:16.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:16.4.verse: Whenever we want, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, we enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

mn31:16.5.verse: This is another superhuman distinction that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.”

mn31:17.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:17.4.verse: Whenever we want, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, we enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness. …

mn31:17.5.verse: going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, we enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness. …

mn31:17.6.verse: going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, we enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn31:17.7.verse: This is another superhuman distinction that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.”

mn31:18.2.verse: But have you achieved any other superhuman distinction for going beyond and stilling that meditation?”

mn31:18.4.verse: Whenever we want, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, we enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, our defilements have come to an end.

mn31:18.5.verse: This is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation, that we have achieved for going beyond and stilling that meditation.

mn31:18.6.verse: And we don’t see any better or finer way of meditating comfortably than this.”

mn31:18.8.verse: There is no better or finer way of meditating comfortably than this.”

mn31:19.1.verse: Then the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila with a Dhamma talk, after which he rose from his seat and left.

mn31:20.1.verse: The venerables then accompanied the Buddha for a little way before turning back. Nandiya and Kimbila said to Anuruddha,

mn31:20.2.verse: “Did we ever tell you that we had

mn31:20.3.verse: gained such and such meditations and attainments, up to the ending of defilements, as you revealed to the Buddha?”

mn31:20.4.verse: “The venerables did not tell me that they had

mn31:20.5.verse: gained such meditations and attainments. But I discovered it by encompassing your minds,

mn31:20.9.verse: I answered when the Buddha directly asked about it.”

mn31:21.1.verse: Then the native spirit Dīgha Parajana went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

mn31:21.2.verse: “The Vajjis are lucky! The Vajjian people are so very lucky

mn31:21.3.verse: that the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha stays there, as well as these three gentlemen,

mn31:21.4.verse: the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.”

mn31:21.5.verse: Hearing the cry of Dīgha Parajana, the earth gods raised the cry …

mn31:21.9.verse: Hearing the cry of the earth gods, the gods of the four great kings …

mn31:21.13.verse: the gods who love to create …

mn31:21.14.verse: the gods who control what is created by others …

mn31:21.15.verse: the gods of the Divinity’s host raised the cry,

mn31:21.16.verse: “The Vajjis are lucky! The Vajjian people are so very lucky

mn31:21.17.verse: that the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha stays there, as well as these three gentlemen,

mn31:21.18.verse: the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.”

mn31:21.19.verse: And so at that moment, that second, that hour, those venerables were known as far as the realm of divinity.

mn31:22.1.verse: “That’s so true, Dīgha! That’s so true!

mn31:22.2.verse: If the family from which those three gentlemen went forth from the lay life to homelessness were to recollect those venerables with confident heart, that would be for that family’s lasting welfare and happiness.

mn31:22.11.verse: all the workers were to recollect those venerables with confident heart, that would be for all those menials’ lasting welfare and happiness.

mn31:22.12.verse: If the whole world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—were to recollect those venerables with confident heart, that would be for the whole world’s lasting welfare and happiness.

mn31:22.13.verse: See, Dīgha, how those three gentlemen are practicing for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans!”

mn31:22.14.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn31:22.15.verse: Satisfied, the native spirit Dīgha Parajana approved what the Buddha said.

mn32:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the sal forest park at Gosiṅga, together with several well-known senior disciples, such as

mn32:1.3.verse: the venerables Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Anuruddha, Revata, Ānanda, and others.

mn32:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna came out of retreat, went to Venerable Mahākassapa, and said,
