mn32:2.2.verse: “Come, Reverend Kassapa, let’s go to Venerable Sāriputta to hear the teaching.”

mn32:2.4.verse: Then, together with Venerable Anuruddha, they went to Sāriputta to hear the teaching.

mn32:3.2.verse: went to Venerable Revata, told him what was happening,

mn32:4.1.verse: Sāriputta saw them coming off in the distance

mn32:4.4.verse: Welcome to Ānanda, the Buddha’s attendant, who is so close to the Buddha.

mn32:4.5.verse: Reverend Ānanda, the sal forest park at Gosiṅga is lovely, the night is bright, the sal trees are in full blossom, and heavenly scents seem to float on the air.

mn32:4.6.verse: What kind of mendicant would grace this park?”

mn32:4.7.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s a mendicant who is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

mn32:4.8.verse: And they teach the four assemblies in order to uproot the underlying tendencies with well-rounded and coherent words and phrases.

mn32:4.9.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:5.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sāriputta said to Revata,

mn32:5.2.verse: “Reverend Revata, Ānanda has answered according to his own inspiration.

mn32:5.3.verse: And now we ask you the same question.”

mn32:5.6.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s a mendicant who enjoys retreat and loves retreat. They’re committed to inner serenity of the heart, they don’t neglect absorption, they’re endowed with discernment, and they frequent empty huts.

mn32:5.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:6.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sāriputta said to Anuruddha,

mn32:6.2.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, Revata has answered according to his own inspiration.

mn32:6.3.verse: And now we ask you the same question.”

mn32:6.6.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s a mendicant who surveys a thousandfold galaxy with clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human,

mn32:6.7.verse: just as a person with clear eyes could survey a thousand orbits from the upper floor of a royal longhouse.

mn32:6.9.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:7.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sāriputta said to Mahākassapa,

mn32:7.2.verse: “Reverend Kassapa, Anuruddha has answered according to his own inspiration.

mn32:7.3.verse: And now we ask you the same question.”

mn32:7.6.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s a mendicant who lives in the wilderness, eats only almsfood, wears rag robes, and owns just three robes; and they praise these things. They are of few wishes, content, secluded, aloof, and energetic; and they praise these things. They are accomplished in ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom; and they praise these things.

mn32:7.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:8.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sāriputta said to Mahāmoggallāna,

mn32:8.2.verse: “Reverend Moggallāna, Mahākassapa has answered according to his own inspiration.

mn32:8.3.verse: And now we ask you the same question.”

mn32:8.6.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s when two mendicants engage in discussion about the teaching. They question each other and answer each other’s questions without faltering, and their discussion on the teaching flows on.

mn32:8.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:9.2.verse: “Each of us has spoken from our heart.

mn32:9.4.verse: Reverend Sāriputta, the sal forest park at Gosiṅga is lovely, the night is bright, the sal trees are in full blossom, and heavenly scents seem to float on the air.

mn32:9.5.verse: What kind of mendicant would grace this park?”

mn32:9.6.verse: “Reverend Moggallāna, it’s when a mendicant masters their mind and is not mastered by it.

mn32:9.7.verse: In the morning, they abide in whatever meditation or attainment they want.

mn32:9.9.verse: and in the evening, they abide in whatever meditation or attainment they want.

mn32:9.10.verse: Suppose that a ruler or their chief minister had a chest full of garments of different colors.

mn32:9.11.verse: In the morning, they’d don whatever pair of garments they wanted.

mn32:9.13.verse: and in the evening, they’d don whatever pair of garments they wanted.

mn32:9.14.verse: In the same way, a mendicant masters their mind and is not mastered by it.

mn32:9.15.verse: In the morning, they abide in whatever meditation or attainment they want.

mn32:9.17.verse: and in the evening, they abide in whatever meditation or attainment they want.

mn32:9.18.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:10.1.verse: Then Sāriputta said to those venerables,

mn32:10.2.verse: “Each of us has spoken from the heart.

mn32:10.3.verse: Come, reverends, let’s go to the Buddha, and inform him about this.

mn32:10.4.verse: As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”

mn32:10.6.verse: Then those venerables went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Venerable Sāriputta told the Buddha of how the mendicants had come to see him, and how he had asked Ānanda:

mn32:11.6.verse: “‘Ānanda, the sal forest park at Gosiṅga is lovely, the night is bright, the sal trees are in full blossom, and heavenly scents seem to float on the air.

mn32:11.7.verse: What kind of mendicant would grace this park?’

mn32:11.8.verse: When I had spoken, Ānanda said to me:

mn32:11.9.verse: ‘Reverend Sāriputta, it’s a mendicant who is very learned …

mn32:11.11.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:11.13.verse: Ānanda answered in the right way for him.

mn32:12.1.verse: “Next I asked Revata the same question.

mn32:12.8.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:12.10.verse: Revata answered in the right way for him.

mn32:13.1.verse: “Next I asked Anuruddha the same question.

mn32:13.5.verse: ‘It’s a mendicant who surveys the thousandfold galaxy with clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human …

mn32:13.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:13.8.verse: “Good, good, Sāriputta! Anuruddha answered in the right way for him.

mn32:13.9.verse: For Anuruddha surveys the thousandfold galaxy with clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human.”

mn32:14.1.verse: “Next I asked Mahākassapa the same question.

mn32:14.6.verse: ‘It’s a mendicant who lives in the wilderness … and is accomplished in the knowledge and vision of freedom; and they praise these things.

mn32:14.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:14.9.verse: Kassapa answered in the right way for him.

mn32:14.10.verse: For Kassapa lives in the wilderness … and is accomplished in the knowledge and vision of freedom; and he praises these things.”

mn32:15.1.verse: “Next I asked Mahāmoggallāna the same question.

mn32:15.6.verse: ‘It’s when two mendicants engage in discussion about the teaching …

mn32:15.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:15.8.verse: “Good, good, Sāriputta! Moggallāna answered in the right way for him.

mn32:15.9.verse: For Moggallāna is a Dhamma speaker.”

mn32:16.1.verse: When he had spoken, Moggallāna said to the Buddha,

mn32:16.3.verse: ‘Each of us has spoken according to our own inspiration.

mn32:16.5.verse: Reverend Sāriputta, the sal forest park at Gosiṅga is lovely, the night is bright, the sal trees are in full blossom, and heavenly scents seem to float on the air.

mn32:16.6.verse: What kind of mendicant would grace this park?’

mn32:16.7.verse: When I had spoken, Sāriputta said to me:

mn32:16.8.verse: ‘Reverend Moggallāna, it’s when a mendicant masters their mind and is not mastered by it …

mn32:16.20.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.’”

mn32:16.22.verse: Sāriputta answered in the right way for him.

mn32:16.23.verse: For Sāriputta masters his mind and is not mastered by it …”

mn32:17.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sāriputta asked the Buddha,

mn32:17.3.verse: “You’ve all spoken well in your own way.

mn32:17.4.verse: However, listen to me also as to what kind of mendicant would grace this sal forest park at Gosiṅga.

mn32:17.5.verse: It’s a mendicant who, after the meal, returns from almsround, sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present, thinking:

mn32:17.6.verse: ‘I will not break this sitting posture until my mind is freed from the defilements by not grasping!’

mn32:17.7.verse: That’s the kind of mendicant who would grace this park.”

mn32:17.8.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn32:17.9.verse: Satisfied, those venerables approved what the Buddha said.

mn33:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jetā’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn33:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn33:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a herdsman is endowed with eleven factors he is incapable of rearing and keeping a herd of cattle.

mn33:2.3.verse: Here a herdsman has no knowledge of form, he is unskilled in characteristics, he fails to pick out flies’ eggs, he fails to cover up wounds, he fails to smoke out (the byres), he does not know the watering-place, he does not know what it is to have drunk, he does not know the road, he is unskilled in pastures, as a milker he leaves none, and he makes no extra offering to those bulls who are the fathers and leaders of the herd.

mn33:2.4.verse: When a herdsman is endowed with these eleven factors, he is incapable of rearing and keeping a herd of cattle.

mn33:3.1.verse: ‘So too, when a bhikkhu is endowed with eleven dhammas, he is incapable of growth, increase and fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn33:3.3.verse: Here a bhikkhu has no knowledge of form, he is unskilled in characteristics, he fails to pick out flies’ eggs, he fails to cover up wounds, he fails to smoke out (the byres), he does not know the watering-place, he does not know what it is to have drunk, he does not know the road, he is unskilled in pastures, as a milker he leaves none, and he makes no extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth, who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha.

mn33:4.1.verse: ‘How has a bhikkhu no knowledge of form?

mn33:4.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu fails to understand any kind (of form) as it actually is thus: “All form of whatever kind consists of the four great primary elements and any form derived from the four great primary elements.”

mn33:4.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu has no knowledge of form.

mn33:5.1.verse: ‘How is a bhikkhu unskilled in characteristics?

mn33:5.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu fails to understand (a characteristic) as it actually is thus: “A fool is characterized by his acts, a wise man is characterized by his acts”.

mn33:5.3.verse: That is how a hhikkhu is unskilled in characteristics.

mn33:6.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu fail to pick out flies’ eggs?

mn33:6.2.verse: Here when thinking with sensual desire has arisen, a bhikkhu endures it, he does not abandon it, remove it, do away with and annihilate it. When thinking with ill-will has arisen … When thinking with cruelty has arisen … When evil unprofitable dhammas have arisen, a bhikkhu endures them, he does not abandon them, remove them, do away with and annihilate them.

mn33:6.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu fails to pick out flies’ eggs.

mn33:7.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu fail to cover up wounds?

mn33:7.2.verse: Here, on seeing a form with the eye, a bhikkhu apprehends signs and features

mn33:7.3.verse: through which, if he leaves the eye-faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him, he does not practise the way of its restraint, he does not guard the eye faculty, does not undertake the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn33:7.4.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn33:7.5.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn33:7.6.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn33:7.7.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn33:7.8.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he apprehends signs and features …

mn33:7.9.verse: if he leaves the mind-faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him, he does not practise the way of its restraint, he does not guard the mind faculty, does not undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn33:7.10.verse: That is how a bhikkhu fails to cover up wounds.

mn33:8.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu fail to smoke out (the byres)?

mn33:8.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu does not teach others in detail the Dhamma as heard and mastered (by him).

mn33:8.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu fails to smoke out (the byres).

mn33:9.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu not know the watering-place?

mn33:9.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu does not go from time to time to such bhikkhus as have learned much, as are versed in scriptures, as remember the Dhamma, as remember the Codes, and he does not enquire and ask questions of them thus:

mn33:9.4.verse: What is the meaning of this?”

mn33:9.5.verse: These venerable ones do not reveal the unrevealed to him, make evident the unevident, or remove his doubts about the many kinds of dhammas that give rise to doubt.

mn33:9.6.verse: That is how a bhikkhu does not know the watering-place.

mn33:10.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu not know what it is to have drunk?

mn33:10.2.verse: Here when the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a bhikkhu does not gain experience of meaning, he does not gain experience of dhamma, he does not find gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn33:10.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu does not know what it is to have drunk.

mn33:11.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu not know the road?

mn33:11.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu does not understand the Noble Path as it actually is.

mn33:11.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu does not know the road.

mn33:12.1.verse: ‘How is a bhikkhu unskilled in pastures?

mn33:12.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu does not understand the foundations of mindfulness as they actually are.

mn33:12.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is unskilled in pastures.

mn33:13.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu as a milker leave none?

mn33:13.2.verse: Here faithful householders invite a bhikkhu with robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, to take as much as he likes. The Bhikkhu does not know the (right) amount in accepting.

mn33:13.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu as a milker leaves none.

mn33:14.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu make no extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth, who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha?

mn33:14.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu does not maintain in public and private towards such elder bhikkhus acts of loving-kindness by body, speech and mind.

mn33:14.5.verse: That is how a bhikkhu makes no extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth, who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha.

mn33:14.6.verse: ‘When a bhikkhu is endowed with these eleven dhammas, he is incapable of growth, increase and fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn33:15.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a herdsman is endowed with eleven factors, he is capable of rearing and keeping a herd of cattle.

mn33:15.3.verse: Here a herdsman has knowledge of form, he is skilled in characteristics, he picks out flies’ eggs, he covers up wounds, he smokes out (the byres), he knows the watering-place, he knows what it is to have drunk, he knows the road, he is skilled in pastures, as a milker he leaves some, and he makes extra offerings to those bulls who are the fathers and leaders of the herd.

mn33:15.4.verse: Bhikkhus, when a herdsman is endowed with eleven factors, he is capable of rearing and keeping a herd of cattle.

mn33:16.1.verse: ‘So too, when a bhikkhu is endowed with eleven dhammas, he is capable of growth, increase and fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.

mn33:16.3.verse: Here a bhikkhu has knowledge of form, he is skilled in characteristics, he picks out flies’ eggs, he covers up wounds, he smokes out (the byres), he knows the watering-place, he knows what it is to have drunk, he knows the road, he is skilled in pastures, as a milker he leaves some, and he makes extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha.

mn33:17.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu have knowledge of form?

mn33:17.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu understands (form) as it actually is thus: “All forms of whatever kind consist of the four great primary elements and any form derived from the four great primary elements.”

mn33:17.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu has knowledge of form.

mn33:18.1.verse: ‘How is a bhikkhu skilled in characteristics?

mn33:18.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu understands (a characteristic) as it actually is thus: “A fool is characterized by his acts; a wise man is characterized by his acts.”

mn33:18.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is skilled in characteristics.

mn33:19.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu pick out flies’ eggs?

mn33:19.2.verse: Here when thinking with sensual desire has arisen, a bhikkhu does not endure it, he abandons it, removes it, does away with it and annihilates it. When thinking with ill-will has arisen … When thinking with cruelty has arisen … When evil unprofitable dhammas have arisen, a bhikkhu does not endure them, he abandons them, removes them, does away with them and annihilates them.

mn33:19.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu picks out flies’ eggs.

mn33:20.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu cover up wounds?

mn33:20.2.verse: Here on seeing a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not apprehend signs and features

mn33:20.3.verse: through which if he leaves the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practises the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn33:20.4.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn33:20.5.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn33:20.6.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn33:20.7.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn33:20.8.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind …

mn33:20.9.verse: undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn33:20.10.verse: That is how a bhikkhu covers up wounds.

mn33:21.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu smoke out (the byres)?

mn33:21.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu teaches others in detail the Dhamma as learnt and mastered (by him).

mn33:21.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu smokes out (the byres).

mn33:22.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu know the watering-place?

mn33:22.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu goes from time to time to such bhikkhus as have learnt much, as are versed in scriptures, as remember the Dhamma, as remember the Discipline, as remember the Codes, and he enquires and asks questions of them thus:

mn33:22.4.verse: What is the meaning of this ?”

mn33:22.5.verse: These venerable ones reveal the unrevealed, make evident the unevident, and remove his doubts about the many kinds of dhammas that give rise to doubt.

mn33:22.6.verse: That is how a bhikkhu knows the watering-place.

mn33:23.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu know what it is to have drunk?

mn33:23.2.verse: Here when the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a bhikkhu gains experience of meaning, he gains experience of dhamma, he finds gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn33:23.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu knows what it is to have drunk.

mn33:24.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu know the road?

mn33:24.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu understands the Noble Eightfold Path as it actually is.

mn33:24.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu knows the road.

mn33:25.1.verse: ‘How is a bhikkhu skilled in pastures?

mn33:25.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu understands the four foundations of mindfulness as they actually are.

mn33:25.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is skilled in pastures.

mn33:26.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu as a milker leave some?

mn33:26.2.verse: Here faithful house-holders invite a bhikkhu, with robes, alms-food, resting place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, to take as much as he likes.

mn33:26.3.verse: The bhikkhu knows the (right) amount in accepting.

mn33:26.4.verse: That is how a bhikkhu as a milker leaves some.

mn33:27.1.verse: ‘How does a bhikkhu make extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth, who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha?

mn33:27.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu maintains in public and in private toward such elder bhikkhus acts of loving-kindness by body, speech and mind.

mn33:27.5.verse: That is how a bhikkhu makes extra offerings to those elder bhikkhus of long-standing knowledge and long gone forth, who are the fathers and leaders of the Sangha.

mn33:27.6.verse: ‘When a bhikkhu is endowed with these eleven dhammas, he is capable of growth, increase and fulfilment in this Dhamma and Discipline.’

mn33:27.7.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn33:27.8.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn33:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on the Cowherd

mn33:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn33:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn33:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, a cowherd with eleven factors can’t maintain and expand a herd of cattle.

mn33:2.3.verse: It’s when a cowherd doesn’t know form, is unskilled in characteristics, doesn’t pick out flies’ eggs, doesn’t dress wounds, doesn’t spread smoke, doesn’t know the ford, doesn’t know satisfaction, doesn’t know the trail, is not skilled in ranges, milks dry, and doesn’t show extra respect to the bulls who are fathers and captains of the herd.

mn33:2.4.verse: A cowherd with these eleven factors can’t maintain and expand a herd of cattle.

mn33:3.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant with eleven qualities can’t achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

mn33:3.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t know form, is unskilled in characteristics, doesn’t pick out flies’ eggs, doesn’t dress wounds, doesn’t spread smoke, doesn’t know the ford, doesn’t know satisfaction, doesn’t know the trail, is not skilled in ranges, milks dry, and doesn’t show extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha.

mn33:4.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not know form?

mn33:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t truly understand that all form is the four principal states, or form derived from the four principal states.

mn33:4.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t know form.

mn33:5.1.verse: And how is a mendicant not skilled in characteristics?

mn33:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t understand that a fool is characterized by their deeds, and an astute person is characterized by their deeds.

mn33:5.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant isn’t skilled in characteristics.

mn33:6.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not pick out flies’ eggs?

mn33:6.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant tolerates a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen. They tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen. They don’t give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

mn33:6.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t pick out flies’ eggs.

mn33:7.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not dress wounds?

mn33:7.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they get caught up in the features and details.

mn33:7.3.verse: Since the faculty of sight is left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure become overwhelming. They don’t practice restraint, they don’t protect the faculty of sight, and they don’t achieve its restraint.

mn33:7.4.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn33:7.5.verse: smell an odor with their nose …

mn33:7.6.verse: taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn33:7.7.verse: feel a touch with their body …

mn33:7.8.verse: know an idea with their mind, they get caught up in the features and details.

mn33:7.9.verse: Since the faculty of the mind is left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure become overwhelming. They don’t practice restraint, they don’t protect the faculty of the mind, and they don’t achieve its restraint.

mn33:7.10.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t dress wounds.

mn33:8.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not spread smoke?

mn33:8.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t teach others the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it.

mn33:8.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t spread smoke.

mn33:9.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not know the ford?

mn33:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t from time to time go up to those mendicants who are very learned—inheritors of the heritage, who have memorized the teachings, the monastic law, and the outlines—and ask them questions:

mn33:9.5.verse: Those venerables don’t reveal what is hidden, clarify what is unclear, and dispel doubt regarding the many doubtful matters.

mn33:9.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t know the ford.

mn33:10.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not know satisfaction?

mn33:10.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, when the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One are being taught, finds no inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and finds no joy connected with the teaching.

mn33:10.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t know satisfaction.

mn33:11.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not know the trail?

mn33:11.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t truly understand the noble eightfold path.

mn33:11.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t know the trail.

mn33:12.1.verse: And how is a mendicant not skilled in ranges?

mn33:12.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t truly understand the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn33:12.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is not skilled in ranges.

mn33:13.1.verse: And how does a mendicant milk dry?

mn33:13.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is invited by a householder to accept robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, and that mendicant doesn’t know moderation in accepting.

mn33:13.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant milks dry.

mn33:14.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not show extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha?

mn33:14.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t consistently treat senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha with kindness by way of body, speech, and mind, both in public and in private.

mn33:14.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t show extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha.

mn33:14.6.verse: A mendicant with these eleven qualities can’t achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.

mn33:15.1.verse: A cowherd with eleven factors can maintain and expand a herd of cattle.

mn33:15.3.verse: It’s when a cowherd knows form, is skilled in characteristics, picks out flies’ eggs, dresses wounds, spreads smoke, knows the ford, knows satisfaction, knows the trail, is skilled in ranges, doesn’t milk dry, and shows extra respect to the bulls who are fathers and captains of the herd.

mn33:15.4.verse: A cowherd with these eleven factors can maintain and expand a herd of cattle.

mn33:16.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant with eleven qualities can achieve growth, improvement, and maturity in this teaching and training.

mn33:16.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant knows form, is skilled in characteristics, picks out flies’ eggs, dresses wounds, spreads smoke, knows the ford, knows satisfaction, knows the trail, is skilled in ranges, doesn’t milk dry, and shows extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha.

mn33:17.1.verse: And how does a mendicant know form?

mn33:17.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands that all form is the four principal states, or form derived from the four principal states.

mn33:17.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows form.

mn33:18.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in characteristics?

mn33:18.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant understands that a fool is characterized by their deeds, and an astute person is characterized by their deeds.

mn33:18.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is skilled in characteristics.

mn33:19.1.verse: And how does a mendicant pick out flies’ eggs?

mn33:19.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t tolerate a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen. They don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

mn33:19.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant picks out flies’ eggs.

mn33:20.1.verse: And how does a mendicant dress wounds?

mn33:20.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn33:20.3.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn33:20.4.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn33:20.5.verse: smell an odor with their nose …

mn33:20.6.verse: taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn33:20.7.verse: feel a touch with their body …

mn33:20.8.verse: know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn33:20.9.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn33:20.10.verse: That’s how a mendicant dresses wounds.

mn33:21.1.verse: And how does a mendicant spread smoke?

mn33:21.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant teaches others the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it.

mn33:21.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant spreads smoke.

mn33:22.1.verse: And how does a mendicant know the ford?

mn33:22.2.verse: It’s when from time to time a mendicant goes up to those mendicants who are very learned—inheritors of the heritage, who have memorized the teachings, the monastic law, and the outlines—and asks them questions:

mn33:22.5.verse: Those venerables reveal what is hidden, clarify what is unclear, and dispel doubt regarding the many doubtful matters.

mn33:22.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows the ford.

mn33:23.1.verse: And how does a mendicant know satisfaction?

mn33:23.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, when the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One are being taught, finds inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and finds joy connected with the teaching.

mn33:23.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows satisfaction.

mn33:24.1.verse: And how does a mendicant know the trail?

mn33:24.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands the noble eightfold path.

mn33:24.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows the trail.

mn33:25.1.verse: And how is a mendicant skilled in ranges?

mn33:25.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn33:25.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is skilled in ranges.

mn33:26.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not milk dry?

mn33:26.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant is invited by a householder to accept robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick,

mn33:26.3.verse: and that mendicant knows moderation in accepting.

mn33:26.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant doesn’t milk dry.

mn33:27.1.verse: And how does a mendicant show extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha?

mn33:27.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant consistently treats senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha with kindness by way of body, speech, and mind, both in public and in private.

mn33:27.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant shows extra respect to senior mendicants of long standing, long gone forth, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha.

mn33:27.6.verse: A mendicant with these eleven qualities can achieve growth, improvement, and maturity in this teaching and training.”

mn33:27.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn33:27.8.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn34:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Vajjian country at Ukkācelā on the banks of the River Ganges.

mn34:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn34:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there was once a Magadhan herdsman who by nature lacked understanding and in the last month of the Rains, in the Autumn time, omitting to examine the near shore of the Ganges River or its further shore, he drove his cattle in where there was no ford to cross over to the other shore here in the Videhan country.

mn34:3.1.verse: Then the cattle bunched together in mid-stream in the Ganges River, and they came to disaster.

mn34:3.3.verse: Because the Magadhan herdsman by nature lacked understanding, and in the last month of the Rains, in the Autumn time, omitting to examine the near shore of the Ganges River or its further shore, he drove his cattle in where there was no ford to cross over to the other shore in the Videhan country.

mn34:3.4.verse: So too, when monks or divines are unskilled in this world and the other world, unskilled in what belongs to Māra and what does not belong to him, and unskilled in what belongs to Death and what does not belong to him, it will be long for the harm and suffering of those who shall conceive them as fit to be heard and fit to place faith in.

mn34:4.1.verse: Bhikkhus, there was once a Magadhan herdsman who by nature had understanding and in the last month of the Rains, in the Autumn time, after examining the near shore of the Ganges River and its further shore, he drove his cattle in where there was a ford to cross over to the other shore in the Videhan country.

mn34:5.1.verse: He made the bulls, the fathers and leaders of the herd, cross over first.

mn34:5.2.verse: and they breasted the stream of the Ganges and got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:5.3.verse: He made the strong cattle and the cattle to be tamed cross over next.

mn34:5.4.verse: and they too breasted the stream of the Ganges and got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:5.5.verse: He made the heifers and young oxen cross over next.

mn34:5.6.verse: and they too breasted the stream of the Ganges and got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:5.7.verse: He made the calves and the feeble cattle cross over next.

mn34:5.8.verse: and they too breasted the stream of the Ganges and got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:5.9.verse: There was once a tender calf just born, and being urged on by the mother’s lowing, he too breasted the stream of the Ganges and got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:5.11.verse: Because the Magadhan herdsman by nature had understanding, and in the last month of the Rains, in the Autumn time, after examining the near shore of the Ganges River and its further shore, he drove his cattle in where there was a ford to cross over to the other shore here in the Videhan country.

mn34:5.12.verse: So too, when monks or divines are skilled in this world and the other world, skilled in what belongs to Māra and what does not belong to him, skilled in what belongs to Death and what does not belong to him, it will be long for the welfare and happiness of those who shall conceive them as fit to be heard and fit to place faith in.

mn34:6.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, the bulls, the fathers and leaders of the herd, breasted the Ganges’ stream and got safely across to the further shore;

mn34:6.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are Arahants, with taints exhausted, who have lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and through right final knowledge are liberated, have, by breasting Māra’s stream, got safely across to the further shore.

mn34:7.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, the strong cattle and the cattle to be tamed breasted the Ganges’ stream and got safely across to the further shore;

mn34:7.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who with the destruction of the five lower fetters will reappear spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes) and there attain Nibbāna without ever returning from that world, will also, by breasting Māra’s stream, get safely across to the further shore.

mn34:8.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, the heifers and young oxen breasted the Ganges’ stream and got safely across to the further shore;

mn34:8.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who with the destruction of three fetters and with attenuation of lust, hate and delusion, are once-returners, returning once to this world to make an end of suffering, will also, by breasting Māra’s stream, get safely across to the further shore.

mn34:9.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, the calves and the feeble cattle also breasted the Ganges’ stream and got safely across to the further shore;

mn34:9.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who with the destruction of three fetters are stream-enterers, no longer subject to perdition, certain (of rightness), and headed for full enlightenment, will also, by breasting Māra’s stream, get safely across to the further shore.

mn34:10.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, that tender calf just born which, being urged on by the mother’s lowing, also breasted the Ganges’ stream and got safely across to the further shore;

mn34:10.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, these bhikkhus who are mature in the Dhamma, mature in faith, will also, by breasting Māra’s stream, get safely across to the further shore.

mn34:11.1.verse: Bhikkhus, I am skilled in this world and the next world, skilled in what belongs to Māra and what does not belong to him, and skilled in what belongs to Death and what does not belong to him. It will be long for the welfare and happiness of those who shall conceive me as fit to be heard and fit to place faith in.

mn34:12.1.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn34:12.2.verse: When the Sublime One had said that, the Master said further:

mn34:12.3.verse: Both this world and the world beyond

mn34:12.4.verse: Are well described by He that knows,

mn34:12.5.verse: And what is still in Māra’s reach

mn34:12.6.verse: And what is out of reach of Death.

mn34:12.14.verse: And set your hearts where safety lies.

mn34:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on the Cowherd

mn34:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis near Ukkacelā on the bank of the Ganges River.

mn34:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn34:2.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was an unintelligent Magadhan cowherd. In the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, without inspecting the near shore or the far shore, he drove his cattle across a place with no ford on the Ganges River to the northern shore among the Suvidehans.

mn34:3.1.verse: But the cattle bunched up in mid-stream and came to ruin right there.

mn34:3.3.verse: Because the unintelligent cowherd failed to inspect the shores before driving the cattle across at a place with no ford.

mn34:3.4.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who are unskilled in this world and the other world, unskilled in Māra’s dominion and its opposite, and unskilled in Death’s dominion and its opposite. If anyone thinks they are worth listening to and trusting, it will be for their lasting harm and suffering.

mn34:4.1.verse: Once upon a time, mendicants, there was an intelligent Magadhan cowherd. In the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, after inspecting the near shore and the far shore, he drove his cattle across a ford on the Ganges River to the northern shore among the Suvidehans.

mn34:5.1.verse: First he drove across the bulls, the fathers and captains of the herd.

mn34:5.2.verse: They breasted the stream of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore.

mn34:5.3.verse: Then he drove across the strong and tractable cattle.

mn34:5.4.verse: They too breasted the stream of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore.

mn34:5.5.verse: Then he drove across the bullocks and heifers.

mn34:5.6.verse: They too breasted the stream of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore.

mn34:5.7.verse: Then he drove across the calves and weak cattle.

mn34:5.8.verse: They too breasted the stream of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore.

mn34:5.9.verse: Once it happened that a baby calf had just been born. Urged on by its mother’s lowing, even it managed to breast the stream of the Ganges and safely reach the far shore.

mn34:5.11.verse: Because the intelligent cowherd inspected both shores before driving the cattle across at a ford.

mn34:5.12.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who are skilled in this world and the other world, skilled in Māra’s dominion and its opposite, and skilled in Death’s dominion and its opposite. If anyone thinks they are worth listening to and trusting, it will be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn34:6.1.verse: Just like the bulls, fathers and captains of the herd, who crossed the Ganges to safety

mn34:6.2.verse: are the mendicants who are perfected, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment. Having breasted Māra’s stream, they have safely crossed over to the far shore.

mn34:7.1.verse: Just like the strong and tractable cattle who crossed the Ganges to safety

mn34:7.2.verse: are the mendicants who, with the ending of the five lower fetters, are reborn spontaneously. They’re extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world. They too, having breasted Māra’s stream, will safely cross over to the far shore.

mn34:8.1.verse: Just like the bullocks and heifers who crossed the Ganges to safety

mn34:8.2.verse: are the mendicants who, with the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, are once-returners. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering. They too, having breasted Māra’s stream, will safely cross over to the far shore.

mn34:9.1.verse: Just like the calves and weak cattle who crossed the Ganges to safety

mn34:9.2.verse: are the mendicants who, with the ending of three fetters are stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening. They too, having breasted Māra’s stream, will safely cross over to the far shore.

mn34:10.1.verse: Just like the baby calf who had just been born, but, urged on by its mother’s lowing, still managed to cross the Ganges to safety

mn34:10.2.verse: are the mendicants who are followers of teachings, followers by faith. They too, having breasted Māra’s stream, will safely cross over to the far shore.

mn34:11.1.verse: Mendicants, I am skilled in this world and the other world, skilled in Māra’s dominion and its opposite, and skilled in Death’s dominion and its opposite. If anyone thinks I am worth listening to and trusting, it will be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn34:12.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn34:12.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

mn34:12.4.verse: have been clearly explained by one who knows;

mn34:12.6.verse: and what’s out of Death’s reach.

mn34:12.9.verse: has opened the door to freedom from death,

mn34:12.11.verse: The Wicked One’s stream has been cut,

mn34:12.12.verse: it’s blown away and mown down.

mn35:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesali in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

mn35:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was staying at Vesāli, a debater and a clever speaker, regarded by many as a saint.

mn35:2.2.verse: He spoke these words before an assembly in Vesali:

mn35:2.3.verse: ‘I see no monk or divine, the head of a sangha, head of a sect, teacher of a sect, even if he claims to be Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who would not shake and shiver and tremble and sweat under the armpits on being engaged in argument with me.

mn35:2.4.verse: Even if I engaged a senseless post in argument it would shake and shiver and tremble on being engaged in argument with me,

mn35:2.5.verse: so what shall I say of a human being?’

mn35:3.1.verse: Then it being morning, the venerable Assaji dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Vesali for alms.

mn35:3.2.verse: As Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was walking and wandering for exercise in Vesāli, he saw the venerable Assaji coming in the distance.

mn35:3.3.verse: When he saw him, he went up to him and exchanged greetings with him,

mn35:3.4.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son said:

mn35:4.1.verse: ‘How does the monk Gotama discipline disciples, Master Assaji; and in what way is the monk Gotama’s instruction usually presented among disciples?’

mn35:4.2.verse: ‘This is how the Blessed One disciplines disciples, Aggivessana; and in this way the Blessed One’s instruction is usually presented among disciples:

mn35:4.3.verse: “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent;

mn35:4.4.verse: form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self;

mn35:4.5.verse: formations are all impermanent, dhammas are all not self.”

mn35:4.6.verse: That is the way the Blessed One disciplines disciples; and that is the way in which the Blessed One’s instruction is usually presented among disciples.’

mn35:4.7.verse: ‘If this is what the monk Gotama asserts, we hear indeed what is ill hearing.

mn35:4.8.verse: Now suppose, sometime or other, we were to meet Master Gotama, suppose we had some conversation with him? Suppose we were to detach him from that evil view?’

mn35:5.1.verse: Now at that time five hundred Licchavis had met together in an assembly hall for some business or other.

mn35:5.2.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went to them and said:

mn35:5.3.verse: ‘Come forth, Licchavis, sirs, come forth. There will be converse today between me and the monk Gotama.

mn35:5.4.verse: If the monk Gotama maintains to me what was maintained to me by one of his famous pupils, the bhikkhu called Assaji, then, just as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by the hair and drag him to, and drag him fro, and drag him round about;

mn35:5.5.verse: so with argument I will drag the monk Gotama to, and drag him fro, and drag him round about.

mn35:5.6.verse: Just as a strong brewer’s workman might throw a big brewer’s sieve into a deep water tank, and taking it by the corners, drag it to, and drag it fro and drag it round about;

mn35:5.7.verse: so with argument I will drag the monk Gotama to, drag him fro and drag him round about.

mn35:5.8.verse: Just as a strong brewer’s mixer might take a strainer by the corners and shake it down and shake it up and thump it about;

mn35:5.9.verse: so with argument I will shake the monk Gotama down and shake him up and thump him.

mn35:5.10.verse: And just as a sixty year old elephant might go down into a pond and have great sport in the game of hemp-washing,

mn35:5.11.verse: so too I shall have great sport, I fancy, in the game of hemp-washing the monk Gotama.

mn35:5.12.verse: Come forth, Licchavis, sirs, come forth. There will be converse today between me and the monk Gotama.’

mn35:6.2.verse: ‘Now will the monk Gotama refute Saccaka the Nigantha son’s assertions; or will Saccaka the Nigantha’s son refute the monk Gotama’s assertions?’

mn35:6.4.verse: ‘How will Saccaka the Nigantha’s son refute the Blessed One’s assertions; on the contrary, the Blessed One will refute Saccaka the Nigantha son’s assertions.’

mn35:6.5.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went with the five hundred Licchavis to the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood.

mn35:7.1.verse: Now on that occasion a number of bhikkhus were walking up and down in the open.

mn35:7.2.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went up to them and asked:

mn35:7.3.verse: ‘Where is Master Gotama living now, sirs.

mn35:7.4.verse: We want to see Master Gotama.’

mn35:7.5.verse: ‘The Blessed One has gone into the Great Wood, Aggivessana, and is sitting at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.’

mn35:8.1.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went together with a large following of Licchavis into the Great Wood to where the Blessed One was and exchanged greetings with him,

mn35:8.2.verse: and after the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

mn35:8.3.verse: And some of the Licchavis paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with him, and when this courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down at one side; some raised their hands palms together in salutation and sat down at one side; some pronounced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence and sat down at one side; some kept silence and sat down at one side.

mn35:9.1.verse: When Saccaka the Nigantha’s son had sat down, he said to the Blessed One:

mn35:9.2.verse: ‘I would question Master Gotama on a certain point, if Master Gotama would grant me the favour of an answer to the question?’

mn35:9.4.verse: ‘How does Master Gotama discipline (lead away) his disciples; and in what way is Master Gotama’s instruction usually presented among the disciples?’

mn35:9.5.verse: ‘This is how I discipline (lead away) disciples, Aggivessana; and this is the way my instruction is usually presented among disciples:

mn35:9.6.verse: Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent;

mn35:9.7.verse: form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self;

mn35:9.8.verse: formations are all impermanent, dhammas are all not self.

mn35:9.9.verse: That is the way I discipline disciples; and that is the way in which my instruction is usually presented among disciples.’

mn35:10.1.verse: ‘A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama.’

mn35:10.2.verse: ‘Let it occur to you, Aggivessana,’ the Blessed One said.

mn35:10.3.verse: ‘Just as when seeds and plants, whatever their kind, reach growth, all do so in dependence on earth, based upon earth;

mn35:10.4.verse: in this way these seeds and plants reach growth, increase and expansion.

mn35:10.5.verse: And just as when the kinds of work to be done by the strong are done, all are done in dependence on earth, based upon earth—

mn35:10.6.verse: in this way these works to be done by the strong are done.

mn35:10.7.verse: so too, Master Gotama, a man has form as self, he produces merit or demerit based on form. He has feeling as self, he produces merit or demerit based on feeling. He has perception as self, he produces merit or demerit based on perception. He has formations as self, he produces merit or demerit based on formations. He has consciousness as self, he produces merit or demerit based on consciousness.’

mn35:11.2.verse: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self?’

mn35:11.4.verse: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self. And so does this great multitude.’

mn35:11.5.verse: ‘What has this great multitude to do with you, Aggivessana?

mn35:11.6.verse: Please confine yourself to your own assertion alone.’

mn35:11.8.verse: form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, consciousness is my self.’

mn35:12.1.verse: ‘In that case, Aggivessana, I shall ask you a question in return. Answer it as you like.

mn35:12.2.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:12.3.verse: would a head-anointed warrior-noble king have the power in his own realm

mn35:12.4.verse: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished, for example, King Pasenadi of Kosala, or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha?’

mn35:12.5.verse: ‘Master Gotama, a head-anointed warrior-noble king would have the power in his own realm

mn35:12.6.verse: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished, for example, King Pasenadi of Kosala, or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.

mn35:12.7.verse: For even these (oligarchic) communities and societies

mn35:12.8.verse: such as the Vajjians and the Mallians,

mn35:12.9.verse: have the power in their own realm

mn35:12.10.verse: to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to banish those who should be banished,

mn35:12.11.verse: so all the more so an anointed warrior king such as King Pasenadi of Kosala or King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.

mn35:12.12.verse: He would have it, Master Gotama, and he would be worthy to have it.’

mn35:13.3.verse: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:

mn35:13.4.verse: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’

mn35:13.5.verse: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was silent.

mn35:13.6.verse: A second time the Blessed One said to him:

mn35:13.7.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Aggivessana, when you say thus:

mn35:13.8.verse: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:

mn35:13.9.verse: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’

mn35:13.10.verse: A second time Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was silent.

mn35:13.11.verse: Then the Blessed One said to him:

mn35:13.12.verse: ‘Aggivessana, answer now. Now is not the time to be silent.

mn35:13.13.verse: If anyone did not answer when asked a question according to Dhamma up to the third time by the Tathāgata his head would split in seven pieces there and then.’

mn35:14.1.verse: Now on that occasion a thunderbolt-wielding spirit with an iron bolt in his head, burning, blazing, glowing, appeared in the air above Saccaka the Nigantha’s son (thinking):

mn35:14.2.verse: ‘If this Saccaka the Nigantha’s son does not answer when asked a question according to Dhamma up to the third time, I shall split his head into seven pieces here and now.’

mn35:14.3.verse: The Blessed One saw the thunderbolt-wielding spirit and so did Saccaka the Nigantha’s son.

mn35:14.4.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was frightened, terrified and his hair stood on end, and seeking to make the Blessed One his shelter, his asylum and refuge, he said:

mn35:14.5.verse: ‘Ask me, Master Gotama; I will answer.’

mn35:15.3.verse: “Form is my self”, have you any such power over that form as:

mn35:15.4.verse: “Let my form be thus; let my form be not thus”?’

mn35:16.3.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn35:16.4.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:16.6.verse: “Feeling is my self”, have you any such power over that feeling as:

mn35:16.7.verse: “Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling be not thus”?’

mn35:17.3.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn35:17.4.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:17.6.verse: “Perception is my self”, have you any such power over that perception as:

mn35:17.7.verse: “Let my perception be thus; let my perception be not thus”?’

mn35:18.3.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn35:18.4.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:18.6.verse: “Formations are my self”, have you any such power over those formations as:

mn35:18.7.verse: “Let my formations be thus; let my formations be not thus”?’

mn35:19.3.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn35:19.4.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:19.6.verse: “Consciousness is my self”, have you any such power over that consciousness as:

mn35:19.7.verse: “Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness be not thus”?’

mn35:20.3.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn35:20.4.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:20.7.verse: ‘Now is what is impermanent unpleasant or pleasant?’

mn35:20.9.verse: ‘Now is what is impermanent, unpleasant and subject to change fit to be regarded as:

mn35:20.10.verse: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’

mn35:20.12.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Aggivessana, is feeling permanent or impermanent? …

mn35:20.15.verse: How do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn35:20.18.verse: ‘Now is what is impermanent unpleasant or pleasant?’

mn35:20.20.verse: ‘Now is what is impermanent, unpleasant and subject to change fit to be regarded as:

mn35:20.21.verse: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’

mn35:21.2.verse: when a man adheres to suffering, resorts to suffering, accepts suffering, always views suffering as: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”, would he himself ever fully understand suffering or abide with suffering quite exhausted?’

mn35:21.6.verse: that being so, do you not adhere to suffering, do you not resort to suffering, do you not accept suffering, do you not always view suffering as:

mn35:21.7.verse: “This is mine, this is I, this is my self”?’

mn35:22.1.verse: ‘It is as though a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, took a sharp axe and went to the wood;

mn35:22.2.verse: and there he saw a large plantain trunk, straight, young, with no fruit-bud core.

mn35:22.3.verse: Then he cut off the root, he cut off the crown, and having cut off the crown he unrolled the leaf-sheaths;

mn35:22.4.verse: but as he went on unrolling the leaf-sheaths he would never come even to any sapwood, let alone heartwood.

mn35:22.5.verse: So too, Aggivessana, when you are pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by me about your own assertion, you are empty, vacant and in the wrong.

mn35:22.6.verse: But these words of yours were spoken before this assembly:

mn35:22.7.verse: “I see no monk or divine, the head of a sangha, head of a sect, teacher of a sect, even if he claims to be Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who would not shake and shiver and tremble and sweat under the armpits on being engaged in argument with me.

mn35:22.8.verse: Even if I engaged a senseless post in argument it would shake and shiver and tremble on being engaged in argument with me,

mn35:22.9.verse: so what shall I say of a human being?”

mn35:22.10.verse: Now there are drops of sweat on your forehead and they have soaked through your upper robe and fallen to the ground.

mn35:22.11.verse: But there is no sweat on my body now.’

mn35:22.12.verse: And the Blessed One uncovered his golden-coloured body before the assembly.

mn35:22.13.verse: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum and with nothing to say.

mn35:23.1.verse: Then Dummukha the son of the Licchavis, seeing Saccaka the Nigantha’s son thus, said to the Blessed One:

mn35:23.2.verse: ‘A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama.’

mn35:23.4.verse: ‘Suppose, venerable sir, not far from a village or town there were a pond

mn35:23.6.verse: And then a party of boys and girls went out from the town or village to the pond, and they went into the water and pulled the crab out of the water and put it on dry land.

mn35:23.7.verse: And whenever the crab extended a leg, they cut it off, broke it, smashed it with sticks and stones,

mn35:23.8.verse: so that the crab with all its legs cut off, broken and smashed would be unable to get back to the pond as before—

mn35:23.9.verse: so too, all Saccaka the Nigantha’s son’s distortions, paradoxes and travesties have been cut off, broken and smashed by the Blessed One,

mn35:23.10.verse: and now he cannot get near the Blessed One as was the purpose of his words.’

mn35:24.1.verse: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son told him:

mn35:24.2.verse: ‘Wait, Dummukkha, wait. We are not treating with you, here we are treating with Master Gotama.

mn35:24.3.verse: Let that talk of ours be, Master Gotama, like that of many a monk and divine

mn35:24.4.verse: it was (just) so many words, I fancy.

mn35:24.5.verse: But how does a disciple of the monk Gotama carry out the message, respond to advice, cross beyond uncertainty, lose his doubts, gain intrepidity, and become independent of others in the Teacher’s message?’

mn35:24.6.verse: ‘Here, Aggivessana, any kind of form—whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a disciple of mine sees with right understanding all form as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this not I, this is not my self.”

mn35:24.10.verse: Any kind of consciousness whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—a disciple of mine sees with right understanding all consciousness as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this not my self.”

mn35:24.11.verse: This is how a disciple of mine carries out the message, responds to advice, crosses beyond uncertainty, loses his doubts, gains intrepidity and becomes independent of others in the Teacher’s message.’

mn35:25.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, how does a bhikkhu become an Arahant, with the taints exhausted who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and who through right final knowledge is liberated?’

mn35:25.2.verse: ‘Here, Aggivessana, any kind of form whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikkhu sees with right understanding all form as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self”, and through not clinging he is liberated.

mn35:25.6.verse: Any kind of consciousness whatever, whether past, future or present, in oneself or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikkhu sees with right understanding all consciousness as it actually is thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self”, and through not clinging he is liberated.

mn35:25.7.verse: That is how a bhikkhu becomes an Arahant, with taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and through right final knowledge is liberated.

mn35:26.1.verse: ‘When a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated, he possesses three unsurpassabilities:

mn35:26.2.verse: unsurpassability in vision, unsurpassability in practice of the way, and unsurpassability in deliverance.

mn35:26.3.verse: When a bhikkhu is thus liberated, he honours, respects, reveres, and venerates only the Tathāgata:

mn35:26.4.verse: The Blessed One is enlightened and teaches the Dhamma by enlightenment. The Blessed One is controlled and he teaches the Dhamma by control. The Blessed One is serene and he teaches the Dhamma by serenity. The Blessed One has crossed over and he teaches the Dhamma by having crossed over. The Blessed One has attained Nibbāna and he teaches the Dhamma by having attained Nibbāna.’

mn35:27.1.verse: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied:

mn35:27.2.verse: ‘Master Gotama, we were bold and forward in conceiving Master Gotama to be attackable by argument.

mn35:27.3.verse: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a mad elephant, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.

mn35:27.4.verse: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a blazing mass of fire, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.

mn35:27.5.verse: A man might be such that he could with impunity attack a terrible poisonous serpent, yet he could not attack Master Gotama with impunity.

mn35:27.6.verse: We were bold and forward in conceiving Master Gotama to be attackable by argument.

mn35:27.7.verse: Let the Blessed One, together with the Sangha of Bhikkhus, accept tomorrow’s meal from me.’

mn35:27.8.verse: The Blessed One accepted in silence.

mn35:28.1.verse: Then knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, he addressed the Licchavis:

mn35:28.2.verse: ‘Hear me, Licchavis, the monk Gotama together with the Sangha of Bhikkhus has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal.

mn35:28.3.verse: You may bring to me whatever you think is proper for him.’

mn35:29.1.verse: Then when the night was ended the Licchavis brought five hundred ceremonial dishes of milk rice as gifts of food.

mn35:29.2.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son had good food of various kinds prepared in his own house, and he had the time announced to the Blessed One:

mn35:29.3.verse: ‘It is time, Master Gotama, the meal is ready.’

mn35:30.1.verse: Then, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went with the Sangha of Bhikkhus to Saccaka the Nigantha’s son’s house, and sat down on the seat made ready.

mn35:30.2.verse: Then with his own hands, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son served and satisfied the Sangha of Bhikkhus headed by the Enlightened One with the various kinds of good food.

mn35:30.3.verse: Then when the Blessed One had eaten and no longer had the bowl in his hand, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son took a low seat and sat down at one side.

mn35:30.4.verse: When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:

mn35:30.5.verse: ‘Master Gotama, whatever the merit and (expected future) greatness due to merit in (this) act-of-giving, may that be for the happiness of the givers.’

mn35:30.6.verse: ‘Aggivessana, such (merit and expected greatness due to merit) as comes of (giving to) one fit for offerings in the way that you are, (you being) not without lust, not without hate, and not without delusion, will be for the givers (who have given to you);

mn35:30.7.verse: but such as comes of (giving to) one fit for offerings in the way that I am, (I being) without lust, without hate and without delusion, will be for you (who have given to me).

mn35:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

mn35:2.1.verse: Now at that time Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, was staying in Vesālī. He was a controversialist who pretended to be astute and was deemed holy by many people.

mn35:2.2.verse: He was telling a crowd in Vesālī,

mn35:2.3.verse: “I don’t see any ascetic or brahmin who would not shake and rock and tremble, sweating from the armpits, were I to take them on in debate—not a leader of an order or a community, or the tutor of a community, and not even one who claims to be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn35:2.4.verse: Even an insentient post would shake and rock and tremble were I to take it on in debate.

mn35:2.5.verse: How much more then a human being!”

mn35:3.1.verse: Then Venerable Assaji robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.

mn35:3.2.verse: As Saccaka was going for a walk he saw Assaji coming off in the distance.

mn35:3.3.verse: He approached him and exchanged greetings with him.

mn35:3.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, Saccaka stood to one side and said to Assaji,

mn35:4.1.verse: “Worthy Assaji, how does the ascetic Gotama guide his disciples? And on what topics does instruction to his disciples generally proceed?”

mn35:4.2.verse: “Aggivessana, this is how the Buddha guides his disciples, and his instructions to disciples generally proceed on these topics:

mn35:4.3.verse: ‘Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.

mn35:4.4.verse: Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

mn35:4.5.verse: All conditions are impermanent. All things are not-self.’

mn35:4.6.verse: This is how the Buddha guides his disciples, and how instruction to his disciples generally proceeds.”

mn35:4.7.verse: “It’s sad to hear, worthy Assaji, that the ascetic Gotama has such a doctrine.

mn35:4.8.verse: Hopefully, some time or other I’ll get to meet the worthy Gotama, and we can have a discussion. And hopefully I can dissuade him from this harmful misconception.”

mn35:5.1.verse: Now at that time around five hundred Licchavis were sitting together at the town hall on some business.

mn35:5.2.verse: Then Saccaka went up to them and said,

mn35:5.3.verse: “Come forth, good Licchavīs, come forth! Today I am going to have a discussion with the ascetic Gotama.

mn35:5.4.verse: If he stands by the position stated to me by one of his well-known disciples—a mendicant named Assaji—I’ll take him on in debate and drag him to and fro and round about, like a strong man would grab a fleecy sheep and drag it to and fro and round about!

mn35:5.6.verse: Taking him on in debate, I’ll drag him to and fro and round about, like a strong brewer’s worker would toss a large brewer’s sieve into a deep lake, grab it by the corners, and drag it to and fro and round about!

mn35:5.8.verse: Taking him on in debate, I’ll shake him down and about, and give him a beating, like a strong brewer’s mixer would grab a strainer by the corners and shake it down and about, and give it a beating!

mn35:5.10.verse: I’ll play a game of hemp-washing with the ascetic Gotama, like a sixty-year-old elephant would plunge into a deep lotus pond and play a game of hemp-washing!

mn35:5.12.verse: Come forth, good Licchavīs, come forth! Today I am going to have a discussion with the ascetic Gotama.”

mn35:6.1.verse: At that, some of the Licchavis said,

mn35:6.2.verse: “How can the ascetic Gotama refute Saccaka’s doctrine, when it is Saccaka who will refute Gotama’s doctrine?”

mn35:6.3.verse: But some of the Licchavis said,

mn35:6.4.verse: “Who is Saccaka to refute the Buddha’s doctrine, when it is the Buddha who will refute Saccaka’s doctrine?”

mn35:6.5.verse: Then Saccaka, escorted by the five hundred Licchavis, went to the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood.

mn35:7.1.verse: At that time several mendicants were walking mindfully in the open air.

mn35:7.2.verse: Then Saccaka went up to them and said,

mn35:7.3.verse: “Good fellows, where is the worthy Gotama at present?

mn35:7.4.verse: For we want to see him.”

mn35:7.5.verse: “Aggivessana, the Buddha has plunged deep into the Great Wood and is sitting at the root of a tree for the day’s meditation.”

mn35:8.1.verse: Then Saccaka, together with a large group of Licchavis, went to the Buddha in the Great Wood, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn35:8.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

mn35:8.3.verse: Before sitting down to one side, some of the Licchavīs bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

mn35:9.1.verse: Then Saccaka said to the Buddha,

mn35:9.2.verse: “I’d like to ask the worthy Gotama about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

mn35:9.4.verse: “How does the worthy Gotama guide his disciples? And on what topics does instruction to his disciples generally proceed?”

mn35:9.5.verse: “This is how I guide my disciples, and my instructions to disciples generally proceed on these topics:

mn35:9.6.verse: ‘Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.

mn35:9.7.verse: Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

mn35:9.8.verse: All conditions are impermanent. All things are not-self.’

mn35:9.9.verse: This is how I guide my disciples, and how instruction to my disciples generally proceeds.”

mn35:10.2.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

mn35:10.3.verse: “All the plants and seeds that achieve growth, increase, and maturity do so depending on the earth and grounded on the earth.

mn35:10.5.verse: All the hard work that gets done depends on the earth and is grounded on the earth.

mn35:10.7.verse: In the same way, an individual person’s self is form. Established on form they brim with merit and wickedness. An individual person’s self is feeling … perception … choices … consciousness. Established on consciousness they brim with merit and wickedness.”

mn35:11.2.verse: ‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, choices are my self, consciousness is my self’?”

mn35:11.3.verse: “Indeed, worthy Gotama, that is what I am saying.

mn35:11.4.verse: And this big crowd agrees with me!”

mn35:11.5.verse: “What has this big crowd to do with you?

mn35:11.6.verse: Please just unpack your own statement.”

mn35:11.7.verse: “Then, worthy Gotama, what I am saying is this:

mn35:11.8.verse: ‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, choices are my self, consciousness is my self’.”

mn35:12.1.verse: “Well then, Aggivessana, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn35:12.3.verse: Consider an anointed aristocratic king such as Pasenadi of Kosala or Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha.

mn35:12.4.verse: Would they have the power in their own realm to execute those who have incurred execution, fine those who have incurred fines, or banish those who have incurred banishment?”

mn35:12.5.verse: “An anointed king would have such power, worthy Gotama.

mn35:12.9.verse: have such power in their own realm.

mn35:12.11.verse: So of course an anointed king such as Pasenadi or Ajātasattu

mn35:12.12.verse: would wield such power, as is their right.”

mn35:13.3.verse: ‘Form is my self,’ do you have power over that form to say:

mn35:13.4.verse: ‘May my form be like this! May it not be like that’?”

mn35:13.5.verse: When he said this, Saccaka kept silent.

mn35:13.6.verse: The Buddha asked the question a second time,

mn35:13.11.verse: So the Buddha said to Saccaka,

mn35:13.12.verse: “Answer now, Aggivessana. Now is not the time for silence.

mn35:13.13.verse: If someone fails to answer a legitimate question when asked three times by the Buddha, their head explodes into seven pieces there and then.”

mn35:14.1.verse: Now at that time the spirit Vajirapāṇī, taking up a burning iron thunderbolt, blazing and glowing, stood in the air above Saccaka, thinking,

mn35:14.2.verse: “If this Saccaka doesn’t answer when asked a third time, I’ll blow his head into seven pieces there and then!”

mn35:14.3.verse: And both the Buddha and Saccaka could see Vajirapāṇī.

mn35:14.4.verse: Saccaka was terrified, shocked, and awestruck. Looking to the Buddha for shelter, asylum, and refuge, he said,

mn35:14.5.verse: “Ask me, worthy Gotama. I will answer.”

mn35:15.3.verse: ‘Form is my self,’ do you have power over that form to say:

mn35:15.4.verse: ‘May my form be like this! May it not be like that’?”

mn35:16.3.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn35:16.6.verse: ‘Feeling is my self,’ do you have power over that feeling to say:

mn35:16.7.verse: ‘May my feeling be like this! May it not be like that’?”

mn35:17.3.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn35:17.6.verse: ‘Perception is my self,’ do you have power over that perception to say:

mn35:17.7.verse: ‘May my perception be like this! May it not be like that’?”

mn35:18.3.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn35:18.6.verse: ‘Choices are my self,’ do you have power over those choices to say:

mn35:18.7.verse: ‘May my choices be like this! May they not be like that’?”

mn35:19.3.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn35:19.6.verse: ‘Consciousness is my self,’ do you have power over that consciousness to say:

mn35:19.7.verse: ‘May my consciousness be like this! May it not be like that’?”

mn35:20.3.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn35:20.7.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn35:20.9.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn35:20.10.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn35:20.18.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn35:20.20.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn35:20.21.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn35:21.2.verse: Consider someone who resorts, draws near, and clings to suffering, regarding it thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’ Would they be able to completely understand suffering themselves, or live having wiped out suffering?”

mn35:21.6.verse: This being so, aren’t you someone who resorts, draws near, and clings to suffering, regarding it thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn35:22.1.verse: “Suppose, Aggivessana, there was a person in need of heartwood. Wandering in search of heartwood, they’d take a sharp axe and enter a forest.

mn35:22.2.verse: There they’d see a big banana trunk, straight and young and grown unskewed.

mn35:22.3.verse: They’d cut it down at the base, cut off the top, and unroll the coiled sheaths.

mn35:22.4.verse: But they wouldn’t even find sapwood, much less heartwood.

mn35:22.5.verse: In the same way, when pursued, pressed, and grilled by me on your own doctrine, you turn out to be vacuous, hollow, and mistaken.

mn35:22.6.verse: But it was you who stated before the assembly of Vesālī:

mn35:22.7.verse: ‘I don’t see any ascetic or brahmin who would not shake and rock and tremble, sweating from the armpits, were I to take them on in debate—not a leader of an order or a community, or the tutor of a community, and not even one who claims to be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn35:22.8.verse: Even an insentient post would shake and rock and tremble were I to take it on in debate.

mn35:22.9.verse: How much more then a human being!’

mn35:22.10.verse: But sweat is pouring from your forehead; it’s soaked through your robe and drips on the ground.

mn35:22.11.verse: While I now have no sweat on my body.”

mn35:22.12.verse: So the Buddha revealed his golden body to the assembly.

mn35:22.13.verse: When this was said, Saccaka sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

mn35:23.1.verse: Knowing this, the Licchavi Dummukha said to the Buddha,

mn35:23.3.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

mn35:23.4.verse: “Sir, suppose there was a lotus pond not far from a town or village,

mn35:23.6.verse: Then several boys or girls would leave the town or village and go to the pond, where they’d pull out the crab and put it on solid ground.

mn35:23.7.verse: Whenever that crab extended a claw, those boys or girls would snap, crack, and break it off with a stick or a stone.

mn35:23.8.verse: And when that crab’s claws had all been snapped, cracked, and broken off it wouldn’t be able to return down into that lotus pond.
