mn35:23.9.verse: In the same way, sir, the Buddha has snapped, cracked, and broken off all Saccaka’s twists, ducks, and dodges.

mn35:23.10.verse: Now he can’t get near the Buddha again looking for a debate.”

mn35:24.2.verse: “Hold on, Dummukha, hold on! I wasn’t talking with you, I was talking with the worthy Gotama.

mn35:24.3.verse: Worthy Gotama, leave aside that statement I made—as did various other ascetics and brahmins—

mn35:24.4.verse: it was, like, just a bit of nonsense.

mn35:24.5.verse: How do you define a disciple of the worthy Gotama who follows instructions and responds to advice; who has gone beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, gained assurance, and is independent of others in the Teacher’s instructions?”

mn35:24.6.verse: “It’s when one of my disciples truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn35:24.7.verse: They truly see any kind of feeling …

mn35:24.10.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn35:24.11.verse: That’s how to define one of my disciples who follows instructions and responds to advice; who has gone beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, gained assurance, and is independent of others in the Teacher’s instructions.”

mn35:25.1.verse: “But how do you define a mendicant who is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment?”

mn35:25.2.verse: “It’s when a mendicant truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ And having seen this with right understanding they’re freed by not grasping.

mn35:25.3.verse: They truly see any kind of feeling …

mn35:25.6.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ And having seen this with right understanding they’re freed by not grasping.

mn35:25.7.verse: That’s how to define a mendicant who is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment.

mn35:26.1.verse: A mendicant whose mind is freed like this has three unsurpassable qualities:

mn35:26.3.verse: They honor, respect, esteem, and venerate only the Realized One:

mn35:26.4.verse: ‘The Blessed One is awakened, tamed, serene, crossed over, and quenched. And he teaches Dhamma for awakening, self-control, serenity, crossing over, and extinguishment.’”

mn35:27.1.verse: When he had spoken, Saccaka said to him,

mn35:27.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, it was rude and impudent of me to imagine I could attack you in debate.

mn35:27.3.verse: For a person might find safety after attacking a rutting elephant, but not after attacking the worthy Gotama.

mn35:27.4.verse: A person might find safety after attacking a blazing mass of fire, but not after attacking the worthy Gotama.

mn35:27.5.verse: They might find safety after attacking a poisonous viper, but not after attacking the worthy Gotama.

mn35:27.6.verse: It was rude and impudent of me to imagine I could attack you in debate.

mn35:27.7.verse: Would the worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

mn35:28.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Saccaka addressed those Licchavis,

mn35:28.2.verse: “Listen, gentlemen. I have invited the ascetic Gotama together with the Saṅgha of mendicants for tomorrow’s meal.

mn35:28.3.verse: You may all bring me what you think is suitable.”

mn35:29.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, those Licchavis presented Saccaka with an offering of five hundred servings of food.

mn35:29.2.verse: And Saccaka had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own park. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying,

mn35:29.3.verse: “It’s time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready.”

mn35:30.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Saccaka’s park, where he sat down on the seat spread out together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn35:30.2.verse: Then Saccaka served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

mn35:30.3.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Saccaka took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn35:30.4.verse: Then Saccaka said to the Buddha,

mn35:30.5.verse: “Worthy Gotama, may the merit and the growth of merit in this gift be for the happiness of the donors.”

mn35:30.6.verse: “Aggivessana, whatever comes from giving to a recipient of a religious donation such as yourself—who is not free of greed, hate, and delusion—will accrue to the donors.

mn35:30.7.verse: Whatever comes from giving to a recipient of a religious donation such as myself—who is free of greed, hate, and delusion—will accrue to you.”

mn36:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood.

mn36:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion, it being morning, the Blessed One had finished dressing and had taken his bowl and (outer) robe, being desirous of going into Vesālī for alms.

mn36:3.1.verse: Then as Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was walking and wandering for exercise he came to the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

mn36:3.2.verse: The venerable Ānanda saw him coming in the distance.

mn36:3.3.verse: When he saw him, he said to the Blessed One:

mn36:3.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, here comes Saccaka the Nigantha’s son; he is a debater, a clever speaker, and regarded by many as a saint.

mn36:3.5.verse: He wants to decry the Enlightened One, to decry the Dhamma, to decry the Sangha.

mn36:3.6.verse: It would be good if the Blessed One would sit down for a while out of compassion.’

mn36:3.7.verse: The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.

mn36:3.8.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went up to him and exchanged greetings with him, and after the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:

mn36:4.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, there are some monks and divines who abide in pursuit of the practice of developing the body without developing the mind.

mn36:4.2.verse: They are touched by bodily painful feeling.

mn36:4.3.verse: It has happened that a man who is touched by bodily painful feeling got a paralysis of the thigh or his heart burst or hot blood gushed from his mouth or he went mad, out of his mind.

mn36:4.4.verse: So then the mind was subservient to the body, it let the body wield mastery.

mn36:4.6.verse: Because the mind was not developed.

mn36:4.7.verse: But there are some monks and divines who abide in pursuit of developing the mind, without developing the body.

mn36:4.8.verse: They are touched by mental painful feeling.

mn36:4.9.verse: It has happened that a man touched by mental painful feeling also got a paralysis of the thigh or his heart burst or hot blood gushed from his mouth or he went mad, out of his mind.

mn36:4.10.verse: So then the body was subservient to the mind, it let the mind wield mastery.

mn36:4.12.verse: Because the body was not developed.

mn36:4.13.verse: Master Gotama, it has occurred to me:

mn36:4.14.verse: surely Master Gotama’s disciples abide in pursuit of developing the mind, without developing the body?’

mn36:5.1.verse: ‘But Aggivessana, how has development of body been learnt by you?’

mn36:5.3.verse: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Sankicca, Makkhali Gosāla.

mn36:5.4.verse: They go naked, rejecting conventions, licking their hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked, they do not accept anything brought, or anything specially made, or an invitation;

mn36:5.5.verse: they receive nothing out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman is lying with a man, from where food is advertized to be distributed, from where a dog is waiting, from where flies are buzzing; they accept no fish or meat, they drink no wine or spirits or fermented liquor.

mn36:5.6.verse: They keep to one house, to one morsel; they keep to two houses, to two morsels; … they keep to seven houses, to seven morsels.

mn36:5.7.verse: They live on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day.

mn36:5.8.verse: They take food once each day, once each two days … once each seven days; and so up to once each fortnight, they dwell devoted to such practice of taking food at stated intervals.’

mn36:6.1.verse: ‘But do they always subsist like that, Aggivessana?’

mn36:6.3.verse: sometimes they chew good hard food, eat good soft food, taste good relishes, drink good drinks.

mn36:6.4.verse: With that they pick up strength, wax and get fat.’

mn36:6.5.verse: ‘What they once abandoned, Aggivessana, they later gather together again. That is how there is amassing and dispersal of this body.

mn36:6.6.verse: Now how has development of mind been learnt by you?’

mn36:6.7.verse: When Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was asked by the Blessed One about development of mind, he was unable to answer.

mn36:7.1.verse: Then the Blessed One told him:

mn36:7.2.verse: ‘What you have just spoken of as development of body, Aggivessana, is not developing the body according to Dhamma in the Noble Discipline.

mn36:7.3.verse: Since you do not know what development of body is, how should you know what developing the mind is?

mn36:7.4.verse: Nevertheless, Aggivessana, listen how a man is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind, and how he is developed in body and developed in mind,

mn36:7.5.verse: and heed well what I shall say.’

mn36:7.6.verse: ‘Even so, sir,’ Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied.

mn36:8.1.verse: ‘How is man undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind?

mn36:8.2.verse: Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in an untaught ordinary man.

mn36:8.3.verse: Touched by that pleasant feeling, he lusts after that pleasant feeling, and he keeps lusting after that pleasant feeling.

mn36:8.4.verse: That pleasant feeling of his ceases.

mn36:8.5.verse: With the cessation of the pleasant feeling painful feeling (later) arises.

mn36:8.6.verse: Touched by that painful feeling he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast, he weeps and becomes distraught.

mn36:8.7.verse: When that pleasant feeling is arisen in him, it invades the mind and remains because the body is not developed. And when that painful feeling is arisen in him, it invades the mind and remains because the mind is not developed.

mn36:8.8.verse: Anyone in whom, in this double manner, pleasant feeling arisen invades the mind and remains because the body is not developed, and painful feeling arisen invades the mind and remains because the mind is not developed, is thus undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.

mn36:9.1.verse: And how is man developed in body and developed in mind?

mn36:9.2.verse: Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in a well-taught noble disciple.

mn36:9.3.verse: Touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not lust after that pleasant feeling, he does not keep lusting after that pleasant feeling.

mn36:9.4.verse: That pleasant feeling of his ceases.

mn36:9.5.verse: With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, painful feeling (later) arises.

mn36:9.6.verse: Touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve or lament, he does not, beating his breast, weep and become distraught.

mn36:9.7.verse: When that pleasant feeling is arisen in him it does not invade the mind and remain because the body is developed. And when that painful feeling is arisen in him, it does not invade the mind and remain because the mind is developed.

mn36:9.8.verse: Anyone in whom, in this double manner, pleasant feeling arisen does not invade the mind and remain because the body is developed, and painful feeling arisen does not invade the mind and remain because the mind is developed, is thus developed in mind and developed in body.’

mn36:10.1.verse: ‘I have confidence in Master Gotama thus:

mn36:10.2.verse: “He is developed in body and developed in mind.”’

mn36:10.3.verse: ‘Surely, Aggivessana, the words you have spoken are directly personal.

mn36:10.5.verse: Since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, that pleasant feeling arisen might invade my mind and remain, or that painful feeling arisen might invade my mind and remain — that is not possible.’

mn36:11.1.verse: ‘Has there perhaps never arisen in Master Gotama a feeling so pleasant as to invade his mind and remain? Has there perhaps never arisen in Master Gotama a feeling so painful as to invade his mind and remain?’

mn36:12.2.verse: Here, before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta I thought:

mn36:12.3.verse: “House life is a constraint and it is a place of dirt; life gone forth is wide open.

mn36:12.4.verse: It is not possible while living in a house to lead the life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.

mn36:12.5.verse: Suppose I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”

mn36:13.1.verse: So, Aggivessana, at a later time, while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn36:13.2.verse: Having thus gone forth in search of what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:

mn36:13.3.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and discipline.’

mn36:13.4.verse: When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma said to me:

mn36:13.6.verse: This Dhamma is such that a wise man can soon enter upon and abide in it, realizing for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’

mn36:13.7.verse: I quickly learned that Dhamma, Aggivessana.

mn36:13.8.verse: As far as mere lip-reciting and mere repeating was concerned, I could speak the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I could claim, ‘I know and see,’ as could others.

mn36:13.10.verse: ‘It is not through mere faith alone that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “By realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this Dhamma”;

mn36:13.11.verse: certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’

mn36:13.12.verse: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:

mn36:13.13.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare that by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge you enter upon and abide in this Dhamma?’

mn36:13.14.verse: When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the base of nothingness.

mn36:13.16.verse: ‘Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has faith; I too have faith.

mn36:13.17.verse: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has energy; I too have energy.

mn36:13.18.verse: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.

mn36:13.19.verse: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has concentration; I too have concentration.

mn36:13.20.verse: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has wisdom; I too have wisdom.

mn36:13.21.verse: Suppose I endeavour to realize the Dhamma that Āḷāra Kālāma declares he enters upon and abides in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.’

mn36:13.22.verse: I quickly entered upon and abided in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, Aggivessana.

mn36:14.1.verse: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:

mn36:14.2.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare that by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge you enter upon and abide in this Dhamma?’

mn36:14.3.verse: ‘That is how I declare it, friend.’

mn36:14.4.verse: ‘I too, friend, in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge.’

mn36:14.5.verse: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is very good for us,

mn36:14.6.verse: that we see such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.

mn36:14.7.verse: So the Dhamma I declare I have realized for myself with direct knowledge is the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge;

mn36:14.8.verse: and the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge, is the Dhamma I declare I have realized for myself with direct knowledge.

mn36:14.9.verse: So the Dhamma I know is the Dhamma you know, and the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma I know.

mn36:14.10.verse: As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.

mn36:14.11.verse: Come, friend, let us now lead this group together.’

mn36:14.12.verse: Thus, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma, my teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself and honoured me with high honour.

mn36:14.14.verse: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only as far as the base of nothingness.’

mn36:14.15.verse: So, being dissatisfied with that Dhamma, I left it and went away.

mn36:15.1.verse: So, Aggivessana, still searching for what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:

mn36:15.2.verse: ‘Friend, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and discipline.’

mn36:15.3.verse: When this was said, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta said to me:

mn36:15.5.verse: This Dhamma is such that a wise man can soon enter upon and abide in it, realizing for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’

mn36:15.6.verse: I quickly learned that Dhamma, Aggivessana.

mn36:15.7.verse: As far as mere lip-reciting and mere repeating was concerned, I could speak the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I could claim, ‘I know and see,’ as could others.

mn36:15.9.verse: ‘It was not through mere faith alone that Rāma declared: “By realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this Dhamma”;

mn36:15.10.verse: certainly Rāma abided knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’

mn36:15.11.verse: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:

mn36:15.12.verse: ‘Friend, in what way did Rāma declare that by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge he entered upon and abided in this Dhamma?’

mn36:15.13.verse: When this was said, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn36:15.15.verse: ‘Not only Rāma had faith; I too have faith.

mn36:15.16.verse: Not only Rāma had energy; I too have energy.

mn36:15.17.verse: Not only Rāma had mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.

mn36:15.18.verse: Not only Rāma had concentration; I too have concentration.

mn36:15.19.verse: Not only Rāma had wisdom; I too have wisdom.

mn36:15.20.verse: Suppose I endeavour to realize the Dhamma that Rāma declared he entered upon and abided in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.’

mn36:15.21.verse: I quickly entered upon and abided in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, Aggivessana.

mn36:15.22.verse: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:

mn36:15.23.verse: ‘Friend, is it in this way that Rāma declared that by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge he entered upon and abided in this Dhamma?’

mn36:15.24.verse: ‘That is how Rāma declared it, friend.’

mn36:15.25.verse: ‘I too, friend, in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge.’

mn36:15.26.verse: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is very good for us,

mn36:15.27.verse: that we see such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.

mn36:15.28.verse: So the Dhamma Rāma declared he had realized for himself with direct knowledge is the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge; and the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge, is the Dhamma Rāma declared he had realized for himself with direct knowledge.

mn36:15.29.verse: So the Dhamma Rāma directly knew is the Dhamma you know, and the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma Rāma directly knew.

mn36:15.30.verse: As Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.

mn36:15.31.verse: Come, friend, now you lead this group.’

mn36:15.32.verse: Thus, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the life divine, placed me in the position of teacher and honoured me with high honour.

mn36:15.34.verse: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only as far as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’

mn36:15.35.verse: So, being dissatisfied with that Dhamma, I left it and went away.

mn36:16.1.verse: So, Aggivessana, still searching for what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, walking by stages through the Magadhan country, I eventually arrived at Uruvelā, at Senānigama.

mn36:16.2.verse: There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove, a clear-flowing river with pleasant, smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.

mn36:16.4.verse: ‘This is an agreeable piece of ground, this delightful grove, this clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.

mn36:16.5.verse: This will serve for the endeavour of a clansman who seeks endeavour.’

mn36:17.1.verse: ‘Now these three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:17.2.verse: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water,

mn36:17.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn36:17.4.verse: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;

mn36:17.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn36:17.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water?’

mn36:17.9.verse: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, and besides, it is lying in water.

mn36:17.10.verse: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn36:17.11.verse: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives still bodily and mentally not withdrawn from sensual desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever for sensual desires are not quite abandoned and quieted within him, then, even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment,

mn36:17.12.verse: and even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.

mn36:17.13.verse: This was the first simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:18.1.verse: Again, a second simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:18.2.verse: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,

mn36:18.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn36:18.4.verse: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;

mn36:18.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn36:18.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?’

mn36:18.9.verse: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, though it is lying on dry land far from water.

mn36:18.10.verse: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn36:18.11.verse: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives still only bodily withdrawn from sensual desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever, for sensual desires are not quite abandoned and quieted within him, then even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment. And even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.

mn36:18.12.verse: This was the second simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:19.1.verse: Again, a third simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:19.2.verse: Suppose there were a dry sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,

mn36:19.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn36:19.4.verse: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;

mn36:19.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,

mn36:19.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by rubbing with it the dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?’

mn36:19.9.verse: Because it is a dry, sapless piece of wood, and besides, it is lying on dry land far from water!’

mn36:19.10.verse: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives both bodily and mentally withdrawn from sense-desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever, for sensual desires are quite abandoned and quieted within him, then, even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is capable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment, and even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is capable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.

mn36:19.11.verse: This was the third simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:19.12.verse: These, Aggivessana, were the three similes that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn36:20.2.verse: “Suppose, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrain and crush mind with mind?”

mn36:20.3.verse: So, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained and crushed mind with mind.

mn36:20.4.verse: While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits.

mn36:20.5.verse: Just as a strong man might seize a weaker by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain and crush him,

mn36:20.6.verse: so too, while with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained and crushed mind with mind, sweat ran from my armpits.

mn36:20.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:20.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:21.2.verse: “Suppose I practise the meditation without breathing?”

mn36:21.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth and nose.

mn36:21.4.verse: While I did so, there was a loud sound of winds coming from my ear-holes.

mn36:21.5.verse: Just as there is a loud sound when a smith’s bellows are blown,

mn36:21.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth and nose, there was a loud sound of winds coming from my ear-holes.

mn36:21.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:21.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:22.2.verse: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”

mn36:22.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.

mn36:22.4.verse: While I did so, violent winds harried my head.

mn36:22.5.verse: Just as if a strong man were splitting my head open with a sharp sword,

mn36:22.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, violent winds harried my head.

mn36:22.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:22.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:23.2.verse: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”

mn36:23.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.

mn36:23.4.verse: While I did so, there were violent pains in my head.

mn36:23.5.verse: Just as if a strong man were tightening a tough leather strap round my head as a headband,

mn36:23.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, there were violent pains in my head.

mn36:23.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:23.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:24.2.verse: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”

mn36:24.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.

mn36:24.4.verse: While I did so, violent winds carved up my belly.

mn36:24.5.verse: Just as a clever butcher or his apprentice carves up an ox’s belly with a sharp knife,

mn36:24.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, violent winds carved up my belly.

mn36:24.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:24.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:25.2.verse: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”

mn36:25.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.

mn36:25.4.verse: While I did so, there was violent burning in my body.

mn36:25.5.verse: Just as if two strong men had seized a weaker man by both arms and were roasting him over a pit of hot coals,

mn36:25.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, there was a violent burning in my body.

mn36:25.7.verse: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.

mn36:25.8.verse: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:26.1.verse: ‘Now when gods saw me, they said:

mn36:26.4.verse: “The monk Gotama is not dead, he is dying.”

mn36:26.6.verse: “The monk Gotama is neither dead nor dying; he is an Arahant, for such is the way of Arahants.”

mn36:27.3.verse: Then gods came to me and said:

mn36:27.4.verse: “Good sir, do not entirely cut off food.

mn36:27.5.verse: If you do so, we shall inject heavenly food into your pores and you will live on that.”

mn36:27.7.verse: “If I claim to be completely fasting and these gods inject heavenly food into my pores and I live on that, then I shall be lying.”

mn36:27.8.verse: I dismissed those gods, saying: “There is no need.”’

mn36:28.2.verse: “Suppose I take very little food, say, a handful each time, whether it is bean soup or lentil soup or vetch soup or pea soup?”

mn36:28.3.verse: So I took very little food, a handful each time, whether it was bean soup or lentil soup or vetch soup or pea soup.

mn36:28.4.verse: While I did so, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.

mn36:28.5.verse: Because of eating so little my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems.

mn36:28.6.verse: Because of eating so little my backside became like a camel’s hoof.

mn36:28.7.verse: Because of eating so little the projections on my spine stood forth like corded beads.

mn36:28.8.verse: Because of eating so little my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn.

mn36:28.9.verse: Because of eating so little the gleam of my eyes sunk far down in their sockets looked like the gleam of water sunk far down in a deep well.

mn36:28.10.verse: Because of eating so little my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun.

mn36:28.11.verse: Because of eating so little, if I touched my belly skin, I encountered my backbone too; if I touched my backbone I encountered my belly skin too.

mn36:28.12.verse: Because of eating so little, if I tried to make water or evacuate my bowels, I fell over on my face there.

mn36:28.13.verse: Because of eating so little, if I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.

mn36:29.1.verse: ‘Now when human beings saw me, they said: “The monk Gotama is a black man.”

mn36:29.2.verse: Other human beings said: “The monk Gotama is not a black man, he is a brown man.”

mn36:29.3.verse: Other human beings said: “The monk Gotama is neither a black nor a brown man, he is a fair-skinned man.”

mn36:29.4.verse: So much had the clear, bright colour of my skin deteriorated through eating so little.

mn36:30.2.verse: “Whenever a monk or divine in the past has felt painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.

mn36:30.3.verse: And whenever a monk or divine in the future will feel painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.

mn36:30.4.verse: And whenever a monk or divine at present feels painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.

mn36:30.5.verse: But by this gruelling penance I have attained no distinction higher than the human state worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision.

mn36:30.6.verse: Might there be another way to enlightenment?”

mn36:31.2.verse: “I recall that, while my Sakyan father was busy, while I was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn36:31.3.verse: Might that be the way to enlightenment?”

mn36:31.4.verse: Then, following on that memory, came the recognition:

mn36:32.2.verse: “Why am I afraid of that pleasure? It is pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unprofitable dhammas.”

mn36:32.4.verse: “I am not afraid of that pleasure, since it has nothing to do with sensual desires and unprofitable dhammas.”

mn36:33.2.verse: “It is not possible to attain that pleasure with a body so excessively emaciated. Suppose I ate some solid food—some boiled rice and bread?”

mn36:33.3.verse: And I ate some solid food—some boiled rice and bread.

mn36:33.4.verse: But at that time five bhikkhus were waiting upon me, thinking:

mn36:33.5.verse: “If the monk Gotama achieves something he will tell us.”

mn36:33.6.verse: As soon as I ate the boiled rice and bread the five bhikkhus were disgusted and left me, thinking:

mn36:33.7.verse: “The monk Gotama has turned self-indulgent, he has given up the endeavour and reverted to luxury.”

mn36:34.1.verse: ‘Now when I had eaten solid food and regained strength, then quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, I entered upon and abode in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn36:34.2.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:35-37.1.verse: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, I entered upon and abode in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind without initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn36:35-37.2.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:35-37.3.verse: With the fading away as well of happiness, I abided in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, I still felt pleasure with the body; I entered upon and abode in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn36:35-37.4.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:35-37.5.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered upon and abode in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn36:35-37.6.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:38.1.verse: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past life.

mn36:38.2.verse: I recollected my manifold past life, that is, one birth, two births … thus with details and particulars I recollected my manifold past life.

mn36:39.1.verse: This was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;

mn36:39.2.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn36:39.3.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:40.1.verse: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing-away and reappearance of beings.

mn36:40.2.verse: With the heavenly eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions …

mn36:41.1.verse: This was the second true knowledge attained by me in the second watch of the night;

mn36:41.2.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn36:41.3.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:42.1.verse: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.

mn36:42.2.verse: I directly knew as it actually is: “This is suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the origin of suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”

mn36:42.3.verse: I directly knew as it actually is: “These are the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the origin of the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the cessation of the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.”

mn36:43.1.verse: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance.

mn36:43.2.verse: When it was liberated there came the knowledge: “It is liberated.”

mn36:43.3.verse: I directly knew: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this to come.”’

mn36:44.1.verse: This was the third true knowledge attained by me in the third watch of the night;

mn36:44.2.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.

mn36:44.3.verse: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.

mn36:45.1.verse: ‘I have direct knowledge of preaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, Aggivessana.

mn36:45.2.verse: Perhaps someone or other has imagined:

mn36:45.3.verse: “The monk Gotama is preaching the Dhamma at me.”

mn36:45.4.verse: But it should not be regarded so:

mn36:45.5.verse: a Tathāgata preaches the Dhamma to others only to give them knowledge.

mn36:45.6.verse: When the talk is finished, Aggivessana, then I settle my mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness and concentrate it on that same sign for concentration as before, in which I constantly abide.’

mn36:45.7.verse: ‘That is believable (as a statement) of Master Gotama’s since he is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.

mn36:45.8.verse: But perhaps Master Gotama has also had direct knowledge of sleeping by day?’

mn36:46.1.verse: ‘In the last month of the hot season, Aggivessana, on return from the alms-round after the meal, I have had direct knowledge of laying out my cloak of patches folded in four, and lying down on the right side and falling asleep, mindful and fully aware.’

mn36:46.2.verse: ‘Some monks and divines call that a deluded man’s abiding, Master Gotama.’

mn36:46.3.verse: ‘That is not how a man is deluded or not deluded, Aggivessana.

mn36:46.4.verse: Listen rather how a man is deluded or not deluded,

mn36:46.5.verse: and heed well what I shall say.’

mn36:46.6.verse: ‘Even so, sir,’ Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied.

mn36:47.1.verse: ‘Him I call deluded, Aggivessana, in whom taints that defile, produce renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death are unabandoned;

mn36:47.2.verse: for it is with the non-abandoning of taints that a man is deluded.

mn36:47.3.verse: Him I call undeluded in whom such taints as defile, as produce renewal of being, as give trouble, as ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned;

mn36:47.4.verse: for it is with the abandoning of taints that a man is undeluded.

mn36:47.5.verse: In a Tathāgata, such taints as produce renewal of being, as give trouble, as ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that their nature to arise in the future is no more.

mn36:47.6.verse: Just as a palm tree with its top cut off is incapable of growing,

mn36:47.7.verse: so too, in a Tathāgata the taints that defile, produce renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that their nature to arise in future is no more.’

mn36:48.1.verse: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son said:

mn36:48.2.verse: ‘It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvellous,

mn36:48.3.verse: how, when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened!

mn36:48.4.verse: I have had direct knowledge of engaging Purāṇa Kassapa in argument,

mn36:48.5.verse: and then he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate and surliness.

mn36:48.6.verse: But when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.

mn36:48.7.verse: I have had direct knowledge of engaging Makkhali Gosāla …

mn36:48.12.verse: and then he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate and surliness.

mn36:48.13.verse: But when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.

mn36:48.14.verse: And now, Master Gotama, we depart;

mn36:48.15.verse: we are busy and have much to do.’

mn36:48.16.verse: ‘It is time now to do as you think fit, Aggivessana.’

mn36:48.17.verse: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was satisfied, and delighting in the Blessed One’s words, he got up from his seat and departed.

mn36:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

mn36:2.1.verse: Now at that time in the morning the Buddha, being properly dressed, took his bowl and robe, wishing to enter Vesālī for alms.

mn36:3.1.verse: Then as Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, was going for a walk he approached the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood.

mn36:3.2.verse: Venerable Ānanda saw him coming off in the distance,

mn36:3.4.verse: “Sir, Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, is coming. He’s a controversialist who pretends to be astute and is deemed holy by many people.

mn36:3.5.verse: He wants to discredit the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha.

mn36:3.6.verse: Please, sir, sit for an hour out of sympathy.”

mn36:3.7.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out.

mn36:3.8.verse: Then Saccaka went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

mn36:4.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who live committed to the practice of developing physical endurance, without developing the mind.

mn36:4.3.verse: This happened to someone once. Their thighs became paralyzed, their heart burst, hot blood gushed from their mouth, and they went mad and lost their mind.

mn36:4.4.verse: Their mind was subject to the body, and the body had power over it.

mn36:4.6.verse: Because their mind was not developed.

mn36:4.7.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who live committed to the practice of developing the mind, without developing physical endurance.

mn36:4.9.verse: This happened to someone once. Their thighs became paralyzed, their heart burst, hot blood gushed from their mouth, and they went mad and lost their mind.

mn36:4.10.verse: Their body was subject to the mind, and the mind had power over it.

mn36:4.12.verse: Because their physical endurance was not developed.

mn36:4.14.verse: The worthy Gotama’s disciples must live committed to the practice of developing the mind, without developing physical endurance.”

mn36:5.1.verse: “But Aggivessana, what have you heard about the development of physical endurance?”

mn36:5.3.verse: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla.

mn36:5.4.verse: They go naked, ignoring conventions. They lick their hands, and don’t come or wait when called. They don’t consent to food brought to them, or food prepared on their behalf, or an invitation for a meal.

mn36:5.5.verse: They don’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or who lives with a man; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. They accept no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drink no fermented gruel.

mn36:5.6.verse: They go to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls.

mn36:5.7.verse: They feed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

mn36:5.8.verse: They eat once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. They live committed to the practice of eating food at set intervals.”

mn36:6.1.verse: “But Aggivessana, do they get by on so little?”

mn36:6.3.verse: Sometimes they eat luxury fresh and cooked foods and drink a variety of luxury beverages.

mn36:6.4.verse: They gather their body’s strength, build it up, and get fat.”

mn36:6.5.verse: “What they earlier gave up, they later got back. That is how there is the increase and decrease of this body.

mn36:6.6.verse: But Aggivessana, what have you heard about development of the mind?”

mn36:6.7.verse: When Saccaka was questioned by the Buddha about development of the mind, he was stumped.

mn36:7.1.verse: So the Buddha said to Saccaka,

mn36:7.2.verse: “The development of physical endurance that you have described is not the legitimate development of physical endurance in the Noble One’s training.

mn36:7.3.verse: And since you don’t even understand the development of physical endurance, how can you possibly understand the development of the mind?

mn36:7.4.verse: Still, as to how someone is undeveloped in physical endurance and mind, and how someone is developed in physical endurance and mind,

mn36:7.5.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn36:8.1.verse: “And how is someone undeveloped in physical endurance and mind?

mn36:8.2.verse: Take an unlearned ordinary person who has a pleasant feeling.

mn36:8.3.verse: When they experience a pleasant feeling they become full of lust for it.

mn36:8.5.verse: And when it ceases, a painful feeling arises.

mn36:8.6.verse: When they suffer painful feeling, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn36:8.7.verse: Because their physical endurance is undeveloped, pleasant feelings occupy the mind. And because their mind is undeveloped, painful feelings occupy the mind.

mn36:8.8.verse: Anyone whose mind is occupied by both pleasant and painful feelings like this is undeveloped both in physical endurance and in mind.

mn36:9.1.verse: And how is someone developed in physical endurance and mind?

mn36:9.2.verse: Take a learned noble disciple who has a pleasant feeling.

mn36:9.3.verse: When they experience a pleasant feeling they don’t become full of lust for it.

mn36:9.5.verse: And when it ceases, painful feeling arises.

mn36:9.6.verse: When they suffer painful feelings they don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn36:9.7.verse: Because their physical endurance is developed, pleasant feelings don’t occupy the mind. And because their mind is developed, painful feelings don’t occupy the mind.

mn36:9.8.verse: Anyone whose mind is not occupied by both pleasant and painful feelings like this is developed both in physical endurance and in mind.”

mn36:10.1.verse: “I am quite confident that the worthy Gotama

mn36:10.2.verse: is developed in physical endurance and in mind.”

mn36:10.3.verse: “Your words are clearly invasive and intrusive, Aggivessana.

mn36:10.5.verse: Ever since I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness, it has not been possible for any pleasant or painful feeling to occupy my mind.”

mn36:11.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama mustn’t have experienced the kind of pleasant or painful feelings that would occupy the mind.”

mn36:12.2.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

mn36:12.3.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn36:12.4.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn36:12.5.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn36:13.1.verse: Some time later, while still with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life—though my mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn36:13.2.verse: Once I had gone forth I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn36:13.3.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn36:13.6.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn36:13.8.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn36:13.10.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn36:13.11.verse: Surely he meditates knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn36:13.12.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn36:13.13.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, to what extent do you say you’ve realized this teaching with your own insight?’

mn36:13.14.verse: When I said this, he declared the dimension of nothingness.

mn36:13.16.verse: ‘It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith,

mn36:13.20.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn36:13.21.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma says he has realized with his own insight?’

mn36:13.22.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn36:14.1.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn36:14.2.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, is it up to this point that you realized this teaching with your own insight, and declare having achieved it?’

mn36:14.4.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn36:14.5.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn36:14.6.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn36:14.7.verse: So the teaching that I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn36:14.8.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it.

mn36:14.9.verse: So the teaching that I know, you know, and the teaching you know, I know.

mn36:14.10.verse: I am like you and you are like me.

mn36:14.11.verse: Come now, reverend! We should both lead this community together.’

mn36:14.12.verse: And that is how my tutor Āḷāra Kālāma placed me, his pupil, on the same position as him, and honored me with high praise.

mn36:14.14.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of nothingness.’

mn36:14.15.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn36:15.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn36:15.2.verse: ‘Reverend, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn36:15.5.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn36:15.7.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn36:15.9.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Rāma declared: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn36:15.10.verse: Surely he meditated knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn36:15.11.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn36:15.12.verse: ‘Reverend, to what extent did Rāma say he’d realized this teaching with his own insight?’

mn36:15.13.verse: When I said this, Uddaka son of Rāma declared the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn36:15.15.verse: ‘It’s not just Rāma who had faith,

mn36:15.19.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn36:15.20.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Rāma said he had realized with his own insight?’

mn36:15.21.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn36:15.22.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn36:15.23.verse: ‘Reverend, had Rāma realized this teaching with his own insight up to this point, and declared having achieved it?’

mn36:15.25.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn36:15.26.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn36:15.27.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn36:15.28.verse: So the teaching that Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it. The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it.

mn36:15.29.verse: So the teaching that Rāma directly knew, you know, and the teaching you know, Rāma directly knew.

mn36:15.30.verse: Rāma was like you and you are like Rāma.

mn36:15.31.verse: Come now, reverend! You should lead this community.’

mn36:15.32.verse: And that is how my spiritual companion Uddaka son of Rāma placed me in the position of a tutor and honored me with high praise.

mn36:15.34.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn36:15.35.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn36:16.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. Traveling stage by stage in the Magadhan lands, I arrived at the town of Senā in Uruvelā.

mn36:16.2.verse: There I saw a delightful park, a lovely grove with a flowing river that was clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby was a village to resort to for alms.

mn36:16.4.verse: ‘This park is truly delightful, a lovely grove with a flowing river that’s clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby there’s a village to resort to for alms.

mn36:16.5.verse: This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.’

mn36:16.6.verse: So I sat down right there, thinking:

mn36:17.1.verse: And then these three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me.

mn36:17.2.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying in water.

mn36:17.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn36:17.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn36:17.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log lying in water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn36:17.9.verse: Because it’s a green, sappy log, and it’s lying in the water.

mn36:17.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn36:17.11.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. They haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn36:17.13.verse: This was the first example that occurred to me.

mn36:18.1.verse: Then a second example occurred to me.

mn36:18.2.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn36:18.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn36:18.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn36:18.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn36:18.9.verse: Because it’s still a green, sappy log, despite the fact that it’s lying on dry land far from water.

mn36:18.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn36:18.11.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. But they haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn36:18.12.verse: This was the second example that occurred to me.

mn36:19.1.verse: Then a third example occurred to me.

mn36:19.2.verse: Suppose there was a dried up, withered log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn36:19.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn36:19.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn36:19.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that dried up, withered log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn36:19.9.verse: Because it’s a dried up, withered log, and it’s lying on dry land far from water.”

mn36:19.10.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. And they have internally given up and stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are capable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn36:19.11.verse: This was the third example that occurred to me.

mn36:19.12.verse: These are the three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, that occurred to me.

mn36:20.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, squeeze, squash, and scorch mind with mind?’

mn36:20.4.verse: until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn36:20.5.verse: It was like when a strong man grabs a weaker man by the head or throat or shoulder and squeezes, squashes, and crushes them.

mn36:20.6.verse: In the same way, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I squeezed, squashed, and crushed mind with mind until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn36:20.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:20.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:21.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice the breathless absorption?’

mn36:21.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose.

mn36:21.4.verse: But then winds came out my ears making a loud noise,

mn36:21.5.verse: like the puffing of a blacksmith’s bellows.

mn36:21.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:21.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:22.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn36:22.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn36:22.4.verse: But then strong winds ground my head,

mn36:22.5.verse: like a strong man was drilling into my head with a sharp point.

mn36:22.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:22.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:23.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn36:23.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn36:23.4.verse: But then I got a severe headache,

mn36:23.5.verse: like a strong man was tightening a strong leather strap around my head.

mn36:23.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:23.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:24.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn36:24.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn36:24.4.verse: But then strong winds carved up my belly,

mn36:24.5.verse: like a deft butcher or their apprentice was slicing my belly open with a sharp meat cleaver.

mn36:24.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:24.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:25.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn36:25.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn36:25.4.verse: But then there was a severe burning in my body,

mn36:25.5.verse: like two strong men grabbing a weaker man by the arms to burn and scorch him on a pit of glowing coals.

mn36:25.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn36:25.8.verse: But even such painful feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:26.1.verse: Then some deities saw me and said,

mn36:26.6.verse: ‘He’s not dead or dying. The ascetic Gotama is a perfected one, for that is how the perfected ones live.’

mn36:27.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice completely cutting off food?’

mn36:27.3.verse: But deities came to me and said,

mn36:27.4.verse: ‘Good fellow, don’t practice totally cutting off food.

mn36:27.5.verse: If you do, we’ll infuse heavenly nectar into your pores and you will live on that.’

mn36:27.7.verse: ‘If I claim to be completely fasting while these deities are infusing heavenly nectar in my pores, that would be a lie on my part.’

mn36:27.8.verse: So I refused those deities, saying, ‘There’s no need.’

mn36:28.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I just take a little bit of food each time, a handful of broth made from mung beans, horse gram, chickpeas, or green gram?’

mn36:28.4.verse: until my body became severely emaciated.

mn36:28.5.verse: Due to eating so little, my major and minor limbs became like the joints of an eighty-year-old or a dying man,

mn36:28.6.verse: my bottom became like a camel’s hoof,

mn36:28.7.verse: my vertebrae stuck out like beads on a string,

mn36:28.8.verse: and my ribs were as gaunt as the broken-down rafters on an old barn.

mn36:28.9.verse: Due to eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets, like the gleam of water sunk deep down a well.

mn36:28.10.verse: Due to eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter-gourd in the wind and sun.

mn36:28.11.verse: Due to eating so little, the skin of my belly stuck to my backbone, so that when I tried to rub the skin of my belly I grabbed my backbone, and when I tried to rub my backbone I rubbed the skin of my belly.

mn36:28.12.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to urinate or defecate I fell face down right there.

mn36:28.13.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell out.

mn36:29.1.verse: Then some people saw me and said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’

mn36:29.2.verse: Some said: ‘He’s not black, he’s brown.’

mn36:29.3.verse: Some said: ‘He’s neither black nor brown. The ascetic Gotama has dingy skin.’

mn36:29.4.verse: That’s how far the pure, bright complexion of my skin had been ruined by taking so little food.

mn36:30.2.verse: ‘Whatever ascetics and brahmins have experienced painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion—whether in the past, future, or present—this is as far as it goes, no-one has done more than this.

mn36:30.5.verse: But I have not achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones by this severe, grueling work.

mn36:30.6.verse: Could there be another path to awakening?’

mn36:31.2.verse: ‘I recall sitting in the cool shade of a black plum tree while my father the Sakyan was off working. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn36:31.3.verse: Could that be the path to awakening?’

mn36:31.4.verse: Stemming from that memory came the understanding:

mn36:32.2.verse: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities?’

mn36:32.4.verse: ‘I’m not afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities.’

mn36:33.2.verse: ‘I can’t achieve that pleasure with a body so severely emaciated. Why don’t I eat some solid food, some rice and porridge?’

mn36:33.3.verse: So I ate some solid food.

mn36:33.4.verse: Now at that time the group of five mendicants were attending on me, thinking,

mn36:33.5.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama will tell us of any truth that he realizes.’

mn36:33.6.verse: But when I ate some solid food, they left disappointed in me, saying,

mn36:33.7.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become indulgent; he has strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.’

mn36:34.1.verse: After eating solid food and gathering my strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn36:34.2.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:35-37.1.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn36:35-37.2.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:35-37.3.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, I entered and remained in the third absorption, where I meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn36:35-37.4.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:35-37.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn36:35-37.6.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:38.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives.

mn36:38.2.verse: I recollected my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn36:39.1.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

mn36:39.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn36:39.3.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:40.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn36:40.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn36:41.1.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night.

mn36:41.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn36:41.3.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:42.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn36:42.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn36:42.3.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn36:43.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn36:43.2.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

mn36:43.3.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.’

mn36:44.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night.

mn36:44.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn36:44.3.verse: But even such pleasant feeling did not occupy my mind.

mn36:45.1.verse: Aggivessana, I recall teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds,

mn36:45.3.verse: that I was teaching the Dhamma especially for them.

mn36:45.4.verse: But it should not be seen like this.

mn36:45.5.verse: The Realized One teaches others only so that they can understand.

mn36:45.6.verse: When that talk was finished, I stilled, settled, unified, and immersed my mind in samādhi internally in the same meditation subject as a basis of immersion as before, in which I regularly meditate.”

mn36:45.7.verse: “I’d believe that of the worthy Gotama, just like a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn36:45.8.verse: But do you ever recall sleeping during the day?”

mn36:46.1.verse: “I do recall that in the last month of the summer, I have spread out my outer robe folded in four and lain down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware.”

mn36:46.2.verse: “Some ascetics and brahmins call that a deluded abiding.”

mn36:46.3.verse: “That’s not how to define whether someone is deluded or not.

mn36:46.4.verse: But as to how to define whether someone is deluded or not,

mn36:46.5.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn36:47.1.verse: “Anyone who has not given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death is deluded, I say.

mn36:47.2.verse: For it’s not giving up the defilements that makes you deluded.

mn36:47.3.verse: Anyone who has given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death—is not deluded, I say.

mn36:47.4.verse: For it’s giving up the defilements that makes you not deluded.

mn36:47.5.verse: The Realized One has given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn36:47.6.verse: Just as a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of further growth,

mn36:47.7.verse: in the same way, the Realized One has given up the defilements so they are unable to arise in the future.”

mn36:48.1.verse: When he had spoken, Saccaka said to him,

mn36:48.3.verse: How when the worthy Gotama is repeatedly attacked with inappropriate and intrusive criticism, the complexion of his skin brightens and the color of his face becomes clear, just like a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha!

mn36:48.4.verse: I recall taking on Pūraṇa Kassapa in debate.

mn36:48.5.verse: He dodged the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points, and displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

mn36:48.6.verse: But when the worthy Gotama is repeatedly attacked with inappropriate and intrusive criticism, the complexion of his skin brightens and the color of his face becomes clear, just like a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn36:48.7.verse: I recall taking on the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla,

mn36:48.11.verse: and the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan in debate.

mn36:48.12.verse: They all dodged the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points, and displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

mn36:48.13.verse: But when the worthy Gotama is repeatedly attacked with inappropriate and intrusive criticism, the complexion of his skin brightens and the color of his face becomes clear, just like a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn36:48.14.verse: Well, now, worthy Gotama, I must go.

mn36:48.15.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn36:48.17.verse: Then Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, rose from his seat and left.

mn37:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother.

mn37:2.1.verse: Then Sakka the deva-king went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side. As he was standing there, he said to the Blessed One,

mn37:2.2.verse: “Briefly, lord, in what respect is a monk released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings?”

mn37:3.1.verse: “There is the case, deva-king, where a monk has heard,

mn37:3.4.verse: all dhammas are unworthy of adherence,

mn37:3.5.verse: he directly knows every dhamma. Directly knowing every dhamma, he comprehends every dhamma. Comprehending every dhamma, then whatever feeling he experiences—pleasure, pain, neither pleasure nor pain—

mn37:3.6.verse: he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation, focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling.

mn37:3.7.verse: As he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation, focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling, he is unsustained by [doesn’t cling to] anything in the world.

mn37:3.8.verse: Unsustained, he isn’t agitated. Unagitated, he totally unbinds right within.

mn37:3.9.verse: He discerns: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, the task done. There is nothing further for this world.’
