mn37:3.10.verse: “It’s in this respect, deva-king, that a monk, in brief, is released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings.”

mn37:4.1.verse: Then Sakka the deva-king, delighting in & approving of the Buddha’s words, bowed down & circumambulated him—keeping him to his right—and then vanished right there.

mn37:5.1.verse: Now, on that occasion Ven. Mahā Moggallāna was sitting not far from the Blessed One.

mn37:5.3.verse: “Did that spirit approve of the Blessed One’s words having broken through to them, or not?

mn37:5.4.verse: What if I were to find out

mn37:5.5.verse: whether he approved of the Blessed One’s words having broken through to them or not?”

mn37:6.1.verse: Then—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—Ven. Mahā Moggallāna vanished from the palace of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery and reappeared among the devas of the Thirty-three.

mn37:7.1.verse: Now, on that occasion, Sakka the deva-king was enjoying himself in the Pleasure Park of the Single White Lotus Flower, furnished & replete with the sound of 500 heavenly musicians.

mn37:7.2.verse: He saw Ven. Mahā Moggallāna coming from afar,

mn37:7.3.verse: and on seeing him, dismissed the 500 heavenly musicians and went to him. On arrival, he said to him,

mn37:7.4.verse: “Come, dear sir Moggallāna. Welcome, dear sir Moggallāna.

mn37:7.5.verse: It’s been a long time, dear sir Moggallāna, since you’ve made your way here.

mn37:7.6.verse: Sit down, dear sir Moggallāna. This seat is made ready.”

mn37:7.7.verse: Then Ven. Mahā Moggallāna sat down on the seat made ready,

mn37:7.8.verse: while Sakka the deva-king sat down to one side, taking a lower seat.

mn37:7.9.verse: When Sakka the deva-king had taken his seat, Ven. Mahā Moggallāna said to him,

mn37:8.1.verse: “Kosiya, how did the Blessed One describe to you in brief the release through the ending of craving?

mn37:8.2.verse: It would be good if we, too, could get to share in hearing that talk.”

mn37:8.3.verse: “Dear sir, Moggallāna, many are our duties, many our responsibilities:

mn37:8.4.verse: not only our own responsibilities but also the responsibilities of the devas of the Thirty-three.

mn37:8.5.verse: On top of that, even what is well-heard, well-grasped, well-attended to, well-remembered by us suddenly vanishes.

mn37:8.6.verse: “Once, dear sir Moggallāna, a war was raging between the devas & the asuras,

mn37:8.7.verse: and in that war the devas won and the asuras lost.

mn37:8.8.verse: Having won that war and returned as victor, I had the Vejayanta (Victory) Palace built.

mn37:8.9.verse: Dear sir Moggallāna, the Vejayanta Palace has 100 wings.

mn37:8.10.verse: Each wing has seven times 700 gabled halls;

mn37:8.11.verse: each gabled hall has seven times seven nymphs;

mn37:8.12.verse: each nymph has seven times seven handmaids.

mn37:8.13.verse: Would you like to see the delightful features of the Vejayanta Palace, dear sir Moggallāna?”

mn37:8.14.verse: Ven. Mahā Moggallāna accepted with silence.

mn37:9.1.verse: Then Sakka the deva-king & the Great King Vessavaṇṇa, giving precedence to Ven. Mahā Moggallāna, went to the Vejayanta palace.

mn37:9.2.verse: The handmaids of Sakka the deva-king saw Ven. Mahā Moggallāna coming in the distance and,

mn37:9.3.verse: on seeing him, feeling embarrassed & ashamed, went each into her own room.

mn37:10.1.verse: Just as a daughter-in-law, on seeing her father-in-law, is embarrassed & ashamed,

mn37:10.2.verse: even so the handmaids of Sakka the deva-king, on seeing Ven. Mahā Moggallāna and feeling embarrassed & ashamed, went each into her own room.

mn37:10.3.verse: Then Sakka the deva-king & the Great King Vessavaṇṇa had Ven. Mahā Moggallāna walk all around, exploring the Vejayanta Palace, (saying,)

mn37:10.4.verse: “Look at this delightful feature of the Vejayanta Palace, dear sir Moggallāna!

mn37:10.5.verse: Look at this delightful feature of the Vejayanta Palace, dear sir Moggallāna!”

mn37:10.6.verse: “This outshines Ven. Kosiya as one who has made merit in the past.

mn37:10.7.verse: Just as whenever human beings, on seeing something delightful, say,

mn37:10.8.verse: ‘How this outshines, good sirs, the devas of the Thirty-three!’

mn37:10.9.verse: in the same way, this outshines Ven. Kosiya as one who has made merit in the past.”

mn37:11.1.verse: Then the thought occurred to Ven. Mahā Moggallāna,

mn37:11.2.verse: “This spirit is living far too heedlessly.

mn37:11.3.verse: What if I were to inspire a sense of terror [saṁvega] in this spirit?”

mn37:11.4.verse: So Ven. Mahā Moggallāna fabricated a fabrication of psychic power such that with his toe he made the Vejayanta Palace shiver & quiver & quake.

mn37:11.5.verse: Then the minds of Sakka the deva-king & the Great King Vessavaṇṇa & the devas of the Thirty-three were overcome with amazement & astonishment:

mn37:11.6.verse: “How amazing, good sirs! How astounding, good sirs!—

mn37:11.7.verse: the great power, the great might of this contemplative, in that with his toe he makes the deva palace shiver & quiver & quake!”

mn37:12.1.verse: Then Ven. Mahā Moggallāna, knowing that Sakka the deva-king was in terror, his hair standing on end, said to him,

mn37:12.2.verse: “Kosiya, how did the Blessed One describe to you in brief the release through the ending of craving?

mn37:12.3.verse: It would be good if we, too, could get to share in hearing that talk.”

mn37:12.4.verse: “Just now, dear sir Moggallāna, I went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side. As I was standing there, I said to the Blessed One,

mn37:12.5.verse: ‘Briefly, lord, in what respect is a monk released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings?’

mn37:13.1.verse: “When this was said, the Blessed One said to me:

mn37:13.2.verse: ‘There is the case, deva-king, where a monk has heard,

mn37:13.5.verse: all dhammas are unworthy of adherence,

mn37:13.6.verse: he directly knows every dhamma. Directly knowing every dhamma, he comprehends every dhamma. Comprehending every dhamma, then whatever feeling he experiences—pleasure, pain, neither pleasure nor pain—

mn37:13.7.verse: he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation, focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling.

mn37:13.8.verse: As he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation, focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling, he is unsustained by [doesn’t cling to] anything in the world.

mn37:13.9.verse: Unsustained, he isn’t agitated. Unagitated, he totally unbinds right within.

mn37:13.10.verse: He discerns: “Birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, the task done. There is nothing further for this world.”

mn37:13.11.verse: ‘It’s in this respect, deva-king, that a monk, in brief, is released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings.’

mn37:13.12.verse: “That is how, dear sir Moggallāna, the Blessed One described to me in brief the release through the ending of craving.”

mn37:14.1.verse: Then Ven. Mahā Moggallāna, delighting in & approving of Sakka the deva-king’s words—as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—vanished from among the devas of the Thirty-three and reappeared in the palace of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn37:14.2.verse: Then not long after Ven. Mahā Moggallāna had left, the handmaids of Sakka the deva-king said to him,

mn37:14.3.verse: “Dear sir, is that Blessed One your teacher?”

mn37:14.4.verse: “No, that Blessed One isn’t my teacher.

mn37:14.5.verse: That is Ven. Mahā Moggallāna, my fellow in the holy life.”

mn37:14.6.verse: “It’s a gain for you, dear sir, a great gain for you, dear sir,

mn37:14.7.verse: in that you have a fellow in the holy life of such great power, such great might!

mn37:14.8.verse: How much more so will the Blessed One, your teacher be!”

mn37:15.1.verse: Then Ven. Mahā Moggallāna went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One,

mn37:15.2.verse: “Does the Lord Blessed One recall describing in brief the release through the ending of craving to a certain spirit with a great following?”

mn37:15.3.verse: “I recall, Moggallāna, that just now Sakka the deva-king approached me and, on arrival, having bowed down to me, stood to one side. As he was standing there, he said to me,

mn37:15.4.verse: ‘Briefly, lord, in what respect is a monk released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings?’

mn37:15.5.verse: “When this was said, I said to him:

mn37:15.6.verse: ‘There is the case, deva-king, where a monk has heard,

mn37:15.9.verse: all dhammas are unworthy of adherence,

mn37:15.10.verse: he directly knows every dhamma. Directly knowing every dhamma, he comprehends every dhamma. Comprehending every dhamma, then whatever feeling he experiences—pleasure, pain, neither pleasure nor pain—

mn37:15.11.verse: he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation, focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling.

mn37:15.12.verse: As he remains focused on inconstancy, focused on dispassion, focused on cessation,

mn37:15.13.verse: focused on relinquishing with regard to that feeling, he is unsustained by [doesn’t cling to] anything in the world,

mn37:15.14.verse: Unsustained, he isn’t agitated. Unagitated, he totally unbinds right within.

mn37:15.15.verse: He discerns: “Birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, the task done. There is nothing further for this world.”

mn37:15.16.verse: ‘It’s in this respect, deva-king, that a monk, in brief, is released through the ending of craving, utterly complete, utterly free from bonds, a follower of the utterly holy life, utterly consummate: foremost among devas & human beings.’

mn37:15.17.verse: “That, Moggallāna, is how I recall describing to Sakka the deva-king in brief the release through the ending of craving.”

mn37:15.18.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn37:15.19.verse: Gratified, Ven. Mahā Moggallāna delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn37:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on the Ending of Craving

mn37:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn37:2.1.verse: And then Sakka, lord of gods, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him:

mn37:2.2.verse: “Sir, how do you briefly define a mendicant who is freed through the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans?”

mn37:3.1.verse: “Lord of gods, take a mendicant who has heard:

mn37:3.3.verse: When a mendicant has heard that

mn37:3.5.verse: they directly know all things. Directly knowing all things, they completely understand all things. Completely understanding all things, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—

mn37:3.6.verse: they meditate observing impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in those feelings.

mn37:3.7.verse: Meditating in this way, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

mn37:3.8.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

mn37:3.9.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn37:3.10.verse: That’s how I briefly define a mendicant who is freed through the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans.”

mn37:4.1.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

mn37:5.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Buddha.

mn37:5.3.verse: “Did that spirit comprehend what the Buddha said when he agreed with him, or not?

mn37:6.1.verse: And then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the Eastern Monastery and reappeared among the gods of the thirty-three.

mn37:7.1.verse: Now at that time Sakka was amusing himself in the Single Lotus Park, supplied and provided with a heavenly orchestra.

mn37:7.2.verse: Seeing Mahāmoggallāna coming off in the distance,

mn37:7.3.verse: he waved off the orchestra, approached Mahāmoggallāna, and said,

mn37:7.4.verse: “Come, my good fellow Moggallāna! Welcome, my good fellow!

mn37:7.5.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

mn37:7.6.verse: Sit, my good Moggallāna, here, a seat is ready.”

mn37:7.7.verse: Mahāmoggallāna sat down on the seat spread out,

mn37:7.8.verse: while Sakka took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn37:8.1.verse: “Kosiya, how did the Buddha briefly explain freedom through the ending of craving?

mn37:8.2.verse: Please share this talk with me so that I can also get to hear it.”

mn37:8.3.verse: “My good Moggallāna, I have many duties, and much to do,

mn37:8.4.verse: not only for myself, but also for the gods of the thirty-three.

mn37:8.5.verse: Still, what is properly heard, learned, attended, and memorized does not vanish all of a sudden.

mn37:8.6.verse: Once upon a time, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

mn37:8.7.verse: In that battle the gods won and the titans lost.

mn37:8.8.verse: When I returned from that battle as a conqueror, I created the Palace of Victory.

mn37:8.9.verse: The Palace of Victory has a hundred towers.

mn37:8.10.verse: Each tower has seven hundred chambers.

mn37:8.13.verse: Would you like to see the lovely Palace of Victory?”

mn37:9.1.verse: Then, putting Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in front, Sakka, lord of gods, and Vessavaṇa, the Great King, went to the Palace of Victory.

mn37:9.2.verse: When they saw Moggallāna coming off in the distance, Sakka’s maids,

mn37:9.3.verse: being discreet and prudent, each went to her own bedroom.

mn37:10.1.verse: They were just like a daughter-in-law who is discreet and prudent when they see their father-in-law.

mn37:10.3.verse: Then Sakka and Vessavaṇa encouraged Moggallāna to wander and explore the palace, saying,

mn37:10.4.verse: “See, in the palace, my good Moggallāna, this lovely thing!

mn37:10.6.verse: “That looks beautiful for the venerable Kosiya, as befits one who has made merit in the past.

mn37:10.7.verse: Humans, when they see something lovely, also say:

mn37:10.8.verse: ‘It looks beautiful enough for the gods of the thirty-three!’

mn37:10.9.verse: That looks beautiful for the venerable Kosiya, as befits one who has made merit in the past.”

mn37:11.3.verse: Why don’t I stir up a sense of urgency in him?”

mn37:11.4.verse: Then Moggallāna used his psychic power to make the Palace of Victory shake and rock and tremble with his big toe.

mn37:11.5.verse: Then Sakka, Vessavaṇa, and the gods of the thirty-three, their minds full of wonder and amazement, thought,

mn37:11.7.verse: The ascetic has such power and might that he makes the god’s home shake and rock and tremble with his big toe!”

mn37:12.1.verse: Knowing that Sakka was shocked and awestruck, Moggallāna said to him,

mn37:12.2.verse: “Kosiya, how did the Buddha briefly explain freedom through the ending of craving?

mn37:12.3.verse: Please share this talk with me so that I can also get to hear it.”

mn37:12.4.verse: “My good fellow Moggallāna, I approached the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

mn37:12.5.verse: ‘Sir, how do you briefly define a mendicant who is freed with the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans?’

mn37:13.1.verse: When I had spoken the Buddha said to me:

mn37:13.2.verse: ‘Lord of gods, it’s when a mendicant has heard:

mn37:13.4.verse: When a mendicant has heard that

mn37:13.6.verse: they directly know all things. Directly knowing all things, they completely understand all things. Having completely understood all things, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—

mn37:13.7.verse: they meditate observing impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in those feelings.

mn37:13.8.verse: Meditating in this way, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

mn37:13.9.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

mn37:13.10.verse: They understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”

mn37:13.11.verse: That’s how I briefly define a mendicant who is freed through the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans.’

mn37:13.12.verse: That’s how the Buddha briefly explained freedom through the ending of craving to me.”

mn37:14.1.verse: Moggallāna approved and agreed with what Sakka said. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from among the gods of the thirty-three and reappeared in the Eastern Monastery.

mn37:14.2.verse: Soon after Moggallāna left, Sakka’s maids said to him,

mn37:14.3.verse: “Good fellow, was that the Blessed One, your Teacher?”

mn37:14.5.verse: That was my spiritual companion Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.”

mn37:14.6.verse: “You’re fortunate, good fellow, so very fortunate,

mn37:14.7.verse: to have a spiritual companion of such power and might!

mn37:14.8.verse: We can’t believe that’s not the Blessed One, your Teacher!”

mn37:15.1.verse: Then Mahāmoggallāna went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn37:15.2.verse: “Sir, do you recall briefly explaining freedom through the ending of craving to a certain well-known and illustrious spirit?”

mn37:15.3.verse: “I do, Moggallāna.” And the Buddha retold all that happened when Sakka came to visit him, adding:

mn37:15.17.verse: “That’s how I recall briefly explaining freedom through the ending of craving to Sakka, lord of gods.”

mn37:15.18.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn37:15.19.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approved what the Buddha said.

mn38:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn38:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion a pernicious view had arisen in a bhikkhu called Sāti, son of a fisherman; thus:

mn38:2.2.verse: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:3.1.verse: Many bhikkhus heard that this was so.

mn38:3.2.verse: ‘It seems that this pernicious view has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:

mn38:3.3.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”’

mn38:3.4.verse: Then they went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman,[^1] and they asked him:

mn38:3.5.verse: ‘Friend, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:

mn38:3.6.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’

mn38:3.7.verse: ‘Exactly so, friends. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:3.8.verse: Then the bhikkhus desiring to detach him from that pernicious view, pressed and questioned and cross-questioned him thus:

mn38:3.9.verse: ‘Friend Sāti, do not say thus, do not misrepresent the Blessed One, it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus,

mn38:3.10.verse: for consciousness has been stated in many discourses by the Blessed One to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’

mn38:3.11.verse: Yet although pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by them in this way, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, still obstinately misapprehended according to his pernicious view and insisted upon it, saying:

mn38:3.12.verse: ‘Exactly so, friends, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:4.1.verse: Since the bhikkhus were unable to detach him from that pernicious view, they went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, they said to the Blessed One:

mn38:4.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, this pernicious view has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:

mn38:4.3.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”

mn38:4.4.verse: We heard, venerable sir, that this pernicious view had arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:

mn38:4.5.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”

mn38:4.6.verse: Then, venerable sir, we went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, and we said to him:

mn38:4.7.verse: ‘Friend, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:

mn38:4.8.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’

mn38:4.9.verse: When this was said, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, said to us:

mn38:4.10.verse: ‘Exactly so, friends. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:4.11.verse: Then, venerable sir, desiring to detach him from that pernicious view, we pressed and questioned and cross-questioned him thus:

mn38:4.12.verse: ‘Friend Sāti, do not say thus, do not misrepresent the Blessed One, it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus,

mn38:4.13.verse: for consciousness has been stated in many discourses by the Blessed One to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’

mn38:4.14.verse: Yet although pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by us in this way, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, still obstinately misapprehended according to his pernicious view and insisted upon it, saying:

mn38:4.15.verse: ‘Exactly so, friends, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:4.16.verse: Since we have been unable to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, from this pernicious view, venerable sir, we have reported this matter to the Blessed One.’

mn38:5.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu thus:

mn38:5.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, tell the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, in my name:

mn38:5.4.verse: ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ he replied, and he went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, and told him:

mn38:5.6.verse: ‘Even so, friend,’ he replied, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One asked him:

mn38:5.7.verse: ‘Sāti, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:

mn38:5.8.verse: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’

mn38:5.9.verse: ‘Exactly so, venerable sir. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’

mn38:5.11.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it is what speaks and feels and experiences here and there the ripening of good and evil actions.’

mn38:5.12.verse: ‘Misguided man, whom have you ever heard me teach the Dhamma to in that way?

mn38:5.13.verse: Misguided man, has not consciousness been stated by me in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being?

mn38:5.14.verse: But you, misguided man, have both misrepresented us by your wrong grasp of it and worked your own undoing by storing up much demerit,

mn38:5.15.verse: for this will be long for your harm and suffering.’

mn38:6.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn38:6.3.verse: has this bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, kindled (in himself) even a spark (of understanding) in this Dhamma and Discipline?’

mn38:6.6.verse: When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum and with nothing to say.

mn38:6.7.verse: Then knowing that, the Blessed One told the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:

mn38:6.8.verse: ‘Misguided man, you will be described by this your own pernicious view.

mn38:6.9.verse: I shall question the bhikkhus on this matter.’

mn38:7.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn38:7.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, do you know the Dhamma taught by me as this bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, does when he both misrepresents us by his wrong grasp (of it) and works his own undoing by storing up much demerit?’

mn38:7.4.verse: for consciousness has been stated by the Blessed One in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’

mn38:7.6.verse: that you know the Dhamma taught by me thus:

mn38:7.7.verse: for consciousness has been stated by me in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’

mn38:7.8.verse: But this misguided man, Sāti, son of a fisherman, both misrepresents us by his wrong grasp (of it) and works his own undoing by storing up much demerit:

mn38:7.9.verse: for this will be long for his harm and suffering.’

mn38:8.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, consciousness is reckoned only by the condition dependent on which it arises:

mn38:8.2.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on eye and forms, it is reckoned only as eye-consciousness;

mn38:8.3.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on ear and sounds, it is reckoned only as ear-consciousness;

mn38:8.4.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on nose and odours, it is reckoned only as nose-consciousness;

mn38:8.5.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on tongue and flavours, it is reckoned only as tongue-consciousness;

mn38:8.6.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on body and tangibles, it is reckoned only as body-consciousness;

mn38:8.7.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on mind and dhammas, it is reckoned only as mind-consciousness.

mn38:8.8.verse: ‘Just as a fire is reckoned only by the condition dependent on which it burns:

mn38:8.9.verse: when fire burns dependent on logs, it is reckoned only as a log fire;

mn38:8.10.verse: when fire burns dependent on faggots, it is reckoned only as a faggot fire;

mn38:8.11.verse: when fire burns dependent on grass, it is reckoned only as a grass fire;

mn38:8.12.verse: when fire burns dependent on cowdung, it is reckoned only as a cowdung fire;

mn38:8.13.verse: when fire burns dependent on chaff, it is reckoned only as a chaff fire;

mn38:8.14.verse: when fire burns dependent on rubbish, it is reckoned only as a rubbish fire—

mn38:8.15.verse: so too, bhikkhus, consciousness is reckonable only by the condition dependent on which it arises.

mn38:8.16.verse: When consciousness arises dependent on eye and forms it is reckoned only as eye-consciousness;

mn38:8.17.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on ear and sounds it is reckoned only as ear-consciousness;

mn38:8.18.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on nose and odours it is reckoned only as nose-consciousness;

mn38:8.19.verse: when consciousness arises dependent on tongue and flavours it is reckoned only as tongue-consciousness.

mn38:8.20.verse: When consciousness arises dependent on body and tangibles it is reckoned only as body-consciousness.

mn38:8.21.verse: When consciousness arises dependent on mind and dhammas it is reckoned only as mind-consciousness.

mn38:9.1.verse: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’

mn38:9.3.verse: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’

mn38:9.5.verse: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’

mn38:10.1.verse: ‘“This (entity) is, is it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’

mn38:10.3.verse: ‘“Is its coming to positive being due to its nutriment, or is it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’

mn38:10.5.verse: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment has it the nature to change, or has it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’

mn38:11.1.verse: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:11.3.verse: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:11.5.verse: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:12.1.verse: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’

mn38:12.3.verse: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’

mn38:12.5.verse: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’

mn38:13.1.verse: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:13.3.verse: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:13.5.verse: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’

mn38:14.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, purified and bright as this view is, were you to adhere to it, cherish it, treasure it, and call it your own, would you then understand the Dhamma that has been taught as similar to a raft[^2], being for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?’

mn38:14.3.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, purified and bright as this view is, were you not to adhere to it, cherish it, treasure it, and call it your own, would you then understand the Dhamma that has been taught as similar to a raft, being for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?’

mn38:15.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of creatures that already are (entities) and for the assistance of those seeking to renew positive being.

mn38:15.3.verse: They are physical food as nutriment whether gross or subtle, contact as the second, volition about (the state of) mind as the third, and consciousness as the fourth.

mn38:16.1.verse: ‘Now these four kinds of nutriment have what as their source, have what as their origin, what brings them birth, what provides them with being?

mn38:16.2.verse: These four kinds of nutriment have craving as their source, have craving as their origin, craving brings them birth, craving provides them with being.

mn38:16.3.verse: ‘And this craving has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.4.verse: Craving has feeling as its source, has feeling as its origin, feeling brings it birth, feeling provides it with being.

mn38:16.5.verse: ‘And this feeling has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.6.verse: Feeling has contact as its source, has contact as its origin, contact brings it birth, contact provides it with being.

mn38:16.7.verse: ‘And this contact has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.8.verse: Contact has the sixfold base as its source, has the sixfold base as its origin, the sixfold base brings it birth, the sixfold base provides it with being.

mn38:16.9.verse: ‘And this sixfold base has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.10.verse: The sixfold base has name-and-form as its source, has name-and-form as its origin, name-and-form brings it birth, name-and-form provides it with being.

mn38:16.11.verse: ‘And this name-and-form has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.12.verse: Name-and-form has consciousness as its source, has consciousness as its origin, consciousness brings it birth, consciousness provides it with being.

mn38:16.13.verse: ‘And this consciousness has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?

mn38:16.14.verse: Consciousness has formations as its source, has formations as its origin, formations bring it birth, formations provide it with being.

mn38:16.15.verse: ‘And these formations have what as their source, have what as their origin, what brings them birth, what provides them with being?

mn38:16.16.verse: Formations have ignorance as their source, have ignorance as their origin, ignorance brings them birth, ignorance provides them with being.

mn38:17.1.verse: ‘So, bhikkhus, it is with ignorance as condition that formations come to be;

mn38:17.4.verse: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;

mn38:17.5.verse: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;

mn38:17.11.verse: it is with birth as condition that ageing and death come to be, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:17.12.verse: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:18.1.verse: ‘“With birth as condition, ageing and death”: so it was said.

mn38:18.2.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.3.verse: ‘With birth as condition, ageing and death, venerable sir:

mn38:18.4.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.5.verse: with birth as condition, ageing and death.’

mn38:18.6.verse: ‘“With being as condition, birth”: so it was said.

mn38:18.7.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.8.verse: ‘With being as condition, birth, venerable sir:

mn38:18.9.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.11.verse: ‘“With clinging as condition, being”: so it was said.

mn38:18.12.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.13.verse: ‘With clinging as condition, being, venerable sir:

mn38:18.14.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.16.verse: ‘“With craving as condition, clinging”: so it was said. Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.17.verse: ‘With craving as condition, clinging, venerable sir:

mn38:18.18.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.20.verse: ‘“With feeling as condition, craving”: so it was said.

mn38:18.21.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.22.verse: ‘With feeling as condition, craving, venerable sir:

mn38:18.23.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.25.verse: ‘“With contact as condition, feeling”: so it was said.

mn38:18.26.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.27.verse: ‘With contact as condition, feeling, venerable sir:

mn38:18.28.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.30.verse: ‘“With the sixfold base as condition, contact”: so it was said.

mn38:18.31.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.32.verse: ‘With the sixfold base as condition, contact, venerable sir:

mn38:18.33.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.34.verse: with the sixfold base as condition, contact.’

mn38:18.35.verse: ‘“With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base”: so it was said.

mn38:18.36.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.37.verse: ‘With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base, venerable sir:

mn38:18.38.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.39.verse: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base.’

mn38:18.40.verse: ‘“With consciousness as condition, name-and-form”: so it was said.

mn38:18.41.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.42.verse: ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form, venerable sir:

mn38:18.43.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.45.verse: ‘“With formations as condition, consciousness”: so it was said.

mn38:18.46.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.47.verse: ‘With formations as condition, consciousness, venerable sir:

mn38:18.48.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:18.50.verse: ‘“With ignorance as condition, formations”: so it was said.

mn38:18.51.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:18.52.verse: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations, venerable sir:

mn38:18.53.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:19.2.verse: So you say thus, and I also say thus:

mn38:19.3.verse: “That is, when this is; that arises with the arising of this,” that is to say:

mn38:19.7.verse: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;

mn38:19.8.verse: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;

mn38:19.14.verse: it is with birth as condition that ageing and death come to be, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:19.15.verse: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.’

mn38:20.1.verse: ‘With the remainderless fading and ceasing of ignorance, cessation of formations;

mn38:20.2.verse: with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;

mn38:20.3.verse: with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;

mn38:20.4.verse: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;

mn38:20.5.verse: with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;

mn38:20.6.verse: with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;

mn38:20.7.verse: with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;

mn38:20.8.verse: with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;

mn38:20.9.verse: with the cessation of clinging, cessation of being;

mn38:20.10.verse: with the cessation of being, cessation of birth;

mn38:20.11.verse: with the cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:20.12.verse: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:21.1.verse: ‘“With cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death”: so it was said.

mn38:21.2.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.3.verse: ‘With cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death, venerable sir:

mn38:21.4.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.5.verse: with cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death.’

mn38:21.6.verse: ‘“With cessation of being, cessation of birth”: so it was said.

mn38:21.7.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.8.verse: ‘With cessation of being, cessation of birth, venerable sir:

mn38:21.9.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.10.verse: with cessation of being, cessation of birth.’

mn38:21.11.verse: ‘“With cessation of clinging, cessation of being”: so it was said.

mn38:21.12.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.13.verse: ‘With cessation of clinging, cessation of being, venerable sir:

mn38:21.14.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.15.verse: with cessation of clinging, cessation of being.’

mn38:21.16.verse: ‘“With cessation of craving, cessation of clinging”: so it was said.

mn38:21.17.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.18.verse: ‘With cessation of craving, cessation of clinging, venerable sir:

mn38:21.19.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.20.verse: with cessation of craving, cessation of clinging.’

mn38:21.21.verse: ‘“With cessation of feeling, cessation of craving”: so it was said.

mn38:21.22.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.23.verse: ‘With cessation of feeling, cessation of craving, venerable sir:

mn38:21.24.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.25.verse: with cessation of feeling, cessation of craving.’

mn38:21.26.verse: ‘“With cessation of contact, cessation of feeling”: so it was said.

mn38:21.27.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.28.verse: ‘With cessation of contact, cessation of feeling, venerable sir:

mn38:21.29.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.30.verse: with cessation of contact, cessation of feeling.’

mn38:21.31.verse: ‘“With cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact”: so it was said.

mn38:21.32.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.33.verse: ‘With cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact, venerable sir:

mn38:21.34.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.35.verse: with cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact.’

mn38:21.36.verse: ‘“With cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base”: so it was said.

mn38:21.37.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.38.verse: ‘With cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base, venerable sir:

mn38:21.39.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.40.verse: with cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base.’

mn38:21.41.verse: ‘“With cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form”: so it was said.

mn38:21.42.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.43.verse: ‘With cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form, venerable sir:

mn38:21.44.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.45.verse: with cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form.’

mn38:21.46.verse: ‘“With cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness”: so it was said.

mn38:21.47.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.48.verse: ‘With cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness, venerable sir:

mn38:21.49.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.50.verse: with cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness.’

mn38:21.51.verse: ‘“With cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations”: so it was said.

mn38:21.52.verse: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’

mn38:21.53.verse: ‘With cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations, venerable sir:

mn38:21.54.verse: so it appears to us in this case—

mn38:21.55.verse: with cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations.’

mn38:22.2.verse: So you say thus, and I also say thus:

mn38:22.3.verse: “That is not, when this is not; that ceases with the cessation of this,” that is to say:

mn38:22.4.verse: with cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations;

mn38:22.5.verse: with cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;

mn38:22.6.verse: with cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;

mn38:22.7.verse: with cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;

mn38:22.8.verse: with cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;

mn38:22.9.verse: with cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;

mn38:22.10.verse: with cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;

mn38:22.11.verse: with cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;

mn38:22.12.verse: with cessation of clinging, cessation of being;

mn38:22.13.verse: with cessation of being, cessation of birth;

mn38:22.14.verse: with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:22.15.verse: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.’

mn38:23.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you run back to the past thus:

mn38:23.2.verse: “Were we in past time? Were we not in past time? What were we in past time? How were we in the past time? Having been what, what were we in the past time?”’

mn38:23.4.verse: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you run forward to the future thus—

mn38:23.5.verse: “Shall we be in future time? Shall we not be in future time? What shall we be in future time? How shall we be in future time? Having been what, what shall we be in future time?”’

mn38:24.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you be doubtful about the present in yourselves now—

mn38:24.2.verse: “Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Whence has this creature come? Whither will it be bound?”’

mn38:24.4.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you speak thus—

mn38:24.5.verse: “The Teacher is respected by us: we speak (as we do) out of respect for the Teacher”?’

mn38:24.7.verse: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you speak thus—

mn38:24.8.verse: “A monk told us, and (other) monks (did too); but we do not speak thus”?’

mn38:24.10.verse: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you acknowledge another[^3]?’

mn38:24.12.verse: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way would you return to the ordinary monks’ and divines’ duties, and to the good omens open to the tumult of debate,[^4] as having a core (of truth)?’

mn38:24.14.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, is it not that you speak only of what you have yourselves known, seen and experienced?’

mn38:25.1.verse: ‘Good, bhikkhus. So you have been guided by me with a Dhamma (with effect) visible here and now, not (after a lapse) of time, inviting inspection, onward-leading, and experienceable by the wise each of himself.

mn38:25.2.verse: This Dhamma, bhikkhus, (has effect) visible here and now, not (after a lapse) of time, it invites inspection, is onward-leading, and is experienceable by the wise each of himself—

mn38:25.3.verse: it was with reference to this that it has been said.’

mn38:26.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, precipitation of an embryo (in a womb) comes about with the concurrence of three (things).

mn38:26.2.verse: Here there is concurrence of the mother and the father, but it is not the mother’s season, and no creature to be reborn is ready, in which case there is no precipitation in the womb.

mn38:26.3.verse: Here there is concurrence of the mother and the father, and it is the mother’s season, but no creature to be reborn is ready, in which case there is no precipitation in the womb.

mn38:26.4.verse: But owing to the fact that there is concurrence of the mother and the father, and it is the mother’s season, and a creature to be reborn is ready, there thus comes about precipitation of an embryo (in a womb) with the concurrence of three (things).

mn38:27.1.verse: ‘The mother then carries the embryo in the womb for nine or ten months, with much anxiety as a great burden.

mn38:27.2.verse: Then at the end of nine or ten months the mother gives birth with much anxiety as a great burden.

mn38:27.3.verse: Then when it is born, she nourishes it with her own blood,

mn38:27.4.verse: for the mother’s breast-milk is called blood in the Noble Ones’ Discipline.

mn38:28.1.verse: ‘Necessitated by his growth and necessitated by the maturing of his faculties,

mn38:28.2.verse: the child plays with such childish games as a toy plough, ‘tipcat’, turning somersaults, a toy windmill, a toy measure, a toy car, a toy bow and arrow.

mn38:29.1.verse: ‘Necessitated by his growth and necessitated by the maturing of his faculties,

mn38:29.2.verse: the youth becomes furnished and invested with the five cords of sensual desire, he enjoys them, namely:

mn38:29.3.verse: forms cognizable through the eye that are wished-for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust;

mn38:29.7.verse: tangibles cognizable through the body that are wished-for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn38:30.1.verse: ‘On seeing a form with the eye, he lusts after it if it is pleasing; he has ill-will towards it if it is unpleasing; he abides with mindfulness of body unestablished and with limited cognizance[^5],

mn38:30.2.verse: without understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.

mn38:30.3.verse: Engaged as he is in favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he relishes that feeling, affirms it and remains cleaving to it.

mn38:30.4.verse: When he does that, relishing arises in him.

mn38:30.5.verse: Now relishing any of those feelings is clinging. With his clinging as condition, being; with being as condition, birth; with birth as condition, ageing and death have positive being, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:30.6.verse: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:30.7.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn38:30.8.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn38:30.9.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn38:30.10.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn38:30.11.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he lusts after it if it is pleasing; he has ill-will towards it if it is unpleasing; he dwells with mindfulness of body unestablished and with limited cognizance,

mn38:30.12.verse: without understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.

mn38:30.13.verse: Engaged as he is in favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he relishes that feeling, affirms it and remains cleaving to it.

mn38:30.14.verse: When he does that, relishing arises in him.

mn38:30.15.verse: Now relishing any of these feelings is clinging. With his clinging as condition, being; with being as condition, birth; with birth as condition, ageing and death have positive being and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:30.16.verse: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:31.1.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.

mn38:31.2.verse: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras and its Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn38:31.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing;

mn38:31.4.verse: and he announces a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn38:32.1.verse: A householder or householder’s son or one born in some clan hears that Dhamma.

mn38:32.2.verse: On hearing the Dhamma he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.

mn38:32.3.verse: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:

mn38:32.4.verse: ‘House life is crowded and dirty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn38:32.5.verse: It is not possible, living in a household, to lead a life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.

mn38:32.6.verse: Suppose I shaved off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?’

mn38:32.7.verse: And on another occasion, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large fortune, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large circle of relatives, he shaves off hair and beard, puts on the yellow cloth, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn38:33.1.verse: ‘Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.

mn38:33.2.verse: Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given, taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.

mn38:33.3.verse: Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart abstaining from vulgar lechery.

mn38:33.4.verse: Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trustworthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.

mn38:33.5.verse: Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.

mn38:33.6.verse: Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.

mn38:33.7.verse: Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.

mn38:33.8.verse: He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.

mn38:33.9.verse: He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.

mn38:33.10.verse: He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.

mn38:33.11.verse: He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.

mn38:33.12.verse: He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.

mn38:33.13.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.

mn38:33.14.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.

mn38:33.15.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.

mn38:33.16.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.

mn38:33.17.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondswomen and bondsmen.

mn38:33.18.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.

mn38:33.19.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.

mn38:33.20.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses and mares.

mn38:33.21.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.

mn38:33.22.verse: He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.

mn38:33.23.verse: He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.

mn38:33.24.verse: He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.

mn38:33.25.verse: He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.

mn38:33.26.verse: He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.

mn38:34.1.verse: He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn38:34.2.verse: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,

mn38:34.3.verse: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn38:34.4.verse: Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn38:35.1.verse: He becomes one who, on seeing a form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features

mn38:35.2.verse: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn38:35.3.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn38:35.4.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn38:35.5.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn38:35.6.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn38:35.7.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind he apprehends no signs and features

mn38:35.8.verse: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn38:35.9.verse: Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is unadulterated.

mn38:36.1.verse: He becomes one who acts in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.

mn38:37.1.verse: He, possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this Noble Ones’ contentment, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,

mn38:37.2.verse: resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn38:38.1.verse: On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.

mn38:38.2.verse: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies mind from covetousness.

mn38:38.3.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.

mn38:38.4.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.

mn38:38.5.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself, he purifies mind from agitation and worry.

mn38:38.6.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas, he purifies mind from uncertainty.

mn38:39.1.verse: Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn38:39.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn38:39.3.verse: Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …

mn38:39.5.verse: and the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn38:40.1.verse: ‘On seeing a form with the eye, he does not lust after it if it is pleasing; he has no ill-will towards it if it is not pleasing. He abides with mindfulness of body established and immeasurable cognizance[^6],

mn38:40.2.verse: understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.

mn38:40.3.verse: Having thus abandoned favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he does not relish that feeling, or affirm it, or remain cleaving to it.

mn38:40.4.verse: When he does not do that, this relishing of those feelings ceases.

mn38:40.5.verse: With cessation of his relishing (there is) cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of being; with cessation of being, cessation of birth; with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:40.6.verse: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:41.1.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn38:41.2.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn38:41.3.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn38:41.4.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn38:41.5.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he does not lust after it if it is pleasing; he has no ill-will towards it if it is not pleasing. He abides with mindfulness of body established and immeasurable cognizance,

mn38:41.6.verse: understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.

mn38:41.7.verse: Having thus abandoned favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he does not relish that feeling, or affirm it, or remain cleaving to it.

mn38:41.8.verse: When he does not do that, this relishing of those feelings ceases.

mn38:41.9.verse: With cessation of his relishing (there is) cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of being; with cessation of being, cessation of birth; with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn38:41.10.verse: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.

mn38:41.11.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, remember this Freedom due to craving’s Full Exhaustion (as taught) in brief by me. But the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, is caught up in a vast net of craving, in craving’s trammel.’

mn38:41.12.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn38:41.13.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn38:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on the Ending of Craving

mn38:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn38:2.1.verse: Now at that time a mendicant named Sāti, the fisherman’s son, had the following harmful misconception:

mn38:2.2.verse: “As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another.”

mn38:3.4.verse: They went up to Sāti and said to him,

mn38:3.5.verse: “Is it really true, Reverend Sāti, that you have such a harmful misconception:

mn38:3.6.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another’?”

mn38:3.7.verse: “Indeed, reverends. As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another.”

mn38:3.8.verse: Then, wishing to dissuade Sāti from his view, the mendicants pursued, pressed, and grilled him,

mn38:3.9.verse: “Don’t say that, Sāti! Don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for misrepresentation of the Buddha is not good. And the Buddha would not say that.

mn38:3.10.verse: In many ways the Buddha has said that consciousness is dependently originated, that without a cause, consciousness does not come to be.”

mn38:3.11.verse: But even though the mendicants pressed him in this way, Sāti obstinately stuck to his misconception and insisted on it.

mn38:4.1.verse: When they weren’t able to dissuade Sāti from his view, the mendicants went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

mn38:5.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

mn38:5.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Sāti that

mn38:5.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Sāti and said to him,

mn38:5.6.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Sāti replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn38:5.7.verse: “Is it really true, Sāti, that you have such a harmful misconception:

mn38:5.8.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another’?”

mn38:5.9.verse: “Indeed, sir. As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another.”

mn38:5.11.verse: “Sir, he is the one who speaks, the one who knows, who experiences the results of good and bad deeds in all the different realms.”

mn38:5.12.verse: “Futile man, who on earth have you ever known me to teach in that way?

mn38:5.13.verse: Haven’t I said in many ways that consciousness is dependently originated, that without a cause, consciousness does not come to be?

mn38:5.14.verse: But still you misrepresent me by your wrong grasp, harm yourself, and brim with much wickedness.

mn38:5.15.verse: This will be for your lasting harm and suffering.”

mn38:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn38:6.3.verse: Has this mendicant Sāti kindled even a spark of ardor in this teaching and training?”

mn38:6.6.verse: When this was said, Sāti sat silent, dismayed, shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

mn38:6.8.verse: “Futile man, you will be known by your own harmful misconception.

mn38:6.9.verse: I’ll question the mendicants about this.”

mn38:7.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn38:7.2.verse: “Mendicants, do you understand my teachings as Sāti does, when he misrepresents me by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and brims with much wickedness?”

mn38:7.4.verse: For in many ways the Buddha has told us that consciousness is dependently originated, that without a cause, consciousness does not come to be.”

mn38:7.6.verse: It’s good that you understand my teaching like this.

mn38:7.7.verse: For in many ways I have told you that consciousness is dependently originated, that without a cause, consciousness does not come to be.

mn38:7.8.verse: But still this Sāti misrepresents me by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and brims with much wickedness.

mn38:7.9.verse: This will be for his lasting harm and suffering.

mn38:8.1.verse: Consciousness is reckoned according to the very same condition dependent upon which it arises.

mn38:8.2.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the eye and sights is reckoned as eye consciousness.

mn38:8.3.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the ear and sounds is reckoned as ear consciousness.

mn38:8.4.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the nose and smells is reckoned as nose consciousness.

mn38:8.5.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the tongue and tastes is reckoned as tongue consciousness.

mn38:8.6.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the body and touches is reckoned as body consciousness.

mn38:8.7.verse: Consciousness that arises dependent on the mind and ideas is reckoned as mind consciousness.

mn38:8.8.verse: It’s like fire, which is reckoned according to the very same condition dependent upon which it burns.

mn38:8.9.verse: A fire that burns dependent on logs is reckoned as a log fire.

mn38:8.10.verse: A fire that burns dependent on twigs is reckoned as a twig fire.

mn38:8.11.verse: A fire that burns dependent on grass is reckoned as a grass fire.

mn38:8.12.verse: A fire that burns dependent on cow-dung is reckoned as a cow-dung fire.

mn38:8.13.verse: A fire that burns dependent on husks is reckoned as a husk fire.

mn38:8.14.verse: A fire that burns dependent on rubbish is reckoned as a rubbish fire.

mn38:8.15.verse: In the same way, consciousness is reckoned according to the very same condition dependent upon which it arises. …

mn38:9.1.verse: Mendicants, do you see that this has come to be?”

mn38:9.3.verse: “Do you see that it came to be with that as fuel?”

mn38:9.5.verse: “Do you see that when that fuel ceases, what has come to be is liable to cease?”

mn38:10.1.verse: “Does doubt arise when you’re uncertain whether or not this has come to be?”

mn38:10.3.verse: “Does doubt arise when you’re uncertain whether or not this has come to be with that as fuel?”

mn38:10.5.verse: “Does doubt arise when you’re uncertain whether or not when that fuel ceases, what has come to be is liable to cease?”

mn38:11.1.verse: “Is doubt given up in someone who truly sees with right understanding that this has come to be?”

mn38:11.3.verse: “Is doubt given up in someone who truly sees with right understanding that this has come to be with that as fuel?”

mn38:11.5.verse: “Is doubt given up in someone who truly sees with right understanding that when that fuel ceases, what has come to be is liable to cease?”

mn38:12.1.verse: “Are you free of doubt as to whether this has come to be?”

mn38:12.3.verse: “Are you free of doubt as to whether this has come to be with that as fuel?”

mn38:12.5.verse: “Are you free of doubt as to whether when that fuel ceases, what has come to be is liable to cease?”

mn38:13.1.verse: “Have you truly seen clearly with right understanding that this has come to be?”

mn38:13.3.verse: “Have you truly seen clearly with right understanding that this has come to be with that as fuel?”

mn38:13.5.verse: “Have you truly seen clearly with right understanding that when that fuel ceases, what has come to be is liable to cease?”

mn38:14.1.verse: “Pure and bright as this view is, mendicants, if you cling to it, dally with it, treasure it, and treat it as your own, would you be understanding my simile of the teaching as a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on?”

mn38:14.3.verse: “Pure and bright as this view is, mendicants, if you don’t cling to it, dally with it, treasure it, and treat it as your own, would you be understanding my simile of the teaching as a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on?”

mn38:15.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four fuels maintain sentient beings that have been born and help those about to be born.

mn38:15.3.verse: Edible food, whether solid or subtle; contact is the second, mental intention the third, and consciousness the fourth.

mn38:16.1.verse: What is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of these four fuels?

mn38:16.3.verse: And what is the source of craving?

mn38:16.5.verse: And what is the source of feeling?

mn38:16.7.verse: And what is the source of contact?

mn38:16.9.verse: And what is the source of the six sense fields?

mn38:16.11.verse: And what is the source of name and form?

mn38:16.13.verse: And what is the source of consciousness?

mn38:16.15.verse: And what is the source of choices?

mn38:17.1.verse: So, ignorance is a requirement for choices.

mn38:17.2.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

mn38:17.3.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

mn38:17.4.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

mn38:17.5.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

mn38:17.6.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

mn38:17.7.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

mn38:17.8.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

mn38:17.9.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

mn38:17.10.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

mn38:17.11.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn38:17.12.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

mn38:18.1.verse: ‘Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death.’ That’s what I said.

mn38:18.2.verse: Is that how you see this or not?”

mn38:18.6.verse: “‘Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.’ …

mn38:18.50.verse: ‘Ignorance is a requirement for choices.’ That’s what I said.

mn38:18.51.verse: Is that how you see this or not?”

mn38:19.2.verse: So both you and I say this.

mn38:19.3.verse: When this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises. That is:

mn38:19.4.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

mn38:19.5.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness.

mn38:19.6.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

mn38:19.7.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

mn38:19.8.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

mn38:19.9.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

mn38:19.10.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

mn38:19.11.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

mn38:19.12.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

mn38:19.13.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

mn38:19.14.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn38:19.15.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

mn38:20.1.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease.

mn38:20.3.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

mn38:20.4.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

mn38:20.5.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

mn38:20.9.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

mn38:20.10.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

mn38:20.11.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn38:20.12.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

mn38:21.1.verse: ‘When rebirth ceases, old age and death cease.’ That’s what I said.

mn38:21.2.verse: Is that how you see this or not?”

mn38:21.51.verse: ‘When ignorance ceases, choices cease.’ That’s what I said.

mn38:21.52.verse: Is that how you see this or not?”

mn38:22.2.verse: So both you and I say this.

mn38:22.3.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

mn38:22.6.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

mn38:22.7.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

mn38:22.8.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

mn38:22.12.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

mn38:22.13.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

mn38:22.14.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn38:22.15.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

mn38:23.1.verse: Knowing and seeing in this way, mendicants, would you turn back to the first beginning, thinking,

mn38:23.2.verse: ‘Did we exist in the past? Did we not exist in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? After being what, what did we become in the past?’?”

mn38:23.4.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, mendicants, would you turn forward to the final end, thinking,

mn38:23.5.verse: ‘Will we exist in the future? Will we not exist in the future? What will we be in the future? How will we be in the future? After being what, what will we become in the future?’?”

mn38:24.1.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, mendicants, would you be undecided about the present, thinking,

mn38:24.2.verse: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This sentient being—where did it come from? And where will it go?’?”

mn38:24.4.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, would you say,

mn38:24.5.verse: ‘Our teacher is respected. We speak like this out of esteem for our teacher’?”

mn38:24.7.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, would you say,

mn38:24.8.verse: ‘Our ascetic says this. We speak like this because it is what he says’?”

mn38:24.10.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, would you dedicate yourself to another teacher?”

mn38:24.12.verse: “Knowing and seeing in this way, would you believe that the observances and boisterous, superstitious rites of the various ascetics and brahmins are essential?”

mn38:24.14.verse: “Aren’t you speaking only of what you have known and seen and realized for yourselves?”

mn38:25.1.verse: “Good, mendicants! You have been guided by me with this teaching that’s apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

mn38:25.2.verse: For when I said that this teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves,

mn38:25.3.verse: this is what I was referring to.

mn38:26.1.verse: Mendicants, when three things come together an embryo is conceived.

mn38:26.2.verse: In a case where the mother and father come together, but the mother is not in the fertile phase of her menstrual cycle, and the virile spirit is not ready, the embryo is not conceived.

mn38:26.3.verse: In a case where the mother and father come together, the mother is in the fertile phase of her menstrual cycle, but the virile spirit is not ready, the embryo is not conceived.

mn38:26.4.verse: But when these three things come together—the mother and father come together, the mother is in the fertile phase of her menstrual cycle, and the virile spirit is ready—an embryo is conceived.

mn38:27.1.verse: The mother nurtures the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months at great risk to her heavy burden.

mn38:27.2.verse: When nine or ten months have passed, the mother gives birth at great risk to her heavy burden.

mn38:27.3.verse: When the infant is born she nourishes it with her own blood.

mn38:27.4.verse: For mother’s milk is regarded as blood in the training of the Noble One.

mn38:28.1.verse: That boy grows up and his faculties mature.

mn38:28.2.verse: He accordingly plays childish games such as toy plows, tipcat, somersaults, pinwheels, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows.

mn38:29.1.verse: That boy grows up and his faculties mature further.

mn38:29.2.verse: He accordingly amuses himself, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn38:29.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn38:29.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
