mn38:30.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, if it’s pleasant they desire it, but if it’s unpleasant they dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body unestablished and their heart stunted.

mn38:30.2.verse: And they don’t truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

mn38:30.3.verse: Being so full of favoring and opposing, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—they approve, welcome, and keep clinging to it.

mn38:30.5.verse: Relishing feelings is grasping. Their grasping is a requirement for continued existence. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn38:30.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

mn38:30.7.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn38:30.8.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn38:30.9.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn38:30.10.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn38:30.11.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, if it’s pleasant they desire it, but if it’s unpleasant they dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body unestablished and their heart stunted.

mn38:30.12.verse: And they don’t truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

mn38:30.13.verse: Being so full of favoring and opposing, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—they approve, welcome, and keep clinging to it.

mn38:30.15.verse: Relishing feelings is grasping. Their grasping is a requirement for continued existence. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn38:30.16.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

mn38:31.1.verse: But consider when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn38:31.2.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn38:31.3.verse: He proclaims a teaching that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased.

mn38:31.4.verse: He reveals an entirely full and pure spiritual life.

mn38:32.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

mn38:32.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One

mn38:32.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn38:32.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn38:32.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from lay life to homelessness?’

mn38:32.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn38:33.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn38:33.2.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

mn38:33.3.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn38:33.4.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

mn38:33.5.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn38:33.6.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn38:33.7.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn38:33.8.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

mn38:33.9.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

mn38:33.10.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn38:33.11.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn38:33.12.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

mn38:33.13.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

mn38:33.22.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

mn38:33.26.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn38:34.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn38:34.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn38:34.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn38:34.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

mn38:35.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn38:35.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn38:35.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn38:35.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn38:35.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn38:35.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn38:35.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn38:35.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn38:35.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

mn38:36.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn38:37.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn38:37.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn38:38.1.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn38:38.2.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn38:38.3.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn38:38.4.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn38:38.5.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn38:38.6.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn38:39.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn38:39.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn38:39.3.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn38:40.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, if it’s pleasant they don’t desire it, and if it’s unpleasant they don’t dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body established and a limitless heart.

mn38:40.2.verse: And they truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

mn38:40.3.verse: Having given up favoring and opposing, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—they don’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging to it.

mn38:40.4.verse: As a result, relishing of feelings ceases.

mn38:40.5.verse: When their relishing ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn38:40.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

mn38:41.1.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn38:41.2.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn38:41.3.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn38:41.4.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn38:41.5.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, if it’s pleasant they don’t desire it, and if it’s unpleasant they don’t dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body established and a limitless heart.

mn38:41.6.verse: And they truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

mn38:41.7.verse: Having given up favoring and opposing, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—they don’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging to it.

mn38:41.8.verse: As a result, relishing of feelings ceases.

mn38:41.9.verse: When their relishing ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn38:41.10.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

mn38:41.11.verse: Mendicants, you should memorize this brief statement on freedom through the ending of craving. But the mendicant Sāti, the fisherman’s son, is caught in a vast net of craving, a tangle of craving.”

mn38:41.12.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn38:41.13.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn39:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Angan country. There is a town of the Angans called Assapura.

mn39:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn39:2.1.verse: ‘“Monks, Monks”, bhikkhus, that is how people perceive you.

mn39:2.2.verse: And when you are asked “What are you?”, you claim that you are monks.

mn39:2.3.verse: Since that is how you are reputed and how you claim, you should train thus: “We shall try to live up to such dhammas as constitute the Monk and as constitute the Divine, so that our reputations may be true and our claims represent what actually is,

mn39:2.4.verse: and so that the acts of those whose robes, alms-food, resting-place and requisite of medicine as cure for the sick we use will furnish them great fruit and benefit in us, and so that our going forth shall not be in vain but fruitful and fertile.”

mn39:2.5.verse: That is how you should train.

mn39:3.1.verse: ‘What dhammas constitute the Monk and constitute the Divine?

mn39:3.2.verse: You should train thus: “We shall be possessed of conscience and shame.”

mn39:3.3.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:3.4.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monk’s goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:3.5.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:3.6.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:4.2.verse: You should train thus: “Our bodily conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,

mn39:4.3.verse: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified bodily conduct.”

mn39:4.4.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:4.5.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct:

mn39:4.6.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:4.7.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:4.8.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:5.2.verse: You should train thus: “Our verbal conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,

mn39:5.3.verse: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified verbal conduct.”

mn39:5.4.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:5.5.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct and verbal conduct:

mn39:5.6.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:5.7.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:5.8.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:6.2.verse: You should train thus: “Our mental conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,

mn39:6.3.verse: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified mental conduct.”

mn39:6.4.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:6.5.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct:

mn39:6.6.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:6.7.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:6.8.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:7.2.verse: You should train thus: “Our livelihood will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,

mn39:7.3.verse: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified livelihood.”

mn39:7.4.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:7.5.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct, mental conduct and livelihood:

mn39:7.6.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:7.7.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:7.8.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:8.2.verse: You should train thus: “We shall keep the doors of the faculties guarded.

mn39:8.3.verse: On seeing a form with the eye, we shall apprehend no signs and features

mn39:8.4.verse: through which, if we leave the eye-door unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade us; we shall practise the way of its restraint, we shall guard the eye-faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye-faculty.

mn39:8.5.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn39:8.6.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn39:8.7.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn39:8.8.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn39:8.9.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, we shall apprehend no signs and features

mn39:8.10.verse: which, if we leave the mind-door unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade us; we shall practise the way of its restraint, we shall guard the mind-faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind-faculty.”

mn39:8.11.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:8.12.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct, and we are guarded in the doors of our faculties:

mn39:8.13.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:8.14.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:8.15.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:9.2.verse: You should train thus: “We shall know the right amount in eating.

mn39:9.3.verse: Reflecting wisely, we shall nourish ourselves with nutriment neither for amusement nor for intoxication (of vanity) nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the life divine, (considering:) ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and blameless shall live in comfort and health.’”

mn39:9.4.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:9.5.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, and we know the right amount in eating:

mn39:9.6.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:9.7.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:9.8.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:10.2.verse: You should train thus: “We shall be devoted to wakefulness. By day while walking and sitting[^1] we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.

mn39:10.3.verse: In the first watch of the night while walking and sitting we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.

mn39:10.4.verse: In the middle watch of the night we shall lie down on the right side in the lion’s sleeping pose with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, after noting in our mind the time of rising.

mn39:10.5.verse: After rising, in the third watch while walking and sitting we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.”

mn39:10.6.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:10.7.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, we know the right amount in eating, and we are devoted to wakefulness:

mn39:10.8.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:10.9.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:10.10.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:11.2.verse: You should train thus: “We shall be possessed of mindfulness and full awareness. We shall act in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward; we shall act in full awareness when looking towards and looking away; we shall act in full awareness when flexing and extending; we shall act in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes; we shall act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; we shall act in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water; we shall act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.”

mn39:11.3.verse: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:

mn39:11.4.verse: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily, verbal and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, we know the right amount in eating, we are devoted to wakefulness, and we are possessed of mindfulness and full awareness:

mn39:11.5.verse: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.

mn39:11.6.verse: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:

mn39:11.7.verse: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.

mn39:12.2.verse: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu resorts to a secluded resting-place: to the forest, to the root of a tree, a rock, a hill-cleft, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, or a heap of straw.

mn39:13.1.verse: On returning from his alms-round after his meal, he sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him.

mn39:13.2.verse: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with his mind free from covetousness, he purifies his mind of covetousness.

mn39:13.3.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with his mind free from ill-will; with pity for all creatures and beings, he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred.

mn39:13.4.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness.

mn39:13.5.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind calmed in himself, he purifies his mind of agitation and worry.

mn39:13.6.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with uncertainty crossed over, undoubting about profitable dhammas, he purifies his mind of uncertainty.

mn39:14.1.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man borrowed a loan and undertook works,

mn39:14.3.verse: so that he repaid all the money of the old loan, and there remained over some extra for his wife and children.

mn39:14.4.verse: Then it would occur to him:

mn39:14.5.verse: ‘Formerly I borrowed a loan and undertook works, and my works succeeded.

mn39:14.6.verse: I have repaid all the money of the old loan, and there remains over some extra for my wife and children.’

mn39:14.7.verse: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.

mn39:14.8.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, and his food did not sustain him and his body had no strength,

mn39:14.9.verse: but later he recovered from the affliction and his food sustained him and his body regained strength.

mn39:14.10.verse: Then it would occur to him:

mn39:14.11.verse: ‘Formerly I was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, and my food did not sustain me and my body had no strength; but now I have recovered from that affliction, my food sustains me, and my body has strength.’

mn39:14.12.verse: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.

mn39:14.13.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were imprisoned in a prison-house,

mn39:14.14.verse: but later he was released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss to his property.

mn39:14.15.verse: Then it would occur to him:

mn39:14.16.verse: ‘Formerly I was imprisoned in a prison-house; but now I am released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss to my property.’

mn39:14.17.verse: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.

mn39:14.18.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were a bondsman, not self-dependent but dependent on others and unable to go where he wanted,

mn39:14.19.verse: but later on he was released from that bondage, self-dependent, independent of others and a freed man able to go where he wanted.

mn39:14.20.verse: Then it would occur to him:

mn39:14.21.verse: ‘Formerly I was a bondsman, not self-dependent but dependent on others and unable to go where I wanted; but now I am released from that bondage, self-dependent, independent of others and a freed man able to go where I want.’

mn39:14.22.verse: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.

mn39:14.23.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man with property and goods entered on a road across a desert,

mn39:14.24.verse: but later on he crossed over the desert, safe and sound, with no loss to his property.

mn39:14.25.verse: Then it would occur to him:

mn39:14.26.verse: ‘Formerly, with property and goods, I entered on a road across a desert.

mn39:14.27.verse: But now I have crossed over that desert, safe and sound, with no loss to my property.’

mn39:14.28.verse: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.

mn39:14.29.verse: So too, bhikkhus, when these five hindrances are unabandoned in himself, a bhikkhu sees them respectively as a debt, a disease, a prison-house, a bondage, and a road across a desert.

mn39:14.30.verse: And when these five hindrances are abandoned in himself, he sees that as unindebtedness, healthiness, release from prison, freedom from bondage, and a land of safety.

mn39:15.1.verse: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn39:15.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn39:15.3.verse: He makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.

mn39:15.4.verse: Just as a skilled bath man or bath man’s apprentice heaps bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, kneads it up till the moisture wets his ball of bath powder, soaks it, and extends over it within and without, though it does not itself become liquid;

mn39:15.5.verse: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill, and extend throughout this whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.

mn39:16.1.verse: Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn39:16.2.verse: He makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.

mn39:16.3.verse: Just as though there were a lake whose waters welled up from below, having no inflow from east, west, north or south, nor yet replenished from time to time by the skies with showers, then the cool fount of water welling up in the lake would make the cool water drench, steep, fill and extend throughout the lake, and there would be nothing of the whole lake to which the cool water did not extend;

mn39:16.4.verse: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.

mn39:17.1.verse: Again, with the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn39:17.2.verse: He makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.

mn39:17.3.verse: Just as, in a water-lily pond or a white lotus pond or a red lotus pond, some water-lilies or white lotuses or red lotuses are born under the water, grow under the water, do not stand up out of the water, flourish immersed under the water, and cool water drenches, fills and extends throughout them, to their tips and to their roots, and there is nothing of the whole of those water-lilies, those white lotuses, those red lotuses, to which the cool water does not extend;

mn39:17.4.verse: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.

mn39:18.1.verse: Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn39:18.2.verse: He sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.

mn39:18.3.verse: Just as though a man were sitting clothed from head to foot in white cloth, and there were nothing of his whole body to which the white cloth did not extend;

mn39:18.4.verse: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.

mn39:19.1.verse: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines mind to knowledge of recollection of past life.

mn39:19.2.verse: He recollects his manifold past life … (as in Sutta 4, para. 27) … Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.

mn39:19.3.verse: Just as though a man went from his own village to another village, and then he went from that village to another village and then he went back again to his own village, and he thought: ‘I went from my own village to that village, and there such was the way I sat, such the way I spoke, such the way I was silent; and from that village I went to that other village, and there such was the way I stood, such the way I sat, such the way I spoke, such the way I was silent; and from that village I came back again to my own village’;

mn39:19.4.verse: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past life … Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.

mn39:20.1.verse: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines, mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn39:20.2.verse: With the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing … (as in Sutta 4, para. 28) …

mn39:20.3.verse: Just as though there were two houses with doors and a man with good eyes standing there in between saw men entering the house and coming out and going to and fro;

mn39:20.4.verse: so too, with heavenly eyesight … He understands how beings pass on according to their kammas.

mn39:21.1.verse: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines, mind to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn39:21.2.verse: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’

mn39:21.3.verse: He understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’

mn39:21.4.verse: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance.

mn39:21.5.verse: When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn39:21.6.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn39:21.7.verse: Just as if there were a lake in a mountain recess, clear, limpid and unturbid,

mn39:21.8.verse: so that a man with good eyes standing up there on the bank, saw shells, gravel and pebbles, and also shoals of fish swimming about and resting,

mn39:21.10.verse: ‘There is this lake, clear, limpid and unturbid, and there are these shells, gravel and pebbles, and also these shoals of fish swimming about and resting’;

mn39:21.11.verse: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands, as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’ …

mn39:21.12.verse: he understands: ‘there is no more of this to come.’

mn39:22.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, it is one such as this who is called a “Monk”, who is called a “Divine”, who is called “Washed”, who is called “Attained to Knowledge”, who is called “In the Stream”, who is called “Noble”, who is called “Arahant”.

mn39:23.1.verse: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a “Monk”?

mn39:23.2.verse: He has quieted (samita) evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.

mn39:23.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is a “Monk”.

mn39:24.1.verse: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a “Divine”?

mn39:24.2.verse: He has divided himself (bāhita) from evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.

mn39:24.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is a “Divine”.

mn39:25.2.verse: He has washed off evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.

mn39:25.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is “Washed”.

mn39:26.1.verse: ‘And how is a bhikkhu “Attained to Knowledge”?[^3]

mn39:26.2.verse: He has known evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.

mn39:26.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is “Attained to Knowledge”.

mn39:27.1.verse: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu “In the Stream”?

mn39:27.2.verse: He has let the evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, stream away (nissuta) from him.

mn39:27.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is “In the Stream”.

mn39:28.2.verse: Evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, are far (āraka) from him.

mn39:28.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is “Noble”.

mn39:29.2.verse: Evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, are far from him.

mn39:29.3.verse: That is how a bhikkhu is “Arahant”.’

mn39:29.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn39:29.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn39:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Aṅgas, near the Aṅgan town named Assapura.

mn39:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn39:2.2.verse: And when they ask you what you are, you claim to be ascetics.

mn39:2.3.verse: Given this label and this claim, you should train like this: ‘We will proceed having undertaken the things that make one an ascetic and a brahmin. That way our label will be accurate and our claim correct.

mn39:2.4.verse: The services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick we enjoy shall be very fruitful and beneficial for them. And our going forth will not be barren, but will be fruitful and fertile.’

mn39:3.1.verse: And what are the things that make one an ascetic and a brahmin?

mn39:3.2.verse: You should train like this: ‘We will have conscience and prudence.’

mn39:3.4.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence. This is sufficient; enough has been done. We have achieved the goal of life as an ascetic. There is nothing more to do.’ And you might rest content with just that much.

mn39:3.5.verse: I declare this to you, mendicants, I announce this to you:

mn39:3.6.verse: ‘You who seek to be true ascetics, do not lose sight of the goal of the ascetic life while there is still more to do.’

mn39:4.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:4.2.verse: You should train like this: ‘Our bodily behavior will be pure, clear, open, neither inconsistent nor secretive.

mn39:4.3.verse: And we won’t glorify ourselves or put others down on account of our pure bodily behavior.’

mn39:4.5.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, and our bodily behavior is pure.

mn39:4.7.verse: I declare this to you, mendicants, I announce this to you:

mn39:4.8.verse: ‘You who seek to be true ascetics, do not lose sight of the goal of the ascetic life while there is still more to do.’

mn39:5.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:5.2.verse: You should train like this: ‘Our verbal behavior …

mn39:7.2.verse: livelihood will be pure, clear, open, neither inconsistent nor secretive.

mn39:7.3.verse: And we won’t glorify ourselves or put others down on account of our pure livelihood.’

mn39:7.5.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, our bodily, verbal, and mental behavior is pure, and our livelihood is pure.

mn39:7.6.verse: This is sufficient; enough has been done. We have achieved the goal of life as an ascetic. There is nothing more to do.’ And you might rest content with just that much.

mn39:7.7.verse: I declare this to you, mendicants, I announce this to you:

mn39:7.8.verse: ‘You who seek to be true ascetics, do not lose sight of the goal of the ascetic life while there is still more to do.’

mn39:8.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:8.2.verse: You should train yourselves like this: ‘We will restrain our sense doors.

mn39:8.3.verse: When we see a sight with our eyes, we won’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn39:8.4.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, we will practice restraint, we will protect the faculty of sight, and we will achieve its restraint.

mn39:8.5.verse: When we hear a sound with our ears …

mn39:8.6.verse: When we smell an odor with our nose …

mn39:8.7.verse: When we taste a flavor with our tongue …

mn39:8.8.verse: When we feel a touch with our body …

mn39:8.9.verse: When we know an idea with our mind, we won’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn39:8.10.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, we will practice restraint, we will protect the faculty of mind, and we will achieve its restraint.’

mn39:8.12.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, our bodily, verbal, and mental behavior is pure, our livelihood is pure, and our sense doors are restrained.

mn39:9.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:9.2.verse: You should train yourselves like this: ‘We will not eat too much. We will only eat after reflecting rationally on our food.

mn39:9.3.verse: We will eat not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, we shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and we will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

mn39:9.5.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, our bodily, verbal, and mental behavior is pure, our livelihood is pure, our sense doors are restrained, and we don’t eat too much.

mn39:10.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:10.2.verse: You should train yourselves like this: ‘We will be dedicated to wakefulness. When practicing walking and sitting meditation by day, we will purify our mind from obstacles.

mn39:10.3.verse: In the first watch of the night, we will continue to practice walking and sitting meditation.

mn39:10.4.verse: In the middle watch, we will lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

mn39:10.5.verse: In the last watch, we will get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying our mind from obstacles.’

mn39:10.7.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, our bodily, verbal, and mental behavior is pure, our livelihood is pure, our sense doors are restrained, we don’t eat too much, and we are dedicated to wakefulness.

mn39:11.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:11.2.verse: You should train yourselves like this: ‘We will have mindfulness and situational awareness. We will act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.’

mn39:11.4.verse: ‘We have conscience and prudence, our bodily, verbal, and mental behavior is pure, our livelihood is pure, our sense doors are restrained, we don’t eat too much, we are dedicated to wakefulness, and we have mindfulness and situational awareness.

mn39:12.1.verse: What more is there to do?

mn39:12.2.verse: Take a mendicant who frequents a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn39:13.1.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn39:13.2.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn39:13.3.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn39:13.4.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn39:13.5.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn39:13.6.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn39:14.1.verse: Suppose a man who has gotten into debt were to apply himself to work,

mn39:14.3.verse: He would pay off the original loan and have enough left over to support his partner.

mn39:14.7.verse: he’d be filled with joy and happiness.

mn39:14.8.verse: Suppose a person was sick, suffering, gravely ill. They’d lose their appetite and get physically weak.

mn39:14.9.verse: But after some time they’d recover from that illness, and regain their appetite and their strength.

mn39:14.12.verse: they’d be filled with joy and happiness.

mn39:14.13.verse: Suppose a person was imprisoned in a jail.

mn39:14.14.verse: But after some time they were released from jail, safe and sound, with no loss of wealth.

mn39:14.17.verse: they’d be filled with joy and happiness.

mn39:14.18.verse: Suppose a person was a bondservant. They would not be their own master, but indentured to another, unable to go where they wish.

mn39:14.19.verse: But after some time they’d be freed from servitude. They would be their own master, not indentured to another, a freeman able to go where they wish.

mn39:14.22.verse: they’d be filled with joy and happiness.

mn39:14.23.verse: Suppose there was a person with wealth and property who was traveling along a desert road.

mn39:14.24.verse: But after some time they crossed over the desert, safe and sound, with no loss of wealth.

mn39:14.28.verse: they’d be filled with joy and happiness.

mn39:14.29.verse: In the same way, as long as these five hindrances are not given up inside themselves, a mendicant regards them as a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery, and a desert crossing.

mn39:14.30.verse: But when these five hindrances are given up inside themselves, a mendicant regards this as freedom from debt, good health, release from prison, emancipation, and a place of sanctuary at last.

mn39:15.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn39:15.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn39:15.3.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

mn39:15.4.verse: It’s like when a deft bathroom attendant or their apprentice pours bath powder into a bronze dish, sprinkling it little by little with water. They knead it until the ball of bath powder is soaked and saturated with moisture, spread through inside and out; yet no moisture oozes out.

mn39:15.5.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

mn39:16.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn39:16.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

mn39:16.3.verse: It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time. But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.

mn39:16.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

mn39:17.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn39:17.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

mn39:17.3.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water. There’s no part of them that’s not soaked with cool water.

mn39:17.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

mn39:18.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn39:18.2.verse: They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn39:18.3.verse: It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.

mn39:18.4.verse: In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn39:19.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn39:19.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn39:19.3.verse: Suppose a person was to leave their home village and go to another village. From that village they’d go to yet another village. And from that village they’d return to their home village. They’d think: ‘I went from my home village to another village. There I stood like this, sat like that, spoke like this, or kept silent like that. From that village I went to yet another village. There too I stood like this, sat like that, spoke like this, or kept silent like that. And from that village I returned to my home village.’

mn39:19.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant recollects their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn39:20.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn39:20.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn39:20.3.verse: Suppose there were two houses with doors. A person with clear eyes standing in between them would see humans entering and leaving a house and wandering to and fro.

mn39:20.4.verse: In the same way, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn39:21.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn39:21.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn39:21.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn39:21.4.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn39:21.5.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn39:21.6.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn39:21.7.verse: Suppose that in a mountain glen there was a lake that was transparent, clear, and unclouded. A person with clear eyes standing on the bank would see the clams and mussels, pebbles and gravel, and schools of fish swimming about or staying still.

mn39:21.10.verse: ‘This lake is transparent, clear, and unclouded. And here are the clams and mussels, pebbles and gravel, and schools of fish swimming about or staying still.’

mn39:21.11.verse: In the same way, a mendicant truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn39:21.12.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

mn39:22.1.verse: This mendicant is one who is called an ‘ascetic’, a ‘brahmin’, a ‘bathed initiate’, a ‘knowledge master’, a ‘scholar’, a ‘noble one’, and also a ‘perfected one’.

mn39:23.1.verse: And how is a mendicant an ascetic?

mn39:23.2.verse: They have assuaged the bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn39:23.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is an ascetic.

mn39:24.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a brahmin?

mn39:24.2.verse: They have banished the bad, unskillful qualities.

mn39:24.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a brahmin.

mn39:25.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a bathed initiate?

mn39:25.2.verse: They have bathed off the bad, unskillful qualities.

mn39:25.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a bathed initiate.

mn39:26.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a knowledge master?

mn39:26.2.verse: They have known the bad, unskillful qualities.

mn39:26.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a knowledge master.

mn39:27.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a scholar?

mn39:27.2.verse: They have scoured off the bad, unskillful qualities.

mn39:27.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a scholar.

mn39:28.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a noble one?

mn39:28.2.verse: They have nobbled their foes, the bad, unskillful qualities.

mn39:28.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a noble one.

mn39:29.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a perfected one?

mn39:29.2.verse: They are impeccably remote from the bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn39:29.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a perfected one.”

mn39:29.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn39:29.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn40:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Aṅgas. Now, the Aṅgas have a town named Assapura.

mn40:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the monks,

mn40:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn40:2.1.verse: “‘Contemplatives, contemplatives’: That is how people perceive you.

mn40:2.2.verse: And when asked, ‘What are you?’ you claim that ‘We are contemplatives.’

mn40:2.3.verse: So, with this being your designation and this your claim, this is how you should train yourselves:

mn40:2.4.verse: ‘We will practice the practice proper to a contemplative,

mn40:2.5.verse: so that our designation will be true and our claim accurate;

mn40:2.6.verse: so that the services of those whose robes, alms-food, lodging, & medicinal requisites we use will bring them great fruit & great reward; and so that our going forth will not be barren, but fruitful & fertile.’

mn40:3.1.verse: “And how, monks, does a monk not practice the practice proper to a contemplative?

mn40:3.2.verse: When the possessiveness of a possessive monk has not been abandoned; when the ill will of an ill-will-minded one has not been abandoned; when the anger of an angry one has not been abandoned; when the spitefulness of a spiteful one has not been abandoned; when the dismissiveness of a dismissive one has not been abandoned; when the antagonism of an antagonistic one has not been abandoned; when the envy of an envious one has not been abandoned; when the selfishness of a selfish one has not been abandoned; when the deceit of a deceitful one has not been abandoned; when the pretentiousness of a pretentious one has not been abandoned; when the evil wishes of one with evil wishes have not been abandoned; when the wrong view of one of wrong view has not been abandoned—

mn40:3.3.verse: when these stains of a contemplative, these flaws in a contemplative, these defects in a contemplative that are grounds for rebirth in a state of deprivation and are to be experienced in a bad destination have not been abandoned, then, I tell you, one is not practicing the practice proper to a contemplative.

mn40:4.1.verse: Just as if a weapon called a mataja, well sharpened on both edges,

mn40:4.2.verse: were wrapped & enclosed in patchwork sheath:

mn40:4.3.verse: The going forth of such a monk, I tell you, is similar to that.

mn40:5.1.verse: “Monks, I don’t say that a patchwork-robe-wearer’s status as a contemplative is through merely wearing a patchwork robe.

mn40:5.2.verse: I don’t say that a clothless ascetic’s status as a contemplative is through merely being without cloth.

mn40:5.3.verse: I don’t say that a dust-&-dirt-caked ascetic’s status as a contemplative is through merely being caked with dust & dirt.

mn40:5.4.verse: I don’t say that a ritual bather’s status as a contemplative is through merely taking ritual baths.

mn40:5.5.verse: I don’t say that a tree-root dweller’s status as a contemplative is through merely dwelling at the root of a tree.

mn40:5.6.verse: I don’t say that an open-air dweller’s status as a contemplative is through merely dwelling in the open air.

mn40:5.7.verse: I don’t say that a stander’s status as a contemplative is through merely standing continually.

mn40:5.8.verse: I don’t say that a regulated-eater’s status as a contemplative is through merely regulating his meals.

mn40:5.9.verse: I don’t say that an incantation reciter’s status as a contemplative is through merely reciting incantations.

mn40:5.10.verse: I don’t say that a dreadlock ascetic’s status as a contemplative is through merely wearing dreadlocks.

mn40:6.1.verse: “If through merely wearing a patchwork robe a possessive individual would abandon possessiveness, an ill-will-minded one would abandon ill will… an individual with wrong view would abandon wrong view, then his friends & companions, his kinsmen & relatives would make him a patchwork-robe-wearer right from birth. They would get him to undertake the practice of simply wearing a patchwork robe, (saying,)

mn40:6.2.verse: ‘Come, you of the auspicious face: Be a patchwork-robe-wearer. Being a patchwork-robe-wearer, when you are possessive, your possessiveness will be abandoned; when you are ill-will-minded, your ill will will be abandoned… when you have wrong view, your wrong view will be abandoned.’

mn40:6.3.verse: But because there is the case where I see a patchwork-robe-wearer who is possessive, ill-will-minded, angry, spiteful, dismissive, antagonistic, envious, selfish, pretentious—one of evil wishes & wrong view, that’s why I don’t say that a patchwork-robe-wearer’s status as a contemplative is through merely wearing a patchwork robe.

mn40:6.5.verse: If through merely being caked with dust & dirt…

mn40:6.6.verse: If through merely taking ritual baths…

mn40:6.7.verse: If through merely dwelling at the root of a tree…

mn40:6.8.verse: If through merely dwelling in the open air…

mn40:6.10.verse: If through merely regulating one’s meals…

mn40:6.12.verse: “If through merely wearing dreadlocks a possessive individual would abandon possessiveness, an ill-will-minded one would abandon ill will… an individual with wrong view would abandon wrong view, then his friends & companions, his kinsmen & relatives would make him a dreadlock ascetic right from birth. They would get him to undertake the practice of simply wearing dreadlocks, (saying,)

mn40:6.13.verse: ‘Come, you of the auspicious face: Be a dreadlock ascetic. Being a dreadlock ascetic, when you are possessive, your possessiveness will be abandoned; when you are ill-will-minded, your ill will will be abandoned… when you have wrong view, your wrong view will be abandoned.’

mn40:6.14.verse: But because there is the case where I see a dreadlock ascetic who is possessive, ill-will-minded, angry, spiteful, dismissive, antagonistic, envious, selfish, pretentious—one of evil wishes & wrong view, that’s why I don’t say that a dreadlock ascetic’s status as a contemplative is through merely wearing dreadlocks.

mn40:7.1.verse: “And how, monks, does a monk practice the practice proper to a contemplative?

mn40:7.2.verse: When the possessiveness of a possessive monk has been abandoned; when the ill will of an ill-will-minded one has been abandoned; when the anger of an angry one has been abandoned; when the spitefulness of a spiteful one has been abandoned; when the dismissiveness of a dismissive one has been abandoned; when the antagonism of an antagonistic one has been abandoned; when the envy of an envious one has been abandoned; when the selfishness of a selfish one has been abandoned; when the deceit of a deceitful one has been abandoned; when the pretentiousness of a pretentious one has been abandoned; when the evil wishes of one with evil wishes have been abandoned; when the wrong view of one of wrong view has been abandoned—

mn40:7.3.verse: when these stains of a contemplative, these flaws in a contemplative, these defects in a contemplative that are grounds for rebirth in a state of deprivation and are to be experienced in a bad destination have been abandoned, then, I tell you, one is practicing the practice proper to a contemplative.

mn40:8.1.verse: “He sees himself purified of all these evil, unskillful qualities; he sees himself released from them.

mn40:8.2.verse: As he sees himself purified of all these evil, unskillful qualities, as he sees himself released from them, joy is born. When he is joyful, rapture is born. In one who is enraptured at heart, the body grows calm. When the body is calm, one feels pleasure. Feeling pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated.

mn40:9.1.verse: “He keeps pervading the first direction [the east] with an awareness imbued with goodwill, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with goodwill—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

mn40:10-12.1.verse: He keeps pervading the first direction with an awareness imbued with compassion…

mn40:10-12.3.verse: equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with equanimity—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

mn40:13.1.verse: “Suppose that there were a lotus pond with pristine water, pleasing water, cool water, pellucid water.

mn40:13.2.verse: If a man were to come from the east—scorched with heat, overcome by heat, exhausted, trembling, & thirsty—

mn40:13.3.verse: on coming to that lotus pond he would subdue his thirst for water, he would subdue his heat-induced fever. If a man were to come from the west… If a man were to come from the north… If a man were to come from the south… If a man were to come from anywhere at all—scorched with heat, overcome by heat, exhausted, trembling, & thirsty—on coming to that lotus pond he would subdue his thirst for water, he would subdue his heat-induced fever.

mn40:13.4.verse: “In the same way, if a person from a noble-warrior family goes forth from the home life into homelessness and, on coming to this Dhamma & Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and thus developing goodwill, compassion, empathetic joy, & equanimity, he gains stilling within, then he, I tell you, is practicing the practice proper to a contemplative. If a person from a brahman family goes forth… If a person from a merchant family goes forth… If a person from a worker family goes forth… If a person from any family at all goes forth from the home life into homelessness and, on coming to this Dhamma & Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and thus developing goodwill, compassion, empathetic joy, & equanimity, he gains stilling within,

mn40:13.5.verse: then he, I tell you, is practicing the practice proper to a contemplative.

mn40:14.1.verse: “If a person from a noble-warrior family goes forth

mn40:14.2.verse: and—through the ending of the effluents—enters & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now,

mn40:14.3.verse: then he, I tell you, is a contemplative through the ending of the effluents. If a person from a brahman family goes forth… If a person from a merchant family goes forth… If a person from a worker family goes forth… If a person from any family at all goes forth and—through the ending of the effluents—enters & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now, then he, I tell you, is a contemplative through the ending of the effluents.”

mn40:14.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn40:14.5.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn40:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Aṅgas, near the Aṅgan town named Assapura.

mn40:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn40:2.2.verse: And when they ask you what you are, you claim to be ascetics.

mn40:2.3.verse: Given this label and this claim, you should train like this: ‘We will practice in the way that is proper for an ascetic. That way our label will be accurate and our claim correct.

mn40:2.6.verse: The services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick we enjoy shall be very fruitful and beneficial for them. And our going forth will not be barren, but will be fruitful and fertile.’

mn40:3.1.verse: And how does a mendicant not practice in the way that is proper for an ascetic?

mn40:3.2.verse: Any mendicant who has not given up covetousness, ill will, irritability, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view

mn40:3.3.verse: is not practicing in the way that is proper for an ascetic, I say. And that is due to not giving up these stains, defects, and dregs of an ascetic, these grounds for rebirth in places of loss, to be experienced in bad places.

mn40:4.1.verse: I say that such a mendicant’s going forth may be compared to the kind of weapon called ‘deadborn’—double-edged, whetted with yellow arsenic—that has been covered and wrapped in an outer robe.

mn40:5.1.verse: I say that you don’t deserve the label ‘outer robe wearer’ just because you wear an outer robe.

mn40:5.2.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘naked ascetic’ just because you go naked.

mn40:5.3.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘dust and dirt wearer’ just because you’re caked in dust and dirt.

mn40:5.4.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘water immerser’ just because you immerse yourself in water.

mn40:5.5.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘tree root dweller’ just because you stay at the root of a tree.

mn40:5.6.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘open air dweller’ just because you stay in the open air.

mn40:5.7.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘stander’ just because you continually stand.

mn40:5.8.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘interval eater’ just because you eat food at set intervals.

mn40:5.9.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘reciter’ just because you recite hymns.

mn40:5.10.verse: You don’t deserve the label ‘matted-hair ascetic’ just because you have matted hair.

mn40:6.1.verse: Imagine that just by wearing an outer robe someone with covetousness, ill will, irritability, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view could give up these things. If that were the case, your friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would make you an outer robe wearer as soon as you were born. They’d encourage you:

mn40:6.2.verse: ‘Please, dearest, wear an outer robe! By doing so you will give up covetousness, ill will, irritability, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view.’

mn40:6.3.verse: But sometimes I see someone with these bad qualities who is an outer robe wearer. That’s why I say that you don’t deserve the label ‘outer robe wearer’ just because you wear an outer robe.

mn40:6.4.verse: Imagine that just by going naked …

mn40:6.7.verse: staying at the root of a tree …

mn40:6.12.verse: having matted hair someone with covetousness, ill will, irritability, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view could give up these things. If that were the case, your friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would make you a matted-hair ascetic as soon as you were born. They’d encourage you:

mn40:6.13.verse: ‘Please, dearest, become a matted-hair ascetic! By doing so you will give up covetousness, ill will, irritability, hostility, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view.’

mn40:6.14.verse: But sometimes I see someone with these bad qualities who is a matted-hair ascetic. That’s why I say that you don’t deserve the label ‘matted-hair ascetic’ just because you have matted hair.

mn40:7.1.verse: And how does a mendicant practice in the way that is proper for an ascetic?

mn40:7.2.verse: Any mendicant who has given up covetousness, ill will, irritability, acrimony, disdain, contempt, jealousy, stinginess, deviousness, deceit, corrupt wishes, and wrong view

mn40:7.3.verse: is practicing in the way that is proper for an ascetic, I say. And that is due to giving up these stains, defects, and dregs of an ascetic, these grounds for rebirth in places of loss, to be experienced in bad places.

mn40:8.1.verse: They see themselves purified from all these bad, unskillful qualities.

mn40:8.2.verse: Seeing this, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, they feel bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn40:9.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn40:10-12.1.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn40:10-12.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn40:10-12.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn40:13.1.verse: Suppose there was a lotus pond with clear, sweet, cool water, clean, with smooth banks, delightful.

mn40:13.2.verse: Then along comes a person—whether from the east, west, north, or south—struggling in the oppressive heat, weary, thirsty, and parched.

mn40:13.3.verse: No matter what direction they come from, when they arrive at that lotus pond they would alleviate their thirst and heat exhaustion.

mn40:13.4.verse: In the same way, suppose someone has gone forth from the lay life to homelessness—whether from a family of aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, or menials—and has arrived at the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One. Having developed love, compassion, rejoicing, and equanimity in this way they find inner peace.

mn40:13.5.verse: Because of that inner peace they are practicing the way proper for an ascetic, I say.

mn40:14.1.verse: And suppose someone has gone forth from the lay life to homelessness—whether from a family of aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, or workers—

mn40:14.2.verse: and they realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn40:14.3.verse: They’re an ascetic because of the ending of defilements.”

mn40:14.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn40:14.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn41:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, and eventually he arrived at a Kosalan divine-caste village called Sālā.

mn41:2.1.verse: The divine-caste householders of Sālā heard:

mn41:2.2.verse: ‘A monk called Gotama, it seems, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, has been wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus and has come to Sālā.

mn41:2.3.verse: Now a good report of Master Gotama has been spread to this effect:

mn41:2.4.verse: “That Blessed One is such since he is Arahant and Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable teacher of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.

mn41:2.5.verse: He describes this world with its gods, its Māras, and its (Brahmā) Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, which he has himself realized through direct knowledge.

mn41:2.6.verse: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end with (the right) meaning and phrasing,

mn41:2.7.verse: he affirms a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.”

mn41:2.8.verse: Now it is good to see such Arahants.’

mn41:3.1.verse: The the divine-caste householders of Sālā went to the Blessed One, and some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with him, and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, sat down at one side: some raised their hands palms together in salutation to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some pronounced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence and sat down at one side; some kept silence and sat down at one side. When they were seated, they said to the Blessed One:

mn41:4.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, what is the reason, what is the condition, why some beings here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell;

mn41:4.2.verse: and what is the reason, what is the condition, why some beings here on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world?’

mn41:5.1.verse: ‘Householders, it is by reason of conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, by reason of unrighteous conduct, that beings here on the dis-solution of the body, after death, reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn41:5.2.verse: It is by reason of conduct in accordance with the Damma, by reason of righteous conduct, that some beings here on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.’

mn41:6.1.verse: ‘We do not understand the detailed meaning of this utterance of Master Gotama’s spoken in brief without expounding the detailed meaning.

mn41:6.2.verse: It would be good if Master Gotama taught us the Dhamma so that we might understand the detailed meaning of Master Gotama’s utterance spoken in brief without expounding the detailed meaning.’

mn41:6.3.verse: ‘Then, householders, listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn41:7.1.verse: ‘Householders, there are three kinds of bodily conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct. There are four kinds of verbal conduct not in accordance with the dhamma, unrighteous conduct. There are three kinds of mental conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct.

mn41:8.1.verse: ‘And how are there three kinds of bodily conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct?

mn41:8.2.verse: Here someone is a killer of living beings: he is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.

mn41:8.3.verse: He is a taker of what is not given: he takes as a thief another’s chattels and property in the village or in that forest.

mn41:8.4.verse: He is given over to misconduct in sexual desires: he has intercourse with such (women) as are protected by the mother, father, (mother and father), brother, sister, relatives, as have a husband, as entail a penalty, and also with those that are garlanded in token of betrothal.

mn41:8.5.verse: That is how there are three kinds of bodily conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct.

mn41:9.1.verse: ‘And how are there four kinds of verbal conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct?

mn41:9.2.verse: Here someone speaks falsehood: when summoned to a court or to a meeting, or to his relatives’ presence, or to his guild, or to the royal family’s presence, and questioned as a witness thus: “So, good man, tell what you know”, then, not knowing, he says “I know”, or knowing, he says “I do not know”; not seeing, he says “I see” or seeing, he says “I do not see”; in full awareness he speaks falsehood for his own ends or for another’s ends or for some trifling worldly end.

mn41:9.3.verse: He speaks maliciously; he is a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, or he is a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, and he is thus a divider of the united, a creator of divisions, who enjoys discord, rejoices in discord, he is a speaker of words that create discord.

mn41:9.4.verse: He speaks harshly: he utters such words as are rough, hard, hurtful to others, censorious of others, bordering on anger and unconducive to concentration.

mn41:9.5.verse: He is a gossip: as one who tells that which is unreasonable, that which is not, that which is not good, that which is not the Dhamma, that which is not the Discipline, and he speaks out of season, speech not worth recording, which is unreasoned, indefinite, and unconnected with good.

mn41:9.6.verse: That is how there are four kinds of verbal conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct.

mn41:10.1.verse: ‘And how are there kinds of mental conduct not in accordance with Dhamma, unrighteous conduct?
