mn41:10.2.verse: Here someone is covetous: he is a coveter of another’s chattels and property thus: “Oh, that what is another’s were mine!”

mn41:10.3.verse: Or he has a mind of ill-will, with the intention of a mind affected by hate thus: “May these beings be slain and slaughtered, may they be cut off, perish, or be annihilated!”

mn41:10.4.verse: Or he has wrong view, distorted vision, thus:

mn41:10.5.verse: “There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed, no fruit and ripening of good and bad kammas, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously (born) beings, no good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.”

mn41:10.6.verse: That is how there are three kinds of mental conduct not in accordance with the Dhamma, unrighteous conduct.

mn41:10.7.verse: So, householders, it is by reason of conduct not in accordance with Dhamma, by reason of unrighteous conduct, that some beings here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn41:11.1.verse: ‘Householders, there are three kinds of bodily conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct. There are four kinds of verbal conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct. There are three kinds of mental conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:12.1.verse: ‘And how are there three kinds of bodily conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct?

mn41:12.2.verse: Here someone, abandoning the killing of living beings, becomes one who abstains from killing living beings: with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all living beings.

mn41:12.3.verse: Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given: he does not take as a thief another’s chattels and property in the village or in the forest.

mn41:12.4.verse: Abandoning misconduct in sexual desires, he becomes one who abstains from misconduct in sexual desires: he does not have intercourse with such women as are protected by mother, father (mother and father), brother, sister, relatives, as have a husband, as entail a penalty, and also those that are garlanded in token of betrothal.

mn41:12.5.verse: That is how there are three kinds of bodily conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:13.1.verse: ‘And how are there four kinds of verbal conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct?

mn41:13.2.verse: Here someone, abandoning false speech, becomes one who abstains from false speech: when summoned to a court or to a meeting or to his relatives’ presence or to his guild or to the royal family’s presence, and questioned as a witness thus: “So, good man, tell what you know”, not knowing, he says “I do not know”, or knowing, he says “I know”, not seeing, he says “I do not see”, or seeing, he says “I see”; he does not in full awareness speak falsehood for his own ends or for another’s ends or for some trifling worldly end.

mn41:13.3.verse: Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to those of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.

mn41:13.4.verse: Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many and dear to many.

mn41:13.5.verse: Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells that which is seasonable, that which is factual, that which is good, that which is the Dhamma, that which is the Discipline, he speaks in season speech worth recording, which is reasoned, definite and connected with good.

mn41:13.6.verse: That is how there are four kinds of verbal conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:14.1.verse: ‘And how are there three kinds of mental conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct?

mn41:14.2.verse: Here someone is not covetous: he is not a coveter of another’s chattels and property thus: “Oh, that what is another’s were mine!”

mn41:14.3.verse: He has no mind of ill-will, with the intention of a mind unaffected by hate thus: “May these beings be free from enmity, affliction and anxiety, may they live happily”.

mn41:14.4.verse: He has right view, undistorted vision, thus:

mn41:14.5.verse: “There is what is given and what is offered and what is sacrificed, and there is fruit and ripening of good and bad kammas, and there is this world and the other world and mother and father and spontaneously (born) beings, and good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world”.

mn41:14.6.verse: That is how there are three kinds of mental conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:14.7.verse: So, householders, it is by reason of conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, by reason of righteous conduct, that some beings here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn41:15.1.verse: ‘If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct, should wish:

mn41:15.2.verse: “Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might reappear in the company of the warrior-nobles of great property”,

mn41:15.3.verse: it is possible that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he may do so.

mn41:15.5.verse: Because he observes conduct that is in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:16-17.1.verse: ‘If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct, should wish:

mn41:16-17.2.verse: “Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might reappear in the company of the divines of great property”, it is possible...

mn41:16-17.3.verse: ‘If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma “ … I might reappear in the company of householders of great property”, it is possible …

mn41:18-42.2.verse: “Oh that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might reappear in the company of Cātumahārājika gods, the gods of the Four Kings”,

mn41:18-42.3.verse: it is possible that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he may do so.

mn41:18-42.5.verse: Because he observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.

mn41:18-42.8.verse: ‘… of the Yāma gods, the gods that have gone to Bliss …

mn41:18-42.10.verse: ‘… of the Nimmānarati gods, the gods that Delight in Creating …

mn41:18-42.11.verse: ‘… of the Paranimittavasavatti gods, the gods that Wield Power over others’ Creations …

mn41:18-42.12.verse: ‘… of the gods of the (Brahmā) Divinity’s Retinue …

mn41:18-42.17.verse: ‘… of the Ābhā gods, the Radiant gods …

mn41:18-42.23.verse: ‘… of the Appamāṇābhā gods, the gods of Measureless Radiance…

mn41:18-42.26.verse: ‘… of the Appamāṇasubhā gods, the gods of Measureless Glory …

mn41:18-42.27.verse: ‘… of the Subhakiṇṇā gods, of the gods of Refulgent Glory …

mn41:18-42.28.verse: ‘… of the Vehapphala gods, the Very Fruitful gods …

mn41:18-42.29.verse: ‘… of the Aviha gods, the gods Bathed in their own prosperity …

mn41:18-42.30.verse: ‘… of the Atappa gods, the Untormenting gods …

mn41:18-42.31.verse: ‘… of the Sudassa gods, the Fair-to-see gods …

mn41:18-42.32.verse: ‘… of the Sudassi gods, the Fair-seeing gods …

mn41:18-42.33.verse: ‘… of the Akanittha gods, the gods who are Junior to none …’

mn41:18-42.38.verse: it is possible that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he may do so.

mn41:18-42.40.verse: Because he observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.’

mn41:43.1.verse: ‘If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct, should wish:

mn41:43.2.verse: “Oh that, by realization myself with direct knowledge, I may here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints”,

mn41:43.3.verse: it is possible that, by realization himself with direct knowledge, he may here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints.

mn41:43.5.verse: Because he observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct.’

mn41:44.1.verse: When this was said, the divine-caste householders of Sālā said to the Blessed One:

mn41:44.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms.’

mn41:44.4.verse: ‘We go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. From today let Master Gotama accept us as followers who have gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn41:44.5.verse: From today let Master Gotama accept us as followers who have gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn41:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Sālā.

mn41:2.1.verse: The brahmins and householders of Sālā heard,

mn41:2.2.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—while wandering in the land of the Kosalans has arrived at Sālā, together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn41:2.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn41:2.5.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn41:2.6.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased.

mn41:2.7.verse: He reveals an entirely full and pure spiritual life.

mn41:2.8.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

mn41:3.1.verse: Then the brahmins and householders of Sālā went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. Seated to one side they said to the Buddha:

mn41:4.1.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell?

mn41:4.2.verse: And what is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”

mn41:5.1.verse: “Unprincipled and immoral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn41:5.2.verse: Principled and moral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

mn41:6.1.verse: “We don’t understand the detailed meaning of the worthy Gotama’s brief statement.

mn41:6.2.verse: Worthy Gotama, please teach us this matter in detail so we can understand the meaning.”

mn41:6.3.verse: “Well then, householders, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn41:7.1.verse: “Householders, unprincipled and immoral conduct is threefold by way of body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of mind.

mn41:8.1.verse: And how is unprincipled and immoral conduct threefold by way of body?

mn41:8.2.verse: It’s when someone kills living creatures. They’re violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to living beings.

mn41:8.3.verse: They steal. With the intention to commit theft, they take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.

mn41:8.4.verse: They commit sexual misconduct. They have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.

mn41:8.5.verse: This is how unprincipled and immoral conduct is threefold by way of body.

mn41:9.1.verse: And how is unprincipled and immoral conduct fourfold by way of speech?

mn41:9.2.verse: It’s when someone lies. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my friend, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.

mn41:9.3.verse: They backbite. They repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. And so they divide those who are harmonious, supporting division, delighting in division, loving division, speaking words that promote division.

mn41:9.4.verse: They speak harshly. They use the kinds of words that are cruel, nasty, hurtful, offensive, bordering on anger, not leading to immersion.

mn41:9.5.verse: They talk nonsense. Their speech is untimely, and is neither factual nor beneficial. It has nothing to do with the teaching or the training. Their words have no value, and are untimely, unreasonable, rambling, and pointless.

mn41:9.6.verse: This is how unprincipled and immoral conduct is fourfold by way of speech.

mn41:10.1.verse: And how is unprincipled and immoral conduct threefold by way of mind?

mn41:10.2.verse: It’s when someone is covetous. They covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’

mn41:10.3.verse: They have ill will and malicious intentions: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, slain, destroyed, or annihilated!’

mn41:10.4.verse: They have wrong view. Their perspective is distorted:

mn41:10.5.verse: ‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn41:10.6.verse: This is how unprincipled and immoral conduct is threefold by way of mind.

mn41:10.7.verse: That’s how unprincipled and immoral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn41:11.1.verse: Householders, principled and moral conduct is threefold by way of body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of mind.

mn41:12.1.verse: And how is principled and moral conduct threefold by way of body?

mn41:12.2.verse: It’s when someone gives up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn41:12.3.verse: They give up stealing. They don’t, with the intention to commit theft, take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.

mn41:12.4.verse: They give up sexual misconduct. They don’t have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They don’t have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.

mn41:12.5.verse: This is how principled and moral conduct is threefold by way of body.

mn41:13.1.verse: And how is principled and moral conduct fourfold by way of speech?

mn41:13.2.verse: It’s when someone gives up lying. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my friend, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.

mn41:13.3.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn41:13.4.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, likable, and agreeable to the people.

mn41:13.5.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn41:13.6.verse: This is how principled and moral conduct is fourfold by way of speech.

mn41:14.1.verse: And how is principled and moral conduct threefold by way of mind?

mn41:14.2.verse: It’s when someone is not covetous. They don’t covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’

mn41:14.3.verse: They have a kind heart and loving intentions: ‘May these sentient beings live free of enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy!’

mn41:14.4.verse: They have right view, an undistorted perspective:

mn41:14.5.verse: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn41:14.6.verse: This is how principled and moral conduct is threefold by way of mind.

mn41:14.7.verse: This is how principled and moral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn41:15.1.verse: Someone of principled and moral conduct might wish:

mn41:15.2.verse: ‘If only, when my body breaks up, after death, I would be reborn in the company of well-to-do aristocrats!’

mn41:15.3.verse: It’s possible that this might happen.

mn41:15.5.verse: Because they have principled and moral conduct.

mn41:16-17.1.verse: Someone of principled and moral conduct might wish:

mn41:16-17.2.verse: ‘If only, when my body breaks up, after death, I would be reborn in the company of well-to-do brahmins …

mn41:18-42.2.verse: the gods of the four great kings …

mn41:18-42.10.verse: the gods who love to create …

mn41:18-42.11.verse: the gods who control what is created by others …

mn41:18-42.12.verse: the gods of the Divinity’s host …

mn41:18-42.34.verse: the gods of the dimension of infinite space …

mn41:18-42.35.verse: the gods of the dimension of infinite consciousness …

mn41:18-42.36.verse: the gods of the dimension of nothingness …

mn41:18-42.37.verse: the gods of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn41:18-42.38.verse: It’s possible that this might happen.

mn41:18-42.40.verse: Because they have principled and moral conduct.

mn41:43.1.verse: Someone of principled and moral conduct might wish:

mn41:43.2.verse: ‘If only I might realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

mn41:43.3.verse: It’s possible that this might happen.

mn41:43.5.verse: Because they have principled and moral conduct.”

mn41:44.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmins and householders of Sālā said to the Buddha,

mn41:44.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn41:44.4.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn41:44.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

mn42:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn42:2.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmins and householders of Verañjā were residing in Sāvatthī on some business.

mn42:2.2.verse: The brahmins and householders of Verañjā heard:

mn42:2.3.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—is staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn42:2.8.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

mn42:4.1.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell?

mn42:4.2.verse: And what is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”

mn42:5.1.verse: “Unprincipled and immoral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn42:5.2.verse: Principled and moral conduct is the reason why some sentient beings, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

mn42:6.1.verse: “We don’t understand the detailed meaning of the worthy Gotama’s brief statement. …”

mn42:7.1.verse: “Householders, a person of unprincipled and immoral conduct is threefold by way of body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of mind. …” …

mn43:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn43:1.3.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Mahā Kotthita rose from meditation, and went to the venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.

mn43:1.4.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the venerable Sāriputta:

mn43:2.1.verse: ‘“Without understanding, without understanding” is said, friend.

mn43:2.2.verse: With reference to what is that said?’

mn43:2.3.verse: ‘“Does not understand, does not understand”, friend, that is why “without understanding” is said.

mn43:2.5.verse: Does not understand: “This is suffering”, does not understand: “This is the origin of suffering”, does not understand: “This is the cessation of suffering”, does not understand: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.

mn43:2.6.verse: “Does not understand, does not understand”, that is why “without understanding” is said.’

mn43:2.7.verse: Saying ‘Good, friend’, the venerable Mahā Kotthita delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words, and after agreeing, he asked him a further question:

mn43:3.1.verse: ‘“Possessed of understanding, possessed of understanding” is said, friend.

mn43:3.2.verse: With reference to what is that said?’

mn43:3.3.verse: ‘“Understands, understands”, friend, that is why “possessed of understanding” is said.

mn43:3.5.verse: Understands: “This is suffering”, understands: “This is the origin of suffering”, understands: “This is the cessation of suffering”, understands: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.

mn43:3.6.verse: “Understands, understands”, that is why “possessed of understanding” is said.’

mn43:4.2.verse: With reference to what is “consciousness” said?’

mn43:4.3.verse: ‘“Cognizes, cognizes”, friend, that is why “consciousness” is said.

mn43:4.5.verse: Cognizes: “(This is) pleasant”, cognizes: “(This is) painful”, cognizes: “(This is) neither-painful-nor-pleasant”.

mn43:4.6.verse: “Cognizes, cognizes,” that is why “consciousness” is said.’

mn43:5.2.verse: are these dhammas conjoined or disjoined?

mn43:5.3.verse: And is it possible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them?’

mn43:5.5.verse: these dhammas are conjoined, not disjoined,

mn43:5.6.verse: and it is impossible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them.

mn43:5.7.verse: For what one understands, that one cognizes, and what one cognizes, that one understands.

mn43:5.8.verse: That is why these dhammas are conjoined, not disjoined,

mn43:5.9.verse: and why it is impossible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them.’

mn43:6.1.verse: ‘This understanding and this consciousness, friend, that are conjoined, not disjoined—

mn43:6.2.verse: what is the difference between them?’

mn43:6.3.verse: ‘This understanding and this consciousness, friend, that are conjoined, not disjoined—

mn43:6.4.verse: the difference between them is this: understanding can be developed,[^1] while consciousness can be fully known.

mn43:6.5.verse: That is the difference between them.’

mn43:7.2.verse: With reference to what is that said?’

mn43:7.3.verse: ‘“Feels, feels”, friend, that is why “feeling” is said.

mn43:7.5.verse: Feels pleasure and feels pain and feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

mn43:7.6.verse: “Feels, feels”, that is why “feeling” is said.’

mn43:8.2.verse: With reference to what is “perception” said?’

mn43:8.3.verse: ‘“Perceives, perceives”, friend, that is why “perception” is said.

mn43:8.5.verse: Perceives blue and perceives yellow and perceives red and perceives white.

mn43:8.6.verse: “Perceives, perceives”, that is why “perception” is said.’

mn43:9.1.verse: ‘This feeling and this perception and this consciousness, friend—

mn43:9.2.verse: are these dhammas conjoined or disjoined?

mn43:9.3.verse: And is it possible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them?’

mn43:9.4.verse: ‘This feeling and this perception and this consciousness, friend—

mn43:9.5.verse: these dhammas are conjoined, not disjoined,

mn43:9.6.verse: and it is impossible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them.

mn43:9.7.verse: For what one feels, that one perceives, and what one perceives, that one cognizes.

mn43:9.8.verse: That is why these dhammas are conjoined, not disjoined,

mn43:9.9.verse: and why it is impossible to separate each from each in order to describe the difference between them.’

mn43:10.1.verse: ‘Friend, what can be known by pure mind-consciousness disjoined from the five faculties?’

mn43:10.2.verse: ‘Friend, by pure mind-consciousness disjoined from the five faculties, the base consisting of infinite space can be known thus: “Infinite space”; the base consisting of infinite consciousness can be known thus: “Infinite consciousness”; and the base consisting of nothingness can be known thus: “There is nothing at all”.’

mn43:11.1.verse: ‘Friend, with what does one understand a knowable dhamma?’

mn43:11.2.verse: ‘A knowable dhamma, friend, one understands with the eye of understanding.’

mn43:12.1.verse: ‘Friend, what does understanding have for its purpose?’

mn43:12.2.verse: ‘Understanding, friend, has direct-knowledge for its purpose,[^2] it has full-knowledge for its purpose, and it has abandoning for its purpose.’

mn43:13.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many conditions are there for the arising of right view?’

mn43:13.2.verse: ‘Friend, there are two conditions for the arising of right view:

mn43:13.4.verse: These are the two conditions for the arising of right view.’

mn43:14.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many factors is right view assisted by when it has deliverance of the heart for its fruit, deliverance of the heart for its benefit, and has the deliverance by understanding for its fruit, the deliverance by understanding for its benefit?’

mn43:14.2.verse: ‘Friend, right view is assisted by five factors when it has the deliverance of the heart for its fruit, the deliverance of the heart for its benefit, the deliverance by understanding for its fruit, the deliverance by understanding for its benefit.

mn43:14.3.verse: Here right view is assisted by virtue, by learning, by converse, by peace and by insight.

mn43:14.4.verse: Right view assisted by these five factors has the deliverance of the heart for its fruit, the deliverance of the heart for its benefit, the deliverance by understanding for its fruit, the deliverance by understanding for its benefit.’

mn43:15.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many kinds of being are there?’

mn43:15.2.verse: ‘There are these three kinds of being, friend:

mn43:15.3.verse: being with sensual desire, being with form and being without form.’

mn43:16.1.verse: ‘Friend, how is renewed being in the future generated?’

mn43:16.2.verse: ‘Friend, renewed being in the future is generated for beings who, shut in by ignorance and fettered by craving, delight in this and that—

mn43:16.3.verse: that is how renewed being in the future is generated.’

mn43:17.1.verse: ‘Friend, how is renewed being in the future not generated?’

mn43:17.2.verse: ‘Friend, with the fading of ignorance, with the arising of true knowledge, and with the cessation of craving—

mn43:17.3.verse: that is how renewed being in the future is not generated.’

mn43:18.2.verse: ‘Here, friend, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion—

mn43:18.3.verse: this is called the first jhāna.’

mn43:19.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many factors has the first jhāna?’

mn43:19.2.verse: ‘Friend, the first jhāna has five factors.

mn43:19.3.verse: Here in a bhikkhu who has entered upon the first jhāna there is the occurrence of initial application and sustained application and happiness and pleasure and unification of mind.

mn43:19.4.verse: That is how the first jhāna has five factors.’

mn43:20.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many factors does the first jhāna abandon and how many does it possess?’

mn43:20.2.verse: ‘Friend, the first jhāna abandons five factors and possesses five factors.

mn43:20.3.verse: Here in a bhikkhu who has entered upon the first jhāna, desire for sensual pleasures is abandoned, ill-will is abandoned, lethargy and drowsiness are abandoned, agitation and worry are abandoned, and uncertainty is abandoned;

mn43:20.4.verse: and there is the occurrence of initial application and sustained application and happiness and pleasure and unification of mind.

mn43:20.5.verse: That is how the first jhāna abandons five factors and possesses five factors.’

mn43:21.1.verse: ‘Friend, there are these five faculties each with a separate field, a separate resort,[^3] no one of them exploiting for its being another’s field and resort, that is to say,

mn43:21.2.verse: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty and body faculty.

mn43:21.3.verse: Now these five faculties each with a separate field, a separate resort, no one of them exploiting for its being another’s field and resort: what is their homing-place, what exploits for its being their fields and resorts?’

mn43:21.4.verse: ‘Friend, there are these five faculties each with a separate field, a separate resort, no one of them exploiting for its being another’s field and resort, that is to say,

mn43:21.5.verse: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty.

mn43:21.6.verse: Now these five faculties each with a separate field, a separate resort, no one of them exploiting for its being another’s field and resort, have mind as their homing-place, mind exploits for its being their fields and resorts.’

mn43:22.1.verse: ‘Friend, there are these five faculties, that is to say,

mn43:22.2.verse: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty:

mn43:22.3.verse: these five faculties persist depending on what?’

mn43:22.4.verse: ‘Friend, there are these five faculties, that is to say,

mn43:22.5.verse: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty:

mn43:22.6.verse: these five faculties persist depending on life-span.’

mn43:22.11.verse: ‘Just now, friend, we understood the venerable Sāriputta to say:

mn43:22.13.verse: and now again we understand him to say:

mn43:22.15.verse: How should the meaning of these statements be regarded?’

mn43:22.16.verse: ‘In that case, friend, I shall give you a simile,

mn43:22.17.verse: for some wise men understand by means of a simile the meaning of a statement.

mn43:22.18.verse: Just as, when an oil lamp is burning, its radiance is seen depending on the flame and its flame is seen depending on the radiance;

mn43:22.19.verse: so too life-span persists depending on heat, and heat persists depending on life-span.’

mn43:23.1.verse: ‘Life-processes,[^4] friend, are they (the same as) states of feeling or are life-processes one and states of feeling another?’

mn43:23.2.verse: ‘Life-processes, friend, are not states of feeling.

mn43:23.3.verse: Were life-processes states of feeling, then when a bhikkhu had entered upon the cessation of perception and feeling, his emergence could not be known.[^5]

mn43:23.4.verse: And it is because life-processes are one and states of feeling are another that when a bhikkhu has entered upon the cessation of perception and feeling his emergence can be known.[^6]’

mn43:24.1.verse: ‘Friend, when this body is bereft of how many dhammas is it then dropped and forsaken (so that) it lies senseless like a log?’

mn43:24.2.verse: ‘Friend, when this body is bereft of three dhammas, that is to say, life, heat and consciousness, it is then dropped and forsaken (so that) it lies senseless like a log.’

mn43:25.1.verse: ‘Friend, one who is dead, who has completed his time, and a bhikkhu who has entered upon the cessation of perception and feeling, what is the difference between them?’

mn43:25.2.verse: ‘Friend, (in the case of) one who has completed his time, his bodily processes have ceased and are tranquil, his verbal processes have ceased and are tranquil, his mental processes have ceased and are tranquil, his life-span is exhausted, his heat has subsided, and his faculties are quite broken up.

mn43:25.3.verse: (In the case of) a bhikkhu who has entered the cessation of perception and feeling, his bodily processes have ceased and are tranquil, his verbal processes have ceased and are tranquil, his mental processes have ceased and are tranquil, his life-span is unexhausted, his heat has not subsided, and his faculties are intact.

mn43:25.4.verse: One who is dead, who has completed his time, and a bhikkhu who has entered upon the cessation of perception and feeling—the difference between them is this.’

mn43:26.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many conditions are there for attainment of the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant?’

mn43:26.2.verse: ‘Friend, there are four conditions for this:

mn43:26.3.verse: here with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn43:26.4.verse: These are the four conditions for attainment of the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.’

mn43:27.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many conditions are there for attainment of the deliverance of mind that is signless?’

mn43:27.2.verse: ‘Friend, there are two conditions for this:

mn43:27.3.verse: non-attention to all signs, and attention to the signless element.

mn43:27.4.verse: These are the two conditions for attainment of the deliverance of mind that is signless.’

mn43:27.5.verse: ‘Friend, how many conditions are there for persistence of the deliverance of mind that is signless?’

mn43:28.1.verse: ‘Friend, there are three conditions for this:

mn43:28.2.verse: non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and the prior determination (of the length of the persistence).

mn43:28.3.verse: These are the three conditions for persistence of the deliverance of mind that is signless.’

mn43:29.1.verse: ‘Friend, how many conditions are there for emergence from the deliverance of mind that is signless?’

mn43:29.2.verse: ‘Friend, there are two conditions for this:

mn43:29.3.verse: attention to all signs, and non-attention to the signless element.

mn43:29.4.verse: These are the two conditions for emergence from the deliverance of mind that is signless.’

mn43:29.5.verse: ‘Friend, the deliverance of mind that is measureless and that which is nothingness and that which is voidness and that which is signless: are these dhammas different in meaning and different in the letter, or are they one in meaning and only the letter is different?’

mn43:30.1.verse: ‘Friend, the deliverance of mind that is measureless and that which is nothingness and that which is voidness and that which is signless: there is a way in which these dhammas are different in meaning and different in the letter,

mn43:30.2.verse: and there is a way in which they are one in meaning and only the letter is different.

mn43:31.1.verse: ‘What is the way in which they are different in meaning and different in the letter?

mn43:31.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides with a mind endued with loving-kindness extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with an abundant, exalted, measureless mind of loving-kindness without hostility or affliction extending over the all-embracing world.

mn43:31.3.verse: He abides with a mind endued with compassion …

mn43:31.4.verse: with a mind endued with gladness …

mn43:31.5.verse: He abides with a mind endued with equanimity extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with an abundant, exalted, measureless mind of equanimity without hostility or affliction extending over the all-embracing world.

mn43:31.6.verse: This is called the deliverance of mind that is measureless.

mn43:32.1.verse: ‘And what is the deliverance of mind that is nothingness?

mn43:32.2.verse: Here, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of infinity of consciousness, (aware that) “there is nothing”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.

mn43:32.3.verse: This is called the deliverance of mind that is nothingness (as-non-owning).[^7]

mn43:33.1.verse: ‘And what is the deliverance of mind that is voidness?

mn43:33.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, considers thus:

mn43:33.3.verse: “This is void of self or of what belongs to self”.

mn43:33.4.verse: This is called the deliverance of mind that is voidness.

mn43:34.1.verse: ‘And what is the deliverance of mind that is signless?

mn43:34.2.verse: Here, with non-attention to all signs, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the signless concentration of mind.

mn43:34.3.verse: This is called the deliverance of mind that is signless.

mn43:34.4.verse: Thus is the way in which these dhammas are different in meaning and different in the letter.

mn43:35.1.verse: ‘And what is the way in which they are one in meaning and only the letter is different?

mn43:35.2.verse: Lust is a making of measurements,[^8] hate is a making of measurements, delusion is a making of measurements.

mn43:35.3.verse: In a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, these are abandoned, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no more liable to future arising.

mn43:35.4.verse: Of (all) the kinds of deliverance of mind that are measureless, the unassailable deliverance of mind is pronounced the best.

mn43:35.5.verse: Now that unassailable deliverance of mind is void of lust, void of hate, and void of delusion.

mn43:36.1.verse: ‘Lust is an owning, hate is an owning, delusion is an owning.

mn43:36.2.verse: In a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, these are abandoned, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no more liable to future arising.

mn43:36.3.verse: Of (all) the kinds of deliverance of mind that are nothingness (as non-owning), the unassailable deliverance of mind is pronounced the best.

mn43:36.4.verse: Now the unassailable deliverance of mind is void of lust, void of hate, and void of delusion.

mn43:37.1.verse: ‘Lust is a making of signs, hate is a making of signs, delusion is a making of signs.

mn43:37.2.verse: In one whose taints are exhausted, these are abandoned, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no more liable to future arising.

mn43:37.3.verse: Of (all) the kinds of deliverance of mind that are signless, the unassailable deliverance of mind is pronounced the best.

mn43:37.4.verse: Now that unassailable deliverance of mind is void of lust, void of hate, and void of delusion.

mn43:37.5.verse: That is the way in which these dhammas are one in meaning and the letter is different.’

mn43:37.6.verse: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

mn43:37.7.verse: The venerable Mahā Kotthita was satisfied, and he delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words.

mn43:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn43:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita came out of retreat, went to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn43:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

mn43:2.2.verse: How is a witless person defined?”

mn43:2.3.verse: “Reverend, they’re called witless because they don’t understand.

mn43:2.5.verse: They don’t understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn43:2.6.verse: They’re called witless because they don’t understand.”

mn43:2.7.verse: Saying “Good, reverend,” Mahākoṭṭhita approved and agreed with what Sāriputta said. Then he asked another question:

mn43:3.2.verse: How is a wise person defined?”

mn43:3.5.verse: They understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn43:3.6.verse: They’re called wise because they understand.”

mn43:4.6.verse: It’s called consciousness because it cognizes.”

mn43:5.2.verse: are these things mixed or separate?

mn43:5.3.verse: And can we completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them?”

mn43:5.5.verse: these things are mixed, not separate.

mn43:5.6.verse: And you can never completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them.

mn43:5.7.verse: For you understand what you cognize, and you cognize what you understand.

mn43:5.8.verse: That’s why these things are mixed, not separate.

mn43:5.9.verse: And you can never completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them.”

mn43:6.2.verse: what is the difference between these things that are mixed, not separate?”

mn43:6.4.verse: “The difference between these things is that wisdom should be developed, while consciousness should be completely understood.”

mn43:7.5.verse: It feels pleasure, pain, and neutral.

mn43:7.6.verse: It’s called feeling because it feels.”

mn43:8.5.verse: It perceives blue, yellow, red, and white.

mn43:8.6.verse: It’s called perception because it perceives.”

mn43:9.2.verse: are these things mixed or separate?

mn43:9.3.verse: And can we completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them?”

mn43:9.5.verse: these things are mixed, not separate.

mn43:9.6.verse: And you can never completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them.

mn43:9.7.verse: For you perceive what you feel, and you cognize what you perceive.

mn43:9.8.verse: That’s why these things are mixed, not separate.

mn43:9.9.verse: And you can never completely disentangle them so as to describe the difference between them.”

mn43:10.1.verse: “What can be known by purified mind consciousness released from the five senses?”

mn43:10.2.verse: “Aware that ‘space is infinite’ it can know the dimension of infinite space. Aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’ it can know the dimension of infinite consciousness. Aware that ‘there is nothing at all’ it can know the dimension of nothingness.”

mn43:11.1.verse: “How do you understand something that can be known?”

mn43:11.2.verse: “You understand something that can be known with the eye of wisdom.”

mn43:12.2.verse: “The goal of wisdom is direct knowledge, complete understanding, and giving up.”

mn43:13.1.verse: “How many conditions are there for the arising of right view?”

mn43:13.2.verse: “There are two conditions for the arising of right view:

mn43:13.3.verse: the voice of another and rational application of mind.

mn43:13.4.verse: These are the two conditions for the arising of right view.”

mn43:14.1.verse: “When right view is supported by how many factors does it have freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom as its fruit and benefit?”

mn43:14.2.verse: “When right view is supported by five factors it has freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom as its fruit and benefit.

mn43:14.3.verse: It’s when right view is supported by ethics, learning, discussion, serenity, and discernment.

mn43:14.4.verse: When right view is supported by these five factors it has freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom as its fruit and benefit.”

mn43:15.1.verse: “How many states of existence are there?”

mn43:15.2.verse: “Reverend, there are these three states of existence.

mn43:15.3.verse: Existence in the sensual realm, the realm of luminous form, and the formless realm.”

mn43:16.1.verse: “But how is there regeneration into a new state of existence in the future?”

mn43:16.2.verse: “It’s because of sentient beings—shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving—taking pleasure wherever they land.

mn43:16.3.verse: That’s how there is regeneration into a new state of existence in the future.”

mn43:17.1.verse: “But how is there no regeneration into a new state of existence in the future?”

mn43:17.2.verse: “It’s when ignorance fades away, knowledge arises, and craving ceases.

mn43:17.3.verse: That’s how there is no regeneration into a new state of existence in the future.”

mn43:18.1.verse: “But what, reverend, is the first absorption?”

mn43:18.2.verse: “Reverend, it’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn43:18.3.verse: This is called the first absorption.”

mn43:19.1.verse: “But how many factors does the first absorption have?”

mn43:19.3.verse: When a mendicant has entered the first absorption, placing the mind, keeping it connected, rapture, bliss, and unification of mind are present.

mn43:19.4.verse: That’s how the first absorption has five factors.”

mn43:20.1.verse: “But how many factors has the first absorption given up and how many does it possess?”

mn43:20.2.verse: “The first absorption has given up five factors and possesses five factors.

mn43:20.3.verse: When a mendicant has entered the first absorption, sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt are given up.

mn43:20.4.verse: Placing the mind, keeping it connected, rapture, bliss, and unification of mind are present.

mn43:20.5.verse: That’s how the first absorption has given up five factors and possesses five factors.”

mn43:21.1.verse: “Reverend, these five faculties have different domains and different ranges, and don’t experience each other’s domain and range. That is,

mn43:21.2.verse: the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

mn43:21.3.verse: What do these five faculties, with their different domains and ranges, have recourse to? What experiences their domains and ranges?”

mn43:21.6.verse: “These five faculties, with their different domains and ranges, have recourse to the mind. And the mind experiences their domains and ranges.”

mn43:22.3.verse: “These five faculties depend on what to continue?”

mn43:22.6.verse: “These five faculties depend on vitality to continue.”

mn43:22.7.verse: “But what does vitality depend on to continue?”

mn43:22.9.verse: “But what does warmth depend on to continue?”

mn43:22.11.verse: “Just now I understood you to say:

mn43:22.13.verse: But I also understood you to say:

mn43:22.15.verse: How then should we see the meaning of this statement?”

mn43:22.16.verse: “Well then, reverend, I shall give you a simile.

mn43:22.17.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

mn43:22.18.verse: Suppose there was an oil lamp burning. The luminosity appears dependent on the flame, and the flame appears dependent on the luminosity.

mn43:22.19.verse: In the same way, vitality depends on warmth to continue, and warmth depends on vitality to continue.”

mn43:23.1.verse: “Are the vital forces and the phenomena that are felt one and the same? Or are the vital forces one thing, and the phenomena that are felt another?”

mn43:23.2.verse: “The vital forces are not the same things as the phenomena that are felt.

mn43:23.3.verse: For if the vital forces and the phenomena that are felt were the same things, a mendicant who had attained the cessation of perception and feeling would not emerge from it.

mn43:23.4.verse: But because the vital forces and the phenomena that are felt are different things, a mendicant who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling can emerge from it.”

mn43:24.1.verse: “How many things must this body lose before it lies abandoned, tossed aside like an insentient log?”

mn43:24.2.verse: “This body must lose three things before it lies abandoned, tossed aside like an insentient log: vitality, warmth, and consciousness.”

mn43:25.1.verse: “What’s the difference between someone who has passed away and a mendicant who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling?”

mn43:25.2.verse: “When someone dies, their physical, verbal, and mental processes have ceased and stilled; their vitality is spent; their warmth is dissipated; and their faculties have disintegrated.

mn43:25.3.verse: When a mendicant has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, their physical, verbal, and mental processes have ceased and stilled. But their vitality is not spent; their warmth is not dissipated; and their faculties are very clear.

mn43:25.4.verse: That’s the difference between someone who has passed away and a mendicant who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling.”

mn43:26.1.verse: “How many conditions are necessary to attain the neutral release of the heart?”

mn43:26.2.verse: “Four conditions are necessary to attain the neutral release of the heart.

mn43:26.3.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn43:26.4.verse: These four conditions are necessary to attain the neutral release of the heart.”

mn43:27.1.verse: “How many conditions are necessary to attain the signless release of the heart?”

mn43:27.2.verse: “Two conditions are necessary to attain the signless release of the heart:

mn43:27.3.verse: not focusing on any signs, and focusing on the signless.

mn43:27.4.verse: These two conditions are necessary to attain the signless release of the heart.”

mn43:27.5.verse: “How many conditions are necessary to remain in the signless release of the heart?”

mn43:28.1.verse: “Three conditions are necessary to remain in the signless release of the heart:

mn43:28.2.verse: not focusing on any signs, focusing on the signless, and a previous determination.

mn43:28.3.verse: These three conditions are necessary to remain in the signless release of the heart.”

mn43:29.1.verse: “How many conditions are necessary to emerge from the signless release of the heart?”

mn43:29.2.verse: “Two conditions are necessary to emerge from the signless release of the heart:

mn43:29.3.verse: focusing on all signs, and not focusing on the signless.

mn43:29.4.verse: These two conditions are necessary to emerge from the signless release of the heart.”

mn43:29.5.verse: “The limitless release of the heart, and the release of the heart through nothingness, and the release of the heart through emptiness, and the signless release of the heart: do these things differ in both meaning and phrasing? Or do they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?”

mn43:30.1.verse: “There is a way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

mn43:30.2.verse: But there’s also a way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.

mn43:31.1.verse: And what’s the way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing?

mn43:31.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn43:31.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn43:31.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn43:31.5.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn43:31.6.verse: This is called the limitless release of the heart.

mn43:32.1.verse: And what is the release of the heart through nothingness?

mn43:32.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn43:32.3.verse: This is called the heart’s release through nothingness.

mn43:33.1.verse: And what is the release of the heart through emptiness?

mn43:33.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

mn43:33.3.verse: ‘This is empty of a self or what belongs to a self.’

mn43:33.4.verse: This is called the release of the heart through emptiness.

mn43:34.1.verse: And what is the signless release of the heart?

mn43:34.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, not focusing on any signs, enters and remains in the signless immersion of the heart.

mn43:34.3.verse: This is called the signless release of the heart.

mn43:34.4.verse: This is the way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

mn43:35.1.verse: And what’s the way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?

mn43:35.2.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are makers of limits.

mn43:35.3.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn43:35.4.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of limitless release of the heart.

mn43:35.5.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

mn43:36.1.verse: Greed is something, hate is something, and delusion is something.

mn43:36.2.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn43:36.3.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of release of the heart through nothingness.

mn43:36.4.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

mn43:37.1.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are makers of signs.

mn43:37.2.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn43:37.3.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of signless release of the heart.

mn43:37.4.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

mn43:37.5.verse: This is the way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.”

mn43:37.6.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

mn43:37.7.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approved what Sāriputta said.

mn44:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn44:1.3.verse: Then the lay follower Visākha went to the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā, and after paying homage to her, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked:

mn44:2.2.verse: What is called embodiment by the Blessed One?’

mn44:2.3.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, these five aggregates affected by clinging are called embodiment by the Blessed One,

mn44:2.4.verse: that is to say: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn44:2.5.verse: These five aggregates affected by clinging are called embodiment by the Blessed One.’

mn44:2.6.verse: Saying ‘Good, lady’, the lay follower Visākha delighted in the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā’s words, and after agreeing, he asked her a further question:

mn44:3.1.verse: ‘Lady, “Origin of embodiment, origin of embodiment” is said.

mn44:3.2.verse: What is called the origin of embodiment by the Blessed One?’

mn44:3.3.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, it is that craving which renews being and is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that, that is to say:

mn44:3.4.verse: craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being;

mn44:3.5.verse: this is called the origin of embodiment by the Blessed One.’

mn44:4.1.verse: ‘Lady, “Cessation of embodiment, cessation of embodiment” is said.

mn44:4.2.verse: What is called the cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One?’

mn44:4.3.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, it is the remainderless fading and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting, of that same craving;

mn44:4.4.verse: this is called cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One.’

mn44:5.1.verse: ‘Lady, “The way leading to the cessation of embodiment, the way leading to the cessation of embodiment” is said.

mn44:5.2.verse: What is called the way leading to the cessation of embodiment by the Blessed One?’

mn44:5.3.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, it is this Noble Eightfold Path, that is to say:

mn44:5.4.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.’

mn44:6.1.verse: ‘Lady, is that clinging the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging, or is the clinging something apart from these five aggregates affected by clinging?’

mn44:6.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, that clinging is neither the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging nor is it something apart from these five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn44:6.3.verse: It is the desire and lust comprised in these five aggregates affected by clinging that is the clinging there.’

mn44:7.1.verse: ‘Lady, how does there come to be the embodiment view?’

mn44:7.2.verse: ‘Here, friend Visākha, the untaught ordinary man who has no regard for the Noble Ones and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it, who has no regard for True Men and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it,

mn44:7.3.verse: sees form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form.

mn44:7.4.verse: He sees feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling.

mn44:7.5.verse: He sees perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception.

mn44:7.6.verse: He sees formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations.

mn44:7.7.verse: He sees consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn44:7.8.verse: That is how there comes to be the embodiment view.’

mn44:8.1.verse: ‘Lady, how does there not come to be the embodiment view?’

mn44:8.2.verse: ‘Here, friend Visākha, the well-taught Noble disciple who has regard for Noble Ones and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it, who has regard for True Men and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it,

mn44:8.3.verse: does not see form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form.

mn44:8.4.verse: He does not see feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling.

mn44:8.5.verse: He does not see perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception.

mn44:8.6.verse: He does not see formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations.

mn44:8.7.verse: He does not see consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn44:8.8.verse: That is how there does not come to be the embodiment view.’

mn44:9.1.verse: ‘Lady, what is the Noble Eightfold Path?’

mn44:9.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, it is just this Noble Eightfold Path, namely:

mn44:9.3.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.’

mn44:10.1.verse: ‘Lady, is the Noble Eightfold Path conditioned or unconditioned[^1]?’

mn44:10.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is conditioned.’

mn44:11.1.verse: ‘Are the three groups included by the Noble Eightfold Path, lady, or is the Noble Eightfold Path included by the three groups?’

mn44:11.2.verse: ‘The three groups are not included by the Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, but the Noble Eightfold Path is included by the three groups.

mn44:11.3.verse: Any right speech, any right action, any right livelihood: these dhammas are included in the Virtue group.

mn44:11.4.verse: Any right effort, any right mindfulness, any right concentration: these dhammas are included in the Concentration group.

mn44:11.5.verse: Any right view, any right intention: these dhammas are included in the Understanding group.’

mn44:12.1.verse: ‘What is concentration, lady, what is the sign of concentration, what is the equipment of concentration, what is the development of concentration?’

mn44:12.2.verse: ‘Any unification of mind is concentration, friend Visākha;

mn44:12.3.verse: the four foundations of mindfulness are the sign of concentration;

mn44:12.4.verse: the four right endeavours are the equipment of concentration;

mn44:12.5.verse: the repetition, development, and cultivation of those same dhammas are the development of concentration therein.’

mn44:13.2.verse: ‘There are these three processes, friend Visākha:

mn44:13.3.verse: bodily process, verbal process, and mental process.’

mn44:14.1.verse: ‘But, lady, what is a bodily process, what is a verbal process, what is a mental process?’

mn44:14.2.verse: ‘In-breaths and out-breaths are a bodily process, friend Visākha, thinking and exploring[^3] are a verbal process, perception and feeling are a mental process.’

mn44:15.1.verse: ‘But, why are in-breaths and out-breaths a bodily process, lady, why are thinking and exploring a verbal process, why are perception and feeling a mental process?’

mn44:15.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, in-breaths and out-breaths belong to a body; these are dhammas bound up with a body, that is why in-breaths and out-breaths are a bodily process.

mn44:15.3.verse: Having previously thought and explored, subsequently one breaks into speech, that is why thinking and exploring are a verbal process.

mn44:15.4.verse: Perception and feeling belong to mind; these are dhammas bound up with mind, that is why perception and feeling are a mental process.’

mn44:16.1.verse: ‘Lady, how does there come to be the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?’

mn44:16.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is attaining cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:

mn44:16.3.verse: “I shall attain the cessation of perception and feeling” or “I am attaining the cessation of perception and feeling”;

mn44:16.4.verse: but rather his mind has previously been developed in such wise that it induces that state.’

mn44:17.1.verse: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, which dhammas come first in him: the bodily process or the verbal process or the mental process?’

mn44:17.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, first his verbal process ceases, then his bodily process, then his mental process.’

mn44:18.1.verse: ‘Lady, how does there come to be emergence from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling?’

mn44:18.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, it does not occur to him:

mn44:18.3.verse: “I shall emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling” or “I am emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling” or “I have emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling”;

mn44:18.4.verse: but rather his mind has previously been developed in such wise that it induces that state.’

mn44:19.1.verse: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, which dhammas arise first in him: the bodily process or the verbal process or the mental process?’

mn44:19.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu is emerging from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, first his mental process arises, then his bodily process, then his verbal process.’

mn44:20.1.verse: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, how many kinds of contact touch him?’

mn44:20.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, three kinds of contact touch him: void contact, signless contact and desireless contact.’

mn44:21.1.verse: ‘Lady, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, to what does his mind incline, lean and tend?’

mn44:21.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, his mind inclines, leans and tends to seclusion.’

mn44:22.1.verse: ‘Lady, how many kinds of feeling are there?’

mn44:22.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, there are three kinds of feeling:

mn44:22.3.verse: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn44:23.1.verse: ‘But, lady, what is pleasant feeling, what is painful feeling, what is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’

mn44:23.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, whatever is bodily or mentally felt as pleasant and gratifying—

mn44:23.4.verse: Whatever is bodily or mentally felt as painful and hurting—

mn44:23.6.verse: Whatever is bodily or mentally felt as neither gratifying nor hurting—

mn44:24.1.verse: ‘Lady, what is pleasant feeling pleasant in virtue of and painful in virtue of? What is painful feeling painful in virtue of and pleasant in virtue of? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling pleasant in virtue of and painful in virtue of?’

mn44:24.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant in virtue of presence and painful in virtue of change;

mn44:24.3.verse: painful feeling is painful in virtue of presence and pleasant in virtue of change;

mn44:24.4.verse: neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant in virtue of knowledge (of it) and painful in virtue of want of knowledge (of it).’

mn44:25.1.verse: ‘Lady, the underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of pleasant feeling? The underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of painful feeling? The underlying tendency to what underlies in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’

mn44:25.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust underlies in the case of pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance underlies in the case of painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance underlies in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn44:26.1.verse: ‘Lady, does the underlying tendency to lust underlie in the case of all pleasant feeling? Does the underlying tendency to resistance underlie in the case of all painful feeling? Does the underlying tendency to ignorance underlie in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’

mn44:26.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie in the case of all pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance does not underlie in the case of all painful feeling. The underlying tendency of ignorance does not underlie in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn44:27.1.verse: ‘Lady, what is abandonable in the case of pleasant feeling? What is abandonable in the case of painful feeling? What is abandonable in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’

mn44:27.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust is abandonable in the case of pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to resistance is abandonable in the case of painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance is abandonable in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn44:28.1.verse: ‘Is the underlying tendency to lust (there and) abandonable in the case of all pleasant feeling? Is the underlying tendency to resistance (there and) abandonable in the case of all painful feeling? Is the underlying tendency to ignorance (there and) abandonable in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?’

mn44:28.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, it is not in the case of all pleasant feeling that the underlying tendency to lust is there (and so) abandonable, it is not in the case of all painful feeling that the underlying tendency to resistance is there (and so) abandonable, it is not in the case of all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that the underlying tendency to ignorance is there (and so) abandonable.

mn44:28.3.verse: ‘Here, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion:

mn44:28.4.verse: with that he abandons lust, and no underlying tendency to lust underlies that.

mn44:28.6.verse: “When shall I enter upon and abide in that base which Noble Ones now enter upon and abide in?”

mn44:28.7.verse: And as he builds up love for the supreme liberations in this way, grief arises with that love as its condition:

mn44:28.8.verse: with that he abandons resistance, and no underlying tendency to resistance underlies that.

mn44:28.9.verse: ‘Here with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of mental joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity:

mn44:28.10.verse: with that he abandons ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that.’

mn44:29.1.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of pleasant feeling, lady?’

mn44:29.2.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, painful feeling is a counterpart of pleasant feeling.’

mn44:29.3.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of painful feeling, lady?’

mn44:29.4.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is a counterpart of painful feeling.’

mn44:29.5.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, lady?’

mn44:29.6.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, ignorance is a counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn44:29.7.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of ignorance, lady?’

mn44:29.8.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, true knowledge is a counterpart of ignorance.’

mn44:29.9.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of true knowledge, lady?’

mn44:29.10.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, deliverance is a counterpart of true knowledge.’

mn44:29.11.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of deliverance, lady?’

mn44:29.12.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, Nibbāna is a counterpart of deliverance.’

mn44:29.13.verse: ‘What is a counterpart of Nibbāna, lady?’

mn44:29.14.verse: ‘Friend Visākha, you have pushed this line of questioning too far. You cannot find a conclusion to this line of questioning;

mn44:29.15.verse: for it is the life divine that merges in Nibbāna, leads to Nibbāna.

mn44:29.16.verse: If you like, you may go to the Blessed One and ask him the meaning of this. As he answers, so you should remember it.’

mn44:30.1.verse: Then the lay follower Visākha delighted in the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā’s words, and after agreeing, he rose from his seat, and after paying homage keeping her on his right, he departed and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.

mn44:30.2.verse: When he had done so, he recounted to the Blessed One all his conversation with the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā.

mn44:30.3.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One told him:

mn44:30.4.verse: ‘The bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā is wise, Visākha, the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā has great understanding.

mn44:30.5.verse: Had you asked me the meaning of this, I should have given you the same reply.

mn44:30.6.verse: As the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā has answered you, such is the meaning, and so you should remember it.’

mn44:30.7.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn44:30.8.verse: The lay follower Visākha was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn44:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn44:1.3.verse: Then the layman Visākha went to see the nun Dhammadinnā, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to her:

mn44:2.1.verse: “Ma’am, they speak of this thing called ‘substantial reality’.

mn44:2.2.verse: What is this substantial reality that the Buddha spoke of?”

mn44:2.3.verse: “Visākha, the Buddha said that these five grasping aggregates are substantial reality.

mn44:2.4.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn44:2.5.verse: The Buddha said that these five grasping aggregates are substantial reality.”

mn44:2.6.verse: Saying “Good, ma’am,” Visākha approved and agreed with what Dhammadinnā said. Then he asked another question:

mn44:3.1.verse: “Ma’am, they speak of this thing called ‘the origin of substantial reality’.

mn44:3.2.verse: What is the origin of substantial reality that the Buddha spoke of?”

mn44:3.3.verse: “It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

mn44:3.4.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

mn44:3.5.verse: The Buddha said that this is the origin of substantial reality.”

mn44:4.1.verse: “Ma’am, they speak of this thing called ‘the cessation of substantial reality’.

mn44:4.2.verse: What is the cessation of substantial reality that the Buddha spoke of?”

mn44:4.3.verse: “It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving with no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

mn44:4.4.verse: The Buddha said that this is the cessation of substantial reality.”

mn44:5.1.verse: “Ma’am, they speak of the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

mn44:5.2.verse: What is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality that the Buddha spoke of?”

mn44:5.3.verse: “The practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality that the Buddha spoke of is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn44:5.4.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.”

mn44:6.1.verse: “But ma’am, is that grasping the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates? Or is grasping one thing and the five grasping aggregates another?”

mn44:6.2.verse: “That grasping is not the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates. Nor is grasping one thing and the five grasping aggregates another.

mn44:6.3.verse: The desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates is the grasping there.”

mn44:7.1.verse: “But ma’am, how does substantialist view come about?”

mn44:7.2.verse: “It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn44:7.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn44:7.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn44:7.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view comes about.”

mn44:8.1.verse: “But ma’am, how does substantialist view not come about?”

mn44:8.2.verse: “It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn44:8.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn44:8.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn44:8.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view does not come about.”

mn44:9.1.verse: “But ma’am, what is the noble eightfold path?”

mn44:9.2.verse: “It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn44:9.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.”

mn44:10.1.verse: “But ma’am, is the noble eightfold path conditioned or unconditioned?”

mn44:11.1.verse: “Are the three spectrums of practice included in the noble eightfold path? Or is the noble eightfold path included in the three spectrums of practice?”

mn44:11.2.verse: “The three spectrums of practice are not included in the noble eightfold path. Rather, the noble eightfold path is included in the three spectrums of practice.

mn44:11.3.verse: Right speech, right action, and right livelihood: these things are included in the spectrum of ethics.
