mn44:11.4.verse: Right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion: these things are included in the spectrum of immersion.

mn44:11.5.verse: Right view and right purpose: these things are included in the spectrum of wisdom.”

mn44:12.1.verse: “But ma’am, what is immersion? What things are the bases of immersion? What things are the prerequisites for immersion? What is the development of immersion?”

mn44:12.3.verse: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the bases for immersion.

mn44:12.4.verse: The four right efforts are the prerequisites for immersion.

mn44:12.5.verse: The cultivation, development, and making much of these very same things is the development of immersion.”

mn44:13.3.verse: The physical process, the verbal process, and the mental process.”

mn44:14.1.verse: “But ma’am, what is the physical process? What’s the verbal process? What’s the mental process?”

mn44:14.2.verse: “Breathing is a physical process. Placing the mind and keeping it connected are a verbal process. Perception and feeling are a mental process.”

mn44:15.1.verse: “But ma’am, why is breathing a physical process? Why are placing the mind and keeping it connected a verbal process? Why are perception and feeling a mental process?”

mn44:15.2.verse: “Breathing is physical. It’s tied up with the body, that’s why breathing is a physical process.

mn44:15.3.verse: First you place the mind and keep it connected, then you break into speech. That’s why placing the mind and keeping it connected are a verbal process.

mn44:15.4.verse: Perception and feeling are mental. They’re tied up with the mind, that’s why perception and feeling are a mental process.”

mn44:16.1.verse: “But ma’am, how does someone attain the cessation of perception and feeling?”

mn44:16.2.verse: “A mendicant who is entering such an attainment does not think:

mn44:16.3.verse: ‘I will enter the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I am entering the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I have entered the cessation of perception and feeling.’

mn44:16.4.verse: Rather, their mind has been previously developed so as to lead to such a state.”

mn44:17.1.verse: “But ma’am, which process ceases first for a mendicant who is entering the cessation of perception and feeling: physical, verbal, or mental?”

mn44:17.2.verse: “The verbal process ceases first, then physical, then mental.”

mn44:18.1.verse: “But ma’am, how does someone emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling?”

mn44:18.2.verse: “A mendicant who is emerging from such an attainment does not think:

mn44:18.3.verse: ‘I will emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I am emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I have emerged from the cessation of perception and feeling.’

mn44:18.4.verse: Rather, their mind has been previously developed so as to lead to such a state.”

mn44:19.1.verse: “But ma’am, which process arises first for a mendicant who is emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling: physical, verbal, or mental?”

mn44:19.2.verse: “The mental process arises first, then physical, then verbal.”

mn44:20.1.verse: “But ma’am, when a mendicant has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, how many kinds of contact do they experience?”

mn44:20.2.verse: “They experience three kinds of contact: emptiness, signless, and undirected contacts.”

mn44:21.1.verse: “But ma’am, when a mendicant has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, what does their mind slant, slope, and incline to?”

mn44:21.2.verse: “Their mind slants, slopes, and inclines to seclusion.”

mn44:22.1.verse: “But ma’am, how many feelings are there?”

mn44:23.2.verse: “Anything felt physically or mentally as pleasant or enjoyable.

mn44:23.4.verse: Anything felt physically or mentally as painful or unpleasant.

mn44:23.6.verse: Anything felt physically or mentally as neither pleasurable nor painful.

mn44:24.1.verse: “What is pleasant and what is painful regarding each of the three feelings?”

mn44:24.2.verse: “Pleasant feeling is pleasant when it remains and painful when it perishes.

mn44:24.3.verse: Painful feeling is painful when it remains and pleasant when it perishes.

mn44:24.4.verse: Neutral feeling is pleasant in the presence of knowledge, and painful in the presence of ignorance.”

mn44:25.1.verse: “What underlying tendencies underlie each of the three feelings?”

mn44:25.2.verse: “The underlying tendency for greed underlies pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency for aversion underlies painful feeling. The underlying tendency for ignorance underlies neutral feeling.”

mn44:26.1.verse: “Do these underlying tendencies always underlie these feelings?”

mn44:27.1.verse: “What should be given up in regard to each of these three feelings?”

mn44:27.2.verse: “The underlying tendency to greed should be given up when it comes to pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion should be given up when it comes to painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance should be given up when it comes to neutral feeling.”

mn44:28.1.verse: “Should these underlying tendencies be given up regarding all instances of these feelings?”

mn44:28.3.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn44:28.4.verse: With this they give up greed, and the underlying tendency to greed does not lie within that.

mn44:28.5.verse: And take a mendicant who reflects:

mn44:28.6.verse: ‘Oh, when will I enter and remain in the same dimension that the noble ones enter and remain in today?’

mn44:28.7.verse: Nursing such a longing for the supreme liberations gives rise to sadness due to longing.

mn44:28.8.verse: With this they give up aversion, and the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie within that.

mn44:28.9.verse: Take a mendicant who, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn44:28.10.verse: With this they give up ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie within that.”

mn44:29.1.verse: “But ma’am, what is the counterpart of pleasant feeling?”

mn44:29.3.verse: “What is the counterpart of painful feeling?”

mn44:29.5.verse: “What is the counterpart of neutral feeling?”

mn44:29.14.verse: “Your question goes too far, Visākha. You weren’t able to grasp the limit of questioning.

mn44:29.15.verse: For extinguishment is the objective, destination, and culmination of the spiritual life.

mn44:29.16.verse: If you wish, go to the Buddha and ask him this question. You should remember it in line with his answer.”

mn44:30.1.verse: And then the layman Visākha approved and agreed with what the nun Dhammadinnā said. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled her, keeping her on his right. Then he went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

mn44:30.2.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

mn44:30.3.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

mn44:30.4.verse: “The nun Dhammadinnā is astute, Visākha, she has great wisdom.

mn44:30.5.verse: If you came to me and asked this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way as the nun Dhammadinnā.

mn44:30.6.verse: That is what it means, and that’s how you should remember it.”

mn44:30.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn44:30.8.verse: Satisfied, the layman Visākha approved what the Buddha said.

mn45:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn45:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn45:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are four ways of undertaking dhammas.

mn45:2.3.verse: There is way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pain.

mn45:2.4.verse: There is a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in the future as pain.

mn45:2.5.verse: There is a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in the future as pleasure.

mn45:2.6.verse: There is a way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pleasure.

mn45:3.1.verse: ‘What is the way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pain?

mn45:3.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn45:3.3.verse: “There is no harm in sensual desires”,

mn45:3.4.verse: and they take to gulping down sensual desires.

mn45:3.5.verse: They divert themselves with turbaned women Wanderers.

mn45:3.7.verse: “What do these good monks and divines fancy they see as future fear from sensual desires that they speak of abandoning sensual desires and describe an (ulterior) full knowledge of sensual desires.

mn45:3.8.verse: The contact of this woman Wanderer’s tender soft downy arm is pleasant”, and they take to gulping down sensual desires.

mn45:3.9.verse: Having done so, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in an unhappy destination, in the states of deprivation, in perdition, even in hell.

mn45:3.10.verse: There they feel painful, racking, piercing feelings.

mn45:3.12.verse: “This is what those good monks and divines see as future fear from sensual desires that they speak of abandoning sensual desires and describe an (ulterior) full knowledge of sensual desires; for it is by reason of sensual desires, owing to sensual desires, that we are (now) feeling painful, racking, piercing feelings.”

mn45:4.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, suppose that in the last month of the summer a māluva-creeper pod burst open

mn45:4.2.verse: and a māluva-creeper seed fell at the foot of a sāla tree;

mn45:4.3.verse: and then a deity living in that tree was alarmed and suspicious and fearful;

mn45:4.4.verse: but the deity’s friends and companions, relatives and kin—garden deities, park deities, tree deities, deities inhabiting medicinal herbs, grass and forest-monarch trees—gathered and met together, and they soothed that deity thus:

mn45:4.5.verse: “Have no fear, good sir, have no fear.

mn45:4.6.verse: Perhaps a peacock will swallow the māluva-creeper seed or a wild animal will eat it or a forest fire will burn it or woodsmen will carry it off or white ants will devour it or it may even not be a seed”;

mn45:4.7.verse: and then no peacock swallowed that seed, no wild animal ate it, no forest fire burnt it, no woodsmen carried it off, no white ants devoured it, and it was in fact a seed; and then, being rained on by the clouds of the Rainy Season, it sprouted in due course,

mn45:4.8.verse: and the tender soft downy māluva-creeper tendril wound itself round the sāla-tree;

mn45:4.9.verse: and then the deity living in the sāla tree (thought:)

mn45:4.10.verse: “What did those friends and acquaintances, those relatives and kin—these garden deities, park deities, tree deities, deities inhabiting medicinal herbs, grass and forest-monarch trees—fancy they saw as future fear from the māluva-creeper seed that they gathered and met together and soothed (me) as they did?

mn45:4.13.verse: The contact of this māluva-creeper’s tender soft downy tendril is pleasant”;

mn45:4.14.verse: and then the creeper enfolded the sāla tree,

mn45:4.15.verse: and after that it made a canopy over it,

mn45:4.16.verse: and after that it draped a curtain all round it,

mn45:4.17.verse: and after that the main branches of the sāla tree broke,

mn45:4.18.verse: and then the deity who lived in that sāla tree (thought:)

mn45:4.19.verse: “This is what those friends and acquaintances, those relatives and kin … fancied they saw as future fear from the māluva-creeper seed that they gathered and met together and soothed (me) as they did !”

mn45:4.22.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, there are certain monks and divines whose theory and view is thus: “There is no harm in sensual desires”,

mn45:4.23.verse: and they take to gulping down sensual desires.

mn45:4.24.verse: They divert themselves with turbaned women Wanderers.

mn45:4.26.verse: “What do these good monks and divines fancy they see as future fear from sensual desires that they speak of abandoning sensual desires and describe an (ulterior) full knowledge of sensual desires.

mn45:4.27.verse: The contact of this woman Wanderer’s tender soft downy arm is pleasant”,

mn45:4.28.verse: and they take to gulping down sensual desires.

mn45:4.29.verse: Having done so, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in an unhappy destination, in the states of deprivation, in perdition, even in hell.

mn45:4.30.verse: There they feel painful, racking, piercing feelings.

mn45:4.32.verse: “This is what those good monks and divines see as future fear from sensual desires that they speak of abandoning sensual desires and describe an (ulterior) full knowledge of sensual desires;

mn45:4.33.verse: for it is by reason of sensual desires, owing to sensual desires, that we are (now) feeling painful, racking, piercing feelings.”

mn45:4.34.verse: ‘This is called a way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pain.

mn45:5.1.verse: ‘And what is a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in future as pain?

mn45:5.2.verse: Here, bhikkhus, someone goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept a thing brought or a thing specially made or an invitation;

mn45:5.3.verse: he receives nothing from out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman was lying with a man, from where food was advertised to be distributed, from where a dog was waiting, from where flies were buzzing; he accepts no fish or meat, he drinks no liquor, wine or besotting drink.

mn45:5.4.verse: He keeps to one house, to one morsel; he keeps to two houses, to two morsels … he keeps to seven houses, to seven morsels.

mn45:5.5.verse: He lives on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day;

mn45:5.6.verse: he takes food once a day, once each two days, … once each seven days; and so on, up to once each fortnight. He dwells pursuing the practice of taking food at stated intervals.

mn45:5.7.verse: He is an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-parings, or moss, or ricebran, or rinsings, or sesamum flour, or grass, or cowdung. He lives on forest roots and on fruits as a feeder on windfalls.

mn45:5.8.verse: He clothes himself in hemp, in hemp mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood (shavings) fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings.

mn45:5.9.verse: He is one who pulls out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of pulling out hair and beard.

mn45:5.10.verse: He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats.

mn45:5.11.verse: He is one who squats continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position.

mn45:5.12.verse: He is one who uses a mattress of spikes; he makes a mattress of spikes his bed.

mn45:5.13.verse: he dwells pursuing the practice of bathing in the water for the third time by nightfall.

mn45:5.14.verse: In this way he dwells pursuing the practice of self mortification in its many aspects.

mn45:5.15.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in an unhappy destination, in the states of deprivation, in perdition, even in hell.

mn45:5.16.verse: ‘This is called a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in the future as pain.

mn45:6.1.verse: ‘And what is a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in the future as pleasure?

mn45:6.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, someone is by nature much given to lust, and he constantly experiences pain and grief consequent upon lust;

mn45:6.3.verse: he is by nature much given to hate, and he constantly experiences pain and grief consequent upon hate;

mn45:6.4.verse: he is by nature much given to delusion, and he constantly experiences pain and grief consequent upon delusion;

mn45:6.5.verse: yet in pain and grief, and with tears on his face and weeping, he leads the life divine in perfect purity.

mn45:6.6.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn45:6.7.verse: ‘This is called a way of undertaking dhammas that is painful now and ripens in the future as pleasure.

mn45:7.1.verse: ‘And what is a way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pleasure?

mn45:7.2.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, someone is not by nature much given to lust, and he does not constantly experience pain and grief consequent upon lust;

mn45:7.3.verse: he is not by nature much given to hate …

mn45:7.4.verse: to delusion, and he does not constantly experience pain and grief consequent upon delusion.

mn45:7.5.verse: Quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn45:7.8.verse: the fourth jhāna … and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn45:7.9.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn45:7.10.verse: ‘This is called a way of undertaking dhammas that is pleasant now and ripens in the future as pleasure.

mn45:7.11.verse: ‘These, bhikkhus, are the four ways of undertaking dhammas.’

mn45:7.12.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn45:7.13.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn45:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on Taking Up Practices

mn45:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn45:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn45:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four ways of taking up practices.

mn45:2.3.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain.

mn45:2.4.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.

mn45:2.5.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure.

mn45:2.6.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.

mn45:3.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain?

mn45:3.2.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn45:3.4.verse: They throw themselves into sensual pleasures,

mn45:3.5.verse: cavorting with female wanderers with jeweled bands in their hair.

mn45:3.7.verse: ‘What future danger do those ascetics and brahmins see in sensual pleasures that they speak of giving up sensual pleasures, and advocate the complete understanding of sensual pleasures?

mn45:3.8.verse: Pleasant is the touch of this female wanderer’s arm, tender, soft, and downy!’ And they throw themselves into sensual pleasures.

mn45:3.9.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn45:3.10.verse: And there they feel painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings.

mn45:3.12.verse: ‘This is that future danger that those ascetics and brahmins saw. For it is because of sensual pleasures that I’m feeling painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings.’

mn45:4.1.verse: Suppose that in the last month of summer a camel’s foot creeper pod were to burst open

mn45:4.2.verse: and a seed were to fall at the root of a sal tree.

mn45:4.3.verse: Then the deity haunting that sal tree would become apprehensive and nervous.

mn45:4.4.verse: But their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin—deities of the parks, forests, trees, and those who haunt the herbs, grass, and big trees—would come together to reassure them,

mn45:4.5.verse: ‘Do not fear, sir, do not fear!

mn45:4.6.verse: Hopefully that seed will be swallowed by a peacock, or eaten by a deer, or burnt by a forest fire, or picked up by a lumberjack, or eaten by termites, or it may not even be fertile.’

mn45:4.7.verse: But none of these things happened. And the seed was fertile, so that when the monsoon clouds soaked it with rain, it sprouted.

mn45:4.8.verse: And the creeper wound its tender, soft, and downy tendrils around that sal tree.

mn45:4.10.verse: ‘What future danger did my friends see when they said:

mn45:4.11.verse: “Do not fear, sir, do not fear!

mn45:4.12.verse: Hopefully that seed will be swallowed by a peacock, or eaten by a deer, or burnt by a forest fire, or picked up by a lumberjack, or eaten by termites, or it may not even be fertile.”

mn45:4.13.verse: Pleasant is the touch of this creeper’s tender, soft, and downy tendrils.’

mn45:4.14.verse: Then the creeper enfolded the sal tree,

mn45:4.17.verse: and split apart all the main branches.

mn45:4.19.verse: ‘This is the future danger that my friends saw!

mn45:4.21.verse: It’s because of that camel’s foot creeper seed that I’m feeling painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings.’

mn45:4.22.verse: In the same way, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘There’s nothing wrong with sensual pleasures’ …

mn45:4.34.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain.

mn45:5.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain?

mn45:5.2.verse: It’s when someone goes naked, ignoring conventions. They lick their hands, and don’t come or wait when called. They don’t consent to food brought to them, or food prepared on their behalf, or an invitation for a meal.

mn45:5.3.verse: They don’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or who lives with a man; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. They accept no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drink no fermented gruel.

mn45:5.4.verse: They go to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls.

mn45:5.5.verse: They feed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

mn45:5.6.verse: They eat once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. They live committed to the practice of eating food at set intervals.

mn45:5.7.verse: They eat herbs, millet, wild rice, poor rice, water lettuce, rice bran, scum from boiling rice, sesame flour, grass, or cow dung. They survive on forest roots and fruits, or eating fallen fruit.

mn45:5.8.verse: They wear robes of sunn hemp, mixed hemp, corpse-wrapping cloth, rags, lodh tree bark, antelope hide (whole or in strips), kusa grass, bark, wood-chips, human hair, horse-tail hair, or owls’ wings.

mn45:5.9.verse: They tear out their hair and beard, committed to this practice.

mn45:5.10.verse: They constantly stand, turning down seats.

mn45:5.11.verse: They squat, committed to the endeavor of squatting.

mn45:5.12.verse: They lie on a mat of thorns, making a mat of thorns their bed.

mn45:5.13.verse: They’re devoted to ritual bathing three times a day, including at dusk.

mn45:5.14.verse: And so they live committed to practicing these various ways of mortifying and tormenting the body.

mn45:5.15.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn45:5.16.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.

mn45:6.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure?

mn45:6.2.verse: It’s when someone is ordinarily full of acute greed, hate, and delusion. They often feel the pain and sadness that greed, hate, and delusion bring.

mn45:6.5.verse: They lead the full and pure spiritual life in pain and sadness, weeping, with tearful faces.

mn45:6.6.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn45:6.7.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure.

mn45:7.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure?

mn45:7.2.verse: It’s when someone is not ordinarily full of acute greed, hate, and delusion. They rarely feel the pain and sadness that greed, hate, and delusion bring.

mn45:7.5.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption …

mn45:7.9.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn45:7.10.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.

mn45:7.11.verse: These are the four ways of taking up practices.”

mn45:7.12.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn45:7.13.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn46:0.2.verse: The Great Discourse on Taking Up Practices

mn46:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn46:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn46:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, sentient beings typically have the wish, desire, and hope:

mn46:2.2.verse: ‘Oh, if only unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things would decrease, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things would increase!’

mn46:2.3.verse: But exactly the opposite happens to them.

mn46:2.4.verse: What do you take to be the reason for this?”

mn46:2.5.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn46:2.6.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn46:3.1.verse: “Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn46:3.2.verse: They don’t know what practices they should cultivate and foster, and what practices they shouldn’t cultivate and foster.

mn46:3.3.verse: So they cultivate and foster practices they shouldn’t, and don’t cultivate and foster practices they should.

mn46:3.4.verse: When they do so, unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things increase, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things decrease.

mn46:3.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the ignorant.

mn46:4.1.verse: But a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn46:4.2.verse: They know what practices they should cultivate and foster, and what practices they shouldn’t cultivate and foster.

mn46:4.3.verse: So they cultivate and foster practices they should, and don’t cultivate and foster practices they shouldn’t.

mn46:4.4.verse: When they do so, unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things decrease, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things increase.

mn46:4.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the knowledgable.

mn46:5.1.verse: Mendicants, there are these four ways of taking up practices.

mn46:5.3.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.

mn46:5.4.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain.

mn46:5.5.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure.

mn46:5.6.verse: There is a way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.

mn46:6.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain, an ignoramus, without knowing this, doesn’t truly understand:

mn46:6.2.verse: ‘This is the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.’

mn46:6.3.verse: So instead of avoiding that practice, they cultivate it.

mn46:6.4.verse: When they do so, unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things increase, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things decrease.

mn46:6.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the ignorant.

mn46:7.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pain, an ignoramus …

mn46:8.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pleasure, an ignoramus …

mn46:9.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure, an ignoramus …

mn46:9.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the ignorant.

mn46:10.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain, a wise person, knowing this, truly understands:

mn46:10.2.verse: ‘This is the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.’

mn46:10.3.verse: So instead of cultivating that practice, they avoid it.

mn46:10.4.verse: When they do so, unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things decrease, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things increase.

mn46:10.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the knowledgable.

mn46:11.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pain, a wise person …

mn46:12.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pleasure, a wise person …

mn46:13.1.verse: When it comes to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure, a wise person, knowing this, truly understands:

mn46:13.2.verse: ‘This is the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.’

mn46:13.3.verse: So instead of avoiding that practice, they cultivate it.

mn46:13.4.verse: When they do so, unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable things decrease, and likable, desirable, and agreeable things increase.

mn46:13.6.verse: Because that’s what it’s like for the knowledgable.

mn46:14.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain?

mn46:14.2.verse: It’s when someone in pain and sadness kills living creatures, steals, and commits sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, with wrong view. Because of these things they experience pain and sadness.

mn46:14.12.verse: And when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn46:14.13.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain.

mn46:15.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain?

mn46:15.2.verse: It’s when someone with pleasure and happiness kills living creatures, steals, and commits sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, with wrong view. Because of these things they experience pleasure and happiness.

mn46:15.12.verse: But when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn46:15.13.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now but results in future pain.

mn46:16.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure?

mn46:16.2.verse: It’s when someone in pain and sadness doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, or commit sexual misconduct. They don’t use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re contented, kind-hearted, with right view. Because of these things they experience pain and sadness.

mn46:16.12.verse: But when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn46:16.13.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is painful now but results in future pleasure.

mn46:17.1.verse: And what is the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure?

mn46:17.2.verse: It’s when someone with pleasure and happiness doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, or commit sexual misconduct. They don’t use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re contented, kind-hearted, with right view. Because of these things they experience pleasure and happiness.

mn46:17.12.verse: And when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn46:17.13.verse: This is called the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure.

mn46:17.14.verse: These are the four ways of taking up practices.

mn46:18.1.verse: Suppose there was some bitter gourd mixed with poison.

mn46:18.2.verse: Then a man would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.

mn46:18.4.verse: ‘Here, my man, this is bitter gourd mixed with poison.

mn46:18.6.verse: If you drink it, the color, aroma, and flavor will be unappetizing, and it will result in death or deadly pain.’

mn46:18.7.verse: He wouldn’t put it down. Without appraisal, he’d drink it.

mn46:18.8.verse: The color, aroma, and flavor would be unappetizing, and it would result in death or deadly pain.

mn46:18.9.verse: This is comparable to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pain, I say.

mn46:19.1.verse: Suppose there was a bronze goblet of beverage that had a nice color, aroma, and flavor.

mn46:19.2.verse: But it was mixed with poison.

mn46:19.3.verse: Then a man would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.

mn46:19.5.verse: ‘Here, my man, this bronze goblet of beverage has a nice color, aroma, and flavor.

mn46:19.8.verse: If you drink it, the color, aroma, and flavor will be appetizing, but it will result in death or deadly pain.’

mn46:19.9.verse: He wouldn’t put it down. Without appraisal, he’d drink it.

mn46:19.10.verse: The color, aroma, and flavor would be appetizing, but it would result in death or deadly pain.

mn46:19.11.verse: This is comparable to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pain, I say.

mn46:20.1.verse: Suppose there was some rancid urine mixed with different medicines.

mn46:20.2.verse: Then a man with jaundice would come along.

mn46:20.4.verse: ‘Here, my man, this is rancid urine mixed with different medicines. Drink it if you like.

mn46:20.5.verse: If you drink it, the color, aroma, and flavor will be unappetizing, but after drinking it you will be happy.’

mn46:20.6.verse: He wouldn’t put it down. After appraisal, he’d drink it.

mn46:20.7.verse: The color, aroma, and flavor would be unappetizing, but after drinking it he would be happy.

mn46:20.8.verse: This is comparable to the way of taking up practices that is painful now and results in future pleasure, I say.

mn46:21.1.verse: Suppose there was some curds, honey, ghee, and molasses all mixed together.

mn46:21.2.verse: Then a man with bloody dysentery would come along.

mn46:21.4.verse: ‘Here, my man, this is curds, honey, ghee, and molasses all mixed together. Drink it if you like.

mn46:21.5.verse: If you drink it, the color, aroma, and flavor will be appetizing, and after drinking it you will be happy.’

mn46:21.6.verse: He wouldn’t put it down. After appraisal, he’d drink it.

mn46:21.7.verse: The color, aroma, and flavor would be appetizing, and after drinking it he would be happy.

mn46:21.8.verse: This is comparable to the way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure, I say.

mn46:22.1.verse: It’s like the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the heavens are sunny and cloudless. And as the sun is rising to the firmament, having dispelled all the darkness of space, it shines and glows and dazzles.

mn46:22.2.verse: In the same way, this way of taking up practices that is pleasant now and results in future pleasure dispels the doctrines of the various other ascetics and brahmins as it shines and glows and dazzles.”

mn46:22.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn46:22.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn47:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.

mn47:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn47:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is an inquirer who knows (how to gauge) the state of another’s heart, research should be made by him with respect to a Tathāgata in order to recognize or not he is fully enlightened.’

mn47:3.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, our dhammas are rooted in the Blessed One, they are guided by the Blessed One, they are centred in the Blessed One. It is good that the meaning of these words should occur to the Blessed One. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.’

mn47:3.2.verse: ‘Then listen, bhikkhus, and heed well what I shall say.’

mn47:4.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is an inquirer who knows (how to gauge) the state of another’s heart, a Tathāgata should be searched with respect to two kinds of dhammas: with respect to dhammas cognizable through the eye and the ear:

mn47:4.2.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be defiled, or not?”

mn47:4.3.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:4.4.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are defiled are not found in a Tathāgata.”

mn47:5.2.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are defiled are not found in a Tathāgata” — with that he makes a further search thus:

mn47:5.3.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be mixed,[^2] or not?”

mn47:5.4.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:5.5.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are mixed are not found in a Tathāgata.”

mn47:6.2.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are mixed are not found in a Tathāgata” — with that he makes a further search thus:

mn47:6.3.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be cleansed, or not?”

mn47:6.4.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:6.5.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are cleansed are found in a Tathāgata.”

mn47:7.2.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are cleansed are found in a Tathāgata” — with that he makes a further search thus:

mn47:7.3.verse: “Has this venerable one long perfected this profitable dhamma, or recently perfected it?”

mn47:7.4.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:7.5.verse: “This venerable one has long perfected this profitable dhamma, he has not recently perfected it.”

mn47:8.2.verse: “This venerable one has long perfected this profitable dhamma, he has not recently perfected it” — with that he makes a further search thus:

mn47:8.3.verse: “Has this venerable one acquired renown, has he reached fame? Are certain dangers in this connexion found in him?”

mn47:8.4.verse: For, bhikkhus, as long as a bhikkhu has not acquired renown or reached fame, certain dangers in this connexion are not found in him,

mn47:8.5.verse: but as soon as he has acquired renown and reached fame, they are found.

mn47:8.6.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:8.7.verse: “This venerable one has acquired renown and reached fame, but certain dangers in this connexion are not found in him.”

mn47:9.2.verse: “This venerable one has acquired renown and reached fame, but certain dangers in this connexion are not found in him” — with that he makes a further search thus:

mn47:9.3.verse: “Is this venerable one fearlessly restrained, and not restrained out of fear,

mn47:9.4.verse: and when he does not indulge in sensual desires is it because he is without lust, because of the exhaustion of lust?”

mn47:9.5.verse: When he searches, he comes to know:

mn47:9.6.verse: “This venerable one is fearlessly restrained, and not restrained out of fear,

mn47:9.7.verse: and his non-indulgence in sensual desires is because he is without lust, because of the exhaustion of lust.”

mn47:10.1.verse: ‘Now if others should ask that bhikkhu:

mn47:10.2.verse: “What is his evidence and what is his inference whereby the venerable one speaks as he does—

mn47:10.3.verse: ‘this venerable one is fearlessly restrained, and not restrained out of fear,

mn47:10.4.verse: and his non-indulgence in sensual desires is because he is without lust, because of the exhaustion of lust’?”

mn47:10.5.verse: Then, answering rightly, the bhikkhu would answer thus:

mn47:10.6.verse: ‘Whether that venerable one dwells in a sangha or alone, while there may be some who are well behaved there and some who are ill behaved there and some who teach a group there and some who show themselves (concerned about) material things and some who are unsullied by material things, still that venerable one belittles no one for that.

mn47:10.7.verse: And I have heard and learnt this in that Blessed One’s own presence, received in his own presence:

mn47:10.8.verse: ‘I am fearlessly restrained and not restrained out of fear, and that I do not indulge in sensual desires is because I am without lust, because of the exhaustion of lust.’”

mn47:11.1.verse: ‘About that, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata should be questioned further thus:

mn47:11.2.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be defiled, or not?”

mn47:11.3.verse: Answering, a Tathāgata would answer thus:

mn47:11.4.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are defiled are not found in a Tathāgata.”

mn47:12.1.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be mixed, or not?”

mn47:12.2.verse: Answering, a Tathāgata would answer thus:

mn47:12.3.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are mixed are not found in a Tathāgata.”

mn47:13.1.verse: “Whether in a Tathāgata’s case dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear are found to be cleansed, or not?”

mn47:13.2.verse: Answering, a Tathāgata would answer thus:

mn47:13.3.verse: “Dhammas cognizable through the eye and ear that are cleansed are found in a Tathāgata;

mn47:13.4.verse: while I have that for my sphere and that for my range, I remain aloof from it.”

mn47:14.1.verse: ‘The teacher who speaks thus is fit for a disciple to approach for the sake of hearing the Dhamma.

mn47:14.2.verse: The teacher shows him the Dhamma at each higher (level), at each superior (stage), with the dark and bright counterparts.

mn47:14.3.verse: According as the teacher shows the Dhamma to a bhikkhu in this way, so he, by directly-knowing some dhamma among the dhammas in that Dhamma, reaches (his) goal, and he has confidence in the Teacher thus:

mn47:14.4.verse: ‘The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way.’

mn47:15.1.verse: ‘Now if others should ask that bhikkhu:

mn47:15.2.verse: “What is his evidence and what is his inference that the venerable one speaks as he does—

mn47:15.3.verse: ‘the Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way’?”

mn47:15.4.verse: Then, answering rightly, the bhikkhu would answer thus:

mn47:15.5.verse: ‘Here, friends, I approached that Blessed One for the sake of hearing the Dhamma.

mn47:15.6.verse: The Teacher showed me the Dhamma at each higher (level), at each superior (stage), with the dark and bright counterparts.

mn47:15.7.verse: According as he did so, I came to direct-knowledge here and now of a certain dhamma among the dhammas in that Dhamma, and I reached (my) goal, and I had confidence in the Teacher thus:

mn47:15.8.verse: ‘The Blessed One is fully enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed, the Sangha has entered on the good way.’”

mn47:16.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, when someone’s faith in a Tathāgata has by these evidences, these terms and phrases been planted, made to take root and established, then his faith is called supported by evidence, rooted in vision,

mn47:16.2.verse: sound, and invincible by monk or divine or Māra or Divinity or anyone in the world.

mn47:16.3.verse: That is how research with respect to a Tathāgata is according to the Dhamma,

mn47:16.4.verse: and that is how a Tathāgata is well sought in accordance with the Dhamma.’

mn47:16.5.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn47:16.6.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn47:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn47:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn47:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who is an inquirer, unable to encompass another’s mind, should scrutinize the Realized One to understand whether he is a fully awakened Buddha or not.”

mn47:3.1.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn47:3.2.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn47:4.1.verse: “Mendicants, a mendicant who is an inquirer, unable to encompass another’s mind, should scrutinize the Realized One for two things—things that can be seen and heard:

mn47:4.2.verse: ‘Can anything corrupt be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:4.4.verse: nothing corrupt can be seen or heard in the Realized One.

mn47:5.3.verse: ‘Can anything mixed be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:5.5.verse: nothing mixed can be seen or heard in the Realized One.

mn47:6.3.verse: ‘Can anything clean be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:6.5.verse: clean things can be seen and heard in the Realized One.

mn47:7.3.verse: ‘Did the venerable attain this skillful state a long time ago, or just recently?’

mn47:7.5.verse: the venerable attained this skillful state a long time ago, not just recently.

mn47:8.3.verse: ‘Are certain dangers found in that venerable mendicant who has achieved fame and renown?’

mn47:8.4.verse: For, mendicants, so long as a mendicant has not achieved fame and renown, certain dangers are not found in them.

mn47:8.5.verse: But when they achieve fame and renown, those dangers appear.

mn47:8.7.verse: those dangers are not found in that venerable mendicant who has achieved fame and renown.

mn47:9.3.verse: ‘Is this venerable securely stilled or insecurely stilled?

mn47:9.4.verse: Is the reason they don’t indulge in sensual pleasures that they’re free of greed because greed has ended?’

mn47:9.6.verse: that venerable is securely stilled, not insecurely stilled.

mn47:9.7.verse: The reason they don’t indulge in sensual pleasures is that they’re free of greed because greed has ended.

mn47:10.1.verse: If others should ask that mendicant,

mn47:10.2.verse: ‘But what reason and evidence does the venerable have for saying this?’

mn47:10.5.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say,

mn47:10.6.verse: ‘Because, whether that venerable is staying in a community or alone, some people there are in a good state or a sorry state, some instruct a group, and some are seen among pleasures of the flesh while others remain unsullied. Yet that venerable doesn’t look down on them for that.

mn47:10.7.verse: Also, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn47:10.8.verse: “I am securely stilled, not insecurely stilled. The reason I don’t indulge in sensual pleasures is that I’m free of greed because greed has ended.”’

mn47:11.1.verse: Next, they should ask the Realized One himself about this,

mn47:11.2.verse: ‘Can anything corrupt be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:11.4.verse: ‘Nothing corrupt can be seen or heard in the Realized One.’

mn47:12.1.verse: ‘Can anything mixed be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:12.3.verse: ‘Nothing mixed can be seen or heard in the Realized One.’

mn47:13.1.verse: ‘Can anything clean be seen or heard in the Realized One or not?’

mn47:13.3.verse: ‘Clean things can be seen and heard in the Realized One.

mn47:13.4.verse: I am the scope and the range of that, but I am not determined by that.’

mn47:14.1.verse: A disciple ought to approach a teacher who has such a doctrine in order to listen to the teaching.

mn47:14.2.verse: The teacher explains Dhamma with its higher and higher stages, with its better and better stages, with its dark and bright sides.

mn47:14.3.verse: When they directly know a certain principle of those teachings, in accordance with how they were taught, the mendicant comes to a conclusion about the teachings. They have confidence in the Teacher:

mn47:14.4.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha! The teaching is well explained! The Saṅgha is practicing well!’

mn47:15.1.verse: If others should ask that mendicant,

mn47:15.2.verse: ‘But what reason and evidence does the venerable have for saying this?’

mn47:15.4.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say,

mn47:15.5.verse: ‘Reverends, I approached the Buddha to listen to the teaching.

mn47:15.6.verse: He explained Dhamma with its higher and higher stages, with its better and better stages, with its dark and bright sides.

mn47:15.7.verse: When I directly knew a certain principle of those teachings, in accordance with how I was taught, I came to a conclusion about the teachings. I had confidence in the Teacher:

mn47:15.8.verse: “The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha! The teaching is well explained! The Saṅgha is practicing well!”’

mn47:16.1.verse: When someone’s faith is settled, rooted, and planted in the Realized One in this manner, with these words and phrases, it’s said to be grounded faith that’s based on evidence.

mn47:16.2.verse: It is strong, and cannot be shifted by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

mn47:16.3.verse: That is how there is legitimate scrutiny of the Realized One,

mn47:16.4.verse: and that is how the Realized One is legitimately well-scrutinized.”

mn47:16.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn47:16.6.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn48:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Kosambī at Ghosita’s monastery.

mn48:2.1.verse: And on that occasion the monks in Kosambī were given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth.

mn48:2.2.verse: They did not persuade one another, and did not agree to be persuaded by one another. They did not convince one another, and did not agree to be convinced by one another.

mn48:3.1.verse: Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One:

mn48:3.2.verse: “Lord, the monks in Kosambī are now given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth. They don’t persuade one another, and don’t agree to be persuaded by one another. They don’t convince one another, and don’t agree to be convinced by one another.

mn48:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One told a certain monk,

mn48:4.2.verse: “Come, monk. In my name, call those monks, saying,

mn48:4.4.verse: Responding, “As you say, lord,” to the Blessed One, the monk went to those monks, and on arrival he said to them,

mn48:4.6.verse: Responding, “As you say, my friend,” to the monk, those monks went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them,

mn48:4.7.verse: “Is it true, monks, that you are given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth?

mn48:4.8.verse: That you don’t persuade one another, and don’t agree to be persuaded by one another? That you don’t convince one another, and don’t agree to be convinced by one another?”

mn48:5.1.verse: “And while you are given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth,

mn48:5.2.verse: are you set on bodily acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs? Are you set on verbal acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs? Are you set on mental acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs?”

mn48:5.4.verse: “So then, while you are given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth, you are not set on bodily acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs; you are not set on verbal acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs; you are not set on mental acts of good will with regard to your companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:5.5.verse: Then what could you worthless men possibly know or see that you are given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing one another with weapons of the mouth?

mn48:5.6.verse: That will be to your long-term harm and suffering.”

mn48:6.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:

mn48:6.2.verse: “Monks, these six are conditions that are conducive to amiability, that engender feelings of endearment, engender feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.4.verse: “There is the case where a monk is set on bodily acts of good will with regard to his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:6.5.verse: This is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.6.verse: “And further, the monk is set on verbal acts of good will with regard to his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:6.7.verse: This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.8.verse: “And further, the monk is set on mental acts of good will with regard to his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:6.9.verse: This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.10.verse: “And further, whatever righteous gains the monk may obtain in a righteous way—even if only the alms in his bowl—he does not consume them alone. He consumes them after sharing them in common with his virtuous companions in the holy life.

mn48:6.11.verse: This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.12.verse: “And further—with reference to the virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the observant, ungrasped at, leading to concentration—the monk dwells with his virtue in tune with that of his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:6.13.verse: This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.14.verse: “And further—with reference to the view that is noble, leading outward, that leads those who act in accordance with it to the right ending of suffering & stress—the monk dwells with a view in tune with those of his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs.

mn48:6.15.verse: This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:6.16.verse: “These are the six conditions that are conducive to amiability, that engender feelings of endearment, engender feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity.

mn48:7.1.verse: “Of these six conditions conducive to amiability, this is the summit, this the girding, this the kingpin: the view that is noble, leading outward, that leads those who act in accordance with it to the right ending of suffering & stress.

mn48:7.2.verse: Just as in a building with a ridged roof, this is the summit, this the girding, this the kingpin: the ridge beam;

mn48:7.3.verse: in the same way, of these six conditions conducive to amiability, this is the summit, this the girding, this the kingpin: the view that is noble, leading outward, that leads those who act in accordance with it to the right ending of suffering & stress.

mn48:8.1.verse: “And how is there the view that is noble, leading outward, that leads those who act in accordance with it to the right ending of suffering & stress?

mn48:8.2.verse: “There is the case where a monk, having gone to the wilderness, to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, considers thus:

mn48:8.3.verse: ‘Is there any internal subjugation unabandoned in me that, subjugated by which, my subjugated mind would not know or see things as they have come to be?’

mn48:8.4.verse: If a monk is subjugated by sensual passion, monks, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.5.verse: If he is subjugated by ill will, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.6.verse: If he is subjugated by sloth & torpor, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.7.verse: If he is subjugated by restlessness & anxiety, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.8.verse: If he is subjugated by uncertainty, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.9.verse: If a monk is absorbed in speculation about this world, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.10.verse: If a monk is absorbed in speculation about the other world, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.11.verse: If a monk is given to arguing and quarreling and disputing, stabbing others with weapons of the mouth, then his mind is subjugated.

mn48:8.13.verse: ‘There is no subjugation unabandoned in me that, subjugated by which, my subjugated mind would not know and see things as they have come to be.

mn48:8.14.verse: My mind is well directed for awakening to the truths.’

mn48:8.15.verse: This is the first knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:9.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:9.2.verse: ‘When I cultivate, develop, and pursue this view, do I personally obtain tranquility, do I personally obtain unbinding?’

mn48:9.4.verse: ‘When I cultivate, develop, and pursue this view, I personally obtain tranquility, I personally obtain unbinding.’

mn48:9.5.verse: This is the second knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:10.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:10.2.verse: ‘Is there, outside of this (Dhamma & Vinaya), any other contemplative or brahman endowed with the sort of view with which I am endowed?’

mn48:10.4.verse: ‘There is no other contemplative or brahman outside (the Dhamma & Vinaya) endowed with the sort of view with which I am endowed.’

mn48:10.5.verse: This is the third knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:11.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:11.2.verse: ‘I am endowed with the character of a person consummate in view?’

mn48:11.3.verse: And what, monks, is the character of a person consummate in view?

mn48:11.4.verse: This is the character of a person consummate in view:

mn48:11.5.verse: Although he may commit some kind of offence for which a means of rehabilitation has been laid down, still he immediately confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to observant companions in the holy life;

mn48:11.6.verse: having done that, he undertakes restraint for the future.

mn48:11.7.verse: Just as a young, tender infant lying on his back, when he has hit a live ember with his hand or his foot, immediately draws back;

mn48:11.8.verse: in the same way, this is the character of a person consummate in view:

mn48:11.9.verse: Although he may commit some kind of offence for which a means of rehabilitation has been laid down, still he immediately confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to observant companions in the holy life;

mn48:11.10.verse: having done that, he undertakes restraint for the future.

mn48:11.12.verse: ‘I am endowed with the character of a person consummate in view.’

mn48:11.13.verse: This is the fourth knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:12.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:12.2.verse: ‘I am endowed with the character of a person consummate in view?’

mn48:12.3.verse: And what, monks, is the character of a person consummate in view?

mn48:12.4.verse: This is the character of a person consummate in view:

mn48:12.5.verse: Although he may be active in the various affairs of his companions in the holy life, he still has a keen regard for training in heightened virtue, training in heightened mind, & training in heightened discernment.

mn48:12.6.verse: Just as a cow with a new calf watches after her calf all the while she is grazing on grass,

mn48:12.7.verse: in the same way, this is the character of a person consummate in view:

mn48:12.8.verse: Although he may be active in the various affairs of his companions in the holy life, he still has a keen regard for training in heightened virtue, training in heightened mind, & training in heightened discernment.

mn48:12.10.verse: ‘I am endowed with the character of a person consummate in view.’

mn48:12.11.verse: This is the fifth knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:13.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:13.2.verse: ‘I am endowed with the strength of a person consummate in view?’

mn48:13.3.verse: And what, monks, is the strength of a person consummate in view?

mn48:13.4.verse: This is the strength of a person consummate in view: When the Dhamma & Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, he heeds it, gives it attention, engages it with all his mind, hears the Dhamma with eager ears.

mn48:13.6.verse: ‘I am endowed with the strength of a person consummate in view.’

mn48:13.7.verse: This is the sixth knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:14.1.verse: “And further, the disciple of the noble ones considers thus:

mn48:14.2.verse: ‘I am endowed with the strength of a person consummate in view?’

mn48:14.3.verse: And what, monks, is the strength of a person consummate in view?

mn48:14.4.verse: This is the strength of a person consummate in view: When the Dhamma & Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, he gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, gains gladness connected with the Dhamma.

mn48:14.6.verse: ‘I am endowed with the strength of a person consummate in view.’

mn48:14.7.verse: This is the seventh knowledge attained by him that is noble, transcendent, not held in common with run-of-the-mill people.

mn48:15.1.verse: “A disciple of the noble ones thus endowed with seven factors has well examined the character for the realization of the fruit of stream entry.

mn48:15.2.verse: A disciple of the noble ones thus endowed with seven factors is endowed with the fruit of stream entry.”

mn48:15.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn48:15.4.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn48:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

mn48:2.1.verse: Now at that time the mendicants of Kosambī were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

mn48:2.2.verse: They couldn’t persuade each other or be persuaded, nor could they convince each other or be convinced.

mn48:3.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

mn48:4.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

mn48:4.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell those mendicants that

mn48:4.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to those monks and said,

mn48:4.6.verse: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied. They went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them,

mn48:4.7.verse: “Is it really true, mendicants, that you have been fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words?

mn48:4.8.verse: And that you can’t persuade each other or be persuaded, nor can you convince each other or be convinced?”

mn48:5.2.verse: When you’re fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words, are you treating your spiritual companions with kindness by way of body, speech, and mind, both in public and in private?”

mn48:5.4.verse: “So it seems that when you’re arguing you are not treating each other with kindness.

mn48:5.5.verse: So what then do you know and see, you futile men, that you behave in such a way?

mn48:5.6.verse: This will be for your lasting harm and suffering.”

mn48:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

mn48:6.2.verse: “Mendicants, these six warm-hearted qualities make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without quarreling.

mn48:6.4.verse: Firstly, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with bodily kindness, both in public and in private.

mn48:6.5.verse: This warm-hearted quality makes for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without quarreling.

mn48:6.6.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with verbal kindness …

mn48:6.8.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with mental kindness …

mn48:6.10.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant shares without reservation any material things they have gained by legitimate means, even the food placed in the alms-bowl, using them in common with their ethical spiritual companions …

mn48:6.12.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives according to the precepts shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private. Those precepts are intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion. …

mn48:6.14.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives according to the view shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private. That view is noble and emancipating, and delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.

mn48:6.15.verse: This warm-hearted quality makes for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without quarreling.

mn48:6.16.verse: These six warm-hearted qualities make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without quarreling.

mn48:7.1.verse: Of these six warm-hearted qualities, the chief is the view that is noble and emancipating, and delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering. It holds and binds everything together.

mn48:7.2.verse: It’s like a bungalow. The roof-peak is the chief point, which holds and binds everything together.

mn48:7.3.verse: In the same way, of these six warm-hearted qualities, the chief is the view that is noble and emancipating, and delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering. It holds and binds everything together.

mn48:8.1.verse: And how does the view that is noble and emancipating lead one who practices it to the complete ending of suffering?

mn48:8.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this,

mn48:8.3.verse: ‘Is there anything that I’m overcome with internally and haven’t given up, because of which I might not accurately know and see?’

mn48:8.4.verse: If a mendicant is overcome with sensual desire, it’s their mind that’s overcome.

mn48:8.5.verse: If a mendicant is overcome with ill will,

mn48:8.10.verse: pursuing speculation about the next world,

mn48:8.11.verse: or fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding others with barbed words, it’s their mind that’s overcome.

mn48:8.13.verse: ‘There is nothing that I’m overcome with internally and haven’t given up, because of which I might not accurately know and see.

mn48:8.14.verse: My heart is properly disposed for awakening to the truths.’

mn48:8.15.verse: This is the first knowledge they have achieved that is noble and transcendent, and is distinct from that of ordinary people.

mn48:9.2.verse: ‘When I develop, cultivate, and make much of this view, do I personally gain serenity and quenching?’

mn48:9.4.verse: ‘When I develop, cultivate, and make much of this view, I personally gain serenity and quenching.’

mn48:10.2.verse: ‘Are there any ascetics or brahmins outside of the Buddhist community who have the same kind of view that I have?’

mn48:10.4.verse: ‘There are no ascetics or brahmins outside of the Buddhist community who have the same kind of view that I have.’

mn48:11.2.verse: ‘Do I have the same nature as an individual accomplished in view?’

mn48:11.3.verse: And what, mendicants, is the nature of an individual accomplished in view?

mn48:11.4.verse: This is the nature of an individual accomplished in view.

mn48:11.5.verse: Though they may fall into a kind of offense for which rehabilitation is possible, they quickly explain, clarify, and disclose it to the Teacher or a sensible spiritual companion.

mn48:11.6.verse: And having revealed it they restrain themselves in the future.

mn48:11.7.verse: Suppose there was a little baby boy. If he puts his hand or foot on a burning coal, he quickly pulls it back.

mn48:11.8.verse: In the same way, this is the nature of an individual accomplished in view.

mn48:11.9.verse: Though they may still fall into a kind of offense for which rehabilitation is possible, they quickly disclose it to the Teacher or a sensible spiritual companion.

mn48:11.10.verse: And having revealed it they restrain themselves in the future.

mn48:11.12.verse: ‘I have the same nature as an individual accomplished in view.’

mn48:12.2.verse: ‘Do I have the same nature as an individual accomplished in view?’

mn48:12.3.verse: And what, mendicants, is the nature of an individual accomplished in view?

mn48:12.4.verse: This is the nature of an individual accomplished in view.

mn48:12.5.verse: Though they might manage a diverse spectrum of duties for their spiritual companions, they still feel a keen regard for the training in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom.

mn48:12.6.verse: Suppose there was a cow with a baby calf. She watches her calf devotedly as she grazes.

mn48:12.7.verse: In the same way, this is the nature of an individual accomplished in view.

mn48:12.8.verse: Though they might manage a diverse spectrum of duties for their spiritual companions, they still feel a keen regard for the training in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom.

mn48:12.10.verse: ‘I have the same nature as an individual accomplished in view.’

mn48:13.2.verse: ‘Do I have the same strength as an individual accomplished in view?’

mn48:13.3.verse: And what, mendicants, is the strength of an individual accomplished in view?

mn48:13.4.verse: The strength of an individual accomplished in view is that, when the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One are being taught, they pay attention, apply the mind, concentrate wholeheartedly, and actively listen to the teaching.

mn48:13.6.verse: ‘I have the same strength as an individual accomplished in view.’

mn48:14.2.verse: ‘Do I have the same strength as an individual accomplished in view?’

mn48:14.3.verse: And what, mendicants, is the strength of an individual accomplished in view?

mn48:14.4.verse: The strength of an individual accomplished in view is that, when the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One are being taught, they find inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and find joy connected with the teaching.

mn48:14.6.verse: ‘I have the same strength as an individual accomplished in view.’

mn48:14.7.verse: This is the seventh knowledge they have achieved that is noble and transcendent, and is distinct from that of ordinary people.

mn48:15.1.verse: When a noble disciple has these seven factors, they have properly investigated their nature through the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.

mn48:15.2.verse: A noble disciple with these seven factors has the fruit of stream-entry.”

mn48:15.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn48:15.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn49:1.1.verse:
In this sutta, the Buddha faces two antagonists: Baka, a Brahmā who believes that his Brahmā-attainment is the highest attainment there is; and Māra, who wants (1) to keep Baka under his power by allowing Baka to maintain his deluded opinion, and (2) to prevent the Buddha from sharing his awakened knowledge with others. Of the two, Māra is the more insidious, a point illustrated by the fact that Māra always speaks through someone else and never directly shows his face. (Another interesting point is illustrated by the fact that Māra is the source of the demand that one obey a creator god.)

In overcoming his antagonists, the Buddha asserts the superiority of his knowledge in two major fashions: through a description of his awakened knowledge and through a display of psychic powers.

The Buddha describes his awakened knowledge in a variety of ways:

—by identifying Māra whenever he possesses an attendant of Baka’s assembly,
—by describing the full extent of Baka’s power,
—by identifying levels of being that Baka does not know,
—by describing an awakened consciousness that is not known by means of any of the six senses at all,
—by asserting an awareness that avoids delight in both becoming and the quest for non-becoming, and
—by asserting that he has abandoned all possible conditions that would lead to further rebirth.

Some of these assertions—in particular, the assertion of a consciousness not mediated by any of the six senses—are extremely important Dhamma lessons, which are further explained in the notes. But as the sutta shows, even the Buddha’s description of these teachings was not enough to win over Baka or the members of his following. They were convinced only when the Buddha then performed a feat of psychic power that (1) even Baka could not fathom and (2) illustrated the Buddha’s major point. Up to then, in identifying Māra and the range of Baka’s power, the Buddha was in effect saying, “I see you, but you don’t see me.” With his display of psychic power, in which Brahmā and his following could not see him but could hear his voice, he demonstrated his point in such graphic terms that Baka and his following were immediately won over.

In this way, the protagonists of this sutta react in a way very different from that of a typical modern reader. We at present, when reading this sutta, may be more impressed with the Buddha’s explanation of his awakened knowledge than we are with the account of his display of psychic power, for after all, both aspects of the sutta—the description of the Buddha’s knowledge and the description of his psychic power—are, for us, just that: descriptions. But, for those who witnessed it, his display of power was an undeniable fact that went beyond words. They saw him go beyond their range. Prior to that display, they regarded his claims of knowledge simply as that: mere claims. When he showed, however, that he could perform a miracle that even Baka could not perform, they were forced to concede his superiority. Thus this sutta imparts a lesson often forgotten at present, that the Buddha taught not only by word but also by example, and that some of his examples required a dimension of power that even the gods could not match.

Strictly speaking, of course, the Buddha’s display of power did not prove that he had gone beyond becoming. After all, in becoming invisible to Baka, he may simply have gone to another level of becoming of which Baka was unaware. However, the Buddha correctly surmised that a display of power would subdue the pride of his listeners, awaken a sense of conviction in his attainment, and thus enable them to enter the path of practice. As he states in MN 27, only when one sees the four noble truths—usually a synonym for stream-entry—is one’s conviction in the Buddha’s awakening confirmed. Only when one puts an end to one’s mental effluents does one have firm proof of the Buddha’s awakening. The Buddha notes in DN 11 that a display of psychic powers can sometimes backfire, in that one’s audience might assume that one is engaging in cheap magic tricks. Thus, instead of inspiring conviction, the display simply increases doubt. Nevertheless, there are other instances in the Canon—most notably in the story of the Kassapa brothers (Mv.I.15-22) and that of Aṅgulimāla (MN 86)—where the Buddha was able to display his powers to good effect. But because he could not trust even his arahant disciples to possess his same sense of when such powers would work and when they would backfire, he forbade his disciples from displaying psychic powers to lay people. (See Cv.V.8; Buddhist Monastic Code, vol. 2, chapter 10.)

The conclusion of the sutta states that the sutta’s name comes from two facets of the story: the fact that it contains an invitation from a Brahmā—when Baka welcomes the Buddha to his realm—and from the silencing of Māra. The first point is clear enough, but the second requires explanation. It is a play on the word Brahmā, which is not only a noun denoting the highest levels of devas, but also an adjective meaning “of great or high power.” The Buddha’s last statement, in which he declares his freedom from rebirth, is something of an invitation to Māra: Māra is welcome to refute it if he can. Up to that point, Māra has phrased his threats to the Buddha in terms of the fortunate rebirths the Buddha will experience if he obeys Māra’s advice, and the unfortunate ones he will experience if he doesn’t.
