Now that the Buddha declares, in a way that Māra cannot refute, that he has abandoned all possible conditions for rebirth, Māra has nothing more on which to base his threats. Thus he is left speechless. In this way, the Buddha’s last statement is a brahma-invitation: a statement that anyone is welcome to refute, but of such great power that no one can refute it at all.

I have heard that

mn49:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn49:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn49:2.1.verse: “On one occasion recently I was staying in Ukkaṭṭha in the Subhaga forest at the root of a royal Sal tree.

mn49:2.2.verse: Now on that occasion an evil viewpoint had arisen to Baka Brahmā:

mn49:2.3.verse: ‘This is constant. This is permanent. This is eternal. This is total. This is not subject to falling away—for this does not take birth, does not age, does not die, does not fall away, does not reappear. And there is no other, higher escape.’

mn49:3.1.verse: “So I—having known with my awareness the line of thinking in Baka Brahmā’s awareness—

mn49:3.2.verse: as a strong man would extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, vanished into the root of the royal Sal tree in the Subhaga forest in Ukkaṭṭha and appeared in that Brahmā world.

mn49:3.3.verse: Baka Brahmā saw me coming in the distance and,

mn49:3.5.verse: ‘Come, good sir. You are well-come, good sir.

mn49:3.6.verse: It has been long, good sir, since you arranged to come here—

mn49:3.7.verse: for this, good sir, is constant. This is permanent. This is eternal. This is total. This is not subject to falling away—for here one does not take birth, does not age, does not die, does not fall away, does not reappear. And there is no other, higher escape.’

mn49:4.1.verse: “When this was said, I told Baka Brahmā,

mn49:4.2.verse: ‘How immersed in ignorance is Baka Brahmā! How immersed in ignorance is Baka Brahmā! —

mn49:4.3.verse: in that what is actually inconstant he calls “constant.” What is actually impermanent he calls “permanent.” What is actually non-eternal he calls “eternal.” What is actually partial he calls “total.” What is actually subject to falling away he calls “not subject to falling away.”

mn49:4.4.verse: Where one takes birth, ages, dies, falls away, and reappears, he says,

mn49:4.5.verse: “For here one does not take birth, does not age, does not die, does not fall away, does not reappear.”

mn49:4.6.verse: And there being another, higher escape, he says, “There is no other, higher escape.”’

mn49:5.1.verse: “Then Māra, the Evil One, taking possession of an attendant of the Brahmā assembly, said to me,

mn49:5.2.verse: ‘Monk! Monk! Don’t attack him! Don’t attack him! For this Brahmā, monk, is the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, All-Powerful, the Sovereign Lord, the Maker, Creator, Chief, Appointer and Ruler, Father of All That Have Been and Shall Be.

mn49:5.3.verse: There were, monk, before your time, contemplatives & brahmans in the world who found fault with earth and were disgusted with earth, who found fault with liquid and were disgusted with liquid, who found fault with fire and were disgusted with fire, who found fault with wind and were disgusted with wind, who found fault with beings and were disgusted with beings, who found fault with devas and were disgusted with devas, who found fault with Pajāpati and were disgusted with Pajāpati, who found fault with Brahmā and were disgusted with Brahmā.

mn49:5.4.verse: “‘They, with the break-up of the body, with the cutting off of life, were established in a coarse body.

mn49:5.5.verse: There were, monk, before your time, contemplatives & brahmans in the world who praised earth and were delighted with earth, who praised liquid and were delighted with liquid, who praised fire and were delighted with fire, who praised wind and were delighted with wind, who praised beings and were delighted with beings, who praised devas and were delighted with devas, who praised Pajāpati and were delighted with Pajāpati, who praised Brahmā and were delighted with Brahmā.

mn49:5.6.verse: “‘They, with the break-up of the body, with the cutting off of life, were established in a refined body.

mn49:5.8.verse: “Please, good sir, do only as Brahmā says. Don’t defy the word of Brahmā.

mn49:5.9.verse: If you defy the word of Brahmā, then—as a man, when the goddess of fortune approaches, chases her away with a stick, or as a man, falling into hell, loses hold of the earth with his hands and feet—that will be what you have accomplished.

mn49:5.10.verse: Please, good sir, do only as Brahmā says. Don’t defy the word of Brahmā.

mn49:5.11.verse: Don’t you see that Brahmā’s assembly has gathered?”’

mn49:5.12.verse: And so Māra the Evil One directed my attention to Brahmā’s assembly.

mn49:6.1.verse: “When this was said, I told Māra the Evil One,

mn49:6.2.verse: ‘I know you, Evil One. Don’t assume,

mn49:6.5.verse: And Brahmā, and Brahmā’s assembly, and the attendants of Brahmā’s assembly have all come into your hands. They have all come under your sway.

mn49:6.7.verse: “This one, too, has come into my hands, has come under my sway.”

mn49:6.8.verse: But, Evil One, I have neither come into your hands nor have I come under your sway.’

mn49:7.1.verse: “When this was said, Baka Brahmā told me,

mn49:7.2.verse: ‘But, good sir, what is actually constant I call “constant.” What is actually permanent I call “permanent.” What is actually eternal I call “eternal.” What is actually total I call “total.” What is actually not subject to falling away I call “not subject to falling away.” Where one does not take birth, age, die, fall away, or reappear, I say,

mn49:7.3.verse: “For this does not take birth, does not age, does not die, does not fall away, does not reappear.”

mn49:7.4.verse: And there being no other, higher escape, I say, “There is no other, higher escape.”

mn49:7.5.verse: ‘There were, monk, before your time, contemplatives & brahmans in the world whose ascetic practice lasted as long as your entire life span.

mn49:7.6.verse: They knew, when there was another, higher escape, that there was another, higher escape; or, when there was no other, higher escape, that there was no other, higher escape.

mn49:7.8.verse: “both that you will not find another, higher escape, and that, to that extent, you will reap your share of trouble & weariness.

mn49:7.9.verse: Monk, if you relish earth, you will lie close to me, lie within my domain, for me to banish and to do with as I like.

mn49:7.16.verse: Brahmā, you will lie close to me, lie within my domain, for me to banish and to do with as I like.’”

mn49:8.2.verse: If I relish earth, I will lie close to you, lie within your domain, for you to banish and to do with as you like.

mn49:8.9.verse: Brahmā, I will lie close to you, lie within your domain, for you to banish and to do with as you like. Moreover, I discern your sphere, I discern your splendor:

mn49:8.10.verse: “Baka Brahmā has this much great power. Baka Brahmā has this much great might. Baka Brahmā has this much great influence.”’

mn49:8.11.verse: ‘Well, monk, how do you discern my sphere, how do you discern my splendor:

mn49:8.12.verse: “Baka Brahmā has this much great power. Baka Brahmā has this much great might. Baka Brahmā has this much great influence”?’

mn49:9.5.verse: There you know those above & below,

mn49:9.7.verse: the state of what is as it is, the state of what becomes otherwise,

mn49:9.9.verse: ‘That, Brahmā, is how I discern your sphere, that is how I discern your splendor:

mn49:9.10.verse: “Baka Brahmā has this much great power. Baka Brahmā has this much great might. Baka Brahmā has this much great influence.”’

mn49:10.1.verse: There are, Brahmā, bodies other than yours that you don’t know, don’t see,

mn49:10.2.verse: but that I know, I see.

mn49:10.3.verse: There is, Brahmā, the body named Ābhassarā [Radiant] from which you fell away & reappeared here.

mn49:10.4.verse: From your having lived here so long, your memory of that has become muddled. That is why you don’t know it, don’t see it,

mn49:10.5.verse: but I know it, I see it.

mn49:10.6.verse: Thus I am not your mere equal in terms of direct knowing, so how could I be inferior?

mn49:10.7.verse: I am actually superior to you.

mn49:10.8.verse: ‘There is, Brahmā, the body named Subhakiṇhā [Beautiful Black]… the body named Vehapphalā [Sky-fruit], {the body named Abhibhū [Conqueror]} which you don’t know, don’t see,

mn49:10.9.verse: but that I know, I see.

mn49:10.10.verse: Thus I am not your mere equal in terms of direct knowing, so how could I be your inferior?

mn49:10.11.verse: I am actually superior to you.

mn49:11.1.verse: ‘Having directly known earth as earth, and having directly known the extent of what has not been experienced through the earthness of earth, I wasn’t earth, I wasn’t in earth, I wasn’t coming from earth, I wasn’t “Earth is mine.” I didn’t affirm earth.

mn49:11.2.verse: Thus I am not your mere equal in terms of direct knowing, so how could I be inferior?

mn49:11.3.verse: I am actually superior to you.

mn49:20.1.verse: the beautiful black as the beautiful black…

mn49:23.1.verse: ‘Having directly known the all as the all, and having directly known the extent of what has not been experienced through the allness of the all, I wasn’t the all, I wasn’t in the all, I wasn’t coming forth from the all, I wasn’t “The all is mine.” I didn’t affirm the all.

mn49:23.2.verse: Thus I am not your mere equal in terms of direct knowing, so how could I be inferior?

mn49:23.3.verse: I am actually superior to you.’

mn49:24.1.verse: ‘If, good sir, you have directly known the extent of what has not been experienced through the allness of the all, may it not turn out to be actually vain and void for you.’

mn49:25.1.verse: ‘Consciousness without surface, endless, radiant all around, has not been experienced through the earthness of earth… the liquidity of liquid… the fieriness of fire… the windiness of wind… the allness of the all.’

mn49:26.1.verse: ‘Well then, good sir, I will disappear from you.’

mn49:26.2.verse: ‘Well then, Brahmā, disappear from me if you can.’

mn49:26.4.verse: ‘I will disappear from Gotama the contemplative. I will disappear from Gotama the contemplative,’ was not able to disappear from me.

mn49:26.5.verse: When this was said, I said to Baka Brahmā,

mn49:26.6.verse: ‘Well then, Brahmā, I will disappear from you.’

mn49:26.7.verse: ‘Well then, good sir, disappear from me if you can.’

mn49:26.8.verse: So then, monks, I fabricated a fabrication of psychic power to the extent that

mn49:26.9.verse: Brahmā, the Brahmā assembly, and the attendants of the Brahmā assembly heard my voice but did not see me.

mn49:26.10.verse: Having disappeared, I recited this verse:

mn49:27.2.verse: and becoming in searching for non-becoming,

mn49:27.3.verse: I didn’t affirm any kind of becoming,

mn49:28.1.verse: “Then in Brahmā, the Brahmā assembly, and the attendants of the Brahmā assembly there arose a sense of amazement & astonishment:

mn49:28.3.verse: The great power, the great might of Gotama the contemplative! Never before have we seen or heard of any other contemplative or brahman of such great power, such great might as that of this Gotama the contemplative, who went forth from a Sakyan clan!

mn49:28.4.verse: Living in a generation that so delights in becoming, so rejoices in becoming, is so fond of becoming, he has pulled out becoming by the root!’

mn49:29.1.verse: “Then Māra, the Evil One, taking possession of an attendant of the Brahmā assembly, said to me,

mn49:29.2.verse: ‘If, good sir, this is what you discern, if this is what you have awakened to, do not lead (lay) disciples or those gone forth.

mn49:29.3.verse: Do not teach the Dhamma to (lay) disciples or those gone forth.

mn49:29.4.verse: Do not yearn for (lay) disciples or those gone forth.

mn49:29.5.verse: There were, good sir, before your time, contemplatives & brahmans in the world who claimed to be worthy & rightly self-awakened.

mn49:29.6.verse: They led (lay) disciples & those gone forth. They taught the Dhamma to (lay) disciples & those gone forth. They yearned for (lay) disciples & those gone forth.

mn49:29.7.verse: Having led (lay) disciples & those gone forth, having taught the Dhamma to (lay) disciples & those gone forth, having yearned for (lay) disciples & those gone forth, they—on the break-up of the body, with the cutting off of life—were established in a coarse body.

mn49:29.8.verse: “‘There were, good sir, before your time, contemplatives & brahmans in the world who claimed to be worthy & rightly self-awakened.

mn49:29.9.verse: They did not lead (lay) disciples or those gone forth. They did not teach the Dhamma to (lay) disciples or those gone forth. They did not yearn for (lay) disciples or those gone forth.

mn49:29.10.verse: Having not led (lay) disciples or those gone forth, having not taught the Dhamma to (lay) disciples or those gone forth, having not yearned for (lay) disciples or those gone forth, they—on the break-up of the body, with the cutting off of life—were established in a refined body.

mn49:29.11.verse: So, monk, I tell you this:

mn49:29.12.verse: Please, good sir, be effortless. Abide committed to a pleasant abiding in the here & now—for it’s skillful, good sir, that this not be taught. Don’t instruct others.’

mn49:30.1.verse: “When this was said, I told Māra the Evil One,

mn49:30.2.verse: ‘I know you, Evil One. Don’t assume,

mn49:30.5.verse: And it’s not sympathetic to welfare that you speak thus to me.

mn49:30.6.verse: It’s sympathetic to what is not welfare that you speak thus to me.

mn49:30.8.verse: “Those to whom Gotama the contemplative will teach the Dhamma will defy my sovereignty”.

mn49:30.9.verse: Without being rightly self-awakened, Evil One, your contemplatives & brahmans claimed to be rightly self-awakened.

mn49:30.10.verse: I, however, being rightly self-awakened, claim to be rightly self-awakened.

mn49:30.11.verse: For when the Tathāgata is teaching the Dhamma to his disciples, he is Such. When he is not teaching the Dhamma to his disciples, he is Such.

mn49:30.12.verse: When leading his disciples he is Such. When not leading his disciples he is Such.

mn49:30.14.verse: The effluents that defile, that lead to further becoming, that disturb, that ripen in stress, that tend to future birth, aging, & death:

mn49:30.15.verse: Those the Tathāgata has abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.

mn49:30.16.verse: Just as a palmyra tree with its crown cut off is incapable of growing again;

mn49:30.17.verse: so, too, the effluents that defile, that lead to further becoming, that disturb, that ripen in stress, that tend to future birth, aging, & death:

mn49:30.18.verse: Those the Tathāgata has abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.’”

mn49:31.1.verse: Thus, because of the silencing of Māra, and because of the Brahmā’s invitation, this discourse is entitled, “The Brahmā Invitation.”

mn49:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn49:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn49:2.1.verse: “This one time, mendicants, I was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Forest at the root of a magnificent sal tree.

mn49:2.2.verse: Now at that time Baka the Divinity had the following harmful misconception:

mn49:2.3.verse: ‘This is permanent, this is everlasting, this is eternal, this is whole, this is not liable to pass away. For this is where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn. And there’s no other escape beyond this.’

mn49:3.1.verse: Then I knew what Baka the Divinity was thinking.

mn49:3.2.verse: As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, I vanished from the Subhaga Forest and reappeared in that realm of divinity.

mn49:3.3.verse: Baka saw me coming off in the distance

mn49:3.6.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

mn49:3.7.verse: For this is permanent, this is everlasting, this is eternal, this is whole, this is not liable to pass away. For this is where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn. And there’s no other escape beyond this.’

mn49:4.1.verse: When he had spoken, I said to him,

mn49:4.2.verse: ‘Oh lord, Baka the Divinity is lost in ignorance! Oh lord, Baka the Divinity is lost in ignorance!

mn49:4.3.verse: Because what is actually impermanent, not lasting, transient, incomplete, and liable to pass away, he says is permanent, everlasting, eternal, whole, and not liable to pass away.

mn49:4.4.verse: And where there is being born, growing old, dying, passing away, and being reborn, he says that

mn49:4.5.verse: there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.

mn49:4.6.verse: And although there is another escape beyond this, he says that there’s no other escape beyond this.’

mn49:5.1.verse: Then Māra the Wicked took possession of a member of the retinue of Divinity and said this to me,

mn49:5.2.verse: ‘Mendicant, mendicant! Don’t attack this one! Don’t attack this one! For this is the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the Universal Seer, the Wielder of Power, God Almighty, the Maker, the Creator, the First, the Begetter, the Controller, the Father of those who have been born and those yet to be born.

mn49:5.3.verse: There have been ascetics and brahmins before you, mendicant, who criticized and loathed earth, water, fire, air, creatures, gods, the Progenitor, and the Divinity.

mn49:5.4.verse: When their bodies broke up and their breath was cut off they were established in a lower realm.

mn49:5.5.verse: There have been ascetics and brahmins before you, mendicant, who praised and approved earth, water, fire, air, creatures, gods, the Progenitor, and the Divinity.

mn49:5.6.verse: When their bodies broke up and their breath was cut off they were established in a higher realm.

mn49:5.7.verse: So, mendicant, I tell you this:

mn49:5.8.verse: please, good fellow, do exactly what the Divinity says. Don’t go beyond the word of the Divinity.

mn49:5.9.verse: If you do, then you’ll end up like a person who, when approached by Lady Luck, would fend her off with a staff; or who, as they are falling over a cliff, would push away the ground with their hands and feet.

mn49:5.10.verse: Please, good fellow, do exactly what the Divinity says. Don’t go beyond the word of the Divinity.

mn49:5.11.verse: Do you not see the assembly of the Divinity gathered here?’

mn49:5.12.verse: And so Māra the Wicked presented the assembly of the Divinity to me.

mn49:7.3.verse: no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.

mn49:7.4.verse: And when I say there’s no other escape beyond this there is in fact no other escape beyond this.

mn49:7.5.verse: There have been ascetics and brahmins in the world before you, mendicant, whose deeds of fervent mortification lasted as long as your entire life.

mn49:7.6.verse: When there was another escape beyond this they knew it, and when there was no other escape beyond this, they knew it.

mn49:7.7.verse: So, mendicant, I tell you this:

mn49:7.8.verse: you will never find another escape beyond this, and you will eventually get weary and frustrated.

mn49:28.1.verse: Then the Divinity, his assembly, and his retinue, their minds full of wonder and amazement, thought,

mn49:29.1.verse: Then Māra the Wicked took possession of a member of the retinue of Divinity and said this to me,

mn49:29.2.verse: ‘If such is your understanding, good fellow, do not present it to your disciples or those gone forth!

mn49:29.3.verse: Do not teach this Dhamma to your disciples or those gone forth!

mn49:29.7.verse: When their bodies broke up and their breath was cut off they were established in a lower realm.

mn49:29.9.verse: They did not present, teach, or wish this for their disciples and those gone forth.

mn49:29.10.verse: When their bodies broke up and their breath was cut off they were established in a higher realm.

mn49:29.11.verse: So, mendicant, I tell you this:

mn49:29.12.verse: please, good fellow, remain passive, dwelling in blissful meditation in this life, for this is better left unsaid. Good fellow, do not instruct others.’

mn51:2.1.verse: ‘It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvellous,

mn51:2.2.verse: how the Sangha of bhikkhus has been led to practise the right way by Master Gotama.

mn51:2.3.verse: Even those Blessed Ones, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who were in the past, did at most only lead the Sangha of bhikkhus to practise the right way

mn51:2.4.verse: as is done by Master Gotama now.

mn51:2.5.verse: Even those Blessed Ones, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who will be in the future, will at most only lead the Sangha of bhikkhus to practise the right way

mn51:2.6.verse: as is done by Master Gotama now.’

mn51:3.1.verse: ‘So it is, Kandaraka, so it is.

mn51:3.2.verse: Even those Blessed Ones, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who were in the past, did at most only lead the Sangha of bhikkhus to practise the right way

mn51:3.3.verse: as is done by me now.

mn51:3.4.verse: Even those Blessed Ones, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, who will be in the future, will at most only lead the Sangha of bhikkhus to practise the right way

mn51:3.5.verse: as is done by me now.

mn51:3.6.verse: ‘Kandaraka, in this Sangha there are bhikkhus who are Arahants with taints exhausted, who have lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, who, through knowing rightly, are liberated.

mn51:3.7.verse: ‘In this Sangha there are those in the higher training of constant virtue, living a life of constant virtue, of constant sagacity, living a life of constant sagacity.

mn51:3.8.verse: They abide with the mind well established in the four foundations of mindfulness.

mn51:3.10.verse: Here, Kandaraka, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:3.11.verse: He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:3.12.verse: He abides contemplating mind as mind, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:3.13.verse: He abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.’

mn51:4.1.verse: When this was said, Pessa, the elephant driver’s son, said:

mn51:4.2.verse: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous

mn51:4.3.verse: how well the four foundations of mindfulness have been made known by the Blessed One for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the subsiding of pain and grief, for the attaining of the true way, for the realizing of Nibbāna.

mn51:4.4.verse: From time to time, venerable sir, we white-clothed laity too abide with mind well established on these four foundations of mindfulness.

mn51:4.5.verse: Here, venerable sir, we abide contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:4.6.verse: feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:4.7.verse: mind as mind, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:4.8.verse: dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn51:4.9.verse: It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous,

mn51:4.10.verse: how amid man’s tangle, amid man’s vices, amid man’s deceptions, the Blessed One knows what is beings’ welfare and what is not.

mn51:4.12.verse: but the animal is plain enough.

mn51:4.13.verse: Venerable sir, I can drive an elephant to be trained:

mn51:4.14.verse: in as short an interval as it takes to make a trip (from here to the city gate) and back in Campā, every kind of fraud and duplicity, crookedness and deception will be manifested (in that elephant.

mn51:4.15.verse: As for men) while for us in one way, they are acting with their bodies as slaves, messengers or servants, in another way (they are acting) in speech and their mind is yet another.

mn51:4.16.verse: It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous

mn51:4.17.verse: how amid man’s tangle, amid man’s vices, amid man’s deceptions, the Blessed One knows what is beings’ welfare and what is not.

mn51:4.19.verse: but the animal is plain enough.’

mn51:5.1.verse: ‘So it is, Pessa, so it is.

mn51:5.3.verse: but the animal is plain enough.

mn51:5.4.verse: ‘Pessa, there are four kinds of persons to be found existing in the world.

mn51:5.6.verse: ‘Here a certain kind of person torments himself, being interested in self-torture.

mn51:5.7.verse: ‘Here a certain kind of person torments others, being interested in torturing others.

mn51:5.8.verse: ‘Here a certain kind of person torments himself, being interested in torturing others.

mn51:5.9.verse: ‘Here a certain kind of person does not torment himself, not being interested in self-torture, nor does he torment others, not being interested in torturing others;

mn51:5.10.verse: since he torments neither himself nor others he is here and now unparched, extinguished, cooled, he abides experiencing pleasure as one become divine in himself.’

mn51:5.11.verse: ‘Which of these four kinds of persons commends itself to your mind, Pessa?’

mn51:5.12.verse: ‘The first three do not commend themselves to my mind, venerable sir,

mn51:5.16.verse: but the last one does so.’

mn51:6.1.verse: ‘But, Pessa, why do these three kinds of persons not commend themselves to your mind?’

mn51:6.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture, torments and tortures his own self which desires pleasure and recoils from pain;

mn51:6.3.verse: that is why that kind of person does not commend itself to my mind.

mn51:6.4.verse: And the kind of person who torments others, being interested in torturing others, torments and tortures another who desires pleasure and recoils from pain;

mn51:6.5.verse: that is why that kind of person does not commed itself to my mind.

mn51:6.6.verse: And the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture, and torments others, being interested in torturing others, torments and tortures his own self and another, both of them desiring pleasure and recoiling from pain;

mn51:6.7.verse: that is why that kind of person does not commend itself to my mind.

mn51:6.8.verse: But the kind of person who does not torment himself, not being interested in self-torture, and does not torment others, not being interested in torturing others, since he torments neither himself nor others, he is here and now unparched, extinguished, cooled, and having become divine in himself he abides experiencing pleasure.

mn51:6.10.verse: That is why that kind of person commends itself to my mind.

mn51:6.11.verse: And now, venerable sir, we depart;

mn51:6.12.verse: we are busy and have much to do.’

mn51:6.13.verse: ‘It is time now, Pessa, to do as you think fit.’

mn51:6.14.verse: Then Pessa, the elephant driver’s son, being satisfied and delighting in the Blessed One’s words, got up from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he departed keeping him on his right.

mn51:7.1.verse: Soon after he had gone, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn51:7.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, Pessa, the elephant driver’s son, is wise,

mn51:7.4.verse: If he had sat a while longer till I had expounded for him in detail these four kinds of persons he would have greatly benefitted.

mn51:7.5.verse: Still he has already greatly benefitted even as it is.’

mn51:7.6.verse: ‘This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Sublime One,

mn51:7.7.verse: for the Blessed One to expound in detail these four kinds of persons. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind.’

mn51:7.8.verse: ‘Then, bhikkhus, listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn51:7.9.verse: ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ the bhikkhus replied.

mn51:8.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, what kind of person torments himself, being interested in self-torture? Here a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept a thing brought or a thing specially made or an invitation;

mn51:8.2.verse: he receives nothing from out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman was lying with a man, from where food was advertized to be distributed, from where a dog was waiting, from where flies were buzzing; he accepts no fish or meat, he drinks no liquor, wine or besotting drink;

mn51:8.3.verse: he keeps to one house, to one morsel; he keeps to two houses, to two morsels … he keeps to seven houses, to seven morsels.

mn51:8.4.verse: He lives on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day;

mn51:8.5.verse: he takes food once a day, once each two days … once each seven days, and so, up to once each fortnight. He dwells pursuing the practice of taking food at stated intervals.

mn51:8.6.verse: He is an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or hide-parings, or moss, or ricebran, or rinsings, or sesamum flour, or grass, or cowdung; he lives on forest roots and on fruits as a feeder on windfalls.

mn51:8.7.verse: He clothes himself in hemp, in hemp mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood (shavings) fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings.

mn51:8.8.verse: He is one who pulls out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of pulling out hair and beard.

mn51:8.9.verse: He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats.

mn51:8.10.verse: He is one who squats continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position.

mn51:8.11.verse: He is one who uses a mattress of spikes; he makes a mattress of spikes his bed.

mn51:8.12.verse: He dwells pursuing the practice of bathing in water for the third time by nightfall.

mn51:8.13.verse: In fact he dwells pursuing the practice of torment and torture of the body in its main aspects.

mn51:8.14.verse: This is called the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture.

mn51:9.1.verse: ‘What kind of person torments others, being interested in torturing others?

mn51:9.2.verse: Here a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a trapper of wild beasts, a hunter, a fisher, an executioner of felons, a prison warder, or follows any other such bloody occupation.

mn51:9.3.verse: This is called the kind of person who torments others, being interested in torturing others.

mn51:10.1.verse: ‘What is the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture, and torments others, being interested in torturing others?

mn51:10.2.verse: Here some person is a head-anointed warrior noble, king, or a divine of great property.

mn51:10.3.verse: He has a new sacrificial temple made to the east of the city, and having shaved off his hair and beard, dressed himself in rough hide and greased his body with ghee and oil, scratching his back with a deer’s horn, he enters the sacrificial temple together with his chief queen and his high priest of the divine caste.

mn51:10.4.verse: There he lies down on the bare ground with the grass on it.

mn51:10.5.verse: The king uses any milk there is in the first teat of a cow with a calf of the same colour while the chief queen uses any milk in the second teat, and the divine high priest uses any milk in the third teat, and milk in the fourth teat they pour onto the fire: the calf uses what is left.

mn51:10.7.verse: “Let so many bulls be slaughtered for sacrifice, let so many bullocks be slaughtered for sacrifice, let so many heifers be slaughtered for sacrifice, let so many goats be slaughtered for sacrifice, let so many sheep be slaughtered for sacrifice, let so many trees be felled for the sacrificial posts, let so much grass be cut for the sacrificial grass.”

mn51:10.8.verse: And then his slaves and messengers and servants make preparations with tearful faces and weeping, being spurred on by threats of punishment and by fear.

mn51:10.9.verse: This is called the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture, and torments others, being interested in torturing others.

mn51:11.1.verse: ‘What kind of person does not torment himself, not being interested in self-torture, and does not torment others, not being interested in torturing others, who since he torments neither himself nor others, is here and now unparched, extinguished, cooled and abides experiencing pleasure having become divine in himself?

mn51:12.1.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.

mn51:12.2.verse: ‘He declares this world with its gods, its Māras and its (Brahmā) Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn51:12.3.verse: ‘He teaches Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end, with (the right) meaning and phrasing, and he announces a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn51:13.1.verse: ‘A householder or householder’s son or one born in some clan hears that Dhamma.

mn51:13.2.verse: On hearing the Dhamma he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.

mn51:13.3.verse: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:

mn51:13.4.verse: “House life is crowded and dirty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn51:13.5.verse: It is not possible, living in a household, to lead a life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.

mn51:13.6.verse: Suppose I shaved off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”

mn51:13.7.verse: ‘And on another occasion, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large fortune, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large circle of relatives, he shaves off hair and beard, puts on the yellow cloth, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn51:14.1.verse: ‘Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.

mn51:14.2.verse: ‘Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given; taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.

mn51:14.3.verse: ‘Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart, abstaining from vulgar lechery.

mn51:14.4.verse: ‘Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trust-worthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.

mn51:14.5.verse: ‘Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.

mn51:14.6.verse: ‘Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech; he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many and dear to many.

mn51:14.7.verse: ‘Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.

mn51:14.8.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.

mn51:14.9.verse: ‘He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.

mn51:14.10.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.

mn51:14.11.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.

mn51:14.12.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.

mn51:14.13.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.

mn51:14.14.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.

mn51:14.15.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.

mn51:14.16.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.

mn51:14.17.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondwomen and bondmen.

mn51:14.18.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.

mn51:14.19.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting fowl and pigs.

mn51:14.20.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting, elephants, cattle, horses and mares.

mn51:14.21.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.

mn51:14.22.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.

mn51:14.23.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.

mn51:14.24.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.

mn51:14.25.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.

mn51:14.26.verse: ‘He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.

mn51:15.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn51:15.2.verse: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,

mn51:15.3.verse: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn51:15.4.verse: Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn51:16.1.verse: He becomes one who, on seeing a visible form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features

mn51:16.2.verse: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn51:16.3.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn51:16.4.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn51:16.5.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn51:16.6.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn51:16.7.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he apprehends no signs and features

mn51:16.8.verse: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn51:16.9.verse: Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn51:17.1.verse: He becomes one who acts in full awareness when, moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, robes and bowl, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, waking up, talking and keeping silent.

mn51:18.1.verse: Possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,

mn51:18.2.verse: he resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn51:19.1.verse: On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.

mn51:19.2.verse: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies mind from covetousness.

mn51:19.3.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.

mn51:19.4.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.

mn51:19.5.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself; he purifies mind from agitation and worry.

mn51:19.6.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas; he purifies mind from uncertainty.

mn51:20.1.verse: Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken understanding,

mn51:20.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of seclusion.

mn51:21.1.verse: With the stilling of initial application and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna which has self-confidence and singleness of mind and is without initial application and sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of concentration.

mn51:22.1.verse: With the fading away of happiness as well, he abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which Noble Ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn51:23.1.verse: With the abandoning of (bodily) pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of (mental) joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn51:24.1.verse: When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the recollection of past life,

mn51:24.2.verse: that is to say, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (world) contraction, many aeons of (world) expansion, many aeons of (world) contraction and expansion: There he was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was his nutriment, such his experience of pleasure and pain, such his life-term; and passing away from there, he appeared elsewhere; and there too he was so-named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was his nutriment, such his experience of pleasure and pain, such his life-term; and passing away from there he appeared here. Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.

mn51:25.1.verse: When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn51:25.2.verse: With the heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; he understands how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings, who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved. He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.

mn51:26.1.verse: When his concentrated mind is thus purified and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to unperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of exhaustion of taints.

mn51:26.2.verse: ‘He has direct knowledge thus: “This is suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”

mn51:27.1.verse: He has direct knowledge thus: “These are taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of taints”.

mn51:27.2.verse: ‘When he knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taints of sensual desire, from the taints of being and from the taints of ignorance.

mn51:27.3.verse: When liberated there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated”.

mn51:27.4.verse: He has direct knowledge thus: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived out, what can be done is done. There is no more of this to come.”’

mn51:28.1.verse: ‘This is called the kind of person who does not torment himself, not being interested in self torture, and does not torment others, not being interested in torturing others, who since he torments neither himself nor others,

mn51:28.2.verse: is here and now unparched, extinguished, cooled, who, become divine in himself, abides experiencing pleasure.’

mn51:28.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn51:28.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn51:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn51:1.3.verse: Then Pessa the elephant marshal’s son and Kandaraka the wanderer went to the Buddha. When they had approached, Pessa bowed and sat down to one side.

mn51:1.4.verse: But the wanderer Kandaraka exchanged greetings with the Buddha and stood to one side.

mn51:1.5.verse: He looked around the mendicant Saṅgha, who were so very silent, and said to the Buddha:

mn51:2.2.verse: How the mendicant Saṅgha has been led to practice properly by the worthy Gotama!

mn51:2.3.verse: The perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas in the past or the future who lead the mendicant Saṅgha to practice properly at best do so

mn51:2.4.verse: like the worthy Gotama does in the present.”

mn51:3.1.verse: “That’s so true, Kandaraka! That’s so true!

mn51:3.2.verse: The perfected ones, the fully awakened Buddhas in the past or the future who lead the mendicant Saṅgha to practice properly at best do so

mn51:3.3.verse: like I do in the present.

mn51:3.6.verse: For in this mendicant Saṅgha there are perfected mendicants, who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment.

mn51:3.7.verse: And in this mendicant Saṅgha there are trainee mendicants who are consistently ethical, living consistently, alert, living alertly.

mn51:3.8.verse: They meditate with their minds firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn51:3.10.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn51:3.11.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn51:3.12.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn51:3.13.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.”

mn51:4.1.verse: When he had spoken, Pessa said to the Buddha:

mn51:4.3.verse: How well described by the Buddha are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation! They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

mn51:4.4.verse: For we white-clothed laypeople also from time to time meditate with our minds well established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn51:4.5.verse: We meditate observing an aspect of the body …

mn51:4.8.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn51:4.10.verse: How the Buddha knows what’s best for sentient beings, even though humans continue to be so shady, rotten, and tricky.

mn51:4.11.verse: For human beings are shady, sir,

mn51:4.13.verse: For I can drive an elephant in training,

mn51:4.14.verse: and while going back and forth in Campā it’ll try all the tricks, bluffs, ruses, and feints that it can.

mn51:4.15.verse: But my bondservants, servants, and workers behave one way by body, another by speech, and their minds another.

mn51:4.17.verse: How the Buddha knows what’s best for sentient beings, even though humans continue to be so shady, rotten, and tricky.

mn51:4.18.verse: For human beings are shady, sir,

mn51:5.1.verse: “That’s so true, Pessa! That’s so true!

mn51:5.4.verse: Pessa, these four individuals are found in the world.

mn51:5.6.verse: One individual mortifies themselves, committed to the practice of mortifying themselves.

mn51:5.7.verse: One individual mortifies others, committed to the practice of mortifying others.

mn51:5.8.verse: One individual mortifies themselves and others, committed to the practice of mortifying themselves and others.

mn51:5.9.verse: One individual doesn’t mortify either themselves or others, committed to the practice of not mortifying themselves or others.

mn51:5.10.verse: They live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.

mn51:5.11.verse: Which one of these four individuals do you like the sound of?”

mn51:5.12.verse: “Sir, I don’t like the sound of the first three individuals.

mn51:5.16.verse: I only like the sound of the last individual, who doesn’t mortify either themselves or others.”

mn51:6.1.verse: “But why don’t you like the sound of those three individuals?”

mn51:6.2.verse: “Sir, the individual who mortifies themselves does so even though they want to be happy and recoil from pain.

mn51:6.3.verse: That’s why I don’t like the sound of that individual.

mn51:6.4.verse: The individual who mortifies others does so even though others want to be happy and recoil from pain.

mn51:6.5.verse: That’s why I don’t like the sound of that individual.

mn51:6.6.verse: The individual who mortifies themselves and others does so even though both themselves and others want to be happy and recoil from pain.

mn51:6.7.verse: That’s why I don’t like the sound of that individual.

mn51:6.8.verse: The individual who doesn’t mortify either themselves or others—living without wishes, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine—does not torment themselves or others, both of whom want to be happy and recoil from pain.

mn51:6.10.verse: That’s why I like the sound of that individual.

mn51:6.11.verse: Well, now, sir, I must go.

mn51:6.12.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn51:6.14.verse: And then Pessa the elephant marshal’s son approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn51:7.1.verse: Then, not long after he had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

mn51:7.2.verse: “Mendicants, Pessa the elephant marshal’s son is astute.

mn51:7.4.verse: If he had sat here an hour so that I could have analyzed these four individuals in detail, he would have greatly benefited.

mn51:7.5.verse: Still, even with this much he has already greatly benefited.”

mn51:7.6.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

mn51:7.7.verse: May the Buddha analyze these four individuals in detail. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn51:7.8.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn51:8.1.verse: “And what individual mortifies themselves, committed to the practice of mortifying themselves? It’s when an individual goes naked, ignoring conventions. They lick their hands, and don’t come or wait when called. They don’t consent to food brought to them, or food prepared for them, or an invitation for a meal.

mn51:8.2.verse: They don’t receive anything from a pot or bowl; or from someone who keeps sheep, or who has a weapon or a shovel in their home; or where a couple is eating; or where there is a woman who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or who lives with a man; or where there’s a hound waiting or flies buzzing. They accept no fish or meat or beer or wine, and drink no fermented gruel.

mn51:8.3.verse: They go to just one house for alms, taking just one mouthful, or two houses and two mouthfuls, up to seven houses and seven mouthfuls.

mn51:8.4.verse: They feed on one saucer a day, two saucers a day, up to seven saucers a day.

mn51:8.5.verse: They eat once a day, once every second day, up to once a week, and so on, even up to once a fortnight. They live committed to the practice of eating food at set intervals.

mn51:8.6.verse: They eat herbs, millet, wild rice, poor rice, water lettuce, rice bran, scum from boiling rice, sesame flour, grass, or cow dung. They survive on forest roots and fruits, or eating fallen fruit.

mn51:8.7.verse: They wear robes of sunn hemp, mixed hemp, corpse-wrapping cloth, rags, lodh tree bark, antelope hide (whole or in strips), kusa grass, bark, wood-chips, human hair, horse-tail hair, or owls’ wings.

mn51:8.8.verse: They tear out their hair and beard, committed to this practice.

mn51:8.9.verse: They constantly stand, turning down seats.

mn51:8.10.verse: They squat, committed to the endeavor of squatting.

mn51:8.11.verse: They lie on a mat of thorns, making a mat of thorns their bed.

mn51:8.12.verse: They’re devoted to ritual bathing three times a day, including at dusk.

mn51:8.13.verse: And so they live committed to practicing these various ways of mortifying and tormenting the body.

mn51:8.14.verse: This is called an individual who mortifies themselves, being committed to the practice of mortifying themselves.

mn51:9.1.verse: And what individual mortifies others, committed to the practice of mortifying others?

mn51:9.2.verse: It’s when an individual is a slaughterer of sheep, pigs, or poultry, a hunter or trapper, a fisher, a bandit, an executioner, a butcher, a jailer, or someone with some other kind of cruel livelihood.

mn51:9.3.verse: This is called an individual who mortifies others, being committed to the practice of mortifying others.

mn51:10.1.verse: And what individual mortifies themselves and others, being committed to the practice of mortifying themselves and others?

mn51:10.2.verse: It’s when an individual is an anointed aristocratic king or a well-to-do brahmin.

mn51:10.3.verse: He has a new ceremonial hall built to the east of the citadel. He shaves off his hair and beard, dresses in a rough antelope hide, and smears his body with ghee and oil. Scratching his back with antlers, he enters the hall with his chief queen and the brahmin high priest.

mn51:10.4.verse: There he lies on the bare ground strewn with grass.

mn51:10.5.verse: The king feeds on the milk from one teat of a cow that has a calf of the same color. The chief queen feeds on the milk from the second teat. The brahmin high priest feeds on the milk from the third teat. The milk from the fourth teat is served to the sacred flame. The calf feeds on the leftovers.

mn51:10.7.verse: ‘Slaughter this many bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats, rams, and horses for the sacrifice! Fell this many trees and reap this much grass for the sacrificial equipment!’

mn51:10.8.verse: His bondservants, servants, and workers do their jobs under threat of punishment and danger, weeping with tearful faces.

mn51:10.9.verse: This is called an individual who mortifies themselves and others, being committed to the practice of mortifying themselves and others.

mn51:11.1.verse: And what individual doesn’t mortify either themselves or others, but lives without wishes, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine?

mn51:12.1.verse: It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn51:12.2.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn51:12.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

mn51:13.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

mn51:13.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One

mn51:13.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn51:13.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn51:13.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn51:13.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn51:14.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn51:14.2.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

mn51:14.3.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn51:14.4.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

mn51:14.5.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn51:14.6.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn51:14.7.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn51:14.8.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

mn51:14.9.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

mn51:14.10.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn51:14.11.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn51:14.12.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

mn51:14.13.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

mn51:14.22.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

mn51:14.26.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn51:15.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn51:15.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn51:15.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn51:15.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

mn51:16.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn51:16.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn51:16.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn51:16.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn51:16.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn51:16.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn51:16.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn51:16.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn51:16.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

mn51:17.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn51:18.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn51:18.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn51:19.1.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn51:19.2.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn51:19.3.verse: Giving up ill will, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will and malevolence.

mn51:19.4.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn51:19.5.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn51:19.6.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn51:20.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn51:20.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn51:21.1.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn51:22.1.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn51:23.1.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn51:24.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn51:24.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn51:25.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn51:25.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn51:26.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn51:26.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn51:27.1.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn51:27.2.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn51:27.3.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn51:27.4.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn51:28.1.verse: This is called an individual who neither mortifies themselves or others, being committed to the practice of not mortifying themselves or others.

mn51:28.2.verse: They live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.”

mn51:28.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn51:28.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn52:1.2.verse: on one occasion Ven. Ānanda was staying near Vesālī at Veḷuvagāmaka.

mn52:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion Dasama the householder from Aṭṭhakanagara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.

mn52:2.1.verse: Then he went to a certain monk at Kukkaṭa Monastery and on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to the monk,

mn52:2.4.verse: “Householder, the Ven. Ānanda is staying near Vesālī at Veḷuvagāmaka.”

mn52:3.1.verse: Then Dasama the householder from Aṭṭhakanagara, on completing his business at Pāṭaliputta, went to Ven. Ānanda at Veḷuvagāmaka near Vesālī. On arrival, having bowed down to him, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to Ven. Ānanda:

mn52:3.2.verse: “Venerable sir, is there a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke that he had not attained before?”

mn52:3.4.verse: “And what is that one quality, venerable sir…?”

mn52:4.1.verse: “There is the case, householder, where a monk, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born from seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn52:4.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:4.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:4.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents.

mn52:4.6.verse: Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters [self-identification views, grasping at habits & practices, uncertainty, sensual passion, and irritation]—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world.

mn52:4.7.verse: “This, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke that he had not attained before.

mn52:5.1.verse: “Then again, householder, with the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, the monk enters & remains in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

mn52:5.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:5.3.verse: ‘This second jhāna is fabricated & intended. Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:5.4.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:6.1.verse: “Then again, householder, with the fading of rapture, the monk remains equanimous, mindful, & alert, and senses pleasure with the body. He enters & remains in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’

mn52:6.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:6.3.verse: ‘This third jhāna is fabricated & intended. Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:6.4.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:7.1.verse: “Then again, householder, with the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of joy & distress—the monk enters & remains in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain.

mn52:7.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:7.3.verse: ‘This fourth jhāna is fabricated & intended. Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:7.4.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:8.1.verse: “Then again, a monk keeps pervading the first direction [the east] with an awareness imbued with goodwill, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with goodwill—abundant, expansive, unlimited, without hostility, without ill will.

mn52:8.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:8.3.verse: ‘This awareness-release through goodwill is fabricated & intended.

mn52:8.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:8.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:8.6.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:9.1.verse: “Then again, a monk keeps pervading the first direction with an awareness imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with compassion—abundant, expansive, unlimited, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects on this and discerns, ‘This awareness-release through compassion is fabricated & intended. Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke that he had not attained before.

mn52:10.1.verse: “Then again, a monk keeps pervading the first direction with an awareness imbued with empathetic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with empathetic joy—abundant, expansive, unlimited, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects on this and discerns, ‘This awareness-release through empathetic joy is fabricated & intended. Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke that he had not attained before.

mn52:11.1.verse: “Then again, a monk keeps pervading the first direction with an awareness imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
