Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with equanimity—abundant, expansive, unlimited, without hostility, without ill will.

mn52:11.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:11.3.verse: ‘This awareness-release through equanimity is fabricated & intended.

mn52:11.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:11.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:11.6.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:12.1.verse: “Then again, householder, a monk—with the complete transcending of perceptions of (physical) form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite space’—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of space.

mn52:12.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:12.3.verse: ‘This attainment of the infinitude of space is fabricated & intended.

mn52:12.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:12.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:12.6.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:13.1.verse: “Then again, a monk—with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite consciousness’—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.

mn52:13.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:13.3.verse: ‘This attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness is fabricated & intended.

mn52:13.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:13.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke

mn52:13.6.verse: that he had not attained before.

mn52:14.1.verse: “Then again, a monk—with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, (perceiving,) ‘There is nothing’—enters & remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn52:14.2.verse: He reflects on this and discerns,

mn52:14.3.verse: ‘This attainment of the dimension of nothingness is fabricated & intended.

mn52:14.4.verse: Now whatever is fabricated & intended is inconstant & subject to cessation.’

mn52:14.5.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents.

mn52:14.6.verse: Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total wasting away of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world.

mn52:14.7.verse: This too, householder, is a single quality declared by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, worthy & rightly self-awakened—where the unreleased mind of a monk who dwells there heedful, ardent, & resolute becomes released, or his unended effluents go to their total ending, or he attains the unexcelled security from the yoke that he had not attained before.”

mn52:15.1.verse: When this was said, Dasama the householder from Aṭṭhakanagara said to Ven. Ānanda,

mn52:15.2.verse: “Venerable Ānanda, just as if a man seeking a single opening onto treasure were all at once to come upon eleven openings onto treasure,

mn52:15.3.verse: in the same way I—seeking a single doorway to the deathless—have all at once come to hear of eleven doorways to the deathless.

mn52:15.4.verse: And just as if a man whose house had eleven doors could take himself to safety by means of any one of those doors,

mn52:15.5.verse: in the same way I can take myself to safety by means of any one of these eleven doors to the deathless.

mn52:15.6.verse: Venerable sir, when sectarians search for a teacher’s fee for their teachers, why shouldn’t I pay homage to Ven. Ānanda?”

mn52:16.1.verse: So Dasama the householder from Aṭṭhakanagara, having assembled the Saṅgha of monks from Vesālī and Pāṭaliputta, with his own hands served & satisfied them with refined staple & non-staple foods.

mn52:16.2.verse: He presented a pair of cloths to each monk, and a triple robe to Ven. Ānanda. And for Ven. Ānanda he had a dwelling built worth five hundred (kahāpanas).

mn52:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Vesālī in the little village of Beluva.

mn52:1.3.verse: Now at that time the householder Dasama, a wealthy citizen, had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.

mn52:2.1.verse: He went to the Chicken Monastery, approached a certain mendicant, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn52:2.2.verse: “Sir, where is Venerable Ānanda now staying?

mn52:2.3.verse: For I want to see him.”

mn52:2.4.verse: “Householder, Venerable Ānanda is staying near Vesālī in the little village of Beluva.”

mn52:3.1.verse: Then the householder Dasama, having concluded his business there, went to the little village of Beluva in Vesālī to see Ānanda. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to Ānanda:

mn52:3.2.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, is there one thing that has been rightly explained by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha—practicing which a diligent, keen, and resolute mendicant’s mind is freed, their defilements are ended, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke?”

mn52:4.1.verse: “Householder, it’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn52:4.3.verse: ‘Even this first absorption is produced by choices and intentions.’

mn52:4.4.verse: They understand: ‘But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.’

mn52:4.5.verse: Abiding in that they attain the ending of defilements.

mn52:4.6.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re reborn spontaneously, because of their passion and love for that meditation. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

mn52:4.7.verse: This is one thing that has been rightly explained by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha—practicing which a diligent, keen, and resolute mendicant’s mind is freed, their defilements are ended, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn52:5.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption …

mn52:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn52:8.3.verse: ‘Even this heart’s release by love is produced by choices and intentions.’

mn52:8.4.verse: They understand: ‘But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ …

mn52:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn52:12.1.verse: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

mn52:12.3.verse: ‘Even this attainment of the dimension of infinite space is produced by choices and intentions.’

mn52:12.4.verse: They understand: ‘But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.’ …

mn52:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. …

mn52:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn52:14.3.verse: ‘Even this attainment of the dimension of nothingness is produced by choices and intentions.’

mn52:14.4.verse: They understand: ‘But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.’

mn52:14.5.verse: Abiding in that they attain the ending of defilements.

mn52:14.6.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re reborn spontaneously because of their passion and love for that meditation. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

mn52:14.7.verse: This too is one thing that has been rightly explained by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha—practicing which a diligent, keen, and resolute mendicant’s mind is freed, their defilements are ended, and they arrive at the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.”

mn52:15.1.verse: When he said this, the householder Dasama said to Venerable Ānanda,

mn52:15.2.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, suppose a person was looking for the entrance to a treasure trove. And all at once they’d come across eleven entrances!

mn52:15.3.verse: In the same way, I was searching for the door to freedom from death. And all at once I found eleven doors to freedom from death for cultivation.

mn52:15.4.verse: Suppose a person had a house with eleven doors. If the house caught fire they’d be able to flee to safety through any one of those doors.

mn52:15.5.verse: In the same way, I’m able to flee to safety through any one of these eleven doors to freedom from death.

mn52:15.6.verse: Sir, those of other religions seek a fee for the tutor. Why shouldn’t I make an offering to Venerable Ānanda?”

mn52:16.1.verse: Then the householder Dasama, having assembled the Saṅgha from Vesālī and Pāṭaliputta, served and satisfied them with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

mn52:16.2.verse: He clothed each and every mendicant in a pair of garments, with a set of three robes for Ānanda. And he had a dwelling worth five hundred built for Ānanda.

mn53:0.2.verse: The Practice for One in Training

mn53:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Park.

mn53:2.1.verse: Now at that time a new reception hall had just been built by the Kapilavatthu Sakyans, and it had not yet been dwelled in by any contemplative, brahman, or anyone at all in human form.

mn53:2.2.verse: So the Kapilavatthu Sakyans went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As they were sitting there they said to him,

mn53:2.3.verse: “Lord, a new reception hall has just been built by the Kapilavatthu Sakyans, and it has not yet been dwelled in by any contemplative, brahman, or anyone at all in human form.

mn53:2.4.verse: May the Blessed One be the first to use it. When the Blessed One has used it first, the Kapilavatthu Sakyans will use it afterwards.

mn53:2.5.verse: That will be for their long-term welfare & happiness.”

mn53:3.1.verse: The Blessed One acquiesced with silence.

mn53:3.2.verse: Sensing his acquiescence, the Kapilavatthu Sakyans got up from their seats, bowed down to him, circumambulated him, and then went to the new reception hall. On arrival, they spread it all over with felt rugs, arranged seats, set out a water vessel, and raised an oil lamp. Then they went to the Blessed One and,

mn53:3.3.verse: on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side.

mn53:3.4.verse: As they were standing there they said to him,

mn53:3.5.verse: “Lord, the reception hall has been covered all over with felt rugs, seats have been arranged, a water vessel has been set out, and an oil lamp raised.

mn53:3.6.verse: It is now time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit.”

mn53:4.1.verse: So the Blessed One—after adjusting his lower robe and taking his bowl & outer robe—went together with a Saṅgha of monks to the reception hall. On arrival he washed his feet, entered the hall, and sat with his back to the central post, facing east.

mn53:4.2.verse: The Saṅgha of monks washed their feet, entered the hall, and sat with their backs to the western wall, facing east, ranged around the Blessed One.

mn53:4.3.verse: The Kapilavatthu Sakyans washed their feet, entered the hall, and sat with their backs to the eastern wall, facing west, ranged around the Blessed One.

mn53:5.1.verse: Then the Blessed One—having spent most of the night instructing, urging, rousing, & encouraging the Kapilavatthu Sakyans with a Dhamma talk—said to Ven. Ānanda,

mn53:5.2.verse: “Ānanda, speak to the Kapilavatthu Sakyans about the person who follows the practice for one in training.

mn53:5.5.verse: Ven. Ānanda responded, “As you say, lord.”

mn53:5.6.verse: Then the Blessed One, having arranged his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion’s sleeping posture, with one foot on top of the other, mindful & alert, having made a mental note to get up.

mn53:6.1.verse: Then Ven. Ānanda addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan:

mn53:6.2.verse: “There is the case, Mahānāma, where a disciple of the noble ones is consummate in virtue, guards the doors to his sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, is endowed with seven qualities, and obtains at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now.

mn53:7.1.verse: “And how is the disciple of the noble ones consummate in virtue?

mn53:7.2.verse: There is the case where the disciple of the noble ones is virtuous. He dwells restrained in accordance with the Pāṭimokkha, consummate in his behavior & sphere of activity. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults.

mn53:7.3.verse: This is how the disciple of the noble ones is consummate in virtue.

mn53:8.1.verse: “And how does the disciple of the noble ones guard the doors to his sense faculties?

mn53:8.2.verse: There is the case where the disciple of the noble ones, on seeing a form with the eye, doesn’t grasp at any theme or variations

mn53:8.3.verse: by which—if he were to dwell without restraint over the faculty of the eye—evil, unskillful qualities such as greed or distress might assail him. He practices with restraint. He guards the faculty of the eye. He achieves restraint with regard to the faculty of the eye.

mn53:8.4.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear.…

mn53:8.5.verse: On smelling an aroma with the nose.…

mn53:8.6.verse: On tasting a flavor with the tongue.…

mn53:8.7.verse: On feeling a tactile sensation with the body.…

mn53:8.8.verse: On cognizing an idea with the intellect, he doesn’t grasp at any theme or variations

mn53:8.9.verse: by which—if he were to dwell without restraint over the faculty of the intellect—evil, unskillful qualities such as greed or distress might assail him. He practices with restraint. He guards the faculty of the intellect. He achieves restraint with regard to the faculty of the intellect.

mn53:8.10.verse: This is how the disciple of the noble ones guards the doors to his sense faculties.

mn53:9.1.verse: “And how does the disciple of the noble ones know moderation in eating?

mn53:9.2.verse: There is the case where the disciple of the noble ones, considering it appropriately, takes his food

mn53:9.3.verse: not playfully, nor for intoxication, nor for putting on bulk, nor for beautification, but simply for the survival & continuance of this body, for ending its afflictions, for the support of the holy life, thinking, ‘I will destroy old feelings (of hunger) & not create new feelings (from overeating). Thus I will maintain myself, be blameless, & live in comfort.’

mn53:9.4.verse: This is how the disciple of the noble ones knows moderation in eating.

mn53:10.1.verse: “And how is the disciple of the noble ones devoted to wakefulness?

mn53:10.2.verse: There is the case where a monk during the day, sitting & pacing back & forth, cleanses his mind of any qualities that would hold the mind in check.

mn53:10.3.verse: During the first watch of the night [dusk to 10 p.m.], sitting & pacing back & forth, he cleanses his mind of any qualities that would hold the mind in check.

mn53:10.4.verse: During the second watch of the night [10 p.m. to 2 a.m.], reclining on his right side, he takes up the lion’s posture, one foot placed on top of the other, mindful, alert, with his mind set on getting up [either as soon as he awakens or at a particular time].

mn53:10.5.verse: During the last watch of the night [2 a.m. to dawn], sitting & pacing back & forth, he cleanses his mind of any qualities that would hold the mind in check.

mn53:10.6.verse: This is how the monk is devoted to wakefulness.

mn53:11.1.verse: “And how is the disciple of the noble ones endowed with seven qualities?

mn53:11.2.verse: “[1] There is the case where the disciple of the noble ones has conviction, is convinced of the Tathāgata’s awakening:

mn53:11.3.verse: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is worthy & rightly self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, well-gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed.’

mn53:12.1.verse: “[2] He feels shame at (the thought of engaging in) bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct.

mn53:13.1.verse: “[3] He feels compunction over (the suffering that would result from) bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct.

mn53:14.1.verse: “[4] He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, has stored what he has heard. Whatever teachings are admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, admirable in the end, that—in their meaning & expression—proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete & pure: those he has listened to often, retained, discussed, accumulated, examined with his mind, and well-penetrated in terms of his views.

mn53:15.1.verse: “[5] He keeps his persistence aroused for abandoning unskillful qualities and taking on skillful qualities. He is steadfast, solid in his effort, not shirking his duties with regard to skillful qualities.

mn53:16.1.verse: “[6] He is mindful, highly meticulous, remembering & able to call to mind even things that were done & said long ago.

mn53:17.1.verse: “[7] He is discerning, endowed with discernment of arising & passing away—noble, penetrating, leading to the right ending of stress.

mn53:17.2.verse: This is how the disciple of the noble ones is endowed with seven qualities.

mn53:18.1.verse: “And how does the disciple of the noble ones obtain at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now?

mn53:18.2.verse: There is the case where, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, the disciple of the noble ones enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn53:18.3.verse: With the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, he enters & remains in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

mn53:18.4.verse: With the fading of rapture he remains equanimous, mindful, & alert, and senses pleasure with the body. He enters & remains in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’

mn53:18.5.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation & distress—he enters & remains in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain.

mn53:18.6.verse: This is how the disciple of the noble ones obtains at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now.

mn53:19.1.verse: “Now, when a disciple of the noble ones is consummate in virtue in this way, guards the doors to his sense faculties in this way, knows moderation in eating in this way, is devoted to wakefulness in this way, is endowed with seven qualities in this way, and obtains at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now in this way, then he is called a disciple of the noble ones who follows the practice for one in training, whose eggs are unspoiled, who is capable of breaking out, capable of awakening, capable of attaining the supreme rest from the yoke.

mn53:19.2.verse: “Just as if a hen had eight, ten, or twelve eggs that she covered rightly, warmed rightly, & incubated rightly: Even though this wish did not occur to her—

mn53:19.3.verse: ‘O that my chicks might break through the egg shells with their spiked claws or beaks and hatch out safely!’—

mn53:19.4.verse: still it is possible that the chicks would break through the shells with their spiked claws or beaks and hatch out safely.

mn53:19.5.verse: In the same way, when a disciple of the noble ones is consummate in virtue in this way, guards the doors to his sense faculties in this way, knows moderation in eating in this way, is devoted to wakefulness in this way, is endowed with seven qualities in this way, and obtains at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now in this way, then he is called a disciple of the noble ones who follows the practice for one in training, whose eggs are unspoiled, who is capable of breaking out, capable of awakening, capable of attaining the supreme rest from the yoke.

mn53:20.1.verse: “Now when the disciple of the noble ones has arrived at this purity of equanimity & mindfulness, he recollects his manifold past lives,

mn53:20.2.verse: i.e., one birth, two… five, ten… fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction & expansion: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure & pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from that state, I re-arose there. There too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance. Such was my food, such my experience of pleasure & pain, such the end of my life. Passing away from that state, I re-arose here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes & details,

mn53:20.3.verse: This is his first breaking out, like that of the hen’s chicks from their shells.

mn53:21.1.verse: “When the disciple of the noble ones has arrived at this purity of equanimity & mindfulness, he sees—by means of the divine eye, purified & surpassing the human—beings passing away & re-appearing, and he discerns how they are inferior & superior, beautiful & ugly, fortunate & unfortunate in accordance with their kamma: ‘These beings—who were endowed with bad conduct of body, speech & mind, who reviled noble ones, held wrong views and undertook actions under the influence of wrong views—with the break-up of the body, after death, have re-appeared in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. But these beings—who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, & mind, who did not revile noble ones, who held right views and undertook actions under the influence of right views—with the break-up of the body, after death, have re-appeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus—by means of the divine eye, purified & surpassing the human—he sees beings passing away & re-appearing, and he discerns how they are inferior & superior, beautiful & ugly, fortunate & unfortunate in accordance with their kamma.

mn53:21.2.verse: This is his second breaking out, like that of the hen’s chicks from their shells.

mn53:22.1.verse: “When the disciple of the noble ones has arrived at this purity of equanimity & mindfulness, he enters & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now.

mn53:22.2.verse: This is his third breaking out, like that of the hen’s chicks from their shells.

mn53:23.1.verse: “Now, when the disciple of the noble ones is consummate in virtue, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:23.2.verse: When he guards the doors to his sense faculties, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:23.3.verse: When he knows moderation in eating, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:23.4.verse: When he is devoted to wakefulness, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:23.5.verse: When he is endowed with seven qualities, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:23.6.verse: When he obtains at will—without trouble or difficulty—the four jhānas that constitute heightened awareness and a pleasant abiding in the here & now, that is a matter of his conduct.

mn53:24.1.verse: “When he recollects his manifold past lives… in their modes & details, that is a matter of his clear-knowing.

mn53:24.2.verse: When he sees—by means of the divine eye, purified & surpassing the human—beings passing away & re-appearing.… and discerns how they fare in accordance with their kamma, that too is a matter of his clear-knowing.

mn53:24.3.verse: When he enters & remains in the effluent-free awareness-release & discernment-release, having directly known & realized them for himself right in the here & now, that is a matter of his clear knowing.

mn53:25.1.verse: “This, Mahānāma, is called a disciple of the noble ones who is consummate in clear-knowing, consummate in conduct, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct.

mn53:25.2.verse: And by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra this verse was said:

mn53:25.3.verse: ‘The noble warrior is the best among people

mn53:25.5.verse: But a person consummate in clear-knowing & conduct,

mn53:25.6.verse: is the best of beings human & divine.’

mn53:25.7.verse: This verse was well-sung by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, not ill-sung; well-said, not ill-said; connected with the goal, not unconnected with the goal. It was endorsed by the Blessed One.”

mn53:26.1.verse: Then the Blessed One got up and said to Ven. Ānanda,

mn53:26.3.verse: What you have said to the Kapilavatthu Sakyans about the person who follows the practice for one in training is good.”

mn53:26.4.verse: That is what Ven. Ānanda said,

mn53:26.6.verse: Gratified, the Kapilavatthu Sakyans delighted in Ven. Ānanda’s words.

mn53:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

mn53:2.1.verse: Now at that time a new town hall had recently been constructed for the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu. It had not yet been occupied by an ascetic or brahmin or any human at all.

mn53:2.2.verse: Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

mn53:2.3.verse: “Sir, a new town hall has recently been constructed for the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu. It has not yet been occupied by an ascetic or brahmin or any human at all.

mn53:2.4.verse: May the Buddha be the first to use it, and only then will the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu use it.

mn53:2.5.verse: That would be for the lasting welfare and happiness of the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.”

mn53:3.2.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, the Sakyans got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. Then they went to the new town hall, where they spread carpets all over, prepared seats, set up a water jar, and placed an oil lamp. Then they went back to the Buddha,

mn53:3.4.verse: and told him of their preparations, saying,

mn53:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the new town hall together with the Saṅgha of mendicants. Having washed his feet, he entered the town hall and sat against the central column facing east.

mn53:4.2.verse: The Saṅgha of mendicants also washed their feet, entered the town hall, and sat against the west wall facing east, with the Buddha right in front of them.

mn53:4.3.verse: The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu also washed their feet, entered the town hall, and sat against the east wall facing west, with the Buddha right in front of them.

mn53:5.1.verse: The Buddha spent much of the night educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the Sakyans with a Dhamma talk. Then he addressed Venerable Ānanda,

mn53:5.2.verse: “Ānanda, speak about the practicing trainee to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu as you feel inspired.

mn53:5.6.verse: And then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and laid down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

mn53:6.1.verse: Then Ānanda addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan:

mn53:6.2.verse: “Mahānāma, a noble disciple is accomplished in ethics, guards the sense doors, eats in moderation, and is dedicated to wakefulness. They have seven good qualities, and they get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn53:7.1.verse: And how is a noble disciple accomplished in ethics?

mn53:7.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

mn53:7.3.verse: That’s how a noble disciple is ethical.

mn53:8.1.verse: And how does a noble disciple guard the sense doors?

mn53:8.2.verse: When a noble disciple sees a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn53:8.3.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn53:8.4.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn53:8.5.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn53:8.6.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn53:8.7.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn53:8.8.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn53:8.9.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn53:8.10.verse: That’s how a noble disciple guards the sense doors.

mn53:9.1.verse: And how does a noble disciple eat in moderation?

mn53:9.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple reflects rationally on the food that they eat:

mn53:9.3.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

mn53:9.4.verse: That’s how a noble disciple eats in moderation.

mn53:10.1.verse: And how is a noble disciple dedicated to wakefulness?

mn53:10.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple practices walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying their mind from obstacles.

mn53:10.3.verse: In the first watch of the night, they continue to practice walking and sitting meditation.

mn53:10.4.verse: In the middle watch, they lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

mn53:10.5.verse: In the last watch, they get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying their mind from obstacles.

mn53:10.6.verse: That’s how a noble disciple is dedicated to wakefulness.

mn53:11.1.verse: And how does a noble disciple have seven good qualities?

mn53:11.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

mn53:11.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn53:12.1.verse: They have a conscience. They’re conscientious about bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and conscientious about having any bad, unskillful qualities.

mn53:13.1.verse: They exercise prudence. They’re prudent when it comes to bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and prudent when it comes to acquiring any bad, unskillful qualities.

mn53:14.1.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

mn53:15.1.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

mn53:16.1.verse: They’re mindful. They have utmost mindfulness and alertness, and can remember and recall what was said and done long ago.

mn53:17.1.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

mn53:17.2.verse: That’s how a noble disciple has seven good qualities.

mn53:18.1.verse: And how does a noble disciple get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty?

mn53:18.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption …

mn53:18.6.verse: That’s how a noble disciple gets the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn53:19.1.verse: When a noble disciple is accomplished in ethics, guards the sense doors, eats in moderation, and is dedicated to wakefulness; and they have seven good qualities, and they get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty, they are called a noble disciple who is a practicing trainee. Their eggs are unspoiled, and they are capable of breaking out of their shell, becoming awakened, and achieving the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn53:19.2.verse: Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs. And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated. Even if that chicken doesn’t wish,

mn53:19.3.verse: ‘If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!’

mn53:19.4.verse: Still they can break out and hatch safely.

mn53:19.5.verse: In the same way, when a noble disciple is practicing all these things they are called a noble disciple who is a practicing trainee. Their eggs are unspoiled, and they are capable of breaking out of their shell, becoming awakened, and achieving the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn53:20.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple recollects their many kinds of past lives.

mn53:20.2.verse: That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. … And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn53:20.3.verse: This is their first breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.

mn53:21.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. … They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn53:21.2.verse: This is their second breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.

mn53:22.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn53:22.2.verse: This is their third breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.

mn53:23.1.verse: A noble disciple’s conduct includes the following: being accomplished in ethics,

mn53:23.6.verse: and getting the four absorptions when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn53:24.1.verse: A noble disciple’s knowledge includes the following: recollecting their past lives,

mn53:24.2.verse: clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman,

mn53:24.3.verse: and realizing the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn53:25.1.verse: This noble disciple is said to be ‘accomplished in knowledge’, and also ‘accomplished in conduct’, and also ‘accomplished in knowledge and conduct’.

mn53:25.2.verse: And the divinity Sanaṅkumāra also spoke this verse:

mn53:25.4.verse: who take clan as the standard.

mn53:25.5.verse: But one accomplished in knowledge and conduct

mn53:25.6.verse: is best among gods and humans.’

mn53:25.7.verse: And that verse was well sung by the Divinity Sanaṅkumāra, not poorly sung; well spoken, not poorly spoken, beneficial, not harmful, and it was approved by the Buddha.”

mn53:26.1.verse: Then the Buddha got up and said to Venerable Ānanda,

mn53:26.3.verse: It’s good that you spoke to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu about the practicing trainee.”

mn53:26.4.verse: That is what Venerable Ānanda said,

mn53:26.6.verse: Satisfied, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu approved what Venerable Ānanda said.

mn54:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the country of the Anguttarāpans. There is a town of theirs called Āpaṇa.

mn54:2.1.verse: Now when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Āpaṇa for alms.

mn54:2.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Āpaṇa and returned from his alms-round after his meal, he went to a certain grove for the day’s abiding,

mn54:2.3.verse: and he went into the grove and sat down at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.

mn54:3.1.verse: Potaliya the householder, wearing full dress with parasol and sandals also went to the grove, walking and wandering for exercise, and when he had gone into the grove he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,

mn54:3.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:

mn54:3.3.verse: ‘There are seats, householder, sit down if you like.’

mn54:3.4.verse: When this was said, the householder Potaliya (thought): ‘The monk Gotama addresses me with the word “householder”,’ and he was annoyed and displeased and remained silent.

mn54:3.6.verse: and a third time the Blessed One said to him:

mn54:3.7.verse: ‘There are seats, householder, sit down if you like.’

mn54:3.8.verse: When this was said, the householder Potaliya (thought): ‘The monk Gotama addresses me with the word “householder”,’ and he was annoyed and displeased, and he said:

mn54:3.9.verse: ‘Master Gotama, it is neither fitting nor proper that you address me with the word “householder”.’

mn54:3.10.verse: ‘Householder, you have the aspects, marks and signs of a householder.’

mn54:3.11.verse: ‘Nevertheless, Master Gotama, I have given up all my works and am cut off from all my affairs.’

mn54:3.12.verse: ‘In what way have you given up all your works, householder, and are cut off from all your affairs?’

mn54:3.13.verse: ‘Master Gotama, whatever property or corn, silver or gold I had I have consigned it all as an inheritance to my children. I live on that, without giving advice or reproof, using just enough for food and clothing.

mn54:3.14.verse: That is how I have given up all my works and am cut off from all my affairs.’

mn54:3.15.verse: ‘Householder, being cut off from affairs as you describe it is one and being cut off from affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline is another.’

mn54:3.16.verse: ‘How is being cut off from affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline, then, venerable sir?

mn54:3.17.verse: It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma showing how being cut off from affairs is in the Noble Ones’ Discipline.’

mn54:3.18.verse: ‘Then listen, householder, and heed well what I shall say.’

mn54:4.2.verse: ‘Householder, there are eight dhammas in the Noble Ones’ Discipline that lead to the cutting off of affairs.

mn54:4.4.verse: Killing of living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings;

mn54:4.5.verse: Taking of what is not given is to be abandoned with the support of taking what is given.

mn54:4.6.verse: False speech is to be abandoned with the support of true speech.

mn54:4.7.verse: Malicious speech is to be abandoned with the support of unmalicious speech.

mn54:4.8.verse: Rapacious greed is to be abandoned with the support of absence of rapacious greed.

mn54:4.9.verse: Spiteful revenge is to be abandoned with the support of absence of spiteful revenge.

mn54:4.10.verse: Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair.

mn54:4.11.verse: Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride.

mn54:4.12.verse: These are the eight dhammas, stated in brief without expounding the details, that lead in the Noble Ones’ Discipline to the cutting off of affairs.’

mn54:5.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it would be good if, out of pity, the Blessed One expounds the details of these eight dhammas that lead in the Noble Ones’ Discipline to the cutting off of affairs, which have been stated in brief by the Blessed One without expounding the details.’

mn54:5.2.verse: ‘Then listen, householder, and heed well what I shall say.’

mn54:6.1.verse: ‘”Killing living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings”, so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn54:6.2.verse: Here a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:6.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my killing living beings.

mn54:6.4.verse: Were I to be a killer of living beings, (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that.

mn54:6.5.verse: But this killing of living beings is itself a fetter and a hindrance.

mn54:6.6.verse: And while taints and fever of defilement might arise owing to the killing of living beings, there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from killing living beings.”

mn54:6.7.verse: “Killing of living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings.”

mn54:6.8.verse: So it is with reference to this that it was said.

mn54:7.1.verse: “‘Taking what is not given is to be abandoned with the support of taking what is given”; so it was said …

mn54:7.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my taking what is not given …

mn54:7.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that …

mn54:7.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from taking what is not given” …

mn54:8.1.verse: “‘False speech is to be abandoned with the support of true speech”; so it was said …

mn54:8.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my speaking falsehood …

mn54:8.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that

mn54:8.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from false speech”

mn54:9.1.verse: “‘Malicious speech is to be abandoned with the support of unmalicious speech”; so it was said …

mn54:9.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my speaking maliciously …

mn54:9.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that

mn54:9.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from malicious speech”

mn54:10.1.verse: “‘Rapacious greed is to be abandoned with the support of absence of rapacious greed”; so it was said …

mn54:10.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being rapaciously greedy …

mn54:10.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that

mn54:10.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not rapaciously greedy”

mn54:11.1.verse: ‘ “Spiteful revenge is to be abandoned with the support of absence of spiteful revenge”; so it was said ...

mn54:11.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being spitefully revengeful …

mn54:11.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that

mn54:11.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not spitefully revengeful”

mn54:12.1.verse: ‘ “Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair”; so it was said …

mn54:12.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my angry despairing …

mn54:12.4.verse: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that …

mn54:12.6.verse: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not angrily despair.”

mn54:12.7.verse: So it was with reference to this that it was said: “Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair.” ’

mn54:13.1.verse: ‘ “Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride”; so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn54:13.2.verse: Here a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:13.3.verse: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being proud.

mn54:13.4.verse: Were I to be proud, (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that.

mn54:13.5.verse: But this pride is itself a fetter and a hindrance.

mn54:13.6.verse: And while taints and fever defilement might arise owing to pride, there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who is not proud.”

mn54:13.7.verse: “Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride.” ’

mn54:13.8.verse: So it was for this reason that it was said,

mn54:14.1.verse: ‘These eight dhammas, stated in brief, which lead in the Noble One’s Discipline to the cutting off of affairs, have now been expounded in detail.

mn54:14.2.verse: But the cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline has not yet been achieved altogether and in all ways.’

mn54:14.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, how does the cutting off of affairs come to pass in the Noble Ones’ Discipline altogether and in all ways?

mn54:14.4.verse: It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would tell me that.’

mn54:14.5.verse: ‘Then listen, householder and heed well what I shall say.’

mn54:15.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose a dog was waiting hungry and weak in a butcher’s shambles,

mn54:15.2.verse: and then a skilled butcher or his apprentice carved out a skeleton of bones, blood-smeared but with no meat and he tossed it to the dog.

mn54:15.3.verse: How do you conceive this, householder?

mn54:15.4.verse: Would that dog get rid of his hunger and weakness by gnawing such a bone?’

mn54:15.7.verse: ‘That skeleton of bones was well carved out, blood-smeared, with no meat;

mn54:15.8.verse: eventually that dog would reap weariness and disappointment.’

mn54:15.9.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:15.10.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a skeleton of bones by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”

mn54:15.11.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:16.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose a vulture, a crow or a kite seized a piece of meat and flew away,

mn54:16.2.verse: and then vultures and crows and kites flew up and pecked and clawed it.

mn54:16.3.verse: How do you conceive this, householder?

mn54:16.4.verse: If that vulture, crow or kite did not soon relinquish that piece of meat, would he because of that incur death or deadly suffering?’

mn54:16.6.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:16.7.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a piece of meat by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”

mn54:16.8.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:17.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose a man took a lighted grass torch and went against the wind.

mn54:17.2.verse: How do you conceive this, householder?

mn54:17.3.verse: If that man did not soon relinquish that lighted grass torch, would that lighted grass torch burn his hand or his arm or one or other of his limbs, and might he because of that incur death or deadly suffering?’

mn54:17.5.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:17.6.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a grass torch by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”

mn54:17.7.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:18.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height full of glowing coals without flame or smoke,

mn54:18.2.verse: and then a man came who wanted to live and not to die, who wanted pleasure and recoiled from pain,

mn54:18.3.verse: and two strong men seized him by both arms and dragged him towards that charcoal pit.

mn54:18.4.verse: How do you conceive this, householder?

mn54:18.5.verse: Would that man fling his body this way and that?’

mn54:18.8.verse: Because that man knows that if he falls into that charcoal pit, he will because of that incur death or deadly suffering.’

mn54:18.9.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:18.10.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a charcoal pit by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”

mn54:18.11.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:19.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose a man saw a dream with delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful meadows, delightful lakes

mn54:19.2.verse: and on waking he saw nothing (of it),

mn54:19.3.verse: so too a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:19.4.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a dream by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,

mn54:19.5.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:20.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose a man borrowed property on loan: a smart carriage, or fine-jewelled earrings,

mn54:20.2.verse: and preceded and surrounded by that borrowed property he went into the marketplace,

mn54:20.3.verse: and then when people saw him, they spoke thus:

mn54:20.4.verse: “Sirs, that is a rich man! That is how the rich enjoy their riches!”

mn54:20.5.verse: and then the owners, whenever they saw him, took back what was theirs.

mn54:20.6.verse: How do you conceive this, householder? Would that be enough for that man to change (his mind)?’

mn54:20.9.verse: Because the owners take back what is theirs.’

mn54:20.10.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:20.11.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a loan by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,

mn54:20.12.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:21.1.verse: ‘Householder, suppose there were a dense grove not far from some village or town

mn54:21.2.verse: where there was a tree all in blossom but none of its flowers had fallen to the ground,

mn54:21.3.verse: and then a man came needing flowers, seeking flowers, wandering in search of flowers

mn54:21.4.verse: and he went into the tree all in blossom,

mn54:21.6.verse: “This tree is all in blossom but none of its flowers have fallen to the ground;

mn54:21.7.verse: still I know how to climb a tree,

mn54:21.8.verse: so why should I not climb this tree and pick as many as I want and fill my pocket?”

mn54:21.10.verse: and then a second man needing flowers, seeking flowers, wandering in search of flowers, taking a sharp axe, he too went into the grove

mn54:21.11.verse: and saw that tree all in blossom,

mn54:21.13.verse: “This tree is all in blossom, but none of its flowers have fallen to the ground;

mn54:21.14.verse: but I do not know how to climb a tree,

mn54:21.15.verse: so why should I not set about cutting this tree down at its root and pick as many as I want and fill my pocket?”

mn54:21.17.verse: How do you conceive this, householder?

mn54:21.18.verse: If that first man who has climbed the tree did not soon come down, might he break his hand when the tree fell, or his foot or one or other of his limbs, whereby he might incur death or deadly suffering?’

mn54:21.20.verse: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn54:21.21.verse: “Sensual desires have been compared to a tree by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,

mn54:21.22.verse: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.

mn54:22.1.verse: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity (characteristic of the fourth jhāna), this noble disciple recollects his manifold past life

mn54:22.2.verse: that is to say, one birth, two births ... five births, ten births … fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (world) contraction, many aeons of (world) expansion, many aeons of [(world) contraction and expansion: There I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I appeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared here. Thus with its details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.

mn54:23.1.verse: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity, with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, this noble disciple sees beings passing away and reappearing inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; I understood how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas (actions), have on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings, who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.

mn54:24.1.verse: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity, by realization himself with direct knowledge, this noble disciple here and now enters upon and abides in deliverance of the heart and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints.

mn54:25.1.verse: ‘At this point, householder, the cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline has been achieved altogether and in all ways.

mn54:25.2.verse: How do you conceive this, householder,

mn54:25.3.verse: do you see in yourself any such cutting off of affairs as this cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline when it is achieved altogether and in all ways?’

mn54:25.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, who am I that I should possess any such cutting off of affairs altogether and in all ways as it is in the Noble Ones’ Discipline?

mn54:25.5.verse: I am far indeed from that, venerable sir.

mn54:25.6.verse: For, venerable sir, while the Wanderers of other sects do not know, we conceived that they knew; while they do not know, we fed them as one feeds those who know; while they do not know, we set them in the place of those who know.

mn54:25.7.verse: But while the Bhikkhus know, we conceived that they did not know; while they know, we fed them as one feeds those who do not know; while they know, we set them in the place of those who do not know.

mn54:25.8.verse: But now, venerable sir, while the Wanderers of other sects do not know, we shall know that they do not know; while they do not know, we shall feed them as one feeds those who do not know; while they do not know, we shall set them in the place of those who do not know.

mn54:25.9.verse: But while the Bhikkhus know, we shall know that they know; while they know, we shall feed them as one feeds those that know; while they know, we shall set them in the place of those who know.

mn54:25.10.verse: Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows my love for monks, my confidence in monks, my respect for monks.

mn54:26.2.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.

mn54:26.3.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn54:26.4.verse: From today let Master, Gotama remember me as one who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn54:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Aṅguttarāpans, near the town of theirs named Āpaṇa.

mn54:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms.

mn54:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Āpaṇa. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to a certain forest grove for the day’s meditation.

mn54:2.3.verse: Having plunged deep into it, he sat at the root of a certain tree to meditate.

mn54:3.1.verse: Potaliya the householder also approached that forest grove while going for a walk. He was well dressed in sarong and cloak, with parasol and sandals. Having plunged deep into it, he went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn54:3.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side, and the Buddha said to him,

mn54:3.3.verse: “There are seats, householder. Please sit if you wish.”

mn54:3.4.verse: When he said this, Potaliya was angry and upset. Thinking, “The ascetic Gotama addresses me as ‘householder’!” he stayed silent.

mn54:3.6.verse: and a third time the Buddha said to him,

mn54:3.7.verse: “There are seats, householder. Please sit if you wish.”

mn54:3.8.verse: When he said this, Potaliya was angry and upset. Thinking, “The ascetic Gotama addresses me as ‘householder’!” he said to the Buddha,

mn54:3.9.verse: “Worthy Gotama, it is neither proper nor appropriate for you to address me as ‘householder’.”

mn54:3.10.verse: “Well, householder, you have the features, attributes, and signs of a householder.”

mn54:3.11.verse: “Worthy Gotama, it’s because I have turned down all work and cut off all business.”

mn54:3.12.verse: “Householder, in what way have you turned down all work and cut off all business?”

mn54:3.13.verse: “Worthy Gotama, all the money, grain, gold, and silver I used to have has been handed over to my children as their inheritance. And in this matter I do not advise or reprimand them, but live with nothing more than food and clothes.

mn54:3.14.verse: That’s how I have turned down all work and cut off all business.”

mn54:3.15.verse: “The cutting off of business as you describe it is one thing, householder, but the cutting off of business in the Noble One’s training is quite different.”

mn54:3.16.verse: “But what, sir, is cutting off of business in the Noble One’s training?

mn54:3.18.verse: “Well then, householder, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn54:4.2.verse: “Householder, these eight things lead to the cutting off of business in the Noble One’s training.

mn54:4.4.verse: Killing living creatures should be given up, relying on not killing living creatures.

mn54:4.5.verse: Stealing should be given up, relying on not stealing.

mn54:4.6.verse: Lying should be given up, relying on speaking the truth.

mn54:4.7.verse: Backbiting should be given up, relying on not backbiting.

mn54:4.8.verse: Greed and lust should be given up, relying on not being greedy and lustful.

mn54:4.9.verse: Blaming and insulting should be given up, relying on not blaming and not insulting.

mn54:4.10.verse: Anger and distress should be given up, relying on not being angry and distressed.

mn54:4.11.verse: Arrogance should be given up, relying on not being arrogant.

mn54:4.12.verse: These are the eight things—stated in brief without being analyzed in detail—that lead to the cutting off of business in the Noble One’s training.”

mn54:5.1.verse: “Sir, please teach me these eight things in detail out of sympathy.”

mn54:5.2.verse: “Well then, householder, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn54:6.1.verse: “‘Killing living creatures should be given up, relying on not killing living creatures.’ That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn54:6.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple reflects:

mn54:6.3.verse: ‘I am practicing to give up and cut off the fetters that might cause me to kill living creatures.

mn54:6.4.verse: But if I were to kill living creatures, because of that I would reprimand myself; sensible people, after examination, would criticize me; and when my body breaks up, after death, I could expect to be reborn in a bad place.

mn54:6.5.verse: And killing living creatures is itself a fetter and a hindrance.

mn54:6.6.verse: The distressing and feverish defilements that might arise because of killing living creatures do not occur in someone who does not kill living creatures.’

mn54:6.7.verse: ‘Killing living creatures should be given up, relying on not killing living creatures.’

mn54:6.8.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn54:13.1.verse: Arrogance should be given up, relying on not being arrogant.’ That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn54:13.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple reflects:

mn54:13.3.verse: ‘I am practicing to give up and cut off the fetters that might cause me to be arrogant.

mn54:13.4.verse: But if I were to be arrogant, because of that I would reprimand myself; sensible people, after examination, would criticize me; and when my body breaks up, after death, I could expect to be reborn in a bad place.

mn54:13.5.verse: And arrogance is itself a fetter and a hindrance.

mn54:13.6.verse: The distressing and feverish defilements that might arise because of arrogance do not occur in someone who is not arrogant.’

mn54:13.7.verse: ‘Arrogance should be given up by not being arrogant.’

mn54:13.8.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn54:14.1.verse: These are the eight things—stated in brief and analyzed in detail—that lead to the cutting off of business in the Noble One’s training.

mn54:14.2.verse: But just this much does not constitute the cutting off of business in each and every respect in the Noble One’s training.”

mn54:14.3.verse: “But, sir, how is there the cutting off of business in each and every respect in the Noble One’s training?

mn54:14.5.verse: “Well then, householder, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn54:15.1.verse: “Householder, suppose a dog weak with hunger was hanging around a butcher’s shop.

mn54:15.2.verse: A deft butcher or their apprentice would toss them a skeleton scraped clean of flesh and smeared in blood.

mn54:15.4.verse: Gnawing on such a fleshless skeleton, would that dog still get rid of its hunger?”

mn54:15.7.verse: Because that skeleton is scraped clean of flesh and smeared in blood.

mn54:15.8.verse: That dog will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn54:15.9.verse: “In the same way, a noble disciple reflects:

mn54:15.10.verse: ‘With the simile of a skeleton the Buddha said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.’

mn54:15.11.verse: Having truly seen this with right understanding, they shun equanimity based on diversity and develop only the equanimity based on unity, where all kinds of grasping to the worldly pleasures of the flesh cease without remainder.

mn54:16.1.verse: Suppose a vulture or a crow or a hawk was to grab a scrap of meat and fly away.

mn54:16.2.verse: Other vultures, crows, and hawks would keep chasing it, pecking and clawing.

mn54:16.4.verse: If that vulture, crow, or hawk doesn’t quickly let go of that scrap of meat, wouldn’t that result in death or deadly suffering for them?”

mn54:17.1.verse: “Suppose a person carrying a blazing grass torch was to walk against the wind.

mn54:17.3.verse: If that person doesn’t quickly let go of that blazing grass torch, wouldn’t they burn their hands or arm or other major or minor limb, resulting in death or deadly suffering for them?”

mn54:18.1.verse: “Suppose there was a pit of glowing coals deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals that neither flamed nor smoked.

mn54:18.2.verse: Then a person would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.

mn54:18.3.verse: Two strong men would grab them by the arms and drag them toward the pit of glowing coals.

mn54:18.5.verse: Wouldn’t that person writhe and struggle to and fro?”

mn54:18.8.verse: For that person knows: ‘If I fall in that pit of glowing coals, that’d result in my death or deadly pain.’” …

mn54:19.1.verse: “Suppose a person was to see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds in a dream.

mn54:19.2.verse: But when they woke they couldn’t see them at all. …

mn54:20.1.verse: Suppose a man had borrowed some goods—a gentleman’s carriage and fine jeweled earrings—

mn54:20.2.verse: and preceded and surrounded by these he proceeded through the middle of Āpaṇa.

mn54:20.3.verse: When people saw him they’d say:

mn54:20.4.verse: ‘This must be a wealthy man! For that’s how the wealthy enjoy their wealth.’

mn54:20.5.verse: But when the owners saw him, they’d take back what was theirs.

mn54:20.6.verse: What do you think? Would that be enough for that man to get upset?”

mn54:20.9.verse: Because the owners took back what was theirs.” …

mn54:21.1.verse: “Suppose there was a dense forest grove not far from a town or village.

mn54:21.2.verse: And there was a tree laden with fruit, yet none of the fruit had fallen to the ground.

mn54:21.3.verse: And along came a person in need of fruit, wandering in search of fruit.

mn54:21.4.verse: Having plunged deep into that forest grove, they’d see that tree laden with fruit.

mn54:21.6.verse: ‘That tree is laden with fruit, yet none of the fruit has fallen to the ground.

mn54:21.7.verse: But I know how to climb a tree.

mn54:21.8.verse: Why don’t I climb the tree, eat as much as I like, then fill my pouch?’

mn54:21.10.verse: And along would come a second person in need of fruit, wandering in search of fruit, carrying a sharp axe.

mn54:21.11.verse: Having plunged deep into that forest grove, they’d see that tree laden with fruit.

mn54:21.13.verse: ‘That tree is laden with fruit, yet none of the fruit has fallen to the ground.

mn54:21.14.verse: But I don’t know how to climb a tree.

mn54:21.15.verse: Why don’t I chop this tree down at the root, eat as much as I like, then fill my pouch?’

mn54:21.16.verse: And so they’d chop the tree down at the root.

mn54:21.18.verse: If the first person, who climbed the tree, doesn’t quickly come down, when that tree fell wouldn’t they break their hand or arm or other major or minor limb, resulting in death or deadly suffering for them?”

mn54:21.20.verse: “In the same way, a noble disciple reflects:

mn54:21.21.verse: ‘With the simile of the fruit tree the Buddha said that sensual pleasures give little gratification and much suffering and distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks.’

mn54:21.22.verse: Having truly seen this with right understanding, they shun equanimity based on diversity and develop only the equanimity based on unity, where all kinds of grasping to the worldly pleasures of the flesh cease without remainder.

mn54:22.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple recollects their many kinds of past lives.

mn54:22.2.verse: That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. … They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn54:23.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. … They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn54:24.1.verse: Relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn54:25.1.verse: That’s how there is the cutting off of business in each and every respect in the Noble One’s training.

mn54:25.3.verse: Do you regard yourself as having cut off business in a way comparable to the cutting off of business in each and every respect in the Noble One’s training?”

mn54:25.4.verse: “Who am I compared to one who has cut off business in each and every respect in the Noble One’s training?

mn54:25.6.verse: Sir, I used to think that the wanderers following other religions were thoroughbreds, and I fed them and treated them accordingly, but they were not actually thoroughbreds.

mn54:25.7.verse: I thought that the mendicants were not thoroughbreds, and I fed them and treated them accordingly, but they actually were thoroughbreds.

mn54:25.8.verse: But now I shall understand that the wanderers following other religions are not actually thoroughbreds, and I will feed them and treat them accordingly.

mn54:25.9.verse: And I shall understand that the mendicants actually are thoroughbreds, and I will feed them and treat them accordingly.

mn54:25.10.verse: The Buddha has inspired me to have love, confidence, and respect for ascetics!

mn54:26.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn54:26.3.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn54:26.4.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn55:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Mango Grove of Jivaka Komārabhacca.

mn55:2.1.verse: Then Jivaka Komārabhacca went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:

mn55:3.2.verse: “They slaughter living beings for the monk Gotama; the monk Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared for him when invited.”

mn55:3.3.verse: Venerable sir, when they say that, do they say what the Blessed One says, without misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is not so, do they express Dhamma according to Dhamma with no legitimate deduction from their assertions that provides in Dhamma grounds for condemning them?’

mn55:4.1.verse: ‘Jivaka, those who say thus: “They slaughter living beings for the monk Gotama; the monk Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared for him when invited” do not say what I say; they misrepresent me with what is not true, what is not so.

mn55:5.1.verse: ‘Jivaka, I say that there are three instances in which meat should not be eaten:

mn55:5.2.verse: when it is seen, heard or suspected (that the living being has been slaughtered for the eater).

mn55:5.3.verse: I say that meat should not be eaten in these three instances.

mn55:5.4.verse: I say that there are three instances in which meat can be eaten:

mn55:5.5.verse: when it is not seen, not heard, not suspected (that the living being has been slaughtered for the eater).

mn55:5.6.verse: I say that meat can be eaten in these three instances.

mn55:6.1.verse: ‘Here some bhikkhu lives near a village or town.

mn55:6.2.verse: He abides with mind endued with loving-kindness extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with an abundant, exalted, measureless mind of loving-kindness extending over the all-embracing world.

mn55:6.3.verse: Then a householder or a householder’s son comes to him and invites him for the next day’s meal.

mn55:6.4.verse: The bhikkhu accepts, if he likes.

mn55:6.5.verse: When the night is ended he dresses, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he goes to the house of that householder or householder’s son and sits down on a seat made ready.

mn55:6.6.verse: Then the householder or householder’s son serves him with good alms-food.

mn55:6.8.verse: “It is good that the householder or householder’s son serves me with good alms-food.

mn55:6.9.verse: If only a householder or householder’s son might serve me with such good alms-food in the future!”

mn55:6.11.verse: He eats that alms-food without entanglement and not unwarily committed, seeing danger in it and understanding the escape from it.

mn55:6.12.verse: How do you conceive this, Jivaka,

mn55:6.13.verse: would that bhikkhu on such an occasion will his own affliction or another’s affliction or the affliction of both?’

mn55:6.15.verse: ‘Does not that bhikkhu nourish himself with blameless nourishment on that occasion?’

mn55:7.2.verse: I have heard this, venerable sir:

mn55:7.4.verse: Venerable sir, I have seen the Blessed One as a witness to that;

mn55:7.5.verse: for the Blessed One, Venerable sir, abides in loving-kindness.’
