mn55:7.6.verse: ‘Jivaka, any lust or any hate or any delusion whereby ill-will might arise in him, a Tathāgata has abandoned, cut off at the roots, made like a palm-stump, done away with so that it is no longer liable to future arising.

mn55:7.7.verse: If what you said referred to that, then I allow it you.’

mn55:7.8.verse: ‘Venerable sir, what I said referred to precisely that.’

mn55:8-10.1.verse: ‘Here some bhikkhu lives near a village or town.

mn55:8-10.2.verse: He abides with mind endued with compassion …’

mn55:8-10.3.verse: ‘Here some bhikkhu lives near a village or town. He abides with gladness …’

mn55:8-10.4.verse: ‘Here some bhikkhu lives near a village or town. He abides with mind endued with equanimity …’

mn55:8-10.6.verse: Then a householder or a householder’s son comes to him and invites him for the next day’s meal.

mn55:8-10.7.verse: The bhikkhu accepts, if he likes.

mn55:8-10.8.verse: When the night is ended he dresses, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he goes to the house of that householder or householder’s son and sits down on a seat made ready.

mn55:8-10.9.verse: Then the householder or householder’s son serves him with good alms-food.

mn55:8-10.11.verse: “It is good that the householder or householder’s son serves me with good alms-food.

mn55:8-10.12.verse: If only a householder or householder’s son might serve me with such good alms-food in the future!”

mn55:8-10.14.verse: He eats that alms-food without entanglement and not unwarily committed, seeing danger in it and understanding the escape from it.

mn55:8-10.15.verse: How do you conceive this, Jivaka,

mn55:8-10.16.verse: would that bhikkhu on such an occasion will his own affliction or another’s affliction or the affliction of both?’

mn55:8-10.18.verse: ‘Does not that bhikkhu nourish himself with blameless nourishment on that occasion?’

mn55:11.8.verse: ‘ … what I said referred to precisely that.’

mn55:12.1.verse: ‘If anyone slaughters a living being for a Tathāgata or his disciple, he lays up much demerit in five instances:

mn55:12.3.verse: “Go and fetch that living being”, this is the first instance in which he lays up much demerit.

mn55:12.4.verse: When that living being experiences pain and grief on being led along with a neck-halter, this is the second instance in which he lays up much demerit.

mn55:12.6.verse: “Go and slaughter that living being”, this is the third instance when he lays up much demerit.

mn55:12.7.verse: When that living being experiences pain and grief on being slaughtered, this is the fourth instance in which he lays up much demerit.

mn55:12.8.verse: When he provides a Tathāgata or his disciple with food that is not permissable, this is the fifth instance in which he lays up much demerit.

mn55:12.9.verse: Anyone who slaughters a living being for a Tathāgata or his disciple lays up much demerit in these five instances.’

mn55:13.1.verse: When this was said, Jivaka Komārabhacca said:

mn55:13.2.verse: ‘It is wonderful, Venerable sir, it is marvellous!

mn55:13.3.verse: Bhikkhus nourish themselves with permissable nourishment.

mn55:13.4.verse: Bhikkhus nourish themselves with blameless nourishment.

mn55:13.6.verse: (as in Sutta 4, para. 36-7 … for refuge for life.’

mn55:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Mango Grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.

mn55:2.1.verse: Then Jīvaka went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

mn55:3.2.verse: ‘They slaughter living creatures specially for the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on his behalf: this is a deed he caused.’

mn55:3.3.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the Buddha has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

mn55:4.1.verse: “Jīvaka, those who say this do not repeat what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue.

mn55:5.1.verse: In three cases I say that meat may not be eaten:

mn55:5.3.verse: These are three cases in which meat may not be eaten.

mn55:5.4.verse: In three cases I say that meat may be eaten:

mn55:5.5.verse: it’s not seen, heard, or suspected.

mn55:5.6.verse: These are three cases in which meat may be eaten.

mn55:6.1.verse: Take the case of a mendicant living supported by a town or village.

mn55:6.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn55:6.3.verse: A householder or their child approaches and invites them for the next day’s meal.

mn55:6.4.verse: The mendicant accepts if they want.

mn55:6.5.verse: When the night has passed, they robe up in the morning, take their bowl and robe, and approach that householder’s home, where they sit on the seat spread out.

mn55:6.6.verse: That householder or their child serves them with delicious almsfood.

mn55:6.8.verse: ‘It’s so good that this householder serves me with delicious almsfood!

mn55:6.9.verse: I hope they serve me with such delicious almsfood in the future!’

mn55:6.11.verse: They eat that almsfood untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawback, and understanding the escape.

mn55:6.13.verse: At that time is that mendicant intending to hurt themselves, hurt others, or hurt both?”

mn55:6.15.verse: “Aren’t they eating blameless food at that time?”

mn55:7.4.verse: Now, I’ve seen the Buddha with my own eyes,

mn55:7.5.verse: and it is the Buddha who truly abides in love.”

mn55:7.6.verse: “Any greed, hate, or delusion that might give rise to ill will has been given up by the Realized One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is unable to arise in the future.

mn55:7.7.verse: If that’s what you were referring to, I grant it.”

mn55:7.8.verse: “That’s exactly what I was referring to.”

mn55:8-10.1.verse: “Take the case, Jīvaka, of a mendicant living supported by a town or village.

mn55:8-10.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn55:8-10.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn55:8-10.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth.

mn55:8-10.5.verse: In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn55:8-10.6.verse: A householder or their child approaches and invites them for the next day’s meal.

mn55:8-10.7.verse: The mendicant accepts if they want.

mn55:8-10.8.verse: When the night has passed, they robe up in the morning, take their bowl and robe, and approach that householder’s home, where they sit on the seat spread out.

mn55:8-10.9.verse: That householder or their child serves them with delicious almsfood.

mn55:8-10.11.verse: ‘It’s so good that this householder serves me with delicious almsfood!

mn55:8-10.12.verse: I hope they serve me with such delicious almsfood in the future!’

mn55:8-10.14.verse: They eat that almsfood untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawback, and understanding the escape.

mn55:8-10.16.verse: At that time is that mendicant intending to hurt themselves, hurt others, or hurt both?”

mn55:8-10.18.verse: “Aren’t they eating blameless food at that time?”

mn55:11.4.verse: Now, I’ve seen the Buddha with my own eyes,

mn55:11.5.verse: and it is the Buddha who truly abides in equanimity.”

mn55:11.6.verse: “Any greed, hate, or delusion that might give rise to cruelty, discontent, or aversion has been given up by the Realized One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is unable to arise in the future.

mn55:11.7.verse: If that’s what you were referring to, I grant it.”

mn55:11.8.verse: “That’s exactly what I was referring to.”

mn55:12.1.verse: “Jīvaka, anyone who slaughters a living creature specially for the Realized One or the Realized One’s disciple brims with much wickedness for five reasons.

mn55:12.3.verse: ‘Go, fetch that living creature,’ this is the first reason.

mn55:12.4.verse: When that living creature experiences pain and sadness as it’s led along by a collar, this is the second reason.

mn55:12.6.verse: ‘Go, slaughter that living creature,’ this is the third reason.

mn55:12.7.verse: When that living creature experiences pain and sadness as it’s being slaughtered, this is the fourth reason.

mn55:12.8.verse: When they serve the Realized One or the Realized One’s disciple with unallowable food, this is the fifth reason.

mn55:12.9.verse: Anyone who slaughters a living creature specially for the Realized One or the Realized One’s disciple brims with much wickedness for five reasons.”

mn55:13.1.verse: When he had spoken, Jīvaka said to the Buddha:

mn55:13.3.verse: The mendicants indeed eat allowable food.

mn55:13.4.verse: The mendicants indeed eat blameless food.

mn55:13.6.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn56:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Nālanda in Pavārika’s Mango Grove.

mn56:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the Nigaṇṭha (Jain) Nātaputta was staying at Nālanda with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.

mn56:2.2.verse: Then when the Nigaṇṭha Tall Ascetic (Dīgha Tapassi) had wandered for alms in Nālanda and had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he went to Pavārika’s Mango Grove to see the Blessed One, and exchanged greetings with him,

mn56:2.3.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:

mn56:2.4.verse: ‘There are seats, ascetic, sit down if you like.’

mn56:3.1.verse: When this was said, the Tall Ascetic took a lower seat and sat down at one side.

mn56:3.2.verse: When he had done so, the Blessed One asked him:

mn56:3.3.verse: ‘Ascetic, how many kinds of kamma does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma?’

mn56:3.4.verse: ‘Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is not accustomed to use the description “kamma, kamma”;

mn56:3.5.verse: the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is accustomed to use the description “rod, rod”.’

mn56:3.6.verse: ‘Then, ascetic, how many kinds of rod does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe for the performance of evil action, for the perpetration of evil action?’

mn56:3.7.verse: ‘Friend Gotama, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describes three kinds of rods for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, that is to say:

mn56:3.8.verse: the bodily rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod.’

mn56:3.9.verse: ‘How then, ascetic, is the bodily rod one, the verbal rod another, and mental rod another?’

mn56:3.10.verse: ‘The bodily rod is one, friend Gotama, the verbal rod is another, and the mental rod is another.’

mn56:3.11.verse: ‘Of these three kinds of rods, ascetic, thus analysed and distinguished, which kind of rod does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma: the bodily rod, or the verbal rod, or the mental rod?’

mn56:3.12.verse: ‘Of these three kinds of rod, friend Gotama, thus analysed and distinguished, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describes the bodily rod as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod, or the mental rod.’

mn56:3.13.verse: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’

mn56:3.14.verse: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’

mn56:3.15.verse: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’

mn56:3.16.verse: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’

mn56:3.17.verse: ‘Do you say the bodily rod, ascetic?’

mn56:3.18.verse: ‘I say the bodily rod, friend Gotama.’

mn56:3.19.verse: So the Blessed One made the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, maintain his statement up to the third time.

mn56:4.1.verse: When this was said, the Tall Ascetic asked the Blessed One:

mn56:4.2.verse: ‘Friend Gotama, how many kinds of rod do you describe for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma?’

mn56:4.3.verse: ‘Ascetic, a Tathāgata is not accustomed to use the description “rod, rod”;

mn56:4.4.verse: a Tathāgata is accustomed to use the description “kamma, kamma”.’

mn56:4.5.verse: ‘But, friend Gotama, how many kinds of kamma do you describe for the performance of evil kammas, for the perpetration of evil kammas?’

mn56:4.6.verse: ‘Ascetic, I describe three kinds of kammas for the performance of evil kammas, for the perpetration of evil kammas, that is to say:

mn56:4.7.verse: bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma.’

mn56:4.8.verse: ‘How then, friend Gotama, is bodily kamma one, verbal kamma another, and mental kamma another?’

mn56:4.9.verse: ‘Bodily kamma is one, ascetic, verbal kamma is another, and mental kamma is another.’

mn56:4.10.verse: ‘Of these three kinds of kamma, friend Gotama, thus analyzed and distinguished, which kind of kamma do you describe as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma: bodily kamma or verbal kamma or mental kamma?’

mn56:4.11.verse: ‘Of these three kinds of kamma, ascetic, thus analyzed and distinguished, I describe mental kamma as the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much bodily kamma or verbal kamma.’

mn56:4.12.verse: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’

mn56:4.14.verse: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’

mn56:4.16.verse: ‘Do you say mental kamma, friend Gotama?’

mn56:4.18.verse: So the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, made the Blessed One maintain his statement up to the third time, after which he rose from his seat and went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

mn56:5.1.verse: Now on that occasion the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was seated together with a very large assembly of laymen from Bālaka, most prominent among them being Upāli.

mn56:5.2.verse: The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta saw the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, coming;

mn56:5.3.verse: and when he saw him he asked him:

mn56:5.4.verse: ‘Now where are you coming from in broad day, Ascetic?’

mn56:5.5.verse: ‘I have come from the monk Gotama’s presence, venerable sir.’

mn56:5.6.verse: ‘Did you have some conversation with the monk Gotama, Ascetic?’

mn56:5.7.verse: ‘I had some conversation with the monk Gotama, venerable sir.’

mn56:5.8.verse: ‘How was your conversation with the monk Gotama, then, Ascetic?’

mn56:5.9.verse: Then the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, related to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta all his conversation with the Blessed One.

mn56:6.1.verse: When this was said the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta told him:

mn56:6.2.verse: ‘Good, good, (on the part of the) Ascetic:

mn56:6.3.verse: As by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the Tall Ascetic to the monk Gotama!

mn56:6.4.verse: What does the trivial mental rod count in comparison with the gross bodily rod?

mn56:6.5.verse: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod and the mental rod.’

mn56:7.1.verse: When this was said, the householder Upāli said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:7.2.verse: Good, good, venerable sir, (on the part of) the Tall Ascetic:

mn56:7.3.verse: As by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the venerable Ascetic to the monk Gotama:

mn56:7.4.verse: “What does the trivial mental rod count for in comparison with the gross bodily rod?

mn56:7.5.verse: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:7.6.verse: Now, venerable sir, I shall go and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement.

mn56:7.7.verse: If the monk Gotama maintains to me as he has been made to maintain by the venerable Tall Ascetic, I shall drag the monk Gotama to and fro and round about with argument as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by the hair and drag him to and fro and round about.

mn56:7.8.verse: I will drag the monk Gotama to and fro and round about with argument as a strong brewer’s workman might throw a big brewer’s seive into a deep water tank, and taking it by the corners, drag it to and fro and round about.

mn56:7.9.verse: I will shake the monk Gotama down and shake him up and thump him about with argument as a strong brewer’s mixer might take a strainer by the corners and shake it down and shake it up and thump it about.

mn56:7.10.verse: And just as a sixty-year old elephant might go down into a pond and have great sport in the game of hemp-washing, so too, I shall have great sport, I fancy, in the game of hemp-washing the monk Gotama!

mn56:7.11.verse: Venerable sir, I shall go and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement.’

mn56:7.12.verse: ‘Go, householder, and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong on the basis of this statement;

mn56:7.13.verse: for either I should prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong, or else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’

mn56:8.1.verse: When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:8.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;

mn56:8.3.verse: for the monk Gotama is a magician and he knows a converting magic by which he converts disciples of other sectarians.’

mn56:8.4.verse: ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should go over to the monk Gotama’s discipleship;

mn56:8.5.verse: but it is possible, it can happen, that the monk Gotama should come over to the householder Upāli’s discipleship.

mn56:8.6.verse: Go, householder, and prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;

mn56:8.7.verse: for either I should prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong or else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’

mn56:9.1.verse: For the second time, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove...’ ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen...’

mn56:9.2.verse: For the third time, the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:9.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;

mn56:9.4.verse: for the monk Gotama is a magician and he knows a converting magic by which he converts disciples of other sectarians.’

mn56:9.5.verse: ‘It is impossible, ascetic, it cannot happen that the householder Upāli should go over to the monk Gotama’s discipleship...

mn56:9.8.verse: else the Tall Ascetic or you yourself.’

mn56:9.9.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the householder Upāli replied, and he rose from his seat, and after paying homage to him, keeping him on his right, he left to go to the Blessed One in Pavārika’s Mango Grove, and there, after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked the Blessed One:

mn56:9.10.verse: ‘Venerable sir, did the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, come here?’

mn56:9.11.verse: ‘The Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, came here, householder.’

mn56:9.12.verse: ‘Venerable sir, did you have some conversation with him?’

mn56:9.13.verse: ‘I had some conversation with him, householder.’

mn56:9.14.verse: ‘How was your conversation with him, then, venerable sir?’

mn56:9.15.verse: Then the Blessed One related to the householder Upāli all his conversation with the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic.

mn56:10.1.verse: When this was said, the householder Upāli said to the Blessed One:

mn56:10.2.verse: ‘Good, good, venerable sir, (on the part of) the Tall Ascetic:

mn56:10.3.verse: as by a well-taught disciple who knows his teacher’s Dispensation rightly, so it has been declared by the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, to the Blessed One!

mn56:10.4.verse: What does the trivial mental rod count for in comparison with the gross bodily rod?

mn56:10.5.verse: On the contrary, the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma, and not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.’

mn56:10.6.verse: ‘Householder, if you will debate on the basis of truth, we might have some conversation about this.’

mn56:10.7.verse: ‘I will debate on the basis of truth, venerable sir,

mn56:10.8.verse: so let us have some conversation about this.’

mn56:11.2.verse: here some Nigaṇṭha might be afflicted, suffering and gravely ill (of an illness needing treatment by cold water which his vows prohibit) and he might refuse cold water (though mentally longing for it) and use only (the permissible) hot water (thus keeping his vows bodily and verbally),

mn56:11.3.verse: and through getting no cold water he might die.

mn56:11.4.verse: Now, householder, where would the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe his reappearance (as taking place)?’

mn56:11.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, there are gods called “mind-bound”; he would be reborn there.

mn56:11.7.verse: Because he died still bound (by attachment) in the mind.’

mn56:11.8.verse: ‘Householder, householder, pay attention how you reply.

mn56:11.9.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn56:11.11.verse: “I will debate on the basis of truth, venerable sir,

mn56:11.12.verse: so let us have some conversation about this.”’

mn56:11.13.verse: ‘Venerable sir, although the Blessed One has spoken thus, yet the bodily rod is the most reprehensible for the performance of evil kamma, for the perpetration of evil kamma.’

mn56:12.2.verse: here some Nigaṇṭha might be restrained with the four checks, curbed by all curbs, clamped by all curbs, cleansed by all curbs, and claimed by all curbs,

mn56:12.3.verse: and yet when moving forward and moving backward he is involved in the destruction of many a small living being.

mn56:12.4.verse: What ripening does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe for him?’

mn56:12.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta does not describe as greatly reprehensible what is not willed.’

mn56:12.7.verse: ‘Then it is greatly reprehensible, venerable sir.’

mn56:12.8.verse: ‘But under which (of the three rods) does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta describe willing, householder?’

mn56:12.11.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after …’

mn56:12.15.verse: ‘Venerable sir, although the Blessed One has spoken thus, yet the bodily rod is the most reprehensible …’

mn56:13.2.verse: is this (town of) Nālanda successful and prosperous, is it populous and crowded with people?’

mn56:13.5.verse: suppose a man came here brandishing a sword

mn56:13.7.verse: “In one moment, in one instant I will make as many living beings as there are in this (town of) Nālanda into one mash of meat, into one heap of meat”,

mn56:13.8.verse: how do you conceive this, householder,

mn56:13.9.verse: would that man be able to do that?’

mn56:13.10.verse: ‘Venerable sir, ten men, or twenty, forty or even fifty men would not be able to do that,

mn56:13.11.verse: so what does a single trivial man count for?’

mn56:13.13.verse: suppose some monk or divine came here possessed of supernormal success and attained to mastery of mind,

mn56:13.15.verse: “I will reduce this (town of) Nālanda to ashes with one mental act of hate”,

mn56:13.16.verse: how do you conceive this, householder,

mn56:13.17.verse: would such a monk or divine be able to do that?’

mn56:13.18.verse: ‘Venerable sir, such a monk or divine would be able to do that to ten Nālandas, or to twenty, thirty, forty or fifty Nālandas,

mn56:13.19.verse: so what does a single trivial Nālanda count for?’

mn56:13.20.verse: ‘Householder, householder, pay attention how you reply. What you said before does not agree with what you said after …’

mn56:13.21.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after …’

mn56:13.25.verse: ‘Venerable sir, although the Blessed One has spoken thus, yet the bodily rod is the most reprehensible …’

mn56:13.27.verse: you have heard how the forests of Daṇḍaka, Kālinga, Mejjha and Mātaṅga are forest and became forest?’

mn56:14.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, householder, by what means is it that the forests of Daṇḍaka, Kālinga, Mejjha and Mātaṅga are forest and have become forest?’

mn56:14.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I have heard this: “The forests of Daṇḍaka, Kālinga, Majjha and Mātanga are forest and have become forest by means of a mental act of hate on the part of the Sages.”’

mn56:14.3.verse: ‘Householder, householder, pay attention how you reply.

mn56:14.4.verse: What you said before does not agree with what you said after, or what you said after with what you said before.

mn56:14.6.verse: “I will debate on the basis of truth, venerable sir,

mn56:14.7.verse: so let us have some conversation about this”.’

mn56:15.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I was satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s very first simile;

mn56:15.2.verse: nevertheless I conceived (the thought of) opposing the Blessed One thus since I desired to hear the Blessed One’s varied answers to the question.

mn56:15.3.verse: Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!

mn56:15.4.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms.

mn56:15.5.verse: Venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.

mn56:15.6.verse: Let the Blessed One remember me as follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn56:16.1.verse: ‘Think it over, householder; it is good for such well-known people as you are to think matters over.’

mn56:16.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s telling me that,

mn56:16.3.verse: for the other sectarians, on acquiring me as their disciple, would carry a banner all over Nālanda to the effect that

mn56:16.4.verse: “the householder Upāli has come to our discipleship”.

mn56:16.5.verse: But on the contrary, the Blessed One tells me:

mn56:16.6.verse: “Think it over, householder; it is good for such well-known people as you are to think matters over.”

mn56:16.7.verse: So for the second time, venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.

mn56:16.8.verse: Let the Blessed One remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn56:17.1.verse: ‘Householder, your family has long been one supporting the Nigaṇṭhas, and so may you conceive that alms should be given to them when they come.’

mn56:17.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and convinced by the Blessed One’s telling me that.

mn56:17.3.verse: Venerable sir, I have heard this: “The monk Gotama says thus:

mn56:17.4.verse: ‘Gifts should be given only to me; gifts should not be given to others.

mn56:17.5.verse: Gifts should be given only to my disciples; gifts should not be given to others’ disciples.

mn56:17.6.verse: Only what is given to me is very fruitful; not what is given to others.

mn56:17.7.verse: Only what is given to my disciples is very fruitful; not what is given to others’ disciples.’

mn56:17.8.verse: But on the contrary, the Blessed One encourages me to give gifts to the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn56:17.9.verse: Anyway we shall know the time for that, venerable sir.

mn56:17.10.verse: So for the third time, venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.

mn56:17.11.verse: Let the Blessed One remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn56:18.1.verse: Then the Blessed One gave the householder Upāli progressive instruction, that is to say,

mn56:18.2.verse: talk on giving, on virtue, on the heavens; he explained the danger, the degradation and the defilement in sensual desires, and the blessings in renunciation.

mn56:18.3.verse: When he knew that the householder Upāli’s mind was ready, receptive, free from hindrance, elated and confident, he expounded to him the teaching peculiar to the Enlightened Ones:

mn56:18.4.verse: Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

mn56:18.5.verse: Just as a clean cloth with all marks removed would take dye evenly,

mn56:18.6.verse: so too, while the householder Upāli sat there, the spotless immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in him:

mn56:18.7.verse: ‘All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation.’

mn56:18.8.verse: Then the householder Upāli saw and reached and knew and fathomed the Dhamma; he crossed beyond uncertainty, he had done with questioning, gained intrepidity, and became independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation, and then he said to the Blessed One:

mn56:18.9.verse: ‘Now, venerable sir, we must go; for we are busy and have much to do.’

mn56:18.10.verse: ‘Now is the time, householder, to do as you conceive fit.’

mn56:19.1.verse: Then delighting in the Blessed One’s words and agreeing with them the householder Upāli rose from his seat, after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he left to return to his own house. There he addressed the doorkeeper thus:

mn56:19.2.verse: ‘Good doorkeeper, from today on I close my door to the Nigaṇṭhas and the Nigaṇṭhīs and I open my door to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.

mn56:19.3.verse: If any Nigaṇṭha comes, then tell him thus:

mn56:19.5.verse: from today on the householder Upāli has come over to the Discipleship of the monk Gotama.

mn56:19.6.verse: He has closed his doors to the Nigaṇṭhas, and he has opened his doors to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.

mn56:19.7.verse: Venerable sir, if you have need of alms, wait here; they will bring it to you here.’

mn56:20.1.verse: The Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, heard:

mn56:20.2.verse: ‘The householder Upāli, it seems, has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.’

mn56:20.3.verse: Then he went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and told him:

mn56:20.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I have heard thus: “The householder Upāli, it seems, has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.”’

mn56:20.5.verse: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should go over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama;

mn56:20.6.verse: but it is possible, it can happen, that the monk Gotama might come over to the discipleship of the householder Upāli.’

mn56:20.7.verse: A second time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: ‘Venerable sir, I have heard thus …’

mn56:20.8.verse: A third time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta …

mn56:20.11.verse: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen …’

mn56:20.12.verse: ‘Venerable sir, shall I go and find out whether he has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama or not?’

mn56:20.13.verse: ‘Go, Ascetic, and find out whether he has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama or not.’

mn56:21.1.verse: Then the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, went to the householder Upāli’s house.

mn56:21.3.verse: When he saw him, he told him:

mn56:21.5.verse: from today on the householder Upāli has come over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.

mn56:21.6.verse: He has closed his doors to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhis, and he has opened his doors to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen followers and laywomen followers.

mn56:21.7.verse: Venerable sir, if you have need of alms, wait here; they will bring it to you here.’

mn56:21.8.verse: ‘I have no need of alms, friend,’ he said, and he turned back and went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and told him:

mn56:21.9.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it is only too true. The householder Upāli has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.

mn56:21.10.verse: Venerable sir, I got no (hearing) from you (when I told you): “Venerable sir, I should prefer that the householder Upāli did not (try to) prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong;

mn56:21.11.verse: for the monk Gotama is a magician, and he knows a converting magic by which he converts disciples of other sectarians.”

mn56:21.12.verse: And now, venerable sir, your householder Upāli has been converted by the monk Gotama with his converting magic !”

mn56:21.13.verse: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen, that the householder Upāli should go over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama;

mn56:21.14.verse: but it is possible it could happen, that the monk Gotama might come over to the discipleship of the householder Upāli.’

mn56:21.15.verse: A second time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:21.16.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it is only too true …’

mn56:21.18.verse: A third time the Nigaṇṭha, the Tall Ascetic, told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:21.19.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it is only too true that the householder Upāli has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama …’

mn56:21.20.verse: ‘It is impossible, Ascetic, it cannot happen …

mn56:21.21.verse: it could happen that the monk Gotama might come over to the discipleship of the householder Upāli.

mn56:21.22.verse: Now I shall go myself and find out whether he has gone over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama or not.’

mn56:22.1.verse: Then the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta went with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas to the householder Upāli’s house.

mn56:22.3.verse: When he saw him he told him

mn56:22.5.verse: from today the householder Upāli has come over to the discipleship of the monk Gotama.

mn56:22.6.verse: He has closed his doors to Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs, and he has opened his doors to the Blessed One’s bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen followers and laywomen followers.

mn56:22.7.verse: Venerable sir, if you have need of alms, wait here; they will bring it to you here.’

mn56:22.8.verse: ‘Good doorkeeper, go to the householder Upāli and tell him:

mn56:22.9.verse: “Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is standing at the outer gate with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas;

mn56:22.11.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied, and he went to the householder Upāli and told him:

mn56:22.12.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is standing at the outer gate with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas;

mn56:22.14.verse: ‘In that case, good doorkeeper, make seats ready in the hall of the central door.’

mn56:22.15.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied, and after he had made seats ready in the hall of the central door, he returned to the householder Upāli and told him:

mn56:22.16.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the seats are made ready in the hall of the cen-tral door.

mn56:22.17.verse: Now it is time to do as you think fit.’

mn56:23.1.verse: Then the householder Upāli went to the hall of the central door, and he sat down on the highest and best, chief and most superior seat of all there. Then he told the doorkeeper:

mn56:23.2.verse: ‘Now, good doorkeeper, go to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and tell him:

mn56:23.4.verse: ‘Enter, venerable sir, if, as it seems, you wish to.’”’

mn56:23.5.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied, and he went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and told him:

mn56:23.7.verse: “Enter, venerable sir, if, as it seems, you wish to.”’

mn56:23.8.verse: Then the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta went with the large assembly of Niganthas to the hall of the central door.

mn56:24.1.verse: Then whereas the householder Upāli had been used,

mn56:24.2.verse: when he saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming in the distance, to go out to meet him and then after dusting with an upper robe the highest and best, chief and most superior seat of all there, seat him on it arranging the upper robe round him, he now being himself seated on the highest and best, chief and most superior seat, then told Nigaṇṭha Nātautta: ‘Venerable sir, there are seats; sit down if you wish.’

mn56:24.3.verse: Then whereas the householder Upāli had been used, when he saw the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming in the distance, to go out to meet him and then after dusting with an upper robe the highest and best, chief and most superior seat of all there, seat him on it arranging the upper robe round him, he now being himself seated on the highest and best, chief and most superior seat, then told Nigaṇṭha Nātautta:

mn56:25.1.verse: When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said:

mn56:25.2.verse: ‘Householder, you are mad, you are imbecile;

mn56:25.3.verse: you go (saying): “Venerable sir, I shall prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong” and you come back all caught up in a vast net of theory.

mn56:25.4.verse: Just as if a man went to castrate someone and came back castrated on both sides, as if a man went to put someone’s eyes out and came back with both his eyes put out;

mn56:25.5.verse: so you too, householder, go (saying): “Venerable sir, I shall prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong” and you come back all caught up in a vast net of theory.

mn56:25.6.verse: Householder, you have been converted by the monk Gotama with his converting magic!’

mn56:26.1.verse: ‘It is an auspicious converting magic, venerable sir,

mn56:26.3.verse: Venerable sir, were my beloved relatives and kin converted by this conversion, it would be long for their welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.4.verse: Were all those in the warrior-noble caste … the divine caste … the burgher caste … the artisan caste to be converted by this conversion, it would be long for their welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.5.verse: Were the world with its gods, its Māras, and its (Brahma) Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and its men, to be converted by this conversion, it would be long for its welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.6.verse: As to which, venerable sir, I shall give you a simile;

mn56:26.7.verse: for some wise men understand by means of a simile the meaning of what is said.

mn56:27.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, there was once a divine who was old, aged and burdened with years, and his wife who was a young divine-caste girl was pregnant and near her confinement.

mn56:27.3.verse: “Go, divine, and buy a young monkey in the market and bring it back to me as a playmate for my child.”

mn56:27.4.verse: When this was said, he replied:

mn56:27.5.verse: “Wait, madam, till you have borne the child;

mn56:27.6.verse: if you bear a boy, then I will go the market and buy a young male monkey and bring it back to you as a playmate for your child;

mn56:27.7.verse: but if you bear a girl, then I will go to the market and buy a young female monkey and bring it back to you as a playmate for your child.”

mn56:27.8.verse: For the second time she made the same request and received the same answer.

mn56:27.9.verse: For the third time she made the same request.

mn56:27.11.verse: Then since he was in love with her and his mind bound, he went to the market and bought a young male monkey and brought it back, and he told her:

mn56:27.12.verse: “I have bought a young male monkey in the market and brought it back to you as a playmate for your child.”

mn56:27.14.verse: “Go, divine, take this young male monkey to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and tell him:

mn56:27.15.verse: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this young male monkey dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”

mn56:27.16.verse: Then, since he was in love with her and his mind bound, he took the young male monkey to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and told him:

mn56:27.17.verse: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this young male monkey dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”

mn56:27.18.verse: When this was said, Dyed-hand the dyer’s son told him:

mn56:27.19.verse: “Venerable sir, this young male monkey of yours will suffer a dyeing but not a pounding or an ironing.”

mn56:27.20.verse: So too, venerable sir, the theory of the foolish Nigaṇṭhas will suffer fools’ dyeing (with their delight in it) but not wise men’s; but it will not suffer testing or ironing out.”

mn56:27.21.verse: And then, venerable sir, on another occasion that divine took a pair of new garments to Dyed-hand the dyer’s son and told him:

mn56:27.22.verse: “Good Dyed-hand, I want this pair of new garments dyed the colour called ‘yellow-unguent’ and pounded and re-pounded and ironed on both sides.”

mn56:27.23.verse: When this was said, Dyed-hand the dyer’s son told him:

mn56:27.24.verse: “Venerable sir, this pair of new garments of yours will suffer dyeing and it will suffer a pounding and an ironing.”

mn56:27.25.verse: So too, venerable sir, the theory of that Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, will suffer wise men’s dyeing (with their delight in it), not fools’, and it will suffer both testing and ironing out.’

mn56:28.1.verse: ‘Householder, the Assembly and the King know you thus:

mn56:28.2.verse: “The householder Upāli is a disciple of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.”

mn56:29.1.verse: When this was said, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, and arranging his upper robe on one shoulder, he extended his hands palms together towards where the Blessed One was, and he told the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn56:29.2.verse: ‘In that case, venerable sir, hear whose disciple I am:

mn56:29.3.verse: There is Wise One who has cast off delusion,

mn56:29.4.verse: his heart’s wildernesses abandoned, his victors vanquished,

mn56:29.5.verse: He knows no anguish, he is quite even-minded,

mn56:29.6.verse: mature in virtue, with true understanding;

mn56:29.7.verse: He is beyond temptation, and he is stainless:

mn56:29.8.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.9.verse: He has done with questioning, abiding contented,

mn56:29.10.verse: he spurns what is worldly, the vessel of gladness;

mn56:29.11.verse: He has done the monk’s duty, his birth was human,

mn56:29.12.verse: he bears his last body in a male existence;

mn56:29.13.verse: He is utterly peerless, utterly spotless:

mn56:29.14.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.15.verse: He is undoubting, he is the most skilful,

mn56:29.16.verse: as the Discipliner, the Excellent Leader;

mn56:29.17.verse: He has none to surpass his dhammas all pure,

mn56:29.18.verse: with no hesitation, he is the Revealer;

mn56:29.19.verse: Conceit he has severed, he is the Hero:

mn56:29.20.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.21.verse: He leads the herds’ leaders, he cannot be measured,

mn56:29.22.verse: his depths are unfathomed, attained to the Silence;

mn56:29.23.verse: Provider of safety, possessor of knowledge,

mn56:29.24.verse: in the True Dhamma standing, restrained in himself;

mn56:29.25.verse: He has overcome passion, he is liberated:

mn56:29.26.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.27.verse: The Immaculate Tusker, who lives in remoteness

mn56:29.28.verse: with fetters all shattered, and liberated;

mn56:29.29.verse: He charms in discussion, is invested with wisdom,

mn56:29.30.verse: his banner is lowered, he knows no more lusting;

mn56:29.31.verse: He has done his subduing, has no diversifying:

mn56:29.32.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.33.verse: Of Sages the Seventh, with no schemes for deceiving

mn56:29.34.verse: with the triple True Knowledge, attained to Divineness

mn56:29.35.verse: He has done the Ablution, a master of oration

mn56:29.36.verse: he knows tranquillization, as the Finder of Knowledge

mn56:29.37.verse: He is first of all givers, and he is able:

mn56:29.38.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.39.verse: He is Noble, and he is self-developed

mn56:29.40.verse: he has gained his objective, he is the Expounder,

mn56:29.41.verse: He is mindful, and endowed with insight

mn56:29.42.verse: and he is impartial, and unfastidious;

mn56:29.43.verse: With no perturbation, of mastery Master:

mn56:29.44.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.45.verse: He has fared rightly, and practised meditation,

mn56:29.47.verse: He is independent, and altogether fearless,

mn56:29.49.verse: He has crossed over, and he shows us the crossing:

mn56:29.50.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.51.verse: Of surpassing serenity, with wide understanding,

mn56:29.52.verse: with great understanding, he has done with all lusting;

mn56:29.53.verse: A Tathāgata Perfect, the Sugata, Well-gone,

mn56:29.54.verse: the Person Unrivalled, and likewise Unequalled;

mn56:29.55.verse: He is intrepid, (supreme in all) talents:

mn56:29.56.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.57.verse: His craving is severed, he is enlightened,

mn56:29.58.verse: and cleared of all clouding, completely untainted;

mn56:29.59.verse: To him gifts can be given, most mighty of spirits,

mn56:29.61.verse: The greatest in grandeur, he has climbed to fame’s summits:

mn56:29.62.verse: Blessed is he, and I am his disciple.

mn56:30.1.verse: ‘When did you concoct that hymn of praise to the monk Gotama, householder?’

mn56:30.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, suppose there were a great heap of many kinds of flowers, and then a clever garland-maker or garland-maker’s apprentice knotted them into a multi-coloured garland,

mn56:30.3.verse: so too, venerable sir, the Blessed One has many a praiseworthy quality, many hundred praise-worthy qualities.

mn56:30.4.verse: Who would not praise the praiseworthy?’

mn56:31.1.verse: Then since the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was unable to bear this honour done to the Blessed One, hot blood gushed then and there from his mouth.

mn56:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

mn56:2.1.verse: At that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan was residing at Nāḷandā together with a large assembly of Jain ascetics.

mn56:2.2.verse: Then the Jain ascetic Dīgha Tapassī wandered for alms in Nāḷandā. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to Pāvārika’s Mango Grove. There he approached the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn56:2.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn56:2.4.verse: “There are seats, Tapassī. Please sit if you wish.”

mn56:3.1.verse: When he said this, Dīgha Tapassī took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn56:3.3.verse: “Tapassī, how many kinds of deed does the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan describe for performing bad deeds?”

mn56:3.4.verse: “Reverend Gotama, the Jain Ñātika doesn’t usually speak in terms of ‘deeds’.

mn56:3.5.verse: He usually speaks in terms of ‘rods’.”

mn56:3.6.verse: “Then how many kinds of rod does the Jain Ñātika describe for performing bad deeds?”

mn56:3.7.verse: “The Jain Ñātika describes three kinds of rod for performing bad deeds:

mn56:3.8.verse: the physical rod, the verbal rod, and the mental rod.”

mn56:3.9.verse: “But are these kinds of rod all distinct from each other?”

mn56:3.11.verse: “Of the three rods thus analyzed and differentiated, which rod does the Jain Ñātika describe as being the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds: the physical rod, the verbal rod, or the mental rod?”

mn56:3.12.verse: “The Jain Ñātika describes the physical rod as being the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:3.13.verse: “Do you say the physical rod, Tapassī?”

mn56:3.14.verse: “I say the physical rod, Reverend Gotama.”

mn56:3.15.verse: “Do you say the physical rod, Tapassī?”

mn56:3.16.verse: “I say the physical rod, Reverend Gotama.”

mn56:3.17.verse: “Do you say the physical rod, Tapassī?”

mn56:3.18.verse: “I say the physical rod, Reverend Gotama.”

mn56:3.19.verse: Thus the Buddha made Dīgha Tapassī stand by this point up to the third time.

mn56:4.1.verse: When this was said, Dīgha Tapassī said to the Buddha,

mn56:4.2.verse: “But Reverend Gotama, how many kinds of rod do you describe for performing bad deeds?”

mn56:4.3.verse: “Tapassī, the Realized One doesn’t usually speak in terms of ‘rods’.

mn56:4.4.verse: He usually speaks in terms of ‘deeds’.”

mn56:4.5.verse: “Then how many kinds of deed do you describe for performing bad deeds?”

mn56:4.6.verse: “I describe three kinds of deed for performing bad deeds:

mn56:4.7.verse: physical deeds, verbal deeds, and mental deeds.”

mn56:4.8.verse: “But are these kinds of deed all distinct from each other?”

mn56:4.10.verse: “Of the three deeds thus analyzed and differentiated, which deed do you describe as being the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds: physical deeds, verbal deeds, or mental deeds?”

mn56:4.11.verse: “I describe mental deeds as being the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much physical deeds or verbal deeds.”

mn56:4.12.verse: “Do you say mental deeds, Reverend Gotama?”

mn56:4.14.verse: “Do you say mental deeds, Reverend Gotama?”

mn56:4.16.verse: “Do you say mental deeds, Reverend Gotama?”

mn56:4.18.verse: Thus the Jain ascetic Dīgha Tapassī made the Buddha stand by this point up to the third time, after which he rose from his seat and went to see the Jain Ñātika.

mn56:5.1.verse: Now at that time the Jain Ñātika was sitting together with a large assembly of Bālaki laypeople headed by Upāli.

mn56:5.2.verse: The Jain Ñātika saw Dīgha Tapassī coming off in the distance

mn56:5.4.verse: “So, Tapassī, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

mn56:5.5.verse: “Just now, sir, I’ve come from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.”

mn56:5.6.verse: “But did you have some discussion with him?”

mn56:5.8.verse: “And what kind of discussion did you have with him?”

mn56:5.9.verse: Then Dīgha Tapassī informed the Jain Ñātika of all they had discussed.

mn56:6.1.verse: When he had spoken, the Jain Ñātika said to him,

mn56:6.3.verse: The Jain ascetic Dīgha Tapassī has answered the ascetic Gotama like a learned disciple who rightly understands their teacher’s instructions.

mn56:6.4.verse: For how significant is the measly mental rod when compared with the solid physical rod?

mn56:6.5.verse: Rather, the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:7.1.verse: When he said this, the householder Upāli said to him,

mn56:7.3.verse: The Honorable Tapassī has answered the ascetic Gotama like a learned disciple who rightly understands their teacher’s instructions.

mn56:7.4.verse: For how significant is the measly mental rod when compared with the solid physical rod?

mn56:7.5.verse: Rather, the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.

mn56:7.6.verse: I’d better go and refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine regarding this point.

mn56:7.7.verse: If he stands by the position that he stated to Dīgha Tapassī, I’ll take him on in debate and drag him to and fro and round about, like a strong man would grab a fleecy sheep and drag it to and fro and round about!

mn56:7.8.verse: Taking him on in debate, I’ll drag him to and fro and round about, like a strong brewer’s worker would toss a large brewer’s sieve into a deep lake, grab it by the corners, and drag it to and fro and round about!

mn56:7.9.verse: Taking him on in debate, I’ll shake him down and about and give him a beating, like a strong brewer’s mixer would grab a strainer by the corners and shake it down and about, and give it a beating!

mn56:7.10.verse: I’ll play a game of hemp-washing with the ascetic Gotama, like a sixty-year-old elephant would plunge into a deep lotus pond and play a game of hemp-washing!

mn56:7.11.verse: Sir, I’d better go and refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine on this point.”

mn56:7.12.verse: “Go, householder, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine on this point.

mn56:7.13.verse: For either I should do so, or Dīgha Tapassī, or you.”

mn56:8.1.verse: When he said this, Dīgha Tapassī said to the Jain Ñātika,

mn56:8.2.verse: “Sir, I don’t believe it’s a good idea for the householder Upāli to rebut the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

mn56:8.3.verse: For the ascetic Gotama is deceitful. He knows a conversion trick, and uses it to convert the disciples of other religions.”

mn56:8.4.verse: “It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that Upāli could become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:8.5.verse: But it is possible that Gotama could become Upāli’s disciple.

mn56:8.6.verse: Go, householder, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine on this point.

mn56:8.7.verse: For either I should do so, or Dīgha Tapassī, or you.”

mn56:9.2.verse: and a third time, Dīgha Tapassī said to the Jain Ñātika,

mn56:9.3.verse: “Sir, I don’t believe it’s a good idea for the householder Upāli to rebut the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

mn56:9.4.verse: For the ascetic Gotama is deceitful. He knows a conversion trick, and uses it to convert the disciples of other religions.”

mn56:9.5.verse: “It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that Upāli could become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:9.6.verse: But it is possible that Gotama could become Upāli’s disciple.

mn56:9.7.verse: Go, householder, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine on this point.

mn56:9.8.verse: For either I should do so, or Dīgha Tapassī, or you.”

mn56:9.9.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the householder Upāli to the Jain Ñātika. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled him, keeping him on his right. Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn56:9.10.verse: “Sir, did the Jain ascetic Dīgha Tapassī come here?”

mn56:9.12.verse: “But did you have some discussion with him?”

mn56:9.14.verse: “And what kind of discussion did you have with him?”

mn56:9.15.verse: Then the Buddha informed Upāli of all they had discussed.

mn56:10.1.verse: When he said this, the householder Upāli said to him,

mn56:10.3.verse: The Jain ascetic Dīgha Tapassī has answered the ascetic Gotama like a learned disciple who rightly understands their teacher’s instructions.

mn56:10.4.verse: For how impressive is the measly mental rod when compared with the solid physical rod?

mn56:10.5.verse: Rather, the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:10.6.verse: “Householder, so long as you debate on the basis of truth, we can have some discussion about this.”

mn56:10.7.verse: “I will debate on the basis of truth, sir.

mn56:10.8.verse: Let us have some discussion about this.”

mn56:11.2.verse: Take a Jain ascetic who is sick, suffering, gravely ill. They turn down cold water and use only hot water.

mn56:11.3.verse: Not getting cold water, they might die.

mn56:11.4.verse: Now, where does the Jain Ñātika say they would be reborn?”

mn56:11.5.verse: “Sir, there are gods called ‘mind-bound’. They would be reborn there.

mn56:11.7.verse: Because they died with mental attachment.”

mn56:11.8.verse: “Think about it, householder! You should think before answering.

mn56:11.9.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn56:11.10.verse: But you said that you would debate on the basis of truth.”

mn56:11.13.verse: “Even though the Buddha says this, still the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:12.2.verse: Take a Jain ascetic who is restrained in the fourfold constraint, is restrained in all that is to be restrained, is bridled in all that is to be restrained, has shaken off evil in all that is to be restrained, and is curbed in all that is to be restrained.

mn56:12.3.verse: When going out and coming back they injure many little creatures.

mn56:12.4.verse: Now, what result does the Jain Ñātika say they would incur?”

mn56:12.5.verse: “Sir, the Jain Ñātika says that unintentional acts are not very blameworthy.”

mn56:12.8.verse: “But where does the Jain Ñātika say that intention is classified?”

mn56:12.10.verse: “Think about it, householder! You should think before answering.

mn56:12.11.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn56:12.12.verse: But you said that you would debate on the basis of truth.”

mn56:12.15.verse: “Even though the Buddha says this, still the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:13.2.verse: Is this Nāḷandā successful and prosperous, populous and full of people?”

mn56:13.5.verse: Suppose a man were to come along with a drawn sword

mn56:13.7.verse: ‘In one hour I will reduce all the living creatures within the bounds of Nāḷandā to one heap and mass of flesh!’

mn56:13.10.verse: “Sir, even ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty men couldn’t do that.

mn56:13.11.verse: How impressive is one measly man?”

mn56:13.13.verse: Suppose an ascetic or brahmin with psychic power, who has achieved mastery of the mind, were to come along

mn56:13.15.verse: ‘I will reduce Nāḷandā to ashes with a single malevolent act of will!’

mn56:13.18.verse: “Sir, an ascetic or brahmin with psychic power, who has achieved mastery of the mind, could reduce ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty Nāḷandās to ashes with a single malevolent act of will.

mn56:13.19.verse: How significant is one measly Nāḷandā?”

mn56:13.20.verse: “Think about it, householder! You should think before answering.

mn56:13.21.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn56:13.22.verse: But you said that you would debate on the basis of truth.”

mn56:13.25.verse: “Even though the Buddha says this, still the physical rod is the most blameworthy for performing bad deeds, not so much the verbal rod or the mental rod.”

mn56:13.27.verse: Have you heard how the wildernesses of Daṇḍaka, Kaliṅga, Mejjha, and Mātaṅga came to be that way?”

mn56:14.2.verse: “I heard that it was because of a malevolent act of will by seers that the wildernesses of Daṇḍaka, Kaliṅga, Mejjha, and Mātaṅga came to be that way.”

mn56:14.3.verse: “Think about it, householder! You should think before answering.

mn56:14.4.verse: What you said before and what you said after don’t match up.

mn56:14.5.verse: But you said that you would debate on the basis of truth.”

mn56:15.1.verse: “Sir, I was already delighted and satisfied by the Buddha’s very first simile.

mn56:15.2.verse: Nevertheless, I wanted to hear the Buddha’s various solutions to the problem, so I thought I’d oppose you in this way.

mn56:15.4.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn56:15.5.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn56:15.6.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn56:16.1.verse: “Householder, you should act after careful consideration. It’s good for well-known people such as yourself to act after careful consideration.”

mn56:16.2.verse: “Now I’m even more delighted and satisfied with the Buddha, since he tells me to act after careful consideration.

mn56:16.3.verse: For if the followers of other religions were to gain me as a disciple, they’d carry a banner all over Nāḷandā, saying:

mn56:16.4.verse: ‘The householder Upāli has become our disciple!’

mn56:16.6.verse: ‘Householder, you should act after careful consideration. It’s good for well-known people such as yourself to act after careful consideration.’

mn56:16.7.verse: For a second time, I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn56:16.8.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn56:17.1.verse: “For a long time now, householder, your family has been a well-spring of support for the Jain ascetics. You should consider giving to them when they come.”

mn56:17.2.verse: “Now I’m even more delighted and satisfied with the Buddha, since he tells me to consider giving to the Jain ascetics when they come.

mn56:17.3.verse: I have heard, sir, that the ascetic Gotama says this:

mn56:17.4.verse: ‘Gifts should only be given to me, not to others.

mn56:17.5.verse: Gifts should only be given to my disciples, not to the disciples of others.

mn56:17.6.verse: Only what is given to me is very fruitful, not what is given to others.

mn56:17.7.verse: Only what is given to my disciples is very fruitful, not what is given to the disciples of others.’

mn56:17.8.verse: Yet the Buddha encourages me to give to the Jain ascetics.

mn56:17.9.verse: Well, sir, we’ll know the proper time for that.

mn56:17.10.verse: For a third time, I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn56:17.11.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn56:18.1.verse: Then the Buddha taught the householder Upāli step by step, with

mn56:18.2.verse: a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.

mn56:18.3.verse: And when he knew that Upāli’s mind was ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:

mn56:18.4.verse: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

mn56:18.5.verse: Just as a clean cloth rid of stains would properly absorb dye,

mn56:18.6.verse: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Upāli:

mn56:18.7.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

mn56:18.8.verse: Then Upāli saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. He went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions.

mn56:18.9.verse: He said to the Buddha, “Well, now, sir, I must go. I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn56:19.1.verse: And then the householder Upāli approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went back to his own home, where he addressed the gatekeeper,

mn56:19.2.verse: “My good gatekeeper, from this day forth close the gate to Jain monks and nuns, and open it for the Buddha’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

mn56:19.3.verse: If any Jain ascetics come, say this to them:

mn56:19.5.verse: From now on the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn56:19.6.verse: His gate is closed to Jain monks and nuns, and opened for the Buddha’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

mn56:19.7.verse: If you require almsfood, wait here, they will bring it to you.’”

mn56:20.2.verse: Upāli had become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn56:20.3.verse: He went to the Jain Ñātika and said to him,

mn56:20.4.verse: “Sir, they say that the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.”

mn56:20.5.verse: “It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that Upāli could become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:20.6.verse: But it is possible that Gotama could become Upāli’s disciple.”

mn56:20.8.verse: and a third time, Dīgha Tapassī said to the Jain Ñātika,

mn56:20.9.verse: “Sir, they say that the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.”

mn56:20.10.verse: “It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that Upāli could become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:20.11.verse: But it is possible that Gotama could become Upāli’s disciple.”

mn56:20.12.verse: “Well, sir, I’d better go and find out whether or not Upāli has become Gotama’s disciple.”

mn56:20.13.verse: “Go, Tapassī, and find out whether or not Upāli has become Gotama’s disciple.”

mn56:21.1.verse: Then Dīgha Tapassī went to Upāli’s home.

mn56:21.2.verse: The gatekeeper saw him coming off in the distance

mn56:21.5.verse: From now on the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn56:21.6.verse: His gate is closed to Jain monks and nuns, and opened for the Buddha’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

mn56:21.7.verse: If you require almsfood, wait here, they will bring it to you.”

mn56:21.8.verse: Saying, “No, worthy man, I do not require almsfood,” he turned back and went to the Jain Ñātika and said to him,

mn56:21.9.verse: “Sir, it’s really true that Upāli has become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:21.10.verse: Sir, I couldn’t get you to accept that it wasn’t a good idea for the householder Upāli to rebut the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

mn56:21.11.verse: For the ascetic Gotama is deceitful. He knows a conversion trick, and uses it to convert the disciples of other religions.

mn56:21.12.verse: The householder Upāli has been converted by the ascetic Gotama’s conversion trick!”

mn56:21.13.verse: “It is impossible, Tapassī, it cannot happen that Upāli could become Gotama’s disciple.

mn56:21.14.verse: But it is possible that Gotama could become Upāli’s disciple.”

mn56:21.18.verse: and a third time, Dīgha Tapassī told the Jain Ñātika

mn56:21.22.verse: Well, Tapassī, I’d better go and find out for myself whether or not Upāli has become Gotama’s disciple.”

mn56:22.1.verse: Then the Jain Ñātika went to Upāli’s home together with a large following of Jain ascetics.

mn56:22.2.verse: The gatekeeper saw him coming off in the distance

mn56:22.5.verse: From now on the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn56:22.6.verse: His gate is closed to Jain monks and nuns, and opened for the Buddha’s monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

mn56:22.7.verse: If you require almsfood, wait here, they will bring it to you.”

mn56:22.8.verse: “Well then, my good gatekeeper, go to Upāli and say:

mn56:22.9.verse: ‘Sir, the Jain Ñātika is waiting outside the gates together with a large following of Jain ascetics.

mn56:22.11.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the gatekeeper. He went to Upāli and relayed what was said.

mn56:22.14.verse: Upāli said to him, “Well, then, my good gatekeeper, prepare seats in the hall of the middle gate.”

mn56:22.15.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the gatekeeper. He did as he was asked, then returned to Upāli and said,

mn56:22.16.verse: “Sir, seats have been prepared in the hall of the middle gate.

mn56:23.1.verse: Then Upāli went to the hall of the middle gate, where he sat on the highest and finest seat. He addressed the gatekeeper,

mn56:23.2.verse: “Well then, my good gatekeeper, go to the Jain Ñātika and say to him:

mn56:23.4.verse: you may enter if you wish.’”

mn56:23.5.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied the gatekeeper. He went to the Jain Ñātika and relayed what was said.

mn56:23.8.verse: Then the Jain Ñātika went to the hall of the middle gate together with a large following of Jain ascetics.

mn56:24.2.verse: Previously, when Upāli saw the Jain Ñātika coming, he would go out to greet him and, having wiped off the highest and finest seat with his upper robe, he would embrace him and sit him down.

mn56:24.3.verse: But today, having seated himself on the highest and finest seat, he said to the Jain Ñātika,

mn56:25.1.verse: When he said this, the Jain Ñātika said to him:

mn56:25.3.verse: You said: ‘I’ll go and refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.’ But you come back caught in the vast net of his doctrine.

mn56:25.4.verse: Suppose a man went to deliver a pair of testicles, but came back castrated. Or they went to deliver eyes, but came back blinded.

mn56:25.5.verse: In the same way, you said: ‘I’ll go and refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.’ But you come back caught in the vast net of his doctrine.

mn56:25.6.verse: You’ve been converted by the ascetic Gotama’s conversion trick!”

mn56:26.3.verse: If my loved ones—relatives and kin—were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.4.verse: If all the aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.5.verse: If the whole world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—were to be converted by this, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn56:26.6.verse: Well then, sir, I shall give you a simile.

mn56:26.7.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

mn56:27.1.verse: Once upon a time, there was an old brahmin, elderly and senior. His wife was a young brahmin lady who was pregnant and about to give birth.

mn56:27.2.verse: Then she said to the brahmin,

mn56:27.3.verse: ‘Go, brahmin, buy a baby monkey from the market and bring it back so it can be a playmate for my child.’

mn56:27.4.verse: When she said this, the brahmin said to her,

mn56:27.5.verse: ‘Wait, my dear, until you give birth.

mn56:27.6.verse: If your child is a boy, I’ll buy you a male monkey,

mn56:27.7.verse: but if it’s a girl, I’ll buy a female monkey.’

mn56:27.9.verse: For a third time she said to the brahmin,

mn56:27.10.verse: ‘Go, brahmin, buy a baby monkey from the market and bring it back so it can be a playmate for my child.’

mn56:27.11.verse: Then that brahmin, because of his love for the brahmin lady, bought a male baby monkey at the market, brought it to her, and said,

mn56:27.12.verse: ‘I’ve bought this male baby monkey for you so it can be a playmate for your child.’

mn56:27.13.verse: When he said this, she said to him,

mn56:27.14.verse: ‘Go, brahmin, take this monkey to Rattapāṇi the dyer and say,

mn56:27.15.verse: “Worthy Rattapāṇi, I wish to have this monkey dyed the color of yellow greasepaint, pounded and re-pounded, and pressed on both sides.”’

mn56:27.16.verse: Then that brahmin, because of his love for the brahmin lady, took the monkey to Rattapāṇi the dyer and said,

mn56:27.17.verse: ‘Worthy Rattapāṇi, I wish to have this monkey dyed the color of yellow greasepaint, pounded and re-pounded, and pressed on both sides.’

mn56:27.18.verse: When he said this, Rattapāṇi said to him,

mn56:27.19.verse: ‘Sir, this monkey can endure a dying, but not a pounding or a pressing.’

mn56:27.20.verse: In the same way, the doctrine of the foolish Jains looks fine initially—for fools, not for the astute—but can’t endure being scrutinized or pressed.

mn56:27.21.verse: Then some time later that brahmin took a new pair of garments to Rattapāṇi the dyer and said,

mn56:27.22.verse: ‘Worthy Rattapāṇi, I wish to have this new pair of garments dyed the color of yellow greasepaint, pounded and re-pounded, and pressed on both sides.’

mn56:27.23.verse: When he said this, Rattapāṇi said to him,

mn56:27.24.verse: ‘Sir, this pair of garments can endure a dying, a pounding, and a pressing.’

mn56:27.25.verse: In the same way, the doctrine of the Buddha looks fine initially—for the astute, not for fools—and it can endure being scrutinized and pressed.”

mn56:28.1.verse: “Householder, the king and his retinue know you as

mn56:28.2.verse: a disciple of the Jain Ñātika.

mn56:28.3.verse: Whose disciple should we remember you as?”

mn56:29.1.verse: When he had spoken, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms in the direction of the Buddha, and said to the Jain Ñātika,

mn56:29.2.verse: “Well then, sir, hear whose disciple I am:

mn56:29.3.verse: The attentive one, free of delusion,

mn56:29.4.verse: with hard-heartedness dissolved, victor in battle;

mn56:29.6.verse: with the virtue of an elder and the wisdom of a saint,

mn56:29.7.verse: immaculate in the midst of it all:

mn56:29.8.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.9.verse: He has no indecision, he’s content,

mn56:29.10.verse: joyful, he has spat out the world’s bait;

mn56:29.11.verse: he has completed the ascetic’s task as a man,

mn56:29.12.verse: a man who bears his final body;

mn56:29.14.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.15.verse: He’s free of doubt, he’s skillful,

mn56:29.16.verse: he’s a trainer, an excellent charioteer;

mn56:29.19.verse: he has cut off conceit, he’s a hero:

mn56:29.20.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.23.verse: he is the maker of sanctuary, knowledgeable,

mn56:29.25.verse: he has slipped his chains and is liberated:

mn56:29.26.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.28.verse: he’s ended the fetters and is liberated;

mn56:29.29.verse: he’s skilled in debate and cleansed,

mn56:29.32.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.33.verse: He is the seventh seer, free of deceit,

mn56:29.34.verse: with three knowledges, he has attained to divinity,

mn56:29.35.verse: he has bathed, he knows philology,

mn56:29.36.verse: he’s tranquil, he understands what is known;

mn56:29.37.verse: he is Sakka the Able, Purindada the Firstgiver:

mn56:29.38.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.40.verse: he has attained the goal and explains it;

mn56:29.42.verse: neither leaning forward nor pulling back,

mn56:29.44.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.46.verse: no inner thoughts arising, he is pure,

mn56:29.48.verse: secluded, he has reached the peak,

mn56:29.49.verse: crossed over, he helps others across:

mn56:29.50.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.51.verse: He’s peaceful, his wisdom is vast,

mn56:29.52.verse: with great wisdom, he’s free of greed;

mn56:29.53.verse: he is the Realized One, the Holy One,

mn56:29.56.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.

mn56:29.57.verse: He has cut off craving and is awakened,

mn56:29.59.verse: a mighty spirit worthy of offerings,

mn56:29.61.verse: grand, he has reached the peak of glory:

mn56:29.62.verse: he is the Buddha, and I am his disciple.”

mn56:30.1.verse: “But when did you compose these praises of the ascetic Gotama’s beautiful qualities, householder?”

mn56:30.2.verse: “Sir, suppose there was a large heap of many different flowers. A deft garland-maker or their apprentice could tie them into a colorful garland.

mn56:30.3.verse: In the same way, the Buddha has many beautiful qualities to praise, many hundreds of such qualities.

mn56:30.4.verse: Who, sir, would not praise the praiseworthy?”

mn56:31.1.verse: Unable to bear this honor paid to the Buddha, the Jain Ñātika spewed hot blood from his mouth there and then.

mn57:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Koliyan country. There is a town of the Koliyans called Haliddavasana.

mn57:2.1.verse: Then Puṇṇa, a son of the Koliyans and an ox-duty ascetic, and also Seniya a naked dog-duty ascetic, went to the Blessed One, and Puṇṇa the ox-duty ascetic paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side, while Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he too sat down at one side curled up like a dog.

mn57:2.2.verse: When Puṇṇa the ox-duty ascetic sat down, he asked the Blessed One:

mn57:2.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, this naked dog-duty ascetic Seniya does what is hard to do: he eats his food when it is thrown on the ground.

mn57:2.4.verse: That dog-duty has long been taken up and practised by him.

mn57:2.5.verse: What will be his destination? What will be his future course?’

mn57:2.6.verse: ‘Enough, Puṇṇa, let that be. Do not ask me that.’

mn57:2.8.verse: A third time Puṇṇa the ox-duty ascetic asked the Blessed One:

mn57:2.9.verse: ‘Venerable sir, this naked dog-duty ascetic Seniya does what is hard to do: he eats his food when it is thrown on the ground.

mn57:2.10.verse: That dog-duty has long been taken up and practised by him.

mn57:2.11.verse: What will be his destination? What will be his future course?’

mn57:2.12.verse: ‘Well, Puṇṇa, since I certainly cannot persuade you when I say

mn57:2.13.verse: “Enough, Puṇṇa, let that be. Do not ask me that”,

mn57:3.1.verse: ‘Here, Puṇṇa, someone develops the dog-duty fully and unstintingly, he develops the dog-habit fully and unstintingly, he develops the dog-mind fully and unstintingly, he develops dog-behaviour fully and unstintingly.

mn57:3.2.verse: Having done that, on that dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of dogs.

mn57:3.3.verse: But if his view is such as this: “By this virtue or duty or asceticism or life divine I shall become a (great) god or some (lesser) god”, that is wrong view in his case.

mn57:3.4.verse: Now there are two destinations for one with wrong view, I say: hell or the animal womb.

mn57:3.5.verse: So, Puṇṇa, if his dog-duty is perfected it will lead him to the company of dogs; if it is not, it will lead him to hell.’

mn57:4.1.verse: When this was said, Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic wept and shed tears.

mn57:4.2.verse: Then the Blessed One told Puṇṇa son of the Koliyans and an ox-duty ascetic:

mn57:4.3.verse: ‘Puṇṇa, I could not persuade you when I said

mn57:4.4.verse: “Enough, Puṇṇa, let that be. Do not ask me that”.’

mn57:4.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I am not weeping that the Blessed One has spoken thus.

mn57:4.6.verse: Still this dog-duty has long been taken up and practised by me.

mn57:4.7.verse: Venerable sir, there is this Puṇṇa, a son of the Koliyans, and on ox-duty ascetic;

mn57:4.8.verse: that ox-duty has long been taken up and practised by him.

mn57:4.9.verse: What will be his destination. What will be his future course?’

mn57:4.10.verse: ‘Enough, Seniya, let that be. Do not ask me that.’

mn57:4.12.verse: A third time Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic asked the Blessed One:

mn57:4.13.verse: ‘Venerable sir, there is this Puṇṇa, a son of the Koliyans and an ox-duty;

mn57:4.14.verse: that ox-duty has long been taken up and practised by him.

mn57:4.15.verse: What will be his destination? What will be his future course?’

mn57:4.16.verse: ‘Well, Seniya, since I certainly cannot persuade you when I say:

mn57:4.17.verse: “Enough, Puṇṇa let that be. Do not ask me that”,

mn57:5.1.verse: ‘Here, Seniya, someone develops the ox-duty fully and unstintingly, he develops the ox-habit fully and unstintingly, he develops the ox-mind fully and unstintingly, he develops ox-behaviour fully and unstintingly.

mn57:5.2.verse: Having done that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of oxen.

mn57:5.3.verse: But if his view is such as this: “By this virtue or duty or asceticism or life divine I shall become a (great) god or some (lesser) god”, that is wrong view in his case.

mn57:5.4.verse: Now there are two destinations for one with wrong view, I say: hell or the animal womb.

mn57:5.5.verse: So, Seniya, if his ox-duty is perfected, it will lead him to the company of oxen; if it is not, it will lead him to hell.’

mn57:6.1.verse: When this was said, Puṇṇa, a son of the Koliyans and an ox-duty ascetic, wept and shed tears.

mn57:6.2.verse: Then the Blessed One told Seniya, the naked dog-duty ascetic:

mn57:6.3.verse: ‘Seniya, I could not persuade you when I said:

mn57:6.4.verse: “Enough, Seniya, let that be. Do not ask me that”.’

mn57:6.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I am not weeping that the Blessed One has spoken thus,

mn57:6.6.verse: still this ox-duty has long been taken up and practised by me.

mn57:6.7.verse: Venerable sir, I have confidence in the Blessed One thus: “The Blessed

mn57:6.8.verse: One is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I may abandon this ox-duty and that this naked dog-duty ascetic Seniya may abandon that dog-duty’ ’

mn57:6.9.verse: ‘Then, Puṇṇa, listen and heed well what I shall say.’
