mn57:7.1.verse: ‘Puṇṇa, there are four kinds of kamma proclaimed by me after realization myself with direct knowledge.

mn57:7.3.verse: There is dark kamma with dark ripening,

mn57:7.4.verse: there is bright kamma with bright ripening,

mn57:7.5.verse: there is dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright ripening,

mn57:7.6.verse: and there is kamma that is not dark and not bright with neither-dark-nor-bright ripening that conduces to the exhaustion of kamma.

mn57:8.1.verse: ‘What is dark kamma with dark ripening?

mn57:8.2.verse: Here someone produces a (kammic) bodily process (bound up) with affliction, he produces a (kammic) verbal process (bound up) with affliction, he produces a (kammic) mental process (bound up) with affliction.

mn57:8.3.verse: By so doing, he reappears in a world with affliction.

mn57:8.4.verse: When that happens, afflicting contacts touch him.

mn57:8.5.verse: Being touched by these, he feels afflicting feelings entirely painful as in the case of beings in hell.

mn57:8.6.verse: Thus a being’s reappearance is due to a being:

mn57:8.7.verse: he reappears owing to the kammas he has performed.

mn57:8.8.verse: When he has reappeared, contacts touch him.

mn57:8.9.verse: Thus I say are beings heirs of their kammas.

mn57:8.10.verse: This is called dark kamma with dark ripening.

mn57:9.1.verse: ‘And what is bright kamma with bright ripening?

mn57:9.2.verse: Here someone produces a (kammic) bodily process not (bound up) with affliction, he produces a (kammic) verbal process not (bound up) with affliction, he produces a (kammic) mental process not (bound up) with affliction.

mn57:9.3.verse: By so doing, he reappears in a world without affliction.

mn57:9.4.verse: When that happens, unafflicting contacts touch him.

mn57:9.5.verse: Being touched by these, he feels unafflicting feelings entirely pleasant as in the case of the Subhakiṇṇā, the gods of Refulgent Glory.

mn57:9.6.verse: Thus a being’s reappearance is due to a being:

mn57:9.7.verse: he reappears owing to the kammas he has performed.

mn57:9.8.verse: When he has reappeared, contacts touch him.

mn57:9.9.verse: Thus I say are beings heirs of their kammas.

mn57:9.10.verse: This is called bright kamma with bright ripening.

mn57:10.1.verse: What is dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright ripening ?

mn57:10.2.verse: Here someone produces a (kammic) bodily process both (bound up) with affliction and not (bound up) with affliction … verbal process … mental process both (bound up) with affliction and not (bound up) with affliction.

mn57:10.3.verse: By doing so, he reappears in a world both with and without affliction.

mn57:10.4.verse: When that happens, both afflicting and unafflicting contacts touch him.

mn57:10.5.verse: Being touched by these, he feels afflicting and unafflicting feelings with mingled pleasure and pain as in the case of human beings and some gods and some inhabitants of the states of deprivation.

mn57:10.6.verse: Thus a being’s reappearance is due to a being:

mn57:10.7.verse: he reappears owing to the kammas he has performed.

mn57:10.8.verse: When he has reappeared, contacts touch him.

mn57:10.9.verse: Thus I say are beings heirs of their kammas.

mn57:10.10.verse: This is called dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright ripening.

mn57:11.1.verse: ‘What is neither-dark-nor-bright kamma with neither-dark-nor-bright ripening that leads to the exhaustion of kamma?

mn57:11.2.verse: As to these (three kinds of kamma), any volition in abandoning the kind of kamma that is dark with dark ripening, and any volition in abandoning the kind of kamma that is bright with bright ripening, and any volition in abandoning the kind of kamma that is dark-and-bright ripening:

mn57:11.3.verse: this is called neither-dark-nor-bright kamma with neither-dark-nor-bright ripening.

mn57:11.4.verse: ‘These are the four kinds of kamma proclaimed by me after realization myself with direct knowledge.’

mn57:12.1.verse: When this was said, Punna, a son of the Koliyans and an ox-duty ascetic, said to the Blessed One:

mn57:12.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who is lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.’

mn57:12.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha. From today let Master Gotama remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn57:13.1.verse: But Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic, said:

mn57:13.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear … for those with eyesight to see forms.’

mn57:13.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn57:13.5.verse: I would receive the Going-forth under Master Gotama and the Full Admission.’

mn57:14.1.verse: ‘Seniya, one who belonged formerly to another sect and wants the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of the four months bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give him the Going-forth into homelessness and also the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state.

mn57:14.2.verse: A difference in persons has become known to me in this (probation period).’

mn57:14.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, if those who belonged formerly to another sect and want the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline live on probation for four months and at the end of four months bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give them the Going-forth into homelessness and the full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state, I will live on probation for four years and at the end of the four years let bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give me the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state.’

mn57:15.1.verse: Seniya the naked dog-duty ascetic received the Going-forth under the Blessed One, and he received the Full Admission.

mn57:15.2.verse: And not long after his Full Admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, the venerable Seniya by realization himself with direct knowledge here and now entered upon and abode in that supreme goal of the life divine for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn57:15.3.verse: He had direct knowledge thus: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn57:15.4.verse: And the venerable Seniya became one of the Arahants.

mn57:0.2.verse: The Ascetic Who Behaved Like a Dog

mn57:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Koliyans, where they have a town named Haliddavasana.

mn57:2.1.verse: Then Puṇṇa the Koliyan, a cow votary, and the naked ascetic Seniya, a dog votary, went to the Buddha. Puṇṇa bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side, while Seniya exchanged greetings and polite conversation with him before sitting down to one side curled up like a dog.

mn57:2.3.verse: “Sir, this naked ascetic Seniya the dog votary does a hard thing: he eats food placed on the ground.

mn57:2.4.verse: For a long time he has undertaken that observance to behave like a dog.

mn57:2.5.verse: Where will he be reborn in his next life?”

mn57:2.6.verse: “Enough, Puṇṇa, let it be. Don’t ask me that.”

mn57:2.8.verse: and a third time, Puṇṇa said to the Buddha,

mn57:2.9.verse: “Sir, this naked ascetic Seniya does a hard thing: he eats food placed on the ground.

mn57:2.10.verse: For a long time he has undertaken that observance to behave like a dog.

mn57:2.11.verse: Where will he be reborn in his next life?”

mn57:2.12.verse: “Clearly, Puṇṇa, I’m not getting through to you when I say:

mn57:2.13.verse: ‘Enough, Puṇṇa, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’

mn57:3.1.verse: Take someone who develops the dog observance fully and uninterruptedly. They develop a dog’s ethics, a dog’s mentality, and a dog’s behavior fully and uninterruptedly.

mn57:3.2.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of dogs.

mn57:3.3.verse: But if they have such a view: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’ This is their wrong view.

mn57:3.4.verse: An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say: hell or the animal realm.

mn57:3.5.verse: So if the dog observance succeeds it leads to rebirth in the company of dogs, but if it fails it leads to hell.”

mn57:4.1.verse: When he said this, Seniya cried and burst out in tears.

mn57:4.3.verse: “This is what I didn’t get through to you when I said:

mn57:4.4.verse: ‘Enough, Puṇṇa, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’”

mn57:4.5.verse: Seniya said, “Sir, I’m not crying because of what the Buddha said.

mn57:4.6.verse: But, sir, for a long time I have undertaken this observance to behave like a dog.

mn57:4.7.verse: Sir, this Puṇṇa is a cow votary.

mn57:4.8.verse: For a long time he has undertaken that observance to behave like a cow.

mn57:4.9.verse: Where will he be reborn in his next life?”

mn57:4.10.verse: “Enough, Seniya, let it be. Don’t ask me that.”

mn57:4.12.verse: and a third time Seniya said to the Buddha,

mn57:4.13.verse: “Sir, this Puṇṇa is a cow votary.

mn57:4.14.verse: For a long time he has undertaken that observance to behave like a cow.

mn57:4.15.verse: Where will he be reborn in his next life?”

mn57:4.16.verse: “Clearly, Seniya, I’m not getting through to you when I say:

mn57:4.17.verse: ‘Enough, Seniya, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’

mn57:5.1.verse: Take someone who develops the cow observance fully and uninterruptedly. They develop a cow’s ethics, a cow’s mentality, and a cow’s behavior fully and uninterruptedly.

mn57:5.2.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of cows.

mn57:5.3.verse: But if they have such a view: ‘By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice, may I become one of the gods!’ This is their wrong view.

mn57:5.4.verse: An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say: hell or the animal realm.

mn57:5.5.verse: So if the cow observance succeeds it leads to rebirth in the company of cows, but if it fails it leads to hell.”

mn57:6.1.verse: When he said this, Puṇṇa cried and burst out in tears.

mn57:6.3.verse: “This is what I didn’t get through to you when I said:

mn57:6.4.verse: ‘Enough, Seniya, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’”

mn57:6.5.verse: Puṇṇa said, “Sir, I’m not crying because of what the Buddha said.

mn57:6.6.verse: But, sir, for a long time I have undertaken this observance to behave like a cow.

mn57:6.7.verse: I am quite confident that the Buddha

mn57:6.8.verse: is capable of teaching me so that I can give up this cow observance, and the naked ascetic Seniya can give up that dog observance.”

mn57:6.9.verse: “Well then, Puṇṇa, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn57:7.1.verse: “Puṇṇa, I declare these four kinds of deeds, having realized them with my own insight.

mn57:7.3.verse: There are dark deeds with dark results;

mn57:7.5.verse: dark and bright deeds with dark and bright results; and

mn57:7.6.verse: neither dark nor bright deeds with neither dark nor bright results, which lead to the ending of deeds.

mn57:8.1.verse: And what are dark deeds with dark results?

mn57:8.2.verse: It’s when someone makes hurtful choices by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn57:8.3.verse: Having made these choices, they’re reborn in a hurtful world,

mn57:8.5.verse: Touched by hurtful contacts, they experience hurtful feelings that are absolutely painful—like the beings in hell.

mn57:8.6.verse: This is how a being is born from a being.

mn57:8.7.verse: For your deeds determine your rebirth,

mn57:8.8.verse: and when you’re reborn contacts strike you.

mn57:8.9.verse: This is why I say that sentient beings are heirs to their deeds.

mn57:8.10.verse: These are called dark deeds with dark results.

mn57:9.1.verse: And what are bright deeds with bright results?

mn57:9.2.verse: It’s when someone makes pleasing choices by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn57:9.3.verse: Having made these choices, they are reborn in a pleasing world,

mn57:9.5.verse: Touched by pleasing contacts, they experience pleasing feelings of absolute happiness—like the gods of universal beauty.

mn57:9.6.verse: This is how a being is born from a being.

mn57:9.7.verse: For your deeds determine your rebirth,

mn57:9.8.verse: and when you’re reborn contacts strike you.

mn57:9.9.verse: This is why I say that sentient beings are heirs to their deeds.

mn57:9.10.verse: These are called bright deeds with bright results.

mn57:10.1.verse: And what are dark and bright deeds with dark and bright results?

mn57:10.2.verse: It’s when someone makes both hurtful and pleasing choices by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn57:10.3.verse: Having made these choices, they are reborn in a world that is both hurtful and pleasing,

mn57:10.4.verse: where hurtful and pleasing contacts strike them.

mn57:10.5.verse: Touched by both hurtful and pleasing contacts, they experience both hurtful and pleasing feelings that are a mixture of pleasure and pain—like humans, some gods, and some beings in the underworld.

mn57:10.6.verse: This is how a being is born from a being.

mn57:10.7.verse: For what you do brings about your rebirth,

mn57:10.8.verse: and when you’re reborn contacts strike you.

mn57:10.9.verse: This is why I say that sentient beings are heirs to their deeds.

mn57:10.10.verse: These are called dark and bright deeds with dark and bright results.

mn57:11.1.verse: And what are neither dark nor bright deeds with neither dark nor bright results, which lead to the ending of deeds?

mn57:11.2.verse: It’s the intention to give up dark deeds with dark results, bright deeds with bright results, and both dark and bright deeds with both dark and bright results.

mn57:11.3.verse: These are called neither dark nor bright deeds with neither dark nor bright results, which lead to the ending of deeds.

mn57:11.4.verse: These are the four kinds of deeds that I declare, having realized them with my own insight.”

mn57:12.1.verse: When he had spoken, Puṇṇa the Koliyan said to the Buddha,

mn57:12.4.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn57:13.1.verse: And Seniya the naked ascetic said to the Buddha,

mn57:13.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn57:13.5.verse: Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

mn57:14.1.verse: “Seniya, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they’ll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.

mn57:14.2.verse: However, I recognize individual differences in this matter.”

mn57:14.3.verse: “Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I’ll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.”

mn57:15.1.verse: And the naked ascetic Seniya received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

mn57:15.2.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Seniya, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn57:15.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn57:15.4.verse: And Venerable Seniya became one of the perfected.

mn58:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

mn58:2.1.verse: Then Prince Abhaya went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said to him:

mn58:3.1.verse: ‘Come, Prince, prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong,

mn58:3.2.verse: and a good report of you will be spread to this effect:

mn58:3.3.verse: “The theory of the monk Gotama, successful and mighty as he is, has been proved wrong by Prince Abhaya.”’

mn58:3.4.verse: ‘But, venerable sir, how shall I prove wrong the theory of the monk Gotama, successful and mighty as he is?’

mn58:3.5.verse: ‘Come, Prince, go to the monk Gotama and say thus:

mn58:3.6.verse: “Venerable sir, would a Tathāgata utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others?”

mn58:3.7.verse: If the monk Gotama, on being asked thus, answers thus:

mn58:3.8.verse: “A Tathāgata, Prince, would utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others”, then say to him thus:

mn58:3.9.verse: “Then, venerable sir, what is the difference between you and an ordinary man?

mn58:3.10.verse: For an ordinary man also utters such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others.”

mn58:3.11.verse: But if the monk Gotama, on being asked thus, answers thus:

mn58:3.12.verse: “A Tathāgata, Prince, would not utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others”, then say to him:

mn58:3.13.verse: “Then, venerable sir, why has Devadatta been declared by you to be thus:

mn58:3.14.verse: ‘Devadatta belongs to the states of deprivation, Devadatta belongs to hell, Devadatta will remain (in hell) for the aeon, Devadatta is incorrigible’?

mn58:3.15.verse: Devadatta was disturbed and dissatisfied with that speech of yours.”

mn58:3.16.verse: When the monk Gotama is posed this two-horned question[^1] by you, he will not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up.

mn58:3.17.verse: If an iron-spiked pod[^2] were stuck in a man’s throat, he would not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up;

mn58:3.18.verse: so too, Prince, when the monk Gotama is posed this two-horned question by you, he will not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up.’

mn58:4.1.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ Prince Abhaya replied. He rose from his seat and after paying homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, keeping him on his right, he departed and went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.

mn58:4.2.verse: When he had done so, he looked at the sun, and he considered:

mn58:4.3.verse: ‘It is too late today to prove the Blessed One’s theory wrong.

mn58:4.4.verse: I shall prove the Blessed One’s theory wrong in my own house tomorrow’, and he said to the Blessed One:

mn58:4.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One with three others accept tomorrow’s meal from me.’

mn58:4.6.verse: The Blessed One accepted in silence.

mn58:5.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, Prince Abhaya rose from his seat, and after paying homage to him, keeping him on his right, he departed.

mn58:5.2.verse: Then when the night was ended, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went to Prince Abhaya’s house and sat down on the seat made ready.

mn58:5.3.verse: Then with his own hands Prince Abhaya served and satisfied the Blessed One with various kinds of good food.

mn58:5.4.verse: Then when the Blessed One had eaten and no longer had the bowl in his hand, Prince Abhaya took another, lower, seat and sat down at one side.

mn58:6.1.verse: When he had done so, Prince Abhaya said to the Blessed One:

mn58:6.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, would a Tathāgata utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others?’

mn58:6.3.verse: ‘There is no outright (answer) to that, Prince.’

mn58:6.4.verse: ‘Then, venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭhas have lost in this.’

mn58:6.6.verse: “Then, venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭhas have lost in this”?’

mn58:6.7.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I went to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and after paying homage to him, I sat down at one side. When I had done so, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said to me:

mn58:6.8.verse: “Come, Prince, prove the monk Gotama’s theory wrong,

mn58:6.9.verse: and a good report of you will be spread to this effect—

mn58:6.10.verse: ‘The theory of the monk Gotama, successful and mighty as he is, has been proved wrong by Prince Abhaya.’”

mn58:6.11.verse: When this was said, venerable sir, I said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:

mn58:6.12.verse: ‘But how shall I prove wrong the theory of the monk Gotama, successful and mighty as he is?’

mn58:6.13.verse: ‘Come, Prince, go to the monk Gotama and say thus:

mn58:6.14.verse: “Venerable sir, would a Tathāgata utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others?”

mn58:6.15.verse: If the monk Gotama, on being asked thus, answers thus:

mn58:6.16.verse: “A Tathāgata, Prince, would utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others”, then say to him thus:

mn58:6.17.verse: “Then, venerable sir, what is the difference between you and an ordinary man?

mn58:6.18.verse: For an ordinary man also utters such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others.”

mn58:6.19.verse: But if the monk Gotama, on being asked thus, answers thus:

mn58:6.20.verse: “A Tathāgata, Prince, would not utter such speech as would be unwelcome and disagreeable to others”, then say to him—

mn58:6.21.verse: then, venerable sir, why has Devadatta been declared by you to be thus:

mn58:6.22.verse: ‘Devadatta belongs to the states of deprivation, Devadatta belongs to hell, Devadatta will remain (in hell) for the aeon, Devadatta is incorrigible’?

mn58:6.23.verse: Devadatta was disturbed and dissatisfied with that speech of yours.’

mn58:6.24.verse: When the monk Gotama is posed this two-horned question by you, he will not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up.

mn58:6.25.verse: If an iron-spiked pod were stuck in a man’s throat, he would not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up;

mn58:6.26.verse: so too, Prince, when the monk Gotama is posed this two-horned question by you, he will not be able either to gulp it down or throw it up.’

mn58:7.1.verse: Now on that occasion a young tender recumbent infant was sitting on Prince Abhaya’s lap.

mn58:7.2.verse: Then the Blessed One said to Prince Abhaya:

mn58:7.4.verse: If this child, while you or your nurse were not attending, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do to him?’

mn58:7.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I should take it away from him.

mn58:7.6.verse: If I could not take it away from him at once, I should take his head in my left hand, and crooking a finger of my right hand, I should take it away even if it meant drawing blood.

mn58:7.8.verse: Because I have pity on the child.’

mn58:8.1.verse: ‘So too, Prince, such speech as a Tathāgata knows does not represent what is, does not accord with reality, and is unconnected with good, which speech is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others: such speech a Tathāgata does not utter.

mn58:8.2.verse: Such speech as a Tathāgata knows does represent what is, does accord with reality, but is unconnected with good, and which speech is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others: such speech a Tathāgata does not utter.

mn58:8.3.verse: Such speech as a Tathāgata knows does represent what is, does accord with reality, and is connected with good, but which speech is unwelcome and disagreeable to others: a Tathāgata knows the time to use that speech.

mn58:8.4.verse: Such speech as a Tathāgata knows does not represent what is, does not accord with reality, and is unconnected with good, but which speech is welcome and agreeable to others: such speech a Tathāgata does not utter.

mn58:8.5.verse: Such speech as a Tathāgata knows does represent what is, does accord with reality, but is unconnected with good, and which speech is welcome and agreeable to others: such speech a Tathāgata does not utter.

mn58:8.6.verse: Such speech as a Tathāgata knows does represent what is, does accord with reality, and is connected with good, and which speech is welcome and agreeable to others: a Tathāgata knows the time to use that speech.[^3]

mn58:8.8.verse: Because a Tathāgata has pity on beings.’

mn58:9.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, when warrior-noble caste scholars and divine-caste scholars and householder-scholars and monk-scholars determine a formulated question and then go to the Blessed One and pose it,

mn58:9.2.verse: has there already been in the Blessed One’s mind the thought: “Whoever comes and asks me thus, I shall answer him thus”, or does that (answer) occur to a Tathāgata on the spot?’

mn58:10.1.verse: ‘As to that, Prince, I shall ask you a question in return; answer it as you choose.

mn58:10.2.verse: How do you conceive this, Prince,

mn58:10.3.verse: are you skilled in the parts of a chariot?’

mn58:10.6.verse: when people come to you and ask:

mn58:10.7.verse: “What is the name of this part of the chariot?”,

mn58:10.8.verse: has there already been in your mind the thought: “Whoever comes and asks me thus, I shall answer him thus”, or does that (answer) occur to you on the spot?’

mn58:10.9.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I am well-known as a chariotman skilled in the parts of a chariot.

mn58:10.10.verse: All the parts of a chariot are well known to me.

mn58:10.11.verse: That answer would occur to me on the spot.’

mn58:11.1.verse: ‘So too, Prince, when warrior-noble caste scholars or divine-caste scholars or householder scholars or monk scholars determine a formulated question and then come to a Tathāgata and pose it, the answer occurs to a Tathāgata on the spot.

mn58:11.3.verse: The element of dhammas has been fully penetrated by a Tathāgata, owing to the full penetration of which element of dhammas the answer occurs to a Tathāgata on the spot.’

mn58:12.1.verse: When this was said, Prince Abhaya said to the Blessed One:

mn58:12.2.verse: ‘Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! … (as in Sutta 4, paras. 36-37) …

mn58:12.3.verse: from this day forth may the Blessed One remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn58:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn58:2.1.verse: Then Prince Abhaya went up to the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Jain Ñātika said to him,

mn58:3.1.verse: “Come, prince, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

mn58:3.2.verse: Then you will get a good reputation:

mn58:3.3.verse: ‘Prince Abhaya refuted the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, so mighty and powerful!’”

mn58:3.4.verse: “But sir, how am I to do this?”

mn58:3.5.verse: “Here, prince, go to the ascetic Gotama and say to him:

mn58:3.6.verse: ‘Sir, may the Realized One utter speech that is disliked by others?’

mn58:3.7.verse: When he’s asked this, if he answers:

mn58:3.8.verse: ‘He may, prince,’ say this to him,

mn58:3.9.verse: ‘So what then, sir, is the difference between you and an ordinary person?

mn58:3.10.verse: For even an ordinary person may utter speech that is disliked by others.’

mn58:3.12.verse: ‘He may not, prince,’ say this to him:

mn58:3.13.verse: ‘So why then, sir, did you declare of Devadatta:

mn58:3.14.verse: “Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable”?

mn58:3.15.verse: Devadatta was angry and upset with what you said.’

mn58:3.16.verse: When you put this dilemma to him, the Buddha won’t be able to either spit it out or swallow it down.

mn58:3.17.verse: He’ll be like a man with an iron cross stuck in his throat, unable to either spit it out or swallow it down.”

mn58:4.1.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Abhaya. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Jain Ñātika, keeping him on his right. Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

mn58:4.2.verse: Then he looked up at the sun and thought,

mn58:4.3.verse: “It’s too late to refute the Buddha’s doctrine today.

mn58:4.4.verse: I shall refute his doctrine in my own home tomorrow.” He said to the Buddha,

mn58:4.5.verse: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with three other monks, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

mn58:5.1.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Abhaya rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn58:5.2.verse: Then when the night had passed, the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Abhaya’s home, and sat down on the seat spread out.

mn58:5.3.verse: Then Abhaya served and satisfied the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

mn58:5.4.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Abhaya took a low seat, sat to one side,

mn58:6.2.verse: “Sir, may the Realized One utter speech that is disliked by others?”

mn58:6.4.verse: “Then the Jains have lost in this, sir.”

mn58:6.5.verse: “But prince, why do you say that

mn58:6.6.verse: the Jains have lost in this?”

mn58:6.7.verse: Then Abhaya told the Buddha all that had happened.

mn58:7.1.verse: Now at that time a little baby boy was sitting in Prince Abhaya’s lap.

mn58:7.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to Abhaya,

mn58:7.4.verse: If—because of your negligence or his nursemaid’s negligence—your boy were to put a stick or stone in his mouth, what would you do to him?”

mn58:7.5.verse: “I’d try to take it out, sir.

mn58:7.6.verse: If that didn’t work, I’d cradle his head with my left hand and take it out using a hooked finger of my right hand, even if it drew blood.

mn58:7.8.verse: Because I have sympathy for the boy, sir.”

mn58:8.1.verse: “In the same way, prince, the Realized One does not utter speech that he knows to be untrue, false, and pointless, and which is disliked by others.

mn58:8.2.verse: The Realized One does not utter speech that he knows to be true and correct, but which is harmful and disliked by others.

mn58:8.3.verse: The Realized One knows the right time to speak so as to explain what he knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disliked by others.

mn58:8.4.verse: The Realized One does not utter speech that he knows to be untrue, false, and pointless, but which is liked by others.

mn58:8.5.verse: The Realized One does not utter speech that he knows to be true and correct, but which is harmful, even if it is liked by others.

mn58:8.6.verse: The Realized One knows the right time to speak so as to explain what he knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is liked by others.

mn58:8.8.verse: Because the Realized One has sympathy for sentient beings.”

mn58:9.1.verse: “Sir, there are astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics who come to see you with a question already planned.

mn58:9.2.verse: Do you think beforehand that if they ask you like this, you’ll answer like that, or does the answer just strike you on the spot?”

mn58:10.1.verse: “Well then, prince, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn58:10.3.verse: Are you skilled in the various parts of a chariot?”

mn58:10.6.verse: When they come to you and ask:

mn58:10.7.verse: ‘What’s the name of this chariot part?’

mn58:10.8.verse: Do you think beforehand that if they ask you like this, you’ll answer like that, or does the answer appear to you on the spot?”

mn58:10.9.verse: “Sir, I’m well-known as a charioteer skilled in a chariot’s parts.

mn58:10.10.verse: All the major and minor parts are well-known to me.

mn58:10.11.verse: The answer just appears to me on the spot.”

mn58:11.1.verse: “In the same way, when astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics come to see me with a question already planned, the answer just strikes me on the spot.

mn58:11.3.verse: Because the Realized One has clearly penetrated the principle of the teachings, so that the answer just strikes him on the spot.”

mn58:12.1.verse: When he had spoken, Prince Abhaya said to the Buddha,

mn58:12.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn59:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn59:1.3.verse: Then the Carpenter Pañcakanga went to the venerable Udāyin, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked him:

mn59:1.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, how many kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One?’

mn59:1.5.verse: ‘Three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder:

mn59:1.6.verse: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—

mn59:1.7.verse: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’

mn59:1.8.verse: When this was said, the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:

mn59:1.9.verse: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;

mn59:1.10.verse: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:

mn59:1.12.verse: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’

mn59:2.1.verse: A second time the venerable Udāyin said to the carpenter Pañcakanga:

mn59:2.2.verse: ‘Not two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder;

mn59:2.3.verse: three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:

mn59:2.4.verse: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—

mn59:2.5.verse: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’

mn59:2.6.verse: A second time the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:

mn59:2.7.verse: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;

mn59:2.8.verse: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:

mn59:2.10.verse: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’

mn59:3.1.verse: A third time the venerable Udāyin said to the carpenter Pañcakanga:

mn59:3.2.verse: ‘Not two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, householder;

mn59:3.3.verse: three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:

mn59:3.4.verse: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—

mn59:3.5.verse: these three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One.’

mn59:3.6.verse: A third time the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Udāyin:

mn59:3.7.verse: ‘Not three kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One, venerable Udāyin;

mn59:3.8.verse: two kinds of feeling have been stated by the Blessed One:

mn59:3.10.verse: This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, has been stated by the Blessed One as a peaceful and superior (type of) pleasure.’

mn59:3.11.verse: The venerable Udāyin could not make the carpenter Pañcakanga perceive, nor could the carpenter Pañcakanga make the venerable Udāyin perceive.

mn59:4.1.verse: The venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the venerable Udāyin and the carpenter Pañcakanga.

mn59:4.2.verse: Then he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.

mn59:4.3.verse: When he had done so, he reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation between the venerable Udāyin and Pañcakanga the carpenter.

mn59:4.4.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One told the venerable Ānanda:

mn59:5.1.verse: ‘Ānanda, it was actually a true presentation that Pañcakanga the carpenter would not accept from Udāyin, and it was actually a true presentation that Udāyin would not accept from Pañcakanga the carpenter.

mn59:5.2.verse: I have stated two kinds of feeling in one presentation, Ānanda; I have stated three kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated five kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated six kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated eighteen kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated thirty-six kinds of feeling in another presentation; I have stated one hundred and eight kinds of feeling in another presentation.

mn59:5.3.verse: That is how the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations.

mn59:5.4.verse: And when the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations thus, it may be expected of those who will not concede, allow and accept what is well-stated, well-spoken, by each that they will abide quarrelling, brawling and disputing, stabbing each other with verbal daggers.

mn59:5.5.verse: That is how the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations.

mn59:5.6.verse: And when the Dhamma has been shown by me in (different) presentations thus, it may be expected of those who concede, allow and accept what is well-stated, well-spoken, by each that they will abide in concord as friendly and undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.

mn59:6.1.verse: ‘Ānanda, there are these five cords of sensual desire.

mn59:6.3.verse: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust,

mn59:6.7.verse: tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust—

mn59:6.8.verse: these, Ānanda, are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn59:6.9.verse: Now, Ānanda, the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five cords of sensual desire is called pleasure in sensual desires.

mn59:7.1.verse: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.

mn59:7.3.verse: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:7.4.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:7.5.verse: Here, Ānanda, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna.

mn59:7.6.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:8.1.verse: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.

mn59:8.3.verse: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:8.4.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:8.5.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the stilling of initial and sustained application … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna.

mn59:8.6.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:9.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:9.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the fading of happiness … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the third jhāna.

mn59:9.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:10.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:10.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.

mn59:10.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:11.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:11.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of variety, aware that ‘space is infinite’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of infinite space.

mn59:11.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:12.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:12.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of infinite consciousness.

mn59:12.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:13.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:13.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing’, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.

mn59:13.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:14.3.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:14.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of the base consisting of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn59:14.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:15.1.verse: ‘Should anyone say, Ānanda: “The pleasure and joy that beings experience is that at the utmost”, I would not concede that to him.

mn59:15.3.verse: Because there is another kind of pleasure, Ānanda, loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:15.4.verse: And what, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior?

mn59:15.5.verse: Here, Ānanda, by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling.

mn59:15.6.verse: This, Ānanda, is that other kind of pleasure loftier than that pleasure and superior.

mn59:16.1.verse: ‘An instance might be found, Ānanda, of Wanderers of other sects saying thus:

mn59:16.2.verse: “The monk Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling and describes that as pleasure:

mn59:16.3.verse: What is this, and how is this?”

mn59:16.4.verse: Wanderers of other sects who say thus, Ānanda, should be told:

mn59:16.5.verse: ‘Friends, the Blessed One describes pleasure with reference not only to pleasant feeling;

mn59:16.6.verse: rather, friends, a Tathāgata describes as pleasure any kind of pleasure wherever and whereinsoever it is obtained.’”

mn59:16.7.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn59:16.8.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied, and he delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn59:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn59:1.3.verse: Then the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga went up to Venerable Udāyī, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn59:1.4.verse: “Sir, how many feelings has the Buddha spoken of?”

mn59:1.5.verse: “Chamberlain, the Buddha has spoken of three feelings:

mn59:1.7.verse: The Buddha has spoken of these three feelings.”

mn59:1.8.verse: When he said this, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

mn59:1.9.verse: “Sir, Udāyī, the Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings.

mn59:1.12.verse: The Buddha said that neutral feeling is included as a peaceful and subtle kind of pleasure.”

mn59:2.1.verse: For a second time, Udāyī said to Pañcakaṅga,

mn59:2.2.verse: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of two feelings,

mn59:2.6.verse: For a second time, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

mn59:2.7.verse: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings,

mn59:3.1.verse: And for a third time, Udāyī said to Pañcakaṅga,

mn59:3.2.verse: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of two feelings,

mn59:3.6.verse: And for a third time, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

mn59:3.7.verse: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings,

mn59:3.11.verse: But neither was able to persuade the other.

mn59:4.1.verse: Venerable Ānanda heard this discussion between Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga.

mn59:4.2.verse: Then he went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

mn59:4.3.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

mn59:4.4.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

mn59:5.1.verse: “Ānanda, the explanation by the mendicant Udāyī, which the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga didn’t agree with, was quite correct. But the explanation by Pañcakaṅga, which Udāyī didn’t agree with, was also quite correct.

mn59:5.2.verse: In one explanation I’ve spoken of two feelings. In another explanation I’ve spoken of three feelings, or five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, or a hundred and eight feelings.

mn59:5.3.verse: I’ve explained the teaching in all these different ways.

mn59:5.4.verse: This being so, you can expect that those who don’t concede, approve, or agree with what has been well spoken will fight, quarrel, and dispute, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

mn59:5.5.verse: I’ve explained the teaching in all these different ways.

mn59:5.6.verse: This being so, you can expect that those who do concede, approve, or agree with what has been well spoken will live in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.

mn59:6.1.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn59:6.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn59:6.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn59:6.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn59:6.9.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called sensual pleasure.

mn59:7.1.verse: There are those who might say that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience. But I don’t grant them that.

mn59:7.3.verse: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:7.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn59:7.6.verse: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:8.1.verse: There are those who would say that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience. But I don’t grant them that.

mn59:8.3.verse: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:8.5.verse: It’s when, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. …

mn59:9.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:9.4.verse: It’s when, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’ …

mn59:10.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:10.4.verse: It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. …

mn59:11.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:11.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. …

mn59:12.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:12.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. …

mn59:13.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:13.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. …

mn59:14.2.verse: There is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:14.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn59:14.5.verse: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:15.1.verse: There are those who would say that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience. But I don’t grant them that.

mn59:15.3.verse: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:15.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling.

mn59:15.6.verse: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.

mn59:16.1.verse: It’s possible that wanderers of other religions might say,

mn59:16.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama spoke of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he includes it in happiness.

mn59:16.4.verse: When wanderers of other religions say this, you should say to them,

mn59:16.5.verse: ‘Reverends, when the Buddha describes what’s included in happiness, he’s not just referring to pleasant feeling.

mn59:16.6.verse: The Realized One describes pleasure as included in happiness wherever it is found, and in whatever context.’”

mn59:16.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn59:16.8.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn60:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, and he eventually arrived at a divine-caste Kosalan village called Sālā.

mn60:2.1.verse: The divine-caste householders of Sālā heard

mn60:3.1.verse: Then the divine-caste householders of Sālā went to the Blessed One … (repeat Sutta 41, para. 3)… sat down at one side.

mn60:4.1.verse: ‘Householders, have you any loved teacher in whom you have found your faith well founded ?’

mn60:4.3.verse: ‘Then, householders, while you have no loved teacher this Incontrovertible Dhamma can be practised and maintained,

mn60:4.4.verse: for when the Incontrovertible Dhamma has been taken up and maintained, it will be long for your welfare and happiness.

mn60:5.1.verse: (I. The Theory That There Is Nothing)

mn60:5.2.verse: “There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed, no fruit or ripening of good and bad kammas, no this world, no other world, no father, no mother, no spontaneously (born) beings, no good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world.”

mn60:6.1.verse: (B) ‘Now there are some monks and divines directly opposed to those monks and divines

mn60:6.3.verse: “There is what is given and what is offered and what is sacrificed, and there is fruit and ripening of good and bad kammas, and there is this world and the other world, and mother and father, and spontaneously (born) beings, and good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.”

mn60:6.5.verse: do not these monks and divines hold theories directly opposed to each other ?’

mn60:7.1.verse: ‘Now of those monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn60:7.2.verse: “There is nothing given … no good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world

mn60:7.3.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three profitable dhammas, namely, bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct, and that they will take to and maintain these three unprofitable dhammas, namely, bodily bad conduct, verbal bad conduct and mental bad conduct.

mn60:7.5.verse: Because those worthy monks and divines do not see the danger, the degradation and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas, and they do not see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.

mn60:8.1.verse: There actually being another world, one whose view is “There is not another world” has a wrong view.

mn60:8.2.verse: There actually being another world, one whose intention is “There is not another world” has a wrong intention.

mn60:8.3.verse: There actually being another world, one who speaks the words “There is not another world” has wrong speech.

mn60:8.4.verse: There actually being another world, one who says “There is not another world” is directly opposed to those Arahants who know the other world.

mn60:8.5.verse: There actually being another world, one who makes another perceive “There is not another world” makes (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma,

mn60:8.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma he praises himself and disparages others.

mn60:8.7.verse: So that any virtuousness that he has is abandoned and unvirtuousness is substituted.

mn60:8.8.verse: And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to Noble Ones, making (another) perceive what is not True Dhamma, and self-praise and disparagement of others—these several evil unprofitable dhammas are thus brought into positive being with wrong view as their condition.

mn60:9.1.verse: ‘About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:9.2.verse: “If there is not another world, then on the dissolution of the body, this worthy person will have made himself safe enough.

mn60:9.3.verse: But if there is another world, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn60:9.4.verse: Now by all means let there be no other world, and let these worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:9.5.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s censure here and now as ‘an unvirtuous person with wrong view and the theory that there is nothing’.

mn60:9.6.verse: But on the other hand, if there is another world, then this worthy person has had an unlucky throw on both counts:

mn60:9.7.verse: since he has come in for wise men’s censure here and now, and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell.

mn60:9.8.verse: He has wrongly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that as it extends only to one side it excludes the profitable aspects’.

mn60:10.1.verse: ‘Now of these monks and divines whose theory and view is

mn60:10.2.verse: given ... and good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world,

mn60:10.3.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three unprofitable dhammas, namely, bodily bad conduct, verbal bad conduct, and mental bad conduct, and that they will take to and maintain these three profitable dhammas, namely, bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct.

mn60:10.5.verse: Because those worthy monks and divines see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas, and they see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.

mn60:11.1.verse: ‘There actually being another world, one whose view is “There is another world” has a right view.

mn60:11.2.verse: There actually being another world, one whose intention is “There is another world” has a right intention.

mn60:11.3.verse: There actually being another world, one who speaks the words “There is another world” has right speech.

mn60:11.4.verse: There actually being another world, one who says “There is another world” is not directly opposed to those Arahants who know the other world.

mn60:11.5.verse: There actually being another world, one who makes another perceive “There is another world” makes (him) perceive what is True Dhamma

mn60:11.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is True Dhamma he does not praise himself and disparage others.

mn60:11.7.verse: So that any unvirtuousness that he had is abandoned and virtuousness is substituted.

mn60:11.8.verse: And this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to Noble Ones, making (another) perceive what is True Dhamma, and non-self-praise and non-disparagement of others—these several profitable dhammas are thus brought into positive being with right view as their condition.

mn60:12.1.verse: ‘About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:12.2.verse: “If there is another world, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, this person will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:12.3.verse: But by all means let there be no other world, and let these worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:12.4.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s praise here and now as ‘a virtuous person with right view and the theory that there is’.

mn60:12.5.verse: And on the other hand, if there is another world, then this worthy person has had a lucky throw on both counts:

mn60:12.6.verse: since he comes in for wise men’s praise here and now, and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:12.7.verse: He has rightly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that as it extends to both sides, it excludes the unprofitable aspects.”’

mn60:13.1.verse: ‘There are some monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn60:13.2.verse: “When a man acts or has action done, when he mutilates or has mutilation done, when he tortures or has torturing done, when he inflicts sorrow, when he oppresses, when he threatens or causes threatening, when he slays living beings, takes what is not given, breaks open locks for plunder, commits burglary, ambushes highways, goes with another’s wife, utters falsehood—no evil is done for the doer.

mn60:13.3.verse: If a man with a razor-rimmed wheel makes the living beings on this earth into one mash of meat, into one heap of meat, there is no evil sourcing from it and no outcome to evil.

mn60:13.4.verse: If a man follows the Ganges’ south bank killing and slaughtering, mutilating and having mutilation done, torturing and having torture done, there is no evil sourcing from it and no outcome of evil.

mn60:13.5.verse: If a man follows the Ganges’ north bank giving (gifts) and having (them) given, offering (sacrifices) and having them offered, then there is no merit sourcing from it and no outcome of merit.

mn60:13.6.verse: By giving, by training, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit and no outcome of merit.”

mn60:14.1.verse: ‘Now there are some monks and divines whose theory is directly opposed to those monks and divines, and they say thus:

mn60:14.2.verse: “When a man acts or has action done, when he mutilates or has mutilation done, when he tortures or has torturing done, when he inflicts sorrow, when he op-presses, when he threatens or causes threatening, when he slays living beings, takes what is not given, breaks open locks, raids for plunder, commits burglary, ambushes highways, goes with another’s wife, utters falsehood—evil is done for the doer.

mn60:14.3.verse: If a man with a razor-rimmed wheel makes the living beings on this earth into one mash of meat, into one heap of meat, there is evil sourcing from it and there is outcome of evil.

mn60:14.4.verse: If a man follows the Ganges’ south bank killing and slaughtering, mutilating and having mutilation done, torturing and having torture done, there is evil sourcing from it, and outcome of evil.

mn60:14.5.verse: If a man follows the Ganges’ north bank giving (gifts) and having (them) given, offering (sacrifices) and having (them) offered, there is merit sourcing from it, and outcome of merit.

mn60:14.6.verse: By giving, by training, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is merit, and outcome of merit.”

mn60:14.8.verse: do not these monks and divines hold theories directly opposed to each other?’

mn60:15.1.verse: ‘Now of those monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn60:15.2.verse: “When a man acts or has action done …

mn60:15.4.verse: no merit and no outcome of merit”,

mn60:15.5.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three profitable dhammas … and that they will take to and maintain these three unprofitable dhammas …

mn60:15.7.verse: Because those worthy monks and divines do not see the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas, and they do not see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.

mn60:16.1.verse: ‘There actually being doing, one whose view is “There is no doing” has wrong view.

mn60:16.2.verse: There actually being doing, one whose intention is “There is no doing” has wrong intention.

mn60:16.3.verse: There actually being doing, one who speaks the words “There is no doing” has wrong speech.

mn60:16.4.verse: There actually being doing, one who says “There is no doing” is directly opposed to those Arahants who hold the theory that there is doing.

mn60:16.5.verse: There actually being doing, one who makes another perceive “There is no doing” makes (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma,

mn60:16.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma he praises himself and disparages others.

mn60:16.7.verse: So that any virtuousness that he had is abandoned and unvirtuousness is substituted.

mn60:16.8.verse: And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to Noble Ones, making another perceive what is not True Dhamma and self-praise and disparagement of others—these several evil unprofitable dhammas are thus brought into positive being with wrong view as their condition.

mn60:17.1.verse: ‘About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:17.2.verse: “If there is no doing, then on the dissolution of the body this worthy person will have made himself safe enough.

mn60:17.3.verse: But if there is doing, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn60:17.4.verse: Now by all means let there be no doing, and let these worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:17.5.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s censure here and now as ‘an unvirtuous person with wrong view and the theory that there is no doing’.

mn60:17.6.verse: But on the other hand, if there is doing, then this worthy person has had an unlucky throw on both counts:

mn60:17.7.verse: since he has come in for wise men’s censure here and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in perdition, even in hell.

mn60:17.8.verse: He has wrongly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that it extends only to one side it excludes the profitable aspect.”

mn60:18.1.verse: ‘Now of those monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn60:18.2.verse: “When a person acts or has action done … evil is done for the doer …

mn60:18.5.verse: There is merit and outcome of merit”,

mn60:18.6.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three unprofitable dhammas … and that they will take to and maintain these three profitable dhammas …

mn60:18.8.verse: Because these worthy monks and divines see the danger, the degradation and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas and they see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.

mn60:19.1.verse: ‘There actually being doing, one whose view is “There is doing” has right view.

mn60:19.2.verse: There actually being doing, one whose intention is “There is doing” has right intention.

mn60:19.3.verse: There actually being doing, one who speaks the words “There is doing” has right speech.

mn60:19.4.verse: There actually being doing, one who says “There is doing” is not opposed to those Arahants who hold the theory that there is doing.

mn60:19.5.verse: There actually being doing, one who makes another perceive “There is doing” makes him perceive what is True Dhamma,

mn60:19.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is True Dhamma he does not praise himself and disparage others.

mn60:19.7.verse: So that any unvirtuousness that he had is abandoned and virtuousness is substituted.

mn60:19.8.verse: And this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to Noble Ones, making (another) perceive what is True Dhamma, and non-self-praise and non-disparagement of others--these several profitable dhammas are thus brought into positive being with right view as their condition.

mn60:20.1.verse: About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:20.2.verse: “If there is doing, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, this worthy person will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:20.3.verse: But by all means let there be no doing, and let those worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:20.4.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s praise here and now as ‘a virtuous person with right view and the theory that there is doing’.

mn60:20.5.verse: And on the other hand, if there is doing, then this worthy person has had a lucky throw on both counts:

mn60:20.6.verse: since he comes in for wise men’s praise here and now, and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:20.7.verse: He has rightly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that as it extends to both sides it excludes the unprofitable aspect.”’

mn60:21.1.verse: There are some monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn60:21.2.verse: “There is no reason, no condition, for beings’ defilement;

mn60:21.3.verse: beings are defiled without reason or condition.

mn60:21.4.verse: There is no reason, no condition for beings’ purification;

mn60:21.5.verse: beings are purified without reason or condition.

mn60:21.6.verse: There is no power, no energy, no manly courage, no manly endurance;

mn60:21.7.verse: all creatures, all breathing things, all beings, all souls, are without mastery, power or energy; moulded by fate, coincidence and essence, they experience pleasure and pain in the six species.”

mn60:22.1.verse: Now there are some monks and divines whose theory is directly opposed to those monks and divines,

mn60:22.3.verse: “There is a reason, a condition, for beings’ defilement;

mn60:22.4.verse: beings are defiled owing to a reason, owing to a condition.

mn60:22.5.verse: There is a reason, a condition, for beings’ purification;

mn60:22.6.verse: beings are purified owing to a reason, owing to a condition.

mn60:22.7.verse: There is power, energy, manly courage, manly endurance;

mn60:22.8.verse: that all creatures, all breathing things, all beings, all souls, being moulded by fate, coincidence and essence, experience pleasure and pain in the six species is not so.”’

mn60:22.10.verse: do not these monks and divines hold theories directly opposed to each other?’

mn60:23.1.verse: ‘Now of those monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn60:23.2.verse: “There is no reason … for beings’ defilement … for beings’ purification … moulded by fate, coincidence and essence, they experience pleasure and pain in the six species”, it is to be expected that they will avoid these three profitable dhammas … and they will take to and maintain these three unprofitable dhammas … Why is that? Because those worthy monks and divines do not see the danger, the degradation and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas, and they do not see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.’

mn60:23.3.verse: beings are defiled without reason or condition.

mn60:23.4.verse: There is no reason, no condition for beings’ purification;

mn60:23.5.verse: beings are purified without reason or condition.

mn60:23.6.verse: There is no power, no energy, no manly courage, no manly endurance; all creatures, all breathing things, all beings, all souls, are without mastery, power or energy; moulded by fate, coincidence and essence, they experience pleasure and pain in the six species.”

mn60:23.7.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three profitable dhammas … and they will take to and maintain these three unprofitable dhammas …

mn60:23.9.verse: Because those worthy monks and divines do not see the danger, the degradation and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas, and they do not see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.’

mn60:24.1.verse: ‘There actually being a reason, one whose view is “There is no reason” has wrong view.

mn60:24.2.verse: There actually being a reason, one whose intention is “There is no reason” has wrong intention.

mn60:24.3.verse: There actually being a reason, one who speaks the words “There is no reason” has wrong speech.

mn60:24.4.verse: There actually being a reason, one who says “There is no reason” is directly opposed to those Arahats who hold the theory that there is a reason.

mn60:24.5.verse: There actually being a reason, one who makes another perceive “There is no reason” makes (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma,

mn60:24.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is not True Dhamma he praises himself and disparages others.

mn60:24.7.verse: So that any virtuousness that he had is abandoned and unvirtuousness is substituted.

mn60:24.8.verse: And this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to Noble Ones, making (another) perceive what is not True Dhamma, and self-praise and disparagement of others—these several evil unprofitable ideas are thus brought into positive being with wrong view as their condition.

mn60:25.1.verse: About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:25.2.verse: “If there is no reason, then on the dissolution of the body this person will have made himself safe enough.

mn60:25.3.verse: But if there is a reason, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn60:25.4.verse: Now by all means let there be no reason, and let these worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:25.5.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s censure here and now as ‘an unvirtuous person with wrong view and the theory that there is no reason’.

mn60:25.6.verse: But on the other hand, if there is a reason, then this worthy person has had an unlucky throw on both counts:

mn60:25.7.verse: since he has come in for wise men’s censure here and now, and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn60:25.8.verse: He has wrongly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that as it extends only to one side it excludes the profitable aspect.”’

mn60:26.1.verse: Now for those monks and divines whose theory and view is thus:

mn60:26.2.verse: “There is a reason … for beings’ defilement … for beings’ purification … moulded by fate, coincidence and essence, experience pleasure and pain in the six species is not so”,

mn60:26.4.verse: There is a reason, a condition, for the purification of sentient beings, etc.

mn60:26.7.verse: it is to be expected that they will avoid these three unprofitable dhammas … and that they will take to and maintain these three profitable dhammas …

mn60:26.9.verse: Because these worthy monks and divines see the danger, the degradation and the defilement in unprofitable dhammas and they see the blessing of renunciation partaking of cleansing in profitable dhammas.’

mn60:27.1.verse: ‘There actually being a reason, one whose view is “There is a reason” has right view.

mn60:27.2.verse: There actually being a reason, one whose intention is “There is a reason” has right intention.

mn60:27.3.verse: There actually being a reason, one who speaks the words “There is a reason” has right speech.

mn60:27.4.verse: There actually being a reason, one who says “There is a reason” is not directly opposed to those Arahants who hold the theory that “There is a reason”.

mn60:27.5.verse: There actually being a reason, one who makes another perceive “There is a reason” makes (him) perceive what is True Dhamma,

mn60:27.6.verse: and in (order to) make (him) perceive what is True Dhamma he does not praise himself and disparage others.

mn60:27.7.verse: So that any unvirtuousness that he had is abandoned and virtuousness is substituted.

mn60:27.8.verse: And this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to Noble Ones, making (another) perceive what is True Dhamma, and non-self-praise and non-disparagement of others—these several profitable dhammas are thus brought into positive being with right view as condition.

mn60:28.1.verse: About this a wise man considers thus: “If there is a reason, then on the dissolution of the body, after death, this person will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:28.2.verse: But by all means let there be no reason, and let those worthy monks’ and divines’ words be true,

mn60:28.3.verse: still this worthy person comes in for wise men’s praise here and now as ‘a virtuous person with right view and the theory that there is a reason’.

mn60:28.4.verse: And on the other hand, if there is a reason, then this person has had a lucky throw on both counts:

mn60:28.5.verse: since he comes in for wise men’s praise here and now, and since on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world.

mn60:28.6.verse: He has rightly taken up and practised this incontrovertible dhamma in such a way that as it extends to both sides it excludes the unprofitable aspect.”’

mn60:29.1.verse: ‘There are some monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn60:30.1.verse: ‘Now there are some monks and divines whose theory is directly opposed to those monks and divines,

mn60:30.5.verse: do not these monks and divines hold theories directly opposed to each other?’

mn60:31.1.verse: ‘About this a wise man considers thus:

mn60:31.2.verse: “When these worthy monks and divines hold the theory and the view that

mn60:31.3.verse: ‘There definitely are no formless states’, that has not been seen by me;

mn60:31.4.verse: and when these (other) worthy monks and divines hold the theory and view that

mn60:31.5.verse: ‘There definitely are formless states’, that has not been known by me.

mn60:31.6.verse: If I, not seeing and not knowing, were to take one side entirely (saying)

mn60:31.7.verse: ‘Only this is true; anything else is wrong’, that would not become me.

mn60:31.8.verse: Not if the monks’ and divines’ theory and view that

mn60:31.9.verse: ‘There definitely are no formless states’ is true, then it is still possible incontrovertibly that my reappearance (after death) might take place among the formed gods consisting of mind;

mn60:31.10.verse: my reappearance (after death) might take place among the formed gods consisting of mind;

mn60:31.11.verse: but if the monks’ and divines’ theory and view that

mn60:31.12.verse: ‘There definitely are formless states’ is true, then it is also possible incontrovertibly that

mn60:31.13.verse: my reappearance (after death) might take place among the formless gods consisting of perception.

mn60:31.14.verse: (What has to be considered is that) resorting to sticks, resorting to weapons, quarrels, brawls, disputes, recriminations, malice, and false speech is to be seen regarding form

mn60:31.15.verse: but definitely there is not this about formless states.”

mn60:31.16.verse: After reflecting thus, he practises the way to dispassion, fading out and cessation, of forms only (but not of being).

mn60:32.1.verse: ‘There are some monks and divines whose theory and whose view is thus:

mn60:32.2.verse: “There definitely is no cessation of being.”’

mn60:33.1.verse: ‘Now there are some monks and divines whose theory is directly opposed to those monks and divines,

mn60:33.3.verse: “There definitely is a cessation of being.”’

mn60:33.5.verse: do not these monks and divines hold theories directly opposed to each other?’

mn60:34.1.verse: ‘About this a wise man considers thus: ‘

mn60:34.2.verse: When these worthy monks and divines hold the theory and the view that ‘

mn60:34.3.verse: There definitely is no cessation of being’, that has not been by me.

mn60:34.5.verse: worthy monks and divines hold the theory and the view that ‘There definitely is a cessation of being’, that has not been known by me.

mn60:34.6.verse: If I, not seeing and not knowing, were to take one side entirely (saying) ‘

mn60:34.7.verse: Only this is true; anything else is wrong’, that would not become me.

mn60:34.8.verse: Now if the monks’ and divines’ theory and view that ‘

mn60:34.9.verse: There definitely is no cessation of being’ is true, then it is still possible incontrovertibly that

mn60:34.10.verse: my reappearance (after death) might take place among the formless gods consisting of perception.

mn60:34.11.verse: But if the monks’ and divines’ theory and view that

mn60:34.12.verse: ‘There definitely is a cessation of being’ is true, then it is possible that

mn60:34.13.verse: I might here and now attain Nibbāna.

mn60:34.14.verse: (What has to be considered is that) the view of those worthy monks and divines whose theory and view is that

mn60:34.15.verse: ‘There definitely is no cessation of being’ is close to lust, to bondage, to relishing, to acceptance, to clinging,

mn60:34.16.verse: while the view of those worthy monks and divines whose theory and view is that

mn60:34.17.verse: ‘There definitely is cessation of being’ is close to non-lust, to non-bondage, to non-relishing, to non-acceptance, to non-clinging.”

mn60:34.18.verse: After reflecting thus he practises the way to dispassion, fading out and cessation, of being too (as well as form).

mn60:35.1.verse: ‘Householders, there are four kinds of person to be found existing in the world.

mn60:35.3.verse: ‘Here a certain kind of person torments himself, being interested in self-torture.

mn60:35.4.verse: Here a certain kind of person torments others, being interested in torturing others.

mn60:35.5.verse: Here a certain kind of person torments himself, being interested in self-torture and he torments others, being interested in torturing others.

mn60:35.6.verse: Here a certain kind of person does not torment himself, not being interested in self-torture, and he does not torment others, not being interested in torturing others;

mn60:35.7.verse: since he torments neither himself nor others he is here, now unparched, extinguished, cooled, he abides experiencing pleasure as one become divine in himself.

mn60:36.1.verse: ‘What kind of person torments himself, being interested in self-torture?

mn60:36.2.verse: ‘Here a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions …

mn60:36.3.verse: in fact he dwells pursuing the practice of torment and torture of the body in its many aspects.

mn60:36.4.verse: This is called the kind of person who torments himself, being interested in self-torture.

mn60:37.1.verse: ‘What kind of person torments others, being interested in torturing others?

mn60:37.2.verse: ‘Here a certain person is a butcher … such bloody occupation.
