mn63:10.2.verse: It is because it is connected with the goal, it belongs to the fundamentals of the life divine, and it leads to dispassion, to fading away, to cessation, to peace, to direct-knowledge, to full-enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

mn63:10.3.verse: That is why it is declared by me.

mn63:10.4.verse: ‘Consequently, Māluṅkyaputta, remember what is undeclared by me as undeclared,

mn63:10.5.verse: and remember what is declared by me as declared.’

mn63:10.6.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn63:10.7.verse: The venerable Māluṅkyaputta was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn63:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn63:2.1.verse: Then as Venerable Māluṅkyaputta was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:

mn63:2.2.verse: “There are several convictions that the Buddha has left undeclared; he has set them aside and turned them down.

mn63:2.3.verse: For example: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

mn63:2.4.verse: The Buddha does not explain these points to me.

mn63:2.5.verse: I don’t endorse that, and do not accept it.

mn63:2.6.verse: I’ll go to him and ask him about this.

mn63:2.7.verse: If he gives me a straight answer on any of these points,

mn63:2.10.verse: I will lead the spiritual life under him.

mn63:2.11.verse: If he does not explain these points to me,

mn63:2.14.verse: I shall resign the training and return to a lesser life.”

mn63:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Māluṅkyaputta came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and told the Buddha of his thoughts. He then continued:

mn63:3.18.verse: that the cosmos is eternal, please tell me.

mn63:3.20.verse: that the cosmos is not eternal, tell me.

mn63:3.22.verse: whether the cosmos is eternal or not, then it is straightforward to simply say:

mn63:3.32.verse: that the soul and the body are one and the same,

mn63:3.34.verse: or is the soul one thing, the body another;

mn63:3.39.verse: that after death, a realized one still exists,

mn63:3.46.verse: or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists, please tell me.

mn63:3.50.verse: any of these things, then it is straightforward to simply say:

mn63:4.1.verse: “What, Māluṅkyaputta, did I ever say to you:

mn63:4.2.verse: ‘Come, Māluṅkyaputta, lead the spiritual life under me, and I will declare these things to you’?”

mn63:4.5.verse: “Or did you ever say to me:

mn63:4.6.verse: ‘Sir, I will lead the spiritual life under the Buddha, and the Buddha will declare these things to me’?”

mn63:4.9.verse: “So it seems that I did not say to you:

mn63:4.10.verse: ‘Come, Māluṅkyaputta, lead the spiritual life under me, and I will declare these things to you.’

mn63:4.13.verse: And you never said to me:

mn63:4.14.verse: ‘Sir, I will lead the spiritual life under the Buddha, and the Buddha will declare these things to me.’

mn63:4.17.verse: In that case, you futile man, who are you and what do you disavow?

mn63:5.1.verse: Suppose someone were to say this:

mn63:5.2.verse: ‘I will not lead the spiritual life under the Buddha until the Buddha declares to me

mn63:5.3.verse: that the cosmos is eternal, or that the cosmos is not eternal …

mn63:5.4.verse: or that after death a realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists.’

mn63:5.5.verse: That would still remain undeclared by the Realized One, and meanwhile that individual would die.

mn63:5.6.verse: Suppose a man was struck by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn63:5.7.verse: His friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat him.

mn63:5.9.verse: ‘I won’t extract this arrow as long as I don’t know whether the man who wounded me was an aristocrat, a brahmin, a peasant, or a menial.’

mn63:5.11.verse: ‘I won’t extract this arrow as long as I don’t know the following things about the man who wounded me: his name and clan;

mn63:5.13.verse: whether he’s tall, short, or medium;

mn63:5.15.verse: whether his skin is black, brown, or dingy;

mn63:5.17.verse: and whether he comes from such-and-such village, town, or city.

mn63:5.19.verse: I won’t extract this arrow as long as I don’t know whether the bow that wounded me was straight or recurved;

mn63:5.21.verse: whether the bow-string is made of swallow-wort fibre, sunn hemp fibre, sinew, sanseveria fibre, or spurge fibre;

mn63:5.23.verse: whether the shaft is made from a bush or a plantation tree;

mn63:5.25.verse: whether the shaft was fitted with feathers from a vulture, a heron, a hawk, a peacock, or a stork;

mn63:5.27.verse: whether the shaft was bound with sinews of a cow, a buffalo, a black lion, or an ape;

mn63:5.29.verse: and whether the arrowhead was spiked, razor-tipped, barbed, made of iron or a calf’s tooth, or lancet-shaped.’

mn63:5.30.verse: That man would still not have learned these things, and meanwhile they’d die.

mn63:5.31.verse: In the same way, suppose someone was to say:

mn63:5.32.verse: ‘I will not lead the spiritual life under the Buddha until the Buddha declares to me

mn63:5.33.verse: that the cosmos is eternal, or that the cosmos is not eternal …

mn63:5.34.verse: or that after death a realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists.’

mn63:5.35.verse: That would still remain undeclared by the Realized One, and meanwhile that individual would die.

mn63:6.1.verse: It’s not true that if there were the view ‘the cosmos is eternal’ there would be the living of the spiritual life.

mn63:6.2.verse: It’s not true that if there were the view ‘the cosmos is not eternal’ there would be the living of the spiritual life.

mn63:6.3.verse: When there is the view that the cosmos is eternal or that the cosmos is not eternal, there is rebirth, there is old age, there is death, and there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn63:6.4.verse: And it is the defeat of these things in this very life that I advocate.

mn63:6.5.verse: It’s not true that if there were the view ‘the cosmos is finite’ …

mn63:6.9.verse: ‘the soul and the body are one and the same’ …

mn63:6.10.verse: ‘the soul is one thing, the body another’ …

mn63:6.13.verse: ‘a realized one still exists after death’ …

mn63:6.14.verse: ‘a realized one no longer exists after death’ …

mn63:6.17.verse: ‘a realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death’ …

mn63:6.18.verse: ‘a realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death’ there would be the living of the spiritual life.

mn63:6.19.verse: When there are any of these views there is rebirth, there is old age, there is death, and there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

mn63:6.20.verse: And it is the defeat of these things in this very life that I advocate.

mn63:7.1.verse: So, Māluṅkyaputta, you should remember what I have not declared as undeclared,

mn63:7.2.verse: and what I have declared as declared.

mn63:7.3.verse: And what have I not declared?

mn63:7.4.verse: I have not declared the following: ‘the cosmos is eternal,’

mn63:7.11.verse: ‘the soul and the body are one and the same,’

mn63:7.13.verse: ‘the soul is one thing, the body another,’

mn63:7.15.verse: ‘a realized one still exists after death,’

mn63:7.17.verse: ‘a realized one no longer exists after death,’

mn63:7.19.verse: ‘a realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death,’

mn63:7.21.verse: ‘a realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death.’

mn63:8.1.verse: And why haven’t I declared these things?

mn63:8.2.verse: Because they aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn63:8.3.verse: That’s why I haven’t declared them.

mn63:9.2.verse: I have declared the following: ‘this is suffering,’

mn63:9.7.verse: ‘this is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn63:10.1.verse: And why have I declared these things?

mn63:10.2.verse: Because they are beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn63:10.3.verse: That’s why I have declared them.

mn63:10.4.verse: So, Māluṅkyaputta, you should remember what I have not declared as undeclared,

mn63:10.5.verse: and what I have declared as declared.”

mn63:10.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn63:10.7.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approved what the Buddha said.

mn64:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn64:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn64:2.1.verse: “Monks, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?”

mn64:2.2.verse: When this was said, Ven. Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One,

mn64:2.3.verse: “Lord, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.”

mn64:2.4.verse: “And how, Māluṅkyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?”

mn64:2.5.verse: “Lord, I remember self-identification view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.

mn64:2.6.verse: I remember uncertainty as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.

mn64:2.7.verse: I remember grasping at habits & practices as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.

mn64:2.8.verse: I remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.

mn64:2.9.verse: I remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.

mn64:2.10.verse: That’s how I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.”

mn64:3.1.verse: “And to whom, Māluṅkyaputta, do you remember my having taught the five lower fetters in that way?

mn64:3.2.verse: Wouldn’t the wanderers of other sects make a rebuttal with the simile of the youngster?

mn64:3.3.verse: For even the thought ‘self-identification’ doesn’t occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would self-identification view arise in it,

mn64:3.4.verse: even though a latent tendency to self-identification view lies latent within it?

mn64:3.5.verse: Even the thought ‘dhammas’ doesn’t occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would uncertainty about dhammas arise in it,

mn64:3.6.verse: even though a latent tendency to uncertainty lies latent within it?

mn64:3.7.verse: Even the thought ‘habits’ doesn’t occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would grasping at habits & practices arise in it,

mn64:3.8.verse: even though a latent tendency to grasping at habits & practices lies latent within it?

mn64:3.9.verse: Even the thought ‘sensuality’ doesn’t occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would sensual desire for sensuality arise in it,

mn64:3.10.verse: even though a latent tendency to sensual passion lies latent within it?

mn64:3.11.verse: Even the thought ‘beings’ doesn’t occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would ill will for beings arise in it,

mn64:3.12.verse: even though a latent tendency to ill will lies latent within it?”

mn64:3.13.verse: Wouldn’t the wanderers of other sects make a rebuttal with the simile of the youngster?”

mn64:4.1.verse: When this was said, Ven. Ānanda said to the Blessed One,

mn64:4.2.verse: “This is the time, O Blessed One. This is the time, O One Well-Gone,

mn64:4.3.verse: for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”

mn64:4.4.verse: “In that case, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention. I will speak.”

mn64:4.5.verse: “As you say, lord,” Ven. Ānanda responded to the Blessed One.

mn64:5.1.verse: “There is the case, Ānanda, where an uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person—who has no regard for noble ones, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma; who has no regard for people of integrity, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma—

mn64:5.2.verse: remains with his awareness possessed by self-identification view, overcome by self-identification view.

mn64:5.3.verse: He doesn’t discern, as it has come to be, the escape from an arisen self-identification view.

mn64:5.4.verse: For him, that self-identification view—fixed & unsubdued in him—is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.5.verse: He remains with his awareness possessed by uncertainty, overcome by uncertainty;

mn64:5.6.verse: and he doesn’t discern, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen uncertainty.

mn64:5.7.verse: For him, that uncertainty—fixed & unsubdued in him—is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.8.verse: He remains with his awareness possessed by grasping at habits & practices, overcome by grasping at habits & practices;

mn64:5.9.verse: and he doesn’t discern, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen grasping at habits & practices.

mn64:5.10.verse: For him, that grasping at habits & practices—fixed & unsubdued in him—is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.11.verse: He remains with his awareness possessed by sensual passion, overcome by sensual passion;

mn64:5.12.verse: and he doesn’t discern, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen sensual passion.

mn64:5.13.verse: For him, that sensual passion—fixed & unsubdued in him—is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.14.verse: He remains with his awareness possessed by ill will, overcome by ill will.

mn64:5.15.verse: He doesn’t discern, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen ill will.

mn64:5.16.verse: For him, that ill will—fixed & unsubdued in him—is a lower fetter.

mn64:6.1.verse: “But there is the case where a well-instructed disciple of the noble ones—who has regard for noble ones, is well-versed & disciplined in their Dhamma; who has regard for people of integrity, is well-versed & disciplined in their Dhamma—remains with his awareness not possessed by self-identification view, not overcome by self-identification view.

mn64:6.2.verse: He discerns, as it has come to be, the escape from an arisen self-identification view.

mn64:6.3.verse: For him, that self-identification view—together with its latent tendency—is abandoned.

mn64:6.4.verse: He remains with his awareness not possessed by uncertainty, not overcome by uncertainty;

mn64:6.5.verse: and he discerns, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen uncertainty.

mn64:6.6.verse: For him, that uncertainty—together with its latent tendency—is abandoned.

mn64:6.7.verse: He remains with his awareness not possessed by grasping at habits & practices, not overcome by grasping at habits & practices;

mn64:6.8.verse: and he discerns, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen grasping at habits & practices.

mn64:6.9.verse: For him, that grasping at habits & practices—together with its latent tendency—is abandoned.

mn64:6.10.verse: He remains with his awareness not possessed by sensual passion, not overcome by sensual passion;

mn64:6.11.verse: and he discerns, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen sensual passion.

mn64:6.12.verse: For him, that sensual passion—together with its latent tendency—is abandoned.

mn64:6.13.verse: He remains with his awareness not possessed by ill will, not overcome by ill will.

mn64:6.14.verse: He discerns, as it has come to be, the escape from arisen ill will.

mn64:6.15.verse: For him, that ill will—together with its latent tendency—is abandoned.

mn64:6.16.verse: “For one who has not followed the path, the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters to know, to see, or to abandon the five lower fetters: That is impossible.

mn64:6.17.verse: It’s just as if there were a great tree standing, possessed of heartwood. For its heartwood to be cut without first cutting through the bark, without cutting through the sapwood:

mn64:6.19.verse: In the same way, for one who has not followed the path, the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters to know, to see, or to abandon the five lower fetters: That is impossible.

mn64:7.1.verse: “For one who has followed the path, the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters to know, to see, or to abandon the five lower fetters: That is possible.

mn64:8.1.verse: It’s just as if there were a great tree standing, possessed of heartwood. For its heartwood to be cut after first cutting through the bark and cutting through the sapwood: That is possible.

mn64:8.2.verse: In the same way, for one who has followed the path, the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters to know, to see, or to abandon the five lower fetters: That is possible.

mn64:8.3.verse: “Suppose that the River Ganges were full of water up to the brim so that crows could drink out of it,

mn64:8.4.verse: and a weak man were to come along, (thinking,)

mn64:8.5.verse: ‘I will go across this River Ganges, cutting the current with my arms, safely to the further shore.’

mn64:8.6.verse: He would not be able to go across the River Ganges, cutting the current with his arms, safely to the further shore.

mn64:8.7.verse: So it is with anyone whose mind, when the cessation of self-identification is being taught, doesn’t take to it, isn’t calmed by it, doesn’t resolve on it, and isn’t released in it:

mn64:8.8.verse: That person is to be seen as like the weak man.

mn64:8.9.verse: “But suppose that the River Ganges were full of water up to the brim so that crows could drink out of it,

mn64:8.10.verse: and a strong man were to come along, (thinking,)

mn64:8.11.verse: ‘I will go across this River Ganges, cutting the current with my arms, safely to the further shore.’

mn64:8.12.verse: He would be able to go across the River Ganges, cutting the current with his arms, safely to the further shore.

mn64:8.13.verse: So it is with anyone whose mind, when the cessation of self-identification is being taught, takes to it, is calmed by it, resolves on it, and is released in it:

mn64:8.14.verse: That person is to be seen as like the strong man.

mn64:9.1.verse: “And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters?

mn64:9.2.verse: There is the case where a monk—from being secluded from acquisitions, from the abandoning of unskillful qualities, from the entire calming of bodily discomfort, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities—enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn64:9.3.verse: He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with form, feeling, perception, fabrications, & consciousness, as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a disintegration, an emptiness, not-self.

mn64:9.4.verse: He turns his mind away from those phenomena and,

mn64:9.5.verse: having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness:

mn64:9.6.verse: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the pacification of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’

mn64:9.7.verse: Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents.

mn64:9.8.verse: Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this Dhamma-delight, and from the total ending of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, never again to return from that world.

mn64:9.9.verse: This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.

mn64:10-12.1.verse: “And further, Ānanda, with the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, the monk enters & remains in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

mn64:10-12.2.verse: With the fading of rapture he remains equanimous, mindful, & alert, and senses pleasure with the body. He enters & remains in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’

mn64:10-12.3.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of joy & distress—he enters & remains in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain.

mn64:10-12.4.verse: He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with form, feeling, perception, fabrications, & consciousness, as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a disintegration, an emptiness, not-self.

mn64:10-12.5.verse: He turns his mind away from those phenomena and, having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the pacification of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this very Dhamma-delight, and from the total ending of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound,

mn64:10-12.6.verse: never again to return from that world.

mn64:10-12.7.verse: This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.

mn64:13.1.verse: “And further, Ānanda, the monk—with the complete transcending of perceptions of (physical) form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite space’—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of space.

mn64:13.2.verse: He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with feeling, perception, fabrications, & consciousness, as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a disintegration, an emptiness, not-self.

mn64:13.3.verse: He turns his mind away from those phenomena and, having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the pacification of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this very Dhamma-delight, and from the total ending of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound,

mn64:13.4.verse: never again to return from that world.

mn64:13.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.

mn64:14.1.verse: “And further, Ānanda, the monk—with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite consciousness’—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.

mn64:14.2.verse: He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with feeling, perception, fabrications, & consciousness, as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a disintegration, an emptiness, not-self.

mn64:14.3.verse: He turns his mind away from those phenomena and, having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the pacification of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this very Dhamma-delight, and from the total ending of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound,

mn64:14.4.verse: never again to return from that world.

mn64:14.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.

mn64:15.1.verse: “And further, Ānanda, the monk—with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, (perceiving,) ‘There is nothing’—enters & remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn64:15.2.verse: He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with feeling, perception, fabrications, & consciousness, as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a disintegration, an emptiness, not-self.

mn64:15.3.verse: He turns his mind away from those phenomena and, having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the pacification of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’ Staying right there, he reaches the ending of the effluents. Or, if not, then—through this very Dhamma-passion, this very Dhamma-delight, and from the total ending of the five lower fetters—he is due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound,

mn64:15.4.verse: never again to return from that world.

mn64:15.5.verse: This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.”

mn64:16.1.verse: “But, lord, if this is the path, if this is the practice, for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, then why are some monks (said to be) ‘released through awareness,’ and some monks are (said to be) ‘released through discernment’?”

mn64:16.2.verse: “I tell you, Ānanda: That is the difference in their faculties.”

mn64:16.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn64:16.4.verse: Gratified, Ven. Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn64:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn64:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn64:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you remember the five lower fetters taught by me?”

mn64:2.2.verse: When he said this, Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to him,

mn64:2.5.verse: “I remember the lower fetters taught by the Buddha as follows: substantialist view,

mn64:2.10.verse: That’s how I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Buddha.”

mn64:3.1.verse: “Who on earth do you remember being taught the five lower fetters in that way?

mn64:3.2.verse: Wouldn’t the wanderers of other religions fault you using the simile of the infant?

mn64:3.3.verse: For a little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘substantial reality’, so how could substantialist view possibly arise in them?

mn64:3.4.verse: Yet the underlying tendency to substantialist view still lies within them.

mn64:3.5.verse: A little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘teachings’, so how could doubt about the teachings possibly arise in them?

mn64:3.6.verse: Yet the underlying tendency to doubt still lies within them.

mn64:3.7.verse: A little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘precepts’, so how could misapprehension of precepts and observances possibly arise in them?

mn64:3.8.verse: Yet the underlying tendency to misapprehension of precepts and observances still lies within them.

mn64:3.9.verse: A little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘sensual pleasures’, so how could desire for sensual pleasures possibly arise in them?

mn64:3.10.verse: Yet the underlying tendency to sensual desire still lies within them.

mn64:3.11.verse: A little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘sentient beings’, so how could ill will for sentient beings possibly arise in them?

mn64:3.12.verse: Yet the underlying tendency to ill will still lies within them.

mn64:3.13.verse: Wouldn’t the wanderers of other religions fault you using the simile of the infant?”

mn64:4.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

mn64:4.2.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

mn64:4.3.verse: May the Buddha teach the five lower fetters. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn64:4.4.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn64:5.1.verse: “Ānanda, take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn64:5.2.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in substantialist view,

mn64:5.3.verse: and they don’t truly understand the escape from substantialist view that has arisen.

mn64:5.4.verse: That substantialist view is entrenched in them, not eliminated: it is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.5.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in doubt,

mn64:5.6.verse: and they don’t truly understand the escape from doubt that has arisen.

mn64:5.7.verse: That doubt is entrenched in them, not eliminated: it is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.8.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in misapprehension of precepts and observances,

mn64:5.9.verse: and they don’t truly understand the escape from misapprehension of precepts and observances that has arisen.

mn64:5.10.verse: That misapprehension of precepts and observances is entrenched in them, not eliminated: it is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.11.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in sensual desire,

mn64:5.12.verse: and they don’t truly understand the escape from sensual desire that has arisen.

mn64:5.13.verse: That sensual desire is entrenched in them, not eliminated: it is a lower fetter.

mn64:5.14.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in ill will,

mn64:5.15.verse: and they don’t truly understand the escape from ill will that has arisen.

mn64:5.16.verse: That ill will is entrenched in them, not eliminated: it is a lower fetter.

mn64:6.1.verse: But a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons. Their heart is not overcome and mired in substantialist view,

mn64:6.2.verse: and they truly understand the escape from substantialist view that has arisen.

mn64:6.3.verse: That substantialist view, along with any underlying tendency to it, is given up in them.

mn64:6.4.verse: Their heart is not overcome and mired in doubt,

mn64:6.5.verse: and they truly understand the escape from doubt that has arisen.

mn64:6.6.verse: That doubt, along with any underlying tendency to it, is given up in them.

mn64:6.7.verse: Their heart is not overcome and mired in misapprehension of precepts and observances,

mn64:6.8.verse: and they truly understand the escape from misapprehension of precepts and observances that has arisen.

mn64:6.9.verse: That misapprehension of precepts and observances, along with any underlying tendency to it, is given up in them.

mn64:6.10.verse: Their heart is not overcome and mired in sensual desire,

mn64:6.11.verse: and they truly understand the escape from sensual desire that has arisen.

mn64:6.12.verse: That sensual desire, along with any underlying tendency to it, is given up in them.

mn64:6.13.verse: Their heart is not overcome and mired in ill will,

mn64:6.14.verse: and they truly understand the escape from ill will that has arisen.

mn64:6.15.verse: That ill will, along with any underlying tendency to it, is given up in them.

mn64:6.16.verse: There is a path and a practice for giving up the five lower fetters. It’s not possible to know or see or give up the five lower fetters without relying on that path and that practice.

mn64:6.17.verse: Suppose there was a large tree standing with heartwood. It’s not possible to cut out the heartwood without having cut through the bark and the softwood.

mn64:6.19.verse: In the same way, there is a path and a practice for giving up the five lower fetters. It’s not possible to know or see or give up the five lower fetters without relying on that path and that practice.

mn64:7.1.verse: But it is possible to know and see and give up the five lower fetters by relying on that path and that practice.

mn64:8.1.verse: Suppose there was a large tree standing with heartwood. It is possible to cut out the heartwood after having cut through the bark and the softwood.

mn64:8.2.verse: In the same way, there is a path and a practice for giving up the five lower fetters. It is possible to know and see and give up the five lower fetters by relying on that path and that practice.

mn64:8.3.verse: Suppose the Ganges River was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

mn64:8.4.verse: Then along comes a feeble person, who thinks:

mn64:8.5.verse: ‘By swimming with my arms I’ll safely cross over to the far shore of the Ganges.’

mn64:8.6.verse: But they’re not able to do so.

mn64:8.7.verse: In the same way, when the Dhamma is being taught to them for the cessation of substantial reality, those whose mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided

mn64:8.8.verse: should be regarded as being like that feeble person.

mn64:8.9.verse: Suppose the Ganges River was full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

mn64:8.10.verse: Then along comes a strong person, who thinks:

mn64:8.11.verse: ‘By swimming with my arms I’ll safely cross over to the far shore of the Ganges.’

mn64:8.12.verse: And they are able to do so.

mn64:8.13.verse: In the same way, when the Dhamma is being taught to them for the cessation of substantial reality, those whose mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided

mn64:8.14.verse: should be regarded as being like that strong person.

mn64:9.1.verse: And what, Ānanda, is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters?

mn64:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—due to the seclusion from attachments, the giving up of unskillful qualities, and the complete settling of physical discomforts—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn64:9.3.verse: They contemplate the phenomena there—included in form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—as impermanent, as suffering, as diseased, as a boil, as a dart, as gloom, as an affliction, as alien, as breaking apart, as empty, as not-self.

mn64:9.4.verse: They turn their mind away from those things,

mn64:9.5.verse: and apply it to the element free of death:

mn64:9.6.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.’

mn64:9.7.verse: Abiding in that they attain the ending of defilements.

mn64:9.8.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, with the ending of the five lower fetters they’re reborn spontaneously, because of their passion and love for that meditation. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

mn64:9.9.verse: This is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters.

mn64:10-12.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn64:10-12.4.verse: They contemplate the phenomena there—included in form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—as impermanent …

mn64:10-12.5.verse: They turn their mind away from those things …

mn64:10-12.6.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, they’re reborn spontaneously … and are not liable to return from that world.

mn64:10-12.7.verse: This too is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters.

mn64:13.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

mn64:13.2.verse: They contemplate the phenomena there—included in feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—as impermanent …

mn64:13.3.verse: They turn their mind away from those things …

mn64:13.4.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, they’re reborn spontaneously … and are not liable to return from that world.

mn64:13.5.verse: This too is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters.

mn64:14.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn64:14.2.verse: They contemplate the phenomena there—included in feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—as impermanent …

mn64:14.3.verse: They turn their mind away from those things …

mn64:14.4.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, they’re reborn spontaneously … and are not liable to return from that world.

mn64:14.5.verse: This too is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters.

mn64:15.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn64:15.2.verse: They contemplate the phenomena there—included in feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—as impermanent …

mn64:15.3.verse: They turn their mind away from those things …

mn64:15.4.verse: If they don’t attain the ending of defilements, they’re reborn spontaneously … and are not liable to return from that world.

mn64:15.5.verse: This too is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters.”

mn64:16.1.verse: “Sir, if this is the path and the practice for giving up the five lower fetters, how then are some mendicants here released in heart while others are released by wisdom?”

mn64:16.2.verse: “In that case, I say it is the disparity of their faculties.”

mn64:16.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn64:16.4.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn65:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn65:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn65:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I eat my food in one sitting per day.

mn65:2.2.verse: Doing so, I find that I’m healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

mn65:2.3.verse: You too should eat your food in one sitting per day.

mn65:2.4.verse: Doing so, you’ll find that you’re healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.”

mn65:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Bhaddāli said to the Buddha,

mn65:3.2.verse: “Sir, I’m not going to attempt to eat my food in one sitting per day.

mn65:3.3.verse: For when eating once a day I might feel remorse and regret.”

mn65:4.1.verse: “Well then, Bhaddāli, eat one part of the meal in the place where you’re invited, and bring the rest back to eat.

mn65:4.2.verse: Eating this way, too, you will sustain yourself.”

mn65:4.3.verse: “Sir, I’m not going to attempt to eat that way, either.

mn65:4.4.verse: For when eating that way I might also feel remorse and regret.”

mn65:4.5.verse: Then, as this rule was being laid down by the Buddha and the Saṅgha was undertaking it, Bhaddāli announced he would not attempt to keep it.

mn65:4.6.verse: Then for the whole of that three months Bhaddāli would not see the Buddha face to face, as happens when someone doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:5.1.verse: At that time several mendicants were making a robe for the Buddha, thinking that

mn65:5.2.verse: when his robe was finished and the three months of the rains residence had passed the Buddha would set out wandering.

mn65:6.1.verse: Then Bhaddāli went up to those mendicants, and exchanged greetings with them.

mn65:6.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The mendicants said to Bhaddāli,

mn65:6.3.verse: “Reverend Bhaddāli, this robe is being made for the Buddha.

mn65:6.4.verse: When it’s finished and the three months of the rains residence have passed the Buddha will set out wandering.

mn65:6.5.verse: Come on, Bhaddāli, learn your lesson. Don’t make it hard for yourself later on.”

mn65:7.1.verse: “Yes, reverends,” Bhaddāli replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn65:7.2.verse: “I made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me that, as this rule was being laid down by the Buddha and the Saṅgha was undertaking it, I announced I would not attempt to keep it.

mn65:7.3.verse: Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

mn65:8.1.verse: “Indeed, Bhaddāli, you made a mistake. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of you that, as this rule was being laid down by the Buddha and the Saṅgha was undertaking it, you announced you would not attempt to keep it.

mn65:9.1.verse: And you didn’t realize this situation:

mn65:9.2.verse: ‘The Buddha is staying in Sāvatthī, and he’ll know me

mn65:9.3.verse: as the mendicant named Bhaddāli who doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.’

mn65:9.5.verse: And you didn’t realize this situation:

mn65:9.6.verse: ‘Several monks have commenced the rains retreat in Sāvatthī …

mn65:9.10.verse: several nuns have commenced the rains retreat in Sāvatthī …

mn65:9.18.verse: several laywomen reside in Sāvatthī, and they’ll know me

mn65:9.19.verse: as the mendicant named Bhaddāli who doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions. …

mn65:9.22.verse: Several ascetics and brahmins who follow various other religions have commenced the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, and they’ll know me

mn65:9.23.verse: as the mendicant named Bhaddāli, one of the senior disciples of Gotama, who doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.’

mn65:9.24.verse: You also didn’t realize this situation.”

mn65:10.1.verse: “I made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me that, as this rule was being laid down by the Buddha and the Saṅgha was undertaking it, I announced I would not attempt to keep it.

mn65:10.2.verse: Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

mn65:10.3.verse: “Indeed, Bhaddāli, you made a mistake. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of you that, as this rule was being laid down by the Buddha and the Saṅgha was undertaking it, you announced you would not attempt to keep it.

mn65:11.2.verse: Suppose I was to say this to a mendicant who is freed both ways:

mn65:11.3.verse: ‘Please, mendicant, be a bridge for me to cross over the mud.’ Would they cross over themselves, or struggle to get out of it, or just say no?”

mn65:11.6.verse: Suppose I was to say the same thing to a mendicant who is freed by wisdom,

mn65:11.12.verse: ‘Please, mendicant, be a bridge for me to cross over the mud.’ Would they cross over themselves, or struggle to get out of it, or just say no?”

mn65:12.2.verse: At that time were you freed both ways, freed by wisdom, a direct witness, attained to view, freed by faith, a follower of teachings, or a follower by faith?”

mn65:13.3.verse: Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

mn65:13.5.verse: But since you have recognized your mistake for what it is, and have dealt with it properly, I accept it.

mn65:13.6.verse: For it is growth in the training of the Noble One to recognize a mistake for what it is, deal with it properly, and commit to restraint in the future.

mn65:14.1.verse: Bhaddāli, take a mendicant who doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:14.3.verse: ‘Why don’t I frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn65:14.4.verse: Hopefully I’ll realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.’

mn65:14.5.verse: So they frequent a secluded lodging.

mn65:14.6.verse: While they’re living withdrawn, they’re reprimanded by the Teacher, by sensible spiritual companions after examination, by deities, and by themselves.

mn65:14.7.verse: Being reprimanded in this way, they don’t realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn65:14.9.verse: Because that’s how it is when someone doesn’t fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:15.1.verse: But take a mendicant who does fulfill the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:15.3.verse: ‘Why don’t I frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn65:15.4.verse: Hopefully I’ll realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.’

mn65:15.5.verse: They frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn65:15.6.verse: While they’re living withdrawn, they’re not reprimanded by the Teacher, by sensible spiritual companions after examination, by deities, or by themselves.

mn65:15.7.verse: Not being reprimanded in this way, they realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn65:16.1.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn65:16.3.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:17.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn65:17.3.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:17.4.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn65:17.6.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:17.7.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn65:17.9.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:18.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn65:18.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. … They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn65:18.4.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:19.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn65:19.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. … they’re reborn in the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. … they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman … they understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn65:19.4.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.

mn65:20.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn65:20.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn65:20.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn65:21.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn65:21.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn65:21.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn65:21.5.verse: Because that’s what happens when someone fulfills the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.”

mn65:22.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Bhaddāli said to the Buddha,

mn65:22.2.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why they punish some monk, repeatedly pressuring him?

mn65:22.3.verse: And what is the cause, what is the reason why they don’t similarly punish another monk, repeatedly pressuring him?”

mn65:23.1.verse: “Take a monk who is a frequent offender with many offenses.

mn65:23.2.verse: When admonished by the monks, he dodges the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. He displays annoyance, hate, and bitterness. He doesn’t proceed properly, he doesn’t fall in line, he doesn’t proceed to get past it, and he doesn’t say: ‘I’ll do what pleases the Saṅgha.’

mn65:23.3.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:23.4.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk is a frequent offender, with many offenses.

mn65:23.5.verse: When admonished by the monks, he dodges the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. He displays annoyance, hate, and bitterness. He doesn’t proceed properly, he doesn’t fall in line, he doesn’t proceed to get past it, and he doesn’t say: “I’ll do what pleases the Saṅgha.”

mn65:23.6.verse: It’d be good for the venerables to examine this monk in such a way that this disciplinary issue is not quickly settled.’

mn65:24.1.verse: Take some other monk who is a frequent offender with many offenses.

mn65:24.2.verse: When admonished by the monks, he doesn’t dodge the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. He doesn’t display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. He proceeds properly, he falls in line, he proceeds to get past it, and he says: ‘I’ll do what pleases the Saṅgha.’

mn65:24.3.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:24.4.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk is a frequent offender, with many offenses.

mn65:24.5.verse: When admonished by the monks, he doesn’t dodge the issue, distracting the discussion with irrelevant points. He doesn’t display annoyance, hate, and bitterness. He proceeds properly, he falls in line, he proceeds to get past it, and he says: “I’ll do what pleases the Saṅgha.”

mn65:24.6.verse: It’d be good for the venerables to examine this monk in such a way that this disciplinary issue is quickly settled.’

mn65:25.1.verse: Take some other monk who is an occasional offender without many offenses.

mn65:25.2.verse: When admonished by the monks, he dodges the issue …

mn65:25.3.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:25.4.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk is an occasional offender without many offenses.

mn65:25.5.verse: When admonished by the monks, he dodges the issue …

mn65:25.6.verse: It’d be good for the venerables to examine this monk in such a way that this disciplinary issue is not quickly settled.’

mn65:26.1.verse: Take some other monk who is an occasional offender without many offenses.

mn65:26.2.verse: When admonished by the monks, he doesn’t dodge the issue …

mn65:26.3.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:26.4.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk is an occasional offender without many offenses.

mn65:26.5.verse: When admonished by the monks, he doesn’t dodge the issue …

mn65:26.6.verse: It’d be good for the venerables to examine this monk in such a way that this disciplinary issue is quickly settled.’

mn65:27.1.verse: Take some other monk who gets by with mere faith and fondness.

mn65:27.2.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:27.3.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk gets by with mere faith and fondness.

mn65:27.4.verse: Suppose we punish him, repeatedly pressuring him—

mn65:27.5.verse: no, let him not lose what little faith and fondness he has!’

mn65:28.1.verse: Suppose there was a person with one eye. Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would protect that one eye:

mn65:28.2.verse: ‘Let them not lose the one eye that they have!’

mn65:28.3.verse: In the same way, some monk gets by with mere faith and fondness.

mn65:28.4.verse: In such a case, the monks say:

mn65:28.5.verse: ‘Reverends, this monk gets by with mere faith and fondness.

mn65:28.6.verse: Suppose we punish him, repeatedly pressuring him—

mn65:28.7.verse: no, let him not lose what little faith and love he has!’

mn65:28.8.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why they punish some monk, repeatedly pressuring him.

mn65:28.9.verse: And this is the cause, this is the reason why they don’t similarly punish another monk, repeatedly pressuring him.”

mn65:29.1.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why there used to be fewer training rules but more enlightened mendicants?

mn65:29.2.verse: And what is the cause, what is the reason why these days there are more training rules and fewer enlightened mendicants?”

mn65:30.1.verse: “That’s how it is, Bhaddāli. When sentient beings are in decline and the true teaching is disappearing there are more training rules and fewer enlightened mendicants.

mn65:30.2.verse: The Teacher does not lay down training rules for disciples as long as certain defiling influences have not appeared in the Saṅgha.

mn65:30.3.verse: But when such defiling influences appear in the Saṅgha, the Teacher lays down training rules for disciples to protect against them.

mn65:31.1.verse: And they don’t appear until the Saṅgha has attained a great size,

mn65:31.4.verse: an abundance of material support and fame, learning, and seniority.

mn65:31.5.verse: But when the Saṅgha has attained these things, then such defiling influences appear in the Saṅgha, and the Teacher lays down training rules for disciples to protect against them.

mn65:32.1.verse: There were only a few of you there at the time when I taught the exposition on the simile of the thoroughbred colt.

mn65:32.4.verse: “What do you believe the reason for that is?”

mn65:32.5.verse: “Sir, it’s surely because for a long time now I haven’t fulfilled the training according to the Teacher’s instructions.”

mn65:32.7.verse: Rather, for a long time I have encompassed your mind and known:

mn65:32.8.verse: ‘While I’m teaching, this futile man doesn’t pay attention, apply the mind, concentrate wholeheartedly, or actively listen to the teaching.’

mn65:32.9.verse: Still, Bhaddāli, I shall teach the exposition on the simile of the thoroughbred colt.

mn65:32.10.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn65:33.1.verse: “Suppose a deft horse trainer were to obtain a fine thoroughbred. First of all he’d make it get used to wearing the bit.

mn65:33.2.verse: Because it has not done this before, it still resorts to some twists, ducks, and dodges.

mn65:33.3.verse: But with regular and gradual practice its bad behavior is extinguished.

mn65:33.4.verse: When it has done this, the horse trainer next makes it get used to wearing the harness.

mn65:33.5.verse: Because it has not done this before, it still resorts to some twists, ducks, and dodges.

mn65:33.6.verse: But with regular and gradual practice its bad behavior is extinguished.

mn65:33.7.verse: When it has done this, the horse trainer next makes it get used to walking in procession, circling, prancing, galloping, charging, the protocols and customs of court, and in the very best speed, fleetness, and camaraderie.

mn65:33.8.verse: Because it has not done this before, it still resorts to some twists, ducks, and dodges.

mn65:33.9.verse: But with regular and gradual practice its bad behavior is extinguished.

mn65:33.10.verse: When it has done this, the horse trainer next rewards it with a grooming and a rub down.

mn65:33.11.verse: A fine royal thoroughbred with these ten factors is worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, and reckoned as a factor of kingship.

mn65:34.1.verse: In the same way, a mendicant with ten qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of veneration with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

mn65:34.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant has an adept’s right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right immersion, right knowledge, and right freedom.

mn65:34.4.verse: A mendicant with these ten qualities is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of veneration with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.”

mn65:34.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn65:34.6.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Bhaddāli approved what the Buddha said.

mn66:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Anguttarāpan country. There is a town of theirs called Apaṇa.

mn66:2.1.verse: Now when it was morning the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Apaṇa for alms.

mn66:2.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Apaṇa and had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he went to a certain grove for the day’s abiding,

mn66:2.3.verse: and he went into the grove and sat down at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.

mn66:3.1.verse: Also when it was morning the venerable Udāyin dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Apaṇa for alms.

mn66:3.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Apaṇa and he had returned from his alms-round after the meal, he went to that grove for the day’s abiding,

mn66:3.3.verse: and he went into the grove and sat down at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.

mn66:3.4.verse: Then while the venerable Udāyin was alone in meditation this thought came to his mind:

mn66:4.1.verse: ‘How many a painful thing (_dhamma_) the Blessed One has rid us of and how many a pleasant thing the Blessed One has brought us!

mn66:4.2.verse: How many an unprofitable thing the Blessed One has rid us of and how many a profitable thing the Blessed One has brought us!’

mn66:5.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Udāyin rose from meditation, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he told the Blessed One what he had thought, and he added:

mn66:6.4.verse: ‘Venerable sir, formerly we used to eat in the evening and in the morning and late in the day.

mn66:6.5.verse: There was the occasion when the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn66:6.6.verse: “Bhikkhus, please abandon that eating late in the day.”

mn66:6.7.verse: Venerable sir, I was discomfited and aggrieved, (thinking:)

mn66:6.8.verse: “When faithful householders give us good food of various kinds late in the day, the Blessed One tells us to abandon it, the Sublime One tells us to relinquish it.”

mn66:6.9.verse: Since we saw in ourselves love and respect for the Blessed One, and conscience and shame, we abandoned that eating late in the day.

mn66:6.10.verse: Then we ate only (in two sessions, that is to say,) in the evening and in the morning.

mn66:6.11.verse: Then there was the occasion when the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn66:6.12.verse: “Bhikkhus, please abandon that eating late at night.”

mn66:6.13.verse: Venerable sir, I was discomfited and aggrieved, (thinking:)

mn66:6.14.verse: “The Blessed One tells us to abandon that one of our meals which is reckoned the superior, the Sublime One tells us to relinquish that.”

mn66:6.15.verse: It has happened, venerable sir, that a certain man obtained some materials for sauces, and he said:

mn66:6.16.verse: “Put that aside and let us all eat it together in the evening.”

mn66:6.17.verse: (Nearly) all cooking is done at night and little by day.

mn66:6.18.verse: Since we saw in ourselves love and respect for the Blessed One, and conscience and shame, we abandoned that eating late at night.

mn66:6.19.verse: It has happened, venerable sir, that bhikkhus wandering for alms in the dark gloom of the night have walked into a cesspit and walked into a sewer and fallen over a thornbush and fallen over a cow and encountered miscreants who had already committed one and have been enticed by women with what is not True Dhamma.

mn66:6.20.verse: It has happened, venerable sir, that I went wandering for alms in the dark gloom of the night,

mn66:6.21.verse: and a woman washing a dish saw me by a flash of lightning.

mn66:6.22.verse: Seeing me, she screamed out in terror:

mn66:6.23.verse: “Mercy me, a devil (has come) for me!”

mn66:6.24.verse: When this was said, I told her:

mn66:6.26.verse: I am a bhikkhu waiting for alms.”

mn66:6.27.verse: “Then it’s a bhikkhu whose ma’s died and whose pa’s died!

mn66:6.28.verse: Better, bhikkhu, you get your belly cut open with a sharp carver than this prowling for alms in the dark gloom of the night for your belly’s sake!”

mn66:6.29.verse: Venerable sir, when I recollected that I (thought:)

mn66:6.30.verse: “How many a painful thing the Blessed One has rid us of; and how many a pleasant thing the Blessed One has brought us!

mn66:6.31.verse: How many an unprofitable thing the Blessed One has rid us of; and how many a profitable thing the Blessed One has brought us!” ’

mn66:7.1.verse: ‘So too, Udāyin, there have been certain misguided men here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:7.2.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail as this? This monk is overmuch of an effacer!”

mn66:7.3.verse: and they did not abandon that and showed discourtesy to me

mn66:7.4.verse: as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training. That becomes a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for them and a thick neck-plank.

mn66:8.1.verse: ‘Suppose a quail were tethered by a rotting-creeper tether, it could thereby expect hurt or captivity or death.

mn66:8.3.verse: “The rotting-creeper tether by which that quail is tethered and can thereby expect hurt, captivity or death, is a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for it,”

mn66:8.6.verse: the rotting-creeper tether by which the quail is tethered and can thereby expect hurt, captivity or death is a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for it and a thick neck-plank.’

mn66:8.7.verse: ‘So too, Udāyin, there have been certain misguided men here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:8.8.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail as this? This monk is overmuch of an effacer!”

mn66:8.9.verse: and they did not abandon that and showed discourtesy to me

mn66:8.10.verse: as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training. That becomes a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for them and a thick neck-plank.

mn66:9.1.verse: ‘Udāyin, there have been some clansmen here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:9.2.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail to be abandoned as this, the Blessed One (formally) announces the abandoning of it, the Sublime One (formally) announces the relinquishment of it?”

mn66:9.3.verse: yet they abandoned that and did not show discourtesy to me as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training.

mn66:9.4.verse: Having abandoned it, they abode uninvolved in activity, unruffled, subsisting on others’ gifts, with mind (as aloof) as a wild deer’s.

mn66:9.5.verse: That is a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for them.

mn66:10.1.verse: ‘Suppose a royal tusker elephant with tusks as long as chariot-poles, full-grown in stature, highly bred, and well-used to battles, were tethered by stout leather thongs, but by simply inclining his body a little he could break and burst the thongs and then go where he liked.

mn66:10.3.verse: “That is a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for him and a thick neck-plank,”

mn66:10.6.verse: The stout leather thongs by which that royal tusker elephant with tusks as long as chariot-poles, full-grown in stature, highly bred and well-used to battles, is tethered, which by simply inclining his body a little he could break and burst and then go where he liked, is a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for him.’

mn66:10.7.verse: ‘So too, Udāyin, there have been some clansmen here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:10.8.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail to be abandoned as this, the Blessed One (formally) announces the abandoning of it, the Sublime One (formally) announces the relinquishment of it?”

mn66:10.9.verse: yet they abandoned that and did not show discourtesy to me as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training.

mn66:10.10.verse: Having abandoned it, they abode uninvolved in activity, unruffled, subsisting on others’ gifts, with mind (as aloof) as a wild deer’s.

mn66:10.11.verse: That is a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for them.’

mn66:11.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a poor, penniless, destitute man,

mn66:11.2.verse: and he had a crazily-leaning hovel, not the best kind, and a crazily-leaning wicker bedstead, not the best kind, and some corn and pumpkin seeds in a pot, not the best kind, and a trapes of a wife, not the best kind,

mn66:11.3.verse: and he went to a monastery park and saw a bhikkhu sitting in the shade of a tree with hands and feet well washed after eating an inviting meal, devoting himself to the higher mind.

mn66:11.5.verse: “How pleasant the monk’s state is, and how healthy!

mn66:11.6.verse: If only I were one who could shave off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth and go forth from the home life into homelessness!”

mn66:11.7.verse: but he is unable to abandon the crazily-leaning hovel, not the best kind, and the crazily-leaning bedstead, not the best kind, and some corn and pumpkin seeds in a pot, not the best kind, and the trapes of a wife, not the best kind, and he was not able to shave off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth and go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn66:11.9.verse: “The tethers by which that man is tethered so that he cannot abandon those things and go forth from the home life into homelessness

mn66:11.10.verse: are a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for him,”

mn66:11.13.verse: The tethers by which that man is tethered so that he cannot abandon those things and go forth from the home life into homelessness

mn66:11.14.verse: are a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for him and a thick neck-plank.’

mn66:11.15.verse: ‘So too, Udāyin, there have been certain misguided men here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:11.16.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail as this? This monk is overmuch of an effacer!”

mn66:11.17.verse: and they did not abandon that and showed discourtesy to me

mn66:11.18.verse: as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training. That becomes a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for them and a thick neck-plank.

mn66:12.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a rich householder or householder’s son, with vast wealth and vast property, many a score of gold ingots and many a score of granaries and many a score of fields and many a score of clothes and many a score of wives and many a score of bondsmen and bondswomen,

mn66:12.2.verse: and he went to a monastery park and saw a bhikkhu sitting in the shade of a tree with hands and feet well washed after eating an inviting meal, devoting himself to the higher mind.

mn66:12.4.verse: “How pleasant the monk’s state is, and how healthy!

mn66:12.5.verse: If only I were one who could shave off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth and go forth from the home life into homelessness!”

mn66:12.6.verse: and he was able to abandon many a score of gold ingots and many a score of granaries and many a score of fields and many a score of clothes and many a score of wives and many a score of bondsmen and bondswomen, and he is able to shave off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth and go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn66:12.8.verse: “The tethers by which that householder or householder’s son is tethered so that he can abandon those things and go forth from the home life into homelessness are a strong, stout, tough, never-rotting tether for him,”

mn66:12.11.verse: The tethers by which that householder or householder’s son is tethered so that he can abandon those things and go forth from the home life into homelessness

mn66:12.12.verse: are a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for him.’

mn66:12.13.verse: ‘Udāyin, there have been some clansmen here, who, when told by me “Abandon this” said:

mn66:12.14.verse: “What, for such a mere trifle, for such a mere detail to be abandoned as this, the Blessed One (formally) announces the abandoning of it, the Sublime One (formally) announces the relinquishment of it?”

mn66:12.15.verse: yet they abandoned that and did not show discourtesy to me

mn66:12.16.verse: as well as the bhikkhus desirous of training. Having abandoned it, they abode uninvolved in activity, unruffled, subsisting on others’ gifts, with mind (as aloof) as a wild deer’s.

mn66:12.17.verse: That is a feeble, weak, rotting, coreless tether for them.

mn66:13.1.verse: ‘There are four kinds of person to be found existing in the world.

mn66:14.1.verse: ‘Here some person practises the way to the abandoning of the essentials of existence, to the relinquishing of the essentials of existence.

mn66:14.2.verse: When that is so, memories and intentions associated with the essentials of existence beset him.

mn66:14.3.verse: He endures them, he does not abandon them or remove them or do away with and annihilate them.

mn66:14.4.verse: Such a person I call “associated” not “dissociated”.

mn66:14.6.verse: Because I have known the particular diversity of faculties in this person.

mn66:15.1.verse: ‘Here some person practises the way to the abandoning of the essentials of existence, to the relinquishing of the essentials of existence.

mn66:15.2.verse: When that is so, memories and intentions associated with the essentials of existence beset him.

mn66:15.3.verse: He does not endure them, he abandons them, removes them, does away with and annihilates them.

mn66:15.4.verse: Such a person I call “associated” not “dissociated”.

mn66:15.6.verse: Because I have known the particular diversity of faculties in this person.

mn66:16.1.verse: ‘Here some person practises the way to the abandoning of the essentials of existence, to the relinquishing of the essentials of existence.

mn66:16.2.verse: When that is so, memories and intentions associated with the essentials of existence beset him now and then owing to lapses of mindfulness.

mn66:16.3.verse: Though his mindfulness may be slow in arising,

mn66:16.4.verse: still he soon abandons them, removes them, does away with and annihilates them.

mn66:16.5.verse: Just as if a man were to let two or three drops of water fall into an iron pan heated for a day,

mn66:16.6.verse: though the drops may be slow in falling, still they would soon be exhausted and disappear.

mn66:16.7.verse: So too, here some person practises the way to the abandoning of the essentials of existence, to the relinquishing of the essentials of existence.

mn66:16.8.verse: When that is so, memories and intentions associated with the essentials of existence beset him now and then owing to lapses of mindfulness.

mn66:16.9.verse: Though his mindfulness may be slow in arising,

mn66:16.10.verse: still he soon abandons them, removes them, does away with and annihilates them.

mn66:16.11.verse: Such a person I call “associated” not “dissociated”.

mn66:16.13.verse: Because I have known the particular diversity of faculties in this person.

mn66:17.1.verse: ‘Here some person, having known that the essentials of existence are the root of suffering,

mn66:17.2.verse: is divested of the essentials of existence and freed with the full exhaustion of the essentials of existence.

mn66:17.3.verse: Such a person I call “dissociated” not “associated”.

mn66:17.5.verse: Because I have known the particular diversity of faculties in this person.

mn66:17.6.verse: ‘These, Udāyin, are the four kinds of person to be found existing in the world.

mn66:18.1.verse: ‘There are these five cords of sensual desires.

mn66:18.3.verse: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn66:18.7.verse: Tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn66:18.8.verse: These are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn66:19.1.verse: ‘Now the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five cords of sensual desire are called pleasure in sensual desires, pleasure in filth, ordinary man’s pleasure, ignoble pleasure; it is not to be repeated or developed or made much of: one should be afraid of such pleasure, I say.

mn66:20.1.verse: ‘Here, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn66:20.2.verse: ‘With the stilling of initial and sustained application he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn66:20.3.verse: ‘With the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna on account of which the Noble Ones announce “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”

mn66:20.4.verse: ‘With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn66:21.1.verse: ‘This is called pleasure in renunciation, pleasure in seclusion, pleasure in stilling, pleasure in full enlightenment; it is to be repeated and developed and made much of: one should not be afraid of such pleasure, I say.

mn66:22.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna … with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn66:22.2.verse: ‘Now that, I say, belongs to perturbability.

mn66:22.4.verse: Whatever initial application and sustained application has not ceased there is the perturbability there.

mn66:23.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna … with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn66:23.2.verse: ‘Now that, I say, belongs to perturbability.

mn66:23.4.verse: Whatever happiness and pleasure has not ceased there is the perturbability there.

mn66:24.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the third jhāna … who has equanimity and is mindful.

mn66:24.2.verse: ‘Now that, I say, belongs to perturbability.

mn66:24.4.verse: Whatever pleasure of equanimity has not ceased there is the perturbability there.

mn66:25.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna … and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn66:26.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna … with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn66:26.2.verse: ‘That, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:27.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna … with happiness and pleasure born of concentration. That surmounts it.

mn66:27.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:28.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the third jhāna … who has equanimity and is mindful. That surmounts it.

mn66:28.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:29.1.verse: ‘Here … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna … and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. That surmounts it.

mn66:29.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:30.1.verse: ‘Here with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with not giving attention to perceptions of difference, (aware that) “space is infinite” a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of the infinity of space. That surmounts it.

mn66:30.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:31.1.verse: ‘Here by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of space, (aware that) “consciousness is infinite”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness. That surmounts it.

mn66:31.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:32.1.verse: ‘Here by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness, (aware that) “there is nothing”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness. That surmounts it.

mn66:32.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:33.1.verse: ‘Here by completely surmounting the base consisting of nothingness a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That surmounts it.

mn66:33.2.verse: ‘That too, I say, is not enough. Abandon it, I say; surmount it, I say.

mn66:34.1.verse: ‘Here by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. That surmounts it.

mn66:34.2.verse: ‘So I speak also of the abandoning of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn66:34.3.verse: Do you see, Udāyin, that fetter, small or great, of whose abandoning I do not speak?’

mn66:34.5.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn66:34.6.verse: The venerable Udāyin was satisfied, and he rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

mn66:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Aṅguttarāpans, near the town of theirs named Āpaṇa.

mn66:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms.
