mn66:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Āpaṇa. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to a certain forest grove for the day’s meditation.

mn66:2.3.verse: Having plunged deep into it, he sat at the root of a certain tree to meditate.

mn66:3.1.verse: Venerable Udāyī also robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms.

mn66:3.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Āpaṇa. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to that forest grove for the day’s meditation.

mn66:3.3.verse: Having plunged deep into it, he sat at the root of a certain tree to meditate.

mn66:3.4.verse: Then as Venerable Udāyī was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:

mn66:4.1.verse: “The Buddha has rid us of so many things that bring suffering and gifted us so many things that bring happiness!

mn66:4.2.verse: He has rid us of so many unskillful things and gifted us so many skillful things!”

mn66:5.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Udāyī came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

mn66:6.1.verse: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

mn66:6.2.verse: ‘The Buddha has rid us of so many things that bring suffering and gifted us so many things that bring happiness!

mn66:6.3.verse: He has rid us of so many unskillful things and gifted us so many skillful things!’

mn66:6.4.verse: For we used to eat at dusk, at daybreak, and at the wrong time of day.

mn66:6.5.verse: But then there came a time when the Buddha addressed the mendicants, saying,

mn66:6.6.verse: ‘Please, mendicants, give up that meal at the wrong time of day.’

mn66:6.7.verse: At that, sir, we became sad and upset,

mn66:6.8.verse: ‘But these faithful householders give us delicious fresh and cooked foods at the wrong time of day. And the Blessed One tells us to give it up! The Holy One tells us to let it go!’

mn66:6.9.verse: But when we considered our fondness and respect for the Buddha, and our sense of conscience and prudence, we gave up that meal at the wrong time of day.

mn66:6.10.verse: Then we ate at dusk and daybreak.

mn66:6.11.verse: But then there came a time when the Buddha addressed the mendicants, saying,

mn66:6.12.verse: ‘Please, mendicants, give up that meal at the wrong time of night.’

mn66:6.13.verse: At that, sir, we became sad and upset,

mn66:6.14.verse: ‘But that’s considered the more delicious of the two meals. And the Blessed One tells us to give it up! The Holy One tells us to let it go!’

mn66:6.15.verse: Once it so happened that a certain person got some soup during the day. He said,

mn66:6.16.verse: ‘Come, let’s set this aside; we’ll enjoy it together this evening.’

mn66:6.17.verse: Nearly all meals are prepared at night, only a few in the day.

mn66:6.18.verse: But when we considered our love and respect for the Buddha, and our sense of conscience and prudence, we gave up that meal at the wrong time of night.

mn66:6.19.verse: In the past, mendicants went wandering for alms in the dark of the night. They walked into a swamp, or fell into a sewer, or collided with a thorn bush, or collided with a sleeping cow, or encountered youths escaping a crime or on their way to commit one, or were invited by a lady to commit a lewd act.

mn66:6.20.verse: Once it so happened that I was wandering for alms in the dark of the night.

mn66:6.21.verse: A woman washing a pot saw me by a flash of lightning.

mn66:6.23.verse: ‘Woe is me! It’s a damn goblin!’

mn66:6.24.verse: When she said this, I said to her,

mn66:6.26.verse: I’m a mendicant waiting for alms.’

mn66:6.28.verse: Better to have your belly sliced open with a sharp meat cleaver than to wander for alms in the dark of night for the sake of your belly!’

mn66:6.30.verse: ‘The Buddha has rid us of so many things that bring suffering and gifted us so many things that bring happiness!

mn66:6.31.verse: He has rid us of so many unskillful things and gifted us so many skillful things!’”

mn66:7.1.verse: “This is exactly what happens when some futile people are told by me to give something up. They say,

mn66:7.2.verse: ‘What, such a trivial, trifling thing as this? This ascetic is much too strict!’

mn66:7.3.verse: They don’t give it up, and they nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:7.4.verse: and for the mendicants who want to train, that becomes a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke.

mn66:8.1.verse: Suppose a quail was tied with a vine, and was waiting there to be injured, caged, or killed.

mn66:8.2.verse: Would it be right to say that,

mn66:8.3.verse: for that quail, that vine is weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial?”

mn66:8.6.verse: For that quail, that vine is a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke.”

mn66:8.7.verse: “In the same way, when some futile people are told by me to give something up, they say,

mn66:8.8.verse: ‘What, such a trivial, trifling thing as this? This ascetic is much too strict!’

mn66:8.9.verse: They don’t give it up, and they nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:8.10.verse: and for the mendicants who want to train, that becomes a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke.

mn66:9.1.verse: But when some gentlemen are told by me to give something up, they say,

mn66:9.2.verse: ‘What, we just have to give up such a trivial, trifling thing as this, when the Blessed One tells us to give it up, the Holy One tells us to let it go?’

mn66:9.3.verse: They give it up, and they don’t nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:9.4.verse: and when the mendicants who want to train have given that up, they live relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, their hearts free as a wild deer.

mn66:9.5.verse: For them, that bond is weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial.

mn66:10.1.verse: Suppose there was a royal bull elephant with tusks like draft-poles, able to draw a heavy load, pedigree and battle-hardened. And it was bound with a strong harness. But just by twisting its body a little, it would break apart its bonds and go wherever it wants.

mn66:10.2.verse: Would it be right to say that,

mn66:10.3.verse: for that bull elephant, that strong harness is a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke?”

mn66:10.6.verse: For that bull elephant, that strong harness is weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial.”

mn66:10.7.verse: “In the same way, when some gentlemen are told by me to give something up, they say,

mn66:10.8.verse: ‘What, we just have to give up such a trivial, trifling thing as this, when the Blessed One tells us to give it up, the Holy One tells us to let it go?’

mn66:10.9.verse: They give it up, and they don’t nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:10.10.verse: and when the mendicants who want to train have given that up, they live relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, their hearts free as a wild deer.

mn66:10.11.verse: For them, that bond is weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial.

mn66:11.1.verse: Suppose there was a poor man, with few possessions and little wealth.

mn66:11.2.verse: He had a single broken-down hovel open to the crows, not the best sort; a single broken-down couch, not the best sort; a single pot for storing grain, not the best sort; and a single wifey, not the best sort.

mn66:11.3.verse: He’d see a mendicant sitting in meditation in the cool shade, their hands and feet well washed after eating a satisfying meal.

mn66:11.5.verse: ‘The ascetic life is so very pleasant! The ascetic life is so very healthy!

mn66:11.6.verse: If only I could shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn66:11.7.verse: But he’s not able to give up his broken-down hovel, his broken-down couch, his pot for storing grain, or his wifey—none of which are the best sort—in order to go forth.

mn66:11.8.verse: Would it be right to say that,

mn66:11.10.verse: those bonds are weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial?”

mn66:11.14.verse: they are a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke.”

mn66:11.15.verse: “In the same way, when some futile people are told by me to give something up, they say,

mn66:11.16.verse: ‘What, such a trivial, trifling thing as this? This ascetic is much too strict!’

mn66:11.17.verse: They don’t give it up, and they nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:11.18.verse: and for the mendicants who want to train, that becomes a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke.

mn66:12.1.verse: Suppose there was a rich householder or householder’s child, affluent, and wealthy. He had a vast amount of gold ingots, grain, fields, lands, wives, and male and female bondservants.

mn66:12.2.verse: He’d see a mendicant sitting in meditation in the cool shade, their hands and feet well washed after eating a satisfying meal.

mn66:12.4.verse: ‘The ascetic life is so very pleasant! The ascetic life is so very healthy!

mn66:12.5.verse: If only I could shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn66:12.6.verse: And he is able to give up his vast amount of gold ingots, grain, fields, lands, wives, and male and female bondservants in order to go forth.

mn66:12.7.verse: Would it be right to say that,

mn66:12.8.verse: for that householder, they are a strong, firm, stout bond, a tie that has not rotted, and a heavy yoke?”

mn66:12.12.verse: those bonds are weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial.”

mn66:12.13.verse: “In the same way, when some gentlemen are told by me to give something up, they say,

mn66:12.14.verse: ‘What, we just have to give up such a trivial, trifling thing as this, when the Blessed One tells us to give it up, the Holy One tells us to let it go?’

mn66:12.15.verse: They give it up, and they don’t nurse bitterness toward me;

mn66:12.16.verse: and when the mendicants who want to train have given that up, they live relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, their hearts free as a wild deer.

mn66:12.17.verse: For them, that bond is weak, feeble, rotten, and insubstantial.

mn66:13.1.verse: Udāyī, these four individuals are found in the world.

mn66:14.1.verse: Take a certain individual practicing to give up and let go of attachments.

mn66:14.2.verse: As they do so, memories and thoughts connected with attachments beset them.

mn66:14.3.verse: They tolerate them and don’t give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

mn66:14.6.verse: Because I understand the disparity of faculties as it applies to this individual.

mn66:15.1.verse: Take another individual practicing to give up and let go of attachments.

mn66:15.2.verse: As they do so, memories and thoughts connected with attachments beset them.

mn66:15.3.verse: They don’t tolerate them, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

mn66:15.4.verse: I also call this individual ‘fettered’, not ‘detached’.

mn66:15.6.verse: Because I understand the disparity of faculties as it applies to this individual.

mn66:16.1.verse: Take another individual practicing to give up and let go of attachments.

mn66:16.2.verse: As they do so, memories and thoughts connected with attachments beset them every so often, due to the loss of mindfulness.

mn66:16.4.verse: then they quickly give up, dispel, eliminate, and obliterate those thoughts.

mn66:16.5.verse: Suppose there was an iron cauldron that had been heated all day, and a person let two or three drops of water fall onto it.

mn66:16.6.verse: Slowly the drops fall, but then they quickly dry up and evaporate.

mn66:16.7.verse: In the same way, take an individual practicing to give up and let go of attachments.

mn66:16.8.verse: As they do so, memories and thoughts connected with attachments beset them every so often, due to the loss of mindfulness.

mn66:16.10.verse: but then they quickly give up, dispel, eliminate, and obliterate those thoughts.

mn66:16.11.verse: I also call this individual ‘fettered’, not ‘detached’.

mn66:16.13.verse: Because I understand the disparity of faculties as it applies to this individual.

mn66:17.1.verse: Take another individual who, understanding that attachment is the root of suffering,

mn66:17.2.verse: is freed with the ending of attachments.

mn66:17.5.verse: Because I understand the disparity of faculties as it applies to this individual.

mn66:17.6.verse: These are the four individuals found in the world.

mn66:18.1.verse: Udāyī, these are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn66:18.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn66:18.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn66:18.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn66:19.1.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called sensual pleasure—a filthy, ordinary, ignoble pleasure. Such pleasure should not be cultivated or developed, but should be feared, I say.

mn66:20.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption …

mn66:21.1.verse: This is called the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening. Such pleasure should be cultivated and developed, and should not be feared, I say.

mn66:22.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption.

mn66:22.2.verse: This belongs to the perturbable, I say.

mn66:22.3.verse: And what there belongs to the perturbable?

mn66:22.4.verse: Whatever placing of the mind and keeping it connected has not ceased there is what belongs to the perturbable.

mn66:23.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, enters and remains in the second absorption.

mn66:23.2.verse: This belongs to the perturbable, I say.

mn66:23.3.verse: And what there belongs to the perturbable?

mn66:23.4.verse: Whatever rapture and bliss has not ceased there is what belongs to the perturbable.

mn66:24.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, with the fading away of rapture, enters and remains in the third absorption.

mn66:24.3.verse: And what there belongs to the perturbable?

mn66:24.4.verse: Whatever bliss with equanimity has not ceased there is what belongs to the perturbable.

mn66:25.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, giving up pleasure and pain, enters and remains in the fourth absorption.

mn66:25.2.verse: This belongs to the imperturbable, I say.

mn66:26.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption.

mn66:26.2.verse: But this is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:27.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, enters and remains in the second absorption. That goes beyond it.

mn66:27.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:28.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, with the fading away of rapture, enters and remains in the third absorption. That goes beyond it.

mn66:28.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:29.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, giving up pleasure and pain, enters and remains in the fourth absorption. That goes beyond it.

mn66:29.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:30.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. That goes beyond it.

mn66:30.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:31.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. That goes beyond it.

mn66:31.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:32.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. That goes beyond it.

mn66:32.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:33.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. That goes beyond it.

mn66:33.2.verse: But this too is not enough, I say: give it up, go beyond it.

mn66:34.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. That goes beyond it.

mn66:34.2.verse: So, Udāyī, I even recommend giving up the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn66:34.3.verse: Do you see any fetter, large or small, that I don’t recommend giving up?”

mn66:34.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn66:34.6.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Udāyī approved what the Buddha said.

mn67:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Cātumā in an embric myrobalan forest.

mn67:2.1.verse: And on that occasion approximately 500 monks, headed by Ven. Sāriputta & Ven. Moggallāna, had arrived in Cātumā to see the Blessed One.

mn67:2.2.verse: As these visiting monks were exchanging greetings with the resident monks, setting their lodgings in order, and putting away their robes & bowls, they made a loud racket, a great racket.

mn67:3.1.verse: Then the Blessed One said to Ven. Ānanda,

mn67:3.2.verse: “Ānanda, what is that loud racket, that great racket, like fishermen hauling a catch of fish?”

mn67:3.3.verse: “Lord, those are approximately 500 monks, headed by Sāriputta & Moggallāna, who have arrived in Cātumā to see the Blessed One.

mn67:3.4.verse: As these visiting monks are exchanging greetings with the resident monks, setting their lodgings in order, and putting away their robes & bowls, they are making a loud racket, a great racket.”

mn67:4.1.verse: “In that case, Ānanda, tell those monks in my name,

mn67:4.3.verse: Responding, “As you say, lord,” to the Blessed One, Ven. Ānanda went to the monks and said,

mn67:4.5.verse: Responding, “As you say, friend,” to Ven. Ānanda, the monks went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them,

mn67:4.6.verse: “Monks, why were you making that loud racket, that great racket, like fishermen hauling a catch of fish?”

mn67:4.7.verse: “Lord, these 500 monks, headed by Sāriputta & Moggallāna, have arrived in Cātumā to see the Blessed One.

mn67:4.8.verse: As they were exchanging greetings with the resident monks, setting their lodgings in order, and putting away their robes & bowls, they made a loud racket, a great racket.”

mn67:5.1.verse: “Go away, monks. I dismiss you. You are not to stay in my vicinity.”

mn67:5.2.verse: Responding, “As you say, lord,” to the Blessed One, the monks got up from their seats, bowed down to the Blessed One, and left, circling him to the right. Setting their lodgings in order and taking their robes & bowls, they left.

mn67:6.1.verse: Now, on that occasion the Cātumā Sakyans were gathered in the assembly hall on some business or other.

mn67:6.2.verse: They saw the monks coming from afar and,

mn67:6.3.verse: on seeing them, went to them and, on arrival, said to them,

mn67:6.4.verse: “Well now, where are you venerable ones going?”

mn67:6.5.verse: “Friends, the community of monks has been dismissed by the Blessed One.”

mn67:6.6.verse: “In that case, venerable ones, sit down for a moment. Perhaps we will be able to reconcile the Blessed One.”

mn67:6.7.verse: “As you say, friends,” the monks responded to the Cātumā Sakyans.

mn67:7.1.verse: Then the Cātumā Sakyans went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to the Blessed One,

mn67:7.2.verse: “May the Blessed One delight in the community of monks!

mn67:7.3.verse: May the Blessed One welcome the community of monks!

mn67:7.4.verse: May the Blessed One aid the community of monks, just as the community of monks was aided by the Blessed One in the past!

mn67:7.5.verse: Lord, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya.

mn67:7.6.verse: If they don’t get to see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.

mn67:7.7.verse: “Just as when young seedlings don’t get water, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration;

mn67:7.8.verse: in the same way, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya. If they don’t get to see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.

mn67:7.9.verse: “Just as when a young calf doesn’t see its mother, there may be a change in it, there may be an alteration;

mn67:7.10.verse: in the same way, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya. If they don’t see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.”

mn67:7.11.verse: May the Blessed One delight in the community of monks;

mn67:7.12.verse: may the Blessed One welcome the community of monks.

mn67:7.13.verse: Just as the community of monks was aided by the Blessed One in the past, may the Blessed One aid the community of monks now as well.”

mn67:8.1.verse: Then Brahmā Sahampati, having known with his own awareness the line of thinking in the Blessed One’s awareness, disappeared from the Brahmā world and—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—appeared in front of the Blessed One.

mn67:8.2.verse: Then, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder and placing his hands palm-to-palm in front of his heart, Brahmā Sahampati said to the Blessed One,

mn67:9.1.verse: “May the Blessed One delight in the community of monks!

mn67:9.2.verse: May the Blessed One welcome the community of monks!

mn67:9.3.verse: May the Blessed One aid the community of monks, just as the community of monks was aided by the Blessed One in the past!

mn67:9.4.verse: Lord, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya. If they don’t get to see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.

mn67:9.5.verse: “Just as when young seedlings don’t get water, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration;

mn67:9.6.verse: in the same way, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya. If they don’t get to see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.

mn67:9.7.verse: “Just as when a young calf doesn’t see its mother, there may be a change in it, there may be an alteration;

mn67:9.8.verse: in the same way, there are new monks here, not long gone forth, recently arrived at this Dhamma & Vinaya. If they don’t see the Blessed One, there may be a change in them, there may be an alteration.”

mn67:9.9.verse: May the Blessed One delight in the community of monks;

mn67:9.10.verse: may the Blessed One welcome the community of monks.

mn67:9.11.verse: Just as the community of monks was aided by the Blessed One in the past, may the Blessed One aid the community of monks now as well.”

mn67:10.1.verse: And so the Cātumā Sakyans & Brahmā Sahampati were able to reconcile the Blessed One by means of the simile of the seedlings & the simile of the young calf.

mn67:11.1.verse: Then Ven. Moggallāna said to the monks,

mn67:11.2.verse: “Get up, friends! Get your robes & bowls.

mn67:11.3.verse: The Blessed One has been reconciled by the Cātumā Sakyans & Brahmā Sahampati by means of the simile of the seedlings & the simile of the young calf.”

mn67:12.1.verse: Responding, “As you say, friend,” to Ven. Moggallāna, the monks got up from their seats and, carrying their robes & bowls, went to the Blessed One. On arrival, having bowed down to him, they sat to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to Ven. Sāriputta,

mn67:12.2.verse: “What did you think, Sāriputta, when the community of monks was dismissed by me?”

mn67:12.4.verse: ‘Now that the community of monks has been dismissed by the Blessed One, the Blessed One will remain inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding in the here-&-now.

mn67:12.5.verse: I, too, will now remain inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding in the here-&-now.”

mn67:12.6.verse: “Wait, Sāriputta! Wait! Such a thought should not occur to you again!”

mn67:13.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed Ven. Moggallāna,

mn67:13.2.verse: “What did you think, Moggallāna, when the community of monks was dismissed by me?”

mn67:13.4.verse: ‘Now that the community of monks has been dismissed by the Blessed One, the Blessed One will remain inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding in the here-&-now.

mn67:13.5.verse: And now Sāriputta & I will look after the community of monks.”

mn67:13.7.verse: For either I should look after the community of monks or Sāriputta & Moggallāna should.”

mn67:14.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks,

mn67:14.2.verse: “Monks, there are these four dangers to be expected by those who go down into the water.

mn67:14.4.verse: Danger from waves, danger from crocodiles, danger from whirlpools, & danger from sharks—

mn67:14.5.verse: these are the four dangers to be expected by those who go down into the water.

mn67:15.1.verse: “In same way, there are these four dangers to be expected by certain individuals who have gone forth from home life into homelessness in this Dhamma & Vinaya.

mn67:15.3.verse: Danger from waves, danger from crocodiles, danger from whirlpools, & danger from sharks.

mn67:16.1.verse: “And which is the danger from waves?

mn67:16.2.verse: There is the case where a son of a good family, out of conviction, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn67:16.3.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn67:16.4.verse: O, that the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!’

mn67:16.5.verse: After he has thus gone forth, his fellows in the holy life admonish & instruct him:

mn67:16.6.verse: ‘This is how you should go forward. This is how you should go back. This is how you should look ahead. This is how you should look away. This is how you should flex & extend your limbs. This is how you should wear & carry your patchwork robe, your upper robe, & your bowl.’

mn67:16.8.verse: ‘Before, when we were a householder, we admonished & instructed others.

mn67:16.9.verse: But now these—who are no more than our sons & grandsons, as it were—suppose that we are to be admonished & instructed!’

mn67:16.10.verse: He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

mn67:16.11.verse: This, monks, is called one who has disavowed the training frightened by the danger from waves—

mn67:16.12.verse: for ‘danger from waves’ is a synonym for anger & distress.

mn67:17.1.verse: “And which is the danger from crocodiles?

mn67:17.2.verse: There is the case where a son of a good family, out of conviction, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn67:17.3.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn67:17.4.verse: O, that the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!’

mn67:17.5.verse: After he has thus gone forth, his fellows in the holy life admonish & instruct him:

mn67:17.6.verse: ‘This you should eat; this you shouldn’t eat. This you should consume; this you shouldn’t consume. This you should savor; this you shouldn’t savor. This you should drink; this you shouldn’t drink. You should eat what is allowable; you shouldn’t eat what is not allowable. You should consume what is allowable; you shouldn’t consume what is not allowable. You should savor what is allowable; you shouldn’t savor what is not allowable. You should drink what is allowable; you shouldn’t drink what is not allowable. You should eat at the right time; you shouldn’t eat at the wrong time. You should consume at the right time; you shouldn’t consume at the wrong time. You should savor at the right time; you shouldn’t savor at the wrong time. You should drink at the right time; you shouldn’t drink at the wrong time.’

mn67:17.7.verse: The thought occurs to him, ‘Before, when we were a householder, we ate what we wanted and didn’t eat what we didn’t want. We consumed what we wanted and didn’t consume what we didn’t want. We savored what we wanted and didn’t savor what we didn’t want. We drank what we wanted and didn’t drink what we didn’t want.

mn67:17.8.verse: We ate what was allowable and we ate what wasn’t allowable. We consumed what was allowable and we consumed what wasn’t allowable. We savored what was allowable and we savored what wasn’t allowable. We drank what was allowable and we drank what wasn’t allowable. We ate at the right time and we ate at the wrong time. We consumed at the right time and we consumed at the wrong time. We savored at the right time and we savored at the wrong time. We drank at the right time and we drank at the wrong time.

mn67:17.9.verse: When householders, out of conviction, give us exquisite staple & non-staple foods at the wrong time of the day, these ones put a muzzle on our mouth, as it were.’

mn67:17.10.verse: He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

mn67:17.11.verse: This, monks, is called one who has disavowed the training frightened by the danger from crocodiles—

mn67:17.12.verse: for ‘danger from crocodiles’ is a synonym for gluttony.

mn67:18.1.verse: “And which is the danger from whirlpools?

mn67:18.2.verse: There is the case where a son of a good family, out of conviction, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn67:18.3.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn67:18.4.verse: O, that the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!’

mn67:18.5.verse: Early in the morning, having adjusted his under robe and carrying his bowl & robes, he goes into a village or town for alms, with his body unguarded, his speech unguarded, his mindfulness unestablished, his faculties unrestrained.

mn67:18.6.verse: He sees a householder or householder’s son going about, endowed & provided with the five strings of sensuality.

mn67:18.8.verse: ‘Before, when we were a householder, we too went about, endowed & provided with the five strings of sensuality.

mn67:18.9.verse: Now, our family has enough wealth

mn67:18.10.verse: that it would be possible to enjoy wealth & make merit.’

mn67:18.11.verse: He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

mn67:18.12.verse: This, monks, is called one who has disavowed the training frightened by the danger from whirlpools—

mn67:18.13.verse: for ‘danger from whirlpools’ is a synonym for the five strings of sensuality.

mn67:19.1.verse: “And which is the danger from sharks?

mn67:19.2.verse: There is the case where a son of a good family, out of conviction, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, (thinking,)

mn67:19.3.verse: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, & death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, & despairs; beset by stress, overcome with stress.

mn67:19.4.verse: O, that the end of this entire mass of suffering & stress might be known!’

mn67:19.5.verse: Early in the morning, having adjusted his under robe and carrying his bowl & robes, he goes into a village or town for alms, with his body unguarded, his speech unguarded, his mindfulness unestablished, his faculties unrestrained.

mn67:19.6.verse: He sees a woman scantily clothed, scantily dressed.

mn67:19.7.verse: On seeing a woman scantily clothed, scantily dressed, lust agitates his mind.

mn67:19.8.verse: With his mind agitated by lust, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

mn67:19.9.verse: This, monks, is called one who has disavowed the training frightened by the danger from sharks—

mn67:19.10.verse: for ‘danger from sharks’ is a synonym for a woman.

mn67:20.1.verse: “These, monks, are the four dangers to be expected by certain individuals who have gone forth from home life into homelessness in this Dhamma & Vinaya.”

mn67:20.2.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn67:20.3.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn67:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Cātumā in a myrobalan grove.

mn67:2.1.verse: Now at that time five hundred mendicants headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna arrived at Cātumā to see the Buddha.

mn67:2.2.verse: And the visiting mendicants, while exchanging pleasantries with the resident mendicants, preparing their lodgings, and putting away their bowls and robes, made a colossal racket.

mn67:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

mn67:3.2.verse: “Ānanda, who’s making that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

mn67:3.3.verse: And Ānanda told him what had happened.

mn67:4.1.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, in my name tell those mendicants that

mn67:4.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” Ānanda replied. He went to those mendicants and said,

mn67:4.5.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants. Then they rose from their seats and went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

mn67:4.6.verse: “Mendicants, what’s with that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

mn67:4.7.verse: And they told him what had happened.

mn67:5.1.verse: “Go away, mendicants, I dismiss you. You are not to stay in my presence.”

mn67:5.2.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied those mendicants. They got up from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. They set their lodgings in order and left, taking their bowls and robes.

mn67:6.1.verse: Now at that time the Sakyans of Cātumā were sitting together at the town hall on some business.

mn67:6.2.verse: Seeing those mendicants coming off in the distance,

mn67:6.3.verse: they went up to them and said,

mn67:6.5.verse: “Reverends, the mendicant Saṅgha has been dismissed by the Buddha.”

mn67:6.6.verse: “Well then, venerables, sit here for an hour. Hopefully we’ll be able to restore the Buddha’s confidence.”

mn67:7.1.verse: Then the Sakyans of Cātumā went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

mn67:7.2.verse: “May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:7.3.verse: May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:7.4.verse: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!

mn67:7.5.verse: There are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training.

mn67:7.6.verse: If they don’t get to see the Buddha they may change and fall apart.

mn67:7.7.verse: If young seedlings don’t get water they may change and fall apart.

mn67:7.8.verse: In the same way, there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. If they don’t get to see the Buddha they may change and fall apart.

mn67:7.9.verse: If a young calf doesn’t see its mother it may change and fall apart.

mn67:7.10.verse: In the same way, there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. If they don’t get to see the Buddha they may change and fall apart.

mn67:7.11.verse: May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:7.12.verse: May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:7.13.verse: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!”

mn67:8.1.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati knew the Buddha’s train of thought. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha.

mn67:8.2.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:

mn67:9.1.verse: “May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:9.2.verse: May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:9.3.verse: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!

mn67:9.4.verse: There are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. If they don’t get to see the Buddha they may change and fall apart.

mn67:9.5.verse: If young seedlings don’t get water they may change and fall apart. …

mn67:9.7.verse: If a young calf doesn’t see its mother it may change and fall apart.

mn67:9.8.verse: In the same way, there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. If they don’t get to see the Buddha they may change and fall apart.

mn67:9.9.verse: May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:9.10.verse: May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

mn67:9.11.verse: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!”

mn67:10.1.verse: The Sakyans of Cātumā and the divinity Sahampati were able to restore the Buddha’s confidence with the similes of the seedlings and the calf.

mn67:11.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the mendicants,

mn67:11.2.verse: “Get up, reverends, and pick up your bowls and robes.

mn67:11.3.verse: The Buddha’s confidence has been restored by the Sakyans of Cātumā and the divinity Sahampati with the similes of the seedlings and the calf.”

mn67:12.1.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants. Then they rose from their seats and, taking their bowls and robes, went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to Venerable Sāriputta,

mn67:12.2.verse: “Sāriputta, what did you think when the mendicant Saṅgha was dismissed by me?”

mn67:12.4.verse: ‘The Buddha has dismissed the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn67:12.5.verse: Now he will remain passive, dwelling in blissful meditation in this life, and so will we.’”

mn67:12.6.verse: “Hold on, Sāriputta, hold on! Don’t you ever think such a thing again!”

mn67:13.1.verse: Then the Buddha addressed Venerable Mahāmoggallāna,

mn67:13.2.verse: “Moggallāna, what did you think when the mendicant Saṅgha was dismissed by me?”

mn67:13.4.verse: ‘The Buddha has dismissed the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn67:13.5.verse: Now he will remain passive, dwelling in blissful meditation in this life. Meanwhile, Venerable Sāriputta and I shall lead the mendicant Saṅgha.’”

mn67:13.7.verse: For either I should lead the mendicant Saṅgha, or else Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

mn67:14.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

mn67:14.2.verse: “Mendicants, when you go into the water you should anticipate four dangers.

mn67:14.4.verse: The dangers of waves, gharials, whirlpools, and sharks.

mn67:14.5.verse: These are the four dangers that you should anticipate when you go into the water.

mn67:15.1.verse: In the same way, an individual gone forth from the lay life to homelessness in this teaching and training should anticipate four dangers.

mn67:15.3.verse: The dangers of waves, gharials, whirlpools, and sharks.

mn67:16.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the danger of waves?

mn67:16.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn67:16.3.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn67:16.4.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn67:16.5.verse: When they’ve gone forth, their spiritual companions advise and instruct them:

mn67:16.6.verse: ‘You should go out like this, and come back like that. You should look to the front like this, and to the side like that. You should contract your limbs like this, and extend them like that. This is how you should bear your outer robe, bowl, and robes.’

mn67:16.8.verse: ‘Formerly, as laypeople, we advised and instructed others.

mn67:16.9.verse: And now these mendicants—who you’d think were our children or grandchildren—imagine they can advise and instruct us!’

mn67:16.10.verse: They resign the training and return to a lesser life.

mn67:16.11.verse: This is called a mendicant who resigns the training and returns to a lesser life for fear of the danger of waves.

mn67:16.12.verse: ‘Danger of waves’ is a term for anger and distress.

mn67:17.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the danger of gharials?

mn67:17.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn67:17.3.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn67:17.4.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn67:17.5.verse: When they’ve gone forth, their spiritual companions advise and instruct them:

mn67:17.6.verse: ‘You may eat, consume, taste, and drink these things, but not those. You may eat what’s allowable, but not what’s unallowable. You may eat at the right time, but not at the wrong time.’

mn67:17.7.verse: They think: ‘Formerly, as laypeople, we used to eat, consume, taste, and drink what we wanted, not what we didn’t want.

mn67:17.8.verse: We ate and drank both allowable and unallowable things, at the right time and the wrong time.

mn67:17.9.verse: And these faithful householders give us delicious fresh and cooked foods at the wrong time of day. But these guys imagine they can gag our mouths!’

mn67:17.10.verse: They resign the training and return to a lesser life.

mn67:17.11.verse: This is called one who resigns the training and returns to a lesser life because they’re afraid of the danger of gharials.

mn67:17.12.verse: ‘Danger of gharials’ is a term for gluttony.

mn67:18.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the danger of whirlpools?

mn67:18.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn67:18.3.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn67:18.4.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn67:18.5.verse: When they’ve gone forth, they robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter a village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

mn67:18.6.verse: There they see a householder or their child amusing themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn67:18.8.verse: ‘Formerly, as laypeople, we amused ourselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn67:18.9.verse: And it’s true that my family is wealthy.

mn67:18.10.verse: I can both enjoy my wealth and make merit.’

mn67:18.11.verse: They resign the training and return to a lesser life.

mn67:18.12.verse: This is called one who resigns the training and returns to a lesser life for fear of the danger of whirlpools.

mn67:18.13.verse: ‘Danger of whirlpools’ is a term for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn67:19.1.verse: And what, mendicants, is the danger of sharks?

mn67:19.2.verse: It’s when a gentleman has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, thinking:

mn67:19.3.verse: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn67:19.4.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

mn67:19.5.verse: When they’ve gone forth, they robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter a village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

mn67:19.6.verse: There they see a lady scantily clad, with revealing clothes.

mn67:19.8.verse: so they resign the training and return to a lesser life.

mn67:19.9.verse: This is called one who resigns the training and returns to a lesser life for fear of the danger of sharks.

mn67:19.10.verse: ‘Danger of sharks’ is a term for ladies.

mn67:20.1.verse: These are the four dangers that an individual who gone forth from the lay life to homelessness in this teaching and training should anticipate.”

mn67:20.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn67:20.3.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn68:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kosalans near Naḷakapāna in the grove of flame-of-the-forest trees.

mn68:2.1.verse: Now at that time several very well-known gentlemen had gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness in the Buddha’s name—

mn68:2.2.verse: The venerables Anuruddha, Bhaddiya, Kimbila, Bhagu, Kuṇḍadhāna, Revata, Ānanda, and other very well-known gentlemen.

mn68:3.1.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was sitting in the open, surrounded by the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn68:3.2.verse: Then the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about those gentlemen:

mn68:3.3.verse: “Mendicants, those gentlemen who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness in my name—I trust they’re satisfied with the spiritual life?”

mn68:3.4.verse: When this was said, the mendicants kept silent.

mn68:3.5.verse: For a second and a third time the Buddha asked the same question.

mn68:3.10.verse: For a third time, the mendicants kept silent.

mn68:4.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

mn68:4.2.verse: “Why don’t I question just those gentlemen?”

mn68:4.3.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Anuruddha,

mn68:4.4.verse: “Anuruddha and friends, I hope you’re satisfied with the spiritual life?”

mn68:4.5.verse: “Indeed, sir, we are satisfied with the spiritual life.”

mn68:5.2.verse: It’s appropriate for gentlemen like yourselves, who have gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, to be satisfied with the spiritual life.

mn68:5.3.verse: Since you’re blessed with youth, in the prime of life, with pristine black hair, you could have enjoyed sensual pleasures; yet you have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn68:5.4.verse: But you didn’t go forth to escape a summons by a king or a summons for a bandit, or because you were in debt or in fear, or in order to make a living.

mn68:5.5.verse: Rather, didn’t you go forth thinking: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

mn68:5.6.verse: Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering’?”

mn68:6.1.verse: “But, Anuruddha and friends, when a gentleman has gone forth like this, what should he do?

mn68:6.2.verse: Take someone who doesn’t achieve the rapture and bliss that are secluded from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that. Their mind is still occupied by desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, doubt, discontent, and sloth.

mn68:6.3.verse: That’s someone who doesn’t achieve the rapture and bliss that are secluded from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that.

mn68:6.4.verse: Take someone who does achieve the rapture and bliss that are secluded from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that. Their mind is not occupied by desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, doubt, discontent, and sloth.

mn68:6.5.verse: That’s someone who does achieve the rapture and bliss that are secluded from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities, or something even more peaceful than that.

mn68:7.1.verse: Is this what you think of me?

mn68:7.2.verse: ‘The Realized One has not given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn68:7.3.verse: That’s why, after appraisal, he uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.’”

mn68:7.4.verse: “No sir, we don’t think of you that way.

mn68:7.7.verse: We think of you this way:

mn68:7.8.verse: ‘The Realized One has given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn68:7.9.verse: That’s why, after appraisal, he uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.’”

mn68:7.11.verse: The Realized One has given up the defilements that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death. He has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn68:7.12.verse: Just as a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of further growth,

mn68:7.13.verse: in the same way, the Realized One has given up the defilements so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn68:7.14.verse: That’s why, after appraisal, he uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things.

mn68:8.1.verse: What do you think, Anuruddha and friends?

mn68:8.2.verse: What advantage does the Realized One see in declaring the rebirth of his disciples who have passed away:

mn68:8.3.verse: ‘This one is reborn here, while that one is reborn there’?”

mn68:8.4.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn68:9.1.verse: “The Realized One does not declare such things for the sake of fawning or flattering people, nor for the benefit of possessions, honor, or popularity, nor thinking, ‘So let people know about me!’

mn68:9.3.verse: Rather, there are gentlemen of faith who are full of sublime joy and gladness.

mn68:9.4.verse: When they hear that, they apply their minds to that end.

mn68:9.5.verse: That is for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn68:10.1.verse: Take a monk who hears this:

mn68:10.2.verse: ‘The monk named so-and-so has passed away.

mn68:10.5.verse: And he’s either seen for himself, or heard from someone else, that that venerable

mn68:10.6.verse: had such ethics, such qualities, such wisdom, such meditation, or such freedom.

mn68:10.7.verse: Recollecting that monk’s faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom, he applies his mind to that end.

mn68:10.8.verse: That’s how a monk lives at ease.

mn68:11.2.verse: ‘The monk named so-and-so has passed away.

mn68:11.4.verse: with the ending of the five lower fetters, he’s been reborn spontaneously and will become extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.’

mn68:24.3.verse: Rather, there are gentlemen of faith who are full of joy and gladness.

mn68:24.4.verse: When they hear that, they apply their minds to that end.

mn68:24.5.verse: That is for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn68:24.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn69:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Forest, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn69:2.1.verse: And on that occasion a monk named Golissāni, a wilderness-dweller of crude behavior, had entered into the midst of the Saṅgha on some business or other.

mn69:2.2.verse: Then Ven. Sāriputta, with reference to the monk named Golissāni, addressed the monks:

mn69:3.1.verse: “Friends, when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, it should be with respect and with deference toward his fellows in the holy life.

mn69:3.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, is not respectful or deferential toward his fellows in the holy life, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:3.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is not respectful or deferential toward his fellows in the holy life?’

mn69:3.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:3.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, it should be with respect and with deference toward his fellows in the holy life.

mn69:4.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should be skilled with regard to seats, (thinking,)

mn69:4.2.verse: ‘I will sit without encroaching on the elder monks, and not preempting the new monks from a seat.’

mn69:4.3.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, is not skilled with regard to seats, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:4.4.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he doesn’t know even a point of good conduct?’

mn69:4.5.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:4.6.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should be skilled with regard to seats.

mn69:4.7.verse: When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should know even the rules of etiquette.

mn69:4.8.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, doesn’t know even the rules of etiquette, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:4.9.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he doesn’t know even the rules of etiquette?’

mn69:4.10.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:4.11.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should know even the rules of etiquette.

mn69:5.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not enter the village too early or return too late in the day.

mn69:5.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, enters the village too early and returns too late in the day, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:5.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he enters the village too early and returns too late in the day?’

mn69:5.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:5.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not enter the village too early or return too late in the day.

mn69:6.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not go calling on families before or after the meal.

mn69:6.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, goes calling on families before or after the meal, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:6.3.verse: ‘Surely this venerable wilderness-dweller, alone in the wilderness, living independently, spends his time making untimely visits, given that he behaves this way even when he has come into the Saṅgha.’

mn69:6.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:6.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not go calling on families before or after the meal.

mn69:7.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not be high-strung & unruly.

mn69:7.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, is high-strung & unruly, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:7.3.verse: ‘Surely this venerable wilderness-dweller, alone in the wilderness, living independently, spends his time being high-strung & unruly, given that he behaves this way even in the Saṅgha.’

mn69:7.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:7.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not be high-strung & unruly.

mn69:8.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not be talkative & loose in his words.

mn69:8.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, is talkative & loose in his words, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:8.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is talkative & loose in his words?’

mn69:8.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:8.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should not be talkative & loose in his words.

mn69:9.1.verse: “When a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should be easy to instruct & have admirable friends.

mn69:9.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk, coming into the Saṅgha and living in the Saṅgha, is hard to instruct & has evil friends, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:9.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is hard to instruct & has evil friends?’

mn69:9.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:9.5.verse: when a wilderness-dwelling monk has come into the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, he should be easy to instruct & have admirable friends.

mn69:10.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should guard the doors of his senses.

mn69:10.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk does not guard the doors of his senses, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:10.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he doesn’t guard the doors to his senses?’

mn69:10.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:10.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should guard the doors of his senses.

mn69:11.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should know moderation in eating.

mn69:11.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk doesn’t know moderation in eating, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:11.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he doesn’t know moderation in eating?’

mn69:11.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:11.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should know moderation in eating.

mn69:12.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should be devoted to wakefulness.

mn69:12.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk is not devoted to wakefulness, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:12.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he isn’t devoted to wakefulness?’

mn69:12.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:12.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should be devoted to wakefulness.

mn69:13.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with aroused persistence.

mn69:13.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk is lazy, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:13.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is lazy?’

mn69:13.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:13.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with aroused persistence.

mn69:14.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with established mindfulness.

mn69:14.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk is confused in his mindfulness, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:14.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is confused in his mindfulness?’

mn69:14.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:14.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with established mindfulness.

mn69:15.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with concentration.

mn69:15.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk is without concentration, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:15.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is without concentration?’

mn69:15.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:15.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with concentration.

mn69:16.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with discernment.

mn69:16.2.verse: If a wilderness-dwelling monk is of dull discernment, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:16.3.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, when he is of dull discernment?’

mn69:16.4.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:16.5.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should be one with discernment.

mn69:17.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to the higher Dhamma & higher Vinaya.

mn69:17.2.verse: There are those who will ask the wilderness-dwelling monk a question about the higher Dhamma & higher Vinaya.

mn69:17.3.verse: If he, when asked a question about the higher Dhamma & higher Vinaya, isn’t able to answer, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:17.4.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, if he, when asked a question about the higher Dhamma & higher Vinaya, isn’t able to answer?’

mn69:17.5.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:17.6.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to the higher Dhamma & higher Vinaya.

mn69:18.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to the peaceful emancipations, formlessnesses beyond forms.

mn69:18.2.verse: There are those who will ask the wilderness-dwelling monk a question about the peaceful emancipations, formlessnesses beyond forms.

mn69:18.3.verse: If he, when asked a question about the peaceful emancipations, formlessnesses beyond forms, isn’t able to answer, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:18.4.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, if he, when asked a question about the peaceful emancipations, formlessnesses beyond forms, isn’t able to answer?’

mn69:18.5.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:18.6.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to the peaceful emancipations, formlessnesses beyond forms.

mn69:19.1.verse: “A wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to a superior human attainment.

mn69:19.2.verse: There are those who will ask the wilderness-dwelling monk a question about a superior human attainment.

mn69:19.3.verse: If he, when asked a question about a superior human attainment, isn’t able to answer, there are those who would say of him,

mn69:19.4.verse: ‘What good has it done for this venerable wilderness-dweller to be alone in the wilderness, living independently, if he, when asked a question about a superior human attainment, isn’t able to answer?’

mn69:19.5.verse: Because there are those who would say that of him,

mn69:19.6.verse: a wilderness-dwelling monk should apply himself to a superior human attainment.”

mn69:19.7.verse: When this was said, Ven. Mahā Moggallāna said to Ven. Sāriputta,

mn69:19.8.verse: “Sāriputta my friend, are these qualities to be undertaken & practiced only by a wilderness-dwelling monk, or also by a village-dwelling monk?”

mn69:19.9.verse: “Moggallāna my friend, these qualities are to be undertaken & practiced by a wilderness-dwelling monk, and even more so by a village-dwelling monk.”

mn69:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn69:2.1.verse: Now at that time a wilderness mendicant of boorish behavior named Gulissāni had come down to the midst of the Saṅgha on some business.

mn69:2.2.verse: There Venerable Sāriputta spoke to the mendicants about Gulissāni:

mn69:3.1.verse: “Reverends, a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should have respect and reverence for his spiritual companions.

mn69:3.2.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:3.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he has no respect and reverence for his spiritual companions?’

mn69:3.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should have respect and reverence for his spiritual companions.

mn69:4.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should be careful where he sits, thinking:

mn69:4.2.verse: ‘I shall sit so that I don’t intrude on the senior monks and I don’t block the junior monks from a seat.’

mn69:4.3.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:4.4.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s not careful where he sits?’

mn69:4.6.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should be careful where he sits.

mn69:4.7.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should know even the supplementary regulations.

mn69:4.8.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:4.9.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he doesn’t even know the supplementary regulations?’

mn69:4.11.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should know even the supplementary regulations.

mn69:5.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t enter the village too early or return too late in the day.

mn69:5.2.verse: If he does so, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:5.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he enters the village too early or returns too late in the day?’

mn69:5.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t enter the village too early or return too late in the day.

mn69:6.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t have relations with  families before or after the meal.

mn69:6.2.verse: If he does so, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:6.3.verse: ‘This wilderness venerable, staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, must be used to wandering about at the wrong time, since he behaves like this when he’s come to the Saṅgha.’

mn69:6.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t have relations with families before or after the meal.

mn69:7.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t be restless and fickle.

mn69:7.2.verse: If he is, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:7.3.verse: ‘This wilderness venerable, staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, must be used to being restless and fickle, since he behaves like this when he’s come to the Saṅgha.’

mn69:7.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t be restless and fickle.

mn69:8.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t be scurrilous and loose-tongued.

mn69:8.2.verse: If he is, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:8.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s scurrilous and loose-tongued?’

mn69:8.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha shouldn’t be scurrilous and loose-tongued.

mn69:9.1.verse: A wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should be easy to admonish, with good friends.

mn69:9.2.verse: If he’s hard to admonish, with bad friends, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:9.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s hard to admonish, with bad friends?’

mn69:9.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk who has come to stay in the Saṅgha should be easy to admonish, with good friends.

mn69:10.1.verse: A wilderness monk should guard the sense doors.

mn69:10.2.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:10.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he doesn’t guard the sense doors?’

mn69:10.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should guard the sense doors.

mn69:11.1.verse: A wilderness monk should eat in moderation.

mn69:11.2.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:11.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he eats too much?’

mn69:11.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should eat in moderation.

mn69:12.1.verse: A wilderness monk should be committed to wakefulness.

mn69:12.2.verse: If he isn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:12.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s not committed to wakefulness?’

mn69:12.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should be committed to wakefulness.

mn69:13.1.verse: A wilderness monk should be energetic.

mn69:13.2.verse: If he isn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:13.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s not energetic?’

mn69:13.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should be energetic.

mn69:14.1.verse: A wilderness monk should be mindful.

mn69:14.2.verse: If he isn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:14.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s not mindful?’

mn69:14.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should be mindful.

mn69:15.1.verse: A wilderness monk should have immersion.

mn69:15.2.verse: If he doesn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:15.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he doesn’t have immersion?’

mn69:15.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should have immersion.

mn69:16.1.verse: A wilderness monk should be wise.

mn69:16.2.verse: If he isn’t, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:16.3.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he’s not wise?’

mn69:16.5.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should be wise.

mn69:17.1.verse: A wilderness monk should make an effort in regards to the teaching and training.

mn69:17.2.verse: There are those who will question a wilderness monk about the teaching and training.

mn69:17.3.verse: If he is stumped, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:17.4.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he is stumped by a question about the teaching and training?’

mn69:17.6.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should make an effort to learn the teaching and training.

mn69:18.1.verse: A wilderness monk should practice meditation to realize the peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form.

mn69:18.2.verse: There are those who will question a wilderness monk about the formless liberations.

mn69:18.3.verse: If he is stumped, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:18.4.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he is stumped by a question about the formless liberations?’

mn69:18.6.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should practice meditation to realize the peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form.

mn69:19.1.verse: A wilderness monk should practice meditation to realize the superhuman state.

mn69:19.2.verse: There are those who will question a wilderness monk about the superhuman state.

mn69:19.3.verse: If he is stumped, there’ll be some who say:

mn69:19.4.verse: ‘What’s the point of this wilderness venerable’s staying alone and autonomous in the wilderness, since he doesn’t know the goal for which he went forth?’

mn69:19.6.verse: That’s why a wilderness monk should practice meditation to realize the superhuman state.”

mn69:19.7.verse: When Venerable Sāriputta said this, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to him,

mn69:19.8.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, should these things be undertaken and followed only by wilderness monks, or by those who live within a village as well?”

mn69:19.9.verse: “Reverend Moggallāna, these things should be undertaken and followed by wilderness monks, and still more by those who live within a village.”

mn70:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on a tour of Kāsi with a large Saṅgha of monks.

mn70:2.2.verse: As I am abstaining from the nighttime meal, I sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.

mn70:2.3.verse: Come, now. You, too, abstain from the nighttime meal.

mn70:2.4.verse: As you are abstaining from the nighttime meal, you, too, will sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.”

mn70:2.5.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn70:3.1.verse: Then, as he was wandering by stages in Kāsi, the Blessed One eventually arrived at a Kāsi town called Kīṭāgiri.

mn70:3.2.verse: And there he stayed in the Kāsi town, Kīṭāgiri.

mn70:4.1.verse: Now at that time the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu were residing in Kīṭāgiri.

mn70:4.2.verse: Then a large number of monks went to them and, on arrival, said to them,

mn70:4.3.verse: “The Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks abstain from the nighttime meal.

mn70:4.4.verse: As they are abstaining from the nighttime meal, they sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.

mn70:4.5.verse: Come now, friends. You, too, abstain from the nighttime meal.

mn70:4.6.verse: As you are abstaining from the nighttime meal, you, too, will sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.”

mn70:4.7.verse: When this was said, the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu said to those monks,

mn70:4.8.verse: “Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day.

mn70:4.9.verse: As we are eating in the evening, and in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day, we sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.

mn70:4.10.verse: Why should we, abandoning what is immediately visible, chase after something subject to time?

mn70:4.11.verse: We will eat in the evening, in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day.”

mn70:5.1.verse: When they were unable to convince the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu, those monks went to the Blessed One [and told him what had happened].

mn70:6.1.verse: Then the Blessed One told a certain monk,

mn70:6.2.verse: “Come, monk. In my name, call the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu, saying,

mn70:6.4.verse: “As you say, lord,” the monk answered and, having gone to the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu, on arrival he said,

mn70:6.6.verse: “As you say, friend,” the monks led by Assaji & Punabbasu replied. Then they went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side.

mn70:6.7.verse: As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them, “Is it true, monks, that a large number of monks went to you and, on arrival, said to you,

mn70:6.8.verse: ‘The Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks abstain from the nighttime meal.

mn70:6.9.verse: As they are abstaining from the nighttime meal, they sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.

mn70:6.10.verse: Come now, friends. You, too, abstain from the nighttime meal.

mn70:6.11.verse: As you are abstaining from the nighttime meal, you, too, will sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding’?

mn70:6.12.verse: When this was said, did you say to them,

mn70:6.13.verse: ‘Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day.

mn70:6.14.verse: As we are eating in the evening, and in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day, we sense next-to-no illness, next-to-no affliction, lightness, strength, & comfortable abiding.

mn70:6.15.verse: Why should we, abandoning what is immediately visible, chase after something subject to time?

mn70:6.16.verse: We will eat in the evening, in the morning, & in the wrong-time during the day.’”

mn70:6.18.verse: “Monks, have you ever understood me to teach the Dhamma in this way: ‘Whatever a person experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—his unskillful qualities decrease and his skillful qualities grow’?”

mn70:7.1.verse: “And haven’t you understood me to teach the Dhamma in this way: ‘For someone feeling a pleasant feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decrease. But there is the case where, for someone feeling a pleasant feeling of that sort, unskillful qualities decrease and skillful qualities grow. For someone feeling a painful feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decrease. But there is the case where, for someone feeling a painful feeling of that sort, unskillful qualities decrease and skillful qualities grow. For someone feeling a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decrease. But there is the case where, for someone feeling a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling of that sort, unskillful qualities decrease and skillful qualities grow.’”

mn70:8.2.verse: And if it were not known by me—not seen, not observed, not realized, not touched through discernment—that

mn70:8.3.verse: ‘For someone feeling a pleasant feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decrease,’

mn70:8.4.verse: then would it be fitting for me, not knowing that, to say, ‘Abandon that sort of pleasant feeling’?”

mn70:8.6.verse: “But because it is known by me—seen, observed, realized, touched through discernment—that

mn70:8.7.verse: ‘For someone feeling a pleasant feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decrease,’ I therefore say, ‘Abandon that sort of pleasant feeling.’

mn70:8.8.verse: If it were not known by me—not seen, not observed, not realized, not touched through discernment—that

mn70:8.9.verse: ‘For someone feeling a pleasant feeling of this sort, unskillful qualities decrease and skillful qualities grow,’ then would it be fitting for me, not knowing that, to say,

mn70:8.10.verse: ‘Enter & remain in that sort of pleasant feeling’?”

mn70:8.12.verse: “But because it is known by me—seen, observed, realized, touched through discernment—that
