mn73:13.23.verse: But since Master Gotama and the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs and the lay followers, householders clothed in white, living the life divine, and the lay followers, householders clothed in white, enjoying sensual pleasures, and the female lay followers, housewives clothed in white, living the life divine, and the female lay followers, housewives clothed in white, enjoying sensual pleasures, are accomplished in this Dhamma,

mn73:13.24.verse: this life divine is thus complete in that respect.

mn73:14.1.verse: Just as the river Ganges inclines towards the sea, slopes towards the sea, tends towards the sea, and merges with the sea, so too Master Gotama’s assembly, with its householders and those gone forth, inclines towards Nibbāna, slopes towards Nibbāna, tends towards Nibbāna, and merges with Nibbāna.

mn73:15.1.verse: ‘Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyesight to see forms. …

mn73:15.2.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn73:15.3.verse: I would receive the Going-forth under Master Gotama, I would receive the Full Admission.’

mn73:16.1.verse: “Vaccha, one who formerly belonged to another sect and wishes for the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of the four months, bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give him the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state;

mn73:16.2.verse: but even here I have recognized a difference between individuals.”

mn73:16.3.verse: “Venerable sir, if those who formerly belonged to another sect and wish for the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline live on probation for four months, and at the end of four months bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give them the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state, then I will live on probation for four years, and at the end of the four years let bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give me the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state.”

mn73:16.4.verse: And Vacchagotta the Wanderer received the Going-forth in the Blessed One’s presence, and he received the Full Admission.

mn73:17.1.verse: Not long after his Full Admission, half a month after his Full Admission, the venerable Vacchagotta went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the venerable Vacchagotta said to the Blessed One:

mn73:17.2.verse: “Venerable sir, I have reached whatever can be reached by the knowledge and the true knowledge of one in higher training;[^1]

mn73:17.3.verse: let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma further.”

mn73:18.1.verse: “In that case, Vaccha, develop two things further: serenity and insight.

mn73:18.2.verse: These two things, Vaccha, when developed further—serenity and insight—will lead to the penetration of the many elements.

mn73:19.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:19.2.verse: ‘may I wield the various kinds of supernormal power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though on earth; seated cross-legged, may I travel through the air like a bird on the wing; with my hand may I touch and stroke the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; may I wield bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world’—

mn73:19.3.verse: in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.

mn73:20.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:20.2.verse: ‘may I, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near’—in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.

mn73:21.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:21.2.verse: ‘may I, having encompassed the minds of other beings and other persons with my own mind, understand them thus—

mn73:21.3.verse: may I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust,

mn73:21.4.verse: and a mind without lust as a mind without lust;

mn73:21.5.verse: may I understand a mind with hate as a mind with hate,

mn73:21.6.verse: and a mind without hate as a mind without hate;

mn73:21.7.verse: may I understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion,

mn73:21.8.verse: and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion;

mn73:21.9.verse: may I understand a contracted mind as contracted,

mn73:21.10.verse: and a distracted mind as distracted;

mn73:21.11.verse: may I understand an exalted mind as exalted,

mn73:21.12.verse: and an unexalted mind as unexalted;

mn73:21.13.verse: may I understand a surpassable mind as surpassable,

mn73:21.14.verse: and an unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable;

mn73:21.15.verse: may I understand a concentrated mind as concentrated,

mn73:21.16.verse: and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated;

mn73:21.17.verse: may I understand a liberated mind as liberated,

mn73:21.18.verse: and an unliberated mind as unliberated’—

mn73:21.19.verse: in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.

mn73:22.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:22.2.verse: ‘may I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: “there I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared here”—thus may I recollect my manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars’—

mn73:22.3.verse: in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.

mn73:23.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:23.2.verse: ‘may I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions thus: “these beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, wrong in view, undertaking action based on wrong view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, right in view, undertaking action based on right view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”—thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, may I see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions’—

mn73:23.3.verse: in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.

mn73:24.1.verse: As far as you shall wish, Vaccha:

mn73:24.2.verse: ‘may I, by realizing for myself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and the deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the exhaustion of the taints’—

mn73:24.3.verse: in each and every case you will attain the capacity to witness it for yourself, whenever there is an opportunity.”

mn73:25.1.verse: Then the venerable Vacchagotta, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he departed.

mn73:26.1.verse: Then the venerable Vacchagotta, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, before long entered upon and abided in that supreme goal of the life divine, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge here and now.

mn73:26.2.verse: He directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn73:26.3.verse: And the venerable Vacchagotta became one of the Arahants.

mn73:27.1.verse: Now on that occasion a number of bhikkhus were going to see the Blessed One.

mn73:27.2.verse: The venerable Vacchagotta saw those bhikkhus coming in the distance.

mn73:27.3.verse: Seeing them, he went up to them and said to them:

mn73:27.4.verse: “Now then, where are you venerable ones going?”

mn73:27.5.verse: “We are going to see the Blessed One, friend.”

mn73:27.6.verse: “Then, venerable ones, please pay homage with your heads at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and say thus:

mn73:27.7.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Vacchagotta pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and he says:

mn73:27.8.verse: “the Blessed One has been served by me, the Fortunate One has been served by me.”’”[^2]

mn73:28.1.verse: “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Vacchagotta.

mn73:28.2.verse: Then those bhikkhus went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down at one side. When they had done so, they said to the Blessed One:

mn73:28.3.verse: “Venerable sir, the venerable Vacchagotta pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and he says:

mn73:28.4.verse: ‘the Blessed One has been served by me, the Fortunate One has been served by me.’”

mn73:28.5.verse: “Bhikkhus, I already knew the bhikkhu Vacchagotta by encompassing his mind with my own mind, thus:

mn73:28.6.verse: ‘the bhikkhu Vacchagotta has the three true knowledges; he has great supernormal power and great might.’

mn73:28.7.verse: And deities also told me of this matter:

mn73:28.8.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Vacchagotta has the three true knowledges; he has great supernormal power and great might.’”

mn73:28.9.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn73:28.10.verse: Those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn73:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn73:2.1.verse: Then the wanderer Vacchagotta went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn73:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

mn73:3.1.verse: “For a long time I have had discussions with the worthy Gotama.

mn73:3.2.verse: Please teach me in brief what is skillful and what is unskillful.”

mn73:3.3.verse: “Vaccha, I can teach you what is skillful and what is unskillful in brief or in detail.

mn73:3.4.verse: Still, let me do so in brief.

mn73:3.5.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn73:4.2.verse: Hate is unskillful, love is skillful.

mn73:4.3.verse: Delusion is unskillful, understanding is skillful.

mn73:4.4.verse: So there are these three unskillful things and three that are skillful.

mn73:5.1.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct; speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; covetousness, ill will, and wrong view: these things are unskillful.

mn73:5.2.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct; refraining from speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical; contentment, good will, and right view: these things are skillful.

mn73:5.11.verse: So there are these ten unskillful things and ten that are skillful.

mn73:6.1.verse: When a mendicant has given up craving so it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future, that mendicant is perfected. They’ve ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment.”

mn73:7.2.verse: is there even a single monk disciple of Worthy Gotama who has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements?”

mn73:7.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such monks who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:8.1.verse: “Leaving aside the worthy Gotama and the monks,

mn73:8.2.verse: is there even a single nun disciple of Worthy Gotama who has realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and lives having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements?”

mn73:8.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such nuns who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:9.1.verse: “Leaving aside the worthy Gotama, the monks, and the nuns,

mn73:9.2.verse: is there even a single layman disciple of Worthy Gotama—white-clothed and chaste—who, with the ending of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously, to be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world?”

mn73:9.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such chaste laymen who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:10.1.verse: “Leaving aside Worthy Gotama, the monks, the nuns, and the chaste laymen,

mn73:10.2.verse: is there even a single layman disciple of the worthy Gotama—white-clothed, enjoying sensual pleasures, following instructions, and responding to advice—who has gone beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and lives self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction?”

mn73:10.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such laymen enjoying sensual pleasures who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:11.1.verse: “Leaving aside Worthy Gotama, the monks, the nuns, the chaste laymen, and the laymen enjoying sensual pleasures,

mn73:11.2.verse: is there even a single laywoman disciple of Worthy Gotama—white-clothed and chaste—who, with the ending of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously, to be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world?”

mn73:11.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such chaste laywomen who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:12.1.verse: “Leaving aside Worthy Gotama, the monks, the nuns, the chaste laymen, the laymen enjoying sensual pleasures, and the chaste laywomen,

mn73:12.2.verse: is there even a single laywoman disciple of the worthy Gotama—white-clothed, enjoying sensual pleasures, following instructions, and responding to advice—who has gone beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and lives self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction?”

mn73:12.3.verse: “There are not just one hundred such laywomen enjoying sensual pleasures who are my disciples, Vaccha, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that.”

mn73:13.1.verse: “If the worthy Gotama was the only one to succeed in this teaching, not any monks,

mn73:13.2.verse: then this spiritual path would be incomplete in that respect.

mn73:13.3.verse: But because both the worthy Gotama and monks have succeeded in this teaching,

mn73:13.4.verse: this spiritual path is complete in that respect.

mn73:13.5.verse: If the worthy Gotama and the monks were the only ones to succeed in this teaching, not any nuns …

mn73:13.22.verse: then this spiritual path would be incomplete in that respect.

mn73:13.23.verse: But because Worthy Gotama, monks, nuns, chaste laymen, laymen enjoying sensual pleasures, chaste laywomen, and laywomen enjoying sensual pleasures have all succeeded in this teaching,

mn73:13.24.verse: this spiritual path is complete in that respect.

mn73:14.1.verse: Just as the Ganges River slants, slopes, and inclines toward the ocean, and keeps pressing into the ocean, in the same way Worthy Gotama’s assembly—with both laypeople and renunciates—slants, slopes, and inclines toward extinguishment, and keeps pressing upon extinguishment.

mn73:15.2.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn73:15.3.verse: May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama’s presence?”

mn73:16.1.verse: “Vaccha, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they’ll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.

mn73:16.2.verse: However, I recognize individual differences in this matter.”

mn73:16.3.verse: “Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I’ll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.”

mn73:16.4.verse: And the wanderer Vaccha received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

mn73:17.1.verse: Not long after his ordination, a fortnight later, Venerable Vacchagotta went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn73:17.2.verse: “Sir, I’ve reached as far as possible with the knowledge and understanding of a trainee.

mn73:18.1.verse: “Well then, Vaccha, further develop two things: serenity and discernment.

mn73:18.2.verse: When you have further developed these two things, they’ll lead to the penetration of many elements.

mn73:19.1.verse: As far as you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:19.2.verse: ‘May I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.’

mn73:20.1.verse: Whenever you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:20.2.verse: ‘With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, may I hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.’

mn73:21.1.verse: As far as you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:21.2.verse: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my mind.

mn73:21.3.verse: May I understand mind with greed as “mind with greed”,

mn73:21.4.verse: and mind without greed as “mind without greed”;

mn73:21.5.verse: mind with hate as “mind with hate”,

mn73:21.6.verse: and mind without hate as “mind without hate”;

mn73:21.7.verse: mind with delusion as “mind with delusion”,

mn73:21.8.verse: and mind without delusion as “mind without delusion”;

mn73:21.13.verse: mind that is not supreme as “mind that is not supreme”,

mn73:21.14.verse: and mind that is supreme as “mind that is supreme”;

mn73:21.15.verse: mind immersed in samādhi as “mind immersed in samādhi”,

mn73:21.16.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as “mind not immersed in samādhi”;

mn73:22.1.verse: As far as you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:22.2.verse: ‘May I recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. May I remember: “There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.” May I recollect my many past lives, with features and details.’

mn73:23.1.verse: Whenever you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:23.2.verse: ‘With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, may I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place—and understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: “These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.” And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, may I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. And may I understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.’

mn73:24.1.verse: As far as you want, you will be capable of realizing these things, since each and every one is within range:

mn73:24.2.verse: ‘May I realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’”

mn73:25.1.verse: And then Venerable Vacchagotta approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn73:26.1.verse: Then Vacchagotta, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn73:26.2.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn73:26.3.verse: And Venerable Vacchagotta became one of the perfected.

mn73:27.1.verse: Now at that time several mendicants were going to see the Buddha.

mn73:27.2.verse: Vacchagotta saw them coming off in the distance,

mn73:27.3.verse: went up to them, and said,

mn73:27.5.verse: “Reverend, we are going to see the Buddha.”

mn73:27.6.verse: “Well then, reverends, in my name please bow with your head to the Buddha’s feet and say:

mn73:27.7.verse: ‘Sir, the mendicant Vacchagotta bows with his head to your feet and says,

mn73:27.8.verse: “I have served the Blessed One! I have served the Holy One!”’”

mn73:28.2.verse: Then those mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn73:28.3.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Vacchagotta bows with his head to your feet and says:

mn73:28.4.verse: ‘I have served the Blessed One! I have served the Holy One!’”

mn73:28.5.verse: “I’ve already encompassed Vacchagotta’s mind and understood that

mn73:28.6.verse: he has the three knowledges, and is very mighty and powerful.

mn73:28.7.verse: And deities also told me about this.”

mn73:28.9.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn73:28.10.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn74:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the Boar’s Cave.

mn74:2.1.verse: Then Dīghanakha the Wanderer went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn74:2.2.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. Standing at one side, Dīghanakha the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn74:2.3.verse: “Master Gotama, this is my doctrine, this is my view:

mn74:2.6.verse: ‘I have no liking for anything’—do you have no liking for that view either?”

mn74:2.7.verse: “Even if I liked this view of mine, Master Gotama, it would be the same, it would be the same.”[^2]

mn74:3.1.verse: “Well, Aggivessana, there are more, indeed far more, in the world who say:

mn74:3.2.verse: ‘it would be the same, it would be the same,’

mn74:3.3.verse: and yet do not abandon that view and take up another view.

mn74:3.4.verse: And there are fewer, indeed far fewer, in the world who say:

mn74:3.5.verse: ‘it would be the same, it would be the same,’

mn74:3.6.verse: and who abandon that view and do not take up another view.

mn74:4.1.verse: There are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:4.3.verse: there are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:4.5.verse: and there are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:4.6.verse: ‘I like some things, and I have no liking for some things.’

mn74:4.7.verse: Of these, Aggivessana, the doctrine and view of those ascetics and brahmins who say: ‘I like everything’

mn74:4.8.verse: is a view close to lust, close to bondage, close to relishing, close to holding, close to clinging;

mn74:4.9.verse: and the doctrine and view of those ascetics and brahmins who say: ‘I have no liking for anything’

mn74:4.10.verse: is a view close to non-lust, close to non-bondage, close to non-relishing, close to non-holding, close to non-clinging.”

mn74:5.1.verse: When this was said, Dīghanakha the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn74:5.2.verse: “Master Gotama extols my view, Master Gotama commends my view.”

mn74:5.3.verse: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:5.4.verse: ‘I like some things, and I have no liking for some things’—

mn74:5.5.verse: the part of their view that likes is close to lust, close to bondage, close to relishing, close to holding, close to clinging;

mn74:5.6.verse: and the part of their view that has no liking is close to non-lust, close to non-bondage, close to non-relishing, close to non-holding, close to non-clinging.

mn74:6.1.verse: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:6.3.verse: a wise man among them considers thus:

mn74:6.4.verse: ‘If I were to adhere obstinately to this view of mine,

mn74:6.7.verse: declaring: “Only this is true, everything else is wrong”—

mn74:6.8.verse: then I would come into conflict with two others—

mn74:6.9.verse: with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I have no liking for anything,”

mn74:6.10.verse: and with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I like some things, and I have no liking for some things”—

mn74:6.11.verse: I would come into conflict with these two.

mn74:6.12.verse: Where there is conflict there is dispute; where there is dispute there is vexation; where there is vexation there is distress.’

mn74:6.13.verse: So, seeing in himself this conflict, dispute, vexation, and distress, he abandons that view and does not take up another view.

mn74:6.14.verse: That is how there comes to be the abandoning of these views, that is how there comes to be the relinquishing of these views.

mn74:7.1.verse: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:7.3.verse: a wise man among them considers thus:

mn74:7.4.verse: ‘If I were to adhere obstinately to this view of mine,

mn74:7.7.verse: declaring: “Only this is true, everything else is wrong”—

mn74:7.8.verse: then I would come into conflict with two others—

mn74:7.9.verse: with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I like everything,”

mn74:7.10.verse: and with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I like some things, and I have no liking for some things”—

mn74:7.11.verse: I would come into conflict with these two.

mn74:7.12.verse: Where there is conflict there is dispute; where there is dispute there is vexation; where there is vexation there is distress.’

mn74:7.13.verse: So, seeing in himself this conflict, dispute, vexation, and distress, he abandons that view and does not take up another view.

mn74:7.14.verse: That is how there comes to be the abandoning of these views, that is how there comes to be the relinquishing of these views.

mn74:8.1.verse: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn74:8.2.verse: ‘I like some things, and I have no liking for some things’—

mn74:8.3.verse: a wise man among them considers thus:

mn74:8.4.verse: ‘If I were to adhere obstinately to this view of mine,

mn74:8.5.verse: “I like some things, and I have no liking for some things,”

mn74:8.7.verse: declaring: “Only this is true, everything else is wrong”—

mn74:8.8.verse: then I would come into conflict with two others—

mn74:8.9.verse: with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I like everything,”

mn74:8.10.verse: and with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I have no liking for anything”—

mn74:8.11.verse: I would come into conflict with these two.

mn74:8.12.verse: Where there is conflict there is dispute; where there is dispute there is vexation; where there is vexation there is distress.’

mn74:8.13.verse: So, seeing in himself this conflict, dispute, vexation, and distress, he abandons that view and does not take up another view.

mn74:8.14.verse: That is how there comes to be the abandoning of these views, that is how there comes to be the relinquishing of these views.

mn74:9.1.verse: Now, Aggivessana, this body possessed of form, made up of the four great elements, procreated by mother and father, built up out of rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking apart and dispersal, should be regarded as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as void, as not self.

mn74:9.2.verse: When one regards this body thus, as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as void, as not self, one abandons desire for the body, affection for the body, and subservience to the body.[^3]

mn74:10.1.verse: There are, Aggivessana, three kinds of feeling—

mn74:10.2.verse: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

mn74:10.3.verse: On the occasion, Aggivessana, when one feels pleasant feeling, one does not on that occasion feel painful feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

mn74:10.4.verse: one feels only pleasant feeling on that occasion.

mn74:10.5.verse: On the occasion when one feels painful feeling, one does not on that occasion feel pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

mn74:10.6.verse: one feels only painful feeling on that occasion.

mn74:10.7.verse: On the occasion when one feels neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not on that occasion feel pleasant feeling or painful feeling;

mn74:10.8.verse: one feels only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling on that occasion.

mn74:11.1.verse: Pleasant feeling too, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation;

mn74:11.2.verse: painful feeling too is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation;

mn74:11.3.verse: and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling too is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation.

mn74:12.1.verse: Seeing thus, Aggivessana, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

mn74:12.2.verse: being disenchanted, his lust fades away; with the fading of lust he is liberated. When he is liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”

mn74:12.3.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn74:13.1.verse: A bhikkhu whose mind is liberated thus, Aggivessana, does not side with anyone, does not dispute with anyone; he employs the current speech of the world without misapprehending it.”

mn74:14.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Sāriputta was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.

mn74:14.2.verse: Then it occurred to the venerable Sāriputta:

mn74:14.3.verse: “The Blessed One, it seems, speaks to us of the abandoning of these various things through direct knowledge; the Fortunate One, it seems, speaks to us of the relinquishing of these various things through direct knowledge.”

mn74:14.4.verse: As the venerable Sāriputta considered this, his mind was liberated from the taints by non-clinging.

mn74:15.1.verse: But in Dīghanakha the Wanderer there arose the spotless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma:

mn74:15.2.verse: “Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.”

mn74:15.3.verse: Then Dīghanakha the Wanderer, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, fathomed the Dhamma, having crossed beyond doubt, being free from perplexity, having gained intrepidity, and become independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, said to the Blessed One:

mn74:16.2.verse: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.

mn74:16.3.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn74:16.4.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”

mn74:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain in the Boar’s Cave.

mn74:2.1.verse: Then the wanderer Dīghanakha went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn74:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side and said to the Buddha,

mn74:2.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, this is my doctrine and view:

mn74:2.7.verse: “If I were to accept this view, worthy Gotama, it would make no difference, it would make no difference!”

mn74:3.1.verse: “Well, Aggivessana, there are many more in the world who say,

mn74:3.2.verse: ‘It would make no difference! It would make no difference!’

mn74:3.3.verse: But they don’t give up that view, and they grasp another view.

mn74:3.4.verse: And there are a scant few in the world who say,

mn74:3.5.verse: ‘It would make no difference! It would make no difference!’

mn74:3.6.verse: And they give up that view by not grasping another view.

mn74:4.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn74:4.3.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn74:4.5.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn74:4.6.verse: ‘Some things are acceptable to me and some things are not.’

mn74:4.7.verse: Regarding this, the view of the ascetics and brahmins to whom everything is acceptable

mn74:4.8.verse: is close to greed, bondage, approving, attachment, and grasping.

mn74:4.9.verse: The view of the ascetics and brahmins to whom nothing is acceptable

mn74:4.10.verse: is far from greed, bondage, approving, attachment, and grasping.”

mn74:5.1.verse: When he said this, the wanderer Dīghanakha said to the Buddha,

mn74:5.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama commends my conviction! He recommends my conviction!”

mn74:5.3.verse: “Now, regarding the ascetics and brahmins to whom

mn74:5.4.verse: some things are acceptable and some things are not.

mn74:5.5.verse: Their view of what is acceptable is close to greed, bondage, approving, attachment, and grasping.

mn74:5.6.verse: Their view of what is not acceptable is far from greed, bondage, approving, attachment, and grasping.

mn74:6.1.verse: When it comes to the view of the ascetics and brahmins to whom

mn74:6.3.verse: a sensible person reflects like this:

mn74:6.6.verse: Suppose I were to obstinately stick to this view and insist,

mn74:6.7.verse: “This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

mn74:6.8.verse: Then I’d argue with two individuals—

mn74:6.9.verse: an ascetic or brahmin to whom nothing is acceptable,

mn74:6.10.verse: and an ascetic or brahmin to whom some things are acceptable and some things are not.

mn74:6.12.verse: And when there’s arguing, there’s dispute; when there’s dispute there’s distress; and when there’s distress there’s harm.’

mn74:6.13.verse: So, considering in themselves the potential for argument, dispute, distress, and harm, they give up that view by not grasping another view.

mn74:6.14.verse: That’s how those views are given up and let go.

mn74:7.1.verse: When it comes to the view of the ascetics and brahmins to whom

mn74:7.3.verse: a sensible person reflects like this:

mn74:7.6.verse: Suppose I were to obstinately stick to this view and insist,

mn74:7.7.verse: “This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

mn74:7.8.verse: Then I’d argue with two individuals—

mn74:7.9.verse: an ascetic or brahmin to whom everything is acceptable,

mn74:7.10.verse: and an ascetic or brahmin to whom some things are acceptable and some things are not.

mn74:7.12.verse: And when there’s arguing, there’s dispute; when there’s dispute there’s distress; and when there’s distress there’s harm.’

mn74:7.13.verse: So, considering in themselves the potential for argument, dispute, distress, and harm, they give up that view by not grasping another view.

mn74:7.14.verse: That’s how those views are given up and let go.

mn74:8.1.verse: When it comes to the view of the ascetics and brahmins to whom

mn74:8.2.verse: some things are acceptable and some things are not,

mn74:8.3.verse: a sensible person reflects like this:

mn74:8.5.verse: some things are acceptable and some things are not.

mn74:8.6.verse: Suppose I were to obstinately stick to this view and insist,

mn74:8.7.verse: “This is the only truth, anything else is futile.”

mn74:8.8.verse: Then I’d argue with two individuals—

mn74:8.9.verse: an ascetic or brahmin to whom everything is acceptable,

mn74:8.10.verse: and an ascetic or brahmin to whom nothing is acceptable.

mn74:8.12.verse: And when there’s arguing, there’s dispute; when there’s dispute there’s distress; and when there’s distress there’s harm.’

mn74:8.13.verse: So, considering in themselves the potential for argument, dispute, distress, and harm, they give up that view by not grasping another view.

mn74:8.14.verse: That’s how those views are given up and let go.

mn74:9.1.verse: Aggivessana, this body is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction. You should see it as impermanent, as suffering, as diseased, as a boil, as a dart, as gloom, as an affliction, as alien, as breaking apart, as empty, as not-self.

mn74:9.2.verse: Doing so, you’ll give up desire, affection, and subservience to the body.

mn74:10.3.verse: At a time when you feel a pleasant feeling, you don’t feel a painful or neutral feeling;

mn74:10.4.verse: you only feel a pleasant feeling.

mn74:10.5.verse: At a time when you feel a painful feeling, you don’t feel a pleasant or neutral feeling;

mn74:10.6.verse: you only feel a painful feeling.

mn74:10.7.verse: At a time when you feel a neutral feeling, you don’t feel a pleasant or painful feeling;

mn74:10.8.verse: you only feel a neutral feeling.

mn74:11.1.verse: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings are impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

mn74:12.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.

mn74:12.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn74:12.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn74:13.1.verse: A mendicant whose mind is freed like this doesn’t side with anyone or dispute with anyone. They use the language of the world to communicate without getting stuck on it.”

mn74:14.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was standing behind the Buddha fanning him.

mn74:14.3.verse: “It seems the Buddha speaks of giving up and letting go of all these things through direct knowledge.”

mn74:14.4.verse: Reflecting like this, Venerable Sāriputta’s mind was freed from the defilements by not grasping.

mn74:15.1.verse: And the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in the wanderer Dīghanakha:

mn74:15.2.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

mn74:15.3.verse: Then Dīghanakha saw, attained, understood, and fathomed the Dhamma. He went beyond doubt, got rid of indecision, and became self-assured and independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instructions. He said to the Buddha:

mn74:16.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn74:16.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn74:16.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn75:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Kurus, at a town of the Kurus called Kammāsadhamma, on a spread of grass in the fire-hall of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.

mn75:2.1.verse: Then when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Kammāsadhamma for alms.

mn75:2.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Kammāsadhamma and had returned from his alms round, after the meal he went to a certain grove for the day’s abiding.

mn75:2.3.verse: Having plunged into that grove, he sat down at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.

mn75:3.1.verse: Then Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer, walking and wandering for exercise, went to the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.

mn75:3.2.verse: Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer saw a spread of grass made ready in the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.

mn75:3.3.verse: Seeing it, he said to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan:

mn75:3.4.verse: “Whose is this spread of grass made ready in Master Bhāradvāja’s fire-hall? It looks like a resting place for an ascetic.”

mn75:4.1.verse: “There is, Master Māgaṇḍiya, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, who has gone forth from a Sakyan clan.

mn75:4.2.verse: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn75:4.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’

mn75:4.4.verse: This is the resting place made ready for that Master Gotama.”

mn75:5.1.verse: “It is indeed an ill sight, Master Bhāradvāja, that we see;

mn75:5.2.verse: it is indeed an ill sight, Master Bhāradvāja, that we see,

mn75:5.3.verse: in that we see the resting place of that Master Gotama, the wreaker of being.”[^1]

mn75:5.5.verse: guard that speech of yours, Māgaṇḍiya.

mn75:5.6.verse: For many wise nobles, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics have full confidence in that Master Gotama, and are trained in the noble method, the wholesome Dhamma.”

mn75:5.7.verse: “Even if we were to see that Master Gotama face to face, Master Bhāradvāja, we would say to his face:

mn75:5.8.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being.’

mn75:5.10.verse: Because that is how it comes down to us in our scriptures.”

mn75:5.11.verse: “If Master Māgaṇḍiya does not mind, I will report that to the ascetic Gotama.”

mn75:5.12.verse: “Let Master Bhāradvāja not trouble himself; say to him just what has been said.”

mn75:6.1.verse: The Blessed One heard, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer.

mn75:6.2.verse: Then when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation and went to the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, and sat down on the spread of grass made ready.

mn75:6.3.verse: Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn75:6.4.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. The Blessed One then said to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, as he sat at one side:

mn75:6.5.verse: “Bhāradvāja, did you have some conversation with Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer concerning this very spread of grass?”

mn75:6.6.verse: When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, alarmed and with hair standing on end, said to the Blessed One:

mn75:6.7.verse: “It was just this that we wanted to report to Master Gotama,

mn75:6.8.verse: but Master Gotama has told it though it was not told to him.”

mn75:7.1.verse: Now this conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was left unfinished,

mn75:7.2.verse: for then Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer, walking and wandering for exercise, went to the Blessed One at the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn75:7.3.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. The Blessed One then said to Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer, as he sat at one side:

mn75:8.1.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, the eye delights in forms, takes delight in forms, rejoices in forms.

mn75:8.2.verse: That is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained in the Tathāgata, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.

mn75:8.3.verse: Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:

mn75:8.4.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being’?”

mn75:8.5.verse: “It was with reference to this, Master Gotama, that I said:

mn75:8.6.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being.’

mn75:8.8.verse: Because that is how it comes down to us in our scriptures.”

mn75:8.11.verse: the tongue delights in flavours, takes delight in flavours, rejoices in flavours.

mn75:8.12.verse: That is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained in the Tathāgata, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.

mn75:8.13.verse: Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:

mn75:8.14.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being’?”

mn75:8.15.verse: “It was with reference to this, Master Gotama, that I said:

mn75:8.16.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being.’

mn75:8.18.verse: Because that is how it comes down to us in our scriptures.”

mn75:8.19.verse: “The body, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in tangibles, takes delight in tangibles …

mn75:8.20.verse: the mind delights in mental objects, takes delight in mental objects, rejoices in mental objects.

mn75:8.21.verse: That is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained in the Tathāgata, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.

mn75:8.22.verse: Was it with reference to this, Māgaṇḍiya, that you said:

mn75:8.23.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being’?”

mn75:8.24.verse: “It was with reference to this, Master Gotama, that I said:

mn75:8.25.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a wreaker of being.’

mn75:8.27.verse: Because that is how it comes down to us in our scriptures.”

mn75:9.2.verse: suppose someone had formerly amused himself with forms cognizable by the eye that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; and on a later occasion, having known as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of forms, he abandoned craving for forms, removed the fever for forms, and dwelt without thirst, his mind stilled within.

mn75:9.3.verse: What would you have to say about him, Māgaṇḍiya?”

mn75:9.6.verse: suppose someone had formerly amused himself with sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn75:9.7.verse: with odours cognizable by the nose …

mn75:9.8.verse: with flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn75:9.9.verse: with tangibles cognizable by the body that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust,

mn75:9.10.verse: and on a later occasion, having known as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of tangibles, he abandoned craving for tangibles, removed the fever for tangibles, and dwelt without thirst, his mind stilled within.

mn75:9.11.verse: What would you have to say about him, Māgaṇḍiya?”

mn75:10.1.verse: “As for me, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly, when I lived the home life, I was furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, and I amused myself with forms cognizable by the eye that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn75:10.2.verse: with odours cognizable by the nose …

mn75:10.3.verse: with flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn75:10.4.verse: with tangibles cognizable by the body that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn75:10.6.verse: one for the rainy season, one for winter, and one for summer.

mn75:10.7.verse: I lived in the rains palace for the four months of the rainy season, being entertained by musicians with no men among them, and I did not go down from that palace.

mn75:10.8.verse: On a later occasion, having known as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever for sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, my mind stilled within.

mn75:10.9.verse: I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.

mn75:10.10.verse: I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:10.12.verse: Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome things,

mn75:10.14.verse: delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:11.1.verse: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a householder or a householder’s son, rich, with great wealth and great possessions, furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, were to amuse himself with forms cognizable by the eye …

mn75:11.3.verse: with tangibles that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn75:11.4.verse: Having conducted himself well in body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he might be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, in the company of the gods of the Thirty-three.

mn75:11.5.verse: There, in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a throng of nymphs, furnished and endowed with the five cords of heavenly sensual desire, he might amuse himself.

mn75:11.6.verse: He might see a householder or a householder’s son furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, amusing himself.

mn75:11.7.verse: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that son of the gods, in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a throng of nymphs, furnished and endowed with the five cords of heavenly sensual desire, and amusing himself, envy that householder or householder’s son, or would he be drawn back to human sensual pleasures, to the five cords of human sensual desire?”

mn75:11.10.verse: Because, Master Gotama, heavenly sensual pleasures are more excellent and sublime than human sensual pleasures.”

mn75:12.1.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly, when I lived the home life, I was furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, and I amused myself with forms cognizable by the eye that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn75:12.2.verse: with odours cognizable by the nose …

mn75:12.3.verse: with flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn75:12.4.verse: with tangibles cognizable by the body that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn75:12.5.verse: On a later occasion, having known as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever for sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, my mind stilled within.

mn75:12.6.verse: I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:12.8.verse: Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome things,

mn75:12.10.verse: delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:13.1.verse: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, were to cauterize his body over a pit of burning coals.

mn75:13.2.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring him a surgeon to treat him.

mn75:13.3.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for him.

mn75:13.4.verse: Through that medicine, he might be freed from the leprosy, and might be healthy and happy, independent, his own master, able to go where he likes.

mn75:13.5.verse: He might see another leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of burning coals.

mn75:13.7.verse: would that man envy that leper his pit of burning coals or his use of medicine?”

mn75:13.10.verse: Because, Master Gotama, when there is illness, there is need for medicine, and when there is no illness, there is no need for medicine.”

mn75:14.1.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly, when I lived the home life, I was furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, and I amused myself with forms cognizable by the eye that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn75:14.2.verse: with odours cognizable by the nose …

mn75:14.3.verse: with flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn75:14.4.verse: with tangibles cognizable by the body that were wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

mn75:14.5.verse: On a later occasion, having known as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever for sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, my mind stilled within.

mn75:14.6.verse: I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.

mn75:14.7.verse: I do not envy them, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:14.9.verse: Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome things,

mn75:14.11.verse: delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that.

mn75:15.1.verse: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, were to cauterize his body over a pit of burning coals.

mn75:15.2.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring him a surgeon to treat him.

mn75:15.3.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for him.

mn75:15.4.verse: Through that medicine, he might be freed from the leprosy, and might be healthy and happy, independent, his own master, able to go where he likes.

mn75:15.5.verse: Then two strong men, seizing him by both arms, might drag him towards a pit of burning coals.

mn75:15.7.verse: would that man twist his body this way and that?”

mn75:15.10.verse: Because, Master Gotama, that fire is painful to touch, causes great heat and great fever.”

mn75:15.12.verse: is that fire painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, only now, or was that fire also painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, formerly?”

mn75:15.13.verse: “That fire, Master Gotama, is painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, both now and formerly.

mn75:15.14.verse: But that leper, Master Gotama, with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, had his faculties impaired, and so acquired a mistaken perception of pleasure regarding that fire which was actually painful to touch.”

mn75:16.1.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, sensual pleasures were painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, in the past; sensual pleasures will be painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, in the future; and sensual pleasures are painful to touch, causing great heat and great fever, now in the present.

mn75:16.2.verse: But these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures,[^3] who are devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, have their faculties impaired, and so acquire a mistaken perception of pleasure regarding sensual pleasures that are actually painful to touch.

mn75:17.1.verse: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizes his body over a pit of burning coals.

mn75:17.2.verse: The more that leper cauterizes his body over the pit of burning coals, the fouler, the more foul-smelling, and the more infected the openings of his wounds become; yet he finds a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment in scratching the openings of his wounds.

mn75:17.3.verse: So too, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who are devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with fever for sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures.

mn75:17.4.verse: The more such beings indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures grows, and the more they burn with fever for sensual pleasures; yet they find a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment dependent on the five cords of sensual desire.

mn75:18.2.verse: have you seen or heard of a king or a king’s minister, furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, amusing himself, who dwelt or dwells or will dwell without thirst, his mind stilled within, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and without having removed the fever for sensual pleasures?”

mn75:18.5.verse: I too, Māgaṇḍiya, have neither seen nor heard of a king or a king’s minister, furnished and endowed with the five cords of sensual desire, amusing himself, who dwelt or dwells or will dwell without thirst, his mind stilled within, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and without having removed the fever for sensual pleasures.

mn75:18.6.verse: Rather, Māgaṇḍiya, any ascetics or brahmins who dwelt or dwell or will dwell without thirst, their minds stilled within, have all done so only after knowing as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, and after abandoning craving for sensual pleasures and removing the fever for sensual pleasures.”

mn75:19.1.verse: Then, on that occasion, the Blessed One uttered this exclamation:

mn75:19.4.verse: and the Eightfold is the best of paths,

mn75:19.6.verse: When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn75:19.7.verse: “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvellous, Master Gotama.

mn75:19.8.verse: How well this has been said by Master Gotama:

mn75:19.9.verse: ‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the highest bliss.’

mn75:19.10.verse: I too have heard this said by former teachers and their teachers among the wanderers:

mn75:19.11.verse: ‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the highest bliss’;

mn75:19.12.verse: this agrees with that, Master Gotama.”

mn75:19.13.verse: “But, Māgaṇḍiya, as to what you have heard said by former teachers and their teachers among the wanderers:

mn75:19.14.verse: ‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the highest bliss’—what is that health, and what is that Nibbāna?”

mn75:19.15.verse: When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer stroked his own limbs with his hand, saying:

mn75:19.16.verse: “This, Master Gotama, is that health, this is that Nibbāna.

mn75:19.17.verse: For I, Master Gotama, am now healthy and happy, and nothing afflicts me.”

mn75:20.1.verse: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there were a man blind from birth;

mn75:20.2.verse: he could not see dark and light forms, could not see blue forms, could not see yellow forms, could not see red forms, could not see crimson forms, could not see what is even and uneven, could not see the stars, could not see the moon and sun.

mn75:20.3.verse: He might hear a man with good eyesight saying:

mn75:20.4.verse: ‘Good sirs, how fine is a white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’

mn75:20.5.verse: He might go in search of a white cloth.

mn75:20.6.verse: Then a certain man might deceive him with a grimy, oil-stained garment, saying:[^4]

mn75:20.7.verse: ‘Good man, here is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean.’

mn75:20.8.verse: He might accept it, and having accepted it, put it on, and having put it on, being pleased, utter words of pleasure:

mn75:20.9.verse: ‘How fine is this white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’

mn75:20.11.verse: would that man blind from birth have accepted that grimy, oil-stained garment, and put it on, and being pleased, uttered words of pleasure:

mn75:20.12.verse: ‘How fine is this white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’ knowing and seeing, or out of faith in the man with good eyesight?”

mn75:20.13.verse: “Not knowing and not seeing, Master Gotama, that man blind from birth would have accepted that grimy, oil-stained garment, and put it on, and being pleased, uttered words of pleasure:

mn75:20.14.verse: ‘How fine is this white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’—out of faith in the man with good eyesight.”

mn75:21.1.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, wanderers of other sects are blind, without eyes, not knowing health, not seeing Nibbāna, and yet they speak this verse:

mn75:21.2.verse: ‘Health is the highest gain, Nibbāna is the highest bliss.’

mn75:21.3.verse: This verse, Māgaṇḍiya, was spoken by former Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Ones:

mn75:21.6.verse: and the Eightfold is the best of paths,

mn75:21.8.verse: That verse has now gradually become a verse of ordinary people.

mn75:21.9.verse: Now this body, Māgaṇḍiya, is a disease, a boil, a dart, a misery, an affliction; yet of this body, which is a disease, a boil, a dart, a misery, an affliction, you say:

mn75:21.10.verse: ‘This, Master Gotama, is that health, this is that Nibbāna.’

mn75:21.11.verse: For you, Māgaṇḍiya, have no noble eye by which you might know health and see Nibbāna.”

mn75:22.1.verse: “I have such confidence in Master Gotama

mn75:22.2.verse: that Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might come to know health and see Nibbāna.”

mn75:22.3.verse: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there were a man blind from birth;

mn75:22.4.verse: he could not see dark and light forms, could not see blue forms, could not see yellow forms, could not see red forms, could not see crimson forms, could not see what is even and uneven, could not see the stars, could not see the moon and sun.

mn75:22.5.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, might bring him a surgeon to treat him.

mn75:22.6.verse: The surgeon might make medicine for him.

mn75:22.7.verse: But through that medicine his eyesight might not arise, and might not be purified.

mn75:22.9.verse: would not that doctor reap nothing but weariness and vexation?”

mn75:22.11.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, were I to teach you the Dhamma thus:

mn75:22.12.verse: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you would not know health, you would not see Nibbāna.

mn75:22.13.verse: That would be nothing but weariness and vexation for me.”

mn75:23.1.verse: “I have such confidence in Master Gotama

mn75:23.2.verse: that Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might come to know health and see Nibbāna.”

mn75:23.3.verse: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there were a man blind from birth;

mn75:23.4.verse: he could not see dark and light forms, could not see blue forms, could not see yellow forms, could not see red forms, could not see crimson forms, could not see what is even and uneven, could not see the stars, could not see the moon and sun.

mn75:23.5.verse: He might hear a man with good eyesight saying:

mn75:23.6.verse: ‘Good sirs, how fine is a white cloth, beautiful, spotless, and clean!’

mn75:23.7.verse: He might go in search of a white cloth.

mn75:23.8.verse: Then a certain man might deceive him with a grimy, oil-stained garment, saying:

mn75:23.9.verse: ‘Good man, here is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean.’

mn75:23.10.verse: He might accept it, and having accepted it, put it on.

mn75:23.11.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, might bring him a surgeon to treat him.

mn75:23.12.verse: The surgeon might make medicine for him—

mn75:23.13.verse: an emetic, a purgative, an ointment, a counter-ointment, and treatment through the nose.

mn75:23.14.verse: And through that medicine his eyesight might arise and be purified.

mn75:23.15.verse: With the arising of his eyesight, whatever desire and lust he had for that grimy, oil-stained garment would be abandoned.

mn75:23.16.verse: He might regard that man as an enemy, as a foe, and might even think he deserved to be put to death, saying:

mn75:23.17.verse: ‘Indeed, sirs, for a long time I was tricked, deceived, and cheated by this man with this grimy, oil-stained garment—

mn75:23.18.verse: “Good man, here is a white cloth for you, beautiful, spotless, and clean.”’

mn75:24.1.verse: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, were I to teach you the Dhamma thus:

mn75:24.3.verse: you might come to know health, you might come to see Nibbāna.

mn75:24.4.verse: With the arising of your eye, whatever desire and lust you had for the five aggregates affected by clinging would be abandoned;

mn75:24.5.verse: and it might occur to you thus:

mn75:24.6.verse: ‘Indeed, sirs, for a long time I was tricked, deceived, and cheated by this mind.

mn75:24.7.verse: For clinging, I clung only to form; clinging, I clung only to feeling; clinging, I clung only to perception; clinging, I clung only to formations; clinging, I clung only to consciousness.

mn75:24.8.verse: With my clinging as condition, being came to be; with being as condition, birth; with birth as condition, ageing and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair came to be;

mn75:24.9.verse: such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”

mn75:25.1.verse: “I have such confidence in Master Gotama

mn75:25.2.verse: that Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind.”

mn75:25.3.verse: “In that case, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with true men.

mn75:25.4.verse: When you associate with true men, Māgaṇḍiya, you will hear the true Dhamma;

mn75:25.5.verse: when you hear the true Dhamma, you will practise in accordance with the Dhamma;

mn75:25.6.verse: when you practise in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know for yourself and see for yourself:

mn75:25.8.verse: and here diseases, boils, darts cease without remainder.

mn75:25.9.verse: With the cessation of my clinging, being ceases; with the cessation of being, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, ageing and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease;

mn75:25.10.verse: such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

mn75:26.1.verse: When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn75:26.3.verse: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.

mn75:26.4.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn75:26.5.verse: I would receive the Going-forth under Master Gotama, I would receive the Full Admission.”

mn75:27.1.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, one who formerly belonged to another sect and wishes for the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of the four months, bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give him the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state.

mn75:27.2.verse: But even here I have recognized a difference between individuals.”

mn75:27.3.verse: “Venerable sir, if those who formerly belonged to another sect and wish for the Going-forth and the Full Admission in this Dhamma and Discipline live on probation for four months, and at the end of four months bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give them the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state, then I will live on probation for four years, and at the end of the four years let bhikkhus who are satisfied in their minds give me the Going-forth into homelessness and the Full Admission to the bhikkhus’ state.”

mn75:28.1.verse: And Māgaṇḍiya the Wanderer received the Going-forth in the Blessed One’s presence, and he received the Full Admission.

mn75:28.2.verse: Not long after his Full Admission, the venerable Māgaṇḍiya, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, before long entered upon and abided in that supreme goal of the life divine, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge here and now.

mn75:28.3.verse: He directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn75:28.4.verse: And the venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the Arahants.

mn75:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma, on a grass mat in the fire chamber of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.

mn75:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadamma for alms.

mn75:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Kammāsadamma. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to a certain forest grove for the day’s meditation.

mn75:2.3.verse: Having plunged deep into it, he sat at the root of a certain tree to meditate.

mn75:3.1.verse: Then as the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was going for a walk he approached that fire chamber.

mn75:3.2.verse: He saw the grass mat spread out there

mn75:3.3.verse: and asked the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan,

mn75:3.4.verse: “Worthy Bhāradvāja, who has this grass mat been spread out for? It looks like an ascetic’s bed.”

mn75:4.1.verse: “There is the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family.

mn75:4.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn75:4.4.verse: This bed has been spread for that worthy Gotama.”

mn75:5.1.verse: “Well, it’s a sad sight, worthy Bhāradvāja,

mn75:5.3.verse: to see a bed for the worthy Gotama, that baby-killer!”

mn75:5.6.verse: Many astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and ascetics are devoted to the worthy Gotama. They’ve been guided by him in the noble system, the skillful teaching.”

mn75:5.7.verse: “Even if I was to see the worthy Gotama face to face, worthy Bhāradvāja, I would say to his face:

mn75:5.10.verse: For so it came to me while sleeping.”

mn75:5.11.verse: “If you don’t mind, I’ll tell the ascetic Gotama about this.”

mn75:5.12.verse: “Don’t worry, worthy Bhāradvāja. You may tell him exactly what I’ve said.”

mn75:6.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, the Buddha heard this discussion between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya.

mn75:6.2.verse: Coming out of retreat, he went to the brahmin’s fire chamber and sat on the grass mat.

mn75:6.3.verse: Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn75:6.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn75:6.5.verse: “Bhāradvāja, did you have a discussion with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya about this grass mat?”

mn75:6.6.verse: When he said this, the brahmin, shocked and awestruck, said to the Buddha,

mn75:6.7.verse: “I wanted to mention this very thing to the worthy Gotama,

mn75:6.8.verse: but you brought it up before I had a chance.”

mn75:7.1.verse: But this conversation between the Buddha and the brahmin was left unfinished.

mn75:7.2.verse: Then as the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was going for a walk he approached that fire chamber. He went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn75:7.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and the Buddha said to him:

mn75:8.1.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, the eye likes sights, it loves them and enjoys them.

mn75:8.2.verse: That’s been tamed, guarded, protected and restrained by the Realized One, and he teaches Dhamma for its restraint.

mn75:8.3.verse: Is that what you were referring to when you called me

mn75:8.5.verse: “That’s exactly what I was referring to.

mn75:8.8.verse: For so it came to me while sleeping.”

mn75:8.20.verse: The mind likes ideas, it loves them and enjoys them.

mn75:8.21.verse: That’s been tamed, guarded, protected and restrained by the Realized One, and he teaches Dhamma for its restraint.

mn75:8.22.verse: Is that what you were referring to when you called me

mn75:8.24.verse: “That’s exactly what I was referring to.

mn75:8.27.verse: For so it came to me while sleeping.”

mn75:9.2.verse: Take someone who used to amuse themselves with sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Some time later—having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of sights, and having given up craving and dispelled passion for sights—they would live rid of thirst, their mind settled internally.

mn75:9.3.verse: What would you have to say to them, Māgaṇḍiya?”

mn75:9.6.verse: Take someone who used to amuse themselves with sounds known by the ear …

mn75:9.9.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn75:9.10.verse: Some time later—having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of touches, and having given up craving and dispelled passion for touches—they would live rid of thirst, their mind settled internally.

mn75:9.11.verse: What would you have to say to them, Māgaṇḍiya?”

mn75:10.1.verse: “Well, when I was still a layperson I used to amuse myself, supplied and provided with sights known by the eye … sounds known by the ear …

mn75:10.4.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn75:10.6.verse: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer.

mn75:10.7.verse: I stayed in a stilt longhouse without coming downstairs for the four months of the rainy season, where I was entertained by musicians—none of them men.

mn75:10.8.verse: Some time later—having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of sensual pleasures, and having given up craving and dispelled passion for sensual pleasures—I live rid of thirst, my mind settled internally.

mn75:10.9.verse: I see other sentient beings who are not free from sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with passion for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.

mn75:10.10.verse: I don’t envy them, nor do I hope to enjoy that.

mn75:10.12.verse: Because there is a satisfaction that is apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities,

mn75:10.14.verse: Enjoying that satisfaction, I don’t envy what is inferior, nor do I hope to enjoy it.

mn75:11.1.verse: Suppose there was a householder or a householder’s child who was rich, affluent, and wealthy. And they would amuse themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation. That is, sights known by the eye …

mn75:11.3.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn75:11.4.verse: Having practiced good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, when their body breaks up, after death, they’d be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three.

mn75:11.5.verse: There they’d amuse themselves in the Garden of Delight, escorted by a band of nymphs, supplied and provided with the five kinds of heavenly sensual stimulation.

mn75:11.6.verse: Then they’d see a householder or a householder’s child amusing themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn75:11.7.verse: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya?
