Would that god—amusing themselves in the Garden of Delight, escorted by a band of nymphs, supplied and provided with the five kinds of heavenly sensual stimulation—envy that householder or householder’s child their five kinds of human sensual stimulation, or return to human sensual pleasures?”

mn75:11.10.verse: Because heavenly sensual pleasures are better than human sensual pleasures.”

mn75:12.1.verse: “In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, when I was still a layperson I used to amuse myself with sights … sounds …

mn75:12.4.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn75:12.5.verse: Some time later—having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of sensual pleasures, and having given up craving and dispelled passion for sensual pleasures—I live rid of thirst, my mind settled internally.

mn75:12.6.verse: I see other sentient beings who are not free from sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with passion for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I don’t envy them, nor do I hope to enjoy that.

mn75:12.8.verse: Because there is a satisfaction that is apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities,

mn75:12.10.verse: Enjoying that satisfaction, I don’t envy what is inferior, nor do I hope to enjoy it.

mn75:13.1.verse: Suppose there was a person affected by leprosy, with sores and blisters on their limbs. Being devoured by worms, scratching with their nails at the opening of their wounds, they’d cauterize their body over a pit of glowing coals.

mn75:13.2.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn75:13.3.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for them,

mn75:13.4.verse: and by using that they’d be cured of leprosy. They’d be healthy, happy, autonomous, master of themselves, able to go where they wanted.

mn75:13.5.verse: Then they’d see another person affected by leprosy, with sores and blisters on their limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching with their nails at the opening of their wounds, cauterizing their body over a pit of glowing coals.

mn75:13.7.verse: Would that person envy that other person affected by leprosy for their pit of glowing coals or for taking medicine?”

mn75:13.10.verse: Because you need to take medicine only when there’s a disease. When there’s no disease, there’s no need for medicine.”

mn75:14.1.verse: “In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, when I was still a layperson I used to amuse myself with sights … sounds …

mn75:14.4.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn75:14.5.verse: Some time later—having truly understood the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of sensual pleasures, and having given up craving and dispelled passion for sensual pleasures—I live rid of thirst, my mind settled internally.

mn75:14.6.verse: I see other sentient beings who are not free from sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with passion for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.

mn75:14.7.verse: I don’t envy them, nor do I hope to enjoy that.

mn75:14.9.verse: Because there is a satisfaction that is apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities,

mn75:14.11.verse: Enjoying that satisfaction, I don’t envy what is inferior, nor do I hope to enjoy it.

mn75:15.1.verse: Suppose there was a person affected by leprosy, with sores and blisters on their limbs. Being devoured by worms, scratching with their nails at the opening of their wounds, they’d cauterize their body over a pit of glowing coals.

mn75:15.2.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn75:15.3.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for them,

mn75:15.4.verse: and by using that they’d be cured of leprosy. They’d be healthy, happy, autonomous, master of themselves, able to go where they wanted.

mn75:15.5.verse: Two strong men would grab them by the arms and drag them toward the pit of glowing coals.

mn75:15.7.verse: Wouldn’t that person writhe and struggle to and fro?”

mn75:15.10.verse: Because that fire is really painful to touch, fiercely burning and scorching.”

mn75:15.12.verse: Is it only now that the fire is really painful to touch, fiercely burning and scorching, or was it painful previously as well?”

mn75:15.13.verse: “That fire is painful now and it was also painful previously.

mn75:15.14.verse: That person was affected by leprosy, with sores and blisters on their limbs. Being devoured by worms, scratching with their nails at the opening of their wounds, their sense faculties were impaired. So even though the fire was actually painful to touch, they had a distorted perception that it was pleasant.”

mn75:16.1.verse: “In the same way, sensual pleasures of the past, future, and present are painful to touch, fiercely burning and scorching.

mn75:16.2.verse: These sentient beings who are not free from sensual pleasures—being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with passion for sensual pleasures—have impaired sense faculties. So even though sensual pleasures are actually painful to touch, they have a distorted perception that they are pleasant.

mn75:17.1.verse: Suppose there was a person affected by leprosy, with sores and blisters on their limbs. Being devoured by worms, scratching with their nails at the opening of their wounds, they’re cauterizing their body over a pit of glowing coals.

mn75:17.2.verse: The more they scratch their wounds and cauterize their body, the more their wounds become foul, stinking, and infected. But still, they derive a degree of pleasure and gratification from the itchiness of their wounds.

mn75:17.3.verse: In the same way, I see other sentient beings who are not free from sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with passion for sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.

mn75:17.4.verse: The more they indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures grows, and the more they burn with passion for sensual pleasures. But still, they derive a degree of pleasure and gratification from the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn75:18.2.verse: Have you seen or heard of a king or a royal minister of the past, future, or present, amusing themselves supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation, who—without giving up craving for sensual pleasures and dispelling passion for sensual pleasures—lives rid of thirst, their mind settled internally?”

mn75:18.6.verse: On the contrary, all the ascetics or brahmins of the past, future, or present who live rid of thirst, their minds settled internally, do so after truly understanding the origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape of sensual pleasures, and after giving up craving and dispelling passion for sensual pleasures.”

mn75:19.1.verse: Then on that occasion the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

mn75:19.4.verse: Of paths, the ultimate is eightfold—

mn75:19.5.verse: it’s safe, and leads to freedom from death.”

mn75:19.6.verse: When he said this, Māgaṇḍiya said to him,

mn75:19.8.verse: How well said this was by the worthy Gotama!

mn75:19.9.verse: ‘Health is the ultimate blessing; extinguishment, the ultimate happiness.’

mn75:19.10.verse: I’ve also heard that wanderers of the past, the tutors of tutors, said:

mn75:19.11.verse: ‘Health is the ultimate blessing; extinguishment, the ultimate happiness.’

mn75:19.13.verse: “But Māgaṇḍiya, when you heard that wanderers of the past said this,

mn75:19.14.verse: what is that health? And what is that extinguishment?”

mn75:19.15.verse: When he said this, Māgaṇḍiya stroked his own limbs with his hands, saying:

mn75:19.16.verse: “This is that health, worthy Gotama, this is that extinguishment!

mn75:19.17.verse: For I am now healthy and happy, and have no afflictions.”

mn75:20.1.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, suppose a person was blind from birth.

mn75:20.2.verse: They couldn’t see sights that are dark or bright, or blue, yellow, red, or magenta. They couldn’t see even and uneven ground, or the stars, or the moon and sun.

mn75:20.3.verse: They might hear a sighted person saying:

mn75:20.4.verse: ‘White cloth is really nice, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.’

mn75:20.5.verse: They’d go in search of white cloth.

mn75:20.6.verse: But someone would cheat them with a dirty, soiled garment, saying:

mn75:20.7.verse: ‘My man, here is a white cloth for you, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.’

mn75:20.8.verse: They’d take it and put it on, expressing their gladness:

mn75:20.9.verse: ‘White cloth is really nice, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.’

mn75:20.11.verse: Did that person blind from birth do this knowing and seeing,

mn75:20.12.verse: or out of faith in the sighted person?”

mn75:20.13.verse: “They did so not knowing or seeing,

mn75:20.14.verse: but out of faith in the sighted person.”

mn75:21.1.verse: “In the same way, the wanderers of other religions are blind and sightless. Not knowing health and not seeing extinguishment, they still recite this verse:

mn75:21.2.verse: ‘Health is the ultimate blessing; extinguishment, the ultimate happiness.’

mn75:21.3.verse: For this verse was recited by the perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas of the past:

mn75:21.6.verse: Of paths, the ultimate is eightfold—

mn75:21.7.verse: it’s safe, and leads to freedom from death.’

mn75:21.8.verse: These days it has gradually become a verse used by ordinary people.

mn75:21.9.verse: But Māgaṇḍiya, this body is a disease, a boil, a dart, a gloom, an affliction. Yet you say of this body:

mn75:21.10.verse: ‘This is that health, this is that extinguishment!’

mn75:21.11.verse: Māgaṇḍiya, you don’t have the noble vision by which you might know health and see extinguishment.”

mn75:22.1.verse: “I am quite confident that the worthy Gotama

mn75:22.2.verse: is capable of teaching me so that I can know health and see extinguishment.”

mn75:22.3.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, suppose a person was blind from birth.

mn75:22.4.verse: They couldn’t see sights that are dark or bright, or blue, yellow, red, or magenta. They couldn’t see even and uneven ground, or the stars, or the moon and sun.

mn75:22.5.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn75:22.6.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for them,

mn75:22.7.verse: but when they used it their eyes were not cured and they still could not see clearly.

mn75:22.9.verse: Wouldn’t that doctor just get weary and frustrated?”

mn75:22.11.verse: “In the same way, suppose I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying:

mn75:22.12.verse: ‘This is that health, this is that extinguishment.’ But you might not know health or see extinguishment,

mn75:22.13.verse: which would be wearying and troublesome for me.”

mn75:23.1.verse: “I am quite confident that the worthy Gotama

mn75:23.2.verse: is capable of teaching me so that I can know health and see extinguishment.”

mn75:23.3.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, suppose a person was blind from birth.

mn75:23.4.verse: They couldn’t see sights that are dark or bright, or blue, yellow, red, or magenta. They couldn’t see even and uneven ground, or the stars, or the moon and sun.

mn75:23.5.verse: They might hear a sighted person saying:

mn75:23.6.verse: ‘White cloth is really nice, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.’

mn75:23.7.verse: They’d go in search of white cloth.

mn75:23.8.verse: But someone would cheat them with a dirty, soiled garment, saying:

mn75:23.9.verse: ‘My man, here is a white cloth for you, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.’

mn75:23.10.verse: They’d take it and put it on.

mn75:23.11.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn75:23.12.verse: The surgeon would make medicine for them:

mn75:23.13.verse: emetics, purgatives, ointment, counter-ointment, or nasal treatment.

mn75:23.14.verse: And when they used it their eyes would be cured so that they could see clearly.

mn75:23.15.verse: As soon as their eyes were cured they’d lose all desire for that dirty, soiled garment.

mn75:23.16.verse: Then they would consider that person to be no friend, but an enemy, and might even think of murdering them:

mn75:23.17.verse: ‘For such a long time I’ve been cheated, tricked, and deceived by that person with this dirty, soiled garment when he said,

mn75:23.18.verse: “My man, here is a white cloth for you, it’s attractive, stainless, and clean.”’

mn75:24.1.verse: In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, suppose I were to teach you the Dhamma, saying:

mn75:24.2.verse: ‘This is that health, this is that extinguishment.’

mn75:24.3.verse: You might know health and see extinguishment.

mn75:24.4.verse: And as soon as your vision arises you might give up desire for the five grasping aggregates.

mn75:24.6.verse: ‘For such a long time I’ve been cheated, tricked, and deceived by this mind.

mn75:24.7.verse: For what I have been grasping is only form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn75:24.8.verse: My grasping is a requirement for continued existence. Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn75:24.9.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’”

mn75:25.1.verse: “I am quite confident that the worthy Gotama

mn75:25.2.verse: is capable of teaching me so that I can rise from this seat cured of blindness.”

mn75:25.3.verse: “Well then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with true persons.

mn75:25.4.verse: When you associate with true persons, you will hear the true teaching.

mn75:25.5.verse: When you hear the true teaching, you’ll practice in line with the teaching.

mn75:25.6.verse: When you practice in line with the teaching, you’ll know and see for yourself:

mn75:25.8.verse: And here is where diseases, boils, and darts cease without remainder.’

mn75:25.9.verse: When my grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn75:25.10.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”

mn75:26.1.verse: When he said this, Māgaṇḍiya said to him,

mn75:26.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn75:26.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn75:26.5.verse: May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama’s presence?”

mn75:27.1.verse: “Māgaṇḍiya, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they’ll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.

mn75:27.2.verse: However, I recognize individual differences in this matter.”

mn75:27.3.verse: “Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I’ll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.”

mn75:28.1.verse: And the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

mn75:28.2.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Māgaṇḍiya, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn75:28.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn75:28.4.verse: And Venerable Māgaṇḍiya became one of the perfected.

mn76:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.

mn76:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion Sandaka the Wanderer was staying in the Pilakkha-tree Cave together with a large assembly of about five hundred wanderers.

mn76:3.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Ānanda rose from meditation and addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn76:3.2.verse: “Come, friends, let us go to the Rain Pool to see the cave.”

mn76:3.3.verse: “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda.

mn76:3.4.verse: Then the venerable Ānanda went to the Rain Pool together with a number of bhikkhus.

mn76:4.1.verse: Now on that occasion Sandaka the Wanderer was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers who were shouting and making a great uproar and noise, talking many kinds of pointless talk,[^1] such as:

mn76:4.2.verse: talk of kings, talk of robbers, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of countries, talk of women, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of wells, talk of the departed, various idle tales, speculation about the world, speculation about the sea, talk of whether things are or are not, and so on.

mn76:4.3.verse: Sandaka the Wanderer saw the venerable Ānanda coming in the distance.

mn76:4.4.verse: Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:

mn76:4.5.verse: “Be quiet, sirs, do not make a noise;

mn76:4.6.verse: here comes the ascetic Ānanda, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn76:4.7.verse: Of those disciples of the ascetic Gotama who are staying at Kosambī, this ascetic Ānanda is one.

mn76:4.8.verse: Those venerable ones like quiet, are trained in quiet, and speak in praise of quiet;

mn76:4.9.verse: perhaps, finding our assembly quiet, he will think it fit to approach.”

mn76:5.1.verse: Then the venerable Ānanda went up to Sandaka the Wanderer.

mn76:5.2.verse: Sandaka the Wanderer said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn76:5.3.verse: “Let Master Ānanda come; welcome to Master Ānanda.

mn76:5.4.verse: It is long, Master Ānanda, since you made an occasion to come here.

mn76:5.5.verse: Let Master Ānanda be seated; this seat is ready.”

mn76:5.6.verse: The venerable Ānanda sat down on the seat made ready.

mn76:5.7.verse: And Sandaka the Wanderer took a certain low seat and sat down at one side.

mn76:5.8.verse: The venerable Ānanda then said to Sandaka the Wanderer, as he sat at one side:

mn76:5.9.verse: “What talk are you gathered here for now, Sandaka? And what was your discussion that was left unfinished?”

mn76:5.10.verse: “Let that be, Master Ānanda, this talk for which we are now gathered here.

mn76:5.11.verse: It will not be hard for Master Ānanda to hear about it later too.

mn76:5.12.verse: It would be good if a talk on the Dhamma in his own teacher’s tradition should occur to Master Ānanda himself.”

mn76:5.13.verse: “Well then, Sandaka, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn76:5.14.verse: “Yes, sir,” Sandaka the Wanderer replied to the venerable Ānanda.

mn76:6.1.verse: “Sandaka, these four kinds of life that are not the life divine have been declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, and these four kinds of life divine without consolation have also been declared, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”

mn76:6.2.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, what are those four kinds of life that are not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”

mn76:7.1.verse: “Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:

mn76:7.2.verse: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world, who have travelled the right path and practised rightly.[^2]

mn76:7.3.verse: This person is made up of the four great elements, and when he dies, the earth in him returns and goes back to the body of earth, the water returns and goes back to the body of water, the fire returns and goes back to the body of fire, the air returns and goes back to the body of air, and the faculties pass over into space.

mn76:7.4.verse: Four men, with the bier as the fifth, carry the corpse away;

mn76:7.5.verse: eulogies are spoken only as far as the charnel ground;

mn76:7.8.verse: giving is a doctrine fabricated by fools.

mn76:7.9.verse: The talk of those who assert there is something is empty, false chatter.

mn76:7.10.verse: Both fools and the wise, at the breaking up of the body, are annihilated, perish, and do not exist after death.’

mn76:8.1.verse: “About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:8.2.verse: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—

mn76:8.3.verse: there is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world, who have travelled the right path and practised rightly.

mn76:8.4.verse: This person is made up of the four great elements, and when he dies, the earth in him returns and goes back to the body of earth, the water returns and goes back to the body of water, the fire returns and goes back to the body of fire, the air returns and goes back to the body of air, and the faculties pass over into space.

mn76:8.5.verse: Four men, with the bier as the fifth, carry the corpse away; eulogies are spoken only as far as the charnel ground.

mn76:8.8.verse: giving is a doctrine fabricated by fools.

mn76:8.9.verse: The talk of those who assert there is something is empty, false chatter.

mn76:8.10.verse: Both fools and the wise, at the breaking up of the body, are annihilated, perish, and do not exist after death.’

mn76:8.11.verse: If this good teacher’s word is true, then, without having done anything, I have done what had to be done here; without having lived the life, I have lived it here.

mn76:8.12.verse: Both of us are equal here, having attained the ascetic life, in that I do not say: ‘Both of us, at the breaking up of the body, will be annihilated, will perish, and will not exist after death.’

mn76:8.13.verse: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.

mn76:8.14.verse: So what do I know, what do I see, that I should live the life divine under this teacher?

mn76:8.16.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:9.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the first kind of life that is not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:10.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:

mn76:10.2.verse: ‘For one who acts or causes others to act, for one who mutilates or causes others to mutilate, for one who tortures or causes others to torture, for one who inflicts sorrow or causes others to inflict sorrow, for one who oppresses or causes others to oppress, for one who intimidates or causes others to intimidate, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, waylays highways, commits adultery, speaks falsehood—no evil is done by the doer.

mn76:10.3.verse: Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make all the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

mn76:10.4.verse: Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and causing others to kill, mutilating and causing others to mutilate, torturing and causing others to torture, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

mn76:10.5.verse: Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing others to give, offering sacrifice and causing others to offer sacrifice, there would be no merit resulting from that, no coming of merit.

mn76:10.6.verse: By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’

mn76:11.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:11.2.verse: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—

mn76:11.3.verse: for one who acts or causes others to act, for one who mutilates or causes others to mutilate, for one who tortures or causes others to torture, for one who inflicts sorrow or causes others to inflict sorrow, for one who oppresses or causes others to oppress, for one who intimidates or causes others to intimidate, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, waylays highways, commits adultery, speaks falsehood—no evil is done by the doer. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make all the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

mn76:11.4.verse: Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and causing others to kill, mutilating and causing others to mutilate, torturing and causing others to torture, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.

mn76:11.5.verse: Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing others to give, offering sacrifice and causing others to offer sacrifice, there would be no merit resulting from that, no coming of merit.

mn76:11.6.verse: By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’

mn76:11.7.verse: If this good teacher’s word is true, then, without having done anything, I have done what had to be done here; without having lived the life, I have lived it here.

mn76:11.8.verse: Both of us are equal here, having attained the ascetic life, in that I do not say: ‘No evil is done by either of us in acting.’

mn76:11.9.verse: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.

mn76:11.10.verse: So what do I know, what do I see, that I should live the life divine under this teacher?

mn76:11.12.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:12.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the second kind of life that is not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:13.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:

mn76:13.2.verse: ‘There is no cause, no condition, for the defilement of beings;

mn76:13.3.verse: beings are defiled without cause or condition;

mn76:13.4.verse: there is no cause, no condition, for the purification of beings;

mn76:13.5.verse: beings are purified without cause or condition;

mn76:13.6.verse: there is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly effort;

mn76:13.7.verse: all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy; shaped by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes.’

mn76:14.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:14.2.verse: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—

mn76:14.3.verse: there is no cause, no condition, for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition.

mn76:14.4.verse: There is no cause, no condition, for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.

mn76:14.5.verse: There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly effort; all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy; shaped by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes.’

mn76:14.6.verse: If this good teacher’s word is true, then, without having done anything, I have done what had to be done here; without having lived the life, I have lived it here.

mn76:14.7.verse: Both of us are equal here, having attained the ascetic life, in that I do not say: ‘Both of us will be purified without cause or condition.’

mn76:14.8.verse: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.

mn76:14.9.verse: So what do I know, what do I see, that I should live the life divine under this teacher?

mn76:14.11.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:15.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the third kind of life that is not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:16.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:

mn76:16.2.verse: ‘There are these seven bodies that are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar;

mn76:16.3.verse: they do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another, and are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.

mn76:16.5.verse: The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the soul as the seventh—

mn76:16.6.verse: these seven bodies are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar.

mn76:16.7.verse: They do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another, and are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.

mn76:16.8.verse: Herein there is no slayer nor one who causes slaying, no hearer nor one who causes hearing, no cognizer nor one who causes cognizing.

mn76:16.9.verse: Even one who cuts off another’s head with a sharp sword does not deprive anyone of life;

mn76:16.10.verse: the sword simply passes through the gap between the seven bodies.

mn76:16.11.verse: There are, moreover, fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs, and six thousand more, and six hundred more; five hundred kinds of action, and five kinds of action, and three kinds of action; a kind of action and a half-kind of action; sixty-two paths; sixty-two sub-aeons; six classes; eight stages of man; four thousand nine hundred kinds of livelihood; four thousand nine hundred kinds of wanderers; four thousand nine hundred abodes of nāgas; two thousand faculties; three thousand hells; thirty-six elements of dust; seven percipient wombs; seven non-percipient wombs; seven wombless wombs; seven kinds of gods; seven kinds of humans; seven kinds of demons; seven lakes; seven knots; seven precipices; seven hundred precipices; seven dreams; seven hundred dreams; and eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons through which, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.[^9]

mn76:16.12.verse: Herein there is no such thing as: “By this virtue, or this observance, or this austerity, or this life divine, I shall ripen unripened action, or, by repeatedly experiencing it, exhaust ripened action.”

mn76:16.13.verse: Pleasure and pain are meted out as by a measure, and the round of rebirths has a fixed limit; there is no decrease or increase, no rising or falling.

mn76:16.14.verse: Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds itself as it runs;

mn76:16.15.verse: so too, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.’

mn76:17.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:17.2.verse: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—

mn76:17.3.verse: there are these seven bodies that are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar.

mn76:17.4.verse: They do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another.

mn76:17.5.verse: They are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.

mn76:17.7.verse: The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the soul as the seventh—

mn76:17.8.verse: these seven bodies are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar.

mn76:17.9.verse: They do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another.

mn76:17.10.verse: They are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.

mn76:17.11.verse: Herein there is no slayer nor one who causes slaying, no hearer nor one who causes hearing, no cognizer nor one who causes cognizing.

mn76:17.12.verse: Even one who cuts off another’s head with a sharp sword does not deprive anyone of life;

mn76:17.13.verse: the sword simply passes through the gap between the seven bodies.

mn76:17.14.verse: There are, moreover, fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs, and six thousand more, and six hundred more; five hundred kinds of action, and five kinds of action, and three kinds of action; a kind of action and a half-kind of action; sixty-two paths; sixty-two sub-aeons; six classes; eight stages of man; four thousand nine hundred kinds of livelihood; four thousand nine hundred kinds of wanderers; four thousand nine hundred abodes of nāgas; two thousand faculties; three thousand hells; thirty-six elements of dust; seven percipient wombs; seven non-percipient wombs; seven wombless wombs; seven kinds of gods; seven kinds of humans; seven kinds of demons; seven lakes; seven knots; seven precipices; seven hundred precipices; seven dreams; seven hundred dreams; and eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons through which, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.

mn76:17.15.verse: Herein there is no such thing as: “By this virtue, or this observance, or this austerity, or this life divine, I shall ripen unripened action, or, by repeatedly experiencing it, exhaust ripened action.” Pleasure and pain are meted out as by a measure, and the round of rebirths has a fixed limit; there is no decrease or increase, no rising or falling.

mn76:17.16.verse: Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds itself as it runs;

mn76:17.17.verse: so too, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.’

mn76:17.18.verse: If this good teacher’s word is true, then, without having done anything, I have done what had to be done here; without having lived the life, I have lived it here.

mn76:17.19.verse: Both of us are equal here, having attained the ascetic life, in that I do not say: ‘Both of us, running on and wandering on, will make an end of suffering.’

mn76:17.20.verse: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.

mn76:17.21.verse: So what do I know, what do I see, that I should live the life divine under this teacher?

mn76:17.23.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:18.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the fourth kind of life that is not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:19.1.verse: These, Sandaka, are the four kinds of life that are not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”

mn76:20.1.verse: “It is wonderful, Master Ānanda, it is marvellous, Master Ānanda,

mn76:20.2.verse: how these four kinds of life that are actually not the life divine have been declared as ‘not the life divine’ by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:20.3.verse: But, Master Ānanda, what are those four kinds of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”

mn76:21.1.verse: “Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus:

mn76:21.2.verse: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.’

mn76:21.3.verse: He enters an empty house, gets no almsfood, is bitten by a dog, meets a fierce elephant, meets a fierce horse, meets a fierce ox, asks the name and clan of a woman or a man, asks the name of a village or town and the way to it.[^4]

mn76:21.4.verse: When asked: ‘Why is that?’[^3] he says: ‘I had to enter an empty house, that is why I entered it; I was not to get almsfood, that is why I did not get it; I had to be bitten by a dog, that is why I was bitten; I had to meet a fierce elephant, that is why I met it; I had to meet a fierce horse, that is why I met it; I had to meet a fierce ox, that is why I met it; I had to ask the name and clan of a woman or a man, that is why I asked; I had to ask the name of a village or town and the way to it, that is why I asked.’

mn76:22.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:22.2.verse: ‘This good teacher claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision … “I had to ask the name of a village or town and the way to it, that is why I asked.”’

mn76:22.4.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:23.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the first kind of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:24.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth.[^5]

mn76:24.2.verse: He teaches a Dhamma by oral tradition, by legend handed down from generation to generation, by what has come down in the scriptures.

mn76:24.3.verse: But for a teacher who relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, some things are well remembered and some are badly remembered, and some are so and some are otherwise.[^6]

mn76:25.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:25.2.verse: ‘This good teacher relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, and teaches a Dhamma by oral tradition, by legend handed down from generation to generation, by what has come down in the scriptures.

mn76:25.3.verse: But for a teacher who relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, some things are well remembered and some are badly remembered, and some are so and some are otherwise.’

mn76:25.5.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:26.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the second kind of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:27.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is a rationalist, an investigator.

mn76:27.2.verse: He teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of investigation as it occurs to him.

mn76:27.3.verse: But for a teacher who is a rationalist, an investigator, some things are well reasoned and some are badly reasoned, and some are so and some are otherwise.

mn76:28.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:28.2.verse: ‘This good teacher is a rationalist, an investigator.

mn76:28.3.verse: He teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of investigation as it occurs to him.

mn76:28.4.verse: But for a teacher who is a rationalist, an investigator, some things are well reasoned and some are badly reasoned, and some are so and some are otherwise.’

mn76:28.6.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:29.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the third kind of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:30.1.verse: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is dull and confused.

mn76:30.2.verse: Being dull and confused, when questioned on this or that point, he resorts to verbal evasion, to eel-wriggling:

mn76:30.3.verse: ‘I don’t say it is so; I don’t say it is thus; I don’t say it is otherwise; I don’t say it is not so; nor do I say it is not not so.’

mn76:31.1.verse: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:

mn76:31.2.verse: ‘This good teacher is dull and confused.

mn76:31.3.verse: Being dull and confused, when questioned on this or that point, he resorts to verbal evasion, to eel-wriggling—

mn76:31.4.verse: “I don’t say it is so; I don’t say it is thus; I don’t say it is otherwise; I don’t say it is not so; nor do I say it is not not so.”’

mn76:31.6.verse: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:32.1.verse: This, Sandaka, is the fourth kind of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:33.1.verse: These, Sandaka, are the four kinds of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”

mn76:34.1.verse: “It is wonderful, Master Ānanda, it is marvellous, Master Ānanda,

mn76:34.2.verse: how these four kinds of life divine that are actually without consolation have been declared as ‘without consolation’ by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:34.3.verse: But, Master Ānanda, what does that Teacher assert, what does he declare, wherein a wise man would certainly live the life divine, and, living it, would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”

mn76:35-42.1.verse: “Here, Sandaka, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed …

mn76:35-42.2.verse: … having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of mind that weaken wisdom,

mn76:35-42.3.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn76:35-42.4.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:43.1.verse: Again, Sandaka, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …

mn76:43.2.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:44-45.1.verse: Again, Sandaka, with the fading away of joy as well, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity … and enters upon and abides in the third jhāna …

mn76:44-45.2.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:46.1.verse: Again, Sandaka, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna …

mn76:46.2.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:47.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

mn76:47.2.verse: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

mn76:47.3.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:48.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn76:48.2.verse: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.

mn76:48.3.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.

mn76:49.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn76:49.2.verse: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;

mn76:49.3.verse: he understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’

mn76:50.1.verse: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn76:50.2.verse: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn76:50.3.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn76:50.4.verse: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”

mn76:51.1.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, would a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—would he indulge in sensual pleasures?”

mn76:51.2.verse: “Sandaka, a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in five instances.

mn76:51.3.verse: A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted is incapable of deliberately depriving a living being of life; he is incapable of taking what is not given in the manner of theft; he is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse; he is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie; he is incapable of storing up goods for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, as he formerly did as a householder.

mn76:51.4.verse: A bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in these five instances.”

mn76:52.1.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is the knowledge and vision continuously and unceasingly present to him, whether he is walking or standing, asleep or awake, that:

mn76:52.3.verse: “Well then, Sandaka, I shall give you a simile;

mn76:52.4.verse: for by means of a simile some wise men here understand the meaning of what is said.

mn76:52.5.verse: Suppose, Sandaka, a man’s hands and feet were cut off;[^10]

mn76:52.6.verse: would he, whether walking or standing, asleep or awake, continuously and unceasingly know:

mn76:52.7.verse: ‘my hands and feet are cut off,’ or would he know it only when he reviews the fact:

mn76:52.8.verse: ‘my hands and feet are cut off’?”

mn76:52.9.verse: “That man, Master Ānanda, does not continuously and unceasingly know:

mn76:52.10.verse: ‘my hands and feet are cut off.’

mn76:52.11.verse: Rather, he knows it when he reviews the fact:

mn76:52.12.verse: ‘my hands and feet are cut off.’”

mn76:52.13.verse: “So too, Sandaka, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, the knowledge and vision is not continuously and unceasingly present to him, whether he is walking or standing, asleep or awake, that:

mn76:52.15.verse: rather, he knows it when he reviews the fact:

mn76:53.1.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, how many guides[^7] are there in this Dhamma and Discipline?”

mn76:53.2.verse: “There are not just one hundred, Sandaka, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but far more than that, who are guides in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

mn76:53.3.verse: “It is wonderful, Master Ānanda, it is marvellous, Master Ānanda.

mn76:53.4.verse: There will be no extolling of one’s own doctrine, no disparaging of others’ doctrines, but the teaching of the Dhamma will be within its proper scope, and yet so many guides are seen.

mn76:53.5.verse: But these Ājīvaka ascetics, mothers’ dead sons,[^8] both extol themselves and disparage others, and yet they proclaim only three guides, namely:

mn76:53.6.verse: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla.”

mn76:54.1.verse: Then Sandaka the Wanderer addressed his own assembly:

mn76:54.2.verse: “Sirs, go and live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama.

mn76:54.3.verse: It is not easy now for us to give up gain, honour, and fame.”

mn76:54.4.verse: So Sandaka the Wanderer sent his own assembly to live the life divine under the Blessed One.

mn76:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

mn76:2.1.verse: Now at that time the wanderer Sandaka was residing at the cave of the wavy leaf fig tree together with a large assembly of around five hundred wanderers.

mn76:3.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat and addressed the mendicants:

mn76:3.2.verse: “Come, reverends, let’s go to the Devakata Pool to see the cave.”

mn76:3.4.verse: Then Ānanda together with several mendicants went to the Devakata Pool.

mn76:4.1.verse: Now at that time, Sandaka and the large assembly of wanderers were sitting together making an uproar, a colossal racket. They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as

mn76:4.2.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

mn76:4.3.verse: Sandaka saw Ānanda coming off in the distance,

mn76:4.5.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

mn76:4.6.verse: The ascetic Ānanda, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming.

mn76:4.7.verse: He is included among the disciples of the ascetic Gotama, who is residing near Kosambī.

mn76:4.8.verse: Such venerables like the quiet, are educated to be quiet, and praise the quiet.

mn76:4.9.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

mn76:5.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the wanderer Sandaka,

mn76:5.4.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

mn76:5.5.verse: Please sit down, here, a seat is ready.”

mn76:5.6.verse: Ānanda sat down on the seat spread out,

mn76:5.7.verse: while Sandaka took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn76:5.9.verse: “Sandaka, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

mn76:5.10.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, leave aside what we were sitting talking about just now.

mn76:5.11.verse: It won’t be hard for you to hear about that later.

mn76:5.12.verse: It’d be great if Mister Ānanda himself would give a Dhamma talk explaining his own denomination.”

mn76:5.13.verse: “Well then, Sandaka, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn76:6.1.verse: “Sandaka, these things have been explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha: four ways that negate the spiritual life, and four kinds of unreliable spiritual life. A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, not practice such spiritual paths, and if they did practice them, they wouldn’t succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn76:6.2.verse: “But worthy Ānanda, what are the four ways that negate the spiritual life, and the four kinds of unreliable spiritual life?”

mn76:7.1.verse: “Sandaka, take a certain teacher who has this doctrine and view:

mn76:7.2.verse: ‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.

mn76:7.3.verse: This person is made up of the four principal states. When they die, the earth in their body progresses and proceeds to the substance of earth. The water in their body progresses and proceeds to the substance of water. The fire in their body progresses and proceeds to the substance of fire. The air in their body progresses and proceeds to the substance of air. The faculties are transferred to space.

mn76:7.4.verse: Four men with a bier carry away the corpse.

mn76:7.5.verse: Their footprints show the way to the cremation ground.

mn76:7.7.verse: Offerings dedicated to the gods end in ashes.

mn76:7.8.verse: Giving is a doctrine of morons.

mn76:7.9.verse: When anyone affirms a positive teaching it’s just hollow, false nonsense.

mn76:7.10.verse: Both the foolish and the astute are annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and they don’t exist after death.’

mn76:8.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:8.2.verse: ‘This teacher has such a doctrine and view.

mn76:8.11.verse: If what that teacher says is true, both I who have not accomplished this and one who has accomplished it

mn76:8.12.verse: have attained exactly the same level. Yet I’m not one who says that both of us are annihilated and destroyed when our body breaks up, and we don’t exist after death.

mn76:8.13.verse: But it’s superfluous for this teacher to go nude, bald, persisting in squatting, tearing out their hair and beard. For I’m living at home with my children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency. Yet I’ll have exactly the same destiny in the next life as this teacher.

mn76:8.14.verse: What do I know or see that I should lead the spiritual life under this teacher?

mn76:9.1.verse: This is the first way that negates the spiritual life.

mn76:10.1.verse: Furthermore, take a certain teacher who has this doctrine and view:

mn76:10.2.verse: ‘The one who acts does nothing wrong when they punish, mutilate, torture, aggrieve, oppress, intimidate, or when they encourage others to do the same. Nothing bad is done when they kill, steal, break into houses, plunder wealth, steal from isolated buildings, commit highway robbery, commit adultery, and lie.

mn76:10.3.verse: If you were to reduce all the living creatures of this earth to one heap and mass of flesh with a razor-edged chakram, no evil comes of that, and no outcome of evil.

mn76:10.4.verse: If you were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing, mutilating, and torturing, and encouraging others to do the same, no evil comes of that, and no outcome of evil.

mn76:10.5.verse: If you were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and sacrificing and encouraging others to do the same, no merit comes of that, and no outcome of merit.

mn76:10.6.verse: In giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness there is no merit or outcome of merit.’

mn76:11.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:11.2.verse: ‘This teacher has such a doctrine and view.

mn76:11.7.verse: If what that teacher says is true, both I who have not accomplished this and one who has accomplished it

mn76:11.8.verse: have attained exactly the same level. Yet I’m not one who says that when both of us act, nothing wrong is done.

mn76:11.9.verse: But it’s superfluous for this teacher to go nude, bald, persisting in squatting, tearing out their hair and beard. For I’m living at home with my children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency. Yet I’ll have exactly the same destiny in the next life as this teacher.

mn76:11.10.verse: What do I know or see that I should lead the spiritual life under this teacher?

mn76:12.1.verse: This is the second way that negates the spiritual life.

mn76:13.1.verse: Furthermore, take a certain teacher who has this doctrine and view:

mn76:13.2.verse: ‘There is no cause or reason for the corruption of sentient beings.

mn76:13.3.verse: Sentient beings are corrupted without cause or reason.

mn76:13.4.verse: There’s no cause or reason for the purification of sentient beings.

mn76:13.5.verse: Sentient beings are purified without cause or reason.

mn76:13.6.verse: There is no power, no energy, no human strength or vigor.

mn76:13.7.verse: All sentient beings, all living creatures, all beings, all souls lack control, power, and energy. Molded by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.’

mn76:14.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:14.2.verse: ‘This teacher has such a doctrine and view.

mn76:14.6.verse: If what that teacher says is true, both I who have not accomplished this and one who has accomplished it

mn76:14.7.verse: have attained exactly the same level. Yet I’m not one who says that both of us are purified without cause or reason.

mn76:14.8.verse: But it’s superfluous for this teacher to go nude, bald, persisting in squatting, tearing out their hair and beard. For I’m living at home with my children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency. Yet I’ll have exactly the same destiny in the next life as this teacher.

mn76:14.9.verse: What do I know or see that I should lead the spiritual life under this teacher?

mn76:15.1.verse: This is the third way that negates the spiritual life.

mn76:16.1.verse: Furthermore, take a certain teacher who has this doctrine and view:

mn76:16.2.verse: ‘There are these seven substances that are not made, not derived, not created, without a creator, barren, steady as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.

mn76:16.3.verse: They don’t move or deteriorate or obstruct each other. They’re unable to cause pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain to each other.

mn76:16.5.verse: The substances of earth, water, fire, air; pleasure, pain, and the soul is the seventh.

mn76:16.6.verse: These seven substances are not made, not derived, not created, without a creator, barren, steady as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.

mn76:16.7.verse: They don’t move or deteriorate or obstruct each other. They’re unable to cause pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain to each other.

mn76:16.8.verse: And here there is no one who kills or who makes others kill; no one who learns or who educates others; no one who understands or who helps others understand.

mn76:16.9.verse: If you chop off someone’s head with a sharp sword, you don’t take anyone’s life.

mn76:16.10.verse: The sword simply passes through the gap between the seven substances.

mn76:16.11.verse: There are 1.4 million main wombs, and 6,000, and 600; 500 deeds, and five, and three; deeds and half-deeds; 62 paths of practice, 62 sub-eons, six classes of rebirth, and eight stages in a person’s life; 4,900 Ājīvaka ascetics, 4,900 wanderers, and 4,900 dragon abodes; 2,000 lordships, 3,000 hells, and 36 realms of dusky sky; seven percipient embryos, seven non-percipient embryos, seven knotless embryos, seven gods, seven mental heavens, seven goblins, seven streams, seven castoff incarnations and 700 castoff incarnations, seven downfalls and 700 downfalls, seven dreams and 700 dreams, and 8.4 million great eons—through all of which the foolish and the astute transmigrate before making an end of suffering.

mn76:16.12.verse: And here there is no such thing as this: “By this precept or observance or fervent austerity or spiritual practice I shall force unripened deeds to bear their fruit, or eliminate old deeds by experiencing their results little by little”—for that cannot be.

mn76:16.13.verse: Pleasure and pain are allotted. Transmigration lasts only for a limited period, so there’s no increase or decrease, no getting better or worse.

mn76:16.14.verse: It’s like how, when you toss a ball of string, it rolls away unraveling.

mn76:16.15.verse: In the same way, after transmigrating the foolish and the astute will make an end of suffering.’

mn76:17.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:17.2.verse: ‘This teacher has such a doctrine and view.

mn76:17.18.verse: If what that teacher says is true, both I who have not accomplished this and one who has accomplished it

mn76:17.19.verse: have attained exactly the same level. Yet I’m not one who says that after transmigrating both of us will make an end of suffering.

mn76:17.20.verse: But it’s superfluous for this teacher to go nude, bald, persisting in squatting, tearing out their hair and beard. For I’m living at home with my children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency. Yet I’ll have exactly the same destiny in the next life as this teacher.

mn76:17.21.verse: What do I know or see that I should lead the spiritual life under this teacher?

mn76:18.1.verse: This is the fourth way that negates the spiritual life.

mn76:19.1.verse: These are the four ways that negate the spiritual life that have been explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, not practice such spiritual paths, and if they did practice them, they wouldn’t succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn76:20.2.verse: how these four ways that negate the spiritual life have been explained by the Buddha.

mn76:20.3.verse: But worthy Ānanda, what are the four kinds of unreliable spiritual life?”

mn76:21.1.verse: “Sandaka, take a certain teacher who claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to know and see everything without exception, thus:

mn76:21.2.verse: ‘Knowledge and vision are constantly and continually present to me, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.’

mn76:21.3.verse: They enter an empty house; they get no almsfood; a dog bites them; they encounter a wild elephant, a wild horse, and a wild cow; they ask the name and clan of a woman or man; they ask the name and path to a village or town.

mn76:21.4.verse: When asked, ‘Why is this?’ they answer: ‘I had to enter an empty house, that’s why I entered it. I had to get no almsfood, that’s why I got none. I had to get bitten by a dog, that’s why I was bitten. I had to encounter a wild elephant, a wild horse, and a wild cow, that’s why I encountered them. I had to ask the name and clan of a woman or man, that’s why I asked. I had to ask the name and path to a village or town, that’s why I asked.’

mn76:22.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:22.2.verse: ‘This teacher makes such a claim, but they answer in such a way.

mn76:23.1.verse: This is the first kind of unreliable spiritual life.

mn76:24.1.verse: Furthermore, take another teacher who is an oral transmitter, who takes oral transmission to be the truth.

mn76:24.2.verse: They teach by oral transmission, by the lineage of testament, by canonical authority.

mn76:24.3.verse: But when a teacher takes oral transmission to be the truth, some of that is well learned, some poorly learned, some true, and some otherwise.

mn76:25.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:25.2.verse: ‘This teacher takes oral transmission to be the truth. He teaches by oral transmission, by the lineage of testament, by canonical authority.

mn76:25.3.verse: But when a teacher takes oral transmission to be the truth, some of that is well learned, some poorly learned, some true, and some otherwise.

mn76:26.1.verse: This is the second kind of unreliable spiritual life.

mn76:27.1.verse: Furthermore, take another teacher who relies on logic and inquiry.

mn76:27.2.verse: They teach what they have worked out by logic, following a line of inquiry, expressing their own perspective.

mn76:27.3.verse: But when a teacher relies on logic and inquiry, some of that is well reasoned, some poorly reasoned, some true, and some otherwise.

mn76:28.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:28.2.verse: ‘This teacher relies on logic and inquiry.

mn76:28.3.verse: They teach what they have worked out by logic, following a line of inquiry, expressing their own perspective.

mn76:28.4.verse: But when a teacher relies on logic and inquiry, some of that is well reasoned, some poorly reasoned, some true, and some otherwise.

mn76:29.1.verse: This is the third kind of unreliable spiritual life.

mn76:30.1.verse: Furthermore, take another teacher who is dull and stupid.

mn76:30.2.verse: Because of that, whenever they’re asked a question, they resort to verbal flip-flops and endless flip-flops:

mn76:30.3.verse: ‘I don’t say it’s like this. I don’t say it’s like that. I don’t say it’s otherwise. I don’t say it’s not so. And I don’t deny it’s not so.’

mn76:31.1.verse: A sensible person reflects on this matter in this way:

mn76:31.3.verse: Because of that, whenever they’re asked a question, they resort to verbal flip-flops and endless flip-flops:

mn76:31.4.verse: “I don’t say it’s like this. I don’t say it’s like that. I don’t say it’s otherwise. I don’t say it’s not so. And I don’t deny it’s not so.”

mn76:32.1.verse: This is the fourth kind of unreliable spiritual life.

mn76:33.1.verse: These are the four kinds of unreliable spiritual life that have been explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, not practice such spiritual paths, and if they did practice them, they wouldn’t complete the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn76:34.2.verse: how these four kinds of unreliable spiritual life have been explained by the Buddha.

mn76:34.3.verse: But, worthy Ānanda, what would a teacher say and explain so that a sensible person would, to the best of their ability, practice such a spiritual path, and once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching?”

mn76:35-42.1.verse: “Sandaka, it’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. …

mn76:35-42.2.verse: He gives up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn76:35-42.3.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn76:35-42.4.verse: A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, lead the spiritual life with a teacher under whom they achieve such a high distinction, and, once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching.

mn76:43.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant … enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn76:46.2.verse: A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, lead the spiritual life under a teacher who achieves such a high distinction, and, once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching.

mn76:47.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn76:47.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. … They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn76:47.3.verse: A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, lead the spiritual life with a teacher under whom they achieve such a high distinction, and, once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching.

mn76:48.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn76:48.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. … They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn76:48.3.verse: A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, lead the spiritual life with a teacher under whom they achieve such a high distinction, and, once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching.

mn76:49.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn76:49.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn76:49.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn76:50.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn76:50.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn76:50.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn76:50.4.verse: A sensible person would, to the best of their ability, lead the spiritual life with a teacher under whom they achieve such a high distinction, and, once practicing it, they would complete the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn76:51.1.verse: “But worthy Ānanda, when a mendicant is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—could they still enjoy sensual pleasures?”

mn76:51.2.verse: “Sandaka, a mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—can’t transgress in five respects.

mn76:51.3.verse: A mendicant with defilements ended can’t deliberately take the life of a living creature, take something with the intention to steal, have sex, tell a deliberate lie, or store up goods for their own enjoyment like they used to as a layperson.

mn76:51.4.verse: A mendicant who is perfected can’t transgress in these five respects.”

mn76:52.1.verse: “But worthy Ānanda, when a mendicant is perfected, would the knowledge and vision that their defilements are ended be constantly and continually present to them, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking?”

mn76:52.3.verse: “Well then, Sandaka, I shall give you a simile.

mn76:52.4.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

mn76:52.5.verse: Suppose there was a person whose hands and feet had been amputated.

mn76:52.6.verse: Would they be aware that their hands and feet had been amputated constantly and continually, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking?

mn76:52.7.verse: Or would they be aware of it only when they checked it?”

mn76:52.9.verse: “They wouldn’t be aware of it constantly,

mn76:52.13.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant is perfected, the knowledge and vision that their defilements are ended is not constantly and continually present to them, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.

mn76:52.15.verse: Rather, they are aware of it only when they checked it.”

mn76:53.1.verse: “But Reverend Ānanda, in this teaching and training, how many are emancipated?”

mn76:53.2.verse: “There are not just one hundred who are emancipated, Sandaka, or two or three or four or five hundred, but many more than that in this teaching and training.”

mn76:53.4.verse: Namely, that there’s no glorifying one’s own teaching and putting down the teaching of others. The Dhamma is taught in its own field, and so many emancipated are recognized.

mn76:53.5.verse: But these Ājīvakas, sons of she whose sons are dead, glorify themselves and put others down. And they only recognize three who have been emancipated:

mn76:53.6.verse: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla.”

mn76:54.1.verse: Then the wanderer Sandaka addressed his own assembly,

mn76:54.2.verse: “Go, good fellows. The spiritual life is lived under the ascetic Gotama.

mn76:54.3.verse: It’s not easy for me to forsake possessions, honor, or popularity now.”

mn76:54.4.verse: And that’s how the wanderer Sandaka sent his own assembly to lead the spiritual life under the Buddha.

mn77:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn77:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion a number of very well-known wanderers were staying in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, that is to say—

mn77:2.2.verse: Annabhāra, Varadhara, and Sakuludāyī the Wanderer, as well as other very well-known wanderers.

mn77:3.1.verse: Then when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Rājagaha for alms.

mn77:3.3.verse: ‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

mn77:3.4.verse: Suppose I went to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary?’
