mn77:28.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption. It is without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn77:28.2.verse: They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn77:28.3.verse: It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.

mn77:28.4.verse: In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn77:28.5.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:29.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to understand this:

mn77:29.2.verse: ‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

mn77:29.3.verse: And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’

mn77:29.4.verse: Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent and clear, endowed with all good qualities.

mn77:29.5.verse: And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.

mn77:29.6.verse: And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it:

mn77:29.7.verse: ‘This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent and clear, endowed with all good qualities.

mn77:29.8.verse: And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.’

mn77:29.9.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to understand this:

mn77:29.10.verse: ‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

mn77:29.11.verse: And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’

mn77:29.12.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:30.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to create from this body another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.

mn77:30.2.verse: Suppose a person was to draw a reed out from its sheath.

mn77:30.4.verse: ‘This is the reed, this is the sheath. The reed and the sheath are different things. The reed has been drawn out from the sheath.’

mn77:30.5.verse: Or suppose a person was to draw a sword out from its scabbard.

mn77:30.7.verse: ‘This is the sword, this is the scabbard. The sword and the scabbard are different things. The sword has been drawn out from the scabbard.’

mn77:30.8.verse: Or suppose a person was to draw a snake out from its slough.

mn77:30.10.verse: ‘This is the snake, this is the slough. The snake and the slough are different things. The snake has been drawn out from the slough.’

mn77:30.11.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to create from this body another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.

mn77:30.12.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:31.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. They control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

mn77:31.2.verse: Suppose a deft potter or their apprentice had some well-prepared clay. They could produce any kind of pot that they like.

mn77:31.3.verse: Or suppose a deft ivory-carver or their apprentice had some well-prepared ivory. They could produce any kind of ivory item that they like.

mn77:31.4.verse: Or suppose a deft goldsmith or their apprentice had some well-prepared gold. They could produce any kind of gold item that they like.

mn77:31.5.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to wield the many kinds of psychic power …

mn77:31.6.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:32.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use so that, with clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.

mn77:32.2.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

mn77:32.3.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use so that, with clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.

mn77:32.4.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:33.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind.

mn77:33.2.verse: They understand mind with greed as ‘mind with greed’,

mn77:33.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed’;

mn77:33.4.verse: mind with hate as ‘mind with hate’,

mn77:33.5.verse: and mind without hate as ‘mind without hate’;

mn77:33.6.verse: mind with delusion as ‘mind with delusion’,

mn77:33.7.verse: and mind without delusion as ‘mind without delusion’;

mn77:33.12.verse: mind that is not supreme as ‘mind that is not supreme’,

mn77:33.13.verse: and mind that is supreme as ‘mind that is supreme’;

mn77:33.14.verse: mind immersed in samādhi as ‘mind immersed in samādhi’,

mn77:33.15.verse: and mind not immersed in samādhi as ‘mind not immersed in samādhi’;

mn77:33.18.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they had a spot they’d know ‘I have a spot’, and if they had no spots they’d know ‘I have no spots’.

mn77:33.19.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind …

mn77:33.36.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:34.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to recollect the many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn77:34.2.verse: Suppose a person was to leave their home village and go to another village. From that village they’d go to yet another village. And from that village they’d return to their home village. They’d think: ‘I went from my home village to another village. There I stood like this, sat like that, spoke like this, or kept silent like that. From that village I went to yet another village. There too I stood like this, sat like that, spoke like this, or kept silent like that. And from that village I returned to my home village.’

mn77:34.3.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to recollect the many kinds of past lives.

mn77:34.4.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:35.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use so that, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn77:35.2.verse: Suppose there were two houses with doors. A person with clear eyes standing in between them would see humans entering and leaving a house and wandering to and fro.

mn77:35.3.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use so that, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn …

mn77:35.4.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:36.1.verse: Furthermore, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn77:36.2.verse: Suppose that in a mountain glen there was a lake that was transparent, clear, and unclouded. A person with clear eyes standing on the bank would see the clams and mussels, pebbles and gravel, and schools of fish swimming about or staying still. They’d think: ‘This lake is transparent, clear, and unclouded. And here are the clams and mussels, pebbles and gravel, and schools of fish swimming about or staying still.’

mn77:36.3.verse: In the same way, I have explained to my disciples a practice that they use to realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn77:36.4.verse: And many of my disciples meditate on that having attained perfection and consummation of insight.

mn77:37.1.verse: This is the fifth quality because of which my disciples are loyal to me.

mn77:38.1.verse: These are the five qualities because of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me; and honoring and respecting me, they remain loyal to me.”

mn77:38.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn77:38.3.verse: Satisfied, the wanderer Sakuludāyī approved what the Buddha said.

mn78:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn78:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion Uggāhamāna, a follower of Muṇḍika the contemplative, together with a large following of about 500 wanderers, had taken up residence in the debating hall near the Tiṇḍuka tree in the single-pavilion park of Queen Mallikā.

mn78:2.1.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga the carpenter left Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Blessed One,

mn78:2.2.verse: but the thought occurred to him,

mn78:2.3.verse: “Now is not the right time to see the Blessed One,

mn78:2.5.verse: And it is not the right time to see the mind-developing monks,

mn78:2.6.verse: for they too are in seclusion.

mn78:2.7.verse: Why don’t I go to the debating hall near the Tiṇḍuka tree in the single-pavilion park of Queen Mallikā to see Uggāhamāna, a follower of Muṇḍika the contemplative?”

mn78:2.8.verse: So he headed to the debating hall near the Tiṇḍuka tree in the single-pavilion park of Queen Mallikā.

mn78:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion Uggāhamāna was sitting with his large following of wanderers, all making a great noise & racket, discussing many kinds of bestial topics of conversation, such as:

mn78:3.2.verse: conversation about kings, robbers, & ministers of state; armies, alarms, & battles; food & drink; clothing, furniture, garlands, & scents; relatives; vehicles; villages, towns, cities, the countryside; women & heroes; the gossip of the street & the well; tales of the dead; tales of diversity, the creation of the world & of the sea; talk of whether things exist or not.

mn78:3.3.verse: Then Uggāhamāna saw Pañcakaṅga the carpenter coming from afar,

mn78:3.4.verse: and on seeing him, hushed his following:

mn78:3.5.verse: “Be quiet, good sirs. Don’t make any noise.

mn78:3.6.verse: Here comes Pañcakaṅga the carpenter, a disciple of Gotama the contemplative.

mn78:3.7.verse: He is one of those disciples of Gotama the contemplative, clad in white, who lives in Sāvatthī.

mn78:3.8.verse: These people are fond of quietude, trained in quietude, and speak in praise of quietude.

mn78:3.9.verse: Maybe, if he perceives our group as quiet, he will consider it worth his while to come our way.”

mn78:4.1.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga went to Uggāhamāna and, on arrival, greeted him courteously.

mn78:4.2.verse: After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Uggāhamāna said to him,

mn78:5.1.verse: “I describe an individual endowed with four qualities as being consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.

mn78:5.3.verse: There is the case where he does no evil action with his body, speaks no evil speech, resolves on no evil resolve, and maintains himself with no evil means of livelihood.

mn78:5.4.verse: An individual endowed with these four qualities I describe as being consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.”

mn78:6.1.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga neither delighted in Uggāhamāna’s words nor did he scorn them.

mn78:6.2.verse: Expressing neither delight nor scorn, he got up from his seat & left, thinking,

mn78:6.3.verse: “I will learn the meaning of this statement in the Blessed One’s presence.”

mn78:7.1.verse: Then he went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, after bowing down to him, sat to one side.

mn78:7.2.verse: As he was sitting there, he told the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with Uggāhamāna.

mn78:8.1.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One said to Pañcakaṅga:

mn78:8.2.verse: “In that case, carpenter, then according to Uggāhamāna’s words a stupid baby boy, lying on its back, is consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.

mn78:8.3.verse: For even the thought ‘body’ does not occur to a stupid baby boy lying on its back, so from where would it do any evil action with its body, aside from a little kicking?

mn78:8.4.verse: Even the thought ‘speech’ does not occur to it, so from where would it speak any evil speech, aside from a little crying?

mn78:8.5.verse: Even the thought ‘resolve’ does not occur to it, so from where would it resolve on any evil resolve, aside from a little bad temper?

mn78:8.6.verse: Even the thought ‘livelihood’ does not occur to it, so from where would it maintain itself with any evil means of livelihood, aside from its mother’s milk?

mn78:8.7.verse: So, according to Uggāhamāna’s words, a stupid baby boy, lying on its back is consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.

mn78:8.8.verse: “If an individual is endowed with these four qualities, I do not describe him as consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments. Rather, he stands on the same level as a stupid baby boy lying on its back.

mn78:8.10.verse: There is the case where he does no evil action with his body, speaks no evil speech, resolves on no evil resolve, and maintains himself with no evil means of livelihood.

mn78:8.11.verse: If an individual is endowed with these four qualities, I do not describe him as consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments. Rather, he stands on the same level as a stupid baby boy lying on its back.

mn78:9.1.verse: “An individual endowed with ten qualities is one whom I describe as being consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.

mn78:9.2.verse: With regard to that point, one should know that ‘These are unskillful habits,’

mn78:9.4.verse: With regard to that point, one should know that ‘That is the cause of unskillful habits’…

mn78:9.8.verse: ‘This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful habits,’

mn78:9.10.verse: With regard to that point, one should know that ‘These are skillful habits’…

mn78:9.12.verse: ‘That is the cause of skillful habits’…

mn78:9.16.verse: ‘This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful habits,’

mn78:9.18.verse: With regard to that point, one should know that ‘These are unskillful resolves’…

mn78:9.20.verse: ‘That is the cause of unskillful resolves’…

mn78:9.24.verse: ‘This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful resolves’

mn78:9.26.verse: With regard to that point, one should know that ‘These are skillful resolves’…

mn78:9.28.verse: ‘That is the cause of skillful resolves’…

mn78:9.32.verse: ‘This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful resolves,’

mn78:10.2.verse: Unskillful bodily actions, unskillful verbal actions, evil means of livelihood.

mn78:10.4.verse: What is the cause of unskillful habits?

mn78:10.6.verse: and they are said to be mind-caused.

mn78:10.8.verse: —for the mind has many modes & permutations.

mn78:10.9.verse: Any mind with passion, aversion or delusion: That is the cause of unskillful habits.

mn78:10.10.verse: Now where do unskillful habits cease without trace?

mn78:10.12.verse: There is the case where a monk abandons wrong bodily conduct & develops right bodily conduct, abandons wrong verbal conduct & develops right verbal conduct, abandons wrong livelihood & maintains his life with right livelihood.

mn78:10.13.verse: This is where unskillful habits cease without trace.

mn78:10.14.verse: And what sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful habits?

mn78:10.15.verse: There is the case where a monk generates desire, endeavors, arouses persistence, upholds & exerts his intent for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities that have not yet arisen;

mn78:10.16.verse: for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen;

mn78:10.17.verse: for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities that have not yet arisen;

mn78:10.18.verse: (and) for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen.

mn78:10.19.verse: This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful habits.

mn78:11.2.verse: Skillful bodily actions, skillful verbal actions, purity of livelihood.

mn78:11.4.verse: What is the cause of skillful habits?

mn78:11.5.verse: Their cause, too, has been stated,

mn78:11.6.verse: and they are said to be mind-caused.

mn78:11.8.verse: —for the mind has many modes & permutations.

mn78:11.9.verse: Any mind without passion, without aversion, without delusion: That is the cause of skillful habits.

mn78:11.10.verse: Now where do skillful habits cease without trace?

mn78:11.11.verse: Their cessation, too, has been stated:

mn78:11.12.verse: There is the case where a monk is virtuous, but not fashioned of virtue.

mn78:11.13.verse: He discerns, as it has come to be, the awareness-release & discernment-release where his skillful habits cease without trace.

mn78:11.14.verse: And what sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful habits?

mn78:11.15.verse: There is the case where a monk generates desire… for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:11.16.verse: for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen…

mn78:11.17.verse: for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:11.18.verse: (and) for the… development & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen.

mn78:11.19.verse: This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful habits.

mn78:12.2.verse: Being resolved on sensuality, on ill will, on harmfulness.

mn78:12.4.verse: What is the cause of unskillful resolves?

mn78:12.5.verse: Their cause, too, has been stated,

mn78:12.6.verse: and they are said to be perception-caused.

mn78:12.9.verse: Any sensuality-perception, ill will-perception or harmfulness-perception:

mn78:12.10.verse: That is the cause of unskillful resolves.

mn78:12.11.verse: Now where do unskillful resolves cease without trace?

mn78:12.12.verse: Their cessation, too, has been stated:

mn78:12.13.verse: There is the case where a monk, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn78:12.14.verse: This is where unskillful resolves cease without trace.

mn78:12.15.verse: And what sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful resolves?

mn78:12.16.verse: There is the case where a monk generates desire… for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:12.17.verse: for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen…

mn78:12.18.verse: for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:12.19.verse: (and) for the… development & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen.

mn78:12.20.verse: This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of unskillful resolves.

mn78:13.2.verse: Being resolved on renunciation [freedom from sensuality], on non-ill will, on harmlessness.

mn78:13.4.verse: What is the cause of skillful resolves?

mn78:13.5.verse: Their cause, too, has been stated,

mn78:13.6.verse: and they are said to be perception-caused.

mn78:13.9.verse: Any renunciation-perception, non-ill will-perception or harmlessness-perception:

mn78:13.10.verse: That is the cause of skillful resolves.

mn78:13.11.verse: Now where do skillful resolves cease without trace?

mn78:13.12.verse: Their cessation, too, has been stated:

mn78:13.13.verse: There is the case where a monk, with the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, enters & remains in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

mn78:13.14.verse: This is where skillful resolves cease without trace.

mn78:13.15.verse: And what sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful resolves?

mn78:13.16.verse: There is the case where a monk generates desire… for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:13.17.verse: for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen…

mn78:13.18.verse: for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities that have not yet arisen…

mn78:13.19.verse: (and) for the… development & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen.

mn78:13.20.verse: This sort of practice is the practice leading to the cessation of skillful resolves.

mn78:14.1.verse: “Now, an individual endowed with which ten qualities is one whom I describe as being consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments?

mn78:14.2.verse: One endowed with the right view of one beyond training, the right resolve of one beyond training, the right speech… the right action… the right livelihood… the right effort… the right mindfulness… the right concentration… the right knowledge… the right release of one beyond training.

mn78:14.3.verse: An individual endowed with these ten qualities is one whom I describe as being consummate in what is skillful, foremost in what is skillful, an invincible contemplative attained to the highest attainments.”

mn78:14.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn78:14.5.verse: Gratified, Pañcakaṅga the carpenter delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn78:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn78:1.3.verse: Now at that time the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamaṇḍikāputta was residing together with around five hundred wanderers in Mallikā’s single-halled monastery for philosophical debates, hedged by pale-moon ebony trees.

mn78:2.1.verse: Then the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga left Sāvatthī in the middle of the day to see the Buddha.

mn78:2.3.verse: “It’s the wrong time to see the Buddha,

mn78:2.5.verse: And it’s the wrong time to see the esteemed mendicants,

mn78:2.7.verse: Why don’t I go to Mallikā’s monastery to visit the wanderer Uggāhamāna?”

mn78:3.1.verse: Now at that time, Uggāhamāna was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers making an uproar, a colossal racket. They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as

mn78:3.2.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

mn78:3.3.verse: Uggāhamāna saw Pañcakaṅga coming off in the distance,

mn78:3.5.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

mn78:3.6.verse: Here comes Pañcakaṅga, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.

mn78:3.7.verse: He is included among the white-clothed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama, who is residing in Sāvatthī.

mn78:3.8.verse: Such venerables like the quiet, are educated to be quiet, and praise the quiet.

mn78:3.9.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

mn78:4.1.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga approached Uggāhamāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn78:4.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Uggāhamāna said to him:

mn78:5.1.verse: “Householder, when an individual person has four qualities I describe them as an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment.

mn78:5.3.verse: It’s when they do no bad deeds with their body; speak no bad words; think no bad thoughts; and don’t earn a living by bad livelihood.

mn78:5.4.verse: When an individual possesses these four qualities I describe them as an invincible ascetic.”

mn78:6.1.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga neither approved nor rejected the wanderer Uggāhamāna’s statement.

mn78:6.2.verse: He rose from his seat, thinking,

mn78:6.3.verse: “I will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.”

mn78:7.1.verse: Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

mn78:7.2.verse: and informed the Buddha of all that had been discussed.

mn78:8.1.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

mn78:8.2.verse: “Chamberlain, if what Uggāhamāna says is true, a little baby boy is an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment.

mn78:8.3.verse: For a little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘a body’, so how could they possibly do a bad deed with their body, aside from just wriggling?

mn78:8.4.verse: And a little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘speech’, so how could they possibly speak bad words, aside from just crying?

mn78:8.5.verse: And a little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘thought’, so how could they possibly think bad thoughts, aside from just whimpering?

mn78:8.6.verse: And a little baby doesn’t even have a concept of ‘livelihood’, so how could they possibly earn a living by bad livelihood, aside from their mother’s breast?

mn78:8.7.verse: If what Uggāhamāna says is true, a little baby boy is an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment.

mn78:8.8.verse: When an individual person has four qualities I describe them, not as an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment—but as having achieved the same level as a little baby.

mn78:8.10.verse: It’s when they do no bad deeds with their body; speak no bad words; think no bad thoughts; and don’t earn a living by bad livelihood.

mn78:8.11.verse: When an individual possesses these four qualities I describe them, not as an invincible ascetic, but as having achieved the same level as a little baby.

mn78:9.1.verse: When an individual person has ten qualities, chamberlain, I describe them as an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment.

mn78:9.2.verse: The following things must be understood, I say. ‘These are unskillful behaviors.’

mn78:9.8.verse: ‘Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of unskillful behaviors.’

mn78:9.16.verse: ‘Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of skillful behaviors.’

mn78:9.24.verse: ‘Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of unskillful thoughts.’

mn78:9.32.verse: ‘Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of skillful thoughts.’

mn78:10.1.verse: And what, chamberlain, are unskillful behaviors?

mn78:10.2.verse: Unskillful deeds by way of body and speech, and bad livelihood.

mn78:10.4.verse: And where do these unskillful behaviors stem from?

mn78:10.5.verse: Where they stem from has been stated.

mn78:10.6.verse: You should say that they stem from the mind.

mn78:10.8.verse: The mind takes many and diverse forms.

mn78:10.9.verse: But unskillful behaviors stem from a mind that has greed, hate, and delusion.

mn78:10.10.verse: And where do these unskillful behaviors cease without remainder?

mn78:10.11.verse: Their cessation has also been stated.

mn78:10.12.verse: It’s when a mendicant gives up bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind, and develops good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind; they give up wrong livelihood and earn a living by right livelihood.

mn78:10.13.verse: This is where these unskillful behaviors cease without remainder.

mn78:10.14.verse: And how is someone practicing for the cessation of unskillful behaviors?

mn78:10.15.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

mn78:10.16.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up.

mn78:10.17.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

mn78:10.18.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

mn78:10.19.verse: Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of unskillful behaviors.

mn78:11.2.verse: Skillful deeds by way of body and speech, and purified livelihood are included in behavior, I say.

mn78:11.4.verse: And where do these skillful behaviors stem from?

mn78:11.5.verse: Where they stem from has been stated.

mn78:11.6.verse: You should say that they stem from the mind.

mn78:11.8.verse: The mind takes many and diverse forms.

mn78:11.9.verse: But skillful behaviors stem from a mind that is free from greed, hate, and delusion.

mn78:11.10.verse: And where do these skillful behaviors cease without remainder?

mn78:11.11.verse: Their cessation has also been stated.

mn78:11.12.verse: It’s when a mendicant behaves ethically, but they are not determined by ethical behavior.

mn78:11.13.verse: And they truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where these skillful behaviors cease without remainder.

mn78:11.14.verse: And how is someone practicing for the cessation of skillful behaviors?

mn78:11.15.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise …

mn78:11.16.verse: so that unskillful qualities are given up …

mn78:11.18.verse: so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

mn78:11.19.verse: Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of skillful behaviors.

mn78:12.2.verse: Purposes of sensuality, of malice, and of cruelty.

mn78:12.4.verse: And where do these unskillful thoughts stem from?

mn78:12.5.verse: Where they stem from has been stated.

mn78:12.6.verse: You should say that they stem from perception.

mn78:12.8.verse: Perception takes many and diverse forms.

mn78:12.9.verse: Perceptions of sensuality, malice, and cruelty—

mn78:12.11.verse: And where do these unskillful thoughts cease without remainder?

mn78:12.12.verse: Their cessation has also been stated.

mn78:12.13.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn78:12.14.verse: This is where these unskillful thoughts cease without remainder.

mn78:12.15.verse: And how is someone practicing for the cessation of unskillful thoughts?

mn78:12.16.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise …

mn78:12.17.verse: so that unskillful qualities are given up …

mn78:12.19.verse: so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

mn78:12.20.verse: Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of unskillful thoughts.

mn78:13.2.verse: Thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness.

mn78:13.4.verse: And where do these skillful thoughts stem from?

mn78:13.5.verse: Where they stem from has been stated.

mn78:13.6.verse: You should say that they stem from perception.

mn78:13.8.verse: Perception takes many and diverse forms.

mn78:13.9.verse: Perceptions of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness—

mn78:13.11.verse: And where do these skillful thoughts cease without remainder?

mn78:13.12.verse: Their cessation has also been stated.

mn78:13.13.verse: It’s when, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn78:13.14.verse: This is where these skillful thoughts cease without remainder.

mn78:13.15.verse: And how is someone practicing for the cessation of skillful thoughts?

mn78:13.16.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise …

mn78:13.17.verse: so that unskillful qualities are given up …

mn78:13.19.verse: so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

mn78:13.20.verse: Someone practicing like this is practicing for the cessation of skillful thoughts.

mn78:14.1.verse: Chamberlain, when an individual person has what ten qualities do I describe them as an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment?

mn78:14.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has an adept’s right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right immersion, right knowledge, and right freedom.

mn78:14.3.verse: When an individual possesses these ten qualities, I describe them as an invincible ascetic—accomplished in the skillful, excelling in the skillful, attained to the highest attainment.”

mn78:14.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn78:14.5.verse: Satisfied, Pañcakaṅga the chamberlain approved what the Buddha said.

mn79:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn79:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion Sakuludāyī the Wanderer was staying in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary, together with a large assembly of wanderers.

mn79:2.1.verse: Then when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Rājagaha for alms.

mn79:2.3.verse: ‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

mn79:2.4.verse: Suppose I went to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer in the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary?’

mn79:2.5.verse: Then the Blessed One went to the Wanderers’ Park, the Peacocks’ Sanctuary.

mn79:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion Sakuludāyī the Wanderer was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers who were shouting and making a great uproar and noise, talking many kinds of pointless talk, such as:

mn79:3.2.verse: talk of kings, talk of robbers, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of countries, talk of women, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of wells, talk of the departed, various idle tales, speculation about the world, speculation about the sea, talk of whether things are or are not, and so on.

mn79:3.3.verse: Sakuludāyī the Wanderer saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

mn79:3.4.verse: Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:

mn79:3.5.verse: “Be quiet, sirs, do not make a noise.

mn79:3.7.verse: that venerable one likes quiet and speaks in praise of quiet.

mn79:3.8.verse: Perhaps, finding our assembly quiet, he will think it fit to approach.”

mn79:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One went up to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer.

mn79:4.2.verse: Sakuludāyī the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn79:4.3.verse: “Let the Blessed One come, venerable sir.

mn79:4.4.verse: Welcome to the Blessed One, venerable sir.

mn79:4.5.verse: It is long, venerable sir, since the Blessed One made an occasion to come here.

mn79:4.6.verse: Let the Blessed One be seated, venerable sir;

mn79:4.8.verse: The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.

mn79:4.9.verse: And Sakuludāyī the Wanderer took a certain low seat and sat down at one side.

mn79:4.10.verse: The Blessed One then said to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer, as he sat at one side:

mn79:4.11.verse: “What talk are you gathered here for now, Udāyī? And what was your discussion that was left unfinished?”

mn79:5.1.verse: “Let that be, venerable sir, this talk for which we are now gathered here.

mn79:5.2.verse: It will not be hard for the Blessed One to hear about it later too, venerable sir.

mn79:5.3.verse: Venerable sir, when I have not come to this assembly, it sits talking many kinds of pointless talk;

mn79:5.4.verse: but when I have come to this assembly, it sits looking only at my face, thinking:

mn79:5.5.verse: ‘Let us hear the Dhamma that the ascetic Udāyī will speak’;

mn79:5.6.verse: and when the Blessed One has come to this assembly, then both I and this assembly sit looking at the Blessed One’s face, thinking:

mn79:5.7.verse: ‘Let us hear the Dhamma that the Blessed One will speak.’”

mn79:6.1.verse: “Well then, Udāyī, let it occur to you to speak of that, in whatever way it may occur to you.”

mn79:6.2.verse: “A few days ago, venerable sir—there was one who claimed to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.’

mn79:6.3.verse: When I asked him a question about the past, he evaded it with another question, turned the talk aside to something outside the point, and displayed anger, hatred, and sulkiness.

mn79:6.4.verse: Then, venerable sir, I became mindful only of the Blessed One:

mn79:6.5.verse: ‘Ah, surely it is the Blessed One, surely it is the Fortunate One, who is thoroughly skilled in these things.’”

mn79:6.6.verse: “But, Udāyī, who was that who claimed to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me’, who, when you asked him a question about the past, evaded it with another question, turned the talk aside to something outside the point, and displayed anger, hatred, and sulkiness?”

mn79:7.1.verse: “Udāyī, if someone were to recollect his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars, were to recollect his manifold past lives, then either he might ask me a question about the past, or I might ask him a question about the past;

mn79:7.2.verse: and either he might satisfy my mind with his answer to a question about the past, or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to a question about the past.

mn79:7.3.verse: And, Udāyī, if someone, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, were to see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions, then either he might ask me a question about the future, or I might ask him a question about the future;

mn79:7.4.verse: and either he might satisfy my mind with his answer to a question about the future, or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to a question about the future.

mn79:7.5.verse: But, Udāyī, let the past be, let the future be.

mn79:7.6.verse: I shall teach you the Dhamma:

mn79:7.7.verse: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises;

mn79:7.8.verse: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.”

mn79:8.1.verse: “Venerable sir, I am not even able to recollect with its aspects and particulars all that I have experienced in this very existence,[^1]

mn79:8.2.verse: so how could I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … with their aspects and particulars, as the Blessed One does?

mn79:8.3.verse: Indeed, venerable sir, I cannot even see a dust-goblin right now,

mn79:8.4.verse: so how could I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions, as the Blessed One does?

mn79:8.5.verse: But when the Blessed One said to me:

mn79:8.6.verse: ‘But, Udāyī, let the past be, let the future be;

mn79:8.7.verse: I shall teach you the Dhamma:

mn79:8.8.verse: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises;

mn79:8.9.verse: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases’—that is even more unclear to me.

mn79:8.10.verse: Perhaps, venerable sir, an answer to a question about our own teacher’s doctrine might satisfy the Blessed One’s mind.”

mn79:9.1.verse: “Well, Udāyī, what is it in your own teacher’s doctrine?”

mn79:9.2.verse: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:

mn79:9.3.verse: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour.’”

mn79:9.4.verse: “But, Udāyī, since in your own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:

mn79:9.5.verse: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour’—what is that highest splendour?”

mn79:9.6.verse: “Venerable sir, that splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour.”

mn79:9.7.verse: “But, Udāyī, what is that highest splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent?”

mn79:9.8.verse: “Venerable sir, that splendour than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour.”

mn79:10.1.verse: “Udāyī, you could go on like this for a long time:

mn79:10.2.verse: ‘That splendour, venerable sir, than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour’, you say, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.

mn79:10.3.verse: Suppose, Udāyī, a man were to say thus:

mn79:10.4.verse: ‘I want, I love, the most beautiful girl in this country.’

mn79:10.6.verse: ‘Good man, this most beautiful girl in the country whom you want and love—do you know whether she is a noble lady, or a brahmin lady, or a merchant lady, or a worker’s daughter?’

mn79:10.7.verse: Being asked thus, he would say “No.”

mn79:10.9.verse: ‘Good man, this most beautiful girl in the country whom you want and love—do you know her name and clan, or … whether she is tall or short or of middle height, dark or brown or golden-skinned … or what village or town or city she lives in?’

mn79:10.10.verse: Being asked thus, he would say “No.”

mn79:10.12.verse: ‘Good man, do you then want and love someone you neither know nor see?’

mn79:10.13.verse: Being asked thus, he would say “Yes.”

mn79:10.15.verse: that being so, would not that man’s statement amount to nonsense?”

mn79:10.16.verse: “Certainly, venerable sir, that being so, that man’s statement would amount to nonsense.”

mn79:10.17.verse: “So too, Udāyī, you say: ‘That splendour, venerable sir, than which there is no other splendour higher or more excellent—that is the highest splendour’, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.”

mn79:11.1.verse: “Venerable sir, just as a beautiful beryl gem of pure water, eight-faceted, well cut, laid on a saffron cloth, gleams, shines, and glows—such is the self, possessed of such splendour, when it is sound after death.”

mn79:12.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a beautiful beryl gem of pure water, eight-faceted, well cut, laid on a saffron cloth, that gleams, shines, and glows, or a glow-worm in the dark of night?”

mn79:12.3.verse: “That glow-worm in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:13.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a glow-worm in the dark of night, or an oil lamp in the dark of night?”

mn79:13.3.verse: “That oil lamp in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:14.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: an oil lamp in the dark of night, or a great bonfire in the dark of night?”

mn79:14.3.verse: “That great bonfire in the dark of night, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:15.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: a great bonfire in the dark of night, or the morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky?”

mn79:15.3.verse: “That morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:16.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: the morning star at night towards dawn in a clear, cloudless sky, or the moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth?”

mn79:16.3.verse: “That moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:17.2.verse: which of these two has the more excellent and superior splendour: the moon at midnight in a clear, cloudless sky on the full-moon Uposatha day of the fifteenth, or the sun at midday in a clear, cloudless sky in the autumn, in the last month of the rains?”

mn79:17.3.verse: “That sun at midday in a clear, cloudless sky in the autumn, in the last month of the rains, venerable sir, has the more excellent and superior splendour of these two.”

mn79:18.1.verse: “Well, Udāyī, there are far more gods than those who do not partake of the light of the moon and sun—those I know.

mn79:18.3.verse: ‘There is no other splendour higher or more excellent than that.’

mn79:18.4.verse: But you, Udāyī, say that that splendour which is inferior to and worse than a glow-worm’s is the highest splendour, and yet you do not make known what that splendour is.”

mn79:19.1.verse: “The Blessed One has cut off the discussion; the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion.”

mn79:19.3.verse: ‘The Blessed One has cut off the discussion, the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion’?”

mn79:19.4.verse: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:

mn79:19.5.verse: ‘This is the highest splendour, this is the highest splendour.’

mn79:19.6.verse: But when we are pressed, questioned, and cross-questioned about our own teacher’s doctrine by the Blessed One, we are found to be empty, hollow, and mistaken.”

mn79:20.1.verse: “But, Udāyī, is there an entirely pleasant world? Is there a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world?”

mn79:20.2.verse: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:

mn79:20.3.verse: ‘There is an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.’”

mn79:21.1.verse: “But, Udāyī, what is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world?”

mn79:21.2.verse: “Here, venerable sir, someone abandons the killing of living beings and abstains from killing living beings; he abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given; he abandons misconduct in sensual desires and abstains from misconduct in sensual desires; he abandons false speech and abstains from false speech; or else he undertakes some form of austerity.

mn79:21.3.verse: This, venerable sir, is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”

mn79:22.2.verse: on the occasion when one abandons the killing of living beings and abstains from killing living beings, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”

mn79:22.5.verse: on the occasion when one abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”

mn79:22.7.verse: “What do you think, Udāyī, on the occasion when one abandons misconduct in sensual desires and abstains from misconduct in sensual desires, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”

mn79:22.9.verse: “What do you think, Udāyī, on the occasion when one abandons false speech and abstains from false speech, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”

mn79:22.12.verse: on the occasion when one undertakes some form of austerity, is the self on that occasion entirely happy, or both happy and unhappy?”

mn79:22.15.verse: is the entirely pleasant world realized by following a way mixed with happiness and unhappiness?”

mn79:23.1.verse: “The Blessed One has cut off the discussion; the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion.”

mn79:23.3.verse: ‘The Blessed One has cut off the discussion, the Fortunate One has cut off the discussion’?”

mn79:23.4.verse: “Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s doctrine it is thus:

mn79:23.5.verse: ‘There is an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.’

mn79:23.6.verse: But when we are pressed, questioned, and cross-questioned about our own teacher’s doctrine by the Blessed One, we are found to be empty, hollow, and mistaken.

mn79:23.7.verse: But, venerable sir, is there an entirely pleasant world? Is there a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world?”

mn79:24.1.verse: “There is, Udāyī, an entirely pleasant world; there is a definite way to realize that entirely pleasant world.”

mn79:24.2.verse: “But, venerable sir, what is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world?”

mn79:25.1.verse: “Here, Udāyī, quite secluded from sensual desires … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna …

mn79:25.2.verse: with the stilling of initial and sustained application … he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …

mn79:25.3.verse: with the fading away of joy as well … he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna—

mn79:25.4.verse: this, Udāyī, is that definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”

mn79:25.5.verse: “That, venerable sir, is not the way to realize the entirely pleasant world; rather, the entirely pleasant world has already been realized by that point.”

mn79:25.6.verse: “The entirely pleasant world is not yet realized by that point, Udāyī;

mn79:25.7.verse: that is only the definite way to realize the entirely pleasant world.”

mn79:26.1.verse: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly became loud, noisy, and clamorous:

mn79:26.2.verse: “Here we have lost, along with our teacher’s doctrine! Here we have lost, along with our teacher’s doctrine!

mn79:26.3.verse: We know nothing higher than this.”

mn79:26.4.verse: Then Sakuludāyī the Wanderer, having quieted those wanderers, said to the Blessed One:

mn79:27.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, at what point is the entirely pleasant world realized?”

mn79:27.2.verse: “Here, Udāyī, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna …

mn79:27.3.verse: He consorts, converses, and engages in discussion with those deities who have been reborn in the entirely pleasant world.

mn79:27.4.verse: It is by this point, Udāyī, that the entirely pleasant world is realized.”

mn79:28.1.verse: “Then surely, venerable sir, it is for the sake of realizing this entirely pleasant world that the bhikkhus live the life divine under the Blessed One?”

mn79:28.2.verse: “It is not, Udāyī, for the sake of realizing the entirely pleasant world that the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:28.3.verse: There are, Udāyī, other things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.”

mn79:28.4.verse: “But what, venerable sir, are those things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under the Blessed One?”

mn79:29-36.1.verse: “Here, Udāyī, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed …

mn79:37.1.verse: … having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of mind that weaken wisdom,

mn79:37.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires … he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna …

mn79:37.3.verse: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:38-40.1.verse: Again, Udāyī, with the stilling of initial and sustained application … the second jhāna …

mn79:38-40.3.verse: he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.

mn79:38-40.4.verse: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:41.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

mn79:41.2.verse: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

mn79:41.3.verse: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:42.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated … he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn79:42.2.verse: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.

mn79:42.3.verse: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:43.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated … he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn79:43.2.verse: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘this is the origin of suffering’ … ‘this is the cessation of suffering’ … he understands as it actually is: ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’,

mn79:43.3.verse: he understands as it actually is: ‘these are the taints’ … ‘this is the origin of the taints’ … ‘this is the cessation of the taints’ … he understands as it actually is: ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’

mn79:44.1.verse: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn79:44.2.verse: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn79:44.3.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn79:44.4.verse: This too, Udāyī, is a thing higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.

mn79:44.5.verse: These, Udāyī, are the things higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which the bhikkhus live the life divine under me.”

mn79:45.1.verse: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:

mn79:45.3.verse: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One.

mn79:45.4.verse: I go to the Blessed One for refuge, venerable sir, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn79:45.5.verse: I would receive the Going-forth in the Blessed One’s presence, venerable sir, I would receive the Full Admission.”

mn79:46.1.verse: When this was said, Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly said to Sakuludāyī the Wanderer:

mn79:46.2.verse: “Let not Master Udāyī live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama;

mn79:46.3.verse: let not Master Udāyī, who has been a teacher, live the life of a pupil.

mn79:46.4.verse: Just as a water-jar might become a mere dipper, so it will be for Master Udāyī.[^3]

mn79:46.5.verse: Let not Master Udāyī live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama;

mn79:46.6.verse: let not Master Udāyī, who has been a teacher, live the life of a pupil.”

mn79:46.7.verse: So it was that Sakuludāyī the Wanderer’s assembly obstructed him in living the life divine under the Blessed One.

mn79:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn79:1.3.verse: Now at that time the wanderer Sakuludāyī was residing together with a large assembly of wanderers in their monastery in the peacocks’ feeding ground.

mn79:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

mn79:2.3.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

mn79:2.4.verse: Why don’t I visit the wanderer Sakuludāyī at the monastery for the wanderers in the peacocks’ feeding ground?”

mn79:2.5.verse: Then the Buddha went to the monastery for the wanderers.

mn79:3.1.verse: Now at that time, Sakuludāyī was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers making an uproar, a colossal racket. They engaged in all kinds of low talk, such as

mn79:3.2.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

mn79:3.3.verse: Sakuludāyī saw the Buddha coming off in the distance,

mn79:3.5.verse: “Be quiet, good fellows, don’t make a sound.

mn79:3.7.verse: The venerable likes quiet and praises quiet.

mn79:3.8.verse: Hopefully if he sees that our assembly is quiet he’ll see fit to approach.”

mn79:4.4.verse: Welcome to the Blessed One, sir!

mn79:4.5.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

mn79:4.6.verse: Please, sir, sit down, this seat is ready.”

mn79:4.8.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

mn79:4.9.verse: while Sakuludāyī took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn79:4.11.verse: “Udāyī, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

mn79:5.1.verse: “Sir, leave aside what we were sitting talking about just now.

mn79:5.2.verse: It won’t be hard for you to hear about that later.

mn79:5.3.verse: When I don’t come to the assembly, they sit and engage in all kinds of low talk.

mn79:5.4.verse: But when I have come to the assembly, they sit gazing up at my face alone, thinking,

mn79:5.5.verse: ‘Whatever the ascetic Udāyī teaches, we shall listen to it.’

mn79:5.6.verse: But when the Buddha has come to the assembly, both myself and the assembly sit gazing up at your face, thinking,

mn79:5.7.verse: ‘Whatever the Buddha teaches, we shall listen to it.’”

mn79:6.1.verse: “Well then, Udāyī, suggest something for me to talk about.”

mn79:6.2.verse: “Sir, a few days ago someone was claiming to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to know and see everything without exception, thus: ‘Knowledge and vision are constantly and continually present to me, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.’

mn79:6.3.verse: When I asked them a question about the first beginning, they dodged the issue, distracted the discussion with irrelevant points, and displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

mn79:6.4.verse: That reminded me of the Buddha:

mn79:6.5.verse: ‘Surely it must be the Blessed One, the Holy One who is so skilled in such matters.’”

mn79:6.6.verse: “But Udāyī, who was it that made such a claim and behaved in such a way?”

mn79:6.7.verse: “It was the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan, sir.”

mn79:7.1.verse: “Udāyī, someone who can recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details, might ask me a question about the first beginning, or I might ask them a question about the first beginning.

mn79:7.2.verse: And they might satisfy me with their answer, or I might satisfy them with my answer.

mn79:7.3.verse: Someone who, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds might ask me a question about the final end, or I might ask them a question about the final end.

mn79:7.4.verse: And they might satisfy me with their answer, or I might satisfy them with my answer.

mn79:7.5.verse: Nevertheless, Udāyī, leave aside the first beginning and the final end.

mn79:7.6.verse: I shall teach you the Dhamma:

mn79:7.7.verse: ‘When this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

mn79:7.8.verse: When this doesn’t exist, that is not; due to the cessation of this, that ceases.’”

mn79:8.1.verse: “Well sir, I can’t even recall with features and details what I’ve undergone in this incarnation.

mn79:8.2.verse: How should I possibly recollect my many kinds of past lives with features and details, like the Buddha?

mn79:8.3.verse: For I can’t even see a mud-goblin right now.

mn79:8.4.verse: How should I possibly, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, see sentient beings passing away and being reborn, like the Buddha?

mn79:8.5.verse: But then the Buddha told me,

mn79:8.6.verse: ‘Nevertheless, Udāyī, leave aside the first beginning and the final end.

mn79:8.7.verse: I shall teach you the Dhamma:

mn79:8.8.verse: “When this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

mn79:8.9.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases.”’ But that is even more unclear to me.

mn79:8.10.verse: Perhaps I might satisfy the Buddha by answering a question about my own denomination.”

mn79:9.1.verse: “But Udāyī, what is your own denomination?”

mn79:9.3.verse: ‘This is the ultimate splendor, this is the ultimate splendor.’”

mn79:9.6.verse: “Sir, the ultimate splendor is the splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.”

mn79:9.7.verse: “But what is that ultimate splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer?”

mn79:9.8.verse: “Sir, the ultimate splendor is the splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.”

mn79:10.1.verse: “Udāyī, you could draw this out for a long time.

mn79:10.2.verse: You say, ‘The ultimate splendor is the splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.’ But you don’t describe that splendor.

mn79:10.3.verse: Suppose a man was to say,

mn79:10.4.verse: ‘Whoever the finest lady in the land is, it is her that I want, her I desire!’

mn79:10.6.verse: ‘My man, that finest lady in the land who you desire—do you know whether she’s an aristocrat, a brahmin, a peasant, or a menial?’

mn79:10.9.verse: ‘My friend, that finest lady in the land who you desire—do you know her name or clan? Whether she’s tall or short or medium? Whether her skin is black, brown, or dingy? Whether she comes from such-and-such village, town, or city?’

mn79:10.12.verse: ‘My man, do you desire someone who you’ve never even known or seen?’

mn79:10.15.verse: This being so, doesn’t that man’s statement turn out to have no demonstrable basis?”

mn79:10.17.verse: “In the same way, you say, ‘The ultimate splendor is the splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.’ But you don’t describe that splendor.”

mn79:11.1.verse: “Worthy sir, suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked. When placed on a cream rug it would shine and glow and dazzle. Such is the splendor of the self that is free of disease after death.”

mn79:12.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: such a beryl gem, or a firefly in the dark of night?”

mn79:12.3.verse: “A firefly in the dark of night, sir.”

mn79:13.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: a firefly in the dark of night, or an oil lamp in the dark of night?”

mn79:13.3.verse: “An oil lamp in the dark of night, sir.”

mn79:14.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: an oil lamp in the dark of night, or a great mass of fire in the dark of night?”

mn79:14.3.verse: “A great mass of fire in the dark of night, sir.”

mn79:15.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: a great mass of fire in the dark of night, or the morning star in the clear and cloudless heavens at the crack of dawn?”

mn79:15.3.verse: “The morning star in the clear and cloudless heavens at the crack of dawn, sir.”

mn79:16.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: the morning star in the clear and cloudless heavens at the crack of dawn, or the full moon at midnight in the clear and cloudless heavens on the fifteenth day sabbath?”

mn79:16.3.verse: “The full moon at midnight in the clear and cloudless heavens on the fifteenth day sabbath, sir.”

mn79:17.2.verse: Which of these two has a finer splendor: the full moon at midnight in the clear and cloudless heavens on the fifteenth day sabbath, or the sun at midday in the clear and cloudless heavens in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn?”

mn79:17.3.verse: “The sun at midday in the clear and cloudless heavens in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, sir.”

mn79:18.1.verse: “Beyond this, Udāyī, I know very many gods on whom the luminosity of the sun and moon makes no impression.

mn79:18.3.verse: ‘The splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.’

mn79:18.4.verse: But of the splendor inferior to a firefly you say, ‘This is the ultimate splendor.’ And you don’t describe that splendor.”

mn79:19.1.verse: “The Blessed One has cut short the discussion! The Holy One has cut short the discussion!”

mn79:19.2.verse: “But Udāyī, why do you say this?”

mn79:19.4.verse: “Sir, it says this in our own denomination:

mn79:19.5.verse: ‘This is the ultimate splendor, this is the ultimate splendor.’

mn79:19.6.verse: But when pursued, pressed, and grilled on our own denomination, we turned out to be vacuous, hollow, and mistaken.”

mn79:20.1.verse: “But Udāyī, is there a world of absolute happiness? And is there a grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness?”

mn79:20.2.verse: “Sir, it says this in our own denomination:

mn79:20.3.verse: ‘There is a world of absolute happiness. And there is a grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.’”

mn79:21.1.verse: “Well, what is that grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness?”

mn79:21.2.verse: “Sir, it’s when someone gives up killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. And they proceed having undertaken some kind of mortification.

mn79:21.3.verse: This is the grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.”

mn79:22.2.verse: On an occasion when someone refrains from killing living creatures, is their self absolutely happy at that time, or does it have both pleasure and pain?”

mn79:22.5.verse: On an occasion when someone refrains from stealing …

mn79:22.9.verse: lying, is their self absolutely happy at that time, or does it have both pleasure and pain?”

mn79:22.12.verse: On an occasion when someone proceeds having undertaken some kind of mortification, is their self absolutely happy at that time, or does it have both pleasure and pain?”

mn79:22.15.verse: Is an absolutely happy world realized by relying on a practice of mixed pleasure and pain?”

mn79:23.1.verse: “The Blessed One has cut short the discussion! The Holy One has cut short the discussion!”

mn79:23.2.verse: “But Udāyī, why do you say this?”

mn79:23.4.verse: “Sir, it says this in our own denomination:

mn79:23.5.verse: ‘There is a world of absolute happiness. And there is a grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.’

mn79:23.6.verse: But when pursued, pressed, and grilled on our own denomination, we turned out to be vacuous, hollow, and mistaken.

mn79:23.7.verse: But sir, is there a world of absolute happiness? And is there a grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness?”

mn79:24.1.verse: “There is a world of absolute happiness, Udāyī. And there is a grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.”

mn79:24.2.verse: “Well sir, what is that grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness?”

mn79:25.1.verse: “It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption.

mn79:25.2.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption.

mn79:25.3.verse: With the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption.

mn79:25.4.verse: This is the grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.”

mn79:25.5.verse: “Sir, that’s not the grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness. At that point an absolutely happy world has already been realized.”

mn79:25.6.verse: “No, Udāyī, at that point an absolutely happy world has not been realized.

mn79:25.7.verse: This is the grounded practice for realizing a world of absolute happiness.”

mn79:26.1.verse: When he said this, Sakuludāyī’s assembly made an uproar, a colossal racket,

mn79:26.2.verse: “In that case, we are lost, together with our denomination! We are lost, together with our denomination!

mn79:26.3.verse: We know nothing higher than this!”

mn79:26.4.verse: Then Sakuludāyī, having quieted those wanderers, said to the Buddha,

mn79:27.1.verse: “Well sir, at what point is an absolutely happy world realized?”

mn79:27.2.verse: “It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption.

mn79:27.3.verse: There are deities who have been reborn in a absolutely happy world. That mendicant associates with them, converses, and engages in discussion.

mn79:27.4.verse: It’s at this point that a absolutely happy world has been realized.”

mn79:28.1.verse: “Surely the mendicants must lead the spiritual life under the Buddha for the sake of realizing this absolutely happy world?”

mn79:28.2.verse: “No, Udāyī, the mendicants don’t lead the spiritual life under me for the sake of realizing this absolutely happy world.

mn79:28.3.verse: There are other things that are finer, for the sake of which the mendicants lead the spiritual life under me.”

mn79:29-36.1.verse: “It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. …

mn79:37.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn79:37.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption.

mn79:37.3.verse: This is one of the finer things for the sake of which the mendicants lead the spiritual life under me.

mn79:38-40.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn79:38-40.4.verse: This too is one of the finer things.

mn79:41.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn79:41.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn79:41.3.verse: This too is one of the finer things.

mn79:42.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn79:42.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn79:42.3.verse: This too is one of the finer things.

mn79:43.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn79:43.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn79:43.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn79:44.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn79:44.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn79:44.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn79:44.4.verse: This too is one of the finer things.

mn79:44.5.verse: These are the finer things for the sake of which the mendicants lead the spiritual life under me.”

mn79:45.1.verse: When he had spoken, Sakuludāyī said to the Buddha,

mn79:45.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn79:45.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn79:45.5.verse: Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

mn79:46.1.verse: When he said this, Sakuludāyī’s assembly said to him,

mn79:46.2.verse: “Worthy Udāyī, don’t lead the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama.

mn79:46.3.verse: You have been a tutor; don’t live as a pupil.

mn79:46.4.verse: You’ll end up like a water jar that turns into a water ladle.

mn79:46.5.verse: Worthy Udāyī, don’t lead the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama.

mn79:46.6.verse: You have been a tutor; don’t live as a pupil.”

mn79:46.7.verse: And that’s how the wanderer Sakuludāyī’s own assembly prevented him from leading the spiritual life under the Buddha.

mn80:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn80:2.1.verse: Then the wanderer Vekhanasa went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn80:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side,

mn80:2.3.verse: and expressed this heartfelt sentiment in the Buddha’s presence:

mn80:2.4.verse: “This is the ultimate splendor, this is the ultimate splendor.”

mn80:2.6.verse: ‘This is the ultimate splendor, this is the ultimate splendor.’

mn80:2.8.verse: “Worthy Gotama, the ultimate splendor is the splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer.”

mn80:2.9.verse: “But what is that ultimate splendor compared to which no other splendor is finer?”
