mn85:4.8.verse: “I gave your message to the worthy Gotama,

mn85:5.1.verse: And when the night had passed Prince Bodhi had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own home. He also had the Pink Lotus longhouse spread with white cloth down to the last step of the staircase. Then he said to Sañjikāputta,

mn85:5.2.verse: “Please, dear Sañjikāputta, go to the Buddha, and announce the time, saying,

mn85:5.3.verse: ‘Sir, it’s time. The meal is ready.’”

mn85:5.4.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” Sañjikāputta replied, and he did as he was asked.

mn85:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Prince Bodhi’s home.

mn85:7.1.verse: Now at that time Prince Bodhi was standing outside the gates waiting for the Buddha.

mn85:7.2.verse: Seeing the Buddha coming off in the distance,

mn85:7.3.verse: he went out to greet him. After bowing and inviting the Buddha to go first, he approached the Pink Lotus longhouse.

mn85:7.4.verse: But the Buddha stopped by the last step of the staircase.

mn85:7.5.verse: Then Prince Bodhi said to him,

mn85:7.6.verse: “Sir, let the Blessed One ascend on the cloth! Let the Holy One ascend on the cloth!

mn85:7.7.verse: It will be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn85:7.8.verse: But when he said this, the Buddha kept silent.

mn85:7.10.verse: and a third time, Prince Bodhi said to him,

mn85:7.11.verse: “Sir, let the Blessed One ascend on the cloth! Let the Holy One ascend on the cloth!

mn85:7.12.verse: It will be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn85:7.13.verse: Then the Buddha glanced at Venerable Ānanda.

mn85:7.14.verse: So Ānanda said to Prince Bodhi,

mn85:7.16.verse: The Buddha will not step upon white cloth.

mn85:7.17.verse: The Realized One has sympathy for future generations.”

mn85:8.1.verse: So Prince Bodhi had the cloth folded up and the seats spread out upstairs in the longhouse.

mn85:8.2.verse: Then the Buddha ascended the longhouse and sat on the seats spread out together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn85:9.1.verse: Then Prince Bodhi served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

mn85:9.2.verse: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Prince Bodhi took a low seat, sat to one side,

mn85:9.5.verse: ‘Pleasure is not gained through pleasure; pleasure is gained through pain.’”

mn85:10.1.verse: “Prince, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too thought,

mn85:10.2.verse: ‘Pleasure is not gained through pleasure; pleasure is gained through pain.’

mn85:11.1.verse: Some time later, while still with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life—though my mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn85:11.2.verse: Once I had gone forth I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn85:11.3.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn85:11.6.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn85:11.8.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn85:11.10.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn85:11.11.verse: Surely he meditates knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn85:12.1.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn85:12.2.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, to what extent do you say you’ve realized this teaching with your own insight?’

mn85:12.3.verse: When I said this, he declared the dimension of nothingness.

mn85:12.5.verse: ‘It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith,

mn85:12.9.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn85:12.10.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma says he has realized with his own insight?’

mn85:12.11.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn85:12.12.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn85:12.13.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, is it up to this point that you realized this teaching with your own insight, and declare having achieved it?’

mn85:12.15.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn85:12.16.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn85:12.17.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn85:12.18.verse: So the teaching that I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn85:12.19.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it.

mn85:12.20.verse: So the teaching that I know, you know, and the teaching you know, I know.

mn85:12.21.verse: I am like you and you are like me.

mn85:12.22.verse: Come now, reverend! We should both lead this community together.’

mn85:12.23.verse: And that is how my tutor Āḷāra Kālāma placed me, his pupil, on the same position as him, and honored me with high praise.

mn85:12.25.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of nothingness.’

mn85:12.26.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn85:12.28.verse: ‘Reverend, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn85:12.33.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn85:12.35.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Rāma declared: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn85:12.36.verse: Surely he meditated knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn85:13.1.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn85:13.2.verse: ‘Reverend, to what extent did Rāma say he’d realized this teaching with his own insight?’

mn85:13.3.verse: When I said this, Uddaka son of Rāma declared the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn85:13.9.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn85:13.10.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Rāma said he had realized with his own insight?’

mn85:13.11.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn85:13.12.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn85:13.13.verse: ‘Reverend, had Rāma realized this teaching with his own insight up to this point, and declared having achieved it?’

mn85:13.15.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn85:13.16.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn85:13.17.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn85:13.18.verse: So the teaching that Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn85:13.19.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it.

mn85:13.20.verse: So the teaching that Rāma directly knew, you know, and the teaching you know, Rāma directly knew.

mn85:13.21.verse: Rāma was like you and you are like Rāma.

mn85:13.22.verse: Come now, reverend! You should lead this community.’

mn85:13.23.verse: And that is how my spiritual companion Uddaka son of Rāma placed me in the position of a tutor and honored me with high praise.

mn85:13.25.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn85:14.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. Traveling stage by stage in the Magadhan lands, I arrived at the town of Senā in Uruvelā.

mn85:14.2.verse: There I saw a delightful park, a lovely grove with a flowing river that was clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby was a village to resort to for alms.

mn85:14.4.verse: ‘This park is truly delightful, a lovely grove with a flowing river that’s clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby there’s a village to resort to for alms.

mn85:14.5.verse: This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.’

mn85:14.6.verse: So I sat down right there, thinking,

mn85:15.1.verse: And then these three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me.

mn85:16.1.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying in water.

mn85:16.2.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn85:16.3.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn85:16.5.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log lying in water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn85:16.8.verse: Because it’s a green, sappy log, and it’s lying in the water.

mn85:16.9.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn85:17.1.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. They haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn85:17.4.verse: This was the first example that occurred to me.

mn85:18.1.verse: Then a second example occurred to me.

mn85:18.2.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn85:18.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn85:18.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn85:18.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn85:18.9.verse: Because it’s still a green, sappy log, despite the fact that it’s lying on dry land far from water.

mn85:18.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn85:18.11.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. But they haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn85:18.14.verse: This was the second example that occurred to me.

mn85:19.1.verse: Then a third example occurred to me.

mn85:19.2.verse: Suppose there was a dried up, withered log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn85:19.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn85:19.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn85:19.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that dried up, withered log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn85:19.9.verse: Because it’s a dried up, withered log, and it’s lying on dry land far from water.”

mn85:19.10.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. And they have internally given up and stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are capable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn85:19.13.verse: This was the third example that occurred to me.

mn85:19.14.verse: These are the three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, that occurred to me.

mn85:20.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, squeeze, squash, and scorch mind with mind?’

mn85:20.4.verse: until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn85:20.5.verse: It was like when a strong man grabs a weaker man by the head or throat or shoulder and squeezes, squashes, and crushes them.

mn85:20.6.verse: In the same way, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I squeezed, squashed, and crushed mind with mind until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn85:20.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:21.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice the breathless absorption?’

mn85:21.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose.

mn85:21.4.verse: But then winds came out my ears making a loud noise,

mn85:21.5.verse: like the puffing of a blacksmith’s bellows.

mn85:21.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:22.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn85:22.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn85:22.4.verse: But then severe winds ground my head,

mn85:22.5.verse: like a strong man was drilling into my head with a sharp point.

mn85:22.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:23.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn85:23.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn85:23.4.verse: But then I got a severe headache,

mn85:23.5.verse: like a strong man was tightening a strong leather strap around my head.

mn85:23.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:24.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn85:24.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn85:24.4.verse: But then severe winds carved up my belly,

mn85:24.5.verse: like a deft butcher or their apprentice was slicing my belly open with a sharp meat cleaver.

mn85:24.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:25.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn85:25.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn85:25.4.verse: But then there was a severe burning in my body,

mn85:25.5.verse: like two strong men grabbing a weaker man by the arms to burn and scorch him on a pit of glowing coals.

mn85:25.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn85:26.1.verse: Then some deities saw me and said,

mn85:26.6.verse: ‘He’s not dead or dying. The ascetic Gotama is a perfected one, for that is how the perfected ones live.’

mn85:27.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice completely cutting off food?’

mn85:27.3.verse: But deities came to me and said,

mn85:27.4.verse: ‘Good fellow, don’t practice totally cutting off food.

mn85:27.5.verse: If you do, we’ll infuse heavenly nectar into your pores and you will live on that.’

mn85:27.7.verse: ‘If I claim to be completely fasting while these deities are infusing heavenly nectar in my pores, that would be a lie on my part.’

mn85:27.8.verse: So I refused those deities, saying, ‘There’s no need.’

mn85:28.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I just take a little bit of food each time, a handful of broth made from mung beans, horse gram, chickpeas, or green gram?’

mn85:28.4.verse: until my body became severely emaciated.

mn85:28.5.verse: Due to eating so little, my major and minor limbs became like the joints of an eighty-year-old or a dying man,

mn85:28.6.verse: my bottom became like a camel’s hoof,

mn85:28.7.verse: my vertebrae stuck out like beads on a string,

mn85:28.8.verse: and my ribs were as gaunt as the broken-down rafters on an old barn.

mn85:28.9.verse: Due to eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets, like the gleam of water sunk deep down a well.

mn85:28.10.verse: Due to eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter-gourd in the wind and sun.

mn85:28.11.verse: Due to eating so little, the skin of my belly stuck to my backbone, so that when I tried to rub the skin of my belly I grabbed my backbone, and when I tried to rub my backbone I rubbed the skin of my belly.

mn85:28.12.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to urinate or defecate I fell face down right there.

mn85:28.13.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell out.

mn85:29.1.verse: Then some people saw me and said, ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’

mn85:29.2.verse: Some said, ‘He’s not black, he’s brown.’

mn85:29.3.verse: Some said, ‘He’s neither black nor brown. The ascetic Gotama has dingy skin.’

mn85:29.4.verse: That’s how far the pure, bright complexion of my skin had been ruined by taking so little food.

mn85:30.2.verse: ‘Whatever ascetics and brahmins have experienced painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion—whether in the past, future, or present—this is as far as it goes, no-one has done more than this.

mn85:30.5.verse: But I have not achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones by this severe, grueling work.

mn85:30.6.verse: Could there be another path to awakening?’

mn85:31.2.verse: ‘I recall sitting in the cool shade of a black plum tree while my father the Sakyan was off working. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn85:31.3.verse: Could that be the path to awakening?’

mn85:31.4.verse: Stemming from that memory came the understanding:

mn85:32.2.verse: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities?’

mn85:32.4.verse: ‘I’m not afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities.’

mn85:33.2.verse: ‘I can’t achieve that pleasure with a body so severely emaciated. Why don’t I eat some solid food, some rice and porridge?’

mn85:33.3.verse: So I ate some solid food.

mn85:33.4.verse: Now at that time the group of five mendicants were attending on me, thinking,

mn85:33.5.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama will tell us of any truth that he realizes.’

mn85:33.6.verse: But when I ate some solid food, they left disappointed in me, saying,

mn85:33.7.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become indulgent; he has strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.’

mn85:34-37.1.verse: After eating solid food and gathering my strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption …

mn85:34-37.5.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives.

mn85:34-37.6.verse: I recollected many past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. And so I recollected my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn85:34-37.7.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

mn85:34-37.8.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn85:38.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn85:38.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn85:39.1.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn85:40.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn85:40.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn85:40.3.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn85:41.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn85:41.2.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

mn85:41.3.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.’

mn85:42.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night.

mn85:42.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn85:43.2.verse: ‘This principle I have discovered is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

mn85:43.3.verse: But people like clinging, they love it and enjoy it.

mn85:43.4.verse: It’s hard for them to see this topic; that is, specific conditionality, dependent origination.

mn85:43.5.verse: It’s also hard for them to see this topic; that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

mn85:43.6.verse: And if I were to teach this principle, others might not understand me, which would be wearying and troublesome for me.’

mn85:43.7.verse: And then these verses, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me:

mn85:43.9.verse: there’s no need to reveal it now!

mn85:43.10.verse: Those mired in greed and hate

mn85:43.12.verse: It goes against the stream, subtle,

mn85:43.14.verse: Those besotted by greed cannot see,

mn85:43.15.verse: for they’re cloaked in a mass of darkness.’

mn85:43.16.verse: So, as I reflected like this, my mind inclined to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.

mn85:44.1.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing my train of thought, thought,

mn85:44.2.verse: ‘Oh lord! The world will be lost, the world will perish! For the mind of the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, inclines to remaining passive, not to teaching the Dhamma.’

mn85:44.3.verse: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, the divinity Sahampati vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of me.

mn85:44.4.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward me, and said,

mn85:44.5.verse: ‘Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Holy One teach the Dhamma!

mn85:44.6.verse: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching.

mn85:44.7.verse: There will be those who understand the teaching!’

mn85:44.8.verse: That is what the divinity Sahampati said.

mn85:44.9.verse: Then he went on to say:

mn85:44.10.verse: ‘Among the Magadhans there appeared in the past

mn85:44.11.verse: an impure teaching thought up by the stained.

mn85:44.12.verse: Fling open the door to freedom from death!

mn85:44.13.verse: Let them hear the teaching the immaculate one discovered.

mn85:44.14.verse: Standing high on a rocky mountain,

mn85:44.15.verse: you can see the people all around.

mn85:44.16.verse: In just the same way, All-seer, so intelligent,

mn85:44.17.verse: having ascended the Temple of Truth,

mn85:44.18.verse: rid of sorrow, look upon the people

mn85:44.19.verse: swamped with sorrow, overcome by rebirth and old age.

mn85:44.20.verse: Rise, hero! Victor in battle, caravan leader,

mn85:44.21.verse: wander the world free of debt.

mn85:44.22.verse: Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma!

mn85:44.23.verse: There will be those who understand!’

mn85:45.1.verse: Then, understanding the Divinity’s invitation, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, because of my compassion for sentient beings.

mn85:45.2.verse: And I saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes; with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach. And some of them lived seeing the danger in the fault to do with the next world, while others did not.

mn85:45.3.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. Some of them sprout and grow in the water reaching the water’s surface. And some of them sprout and grow in the water but rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to them.

mn85:45.4.verse: In the same way, I saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes, and some with much dust in their eyes.

mn85:45.5.verse: Then I replied in verse to the divinity Sahampati:

mn85:45.6.verse: ‘Flung open are the doors to freedom from death!

mn85:45.7.verse: Let those with ears to hear commit to faith.

mn85:45.8.verse: Thinking it would be troublesome, Divinity, I did not teach

mn85:45.9.verse: the sophisticated, sublime Dhamma among mankind.’

mn85:45.10.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing that his request for me to teach the Dhamma had been granted, bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right, before vanishing right there.

mn85:46.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn85:46.3.verse: Who will quickly understand the teaching?’

mn85:46.5.verse: ‘That Āḷāra Kālāma is astute, competent, intelligent, and has long had little dust in his eyes.

mn85:46.6.verse: Why don’t I teach him first of all?

mn85:46.8.verse: But a deity came to me and said,

mn85:46.9.verse: ‘Sir, Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’

mn85:46.10.verse: And knowledge and vision arose in me,

mn85:46.11.verse: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago.’

mn85:46.13.verse: ‘This is a great loss for Āḷāra Kālāma.

mn85:46.14.verse: If he had heard the teaching, he would have understood it quickly.’

mn85:47.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn85:47.3.verse: Who will quickly understand the teaching?’

mn85:47.5.verse: ‘That Uddaka son of Rāma is astute, competent, intelligent, and has long had little dust in his eyes.

mn85:47.6.verse: Why don’t I teach him first of all?

mn85:47.8.verse: But a deity came to me and said,

mn85:47.9.verse: ‘Sir, Uddaka son of Rāma, passed away just last night.’

mn85:47.10.verse: And knowledge and vision arose in me,

mn85:47.11.verse: ‘Uddaka son of Rāma, passed away just last night.’

mn85:47.13.verse: ‘This is a great loss for Uddaka.

mn85:47.14.verse: If he had heard the teaching, he would have understood it quickly.’

mn85:48.2.verse: ‘Who should I teach first of all?

mn85:48.3.verse: Who will quickly understand the teaching?’

mn85:48.5.verse: ‘The group of five mendicants were very helpful to me. They looked after me during my time of resolute striving.

mn85:48.6.verse: Why don’t I teach them first of all?’

mn85:48.8.verse: ‘Where are the group of five mendicants staying these days?’

mn85:48.9.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman I saw that the group of five mendicants were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

mn85:49.1.verse: So, when I had stayed in Uruvelā as long as I pleased, I set out for Varanasi.

mn85:49.2.verse: While I was traveling along the road between Gayā and Bodhgaya, the Ājīvaka ascetic Upaka saw me

mn85:49.4.verse: ‘Reverend, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

mn85:49.5.verse: In whose name have you gone forth, reverend? Who is your Teacher? Whose teaching do you believe in?’

mn85:49.6.verse: I replied to Upaka in verse:

mn85:49.7.verse: ‘I am the vanquisher of all, the knower of all,

mn85:49.8.verse: unsullied in the midst of all things.

mn85:49.9.verse: I’ve given up all, freed in the ending of craving.

mn85:49.10.verse: Since I know for myself, whose follower should I be?

mn85:49.12.verse: There is no one like me.

mn85:49.13.verse: In the world with its gods,

mn85:49.15.verse: For in this world, I am the perfected one;

mn85:49.19.verse: I am going to the city of Kāsi

mn85:49.20.verse: to roll forth the Wheel of Dhamma.

mn85:49.21.verse: In this world that is so blind,

mn85:49.22.verse: I’ll beat the drum of freedom from death!’

mn85:49.23.verse: ‘According to what you claim, reverend, you ought to be the Infinite Victor.’

mn85:49.24.verse: ‘The victors are those who, like me,

mn85:49.25.verse: have reached the ending of defilements.

mn85:49.26.verse: I have conquered bad qualities, Upaka—

mn85:49.28.verse: When I had spoken, Upaka said: ‘If you say so, reverend.’ Shaking his head, he took a wrong turn and left.

mn85:50.1.verse: Traveling stage by stage, I arrived at Varanasi, and went to see the group of five mendicants in the deer park at Isipatana.

mn85:50.2.verse: The group of five mendicants saw me coming off in the distance

mn85:50.4.verse: ‘Here comes the ascetic Gotama. He’s so indulgent; he strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.

mn85:50.5.verse: We shouldn’t bow to him or rise for him or receive his bowl and robe.

mn85:50.6.verse: But we can set out a seat; he can sit if he likes.’

mn85:50.7.verse: Yet as I drew closer, the group of five mendicants were unable to stop themselves per their own agreement.

mn85:50.8.verse: Some came out to greet me and receive my bowl and robe, some spread out a seat, while others set out water for washing my feet.

mn85:50.9.verse: But they still addressed me by name and as ‘reverend’.

mn85:51.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, don’t address me by name and as “reverend”.

mn85:51.3.verse: The Realized One is Perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn85:51.4.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn85:51.5.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn85:51.7.verse: ‘Reverend Gotama, even by that conduct, that practice, that grueling work you did not achieve any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How could you have achieved such a state now that you’ve become indulgent, strayed from the struggle and fallen into indulgence?’

mn85:51.9.verse: ‘The Realized One has not become indulgent, strayed from the struggle and fallen into indulgence.

mn85:51.10.verse: The Realized One is Perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn85:51.11.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn85:51.12.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn85:51.13.verse: But for a second time they said to me,

mn85:51.15.verse: So for a second time I said to them,

mn85:51.16.verse: ‘The Realized One has not become indulgent …’

mn85:51.20.verse: But for a third time they said to me,

mn85:52.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, have you ever known me to speak like this before?’

mn85:52.4.verse: ‘The Realized One is Perfected, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn85:52.5.verse: Listen up, mendicants: I have achieved freedom from death! I shall instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma.

mn85:52.6.verse: By practicing as instructed you will soon realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. You will live having achieved with your own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

mn85:53.1.verse: I was able to persuade the group of five mendicants.

mn85:53.2.verse: Then sometimes I advised two mendicants, while the other three went for alms.

mn85:53.3.verse: Then those three would feed all six of us with what they brought back.

mn85:53.4.verse: Sometimes I advised three mendicants, while the other two went for alms.

mn85:53.5.verse: Then those two would feed all six of us with what they brought back.

mn85:54.1.verse: As the group of five mendicants were being advised and instructed by me like this, they soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They lived having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

mn85:55.1.verse: When he had spoken, Prince Bodhi said to the Buddha,

mn85:55.2.verse: “Sir, when a mendicant has the Realized One as trainer, how long would it take for them to realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life?”

mn85:55.3.verse: “Well then, prince, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn85:55.5.verse: Are you skilled in the art of wielding a hooked goad while riding an elephant?”

mn85:56.2.verse: Suppose a man were to come along thinking,

mn85:56.3.verse: ‘Prince Bodhi knows the art of wielding a hooked goad while riding an elephant.

mn85:56.4.verse: I’ll train in that art under him.’

mn85:56.6.verse: he wouldn’t achieve what he could with faith.

mn85:56.8.verse: he wouldn’t achieve what he could with good health.

mn85:56.10.verse: he wouldn’t achieve what he could with honesty and integrity.

mn85:56.12.verse: he wouldn’t achieve what he could with energy.

mn85:56.14.verse: he wouldn’t achieve what he could with wisdom.

mn85:56.16.verse: Could that man still train under you in the art of wielding a hooked goad while riding an elephant?”

mn85:56.17.verse: “Sir, if he had even a single one of these factors he couldn’t train under me, let alone all five.”

mn85:57.2.verse: Suppose a man were to come along thinking,

mn85:57.3.verse: ‘Prince Bodhi knows the art of wielding a hooked goad while riding an elephant.

mn85:57.4.verse: I’ll train in that art under him.’

mn85:57.6.verse: he’d achieve what he could with faith.

mn85:57.8.verse: he’d achieve what he could with good health.

mn85:57.9.verse: If he’s honest and has integrity,

mn85:57.10.verse: he’d achieve what he could with honesty and integrity.

mn85:57.12.verse: he’d achieve what he could with energy.

mn85:57.14.verse: he’d achieve what he could with wisdom.

mn85:57.16.verse: Could that man still train under you in the art of wielding a hooked goad while riding an elephant?”

mn85:57.17.verse: “Sir, if he had even a single one of these factors he could train under me, let alone all five.”

mn85:58.1.verse: “In the same way, prince, there are these five factors that support meditation.

mn85:58.3.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

mn85:58.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn85:58.5.verse: They are rarely ill or unwell. Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

mn85:58.6.verse: They’re not devious or deceitful. They reveal themselves honestly to the Teacher or sensible spiritual companions.

mn85:58.7.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

mn85:58.8.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

mn85:58.9.verse: These are the five factors that support meditation.

mn85:59.1.verse: When a mendicant with these five factors that support meditation has the Realized One as trainer, they could

mn85:59.2.verse: realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in seven years.

mn85:59.5.verse: realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in six years,

mn85:59.10.verse: or as little as one year.

mn85:59.12.verse: when a mendicant with these five factors that support meditation has the Realized One as trainer, they could

mn85:59.13.verse: realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in seven months,

mn85:59.36.verse: or as little as one day.

mn85:59.38.verse: when a mendicant with these five factors that support meditation has the Realized One as trainer, they could be instructed at dusk and achieve distinction at daybreak, or be instructed at daybreak and achieve distinction at dusk.”

mn85:60.1.verse: When he had spoken, Prince Bodhi said to the Buddha,

mn85:60.2.verse: “Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the teaching! Oh, how well explained is the teaching!

mn85:60.3.verse: For someone could be instructed at dusk and achieve distinction at daybreak, or be instructed at daybreak and achieve distinction at dusk.”

mn85:61.1.verse: When he said this, Sañjikāputta said to Prince Bodhi,

mn85:61.2.verse: “Though the worthy Bodhi speaks like this,

mn85:61.4.verse: you don’t go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.”

mn85:61.5.verse: “Don’t say that, dear Sañjikāputta, don’t say that!

mn85:61.6.verse: I have heard and learned this in the presence of my lady mother.

mn85:61.7.verse: This one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

mn85:61.8.verse: Then my pregnant lady mother went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn85:61.9.verse: ‘Sir, the prince or princess in my womb goes for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn85:61.10.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember them as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.’

mn85:61.11.verse: Another time the Buddha was staying here in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

mn85:61.12.verse: Then my nursemaid, carrying me on her hip, went to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

mn85:61.13.verse: ‘Sir, this Prince Bodhi goes for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn85:61.14.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember him as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.’

mn85:61.15.verse: Now for a third time I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn85:61.16.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn86:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn86:2.1.verse: 2. Now on that occasion there was a bandit in the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala called Aṅgulimāla, or ‘Finger-garland’ who was murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.

mn86:2.2.verse: Villages, towns and districts were being laid waste by him.

mn86:2.3.verse: He was constantly murdering people, and he wore their fingers (aṅguli) as a garland (māla).

mn86:3.1.verse: Then, when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Sāvatthi for alms.

mn86:3.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Sāvatthi and had returned from his alms-round after his meal, he set his resting place in order, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he set out by the road to where Aṅgulimāla was.

mn86:3.3.verse: Cowherds, shepherds and ploughmen passing by saw him taking the road to where Aṅgulimāla was.

mn86:3.4.verse: When they saw him, they said:

mn86:3.6.verse: On that road is the bandit Aṅgulimāla who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.

mn86:3.7.verse: Villages and towns and districts are being laid waste by him.

mn86:3.8.verse: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.

mn86:3.9.verse: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty from time to time,

mn86:3.10.verse: but still they have fallen into Aṅgulimāla’s hands.’

mn86:3.11.verse: When this was said the Blessed One went on in silence.

mn86:3.13.verse: A third time the cowherds, shepherds and ploughmen passing by said:

mn86:3.14.verse: ‘Do not take that road, monk. On that road is the bandit Aṅgulimāla who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings. Villages and towns and districts are being laid waste by him.

mn86:3.15.verse: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.

mn86:3.16.verse: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty from time to time,

mn86:3.17.verse: but still they have fallen into Aṅgulimāla’s hands.’

mn86:4.1.verse: Still the Blessed One went on in silence.

mn86:4.2.verse: The bandit Aṅgulimāla saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

mn86:4.5.verse: Men have come along this road in groups of ten, twenty, thirty and even forty, from time to time

mn86:4.6.verse: but still they have fallen into my hands.

mn86:4.7.verse: And now this monk comes alone and unaccompanied. One would fancy he had been fated to come.

mn86:4.8.verse: Why should I not take this monk’s life ?”

mn86:5.1.verse: Angulimāla took up his sword and shield and buckled on his bow and quiver, and he followed behind the Blessed One.

mn86:5.2.verse: Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal success that the bandit Angulimāla, going as fast as he could, was unable to catch up with the Blessed One, who was walking at his normal pace.

mn86:5.5.verse: Formerly I caught up with even a galloping elephant and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping horse and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping chariot and seized it; I caught up with even a galloping deer and seized it;

mn86:5.6.verse: but yet, though I am going as fast as I can, I am unable to catch up with this monk who is walking at his normal pace!’

mn86:5.9.verse: ‘I have stopped, Angulimāla. Do you stop, too.’

mn86:5.11.verse: ‘These monks, sons of Sakyans, speak truth, assert truth:

mn86:5.12.verse: but though this monk is walking yet he says

mn86:5.13.verse: “I have stopped. Angulimāla. Do you stop too.”

mn86:6.1.verse: Then he addressed the Blessed One in stanzas thus:

mn86:6.2.verse: ‘While you are walking, monk, you tell me you have stopped;

mn86:6.3.verse: But now, when I have stopped, you say I have not stopped.

mn86:6.4.verse: I ask you now, O monk, what is the meaning of it;

mn86:6.5.verse: How is it you have stopped and I have not ?’

mn86:6.7.verse: Forswearing violence to every living being;

mn86:6.8.verse: But you have no restraint towards things that breathe:

mn86:6.9.verse: So that is why I have stopped and you have not.’

mn86:6.10.verse: ‘Oh, at long last a sage revered by me,

mn86:6.11.verse: This monk, has now appeared in the great forest:

mn86:6.12.verse: Indeed I will for long renounce all evil,

mn86:6.13.verse: Hearing your stanza showing the Dhamma.’

mn86:6.15.verse: And flung them in a gaping chasm’s pit;

mn86:6.16.verse: The bandit worshipped the Sublime One’s feet,

mn86:6.17.verse: And then and there asked for the Going-forth.

mn86:6.18.verse: The Enlightened One, the Sage of Great Compassion,

mn86:6.19.verse: The Teacher of the world with (all) its gods,

mn86:6.20.verse: Addressed him with these words ‘Come bhikkhu’,

mn86:6.21.verse: And that was how he came to be a bhikkhu.

mn86:7.1.verse: Then the Blessed One set out to wander by stages back to Sāvatthi with Aṅgulimāla as his attendant monk,

mn86:7.2.verse: and eventually he arrived at Sāvatthi.

mn86:7.3.verse: Then the Blessed One stayed in Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn86:8.1.verse: Now on that occasion great crowds of people were gathering at the gates of King Pasenadi’s inner palace, very clamorous and noisy, (crying:)

mn86:8.2.verse: ‘Sire, there is a bandit called Aṅgulimāla in your realm; he is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings!

mn86:8.3.verse: Villages, towns and districts are being laid waste by him!

mn86:8.4.verse: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland!

mn86:8.5.verse: The king must put him down!’

mn86:9.1.verse: Then in broad day King Pasenadi of Kosala drove out with (a bodyguard of) five hundred horse,

mn86:9.3.verse: He went as far as the road was passable for carriages, and then he dismounted from his carriage and went to the Blessed One on foot. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:

mn86:9.4.verse: ‘What is it, great king? Is Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha attacking you, or the Licchavis of Vesāli, or other hostile kings?’

mn86:10.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, Seniya Bimbisāra king of Magadha is not attacking me, nor are the Licchavis of Vesāli, nor are other hostile kings.

mn86:10.2.verse: But there is a bandit in my realm called Aṅgulimāla, who is murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, and merciless to all living beings.

mn86:10.3.verse: Villages, town and districts are being laid waste by him.

mn86:10.4.verse: He is constantly murdering people, and he wears their fingers as a garland.

mn86:10.5.verse: I shall never be able to put him down, venerable sir.’

mn86:11.1.verse: ‘Great king, if you saw that Aṅgulimāla had shaved off his hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and that he was abstaining from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from false speech, and, eating in (only) one half of the day, he was living the life divine in virtue and good Dhamma, (if you saw him thus,) how would you treat him?’

mn86:11.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, we should pay homage, or we should rise up for him, or we should invite him to be seated, or we should invite him to accept robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, or we should arrange for his guarding in accordance with the Dhamma, and his defence and protection.

mn86:11.3.verse: But, venerable sir, he is an evil-doer, one of evil qualities; how could he have such virtue and restraint?’

mn86:12.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Angulimāla was sitting not far from the Blessed One,

mn86:12.2.verse: who extended his right arm, saying to King Pasenadi of Kosala:

mn86:12.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi was alarmed and fearful, and his hair stood on end.

mn86:12.5.verse: Knowing this, the Blessed One told him:

mn86:12.6.verse: ‘Do not be afraid, great king, do not be afraid. There is nothing for you to fear.’

mn86:12.7.verse: Then the king’s alarm and fear and horror was allayed.

mn86:12.8.verse: He went over to the venerable Angulimāla and said:

mn86:12.9.verse: ‘Venerable sir, Angulimāla was a noble lord, was he not?’

mn86:12.11.verse: ‘Venerable sir, of what family was the noble lord’s father? Of what family was his mother?’

mn86:12.12.verse: ‘My father was a Gagga, great king; my mother was a Mantāni.’

mn86:12.13.verse: ‘Let the noble lord Gagga Mantāniputta rest content.

mn86:12.14.verse: I shall take care of robes, alms-food, resting-place, and the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick, for the noble lord Gagga Mantāniputta.’

mn86:13.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Angulimāla was a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater and a refuse-rag wearer restricting himself to three robes.

mn86:13.3.verse: ‘Enough, great king, my triple robe is complete.’

mn86:13.4.verse: King Pasenadi then returned to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn86:13.5.verse: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous

mn86:13.6.verse: how the Blessed One subdues the unsubdued, quiets the unquieted, brings about extinguishment in the unextinguished.

mn86:15.9.verse: And the woman and the infant had peace.

mn86:15.9.verse: Then that woman was safe, and so was her baby.

mn87:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn87:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion a certain householder’s dear and beloved only son had died.

mn87:2.2.verse: After his son’s death, he gave no more thought to his work or his meals.

mn87:2.3.verse: He kept going to the charnel-ground and crying:

mn87:2.4.verse: ‘My only child, where are you? My only child, where are you?’

mn87:3.1.verse: Then he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:

mn87:3.2.verse: ‘Householder, your faculties seem those one of who is out of his mind. Your faculties are in no normal state.’

mn87:3.3.verse: ‘How should my faculties be in their normal state, venerable sir?

mn87:3.4.verse: For my dear and beloved only son is dead.

mn87:3.5.verse: Since he died I have given no more thought to my work or my meals.

mn87:3.6.verse: I keep going to the charnel ground and crying:

mn87:3.7.verse: “My only child, where are you? My only child, where are you?”’

mn87:3.8.verse: ‘So it is, householder, so it is.

mn87:3.9.verse: Dear ones, those who are dear (bring) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.’

mn87:3.11.verse: dear ones, those who are dear, (bring) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair?

mn87:3.12.verse: Venerable sir, dear ones, those who are dear, (bring) happiness and joy.’

mn87:3.13.verse: Then, not delighting in the Blessed One’s words, and disapproving, he got up from his seat and went away.

mn87:4.1.verse: Now on that occasion some gamblers were playing with dice not far from the Blessed One.

mn87:4.2.verse: Then the householder went to the gamblers and said:

mn87:4.4.verse: “Householder, your faculties seem those of one who is out of his mind. Your faculties are not in their normal state.”

mn87:4.5.verse: When that was said, sirs, I told him:

mn87:4.6.verse: “How should my faculties be in their normal-state, venerable sir?

mn87:4.7.verse: For my dear and beloved only son is dead.

mn87:4.12.verse: Dear ones, those who are dear (bring) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.”

mn87:4.14.verse: dear ones, those who are dear, (bring) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair?

mn87:4.17.verse: ‘So it is, householder, so it is.

mn87:4.18.verse: Dear ones, those who are dear, (bring) happiness and joy.’

mn87:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn87:2.1.verse: Now at that time a certain householder’s dear and beloved only child passed away.

mn87:2.2.verse: After their death he didn’t feel like working or eating.

mn87:2.3.verse: He would go to the cremation ground and wail,

mn87:2.4.verse: “Where are you, my only child? Where are you, my only child?”

mn87:3.1.verse: Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn87:3.2.verse: “Your faculties, householder, are those of one who is unstable in their own mind; there is a deterioration in your faculties.”

mn87:3.3.verse: “And how, sir, could there be no deterioration of my faculties?

mn87:3.4.verse: For my dear and beloved only child has passed away.

mn87:3.5.verse: Since their death I haven’t felt like working or eating.

mn87:3.6.verse: I go to the cremation ground and wail:

mn87:3.7.verse: ‘Where are you, my only child? Where are you, my only child?’”

mn87:3.8.verse: “That’s so true, householder! That’s so true, householder!

mn87:3.9.verse: For our loved ones are a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.”

mn87:3.10.verse: “Sir, who on earth could ever think such a thing!

mn87:3.12.verse: For our loved ones are a source of joy and happiness.”

mn87:3.13.verse: Disagreeing with the Buddha’s statement, rejecting it, he rose from his seat and left.

mn87:4.1.verse: Now at that time several gamblers were playing dice not far from the Buddha.

mn87:4.2.verse: That householder approached them and told them what had happened.

mn87:4.17.verse: “That’s so true, householder! That’s so true, householder!

mn87:4.18.verse: For our loved ones are a source of joy and happiness.”

mn87:4.19.verse: Thinking, “The gamblers and I are in agreement,” the householder left.

mn87:5.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi addressed Queen Mallikā,

mn87:5.4.verse: ‘Our loved ones are a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.’”

mn87:5.5.verse: “If that’s what the Buddha said, Great King, then that’s how it is.”

mn87:5.6.verse: “No matter what the ascetic Gotama says, Mallikā agrees with him:

mn87:5.7.verse: ‘If that’s what the Buddha said, Great King, then that’s how it is.’

mn87:5.8.verse: You’re just like a pupil who agrees with everything their tutor says.

mn87:5.12.verse: Go away, Mallikā, get out of here!”

mn87:6.1.verse: Then Queen Mallikā addressed the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha,

mn87:6.2.verse: “Please, brahmin, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Ask him if he is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

mn87:6.5.verse: ‘Sir, did the Buddha make this statement:

mn87:6.6.verse: “Our loved ones are a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress”?’

mn87:6.7.verse: Remember well how the Buddha answers and tell it to me.

mn87:6.8.verse: For Realized Ones say nothing that is not so.”

mn87:6.9.verse: “Yes, ma’am,” he replied. He went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn87:6.10.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

mn87:6.11.verse: “Worthy Gotama, Queen Mallikā bows with her head to your feet. She asks if you are healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.

mn87:6.14.verse: ‘Our loved ones are a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.’”
