mn88:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn88:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

mn88:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Eastern Monastery, the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother, for the day’s meditation.

mn88:3.1.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala mounted the Single Lotus Elephant and drove out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day.

mn88:3.2.verse: He saw Ānanda coming off in the distance

mn88:3.3.verse: and said to the chief minister Sirivaḍḍha,

mn88:3.4.verse: “My dear Sirivaḍḍha, isn’t that Venerable Ānanda?”

mn88:4.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi addressed a man,

mn88:4.2.verse: “Please, my man, go to Venerable Ānanda, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him,

mn88:4.3.verse: ‘Sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala bows with his head at your feet.’

mn88:4.5.verse: ‘Sir, if you have no urgent business, please wait a while out of sympathy.’”

mn88:5.1.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” that man replied. He did as the king asked.

mn88:6.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi rode on the elephant as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and approached Ānanda on foot. He bowed, stood to one side, and said to Ānanda,

mn88:6.3.verse: “Sir, if you have no urgent business, it would be nice of you to go to the bank of the Aciravatī River out of sympathy.”

mn88:7.2.verse: He went to the river bank and sat at the root of a certain tree on a seat spread out.

mn88:7.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi rode on the elephant as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and approached Ānanda on foot. He bowed, stood to one side, and said to Ānanda,

mn88:7.4.verse: “Here, Venerable Ānanda, sit on this elephant rug.”

mn88:7.7.verse: I’m sitting on my own seat.”

mn88:8.1.verse: So the king sat down on the seat spread out,

mn88:8.3.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, would the Buddha engage in the sort of behavior—by way of body, speech, or mind—that is faulted by ascetics and brahmins?”

mn88:8.4.verse: “No, Great King, the Buddha would not engage in the sort of behavior that is faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins.”

mn88:9.2.verse: For I couldn’t fully express the question, but Venerable Ānanda’s answer completed it for me.

mn88:9.3.verse: I don’t believe that praise or criticism of others spoken by incompetent fools, without examining or scrutinizing, is the most important thing.

mn88:9.4.verse: Rather, I believe that praise or criticism of others spoken by competent and intelligent people after examining and scrutinizing is the most important thing.

mn88:10.1.verse: But Honorable Ānanda, what kind of bodily behavior is faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins?”

mn88:10.3.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is unskillful?”

mn88:10.5.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is blameworthy?”

mn88:10.7.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is hurtful?”

mn88:10.9.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior results in suffering?”

mn88:10.10.verse: “Bodily behavior that leads to hurting yourself, hurting others, and hurting both,

mn88:10.11.verse: and which makes unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn88:10.12.verse: That kind of bodily behavior is faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins.”

mn88:11.2.verse: mental behavior is faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins?” …

mn88:12.4.verse: “Mental behavior that leads to hurting yourself, hurting others, and hurting both,

mn88:12.5.verse: and which makes unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn88:12.6.verse: That kind of mental behavior is faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins.”

mn88:13.1.verse: “Sir, does the Buddha praise giving up all these unskillful things?”

mn88:13.2.verse: “Great king, the Realized One has given up all unskillful things and possesses skillful things.”

mn88:14.1.verse: “But sir, what kind of bodily behavior is not faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins?”

mn88:14.3.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is skillful?”

mn88:14.5.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is blameless?”

mn88:14.7.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior is pleasing?”

mn88:14.9.verse: “But what kind of bodily behavior results in happiness?”

mn88:14.10.verse: “Bodily behavior that leads to pleasing yourself, pleasing others, and pleasing both,

mn88:14.11.verse: and which makes unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn88:14.12.verse: That kind of bodily behavior is not faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins.”

mn88:15.2.verse: mental behavior is not faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins?” …

mn88:16.6.verse: “Mental behavior that leads to pleasing yourself, pleasing others, and pleasing both,

mn88:16.7.verse: and which makes unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn88:16.8.verse: That kind of mental behavior is not faulted by sensible ascetics and brahmins.”

mn88:17.1.verse: “Sir, does the Buddha praise embracing all these skillful things?”

mn88:17.2.verse: “Great king, the Realized One has given up all unskillful things and possesses skillful things.”

mn88:18.2.verse: How well this was said by Venerable Ānanda!

mn88:18.3.verse: I’m delighted and satisfied with what you’ve expressed so well.

mn88:18.5.verse: if an elephant-treasure was suitable for you, I would give you one.

mn88:18.6.verse: If a horse-treasure was suitable for you, I would give you one.

mn88:18.7.verse: If a prize village was suitable for you, I would give you one.

mn88:18.9.verse: these things are not suitable for you.

mn88:18.10.verse: This foreign cloth was sent to me by King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, packed in a parasol case. It’s exactly sixteen measures long and eight wide.

mn88:18.11.verse: May Venerable Ānanda please accept it out of sympathy.”

mn88:18.12.verse: “Enough, Great King. My three robes are complete.”

mn88:19.1.verse: “Sir, we have both seen this Aciravatī River

mn88:19.2.verse: when it has rained heavily in the mountains, and the river overflows both its banks.

mn88:19.3.verse: In the same way, Venerable Ānanda can make a set of three robes for himself from this foreign cloth,

mn88:19.4.verse: and you can share your old robes with your fellow monks.

mn88:19.5.verse: In this way my religious donation will come to overflow, it seems to me.

mn88:20.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi said to him,

mn88:20.4.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn88:20.5.verse: “Please, Great King, go at your convenience.”

mn88:20.6.verse: Then King Pasenadi approved and agreed with what Ānanda said. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled Ānanda, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn88:21.1.verse: Soon after he left, Ānanda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

mn88:21.2.verse: and told him what had happened.

mn88:21.3.verse: He presented the cloth to the Buddha.

mn88:22.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn88:22.2.verse: “Mendicants, King Pasenadi is lucky, so very lucky,

mn88:22.3.verse: to get to see Ānanda and pay homage to him.”

mn88:22.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn88:22.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn89:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Sakyan country. There is a town of the Sakyans called Medaḷumpa.

mn89:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion King Pasenadi of Kosala had arrived at Nāgaraka for some business or other.

mn89:2.3.verse: ‘My friend, have the state carriages got ready. Let us go to the Pleasure Garden to see a pleasing spot.’

mn89:2.4.verse: ‘Yes, sire,’ he replied. When the state carriages were ready, he informed the king:

mn89:2.5.verse: ‘Sire, the state carriages are ready for you.

mn89:2.6.verse: Now it is time to do as you think fit.’

mn89:3.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi mounted a state carriage and driving out from Nāgaraka with the full pomp of royalty,

mn89:3.3.verse: He went thus as far as the road was passable for carriages, and then he got down from his carriage and went forward on foot.

mn89:4.1.verse: As he walked and wandered in the Park for exercise, he saw the roots of trees that inspired trust and confidence in him, that were quiet and undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of unfrequentedness, where one could lie hidden from people, favourable for retreat.

mn89:4.2.verse: The sight of them reminded him of the Blessed One thus:

mn89:4.3.verse: ‘These roots of trees are like (those) that inspired trust and confidence in me, that were quiet and undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of unfrequentedness, where one could lie hidden from people, favourable for retreat, where we used to do honour to the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened.’

mn89:4.5.verse: ‘These roots of trees, friend Kārāyana, are like (those) that inspired trust and confidence in me, that were quiet and undisturbed by voices, with an atmosphere of unfrequentedness, where one could lie hidden from people, favourable for retreat, where we used to do honour to the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened.

mn89:4.6.verse: ‘Where is he living now, the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened?’

mn89:5.1.verse: ‘There is a town of the Sakyans called Medaḷumpa, sire.

mn89:5.2.verse: The Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened is living there now.’

mn89:5.3.verse: ‘How far is it from Nāgaraka to Medaḷumpa?’

mn89:5.6.verse: There is still daylight enough to go there.’

mn89:5.7.verse: ‘Then, my friend, get the state carriages ready. Let us go and see the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened.’

mn89:5.8.verse: ‘Yes, sire,’ he replied. When the state carriages were ready, he informed the king:

mn89:5.9.verse: ‘Sire, the state carriages are ready for you.

mn89:5.10.verse: Now it is time to do as you think fit.’

mn89:6.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi mounted a state carriage, and he drove out of Nāgaraka and proceeded to the Sakyan town of Medalumpa.

mn89:6.2.verse: He arrived there while it was still daylight,

mn89:6.3.verse: and he proceeded to the Park.

mn89:6.4.verse: He went thus as far as the road was passable for carriages, and then he got down from his carriage and went into the park on foot.

mn89:7.1.verse: Now on that occasion a number of bhikkhus were walking up and down in the open.

mn89:7.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi went to them and asked:

mn89:7.3.verse: ‘Venerable sirs, where is he living now, the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened?

mn89:7.4.verse: We want to see the Blessed One, Arahant and Fully Enlightened.’

mn89:8.1.verse: ‘That is his dwelling, great king, with the closed door. Go up to it quietly, go into the porch without hurry, cough and tap on the panel. The Blessed One will open the door to you.’

mn89:8.2.verse: King Pasenadi handed over his sword and turban to Digha Kārāyana then and there.

mn89:8.4.verse: ‘So the King is going into secret session now! And I have to wait here alone now!

mn89:8.5.verse: King Pasenadi went quietly up to the dwelling with the closed door. He went into the porch without hurry, coughed and tapped on the panel. The Blessed One opened the door.

mn89:9.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi entered the dwelling. He prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet, and then he covered the Blessed One’s feet with kisses, caressing them with his hands and pronouncing his name:

mn89:9.2.verse: ‘I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir;

mn89:9.3.verse: I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir.’

mn89:9.4.verse: ‘But, great king, what purpose do you see in doing such extreme honour to this body and in showing such friendship?’

mn89:10.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:10.2.verse: The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed one’s disciples has entered upon the good way.

mn89:10.3.verse: Now, venerable sir, I see some monks and divines leading the life divine for ten, twenty, thirty, forty years,

mn89:10.4.verse: and then on another occasion (I see them) enjoying themselves endowed and invested with the five cords of sensual desire.

mn89:10.5.verse: But here I see bhikkhus leading the life divine in perfect purity as long as life and breath last.

mn89:10.6.verse: Indeed, I do not see any other life divine elsewhere so perfect and pure as this.

mn89:10.7.verse: So, venerable sir, I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:10.8.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:11.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, kings quarrel with kings, warrior-nobles with warrior-nobles, divines with divines, householders with householders, mother with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, friend with friend.

mn89:11.2.verse: But here I see bhikkhus enjoying concord, living as undisputing as milk with water, and viewing each other with kindly eyes.

mn89:11.3.verse: I do not see any other assembly elsewhere with such concord.

mn89:11.4.verse: This is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:11.5.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:12.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, I have walked and wandered from park to park and from garden to garden,

mn89:12.2.verse: and there I have seen some monks and divines lean, wretched, unsightly, jaundiced, with veins standing out on their limbs, hardly such, one would think, as to make people want to look at them again.

mn89:12.4.verse: “Surely these venerable ones are leading the life divine in discontent, or they have done some evil deed and are concealing it,

mn89:12.5.verse: so lean and wretched are they, so unsightly and jaundiced, with veins standing out on their limbs, not such, one would think, as to make people want to look at them again.

mn89:12.6.verse: I went up to them and asked:

mn89:12.7.verse: “Why are you venerable ones so lean, wretched, unsightly and jaundiced, with veins standing out on your limbs, not such, one would think, as to make people want to look at you again?”

mn89:12.9.verse: “It is our family sickness, great king.”

mn89:12.10.verse: But here I see bhikkhus smiling, cheerful and sincerely joyful, plainly delighting, their faculties fresh, uninvolved in activity, unruffled, subsisting on what others give, abiding with mind (as aloof) as a wild deer’s.

mn89:12.12.verse: “Surely these venerable ones perceive high successive distinction in the Blessed One’s dispensation,

mn89:12.13.verse: since they abide so smiling and cheerful, so sincerely joyful, so plainly delighting, their faculties so fresh, so uninvolved in activity and unruffled, subsisting on other’ gifts with mind (as aloof) as a wild deer’s.”

mn89:12.14.verse: That is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:12.15.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:13.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, as a head-anointed warrior-noble king

mn89:13.2.verse: I am able to have executed those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, to exile those who should be exiled.

mn89:13.3.verse: Yet when I am sitting in council they interrupt me

mn89:13.5.verse: “Gentlemen, do not interrupt me when I am sitting in council; wait till the end of my speech,”

mn89:13.8.verse: while the Blessed One was expounding the Dhamma to an assembly of several hundreds and then there is not even the sound of a disciple of the Blessed One hawking or clearing his throat.

mn89:13.9.verse: Once the Blessed One was expounding the Dhamma to an assembly of several hundreds,

mn89:13.10.verse: a disciple of the Blessed One cleared his throat.

mn89:13.11.verse: Thereupon one of his companions in the life divine nudged him with his knee (saying):

mn89:13.12.verse: “Quiet, venerable sir, make no noise; the Teacher is expounding the Dhamma.”

mn89:13.15.verse: An assembly, it seems, can be so well disciplined without either punishment or weapon!”

mn89:13.16.verse: Indeed, I do not see any other assembly elsewhere so well disciplined.

mn89:13.17.verse: That is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:13.18.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:14.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, I have seen here certain warrior-noble scholars that were clever and knew others’ theories as a hair-splitting (marksman knows archery): they must surely, one would think, go about demolishing views with the understanding that they have.

mn89:14.3.verse: “The monk Gotama will visit such and such a village or town.”

mn89:14.4.verse: They construct a formulated question thus:

mn89:14.5.verse: ‘We shall approach the monk Gotama and ask him this question.

mn89:14.6.verse: “If he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong;

mn89:14.7.verse: and if he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong”.

mn89:14.9.verse: “The monk Gotama has come to visit such and such a village or town.”

mn89:14.10.verse: They go to the monk Gotama.

mn89:14.11.verse: The monk Gotama instructs, urges, rouses and encourages them with talk on the Dhamma.

mn89:14.12.verse: When they have been instructed, urged, roused and encouraged by the monk Gotama with talk on the Dhamma, they do not even ask him the question, so how should they prove his theory wrong?

mn89:14.13.verse: In actual fact these become his disciples.

mn89:14.14.verse: That is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:14.15.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:15.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, I have seen here certain divine caste scholars …

mn89:16.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, I have seen here certain householder scholars …

mn89:17.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, I have seen here certain monk scholars that were clever and knew others’ theories as a hair-splitting (marksman knows archery): they must surely, one would think, go about demolishing views with the understanding that they have.

mn89:17.3.verse: “The monk Gotama will visit such and such a village or town.”

mn89:17.4.verse: They construct a formulated question thus:

mn89:17.5.verse: ‘We shall approach the monk Gotama and ask him this question.

mn89:17.6.verse: “If he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong;

mn89:17.7.verse: and if he is asked like this, he will answer like this, and so we shall prove his theory wrong”.

mn89:17.9.verse: “The monk Gotama has come to visit such and such a village or town.”

mn89:17.10.verse: They go to the monk Gotama.

mn89:17.11.verse: The monk Gotama instructs, urges, rouses and encourages them with talk on the Dhamma.

mn89:17.12.verse: When they have been instructed, urged, roused and encouraged by the monk Gotama with talk on the Dhamma, they do not even ask him the question, so how should they prove his theory wrong?

mn89:17.13.verse: In actual fact they ask the Blessed One to allow them to go forth from the home life into homelessness,

mn89:17.14.verse: and he gives them the Going-forth.

mn89:17.15.verse: Not long after they have gone forth thus, dwelling alone in retreat, diligent, ardent and self-controlled, by realization themselves with direct knowledge they here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the life divine for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn89:17.17.verse: “We were very nearly lost, we were very nearly undone,

mn89:17.18.verse: for formerly we claimed that we were monks though we were not; we claimed that we were divines though we were not;

mn89:17.19.verse: now we are Monks, now we are Divines, now we are Arahants.”

mn89:17.20.verse: That is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:17.21.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:18.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, there are Isidatta and Purāna, my two inspectors, who accept food and keep from me, whose provider of livelihood and bestower of fame I am.

mn89:18.2.verse: In spite of that they are less respectful to me than they are to the Blessed One.

mn89:18.3.verse: Once when I had gone out leading an army and was testing these inspectors, Isidatta and Purāna, I happened to put up in very cramped quarters.

mn89:18.4.verse: Then these two inspectors, Isidatta and Purāna, spent much of the night in talk on the Dhamma, after which they lay down with their heads towards where they had heard the Blessed One was and their feet towards me.

mn89:18.7.verse: There are these two inspectors, Isidatta and Purāna, who accept food and keep from me, whose provider of livelihood and bestower of fame I am;

mn89:18.8.verse: in spite of that they are less respectful to me than they are to the Blessed One.

mn89:18.9.verse: Surely these good people perceive high successive distinction in the Blessed One’s dispensation.”

mn89:18.10.verse: That is why I infer according to Dhamma about the Blessed One:

mn89:18.11.verse: “The Blessed One is fully enlightened. The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One. The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has entered on the good way.”

mn89:19.1.verse: ‘Again, venerable sir, the Blessed One is a warrior-noble and I am a warrior-noble;

mn89:19.2.verse: the Blessed One is a Kosalan and I am a Kosalan;

mn89:19.3.verse: the Blessed One is eighty and I am eighty.

mn89:19.5.verse: I therefore think it proper to do extreme honour to the Blessed One and to show such friendship.

mn89:20.2.verse: we are busy and have much to do.’

mn89:20.3.verse: ‘It is time now, great king, to do as you think fit.’

mn89:20.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he departed.

mn89:21.1.verse: Then soon after he had gone, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn89:21.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, this King Pasenadi has uttered monuments to the Dhamma before rising from his seat and departing.

mn89:21.3.verse: Learn the monuments to the Dhamma;

mn89:21.4.verse: master the monuments to the Dhamma;

mn89:21.5.verse: remember the monuments to the Dhamma.

mn89:21.6.verse: The monuments to the Dhamma are conducive to welfare, and they belong to the principles of the life divine.’

mn89:21.7.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn89:21.8.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in his words.

mn89:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near the Sakyan town named Medaḷumpa.

mn89:2.1.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala had arrived at Townsville on some business.

mn89:2.3.verse: “My good Kārāyana, harness the finest chariots. We will go to a park and see the scenery.”

mn89:2.4.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Dīgha Kārāyana. He harnessed the chariots and informed the king,

mn89:2.5.verse: “Your Majesty, the finest chariots are harnessed.

mn89:3.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out in full royal pomp from Townsville,

mn89:3.3.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and entered the park on foot.

mn89:4.1.verse: As he was going for a walk in the park he saw roots of trees that were impressive and inspiring, quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat.

mn89:4.2.verse: The sight reminded him right away of the Buddha:

mn89:4.3.verse: “These roots of trees, so impressive and inspiring, are like those where we used to pay homage to the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.”

mn89:4.5.verse: “These roots of trees, so impressive and inspiring, are like those where we used to pay homage to the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn89:4.6.verse: My good Kārāyana, where is that Buddha at present?”

mn89:5.1.verse: “Great king, there is a Sakyan town named Medaḷumpa.

mn89:5.2.verse: That’s where the Buddha is now staying.”

mn89:5.3.verse: “But how far away is that town?”

mn89:5.6.verse: We can get there while it’s still light.”

mn89:5.7.verse: “Well then, harness the chariots, and we shall go to see the Buddha.”

mn89:5.8.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Dīgha Kārāyana. He harnessed the chariots and informed the king,

mn89:5.9.verse: “Your Majesty, the finest chariots are harnessed.

mn89:6.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out from Townsville to Medaḷumpa.

mn89:6.2.verse: He reached the town while it was still light

mn89:6.3.verse: and headed for the monastery grounds.

mn89:6.4.verse: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and entered the monastery on foot.

mn89:7.1.verse: At that time several mendicants were walking mindfully in the open air.

mn89:7.2.verse: King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to them and said,

mn89:7.3.verse: “Sirs, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?

mn89:7.4.verse: For I want to see him.”

mn89:8.1.verse: “Great king, that’s his dwelling, with the door closed. Approach it quietly, without hurrying; go onto the porch, clear your throat, and knock on the door-panel. The Buddha will open the door.”

mn89:8.2.verse: The king right away presented his sword and turban to Dīgha Kārāyana,

mn89:8.4.verse: “Now the king seeks privacy. I should wait here.”

mn89:8.5.verse: Then the king approached the Buddha’s dwelling, cleared his throat and knocked on the door-panel, and the Buddha opened the door.

mn89:9.1.verse: King Pasenadi entered the dwelling, and bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet, caressing them and covering them with kisses, and pronounced his name:

mn89:9.2.verse: “Sir, I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!

mn89:9.3.verse: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!”

mn89:9.4.verse: “But, Great King, for what reason do you demonstrate such utmost deference for this body, conveying your manifest love?”

mn89:10.1.verse: “Sir, I infer about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:10.2.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:10.3.verse: It happens, sir, that I see some ascetics and brahmins leading the spiritual life only for a limited period: ten, twenty, thirty, or forty years.

mn89:10.4.verse: Some time later—nicely bathed and anointed, with hair and beard dressed—they amuse themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn89:10.5.verse: But here I see the mendicants leading the spiritual life entirely full and pure as long as they live, to their last breath.

mn89:10.6.verse: I don’t see any other spiritual life elsewhere so full and pure.

mn89:10.7.verse: That’s why I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:10.8.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:11.1.verse: Furthermore, kings fight with kings, aristocrats fight with aristocrats, brahmins fight with brahmins, householders fight with householders. A mother fights with her child, child with mother, father with child, and child with father. Brother fights with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, and friend fights with friend.

mn89:11.2.verse: But here I see the mendicants living in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.

mn89:11.3.verse: I don’t see any other assembly elsewhere so harmonious.

mn89:11.4.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:11.5.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:12.1.verse: Furthermore, I have walked and wandered from monastery to monastery and from park to park.

mn89:12.2.verse: There I’ve seen some ascetics and brahmins who are thin, haggard, pale, and veiny—hardly a captivating sight for people, you’d think.

mn89:12.4.verse: ‘Clearly these venerables lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, or they’re hiding some bad deed they’ve done.

mn89:12.5.verse: That’s why they’re thin, haggard, pale, and veiny—hardly a captivating sight for people, you’d think.’

mn89:12.6.verse: I went up to them and said:

mn89:12.7.verse: ‘Venerables, why are you so thin, haggard, pale, and veiny—hardly a captivating sight for people, you’d think?’

mn89:12.10.verse: But here I see mendicants always smiling and joyful, obviously happy, with cheerful faces, living relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, their hearts free as a wild deer.

mn89:12.12.verse: ‘Clearly these venerables have realized a higher distinction in the Buddha’s instructions than they had before.

mn89:12.13.verse: That’s why these venerables are always smiling and joyful, obviously happy, with cheerful faces, living relaxed, unruffled, surviving on charity, their hearts free as a wild deer.’

mn89:12.14.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:12.15.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:13.1.verse: Furthermore, as an anointed aristocratic king

mn89:13.2.verse: I am able to execute, fine, or banish those who are guilty.

mn89:13.3.verse: Yet when I’m sitting in court they interrupt me.

mn89:13.5.verse: to stop interrupting me and wait until I’ve finished speaking.

mn89:13.7.verse: But here I see the mendicants

mn89:13.8.verse: while the Buddha is teaching an assembly of many hundreds, and there is no sound of his disciples coughing or clearing their throats.

mn89:13.9.verse: Once it so happened that the Buddha was teaching an assembly of many hundreds.

mn89:13.10.verse: Then one of his disciples cleared their throat.

mn89:13.11.verse: And one of their spiritual companions nudged them with their knee, to indicate:

mn89:13.12.verse: ‘Hush, venerable, don’t make a sound! Our teacher, the Blessed One, is teaching!’

mn89:13.15.verse: how an assembly can be so well trained without rod or sword!’

mn89:13.16.verse: I don’t see any other assembly elsewhere so well trained.

mn89:13.17.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:13.18.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:14.1.verse: Furthermore, I’ve seen some astute aristocrats who are subtle, accomplished in the doctrines of others, hair-splitters. You’d think they live to demolish convictions with their intellect.

mn89:14.3.verse: ‘So, gentlemen, that ascetic Gotama will come down to such-and-such village or town.’

mn89:14.5.verse: ‘We’ll approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question.

mn89:14.6.verse: If he answers like this, we’ll refute him like that;

mn89:14.7.verse: and if he answers like that, we’ll refute him like this.’

mn89:14.11.verse: The Buddha educates, encourages, fires up, and inspires them with a Dhamma talk.

mn89:14.12.verse: They don’t even get around to asking their question to the Buddha, so how could they refute his answer?

mn89:14.14.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:14.15.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:15.1.verse: Furthermore, I see some astute brahmins …

mn89:17.1.verse: some astute ascetics who are subtle, accomplished in the doctrines of others, hair-splitters. …

mn89:17.12.verse: They don’t even get around to asking their question to the Buddha, so how could they refute his answer?

mn89:17.13.verse: Invariably, they ask the Buddha for the chance to go forth.

mn89:17.14.verse: And he gives them the going-forth.

mn89:17.15.verse: Soon after going forth, living withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, they realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn89:17.17.verse: ‘We were almost lost! We almost perished!

mn89:17.18.verse: For we used to claim that we were ascetics, brahmins, and perfected ones, but we were none of these things.

mn89:17.19.verse: But now we really are ascetics, brahmins, and perfected ones!’

mn89:17.20.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:17.21.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:18.1.verse: Furthermore, these chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa share my meals and my carriages. I give them a livelihood and bring them renown.

mn89:18.2.verse: And yet they don’t show me the same level of deference that they show to the Buddha.

mn89:18.3.verse: Once it so happened that while I was leading a military campaign and testing Isidatta and Purāṇa I took up residence in a cramped house.

mn89:18.4.verse: They spent much of the night discussing the teaching, then they lay down with their heads toward where the Buddha was and their feet toward me.

mn89:18.7.verse: These chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa share my meals and my carriages. I give them a livelihood and bring them renown.

mn89:18.8.verse: And yet they don’t show me the same level of deference that they show to the Buddha.

mn89:18.9.verse: Clearly these venerables have realized a higher distinction in the Buddha’s instructions than they had before.’

mn89:18.10.verse: So I infer this about the Buddha from the teaching:

mn89:18.11.verse: ‘The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained. The Saṅgha is practicing well.’

mn89:19.1.verse: Furthermore, the Buddha is an aristocrat, and so am I.

mn89:19.2.verse: The Buddha is Kosalan, and so am I.

mn89:19.3.verse: The Buddha is eighty years old, and so am I.

mn89:19.5.verse: it’s proper for me to act with such utmost deference for the Buddha and convey my manifest love.

mn89:20.1.verse: Well, now, sir, I must go.

mn89:20.2.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn89:20.3.verse: “Please, Great King, go at your convenience.”

mn89:20.4.verse: Then King Pasenadi rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn89:21.1.verse: Soon after the king had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

mn89:21.2.verse: “Mendicants, before he got up and left, King Pasenadi spoke shrines to the teaching.

mn89:21.3.verse: Learn these shrines to the teaching!

mn89:21.4.verse: Memorize these shrines to the teaching!

mn89:21.5.verse: Remember these shrines to the teaching!

mn89:21.6.verse: These shrines to the teaching are beneficial and relate to the fundamentals of the spiritual life.”

mn89:21.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn89:21.8.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn90:1.1.verse:
The frame story of this sutta presents a gentle satire of royal life. Despite his position, King Pasenadi Kosala must still act the role of messenger for his wives. Because of his position, he finds himself surrounded by people he cannot trust—he never gets to the bottom of the question of who brought misinformation into the palace—and whose minds fasten on issues of overthrowing and banishing, possibly him. He is so preoccupied with his responsibilities that he doesn’t pick up on the Buddha’s gentle joke about his servitude to the sisters Somā and Sakulā, can’t stick with an issue for any length of time, sometimes can’t even phrase his questions properly, and can arrive at no greater certainty about the Buddha’s teachings than that they seem reasonable. At the end of the sutta he has to leave, not because he has exhausted the issues he would like to discuss, but because one of his courtiers tells him it is time to go. All in all, not an enviable position.

The substance of the discussion, however, does touch on some serious issues. The topic treated in greatest detail concerns the differences among the castes of the Buddha’s time, and the Buddha’s remarks can profitably be applied to issues of racism in ours.

The discussion and the frame story, of course, play off one another. Because of his social position, King Pasenadi is unable to pursue the path to release that is open to all regardless of race or caste. His social advantages are a spiritual liability. Like many people in the modern world, he has plenty of things but no time.

I have heard that

mn90:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Udaññans, in the Deer Park at Kaṇṇakatthala.

mn90:2.1.verse: And at that time King Pasenadi Kosala had arrived at Udañña on some business or other.

mn90:2.2.verse: So King Pasenadi Kosala said to one of his men,

mn90:2.3.verse: “Come, my good man. Go to the Blessed One and, on arrival, showing reverence with your head to his feet in my name, ask whether he is free from illness & affliction, is carefree, strong, & living in comfort, saying:

mn90:2.4.verse: ‘King Pasenadi Kosala, lord, shows reverence with his head to your feet and asks whether you are free from illness & affliction, are carefree, strong, & living in comfort.’

mn90:2.6.verse: ‘Lord, today King Pasenadi Kosala will come to see the Blessed One after his morning meal.’”

mn90:2.7.verse: Having responded, “As you say, sire,” the man went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to him,

mn90:2.10.verse: “Lord, today King Pasenadi Kosala will come to see the Blessed One after his morning meal.”

mn90:3.4.verse: “Well in that case, great king, show reverence with your head to his feet in our name, too, and ask whether he is free from illness & affliction, is carefree, strong, & living in comfort, saying:

mn90:3.5.verse: ‘The sisters Somā and Sakulā, lord, show reverence with their heads to your feet and asks whether you are free from illness & affliction, are carefree, strong, & living in comfort.’”

mn90:4.2.verse: “The sisters Somā and Sakulā, lord, show reverence with their heads to your feet and asks whether you are free from illness & affliction, are carefree, strong, & living in comfort.”

mn90:4.3.verse: “But, great king, couldn’t the sisters Somā and Sakulā get another messenger?”

mn90:4.4.verse: “Lord, the sisters Somā and Sakulā heard,

mn90:4.5.verse: ‘Today, they say, King Pasenadi Kosala will go to see the Blessed One after his morning meal.’

mn90:4.7.verse: ‘In that case, great king, show reverence with your head to his feet in our name, too, and ask whether he is free from illness & affliction, is carefree, strong, & living in comfort, saying:

mn90:4.9.verse: “May the sisters Somā and Sakulā be happy, great king.”

mn90:5.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi Kosala said to the Blessed One,

mn90:5.2.verse: “Lord, I have heard that ‘Gotama the contemplative says this:

mn90:5.3.verse: “It is not possible that a contemplative or brahman would claim a knowledge and vision that is all-knowing and all-seeing without exception.”’

mn90:5.4.verse: Those who say this: are they speaking in line with what the Blessed One has said? Are they not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is unfactual? Are they answering in line with the Dhamma, so that no one whose thinking is in line with the Dhamma would have grounds for criticizing them?”

mn90:5.5.verse: “Great king, those who say that are not speaking in line with what I have said, and are misrepresenting me with what is untrue and unfactual.”

mn90:6.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi Kosala turned to General Viḍūḍabha:

mn90:8.2.verse: “Could it be that something was said by the Blessed One in reference to something else, which a person could have misunderstood?

mn90:8.5.verse: ‘It is not possible that a contemplative or brahman could know everything and see everything all at once.’”

mn90:8.6.verse: “What the Blessed One says, lord, seems reasonable. What the Blessed One says seems logical:

mn90:8.7.verse: ‘It is not possible that a contemplative or brahman could know everything and see everything all at once.’

mn90:9.3.verse: Is there any distinction or difference among them?”

mn90:9.4.verse: “Great king, there are these four castes:

mn90:10.1.verse: “I’m not asking about the present life, lord.

mn90:10.2.verse: I’m asking about the future life.

mn90:10.3.verse: Lord, there are these four castes:

mn90:10.5.verse: Is there any distinction or difference among these four castes?”

mn90:10.6.verse: “Great king, there are these five factors for exertion.

mn90:10.8.verse: There is the case where a monk has conviction, is convinced of the Tathāgata’s awakening:

mn90:10.9.verse: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is worthy & rightly self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, well-gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed.’

mn90:10.10.verse: He is free from illness & discomfort, endowed with good digestion—not too cold, not too hot, of moderate strength—fit for exertion.

mn90:10.11.verse: He is neither fraudulent nor deceitful. He declares himself to the Teacher or to his observant companions in the holy life in line with what he actually is.

mn90:10.12.verse: He keeps his persistence aroused for abandoning unskillful qualities and taking on skillful qualities. He is steadfast, solid in his effort, not shirking his duties with regard to skillful qualities.

mn90:10.13.verse: He is discerning, endowed with discernment leading to the arising of the goal—noble, penetrating, leading to the right ending of stress—

mn90:10.14.verse: these are the five factors for exertion.

mn90:10.15.verse: As for the four castes, great king:

mn90:10.17.verse: if they were endowed with these five factors for exertion,

mn90:10.18.verse: that would be for their long-term welfare & happiness.”

mn90:11.3.verse: If these four castes were endowed with these five factors for exertion,

mn90:11.4.verse: would there be any distinction or difference among them in that respect?”

mn90:11.5.verse: “I tell you, great king: The difference among them would lie in the diversity of their exertion.

mn90:11.6.verse: Suppose that there were two tamable elephants, tamable horses, or tamable oxen that were well-tamed & well-trained; and two tamable elephants, tamable horses, or tamable oxen that were untamed & untrained.

mn90:11.7.verse: What do you think, great king?

mn90:11.8.verse: Would the two tamable elephants, tamable horses, or tamable oxen that were well-tamed & well-trained acquire the habits of the tamed and reach the status of the tamed?”

mn90:11.10.verse: “And would the two tamable elephants, tamable horses, or tamable oxen that were untamed & untrained acquire the habits of the tamed and reach the status of the tamed, just as the two tamable elephants, tamable horses, or tamable oxen that were well-tamed & well-trained?”

mn90:11.12.verse: “In the same way, great king, it is impossible that what could be attained by one who has confidence, who is free from illness, who is neither fraudulent nor deceitful, whose persistence is aroused, and who is discerning could also be attained by one who is without conviction, who is sickly, fraudulent & deceitful, lazy, and dull.”

mn90:12.1.verse: “What the Blessed One says, lord, seems reasonable. What the Blessed One says seems logical.

mn90:12.2.verse: Lord, there are these four castes:

mn90:12.4.verse: If they were endowed with these five factors for exertion, and they had right exertion,

mn90:12.5.verse: would there be any distinction or difference among them in that respect?”

mn90:12.6.verse: “I tell you, great king, that there would be no difference among them with regard to the release of one and the release of another.

mn90:12.7.verse: Suppose that a man, taking dry Sal wood, were to generate a fire and make heat appear.

mn90:12.8.verse: And suppose that another man, taking dry saka [teak?] wood, were to generate a fire and make heat appear.

mn90:12.9.verse: And suppose that another man, taking dry mango wood, were to generate a fire and make heat appear.

mn90:12.10.verse: And suppose that another man, taking dry fig wood, were to generate a fire and make heat appear.

mn90:12.11.verse: Now what do you think, great king?

mn90:12.12.verse: Among those fires generated from different kinds of wood, would there be any difference between the glow of one and the glow of another, the color of one and the color of another, the radiance of one and the radiance of another?”

mn90:12.14.verse: “In the same way, great king, in the power that is kindled by persistence and generated by exertion, I say that there is no difference with regard to the release of one and the release of another.”

mn90:13.1.verse: “What the Blessed One says, lord, seems reasonable. What the Blessed One says seems logical.

mn90:13.5.verse: “Whether the devas come back to this life, lord, or whether they don’t.”

mn90:13.6.verse: “Those devas who are afflicted come back to this life, whereas those devas who are unafflicted don’t come back to this life.”

mn90:14.1.verse: When this was said, General Viḍūḍabha said to the Blessed One,

mn90:14.2.verse: “Lord, can the afflicted devas oust or expel the unafflicted devas from that place?”

mn90:14.3.verse: Then the thought occurred to Ven. Ānanda,

mn90:14.4.verse: “This General Viḍūḍabha is the son of King Pasenadi Kosala,

mn90:14.5.verse: and I am the son of the Blessed One.

mn90:14.6.verse: Now is the time for the son to counsel the son.”

mn90:14.7.verse: So Ven. Ānanda turned to General Viḍūḍabha and said,

mn90:14.8.verse: “In that case, general, I will ask you a counter question. Answer as you see fit.

mn90:14.10.verse: Through the extent of land conquered by King Pasenadi Kosala—where he exercises sovereign & independent kingship—is he able to oust or expel a contemplative or brahman from that place, regardless of whether that person has merit or not, or follows the holy life or not?”

mn90:14.11.verse: “Sir, through the extent of land conquered by King Pasenadi Kosala—where he exercises sovereign & independent kingship—he is able to oust or expel a contemplative or brahman from that place, regardless of whether that person has merit or not, or follows the holy life or not.”

mn90:14.13.verse: Through the extent of land not conquered by King Pasenadi Kosala—where he does not exercise sovereign & independent kingship—is he able to oust or expel a contemplative or brahman from that place, regardless of whether that person has merit or not, or follows the holy life or not?”

mn90:14.14.verse: “Sir, through the extent of land not conquered by King Pasenadi Kosala—where he does not exercise sovereign & independent kingship—he is not able to oust or expel a contemplative or brahman from that place, regardless of whether that person has merit or not, or follows the holy life or not.”

mn90:14.16.verse: Have you heard of the Devas of the Thirty-three?”

mn90:14.18.verse: I have heard of the Devas of the Thirty-three,

mn90:14.21.verse: Could King Pasenadi Kosala oust or expel the Devas of the Thirty-three from that place?”

mn90:14.22.verse: “Sir, King Pasenadi Kosala can’t even see the Devas of the Thirty-three. How could he oust or expel them from that place?”

mn90:14.23.verse: “In the same way, general, afflicted devas, who will come back to this life, can’t even see the unafflicted devas who don’t come back to this life. How could they oust or expel them from that place?”

mn90:15.2.verse: “Lord, what is the name of this monk?”

mn90:15.5.verse: What Ven. Ānanda says, lord, seems reasonable. What Ven. Ānanda says seems logical.

mn90:15.10.verse: “Those Brahmās who are afflicted come back to this life, whereas those Brahmās who are unafflicted don’t come back to this life.”

mn90:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Ujuññā in the deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala.

mn90:2.7.verse: “Yes, Your Majesty,” that man replied. He did as the king asked.

mn90:5.4.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the Buddha has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

mn90:5.5.verse: “Great king, those who say this do not repeat what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue.”

mn90:10.6.verse: “Great king, there are these five factors that support meditation.

mn90:10.8.verse: It’s when a mendicant has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

mn90:10.9.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn90:10.10.verse: They are rarely ill or unwell. Their stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, but just right, and fit for meditation.

mn90:10.11.verse: They’re not devious or deceitful. They reveal themselves honestly to the Teacher or sensible spiritual companions.

mn90:10.12.verse: They live with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They’re strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities.

mn90:10.13.verse: They’re wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.

mn90:10.14.verse: These are the five factors that support meditation.

mn90:10.17.verse: If they had these five factors that support meditation,

mn90:10.18.verse: that would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn90:11.3.verse: If they had these five factors that support meditation,

mn90:11.4.verse: would there be any difference between them?”

mn90:11.5.verse: “In that case, I say it is the disparity of their efforts in meditation.

mn90:11.6.verse: Suppose there was a pair of elephants or horses or oxen in training who were well tamed and well trained. And there was a pair who were not tamed or trained.

mn90:11.7.verse: What do you think, Great King?

mn90:11.8.verse: Wouldn’t the pair that was well tamed and well trained perform the tasks of the tamed, and reach the level of the tamed?”

mn90:11.10.verse: “But would the pair that was not tamed and trained perform the tasks of the tamed and reach the level of the tamed, just like the tamed pair?”

mn90:11.12.verse: “In the same way, there are things that must be attained by someone with faith, health, integrity, energy, and wisdom. It’s not possible for a faithless, unhealthy, deceitful, lazy, witless person to attain them.”

mn90:12.2.verse: Sir, there are these four classes:

mn90:12.4.verse: If they had these five factors that support meditation, and if they practiced rightly,

mn90:12.5.verse: would there be any difference between them?”

mn90:12.6.verse: “In that case, I say that there is no difference between the freedom of one and the freedom of the other.

mn90:12.7.verse: Suppose a person took dry teak wood and lit a fire and produced heat.

mn90:12.8.verse: Then another person did the same using sāl wood,

mn90:12.10.verse: while another used wood of the cluster fig.

mn90:12.11.verse: What do you think, Great King?

mn90:12.12.verse: Would there be any difference between the fires produced by these different kinds of wood, that is, in the flame, color, or luminosity?”

mn90:12.14.verse: “In the same way, when fire has been churned by energy and produced by effort, I say that there is no difference between the freedom of one and the freedom of the other.”

mn90:14.4.verse: “This General Viḍūḍabha is King Pasenadi’s son,

mn90:14.8.verse: “Well then, general, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn90:14.16.verse: Have you heard of the gods of the thirty-three?”

mn90:14.19.verse: and so has the worthy King Pasenadi.”

mn90:15.4.verse: “A joy he is, and a joy he seems!

mn90:15.9.verse: “Whether that divinity comes back to this place or not.”
