mn94:15.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn94:15.8.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn94:16.1.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

mn94:16.2.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn94:16.3.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

mn94:16.4.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn94:16.5.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn94:16.6.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn94:16.7.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

mn94:16.8.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

mn94:16.9.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn94:16.10.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn94:16.11.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

mn94:16.12.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

mn94:16.21.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

mn94:16.25.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn94:17.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn94:17.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn94:17.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn94:17.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

mn94:18.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn94:18.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn94:18.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn94:18.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn94:18.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn94:18.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn94:18.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn94:18.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn94:18.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

mn94:19.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn94:20.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn94:20.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn94:21.1.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn94:21.2.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn94:21.3.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn94:21.4.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn94:21.5.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn94:21.6.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn94:22.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn94:22.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn94:23.1.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn94:24.1.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn94:25.1.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn94:26.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn94:26.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn94:27.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn94:27.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn94:28.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn94:28.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn94:28.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn94:29.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn94:29.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn94:29.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn94:30.1.verse: This is called an individual who neither mortifies themselves or others, being committed to the practice of not mortifying themselves or others.

mn94:30.2.verse: They live without wishes in this very life, quenched, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become divine.”

mn94:31.1.verse: When he had spoken, Ghoṭamukha said to him,

mn94:31.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Udena has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn94:31.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Udena, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn94:31.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Udena remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn94:32.1.verse: “Brahmin, don’t go for refuge to me.

mn94:32.2.verse: You should go for refuge to that same Blessed One to whom I have gone for refuge.”

mn94:32.3.verse: “But worthy Udena, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

mn94:32.4.verse: “Brahmin, the Buddha has already become fully quenched.”

mn94:32.5.verse: “Worthy Udena, if I heard that the worthy Gotama was within ten leagues, or twenty, or even up to a hundred leagues away, I’d go a hundred leagues to see him.

mn94:32.11.verse: But since the worthy Gotama has become fully quenched, I go for refuge to that worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the Saṅgha.

mn94:32.12.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Udena remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.

mn94:33.1.verse: Worthy Udena, the king of Aṅga gives me a regular daily allowance. I will give you one portion of that.”

mn94:33.2.verse: “But brahmin, what does the king of Aṅga give you as a regular daily allowance?”

mn94:33.4.verse: “It’s not proper for us to receive gold and currency.”

mn94:33.5.verse: “If that’s not proper, I will have a dwelling built for the worthy Udena.”

mn94:33.6.verse: “If you want to build me a dwelling, then build an assembly hall for the Saṅgha at Pāṭaliputta.”

mn94:33.7.verse: “Now I’m even more delighted and satisfied with the worthy Udena, since he encourages me to give to the Saṅgha.

mn94:33.8.verse: So with this allowance and another one I will have an assembly hall built for the Saṅgha at Pāṭaliputta.”

mn94:33.9.verse: And so he had that hall built.

mn94:33.10.verse: And these days it’s called the “Ghoṭamukhī”.

mn95:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans called Opasāda.

mn95:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One stayed at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the brahmin Caṅkī was living at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift.[^1]

mn95:3.1.verse: The brahmin householders of Opasāda heard:

mn95:3.2.verse: “The ascetic Gotama, it seems, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:3.3.verse: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn95:3.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’

mn95:3.5.verse: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its rulers and its people, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn95:3.6.verse: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn95:3.7.verse: Now it is good to see such Arahants.”

mn95:4.1.verse: Then the brahmin householders of Opasāda came out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, and went northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:5.1.verse: Now on that occasion the brahmin Caṅkī had gone to rest at midday on the upper terrace.

mn95:5.2.verse: The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmin householders of Opasāda coming out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, going northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:5.3.verse: Seeing this, he addressed his steward:

mn95:5.4.verse: “Why, good steward, are the brahmin householders of Opasāda coming out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, and going northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove?”

mn95:6.1.verse: “There is, good Caṅkī, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, who has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:6.2.verse: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn95:6.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’

mn95:6.4.verse: They are going to see that Master Gotama.”

mn95:6.5.verse: “Then, good steward, go to the brahmin householders of Opasāda, and having gone, say to them:

mn95:6.7.verse: “Let the sirs wait, please; the brahmin Caṅkī too is going to see the ascetic Gotama.”’”

mn95:6.8.verse: “Yes, sir,” that steward replied to the brahmin Caṅkī, and he went to the brahmin householders of Opasāda and said to them:

mn95:6.10.verse: ‘Let the sirs wait, please; the brahmin Caṅkī too is going to see the ascetic Gotama.’”

mn95:7.1.verse: Now on that occasion about five hundred brahmins from various provinces were staying at Opasāda for some business or other.

mn95:7.3.verse: “The brahmin Caṅkī, it seems, is going to see the ascetic Gotama.”

mn95:7.4.verse: Then those brahmins went to the brahmin Caṅkī and said to him:

mn95:7.5.verse: “Is it true, as they say, that Master Caṅkī is going to see the ascetic Gotama?”

mn95:7.7.verse: ‘I shall go to see the ascetic Gotama.’”

mn95:8.1.verse: “Let Master Caṅkī not go to see the ascetic Gotama.

mn95:8.2.verse: It is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;[^2]

mn95:8.3.verse: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.

mn95:8.4.verse: For Master Caṅkī is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth.

mn95:8.5.verse: Since Master Caṅkī is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth—on this ground it is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;

mn95:8.6.verse: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.

mn95:8.7.verse: For Master Caṅkī is rich, with great wealth and great possessions …

mn95:8.8.verse: for Master Caṅkī is an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man …

mn95:8.9.verse: for Master Caṅkī is handsome, good-looking, pleasing, possessed of supreme beauty of complexion, of divine complexion and divine appearance, no ordinary sight to see …

mn95:8.10.verse: for Master Caṅkī is virtuous, mature in virtue, possessed of mature virtue …[^3]

mn95:8.11.verse: for Master Caṅkī has good speech and a good delivery, possessed of urbane speech, distinct, faultless, and conveying the meaning …

mn95:8.12.verse: for Master Caṅkī is a teacher of the teachers of many, and instructs three hundred students in the hymns …

mn95:8.13.verse: for Master Caṅkī is honoured, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by King Pasenadi of Kosala …

mn95:8.14.verse: for Master Caṅkī is honoured, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by the brahmin Pokkharasāti …

mn95:8.15.verse: for Master Caṅkī lives at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift.

mn95:8.16.verse: Since Master Caṅkī lives at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift—on this ground it is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;

mn95:8.17.verse: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.”

mn95:9.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to those brahmins:

mn95:9.2.verse: “Well then, sirs, hear from me too why it is proper for us to go to see that Master Gotama;

mn95:9.3.verse: it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us.

mn95:9.4.verse: For, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth.

mn95:9.5.verse: Since, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth—on this ground it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;

mn95:9.6.verse: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.

mn95:9.7.verse: The ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth abandoning abundant gold and silver, stored both underground and in the air …

mn95:9.8.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, while still young, a black-haired youth, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, went forth from the home life into homelessness …

mn95:9.9.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, though his mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness …

mn95:9.10.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is handsome, good-looking, pleasing, possessed of supreme beauty of complexion, of divine complexion and divine appearance, no ordinary sight to see …

mn95:9.11.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is virtuous, with noble virtue, with wholesome virtue, possessed of wholesome virtue …

mn95:9.12.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has good speech and a good delivery, possessed of urbane speech, distinct, faultless, and conveying the meaning …

mn95:9.13.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is a teacher of the teachers of many …

mn95:9.14.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has exhausted lust for sensual pleasures and is rid of vacillation …[^4]

mn95:9.15.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, holds the doctrine of action, the doctrine of doing, and does not put forth what is bad for the brahmin race …[^5]

mn95:9.16.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth from a high family, an unbroken noble family …

mn95:9.17.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth from a rich family, of great wealth and great possessions …

mn95:9.18.verse: people, sirs, come from foreign realms and foreign countries to question the ascetic Gotama …

mn95:9.19.verse: many thousands of deities, sirs, have gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …[^6]

mn95:9.20.verse: and, sirs, a good report of the ascetic Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn95:9.21.verse: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed’ …

mn95:9.22.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man …

mn95:9.23.verse: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …

mn95:9.24.verse: King Pasenadi of Kosala, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …

mn95:9.25.verse: the brahmin Pokkharasāti, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …

mn95:9.26.verse: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.

mn95:9.27.verse: Now whatever ascetics or brahmins come into our village territory are our guests,

mn95:9.28.verse: and guests should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated by us.

mn95:9.29.verse: Since the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove, the ascetic Gotama is our guest,

mn95:9.30.verse: and a guest should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated by us.

mn95:9.31.verse: On this ground it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;

mn95:9.32.verse: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.

mn95:9.33.verse: This much, sirs, is as far as I can go in praise of that Master Gotama, but that Master Gotama is not to be measured by so much praise;

mn95:9.34.verse: that Master Gotama’s praise is immeasurable.

mn95:9.35.verse: Even if he possessed only one of these factors, it would not be proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;

mn95:9.36.verse: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.

mn95:9.37.verse: So then, sirs, let us all go to see the ascetic Gotama.”

mn95:10.1.verse: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn95:10.2.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.

mn95:11.1.verse: Now on that occasion the Blessed One was seated exchanging some pleasant conversation with very senior brahmins.

mn95:11.2.verse: Now on that occasion there was a young student named Kāpaṭika, with a shaved head, sixteen years of age, an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man; and he was sitting in that assembly.

mn95:11.3.verse: While the very senior brahmins were conversing with the Blessed One, he interrupted their talk from time to time.

mn95:11.4.verse: Then the Blessed One rebuked the student Kāpaṭika:

mn95:11.5.verse: “Let the venerable Bhāradvāja not interrupt the very senior brahmins’ talk from time to time while they are conversing.[^7]

mn95:11.6.verse: Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait for the talk to finish.”

mn95:11.7.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One:

mn95:11.8.verse: “Let Master Gotama not rebuke the student Kāpaṭika.

mn95:11.9.verse: The student Kāpaṭika is of good family, he is learned, he has good delivery, he is wise, and he is capable of taking part in this discussion with Master Gotama.”

mn95:12.2.verse: “Surely the student Kāpaṭika will have completed the threefold-knowledge tradition,

mn95:12.3.verse: since the brahmins so honour him.”

mn95:12.4.verse: Then it occurred to the student Kāpaṭika:

mn95:12.5.verse: “When the ascetic Gotama turns his eyes to me, I shall ask the ascetic Gotama a question.”

mn95:12.6.verse: Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the student Kāpaṭika’s mind with his own mind, turned his eyes towards the student Kāpaṭika.

mn95:12.7.verse: Then it occurred to the student Kāpaṭika:

mn95:12.8.verse: “The ascetic Gotama is paying attention to me.

mn95:12.9.verse: Suppose I were to ask the ascetic Gotama a question?”

mn95:12.10.verse: Then the student Kāpaṭika said to the Blessed One:

mn95:12.11.verse: “Master Gotama, as to the brahmins’ ancient hymnal, handed down by oral tradition, generation after generation, coming down in the scriptures[^8]—in that matter the brahmins come to the definite conclusion:

mn95:12.12.verse: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’[^9]

mn95:12.13.verse: What does Master Gotama say about this?”

mn95:13.1.verse: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says thus:

mn95:13.3.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”

mn95:13.5.verse: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single teacher among the brahmins, or a teacher’s teacher, or even back to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus:

mn95:13.7.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”

mn95:13.9.verse: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, did those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the hymns, the composers of the hymns,[^11] whose ancient hymns, once chanted, uttered, and compiled, the brahmins nowadays still chant and repeat, repeating what has been repeated, reciting what has been recited—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—

mn95:13.12.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”

mn95:13.14.verse: “So then, Bhāradvāja, it seems there is not even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says thus:

mn95:13.16.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong’;

mn95:13.17.verse: there is not even a single teacher among the brahmins, or a teacher’s teacher, or even back to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus:

mn95:13.19.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong’;

mn95:13.20.verse: and even those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the hymns, the composers of the hymns, whose ancient hymns, once chanted, uttered, and compiled, the brahmins nowadays still chant and repeat, repeating what has been repeated, reciting what has been recited—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—even they did not say thus:

mn95:13.22.verse: only this is true, everything else is wrong.’

mn95:13.23.verse: Suppose, Bhāradvāja, there were a file of blind men holding on to one another—the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see;

mn95:13.24.verse: so too, Bhāradvāja, it seems to me that the brahmins’ statement turns out to be just like a file of blind men—the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

mn95:13.26.verse: that being so, does it not turn out that the brahmins’ faith is baseless?”

mn95:14.1.verse: “It is not only out of faith, Master Gotama, that the brahmins honour this; the brahmins also honour it as oral tradition.”

mn95:14.2.verse: “First, Bhāradvāja, you took your stand on faith; now you speak of oral tradition.

mn95:14.3.verse: There are, Bhāradvāja, these five things which have a twofold result in this very life.

mn95:14.5.verse: Faith, liking, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and acceptance of a view after pondering it[^12]—

mn95:14.6.verse: these, Bhāradvāja, are the five things which have a twofold result in this very life.

mn95:14.7.verse: Now something may be firmly believed, and yet it may be hollow, empty, and false;

mn95:14.8.verse: and something may not be firmly believed, and yet it may be factual, true, and not otherwise.

mn95:14.9.verse: Again, something may be well liked …

mn95:14.10.verse: something may be well transmitted by oral tradition …

mn95:14.12.verse: something may be well pondered, and yet it may be hollow, empty, and false;

mn95:14.13.verse: and something may not be well pondered, and yet it may be factual, true, and not otherwise.

mn95:14.14.verse: In such a case, Bhāradvāja, it is not fitting for a wise man who safeguards truth to come to the definite conclusion:

mn95:14.15.verse: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’”

mn95:15.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the safeguarding of truth? In what way does one safeguard truth?

mn95:15.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the safeguarding of truth.”

mn95:15.3.verse: “If a man has faith, Bhāradvāja, and he says:

mn95:15.5.verse: in speaking thus he safeguards truth, but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:

mn95:15.6.verse: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’

mn95:15.7.verse: If, Bhāradvāja, a man has a liking …

mn95:15.8.verse: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has an oral tradition …

mn95:15.9.verse: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has reasoned reflection …

mn95:15.10.verse: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has acceptance of a view after pondering it,

mn95:15.11.verse: and he says: ‘Such is my acceptance of a view after pondering it’—

mn95:15.12.verse: in speaking thus he safeguards truth, but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:

mn95:15.13.verse: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’

mn95:15.14.verse: In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is the safeguarding of truth; in this way one safeguards truth; and in this way we describe the safeguarding of truth;

mn95:15.15.verse: but there is not yet the discovery of truth.”

mn95:16.1.verse: “In this way, Master Gotama, there is the safeguarding of truth; in this way one safeguards truth; and we see the safeguarding of truth in this way.

mn95:16.2.verse: But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the discovery of truth? In what way does one discover truth?

mn95:16.3.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the discovery of truth.”

mn95:17.1.verse: “Here, Bhāradvāja, a bhikkhu lives in dependence on some village or town.

mn95:17.2.verse: A householder or a householder’s child approaches him and observes him with regard to three kinds of things—

mn95:17.3.verse: things provoking greed, things provoking hate, and things provoking delusion:

mn95:17.4.verse: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking greed, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:17.6.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’

mn95:17.7.verse: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:

mn95:17.8.verse: ‘There are no such things provoking greed in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:17.10.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.

mn95:17.11.verse: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not greedy.

mn95:17.12.verse: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;

mn95:17.13.verse: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is greedy.’

mn95:18.1.verse: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking greed, he next observes him further with regard to things provoking hate:

mn95:18.2.verse: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking hate, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:18.4.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’

mn95:18.5.verse: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:

mn95:18.6.verse: ‘There are no such things provoking hate in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:18.8.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.

mn95:18.9.verse: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not hateful.

mn95:18.10.verse: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;

mn95:18.11.verse: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is hateful.’

mn95:19.1.verse: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking hate, he next observes him further with regard to things provoking delusion:

mn95:19.2.verse: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking delusion, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:19.4.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’

mn95:19.5.verse: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:

mn95:19.6.verse: ‘There are no such things provoking delusion in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—

mn95:19.8.verse: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.

mn95:19.9.verse: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not deluded.

mn95:19.10.verse: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;

mn95:19.11.verse: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is deluded.’

mn95:20.1.verse: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking delusion,

mn95:20.2.verse: he then places his faith in him;[^13] possessed of faith, he visits him; visiting him, he pays respect; paying respect, he gives ear; giving ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard it, he retains it; he examines the meaning of the things he has retained; when he examines the meaning, the things are accepted upon reflection; when there is acceptance upon reflection, zeal springs up; when zeal has sprung up, he applies himself; having applied himself, he weighs it up; having weighed it up, he strives; being resolute, he realizes with the body the ultimate truth and sees it, having penetrated it with wisdom.

mn95:20.3.verse: It is to this extent, Bhāradvāja, that there is discovery of truth, to this extent that one discovers truth; and it is to this extent that we describe the discovery of truth;

mn95:20.4.verse: but there is not yet the final arrival at truth.”

mn95:21.1.verse: “To this extent, Master Gotama, there is discovery of truth; to this extent one discovers truth; and we see the discovery of truth to this extent.

mn95:21.2.verse: But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the final arrival at truth? In what way does one finally arrive at truth?

mn95:21.3.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the final arrival at truth.”

mn95:21.4.verse: “The final arrival at truth, Bhāradvāja, is the cultivation, development, and repeated practice of those very same things.

mn95:21.5.verse: It is to this extent, Bhāradvāja, that there is the final arrival at truth, to this extent that one finally arrives at truth; and it is to this extent that we describe the final arrival at truth.”

mn95:22.1.verse: “To this extent, Master Gotama, there is the final arrival at truth; to this extent one finally arrives at truth; and we see the final arrival at truth to this extent.

mn95:22.2.verse: But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for the final arrival at truth?

mn95:22.3.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth.”

mn95:22.4.verse: “Striving, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for the final arrival at truth.

mn95:22.5.verse: If one did not strive, one would not finally arrive at truth.

mn95:22.6.verse: It is because one strives that one finally arrives at truth.

mn95:22.7.verse: That is why striving is most helpful for the final arrival at truth.”

mn95:23.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for striving?

mn95:23.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for striving.”

mn95:23.3.verse: “Weighing up, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for striving.

mn95:23.4.verse: If one did not weigh it up, one would not strive.

mn95:23.5.verse: It is because one weighs it up that one strives.

mn95:23.6.verse: That is why weighing up is most helpful for striving.”

mn95:24.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for weighing up?

mn95:24.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for weighing up.”

mn95:24.3.verse: “Application, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for weighing up.

mn95:24.4.verse: If one did not apply oneself, one would not weigh it up.

mn95:24.5.verse: It is because one applies oneself that one weighs it up.

mn95:24.6.verse: That is why application is most helpful for weighing up.”

mn95:25.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for application?

mn95:25.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for application.”

mn95:25.3.verse: “Zeal, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for application.

mn95:25.4.verse: If zeal did not arise, one would not apply oneself.

mn95:25.5.verse: It is because zeal arises that one applies oneself.

mn95:25.6.verse: That is why zeal is most helpful for application.”

mn95:26.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for zeal?

mn95:26.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for zeal.”

mn95:26.3.verse: “Acceptance of a teaching after pondering it, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for zeal.

mn95:26.4.verse: If those teachings were not accepted upon reflection, zeal would not arise.

mn95:26.5.verse: It is because those teachings are accepted upon reflection that zeal arises.

mn95:26.6.verse: That is why acceptance of a teaching after pondering it is most helpful for zeal.”

mn95:27.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it?

mn95:27.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.”

mn95:27.3.verse: “Examination of the meaning, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.

mn95:27.4.verse: If one did not examine the meaning, those teachings would not be accepted upon reflection.

mn95:27.5.verse: It is because one examines the meaning that those teachings are accepted upon reflection.

mn95:27.6.verse: That is why examination of the meaning is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.”

mn95:28.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for examination of the meaning?

mn95:28.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for examination of the meaning.”

mn95:28.3.verse: “Retention of the teaching,[^14] Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for examination of the meaning.

mn95:28.4.verse: If one did not retain the teaching, one would not examine the meaning.

mn95:28.5.verse: It is because one retains the teaching that one examines the meaning.

mn95:28.6.verse: That is why retention of the teaching is most helpful for examination of the meaning.”

mn95:29.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for retention of the teaching?

mn95:29.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for retention of the teaching.”

mn95:29.3.verse: “Listening to the teaching, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for retention of the teaching.

mn95:29.4.verse: If one did not listen to the teaching, one would not retain it.

mn95:29.5.verse: It is because one listens to the teaching that one retains it.

mn95:29.6.verse: That is why listening to the teaching is most helpful for retention of the teaching.”

mn95:30.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for listening to the teaching?

mn95:30.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for listening to the teaching.”

mn95:30.3.verse: “Giving ear, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for listening to the teaching.

mn95:30.4.verse: If one did not give ear, one would not listen to the teaching.

mn95:30.5.verse: It is because one gives ear that one listens to the teaching.

mn95:30.6.verse: That is why giving ear is most helpful for listening to the teaching.”

mn95:31.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for giving ear?

mn95:31.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for giving ear.”

mn95:31.3.verse: “Paying respect, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for giving ear.

mn95:31.4.verse: If one did not pay respect, one would not give ear.

mn95:31.5.verse: It is because one pays respect that one gives ear.

mn95:31.6.verse: That is why paying respect is most helpful for giving ear.”

mn95:32.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for paying respect?

mn95:32.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for paying respect.”

mn95:32.3.verse: “Visiting, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for paying respect.

mn95:32.4.verse: If one did not visit, one would not pay respect.

mn95:32.5.verse: It is because one visits that one pays respect.

mn95:32.6.verse: That is why visiting is most helpful for paying respect.”

mn95:33.1.verse: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for visiting?

mn95:33.2.verse: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for visiting.”

mn95:33.3.verse: “Faith, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for visiting.

mn95:33.4.verse: If faith did not arise, one would not visit.

mn95:33.5.verse: It is because faith arises that one visits.

mn95:33.6.verse: That is why faith is most helpful for visiting.”

mn95:34.1.verse: “We asked Master Gotama about the safeguarding of truth; Master Gotama has explained the safeguarding of truth;

mn95:34.2.verse: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.

mn95:34.3.verse: We asked Master Gotama about the discovery of truth; Master Gotama has explained the discovery of truth;

mn95:34.4.verse: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.

mn95:34.5.verse: We asked Master Gotama about the final arrival at truth; Master Gotama has explained the final arrival at truth;

mn95:34.6.verse: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.

mn95:34.7.verse: We asked Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth; Master Gotama has explained the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth;

mn95:34.8.verse: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.

mn95:34.9.verse: And whatever we asked Master Gotama, that Master Gotama has explained;

mn95:34.10.verse: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.

mn95:34.11.verse: For formerly, Master Gotama, we used to think thus:

mn95:34.12.verse: ‘Who indeed are these shaveling ascetics, menial, dark, born of the Kinsman’s foot,[^15] that they should be knowers of the Dhamma?’

mn95:34.13.verse: But Master Gotama has aroused in me love for ascetics, confidence in ascetics, and reverence for ascetics.

mn95:35.1.verse: Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms. …

mn95:35.2.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha. Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”

mn95:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Opāsāda.

mn95:1.3.verse: He stayed in the Godswood of sal trees to the north of Opāsāda.

mn95:2.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was living in Opāsāda. It was a crown property given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, teeming with living creatures, full of hay, wood, water, and grain, a royal park endowed to a brahmin.

mn95:3.1.verse: The brahmins and householders of Opāsāda heard:

mn95:3.2.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Opāsāda together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. He is staying in the Godswood to the north.

mn95:3.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn95:3.5.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn95:3.6.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

mn95:3.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

mn95:4.1.verse: Then, exiting Opāsāda, they formed into companies and headed north to the Godswood.

mn95:5.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī had retired to the upper floor of his stilt longhouse for his midday nap.

mn95:5.2.verse: He saw the brahmins and householders heading for the Godswood,

mn95:5.4.verse: “My butler, why are the brahmins and householders heading north for the Godswood?”

mn95:6.1.verse: “The ascetic Gotama has arrived at Opāsāda together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. He is staying in the Godswood to the north.

mn95:6.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn95:6.4.verse: They’re going to see that worthy Gotama.”

mn95:6.5.verse: “Well then, go to the brahmins and householders and say to them:

mn95:6.7.verse: you to wait, as he will also go to see the ascetic Gotama.’”

mn95:6.8.verse: “Yes, worthy sir,” replied the butler, and did as he was asked.

mn95:7.1.verse: Now at that time around five hundred brahmins from abroad were residing in Opāsāda on some business.

mn95:7.3.verse: the brahmin Caṅkī was going to see the ascetic Gotama.

mn95:7.4.verse: They approached Caṅkī and said to him,

mn95:7.5.verse: “Is it really true that you are going to see the ascetic Gotama?”

mn95:8.2.verse: It’s not appropriate for you to go to see the ascetic Gotama;

mn95:8.3.verse: it’s appropriate that he comes to see you.

mn95:8.4.verse: You are well born on both your mother’s and father’s side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation.

mn95:8.5.verse: For this reason it’s not appropriate for you to go to see the ascetic Gotama;

mn95:8.6.verse: it’s appropriate that he comes to see you.

mn95:8.8.verse: You recite and remember the hymns, and have mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. You know them word-by-word, and their grammar. You are well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man. …

mn95:8.9.verse: You are attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. You have divine looks and lustre, remarkable to behold. …

mn95:8.10.verse: You are ethical, mature in ethical conduct. …

mn95:8.11.verse: You’re a good speaker who enunciates well, with a polished, clear, and articulate voice that expresses the meaning. …

mn95:8.12.verse: You’re the tutor of tutors for many, and teach three hundred young students to recite the hymns. …

mn95:8.13.verse: You’re honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by King Pasenadi of Kosala

mn95:8.15.verse: You live in Opāsāda, a crown property given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, teeming with living creatures, full of hay, wood, water, and grain, a royal park endowed to a brahmin.

mn95:8.16.verse: For all these reasons it’s not appropriate for you to go to see the ascetic Gotama;

mn95:8.17.verse: it’s appropriate that he comes to see you.”

mn95:9.1.verse: When they had spoken, Caṅkī said to those brahmins:

mn95:9.2.verse: “Well then, gentlemen, listen to why it’s appropriate for me to go to see the ascetic Gotama,

mn95:9.3.verse: and it’s not appropriate for him to come to see me.

mn95:9.4.verse: He is well born on both his mother’s and father’s side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation.

mn95:9.5.verse: For this reason it’s not appropriate for the ascetic Gotama to come to see me;

mn95:9.6.verse: rather, it’s appropriate for me to go to see him.

mn95:9.7.verse: When he went forth he abandoned abundant gold, both coined and uncoined, stored above and below ground. …

mn95:9.8.verse: He went forth from the lay life to homelessness while still a youth, young, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life. …

mn95:9.9.verse: Though his mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces, he shaved off his hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness. …

mn95:9.10.verse: He is attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. He has divine looks and lustre, remarkable to behold. …

mn95:9.11.verse: He is ethical, possessing ethical conduct that is noble and skillful. …

mn95:9.12.verse: He’s a good speaker who enunciates well, with a polished, clear, and articulate voice that expresses the meaning. …

mn95:9.14.verse: He has ended sensual desire, and is rid of caprice. …

mn95:9.15.verse: He teaches the efficacy of deeds and action. He doesn’t wish any harm upon the community of brahmins. …

mn95:9.16.verse: He went forth from an eminent family of unbroken aristocratic lineage. …

mn95:9.17.verse: He went forth from a rich, affluent, and wealthy family. …

mn95:9.18.verse: People come from distant lands and distant countries to question him. …

mn95:9.19.verse: Many thousands of deities have gone for refuge for life to him. …

mn95:9.21.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ …

mn95:9.22.verse: He has the thirty-two marks of a great man. …

mn95:9.23.verse: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha and his wives and children have gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama. …

mn95:9.24.verse: King Pasenadi of Kosala and his wives and children have gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama. …

mn95:9.25.verse: The brahmin Pokkharasāti and his wives and children have gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama. …

mn95:9.26.verse: The ascetic Gotama has arrived to stay in the Godswood to the north of Opāsāda.

mn95:9.27.verse: Any ascetic or brahmin who comes to stay in our village district is our guest,

mn95:9.28.verse: and should be honored and respected as such.

mn95:9.31.verse: For this reason, too, it’s not appropriate for the worthy Gotama to come to see me;

mn95:9.32.verse: rather, it’s appropriate for me to go to see him.

mn95:9.33.verse: This is the extent of the worthy Gotama’s praise that I have memorized. But his praises are not confined to this,

mn95:9.34.verse: for the praise of the worthy Gotama is limitless.

mn95:9.35.verse: The possession of even a single one of these factors makes it inappropriate for Worthy Gotama to come to see me;

mn95:9.36.verse: rather, it’s appropriate for me to go to see him.

mn95:9.37.verse: Well then, gentlemen, let’s all go to see the ascetic Gotama.”

mn95:10.1.verse: Then Caṅkī together with a large group of brahmins went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn95:10.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

mn95:11.1.verse: Now at that time the Buddha was sitting engaged in some polite conversation together with some very senior brahmins.

mn95:11.2.verse: And the student Kāpaṭika was sitting in that assembly. He was young, tonsured, and sixteen years old. He had mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. He knew them word-by-word, and their grammar. He was well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man.

mn95:11.3.verse: While the senior brahmins were conversing together with the Buddha, he interrupted.

mn95:11.5.verse: “Venerable Bhāradvāja, don’t interrupt the senior brahmins.

mn95:11.7.verse: When he had spoken, Caṅkī said to the Buddha,

mn95:11.8.verse: “Worthy Gotama, don’t rebuke the student Kāpaṭika.

mn95:11.9.verse: He’s a gentleman, learned and astute, who enunciates well. He is capable of debating with the worthy Gotama about this.”

mn95:12.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

mn95:12.2.verse: “Clearly the student Kāpaṭika will talk about the scriptural heritage of the three Vedas.

mn95:12.3.verse: That’s why the brahmins put him at the front.”

mn95:12.5.verse: “When the ascetic Gotama looks at me, I’ll ask him a question.”

mn95:12.6.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing Kāpaṭika’s train of thought, looked at him.

mn95:12.8.verse: “The ascetic Gotama is engaging with me.

mn95:12.9.verse: Why don’t I ask him a question?”

mn95:12.11.verse: “Worthy Gotama, regarding that which by the lineage of testament and by canonical authority is the ancient hymnal of the brahmins, the brahmins come to the categorical conclusion:

mn95:12.12.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

mn95:12.13.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn95:13.1.verse: “Well, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single one of the brahmins who says this:

mn95:13.3.verse: this is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

mn95:13.5.verse: “Well, is there even a single tutor of the brahmins, or a tutors’ tutor, or anyone back to the seventh generation of tutors, who says this:

mn95:13.7.verse: this is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

mn95:13.9.verse: “Well, what of the ancient seers of the brahmins, namely Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu? They were the authors and propagators of the hymns. Their hymnal was sung and propagated and compiled in ancient times; and these days, brahmins continue to sing and chant it, chanting what was chanted and teaching what was taught.

mn95:13.12.verse: this is the only truth, anything else is futile’?”

mn95:13.14.verse: “So, Bhāradvāja, it seems that there is not a single one of the brahmins,

mn95:13.17.verse: not even anyone back to the seventh generation of tutors,

mn95:13.20.verse: nor even the ancient seers of the brahmins who say:

mn95:13.22.verse: this is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

mn95:13.23.verse: Suppose there was a queue of blind men, each holding the one in front: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

mn95:13.24.verse: In the same way, it seems to me that the brahmins’ statement turns out to be like a queue of blind men: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

mn95:13.26.verse: This being so, doesn’t the brahmins’ faith turn out to be baseless?”

mn95:14.1.verse: “The brahmins don’t just honor this because of faith, but also because of oral transmission.”

mn95:14.2.verse: “First you relied on faith, now you speak of oral transmission.

mn95:14.3.verse: These five things can be seen to turn out in two different ways in this very life.

mn95:14.5.verse: Faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, and acceptance of a view after deliberation.

mn95:14.7.verse: Even though you have full faith in something, it may be vacuous, hollow, and false.

mn95:14.8.verse: And even if you don’t have full faith in something, it may be true and real, not otherwise.

mn95:14.9.verse: Even though you fully endorse something …

mn95:14.11.verse: something may be well thought out …

mn95:14.12.verse: something may be well deliberated, it may be vacuous, hollow, and false.

mn95:14.13.verse: And even if something is not well deliberated, it may be true and real, not otherwise.

mn95:14.14.verse: For a sensible person who is preserving truth this is not sufficient to come to the categorical conclusion:

mn95:14.15.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’”

mn95:15.1.verse: “But worthy Gotama, how do you define the preservation of truth?”

mn95:15.4.verse: they preserve truth by saying, ‘Such is my faith.’

mn95:15.5.verse: But they don’t yet come to the categorical conclusion:

mn95:15.6.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

mn95:15.8.verse: or has received an oral transmission …

mn95:15.9.verse: or has a reasoned train of thought about something …

mn95:15.10.verse: or has accepted a view after deliberation,

mn95:15.11.verse: they preserve truth by saying, ‘Such is the view I have accepted after deliberation.’

mn95:15.12.verse: But they don’t yet come to the categorical conclusion:

mn95:15.13.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

mn95:15.14.verse: That’s how the preservation of truth is defined, Bhāradvāja. I describe the preservation of truth as defined in this way.

mn95:15.15.verse: But this is not yet the awakening to the truth.”

mn95:16.1.verse: “That’s how the preservation of truth is defined, worthy Gotama. We regard the preservation of truth as defined in this way.

mn95:16.2.verse: But worthy Gotama, how do you define awakening to the truth?”

mn95:17.1.verse: “Bhāradvāja, take the case of a mendicant living supported by a town or village.

mn95:17.2.verse: A householder or their child approaches and scrutinizes them for three qualities:

mn95:17.3.verse: qualities that arouse greed, things that provoke hate, and things that promote delusion.

mn95:17.4.verse: ‘Does this venerable have any qualities that arouse greed? Such qualities that, were their mind to be overwhelmed by them, they might say

mn95:17.5.verse: that they know, even though they don’t know, or that they see, even though they don’t see;

mn95:17.6.verse: or that they might encourage others to do what is for their lasting harm and suffering?’

mn95:17.8.verse: ‘This venerable has no such qualities that arouse greed.

mn95:17.11.verse: Rather, that venerable has bodily and verbal behavior like that of someone without greed.

mn95:17.12.verse: And the principle that they teach is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

mn95:17.13.verse: It’s not easy for someone with greed to teach this.’

mn95:18.1.verse: Scrutinizing them in this way they see that they are purified of qualities that arouse greed. Next, they scrutinize them for qualities that provoke hate.

mn95:18.2.verse: ‘Does this venerable have any qualities that provoke hate? Such qualities that, were their mind to be overwhelmed by them, they might say

mn95:18.3.verse: that they know, even though they don’t know, or that they see, even though they don’t see;

mn95:18.4.verse: or that they might encourage others to do what is for their lasting harm and suffering?’

mn95:18.6.verse: ‘This venerable has no such qualities that provoke hate.

mn95:18.9.verse: Rather, that venerable has bodily and verbal behavior like that of someone without hate.

mn95:18.10.verse: And the principle that they teach is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

mn95:18.11.verse: It’s not easy for someone with hate to teach this.’

mn95:19.1.verse: Scrutinizing them in this way they see that they are purified of qualities that provoke hate. Next, they scrutinize them for qualities that promote delusion.

mn95:19.2.verse: ‘Does this venerable have any qualities that promote delusion? Such qualities that, were their mind to be overwhelmed by them, they might say

mn95:19.3.verse: that they know, even though they don’t know, or that they see, even though they don’t see;

mn95:19.4.verse: or that they might encourage others to do what is for their lasting harm and suffering?’

mn95:19.6.verse: ‘This venerable has no such qualities that promote delusion.

mn95:19.9.verse: Rather, that venerable has bodily and verbal behavior like that of someone without delusion.

mn95:19.10.verse: And the principle that they teach is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of logic, subtle, comprehensible to the astute.

mn95:19.11.verse: It’s not easy for someone with delusion to teach this.’

mn95:20.1.verse: Scrutinizing them in this way they see that they are purified of qualities that promote delusion.

mn95:20.2.verse: Next, they place faith in them. When faith has arisen they approach the teacher. They pay homage, actively listen, hear the teachings, remember the teachings, examine their meaning, and accept them after deliberation. Then enthusiasm springs up; they make an attempt, weigh up, and strive. Striving, they directly realize the ultimate truth, and see it with penetrating wisdom.

mn95:20.3.verse: That’s how the awakening to truth is defined, Bhāradvāja. I describe the awakening to truth as defined in this way.

mn95:20.4.verse: But this is not yet the attainment of truth.”

mn95:21.1.verse: “That’s how the awakening to truth is defined, worthy Gotama. I regard the awakening to truth as defined in this way.

mn95:21.2.verse: But worthy Gotama, how do you define the attainment of truth?”

mn95:21.4.verse: “By the cultivation, development, and making much of these very same things there is the attainment of truth.

mn95:21.5.verse: That’s how the attainment of truth is defined, Bhāradvāja. I describe the attainment of truth as defined in this way.”

mn95:22.1.verse: “That’s how the attainment of truth is defined, worthy Gotama. I regard the attainment of truth as defined in this way.

mn95:22.2.verse: But what quality is helpful for arriving at the truth?”

mn95:22.4.verse: “Striving is helpful for arriving at the truth.

mn95:22.5.verse: If you don’t strive, you won’t arrive at the truth.

mn95:22.6.verse: You arrive at the truth because you strive.

mn95:22.7.verse: That’s why striving is helpful for arriving at the truth.”

mn95:23.1.verse: “But what quality is helpful for striving?”

mn95:23.3.verse: “Weighing up the teachings is helpful for striving …

mn95:24.3.verse: Making an attempt is helpful for weighing up the teachings …

mn95:25.3.verse: Enthusiasm is helpful for making an attempt …

mn95:26.3.verse: Acceptance of the teachings after deliberation is helpful for enthusiasm …

mn95:27.3.verse: Examining the meaning of the teachings is helpful for accepting them after deliberation …

mn95:28.3.verse: Remembering the teachings is helpful for examining their meaning …

mn95:29.3.verse: Hearing the teachings is helpful for remembering the teachings …

mn95:30.3.verse: Active listening is helpful for hearing the teachings …

mn95:31.3.verse: Paying homage is helpful for active listening …

mn95:32.3.verse: Approaching is helpful for paying homage …

mn95:33.3.verse: Faith is helpful for approaching a teacher.

mn95:33.4.verse: If you don’t give rise to faith, you won’t approach a teacher.

mn95:33.5.verse: You approach a teacher because you have faith.

mn95:33.6.verse: That’s why faith is helpful for approaching a teacher.”

mn95:34.1.verse: “I’ve asked the worthy Gotama about the preservation of truth, and he has answered me.

mn95:34.2.verse: I endorse and accept this, and am satisfied with it.

mn95:34.3.verse: I’ve asked the worthy Gotama about awakening to the truth, and he has answered me.

mn95:34.4.verse: I endorse and accept this, and am satisfied with it.

mn95:34.5.verse: I’ve asked the worthy Gotama about the attainment of truth, and he has answered me.

mn95:34.6.verse: I endorse and accept this, and am satisfied with it.

mn95:34.7.verse: I’ve asked the worthy Gotama about the things that are helpful for the attainment of truth, and he has answered me.

mn95:34.8.verse: I endorse and accept this, and am satisfied with it.

mn95:34.9.verse: Whatever point I have asked the worthy Gotama about he has answered me.

mn95:34.10.verse: I endorse and accept this, and am satisfied with it.

mn95:34.11.verse: Worthy Gotama, I used to think this:

mn95:34.12.verse: ‘Who are these shavelings, fake ascetics, primitives, black spawn from the feet of our kinsman next to those who understand the teaching?’

mn95:34.13.verse: The Buddha has inspired me to have fondness, confidence, and respect for ascetics!

mn95:35.2.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn96:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn96:2.1.verse: Then Esukārī the brahmin went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn96:2.2.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, Esukārī the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn96:3.1.verse: “Master Gotama, brahmins prescribe four kinds of service—

mn96:3.2.verse: they prescribe service for the brahmin, service for the noble, service for the merchant, service for the worker.

mn96:3.3.verse: Now this, Master Gotama, is the service for the brahmin that brahmins prescribe:

mn96:3.4.verse: ‘a brahmin may serve a brahmin, a noble may serve a brahmin, a merchant may serve a brahmin, or a worker may serve a brahmin.’

mn96:3.5.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the service for the brahmin that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:3.6.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the service for the noble that brahmins prescribe:

mn96:3.7.verse: ‘a noble may serve a noble, a merchant may serve a noble, or a worker may serve a noble.’

mn96:3.8.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the service for the noble that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:3.9.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the service for the merchant that brahmins prescribe:

mn96:3.10.verse: ‘a merchant may serve a merchant, or a worker may serve a merchant.’

mn96:3.11.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the service for the merchant that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:3.12.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the service for the worker that brahmins prescribe:

mn96:3.13.verse: ‘only a worker may serve a worker;

mn96:3.14.verse: for who else would serve a worker?’

mn96:3.15.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the service for the worker that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:3.16.verse: These, Master Gotama, are the four kinds of service that brahmins prescribe.[^1]

mn96:3.17.verse: What does Master Gotama say about this?”

mn96:4.1.verse: “But, brahmin, does the whole world grant the brahmins permission to prescribe these four kinds of service?”

mn96:4.3.verse: “Suppose, brahmin, there were a poor, penniless, destitute man, and they were to force a piece of meat on him against his will, saying: ‘Good man, you must eat this meat, and you must pay for it.’

mn96:4.4.verse: So too, brahmin, without the consent of those ascetics and brahmins, the brahmins nevertheless prescribe these four kinds of service.[^2]

mn96:5.1.verse: I do not say, brahmin, that everyone should be served; nor do I say, brahmin, that no one should be served.

mn96:5.2.verse: For, brahmin, whoever, by serving someone, would become worse and not better on account of that service, I say that person should not be served;

mn96:5.3.verse: and whoever, by serving someone, would become better and not worse on account of that service, I say that person should be served.

mn96:6.1.verse: If, brahmin, they were to ask a noble thus:

mn96:6.2.verse: ‘Of these two—the one whom, by serving, you would become worse and not better on account of that service, or the one whom, by serving, you would become better and not worse on account of that service—

mn96:6.3.verse: which of these should you serve?’ then, brahmin, a noble, answering rightly, would answer thus:

mn96:6.4.verse: ‘I would not serve him by serving whom, on account of that service, I would become worse and not better; but I would serve him by serving whom, on account of that service, I would become better and not worse.’

mn96:7.1.verse: If, brahmin, they were to ask a brahmin …

mn96:7.2.verse: if they were to ask a merchant …

mn96:7.3.verse: if they were to ask a worker thus:

mn96:7.4.verse: ‘Of these two—the one whom, by serving, you would become worse and not better on account of that service, or the one whom, by serving, you would become better and not worse on account of that service—

mn96:7.5.verse: which of these should you serve?’ then, brahmin, a worker too, answering rightly, would answer thus:

mn96:7.6.verse: ‘I would not serve him by serving whom, on account of that service, I would become worse and not better; but I would serve him by serving whom, on account of that service, I would become better and not worse.’

mn96:7.7.verse: I do not say, brahmin, that a man is better for being of high birth, nor do I say, brahmin, that he is worse for being of high birth;[^3]

mn96:7.8.verse: I do not say, brahmin, that he is better for great beauty, nor do I say, brahmin, that he is worse for great beauty;

mn96:7.9.verse: I do not say, brahmin, that he is better for great wealth, nor do I say, brahmin, that he is worse for great wealth.

mn96:8.1.verse: For, brahmin, one of high birth may be a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, one who misconducts himself in sensual desires, a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of malicious speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a gossip, covetous, of ill will, and of wrong view.

mn96:8.2.verse: That is why I say a man is not better for being of high birth.

mn96:8.3.verse: And, brahmin, one of high birth may abstain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from misconduct in sensual desires, from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, from gossip, and be uncovetous, of good will, and of right view.

mn96:8.4.verse: That is why I say a man is not worse for being of high birth.

mn96:8.5.verse: One of great beauty too, brahmin, may be a killer of living beings …

mn96:8.7.verse: one of great wealth too, brahmin, may be a killer of living beings …

mn96:8.10.verse: That is why I say a man is not better for great wealth.

mn96:8.11.verse: And one of great wealth too, brahmin, may abstain from killing living beings … and be of right view.

mn96:8.12.verse: That is why I say a man is not worse for great wealth.

mn96:9.1.verse: I do not say, brahmin, that everyone should be served, nor do I say, brahmin, that no one should be served.

mn96:9.2.verse: For, brahmin, whoever, by serving someone, finds that his faith increases, his virtue increases, his learning increases, his generosity increases, and his wisdom increases, on account of that service—that person, I say, should be served.

mn96:9.3.verse: But whoever, by serving someone, finds that his faith does not increase, his virtue does not increase, his learning does not increase, his generosity does not increase, and his wisdom does not increase, on account of that service—that person, I say, should not be served.”

mn96:10.1.verse: When this was said, Esukārī the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn96:10.2.verse: “Master Gotama, brahmins prescribe four kinds of proper wealth—

mn96:10.3.verse: they prescribe the proper wealth for the brahmin, the proper wealth for the noble, the proper wealth for the merchant, and the proper wealth for the worker.

mn96:10.4.verse: Now, Master Gotama, this is the proper wealth for the brahmin that brahmins prescribe: alms-gathering;

mn96:10.5.verse: and a brahmin who scorns his proper wealth of alms-gathering acts wrongly, like a herdsman taking what is not given.[^4]

mn96:10.6.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the brahmin that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:10.7.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the noble that brahmins prescribe: the bow and quiver;

mn96:10.8.verse: and a noble who scorns his proper wealth of the bow and quiver acts wrongly, like a herdsman taking what is not given.

mn96:10.9.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the noble that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:10.10.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the merchant that brahmins prescribe: farming and cattle-raising;

mn96:10.11.verse: and a merchant who scorns his proper wealth of farming and cattle-raising acts wrongly, like a herdsman taking what is not given.

mn96:10.12.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the merchant that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:10.13.verse: And this, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the worker that brahmins prescribe: the sickle and carrying-yoke;[^5]

mn96:10.14.verse: and a worker who scorns his proper wealth of the sickle and carrying-yoke acts wrongly, like a herdsman taking what is not given.

mn96:10.15.verse: This, Master Gotama, is the proper wealth for the worker that brahmins prescribe.

mn96:10.16.verse: These, Master Gotama, are the four kinds of proper wealth that brahmins prescribe.[^6]

mn96:10.17.verse: What does Master Gotama say about this?”

mn96:11.1.verse: “But, brahmin, does the whole world grant the brahmins permission to prescribe these four kinds of proper wealth?”

mn96:11.3.verse: “Suppose, brahmin, there were a poor, penniless, destitute man, and they were to force a piece of meat on him against his will, saying: ‘Good man, you must eat this meat, and you must pay for it.’

mn96:11.4.verse: So too, brahmin, without the consent of those ascetics and brahmins, the brahmins nevertheless prescribe these four kinds of proper wealth.

mn96:12.1.verse: I prescribe the noble, supramundane Dhamma as a man’s own proper wealth.

mn96:12.2.verse: But if one recalls his ancient maternal and paternal lineage, then, in whatever family his individual existence has come to be, he is reckoned accordingly.

mn96:12.3.verse: If his individual existence has come to be in a noble family, he is reckoned as a noble;

mn96:12.4.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a brahmin family, he is reckoned as a brahmin;

mn96:12.5.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a merchant family, he is reckoned as a merchant;

mn96:12.6.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a worker family, he is reckoned as a worker.

mn96:12.7.verse: Just as, brahmin, a fire is reckoned only by the condition dependent on which it burns.

mn96:12.8.verse: If a fire burns dependent on logs, it is reckoned just as a log fire;

mn96:12.9.verse: if a fire burns dependent on chips, it is reckoned just as a chip fire;

mn96:12.10.verse: if a fire burns dependent on grass, it is reckoned just as a grass fire;

mn96:12.11.verse: if a fire burns dependent on cow-dung, it is reckoned just as a cow-dung fire.

mn96:12.12.verse: So too, brahmin, I prescribe the noble, supramundane Dhamma as a man’s own proper wealth.

mn96:12.13.verse: But if one recalls his ancient maternal and paternal lineage, then, in whatever family his individual existence has come to be, he is reckoned accordingly.

mn96:12.14.verse: If his individual existence has come to be in a noble family, he is reckoned as a noble;

mn96:12.15.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a brahmin family, he is reckoned as a brahmin;

mn96:12.16.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a merchant family, he is reckoned as a merchant;

mn96:12.17.verse: if his individual existence has come to be in a worker family, he is reckoned as a worker.

mn96:13.1.verse: If, brahmin, one from a noble family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from unchastity,[^7] from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, from gossip, is uncovetous, of good will, and of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:13.2.verse: If one from a brahmin family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:13.3.verse: If one from a merchant family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:13.4.verse: If one from a worker family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:14.2.verse: is only a brahmin capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness towards this district, free of hostility and ill will, and not a noble, a merchant, or a worker?”

mn96:14.4.verse: A noble too, Master Gotama, is capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness towards this district, free of hostility and ill will;

mn96:14.8.verse: all four castes, Master Gotama, are capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness towards this district, free of hostility and ill will.”

mn96:14.9.verse: “So too, brahmin, if one from a noble family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.
