mn96:14.10.verse: If one from a brahmin family, brahmin …

mn96:14.11.verse: if one from a merchant family, brahmin …

mn96:14.12.verse: if one from a worker family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:15.2.verse: is only a brahmin capable of taking a bath-powder and loofah, going to a river, and washing off dust and dirt, and not a noble, a merchant, or a worker?”

mn96:15.4.verse: A noble too, Master Gotama, is capable of taking a bath-powder and loofah, going to a river, and washing off dust and dirt;

mn96:15.8.verse: all four castes, Master Gotama, are capable of taking a bath-powder and loofah, going to a river, and washing off dust and dirt.”

mn96:15.9.verse: “So too, brahmin, if one from a noble family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:15.10.verse: If one from a brahmin family, brahmin …

mn96:15.11.verse: if one from a merchant family, brahmin …

mn96:15.12.verse: if one from a worker family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:16.2.verse: suppose a head-anointed noble king here were to gather a hundred men of different births, saying:

mn96:16.3.verse: ‘Come, sirs, let those among you who were born in noble families, brahmin families, or royal families take an upper fire-stick made of sāla wood, or sāla-pine wood, or sandalwood, or lotus wood, and kindle a fire, producing heat;

mn96:16.4.verse: and let those among you who were born in outcaste families, hunter families, bamboo-worker families, cartwright families, or scavenger families take an upper fire-stick made from a dog’s feeding-trough, or a pig’s trough, or a washerman’s trough, or castor-oil wood, and kindle a fire, producing heat.’”

mn96:16.6.verse: would the fire kindled and the heat produced by those born in noble, brahmin, and royal families, using an upper fire-stick made of sāla wood, or sāla-pine wood, or sandalwood, or lotus wood, have a flame, a colour, and a radiance, and would one be able to do with that fire what should be done with fire;

mn96:16.7.verse: while the fire kindled and the heat produced by those born in outcaste, hunter, bamboo-worker, cartwright, and scavenger families, using an upper fire-stick made from a dog’s feeding-trough, a pig’s trough, a washerman’s trough, or castor-oil wood, would have no flame, no colour, and no radiance, and one would not be able to do with that fire what should be done with fire?”

mn96:16.9.verse: The fire kindled and the heat produced by those born in noble, brahmin, and royal families, using an upper fire-stick made of sāla wood, or sāla-pine wood, or sandalwood, or lotus wood, would have a flame, a colour, and a radiance, and one would be able to do with that fire what should be done with fire;

mn96:16.10.verse: and the fire kindled and the heat produced by those born in outcaste, hunter, bamboo-worker, cartwright, and scavenger families, using an upper fire-stick made from a dog’s feeding-trough, a pig’s trough, a washerman’s trough, or castor-oil wood, would likewise have a flame, a colour, and a radiance, and one would be able to do with that fire what should be done with fire.

mn96:16.11.verse: For all fire, Master Gotama, has a flame, a colour, and a radiance, and with any fire one is able to do what should be done with fire.”

mn96:16.12.verse: “So too, brahmin, if one from a noble family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings … is of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.

mn96:16.13.verse: If one from a brahmin family, brahmin …

mn96:16.14.verse: if one from a merchant family, brahmin …

mn96:16.15.verse: if one from a worker family has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, brahmin, and, coming to the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata, abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from unchastity, from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, from gossip, is uncovetous, of good will, and of right view, he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma.”

mn96:17.1.verse: When this was said, Esukārī the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn96:17.3.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”

mn96:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn96:2.1.verse: Then Esukārī the brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn96:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn96:3.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, the brahmins prescribe four kinds of service:

mn96:3.2.verse: for a brahmin, an aristocrat, a peasant, and a menial.

mn96:3.3.verse: This is the service they prescribe for a brahmin:

mn96:3.4.verse: ‘A brahmin, an aristocrat, a peasant, and a menial may all serve a brahmin.’

mn96:3.6.verse: This is the service they prescribe for an aristocrat:

mn96:3.7.verse: ‘An aristocrat, a peasant, and a menial may all serve an aristocrat.’

mn96:3.9.verse: This is the service they prescribe for a peasant:

mn96:3.10.verse: ‘A peasant or a menial may serve a peasant.’

mn96:3.12.verse: This is the service they prescribe for a menial:

mn96:3.13.verse: ‘Only a menial may serve a menial.

mn96:3.14.verse: For who else will serve a menial?’

mn96:3.16.verse: These are the four kinds of service that the brahmins prescribe.

mn96:3.17.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn96:4.1.verse: “But brahmin, did the whole world authorize the brahmins to prescribe these four kinds of service?”

mn96:4.3.verse: “It’s as if they were to force a chop on a poor, penniless person, telling them, ‘Eat this meat and pay for it!’

mn96:4.4.verse: In the same way, the brahmins have prescribed these four kinds of service without the consent of those ascetics and brahmins.

mn96:5.1.verse: Brahmin, I don’t say that you should serve everyone, nor do I say that you shouldn’t serve anyone.

mn96:5.2.verse: I say that you shouldn’t serve someone if serving them makes you worse, not better.

mn96:5.3.verse: And I say that you should serve someone if serving them makes you better, not worse.

mn96:6.1.verse: If they were to ask an aristocrat this,

mn96:6.2.verse: ‘Who should you serve? Someone in whose service you get worse, or someone in whose service you get better?’

mn96:6.3.verse: Answering rightly, an aristocrat would say,

mn96:6.4.verse: ‘Someone in whose service I get better.’

mn96:7.1.verse: If they were to ask a brahmin …

mn96:7.4.verse: ‘Who should you serve? Someone in whose service you get worse, or someone in whose service you get better?’

mn96:7.5.verse: Answering rightly, a menial would say,

mn96:7.6.verse: ‘Someone in whose service I get better.’

mn96:7.7.verse: Brahmin, I don’t say that an eminent family makes you a better or worse person.

mn96:7.8.verse: I don’t say that exceptional beauty makes you a better or worse person.

mn96:7.9.verse: I don’t say that exceptional wealth makes you a better or worse person.

mn96:8.1.verse: For some people from eminent families kill living creatures, steal, and commit sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, with wrong view.

mn96:8.2.verse: That’s why I don’t say that an eminent family makes you a better person.

mn96:8.3.verse: But some people from eminent families also refrain from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct. They refrain from using speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re content, kind-hearted, with right view.

mn96:8.4.verse: That’s why I don’t say that an eminent family makes you a worse person.

mn96:8.5.verse: And some people who are exceptionally beautiful …

mn96:8.7.verse: And some people who are exceptionally wealthy kill living creatures … and have wrong view.

mn96:8.10.verse: That’s why I don’t say that exceptional wealth makes you a better person.

mn96:8.11.verse: But some people who are exceptionally wealthy also refrain from killing living creatures … and have right view.

mn96:8.12.verse: That’s why I don’t say that any of these things makes you a better or worse person.

mn96:9.1.verse: Brahmin, I don’t say that you should serve everyone, nor do I say that you shouldn’t serve anyone.

mn96:9.2.verse: And I say that you should serve someone if serving them makes you grow in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

mn96:9.3.verse: I say that you shouldn’t serve someone if serving them doesn’t make you grow in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.”

mn96:10.1.verse: When he had spoken, Esukārī said to him:

mn96:10.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, the brahmins prescribe four kinds of wealth:

mn96:10.3.verse: for a brahmin, an aristocrat, a peasant, and a menial.

mn96:10.4.verse: The wealth they prescribe for a brahmin is living on alms.

mn96:10.5.verse: A brahmin who scorns his own wealth, living on alms, fails in his duty like a guard who steals.

mn96:10.7.verse: The wealth they prescribe for an aristocrat is the bow and quiver.

mn96:10.8.verse: An aristocrat who scorns his own wealth, the bow and quiver, fails in his duty like a guard who steals.

mn96:10.10.verse: The wealth they prescribe for a peasant is farming and animal husbandry.

mn96:10.11.verse: A peasant who scorns his own wealth, farming and animal husbandry, fails in his duty like a guard who steals.

mn96:10.13.verse: The wealth they prescribe for a menial is the scythe and flail.

mn96:10.14.verse: A menial who scorns his own wealth, the scythe and flail, fails in his duty like a guard who steals.

mn96:10.16.verse: These are the four kinds of wealth that the brahmins prescribe.

mn96:10.17.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn96:11.1.verse: “But brahmin, did the whole world authorize the brahmins to prescribe these four kinds of wealth?”

mn96:11.3.verse: “It’s as if they were to force a chop on a poor, penniless person, telling them, ‘Eat this meat and pay for it!’

mn96:11.4.verse: In the same way, the brahmins have prescribed these four kinds of wealth without the consent of these ascetics and brahmins.

mn96:12.1.verse: I assert that a person’s own wealth is the noble, transcendent teaching.

mn96:12.2.verse: But they are reckoned by recollecting the traditional family customs of their mother and father wherever they are incarnated.

mn96:12.3.verse: If they incarnate in a family of aristocrats they are reckoned as an aristocrat.

mn96:12.4.verse: If they incarnate in a family of brahmins they are reckoned as a brahmin.

mn96:12.5.verse: If they incarnate in a family of peasants they are reckoned as a peasant.

mn96:12.6.verse: If they incarnate in a family of menials they are reckoned as a menial.

mn96:12.7.verse: It’s like fire, which is reckoned according to the very same condition dependent upon which it burns.

mn96:12.8.verse: A fire that burns dependent on logs is reckoned as a log fire.

mn96:12.9.verse: A fire that burns dependent on twigs is reckoned as a twig fire.

mn96:12.10.verse: A fire that burns dependent on grass is reckoned as a grass fire.

mn96:12.11.verse: A fire that burns dependent on cow-dung is reckoned as a cow-dung fire.

mn96:12.12.verse: In the same way, I assert that a person’s own wealth is the noble, transcendent teaching.

mn96:12.13.verse: But they are reckoned by recollecting the traditional family customs of their mother and father wherever they are incarnated.

mn96:13.1.verse: Suppose someone from a family of aristocrats goes forth from the lay life to homelessness. Relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One they refrain from killing living creatures, stealing, and sex. They refrain from using speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re content, kind-hearted, with right view. They succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.

mn96:13.2.verse: Suppose someone from a family of brahmins …

mn96:13.4.verse: menials goes forth from the lay life to homelessness. Relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One … they succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.

mn96:14.2.verse: Is only a brahmin capable of developing a heart of love free of enmity and ill will for this region, and not an aristocrat, peasant, or menial?”

mn96:14.4.verse: Aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials can all do so.

mn96:14.8.verse: For all four classes are capable of developing a heart of love free of enmity and ill will for this region.”

mn96:14.9.verse: “In the same way, suppose someone from a family of aristocrats,

mn96:14.12.verse: or menials goes forth from the lay life to homelessness. Relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One … they succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.

mn96:15.2.verse: Is only a brahmin capable of taking some bathing cleanser, going to the river, and rinsing off dust and dirt, and not an aristocrat, peasant, or menial?”

mn96:15.8.verse: All four classes are capable of doing this.”

mn96:15.9.verse: “In the same way, suppose someone from a family of aristocrats,

mn96:15.12.verse: or menials goes forth from the lay life to homelessness. Relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One … they succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.

mn96:16.2.verse: Suppose an anointed aristocratic king were to gather a hundred people born in different classes and say to them:

mn96:16.3.verse: ‘Please gentlemen, let anyone here who was born in a family of aristocrats, brahmins, or chieftains take a drill-stick made of teak, sal, salaḷa, sandalwood, or cherry wood, light a fire and produce heat.

mn96:16.4.verse: And let anyone here who was born in a family of corpse-workers, hunters, bamboo-workers, chariot-makers, or scavengers take a drill-stick made from a mutt’s drinking trough, a pig’s trough, a dustbin, or castor-oil wood, light a fire and produce heat.’

mn96:16.6.verse: Would only the fire produced by the high class people with good quality wood have flames, color, and radiance, and be usable as fire,

mn96:16.7.verse: and not the fire produced by the low class people with poor quality wood?”

mn96:16.9.verse: The fire produced by the high class people with good quality wood would have flames, color, and radiance, and be usable as fire,

mn96:16.10.verse: and so would the fire produced by the low class people with poor quality wood.

mn96:16.11.verse: For all fire has flames, color, and radiance, and is usable as fire.”

mn96:16.12.verse: “In the same way, suppose someone from a family of aristocrats,

mn96:16.15.verse: or menials goes forth from the lay life to homelessness. Relying on the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One they refrain from killing living creatures, stealing, and sex. They refrain from using speech that’s false, divisive, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re content, kind-hearted, with right view. They succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn96:17.1.verse: When he had spoken, Esukārī said to him,

mn96:17.3.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn97:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn97:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Sāriputta was wandering in the Southern Hills with a large Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn97:2.2.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu who had spent the Rains at Rājagaha went to the venerable Sāriputta in the Southern Hills, and after exchanging greetings with him

mn97:2.3.verse: he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the venerable Sāriputta asked him:

mn97:2.4.verse: ‘Is the Blessed One well and strong, friend?’

mn97:2.5.verse: ‘The Blessed One is well and strong, friend.’

mn97:2.6.verse: ‘Is the Sangha of bhikkhus well and strong, friend?’

mn97:2.7.verse: ‘The Sangha of bhikkhus well and strong, friend.’

mn97:2.8.verse: ‘Friend, there is a divine named Dhanañjāni there (at Rājagaha living) at the Rice-keeper’s Gate.

mn97:2.9.verse: Is the divine named Dhanañjāni well and strong?’

mn97:2.10.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni the divine is well and strong too, friend.’

mn97:2.13.verse: He plunders divine-caste householders in the name of the king, and he plunders the king in the name of divine-caste householders.

mn97:2.14.verse: His wife who had faith and came from a clan with faith, is dead

mn97:2.15.verse: and he has another wife without faith who comes from a clan without faith.’

mn97:2.16.verse: ‘This is bad news that we hear, friend, it is bad news indeed to hear

mn97:2.17.verse: that Dhanañjāni the divine is no more diligent.

mn97:2.18.verse: Now suppose that sometime or other we were to meet him and have some conversation with him?’

mn97:3.1.verse: Then when the venerable Sāriputta had stayed in the Southern Hills as long as he chose, he set out to go by stages to Rājagaha.

mn97:3.2.verse: Wandering by stages he at length arrived at Rājagaha,

mn97:3.3.verse: and there he went to live in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn97:4.1.verse: Then when it was morning, the venerable Sāriputta dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Rājagaha for alms.

mn97:4.2.verse: Now at that time Dhanañjāni the divine was having his cowsheds outside the city washed out.

mn97:4.3.verse: So when the venerable Sāriputta had wandered for alms in Rājagaha and was returning from his alms-round after his meal, he went to Dhanañjāni the divine.

mn97:4.4.verse: The divine saw the venerable Sāriputta coming in the distance,

mn97:4.5.verse: and seeing him, he went to him and said:

mn97:4.6.verse: ‘As soon as you have drunk some new milk, Master Sāriputta, it will be time for the meal.’

mn97:4.8.verse: I have finished my meal today.

mn97:4.9.verse: I shall be at the tree’s root for the day’s abiding.

mn97:5.1.verse: And then, after he had eaten his morning meal, he went to the venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him,

mn97:5.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the venerable Sāriputta asked him:

mn97:5.4.verse: ‘How can we be diligent, Master Sāriputta, when we have our parents’ to keep, our wife and children to keep, our slaves, servants and men to keep, our friends’ and companions’ business to see to, our relatives’ and kinsmens’ business to see to, our guests’ business to see to, our ancestors’ business to see to, the gods’ business to see to, the kings’ business to see to, and then this body to refresh and nourish as well?’

mn97:6.2.verse: say someone here behaved not according to Dhamma, behaved unrighteously, and then, because of such behaviour the warders of hell dragged him off to hell,

mn97:6.3.verse: would he get (a hearing by pleading thus): “I behaved thus for the sake of my parents; so let not the warders of hell (drag me off) to hell”, or would his parents get (a hearing) for him (by pleading thus): “He behaved thus for our sake; so let not the warders of hell (drag me off) to hell”?’

mn97:6.5.verse: rather would the warders of hell fling him thus crying out into hell.’

mn97:16.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, one who for the sake of his parents behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, or one who for the sake of his parents behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously—

mn97:16.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of his parents behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, is not the better;

mn97:16.4.verse: the one who for the sake of his parents behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously, is the better.

mn97:16.5.verse: For conduct according to Dhamma and righteous conduct is better than conduct not according to Dhamma and unrighteous conduct, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:16.6.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni, there are other kinds of work (to be done) for one’s own sake which are in accordance with Dhamma, by means of which one can keep one’s parents and at the same time both do no evil and enter the way of merit.’

mn97:17.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, one who for the sake of his wife and children behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, or one who for the sake of his wife and children behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously—

mn97:17.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of his wife and children behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, is not the better;

mn97:17.4.verse: the one who for the sake of his wife and children behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously, is the better.

mn97:17.5.verse: For conduct according to Dhamma and righteous conduct is better than conduct not according to Dhamma and unrighteous conduct, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:17.6.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni, there are other kinds of work (to be done) for one’s own sake which are in accordance with Dhamma, by means of which one can keep one’s wife and children and at the same time both do no evil and enter the way of merit.’

mn97:18.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of his slaves, servants and men behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, is not the better;

mn97:18.4.verse: the one who for the sake of his slaves, servants and men behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously, is the better.

mn97:18.5.verse: For conduct according to Dhamma and righteous conduct is better than conduct not according to Dhamma and unrighteous conduct, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:18.6.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni, there are other kinds of work (to be done) for one’s own sake which are in accordance with Dhamma, by means of which one can keep one’s slaves, servants and men and at the same time both do no evil and enter the way of merit.’

mn97:19.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of his friends and companions behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, is not the better;

mn97:19.6.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni, there are other kinds of work (to be done) for one’s own sake which are in accordance with Dhamma, by means of which one can do one’s friends’ and companions’ business and at the same time both do no evil and enter the way of merit.’

mn97:20.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of his relatives and kinsmen behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, is not the better;

mn97:20.4.verse: the one who for the sake of his relatives and kinsmen behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously, is the better.

mn97:20.5.verse: For conduct according to Dhamma and righteous conduct is better than conduct not according to Dhamma and unrighteous conduct, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:20.6.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni, there are other kinds of work (to be done) for one’s own sake which are in accordance with Dhamma, by means of which one can do one’s relatives’ and kinsmen’ business and at the same time both do no evil and enter the way of merit.’

mn97:25.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, one who for the sake of refreshing and nourishing this body behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously, or one who for the sake of refreshing and nourishing this body behaves according to Dhamma, behaves righteously—

mn97:25.3.verse: ‘The one, Master Sāriputta, who for the sake of refreshing and nourishing this body behaves not according to Dhamma, behaves unrighteously is not the better,

mn97:26.1.verse: Then Dhanañjāni the divine, delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words, and agreeing, he rose from his seat and departed.

mn97:27.1.verse: Now on another occasion, Dhanañjāni the divine was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill.

mn97:27.3.verse: ‘Come, good man, go to the Blessed One and pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and say:

mn97:27.4.verse: “Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:27.5.verse: he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet”;

mn97:27.6.verse: and go to the venerable Sāriputta and pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and say:

mn97:27.7.verse: “Venerable Sir, Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:27.8.verse: he pays homage with his head at the venerable Sāriputta’s feet”,

mn97:27.10.verse: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the venerable Sāriputta would come to the house of Dhanañjāni the divine, out of pity.”’

mn97:27.11.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the man replied, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn97:27.12.verse: ‘Venerable sir, Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:27.13.verse: he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.’

mn97:27.14.verse: And he went to the venerable Sāriputta, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn97:27.15.verse: ‘Venerable sir, Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:27.16.verse: he pays homage with his head at the venerable Sāriputta’s feet and he says:

mn97:27.17.verse: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the venerable Sāriputta would come to the house of Dhanañjāni the divine out of pity.”’

mn97:27.18.verse: The venerable Sāriputta consented in silence.

mn97:28.1.verse: Then the venerable Sāriputta dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went to the house of Dhanañjāni the divine, and sat down on a seat made ready. When he had done so, he said:

mn97:28.2.verse: ‘I hope you are getting well, divine, I hope you are comfortable; I hope your painful feelings are departing and not increasing, and that their departure and not their increase, is apparent.’

mn97:29.1.verse: ‘Master Sāriputta, I am not getting well, I am not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing, not departing; their increase and not their departure, is apparent.

mn97:29.2.verse: Just as if a strong man were splitting my head with a sharp sword, so too, violent winds (forces) are racking my head.

mn97:29.3.verse: I am not getting well, I am not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing, not departing; their increase and not their departure is apparent.

mn97:29.4.verse: Just as if a strong man were tightening a tough leather thong round my head as a headband, so too, there are violent pains in my head.

mn97:29.5.verse: I am not getting well, I am not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing, not departing; their increase and not their departure is apparent.

mn97:29.6.verse: Just as if a clever butcher or butcher’s apprentice were carving up an ox’s belly with a sharp knife, so too, violent winds (forces) are carving up my belly.

mn97:29.7.verse: I am not getting well, I am not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing, not departing; their increase and not their departure is apparent.

mn97:29.8.verse: Just as if two strong men had seized a weaker one by both arms and were roasting him over a pit of hot coals, so too, there is a violent burning in my body.

mn97:29.9.verse: I am not getting well, I am not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing, not departing; their increase and not their departure is apparent.’

mn97:30.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which is better,

mn97:30.3.verse: ‘The animal womb is better than hell, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.4.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which is better,

mn97:30.5.verse: the animal womb or the world of ghosts?’

mn97:30.6.verse: ‘The realm of ghosts is better than the animal womb, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.7.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which is better,

mn97:30.8.verse: the realm of ghosts or human beings?’

mn97:30.9.verse: ‘Human beings are better than the realm of ghosts, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.10.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which is better,

mn97:30.11.verse: human beings or the gods of the Four Kings?’

mn97:30.12.verse: ‘The gods of the Four Kings are better than human beings, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.13.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:30.14.verse: the gods of the Four Kings or the gods of the Thirty-three?’

mn97:30.15.verse: ‘The gods of the Thirty-three are better than the gods of the Four Kings, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.16.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:30.17.verse: the gods of the Thirty-three or the gods that have Gone to Bliss?’

mn97:30.18.verse: ‘The gods that have Gone to Bliss are better than the gods of the Thirty-three, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.19.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:30.20.verse: the gods that have Gone to Bliss or the Contented gods?’

mn97:30.21.verse: ‘The Contented gods are better than the gods that have Gone to the Bliss, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.22.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:30.23.verse: the Contented gods or the gods that Delight in Creating?’

mn97:30.24.verse: ‘The gods that Delight in Creating are better than the Contented gods, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:30.25.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:30.26.verse: the Gods that Delight in Creating or the gods that Wield Power over others’ Creations?’

mn97:30.27.verse: ‘The gods that Wield Power over others’ Creations are better than the gods that delight in Creating, Master Sāriputta.’

mn97:31.1.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, Dhanañjāni, which are better,

mn97:31.2.verse: the gods that Wield Power over other’s Creations or the gods of the world of the Divinity (Brahmā)?’

mn97:31.3.verse: ‘Does Master Sāriputta say “the World of the Divinity” ?

mn97:31.4.verse: Does Master Sāriputta say “the World of the Divinity” (Brahmā) ?’

mn97:31.6.verse: ‘These divines are devoted to the World of the Divinity.

mn97:31.7.verse: Suppose I show Dhanañjāni the divine the path to the Divinity’s Retinue?’

mn97:31.8.verse: (And he said:) ‘Dhanañjāni, I shall show you the path to the Divinity’s Retinue.

mn97:31.9.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn97:32.1.verse: ‘What is the Path to the World of the Divinity?

mn97:32.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides with his heart endued with loving-kindness extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with his heart abundant with loving-kindness, exalted, measureless, without hostility or a affliction extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn97:32.3.verse: This, Dhanañjāni, is the path to the Divinity’s Retinue.

mn97:33-35.1.verse: ‘Again, he abides with … compassion … extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn97:33-35.2.verse: ‘Again, he abides with … gladness … extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn97:33-35.3.verse: ‘Again, he abides with his heart endued with equanimity extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself; he abides with his heart abundant with equanimity, exalted, measureless, without hostility or affliction extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn97:33-35.4.verse: ‘This is the path to the Divinity’s Retinue.’

mn97:36.1.verse: ‘Then, Master Sāriputta, pay homage in my name with your head at the Blessed One’s feet

mn97:36.2.verse: (and say:) “Venerable sir, Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:36.3.verse: he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.” ’

mn97:36.4.verse: Then the venerable Sāriputta, having established Dhanañjāni the divine in the Divinity’s World (which he himself) had abandoned, rose from his seat and departed while there was still more to be done.

mn97:36.5.verse: And soon after he had left, Dhanañjāni the divine died and reappeared in the World of the Divinity.

mn97:37.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn97:37.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, Sāriputta, having established Dhanañjāni the divine in the World of the Divinity (which he himself) had abandoned, has risen from his seat and departed while there was still more to be done.’

mn97:38.1.verse: Then the venerable Sāriputta went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said:

mn97:38.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, Dhanañjāni the divine is afflicted, suffering and gravely ill;

mn97:38.3.verse: he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.’

mn97:38.4.verse: ‘How then, Sāriputta, did you, having established Dhanañjāni the divine in the Divinity’s World (which you yourself) have abandoned, rise from your seat and depart while there was still more to be done?’

mn97:38.6.verse: “These divines are devoted to the Divinity’s World. Suppose I show Dhanañjāni the divine the path to the Divinity’s Retinue?”’

mn97:38.7.verse: ‘Dhanañjāni the divine is dead, Sāriputta, and he has reappeared in the World of the Divinity.’

mn97:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn97:2.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was wandering in the Southern Hills together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn97:2.2.verse: Then a certain mendicant who had completed the rainy season residence in Rājagaha went to the Southern Hills, where he approached Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn97:2.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Sāriputta said to him,

mn97:2.4.verse: “Reverend, I hope the Buddha is healthy and strong?”

mn97:2.6.verse: “And I hope that the mendicant Saṅgha is healthy and strong.”

mn97:2.8.verse: “Reverend, at the rice checkpoint at the city gate there is a brahmin named Dhanañjāni.

mn97:2.9.verse: I hope that he is healthy and strong?”

mn97:2.13.verse: Dhanañjāni robs the brahmins and householders in the name of the king, and he robs the king in the name of the brahmins and householders.

mn97:2.14.verse: His wife, a lady of faith who he married from a family of faith, has passed away.

mn97:2.15.verse: And he has taken a new wife who has no faith.”

mn97:2.17.verse: to hear that Dhanañjāni is negligent.

mn97:2.18.verse: Hopefully, some time or other I’ll get to meet him, and we can have a discussion.”

mn97:3.1.verse: When Sāriputta had stayed in the Southern Hills as long as he pleased, he set out for Rājagaha.

mn97:3.2.verse: Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Rājagaha,

mn97:3.3.verse: where he stayed in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn97:4.1.verse: Then he robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

mn97:4.2.verse: Now at that time Dhanañjāni was having his cows milked in a cow-shed outside the city.

mn97:4.3.verse: Then Sāriputta wandered for alms in Rājagaha. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he approached Dhanañjāni.

mn97:4.4.verse: Seeing Sāriputta coming off in the distance,

mn97:4.5.verse: Dhanañjāni went to him and said,

mn97:4.6.verse: “Here, worthy Sāriputta, drink some fresh milk before the meal time.”

mn97:4.9.verse: I shall be at the root of that tree there for the day’s meditation.

mn97:5.1.verse: When Dhanañjāni had finished breakfast he went to Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.

mn97:5.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Sāriputta said to him,

mn97:5.4.verse: “How can I possibly be diligent, worthy Sāriputta? I have to provide for my mother and father, my wives and children, and my bondservants and workers. And I have to make the proper offerings to friends and colleagues, relatives and kin, guests, ancestors, deities, and king. And then this body must also be fattened and built up.”

mn97:6.2.verse: Suppose someone was to behave in an unprincipled and immoral way for the sake of their parents. Because of this the wardens of hell would drag them to hell.

mn97:6.3.verse: Could they get out of being dragged to hell by pleading that they had acted for the sake of their parents? Or could their parents save them by pleading that the acts had been done for their sake?”

mn97:6.5.verse: Rather, even as they were wailing the wardens of hell would cast them down into hell.”

mn97:7.2.verse: Suppose someone was to behave in an unprincipled and immoral way for the sake of their wives and children …

mn97:15.1.verse: fattening and building up their body. Because of this the wardens of hell would drag them to hell.

mn97:15.2.verse: Could they get out of being dragged to hell by pleading that they had acted for the sake of fattening and building up their body? Or could anyone else save them by pleading that the acts had been done for that reason?”

mn97:15.4.verse: Rather, even as they were wailing the wardens of hell would cast them down into hell.”

mn97:16.1.verse: “Who do you think is better, Dhanañjāni? Someone who, for the sake of their parents, behaves in an unprincipled and immoral manner, or someone who behaves in a principled and moral manner?”

mn97:16.3.verse: “Someone who behaves in a principled and moral manner for the sake of their parents.

mn97:16.5.verse: For principled and moral conduct is better than unprincipled and immoral conduct.”

mn97:16.6.verse: “Dhanañjāni, others have livelihoods that are both profitable and legitimate. By means of these it’s possible to provide for your parents, avoid bad deeds, and practice the path of goodness.

mn97:17.1.verse: Who do you think is better, Dhanañjāni? Someone who, for the sake of their wives and children …

mn97:25.1.verse: fattening and building up their body, behaves in an unprincipled and immoral manner, or someone who behaves in a principled and moral manner?”

mn97:25.3.verse: “Someone who behaves in a principled and moral manner.

mn97:25.5.verse: For principled and moral conduct is better than unprincipled and immoral conduct.”

mn97:25.6.verse: “Dhanañjāni, others have livelihoods that are both profitable and legitimate. By means of these it’s possible to fatten and build up your body, avoid bad deeds, and practice the path of goodness.”

mn97:26.1.verse: Then Dhanañjāni the brahmin, having approved and agreed with what Venerable Sāriputta said, rose from his seat and left.

mn97:27.1.verse: Some time later Dhanañjāni became sick, suffering, gravely ill.

mn97:27.3.verse: “Please, my man, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

mn97:27.4.verse: ‘Sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

mn97:27.5.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’

mn97:27.6.verse: Then go to Venerable Sāriputta, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

mn97:27.7.verse: ‘Sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

mn97:27.8.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’

mn97:27.10.verse: ‘Sir, please visit Dhanañjāni at his home out of sympathy.’”

mn97:27.11.verse: “Yes, sir,” that man replied. He did as Dhanañjāni asked.

mn97:28.1.verse: He robed up, and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Dhanañjāni’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out and said to Dhanañjāni,

mn97:28.2.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Dhanañjāni, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

mn97:29.1.verse: “I’m not keeping well, Mister Sāriputta, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.

mn97:29.2.verse: The winds piercing my head are so severe, it feels like a strong man drilling into my head with a sharp point.

mn97:29.4.verse: The pain in my head is so severe, it feels like a strong man tightening a strong leather strap around my head.

mn97:29.6.verse: The winds slicing my belly are so severe, like a deft butcher or their apprentice were slicing open a cow’s belly with a sharp meat cleaver.

mn97:29.8.verse: The burning in my body is so severe, it feels like two strong men grabbing a weaker man by the arms to burn and scorch him on a pit of glowing coals.

mn97:29.9.verse: I’m not keeping well, Mister Sāriputta, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

mn97:30.1.verse: “Dhanañjāni, which do you think is better:

mn97:30.5.verse: the animal realm or the ghost realm?”

mn97:30.8.verse: the ghost realm or human life?”

mn97:30.11.verse: human life or as one of the gods of the four great kings?”

mn97:30.12.verse: “The gods of the four great kings.”

mn97:30.14.verse: the gods of the four great kings or the gods of the thirty-three?”

mn97:30.17.verse: the gods of the thirty-three or the gods of Yama?”

mn97:30.20.verse: the gods of Yama or the joyful gods?”

mn97:30.23.verse: the joyful gods or the gods who love to create?”

mn97:30.26.verse: the gods who love to create or the gods who control what is created by others?”

mn97:30.27.verse: “The gods who control what is created by others.”

mn97:31.2.verse: the gods who control what is created by others or the realm of divinity?”

mn97:31.3.verse: “Worthy Sāriputta speaks of the realm of divinity!

mn97:31.4.verse: Worthy Sāriputta speaks of the realm of divinity!”

mn97:31.6.verse: “These brahmins are devoted to the realm of divinity.

mn97:31.7.verse: Why don’t I teach him a path to the company of Divinity?”

mn97:31.8.verse: “Dhanañjāni, I shall teach you a path to the company of Divinity.

mn97:31.9.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn97:32.1.verse: “And what is a path to company with Divinity?

mn97:32.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn97:32.3.verse: This is a path to company with Divinity.

mn97:33-35.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn97:33-35.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn97:33-35.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn97:33-35.4.verse: This is a path to company with Divinity.”

mn97:36.1.verse: “Well then, Mister Sāriputta, in my name bow with your head to the Buddha’s feet. Say to him:

mn97:36.2.verse: ‘Sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

mn97:36.3.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’”

mn97:36.4.verse: Then Sāriputta, after establishing Dhanañjāni in the inferior realm of divinity, rose from his seat and left while there was still more left to do.

mn97:36.5.verse: Not long after Sāriputta had left, Dhanañjāni passed away and was reborn in the realm of divinity.

mn97:37.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

mn97:37.2.verse: “Mendicants, Sāriputta, after establishing Dhanañjāni in the inferior realm of divinity, rose from his seat and left while there was still more left to do.”

mn97:38.1.verse: Then Sāriputta went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said,

mn97:38.2.verse: “Sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

mn97:38.3.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.”

mn97:38.4.verse: “But Sāriputta, after establishing Dhanañjāni in the inferior realm of divinity, why did you get up from your seat and leave while there was still more left to do?”

mn97:38.6.verse: ‘These brahmins are devoted to the realm of divinity. Why don’t I teach him a path to the company of Divinity?’”

mn97:38.7.verse: “And Sāriputta, the brahmin Dhanañjāni has passed away and been reborn in the realm of divinity.”

mn98:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.

mn98:2.1.verse: And on that occasion many well-known wealthy brahmans were dwelling in Icchānaṅgala, i.e.,

mn98:2.2.verse: Caṅkī the brahman, Tārukkha the brahman, Pokkharasāti the brahman, Jānusoṇin the brahman, Todeyya the brahman, and many other well-known wealthy brahmans.

mn98:3.1.verse: Then, while the young brahmans Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were walking and wandering about to exercise their legs, this conversation arose between them:

mn98:3.4.verse: “When one is well-born on both sides, the mother’s & the father’s, is of pure descent for seven generations of fathers—uncriticized & irreproachable in the telling of one’s birth:

mn98:3.5.verse: It’s to that extent that one is a brahman.”

mn98:3.7.verse: “When one is virtuous & consummate in one’s practices,

mn98:3.8.verse: it’s to that extent that one is a brahman.”

mn98:4.1.verse: But neither was the young brahman Bhāradvāja able to win over the young brahman Vāseṭṭha, nor was the young brahman Vāseṭṭha able to win over the young brahman Bhāradvāja.

mn98:5.1.verse: Then the young brahman Vāseṭṭha said to the young brahman Bhāradvāja,

mn98:5.2.verse: “Bhāradvāja, this Gotama the contemplative—a son of the Sakyans, gone forth from the Sakyan clan—is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.

mn98:5.3.verse: And of that Master Gotama this fine reputation has spread:

mn98:5.4.verse: ‘He is indeed a Blessed One, worthy & rightly self-awakened, consummate in clear-knowing & conduct, well-gone, an expert with regard to the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of people fit to be tamed, teacher of devas & human beings, awakened, blessed.’

mn98:5.5.verse: Come, let’s go to Gotama the contemplative and, on arrival, ask him about this matter.

mn98:5.6.verse: However he answers, that’s how we’ll hold it.”

mn98:5.7.verse: “As you say, master,” the young brahman Bhāradvāja responded to the young brahman Vāseṭṭha.

mn98:6.1.verse: So the young brahmans Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him.

mn98:6.2.verse: After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, they sat to one side.

mn98:6.3.verse: As they were sitting there, the young brahman Vāseṭṭha addressed the Blessed One in verses:

mn98:7.2.verse: as masters of the three knowledges:

mn98:14.1.verse: When this was said, the young brahmans Vāseṭṭha & Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One:

mn98:14.3.verse: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

mn98:14.4.verse: We go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, & to the Saṅgha of monks.

mn98:14.5.verse: May Master Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forward, for life.”

mn98:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

mn98:2.1.verse: Now at that time several very well-known well-to-do brahmins were residing in Icchānaṅgala. They included

mn98:2.2.verse: the brahmins Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jānussoṇi, Todeyya, and others.

mn98:3.1.verse: Then as the students Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were going for a walk they began to discuss the question:

mn98:3.4.verse: “When you’re well born on both your mother’s and father’s side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation—

mn98:3.7.verse: “When you’re ethical and accomplished in doing your duties—

mn98:4.1.verse: But neither was able to persuade the other.

mn98:5.2.verse: “Worthy Bhāradvāja, the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

mn98:5.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn98:5.5.verse: Come, let’s go to see him and ask him about this matter.

mn98:5.6.verse: As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”

mn98:6.1.verse: So they went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn98:6.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side,

mn98:6.3.verse: and Vāseṭṭha addressed the Buddha in verse:

mn98:7.6.verse: in all the Vedic experts teach.

mn98:7.8.verse: we match our tutors in recitation.

mn98:7.12.verse: one is a brahmin due to birth,

mn98:7.13.verse: but I declare it’s because of one’s deeds.

mn98:7.14.verse: Oh Clear-eyed One, know this as our debate.

mn98:7.15.verse: Since neither of us was able

mn98:7.17.verse: we’ve come to ask you, sir,

mn98:7.19.verse: As people honor with cupped palms

mn98:7.20.verse: the moon on the cusp of waxing,

mn98:7.24.verse: the Eye arisen in the world:

mn98:7.25.verse: is one a brahmin due to birth,

mn98:7.27.verse: We don’t know, please tell us,

mn98:7.28.verse: so we can recognize a brahmin.”

mn98:14.1.verse: When he had spoken, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to him,

mn98:14.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn98:14.4.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn98:14.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

mn99:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn99:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the student (divine) Subha, Todeyya’s son, was staying in a certain householder’s residence at Sāvatthi for some business or other.

mn99:2.2.verse: Then he asked the householder in whose residence he was staying:

mn99:2.4.verse: Sāvatthi is not lacking in Arahants.

mn99:2.5.verse: What monk or divine is there whom we may honour today?’

mn99:2.6.verse: ‘Venerable sir, there is this Blessed One living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn99:2.7.verse: You may honour the Blessed One, venerable sir.’

mn99:3.1.verse: Then having heard (what) the householder (said), the student (divine) Todeyya’s son went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,

mn99:3.2.verse: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he asked the Blessed One:

mn99:4.2.verse: “A householder is one who has embarked upon a profitable dhamma of the true way; one gone forth into homelessness has not embarked upon a profitable dhamma of the true way.”

mn99:4.3.verse: What does Master Gotama say about that?’

mn99:4.4.verse: ‘Here, student (divine), I am one who answers after analysing.

mn99:4.6.verse: I do not commend the wrong way in either a householder or one gone forth,

mn99:4.7.verse: for either a householder or one gone forth who has entered on the wrong way is for that reason not one who has embarked upon a profitable dhamma of the true way.

mn99:4.8.verse: I commend the right way in either a householder or one gone forth,

mn99:4.9.verse: for either a householder or one gone forth who has entered on the right way is for that reason one who has embarked upon a profitable dhamma of the true way.’

mn99:5.2.verse: “The field of action in the household life since it has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is very fruitful;

mn99:5.3.verse: the field of action in the life gone forth, since it has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is fruitless.”

mn99:5.4.verse: What does Master Gotama say about this?’

mn99:5.5.verse: ‘Here too, student (divine), I am one who answers after analysing.

mn99:5.7.verse: There is a field of action that has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it fails it is fruitless.

mn99:5.8.verse: There is a field of action that has greatly to do with (public) affairs with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it succeeds it is very fruitful.

mn99:5.9.verse: There is a field of action that has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it fails it is fruitless.

mn99:5.10.verse: There is a field of action that has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it succeeds, it is very fruitful.

mn99:6.1.verse: ‘What is a field of action that has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it fails is fruitless?

mn99:6.2.verse: Agriculture is such a field of action.

mn99:6.3.verse: ‘What is a field of action that has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it succeeds is very fruitful?

mn99:6.4.verse: Agriculture, too, is such a field of action.

mn99:6.5.verse: ‘What is a field of action that has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it fails is fruitless?

mn99:6.6.verse: Trade is such a field of action.

mn99:6.7.verse: ‘What is a field of action that has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, and when it succeeds is very fruitful?

mn99:6.8.verse: Trade, too, is such a field of action.

mn99:7.1.verse: ‘Just as the field of action consisting in agriculture, which has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is fruitless when it fails,

mn99:7.2.verse: so too the household life which is such a field of action, is fruitless when it fails.

mn99:7.3.verse: ‘Just as the field of action consisting in agriculture, which has greatly to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is very fruitful when it succeeds,

mn99:7.4.verse: so too the household life which is such a field of action, is very fruitful when it succeeds.

mn99:7.5.verse: ‘Just as the field of action consisting in trade, which has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is fruitless when it fails,

mn99:7.6.verse: so too the going forth which is such a field of action, is fruitless when it fails.

mn99:7.7.verse: ‘Just as the field of action consisting in trade, which has little to do with (public) affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is very fruitful when it succeeds,

mn99:7.8.verse: so too the going forth which is such a field of action, is very fruitful when it succeeds.’

mn99:8.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, divines describe five dhammas for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.’

mn99:8.2.verse: ‘Those five dhammas, student (divine), that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable—

mn99:8.3.verse: if it is no trouble to you—

mn99:8.4.verse: it would be good if you would state them in this assembly.’

mn99:8.5.verse: ‘It is no trouble for me, Master Gotama, sir, (in an assembly) where you, sirs, or such as you, sirs, are seated.’

mn99:9.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, divines describe truth as the first dhamma for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.2.verse: Divines describe asceticism as the second dhamma for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.3.verse: Divines describe the life divine as the third dhamma for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.4.verse: Divines describe study as the fourth dhamma for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.5.verse: Divines describe generosity as the fifth dhamma for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.6.verse: These are the five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable.

mn99:9.7.verse: What does Master Gotama say about this?’

mn99:9.8.verse: ‘How then, student (divine), do divines have any single divine among them who says thus:

mn99:9.9.verse: “I describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge”?’

mn99:9.11.verse: ‘How then, do divines have any single teacher or teacher’s teacher back to the seventh generation of teachers among them, who say thus:

mn99:9.12.verse: “I describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge”?’

mn99:9.14.verse: ‘How then, did the divines’ former sages, makers of the hymns, tellers of the hymns, whose ancient hymnal has been chanted, told and compiled, which divines now keep chanting and pronouncing, the pronouncements that they keep pronouncing and the recitations that they keep reciting—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Angirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa and Bhagu—

mn99:9.16.verse: “We describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge”?’

mn99:9.18.verse: ‘So divines, it seems, have no single divine among them who says thus:

mn99:9.19.verse: “I describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge”;

mn99:9.20.verse: and divines have no single teacher, or teacher’s teacher back to the seventh generation of teachers among them, who says thus:

mn99:9.21.verse: “I describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge”;

mn99:9.22.verse: and the divines’ former sages, makers of the hymns, tellers of the hymns, whose ancient hymnal has been chanted, told and compiled, which divines now keep chanting and pronouncing, the pronouncements that they keep pronouncing and the recitations that they keep reciting—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Angirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa and Bhagu—

mn99:9.23.verse: these too did not say thus:

mn99:9.24.verse: “We describe the ripening of these five dhammas, having realized it by direct knowledge.”

mn99:9.25.verse: Suppose there were a file of blind men each in touch with the next: the first one does not see and the middle one does not see and the last one does not see.

mn99:9.26.verse: So too, it must be with the divines’ declarations: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.’

mn99:10.1.verse: When this was said, the student (divine) Subbha, Todeyya’s son, was angry and displeased with the mention of the simile of the blind men’s file, and scorning, disparaging and censuring the Blessed One thus:

mn99:10.2.verse: ‘The monk Gotama will be (shown to be) mistaken.’ He said to him:

mn99:10.3.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga Grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) has spoken thus.

mn99:10.4.verse: “So indeed there are certain monks and divines here who claim distinction higher than the human state worthy of Noble Ones’ knowledge and vision;

mn99:10.5.verse: but what they say turns out to be laughable, it is mere empty, vain words.

mn99:10.6.verse: For how can a human being know or see or realize a distinction higher than the human state worthy of Noble Ones’ knowledge and vision?

mn99:11.1.verse: ‘How then, has Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga Grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) understood how to encompass with mind the minds of all monks and divines?’

mn99:11.2.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, Pokkharasāti the divine does not even understand how to encompass with mind the mind of even his own bondswoman, Puṇṇikā, so how could he encompass with mind the minds of all monks and divines?’

mn99:12.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a man blind from birth who could not see dark and light forms, or blue or yellow or red or pink forms, or even and uneven (places), or the stars, the moon and the sun,

mn99:12.3.verse: “There are no dark and light forms,

mn99:12.10.verse: moon and sun and there is no seer of them either.

mn99:12.11.verse: I do not know that, I do not see that,

mn99:12.12.verse: therefore there is none of that”,

mn99:12.15.verse: There are dark and light forms, and there is a seer of dark and light forms;

mn99:12.16.verse: there are blue forms, and there is a seer of blue forms;

mn99:12.17.verse: there are yellow forms, and there is a seer of yellow forms;

mn99:12.18.verse: there are red forms, and there is a seer of red forms;

mn99:12.19.verse: there are pink forms, and there is a seer of pink forms;

mn99:12.20.verse: there are even and uneven (places), and there is a seer of even and uneven (places);

mn99:12.21.verse: there are stars, and there is a seer of the stars;

mn99:12.22.verse: there are the moon and sun, and there is a seer of the moon and sun.

mn99:12.23.verse: ‘I do not know that, I do not see that,

mn99:12.24.verse: therefore there is none of that’;

mn99:12.25.verse: By so saying he would not be speaking rightly.’

mn99:13.1.verse: ‘So too, Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) is blind and sightless.

mn99:13.2.verse: That he should know or realize any distinction higher than the human state worthy of Noble Ones’ knowledge and vision, is not possible.

mn99:13.3.verse: How do you conceive this, student (divine),

mn99:13.4.verse: for these Kosalan divines of great property such as

mn99:13.5.verse: Caṅkī the divine, Tārukkha the divine, Janussoni the divine, Todeyya the divine, your father, which is better, that the speech they utter (accords with) the convention current in the world or (does) not (accord with) the convention current in the world?’

mn99:13.6.verse: ‘The convention current in the world, Master Gotama, sir.’

mn99:13.7.verse: ‘Which is the better for them: that the speech they utter is well-advised or ill-advised?’

mn99:13.9.verse: ‘Which is better for them: that the speech they utter is after reflexion or not after reflexion?’

mn99:13.11.verse: ‘Which is better for them: that the speech they utter is connected with good, or not?’

mn99:14.2.verse: if that is so, is the speech uttered by Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga Grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) the convention current in the world or that not current in the world?’

mn99:14.3.verse: ‘That not current in the world, Master Gotama, sir.’

mn99:14.9.verse: ‘Not connected with good, Master Gotama, sir.’

mn99:15.3.verse: There is the hindrance of desire for sensual pleasure, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of lethargy-and-drowsiness, the hindrance of agitation-and-worry, the hindrance of uncertainty.

mn99:15.5.verse: Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga Grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) is blocked and hindered and caught up and enveloped by these five hindrances.

mn99:15.6.verse: That he should know or see or realize any distinction higher than the human state worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, is not possible.

mn99:16.1.verse: Now there are these five cords of sensual desire.

mn99:16.3.verse: There are forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desirable, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn99:16.4.verse: There are sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn99:16.5.verse: There are odours cognizable by the nose …

mn99:16.6.verse: There are flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn99:16.7.verse: There are tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desireable, agreeable, and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn99:16.8.verse: These, student (divine), are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn99:16.9.verse: Pokkharasāti the divine of the Opamaññas and (lord) of the Subhaga Grove (at Ukkaṭṭhā) being entangled with and unwarily committed to these five cords of sensual desires, enjoys them, without either seeing the danger in them or understanding the escape from them.

mn99:16.10.verse: That he should know or see or realize any distinction higher than the human state worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, is not possible.

mn99:17.1.verse: How do you conceive this, student (divine, of two fires, namely,)

mn99:17.2.verse: a fire made to blaze dependent on fuel consisting of grass and wood, and a fire made to blaze dependent on fuel free from grass and wood (and the like), which would have (a better) flame and colour and radiance?’

mn99:17.3.verse: ‘If such a thing were possible, Master Gotama, the fire made to blaze dependent on fuel free from grass and wood (and the like) would have (a better) flame and colour and radiance.’

mn99:17.4.verse: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a fire should be made to blaze dependent on fuel free from grass and wood (and the like) except by one possessed of (supernormal) success.

mn99:17.5.verse: The kind of happiness which is dependent on the five cords of sensual desires is like the fire made to blaze dependent on fuel consisting of grass and wood, I say.

mn99:17.6.verse: That kind of happiness which is quite independent of sensual desires, independent of unprofitable dhammas, is like the fire made to blaze dependent on fuel free from grass and wood, I say.

mn99:17.7.verse: And what is that kind of happiness which is quite independent of sensual desires, independent of unprofitable dhammas?

mn99:17.8.verse: Here, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of seclusion.

mn99:17.9.verse: Now this kind of happiness is quite independent of sensual desires, independent of unprofitable dhammas.

mn99:17.10.verse: Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and (bodily) pleasure born of concentration.

mn99:17.11.verse: Now this kind of happiness, too, is quite independent of sensual desires, independent of unprofitable dhammas.

mn99:18.1.verse: ‘When divines describe those five dhammas for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable, which of these dhammas do they describe as the most fruitful for performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable?’

mn99:18.2.verse: ‘Of these they describe generosity as the most fruitful, Master Gotama, sir.’

mn99:19.2.verse: some great sacrificial offering might fall to some divine (to make),

mn99:19.3.verse: and then two divines went (there, thinking):

mn99:19.4.verse: “We will take part in the great sacrifice of the divine named so-and-so”,

mn99:19.6.verse: “If only I might get the best seat, the best water, the best alms-food in the refectory, and the other divine might not get the best seat, the best water, the best alms-food in the refectory!”

mn99:19.7.verse: And it is possible that the other divine, and not that divine, might get the best seat, the best water, the best alms-food in the refectory,

mn99:19.10.verse: Now, how do divines describe the ripening of that divine’s (kamma)?’

mn99:19.11.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, divines do not give gifts thus;

mn99:19.12.verse: ‘that by this another may be angry and displeased’;

mn99:19.13.verse: on the contrary, divines give gifts out of pity.’

mn99:19.14.verse: ‘That being so, then divines have this as the sixth instance of the performance of merit,

mn99:19.15.verse: namely, that done out of pity?’

mn99:19.16.verse: ‘That being so, Master Gotama, sir, then divines have this as the sixth instance of the performance of merit, namely,

mn99:19.17.verse: namely, that done out of pity.’

mn99:20.1.verse: ‘Where do you see most those five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking on the profitable:

mn99:20.2.verse: among householders or among those gone forth?’

mn99:20.3.verse: ‘These five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking on the profitable, Master Gotama, I see much among those gone forth and little among householders.

mn99:20.4.verse: For a householder, having greatly to do with public affairs, with functions, with engagements, with undertakings, is not constantly and invariably a speaker of truth,

mn99:20.5.verse: but one gone forth, having little to do with public affairs, with engagements, with undertakings, is constantly and invariably a speaker of truth.

mn99:20.6.verse: For the same reasons a householder does not practice constant and invariable asceticism,

mn99:20.7.verse: does not lead the life divine,

mn99:20.10.verse: while one gone forth practises constant and invariable asceticism,

mn99:20.14.verse: These five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking on the profitable, I see much among those gone forth and little among householders.’

mn99:21.1.verse: ‘Now those five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable, those I call equipments of mind,

mn99:21.2.verse: that is to say, for the development of a mind which is free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.3.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu is a speaker of truth.

mn99:21.4.verse: (By thinking:) “I am a speaker of truth”, he finds inspiration in the meaning, he finds inspiration in the dhamma, he finds gladness connected with Dhamma;

mn99:21.5.verse: and it is that gladness associated with what is profitable that I call an equipment of mind,

mn99:21.6.verse: that is to say, for the development of a mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.7.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu is an ascetic. (By thinking:) “I am an ascetic”, he finds inspiration in the meaning … a mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.8.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu is one who leads the life divine. (By thinking:) “I am one who leads the life divine”, he finds inspiration in the meaning … a mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.9.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu is one who studies much. (By thinking:) “I am one who studies much”, he finds inspiration in the meaning … a mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.11.verse: (By thinking:) “I have much generosity”, he finds inspiration in the meaning, he finds inspiration in the dhamma, he finds gladness connected with Dhamma;

mn99:21.12.verse: and it is that gladness associated with what is profitable that I call an equipment of mind,

mn99:21.13.verse: that is to say, for the development of mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.

mn99:21.14.verse: ‘As to those five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable, those I call equipments of mind—

mn99:21.15.verse: that is to say, for the development of a mind free from hostility and free from ill-will.’

mn99:22.1.verse: When this was said, the student (divine) Subha, Todeyya’s son, said to the Blessed One:

mn99:22.2.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, I have heard (it said) that

mn99:22.3.verse: the monk Gotama knows the path to the Divinity’s (Brahma’s) Retinue.’

mn99:22.5.verse: is the village of Naḷakāra near here, not far from here?’

mn99:22.6.verse: ‘Yes, sir, the village of Naḷakāra is near here, not far from here.’

mn99:22.7.verse: ‘How do you conceive this, student (divine), suppose a man were born and brought up in the village of Naḷakāra,

mn99:22.8.verse: and then when he had only recently left Naḷakāra they asked him the path to the village,

mn99:22.9.verse: would he be slow or hesitant (in answering)?’

mn99:22.12.verse: Because that man has been born and brought up in the village of Naḷakāra: he is well acquainted with all paths to it.’

mn99:22.13.verse: ‘Still a man born and brought up in the village of Naḷakāra might, on being asked about the path to the village, be slow or hesitant, but a Tathāgata on being asked about the path to the world of the Divinity would never be slow or hesitant.

mn99:22.14.verse: I understand the Divinity and the World of the Divinity and I also understand how one practises in order to reappear in the World of the Divinity.’

mn99:23.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, sir, I have heard (it said) that

mn99:23.2.verse: the monk Gotama teaches the path to the Divinity’s Retinue.

mn99:23.3.verse: It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the path to the Divinity’s Retinue.’

mn99:23.4.verse: ‘Then listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn99:24.1.verse: ‘And what is the path to the Divinity’s Retinue?

mn99:24.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides with mind endued with loving-kindness extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself: he abides with his heart abundant with loving-kindness, exalted, measureless, without hostility or ill-will extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn99:24.3.verse: While the deliverance of the heart by loving-kindness is developed in this way, no kamma restricted by limited measurements is found there, none persists there.

mn99:24.4.verse: Just as a vigorous trumpeter could make himself heard without difficulty in the four directions,

mn99:24.5.verse: so too when the deliverance of the heart by loving-kindness is developed thus, no kamma restricted by limited measurements is found there, none persists there.

mn99:24.6.verse: This is a path to the Divinity’s Retinue.

mn99:25-27.1.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu abides with a mind endued with compassion ...

mn99:25-27.2.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu abides with a mind endued with gladness …

mn99:25-27.3.verse: ‘Here a bhikkhu abides with mind endued with equanimity extending over one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth, and so above, below, around and everywhere, and to all as to himself: he abides with his heart abundant with equanimity, exalted, measureless, without hostility or ill-will extending over the all-encompassing world.

mn99:25-27.4.verse: While the deliverance of the heart by equanimity is developed in this way, no kamma restricted by limited measurements is found there, none persists there.

mn99:25-27.5.verse: Just as a vigorous trumpeter could make himself heard without difficulty in the four directions,

mn99:25-27.6.verse: so too when the deliverance of the heart by equanimity is developed thus, no kamma restricted by limited measurements is found there, none persists there.

mn99:25-27.7.verse: This too is a path to the Divinity’s Retinue.’

mn99:28.1.verse: When this was said, the student (divine) Subha, Todeyya’s son, said to the Blessed One:

mn99:28.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.

mn99:28.4.verse: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.

mn99:28.5.verse: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn99:28.6.verse: ‘And now Master Gotama sir, we depart;

mn99:28.7.verse: we are busy and have much to do.’

mn99:29.1.verse: ‘It is time now, student (divine), to do as you think fit.’

mn99:29.2.verse: Then the student (divine) Subha, Todeyya’s son, thus delighting in the Blessed One’s words and agreeing, rose from his seat and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he departed.

mn99:30.1.verse: Now at that time, it being midday, Janussoni the divine was driving through Sāvatthī in a chariot drawn by mares, all in white.

mn99:30.2.verse: Janussoni the divine saw the student (divine) Subha, Todeyya’s son, coming.

mn99:30.3.verse: When he saw him, he said:

mn99:30.4.verse: ‘Now where is Master Bhāradvāja coming from at midday?’

mn99:30.5.verse: ‘Sir, I am coming from the monk Gotama’s presence.’

mn99:30.6.verse: ‘How does Master Bhāradvāja conceive the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding? He is wise, is he not?’

mn99:30.7.verse: ‘Sir, who am I to know the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding?

mn99:30.8.verse: One would surely have to be his equal to know the monk Gotama’s ability of understanding.’

mn99:30.9.verse: ‘Master Bhāradvāja praises the monk Gotama with high praise indeed.’

mn99:30.10.verse: ‘Sir, who am I to praise the monk Gotama?

mn99:30.11.verse: The monk Gotama is praised by the praised—as best among gods and men.

mn99:30.12.verse: And sir, these five dhammas that divines describe for the performance of merit, for embarking upon the profitable,

mn99:30.13.verse: the monk Gotama calls them equipments of mind, that is to say,

mn99:30.14.verse: for the development of a mind which is a free from hostility and free from ill-will.’

mn99:31.1.verse: When this was said, Janussoni the divine got down from his chariot drawn by mares, all in white, and, arranging his robe on one shoulder, he raised his hands palms together towards where the Blessed One was, and he uttered this exclamation:

mn99:31.2.verse: ‘It is a gain for King Pasenadi of Kosala,

mn99:31.3.verse: that a Tathāgata, Arahant and Fully Enlightened One abides in his realm!’

mn99:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn99:2.1.verse: Now at that time the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, was residing in Sāvatthī at a certain householder’s home on some business.

mn99:2.2.verse: Then Subha said to that householder,

mn99:2.4.verse: Sāvatthī does not lack for perfected ones.

mn99:2.5.verse: What ascetic or brahmin might we pay homage to today?”

mn99:2.6.verse: “Sir, the Buddha is staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn99:2.7.verse: You can pay homage to him.”

mn99:3.1.verse: Acknowledging that householder, Subha went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn99:3.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn99:4.2.verse: ‘Laypeople succeed in the system of the skillful teaching, not renunciates.’

mn99:4.3.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn99:4.4.verse: “On this point, student, I speak after analyzing the question,

mn99:4.6.verse: I don’t praise wrong practice for either laypeople or renunciates.

mn99:4.7.verse: Because of wrong practice, neither laypeople nor renunciates succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.

mn99:4.8.verse: I praise right practice for both laypeople and renunciates.

mn99:4.9.verse: Because of right practice, both laypeople and renunciates succeed in the system of the skillful teaching.”

mn99:5.2.verse: ‘Since the work of the lay life has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings it is very fruitful.
