mn99:5.3.verse: But since the work of the renunciate has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings it is not very fruitful.’

mn99:5.4.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn99:5.5.verse: “On this point, too, I speak after analyzing the question,

mn99:5.7.verse: Some work has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it fails it’s not very fruitful.

mn99:5.8.verse: Some work has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it succeeds it is very fruitful.

mn99:5.9.verse: Some work has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it fails it’s not very fruitful.

mn99:5.10.verse: Some work has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it succeeds it is very fruitful.

mn99:6.1.verse: And what work has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it fails it’s not very fruitful?

mn99:6.3.verse: And what work has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it succeeds it is very fruitful?

mn99:6.5.verse: And what work has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it fails it’s not very fruitful?

mn99:6.7.verse: And what work has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and when it succeeds it is very fruitful?

mn99:7.1.verse: The lay life is like farming in that it’s work with many obligations and when it fails it’s not very fruitful;

mn99:7.3.verse: but when it succeeds it is very fruitful.

mn99:7.5.verse: The renunciate life is like trade in that it’s work with few obligations and when it fails it’s not very fruitful;

mn99:7.7.verse: but when it succeeds it is very fruitful.”

mn99:8.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, the brahmins prescribe five things for making merit and succeeding in the skillful.”

mn99:8.4.verse: please explain these in this assembly.”

mn99:8.5.verse: “It’s no trouble when good fellows such as yourself are sitting here.”

mn99:9.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, truth is the first thing.

mn99:9.6.verse: These are the five things that the brahmins prescribe for making merit and succeeding in the skillful.

mn99:9.7.verse: What do you say about this?”

mn99:9.8.verse: “Well, student, is there even a single one of the brahmins who says this:

mn99:9.9.verse: ‘I declare the result of these five things after realizing it with my own insight’?”

mn99:9.11.verse: “Well, is there even a single tutor of the brahmins, or a tutor’s tutor, or anyone back to the seventh generation of tutors, who says this:

mn99:9.12.verse: ‘I declare the result of these five things after realizing it with my own insight’?”

mn99:9.14.verse: “Well, what of the ancient seers of the brahmins, namely Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu? They were the authors and propagators of the hymns. Their hymnal was sung and propagated and compiled in ancient times; and these days, brahmins continue to sing and chant it, chanting what was chanted and teaching what was taught.

mn99:9.16.verse: ‘We declare the result of these five things after realizing it with our own insight’?”

mn99:9.18.verse: “So, student, it seems that there is not a single one of the brahmins,

mn99:9.20.verse: not even anyone back to the seventh generation of tutors,

mn99:9.22.verse: nor even the ancient seers of the brahmins

mn99:9.24.verse: ‘We declare the result of these five things after realizing it with our own insight.’

mn99:9.25.verse: Suppose there was a queue of blind men, each holding the one in front: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.

mn99:9.26.verse: In the same way, it seems to me that the brahmins’ statement turns out to be comparable to a queue of blind men: the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.”

mn99:10.1.verse: When he said this, Subha became angry and upset with the Buddha because of the simile of the queue of blind men. He even attacked and badmouthed the Buddha himself, saying,

mn99:10.2.verse: “The ascetic Gotama will be worsted!” He said to the Buddha:

mn99:10.3.verse: “Worthy Gotama, the brahmin Pokkharasāti Upamañña of the Subhaga Forest says:

mn99:10.4.verse: ‘This is exactly what happens with some ascetics and brahmins. They claim to have a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn99:10.5.verse: But their statement turns out to be a joke—mere words, vacuous and hollow.

mn99:10.6.verse: For how on earth can a human being know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?

mn99:11.1.verse: “But student, does Pokkharasāti understand the minds of all these ascetics and brahmins, having encompassed them with his mind?”

mn99:11.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, Pokkharasāti doesn’t even understand the mind of his own bonded maid Puṇṇikā, so how could he know all those ascetics and brahmins?”

mn99:12.1.verse: “Suppose there was a person blind from birth. They couldn’t see sights that are dark or bright, or blue, yellow, red, or magenta. They couldn’t see even and uneven ground, or the stars, or the moon and sun.

mn99:12.3.verse: ‘There’s no such thing as dark and bright sights, and no one who sees them.

mn99:12.4.verse: There’s no such thing as blue,

mn99:12.10.verse: moon and sun, and no one who sees these things.

mn99:12.11.verse: I don’t know it or see it,

mn99:12.15.verse: There are such things as dark and bright sights, and one who sees them.

mn99:12.22.verse: moon and sun, and one who sees these things.

mn99:12.23.verse: So it’s not right to say this: ‘I don’t know it or see it,

mn99:13.1.verse: “In the same way, Pokkharasāti is blind and sightless.

mn99:13.2.verse: It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn99:13.4.verse: There are well-to-do brahmins of Kosala such as

mn99:13.5.verse: the brahmins Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jānussoṇi, and your father Todeyya. What’s better for them: that their speech agrees or disagrees with the consensus of opinion?”

mn99:13.7.verse: “What’s better for them: that their speech is thoughtful or thoughtless?”

mn99:13.9.verse: “What’s better for them: that their speech follows reflection or is unreflective?”

mn99:13.11.verse: “What’s better for them: that their speech is beneficial or worthless?”

mn99:14.2.verse: If this is so, does Pokkharasāti’s speech agree or disagree with the consensus of opinion?”

mn99:15.3.verse: The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

mn99:15.5.verse: Pokkharasāti is obstructed, hindered, engulfed, and enveloped by these five hindrances.

mn99:15.6.verse: It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn99:16.1.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn99:16.3.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn99:16.4.verse: There are sounds known by the ear …

mn99:16.7.verse: touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn99:16.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn99:16.9.verse: Pokkharasāti enjoys these five kinds of sensual stimulation, tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

mn99:16.10.verse: It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn99:17.2.verse: Which would have better flames, color, and radiance: a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel, or one that does not?”

mn99:17.3.verse: “If it were possible for a fire to burn without depending on grass and logs as fuel, that would have better flames, color, and radiance.”

mn99:17.4.verse: “But it isn’t possible, except by psychic power.

mn99:17.5.verse: Rapture that depends on the five kinds of sensual stimulation is like a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel.

mn99:17.6.verse: Rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities is like a fire that doesn’t depend on grass and logs as fuel.

mn99:17.7.verse: And what is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities?

mn99:17.8.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn99:17.9.verse: This is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

mn99:17.10.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn99:17.11.verse: This too is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

mn99:18.1.verse: Of the five things that the brahmins prescribe for making merit and succeeding in the skillful, which do they say is the most fruitful?”

mn99:19.2.verse: Suppose a brahmin was setting up a grand sacrifice.

mn99:19.3.verse: Then two brahmins came along, thinking,

mn99:19.4.verse: ‘We shall participate in the grand sacrifice of the brahmin named so-and-so.’

mn99:19.5.verse: Then one of those brahmins thought:

mn99:19.6.verse: ‘Oh, I hope that I alone get the best seat, the best drink, and the best almsfood in the refectory, not some other brahmin.’

mn99:19.7.verse: But it’s possible that some other brahmin gets the best seat, the best drink, and the best almsfood in the refectory.

mn99:19.8.verse: Thinking, ‘Some other brahmin has got the best seat, the best drink, the best almsfood,’

mn99:19.10.verse: What do the brahmins say is the result of this?”

mn99:19.11.verse: “Worthy Gotama, brahmins don’t give gifts so that

mn99:19.12.verse: others will get angry and upset.

mn99:19.13.verse: Rather, they only give gifts that are born from sympathy.”

mn99:19.14.verse: “In that case, isn’t this a sixth ground for making merit,

mn99:19.16.verse: “In that case, this is a sixth ground for making merit,

mn99:20.1.verse: “Of the five things that the brahmins prescribe for making merit and succeeding in the skillful, where do you usually find them:

mn99:20.3.verse: “Mostly among renunciates, and less so among lay people.

mn99:20.4.verse: For a layperson has many obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and they can’t always tell the truth,

mn99:20.10.verse: But a renunciate has few obligations, duties, issues, and undertakings, and they can always tell the truth, be fervent,

mn99:20.14.verse: Of the five things that the brahmins prescribe for making merit and succeeding in the skillful, I usually find them among renunciates, and less so among laypeople.”

mn99:21.1.verse: “I say that the five things prescribed by the brahmins for making merit are prerequisites of the mind for

mn99:21.2.verse: developing a mind free of enmity and ill will.

mn99:21.3.verse: Take a mendicant who speaks the truth.

mn99:21.4.verse: Thinking, ‘I’m truthful,’ they find inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and find joy connected with the teaching.

mn99:21.5.verse: And I say that joy connected with the skillful is a prerequisite of the mind for

mn99:21.6.verse: developing a mind free of enmity and ill will.

mn99:21.7.verse: Take a mendicant who is fervent …

mn99:21.11.verse: Thinking, ‘I’m very generous,’ they find inspiration in the meaning and the teaching, and find joy connected with the teaching.

mn99:21.12.verse: And I say that joy connected with the skillful is a prerequisite of the mind for

mn99:21.13.verse: developing a mind free of enmity and ill will.

mn99:21.14.verse: I say that these five things prescribed by the brahmins for making merit are prerequisites of the mind for

mn99:21.15.verse: developing a mind free of enmity and ill will.”

mn99:22.1.verse: When he had spoken, Subha said to him,

mn99:22.3.verse: the ascetic Gotama knows a path to company with divinity.”

mn99:22.5.verse: Is the village of Naḷakāra nearby?”

mn99:22.7.verse: “What do you think, student? Suppose a person was born and raised in Naḷakāra.

mn99:22.8.verse: And as soon as they left the town some people asked them for the road to Naḷakāra.

mn99:22.9.verse: Would they be slow or hesitant to answer?”

mn99:22.12.verse: Because they were born and raised in Naḷakāra. They’re well acquainted with all the roads to the village.”

mn99:22.13.verse: “Still, it’s possible they might be slow or hesitant to answer. But the Realized One is never slow or hesitant when questioned about the realm of divinity or the practice that leads to the realm of divinity.

mn99:22.14.verse: I understand the Divinity, the realm of divinity, and the practice that leads to the realm of divinity, practicing in accordance with which one is reborn in the realm of divinity.”

mn99:23.2.verse: the ascetic Gotama teaches a path to company with divinity.

mn99:23.4.verse: “Well then, student, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn99:24.1.verse: “And what is a path to company with divinity?

mn99:24.2.verse: Firstly, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn99:24.3.verse: When the heart’s release by love has been developed like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

mn99:24.4.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

mn99:24.5.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by love has been developed like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

mn99:24.6.verse: This is a path to company with divinity.

mn99:25-27.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn99:25-27.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn99:25-27.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn99:25-27.4.verse: When the heart’s release by equanimity has been developed and cultivated like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

mn99:25-27.5.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

mn99:25-27.6.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by equanimity has been developed and cultivated like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

mn99:25-27.7.verse: This too is a path to company with divinity.”

mn99:28.1.verse: When he had spoken, Subha said to him,

mn99:28.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

mn99:28.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn99:28.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.

mn99:28.6.verse: Well, now, worthy Gotama, I must go.

mn99:28.7.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn99:29.2.verse: And then Subha approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn99:30.1.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Jānussoṇi drove out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares.

mn99:30.2.verse: He saw the student Subha coming off in the distance,

mn99:30.4.verse: “So, worthy Bhāradvāja, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

mn99:30.5.verse: “Just now, good fellow, I’ve come from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.”

mn99:30.6.verse: “What do you think of the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? Do you think he’s astute?”

mn99:30.7.verse: “Worthy sir, who am I to judge the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom?

mn99:30.8.verse: You’d really have to be on the same level to judge his lucidity of wisdom.”

mn99:30.9.verse: “Worthy Bhāradvāja praises the ascetic Gotama with high praise indeed.”

mn99:30.10.verse: “Who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama?

mn99:30.11.verse: He is praised by the praised as the best among gods and humans.

mn99:30.12.verse: The five things that the brahmins prescribe for making merit and succeeding in the skillful

mn99:30.13.verse: he says are prerequisites of the mind for

mn99:30.14.verse: developing a mind free of enmity and ill will.”

mn99:31.1.verse: When he had spoken, Jānussoṇi got down from his chariot, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times,

mn99:31.2.verse: “King Pasenadi of Kosala is lucky, so very lucky

mn99:31.3.verse: that the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha is living in his realm!”

mn100:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn100:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion a brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī was living at Caṇḍalakappa; she had full confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.

mn100:2.2.verse: Then the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, having stumbled, uttered this exclamation three times:

mn100:2.3.verse: “Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

mn100:2.4.verse: Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

mn100:2.5.verse: Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.”

mn100:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion a student named Saṅgārava was living at Caṇḍalakappa, an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man.

mn100:3.2.verse: The student Saṅgārava heard the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī speaking these words.

mn100:3.3.verse: Having heard this, he said to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī:

mn100:3.4.verse: “This brahmin woman Dhanañjānī is degraded indeed, this brahmin woman Dhanañjānī is disgraced indeed, that when there are brahmins possessing the three knowledges, she praises that shaveling ascetic.”

mn100:3.5.verse: “You do not know, dear sir, that Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.

mn100:3.6.verse: If you knew, dear sir, that Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom, you would not think that that Blessed One should be abused and reviled.”

mn100:3.7.verse: “Well then, madam, when the ascetic Gotama arrives at Caṇḍalakappa, tell me.”

mn100:3.8.verse: “Yes, dear sir,” the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī replied to the student Saṅgārava.

mn100:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages through the Kosalan country, arrived at Caṇḍalakappa.

mn100:4.2.verse: There the Blessed One stayed at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.

mn100:5.1.verse: The brahmin woman Dhanañjānī heard: “The Blessed One, it seems, has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa, and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.”

mn100:5.2.verse: Then the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī went to the student Saṅgārava and said to him:

mn100:5.3.verse: “Dear sir, that Blessed One has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa, and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa, in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.

mn100:5.4.verse: Now, dear sir, it is time for you to do as you think fit.”

mn100:5.5.verse: “Yes, madam,” the student Saṅgārava replied to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, and he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn100:5.6.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:

mn100:6.1.verse: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine.[^1]

mn100:6.2.verse: Now, Master Gotama, of those ascetics and brahmins who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine, to which does Master Gotama belong?”

mn100:7.1.verse: “Bhāradvāja, I say that there is diversity even among those who, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine.

mn100:7.2.verse: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who rely on oral tradition.

mn100:7.3.verse: They, on the basis of oral tradition, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine;

mn100:7.4.verse: such are the brahmins who are masters of the Three Vedas.

mn100:7.5.verse: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who, on the basis of mere faith alone, having reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, claim the fundamentals of the life divine;

mn100:7.6.verse: such are the rationalists and investigators.

mn100:7.7.verse: There are, Bhāradvāja, some ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine.

mn100:7.8.verse: Of these, Bhāradvāja, the ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine—I am one of them.

mn100:8.1.verse: This too, Bhāradvāja, may be understood in such a way that I am one of those ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves a Dhamma among things not heard before, have reached here and now the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge, and claim the fundamentals of the life divine.

mn100:9.1.verse: Here, Bhāradvāja, before my enlightenment, while I was still a Bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me:

mn100:9.2.verse: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn100:9.3.verse: It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the life divine utterly perfect and utterly pure as a polished shell.

mn100:9.4.verse: Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’

mn100:9.5.verse: Later, while still a boy, a black-haired youth endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first phase of life, I shaved off my hair and beard—though my mother and father wished otherwise and grieved with tearful faces—I put on the yellow cloth and went forth from the house life into homelessness.

mn100:9.6.verse: Having gone forth in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and I said to him:

mn100:9.7.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.’

mn100:9.8.verse: When this was said, Āḷāra Kālāma replied:

mn100:9.10.verse: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’

mn100:9.12.verse: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teachings went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others that did likewise.

mn100:9.14.verse: ‘It is not through mere faith alone the Āḷāra Kālāma declares his Dhamma; (he does so) because he enters upon and abides in it, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:9.15.verse: Certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.’

mn100:10.1.verse: Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma, and I said to him:

mn100:10.2.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:10.3.verse: When this was said, he declared the base consisting of nothingness.

mn100:10.5.verse: ‘Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has faith; I too have faith.

mn100:10.6.verse: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has energy …

mn100:10.10.verse: Suppose I exercise control in order to realize the Dhamma that he declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:10.11.verse: I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:10.12.verse: Then I went to Āḷāra Kālāma, and I said to him:

mn100:10.13.verse: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:10.14.verse: ‘It is in this way, friend, that I declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.’

mn100:10.15.verse: ‘Friend, I too in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.’

mn100:10.16.verse: ‘It is gain for us, friend, it is great gain for us,

mn100:10.17.verse: that we have such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.

mn100:10.18.verse: So the Dhamma that I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:10.19.verse: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:10.20.verse: So you know the Dhamma that I know; I know the Dhamma that you know.

mn100:10.21.verse: As I am, so you are; as you are, so am I.

mn100:10.22.verse: Come, friend, let us now lead this community together.’

mn100:10.23.verse: Thus Āḷāra Kālāma, my Teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself, and awarded me the highest honour.

mn100:10.25.verse: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only to the base consisting of nothingness.’

mn100:10.26.verse: I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.

mn100:11.1.verse: Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:

mn100:11.2.verse: ‘Friend, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.’

mn100:11.3.verse: When this was said, Uddaka Rāmaputta replied:

mn100:11.5.verse: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’

mn100:11.7.verse: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teaching went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others who did likewise.

mn100:11.9.verse: ‘It is not through mere faith alone that Rāma declares his Dhamma, but (he does so) because he enters upon and abides in it, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:11.10.verse: Certainly Rāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.’

mn100:11.11.verse: Then I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:

mn100:11.12.verse: ‘Friend Rāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:11.13.verse: When this was said, he declared the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn100:11.15.verse: ‘Not only Rāma has faith; I too have faith.

mn100:11.20.verse: Suppose I exercise control in order to realize the Dhamma that he declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:11.21.verse: I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:12.1.verse: Then I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and I said to him:

mn100:12.2.verse: ‘Friend, is it in this way that Rāma declared to have entered upon this Dhamma, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?’

mn100:12.3.verse: ‘It is in this way, friend, that Rāma declared to have entered upon this Dhamma, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.’

mn100:12.4.verse: ‘Friend, I too in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.’

mn100:12.5.verse: ‘It is gain for us, friend, it is great gain for us,

mn100:12.6.verse: that we have such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.

mn100:12.7.verse: So the Dhamma that Rāma declared to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:12.8.verse: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma Rāma declared to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.

mn100:12.9.verse: So you know the Dhamma that Rāma knew directly; Rāma knew directly the Dhamma that you know.

mn100:12.10.verse: As Rāma was, so you are; as you are, so Rāma was.

mn100:12.11.verse: Come, friend, now lead this community.’

mn100:12.12.verse: Thus Uddaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the life divine, placed me in the Teacher’s place, and awarded me the highest honour.

mn100:12.14.verse: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’

mn100:12.15.verse: I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.

mn100:13.1.verse: Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country, till at length I arrived at Senānigama near Uruvelā.

mn100:13.2.verse: There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove, a clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.

mn100:13.4.verse: ‘There is this agreeable piece of ground, this delightful grove, this clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village for alms resort.

mn100:13.5.verse: This will serve for the endeavour of a clansman who seeks endeavour.’

mn100:14.1.verse: Now these three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:14.2.verse: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water,

mn100:14.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn100:14.4.verse: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;

mn100:14.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,

mn100:14.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water?”

mn100:14.9.verse: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, and besides, it is lying in water.

mn100:14.10.verse: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.”

mn100:14.11.verse: “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live still bodily and mentally not withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are not thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment; and even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.

mn100:14.12.verse: This was the first simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:15.1.verse: Again, a second simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:15.2.verse: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,

mn100:15.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn100:15.4.verse: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;

mn100:15.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,

mn100:15.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?”

mn100:15.9.verse: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, though it is lying on dry land far from water.

mn100:15.10.verse: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.” “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live only bodily withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are not thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment. And even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.

mn100:15.11.verse: This was the second simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:16.1.verse: Again, a third simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:16.2.verse: Suppose there were a dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,

mn100:16.3.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn100:16.4.verse: ‘I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat’;

mn100:16.5.verse: how do you conceive this, Bhāradvāja,

mn100:16.6.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?”

mn100:16.9.verse: Because it is a dry, sapless piece of wood, and besides, it is lying on dry land far from water!”

mn100:16.10.verse: “So too, Bhāradvāja, while any ascetics or brahmins live both bodily and mentally withdrawn from sensual desires, and while their lust, affection, passion, thirst, and fever for sensual desires are thoroughly abandoned and quieted within them, then even if those good ascetics and brahmins feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment, and even if those good ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.

mn100:16.11.verse: This was the third simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:16.12.verse: These, Bhāradvāja, were the three similes that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

mn100:17.2.verse: ‘Suppose, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrain, and crush mind with mind?’

mn100:17.3.verse: So, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind.

mn100:17.4.verse: While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits.

mn100:17.5.verse: Just as a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain, and crush him,

mn100:17.6.verse: so too, while with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained, and crushed mind with mind, sweat ran from my armpits.

mn100:17.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:18.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation?’

mn100:18.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose.

mn100:18.4.verse: While I did so, there was a loud sound of winds escaping through my ear-holes.

mn100:18.5.verse: Just as there is a loud sound when a smith’s bellows are blown,

mn100:18.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose, there was a loud sound of winds escaping through my ear-holes.

mn100:18.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:19.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’

mn100:19.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.

mn100:19.4.verse: While I did so, violent winds struck against my head.

mn100:19.5.verse: Just as if a strong man were splitting my head open with a sharp point,

mn100:19.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds struck against my head.

mn100:19.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:20.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’

mn100:20.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.

mn100:20.4.verse: While I did so, there were violent pains in my head.

mn100:20.5.verse: Just as if a strong man were tightening a tough leather strap round my head as a headband,

mn100:20.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, there were violent pains in my head.

mn100:20.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:21.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’

mn100:21.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.

mn100:21.4.verse: While I did so, violent winds carved through my belly.

mn100:21.5.verse: Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice might carve through the belly of an ox with a sharp butcher’s knife,

mn100:21.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds carved through my belly.

mn100:21.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:22.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise the breathless meditation further?’

mn100:22.3.verse: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears.

mn100:22.4.verse: While I did so, there was a violent burning in my body.

mn100:22.5.verse: Just as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him, thoroughly roast him, over a pit of burning coals,

mn100:22.6.verse: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, there was a violent burning in my body.

mn100:22.7.verse: But energy was aroused in me, unremitting, and mindfulness was established, unconfused; yet my body was overwrought and not calm, because I was exhausted by that painful striving.

mn100:23.1.verse: Then, Bhāradvāja, some deities, seeing me, said:

mn100:23.4.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’

mn100:23.6.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither dead nor dying;

mn100:23.7.verse: the ascetic Gotama is an Arahant, for such is the way an Arahant abides.’

mn100:24.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to practise entirely cutting off food?’

mn100:24.3.verse: Then deities came to me and said:

mn100:24.4.verse: ‘Good sir, do not practise entirely cutting off food.

mn100:24.5.verse: If you do so, good sir, we shall infuse heavenly essence into you through your pores,

mn100:24.6.verse: and you will live on that.’

mn100:24.8.verse: ‘If I were to claim to be completely fasting, and these deities were to infuse heavenly essence into me through my pores, and I were to live on that,

mn100:24.9.verse: that would be false speech on my part.’

mn100:24.10.verse: So I refused those deities, saying: ‘Enough.’

mn100:25.2.verse: ‘Suppose I were to take very little food, a handful at a time, whether bean soup, or lentil soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup?’

mn100:25.3.verse: So I took very little food, a handful at a time, whether bean soup, or lentil soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup.

mn100:25.4.verse: While I took very little food in this way, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.

mn100:25.5.verse: Just like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems, so my limbs became, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.6.verse: Just like a camel’s hoof, so my backside became, because of eating so little;

mn100:25.7.verse: just like a string of beads, so my spine, with its projections standing up and sinking down, became, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.8.verse: Just as the rafters of an old barn collapse and jut out, so my ribs, collapsing and jutting out, became, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.9.verse: Just as the sparkle of water sunk far down and deep in a deep well appears, so the sparkle of my eyes, sunk far down and deep in their sockets, appeared, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.10.verse: Just as a bitter gourd, cut green, shrivels and withers in the wind and sun, so my scalp, shrivelling and withering, became, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.11.verse: When I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I actually took hold of my spine as well; and when I thought, ‘I will touch my spine,’ I actually took hold of the skin of my belly as well; so much had the skin of my belly become stuck to my spine, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.12.verse: When I thought, ‘I will move my bowels or pass water,’ I fell down on my face right there, because of eating so little.

mn100:25.13.verse: When, trying to ease my body, I stroked my limbs with my hand, the hairs, rotted at their roots, fell away from my body, because of eating so little.

mn100:26.1.verse: Then, Bhāradvāja, some people, seeing me, said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’

mn100:26.2.verse: Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, the ascetic Gotama is brown.’

mn100:26.3.verse: Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown, the ascetic Gotama is golden-skinned’;

mn100:26.4.verse: so much had the clear, bright colour of my skin deteriorated, because of eating so little.

mn100:27.2.verse: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have felt painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this;

mn100:27.3.verse: whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this;

mn100:27.4.verse: and whatever ascetics or brahmins at present feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this.

mn100:27.5.verse: But by this severe austerity I have not attained any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.

mn100:27.6.verse: Might there be another path to enlightenment?’

mn100:28.2.verse: ‘I recall that, while my father the Sakyan was working, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn100:28.3.verse: Might this be the path to enlightenment?’

mn100:28.4.verse: Then, following on that memory, came the recognition:

mn100:29.2.verse: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, since it is a pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unwholesome states?’

mn100:29.4.verse: ‘I am not afraid of that pleasure, since it is a pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unwholesome states.’

mn100:30.2.verse: ‘It is not easy to attain that pleasure with a body so extremely emaciated.

mn100:30.3.verse: Suppose I were to eat some solid food, some boiled rice and porridge?’

mn100:30.4.verse: So I ate some solid food, some boiled rice and porridge.

mn100:30.5.verse: Now at that time, Bhāradvāja, five bhikkhus were attending on me, thinking:

mn100:30.6.verse: ‘Whatever truth the ascetic Gotama attains, he will tell us.’

mn100:30.7.verse: But when I ate the solid food, the boiled rice and porridge, the group of five bhikkhus were disgusted and left me, saying:

mn100:30.8.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become self-indulgent; he has given up striving and reverted to luxury.’

mn100:31-33.1.verse: Then, Bhāradvāja, having eaten solid food and regained strength, quite secluded from sensual desires … I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna.

mn100:31-33.2.verse: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, I entered upon and abided in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind, without initial application, without sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of concentration …

mn100:31-33.4.verse: I entered upon and abided in the fourth jhāna.

mn100:34.1.verse: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

mn100:34.2.verse: I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.

mn100:35.1.verse: This, Bhāradvāja, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;

mn100:35.2.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.

mn100:36-38.1.verse: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn100:36-38.2.verse: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I understood how beings pass on according to their actions …

mn100:36-38.3.verse: this, Bhāradvāja, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night;

mn100:36-38.4.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.

mn100:39.1.verse: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it, inclined it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn100:39.2.verse: I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;

mn100:39.3.verse: I directly knew as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’

mn100:40.1.verse: Knowing and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn100:40.2.verse: When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn100:40.3.verse: I directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn100:41.1.verse: This, Bhāradvāja, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night;

mn100:41.2.verse: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and self-controlled.”

mn100:42.1.verse: When this was said, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:

mn100:42.2.verse: “Master Gotama’s striving was the striving of one who does not falter, Master Gotama’s striving was the striving of a true man,[^2]

mn100:42.3.verse: as befits an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One.

mn100:42.4.verse: But, Master Gotama, are there gods?”[^3]

mn100:42.5.verse: “It is known to me, Bhāradvāja, on good grounds, that—

mn100:42.7.verse: “How is it, Master Gotama, that when asked ‘are there gods?’ you say: ‘It is known to me, Bhāradvāja, on good grounds, that there are gods’?

mn100:42.8.verse: Is that not, Master Gotama, in that case empty and false?”

mn100:42.9.verse: “Bhāradvāja, when asked ‘are there gods?’, whether one says ‘there are gods’, or whether one says ‘it is known to me on good grounds’,

mn100:42.10.verse: in either case a wise man should come to the definite conclusion here:

mn100:42.12.verse: “Then why did Master Gotama not answer me in that way from the start?”

mn100:42.13.verse: “It is widely accepted in the world, Bhāradvāja, that—

mn100:43.1.verse: When this was said, the student Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:

mn100:43.3.verse: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.

mn100:43.4.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.

mn100:43.5.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”

mn100:45.1.verse: The householder chapter, the bhikkhu chapter,

mn100:45.3.verse: the king chapter, and the brahmin chapter—

mn100:45.4.verse: these five are in the Majjhima collection.

mn100:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn100:2.1.verse: Now at that time a brahmin lady named Dhanañjānī was residing at Caṇḍalakappa. She was devoted to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha.

mn100:2.2.verse: Once, she tripped and expressed this heartfelt sentiment three times:

mn100:2.3.verse: “Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

mn100:2.4.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!

mn100:2.5.verse: Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!”

mn100:3.1.verse: Now at that time the student Saṅgārava was residing in Caṇḍalakappa. He was young, newly tonsured; he was sixteen years old. He had mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. He knew them word-by-word, and their grammar. He was well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man.

mn100:3.4.verse: “The brahmin lady Dhanañjānī is a disgrace! Though brahmins proficient in the three Vedas are found, she will praise that shaveling, that fake ascetic.”

mn100:3.5.verse: “But dearest boy, you don’t understand the Buddha’s ethics and wisdom.

mn100:3.6.verse: If you did, you’d never think of abusing or insulting him.”

mn100:3.7.verse: “Well then, ma’am, let me know when the Buddha arrives in Caṇḍalakappa.”

mn100:4.1.verse: And then the Buddha, traveling stage by stage in the Kosalan lands, arrived at Caṇḍalakappa,

mn100:4.2.verse: where he stayed in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.

mn100:5.1.verse: Dhanañjānī heard that he had arrived.

mn100:5.2.verse: So she went to Saṅgārava and told him, adding,

mn100:5.4.verse: “Please, dearest boy, go at your convenience.”

mn100:5.5.verse: “Yes, ma’am,” replied Saṅgārava. He went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

mn100:5.6.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn100:6.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who claim to have mastered the fundamentals of the spiritual life having attained perfection and consummation of insight in this life.

mn100:6.2.verse: Where do you stand regarding these?”

mn100:7.1.verse: “I say there is a disparity among those who claim to have mastered the fundamentals of the spiritual life having attained perfection and consummation of insight in this life.

mn100:7.2.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who are oral transmitters.

mn100:7.3.verse: Through oral transmission they claim to have mastered the fundamentals of the spiritual life.

mn100:7.4.verse: For example, the brahmins who are proficient in the three Vedas.

mn100:7.5.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who solely by mere faith claim to have mastered the fundamentals of the spiritual life.

mn100:7.6.verse: For example, those who rely on logic and inquiry.

mn100:7.7.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who, having directly known for themselves the principle regarding teachings not learned before from another, claim to have mastered the fundamentals of the spiritual life.

mn100:8.1.verse: And here’s a way to understand that I am one of them.

mn100:9.1.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

mn100:9.2.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn100:9.3.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn100:9.4.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn100:9.5.verse: Some time later, while still with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life—though my mother and father wished otherwise, weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn100:9.6.verse: Once I had gone forth I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn100:9.7.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn100:9.10.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn100:9.12.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn100:9.14.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn100:9.15.verse: Surely he meditates knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn100:10.1.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:

mn100:10.2.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, to what extent do you say you’ve realized this teaching with your own insight?’

mn100:10.3.verse: When I said this, he declared the dimension of nothingness.

mn100:10.5.verse: ‘It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith,

mn100:10.9.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn100:10.10.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma says he has realized with his own insight?’

mn100:10.11.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn100:10.12.verse: So I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him,

mn100:10.13.verse: ‘Reverend Kālāma, is it up to this point that you realized this teaching with your own insight, and declare having achieved it?’

mn100:10.15.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn100:10.16.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn100:10.17.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn100:10.18.verse: So the teaching that I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn100:10.19.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, I’ve realized with my own insight, and declare having achieved it.

mn100:10.20.verse: So the teaching that I know, you know, and the teaching you know, I know.

mn100:10.21.verse: I am like you and you are like me.

mn100:10.22.verse: Come now, reverend! We should both lead this community together.’

mn100:10.23.verse: And that is how my tutor Āḷāra Kālāma placed me, his pupil, on the same position as him, and honored me with high praise.

mn100:10.25.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of nothingness.’

mn100:10.26.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn100:11.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn100:11.2.verse: ‘Reverend, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training.’

mn100:11.5.verse: This teaching is such that a sensible person can soon realize their own denomination with their own insight and live having achieved it.’

mn100:11.7.verse: As far as lip-recital and verbal repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge, the elder doctrine. I claimed to know and see, and so did others.

mn100:11.9.verse: ‘It is not solely by mere faith that Rāma declared: “I realize this teaching with my own insight, and live having achieved it.”

mn100:11.10.verse: Surely he meditated knowing and seeing this teaching.’

mn100:11.11.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn100:11.12.verse: ‘Reverend, to what extent did Rāma say he’d realized this teaching with his own insight?’

mn100:11.13.verse: When I said this, Uddaka son of Rāma declared the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn100:11.15.verse: ‘It’s not just Rāma who had faith,

mn100:11.19.verse: and wisdom; I too have these things.

mn100:11.20.verse: Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Rāma said he had realized with his own insight?’

mn100:11.21.verse: I quickly realized that teaching with my own insight, and lived having achieved it.

mn100:12.1.verse: So I approached Uddaka son of Rāma and said to him,

mn100:12.2.verse: ‘Reverend, had Rāma realized this teaching with his own insight up to this point, and declared having achieved it?’

mn100:12.4.verse: ‘I too have realized this teaching with my own insight up to this point, and live having achieved it.’

mn100:12.5.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn100:12.6.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!

mn100:12.7.verse: So the teaching that Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it, you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it.

mn100:12.8.verse: The teaching that you’ve realized with your own insight, and dwell having achieved it, Rāma had realized with his own insight, and declared having achieved it.

mn100:12.9.verse: So the teaching that Rāma directly knew, you know, and the teaching you know, Rāma directly knew.

mn100:12.10.verse: Rāma was like you and you are like Rāma.

mn100:12.11.verse: Come now, reverend! You should lead this community.’

mn100:12.12.verse: And that is how my spiritual companion Uddaka son of Rāma placed me in the position of a tutor and honored me with high praise.

mn100:12.14.verse: ‘This teaching doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. It only leads as far as rebirth in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn100:12.15.verse: Realizing that this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed.

mn100:13.1.verse: I set out to discover what is skillful, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace. Traveling stage by stage in the Magadhan lands, I arrived at the town of Senā in Uruvelā.

mn100:13.2.verse: There I saw a delightful park, a lovely grove with a flowing river that was clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby was a village to resort to for alms.

mn100:13.4.verse: ‘This park is truly delightful, a lovely grove with a flowing river that’s clean and charming, with smooth banks. And nearby there’s a village to resort to for alms.

mn100:13.5.verse: This is good enough for striving for a gentleman wanting to strive.’

mn100:13.6.verse: So I sat down right there, thinking:

mn100:14.1.verse: And then these three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, occurred to me.

mn100:14.2.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying in water.

mn100:14.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn100:14.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn100:14.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log lying in water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn100:14.9.verse: Because it’s a green, sappy log, and it’s lying in the water.

mn100:14.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

mn100:14.11.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. They haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn100:14.12.verse: This was the first example that occurred to me.

mn100:15.1.verse: Then a second example occurred to me.

mn100:15.2.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn100:15.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn100:15.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn100:15.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn100:15.9.verse: Because it’s still a green, sappy log, despite the fact that it’s lying on dry land far from water.

mn100:15.10.verse: That person will eventually get weary and frustrated.” “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. But they haven’t internally given up or stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are incapable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn100:15.11.verse: This was the second example that occurred to me.

mn100:16.1.verse: Then a third example occurred to me.

mn100:16.2.verse: Suppose there was a dried up, withered log, and it was lying on dry land far from the water.

mn100:16.3.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn100:16.4.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn100:16.6.verse: By drilling the stick against that dried up, withered log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn100:16.9.verse: Because it’s a dried up, withered log, and it’s lying on dry land far from water.”

mn100:16.10.verse: “In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who live withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures. And they have internally given up and stilled desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and passion for sensual pleasures. Regardless of whether or not they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion, they are capable of knowledge and vision, of supreme awakening.

mn100:16.11.verse: This was the third example that occurred to me.

mn100:16.12.verse: These are the three similes, which were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past, that occurred to me.

mn100:17.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, squeeze, squash, and scorch mind with mind?’

mn100:17.4.verse: until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn100:17.5.verse: It was like when a strong man grabs a weaker man by the head or throat or shoulder and squeezes, squashes, and crushes them.

mn100:17.6.verse: In the same way, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I squeezed, squashed, and crushed mind with mind until sweat ran from my armpits.

mn100:17.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:18.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice the breathless absorption?’

mn100:18.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose.

mn100:18.4.verse: But then winds came out my ears making a severe noise,

mn100:18.5.verse: like the puffing of a blacksmith’s bellows.

mn100:18.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:19.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn100:19.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn100:19.4.verse: But then severe winds ground my head,

mn100:19.5.verse: like a strong man was drilling into my head with a sharp point.

mn100:19.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:20.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn100:20.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn100:20.4.verse: But then I got a severe headache,

mn100:20.5.verse: like a strong man was tightening a strong leather strap around my head.

mn100:20.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:21.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn100:21.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn100:21.4.verse: But then severe winds carved up my belly,

mn100:21.5.verse: like a deft butcher or their apprentice was slicing my belly open with a sharp meat cleaver.

mn100:21.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:22.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I keep practicing the breathless absorption?’

mn100:22.3.verse: So I cut off my breathing through my mouth and nose and ears.

mn100:22.4.verse: But then there was a severe burning in my body,

mn100:22.5.verse: like two strong men grabbing a weaker man by the arms to burn and scorch him on a pit of glowing coals.

mn100:22.7.verse: My energy was roused up and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and lucid, but my body was disturbed, not tranquil, because I’d pushed too hard with that painful striving.

mn100:23.1.verse: Then some deities saw me and said,

mn100:23.6.verse: ‘He’s not dead or dying. The ascetic Gotama is a perfected one, for that is how the perfected ones live.’

mn100:24.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I practice completely cutting off food?’

mn100:24.3.verse: But deities came to me and said,

mn100:24.4.verse: ‘Good fellow, don’t practice totally cutting off food.

mn100:24.5.verse: If you do, we’ll infuse heavenly nectar into your pores and you will live on that.’

mn100:24.8.verse: ‘If I claim to be completely fasting while these deities are infusing heavenly nectar in my pores, that would be a lie on my part.’

mn100:24.10.verse: So I refused those deities, saying, ‘There’s no need.’

mn100:25.2.verse: ‘Why don’t I just take a little bit of food each time, a handful of broth made from mung beans, horse gram, chickpeas, or green gram?’

mn100:25.4.verse: until my body became severely emaciated.

mn100:25.5.verse: Due to eating so little, my major and minor limbs became like the joints of an eighty-year-old or a dying man,

mn100:25.6.verse: my bottom became like a camel’s hoof,

mn100:25.7.verse: my vertebrae stuck out like beads on a string,

mn100:25.8.verse: and my ribs were as gaunt as the broken-down rafters on an old barn.

mn100:25.9.verse: Due to eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets, like the gleam of water sunk deep down a well.

mn100:25.10.verse: Due to eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter-gourd in the wind and sun.

mn100:25.11.verse: Due to eating so little, the skin of my belly stuck to my backbone, so that when I tried to rub the skin of my belly I grabbed my backbone, and when I tried to rub my backbone I rubbed the skin of my belly.

mn100:25.12.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to urinate or defecate I fell face down right there.

mn100:25.13.verse: Due to eating so little, when I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell out.

mn100:26.1.verse: Then some people saw me and said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’

mn100:26.2.verse: Some said: ‘He’s not black, he’s brown.’

mn100:26.3.verse: Some said: ‘He’s neither black nor brown. The ascetic Gotama has dingy skin.’

mn100:26.4.verse: That’s how far the pure, bright complexion of my skin had been ruined by taking so little food.

mn100:27.2.verse: ‘Whatever ascetics and brahmins have experienced painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion—whether in the past, future, or present—this is as far as it goes, no-one has done more than this.

mn100:27.5.verse: But I have not achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones by this severe, grueling work.

mn100:27.6.verse: Could there be another path to awakening?’

mn100:28.2.verse: ‘I recall sitting in the cool shade of a black plum tree while my father the Sakyan was off working. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn100:28.3.verse: Could that be the path to awakening?’

mn100:28.4.verse: Stemming from that memory came the understanding:

mn100:29.2.verse: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities?’

mn100:29.4.verse: ‘I’m not afraid of that pleasure, for it has nothing to do with sensual pleasures or unskillful qualities.’

mn100:30.2.verse: ‘I can’t achieve that pleasure with a body so severely emaciated. Why don’t I eat some solid food, some rice and porridge?’

mn100:30.4.verse: So I ate some solid food.

mn100:30.5.verse: Now at that time the group of five mendicants were attending on me, thinking,

mn100:30.6.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama will tell us of any truth that he realizes.’

mn100:30.7.verse: But when I ate some solid food, they left disappointed in me, saying,

mn100:30.8.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama has become indulgent; he has strayed from the struggle and returned to indulgence.’

mn100:31-33.1.verse: After eating solid food and gathering my strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption …

mn100:31-33.2.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption …

mn100:34.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward recollection of past lives.

mn100:34.2.verse: I recollected many past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. And so I recollected my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn100:35.1.verse: This was the first knowledge, which I achieved in the first watch of the night.

mn100:35.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn100:36-38.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn100:36-38.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I saw sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn100:36-38.3.verse: This was the second knowledge, which I achieved in the middle watch of the night.

mn100:36-38.4.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

mn100:39.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn100:39.2.verse: I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn100:39.3.verse: I truly understood: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.’

mn100:40.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn100:40.2.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

mn100:40.3.verse: I understood: ‘Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.’

mn100:41.1.verse: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night.

mn100:41.2.verse: Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.”

mn100:42.1.verse: When he had spoken, Saṅgārava said to the Buddha,

mn100:42.2.verse: “The striving of the worthy Gotama was indeed assiduous and that of a true person,

mn100:42.3.verse: since he is a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn100:42.4.verse: But worthy Gotama, do gods survive?”

mn100:42.5.verse: “I’ve understood about gods in terms of causes.”

mn100:42.7.verse: “But worthy Gotama, when asked ‘Do gods survive?’ why did you say that you have understood about gods in terms of causes?

mn100:42.8.verse: That being so, is it not hollow and false?”

mn100:42.9.verse: “When asked ‘Do gods survive’, whether you reply ‘Gods survive’ or ‘I’ve understood in terms of causes’

mn100:42.10.verse: a sensible person would come to the categorical conclusion in this matter that

mn100:42.12.verse: “But why didn’t you say that in the first place?”

mn100:42.13.verse: “It is agreed by the eminent in the world that gods survive.”

mn100:43.1.verse: When he had spoken, Saṅgārava said to the Buddha,

mn100:43.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the Teaching clear in many ways.

mn100:43.4.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn100:43.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn101:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans, at a town of the Sakyans called Devadaha.

mn101:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

mn101:2.2.verse: “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

mn101:2.4.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and this view:

mn101:2.5.verse: ‘Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.[^1]

mn101:2.6.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:2.7.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.’

mn101:2.8.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn101:3.1.verse: Having this doctrine, bhikkhus, I went to the Nigaṇṭhas and said:

mn101:3.2.verse: ‘Is it true, friend Nigaṇṭhas, as they say, that you have this doctrine and this view—

mn101:3.3.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:3.4.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:3.5.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away”?’

mn101:3.6.verse: And those Nigaṇṭhas, bhikkhus, being asked thus, admitted it, saying: ‘Yes.’

mn101:4.3.verse: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”?’[^2]

mn101:4.6.verse: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”?’

mn101:4.12.verse: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”?’

mn101:4.15.verse: “the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now”?’

mn101:5.1.verse: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems you do not know—

mn101:5.2.verse: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; you do not know—

mn101:5.3.verse: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; you do not know—

mn101:5.4.verse: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; you do not know—

mn101:5.5.verse: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; you do not know—

mn101:5.6.verse: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;
