mn101:5.7.verse: that being so, it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:5.8.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:5.9.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:5.10.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:6.2.verse: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; if you knew—

mn101:6.3.verse: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; if you knew—

mn101:6.4.verse: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; if you knew—

mn101:6.5.verse: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; if you knew—

mn101:6.6.verse: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;

mn101:6.7.verse: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:6.8.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:6.9.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:6.10.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:7.1.verse: ‘Suppose, friend Nigaṇṭhas, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison;

mn101:7.2.verse: because of the arrow’s piercing, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.3.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring a surgeon to treat him.

mn101:7.4.verse: The surgeon would cut round the opening of the wound with a knife;

mn101:7.5.verse: because of the knife’s cutting round the opening of the wound, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.6.verse: The surgeon would probe for the arrow with a probe;

mn101:7.7.verse: because of the probe’s probing for the arrow, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.8.verse: The surgeon would pull out the arrow;

mn101:7.9.verse: because of the pulling out of the arrow, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.10.verse: The surgeon would apply a caustic medicine to the opening of the wound;

mn101:7.11.verse: because of the caustic medicine applied to the opening of the wound, he would feel painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.12.verse: On a later occasion, with the wound healed and covered with skin, he would be well, happy, independent, his own master, able to go where he likes.

mn101:7.14.verse: “Formerly I was wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn101:7.15.verse: Because of the arrow’s piercing, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.16.verse: My friends and companions, my relatives and kin, brought a surgeon to treat me.

mn101:7.17.verse: The surgeon cut round the opening of the wound with a knife;

mn101:7.18.verse: because of the knife’s cutting round the opening of the wound, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.19.verse: The surgeon probed for the arrow with a probe;

mn101:7.20.verse: because of the probe’s probing for the arrow, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.21.verse: The surgeon pulled out the arrow;[^4]

mn101:7.22.verse: because of the pulling out of the arrow, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.23.verse: The surgeon applied a caustic medicine to the opening of the wound;

mn101:7.24.verse: because of the caustic medicine applied to the opening of the wound, I felt painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:7.25.verse: Now, with the wound healed and covered with skin, I am well, happy, independent, my own master, able to go where I like.”’

mn101:8.1.verse: ‘So too, friend Nigaṇṭhas, if you knew—

mn101:8.2.verse: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; if you knew—

mn101:8.3.verse: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; if you knew—

mn101:8.4.verse: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; if you knew—

mn101:8.5.verse: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; if you knew—

mn101:8.6.verse: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;

mn101:8.7.verse: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:8.8.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:8.9.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:8.10.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:9.1.verse: ‘But since, friend Nigaṇṭhas, you do not know—

mn101:9.2.verse: “we existed in the past, we did not not exist”; you do not know—

mn101:9.3.verse: “we did evil deeds in the past, we did not not do them”; you do not know—

mn101:9.4.verse: “we did such-and-such an evil deed”; you do not know—

mn101:9.5.verse: “so much suffering has been worn away, or so much suffering has yet to be worn away, or when so much suffering has been worn away, all suffering will have been worn away”; you do not know—

mn101:9.6.verse: the abandoning of unwholesome things and the achievement of wholesome things here and now;

mn101:9.7.verse: therefore it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:9.8.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:9.9.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:9.10.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:10.1.verse: When this was said, bhikkhus, those Nigaṇṭhas said to me:

mn101:10.2.verse: ‘Friend, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is omniscient and all-seeing, and claims to have complete knowledge and vision thus:

mn101:10.3.verse: “whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.”

mn101:10.5.verse: “Nigaṇṭhas, you have done evil deeds in the past; wear them away by this severe austerity;[^5]

mn101:10.6.verse: and as to being restrained here and now in body, speech, and mind, that is the non-doing of evil deeds for the future.

mn101:10.7.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:10.8.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”

mn101:10.9.verse: And this is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.’

mn101:11.1.verse: When this was said, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:

mn101:11.2.verse: ‘There are, friend Nigaṇṭhas, these five things which have a twofold result in this very life.

mn101:11.4.verse: Faith, liking, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and acceptance of a view after pondering it[^6]—

mn101:11.5.verse: these, friend Nigaṇṭhas, are the five things which have a twofold result in this very life.

mn101:11.6.verse: Now, as regards your teacher’s teaching about the past, what is the venerable Nigaṇṭhas’ faith, what is their liking, what is their oral tradition, what is their reasoned reflection, what is their acceptance of a view after pondering it?’

mn101:11.7.verse: Speaking thus, bhikkhus, I do not see any legitimate rebuttal from the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn101:12.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:

mn101:12.3.verse: On the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, do you on that occasion feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:12.4.verse: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, do you on that occasion not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion?’

mn101:12.5.verse: ‘On the occasion, friend Gotama, when there is intense exertion, intense striving, we feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:12.6.verse: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, we do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion.’

mn101:13.1.verse: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems that on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;[^7]

mn101:13.2.verse: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion.

mn101:13.3.verse: That being so, it is not fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:13.4.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:13.5.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:13.6.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:14.1.verse: ‘If, friend Nigaṇṭhas, on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you were not to feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:14.2.verse: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you were to feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:14.3.verse: that being so, it would be fitting for the venerable Nigaṇṭhas to declare:

mn101:14.4.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:14.5.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:14.6.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:15.1.verse: ‘But since, friend Nigaṇṭhas, on the occasion when there is intense exertion, intense striving, you feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:15.2.verse: and on the occasion when there is no intense exertion, no intense striving, you do not feel painful, sharp, severe feelings caused by that exertion;

mn101:15.3.verse: you yourselves, feeling painful, sharp, severe feelings due to that self-imposed exertion, mistakenly believe, through ignorance, unknowing, and delusion:

mn101:15.4.verse: “whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure, or pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.

mn101:15.5.verse: So, by annihilating past deeds through austerity, and by doing no new deeds, there is no consequence for the future;

mn101:15.6.verse: with no consequence for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be worn away.”’

mn101:15.7.verse: Speaking thus too, bhikkhus, I do not see any legitimate rebuttal from the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn101:16.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas:

mn101:16.2.verse: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced here and now could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced in a future life?’

mn101:16.4.verse: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced in a future life could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced here and now?’

mn101:17.1.verse: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced as pleasure could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pain?’

mn101:17.3.verse: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced as pain could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pleasure?’

mn101:18.1.verse: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced when mature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when immature?’[^8]

mn101:18.3.verse: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced when immature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when mature?’

mn101:19.1.verse: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced much could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced little?’

mn101:19.3.verse: ‘But is it possible that a deed to be experienced little could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced much?’

mn101:20.1.verse: ‘What do you think, friend Nigaṇṭhas: is it possible that a deed to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed not to be experienced?’

mn101:20.3.verse: ‘But is it possible that a deed not to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced?’

mn101:21.1.verse: ‘So then, friend Nigaṇṭhas, it seems it is not possible that a deed to be experienced here and now could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced in a future life; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced in a future life could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced here and now; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced as pleasure could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pain; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced as pain could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced as pleasure; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced when mature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when immature; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced when immature could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced when mature; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced much could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced little; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced little could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced much; it is not possible that a deed to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed not to be experienced; it is not possible that a deed not to be experienced could, by exertion or striving, become a deed to be experienced;

mn101:21.2.verse: that being so, the venerable Nigaṇṭhas’ exertion is fruitless, their striving is fruitless.’

mn101:22.1.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn101:22.2.verse: For the Nigaṇṭhas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, there are ten legitimate deductions that give ground for censure.

mn101:22.3.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past,

mn101:22.4.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas were doers of evil deeds in the past, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:22.5.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god,

mn101:22.6.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas were created by an evil supreme god, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:22.7.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance,[^9]

mn101:22.8.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have bad circumstances, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:22.9.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin,[^10]

mn101:22.10.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have a bad class of origin, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:22.11.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion,

mn101:22.12.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas have made bad present exertion, since they now feel such painful, sharp, severe feelings.

mn101:22.13.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;

mn101:22.14.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.

mn101:22.15.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;

mn101:22.16.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.

mn101:22.17.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;

mn101:22.18.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.

mn101:22.19.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;

mn101:22.20.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.

mn101:22.21.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed;

mn101:22.22.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Nigaṇṭhas are to be blamed.

mn101:22.23.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.

mn101:22.24.verse: For the Nigaṇṭhas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, these ten legitimate deductions give ground for censure.

mn101:22.25.verse: So, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitless in this way, striving is fruitless in this way.

mn101:23.1.verse: And how, bhikkhus, is exertion fruitful, how is striving fruitful?

mn101:23.2.verse: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is not yet free from suffering does not add further suffering to himself,[^11] nor does he give up pleasure that accords with the Dhamma, yet he is not infatuated with that pleasure.

mn101:23.4.verse: ‘When I strive with active effort against this source of suffering, then, through that active effort, there comes to be fading away of this source; but when I look on with equanimity at this source of suffering, then, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away of this source.’

mn101:23.5.verse: So he strives with active effort against that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away;

mn101:23.6.verse: and he develops equanimity in regard to that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away.

mn101:23.7.verse: For that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away, by striving with active effort—

mn101:23.8.verse: in that way that suffering is worn away in him.

mn101:23.9.verse: And for that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away, by developing equanimity—

mn101:23.10.verse: in that way too that suffering is worn away in him.

mn101:24.1.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were enamoured of a woman, with his mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing.

mn101:24.2.verse: He might see that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together.

mn101:24.4.verse: would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together?”

mn101:24.7.verse: “Because, venerable sir, that man is enamoured of that woman, with his mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing;

mn101:24.8.verse: that is why, on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in him.”

mn101:25.1.verse: “Then, bhikkhus, it might occur to that man:

mn101:25.2.verse: ‘I am enamoured of that woman, with my mind bound to her, with intense desire, intense longing.

mn101:25.3.verse: On seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in me.

mn101:25.4.verse: Suppose I were to abandon the desire and lust I have for that woman?’

mn101:25.5.verse: So he abandons the desire and lust he has for that woman.

mn101:25.6.verse: Then, on a later occasion, he might see that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together.

mn101:25.8.verse: would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in that man on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together?”

mn101:25.11.verse: “Because, venerable sir, that man is without lust for that woman.

mn101:25.12.verse: That is why, on seeing that woman standing with another man, chatting, laughing, and joking together, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise in him.”

mn101:26.1.verse: “So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is not yet free from suffering does not add further suffering to himself, nor does he give up pleasure that accords with the Dhamma, yet he is not infatuated with that pleasure.

mn101:26.3.verse: ‘When I strive with active effort against this source of suffering, then, through that active effort, there comes to be fading away of this source; but when I look on with equanimity at this source of suffering, then, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away of this source.’

mn101:26.4.verse: So he strives with active effort against that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away;

mn101:26.5.verse: and he develops equanimity in regard to that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away.

mn101:26.6.verse: For that source of suffering for which, through active effort, there comes to be fading away, by striving with active effort—

mn101:26.7.verse: in that way that suffering is worn away in him.

mn101:26.8.verse: And for that source of suffering for which, while developing equanimity, there comes to be fading away, by developing equanimity—

mn101:26.9.verse: in that way too that suffering is worn away in him.

mn101:26.10.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:27.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu considers thus:

mn101:27.2.verse: ‘When I dwell at ease, unwholesome things increase in me and wholesome things decline;

mn101:27.3.verse: but when I apply myself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in me and wholesome things increase.

mn101:27.4.verse: Suppose I were to apply myself to painful striving?’[^12]

mn101:27.5.verse: So he applies himself to painful striving.

mn101:27.6.verse: When he applies himself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in him and wholesome things increase.

mn101:27.7.verse: On a later occasion he does not apply himself to painful striving again.

mn101:27.9.verse: Because, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had a purpose for which he applied himself to painful striving, and that purpose has been achieved.

mn101:27.10.verse: That is why, on a later occasion, he does not apply himself to painful striving again.

mn101:28.1.verse: Suppose, bhikkhus, a fletcher were to heat and warm an arrow-shaft between two flames, making it straight and workable.

mn101:29.1.verse: When, bhikkhus, the fletcher’s arrow-shaft has been heated and warmed between two flames, and made straight and workable, that fletcher does not again heat and warm the arrow-shaft between two flames and make it straight and workable on a later occasion.

mn101:29.3.verse: Because, bhikkhus, he had a purpose for which he heated and warmed the arrow-shaft between two flames and made it straight and workable, and that purpose has been achieved.

mn101:29.4.verse: That is why he does not again heat and warm the arrow-shaft between two flames and make it straight and workable on a later occasion.

mn101:29.5.verse: So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu considers thus:

mn101:29.6.verse: ‘When I dwell at ease, unwholesome things increase in me and wholesome things decline;

mn101:29.7.verse: but when I apply myself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in me and wholesome things increase.

mn101:29.8.verse: Suppose I were to apply myself to painful striving?’

mn101:29.9.verse: So he applies himself to painful striving.

mn101:29.10.verse: When he applies himself to painful striving, unwholesome things decline in him and wholesome things increase.

mn101:29.11.verse: On a later occasion he does not apply himself to painful striving again.

mn101:29.13.verse: Because, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had a purpose for which he applied himself to painful striving, and that purpose has been achieved.

mn101:29.14.verse: That is why, on a later occasion, he does not apply himself to painful striving again.

mn101:29.15.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:30.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.

mn101:30.2.verse: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its rulers and its people, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn101:30.3.verse: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn101:31.1.verse: A householder or a householder’s child, or one reborn into some other family, hears that Dhamma.

mn101:31.2.verse: Having heard the Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.

mn101:31.3.verse: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:

mn101:31.4.verse: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn101:31.5.verse: It is not easy, while living in a house, to lead the life divine utterly perfect and utterly pure as a polished shell.

mn101:31.6.verse: Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’

mn101:31.7.verse: On a later occasion, abandoning a small or a large fortune, abandoning a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the yellow robe, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn101:32.1.verse: Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.

mn101:32.2.verse: Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given, taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.

mn101:32.3.verse: Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart abstaining from vulgar lechery.

mn101:32.4.verse: Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trustworthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.

mn101:32.5.verse: Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.

mn101:32.6.verse: Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.

mn101:32.7.verse: Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.

mn101:32.8.verse: He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.

mn101:32.9.verse: He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.

mn101:32.10.verse: He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.

mn101:32.11.verse: He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.

mn101:32.12.verse: He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.

mn101:32.13.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.

mn101:32.14.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.

mn101:32.15.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.

mn101:32.16.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.

mn101:32.17.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondswomen and bondsmen.

mn101:32.18.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.

mn101:32.19.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.

mn101:32.20.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses and mares.

mn101:32.21.verse: He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.

mn101:32.22.verse: He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.

mn101:32.23.verse: He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.

mn101:32.24.verse: He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.

mn101:32.25.verse: He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.

mn101:32.26.verse: He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.

mn101:33.1.verse: He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn101:33.2.verse: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,

mn101:33.3.verse: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.

mn101:33.4.verse: Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.

mn101:34.1.verse: He becomes one who, on seeing a visible form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features

mn101:34.2.verse: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn101:34.3.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn101:34.4.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose …

mn101:34.5.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn101:34.6.verse: On touching a tangible with the body …

mn101:34.7.verse: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind he apprehends no signs and features

mn101:34.8.verse: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.

mn101:34.9.verse: Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is unsullied.

mn101:35.1.verse: He becomes one who acts in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, robes and bowl, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, waking up, talking and keeping silent.

mn101:36.1.verse: Possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this noble contentment, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,

mn101:36.2.verse: he resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn101:36.3.verse: On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.

mn101:37.1.verse: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies mind from covetousness.

mn101:37.2.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.

mn101:37.3.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.

mn101:37.4.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself, he purifies mind from agitation and worry.

mn101:37.5.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas, he purifies mind from uncertainty.

mn101:38.1.verse: Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn101:38.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn101:38.3.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:39.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind, without initial application, without sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of concentration.

mn101:39.2.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:40.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, with the fading away of joy as well, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, and feels pleasure with the body; he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the noble ones announce: ‘He dwells happily who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn101:40.2.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:41.1.verse: Again, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn101:41.2.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:42.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

mn101:42.2.verse: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘there I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span; and passing away from there, I reappeared here’—thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars.

mn101:42.3.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:43.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn101:43.2.verse: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘these beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, wrong in view, undertaking action based on wrong view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, right in view, undertaking action based on right view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world’—thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.

mn101:43.3.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:44.1.verse: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.

mn101:44.2.verse: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;

mn101:44.3.verse: he understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’

mn101:45.1.verse: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn101:45.2.verse: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn101:45.3.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’

mn101:45.4.verse: In this way too, bhikkhus, exertion is fruitful, striving is fruitful.

mn101:46.1.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Tathāgatas.

mn101:46.2.verse: For the Tathāgatas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, there are ten legitimate grounds for praise.

mn101:46.3.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past,

mn101:46.4.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata was a doer of good deeds in the past, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.

mn101:46.5.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god,

mn101:46.6.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata was created by a good supreme god, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.

mn101:46.7.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance,

mn101:46.8.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has good circumstances, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.

mn101:46.9.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin,

mn101:46.10.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has a good class of origin, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.

mn101:46.11.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion,

mn101:46.12.verse: then surely, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has made good present exertion, since he now feels such taintless, pleasant feelings.

mn101:46.13.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Tathāgata is to be praised;

mn101:46.14.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of what was done in the past, the Tathāgata is to be praised.

mn101:46.15.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Tathāgata is to be praised;

mn101:46.16.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of creation by a supreme god, the Tathāgata is to be praised.

mn101:46.17.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Tathāgata is to be praised;

mn101:46.18.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance, the Tathāgata is to be praised.

mn101:46.19.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Tathāgata is to be praised;

mn101:46.20.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of class of origin, the Tathāgata is to be praised.

mn101:46.21.verse: If, bhikkhus, beings experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Tathāgata is to be praised;

mn101:46.22.verse: if beings do not experience pleasure and pain because of present exertion, the Tathāgata is to be praised.

mn101:46.23.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the doctrine of the Tathāgatas.

mn101:46.24.verse: For the Tathāgatas who hold this doctrine, bhikkhus, these ten legitimate grounds for praise apply.”

mn101:46.25.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn101:46.26.verse: Those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn101:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near the Sakyan town named Devadaha.

mn101:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn101:2.4.verse: “Mendicants, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn101:2.5.verse: ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of past deeds.

mn101:2.6.verse: So, due to eliminating past deeds by fervent mortification, and not doing any new deeds, there’s nothing to come up in the future.

mn101:2.7.verse: With no future consequence, deeds end. With the ending of deeds, suffering ends. With the ending of suffering, feeling ends. And with the ending of feeling, all suffering will have been worn away.’

mn101:2.8.verse: Such is the doctrine of the Jain ascetics.

mn101:3.1.verse: I’ve gone up to the Jain ascetics who say this and said,

mn101:3.2.verse: ‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’

mn101:4.3.verse: for sure that you existed in the past, and it is not the case that you did not exist?’

mn101:4.6.verse: for sure that you did bad deeds in the past?’

mn101:4.9.verse: that you did bad deeds of this type or that?’

mn101:4.12.verse: that so much suffering has already been worn away? Or that so much suffering still remains to be worn away? Or that when so much suffering is worn away all suffering will have been worn away?’

mn101:4.15.verse: about giving up unskillful qualities in this very life and embracing skillful qualities?’

mn101:5.1.verse: ‘So it seems that you don’t know any of these things.

mn101:5.7.verse: In that case, it’s not appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare this.

mn101:6.1.verse: Now, supposing you did know these things.

mn101:6.7.verse: In that case, it would be appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare this.

mn101:7.1.verse: Suppose a man was struck by an arrow thickly smeared with poison,

mn101:7.2.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.3.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn101:7.4.verse: The surgeon would cut open the wound with a scalpel,

mn101:7.5.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.7.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.9.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.10.verse: They’d apply cauterizing medicine to the wound,

mn101:7.11.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.12.verse: After some time that wound would be healed and the skin regrown. They’d be healthy, happy, autonomous, master of themselves, able to go where they wanted.

mn101:7.14.verse: “Earlier I was struck by an arrow thickly smeared with poison,

mn101:7.15.verse: causing painful feelings, sharp and severe.

mn101:7.16.verse: My friends and colleagues, relatives and kin got a surgeon to treat me.

mn101:7.17.verse: At each step, the treatment was painful.

mn101:7.25.verse: But these days that wound is healed and the skin regrown. I’m healthy, happy, autonomous, my own master, able to go where I want.”

mn101:8.1.verse: In the same way, reverends, if you knew about these things,

mn101:8.7.verse: it would be appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare this.

mn101:9.1.verse: But since you don’t know any of these things,

mn101:9.7.verse: it’s not appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare this.’

mn101:10.1.verse: When I said this, those Jain ascetics said to me,

mn101:10.2.verse: ‘Reverend, the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to know and see everything without exception, thus:

mn101:10.3.verse: “Knowledge and vision are constantly and continually present to me, while walking, standing, sleeping, and waking.”

mn101:10.5.verse: “O reverend Jain ascetics, you have done bad deeds in a past life. Wear them away with these severe and grueling austerities.

mn101:10.6.verse: And when in the present you are restrained in body, speech, and mind, you’re not doing any bad deeds for the future.

mn101:10.7.verse: So, due to eliminating past deeds by fervent mortification, and not doing any new deeds, there’s nothing to come up in the future.

mn101:10.8.verse: With no future consequence, deeds end. With the ending of deeds, suffering ends. With the ending of suffering, feeling ends. And with the ending of feeling, all suffering will have been worn away.”

mn101:10.9.verse: We endorse and accept this, and we are satisfied with it.’

mn101:11.1.verse: When they said this, I said to them,

mn101:11.2.verse: ‘These five things can be seen to turn out in two different ways in this very life.

mn101:11.4.verse: Faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, and acceptance of a view after deliberation.

mn101:11.5.verse: These are the five things that can be seen to turn out in two different ways in this very life.

mn101:11.6.verse: In this case, what faith in your teacher do you have when it comes to the past? What endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation?’

mn101:11.7.verse: When I said this, I did not see any legitimate defense of their doctrine from the Jains.

mn101:12.1.verse: Furthermore, I said to those Jain ascetics,

mn101:12.3.verse: At a time of intense exertion and striving do you suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion?

mn101:12.4.verse: Whereas at a time without intense exertion and striving do you not suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings due to exertion?’

mn101:12.5.verse: ‘Reverend Gotama, at a time of intense exertion we suffer painful, sharp feelings due to exertion,

mn101:13.1.verse: ‘So it seems that only at a time of intense exertion do you suffer painful, sharp feelings due to exertion,

mn101:13.3.verse: In that case, it’s not appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare:

mn101:13.4.verse: “Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of past deeds. …”

mn101:14.1.verse: If at a time of intense exertion you did not suffer painful, sharp feelings due to exertion,

mn101:14.2.verse: and if without intense exertion you did experience such feelings,

mn101:14.3.verse: it would be appropriate for the Jain venerables to declare this.

mn101:15.1.verse: But since this is not the case,

mn101:15.3.verse: aren’t you experiencing painful, sharp feelings due only to your own exertion, which out of ignorance, unknowing, and confusion you misconstrue to imply:

mn101:15.4.verse: “Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of past deeds. …”?’

mn101:15.7.verse: When I said this, I did not see any legitimate defense of their doctrine from the Jains.

mn101:16.1.verse: Furthermore, I said to those Jain ascetics,

mn101:16.2.verse: ‘What do you think, reverends? If a deed is to be experienced in this life, can exertion make it be experienced in lives to come?’

mn101:16.4.verse: ‘But if a deed is to be experienced in lives to come, can exertion make it be experienced in this life?’

mn101:17.1.verse: ‘What do you think, reverends? If a deed is to be experienced as pleasant, can exertion make it be experienced as painful?’

mn101:17.3.verse: ‘But if a deed is to be experienced as painful, can exertion make it be experienced as pleasant?’

mn101:18.1.verse: ‘What do you think, reverends? If a deed is to be experienced when ripe, can exertion make it be experienced when unripe?’

mn101:18.3.verse: ‘But if a deed is to be experienced when unripe, can exertion make it be experienced when ripe?’

mn101:19.1.verse: ‘What do you think, reverends? If a deed is to be experienced a lot, can exertion make it be experienced a little?’

mn101:19.3.verse: ‘But if a deed is to be experienced a little, can exertion make it be experienced a lot?’

mn101:20.1.verse: ‘What do you think, reverends? If a deed is to be experienced, can exertion make it not be experienced?’

mn101:20.3.verse: ‘But if a deed is not to be experienced, can exertion make it be experienced?’

mn101:21.1.verse: ‘So it seems that exertion cannot change the way deeds are experienced in any of these ways.

mn101:21.2.verse: This being so, your exertion and striving are fruitless.’

mn101:22.1.verse: Such is the doctrine of the Jain ascetics.

mn101:22.2.verse: Saying this, the Jain ascetics deserve rebuttal and criticism on ten legitimate grounds.

mn101:22.3.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of past deeds,

mn101:22.4.verse: clearly the Jains have done bad deeds in the past, since they now experience such intense pain.

mn101:22.5.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of God Almighty’s creation,

mn101:22.6.verse: clearly the Jains were created by a bad God, since they now experience such intense pain.

mn101:22.7.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance and nature,

mn101:22.8.verse: clearly the Jains arise from bad circumstances, since they now experience such intense pain.

mn101:22.9.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of the class of rebirth,

mn101:22.10.verse: clearly the Jains have been reborn in a bad class, since they now experience such intense pain.

mn101:22.11.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of exertion in this life,

mn101:22.12.verse: clearly the Jains exert themselves badly in this life, since they now experience such intense pain.

mn101:22.13.verse: The Jains deserve criticism whether or not sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of past deeds,

mn101:22.23.verse: Such is the doctrine of the Jain ascetics.

mn101:22.24.verse: The Jain ascetics who say this deserve rebuttal and criticism on these ten legitimate grounds.

mn101:22.25.verse: That’s how exertion and striving is fruitless.

mn101:23.1.verse: And how is exertion and striving fruitful?

mn101:23.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant does not bring suffering upon themselves; and they don’t forsake legitimate pleasure, but they’re not besotted with that pleasure.

mn101:23.4.verse: ‘When I actively strive I become dispassionate toward this source of suffering. But when I develop equanimity I become dispassionate toward this other source of suffering.’

mn101:23.5.verse: So they either actively strive or develop equanimity as appropriate.

mn101:23.7.verse: Through active striving they become dispassionate toward that specific source of suffering,

mn101:23.8.verse: and so that suffering is worn away.

mn101:23.9.verse: Through developing equanimity they become dispassionate toward that other source of suffering,

mn101:23.10.verse: and so that suffering is worn away.

mn101:24.1.verse: Suppose a man is in love with a woman, full of intense desire and lust.

mn101:24.2.verse: Then he sees her standing together with another man, chatting, giggling, and laughing.

mn101:24.4.verse: Would that give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress for him?”

mn101:24.7.verse: Because that man is in love with that woman, full of intense desire and lust.”

mn101:25.2.verse: ‘I’m in love with that woman, full of intense desire and lust.

mn101:25.3.verse: When I saw her standing together with another man, chatting, giggling, and laughing, it gave rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress for me.

mn101:25.4.verse: Why don’t I give up that desire and lust for that woman?’

mn101:25.6.verse: Some time later he sees her again standing together with another man, chatting, giggling, and laughing.

mn101:25.8.verse: Would that give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress for him?”

mn101:25.11.verse: Because he no longer desires that woman.”

mn101:26.1.verse: “In the same way, a mendicant does not bring suffering upon themselves; and they don’t forsake legitimate pleasure, but they’re not besotted with that pleasure.

mn101:26.3.verse: ‘When I actively strive I become dispassionate toward this source of suffering. But when I develop equanimity I become dispassionate toward this other source of suffering.’

mn101:26.4.verse: So they either actively strive or develop equanimity as appropriate.

mn101:26.6.verse: Through active striving they become dispassionate toward that specific source of suffering,

mn101:26.7.verse: and so that suffering is worn away.

mn101:26.8.verse: Through developing equanimity they become dispassionate toward that other source of suffering,

mn101:26.9.verse: and so that suffering is worn away.

mn101:26.10.verse: That’s how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:27.2.verse: ‘When I live as I please, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decline.

mn101:27.3.verse: But when I strive painfully, unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities grow.

mn101:27.6.verse: and as they do so unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities grow.

mn101:27.7.verse: After some time, they no longer strive painfully.

mn101:27.9.verse: Because they have accomplished the goal for which they strived painfully.

mn101:28.1.verse: Suppose a fletcher was heating an arrow shaft between two firebrands, making it straight and fit for use.

mn101:29.1.verse: After it’s been made straight and fit for use, they’d no longer heat it to make it straight and fit for use.

mn101:29.3.verse: Because they have accomplished the goal for which they heated it.

mn101:29.5.verse: In the same way, a mendicant reflects:

mn101:29.6.verse: ‘When I live as I please, unskillful qualities grow and skillful qualities decline.

mn101:29.7.verse: But when I strive painfully, unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities grow.

mn101:29.14.verse: After some time, they no longer strive painfully.

mn101:29.15.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:30.1.verse: Furthermore, a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn101:30.2.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn101:30.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

mn101:31.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

mn101:31.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One,

mn101:31.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn101:31.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn101:31.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn101:31.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn101:32.1.verse: Once they’ve gone forth, they take up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. They give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn101:32.2.verse: They give up stealing. They take only what’s given, and expect only what’s given. They keep themselves clean by not thieving.

mn101:32.3.verse: They give up unchastity. They are chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn101:32.4.verse: They give up lying. They speak the truth and stick to the truth. They’re honest and dependable, and don’t trick the world with their words.

mn101:32.5.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn101:32.6.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn101:32.7.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn101:32.8.verse: They refrain from injuring plants and seeds.

mn101:32.9.verse: They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

mn101:32.10.verse: They refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn101:32.11.verse: They refrain from attiring and adorning themselves with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn101:32.12.verse: They refrain from high and luxurious beds.

mn101:32.13.verse: They refrain from receiving gold and currency,

mn101:32.22.verse: They refrain from running errands and messages;

mn101:32.26.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn101:33.1.verse: They’re content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn101:33.2.verse: They’re like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn101:33.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they set out taking only these things.

mn101:33.4.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.

mn101:34.1.verse: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn101:34.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn101:34.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn101:34.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn101:34.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn101:34.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn101:34.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn101:34.8.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn101:34.9.verse: When they have this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied bliss inside themselves.

mn101:35.1.verse: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn101:36.1.verse: When they have this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn101:36.2.verse: they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn101:36.3.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn101:37.1.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn101:37.2.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn101:37.3.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn101:37.4.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn101:37.5.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn101:38.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn101:38.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn101:38.3.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:39.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn101:39.2.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:40.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn101:40.2.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:41.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn101:41.2.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:42.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn101:42.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn101:42.3.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:43.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn101:43.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understood how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn101:43.3.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:44.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn101:44.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

mn101:44.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn101:45.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn101:45.2.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn101:45.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn101:45.4.verse: That too is how exertion and striving is fruitful.

mn101:46.1.verse: Such is the doctrine of the Realized One.

mn101:46.2.verse: Saying this, the Realized One deserves praise on ten legitimate grounds.

mn101:46.3.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of past deeds,

mn101:46.4.verse: clearly the Realized One has done good deeds in the past, since he now experiences such undefiled pleasure.

mn101:46.5.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of God Almighty’s creation,

mn101:46.6.verse: clearly the Realized One was created by a good God, since he now experiences such undefiled pleasure.

mn101:46.7.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of circumstance and nature,

mn101:46.8.verse: clearly the Realized One arises from good circumstances, since he now experiences such undefiled pleasure.

mn101:46.9.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of the class of rebirth,

mn101:46.10.verse: clearly the Realized One was reborn in a good class, since he now experiences such undefiled pleasure.

mn101:46.11.verse: If sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of exertion in this life,

mn101:46.12.verse: clearly the Realized One exerts himself well in this life, since he now experiences such undefiled pleasure.

mn101:46.13.verse: The Realized One deserves praise whether or not sentient beings experience pleasure and pain because of past deeds,

mn101:46.23.verse: Such is the doctrine of the Realized One.

mn101:46.24.verse: Saying this, the Realized One deserves praise on these ten legitimate grounds.”

mn101:46.25.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn101:46.26.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn102:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn102:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

mn102:1.5.verse: “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

mn102:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the future, who hold views about the future, and who assert various propositions concerning the future.

mn102:2.2.verse: ‘The self is percipient and free from disease after death’—

mn102:2.4.verse: ‘the self is non-percipient and free from disease after death’—

mn102:2.6.verse: ‘the self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient and free from disease after death’—

mn102:2.8.verse: or else they declare[^1] the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, or some assert Nibbāna here and now.[^2]

mn102:2.9.verse: So (a) they declare an existing self to be free from disease after death, or (b) they declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, or (c) some assert Nibbāna here and now.

mn102:2.10.verse: So these five become three, and these three become five—

mn102:2.11.verse: this is the summary of the five and the three.

mn102:3.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless, or they declare it percipient of unity, or they declare it percipient of diversity, or they declare it percipient of the limited, or they declare it percipient of the measureless; or else, going beyond all this, some assert the totality of consciousness,[^3] as measureless and imperturbable.

mn102:4.2.verse: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless, or they declare it percipient of unity, or they declare it percipient of diversity, or they declare it percipient of the limited, or they declare it percipient of the measureless, or else there is that perception which is declared to be the purest, the highest, the supreme, the unsurpassed of those perceptions—

mn102:4.3.verse: whether perceptions of form, or perceptions of the formless, or perceptions of unity, or perceptions of diversity.

mn102:4.4.verse: ‘There is nothing’—some assert the base of nothingness, as measureless and imperturbable.

mn102:4.5.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’[^4]

mn102:4.6.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:5.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.

mn102:6.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them.

mn102:6.3.verse: ‘Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, non-perception.’

mn102:7.2.verse: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.

mn102:7.3.verse: For, bhikkhus, if any ascetic or brahmin were to say:

mn102:7.4.verse: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I shall describe the coming or going, the passing away or reappearance, the growth, increase, or maturing of consciousness’—

mn102:7.6.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:7.7.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:8.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.

mn102:9.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them, and those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them.

mn102:9.3.verse: ‘Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; non-perception is delusion; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely,

mn102:10.2.verse: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.

mn102:10.3.verse: For, bhikkhus, when any ascetics or brahmins declare the attainment of this base merely in terms of what has been seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, this is declared, bhikkhus, to be a disaster for the attainment of this base.

mn102:10.4.verse: For this base, bhikkhus, is not declared to be attainable by an attainment accompanied by formations;

mn102:10.5.verse: this base, bhikkhus, is declared to be attainable by an attainment accompanied by the residue of formations.

mn102:10.6.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:10.7.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:11.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being—those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them; those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them; and those ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them.

mn102:11.3.verse: All these good ascetics and brahmins, being intent on what lies ahead, assert only attachment thus:

mn102:11.4.verse: ‘So we shall be after death, so we shall be after death.’

mn102:12.1.verse: Just as a merchant going about his trade thinks:

mn102:12.2.verse: ‘From this I shall get that, with this I shall obtain that’;

mn102:12.3.verse: so too, these good ascetics and brahmins seem, as it were, like merchants:

mn102:12.4.verse: ‘So we shall be after death, so we shall be after death.’

mn102:12.6.verse: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being—out of fear of individual existence, out of disgust with individual existence, they run and circle round that very individual existence.

mn102:12.7.verse: Just as a dog tied by a leash and bound to a strong post or pillar runs and circles round that very post or pillar,

mn102:12.8.verse: so too, these good ascetics and brahmins, out of fear of individual existence, out of disgust with individual existence, run and circle round that very individual existence.

mn102:12.9.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:12.10.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:13.1.verse: Whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be, bhikkhus, who speculate about the future, who hold views about the future, and who assert various propositions concerning the future—all of them assert one or another of these five bases.
