mn102:14.1.verse: There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the past, who hold views about the past, and who assert various propositions concerning the past.

mn102:14.2.verse: ‘The self and the world are eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—[^5]

mn102:14.3.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.4.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both eternal and not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.5.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.6.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are finite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.7.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.8.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both finite and infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.9.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.10.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of unity, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.11.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of diversity, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.12.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of the limited, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.13.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of the measureless, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.14.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are exclusively happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.15.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are exclusively suffering, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.16.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both happy and suffering, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:14.17.verse: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither suffering nor happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—

mn102:15.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn102:15.2.verse: ‘the self and the world are eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—that they should have, apart from faith, apart from liking, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it,[^6] any personal, purified, and clear knowledge of this—that is not possible.

mn102:15.3.verse: But, bhikkhus, when there is no personal, purified, and clear knowledge, then even the mere fragment of knowledge that those good ascetics and brahmins clarify in that respect is itself declared to be clinging on the part of those good ascetics and brahmins.

mn102:15.4.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:15.5.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:16.1.verse: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:

mn102:16.2.verse: ‘the self and the world are not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’ …

mn102:16.3.verse: ‘the self and the world are both eternal and not eternal’ …

mn102:16.4.verse: ‘the self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal’ …

mn102:16.5.verse: ‘the self and the world are finite’ …

mn102:16.6.verse: ‘the self and the world are infinite’ …

mn102:16.7.verse: ‘the self and the world are both finite and infinite’ …

mn102:16.8.verse: ‘the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite’ …

mn102:16.9.verse: ‘the self and the world are percipient of unity’ …

mn102:16.10.verse: ‘the self and the world are percipient of diversity’ …

mn102:16.11.verse: ‘the self and the world are percipient of the limited’ …

mn102:16.12.verse: ‘the self and the world are percipient of the measureless’ …

mn102:16.13.verse: ‘the self and the world are exclusively happy’ …

mn102:16.14.verse: ‘the self and the world are exclusively suffering’ …

mn102:16.15.verse: ‘the self and the world are both happy and suffering’ …

mn102:16.16.verse: ‘the self and the world are neither suffering nor happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—that they should have, apart from faith, apart from liking, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, any personal, purified, and clear knowledge of this—that is not possible.

mn102:16.17.verse: But, bhikkhus, when there is no personal, purified, and clear knowledge, then even the mere fragment of knowledge that those good ascetics and brahmins clarify in that respect is itself declared to be clinging on the part of those good ascetics and brahmins.

mn102:16.18.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:16.19.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:17.1.verse: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all[^7] upon the fetters of sensual desire, enters upon and abides in the joy of seclusion,[^8] (thinking:)

mn102:17.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in the joy of seclusion.’

mn102:17.3.verse: That joy of seclusion of his ceases.

mn102:17.4.verse: With the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;

mn102:18.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, enters upon and abides in the joy of seclusion, (thinking:)

mn102:18.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in the joy of seclusion.’

mn102:18.6.verse: That joy of seclusion of his ceases.

mn102:18.7.verse: With the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.8.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:18.9.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:19.1.verse: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, enters upon and abides in unworldly pleasure,[^9] (thinking:)

mn102:19.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in unworldly pleasure.’

mn102:19.3.verse: That unworldly pleasure of his ceases.

mn102:19.4.verse: With the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.

mn102:20.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;

mn102:20.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.

mn102:20.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, enters upon and abides in unworldly pleasure, (thinking:)

mn102:20.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in unworldly pleasure.’

mn102:20.6.verse: That unworldly pleasure of his ceases.

mn102:20.7.verse: With the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.

mn102:20.8.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:20.9.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:21.1.verse: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, enters upon and abides in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,[^10] (thinking:)

mn102:21.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn102:21.3.verse: That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.

mn102:21.4.verse: With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

mn102:22.1.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;

mn102:22.2.verse: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

mn102:22.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, enters upon and abides in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, (thinking:)

mn102:22.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’

mn102:22.6.verse: That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.

mn102:22.7.verse: With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

mn102:22.8.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:22.9.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:23.1.verse: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, through surmounting neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, regards himself thus:

mn102:23.2.verse: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging.’

mn102:24.2.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, through surmounting neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, regards himself thus:

mn102:24.3.verse: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging’;

mn102:24.4.verse: certainly this venerable one asserts a way that is conducive to Nibbāna.

mn102:24.5.verse: And yet this good ascetic or brahmin, clinging to a view based on the past, clings; clinging to a view based on the future, clings; clinging to the fetter of sensual desire, clings; clinging to the joy of seclusion, clings; clinging to unworldly pleasure, clings; clinging to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, clings.

mn102:24.6.verse: And as for this venerable one’s regarding himself thus:

mn102:24.7.verse: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging’—this too is declared to be clinging on the part of this good ascetic or brahmin.

mn102:24.8.verse: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’

mn102:24.9.verse: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.

mn102:25.1.verse: Now this, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely—

mn102:25.2.verse: liberation without clinging, through knowing as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases of contact.”

mn102:25.3.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn102:25.4.verse: Those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn102:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn102:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn102:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speculate and theorize about the final end, and propose various hypotheses concerning the final end.

mn102:2.2.verse: Some propose this: ‘The self is percipient and healthy after death.’

mn102:2.4.verse: Some propose this: ‘The self is non-percipient and healthy after death.’

mn102:2.6.verse: Some propose this: ‘The self is neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy after death.’

mn102:2.8.verse: But some assert the annihilation, eradication, and nonexistence of an existing being, while others propose extinguishment in this life.

mn102:2.9.verse: Thus they assert an existent self that is healthy after death; or they assert the annihilation of an existing being; while some propose extinguishment in this life.

mn102:2.10.verse: In this way five become three, and three become five.

mn102:2.11.verse: This is the summary recital of the five and three.

mn102:3.1.verse: Now, the ascetics and brahmins who propose a self that is percipient and healthy after death describe it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless. Or they propose a self of unified perception, or of diverse perception, or of limited perception, or of limitless perception. Or some among those who go beyond this propose universal consciousness, limitless and imperturbable.

mn102:4.1.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:4.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who assert a self that is percipient and healthy after death, describing it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless. Or they describe it as of unified perception, or of diverse perception, or of limited perception, or of limitless perception.

mn102:4.4.verse: Or some, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, propose the dimension of nothingness, limitless and imperturbable. They declare that this is the purest, highest, best, and supreme of all those perceptions, whether of form or of formlessness or of unity or of diversity.

mn102:4.5.verse: ‘That much is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:4.6.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:5.1.verse: Now, the ascetics and brahmins who assert a self that is non-percipient and healthy after death describe it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless.

mn102:6.1.verse: So they reject those who assert a self that is percipient and healthy after death.

mn102:6.3.verse: Because they believe that perception is a disease, a boil, a dart, and that the state of non-perception is peaceful and sublime.

mn102:7.1.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:7.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who assert a self that is non-percipient and healthy after death, describing it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless.

mn102:7.3.verse: But if any ascetic or brahmin should say this:

mn102:7.4.verse: ‘Apart from form, feeling, perception, and choices, I will describe the coming and going of consciousness, its passing away and reappearing, its growth, increase, and maturity.’

mn102:7.6.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:7.7.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:8.1.verse: Now, the ascetics and brahmins who assert a self that is neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy after death describe it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless.

mn102:9.1.verse: So they reject those who assert a self that is percipient and healthy after death, as well as those who assert a self that is non-percipient and healthy after death.

mn102:9.3.verse: Because they believe that perception is a disease, a boil, a dart; that non-perception is a stupor; and that the state of neither perception nor non-perception is peaceful and sublime.

mn102:10.1.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:10.2.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who assert a self that is neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy after death, describing it as formed, or formless, or both formed and formless, or neither formed nor formless.

mn102:10.3.verse: Some ascetics or brahmins assert the embracing of that dimension merely through the conditioned phenomena of what ought be seen, heard, thought, and known. But that is said to be a disastrous approach.

mn102:10.4.verse: For that dimension is said to be not attainable by means of conditioned phenomena,

mn102:10.5.verse: but only with a residue of conditioned phenomena.

mn102:10.6.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:10.7.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:11.1.verse: Now, the ascetics and brahmins who assert the annihilation, eradication, and nonexistence of an existing being reject those who assert a self that is healthy after death, whether percipient or non-percipient or neither percipient nor non-percipient.

mn102:11.3.verse: Because they think: ‘All of those ascetics and brahmins only propose their attachment to heading upstream:

mn102:11.4.verse: “After death we shall be like this! After death we shall be like that!”

mn102:12.1.verse: Suppose a trader was going to market, thinking:

mn102:12.2.verse: “With this, that shall be mine! This way, I shall get that!”

mn102:12.3.verse: In the same way, those ascetics and brahmins seem to be like traders when they say:

mn102:12.4.verse: “After death we shall be like this! After death we shall be like that!”’

mn102:12.5.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:12.6.verse: The ascetics and brahmins who assert the annihilation, eradication, and nonexistence of an existing being; from fear and disgust with substantial reality, they just keep running and circling around substantial reality.

mn102:12.7.verse: Suppose a mutt on a leash was tethered to a strong post or pillar. It would just keeping running and circling around that post or pillar.

mn102:12.8.verse: In the same way, those ascetics and brahmins, from fear and disgust with substantial reality, just keep running and circling around substantial reality.

mn102:12.9.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:12.10.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:13.1.verse: Whatever ascetics and brahmins speculate and theorize about the final end, and propose various hypotheses concerning the final end, all of them propose one or other of these five topics.

mn102:14.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who speculate and theorize about the first beginning, and propose various hypotheses concerning the first beginning. They propose the following, each insisting that theirs is the only truth and that everything else is wrong.

mn102:14.2.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are eternal.’

mn102:14.3.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are not eternal.’

mn102:14.4.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are both eternal and not eternal.’

mn102:14.5.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are neither eternal nor not eternal.’

mn102:14.6.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are finite.’

mn102:14.7.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are infinite.’

mn102:14.8.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are both finite and infinite.’

mn102:14.9.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are neither finite nor infinite.’

mn102:14.10.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are unified in perception.’

mn102:14.11.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are diverse in perception.’

mn102:14.12.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos have limited perception.’

mn102:14.13.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos have limitless perception.’

mn102:14.14.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos experience nothing but happiness.’

mn102:14.15.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos experience absolute suffering.’

mn102:14.16.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos experience both happiness and suffering.’

mn102:14.17.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos experience neither happiness nor suffering.’

mn102:15.1.verse: Now, consider the ascetics and brahmins whose view is as follows.

mn102:15.2.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are eternal. This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’ It’s simply not possible for them to have personal knowledge of this that is pure and bright, apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation.

mn102:15.3.verse: But in the absence of personal knowledge that is pure and bright, even the portion of knowledge they illuminate is said to be grasping on their part.

mn102:15.4.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:15.5.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:16.1.verse: Now, consider the ascetics and brahmins whose view is as follows.

mn102:16.2.verse: The self and the cosmos are not eternal,

mn102:16.3.verse: or both eternal and not eternal,

mn102:16.15.verse: or experience both happiness and suffering,

mn102:16.16.verse: or experience neither happiness nor suffering. It’s simply not possible for them to have personal knowledge of this that is pure and bright, apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation.

mn102:16.17.verse: But in the absence of personal knowledge that is pure and bright, even the portion of knowledge they illuminate is said to be grasping on their part.

mn102:16.18.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:16.19.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:17.1.verse: Now, some ascetics and brahmins, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, enter and remain in the rapture of seclusion:

mn102:17.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in the rapture of seclusion.’

mn102:17.3.verse: But that rapture of seclusion of theirs ceases.

mn102:17.4.verse: When the rapture of seclusion ceases, sadness arises; and when sadness ceases, the rapture of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.1.verse: It’s like how the sunlight fills the space when the shadow leaves, or the shadow fills the space when the sunshine leaves.

mn102:18.2.verse: In the same way, when the rapture of seclusion ceases, sadness arises; and when sadness ceases, the rapture of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.3.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:18.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, enters and remains in the rapture of seclusion:

mn102:18.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in the rapture of seclusion.’

mn102:18.6.verse: But that rapture of seclusion of theirs ceases.

mn102:18.7.verse: When the rapture of seclusion ceases, sadness arises; and when sadness ceases, the rapture of seclusion arises.

mn102:18.8.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:18.9.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:19.1.verse: Now, some ascetics and brahmins, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, going beyond the rapture of seclusion, enter and remain in pleasure not of the flesh.

mn102:19.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in pleasure not of the flesh.’

mn102:19.3.verse: But that pleasure not of the flesh of theirs ceases.

mn102:19.4.verse: When pleasure not of the flesh ceases, the rapture of seclusion arises; and when the rapture of seclusion ceases, pleasure not of the flesh arises.

mn102:20.1.verse: It’s like how the sunlight fills the space when the shadow leaves, or the shadow fills the space when the sunshine leaves. …

mn102:20.3.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:20.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, going beyond the rapture of seclusion, enters and remains in pleasure not of the flesh.

mn102:20.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in pleasure not of the flesh.’

mn102:20.6.verse: But that pleasure not of the flesh of theirs ceases.

mn102:20.7.verse: When pleasure not of the flesh ceases, the rapture of seclusion arises; and when the rapture of seclusion ceases, pleasure not of the flesh arises.

mn102:20.8.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:20.9.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:21.1.verse: Now, some ascetics and brahmins, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, going beyond the rapture of seclusion and pleasure not of the flesh, enter and remain in neutral feeling.

mn102:21.2.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in neutral feeling.’

mn102:21.4.verse: When neutral feeling ceases, pleasure not of the flesh arises; and when pleasure not of the flesh ceases, neutral feeling arises.

mn102:22.1.verse: It’s like how the sunlight fills the space when the shadow leaves, or the shadow fills the space when the sunshine leaves. …

mn102:22.3.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:22.4.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, going beyond the rapture of seclusion and pleasure not of the flesh, enters and remains in neutral feeling.

mn102:22.5.verse: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, entering and remaining in neutral feeling.’

mn102:22.7.verse: When neutral feeling ceases, pleasure not of the flesh arises; and when pleasure not of the flesh ceases, neutral feeling arises.

mn102:22.8.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:22.9.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:23.1.verse: Now, some ascetics and brahmins, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, go beyond the rapture of seclusion, pleasure not of the flesh, and neutral feeling.

mn102:23.2.verse: They regard themselves like this: ‘I am at peace; I am quenched; I am free of grasping.’

mn102:24.1.verse: The Realized One understands this as follows.

mn102:24.2.verse: This good ascetic or brahmin, letting go of theories about the first beginning and the final end, not fixating on the fetters of sensuality, goes beyond the rapture of seclusion, pleasure not of the flesh, and neutral feeling.

mn102:24.3.verse: They regard themselves like this: ‘I am at peace; I am quenched; I am free of grasping.’

mn102:24.4.verse: Clearly this venerable speaks of a practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.

mn102:24.5.verse: Nevertheless, they still grasp at theories about the first beginning or the final end, or the fetters of sensuality, or the rapture of seclusion, or pleasure not of the flesh, or neutral feeling.

mn102:24.6.verse: And when they regard themselves like this:

mn102:24.7.verse: ‘I am at peace; I am quenched; I am free of grasping,’ that’s also said to be grasping on their part.

mn102:24.8.verse: ‘All that is conditioned and crude. But there is the cessation of conditions—that is real.’

mn102:24.9.verse: Understanding this and seeing the escape from it, the Realized One has gone beyond all that.

mn102:25.1.verse: But the Realized One has awakened to the supreme state of sublime peace, that is,

mn102:25.2.verse: liberation by not grasping after truly understanding the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.”

mn102:25.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn102:25.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn103:0.2.verse: Is This What You Think Of Me?

mn103:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kusinārā in the Forest of Offerings.

mn103:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn103:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, is this what you think of me?

mn103:2.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.’”

mn103:2.3.verse: “No sir, we don’t think of you that way.”

mn103:2.5.verse: “If you don’t think of me that way,

mn103:2.8.verse: what then do you think of me?”

mn103:2.10.verse: ‘The Buddha is sympathetic and wants what’s best for us.

mn103:2.14.verse: that I teach out of sympathy.

mn103:3.1.verse: In that case, each and every one of you should train in the things I have taught from my direct knowledge, that is:

mn103:3.2.verse: the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path. You should train in these things in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute.

mn103:4.1.verse: As you do so, it may happen that two mendicants disagree about the teaching.

mn103:5.2.verse: ‘These two venerables disagree on both the meaning and the phrasing.’ So you should approach whichever mendicant you think is most amenable and say to them:

mn103:5.3.verse: ‘The venerables disagree on the meaning and the phrasing.

mn103:5.4.verse: But the venerables should know that this is how

mn103:5.5.verse: such disagreement on the meaning and the phrasing comes to be.

mn103:5.6.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about this.’

mn103:5.7.verse: Then you should approach whichever mendicant they think is most amenable among those who side with the other party and say to them:

mn103:5.8.verse: ‘The venerables disagree on the meaning and the phrasing.

mn103:5.9.verse: But the venerables should know that this is how

mn103:5.10.verse: such disagreement on the meaning and the phrasing comes to be.

mn103:5.11.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about this.’

mn103:5.12.verse: So you should remember what has been incorrectly memorized as incorrectly memorized and what has been correctly memorized as correctly memorized.

mn103:5.13.verse: Remembering this, you should speak on the teaching and the training.

mn103:6.2.verse: ‘These two venerables disagree on the meaning but agree on the phrasing.’ So you should approach whichever mendicant you think is most amenable and say to them:

mn103:6.3.verse: ‘The venerables disagree on the meaning but agree on the phrasing.

mn103:6.4.verse: But the venerables should know that this is how

mn103:6.5.verse: such disagreement on the meaning and agreement on the phrasing comes to be.

mn103:6.6.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about this.’

mn103:6.7.verse: Then you should approach whichever mendicant they think is most amenable among those who side with the other party and say to them:

mn103:6.8.verse: ‘The venerables disagree on the meaning but agree on the phrasing.

mn103:6.9.verse: But the venerables should know that this is how

mn103:6.10.verse: such disagreement on the meaning and agreement on the phrasing comes to be.

mn103:6.11.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about this.’

mn103:6.12.verse: So you should remember what has been incorrectly memorized as incorrectly memorized and what has been correctly memorized as correctly memorized.

mn103:6.13.verse: Remembering this, you should speak on the teaching and the training.

mn103:7.2.verse: ‘These two venerables agree on the meaning but disagree on the phrasing.’ So you should approach whichever mendicant you think is most amenable and say to them:

mn103:7.3.verse: ‘The venerables agree on the meaning but disagree on the phrasing.

mn103:7.4.verse: But the venerables should know that this is how

mn103:7.5.verse: such agreement on the meaning and disagreement on the phrasing comes to be.

mn103:7.6.verse: But the phrasing is a minor matter.

mn103:7.7.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about something so minor.’

mn103:7.8.verse: Then you should approach whichever mendicant they think is most amenable among those who side with the other party and say to them:

mn103:7.9.verse: ‘The venerables agree on the meaning but disagree on the phrasing.

mn103:8.5.verse: they come to agree on the meaning and the phrasing.

mn103:8.6.verse: Please don’t get into a dispute about this.’

mn103:8.10.verse: they come to agree on the meaning and the phrasing.

mn103:8.12.verse: So you should remember what has been correctly memorized as correctly memorized.

mn103:9.1.verse: As you train in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, one of the mendicants might commit an offense or transgression.

mn103:10.1.verse: In such a case, you should not be in a hurry to accuse them. The individual should be examined like this:

mn103:10.2.verse: ‘I won’t be troubled and the other individual won’t be hurt, for they’re not irritable and acrimonious. They don’t hold fast to their views, but let them go easily. I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.’

mn103:10.3.verse: If that’s what you think, then it’s appropriate to speak to them.

mn103:11.2.verse: ‘I will be troubled and the other individual will be hurt, for they’re irritable and acrimonious. However, they don’t hold fast to their views, but let them go easily. I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.

mn103:11.3.verse: But for the other individual to get hurt is a minor matter.

mn103:11.5.verse: that I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.’

mn103:11.6.verse: If that’s what you think, then it’s appropriate to speak to them.

mn103:12.2.verse: ‘I will be troubled but the other individual won’t be hurt, for they’re not irritable and acrimonious. However, they hold fast to their views, refusing to let go. Nevertheless, I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.

mn103:12.3.verse: But for me to be troubled is a minor matter.

mn103:12.5.verse: that I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.’

mn103:12.6.verse: If that’s what you think, then it’s appropriate to speak to them.

mn103:13.3.verse: But for me to be troubled and the other individual to get hurt is a minor matter.

mn103:13.5.verse: that I can draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.’

mn103:13.6.verse: If that’s what you think, then it’s appropriate to speak to them.

mn103:14.2.verse: ‘I will be troubled and the other individual will be hurt, for they’re irritable and acrimonious. And they hold fast to their views, refusing to let go. I cannot draw them away from the unskillful and establish them in the skillful.’

mn103:14.3.verse: Don’t underestimate the value of equanimity regarding such an individual.

mn103:15.1.verse: As you train in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, the sides might continue to bring up settled issues with each other, with contempt for each other’s views, resentful, bitter, and exasperated.

mn103:15.2.verse: In this case you should approach whichever mendicant you think is most amenable among those who side with one party and say to them:

mn103:15.3.verse: ‘Reverend, as we were training, the sides continued to bring up settled issues with each other. If the Ascetic knew about this, would he criticize it?’

mn103:15.4.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say:

mn103:15.6.verse: ‘But without giving that up, reverend, can one realize extinguishment?’

mn103:15.7.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say:

mn103:16.1.verse: Then you should approach whichever mendicant they think is most amenable among those who side with the other party and say to them:

mn103:16.2.verse: ‘Reverend, as we were training, the sides continued to bring up settled issues with each other. If the Ascetic knew about this, would he criticize it?’

mn103:16.3.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say:

mn103:16.5.verse: ‘But without giving that up, reverend, can one realize extinguishment?’

mn103:16.6.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say:

mn103:17.1.verse: If others should ask that mendicant:

mn103:17.2.verse: ‘Were you the venerable who drew those mendicants away from the unskillful and established them in the skillful?’

mn103:17.3.verse: Answering rightly, the mendicant should say:

mn103:17.4.verse: ‘Well, reverends, I approached the Buddha. He taught me the Dhamma. After hearing that teaching I explained it to those mendicants.

mn103:17.5.verse: When those mendicants heard that teaching they were drawn away from the unskillful and established in the skillful.’

mn103:17.6.verse: Answering in this way, that mendicant doesn’t glorify themselves or put others down. They answer in line with the teaching, with no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism.”

mn103:17.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn103:17.8.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn104:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans near the village of Sāma.

mn104:2.1.verse: Now at that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan had recently passed away at Pāvā.

mn104:2.2.verse: With his passing the Jain ascetics split, dividing into two factions, fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words:

mn104:2.3.verse: “You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. I stay on topic, you don’t. You said last what you should have said first. You said first what you should have said last. What you’ve thought so much about has been disproved. Your doctrine is refuted. Go on, save your doctrine! You’re trapped; get yourself out of this—if you can!”

mn104:2.4.verse: You’d think there was nothing but slaughter going on among the Jain ascetics.

mn104:2.5.verse: And the Jain Ñātika’s white-clothed lay disciples were disillusioned, dismayed, and disappointed in the Jain ascetics. They were equally disappointed with a teaching and training so poorly explained and poorly propounded, not emancipating, not leading to peace, proclaimed by someone who is not a fully awakened Buddha, with broken monument and without a refuge.

mn104:3.1.verse: And then, after completing the rainy season residence near Pāvā, the novice Cunda went to see Venerable Ānanda at Sāma village. He bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

mn104:4.2.verse: “Reverend Cunda, we should see the Buddha about this matter.

mn104:4.3.verse: Come, let’s go to the Buddha and inform him about this.”

mn104:4.5.verse: Then Ānanda and Cunda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and Ānanda informed him of what Cunda had said. He went on to say,

mn104:4.10.verse: ‘When the Buddha has passed away, let no dispute arise in the Saṅgha.

mn104:4.11.verse: For such a dispute would be for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.’”

mn104:5.2.verse: Do you see even two mendicants whose opinion differs regarding the things I have taught from my direct knowledge, that is,

mn104:5.3.verse: the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path?”

mn104:5.6.verse: Nevertheless, there are some individuals who appear to live obedient to the Buddha, but when the Buddha has passed away they might create a dispute in the Saṅgha regarding livelihood or the monastic code.

mn104:5.7.verse: Such a dispute would be for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.”

mn104:5.8.verse: “Ānanda, dispute about livelihood or the monastic code is a minor matter.

mn104:5.9.verse: But should a dispute arise in the Saṅgha concerning the path or the practice, that would be for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

mn104:6.1.verse: Ānanda, there are these six roots of dispute.

mn104:6.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant is irritable and acrimonious.

mn104:6.4.verse: Such a mendicant lacks respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and they don’t fulfill the training.

mn104:6.5.verse: They create a dispute in the Saṅgha, which is for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

mn104:6.6.verse: If you see such a root of dispute in yourselves or others, you should try to give up this bad thing.

mn104:6.7.verse: If you don’t see it, you should practice so that it doesn’t come up in the future.

mn104:6.8.verse: That’s how to give up this bad root of dispute, so it doesn’t come up in the future.

mn104:7-11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant is offensive and contemptuous …

mn104:7-11.4.verse: They have corrupt wishes and wrong view …

mn104:7-11.5.verse: They’re attached to their own views, holding them tight, and refusing to let go.

mn104:7-11.6.verse: Such a mendicant lacks respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and they don’t fulfill the training.

mn104:7-11.7.verse: They create a dispute in the Saṅgha, which is for the detriment and unhappiness of the people, against the people, for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

mn104:7-11.8.verse: If you see such a root of dispute in yourselves or others, you should try to give up this bad thing.

mn104:7-11.9.verse: If you don’t see it, you should practice so that it doesn’t come up in the future.

mn104:7-11.10.verse: That’s how to give up this bad root of dispute, so it doesn’t come up in the future.

mn104:7-11.11.verse: These are the six roots of dispute.

mn104:12.1.verse: There are four kinds of disciplinary issues.

mn104:12.3.verse: Disciplinary issues due to disputes, accusations, offenses, or business.

mn104:12.4.verse: These are the four kinds of disciplinary issues.

mn104:13.1.verse: There are these seven means of settling any disciplinary issues that might arise.

mn104:13.2.verse: Resolution face-to-face to be applied. Resolution through recollection to be granted. Resolution because of past insanity to be granted. Acting according to what has been admitted. Majority decision. Further penalty. Covering over as if with grass.

mn104:14.1.verse: And how is there resolution face-to-face?

mn104:14.2.verse: It’s when mendicants are disputing: ‘This is the teaching,’ ‘This is not the teaching,’ ‘This is the monastic law,’ ‘This is not the monastic law.’

mn104:14.3.verse: Those mendicants should all sit together in harmony

mn104:14.4.verse: and thoroughly go over the guidelines of the teaching.

mn104:14.5.verse: They should settle that disciplinary issue in agreement with the guidelines.

mn104:14.6.verse: That’s how there is resolution face-to-face.

mn104:14.7.verse: And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:15.1.verse: And how is there majority decision?

mn104:15.2.verse: If those mendicants are not able to settle that issue in that monastery,

mn104:15.3.verse: they should go to another monastery with more mendicants.

mn104:15.4.verse: There they should all sit together in harmony

mn104:15.5.verse: and thoroughly go over the guidelines of the teaching.

mn104:15.6.verse: They should settle that disciplinary issue in agreement with the guidelines.

mn104:15.7.verse: That’s how there is majority decision. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:16.1.verse: And how is there resolution through recollection?

mn104:16.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant accuses a mendicant of a heavy offense; one entailing expulsion, or close to it:

mn104:16.3.verse: ‘Venerable, do you recall committing the kind of serious offense that entails expulsion or close to it?’

mn104:16.5.verse: ‘No, reverend, I don’t recall committing such an offense.’

mn104:16.6.verse: The resolution through recollection should be granted to them.

mn104:16.7.verse: That’s how there is the resolution through recollection. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:17.1.verse: And how is there resolution because of past insanity?

mn104:17.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant accuses a mendicant of the kind of serious offense that entails expulsion, or close to it:

mn104:17.3.verse: ‘Venerable, do you recall committing the kind of serious offense that entails expulsion or close to it?’

mn104:17.5.verse: ‘No, reverend, I don’t recall committing such an offense.’

mn104:17.6.verse: But though they try to get out of it, the mendicant pursues the issue:

mn104:17.7.verse: ‘Surely the venerable must know perfectly well if you recall committing an offense that entails expulsion or close to it!’

mn104:17.9.verse: ‘Reverend, I had gone mad, I was out of my mind.

mn104:17.10.verse: And while I was mad I did and said many things that are not proper for an ascetic.

mn104:17.11.verse: I don’t remember any of that,

mn104:17.12.verse: I was mad when I did it.’

mn104:17.13.verse: The resolution because of past insanity should be granted to them.

mn104:17.14.verse: That’s how there is resolution because of past insanity. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:17.15.verse: by resolution because of past insanity.

mn104:18.1.verse: And how is there acting according to what has been admitted?

mn104:18.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, whether accused or not, recalls an offense and clarifies it and reveals it.

mn104:18.3.verse: After approaching a more senior mendicant, that mendicant should arrange his robe over one shoulder, bow to that mendicant’s feet, squat on their heels, raise their cupped palms, and say:

mn104:18.4.verse: ‘Sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense. I confess it.’

mn104:18.10.verse: That’s how there is acting according to what has been admitted. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:18.11.verse: by acting according to what has been admitted.

mn104:19.1.verse: And how is there a verdict of further penalty?

mn104:19.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant accuses a mendicant of the kind of heavy offense that entails expulsion, or close to it:

mn104:19.3.verse: ‘Venerable, do you recall committing the kind of heavy offense that entails expulsion or close to it?’

mn104:19.5.verse: ‘No, reverend, I don’t recall committing such an offense.’

mn104:19.6.verse: But though they try to get out of it, the mendicant pursues the issue:

mn104:19.7.verse: ‘Surely the venerable must know perfectly well if you recall committing an offense that entails expulsion or close to it!’

mn104:19.9.verse: ‘Reverend, I don’t recall committing a heavy offense of that nature.

mn104:19.10.verse: But I do recall committing a light offense.’

mn104:19.11.verse: But though they try to get out of it, the mendicant pursues the issue:

mn104:19.12.verse: ‘Surely the venerable must know perfectly well if you recall committing an offense that entails expulsion or close to it!’

mn104:19.14.verse: ‘Reverend, I’ll go so far as to admit this light offense even when not asked.

mn104:19.15.verse: Why wouldn’t I admit a heavy offense when asked?’

mn104:19.17.verse: ‘You wouldn’t have admitted that light offense without being asked, so why would you admit a heavy offense?

mn104:19.18.verse: Surely the venerable must know perfectly well if you recall committing an offense that entails expulsion or close to it!’

mn104:19.20.verse: ‘Reverend, I do recall committing the kind of heavy offense that entails expulsion or close to it.

mn104:19.21.verse: I spoke too hastily when I said

mn104:19.23.verse: That’s how there is further penalty. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:20.1.verse: And how is there the covering over as if with grass?

mn104:20.2.verse: It’s when the mendicants continually fight, quarrel, and dispute, doing and saying many things that are not proper for an ascetic.

mn104:20.3.verse: Those mendicants should all sit together in harmony.

mn104:20.4.verse: A competent mendicant of one party, having risen from their seat, arranged their robe over one shoulder, and raised their cupped palms, should inform the Saṅgha:

mn104:20.5.verse: ‘Sir, let the Saṅgha listen to me.

mn104:20.6.verse: We have been continually fighting, quarreling, and disputing, doing and saying many things that are not proper for an ascetic.

mn104:20.7.verse: If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, then—for the benefit of these venerables and myself—I disclose in the middle of the Saṅgha by means of covering over as if with grass any offenses committed by these venerables and by myself, excepting only those that are gravely blameworthy and those connected with laypeople.’

mn104:20.8.verse: Then a competent mendicant of the other party, having risen from their seat, arranged their robe over one shoulder, and raising their cupped palms, should inform the Saṅgha:

mn104:20.9.verse: ‘Sir, let the Saṅgha listen to me.

mn104:20.10.verse: We have been continually fighting, quarreling, and disputing, doing and saying many things that are not proper for an ascetic.

mn104:20.11.verse: If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, then—for the benefit of these venerables and myself—I disclose in the middle of the Saṅgha by means of covering over as if with grass any offenses committed by these venerables and by myself, excepting only those that are gravely blameworthy and those connected with laypeople.’

mn104:20.12.verse: That’s how there is the covering over as if with grass. And that’s how certain disciplinary issues are settled, that is,

mn104:20.13.verse: by covering over as if with grass.

mn104:21.1.verse: Ānanda, these six warm-hearted qualities make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without quarreling.

mn104:21.3.verse: Firstly, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with bodily kindness, both in public and in private.

mn104:21.4.verse: This warm-hearted quality makes for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without dispute.

mn104:21.5.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with verbal kindness …

mn104:21.6.verse: This too is a warm-hearted quality.

mn104:21.7.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant consistently treats their spiritual companions with mental kindness …

mn104:21.8.verse: This too is a warm-hearted quality.

mn104:21.9.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant shares without reservation any material things they have gained by legitimate means, even the food placed in the alms-bowl, using them in common with their ethical spiritual companions.

mn104:21.10.verse: This too is a warm-hearted quality.

mn104:21.11.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives according to the precepts shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private. Those precepts are intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

mn104:21.12.verse: This too is a warm-hearted quality.

mn104:21.13.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant lives according to the view shared with their spiritual companions, both in public and in private. That view is noble and emancipating, and delivers one who applies it to the complete ending of suffering.

mn104:21.14.verse: This too is a warm-hearted quality.

mn104:21.15.verse: These six warm-hearted qualities make for fondness and respect, conducing to inclusion, harmony, and unity, without dispute.

mn104:22.1.verse: If you should proceed having undertaken these six warm-hearted qualities, do you see any criticism, large or small, that you could not endure?”

mn104:22.3.verse: “That’s why, Ānanda, you should proceed having undertaken these six warm-hearted qualities.

mn104:22.4.verse: That will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn104:22.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn104:22.6.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn105:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

mn105:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion final knowledge had been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence:

mn105:2.2.verse: “We understand: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’”

mn105:2.4.verse: “It seems that final knowledge has been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence:

mn105:2.5.verse: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”’”

mn105:3.1.verse: Then Sunakkhatta the Licchavi went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:

mn105:4.2.verse: ‘It seems that final knowledge has been declared by many bhikkhus in the Blessed One’s presence—

mn105:4.3.verse: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”—so we understand.’

mn105:4.4.verse: Now, venerable sir, do those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge in the Blessed One’s presence:

mn105:4.5.verse: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”’—do they, venerable sir, declare final knowledge rightly, or are there some bhikkhus here who declare final knowledge through overestimation?”

mn105:5.1.verse: “Sunakkhatta, of those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge in my presence:

mn105:5.2.verse: ‘We understand: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come”’—

mn105:5.3.verse: there are some bhikkhus here who declared final knowledge rightly, but there are also some bhikkhus here who declared final knowledge through overestimation.

mn105:5.4.verse: Now, Sunakkhatta, as to those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge rightly, it is so with them just as they say;

mn105:5.5.verse: but as to those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge through overestimation, in that case, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata:

mn105:5.7.verse: So it is here, Sunakkhatta, that it occurs to the Tathāgata:

mn105:5.9.verse: And yet, here, certain misguided men, having elaborately formulated a question, approach the Tathāgata and ask it.

mn105:5.10.verse: In such a case, Sunakkhatta, even though it had occurred to the Tathāgata:

mn105:5.11.verse: ‘I shall teach them the Dhamma’—there comes to be a change in that intention.”

mn105:6.1.verse: “This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One,

mn105:6.2.verse: for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

mn105:6.3.verse: “Well then, Sunakkhatta, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn105:6.4.verse: “Yes, venerable sir,” Sunakkhatta the Licchavi replied to the Blessed One.

mn105:7.1.verse: “There are, Sunakkhatta, these five cords of sensual desire.

mn105:7.3.verse: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust,

mn105:7.7.verse: tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—

mn105:7.8.verse: these, Sunakkhatta, are the five cords of sensual desire.

mn105:8.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on worldly material things.

mn105:8.2.verse: For a person intent on worldly material things, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:8.3.verse: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:9.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man had long been away from his own village or town.

mn105:9.2.verse: He might see another man who had recently left that village or town.

mn105:9.3.verse: He would ask that man about the safety, plenty, and freedom from sickness of that village or town;

mn105:9.4.verse: and that man would tell him about the safety, plenty, and freedom from sickness of that village or town.

mn105:9.6.verse: would that man listen to that man, give ear, apply his mind to understanding it, associate with that man, and find satisfaction through him?”

mn105:9.8.verse: “So too, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that some individual person here might be intent on worldly material things.

mn105:9.9.verse: For a person intent on worldly material things, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:9.10.verse: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:9.12.verse: ‘This individual person intent on worldly material things is not freed from the fetter of the imperturbable.’

mn105:10.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the imperturbable.[^2]

mn105:10.2.verse: For a person intent on the imperturbable, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:10.3.verse: but when talk connected with worldly material things is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:11.1.verse: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a yellow leaf, fallen from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again;

mn105:11.2.verse: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the imperturbable, the fetter of worldly material things has fallen away.

mn105:11.4.verse: ‘This individual person intent on the imperturbable is freed from the fetter of worldly material things.’

mn105:12.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the base of nothingness.

mn105:12.2.verse: For a person intent on the base of nothingness, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:12.3.verse: but when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:13.1.verse: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a large rock, split in two, cannot be joined together again;

mn105:13.2.verse: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the base of nothingness, the fetter of the imperturbable is broken.

mn105:13.4.verse: ‘This individual person intent on the base of nothingness is freed from the fetter of the imperturbable.’

mn105:14.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn105:14.2.verse: For a person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:14.3.verse: but when talk connected with the base of nothingness is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:15.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man had eaten delicious food and then vomited it up.

mn105:15.3.verse: would that man have any desire to eat that food again?”

mn105:15.6.verse: “Because, venerable sir, that food is now reckoned as disgusting.”

mn105:15.7.verse: “So too, Sunakkhatta, for a person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the fetter of the base of nothingness has been vomited up.

mn105:15.9.verse: ‘This individual person intent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is freed from the fetter of the base of nothingness.’

mn105:16.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some individual person here might be rightly intent on Nibbāna.

mn105:16.2.verse: For a person rightly intent on Nibbāna, Sunakkhatta, only talk that is fitting for this settles his mind, and he thinks and ponders in line with it, he associates with that kind of person, and he finds satisfaction through him;

mn105:16.3.verse: but when talk connected with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is going on, he does not want to listen, does not give ear, does not apply his mind to understanding it, and he does not associate with that kind of person, and he finds no satisfaction through him.

mn105:17.1.verse: Just as, Sunakkhatta, a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of growing again;

mn105:17.2.verse: so too, Sunakkhatta, for a person rightly intent on Nibbāna, the fetter of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has been cut off, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no more subject to future arising.

mn105:17.4.verse: ‘This individual person rightly intent on Nibbāna is freed from the fetter of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’

mn105:18.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:

mn105:18.2.verse: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic;[^3] the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.

mn105:18.3.verse: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’

mn105:18.4.verse: He might conceive this though it is not really so.

mn105:18.5.verse: He would pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.

mn105:18.6.verse: As he pursues an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would invade his mind.

mn105:18.7.verse: With his mind invaded by lust, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.

mn105:19.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn105:19.2.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring a surgeon to treat him.

mn105:19.3.verse: The surgeon would cut round the opening of the wound with a knife.

mn105:19.4.verse: Having cut round the opening of the wound with a knife, he would probe for the arrow with a probe.

mn105:19.5.verse: Having probed for the arrow with a probe, he would pull out the arrow, and remove the poison, but with some trace remaining.[^4]

mn105:19.6.verse: Knowing that some trace remained, he would say:

mn105:19.7.verse: ‘Good man, your arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, but with some trace remaining.

mn105:19.8.verse: It is not enough to endanger you.

mn105:19.9.verse: Eat only suitable food; do not let unsuitable food make your wound discharge.

mn105:19.10.verse: Wash the wound from time to time, and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, lest, from your not washing the wound and not anointing the opening of the wound from time to time, stale blood should seal up the opening of the wound.

mn105:19.11.verse: And do not walk about in the wind and sun, lest, as you walk about in the wind and sun, dust and grit should infect the opening of the wound.

mn105:19.12.verse: You must live guarding the wound, good man, until it heals.’

mn105:20.2.verse: ‘My arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with some trace remaining.

mn105:20.3.verse: It is not enough to endanger me.’

mn105:20.4.verse: And he would eat unsuitable food, and from his eating unsuitable food his wound would discharge.

mn105:20.5.verse: And he would not wash the wound from time to time, nor anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, and from his not doing so, stale blood would seal up the opening of the wound.

mn105:20.6.verse: And he would walk about in the wind and sun, and from his doing so, dust and grit would infect the opening of the wound.

mn105:20.7.verse: And he would not live guarding the wound, nor let it heal.

mn105:20.8.verse: Then, both through this unsuitable conduct and through the impure poison that had been removed but with some trace remaining, the wound would swell up from these two causes.

mn105:20.9.verse: With the wound swollen up in this way, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.

mn105:21.1.verse: So too, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:

mn105:21.2.verse: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic; the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.

mn105:21.3.verse: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’

mn105:21.4.verse: He might conceive this though it is not really so.

mn105:21.5.verse: He would pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.

mn105:21.6.verse: As he pursues an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would invade his mind.

mn105:21.7.verse: With his mind invaded by lust, he would meet death, or suffering close to death.

mn105:22.1.verse: For, Sunakkhatta, in the Discipline of the Noble Ones, this is death: when one abandons the training and reverts to the lower life;

mn105:22.2.verse: and this, Sunakkhatta, is suffering close to death: when one commits a certain defiled offence.

mn105:23.1.verse: Now it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:

mn105:23.2.verse: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic; the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.

mn105:23.3.verse: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’

mn105:23.4.verse: Being one who is truly rightly intent on Nibbāna, he would not pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would not pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would not pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would not pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would not pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would not pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.

mn105:23.5.verse: As he does not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would not invade his mind.

mn105:23.6.verse: With his mind not invaded by lust, he would meet neither death nor suffering close to death.

mn105:24.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man were wounded by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn105:24.2.verse: His friends and companions, his relatives and kin, would bring a surgeon to treat him.

mn105:24.3.verse: The surgeon would cut round the opening of the wound with a knife.

mn105:24.4.verse: Having cut round the opening of the wound with a knife, he would probe for the arrow with a probe.

mn105:24.5.verse: Having probed for the arrow with a probe, he would pull out the arrow, and remove the poison, with no trace remaining.

mn105:24.6.verse: Knowing that no trace remained, he would say:

mn105:24.7.verse: ‘Good man, your arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with no trace remaining.

mn105:24.8.verse: It is not enough to endanger you.

mn105:24.9.verse: Eat only suitable food; do not let unsuitable food make your wound discharge.

mn105:24.10.verse: Wash the wound from time to time, and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, lest, from your not washing the wound and not anointing the opening of the wound from time to time, stale blood should seal up the opening of the wound.

mn105:24.11.verse: And do not walk about in the wind and sun, lest, as you walk about in the wind and sun, dust and grit should infect the opening of the wound.

mn105:24.12.verse: You must live guarding the wound, good man, until it heals.’

mn105:25.2.verse: ‘My arrow has been pulled out; the poison has been removed, with no trace remaining.

mn105:25.3.verse: It is not enough to endanger me.’

mn105:25.4.verse: And he would eat only suitable food, and from his eating suitable food his wound would not discharge.

mn105:25.5.verse: And he would wash the wound from time to time, and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, and from his doing so, stale blood would not seal up the opening of the wound.

mn105:25.6.verse: And he would not walk about in the wind and sun, and from his not doing so, dust and grit would not infect the opening of the wound.

mn105:25.7.verse: And he would live guarding the wound, and let it heal.

mn105:25.8.verse: Then, both through this suitable conduct and through the impure poison that had been removed with no trace remaining, the wound would grow together from these two causes.

mn105:25.9.verse: With the wound healed and covered over with skin, he would meet neither death nor suffering close to death.

mn105:26.1.verse: So too, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:

mn105:26.2.verse: ‘Craving has been called a dart by the Ascetic; the poison of ignorance spreads through desire, lust, and ill will.

mn105:26.3.verse: That dart of craving has been abandoned in me, the poison of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna.’

mn105:26.4.verse: Being one who is truly rightly intent on Nibbāna, he would not pursue those things unsuitable for one who is rightly intent on Nibbāna; he would not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, he would not pursue an unsuitable sound with the ear, he would not pursue an unsuitable odour with the nose, he would not pursue an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, he would not pursue an unsuitable tangible with the body, he would not pursue an unsuitable mental object with the mind.

mn105:26.5.verse: As he does not pursue an unsuitable sight with the eye, an unsuitable sound with the ear, an unsuitable odour with the nose, an unsuitable flavour with the tongue, an unsuitable tangible with the body, an unsuitable mental object with the mind, lust would not invade his mind.

mn105:26.6.verse: With his mind not invaded by lust, he would meet neither death nor suffering close to death.

mn105:27.1.verse: This simile, Sunakkhatta, has been made by me to convey a meaning.

mn105:27.3.verse: ‘wound’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for the six internal bases;

mn105:27.4.verse: ‘poison’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for ignorance;

mn105:27.5.verse: ‘dart’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for craving;

mn105:27.6.verse: ‘probe’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for mindfulness;

mn105:27.7.verse: ‘knife’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for noble wisdom;

mn105:27.8.verse: ‘surgeon’, Sunakkhatta, is a term for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

mn105:28.1.verse: Truly, Sunakkhatta, a bhikkhu who practises restraint in the six bases of contact,

mn105:28.2.verse: and who, knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’[^5] is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.

mn105:29.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, there were a bronze cup of a drink, endowed with colour, endowed with smell, endowed with taste;

mn105:29.2.verse: but it was mixed with poison.

mn105:29.3.verse: Then a man came along who wanted to live, did not want to die, wanted happiness, and recoiled from suffering.

mn105:29.5.verse: would that man drink from that cup of drink, knowing:

mn105:29.6.verse: ‘Having drunk this, I will meet death, or suffering close to death’?”

mn105:29.8.verse: “So too, Sunakkhatta, when a bhikkhu, practising restraint in the six bases of contact,

mn105:29.9.verse: and knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’ is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.

mn105:30.1.verse: Suppose, Sunakkhatta, there were a fierce, venomous snake.

mn105:30.2.verse: Then a man came along who wanted to live, did not want to die, wanted happiness, and recoiled from suffering.

mn105:30.4.verse: would that man give his hand or his thumb to that fierce, venomous snake, knowing:

mn105:30.5.verse: ‘Bitten by this, I will meet death, or suffering close to death’?”

mn105:30.7.verse: “So too, Sunakkhatta, when a bhikkhu, practising restraint in the six bases of contact,

mn105:30.8.verse: and knowing that ‘acquisitions are the root of suffering,’ is free of acquisitions, liberated in the exhaustion of acquisitions—

mn105:30.9.verse: it is not possible that he would apply his body or arouse his mind towards any acquisition.”

mn105:30.10.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn105:30.11.verse: Sunakkhatta the Licchavi was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn105:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

mn105:2.1.verse: Now at that time several mendicants had declared their enlightenment in the Buddha’s presence:

mn105:2.2.verse: “We understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

mn105:2.3.verse: Sunakkhatta the Licchavi heard about this.

mn105:3.1.verse: He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn105:4.2.verse: several mendicants have declared their enlightenment in the Buddha’s presence.

mn105:4.5.verse: I trust they did so rightly—or are there some who declared enlightenment out of overestimation?”

mn105:5.3.verse: “Some of them did so rightly, Sunakkhatta, while others did so out of overestimation.

mn105:5.4.verse: Now, when mendicants declare enlightenment rightly, that is their truth.

mn105:5.5.verse: But when mendicants declare enlightenment out of overestimation, the Realized One thinks:

mn105:5.8.verse: he should teach them the Dhamma,

mn105:5.9.verse: but then certain futile men, having carefully planned a question, approach the Realized One and ask it,

mn105:6.1.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

mn105:6.2.verse: Let the Buddha teach the Dhamma. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn105:6.3.verse: “Well then, Sunakkhatta, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn105:7.1.verse: “Sunakkhatta, there are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn105:7.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn105:7.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn105:7.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn105:8.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain individual person may be intent on worldly pleasures of the flesh.

mn105:8.2.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:8.3.verse: But when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:9.1.verse: Suppose a person had left their own village or town long ago,
