mn105:9.2.verse: and they saw another person who had only recently left there.

mn105:9.3.verse: They would ask about whether their village was safe, with plenty of food and little disease,

mn105:9.4.verse: and the other person would tell them the news.

mn105:9.6.verse: Would that person want to listen to that other person? Would they actively listen and try to understand? Would they associate with that person, and find it rewarding?”

mn105:9.8.verse: “In the same way, it’s possible that a certain individual may be intent on worldly pleasures of the flesh.

mn105:9.9.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:9.10.verse: But when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:9.12.verse: ‘That individual is intent on pleasures of the flesh, for they’re detached from things connected with the imperturbable.’

mn105:10.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain individual person may be intent on the imperturbable.

mn105:10.2.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:10.3.verse: But when talk connected with worldly pleasures of the flesh is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:11.1.verse: Suppose there was a fallen, withered leaf. It’s incapable of becoming green again.

mn105:11.2.verse: In the same way, an individual intent on the imperturbable has dropped the connection with worldly pleasures of the flesh.

mn105:11.4.verse: ‘That individual is intent on the imperturbable, for they’re detached from things connected with pleasures of the flesh.’

mn105:12.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain individual person may be intent on the dimension of nothingness.

mn105:12.2.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:12.3.verse: But when talk connected with the imperturbable is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:13.1.verse: Suppose there was a broad rock that had been broken in half, so that it could not be put back together again.

mn105:13.2.verse: In the same way, an individual intent on the dimension of nothingness has broken the connection with the imperturbable.

mn105:13.4.verse: ‘That individual is intent on the dimension of nothingness, for they’re detached from things connected with the imperturbable.’

mn105:14.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain individual person may be intent on the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn105:14.2.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:14.3.verse: But when talk connected with the dimension of nothingness is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:15.1.verse: Suppose someone had eaten some satisfying food and thrown it up.

mn105:15.3.verse: Would that person want to eat that food again?”

mn105:15.6.verse: Because that food is deemed repulsive.”

mn105:15.7.verse: “In the same way, an individual intent on the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception has vomited the connection with the dimension of nothingness.

mn105:15.9.verse: ‘That individual is intent on the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, for they’re detached from things connected with the dimension of nothingness.’

mn105:16.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain individual person may be rightly intent on extinguishment.

mn105:16.2.verse: Such an individual engages in pertinent conversation, thinking and considering in line with that. They associate with that kind of person, and they find it rewarding.

mn105:16.3.verse: But when talk connected with the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception is going on they don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They don’t associate with that kind of person, and they don’t find it rewarding.

mn105:17.1.verse: Suppose there was a palm tree with its crown cut off. It’s incapable of further growth.

mn105:17.2.verse: In the same way, an individual rightly intent on extinguishment has cut off the connection with the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn105:17.4.verse: ‘That individual is rightly intent on extinguishment, for they’re detached from things connected with the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn105:18.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain mendicant might think:

mn105:18.2.verse: ‘The Ascetic has said that craving is a dart; and that the poison of ignorance is inflicted by desire and ill will.

mn105:18.3.verse: I have given up the dart of craving and expelled the poison of ignorance; I am rightly intent on extinguishment.’

mn105:18.4.verse: Having such conceit, though it’s not based in fact,

mn105:18.5.verse: they would engage in things unconducive to extinguishment: unsuitable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

mn105:18.6.verse: Doing so, lust infects their mind,

mn105:18.7.verse: resulting in death or deadly pain.

mn105:19.1.verse: Suppose a man was struck by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn105:19.2.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn105:19.3.verse: The surgeon would cut open the wound with a scalpel,

mn105:19.5.verse: extract it, and expel the poison, leaving some residue behind.

mn105:19.6.verse: Imagining that no residue remained, the surgeon would say:

mn105:19.7.verse: ‘My man, the dart has been extracted and the poison expelled without residue.

mn105:19.8.verse: It is still capable of harming you.

mn105:19.9.verse: Eat only suitable food. Don’t eat unsuitable food, or else the wound may get infected.

mn105:19.10.verse: Regularly wash the wound and anoint the opening, or else it’ll get covered with pus and blood.

mn105:19.11.verse: Don’t walk too much in the wind and sun, or else dust and dirt will infect the wound.

mn105:19.12.verse: Take care of the wound, my man, heal it.’

mn105:20.2.verse: ‘The dart has been extracted and the poison expelled with no residue.

mn105:20.3.verse: It’s not capable of harming me.’

mn105:20.4.verse: They’d eat unsuitable food, and the wound would get infected.

mn105:20.5.verse: And they wouldn’t regularly wash and anoint the opening, so it would get covered in pus and blood.

mn105:20.6.verse: And they’d walk too much in the wind and sun, so dust and dirt infected the wound.

mn105:20.7.verse: And they wouldn’t take care of the wound or heal it.

mn105:20.8.verse: Then both because they did what was unsuitable, and because of the residue of unclean poison, the wound would expand,

mn105:20.9.verse: resulting in death or deadly pain.

mn105:21.1.verse: In the same way, it’s possible that a certain mendicant might think:

mn105:21.2.verse: ‘The Ascetic has said that craving is a dart; and that the poison of ignorance is inflicted by desire and ill will.

mn105:21.3.verse: I have given up the dart of craving and expelled the poison of ignorance; I am rightly intent on extinguishment.’

mn105:21.4.verse: Having such conceit, though it’s not based in fact,

mn105:21.5.verse: they would engage in things unconducive to extinguishment: unsuitable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

mn105:21.6.verse: Doing so, lust infects their mind,

mn105:21.7.verse: resulting in death or deadly pain.

mn105:22.1.verse: For it is death in the training of the Noble One to resign the training and return to a lesser life.

mn105:22.2.verse: And it is deadly pain to commit one of the corrupt offenses.

mn105:23.1.verse: It’s possible that a certain mendicant might think:

mn105:23.2.verse: ‘The Ascetic has said that craving is a dart; and that the poison of ignorance is inflicted by desire and ill will.

mn105:23.3.verse: I have given up the dart of craving and expelled the poison of ignorance; I am rightly intent on extinguishment.’

mn105:23.4.verse: Being rightly intent on extinguishment, they wouldn’t engage in things unconducive to extinguishment: unsuitable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

mn105:23.5.verse: Doing so, lust wouldn’t infect their mind,

mn105:23.6.verse: so no death or deadly pain would result.

mn105:24.1.verse: Suppose a man was struck by an arrow thickly smeared with poison.

mn105:24.2.verse: Their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin would get a surgeon to treat them.

mn105:24.3.verse: The surgeon would cut open the wound with a scalpel,

mn105:24.5.verse: extract it, and expel the poison, leaving no residue behind.

mn105:24.6.verse: Knowing that no residue remained, the surgeon would say:

mn105:24.7.verse: ‘My man, the dart has been extracted and the poison expelled with no residue.

mn105:24.8.verse: It’s not capable of harming you.

mn105:24.9.verse: Eat only suitable food. Don’t eat unsuitable food, or else the wound may get infected.

mn105:24.10.verse: Regularly wash the wound and anoint the opening, or else it’ll get covered with pus and blood.

mn105:24.11.verse: Don’t walk too much in the wind and sun, or else dust and dirt will infect the wound.

mn105:24.12.verse: Take care of the wound, my man, heal it.’

mn105:25.2.verse: ‘The dart has been extracted and the poison expelled with no residue.

mn105:25.3.verse: It’s not capable of harming me.’

mn105:25.4.verse: They’d eat suitable food, and the wound wouldn’t get infected.

mn105:25.5.verse: And they’d regularly wash and anoint the opening, so it wouldn’t get covered in pus and blood.

mn105:25.6.verse: And they wouldn’t walk too much in the wind and sun, so dust and dirt wouldn’t infect the wound.

mn105:25.7.verse: And they’d take care of the wound and heal it.

mn105:25.8.verse: Then both because they did what was suitable, and the unclean poison had left no residue, the wound would heal,

mn105:25.9.verse: and no death or deadly pain would result.

mn105:26.1.verse: In the same way, it’s possible that a certain mendicant might think:

mn105:26.2.verse: ‘The Ascetic has said that craving is a dart; and that the poison of ignorance is inflicted by desire and ill will.

mn105:26.3.verse: I have given up the dart of craving and expelled the poison of ignorance; I am rightly intent on extinguishment.’

mn105:26.4.verse: Being rightly intent on extinguishment, they wouldn’t engage in things unconducive to extinguishment: unsuitable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

mn105:26.5.verse: Doing so, lust wouldn’t infect their mind,

mn105:26.6.verse: so no death or deadly pain would result.

mn105:27.1.verse: I’ve made up this simile to make a point.

mn105:27.3.verse: ‘Wound’ is a term for the six interior sense fields.

mn105:27.7.verse: ‘Scalpel’ is a term for noble wisdom.

mn105:27.8.verse: ‘Surgeon’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn105:28.1.verse: Truly, Sunakkhatta, that mendicant practices restraint regarding the six fields of contact.

mn105:28.2.verse: Understanding that attachment is the root of suffering, they are freed with the ending of attachments. It’s not possible that they would apply their body or interest their mind in any attachment.

mn105:29.1.verse: Suppose there was a bronze goblet of beverage that had a nice color, aroma, and flavor.

mn105:29.2.verse: But it was mixed with poison.

mn105:29.3.verse: Then a person would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.

mn105:29.5.verse: Would that person drink that beverage if they knew that

mn105:29.6.verse: it would result in death or deadly suffering?”

mn105:29.8.verse: “In the same way, Sunakkhatta, that mendicant practices restraint regarding the six fields of contact.

mn105:29.9.verse: Understanding that attachment is the root of suffering, they are freed with the ending of attachments. It’s not possible that they would apply their body or interest their mind in any attachment.

mn105:30.1.verse: Suppose there was a lethal viper.

mn105:30.2.verse: Then a person would come along who wants to live and doesn’t want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain.

mn105:30.4.verse: Would that person give that lethal viper their hand or finger if they knew that

mn105:30.5.verse: it would result in death or deadly suffering?”

mn105:30.7.verse: “In the same way, Sunakkhatta, that mendicant practices restraint regarding the six fields of contact.

mn105:30.8.verse: Understanding that attachment is the root of suffering, they are freed with the ending of attachments. It’s not possible that they would apply their body or interest their mind in any attachment.”

mn105:30.10.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn105:30.11.verse: Satisfied, Sunakkhatta of the Licchavi clan approved what the Buddha said.

mn106:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kuru Country, at a town of the Kurus called Kammāsadamma.[^1]

mn106:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn106:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, sensual desires are impermanent, hollow, false, false-natured,

mn106:2.2.verse: made up of illusion, and fools’ talk.

mn106:2.3.verse: Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:2.4.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come—

mn106:2.5.verse: are alike Māra’s realm, Māra’s domain, Māra’s bait, Māra’s hunting-ground.

mn106:2.6.verse: Evil unprofitable notions of covetousness and ill-will and ambition lead on here, in this sensual desire sphere,

mn106:2.7.verse: and they obstruct the training of a noble disciple here.

mn106:3.1.verse: ‘Now, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:3.2.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:3.3.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come—

mn106:3.4.verse: are alike Māra’s realm, Māra’s domain, Māra’s bait, Māra’s hunting-ground.

mn106:3.5.verse: Evil unprofitable notions of covetousness and ill-will and ambition lead on here, in this sensual desire sphere,

mn106:3.6.verse: and they obstruct the training of a noble disciple here.

mn106:3.7.verse: Suppose I were to abide with mind abundant and exalted, by transcending the world and resolving firmly with the mind:[^2]

mn106:3.8.verse: then there would be no more evil unprofitable notions of covetousness and ill-will and ambition in me,

mn106:3.9.verse: and with the abandoning of them my mind would be limited no longer; it would become measureless and well developed.”

mn106:3.10.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:3.11.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the Imperturbable,[^3] or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:3.12.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to one of the Imperturbable states.

mn106:3.13.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the first way directed to the Imperturbable.

mn106:4.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:4.2.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:4.3.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come;

mn106:4.4.verse: whatever is form, all form is the four great primary elements and the form derived from the four great primary elements.”[^4]

mn106:4.5.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:4.6.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the Imperturbable, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:4.7.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to one of the Imperturbable states.

mn106:4.8.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the second way directed to the Imperturbable.

mn106:5.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:5.2.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:5.3.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come;

mn106:5.4.verse: forms here and now and forms in lives to come,

mn106:5.5.verse: perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come—

mn106:5.7.verse: What is impermanent is not worth relishing, not worth affirming, not worth accepting.”

mn106:5.8.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:5.9.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the Imperturbable, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:5.10.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to one of the Imperturbable states.

mn106:5.11.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the third way directed to the Imperturbable.

mn106:6.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:6.2.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:6.3.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come;

mn106:6.4.verse: forms here and now and forms in lives to come,

mn106:6.5.verse: perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come;

mn106:6.8.verse: Where these perceptions cease without remainder, that is more peaceful, that is a superior goal,

mn106:6.9.verse: that is to say, the base consisting of nothingness.”

mn106:6.10.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:6.11.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the base consisting of nothingness, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:6.12.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:6.13.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the first way directed to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:7.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, considers thus:

mn106:7.2.verse: “This is void of self or of a self’s property.”[^5]

mn106:7.3.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:7.4.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the base consisting of nothingness, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:7.5.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:7.6.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the second way directed to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:8.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:8.2.verse: “I am not anywhere anyone’s owning; nor is there anywhere my owning in anyone.”[^6]

mn106:8.3.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:8.4.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the base consisting of nothingness, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:8.5.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:8.6.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the third way directed to the base consisting of nothingness.

mn106:9.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:9.2.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:9.3.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come;

mn106:9.4.verse: forms here and now and forms in lives to come,

mn106:9.5.verse: perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come;

mn106:9.6.verse: perceptions of the Imperturbable, and perceptions of the base consisting of nothingness—

mn106:9.8.verse: Where these perceptions cease without remainder, that is more peaceful, that is a superior goal,

mn106:9.9.verse: that is to say, the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

mn106:9.10.verse: When he enters upon this way and abides in it often, his mind acquires confidence in this base.

mn106:9.11.verse: Once there is full confidence, then he either enters upon the way to rebirth in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or else he decides to perfect understanding by reaching Arahantship.

mn106:9.12.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, it is possible that that consciousness of his which leads on to rebirth may pass on, upon rebirth, to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn106:9.13.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the way directed to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’

mn106:10.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

mn106:10.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, here a bhikkhu enters upon this way:

mn106:10.3.verse: “If I were not, and naught were mine, I shall not be and naught will be mine. And what there is, has come to be, that I abandon”,[^7]

mn106:10.5.verse: Venerable sir, does such a bhikkhu attain final Nibbāna, or does he not?’

mn106:10.6.verse: ‘Ānanda, one such bhikkhu might attain final Nibbāna, another such bhikkhu might not attain final Nibbāna.’

mn106:10.7.verse: ‘Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why one might attain final Nibbāna and another might not?’

mn106:10.8.verse: ‘Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu enters upon this way:

mn106:10.9.verse: “If I were not, and naught were mine, I shall not be and naught will be mine. And what there is, has come to be, that I abandon”,

mn106:10.11.verse: He relishes that equanimity, welcomes it, and holds to it.

mn106:10.12.verse: As he relishes that equanimity, welcomes it, and holds to it, his consciousness comes to depend on it and to cling to it.

mn106:10.13.verse: A bhikkhu who is affected by clinging, Ānanda, does not attain final Nibbāna.’

mn106:11.1.verse: ‘But, venerable sir, when that bhikkhu clings, what does he cling to?’

mn106:11.2.verse: ‘To the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, Ānanda.’

mn106:11.3.verse: ‘It seems, venerable sir, that when that bhikkhu clings, he clings to the best of the objects for clinging?’[^8]

mn106:11.4.verse: ‘When that bhikkhu clings, Ānanda, he does cling to the best of the objects for clinging.

mn106:11.5.verse: For this is the best of the objects for clinging, namely,

mn106:12.1.verse: ‘Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu enters upon this way:

mn106:12.2.verse: “If I were not, and naught were mine, I shall not be and naught will be mine. And what there is, has come to be, that I abandon”,

mn106:12.4.verse: He does not relish that equanimity, does not welcome it, and does not hold to it.

mn106:12.5.verse: As he does not relish that equanimity, does not welcome it, and does not hold to it, his consciousness does not come to depend on it and does not cling to it.

mn106:12.6.verse: A bhikkhu who is without clinging, Ānanda, attains final Nibbāna.’

mn106:13.1.verse: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous!

mn106:13.2.verse: For each stage, it seems, the crossing of the flood has been told to us by the Blessed One, depending on this, then on that.

mn106:13.3.verse: But, venerable sir, what is the Noble One’s liberation?’

mn106:13.4.verse: ‘Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple considers thus:

mn106:13.5.verse: “Sensual desires here and now and sensual desires in lives to come,

mn106:13.6.verse: perceptions of sensual desires here and now and perceptions of sensual desires in lives to come;

mn106:13.7.verse: forms here and now and forms in lives to come,

mn106:13.8.verse: perceptions of forms here and now and perceptions of forms in lives to come;

mn106:13.9.verse: perceptions of the Imperturbable, perceptions of the base consisting of nothingness, and perceptions of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—

mn106:13.10.verse: that is embodiment, that is as far as embodiment extends.

mn106:13.11.verse: This is the deathless, that is to say, the liberation of the mind through not clinging.’

mn106:14.1.verse: ‘So, Ānanda, I have shown the way directed to the Imperturbable, I have shown the way directed to the base consisting of nothingness, I have shown the way directed to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I have shown for each stage the crossing of the flood, depending on this, then on that, and I have shown the Noble One’s liberation.

mn106:15.1.verse: ‘Ānanda, what should be done for his disciples out of compassion by a teacher who seeks their welfare and has compassion for them, that I have done for you, Ānanda.

mn106:15.2.verse: There are these roots of trees, there are these empty huts. Meditate,[^9] Ānanda, do not delay, lest you regret it later. This is our instruction to you.’

mn106:15.3.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn106:15.4.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn106:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.

mn106:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn106:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, false, and deceptive.

mn106:2.2.verse: This is made by illusion, mendicants, lamented by fools.

mn106:2.3.verse: Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:2.4.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come;

mn106:2.5.verse: both of these are Māra’s dominion, Māra’s domain, Māra’s lair, and Māra’s range.

mn106:2.6.verse: They conduce to bad, unskillful notions such as desire, ill will, and aggression.

mn106:2.7.verse: And they create an obstacle for a noble disciple training here.

mn106:3.1.verse: A noble disciple reflects on this:

mn106:3.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:3.3.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come;

mn106:3.4.verse: both of these are Māra’s dominion, Māra’s domain, Māra’s lair, and Māra’s range.

mn106:3.5.verse: They conduce to bad, unskillful notions such as desire, ill will, and aggression.

mn106:3.6.verse: And they create an obstacle for a noble disciple training here.

mn106:3.7.verse: Why don’t I meditate with an abundant, expansive heart, having mastered the world and stabilized the mind?

mn106:3.8.verse: Then I will have no more bad, unskillful notions such as desire, ill will, and aggression.

mn106:3.9.verse: And by giving them up my mind, no longer limited, will become limitless and well developed.’

mn106:3.10.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:3.11.verse: Being confident, they either attain the imperturbable now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:3.12.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the imperturbable.

mn106:3.13.verse: This is said to be the first way of practice suitable for attaining the imperturbable.

mn106:4.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:4.3.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come;

mn106:4.4.verse: whatever form there is, all form is the four principal states, or form derived from the four principal states.’

mn106:4.5.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:4.6.verse: Being confident, they either attain the imperturbable now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:4.7.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the imperturbable.

mn106:4.8.verse: This is said to be the second way of practice suitable for attaining the imperturbable.

mn106:5.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:5.3.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:5.4.verse: visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:5.5.verse: perceptions of visions in this life and in lives to come;

mn106:5.7.verse: And what’s impermanent is not worth approving, welcoming, or clinging to.’

mn106:5.8.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:5.9.verse: Being confident, they either attain the imperturbable now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:5.10.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the imperturbable.

mn106:5.11.verse: This is said to be the third way of practice suitable for attaining the imperturbable.

mn106:6.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:6.3.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:6.4.verse: visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:6.5.verse: perceptions of visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:6.8.verse: Where they cease without remainder, that is peaceful, that is sublime,

mn106:6.10.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:6.11.verse: Being confident, they either attain the dimension of nothingness now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:6.12.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:6.13.verse: This is said to be the first way of practice suitable for attaining the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a noble disciple has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

mn106:7.2.verse: ‘This is empty of a self or what belongs to a self.’

mn106:7.3.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:7.4.verse: Being confident, they either attain the dimension of nothingness now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:7.5.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:7.6.verse: This is said to be the second way of practice suitable for attaining the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:8.2.verse: ‘I don’t belong to anyone anywhere! And nothing belongs to me anywhere!’

mn106:8.3.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:8.4.verse: Being confident, they either attain the dimension of nothingness now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:8.5.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:8.6.verse: This is said to be the third way of practice suitable for attaining the dimension of nothingness.

mn106:9.2.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:9.3.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:9.4.verse: visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:9.5.verse: perceptions of visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:9.6.verse: perceptions of the imperturbable, and perceptions of the dimension of nothingness;

mn106:9.8.verse: Where they cease without remainder, that is peaceful, that is sublime,

mn106:9.9.verse: namely the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn106:9.10.verse: Practicing in this way and meditating on it often their mind becomes confident in this dimension.

mn106:9.11.verse: Being confident, they either attain the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception now, or are freed by wisdom.

mn106:9.12.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, it’s possible that that conducive consciousness will be reborn in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn106:9.13.verse: This is said to be the way of practice suitable for attaining the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.”

mn106:10.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha:

mn106:10.2.verse: “Sir, take a mendicant who practices like this:

mn106:10.3.verse: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’

mn106:10.4.verse: In this way they gain equanimity.

mn106:10.5.verse: Would that mendicant become extinguished or not?”

mn106:10.6.verse: “One such mendicant might become extinguished, Ānanda, while another might not.”

mn106:10.7.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason for this?”

mn106:10.8.verse: “Ānanda, take a mendicant who practices like this:

mn106:10.9.verse: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’

mn106:10.10.verse: In this way they gain equanimity.

mn106:10.11.verse: They approve, welcome, and keep clinging to that equanimity.

mn106:10.12.verse: Their consciousness has that as support and fuel for grasping.

mn106:10.13.verse: A mendicant with fuel for grasping does not become extinguished.”

mn106:11.1.verse: “But sir, what is that mendicant grasping?”

mn106:11.2.verse: “The dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.”

mn106:11.3.verse: “Sir, it seems that mendicant is grasping the best thing to grasp!”

mn106:11.5.verse: For the best thing to grasp is

mn106:11.6.verse: the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn106:12.1.verse: Take a mendicant who practices like this:

mn106:12.2.verse: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’

mn106:12.3.verse: In this way they gain equanimity.

mn106:12.4.verse: They don’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging to that equanimity.

mn106:12.5.verse: So their consciousness doesn’t have that as support and fuel for grasping.

mn106:12.6.verse: A mendicant free of grasping becomes extinguished.”

mn106:13.2.verse: It seems the Buddha has explained to us how to cross over the flood by relying on one support or another.

mn106:13.3.verse: But sir, what is noble liberation?”

mn106:13.4.verse: “Ānanda, it’s when a noble disciple reflects like this:

mn106:13.5.verse: ‘Sensual pleasures in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:13.6.verse: sensual perceptions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:13.7.verse: visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:13.8.verse: perceptions of visions in this life and in lives to come,

mn106:13.9.verse: perceptions of the imperturbable, perceptions of the dimension of nothingness, perceptions of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception;

mn106:13.10.verse: that is substantial reality as far as substantial reality extends.

mn106:13.11.verse: But this is freedom from death, namely the liberation of the mind by not grasping.’

mn106:14.1.verse: So, Ānanda, I have taught the ways of practice suitable for attaining the imperturbable, the dimension of nothingness, and the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. I have taught how to cross the flood by relying on one support or another, and I have taught noble liberation.

mn106:15.1.verse: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

mn106:15.2.verse: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, Ānanda! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

mn106:15.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn106:15.4.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn107:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.

mn107:1.3.verse: Then the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

mn107:1.4.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn107:2.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, in this palace of Migāra’s Mother there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,

mn107:2.2.verse: down to the last step of the stair.[^1]

mn107:2.3.verse: And also in the case of these brahmins there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,

mn107:2.5.verse: And also in the case of these archers there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,

mn107:2.7.verse: And also in the case of us accountants, who get our living by accountancy, there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,

mn107:2.9.verse: For, Master Gotama, when we get an apprentice, we first make him count thus:

mn107:2.10.verse: ‘One, ones; two, twos; three, threes; four, fours; five, fives; six, sixes; seven, sevens; eight, eights; nine, nines; ten, tens.’

mn107:2.11.verse: And we make him count a hundred too, and more than that too.

mn107:2.12.verse: Now, Master Gotama, is it possible, in the case of this Dhamma and Discipline, to describe progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice in the same way?’

mn107:3.1.verse: ‘It is possible, brahmin, in the case of this Dhamma and Discipline to describe progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice.

mn107:3.2.verse: Just as, brahmin, a skilled tamer of horses, on getting a fine thoroughbred, first makes him do exercises with the bit in his mouth, and afterwards makes him do further exercises;

mn107:3.3.verse: so too, brahmin, when the Tathāgata gets a person to be tamed, he first disciplines him thus:

mn107:3.4.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha,[^2] perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, train by undertaking the training precepts.’

mn107:4.1.verse: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, trains by undertaking the training precepts, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn107:4.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, guard the doors of the faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features.

mn107:4.3.verse: Since, if you left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the eye faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye faculty.

mn107:4.4.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn107:4.5.verse: on smelling an odour with the nose …

mn107:4.6.verse: on tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn107:4.7.verse: on touching a tangible with the body …

mn107:4.8.verse: on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features.

mn107:4.9.verse: Since, if you left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the mind faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.’

mn107:5.1.verse: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu guards the doors of the faculties, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn107:5.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, be one who knows the right amount in eating.

mn107:5.3.verse: Reflecting wisely, you should take food

mn107:5.4.verse: neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the life divine, thinking: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.”’[^3]

mn107:6.1.verse: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu knows the right amount in eating, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn107:6.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, abide devoted to wakefulness. By day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the middle watch of the night, lie down on the right side in the lion’s pose, with one foot overlapping[^4] the other, mindful and fully aware, having noted in your mind the time for rising. After rising, in the third watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas.’

mn107:7.1.verse: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn107:7.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, possess mindfulness and full awareness. Act in full awareness when going forward and returning; act in full awareness when looking ahead and looking away; act in full awareness when flexing and extending your limbs; act in full awareness when wearing your outer cloak, bowl and robes; act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; act in full awareness when defecating and urinating; act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.’

mn107:8.1.verse: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu possesses mindfulness and full awareness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn107:8.2.verse: ‘Come, bhikkhu, resort to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.’

mn107:9.1.verse: He resorts to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn107:9.2.verse: On returning from his alms round, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.

mn107:9.3.verse: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.

mn107:9.4.verse: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred.

mn107:9.5.verse: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness.

mn107:9.6.verse: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled within; he purifies his mind of agitation and worry.

mn107:9.7.verse: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides having crossed beyond uncertainty, unperplexed about profitable dhammas; he purifies his mind of uncertainty.

mn107:10.1.verse: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn107:10.2.verse: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn107:10.3.verse: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn107:10.4.verse: With the fading as well of happiness, he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn107:10.5.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn107:11.1.verse: This, brahmin, is the kind of instruction I give to those bhikkhus who are in higher training, whose minds have not yet attained the goal, who abide aspiring to the supreme surcease of bondage.

mn107:11.2.verse: But for those bhikkhus who are Arahants with taints exhausted, who have lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, who, through knowing rightly, are liberated, these dhammas conduce to a pleasant abiding here and now and to mindfulness and full awareness.’

mn107:12.1.verse: When this was said, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn107:12.2.verse: ‘Master Gotama, when Master Gotama’s disciples are thus advised and instructed by him, do they all attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, or do some not attain it?’

mn107:12.3.verse: ‘Brahmin, some of my disciples, when thus advised and instructed by me, attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it.’

mn107:13.1.verse: ‘Master Gotama, since there is Nibbāna, and there is the path leading to Nibbāna, and there is Master Gotama as guide,

mn107:13.2.verse: what is the cause, what is the reason, why, when Master Gotama’s disciples are thus advised and instructed by him, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it?’

mn107:14.1.verse: ‘Well then, brahmin, I shall question you about this in return. Answer as you see fit.

mn107:14.3.verse: Are you skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha?’

mn107:14.4.verse: ‘Yes, sir, I am skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha.’

mn107:14.6.verse: Suppose a man came here wanting to go to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.8.verse: “Venerable sir, I want to go to Rājagaha;

mn107:14.9.verse: show me the road to Rājagaha.”

mn107:14.11.verse: “Well, good man, this road goes to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.12.verse: Follow it for a while, and you will see a certain village; follow it for a while, and you will see a certain town;

mn107:14.13.verse: follow it for a while, and you will see Rājagaha with its delightful parks, delightful woods, delightful lands and delightful lotus pools.”

mn107:14.14.verse: Though advised and instructed by you thus, he might take the wrong road and go west.

mn107:14.15.verse: Then a second man came here wanting to go to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.17.verse: “Venerable sir, I want to go to Rājagaha;

mn107:14.18.verse: show me the road to Rājagaha.”

mn107:14.20.verse: “Well, good man, this road goes to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.21.verse: Follow it for a while, and you will see a certain village;

mn107:14.22.verse: follow it for a while, and you will see a certain town;

mn107:14.23.verse: follow it for a while, and you will see Rājagaha with its delightful parks, delightful woods, delightful lands and delightful lotus pools.”

mn107:14.24.verse: Advised and instructed by you thus, he might get safely to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.25.verse: What is the cause, what is the reason, brahmin, why, since there is Rājagaha, and there is the road leading to Rājagaha, and there is you as guide,

mn107:14.26.verse: yet when advised and instructed by you thus, one man takes the wrong road and goes west, and the other gets safely to Rājagaha?’

mn107:14.27.verse: ‘What can I do about that, Master Gotama?

mn107:14.28.verse: I am only one who points out the way, Master Gotama.’

mn107:14.29.verse: ‘So too, brahmin, there is Nibbāna, and there is the path leading to Nibbāna, and there am I as guide;

mn107:14.30.verse: yet when my disciples are thus advised and instructed by me, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it.

mn107:14.31.verse: What can I do about that, brahmin?

mn107:14.32.verse: The Tathāgata is only one who points out the way, brahmin.’

mn107:15.1.verse: When this was said, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:

mn107:15.2.verse: “As to those persons, Master Gotama, who are faithless, who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness not out of faith but seeking a livelihood, who are fraudulent, deceitful, treacherous, haughty,[^5] hollow, vain, rough-tongued, loose-spoken, unguarded in the faculties, immoderate in eating, undevoted to wakefulness, unconcerned with the ascetic life, without deep respect for the training, luxurious, lax, foremost in backsliding, neglectful of seclusion, lazy, lacking energy, unmindful, lacking full awareness, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, witless, and drivelling—Master Gotama does not dwell together with these.

mn107:15.3.verse: But as to those clansmen who have gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, who are not fraudulent, not deceitful, not treacherous, not haughty, not hollow, not vain, not rough-tongued, not loose-spoken, guarded in the faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, concerned with the ascetic life, with deep respect for the training, not luxurious, not lax, foremost in avoiding backsliding, foremost in seclusion, energetic, resolute, with mindfulness set up, fully aware, concentrated, with unified minds, possessing understanding, and not drivelling—Master Gotama dwells together with these.

mn107:16.1.verse: Just as, of root perfumes of any kind, black orris root is reckoned the best;

mn107:16.2.verse: of heartwood perfumes of any kind, red sandalwood is reckoned the best;

mn107:16.3.verse: of flower perfumes of any kind, jasmine is reckoned the best;

mn107:16.4.verse: so too, Master Gotama’s advice is supreme among the dhammas of the present day.

mn107:17.2.verse: Master Gotama has made the Dhamma clear in many ways, as though he were turning upright what had been overthrown, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyes to see forms.

mn107:17.3.verse: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

mn107:17.4.verse: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’”

mn107:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn107:1.3.verse: Then the brahmin Moggallāna the Accountant went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn107:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

mn107:2.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, in this stilt longhouse we can see gradual training, gradual progress, and gradual practice

mn107:2.2.verse: down to the last step of the staircase.

mn107:2.3.verse: Among the brahmins we can see gradual training, gradual progress, and gradual practice

mn107:2.5.verse: Among archers we can see gradual training, gradual progress, and gradual practice

mn107:2.7.verse: Among us accountants, who earn a living by accounting, we can see gradual training, gradual progress, and gradual practice

mn107:2.9.verse: For when we get an apprentice we first make them count:

mn107:2.10.verse: ‘One one, two twos, three threes, four fours, five fives, six sixes, seven sevens, eight eights, nine nines, ten tens.’

mn107:2.11.verse: We even make them count up to a hundred.

mn107:2.12.verse: Is it possible to similarly describe a gradual training, gradual progress, and gradual practice in this teaching and training?”

mn107:3.2.verse: Suppose a deft horse trainer were to obtain a fine thoroughbred. First of all he’d make it get used to wearing the bit.

mn107:3.3.verse: In the same way, when the Realized One gets a person fit for training they first guide them like this:

mn107:3.4.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, be ethical and restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourself well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.’

mn107:4.1.verse: When they have ethical conduct, the Realized One guides them further:

mn107:4.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, guard your sense doors. When you see a sight with your eyes, don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn107:4.3.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, practice restraint, protect the faculty of sight, and achieve its restraint.

mn107:4.4.verse: When you hear a sound with your ears …

mn107:4.5.verse: When you smell an odor with your nose …

mn107:4.6.verse: When you taste a flavor with your tongue …

mn107:4.7.verse: When you feel a touch with your body …

mn107:4.8.verse: When you know an idea with your mind, don’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn107:4.9.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, practice restraint, protect the faculty of mind, and achieve its restraint.’

mn107:5.1.verse: When they guard their sense doors, the Realized One guides them further:

mn107:5.3.verse: Reflect rationally on the food that you eat:

mn107:5.4.verse: “Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.”’

mn107:6.1.verse: When they eat in moderation, the Realized One guides them further:

mn107:6.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, be committed to wakefulness. Practice walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying your mind from obstacles. In the first watch of the night, continue to practice walking and sitting meditation. In the middle watch, lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up. In the last watch, get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying your mind from obstacles.’

mn107:7.1.verse: When they are committed to wakefulness, the Realized One guides them further:

mn107:7.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, have mindfulness and situational awareness. Act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.’

mn107:8.1.verse: When they have mindfulness and situational awareness, the Realized One guides them further:

mn107:8.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.’

mn107:9.2.verse: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and bring mindfulness to the present.

mn107:9.3.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn107:9.4.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn107:9.5.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn107:9.6.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn107:9.7.verse: Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn107:10.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn107:10.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn107:10.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn107:10.4.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn107:10.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn107:11.1.verse: That’s how I instruct the mendicants who are trainees—who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

mn107:11.2.verse: But for those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—these things lead to blissful meditation in this life, and to mindfulness and awareness.”

mn107:12.1.verse: When he had spoken, Moggallāna the Accountant said to the Buddha,

mn107:12.2.verse: “When his disciples are instructed and advised like this by the worthy Gotama, do all of them achieve the ultimate goal, extinguishment, or do some of them fail?”

mn107:13.1.verse: “What is the cause, worthy Gotama, what is the reason why, though extinguishment is present, the path leading to extinguishment is present, and the worthy Gotama is present to encourage them,

mn107:13.2.verse: still some succeed while others fail?”

mn107:14.1.verse: “Well then, brahmin, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn107:14.3.verse: Are you skilled in the road to Rājagaha?”

mn107:14.6.verse: Suppose a person was to come along who wanted to go to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.8.verse: ‘Sir, I wish to go to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.9.verse: Please point out the road to Rājagaha.’

mn107:14.11.verse: ‘Here, my man, this road goes to Rājagaha.

mn107:14.12.verse: Go along it for an hour, and you’ll see a certain village. Go along an hour further, and you’ll see a certain town.

mn107:14.13.verse: Go along an hour further and you’ll see Rājagaha with its delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds.’

mn107:14.14.verse: Instructed like this by you, they might still take the wrong road, heading west.

mn107:14.15.verse: But a second person might come with the same question and receive the same instructions.

mn107:14.24.verse: Instructed by you, they might safely arrive at Rājagaha.

mn107:14.25.verse: What is the cause, brahmin, what is the reason why, though Rājagaha is present, the path leading to Rājagaha is present, and you are there to encourage them,

mn107:14.26.verse: one person takes the wrong path and heads west, while another arrives safely at Rājagaha?”

mn107:14.27.verse: “What can I do about that, worthy Gotama?

mn107:14.28.verse: I am the one who shows the way.”

mn107:14.29.verse: “In the same way, though extinguishment is present, the path leading to extinguishment is present, and I am present to encourage them,

mn107:14.30.verse: still some of my disciples, instructed and advised like this, achieve the ultimate goal, extinguishment, while some of them fail.

mn107:14.31.verse: What can I do about that, brahmin?

mn107:14.32.verse: The Realized One is the one who shows the way.”

mn107:15.1.verse: When he had spoken, Moggallāna the Accountant said to the Buddha,

mn107:15.2.verse: “Worthy Gotama, there are those faithless individuals who went forth from the lay life to homelessness not out of faith but to earn a livelihood. They’re devious, deceitful, and sneaky. They’re haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, and loose-tongued. They do not guard their sense doors or eat in moderation, and they are not committed to wakefulness. They don’t care about the ascetic life, and don’t keenly respect the training. They’re indulgent and slack, leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion, lazy, and lacking energy. They’re unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds, witless and idiotic. The worthy Gotama does not live together with these.

mn107:15.3.verse: But there are those gentlemen who went forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith. They’re not devious, deceitful, and sneaky. They’re not haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, and loose-tongued. They guard their sense doors and eat in moderation, and they are committed to wakefulness. They care about the ascetic life, and keenly respect the training. They’re not indulgent or slack, nor are they leaders in backsliding, neglecting seclusion. They’re energetic and determined. They’re mindful, with situational awareness, immersion, and unified minds; wise and clever. The worthy Gotama does live together with these.

mn107:16.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant root, spikenard is said to be the best.

mn107:16.2.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant heartwood, red sandalwood is said to be the best.

mn107:16.3.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant flower, jasmine is said to be the best.

mn107:16.4.verse: In the same way, worthy Gotama’s advice is the best of contemporary teachings.

mn107:17.2.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the Teaching clear in many ways.

mn107:17.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn107:17.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

mn108:1.2.verse: On one occasion the venerable Ānanda was living at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.

mn108:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, King of Magadha, was having Rājagaha fortified, being suspicious of King Pajjota.

mn108:3.1.verse: Then, when it was morning, the venerable Ānanda dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Rājagaha for alms.

mn108:3.2.verse: Then it occurred to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:3.3.verse: “It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

mn108:3.4.verse: What if I went to where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna is at work, to see the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna?”

mn108:4.1.verse: Then the venerable Ānanda went to where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna was at work, to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna.

mn108:4.2.verse: The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw the venerable Ānanda coming in the distance.

mn108:4.3.verse: On seeing him, he said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:4.6.verse: It is long since Master Ānanda found the opportunity to come here.

mn108:4.7.verse: Let Master Ānanda be seated; this seat is ready.”

mn108:4.8.verse: The venerable Ānanda sat down on the seat made ready.

mn108:4.9.verse: The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna took a certain low seat and sat down at one side.

mn108:4.10.verse: When he had done so, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:5.1.verse: “Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu who possesses in every way and in every part those dhammas that Master Gotama, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, possessed?”

mn108:5.2.verse: “There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, who possesses in every way and in every part those dhammas that the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, possessed.

mn108:5.3.verse: For, brahmin, the Blessed One was the arouser of the path unarisen, the producer of the path unproduced, the declarer of the path undeclared; he was the knower of the path, the finder of the path, one skilled in the path;

mn108:5.4.verse: but his disciples now abide following the path, and become possessed of it afterwards.”[^1]

mn108:6.1.verse: Now this conversation between the venerable Ānanda and the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna was left unfinished.

mn108:6.2.verse: For then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, who was supervising the works at Rājagaha, went to where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna was at work, to the venerable Ānanda, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn108:6.3.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:6.4.verse: “For what talk, Master Ānanda, are you sitting together now, and what was your conversation that was left unfinished?”

mn108:6.5.verse: “Here, brahmin, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said this to me:

mn108:6.6.verse: ‘Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu who possesses in every way and in every part those dhammas that Master Gotama possessed?’

mn108:6.7.verse: When this was said, brahmin, I said this to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna:

mn108:6.8.verse: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, who possesses in every way and in every part those dhammas that the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, possessed.[^2]

mn108:6.9.verse: For, brahmin, the Blessed One was the arouser of the path unarisen, the producer of the path unproduced, the declarer of the path undeclared; he was the knower of the path, the finder of the path, one skilled in the path;

mn108:6.10.verse: but his disciples now abide following the path, and become possessed of it afterwards.’

mn108:6.11.verse: This, brahmin, is the conversation between me and the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna that was left unfinished.

mn108:7.1.verse: “Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu appointed by Master Gotama thus:

mn108:7.2.verse: ‘This one will be your refuge when I am gone’, on whom you might now depend?”

mn108:7.3.verse: “There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, appointed by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, thus:

mn108:7.4.verse: ‘This one will be your refuge when I am gone’, on whom we might now depend.”[^3]

mn108:8.1.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus:

mn108:8.2.verse: ‘This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone’, on whom you might now depend?”

mn108:8.3.verse: “There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus:

mn108:8.4.verse: ‘This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone’, on whom we might now depend.”

mn108:9.1.verse: “But, Master Ānanda, if you are thus without refuge, what is the reason for your concord?”

mn108:9.4.verse: we have the Dhamma as our refuge.”

mn108:10.1.verse: “‘Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu appointed by Master Gotama thus—

mn108:10.2.verse: “This one will be your refuge when I am gone”, on whom you might now depend?’—

mn108:10.3.verse: when asked thus, you say: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, appointed by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, thus—

mn108:10.4.verse: “This one will be your refuge when I am gone”, on whom we might now depend’;

mn108:10.5.verse: ‘But, Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus—

mn108:10.6.verse: “This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone”, on whom you might now depend?’—

mn108:10.7.verse: when asked thus, you say: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus—

mn108:10.8.verse: “This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone”, on whom we might now depend’—

mn108:10.10.verse: ‘But, Master Ānanda, if you are thus without refuge, what is the reason for your concord?’—when asked thus, you say: ‘We are not without refuge, brahmin;

mn108:10.12.verse: we have the Dhamma as our refuge’—so you say.

mn108:10.13.verse: Now, Master Ānanda, how should the meaning of this statement be regarded?”

mn108:10.14.verse: “There is, brahmin, a training precept laid down for the bhikkhus by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One; the Pātimokkha has been recited.

mn108:10.15.verse: As many of us as live in dependence on one village district assemble together on that day for the Uposatha.

mn108:10.16.verse: Having assembled, we invite whoever knows the recitation to recite it.

mn108:10.17.verse: If, while it is being recited, there is an offence, a transgression, in the case of a bhikkhu, we make him act[^4] according to the Dhamma, according to the instruction that has been given.

mn108:10.18.verse: It is not, indeed, that the venerable ones make us act;

mn108:10.19.verse: it is the Dhamma that makes us act.”

mn108:11.1.verse: “Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu whom you now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, live in dependence on?”

mn108:11.2.verse: “There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, whom we now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, live in dependence on.”

mn108:11.3.verse: “‘Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu appointed by Master Gotama thus—

mn108:11.4.verse: “This one will be your refuge when I am gone”, on whom you might now depend?’—

mn108:11.5.verse: when asked thus, you say: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, appointed by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, thus—

mn108:12.1.verse: “This one will be your refuge when I am gone”, on whom we might now depend’;

mn108:12.2.verse: ‘But, Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus—

mn108:12.3.verse: “This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone”, on whom you might now depend?’—

mn108:12.4.verse: when asked thus, you say: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, agreed upon by the Saṅgha and appointed by a number of elder bhikkhus thus—

mn108:12.5.verse: “This one will be our refuge after the Blessed One is gone”, on whom we might now depend’;

mn108:12.6.verse: ‘Master Ānanda, is there any single bhikkhu whom you now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, live in dependence on?’—

mn108:12.7.verse: when asked thus, you say: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, whom we now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, live in dependence on’—so you say.

mn108:12.8.verse: Now, Master Ānanda, how should the meaning of this statement be regarded?”

mn108:13.1.verse: “There are, brahmin, ten dhammas that inspire confidence, declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

mn108:13.2.verse: In whomever among us these dhammas are found, him we now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, we live in dependence on him.

mn108:14.1.verse: Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, trains himself by undertaking the training precepts.

mn108:15.1.verse: He has learnt much, remembers what he has learnt, and consolidates what he has learnt.

mn108:15.2.verse: Those dhammas that are good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, that proclaim the life divine that is utterly perfect and pure—such dhammas as those he has learnt much of, remembered, consolidated by recitation,[^5] examined with the mind, and penetrated well by view.

mn108:16.1.verse: He is content with robes, almsfood, resting place, and the requisite of medicine for the sick.

mn108:17.1.verse: He is one who obtains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that pertain to the higher mind and provide a pleasant abiding here and now.

mn108:18.1.verse: He wields the various kinds of supernormal power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though on earth; seated cross-legged, he travels through the air like a bird on the wing; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world.

mn108:19.1.verse: He hears, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near.

mn108:20.1.verse: Having encompassed the minds of other beings and other persons with his own mind, he understands them—

mn108:20.2.verse: he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust,

mn108:20.3.verse: and a mind without lust as a mind without lust;

mn108:20.4.verse: he understands a mind with hate as a mind with hate,

mn108:20.5.verse: and a mind without hate as a mind without hate;

mn108:20.6.verse: he understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion,

mn108:20.7.verse: and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion;

mn108:20.8.verse: he understands a contracted mind as contracted,

mn108:20.9.verse: and a distracted mind as distracted;

mn108:20.10.verse: he understands an exalted mind as exalted,

mn108:20.11.verse: and an unexalted mind as unexalted;

mn108:20.12.verse: he understands a surpassable mind as surpassable,

mn108:20.13.verse: and an unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable;

mn108:20.14.verse: he understands a concentrated mind as concentrated,

mn108:20.15.verse: and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated;

mn108:20.16.verse: he understands a liberated mind as liberated,

mn108:20.17.verse: and an unliberated mind as unliberated.

mn108:21.1.verse: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world contraction, many aeons of world expansion, many aeons of world contraction and expansion: ‘There he was so named, of such a race, with such appearance, such was his nutriment, such his experience of pleasure and pain, such his life-term; and passing away from there, he appeared elsewhere; and there too he was so named, of such a race, with such appearance, such was his nutriment, such his experience of pleasure and pain, such his life-term; and passing away from there, he appeared here.’ Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

mn108:22.1.verse: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.

mn108:23.1.verse: By realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and the deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the exhaustion of the taints.

mn108:23.2.verse: These, brahmin, are the ten dhammas that inspire confidence, declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.

mn108:23.3.verse: In whomever among us these dhammas are found, him we now honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring and respecting him, we live in dependence on him.”

mn108:24.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, said to General Upananda:

mn108:24.2.verse: “What do you think, General? If these venerable ones honour him who should be honoured, respect him who should be respected,

mn108:24.3.verse: revere him who should be revered, and venerate him who should be venerated—

mn108:24.4.verse: then indeed these venerable ones honour him who should be honoured, respect him who should be respected, revere him who should be revered, and venerate him who should be venerated.

mn108:24.5.verse: For if these venerable ones did not honour, respect, revere and venerate this one,

mn108:24.6.verse: then whom indeed would these venerable ones honour, respect, revere and venerate, and, honouring, respecting, revering and venerating him, live in dependence on?”

mn108:25.1.verse: Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:25.2.verse: “And where does Master Ānanda now live?”

mn108:25.3.verse: “I now live in the Bamboo Grove, brahmin.”

mn108:25.4.verse: “I hope, Master Ānanda, that the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by noise, secluded from people, remote from crowds, favourable for retreat?”

mn108:25.5.verse: “Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by noise, secluded from people, remote from crowds, favourable for retreat, thanks to such guardians and protectors as yourself.”

mn108:25.6.verse: “Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet, undisturbed by noise, secluded from people, remote from crowds, favourable for retreat, thanks to such venerable ones as you, who meditate and are devoted to meditation.

mn108:25.7.verse: For the venerable ones do meditate, and are devoted to meditation.

mn108:25.8.verse: Once, Master Ānanda, on one occasion Master Gotama was living at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

mn108:25.9.verse: Then I went to the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof, to Master Gotama.

mn108:25.10.verse: And there Master Gotama spoke on the subject of jhāna in many ways.

mn108:25.11.verse: Master Gotama was indeed one who meditated and was devoted to meditation,

mn108:25.12.verse: and Master Gotama commended all sorts of jhāna.”

mn108:26.1.verse: “It is not, brahmin, that the Blessed One commended all sorts of jhāna, nor is it that he did not commend all sorts of jhāna.
