mn108:26.2.verse: What sort of jhāna, brahmin, did the Blessed One not commend?

mn108:26.3.verse: Here, brahmin, someone abides with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, a prey to sensual lust, and he does not understand as it actually is the escape from sensual lust once it has arisen;

mn108:26.4.verse: making that sensual lust the main thing,[^6] he meditates on it, meditates about it, meditates because of it, meditates over it.

mn108:26.5.verse: He abides with his mind obsessed by ill will, a prey to ill will, and he does not understand as it actually is the escape from ill will once it has arisen;

mn108:26.6.verse: making that ill will the main thing, he meditates on it, meditates about it, meditates because of it, meditates over it.

mn108:26.7.verse: He abides with his mind obsessed by lethargy and drowsiness, a prey to lethargy and drowsiness, and he does not understand as it actually is the escape from lethargy and drowsiness once it has arisen;

mn108:26.8.verse: making that lethargy and drowsiness the main thing, he meditates on it, meditates about it, meditates because of it, meditates over it.

mn108:26.9.verse: He abides with his mind obsessed by agitation and worry, a prey to agitation and worry, and he does not understand as it actually is the escape from agitation and worry once it has arisen;

mn108:26.10.verse: making that agitation and worry the main thing, he meditates on it, meditates about it, meditates because of it, meditates over it.

mn108:26.11.verse: He abides with his mind obsessed by uncertainty, a prey to uncertainty, and he does not understand as it actually is the escape from uncertainty once it has arisen;

mn108:26.12.verse: making that uncertainty the main thing, he meditates on it, meditates about it, meditates because of it, meditates over it.

mn108:26.13.verse: Such is the sort of jhāna, brahmin, that the Blessed One did not commend.[^7]

mn108:27.1.verse: What sort of jhāna, brahmin, did the Blessed One commend?

mn108:27.2.verse: Here, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn108:27.3.verse: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …

mn108:27.5.verse: he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn108:27.6.verse: Such is the sort of jhāna, brahmin, that the Blessed One commended.”

mn108:28.1.verse: “It seems, Master Ānanda, that Master Gotama censured the sort of jhāna that should be censured, and praised the sort of jhāna that should be praised.

mn108:28.2.verse: But now, Master Ānanda, we must go;

mn108:28.3.verse: we are busy and have much to do.”

mn108:28.4.verse: “Now, brahmin, is the time for you to do as you see fit.”

mn108:28.5.verse: Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, having delighted in and approved of the venerable Ānanda’s words, rose from his seat and departed.

mn108:29.1.verse: Then, soon after the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, had left, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said to the venerable Ānanda:

mn108:29.2.verse: “What we asked Master Ānanda, Master Ānanda has not answered.”

mn108:29.4.verse: ‘There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, who possesses in every way and in every part those dhammas that the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, possessed.

mn108:29.5.verse: For, brahmin, the Blessed One was the arouser of the path unarisen, the producer of the path unproduced, the declarer of the path undeclared; he was the knower of the path, the finder of the path, one skilled in the path.

mn108:29.6.verse: But his disciples now abide following the path, and become possessed of it afterwards’?”

mn108:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. It was not long after the Buddha had become fully quenched.

mn108:2.1.verse: Now at that time King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, being suspicious of King Pajjota, was having Rājagaha fortified.

mn108:3.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

mn108:3.3.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

mn108:3.4.verse: Why don’t I go to see the brahmin Moggallāna the Guardian at his place of work?”

mn108:4.2.verse: Moggallāna the Guardian saw Ānanda coming off in the distance

mn108:4.6.verse: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.

mn108:4.7.verse: Please, sir, sit down, here, a seat is ready.”

mn108:4.8.verse: Ānanda sat down on the seat spread out,

mn108:4.9.verse: while Moggallāna took a low seat and sat to one side.

mn108:5.1.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, is there even a single mendicant who has all the same qualities in each and every way as possessed by the worthy Gotama, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

mn108:5.3.verse: For the Blessed One gave rise to the unarisen path, gave birth to the unborn path, and explained the unexplained path. He is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert on the path.

mn108:5.4.verse: And now the disciples live following the path; they acquire it later.”

mn108:6.1.verse: But this conversation between Ānanda and Moggallāna the Guardian was left unfinished.

mn108:6.2.verse: For just then the brahmin Vassakāra, a chief minister of Magadha, while supervising the work at Rājagaha, approached Ānanda at Moggallāna’s place of work and exchanged greetings with him.

mn108:6.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda,

mn108:6.4.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

mn108:6.5.verse: So Ānanda told him of the conversation that they were having when Vassakāra arrived. Vassakāra said:

mn108:7.1.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, is there even a single mendicant who was appointed by the worthy Gotama, saying:

mn108:7.2.verse: ‘This one will be your refuge when I have passed away,’ to whom you would now turn?”

mn108:8.1.verse: “But is there even a single mendicant who has been elected to such a position by the Saṅgha and appointed by several senior mendicants?”

mn108:9.1.verse: “But since you lack a refuge, worthy Ānanda, what’s the reason for your harmony?”

mn108:10.1.verse: “But Worthy Ānanda, when asked whether there was even a single mendicant—either appointed by the worthy Gotama,

mn108:10.5.verse: or elected by the Saṅgha and appointed by several senior mendicants—

mn108:10.6.verse: who serves as your refuge after the Buddha passed away, to whom you now turn,

mn108:10.10.verse: But you say that the reason for your harmony is that you have

mn108:10.13.verse: How should I see the meaning of this statement?”

mn108:10.14.verse: “The Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha laid down training rules and recited the monastic code for the mendicants.

mn108:10.15.verse: On the day of the sabbath all of us who live in dependence on one village district gather together as one.

mn108:10.16.verse: We invite one who transmits the code to recite it.

mn108:10.17.verse: If anyone remembers an offense or transgression while they’re reciting, we make them act in line with the teaching and in line with the instructions.

mn108:10.18.verse: It’s not the good fellows who make us act,

mn108:10.19.verse: it’s the teaching that makes us act.”

mn108:11.1.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, is there even a single mendicant who you honor, respect, revere, venerate, and rely on?”

mn108:11.3.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, when asked whether there was even a single mendicant—either appointed by the worthy Gotama,

mn108:12.2.verse: or elected by the Saṅgha and appointed by several senior mendicants—

mn108:12.3.verse: who serves as your refuge after the Buddha passed away, to whom you now turn,

mn108:12.6.verse: And when asked whether there is even a single mendicant who you honor, respect, revere, venerate, and rely on,

mn108:12.8.verse: How should I see the meaning of this statement?”

mn108:13.1.verse: “There are ten inspiring things explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn108:13.2.verse: We honor anyone in whom these things are found.

mn108:14.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

mn108:15.1.verse: They’re very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned.

mn108:15.2.verse: These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

mn108:16.1.verse: They’re content with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

mn108:17.1.verse: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn108:18.1.verse: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. They control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

mn108:19.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.

mn108:20.1.verse: They understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind.

mn108:20.2.verse: They understand mind with greed as ‘mind with greed’,

mn108:20.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed’.

mn108:20.17.verse: They understand unfreed mind as ‘unfreed mind’.

mn108:21.1.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn108:22.1.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn108:23.1.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn108:23.2.verse: These are the ten inspiring things explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn108:23.3.verse: We honor anyone in whom these things are found, and rely on them.”

mn108:24.1.verse: When he had spoken, Vassakāra addressed General Upananda,

mn108:24.3.verse: Do these venerables honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are worthy?”

mn108:24.5.verse: For if these venerables were not to honor, respect, revere, and venerate them,

mn108:25.4.verse: “I hope the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat?”

mn108:25.5.verse: “Indeed it is, brahmin. And it is like that owing to such protectors and guardians as yourself.”

mn108:25.6.verse: “Surely, worthy Ānanda, it is owing to the good fellows who meditate, making a habit of meditating.

mn108:25.7.verse: For the good fellows do in fact meditate and make a habit of meditating.

mn108:25.8.verse: This one time, worthy Ānanda, worthy Gotama was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

mn108:25.9.verse: So I went there to see him.

mn108:25.10.verse: And there he spoke about meditation in many ways.

mn108:25.11.verse: He meditated, and made a habit of meditating.

mn108:25.12.verse: And he praised all kinds of meditation.”

mn108:26.1.verse: “No, brahmin, the Buddha did not praise all kinds of meditation, nor did he dispraise all kinds of meditation.

mn108:26.2.verse: And what kind of meditation did he not praise?

mn108:26.3.verse: It’s when someone’s heart is overcome and mired in sensual desire, and they don’t truly understand the escape from sensual desire that has arisen.

mn108:26.4.verse: Hiding sensual desire within, they meditate and concentrate and contemplate and ruminate.

mn108:26.5.verse: Their heart is overcome and mired in ill will …

mn108:26.11.verse: doubt, and they don’t truly know and see the escape from doubt that has arisen.

mn108:26.12.verse: Hiding doubt within, they meditate and concentrate and contemplate and ruminate.

mn108:26.13.verse: The Buddha didn’t praise this kind of meditation.

mn108:27.1.verse: And what kind of meditation did he praise?

mn108:27.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn108:27.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn108:27.4.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn108:27.5.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn108:27.6.verse: The Buddha praised this kind of meditation.”

mn108:28.1.verse: “Well, worthy Ānanda, it seems that worthy Gotama criticized the kind of meditation that deserves criticism and praised that deserving of praise.

mn108:28.2.verse: Well, now, worthy Ānanda, I must go.

mn108:28.3.verse: I have many duties, and much to do.”

mn108:28.5.verse: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, having approved and agreed with what Venerable Ānanda said, rose from his seat and left.

mn108:29.1.verse: Soon after he had left, Moggallāna the Guardian said to Ānanda,

mn108:29.2.verse: “Worthy Ānanda, you still haven’t answered my question.”

mn108:29.4.verse: ‘There is no single mendicant who has all the same qualities in each and every way as possessed by the worthy Gotama, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn108:29.5.verse: For the Blessed One gave rise to the unarisen path, gave birth to the unborn path, and explained the unexplained path. He is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert on the path.

mn108:29.6.verse: And now the disciples live following the path; they acquire it later.’”

mn109:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.

mn109:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon,[^1] the Blessed One was sitting in the open, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

mn109:3.1.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined hands in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One:

mn109:3.2.verse: “Venerable sir, I would ask the Blessed One about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the favour of answering my question.”

mn109:3.3.verse: “Well then, bhikkhu, sit down on your own seat and ask what you like.”

mn109:3.4.verse: Then that bhikkhu sat down on his own seat and said to the Blessed One:

mn109:4.1.verse: “Venerable sir, are there these five aggregates affected by clinging, that is to say,

mn109:4.2.verse: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging?”

mn109:4.3.verse: “There are, bhikkhu, these five aggregates affected by clinging, that is to say,

mn109:4.4.verse: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.”

mn109:4.5.verse: Saying, “Good, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu delighted in and approved of the Blessed One’s words, and he asked the Blessed One a further question:

mn109:5.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, what are these five aggregates affected by clinging rooted in?”

mn109:5.2.verse: “These five aggregates affected by clinging, bhikkhu, are rooted in desire.”

mn109:6.1.verse: “Venerable sir, is that clinging the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging, or is the clinging something apart from the five aggregates affected by clinging?”

mn109:6.2.verse: “Bhikkhu, that clinging is neither the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging, nor is it something apart from the five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn109:6.3.verse: It is the desire and lust comprised in these five aggregates affected by clinging that is the clinging there.”

mn109:7.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be diversity in the desire and lust comprised in these five aggregates affected by clinging?”

mn109:7.2.verse: “There might, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.

mn109:7.4.verse: ‘May my form be such in the future; may my feeling be such in the future; may my perception be such in the future; may my formations be such in the future; may my consciousness be such in the future.’

mn109:7.5.verse: Thus, bhikkhu, there is diversity in the desire and lust comprised in these five aggregates affected by clinging.”

mn109:8.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, in what way is ‘aggregate’ a term for the aggregates?”

mn109:8.2.verse: “Whatever kind of form there is, bhikkhu—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the form aggregate.

mn109:8.3.verse: Whatever kind of feeling there is—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the feeling aggregate.

mn109:8.4.verse: Whatever kind of perception there is—past, future or present …—this is called the perception aggregate.

mn109:8.5.verse: Whatever kind of formations there are—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the formations aggregate.

mn109:8.6.verse: Whatever kind of consciousness there is—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate.

mn109:8.7.verse: It is in this way, bhikkhu, that ‘aggregate’ is a term for the aggregates.”

mn109:9.1.verse: “What is the reason, venerable sir, what is the condition, for describing the form aggregate?

mn109:9.2.verse: What is the reason, what is the condition, for describing the feeling aggregate?

mn109:9.3.verse: What is the reason, what is the condition, for describing the perception aggregate?

mn109:9.4.verse: What is the reason, what is the condition, for describing the formations aggregate?

mn109:9.5.verse: What is the reason, what is the condition, for describing the consciousness aggregate?”

mn109:9.6.verse: “The four great primary elements, bhikkhu, are the reason, the four great primary elements are the condition, for describing the form aggregate.

mn109:9.7.verse: Contact is the reason, contact is the condition, for describing the feeling aggregate.

mn109:9.8.verse: Contact is the reason, contact is the condition, for describing the perception aggregate.

mn109:9.9.verse: Contact is the reason, contact is the condition, for describing the formations aggregate.

mn109:9.10.verse: Name-and-form is the reason, bhikkhu, name-and-form is the condition, for describing the consciousness aggregate.”

mn109:10.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, how does there come to be the embodiment view?”

mn109:10.2.verse: “Here, bhikkhu, the untaught ordinary man, who has no regard for the Noble Ones and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it, who has no regard for True Men and is unconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it,

mn109:10.3.verse: sees form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form;

mn109:10.4.verse: he sees feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling;

mn109:10.5.verse: he sees perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception;

mn109:10.6.verse: he sees formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations;

mn109:10.7.verse: he sees consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn109:10.8.verse: That, bhikkhu, is how there comes to be the embodiment view.”

mn109:11.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, how does there not come to be the embodiment view?”

mn109:11.2.verse: “Here, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple, who has regard for the Noble Ones and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it, who has regard for True Men and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it,

mn109:11.3.verse: does not see form as self, or self as possessed of form, or form in self, or self in form;

mn109:11.4.verse: he does not see feeling as self, or self as possessed of feeling, or feeling in self, or self in feeling;

mn109:11.5.verse: he does not see perception as self, or self as possessed of perception, or perception in self, or self in perception;

mn109:11.6.verse: he does not see formations as self, or self as possessed of formations, or formations in self, or self in formations;

mn109:11.7.verse: he does not see consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn109:11.8.verse: That, bhikkhu, is how there does not come to be the embodiment view.”

mn109:12.1.verse: “What is the gratification, venerable sir, what is the danger, what is the escape,[^2] in the case of form?

mn109:12.2.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape, in the case of feeling?

mn109:12.3.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape, in the case of perception?

mn109:12.4.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape, in the case of formations?

mn109:12.5.verse: What is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape, in the case of consciousness?”

mn109:12.6.verse: “The pleasure and joy, bhikkhu, that arise dependent on form—this is the gratification in the case of form.

mn109:12.7.verse: Form is impermanent, painful, and subject to change—this is the danger in the case of form.

mn109:12.8.verse: The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust, for form—this is the escape in the case of form.

mn109:12.9.verse: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling …

mn109:12.12.verse: the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification in the case of consciousness.

mn109:12.13.verse: Consciousness is impermanent, painful, and subject to change—this is the danger in the case of consciousness.

mn109:12.14.verse: The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust, for consciousness—this is the escape in the case of consciousness.”

mn109:13.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, how does a man know, how does he see, so that there come to be in him, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, no underlying tendency to I-making, mine-making and conceit?”

mn109:13.2.verse: “Whatever kind of form there is, bhikkhu—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—he sees all form as it actually is with right understanding thus: ‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.’

mn109:13.3.verse: Whatever kind of feeling there is …

mn109:13.4.verse: whatever kind of perception there is …

mn109:13.5.verse: whatever kind of formations there are …

mn109:13.6.verse: whatever kind of consciousness there is—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—he sees all consciousness as it actually is with right understanding thus: ‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.’

mn109:13.7.verse: That, bhikkhu, is how a man knows, how he sees, so that there come to be in him, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external signs, no underlying tendency to I-making, mine-making and conceit.”

mn109:14.1.verse: Then a thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu:

mn109:14.2.verse: “So, it seems, form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self.

mn109:14.3.verse: Then what self will actions done by what is not self affect?”[^3]

mn109:14.4.verse: Then the Blessed One, knowing in his own mind the thought in that bhikkhu’s mind, addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn109:14.5.verse: “It is possible, bhikkhus, that some misguided man here, unknowing and ignorant, with his mind dominated by craving, might think he could outstrip the Teacher’s Dispensation thus:

mn109:14.6.verse: ‘So, it seems, form is not self, feeling is not self, perception is not self, formations are not self, consciousness is not self.

mn109:14.7.verse: Then what self will actions done by what is not self affect?’

mn109:14.8.verse: Now, bhikkhus, you have been trained by me through questioning about these various matters here and there in the Dhamma.

mn109:15.1.verse: How do you conceive this, bhikkhus,

mn109:15.4.verse: “And is what is impermanent painful or pleasant?”

mn109:15.6.verse: “And is what is impermanent, painful, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus:

mn109:15.7.verse: ‘This is mine, this is I, this is my self’?”

mn109:16.7.verse: “And is what is impermanent painful or pleasant?”

mn109:16.9.verse: “And is what is impermanent, painful, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus:

mn109:16.10.verse: ‘This is mine, this is I, this is my self’?”

mn109:16.12.verse: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever kind of form there is—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: ‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.’

mn109:17.1.verse: Whatever kind of feeling there is …

mn109:17.2.verse: whatever kind of perception there is …

mn109:17.3.verse: whatever kind of formations there are …

mn109:17.4.verse: whatever kind of consciousness there is—past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: ‘This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.’

mn109:17.5.verse: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes dispassionate towards form, dispassionate towards feeling, dispassionate towards perception, dispassionate towards formations, dispassionate towards consciousness.

mn109:18.1.verse: Being dispassionate, his greed fades away; with the fading of greed his mind is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn109:18.2.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’”

mn109:18.3.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn109:18.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn109:18.5.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of as many as sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints by not clinging.

mn109:0.2.verse: The Longer Discourse on the Full-Moon Night

mn109:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn109:2.1.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

mn109:3.1.verse: Then one of the monks rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said,

mn109:3.2.verse: “Sir, I’d like to ask the Buddha about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

mn109:3.3.verse: “Well then, monk, take your own seat and ask what you wish.”

mn109:3.4.verse: That monk took his seat and said to the Buddha:

mn109:4.1.verse: “Sir, are these the five grasping aggregates:

mn109:4.2.verse: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness?”

mn109:4.5.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

mn109:5.1.verse: “But sir, what is the root of these five grasping aggregates?”

mn109:5.2.verse: “These five grasping aggregates are rooted in desire.”

mn109:6.1.verse: “But sir, is that grasping the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates? Or is grasping one thing and the five grasping aggregates another?”

mn109:6.3.verse: The desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates is the grasping there.”

mn109:7.1.verse: “But sir, can there be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates?”

mn109:7.4.verse: ‘In the future, may I be of such form, such feeling, such perception, such choices, and such consciousness!’

mn109:7.5.verse: That’s how there can be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates.”

mn109:8.1.verse: “Sir, what is the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates?”

mn109:8.2.verse: “Any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of form.

mn109:8.3.verse: Any kind of feeling at all …

mn109:8.4.verse: Any kind of perception at all …

mn109:8.5.verse: Any kind of choices at all …

mn109:8.6.verse: Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of consciousness.

mn109:8.7.verse: That’s the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates.”

mn109:9.1.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why the aggregate of form is found?

mn109:9.2.verse: What is the cause, what is the reason why the aggregate of feeling …

mn109:9.6.verse: “The four principal states are the reason why the aggregate of form is found.

mn109:9.7.verse: Contact is the reason why the aggregates of feeling,

mn109:9.10.verse: Name and form are the reasons why the aggregate of consciousness is found.”

mn109:10.1.verse: “But sir, how does substantialist view come about?”

mn109:10.2.verse: “It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn109:10.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn109:10.4.verse: They regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

mn109:10.5.verse: They regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

mn109:10.6.verse: They regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

mn109:10.7.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn109:10.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view comes about.”

mn109:11.1.verse: “But sir, how does substantialist view not come about?”

mn109:11.2.verse: “It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn109:11.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn109:11.4.verse: They don’t regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

mn109:11.5.verse: They don’t regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

mn109:11.6.verse: They don’t regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

mn109:11.7.verse: They don’t regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn109:11.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view does not come about.”

mn109:12.1.verse: “Sir, what’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

mn109:12.6.verse: “The pleasure and happiness that arise from form: this is its gratification.

mn109:12.7.verse: That form is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

mn109:12.8.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for form: this is its escape.

mn109:12.9.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling …

mn109:12.13.verse: That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

mn109:12.14.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for consciousness: this is its escape.”

mn109:13.1.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

mn109:13.2.verse: “One truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn109:13.3.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

mn109:13.6.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn109:13.7.verse: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

mn109:14.1.verse: Now at that time one of the monks had the thought,

mn109:14.2.verse: “So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

mn109:14.3.verse: Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?”

mn109:14.4.verse: But the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the monks:

mn109:14.5.verse: “It’s possible that some futile person here—unknowing and ignorant, his mind dominated by craving—thinks he can overstep the Teacher’s instructions. He thinks:

mn109:14.6.verse: ‘So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

mn109:14.7.verse: Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?’

mn109:14.8.verse: Now, monks, you have been educated by me in questioning with regard to all these things in all such cases.

mn109:15.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn109:15.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn109:15.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn109:16.7.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

mn109:16.9.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn109:16.10.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn109:16.12.verse: “So you should truly see any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn109:17.1.verse: You should truly see any kind of feeling …

mn109:17.4.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn109:17.5.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn109:18.1.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn109:18.2.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

mn109:18.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn109:18.4.verse: Satisfied, the monks approved what the Buddha said.

mn109:18.5.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed from defilements by not grasping.

mn110:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother.

mn110:2.1.verse: And on that occasion—the uposatha of the fifteenth, the night of a very full moon—he was sitting out in the open with the Saṅgha of monks.

mn110:2.2.verse: Then, having surveyed the silent Saṅgha of monks, he addressed them:

mn110:3.1.verse: “Monks, could a person of no integrity know of a person of no integrity:

mn110:3.2.verse: ‘This is a person of no integrity’?”

mn110:3.5.verse: It’s impossible, there’s no way, that a person of no integrity would know of a person of no integrity:

mn110:3.6.verse: ‘This is a person of no integrity.’

mn110:3.7.verse: Could a person of no integrity know of a person of integrity:

mn110:3.11.verse: It’s impossible, there’s no way, that a person of no integrity would know of a person of integrity:

mn110:4.1.verse: A person of no integrity is endowed with qualities of no integrity; he is a person of no integrity in his friendship, in the way he wills, the way he gives advice, the way he speaks, the way he acts, the views he holds, & the way he gives a gift.

mn110:5.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity endowed with qualities of no integrity?

mn110:5.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity is lacking in conviction, lacking in shame, lacking in compunction; he is unlearned, lazy, of muddled mindfulness, & poor discernment.

mn110:5.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is endowed with qualities of no integrity.”

mn110:6.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in his friendship?

mn110:6.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity has, as his friends & companions, those contemplatives & brahmans who are lacking in conviction, lacking in shame, lacking in compunction, unlearned, lazy, of muddled mindfulness, & poor discernment.

mn110:6.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in his friendship.

mn110:7.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the way he wills?

mn110:7.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity wills for his own affliction, or for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both.

mn110:7.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the way he wills.

mn110:8.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the way he gives advice?

mn110:8.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity gives advice for his own affliction, or for the affliction of others, or for the affliction of both.

mn110:8.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the way he gives advice.

mn110:9.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the way he speaks?

mn110:9.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity is one who tells lies, engages in divisive tale-bearing, engages in harsh speech, engages in idle chatter.

mn110:9.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the way he speaks.

mn110:10.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the way he acts?

mn110:10.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity is one who takes life, steals, engages in illicit sex.

mn110:10.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the way he acts.

mn110:11.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the views he holds?

mn110:11.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity is one who holds a view like this:

mn110:11.3.verse: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed. There is no fruit or result of good or bad actions. There is no this world, no next world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously reborn beings; no contemplatives or brahmans who, faring rightly & practicing rightly, proclaim this world & the next after having directly known & realized it for themselves.’

mn110:11.4.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the views he holds.

mn110:12.1.verse: “And how is a person of no integrity a person of no integrity in the way he gives a gift?

mn110:12.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity gives a gift inattentively, not with his own hand, disrespectfully, as if throwing it away, with the view that nothing will come of it.

mn110:12.3.verse: This is how a person of no integrity is a person of no integrity in the way he gives a gift.

mn110:13.1.verse: This person of no integrity—thus endowed with qualities of no integrity; a person of no integrity in his friendship, in the way he wills, the way he gives advice, the way he speaks, the way he acts, the views he holds, & the way he gives a gift—

mn110:13.2.verse: on the break-up of the body, after death, reappears in the destination of people of no integrity.

mn110:13.3.verse: And what is the destination of people of no integrity?

mn110:14.1.verse: “Now, monks, could a person of integrity know of a person of no integrity:

mn110:14.2.verse: ‘This is a person of no integrity’?”

mn110:14.5.verse: It is possible that a person of integrity would know of a person of no integrity:

mn110:14.6.verse: ‘This is a person of no integrity.’

mn110:14.7.verse: Could a person of integrity know of a person of integrity:

mn110:15.2.verse: It is possible that a person of integrity would know of a person of integrity:

mn110:15.4.verse: A person of integrity is endowed with qualities of integrity; he is a person of integrity in his friendship, in the way he wills, the way he gives advice, the way he speaks, the way he acts, the views he holds, &

mn110:15.5.verse: the way he gives a gift.

mn110:16.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity endowed with qualities of integrity?

mn110:16.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity is endowed with conviction, shame, compunction; he is learned, with aroused persistence, unmuddled mindfulness, & good discernment.

mn110:16.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is endowed with qualities of integrity.”

mn110:17.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in his friendship?

mn110:17.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity has, as his friends & companions, those contemplatives & brahmans who are endowed with conviction, shame, compunction; who are learned, with aroused persistence, unmuddled mindfulness, & good discernment.

mn110:17.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in his friendship.

mn110:18.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the way he wills?

mn110:18.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity wills neither for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both.

mn110:18.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the way he wills.

mn110:19.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the way he gives advice?

mn110:19.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity gives advice neither for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both.

mn110:19.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the way he gives advice.

mn110:20.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the way he speaks?

mn110:20.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity is one who refrains from lies, refrains from divisive tale-bearing, refrains from harsh speech, refrains from idle chatter.

mn110:20.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the way he speaks.

mn110:21.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the way he acts?

mn110:21.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity is one who refrains from taking life, refrains from stealing, refrains from illicit sex.

mn110:21.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the way he acts.

mn110:22.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the views he holds?

mn110:22.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity is one who holds a view like this:

mn110:22.3.verse: ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed. There are fruits & results of good & bad actions. There is this world & the next world. There is mother & father. There are spontaneously reborn beings; there are contemplatives & brahmans who, faring rightly & practicing rightly, proclaim this world & the next after having directly known & realized it for themselves.’

mn110:22.4.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the views he holds.

mn110:23.1.verse: “And how is a person of integrity a person of integrity in the way he gives a gift?

mn110:23.2.verse: There is the case where a person of integrity gives a gift attentively, with his own hand, respectfully, not as if throwing it away, with the view that something will come of it.

mn110:23.3.verse: This is how a person of integrity is a person of integrity in the way he gives a gift.

mn110:24.1.verse: This person of integrity—thus endowed with qualities of integrity; a person of integrity in his friendship, in the way he wills, the way he gives advice, the way he speaks, the way he acts, the views he holds, & the way he gives a gift—

mn110:24.2.verse: on the break-up of the body, after death, reappears in the destination of people of integrity.

mn110:24.3.verse: And what is the destination of people of integrity?

mn110:24.4.verse: Greatness among devas or among human beings.”

mn110:25.1.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn110:25.2.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn110:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse on the Full-Moon Night

mn110:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn110:2.1.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

mn110:2.2.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them,

mn110:3.1.verse: “Monks, could an untrue person know of an untrue person:

mn110:3.2.verse: ‘This worthy one is an untrue person’?”

mn110:3.5.verse: It’s impossible, it can’t happen, that an untrue person could know of an untrue person:

mn110:3.6.verse: ‘This worthy one is an untrue person.’

mn110:3.7.verse: But could an untrue person know of a true person:

mn110:3.8.verse: ‘This worthy one is a true person’?”

mn110:4.1.verse: An untrue person has bad qualities, is devoted to untrue persons, and has the intentions, counsel, speech, actions, views, and giving of an untrue person.

mn110:5.1.verse: And how does an untrue person have bad qualities?

mn110:5.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person is faithless, shameless, imprudent, unlearned, lazy, unmindful, and witless.

mn110:5.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person has bad qualities.

mn110:6.1.verse: And how is an untrue person devoted to untrue persons?

mn110:6.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person is a friend and companion of ascetics and brahmins who are faithless, shameless, imprudent, unlearned, lazy, unmindful, and witless.

mn110:6.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person is devoted to untrue persons.

mn110:7.1.verse: And how does an untrue person have the intentions of an untrue person?

mn110:7.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person intends to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both.

mn110:7.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person has the intentions of an untrue person.

mn110:8.1.verse: And how does an untrue person offer the counsel of an untrue person?

mn110:8.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person offers counsel that hurts themselves, hurts others, and hurts both.

mn110:8.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person offers the counsel of an untrue person.

mn110:9.1.verse: And how does an untrue person have the speech of an untrue person?

mn110:9.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person uses speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, and nonsensical.

mn110:9.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person has the speech of an untrue person.

mn110:10.1.verse: And how does an untrue person have the action of an untrue person?

mn110:10.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person kills living creatures, steals, and commits sexual misconduct.

mn110:10.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person has the actions of an untrue person.

mn110:11.1.verse: And how does an untrue person have the view of an untrue person?

mn110:11.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person has such a view:

mn110:11.3.verse: ‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn110:11.4.verse: That’s how an untrue person has the view of an untrue person.

mn110:12.1.verse: And how does an untrue person give the gifts of an untrue person?

mn110:12.2.verse: It’s when an untrue person gives a gift carelessly, not with their own hand, and thoughtlessly. They give the dregs, and they give without consideration for consequences.

mn110:12.3.verse: That’s how an untrue person gives the gifts of an untrue person.

mn110:13.1.verse: That untrue person—who has such bad qualities, is devoted to untrue persons, and has the intentions, counsel, speech, actions, views, and giving of an untrue person—

mn110:13.2.verse: when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in the place where untrue persons are reborn.

mn110:13.3.verse: And what is the place where untrue persons are reborn?

mn110:14.1.verse: Monks, could a true person know of a true person:

mn110:14.2.verse: ‘This worthy one is a true person’?”

mn110:14.5.verse: It is possible that a true person could know of a true person:

mn110:14.6.verse: ‘This worthy one is a true person.’

mn110:14.7.verse: But could a true person know of an untrue person:

mn110:14.8.verse: ‘This worthy one is an untrue person’?”

mn110:15.4.verse: A true person has good qualities, is devoted to true persons, and has the intentions, counsel, speech, actions, views, and giving of a true person.

mn110:16.1.verse: And how does a true person have good qualities?

mn110:16.2.verse: It’s when a true person is faithful, conscientious, prudent, learned, energetic, mindful, and wise.

mn110:16.3.verse: That’s how a true person has good qualities.

mn110:17.1.verse: And how is a true person devoted to true persons?

mn110:17.2.verse: It’s when a true person is a friend and companion of ascetics and brahmins who are faithful, conscientious, prudent, learned, energetic, mindful, and wise.

mn110:17.3.verse: That’s how a true person is devoted to true persons.

mn110:18.1.verse: And how does a true person have the intentions of a true person?

mn110:18.2.verse: It’s when a true person doesn’t intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both.

mn110:18.3.verse: That’s how a true person has the intentions of a true person.

mn110:19.1.verse: And how does a true person offer the counsel of a true person?

mn110:19.2.verse: It’s when a true person offers counsel that doesn’t hurt themselves, hurt others, and hurt both.

mn110:19.3.verse: That’s how a true person offers the counsel of a true person.

mn110:20.1.verse: And how does a true person have the speech of a true person?

mn110:20.2.verse: It’s when a true person refrains from speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical.

mn110:20.3.verse: That’s how a true person has the speech of a true person.

mn110:21.1.verse: And how does a true person have the action of a true person?

mn110:21.2.verse: It’s when a true person refrains from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

mn110:21.3.verse: That’s how a true person has the action of a true person.

mn110:22.1.verse: And how does a true person have the view of a true person?

mn110:22.2.verse: It’s when a true person has such a view:

mn110:22.3.verse: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn110:22.4.verse: That’s how a true person has the view of a true person.

mn110:23.1.verse: And how does a true person give the gifts of a true person?

mn110:23.2.verse: It’s when a true person gives a gift carefully, with their own hand, and thoughtfully. They don’t give the dregs, and they give with consideration for consequences.

mn110:23.3.verse: That’s how a true person gives the gifts of a true person.

mn110:24.1.verse: That true person—who has such good qualities, is devoted to true persons, and has the intentions, counsel, speech, actions, views, and giving of a true person—

mn110:24.2.verse: when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in the place where true persons are reborn.

mn110:24.3.verse: And what is the place where true persons are reborn?

mn110:24.4.verse: A state of greatness among gods or humans.”

mn110:25.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn110:25.2.verse: Satisfied, the monks approved what the Buddha said.

mn111:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn111:1.3.verse: There he addressed the monks, saying,

mn111:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn111:2.8.verse: For half a month, Sāriputta clearly saw insight into mental qualities one after another.

mn111:2.9.verse: This is what occurred to Sāriputta through insight into mental qualities one after another:

mn111:3.1.verse: There was the case where Sāriputta—quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities—entered & remained in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn111:4.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the first jhāna—directed thought, evaluation, rapture, pleasure, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:4.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:4.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:4.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:4.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:4.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:5.1.verse: And further, with the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, Sāriputta entered & remained in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.

mn111:6.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the second jhāna—internal assurance, rapture, pleasure, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:6.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:6.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:6.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:6.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:6.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:7.1.verse: And further, with the fading of rapture, Sāriputta—remaining equanimous, mindful, & alert, and sensing pleasure with the body—entered & remained in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’

mn111:8.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the third jhāna—equanimity, pleasure, mindfulness, alertness, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—

mn111:8.2.verse: he ferreted them out one after another. Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:8.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:8.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:8.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:8.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:9.1.verse: And further, with the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of joys & distresses—Sāriputta entered & remained in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither-pleasure-nor-pain.

mn111:10.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the fourth jhāna—a feeling of equanimity, neither pleasure nor pain; an unconcern due to calmness of awareness; singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:10.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:10.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:10.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:10.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:10.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:11.1.verse: And further, with the complete transcending of perceptions of (physical) form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite space,’ Sāriputta entered & remained in the dimension of the infinitude of space.

mn111:12.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the dimension of the infinitude of space—the perception of the dimension of the infinitude of space, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:12.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:12.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:12.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:12.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:12.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:13.1.verse: And further, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite consciousness,’ Sāriputta entered & remained in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.

mn111:14.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness—the perception of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:14.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:14.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:14.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:14.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:14.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:15.1.verse: And further, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, (perceiving,) ‘There is nothing,’ Sāriputta entered & remained in the dimension of nothingness.

mn111:16.1.verse: Whatever qualities there are in the dimension of nothingness—the perception of the dimension of nothingness, singleness of mind, contact, feeling, perception, intention, consciousness, desire, decision, persistence, mindfulness, equanimity, & attention—he ferreted them out one after another.

mn111:16.2.verse: Known to him they arose, known to him they became established, known to him they subsided.

mn111:16.4.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:16.5.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:16.6.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:16.7.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:17.1.verse: And further, with the complete transcending of the dimension of nothingness, Sāriputta entered & remained in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn111:18.1.verse: He emerged mindfully from that attainment.

mn111:18.2.verse: On emerging mindfully from that attainment, he regarded the past qualities that had ceased & changed:

mn111:18.3.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:18.4.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:18.5.verse: He discerned that ‘There is a further escape,’

mn111:18.6.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There is.’

mn111:19.1.verse: And further, with the complete transcending of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, Sāriputta entered & remained in the cessation of perception & feeling. And when he saw with discernment, his effluents were totally ended.

mn111:20.1.verse: He emerged mindfully from that attainment.

mn111:20.2.verse: On emerging mindfully from that attainment, he regarded the past qualities that had ceased & changed:

mn111:20.3.verse: ‘So this is how these qualities, not having been, come into play. Having been, they vanish.’

mn111:20.4.verse: He remained unattracted & unrepelled with regard to those qualities, independent, detached, released, dissociated, with unrestricted awareness.

mn111:20.5.verse: He discerned that ‘There is no further escape,’

mn111:20.6.verse: and pursuing it, he confirmed that ‘There isn’t.’

mn111:21.1.verse: “If a person, rightly saying it of anyone, were to say,

mn111:21.2.verse: ‘He has attained mastery & perfection in noble virtue… noble concentration… noble discernment… noble release,’ he would be rightly saying it of Sāriputta if he were to say:

mn111:21.3.verse: ‘He has attained mastery & perfection in noble virtue… noble concentration… noble discernment… noble release.’

mn111:22.1.verse: “If a person, rightly saying it of anyone, were to say,

mn111:22.2.verse: ‘He is the Blessed One’s son, his offspring—born of his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, his heir in the Dhamma, not his heir in material things,’ he would be rightly saying it of Sāriputta if he were to say:

mn111:22.3.verse: ‘He is the Blessed One’s son, his offspring—born of his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, his heir in the Dhamma, not his heir in material things.’

mn111:23.1.verse: Sāriputta, monks, takes the unexcelled wheel of Dhamma set rolling by the Tathāgata, and keeps it rolling rightly.”

mn111:23.2.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn111:23.3.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn111:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn111:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn111:2.8.verse: For a fortnight he practiced discernment of phenomena one by one.

mn111:2.9.verse: And this is how he did it.

mn111:3.1.verse: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn111:4.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the first absorption one by one: placing and keeping and rapture and bliss and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:4.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:4.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:4.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:4.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:4.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:5.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, he entered and remained in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn111:6.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the second absorption one by one: internal confidence and rapture and bliss and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:6.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:6.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:6.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:6.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:6.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:7.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, he entered and remained in the third absorption, where he meditated with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn111:8.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the third absorption one by one: bliss and mindfulness and awareness and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:8.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:8.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:8.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:8.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:8.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:9.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, he entered and remained in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn111:10.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the fourth absorption one by one: equanimity and neutral feeling and mental unconcern due to tranquility and pure mindfulness and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:10.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:10.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:10.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, his mind without boundaries.

mn111:10.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:10.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:11.1.verse: Furthermore, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, he entered and remained in the dimension of infinite space.

mn111:12.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the dimension of infinite space one by one: the perception of the dimension of infinite space and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:12.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:12.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:12.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:12.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:12.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:13.1.verse: Furthermore, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, he entered and remained in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn111:14.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the dimension of infinite consciousness one by one: the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:14.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:14.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:14.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, his mind free of limits.

mn111:14.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:14.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:15.1.verse: Furthermore, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, he entered and remained in the dimension of nothingness.

mn111:16.1.verse: And he distinguished the phenomena of the dimension of nothingness one by one: the perception of the dimension of nothingness and unification of mind; contact, feeling, perception, intention, mind, enthusiasm, decision, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and application of mind.

mn111:16.2.verse: He knew those phenomena as they arose, as they remained, and as they went away.

mn111:16.4.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:16.5.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:16.6.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:16.7.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:17.1.verse: Furthermore, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, he entered and remained in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn111:18.1.verse: And he emerged from that attainment with mindfulness.

mn111:18.2.verse: Then he contemplated the phenomena of that attainment that had passed, ceased, and perished:

mn111:18.3.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:18.4.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, his mind without boundaries.

mn111:18.5.verse: He understood: ‘There is an escape beyond.’

mn111:18.6.verse: Repeated practice of that confirmed this for him.

mn111:19.1.verse: Furthermore, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, he entered and remained in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, his defilements came to an end.

mn111:20.1.verse: And he emerged from that attainment with mindfulness.

mn111:20.2.verse: Then he contemplated the phenomena of that attainment that had passed, ceased, and perished:

mn111:20.3.verse: ‘So it seems that these phenomena, not having been, come to be; and having come to be, they flit away.’

mn111:20.4.verse: Regarding those phenomena, he meditated without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn111:20.5.verse: He understood: ‘There is no escape beyond.’

mn111:20.6.verse: By cultivating that he confirmed that there is not.

mn111:21.1.verse: And if there’s anyone of whom it may be rightly said that

mn111:21.2.verse: they have attained mastery and perfection in noble ethics, immersion, wisdom, and freedom, it’s Sāriputta.

mn111:22.1.verse: And if there’s anyone of whom it may be rightly said that

mn111:22.2.verse: they’re the Buddha’s bosom son, born from his mouth, born of the teaching, created by the teaching, heir in the teaching, not in things of the flesh, it’s Sāriputta.

mn111:23.1.verse: Sāriputta rightly keeps rolling the supreme Wheel of Dhamma that was rolled forth by the Realized One.”

mn111:23.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn111:23.3.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn112:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn112:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn112:2.2.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’

mn112:3.1.verse: You should neither approve nor reject that mendicant’s statement.

mn112:3.3.verse: ‘Reverend, these four kinds of expression have been rightly explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn112:3.5.verse: Saying you’ve seen, heard, thought, or known something, and you have.

mn112:3.6.verse: These are the four kinds of expression rightly explained by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

mn112:3.7.verse: How does the venerable know and see regarding these four kinds of expression so that your mind is freed from defilements by not grasping?’

mn112:4.1.verse: For a mendicant with defilements ended—who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—it is in line with the teaching to answer:

mn112:4.2.verse: ‘Regarding what is seen, reverends, I live without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn112:4.5.verse: or known, I live without getting involved or shying away, independent, untied, liberated, detached, with mind free of boundaries.

mn112:4.6.verse: That is how I know and see regarding these four kinds of expression so that my mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.’

mn112:5.1.verse: Saying ‘Good!’ you should applaud and cheer that mendicant’s statement,

mn112:5.3.verse: ‘Reverend, these five grasping aggregates have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:5.5.verse: That is: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn112:5.6.verse: These are the five grasping aggregates that have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:5.7.verse: How does the venerable know and see regarding these five grasping aggregates so that your mind is freed from defilements by not grasping?’

mn112:6.1.verse: For a mendicant with defilements ended it is in line with the teaching to answer:

mn112:6.2.verse: ‘Reverends, knowing that form is powerless, faded, and unreliable, I understand that my mind is freed through the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendency for form.
