mn112:6.6.verse: consciousness is powerless, faded, and unreliable, I understand that my mind is freed through the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendency for consciousness.

mn112:6.7.verse: That is how I know and see regarding these five grasping aggregates so that my mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.’

mn112:7.1.verse: Saying ‘Good!’ you should applaud and cheer that mendicant’s statement,

mn112:7.3.verse: ‘Reverend, these six elements have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:7.5.verse: The elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.

mn112:7.6.verse: These are the six elements that have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:7.7.verse: How does the venerable know and see regarding these six elements so that your mind is freed from defilements by not grasping?’

mn112:8.1.verse: For a mendicant with defilements ended it is in line with the teaching to answer:

mn112:8.2.verse: ‘Reverends, I’ve not taken the earth element as self, nor is there a self based on the earth element.

mn112:8.3.verse: And I understand that my mind is freed through the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendency based on the earth element.

mn112:8.4.verse: I’ve not taken the water element …

mn112:8.8.verse: consciousness element as self, nor is there a self based on the consciousness element.

mn112:8.9.verse: And I understand that my mind is freed through the ending of attraction based on the consciousness element.

mn112:8.10.verse: That is how I know and see regarding these six elements so that my mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.’

mn112:9.1.verse: Saying ‘Good!’ you should applaud and cheer that mendicant’s statement,

mn112:9.3.verse: ‘Reverend, these six interior and exterior sense fields have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:9.5.verse: The eye and sights, the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and touches, and the mind and ideas.

mn112:9.6.verse: These are the six interior and exterior sense fields that have been rightly explained by the Buddha.

mn112:9.7.verse: How does the venerable know and see regarding these six interior and exterior sense fields so that your mind is freed from defilements by not grasping?’

mn112:10.1.verse: For a mendicant with defilements ended it is in line with the teaching to answer:

mn112:10.2.verse: ‘I understand that my mind is freed through the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of desire and greed and relishing and craving; attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendency for the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and things knowable by eye consciousness.

mn112:10.3.verse: I understand that my mind is freed through the ending of desire for the ear …

mn112:10.7.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and things knowable by mind consciousness.

mn112:10.8.verse: That is how I know and see regarding these six interior and exterior sense fields so that my mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.’

mn112:11.1.verse: Saying ‘Good!’ you should applaud and cheer that mendicant’s statement,

mn112:11.3.verse: ‘Sir, how does the venerable know and see so that he has eradicated I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?’

mn112:12.1.verse: For a mendicant with defilements ended it is in line with the teaching to answer:

mn112:12.2.verse: ‘Formerly, reverends, when I was still a layperson, I was ignorant.

mn112:12.3.verse: Then the Realized One or one of his disciples taught me the Dhamma.

mn112:12.4.verse: I gained faith in the Realized One,

mn112:12.6.verse: “Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn112:12.7.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn112:12.8.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from lay life to homelessness?”

mn112:13.1.verse: After some time I gave up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. I shaved off hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn112:13.2.verse: Once I had gone forth, I took up the training and livelihood of the mendicants. I gave up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. I was scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn112:13.3.verse: I gave up stealing. I took only what’s given, and expected only what’s given. I kept myself clean by not thieving.

mn112:13.4.verse: I gave up unchastity. I became chaste, set apart, refraining from the vulgar act of sex.

mn112:13.5.verse: I gave up lying. I spoke the truth and stuck to the truth. I was honest and dependable, not tricking the world with my words.

mn112:13.6.verse: I gave up backbiting. I didn’t repeat in one place what I heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, I reconciled those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn112:13.7.verse: I gave up harsh speech. I spoke in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn112:13.8.verse: I gave up talking nonsense. My words were timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. I said things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn112:14.1.verse: I refrained from injuring plants and seeds. I ate in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time.

mn112:14.2.verse: I refrained from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.

mn112:14.3.verse: I refrained from attiring and adorning myself with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.

mn112:14.4.verse: I refrained from high and luxurious beds.

mn112:14.5.verse: I refrained from receiving gold and currency,

mn112:14.14.verse: I refrained from running errands and messages;

mn112:14.18.verse: mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.

mn112:14.19.verse: I became content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever I went, I set out taking only these things.

mn112:14.20.verse: Like a bird: wherever it flies, wings are its only burden.

mn112:14.21.verse: In the same way, I became content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever I went, I set out taking only these things.

mn112:14.22.verse: When I had this spectrum of noble ethics, I experienced a blameless happiness inside myself.

mn112:15.1.verse: When I saw a sight with my eyes, I didn’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn112:15.2.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, I practiced restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

mn112:15.3.verse: When I heard a sound with my ears …

mn112:15.4.verse: When I smelled an odor with my nose …

mn112:15.5.verse: When I tasted a flavor with my tongue …

mn112:15.6.verse: When I felt a touch with my body …

mn112:15.7.verse: When I knew an idea with my mind, I didn’t get caught up in the features and details.

mn112:15.8.verse: If the faculty of the mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, I practiced restraint, protecting the faculty of the mind, and achieving its restraint.

mn112:15.9.verse: When I had this noble sense restraint, I experienced an unsullied bliss inside myself.

mn112:16.1.verse: I acted with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn112:16.2.verse: When I had this spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness,

mn112:16.3.verse: I frequented a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn112:16.4.verse: After the meal, I returned from almsround, sat down cross-legged, set my body straight, and brought mindfulness to the present.

mn112:17.1.verse: Giving up covetousness for the world, I meditated with a heart rid of covetousness, cleansing the mind of covetousness.

mn112:17.2.verse: Giving up ill will and malevolence, I meditated with a mind rid of ill will, full of sympathy for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will.

mn112:17.3.verse: Giving up dullness and drowsiness, I meditated with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness.

mn112:17.4.verse: Giving up restlessness and remorse, I meditated without restlessness, my mind settled internally, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse.

mn112:17.5.verse: Giving up doubt, I meditated having gone beyond doubt, not undecided about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.

mn112:18.1.verse: I gave up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn112:18.2.verse: Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn112:18.3.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption …

mn112:19.1.verse: When my mind had immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—I extended it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn112:19.2.verse: I truly understood: “This is suffering” … “This is the origin of suffering” … “This is the cessation of suffering” … “This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering”.

mn112:19.3.verse: I truly understood: “These are defilements” … “This is the origin of defilements” … “This is the cessation of defilements” … “This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements”.

mn112:20.1.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, my mind was freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn112:20.2.verse: When it was freed, I knew it was freed.

mn112:20.3.verse: I understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn112:20.4.verse: That is how I know and see so that I have eradicated I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.’

mn112:21.1.verse: Saying ‘Good!’ you should applaud and cheer that mendicant’s statement,

mn112:21.3.verse: ‘We are fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate

mn112:21.4.verse: to see a venerable such as yourself as one of our spiritual companions!’”

mn112:21.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn112:21.6.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn113:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn113:1.5.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn113:2.1.verse: “Monks, I will teach you the quality of a person of integrity and the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:2.2.verse: Listen, and pay close attention. I will speak.”

mn113:2.3.verse: “Yes, lord,” the monks responded to him.

mn113:3.1.verse: “And which is the quality of a person of no integrity?

mn113:3.2.verse: There is the case where a person of no integrity goes forth from a high-ranking family.

mn113:3.4.verse: ‘I have gone forth from a high-ranking family, but these other monks have not gone forth from a high-ranking family.’

mn113:3.5.verse: He exalts himself for having a high-ranking family and disparages others.

mn113:3.6.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:3.7.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:3.8.verse: ‘It’s not through having a high-ranking family that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through having a high-ranking family that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:3.9.verse: Even though one has not gone forth from a high-ranking family,

mn113:3.10.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:3.11.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for having a high-ranking family nor disparages others.

mn113:3.12.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:4-6.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity goes forth from a great family…

mn113:4-6.5.verse: ‘I have gone forth from a family of extensive wealth, but these other monks have not gone forth from a family of extensive wealth.’

mn113:4-6.6.verse: He exalts himself for having a family of extensive wealth and disparages others.

mn113:4-6.7.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:4-6.8.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:4-6.9.verse: ‘It’s not through having a family of extensive wealth that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through having a family of extensive wealth that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:4-6.10.verse: Even though one has not gone forth from a family of extensive wealth,

mn113:4-6.11.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:4-6.12.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for having a family of extensive wealth nor disparages others.

mn113:4-6.13.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:7.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is well-known & highly regarded.

mn113:7.3.verse: ‘I am well-known & highly regarded, but these other monks are hardly known & have hardly any influence.’

mn113:7.4.verse: He exalts himself for being well-known & highly regarded and disparages others.

mn113:7.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:7.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:7.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being well-known & highly regarded that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being well-known & highly regarded that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:7.8.verse: Even though one is not well-known & highly regarded,

mn113:7.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:7.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being well-known nor disparages others.

mn113:7.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:8.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is one who gains robe-cloth, alms-food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for the sick.

mn113:8.3.verse: ‘I am one who gains robe-cloth, alms-food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for the sick, but these other monks are not ones who gain robe-cloth, alms-food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for the sick.’

mn113:8.4.verse: He exalts himself for being one who gains robe-cloth, alms-food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for the sick and disparages others.

mn113:8.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:8.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:8.7.verse: ‘It’s not through gains that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through gains that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:8.8.verse: Even though one is not one who gains robe-cloth, alms-food, lodgings, & medicinal requisites for the sick,

mn113:8.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:8.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for his gains nor disparages others.

mn113:8.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:9.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is learned.

mn113:9.3.verse: ‘I am learned, but these other monks are not learned.’

mn113:9.4.verse: He exalts himself for being learned and disparages others.

mn113:9.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:9.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:9.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being learned that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being learned that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:9.8.verse: Even though one is not learned,

mn113:9.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:9.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being learned nor disparages others.

mn113:9.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:10.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is a master of the Vinaya.

mn113:10.3.verse: ‘I am a master of the Vinaya, but these other monks are not masters of the Vinaya.’

mn113:10.4.verse: He exalts himself for being a master of the Vinaya and disparages others.

mn113:10.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:10.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:10.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being a master of the Vinaya that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being a master of the Vinaya that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:10.8.verse: Even though one is not a master of the Vinaya,

mn113:10.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:10.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being a master of the Vinaya nor disparages others.

mn113:10.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:11.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is a Dhamma-speaker.

mn113:11.3.verse: ‘I am a Dhamma-speaker, but these other monks are not Dhamma-speakers.’

mn113:11.4.verse: He exalts himself for being a Dhamma-speaker and disparages others.

mn113:11.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:11.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:11.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being a Dhamma-speaker that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being a Dhamma-speaker that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:11.8.verse: Even though one is not a Dhamma-speaker,

mn113:11.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:11.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being a Dhamma-speaker nor disparages others.

mn113:11.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:12.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is a wilderness dweller.

mn113:12.3.verse: ‘I am a wilderness dweller, but these other monks are not wilderness dwellers.’

mn113:12.4.verse: He exalts himself for being a wilderness dweller and disparages others.

mn113:12.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:12.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:12.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being a wilderness dweller that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being a wilderness dweller that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:12.8.verse: Even though one is not a wilderness dweller,

mn113:12.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:12.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being a wilderness dweller nor disparages others.

mn113:12.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:13.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is one who wears robes of thrown-away rags.

mn113:13.3.verse: ‘I am one who wears robes of thrown-away rags, but these other monks are not ones who wear robes of thrown-away rags.’

mn113:13.4.verse: He exalts himself for being one who wears robes of thrown-away rags and disparages others.

mn113:13.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:13.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:13.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being one who wears robes of thrown-away rags that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being one who wears robes of thrown-away rags that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:13.8.verse: Even though one is not one who wears robes of thrown-away rags,

mn113:13.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:13.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being one who wears robes of thrown-away rags nor disparages others.

mn113:13.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:14.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is an alms-goer.

mn113:14.3.verse: ‘I am an alms-goer, but these other monks are not alms-goers.’

mn113:14.4.verse: He exalts himself for being an alms-goer and disparages others.

mn113:14.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:14.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:14.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being an alms-goer that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being an alms-goer that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:14.8.verse: Even though one is not an alms-goer,

mn113:14.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:14.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being an alms-goer nor disparages others.

mn113:14.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:15.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is one who dwells at the root of a tree.

mn113:15.3.verse: ‘I am one who dwells at the root of a tree, but these other monks are not ones who dwell at the root of a tree.’

mn113:15.4.verse: He exalts himself for being one who dwells at the root of a tree and disparages others.

mn113:15.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:15.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:15.7.verse: ‘It’s not through being one who dwells at the root of a tree that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being one who dwells at the root of a tree that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:15.8.verse: Even though one is not one who dwells at the root of a tree,

mn113:15.9.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:15.10.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being one who dwells at the root of a tree nor disparages others.

mn113:15.11.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:16-20.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity is a cemetery dweller…

mn113:16-20.2.verse: one who lives in the open air…

mn113:16-20.4.verse: one who is content with whatever dwelling is assigned to him…

mn113:16-20.5.verse: one who eats only one meal a day.

mn113:16-20.7.verse: ‘I am one who eats only one meal a day, but these other monks do not eat only one meal a day.’

mn113:16-20.8.verse: He exalts himself for being one who eats only one meal a day and disparages others.

mn113:16-20.9.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:16-20.10.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:16-20.11.verse: ‘It’s not through being one who eats only one meal a day that the quality of greed goes to its end; it’s not through being one who eats only one meal a day that the quality of aversion… the quality of delusion goes to its end.

mn113:16-20.12.verse: Even though one is not one who eats only one meal a day,

mn113:16-20.13.verse: if—practicing the Dhamma in line with the Dhamma, practicing masterfully—he is one who follows the Dhamma, he is to be honored for that, praised for that.’

mn113:16-20.14.verse: So, giving priority just to the practice, he neither exalts himself for being one who eats only one meal a day nor disparages others.

mn113:16-20.15.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:21.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity—secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.

mn113:21.3.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the first jhāna, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the first jhāna.’

mn113:21.4.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the first jhāna and disparages others.

mn113:21.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:21.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:21.7.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the first jhāna,

mn113:21.8.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:21.9.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the first jhāna nor disparages others.

mn113:21.10.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:22-24.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity… enters & remains in the second jhāna…

mn113:22-24.5.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the fourth jhāna, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the fourth jhāna.’

mn113:22-24.6.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the fourth jhāna and disparages others.

mn113:22-24.7.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:22-24.8.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:22-24.9.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the fourth jhāna,

mn113:22-24.10.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:22-24.11.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the fourth jhāna nor disparages others.

mn113:22-24.12.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:25.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity, with the complete transcending of perceptions of (physical) form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite space,’ enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of space.

mn113:25.3.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of space, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of space.’

mn113:25.4.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of space and disparages others.

mn113:25.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:25.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:25.7.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of space,

mn113:25.8.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:25.9.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of space nor disparages others.

mn113:25.10.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:26.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite consciousness,’ enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.

mn113:26.3.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.’

mn113:26.4.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness and disparages others.

mn113:26.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:26.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:26.7.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness,

mn113:26.8.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:26.9.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness nor disparages others.

mn113:26.10.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:27.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, (perceiving,) ‘There is nothing,’ enters & remains in the dimension of nothingness.

mn113:27.3.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the dimension of nothingness, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the dimension of nothingness.’

mn113:27.4.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of nothingness and disparages others.

mn113:27.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:27.6.verse: But a person of integrity notices,

mn113:27.7.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the dimension of nothingness,

mn113:27.8.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:27.9.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of nothingness nor disparages others.

mn113:27.10.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:28.1.verse: And further, a person of no integrity, with the complete transcending of the dimension of nothingness, enters & remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn113:28.3.verse: ‘I have gained the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, but these other monks have not gained the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn113:28.4.verse: He exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception and disparages others.

mn113:28.5.verse: This is the quality of a person of no integrity.

mn113:28.7.verse: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-fashioning even with regard to the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception,

mn113:28.8.verse: for by whatever means they suppose it, it becomes otherwise from that.’

mn113:28.9.verse: So, giving priority to non-fashioning, he neither exalts himself for the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception nor disparages others.

mn113:28.10.verse: This is the quality of a person of integrity.

mn113:29.1.verse: A person of integrity, completely transcending the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters & remains in the cessation of perception & feeling. When he sees with discernment, his effluents are ended.

mn113:29.2.verse: This is a monk who does not suppose anything, does not suppose anywhere, does not suppose in any way.”

mn113:29.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn113:29.4.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn113:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn113:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn113:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the qualities of a true person and the qualities of an untrue person.

mn113:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn113:3.1.verse: “And what is a quality of an untrue person?

mn113:3.2.verse: Take an untrue person who has gone forth from an eminent family.

mn113:3.4.verse: ‘I have gone forth from an eminent family, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:3.5.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:3.6.verse: This is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:3.8.verse: ‘It’s not because of one’s eminent family that thoughts of greed, hate, or delusion come to an end.

mn113:3.9.verse: Even if someone has not gone forth from an eminent family,

mn113:3.10.verse: if they practice in line with the teaching, practice properly, and live in line with the teaching, they are worthy of honor and praise for that.’

mn113:3.11.verse: Keeping the practice to themselves, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their eminent family.

mn113:3.12.verse: This is a quality of a true person.

mn113:4-6.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who has gone forth from a great family …

mn113:4-6.5.verse: ‘I have gone forth from an exceptionally wealthy family, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:4-6.6.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:4-6.7.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:4-6.9.verse: ‘It’s not because of one’s exceptionally wealthy family that thoughts of greed, hate, or delusion come to an end.

mn113:4-6.10.verse: Even if someone has not gone forth from an exceptionally wealthy family,

mn113:4-6.11.verse: if they practice in line with the teaching, practice properly, and live in line with the teaching, they are worthy of honor and praise for that.’

mn113:4-6.12.verse: Keeping the practice to themselves, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their exceptionally wealthy family.

mn113:4-6.13.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:7.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who is well-known and famous.

mn113:7.3.verse: ‘I’m well-known and famous. These other mendicants are obscure and insignificant.’

mn113:7.4.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:7.5.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:7.7.verse: ‘It’s not because of one’s fame that thoughts of greed, hate, or delusion come to an end.

mn113:7.8.verse: Even if someone is not well-known and famous,

mn113:7.9.verse: if they practice in line with the teaching, practice properly, and live in line with the teaching, they are worthy of honor and praise for that.’

mn113:7.10.verse: Keeping the practice to themselves, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their fame.

mn113:7.11.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:8.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.

mn113:8.3.verse: ‘I receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:8.4.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:8.5.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:8.7.verse: ‘It’s not because of one’s material things that thoughts of greed, hate, or delusion come to an end.

mn113:8.8.verse: Even if someone doesn’t receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick,

mn113:8.9.verse: if they practice in line with the teaching, practice properly, and live in line with the teaching, they are worthy of honor and praise for that.’

mn113:8.10.verse: Keeping the practice to themselves, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their material things.

mn113:8.11.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:9.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who is very learned …

mn113:10.1.verse: who is an expert in the monastic law …

mn113:13.1.verse: who is a rag robe wearer …

mn113:15.1.verse: who stays at the root of a tree …

mn113:16-20.1.verse: who stays in a charnel ground …

mn113:16-20.2.verse: who stays in the open air …

mn113:16-20.4.verse: who sleeps wherever they lay their mat …

mn113:16-20.5.verse: who eats in one sitting per day.

mn113:16-20.7.verse: ‘I eat in one sitting per day, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:16-20.8.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:16-20.9.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:16-20.11.verse: ‘It’s not because of eating in one sitting per day that thoughts of greed, hate, or delusion come to an end.

mn113:16-20.12.verse: Even if someone eats in more than one sitting per day,

mn113:16-20.13.verse: if they practice in line with the teaching, practice properly, and live in line with the teaching, they are worthy of honor and praise for that.’

mn113:16-20.14.verse: Keeping the practice to themselves, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their eating in one sitting per day.

mn113:16-20.15.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:21.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn113:21.3.verse: ‘I have attained the first absorption, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:21.4.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:21.5.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:21.7.verse: ‘The Buddha has spoken of not being determined even by the attainment of the first absorption.

mn113:21.8.verse: For however they imagine it, it turns out to be something else.’

mn113:21.9.verse: Keeping to themselves the fact that they are not determined by that, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their attainment of the first absorption.

mn113:21.10.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:22-24.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, enters and remains in the second absorption …

mn113:22-24.5.verse: ‘I have attained the fourth absorption, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:22-24.6.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:22-24.7.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:22-24.9.verse: ‘The Buddha has spoken of not being determined even by the attainment of the fourth absorption.

mn113:22-24.10.verse: For however they imagine it, it turns out to be something else.’

mn113:22-24.11.verse: Keeping to themselves the fact that they are not determined by that, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their attainment of the fourth absorption.

mn113:22-24.12.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:25.1.verse: Furthermore, take an untrue person who, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space …

mn113:28.1.verse: the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn113:28.3.verse: ‘I have attained the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, unlike these other mendicants.’

mn113:28.4.verse: And they glorify themselves and put others down on account of that.

mn113:28.5.verse: This too is a quality of an untrue person.

mn113:28.7.verse: ‘The Buddha has spoken of not being determined even by the attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn113:28.8.verse: For however they imagine it, it turns out to be something else.’

mn113:28.9.verse: Keeping to themselves the fact that they are not determined by that, they don’t glorify themselves and put others down on account of their attainment of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn113:28.10.verse: This too is a quality of a true person.

mn113:29.1.verse: Furthermore, take a true person who, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, their defilements come to an end.

mn113:29.2.verse: This is a mendicant who does not conceive with anything, does not conceive regarding anything, does not conceive through anything.”

mn113:29.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn113:29.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn114:0.2.verse: What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated

mn114:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn114:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn114:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you an exposition of the teaching on what should and should not be cultivated.

mn114:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn114:3.1.verse: “I say that there are two kinds of bodily behavior:

mn114:3.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.3.verse: And each of these is a kind of bodily behavior.

mn114:3.4.verse: I say that there are two kinds of verbal behavior:

mn114:3.5.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.6.verse: And each of these is a kind of verbal behavior.

mn114:3.7.verse: I say that there are two kinds of mental behavior:

mn114:3.8.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.9.verse: And each of these is a kind of mental behavior.

mn114:3.10.verse: I say that there are two arisings of thought:

mn114:3.11.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.12.verse: And each of these is an arising of thought.

mn114:3.13.verse: I say that there are two acquisitions of perception:

mn114:3.14.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.15.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of perception.

mn114:3.16.verse: I say that there are two acquisitions of views:

mn114:3.17.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:3.18.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of views.

mn114:3.19.verse: I say that there are two kinds of incarnation:

mn114:3.20.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:4.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Sāriputta said to the Buddha,

mn114:4.2.verse: “Sir, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.

mn114:5.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of bodily behavior:

mn114:5.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:5.3.verse: And each of these is a kind of bodily behavior.’

mn114:5.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:5.6.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of bodily behavior which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:5.7.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of bodily behavior which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:5.8.verse: And what kind of bodily behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:5.9.verse: It’s when someone kills living creatures. They’re violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to living beings.

mn114:5.10.verse: They steal. With the intention to commit theft, they take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.

mn114:5.11.verse: They commit sexual misconduct. They have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.

mn114:5.12.verse: That kind of bodily behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:5.13.verse: And what kind of bodily behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:5.14.verse: It’s when someone gives up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.

mn114:5.15.verse: They give up stealing. They don’t, with the intention to commit theft, take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.

mn114:5.16.verse: They give up sexual misconduct. They don’t have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They don’t have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.

mn114:5.17.verse: That kind of bodily behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:5.18.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of bodily behavior:

mn114:5.19.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:5.20.verse: And each of these is a kind of bodily behavior.’

mn114:5.21.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:6.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of verbal behavior:

mn114:6.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:6.3.verse: And each of these is a kind of verbal behavior.’

mn114:6.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:6.6.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of verbal behavior which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:6.7.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of verbal behavior which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:6.8.verse: And what kind of verbal behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:6.9.verse: It’s when someone lies. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.

mn114:6.10.verse: They backbite. They repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. And so they divide those who are harmonious, supporting division, delighting in division, loving division, speaking words that promote division.

mn114:6.11.verse: They speak harshly. They use the kinds of words that are cruel, nasty, hurtful, offensive, bordering on anger, not leading to immersion.

mn114:6.12.verse: They talk nonsense. Their speech is untimely, and is neither factual nor beneficial. It has nothing to do with the teaching or the training. Their words have no value, and are untimely, unreasonable, rambling, and pointless.

mn114:6.13.verse: That kind of verbal behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:6.14.verse: And what kind of verbal behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:6.15.verse: It’s when someone gives up lying. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my friend, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.

mn114:6.16.verse: They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.

mn114:6.17.verse: They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn114:6.18.verse: They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.

mn114:6.19.verse: That kind of verbal behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:6.20.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of verbal behavior:

mn114:6.21.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:6.22.verse: And each of these is a kind of verbal behavior.’

mn114:6.23.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:7.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of mental behavior:

mn114:7.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:7.3.verse: And each of these is a kind of mental behavior.’

mn114:7.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:7.6.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of mental behavior which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:7.7.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of mental behavior which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:7.8.verse: And what kind of mental behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:7.9.verse: It’s when someone is covetous. They covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’

mn114:7.10.verse: They have ill will and malicious intentions: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, slain, destroyed, or annihilated!’

mn114:7.11.verse: That kind of mental behavior causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:7.12.verse: And what kind of mental behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:7.13.verse: It’s when someone is content. They don’t covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’

mn114:7.14.verse: They have a kind heart and loving intentions: ‘May these sentient beings live free of enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy!’

mn114:7.15.verse: That kind of mental behavior causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:7.16.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of mental behavior:

mn114:7.17.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:7.18.verse: And each of these is a kind of mental behavior.’

mn114:7.19.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:8.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two arisings of thought:

mn114:8.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:8.3.verse: And each of these is an arising of thought.’

mn114:8.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:8.6.verse: You should not cultivate the arising of thought which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:8.7.verse: And you should cultivate the arising of thought which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:8.8.verse: And what arising of thought causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:8.9.verse: It’s when someone is covetous, and lives with their heart full of covetousness.

mn114:8.10.verse: They are malicious, and live with their heart full of ill will.

mn114:8.11.verse: They’re hurtful, and live with their heart intent on harm.

mn114:8.12.verse: That arising of thought causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:8.13.verse: And what arising of thought causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:8.14.verse: It’s when someone is content, and lives with their heart full of contentment.

mn114:8.15.verse: They have good will, and live with their heart full of good will.

mn114:8.16.verse: They’re kind, and live with their heart full of kindness.

mn114:8.17.verse: That arising of thought causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:8.18.verse: ‘I say that there are two arisings of thought:

mn114:8.19.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:8.20.verse: And each of these is an arising of thought.’

mn114:8.21.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:9.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two acquisitions of perception:

mn114:9.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:9.3.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of perception.’

mn114:9.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:9.6.verse: You should not cultivate the acquisition of perception which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:9.7.verse: And you should cultivate the acquisition of perception which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:9.8.verse: And what acquisition of perception causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:9.9.verse: It’s when someone is covetous, and lives with their perception full of covetousness.

mn114:9.10.verse: They are malicious, and live with their perception full of ill will.

mn114:9.11.verse: They’re hurtful, and live with their perception intent on harm.

mn114:9.12.verse: That acquisition of perception causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:9.13.verse: And what acquisition of perception causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:9.14.verse: It’s when someone is content, and lives with their perception full of contentment.

mn114:9.15.verse: They have good will, and live with their perception full of good will.

mn114:9.16.verse: They’re kind, and live with their perception full of kindness.

mn114:9.17.verse: That acquisition of perception causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:9.18.verse: ‘I say that there are two acquisitions of perception:

mn114:9.19.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:9.20.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of perception.’

mn114:9.21.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:10.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two acquisitions of views:

mn114:10.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:10.3.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of views.’

mn114:10.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:10.6.verse: You should not cultivate the acquisition of views which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:10.7.verse: And you should cultivate the acquisition of views which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:10.8.verse: And what acquisition of views causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:10.9.verse: It’s when someone has such a view:

mn114:10.10.verse: ‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn114:10.11.verse: That acquisition of views causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:10.12.verse: And what acquisition of views causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow?

mn114:10.13.verse: It’s when someone has such a view:

mn114:10.14.verse: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn114:10.15.verse: That acquisition of views causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:10.16.verse: ‘I say that there are two acquisitions of views:

mn114:10.17.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:10.18.verse: And each of these is an acquisition of views.’

mn114:10.19.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:11.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of incarnation:

mn114:11.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:11.5.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:11.6.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of incarnation that causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:11.8.verse: You should cultivate the kind of incarnation that causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:11.10.verse: And what kind of incarnation causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline?

mn114:11.11.verse: For one who generates a hurtful incarnation not for the sake of the state of perfection, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:11.12.verse: And what kind of incarnation causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow? For one who generates a pleasing incarnation for the sake of the state of perfection, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:11.13.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of incarnation:

mn114:11.14.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:11.16.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:12.1.verse: Sir, that’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

mn114:13.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of my brief statement in this way.”

mn114:14.1.verse: And the Buddha went on to repeat and endorse Venerable Sāriputta’s explanation in full. Then he went on to explain further:

mn114:22.1.verse: “I say that there are two kinds of sight known by the eye:

mn114:22.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:22.3.verse: I say that there are two kinds of sound known by the ear …

mn114:22.5.verse: two kinds of smell known by the nose …

mn114:22.7.verse: two kinds of taste known by the tongue …

mn114:22.9.verse: two kinds of touch known by the body …

mn114:22.11.verse: two kinds of idea known by the mind:

mn114:22.12.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.”

mn114:23.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Sāriputta said to the Buddha:

mn114:23.2.verse: “Sir, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.

mn114:24.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of sight known by the eye:

mn114:24.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.’

mn114:24.4.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:24.5.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of sight known by the eye which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:24.6.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of sight known by the eye which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:24.7.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of sight known by the eye:

mn114:24.8.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.’

mn114:24.9.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:25.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of sound known by the ear …

mn114:26.1.verse: two kinds of smell known by the nose …

mn114:27.1.verse: two kinds of taste known by the tongue …

mn114:27.3.verse: two kinds of touch known by the body …

mn114:29.1.verse: two kinds of idea known by the mind:

mn114:29.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.’

mn114:29.4.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:30.1.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of idea known by the mind which causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:30.2.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of idea known by the mind which causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:30.3.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of idea known by the mind:

mn114:30.4.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.’

mn114:30.5.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:30.6.verse: Sir, that’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

mn114:31.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of my brief statement in this way.”

mn114:32-36.1.verse: And the Buddha went on to repeat and endorse Venerable Sāriputta’s explanation in full. Then he went on to explain further:

mn114:39.1.verse: “I say that there are two kinds of robes:

mn114:39.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.

mn114:39.3.verse: I say that there are two kinds of almsfood …

mn114:39.10.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.”

mn114:40.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Sāriputta said to the Buddha:

mn114:40.2.verse: “Sir, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.

mn114:41.1.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of robes …

mn114:48.2.verse: that which you should cultivate, and that which you should not cultivate.’

mn114:48.4.verse: but why did he say it?

mn114:48.5.verse: You should not cultivate the kind of individual who causes unskillful qualities to grow while skillful qualities decline.

mn114:48.6.verse: And you should cultivate the kind of individual who causes unskillful qualities to decline while skillful qualities grow.

mn114:48.7.verse: ‘I say that there are two kinds of individual:

mn114:48.8.verse: those who you should cultivate, and those who you should not cultivate.’

mn114:48.9.verse: That’s what the Buddha said, and this is why he said it.

mn114:49.1.verse: Sir, that’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

mn114:50.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of my brief statement in this way.”

mn114:51-58.1.verse: And the Buddha went on to repeat and endorse Venerable Sāriputta’s explanation in full. Then he added:

mn114:60.1.verse: “If all the aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials were to understand the detailed meaning of my brief statement in this way, it would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

mn114:60.5.verse: If the whole world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—was to understand the detailed meaning of my brief statement in this way, it would be for the whole world’s lasting welfare and happiness.”

mn114:61.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn114:61.2.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Sāriputta approved what the Buddha said.

mn115:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn115:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn115:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;

mn115:2.2.verse: whatever perils arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;

mn115:2.3.verse: whatever calamities arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.

mn115:2.4.verse: Just as, bhikkhus, a fire that starts in a reed hut or a grass hut burns down even a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draught-proof, with bolted doors and shuttered windows,

mn115:2.5.verse: so too, bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;

mn115:2.6.verse: whatever perils arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man;

mn115:2.7.verse: whatever calamities arise, all arise because of the fool, not because of the wise man.

mn115:2.8.verse: So, bhikkhus, the fool brings fear, the wise man is free from fear;

mn115:2.9.verse: the fool brings peril, the wise man is free from peril;

mn115:2.10.verse: the fool brings calamity, the wise man is free from calamity.

mn115:2.11.verse: There is no fear from the wise man, bhikkhus, there is no peril from the wise man, there is no calamity from the wise man.

mn115:2.12.verse: Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train thus: ‘We shall be wise men and inquirers’—

mn115:2.13.verse: that is how you should train yourselves.”[^1]

mn115:3.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

mn115:3.2.verse: “In what way, venerable sir, is a wise bhikkhu worthy to be called an inquirer?”

mn115:3.3.verse: “When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in the possible and the impossible—

mn115:3.4.verse: in this way, Ānanda, a wise bhikkhu is worthy to be called an inquirer.”

mn115:4.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:4.3.verse: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element;

mn115:4.4.verse: the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;

mn115:4.5.verse: the nose element, the odour element, the nose-consciousness element;

mn115:4.6.verse: the tongue element, the flavour element, the tongue-consciousness element;

mn115:4.7.verse: the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element;

mn115:4.8.verse: the mind element, the dhamma element, the mind-consciousness element.

mn115:4.9.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these eighteen elements—

mn115:4.10.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:5.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:5.3.verse: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:

mn115:5.4.verse: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.

mn115:5.5.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—

mn115:5.6.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:6.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:6.3.verse: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:

mn115:6.4.verse: the pleasure element, the pain element, the joy element, the grief element, the equanimity element, the ignorance element.

mn115:6.5.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—

mn115:6.6.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:7.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:7.3.verse: There are, Ānanda, these six elements:

mn115:7.4.verse: the sensual-desire element, the renunciation element, the ill-will element, the non-ill-will element, the cruelty element, the non-cruelty element.

mn115:7.5.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six elements—

mn115:7.6.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:8.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:8.3.verse: There are, Ānanda, these three elements:

mn115:8.4.verse: the sensual-desire element, the form element, the formless element.

mn115:8.5.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these three elements—

mn115:8.6.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:9.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements?”

mn115:9.3.verse: There are, Ānanda, these two elements:

mn115:9.4.verse: the conditioned element, the unconditioned element.

mn115:9.5.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these two elements—

mn115:9.6.verse: in this way too, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the elements.”

mn115:10.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the bases?”

mn115:10.2.verse: “There are, Ānanda, these six internal and external bases:

mn115:10.3.verse: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odours, the tongue and flavours, the body and tangibles, the mind and dhammas.

mn115:10.4.verse: When, Ānanda, he knows and sees these six internal and external bases—

mn115:10.5.verse: in this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the bases.”

mn115:11.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in dependent origination?”

mn115:11.3.verse: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.

mn115:11.4.verse: When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases; that is to say:

mn115:11.8.verse: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;

mn115:11.9.verse: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;

mn115:11.15.verse: with birth as condition, ageing and death come to be, and also sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn115:11.16.verse: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.

mn115:11.17.verse: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations;

mn115:11.18.verse: with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;

mn115:11.19.verse: with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;

mn115:11.20.verse: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;

mn115:11.21.verse: with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;

mn115:11.22.verse: with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;

mn115:11.23.verse: with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;

mn115:11.24.verse: with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;

mn115:11.25.verse: with the cessation of clinging, cessation of being;

mn115:11.26.verse: with the cessation of being, cessation of birth;

mn115:11.27.verse: with the cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and also sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair.

mn115:11.28.verse: That is how there is a cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’

mn115:11.29.verse: In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in dependent origination.”

mn115:12.1.verse: “But, venerable sir, in what way is a bhikkhu worthy to be called skilled in the possible and the impossible?”

mn115:12.2.verse: “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any formation as permanent—no such possibility exists’;

mn115:12.3.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some formation as permanent—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:12.4.verse: He understands: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any formation as pleasurable—no such possibility exists’;

mn115:12.5.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some formation as pleasurable—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:12.6.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could treat any dhamma as self—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^2]

mn115:12.7.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could treat some dhamma as self—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:13.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could deprive his mother of life—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:13.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could deprive his mother of life—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:13.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could deprive his father of life …

mn115:13.4.verse: could deprive an Arahant of life—such a possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:13.5.verse: ‘it is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could, with a mind of hate, shed a Tathāgata’s blood—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:13.6.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could, with a mind of hate, shed a Tathāgata’s blood—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:13.7.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could cause a schism in the Saṅgha—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:13.8.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could cause a schism in the Saṅgha—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:13.9.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view could acknowledge another teacher—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^3]

mn115:13.10.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person could acknowledge another teacher—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:14.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that two Arahants, Fully Enlightened Ones, could arise contemporaneously in one world-system—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^4]

mn115:14.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a single Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, could arise in one world-system—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:14.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that two Wheel-turning Monarchs could arise contemporaneously in one world-system—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:14.4.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a single Wheel-turning Monarch could arise in one world-system—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:15.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One—no such possibility exists’, he understands;[^5]

mn115:15.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:15.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could be a Wheel-turning Monarch—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:15.4.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could be a Wheel-turning Monarch—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:15.5.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a woman could occupy the status of Sakka … the status of Māra … the status of a Brahmā—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:15.6.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a man could occupy the status of Sakka … the status of Māra … the status of a Brahmā—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:16.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from bad bodily conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:16.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from bad bodily conduct—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:16.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from bad verbal conduct …

mn115:16.4.verse: from bad mental conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:16.5.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from bad verbal conduct …

mn115:16.6.verse: from bad mental conduct—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:17.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from good bodily conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:17.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from good bodily conduct—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:17.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that an unwished-for, undesired, disagreeable result could come from good verbal conduct …

mn115:17.4.verse: from good mental conduct—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:17.5.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a wished-for, desired, agreeable result could come from good verbal conduct …

mn115:17.6.verse: from good mental conduct—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:18.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of bad bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason,[^6] on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:18.2.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of bad bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:19.1.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of bad verbal conduct …

mn115:19.2.verse: possessed of bad mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:19.3.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of bad verbal conduct …

mn115:19.4.verse: possessed of bad mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—such a possibility exists.’
