mn115:19.5.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of good bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:19.6.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of good bodily conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:19.7.verse: ‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, that a person possessed of good verbal conduct …

mn115:19.8.verse: possessed of good mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell—no such possibility exists’, he understands;

mn115:19.9.verse: and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a person possessed of good verbal conduct …

mn115:19.10.verse: possessed of good mental conduct could, because of that, for that reason, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world—such a possibility exists.’

mn115:19.11.verse: In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is worthy to be called skilled in the possible and the impossible.”

mn115:20.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

mn115:20.2.verse: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvellous.

mn115:20.3.verse: What is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma, venerable sir?”

mn115:20.4.verse: “Therefore, Ānanda, you may remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Many Kinds of Elements’, and also as ‘The Four Cycles’, and also as ‘The Mirror of the Dhamma’, and also as ‘The Drum of the Deathless’, and also as ‘The Unsurpassed Victory in Battle.’”

mn115:20.5.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn115:20.6.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn115:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn115:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn115:2.1.verse: “Whatever dangers there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.2.verse: Whatever perils there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.3.verse: Whatever hazards there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.4.verse: It’s like a fire that spreads from a hut made of reeds or grass, and burns down even a bungalow, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with doors fastened and windows shuttered.

mn115:2.5.verse: In the same way, whatever dangers there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.6.verse: Whatever perils there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.7.verse: Whatever hazards there are, all come from the foolish, not from the astute.

mn115:2.8.verse: So, the fool is dangerous, but the astute person is safe.

mn115:2.9.verse: The fool is perilous, but the astute person is not.

mn115:2.10.verse: The fool is hazardous, but the astute person is not.

mn115:2.11.verse: There’s no danger, peril, or hazard that comes from the astute.

mn115:2.12.verse: So you should train like this: ‘We shall be astute, we shall be inquirers.’”

mn115:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

mn115:3.2.verse: “Sir, how is a mendicant qualified to be called ‘astute, an inquirer’?”

mn115:3.3.verse: “Ānanda, it’s when a mendicant is skilled in the elements, in the sense fields, in dependent origination, and in the possible and the impossible.

mn115:3.4.verse: That’s how a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘astute, an inquirer’.”

mn115:4.1.verse: “But sir, how is a mendicant qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:4.3.verse: The eye element, sight element, and eye consciousness element.

mn115:4.4.verse: The ear element, sound element, and ear consciousness element.

mn115:4.5.verse: The nose element, smell element, and nose consciousness element.

mn115:4.6.verse: The tongue element, taste element, and tongue consciousness element.

mn115:4.7.verse: The body element, touch element, and body consciousness element.

mn115:4.8.verse: The mind element, ideas element, and mind consciousness element.

mn115:4.9.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these eighteen elements,

mn115:4.10.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:5.1.verse: “But sir, could there be another way in which a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:5.4.verse: the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.

mn115:5.5.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these six elements,

mn115:5.6.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:6.1.verse: “But sir, could there be another way in which a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:6.4.verse: the elements of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, equanimity, and ignorance.

mn115:6.5.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these six elements,

mn115:6.6.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:7.1.verse: “But sir, could there be another way in which a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:7.4.verse: the elements of sensuality and renunciation, malice and good will, and cruelty and harmlessness.

mn115:7.5.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these six elements,

mn115:7.6.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:8.1.verse: “But sir, could there be another way in which a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:8.4.verse: the sensual realm, the realm of luminous form, and the formless realm.

mn115:8.5.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these three elements,

mn115:8.6.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:9.1.verse: “But sir, could there be another way in which a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?”

mn115:9.4.verse: the conditioned element and the unconditioned element.

mn115:9.5.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these two elements,

mn115:9.6.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the elements’.”

mn115:10.1.verse: “But sir, how is a mendicant qualified to be called ‘skilled in the sense fields’?”

mn115:10.2.verse: “There are these six interior and exterior sense fields:

mn115:10.3.verse: the eye and sights, the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and touches, and the mind and ideas.

mn115:10.4.verse: When a mendicant knows and sees these six interior and exterior sense fields,

mn115:10.5.verse: they’re qualified to be called ‘skilled in the sense fields’.”

mn115:11.1.verse: “But sir, how is a mendicant qualified to be called ‘skilled in dependent origination’?”

mn115:11.3.verse: ‘When this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

mn115:11.4.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

mn115:11.5.verse: ignorance is a requirement for choices.

mn115:11.6.verse: Choices are a condition for consciousness.

mn115:11.7.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form.

mn115:11.8.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields.

mn115:11.9.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact.

mn115:11.10.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling.

mn115:11.11.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving.

mn115:11.12.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping.

mn115:11.13.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

mn115:11.14.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

mn115:11.15.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

mn115:11.16.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

mn115:11.17.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease.

mn115:11.19.verse: When consciousness ceases, name and form cease.

mn115:11.20.verse: When name and form cease, the six sense fields cease.

mn115:11.21.verse: When the six sense fields cease, contact ceases.

mn115:11.25.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

mn115:11.26.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

mn115:11.27.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

mn115:11.28.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’

mn115:11.29.verse: That’s how a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in dependent origination’.”

mn115:12.1.verse: “But sir, how is a mendicant qualified to be called ‘skilled in the possible and impossible’?”

mn115:12.2.verse: “It’s when a mendicant understands: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to take any condition as permanent. That is not possible.

mn115:12.3.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to take some condition as permanent. That is possible.’

mn115:12.4.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to take any condition as pleasant.

mn115:12.5.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to take some condition as pleasant.’

mn115:12.6.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to take anything as self.

mn115:12.7.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to take something as self.’

mn115:13.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to murder their mother.

mn115:13.2.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to murder their mother.’

mn115:13.3.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to murder their father … or murder a perfected one.

mn115:13.4.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to murder their father … or murder a perfected one.’

mn115:13.5.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to injure a Realized One with malicious intent.

mn115:13.6.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to injure a Realized One with malicious intent.’

mn115:13.7.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to cause a schism in the Saṅgha.

mn115:13.8.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to cause a schism in the Saṅgha.’

mn115:13.9.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an individual accomplished in view to dedicate themselves to another teacher.

mn115:13.10.verse: But it’s possible for an ordinary person to dedicate themselves to another teacher.’

mn115:14.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for two perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas to arise in the same solar system at the same time.

mn115:14.2.verse: But it is possible for just one perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, to arise in one solar system.’

mn115:14.3.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for two wheel-turning monarchs to arise in the same solar system at the same time.

mn115:14.4.verse: But it is possible for just one wheel-turning monarch to arise in one solar system.’

mn115:15.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for a woman to be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

mn115:15.2.verse: But it is possible for a man to be a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.’

mn115:15.3.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for a woman to be a wheel-turning monarch.

mn115:15.4.verse: But it is possible for a man to be a wheel-turning monarch.’

mn115:15.5.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for a woman to perform the role of Sakka, Māra, or the Divinity.

mn115:15.6.verse: But it is possible for a man to perform the role of Sakka, Māra, or the Divinity.’

mn115:16.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for a likable, desirable, agreeable result to come from bad conduct of body, speech, and mind.

mn115:16.2.verse: But it is possible for an unlikable, undesirable, disagreeable result to come from bad conduct of body, speech, and mind.’

mn115:17.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible for an unlikable, undesirable, disagreeable result to come from good conduct of body, speech, and mind.

mn115:17.2.verse: But it is possible for a likable, desirable, agreeable result to come from good conduct of body, speech, and mind.’

mn115:18.1.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible that someone who has engaged in bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, could for that reason alone, when their body breaks up, after death, be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn115:18.2.verse: But it is possible that someone who has engaged in bad conduct of body, speech, and mind could, for that reason alone, when their body breaks up, after death, be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.’

mn115:19.5.verse: They understand: ‘It’s impossible that someone who has engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind could, for that reason alone, when their body breaks up, after death, be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn115:19.6.verse: But it is possible that someone who has engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind could, for that reason alone, when their body breaks up, after death, be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’

mn115:19.11.verse: That’s how a mendicant is qualified to be called ‘skilled in the possible and impossible’.”

mn115:20.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

mn115:20.3.verse: What is the name of this exposition of the teaching?”

mn115:20.4.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, you may remember this exposition of the teaching as ‘The Many Elements’, or else ‘The Four Rounds’, or else ‘The Mirror of the Teaching’, or else ‘The Drum of Freedom From Death’, or else ‘The Supreme Victory in Battle’.”

mn115:20.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn115:20.6.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn116:1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha on the Isigili mountain.

mn116:1.3.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

mn116:1.5.verse: “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

mn116:1.6.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

mn116:2.1.verse: “Do you see, monks, that mountain called Vebhāra?”

mn116:2.3.verse: “For that mountain Vebhāra, monks, there was once another name, another designation.

mn116:2.4.verse: Do you see, monks, that mountain called Paṇḍava?”

mn116:2.6.verse: “For that mountain Paṇḍava, monks, there was once another name, another designation.

mn116:2.7.verse: Do you see, monks, that mountain called Vepulla?”

mn116:2.9.verse: “For that mountain Vepulla, monks, there was once another name, another designation.

mn116:2.10.verse: Do you see, monks, that mountain called Gijjhakūṭa?”

mn116:2.12.verse: “For that mountain Gijjhakūṭa, monks, there was once another name, another designation.

mn116:2.13.verse: Do you see, monks, this mountain called Isigili?”

mn116:3.1.verse: “For this mountain Isigili, monks, there has been only this name, this designation.

mn116:3.2.verse: Formerly, monks, five hundred Independent Buddhas were settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:3.3.verse: They were seen entering this mountain, but after entering were not seen again.

mn116:3.4.verse: Having seen that the people said this:

mn116:3.5.verse: “This mountain devours these seers - Seer Devourer (Isi-gili),”

mn116:3.7.verse: Monks, I will declare the names of those Independent Buddhas,

mn116:3.8.verse: monks, I will proclaim the names of those Independent Buddhas,

mn116:3.9.verse: monks, I will reveal the names of those Independent Buddhas.

mn116:3.10.verse: Listen to it, apply your minds well, and I will speak.”

mn116:3.11.verse: “Yes, reverend Sir,” those monks, replied to the Fortunate One,

mn116:3.12.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

mn116:4.1.verse: “One Independent Sambuddha named Ariṭṭha, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.2.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Upariṭṭha, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.3.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Tagarasikhī, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.4.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Yasassī, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.5.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Sudassana, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.6.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Piyadassī, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.7.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Gandhāra, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.8.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Piṇḍola, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.9.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Upāsabha, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.10.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Nīta, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.11.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Tatha, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.12.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Sutavā, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:4.13.verse: One Independent Sambuddha named Bhāvitatta, monks, was settled for a long time on this mountain Isigili.

mn116:5.1.verse: Those excellent beings, not troubled, not yearning,

mn116:5.4.verse: please listen as I proclaim their names:

mn116:6.2.verse: also there are Megha, Anīgha, Sudāṭha,

mn116:6.3.verse: Independent Buddhas who have ended what leads to rebirth.

mn116:6.4.verse: Hiṅgu and Hiṅga, ones of great power,

mn116:6.5.verse: the two Jālinas who were sages, and Aṭṭhaka,

mn116:6.6.verse: also Kosala the Buddha, and then Subāhu,

mn116:6.9.verse: Kāla and Upakāla, Vijita, and Jita,

mn116:6.11.verse: Passī, who left off cleaving, the root of suffering,

mn116:6.12.verse: Aparājita, who defeated the strength of Māra,

mn116:6.22.verse: another sage Sayha, who had great fervour,

mn116:6.23.verse: the twelve named Ānanda, Nanda, and Upananda (i.e. 4 to each name),

mn116:6.24.verse: Bhāradvāja, one who bore his last body,

mn116:6.27.verse: Tissa and Upatissa, who cut the bonds of rebirth,

mn116:6.28.verse: Upasīdarī, and Sīdarī, who cut off craving,

mn116:6.30.verse: Usabha, who cut off the net, the root of suffering,

mn116:6.31.verse: Upanīta, who attained the state of peace,

mn116:6.36.verse: the Buddha Kaṇha, whose mind was completely free -

mn116:7.1.verse: these and others who were ones of great power,

mn116:7.2.verse: Independent Buddhas, who had ended what leads to rebirth,

mn116:7.3.verse: these great seers, who had gone beyond the shackle,

mn116:7.4.verse: worship those completely emancipated, who are beyond measure.”

mn116:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Isigili Mountain.

mn116:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn116:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you see that Mount Vebhāra?”

mn116:2.3.verse: “It used to have a different label and description.

mn116:2.4.verse: Do you see that Mount Paṇḍava?”

mn116:2.6.verse: “It too used to have a different label and description.

mn116:2.7.verse: Do you see that Mount Vepulla?”

mn116:2.9.verse: “It too used to have a different label and description.

mn116:2.10.verse: Do you see that Mount Vulture’s Peak?”

mn116:2.12.verse: “It too used to have a different label and description.

mn116:2.13.verse: Do you see that Mount Isigili?”

mn116:3.1.verse: “It used to have exactly the same label and description.

mn116:3.2.verse: Once upon a time, five hundred independent Buddhas dwelt for a long time on this Isigili.

mn116:3.3.verse: They were seen entering the mountain, but after entering were seen no more.

mn116:3.4.verse: When people noticed this they said:

mn116:3.6.verse: That’s how it came to be known as Isigili, the “seer-swallower”.

mn116:3.7.verse: I shall declare the names of the independent Buddhas;

mn116:3.8.verse: I shall extol the names of the independent Buddhas;

mn116:3.9.verse: I shall teach the names of the independent Buddhas.

mn116:3.10.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn116:4.1.verse: “The independent Buddhas who dwelt for a long time on this Isigili were named Ariṭṭha,

mn116:5.1.verse: Those saintly beings, untroubled, with no need for hope,

mn116:5.4.verse: the supreme men, free of thorns.

mn116:6.3.verse: Independent Buddhas, enders of the leash to existence;

mn116:6.4.verse: and Hiṅgū and Hiṅga the mighty.

mn116:6.5.verse: Two sages named Jāli, and Aṭṭhaka;

mn116:6.6.verse: then the awakened one Kosala, then Subāhu;

mn116:6.8.verse: right and true, stainless and astute.

mn116:6.9.verse: Kāḷa and Upakāḷa, Vijita and Jita,

mn116:6.10.verse: Aṅga and Paṅga, and Guttijita too;

mn116:6.11.verse: Passin gave up attachment, suffering’s root,

mn116:6.15.verse: Manomaya, and Bandhumā the cutter of conceit,

mn116:6.16.verse: then Adhimutta, and Ketumā the immaculate.

mn116:6.22.verse: another sage, Sayha of peerless effort.

mn116:6.23.verse: There are twelve Ānandas, Nandas, and Upanandas,

mn116:6.24.verse: and Bhāradvāja, bearing his final body.

mn116:6.27.verse: Tissa and Upatissa, who’ve both cut the bonds to rebirth,

mn116:6.28.verse: Upasīdarī and Sīdarī, who’ve both cut off craving.

mn116:6.29.verse: Maṅgala was awakened, free of greed,

mn116:6.30.verse: Usabha cut the net, the root of suffering,

mn116:6.31.verse: Upanīta who attained the state of peace,

mn116:6.35.verse: Mānatthaddha, beautiful and free of greed,

mn116:6.36.verse: and the Buddha Kaṇha, his mind well freed.

mn116:7.1.verse: These and other mighty ones awakened independently,

mn116:7.2.verse: enders of the leash to existence—

mn116:7.3.verse: honor these great seers who have slipped all chains,

mn117:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn117:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn117:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Noble right concentration with its supports and with its requisites.

mn117:2.2.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn117:3.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble right concentration with its supports and with its requisites?

mn117:3.2.verse: These are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness;

mn117:3.3.verse: any unification of mind equipped with these seven factors—

mn117:3.4.verse: this is called the Noble right concentration with its supports and with its requisites.

mn117:4.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:4.3.verse: He understands wrong view as wrong view, and he understands right view as right view: this is his right view.

mn117:5.2.verse: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed, no fruit or ripening of good and bad kammas, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously born beings, no good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.’

mn117:6.2.verse: There is twofold right view, I say, bhikkhus:

mn117:6.3.verse: there is right view affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence;

mn117:6.4.verse: and there is the Noble Ones’ right view unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:7.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is right view affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence?

mn117:7.2.verse: ‘There is what is given and what is offered and what is sacrificed, and there is fruit and ripening of good and bad kammas, and there is this world and the other world, and mother and father, and spontaneously born beings, and good and virtuous monks and divines that have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world.’

mn117:7.3.verse: This, bhikkhus, is right view affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence.

mn117:8.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right view unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path?

mn117:8.2.verse: Any understanding, understanding faculty, understanding power, investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, right view as path factor, in one whose mind is noble and taint-free, who possesses and develops the Path—

mn117:8.3.verse: this is called, bhikkhus, the Noble Ones’ right view unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:9.1.verse: ‘He makes effort to abandon wrong view and to enter upon right view: this is his right effort.

mn117:9.2.verse: Mindful he abandons wrong view, mindful he enters upon and abides in right view: this is his right mindfulness.

mn117:9.3.verse: So these three dhammas run and revolve around right view, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:10.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:10.3.verse: He understands wrong intention as wrong intention, and he understands right intention as right intention: this is his right view.

mn117:11.2.verse: Intention directed to sensual desires, intention directed to ill-will, intention directed to cruelty—

mn117:12.2.verse: There is twofold right intention, I say, bhikkhus:

mn117:12.3.verse: there is right intention affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence;

mn117:12.4.verse: and there is the Noble Ones’ right intention unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:13.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is right intention affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence?

mn117:13.2.verse: Intention directed to renunciation, intention directed to non-ill-will, intention directed to non-cruelty:

mn117:13.3.verse: ‘this, bhikkhus, is right intention affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence.’

mn117:14.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right intention unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path?

mn117:14.2.verse: Any thought, thinking, intention, fixing, fixedness, directing of mind, verbal process, in one whose mind is noble and taint-free, who possesses and develops the Path—

mn117:14.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right intention unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:15.1.verse: ‘He makes effort to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention: this is his right effort.

mn117:15.2.verse: Mindful he abandons wrong intention, mindful he enters upon and abides in right intention: this is his right mindfulness.

mn117:15.3.verse: So these three dhammas run and revolve around right intention, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:16.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:16.3.verse: He understands wrong speech as wrong speech, and he understands right speech as right speech: this is his right view.

mn117:17.2.verse: False speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, gossip—

mn117:18.2.verse: There is twofold right speech, I say, bhikkhus:

mn117:18.3.verse: there is right speech affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence;

mn117:18.4.verse: and there is the Noble Ones’ right speech unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:19.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is right speech affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence?

mn117:19.2.verse: Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, abstinence from gossip—

mn117:19.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is right speech affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence.

mn117:20.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right speech unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path?

mn117:20.2.verse: Any abstaining, abstention, reabstention, abstinence, from the four kinds of verbal misconduct, in one whose mind is noble and taint-free, who possesses and develops the Path—

mn117:20.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right speech unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:21.1.verse: ‘He makes effort to abandon wrong speech and to enter upon right speech: this is his right effort.

mn117:21.2.verse: Mindful he abandons wrong speech, mindful he enters upon and abides in right speech: this is his right mindfulness.

mn117:21.3.verse: So these three dhammas run and revolve around right speech, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:22.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:22.3.verse: He understands wrong action as wrong action, and he understands right action as right action: this is his right view.

mn117:23.2.verse: Killing living beings, taking what is not given, misconduct in sensual desires—

mn117:24.2.verse: There is twofold right action, I say, bhikkhus:

mn117:24.3.verse: there is right action affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence;

mn117:24.4.verse: and there is the Noble Ones’ right action unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:25.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is right action affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence?

mn117:25.2.verse: Abstinence from killing living beings, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from misconduct in sensual desires—

mn117:25.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is right action affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence.

mn117:26.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right action unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path?

mn117:26.2.verse: Any abstaining, abstention, reabstention, abstinence, from the three kinds of bodily misconduct, in one whose mind is noble and taint-free, who possesses and develops the Path—

mn117:26.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right action unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:27.1.verse: ‘He makes effort to abandon wrong action and to enter upon right action: this is his right effort.

mn117:27.2.verse: Mindful he abandons wrong action, mindful he enters upon and abides in right action: this is his right mindfulness.

mn117:27.3.verse: So these three dhammas run and revolve around right action, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:28.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:28.3.verse: He understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, and he understands right livelihood as right livelihood: this is his right view.

mn117:29.2.verse: Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain—

mn117:30.2.verse: There is twofold right livelihood, I say, bhikkhus:

mn117:30.3.verse: there is right livelihood affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence;

mn117:30.4.verse: and there is the Noble Ones’ right livelihood unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:31.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence?

mn117:31.2.verse: Here, bhikkhus, a disciple of the Noble Ones abandons wrong livelihood and gains his living by right livelihood—

mn117:31.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood affected by taints, which partakes of merit and ripens into the essentials of existence.

mn117:32.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right livelihood unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path?

mn117:32.2.verse: Any abstaining, abstention, reabstention, abstinence, from wrong livelihood, in one whose mind is noble and taint-free, who possesses and develops the Path—

mn117:32.3.verse: this, bhikkhus, is the Noble Ones’ right livelihood unaffected by taints, which is supramundane and a factor of the Path.

mn117:33.1.verse: ‘He makes effort to abandon wrong livelihood and to enter upon right livelihood: this is his right effort.

mn117:33.2.verse: Mindful he abandons wrong livelihood, mindful he enters upon and abides in right livelihood: this is his right mindfulness.

mn117:33.3.verse: So these three dhammas run and revolve around right livelihood, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:34.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:34.3.verse: In one of right view, right intention is brought to be; in one of right intention, right speech is brought to be; in one of right speech, right action is brought to be; in one of right action, right livelihood is brought to be; in one of right livelihood, right effort is brought to be; in one of right effort, right mindfulness is brought to be; in one of right mindfulness, right concentration is brought to be; in one of right concentration, right knowledge is brought to be; in one of right knowledge, right deliverance is brought to be.

mn117:34.4.verse: So, bhikkhus, the way of one in the higher training has eight factors, while the Arahant’s has ten.

mn117:34.5.verse: Here too, through right knowledge, many evil unprofitable dhammas that have vanished come to perfection through development.

mn117:35.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:35.3.verse: In one of right view, wrong view is abolished.

mn117:35.4.verse: And the many evil unprofitable dhammas that come to be with wrong view as their condition are also abolished in him.

mn117:35.5.verse: And the many profitable dhammas that have right view as their condition come to perfection in him through development.

mn117:35.6.verse: In one of right intention, wrong intention is abolished …

mn117:35.7.verse: in one of right speech, wrong speech is abolished …

mn117:35.8.verse: in one of right action, wrong action is abolished …

mn117:35.9.verse: in one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is abolished …

mn117:35.10.verse: in one of right effort, wrong effort is abolished …

mn117:35.11.verse: in one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is abolished …

mn117:35.12.verse: in one of right concentration, wrong concentration is abolished …

mn117:35.13.verse: in one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is abolished …

mn117:35.14.verse: in one of right deliverance, wrong deliverance is abolished.

mn117:35.15.verse: And the many evil unprofitable dhammas that come to be with wrong deliverance as their condition are also abolished in him.

mn117:35.16.verse: And the many profitable dhammas that have right deliverance as their condition come to perfection in him through development.

mn117:36.1.verse: ‘So, bhikkhus, there are twenty parts on the profitable side, and twenty parts on the unprofitable side—

mn117:36.2.verse: this discourse on the Dhamma in forty essential parts has been set rolling and cannot be stopped by any monk or divine or god or Māra or Divinity or anyone in the world.

mn117:37.1.verse: ‘Whatever monk or divine, bhikkhus, should think that this discourse on the Dhamma in forty essential parts ought to be censured and rejected, then there are ten legitimate grounds for criticism that would provide him, here and now, with grounds for blame:

mn117:37.2.verse: if that worthy one censures right view, then those monks and divines who have wrong view are honoured by him, are commended by him;

mn117:37.3.verse: if that worthy one censures right intention, then those monks and divines who have wrong intention are honoured by him, are commended by him;

mn117:37.4.verse: if that worthy one censures right speech …

mn117:37.11.verse: if that worthy one censures right deliverance, then those monks and divines who have wrong deliverance are honoured by him, are commended by him.

mn117:37.12.verse: Whatever monk or divine, bhikkhus, should think that this discourse on the Dhamma in forty essential parts ought to be censured and rejected, then these ten legitimate grounds for criticism would provide him, here and now, with grounds for blame.

mn117:38.1.verse: ‘Even those of Okkalā, the Vassa and Bhañña, holders of the doctrine of non-causality, the doctrine of non-action, and the doctrine of nihilism, did not think that this discourse on the Dhamma in forty essential parts should be censured and rejected.

mn117:38.3.verse: For fear of blame, attack, and confutation.’

mn117:38.4.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn117:38.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn117:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn117:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn117:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you noble right immersion with its vital conditions and its prerequisites.

mn117:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn117:3.1.verse: “And what is noble right immersion with its vital conditions and its prerequisites?

mn117:3.2.verse: They are: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:3.3.verse: Unification of mind with these seven factors as prerequisites

mn117:3.4.verse: is called noble right immersion ‘with its vital conditions’ and also ‘with its prerequisites’.

mn117:4.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:4.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:4.3.verse: When you understand wrong view as wrong view and right view as right view, that’s your right view.

mn117:5.2.verse: ‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn117:6.2.verse: Right view is twofold, I say.

mn117:6.3.verse: There is right view that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:6.4.verse: And there is right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:7.1.verse: And what is right view that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments?

mn117:7.2.verse: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’

mn117:7.3.verse: This is right view that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:8.1.verse: And what is right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path?

mn117:8.2.verse: It’s the wisdom—the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of investigation of principles, and right view as a factor of the path—in one intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path.

mn117:8.3.verse: This is called right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:9.1.verse: They make an effort to give up wrong view and embrace right view: that’s their right effort.

mn117:9.2.verse: Mindfully they give up wrong view and embrace right view: that’s their right mindfulness.

mn117:9.3.verse: So these three things keep running and circling around right view, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:10.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:10.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:10.3.verse: When you understand wrong purpose as wrong purpose and right purpose as right purpose, that’s your right view.

mn117:11.2.verse: Purposes of sensuality, of malice, and of cruelty.

mn117:12.2.verse: Right purpose is twofold, I say.

mn117:12.3.verse: There is right purpose that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:12.4.verse: And there is right purpose that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:13.1.verse: And what is right purpose that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments?

mn117:13.2.verse: Purposes of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness.

mn117:13.3.verse: This is right purpose that is accompanied by defilements.

mn117:14.1.verse: And what is right purpose that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path?

mn117:14.2.verse: It’s the thinking—the placing of the mind, thought, planting, implanting, embedding of the mind, verbal process—in one intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path.

mn117:14.3.verse: This is right purpose that is noble.

mn117:15.1.verse: They make an effort to give up wrong purpose and embrace right purpose: that’s their right effort.

mn117:15.2.verse: Mindfully they give up wrong purpose and take up right purpose: that’s their right mindfulness.

mn117:15.3.verse: So these three things keep running and circling around right purpose, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:16.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:16.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:16.3.verse: When you understand wrong speech as wrong speech and right speech as right speech, that’s your right view.

mn117:17.2.verse: Speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical.

mn117:18.2.verse: Right speech is twofold, I say.

mn117:18.3.verse: There is right speech that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:18.4.verse: And there is right speech that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:19.1.verse: And what is right speech that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments?

mn117:19.2.verse: Refraining from lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and talking nonsense.

mn117:19.3.verse: This is right speech that is accompanied by defilements.

mn117:20.1.verse: And what is right speech that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path?

mn117:20.2.verse: It’s the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from the four kinds of bad verbal conduct in one intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path.

mn117:20.3.verse: This is right speech that is noble.

mn117:21.1.verse: They make an effort to give up wrong speech and embrace right speech: that’s their right effort.

mn117:21.2.verse: Mindfully they give up wrong speech and take up right speech: that’s their right mindfulness.

mn117:21.3.verse: So these three things keep running and circling around right speech, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:22.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:22.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:22.3.verse: When you understand wrong action as wrong action and right action as right action, that’s your right view.

mn117:23.2.verse: Killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

mn117:24.2.verse: Right action is twofold, I say.

mn117:24.3.verse: There is right action that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:24.4.verse: And there is right action that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:25.1.verse: And what is right action that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments?

mn117:25.2.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

mn117:25.3.verse: This is right action that is accompanied by defilements.

mn117:26.1.verse: And what is right action that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path?

mn117:26.2.verse: It’s the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from the three kinds of bad bodily conduct in one intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path.

mn117:26.3.verse: This is right action that is noble.

mn117:27.1.verse: They make an effort to give up wrong action and embrace right action: that’s their right effort.

mn117:27.2.verse: Mindfully they give up wrong action and take up right action: that’s their right mindfulness.

mn117:27.3.verse: So these three things keep running and circling around right action, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:28.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:28.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:28.3.verse: When you understand wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood and right livelihood as right livelihood, that’s your right view.

mn117:29.2.verse: Fawning, flattery, hinting, and belittling, and using material things to chase after other material things.

mn117:30.2.verse: Right livelihood is twofold, I say.

mn117:30.3.verse: There is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments.

mn117:30.4.verse: And there is right livelihood that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.

mn117:31.1.verse: And what is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements, partakes of good deeds, and ripens in attachments?

mn117:31.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and earns a living by right livelihood.

mn117:31.3.verse: This is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements.

mn117:32.1.verse: And what is right livelihood that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path?

mn117:32.2.verse: It’s the desisting, abstaining, abstinence, and refraining from wrong livelihood in one intent on the noble, intent on the undefiled, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path.

mn117:32.3.verse: This is right livelihood that is noble.

mn117:33.1.verse: They make an effort to give up wrong livelihood and embrace right livelihood: that’s their right effort.

mn117:33.2.verse: Mindfully they give up wrong livelihood and take up right livelihood: that’s their right mindfulness.

mn117:33.3.verse: So these three things keep running and circling around right livelihood, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.

mn117:34.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:34.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:34.3.verse: Right view produces right purpose. Right purpose produces right speech. Right speech produces right action. Right action produces right livelihood. Right livelihood produces right effort. Right effort produces right mindfulness. Right mindfulness produces right immersion. Right immersion produces right knowledge. Right knowledge produces right freedom.

mn117:34.4.verse: So the trainee has eight factors, while the perfected one has ten factors.

mn117:34.5.verse: And here too, the eradication of many bad, unskillful qualities is fully developed due to right knowledge.

mn117:35.1.verse: In this context, right view comes first.

mn117:35.2.verse: And how does right view come first?

mn117:35.3.verse: For one of right view, wrong view is worn away.

mn117:35.4.verse: And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong view are worn away.

mn117:35.5.verse: And because of right view, many skillful qualities are fully developed.

mn117:35.6.verse: For one of right purpose, wrong purpose is worn away. …

mn117:35.7.verse: For one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away. …

mn117:35.8.verse: For one of right action, wrong action is worn away. …

mn117:35.9.verse: For one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away. …

mn117:35.10.verse: For one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away. …

mn117:35.11.verse: For one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away. …

mn117:35.12.verse: For one of right immersion, wrong immersion is worn away. …

mn117:35.13.verse: For one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away. …

mn117:35.14.verse: For one of right freedom, wrong freedom is worn away.

mn117:35.15.verse: And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong freedom are worn away.

mn117:35.16.verse: And because of right freedom, many skillful qualities are fully developed.

mn117:36.1.verse: So there are twenty on the side of the skillful, and twenty on the side of the unskillful.

mn117:36.2.verse: This exposition of the teaching on the Great Forty has been rolled forth. And it cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

mn117:37.1.verse: If any ascetic or brahmin imagines they can criticize and reject the exposition of the teaching on the Great Forty, they deserve rebuttal and criticism on ten legitimate grounds in this very life.

mn117:37.2.verse: If such a gentleman criticizes right view, they praise and honor the ascetics and brahmins who have wrong view.

mn117:37.11.verse: right freedom, they praise and honor the ascetics and brahmins who have wrong freedom.

mn117:37.12.verse: If any ascetic or brahmin imagines they can criticize and reject the exposition of the teaching on the Great Forty, they deserve rebuttal and criticism on these ten legitimate grounds in this very life.

mn117:38.1.verse: Even those who were loud and bold advocates of the doctrines of no-cause, inaction, and nihilism, didn’t imagine that the Great Forty should be criticized or rejected.

mn117:38.3.verse: For fear of being blamed, provoked, and faulted.”

mn117:38.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn117:38.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn118:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, together with many well-known elder disciples—

mn118:1.3.verse: Ven. Sāriputta, Ven. Mahā Moggallāna, Ven. Mahā Kassapa, Ven. Mahā Kaccāna, Ven. Mahā Koṭṭhita, Ven. Mahā Kappina, Ven. Mahā Cunda, Ven. Anuruddha, Ven. Revata, Ven. Ānanda, and other well-known elder disciples.

mn118:2.1.verse: On that occasion the elder monks were teaching & instructing.

mn118:2.2.verse: Some elder monks were teaching & instructing ten monks, some were teaching & instructing twenty monks, some were teaching & instructing thirty monks, some were teaching & instructing forty monks.

mn118:2.3.verse: The new monks, being taught & instructed by the elder monks, were discerning grand, successive distinctions.

mn118:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion—the uposatha day of the fifteenth, the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony—the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:3.2.verse: Surveying the silent Saṅgha of monks, he addressed them:

mn118:4.1.verse: “Monks, I am content with this practice.

mn118:4.2.verse: I am content at heart with this practice.

mn118:4.3.verse: So arouse even more intense persistence for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized.

mn118:4.4.verse: I will remain right here at Sāvatthī (for another month) through the ‘White Water-lily’ Month, the fourth month of the rains.”

mn118:5.1.verse: The monks in the countryside heard,

mn118:5.2.verse: “The Blessed One, they say, will remain right there at Sāvatthī through the White Water-lily Month, the fourth month of the rains.”

mn118:5.3.verse: So they left for Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.

mn118:6.1.verse: Then the elder monks taught & instructed the new monks even more intensely.

mn118:6.2.verse: Some elder monks were teaching & instructing ten monks, some were teaching & instructing twenty monks, some were teaching & instructing thirty monks, some were teaching & instructing forty monks.

mn118:6.3.verse: The new monks, being taught & instructed by the elder monks, were discerning grand, successive distinctions.

mn118:7.1.verse: Now on that occasion—the uposatha day of the fifteenth, the full-moon night of the White Water-lily Month, the fourth month of the rains—the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:7.2.verse: Surveying the silent Saṅgha of monks, he addressed them:

mn118:8.1.verse: “Monks, this assembly is free from idle chatter, devoid of idle chatter, and is established on pure heartwood: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly.

mn118:8.2.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly.

mn118:8.3.verse: The sort of assembly that is deserving of gifts, deserving of hospitality, deserving of offerings, deserving of respect, an incomparable field of merit for the world:

mn118:8.4.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly.

mn118:8.5.verse: The sort of assembly to which a small gift, when given, becomes great, and a great gift greater:

mn118:8.6.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly.

mn118:8.7.verse: The sort of assembly that is rare to see in the world:

mn118:8.8.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly—

mn118:8.9.verse: the sort of assembly that it would be worth traveling for leagues, taking along provisions, in order to see.

mn118:9.1.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who are arahants, whose effluents are ended, who have reached fulfillment, done the task, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, laid to waste the fetter of becoming, and who are released through right gnosis:

mn118:9.2.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:10.1.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who, with the wasting away of the five lower fetters, are due to arise spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes), there to be totally unbound, destined never again to return from that world:

mn118:10.2.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:11.1.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who, with the wasting away of (the first) three fetters, and with the attenuation of passion, aversion, & delusion, are once-returners, who—on returning only once more to this world—will make an ending to stress:

mn118:11.2.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:12.1.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who, with the wasting away of (the first) three fetters, are stream-enterers, certain, never again destined for the lower realms, headed for self-awakening:

mn118:12.2.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:13.1.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who remain devoted to the development of the four establishings of mindfulness—

mn118:13.2.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:14.7.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:14.8.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who remain devoted to the development of good will…

mn118:14.12.verse: (the perception of the) unattractiveness (of the body)…

mn118:14.14.verse: Such are the monks in this Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:14.15.verse: “In this Saṅgha of monks there are monks who remain devoted to mindfulness of in-&-out breathing.

mn118:15.1.verse: Mindfulness of in-&-out breathing, when developed & pursued, is of great fruit, of great benefit.

mn118:15.2.verse: Mindfulness of in-&-out breathing, when developed & pursued, brings the four establishings of mindfulness to their culmination.

mn118:15.3.verse: The four establishings of mindfulness, when developed & pursued, bring the seven factors for awakening to their culmination.

mn118:15.4.verse: The seven factors for awakening, when developed & pursued, bring clear knowing & release to their culmination.

mn118:16.1.verse: “Now how is mindfulness of in-&-out breathing developed & pursued so as to be of great fruit, of great benefit?

mn118:17.1.verse: There is the case where a monk, having gone to the wilderness, to the shade of a tree, or to an empty building, sits down folding his legs crosswise, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness to the fore.

mn118:17.2.verse: Always mindful, he breathes in; mindful he breathes out.

mn118:18.1.verse: [1] Breathing in long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in long’; or breathing out long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out long.’

mn118:18.2.verse: [2] Or breathing in short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in short’; or breathing out short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out short.’

mn118:18.3.verse: [3] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the entire body.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the entire body.’

mn118:18.4.verse: [4] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in calming bodily fabrication.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out calming bodily fabrication.’

mn118:19.1.verse: [5] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in sensitive to rapture.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out sensitive to rapture.’

mn118:19.2.verse: [6] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in sensitive to pleasure.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out sensitive to pleasure.’

mn118:19.3.verse: [7] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in sensitive to mental fabrication.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out sensitive to mental fabrication.’

mn118:19.4.verse: [8] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in calming mental fabrication.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out calming mental fabrication.’

mn118:20.1.verse: [9] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the mind.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the mind.’

mn118:20.2.verse: [10] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in gladdening the mind.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out gladdening the mind.’

mn118:20.3.verse: [11] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in concentrating the mind.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out concentrating the mind.’

mn118:20.4.verse: [12] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in releasing the mind.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out releasing the mind.’

mn118:21.1.verse: [13] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in focusing on inconstancy.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out focusing on inconstancy.’

mn118:21.2.verse: [14] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in focusing on dispassion [or: fading].’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out focusing on dispassion.’

mn118:21.3.verse: [15] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in focusing on cessation.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out focusing on cessation.’

mn118:21.4.verse: [16] He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in focusing on relinquishing.’ He trains himself, ‘I will breathe out focusing on relinquishing.’

mn118:22.1.verse: This is how mindfulness of in-&-out breathing is developed & pursued so as to be of great fruit, of great benefit.

mn118:23.1.verse: “And how is mindfulness of in-&-out breathing developed & pursued so as to bring the four establishings of mindfulness to their culmination?

mn118:24.1.verse: [1] On whatever occasion a monk breathing in long discerns, ‘I am breathing in long’; or breathing out long, discerns, ‘I am breathing out long’;

mn118:24.2.verse: or breathing in short, discerns, ‘I am breathing in short’; or breathing out short, discerns, ‘I am breathing out short’;

mn118:24.3.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out sensitive to the entire body’;

mn118:24.4.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out calming bodily fabrication’:

mn118:24.5.verse: On that occasion the monk remains focused on the body in & of itself—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:24.6.verse: I tell you, monks, that this—the in-&-out breath—is classed as a body among bodies,

mn118:24.7.verse: which is why the monk on that occasion remains focused on the body in & of itself—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:25.1.verse: [2] On whatever occasion a monk trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out sensitive to rapture’;

mn118:25.2.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out sensitive to pleasure’;

mn118:25.3.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out sensitive to mental fabrication’;

mn118:25.4.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out calming mental fabrication’:

mn118:25.5.verse: On that occasion the monk remains focused on feelings in & of themselves—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:25.6.verse: I tell you, monks, that this—careful attention to in-&-out breaths—is classed as a feeling among feelings,

mn118:25.7.verse: which is why the monk on that occasion remains focused on feelings in & of themselves—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:26.1.verse: [3] On whatever occasion a monk trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out sensitive to the mind’;

mn118:26.2.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out gladdening the mind’;

mn118:26.3.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out concentrating the mind’;

mn118:26.4.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out releasing the mind’:

mn118:26.5.verse: On that occasion the monk remains focused on the mind in & of itself—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:26.6.verse: I don’t say that there is mindfulness of in-&-out breathing in one of lapsed mindfulness and no alertness,

mn118:26.7.verse: which is why the monk on that occasion remains focused on the mind in & of itself—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:27.1.verse: [4] On whatever occasion a monk trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out focusing on inconstancy’;

mn118:27.2.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out focusing on dispassion’;

mn118:27.3.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out focusing on cessation’;

mn118:27.4.verse: trains himself, ‘I will breathe in…&…out focusing on relinquishing’:

mn118:27.5.verse: On that occasion the monk remains focused on mental qualities in & of themselves—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:27.6.verse: He who sees with discernment the abandoning of greed & distress is one who watches carefully with equanimity,

mn118:27.7.verse: which is why the monk on that occasion remains focused on mental qualities in & of themselves—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world.

mn118:28.1.verse: This is how mindfulness of in-&-out breathing is developed & pursued so as to bring the four establishings of mindfulness to their culmination.

mn118:29.1.verse: “And how are the four establishings of mindfulness developed & pursued so as to bring the seven factors for awakening to their culmination?

mn118:30.1.verse: [1] On whatever occasion the monk remains focused on the body in & of itself—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world, on that occasion his mindfulness is steady & without lapse.

mn118:30.2.verse: When his mindfulness is steady & without lapse, then mindfulness as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:31.1.verse: [2] Remaining mindful in this way, he examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment.

mn118:31.2.verse: When he remains mindful in this way, examining, analyzing, & coming to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, then analysis of qualities as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:32.1.verse: [3] In one who examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, persistence is aroused unflaggingly.

mn118:32.2.verse: When persistence is aroused unflaggingly in one who examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, then persistence as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:33.1.verse: [4] In one whose persistence is aroused, a rapture not of the flesh arises.

mn118:33.2.verse: When a rapture not of the flesh arises in one whose persistence is aroused, then rapture as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:34.1.verse: [5] For one enraptured at heart, the body grows calm and the mind grows calm.

mn118:34.2.verse: When the body & mind of a monk enraptured at heart grow calm, then calm as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:35.1.verse: [6] For one who is at ease—his body calmed—the mind becomes concentrated.

mn118:35.2.verse: When the mind of one who is at ease—his body calmed—becomes concentrated, then concentration as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:36.1.verse: [7] He carefully watches the mind thus concentrated with equanimity.

mn118:36.2.verse: When he carefully watches the mind thus concentrated with equanimity, equanimity as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.2.verse: and mental qualities in & of themselves: the monk remains focused there—ardent, alert, & mindful—subduing greed & distress with reference to the world—on that occasion his mindfulness is steady & without lapse.

mn118:38.3.verse: When his mindfulness is steady & without lapse, then mindfulness as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.4.verse: Remaining mindful in this way, he examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment.

mn118:38.5.verse: When he remains mindful in this way, examining, analyzing, & coming to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, then analysis of qualities as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.6.verse: In one who examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, persistence is aroused unflaggingly.

mn118:38.7.verse: When persistence is aroused unflaggingly in one who examines, analyzes, & comes to a comprehension of that quality with discernment, then persistence as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.8.verse: In one whose persistence is aroused, a rapture not of the flesh arises.

mn118:38.9.verse: When a rapture not of the flesh arises in one whose persistence is aroused, then rapture as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.10.verse: For one enraptured at heart, the body grows calm and the mind grows calm.

mn118:38.11.verse: When the body & mind of a monk enraptured at heart grow calm, then calm as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:38.12.verse: For one who is at ease—his body calmed—the mind becomes concentrated.

mn118:38.13.verse: When the mind of one who is at ease—his body calmed—becomes concentrated, then concentration as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:39.1.verse: He carefully watches the mind thus concentrated with equanimity.]

mn118:39.2.verse: When he carefully watches the mind thus concentrated with equanimity, equanimity as a factor for awakening is aroused in him. He develops it, and for him it goes to the culmination of its development.

mn118:40.1.verse: This is how the four establishings of mindfulness are developed & pursued so as to bring the seven factors for awakening to their culmination.

mn118:41.1.verse: “And how are the seven factors for awakening developed & pursued so as to bring clear knowing & release to their culmination?

mn118:42.1.verse: There is the case where a monk develops mindfulness as a factor for awakening dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.

mn118:42.2.verse: He develops analysis of qualities as a factor for awakening…

mn118:42.3.verse: persistence as a factor for awakening…

mn118:42.4.verse: rapture as a factor for awakening…

mn118:42.5.verse: calm as a factor for awakening…

mn118:42.6.verse: concentration as a factor for awakening…

mn118:42.7.verse: equanimity as a factor for awakening dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.

mn118:43.1.verse: This is how the seven factors for awakening are developed & pursued so as to bring clear knowing & release to their culmination.”

mn118:43.2.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn118:43.3.verse: Gratified, the monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn118:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, together with several well-known senior disciples, such as

mn118:1.3.verse: the venerables Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāna, Mahākoṭṭhita, Mahākappina, Mahācunda, Anuruddha, Revata, Ānanda, and others.

mn118:2.1.verse: Now at that time the senior monks were advising and instructing the junior monks.

mn118:2.2.verse: Some senior monks instructed ten monks, while some instructed twenty, thirty, or forty.

mn118:2.3.verse: Being instructed by the senior monks, the junior monks realized a higher distinction than they had before.

mn118:3.1.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks for the invitation to admonish.

mn118:3.2.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them:

mn118:4.1.verse: “I am satisfied, monks, with this practice.

mn118:4.2.verse: My heart is satisfied with this practice.

mn118:4.3.verse: So you should rouse up even more energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.

mn118:4.4.verse: I will wait here in Sāvatthī for the Komudī full moon of the fourth month.”

mn118:5.1.verse: Mendicants from around the country heard about this,

mn118:5.3.verse: and came down to Sāvatthī to see the Buddha.

mn118:6.1.verse: And those senior monks instructed the junior monks even more.

mn118:6.2.verse: Some senior monks instructed ten monks, while some instructed twenty, thirty, or forty.

mn118:6.3.verse: Being instructed by the senior monks, the junior monks realized a higher distinction than they had before.

mn118:7.1.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the Komudī full moon on the fifteenth day of the fourth month—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

mn118:7.2.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them:

mn118:8.1.verse: “This assembly has no chaff, monks, it is free of chaff, pure, and consolidated in the core.

mn118:8.2.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly!

mn118:8.3.verse: An assembly such as this is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

mn118:8.4.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly!

mn118:8.5.verse: For an assembly such as this, giving little becomes much, while giving much becomes even more.

mn118:8.6.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly!

mn118:8.7.verse: An assembly such as this is rarely seen in the world.

mn118:8.8.verse: Such is this Saṅgha of monks, such is this assembly!

mn118:8.9.verse: An assembly such as this is worth traveling many leagues to see, even if you have to carry your own provisions in a knapsack.

mn118:9.1.verse: For in this Saṅgha there are perfected mendicants who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment.

mn118:9.2.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:10.1.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who, with the ending of the five lower fetters are reborn spontaneously. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world.

mn118:10.2.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:11.1.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who, with the ending of three fetters, and the weakening of greed, hate, and delusion, are once-returners. They come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.

mn118:11.2.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:12.1.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who, with the ending of three fetters are stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

mn118:12.2.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:13.1.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who are committed to developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation …

mn118:14.2.verse: the four bases of psychic power …

mn118:14.7.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:14.8.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who are committed to developing the meditation on love …

mn118:14.14.verse: There are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.

mn118:14.15.verse: In this Saṅgha there are mendicants who are committed to developing the meditation on mindfulness of breathing.

mn118:15.1.verse: Mendicants, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it is very fruitful and beneficial.

mn118:15.2.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn118:15.3.verse: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors.

mn118:15.4.verse: And the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.

mn118:16.1.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

mn118:17.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

mn118:17.2.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

mn118:18.1.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

mn118:18.2.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

mn118:18.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

mn118:18.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

mn118:19.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’

mn118:19.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’

mn118:19.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mental process.’

mn118:19.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

mn118:20.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

mn118:20.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out gladdening the mind.’

mn118:20.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out immersing the mind in samādhi.’

mn118:20.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in freeing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out freeing the mind.’

mn118:21.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing impermanence.’

mn118:21.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing fading away.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing fading away.’

mn118:21.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing cessation.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing cessation.’

mn118:21.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

mn118:22.1.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.

mn118:23.1.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?

mn118:24.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant knows that they breathe heavily,

mn118:24.5.verse: at that time they’re meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:24.6.verse: For I say that the in-breaths and out-breaths are an aspect of the body.

mn118:24.7.verse: That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:25.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant practices breathing while experiencing rapture,

mn118:25.5.verse: at that time they meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:25.6.verse: For I say that careful application of mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths is an aspect of feelings.

mn118:25.7.verse: That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:26.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant practices breathing while experiencing the mind,

mn118:26.3.verse: or immersing the mind in samādhi,

mn118:26.5.verse: at that time they meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:26.6.verse: There is no development of mindfulness of breathing for someone who is unmindful and lacks awareness, I say.
