mn118:26.7.verse: That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:27.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant practices breathing while observing impermanence,

mn118:27.5.verse: at that time they meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:27.6.verse: Having seen with wisdom the giving up of covetousness and displeasure, they watch over closely with equanimity.

mn118:27.7.verse: That’s why at that time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn118:28.1.verse: That’s how mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

mn118:29.1.verse: And how are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven awakening factors?

mn118:30.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body, at that time their mindfulness is established and lucid.

mn118:30.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of mindfulness; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:31.1.verse: As they live mindfully in this way they investigate, explore, and inquire into that principle with wisdom.

mn118:31.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of investigation of principles; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:32.1.verse: As they investigate principles with wisdom in this way their energy is roused up and unflagging.

mn118:32.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of energy; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:33.1.verse: When they’re energetic, rapture not of the flesh arises.

mn118:33.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of rapture; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:34.1.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body and mind become tranquil.

mn118:34.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of tranquility; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:35.1.verse: When the body is tranquil and they feel bliss, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn118:35.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of immersion; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:36.1.verse: They closely watch over that mind immersed in samādhi.

mn118:36.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of equanimity; they develop it and perfect it.

mn118:37.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of feelings …

mn118:38.2.verse: principles, at that time their mindfulness is established and lucid.

mn118:38.3.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of mindfulness …

mn118:40.1.verse: That’s how the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors.

mn118:41.1.verse: And how are the seven awakening factors developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom?

mn118:42.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

mn118:42.7.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

mn118:43.1.verse: That’s how the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.”

mn118:43.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn118:43.3.verse: Satisfied, the monks approved what the Buddha said.

mn119:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn119:2.1.verse: Then a number of bhikkhus were sitting in the assembly hall where they had met together on return from their alms-round after their meal was over. Meanwhile it was being said among them:

mn119:2.2.verse: ‘It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous,

mn119:2.3.verse: how mindfulness of the body has been said by the Blessed One who knows and sees, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, to be of great fruit, of great benefit when developed and repeatedly practised!’

mn119:2.4.verse: Then their talk meanwhile was left unfinished for the Blessed One rose from meditation now when it was evening, and he came to the assembly hall and sat down on a seat made ready.

mn119:2.5.verse: When he had done so, he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn119:2.6.verse: ‘For what talk are you gathered here together now, bhikkhus? And what was your talk meanwhile which was left unfinished?’

mn119:2.7.verse: ‘Here, venerable sir, we were sitting in the assembly hall where we had met together on return from our alms-round after our meal. Meanwhile it was being said amongst us:

mn119:2.8.verse: “It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous,

mn119:2.9.verse: how mindfulness of the body has been said by the Blessed One who knows and sees, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, to be of great fruit, of great benefit when developed and repeatedly practised!”

mn119:2.10.verse: This was our talk meanwhile, venerable sir, which was left unfinished, for then the Blessed One arrived.’

mn119:3.1.verse: ‘And how developed, bhikkhus, how repeatedly practised is mindfulness of the body of great fruit, of great benefit?

mn119:4.1.verse: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, established mindfulness before him,

mn119:4.2.verse: just mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.

mn119:4.3.verse: ‘Breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”.

mn119:4.4.verse: Breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”.

mn119:4.5.verse: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”.

mn119:4.6.verse: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the body process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn understands: “I make a long turn”; or when making a short turn understands: “I make a short turn”; so too, breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”; breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the bodily process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.

mn119:4.7.verse: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:4.8.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:4.9.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:5.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu when walking, understands: “I walk”; when standing, understands: “I stand”; when sitting, understands: “I sit”; when lying down, understands: “I am lying down”;

mn119:5.2.verse: or however his body is disposed he understands accordingly.

mn119:5.3.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:5.4.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:5.5.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:6.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who acts in full awareness when moving to and fro, who acts in full awareness when looking at and away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when feeding, drinking and supping, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent.

mn119:6.2.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:6.3.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:6.4.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:7.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth, thus:

mn119:7.2.verse: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine”.

mn119:7.3.verse: ‘Just as though there were a bag with an opening at both (ends) full of many sorts of grain such as

mn119:7.4.verse: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet and white rice,

mn119:7.5.verse: and a man with (clear) eyes had opened it and were reviewing it thus:

mn119:7.6.verse: “This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice”,

mn119:7.7.verse: so too, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth,

mn119:7.8.verse: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine”.

mn119:7.9.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:7.10.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:7.11.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:8.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body however it is placed (consisting of) elements, thus:

mn119:8.2.verse: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element”.

mn119:8.3.verse: ‘Just as though a skilled butcher or his apprentice had killed a cow and were seated at the four crossroads with it cut up into pieces;

mn119:8.4.verse: so too, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body,

mn119:8.5.verse: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element”.

mn119:8.6.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:8.7.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:8.8.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:9.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu here were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing matter,

mn119:9.2.verse: he compares this same body with it, thus:

mn119:9.3.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.

mn119:9.4.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:9.5.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:9.6.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:10.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, kites, vultures, herons, dogs, tigers, leopards, jackals, and the multitudinous kinds of worms,

mn119:10.2.verse: he compares this same body with it, thus:

mn119:10.3.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.

mn119:10.4.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:10.5.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:11-14.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood held together with sinews,

mn119:11-14.2.verse: a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood and held together with sinews,

mn119:11-14.3.verse: a skeleton without flesh and blood held together with sinews,

mn119:11-14.4.verse: bones without sinews scattered in all directions: here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a back-bone, there a rib-bone, there a breast-bone, there an arm-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull,

mn119:11-14.5.verse: he compares this same body with it, thus:

mn119:11-14.6.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.

mn119:11-14.7.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:11-14.8.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:15-17.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground,

mn119:15-17.2.verse: bones bleached white, the colour of shells,

mn119:15-17.3.verse: bones heaped up, more than a year old,

mn119:15-17.4.verse: bones rotted and crumbled to dust,

mn119:15-17.5.verse: he compares this same body with it, thus:

mn119:15-17.6.verse: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.

mn119:15-17.7.verse: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:15-17.8.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:15-17.9.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:18.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhana which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn119:18.2.verse: ‘He makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.

mn119:18.3.verse: Just as a skilled bath man or bath man’s apprentice heaps bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, kneads it up till the moisture wets his ball of bath powder, soaks it, and extends over it within and without though it does not itself become liquid,

mn119:18.4.verse: so too, a bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill, and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.

mn119:18.5.verse: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:18.6.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:18.7.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:19.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.

mn119:19.2.verse: ‘He makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.

mn119:19.3.verse: Just as though there were a lake whose waters welled up (from below), having no inflow from east, west, north or south, nor yet replenished from time to time by the skies with showers, then the cool fount of water welling up in the lake would make the cool water drench, steep, fill and extend throughout the lake, and there would be nothing of the whole lake to which the cool water did not extend,

mn119:19.4.verse: so, too, the bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.

mn119:19.5.verse: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:19.6.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:20.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”

mn119:20.2.verse: ‘He makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.

mn119:20.3.verse: Just as, in a water-lily pond or a white lotus pond or a red lotus pond some water-lilies or white lotuses or red lotuses are born under the water, grow under the water, do not stand up out of the water, flourish immersed under the water, and cool water drenches, steeps, fill and extends throughout them, to their tips and to their roots, and there is nothing of the whole of those water-lilies, those white lotuses, those red lotuses, to which the cool water does not extend,

mn119:20.4.verse: so too, the bhikkhu makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.

mn119:20.5.verse: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.

mn119:20.6.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:21.1.verse: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn119:21.2.verse: ‘He sits with pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.

mn119:21.3.verse: Just as though a man were sitting clothed from head to foot in white cloth, and there were nothing of his whole body to which the white cloth did not extend,

mn119:21.4.verse: so too, the bhikkhu sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.

mn119:21.5.verse: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;

mn119:21.6.verse: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness, and concentrated.

mn119:21.7.verse: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:22.1.verse: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, he has included whatever profitable dhammas there are that partake of true knowledge.

mn119:22.2.verse: ‘Just as anyone who extends his mind over the great ocean has included whatever streams there are that flow into the ocean,

mn119:22.3.verse: so too, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, he has included whatever profitable dhammas there are that partake of true knowledge.

mn119:23.1.verse: ‘When anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.

mn119:23.2.verse: ‘Suppose a man were to throw a heavy stone ball at a heap of wet clay;

mn119:23.4.verse: would that heavy stone ball find an entry into that heap of wet clay?’

mn119:23.6.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.

mn119:24.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a dry sapless piece of wood

mn119:24.2.verse: and man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:

mn119:24.3.verse: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;

mn119:24.5.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by rubbing the dry sapless piece of wood with an upper fire-stick?’

mn119:24.7.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.

mn119:25.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a hollow empty water pot standing on a stand

mn119:25.2.verse: and a man came with a load of water;

mn119:25.4.verse: would he be able to pour water into it?’

mn119:25.6.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.

mn119:26.1.verse: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.

mn119:26.2.verse: ‘Suppose a man were to throw a light ball of string at a door-panel all made of heartwood;

mn119:26.4.verse: would that light ball of string find an entry into that door-panel all made of heartwood?’

mn119:26.6.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.

mn119:27.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a wet sappy piece of wood,

mn119:27.2.verse: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking,

mn119:27.3.verse: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;

mn119:27.5.verse: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing the wet sappy piece of wood with it?’

mn119:27.7.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.

mn119:28.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a water pot full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it, standing on a stand,

mn119:28.2.verse: and man came with a load of water;

mn119:28.4.verse: would he be able to pour water into it?’

mn119:28.6.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.

mn119:29.1.verse: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.

mn119:29.2.verse: ‘Suppose there were a water pot full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it, standing on a stand,

mn119:29.3.verse: then as soon as a strong man tipped it would water come (from it) each time?’

mn119:29.5.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’

mn119:30.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a square pond on a level piece of ground, surrounded by an embankment, full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it,

mn119:30.2.verse: then as soon as a strong man loosened the embankment would water come (from it) each time?’

mn119:30.4.verse: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’

mn119:31.1.verse: ‘Suppose there were a chariot on even ground at the four cross-roads, harnessed to thoroughbreds, waiting with whips lying ready,

mn119:31.2.verse: so that a skilled trainer, a driver of horses to be tamed, might mount, and taking the reins in his hand, drive out and back by any road in any way he liked,

mn119:31.3.verse: so too, bhikkhus, So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’

mn119:32.1.verse: ‘When mindfulness of the body is developed, repeatedly practised, made the vehicle, made the basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these ten rewards may be expected. What ten?

mn119:33.1.verse: ‘He becomes a conqueror of aversion and delight and aversion does not conquer him, and he abides transcending aversion as it arises.

mn119:34.1.verse: ‘He becomes a conqueror of fear and dread, fear and dread do not conquer him, and he abides transcending fear and dread as they arise.

mn119:35.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who bears cold and heat, hunger and thirst and contact with mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun and creeping things, who endures ill-spoken unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and menacing to life.

mn119:36.1.verse: ‘He becomes one who obtains at will with no trouble and easily the four jhānas which are the higher mind and provide a pleasant abiding here and now.

mn119:37.1.verse: ‘He wields the various kinds of supernormal success … (as in Sutta 77, para. 31) … even as far as the world of the Divinity (Brahmā).

mn119:38.1.verse: ‘With the heavenly ear element … (Sutta 77, para. 32) … far as well as near.

mn119:39.1.verse: ‘He encompasses with his mind the minds of other beings, of other persons, and understands them:

mn119:39.2.verse: he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust,

mn119:39.3.verse: and a mind without lust as a mind without lust;

mn119:39.4.verse: a mind with hate as a mind with hate,

mn119:39.5.verse: and a mind without hate as a mind without hate;

mn119:39.6.verse: a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion,

mn119:39.7.verse: and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion;

mn119:39.8.verse: a contracted mind as a contracted mind,

mn119:39.9.verse: and a distracted mind as a distracted mind;

mn119:39.10.verse: an exalted mind as an exalted mind,

mn119:39.11.verse: and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind;

mn119:39.12.verse: a surpassed mind as a surpassed mind,

mn119:39.13.verse: and an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind;

mn119:39.14.verse: a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind,

mn119:39.15.verse: and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind;

mn119:39.16.verse: a liberated mind as a liberated mind,

mn119:39.17.verse: and the unliberated mind as unliberated.

mn119:40.1.verse: ‘He recollects his manifold past life … (Sutta 77, para. 34) … with its details and particulars.

mn119:41.1.verse: ‘With the heavenly eyesight … (Sutta 77, para. 35) … according to their kammas.

mn119:42.1.verse: ‘By realization himself with direct knowledge here and now, he enters upon and abides in the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints.

mn119:43.1.verse: ‘When mindfulness of the body is developed, repeatedly practised, made the vehicle, made the basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these ten rewards may be expected.’

mn119:43.2.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn119:43.3.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn119:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn119:2.1.verse: Then after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall and this discussion came up among them.

mn119:2.3.verse: how the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body, when developed and cultivated, is very fruitful and beneficial.”

mn119:2.4.verse: But their conversation was left unfinished. Then the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out

mn119:2.6.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

mn119:2.7.verse: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about. The Buddha said:

mn119:3.1.verse: “And how, mendicants, is mindfulness of the body developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

mn119:4.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

mn119:4.2.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

mn119:4.3.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

mn119:4.4.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

mn119:4.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

mn119:4.6.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

mn119:4.7.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:4.8.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:4.9.verse: That’s how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:5.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant is walking they know: ‘I am walking.’ When standing they know: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting they know: ‘I am sitting.’ And when lying down they know: ‘I am lying down.’

mn119:5.2.verse: Whatever posture their body is in, they know it.

mn119:5.3.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:5.4.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:5.5.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant acts with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

mn119:6.2.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:6.3.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:6.4.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

mn119:7.2.verse: ‘In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

mn119:7.3.verse: It’s as if there were a bag with openings at both ends, filled with various kinds of grains, such as

mn119:7.4.verse: fine rice, wheat, mung beans, peas, sesame, and ordinary rice.

mn119:7.5.verse: And a person with clear eyes were to open it and examine the contents:

mn119:7.6.verse: ‘These grains are fine rice, these are wheat, these are mung beans, these are peas, these are sesame, and these are ordinary rice.’

mn119:7.7.verse: In the same way, a mendicant examines their own body, up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth. …

mn119:7.9.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:7.10.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:7.11.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant examines their own body, whatever its placement or posture, according to the elements:

mn119:8.2.verse: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

mn119:8.3.verse: It’s as if a deft butcher or butcher’s apprentice were to kill a cow and sit down at the crossroads with the meat cut into chops.

mn119:8.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant examines their own body, whatever its placement or posture, according to the elements:

mn119:8.5.verse: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

mn119:8.6.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:8.7.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:8.8.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:9.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose a mendicant were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground. And it had been dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering.

mn119:9.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn119:9.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn119:9.4.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:9.5.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:9.6.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:10.1.verse: Or suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, herons, hounds, tigers, leopards, jackals, and many kinds of little creatures.

mn119:10.2.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn119:10.3.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn119:10.5.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:11-14.1.verse: Furthermore, suppose they were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

mn119:11-14.2.verse: A skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, and held together by sinews …

mn119:11-14.3.verse: A skeleton rid of flesh and blood, held together by sinews …

mn119:11-14.4.verse: Bones rid of sinews scattered in every direction. Here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here an arm-bone, there a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, there a tooth, here the skull. …

mn119:15-17.2.verse: White bones, the color of shells …

mn119:15-17.3.verse: Decrepit bones, heaped in a pile …

mn119:15-17.4.verse: Bones rotted and crumbled to powder.

mn119:15-17.5.verse: They’d compare it with their own body:

mn119:15-17.6.verse: ‘This body is also of that same nature, that same kind, and cannot go beyond that.’

mn119:15-17.7.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to lay life are given up.

mn119:15-17.8.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:15-17.9.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:18.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn119:18.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

mn119:18.3.verse: It’s like when a deft bathroom attendant or their apprentice pours bath powder into a bronze dish, sprinkling it little by little with water. They knead it until the ball of bath powder is soaked and saturated with moisture, spread through inside and out; yet no moisture oozes out.

mn119:18.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads their body with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

mn119:18.5.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to lay life are given up.

mn119:18.6.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:18.7.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:19.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn119:19.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

mn119:19.3.verse: It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time. But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.

mn119:19.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.

mn119:19.6.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:20.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption. They meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn119:20.2.verse: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

mn119:20.3.verse: It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water. There’s no part of them that’s not soaked with cool water.

mn119:20.4.verse: In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.

mn119:20.6.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:21.1.verse: Furthermore, giving up pleasure and pain, and ending former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn119:21.2.verse: They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn119:21.3.verse: It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.

mn119:21.4.verse: In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.

mn119:21.5.verse: As they meditate like this—diligent, keen, and resolute—memories and thoughts tied to domestic life are given up.

mn119:21.6.verse: Their mind becomes stilled internally; it settles, unifies, and becomes immersed in samādhi.

mn119:21.7.verse: That too is how a mendicant develops mindfulness of the body.

mn119:22.1.verse: Anyone who has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body includes all of the skillful qualities that play a part in realization.

mn119:22.2.verse: Anyone who brings into their mind the great ocean includes all of the streams that run down into it.

mn119:22.3.verse: In the same way, anyone who has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body includes all of the skillful qualities that play a part in realization.

mn119:23.1.verse: When a mendicant has not developed or cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra finds a vulnerability and gets an opportunity.

mn119:23.2.verse: Suppose a person were to throw a heavy stone ball at a mound of wet clay.

mn119:23.4.verse: Would that heavy stone ball find an entry into that mound of wet clay?”

mn119:23.6.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has not developed or cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra finds a vulnerability and gets an opportunity.

mn119:24.1.verse: Suppose there was a dried up, withered log.

mn119:24.2.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn119:24.3.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn119:24.5.verse: By drilling the stick against that dried up, withered log, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn119:24.7.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has not developed or cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra finds a vulnerability and gets an opportunity.

mn119:25.1.verse: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, empty and hollow.

mn119:25.2.verse: Then a person comes along with a load of water.

mn119:25.4.verse: Could that person pour water into the jar?”

mn119:25.6.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has not developed or cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra finds a vulnerability and gets an opportunity.

mn119:26.1.verse: When a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra cannot find a vulnerability and doesn’t get an opportunity.

mn119:26.2.verse: Suppose a person were to throw a light ball of string at a door-panel made entirely of hardwood.

mn119:26.4.verse: Would that light ball of string find an entry into that door-panel made entirely of hardwood?”

mn119:26.6.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra cannot find a vulnerability and doesn’t get an opportunity.

mn119:27.1.verse: Suppose there was a green, sappy log.

mn119:27.2.verse: Then a person comes along with a drill-stick, thinking

mn119:27.3.verse: to light a fire and produce heat.

mn119:27.5.verse: By drilling the stick against that green, sappy log on dry land far from water, could they light a fire and produce heat?”

mn119:27.7.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra cannot find a vulnerability and doesn’t get an opportunity.

mn119:28.1.verse: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

mn119:28.2.verse: Then a person comes along with a load of water.

mn119:28.4.verse: Could that person pour water into the jar?”

mn119:28.6.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, Māra cannot find a vulnerability and doesn’t get an opportunity.

mn119:29.1.verse: When a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, they extend the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

mn119:29.2.verse: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

mn119:29.3.verse: If a strong man was to pour it on any side, would water pour out?”

mn119:29.5.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, they extend the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

mn119:30.1.verse: Suppose there was a square, walled lotus pond on level ground, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

mn119:30.2.verse: If a strong man was to open the wall on any side, would water pour out?”

mn119:30.4.verse: “In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, they extend the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

mn119:31.1.verse: Suppose a chariot stood harnessed to thoroughbreds at a level crossroads, with a goad ready.

mn119:31.2.verse: A deft horse trainer, a master charioteer, might mount the chariot, taking the reins in his right hand and goad in the left. He’d drive out and back wherever he wishes, whenever he wishes.

mn119:31.3.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body, they extend the mind to realize by insight each and every thing that can be realized by insight; and they are capable of realizing those things, since each and every one is within range.

mn119:32.1.verse: You can expect ten benefits when mindfulness of the body has been cultivated, developed, and practiced, made a vehicle and a basis, kept up, consolidated, and properly implemented.

mn119:33.1.verse: They prevail over desire and discontent, and live having mastered desire and discontent whenever they arose.

mn119:34.1.verse: They prevail over fear and dread, and live having mastered fear and dread whenever they arose.

mn119:35.1.verse: They endure cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; rude and unwelcome criticism; and put up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.

mn119:36.1.verse: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn119:37.1.verse: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again … They control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

mn119:38.1.verse: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far. …

mn119:39.1.verse: They understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with their own mind. …

mn119:40.1.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn119:41.1.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn119:42.1.verse: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn119:43.1.verse: You can expect these ten benefits when mindfulness of the body has been cultivated, developed, and practiced, made a vehicle and a basis, kept up, consolidated, and properly implemented.”

mn119:43.2.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn119:43.3.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn120:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn120:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn120:2.1.verse: “I shall teach you rebirth by choice.

mn120:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn120:3.3.verse: ‘If only, when my body breaks up, after death, I would be reborn in the company of well-to-do aristocrats!’

mn120:3.5.verse: Those choices and meditations of theirs, developed and cultivated like this, lead to rebirth there.

mn120:3.6.verse: This is the path and the practice that leads to rebirth there.

mn120:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn120:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn120:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you reappearance in accordance with one’s aspiration.

mn120:2.2.verse: Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn120:3.1.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

mn120:3.3.verse: ‘Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might reappear in the company of well-to-do nobles!’

mn120:3.4.verse: He fixes his mind on that, resolves upon it, develops it.

mn120:3.5.verse: These aspirations and this abiding of his, thus developed and cultivated, lead to his reappearance there.

mn120:3.6.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.

mn120:4-5.5.verse: He fixes his mind on that, resolves upon it, develops it.

mn120:4-5.6.verse: These aspirations and this abiding of his, thus developed and cultivated, lead to his reappearance there.

mn120:4-5.7.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the path, the way that leads to reappearance there.

mn120:37.10.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn121:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.

mn121:2.1.verse: Then when it was evening, the venerable Ānanda rose from meditation, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:

mn121:3.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, once the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans; there is a town of the Sakyans called Nāgaraka.

mn121:3.2.verse: There, venerable sir, I heard and learned this in the Blessed One’s own presence:

mn121:3.3.verse: “Now I abide much in voidness, Ānanda.”

mn121:3.4.verse: Venerable sir, was this well heard by me, well apprehended, well attended to, well remembered?’

mn121:3.5.verse: ‘Certainly, Ānanda, that was well heard by you, well apprehended, well attended to, well remembered.

mn121:3.6.verse: As formerly, Ānanda, so now too I abide much in voidness.

mn121:4.1.verse: ‘Just as, Ānanda, this palace of Migāra’s Mother is void of elephants, cattle, horses and mares, void of gold and silver, void of the foregathering of women and men, and there is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:4.2.verse: the single state dependent on the community of bhikkhus;

mn121:4.3.verse: so too, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of village, without giving attention to perception of man, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of forest.

mn121:4.4.verse: His mind enters into that perception of forest and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:4.6.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of village are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of man are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:4.7.verse: the single state dependent on perception of forest.”

mn121:4.8.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of village.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of man.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:4.9.verse: the single state dependent on perception of forest.”

mn121:4.10.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:4.11.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:5.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of man, without giving attention to perception of forest, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of earth.

mn121:5.2.verse: His mind enters into that perception of earth and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:5.3.verse: Just as though a bull’s hide were freed from folds by stretching it with a hundred pegs;

mn121:5.4.verse: so too, Ānanda, without giving attention to all the ridges and hollows, the river ravines, the tracts of stumps and thorns, the rocky inequalities on this earth, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of earth.

mn121:5.5.verse: His mind enters into that perception of earth and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:5.7.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of man are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of forest are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:5.8.verse: the single state dependent on perception of earth.”

mn121:5.9.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of man.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of forest.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:5.10.verse: the single state dependent on perception of earth.”

mn121:5.11.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:5.12.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:6.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of forest, without giving attention to perception of earth, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.

mn121:6.2.verse: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of infinite space and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:6.4.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of forest are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of earth are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:6.5.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.”

mn121:6.6.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of forest.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of earth.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:6.7.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.”

mn121:6.8.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:6.9.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:7.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of earth, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite space, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.

mn121:7.2.verse: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:7.4.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of earth are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:7.5.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.”

mn121:7.6.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of earth.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite space.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:7.7.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.”

mn121:7.8.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:7.9.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:8.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite space, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.

mn121:8.2.verse: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of nothingness and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:8.4.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:8.5.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.”

mn121:8.6.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite space.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:8.7.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.”

mn121:8.8.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:8.9.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:9.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn121:9.2.verse: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:9.4.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:9.5.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

mn121:9.6.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of nothingness.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:9.7.verse: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

mn121:9.8.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:9.9.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:10.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state, the signless concentration of mind.

mn121:10.2.verse: His mind enters into that signless concentration of mind and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:10.4.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:10.5.verse: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”

mn121:10.6.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of nothingness.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:10.7.verse: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”

mn121:10.8.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:10.9.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.

mn121:11.1.verse: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state, the signless concentration of mind.

mn121:11.2.verse: His mind enters into that signless concentration of mind and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn121:11.4.verse: “This signless concentration of mind is also conditioned and mentally produced.”

mn121:11.5.verse: He understands: “Whatever is conditioned and mentally produced is impermanent and liable to cessation.”

mn121:11.6.verse: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of being, his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn121:11.7.verse: When liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”

mn121:11.8.verse: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”

mn121:12.2.verse: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of sensual desire are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of being are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of ignorance are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,

mn121:12.3.verse: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”

mn121:12.4.verse: He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of sensual desire.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of being.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of ignorance.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,

mn121:12.5.verse: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”

mn121:12.6.verse: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”

mn121:12.7.verse: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, is pure, and is unsurpassed by any other.

mn121:13.1.verse: ‘Whatever monks or divines in the past, Ānanda, entered upon and abided in a voidness that was pure and unsurpassed by any other, they all entered upon and abided in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.

mn121:13.2.verse: Whatever monks or divines in the future, Ānanda, will enter upon and abide in a voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other, they will all enter upon and abide in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.

mn121:13.3.verse: Whatever monks or divines at present, Ānanda, enter upon and abide in a voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other, they all enter upon and abide in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.

mn121:13.4.verse: Therefore, Ānanda: “We will enter upon and abide in the voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other”—

mn121:13.5.verse: thus should you train yourselves, Ānanda.’

mn121:13.6.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn121:13.7.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn121:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

mn121:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

mn121:3.1.verse: “Sir, this one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans where they have a town named Townsville.

mn121:3.2.verse: There I heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn121:3.3.verse: ‘Ānanda, these days I usually practice the meditation on emptiness.’

mn121:3.4.verse: I trust I properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that from the Buddha?”

mn121:3.5.verse: “Indeed, Ānanda, you properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered that.

mn121:3.6.verse: Now, as before, I usually practice the meditation on emptiness.

mn121:4.1.verse: Consider this stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother. It’s empty of elephants, cows, horses, and mares; of gold and silver; and of gatherings of men and women.

mn121:4.2.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn121:4.3.verse: In the same way, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of the village and the perception of people—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of wilderness.

mn121:4.4.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of wilderness.

mn121:4.6.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of village or the perception of people.

mn121:4.7.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of wilderness.’

mn121:4.8.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of the village. It is empty of the perception of people.

mn121:4.9.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of wilderness.’

mn121:4.10.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:4.11.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:5.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of people and the perception of wilderness—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.

mn121:5.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of earth.

mn121:5.3.verse: As a bull’s hide is rid of folds when fully stretched out by a hundred pegs,

mn121:5.4.verse: so too, ignoring the hilly terrain, inaccessible riverlands, stumps and thorns, and rugged mountains, they focus on the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.

mn121:5.5.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of earth.

mn121:5.7.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of people or the perception of wilderness.

mn121:5.8.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.’

mn121:5.9.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of people. It is empty of the perception of wilderness.

mn121:5.10.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.’

mn121:5.11.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:5.12.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:6.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of wilderness and the perception of earth—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite space.

mn121:6.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of the dimension of infinite space.

mn121:6.4.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of wilderness or the perception of earth.

mn121:6.5.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite space.’

mn121:6.6.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of wilderness. It is empty of the perception of earth.

mn121:6.7.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite space.’

mn121:6.8.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:6.9.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:7.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of earth and the perception of the dimension of infinite space—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn121:7.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn121:7.4.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of earth or the perception of the dimension of infinite space.

mn121:7.5.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.’

mn121:7.6.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of earth. It is empty of the perception of the dimension of infinite space.

mn121:7.7.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.’

mn121:7.8.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:7.9.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:8.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of the dimension of infinite space and the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of nothingness.

mn121:8.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of the dimension of nothingness.

mn121:8.4.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of the dimension of infinite space or the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn121:8.5.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of nothingness.’

mn121:8.6.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of the dimension of infinite space. It is empty of the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn121:8.7.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of nothingness.’

mn121:8.8.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:8.9.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:9.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness and the perception of the dimension of nothingness—focuses on the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn121:9.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn121:9.4.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness or the perception of the dimension of nothingness.

mn121:9.5.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn121:9.6.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness. It is empty of the perception of the dimension of nothingness.

mn121:9.7.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely the oneness dependent on the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

mn121:9.8.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:9.9.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:10.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of the dimension of nothingness and the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception—focuses on the oneness dependent on the signless immersion of the heart.

mn121:10.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that signless immersion of the heart.

mn121:10.4.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the perception of the dimension of nothingness or the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn121:10.5.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely that related to the six sense fields dependent on this body and conditioned by life.’

mn121:10.6.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of the dimension of nothingness. It is empty of the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn121:10.7.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely that related to the six sense fields dependent on this body and conditioned by life.’

mn121:10.8.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:10.9.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, and pure.

mn121:11.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant—ignoring the perception of the dimension of nothingness and the perception of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception—focuses on the oneness dependent on the signless immersion of the heart.

mn121:11.2.verse: Their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided in that signless immersion of the heart.

mn121:11.4.verse: ‘Even this signless immersion of the heart is produced by choices and intentions.’

mn121:11.5.verse: They understand: ‘But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.’

mn121:11.6.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn121:11.7.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn121:11.8.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn121:12.2.verse: ‘Here there is no stress due to the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, or ignorance.

mn121:12.3.verse: There is only this modicum of stress, namely that related to the six sense fields dependent on this body and conditioned by life.’

mn121:12.4.verse: They understand: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn121:12.5.verse: There is only this that is not emptiness, namely that related to the six sense fields dependent on this body and conditioned by life.’

mn121:12.6.verse: And so they regard it as empty of what is not there, but as to what remains they understand that it is present.

mn121:12.7.verse: That’s how emptiness manifests in them—genuine, undistorted, pure, and supreme.

mn121:13.1.verse: Whatever ascetics and brahmins enter and remain in the pure, ultimate, supreme emptiness—whether in the past, future, or present—all of them enter and remain in this same pure, ultimate, supreme emptiness.

mn121:13.4.verse: So, Ānanda, you should train like this: ‘We will enter and remain in the pure, ultimate, supreme emptiness.’

mn121:13.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn121:13.7.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn122:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

mn122:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms.

mn122:2.2.verse: He wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the lodge of the Sakyan Khemaka the Dark for the day’s meditation.

mn122:2.3.verse: Now at that time many resting places had been spread out at the lodge of Khemaka the Dark.

mn122:2.6.verse: “Many resting places have been spread out;

mn122:2.7.verse: are there many mendicants living here?”

mn122:2.8.verse: Now at that time Venerable Ānanda, together with many other mendicants, was making robes at the lodge of the Sakyan Ghaṭā.

mn122:2.9.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to Ghaṭā’s lodge, where he sat down on the seat spread out

mn122:2.11.verse: “Many resting places have been spread out at the lodge of Khemaka the Dark;

mn122:2.15.verse: It’s currently the time for making robes.”
