mn122:3.1.verse: “Ānanda, a mendicant doesn’t shine who enjoys company and groups, who loves them and likes to enjoy them.

mn122:3.2.verse: It is quite impossible that such a mendicant will get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

mn122:3.3.verse: But you should expect that a mendicant who lives alone, withdrawn from the group, will get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty. That is possible.

mn122:4.1.verse: Indeed, Ānanda, it is quite impossible that a mendicant who enjoys company will enter and remain in the freedom of heart—either that which is temporary and pleasant, or that which is irreversible and unshakable.

mn122:4.2.verse: But it is possible that a mendicant who lives alone, withdrawn from the group will enter and remain in the freedom of heart—either that which is temporary and pleasant, or that which is irreversible and unshakable.

mn122:5.1.verse: Ānanda, I do not see even a single sight which, with its decay and perishing, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in someone who has desire and lust for it.

mn122:6.1.verse: But this meditation has been understood by the Realized One, namely

mn122:6.2.verse: to enter and remain in emptiness internally by not focusing on any signs.

mn122:6.3.verse: Now, suppose that while the Realized One is practicing this meditation, monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, rulers and their chief ministers, monastics of other religions and their disciples go to visit him.

mn122:6.4.verse: In that case, with a mind slanting, sloping, and inclining to seclusion, withdrawn, and loving renunciation, having totally eliminated defiling influences, he invariably gives a talk concerned only with sending them away.

mn122:7.1.verse: Therefore, if a mendicant should wish,

mn122:7.2.verse: ‘May I enter and remain in emptiness internally!’ then they should still, settle, unify, and immerse their mind in samādhi internally.

mn122:7.3.verse: And how does a mendicant still, settle, unify, and immerse their mind in samādhi internally?

mn122:8.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption …

mn122:8.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant stills, settles, unifies, and immerses their mind in samādhi internally.

mn122:9.2.verse: but their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.

mn122:9.4.verse: ‘I am focusing on emptiness internally, but my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.’

mn122:9.5.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:9.7.verse: They focus on emptiness internally and externally …

mn122:9.9.verse: but their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.

mn122:9.11.verse: ‘I am focusing on the imperturbable internally, but my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.’

mn122:9.12.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:10.1.verse: Then that mendicant should still, settle, unify, and immerse their mind in samādhi internally in the same meditation subject as a basis of immersion as before.

mn122:10.3.verse: and their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

mn122:10.5.verse: ‘I am focusing on emptiness internally, and my mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.’

mn122:10.6.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:10.8.verse: They focus on emptiness internally and externally …

mn122:10.10.verse: and their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.

mn122:10.12.verse: ‘I am focusing on the imperturbable, and my mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.’

mn122:10.13.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:11.1.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to walking, they walk, thinking:

mn122:11.2.verse: ‘While I’m walking, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

mn122:11.3.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:11.4.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to standing, they stand, thinking:

mn122:11.5.verse: ‘While I’m standing, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

mn122:11.6.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:11.7.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to sitting, they sit, thinking:

mn122:11.8.verse: ‘While I’m sitting, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

mn122:11.9.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:11.10.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to lying down, they lie down, thinking:

mn122:11.11.verse: ‘While I’m lying down, bad, unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure will not overwhelm me.’

mn122:11.12.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:12.1.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to talking, they think:

mn122:12.2.verse: ‘I will not engage in the kind of speech that is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. Such speech doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. Namely: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that state of existence.’

mn122:12.3.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:12.4.verse: ‘But I will take part in talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart and leads solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.’

mn122:12.5.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:13.1.verse: While a mendicant is practicing such a meditation, if their mind inclines to thinking, they think:

mn122:13.2.verse: ‘I will not think the kind of thought that is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. Such thoughts don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. That is, sensual, malicious, or cruel thoughts.’

mn122:13.3.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:13.4.verse: ‘But I will think the kind of thought that is noble and emancipating, and brings one who practices it to the complete ending of suffering. That is, thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness.’

mn122:13.5.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:14.1.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn122:14.3.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn122:14.7.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn122:14.8.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn122:15.1.verse: So a mendicant should regularly check their own mind:

mn122:15.2.verse: ‘Does my mind take an interest in any of these five kinds of sensual stimulation?’

mn122:15.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

mn122:15.6.verse: ‘I have not given up desire and greed for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.’

mn122:15.7.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:15.8.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows this:

mn122:15.9.verse: ‘My mind does not take an interest.’

mn122:15.11.verse: ‘I have given up desire and greed for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.’

mn122:15.12.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:16.1.verse: A mendicant should meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates:

mn122:16.2.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

mn122:16.6.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

mn122:17.1.verse: As they do so, they give up the conceit ‘I am’ regarding the five grasping aggregates.

mn122:17.3.verse: ‘I have given up the conceit “I am” regarding the five grasping aggregates.’

mn122:17.4.verse: In this way they are aware of the situation.

mn122:18.1.verse: These principles are entirely skillful, with skillful outcomes; they are noble, transcendent, and inaccessible to the Wicked One.

mn122:19.2.verse: For what reason would a disciple deem it worthwhile to follow the Teacher, even if driven away?”

mn122:19.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

mn122:20.1.verse: “A disciple would not deem it worthwhile to follow the Teacher for the sake of this, namely statements, mixed prose & verse, or discussions.

mn122:20.3.verse: Because for a long time you have learned the teachings, remembering them, rehearsing them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.

mn122:20.4.verse: But a disciple would deem it worthwhile to follow the Teacher, even if driven away, for the sake of talk about self-effacement that helps open the heart and leads solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment. That is, talk about fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, aloofness, arousing energy, ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom.

mn122:21.1.verse: This being so, Ānanda, there is a peril for the tutor, a peril for the pupil, and a peril for a spiritual practitioner.

mn122:22.1.verse: And how is there a peril for the tutor?

mn122:22.2.verse: It’s when some teacher frequents a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn122:22.3.verse: While meditating withdrawn, they’re visited by a stream of brahmins and householders, and people of town and country.

mn122:22.4.verse: When this happens, they enjoy infatuation, fall into greed, and return to indulgence.

mn122:22.5.verse: This is said to be the tutor’s peril.

mn122:22.6.verse: They’re ruined by bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn122:22.7.verse: That’s how there is a peril for the tutor.

mn122:23.1.verse: And how is there a peril for the pupil?

mn122:23.2.verse: It’s when the disciple of a teacher, emulating their teacher’s fostering of seclusion,

mn122:23.3.verse: frequents a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn122:23.4.verse: While meditating withdrawn, they’re visited by a stream of brahmins and householders, and people of town and country.

mn122:23.5.verse: When this happens, they enjoy infatuation, fall into greed, and return to indulgence.

mn122:23.6.verse: This is said to be the pupil’s peril.

mn122:23.7.verse: They’re ruined by bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn122:23.8.verse: That’s how there is a peril for the pupil.

mn122:24.1.verse: And how is there a peril for a spiritual practitioner?

mn122:24.2.verse: It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn122:24.3.verse: He frequents a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn122:24.4.verse: While meditating withdrawn, he’s visited by a stream of brahmins and householders, and people of town and country.

mn122:24.5.verse: When this happens, he doesn’t enjoy infatuation, fall into greed, and return to indulgence.

mn122:24.6.verse: But a disciple of this teacher, emulating their teacher’s fostering of seclusion,

mn122:24.7.verse: frequents a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.

mn122:24.8.verse: While meditating withdrawn, they’re visited by a stream of brahmins and householders, and people of town and country.

mn122:24.9.verse: When this happens, they enjoy infatuation, fall into greed, and return to indulgence.

mn122:24.10.verse: This is said to be the spiritual practitioner’s peril.

mn122:24.11.verse: They’re ruined by bad, unskillful qualities that are corrupting, leading to future lives, hurtful, resulting in suffering and future rebirth, old age, and death.

mn122:24.12.verse: That’s how there is a peril for the spiritual practitioner.

mn122:24.13.verse: And in this context, Ānanda, as compared to the peril of the tutor or the pupil, the peril of the spiritual practitioner has more painful, bitter results, and even leads to the underworld.

mn122:25.1.verse: So, Ānanda, treat me as a friend, not as an enemy.

mn122:25.2.verse: That will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn122:25.3.verse: And how do disciples treat their Teacher as an enemy, not a friend?

mn122:25.4.verse: It’s when the Teacher teaches Dhamma to his disciples out of kindness and sympathy:

mn122:25.5.verse: ‘This is for your welfare. This is for your happiness.’

mn122:25.6.verse: But their disciples don’t want to listen. They don’t actively listen or try to understand. They proceed having turned away from the Teacher’s instruction.

mn122:25.7.verse: That’s how the disciples treat their Teacher as an enemy, not a friend.

mn122:26.1.verse: And how do disciples treat their Teacher as a friend, not an enemy?

mn122:26.2.verse: It’s when the Teacher teaches Dhamma to his disciples out of kindness and sympathy:

mn122:26.3.verse: ‘This is for your welfare. This is for your happiness.’

mn122:26.4.verse: And their disciples want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand. They don’t proceed having turned away from the Teacher’s instruction.

mn122:26.5.verse: That’s how the disciples treat their Teacher as a friend, not an enemy.

mn122:26.6.verse: So, Ānanda, treat me as a friend, not as an enemy.

mn122:26.7.verse: That will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.

mn122:27.1.verse: I shall not mollycoddle you like a potter with their damp, unfired pots.

mn122:27.2.verse: I shall speak, curbing you again and again,

mn122:27.4.verse: The core will stand the test.”

mn122:27.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn122:27.6.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Ānanda approved what the Buddha said.

mn122:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Sakyan country at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park.

mn122:2.1.verse: Then, when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Kapilavatthu for alms.

mn122:2.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu and had returned from his almsround, after his meal he went for his daytime abiding to the dwelling of Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan.

mn122:2.3.verse: Now on that occasion there were many resting places prepared in Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.4.verse: The Blessed One saw the many resting places prepared in Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.6.verse: “There are many resting places prepared in Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.8.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Ānanda, along with many bhikkhus, was busy making robes at Ghaṭā the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.9.verse: Then, when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from retreat and went to Ghaṭā the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.10.verse: There he sat down on a seat made ready and asked the venerable Ānanda:

mn122:2.11.verse: “Ānanda, there are many resting places prepared in Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.13.verse: “Venerable sir, many resting places have been prepared in Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan’s dwelling.

mn122:2.15.verse: This is our time for making robes, venerable sir.”

mn122:3.1.verse: “Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not shine by delighting in company, by taking delight in company, by devoting himself to delight in company; by delighting in society, by taking delight in society, by rejoicing in society.

mn122:3.2.verse: Indeed, Ānanda, it is not possible that a bhikkhu who delights in company, takes delight in company, and devotes himself to delight in company, who delights in society, takes delight in society, and rejoices in society, will ever obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the bliss of renunciation, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace, the bliss of enlightenment.

mn122:3.3.verse: But it can be expected that when a bhikkhu lives alone, withdrawn from society, he will obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the bliss of renunciation, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace, the bliss of enlightenment.

mn122:4.1.verse: “Indeed, Ānanda, it is not possible that a bhikkhu who delights in company, takes delight in company, and devotes himself to delight in company, who delights in society, takes delight in society, and rejoices in society, will ever enter upon and abide in either the deliverance of mind that is temporary and delectable or in [the deliverance of mind] that is perpetual and unshakeable.

mn122:4.2.verse: But it can be expected that when a bhikkhu lives alone, withdrawn from society, he will enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind that is temporary and delectable or in [the deliverance of mind] that is perpetual and unshakeable.

mn122:5.1.verse: “I do not see even a single kind of form, Ānanda, from the change and alteration of which there would not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair in one who lusts for it and takes delight in it.

mn122:6.1.verse: “However, Ānanda, there is this abiding discovered by the Tathāgata:

mn122:6.2.verse: to enter and abide in voidness internally by giving no attention to all signs.

mn122:6.3.verse: If, while the Tathāgata is abiding thus, he is visited by bhikkhus or bhikkhunīs, by men or women lay followers, by kings or kings’ ministers, by other sectarians or their disciples,

mn122:6.4.verse: then with a mind leaning to seclusion, tending and inclining to seclusion, withdrawn, delighting in renunciation, and altogether done away with things that are the basis for taints, he invariably talks to them in a way concerned with dismissing them.

mn122:7.1.verse: “Therefore, Ānanda, if a bhikkhu should wish:

mn122:7.2.verse: ‘May I enter upon and abide in voidness internally,’ he should steady his mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness, and concentrate it.

mn122:7.3.verse: And how does he steady his mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness, and concentrate it?

mn122:8.1.verse: “Here, Ānanda, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna…

mn122:8.4.verse: the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn122:8.5.verse: That is how a bhikkhu steadies his mind internally, quiets it, brings it to singleness, and concentrates it.

mn122:9.1.verse: Then he gives attention to voidness internally.

mn122:9.2.verse: While he is giving attention to voidness internally, his mind does not enter into voidness internally or acquire confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn122:9.3.verse: When that is so, he understands thus:

mn122:9.4.verse: ‘While I am giving attention to voidness internally, my mind does not enter into voidness internally or acquire confidence, steadiness, and decision.’

mn122:9.5.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:9.6.verse: He gives attention to voidness externally…

mn122:9.7.verse: He gives attention to voidness internally and externally…

mn122:9.9.verse: While he is giving attention to imperturbability, his mind does not enter into imperturbability or acquire confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn122:9.10.verse: When that is so, he understands thus:

mn122:9.11.verse: ‘While I am giving attention to imperturbability, my mind does not enter into imperturbability or acquire confidence, steadiness, and decision.’

mn122:9.12.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:10.1.verse: “Then that bhikkhu should steady his mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness, and concentrate it on that same sign of concentration as before.

mn122:10.2.verse: Then he gives attention to voidness internally.

mn122:10.3.verse: While he is giving attention to voidness internally, his mind enters into voidness internally and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn122:10.4.verse: When that is so, he understands thus:

mn122:10.5.verse: ‘While I am giving attention to voidness internally, my mind enters into voidness internally and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.’

mn122:10.6.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:10.7.verse: He gives attention to voidness externally…

mn122:10.8.verse: He gives attention to voidness internally and externally…

mn122:10.10.verse: While he is giving attention to imperturbability, his mind enters into imperturbability and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.

mn122:10.11.verse: When that is so, he understands thus:

mn122:10.12.verse: ‘While I am giving attention to imperturbability, my mind enters into imperturbability and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.’

mn122:10.13.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:11.1.verse: “When a bhikkhu abides thus, if his mind inclines to walking, he walks, thinking:

mn122:11.2.verse: ‘While I am walking thus, no evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will beset me.’

mn122:11.3.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:11.4.verse: And when a bhikkhu abides thus, if his mind inclines to standing, he stands, thinking:

mn122:11.5.verse: ‘While I am standing thus, no evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will beset me.’

mn122:11.6.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:11.7.verse: If his mind inclines to sitting, he sits, thinking:

mn122:11.8.verse: ‘While I am sitting thus, no evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief will beset me.’

mn122:11.9.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:11.10.verse: If his mind inclines to lying down, he lies down, thinking:

mn122:11.11.verse: ‘While I am lying down thus, no evil unwholesome states will beset me.’

mn122:11.12.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:12.1.verse: “When a bhikkhu abides thus, if his mind inclines to talking, he resolves:

mn122:12.2.verse: ‘Such talk as is low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, unbeneficial, and which does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna, that is, talk of kings, robbers, ministers, armies, dangers, battles, food, drink, clothing, beds, garlands, perfumes, relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, countries, women, heroes, streets, wells, the dead, trivialities, the origin of the world, the origin of the sea, whether things are so or are not so: such talk I shall not utter.’

mn122:12.3.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:12.4.verse: But he resolves: ‘Such talk as deals with effacement, as favours the mind’s release, and which leads to complete disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna, that is, talk on wanting little, on contentment, seclusion, aloofness from society, arousing energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, deliverance, knowledge and vision of deliverance: such talk I shall utter.’

mn122:12.5.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:13.1.verse: “When a bhikkhu abides thus, if his mind inclines to thinking, he resolves:

mn122:13.2.verse: ‘Such thoughts as are low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, unbeneficial, and which do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna, that is, thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty: such thoughts I shall not think.’

mn122:13.3.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:13.4.verse: But he resolves: ‘Such thoughts as are noble and emancipating, and lead the one who practises in accordance with them to the complete destruction of suffering, that is, thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty: such thoughts I shall think.’

mn122:13.5.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:14.1.verse: “Ānanda, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.

mn122:14.3.verse: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn122:14.7.verse: Tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn122:14.8.verse: These are the five cords of sensual pleasure.

mn122:15.1.verse: “Herein a bhikkhu should constantly review his own mind thus:

mn122:15.2.verse: ‘Does any mental excitement concerning any base among these five cords of sensual pleasure ever arise in me?’

mn122:15.3.verse: If, on reviewing his mind, the bhikkhu understands:

mn122:15.4.verse: ‘Mental excitement concerning a certain base among these five cords of sensual pleasure does arise in me,’

mn122:15.6.verse: ‘Desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure are unabandoned in me.’

mn122:15.7.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:15.8.verse: But if, on reviewing his mind, the bhikkhu understands:

mn122:15.9.verse: ‘No mental excitement concerning any base among these five cords of sensual pleasure arises in me,’

mn122:15.11.verse: ‘Desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure are abandoned in me.’

mn122:15.12.verse: In this way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:16.1.verse: “Ānanda, there are these five aggregates affected by clinging, in regard to which a bhikkhu should abide contemplating rise and fall thus:

mn122:16.2.verse: ‘Such is material form, such its arising, such its disappearance;

mn122:16.3.verse: such is feeling, such its arising, such its disappearance;

mn122:16.4.verse: such is perception, such its arising, such its disappearance;

mn122:16.5.verse: such are formations, such their arising, such their disappearance;

mn122:16.6.verse: such is consciousness, such its arising, such its disappearance.’

mn122:17.1.verse: “When he abides contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates affected by clinging, the conceit ‘I am’ based on these five aggregates affected by clinging is abandoned in him.

mn122:17.2.verse: When that is so, that bhikkhu understands:

mn122:17.3.verse: ‘The conceit “I am” based on these five aggregates affected by clinging is abandoned in me.’

mn122:17.4.verse: In that way he has full awareness of that.

mn122:18.1.verse: “These states are entirely wholesome and have a wholesome outcome; they are noble, supramundane, and inaccessible to the Evil One.

mn122:19.2.verse: What good does a disciple see that he should seek the Teacher’s company even if he is told to go away?”

mn122:19.3.verse: “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, have the Blessed One as their resort. It would be good if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of these words. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

mn122:20.1.verse: “Ānanda, a disciple should not seek the Teacher’s company for the sake of discourses, stanzas, and expositions.

mn122:20.3.verse: For a long time, Ānanda, you have learned the teachings, remembered them, recited them verbally, examined them with the mind, and penetrated them well by view.

mn122:20.4.verse: But such talk as deals with effacement, as favours the mind’s release, and which leads to complete disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna, that is, talk on wanting little, on contentment, seclusion, aloofness from society, arousing energy, virtue, concentration, wisdom, deliverance, knowledge and vision of deliverance: for the sake of such talk a disciple should seek the Teacher’s company even if he is told to go away.

mn122:21.1.verse: “Since this is so, Ānanda, a teacher’s undoing may come about, a pupil’s undoing may come about, and the undoing of one who lives the holy life may come about.

mn122:22.1.verse: “And how does a teacher’s undoing come about?

mn122:22.2.verse: Here some teacher resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.

mn122:22.3.verse: While he lives thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders from town and country visit him,

mn122:22.4.verse: and as a result he goes astray, becomes filled with desire, succumbs to craving, and reverts to luxury.

mn122:22.5.verse: This teacher is said to be undone by the teacher’s undoing.

mn122:22.6.verse: He has been struck down by evil unwholesome states that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing, and death.

mn122:22.7.verse: This is how the teacher’s undoing comes about.

mn122:23.1.verse: “And how does a pupil’s undoing come about?

mn122:23.2.verse: A pupil of that teacher, emulating the teacher’s seclusion,

mn122:23.3.verse: resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest…a heap of straw.

mn122:23.4.verse: While he lives thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders from town and country visit him,

mn122:23.5.verse: and as a result he goes astray, becomes filled with desire, succumbs to craving, and reverts to luxury.

mn122:23.6.verse: This pupil is said to be undone by the pupil’s undoing.

mn122:23.7.verse: He has been struck down by evil unwholesome states that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing, and death.

mn122:23.8.verse: This is how the pupil’s undoing comes about.

mn122:24.1.verse: “And how does the undoing of one who lives the holy life come about?

mn122:24.2.verse: Here a Tathāgata appears in the world, accomplished and fully enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.

mn122:24.3.verse: He resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest…a heap of straw.

mn122:24.4.verse: While he lives thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders from town and country visit him,

mn122:24.5.verse: yet he does not go astray, or become filled with desire, succumb to craving, and revert to luxury.

mn122:24.6.verse: But a disciple of this teacher, emulating his teacher’s seclusion,

mn122:24.7.verse: resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest...a heap of straw.

mn122:24.8.verse: While he lives thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders from town and country visit him,

mn122:24.9.verse: and as a result he goes astray, becomes filled with desire, succumbs to craving, and reverts to luxury.

mn122:24.10.verse: This one who lives the holy life is said to be undone by the undoing of one who lives the holy life.

mn122:24.11.verse: He has been struck down by evil unwholesome states that defile, bring renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing, and death.

mn122:24.12.verse: Thus there comes to be the undoing of one who leads the holy life.

mn122:24.13.verse: And herein, Ānanda, the undoing of one who leads the holy life has a more painful result, a more bitter result, than the teacher’s undoing or the pupil’s undoing, and it even leads to perdition.

mn122:25.1.verse: “Therefore, Ānanda, behave towards me with friendliness, not with hostility.

mn122:25.2.verse: That will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.

mn122:25.3.verse: And how do disciples behave towards the Teacher with hostility, not with friendliness?

mn122:25.4.verse: Here, Ānanda, compassionate and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples out of compassion:

mn122:25.5.verse: ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’

mn122:25.6.verse: His disciples do not want to hear or give ear or exert their minds to understand; they err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn122:25.7.verse: Thus do disciples behave towards the Teacher with hostility, not with friendliness.

mn122:26.1.verse: “And how do disciples behave towards the Teacher with friendliness, not with hostility?

mn122:26.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, compassionate and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples out of compassion:

mn122:26.3.verse: ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’

mn122:26.4.verse: His disciples want to hear and give ear and exert their minds to understand; they do not err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn122:26.5.verse: Thus do disciples behave towards the Teacher with friendliness, not with hostility.

mn122:26.6.verse: Therefore, Ānanda, behave towards me with friendliness, not with hostility.

mn122:26.7.verse: That will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.

mn122:27.1.verse: “I shall not treat you as the potter treats the raw damp clay.

mn122:27.2.verse: Repeatedly restraining you, I shall speak to you, Ānanda.

mn122:27.3.verse: Repeatedly admonishing you, I shall speak to you, Ānanda.

mn122:27.4.verse: The sound core will stand [the test].”

mn122:27.5.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn122:27.6.verse: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn123:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn123:2.1.verse: Then after the meal, on return from almsround, several mendicants sat together in the assembly hall and this discussion came up among them:

mn123:2.2.verse: “It’s incredible, reverends, it’s amazing! The Realized One has such psychic power and might!

mn123:2.3.verse: For he is able to know the Buddhas of the past who have become completely quenched, cut off proliferation, cut off the course, finished off the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering:

mn123:2.4.verse: ‘Such is the birth, names, clans, conduct, teachings, wisdom, meditation, and freedom of those Blessed Ones.’

mn123:2.5.verse: When they said this, Venerable Ānanda said,

mn123:2.6.verse: “The Realized Ones are incredible, reverends, and they have incredible qualities.

mn123:2.7.verse: They’re amazing, and they have amazing qualities.”

mn123:2.8.verse: But this conversation among those mendicants was left unfinished.

mn123:2.9.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat, went to the assembly hall, sat down on the seat spread out,

mn123:2.11.verse: “Mendicants, what were you sitting talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?”

mn123:2.12.verse: So the mendicants told him what they had been talking about. The Buddha said,

mn123:2.19.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, say some more about the incredible and amazing qualities of the Realized One.”

mn123:3.1.verse: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:3.2.verse: ‘Mindful and aware, the being intent on awakening was reborn in the host of joyful gods.’

mn123:3.3.verse: This I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:4.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:4.2.verse: ‘Mindful and aware, the being intent on awakening remained in the host of joyful gods.’

mn123:4.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:5.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:5.2.verse: ‘For the whole of that life, the being intent on awakening remained in the host of joyful gods.’

mn123:5.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:6.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:6.2.verse: ‘Mindful and aware, the being intent on awakening passed away from the host of joyful gods and was conceived in his mother’s womb.’

mn123:6.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:7.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:7.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening passes away from the host of joyful gods, he is conceived in his mother’s womb.

mn123:7.3.verse: And then—in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

mn123:7.4.verse: Even in the boundless gloom of interstellar space—so utterly dark that even the luminosity of the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful, makes no impression—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

mn123:7.5.verse: And even the sentient beings reborn there recognize each other by that light: “So, it seems other sentient beings have been reborn here!”

mn123:7.6.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shakes and rocks and trembles. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.’

mn123:7.7.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:8.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:8.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, four godlings approach to guard the four quarters, so that no human or non-human or anyone at all shall harm the being intent on awakening or his mother.’

mn123:8.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:9.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:9.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she becomes naturally ethical. She refrains from killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and beer, wine, and liquor intoxicants.’

mn123:9.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:10.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:10.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she no longer thinks of men in a sexual way, and she cannot be violated by a man of lustful intent.’

mn123:10.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:11.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:11.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, she obtains the five kinds of sensual stimulation and amuses herself, supplied and provided with them.’

mn123:11.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:12.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:12.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, no afflictions beset her. She’s happy and free of bodily fatigue. And she sees the being intent on awakening in her womb, whole in his major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.

mn123:12.3.verse: Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked. And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.

mn123:12.4.verse: And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it: “This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked. And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.”

mn123:12.5.verse: In the same way, when the being intent on awakening is conceived in his mother’s womb, no afflictions beset her. She’s happy and free of bodily fatigue. And she sees the being intent on awakening in her womb, whole in his major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.’

mn123:12.6.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:13.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:13.2.verse: ‘Seven days after the being intent on awakening is born, his mother passes away and is reborn in the host of joyful gods.’

mn123:13.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:14.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:14.2.verse: ‘Other women carry the infant in the womb for nine or ten months before giving birth. Not so the mother of the being intent on awakening. She gives birth after exactly ten months.’

mn123:14.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:15.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:15.2.verse: ‘Other women give birth while sitting or lying down. Not so the mother of the being intent on awakening. She only gives birth standing up.’

mn123:15.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:16.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:16.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, gods receive him first, then humans.’

mn123:16.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:17.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:17.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, before he reaches the ground, four godlings receive him and place him before his mother, saying: “Rejoice, O Queen! An illustrious son is born to you.”’

mn123:17.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:18.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:18.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges already clean, unsoiled by waters, mucus, blood, or any other kind of impurity, pure and clean.

mn123:18.3.verse: Suppose a jewel-treasure was placed on a cloth from Kāsi. The jewel would not soil the cloth, nor would the cloth soil the jewel.

mn123:18.5.verse: Because of the cleanliness of them both.

mn123:18.6.verse: In the same way, when the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, he emerges already clean, unsoiled by waters, mucus, blood, or any other kind of impurity, pure and clean.’

mn123:18.7.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:19.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:19.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, two showers of water appear from the sky, one cool, one warm, for bathing the being intent on awakening and his mother.’

mn123:19.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:20.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:20.2.verse: ‘As soon as he’s born, the being intent on awakening stands firm with his own feet on the ground. Facing north, he takes seven strides with a white parasol held above him, surveys all quarters, and makes this dramatic proclamation: “I am the foremost in the world! I am the eldest in the world! I am the first in the world! This is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.”’

mn123:20.3.verse: This too I remember as an incredible quality of the Buddha.

mn123:21.1.verse: I have learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

mn123:21.2.verse: ‘When the being intent on awakening emerges from his mother’s womb, then—in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

mn123:21.3.verse: Even in the boundless gloom of interstellar space—so utterly dark that even the luminosity of the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful, makes no impression—an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing the glory of the gods.

mn123:21.4.verse: And the sentient beings reborn there recognize each other by that light: “So, it seems other sentient beings have been reborn here!”

mn123:21.5.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shakes and rocks and trembles. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.’

mn123:21.6.verse: This too I remember as an incredible and amazing quality of the Buddha.”

mn123:22.1.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, you should also remember this as an incredible and amazing quality of the Realized One.

mn123:22.2.verse: It’s that the Realized One knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:22.3.verse: He knows perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:22.4.verse: He knows thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:22.5.verse: This too you should remember as an incredible and amazing quality of the Realized One.”

mn123:23.1.verse: “Sir, the Buddha knows feelings as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:23.2.verse: He knows perceptions as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:23.3.verse: He knows thoughts as they arise, as they remain, and as they go away.

mn123:23.4.verse: This too I remember as an incredible and amazing quality of the Buddha.”

mn123:23.5.verse: That is what Venerable Ānanda said,

mn123:23.7.verse: Satisfied, those mendicants approved what Venerable Ānanda said.

mn123:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn123:2.1.verse: Now a number of bhikkhus were sitting in the assembly hall, where they had met together on returning from their almsround, after their meal, when this discussion arose among them:

mn123:2.2.verse: “It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous, how mighty and powerful is the Tathāgata!

mn123:2.3.verse: For he is able to know about the Buddhas of the past—who attained to final Nibbāna, cut [the tangle of] proliferation, broke the cycle, ended the round, and surmounted all suffering—that for those Blessed Ones

mn123:2.4.verse: their birth was thus, their names were thus, their clans were thus, their virtue was thus, their state [of concentration] was thus, their wisdom was thus, their abiding [in attainments] was thus, their deliverance was thus.”

mn123:2.5.verse: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda told the bhikkhus:

mn123:2.6.verse: “Friends, Tathāgatas are wonderful and have wonderful qualities.

mn123:2.7.verse: Tathāgatas are marvellous and have marvellous qualities.”

mn123:2.9.verse: for the Blessed One rose from meditation when it was evening, went to the assembly hall, and sat down on a seat made ready.

mn123:2.10.verse: Then he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn123:2.11.verse: “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you sitting together here now? And what was your discussion that was interrupted?”

mn123:2.12.verse: “Here, venerable sir, we were sitting in the assembly hall, where we had met together on returning from our almsround, after our meal, when this discussion arose among us:

mn123:2.13.verse: ‘It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous, how mighty and powerful is the Tathāgata! For he is able to know about the Buddhas of the past—who attained to final Nibbāna, cut [the tangle of] proliferation, broke the cycle, ended the round, and surmounted all suffering—that for those Blessed Ones

mn123:2.14.verse: their birth was thus, their names were thus, their clans were thus, their virtue was thus, their state [of concentration] was thus, their wisdom was thus, their abiding [in attainments] was thus, their deliverance was thus.’ When this was said, venerable sir, the venerable Ānanda said to us:

mn123:2.15.verse: ‘Friends, Tathāgatas are wonderful and have wonderful qualities.

mn123:2.16.verse: Tathāgatas are marvellous and have marvellous qualities.’

mn123:2.17.verse: This was our discussion, venerable sir, that was interrupted when the Blessed One arrived.”

mn123:2.18.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:

mn123:2.19.verse: “That being so, Ānanda, explain more fully the Tathāgata’s wonderful and marvellous qualities.”

mn123:3.1.verse: “I heard and learned this, venerable sir, from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:3.2.verse: ‘Mindful and fully aware, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta appeared in the Tusita heaven.’

mn123:3.3.verse: That mindful and fully aware the Bodhisatta appeared in the Tusita heaven—this I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:4.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:4.2.verse: ‘Mindful and fully aware the Bodhisatta remained in the Tusita heaven.’

mn123:4.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:5.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:5.2.verse: ‘For the whole of his life-span the Bodhisatta remained in the Tusita heaven.’

mn123:5.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:6.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:6.2.verse: ‘Mindful and fully aware the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and descended into his mother’s womb.’

mn123:6.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:7.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:7.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and descended into his mother’s womb,

mn123:7.3.verse: then a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared in the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its princes and its people.

mn123:7.4.verse: And even in those abysmal world interspaces of vacancy, gloom, and utter darkness, where the moon and the sun, mighty and powerful as they are, cannot make their light prevail—there too a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared.

mn123:7.5.verse: And the beings reborn there perceived each other by that light: “So indeed, sir, there are other beings reborn here!”

mn123:7.6.verse: And this ten-thousandfold world system shook and quaked and trembled, and there too a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared.’

mn123:7.7.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:8.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:8.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb, four young deities came to guard him at the four quarters so that no humans or non-humans or anyone at all could harm the Bodhisatta or his mother.’

mn123:8.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:9.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:9.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb, she became intrinsically virtuous, refraining from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from misconduct in sensual pleasures, from false speech, and from wines, liquors, and intoxicants, which are the basis of negligence.’

mn123:9.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:10.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:10.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb, no sensual thought arose in her concerning men, and she was inaccessible to any man having a lustful mind.’

mn123:10.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:11.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:11.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb, she obtained the five cords of sensual pleasure, and furnished and endowed with them, she enjoyed herself with them.’

mn123:11.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:12.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:12.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb, no kind of affliction arose in her; she was blissful and free from bodily fatigue. She saw the Bodhisatta within her womb with all his limbs, lacking no faculty.

mn123:12.3.verse: Suppose a blue, yellow, red, white, or brown thread were strung through a fine beryl gem of purest water, eight-faceted, well cut,

mn123:12.4.verse: and a man with good sight were to take it in his hand and review it thus: “This is a fine beryl gem of purest water, eight-faceted, well cut, and through it is strung a blue, yellow, red, white, or brown thread”;

mn123:12.5.verse: so too when the Bodhisatta had descended into his mother’s womb…she saw the Bodhisatta within her womb with all his limbs, lacking no faculty.’

mn123:12.6.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:13.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:13.2.verse: ‘Seven days after the birth of the Bodhisatta, his mother died and reappeared in the Tusita heaven.’

mn123:13.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:14.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:14.2.verse: ‘Other women give birth after carrying the child in the womb for nine or ten months, but not so the Bodhisatta’s mother. The Bodhisatta’s mother gave birth to him after carrying him in her womb for exactly ten months.’

mn123:14.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:15.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:15.2.verse: ‘Other women give birth seated or lying down, but not so the Bodhisatta’s mother. The Bodhisatta’s mother gave birth to him standing up.’

mn123:15.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:16.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:16.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, first gods received him, then human beings.’

mn123:16.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:17.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:17.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, he did not touch the earth. The four young gods received him and set him before his mother saying: “Rejoice, O queen, a son of great power has been born to you.”’

mn123:17.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:18.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:18.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, he came forth unsullied, unsmeared by water or humours or blood or any kind of impurity, clean, and unsullied.

mn123:18.3.verse: Suppose there were a gem placed on Kāsi cloth, then the gem would not smear the cloth or the cloth the gem.

mn123:18.5.verse: Because of the purity of both.

mn123:18.6.verse: So too when the Bodhisatta came forth…clean and unsullied.’

mn123:18.7.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:19.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:19.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, two jets of water appeared to pour from the sky, one cool and one warm, for bathing the Bodhisatta and his mother.’

mn123:19.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:20.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:20.2.verse: ‘As soon as the Bodhisatta was born, he stood firmly with his feet on the ground; then he took seven steps facing north, and with a white parasol held over him, he surveyed each quarter and uttered the words of the Leader of the Herd: “I am the highest in the world; I am the best in the world; I am the foremost in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no renewal of being for me.”’

mn123:20.3.verse: This too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.

mn123:21.1.verse: I heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips:

mn123:21.2.verse: ‘When the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, then a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared in the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its princes and its people.

mn123:21.3.verse: And even in those abysmal world interspaces of vacancy, gloom, and utter darkness, where the moon and the sun, mighty and powerful as they are, cannot make their light prevail—there too a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared.

mn123:21.4.verse: And the beings reborn there perceived each other by that light: “So indeed, sir, there are other beings reborn here!”

mn123:21.5.verse: And this ten-thousandfold world system shook and quaked and trembled, and there too a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared.’

mn123:21.6.verse: That when the Bodhisatta came forth from his mother’s womb, then a great immeasurable light surpassing the splendour of the gods appeared…this too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.”

mn123:22.1.verse: “That being so, Ānanda, remember this too as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Tathāgata:

mn123:22.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, for the Tathāgata feelings are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear;

mn123:22.3.verse: perceptions are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear;

mn123:22.4.verse: thoughts are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear.

mn123:22.5.verse: Remember this too, Ānanda, as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Tathāgata.”

mn123:23.1.verse: “Venerable sir, since for the Blessed One feelings are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear;

mn123:23.2.verse: perceptions are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear;

mn123:23.3.verse: thoughts are known as they arise, as they are present, as they disappear—

mn123:23.4.verse: this too I remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the Blessed One.”

mn123:23.5.verse: That is what the venerable Ānanda said.

mn123:23.7.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the venerable Ānanda’s words.

mn124:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Bakkula was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn124:2.1.verse: Then the naked ascetic Kassapa, an old friend of Bakkula in the lay life, approached him, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn124:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Venerable Bakkula,

mn124:3.1.verse: “Reverend Bakkula, how long has it been since you went forth?”

mn124:3.3.verse: “But in these eighty years, how many times have you had sex?”

mn124:3.4.verse: “You shouldn’t ask me such a question.

mn124:3.6.verse: Rather, you should ask me this:

mn124:3.7.verse: ‘But in these eighty years, how many times have sensual perceptions ever arisen in you?’”

mn124:3.8.verse: “But in these eighty years, how many times have sensual perceptions ever arisen in you?”

mn124:3.9.verse: “In these eighty years, I don’t recall that any sensual perception has ever arisen in me.”

mn124:3.10.verse: This we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:4-5.1.verse: “In these eighty years, I don’t recall that any perception of ill will …

mn124:4-5.2.verse: or cruelty has ever arisen in me.”

mn124:4-5.3.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:6.1.verse: “In these eighty years, I don’t recall that any thought of sensuality …

mn124:7-8.2.verse: or cruelty has ever arisen in me.”

mn124:7-8.3.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:9.1.verse: “In these eighty years, I don’t recall accepting a robe from a householder …

mn124:10.1.verse: cutting a robe with a knife …

mn124:11-15.1.verse: sewing a robe with a needle …

mn124:11-15.3.verse: sewing a robe during the robe-making ceremony …

mn124:11-15.4.verse: wandering to look for robe material for my companions in the spiritual life when they are making robes …

mn124:20-25.1.verse: getting caught up in the features by way of the details of a lady’s appearance …

mn124:20-25.2.verse: teaching a lady, even so much as a four line verse …

mn124:30-36.3.verse: looking for a massage from my spiritual companions …

mn124:30-36.4.verse: being ill, even for as long as it takes to pull a cow’s udder …

mn124:30-36.5.verse: being presented with medicine, even as much as a bit of yellow myrobalan …

mn124:30-36.8.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:37.1.verse: “In these eighty years, I don’t recall commencing the rainy season residence within a village.”

mn124:37.2.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:38.1.verse: “Reverend, for seven days I ate the nation’s almsfood as a debtor.

mn124:38.2.verse: Then on the eighth day I became enlightened.”

mn124:38.3.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:39.1.verse: “Reverend Bakkula, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training?”

mn124:39.2.verse: And the naked ascetic Kassapa received the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training.

mn124:39.3.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Kassapa, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn124:39.4.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

mn124:39.5.verse: And Venerable Kassapa became one of the perfected.

mn124:40.1.verse: Then some time later Venerable Bakkula, taking a latchkey, went from dwelling to dwelling, saying,

mn124:40.2.verse: “Come forth, venerables, come forth! Today will be my full extinguishment.”

mn124:40.3.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:41.1.verse: And Venerable Bakkula became fully extinguished while seated right in the middle of the Saṅgha.

mn124:41.2.verse: This too we remember as an incredible and amazing quality of Venerable Bakkula.

mn124:1.2.verse: On one occasion the venerable Bakkula was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn124:2.1.verse: Then Acela Kassapa, a former companion of the venerable Bakkula in his lay life, went to the venerable Bakkula and exchanged greetings with him.

mn124:2.2.verse: When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side and asked the venerable Bakkula:

mn124:3.1.verse: “Friend Bakkula, how long is it since you went forth?”

mn124:3.2.verse: “It is eighty years since I went forth, friend.”

mn124:3.3.verse: “Friend Bakkula, in these eighty years how many times have you engaged in sexual intercourse?”

mn124:3.4.verse: “Friend Kassapa, you should not ask me such a question as that.

mn124:3.5.verse: You should ask me such a question as this: ‘Friend Bakkula, in these eighty years how many times have you engaged in sexual intercourse?’

mn124:3.6.verse: You should ask me such a question as this:

mn124:3.7.verse: ‘Friend Bakkula, in these eighty years how many times have perceptions of sensual desire arisen in you?’”

mn124:3.8.verse: “Friend Bakkula, in these eighty years how many times have perceptions of sensual desire arisen in you?”

mn124:3.9.verse: “Friend Kassapa, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall any perception of sensual desire to have ever arisen in me.”

mn124:3.10.verse: [That in the eighty years since he went forth the venerable Bakkula did not recall any perception of sensual desire to have ever arisen in him—this we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:4-5.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall any perception of ill will…

mn124:4-5.2.verse: any perception of cruelty to have ever arisen in me.”

mn124:4-5.3.verse: [That in the eighty years since he went forth the venerable Bakkula did not recall any perception of ill will…any perception of cruelty to have ever arisen in him—this we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:6.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall any thought of sensual desire to have ever arisen in me.”

mn124:6.2.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:7-8.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall any thought of ill will…

mn124:7-8.2.verse: any thought of cruelty to have ever arisen in me.”

mn124:7-8.3.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:9.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall ever having accepted a robe from a householder…

mn124:9.2.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:10.1.verse: ever having cut a robe with a cutter…”

mn124:10.2.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:11-15.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall ever having sewn a robe with a needle…

mn124:11-15.2.verse: ever having coloured a robe with dye…

mn124:11-15.3.verse: ever having sewn a robe at the kaṭhina time…

mn124:11-15.4.verse: ever having worked on making robes for my companions in the holy life…

mn124:16-19.1.verse: ever having accepted an invitation to a meal…

mn124:16-19.2.verse: ever having given rise to the thought:

mn124:16-19.3.verse: ‘Oh, may someone invite me to a meal!’…

mn124:16-19.4.verse: ever having sat down inside a house…

mn124:16-19.5.verse: ever having eaten inside a house…

mn124:20-25.1.verse: ever having grasped at the signs and features of a woman…

mn124:20-25.2.verse: ever having taught the Dhamma to a woman, even as much as a four-line stanza…

mn124:20-25.3.verse: ever having gone to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters…

mn124:20-25.4.verse: ever having taught the Dhamma to a bhikkhunī…

mn124:20-25.5.verse: ever having taught the Dhamma to a female probationer…

mn124:20-25.6.verse: ever having taught the Dhamma to a female novice…

mn124:26-29.1.verse: ever having given the going forth…

mn124:26-29.2.verse: ever having given the full admission…

mn124:26-29.4.verse: ever having had a novice wait on me…

mn124:30-36.1.verse: ever having bathed in a bath house…

mn124:30-36.2.verse: ever having bathed with bath powder…

mn124:30-36.3.verse: ever having undertaken the work of massaging the limbs of my companions in the holy life…

mn124:30-36.4.verse: ever having had an affliction arise in me even for as long as it takes to milk a cow…

mn124:30-36.5.verse: ever having carried medicine around, even as much as a piece of gallnut…

mn124:30-36.7.verse: ever having made up a bed.”

mn124:30-36.8.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:37.1.verse: “Friend, in the eighty years since I went forth I do not recall ever having entered upon residence for the Rains in a resting place inside a village.”

mn124:37.2.verse: […this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:38.1.verse: “Friend, for seven days after going forth I ate the country’s almsfood as a debtor;

mn124:38.2.verse: on the eighth day final knowledge arose.”

mn124:38.3.verse: [That for seven days the venerable Bakkula ate the country’s almsfood as a debtor, and on the eighth day final knowledge arose—this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:39.1.verse: [Then Acela Kassapa said:] “I would receive the going forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, I would receive the full admission.”

mn124:39.2.verse: And Acela Kassapa received the going forth in this Dhamma and Discipline, he received the full admission.

mn124:39.3.verse: And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the venerable Kassapa, by realising for himself with direct knowledge, here and now entered upon and abided in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn124:39.4.verse: He knew directly: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.”

mn124:39.5.verse: And the venerable Kassapa became one of the arahants.

mn124:40.1.verse: Then, on a later occasion, the venerable Bakkula took a key and went from dwelling to dwelling, saying:

mn124:40.2.verse: “Come forth, venerable sirs; come forth, venerable sirs. Today I shall attain final Nibbāna.”

mn124:40.3.verse: [That the venerable Bakkula took a key and went from dwelling to dwelling saying: “Come forth, venerable sirs; come forth, venerable sirs. Today I shall attain final Nibbāna”—this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn124:41.1.verse: Then, seated in the midst of the Sangha of bhikkhus, the venerable Bakkula attained final Nibbāna.

mn124:41.2.verse: [That seated in the midst of the Sangha of bhikkhus, the venerable Bakkula attained final Nibbāna—this too we remember as a wonderful and marvellous quality of the venerable Bakkula.]

mn125:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

mn125:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the novice Aciravata was living in a forest hut.

mn125:2.2.verse: Then Prince Jayasena, while wandering and walking for exercise, went to the novice Aciravata and exchanged greetings with him.

mn125:2.3.verse: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, Prince Jayasena said to the novice Aciravata:

mn125:2.5.verse: “A bhikkhu who lives here diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.”’

mn125:2.6.verse: ‘That is so, Prince, that is so.

mn125:2.7.verse: A bhikkhu who lives here diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.’

mn125:3.1.verse: ‘It would be good if Master Aggivessana taught me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.’

mn125:3.2.verse: ‘I cannot teach you the Dhamma, Prince, according as I have heard and mastered it.

mn125:3.3.verse: For, Prince, were I to teach you the Dhamma according as I have heard and mastered it, and you did not know the meaning of what I said, that would be wearisome and a bother for me.’

mn125:4.1.verse: ‘Let Master Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.

mn125:4.2.verse: Perhaps I might know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said.’

mn125:4.3.verse: ‘I might teach you the Dhamma, Prince, according as I have heard and mastered it.

mn125:4.4.verse: If you know the meaning of what I say, that will be good;

mn125:4.5.verse: if you do not know the meaning of what I say, then leave it at that and question me no further about it.’

mn125:4.6.verse: ‘Let Master Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.

mn125:4.7.verse: If I know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said, that will be good;

mn125:4.8.verse: if I do not know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said, then I shall leave it at that, and question Master Aggivessana no further about it.’

mn125:5.1.verse: Then the novice Aciravata taught Prince Jayasena the Dhamma according as he had heard and mastered it.

mn125:5.2.verse: When this was said, Prince Jayasena said to the novice Aciravata:

mn125:5.3.verse: ‘It is impossible, Master Aggivessana, it cannot be, that a bhikkhu who lives diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.’

mn125:5.4.verse: Then, having told the novice Aciravata that it was impossible and could not be, Prince Jayasena got up from his seat and departed.

mn125:6.1.verse: Then, soon after Prince Jayasena had gone, the novice Aciravata went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.

mn125:6.2.verse: When he had done so, the novice Aciravata recounted to the Blessed One all his conversation with Prince Jayasena.

mn125:7.1.verse: When this was said, the Blessed One said to the novice Aciravata:

mn125:7.3.verse: That what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.

mn125:8.1.verse: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, there were two tamable elephants, or two tamable horses, or two tamable oxen, that were well-tamed and well-disciplined, and also two tamable elephants or two tamable horses or two tamable oxen that were untamed and undisciplined.

mn125:8.3.verse: those two tamable elephants, horses, or oxen that were well-tamed and well-disciplined—being tamed, would they go as the tamed go, would they reach the grade of the tamed?’

mn125:8.5.verse: ‘But those two tamable elephants, horses, or oxen that were untamed and undisciplined—being untamed, would they go as the tamed go, would they reach the grade of the tamed, as those two well-tamed, well-disciplined elephants, horses, or oxen did?’

mn125:8.7.verse: ‘So too, Aggivessana, that what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.

mn125:9.1.verse: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, there were a high rock not far from a village or town.

mn125:9.2.verse: Then two friends went out from that village or town and approached that rock hand in hand; having approached, one friend remained below at the foot of the rock while the other climbed up on the rock.

mn125:9.3.verse: Then the friend standing below at the foot of the rock said to the friend standing on top of the rock:

mn125:9.4.verse: “Well, friend, what do you see, standing on top of the rock?”

mn125:9.6.verse: “Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”

mn125:9.8.verse: “It is impossible, friend, it cannot be, that you, standing on top of the rock, should see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”

mn125:9.9.verse: Then the friend standing on top of the rock came down to the foot of the rock, and taking that friend by the arm, made him climb to the top of the rock, and then, after letting him breathe a little, said:

mn125:9.10.verse: “Well, friend, what do you see, standing on top of the rock?”

mn125:9.12.verse: “Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”

mn125:9.14.verse: “Just a little earlier, friend, you spoke thus—we heard you say this:

mn125:9.15.verse: ‘It is impossible, friend, it cannot be, that you, standing on top of the rock, should see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.’

mn125:9.16.verse: But just now you spoke thus—we heard you say this:

mn125:9.17.verse: ‘Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.’”

mn125:9.19.verse: “That is because, friend, I was obstructed by this great rock, so that I did not see what was there to be seen.”

mn125:10.1.verse: ‘By something greater than that, Aggivessana, Prince Jayasena is obstructed, screened, blocked, and shut off by the mass of ignorance.

mn125:10.2.verse: So too, that what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.

mn125:11.1.verse: ‘If, Aggivessana, these two similes had occurred to you in regard to Prince Jayasena, he would, without wonder, have acquired confidence in you, and having acquired confidence he would have shown you the sign of his confidence.’

mn125:11.2.verse: ‘But, venerable sir, how could these two similes—never heard before—occur to me in regard to Prince Jayasena, without wonder, as they occur to the Blessed One?’

mn125:12.1.verse: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, a head-anointed warrior-noble king addressed his elephant woodsman thus:

mn125:12.2.verse: “Come, good elephant woodsman, mount the king’s elephant, enter the elephant wood, and having seen a forest elephant, fasten him by the neck to the king’s elephant.”

mn125:12.3.verse: ‘Yes, sire,’ the elephant woodsman replied to the head-anointed warrior-noble king, and, mounting the king’s elephant, he entered the elephant wood, and having seen a forest elephant, he fastened him by the neck to the king’s elephant.

mn125:12.4.verse: Then the king’s elephant led him out into the open.

mn125:12.5.verse: And that is how, Aggivessana, the forest elephant comes into the open;

mn125:12.6.verse: for forest elephants, Aggivessana, cleave to that, that is to say, the elephant wood.

mn125:12.7.verse: Then the elephant woodsman reported to the head-anointed warrior-noble king:

mn125:12.8.verse: “Sire, the forest elephant has come into the open.”

mn125:12.9.verse: Then, Aggivessana, the head-anointed warrior-noble king addressed the elephant-tamer thus:
