mn125:12.10.verse: “Come, good elephant-tamer, tame the forest elephant, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men.”

mn125:12.11.verse: ‘Yes, sire,’ the elephant-tamer replied to the head-anointed warrior-noble king; and he embedded a large post in the earth and fastened the forest elephant to it by the neck, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men.

mn125:12.12.verse: Then the elephant-tamer treats him with such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear, and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.

mn125:12.13.verse: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant, being treated by the elephant-tamer with such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear, and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many, is willing to hear, gives ear, and establishes his mind in knowledge,

mn125:12.14.verse: then the elephant-tamer rewards him further with grass fodder and water.

mn125:12.15.verse: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant accepts the grass fodder and water from the elephant-tamer, it occurs to the elephant-tamer thus:

mn125:12.17.verse: Then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:

mn125:12.19.verse: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to take up and put down and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:

mn125:12.21.verse: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to go forward and go back and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:

mn125:12.23.verse: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to get up and sit down and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise called imperturbability: he fastens a great shield to his trunk, a man with a lance in his hand sits on his neck, men with lances in their hands stand surrounding him on all sides, and the elephant-tamer himself stands in front of him holding a long lance pole.

mn125:12.24.verse: As he carries out the exercise of imperturbability, he moves neither his fore feet nor his hind feet, neither the fore part nor the hind part of his body, nor his head, nor his ears, nor his tusks, nor his tail, nor his trunk.

mn125:12.25.verse: The forest elephant becomes one who endures blows from spears, swords, arrows, and other weapons, and the sounds of drums, kettledrums, conches, and tabors; and being rid of all faults and defects, with flaws removed, he becomes worthy of the king, in the king’s service, and is reckoned as one of the king’s limbs.

mn125:13.1.verse: ‘So too, Aggivessana, here a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.

mn125:13.2.verse: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, its Brahmās, this generation with its monks and divines, with its princes and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.

mn125:13.3.verse: He teaches the Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he proclaims the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn125:14.1.verse: ‘A householder or a householder’s son or one born in some other clan hears that Dhamma.

mn125:14.2.verse: On hearing that Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.

mn125:14.3.verse: Possessing that faith he considers thus:

mn125:14.4.verse: “Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.

mn125:14.5.verse: It is not easy, living in a household, to lead the holy life as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.

mn125:14.6.verse: Suppose I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”

mn125:14.7.verse: On a later occasion, abandoning a small or a large fortune, abandoning a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the yellow robe, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.

mn125:14.8.verse: That is how, Aggivessana, a disciple of the Noble Ones comes into the open;

mn125:14.9.verse: for gods and men, Aggivessana, cleave to that, that is to say, the five cords of sensual desire.

mn125:15.2.verse: “Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, train by undertaking the training precepts.”

mn125:16.1.verse: ‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, trains by undertaking the training precepts, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:

mn125:16.2.verse: “Come, bhikkhu, guard the doors of the faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the eye faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear …

mn125:17-21.1.verse:
on smelling an odour with the nose … on tasting a flavour with the tongue … on touching a tangible with the body … on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the mind faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu guards the doors of the faculties, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, be one who knows the right amount in eating. Reflecting wisely, you should take food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.’”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu knows the right amount in eating, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, abide devoted to wakefulness. By day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the middle watch of the night, lie down on the right side in the lion’s pose, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, having noted in your mind the time for rising. After rising, in the third watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, possess mindfulness and full awareness. Act in full awareness when going forward and returning; act in full awareness when looking ahead and looking away; act in full awareness when flexing and extending your limbs; act in full awareness when wearing your outer cloak, bowl and robes; act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; act in full awareness when defecating and urinating; act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu possesses mindfulness and full awareness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, resort to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.”

He resorts to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw. On returning from his alms round, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness. Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred. Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness. Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled within; he purifies his mind of agitation and worry. Abandoning uncertainty, he abides having crossed beyond uncertainty, unperplexed about profitable dhammas; he purifies his mind of uncertainty.

mn125:22.1.verse: ‘Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,

mn125:22.2.verse: he abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn125:23.1.verse: He abides contemplating feelings as feelings …

mn125:23.3.verse: he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

mn125:23.4.verse: Just as, Aggivessana, the elephant-tamer embeds a large post in the earth and fastens the forest elephant to it by the neck, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men;

mn125:23.5.verse: so too, Aggivessana, these four foundations of mindfulness are the fastening for the mind of a disciple of the Noble Ones, in order to subdue his house-based habits, in order to subdue his house-based memories and intentions, in order to subdue his house-based distress, fatigue, and fever, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

mn125:24.2.verse: “Come, bhikkhu, abide contemplating the body as a body, but do not think thoughts connected with the body.

mn125:24.5.verse: abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas, but do not think thoughts connected with dhammas.”

mn125:25.1.verse: ‘With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …

mn125:25.3.verse: he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.

mn125:26.1.verse: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the recollection of past life.

mn125:26.2.verse: He recollects his manifold past life, that is to say, one birth, two births …he recollects his manifold past life with its details and particulars.

mn125:27-28.1.verse: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

mn125:27-28.2.verse: With the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved … he understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.

mn125:29.1.verse: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.

mn125:29.2.verse: He has direct knowledge thus: “This is suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.

mn125:29.3.verse: He has direct knowledge thus: “These are taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of taints”.

mn125:29.4.verse: When he knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of being, the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.

mn125:29.5.verse: When liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”

mn125:29.6.verse: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”

mn125:30.1.verse: ‘That bhikkhu becomes one who bears cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, who endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words, and who is of a nature to bear arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and menacing to life;

mn125:30.2.verse: being rid of all lust, hatred, and delusion, with flaws removed, he becomes fit for gifts, fit for hospitality, fit for offerings, fit for reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

mn125:31.1.verse: ‘If, Aggivessana, an old king’s elephant, untamed and undisciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “an untamed old king’s elephant that has died an untamed death”;

mn125:31.2.verse: if a middle-aged king’s elephant, Aggivessana …

mn125:31.3.verse: if a young king’s elephant, Aggivessana, untamed and undisciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “an untamed young king’s elephant that has died an untamed death”;

mn125:31.4.verse: so too, Aggivessana, if an elder bhikkhu with taints unexhausted dies, it is reckoned as “an elder bhikkhu who has died an untamed death”;

mn125:31.6.verse: if a new bhikkhu, Aggivessana, with taints unexhausted dies, it is reckoned as “a new bhikkhu who has died an untamed death”.

mn125:32.1.verse: ‘If, Aggivessana, an old king’s elephant, well-tamed and well-disciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “a tamed old king’s elephant that has died a tamed death”;

mn125:32.2.verse: if a middle-aged king’s elephant, Aggivessana …

mn125:32.3.verse: if a young king’s elephant, Aggivessana, well-tamed and well-disciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “a tamed young king’s elephant that has died a tamed death”;

mn125:32.4.verse: so too, Aggivessana, if an elder bhikkhu with taints exhausted dies, it is reckoned as “an elder bhikkhu who has died a tamed death”;

mn125:32.6.verse: if a new bhikkhu, Aggivessana, with taints exhausted dies, it is reckoned as “a new bhikkhu who has died a tamed death”.’

mn125:32.7.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn125:32.8.verse: The novice Aciravata was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn125:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn125:2.1.verse: Now at that time the novice Aciravata was staying in a wilderness hut.

mn125:2.2.verse: Then as Prince Jayasena was going for a walk he approached Aciravata, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn125:2.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Aciravata,

mn125:2.5.verse: a mendicant who meditates diligently, keenly, and resolutely can experience unification of mind.”

mn125:2.6.verse: “That’s so true, Prince! That’s so true!

mn125:2.7.verse: A mendicant who meditates diligently, keenly, and resolutely can experience unification of mind.”

mn125:3.1.verse: “Worthy Aggivessana, please teach me the Dhamma as you have learned and memorized it.”

mn125:3.2.verse: “I’m not competent to do so, Prince.

mn125:3.3.verse: For if I were to teach you the Dhamma as I have learned and memorized it, you might not understand the meaning, which would be wearying and troublesome for me.”

mn125:4.1.verse: “Worthy Aggivessana, please teach me the Dhamma as you have learned and memorized it.

mn125:4.2.verse: Hopefully I will understand the meaning of what you say.”

mn125:4.4.verse: If you understand the meaning of what I say, that’s good.

mn125:4.5.verse: If not, then leave each to his own, and do not question me about it further.”

mn125:4.6.verse: “Worthy Aggivessana, please teach me the Dhamma as you have learned and memorized it.

mn125:4.7.verse: If I understand the meaning of what you say, that’s good.

mn125:4.8.verse: If not, then I will leave each to his own, and not question you about it further.”

mn125:5.1.verse: Then the novice Aciravata taught Prince Jayasena the Dhamma as he had learned and memorized it.

mn125:5.2.verse: When he had spoken, Jayasena said to him,

mn125:5.3.verse: “It is impossible, worthy Aggivessana, it cannot happen that a mendicant who meditates diligently, keenly, and resolutely can experience unification of mind.”

mn125:5.4.verse: Having declared that this was impossible, Jayasena rose from his seat and left.

mn125:6.1.verse: Not long after he had left, Aciravata went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

mn125:6.2.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

mn125:7.1.verse: When he had spoken, the Buddha said to him,

mn125:7.2.verse: “How could it possibly be otherwise, Aggivessana?

mn125:7.3.verse: Prince Jayasena dwells in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, consumed by thoughts of them, burning with fever for them, and eagerly seeking more. It’s simply impossible for him to know or see or realize what can only be known, seen, and realized by renunciation.

mn125:8.1.verse: Suppose there was a pair of elephants or horse or oxen in training who were well tamed and well trained. And there was a pair who were not tamed or trained.

mn125:8.3.verse: Wouldn’t the pair that was well tamed and well trained perform the tasks of the tamed and reach the level of the tamed?”

mn125:8.5.verse: “But would the pair that was not tamed and trained perform the tasks of the tamed and reach the level of the tamed, just like the tamed pair?”

mn125:8.7.verse: “In the same way, Prince Jayasena dwells in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, consumed by thoughts of them, burning with fever for them, and eagerly seeking more. It’s simply impossible for him to know or see or realize what can only be known, seen, and realized by renunciation.

mn125:9.1.verse: Suppose there was a big mountain not far from a town or village.

mn125:9.2.verse: And two friends set out from that village or town, lending each other a hand up to the mountain. Once there, one friend would remain at the foot of the mountain, while the other would climb to the peak.

mn125:9.3.verse: The one standing at the foot would say to the one at the peak,

mn125:9.4.verse: ‘My dear, what do you see, standing there at the peak?’

mn125:9.6.verse: ‘Standing at the peak, I see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds!’

mn125:9.8.verse: ‘It’s impossible, it cannot happen that, standing at the peak, you can see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds.’

mn125:9.9.verse: So their friend would come down from the peak, take their friend by the arm, and make them climb to the peak. After giving them a while to catch their breath, they’d say,

mn125:9.10.verse: ‘My dear, what do you see, standing here at the peak?’

mn125:9.12.verse: ‘Standing at the peak, I see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds!’

mn125:9.14.verse: ‘Just now I understood you to say:

mn125:9.15.verse: “It’s impossible, it cannot happen that, standing at the peak, you can see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds.”

mn125:9.17.verse: “Standing at the peak, I see delightful parks, woods, meadows, and lotus ponds!”’

mn125:9.19.verse: ‘But my dear, it was because I was obstructed by this big mountain that I didn’t see what could be seen.’

mn125:10.1.verse: But bigger than that is the mass of ignorance by which Prince Jayasena is obstructed, hindered, engulfed, and enveloped.

mn125:10.2.verse: Prince Jayasena dwells in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, consumed by thoughts of them, burning with fever for them, and eagerly seeking more. It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize what can only be known, seen, and realized by renunciation.

mn125:11.1.verse: It would be no wonder if, had these two similes occurred to you, Prince Jayasena would have gained confidence in you and shown his confidence.”

mn125:11.2.verse: “But sir, how could these two similes have occurred to me as they did to the Buddha, since they were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past?”

mn125:12.1.verse: “Suppose, Aggivessana, an anointed aristocratic king was to address his elephant tracker,

mn125:12.2.verse: ‘Please, my good elephant tracker, mount the royal bull elephant and enter the elephant wood. When you see a wild bull elephant, tether it by the neck to the royal elephant.’

mn125:12.3.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the elephant tracker, and did as he was asked.

mn125:12.4.verse: The royal elephant leads the wild elephant out into the open;

mn125:12.5.verse: and it’s only then that it comes out into the open,

mn125:12.6.verse: for a wild bull elephant clings to the elephant wood.

mn125:12.7.verse: The elephant tracker informs the king,

mn125:12.8.verse: ‘Your Majesty, the wild elephant has come out into the open.’

mn125:12.9.verse: Then the king addresses his elephant trainer,

mn125:12.10.verse: ‘Please, dear elephant trainer, tame the wild bull elephant. Subdue its wild behaviors, its wild memories and thoughts, and its wild stress, weariness, and fever. Make it happy to be within a village, and instill behaviors congenial to humans.’

mn125:12.11.verse: ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ replied the elephant trainer. He dug a large post into the earth and tethered the elephant to it by the neck, so as to subdue its wild behaviors, its wild memories and thoughts, and its wild stress, weariness, and fever, and to make it happy to be within a village, and instill behaviors congenial to humans.

mn125:12.12.verse: He spoke in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.

mn125:12.13.verse: Spoken to in such a way by the elephant trainer, the wild elephant wanted to listen. It actively listened and tried to understand.

mn125:12.14.verse: So the elephant trainer rewards it with grass, fodder, and water.

mn125:12.15.verse: When the wild elephant accepts the grass, fodder, and water, the trainer knows,

mn125:12.17.verse: He sets it a further task:

mn125:12.18.verse: ‘Pick it up, worthy sir! Put it down, worthy sir!’

mn125:12.19.verse: When the wild elephant picks up and puts down when the trainer says, following instructions, the trainer sets it a further task:

mn125:12.21.verse: When the wild elephant goes forward and back when the trainer says, following instructions, the trainer sets it a further task:

mn125:12.23.verse: When the wild elephant stands and sits when the trainer says, following instructions, the trainer sets the task called imperturbability. He fastens a large plank to its trunk; a lancer sits on its neck; other lancers surround it on all sides; and the trainer himself stands in front with a long lance.

mn125:12.24.verse: While practicing this task, it doesn’t budge its fore-feet or hind-feet, its fore-quarters or hind-quarters, its head, ears, tusks, tail, or trunk.

mn125:12.25.verse: The wild bull elephant endures being struck by spears, swords, arrows, and axes; it endures the thunder of the drums, kettledrums, pipes, horns, and tom-toms. Rid of all crooks and flaws, and purged of defects, it is worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, and reckoned a factor of kingship.

mn125:13.1.verse: In the same way, Aggivessana, a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

mn125:13.2.verse: He realizes with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn125:13.3.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

mn125:14.1.verse: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder’s child, or someone reborn in a good family.

mn125:14.2.verse: They gain faith in the Realized One

mn125:14.4.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

mn125:14.5.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

mn125:14.6.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

mn125:14.7.verse: After some time they give up a large or small fortune, and a large or small family circle. They shave off hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

mn125:14.8.verse: And it’s only then that a noble disciple comes out into the open,

mn125:14.9.verse: for gods and humans cling to the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn125:15.1.verse: The Realized One guides them further:

mn125:15.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, be ethical and restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourself well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.’

mn125:16.1.verse: When they have ethical conduct, the Realized One guides them further:

mn125:16.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, guard your sense doors. When you see a sight with your eyes, don’t get caught up in the features and details. …

mn125:17-21.1.verse: (Tell in full as in MN 107, the Discourse with Moggallāna the Accountant.)

mn125:22.1.verse: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the heart that weaken wisdom.

mn125:22.2.verse: Then they meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn125:23.1.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

mn125:23.3.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

mn125:23.4.verse: It’s like when the elephant trainer dug a large post into the earth and tethered the elephant to it by the neck, so as to subdue its wild behaviors, its wild memories and thoughts, and its wild stress, weariness, and fever, and to make it happy to be within a village, and instill behaviors congenial to humans.

mn125:23.5.verse: In the same way, a noble disciple has these four kinds of mindfulness meditation as tethers for the mind so as to subdue behaviors tied to domestic life, memories and thoughts tied to domestic life, stress, weariness, and fever tied to domestic life, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

mn125:24.1.verse: The Realized One guides them further:

mn125:24.2.verse: ‘Come, mendicant, meditate observing an aspect of the body, but don’t think thoughts connected with sensual pleasures.

mn125:24.3.verse: Meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

mn125:24.5.verse: principles, but don’t think thoughts connected with sensual pleasures.’

mn125:25.1.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption …

mn125:26.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward recollection of past lives.

mn125:26.2.verse: They recollect many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

mn125:27-28.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.

mn125:27-28.2.verse: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

mn125:29.1.verse: When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they extend it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.

mn125:29.2.verse: They truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

mn125:29.3.verse: They truly understand: ‘These are defilements’ … ‘This is the origin of defilements’ … ‘This is the cessation of defilements’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements’.

mn125:29.4.verse: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance.

mn125:29.5.verse: When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn125:29.6.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn125:30.1.verse: Such a mendicant endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; rude and unwelcome criticism; and puts up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.

mn125:30.2.verse: Rid of all greed, hate, and delusion, and purged of defects, they are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.

mn125:31.1.verse: If a royal bull elephant—whether elderly, middle aged, or youthful—passes away untamed and untrained, they’re reckoned a royal bull elephant who passed away untamed.

mn125:31.4.verse: In the same way, if a mendicant—whether senior, middle, or junior—passes away without having ended the defilements, they’re reckoned a mendicant who passed away untamed.

mn125:32.1.verse: If a royal bull elephant—whether elderly, middle aged, or youthful—passes away tamed and trained, they’re reckoned a royal bull elephant who passed away tamed.

mn125:32.4.verse: In the same way, if a mendicant—whether senior, middle, or junior—passes away having ended the defilements, they’re reckoned a mendicant who passed away tamed.”

mn125:32.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn125:32.8.verse: Satisfied, the novice Aciravata approved what the Buddha said.

mn126:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn126:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Bhūmija robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of Prince Jayasena, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

mn126:3.1.verse: Then Jayasena approached and exchanged greetings with him.

mn126:3.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Bhūmija:

mn126:3.3.verse: “Worthy Bhūmija, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

mn126:3.4.verse: ‘If you make a wish and lead the spiritual life, you can’t win the fruit.

mn126:3.5.verse: If you don’t make a wish and lead the spiritual life, you can’t win the fruit.

mn126:3.6.verse: If you both make a wish and don’t make a wish and lead the spiritual life, you can’t win the fruit.

mn126:3.7.verse: If you neither make a wish nor don’t make a wish and lead the spiritual life, you can’t win the fruit.’

mn126:3.8.verse: What does the worthy Bhūmija’s Teacher say about this? How does he explain it?”

mn126:4.1.verse: “Prince, I haven’t heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha.

mn126:4.2.verse: But it’s possible that he might explain it like this:

mn126:4.3.verse: ‘If you lead the spiritual life irrationally, you can’t win the fruit, regardless of whether you make a wish,

mn126:4.5.verse: you both do and do not make a wish,

mn126:4.6.verse: or you neither do nor don’t make a wish.

mn126:4.7.verse: But if you lead the spiritual life rationally, you can win the fruit, regardless of whether you make a wish,

mn126:4.9.verse: you both do and do not make a wish,

mn126:4.10.verse: or you neither do nor don’t make a wish.’

mn126:4.11.verse: I haven’t heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha.

mn126:4.12.verse: But it’s possible that he might explain it like that.”

mn126:5.1.verse: “If that’s what your teacher says, worthy Bhūmija, he clearly stands head and shoulders above all the various other ascetics and brahmins.”

mn126:6.1.verse: Then Prince Jayasena served Venerable Bhūmija from his own dish.

mn126:7.1.verse: Then after the meal, on his return from almsround, Bhūmija went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him all that had happened, adding:

mn126:7.25.verse: “Answering this way, I trust that I repeated what the Buddha has said, and didn’t misrepresent him with an untruth. I trust my explanation was in line with the teaching, and that there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.”

mn126:8.1.verse: “Indeed, Bhūmija, in answering this way you repeated what I’ve said, and didn’t misrepresent me with an untruth. Your explanation was in line with the teaching, and there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.

mn126:9.1.verse: There are some ascetics and brahmins who have wrong view, wrong purpose, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion. If they lead the spiritual life, they can’t win the fruit, regardless of whether they make a wish,

mn126:9.3.verse: they both do and do not make a wish,

mn126:9.4.verse: or they neither do nor don’t make a wish.

mn126:9.6.verse: Because that’s an irrational way to win the fruit.

mn126:10.1.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of oil. While wandering in search of oil, they tried heaping sand in a bucket, sprinkling it little by little with water, and pressing it out.

mn126:10.2.verse: But by doing this, they couldn’t extract any oil, regardless of whether they made a wish,

mn126:10.4.verse: both did and did not make a wish,

mn126:10.5.verse: or neither did nor did not make a wish.

mn126:10.7.verse: Because that’s an irrational way to extract oil.

mn126:10.8.verse: And so it is for any ascetics and brahmins who have wrong view, wrong purpose, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion. If they lead the spiritual life, they can’t win the fruit, regardless of whether or not they make a wish.

mn126:10.13.verse: Because that’s an irrational way to win the fruit.

mn126:19.1.verse: Bhūmija, it would be no wonder if, had these four similes occurred to you, Prince Jayasena would have gained confidence in you and shown his confidence.”

mn126:19.2.verse: “But sir, how could these four similes have occurred to me as they did to the Buddha, since they were neither supernaturally inspired, nor learned before in the past?”

mn126:19.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn126:19.4.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Bhūmija approved what the Buddha said.

mn126:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn126:2.1.verse: Then, when it was morning, the venerable Bhūmija dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went to the house of Prince Jayasena and sat down on a seat made ready.

mn126:3.1.verse: Then Prince Jayasena went to the venerable Bhūmija and exchanged greetings with him.

mn126:3.2.verse: When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side and said to the venerable Bhūmija:

mn126:3.3.verse: “Master Bhūmija, there are some recluses and brahmins who make such assertions and hold such views as this:

mn126:3.4.verse: ‘If one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:3.5.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:3.6.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:3.7.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit.’

mn126:3.8.verse: What does the venerable Bhūmija’s teacher say here, what does he declare?”

mn126:4.1.verse: “I have not heard and learned that from the Blessed One’s own lips, prince.

mn126:4.2.verse: But it is possible that the Blessed One might say this:

mn126:4.3.verse: ‘If one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:4.4.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:4.5.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:4.6.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit.

mn126:4.7.verse: However, if one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is able to procure fruit;

mn126:4.8.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit;

mn126:4.9.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit;

mn126:4.10.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit.’

mn126:4.11.verse: I have not heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips, prince,

mn126:4.12.verse: but it is possible that the Blessed One would answer as I have stated.”

mn126:5.1.verse: “If Master Bhūmija’s teacher speaks thus, if he declares thus, then it certainly seems that the venerable Bhūmija’s teacher stands ahead of all the ordinary recluses and brahmins.”

mn126:6.1.verse: Then Prince Jayasena served the venerable Bhūmija from his own dish of milk rice.

mn126:7.1.verse: Then, when the venerable Bhūmija had returned from his almsround after his meal, he went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Bhūmija said to the Blessed One:

mn126:7.2.verse: “Venerable sir, this morning I dressed, and taking my bowl and outer robe, went to the house of Prince Jayasena and sat down on a seat made ready.

mn126:7.3.verse: Then, venerable sir, Prince Jayasena came to me and exchanged greetings with me.

mn126:7.4.verse: When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, venerable sir, Prince Jayasena said to me:

mn126:7.5.verse: ‘Master Bhūmija, there are some recluses and brahmins who make such assertions and hold such views as this—

mn126:7.6.verse: if one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.7.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.8.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.9.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life, one is still unable to procure any fruit.’

mn126:7.10.verse: ‘What does the venerable Bhūmija’s teacher say here, what does he declare?’

mn126:7.11.verse: When this was said, venerable sir, I said to Prince Jayasena:

mn126:7.12.verse: ‘I have not heard and learned that from the Blessed One’s own lips, prince.

mn126:7.13.verse: But it is possible that the Blessed One might say this—

mn126:7.14.verse: if one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.15.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.16.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:7.17.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life unwisely, one is still unable to procure any fruit.

mn126:7.18.verse: However, if one makes an aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is able to procure fruit;

mn126:7.19.verse: if one makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit;

mn126:7.20.verse: if one both makes an aspiration and makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit;

mn126:7.21.verse: if one neither makes an aspiration nor makes no aspiration and one leads the holy life wisely, one is still able to procure fruit.’

mn126:7.22.verse: I have not heard and learned this from the Blessed One’s own lips, prince,

mn126:7.23.verse: but it is possible that the Blessed One would answer as I have stated.’

mn126:7.24.verse: ‘If Master Bhūmija’s teacher speaks thus, if he declares thus, then it certainly seems that the venerable Bhūmija’s teacher stands ahead of all the ordinary recluses and brahmins.’

mn126:7.25.verse: Venerable sir, I hope that when I was asked such a question and answered thus, I said what has been said by the Blessed One and did not misrepresent him with what is contrary to fact. I hope I explained in accordance with the Dhamma in such a way that nothing which provides a ground for censure can be legitimately deduced from my assertion.”

mn126:8.1.verse: “Surely, Bhūmija, when you were asked such a question and answered thus, you said what has been said by me and did not misrepresent me with what is contrary to fact. You explained in accordance with the Dhamma in such a way that nothing which provides a ground for censure can be legitimately deduced from your assertion.

mn126:9.1.verse: “Whatever recluses and brahmins have wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration, if they make an aspiration and they lead the holy life, they are unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:9.2.verse: if they make no aspiration and they lead the holy life, they are still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:9.3.verse: if they both make an aspiration and make no aspiration and they lead the holy life, they are still unable to procure any fruit;

mn126:9.4.verse: if they neither make an aspiration nor make no aspiration and they lead the holy life, they are still unable to procure any fruit.

mn126:9.6.verse: Because that [wrong path] is not a proper method for procuring fruit.

mn126:19.1.verse: “Bhūmija, if these four similes had occurred to you [with reference] to Prince Jayasena, he would have spontaneously acquired confidence in you, and being confident, would have shown his confidence to you.”

mn126:19.2.verse: “Venerable sir, how could these four similes have occurred to me [with reference] to Prince Jayasena as they occur to the Blessed One, since they are spontaneous and have never been heard before?”

mn126:19.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn126:19.4.verse: The venerable Bhūmija was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn127:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn127:2.1.verse: And then the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga addressed a man,

mn127:2.2.verse: “Please, my man, go to Venerable Anuruddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him,

mn127:2.3.verse: ‘Sir, the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga bows with his head to your feet.’

mn127:2.4.verse: And then ask him whether he

mn127:2.5.verse: would please accept tomorrow’s meal from Pañcakaṅga together with the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn127:2.6.verse: And ask whether he might please come earlier than usual,

mn127:2.7.verse: for Pañcakaṅga has many duties, and much work to do for the king.”

mn127:2.8.verse: “Yes, sir,” that man replied. He did as Pañcakaṅga asked, and

mn127:3.1.verse: Then when the night had passed, Anuruddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Pañcakaṅga’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

mn127:3.2.verse: Then Pañcakaṅga served and satisfied Anuruddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

mn127:3.3.verse: When Anuruddha had eaten and washed his hands and bowl, Pañcakaṅga took a low seat, sat to one side,

mn127:4.1.verse: “Sir, some senior mendicants have come to me and said,

mn127:4.2.verse: ‘Householder, develop the limitless release of the heart.’

mn127:4.4.verse: ‘Householder, develop the expansive release of the heart.’

mn127:4.5.verse: Now, the limitless release of the heart and the expansive release of the heart:

mn127:4.6.verse: do these things differ in both meaning and phrasing? Or do they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?”

mn127:5.1.verse: “Well then, householder, let me know what you think about this. Afterwards, it’s a sure bet that you’ll get it.”

mn127:5.3.verse: The limitless release of the heart and the expansive release of the heart mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.”

mn127:6.1.verse: “The limitless release of the heart and the expansive release of the heart differ in both meaning and phrasing.

mn127:6.2.verse: This is a way to understand how these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

mn127:7.1.verse: And what is the limitless release of the heart?

mn127:7.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn127:7.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

mn127:7.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

mn127:7.5.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

mn127:7.6.verse: This is called the limitless release of the heart.

mn127:8.1.verse: And what is the expansive release of the heart?

mn127:8.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates focused on pervading the extent of a single tree root as expansive.

mn127:8.3.verse: This is called the expansive release of the heart.

mn127:8.4.verse: Also, a mendicant meditates focused on pervading the extent of two or three tree roots …

mn127:8.15.verse: This too is called the expansive release of the heart.

mn127:8.16.verse: This is a way to understand how these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

mn127:9.1.verse: Householder, there are these four kinds of rebirth in a future life.

mn127:9.3.verse: Take someone who meditates focused on pervading ‘limited luminosity’.

mn127:9.4.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of limited luminosity.

mn127:9.5.verse: Next, take someone who meditates focused on pervading ‘limitless luminosity’.

mn127:9.6.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of limitless luminosity.

mn127:9.7.verse: Next, take someone who meditates focused on pervading ‘corrupted radiance’.

mn127:9.8.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of corrupted luminosity.

mn127:9.9.verse: Next, take someone who meditates focused on pervading ‘pure radiance’.

mn127:9.10.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of pure luminosity.

mn127:9.11.verse: These are the four kinds of rebirth in a future life.

mn127:10.1.verse: There comes a time, householder, when the deities gather together as one. When they do so, a difference in their color is evident, but not in their luminosity.

mn127:10.2.verse: It’s like when a person brings several oil lamps into one house.

mn127:10.3.verse: You can detect a difference in their flames, but not in their radiance.

mn127:10.4.verse: In the same way, when the deities gather together as one, a difference in their color is evident, but not in their luminosity.

mn127:11.1.verse: There comes a time when those deities go their separate ways. When they do so, a difference both in their color and also in their luminosity is evident.

mn127:11.2.verse: It’s like when a person takes those several oil lamps out of that house.

mn127:11.3.verse: You can detect a difference both in their flames and also in their radiance.

mn127:11.4.verse: In the same way, when the deities go their separate ways, a difference both in their color and also in their luminosity is evident.

mn127:12.1.verse: It’s not that those deities think,

mn127:12.2.verse: ‘What we have is permanent, lasting, and eternal.’ Rather, wherever those deities cling, that’s where they take pleasure.

mn127:12.3.verse: It’s like when flies are being carried along on a carrying-pole or basket. It’s not that they think,

mn127:12.4.verse: ‘What we have is permanent, lasting, and eternal.’ Rather, wherever those flies cling, that’s where they take pleasure.

mn127:12.5.verse: In the same way, it’s not that those deities think,

mn127:12.6.verse: ‘What we have is permanent, lasting, and eternal.’ Rather, wherever those deities cling, that’s where they take pleasure.”

mn127:13.1.verse: When he had spoken, Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said to Venerable Anuruddha:

mn127:13.3.verse: I have a further question about this.

mn127:13.4.verse: Do all the radiant deities have limited luminosity, or do some there have limitless luminosity?”

mn127:13.5.verse: “In that respect, Reverend Kaccāna, some deities there have limited luminosity, while some have limitless luminosity.”

mn127:14.1.verse: “What is the cause, Honorable Anuruddha, what is the reason why, when those deities have been reborn in a single order of gods, some deities there have limited luminosity, while some have limitless luminosity?”

mn127:14.2.verse: “Well then, Reverend Kaccāna, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

mn127:14.3.verse: What do you think, Reverend Kaccāna?

mn127:14.4.verse: Which of these two kinds of mental development is more expansive: when a mendicant meditates focused on pervading as expansive the extent of a single tree root, or two or three tree roots?”

mn127:14.6.verse: “When a mendicant meditates on two or three tree roots.”

mn127:14.9.verse: Which of these two kinds of mental development is more expansive: when a mendicant meditates focused on pervading as expansive the extent of two or three tree roots, or a single village district …

mn127:14.27.verse: “When a mendicant meditates on this land surrounded by ocean.”

mn127:14.29.verse: “This is the cause, Reverend Kaccāna, this is the reason why, when those deities have been reborn in a single order of gods, some deities there have limited luminosity, while some have limitless luminosity.”

mn127:15.2.verse: I have a further question about this.

mn127:15.3.verse: Do all the radiant deities have corrupted radiance, or do some there have pure radiance?”

mn127:15.4.verse: “In that respect, Reverend Kaccāna, some deities there have corrupted radiance, while some have pure radiance.”

mn127:16.1.verse: “What is the cause, Honorable Anuruddha, what is the reason why, when those deities have been reborn in a single order of gods, some deities there have corrupted radiance, while some have pure radiance?”

mn127:16.2.verse: “Well then, Reverend Kaccāna, I shall give you a simile.

mn127:16.3.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

mn127:16.4.verse: Suppose an oil lamp was burning with impure oil and impure wick.

mn127:16.5.verse: Because of the impurity of the oil and the wick it burns dimly, as it were.

mn127:16.6.verse: In the same way, take some mendicant who meditates focused on pervading ‘corrupted radiance’.

mn127:16.7.verse: Their physical discomfort is not completely settled, their dullness and drowsiness is not completely eradicated, and their restlessness and remorse are not completely eliminated.

mn127:16.8.verse: Because of this they practice absorption dimly, as it were.

mn127:16.9.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of corrupted luminosity.

mn127:16.10.verse: Suppose an oil lamp was burning with pure oil and pure wick.

mn127:16.11.verse: Because of the purity of the oil and the wick it doesn’t burn dimly, as it were.

mn127:16.12.verse: In the same way, take some mendicant who meditates focused on pervading ‘pure radiance’.

mn127:16.13.verse: Their physical discomfort is completely settled, their dullness and drowsiness is completely eradicated, and their restlessness and remorse is completely eliminated.

mn127:16.14.verse: Because of this they don’t practice absorption dimly, as it were.

mn127:16.15.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of the gods of pure luminosity.

mn127:16.16.verse: This is the cause, Reverend Kaccāna, this is the reason why, when those deities have been reborn in a single order of gods, some deities there have corrupted radiance, while some have pure radiance.”

mn127:17.1.verse: When he had spoken, Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said to Venerable Anuruddha,

mn127:17.4.verse: ‘So I have heard’ or ‘It ought to be like this.’

mn127:17.5.verse: Rather, you say: ‘These deities are like this, those deities are like that.’

mn127:17.7.verse: ‘Clearly, Venerable Anuruddha has previously lived together with those deities, conversed, and engaged in discussion.’”

mn127:17.8.verse: “Your words are clearly invasive and intrusive, Reverend Kaccāna.

mn127:17.10.verse: For a long time I have previously lived together with those deities, conversed, and engaged in discussion.”

mn127:18.1.verse: When he had spoken, Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said to Pañcakaṅga the chamberlain,

mn127:18.3.verse: to have given up your state of uncertainty, and to have got the chance to listen to this exposition of the teaching.”

mn127:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn127:2.1.verse: Then the carpenter Pañcakanga addressed a certain man thus:

mn127:2.2.verse: “Come, good man, go to the venerable Anuruddha, pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and say:

mn127:2.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the carpenter Pañcakanga pays homage with his head at the venerable Anuruddha’s feet’;

mn127:2.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, let the venerable Anuruddha with three others consent to accept tomorrow’s meal from the carpenter Pañcakanga;

mn127:2.6.verse: and let the venerable Anuruddha arrive punctually,

mn127:2.7.verse: as the carpenter Pañcakanga is very busy and has much work to do for the king.’”

mn127:2.8.verse: “Yes, sir,” that man replied, and he went to the venerable Anuruddha. After paying homage to the venerable Anuruddha, he sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, that man said to the venerable Anuruddha:

mn127:2.9.verse: “Venerable sir, the carpenter Pañcakanga pays homage with his head at the venerable Anuruddha’s feet, and says this:

mn127:2.10.verse: ‘Venerable sir, let the venerable Anuruddha with three others consent to accept tomorrow’s meal from the carpenter Pañcakanga;

mn127:2.11.verse: and let the venerable Anuruddha arrive punctually,

mn127:2.12.verse: as the carpenter Pañcakanga is very busy and has much work to do for the king.’”

mn127:2.13.verse: The venerable Anuruddha consented in silence.

mn127:3.1.verse: Then, when the night had ended, it being morning, the venerable Anuruddha dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went to the carpenter Pañcakanga’s house and sat down on a seat made ready.

mn127:3.2.verse: Then, with his own hands, the carpenter Pañcakanga served and satisfied the venerable Anuruddha with the various kinds of good food.

mn127:3.3.verse: Then, when the venerable Anuruddha had eaten and had put his bowl aside, the carpenter Pañcakanga took a low seat and sat down at one side.

mn127:3.4.verse: As he was sitting there, the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the venerable Anuruddha:

mn127:4.1.verse: “Here, venerable sir, elder bhikkhus have come to me and said:

mn127:4.2.verse: ‘Householder, develop the immeasurable deliverance of mind’;

mn127:4.4.verse: ‘Householder, develop the exalted deliverance of mind.’

mn127:4.5.verse: Venerable sir, the immeasurable deliverance of mind and the exalted deliverance of mind—

mn127:4.6.verse: are these states different in meaning and different in name, or are they one in meaning and different only in name?”

mn127:5.1.verse: “Explain it as you see it, householder. Afterwards it will be cleared up for you.”

mn127:5.3.verse: ‘the immeasurable deliverance of mind and the exalted deliverance of mind—these states are one in meaning and different only in name.’”

mn127:6.1.verse: “Householder, the immeasurable deliverance of mind and the exalted deliverance of mind—these states are different in meaning and different in name.

mn127:6.2.verse: And it should be understood as follows how these states are different in meaning and different in name.

mn127:7.1.verse: “What, householder, is the immeasurable deliverance of mind?

mn127:7.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will.

mn127:7.3.verse: He abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion…

mn127:7.4.verse: with a mind imbued with altruistic joy…

mn127:7.5.verse: he abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will.

mn127:7.6.verse: This is called the immeasurable deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.1.verse: “And what, householder, is the exalted deliverance of mind?

mn127:8.2.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the root of one tree, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.3.verse: this is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.4.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the roots of two or three trees, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.5.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.6.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one village, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.7.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.8.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three villages, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.9.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.10.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one major kingdom, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.11.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.12.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three major kingdoms, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.13.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.14.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the earth bounded by the ocean, pervading it as exalted:

mn127:8.15.verse: this too is called the exalted deliverance of mind.

mn127:8.16.verse: It is in this way, householder, that it can be understood how these states are different in meaning and different in name.

mn127:9.1.verse: “There are, householder, these four kinds of reappearance [in a future state of] being.

mn127:9.3.verse: Here someone abides resolved upon and pervading ‘limited radiance’;

mn127:9.4.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Limited Radiance.

mn127:9.5.verse: Here someone abides resolved upon and pervading ‘immeasurable radiance’;

mn127:9.6.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Immeasurable Radiance.

mn127:9.7.verse: Here someone abides resolved upon and pervading ‘defiled radiance’;

mn127:9.8.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Defiled Radiance.

mn127:9.9.verse: Here someone abides resolved upon and pervading ‘pure radiance’;

mn127:9.10.verse: on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Pure Radiance.

mn127:9.11.verse: These are the four kinds of reappearance [in a future state of] being.

mn127:10.1.verse: “There is an occasion, householder, when those deities assemble in one place. When they have assembled in one place, a difference in their colour can be discerned but no difference in their radiance.

mn127:10.2.verse: Just as, if a man were to bring several oil-lamps into a house,

mn127:10.3.verse: a difference in the flames of the lamps might be discerned but no difference in their radiance;

mn127:10.4.verse: so too, there is an occasion when those deities assemble in one place…but no difference in their radiance.

mn127:11.1.verse: “There is an occasion, householder, when those deities disperse from there. When they have dispersed, a difference in their colours can be discerned and also a difference in their radiance.

mn127:11.2.verse: Just as, if the man were to remove those several oil-lamps from that house,

mn127:11.3.verse: a difference might be discerned in the flames of the lamps and also a difference in their radiance;

mn127:11.4.verse: so too, there is an occasion when those deities disperse from there…and also a difference in their radiance.

mn127:12.1.verse: “It does not occur to those deities:

mn127:12.2.verse: ‘This [life] of ours is permanent, everlasting, and eternal,’ yet wherever those deities settle down, there they find delight.

mn127:12.3.verse: Just as, when flies are being carried along on a carrying-pole or on a basket, it does not occur to them:

mn127:12.4.verse: ‘This [life] of ours is permanent, everlasting, or eternal,’ yet wherever those flies settle down, there they find delight;

mn127:12.5.verse: so too, it does not occur to those deities:

mn127:12.6.verse: ‘This [life] of ours is permanent, everlasting, or eternal,’ yet wherever they settle down, there they find delight.”

mn127:13.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Abhiya Kaccāna said to the venerable Anuruddha:

mn127:13.3.verse: yet I have something further to ask:

mn127:13.4.verse: Are all those radiant ones deities of Limited Radiance, or are some of them deities of Immeasurable Radiance?”

mn127:13.5.verse: “By reason of the factor [responsible for rebirth], friend Kaccāna, some are deities of Limited Radiance, some deities of Immeasurable Radiance.”

mn127:14.1.verse: “Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause and reason why among those deities that have reappeared in a single order of gods, some are deities of Limited Radiance, some deities of Immeasurable Radiance?”

mn127:14.2.verse: “As to that, friend Kaccāna, I shall ask you a question in return. Answer it as you choose.

mn127:14.3.verse: What do you think, friend Kaccāna?

mn127:14.4.verse: When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the root of one tree, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon the area the size of the roots of two or three trees, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.5.verse: which of these types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.6.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of the roots of two or three trees, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.7.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.9.verse: When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the roots of two or three trees, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one village, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.10.verse: which of these two types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.11.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of one village, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.12.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.13.verse: “What do you think, friend Kaccāna? When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one village, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three villages, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.14.verse: which of these two types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.15.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three villages, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.16.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.17.verse: “What do you think, friend Kaccāna? When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three villages, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one major kingdom, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.18.verse: which of these two types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.19.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of one major kingdom, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.20.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.21.verse: “What do you think, friend Kaccāna? When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of one major kingdom, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three major kingdoms, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.22.verse: which of these two types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.23.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three major kingdoms, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.24.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.25.verse: “What do you think, friend Kaccāna? When one bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of two or three major kingdoms, pervading it as exalted, and another bhikkhu abides resolved upon an area the size of the earth bounded by the ocean, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.26.verse: which of these two types of mental development is more exalted?”

mn127:14.27.verse: “The bhikkhu who abides resolved upon an area the size of the earth bounded by the ocean, pervading it as exalted—

mn127:14.28.verse: this development of mind is more exalted of the two.”

mn127:14.29.verse: “This is the cause and reason, friend Kaccāna, why among those deities that have reappeared in a single order of gods, some are deities of Limited Radiance, some deities of Immeasurable Radiance.”

mn127:15.2.verse: yet I have something further to ask:

mn127:15.3.verse: Are all those radiant ones deities of Defiled Radiance, or are some of them deities of Pure Radiance?”

mn127:15.4.verse: “By reason of the factor [responsible for rebirth], friend Kaccāna, some are deities of Defiled Radiance, some deities of Pure Radiance.”

mn127:16.1.verse: “Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause and reason why among those deities that have reappeared in a single order of gods, some are deities of Defiled Radiance, some deities of Pure Radiance?”

mn127:16.2.verse: “As to that, friend Kaccāna, I shall give a simile,

mn127:16.3.verse: for some wise men here understand the meaning of a statement by means of a simile.

mn127:16.4.verse: Suppose an oil-lamp is burning with impure oil and an impure wick;

mn127:16.5.verse: because of the impurity of its oil and its wick it burns dimly.

mn127:16.6.verse: So too, here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon and pervading [an area with] a defiled radiance.

mn127:16.7.verse: His bodily inertia has not fully subsided, his sloth and torpor have not been fully eliminated, his restlessness and remorse have not been fully removed;

mn127:16.8.verse: because of this he meditates, as it were, dimly.

mn127:16.9.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Defiled Radiance.

mn127:16.10.verse: Suppose an oil-lamp is burning with pure oil and a pure wick;

mn127:16.11.verse: because of the purity of its oil and its wick it does not burn dimly.

mn127:16.12.verse: So too, here a bhikkhu abides resolved upon and pervading [an area with] a pure radiance.

mn127:16.13.verse: His bodily inertia has fully subsided, his sloth and torpor have been fully eliminated, his restlessness and remorse have been fully removed;

mn127:16.14.verse: because of this he meditates, as it were, brightly.

mn127:16.15.verse: On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the gods of Pure Radiance.

mn127:16.16.verse: This is the cause and reason, friend Kaccāna, why among those deities that have reappeared in the same order of gods, some are deities of Defiled Radiance, some deities of Pure Radiance.”

mn127:17.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Abhiya Kaccāna said to the venerable Anuruddha:

mn127:17.3.verse: The venerable Anuruddha does not say:

mn127:17.4.verse: ‘Thus have I heard’ or ‘It should be thus.’

mn127:17.5.verse: Rather, the venerable Anuruddha says: ‘These gods are thus and those gods are such.’

mn127:17.6.verse: It occurs to me, venerable sir, that

mn127:17.7.verse: the venerable Anuruddha certainly has previously associated with those deities and talked with them and held conversations with them.”

mn127:17.8.verse: “Certainly, friend Kaccāna, your words are offensive and discourteous,

mn127:17.9.verse: but still I will answer you:

mn127:17.10.verse: ‘Over a long time I have previously associated with those deities and talked with them and held conversations with them.’”

mn127:18.1.verse: When this was said, the venerable Abhiya Kaccāna said to the carpenter Pañcakanga:

mn127:18.2.verse: “It is a gain for you, householder, it is a great gain for you

mn127:18.3.verse: that you have abandoned your state of doubt and have had the opportunity to hear this discourse on the Dhamma.”

mn128:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Kosambī, in Ghosita’s Park.

mn128:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion the bhikkhus at Kosambī had taken to quarrelling and brawling, and were deep in disputes, stabbing each other with verbal daggers.

mn128:3.1.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he stood at one side. Standing at one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

mn128:3.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, here at Kosambī the bhikkhus have taken to quarrelling and brawling, and are deep in disputes, stabbing each other with verbal daggers.

mn128:3.3.verse: Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One went to those bhikkhus out of compassion.’

mn128:3.4.verse: The Blessed One consented in silence.

mn128:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One went to those bhikkhus and said to them:

mn128:4.2.verse: ‘Enough, bhikkhus, no quarrelling, no brawling, no wrangling, no disputing.’

mn128:4.3.verse: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

mn128:4.4.verse: ‘Let the Blessed One wait, venerable sir.

mn128:4.5.verse: The Blessed One is lord of the Dhamma;

mn128:4.6.verse: let the Blessed One, venerable sir, abide inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding here and now;

mn128:4.7.verse: it is we who shall be known for this quarrelling, brawling, wrangling, and disputing.’

mn128:4.8.verse: For the second time the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:

mn128:4.9.verse: ‘Enough, bhikkhus, no quarrelling, no brawling, no wrangling, no disputing.’

mn128:4.10.verse: For the second time that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

mn128:4.11.verse: ‘Let the Blessed One wait, venerable sir.

mn128:4.12.verse: The Blessed One is lord of the Dhamma;

mn128:4.13.verse: let the Blessed One, venerable sir, abide inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding here and now;

mn128:4.14.verse: it is we who shall be known for this quarrelling, brawling, wrangling, and disputing.’

mn128:4.15.verse: For the third time the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:

mn128:4.16.verse: ‘Enough, bhikkhus, no quarrelling, no brawling, no wrangling, no disputing.’

mn128:4.17.verse: For the third time that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:

mn128:4.18.verse: ‘Let the Blessed One wait, venerable sir.

mn128:4.19.verse: The Blessed One is lord of the Dhamma;

mn128:4.20.verse: let the Blessed One, venerable sir, abide inactive, devoted to a pleasant abiding here and now;

mn128:4.21.verse: it is we who shall be known for this quarrelling, brawling, wrangling, and disputing.’

mn128:5.1.verse: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Kosambī for alms.

mn128:5.2.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Kosambī and had returned from his alms round, after his meal he set his resting place in order, and taking his bowl and outer robe, he uttered these stanzas while standing:

mn128:6.2.verse: there is none thinks himself a fool;

mn128:6.3.verse: the Saṅgha being split, none thinks

mn128:6.4.verse: “I too took part, I helped in this.”

mn128:6.5.verse: They have forgotten wise speech, they talk

mn128:6.6.verse: with minds obsessed by words alone;

mn128:6.7.verse: uncurbed their mouths, they bawl at will;

mn128:6.8.verse: none knows what leads him so to do.

mn128:6.10.verse: he worsted me, he robbed me!”

mn128:6.11.verse: Hate is never allayed in men

mn128:6.14.verse: he worsted me, he robbed me!”

mn128:6.15.verse: Hate is surely allayed in men

mn128:6.18.verse: is never in this world allayed.

mn128:6.22.verse: that here we should restrain ourselves;

mn128:6.23.verse: but those who do recognize this—

mn128:6.27.verse: while bent on pillaging the realm,

mn128:6.28.verse: even these can act in concord;

mn128:6.29.verse: so why can you not do so too?

mn128:6.30.verse: If you can find a trustworthy companion

mn128:6.31.verse: with whom to walk, both virtuous and steadfast,

mn128:6.32.verse: then walk with him content and mindfully,

mn128:6.34.verse: If you can find no trustworthy companion

mn128:6.35.verse: with whom to walk, both virtuous and steadfast,

mn128:6.36.verse: then, as a king who leaves a vanquished kingdom,

mn128:6.37.verse: walk like a tusker in the woods alone.

mn128:6.38.verse: Better it is to walk alone,

mn128:6.39.verse: there is no fellowship with fools.

mn128:6.40.verse: Walk alone, harm none, and know no conflict;

mn128:6.41.verse: be like a tusker in the woods alone.’

mn128:7.1.verse: Then, having uttered these stanzas standing, the Blessed One went to Bālakaloṇakāra village.

mn128:7.2.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Bhagu was living at Bālakaloṇakāra village.

mn128:7.3.verse: The venerable Bhagu saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

mn128:7.4.verse: Seeing him, he prepared a seat and water for the feet.

mn128:7.5.verse: The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared.

mn128:7.6.verse: Having sat down, he washed his feet.

mn128:7.7.verse: The venerable Bhagu paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

mn128:7.8.verse: When he had done so, the Blessed One said to the venerable Bhagu:

mn128:7.9.verse: ‘I hope that you are keeping well, bhikkhu, that you are comfortable, and that you have no trouble on account of alms-food?’

mn128:7.10.verse: ‘I am keeping well, Blessed One, I am comfortable, and I have no trouble on account of alms-food.’

mn128:7.11.verse: Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged the venerable Bhagu with talk on the Dhamma, after which he got up from his seat and went to the Eastern Bamboo Park.

mn128:8.1.verse: Now on that occasion the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila were living at the Eastern Bamboo Park.

mn128:8.2.verse: The park-keeper saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

mn128:8.3.verse: Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One:

mn128:8.4.verse: ‘Do not enter this park, great ascetic.

mn128:8.5.verse: There are three clansmen here seeking their own good.

mn128:9.1.verse: The venerable Anuruddha heard the park-keeper conversing with the Blessed One.

mn128:9.2.verse: Hearing this, he said to the park-keeper:

mn128:9.3.verse: ‘Friend park-keeper, do not keep the Blessed One out.

mn128:9.4.verse: It is our Teacher, the Blessed One, who has arrived.’

mn128:10.1.verse: Then the venerable Anuruddha went to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila and said to them:

mn128:10.2.verse: ‘Come out, venerable sirs, come out! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.’

mn128:10.3.verse: Then the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila went to meet the Blessed One,

mn128:10.4.verse: and one took his bowl and outer robe, one prepared a seat, and one placed water for washing the feet.

mn128:10.5.verse: The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared.

mn128:10.6.verse: Having sat down, he washed his feet.

mn128:10.7.verse: Then those venerable ones paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

mn128:10.8.verse: When they had done so, the Blessed One said to the venerable Anuruddha:

mn128:10.9.verse: ‘I hope that you are all keeping well, Anuruddha, that you are comfortable, and that you have no trouble on account of alms-food?’

mn128:10.10.verse: ‘We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are comfortable, and we have no trouble on account of alms-food.’

mn128:11.1.verse: ‘I hope that you all live in concord and agreement, Anuruddha, as undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?’

mn128:11.2.verse: ‘Surely we do so, venerable sir, we live in concord and agreement, as undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.’

mn128:11.3.verse: ‘But, Anuruddha, how do you live thus, in concord and agreement, as undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?’

mn128:12.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, as to that, I think thus:

mn128:12.2.verse: “It is gain for me, it is great gain for me
