mn128:12.3.verse: that I am living with such companions in the holy life.”

mn128:12.4.verse: I maintain bodily acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private,

mn128:12.5.verse: I maintain verbal acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private,

mn128:12.6.verse: I maintain mental acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private.

mn128:12.8.verse: “Why should I not set aside what I am minded to do and do only what these venerable ones are minded to do?”

mn128:12.9.verse: And I set aside what I am minded to do, venerable sir, and I do only what these venerable ones are minded to do.

mn128:12.10.verse: We are different in body, venerable sir, but only one in mind, I think.’

mn128:12.12.verse: and the venerable Kimbila said to the Blessed One:

mn128:12.14.verse: “It is gain for me, it is great gain for me

mn128:12.15.verse: that I am living with such companions in the holy life.”

mn128:12.16.verse: I maintain bodily acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private,

mn128:12.17.verse: I maintain verbal acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private,

mn128:12.18.verse: I maintain mental acts of loving-kindness towards these venerable ones, in public and in private.

mn128:12.20.verse: “Why should I not set aside what I am minded to do and do only what these venerable ones are minded to do?”

mn128:12.21.verse: And I set aside what I am minded to do, venerable sir, and I do only what these venerable ones are minded to do.

mn128:12.22.verse: We are different in body, venerable sir, but only one in mind, I think.

mn128:12.23.verse: That is how we live in concord, venerable sir, as undisputing as milk with water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.’

mn128:13.2.verse: I hope that you all dwell diligent, ardent, and self-controlled?’

mn128:14.2.verse: ‘But, Anuruddha, how do you dwell thus, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled?’

mn128:14.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, as to that, whichever of us returns first from the village with alms-food prepares the seats, sets out the water for drinking and for washing, and puts the refuse bucket in its place.

mn128:14.4.verse: Whichever of us returns last from the village with alms-food eats any food left over, if he wishes; if he does not wish to, he throws it away where there is no greenery, or he drops it into water where there is no life.

mn128:14.5.verse: He puts away the seats, he puts away the water for drinking and for washing, he puts away the refuse bucket after washing it, and he sweeps out the refectory.

mn128:14.6.verse: Whoever notices that the pot of drinking water or the pot of washing water or the pot for the privy is low or empty sees to it.

mn128:14.7.verse: If it is too heavy for him, he calls someone else by a sign of the hand, and they move it by joining hands; but we do not speak for that purpose, venerable sir.

mn128:14.8.verse: And every five days, venerable sir, we sit out the whole night together in talk on the Dhamma.

mn128:14.9.verse: That is how we dwell diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, venerable sir.’

mn128:15.2.verse: But, Anuruddha, while dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, have you attained as a comfortable abiding any distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision, higher than the human dhamma?’

mn128:15.3.verse: ‘As to that, venerable sir, we, while dwelling diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, perceive both illumination and the vision of forms.

mn128:15.4.verse: But that illumination of ours soon disappears, and so does the vision of forms;

mn128:15.5.verse: and we have not penetrated the sign for that.’

mn128:16.1.verse: ‘Still, Anuruddha, that sign should be penetrated by you.

mn128:16.2.verse: I too, Anuruddha, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, perceived both illumination and the vision of forms.

mn128:16.3.verse: But that illumination of mine soon disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:16.5.verse: “What is the reason, what is the condition, why this illumination of mine and the vision of forms disappears?”

mn128:16.7.verse: “Uncertainty arose in me, and owing to uncertainty my concentration died away.

mn128:16.8.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:16.9.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again.”

mn128:17.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt, Anuruddha, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, I perceived illumination and the vision of forms.

mn128:17.2.verse: But that illumination of mine soon disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:17.4.verse: “What is the reason, what is the condition, why this illumination of mine and the vision of forms disappears?”

mn128:17.6.verse: “Inattention arose in me, and owing to inattention my concentration died away.

mn128:17.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:17.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention.”

mn128:18.3.verse: “Lethargy and drowsiness arose in me, and owing to lethargy and drowsiness my concentration died away.

mn128:18.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:18.5.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness.”

mn128:19.3.verse: “Alarm arose in me, and owing to alarm my concentration died away.

mn128:19.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:19.5.verse: Just as, Anuruddha, if a man walking along a road had quails fly up on either side of him, alarm would arise in him on that account;

mn128:19.6.verse: so too, Anuruddha, alarm arose in me, and owing to alarm my concentration died away.

mn128:19.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:19.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm.”

mn128:20.3.verse: “Elation arose in me, and owing to elation my concentration died away.

mn128:20.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:20.5.verse: Just as, Anuruddha, if a man seeking one hidden treasure came upon five hidden treasures all at once, elation would arise in him on that account;

mn128:20.6.verse: so too, Anuruddha, elation arose in me, and owing to elation my concentration died away.

mn128:20.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:20.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation.”

mn128:21.3.verse: “Inertia arose in me, and owing to inertia my concentration died away.

mn128:21.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:21.5.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia.”

mn128:22.3.verse: “Too active an energy arose in me, and owing to too active an energy my concentration died away.

mn128:22.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:22.5.verse: Just as, Anuruddha, if a man gripped a quail tightly with both hands, it would die then and there;

mn128:22.6.verse: so too, Anuruddha, too active an energy arose in me, and owing to too active an energy my concentration died away.

mn128:22.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:22.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia, nor too active an energy.”

mn128:23.3.verse: “Too sluggish an energy arose in me, and owing to too sluggish an energy my concentration died away.

mn128:23.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:23.5.verse: Just as, Anuruddha, if a man gripped a quail loosely, it would fly up out of his hand;

mn128:23.6.verse: so too, Anuruddha, too sluggish an energy arose in me, and owing to too sluggish an energy my concentration died away.

mn128:23.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:23.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia, nor too active an energy, nor too sluggish an energy.”

mn128:24.3.verse: “Longing arose in me, and owing to longing my concentration died away.

mn128:24.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:24.5.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia, nor too active an energy, nor too sluggish an energy, nor longing.”

mn128:25.3.verse: “Perception of diversity arose in me, and owing to perception of diversity my concentration died away.

mn128:25.4.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:25.5.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia, nor too active an energy, nor too sluggish an energy, nor longing, nor perception of diversity.”

mn128:26.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt, Anuruddha, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, I perceived illumination and the vision of forms.

mn128:26.2.verse: But that illumination of mine soon disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:26.4.verse: “What is the reason, what is the condition, why this illumination of mine and the vision of forms disappears?”

mn128:26.6.verse: “Too much meditating upon forms arose in me, and owing to too much meditating upon forms my concentration died away.

mn128:26.7.verse: When concentration died away, the illumination disappeared, and so did the vision of forms.

mn128:26.8.verse: I shall so act that uncertainty does not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor lethargy and drowsiness, nor alarm, nor elation, nor inertia, nor too active an energy, nor too sluggish an energy, nor longing, nor perception of diversity, nor too much meditating upon forms.”

mn128:27.1.verse: ‘Knowing thus, Anuruddha, “Uncertainty is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned uncertainty, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.2.verse: Knowing thus, “Inattention is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned inattention, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.3.verse: Knowing thus, “Lethargy and drowsiness is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned lethargy and drowsiness, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.4.verse: Knowing thus, “Alarm is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned alarm, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.5.verse: Knowing thus, “Elation is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned elation, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.6.verse: Knowing thus, “Inertia is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned inertia, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.7.verse: Knowing thus, “Too active an energy is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned too active an energy, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.8.verse: Knowing thus, “Too sluggish an energy is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned too sluggish an energy, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.9.verse: Knowing thus, “Longing is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned longing, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.10.verse: Knowing thus, “Perception of diversity is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned perception of diversity, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:27.11.verse: Knowing thus, “Too much meditating upon forms is an imperfection of mind,” I abandoned too much meditating upon forms, that imperfection of mind.

mn128:28.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt, Anuruddha, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, I perceived illumination and did not see forms;

mn128:28.2.verse: I saw forms and did not perceive illumination—

mn128:28.3.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day.

mn128:28.5.verse: “What is the reason, what is the condition, why I perceive illumination and do not see forms,

mn128:28.6.verse: and why I see forms and do not perceive illumination,

mn128:28.7.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day?”

mn128:28.9.verse: “On the occasion on which I give attention to the sign of forms without giving attention to the sign of illumination, on that occasion I perceive illumination and do not see forms.

mn128:28.10.verse: But on the occasion on which I give attention to the sign of illumination without giving attention to the sign of forms, on that occasion I see forms and do not perceive illumination—

mn128:28.11.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day.”

mn128:29.1.verse: ‘As I dwelt, Anuruddha, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, I perceived limited illumination and saw limited forms;

mn128:29.2.verse: I perceived measureless illumination and saw measureless forms—

mn128:29.3.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day.

mn128:29.5.verse: “What is the reason, what is the condition, why I perceive limited illumination and see limited forms,

mn128:29.6.verse: and why I perceive measureless illumination and see measureless forms—

mn128:29.7.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day?”

mn128:29.9.verse: “On the occasion on which my concentration is limited, on that occasion my eye is limited.

mn128:29.10.verse: With a limited eye I perceive limited illumination and see limited forms.

mn128:29.11.verse: But on the occasion on which my concentration is measureless, on that occasion my eye is measureless.

mn128:29.12.verse: With a measureless eye I perceive measureless illumination and see measureless forms—

mn128:29.13.verse: for a whole night, for a whole day, for a whole night and day.”

mn128:30.1.verse: ‘As soon as I knew, Anuruddha, “Uncertainty is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.2.verse: As soon as I knew, “Inattention is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.3.verse: As soon as I knew, “Lethargy and drowsiness is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.4.verse: As soon as I knew, “Alarm is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.5.verse: As soon as I knew, “Elation is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.6.verse: As soon as I knew, “Inertia is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.7.verse: As soon as I knew, “Too active an energy is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.8.verse: As soon as I knew, “Too sluggish an energy is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.9.verse: As soon as I knew, “Longing is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.10.verse: As soon as I knew, “Perception of diversity is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:30.11.verse: As soon as I knew, “Too much meditating upon forms is an imperfection of mind,” it was abandoned in me.

mn128:31.2.verse: “The imperfections of my mind have been abandoned by me.

mn128:31.3.verse: Now let me develop concentration in three ways.”

mn128:31.4.verse: So, Anuruddha, I developed concentration with initial application and sustained application; I developed concentration without initial application and with sustained application only; I developed concentration without initial application and without sustained application; I developed concentration accompanied by happiness; I developed concentration without happiness; I developed concentration accompanied by pleasure; I developed concentration accompanied by equanimity.

mn128:32.1.verse: ‘When, Anuruddha, concentration with initial application and sustained application had been developed by me, concentration without initial application and with sustained application only had been developed by me, concentration without initial application and without sustained application had been developed by me, concentration accompanied by happiness had been developed by me, concentration without happiness had been developed by me, concentration accompanied by pleasure had been developed by me, concentration accompanied by equanimity had been developed by me,

mn128:32.2.verse: then knowledge and vision arose in me:

mn128:32.3.verse: “My deliverance is unshakeable; this is the last birth; there is now no more renewal of being.”’

mn128:32.4.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn128:32.5.verse: The venerable Anuruddha was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn128:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

mn128:2.1.verse: Now at that time the mendicants of Kosambī were fighting, quarreling, and disputing, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

mn128:3.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and told him what was happening, adding:

mn128:3.3.verse: “Please, sir go to those mendicants out of sympathy.”

mn128:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha went up to those mendicants and said,

mn128:4.2.verse: “Enough, mendicants! Stop fighting, quarreling, and disputing.”

mn128:4.3.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

mn128:4.5.verse: Let the Buddha, the Lord of the Dhamma,

mn128:4.6.verse: remain passive, dwelling in blissful meditation in this life.

mn128:4.7.verse: We will be known for this fighting, quarreling, arguing, and disputing.”

mn128:4.15.verse: and a third time the Buddha said to those mendicants,

mn128:4.16.verse: “Enough, mendicants! Stop fighting, quarreling, and disputing.”

mn128:4.17.verse: For a third time, that mendicant said to the Buddha,

mn128:4.19.verse: Let the Buddha, the Lord of the Dhamma,

mn128:4.20.verse: remain passive, dwelling in blissful meditation in this life.

mn128:4.21.verse: We will be known for this fighting, quarreling, arguing, and disputing.”

mn128:5.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

mn128:5.2.verse: After the meal, on his return from almsround, he set his lodgings in order. Taking his bowl and robe, he recited these verses while standing right there:

mn128:6.2.verse: yet no one thinks that they’re the fool.

mn128:6.4.verse: they think no better of the other.

mn128:6.6.verse: they talk, their words out of bounds.

mn128:6.7.verse: They blab at will, their mouths agape,

mn128:6.8.verse: and not one knows what leads them on.

mn128:6.10.verse: They beat me, they robbed me!’

mn128:6.11.verse: For those bearing such a grudge,

mn128:6.12.verse: hatred is never laid to rest.

mn128:6.14.verse: They beat me, they robbed me!’

mn128:6.15.verse: For those who bear no such grudge,

mn128:6.19.verse: it’s laid to rest by love:

mn128:6.22.verse: let us, who do understand this,

mn128:6.24.verse: for that is how conflicts are laid to rest.

mn128:6.25.verse: Breakers of bones and takers of life,

mn128:6.30.verse: If you find an alert companion,

mn128:6.31.verse: an attentive friend to live happily together,

mn128:6.33.verse: wander with them, joyful and mindful.

mn128:6.34.verse: If you find no alert companion,

mn128:6.35.verse: no attentive friend to live happily together,

mn128:6.36.verse: then, like a king who flees his conquered realm,

mn128:6.37.verse: wander alone like a tusker in the wilds.

mn128:6.40.verse: Wander alone and do no wrong,

mn128:6.41.verse: at ease like a tusker in the wilds.”

mn128:7.1.verse: After speaking these verses while standing, the Buddha went to the village of the child salt-miners,

mn128:7.2.verse: where Venerable Bhagu was staying at the time.

mn128:7.3.verse: Bhagu saw the Buddha coming off in the distance,

mn128:7.4.verse: so he spread out a seat and placed water for washing the feet.

mn128:7.5.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

mn128:7.7.verse: Bhagu bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side.

mn128:7.9.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, mendicant, I hope you’re all right. And I hope you’re having no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn128:7.10.verse: “I’m keeping well, Blessed One, I’m all right. And I’m having no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn128:7.11.verse: Then the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired Bhagu with a Dhamma talk, after which he rose from his seat and set out for the Park of the East-Raftered Hall.

mn128:8.1.verse: Now at that time the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila were staying in the Park of the East-Raftered Hall.

mn128:8.2.verse: The park keeper saw the Buddha coming off in the distance

mn128:8.5.verse: There are three gentlemen staying here whose nature is to desire self-knowledge.

mn128:9.1.verse: Anuruddha heard the park keeper conversing with the Buddha,

mn128:9.3.verse: “Don’t keep the Buddha out, good park keeper!

mn128:9.4.verse: Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”

mn128:10.1.verse: Then Anuruddha went to Nandiya and Kimbila, and said to them,

mn128:10.2.verse: “Come forth, venerables, come forth! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived!”

mn128:10.3.verse: Then Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila came out to greet the Buddha.

mn128:10.4.verse: One received his bowl and robe, one spread out a seat, and one set out water for washing his feet.

mn128:10.5.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out,

mn128:10.7.verse: Those venerables bowed and sat down to one side.

mn128:10.9.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Anuruddha and friends, I hope you’re all right. And I hope you’re having no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn128:10.10.verse: “We’re keeping well, Blessed One, we’re getting by. And we have no trouble getting almsfood.”

mn128:11.1.verse: “I hope you’re living in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes?”

mn128:11.2.verse: “Indeed, sir, we live in harmony as you say.”

mn128:11.3.verse: “But how do you live this way?”

mn128:12.3.verse: to live together with spiritual companions such as these.’

mn128:12.4.verse: I consistently treat these venerables with kindness by way of body, speech, and mind, both in public and in private.

mn128:12.8.verse: ‘Why don’t I set aside my own ideas and just go along with these venerables’ ideas?’

mn128:12.10.verse: Though we’re different in body, sir, we’re one in mind, it seems to me.”

mn128:12.11.verse: And the venerables Nandiya and Kimbila spoke likewise, and they added:

mn128:12.23.verse: “That’s how we live in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.”

mn128:13.2.verse: But I hope you’re living diligently, keen, and resolute?”

mn128:14.2.verse: “But how do you live this way?”

mn128:14.3.verse: “In this case, sir, whoever returns first from almsround prepares the seats, and puts out the drinking water and the rubbish bin.

mn128:14.4.verse: If there’s remainder, whoever returns last eats it if they like. Otherwise they throw it out where there is little that grows, or drop it into water that has no living creatures.

mn128:14.5.verse: Then they put away the seats, drinking water, and rubbish bin, and sweep the refectory.

mn128:14.6.verse: If someone sees that the pot of water for washing, drinking, or the toilet is empty they set it up.

mn128:14.7.verse: If he can’t do it, he summons another with a wave of the hand, and they set it up by lending each other a hand to lift. But we don’t break into speech for that reason.

mn128:14.8.verse: And every five days we sit together for the whole night and discuss the teachings.

mn128:14.9.verse: That’s how we live diligently, keen, and resolute.”

mn128:15.2.verse: But as you live diligently like this, have you achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation?”

mn128:15.3.verse: “Well, sir, while meditating diligent, keen, and resolute, we perceive both light and vision of forms.

mn128:15.4.verse: But before long the light and the vision of forms vanish.

mn128:15.5.verse: We haven’t worked out the basis of that.”

mn128:16.1.verse: “Well, you should work out the basis of that.

mn128:16.2.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too perceived light and vision of forms.

mn128:16.3.verse: But before long my light and vision of forms vanished.

mn128:16.5.verse: ‘What’s the cause, what’s the reason why my light and vision of forms vanish?’

mn128:16.7.verse: ‘Doubt arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:16.8.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:16.9.verse: I’ll make sure that doubt will not arise in me again.’

mn128:17.1.verse: While meditating diligent, keen, and resolute, I perceived light and vision of forms.

mn128:17.2.verse: But before long my light and vision of forms vanished.

mn128:17.4.verse: ‘What’s the cause, what’s the reason why my light and vision of forms vanish?’

mn128:17.6.verse: ‘Loss of focus arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:17.7.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:17.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus will arise in me again.’

mn128:18.5.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness will arise in me again.’

mn128:19.3.verse: ‘Terror arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:19.4.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:19.5.verse: Suppose a person was traveling along a road, and killers were to spring out at them from both sides. They’d feel terrified because of that.

mn128:19.6.verse: In the same way, terror arose in me …

mn128:19.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror will arise in me again.’

mn128:20.3.verse: ‘Elation arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:20.4.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:20.5.verse: Suppose a person was looking for the entrance to a treasure trove. And all at once they’d come across five entrances! They’d feel excited because of that.

mn128:20.6.verse: In the same way, elation arose in me …

mn128:20.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation will arise in me again.’

mn128:21.5.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort will arise in me again.’

mn128:22.3.verse: ‘Excessive energy arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:22.4.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:22.5.verse: Suppose a person was to grip a quail too tightly in their hands—it would die right there.

mn128:22.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort nor excessive energy will arise in me again.’

mn128:23.3.verse: ‘Overly lax energy arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:23.4.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:23.5.verse: Suppose a person was to grip a quail too loosely—it would fly out of their hands.

mn128:23.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort nor excessive energy nor overly lax energy will arise in me again.’

mn128:24.5.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort nor excessive energy nor overly lax energy nor longing will arise in me again.’

mn128:25.5.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort nor excessive energy nor overly lax energy nor longing nor perception of diversity will arise in me again.’

mn128:26.1.verse: While meditating diligent, keen, and resolute, I perceived light and vision of forms.

mn128:26.2.verse: But before long my light and vision of forms vanished.

mn128:26.4.verse: ‘What’s the cause, what’s the reason why my light and vision of forms vanish?’

mn128:26.6.verse: ‘Excessive concentration on forms arose in me, and because of that my immersion fell away.

mn128:26.7.verse: When immersion falls away, the light and vision of forms vanish.

mn128:26.8.verse: I’ll make sure that neither doubt nor loss of focus nor dullness and drowsiness nor terror nor elation nor discomfort nor excessive energy nor overly lax energy nor longing nor perception of diversity nor excessive concentration on forms will arise in me again.’

mn128:27.1.verse: When I understood that doubt is a corruption of the mind, I gave it up.

mn128:27.2.verse: When I understood that loss of focus,

mn128:27.11.verse: and excessive concentration on forms are corruptions of the mind, I gave them up.

mn128:28.1.verse: While meditating diligent, keen, and resolute, I perceived light but did not see forms,

mn128:28.2.verse: or I saw forms, but did not see light.

mn128:28.3.verse: And this went on for a whole night, a whole day, even a whole night and day.

mn128:28.5.verse: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason for this?’

mn128:28.9.verse: ‘When I don’t focus on the basis of the forms, but focus on the basis of the light, then I perceive light and do not see forms.

mn128:28.10.verse: But when I don’t focus on the basis of the light, but focus on the basis of the forms, then I see forms and do not perceive light.

mn128:28.11.verse: And this goes on for a whole night, a whole day, even a whole night and day.’

mn128:29.1.verse: While meditating diligent, keen, and resolute, I perceived limited light and saw limited forms,

mn128:29.2.verse: or I perceived limitless light and saw limitless forms.

mn128:29.3.verse: And this went on for a whole night, a whole day, even a whole night and day.

mn128:29.5.verse: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason for this?’

mn128:29.9.verse: ‘When my immersion is limited, then my vision is limited,

mn128:29.10.verse: and with limited vision I perceive limited light and see limited forms.

mn128:29.11.verse: But when my immersion is limitless, then my vision is limitless,

mn128:29.12.verse: and with limitless vision I perceive limitless light and see limitless forms.

mn128:29.13.verse: And this goes on for a whole night, a whole day, even a whole night and day.’

mn128:30.11.verse: and excessive concentration on forms are corruptions of the mind, I had given them up.

mn128:31.3.verse: Now let me develop immersion in three ways.’

mn128:31.4.verse: I developed immersion while placing the mind and keeping it connected; without placing the mind, merely keeping it connected; without placing the mind or keeping it connected; with rapture; without rapture; with pleasure; with equanimity.

mn128:32.1.verse: When I had developed immersion in these ways,

mn128:32.2.verse: the knowledge and vision arose in me:

mn128:32.3.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

mn128:32.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn128:32.5.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Anuruddha approved what the Buddha said.

mn129:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn129:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn129:2.1.verse: “These are the three characteristics, signs, and manifestations of a fool.

mn129:2.3.verse: A fool thinks poorly, speaks poorly, and acts poorly.

mn129:2.4.verse: If a fool didn’t think poorly, speak poorly, and act poorly, then how would the astute know of them,

mn129:2.5.verse: ‘This worthy one is a fool, an untrue person’?

mn129:2.6.verse: But since a fool does think poorly, speak poorly, and act poorly, then the astute do know of them,

mn129:2.7.verse: ‘This worthy one is a fool, an untrue person’.

mn129:3.1.verse: A fool experiences three kinds of suffering and sadness in this very life.

mn129:3.2.verse: Suppose a fool is sitting in a council hall, a street, or a crossroad,

mn129:3.3.verse: where people are discussing what is proper and fitting.

mn129:3.4.verse: And suppose that fool is someone who kills living creatures, steals, commits sexual misconduct, lies, and consumes intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

mn129:3.6.verse: ‘These people are discussing what is proper and fitting.

mn129:3.7.verse: But those bad things are found in me and I exhibit them!’

mn129:3.8.verse: This is the first kind of suffering and sadness that a fool experiences in this very life.

mn129:4.1.verse: Furthermore, a fool sees that the kings have arrested a bandit, a criminal, and subjected them to various punishments—

mn129:4.2.verse: whipping, caning, and clubbing; cutting off hands or feet, or both; cutting off ears or nose, or both; the ‘porridge pot’, the ‘shell-shave’, the ‘Rāhu’s mouth’, the ‘garland of fire’, the ‘burning hand’, the ‘bulrush twist’, the ‘bark dress’, the ‘antelope’, the ‘meat hook’, the ‘coins’, the ‘caustic pickle’, the ‘twisting bar’, the ‘straw mat’; being splashed with hot oil, being fed to the hounds, being impaled alive, and being beheaded.

mn129:4.4.verse: ‘The kinds of deeds for which the kings inflict such punishments—

mn129:4.6.verse: those things are found in me and I exhibit them!

mn129:4.7.verse: If the kings find out about me, they will inflict the same kinds of punishments on me!’

mn129:4.9.verse: This is the second kind of suffering and sadness that a fool experiences in this very life.

mn129:5.1.verse: Furthermore, when a fool is resting on a chair or a bed or on the ground, their past bad deeds—misconduct of body, speech, and mind—settle down upon them, rest down upon them, and lay down upon them.

mn129:5.2.verse: It is like the shadow of a great mountain peak in the evening as it settles down, rests down, and lays down upon the earth.

mn129:5.3.verse: In the same way, when a fool is resting on a chair or a bed or on the ground, their past bad deeds—misconduct of body, speech, and mind—settle down upon them, rest down upon them, and lay down upon them.

mn129:5.5.verse: ‘Alas, I haven’t done good and skillful things that keep me safe.

mn129:5.6.verse: And I have done bad things, violence and sin.

mn129:5.7.verse: When I depart, I’ll go to the place where people who’ve done such things go.’

mn129:5.8.verse: They sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breasts and falling into confusion.

mn129:5.9.verse: This is the third kind of suffering and sadness that a fool experiences in this very life.

mn129:6.1.verse: Having done bad things by way of body, speech, and mind, when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn129:7.1.verse: And if there’s anything of which it may be rightly said that

mn129:7.2.verse: it is utterly unlikable, undesirable, and disagreeable, it is of hell that this should be said.

mn129:7.4.verse: So much so that it’s not easy to give a simile for how painful hell is.”

mn129:7.5.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

mn129:7.6.verse: “But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”

mn129:8.2.verse: “Suppose they arrest a bandit, a criminal and present him to the king, saying,

mn129:8.3.verse: ‘Your Majesty, this is a bandit, a criminal. Punish him as you will.’

mn129:8.5.verse: ‘Go, my men, and strike this man in the morning with a hundred spears!’

mn129:8.6.verse: The king’s men did as they were told.

mn129:8.7.verse: Then at midday the king would say,

mn129:8.11.verse: ‘Go, my men, and strike this man in the midday with a hundred spears!’

mn129:8.12.verse: The king’s men did as they were told.

mn129:8.13.verse: Then late in the afternoon the king would say,

mn129:8.17.verse: ‘Go, my men, and strike this man in the late afternoon with a hundred spears!’

mn129:8.18.verse: The king’s men did as they were told.

mn129:8.20.verse: Would that man experience pain and distress from being struck with three hundred spears?”

mn129:8.21.verse: “Sir, that man would experience pain and distress from being struck with one spear, let alone three hundred spears!”

mn129:9.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a stone the size of his palm, addressed the mendicants,

mn129:9.3.verse: Which is bigger: the stone the size of my palm that I’ve picked up, or the Himalayas, the king of mountains?”

mn129:9.4.verse: “Sir, the stone you’ve picked up is tiny. Compared to the Himalayas, it doesn’t count, it’s not worth a fraction, there’s no comparison.”

mn129:9.5.verse: “In the same way, compared to the suffering in hell, the pain and distress experienced by that man due to being struck with three hundred spears doesn’t count, it’s not worth a fraction, there’s no comparison.

mn129:10.1.verse: The wardens of hell punish them with the five-fold crucifixion.

mn129:10.2.verse: They drive red-hot stakes through the hands and feet, and another in the middle of the chest.

mn129:10.3.verse: And there they feel painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.

mn129:11.1.verse: The wardens of hell throw them down and hack them with axes. …

mn129:12.1.verse: They hang them upside-down and hack them with hatchets. …

mn129:13.1.verse: They harness them to a chariot, and drive them back and forth across burning ground, blazing and glowing. …

mn129:14.1.verse: They make them climb up and down a big mountain of burning coals, blazing and glowing. …

mn129:15.1.verse: The wardens of hell turn them upside down and throw them into a red-hot copper pot, burning, blazing, and glowing.

mn129:15.3.verse: There they’re seared in boiling scum, and they’re swept up and down and round and round.

mn129:15.4.verse: And there they feel painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.

mn129:16.1.verse: The wardens of hell toss them in the Great Hell.

mn129:16.3.verse: ‘Four are its corners, four its doors,

mn129:16.7.verse: The ground is even made of iron,

mn129:17.1.verse: I could tell you many different things about hell.

mn129:17.2.verse: So much so that it’s not easy to completely describe the suffering in hell.

mn129:18.1.verse: There are, mendicants, animals that feed on grass.

mn129:18.2.verse: They eat by cropping fresh or dried grass with their teeth.

mn129:18.3.verse: And what animals feed on grass?

mn129:18.4.verse: Elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, goats, deer, and various others.

mn129:18.5.verse: A fool who used to be a glutton here and did bad deeds here, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in the company of those sentient beings who feed on grass.

mn129:19.1.verse: There are animals that feed on dung.

mn129:19.2.verse: When they catch a whiff of dung they run to it, thinking,

mn129:19.4.verse: It’s like when brahmins smell a burnt offering, they run to it, thinking,

mn129:19.6.verse: In the same way, there are animals that feed on dung.

mn129:19.7.verse: When they catch a whiff of dung they run to it, thinking,

mn129:19.9.verse: And what animals feed on dung?

mn129:19.10.verse: Chickens, pigs, hounds, jackals, and various others.

mn129:19.11.verse: A fool who used to be a glutton here and did bad deeds here, after death is reborn in the company of those sentient beings who feed on dung.

mn129:20.1.verse: There are animals who are born, live, and die in darkness.

mn129:20.2.verse: And what animals are born, live, and die in darkness?

mn129:20.3.verse: Moths, maggots, earthworms, and various others.

mn129:20.4.verse: A fool who used to be a glutton here and did bad deeds here, after death is reborn in the company of those sentient beings who are born, live, and die in darkness.

mn129:21.1.verse: There are animals who are born, live, and die in water.

mn129:21.2.verse: And what animals are born, live, and die in water?

mn129:21.3.verse: Fish, turtles, dolphins, and various others.

mn129:21.4.verse: A fool who used to be a glutton here and did bad deeds here, after death is reborn in the company of those sentient beings who are born, live, and die in water.

mn129:22.1.verse: There are animals who are born, live, and die in filth.

mn129:22.2.verse: And what animals are born, live, and die in filth?

mn129:22.3.verse: Those animals that are born, live, and die in a rotten fish, a rotten carcass,

mn129:22.7.verse: A fool who used to be a glutton here and did bad deeds here, after death is reborn in the company of those sentient beings who are born, live, and die in filth.

mn129:23.1.verse: I could tell you many different things about the animal realm.

mn129:23.2.verse: So much so that it’s not easy to completely describe the suffering in the animal realm.

mn129:24.1.verse: Mendicants, suppose a person were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the ocean.

mn129:24.2.verse: The east wind wafts it west; the west wind wafts it east; the north wind wafts it south; and the south wind wafts it north.

mn129:24.3.verse: And there was a one-eyed turtle who popped up once every hundred years.

mn129:24.5.verse: Would that one-eyed turtle still poke its neck through the hole in that yoke?”

mn129:24.7.verse: Only after a very long time, sir, if ever.”

mn129:24.8.verse: “That one-eyed turtle would poke its neck through the hole in that yoke sooner than a fool who has fallen to the underworld would be reborn as a human being, I say.

mn129:24.10.verse: Because in that place there’s no principled or moral conduct, and no doing what is good and skillful.

mn129:24.11.verse: There they just prey on each other, preying on the weak.

mn129:25.1.verse: And suppose that fool, after a very long time, returned to the human realm.

mn129:25.2.verse: They’d be reborn in a low class family—a family of corpse-workers, hunters, bamboo-workers, chariot-makers, or scavengers.

mn129:25.3.verse: Such families are poor, with little to eat or drink, where life is tough, and food and shelter are hard to find.

mn129:25.4.verse: And they’d be ugly, unsightly, deformed, sickly—one-eyed, crippled, lame, or half-paralyzed. They don’t get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; or bed, house, and lighting.

mn129:25.5.verse: And they do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn129:25.6.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn129:26.1.verse: Suppose a gambler were to lose his wife and child, all his property, and then get thrown in jail with his first losing hand.

mn129:26.2.verse: Such a losing hand is trivial compared to

mn129:26.3.verse: the losing hand whereby a fool, having done bad things by way of body, speech, and mind, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

mn129:26.4.verse: This is the total fulfillment of the fool’s level.

mn129:27.1.verse: There are these three characteristics, signs, and manifestations of an astute person.

mn129:27.3.verse: An astute person thinks well, speaks well, and acts well.

mn129:27.4.verse: If an astute person didn’t think well, speak well, and act well, then how would the astute know of them,

mn129:27.5.verse: ‘This worthy one is astute, a true person’?

mn129:28.1.verse: But since an astute person does think well, speak well, and act well, then the astute do know of them,

mn129:28.2.verse: ‘This worthy one is astute, a true person’.

mn129:28.3.verse: An astute person experiences three kinds of pleasure and happiness in this very life.

mn129:28.4.verse: Suppose an astute person is sitting in a council hall, a street, or a crossroad,

mn129:28.5.verse: where people are discussing about what is proper and fitting.

mn129:28.6.verse: And suppose that astute person is someone who refrains from killing living creatures, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

mn129:28.8.verse: ‘These people are discussing what is proper and fitting.

mn129:28.9.verse: And those good things are found in me and I exhibit them.’

mn129:28.10.verse: This is the first kind of pleasure and happiness that an astute person experiences in this very life.

mn129:29.1.verse: Furthermore, an astute person sees that the kings have arrested a bandit, a criminal, and subjected them to various punishments—

mn129:29.2.verse: whipping, caning, and clubbing; cutting off hands or feet, or both; cutting off ears or nose, or both; the ‘porridge pot’, the ‘shell-shave’, the ‘Rāhu’s mouth’, the ‘garland of fire’, the ‘burning hand’, the ‘bulrush twist’, the ‘bark dress’, the ‘antelope’, the ‘meat hook’, the ‘coins’, the ‘caustic pickle’, the ‘twisting bar’, the ‘straw mat’; being splashed with hot oil, being fed to the hounds, being impaled alive, and being beheaded.

mn129:29.4.verse: ‘The kinds of deeds for which the kings inflict such punishments—those things are not found in me and I do not exhibit them!’

mn129:29.5.verse: This is the second kind of pleasure and happiness that an astute person experiences in this very life.

mn129:30.1.verse: Furthermore, when an astute person is resting on a chair or a bed or on the ground, their past good deeds—good conduct of body, speech, and mind—settle down upon them, rest down upon them, and lay down upon them.

mn129:30.2.verse: It is like the shadow of a great mountain peak in the evening as it settles down, rests down, and lays down upon the earth.

mn129:30.3.verse: In the same way, when an astute person is resting on a chair or a bed or on the ground, their past good deeds—good conduct of body, speech, and mind—settle down upon them, rest down upon them, and lay down upon them.

mn129:30.5.verse: ‘Well, I haven’t done bad things, violence and sin.

mn129:30.6.verse: And I have done good and skillful deeds that keep me safe.

mn129:30.7.verse: When I pass away, I’ll go to the place where people who’ve done such things go.’

mn129:30.8.verse: So they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

mn129:30.9.verse: This is the third kind of pleasure and happiness that an astute person experiences in this very life.

mn129:31.1.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn129:32.1.verse: And if there’s anything of which it may be rightly said that

mn129:32.2.verse: it is utterly likable, desirable, and agreeable, it is of heaven that this should be said.

mn129:32.4.verse: So much so that it’s not easy to give a simile for how pleasurable heaven is.”

mn129:32.5.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

mn129:32.6.verse: “But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”

mn129:33.2.verse: “Suppose there was a king, a wheel-turning monarch who possessed seven treasures and four blessings, and experienced pleasure and happiness because of them.

mn129:34.2.verse: It’s when, on the fifteenth day sabbath, an anointed aristocratic king has bathed his head and gone upstairs in the royal longhouse to observe the sabbath. And the heavenly wheel-treasure appears to him, with a thousand spokes, with rim and hub, complete in every detail.

mn129:34.4.verse: ‘I have heard that when the heavenly wheel-treasure appears to a king in this way, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:34.5.verse: Am I then a wheel-turning monarch?’

mn129:35.1.verse: Then the anointed aristocratic king, taking a ceremonial vase in his left hand, besprinkled the wheel-treasure with his right hand, saying,

mn129:35.2.verse: ‘Roll forth, O wheel-treasure! Triumph, O wheel-treasure!’

mn129:35.3.verse: Then the wheel-treasure rolls toward the east. And the king follows it together with his army of four divisions. In whatever place the wheel-treasure stands still, there the king comes to stay together with his army.

mn129:35.4.verse: And any opposing rulers of the eastern quarter come to the wheel-turning monarch and say,

mn129:35.5.verse: ‘Come, Great King! Welcome, Great King! We are yours, Great King, instruct us.’

mn129:35.7.verse: ‘Do not kill living creatures. Do not steal. Do not commit sexual misconduct. Do not lie. Do not drink liquor. Maintain the current level of taxation.’

mn129:35.8.verse: And so the opposing rulers of the eastern quarter become his vassals.

mn129:35.9.verse: Then the wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged again, rolls toward the south. …

mn129:35.10.verse: Having plunged into the southern ocean and emerged again, it rolls toward the west. …

mn129:35.11.verse: Having plunged into the western ocean and emerged again, it rolls toward the north, followed by the king together with his army of four divisions. In whatever place the wheel-treasure stands still, there the king comes to stay together with his army.

mn129:35.12.verse: And any opposing rulers of the northern quarter come to the wheel-turning monarch and say,

mn129:35.13.verse: ‘Come, Great King! Welcome, Great King! We are yours, Great King, instruct us.’

mn129:35.15.verse: ‘Do not kill living creatures. Do not steal. Do not commit sexual misconduct. Do not lie. Do not drink liquor. Maintain the current level of taxation.’

mn129:35.16.verse: And so the opposing rulers of the eastern quarter become his vassals.

mn129:35.17.verse: And then the wheel-treasure, having triumphed over this land surrounded by ocean, returns to the royal capital. There it stands still at the gate to the royal compound as if fixed to an axle, illuminating the royal compound.

mn129:35.18.verse: Such is the wheel-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:36.1.verse: Next, the elephant-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:36.2.verse: It was an all-white sky-walker with psychic power, touching the ground in seven places, a king of elephants named Sabbath.

mn129:36.3.verse: Seeing him, the king was impressed,

mn129:36.4.verse: ‘This would truly be a fine elephant vehicle, if he would submit to taming.’

mn129:36.5.verse: Then the elephant-treasure submitted to taming, as if he were a fine thoroughbred elephant that had been tamed for a long time.

mn129:36.6.verse: Once it so happened that the wheel-turning monarch, testing that same elephant-treasure, mounted him in the morning and traversed the land surrounded by ocean before returning to the royal capital in time for breakfast.

mn129:36.7.verse: Such is the elephant-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:37.1.verse: Next, the horse-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:37.2.verse: It was an all-white sky-walker with psychic power, with head of black and mane like woven reeds, a royal steed named Thundercloud.

mn129:37.3.verse: Seeing him, the king was impressed,

mn129:37.4.verse: ‘This would truly be a fine horse vehicle, if he would submit to taming.’

mn129:37.5.verse: Then the horse-treasure submitted to taming, as if he were a fine thoroughbred horse that had been tamed for a long time.

mn129:37.6.verse: Once it so happened that the wheel-turning monarch, testing that same horse-treasure, mounted him in the morning and traversed the land surrounded by ocean before returning to the royal capital in time for breakfast.

mn129:37.7.verse: Such is the horse-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:38.1.verse: Next, the jewel-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:38.2.verse: It is a beryl gem that’s naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked.

mn129:38.3.verse: And the radiance of that jewel spreads all-round for a league.

mn129:38.4.verse: Once it so happened that the wheel-turning monarch, testing that same jewel-treasure, mobilized his army of four divisions and, with the jewel hoisted on his banner, set out in the dark of the night.

mn129:38.5.verse: Then the villagers around them set off to work, thinking that it was day.

mn129:38.6.verse: Such is the jewel-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:39.1.verse: Next, the woman-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:39.2.verse: She is attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. She’s neither too tall nor too short; neither too thin nor too fat; neither too dark nor too light. She outdoes human beauty without reaching heavenly beauty.

mn129:39.3.verse: And her touch is like a tuft of cotton-wool or kapok.

mn129:39.4.verse: When it’s cool her limbs are warm, and when it’s warm her limbs are cool.

mn129:39.5.verse: The fragrance of sandal floats from her body, and lotus from her mouth.

mn129:39.6.verse: She gets up before the king and goes to bed after him, and is obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.

mn129:39.7.verse: The woman-treasure does not betray the wheel-turning monarch even in thought, still less in deed.

mn129:39.8.verse: Such is the woman-treasure who appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:40.1.verse: Next, the householder-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:40.2.verse: The power of clairvoyance manifests in him as a result of past deeds, by which he sees treasure troves, both owned and ownerless.

mn129:40.3.verse: He approaches the wheel-turning monarch and says,

mn129:40.4.verse: ‘Relax, Your Majesty. I will take care of the treasury.’

mn129:40.5.verse: Once it so happened that the wheel-turning monarch, testing that same householder-treasure, boarded a boat and sailed to the middle of the Ganges River. Then he said to the householder-treasure,

mn129:40.6.verse: ‘Householder, I need gold, both coined and uncoined.’

mn129:40.7.verse: ‘Well then, Great King, draw the boat up to one shore.’

mn129:40.8.verse: ‘It’s right here, householder, that I need gold, both coined and uncoined.’

mn129:40.9.verse: Then that householder-treasure, immersing both hands in the water, pulled up a pot full of gold, both coined and uncoined, and said to the king,

mn129:40.10.verse: ‘Is this sufficient, Great King? Has enough been done, Great King, enough offered?’

mn129:40.12.verse: ‘That is sufficient, householder. Enough has been done, enough offered.’

mn129:40.13.verse: Such is the householder-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:41.1.verse: Next, the commander-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:41.2.verse: He is astute, competent, intelligent, and capable regarding who should be ushered in to the king’s presence, who should be ushered out, and who should be kept by his side.

mn129:41.3.verse: He approaches the wheel-turning monarch and says,

mn129:41.4.verse: ‘Relax, Your Majesty. I shall issue instructions.’

mn129:41.5.verse: Such is the commander-treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:41.6.verse: These are the seven treasures possessed by a wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:42.1.verse: And what are the four blessings?

mn129:42.2.verse: A wheel-turning monarch is attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty, more so than other humans.

mn129:43.1.verse: Furthermore, he is long-lived, more so than other humans.

mn129:44.1.verse: Furthermore, he is rarely ill or unwell, and his stomach digests well, being neither too hot nor too cold, more so than other humans.

mn129:45.1.verse: Furthermore, a wheel-turning monarch is as dear and beloved to the brahmins and householders

mn129:45.2.verse: as a father is to his children.

mn129:45.4.verse: And the brahmins and householders are as dear to the wheel-turning monarch

mn129:45.5.verse: as children are to their father.

mn129:45.7.verse: Once it so happened that a wheel-turning monarch went with his army of four divisions to visit a park.

mn129:45.8.verse: Then the brahmins and householders went up to him and said,

mn129:45.9.verse: ‘Slow down, Your Majesty, so we may see you longer!’

mn129:45.10.verse: And the king addressed his charioteer,

mn129:45.11.verse: ‘Drive slowly, charioteer, so I can see the brahmins and householders longer!’

mn129:45.13.verse: These are the four blessings possessed by a wheel-turning monarch.

mn129:46.2.verse: Would a wheel-turning monarch who possessed these seven treasures and these four blessings experience pleasure and happiness because of them?”

mn129:46.3.verse: “Sir, a wheel-turning monarch who possessed even a single one of these treasures would experience pleasure and happiness because of that, let alone all seven treasures and four blessings!”

mn129:47.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a stone the size of his palm, addressed the mendicants,

mn129:47.3.verse: Which is bigger: the stone the size of my palm that I’ve picked up, or the Himalayas, the king of mountains?”

mn129:47.4.verse: “Sir, the stone you’ve picked up is tiny. Compared to the Himalayas, it doesn’t count, it’s not worth a fraction, there’s no comparison.”

mn129:47.5.verse: “In the same way, compared to the happiness of heaven, the pleasure and happiness experienced by a wheel-turning monarch due to those seven treasures and those four blessings doesn’t even count, it’s not even a fraction, there’s no comparison.

mn129:48.1.verse: And suppose that astute person, after a very long time, returned to the human realm.

mn129:48.2.verse: They’d be reborn in a well-to-do family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain.

mn129:48.3.verse: And they’d be attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. They’d get to have food, drink, clothes, and vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and a bed, house, and lighting.

mn129:48.4.verse: And they do good things by way of body, speech, and mind.

mn129:48.5.verse: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn129:49.1.verse: Suppose a gambler was to win a big pile of money with the first winning hand.

mn129:49.2.verse: Such a winning hand is trivial compared to

mn129:49.3.verse: the winning hand whereby an astute person, when their body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

mn129:49.4.verse: This is the total fulfillment of the astute person’s level.”

mn129:49.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn129:49.6.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn129:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn129:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn129:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, attributes of a fool.

mn129:2.3.verse: Here a fool is one who thinks bad thoughts, speaks bad words, and does bad deeds.

mn129:2.4.verse: If a fool were not so, how would the wise know him thus:

mn129:2.5.verse: ‘This person is a fool, an untrue man’?

mn129:2.6.verse: But because a fool is one who thinks bad thoughts, speaks bad words, and does bad deeds, the wise know him thus:

mn129:2.7.verse: ‘This person is a fool, an untrue man.’

mn129:3.1.verse: “A fool feels pain and grief here and now in three ways.

mn129:3.2.verse: If a fool is seated in an assembly or along a street or in a square

mn129:3.3.verse: and people there are discussing certain pertinent and relevant matters,

mn129:3.4.verse: then, if the fool is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, misconducts himself in sensual pleasures, speaks falsehood, and indulges in wine, liquor, and intoxicants, which are the basis of negligence,

mn129:3.6.verse: ‘These people are discussing certain pertinent and relevant matters;

mn129:3.7.verse: these things are found in me, and I am seen engaging in those things.’

mn129:3.8.verse: This is the first kind of pain and grief that a fool feels here and now.

mn129:4.1.verse: “Again, when a robber culprit is caught, a fool sees kings having many kinds of torture inflicted on him:

mn129:4.2.verse: having him flogged with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with clubs; having his hands cut off, his feet cut off, his hands and feet cut off; his ears cut off, his nose cut off, his ears and nose cut off; having him subjected to the ‘porridge pot,’ to the ‘polished-shell shave,’ to the ‘Rāhu’s mouth,’ to the ‘fiery wreath,’ to the ‘flaming hand,’ to the ‘blades of grass,’ to the ‘bark dress,’ to the ‘antelope,’ to the ‘meat hooks,’ to the ‘coins,’ to the ‘lye pickling,’ to the ‘pivoting pin,’ to the ‘rolled-up palliasse’; and having him splashed with boiling oil, and having him thrown to be devoured by dogs, and having him impaled alive on stakes, and having his head cut off with a sword.

mn129:4.4.verse: ‘Because of such evil actions as those, when a robber culprit is caught, kings have many kinds of tortures inflicted on him:

mn129:4.5.verse: they have him flogged with whips…and have his head cut off with a sword.

mn129:4.6.verse: Those things are found in me, and I am seen engaging in those things.’

mn129:4.9.verse: This is the second kind of pain and grief that a fool feels here and now.

mn129:5.1.verse: “Again, when a fool is on his chair or on his bed or resting on the ground, then the evil actions that he did in the past—his bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct—cover him, overspread him, and envelop him.

mn129:5.2.verse: Just as the shadow of a great mountain peak in the evening covers, overspreads, and envelops the earth,

mn129:5.3.verse: so too, when a fool is on his chair or on his bed or resting on the ground, then the evil actions that he did in the past—his bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct—cover him, overspread him, and envelop him.

mn129:5.5.verse: ‘I have not done what is good, I have not done what is wholesome, I have not made myself a shelter from anguish.

mn129:5.6.verse: I have done what is evil, I have done what is cruel, I have done what is wicked.

mn129:5.7.verse: When I pass away, I shall go to the destination of those who have not done what is good…who have done what is wicked.’

mn129:5.8.verse: He sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps beating his breast and becomes distraught.

mn129:5.9.verse: This is the third kind of pain and grief that a fool feels here and now.

mn129:6.1.verse: “A fool who has given himself over to misconduct of body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, even in hell.

mn129:7.1.verse: “Were it rightly speaking to be said of anything:

mn129:7.2.verse: ‘That is utterly unwished for, utterly undesired, utterly disagreeable,’ it is of hell that, rightly speaking, this should be said:

mn129:7.3.verse: ‘That is utterly unwished for, utterly undesired, utterly disagreeable.’

mn129:7.4.verse: So much so that it is hard to find a simile for the suffering in hell.”

mn129:7.5.verse: When this was said, a bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:

mn129:7.6.verse: “But, venerable sir, can a simile be given?”

mn129:8.1.verse: “It can, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.

mn129:8.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose men caught a robber culprit and presented him to the king, saying:

mn129:8.3.verse: ‘Sire, here is a robber culprit. Order what punishment you will for him.’

mn129:8.5.verse: ‘Go and strike this man in the morning with a hundred spears.’

mn129:8.6.verse: And they struck him in the morning with a hundred spears.

mn129:8.7.verse: Then at noon the king asked:

mn129:8.11.verse: ‘Go and strike that man at noon with a hundred spears.’

mn129:8.12.verse: And they struck him at noon with a hundred spears.

mn129:8.13.verse: Then in the evening the king asked:

mn129:8.17.verse: ‘Go and strike that man in the evening with a hundred spears.’

mn129:8.18.verse: And they struck him in the evening with a hundred spears.

mn129:8.20.verse: Would that man experience pain and grief because of being struck with the three hundred spears?”

mn129:8.21.verse: “Venerable sir, that man would experience pain and grief because of being struck with even one spear, let alone three hundred.”

mn129:9.1.verse: Then, taking a small stone the size of his hand, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn129:9.3.verse: Which is the greater, this small stone that I have taken, the size of my hand, or Himalaya, the king of mountains?”

mn129:9.4.verse: “Venerable sir, the small stone that the Blessed One has taken, the size of his hand, does not count beside Himalaya, the king of mountains; it is not even a fraction, there is no comparison.”

mn129:9.5.verse: “So too, bhikkhus, the pain and grief that the man would experience because of being struck with the three hundred spears does not count beside the suffering of hell; it is not even a fraction, there is no comparison.

mn129:10.1.verse: “Now the wardens of hell torture him with the fivefold transfixing.

mn129:10.2.verse: They drive a red-hot iron stake through one hand, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other hand, they drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot, they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other foot, they drive a red-hot iron stake in the middle through his breast.

mn129:10.3.verse: There he feels painful, racking, piercing feelings. Yet he does not die so long as that evil action has not exhausted its result.

mn129:11.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell throw him down and pare him with axes.

mn129:11.2.verse: There he feels painful, racking…has not exhausted its result.

mn129:12.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell set him with his feet up and his head down and pare him with adzes.

mn129:12.2.verse: There he feels painful, racking…has not exhausted its result.

mn129:13.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell harness him to a chariot and drive him back and forth across ground that is burning, blazing, and glowing.

mn129:13.2.verse: There he feels painful, racking…has not exhausted its result.

mn129:14.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell make him climb up and down a great mound of coals that are burning, blazing, and glowing.

mn129:14.2.verse: There he feels painful, racking, piercing feelings. Yet he does not die so long as that evil action has not exhausted its result.

mn129:15.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell take him feet up and head down and plunge him into a red-hot metal cauldron that is burning, blazing, and glowing.

mn129:15.2.verse: He is cooked there in a swirl of froth.

mn129:15.3.verse: And as he is being cooked there in a swirl of froth, he is swept now up, now down, and now across.

mn129:15.4.verse: There he feels painful, racking, piercing feelings. Yet he does not die so long as that evil action has not exhausted its result.

mn129:16.1.verse: “Next the wardens of hell throw him into the Great Hell.

mn129:16.2.verse: Now as to that Great Hell, bhikkhus:

mn129:16.3.verse: It has four corners and is built

mn129:16.4.verse: With four doors, one set in each side,

mn129:16.5.verse: Walled up with iron and all around

mn129:16.6.verse: And shut in with an iron roof.

mn129:16.7.verse: Its floor as well is made of iron

mn129:16.8.verse: And heated till it glows with fire.

mn129:16.9.verse: The range is a full hundred leagues

mn129:17.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I could tell you in many ways about hell.

mn129:17.2.verse: So much so that it is hard to finish describing the suffering in hell.

mn129:18.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are animals that feed on grass.

mn129:18.2.verse: They eat by cropping fresh or dried grass with their teeth.

mn129:18.3.verse: And what animals feed on grass?

mn129:18.4.verse: Horses, cattle, donkeys, goats, and deer, and any other such animals.

mn129:18.5.verse: A fool who formerly delighted in tastes here and did evil actions here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the company of animals that feed on grass.

mn129:19.1.verse: “There are animals that feed on dung.

mn129:19.2.verse: They smell dung from a distance and run to it, thinking:

mn129:19.4.verse: Just as brahmins run to the smell of a sacrifice, thinking:

mn129:19.5.verse: ‘We can eat here, we can eat here!’

mn129:19.6.verse: so too these animals that feed on dung

mn129:19.7.verse: smell dung from a distance and run to it, thinking:

mn129:19.8.verse: ‘We can eat here, we can eat here!’

mn129:19.9.verse: And what animals feed on dung?

mn129:19.10.verse: Fowls, pigs, dogs, and jackals, and any other such animals.

mn129:19.11.verse: A fool who formerly delighted in tastes here and did evil actions here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the company of animals that feed on dung.

mn129:20.1.verse: “There are animals that are born, age, and die in darkness.

mn129:20.2.verse: And what animals are born, age, and die in darkness?

mn129:20.3.verse: Moths, maggots, and earthworms, and any other such animals.

mn129:20.4.verse: A fool who formerly delighted in tastes here and did evil actions here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the company of animals that are born, age, and die in darkness.

mn129:21.1.verse: “There are animals that are born, age, and die in water.

mn129:21.2.verse: And what animals are born, age, and die in water?

mn129:21.3.verse: Fish, turtles, and crocodiles, and any other such animals.

mn129:21.4.verse: A fool who formerly delighted in tastes here and did evil actions here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the company of animals that are born, age, and die in water.

mn129:22.1.verse: “There are animals that are born, age, and die in filth.

mn129:22.2.verse: And what animals are born, age, and die in filth?

mn129:22.3.verse: Those animals that are born, age, and die in a rotten fish or in a rotten corpse…

mn129:22.6.verse: or in a sewer, and any other such animals that are born, age, and die in filth.

mn129:22.7.verse: A fool who formerly delighted in tastes here and did evil actions here, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in the company of animals that are born, age, and die in filth.

mn129:23.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I could tell you in many ways about the animal kingdom,

mn129:23.2.verse: so much so that it is hard to finish describing the suffering in the animal kingdom.

mn129:24.1.verse: “Suppose a man threw into the sea a yoke with one hole in it,

mn129:24.2.verse: and the east wind carried it to the west, and the west wind carried it to the east, and the north wind carried it to the south, and the south wind carried it to the north.

mn129:24.3.verse: Suppose there were a blind turtle that came up once at the end of each century.

mn129:24.5.verse: Would that blind turtle put his neck into that yoke with one hole in it?”

mn129:24.7.verse: “He might, venerable sir, sometime or other at the end of a long period.”

mn129:24.8.verse: “Bhikkhus, the blind turtle would sooner put his neck into that yoke with a single hole in it than a fool, once gone to perdition, would take to regain the human state, I say.

mn129:24.10.verse: Because there is no practising of the Dhamma there, no practising of what is righteous, no doing of what is wholesome, no performance of merit.

mn129:24.11.verse: There mutual devouring prevails, and the slaughter of the weak.

mn129:25.1.verse: “If, sometime or other, at the end of a long period, that fool comes back to the human state, it is into a low family that he is reborn—

mn129:25.2.verse: into a family of outcasts or hunters or bamboo-workers or cartwrights or scavengers—

mn129:25.3.verse: one that is poor with little to eat and drink, surviving with difficulty, where he scarcely finds food and clothing;

mn129:25.4.verse: and he is ugly, unsightly, and misshapen, sickly, blind, cripple-handed, lame, or paralysed; he gets no food, drink, clothes, vehicles, garlands, scents and unguents, bed, lodging, and light;

mn129:25.5.verse: he misconducts himself in body, speech, and mind,

mn129:25.6.verse: and having done that, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn129:26.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose a gambler at the very first unlucky throw loses his child and his wife and all his property and furthermore goes into bondage himself,

mn129:26.2.verse: yet an unlucky throw such as that is negligible;

mn129:26.3.verse: it is a far more unlucky throw when a fool who misconducts himself in body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

mn129:26.4.verse: This is the complete perfection of the fool’s grade.

mn129:27.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a wise man, signs of a wise man, attributes of a wise man.

mn129:27.3.verse: Here a wise man is one who thinks good thoughts, speaks good words, and does good deeds.

mn129:27.4.verse: If a wise man were not so, how would the wise know him thus:

mn129:27.5.verse: ‘This person is a wise man, a true man’?

mn129:28.1.verse: But because a wise man is one who thinks good thoughts, speaks good words, and does good deeds, the wise know him thus:

mn129:28.2.verse: ‘This person is a wise man, a true man.’

mn129:28.3.verse: “A wise man feels pleasure and joy here and now in three ways.

mn129:28.4.verse: If a wise man is seated in an assembly or along a street or in a square

mn129:28.5.verse: and people there are discussing certain pertinent and relevant matters,

mn129:28.6.verse: then, if the wise man is one who abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from misconduct in sensual pleasures, from false speech, from wine, liquor, and intoxicants, which are the basis of negligence,

mn129:28.8.verse: ‘These people are discussing certain pertinent and relevant matters;

mn129:28.9.verse: those things are not found in me, and I am not seen engaging in them.’

mn129:28.10.verse: This is the first kind of pleasure and joy that a wise man feels here and now.

mn129:29.1.verse: “Again, when a robber culprit is caught, a wise man sees kings having many kinds of torture inflicted on him:

mn129:29.2.verse: having him flogged with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with clubs; having his hands cut off, his feet cut off, his hands and feet cut off; his ears cut off, his nose cut off, his ears and nose cut off; having him subjected to the ‘porridge pot,’ to the ‘polished-shell shave,’ to the ‘Rāhu’s mouth,’ to the ‘fiery wreath,’ to the ‘flaming hand,’ to the ‘blades of grass,’ to the ‘bark dress,’ to the ‘antelope,’ to the ‘meat hooks,’ to the ‘coins,’ to the ‘lye pickling,’ to the ‘pivoting pin,’ to the ‘rolled-up palliasse’; and having him splashed with boiling oil, and having him thrown to be devoured by dogs, and having him impaled alive on stakes, and having his head cut off with a sword. (As in §4.)

mn129:29.3.verse: Then the wise man thinks thus:

mn129:29.4.verse: ‘Because of such evil actions as those, when a robber culprit is caught, kings have many kinds of tortures inflicted on him. Those things are not found in me, and I am not seen engaging in those things.’

mn129:29.5.verse: This is the second kind of pleasure and joy that a wise man feels here and now.

mn129:30.1.verse: “Again, when a wise man is on his chair or on his bed or resting on the ground, then the good actions that he did in the past—his good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct—cover him…

mn129:30.2.verse: Just as the shadow of a great mountain peak in the evening covers, overspreads, and envelops the earth,

mn129:30.3.verse: so too, when a wise man is on his chair or on his bed or resting on the ground, then the good actions that he did in the past—his good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct—cover him, overspread him, and envelop him.

mn129:30.5.verse: ‘I have not done what is evil, I have not done what is cruel, I have not done what is wicked.

mn129:30.6.verse: I have done what is good, I have done what is wholesome, I have made myself a shelter from anguish.

mn129:30.7.verse: When I pass away, I shall go to the destination of those who have not done what is evil…who have made themselves a shelter from anguish.’

mn129:30.8.verse: He does not sorrow, grieve, and lament, he does not weep beating his breast and become distraught.

mn129:30.9.verse: This is the third kind of pleasure and joy that a wise man feels here and now.

mn129:31.1.verse: “A wise man who has given himself over to good conduct of body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, even in heaven.

mn129:32.1.verse: “Were it rightly speaking to be said of anything:

mn129:32.2.verse: ‘That is utterly wished for, utterly desired, utterly agreeable,’ it is of heaven that, rightly speaking, this should be said:

mn129:32.3.verse: ‘That is utterly wished for, utterly desired, utterly agreeable.’

mn129:32.4.verse: So much so that it is hard to finish describing the happiness of heaven.”

mn129:32.5.verse: When this was said, a bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:

mn129:32.6.verse: “But, venerable sir, can a simile be given?”

mn129:33.1.verse: “It can, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.

mn129:33.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, suppose that a Wheel-turning Monarch possessed the seven treasures and the four kinds of success, and because of that experienced pleasure and joy.

mn129:34.2.verse: Here, when a head-anointed noble king has bathed his head on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth and has ascended to the upper palace chamber for the Uposatha, there appears to him the divine wheel-treasure with its thousand spokes, its tire, and its nave, complete in every aspect.

mn129:34.3.verse: On seeing it, the head-anointed noble king thinks thus:

mn129:34.4.verse: ‘Now it has been heard by me that when a head-anointed noble king has bathed his head on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth and has ascended to the upper palace chamber for the Uposatha, and there appears to him the divine wheel-treasure with its thousand spokes, its tire, and its nave, complete in every aspect, then that king becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch.

mn129:34.5.verse: Am I then a Wheel-turning Monarch?’

mn129:35.1.verse: “Then the head-anointed noble king rises from his seat, and taking a water vessel in his left hand, he sprinkles the wheel-treasure with his right hand, saying:

mn129:35.2.verse: ‘Turn forward, good wheel-treasure; triumph, good wheel-treasure!’

mn129:35.3.verse: Then the wheel-treasure turns forward rolling in the eastern direction and the Wheel-turning Monarch follows it with his four-constituent army. Now in whatever region the wheel-treasure pauses, there the Wheel-turning Monarch takes up his abode with his four-constituent army.

mn129:35.4.verse: And opposing kings in the eastern direction come to the Wheel-turning Monarch and speak thus:

mn129:35.5.verse: ‘Come, great king; welcome, great king; command, great king; advise, great king.’

mn129:35.7.verse: ‘You should not kill living beings; you should not take what has not been given; you should not misconduct yourselves in sensual pleasures; you should not speak falsehood; you should not drink intoxicants; you should eat what you are accustomed to eat.’
