mn137:24.3.verse: And their disciples want to listen. They actively listen and try to understand. They don’t proceed having turned away from the Teacher’s instruction.

mn137:24.4.verse: In this case the Realized One is happy, he does feel happiness. He remains unfestering, mindful and aware.

mn137:24.5.verse: This is the third case in which the Noble One cultivates the establishment of mindfulness.

mn137:24.6.verse: ‘The Noble One cultivates the establishment of mindfulness in three cases, by virtue of which they are a Teacher worthy to instruct a group.’

mn137:24.7.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn137:25.1.verse: ‘Of all meditation tutors, it is he that is called the supreme guide for those fit for training.’

mn137:25.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn137:25.3.verse: Driven by an elephant trainer, an elephant in training proceeds in just one direction:

mn137:26.1.verse: Driven by a horse trainer, a horse in training proceeds in just one direction:

mn137:26.3.verse: Driven by an ox trainer, an ox in training proceeds in just one direction:

mn137:26.5.verse: But driven by the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, a person in training proceeds in eight directions:

mn137:27.1.verse: Having physical form, they see forms.

mn137:27.3.verse: Not perceiving physical form internally, they see forms externally.

mn137:27.7.verse: Going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

mn137:27.9.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

mn137:27.11.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, they enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.

mn137:27.13.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, they enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

mn137:27.15.verse: Going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, they enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling.

mn137:27.17.verse: Driven by the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, a person in training proceeds in these eight directions.

mn137:28.1.verse: ‘Of all meditation tutors, it is he that is called the supreme guide for those fit for training.’

mn137:28.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.”

mn137:28.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn137:28.4.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn137:0.2.verse: The Exposition of the Sixfold Base

mn137:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn137:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn137:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you an exposition of the sixfold base.

mn137:2.2.verse: Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn137:3.1.verse: “‘The six internal bases should be understood. The six external bases should be understood. The six classes of consciousness should be understood. The six classes of contact should be understood. The eighteen kinds of mental exploration should be understood. The thirty-six positions of beings should be understood. Therein, by depending on this, abandon that. There are three foundations of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group. Among the teachers of training it is he that is called the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed’—

mn137:3.2.verse: this is the summary of the exposition of the sixfold base.

mn137:4.1.verse: “‘The six internal bases should be understood.’

mn137:4.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:4.3.verse: There are the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base.

mn137:4.4.verse: ‘The six internal bases should be understood’—

mn137:4.5.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:5.1.verse: “‘The six external bases should be understood.’

mn137:5.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:5.3.verse: There are the form-base, the sound-base, the odour-base, the flavour-base, the tangible-base, and the mind-object-base.

mn137:5.4.verse: ‘The six external bases should be understood’—

mn137:5.5.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:6.1.verse: “‘The six classes of consciousness should be understood.’

mn137:6.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:6.3.verse: There are eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

mn137:6.4.verse: ‘The six classes of consciousness should be understood’—

mn137:6.5.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:7.1.verse: “‘The six classes of contact should be understood.’

mn137:7.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:7.3.verse: There are eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.

mn137:7.4.verse: ‘The six classes of contact should be understood’—

mn137:7.5.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:8.1.verse: “‘The eighteen kinds of mental exploration should be understood.’

mn137:8.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:8.3.verse: “On seeing a form with the eye, one explores a form productive of joy, one explores a form productive of grief, one explores a form productive of equanimity.

mn137:8.4.verse: On hearing a sound with the ear…

mn137:8.5.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose…

mn137:8.6.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue…

mn137:8.7.verse: On touching a tangible with the body…

mn137:8.8.verse: On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, one explores a mind-object productive of joy, one explores a mind-object productive of grief, one explores a mind-object productive of equanimity.

mn137:8.9.verse: Thus there are six kinds of exploration with joy, six kinds of exploration with grief, and six kinds of exploration with equanimity. ‘The eighteen kinds of mental exploration should be understood’—

mn137:8.10.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:9.1.verse: “‘The thirty-six positions of beings should be understood.’

mn137:9.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:9.3.verse: There are six kinds of joy based on the household life and six kinds of joy based on renunciation. There are six kinds of grief based on the household life and six kinds of grief based on renunciation. There are six kinds of equanimity based on the household life and six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.

mn137:10.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of joy based on the household life?

mn137:10.2.verse: When one regards as a gain the gain of forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, gratifying, and associated with worldliness—or when one recalls what was formerly obtained that has passed, ceased, and changed—joy arises.

mn137:10.3.verse: Such joy as this is called joy based on the household life.

mn137:10.4.verse: “When one regards as a gain the gain of sounds cognizable by the ear…

mn137:10.5.verse: the gain of odours cognizable by the nose…

mn137:10.6.verse: the gain of flavours cognizable by the tongue…

mn137:10.7.verse: the gain of tangibles cognizable by the body…

mn137:10.8.verse: the gain of mind-objects cognizable by the mind that are wished for, desired, agreeable…joy arises.

mn137:10.9.verse: Such joy as this is called joy based on the household life.

mn137:10.10.verse: These are the six kinds of joy based on the household life.

mn137:11.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation?

mn137:11.2.verse: When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of forms, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that forms both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, joy arises.

mn137:11.3.verse: Such joy as this is called joy based on renunciation.

mn137:11.4.verse: “When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of sounds…

mn137:11.8.verse: of mind-objects, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that mind-objects both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, joy arises.

mn137:11.9.verse: Such joy as this is called joy based on renunciation.

mn137:11.10.verse: These are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation.

mn137:12.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of grief based on the household life?

mn137:12.2.verse: When one regards as a non-gain the non-gain of forms cognizable by the eye…

mn137:12.3.verse: …that are wished for, desired, agreeable, gratifying, and associated with worldliness—or when one recalls what was formerly not obtained that has passed, ceased, and changed—grief arises. Such grief as this is called grief based on the household life.

mn137:12.4.verse: “When one regards as a non-gain the non-gain of sounds cognizable by the ear…

mn137:12.5.verse: the non-gain of odours cognizable by the nose…

mn137:12.6.verse: the non-gain of flavours cognizable by the tongue…

mn137:12.7.verse: the non-gain of tangibles cognizable by the body…

mn137:12.8.verse: the non-gain of mind-objects cognizable by the mind that are wished for, desired, agreeable, gratifying, and associated with worldliness—or when one recalls what was formerly not obtained that has passed, ceased, and changed—grief arises.

mn137:12.9.verse: Such grief as this is called grief based on the household life.

mn137:12.10.verse: These are the six kinds of grief based on the household life.

mn137:13.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation?

mn137:13.2.verse: When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of forms, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that forms both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, one generates a longing for the supreme liberations thus:

mn137:13.3.verse: ‘When shall I enter upon and abide in that base that the noble ones now enter upon and abide in?’ In one who generates thus a longing for the supreme liberations, grief arises with that longing as condition.

mn137:13.4.verse: Such grief as this is called grief based on renunciation.

mn137:13.5.verse: “When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of sounds…

mn137:13.9.verse: of mind-objects, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that mind-objects both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, one generates a longing for the supreme liberations thus:

mn137:13.10.verse: ‘When shall I enter upon and abide in that base that the noble ones now enter upon and abide in?’ In one who thus generates a longing for the supreme liberations, grief arises with that longing as condition.

mn137:13.11.verse: Such grief as this is called grief based on renunciation.

mn137:13.12.verse: These are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation.

mn137:14.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life?

mn137:14.2.verse: On seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in a foolish infatuated ordinary person, in an untaught ordinary person who has not conquered his limitations or conquered the results [of action] and who is blind to danger.

mn137:14.3.verse: Such equanimity as this does not transcend the form;

mn137:14.4.verse: that is why it is called equanimity based on the household life.

mn137:14.5.verse: “On hearing a sound with the ear…

mn137:14.6.verse: On smelling an odour with the nose…

mn137:14.7.verse: On tasting a flavour with the tongue…

mn137:14.8.verse: On touching a tangible with the body…

mn137:14.9.verse: On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, equanimity arises in a foolish infatuated ordinary person, in an untaught ordinary person who has not conquered his limitations or conquered the results [of action] and who is blind to danger.

mn137:14.10.verse: Such equanimity as this does not transcend the mind-object;

mn137:14.11.verse: that is why it is called equanimity based on the household life.

mn137:14.12.verse: These are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.

mn137:15.1.verse: “Herein, what are the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation?

mn137:15.2.verse: When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of forms, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that forms both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, equanimity arises.

mn137:15.3.verse: Such equanimity as this transcends the form;

mn137:15.4.verse: that is why it is called equanimity based on renunciation.

mn137:15.5.verse: “When, by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of sounds…

mn137:15.9.verse: of mind-objects, one sees as it actually is with proper wisdom that mind-objects both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, equanimity arises.

mn137:15.10.verse: Such equanimity as this transcends the mind-object;

mn137:15.11.verse: that is why it is called equanimity based on renunciation.

mn137:15.12.verse: These are the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.

mn137:15.13.verse: “‘The thirty-six positions of beings should be understood’—

mn137:15.14.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:16.1.verse: “‘Therein, by depending on this, abandon that.’

mn137:16.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:16.3.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, by depending and relying on the six kinds of joy based on renunciation, abandon and surmount the six kinds of joy based on the household life.

mn137:16.4.verse: It is thus they are abandoned; it is thus they are surmounted.

mn137:16.5.verse: By depending and relying on the six kinds of grief based on renunciation, abandon and surmount the six kinds of grief based on the household life.

mn137:16.6.verse: It is thus they are abandoned; it is thus they are surmounted.

mn137:16.7.verse: By depending and relying on the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, abandon and surmount the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.

mn137:16.8.verse: It is thus they are abandoned; it is thus they are surmounted.

mn137:16.9.verse: “By depending and relying on the six kinds of joy based on renunciation, abandon and surmount the six kinds of grief based on renunciation.

mn137:16.10.verse: It is thus they are abandoned; it is thus they are surmounted.

mn137:16.11.verse: By depending and relying on the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, abandon and surmount the six kinds of joy based on renunciation.

mn137:16.12.verse: It is thus they are abandoned; it is thus they are surmounted.

mn137:17.1.verse: “There is, bhikkhus, equanimity that is diversified, based on diversity; and there is equanimity that is unified, based on unity.

mn137:18.1.verse: “And what, bhikkhus, is equanimity that is diversified, based on diversity?

mn137:18.2.verse: There is equanimity regarding forms, sounds, odours, flavours, and tangibles.

mn137:18.3.verse: This, bhikkhus, is equanimity that is diversified, based on diversity.

mn137:19.1.verse: “And what, bhikkhus, is equanimity that is unified, based on unity?

mn137:19.2.verse: There is equanimity regarding the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

mn137:19.3.verse: This, bhikkhus, is equanimity that is unified, based on unity.

mn137:20.1.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, by depending and relying on equanimity that is unified, based on unity, abandon and surmount equanimity that is diversified, based on diversity.

mn137:20.2.verse: It is thus this is abandoned; it is thus this is surmounted.

mn137:20.3.verse: “Bhikkhus, by depending and relying on non-identification, abandon and surmount equanimity that is unified, based on unity.

mn137:20.4.verse: It is thus this is abandoned; it is thus this is surmounted.

mn137:20.5.verse: “‘Therein, by depending on this, abandon that’—

mn137:20.6.verse: so it was in reference to this that it was said.

mn137:21.1.verse: “‘There are three foundations of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group.’

mn137:21.3.verse: And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:22.1.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, compassionate and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples out of compassion:

mn137:22.2.verse: ‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.’

mn137:22.3.verse: His disciples do not want to hear or give ear or exert their minds to understand; they err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn137:22.4.verse: With that the Tathāgata is not satisfied and feels no satisfaction; yet he dwells unmoved, mindful, and fully aware.

mn137:22.5.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the first foundation of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group.

mn137:23.1.verse: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, compassionate and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples out of compassion:

mn137:23.2.verse: ‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.’

mn137:23.3.verse: Some of his disciples will not hear or give ear or exert their minds to understand; they err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn137:23.4.verse: Some of his disciples will hear and give ear and exert their minds to understand; they do not err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn137:23.5.verse: With that the Tathāgata is not satisfied and feels no satisfaction,

mn137:23.6.verse: and he is not dissatisfied and feels no dissatisfaction;

mn137:23.7.verse: remaining free from both satisfaction and dissatisfaction,

mn137:23.8.verse: he dwells in equanimity, mindful, and fully aware.

mn137:23.9.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the second foundation of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group.

mn137:24.1.verse: “Furthermore, bhikkhus, compassionate and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the disciples out of compassion:

mn137:24.2.verse: ‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.’

mn137:24.3.verse: His disciples will hear and give ear and exert their minds to understand; they do not err and turn aside from the Teacher’s Dispensation.

mn137:24.4.verse: With that the Tathāgata is satisfied and feels satisfaction; yet he dwells unmoved, mindful, and fully aware.

mn137:24.5.verse: This, bhikkhus, is called the third foundation of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group.

mn137:24.6.verse: “‘There are three foundations of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group’—

mn137:24.7.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn137:25.1.verse: “‘Among the teachers of training it is he that is called the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed.’

mn137:25.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn137:25.3.verse: “Guided by the elephant tamer, bhikkhus, the elephant to be tamed goes in one direction—

mn137:26.1.verse: Guided by the horse tamer, bhikkhus, the horse to be tamed goes in one direction—

mn137:26.3.verse: Guided by the ox tamer, bhikkhus, the ox to be tamed goes in one direction—

mn137:26.5.verse: “Bhikkhus, guided by the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, the person to be tamed goes in eight directions.

mn137:27.1.verse: “Possessed of material form, he sees forms:

mn137:27.3.verse: Not perceiving forms internally, he sees forms externally:

mn137:27.5.verse: He is resolved only upon the beautiful:

mn137:27.7.verse: With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ he enters upon and abides in the base of infinite space:

mn137:27.9.verse: By completely surmounting the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters upon and abides in the base of infinite consciousness:

mn137:27.11.verse: By completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ he enters upon and abides in the base of nothingness:

mn137:27.13.verse: By completely surmounting the base of nothingness, he enters upon and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:

mn137:27.15.verse: By completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling:

mn137:27.17.verse: “Bhikkhus, guided by the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, the person to be tamed goes in these eight directions.

mn137:28.1.verse: “‘Among the teachers of training it is he that is called the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed’—

mn137:28.2.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.”

mn137:28.3.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn137:28.4.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn138:0.2.verse: A Summary Recital and its Analysis

mn138:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn138:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn138:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I shall teach you a summary recital and its analysis.

mn138:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn138:3.1.verse: “A mendicant should examine in whatever way such that, while examining, consciousness would neither be scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they would not be anxious because of grasping.

mn138:3.2.verse: When consciousness is neither scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they are not anxious because of grasping, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.”

mn138:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn138:4.2.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

mn138:5.1.verse: Soon after the Buddha left, those mendicants considered,

mn138:5.2.verse: “The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail.

mn138:5.5.verse: Who can explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha?”

mn138:5.7.verse: “This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

mn138:5.8.verse: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

mn138:5.9.verse: Let’s go to him, and ask him about this matter.”

mn138:6.1.verse: Then those mendicants went to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

mn138:6.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. They told him what had happened, and said,

mn138:7.1.verse: “Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But he’d pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves.

mn138:7.2.verse: Such is the consequence for the venerables. Though you were face to face with the Buddha, you bypassed him, imagining that you should ask me about this matter.

mn138:7.3.verse: For he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

mn138:7.4.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

mn138:7.5.verse: You should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

mn138:8.1.verse: “Certainly he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

mn138:8.2.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

mn138:8.3.verse: We should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.

mn138:8.4.verse: Still, Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

mn138:8.5.verse: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

mn138:8.6.verse: Please explain this, if it’s no trouble.”

mn138:9.1.verse: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn138:9.4.verse: “Reverends, the Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:

mn138:9.5.verse: ‘A mendicant should examine in whatever way such that, while examining, consciousness would neither be scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they would not be anxious because of grasping. When consciousness is neither scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they are not anxious because of grasping, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.’

mn138:9.6.verse: This is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.

mn138:10.1.verse: How is consciousness said to be scattered and diffused externally?

mn138:10.2.verse: In this case, when a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, and consciousness follows after the features of that sight—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in its features—consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:10.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn138:10.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn138:10.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn138:10.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn138:10.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, and consciousness follows after the features of that idea—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in its features—consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:10.8.verse: That’s how consciousness is said to be scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:11.1.verse: And how is consciousness said to be not scattered and diffused externally?

mn138:11.2.verse: In this case, when a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, but consciousness does not follow after the features of that sight—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in its features—consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:11.3.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

mn138:11.4.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

mn138:11.5.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

mn138:11.6.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

mn138:11.7.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, but consciousness does not follow after the features of that idea—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in its features—consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:11.8.verse: That’s how consciousness is said to be not scattered and diffused externally.

mn138:12.1.verse: And how is it said to be stuck internally?

mn138:12.2.verse: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn138:12.3.verse: When consciousness follows after that rapture and bliss born of seclusion—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that rapture and bliss born of seclusion—the mind is said to be stuck internally.

mn138:13.1.verse: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn138:13.2.verse: When consciousness follows after that rapture and bliss born of immersion—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that rapture and bliss born of immersion—the mind is said to be stuck internally.

mn138:14.1.verse: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

mn138:14.2.verse: When consciousness follows after that equanimity—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that bliss with equanimity—the mind is said to be stuck internally.

mn138:15.1.verse: Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

mn138:15.2.verse: When consciousness follows after that neutral feeling—tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that neutral feeling—the mind is said to be stuck internally.

mn138:15.3.verse: That’s how it is said to be stuck internally.

mn138:16.1.verse: And how is it said to be not stuck internally?

mn138:16.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn138:16.3.verse: When consciousness does not follow after that rapture and bliss born of seclusion—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that rapture and bliss born of seclusion—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.

mn138:17.1.verse: Furthermore, they enter the second absorption …

mn138:17.2.verse: When consciousness does not follow after that rapture and bliss born of immersion—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that rapture and bliss born of immersion—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.

mn138:18.1.verse: Furthermore, they enter and remain in the third absorption …

mn138:18.2.verse: When consciousness does not follow after that equanimity—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that bliss with equanimity—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.

mn138:19.1.verse: Furthermore, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption …

mn138:19.2.verse: When consciousness does not follow after that neutral feeling—not tied, attached, and fettered to gratification in that neutral feeling—the mind is said to be not stuck internally.

mn138:19.3.verse: That’s how it is said to be not stuck internally.

mn138:20.1.verse: And how is it anxious because of grasping?

mn138:20.2.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn138:20.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn138:20.4.verse: But that form decays and perishes,

mn138:20.5.verse: and consciousness latches on to the perishing of form.

mn138:20.6.verse: Anxieties occupy the mind, born of latching on to the perishing of form, and originating in accordance with natural principles.

mn138:20.7.verse: So it becomes frightened, worried, concerned, and anxious because of grasping.

mn138:20.11.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn138:20.12.verse: But that consciousness decays and perishes,

mn138:20.13.verse: and consciousness latches on to the perishing of consciousness.

mn138:20.14.verse: Anxieties occupy the mind, born of latching on to the perishing of consciousness, and originating in accordance with natural principles.

mn138:20.15.verse: So it becomes frightened, worried, concerned, and anxious because of grasping.

mn138:20.16.verse: That’s how it is anxious because of grasping.

mn138:21.1.verse: And how is it not anxious because of grasping?

mn138:21.2.verse: It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

mn138:21.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

mn138:21.4.verse: When that form decays and perishes,

mn138:21.5.verse: consciousness doesn’t latch on to the perishing of form.

mn138:21.6.verse: Anxieties—born of latching on to the perishing of form and originating in accordance with natural principles—don’t occupy the mind.

mn138:21.7.verse: So it does not become frightened, worried, concerned, or anxious because of grasping.

mn138:21.11.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

mn138:21.12.verse: When that consciousness decays and perishes,

mn138:21.13.verse: consciousness doesn’t latch on to the perishing of consciousness.

mn138:21.14.verse: Anxieties—born of latching on to the perishing of consciousness and originating in accordance with natural principles—don’t occupy the mind.

mn138:21.15.verse: So it does not become frightened, worried, concerned, or anxious because of grasping.

mn138:21.16.verse: That’s how it is not anxious because of grasping.

mn138:22.1.verse: The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:

mn138:22.2.verse: ‘A mendicant should examine in whatever way such that, while examining, consciousness would neither be scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they would not be anxious because of grasping.

mn138:22.3.verse: When consciousness is neither scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they are not anxious because of grasping, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.’

mn138:22.4.verse: And this is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.

mn138:22.5.verse: If you wish, you may go to the Buddha and ask him about this.

mn138:22.6.verse: You should remember it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

mn138:23.1.verse: Then those mendicants, approving and agreeing with what Mahākaccāna said, rose from their seats and went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened, adding:

mn138:23.15.verse: “Mahākaccāna clearly explained the meaning to us in this manner, with these words and phrases.”

mn138:24.1.verse: “Mahākaccāna is astute, mendicants, he has great wisdom.

mn138:24.2.verse: If you came to me and asked this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way as Mahākaccāna.

mn138:24.3.verse: That is what it means, and that’s how you should remember it.”

mn138:24.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn138:24.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn138:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn138:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn138:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you a summary and an exposition.

mn138:2.2.verse: Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn138:3.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:3.2.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.”

mn138:4.1.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn138:4.2.verse: Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling.

mn138:5.1.verse: Then, soon after the Blessed One had gone, the bhikkhus considered:

mn138:5.2.verse: “Now, friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning:

mn138:5.3.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:5.4.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.’

mn138:5.5.verse: Now who will expound this in detail?”

mn138:5.7.verse: “The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life.

mn138:5.8.verse: He is capable of expounding the detailed meaning.

mn138:5.9.verse: Suppose we went to him and asked him the meaning of this.”

mn138:6.1.verse: Then the bhikkhus went to the venerable Mahā Kaccāna and exchanged greetings with him.

mn138:6.2.verse: When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, they sat down to one side and told the venerable Mahā Kaccāna what had taken place:

mn138:6.3.verse: “Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning:

mn138:6.4.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:6.5.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.’

mn138:6.6.verse: Then, friend Kaccāna, soon after the Blessed One had gone, we considered:

mn138:6.7.verse: ‘Now, friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning:

mn138:6.8.verse: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:6.9.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.”

mn138:6.10.verse: Now who will expound this in detail?’

mn138:6.12.verse: ‘The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life.

mn138:6.13.verse: The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is capable of expounding the detailed meaning.

mn138:6.14.verse: Suppose we went to him and asked him the meaning of this.’—

mn138:6.15.verse: let the venerable Mahā Kaccāna expound it to us.”

mn138:7.1.verse: “Friends, it is as though a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, thought that heartwood should be sought for among the branches and leaves of a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, after he had passed over the root and the trunk.

mn138:7.2.verse: And so it is with you, venerable sirs, that you think that I should be asked about the meaning of this, after you passed the Blessed One by when you were face to face with the Teacher.

mn138:7.3.verse: For knowing, the Blessed One knows; seeing, he sees; he is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the holy one; he is the sayer, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.

mn138:7.4.verse: That was the time when you should have asked the Blessed One the meaning;

mn138:7.5.verse: as he told you, so you should have remembered it.”

mn138:8.1.verse: “Surely, friend Kaccāna, knowing, the Blessed One knows; seeing, he sees; he is vision…the Tathāgata.

mn138:8.2.verse: That was the time when we should have asked the Blessed One the meaning;

mn138:8.3.verse: as he told us, so we should have remembered it.

mn138:8.4.verse: Yet the venerable Mahā Kaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life.

mn138:8.5.verse: The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is capable of expounding the detailed meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One without expounding the detailed meaning.

mn138:8.6.verse: Let the venerable Mahā Kaccāna expound it without finding it troublesome.”

mn138:9.1.verse: “Then listen, friends, and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn138:9.3.verse: The venerable Mahā Kaccāna said this:

mn138:9.4.verse: “Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, that is:

mn138:9.5.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated. If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.’

mn138:9.6.verse: I understand the detailed meaning of this summary to be thus.

mn138:10.1.verse: “How, friends, is consciousness called ‘distracted and scattered externally’?

mn138:10.2.verse: Here, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, if his consciousness follows after the sign of form, is tied and shackled by gratification in the sign of form, is fettered by the fetter of gratification in the sign of form, then his consciousness is called ‘distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:10.3.verse: “When he has heard a sound with the ear…

mn138:10.4.verse: smelt an odour with the nose…

mn138:10.5.verse: tasted a flavour with the tongue…

mn138:10.6.verse: touched a tangible with the body…

mn138:10.7.verse: cognized a mind-object with the mind, if his consciousness follows after the sign of the mind-object, is tied and shackled by gratification in the sign of the mind-object, is fettered by the fetter of gratification in the sign of the mind-object, then his consciousness is called ‘distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:10.8.verse: That is how, friends, consciousness is called ‘distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:11.1.verse: “And how, friends, is consciousness called ‘not distracted and scattered externally’?

mn138:11.2.verse: Here, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, if his consciousness does not follow after the sign of form, is not tied and shackled by gratification in the sign of form, is not fettered by the fetter of gratification in the sign of form, then his consciousness is called ‘not distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:11.3.verse: “When he has heard a sound with the ear…

mn138:11.4.verse: smelt an odour with the nose…

mn138:11.5.verse: tasted a flavour with the tongue…

mn138:11.6.verse: touched a tangible with the body…

mn138:11.7.verse: cognized a mind-object with the mind, if his consciousness does not follow after the sign of the mind-object, is not tied and shackled by gratification in the sign of the mind-object, is not fettered by the fetter of gratification in the sign of the mind-object, then his consciousness is called ‘not distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:11.8.verse: That is how, friends, consciousness is called ‘not distracted and scattered externally.’

mn138:12.1.verse: “And how, friends, is the mind called ‘stuck internally’?

mn138:12.2.verse: Here, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

mn138:12.3.verse: If his consciousness follows after the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, is tied and shackled by gratification in the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, then his mind is called ‘stuck internally.’

mn138:13.1.verse: “Again, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.

mn138:13.2.verse: If his consciousness follows after the rapture and pleasure born of concentration…then his mind is called ‘stuck internally.’

mn138:14.1.verse: “Again, with the fading away as well of rapture, a bhikkhu abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’

mn138:14.2.verse: If his consciousness follows after the equanimity…then his mind is called ‘stuck internally.’

mn138:15.1.verse: “Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

mn138:15.2.verse: If his consciousness follows after the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, is tied and shackled by gratification in the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, is fettered by the fetter of gratification in the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, then his mind is called ‘stuck internally.’

mn138:15.3.verse: That is how the mind is called ‘stuck internally.’

mn138:16.1.verse: “And how, friends, is the mind called ‘not stuck internally’?

mn138:16.2.verse: Here, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna…

mn138:16.3.verse: If his consciousness does not follow after the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, is not tied and shackled by gratification in the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, is not fettered by the fetter of gratification in the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, then his mind is called ‘not stuck internally.’

mn138:17.1.verse: “Again, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna…

mn138:17.2.verse: If his consciousness does not follow after the rapture and pleasure born of concentration…then his mind is called ‘not stuck internally.’

mn138:18.1.verse: “Again, with the fading away as well of rapture, a bhikkhu…enters upon and abides in the third jhāna…

mn138:18.2.verse: If his consciousness does not follow after the equanimity…then his mind is called ‘not stuck internally.’

mn138:19.1.verse: “Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain…a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna…

mn138:19.2.verse: If his consciousness does not follow after the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, is not tied and shackled by gratification in the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, is not fettered by the fetter of gratification in the neither-pain-nor-pleasure, then his mind is called ‘not stuck internally.’

mn138:19.3.verse: That is how the mind is called ‘not stuck internally.’

mn138:20.1.verse: “How, friends, is there agitation due to clinging?

mn138:20.2.verse: Here an untaught ordinary person who has no regard for noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for true men and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma,

mn138:20.3.verse: regards material form as self, or self as possessed of material form, or material form as in self, or self as in material form.

mn138:20.4.verse: That material form of his changes and becomes otherwise.

mn138:20.5.verse: With the change and becoming otherwise of that material form, his consciousness is preoccupied with the change of material form.

mn138:20.6.verse: Agitated mental states born of preoccupation with the change of material form arise together and remain obsessing his mind.

mn138:20.7.verse: Because his mind is obsessed, he is anxious, distressed, and concerned, and due to clinging he becomes agitated.

mn138:20.11.verse: He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.

mn138:20.12.verse: That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.

mn138:20.13.verse: With the change and becoming otherwise of that consciousness, his consciousness is preoccupied with the change of consciousness.

mn138:20.14.verse: Agitated states of mind born of preoccupation with the change of consciousness arise together and remain obsessing his mind.

mn138:20.15.verse: Because his mind is obsessed, he is anxious, distressed, and concerned, and due to clinging he becomes agitated.

mn138:20.16.verse: That is how there is agitation due to clinging.

mn138:21.1.verse: “And how, friends, is there non-agitation due to non-clinging?

mn138:21.2.verse: Here a well-taught noble disciple who has regard for noble ones and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma, who has regard for true men and is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma,

mn138:21.3.verse: does not regard material form as self, or self as possessed of material form, or material form as in self, or self as in material form.

mn138:21.4.verse: That material form of his changes and becomes otherwise.

mn138:21.5.verse: With the change and becoming otherwise of that material form, his consciousness is not preoccupied with the change of material form.

mn138:21.6.verse: Agitated mental states born of preoccupation with the change of material form do not arise together and remain obsessing his mind.

mn138:21.7.verse: Because his mind is not obsessed, he is not anxious, distressed, and concerned, and due to non-clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:21.8.verse: “He does not regard feeling as self…

mn138:21.9.verse: He does not regard perception as self…

mn138:21.10.verse: He does not regard formations as self…

mn138:21.11.verse: He does not regard consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.

mn138:21.12.verse: That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.

mn138:21.13.verse: With the change and becoming otherwise of that consciousness, his consciousness is not preoccupied with the change of consciousness.

mn138:21.14.verse: Agitated mental states born of preoccupation with the change of consciousness do not arise together and remain obsessing his mind.

mn138:21.15.verse: Because his mind is not obsessed, he is not anxious, distressed, and concerned, and due to non-clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:21.16.verse: That is how there is non-agitation due to non-clinging.

mn138:22.1.verse: “Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, that is:

mn138:22.2.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:22.3.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future,’

mn138:22.4.verse: I understand the detailed meaning of this summary to be thus.

mn138:22.5.verse: Now, friends, if you wish, go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this.

mn138:22.6.verse: As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should remember it.”

mn138:23.1.verse: Then the bhikkhus, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Mahā Kaccāna’s words, rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, they sat down at one side and told the Blessed One all that had taken place after he had left:

mn138:23.2.verse: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning:

mn138:23.3.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:23.4.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.’

mn138:23.5.verse: Then, venerable sir, soon after the Blessed One had gone, we considered:

mn138:23.6.verse: ‘Now, friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone into his dwelling after giving a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning:

mn138:23.7.verse: Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that while he is examining them, his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging he does not become agitated.

mn138:23.8.verse: If his consciousness is not distracted and scattered externally nor stuck internally, and if by not clinging he does not become agitated, then for him there is no origination of suffering—of birth, ageing, and death in the future.

mn138:23.9.verse: Now who will expound this in detail?’

mn138:23.11.verse: ‘The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life.

mn138:23.12.verse: The venerable Mahā Kaccāna is capable of expounding the detailed meaning.

mn138:23.13.verse: Suppose we went to him and asked him the meaning of this.’

mn138:23.14.verse: Then, venerable sir, we went to the venerable Mahā Kaccāna and asked him about the meaning.

mn138:23.15.verse: The venerable Mahā Kaccāna expounded the meaning to us with these terms, statements, and phrases.”

mn138:24.1.verse: “Mahā Kaccāna is wise, bhikkhus, Mahā Kaccāna has great wisdom.

mn138:24.2.verse: If you had asked me the meaning of this, I would have explained it to you in the same way that Mahā Kaccāna has explained it.

mn138:24.3.verse: Such is its meaning, and so you should remember it.”

mn138:24.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn138:24.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn139:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn139:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn139:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I shall teach you the analysis of no strife.

mn139:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn139:3.1.verse: “Don’t indulge in sensual pleasure, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And don’t indulge in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.

mn139:3.2.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

mn139:3.3.verse: Know what it means to flatter and to rebuke.

mn139:3.4.verse: Knowing these, avoid them, and just teach Dhamma.

mn139:3.5.verse: Know how to evaluate different kinds of pleasure.

mn139:3.7.verse: Don’t talk behind people’s backs, and don’t speak sharply in their presence.

mn139:3.9.verse: Don’t insist on popular definitions and don’t overstep normal labels.

mn139:3.10.verse: This is the summary recital for the analysis of no strife.

mn139:4.1.verse: ‘Don’t indulge in sensual pleasure, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And don’t indulge in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.’

mn139:4.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:4.3.verse: Indulging in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. It is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:4.4.verse: Breaking off such indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:4.5.verse: Indulging in self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and pointless. It is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:4.6.verse: Breaking off such indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:4.7.verse: ‘Don’t indulge in sensual pleasure, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And don’t indulge in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.’

mn139:4.8.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:5.1.verse: ‘Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.’

mn139:5.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:5.3.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

mn139:5.4.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

mn139:5.5.verse: ‘Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.’

mn139:5.6.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:6.1.verse: ‘Know what it means to flatter and to rebuke.

mn139:6.2.verse: Knowing these, avoid them, and just teach Dhamma.’

mn139:6.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:7.1.verse: And how is there flattering and rebuking without teaching Dhamma?

mn139:7.2.verse: ‘All those who indulge in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality—low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless—are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:7.3.verse: In speaking like this, one rebukes some here.

mn139:7.4.verse: ‘All those who have broken off indulging in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:7.5.verse: In speaking like this, one flatters some here.

mn139:7.6.verse: ‘All those who indulge in self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and pointless—are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:7.7.verse: In speaking like this, one rebukes some here.

mn139:7.8.verse: ‘All those who have broken off indulging in self-mortification are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:7.9.verse: In speaking like this, one flatters some here.

mn139:7.10.verse: ‘All those who have not given up the fetter of continued existence are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:7.11.verse: In speaking like this, one rebukes some here.

mn139:7.12.verse: ‘All those who have given up the fetter of continued existence are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:7.13.verse: In speaking like this, one flatters some here.

mn139:7.14.verse: That’s how there is flattering and rebuking without teaching Dhamma.

mn139:8.1.verse: And how is there neither flattering nor rebuking, and just teaching Dhamma?

mn139:8.2.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who indulge in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality—low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless—are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:8.3.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.4.verse: ‘The indulgence is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.’

mn139:8.7.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who have broken off indulging in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:8.8.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.9.verse: ‘Breaking off the indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.’

mn139:8.12.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who indulge in self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and pointless—are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:8.13.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.14.verse: ‘The indulgence is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.’

mn139:8.17.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who have broken off indulging in self-mortification are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:8.18.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.19.verse: ‘Breaking off the indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.’

mn139:8.22.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who have not given up the fetter of continued existence are beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the wrong way.’

mn139:8.23.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.24.verse: ‘When the fetter of continued existence is not given up, continued existence is also not given up.’

mn139:8.26.verse: You don’t say: ‘All those who have given up the fetter of continued existence are free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and they are practicing the right way.’

mn139:8.27.verse: Rather, by saying this you just teach Dhamma:

mn139:8.28.verse: ‘When the fetter of continued existence is given up, continued existence is also given up.’

mn139:8.30.verse: That’s how there is neither flattering nor rebuking, and just teaching Dhamma.

mn139:8.31.verse: ‘Know what it means to flatter and to rebuke.

mn139:8.32.verse: Knowing these, avoid them, and just teach Dhamma.’

mn139:8.33.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:9.1.verse: ‘Know how to evaluate different kinds of pleasure.

mn139:9.3.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:9.4.verse: There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn139:9.6.verse: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn139:9.10.verse: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn139:9.11.verse: These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

mn139:9.12.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called sensual pleasure—a filthy, common, ignoble pleasure.

mn139:9.13.verse: Such pleasure should not be cultivated or developed, but should be feared, I say.

mn139:9.14.verse: Now, take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

mn139:9.15.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption …

mn139:9.18.verse: This is called the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening.

mn139:9.19.verse: Such pleasure should be cultivated and developed, and should not be feared, I say.

mn139:9.20.verse: ‘Know how to evaluate different kinds of pleasure.

mn139:9.22.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:10.1.verse: ‘Don’t talk behind people’s backs, and don’t speak sharply in their presence.’

mn139:10.3.verse: but why did I say it?

mn139:10.4.verse: When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is untrue, false, and pointless, then to the best of your ability you should not speak.

mn139:10.5.verse: When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is true and correct, but pointless, then you should train yourself not to speak.

mn139:10.6.verse: When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is true, correct, and beneficial, then you should know the right time to speak.

mn139:10.7.verse: When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are untrue, false, and pointless, then to the best of your ability you should not speak.

mn139:10.8.verse: When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are true and correct, but pointless, then you should train yourself not to speak.

mn139:10.9.verse: When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are true, correct, and beneficial, then you should know the right time to speak.

mn139:10.10.verse: ‘Don’t talk behind people’s backs, and don’t speak sharply in their presence.’

mn139:10.11.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:11.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:11.3.verse: When speaking hurriedly, your body gets tired, your mind gets stressed, your voice gets stressed, your throat gets sore, and your words become unclear and hard to understand.

mn139:11.4.verse: When not speaking hurriedly, your body doesn’t get tired, your mind doesn’t get stressed, your voice doesn’t get stressed, your throat doesn’t get sore, and your words are clear and easy to understand.

mn139:11.6.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:12.1.verse: ‘Don’t insist on popular definitions and don’t overstep normal labels.’

mn139:12.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn139:12.3.verse: And how do you insist on popular definitions and overstep normal labels?

mn139:12.4.verse: It’s when among different populations they label the same thing as a ‘cup’, a ‘bowl’, a ‘jar’, a ‘scoop’, a ‘vessel’, a ‘dish’, or a ‘plate’.

mn139:12.5.verse: And however it is known among those various populations, you speak accordingly, obstinately sticking to that and insisting:

mn139:12.6.verse: ‘This is the only truth, anything else is futile.’

mn139:12.7.verse: That’s how you insist on popular definitions and overstep normal labels.

mn139:12.8.verse: And how do you not insist on popular definitions and overstep normal labels?

mn139:12.9.verse: It’s when among different populations they label the same thing as a ‘cup’, a ‘bowl’, a ‘jar’, a ‘scoop’, a ‘vessel’, a ‘dish’, or a ‘plate’.

mn139:12.10.verse: And however it is known among those various populations, you speak accordingly, thinking: ‘It seems that the venerables are referring to this.’

mn139:12.11.verse: That’s how you don’t insist on popular definitions and don’t overstep normal labels.

mn139:12.12.verse: ‘Don’t insist on popular definitions and don’t overstep normal labels.’

mn139:12.13.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn139:13.1.verse: Now, mendicants, indulging in the happiness of the pleasure linked to sensuality is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. It is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.3.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.4.verse: Breaking off such indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.6.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.7.verse: Indulging in self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and pointless. It is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.9.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.10.verse: Breaking off such indulgence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.12.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.13.verse: The middle way of practice that was understood by the Realized One gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment. It is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.15.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.16.verse: Flattering and rebuking without teaching Dhamma is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.18.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.19.verse: Neither flattering nor rebuking, and just teaching Dhamma is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.21.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.22.verse: Sensual pleasure—a filthy, common, ignoble pleasure—is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.24.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.25.verse: The pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.27.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.28.verse: Saying untrue, false, and pointless things behind someone’s back is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.30.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.31.verse: Saying true and correct, but pointless things behind someone’s back is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.33.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.34.verse: Saying true, correct, and beneficial things behind someone’s back is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.36.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.37.verse: Saying untrue, false, and pointless things in someone’s presence is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.39.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.40.verse: Saying true and correct, but pointless things in someone’s presence is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.42.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.43.verse: Saying true, correct, and beneficial things in someone’s presence is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.45.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.46.verse: Speaking hurriedly is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.48.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.49.verse: Speaking unhurriedly is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.51.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:13.52.verse: Insisting on popular definitions and overriding common usage is a principle beset by pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.54.verse: That’s why this is a principle beset by strife.

mn139:13.55.verse: Not insisting on popular definitions and not overriding common usage is a principle free of pain, harm, stress, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:13.57.verse: That’s why this is a principle free of strife.

mn139:14.1.verse: So you should train like this: ‘We shall know the principles beset by strife and the principles free of strife.

mn139:14.2.verse: Knowing this, we will practice the way free of strife.’

mn139:14.3.verse: And, mendicants, the gentleman Subhūti practices the way free of strife.”

mn139:14.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn139:14.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn139:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn139:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn139:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you an exposition of non-conflict.

mn139:2.2.verse: Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn139:3.1.verse: “One should not pursue sensual pleasure, which is low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and one should not pursue self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.

mn139:3.2.verse: The Middle Way discovered by the Tathāgata avoids both these extremes; giving vision, giving knowledge, it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

mn139:3.3.verse: One should know what it is to extol and what it is to disparage,

mn139:3.4.verse: and knowing both, one should neither extol nor disparage but should teach only the Dhamma.

mn139:3.5.verse: One should know how to define pleasure,

mn139:3.6.verse: and knowing that, one should pursue pleasure within oneself.

mn139:3.7.verse: One should not utter covert speech, and one should not utter overt sharp speech.

mn139:3.8.verse: One should speak unhurriedly, not hurriedly.

mn139:3.9.verse: One should not insist on local language, and one should not override normal usage.

mn139:3.10.verse: This is the summary of the exposition of non-conflict.

mn139:4.1.verse: “‘One should not pursue sensual pleasure, which is low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and one should not pursue self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.’

mn139:4.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:4.3.verse: “The pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:4.4.verse: Disengagement from the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:4.5.verse: “The pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and it is the wrong way.

mn139:4.6.verse: Disengagement from the pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and it is the right way.

mn139:4.7.verse: ‘One should not pursue sensual pleasure, which is low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and one should not pursue self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial’—

mn139:4.8.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:5.1.verse: “‘The Middle Way discovered by the Tathāgata avoids both these extremes; giving vision, giving knowledge, it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.’

mn139:5.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:5.3.verse: It is just this Noble Eightfold Path; that is,

mn139:5.4.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

mn139:5.5.verse: ‘The Middle Way discovered by the Tathāgata avoids both these extremes…to Nibbāna’—

mn139:5.6.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:6.1.verse: “‘One should know what it is to extol and what it is to disparage,

mn139:6.2.verse: and knowing both, one should neither extol nor disparage but should teach only the Dhamma.’

mn139:6.3.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:7.1.verse: “How, bhikkhus, does there come to be extolling and disparaging and failure to teach only the Dhamma?

mn139:7.2.verse: When one says: ‘All those engaged in the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low…and unbeneficial—are beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the wrong way,’

mn139:7.4.verse: When one says: ‘All those disengaged from the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low…and unbeneficial—are without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the right way,’

mn139:7.6.verse: When one says: ‘All those engaged in the pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the wrong way,’

mn139:7.8.verse: When one says: ‘All those disengaged from the pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—are without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the right way,’

mn139:7.10.verse: When one says: ‘All those who have not abandoned the fetter of being are beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the wrong way,’

mn139:7.12.verse: When one says: ‘All those who have abandoned the fetter of being are without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, and they have entered upon the right way,’

mn139:7.14.verse: This is how, bhikkhus, there comes to be extolling and disparaging and failure to teach only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.1.verse: “And how, bhikkhus, does there come to be neither extolling nor disparaging but teaching only the Dhamma?

mn139:8.2.verse: ‘All those engaged in the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires…have entered upon the wrong way’—

mn139:8.4.verse: But saying instead: ‘The pursuit is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:8.5.verse: and it is the wrong way,’

mn139:8.6.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.7.verse: ‘All those disengaged from the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires…have entered upon the right way’—

mn139:8.9.verse: But saying instead: ‘The disengagement is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:8.10.verse: and it is the right way,’

mn139:8.11.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.12.verse: ‘All those engaged in the pursuit of self-mortification…have entered upon the wrong way’—

mn139:8.14.verse: But saying instead: ‘The pursuit is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:8.15.verse: and it is the wrong way,’

mn139:8.16.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.17.verse: ‘All those disengaged from the pursuit of self-mortification…have entered upon the right way’—

mn139:8.19.verse: But saying instead: ‘The disengagement is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:8.20.verse: and it is the right way,’

mn139:8.21.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.22.verse: ‘All those who have not abandoned the fetter of being…have entered upon the wrong way’—

mn139:8.24.verse: But saying instead: ‘As long as the fetter of being is unabandoned, being too is unabandoned,’

mn139:8.25.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.
