mn139:8.26.verse: ‘All those who have abandoned the fetter of being…have entered upon the right way’—

mn139:8.28.verse: But saying instead: ‘When the fetter of being is abandoned, being also is abandoned,’

mn139:8.29.verse: one thus teaches only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.30.verse: This is how, bhikkhus, there comes to be neither extolling nor disparaging but teaching only the Dhamma.

mn139:8.31.verse: ‘One should know what it is to extol and what it is to disparage,

mn139:8.32.verse: and knowing both, one should neither extol nor disparage but should teach only the Dhamma’—

mn139:8.33.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:9.1.verse: “‘One should know how to define pleasure,

mn139:9.2.verse: and knowing that, one should pursue pleasure within oneself.’

mn139:9.3.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:9.4.verse: Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.

mn139:9.10.verse: tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.

mn139:9.11.verse: These are the five cords of sensual pleasure.

mn139:9.12.verse: Now the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five cords of sensual pleasure are called sensual pleasure—a filthy pleasure, a coarse pleasure, an ignoble pleasure.

mn139:9.13.verse: I say of this kind of pleasure that it should not be pursued, that it should not be developed, that it should not be cultivated, and that it should be feared.

mn139:9.14.verse: Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna…

mn139:9.18.verse: This is called the bliss of renunciation, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace, the bliss of enlightenment.

mn139:9.19.verse: I say of this kind of pleasure that it should be pursued, that it should be developed, that it should be cultivated, and that it should not be feared.

mn139:9.20.verse: ‘One should know how to define pleasure,

mn139:9.21.verse: and knowing that, one should pursue pleasure within oneself’—

mn139:9.22.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:10.1.verse: “‘One should not utter covert speech, and one should not utter overt sharp speech.’

mn139:10.3.verse: And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:10.4.verse: Here, bhikkhus, when one knows covert speech to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, one should on no account utter it.

mn139:10.5.verse: When one knows covert speech to be true, correct, and unbeneficial, one should try not to utter it.

mn139:10.6.verse: But when one knows covert speech to be true, correct, and beneficial, one may utter it, knowing the time to do so.

mn139:10.7.verse: Here, bhikkhus, when one knows overt sharp speech to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, one should on no account utter it.

mn139:10.8.verse: When one knows overt sharp speech to be true, correct, and unbeneficial, one should try not to utter it.

mn139:10.9.verse: But when one knows overt sharp speech to be true, correct, and beneficial, one may utter it, knowing the time to do so.

mn139:10.10.verse: ‘One should not utter covert speech, and one should not utter overt sharp speech’—

mn139:10.11.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:11.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:11.3.verse: Here, bhikkhus, when one speaks hurriedly, one’s body grows tired and one’s mind becomes excited, one’s voice is strained and one’s throat becomes hoarse, and the speech of one who speaks hurriedly is indistinct and hard to understand.

mn139:11.4.verse: Here, bhikkhus, when one speaks unhurriedly, one’s body does not grow tired nor does one’s mind become excited, one’s voice is not strained nor does one’s throat become hoarse, and the speech of one who speaks unhurriedly is distinct and easy to understand.

mn139:11.6.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:12.1.verse: “‘One should not insist on local language, and one should not override normal usage.’

mn139:12.2.verse: So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn139:12.3.verse: “How, bhikkhus, does there come to be insistence on local language and overriding of normal usage?

mn139:12.4.verse: Here, bhikkhus, in different localities they call the same thing a ‘dish’ [pāti], a ‘bowl’ [patta], a ‘vessel’ [vittha], a ‘saucer’ [serāva], a ‘pan’ [dhāropa], a ‘pot’ [poṇa], or a ‘basin’ [pisīla].

mn139:12.5.verse: So whatever they call it in such and such a locality, one speaks accordingly, firmly adhering [to that expression] and insisting:

mn139:12.6.verse: ‘Only this is correct; anything else is wrong.’

mn139:12.7.verse: This is how, bhikkhus, there comes to be insistence on local language and overriding normal usage.

mn139:12.8.verse: “And how, bhikkhus, does there come to be non-insistence on local language and non-overriding of normal usage?

mn139:12.9.verse: Here, bhikkhus, in different localities they call the same thing a ‘dish’…or a ‘basin.’

mn139:12.10.verse: So whatever they call it in such and such a locality, without adhering [to that expression] one speaks accordingly, thinking: ‘These venerable ones, it seems, are speaking with reference to this.’

mn139:12.11.verse: This is how, bhikkhus, there comes to be non-insistence on local language and non-overriding of normal usage.

mn139:12.12.verse: ‘One should not insist on local language, and one should not override normal usage’—

mn139:12.13.verse: so it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn139:13.1.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.2.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.3.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.4.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, disengagement from the pursuit of the enjoyment of one whose pleasure is linked to sensual desires—low, vulgar, coarse, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.5.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.6.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.7.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.8.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.9.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.10.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, disengagement from the pursuit of self-mortification—painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.11.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.12.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.13.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the Middle Way discovered by the Tathāgata avoids both these extremes; giving vision, giving knowledge, it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. It is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.14.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.15.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.16.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, extolling and disparaging and failure to teach only the Dhamma is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.17.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.18.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.19.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, not extolling and not disparaging and teaching only the Dhamma is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.20.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.21.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.22.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, sensual pleasure—a filthy pleasure, a coarse pleasure, an ignoble pleasure—is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.23.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.24.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.25.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the bliss of renunciation, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace, the bliss of enlightenment, is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.26.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.27.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.28.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, covert speech that is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.29.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.30.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.31.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, covert speech that is true, correct, and unbeneficial is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.32.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.33.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.34.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, covert speech that is true, correct, and beneficial is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.35.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.36.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.37.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, overt sharp speech that is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.38.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.39.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.40.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, overt sharp speech that is true, correct, and unbeneficial is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.41.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.42.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.43.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, overt sharp speech that is true, correct, and beneficial is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.44.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.45.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.46.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the speech of one who speaks hurriedly is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.47.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.48.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.49.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, the speech of one who speaks unhurriedly is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.50.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.51.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:13.52.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, insistence on local language and overriding of normal usage is a state beset by suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.53.verse: and it is the wrong way.

mn139:13.54.verse: Therefore this is a state with conflict.

mn139:13.55.verse: “Here, bhikkhus, non-insistence on local language and non-overriding of normal usage is a state without suffering, vexation, despair, and fever,

mn139:13.56.verse: and it is the right way.

mn139:13.57.verse: Therefore this is a state without conflict.

mn139:14.1.verse: “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall know the state with conflict and we shall know the state without conflict,

mn139:14.2.verse: and knowing these, we shall enter upon the way without conflict.’

mn139:14.3.verse: Now, bhikkhus, Subhūti is a clansman who has entered upon the way without conflict.”

mn139:14.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn139:14.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn140:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering by stages in the Magadhan country, arrived at Rājagaha;

mn140:1.3.verse: he went to Bhaggava the potter and said to Bhaggava the potter:

mn140:2.1.verse: ‘If it is no inconvenience to you, Bhaggava, I will stay in your workshop for one night.’

mn140:2.2.verse: ‘It is no inconvenience to me, venerable sir.

mn140:2.3.verse: But there is a homeless one who has already taken up his abode there first.

mn140:2.4.verse: If he agrees, venerable sir, stay as long as you like.’

mn140:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, on account of the Blessed One.

mn140:3.2.verse: He had already taken up his abode in that potter’s workshop first.

mn140:3.3.verse: Then the Blessed One went to the venerable Pukkusāti and said to the venerable Pukkusāti:

mn140:3.4.verse: ‘If it is no inconvenience to you, bhikkhu, I will stay in the workshop for one night.’

mn140:3.5.verse: ‘The potter’s workshop is roomy enough, friend.

mn140:3.6.verse: Let the venerable one stay as long as he likes.’

mn140:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop, and having spread out a grass mat at one end, he sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.

mn140:4.2.verse: Then the Blessed One spent much of the night seated.

mn140:4.3.verse: The venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night seated.

mn140:4.5.verse: ‘This clansman conducts himself in a way that inspires confidence.

mn140:4.7.verse: Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Pukkusāti:

mn140:5.1.verse: ‘Under whom have you gone forth, bhikkhu? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’

mn140:5.2.verse: ‘There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, who went forth from a Sakyan clan.

mn140:5.3.verse: Now a good report of that Blessed One Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn140:5.4.verse: “That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.”

mn140:5.5.verse: I have gone forth on account of that Blessed One.

mn140:5.6.verse: That Blessed One is my teacher.

mn140:5.7.verse: I profess the Dhamma of that Blessed One.’

mn140:5.8.verse: ‘But, bhikkhu, where is that Blessed One, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, living now?’

mn140:5.9.verse: ‘There is, friend, in the northern country, a city called Sāvatthī.

mn140:5.10.verse: There that Blessed One, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, is living now.’

mn140:5.11.verse: ‘But, bhikkhu, have you seen that Blessed One before;

mn140:5.12.verse: and would you recognize him if you saw him?’

mn140:5.13.verse: ‘I have not seen that Blessed One before, friend;

mn140:5.14.verse: and I would not recognize him if I saw him.’

mn140:6.2.verse: ‘This clansman has gone forth on account of me.

mn140:6.3.verse: What if I taught him the Dhamma?’

mn140:6.4.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti:

mn140:6.5.verse: ‘Bhikkhu, I shall teach you the Dhamma.

mn140:6.6.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn140:6.7.verse: ‘Yes, friend,’ the venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One.

mn140:7.1.verse: ‘This man, bhikkhu, has six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen kinds of mental exploration, and four foundations;

mn140:7.2.verse: steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace.

mn140:7.3.verse: He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone—

mn140:7.4.verse: this is the summary of the exposition of the elements.

mn140:8.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:8.3.verse: There are, bhikkhu, these six elements:

mn140:8.4.verse: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.

mn140:8.6.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:9.1.verse: ‘“This man, bhikkhu, has six bases of contact”—

mn140:9.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:9.3.verse: The eye-contact base, the ear-contact base, the nose-contact base, the tongue-contact base, the body-contact base, the mind-contact base.

mn140:9.4.verse: “This man, bhikkhu, has six bases of contact”—

mn140:9.5.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:10.1.verse: ‘“This man, bhikkhu, has eighteen kinds of mental exploration”—

mn140:10.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:10.3.verse: On seeing a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy, one explores a form that is a basis for grief, one explores a form that is a basis for equanimity;

mn140:10.4.verse: on hearing a sound with the ear …

mn140:10.5.verse: on smelling an odour with the nose …

mn140:10.6.verse: on tasting a flavour with the tongue …

mn140:10.7.verse: on touching a tangible with the body …

mn140:10.8.verse: on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for joy, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for grief, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for equanimity—

mn140:10.9.verse: so there are six kinds of exploration with joy, six kinds of exploration with grief, and six kinds of exploration with equanimity.

mn140:10.10.verse: “This man, bhikkhu, has eighteen kinds of mental exploration”—

mn140:10.11.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:11.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:11.3.verse: The foundation of understanding, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, the foundation of peace.

mn140:11.5.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:12.1.verse: ‘“He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone”—

mn140:12.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:13.1.verse: And how, bhikkhu, does one not neglect understanding?

mn140:13.2.verse: There are, bhikkhu, these six elements:

mn140:13.3.verse: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.

mn140:14.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element?

mn140:14.2.verse: The earth element can be either in oneself or external.

mn140:14.3.verse: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element in oneself?

mn140:14.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn140:14.5.verse: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to—

mn140:14.6.verse: this, bhikkhu, is called the earth element in oneself.

mn140:14.7.verse: Now the earth element in oneself and the external earth element are simply earth element.

mn140:14.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn140:14.9.verse: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the earth element, and one fades lust for the earth element out of the mind.

mn140:15.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the water element?

mn140:15.2.verse: The water element can be either in oneself or external.

mn140:15.3.verse: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element in oneself?

mn140:15.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn140:15.5.verse: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to—

mn140:15.6.verse: this, bhikkhu, is called the water element in oneself.

mn140:15.7.verse: Now the water element in oneself and the external water element are simply water element.

mn140:15.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn140:15.9.verse: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the water element, and one fades lust for the water element out of the mind.

mn140:16.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element?

mn140:16.2.verse: The fire element can be either in oneself or external.

mn140:16.3.verse: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element in oneself?

mn140:16.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn140:16.5.verse: that whereby one is warmed, ages, and is consumed, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to—

mn140:16.6.verse: this, bhikkhu, is called the fire element in oneself.

mn140:16.7.verse: Now the fire element in oneself and the external fire element are simply fire element.

mn140:16.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn140:16.9.verse: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the fire element, and one fades lust for the fire element out of the mind.

mn140:17.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the air element?

mn140:17.2.verse: The air element can be either in oneself or external.

mn140:17.3.verse: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element in oneself?

mn140:17.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn140:17.5.verse: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that pervade all the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to—

mn140:17.6.verse: this, bhikkhu, is called the air element in oneself.

mn140:17.7.verse: Now the air element in oneself and the external air element are simply air element.

mn140:17.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn140:17.9.verse: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the air element, and one fades lust for the air element out of the mind.

mn140:18.1.verse: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the space element?

mn140:18.2.verse: The space element can be either in oneself or external.

mn140:18.3.verse: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element in oneself?

mn140:18.4.verse: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, and clung-to, that is to say,

mn140:18.5.verse: the ear-hole, the nose-hole, the door of the mouth, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed, and where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted collects, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted passes out below, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, void, an opening, unfilled by flesh or blood, and clung-to—

mn140:18.6.verse: this, bhikkhu, is called the space element in oneself.

mn140:18.7.verse: Now the space element in oneself and the external space element are simply space element.

mn140:18.8.verse: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”

mn140:18.9.verse: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the space element, and one fades lust for the space element out of the mind.

mn140:19.1.verse: ‘Then there remains only consciousness, purified and bright.

mn140:19.2.verse: And what does one cognize with that consciousness?

mn140:19.3.verse: One cognizes: “Pleasant,” one cognizes: “Painful,” one cognizes: “Neither-painful-nor-pleasant.”

mn140:19.4.verse: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as pleasant, there arises pleasant feeling.

mn140:19.5.verse: Feeling pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel pleasant feeling.”

mn140:19.6.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as pleasant, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:19.7.verse: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as painful, there arises painful feeling.

mn140:19.8.verse: Feeling painful feeling, one understands: “I feel painful feeling.”

mn140:19.9.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as painful, the painful feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:19.10.verse: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

mn140:19.11.verse: Feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

mn140:19.12.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:19.13.verse: Just as, bhikkhu, from the contact and friction of two fire-sticks heat is generated and fire is produced, and with the separation and parting of those same two sticks the corresponding heat ceases and is stilled;

mn140:19.14.verse: so too, bhikkhu, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, there arises pleasant feeling.

mn140:19.15.verse: Feeling pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel pleasant feeling.”

mn140:19.16.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as pleasant, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:19.17.verse: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as painful, there arises painful feeling.

mn140:19.18.verse: Feeling painful feeling, one understands: “I feel painful feeling.”

mn140:19.19.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as painful, the painful feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:19.20.verse: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

mn140:19.21.verse: Feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

mn140:19.22.verse: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”

mn140:20.1.verse: ‘Then there remains only equanimity, purified and bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant.

mn140:20.2.verse: Just as, bhikkhu, a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice might prepare a furnace, and having prepared the furnace, heat up the crucible, and having heated up the crucible, take gold with tongs and put it into the crucible, and blow on it from time to time, sprinkle water on it from time to time, and look on at it from time to time, then that gold becomes refined, well refined, completely refined, faultless, rid of dross, malleable, wieldy, and radiant; then whatever kind of ornament he wishes to work it into, whether a chain, a ring, a necklace, or a gold garland, it serves his purpose;

mn140:20.3.verse: so too, bhikkhu, there then remains only equanimity, purified and bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant.

mn140:21.2.verse: “If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite space, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:21.3.verse: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.

mn140:21.4.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite consciousness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:21.5.verse: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.

mn140:21.6.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of nothingness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:21.7.verse: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.

mn140:21.8.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:21.9.verse: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.”

mn140:22.2.verse: “If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite space, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:22.4.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite consciousness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:22.6.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of nothingness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:22.8.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,

mn140:22.10.verse: He neither forms nor generates any volition tending towards being or towards non-being.

mn140:22.11.verse: Not forming, not generating any volition tending towards being or towards non-being, he does not cling to anything in the world.

mn140:22.12.verse: Not clinging, he is not agitated; not being agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna.

mn140:22.13.verse: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”

mn140:23.1.verse: ‘If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”

mn140:23.2.verse: If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”

mn140:23.3.verse: If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”

mn140:24.1.verse: ‘If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached;

mn140:24.2.verse: if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;

mn140:24.3.verse: if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.

mn140:24.4.verse: Feeling a feeling that is bounded by the body, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by the body”; feeling a feeling that is bounded by life, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by life”;

mn140:24.5.verse: he understands: “With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being relished, will become cool right here.”

mn140:24.6.verse: Just as, bhikkhu, an oil-lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick,

mn140:24.7.verse: and with the exhaustion of that very oil and wick, and with no further feeding, it goes out, unfed;

mn140:24.8.verse: so too, bhikkhu, feeling a feeling that is bounded by the body, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by the body”; feeling a feeling that is bounded by life, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by life”;

mn140:24.9.verse: he understands: “With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being relished, will become cool right here.”

mn140:25.1.verse: ‘Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of understanding.

mn140:25.2.verse: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble understanding, that is to say,

mn140:25.3.verse: the knowledge of the exhaustion of all suffering.

mn140:26.1.verse: ‘His deliverance, being founded on truth, is unshakeable.

mn140:26.2.verse: For that, bhikkhu, is false which has a deceptive nature, and that is true which has an undeceptive nature—Nibbāna.

mn140:26.3.verse: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of truth.

mn140:26.4.verse: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble truth, that is to say,

mn140:26.5.verse: Nibbāna, which has an undeceptive nature.

mn140:27.1.verse: ‘Formerly, when unknowing, he undertook and held to the essentials of existence.

mn140:27.2.verse: These have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.

mn140:27.3.verse: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of relinquishment.

mn140:27.4.verse: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble relinquishment, that is to say,

mn140:27.5.verse: the relinquishing of all the essentials of existence.

mn140:28.1.verse: ‘Formerly, when unknowing, he had covetousness, desire, and lust.

mn140:28.2.verse: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.

mn140:28.3.verse: Formerly, when unknowing, he had ill will, malevolence, and hatred.

mn140:28.4.verse: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.

mn140:28.5.verse: Formerly, when unknowing, he had ignorance and delusion.

mn140:28.6.verse: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.

mn140:28.7.verse: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of peace.

mn140:28.8.verse: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble peace, that is to say,

mn140:28.9.verse: the pacification of greed, hatred, and delusion.

mn140:29.1.verse: ‘“He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone”—

mn140:29.2.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:30.1.verse: ‘“Steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace”—

mn140:30.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn140:31.1.verse: ‘“I am,” bhikkhu, is a conceiving; “I am this” is a conceiving; “I shall be” is a conceiving; “I shall not be” is a conceiving; “I shall be possessed of form” is a conceiving; “I shall be formless” is a conceiving; “I shall be percipient” is a conceiving; “I shall be non-percipient” is a conceiving; “I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient” is a conceiving.

mn140:31.2.verse: Conceiving, bhikkhu, is a disease, conceiving is a tumour, conceiving is a dart.

mn140:31.3.verse: It is with the overcoming of all conceivings, bhikkhu, that one is called a sage at peace.

mn140:31.4.verse: And, bhikkhu, the sage at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, and does not yearn.

mn140:31.5.verse: For there is nothing in him, bhikkhu, by which he might be born; not being born, how could he age? not ageing, how could he die? not dying, how could he be shaken? not being shaken, for what could he yearn?

mn140:32.1.verse: ‘“Steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace”—

mn140:32.2.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn140:32.3.verse: Bear in mind, bhikkhu, this brief exposition of the six elements that I have given you.’

mn140:33.2.verse: ‘The Teacher has indeed come to me! The Fortunate One has indeed come to me! The Fully Enlightened One has indeed come to me!’ and he got up from his seat, and arranging his robe over one shoulder, he prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said to the Blessed One:

mn140:33.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, a transgression overcame me, foolish, confused, and unskilled as I was, in that I presumed to address the Blessed One as “friend.”

mn140:33.4.verse: May the Blessed One forgive me my transgression, venerable sir, seen as a transgression, for the sake of restraint in the future.’

mn140:33.5.verse: ‘Surely, bhikkhu, a transgression overcame you, foolish, confused, and unskilled as you were, in that you presumed to address me as “friend.”

mn140:33.6.verse: But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends for it according to the Dhamma, we forgive you that.

mn140:33.7.verse: For it is growth in the Noble One’s discipline when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it according to the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint in the future.’

mn140:34.1.verse: ‘Venerable sir, may I receive the full admission in the Blessed One’s presence?’

mn140:34.2.verse: ‘But, bhikkhu, are your bowl and robes complete?’

mn140:34.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not complete.’

mn140:34.4.verse: ‘Bhikkhu, Tathāgatas do not give the full admission to one whose bowl and robes are not complete.’

mn140:35.1.verse: Then the venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted in and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he set out in search of a bowl and robes.

mn140:35.2.verse: Then, while the venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow killed him.

mn140:36.1.verse: Then a number of bhikkhus went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:

mn140:36.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, the clansman Pukkusāti, who was given advice in brief by the Blessed One, has died.

mn140:36.3.verse: What is his destination? What is his future course?’

mn140:36.4.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, the clansman Pukkusāti was wise; he practised in accordance with the Dhamma, and he did not trouble me in the interpretation of the Dhamma.

mn140:36.5.verse: Bhikkhus, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, the clansman Pukkusāti has reappeared spontaneously and will attain final Nibbāna there, without ever returning from that world.’

mn140:36.6.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn140:36.7.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn140:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the Magadhan lands when he arrived at Rājagaha.

mn140:1.3.verse: He went to see Bhaggava the potter, and said,

mn140:2.1.verse: “Bhaggava, if it is no trouble, I’d like to spend a single night in your workshop.”

mn140:2.3.verse: But there’s a renunciate already staying there.

mn140:2.4.verse: If he allows it, sir, you may stay as long as you please.”

mn140:3.1.verse: Now at that time a gentleman named Pukkusāti had gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness in the Buddha’s name.

mn140:3.2.verse: And it was he who had first taken up residence in the workshop.

mn140:3.3.verse: Then the Buddha approached Venerable Pukkusāti and said,

mn140:3.4.verse: “Mendicant, if it is no trouble, I’d like to spend a single night in the workshop.”

mn140:3.6.verse: Stay as long as you please.”

mn140:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha entered the workshop and spread out a grass mat to one side. He sat down cross-legged, set his body straight, and brought mindfulness to the present.

mn140:4.2.verse: He spent much of the night sitting in meditation,

mn140:4.4.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

mn140:4.7.verse: So the Buddha said to Pukkusāti,

mn140:5.1.verse: “In whose name have you gone forth, mendicant? Who is your Teacher? Whose teaching do you believe in?”

mn140:5.2.verse: “Reverend, there is the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family.

mn140:5.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn140:5.5.verse: I’ve gone forth in his name.

mn140:5.6.verse: That Blessed One is my Teacher,

mn140:5.7.verse: and I believe in his teaching.”

mn140:5.8.verse: “But mendicant, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?”

mn140:5.9.verse: “In the northern lands there is a city named Sāvatthī.

mn140:5.10.verse: There the Blessed One is now staying, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.”

mn140:5.11.verse: “But have you ever seen that Buddha?

mn140:5.12.verse: Would you recognize him if you saw him?”

mn140:5.14.verse: and I wouldn’t recognize him if I did.”

mn140:6.1.verse: Then it occurred to the Buddha,

mn140:6.2.verse: “This gentleman has gone forth in my name.

mn140:6.3.verse: Why don’t I teach him the Dhamma?”

mn140:6.4.verse: So the Buddha said to Pukkusāti,

mn140:6.5.verse: “Mendicant, I shall teach you the Dhamma.

mn140:6.6.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn140:7.1.verse: “‘This person has six elements, six fields of contact, eighteen mental preoccupations, and four foundations.

mn140:7.2.verse: Where they stand, the streams of conceiving do not flow. And where the streams of conceiving do not flow, they are called a sage at peace.

mn140:7.3.verse: Do not neglect wisdom; preserve truth; foster generosity; and train only for peace.’

mn140:7.4.verse: This is the summary recital for the analysis of the elements.

mn140:8.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:8.4.verse: the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.

mn140:8.6.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:9.1.verse: ‘This person has six fields of contact.’

mn140:9.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:9.3.verse: The fields of contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

mn140:9.4.verse: ‘This person has six fields of contact.’

mn140:9.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:10.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:10.3.verse: Seeing a sight with their eyes, one is preoccupied with a sight that’s a basis for happiness or sadness or equanimity.

mn140:10.4.verse: Hearing a sound with their ears …

mn140:10.5.verse: Smelling an odor with their nose …

mn140:10.6.verse: Tasting a flavor with their tongue …

mn140:10.7.verse: Encountering a touch with their body …

mn140:10.8.verse: Becoming conscious of an idea with their mind, one is preoccupied with an idea that’s a basis for happiness or sadness or equanimity.

mn140:10.9.verse: So there are six preoccupations with happiness, six preoccupations with sadness, and six preoccupations with equanimity.

mn140:10.11.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:11.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:11.3.verse: The foundations of wisdom, truth, generosity, and peace.

mn140:11.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:12.1.verse: ‘Do not neglect wisdom; preserve truth; foster generosity; and train only for peace.’

mn140:12.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:13.1.verse: And how does one not neglect wisdom?

mn140:13.3.verse: the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.

mn140:14.1.verse: And what is the earth element?

mn140:14.2.verse: The earth element may be interior or exterior.

mn140:14.3.verse: And what is the interior earth element?

mn140:14.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s hard, solid, and appropriated. This includes:

mn140:14.5.verse: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, or anything else internal, personal, that’s hard, solid, and appropriated.

mn140:14.6.verse: This is called the interior earth element.

mn140:14.7.verse: The interior earth element and the exterior earth element are just the earth element.

mn140:14.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn140:14.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the earth element, detaching the mind from the earth element.

mn140:15.1.verse: And what is the water element?

mn140:15.2.verse: The water element may be interior or exterior.

mn140:15.3.verse: And what is the interior water element?

mn140:15.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s water, watery, and appropriated. This includes:

mn140:15.5.verse: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine, or anything else internal, personal, that’s water, watery, and appropriated.

mn140:15.6.verse: This is called the interior water element.

mn140:15.7.verse: The interior water element and the exterior water element are just the water element.

mn140:15.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn140:15.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the water element, detaching the mind from the water element.

mn140:16.1.verse: And what is the fire element?

mn140:16.2.verse: The fire element may be interior or exterior.

mn140:16.3.verse: And what is the interior fire element?

mn140:16.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s fire, fiery, and appropriated. This includes:

mn140:16.5.verse: that which warms, that which ages, that which heats you up when feverish, that which properly digests food and drink; or anything else internal, personal, that’s fire, fiery, and appropriated.

mn140:16.6.verse: This is called the interior fire element.

mn140:16.7.verse: The interior fire element and the exterior fire element are just the fire element.

mn140:16.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn140:16.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the fire element, detaching the mind from the fire element.

mn140:17.1.verse: And what is the air element?

mn140:17.2.verse: The air element may be interior or exterior.

mn140:17.3.verse: And what is the interior air element?

mn140:17.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s air, airy, and appropriated. This includes:

mn140:17.5.verse: winds that go up or down, winds in the belly or the bowels, winds that flow through the limbs, in-breaths and out-breaths; or anything else internal, personal, that’s air, airy, and appropriated.

mn140:17.6.verse: This is called the interior air element.

mn140:17.7.verse: The interior air element and the exterior air element are just the air element.

mn140:17.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn140:17.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the air element, detaching the mind from the air element.

mn140:18.1.verse: And what is the space element?

mn140:18.2.verse: The space element may be interior or exterior.

mn140:18.3.verse: And what is the interior space element?

mn140:18.4.verse: Anything internal, personal, that’s space, spacious, and appropriated. This includes:

mn140:18.5.verse: the ear canals, nostrils, and mouth; and the space for swallowing what is eaten and drunk, the space where it stays, and the space for excreting it from the nether regions; or anything else internal, personal, that’s space, spacious, and appropriated.

mn140:18.6.verse: This is called the interior space element.

mn140:18.7.verse: The interior space element and the exterior space element are just the space element.

mn140:18.8.verse: This should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

mn140:18.9.verse: When you truly see with right understanding, you grow disillusioned with the space element, detaching the mind from the space element.

mn140:19.1.verse: What remains is sheer consciousness, pure and bright.

mn140:19.2.verse: And what does that consciousness know?

mn140:19.4.verse: Pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

mn140:19.5.verse: When they feel a pleasant feeling, they know: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling.’

mn140:19.6.verse: They know: ‘With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding pleasant feeling ceases and stops.’

mn140:19.7.verse: Painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

mn140:19.8.verse: When they feel a painful feeling, they know: ‘I feel a painful feeling.’

mn140:19.9.verse: They know: ‘With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding painful feeling ceases and stops.’

mn140:19.10.verse: Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

mn140:19.11.verse: When they feel a neutral feeling, they know: ‘I feel a neutral feeling.’

mn140:19.12.verse: They know: ‘With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neutral, the corresponding neutral feeling ceases and stops.’

mn140:19.13.verse: When you rub two sticks together, heat is generated and fire is produced. But when you part the sticks and lay them aside, any corresponding heat ceases and stops.

mn140:19.14.verse: In the same way, pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant. …

mn140:19.22.verse: They know: ‘With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neutral, the corresponding neutral feeling ceases and stops.’

mn140:20.1.verse: There remains only equanimity, pure, bright, pliable, workable, and radiant.

mn140:20.2.verse: It’s like when a deft goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice prepares a forge, fires the crucible, picks up some native gold with tongs and puts it in the crucible. From time to time they fan it, from time to time they sprinkle water on it, and from time to time they just watch over it. That native gold becomes pliable, workable, and radiant, not brittle, and is ready to be worked. Then the goldsmith can successfully create any kind of ornament they want, whether a bracelet, earrings, a necklace, or a golden garland.

mn140:20.3.verse: In the same way, there remains only equanimity, pure, bright, pliable, workable, and radiant.

mn140:21.2.verse: ‘If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of infinite space, and develop my mind accordingly,

mn140:21.3.verse: this equanimity of mine, relying on that and grasping it, would remain for a very long time.

mn140:21.4.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of infinite consciousness, and develop my mind accordingly,

mn140:21.5.verse: this equanimity of mine, relying on that and grasping it, would remain for a very long time.

mn140:21.6.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of nothingness, and develop my mind accordingly,

mn140:21.7.verse: this equanimity of mine, relying on that and grasping it, would remain for a very long time.

mn140:21.8.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, and develop my mind accordingly,

mn140:21.9.verse: this equanimity of mine, relying on that and grasping it, would remain for a very long time.’

mn140:22.2.verse: ‘If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of infinite space, my mind would develop accordingly.

mn140:22.4.verse: If I were to apply this equanimity, so pure and bright, to the dimension of infinite consciousness …

mn140:22.8.verse: neither perception nor non-perception, my mind would develop accordingly.

mn140:22.10.verse: They neither make a choice nor form an intention for existence or nonexistence.

mn140:22.11.verse: Because of this, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

mn140:22.12.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

mn140:22.13.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

mn140:23.1.verse: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

mn140:23.2.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

mn140:23.3.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

mn140:24.1.verse: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

mn140:24.2.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

mn140:24.3.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

mn140:24.4.verse: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

mn140:24.5.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’

mn140:24.6.verse: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn.

mn140:24.7.verse: As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

mn140:24.8.verse: In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

mn140:24.9.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’

mn140:25.1.verse: Therefore a mendicant thus endowed is endowed with the ultimate foundation of wisdom.

mn140:25.2.verse: For this is the ultimate noble wisdom, namely,

mn140:25.3.verse: the knowledge of the ending of all suffering.

mn140:26.1.verse: Their freedom, being founded on truth, is unshakable.

mn140:26.2.verse: For that which is false has a deceptive nature, while that which is true has an undeceptive nature—extinguishment.

mn140:26.3.verse: Therefore a mendicant thus endowed is endowed with the ultimate foundation of truth.

mn140:26.4.verse: For this is the ultimate noble truth, namely,

mn140:26.5.verse: that which has an undeceptive nature—extinguishment.

mn140:27.1.verse: In their ignorance, they used to acquire attachments.

mn140:27.2.verse: Those have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so they are unable to arise in the future.

mn140:27.3.verse: Therefore a mendicant thus endowed is endowed with the ultimate foundation of generosity.

mn140:27.4.verse: For this is the ultimate noble generosity, namely,

mn140:28.1.verse: In their ignorance, they used to be covetous, full of desire and lust.

mn140:28.2.verse: That has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn140:28.3.verse: In their ignorance, they used to be contemptuous, full of ill will and malevolence.

mn140:28.4.verse: That has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn140:28.5.verse: In their ignorance, they used to be ignorant, full of delusion.

mn140:28.6.verse: That has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so it’s unable to arise in the future.

mn140:28.7.verse: Therefore a mendicant thus endowed is endowed with the ultimate foundation of peace.

mn140:28.8.verse: For this is the ultimate noble peace, namely,

mn140:28.9.verse: the pacification of greed, hate, and delusion.

mn140:29.1.verse: ‘Do not neglect wisdom; preserve truth; foster generosity; and train only for peace.’

mn140:29.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:30.1.verse: ‘Where they stand, the streams of conceiving do not flow. And where the streams of conceiving do not flow, they are called a sage at peace.’

mn140:30.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn140:31.1.verse: These are all forms of conceiving: ‘I am’, ‘I am this’, ‘I will be’, ‘I will not be’, ‘I will have form’, ‘I will be formless’, ‘I will be percipient’, ‘I will be non-percipient’, ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.’

mn140:31.2.verse: Conceiving is a disease, a boil, a dart.

mn140:31.3.verse: Having gone beyond all conceiving, one is called a sage at peace.

mn140:31.4.verse: The sage at peace is not reborn, does not grow old, and does not die. They are not shaken, and do not yearn.

mn140:31.5.verse: For they have nothing which would cause them to be reborn. Not being reborn, how could they grow old? Not growing old, how could they die? Not dying, how could they be shaken? Not shaking, for what could they yearn?

mn140:32.1.verse: ‘Where they stand, the streams of conceiving do not flow. And where the streams of conceiving do not flow, they are called a sage at peace.’

mn140:32.2.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn140:32.3.verse: Mendicant, you should remember this brief analysis of the six elements.”

mn140:33.2.verse: “It seems the Teacher has come to me! The Holy One has come to me! The fully awakened Buddha has come to me!” He got up from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet, and said,

mn140:33.3.verse: “I made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me to presume to address the Buddha as ‘reverend’.

mn140:33.4.verse: Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

mn140:33.5.verse: “Indeed, mendicant, you made a mistake. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of you to act in that way.

mn140:33.6.verse: But since you have recognized your mistake for what it is, and have dealt with it properly, I accept it.

mn140:33.7.verse: For it is growth in the training of the Noble One to recognize a mistake for what it is, deal with it properly, and commit to restraint in the future.”

mn140:34.1.verse: “Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

mn140:34.2.verse: “But mendicant, do you have a full set of bowl and robes?”

mn140:34.4.verse: “The Realized Ones do not ordain those without a full set of bowl and robes.”

mn140:35.1.verse: And then Venerable Pukkusāti approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

mn140:35.2.verse: But while he was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow took his life.

mn140:36.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn140:36.2.verse: “Sir, the gentleman named Pukkusāti, who was advised in brief by the Buddha, has passed away.

mn140:36.3.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

mn140:36.4.verse: “Mendicants, Pukkusāti was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

mn140:36.5.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters, he’s been reborn spontaneously and will become extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.”

mn140:36.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn140:36.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn141:1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

mn141:1.3.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

mn141:1.5.verse: “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

mn141:1.6.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

mn141:2.1.verse: “The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:2.2.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the four noble truths.

mn141:3.1.verse: ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the arising of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:4.1.verse: “The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:4.2.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of these four noble truths.

mn141:5.1.verse: Associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks,

mn141:5.2.verse: keep company with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks,

mn141:5.3.verse: they are wise monks who assist those living the spiritual life.

mn141:5.4.verse: Sāriputta is just like one who gives birth, monks,

mn141:5.5.verse: Moggallāna is just like a wet nurse to the one new-born, monks;

mn141:5.6.verse: Sāriputta guides to the fruit of stream entry, monks, Moggallāna guides to the supreme good.

mn141:5.7.verse: Sāriputta is able, monks, ° to explain, reveal, make known, set forth, open up, analyse, and make plain, the four noble truths in detail.”

mn141:6.2.verse: and after saying this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went into his living quarters.

mn141:7.1.verse: Then venerable Sāriputta, not long after the Fortunate One had gone, addressed the monks, saying:

mn141:7.3.verse: “Venerable friend!” those monks replied to venerable Sāriputta,

mn141:8.1.verse: “The Realised One, friends, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:8.2.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the four noble truths.

mn141:9.1.verse: ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the arising of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:10.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of suffering?

mn141:10.2.verse: Birth is suffering also old age is suffering also sickness is suffering also death is suffering also grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, is suffering also not to obtain what one longs for is suffering in brief, the five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment are suffering.

mn141:11.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is birth?

mn141:11.2.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is birth, being born, appearing, turning up;

mn141:11.3.verse: the manifestation of the constituent groups (of mind and body), the acquisition of the sense spheres: this venerable friends, is called birth.

mn141:12.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is old age?

mn141:12.2.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is aging, agedness, broken teeth, greying hair, and wrinkled skin;

mn141:12.3.verse: the dwindling away of the lifespan, the decay of the sense faculties: this venerable friends, is called old age.

mn141:13.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is death?

mn141:13.2.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is a fall, a falling away, a breaking up, a disappearance, a dying, a death, a making of time;

mn141:13.3.verse: the break up of the constituent groups (of mind and body), the throwing off of the body, this, venerable friends, is called death.

mn141:14.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is grief?

mn141:14.2.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

mn141:14.3.verse: there is grief, grieving, the state of grieving, inner grief, great inner grief: this, venerable friends, is called grief.

mn141:15.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is lamenation?

mn141:15.2.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

mn141:15.3.verse: there are laments, great laments, lamenting, great lamenting, the state of lamenting, great lamentation: this, venerable friends, is called lamentation.

mn141:16.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is pain?

mn141:16.2.verse: That, venerable friends, which is bodily pain, bodily disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the body, disagreeable feeling:

mn141:16.3.verse: this, venerable friends, is called pain.

mn141:17.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is sorrow?

mn141:17.2.verse: That, venerable friends, which is mental pain, mental disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the mind, disagreeable feeling:

mn141:17.3.verse: this, venerable friends, is called sorrow.

mn141:18.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is despair?

mn141:18.2.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

mn141:18.3.verse: there is desponding, despairing, despondency, despair: this, venerable friends, is called despair.

mn141:19.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for?

mn141:19.2.verse: To those beings subject to birth, venerable friends, this longing arises:

mn141:19.3.verse: “Oh, might we not be subject to birth, and may birth surely not come to us!”

mn141:19.4.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

mn141:19.5.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

mn141:19.9.verse: To those beings subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, venerable friends, this longing arises:

mn141:19.10.verse: ° “Oh, might we not be subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, may grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair surely not come to us!”

mn141:19.11.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

mn141:19.12.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

mn141:20.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, in brief, are the constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment that are suffering?

mn141:20.2.verse: They are as follows: the form constituent group that is attached to the feelings constituent group that is attached to the perceptions constituent group that is attached to the (mental) processes constituent group that is attached to the consciousness constituent group that is attached to.

mn141:20.3.verse: These, venerable friends, in brief, are called the constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment and that are suffering.

mn141:20.4.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of suffering.

mn141:21.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the arising of suffering?

mn141:21.2.verse: It is that craving which leads to continuation in existence, which is connected with enjoyment and passion, greatly enjoying this and that, as follows:

mn141:21.3.verse: craving for sense pleasures craving for continuation craving for discontinuation.

mn141:21.4.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the arising of suffering.

mn141:22.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

mn141:22.2.verse: It is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that craving - liberation, letting go, release, and non-adherence.

mn141:22.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

mn141:23.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering?

mn141:23.2.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

mn141:23.3.verse: right view right thought right speech right action right livelihood right endeavour right mindfulness right concentration.

mn141:24.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right view?

mn141:24.2.verse: That, venerable friends, which is knowledge about suffering knowledge about the arising of suffering knowledge about the cessation of suffering knowledge about the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:24.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right view.

mn141:25.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right thought?

mn141:25.2.verse: The thought of renunciation the thought of good will the thought of non-violence.

mn141:25.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right thought.

mn141:26.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right speech?

mn141:26.2.verse: Refraining from false speech refraining from malicious speech refraining from rough speech refraining from frivolous talk.

mn141:26.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right speech.

mn141:27.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right action?

mn141:27.2.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures refraining from taking what has not been given refraining from sexual misconduct.

mn141:27.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right action.

mn141:28.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right livelihood?

mn141:28.2.verse: Here, venerable friends, a noble disciple, having given up wrong ways of livelihood, earns his living by a right way of livelihood.

mn141:28.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right livelihood.

mn141:29.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right endeavour?

mn141:29.2.verse: ° Here, venerable friends, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of bad and unwholesome things that have not yet arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

mn141:29.3.verse: ° He generates desire to give up bad and unwholesome things that have already arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

mn141:29.4.verse: He generates desire for the arising of wholesome things that have not yet arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

mn141:29.5.verse: ° He generates desire for the endurance of wholesome things that have arisen, their non-forgetting, multiplicaton, extension, development, and fulfilment, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

mn141:29.6.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right endeavour.

mn141:30.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right mindfulness?

mn141:30.2.verse: Here, venerable friends, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body, ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

mn141:30.5.verse: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

mn141:30.6.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right mindfulness.

mn141:31.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right concentration?

mn141:31.2.verse: Here, venerable friends, a monk, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unwholesome things, having thinking, reflection, and the happiness and rapture born of seclusion, dwells having attained the first absorption.

mn141:31.3.verse: With the ending of thinking, and reflection, with internal clarity, and one-pointedness of mind, being without thinking, without reflection, having the happiness and rapture born of concentration, he dwells having attained the second absorption.

mn141:31.5.verse: he dwells having attained the fourth absorption.

mn141:31.6.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right concentration.

mn141:31.7.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:32.1.verse: The Realised One, friends, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:32.2.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of these four noble truths.”

mn141:32.4.verse: and those monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in venerable Sāriputta’s words.

mn141:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

mn141:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn141:2.1.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:2.2.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

mn141:3.1.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:4.1.verse: Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:4.2.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

mn141:5.1.verse: Mendicants, you should cultivate friendship with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

mn141:5.2.verse: You should associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

mn141:5.3.verse: They’re astute, and they support their spiritual companions.

mn141:5.4.verse: Sāriputta is like one who gives birth,

mn141:5.5.verse: while Moggallāna is like one who raises the child.

mn141:5.6.verse: Sāriputta guides people to the fruit of stream-entry, Moggallāna to the highest goal.

mn141:5.7.verse: Sāriputta is able to explain, teach, assert, establish, clarify, analyze, and reveal the four noble truths in detail.”

mn141:6.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn141:6.2.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

mn141:7.1.verse: Then, not long after the Buddha left, Venerable Sāriputta said to the mendicants,

mn141:8.1.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

mn141:8.2.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

mn141:9.1.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

mn141:10.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

mn141:10.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

mn141:11.2.verse: The rebirth, inception, conception, regeneration, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense fields of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn141:12.2.verse: The old age, decrepitude, broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkly skin, diminished vitality, and failing faculties of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn141:13.2.verse: The passing away, passing on, disintegration, demise, mortality, death, decease, breaking up of the aggregates, laying to rest of the corpse, and cutting off of the life faculty of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

mn141:14.2.verse: The sorrow, sorrowing, state of sorrow, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

mn141:15.2.verse: The wail, lament, wailing, lamenting, state of wailing and lamentation in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

mn141:16.2.verse: Physical pain, physical unpleasantness, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from physical contact.

mn141:17.2.verse: Mental pain, mental displeasure, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from mind contact.

mn141:18.2.verse: The stress, distress, state of stress and distress in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

mn141:19.1.verse: And what is ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’?

mn141:19.2.verse: In sentient beings who are liable to be reborn, such a wish arises:

mn141:19.3.verse: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to be reborn! If only rebirth would not come to us!’

mn141:19.4.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

mn141:19.5.verse: This is: ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

mn141:19.6.verse: In sentient beings who are liable to grow old …

mn141:19.9.verse: experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, such a wish arises:

mn141:19.10.verse: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress! If only sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress would not come to us!’

mn141:19.11.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

mn141:19.12.verse: This is: ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

mn141:20.1.verse: And what is ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’?

mn141:20.2.verse: They are the grasping aggregates that consist of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn141:20.3.verse: This is called ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’.

mn141:20.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

mn141:21.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

mn141:21.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

mn141:21.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

mn141:21.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

mn141:22.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
