mn145:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Puṇṇa came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha,

mn145:2.1.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

mn145:2.2.verse: “Well then, Puṇṇa, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn145:3.1.verse: “Puṇṇa, there are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn145:3.2.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

mn145:3.4.verse: Relishing is the origin of suffering, I say.

mn145:3.5.verse: There are sounds known by the ear …

mn145:3.9.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn145:3.10.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

mn145:3.12.verse: Relishing is the origin of suffering, I say.

mn145:4.1.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn145:4.2.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them,

mn145:4.4.verse: When relishing ceases, suffering ceases, I say.

mn145:4.5.verse: There are sounds known by the ear …

mn145:4.9.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

mn145:4.10.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them,

mn145:4.12.verse: When relishing ceases, suffering ceases, I say.

mn145:5.1.verse: Puṇṇa, now that I’ve given you this brief advice, what country will you live in?”

mn145:5.2.verse: “Sir, there’s a country named Sunāparanta. I shall live there.”

mn145:5.3.verse: “The people of Sunāparanta are wild and rough, Puṇṇa.

mn145:5.5.verse: If they abuse and insult you, what will you think of them?”

mn145:5.6.verse: “If they abuse and insult me, I will think:

mn145:5.7.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t hit me with their fists.’

mn145:5.8.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.9.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:5.10.verse: “But if they do hit you with their fists, what will you think of them then?”

mn145:5.11.verse: “If they hit me with their fists, I’ll think:

mn145:5.12.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t throw stones at me.’

mn145:5.13.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.14.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:5.15.verse: “But if they do throw stones at you, what will you think of them then?”

mn145:5.16.verse: “If they throw stones at me, I’ll think:

mn145:5.17.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t beat me with a club.’

mn145:5.18.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.19.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:5.20.verse: “But if they do beat you with a club, what will you think of them then?”

mn145:5.21.verse: “If they beat me with a club, I’ll think:

mn145:5.22.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t stab me with a knife.’

mn145:5.23.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.24.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:5.25.verse: “But if they do stab you with a knife, what will you think of them then?”

mn145:5.26.verse: “If they stab me with a knife, I’ll think:

mn145:5.27.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t take my life with a sharp knife.’

mn145:5.28.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.29.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:5.30.verse: “But if they do take your life with a sharp knife, what will you think of them then?”

mn145:5.31.verse: “If they take my life with a sharp knife, I’ll think:

mn145:5.32.verse: ‘There are disciples of the Buddha who looked for a suicide weapon because they were horrified, repelled, and disgusted with the body and with life. And I have found this without looking!’

mn145:5.33.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

mn145:5.34.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

mn145:6.2.verse: Having such self-control and peacefulness, you will be quite capable of living in Sunāparanta.

mn145:6.3.verse: Now, Puṇṇa, go at your convenience.”

mn145:7.1.verse: And then Puṇṇa welcomed and agreed with the Buddha’s words. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, set out for Sunāparanta.

mn145:7.2.verse: Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Sunāparanta,

mn145:7.4.verse: Within that rainy season he confirmed around five hundred male and five hundred female lay followers. And within that same rainy season he realized the three knowledges.

mn145:7.5.verse: Some time later he became fully extinguished.

mn145:8.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

mn145:8.2.verse: “Sir, the gentleman named Puṇṇa, who was advised in brief by the Buddha, has passed away.

mn145:8.3.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

mn145:8.4.verse: “Mendicants, Puṇṇa was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

mn145:8.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn145:8.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn146:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn146:2.1.verse: Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, together with about five hundred bhikkhunīs, went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, she stood at one side. Standing at one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One:

mn146:2.2.verse: ‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One advise the bhikkhunīs;

mn146:2.3.verse: let the Blessed One instruct the bhikkhunīs;

mn146:2.4.verse: let the Blessed One give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma.’

mn146:3.1.verse: Now on that occasion the elder bhikkhus were advising the bhikkhunīs in turn.

mn146:3.2.verse: The venerable Nandaka did not want to advise the bhikkhunīs in his turn.

mn146:3.3.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda thus:

mn146:3.4.verse: ‘Ānanda, whose turn is it today to advise the bhikkhunīs?’

mn146:3.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir, it is everyone’s turn to advise the bhikkhunīs.

mn146:3.6.verse: It is the venerable Nandaka’s turn, venerable sir, but he does not want to advise the bhikkhunīs.’

mn146:4.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka thus:

mn146:4.4.verse: give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma, brahmin.’

mn146:4.5.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Then, when it was morning, he dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms.

mn146:4.6.verse: When he had wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from his alms round, after the meal he went with a companion to the Rājaka Park.

mn146:4.7.verse: The bhikkhunīs saw the venerable Nandaka coming from a distance.

mn146:4.8.verse: Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for the feet.

mn146:4.9.verse: The venerable Nandaka sat down on the seat made ready.

mn146:12.1.verse: ‘This simile, sisters, has been made by me to convey a meaning.

mn146:13.1.verse: ‘There are, sisters, these seven enlightenment factors, developing and cultivating which a bhikkhu, by realizing for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the taintless deliverance of mind and deliverance by understanding, with the exhaustion of the taints.

mn146:16.1.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka thus:

mn146:16.2.verse: ‘Then, Nandaka, you should advise those same bhikkhunīs tomorrow too with this same advice.’

mn146:16.3.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One.

mn146:16.4.verse: Then, when that night had passed, the venerable Nandaka, in the morning, dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms.

mn146:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn146:2.1.verse: Then Mahāpajāpati Gotamī together with around five hundred nuns approached the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him,

mn146:2.4.verse: Please give the nuns a Dhamma talk.”

mn146:3.1.verse: Now at that time the senior monks were taking turns to advise the nuns.

mn146:3.2.verse: But Venerable Nandaka didn’t want to take his turn.

mn146:3.3.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda,

mn146:3.4.verse: “Ānanda, whose turn is it to advise the nuns today?”

mn146:3.6.verse: but he doesn’t want to do it.”

mn146:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Nandaka,

mn146:4.4.verse: Please, brahmin, give the nuns a Dhamma talk.”

mn146:4.5.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Nandaka. Then, in the morning, he robed up and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

mn146:4.6.verse: He wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Royal Monastery with a companion.

mn146:4.7.verse: Those nuns saw him coming off in the distance,

mn146:4.8.verse: so they spread out a seat and placed water for washing the feet.

mn146:4.9.verse: Nandaka sat down on the seat spread out,

mn146:4.11.verse: Those nuns bowed, and sat down to one side.

mn146:5.4.verse: ‘Why, sir, does it say this? What does that mean?’”

mn146:5.5.verse: “We’re already delighted and satisfied with Master Nandaka, since he invites us like this.”

mn146:8.21.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

mn146:8.22.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

mn146:8.25.verse: Because we have already truly seen this with right wisdom:

mn146:8.26.verse: ‘So these six classes of consciousness are impermanent.’”

mn146:8.28.verse: That’s how it is for a noble disciple who truly sees with right wisdom.

mn146:9.1.verse: Suppose there was an oil lamp burning. The oil, wick, flame, and light were all impermanent and perishable.

mn146:9.2.verse: Now, suppose someone was to say:

mn146:9.3.verse: ‘While this oil lamp is burning, the oil, the wick, and the flame are all impermanent and perishable.

mn146:9.4.verse: But the light is permanent, lasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

mn146:9.8.verse: Because that oil lamp’s oil, wick, and flame are all impermanent and perishable,

mn146:9.10.verse: “In the same way, suppose someone was to say:

mn146:9.11.verse: ‘These six interior sense fields are impermanent.

mn146:9.12.verse: But the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that I experience due to these six interior sense fields is permanent, lasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

mn146:9.16.verse: Because each kind of feeling arises dependent on the corresponding condition.

mn146:9.17.verse: When the corresponding condition ceases, the appropriate feeling ceases.”

mn146:9.19.verse: That’s how it is for a noble disciple who truly sees with right wisdom.

mn146:10.1.verse: Suppose there was a large tree standing with heartwood. The roots, trunk, branches and leaves, and shadow were all impermanent and perishable.

mn146:10.2.verse: Now, suppose someone was to say:

mn146:10.3.verse: ‘There’s a large tree standing with heartwood. The roots, trunk, and branches and leaves are all impermanent and perishable. But the shadow is permanent, lasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

mn146:10.7.verse: Because that large tree’s roots, trunk, and branches and leaves are all impermanent and perishable,

mn146:10.9.verse: “In the same way, suppose someone was to say:

mn146:10.10.verse: ‘These six exterior sense fields are impermanent.

mn146:10.11.verse: But the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that I experience due to these six exterior sense fields is permanent, lasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

mn146:10.15.verse: Because each kind of feeling arises dependent on the corresponding condition.

mn146:10.16.verse: When the corresponding condition ceases, the appropriate feeling ceases.”

mn146:10.18.verse: That’s how it is for a noble disciple who truly sees with right wisdom.

mn146:11.1.verse: Suppose a deft butcher or their apprentice, having killed a cow, were to carve it with a sharp meat cleaver, without damaging the flesh inside or the hide outside.

mn146:11.2.verse: They’d cut, carve, sever, and slice through each of the connecting tendons, sinews, and ligaments with a sharp meat cleaver,

mn146:11.3.verse: and then peel off the outer hide. Then they’d wrap that cow up in that very same hide and say:

mn146:11.4.verse: ‘This cow is joined to its hide just like before.’

mn146:11.10.verse: Because even if they wrap that cow up in that very same hide and say:

mn146:11.11.verse: ‘This cow is joined to its hide just like before,’

mn146:11.12.verse: still that cow is not joined to that hide.”

mn146:12.1.verse: “I’ve made up this simile to make a point.

mn146:12.3.verse: ‘The inner flesh’ is a term for the six interior sense fields.

mn146:12.4.verse: ‘The outer hide’ is a term for the six exterior sense fields.

mn146:12.5.verse: ‘The connecting tendons, sinews, and ligaments’ is a term for greed and relishing.

mn146:12.6.verse: ‘A sharp meat cleaver’ is a term for noble wisdom.

mn146:12.7.verse: And it is that noble wisdom which cuts, carves, severs, and slices the connecting corruption, fetter, and bond.

mn146:13.1.verse: Sisters, by developing and cultivating these seven awakening factors, a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

mn146:13.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

mn146:13.9.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

mn146:13.10.verse: It is by developing and cultivating these seven awakening factors that a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

mn146:14.1.verse: Then after giving this advice to the nuns, Nandaka sent them off, saying,

mn146:14.3.verse: And then those nuns approved and agreed with what Nandaka had said. They rose from their seats, bowed, and respectfully circled him, keeping him on their right. Then they went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to them,

mn146:14.5.verse: Then those nuns bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before leaving.

mn146:15.1.verse: Soon after those nuns had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

mn146:15.2.verse: “Suppose, mendicants, it was the sabbath of the fourteenth day. You wouldn’t get lots of people

mn146:15.3.verse: wondering whether the moon is full or not, since it is obviously not full.

mn146:15.4.verse: In the same way, those nuns were uplifted by Nandaka’s Dhamma teaching, but they still haven’t got all they wished for.”

mn146:16.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Nandaka,

mn146:16.2.verse: “Well then, Nandaka, tomorrow you should give those nuns the same advice again.”

mn146:16.4.verse: And the next day he went to those nuns, and all unfolded just like the previous day.

mn146:27.1.verse: Soon after those nuns had left, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

mn146:27.2.verse: “Suppose, mendicants, it was the sabbath of the fifteenth day. You wouldn’t get lots of people

mn146:27.3.verse: wondering whether the moon is full or not, since it is obviously full.

mn146:27.4.verse: In the same way, those nuns were uplifted by Nandaka’s Dhamma teaching, and they got all they wished for.

mn146:27.5.verse: Even the last of these five hundred nuns is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

mn146:27.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn146:27.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn147:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn147:1.3.verse: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

mn147:1.4.verse: “The qualities that ripen in freedom have ripened in Rāhula.

mn147:1.5.verse: Why don’t I lead him further to the ending of defilements?”

mn147:1.6.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

mn147:1.7.verse: Then, after the meal, on his return from almsround, he addressed Venerable Rāhula,

mn147:1.9.verse: Let’s go to the Dark Forest for the day’s meditation.”

mn147:1.10.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Rāhula. Taking his sitting cloth he followed behind the Buddha.

mn147:2.2.verse: “Today the Buddha will lead Rāhula further to the ending of defilements!”

mn147:2.3.verse: Then the Buddha plunged deep into the Dark Forest and sat at the root of a tree on the seat spread out.

mn147:2.4.verse: Rāhula bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side.

mn147:9.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact. And they grow disillusioned with anything included in feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness that arises dependent on eye contact.

mn147:9.2.verse: They grow disillusioned with the ear …

mn147:9.6.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact. And they grow disillusioned with anything included in feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness that arises dependent on mind contact.

mn147:9.7.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

mn147:9.8.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

mn147:9.9.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn147:9.10.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Rāhula approved what the Buddha said.

mn147:9.11.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, Rāhula’s mind was freed from defilements by not grasping.

mn147:9.12.verse: And the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in those thousands of deities:

mn147:9.13.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

mn147:0.2.verse: The Shorter Discourse of Advice to Rāhula

mn147:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn147:1.3.verse: Then, while the Blessed One was alone in meditation, a thought arose in his mind thus:

mn147:1.4.verse: “The states that ripen in deliverance have ripened in Rāhula.

mn147:1.5.verse: Suppose I were to lead him on further to the destruction of the taints.”

mn147:1.6.verse: Then, when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms.

mn147:1.7.verse: When he had walked for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from his almsround, after his meal he addressed the venerable Rāhula thus:

mn147:1.8.verse: “Take your sitting cloth with you, Rāhula;

mn147:1.9.verse: let us go to the Blind Men’s Grove to pass the day.”

mn147:1.10.verse: “Yes, venerable sir,” the venerable Rāhula replied, and taking his sitting cloth with him, he followed close behind the Blessed One.

mn147:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion many thousands of deities followed the Blessed One, thinking:

mn147:2.2.verse: “Today the Blessed One will lead the venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints.”

mn147:2.3.verse: Then the Blessed One went into the Blind Men’s Grove and sat down at the root of a certain tree on a seat made ready.

mn147:2.4.verse: And the venerable Rāhula paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

mn147:2.5.verse: The Blessed One then said to the venerable Rāhula:

mn147:9.1.verse: “Seeing thus, Rāhula, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, and disenchanted with anything comprised within the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise with eye-contact as condition.

mn147:9.2.verse: He becomes disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with sounds…

mn147:9.3.verse: disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with odours…

mn147:9.4.verse: disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with flavours…

mn147:9.5.verse: disenchanted with the body, disenchanted with tangibles…

mn147:9.6.verse: He becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mind-objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and disenchanted with anything comprised within the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise with mind-contact as condition.

mn147:9.7.verse: Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn147:9.8.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’”

mn147:9.9.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn147:9.10.verse: The venerable Rāhula was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn147:9.11.verse: Now while this discourse was being spoken, through not clinging the venerable Rāhula’s mind was liberated from the taints.

mn147:9.12.verse: And in those many thousands of deities there arose the spotless immaculate vision of the Dhamma:

mn147:9.13.verse: “All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation.”

mn148:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn148:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn148:1.5.verse: ‘Venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

mn148:2.1.verse: ‘Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and I shall proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure, that is to say,

mn148:2.3.verse: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’

mn148:2.4.verse: ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

mn148:3.1.verse: ‘The six bases in oneself should be understood. The six external bases should be understood. The six bodies of consciousness should be understood. The six bodies of contact should be understood. The six bodies of feeling should be understood. The six bodies of craving should be understood.

mn148:4.1.verse: “The six bases in oneself should be understood”—

mn148:4.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:4.3.verse: The eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, the mind base.

mn148:4.4.verse: “The six bases in oneself should be understood”—

mn148:4.5.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:5.1.verse: “The six external bases should be understood”—

mn148:5.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:5.3.verse: The form base, the sound base, the odour base, the flavour base, the tangible base, the dhamma base.

mn148:5.4.verse: “The six external bases should be understood”—

mn148:5.5.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:6.1.verse: “The six bodies of consciousness should be understood”—

mn148:6.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:6.3.verse: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;

mn148:6.4.verse: dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises;

mn148:6.5.verse: dependent on the nose and odours, nose-consciousness arises;

mn148:6.6.verse: dependent on the tongue and flavours, tongue-consciousness arises;

mn148:6.7.verse: dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises;

mn148:6.8.verse: dependent on the mind and dhammas, mind-consciousness arises.

mn148:6.9.verse: “The six bodies of consciousness should be understood”—

mn148:6.10.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:7.1.verse: “The six bodies of contact should be understood”—

mn148:7.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:7.3.verse: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;

mn148:7.4.verse: dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;

mn148:7.5.verse: dependent on the nose and odours, nose-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;

mn148:7.6.verse: dependent on the tongue and flavours, tongue-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;

mn148:7.7.verse: dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact;

mn148:7.8.verse: dependent on the mind and dhammas, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact.

mn148:7.9.verse: “The six bodies of contact should be understood”—

mn148:7.10.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:8.1.verse: “The six bodies of feeling should be understood”—

mn148:8.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:8.3.verse: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling;

mn148:8.4.verse: dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling;

mn148:8.5.verse: dependent on the nose and odours, nose-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling;

mn148:8.6.verse: dependent on the tongue and flavours, tongue-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling;

mn148:8.7.verse: dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling;

mn148:8.8.verse: dependent on the mind and dhammas, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling.

mn148:8.9.verse: “The six bodies of feeling should be understood”—

mn148:8.10.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:9.1.verse: “The six bodies of craving should be understood”—

mn148:9.2.verse: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

mn148:9.3.verse: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving;

mn148:9.4.verse: dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises …

mn148:9.5.verse: dependent on the nose and odours, nose-consciousness arises …

mn148:9.6.verse: dependent on the tongue and flavours, tongue-consciousness arises …

mn148:9.7.verse: dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises …

mn148:9.8.verse: dependent on the mind and dhammas, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving.

mn148:9.9.verse: “The six bodies of craving should be understood”—

mn148:9.10.verse: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.

mn148:10.3.verse: Since its rise and fall are evident, it would follow that “my self rises and falls.”

mn148:10.4.verse: That is why it is not tenable for anyone to say:

mn148:10.8.verse: The rise and fall of forms is evident.

mn148:10.9.verse: Since their rise and fall are evident, it would follow that “my self rises and falls.”

mn148:10.10.verse: That is why it is not tenable for anyone to say:

mn148:10.13.verse: If anyone says: “Eye-consciousness is self,” that is not tenable.

mn148:10.14.verse: The rise and fall of eye-consciousness is evident.

mn148:10.15.verse: Since its rise and fall are evident, it would follow that “my self rises and falls.”

mn148:10.16.verse: That is why it is not tenable for anyone to say:

mn148:28.1.verse: Bhikkhus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there arises what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

mn148:28.2.verse: If, when touched by pleasant feeling, one relishes it, affirms it, and remains holding to it,

mn148:28.3.verse: then the underlying tendency to lust underlies that.

mn148:28.4.verse: If, when touched by painful feeling, one sorrows, grieves and laments, beating one’s breast one weeps and becomes distraught,

mn148:28.5.verse: then the underlying tendency to resistance underlies that.

mn148:28.6.verse: If, when touched by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not understand as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of that feeling,

mn148:28.7.verse: then the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies that.

mn148:28.8.verse: That one shall make an end of suffering without abandoning the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling, without eliminating the underlying tendency to resistance to painful feeling, without abolishing the underlying tendency to ignorance of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, without abandoning ignorance, and without arousing true knowledge, here and now—this is not possible.

mn148:40.1.verse: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes dispassionate towards the eye, becomes dispassionate towards forms, becomes dispassionate towards eye-consciousness, becomes dispassionate towards eye-contact, becomes dispassionate towards feeling, becomes dispassionate towards craving.

mn148:41.1.verse: He becomes dispassionate towards the ear, becomes dispassionate towards sounds …

mn148:41.2.verse: he becomes dispassionate towards the nose, becomes dispassionate towards odours …

mn148:41.3.verse: he becomes dispassionate towards the tongue, becomes dispassionate towards flavours …

mn148:41.4.verse: he becomes dispassionate towards the body, becomes dispassionate towards tangibles …

mn148:41.5.verse: he becomes dispassionate towards the mind, becomes dispassionate towards dhammas, becomes dispassionate towards mind-consciousness, becomes dispassionate towards mind-contact, becomes dispassionate towards feeling, becomes dispassionate towards craving.

mn148:41.6.verse: Being dispassionate, his greed fades away; with the fading of greed his mind is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’

mn148:41.7.verse: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’”

mn148:41.8.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

mn148:41.9.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn148:41.10.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of as many as sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints by not clinging.

mn148:41.11.verse: The Discourse on the Six Sixes, the sixth, is finished.

mn148:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn148:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn148:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I shall teach you the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I shall reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure, namely,

mn148:2.3.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn148:3.1.verse: “The six interior sense fields should be understood. The six exterior sense fields should be understood. The six classes of consciousness should be understood. The six classes of contact should be understood. The six classes of feeling should be understood. The six classes of craving should be understood.

mn148:4.1.verse: ‘The six interior sense fields should be understood.’

mn148:4.2.verse: That’s what I said, but why did I say it?

mn148:4.3.verse: There are the sense fields of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

mn148:4.4.verse: ‘The six interior sense fields should be understood.’

mn148:4.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn148:5.5.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn148:6.10.verse: That’s what I said, and this is why I said it.

mn148:6.11.verse: This is the third set of six.

mn148:28.1.verse: Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a requirement for the arising of what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral.

mn148:28.2.verse: When you experience a pleasant feeling, if you approve, welcome, and keep clinging to it,

mn148:28.3.verse: the underlying tendency to greed underlies that.

mn148:28.4.verse: When you experience a painful feeling, if you sorrow and wail and lament, beating your breast and falling into confusion,

mn148:28.5.verse: the underlying tendency to aversion underlies that.

mn148:28.6.verse: When you experience a neutral feeling, if you don’t truly understand that feeling’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape,

mn148:28.7.verse: the underlying tendency to ignorance underlies that.

mn148:28.8.verse: Mendicants, without giving up the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling, without dispelling the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling, without eradicating ignorance in the case of neutral feeling, without giving up ignorance and without giving rise to knowledge, it is quite impossible to make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn148:29-33.5.verse: Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and ideas. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a requirement for the arising of what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral.

mn148:34.5.verse: the underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie that.

mn148:34.6.verse: When you experience a neutral feeling, if you truly understand that feeling’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape,

mn148:34.7.verse: the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that.

mn148:34.8.verse: Mendicants, after giving up the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling, after dispelling the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling, after eradicating ignorance in the case of neutral feeling, after giving up ignorance and giving rise to knowledge, it’s quite possible to make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn148:39.1.verse: Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and ideas. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a requirement for what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral.

mn148:39.2.verse: When you experience a pleasant feeling, if you don’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to it,

mn148:39.3.verse: the underlying tendency to greed does not underlie that.

mn148:39.4.verse: When you experience a painful feeling, if you don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating your breast and falling into confusion,

mn148:39.5.verse: the underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie that.

mn148:39.6.verse: When you experience a neutral feeling, if you truly understand that feeling’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape,

mn148:39.7.verse: the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that.

mn148:39.8.verse: Mendicants, after giving up the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling, after dispelling the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling, after eradicating ignorance in the case of neutral feeling, after giving up ignorance and giving rise to knowledge, it’s quite possible to make an end of suffering in this very life.

mn148:40.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, eye contact, feeling, and craving.

mn148:41.1.verse: They grow disillusioned with the ear …

mn148:41.5.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, mind contact, feeling, and craving.

mn148:41.6.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When it is freed, they know it is freed.

mn148:41.7.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

mn148:41.8.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn148:41.9.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn148:41.10.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty mendicants were freed from defilements by not grasping.

mn149:0.2.verse: The Great Discourse on What Relates to the Six Sense Fields

mn149:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

mn149:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

mn149:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, I shall teach you the great discourse on what relates to the six sense fields.

mn149:2.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

mn149:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, when you don’t truly know and see the eye, sights, eye consciousness, eye contact, and what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral that arises dependent on eye contact, you’re aroused by these things.

mn149:3.2.verse: Someone who lives aroused like this—fettered, confused, concentrating on gratification—accumulates the five grasping aggregates for themselves in the future.

mn149:3.3.verse: And their craving—which leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights—grows.

mn149:3.7.verse: And they experience physical and mental suffering.

mn149:4-7.1.verse: When you don’t truly know and see the ear …

mn149:4-7.5.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, mind contact, and what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral that arises dependent on mind contact, you’re aroused by these things.

mn149:8.1.verse: Someone who lives aroused like this—fettered, confused, concentrating on gratification—accumulates the five grasping aggregates for themselves in the future.

mn149:8.2.verse: And their craving—which leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights—grows.

mn149:8.6.verse: And they experience physical and mental suffering.

mn149:9.1.verse: When you do truly know and see the eye, sights, eye consciousness, eye contact, and what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral that arises dependent on eye contact, you’re not aroused by these things.

mn149:9.2.verse: Someone who lives unaroused like this—unfettered, unconfused, concentrating on drawbacks—disperses the five grasping aggregates for themselves in the future.

mn149:9.3.verse: And their craving—which leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights—is given up.

mn149:9.7.verse: And they experience physical and mental pleasure.

mn149:10.1.verse: The view of such a person is right view.

mn149:10.5.verse: and their immersion is right immersion.

mn149:10.6.verse: And their actions of body and speech, and their livelihood, have already been fully purified before.

mn149:10.7.verse: So this noble eightfold path is fully developed.

mn149:10.8.verse: When the noble eightfold path is developed, the following are fully developed: the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven awakening factors.

mn149:10.9.verse: And these two qualities proceed in conjunction:

mn149:10.11.verse: They completely understand by direct knowledge those things that should be completely understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.12.verse: They give up by direct knowledge those things that should be given up by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.13.verse: They develop by direct knowledge those things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.14.verse: They realize by direct knowledge those things that should be realized by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.1.verse: And what are the things that should be completely understood by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.2.verse: You should say: ‘The five grasping aggregates.’

mn149:11.3.verse: That is: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

mn149:11.4.verse: These are the things that should be completely understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.5.verse: And what are the things that should be given up by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.6.verse: Ignorance and craving for continued existence.

mn149:11.7.verse: These are the things that should be given up by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.8.verse: And what are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.10.verse: These are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.11.verse: And what are the things that should be realized by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.13.verse: These are the things that should be realized by direct knowledge.

mn149:12-18.1.verse: When you truly know and see the ear …

mn149:12-18.5.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, mind contact, and what is felt as pleasant, painful, or neutral that arises dependent on mind contact, you are not aroused by these things. …

mn149:26.3.verse: These are the things that should be realized by direct knowledge.”

mn149:26.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn149:26.5.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

mn149:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

mn149:1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

mn149:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you a discourse on the great sixfold base.

mn149:2.2.verse: Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”

mn149:3.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, when one does not know and see the eye as it actually is, when one does not know and see forms as they actually are, when one does not know and see eye-consciousness as it actually is, when one does not know and see eye-contact as it actually is, when one does not know and see as it actually is [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with eye-contact as condition, then one is inflamed by lust for the eye, for forms, for eye-consciousness, for eye-contact, for [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with eye-contact as condition.

mn149:3.2.verse: When one abides inflamed by lust, fettered, infatuated, contemplating gratification, then the five aggregates affected by clinging are built up for oneself in the future;

mn149:3.3.verse: and one’s craving—which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that—increases.

mn149:3.4.verse: One’s bodily and mental troubles increase,

mn149:3.5.verse: one’s bodily and mental torments increase,

mn149:3.6.verse: one’s bodily and mental fevers increase,

mn149:3.7.verse: and one experiences bodily and mental suffering.

mn149:4-7.1.verse: “When one does not know and see the ear as it actually is…

mn149:4-7.2.verse: when one does not know and see the nose as it actually is…

mn149:4-7.3.verse: when one does not know and see the tongue as it actually is…

mn149:4-7.4.verse: when one does not know and see the body as it actually is…

mn149:4-7.5.verse: When one does not know and see the mind as it actually is, when one does not know and see mind-objects as they actually are, when one does not know and see mind-consciousness as it actually is, when one does not know and see mind-contact as it actually is, when one does not know and see as it actually is [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with mind-contact as condition, then one is inflamed by lust for the mind, for mind-objects, for mind-consciousness, for mind-contact, for [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with mind-contact as condition.

mn149:8.1.verse: When one abides inflamed by lust, fettered, infatuated, contemplating gratification, then the five aggregates affected by clinging are built up for oneself in the future;

mn149:8.2.verse: and one’s craving—which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that—increases.

mn149:8.3.verse: One’s bodily and mental troubles increase,

mn149:8.4.verse: one’s bodily and mental torments increase,

mn149:8.5.verse: one’s bodily and mental fevers increase,

mn149:8.6.verse: and one experiences bodily and mental suffering.

mn149:9.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, when one knows and sees the eye as it actually is, when one knows and sees forms as they actually are, when one knows and sees eye-consciousness as it actually is, when one knows and sees eye-contact as it actually is, when one knows and sees as it actually is [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with eye-contact as condition, then one is not inflamed by lust for the eye, for forms, for eye-consciousness, for eye-contact, for [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with eye-contact as condition.

mn149:9.2.verse: When one abides uninflamed by lust, unfettered, uninfatuated, contemplating danger, then the five aggregates affected by clinging are diminished for oneself in the future;

mn149:9.3.verse: and one’s craving—which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this or that—is abandoned.

mn149:9.4.verse: One’s bodily and mental troubles are abandoned,

mn149:9.5.verse: one’s bodily and mental torments are abandoned,

mn149:9.6.verse: one’s bodily and mental fevers are abandoned,

mn149:9.7.verse: and one experiences bodily and mental pleasure.

mn149:10.1.verse: The view of a person such as this is right view.

mn149:10.6.verse: But his bodily action, his verbal action, and his livelihood have already been well purified earlier.

mn149:10.7.verse: Thus this Noble Eightfold Path comes to fulfilment in him by development.

mn149:10.8.verse: When he develops this Noble Eightfold Path, the four foundations of mindfulness also come to fulfilment in him by development; the four right kinds of striving also come to fulfilment in him by development; the four bases for spiritual power also come to fulfilment in him by development; the five faculties also come to fulfilment in him by development; the five powers also come to fulfilment in him by development; the seven enlightenment factors also come to fulfilment in him by development.

mn149:10.9.verse: These two things occur in him yoked evenly together—

mn149:10.11.verse: He fully understands by direct knowledge those things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.12.verse: He abandons by direct knowledge those things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.13.verse: He develops by direct knowledge those things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:10.14.verse: He realises by direct knowledge those things that should be realised by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.1.verse: “And what things should be fully understood by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.2.verse: The answer to that is: the five aggregates affected by clinging,

mn149:11.3.verse: that is, the material form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn149:11.4.verse: These are the things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.5.verse: “And what things should be abandoned by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.7.verse: these are the things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.8.verse: “And what things should be developed by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.10.verse: these are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:11.11.verse: “And what things should be realised by direct knowledge?

mn149:11.13.verse: these are the things that should be realised by direct knowledge.

mn149:12-18.1.verse: “When one knows and sees the ear as it actually is…

mn149:12-18.2.verse: when one knows and sees the nose as it actually is…

mn149:12-18.3.verse: when one knows and sees the tongue as it actually is…

mn149:12-18.4.verse: when one knows and sees the body as it actually is…

mn149:12-18.5.verse: When one knows and sees the mind as it actually is, when one knows and sees mind-objects as they actually are, when one knows and sees mind-consciousness as it actually is, when one knows and sees mind-contact as it actually is, when one knows and sees as it actually is [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with mind-contact as condition, then one is not inflamed by lust for the mind, for mind-objects, for mind-consciousness, for mind-contact, for [the feeling] felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant that arises with mind-contact as condition.

mn149:19.1.verse: When one abides uninflamed by lust, unfettered, uninfatuated, contemplating danger, then the five aggregates affected by clinging are diminished for oneself in the future;

mn149:19.2.verse: and one’s craving—which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this or that—is abandoned.

mn149:19.3.verse: One’s bodily and mental troubles are abandoned,

mn149:19.4.verse: one’s bodily and mental torments are abandoned,

mn149:19.5.verse: one’s bodily and mental fevers are abandoned,

mn149:19.6.verse: and one experiences bodily and mental pleasure.

mn149:20.1.verse: The view of a person such as this is right view.

mn149:20.6.verse: But his bodily action, his verbal action, and his livelihood have already been well purified earlier.

mn149:20.7.verse: Thus this Noble Eightfold Path comes to fulfilment in him by development.

mn149:21.1.verse: When he develops this Noble Eightfold Path, the four foundations of mindfulness also come to fulfilment in him by development; the four right kinds of striving also come to fulfilment in him by development; the four bases for spiritual power also come to fulfilment in him by development; the five faculties also come to fulfilment in him by development; the five powers also come to fulfilment in him by development; the seven enlightenment factors also come to fulfilment in him by development.

mn149:22.1.verse: These two things occur in him yoked evenly together—

mn149:22.3.verse: He fully understands by direct knowledge those things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:22.4.verse: He abandons by direct knowledge those things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge.

mn149:22.5.verse: He develops by direct knowledge those things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:22.6.verse: He realises by direct knowledge those things that should be realised by direct knowledge.

mn149:23.1.verse: “And what things should be fully understood by direct knowledge?

mn149:23.2.verse: The answer to that is: the five aggregates affected by clinging, that is—

mn149:23.3.verse: the material form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

mn149:23.4.verse: These are the things that should be fully understood by direct knowledge.

mn149:24.1.verse: “And what things should be abandoned by direct knowledge?

mn149:24.3.verse: these are the things that should be abandoned by direct knowledge.

mn149:25.1.verse: “And what things should be developed by direct knowledge?

mn149:25.3.verse: these are the things that should be developed by direct knowledge.

mn149:26.1.verse: “And what things should be realised by direct knowledge?

mn149:26.3.verse: these are the things that should be realised by direct knowledge.”

mn149:26.4.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

mn149:26.5.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

mn150:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmin householders named Nagaravinda.

mn150:2.1.verse: The brahmin householders of Nagaravinda heard:

mn150:2.2.verse: ‘The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, has arrived at Nagaravinda.

mn150:2.3.verse: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:

mn150:2.4.verse: “That Blessed One is such since he is accomplished, fully enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.”

mn150:2.5.verse: He describes this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans, which he has himself realized through direct knowledge.

mn150:2.6.verse: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure.

mn150:2.7.verse: It is good to see such arahants.’

mn150:3.1.verse: Then the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda went to the Blessed One; some of them, having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down at one side; some exchanged greetings with him, and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, sat down at one side; some raised their hands palms together in salutation to the Blessed One and sat down at one side; some pronounced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence and sat down at one side; some kept silent and sat down at one side. When the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda were seated at one side, the Blessed One said this to them:

mn150:4.1.verse: ‘Householders, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you thus:

mn150:4.2.verse: “Householders, what sort of ascetics and brahmins should not be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated?”—

mn150:4.3.verse: being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus:

mn150:4.4.verse: “Those ascetics and brahmins who are not rid of lust, not rid of hate, not rid of delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, whose minds are not stilled within, and who conduct themselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins should not be honoured, respected, revered, or venerated.

mn150:4.6.verse: Because we too are not rid of lust, not rid of hate, not rid of delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, our minds are not stilled within, and we conduct ourselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind; since we see no higher conduct than our own in these good ascetics and brahmins,

mn150:4.7.verse: therefore those ascetics and brahmins should not be honoured, respected, revered, or venerated.

mn150:4.8.verse: Those ascetics and brahmins who are not rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn150:4.9.verse: regarding odours cognizable by the nose …

mn150:4.10.verse: regarding flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn150:4.11.verse: regarding tangibles cognizable by the body …

mn150:4.12.verse: who are not rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding dhammas cognizable by the mind, whose minds are not stilled within, and who conduct themselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins should not be honoured, respected, revered, or venerated.

mn150:4.14.verse: Because we too are not rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding dhammas cognizable by the mind, our minds are not stilled within, and we conduct ourselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind; since we see no higher conduct than our own in these good ascetics and brahmins,

mn150:4.15.verse: therefore those ascetics and brahmins should not be honoured, respected, revered, or venerated.”

mn150:4.16.verse: Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus.

mn150:5.1.verse: But, householders, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you thus:

mn150:5.2.verse: “Householders, what sort of ascetics and brahmins should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated?”—

mn150:5.3.verse: being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus:

mn150:5.4.verse: “Those ascetics and brahmins who are rid of lust, rid of hate, rid of delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, whose minds are stilled within, and who conduct themselves rightly in body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated.

mn150:5.6.verse: Because we are not rid of lust, not rid of hate, not rid of delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, our minds are not stilled within, and we conduct ourselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind; since we see a higher conduct than our own in these good ascetics and brahmins,

mn150:5.7.verse: therefore those ascetics and brahmins should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated.

mn150:5.8.verse: Those ascetics and brahmins who are rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding sounds cognizable by the ear …

mn150:5.9.verse: regarding odours cognizable by the nose …

mn150:5.10.verse: regarding flavours cognizable by the tongue …

mn150:5.11.verse: regarding tangibles cognizable by the body …

mn150:5.12.verse: who are rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding dhammas cognizable by the mind, whose minds are stilled within, and who conduct themselves rightly in body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated.

mn150:5.14.verse: Because we are not rid of lust, hate, and delusion regarding dhammas cognizable by the mind, our minds are not stilled within, and we conduct ourselves sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly in body, speech, and mind; since we see a higher conduct than our own in these good ascetics and brahmins,

mn150:5.15.verse: therefore those ascetics and brahmins should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated.”

mn150:5.16.verse: Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus.

mn150:6.1.verse: But, householders, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you thus:

mn150:6.2.verse: “But what is the reason, what is the ground, venerable ones, by which you speak thus?

mn150:6.3.verse: Surely those venerable ones are either rid of lust or have entered on the way to remove lust; are either rid of hate or have entered on the way to remove hate; are either rid of delusion or have entered on the way to remove delusion”—

mn150:6.4.verse: being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus:

mn150:6.5.verse: “Indeed, those venerable ones resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest.

mn150:6.6.verse: There there are no such forms cognizable by the eye that, having seen them again and again, they would delight in; there are no such sounds cognizable by the ear that, having heard them again and again, they would delight in; there are no such odours cognizable by the nose that, having smelled them again and again, they would delight in; there are no such flavours cognizable by the tongue that, having tasted them again and again, they would delight in; there are no such tangibles cognizable by the body that, having touched them again and again, they would delight in.

mn150:6.7.verse: These, friends, are the reason, this is the ground, by which we speak thus—

mn150:6.8.verse: surely those venerable ones are either rid of lust or have entered on the way to remove lust; are either rid of hate or have entered on the way to remove hate; are either rid of delusion or have entered on the way to remove delusion.”

mn150:6.9.verse: Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus.’

mn150:7.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda said to the Blessed One:

mn150:7.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms.

mn150:7.4.verse: We go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

mn150:7.5.verse: From today let Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone to him for refuge for life.’

mn150:7.6.verse: The Discourse to the Nagaravindans, the eighth, is finished.

mn150:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Nagaravinda.

mn150:2.1.verse: The brahmins and householders of Nagaravinda heard,

mn150:2.2.verse: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—while wandering in the land of the Kosalans has arrived at Nagaravinda, together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

mn150:2.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

mn150:2.5.verse: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

mn150:2.6.verse: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

mn150:2.7.verse: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

mn150:3.1.verse: Then the brahmins and householders of Nagaravinda went up to the Buddha. Before sitting down to one side, some bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent. The Buddha said to them:

mn150:4.1.verse: “Householders, if wanderers who follow another religion were to ask you:

mn150:4.2.verse: ‘What kind of ascetic or brahmin doesn’t deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration?’

mn150:4.4.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are not free of greed, hate, and delusion for sights known by the eye, whose minds are not settled internally, and who conduct themselves badly among the good by way of body, speech, and mind. They don’t deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:4.6.verse: Because we ourselves are not free of these things, so we do not see that they have any higher good conduct than us.

mn150:4.7.verse: That’s why they don’t deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:4.8.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who are not free of greed, hate, and delusion for sounds known by the ear …

mn150:4.12.verse: ideas known by the mind, who are not settled internally, and who conduct themselves badly among the good by way of body, speech, and mind. They don’t deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:4.14.verse: Because we ourselves are not free of these things, so we do not see that they have any higher good conduct than us.

mn150:4.15.verse: That’s why they don’t deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.’

mn150:4.16.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.

mn150:5.1.verse: If wanderers of other religions were to ask you:

mn150:5.2.verse: ‘What kind of ascetic or brahmin deserves honor, respect, reverence, and veneration?’

mn150:5.4.verse: ‘There are ascetics and brahmins who are free of greed, hate, and delusion for sights known by the eye, whose minds are settled internally, and who conduct themselves well by way of body, speech, and mind. They deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:5.6.verse: Because we ourselves are not free of these things, but we see that they have a higher good conduct than us.

mn150:5.7.verse: That’s why they deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:5.8.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who are free of greed, hate, and delusion for sounds known by the ear …

mn150:5.12.verse: ideas known by the mind, whose minds are settled internally, and who conduct themselves well by way of body, speech, and mind. They deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.

mn150:5.14.verse: Because we ourselves are not free of these things, but we see that they have a higher good conduct than us.

mn150:5.15.verse: That’s why they deserve honor, respect, reverence, and veneration.’

mn150:5.16.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.

mn150:6.1.verse: If wanderers of other religions were to ask you:

mn150:6.2.verse: ‘But what reasons and evidence do you have regarding those venerables that justifies saying,

mn150:6.3.verse: “Clearly those venerables are free of greed, hate, and delusion, or practicing to be free of them”?’

mn150:6.5.verse: ‘It’s because those venerables frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest.

mn150:6.6.verse: In such places there are no sights known by the eye to see and enjoy, there are no sounds known by the ear to hear and enjoy, no odors known by the nose to smell and enjoy, no flavors known by the tongue to taste and enjoy, and no touches known by the body to feel and enjoy.

mn150:6.7.verse: These are the reasons and evidence that you have regarding those venerables that justifies saying,

mn150:6.8.verse: “Clearly those venerables are free of greed, hate, and delusion, or practicing to be free of them”.’

mn150:6.9.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.”

mn150:7.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmins and householders of Nagaravinda said to the Buddha,

mn150:7.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the Teaching clear in many ways.

mn150:7.4.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

mn150:7.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

mn151:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

mn151:1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Sāriputta came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

mn151:2.1.verse: “Sāriputta, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

mn151:2.2.verse: What kind of meditation are you usually practicing these days?”

mn151:2.3.verse: “Sir, these days I usually practice the meditation on emptiness.”

mn151:2.5.verse: It seems you usually practice the meditation of a great man.

mn151:2.6.verse: For emptiness is the meditation of a great man.

mn151:3.2.verse: ‘May I usually practice the meditation on emptiness.’ So they should reflect:

mn151:3.3.verse: ‘Along the path that I went for alms, or in the place I wandered for alms, or along the path that I returned from alms, was there any desire or greed or hate or delusion or aversion in my heart for sights known by the eye?’

mn151:3.4.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:3.5.verse: there was such desire or greed or hate or delusion or aversion in their heart, they should make an effort to give up those unskillful qualities.

mn151:3.6.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:3.7.verse: there was no such desire or greed or hate or delusion or aversion in their heart, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:4-8.2.verse: ‘Along the path that I went for alms, or in the place I wandered for alms, or along the path that I returned from alms, was there any desire or greed or hate or delusion or repulsion in my heart for sounds known by the ear …

mn151:4-8.7.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:4-8.8.verse: there was such desire or greed or hate or delusion or aversion in their heart, they should make an effort to give up those unskillful qualities.

mn151:4-8.9.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:4-8.10.verse: there was no such desire or greed or hate or delusion or aversion in their heart, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:9.2.verse: ‘Have I given up the five kinds of sensual stimulation?’

mn151:9.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:9.4.verse: they have not given them up, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:9.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:9.6.verse: they have given them up, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:10.2.verse: ‘Have I given up the five hindrances?’

mn151:10.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:10.4.verse: they have not given them up, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:10.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:10.6.verse: they have given them up, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:11.2.verse: ‘Have I completely understood the five grasping aggregates?’

mn151:11.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:11.4.verse: they have not completely understood them, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:11.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:11.6.verse: they have completely understood them, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:12.2.verse: ‘Have I developed the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?’

mn151:12.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:12.4.verse: they haven’t developed them, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:12.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:12.6.verse: they have developed them, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:13.2.verse: ‘Have I developed the four right efforts …

mn151:14.2.verse: the four bases of psychic power …

mn151:18.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:18.4.verse: they haven’t developed it, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:18.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:18.6.verse: they have developed it, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:19.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:19.4.verse: they haven’t developed them, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:19.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:19.6.verse: they have developed them, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:20.3.verse: Suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:20.4.verse: they haven’t realized them, they should make an effort to do so.

mn151:20.5.verse: But suppose that, upon checking, a mendicant knows that

mn151:20.6.verse: they have realized them, they should meditate with rapture and joy, training day and night in skillful qualities.

mn151:21.1.verse: Whether in the past, future, or present, all those who purify their almsfood do so by continually checking in this way.

mn151:21.4.verse: So, Sāriputta, you should all train like this: ‘We shall purify our almsfood by continually checking.’”

mn151:21.6.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

mn151:21.7.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Sāriputta approved what the Buddha said.

mn151:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

mn151:1.3.verse: Then, when it was evening, the venerable Sāriputta rose from meditation and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. The Blessed One then said to him:

mn151:2.1.verse: “Sāriputta, your faculties are clear. The colour of your skin is pure and bright.

mn151:2.2.verse: What abiding do you often abide in now, Sāriputta?”

mn151:2.3.verse: “Now, venerable sir, I often abide in voidness.”

mn151:2.5.verse: Now, indeed, you often abide in the abiding of a great man.

mn151:2.6.verse: For this is the abiding of a great man, namely—

mn151:3.1.verse: “So, Sāriputta, if a bhikkhu should wish:

mn151:3.2.verse: ‘May I now often abide in voidness,’ he should consider thus:

mn151:3.3.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, or in the place where I wandered for alms, or on the path by which I returned from the almsround, was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding forms cognizable by the eye?’

mn151:3.4.verse: If, by so reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:3.5.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, or in the place where I wandered for alms, or on the path by which I returned from the almsround, there was desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding forms cognizable by the eye,’ then he should make an effort to abandon those evil unwholesome states.

mn151:3.6.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:3.7.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, and in the place where I wandered for alms, and on the path by which I returned from the almsround, there was no desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding forms cognizable by the eye,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:4-8.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:4-8.2.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, or in the place where I wandered for alms, or on the path by which I returned from the almsround, was there any desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding sounds cognizable by the ear?…

mn151:4-8.3.verse: regarding odours cognizable by the nose?…

mn151:4-8.4.verse: regarding flavours cognizable by the tongue?…

mn151:4-8.5.verse: regarding tangibles cognizable by the body?…

mn151:4-8.6.verse: regarding mind-objects cognizable by the mind?’

mn151:4-8.7.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:4-8.8.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, or in the place where I wandered for alms, or on the path by which I returned from the almsround, there was desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding mind-objects cognizable by the mind,’ then he should make an effort to abandon those evil unwholesome states.

mn151:4-8.9.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:4-8.10.verse: ‘On the path by which I went to the village for alms, and in the place where I wandered for alms, and on the path by which I returned from the almsround, there was no desire, lust, hate, delusion, or aversion in my mind regarding mind-objects cognizable by the mind,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:9.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:9.2.verse: ‘Are the five cords of sensual pleasure abandoned in me?’

mn151:9.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:9.4.verse: ‘The five cords of sensual pleasure are not abandoned in me,’ then he should make an effort to abandon those five cords of sensual pleasure.

mn151:9.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:9.6.verse: ‘The five cords of sensual pleasure are abandoned in me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:10.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:10.2.verse: ‘Are the five hindrances abandoned in me?’

mn151:10.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:10.4.verse: ‘The five hindrances are not abandoned in me,’ then he should make an effort to abandon those five hindrances.

mn151:10.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:10.6.verse: ‘The five hindrances are abandoned in me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:11.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:11.2.verse: ‘Are the five aggregates affected by clinging fully understood by me?’

mn151:11.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:11.4.verse: ‘The five aggregates affected by clinging are not fully understood by me,’ then he should make an effort to fully understand those five aggregates affected by clinging.

mn151:11.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:11.6.verse: ‘The five aggregates affected by clinging are fully understood by me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:12.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:12.2.verse: ‘Are the four foundations of mindfulness developed in me?’

mn151:12.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:12.4.verse: ‘The four foundations of mindfulness are not developed in me,’ then he should make an effort to develop those four foundations of mindfulness.

mn151:12.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:12.6.verse: ‘The four foundations of mindfulness are developed in me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:13.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:13.2.verse: ‘Are the four right kinds of striving developed in me?’

mn151:13.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:13.4.verse: ‘The four right kinds of striving are not developed in me,’ then he should make an effort to develop those four right kinds of striving.

mn151:13.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:13.6.verse: ‘The four right kinds of striving are developed in me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:14.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:14.2.verse: ‘Are the four bases for spiritual power developed in me?’

mn151:14.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:14.4.verse: ‘The four bases for spiritual power are not developed in me,’ then he should make an effort to develop those four bases for spiritual power.

mn151:14.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:14.6.verse: ‘The four bases for spiritual power are developed in me,’ then he can abide happy and glad, training day and night in wholesome states.

mn151:15.1.verse: “Again, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should consider thus:

mn151:15.2.verse: ‘Are the five faculties developed in me?’

mn151:15.3.verse: If, by reviewing, he knows thus:

mn151:15.4.verse: ‘The five faculties are not developed in me,’ then he should make an effort to develop those five faculties.

mn151:15.5.verse: But if, by reviewing, he knows thus:
