sn2.8:1.2.verse: Then Tāyana the deva’s son, formerly of another religious sect, in the far extreme of the night, his extreme radiance lighting up the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side.

sn2.8:1.3.verse: As he was standing there, he recited these verses in the Blessed One’s presence:

sn2.8:2.3.verse: Without abandoning sensual passions, a sage

sn2.8:3.4.verse: kicks up all the more dust.

sn2.8:4.1.verse: It’s better to leave a misdeed undone.

sn2.8:4.3.verse: Better that a good deed be done

sn2.8:4.4.verse: that, when done, you don’t regret.

sn2.8:5.1.verse: Just as sharp-bladed grass, if wrongly held,

sn2.8:5.2.verse: wounds the very hand that holds it—

sn2.8:5.3.verse: the contemplative life, if wrongly grasped,

sn2.8:7.1.verse: That is what Tāyana the deva’s son said.

sn2.8:7.2.verse: Having said it, he bowed down to the Blessed One and, circling him on the right, vanished right there.

sn2.8:8.1.verse: Then, toward the end of the night, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

sn2.8:8.2.verse: “Last night, monks, Tāyana the deva’s son, formerly of another religious sect, in the far extreme of the night, his extreme radiance lighting up the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, came to me and, on arrival, having bowed down to me, stood to one side.

sn2.8:8.3.verse: As he was standing there, he recited these verses in my presence:

sn2.8:9.3.verse: Without abandoning sensual passions, a sage

sn2.8:10.4.verse: kicks up all the more dust.

sn2.8:11.1.verse: It’s better to leave a misdeed undone.

sn2.8:11.3.verse: Better that a good deed be done

sn2.8:11.4.verse: that, when done, you don’t regret.

sn2.8:12.1.verse: Just as sharp-bladed grass, if wrongly held,

sn2.8:12.2.verse: wounds the very hand that holds it—

sn2.8:12.3.verse: the contemplative life, if wrongly grasped,

sn2.8:14.1.verse: That is what Tāyana the deva’s son said. Having said it, he bowed down to me and, circling me on the right, vanished right there.

sn2.8:14.5.verse: Connected with the goal are Tāyana’s verses, monks, and basic to the holy life.”

sn2.8:1.2.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious godling Tāyana, formerly a religious founder, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side,

sn2.8:1.3.verse: and recited these verses in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.8:2.3.verse: A sage who doesn’t give up sensual pleasures

sn2.8:2.4.verse: is not reborn in a unified state.

sn2.8:3.1.verse: If one is to do what should be done,

sn2.8:3.3.verse: For the life gone forth when laxly led

sn2.8:3.4.verse: just stirs up dust all the more.

sn2.8:4.1.verse: A bad deed is better left undone,

sn2.8:4.2.verse: for it will plague you later on.

sn2.8:4.3.verse: A good deed is better done,

sn2.8:4.4.verse: one that does not plague you.

sn2.8:5.1.verse: When kusa grass is wrongly grasped

sn2.8:5.3.verse: So too, the ascetic life, when wrongly taken,

sn2.8:7.1.verse: That is what the godling Tāyana said.

sn2.8:7.2.verse: Then he bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

sn2.8:8.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened.

sn2.8:8.2.verse: “Mendicants, tonight, the glorious godling Tāyana, formerly a religious founder, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, came to me, bowed, stood to one side,

sn2.8:8.3.verse: and recited these verses in my presence.” The Buddha repeated the verses in full, adding:

sn2.8:14.1.verse: “That is what the godling Tāyana said. Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right side, before vanishing right there.

sn2.8:14.2.verse: Mendicants, learn the verses of Tāyana!

sn2.8:14.5.verse: These verses are beneficial and relate to the fundamentals of the spiritual life.”

sn2.8:1.2.verse: Then, when the night had advanced, the young deva Tāyana, formerly the founder of a religious sect, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One.

sn2.8:1.3.verse: Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.8:2.4.verse: A sage does not reach unity.

sn2.8:3.1.verse: “If one would do what should be done,

sn2.8:4.2.verse: A deed that later brings repentance.

sn2.8:4.3.verse: Better done is the good deed

sn2.8:4.4.verse: Which when done is not repented.

sn2.8:5.3.verse: So the ascetic life, wrongly taken up,

sn2.8:6.3.verse: A holy life that breeds suspicion,

sn2.8:7.1.verse: ” This is what the young deva Tāyana said.

sn2.8:7.2.verse: Having said this, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on the right, he disappeared right there.

sn2.8:8.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus: “Bhikkhus,

sn2.8:8.2.verse: last night, when the night had advanced, the young deva Tāyana, formerly the founder of a religious sect . approached me .

sn2.8:8.3.verse: and in my presence recited these verses:

sn2.8:14.1.verse: “This is what the young deva Tāyana said. Having said this, he paid homage to me and, keeping me on the right, he disappeared right there.

sn2.8:14.5.verse: Tāyana’s verses are beneficial, bhikkhus, they pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life. ”

sn2.13:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn2.13:1.3.verse: Then, late at night, the glorious godling Dīghalaṭṭhi, lighting up the entire Bamboo Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side,

sn2.13:1.4.verse: and spoke this verse in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.13:2.1.verse: “If a mendicant is a meditator, freed in mind,

sn2.13:2.2.verse: and if they desire the heart’s fulfillment—

sn2.13:2.3.verse: having known the arising and passing of the world,

sn2.13:2.4.verse: good-hearted, independent, that is their reward.”

sn2.13:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary.

sn2.13:1.3.verse: Then, when the night had advanced, the young deva Dīghalaṭṭhi, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Bamboo Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side,

sn2.13:1.4.verse: and recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.13:2.1.verse: “A bhikkhu should be a meditator, One who is liberated in mind,

sn2.13:2.2.verse: If he desires the heart’s attainment, Bent on that as his advantage.

sn2.13:2.3.verse: Having known the world’s rise and fall,

sn2.13:2.4.verse: Let him be lofty in mind and unattached. ”

sn2.14:1.1.verse: Standing to one side, the godling Nandana addressed the Buddha in verse:

sn2.14:2.1.verse: “I ask you, Gotama, whose wisdom is vast,

sn2.14:2.2.verse: the Blessed One of unhindered knowledge and vision.

sn2.14:2.3.verse: What sort do they call ethical?

sn2.14:2.4.verse: What sort do they call wise?

sn2.14:2.5.verse: What sort lives on after transcending suffering?

sn2.14:2.6.verse: What sort is worshiped by the deities?”

sn2.14:3.3.verse: who’s gotten rid of and given up all sorrows,

sn2.14:3.4.verse: with defilements ended, they bear their final body.

sn2.14:4.3.verse: That sort lives on after transcending suffering.

sn2.14:4.4.verse: That sort is worshiped by the deities.”

sn2.14:1.1.verse: Standing to one side, the young deva Nandana addressed the Blessed One in verse:

sn2.14:2.1.verse: “I ask you, Gotama, broad of wisdom—

sn2.14:2.2.verse: Unobstructed is the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision:

sn2.14:2.3.verse: What is he like whom they call virtuous?

sn2.14:2.4.verse: What is he like whom they call wise?

sn2.14:2.5.verse: What is he like who has passed beyond suffering?

sn2.14:2.6.verse: What is he like whom the devatās worship?”

sn2.14:3.3.verse: For whom all sorrows are gone, abandoned,

sn2.14:3.4.verse: A taint-destroyer bearing his final body:

sn2.14:4.1.verse: It is such a one that they call virtuous,

sn2.14:4.2.verse: Such a one that they call wise,

sn2.14:4.3.verse: Such a one has passed beyond suffering,

sn2.14:4.4.verse: Such a one the devatās worship. ”

sn2.15:1.1.verse: Standing to one side, the godling Candana addressed the Buddha in verse:

sn2.15:2.4.verse: does not sink in the deep?”

sn2.15:3.1.verse: “Someone who is always endowed with ethics,

sn2.15:3.4.verse: crosses the flood so hard to cross.

sn2.15:4.1.verse: Someone who desists from sensual perception,

sn2.15:4.2.verse: has moved past the fetter of form,

sn2.25:2.1.verse: Then, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, the young deva Jantu approached those bhikkhus and addressed them in verses:

sn2.26:1.2.verse: As he was standing to one side, Rohitassa the deva’s son said to the Blessed One:

sn2.26:1.3.verse: “Is it possible, lord, by traveling, to know or see or reach a far end of the cosmos where one doesn’t take birth, age, die, pass away or reappear?”

sn2.26:1.4.verse: “I tell you, friend, that it isn’t possible by traveling to know or see or reach a far end of the cosmos where one doesn’t take birth, age, die, pass away, or reappear.”

sn2.26:2.2.verse: how well that has been said by the Lord Blessed One:

sn2.26:2.3.verse: ‘I tell you, friend, that it isn’t possible by traveling to know or see or reach a far end of the cosmos where one doesn’t take birth, age, die, pass away, or reappear.’

sn2.26:3.1.verse: Once I was a seer named Rohitassa, a student of Bhoja, a powerful sky-walker.

sn2.26:3.2.verse: My speed was as fast as that of a strong archer—well trained, a practiced hand, a practiced sharpshooter—shooting a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree.

sn2.26:3.3.verse: My stride stretched as far as the east sea is from the west.

sn2.26:3.4.verse: To me, there came the desire:

sn2.26:3.5.verse: ‘I will go traveling to the end of the cosmos.’

sn2.26:3.6.verse: I— endowed with such speed, such a stride, with a one-hundred year life, a one-hundred year span—spent one hundred years traveling—apart from the time spent on eating, drinking, chewing & tasting, urinating & defecating, and sleeping to fight off weariness—but without reaching the end of the cosmos I died along the way.

sn2.26:4.1.verse: So it’s amazing, lord, and astounding,

sn2.26:4.2.verse: how well that has been said by the Lord Blessed One:

sn2.26:4.3.verse: ‘I tell you, friend, that it isn’t possible by traveling to know or see or reach a far end of the cosmos where one doesn’t take birth, age, die, pass away, or reappear.’”

sn2.26:5.1.verse: [When this was said, the Blessed One responded:] “I tell you, friend, that it isn’t possible by traveling to know or see or reach a far end of the cosmos where one doesn’t take birth, age, die, pass away, or reappear. But at the same time, I tell you that there is no making an end of suffering & stress without reaching the end of the cosmos.

sn2.26:5.2.verse: Yet it is just within this fathom-long body, with its perception & intellect, that I declare that there is the cosmos, the origination of the cosmos, the cessation of the cosmos, and the path of practice leading to the cessation of the cosmos.”

sn2.26:6.1.verse: It’s not to be reached by traveling,

sn2.26:6.3.verse: And it’s not without reaching the end of the cosmos

sn2.26:6.4.verse: that there is release from suffering & stress.

sn2.26:7.1.verse: So, truly, an expert with regard to the cosmos, intelligent,

sn2.26:7.2.verse: a knower of the end of the cosmos, having fulfilled the holy life,

sn2.26:7.4.verse: doesn’t long for this cosmos or any other.

sn2.26:1.4.verse: “Reverend, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.”

sn2.26:2.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha.

sn2.26:3.2.verse: I was as fast as a light arrow easily shot across the shadow of a palm tree by a well-trained expert archer with a strong bow.

sn2.26:3.3.verse: My stride was such that it could span from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.

sn2.26:3.5.verse: ‘I will reach the end of the world by traveling.’

sn2.26:3.6.verse: Having such speed and stride, I traveled for my whole lifespan of a hundred years—pausing only to eat and drink, go to the toilet, and sleep to dispel weariness—and I passed away along the way, never reaching the end of the world.

sn2.26:4.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha.

sn2.26:4.3.verse: ‘Reverend, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling to a place where there’s no being born, growing old, dying, passing away, or being reborn.’”

sn2.26:5.1.verse: “But Reverend, I also say there’s no making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world.

sn2.26:5.2.verse: For it is in this fathom-long carcass with its perception and mind that I describe the world, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

sn2.26:7.2.verse: has completed the spiritual journey and gone to the end of the world.

sn2.26:7.3.verse: Assuaged, knowing the end of the world,

sn2.26:7.4.verse: they do not hope for this world or the next.”

sn2.26:1.2.verse: Standing to one side, the young deva Rohitassa said to the Blessed One:

sn2.26:1.4.verse: “As to that end of the world, friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—I say that it cannot be known, seen, or reached by travelling. ”

sn2.26:2.2.verse: How well this was stated by the Blessed One:

sn2.26:2.3.verse: ‘As to that end of the world, friend, I say that it cannot be known, seen, or reached by travelling.

sn2.26:3.1.verse: ’“Once in the past, venerable sir, I was a seer named Rohitassa, son of Bhoja, possessed of spiritual power, able to travel through the sky.

sn2.26:3.2.verse: My speed was such, venerable sir, that I could move just as swiftly as a firm-bowed archer—trained, skilful, practised, experienced—could easily shoot past the shadow of a palmyra tree with a light arrow.

sn2.26:3.3.verse: My stride was such, venerable sir, that it seemed to reach from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.

sn2.26:3.4.verse: Then, venerable sir, the wish arose in me:

sn2.26:3.5.verse: ‘I will reach the end of the world by travelling.

sn2.26:3.6.verse: ’Possessing such speed and such a stride, and having a life span of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, I travelled for a hundred years, without pausing except to eat, drink, take meals and snacks, to defecate and urinate, to sleep and dispel fatigue; yet I died along the way without having reached the end of the world.

sn2.26:4.1.verse: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir!

sn2.26:4.2.verse: How well this was stated by the Blessed One:

sn2.26:4.3.verse: ‘As to that end of the world, friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—I say that it cannot be known, seen, or reached by travelling. ’”

sn2.26:5.1.verse: “However, friend, I say that without having reached the end of the world there is no making an end to suffering.

sn2.26:5.2.verse:
It is, friend, in just this  fathom-high carcass endowed with perception and mind that I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world,
and the way leading to the cessation of the world.

sn2.26:6.1.verse: “By means of travelling it cannot be reached,

sn2.26:6.2.verse: The world’s end at any time.

sn2.26:6.3.verse: Yet without reaching the world’s end

sn2.26:6.4.verse: There is no release from suffering.

sn2.26:7.1.verse: “Therefore, truly, the world-knower, the wise one,

sn2.26:7.2.verse: Gone to the world’s end, fulfiller of the holy life,

sn2.26:7.3.verse: Having known the world’s end, at peace,

sn2.26:7.4.verse: Longs not for this world or another. ”

sn2.29:14.1.verse: Then the Buddha replied to Susīma with this verse about Venerable Sāriputta:

sn2.29:15.4.verse: developed and well-tamed, he awaits his time.”

sn2.29:1.2.verse: Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to him:

sn2.29:1.3.verse: “Do you too, Ānanda, approve of Sāriputta?”

sn2.29:2.1.verse: “Indeed, venerable sir, who would not approve of the Venerable Sāriputta, unless he were foolish, full of hatred, deluded, or mentally deranged?

sn2.29:2.2.verse: The Venerable Sāriputta, venerable sir, is wise,

sn2.29:2.9.verse: The Venerable Sāriputta, venerable sir, has few wishes;

sn2.29:2.14.verse: The Venerable Sāriputta, venerable sir, is one who gives advice,

sn2.29:2.18.verse: Indeed, venerable sir, who would not approve of the Venerable Sāriputta, unless he were foolish, full of hatred, deluded, or mentally deranged?”

sn2.29:3.1.verse: “So it is, Ānanda, so it is!

sn2.29:3.2.verse: Indeed, Ānanda, who would not approve of Sāriputta, unless he were foolish, full of hatred, deluded, or mentally deranged?

sn2.29:3.19.verse: (as above) … unless he were mentally deranged?”

sn2.29:4.1.verse: Then, while this praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the young deva Susīma, accompanied by a great assembly of young devas, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and said to him:

sn2.29:5.1.verse: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Fortunate One!

sn2.29:5.2.verse: Indeed, venerable sir, who would not approve of the Venerable Sāriputta …

sn2.29:6.1.verse: In my case too, venerable sir, no matter what assembly of young devas I have approached, I have often heard this same report:

sn2.29:6.4.verse: Indeed, who would not approve of the Venerable Sāriputta, unless he were foolish, full of hatred, deluded, or mentally deranged?’”

sn2.29:7.1.verse: Then, while this praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the young devas in Susīma’s assembly—elated, gladdened, full of rapture and joy—displayed diverse lustrous colours.

sn2.29:8.1.verse: Just as a beryl gem—beautiful, of fine quality, eight-faceted, of excellent workmanship—when placed on a brocade cloth, shines and beams and radiates,

sn2.29:8.2.verse: so too the young devas in Susīma’s assembly  … displayed diverse lustrous colours.

sn2.29:9.1.verse: And just as an ornament of finest gold—very skilfully burnished in a furnace by an adroit goldsmith—when placed on a brocade cloth, shines and beams and radiates,

sn2.29:9.2.verse: so too the young devas in Susīma’s assembly … displayed diverse lustrous colours.

sn2.29:10.1.verse: And just as, when the night is fading, the morning star shines and beams and radiates,

sn2.29:10.2.verse: so too the young devas in Susīma’s assembly . . . displayed diverse lustrous colours.

sn2.29:11.1.verse: And just as in the autumn, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, ascending in the sky, dispels all darkness from space as it shines and beams and radiates,

sn2.29:11.2.verse: so too the young devas in Susīma’s assembly—elated, gladdened, full of rapture and joy—displayed diverse lustrous colours.

sn2.29:12.1.verse: Then, with reference to the Venerable Sāriputta, the young deva Susīma recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.29:13.1.verse: “He is widely known to be a wise man,

sn2.29:13.2.verse: Sāriputta, who is free of anger;

sn2.29:13.4.verse: The seer adorned by the Teacher’s praise. ”

sn2.29:14.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, with reference to the Venerable Sāriputta, replied to the young deva Susīma in verse:

sn2.29:15.1.verse: “He is widely known to be a wise man,

sn2.29:15.2.verse: Sāriputta, who is free of anger;

sn2.29:15.4.verse: Developed, well tamed, he awaits the time. ”

sn2.30:0.3.verse: The Disciples of Various Monastics of Other Religions

sn2.30:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn2.30:1.3.verse: Then, late at night, several glorious godlings lit up the entire Bamboo Grove. They were Asama, Sahalī, Niṅka, Ākoṭaka, Veṭambarī, and Māṇavagāmiya, and all of them were disciples of various monastics of other religions. They went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side.

sn2.30:1.4.verse: Standing to one side, the godling Asama spoke this verse about Pūraṇa Kassapa in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.30:2.5.verse: What he taught should truly be trusted,

sn2.30:2.6.verse: he’s worthy of esteem as Teacher.”

sn2.30:3.1.verse: Then the godling Sahalī spoke this verse about the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.30:4.1.verse: “Through fervent mortification in disgust of sin he became well restrained.

sn2.30:4.2.verse: He gave up quarreling with people.

sn2.30:4.3.verse: Refraining from false speech, he spoke the truth.

sn2.30:4.4.verse: Surely such a man does no wrong!”

sn2.30:5.1.verse: Then the godling Niṅka spoke this verse about the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.30:6.2.verse: well restrained in the fourfold constraint;

sn2.30:6.3.verse: explaining what is seen and heard:

sn2.30:6.4.verse: surely he can be no sinner!”

sn2.30:7.1.verse: Then the godling Ākoṭaka spoke this verse about various sectarian teachers in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.30:8.2.verse: as well as this bamboo-staffed ascetic and Pūraṇa:

sn2.30:8.4.verse: surely they weren’t far from truly good men!”

sn2.30:9.1.verse: Then the godling Veṭambarī replied to the godling Ākoṭaka in verse:

sn2.30:10.3.verse: A nude liar with suspicious conduct,

sn2.30:10.4.verse: though they teach a community, is not like the good.”

sn2.30:11.1.verse: Then Māra the Wicked took possession of the godling Veṭambarī and spoke this verse in the Buddha’s presence:

sn2.30:12.1.verse: “Those dedicated to mortification in disgust of sin,

sn2.30:12.4.verse: they rejoice in the heavenly realm.

sn2.30:12.5.verse: Indeed, those mortals give correct instructions

sn2.30:13.1.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing that this was Māra the Wicked, replied to him in verse:

sn2.30:14.1.verse: “Whatever forms there are in this life or the next,

sn2.30:14.2.verse: and those of shining beauty in the sky,

sn2.30:14.3.verse: all of these you praise, Namuci,

sn2.30:14.4.verse: like bait tossed out for catching fish.”

sn2.30:15.1.verse: Then the godling Māṇavagāmiya spoke this verse about the Buddha in his presence:

sn2.30:16.2.verse: Vepulla’s said to be the best.

sn2.30:16.3.verse: Seta is the best of the Himalayan peaks,

sn2.30:16.4.verse: and the sun, of travelers in space.

sn2.30:17.1.verse: The ocean is the best of seas,

sn2.30:17.2.verse: and the moon, of lights that shine at night.

sn2.30:17.3.verse: But in all the world with its gods,

sn2.30:18.5.verse: The Linked Discourses on Godlings are complete.

sn2.30:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary.

sn2.30:1.3.verse: Then, when the night had advanced, a number  of young devas, disciples of various sectarian teachers—Asama and Sahalī and Niṅka and Ākoṭaka and Vetambarī and Māṇavagāmiya—of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Bamboo Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.

sn2.30:1.4.verse: Then, standing to one side, the young deva Asama spoke this verse referring to Pūraṇa Kassapa in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.30:2.4.verse: Nor see any merit for oneself.

sn2.30:2.5.verse: He indeed taught what is worthy of trust:

sn2.30:3.1.verse: Then the young deva Sahalī spoke this verse referring to Makkhali Gosāla in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.30:4.1.verse: “By austerity and scrupulousness, he attained complete self-restraint.

sn2.30:4.2.verse: He abandoned contentious talk with people,

sn2.30:4.3.verse: Refrained from falsehood, a speaker of truth.

sn2.30:4.4.verse: Surely such a one does no evil.

sn2.30:5.1.verse: Then the young deva Niṅka spoke this verse referring to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.30:6.2.verse: Well restrained by the four controls,

sn2.30:6.3.verse: Explaining what is seen and heard:

sn2.30:6.4.verse: Surely, he could not be a sinner. ”

sn2.30:7.1.verse: Then the young deva Ākoṭaka spoke this verse referring to various sectarian teachers in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.30:8.3.verse: Teachers of companies, attained to ascetic stature:

sn2.30:8.4.verse: They were surely not far from superior men. ”

sn2.30:9.1.verse: Then the young deva Vetambarī replied to the young deva Ākoṭaka in verse:

sn2.30:10.1.verse: “Even by howling along the wretched jackal

sn2.30:10.2.verse: Remains a vile beast, never the lion’s peer.

sn2.30:10.3.verse: So though he be the teacher of a group, The naked ascetic, speaker of falsehood,

sn2.30:10.4.verse: Arousing suspicion by his conduct, Bears no resemblance to superior men. ”

sn2.30:11.1.verse: Then Māra the Evil One took possession of the young deva Vetambarī and recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:

sn2.30:12.3.verse: And those who have settled on form,

sn2.30:12.4.verse: Delighting in the world of devas:

sn2.30:12.6.verse: In regard to the other world. ”

sn2.30:13.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, having understood, “This is Māra the Evil One, ” replied to Māra the Evil One in verse:

sn2.30:14.2.verse: And those of luminous beauty in the sky,

sn2.30:14.3.verse: All these, indeed, you praise, Namuci,

sn2.30:14.4.verse: Like bait thrown out for catching fish. ”

sn2.30:15.1.verse: Then, in the Blessed One’s presence, the young deva Māṇavagāmiya recited these verses referring to the Blessed One:

sn2.30:16.1.verse: “Vipula is called the best of mountains

sn2.30:16.3.verse: Seta, the best of snow-clad mountains,

sn2.30:16.4.verse: The sun, the best of travellers in the sky.

sn2.30:17.1.verse: “The ocean is the best body of water,

sn2.30:17.2.verse: The moon, the best of nocturnal lights,

sn2.30:17.3.verse: But in this world together with its devas

sn3.1:1.2.verse: on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn3.1:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi Kosala went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him.

sn3.1:1.4.verse: After this exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there he said to the Blessed One:

sn3.1:1.5.verse: “Now then, does Master Gotama claim, ‘I have awakened to the unexcelled right self-awakening’?”

sn3.1:1.6.verse: “If, great king, one speaking rightly could say of anyone, ‘He has awakened to the unexcelled right self-awakening,’ one could rightly say that of me.

sn3.1:1.7.verse: For I, great king, have awakened to the unexcelled right self-awakening.”

sn3.1:2.1.verse: “But Master Gotama, those contemplatives & brahmans, each with his group, each with his community, each the teacher of his group, an honored leader, well-regarded by people at large—i.e.,

sn3.1:2.2.verse: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalin, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Velaṭṭhaputta, and the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta:

sn3.1:2.3.verse: Even they, when I asked them whether they claimed to have awakened to the unexcelled right self-awakening, didn’t make that claim.

sn3.1:2.4.verse: So who is Master Gotama to do so when he is still young & newly gone forth?”

sn3.1:3.1.verse: “There are these four things, great king, that shouldn’t be despised & disparaged for being young.

sn3.1:3.3.verse: A noble warrior, great king, shouldn’t be despised & disparaged for being young.

sn3.1:3.6.verse: And a monk shouldn’t be despised & disparaged for being young.

sn3.1:3.7.verse: These are the four things that shouldn’t be despised & disparaged for being young.”

sn3.1:4.1.verse: That is what the Blessed One said.

sn3.1:4.2.verse: Having said that, the One Well-Gone, the Teacher, said further:

sn3.1:5.3.verse: a noble warrior of consummate birth, a high-born prince of great status.

sn3.1:6.1.verse: For it’s possible that this lord of human beings,

sn3.1:6.2.verse: this noble warrior, will gain the throne

sn3.1:6.4.verse: come down harshly with his royal might.

sn3.1:7.3.verse: a serpent you meet in village or wilderness:

sn3.1:8.1.verse: As that potent snake slithers along

sn3.1:8.3.verse: it may someday burn the fool,

sn3.1:9.3.verse: a blaze that feeds on many things, a flame with its blackened trail:

sn3.1:10.2.verse: becoming a great mass of flame,

sn3.1:10.3.verse: it may someday burn the fool,

sn3.1:11.1.verse: When a fire burns down a forest

sn3.1:11.3.verse: the shoots there take birth once more

sn3.1:11.4.verse: with the passage of days & nights.

sn3.1:12.1.verse: But if a monk, his virtue consummate,

sn3.1:12.3.verse: you won’t acquire sons or cattle

sn3.1:12.4.verse: nor will your heirs enjoy wealth.

sn3.1:13.2.verse: out of regard for his own good,

sn3.1:13.3.verse: should always show due respect for

sn3.1:13.5.verse: a noble warrior with high status,

sn3.1:14.1.verse: When this was said, King Pasenadi Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.1:14.3.verse: Just as if he were to place upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has the Blessed One—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear.

sn3.1:14.4.verse: I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.

sn3.1:14.5.verse: May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge, from this day forward, for life.”

sn3.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn3.1:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn3.1:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

sn3.1:1.5.verse: “Does the worthy Gotama claim to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening?”

sn3.1:1.6.verse: “If anyone should rightly be said to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening, it’s me.

sn3.1:1.7.verse: For, Great King, I have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening.”

sn3.1:2.1.verse: “Well, there are those ascetics and brahmins who lead an order and a community, and tutor a community. They’re well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people. That is,

sn3.1:2.2.verse: Pūraṇa Kassapa, the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita of the hair blanket.

sn3.1:2.3.verse: I also asked them whether they claimed to have awakened to the supreme perfect awakening, but they made no such claim.

sn3.1:2.4.verse: So why do you, given that you’re so young in age and newly gone forth?”

sn3.1:3.1.verse: “Great king, these four things should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young.

sn3.1:3.7.verse: These four things should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young.”

sn3.1:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn3.1:4.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn3.1:6.1.verse: For it’s possible that that lord of mankind,

sn3.1:6.2.verse: as aristocrat, will gain the throne.

sn3.1:6.3.verse: And in his anger he’ll execute a royal punishment,

sn3.1:6.6.verse: for the sake of your own life.

sn3.1:7.3.verse: a man should not look down on it

sn3.1:7.4.verse: or despise it for its youth.

sn3.1:8.2.verse: the serpent of fiery breath glides along.

sn3.1:8.3.verse: It lashes out and bites the fool,

sn3.1:8.6.verse: for the sake of your own life.

sn3.1:9.1.verse: A fire devours a vast amount,

sn3.1:9.2.verse: a conflagration with a blackened trail.

sn3.1:9.3.verse: A man should not look down on it

sn3.1:10.3.verse: It’ll lash out and burn the fool,

sn3.1:10.6.verse: for the sake of your own life.

sn3.1:11.1.verse: When a forest is burned by fire,

sn3.1:11.2.verse: a conflagration with a blackened trail,

sn3.1:11.3.verse: the shoots will spring up there again,

sn3.1:11.4.verse: with the passing of the days and nights.

sn3.1:12.1.verse: But if a mendicant endowed with ethics

sn3.1:12.3.verse: you’ll have no children or livestock,

sn3.1:12.4.verse: nor will your heirs find wealth.

sn3.1:13.6.verse: and a mendicant endowed with ethics.”

sn3.1:14.1.verse: When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Buddha,

sn3.1:14.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn3.1:14.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn3.1:14.5.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn3.1:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

sn3.1:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

sn3.1:1.4.verse: When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One:

sn3.1:1.5.verse: “Does Master Gotama too claim, ‘I have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment’?”

sn3.1:1.6.verse: “If, great king, one speaking rightly could say of anyone, ‘He has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, ’ it is of me that one might rightly say this.

sn3.1:1.7.verse: For I, great king, have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. ”

sn3.1:2.1.verse: “Master Gotama, even those ascetics and brahmins who are the heads of orders and companies, the teachers of companies, well known and famous founders of sects considered by the multitude to be holy men, that is,

sn3.1:2.2.verse: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Ajita Kesakambalī

sn3.1:2.3.verse: Even these, when I asked them whether they had awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, did not claim to have done so.

sn3.1:2.4.verse: So why then should Master Gotama [make such a claim] when he is so young in years and has newly gone forth?”

sn3.1:3.1.verse: “There are four things, great king, that should not be despised and disparaged as ‘young’.

sn3.1:3.3.verse: A khattiya, great king, should not be despised and disparaged as ‘young’;

sn3.1:3.4.verse: a snake should not be despised and disparaged as ‘young’;

sn3.1:3.5.verse: a fire should not be despised and disparaged as ‘young’;

sn3.1:3.6.verse: and a bhikkhu should not be despised and disparaged as ‘young. "

sn3.1:4.1.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

sn3.1:4.2.verse: Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:

sn3.1:5.2.verse: A high-born prince of glorious fame:

sn3.1:5.4.verse: A man should not disparage him.

sn3.1:6.1.verse: For it may happen that this lord of men,

sn3.1:6.2.verse: This khattiya, shall gain the throne,

sn3.1:6.3.verse: And in his anger thrash one harshly With a royal punishment.

sn3.1:7.1.verse: If in the village or a forest:

sn3.1:7.2.verse: A serpent one may see by chance.

sn3.1:7.4.verse: A man should not disparage it.

sn3.1:8.2.verse: For as that fierce snake glides along,

sn3.1:8.3.verse: It may attack and bite the fool,

sn3.1:8.4.verse: Whether a man or a woman.

sn3.1:9.1.verse: A blazing fire that devours much,

sn3.1:9.4.verse: A man should not disparage it.

sn3.1:10.1.verse: For if it gains a stock of fuel,

sn3.1:10.3.verse: It may attack and burn the fool,

sn3.1:10.4.verse: Whether a man or a woman.

sn3.1:11.1.verse: “When a fire burns down a forest—

sn3.1:11.3.verse: The shoots there spring to life once more

sn3.1:11.4.verse: As the days and nights pass by.

sn3.1:12.1.verse: But if one of perfect virtue

sn3.1:12.2.verse: A bhikkhu burns one with [his virtue’s] fire,

sn3.1:12.3.verse: One does not gain sons and cattle,

sn3.1:12.4.verse: Nor do one’s heirs acquire wealth.

sn3.1:13.2.verse: Out of regard for his own good:

sn3.1:13.3.verse: A fierce serpent and a blazing fire

sn3.1:13.5.verse: And a bhikkhu of perfect virtue.

sn3.1:13.6.verse: One should always treat these properly.”

sn3.1:14.1.verse: When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.1:14.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as though he were turning upright what had been turned upside down, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyesight to see forms.

sn3.1:14.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

sn3.1:14.5.verse: From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. ”

sn3.2:1.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn3.2:1.3.verse: “Sir, how many things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort?”

sn3.2:2.1.verse: “Great king, three things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.

sn3.2:2.6.verse: These three things arise inside a person for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.”

sn3.2:2.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said. …

sn3.2:3.3.verse: they harm a person of wicked heart,

sn3.2:3.4.verse: as a bamboo is destroyed by its own fruit.”

sn3.2:1.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn3.2:1.3.verse: “Venerable sir, how many things are there which, when they arise within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort?”

sn3.2:2.1.verse: “There are, great king, three things which, when they arise within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort.

sn3.2:2.3.verse: Greed, great king,  when arises within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort.

sn3.2:2.4.verse: Hatred great king,  when arises within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort.

sn3.2:2.5.verse: Delusion great king,  when arises within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort.

sn3.2:2.6.verse: “These three, great king, are three things which, when they arise within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort. ”

sn3.2:3.3.verse: Injure the person of evil mind

sn3.2:3.4.verse: As its own fruit destroys the reed.

sn3.3:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.3:1.3.verse: “Sir, for someone who has been reborn, is there any exemption from old age and death?”

sn3.3:1.4.verse: “Great king, for someone who has been reborn, there’s no exemption from old age and death.

sn3.3:1.7.verse: or householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain—when they’re born, there’s no exemption from old age and death.

sn3.3:1.8.verse: Even for mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—their bodies are liable to break up and be laid to rest.”

sn3.3:1.9.verse: That is what the Buddha said. …

sn3.3:2.2.verse: and even this body gets old.

sn3.3:2.3.verse: But the truth of the good never gets old—

sn3.3:2.4.verse: so the good proclaim to the good.”

sn3.3:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.3:1.3.verse: “Venerable sir, for one who has taken birth, is there anything other [to expect] than aging and death?”

sn3.3:1.4.verse: “For one who has taken birth, great king, there is nothing other [to expect] than aging and death.

sn3.3:1.5.verse: Even in the case of those affluent khattiyas—rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and commodities, abundant wealth and grain—because they have taken birth, there is nothing other [to expect] than aging and death.

sn3.3:1.6.verse: Even in the case of those affluent brahmins …

sn3.3:1.7.verse: affluent householders—rich . . . with abundant wealth and grain—because they have taken birth, there is nothing other [to expect] than aging and death.

sn3.3:1.8.verse: Even in the case of those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge: even for them this body is subject to breaking up, subject to being laid down.

sn3.3:2.1.verse: “The beautiful chariots of kings wear out,

sn3.3:2.3.verse: But the Dhamma of the good does not decay:

sn3.3:2.4.verse: So the good proclaim along with the good. ”

sn3.4:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.4:1.3.verse: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

sn3.4:1.4.verse: ‘Who are those who love themselves? And who are those who don’t love themselves?’

sn3.4:1.6.verse: ‘Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind

sn3.4:1.11.verse: It’s because they treat themselves like an enemy.

sn3.4:1.12.verse: That’s why they don’t love themselves.

sn3.4:1.13.verse: Those who do good things by way of body, speech, and mind

sn3.4:1.16.verse: “I don’t love myself”, they do really.

sn3.4:1.18.verse: It’s because they treat themselves like a loved one.

sn3.4:1.19.verse: That’s why they do love themselves.’”

sn3.4:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

sn3.4:3.1.verse: “If you knew your self as beloved,

sn3.4:3.2.verse: you’d not yoke yourself to wickedness.

sn3.4:3.3.verse: For happiness is not easy to find

sn3.4:3.4.verse: by someone who does bad deeds.

sn3.4:4.1.verse: When you’re seized by the terminator

sn3.4:4.2.verse: as you give up your human life,

sn3.4:4.3.verse: what can you call your own?

sn3.4:4.4.verse: What do you take when you go?

sn3.4:4.6.verse: like a shadow that never leaves?

sn3.4:5.1.verse: Both the good and the bad

sn3.4:5.2.verse: that a mortal does in this life

sn3.4:5.3.verse: is what they can call their own.

sn3.4:5.4.verse: That’s what they take when they go.

sn3.4:5.6.verse: like a shadow that never leaves.

sn3.4:6.1.verse: That’s why you should do good,

sn3.4:6.3.verse: The good deeds of sentient beings

sn3.4:6.4.verse: support them in the next world.”

sn3.4:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.4:1.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind thus:

sn3.4:1.4.verse: ‘Who now treat themselves as dear, and who treat themselves as a foe?’

sn3.4:1.5.verse: Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:

sn3.4:1.6.verse: ‘Those who engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind

sn3.4:1.9.verse: “We regard ourselves as dear, ” still they treat themselves as a foe.

sn3.4:1.11.verse: Because of their own accord they act towards themselves in the same way that a foe might act towards a foe;

sn3.4:1.12.verse: therefore they treat themselves as a foe.

sn3.4:1.13.verse: But those who engage in good conduct of body, speech, and mind

sn3.4:1.16.verse: “We regard ourselves as a foe, ” still they treat themselves as dear.

sn3.4:1.18.verse: Because of their own accord they act towards themselves in the same way that a dear person might act towards one who is dear;

sn3.4:1.19.verse: therefore they treat themselves as dear. ’”

sn3.4:2.1.verse: “So it is, great king! So it is, great king!”

sn3.4:3.2.verse: One should not yoke oneself to evil,

sn3.4:3.3.verse: For happiness is not easily gained

sn3.4:3.4.verse: By one who does a wrongful deed.

sn3.4:4.1.verse: “When one is seized by the End-maker

sn3.4:4.2.verse: As one discards the human state,

sn3.4:4.3.verse: What can one call truly one’s own?

sn3.4:4.4.verse: What does one take when one goes?

sn3.4:4.6.verse: Like a shadow that never departs?

sn3.4:5.2.verse: That a mortal does right here:

sn3.4:5.3.verse: This is what is truly one’s own,

sn3.4:5.4.verse: This one takes when one goes;

sn3.4:5.5.verse: This is what follows one along

sn3.4:5.6.verse: Like a shadow that never departs.

sn3.4:6.1.verse: “Therefore one should do what is good

sn3.4:6.2.verse: As a collection for the future life.

sn3.4:6.3.verse: Merits are the support for living beings

sn3.4:6.4.verse: [When they arise] in the other world. ”

sn3.5:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.5:1.3.verse: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

sn3.5:1.4.verse: ‘Who are those who protect themselves? And who are those who don’t protect themselves?’

sn3.5:1.6.verse: ‘Those who do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind

sn3.5:1.8.verse: Even if they’re protected by a company of elephants, cavalry, chariots, or infantry,

sn3.5:1.11.verse: Because such protection is exterior, not interior.

sn3.5:1.12.verse: That’s why they don’t protect themselves.

sn3.5:1.13.verse: Those who do good things by way of body, speech, and mind

sn3.5:1.15.verse: Even if they’re not protected by a company of elephants, cavalry, chariots, or infantry,

sn3.5:1.18.verse: Because such protection is interior, not exterior.

sn3.5:1.19.verse: That’s why they do protect themselves.’”

sn3.5:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

sn3.5:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.5:1.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind thus:

sn3.5:1.4.verse: ‘Who now protect themselves and who leave themselves unprotected?’

sn3.5:1.5.verse: Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:

sn3.5:1.6.verse: ‘Those who engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind

sn3.5:1.8.verse: Even though a company of elephant troops may protect them, or a company of cavalry, or a company of chariot troops, or a company of infantry,

sn3.5:1.11.verse: Because that protection is external, not internal;

sn3.5:1.13.verse: But those who engage in good conduct of body, speech, and mind

sn3.5:1.15.verse: Even though no company of elephant troops protects them, nor a company of cavalry, nor a company of charioteers, nor a company of infantry,

sn3.5:1.18.verse: Because that protection is internal, not external;

sn3.5:2.1.verse: “So it is, great king! So it is, great king!”

sn3.5:3.2.verse: Restraint by speech is also good;

sn3.5:3.3.verse: Good is restraint with the mind,

sn3.5:3.6.verse: One is said to be protected. ”

sn3.6:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.6:1.3.verse: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

sn3.6:1.4.verse: ‘Few are the sentient beings in the world who, when they obtain luxury possessions, don’t grow indulgent and negligent, giving in to greed for sensual pleasures, and doing the wrong thing by others.

sn3.6:1.5.verse: There are many more who, when they obtain luxury possessions, do grow indulgent and negligent, giving in to greed for sensual pleasures, and doing the wrong thing by others.’”

sn3.6:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

sn3.6:3.1.verse: “Full of desire for possessions and pleasures,

sn3.6:3.3.verse: they don’t notice that they’ve gone too far,

sn3.6:3.4.verse: like deer ensnared in a trap set out.

sn3.6:3.6.verse: for the result will be bad for them.”

sn3.6:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.6:1.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind thus:

sn3.6:1.4.verse: ‘Few are those people in the world who, when they obtain superior possessions, do not become intoxicated and negligent, yield to greed for sensual pleasures, and mistreat other beings.

sn3.6:1.5.verse: Far more numerous are those people in the world who, when they obtain superior possessions, become intoxicated and negligent, yield to greed for sensual pleasures, and mistreat other beings. ’”

sn3.6:2.1.verse: “So it is, great king! So it is, great king!”

sn3.6:3.3.verse: They do not realize they have gone too far

sn3.6:3.4.verse: Like deer that enter the trap laid out.

sn3.6:3.5.verse: Afterwards the bitter fruit is theirs,

sn3.6:3.6.verse: For bad indeed is the result. ”

sn3.7:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.7:1.3.verse: “Sir, when I’m sitting in court I see well-to-do aristocrats, brahmins, and householders—rich, affluent, and wealthy, with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain. But they tell deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures.

sn3.7:1.5.verse: ‘Enough with passing judgment today. Now my dearest will be known by the judgments he makes.’”

sn3.7:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!

sn3.7:2.2.verse: Those who are well-to-do aristocrats, brahmins, and householders tell deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures.

sn3.7:2.3.verse: That is for their lasting harm and suffering.”

sn3.7:2.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said. …

sn3.7:3.1.verse: “Full of desire for possessions and pleasures,

sn3.7:3.3.verse: they don’t notice that they’ve gone too far,

sn3.7:3.6.verse: for the result will be bad for them.”

sn3.7:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.7:1.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, when I am sitting in the judgement hall, I see even affluent khattiyas, affluent brahmins, and affluent householders—rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and commodities, abundant wealth and grain—speaking deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, on account of sensual pleasures.

sn3.7:1.4.verse: Then, venerable sir, it occurs to me:

sn3.7:1.5.verse: ‘I’ve had enough now with the judgement hall! Now it is Good Face who will be known by his judgements. ’”

sn3.7:2.1.verse: “So it is, great king! So it is, great king!

sn3.7:2.2.verse: Even affluent khattiyas, affluent brahmins, and affluent householders … speak deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, on account of sensual pleasures.

sn3.7:2.3.verse: That will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time to come.

sn3.7:3.3.verse: They do not realize they have gone too far

sn3.7:3.4.verse: Like fish that enter the net spread out.

sn3.7:3.5.verse: Afterwards the bitter fruit is theirs,

sn3.7:3.6.verse: For bad indeed is the result. ”

sn3.8:1.2.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala was upstairs in the royal longhouse together with Queen Mallikā.

sn3.8:1.3.verse: Then the king said to the queen,

sn3.8:1.4.verse: “Mallikā, is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

sn3.8:1.6.verse: But is there anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

sn3.8:1.7.verse: “For me also, Mallikā, there’s no one.”

sn3.8:2.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala came downstairs from the stilt longhouse, went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

sn3.8:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha spoke this verse:

sn3.8:4.1.verse: “Having explored every quarter with the mind,

sn3.8:4.2.verse: one finds no one dearer than oneself.

sn3.8:4.3.verse: Likewise for others, each holds themselves dear;

sn3.8:4.4.verse: so one who desires self-knowledge would harm no other.”

sn3.8:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion King Pasenadi of Kosala had gone together with Queen Mallikā to the upper terrace of the palace.

sn3.8:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said to Queen Mallikā:

sn3.8:1.4.verse: “Is there, Mallikā, anyone more dear to you than yourself?”

sn3.8:1.5.verse: “There is no one, great king, more dear to me than myself.

sn3.8:1.6.verse: But is there anyone, great king, more dear to you than yourself?”

sn3.8:1.7.verse: “For me too, Mallikā, there is no one more dear than myself. ”

sn3.8:2.1.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala descended from the palace and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn3.8:3.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this,

sn3.8:4.1.verse: “Having traversed all quarters with the mind,

sn3.8:4.2.verse: One finds none anywhere dearer than oneself.

sn3.8:4.3.verse: Likewise, each person holds himself most dear;

sn3.8:4.4.verse: Hence one who loves himself should not harm others. ”

sn3.9:1.2.verse: Now at that time a grand sacrifice had been set up for King Pasenadi of Kosala. Bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats and rams—five hundred of each—had been led to the pillar for the sacrifice.

sn3.9:1.3.verse: His bondservants, servants, and workers did their jobs under threat of punishment and danger, weeping with tearful faces.

sn3.9:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn3.9:2.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

sn3.9:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:

sn3.9:4.2.verse: the ‘casting of the yoke-pin’, the ‘royal soma drinking’,

sn3.9:4.4.verse: these grand, violent sacrifices yield no great fruit.

sn3.9:5.1.verse: The great sages of right comportment

sn3.9:6.1.verse: But the great sages of right comportment

sn3.9:6.5.verse: and various creatures are not killed.

sn3.9:7.1.verse: An intelligent person should sacrifice like this,

sn3.9:7.2.verse: for this sacrifice is very fruitful.

sn3.9:7.3.verse: For a sponsor of sacrifices like this,

sn3.9:7.5.verse: Such a sacrifice is truly abundant,

sn3.9:7.6.verse: and even the deities are pleased.”

sn3.9:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion a great sacrifice had been set up for King Pasenadi of Kosala. Five hundred bulls, five hundred bullocks, five hundred heifers, five hundred goats, and five hundred rams had been led to the pillar for the sacrifice.

sn3.9:1.3.verse: And his slaves, servants, and workers, spurred on by punishment and fear, were busy making the preparations, wailing with tearful faces.

sn3.9:2.1.verse: Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn3.9:2.2.verse: When they had walked for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from their alms round, after the meal they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said:

sn3.9:2.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, a great sacrifice has been set up for King Pasenadi of Kosala. Five hundred bulls . . . have been led to the pillar for the sacrifice.

sn3.9:2.4.verse: And his slaves servants, and workers, spurred on by punishment and fear, are busy making preparations, wailing with tearful faces. ”

sn3.9:3.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, on that occasion recited these verses:

sn3.9:4.3.verse: These great sacrifices, fraught with violence,

sn3.9:5.3.verse: They do not attend that sacrifice:

sn3.9:5.4.verse: The great seers of right conduct.

sn3.9:6.2.verse: Are always offered by family custom,

sn3.9:6.3.verse: Where no goats, sheep, or cattle

sn3.9:6.5.verse: They attend a sacrifice like this:

sn3.9:6.6.verse: The great seers of right conduct.

sn3.9:7.3.verse: For one who makes such sacrifice

sn3.9:7.4.verse: It is indeed better, never worse.

sn3.9:7.5.verse: Such a sacrifice is truly vast

sn3.9:7.6.verse: And the devatās too are pleased. ”

sn3.10:1.1.verse: Now at that time a large group of people had been put in shackles by King Pasenadi of Kosala—some in ropes, some in manacles, some in chains.

sn3.10:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn3.10:2.2.verse: Then, after the meal, when they returned from almsround, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what was happening.

sn3.10:3.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:

sn3.10:4.1.verse: “The attentive say that shackle is not strong

sn3.10:4.2.verse: that’s made of iron, wood, or knots.

sn3.10:4.4.verse: concern for your partners and children:

sn3.10:5.1.verse: this, say the attentive, is a strong shackle

sn3.10:5.2.verse: dragging the indulgent down, hard to escape.

sn3.10:5.3.verse: Having cut this one too they go forth,

sn3.10:5.4.verse: unconcerned, having given up sensual pleasures.”

sn3.10:1.1.verse: Now on that occasion a great mass of people had been put in bondage by King Pasenadi of Kosala—some with ropes, some with clogs, some with chains.

sn3.10:2.1.verse: Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn3.10:2.2.verse: When they had walked for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from their alms round, after the meal they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said:

sn3.10:2.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, a great mass of people have been put in bondage by King Pasenadi of Kosala, some with ropes, some with clogs, some with chains. ”

sn3.10:3.1.verse: Then the Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, on that occasion recited these verses:

sn3.10:4.1.verse: “That bond, the wise say, is not strong

sn3.10:4.2.verse: Made of iron, wood, or rope;

sn3.10:4.3.verse: But infatuation with jewellery and earrings,

sn3.10:4.4.verse: Anxious concern for wives and children—

sn3.10:5.1.verse: This, the wise say, is the strong bond,

sn3.10:5.3.verse: But even this they cut and wander forth,

sn3.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery.

sn3.11:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and sat outside the gate.

sn3.11:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

sn3.11:2.1.verse: Now at that time seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain ascetics, seven naked ascetics, seven one-cloth ascetics, and seven wanderers passed by not far from the Buddha. Their armpits and bodies were hairy, and their nails were long; and they carried their pack with shoulder-poles.

sn3.11:2.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi got up from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, raised his joined palms toward those various ascetics, and pronounced his name three times:

sn3.11:2.3.verse: “Sirs, I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala! …

sn3.11:2.4.verse: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala!”

sn3.11:3.1.verse: Then, not long after those ascetics had left, King Pasenadi went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn3.11:3.2.verse: “Sir, these are among those in the world who are perfected or who are on the path to perfection!”

sn3.11:4.1.verse: “Great king, as a layman enjoying sensual pleasures, living at home with your children, using sandalwood imported from Kāsi, wearing garlands, fragrance, and makeup, and accepting gold and currency, it’s hard for you to know who is perfected or on the path to perfection.

sn3.11:5.1.verse: You can get to know a person’s ethics by living with them. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.

sn3.11:5.2.verse: You can get to know a person’s purity by dealing with them. …

sn3.11:5.3.verse: You can get to know a person’s resilience in times of trouble. …

sn3.11:5.4.verse: You can get to know a person’s wisdom by discussion. But only after a long time, not casually; only when attentive, not when inattentive; and only by the wise, not the witless.”

sn3.11:6.2.verse: how well said this was by the Buddha. …

sn3.11:7.1.verse: Sir, these are my spies, my undercover agents returning after spying on the country.

sn3.11:7.2.verse: I shall later make use of what they first spied out.

sn3.11:7.3.verse: Now—when they have rinsed off the dust and dirt, and are nicely bathed and anointed, with hair and beard dressed, and dressed in white—they will amuse themselves, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.”

sn3.11:8.1.verse: Then, understanding this matter, on that occasion the Buddha recited these verses:

sn3.11:9.1.verse: “It’s not easy to know a man by his appearance.

sn3.11:9.2.verse: You shouldn’t trust them at first sight.

sn3.11:9.3.verse: For undisciplined men live in this world

sn3.11:10.1.verse: Like a fake earring made of clay,

sn3.11:10.2.verse: like a copper halfpenny covered with gold,

sn3.11:10.3.verse: they live hidden in the world,

sn3.11:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.

sn3.11:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion, in the evening, the Blessed One had emerged from seclusion and was sitting by the outer gateway.

sn3.11:1.3.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.

sn3.11:2.1.verse: Now on that occasion seven jaṭilas, seven nigaṇṭhas, seven naked ascetics, seven one-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers—with hairy armpits, long fingernails and long body hairs, carrying their bundles of requisites—passed by not far from the Blessed One.

sn3.11:2.2.verse: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt down with his right knee on the ground, and, raising his joined hands in reverential salutation towards the seven jaṭilas, seven nigaṇṭhas, seven naked ascetics, seven one-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers, he announced his name three times:

sn3.11:2.3.verse: “I am the king, venerable sirs, Pasenadi of Kosala!…

sn3.11:2.4.verse: I am the king, venerable sirs, Pasenadi of Kosala!”

sn3.11:3.1.verse: Then, not long after those seven jaṭilas … and seven wanderers had departed, King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One:

sn3.11:3.2.verse: “Those, venerable sir, are to be included among the men in the world who are arahants or who have entered upon the path to arahantship. ”

sn3.11:4.1.verse: “Great king, being a layman who enjoys sensual pleasures, dwelling in a home crowded with children, enjoying the use of Kāsian sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, receiving gold and silver, it is difficult for you to know: ‘These are arahants or these have entered upon the path to arahantship.

sn3.11:5.1.verse: ’ “It is by living together with someone, great king, that his virtue is to be known, and that after a long time, not after a short time; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by a dullard.

sn3.11:5.2.verse: “It is by dealing with someone, great king, that his honesty is to be known, and that after a long time, not after a short time; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by a dullard.

sn3.12:2.2.verse: “Come, good fellows, let’s go to the Buddha and ask him about this.

sn3.12:9.3.verse: “I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!”

sn3.12:9.4.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

sn3.12:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion five kings headed by King Pasenadi were enjoying themselves supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure when this conversation arose among them:

sn3.12:1.3.verse: “What is the chief of sensual pleasures?”

sn3.12:1.5.verse: “Forms are the chief of sensual pleasures. ”

sn3.12:1.14.verse: Since those kings were unable to convince one another,

sn3.12:2.1.verse: King Pasenadi of Kosala said to them:

sn3.12:2.2.verse: “Come, dear sirs, let us approach the Blessed One and question him about this matter.

sn3.12:2.3.verse: As the Blessed One answers us, so we should remember it. ”

sn3.12:2.4.verse: “All right, dear sir, ” those kings replied.

sn3.12:3.1.verse: Then those five kings, headed by King Pasenadi, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. King Pasenadi then reported their entire discussion to the Blessed One, asking:

sn3.12:3.3.verse: “What now, venerable sir, is the chief of sensual pleasures?”

sn3.12:4.1.verse: “Great king, I say that what is chief among the five cords of sensual pleasure is determined by whatever is most agreeable.

sn3.12:4.2.verse: Those same forms that are agreeable to one person, great king, are disagreeable to another.

sn3.12:4.3.verse: When one is pleased and completely satisfied with certain forms, then one does not yearn for any other form higher or more sublime than those forms.

sn3.12:4.4.verse: For him those forms are then supreme;

sn3.12:4.5.verse: for him those forms are unsurpassed.

sn3.12:8.1.verse: Those same tactile objects that are agreeable to one person, great king, are disagreeable to another.

sn3.12:8.2.verse: When one is pleased and completely satisfied with certain tactile objects, then one does not yearn for any other tactile object higher or more sublime than those tactile objects. For him those tactile objects are then supreme; for him those tactile objects are unsurpassed.

sn3.12:9.1.verse: Now on that occasion the lay follower Candanaṅgalika was sitting in that assembly.

sn3.12:9.3.verse: “An inspiration has come to me, Blessed One! An inspiration has come to me, Fortunate One!”

sn3.12:9.4.verse: “Then express your inspiration, Candanaṅgalika, ”, the Blessed One said.

sn3.12:11.2.verse: Blooms in the morning, its fragrance unspent,

sn3.13:1.2.verse: Now at that time King Pasenadi of Kosala used to eat boiled rice by the bucketful.

sn3.18:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, King Pasenadi said to the Buddha,

sn3.18:1.3.verse: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.

sn3.18:1.4.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha. But it’s for someone with good friends, companions, and associates, not for someone with bad friends, companions, and associates.’”

sn3.18:2.1.verse: “That’s so true, Great King! That’s so true!” said the Buddha. And he repeated the king’s statement, adding:

sn3.18:3.1.verse: “Great king, this one time I was staying in the land of the Sakyans where they have a town named Townsville.

sn3.18:3.2.verse: Then the mendicant Ānanda came to me, bowed, sat down to one side, and said:

sn3.18:3.3.verse: ‘Sir, good friends, companions, and associates are half the spiritual life.’

sn3.18:4.1.verse: When he had spoken, I said to him:

sn3.18:4.3.verse: Good friends, companions, and associates are the whole of the spiritual life.

sn3.18:4.4.verse: A mendicant with good friends, companions, and associates can expect to develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path.

sn3.18:5.1.verse: And how does a mendicant with good friends develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path?

sn3.18:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

sn3.18:5.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant with good friends develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path.

sn3.18:5.4.verse: And here’s another way to understand how good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.

sn3.18:6.1.verse: For, by relying on me as a good friend, sentient beings who are liable to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are freed from all these things.

sn3.18:6.2.verse: This is another way to understand how good friends are the whole of the spiritual life.’

sn3.18:7.1.verse: So, Great King, you should train like this:

sn3.18:7.2.verse: ‘I will have good friends, companions, and associates.’

sn3.18:8.1.verse: When you have good friends, companions, and associates, you should live supported by one thing:

sn3.18:9.1.verse: When you’re diligent, supported by diligence, your ladies of the harem,

sn3.18:12.1.verse: and people of town and country will think:

sn3.18:12.2.verse: ‘The king lives diligently, supported by diligence.

sn3.18:12.3.verse: We’d better live diligently, supported by diligence!’

sn3.18:13.1.verse: When you’re diligent, supported by diligence, then not only you yourself,

sn3.18:13.2.verse: but your ladies of the harem, and your treasury and storehouses will be guarded and protected.”

sn3.18:13.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said. …

sn3.18:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:

sn3.18:1.3.verse: “Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, the following reflection arose in my mind:

sn3.18:1.4.verse: ‘The Dhamma has been well expounded by the Blessed One, and that is for one with good friends, good companions, good comrades, not for one with bad friends, bad companions, bad comrades. ’”

sn3.18:2.1.verse: “So it is, great king! So it is, great king!

sn3.18:2.2.verse: The Dhamma has been well expounded by me, and that is for one with good friends, good companions, good comrades, not for one with bad friends, bad companions, bad comrades.

sn3.18:3.1.verse: “On one occasion, great king, I was living among the Sakyans, where there is a town of the Sakyans named Nāgaraka.

sn3.18:3.2.verse: Then the bhikkhu Ānanda approached me, paid homage to me, sat down to one side, and said:

sn3.18:3.3.verse: ‘Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life, that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.’

sn3.18:4.1.verse: “When this was said, great king, I told the bhikkhu Ānanda:

sn3.18:4.3.verse: This is the entire holy life, Ānanda, that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.

sn3.18:4.4.verse: When a bhikkhu has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, it is to be expected that he will develop and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.

sn3.18:5.1.verse: And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develop and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?

sn3.18:5.2.verse: Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. He develops right intention … right speech … right action … right livelihood … right effort … right mindfulness … right concentration, which is based upon seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release.

sn3.18:5.3.verse: It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.

sn3.18:5.4.verse: “‘By the following method too, Ānanda, it may be understood how the entire holy life is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship:

sn3.18:6.1.verse: by relying upon me as a good friend, Ānanda, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to illness are freed from illness; beings subject to death are freed from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.

sn3.18:6.2.verse: By this method, Ānanda, it may be understood how the entire holy life is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.’

sn3.18:7.1.verse: “Therefore, great king, you should train yourself thus:

sn3.18:7.2.verse: ‘I will be one who has good friends, good companions, good comrades.’

sn3.18:7.3.verse: It is in such a way that you should train yourself.

sn3.18:8.1.verse: “When, great king, you have good friends, good companions, good comrades, you should dwell with one thing for support:

sn3.18:9.1.verse: “When, great king, you are dwelling diligently, with diligence for support, your retinue of harem women will think thus:

sn3.18:9.2.verse: ‘The king dwells diligently, with diligence for support.

sn3.18:9.3.verse: Come now, let us also dwell diligently, with diligence for support.’

sn3.18:12.2.verse: ‘The king dwells diligently, with diligence for support.

sn3.18:12.3.verse: Come now, let us also dwell diligently, with diligence for support.’

sn3.18:13.1.verse: “When, great king, you are dwelling diligently, with diligence for support, you yourself will be guarded and protected,

sn3.18:13.2.verse: your retinue of harem women will be guarded and protected, your treasury and storehouse will be guarded and protected.

sn3.18:15.1.verse: The good visible in this very life
