Having approached, they saw the Blessed One sitting in that woodland thicket with his legs folded crosswise, holding his body erect, having set up mindfulness in front of him. Having seen him, they approached the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and said to him:

sn7.18:1.4.verse: you should know that in such and such a woodland thicket an ascetic is sitting with his legs folded crosswise,

sn7.18:1.5.verse: Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, together with those brahmin boys, went to that woodland thicket.

sn7.18:1.6.verse: He saw the Blessed One sitting there … having set up mindfulness in front of him.

sn7.18:1.7.verse: He then approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:

sn7.18:2.1.verse: Deep in the woods where many terrors lurk,

sn7.18:2.2.verse: Having entered the empty, desolate forest,

sn7.18:2.3.verse: With a motionless body, steady, lovely,

sn7.18:2.4.verse: How you meditate, bhikkhu, so beautifully!

sn7.18:3.1.verse: In the forest where no song or music sounds,

sn7.18:3.2.verse: A solitary sage has resorted to the woods!

sn7.18:3.3.verse: This strikes me as a wonder—that you dwell

sn7.18:3.4.verse: With joyful mind alone in the woods.

sn7.18:4.1.verse: The company of the world’s divine lord,

sn7.18:4.2.verse: I suppose you desire the supreme triple heaven,

sn7.18:4.3.verse: Therefore you resort to the desolate forest:

sn7.18:4.4.verse: You practise penance here for attaining Brahmā.

sn7.18:5.1.verse: Whatever be the many desires and delights

sn7.18:5.2.verse: That are always attached to the manifold elements,

sn7.18:5.3.verse: The longings sprung from the root of unknowing:

sn7.18:5.4.verse: All I have demolished along with their root.

sn7.18:6.2.verse: My vision of all things has been purified.

sn7.18:7.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan said to the Blessed One:

sn7.18:7.3.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who from today has gone for refuge for life.

sn7.19:0.3.verse: The Brahmin Who Provided for His Mother

sn7.19:1.2.verse: Then a brahmin who provided for his mother went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn7.19:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

sn7.19:1.4.verse: “Worthy Gotama, I seek alms by legitimate means, which I use to provide for my mother and father.

sn7.19:1.5.verse: In doing so, am I doing my duty?”

sn7.19:1.6.verse: “Indeed, brahmin, in so doing you are doing your duty.

sn7.19:1.7.verse: Whoever seeks alms by legitimate means, and uses them to provide for their mother and father brims with much merit.

sn7.19:2.1.verse: A mortal provides for their mother

sn7.19:2.5.verse: they’re praised in this life by the astute,

sn7.19:2.6.verse: and they depart to rejoice in heaven.”

sn7.19:3.1.verse: When he said this, the brahmin who provided for his mother said to the Buddha,

sn7.19:3.3.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn7.19:1.2.verse: Then a brahmin who supported his mother approached the Blessed One

sn7.19:1.4.verse: Master Gotama, I seek almsfood righteously and thereby support my mother and father.

sn7.19:1.5.verse: In doing so, am I doing my duty?

sn7.19:1.6.verse: For sure, brahmin, in doing so you are doing your duty.

sn7.19:1.7.verse: One who seeks almsfood righteously and thereby supports his mother and father generates much merit.

sn7.19:2.5.verse: praise him here in this world,

sn7.19:2.6.verse: And after death he rejoices in heaven.

sn7.19:3.1.verse: When this was said,the brahmin who supported his mother said to the Blessed One:

sn7.19:3.2.verse: Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!…

sn7.19:3.3.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who from today has gone for refuge for life.

sn7.20:1.2.verse: Then a brahmin almsman went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn7.20:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha,

sn7.20:1.4.verse: “Worthy Gotama, both you and I are almsmen. What, then, is the difference between us?”

sn7.20:2.2.verse: just by begging alms from others.

sn7.20:2.3.verse: One who has undertaken domestic duties

sn7.20:2.4.verse: has not yet become a mendicant.

sn7.20:3.1.verse: But one living a spiritual life

sn7.20:3.2.verse: who has banished both merit and evil,

sn7.20:3.3.verse: and wanders having appraised the world,

sn7.20:3.4.verse: is said to be a mendicant.”

sn7.20:4.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmin almsman said to the Buddha,

sn7.20:4.3.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn7.20:1.2.verse: Then a mendicant brahmin approached the Blessed One

sn7.20:1.4.verse: Master Gotama, I am a mendicant and you are a mendicant. What is the difference between us in this respect?

sn7.20:2.1.verse: [The Blessed One: ]  “It is not thus that one becomes a mendicant,

sn7.20:2.2.verse: Just because one begs others for alms.

sn7.20:2.3.verse: If one has taken up a domestic practice,

sn7.20:2.4.verse: One still has not become a bhikkhu.

sn7.20:3.2.verse: and one leads the holy life,

sn7.20:3.3.verse: Who fares in the world with comprehension:

sn7.20:3.4.verse: He is truly called a bhikkhu.”

sn7.20:4.1.verse: When this was said, the mendicant brahmin said to the Blessed One:

sn7.20:4.3.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who from today has gone for refuge for life.

sn7.21:1.2.verse: Now at that time there was a brahmin named Saṅgārava staying in Sāvatthī. He practiced purification by water, believing in purification by water. He lived committed to the practice of immersing himself in water at daybreak and dusk.

sn7.21:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn7.21:1.4.verse: He wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn7.21:1.5.verse: “Sir, there is a brahmin named Saṅgārava staying in Sāvatthī. He practices purification by water, believing in purification by water. He lives devoted to ritual bathing at daybreak and dusk.

sn7.21:1.6.verse: Please visit him at his home out of sympathy.”

sn7.21:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the brahmin Saṅgārava, and sat down on the seat spread out.

sn7.21:2.2.verse: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn7.21:2.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

sn7.21:2.4.verse: “Is it really true, brahmin, that you practice purification by water, believing in purification by water; that you live committed to the practice of immersing yourself in water at daybreak and dusk?”

sn7.21:2.6.verse: “But brahmin, for what reason do you practice purification by water?”

sn7.21:2.7.verse: “It’s because, Worthy Gotama, whatever bad deeds I’ve done during the day I rinse off by bathing at dusk; and whatever bad deeds I’ve done during the night, I rinse off by bathing at dawn.

sn7.21:2.8.verse: That’s the reason why I practice purification by water.”

sn7.21:3.1.verse: “The teaching is a lake, brahmin, into which ethics are the stairs,

sn7.21:3.2.verse: unclouded, praised by the fine to the good.

sn7.21:3.3.verse: There the knowledge masters go to bathe,

sn7.21:3.4.verse: and cross to the far shore with dry limbs.”

sn7.21:4.1.verse: When he had spoken, Saṅgārava said to the Buddha,

sn7.21:4.3.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn7.21:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion a brahmin named Saṅgārava was residing at Sāvatthī. He was a practitioner of water-purification, one who believed in purification by water, who dwelt devoted to the practice of immersing himself in water at dusk and at dawn.

sn7.21:1.3.verse: Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed and, taking bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

sn7.21:1.4.verse: Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, when he had returned from his alms round, after his meal he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn7.21:1.5.verse: “Here, venerable sir, a brahmin named Saṅgārava is residing at Sāvatthī. He is a practitioner of water-purification … devoted to the practice of immersing himself in water at dusk and at dawn.

sn7.21:1.6.verse: It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach the residence of the brahmin Saṅgārava out of compassion.”

sn7.21:1.7.verse: The Blessed One consented by silence.

sn7.21:2.1.verse: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed and, taking bowl and robe, approached the brahmin Saṅgārava’s residence, where he sat down in the appointed seat.

sn7.21:2.2.verse: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him, after which he sat down to one side.

sn7.21:2.3.verse: The Blessed One then said to him:

sn7.21:2.4.verse: “Is it true, brahmin, that you are a practitioner of water-purification, one who believes in purification by water, devoted to the practice of immersing yourself in water at dusk and at dawn?”

sn7.21:2.6.verse: “Considering what benefit do you do this, brahmin?”

sn7.21:2.7.verse: “Here, Master Gotama, whatever evil deed I have done during the day I wash away by bathing at dusk. Whatever evil deed I have done at night I wash away by bathing at dawn.”

sn7.21:3.1.verse: “The Dhamma, brahmin, is a lake with fords of virtue—

sn7.21:3.2.verse: A limpid lake the good praise to the good—

sn7.21:3.3.verse: Where the knowledge-masters go to bathe,

sn7.21:3.4.verse: And, dry-limbed, cross to the far shore.”

sn7.21:4.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One:

sn7.21:4.3.verse: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who from today has gone for refuge for life.”

sn7.22:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, where they have a town named Khomadussa.

sn7.22:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Khomadussa for alms.

sn7.22:1.4.verse: Now at that time the brahmins and householders of Khomadussa were gathered in the council hall for some business, while a gentle rain drizzled down.

sn7.22:1.5.verse: Then the Buddha approached that council.

sn7.22:1.6.verse: The brahmins and householders saw the Buddha coming off in the distance,

sn7.22:1.8.verse: “Who are these shavelings, these fake ascetics? Don’t they understand the council rules?”

sn7.22:1.9.verse: Then the Buddha addressed the brahmins and householders of Khomadussa in verse:

sn7.22:2.1.verse: “If good people are not present it is no true council;

sn7.22:2.2.verse: and those whose speak against principle are not good people.

sn7.22:2.3.verse: Having given up greed, hate, and delusion,

sn7.22:2.4.verse: speakers of principle are good people.”

sn7.22:3.1.verse: When he had spoken, the brahmins and householders of Khomadussa said to the Buddha,

sn7.22:3.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn7.22:3.4.verse: We go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn7.22:3.5.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”

sn7.22:4.7.verse: The Linked Discourses with Brahmins are complete.

sn7.22:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans where there was a town of the Sakyans named Khomadussa.

sn7.22:1.3.verse: Then the Blessed One dressed and, taking bowl and robe, entered Khomadussa for alms.

sn7.22:1.4.verse: Now on that occasion the brahmin householders of Khomadussa had assembled in council on some business matter while it was drizzling.

sn7.22:1.5.verse: Then the Blessed One approached the council.

sn7.22:1.6.verse: The brahmin householders of Khomadussa saw the Blessed One coming in the distance

sn7.22:1.8.verse: “Who are these shaveling ascetics? Don’t they know the rule of order?”

sn7.22:1.9.verse: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin householders of Khomadussa in verse:

sn7.22:2.1.verse: “That is no council where the good are absent;

sn7.22:2.2.verse: They are not the good who don’t speak Dhamma.

sn7.22:2.3.verse: But having abandoned lust, hate, and delusion,

sn7.22:2.4.verse: Those speaking on Dhamma are alone the good.”

sn7.22:3.1.verse: When this was said, the brahmin householders of Khomadussa said to the Blessed One:

sn7.22:3.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were turning upright what had been turned upside down, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyesight to see forms.

sn7.22:3.4.verse: We go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

sn7.22:3.5.verse: Let Master Gotama remember us as lay followers who from today have gone for refuge for life.

sn8.1:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Vaṅgīsa was staying near Āḷavī, at Āḷavī’s premier shrine, together with his mentor, Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time Vaṅgīsa was junior, recently gone forth. He had been left behind to look after the dwelling.

sn8.1:1.4.verse: Then several women dressed in all their finery went to the monastery at Āḷavī’s premier shrine in order to inspect the dwelling.

sn8.1:1.5.verse: When Vaṅgīsa saw them he became dissatisfied, with lust infecting his mind.

sn8.1:1.8.verse: that I’ve become dissatisfied, with lust infecting my mind. How is it possible for someone else to dispel my discontent and give rise to satisfaction?

sn8.1:1.9.verse: Why don’t I do it myself?”

sn8.1:1.10.verse: Then, on the occasion of dispelling his own discontent and giving rise to satisfaction, he recited these verses:

sn8.1:2.4.verse: by the rude thoughts of the Dark One.

sn8.1:3.1.verse: Even if a thousand warrior chiefs and great archers,

sn8.1:4.4.verse: for I stand firm in the teaching.

sn8.1:5.1.verse: I heard with my own ears

sn8.1:5.2.verse: from the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun,

sn8.1:5.3.verse: about the path going to extinguishment;

sn8.1:6.1.verse: Wicked One, if you come near me

sn8.1:6.3.verse: I’ll make sure that you, Death,

sn8.1:6.4.verse: won’t even see the path I take.”

sn8.1:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.1:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, newly ordained, not long gone forth, had been left behind as a caretaker of the dwelling.

sn8.1:1.4.verse: Then a number of women, beautifully adorned, approached the Aggāḷavaka Park in order to see the dwelling.

sn8.1:1.5.verse: When the Venerable Vaṅgīsa saw those women, dissatisfaction arose in him; lust infested his mind.

sn8.1:1.7.verse: “It is a loss for me indeed, it is no gain for me!

sn8.1:1.8.verse: It is a mishap for me indeed, it is not well gained by me, that dissatisfaction has arisen in me, that lust has infested my mind. How could anyone else dispel my dissatisfaction and arouse delight?

sn8.1:1.9.verse: Let me dispel my own dissatisfaction and arouse delight by myself.”

sn8.1:1.10.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having dispelled his own dissatisfaction and aroused delight by himself, on that occasion recited these verses:

sn8.1:2.1.verse: “Alas, though I am one who has renounced,

sn8.1:2.3.verse: These thoughts still run over me,

sn8.1:2.4.verse: Impudent thoughts from the Dark One.

sn8.1:3.2.verse: Trained men, masters of the bow,

sn8.1:3.3.verse: A thousand such men who do not flee

sn8.1:3.4.verse: Should surround me on all sides,

sn8.1:4.1.verse: And if women were to come here

sn8.1:4.3.verse: They would never make me tremble

sn8.1:4.4.verse: For I stand firmly in the Dhamma.

sn8.1:5.1.verse: “I have heard this as a witness

sn8.1:5.2.verse: From the Buddha, Kinsman of the Sun:

sn8.1:5.4.verse: That is where my mind delights.

sn8.1:6.3.verse: I will act in such a way, O Death,

sn8.1:6.4.verse: That you won’t even see my path.”

sn8.2:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Vaṅgīsa was staying near Āḷavī, at Āḷavī’s premier shrine, together with his mentor, Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.2:1.2.verse: Now at that time after Venerable Nigrodhakappa had finished his meal, on his return from almsround, he would enter his dwelling and not emerge for the rest of that day, or the next.

sn8.2:1.3.verse: And at that time Venerable Vaṅgīsa became dissatisfied, as lust infected his mind.

sn8.2:1.6.verse: that I’ve become dissatisfied, with lust infecting my mind. How is it possible for someone else to dispel my discontent and give rise to satisfaction?

sn8.2:1.7.verse: Why don’t I do it myself?”

sn8.2:1.8.verse: Then, on the occasion of dispelling his own discontent and giving rise to satisfaction, he recited these verses:

sn8.2:2.2.verse: along with all thoughts of domestic life,

sn8.2:2.3.verse: they wouldn’t get snarled in anything;

sn8.2:2.4.verse: unsnarled, undesiring: that’s a real mendicant.

sn8.2:3.1.verse: Whatever here is included in form—

sn8.2:3.2.verse: on earth, in the sky, or in planet’s deep—

sn8.2:3.3.verse: wears out, it is all impermanent:

sn8.2:3.4.verse: the self-examined live having comprehended this.

sn8.2:4.1.verse: People are bound to their attachments,

sn8.2:4.2.verse: to impingement of the seen and heard, and to what is thought.

sn8.2:4.3.verse: Unstirred, dispel desire for these things;

sn8.2:4.4.verse: for one called ‘a sage’ does not cling to them.

sn8.2:5.1.verse: Trapped in the sixty wrong views, full of their own opinions,

sn8.2:5.2.verse: ordinary people are fixed in wrong principles.

sn8.2:5.3.verse: But that mendicant wouldn’t join a sect,

sn8.2:5.4.verse: still less would they utter lewd speech.

sn8.2:6.2.verse: free of deceit, alert, without envy,

sn8.2:6.3.verse: the sage has reached the state of peace;

sn8.2:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.2:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion, when the Venerable Nigrodhakappa returned from his alms round, after his meal he would enter the dwelling and would come out either in the evening or on the following day.

sn8.2:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion dissatisfaction had arisen in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa; lust had infested his mind.

sn8.2:1.4.verse: Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:

sn8.2:1.5.verse: It is a loss for me indeed, it is no gain for me! It is a mishap for me indeed, it is not well gained by me.

sn8.2:1.6.verse: How could anyone else dispel my dissatisfaction and arouse delight?

sn8.2:1.7.verse: Let me dispel my own dissatisfaction and arouse delight by myself.

sn8.2:1.8.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having dispelled his own dissatisfaction and aroused delight by himself, on that occasion recited these verses.

sn8.2:2.3.verse: One should not nurture lust towards anything;

sn8.2:2.4.verse: The lustless one, without delight— He is indeed a bhikkhu.

sn8.2:3.1.verse: Whatever exists here on earth and in space,

sn8.2:3.2.verse: Comprised by form, included in the world—

sn8.2:3.4.verse: The sages fare having pierced this truth.

sn8.2:4.1.verse: People are tied to their acquisitions,

sn8.2:4.2.verse: To what is seen, heard, sensed, and felt;

sn8.2:4.3.verse: Dispel desire for this, be unstirred:

sn8.2:4.4.verse: They call him a sage Who clings to nothing here.

sn8.2:5.1.verse: Then those caught in the sixty,

sn8.2:5.2.verse: Led by their own thoughts— There are many such among the people Who have settled on wrong doctrine:

sn8.2:5.3.verse: One who would not join their faction anywhere,

sn8.2:5.4.verse: Nor utter corrupt speech—he is a bhikkhu.

sn8.2:6.3.verse: The sage has attained the peaceful state, depending on which he bides his time

sn8.3:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Vaṅgīsa was staying near Āḷavī, at Āḷavī’s premier shrine, together with his mentor, Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.3:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Vaṅgīsa looked down upon other good-hearted mendicants because of his own eloquence.

sn8.3:1.5.verse: that I look down on other good-hearted mendicants because of my own eloquence.”

sn8.3:1.6.verse: Then, on the occasion of arousing remorse in himself, he recited these verses:

sn8.3:2.2.verse: Completely abandon the different kinds of conceit!

sn8.3:2.3.verse: Besotted with the different kinds of conceit,

sn8.3:2.4.verse: you’ve had regrets for a long time.

sn8.3:3.1.verse: Smeared by smears and slain by conceit,

sn8.3:3.3.verse: When people slain by conceit are reborn in hell,

sn8.3:3.4.verse: they grieve for a long time.

sn8.3:4.1.verse: But a mendicant who practices rightly,

sn8.3:4.3.verse: They enjoy happiness and a good reputation,

sn8.3:4.4.verse: and they rightly call him a ‘Seer of Truth’.

sn8.3:5.1.verse: So being not hard-hearted, but energetic,

sn8.3:5.3.verse: and having completely given up conceit,

sn8.3:5.4.verse: the one who makes an end with knowledge is assuaged.”

sn8.3:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was living at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine together with his preceptor, the Venerable Nigrodhakappa.

sn8.3:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, because of his own ingenuity, had been looking down at other well-behaved bhikkhus.

sn8.3:1.3.verse: Then the thought occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:

sn8.3:1.4.verse: “It is a loss for me indeed, it is no gain for me! It is a mishap for me indeed, it is not well gained by me,

sn8.3:1.5.verse: that because of my ingenuity I look down upon other well-behaved bhikkhus.”

sn8.3:1.6.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having aroused remorse in himself, on that occasion recited these verses:

sn8.3:2.2.verse: And leave the pathway of conceit entirely.

sn8.3:2.3.verse: Infatuated with the pathway of conceit,

sn8.3:2.4.verse: For a long time you’ve been remorseful.

sn8.3:3.2.verse: Slain by conceit, fall into hell.

sn8.3:3.3.verse: People sorrow for a long time,

sn8.3:3.4.verse: Slain by conceit, reborn in hell.

sn8.3:4.1.verse: “But a bhikkhu never sorrows at all,

sn8.3:4.4.verse: Truly they call him a seer of Dhamma.

sn8.3:5.2.verse: Having abandoned the hindrances, be pure.

sn8.3:5.4.verse: Be an end-maker by knowledge, peaceful.

sn8.4:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn8.4:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms with Venerable Vaṅgīsa as his second monk.

sn8.4:1.3.verse: And at that time Venerable Vaṅgīsa became dissatisfied, as lust infected his mind.

sn8.4:1.4.verse: Then he addressed Ānanda in verse:

sn8.4:2.1.verse: “I’ve got a burning desire for pleasure;

sn8.4:2.4.verse: tell me how to quench the flames.”

sn8.4:3.2.verse: because of a perversion of perception.

sn8.5:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, speech that has four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It’s blameless and is not criticized by sensible people.

sn8.5:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant speaks well, not poorly; their speech is principled, not unprincipled; they speak pleasantly, not unpleasantly; and they speak truthfully, not falsely.

sn8.5:2.4.verse: Speech with these four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It’s blameless and is not criticized by sensible people.”

sn8.5:2.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn8.5:3.1.verse: “Good people say well-spoken words are foremost;

sn8.5:3.2.verse: second, speech ought be principled, not unprincipled;

sn8.5:3.4.verse: and fourth, speak truthfully, not falsely.”

sn8.5:1.2.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

sn8.5:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, when speech possesses four factors, then it is well spoken, not badly spoken, and it is blameless, not blameworthy among the wise.

sn8.5:2.3.verse: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu speaks only what is well spoken, not what is badly spoken. He speaks only on the Dhamma, not on non-Dhamma. He speaks only what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant. He speaks only what is true, not what is false.

sn8.5:2.4.verse: When speech possesses these four factors, it is well spoken, not badly spoken, and it is blameless, not blameworthy among the wise.”

sn8.5:2.5.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

sn8.5:3.1.verse: “What is well spoken, the good say, is foremost;

sn8.5:3.3.verse: Third, speak what is pleasant, not unpleasant;

sn8.5:3.4.verse: Fourth, speak the truth, not falsehood.”

sn8.7:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, together with a large Saṅgha of around five hundred monks, all of whom were perfected ones.

sn8.7:1.2.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks for the invitation to admonish.

sn8.7:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were silent. He addressed them:

sn8.7:1.4.verse: “Come now, monks, I invite you all:

sn8.7:1.5.verse: Is there anything I’ve done by way of body or speech that you would criticize?”

sn8.7:2.1.verse: When he had spoken, Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:

sn8.7:2.2.verse: “There is nothing, sir, that you’ve done by way of body or speech that we would criticize.

sn8.7:2.3.verse: For the Blessed One gave rise to the unarisen path, gave birth to the unborn path, and explained the unexplained path. He is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert on the path.

sn8.7:2.4.verse: And now the disciples live following the path; they acquire it later.

sn8.7:2.5.verse: And sir, I invite the Blessed One.

sn8.7:2.6.verse: Is there anything I’ve done by way of body or speech that you would criticize?”

sn8.7:3.1.verse: “There is nothing, Sāriputta, that you’ve done by way of body or speech that I would criticize.

sn8.7:3.2.verse: Sāriputta, you are astute. You have great wisdom, widespread wisdom, laughing wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrating wisdom.

sn8.7:3.3.verse: A wheel-turning monarch’s oldest son rightly keeps wielding the power set in motion by his father.

sn8.7:3.4.verse: In the same way, Sāriputta rightly keeps rolling the supreme Wheel of Dhamma that was rolled forth by me.”

sn8.7:4.1.verse: “Since it seems I have done nothing worthy of the Blessed One’s criticism,

sn8.7:4.2.verse: is there anything these five hundred monks have done by way of body or speech that you would criticize?”

sn8.7:4.3.verse: “There is nothing, Sāriputta, that these five hundred monks have done by way of body or speech that I would criticize.

sn8.7:4.4.verse: For of these five hundred monks, sixty have the three knowledges, sixty have the six direct knowledges, sixty are freed both ways, and the rest are freed by wisdom.”

sn8.7:5.1.verse: Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said,

sn8.7:5.2.verse: “I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!”

sn8.7:5.3.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

sn8.7:5.4.verse: Then Vaṅgīsa extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:

sn8.7:6.2.verse: five hundred monks have gathered together to purify their precepts.

sn8.7:6.3.verse: These untroubled sages have cut off their fetters and bonds,

sn8.7:6.4.verse: they will not be reborn again.

sn8.7:8.3.verse: revere the winner of the battle,

sn8.7:2.5.verse: And I, venerable sir, invite the Blessed One

sn8.7:2.6.verse: Is there any deed of mine, either bodily or verbal, which the Blessed One would censure?

sn8.7:3.1.verse: There is no deed of yours, Sāriputta, either bodily or verbal, that I censure.

sn8.7:3.2.verse: For you, Sāriputta, are wise, one of great wisdom, of wide wisdom, of joyous wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrative wisdom.

sn8.7:3.3.verse: Just as the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch properly keeps in motion the wheel [of sovereignty] set in motion by his father,

sn8.7:3.4.verse: so do you, Sāriputta, properly keep in motion the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me.

sn8.7:4.1.verse: If, venerable sir, the Blessed One does not censure any deed of mine, bodily or verbal,

sn8.7:4.2.verse: does he censure any deed, bodily or verbal, of these five hundred bhikkhus?

sn8.7:4.3.verse: There is no deed, Sāriputta, bodily or verbal, of these five hundred bhikkhus that I censure.

sn8.7:4.4.verse: For of these five hundred bhikkhus, Sāriputta, sixty bhikkhus are triple-knowledge bearers, sixty bhikkhus are bearers of the six direct knowledges, sixty bhikkhus are liberated in both ways, while the rest are liberated by wisdom.

sn8.9:2.4.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa extolled the Venerable Aññā Koṇḍañña in the Blessed One’s presence with suitable verses:

sn8.9:3.2.verse: The elder Koṇḍañña, of strong endeavour,

sn8.9:3.3.verse: Is one who gains pleasant dwellings,

sn8.9:3.4.verse: One who often gains the seclusions.

sn8.9:4.1.verse: “Whatever may be attained by a disciple

sn8.9:4.3.verse: All that has been attained by him,

sn8.9:5.2.verse: Skilled in the course of others’ minds—

sn8.9:5.3.verse: Koṇḍañña, a true heir of the Buddha,

sn8.9:5.4.verse: Pays homage at the Teacher’s feet.

sn8.10:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying on the slopes of Isigili at the Black Rock, together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants, all of whom were perfected ones.

sn8.10:1.2.verse: Thereupon, with his mind, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna scrutinized whose mind was liberated and free of attachments.

sn8.10:1.4.verse: “The Buddha is staying on the slopes of Isigili … with five hundred perfected ones.

sn8.10:1.5.verse: Mahāmoggallāna is scrutinizing whose mind is liberated and free of attachments.

sn8.10:1.6.verse: Why don’t I extoll him in the Buddha’s presence with fitting verses?”

sn8.10:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said,

sn8.10:2.2.verse: “I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!”

sn8.10:2.3.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

sn8.10:2.4.verse: Then Vaṅgīsa extolled Mahāmoggallāna in his presence with fitting verses:

sn8.10:3.1.verse: “As the sage, who has gone beyond suffering,

sn8.10:3.3.verse: he is revered by disciples with the three knowledges,

sn8.10:5.1.verse: That is how those endowed with many fine qualities

sn8.10:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on the Black Rock on the Isigili Slope, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with five hundred bhikkhus all of whom were arahants.

sn8.10:1.2.verse: Thereupon the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna searched their minds with his own mind [and saw that they were] released, without acquisitions.

sn8.10:1.3.verse: Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:

sn8.10:1.4.verse: “The Blessed One is dwelling at Rājagaha on the Black Rock on the Isigili Slope…

sn8.10:1.5.verse: Thereupon the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has searched their minds with his own mind [and seen that they are] released, without acquisitions.

sn8.10:1.6.verse: Let me extol the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the Blessed One’s presence with suitable verses.”

sn8.10:2.1.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, raising his joined hands in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One, said to him:

sn8.10:2.2.verse: “An inspiration has come to me, Blessed One! An inspiration has come to me, Fortunate One!”

sn8.10:2.4.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa extolled the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the Blessed One’s presence with suitable verses:

sn8.10:3.1.verse: “While the sage is seated on the mountain slope,

sn8.10:3.2.verse: Gone to the far shore of suffering,

sn8.10:3.3.verse: His disciples sit in attendance on him,

sn8.10:3.4.verse: Triple-knowledge men who have left Death behind.

sn8.10:4.2.verse: Encompassed their minds with his own,

sn8.10:4.3.verse: And searching [he came to see] their minds:

sn8.10:5.3.verse: The sage perfect in all respects,

sn8.10:5.4.verse: Gone to the far shore of suffering.

sn8.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond, together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants, seven hundred male and seven hundred female lay followers, and many thousands of deities.

sn8.11:1.2.verse: But the Buddha outshone them all in beauty and glory.

sn8.11:1.4.verse: “The Buddha is staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond, together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants, seven hundred male and seven hundred female lay followers, and many thousands of deities.

sn8.11:1.5.verse: And he outshines them all in beauty and glory.

sn8.11:1.6.verse: Why don’t I extoll him in his presence with fitting verses?”

sn8.11:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said,

sn8.11:2.2.verse: “I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!”

sn8.11:2.3.verse: “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha.

sn8.11:2.4.verse: Then Vaṅgīsa extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:

sn8.11:3.1.verse: “Like the moon on a cloudless night,

sn8.11:3.3.verse: so too Aṅgīrasa, O great sage,

sn8.11:3.4.verse: your glory outshines the entire world.”

sn8.11:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with five hundred bhikkhus, seven hundred male lay followers, seven hundred female lay followers, and many thousands of devatās.

sn8.11:1.2.verse: The Blessed One outshone them in beauty and glory.

sn8.11:1.3.verse: Then it occurred to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa:

sn8.11:1.4.verse: This Blessed One is dwelling at Campā … and many thousands of devatās.

sn8.11:1.5.verse: The Blessed One outshines them in beauty and glory.

sn8.11:1.6.verse: Let me extol the Blessed One to his face with suitable verses.

sn8.11:2.1.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, raising his joined hands in reverential salutation towards the Blessed One, said to him:

sn8.11:2.2.verse: An inspiration has come to me, Blessed One! An inspiration has come to me, Fortunate One!

sn8.11:2.4.verse: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa extolled the Blessed One to his face with a suitable verse:

sn8.11:3.1.verse: As the moon shines in a cloudless sky,

sn8.11:3.2.verse: As the sun shines devoid of stain,

sn8.11:3.3.verse: So you, Aṅgīrasa, O great sage,

sn8.11:3.4.verse: Outshine the whole world with your glory.

sn8.12:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Vaṅgīsa was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn8.12:1.2.verse: Now at that time Vaṅgīsa had recently attained perfection. While experiencing the bliss of freedom, on that occasion he recited these verses:

sn8.12:2.1.verse: “We used to wander, drunk on poetry,

sn8.12:2.2.verse: village to village, town to town.

sn8.12:3.2.verse: the aggregates, sense fields, and elements.

sn8.12:4.1.verse: It was truly for the benefit of many

sn8.12:4.3.verse: for the monks and for the nuns

sn8.12:4.4.verse: who see that they’ve reached certainty.

sn8.12:5.1.verse: It was so welcome for me

sn8.12:5.2.verse: to be in the presence of the Buddha.

sn8.12:6.3.verse: I am master of three knowledges, attained in psychic power,

sn8.12:6.4.verse: expert in encompassing the minds of others.”

sn8.12:7.8.verse: The Linked Discourses with Vaṅgīsa are complete.

sn8.12:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

sn8.12:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion the Venerable Vaṅgīsa had only recently attained arahantship and, while experiencing the happiness of liberation, on that occasion he recited these verses:

sn8.12:2.1.verse: Drunk on poetry, I used to wander

sn8.12:2.2.verse: From village to village, town to town.

sn8.12:2.3.verse: Then I saw the Enlightened One

sn8.12:3.1.verse: He then taught me the Dhamma:

sn8.12:3.3.verse: Having heard the Dhamma from him,

sn8.12:4.1.verse: Indeed, for the good of many,

sn8.12:4.4.verse: Who have reached and seen the fixed course.

sn8.12:5.1.verse: Welcome indeed has it been for me,

sn8.12:5.2.verse: My coming into the Buddha’s presence.

sn8.12:5.3.verse: The three knowledges have been obtained,

sn8.12:5.4.verse: The Buddha’s Teaching has been done.

sn8.12:6.1.verse: I know now my past abodes,

sn8.12:6.3.verse: A triple knowledge man, attained to spiritual powers,

sn8.12:6.4.verse: I am skilled in the course of others’ minds.

sn9.1:1.2.verse: At one time one of the mendicants was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time that mendicant, during their day’s meditation, was thinking bad, unskillful thoughts to do with the domestic life.

sn9.1:1.4.verse: The deity haunting that forest had sympathy for that mendicant, and wanted what’s best for them. So they approached that mendicant wanting to stir them up, and addressed them in verse:

sn9.1:2.2.verse: yet your mind strays to outward things.

sn9.1:2.3.verse: As a person, dispel the desire for people;

sn9.1:2.4.verse: then you’ll be happy, free of greed.

sn9.1:3.2.verse: let us remind you to be mindful.

sn9.1:3.3.verse: The dusty abyss is so hard to cross;

sn9.1:3.4.verse: don’t let sensual dust drag you down.

sn9.1:4.1.verse: Just as a bird strewn with dirt

sn9.1:4.2.verse: sheds that clingy dust with a shake;

sn9.1:4.3.verse: so too, an energetic, mindful mendicant

sn9.1:4.4.verse: sheds that clingy dust with a shake.”

sn9.1:5.1.verse: Impelled by that deity, that mendicant was struck with a sense of urgency.

sn9.1:1.2.verse: On one occasion a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.1:1.3.verse: Now on that occasion, while that bhikkhu had gone for his day’s abiding, he kept on thinking evil unwholesome thoughts connected with the household life.

sn9.1:1.4.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for that bhikkhu, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verses:

sn9.1:2.1.verse: Desiring seclusion you entered the woods,

sn9.1:2.3.verse: Remove, man, the desire for people;

sn9.1:2.4.verse: Then you’ll be happy, devoid of lust.

sn9.1:3.1.verse: You must abandon discontent, be mindful—

sn9.1:3.2.verse: Let us remind [you] of that [way] of the good.

sn9.1:3.3.verse: Hard to cross, indeed, is the dusty abyss;

sn9.1:3.4.verse: Don’t let sensual dust drag you down.

sn9.1:4.1.verse: Just as a bird littered with soil

sn9.1:4.2.verse: With a shake flicks off the sticky dust,

sn9.1:4.3.verse: So a bhikkhu, strenuous and mindful,

sn9.1:4.4.verse: With a shake flicks off the sticky dust.

sn9.1:5.1.verse: Then that bhikkhu, stirred up by that devatā, acquired a sense of urgency

sn9.2:1.1.verse: At one time one of the mendicants was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.2:1.2.verse: Now at that time that mendicant went for the day’s meditation, but fell asleep.

sn9.2:1.3.verse: The deity haunting that forest had sympathy for that mendicant, and wanted what’s best for them. So they approached that mendicant wanting to stir them up, and addressed them in verse:

sn9.2:3.2.verse: that led you to go forth

sn9.2:3.3.verse: from the lay life to homelessness.

sn9.2:3.4.verse: Don’t fall under the sway of slumber.”

sn9.2:4.2.verse: but dullards still fall for them.

sn9.2:4.3.verse: Among those who are bound, they’re free and unattached:

sn9.2:5.3.verse: that knowledge has been perfectly cleansed:

sn9.2:1.1.verse: On one occasion a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.2:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion when that bhikkhu had gone for his day’s abiding he fell asleep.

sn9.2:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for that bhikkhu, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verses:

sn9.2:2.3.verse: What need do you have for sleep?

sn9.2:2.4.verse: What slumber [can there be] for one afflicted, Stricken, pierced by the dart?

sn9.2:3.2.verse: With which you left behind the home life

sn9.2:4.2.verse: Though the dullard is enthralled with them.

sn9.2:4.3.verse: When he’s free, detached among those bound,

sn9.2:5.1.verse: When, by the removal of desire and lust

sn9.2:6.1.verse: When, by breaking ignorance with knowledge

sn9.2:6.2.verse: And by destruction of the taints,

sn9.2:7.1.verse: When he is energetic and resolute,

sn9.3:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Kassapagotta was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.3:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Kassapagotta, having withdrawn for his day’s meditation, tried to advise a nimrod.

sn9.3:1.3.verse: Then the deity haunting that forest approached Kassapagotta wanting to stir him up, and recited these verses:

sn9.3:2.3.verse: It’s a waste of time to advise him, mendicant;

sn9.3:2.4.verse: he strikes me as a dullard.

sn9.3:4.1.verse: Even if you lit ten lamps

sn9.3:4.2.verse: and brought them to him, Kassapa,

sn9.3:4.4.verse: for he has no eyes to see.”

sn9.3:5.1.verse: Impelled by that deity, Venerable Kassapagotta was struck with a sense of urgency.

sn9.3:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Kassapagotta was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.3:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion,when he had gone for his day’s abiding, the Venerable Kassapagotta exhorted a certain hunter.

sn9.3:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for the Venerable Kassapagotta, desiring his good,desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verses:

sn9.3:2.1.verse: A hunter, roaming in the rugged mountains

sn9.3:2.2.verse: With little wisdom, devoid of sense.

sn9.3:2.3.verse: Out of season.  Like this bhikkhu I exhort.

sn9.3:2.4.verse: He strikes me as a dolt.

sn9.3:3.1.verse: He listens but does not understand,

sn9.3:3.2.verse: He looks but does not see;

sn9.3:3.3.verse: Though the Dhamma is being spoken,

sn9.3:3.4.verse: The fool does not grasp the meaning.

sn9.3:4.3.verse: Still he would not see forms,

sn9.3:4.4.verse: For he does not have eyes to see.

sn9.3:5.1.verse: Then the Venerable Kassapagotta, stirred up by that devatā,acquired a sense of urgency

sn9.4:1.1.verse: At one time several mendicants were staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.4:1.2.verse: Then after completing the three months of the rainy season residence, those mendicants set out wandering.

sn9.4:1.3.verse: Not seeing those mendicants, the deity haunting that forest cried. And on that occasion they spoke this verse:

sn9.4:2.3.verse: They were so learned, such brilliant speakers!

sn9.4:2.4.verse: Where have these disciples of Gotama gone?”

sn9.4:3.1.verse: When they had spoken, another deity replied with this verse:

sn9.4:4.1.verse: “They’ve gone to Magadha, they’ve gone to Kosala,

sn9.4:4.2.verse: and some are in the Vajjian lands.

sn9.4:4.3.verse: Like deer that wander free of ties,

sn9.4:4.4.verse: the mendicants live with no abode.”

sn9.4:1.1.verse: On one occasion a number of bhikkhus were dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.4:1.2.verse: Then, when they had spent the rains there, after the three months had passed those bhikkhus set out on tour.

sn9.4:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, not seeing those bhikkhus, lamenting, on that occasion recited this verse:

sn9.4:2.2.verse: When I see here so many vacant seats.

sn9.4:2.3.verse: Where have they gone, Gotama’s disciples,

sn9.4:2.4.verse: Those splendid speakers rich in learning?”

sn9.4:3.1.verse: When this was said, another devatā replied in verse:

sn9.4:4.1.verse: “They’ve gone to Magadha, gone to Kosala,

sn9.4:4.2.verse: And some are in the Vajjian land.

sn9.4:4.3.verse: Like deer that roam free from ties,

sn9.5:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.5:1.2.verse: Now at that time Ānanda was spending too much time persuading lay people.

sn9.5:1.3.verse: Then the deity haunting that forest had sympathy for Ānanda, wanting what’s best for him. So they approached him wanting to stir him up, and recited these verses:

sn9.5:2.1.verse: “You’ve left for the jungle, the root of a tree,

sn9.5:2.2.verse: having laid extinguishment in your heart.

sn9.5:2.4.verse: What use is this hullabaloo to you?”

sn9.5:3.1.verse: Impelled by that deity, Venerable Ānanda was struck with a sense of urgency.

sn9.5:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.5:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion the Venerable Ānanda was excessively involved instructing lay people.

sn9.5:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for the Venerable Ānanda, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verse

sn9.5:2.1.verse: “Having entered the thicket at the foot of a tree,

sn9.5:2.2.verse: Having placed Nibbāna in your heart,

sn9.5:2.3.verse: Meditate, Gotama, and don’t be negligent!

sn9.5:2.4.verse: What will this hullabaloo do for you?”

sn9.5:3.1.verse: Then the Venerable Ānanda, stirred up by that deity, acquired a sense of urgency

sn9.6:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.6:1.2.verse: Then a certain deity of the company of the thirty-three named Penelope had been Anuruddha’s partner in a former life. She went up to Anuruddha, and recited these verses:

sn9.6:2.3.verse: among the gods of the thirty-three,

sn9.6:2.5.verse: At the fore of a retinue

sn9.6:3.1.verse: “Divine maidens are in a sorry state,

sn9.6:3.3.verse: And those beings too are in a sorry state,

sn9.6:3.4.verse: who are attached to divine maidens.”

sn9.6:4.2.verse: who don’t see the Garden of Delight!

sn9.6:4.3.verse: It’s the abode of lordly gods,

sn9.6:5.2.verse: the saying of the perfected ones:

sn9.6:5.4.verse: their nature is to rise and fall;

sn9.6:6.1.verse: O Penelope, weaver of the web—

sn9.6:6.2.verse: there are no more abodes for me in the heavenly host.

sn9.6:6.4.verse: now there’ll be no more future lives.”

sn9.6:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.6:1.2.verse: Then a certain devatā of the Tāvatiṃsa host named Jālinī, a former consort of the Venerable Anuruddha, approached him and addressed him in verse

sn9.6:2.1.verse: Direct your mind there [to that realm]

sn9.6:2.2.verse: Where you dwelt in the past

sn9.6:2.4.verse: For whom all desires are fulfilled.

sn9.6:2.5.verse: You will shine forth highly honoured,

sn9.6:3.3.verse: And miserable too are those beings,

sn9.6:4.3.verse: The abode of the glorious male devas

sn9.6:4.4.verse: Belonging to the host of Thirty.”

sn9.6:5.4.verse: Their nature is to arise and vanish.

sn9.6:6.3.verse: The wandering on in birth is ended:

sn9.6:6.4.verse: Now there is no more renewed existence.”

sn9.7:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Nāgadatta was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.7:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Nāgadatta had been entering the village too early and returning late in the day.

sn9.7:1.3.verse: Then the deity haunting that forest had sympathy for Nāgadatta, wanting what’s best for him. So they approached him wanting to stir him up, and recited these verses:

sn9.7:2.2.verse: and returning too late in the day,

sn9.7:3.1.verse: I’m afraid for Nāgadatta; he’s reckless,

sn9.7:3.3.verse: May he not come under the King of Death’s power,

sn9.7:3.4.verse: under the sway of the terminator!”

sn9.7:4.1.verse: Impelled by that deity, Venerable Nāgadatta was struck with a sense of urgency.

sn9.7:1.1.verse: On one occasion the Venerable Nāgadatta was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.7:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion the Venerable Nāgadatta had been entering the village too early and returning too late in the day.

sn9.7:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for the Venerable Nāgadatta, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verses:

sn9.7:2.1.verse: Entering the village early, Nāgadatta associates too closely with lay folk, Sharing their happiness and suffering.

sn9.7:2.3.verse: Nāgadatta associates too closely with lay folk,

sn9.7:3.3.verse: Do not come under the End-maker’s control,

sn9.7:3.4.verse: [In the grip] of the powerful King of Death.

sn9.7:4.1.verse: Then the Venerable Nāgadatta, stirred up by that deity, acquired a sense of urgency

sn9.8:1.1.verse: At one time one of the monks was staying in the land of the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.

sn9.8:1.2.verse: Now at that time that monk had become too closely involved in the affairs of a certain family.

sn9.8:1.3.verse: The deity haunting that forest had sympathy for that monk, wanting what’s best for him. So, wanting to stir him up, they manifested in the appearance of the mistress of that family, approached the monk, and addressed him in verse:

sn9.8:2.4.verse: what’s going on between you and me.”

sn9.8:3.2.verse: that a fervent ascetic must endure.

sn9.8:3.3.verse: They ought not be dismayed by that,

sn9.8:3.4.verse: for that’s not what defiles you.

sn9.8:4.1.verse: If you’re startled by every little sound,

sn9.8:4.2.verse: like a wind-deer in the wood,

sn9.8:1.1.verse: On one occasion a certain bhikkhu was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.8:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion that bhikkhu had become excessively intimate with a certain family.

sn9.8:1.3.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for that bhikkhu, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, manifested herself in the form of the mistress of that family. Having approached that bhikkhu, she addressed him in verse:

sn9.8:2.1.verse: “By the riverbanks and in the rest house,

sn9.8:2.2.verse: In the meeting halls and along the roads,

sn9.8:2.3.verse: People meet and gossip about this:

sn9.8:2.4.verse: What’s going on between you and me?”

sn9.8:3.2.verse: That an ascetic must patiently endure.

sn9.8:3.3.verse: One should not be dismayed because of that,

sn9.8:3.4.verse: For it is not by this one is defiled.

sn9.8:4.1.verse: “If one is frightened by random sounds

sn9.8:4.2.verse: Like an antelope dwelling in the woods,

sn9.8:4.3.verse: They call him ‘one with a fickle mind’:

sn9.9:1.1.verse: At one time a certain Vajjian mendicant was staying near Vesālī in a certain forest grove.

sn9.9:1.2.verse: Now at that time the Vajjis were holding an all-night event in Vesālī.

sn9.9:1.1.verse: On one occasion a certain bhikkhu, a Vajjian prince, was dwelling at Vesālī in a certain woodland thicket.

sn9.9:1.2.verse: Now on that occasion an all-night festival was being held in Vesālī.

sn9.9:1.3.verse: Then that bhikkhu, lamenting as he heard the clamour of instruments, gongs, and music coming from Vesālī, on that occasion recited this verse:

sn9.9:2.1.verse: “We dwell in the forest all alone

sn9.9:2.2.verse: Like a log rejected in the woods.

sn9.9:2.3.verse: On such a splendid night as this

sn9.9:2.4.verse: Who is there worse off than us?”

sn9.9:3.1.verse: Then the devatā that inhabited that woodland thicket, having compassion for that bhikkhu, desiring his good, desiring to stir up a sense of urgency in him, approached him and addressed him in verse:

sn9.9:4.1.verse: “As you dwell in the forest all alone

sn9.9:4.2.verse: Like a log rejected in the woods,

sn9.9:4.3.verse: Many are those who envy you,

sn9.9:4.4.verse: As hell-beings envy those going to heaven.”

sn9.9:5.1.verse: Then that bhikkhu, stirred up by that devatā, acquired a sense of urgency.

sn9.10:2.1.verse: “Mendicant, why don’t you recite passages of the teaching,

sn9.13:1.1.verse: At one time several mendicants were staying in the Kosalan lands in a certain forest grove. They were haughty, insolent, fickle, scurrilous, loose-tongued, unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties.

sn9.13:2.5.verse: Knowing that the world was impermanent

sn10.1:4.2.verse: the food and drink that she consumes—

sn10.12:1.15.verse: “All right, friend,” the Blessed One said, and he went out.

sn10.12:1.17.verse: “All right, friend,” the Blessed One said, and he went in.

sn10.12:1.18.verse: A fourth time the yakkha Alavaka said to the Blessed One:

sn10.12:1.21.verse: Do whatever you have to do.”

sn10.12:1.23.verse: If you won't answer me, I'll drive you insane or I'll split your heart or I'll grab you by the feet and hurl you across the Ganges.”

sn10.12:1.24.verse: “I do not see anyone in this world, friend, with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who could drive me insane or split my heart or grab me by the feet and hurl me across the Ganges.

sn10.12:1.25.verse: But ask whatever you want, friend.”

sn10.12:2.1.verse: “What here is a man’s best treasure?

sn10.12:2.3.verse: What is really the sweetest of tastes?

sn10.12:2.4.verse: How lives the one who they say lives best?”

sn10.12:3.1.verse: “Faith Is here a man’s best treasure;

sn10.12:3.3.verse: Truth is really the sweetest of tastes;

sn10.12:3.4.verse: One living by wisdom they say lives best.”

sn10.12:4.1.verse: “How does one cross over the flood?

sn10.12:4.2.verse: How does one cross the rugged sea?

sn10.12:5.1.verse: “By faith one crosses over the flood,

sn10.12:6.6.verse: When passing from this world to the next,

sn10.12:7.1.verse: If one is diligent and astute.

sn10.12:7.2.verse: From desire to learn one gains wisdom

sn10.12:7.3.verse: Placing faith in the Dhamma of the arahants

sn10.12:8.5.verse: When passing from this world to the next.”

sn10.12:8.6.verse: That is how one does not sorrow

sn10.12:9.1.verse: In whom dwell these four qualities—

sn10.12:9.2.verse: The faithful seeker of the household life

sn10.12:9.4.verse: Does not sorrow when he passes on.

sn10.12:10.3.verse: Than truth, self-control, generosity, and patience.

sn10.12:10.4.verse: Whether there is found here anything better”

sn10.12:11.1.verse: “Why now should I ask this question

sn10.12:11.2.verse: Of the many ascetics and brahmins?

sn10.12:11.4.verse: The good pertaining to the future life.

sn10.12:12.1.verse: Indeed, for my sake the Buddha

sn10.12:12.4.verse: Where a gift bears great fruit.

sn10.12:13.2.verse: From village to village, town to town,

sn10.12:13.3.verse: Paying homage to the Enlightened One

sn10.12:13.4.verse: And to the excellence of the Dhamma.”

sn11.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn11.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

sn11.1:2.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, the titans marched against the gods.

sn11.1:2.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the godling Suvīra,

sn11.1:2.3.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!

sn11.1:2.4.verse: Go, and march against the titans!’

sn11.1:2.5.verse: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But he fell into negligence.

sn11.1:2.6.verse: For a second time Sakka addressed Suvīra,

sn11.1:2.7.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!

sn11.1:2.8.verse: Go, and march against the titans!’

sn11.1:2.9.verse: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But for a second time he fell into negligence.

sn11.1:2.10.verse: For a third time Sakka addressed Suvīra,

sn11.1:2.11.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, the titans march against the gods!

sn11.1:2.12.verse: Go, and march against the titans!’

sn11.1:2.13.verse: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Suvīra. But for a third time he fell into negligence.

sn11.1:2.14.verse: Then Sakka addressed the godling Suvīra in verse:

sn11.1:3.3.verse: without working for it or trying hard—

sn11.1:4.1.verse: ‘That a lazy man who does no work,

sn11.1:5.2.verse: where a lazy man who does no work

sn11.1:6.2.verse: that we might find the happiness

sn11.1:7.2.verse: where one can live happily without working,

sn11.1:7.3.verse: that surely would be extinguishment’s path!

sn11.1:8.1.verse: Since, mendicants, even that Sakka, lord of gods—while living off of the fruit of his good deeds, and ruling as sovereign lord over these gods of the thirty-three—will speak in praise of initiative and energy,

sn11.1:8.2.verse: you can excel at this, for you who have gone forth in such a well explained teaching and training can try hard, strive, and make an effort to attain the unattained, achieve the unachieved, and realize the unrealized.”

sn11.1:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

sn11.1:1.3.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

sn11.1:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, once in the past the asuras marched against the devas.

sn11.1:2.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Suvīra, a young deva, thus:

sn11.1:2.3.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, these asuras are marching against the devas.

sn11.1:2.4.verse: Go, dear Suvīra, launch a counter-march against the asuras.’

sn11.1:2.5.verse: ‘Yes, your lordship,’ Suvīra replied, but he became negligent.

sn11.1:2.6.verse: A second time Sakka addressed Suvīra,

sn11.1:2.7.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, these asuras are marching against the devas.

sn11.1:2.8.verse: Go, dear Suvīra, launch a counter-march against the asuras.’

sn11.1:2.9.verse: ‘Yes, your lordship,’ Suvīra replied, but he became negligent.

sn11.1:2.10.verse: A third time Sakka addressed Suvīra,

sn11.1:2.11.verse: ‘Dear Suvīra, these asuras are marching against the devas.

sn11.1:2.12.verse: Go, dear Suvīra, launch a counter-march against the asuras.’

sn11.1:2.13.verse: ‘Yes, your lordship,’ Suvīra replied, but he became negligent.

sn11.1:2.14.verse: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka addressed Suvīra in verse:

sn11.1:3.1.verse: ‘Where one need not toll and strive,

sn11.1:3.2.verse: Yet still may attain to bliss:

sn11.1:3.4.verse: And take me along with you!’

sn11.1:4.1.verse: ‘That a lazy man who does not toil,

sn11.1:4.3.verse: Might still have all desires fulfilled:

sn11.1:4.4.verse: Grant me that, Sakka, as a boon,’

sn11.1:5.1.verse: ‘Where a lazy man who does not toil,

sn11.1:5.4.verse: And take me along with you!’

sn11.1:6.1.verse: ‘The bliss, supreme deva, we might find

sn11.1:6.3.verse: Oh Sakka, The sorrowless state without despair:

sn11.1:6.4.verse: Grant me that, Sakka, as a boon.’

sn11.1:7.2.verse: Where without work one won't decline,

sn11.1:7.5.verse: And take me along with you!’

sn11.1:8.1.verse: So, bhikkhus, if Sakka, lord of the devas, subsisting on the fruit of his own merit, exercising supreme sovereignty and rulership over the Tavatimsa devas, will be one who speaks in praise of initiative and energy,

sn11.1:8.2.verse: then how much more would it be fitting here for you, who have gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, to toil, struggle, and strive for the attainment of the as-yet-unattained, for the achievement of the as-yet-unachieved,

sn11.2:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

sn11.2:2.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, the titans marched against the gods.

sn11.2:2.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the godling Susīma,

sn11.2:2.3.verse: ‘Dear Susīma, the titans march against the gods!

sn11.2:2.4.verse: Go, and march against the titans!’

sn11.2:2.5.verse: ‘Yes, lord,’ replied Susīma. But he fell into negligence.

sn11.2:2.10.verse: Then Sakka addressed the godling Susīma in verse:

sn11.2:3.3.verse: without working for it or trying hard—

sn11.2:4.1.verse: ‘That a lazy man who does no work,

sn11.2:5.2.verse: where a lazy man who does no work

sn11.2:6.2.verse: that we might find the happiness

sn11.2:7.2.verse: where one can live happily without working,

sn11.2:7.3.verse: that surely would be extinguishment’s path!

sn11.2:8.1.verse: Since, mendicants, even that Sakka, lord of gods—while living off of the fruit of his good deeds, and ruling as sovereign lord over these gods of the thirty-three—will speak in praise of initiative and energy,

sn11.2:8.2.verse: you can excel at this, for you who have gone forth in such a well explained teaching and training can try hard, strive, and make an effort to attain the unattained, achieve the unachieved, and realize the unrealized.”

sn11.3:1.2.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

sn11.3:1.4.verse: “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

sn11.3:1.5.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

sn11.3:2.1.verse: “Formerly, monks, there was a massed battle between the gods and the asuras.

sn11.3:2.2.verse: Then, monks, the lord of the gods Sakka addressed the Tāvatiṁsa gods, saying:

sn11.3:3.1.verse: ‘If, dear Sirs, to the gods who have gone into battle there should arise fear, or terror, or horror, at that time you could look for the top of my banner.

sn11.3:3.2.verse: For to those who look to the top of my banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:4.1.verse: If you cannot look to the top of my banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner.

sn11.3:4.2.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:5.1.verse: If you cannot look to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner.

sn11.3:5.2.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:6.1.verse: If you cannot look to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner.

sn11.3:6.2.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.’

sn11.3:7.1.verse: But, monks, to he who looks to the top of the lord of the gods Sakka’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner, whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, may be given up, and may not be given up.

sn11.3:8.1.verse: What is the reason for that?

sn11.3:8.2.verse: The lord of the gods Sakka, monks, is not free from passion, is not free from hatred, is not free from delusion, being fearful, terrified, scared, he ran away.

sn11.3:9.2.verse: ‘If to you, monks, after going to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, there should arise fear, or terror, or horror, at that time you could recollect me thus:

sn11.3:9.3.verse: “Such is he, the Fortunate One, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, the one endowed with understanding and good conduct, the Happy One, the One who understands the worlds, the unsurpassed guide for those people who need taming, the Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Fortunate One.”

sn11.3:9.4.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect me whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:10.1.verse: If you cannot recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma thus:

sn11.3:10.2.verse: “The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Fortunate One, it is visible, not subject to time, inviting inspection, onward leading, and can be understood by the wise for themselves.”

sn11.3:10.3.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect the Dhamma whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:11.1.verse: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Saṅgha thus:

sn11.3:11.2.verse: “The Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are good in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are upright in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are systematic in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are correct in their practice, that is to say, the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons, this is the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples, they are worthy of offerings, of hospitality, of gifts, and of reverential salutation, they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”

sn11.3:11.3.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect the Saṅgha whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

sn11.3:12.1.verse: What is the reason for that?

sn11.3:12.2.verse: The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, is free from passion, is free from hatred, is free from delusion, not being fearful, not terrified, not scared, he did not run away.’”

sn11.3:12.4.verse: and after saying this, the Happy One, the Teacher, said something more:

sn11.3:13.1.verse: “In the wilds, at the root of a tree,

sn11.3:13.2.verse: or in an empty place, monks,

sn11.3:13.4.verse: and there will be no fear for you.

sn11.3:14.1.verse: if you can’t remember the Buddha,

sn11.3:14.3.verse: then you must remember the Dhamma,

sn11.3:14.4.verse: which leads out, which is well preached.

sn11.3:15.1.verse: If you can’t remember the Dhamma,

sn11.3:15.2.verse: which leads out, which is well preached,

sn11.3:15.3.verse: then you must remember the Saṅgha,

sn11.3:15.4.verse: which is an unsurpassed field of merit.

sn11.3:16.1.verse: Thus for those who remember the Buddha,

sn11.3:16.2.verse: the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, monks,

sn11.3:16.3.verse: (there will be no) fear, or terror,

sn11.3:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

sn11.3:2.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

sn11.3:2.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

sn11.3:3.1.verse: ‘Good fellows, when the gods are fighting, if you get scared or terrified, just look up at my banner’s crest.

sn11.3:3.2.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:4.1.verse: If you can’t see my banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of the Progenitor, king of gods.

sn11.3:4.2.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:5.1.verse: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Varuṇa, king of gods.

sn11.3:5.2.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:6.1.verse: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Īsāna, king of gods.

sn11.3:6.2.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.’

sn11.3:7.1.verse: However, when they look up at those banner’s crests their fear and terror might go away or it might not.

sn11.3:8.2.verse: Because Sakka is not free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearful, scared, nervous, quick to flee.

sn11.3:9.2.verse: If you’ve gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and you get scared or terrified, just recollect me:

sn11.3:9.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

sn11.3:9.4.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:10.1.verse: If you can’t recollect me, then recollect the teaching:

sn11.3:10.2.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

sn11.3:10.3.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:11.1.verse: If you can’t recollect the teaching, then recollect the Saṅgha:

sn11.3:11.2.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

sn11.3:11.3.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

sn11.3:12.2.verse: Because the Realized One is free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearless, brave, bold, and stands his ground.”

sn11.3:12.3.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn11.3:12.4.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn11.3:13.1.verse: “In the wilderness, at a tree’s root,

sn11.3:13.2.verse: or an empty hut, O mendicants,

sn11.3:13.4.verse: and no fear will come to you.

sn11.3:14.1.verse: If you can’t recollect the Buddha—

sn11.3:14.2.verse: the eldest in the world, the captain of men—

sn11.3:15.1.verse: If you can’t recollect the teaching—

sn11.3:16.2.verse: the teaching, and the Saṅgha, mendicants,

sn11.3:16.4.verse: and goosebumps will be no more.”

sn11.3:1.2.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

sn11.3:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, once in the past the devas and the asuras were arrayed for battle.

sn11.3:2.2.verse: Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tavatimsa devas thus:

sn11.3:3.1.verse: ‘Dear sirs, when the devas are engaged in battle, if fear or trepidation or terror should arise, on that occasion you should look up at the crest of my standard.

sn11.3:3.2.verse: For when you look up at the crest of my standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

sn11.3:4.1.verse: If you cannot look up at the crest of my standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Pajapati's standard. For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

sn11.3:4.2.verse: If you cannot look up at the crest of the deva-king Pajapati's standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Varuna's standard.

sn11.3:5.1.verse: For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned. If you cannot look up at the crest of the deva-king Varuna's standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Isana's standard.

sn11.3:5.2.verse: For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.’

sn11.3:6.1.verse: Bhikkhus, for those who look up at the crest of the standard of Sakka, lord of the devas;

sn11.3:6.2.verse: or of Pajapati, the deva-king; or of Varuna, the deva-king;

sn11.3:7.1.verse: or of Isana, the deva-king, whatever fear or trepidation or terror they may have may or may not be abandoned.

sn11.3:8.2.verse: Because Sakka, lord of the devas, is not devoid of lust, not devoid of hatred, not devoid of delusion; he can be timid, petrified, frightened, quick to flee.

sn11.3:9.2.verse: If you have gone to a forest or to the foot of a tree or to an empty hut, and fear or trepidation or terror should arise in you, on that occasion you should recollect me thus:

sn11.3:9.3.verse: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ For when you recollect me,

sn11.3:9.4.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

sn11.3:10.1.verse: If you cannot recollect me, then you should recollect the Dhamma thus:

sn11.3:10.2.verse: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ For when you recollect the Dhamma,

sn11.3:10.3.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

sn11.3:11.1.verse: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, then you should recollect the Sangha thus:

sn11.3:11.2.verse: ‘The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practising the good way, practising the straight way, practising the true way, practising the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals: this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ For when you recollect the Sangha,

sn11.3:11.3.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

sn11.3:12.2.verse: Because, bhikkhus, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is devoid of lust, devoid of hatred, devoid of delusion; he is brave, courageous, bold, ready to stand his place.”

sn11.3:12.3.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

sn11.3:12.4.verse: Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:

sn11.3:13.1.verse: “In a forest, at the foot of a tree,

sn11.3:13.2.verse: Or in an empty hut, O bhikkhus,

sn11.3:13.4.verse: No fear will then arise in you.

sn11.3:14.1.verse: But if you cannot recall the Buddha,

sn11.3:14.2.verse: Best in the world, the bull of men,

sn11.3:14.3.verse: Then you should recall the Dhamma,

sn11.3:15.1.verse: But if you cannot recall the Dhamma,

sn11.3:15.3.verse: Then you should recall the Sangha,

sn11.3:16.1.verse: For those who thus recall the Buddha,

sn11.3:16.2.verse: The Dhamma, and the Sangha, bhikkhus,

sn11.3:16.4.verse: will arise, Nor any grisly terror.

sn11.4:1.2.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

sn11.4:1.3.verse: Then Vepacitti, lord of titans, addressed the titans,

sn11.4:1.4.verse: ‘My good fellows, if the titans defeat the gods in this battle, bind Sakka, the lord of gods, by his limbs and neck and bring him to my presence in the citadel of the titans.’

sn11.4:1.5.verse: Meanwhile, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three,

sn11.4:1.6.verse: ‘My good fellows, if the gods defeat the titans in this battle, bind Vepacitti by his limbs and neck and bring him to my presence in the Hall of Clear Right of the gods.’

sn11.4:1.7.verse: In that battle the gods won and the titans lost.

sn11.4:1.8.verse: So the gods of the thirty-three bound Vepacitti by his limbs and neck and brought him to Sakka’s presence in the Hall of Clear Right of the gods.

sn11.4:1.9.verse: And as Sakka was entering and leaving the hall, Vepacitti abused and insulted him with rude, harsh words.

sn11.4:1.10.verse: So Mātali the chariot handler addressed Sakka in verse:

sn11.4:2.2.verse: is it from fear or from weakness

sn11.4:2.3.verse: that you endure such harsh words

sn11.4:3.1.verse: ‘It’s not out of fear or weakness

sn11.4:3.3.verse: For how can a sensible person like me

sn11.4:3.4.verse: get in a fight with a fool?’

sn11.4:4.2.verse: if there’s no one to put a stop to them.

sn11.4:4.3.verse: So an attentive one should stop

sn11.4:5.1.verse: ‘I think that this is the only way

sn11.4:5.2.verse: to put a stop to a fool,

sn11.4:5.3.verse: when you know that the other is upset,

sn11.4:6.5.verse: the simpleton will go after you even harder,

sn11.4:6.6.verse: like a cow chasing someone who runs away.’

sn11.4:7.1.verse: ‘Let him think this if he wishes, or not—

sn11.4:7.3.verse: For the highest goal, one’s own,

sn11.4:7.4.verse: naught better than patience is found.

sn11.4:8.3.verse: they call that the ultimate patience,

sn11.4:8.4.verse: for a weakling must always be patient.

sn11.4:9.2.verse: is really just weakness, they say.

sn11.4:9.3.verse: But no one can challenge a person

sn11.4:9.4.verse: who’s strong, guarded by the teaching.

sn11.4:10.1.verse: When you get angry at an angry person

sn11.4:10.2.verse: you just make things worse for yourself.

sn11.4:10.3.verse: When you don’t get angry at an angry person

sn11.4:10.4.verse: you win a battle hard to win.

sn11.4:11.1.verse: When you know that the other is angry,

sn11.4:11.2.verse: you act for the good of both

sn11.4:11.4.verse: if you’re mindful and stay calm.
