sn12.14:2.13.verse: These I do not consider to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and these venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood.

sn12.14:3.1.verse: But, bhikkhus, as to those ascetics and brahmins who understand these things, the origin of these things, the cessation of these things, and the way leading to the cessation of these things: what are those things that they understand, whose origin they understand, whose cessation they understand, and the way leading to whose cessation they understand?

sn12.14:4.1.verse: They understand aging-and-death, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation.

sn12.14:4.11.verse: volitional formations, their origin, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation.

sn12.14:4.12.verse: These are the things that they understand, whose origin they understand, whose cessation they understand, and the way leading to whose cessation they understand.

sn12.14:4.13.verse: These I consider to be ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins, and these venerable ones, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood.”

sn12.14:1.2.verse: Any recluses or brahmins, Monks, who do not know these things, do not know the uprising of them, the ceasing of them, the way leading to their ceasing—which things is it they do not know [in this fourfold way]?

sn12.14:2.13.verse: those recluses or brahmins are approved neither among recluses as recluses, nor among brahmins as brahmins. Nor have those venerable ones understood of themselves, nor realized what is the good of being a recluse or o brahmin, nor lived in the attainment thereof.

sn12.14:3.1.verse: But those recluses or brahmins, Monks, who know these things—which things is it they know?

sn12.14:4.11.verse: activities in their nature, their uprising, their ceasing.

sn12.14:4.12.verse: the way going to their ceasing—

sn12.14:4.13.verse: those recluses or brahmins are approved both among recluses as recluses and among brahmins as brahmins. And those venerable ones have understood of themselves, have realized what is the good of being a recluse and a brahmin, and have lived in the attainment thereof even in this present life.

sn12.15:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Kaccānagotta went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn12.15:1.3.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘right view’.

sn12.15:2.1.verse: “Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on the duality of existence and non-existence.

sn12.15:2.2.verse: But for one who truly sees the origin of the world with right understanding, the concept of non-existence regarding the world does not occur.

sn12.15:2.3.verse: And for one who truly sees the cessation of the world with right understanding, the concept of existence regarding the world does not occur.

sn12.15:2.4.verse: This world is for the most part shackled by getting involved, grasping, and insisting.

sn12.15:2.5.verse: But if, when it comes to this getting involved & grasping, mental fixation, and insistence & underlying tendency, they are not attracted, do not grasp, and do not fixate on the thought, “my self”,

sn12.15:2.6.verse: they’ll have no doubt or uncertainty that what arises is just suffering arising, and what ceases is just suffering ceasing. Their knowledge of this is independent of others.

sn12.15:2.7.verse: This is how right view is defined.

sn12.15:3.2.verse: ‘All does not exist’: this is the second extreme.

sn12.15:3.3.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way:

sn12.15:3.5.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn12.15:3.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn12.15:3.7.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease.

sn12.15:3.9.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’”

sn12.15:1.2.verse: Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn12.15:1.3.verse: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘right view, right view.’

sn12.15:1.4.verse: In what way, venerable sir, is there right view?”

sn12.15:2.1.verse: “This world, Kaccāna, for the most part depends upon a duality—upon the notion of existence and the notion of nonexistence.

sn12.15:2.2.verse: But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no notion of nonexistence in regard to the world.

sn12.15:2.3.verse: And for one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no notion of existence in regard to the world.

sn12.15:2.4.verse: This world, Kaccāna, is for the most part shackled by engagement, clinging, and adherence.

sn12.15:2.5.verse: But this one [with right view] does not become engaged and cling through that engagement and clinging, mental standpoint, adherence, underlying tendency; he does not take a stand about ‘my self.’

sn12.15:2.6.verse: He has no perplexity or doubt that what arises is only suffering arising, what ceases is only suffering ceasing. His knowledge about this is independent of others.

sn12.15:2.7.verse: It is in this way, Kaccāna, that there is right view.

sn12.15:3.1.verse: ‘All exists’: Kaccāna, this is one extreme.

sn12.15:3.2.verse: ‘All does not exist’: this is the second extreme.

sn12.15:3.3.verse: Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle:

sn12.15:3.4.verse: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be];

sn12.15:3.5.verse: with volitional formations as condition, consciousness….

sn12.15:3.6.verse: Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.

sn12.15:3.7.verse: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations;

sn12.15:3.8.verse: with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness….

sn12.15:3.9.verse: Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

sn12.15:1.1.verse: While the Exalted One was at Savatthi

sn12.15:1.2.verse: the venerable Kaccāyana of that clan came to visit him, and saluting him sat down at one side. So seated he asked the Exalted One, saying:—

sn12.15:1.3.verse: Lord, we hear the phrase 'right view, right view.'

sn12.15:1.4.verse: Now how far is there a 'right view'?

sn12.15:2.1.verse: This world, Kaccāyana, usually bases [its view] on two things: on existence and on non-existence.

sn12.15:2.2.verse: Now he, who with right insight sees the uprising of the world as it really is, does not hold with the non-existence of the world.

sn12.15:2.3.verse: But he, who with right insight sees the passing away of the world as it really is, does not hold with the existence of the world.

sn12.15:2.4.verse: Grasping after systems, imprisoned by dogmas is this world, Kaccāyana, for the most part.

sn12.15:2.5.verse: And the man who does not go after that system-grasping, that mental standpoint, that dogmatic bias, who does not grasp at it, does not take up his stand upon it, [does not think]:—'It is my soul!'

sn12.15:2.6.verse: who thinks: 'that which arises is just Ill, that which passes away is Ill'—this man is not in doubt, is not perplexed. Knowledge herein is his that is not merely another's.

sn12.15:2.7.verse: Thus far, Kaccāyana, he has right view.

sn12.15:3.2.verse: Nothing exists:—this is the other extreme.

sn12.15:3.3.verse: Not approaching either extreme the Tathagata teaches you a doctrine by the middle [way]:—

sn12.15:3.4.verse: Conditioned by ignorance activities come to pass,

sn12.15:3.5.verse: conditioned by activities consciousness; thus conditioned [arises] name-and-shape; and sense arises, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, decay-and-death, grief, suffering, ...

sn12.15:3.6.verse: even such is the uprising of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.15:3.7.verse: But from the utter fading away and ceasing of ignorance [arises] ceasing of activities,

sn12.15:3.9.verse: of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.16:1.2.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn12.16:1.4.verse: How is a Dhamma speaker defined?”

sn12.16:2.1.verse: “If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding old age and death, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn12.16:2.2.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding old age and death, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn12.16:2.3.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping, by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding old age and death, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.

sn12.16:3.1.verse: If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment regarding rebirth …

sn12.16:3.11.verse: If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding ignorance, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn12.16:3.12.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding ignorance, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn12.16:3.13.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping, by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding ignorance, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.”

sn12.16:1.2.verse: Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn12.16:1.3.verse: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘a speaker on the Dhamma, a speaker on the Dhamma.’

sn12.16:1.4.verse: In what way, venerable sir, is one a speaker on the Dhamma?”

sn12.16:2.1.verse: “Bhikkhu, if one teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards aging-and-death, for its fading away and cessation, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who is a speaker on the Dhamma.

sn12.16:2.2.verse: If one is practising for the purpose of revulsion towards aging-and-death, for its fading away and cessation, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who is practising in accordance with the Dhamma.

sn12.16:2.3.verse: If, through revulsion towards aging-and-death, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by nonclinging, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.

sn12.16:3.1.verse: Bhikkhu, if one teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards birth …

sn12.16:3.11.verse: If one is practising for the purpose of revulsion towards ignorance, for its fading away and cessation, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who is a speaker on the Dhamma.

sn12.16:3.12.verse: If one is practising for the purpose of revulsion towards ignorance, for its fading away and cessation, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who is practising in accordance with the Dhamma.

sn12.16:3.13.verse: If, through revulsion towards ignorance, through its fading away and cessation, one is liberated by nonclinging, one is fit to be called a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.”

sn12.16:1.1.verse: [While the Exalted One was staying] at Sāvatthi,

sn12.16:1.2.verse: a certain monk came into his presence, and when he had saluted him he sat down at one side and said:—

sn12.16:1.3.verse: Lord, we hear the word Dhamma-teacher, Dhamma-teacher.

sn12.16:2.1.verse: If one of you, monk, teaches a doctrine of revulsion from decay-and-death, of its fading away, of the ceasing thereof, this is enough for him to be called Dhamma-teaching Brother.

sn12.16:2.2.verse: If a monk have practised himself in this revulsion, [making it] fade away and cease, this is enough for him to be called one versed in that which is in conformity with the Dhamma.

sn12.16:2.3.verse: If a monk from revulsion, from [making it] fade away and cease, be set free from any form of grasping, this is enough for him to be called 'one who hath won Nibbana in this life.'

sn12.16:3.1.verse: In the same way you can so call a monk after this threefold manner if he teach, if he practise, if he be in consequence set free from any form of grasping with respect to birth …

sn12.16:3.11.verse: If one of you, monk, teaches a doctrine of revulsion from ignorance, of its fading away, of the ceasing thereof, this is enough for him to be called Dhamma-teaching Brother.

sn12.16:3.12.verse: If a monk have practised himself in this revulsion from ignorance, [making it] fade away and cease, this is enough for him to be called one versed in that which is in conformity with the Dhamma.

sn12.16:3.13.verse: If a monk from revulsion from ignorance, from [making it] fade away and cease, be set free from any form of grasping, this is enough for him to be called 'one who hath won Nibbana in this life.'

sn12.17:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn12.17:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

sn12.17:1.4.verse: The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Buddha coming off in the distance.

sn12.17:1.5.verse: He went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn12.17:1.6.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side and said to the Buddha,

sn12.17:1.7.verse: “I’d like to ask the worthy Gotama about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

sn12.17:1.8.verse: “Kassapa, it’s the wrong time for questions.

sn12.17:2.5.verse: and a third time, Kassapa spoke to the Buddha and the Buddha replied.

sn12.17:2.7.verse: When this was said, Kassapa said to the Buddha,

sn12.17:3.1.verse: “Well, worthy Gotama, is suffering made by oneself?”

sn12.17:3.5.verse: “Well, is suffering made by both oneself and another?”

sn12.17:3.7.verse: “Then does suffering arise anomalously, not made by oneself or another?”

sn12.17:3.9.verse: “Well, is there no such thing as suffering?”

sn12.17:3.10.verse: “It’s not that there’s no such thing as suffering.

sn12.17:3.12.verse: “Then does the worthy Gotama not know or see suffering?”

sn12.17:3.13.verse: “It’s not that I don’t know or see suffering.

sn12.17:4.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, when asked these questions, you say ‘not so’.

sn12.17:4.5.verse: Yet you say that there is such a thing as suffering.

sn12.17:4.7.verse: And you say that you do know suffering,

sn12.17:4.9.verse: Sir, let the Blessed One explain suffering to me!

sn12.17:4.10.verse: Let the Blessed One teach me about suffering!”

sn12.17:5.1.verse: “Suppose that he who does the deed and he who experiences the result are one and the same. Then for one who has existed since the beginning, suffering is made by oneself. In speaking like this, one implies this is eternal.

sn12.17:5.2.verse: Suppose that he who does the deed is one, and he who experiences the result is another. Then for one stricken by feeling, suffering is made by another. In speaking like this, one implies this is annihilated.

sn12.17:5.3.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way:

sn12.17:5.5.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn12.17:5.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn12.17:5.7.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease.

sn12.17:5.9.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’”

sn12.17:6.1.verse: When this was said, Kassapa said to the Buddha,

sn12.17:6.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn12.17:6.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn12.17:6.5.verse: Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

sn12.17:7.1.verse: “Kassapa, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they’ll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.

sn12.17:7.2.verse: However, I have recognized individual differences.”

sn12.17:8.1.verse: “Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I’ll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.”

sn12.17:9.1.verse: And the naked ascetic Kassapa received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

sn12.17:9.2.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Kassapa, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn12.17:9.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn12.17:9.4.verse: And Venerable Kassapa became one of the perfected.

sn12.17:1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary.

sn12.17:1.3.verse: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed and, taking bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

sn12.17:1.4.verse: The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

sn12.17:1.5.verse: Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

sn12.17:1.6.verse: When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he stood to one side and said to him:

sn12.17:1.7.verse: “We would like to ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if he would grant us the favour of answering our question.”

sn12.17:1.8.verse: “This is not the right time for a question, Kassapa.

sn12.17:1.9.verse: We have entered among the houses.”

sn12.17:2.5.verse: and a third time the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One:“We would like to ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if he would grant us the favour of answering our question.”

sn12.17:2.6.verse: “This is not the right time for a question, Kassapa. We have entered among the houses.”

sn12.17:2.7.verse: Then the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One:

sn12.17:2.8.verse: “We do not wish to ask Master Gotama much.”

sn12.17:3.1.verse: “How is it, Master Gotama: is suffering created by oneself?”

sn12.17:3.2.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.17:3.3.verse: “Then, Master Gotama, is suffering created by another?”

sn12.17:3.4.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.17:3.5.verse: “How is it then, Master Gotama: is suffering created both by oneself and by another?”

sn12.17:3.6.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.17:3.7.verse: “Then, Master Gotama, has suffering arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another?”

sn12.17:3.8.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.17:3.9.verse: “How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no suffering?”

sn12.17:3.10.verse: “It is not that there is no suffering, Kassapa;

sn12.17:3.12.verse: “Then is it that Master Gotama does not know and see suffering?”

sn12.17:3.13.verse: “It is not that I do not know and see suffering, Kassapa.

sn12.17:4.1.verse: “Whether you are asked: ‘How is it, Master Gotama: is suffering created by oneself?’ or ‘Is it created by another?’ or ‘Is it created by both?’ or ‘Is it created by neither?’ in each case you say:

sn12.17:4.5.verse: ‘Not so, Kassapa.’ When you are asked:

sn12.17:4.7.verse: ‘How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no suffering?’

sn12.17:4.8.verse: you say: ‘It is not that there is no suffering, Kassapa; there is suffering.’ When asked: ‘Then is it that Master Gotama does not know and see suffering?’

sn12.17:4.9.verse: you say: ‘It is not that I do not know and see suffering, Kassapa. I know suffering, I see suffering.’

sn12.17:4.10.verse: Venerable sir, let the Blessed One explain suffering to me. Let the Blessed One teach me about suffering.”

sn12.17:5.1.verse: “Kassapa, [if one thinks,] ‘The one who acts is the same as the one who experiences [the result],’ [then one asserts] with reference to one existing from the beginning: ‘Suffering is created by oneself.’ When one asserts thus, this amounts to eternalism.

sn12.17:5.2.verse: But, Kassapa, [if one thinks,] ‘The one who acts is one, the one who experiences [the result] is another,’ [then one asserts] with reference to one stricken by feeling: ‘Suffering is created by another.’ When one asserts thus, this amounts to annihilationism.

sn12.17:5.3.verse: Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle:

sn12.17:5.4.verse: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be];

sn12.17:5.5.verse: with volitional formations as condition, consciousness….

sn12.17:5.6.verse: Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.

sn12.17:5.7.verse: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations;

sn12.17:5.8.verse: with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness….

sn12.17:5.9.verse: Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

sn12.17:6.1.verse: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One:

sn12.17:6.3.verse: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as though he were turning upright what had been turned upside down, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyesight to see forms.

sn12.17:6.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

sn12.17:6.5.verse: May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination?”

sn12.17:7.1.verse: “Kassapa, one formerly belonging to another sect who desires the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with him, they may if they wish give him the going forth and the higher ordination to the state of a bhikkhu.

sn12.17:7.2.verse: But individual differences are recognized by me.”

sn12.17:8.1.verse: “If, venerable sir, one formerly belonging to another sect who desires the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months, and if at the end of the four months the bhikkhus, being satisfied with him, may if they wish give him the going forth and the higher ordination to the state of a bhikkhu, then I will live on probation for four years. At the end of the four years, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with me, let them if they wish give me the going forth and the higher ordination to the state of a bhikkhu.”

sn12.17:9.1.verse: Then the naked ascetic Kassapa received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the higher ordination.

sn12.17:9.2.verse: And soon, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Kassapa, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.

sn12.17:9.3.verse: He directly knew: “Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.”

sn12.17:9.4.verse: And the Venerable Kassapa became one of the arahants.

sn12.17:1.2.verse: The Exalted One was once staying near Rajagaha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels' Feeding-Ground.

sn12.17:1.3.verse: Now the Exalted One in the early morning dressed himself, and taking bowl and robe entered Rājagaha for alms.

sn12.17:1.4.verse: And Kassapa the Unclothed saw the Exalted One coming from afar,

sn12.17:1.5.verse: and seeing him he came up to the Exalted One and greeted him,

sn12.17:1.6.verse: and when compliments of friendship and courtesy had been exchanged, he stood at one side. So standing Kassapa the Unclothed said:—

sn12.17:1.7.verse: “We will ask Master Gotama concerning one point, if he would give us opportunity of hearing him reply to our question.”

sn12.17:1.8.verse: “It is untimely just now for questions, Kassapa.

sn12.17:2.5.verse: But Kassapa made his request again. And again, and even a third time he received the same reply.

sn12.17:2.7.verse: When the Exalted One had thus spoken, Kassapa the Unclothed said:—

sn12.17:2.8.verse: “It is not many things we want to ask of Master Gotama.”

sn12.17:3.1.verse: “Now then, Master Gotama, is suffering wrought by one's self?”

sn12.17:3.2.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.17:3.3.verse: “What then, Master Gotama, is one's suffering wrought by another?”

sn12.17:3.4.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.17:3.5.verse: “What then, Master Gotama, is suffering wrought both by one's self and by another?'

sn12.17:3.6.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.17:3.7.verse: “What then, Master Gotama, has [the] suffering [which is] wrought neither by myself nor by another, befallen me by chance?”

sn12.17:3.8.verse: “Not so, Kassapa,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.17:3.9.verse: “What then, Master Gotama, is suffering non-existent?”

sn12.17:3.12.verse: “Then Master Gotama neither knows nor sees suffering.”

sn12.17:3.13.verse: “No, Kassapa, I am not one who knows not suffering nor sees it.

sn12.17:3.14.verse: I am one that knows suffering, Kassapa,

sn12.17:3.15.verse: I am one that sees suffering.”

sn12.17:4.1.verse: “How now, Master Gotama? To all my questions you have said 'not so verily.”

sn12.17:4.5.verse: You have both affirmed that suffering is,

sn12.17:4.9.verse: Declare then to me, Master, Exalted One, [the nature of] suffering.

sn12.17:4.10.verse: Teach me, Master, Exalted One, the nature of suffering.”

sn12.17:5.1.verse: “One and the same person both acts and experiences [the results]':—this, Kassapa, which you called at first 'suffering self-wrought,' amounts to the Eternalist theory.

sn12.17:5.2.verse: “One acts, another experiences [the result]':—this, Kassapa, which to one smitten by the feeling occurs as 'suffering caused by another,' amounts to the Annihilationist theory.

sn12.17:5.3.verse: To you, Kassapa, the Tathagata, not approaching either extreme, teaches the Norm by a middle [way]:—

sn12.17:5.4.verse: conditioned by ignorance activities come to pass,

sn12.17:5.6.verse: thus arise name-and-shape, sense, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, decay-and-death, grief, suffering.

sn12.17:5.7.verse: But from the utter fading away and ceasing of ignorance,

sn12.17:5.8.verse: activities and the rest, comes the ceasing of activities, consciousness and the rest.

sn12.17:5.9.verse: Even such is the ceasing of this entire mass of ill.”

sn12.17:6.1.verse: When this had been said Kassapa the Unclothed said to the Exalted One:—

sn12.17:6.3.verse: Just as if a man were to set up that which had been thrown down, or were to reveal that which was hidden away, or were to point out the right road to him who had gone astray, or were to bring a lamp into the darkness, so that those who had eyes could see shapes,—even so, lord, has the lord Gotama shown me his doctrine in various ways.

sn12.17:6.4.verse: I, even I, lord, betake myself to the Exalted One as my refuge, to the Norm and to the Order.

sn12.17:6.5.verse: I would leave the world under the Rule of the Exalted One. I would be ordained.”

sn12.17:7.1.verse: “He, Kassapa, who, being formerly a votary of another doctrine, desires to leave the world to obtain orders in this Doctrine and Rule, remains on probation for four months. At the end of four months spent in seclusion, the brethren, moved in heart and will, receive him from the world and ordain him to be a brother.

sn12.17:7.2.verse: Nevertheless, I acknowledge a difference in persons.”

sn12.17:8.1.verse: “If, lord, he who, formerly a votary of another doctrine, desires to leave the world, to obtain orders in this Doctrine and Rule, goes on probation for four months, and if at the end of four months spent in seclusion, the brethren, moved in heart and willing, receive him from the world and ordain him to be a brother, I will live on probation for four years. At the end of four years so living may the brethren, moved in heart and will, receive me and ordain me as a brother.”

sn12.17:9.1.verse: So Kassapa the Unclothed was received under the Exalted One and obtained ordination.

sn12.17:9.2.verse: And not long after his ordination the venerable Kassapa, remaining alone and separate, earnest, ardent and strenuous, attained ere long to that supreme goal of the divine life, for the sake of which the clansmen rightly go forth from home into the homeless: yea, that supreme goal did he, by himself, even in this present life, come to understand and realize,

sn12.17:9.3.verse: namely, that birth was destroyed, that the divine life was lived, that the task was done, that for life in these conditions there was no hereafter.

sn12.17:9.4.verse: And that venerable Kassapa became one of the Arahants.

sn12.18:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Timbaruka went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn12.18:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

sn12.18:2.1.verse: “Well, worthy Gotama, are pleasure and pain made by oneself?”

sn12.18:2.3.verse: “Then are pleasure and pain made by another?”

sn12.18:2.5.verse: “Well, are pleasure and pain made by both oneself and another?”

sn12.18:2.7.verse: “Then do pleasure and pain arise anomalously, not made by oneself or another?”

sn12.18:2.9.verse: “Well, is there no such thing as pleasure and pain?”

sn12.18:2.10.verse: “It’s not that there’s no such thing as pleasure and pain.

sn12.18:2.12.verse: “Then does the worthy Gotama not know or see suffering?”

sn12.18:2.13.verse: “It’s not that I don’t know or see pleasure and pain.

sn12.18:2.14.verse: I do know pleasure and pain,

sn12.18:2.15.verse: I do see pleasure and pain.”

sn12.18:3.1.verse: “Worthy Gotama, when asked these questions, you say ‘not so’.

sn12.18:3.5.verse: Yet you say that there is such a thing as pleasure and pain.

sn12.18:3.8.verse: And you say that you do know pleasure and pain,

sn12.18:3.9.verse: and you do see pleasure and pain.

sn12.18:3.10.verse: Sir, explain pleasure and pain to me!

sn12.18:3.11.verse: Teach me about pleasure and pain!”

sn12.18:4.1.verse: “Suppose that the feeling and the one who feels it are one and the same. Then for one who has existed since the beginning, pleasure and pain is made by oneself. I don’t say this.

sn12.18:4.2.verse: Suppose that the feeling is one thing and the one who feels it is another. Then for one stricken by feeling, pleasure and pain is made by another. I don’t say this.

sn12.18:4.3.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way:

sn12.18:4.5.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn12.18:4.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn12.18:4.7.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease.

sn12.18:4.9.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’”

sn12.18:5.1.verse: When he said this, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Buddha,

sn12.18:5.3.verse: I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn12.18:5.4.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn12.18:1.2.verse: Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.

sn12.18:1.3.verse: When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to him:

sn12.18:2.1.verse: “How is it, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created by oneself?”

sn12.18:2.2.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.18:2.3.verse: “Then, Master Gotama, are pleasure and pain created by another?”

sn12.18:2.4.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.18:2.5.verse: “How is it then, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created both by oneself and by another?”

sn12.18:2.6.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.18:2.7.verse: “Then, Master Gotama, have pleasure and pain arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another?”

sn12.18:2.8.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.

sn12.18:2.9.verse: “How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no pleasure and pain?”

sn12.18:2.10.verse: “It is not that there is no pleasure and pain, Timbaruka;

sn12.18:2.12.verse: “Then is it that Master Gotama does not know and see pleasure and pain?”

sn12.18:2.13.verse: “It is not that I do not know and see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka.

sn12.18:3.1.verse: “Whether you are asked: ‘How is it, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created by oneself?’

sn12.18:3.2.verse: or ‘Are they created by another? ’ or

sn12.18:3.4.verse: or ‘Are they created by neither?’ in each case you say: ‘Not so, Timbaruka.’

sn12.18:3.5.verse: When you are asked: ‘How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no pleasure and pain?’ you say: ‘It is not that there is no pleasure and pain, Timbaruka;

sn12.18:3.7.verse: ‘It is not that I do not know and see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka.

sn12.18:3.10.verse: Venerable sir, let the Blessed One explain pleasure and pain to me.

sn12.18:3.11.verse: Let the Blessed One teach me about pleasure and pain.”

sn12.18:4.1.verse: “Timbaruka, [if one thinks,] ‘The feeling and the one who feels it are the same,’ [then one asserts] with reference to one existing from the beginning: ‘Pleasure and pain are created by oneself.’ I do not speak thus.

sn12.18:4.2.verse: But, Timbaruka, [if one thinks,] ‘The feeling is one, the one who feels it is another,’ [then one asserts]with reference to one stricken by feeling:‘Pleasure and pain are created by another.’ Neither do I speak thus.

sn12.18:4.3.verse: Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle:

sn12.18:4.4.verse: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be];

sn12.18:4.5.verse: with volitional formations as condition, consciousness….

sn12.18:4.6.verse: Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.

sn12.18:4.7.verse: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations;

sn12.18:4.8.verse: with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness….

sn12.18:4.9.verse: Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

sn12.18:5.1.verse: When this was said, the naked ascetic Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:

sn12.18:5.3.verse: I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

sn12.18:5.4.verse: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn12.18:1.2.verse: Now the wanderer Timbaruka came up to the Exalted One and greeted him;

sn12.18:1.3.verse: and when compliments of friendship and courtesy had been exchanged, he sat down at one side. So seated he spoke thus to the Exalted One:

sn12.18:2.1.verse: “Now then, Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain brought about by one's self?”

sn12.18:2.2.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.18:2.3.verse: “Well then, are they brought about by another?”

sn12.18:2.4.verse: “Not so, Timbaruka,” said the Exalted One.

sn12.18:2.5.verse: “Well then, are they brought about by both one's self and another?”

sn12.18:2.7.verse: “But then, are they brought about neither by one's self nor by another, but by chance?”

sn12.18:2.9.verse: “How then, Master Gotama, is there no such thing as pleasure or pain?”

sn12.18:2.10.verse: “No, Timbaruka, there is pleasure and pain.”

sn12.18:2.12.verse: “Is it then that Master Gotama neither knows nor sees pleasure and pain?”

sn12.18:2.13.verse: “No, Timbaruka, I am not one who knows not pleasure and pain, nor sees them.

sn12.18:3.1.verse: “How now, Master Gotama: to all my questions you have said, 'not so, Timbaruka.'

sn12.18:3.5.verse: And, being asked as to the existence of pleasure and pain, you affirm they are, and are known and seen by you.

sn12.18:3.10.verse: Declare to me then, Master Gotama, the truth about pleasure and pain.

sn12.18:3.11.verse: Teach me, Master Gotama, the truth about pleasure and pain.”

sn12.18:4.1.verse: “The experience and he who experiences hereafter are one and the same: this, Timbaruka, which you at first called 'pleasure and pain brought about by one's self' — I declare this is not so.

sn12.18:4.2.verse: The experience and he who experiences hereafter are different one from the other: this, Timbaruka, which by one smitten by the after-experience is called 'pleasure and pain brought about by another' — I declare this is not so.

sn12.18:4.3.verse: To you, Timbaruka, the Tathagata, not approaching either extreme, teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:

sn12.18:4.4.verse: ‘Conditioned by ignorance activities come to pass,

sn12.18:4.5.verse: by activities consciousness, and so on.

sn12.18:4.6.verse: Such is the arising of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.18:4.7.verse: But through the utter fading away and ceasing of ignorance comes ceasing of activities,

sn12.18:4.8.verse: through ceasing of activities ceasing of consciousness, and so on.

sn12.18:4.9.verse: Such is the ceasing of this entire mass of ill.’”

sn12.18:5.1.verse: When this had been said, Timbaruka, the Wanderer, spoke thus to the Exalted One:

sn12.18:5.3.verse: I, even I, lord, take myself to the Exalted One as my refuge, to the Norm and to the Order.

sn12.18:5.4.verse: May Master Gotama accept me as a follower, as one who from this day forth, as long as life lasts, has taken his refuge therein!”

sn12.19:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, for a fool shrouded by ignorance and coupled to craving, this body has been produced.

sn12.19:1.3.verse: So there is this duality: this body and external name and form. Contact depends on this duality. When contacted through one or other of the six sense fields, the fool experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:2.1.verse: For an astute person shrouded by ignorance and coupled to craving, this body has been produced.

sn12.19:2.2.verse: So there is this duality: this body and external name and form. Contact depends on this duality. When contacted through one or other of the six sense fields, the astute person experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:3.1.verse: What, then, is the difference between the foolish and the astute?”

sn12.19:3.2.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

sn12.19:4.1.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn12.19:5.1.verse: “For a fool shrouded by ignorance and coupled to craving, this body has been produced. But the fool has not given up that ignorance or finished that craving.

sn12.19:5.3.verse: The fool has not completed the spiritual journey for the complete ending of suffering.

sn12.19:5.4.verse: Therefore, when their body breaks up, the fool passes on to another body.

sn12.19:5.5.verse: When they have passed on to another body, they’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn12.19:5.6.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

sn12.19:6.1.verse: For an astute person shrouded by ignorance and coupled to craving, this body has been produced. But the astute person has given up that ignorance and finished that craving.

sn12.19:6.3.verse: The astute person has completed the spiritual journey for the complete ending of suffering.

sn12.19:6.4.verse: Therefore, when their body breaks up, the astute person does not pass on to another body.

sn12.19:6.5.verse: Not passing on to another body, they’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn12.19:6.6.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.

sn12.19:6.7.verse: This is the difference here between the foolish and the astute, that is, leading the spiritual life.”

sn12.19:0.3.verse: The Wise Man and the Fool

sn12.19:1.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, for the fool, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thereby originated.

sn12.19:1.3.verse: So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact. There are just six sense bases, contacted through which—or through a certain one among them—the fool experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:2.1.verse: Bhikkhus, for the wise man, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thereby originated.

sn12.19:2.2.verse: So there is this body and external name-and-form: thus this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact. There are just six sense bases, contacted through which—or through a certain one among them—the wise man experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:3.1.verse: What, bhikkhus, is the distinction here, what is the disparity, what is the difference between the wise man and the fool?”

sn12.19:3.2.verse: “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would clear up the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

sn12.19:4.1.verse: “Then listen and attend closely, bhikkhus, I will speak.”

sn12.19:5.1.verse: “Bhikkhus, for the fool, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has originated. For the fool that ignorance has not been abandoned and that craving has not been utterly destroyed.

sn12.19:5.3.verse: Because the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering.

sn12.19:5.4.verse: Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool fares on to [another] body.

sn12.19:5.5.verse: Faring on to [another] body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair;

sn12.19:5.6.verse: not freed from suffering, I say.

sn12.19:6.1.verse: Bhikkhus, for the wise man, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has originated. For the wise man that ignorance has been abandoned and that craving has been utterly destroyed.

sn12.19:6.3.verse: Because the wise man has lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering.

sn12.19:6.4.verse: Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the wise man does not fare on to [another] body.

sn12.19:6.5.verse: Not faring on to [another] body, he is freed from birth, aging, and death; freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair;

sn12.19:6.7.verse: This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, the disparity, the difference between the wise man and the fool, that is, the living of the holy life.”

sn12.19:0.3.verse: The wise man [compared] with the fool.

sn12.19:1.1.verse: Near Sāvatthī the Exalted One said:—

sn12.19:1.2.verse: “For the fool, Monks, cloaked by ignorance and tied to craving, this body is formed in this way:

sn12.19:1.3.verse: There is just this body and names-and-shapes without:— thus this pair. Because of the pair [there is] contact, just six spheres of sense. Touched by these, or by one of them, the fool experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:2.1.verse: For the wise man, Monks, cloaked by ignorance and tied to craving this body is formed in this way:

sn12.19:2.2.verse: there is just this body and names-and-shapes without:— thus this pair. Because of the pair [there is] contact, just six spheres of sense. Touched by these, or by one of them, the wise man experiences pleasure and pain.

sn12.19:3.1.verse: What, Monks, is there here that is different, distinctive, diverse between the wise man and the fool?”

sn12.19:3.2.verse: “For us, lord, things have the Exalted One as their root, their guide, their resort. Well indeed were it if the meaning of this that he has spoken were to manifest itself in the Exalted One. Hearing it from him the Monks will remember it.”

sn12.19:4.1.verse: “Well then, Monks, listen, give your mind thoroughly and I will speak.”

sn12.19:5.1.verse: “The ignorance, Monks, wherewith the fool, whose body is so wrought, is cloaked, the craving whereto he is tied, that ignorance the fool has not thrown off, that craving is not withered away.

sn12.19:5.3.verse: The fool has not lived the divine life for the right withering away of ill,

sn12.19:5.4.verse: therefore the fool at the breaking up of the body is on his way to [another] body.

sn12.19:5.5.verse: He being on his way thither is not set free from birth, nor from old age and death, nor from grievings, from lamentings, from ills, from sorrows, from despairs—

sn12.19:5.6.verse: I say, he is not set free from Ill.

sn12.19:6.1.verse: The ignorance, Monks, wherewith the wise man, whose body is so wrought, is cloaked, the craving whereto he is tied, that ignorance the wise man has thrown off, and that craving is withered away.

sn12.19:6.3.verse: The wise man has lived the divine life for the right withering away of ill,

sn12.19:6.4.verse: therefore the wise man at the breaking up of the body is not on his way to [another sense-] body.

sn12.19:6.5.verse: He not being on his way thither is set free from rebirth, from old age and death, from grievings, from lamentings, from ills, from sorrows, from despairs—

sn12.19:6.6.verse: I say, he is set free from Ill.

sn12.19:6.7.verse: This, Monks, is how the wise man is different, distinctive, diverse from the fool, namely in that he lives the divine life.”

sn12.20:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena.

sn12.20:1.3.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn12.20:2.2.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death.

sn12.20:2.3.verse: Whether Realized Ones arise or not, this law of nature persists, this regularity of natural principles, this surety of natural principles, specific conditionality.

sn12.20:2.4.verse: A Realized One awakens to this and comprehends it,

sn12.20:2.5.verse: then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

sn12.20:2.7.verse: ‘Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death.’

sn12.20:3.1.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth …

sn12.20:3.2.verse: Grasping is a requirement for continued existence …

sn12.20:3.3.verse: Craving is a requirement for grasping …

sn12.20:3.4.verse: Feeling is a requirement for craving …

sn12.20:3.5.verse: Contact is a requirement for feeling …

sn12.20:3.6.verse: The six sense fields are requirements for contact …

sn12.20:3.7.verse: Name and form are requirements for the six sense fields …

sn12.20:3.8.verse: Consciousness is a requirement for name and form …

sn12.20:3.9.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness …

sn12.20:3.10.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

sn12.20:3.11.verse: Whether Realized Ones arise or not, this law of nature persists, this regularity of natural principles, this surety of natural principles, specific conditionality.

sn12.20:3.12.verse: A Realized One awakens to this and comprehends it,

sn12.20:3.13.verse: then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

sn12.20:3.16.verse: So the fact that this is real, not unreal, not otherwise; the specific conditionality of it:

sn12.20:4.1.verse: And what are the dependently originated phenomena?

sn12.20:4.2.verse: Old age and death are impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

sn12.20:4.13.verse: Ignorance is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

sn12.20:4.14.verse: These are called the dependently originated phenomena.

sn12.20:5.1.verse: When a noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom this dependent origination and these dependently originated phenomena as they are, it will be quite impossible for them to turn back to the first beginning, thinking:

sn12.20:5.2.verse: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? After being what, what did I become in the past?’

sn12.20:5.3.verse: Or to turn forward to the final end, thinking:

sn12.20:5.4.verse: ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? After being what, what will I become in the future?’

sn12.20:5.5.verse: Or to be undecided about the present, thinking:

sn12.20:5.6.verse: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This sentient being—where did it come from? And where will it go?’

sn12.20:5.9.verse: Because that noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom this dependent origination and these dependently originated phenomena as they are.”

sn12.20:1.2.verse: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena.

sn12.20:1.3.verse: Listen and attend closely, I will speak.”

sn12.20:2.2.verse: ‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death [comes to be]’:

sn12.20:2.3.verse: whether there is an arising of Tathāgatas or no arising of Tathāgatas, that element still persists, the stableness of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma, specific conditionality.

sn12.20:2.5.verse: Having done so, he explains it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyses it, elucidates it.

sn12.20:2.7.verse: With birth as condition, bhikkhus, aging-and-death.’

sn12.20:3.6.verse: ‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact’…

sn12.20:3.7.verse: ‘With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases’…

sn12.20:3.11.verse: whether there is an arising of Tathāgatas or no arising of Tathāgatas, that element still persists, the stableness of the Dhamma, the fixed course of the Dhamma, specific conditionality.

sn12.20:3.12.verse: A Tathāgata awakens to this and breaks through to it.

sn12.20:3.13.verse: Having done so, he explains it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyses it, elucidates it.

sn12.20:3.15.verse: With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations.’

sn12.20:3.16.verse: Thus, bhikkhus, the actuality in this, the inerrancy, the nototherwiseness, specific conditionality:

sn12.20:4.1.verse: And what, bhikkhus, are the dependently arisen phenomena?

sn12.20:4.2.verse: Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, vanishing, fading away, and cessation.

sn12.20:4.9.verse: The six sense bases are impermanent …

sn12.20:4.13.verse: Ignorance is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, vanishing, fading away, and cessation.

sn12.20:4.14.verse: These, bhikkhus, are called the dependently arisen phenomena.

sn12.20:5.1.verse: When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has clearly seen with correct wisdom as it really is this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena, it is impossible that he will run back into the past, thinking:

sn12.20:5.2.verse: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?’

sn12.20:5.3.verse: Or that he will run forward into the future, thinking:

sn12.20:5.4.verse: ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?’

sn12.20:5.5.verse: Or that he will now be inwardly confused about the present thus:

sn12.20:5.6.verse: ‘Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? This being—where has it come from, and where will it go?’

sn12.20:5.9.verse: Because, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has clearly seen with correct wisdom as it really is this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena.”

sn12.20:1.2.verse: The Exalted One said:—“I will teach you, Monks, both causal happening and things as having causally happened.

sn12.20:1.3.verse: Hear this, give your mind thoroughly, I will speak.”

sn12.20:1.4.verse: “Even so, lord,” those Monks made response to the Exalted One.

sn12.20:2.2.verse: Conditioned by rebirth is decay and death.

sn12.20:2.3.verse: Whether, Monks, there be an arising of Tathagatas, or whether there be no such arising, this nature of things just stands, this causal status, this causal orderliness, the relatedness of this to that.

sn12.20:2.4.verse: Concerning that the Tathagata is fully enlightened, that he fully understands.

sn12.20:2.5.verse: Fully enlightened, fully understanding, he declares it, teaches it, reveals it, sets it forth, manifests, explains, makes it plain,

sn12.20:2.7.verse: Conditioned by rebirth is decay and death.’

sn12.20:3.7.verse: conditioned by name and shape is sense …

sn12.20:3.8.verse: conditioned by consciousness is name and shape …

sn12.20:3.11.verse: Whether, Monks, there be an arising of Tathagatas, or whether there be no such arising, in each this nature of things just stands, this causal status, this causal orderliness, the relatedness of this to that.

sn12.20:3.12.verse: Concerning that the Tathagata is fully enlightened, that he fully understands.

sn12.20:3.13.verse: Fully enlightened, fully understanding, he declares it, teaches it, reveals it, sets it forth, manifests, explains, makes it plain,

sn12.20:3.15.verse: Conditioned by this, that comes to be.’

sn12.20:3.16.verse: Thus, Monks, that which here is such, not else, not otherwise, the relatedness of this to that:—

sn12.20:3.17.verse: this, Monks, is called causal happening.

sn12.20:4.1.verse: And what, Monks, are things as having causally happened?

sn12.20:4.2.verse: Decay-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, arisen causally, is by nature withering away, passing away, fading away, coming to an end.

sn12.20:4.13.verse: ignorance. These also are impermanent, conditioned, arisen causally, are by nature withering away, passing away, fading away, coming to an end.

sn12.20:4.14.verse: These, Monks, are called things as having causally happened.

sn12.20:5.1.verse: Now inasmuch, Monks, as the Ariyan disciple has by right insight well seen even as they really are both this causal happening and things as having causally happened, never doth it arise, that such as he will run back to the past, thinking:

sn12.20:5.2.verse: ‘Did I live in times gone by? Or did I not? What was I in times gone by? How was I then? Or from being what did I become what?’

sn12.20:5.3.verse: Or that he will run towards the times to come, thinking:

sn12.20:5.4.verse: ‘Shall I be reborn in a future time, or shall I not? What shall I become in the future? How shall I become in the future? Or, being what, shall I in the future become what?’

sn12.20:5.5.verse: Or that he will now become perplexed within himself as to the present day, thinking:

sn12.20:5.6.verse: ‘Am I indeed? Or am I not indeed? What indeed am I? How indeed am I? This person that is I, whence came he, whither will he go?’

sn12.20:5.9.verse: In that the Ariyan disciple, Monks, has by right insight well seen even as they really are both this causal happening and things as having causally happened.”

sn12.21:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, a Realized One has ten powers and four kinds of self-assurance. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

sn12.21:1.3.verse: Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn12.21:1.4.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

sn12.21:1.5.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

sn12.21:1.6.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

sn12.21:1.7.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.

sn12.21:1.8.verse: So, when this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

sn12.21:1.9.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

sn12.21:1.10.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

sn12.21:1.11.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn12.21:1.12.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn12.21:1.13.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease.

sn12.21:1.15.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”

sn12.21:1.2.verse: “The Tathāgata, monks, endowed with the ten powers and the four confidences, claims the Place of the Bull; he roars the Lion's Roar amid the congregations; he turns the Divine Wheel, saying:

sn12.21:1.3.verse: Such is material shape, such is its arising, such is its passing away.

sn12.21:1.4.verse: Such is feeling, such is its arising, such is its passing away.

sn12.21:1.7.verse: Such is consciousness, such is its arising, such is its passing away.

sn12.21:1.8.verse: Thus: 'this' being, 'that' becomes; from the arising of this, that arises.

sn12.21:1.9.verse: This not being, that becomes not; from the ceasing of this, that ceases. That is to say:

sn12.21:1.11.verse: Conditioned by activities, consciousness comes to pass, and so on:

sn12.21:1.12.verse: Such is the uprising of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.21:1.13.verse: But from the utter fading out and cessation of ignorance, activities cease.

sn12.21:1.14.verse: From the ceasing of activities, consciousness ceases, and so on:

sn12.21:1.15.verse: Such is the ceasing of this entire mass of ill.”

sn12.22:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, a Realized One has ten powers and four kinds of self-assurance. With these he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and turns the divine wheel.

sn12.22:1.3.verse: Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn12.22:1.4.verse: Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the disappearance of feeling.

sn12.22:1.5.verse: Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the disappearance of perception.

sn12.22:1.6.verse: Such are choices, such is the origin of choices, such is the disappearance of choices.

sn12.22:1.7.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.

sn12.22:1.8.verse: So, when this exists, this comes to be; due to the arising of this, this arises.

sn12.22:1.9.verse: When this doesn’t exist, this doesn’t come to be; due to the cessation of this, this ceases. That is:

sn12.22:1.10.verse: Ignorance is a requirement for choices.

sn12.22:1.11.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn12.22:1.12.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn12.22:1.13.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease.

sn12.22:1.15.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

sn12.22:2.1.verse: The teaching well-explained thus by me is clarified, revealed, illuminated, and stripped of patchwork.

sn12.22:2.2.verse: In this teaching thus well-explained, it is quite enough for a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith to rouse up energy.

sn12.22:2.3.verse: ‘Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and tendons remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.’

sn12.22:3.1.verse: A lazy person lives in suffering, mixed up with bad, unskillful qualities, neglecting their heart’s great goal.

sn12.22:3.2.verse: But an energetic person lives happily, secluded from bad, unskillful qualities, fulfilling their heart’s great goal.

sn12.22:3.3.verse: The best isn’t reached by the worst.

sn12.22:3.4.verse: The best is reached by the best.

sn12.22:3.5.verse: This spiritual life is the cream, mendicants, and the Teacher is before you.

sn12.22:3.6.verse: So you should rouse up energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized, thinking:

sn12.22:3.7.verse: ‘In this way our going forth will not be barren, but will be fruitful and fertile.

sn12.22:3.8.verse: And the services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick we enjoy shall be very fruitful and beneficial for them.’

sn12.22:3.10.verse: Considering what is good for yourself, mendicants, is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.

sn12.22:3.11.verse: Considering what is good for others is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.

sn12.22:3.12.verse: Considering what is good for both is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.”

sn12.22:1.1.verse: Near Sāvatthī … the Exalted One said:

sn12.22:1.2.verse: “Monks, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers and the four confidences … turns the Divine Wheel:

sn12.22:1.3.verse: Such is material shape: and so on.

sn12.22:1.8.verse: So 'this' being, 'that' becomes; from the arising of this, that arises;

sn12.22:1.9.verse: 'this' not being, that becomes not; from the ceasing of this, that ceases. That is to say:

sn12.22:1.11.verse: Conditioned by activities, consciousness … name-and-shape, sense, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, old age-and-death, and grief, lamenting, suffering, sorrow, despair come to pass.

sn12.22:1.12.verse: Such is the uprising of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.22:1.13.verse: But from the utter fading away and ceasing of ignorance, activities cease,

sn12.22:1.14.verse: and thus ceases each of the rest. …

sn12.22:1.15.verse: Such is the ceasing of this entire mass of ill.

sn12.22:2.1.verse: Thus, Monks, the Dhamma being well declared by me, made manifest, disclosed, brought to light, stripped of its swathing,

sn12.22:2.2.verse: it is enough for the clansman who has left the world through faith to stir up energy and vow:

sn12.22:2.3.verse: 'Let skin and sinews and bones wilt in my body, let flesh and blood dry up, yet shall there be upkeep of energy till I have won that which by man's strength, by man's energy, by man's progress may be won!'

sn12.22:3.1.verse: Sadly, Monks, lives the man of sloth, involved in bad, wicked things. Great is the salvation which he fails to win.

sn12.22:3.2.verse: But he of stirred up energy lives happily, aloof from bad, wicked things. Great is the salvation that he makes perfect.

sn12.22:3.3.verse: Not by that which is low, Monks, may the highest be won;

sn12.22:3.4.verse: by that which is highest may the highest be won.

sn12.22:3.5.verse: Worthy of praise, Monks, is this divine life. The Teacher has come to you face to face.

sn12.22:3.6.verse: Wherefore stir up energy that you may win what is not won, that you may attain what is not attained, that you may realize what is unrealized, thinking:

sn12.22:3.7.verse: 'Thus will this our leaving the world not be barren, but a fruitful and a growing thing.

sn12.22:3.8.verse: The necessaries that we enjoy: the equipment of robes, alms, lodging and medicine, though they be humble, shall be to us of great profit and advantage.'

sn12.22:3.9.verse: For thus, Monks, must you train yourselves:

sn12.22:3.10.verse: If a man discerns his own good, this is enough to call up earnestness;

sn12.22:3.11.verse: if he discerns another's good, this is enough to call up earnestness;

sn12.22:3.12.verse: if he discerns both his own and another's good, this is enough to call up earnestness.

sn12.23:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see.

sn12.23:1.3.verse: For one who knows and sees what?

sn12.23:1.4.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn12.23:1.8.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn12.23:1.9.verse: The ending of the defilements is for one who knows and sees this.

sn12.23:2.1.verse: I say that this knowledge of ending has a vital condition, it doesn’t lack a vital condition.

sn12.23:2.4.verse: I say that freedom has a vital condition, it doesn’t lack a vital condition.

sn12.23:2.7.verse: I say that dispassion has a vital condition.

sn12.23:2.10.verse: I say that disillusionment has a vital condition.

sn12.23:2.12.verse: You should say: ‘Truly knowing and seeing.’

sn12.23:2.13.verse: I say that truly knowing and seeing has a vital condition.

sn12.23:2.16.verse: I say that immersion has a vital condition.

sn12.23:3.3.verse: I say that bliss has a vital condition.

sn12.23:3.6.verse: I say that tranquility has a vital condition.

sn12.23:3.9.verse: I say that rapture has a vital condition.

sn12.23:3.12.verse: I say that joy has a vital condition.

sn12.23:3.15.verse: I say that faith has a vital condition.

sn12.23:4.3.verse: I say that suffering has a vital condition.

sn12.23:4.6.verse: I say that rebirth has a vital condition.

sn12.23:4.9.verse: I say that continued existence has a vital condition.

sn12.23:4.12.verse: I say that grasping has a vital condition.

sn12.23:4.15.verse: I say that craving has a vital condition.

sn12.23:5.4.verse: You should say: ‘The six sense fields.’ …

sn12.23:5.8.verse: I say that choices have a vital condition, they don’t lack a vital condition.

sn12.23:5.9.verse: And what is the vital condition for choices?

sn12.23:6.1.verse: So, mendicants: ignorance is the vital condition for choices.

sn12.23:6.2.verse: Choices are the vital condition for consciousness.

sn12.23:6.3.verse: Consciousness is the vital condition for name and form.

sn12.23:6.4.verse: Name and form are the vital conditions for the six sense fields.

sn12.23:6.5.verse: The six sense fields are the vital conditions for contact.

sn12.23:6.6.verse: Contact is the vital condition for feeling.

sn12.23:6.7.verse: Feeling is the vital condition for craving.

sn12.23:6.8.verse: Craving is the vital condition for grasping.

sn12.23:6.9.verse: Grasping is the vital condition for continued existence.

sn12.23:6.10.verse: Continued existence is the vital condition for rebirth.

sn12.23:6.11.verse: Rebirth is the vital condition for suffering.

sn12.23:6.12.verse: Suffering is the vital condition for faith.

sn12.23:6.13.verse: Faith is the vital condition for joy.

sn12.23:6.14.verse: Joy is the vital condition for rapture.

sn12.23:6.15.verse: Rapture is the vital condition for tranquility.

sn12.23:6.16.verse: Tranquility is the vital condition for bliss.

sn12.23:6.17.verse: Bliss is the vital condition for immersion.

sn12.23:6.18.verse: Immersion is the vital condition for truly knowing and seeing.

sn12.23:6.19.verse: Truly knowing and seeing is the vital condition for disillusionment.

sn12.23:6.20.verse: Disillusionment is the vital condition for dispassion.

sn12.23:6.21.verse: Dispassion is the vital condition for freedom.

sn12.23:6.22.verse: Freedom is the vital condition for the knowledge of ending.

sn12.23:7.1.verse: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily on a mountain top, and the water flows downhill to fill the hollows, crevices, and creeks. As they become full, they fill up the pools. The pools fill up the lakes, the lakes fill up the streams, and the streams fill up the rivers. And as the rivers become full, they fill up the ocean.

sn12.23:8.1.verse: In the same way, ignorance is the vital condition for choices. … Freedom is the vital condition for the knowledge of ending.”

sn12.23:1.1.verse: Near Sāvatthī … the Exalted One said:

sn12.23:1.2.verse: “In him who knows, Monks, who sees do I say that the intoxicants are extinct, not in him who knows not, neither sees.

sn12.23:1.3.verse: And in what, Monks, in him who knows, in him who sees are the intoxicants extinct?

sn12.23:1.4.verse: Thus is material shape, thus is its uprising, thus its passing away.

sn12.23:1.8.verse: thus is consciousness, thus is their uprising, thus their passing away.

sn12.23:1.9.verse: Now in extinction, the knowledge about extinction:

sn12.23:2.1.verse: that I say is causally associated, not the opposite.

sn12.23:2.2.verse: And what is that which is the cause of knowledge about extinction?

sn12.23:2.4.verse: I say that liberation is causally associated, not uncausally associated.

sn12.23:2.5.verse: And what is that which is the cause of liberation?

sn12.23:2.7.verse: I say that passionlessness is causally associated with liberation.

sn12.23:2.8.verse: And what is that which is the cause of passionlessness?

sn12.23:2.10.verse: I say that repulsion is causally associated with passionlessness.

sn12.23:2.11.verse: And what is that which is the cause of repulsion?

sn12.23:2.12.verse: The knowledge and the vision of things as they really are is the answer.

sn12.23:2.13.verse: I say that the knowledge-and-vision of things as they really are is causally associated with repulsion.

sn12.23:2.14.verse: And what is that which is the cause of the knowledge and insight of things as they really are?

sn12.23:2.16.verse: I say that concentration is causally associated with the knowledge and vision of things as they really are.

sn12.23:3.1.verse: And what is that which is the cause of concentration?

sn12.23:3.3.verse: I say that happiness is causally associated with concentration.

sn12.23:3.4.verse: And what is that which is the cause of happiness?

sn12.23:3.6.verse: I say that serenity is causally associated with happiness.

sn12.23:3.7.verse: And what is the cause of serenity?

sn12.23:3.9.verse: I say that rapture is causally associated with serenity.

sn12.23:3.10.verse: And what is the cause of rapture?

sn12.23:3.12.verse: I say that joy is causally associated with rapture.

sn12.23:3.13.verse: And what is the cause of joy?

sn12.23:3.15.verse: I say that faith is causally associated with joy.

sn12.23:4.1.verse: And what is the cause of faith?

sn12.23:4.3.verse: I say that suffering is causally associated with faith.

sn12.23:4.4.verse: And what is the cause of suffering?

sn12.23:4.6.verse: I say that birth is causally associated with suffering.

sn12.23:4.8.verse: so also is becoming with birth.

sn12.23:6.1.verse: Now therefore, Monks, activities are in causal association with ignorance,

sn12.23:6.2.verse: consciousness is in causal association with activities,

sn12.23:6.18.verse: the knowledge and vision into things as they really are with concentration,

sn12.23:6.19.verse: repulsion with the knowledge and vision into things as they really are,

sn12.23:6.22.verse: knowledge about extinction [of intoxicants] with liberation.

sn12.23:7.1.verse: Just as when, Monks, on some hilltop when rain is falling in thick drops, that water, coursing, according to the slope, fills the hillside clefts and chasms and gullies, these being filled up fill the tarns, these being filled up fill the lakes, these being filled up fill the little rivers, these being filled up fill the great rivers, and the great rivers being filled up fill the sea, the ocean—

sn12.23:8.1.verse: even so, Monks, there is causal association of activities with ignorance, of consciousness with activities, of name-and-shape with consciousness, of the sixfold sense-sphere with name-and-shape, of contact with the sixfold sense-sphere, of feeling with contact, of craving with feeling, of grasping with craving, of [renewed] becoming with grasping, of birth with [renewed] becoming, of sorrow with birth, of faith with sorrow, of joy with faith, of rapture with joy, of serenity with rapture, of happiness with serenity, of concentration with happiness, of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are with concentration, of repulsion with the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, of passionlessness with repulsion, of liberation with passionlessness, of knowledge about extinction [of intoxicants] with liberation.”

sn12.24:1.1.verse: Near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove.

sn12.24:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Sāriputta robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

sn12.24:1.4.verse: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

sn12.24:1.5.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?”

sn12.24:2.1.verse: Then he went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

sn12.24:2.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The wanderers said to him:

sn12.24:3.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, there are ascetics and brahmins who teach the efficacy of deeds. Some of them assert that suffering is made by oneself.

sn12.24:3.2.verse: Some of them assert that suffering is made by another.

sn12.24:3.3.verse: Some of them assert that suffering is made by both oneself and another.

sn12.24:3.4.verse: Some of them assert that suffering arises anomalously, not made by oneself or another.

sn12.24:3.5.verse: What does the ascetic Gotama say about this? How does he explain it?

sn12.24:3.6.verse: How should we answer so as to repeat what the ascetic Gotama has said, and not misrepresent him with an untruth? How should we explain in line with his teaching, with no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

sn12.24:4.1.verse: “Reverends, the Buddha has said that suffering is dependently originated.

sn12.24:4.4.verse: In speaking like this, you would repeat what the Buddha has said, and not misrepresent him with an untruth. You would explain in line with his teaching, and there would be no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism.

sn12.24:5.1.verse: Consider the ascetics and brahmins who teach the efficacy of deeds. In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself, that’s dependent on contact.

sn12.24:5.2.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by another, that’s also dependent on contact.

sn12.24:5.3.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself and another, that’s also dependent on contact.

sn12.24:5.4.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering arises anomalously, not made by oneself or another, that’s also dependent on contact.

sn12.24:6.1.verse: Consider the ascetics and brahmins who teach the efficacy of deeds. In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact.

sn12.24:6.2.verse: In the case of those who declare that suffering is made by another, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact.

sn12.24:6.3.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself and another, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact.

sn12.24:6.4.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering arises anomalously, not made by oneself or another, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact.”

sn12.24:7.1.verse: Venerable Ānanda heard this discussion between Venerable Sāriputta and those wanderers of other religions.

sn12.24:7.2.verse: Then Ānanda wandered for alms in Rājagaha. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

sn12.24:7.3.verse: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

sn12.24:8.1.verse: “Good, good, Ānanda! It’s just as Sāriputta has so rightly explained.

sn12.24:8.2.verse: I have said that suffering is dependently originated.

sn12.24:8.5.verse: Saying this you would repeat what I have said, and not misrepresent me with an untruth. You would explain in line with my teaching, and there would be no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism.

sn12.24:9.1.verse: Consider the ascetics and brahmins who teach the efficacy of deeds. In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself, that’s dependent on contact. …

sn12.24:9.4.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering arises anomalously, not made by oneself or another, that’s also dependent on contact.

sn12.24:10.1.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering is made by oneself, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact. …

sn12.24:10.4.verse: In the case of those who assert that suffering arises anomalously, not made by oneself or another, it’s impossible that they will experience that without contact.

sn12.24:11.1.verse: Ānanda, this one time I was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn12.24:11.2.verse: Then I robed up in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.

sn12.24:11.4.verse: ‘It’s too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.

sn12.24:11.5.verse: Why don’t I visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?’

sn12.24:12.1.verse: Then I went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.

sn12.24:12.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, I sat down to one side. …”

sn12.24:13.1.verse: (The wanderers asked the Buddha the very same questions, and he gave the same answers.)

sn12.24:17.2.verse: how the whole matter is stated with one phrase.

sn12.24:17.3.verse: Could there be a detailed explanation of this matter that is both deep and appears deep?”

sn12.24:18.1.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, clarify this matter yourself.”

sn12.24:18.2.verse: “Sir, suppose they were to ask me:

sn12.24:18.3.verse: ‘Reverend Ānanda, what is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of old age and death?’

sn12.24:18.5.verse: ‘Reverends, rebirth is the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of old age and death.’

sn12.24:18.6.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.

sn12.24:19.1.verse: Suppose they were to ask me:

sn12.24:19.4.verse: ‘Continued existence is the source of rebirth.’

sn12.24:19.5.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.

sn12.24:20.1.verse: Suppose they were to ask me:

sn12.24:20.2.verse: ‘What is the source of continued existence?’

sn12.24:20.4.verse: ‘Grasping is the source of continued existence.’

sn12.24:20.5.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.

sn12.24:21.1.verse: Suppose they were to ask me:

sn12.24:21.5.verse: Suppose they were to ask me:

sn12.24:21.8.verse: ‘The six sense fields are the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of contact.’

sn12.24:21.9.verse: ‘When the six fields of contact fade away and cease with no residue left behind, contact ceases.

sn12.24:21.13.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases.

sn12.24:21.14.verse: When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases.

sn12.24:21.15.verse: When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.

sn12.24:21.16.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.’

sn12.24:21.17.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.”

sn12.24:1.1.verse: [The Exalted One was once] staying near Rājagaha at the Bamboo Grove.

sn12.24:1.2.verse: Now the venerable Sariputta clothed himself one morning, and taking his bowl and cloak entered Rājagaha on his alms round.

sn12.24:1.4.verse: “It is too early as yet to go about Rājagaha for alms:

sn12.24:1.5.verse: I might go to the gardens of the heretical Wanderers.”
