sn16.8:3.2.verse: ‘Welcome, mendicant! What is this mendicant’s name? This mendicant is good-natured; he really wants to train. Please, mendicant, here, take a seat.’

sn16.8:4.2.verse: ‘It seems that when a mendicant lives in the wilderness … and is energetic, and praises these things, senior mendicants invite them to a seat …’

sn16.8:4.5.verse: That is for their lasting welfare and happiness.

sn16.8:5.1.verse: But these days, Kassapa, the senior mendicants don’t live in the wilderness … and aren’t energetic; and they don’t praise these things.

sn16.8:6.1.verse: When a mendicant is well-known and famous, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, senior mendicants invite them to a seat:

sn16.8:6.2.verse: ‘Welcome, mendicant! What is this mendicant’s name? This mendicant is good-natured; he’s fond of his fellow monks. Please, mendicant, here, take a seat.’

sn16.8:7.2.verse: ‘It seems that when a mendicant is well-known and famous, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, senior mendicants invite them to a seat …’

sn16.8:7.5.verse: That is for their lasting harm and suffering.

sn16.8:7.6.verse: And if it could ever be rightly said that

sn16.8:7.7.verse: spiritual practitioners have been imperiled by the peril of a spiritual practitioner, and vanquished by the vanquishing of a spiritual practitioner, it is these days that this could be rightly said.”

sn16.9:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn16.9:2.1.verse: Whenever I want, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, I enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn16.9:3.1.verse: Whenever I want, with the fading away of rapture, I enter and remain in the third absorption, where I meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

sn16.9:4.1.verse: Whenever I want, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

sn16.9:5.1.verse: Whenever I want, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, I enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.

sn16.9:6.1.verse: Whenever I want, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, I enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

sn16.9:7.1.verse: Whenever I want, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, I enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.

sn16.9:8.1.verse: Whenever I want, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, I enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

sn16.9:9.1.verse: Whenever I want, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, I enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling.

sn16.9:10.1.verse: Whenever I want, I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. I control the body as far as the realm of divinity.

sn16.9:11.1.verse: Whenever I want, with clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, I hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.

sn16.9:12.1.verse: Whenever I want, I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my mind.

sn16.9:12.2.verse: I understand mind with greed as ‘mind with greed’,

sn16.9:12.3.verse: and mind without greed as ‘mind without greed’;

sn16.9:13.1.verse: Whenever I want, I recollect my many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. I remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so I recollect my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

sn16.9:14.1.verse: Whenever I want, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. I understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

sn16.9:15.1.verse: I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

sn16.10:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn16.10:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Mahākassapa and said,

sn16.10:1.4.verse: “Come, Honorable Kassapa. Let’s go to one of the nuns’ quarters.”

sn16.10:1.5.verse: “You go, Reverend Ānanda. You’re the one with many duties and responsibilities.”

sn16.10:1.9.verse: And a third time, Ānanda said,

sn16.10:1.10.verse: “Come, Honorable Kassapa. Let’s go to one of the nuns’ quarters.”

sn16.10:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahākassapa robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went with Venerable Ānanda as his second monk to one of the nuns’ quarters, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

sn16.10:2.2.verse: And then several nuns went up to Mahākassapa, bowed, and sat down to one side.

sn16.10:2.3.verse: Mahākassapa educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired those nuns with a Dhamma talk,

sn16.10:2.4.verse: after which he rose from his seat and left.

sn16.10:3.1.verse: But the nun Thullatissā was upset and blurted out,

sn16.10:3.2.verse: “What is the venerable Mahākassapa thinking, that he’d teach Dhamma in front of the venerable Ānanda, the Videhan sage?

sn16.10:3.3.verse: He’s like a needle peddler who thinks they can sell a needle to a needle maker!”

sn16.10:4.1.verse: Mahākassapa heard Thullatissā say these words,

sn16.10:4.3.verse: “Is that right, Reverend Ānanda? Am I the needle peddler and you the needle maker?

sn16.10:4.4.verse: Or am I the needle maker and you the needle peddler?”

sn16.10:4.5.verse: “Forgive her, sir. The lady’s a fool.”

sn16.10:4.6.verse: “Hold on, Reverend Ānanda! Don’t make the Saṅgha investigate you further!

sn16.10:5.1.verse: What do you think, Reverend Ānanda?

sn16.10:5.2.verse: Was it you who the Buddha brought up before the Saṅgha of mendicants, saying:

sn16.10:5.3.verse: ‘Mendicants, whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn16.10:6.1.verse: “I was the one the Buddha brought up before the Saṅgha of mendicants, saying:

sn16.10:6.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn16.10:6.4.verse: (The nine progressive meditations and the five insights should be told in full.)

sn16.10:7.1.verse: What do you think, Reverend Ānanda?

sn16.10:7.2.verse: Was it you who the Buddha brought up before the Saṅgha of mendicants, saying:

sn16.10:7.3.verse: ‘I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

sn16.10:8.1.verse: “I was the one the Buddha brought up before the Saṅgha of mendicants, saying:

sn16.10:8.2.verse: ‘I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

sn16.10:9.1.verse: Reverend, you might as well think to hide a bull elephant that’s three or three and a half meters tall behind a palm leaf as to hide my six insights.”

sn16.10:10.1.verse: But the nun Thullatissā fell from the spiritual life.

sn16.11:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn16.11:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants.

sn16.11:2.1.verse: And at that time thirty of Ānanda’s mendicant protégés resigned the training and returned to a lesser life. Most of them were youths.

sn16.11:2.2.verse: When Venerable Ānanda had wandered in the Southern Hills as long as he pleased, he set out for Rājagaha, to the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. He went up to Venerable Mahākassapa, bowed, and sat down to one side. Mahākassapa said to him:

sn16.11:2.3.verse: “Reverend Ānanda, for how many reasons did the Buddha lay down a rule against eating in groups of more than three among families?”

sn16.11:3.1.verse: “Sir, the Buddha laid down that rule for three reasons.

sn16.11:3.2.verse: For keeping difficult individuals in check and for the comfort of good-hearted mendicants. To prevent those of corrupt wishes from taking sides and dividing the Saṅgha. And out of consideration for families.

sn16.11:3.3.verse: These are the three reasons why the Buddha laid down that rule.”

sn16.11:4.1.verse: “So what then are you doing, wandering together with these junior mendicants? They don’t guard their sense doors, they eat too much, and they’re not committed to wakefulness.

sn16.11:4.2.verse: It’s like you’re wandering about wrecking crops and ruining families!

sn16.11:4.3.verse: Your following is falling away, Reverend Ānanda,

sn16.11:4.4.verse: and those just getting started are falling apart.

sn16.11:4.5.verse: Yet this boy knows no limit!”

sn16.11:5.1.verse: “Though there are grey hairs on my head,

sn16.11:5.2.verse: I still can’t escape being called a boy by Venerable Mahākassapa.”

sn16.11:5.3.verse: “It’s because you wander with these junior mendicants. …

sn16.11:5.4.verse: Your following is falling away, Reverend Ānanda,

sn16.11:5.5.verse: and those just getting started are falling apart.

sn16.11:5.6.verse: Yet this boy knows no limit!”

sn16.11:6.1.verse: The nun Thullanandā heard a rumor that

sn16.11:6.2.verse: the venerable Mahākassapa had rebuked the venerable Ānanda the Videhan sage by calling him a boy.

sn16.11:7.1.verse: She was upset and blurted out,

sn16.11:7.2.verse: “How can the venerable Mahākassapa, who formerly followed another religion, presume to rebuke the venerable Ānanda the Videhan sage by calling him a boy?”

sn16.11:7.3.verse: Mahākassapa heard Thullanandā say these words,

sn16.11:8.2.verse: “Indeed, Reverend Ānanda, the nun Thullanandā spoke rashly and without reflection.

sn16.11:8.3.verse: Since I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness, I don’t recall acknowledging any other teacher apart from the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

sn16.11:8.4.verse: Formerly when I was still a layman, I thought:

sn16.11:8.5.verse: ‘Life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

sn16.11:8.6.verse: It’s not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell.

sn16.11:8.7.verse: Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?’

sn16.11:8.8.verse: After some time I made an outer robe of patches and, in the name of the perfected ones in the world, I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn16.11:9.1.verse: When I had gone forth, I traveled along the road between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, where I saw the Buddha sitting at the Many Sons Shrine.

sn16.11:9.3.verse: ‘Were I ever to see a Teacher, it would be this Blessed One!

sn16.11:9.4.verse: Were I ever to see a Holy One, it would be this Blessed One!

sn16.11:9.5.verse: Were I ever to see a fully awakened Buddha, it would be this Blessed One!’

sn16.11:9.7.verse: Then I bowed with my head to the Buddha’s feet and said:

sn16.11:9.8.verse: ‘Sir, the Buddha is my Teacher, I am his disciple!

sn16.11:9.9.verse: The Buddha is my Teacher, I am his disciple!’

sn16.11:9.11.verse: ‘Kassapa, if anyone was to say to such a wholehearted disciple that they know when they don’t know, or that they see when they don’t see, their head would explode.

sn16.11:9.12.verse: But Kassapa, when I say that I know I really do know; and when I say that I see I really do see.

sn16.11:10.1.verse: So you should train like this:

sn16.11:10.2.verse: “I will set up a keen sense of conscience and prudence for seniors, juniors, and those in the middle.”

sn16.11:11.1.verse: And you should train like this:

sn16.11:11.2.verse: “Whenever I hear a teaching connected with what’s skillful, I will pay attention, apply the mind, concentrate wholeheartedly, and actively listen to that teaching.”

sn16.11:12.1.verse: And you should train like this:

sn16.11:12.2.verse: “I will never neglect mindfulness of the body that is full of pleasure.”

sn16.11:13.1.verse: And when the Buddha had given me this advice he rose from his seat and left.

sn16.11:13.2.verse: For seven days I ate the nation’s almsfood as a debtor. On the eighth day I became enlightened.

sn16.11:14.1.verse: And then the Buddha left the road and went to the root of a certain tree.

sn16.11:14.2.verse: So I spread out my outer robe of patches folded in four and said to him,

sn16.11:14.3.verse: ‘Sir, sit here. That would be for my lasting welfare and happiness.’

sn16.11:14.4.verse: The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out

sn16.11:14.6.verse: ‘Kassapa, this outer robe of patches is soft.’

sn16.11:14.7.verse: ‘Sir, please accept my outer robe of patches out of sympathy.’

sn16.11:14.8.verse: ‘In that case, Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out hempen rag robe?’

sn16.11:14.10.verse: And so I presented my outer robe of patches to the Buddha,

sn16.11:14.11.verse: and the Buddha presented me with his worn-out hempen rag robe.

sn16.11:15.1.verse: For if anyone should be rightly called

sn16.11:15.2.verse: the Buddha’s bosom son, born from his mouth, born of the teaching, created by the teaching, heir to the teaching, and receiver of his worn-out hempen rag robes, it’s me.

sn16.11:16.1.verse: Whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. …

sn16.11:16.3.verse: (The nine progressive meditations and the five insights should be told in full.)

sn16.11:17.1.verse: I have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

sn16.11:17.2.verse: Reverend, you might as well think to hide a bull elephant that’s three or three and a half meters tall behind a palm leaf as to hide my six insights.”

sn16.11:18.1.verse: But the nun Thullanandā fell from the spiritual life.

sn16.12:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

sn16.12:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Mahākassapa, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn16.12:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Mahākassapa:

sn16.12:1.4.verse: “Reverend Kassapa, does a realized one still exist after death?”

sn16.12:1.5.verse: “Reverend, this has not been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:1.7.verse: “Well then, does a realized one no longer exist after death?”

sn16.12:1.8.verse: “This too has not been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:1.10.verse: “Well then, does a realized one both still exist and no longer exist after death?”

sn16.12:1.11.verse: “This too has not been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:1.13.verse: “Well then, does a realized one neither still exist nor no longer exist after death?”

sn16.12:1.14.verse: “This too has not been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:1.16.verse: “And why has this not been declared by the Buddha?”

sn16.12:1.17.verse: “Because it’s not beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. It doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn16.12:1.18.verse: That’s why it has not been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:2.1.verse: “So what now has been declared by the Buddha?”

sn16.12:2.2.verse: “‘This is suffering’ has been declared by the Buddha.

sn16.12:2.5.verse: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’ has been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.12:2.6.verse: “And why has this been declared by the Buddha?”

sn16.12:2.7.verse: “Because it’s beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. It leads to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn16.12:2.8.verse: That’s why it has been declared by the Buddha.”

sn16.13:0.3.verse: The Counterfeit of the True Teaching

sn16.13:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn16.13:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Mahākassapa went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn16.13:1.4.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why there used to be fewer training rules but more enlightened mendicants?

sn16.13:1.5.verse: And what is the cause, what is the reason why these days there are more training rules and fewer enlightened mendicants?”

sn16.13:1.6.verse: “That’s how it is, Kassapa. When sentient beings are in decline and the true teaching is disappearing there are more training rules and fewer enlightened mendicants.

sn16.13:1.7.verse: The true teaching doesn’t disappear as long as the counterfeit of the true teaching hasn’t appeared in the world.

sn16.13:1.8.verse: But when the counterfeit of the true teaching appears in the world then the true teaching disappears.

sn16.13:2.1.verse: It’s like native gold, which doesn’t disappear as long as counterfeit gold hasn’t appeared in the world.

sn16.13:2.2.verse: But when counterfeit gold appears in the world then native gold disappears.

sn16.13:2.3.verse: In the same way, the true teaching doesn’t disappear as long as the counterfeit of the true teaching hasn’t appeared in the world.

sn16.13:2.4.verse: But when the counterfeit of the true teaching appears in the world then the true teaching disappears.

sn16.13:3.1.verse: It’s not the elements of earth, water, fire, or air that make the true teaching disappear.

sn16.13:3.2.verse: Rather, it’s the futile people who appear right here that make the true teaching disappear.

sn16.13:3.3.verse: The true teaching doesn’t disappear like a ship that sinks all at once.

sn16.13:4.1.verse: There are five detrimental things that lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching.

sn16.13:4.3.verse: It’s when the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen lack respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the training, and immersion.

sn16.13:4.4.verse: These five detrimental things lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching.

sn16.13:5.1.verse: There are five things that lead to the continuation, persistence, and enduring of the true teaching.

sn16.13:5.3.verse: It’s when the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen maintain respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the training, and immersion.

sn16.13:5.4.verse: These five things lead to the continuation, persistence, and enduring of the true teaching.”

sn16.13:6.7.verse: The Linked Discourses with Kassapa are complete.

sn17.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn17.1:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

sn17.1:2.1.verse: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.1:2.2.verse: So you should train like this:

sn17.1:2.3.verse: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

sn17.2:1.2.verse: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.2:1.3.verse: Suppose an angler was to cast a baited hook into a deep lake.

sn17.2:1.4.verse: Seeing the bait, a fish would swallow it.

sn17.2:1.5.verse: And so the fish that swallowed the hook would meet with tragedy and disaster, and the angler can do what he wants with it.

sn17.2:2.1.verse: ‘Angler’ is a term for Māra the Wicked.

sn17.2:2.2.verse: ‘Hook’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.2:2.3.verse: Whoever enjoys and likes arisen possessions, honor, and popularity is called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

sn17.2:2.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.2:2.5.verse: So you should train like this:

sn17.2:2.6.verse: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

sn17.3:1.3.verse: Once upon a time, in a certain lake there was a large family of turtles that had lived there for a long time.

sn17.3:1.4.verse: Then one of the turtles said to another,

sn17.3:1.5.verse: ‘My dear turtle, don’t you go to that place.’

sn17.3:1.6.verse: But that turtle did go to that place,

sn17.3:1.7.verse: and a hunter pierced her with a harpoon.

sn17.3:1.8.verse: Then that turtle went back to the other turtle.

sn17.3:1.9.verse: When the other turtle saw her coming off in the distance,

sn17.3:1.11.verse: ‘My dear turtle, I hope you didn’t go to that place!’

sn17.3:1.13.verse: ‘But my dear turtle, I hope you’re not hurt or injured!’

sn17.3:1.14.verse: ‘I’m not hurt or injured. But this cord keeps dragging behind me.’

sn17.3:1.15.verse: ‘Indeed, my dear turtle, you’re hurt and injured!

sn17.3:1.16.verse: Your father and grandfather met with tragedy and disaster because of such a cord.

sn17.3:1.17.verse: Go now, you are no longer one of us.’

sn17.3:2.1.verse: ‘Hunter’ is a term for Māra the Wicked.

sn17.3:2.2.verse: ‘Harpoon’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.3:2.3.verse: ‘Cord’ is a term for greed and relishing.

sn17.3:2.4.verse: Whoever enjoys and likes arisen possessions, honor, and popularity is called a mendicant who has been pierced with a harpoon. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

sn17.3:2.6.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.4:1.3.verse: Suppose a fleecy sheep was to enter a briar patch.

sn17.4:1.4.verse: She’d get caught, snagged, and trapped at every turn, coming to ruin.

sn17.4:1.5.verse: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the village or town for alms.

sn17.4:1.6.verse: They get caught, snagged, and trapped at every turn, coming to ruin.

sn17.4:1.7.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.5:1.3.verse: Suppose there was a dung-eating beetle full of dung, stuffed with dung, and before her was a big pile of dung.

sn17.5:1.4.verse: She’d look down on other beetles, thinking:

sn17.5:1.5.verse: ‘For I am a dung-eating beetle full of dung, stuffed with dung, and before me is a big pile of dung.’

sn17.5:1.6.verse: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the village or town for alms.

sn17.5:1.7.verse: There they eat as much as they like, get invited back tomorrow, and have plenty of almsfood.

sn17.5:1.8.verse: When they get back to the monastery, they boast in the middle of a group of mendicants:

sn17.5:1.9.verse: ‘I ate as much as I liked, got invited back tomorrow, and had plenty of almsfood. I get robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. But these other mendicants have little merit or significance, so they don’t get these things.’

sn17.5:1.10.verse: With a mind overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity, they look down on other good-hearted mendicants.

sn17.5:1.11.verse: This will be for their lasting harm and suffering.

sn17.5:1.12.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.6:1.3.verse: Let forked lightning fall on whom? Let possessions, honor, and popularity come to a trainee who has not achieved their heart’s desire.

sn17.6:2.1.verse: ‘Forked lightning’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.6:2.2.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.7:1.3.verse: Let whom be pierced by a poisoned arrow? Let possessions, honor, and popularity come to a trainee who has not achieved their heart’s desire.

sn17.7:2.1.verse: ‘Arrow’ is a term for possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.7:2.2.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.8:1.3.verse: Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”

sn17.8:1.5.verse: “That old jackal has the disease called mange. He’s not happy in his den, or at the root of a tree, or out in the open.

sn17.8:1.6.verse: Wherever he goes, stands, sits, or lies down he meets with tragedy and disaster.

sn17.8:1.7.verse: In the same way, take a certain mendicant whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. They’re not happy in an empty hut, at the root of a tree, or out in the open.

sn17.8:1.8.verse: Wherever they go, stand, sit, or lie down they meet with tragedy and disaster.

sn17.8:1.9.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.9:1.3.verse: High in the atmosphere there are gale-force winds blowing.

sn17.9:1.4.verse: Any bird that flies there is flung about by those gale-force winds.

sn17.9:1.5.verse: Their feet go one way, their wings another, their head another, and their body another.

sn17.9:1.6.verse: In the same way, take a certain monk whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity. He robes up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, enters the village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

sn17.9:1.7.verse: There he sees a lady scantily clad, with revealing clothes.

sn17.9:1.9.verse: He resigns the training and returns to a lesser life.

sn17.9:1.10.verse: Some take his robe, others his bowl, others his sitting cloth, others his needle case, just like the bird flung about by the gale-force winds.

sn17.9:1.11.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.10:1.3.verse: Take a case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

sn17.10:1.4.verse: Take another case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by lack of honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

sn17.10:1.5.verse: And take another case where I see a certain individual whose mind is overcome and overwhelmed by both honor and lack of honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

sn17.10:1.6.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.10:2.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn17.10:2.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn17.10:3.4.verse: as they abide in the immeasurables.

sn17.10:4.3.verse: Rejoicing in the ending of grasping,

sn17.10:4.4.verse: they’re said to be a true person.”

sn17.11:1.3.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

sn17.11:1.4.verse: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a gold cup filled with silver powder.’

sn17.11:1.5.verse: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.11:1.6.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.12:1.3.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

sn17.12:1.4.verse: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a silver cup filled with gold powder.’

sn17.12:1.5.verse: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.12:1.6.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.13-20:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

sn17.13-20:1.3.verse: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of a gold ingot.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.4.verse: “‘… for the sake of a hundred gold ingots.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.5.verse: “‘… for the sake of a mountain of gold.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.6.verse: “‘… for the sake of a hundred mountains of gold.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.7.verse: “‘… for the sake of the whole earth full of gold.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.8.verse: “‘… for any kind of material reward.’ …”

sn17.13-20:1.10.verse: “‘… for the sake of the finest lady in the land.’

sn17.13-20:1.11.verse: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.13-20:1.12.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.21:1.3.verse: Even if you’re alone with a lady she might not occupy your mind, but possessions, honor and popularity would still occupy your mind.

sn17.21:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.22:0.3.verse: The Finest Lady in the Land

sn17.22:1.3.verse: Even if you’re alone with the finest lady in the land she might not occupy your mind, but possessions, honor and popularity would still occupy your mind.

sn17.22:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.23:1.3.verse: A faithful laywoman with a dear and beloved only son would rightly appeal to him,

sn17.23:1.4.verse: ‘My darling, please be like the householder Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.’

sn17.23:1.5.verse: These are a standard and a measure for my male lay disciples, that is, the householder Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.

sn17.23:1.6.verse: ‘But my darling, if you go forth from the lay life to homelessness,

sn17.23:1.7.verse: please be like Sāriputta and Moggallāna.’

sn17.23:1.8.verse: These are a standard and a measure for my monk disciples, that is, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

sn17.23:1.9.verse: ‘And my darling, may you not come into possessions, honor, and popularity while you’re still a trainee and haven’t achieved your heart’s desire.’

sn17.23:1.10.verse: If a trainee who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire comes into possessions, honor, and popularity it’s an obstacle for them.

sn17.23:1.11.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.24:1.3.verse: A faithful laywoman with a dear and beloved only daughter would rightly appeal to her,

sn17.24:1.4.verse: ‘My darling, please be like the laywomen Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇṭakī, Nanda’s mother.’

sn17.24:1.5.verse: These are a standard and a measure for my female lay disciples, that is, the laywomen Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇṭakī, Nanda’s mother.

sn17.24:1.6.verse: ‘But my darling, if you go forth from the lay life to homelessness,

sn17.24:1.7.verse: please be like the nuns Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.’

sn17.24:1.8.verse: These are a standard and a measure for my nun disciples, that is, the nuns Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.

sn17.24:1.9.verse: ‘And my darling, may you not come into possessions, honor, and popularity while you’re still a trainee and haven’t achieved your heart’s desire.’

sn17.24:1.10.verse: If a trainee who hasn’t achieved their heart’s desire comes into possessions, honor, and popularity it’s an obstacle for them.

sn17.24:1.11.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.25:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand the gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.25:1.3.verse: I don’t deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and don’t live having realized it with their own insight in this very life.

sn17.25:1.4.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand the gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.25:1.5.verse: I deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”

sn17.26:1.2.verse: “There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape when it comes to possessions, honor, and popularity …

sn17.26:1.3.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand …”

sn17.27:1.2.verse: “There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand possessions, honor, and popularity, their origin, their cessation, and the path that leads to their cessation …

sn17.27:1.3.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand …”

sn17.28:1.3.verse: They cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.

sn17.28:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.29:1.3.verse: They cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.

sn17.29:2.1.verse: Suppose a strong man was to twist a strong horse-hair rope around your shin and tighten it.

sn17.29:2.2.verse: It would cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until it reached the marrow and kept pressing.

sn17.29:2.3.verse: In the same way, possessions, honor, and popularity cut through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, sinews, and bones, until they reach the marrow and keep pressing.

sn17.29:2.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.30:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, possessions, honor, and popularity are an obstacle even for a mendicant who is perfected, with defilements ended.”

sn17.30:1.3.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

sn17.30:1.4.verse: “Sir, what do possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct for a mendicant with defilements ended?”

sn17.30:1.5.verse: “Ānanda, I don’t say that possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct the unshakable freedom of heart.

sn17.30:1.6.verse: But I do say that possessions, honor, and popularity obstruct the achievement of blissful meditations in this life for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.

sn17.30:1.7.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.30:1.8.verse: So you should train like this:

sn17.30:1.9.verse: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

sn17.31:1.3.verse: Devadatta split the Saṅgha because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.31:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.32:1.3.verse: Devadatta cut off his skillful root because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.32:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.33:1.3.verse: Devadatta cut off his skillful quality because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.33:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.34:1.3.verse: Devadatta cut off his bright quality because his mind was overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.34:1.4.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.35:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

sn17.35:1.2.verse: There the Buddha spoke to the mendicants about Devadatta:

sn17.35:1.3.verse: “Possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.

sn17.35:4.1.verse: or a reed, all of which bear fruit to their own ruin and downfall …

sn17.35:5.1.verse: It’s like a mule, which becomes pregnant to its own ruin and downfall.

sn17.35:5.2.verse: In the same way, possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.

sn17.35:5.3.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.35:6.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn17.35:6.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn17.35:7.1.verse: “The banana plant is destroyed by its own fruit,

sn17.35:7.2.verse: as are the bamboo and the reed.

sn17.36:1.1.verse: Near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn17.36:1.2.verse: Now at that time Prince Ajātasattu was going with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food.

sn17.36:1.3.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn17.36:1.4.verse: “Sir, Prince Ajātasattu is going with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food.”

sn17.36:1.5.verse: “Mendicants, don’t envy Devadatta’s possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.36:1.6.verse: As long as Prince Ajātasattu goes with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food, Devadatta can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities.

sn17.36:2.1.verse: If they were to lance a boil on a wild dog’s nose, it would get even wilder.

sn17.36:2.2.verse: In the same way, as long as Prince Ajātasattu goes with five hundred carts at daybreak and dusk to attend on Devadatta, presenting him with an offering of five hundred servings of food, Devadatta can expect decline, not growth, in skillful qualities.

sn17.36:2.3.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity. …”

sn17.37:1.2.verse: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.37:1.3.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

sn17.37:1.4.verse: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of their mother.’

sn17.37:1.5.verse: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.37:1.6.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.37:1.7.verse: So you should train like this:

sn17.37:1.8.verse: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

sn17.38-43:1.2.verse: “Possessions, honor, and popularity are grim, bitter, and harsh. They’re an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.38-43:1.3.verse: When I’ve comprehended the mind of a certain individual, I understand:

sn17.38-43:1.4.verse: ‘This venerable would not tell a deliberate lie even for the sake of their father.’ …”

sn17.38-43:1.11.verse: But some time later I see them tell a deliberate lie because their mind is overcome and overwhelmed by possessions, honor, and popularity.

sn17.38-43:1.12.verse: So grim are possessions, honor, and popularity—bitter and harsh, an obstacle to reaching the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn17.38-43:1.13.verse: So you should train like this:

sn17.38-43:1.14.verse: ‘We will give up arisen possessions, honor, and popularity, and we won’t let them occupy our minds.’

sn17.38-43:2.5.verse: The Linked Discourses on possessions, honor, and popularity are complete.

sn18.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn18.1:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn18.1:1.4.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn18.1:2.2.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.1:2.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn18.1:2.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn18.1:2.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn18.1:3.11.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn18.1:3.13.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn18.1:3.14.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn18.1:4.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind.

sn18.1:4.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn18.1:4.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn18.1:4.4.verse: (The ten discourses of this series should be told in full the same way.)

sn18.2:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas.

sn18.3:1.3.verse: Is eye consciousness permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.3:1.9.verse: Is mind consciousness permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.3:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, and mind consciousness.

sn18.4:1.3.verse: Is eye contact permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.4:1.9.verse: Is mind contact permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.4:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with eye contact, ear contact, nose contact, tongue contact, body contact, and mind contact.

sn18.5:1.3.verse: Is feeling born of eye contact permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.5:1.9.verse: Is feeling born of mind contact permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.5:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with feeling born of eye contact, ear contact, nose contact, tongue contact, body contact, and mind contact. …”

sn18.6:1.3.verse: Is perception of sights permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.6:1.9.verse: Is perception of ideas permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.6:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the perception of sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas. …”

sn18.7:1.3.verse: Is intention regarding sights permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.7:1.9.verse: Is intention regarding ideas permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.7:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with intention regarding sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas. …”

sn18.8:1.3.verse: Is craving for sights permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.8:1.9.verse: Is craving for ideas permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.8:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with craving for sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas. …”

sn18.9:1.3.verse: Is the earth element permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.9:1.9.verse: Is the consciousness element permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.9:1.11.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, space element, and consciousness element …”

sn18.10:1.10.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn18.10:1.11.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn18.10:1.12.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn18.11:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī.

sn18.11:1.3.verse: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn18.11:1.5.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.11:1.7.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn18.11:1.9.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn18.11:1.10.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn18.11:1.16.verse: Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”

sn18.11:1.18.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn18.11:1.20.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn18.11:1.21.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn18.11:1.23.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind.

sn18.11:1.24.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn18.11:1.25.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn18.11:1.26.verse: (The ten discourses of this series should be told in full the same way.)

sn18.12-20:0.3.verse: The Nine Discourses on Sights, Etc.

sn18.12-20:9.8.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn18.21:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn18.21:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

sn18.21:1.4.verse: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn18.21:1.5.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn18.21:1.8.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn18.21:1.9.verse: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

sn18.22:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn18.22:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed?”

sn18.22:1.4.verse: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.

sn18.22:2.1.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn18.22:2.4.verse: One truly sees any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.

sn18.22:2.5.verse: That’s how to know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed.”

sn18.22:3.7.verse: The Linked Discourses with Rāhula are complete.

sn19.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn19.1:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mark and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

sn19.1:1.4.verse: Then Mahāmoggallāna robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Mark and said to him,

sn19.1:1.5.verse: “Come, Reverend Mark, let’s enter Rājagaha for alms.”

sn19.1:1.7.verse: As Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain he smiled at a certain spot.

sn19.1:1.9.verse: “What is the cause, Reverend Moggallāna, what is the reason you smiled?”

sn19.1:1.10.verse: “Reverend Mark, it’s the wrong time for this question.

sn19.1:1.11.verse: Ask me when we’re in the Buddha’s presence.”

sn19.1:2.1.verse: Then Mark and Mahāmoggallāna wandered for alms in Rājagaha. After the meal, on their return from almsround, they went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Mark said to Mahāmoggallāna:

sn19.1:2.2.verse: “Just now, as Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain he smiled at a certain spot.

sn19.1:2.3.verse: What is the cause, Reverend Moggallāna, what is the reason you smiled?”

sn19.1:3.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a skeleton flying through the air.

sn19.1:3.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing it, pecking, clawing, and stabbing it in the ribs

sn19.1:3.6.verse: That there can be such a sentient being,

sn19.1:4.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

sn19.1:4.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are disciples who live full of vision and knowledge,

sn19.1:4.3.verse: since a disciple knows, sees, and witnesses such a thing.

sn19.1:4.4.verse: Formerly, I too saw that being, but I did not speak of it.

sn19.1:4.5.verse: For if I had spoken of it others would not have believed me,

sn19.1:4.6.verse: which would be for their lasting harm and suffering.

sn19.1:4.7.verse: That being used to be a cattle butcher right here in Rājagaha.

sn19.1:4.8.verse: As a result of that deed he burned in hell for many years, many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of years. Now he experiences the residual result of that deed in such an incarnation.”

sn19.1:4.9.verse: (Tell all these discourses in full like this.)

sn19.2:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a scrap of meat flying through the air.

sn19.2:1.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing it, pecking and clawing

sn19.2:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a cattle butcher right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.3:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a piece of flesh flying through the air.

sn19.3:1.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing it, pecking and clawing

sn19.3:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a bird hunter right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.4:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a flayed man flying through the air.

sn19.4:1.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing it, pecking and clawing

sn19.4:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a sheep butcher right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.5:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man whose body hairs were swords flying through the air.

sn19.5:1.2.verse: And those swords kept rising up and falling on his body

sn19.5:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a pig butcher right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.6:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man whose body hairs were spears flying through the air.

sn19.6:1.2.verse: And those spears kept rising up and falling on his body

sn19.6:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a deer hunter right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.7:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man whose body hairs were arrows flying through the air.

sn19.7:1.2.verse: And those arrows kept rising up and falling on his body

sn19.7:1.4.verse: “That being used to be a punisher right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.8:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man whose body hairs were needles flying through the air.

sn19.8:1.2.verse: And those needles kept rising up and falling on his body

sn19.8:1.4.verse: “That being used to be an equerry right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.9:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man whose body hairs were needles flying through the air.

sn19.9:1.2.verse: The needles bored into his head and out his mouth,

sn19.9:1.3.verse: into his mouth and out his chest,

sn19.9:1.4.verse: into his chest and out his belly,

sn19.9:1.5.verse: into his belly and out his thighs,

sn19.9:1.6.verse: into his thighs and out his calves,

sn19.9:1.7.verse: and into his calves and out his feet.

sn19.9:1.9.verse: “That being used to be an informant right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.10:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man with testicles big as pots flying through the air.

sn19.10:1.2.verse: When he was walking he had to lift his testicles on to his shoulder.

sn19.10:1.3.verse: And when he sat down, he sat right on them.

sn19.10:1.4.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing him, pecking and clawing

sn19.10:1.6.verse: “That being used to be a corrupt village head right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.11:1.2.verse: At one time near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove …

sn19.11:1.3.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man sunk over his head in a sewer. …” …

sn19.11:1.4.verse: “That being used to be an adulterer right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.12:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a man sunk in a sewer, eating dung with both hands. …” …

sn19.12:1.2.verse: “That being used to be a nasty brahmin right here in Rājagaha.

sn19.12:1.3.verse: In the time of the Buddha Kassapa’s dispensation he invited the Saṅgha of mendicants for a meal. He filled a trough with dung and said:

sn19.12:1.4.verse: ‘My good men, eat as much as you like, and take what’s left.’ …”

sn19.13:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a flayed woman flying through the air.

sn19.13:1.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing her, pecking and clawing

sn19.13:1.4.verse: “That woman used to be an adulteress right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.14:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a woman stinking and dingy as a catfish flying through the air.

sn19.14:1.2.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing her, pecking and clawing

sn19.14:1.4.verse: “That woman used to be a sorceress right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.15:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a scorched woman, sooty and sweaty, flying through the air,

sn19.15:1.3.verse: “That woman used to be the king of Kaliṅga’s chief queen.

sn19.15:1.4.verse: She was of jealous nature, and poured a brazier of hot coals over her co-wife. …” …

sn19.16:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a headless trunk flying through the air.

sn19.16:1.2.verse: Its eyes and mouth were on its chest.

sn19.16:1.3.verse: Vultures, crows, and hawks kept chasing it, pecking and clawing

sn19.16:1.5.verse: “That being used to be an executioner named Taker right here in Rājagaha. …”

sn19.17:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a monk flying through the air.

sn19.17:1.2.verse: His outer robe, bowl, belt, and body were burning, blazing, and glowing

sn19.17:1.4.verse: “That monk used to be a bad monk in the time of Buddha Kassapa’s dispensation. …”

sn19.18:1.1.verse: “I saw a nun flying through the air.

sn19.18:1.3.verse: “She used to be a bad nun …”

sn19.19:1.1.verse: “I saw a trainee nun flying through the air.

sn19.19:1.3.verse: “She used to be a bad trainee nun …”

sn19.20:1.1.verse: “I saw a novice monk flying through the air.

sn19.20:1.3.verse: “He used to be a bad novice monk …”

sn19.21:1.1.verse: “Just now, reverend, as I was descending from Vulture’s Peak Mountain I saw a novice nun flying through the air.

sn19.21:1.2.verse: Her outer robe, bowl, belt, and body were burning, blazing, and glowing

sn19.21:1.6.verse: That there can be such a sentient being,

sn19.21:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants:

sn19.21:2.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are disciples who live full of vision and knowledge,

sn19.21:2.3.verse: since a disciple knows, sees, and witnesses such a thing.

sn19.21:2.4.verse: Formerly, I too saw that novice nun, but I did not speak of it.

sn19.21:2.6.verse: For if I had spoken of it others would not have believed me,

sn19.21:2.7.verse: which would be for their lasting harm and suffering.

sn19.21:2.8.verse: That female novice used to be a bad novice nun in the time of the Buddha Kassapa’s dispensation.

sn19.21:2.9.verse: As a result of that deed she burned in hell for many years, many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of years. Now she experiences the residual result of that deed in such an incarnation.”

sn19.21:4.5.verse: The Linked Discourses with Mark are complete.

sn20.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn20.1:1.4.verse: “Mendicants, the rafters of a bungalow all lean to the peak and meet at the peak, and when the peak is demolished they’re all demolished too.

sn20.1:1.5.verse: In the same way all unskillful qualities are rooted in ignorance and meet in ignorance, and when ignorance is demolished they’re all demolished too.

sn20.1:1.6.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.2:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, addressed the mendicants:

sn20.2:1.4.verse: Which is more: the little bit of dirt on my fingernail, or this great earth?”

sn20.2:1.5.verse: “Sir, the great earth is far more.

sn20.2:1.6.verse: The little bit of dirt on your fingernail is tiny.

sn20.2:1.7.verse: Compared to the great earth, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn20.2:1.8.verse: “In the same way the sentient beings reborn as humans are few,

sn20.2:1.9.verse: while those not reborn as humans are many.

sn20.2:1.10.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.3:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, those families with many women and few men are easy prey for bandits and  grain-jar thieves.

sn20.3:1.3.verse: In the same way any mendicant who has not developed and cultivated the heart’s release by love is easy prey for non-humans.

sn20.3:1.4.verse: Those families with few women and many men are hard prey for bandits and grain-jar thieves.

sn20.3:1.5.verse: In the same way a mendicant who has developed and cultivated the heart’s release by love is hard prey for non-humans.

sn20.3:1.6.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.3:1.7.verse: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’

sn20.4:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, suppose one person was to give a gift of a hundred cauldrons of rice in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. And someone else was to develop a heart of love, even just as long as it takes to pull a cow’s udder. The latter would be more fruitful.

sn20.4:1.3.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.4:1.4.verse: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’

sn20.5:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, suppose there was a sharp-pointed spear.

sn20.5:1.3.verse: And a man came along and thought,

sn20.5:1.4.verse: ‘With my hand or fist I’ll fold this sharp spear over, crumple it, and bend it back!’

sn20.5:1.6.verse: Is that man capable of doing so?”

sn20.5:1.9.verse: Because it’s not easy to fold that sharp spear over, crumple it, and bend it back with the hand or fist.

sn20.5:1.10.verse: That man will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

sn20.5:2.1.verse: “In the same way, suppose a mendicant has developed the heart’s release by love, has cultivated it, made it a vehicle and a basis, kept it up, consolidated it, and properly implemented it. Should any non-human think to overthrow their mind,

sn20.5:2.2.verse: they’ll eventually get weary and frustrated.

sn20.5:2.3.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.5:2.4.verse: ‘We will develop the heart’s release by love. We’ll cultivate it, make it our vehicle and our basis, keep it up, consolidate it, and properly implement it.’

sn20.6:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, suppose there were four well-trained expert archers with strong bows standing in the four quarters.

sn20.6:1.3.verse: And a man came along and thought,

sn20.6:1.4.verse: ‘When these four well-trained expert archers shoot arrows in four quarters, I’ll catch them before they reach the ground, and then I’ll bring them back.’

sn20.6:1.6.verse: Are they qualified to be called ‘a speedster endowed with super-speed’?”

sn20.6:2.1.verse: “If he could catch an arrow shot by just one well-trained expert archer before it reaches the ground and bring it back,

sn20.6:2.2.verse: he’d be qualified to be called ‘a speedster endowed with super-speed’. How much more so arrows shot by four archers!”

sn20.6:3.1.verse: “As fast as that man is, the sun and moon are faster.

sn20.6:3.2.verse: As fast as that man is, as fast as the sun and moon are, and as fast as the deities that run before the sun and moon are, the waning of the life forces is faster.

sn20.6:3.3.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.7:1.2.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, the Dasārahas had a mridangam drum called the Plugger.

sn20.7:1.3.verse: When the Plugger cracked, the Dasārahas patched it with another plug.

sn20.7:1.4.verse: Eventually, there came a time when the old wooden shell for the drumskin disappeared

sn20.7:1.5.verse: and all that was left of the mridangam Plugger was a mass of plugs.

sn20.7:1.6.verse: In the same way, in a future time there will be mendicants who won’t want to listen when discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited. They won’t actively listen or try to understand, nor will they think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

sn20.7:2.1.verse: But when discourses composed by poets—poetry, with fancy words and phrases, composed by outsiders or spoken by disciples—are being recited they will want to listen. They’ll actively listen and try to understand, and they’ll think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.

sn20.7:2.2.verse: And that is how the discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—will disappear.

sn20.7:2.3.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.7:2.4.verse: ‘When discourses spoken by the Realized One—deep, profound, transcendent, dealing with emptiness—are being recited we will want to listen. We will actively listen and try to understand, and we will think those teachings are worth learning and memorizing.’

sn20.8:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

sn20.8:1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

sn20.8:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, these days the Licchavis live using wood blocks as pillows, and they exercise diligently and keenly.

sn20.8:2.2.verse: King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, finds no vulnerability, he’s got no opportunity.

sn20.8:2.3.verse: But in the future the Licchavis will become delicate, with soft and tender hands and feet.

sn20.8:2.4.verse: They’ll sleep on soft beds with down pillows until the sun comes up.

sn20.8:2.5.verse: King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the princess of Videha, will find a vulnerability and get an opportunity.

sn20.8:3.1.verse: These days the mendicants live using wood blocks as pillows, and they meditate diligently and keenly.

sn20.8:3.2.verse: Māra the Wicked finds no vulnerability, he’s got no opportunity.

sn20.8:3.3.verse: But in the future the mendicants will become delicate, with soft and tender hands and feet.

sn20.8:3.4.verse: They’ll sleep on soft beds with down pillows until the sun comes up.

sn20.8:3.5.verse: Māra the Wicked will find a vulnerability and get an opportunity.

sn20.8:3.6.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.8:3.7.verse: ‘We will live using wood blocks as pillows, and we will meditate diligently and keenly.’

sn20.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn20.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time a certain junior mendicant went to visit families too often.

sn20.9:1.5.verse: “Venerable, don’t go to visit families too often.”

sn20.9:1.6.verse: But that mendicant, when spoken to by the mendicants, said this,

sn20.9:1.7.verse: “But these senior mendicants think they can go to visit families, so why can’t I?”

sn20.9:2.1.verse: And then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. The Buddha said:

sn20.9:3.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a great lake in the jungle,

sn20.9:3.3.verse: They’d plunge into the lake and pull up lotus bulbs with their trunks. They’d wash them thoroughly until they were free of mud before chewing and swallowing them.

sn20.9:3.4.verse: That was good for their appearance and strength, and wouldn’t result in death or deadly pain.

sn20.9:3.5.verse: The young calves, following the example of the great bull elephants, plunged into the lake and pulled up lotus bulbs with their trunks. But they didn’t wash them thoroughly, and while they were still muddy they chewed and swallowed them.

sn20.9:3.6.verse: That was not good for their appearance and strength, and resulted in death or deadly pain.

sn20.9:4.1.verse: In the same way, there are senior mendicants who robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.

sn20.9:4.2.verse: There they speak on the teachings,

sn20.9:4.3.verse: and lay people demonstrate their confidence in them.

sn20.9:4.4.verse: And when they get things, they use them untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

sn20.9:4.5.verse: That’s good for their appearance and strength, and doesn’t result in death or deadly pain.

sn20.9:4.6.verse: Junior mendicants, following the example of the senior mendicants, robe up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, enter the town or village for alms.

sn20.9:4.7.verse: There they speak on the teachings,

sn20.9:4.8.verse: and lay people demonstrate their confidence in them.

sn20.9:4.9.verse: But when they get things, they use them tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, not understanding the escape.

sn20.9:4.10.verse: That’s not good for their appearance and strength, and results in death or deadly pain.

sn20.9:4.11.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.9:4.12.verse: ‘When we get things, we will use them untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.’

sn20.10:1.2.verse: Now at that time a certain mendicant had relations with families too often.

sn20.10:1.4.verse: “Venerable, don’t have relations with families too often.”

sn20.10:1.5.verse: But that mendicant, when spoken to by the mendicants, did not stop.

sn20.10:1.6.verse: And then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. The Buddha said:

sn20.10:2.1.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a cat was standing by an alley or a drain or a dustbin hunting a little mouse, thinking,

sn20.10:2.2.verse: ‘When that little mouse comes out to feed, I’ll catch it right there and eat it!’

sn20.10:2.3.verse: And then that little mouse came out to feed.

sn20.10:2.4.verse: The cat caught it and hastily swallowed it without chewing.

sn20.10:2.5.verse: But that little mouse ate its intestines and mesentery,

sn20.10:2.6.verse: resulting in death and deadly pain.

sn20.10:3.1.verse: In the same way, take a certain monk who robes up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, enters the village or town for alms without guarding body, speech, and mind, without establishing mindfulness, and without restraining the sense faculties.

sn20.10:3.2.verse: There he sees a lady scantily clad, with revealing clothes.

sn20.10:3.4.verse: resulting in death or deadly pain.

sn20.10:3.5.verse: For it is death in the training of the Noble One to resign the training and return to a lesser life.

sn20.10:3.6.verse: And it is deadly pain to commit one of the corrupt offenses

sn20.10:3.8.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.10:3.9.verse: ‘We will enter the village or town for alms guarding body, speech, and mind, establishing mindfulness, and restraining the sense faculties.’

sn20.11:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”

sn20.11:1.4.verse: “That old jackal has the disease called mange.

sn20.11:1.5.verse: Yet it still goes where it wants,

sn20.11:1.8.verse: and lies down where it wants.

sn20.11:1.9.verse: And the cool breeze still blows on it.

sn20.11:1.10.verse: A certain person here who claims to follow the Sakyan would be lucky to experience even such an incarnation.

sn20.11:1.11.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.12:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, did you hear an old jackal howling at the crack of dawn?”

sn20.12:1.4.verse: “There might be some gratitude and thankfulness in that old jackal, but there is none in a certain person here who claims to follow the Sakyan.

sn20.12:1.5.verse: So you should train like this:

sn20.12:1.7.verse: We won’t forget even a small thing done for us.’

sn20.12:2.5.verse: The Linked Discourses with similes are complete.

sn21.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn21.1:1.3.verse: There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the mendicants:

sn21.1:2.2.verse: “Just now, reverends, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

sn21.1:2.3.verse: ‘They speak of this thing called “noble silence”.

sn21.1:2.4.verse: What then is this noble silence?’

sn21.1:2.6.verse: ‘As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn21.1:2.8.verse: And so, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I was entering and remaining in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn21.1:2.9.verse: While I was in that meditation, perception and focus accompanied by placing the mind beset me.

sn21.1:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha came up to me with his psychic power and said,

sn21.1:3.2.verse: ‘Moggallāna, Moggallāna! Don’t neglect noble silence, brahmin! Settle your mind in noble silence; unify your mind and bring it to immersion in noble silence.’

sn21.1:3.3.verse: And so, after some time, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption …

sn21.1:3.4.verse: So if anyone should be rightly called

sn21.1:3.5.verse: a disciple who attained to great direct knowledge with help from the Teacher, it’s me.”

sn21.2:2.1.verse: “Just now, reverends, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind:

sn21.2:2.2.verse: ‘Is there anything in the world whose decay and perishing would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me?’

sn21.2:2.4.verse: ‘There is nothing in the world whose decay and perishing would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me.’”

sn21.2:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to him,

sn21.2:3.2.verse: “Even if the Teacher were to decay and perish? Wouldn’t that give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in you?”

sn21.2:3.3.verse: “Even if the Teacher were to decay and perish, that wouldn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in me. Still, I would think:

sn21.2:3.4.verse: ‘Oh lord, the illustrious Teacher, so mighty and powerful, has vanished!

sn21.2:3.5.verse: If the Buddha was to remain for a long time, that would be for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.’”

sn21.2:3.6.verse: “That must be because Venerable Sāriputta has long ago totally eradicated I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit.

sn21.2:3.7.verse: So even if the Teacher were to decay and perish, it wouldn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress in him.”

sn21.3:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn21.3:1.3.verse: At that time the venerables Sāriputta and Moggallāna were staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn21.3:1.4.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Moggallāna, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn21.3:1.5.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, Sāriputta sat down to one side, and said to Mahāmoggallāna:

sn21.3:2.1.verse: “Reverend Moggallāna, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

sn21.3:2.2.verse: Have you spent the day in a peaceful meditation?”

sn21.3:2.3.verse: “Reverend, I’ve spent the day in a coarse meditation.

sn21.3:2.4.verse: But I have had some Dhamma talk.”

sn21.3:2.5.verse: “Who did you have a Dhamma talk with?”

sn21.3:2.7.verse: “But Reverend, the Buddha is far away. He’s staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn21.3:2.8.verse: Did you go to him with your psychic power,

sn21.3:2.9.verse: or did he come to you?”

sn21.3:2.10.verse: “No reverend, I didn’t go to him with my psychic power,

sn21.3:2.11.verse: nor did he come to me.

sn21.3:2.12.verse: Rather, the Buddha cleared his clairvoyance and clairaudience toward me,

sn21.3:2.13.verse: and I cleared my clairvoyance and clairaudience toward him.”

sn21.3:2.14.verse: “But what manner of Dhamma talk did you have together?”

sn21.3:3.1.verse: “Well, reverend, I said to the Buddha,

sn21.3:3.2.verse: ‘Sir, they speak of one who is energetic.

sn21.3:3.3.verse: How is an energetic person defined?’

sn21.3:3.4.verse: When I said this, the Buddha said,

sn21.3:3.5.verse: ‘Moggallāna, it’s when a mendicant lives with energy roused up:

sn21.3:3.6.verse: “Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain! Let the flesh and blood waste away in my body! I will not stop trying until I have achieved what is possible by human strength, energy, and vigor.”

sn21.3:3.7.verse: That’s how an individual is energetic.’

sn21.3:3.8.verse: That’s the Dhamma talk I had together with the Buddha.”

sn21.3:4.1.verse: “Reverend, next to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna I’m like a few pieces of gravel next to the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

sn21.3:4.3.verse: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is so mighty and powerful he could, if he wished, live on for the proper lifespan.”

sn21.3:5.1.verse: “Reverend, next to Venerable Sāriputta I’m like a few grains of salt next to a mound of salt.

sn21.3:5.3.verse: Venerable Sāriputta has been commended, complimented, and praised by the Buddha:

sn21.3:6.3.verse: Even a mendicant who has crossed over

sn21.3:7.1.verse: And so these two spiritual giants agreed with each other’s fine words.

sn21.4:1.2.verse: Now at that time a certain junior monk, after his meal, on his return from almsround, entered his dwelling, where he adhered to passivity and silence. And he didn’t help the mendicants out when it was time to sew robes.

sn21.4:1.3.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

sn21.4:2.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

sn21.4:2.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell that monk that the Teacher summons him.”

sn21.4:2.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to that monk and said to him,

sn21.4:2.5.verse: “Yes, reverend,” that monk replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn21.4:2.6.verse: “Is it really true, monk, that after your meal, on your return from almsround, you entered your dwelling, where you adhered to passivity and silence, and you didn’t help the mendicants out when it was time to sew robes?”

sn21.4:2.7.verse: “Sir, I am doing my own work.”
