sn21.4:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the mendicants:

sn21.4:3.3.verse: This monk gets the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when he wants, without trouble or difficulty. He has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life, and lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

sn21.4:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.4:4.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.4:6.4.verse: having vanquished Māra with his legions.”

sn21.5:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Sujāta went to the Buddha.

sn21.5:1.3.verse: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,

sn21.5:1.6.verse: He’s attractive, good-looking, lovely, of surpassing beauty. And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

sn21.5:1.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.5:1.8.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.5:2.6.verse: having vanquished Māra with his legions.”

sn21.6:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf went to the Buddha.

sn21.6:1.3.verse: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,

sn21.6:1.5.verse: “Mendicants, do you see this monk coming—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and despised by the mendicants?”

sn21.6:1.7.verse: “That mendicant is very mighty and powerful. It’s not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained.

sn21.6:1.8.verse: And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

sn21.6:1.9.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.6:1.10.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.6:2.3.verse: though their bodies are not equal,

sn21.6:3.2.verse: if a little person is wise,

sn21.6:3.4.verse: not the fool with a good body.”

sn21.7:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

sn21.7:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son, was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk. His words were polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.

sn21.7:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the assembly hall. He sat down on the seat spread out,

sn21.7:2.3.verse: “Mendicants, who was educating, encouraging, firing up, and inspiring the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk?”

sn21.7:2.4.verse: “Sir, it was Venerable Visākha, Pañcāli’s son.”

sn21.7:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to Visākha:

sn21.7:3.3.verse: It’s good that you educate, encourage, fire up, and inspire the mendicants in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk, with words that are polished, clear, articulate, expressing the meaning, comprehensive, and independent.”

sn21.7:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.7:4.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.7:5.1.verse: “Though an astute person is mixed up with fools,

sn21.7:5.2.verse: they don’t know unless he speaks.

sn21.7:5.3.verse: But when he speaks they know,

sn21.7:5.4.verse: he’s teaching the state free of death.

sn21.7:6.1.verse: He should speak and illustrate the teaching,

sn21.7:6.2.verse: holding up the banner of the seers.

sn21.7:6.3.verse: Words well spoken are the seers’ banner,

sn21.7:6.4.verse: for the teaching is the banner of the seers.”

sn21.8:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Nanda—the Buddha’s cousin on his mother’s side—dressed in nicely pressed and ironed robes, applied eyeshadow, and took a glazed bowl. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn21.8:1.3.verse: “Nanda, as a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, it’s not appropriate for you to dress in nicely pressed and ironed robes, apply eyeshadow, and carry a glazed bowl.

sn21.8:1.4.verse: It’s appropriate for you to stay in the wilderness, eat only almsfood, wear rag robes, and live without concern for sensual pleasures.”

sn21.8:1.5.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.8:1.6.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.8:2.2.verse: in the wilderness, wearing rag robes,

sn21.8:2.3.verse: feeding on scraps offered by strangers,

sn21.8:3.1.verse: Then some time later Venerable Nanda stayed in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and lived without concern for sensual pleasures.

sn21.9:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Tissa—the Buddha’s cousin on his father’s side—went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. He was miserable and sad, with tears flowing. Then the Buddha said to him:

sn21.9:1.3.verse: “Tissa, why are you sitting there so miserable and sad, with tears flowing?”

sn21.9:1.4.verse: “Sir, it’s because the mendicants beset me on all sides with sneering and jeering.”

sn21.9:1.5.verse: “That’s because you admonish others, but don’t accept admonition yourself.

sn21.9:1.6.verse: As a gentleman who has gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, it’s not appropriate for you to admonish others without accepting admonition yourself.

sn21.9:1.8.verse: admonish others and accept admonition yourself.”

sn21.9:2.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.9:2.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.9:3.1.verse: “Why are you angry? Don’t be angry!

sn21.9:3.2.verse: It’s better to not be angry, Tissa.

sn21.9:3.3.verse: For this spiritual life is lived

sn21.9:3.4.verse: in order to remove anger, conceit, and denigration.”

sn21.10:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn21.10:1.2.verse: Now at that time there was a certain mendicant who was Senior in name only. He lived alone and praised living alone.

sn21.10:1.3.verse: He entered the village for alms alone, returned alone, sat in private alone, and focussed on walking mindfully alone.

sn21.10:1.4.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn21.10:1.5.verse: “Sir, there’s a certain mendicant who is Senior in name only. He lives alone and praises living alone.”

sn21.10:2.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

sn21.10:2.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Senior that

sn21.10:2.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Venerable Senior and said to him,

sn21.10:2.6.verse: “Yes, reverend,” that monk replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn21.10:2.7.verse: “Is it really true, Senior, that you live alone and praise living alone?”

sn21.10:2.9.verse: “But in what way do you live alone and praise living alone?”

sn21.10:2.10.verse: “Well, sir, I enter the village for alms alone, return alone, sit in private alone, and focus on walking mindfully alone.

sn21.10:2.11.verse: That’s how I live alone and praise living alone.”

sn21.10:3.1.verse: “That is a kind of living alone, I don’t deny it.

sn21.10:3.2.verse: But as to how living alone is fulfilled in detail,

sn21.10:3.3.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn21.10:3.5.verse: “And how, Senior, is living alone fulfilled in detail?

sn21.10:3.6.verse: It’s when what’s in the past is given up, what’s in the future is relinquished, and desire and greed for present incarnations is eliminated.

sn21.10:3.7.verse: That’s how living alone is fulfilled in detail.”

sn21.10:4.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.10:4.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.10:5.1.verse: “The vanquisher of all, knower of all, so very intelligent,

sn21.10:5.2.verse: is unsullied in the midst of all things.

sn21.10:5.3.verse: He’s given up all, freed in the ending of craving:

sn21.10:5.4.verse: I declare that man to be one who lives alone.”

sn21.11:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Mahākappina went to the Buddha.

sn21.11:1.3.verse: The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance,

sn21.11:1.5.verse: “Mendicants, do you see that monk coming—white, thin, with a pointy nose?”

sn21.11:1.7.verse: “That mendicant is very mighty and powerful.

sn21.11:1.8.verse: It’s not easy to find an attainment that he has not already attained.

sn21.11:1.9.verse: And he has realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lives having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

sn21.11:2.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.11:2.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.11:3.2.verse: who take clan as the standard.

sn21.11:3.3.verse: But one accomplished in knowledge and conduct

sn21.11:3.4.verse: is best among gods and humans.

sn21.11:4.4.verse: and the brahmin shines in absorption.

sn21.11:4.5.verse: But all day and all night,

sn21.12:1.2.verse: Then two mendicants who were companions, protégés of Venerable Mahākappina, went to the Buddha.

sn21.12:1.3.verse: The Buddha saw them coming off in the distance,

sn21.12:1.5.verse: “Mendicants, do you see those monks coming who are companions, protégés of Venerable Mahākappina?”

sn21.12:1.7.verse: “Those mendicants are very mighty and powerful.

sn21.12:1.8.verse: It’s not easy to find an attainment that they have not already attained.

sn21.12:1.9.verse: And they’ve realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”

sn21.12:2.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn21.12:2.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn21.12:3.2.verse: have been together for a long time.

sn21.12:3.3.verse: The true teaching has brought them together,

sn21.12:3.4.verse: the teaching proclaimed by the Buddha.

sn21.12:4.1.verse: They’ve been well trained by Kappina

sn21.12:4.2.verse: in the teaching proclaimed by the Noble One.

sn21.12:4.4.verse: having vanquished Māra with his legions.”

sn21.12:5.7.verse: The Linked Discourses on monks are complete.

sn21.12:6.6.verse: The Book of Causality is finished.

sn22.1:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

sn22.1:1.3.verse: Then the householder Nakula’s father went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn22.1:2.1.verse: “Sir, I’m an old man, elderly and senior. I’m advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life. My body is ailing and I’m constantly unwell.

sn22.1:2.2.verse: I hardly ever get to see the esteemed mendicants.

sn22.1:2.3.verse: May the Buddha please advise me

sn22.1:2.5.verse: It will be for my lasting welfare and happiness.”

sn22.1:3.1.verse: “That’s so true, householder! That’s so true, householder!

sn22.1:3.2.verse: For this body is ailing, swaddled in its shell.

sn22.1:3.3.verse: If anyone dragging around this body claimed to be healthy even for an hour, what is that but foolishness?

sn22.1:3.4.verse: So you should train like this:

sn22.1:3.5.verse: ‘Though my body is ailing, my mind will be healthy.’

sn22.1:4.1.verse: And then the householder Nakula’s father approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he went up to Venerable Sāriputta, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sāriputta said to him:

sn22.1:4.2.verse: “Householder, your faculties are so very clear,

sn22.1:4.3.verse: and your complexion is pure and bright.

sn22.1:4.4.verse: Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk in the Buddha’s presence today?”

sn22.1:5.2.verse: Just now the Buddha anointed me with the deathless ambrosia of a Dhamma talk.”

sn22.1:5.3.verse: “But with what kind of ambrosial Dhamma talk did the Buddha anoint you?”

sn22.1:5.4.verse: So Nakula’s father told Sāriputta all that had happened, and said,

sn22.1:6.8.verse: “That’s the ambrosial Dhamma talk with which I was anointed by the Buddha.”

sn22.1:7.1.verse: “But didn’t you feel the need to ask the Buddha the further question:

sn22.1:7.2.verse: ‘Sir, how do you define someone ailing in body and ailing in mind, and someone ailing in body and healthy in mind’?”

sn22.1:7.3.verse: “Sir, we would travel a long way to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta.

sn22.1:7.4.verse: May Venerable Sāriputta himself please clarify the meaning of this.”

sn22.1:8.1.verse: “Well then, householder, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn22.1:9.1.verse: “And how is one ailing in body and ailing in mind?

sn22.1:9.2.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the qualities of a noble one. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the qualities of a true person.

sn22.1:9.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.1:9.4.verse: They’re obsessed with the thought: ‘I am form, form is mine!’

sn22.1:9.5.verse: But that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:9.6.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:10.1.verse: They regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

sn22.1:10.2.verse: They’re obsessed with the thought: ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine!’

sn22.1:10.3.verse: But that feeling of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:10.4.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:11.1.verse: They regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

sn22.1:11.2.verse: They’re obsessed with the thought: ‘I am perception, perception is mine!’

sn22.1:11.3.verse: But that perception of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:11.4.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:12.1.verse: They regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

sn22.1:12.2.verse: They’re obsessed with the thought: ‘I am choices, choices are mine!’

sn22.1:12.3.verse: But those choices of theirs decay and perish,

sn22.1:12.4.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:13.1.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.1:13.2.verse: They’re obsessed with the thought: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine!’

sn22.1:13.3.verse: But that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:13.4.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:13.5.verse: That’s how one is ailing in body and ailing in mind.

sn22.1:14.1.verse: And how is one ailing in body and healthy in mind?

sn22.1:14.2.verse: It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.1:14.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.1:14.4.verse: They’re not obsessed with the thought: ‘I am form, form is mine!’

sn22.1:14.5.verse: So when that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:14.6.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:15.1.verse: They don’t regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling.

sn22.1:15.2.verse: They’re not obsessed with the thought: ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine!’

sn22.1:15.3.verse: So when that feeling of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:15.4.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:16.1.verse: They don’t regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception.

sn22.1:16.2.verse: They’re not obsessed with the thought: ‘I am perception, perception is mine!’

sn22.1:16.3.verse: So when that perception of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:16.4.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:17.1.verse: They don’t regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices.

sn22.1:17.2.verse: They’re not obsessed with the thought: ‘I am choices, choices are mine!’

sn22.1:17.3.verse: So when those choices of theirs decay and perish,

sn22.1:17.4.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:18.1.verse: They don’t regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.1:18.2.verse: They’re not obsessed with the thought: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine!’

sn22.1:18.3.verse: So when that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.1:18.4.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.1:18.5.verse: That’s how an individual is ailing in body and healthy in mind.”

sn22.1:19.1.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

sn22.1:19.2.verse: Satisfied, Nakula’s father approved what Sāriputta said.

sn22.2:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, where they have a town named Devadaha.

sn22.2:1.3.verse: Then several mendicants who were heading for the west went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn22.2:1.4.verse: “Sir, we wish to go to a western land to take up residence there.”

sn22.2:2.1.verse: “But mendicants, have you taken leave of Sāriputta?”

sn22.2:2.4.verse: He’s astute, and supports his spiritual companions, the mendicants.”

sn22.2:3.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha in a clump of golden shower trees.

sn22.2:3.2.verse: And then those mendicants approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. They got up from their seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right. Then they went up to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn22.2:3.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him,

sn22.2:3.4.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, we wish to go to a western land to take up residence there.

sn22.2:3.5.verse: We have taken leave of the Teacher.”

sn22.2:4.1.verse: “Reverends, there are those who question a mendicant who has gone abroad—

sn22.2:4.2.verse: astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and ascetics—

sn22.2:4.4.verse: ‘But what does the venerables’ Teacher teach? What does he explain?’ I trust the venerables have properly heard, learned, applied the mind, and remembered the teachings, and penetrated them with wisdom. That way, when answering you will repeat what the Buddha has said and not misrepresent him with an untruth. You will explain in line with the teaching, with no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism.”

sn22.2:5.1.verse: “Reverend, we would travel a long way to learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of Venerable Sāriputta.

sn22.2:5.2.verse: May Venerable Sāriputta himself please clarify the meaning of this.”

sn22.2:5.3.verse: “Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn22.2:6.1.verse: “Reverends, there are those who question a mendicant who has gone abroad—

sn22.2:6.2.verse: astute aristocrats, brahmins, householders, and ascetics—

sn22.2:6.4.verse: ‘But what does the venerables’ Teacher teach? What does he explain?’

sn22.2:6.5.verse: When questioned like this, reverends, you should answer:

sn22.2:6.6.verse: ‘Reverend, our Teacher explained the removal of desire and lust.’

sn22.2:7.1.verse: When you answer like this, such astute people may inquire further:

sn22.2:7.4.verse: ‘But regarding what does the venerables’ teacher explain the removal of desire and lust?’

sn22.2:7.5.verse: When questioned like this, reverends, you should answer:

sn22.2:7.6.verse: ‘Our teacher explains the removal of desire and lust for form,

sn22.2:8.1.verse: When you answer like this, such astute people may inquire further:

sn22.2:8.4.verse: ‘But what drawback has he seen that he teaches the removal of desire and lust for form,

sn22.2:8.9.verse: When questioned like this, reverends, you should answer:

sn22.2:8.10.verse: ‘If you’re not free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes it gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.2:8.11.verse: If you’re not free of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for feeling …

sn22.2:8.15.verse: consciousness, when that consciousness decays and perishes it gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.2:8.16.verse: This is the drawback our Teacher has seen that he teaches the removal of desire and lust for form,

sn22.2:9.1.verse: When you answer like this, such astute people may inquire further:

sn22.2:9.4.verse: ‘But what benefit has he seen that he teaches the removal of desire and lust for form,

sn22.2:9.9.verse: When questioned like this, reverends, you should answer:

sn22.2:9.10.verse: ‘If you are rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.2:9.11.verse: If you are rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for feeling …

sn22.2:9.14.verse: consciousness, when that consciousness decays and perishes it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.2:9.15.verse: This is the benefit our Teacher has seen that he teaches the removal of desire and lust for form, feeling,

sn22.2:10.1.verse: If those who acquired and kept unskillful qualities were to live happily in the present life, free of distress, anguish, and fever; and if, when their body breaks up, after death, they could expect to go to a good place, the Buddha would not praise giving up unskillful qualities.

sn22.2:10.2.verse: But since those who acquire and keep unskillful qualities live unhappily in the present life, full of distress, anguish, and fever; and since, when their body breaks up, after death, they can expect to go to a bad place, the Buddha praises giving up unskillful qualities.

sn22.2:11.1.verse: If those who embraced and kept skillful qualities were to live unhappily in the present life, full of distress, anguish, and fever; and if, when their body breaks up, after death, they could expect to go to a bad place, the Buddha would not praise embracing skillful qualities.

sn22.2:11.2.verse: But since those who embrace and keep skillful qualities live happily in the present life, free of distress, anguish, and fever; and since, when their body breaks up, after death, they can expect to go to a good place, the Buddha praises embracing skillful qualities.”

sn22.2:12.1.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

sn22.2:12.2.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Sāriputta said.

sn22.3:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis near Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain.

sn22.3:1.3.verse: Then the householder Hāliddikāni went up to Venerable Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn22.3:1.4.verse: “Sir, this was said by the Buddha in the Chapter of the Eights, in ‘The Questions of Māgandiya’:

sn22.3:2.1.verse: ‘After leaving their bastion to migrate without abode,

sn22.3:2.2.verse: a sage doesn’t get close to anyone in town.

sn22.3:2.3.verse: Rid of sensual pleasures, not expecting,

sn22.3:2.4.verse: they wouldn’t get in arguments with people.’

sn22.3:3.1.verse: How should we see the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement?”

sn22.3:4.1.verse: “Householder, the form element is a bastion for consciousness.

sn22.3:4.2.verse: One whose consciousness is shackled by greed for the form element is called a migrant going from bastion to bastion.

sn22.3:4.3.verse: The feeling element is a bastion for consciousness.

sn22.3:4.4.verse: One whose consciousness is shackled to greed for the feeling element is called a migrant going from bastion to bastion.

sn22.3:4.5.verse: The perception element is a bastion for consciousness.

sn22.3:4.6.verse: One whose consciousness is shackled to greed for the perception element is called a migrant going from bastion to bastion.

sn22.3:4.7.verse: The choices element is a bastion for consciousness.

sn22.3:4.8.verse: One whose consciousness is shackled to greed for the choices element is called a migrant going from bastion to bastion.

sn22.3:4.9.verse: That’s how one is a migrant going from  bastion to bastion.

sn22.3:5.1.verse: And how is one a migrant with no bastion?

sn22.3:5.2.verse: The Realized One has given up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for the form element; any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies. He has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn22.3:5.3.verse: That’s why the Realized One is called a migrant with no bastion.

sn22.3:5.4.verse: The Realized One has given up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for the feeling element …

sn22.3:5.7.verse: the consciousness element; any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies. He has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn22.3:5.8.verse: That’s why the Realized One is called a migrant with no bastion.

sn22.3:5.9.verse: That’s how one is a migrant with no bastion.

sn22.3:6.1.verse: And how is one a migrant going from abode to abode?

sn22.3:6.2.verse: Shackled to chasing the abodes that are the features of sights, one is called a migrant going from abode to abode.

sn22.3:6.3.verse: Shackled to chasing the abodes that are the features of sounds …

sn22.3:6.7.verse: thoughts, one is called a migrant going from abode to abode.

sn22.3:6.8.verse: That’s how one is a migrant going from abode to abode.

sn22.3:7.1.verse: And how is one a migrant without abode?

sn22.3:7.2.verse: The Realized One has given up being shackled to chasing the abodes that are the features of  sights. He has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn22.3:7.3.verse: That’s why the Realized One is called a migrant without abode.

sn22.3:7.4.verse: The Realized One has given up being shackled to chasing the abodes that are the features of sounds …

sn22.3:7.8.verse: ideas. He has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn22.3:7.9.verse: That’s why the Realized One is called a migrant without abode.

sn22.3:7.10.verse: That’s how one is a migrant without abode.

sn22.3:8.1.verse: And how does one get close to people in town?

sn22.3:8.2.verse: It’s when someone mixes closely with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows—happy when they’re happy and sad when they’re sad—and getting themselves involved in their business.

sn22.3:8.3.verse: That’s how one gets close to people in town.

sn22.3:9.1.verse: And how does one not get close to people in town?

sn22.3:9.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t mix closely with laypeople, not sharing their joys and sorrows—not happy when they’re happy or sad when they’re sad—and not getting themselves involved in their business.

sn22.3:9.3.verse: That’s how one doesn’t get close to people in town.

sn22.3:10.1.verse: And how is one not rid of sensual pleasures?

sn22.3:10.2.verse: It’s when someone isn’t rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

sn22.3:10.3.verse: That’s how one is not rid of sensual pleasures.

sn22.3:11.1.verse: And how is one rid of sensual pleasures?

sn22.3:11.2.verse: It’s when someone is rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for sensual pleasures.

sn22.3:11.3.verse: That’s how one is rid of sensual pleasures.

sn22.3:12.3.verse: ‘In the future, may I be of such form, such feeling, such perception, such choices, and such consciousness!’

sn22.3:13.1.verse: And how is one not expecting?

sn22.3:13.3.verse: ‘In the future, may I be of such form, such feeling, such perception, such choices, and such consciousness!’

sn22.3:13.4.verse: That’s how one is not expecting.

sn22.3:14.1.verse: And how does one argue with people?

sn22.3:14.2.verse: It’s when someone takes part in this sort of discussion:

sn22.3:14.3.verse: ‘You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. You said last what you should have said first. You said first what you should have said last. I stay on topic, you don’t. What you’ve thought so much about has been disproved. Your doctrine is refuted. Go on, save your doctrine! You’re trapped; get yourself out of this—if you can!’

sn22.3:14.4.verse: That’s how one argues with people.

sn22.3:15.1.verse: And how does one not argue with people?

sn22.3:15.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t take part in this sort of discussion:

sn22.3:15.3.verse: ‘You don’t understand this teaching and training … get yourself out of this—if you can!’

sn22.3:15.4.verse: That’s how one doesn’t argue with people.

sn22.3:16.1.verse: So, householder, that’s how to understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha said in brief in the Chapter of the Eights, in ‘The Questions of Māgandiya’:

sn22.3:17.1.verse: ‘After leaving their bastion to migrate without abode,

sn22.3:17.2.verse: a sage doesn’t get close to anyone in town.

sn22.3:17.3.verse: Rid of sensual pleasures, not expecting,

sn22.3:17.4.verse: they wouldn’t get in arguments with people.’”

sn22.4:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis near Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain.

sn22.4:1.3.verse: Then the householder Hāliddikāni went up to Venerable Mahākaccāna … and asked him,

sn22.4:1.4.verse: “Sir, this was said by the Buddha in ‘The Questions of Sakka’:

sn22.4:1.5.verse: ‘Those ascetics and brahmins who are freed due to the ending of craving have reached the ultimate goal, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate end, and are best among gods and humans.’

sn22.4:2.1.verse: How should we see the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement?”

sn22.4:3.1.verse: “Householder, consider any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for the form element; any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies. With the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of that, the mind is said to be ‘well freed’.

sn22.4:4.1.verse: Consider any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for the feeling element …

sn22.4:4.4.verse: the consciousness element; any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies. With the ending, fading away, cessation, giving away, and letting go of that, the mind is said to be ‘well freed’.

sn22.4:5.1.verse: So, householder, that’s how to understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha said in brief in ‘The Questions of Sakka’:

sn22.4:5.2.verse: ‘Those ascetics and brahmins who are freed due to the ending of craving have reached the ultimate goal, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate end, and are best among gods and humans.’”

sn22.5:1.5.verse: A mendicant who has immersion truly understands.

sn22.5:1.7.verse: The origin and ending of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.5:2.1.verse: And what is the origin of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness?

sn22.5:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging.

sn22.5:3.1.verse: What do they approve, welcome, and keep clinging to?

sn22.5:3.2.verse: They approve, welcome, and keep clinging to form.

sn22.5:3.5.verse: Their grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

sn22.5:3.6.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

sn22.5:3.7.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

sn22.5:3.8.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn22.5:4.1.verse: They approve, welcome, and keep clinging to feeling …

sn22.5:4.7.verse: Their grasping is a requirement for continued existence.

sn22.5:4.8.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

sn22.5:4.9.verse: Rebirth is a condition that gives rise to old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.5:4.10.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn22.5:5.1.verse: This is the origin of form,

sn22.5:6.1.verse: And what is the ending of form, feeling,

sn22.5:7.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging.

sn22.5:8.1.verse: What don’t they approve, welcome, or keep clinging to?

sn22.5:8.2.verse: They don’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging to form.

sn22.5:8.3.verse: As a result, relishing of form ceases.

sn22.5:8.4.verse: When that relishing ceases, grasping ceases.

sn22.5:8.5.verse: When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. …

sn22.5:8.6.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

sn22.5:9.1.verse: They don’t approve, welcome, or keep clinging to feeling …

sn22.5:11.2.verse: As a result, relishing of consciousness ceases.

sn22.5:11.3.verse: When that relishing ceases, grasping ceases. …

sn22.5:11.4.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.

sn22.5:12.1.verse: This is the ending of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.”

sn22.6:1.3.verse: A mendicant in retreat truly understands.

sn22.6:1.5.verse: The origin and disappearance of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. …”

sn22.6:1.6.verse: (Tell in full as in the previous discourse.)

sn22.7:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you how grasping leads to anxiety, and how not grasping leads to freedom from anxiety.

sn22.7:1.3.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn22.7:2.1.verse: “And how does grasping lead to anxiety?

sn22.7:2.2.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.7:2.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.7:2.4.verse: But that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.7:2.5.verse: and consciousness latches on to the perishing of form.

sn22.7:2.6.verse: Anxieties occupy their mind, born of latching on to the perishing of form, and originating in accordance with natural principles.

sn22.7:2.7.verse: So they become frightened, worried, concerned, and anxious because of grasping.

sn22.7:5.1.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.7:5.2.verse: But that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.7:5.3.verse: and consciousness latches on to the perishing of consciousness.

sn22.7:5.4.verse: Anxieties occupy their mind, born of latching on to the perishing of consciousness, and originating in accordance with natural principles.

sn22.7:5.5.verse: So they become frightened, worried, concerned, and anxious because of grasping.

sn22.7:5.6.verse: That’s how grasping leads to anxiety.

sn22.7:6.1.verse: And how does not grasping lead to freedom from anxiety?

sn22.7:6.2.verse: It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.7:6.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.7:6.4.verse: When that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.7:6.5.verse: consciousness doesn’t latch on to the perishing of form.

sn22.7:6.6.verse: Anxieties—born of latching on to the perishing of form and originating in accordance with natural principles—don’t occupy their mind.

sn22.7:6.7.verse: So they don’t become frightened, worried, concerned, or anxious because of grasping.

sn22.7:7.1.verse: They don’t regard feeling as self …

sn22.7:8.1.verse: They don’t regard perception as self …

sn22.7:8.2.verse: They don’t regard choices as self …

sn22.7:9.1.verse: They don’t regard consciousness as self …

sn22.7:9.2.verse: When that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.7:9.3.verse: consciousness doesn’t latch on to the perishing of consciousness.

sn22.7:9.4.verse: Anxieties—born of latching on to the perishing of consciousness and originating in accordance with natural principles—don’t occupy their mind.

sn22.7:9.5.verse: So they don’t become frightened, worried, concerned, or anxious because of grasping.

sn22.7:9.6.verse: That’s how not grasping leads to freedom from anxiety.”

sn22.8:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you how grasping leads to anxiety, and how not grasping leads to freedom from anxiety.

sn22.8:1.3.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.

sn22.8:1.4.verse: And how does grasping lead to anxiety?

sn22.8:1.5.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person regards form like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

sn22.8:1.6.verse: But that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.8:1.7.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.8:1.11.verse: consciousness like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

sn22.8:1.12.verse: But that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.8:1.13.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.8:1.14.verse: That’s how grasping leads to anxiety.

sn22.8:2.1.verse: And how does not grasping lead to freedom from anxiety?

sn22.8:2.2.verse: It’s when a learned noble disciple regards form like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.8:2.3.verse: When that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.8:2.4.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.8:2.8.verse: consciousness like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.8:2.9.verse: When that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.8:2.10.verse: it doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.8:2.11.verse: That’s how not grasping leads to freedom from anxiety.”

sn22.9:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, form of the past and future is impermanent,

sn22.9:1.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past form,

sn22.9:1.5.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future form,

sn22.9:1.6.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.

sn22.9:1.14.verse: Consciousness of the past and future is impermanent,

sn22.9:1.16.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past consciousness,

sn22.9:1.17.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future consciousness,

sn22.9:1.18.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

sn22.10:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, form of the past and future is suffering,

sn22.10:1.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past form,

sn22.10:1.5.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future form,

sn22.10:1.6.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.

sn22.10:1.10.verse: Consciousness of the past and future is suffering,

sn22.10:1.12.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past consciousness,

sn22.10:1.13.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future consciousness,

sn22.10:1.14.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

sn22.11:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, form of the past and future is not-self,

sn22.11:1.4.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past form,

sn22.11:1.5.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future form,

sn22.11:1.6.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.

sn22.11:1.10.verse: Consciousness of the past and future is not-self,

sn22.11:1.12.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple is not concerned with past consciousness,

sn22.11:1.13.verse: doesn’t look forward to enjoying future consciousness,

sn22.11:1.14.verse: and they practice for the disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

sn22.12:1.4.verse: “Mendicants, form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.

sn22.12:1.5.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.12:1.6.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.12:1.7.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.13:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are suffering.

sn22.13:1.4.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.14:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

sn22.14:1.3.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.14:1.4.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.14:1.5.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.15:1.5.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.15:1.15.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.15:1.17.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.16:1.4.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.16:1.10.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.16:1.12.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.17:1.3.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.17:1.8.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.17:1.10.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.18:1.3.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to form is also impermanent.

sn22.18:1.4.verse: Since form is produced by what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn22.18:1.13.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to consciousness is also impermanent.

sn22.18:1.14.verse: Since consciousness is produced by what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn22.18:1.16.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.19:1.3.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to form is also suffering.

sn22.19:1.4.verse: Since form is produced by what is suffering, how could it be happiness?

sn22.19:1.9.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to consciousness is also suffering.

sn22.19:1.10.verse: Since consciousness is produced by what is suffering, how could it be happiness?

sn22.19:1.12.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.20:1.3.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to form is also not-self.

sn22.20:1.4.verse: Since form is produced by what is not-self, how could it be self?

sn22.20:1.9.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to consciousness is also not-self.

sn22.20:1.10.verse: Since consciousness is produced by what is not-self, how could it be self?

sn22.20:1.12.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.21:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn22.21:1.4.verse: The cessation of what things does this refer to?”

sn22.21:1.5.verse: “Ānanda, form is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

sn22.21:1.6.verse: Its cessation is what ‘cessation’ refers to.

sn22.21:1.12.verse: Consciousness is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.

sn22.21:1.13.verse: Its cessation is what ‘cessation’ refers to.

sn22.21:1.14.verse: When they speak of ‘cessation’, its the cessation of these things that this refers to.”

sn22.22:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the burden, the bearer of the burden, the taking up of the burden, and the putting down of the burden.

sn22.22:1.5.verse: The five grasping aggregates, it should be said.

sn22.22:1.7.verse: The grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.22:2.1.verse: And who is the bearer of the burden?

sn22.22:2.2.verse: The individual, it should be said;

sn22.22:2.3.verse: the venerable of such name and such clan.

sn22.22:2.4.verse: This is called the bearer of the burden.

sn22.22:3.1.verse: And what is the taking up of the burden?

sn22.22:3.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

sn22.22:3.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn22.22:3.4.verse: This is called the taking up of the burden.

sn22.22:4.1.verse: And what is the putting down of the burden?

sn22.22:4.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn22.22:4.3.verse: This is called the putting down of the burden.”

sn22.22:5.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn22.22:5.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn22.22:6.2.verse: and the individual is the bearer of the burden.

sn22.22:6.3.verse: Taking up the burden is suffering in the world,

sn22.22:6.4.verse: and putting the burden down is happiness.

sn22.22:7.1.verse: When the heavy burden is put down

sn22.22:7.3.verse: one who has plucked out craving, root and all,

sn22.23:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the things that should be completely understood, and complete understanding.

sn22.23:1.4.verse: And what things should be completely understood?

sn22.23:1.5.verse: Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.23:1.6.verse: These are called the things that should be completely understood.

sn22.23:1.8.verse: The ending of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn22.24:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, without directly knowing and completely understanding form, without dispassion for it and giving it up, you can’t end suffering.

sn22.24:1.3.verse: Without directly knowing and completely understanding feeling …

sn22.24:1.6.verse: consciousness, without dispassion for it and giving it up, you can’t end suffering.

sn22.24:1.7.verse: By directly knowing and completely understanding form, having dispassion for it and giving it up, you can end suffering.

sn22.24:1.8.verse: By directly knowing and completely understanding feeling …

sn22.24:1.11.verse: consciousness, having dispassion for it and giving it up, you can end suffering.”

sn22.25:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, give up desire and greed for form.

sn22.25:1.3.verse: Thus that form will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

sn22.25:1.4.verse: Give up desire and greed for feeling …

sn22.25:1.11.verse: Thus that consciousness will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.”

sn22.26:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

sn22.26:1.3.verse: ‘What’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form …

sn22.26:1.9.verse: ‘The pleasure and happiness that arise from form: this is its gratification.

sn22.26:1.10.verse: That form is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

sn22.26:1.11.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for form: this is its escape.

sn22.26:1.12.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling …

sn22.26:1.20.verse: That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

sn22.26:1.21.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for consciousness: this is its escape.’

sn22.26:2.1.verse: As long as I didn’t truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are, I didn’t announce my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

sn22.26:2.2.verse: But when I did truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape in this way for what they are, I announced my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

sn22.26:2.4.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

sn22.26:2.5.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

sn22.27:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I went in search of form’s gratification,

sn22.27:1.4.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of form’s gratification.

sn22.27:1.5.verse: I went in search of form’s drawback,

sn22.27:1.7.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of form’s drawback.

sn22.27:1.8.verse: I went in search of form’s escape,

sn22.27:1.10.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of form’s escape.

sn22.27:1.11.verse: I went in search of the gratification of feeling …

sn22.27:1.16.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of consciousness’s gratification.

sn22.27:1.17.verse: I went in search of consciousness’s drawback,

sn22.27:1.19.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of consciousness’s drawback.

sn22.27:1.20.verse: I went in search of consciousness’s escape,

sn22.27:1.22.verse: I’ve seen clearly with wisdom the full extent of consciousness’s escape.

sn22.27:1.23.verse: As long as I didn’t truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape for what they are, I didn’t announce my supreme perfect awakening …

sn22.27:1.24.verse: But when I did truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape for what they are, I announced my supreme perfect awakening …

sn22.27:1.25.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

sn22.27:1.26.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

sn22.28:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, if there were no gratification in form, sentient beings wouldn’t be aroused by it.

sn22.28:1.3.verse: But since there is gratification in form, sentient beings are aroused by it.

sn22.28:1.4.verse: If form had no drawback, sentient beings wouldn’t grow disillusioned with it.

sn22.28:1.5.verse: But since form has a drawback, sentient beings do grow disillusioned with it.

sn22.28:1.6.verse: If there were no escape from form, sentient beings wouldn’t escape from it.

sn22.28:1.7.verse: But since there is an escape from form, sentient beings do escape from it.

sn22.28:1.8.verse: If there were no gratification in feeling …

sn22.28:1.12.verse: consciousness, sentient beings wouldn’t be aroused by it.

sn22.28:1.13.verse: But since there is gratification in consciousness, sentient beings are aroused by it.

sn22.28:1.14.verse: If consciousness had no drawback, sentient beings wouldn’t grow disillusioned with it.

sn22.28:1.15.verse: But since consciousness has a drawback, sentient beings do grow disillusioned with it.

sn22.28:1.16.verse: If there were no escape from consciousness, sentient beings wouldn’t escape from it.

sn22.28:1.17.verse: But since there is an escape from consciousness, sentient beings do escape from it.

sn22.28:2.1.verse: As long as sentient beings don’t truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape for what they are, they haven’t escaped from this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—and they don’t live detached, liberated, with mind free of limits.

sn22.28:2.3.verse: But when sentient beings truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape for what they are, they’ve escaped from this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—and they live detached, liberated, with mind free of limits.”

sn22.29:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, if you take pleasure in form, you take pleasure in suffering.

sn22.29:1.3.verse: If you take pleasure in suffering, you’re not free from suffering, I say.

sn22.29:1.4.verse: If you take pleasure in feeling …

sn22.29:1.7.verse: consciousness, you take pleasure in suffering.

sn22.29:1.8.verse: If you take pleasure in suffering, you’re not free from suffering, I say.

sn22.29:1.9.verse: If you don’t take pleasure in form, you don’t take pleasure in suffering.

sn22.29:1.10.verse: If you don’t take pleasure in suffering, you’re free from suffering, I say.

sn22.29:1.11.verse: If you don’t take pleasure in feeling …

sn22.29:1.14.verse: consciousness, you don’t take pleasure in suffering.

sn22.29:1.15.verse: If you don’t take pleasure in suffering, you’re free from suffering, I say.”

sn22.30:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, the arising, continuation, and manifestation and regeneration of form is the arising of suffering, the continuation of diseases, and the manifestation of old age and death.

sn22.30:1.3.verse: The arising, continuation, and manifestation and regeneration of feeling …

sn22.30:1.6.verse: consciousness is the arising of suffering, the continuation of diseases, and the manifestation of old age and death.

sn22.30:1.7.verse: The cessation, settling, and disappearance of form is the cessation of suffering, the settling of diseases, and the disappearance of old age and death.

sn22.30:1.8.verse: The cessation, settling, and disappearance of feeling …

sn22.30:1.11.verse: consciousness is the cessation of suffering, the settling of diseases, and the disappearance of old age and death.”

sn22.31:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you gloom and the root of gloom.

sn22.31:1.5.verse: Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are gloom.

sn22.31:1.7.verse: And what is the root of gloom?

sn22.31:1.8.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

sn22.31:1.9.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn22.31:1.10.verse: This is called the root of gloom.”

sn22.32:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you what is brittle and what is not brittle.

sn22.32:1.4.verse: And what is brittle? What is not brittle?

sn22.32:1.6.verse: but its cessation, settling, and disappearance is not brittle.

sn22.32:1.13.verse: but its cessation, settling, and disappearance is not brittle.”

sn22.33:1.3.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.33:1.5.verse: Form isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.33:1.6.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.33:1.12.verse: Consciousness isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.33:1.13.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.33:2.1.verse: Suppose a person was to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do what they want with them.

sn22.33:2.3.verse: ‘This person is carrying us off, burning us, or doing what they want with us’?”

sn22.33:2.6.verse: Because to us that’s neither self nor belonging to self.”

sn22.33:2.7.verse: “In the same way, mendicants, form isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.33:2.8.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.33:2.13.verse: Consciousness isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.33:2.14.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.”

sn22.34:1.3.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.34:1.5.verse: Form isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.34:1.6.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.34:1.10.verse: Consciousness isn’t yours: give it up.

sn22.34:1.11.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn22.34:1.13.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.”

sn22.35:1.2.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn22.35:1.3.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn22.35:1.5.verse: “Mendicant, you’re reckoned by what you have an underlying tendency for.

sn22.35:1.6.verse: You’re not reckoned by what you have no underlying tendency for.”

sn22.35:2.1.verse: “But how do you see the detailed meaning of my brief statement?”

sn22.35:2.2.verse: “If you have an underlying tendency for form, you’re reckoned by that.

sn22.35:2.3.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.35:2.7.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for form, you’re not reckoned by that.

sn22.35:2.8.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.35:2.11.verse: consciousness, you’re not reckoned by that.

sn22.35:2.12.verse: That’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

sn22.35:3.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of what I’ve said in brief like this.

sn22.35:3.3.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for form, you’re reckoned by that.

sn22.35:3.4.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.35:3.8.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for form, you’re not reckoned by that.

sn22.35:3.9.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.35:3.12.verse: consciousness, you’re not reckoned by that.

sn22.35:3.13.verse: This is how to see the detailed meaning of what I said in brief.”

sn22.35:4.1.verse: And then that mendicant approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn22.35:5.1.verse: Then that mendicant, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn22.35:5.2.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn22.35:5.3.verse: And that mendicant became one of the perfected.

sn22.36:1.2.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn22.36:1.3.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn22.36:1.4.verse: “Mendicant, you’re measured against what you have an underlying tendency for,

sn22.36:1.5.verse: and you’re reckoned by what you’re measured against.

sn22.36:1.6.verse: You’re not measured against what you have no underlying tendency for,

sn22.36:1.7.verse: and you’re not reckoned by what you’re not measured against.”

sn22.36:2.1.verse: “But how do you see the detailed meaning of my brief statement?”

sn22.36:2.2.verse: “If you have an underlying tendency for form, you’re measured against that,

sn22.36:2.3.verse: and you’re reckoned by what you’re measured against.

sn22.36:2.4.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.36:2.8.verse: and you’re reckoned by what you’re measured against.

sn22.36:2.9.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for form, you’re not measured against that,

sn22.36:2.10.verse: and you’re not reckoned by what you’re not measured against.

sn22.36:2.11.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.36:2.14.verse: consciousness, you’re not measured against that,

sn22.36:2.15.verse: and you’re not reckoned by what you’re not measured against.

sn22.36:2.16.verse: That’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”

sn22.36:3.2.verse: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of what I’ve said in brief like this.

sn22.36:3.3.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for form, you’re measured against that,

sn22.36:3.4.verse: and you’re reckoned by what you’re measured against.

sn22.36:3.5.verse: If you have an underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.36:3.9.verse: and you’re reckoned by what you’re measured against.

sn22.36:3.10.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for form, you’re not measured against that,

sn22.36:3.11.verse: and you’re not reckoned by what you’re not measured against.

sn22.36:3.12.verse: If you have no underlying tendency for feeling …

sn22.36:3.15.verse: consciousness, you’re not measured against that,

sn22.36:3.16.verse: and you’re not reckoned by what you’re not measured against.

sn22.36:3.17.verse: This is how to see the detailed meaning of what I said in brief.” …

sn22.36:3.18.verse: And that mendicant became one of the perfected.

sn22.37:1.3.verse: sitting to one side, the Buddha said to him:

sn22.37:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, suppose they were to ask you:

sn22.37:2.2.verse: ‘Reverend Ānanda, what are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident?’

sn22.37:2.4.verse: “Sir, suppose they were to ask me:

sn22.37:2.5.verse: ‘What are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident?’

sn22.37:2.7.verse: ‘Reverend, the arising of form is evident, its vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.37:2.11.verse: consciousness is evident, its vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.37:2.12.verse: These are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.’

sn22.37:2.13.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.”

sn22.37:3.2.verse: The arising of form is evident, its vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.37:3.6.verse: consciousness is evident, its vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.37:3.7.verse: These are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.37:3.8.verse: That’s how you should answer such a question.”

sn22.38:1.2.verse: Sitting to one side, the Buddha said to Ānanda:

sn22.38:2.1.verse: “Ānanda, suppose they were to ask you:

sn22.38:2.2.verse: ‘Reverend Ānanda, what are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident?

sn22.38:2.3.verse: What are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident?

sn22.38:2.4.verse: What are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting are evident?’

sn22.38:2.6.verse: “Sir, suppose they were to ask me:

sn22.38:2.7.verse: ‘Reverend Ānanda, what are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident?

sn22.38:2.8.verse: What are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident?

sn22.38:2.9.verse: What are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting are evident?’

sn22.38:2.11.verse: ‘Whatever form has passed, ceased, and perished,

sn22.38:2.12.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:2.18.verse: consciousness has passed, ceased, and perished,

sn22.38:2.19.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:2.20.verse: These are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:3.1.verse: Whatever form is not yet born, and has not yet appeared,

sn22.38:3.2.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:3.8.verse: consciousness is not yet born, and has not yet appeared,

sn22.38:3.9.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:3.10.verse: These are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:4.1.verse: Whatever form has been born, and has appeared,

sn22.38:4.2.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.38:4.7.verse: consciousness has been born, and has appeared, its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting are evident.

sn22.38:4.8.verse: These are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.’

sn22.38:4.9.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.”

sn22.38:5.2.verse: Whatever form has passed, ceased, and perished,

sn22.38:5.3.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:5.7.verse: consciousness has passed, ceased, and perished,

sn22.38:5.8.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:5.9.verse: These are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting were evident.

sn22.38:6.1.verse: Whatever form is not yet born, and has not yet appeared,

sn22.38:6.2.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:6.6.verse: consciousness is not yet born, and has not yet appeared,

sn22.38:6.7.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:6.8.verse: These are the things for which arising, vanishing, and change while persisting will be evident.

sn22.38:7.1.verse: Whatever form has been born, and has appeared,

sn22.38:7.2.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting are evident.

sn22.38:7.6.verse: consciousness has been born, and has appeared,

sn22.38:7.7.verse: its arising, vanishing, and change while persisting are evident.

sn22.38:7.8.verse: These are the things for which arising is evident, vanishing is evident, and change while persisting is evident.

sn22.38:7.9.verse: That’s how you should answer such a question.”

sn22.39:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant is practicing in line with the teaching, this is what’s in line with the teaching.

sn22.39:1.3.verse: They should live full of disillusionment for form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.39:1.4.verse: Living in this way, they completely understand form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.39:1.5.verse: Completely understanding form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness, they’re freed from these things.

sn22.39:1.6.verse: They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re freed from suffering, I say.”

sn22.40:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant is practicing in line with the teaching, this is what’s in line with the teaching. They should meditate observing impermanence in form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. …

sn22.40:1.3.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.”

sn22.41:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant is practicing in line with the teaching, this is what’s in line with the teaching. They should meditate observing suffering in form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. …

sn22.41:1.3.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.”

sn22.42:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when a mendicant is practicing in line with the teaching, this is what’s in line with the teaching. They should meditate observing not-self in form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. …

sn22.42:1.3.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.”

sn22.43:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, be your own island, your own refuge, with no other refuge. Let the teaching be your island and your refuge, with no other refuge.

sn22.43:1.3.verse: When you live like this, you should examine rationally: ‘From what are sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress born and produced?’

sn22.43:2.1.verse: And, mendicants, from what are sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress born and produced?

sn22.43:2.2.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.43:2.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.43:2.4.verse: But that form of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.43:2.5.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.43:2.11.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.43:2.12.verse: But that consciousness of theirs decays and perishes,

sn22.43:2.13.verse: which gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.43:3.1.verse: Sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are given up when you understand the impermanence of form—its perishing, fading away, and cessation—and you truly see with right understanding that all form, whether past or present, is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

sn22.43:3.2.verse: When these things are given up there’s no anxiety. Without anxiety you live happily. A mendicant who lives happily is said to be quenched in that respect.

sn22.43:3.3.verse: Sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are given up when you understand the impermanence of feeling …

sn22.43:3.8.verse: consciousness—its perishing, fading away, and cessation—and you truly see with right understanding that all consciousness, whether past or present, is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

sn22.43:3.9.verse: When these things are given up there’s no anxiety. Without anxiety you live happily. A mendicant who lives happily is said to be quenched in that respect.”

sn22.44:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the practice that leads to the origin of substantial reality and the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.44:1.4.verse: And what is the practice that leads to the origin of substantial reality?

sn22.44:1.5.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.44:1.6.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.44:1.10.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.44:1.11.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the origin of substantial reality.

sn22.44:1.12.verse: And that’s why it’s called a way of regarding things that leads to the origin of suffering.

sn22.44:2.1.verse: And what is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality?

sn22.44:2.2.verse: It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.44:2.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.44:2.4.verse: They don’t regard feeling as self …

sn22.44:2.5.verse: They don’t regard perception as self …

sn22.44:2.6.verse: They don’t regard choices as self …

sn22.44:2.7.verse: They don’t regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.44:2.8.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.44:2.9.verse: And that’s why it’s called a way of regarding things that leads to the cessation of suffering.”

sn22.45:1.5.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.45:1.6.verse: Seeing truly with right understanding like this, the mind becomes dispassionate and freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.45:1.13.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.45:1.14.verse: Seeing truly with right understanding like this, the mind becomes dispassionate and freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.45:1.15.verse: If a mendicant’s mind is dispassionate toward the form element, the feeling element,

sn22.45:1.18.verse: and the consciousness element, it’s freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.45:1.19.verse: Being free, it’s stable. Being stable, it’s content. Being content, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

sn22.45:1.20.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.46:1.5.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.46:1.12.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.46:2.1.verse: Seeing truly with right understanding like this, they have no theories about the first beginning.

sn22.46:2.2.verse: Not having theories about the first beginning, they have no theories about the final end.

sn22.46:2.3.verse: Not having theories about the final end, they don’t obstinately stick to them.

sn22.46:2.4.verse: Not misapprehending, the mind becomes dispassionate toward form,

sn22.46:2.8.verse: and consciousness; it’s freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.46:2.9.verse: Being free, it’s stable. Being stable, it’s content. Being content, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

sn22.46:2.10.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.47:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, whatever ascetics and brahmins regard various kinds of things as self, all regard the five grasping aggregates, or one of them.

sn22.47:1.4.verse: It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.47:1.5.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.47:1.9.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.47:2.1.verse: So they’re not rid of this way of regarding things, and the conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.47:2.2.verse: As long as they’re not rid of the conceit ‘I am’, the five faculties are conceived—

sn22.47:2.3.verse: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

sn22.47:2.4.verse: The mind, ideas, and the element of ignorance are all present.

sn22.47:2.5.verse: Struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, an unlearned ordinary person thinks ‘I am’,

sn22.47:2.13.verse: ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient’.

sn22.47:3.1.verse: The five faculties stay right where they are.

sn22.47:3.2.verse: But a learned noble disciple gives up ignorance about them and gives rise to knowledge.

sn22.47:3.3.verse: With the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, they don’t think ‘I am’,

sn22.47:3.11.verse: ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient’.”

sn22.48:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.48:1.4.verse: And what are the five aggregates?

sn22.48:1.5.verse: Any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of form.

sn22.48:1.6.verse: Any kind of feeling at all …

sn22.48:1.7.verse: Any kind of perception at all …

sn22.48:1.8.verse: Any kind of choices at all …

sn22.48:1.9.verse: Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of consciousness.

sn22.48:1.10.verse: These are called the five aggregates.

sn22.48:2.1.verse: And what are the five grasping aggregates?

sn22.48:2.2.verse: Any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near, which is accompanied by defilements and fuels grasping: this is called the grasping aggregate of form.

sn22.48:2.3.verse: Any kind of feeling at all …

sn22.48:2.4.verse: Any kind of perception at all …

sn22.48:2.5.verse: Any kind of choices at all …

sn22.48:2.6.verse: Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near, which is accompanied by defilements and fuels grasping: this is called the grasping aggregate of consciousness.

sn22.48:2.7.verse: These are called the five grasping aggregates.”

sn22.49:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn22.49:1.3.verse: Then the householder Soṇa went up to the Buddha …

sn22.49:2.1.verse: “Soṇa, there are ascetics and brahmins who—based on form, which is impermanent, suffering, and perishable—regard themselves thus: ‘I’m better’,

sn22.49:2.4.verse: What is that but a failure to see truly?

sn22.49:2.14.verse: consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and perishable, they regard themselves thus: ‘I’m better’,

sn22.49:2.17.verse: What is that but a failure to see truly?

sn22.49:3.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who—based on form, which is impermanent, suffering, and perishable—don’t regard themselves thus: ‘I’m better’,

sn22.49:3.4.verse: What is that but seeing truly?

sn22.49:3.8.verse: consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and perishable, they don’t regard themselves thus: ‘I’m better’,

sn22.49:3.11.verse: What is that but seeing truly?

sn22.49:4.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
