sn22.72:1.12.verse: That’s how to know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed.” …

sn22.72:1.13.verse: And Venerable Surādha became one of the perfected.

sn22.73:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person doesn’t truly understand the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.73:1.7.verse: A learned noble disciple does truly understand the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.74:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person doesn’t truly understand the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.74:1.7.verse: A learned noble disciple does truly understand the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.75:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, a learned noble disciple truly understands the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.76:1.5.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.76:1.12.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.76:2.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.76:2.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.76:2.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.76:2.4.verse: As far as there are abodes of sentient beings, even up until the pinnacle of existence, the perfected ones are the foremost and the best.”

sn22.76:3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn22.76:3.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn22.76:4.1.verse: “Oh! How happy are the perfected ones!

sn22.76:4.2.verse: Craving is not found in them,

sn22.76:4.3.verse: the conceit ‘I am’ is cut off,

sn22.76:4.4.verse: and the net of delusion is shattered.

sn22.76:5.3.verse: nothing in the world clings to them,

sn22.76:6.2.verse: their domain is the seven good qualities.

sn22.76:7.2.verse: and trained in the three trainings,

sn22.76:7.4.verse: with fear and dread given up.

sn22.76:8.2.verse: those giants are immersed in samādhi.

sn22.76:8.3.verse: They are the best in the world,

sn22.76:8.4.verse: craving is not found in them.

sn22.76:9.2.verse: ‘This bag of bones is my last.’

sn22.76:9.4.verse: in the core of the spiritual path.

sn22.76:10.1.verse: They do not waver due to the discriminations,

sn22.76:10.3.verse: They’ve reached the level of the tamed,

sn22.76:10.4.verse: in the world, they’re the winners.

sn22.76:11.2.verse: relishing is not found in them.

sn22.76:11.4.verse: ‘The awakened are supreme in the world!’”

sn22.77:1.5.verse: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.77:2.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.77:2.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.77:2.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.77:2.4.verse: As far as there are abodes of sentient beings, even up until the pinnacle of existence, the perfected ones are the foremost and the best.”

sn22.78:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, toward evening the lion, king of beasts, emerges from his den, yawns, surveys the four quarters, and roars his lion’s roar three times. Then he sets out on the hunt.

sn22.78:1.3.verse: And whatever animals hear the roar of the lion, king of beasts, are typically filled with fear, awe, and terror. They return to their lairs, be they in a hole, the water, or a wood; and the birds take to the air.

sn22.78:1.4.verse: Even the royal elephants, bound with strong harnesses in the villages, towns, and capital cities, break apart their bonds, and urinate and defecate in terror as they flee here and there.

sn22.78:1.5.verse: That’s how powerful is the lion, king of beasts, over animals, how illustrious and mighty.

sn22.78:2.1.verse: In the same way, when a Realized One arises in the world—perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed—he teaches the Dhamma:

sn22.78:2.2.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn22.78:2.6.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn22.78:2.7.verse: Now, there are gods who are long-lived, beautiful, and very happy, lasting long in their divine palaces. When they hear this teaching by the Realized One, they’re typically filled with fear, awe, and terror.

sn22.78:2.8.verse: ‘Oh no! It turns out we’re impermanent, though we thought we were permanent!

sn22.78:2.9.verse: It turns out we don’t last, though we thought we were everlasting!

sn22.78:2.10.verse: It turns out we’re transient, though we thought we were eternal!

sn22.78:2.11.verse: It turns out that we’re impermanent, not lasting, transient, and included within substantial reality.’

sn22.78:2.12.verse: That’s how powerful is the Realized One in the world with its gods, how illustrious and mighty.”

sn22.78:2.13.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn22.78:2.14.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn22.78:3.2.verse: in all the world with its gods,

sn22.78:3.3.verse: rolls forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn22.78:4.4.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

sn22.78:5.3.verse: are afraid and full of terror,

sn22.78:5.4.verse: like the other beasts when they hear a lion.

sn22.78:6.3.verse: So they say when they hear the word

sn22.78:6.4.verse: of the perfected one, free and unaffected.”

sn22.79:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, whatever ascetics and brahmins recollect many kinds of past lives, all recollect the five grasping aggregates, or one of them.

sn22.79:1.4.verse: ‘I had such form in the past.’

sn22.79:1.5.verse: Recollecting thus, it’s only form that they recollect.

sn22.79:1.11.verse: Recollecting thus, it’s only consciousness that they recollect.

sn22.79:2.1.verse: And why do you call it form?

sn22.79:2.2.verse: It’s deformed; that’s why it’s called ‘form’.

sn22.79:2.4.verse: Deformed by cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and deformed by the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles.

sn22.79:2.5.verse: It’s deformed; that’s why it’s called ‘form’.

sn22.79:3.1.verse: And why do you call it feeling?

sn22.79:3.2.verse: It feels; that’s why it’s called ‘feeling’.

sn22.79:3.4.verse: It feels pleasure, pain, and neutral.

sn22.79:3.5.verse: It feels; that’s why it’s called ‘feeling’.

sn22.79:4.1.verse: And why do you call it perception?

sn22.79:4.2.verse: It perceives; that’s why it’s called ‘perception’.

sn22.79:4.4.verse: It perceives blue, yellow, red, and white.

sn22.79:4.5.verse: It perceives; that’s why it’s called ‘perception’.

sn22.79:5.1.verse: And why do you call them choices?

sn22.79:5.2.verse: Choices produce conditioned phenomena; that’s why they’re called ‘choices’.

sn22.79:5.3.verse: And what are the conditioned phenomena that they produce?

sn22.79:5.4.verse: Form is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into form. Feeling is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into feeling. Perception is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into perception. Choices are conditioned phenomena; choices are what make them into choices. Consciousness is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into consciousness.

sn22.79:5.5.verse: Choices produce conditioned phenomena; that’s why they’re called ‘choices’.

sn22.79:6.1.verse: And why do you call it consciousness?

sn22.79:6.2.verse: It cognizes; that’s why it’s called ‘consciousness’.

sn22.79:6.4.verse: It cognizes sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, hot, mild, salty, and bland.

sn22.79:6.5.verse: It cognizes; that’s why it’s called ‘consciousness’.

sn22.79:7.1.verse: A learned noble disciple reflects on this:

sn22.79:7.3.verse: In the past I was also bitten by form just like now.

sn22.79:7.4.verse: If I were to look forward to enjoying form in the future, I’d be bitten by form in the future just as I am today.’

sn22.79:7.5.verse: Reflecting like this they are not concerned with past form,

sn22.79:7.6.verse: they don’t look forward to enjoying future form,

sn22.79:7.7.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.

sn22.79:10.2.verse: In the past I was also bitten by consciousness just like now.

sn22.79:10.3.verse: If I were to look forward to enjoying consciousness in the future, I’d be bitten by consciousness in the future just as I am today.’

sn22.79:10.5.verse: Reflecting like this they are not concerned with past consciousness,

sn22.79:10.6.verse: they don’t look forward to enjoying future consciousness,

sn22.79:10.7.verse: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.

sn22.79:11.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.79:11.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn22.79:11.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.79:11.14.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.79:11.16.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn22.79:11.17.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.79:11.19.verse: “So you should truly see any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.79:11.20.verse: You should truly see any kind of feeling …

sn22.79:11.23.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.79:12.1.verse: This is called a noble disciple who gets rid of and doesn’t accumulate;

sn22.79:12.2.verse: who gives up and doesn’t grasp;

sn22.79:12.4.verse: who dissipates and doesn’t get clouded.

sn22.79:12.5.verse: And what things do they get rid of and not accumulate?

sn22.79:12.6.verse: They get rid of form and don’t accumulate it.

sn22.79:12.11.verse: And what things do they give up and not grasp?

sn22.79:12.12.verse: They give up form and don’t grasp it.

sn22.79:12.17.verse: And what things do they unmesh and not enmesh?

sn22.79:12.18.verse: They unmesh form and don’t enmesh it.

sn22.79:12.23.verse: And what things do they dissipate and not get clouded by?

sn22.79:12.24.verse: They dissipate form and don’t get clouded by it.

sn22.79:12.28.verse: consciousness and don’t get clouded by it.

sn22.79:13.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.79:13.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.79:13.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.79:14.1.verse: This is called a mendicant who neither gets rid of nor accumulates, but remains after getting rid. They neither give up nor grasp, but remain after giving up. They neither unmesh nor enmesh, but remain after unmeshing. They neither dissipate nor get clouded, but remain after dissipating.

sn22.79:14.2.verse: And what things do they neither get rid of nor accumulate, but remain after getting rid of them?

sn22.79:14.3.verse: They neither get rid of nor accumulate form, but remain after getting rid of it.

sn22.79:14.4.verse: They neither get rid of nor accumulate feeling …

sn22.79:14.7.verse: consciousness, but remain after getting rid of it.

sn22.79:14.8.verse: And what things do they neither give up nor grasp, but remain after giving them up?

sn22.79:14.9.verse: They neither give up nor grasp form, but remain after giving it up.

sn22.79:14.10.verse: They neither give up nor grasp feeling …

sn22.79:14.13.verse: consciousness, but remain after giving it up.

sn22.79:14.14.verse: And what things do they neither discard nor amass, but remain after discarding them?

sn22.79:14.15.verse: They neither unmesh nor enmesh form, but remain after unmeshing it.

sn22.79:14.16.verse: They neither unmesh nor enmesh feeling …

sn22.79:14.19.verse: consciousness, but remain after unmeshing it.

sn22.79:14.20.verse: And what things do they neither dissipate nor get clouded by, but remain after dissipating them?

sn22.79:14.21.verse: They neither dissipate nor get clouded by form, but remain after dissipating it.

sn22.79:14.22.verse: They neither dissipate nor get clouded by feeling …

sn22.79:14.25.verse: consciousness, but remain after dissipating it.

sn22.79:14.26.verse: When a mendicant’s mind is freed like this, the gods together with Indra, the Divinity, and the Progenitor worship them from afar:

sn22.79:15.2.verse: Homage to you, supreme among men!

sn22.80:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

sn22.80:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha, having dismissed the mendicant Saṅgha for some reason, robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms.

sn22.80:1.3.verse: He wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s meditation,

sn22.80:1.4.verse: plunged deep into it, and sat at the root of a young wood-apple tree to meditate.

sn22.80:2.1.verse: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

sn22.80:2.3.verse: But there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training.

sn22.80:2.4.verse: Not seeing me they may change and fall apart.

sn22.80:2.5.verse: If a young calf doesn’t see its mother it may change and fall apart. …

sn22.80:2.7.verse: Or if young seedlings don’t get water they may change and fall apart.

sn22.80:2.8.verse: In the same way, there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training.

sn22.80:2.9.verse: Not seeing me they may change and fall apart.

sn22.80:2.10.verse: Why don’t I support the mendicant Saṅgha now as I did in the past?”

sn22.80:3.1.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati knew the Buddha’s train of thought. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha.

sn22.80:3.2.verse: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:

sn22.80:3.3.verse: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

sn22.80:3.4.verse: The Buddha has purged the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn22.80:3.5.verse: But there are mendicants who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. …

sn22.80:3.11.verse: May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!

sn22.80:3.12.verse: May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

sn22.80:3.13.verse: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!”

sn22.80:4.2.verse: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing that the Buddha had consented, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

sn22.80:5.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the Banyan Tree Monastery, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

sn22.80:5.2.verse: Then he used his psychic power to will that the mendicants would come to him timidly, alone or in pairs.

sn22.80:5.3.verse: Those mendicants approached the Buddha timidly, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

sn22.80:6.1.verse: “This is the last of lifestyles, mendicants, namely relying on alms.

sn22.80:6.2.verse: The world curses you: ‘You beggar, walking bowl in hand!’

sn22.80:6.3.verse: Yet earnest gentlemen take it up for a good reason.

sn22.80:6.4.verse: Not to escape a summons by a king or a summons for a bandit, or because you were in debt or in fear, or in order to make a living.

sn22.80:6.5.verse: But because they’re swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

sn22.80:6.6.verse: And they think, ‘Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’

sn22.80:7.1.verse: That’s how this gentleman has gone forth.

sn22.80:7.2.verse: Yet they covet sensual pleasures; they’re infatuated, full of ill will and malicious intent. They are unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying mind and undisciplined faculties.

sn22.80:7.3.verse: Suppose there was a firebrand for lighting a funeral pyre, burning at both ends, and smeared with dung in the middle. It couldn’t be used as timber either in the village or the wilderness.

sn22.80:7.4.verse: I say that individual is just like this. They’ve missed out on the pleasures of the lay life, and haven’t fulfilled the goal of the ascetic life.

sn22.80:8.1.verse: There are these three unskillful thoughts.

sn22.80:8.3.verse: And where do these three unskillful thoughts cease without remainder?

sn22.80:8.4.verse: In those who meditate with their mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation; or who develop signless immersion.

sn22.80:8.5.verse: This is quite enough motivation to develop signless immersion.

sn22.80:8.6.verse: When signless immersion is developed and cultivated it is very fruitful and beneficial.

sn22.80:9.2.verse: Views favoring existence and views favoring nonexistence.

sn22.80:9.3.verse: A learned noble disciple reflects on this:

sn22.80:9.4.verse: ‘Is there anything in the world that I could grasp without fault?’

sn22.80:9.6.verse: ‘There’s nothing in the world that I could grasp without fault.

sn22.80:9.7.verse: For in grasping I would grasp only at form, feeling,

sn22.80:9.10.verse: That grasping of mine would be a condition for continued existence.

sn22.80:9.11.verse: Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.

sn22.80:9.12.verse: Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.

sn22.80:9.13.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’

sn22.80:10.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.80:10.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn22.80:10.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.80:10.15.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.81:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

sn22.81:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

sn22.81:1.3.verse: After the meal, on his return from almsround, he set his lodgings in order himself. Taking his bowl and robe, without informing his supporters or taking leave of the mendicant Saṅgha, he set out to go wandering alone, with no companion.

sn22.81:2.1.verse: Then, not long after the Buddha had left, one of the mendicants went to Venerable Ānanda and told him what had happened.

sn22.81:2.3.verse: Ānanda said, “Reverend, when the Buddha leaves like this it means he wants to stay alone.

sn22.81:2.4.verse: At this time no one should follow him.”

sn22.81:3.1.verse: Then the Buddha, traveling stage by stage, arrived at Pārileyyaka,

sn22.81:3.2.verse: where he stayed at the root of a sacred sal tree.

sn22.81:3.3.verse: Then several mendicants went up to Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.

sn22.81:3.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him,

sn22.81:3.5.verse: “Reverend, it’s been a long time since we’ve heard a Dhamma talk from the Buddha.

sn22.81:3.6.verse: We wish to hear a Dhamma talk from the Buddha.”

sn22.81:4.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda together with those mendicants went to Pārileyyaka to see the Buddha. They bowed and sat down to one side,

sn22.81:4.2.verse: and the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired them with a Dhamma talk.

sn22.81:4.3.verse: Now at that time one of the monks had the thought,

sn22.81:4.4.verse: “How do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?”

sn22.81:4.5.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the mendicants:

sn22.81:4.7.verse: I’ve analytically taught the four kinds of mindfulness meditation,

sn22.81:4.9.verse: the four bases of psychic power,

sn22.81:4.14.verse: That’s how I’ve taught the Dhamma analytically.

sn22.81:4.15.verse: Though I’ve taught the Dhamma analytically, still a certain mendicant present here has this thought:

sn22.81:4.16.verse: ‘How do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?’

sn22.81:5.1.verse: And how, mendicants, do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?

sn22.81:5.2.verse: Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.81:5.4.verse: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon.

sn22.81:5.5.verse: And what’s the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of that conditioned phenomenon?

sn22.81:5.6.verse: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.

sn22.81:5.7.verse: That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

sn22.81:5.8.verse: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:5.11.verse: and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:5.12.verse: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

sn22.81:6.1.verse: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self,

sn22.81:6.2.verse: but they still regard self as possessing form.

sn22.81:6.3.verse: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

sn22.81:7.1.verse: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form,

sn22.81:7.2.verse: but they still regard form in self.

sn22.81:7.3.verse: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

sn22.81:8.1.verse: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self,

sn22.81:8.2.verse: but they still regard self in form.

sn22.81:8.3.verse: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

sn22.81:9.1.verse: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form.

sn22.81:9.2.verse: But they regard feeling as self …

sn22.81:9.6.verse: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon.

sn22.81:9.7.verse: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon?

sn22.81:9.8.verse: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.

sn22.81:9.9.verse: That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

sn22.81:9.10.verse: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:9.14.verse: and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:9.15.verse: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

sn22.81:10.6.verse: Still, they have such a view:

sn22.81:10.7.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

sn22.81:10.8.verse: But that eternalist view is just a conditioned phenomenon.

sn22.81:10.9.verse: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon? …

sn22.81:10.10.verse: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

sn22.81:11.6.verse: Nor do they have such a view:

sn22.81:11.7.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

sn22.81:11.8.verse: Still, they have such a view:

sn22.81:11.9.verse: ‘I might not be, and it might not be mine. I will not be, and it will not be mine.’

sn22.81:11.10.verse: But that annihilationist view is just a conditioned phenomenon.

sn22.81:11.11.verse: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon? …

sn22.81:11.15.verse: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

sn22.81:12.1.verse: Perhaps they don’t regard form or feeling

sn22.81:12.5.verse: Nor do they have such a view:

sn22.81:12.6.verse: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

sn22.81:12.7.verse: Nor do they have such a view:

sn22.81:12.8.verse: ‘I might not be, and it might not be mine. I will not be, and it will not be mine.’

sn22.81:12.9.verse: Still, they have doubts and uncertainties. They’re undecided about the true teaching.

sn22.81:12.10.verse: That doubt and uncertainty, the indecision about the true teaching, is just a conditioned phenomenon.

sn22.81:12.11.verse: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon?

sn22.81:12.12.verse: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.

sn22.81:12.13.verse: That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

sn22.81:12.14.verse: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:12.18.verse: and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

sn22.81:12.19.verse: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.”

sn22.82:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, together with a large Saṅgha of monks.

sn22.82:1.2.verse: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

sn22.82:2.1.verse: Then one of the monks rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:

sn22.82:2.2.verse: “Sir, I’d like to ask the Buddha about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

sn22.82:2.3.verse: “Well then, monk, take your own seat and ask what you wish.”

sn22.82:2.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied that monk. He took his seat and said to the Buddha:

sn22.82:2.5.verse: “Sir, are these the five grasping aggregates, that is:

sn22.82:2.6.verse: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness?”

sn22.82:3.3.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

sn22.82:4.1.verse: “But sir, what is the root of these five grasping aggregates?”

sn22.82:4.2.verse: “These five grasping aggregates are rooted in desire.” …

sn22.82:4.3.verse: “But sir, is that grasping the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates? Or is grasping one thing and the five grasping aggregates another?”

sn22.82:4.4.verse: “Neither. Rather, the desire and greed for them is the grasping there.”

sn22.82:4.5.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:

sn22.82:5.1.verse: “But sir, can there be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates?”

sn22.82:5.4.verse: ‘In the future, may I be of such form, such feeling, such perception, such choices, and such consciousness!’

sn22.82:5.5.verse: That’s how there can be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates.”

sn22.82:5.6.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:

sn22.82:6.1.verse: “Sir, what is the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates?”

sn22.82:6.2.verse: “Any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of form.

sn22.82:6.3.verse: Any kind of feeling at all …

sn22.82:6.4.verse: Any kind of perception at all …

sn22.82:6.5.verse: Any kind of choices at all …

sn22.82:6.6.verse: Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of consciousness.

sn22.82:6.7.verse: That’s the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates.”

sn22.82:6.8.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:

sn22.82:7.1.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why the aggregate of form is found?

sn22.82:7.2.verse: What is the cause, what is the reason why the aggregate of feeling …

sn22.82:7.6.verse: “The four principal states are the reason why the aggregate of form is found.

sn22.82:7.7.verse: Contact is the reason why the aggregates of feeling,

sn22.82:7.10.verse: Name and form are the reasons why the aggregate of consciousness is found.”

sn22.82:7.11.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:

sn22.82:8.1.verse: “Sir, how does substantialist view come about?”

sn22.82:8.2.verse: “It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.82:8.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.82:8.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.82:8.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view comes about.”

sn22.82:8.9.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk … asked another question:

sn22.82:9.1.verse: “But sir, how does substantialist view not come about?”

sn22.82:9.2.verse: “It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.82:9.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.82:9.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.82:9.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view does not come about.”

sn22.82:9.9.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk … asked another question:

sn22.82:10.1.verse: “Sir, what’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,

sn22.82:10.6.verse: “The pleasure and happiness that arise from form: this is its gratification.

sn22.82:10.7.verse: That form is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

sn22.82:10.8.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for form: this is its escape.

sn22.82:10.9.verse: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling …

sn22.82:10.13.verse: That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

sn22.82:10.14.verse: Removing and giving up desire and greed for consciousness: this is its escape.”

sn22.82:10.15.verse: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

sn22.82:11.1.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

sn22.82:11.2.verse: “One truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.82:11.3.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn22.82:11.6.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.82:11.7.verse: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

sn22.82:12.1.verse: Now at that time one of the monks had the thought:

sn22.82:12.2.verse: “So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

sn22.82:12.3.verse: Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?”

sn22.82:12.4.verse: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the monks:

sn22.82:13.1.verse: “It’s possible that some futile person here—unknowing and ignorant, his mind dominated by craving—thinks he can overstep the Teacher’s instructions. He thinks:

sn22.82:13.2.verse: ‘So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.

sn22.82:13.3.verse: Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?’

sn22.82:13.4.verse: Now, monks, you have been educated by me in questioning with regard to all these things in all such cases.

sn22.82:14.9.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.82:14.11.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn22.82:14.12.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.82:14.16.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.82:15.1.verse: “Two on the aggregates; exactly the same; and can there be;

sn22.82:15.2.verse: on the term; and on the cause;

sn22.83:2.1.verse: “Reverends, the venerable named Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī was very helpful to me when I was just ordained.

sn22.83:2.3.verse: ‘Reverend Ānanda, the thought “I am” occurs because of grasping, not without grasping.

sn22.83:2.5.verse: The thought “I am” occurs because of grasping form,

sn22.83:3.1.verse: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. They’d look because of grasping, not without grasping.

sn22.83:3.2.verse: In the same way, the thought “I am” occurs because of grasping form,

sn22.83:4.1.verse: What do you think, Reverend Ānanda?

sn22.83:4.11.verse: They understand: “… there is nothing further for this place.”’

sn22.83:4.12.verse: Reverends, the venerable named Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī was very helpful to me when I was just ordained.

sn22.83:4.14.verse: And when I heard this teaching from Venerable Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī, I comprehended the teaching.”

sn22.84:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Tissa—the Buddha’s cousin on his father’s side—informed several mendicants:

sn22.84:1.3.verse: “Reverends, my body feels like it’s drugged. I’m disorientated, the teachings don’t spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and have doubts about the teachings.”

sn22.84:2.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

sn22.84:3.1.verse: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

sn22.84:3.2.verse: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Tissa that the Teacher summons him.”

sn22.84:3.3.verse: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Tissa and said to him,

sn22.84:3.5.verse: “Yes, reverend,” Tissa replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn22.84:3.6.verse: “Is it really true, Tissa, that you informed several mendicants that

sn22.84:3.7.verse: your body feels like it’s drugged … and you have doubts about the teachings?”

sn22.84:3.10.verse: If you’re not rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn22.84:4.3.verse: when you’re not rid of greed for form.

sn22.84:4.4.verse: If you’re not rid of greed for feeling …

sn22.84:5.3.verse: consciousness, when that consciousness decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn22.84:6.3.verse: when you’re not rid of greed for consciousness.

sn22.84:6.5.verse: If you are rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn22.84:7.3.verse: when you are rid of greed for form …

sn22.84:8.14.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.84:9.1.verse: Suppose, Tissa, there were two individuals.

sn22.84:9.2.verse: One was not skilled in the path, the other was.

sn22.84:9.3.verse: The one not skilled in the path would question the one skilled in the path,

sn22.84:9.5.verse: ‘Come, my man, this is the path.

sn22.84:9.7.verse: and you’ll see a fork in the road. Ignore the left, and take the right-hand path.

sn22.84:9.9.verse: and you’ll see a dense forest grove.

sn22.84:9.11.verse: and you’ll see an expanse of low-lying marshes.

sn22.84:9.13.verse: and you’ll see a large, steep cliff.

sn22.84:9.15.verse: and you’ll see level, cleared parkland.’

sn22.84:10.1.verse: I’ve made up this simile to make a point.

sn22.84:10.2.verse: And this is what it means.

sn22.84:10.3.verse: ‘A person who is not skilled in the path’ is a term for an ordinary unlearned person.

sn22.84:10.4.verse: ‘A person who is skilled in the path’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.

sn22.84:10.5.verse: ‘A fork in the road’ is a term for doubt.

sn22.84:10.6.verse: ‘The left-hand path’ is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is,

sn22.84:10.8.verse: ‘The right-hand path’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is,

sn22.84:10.10.verse: ‘A dense forest grove’ is a term for ignorance.

sn22.84:10.11.verse: ‘An expanse of low-lying marshes’ is a term for sensual pleasures.

sn22.84:10.12.verse: ‘A large, steep cliff’ is a term for anger and distress.

sn22.84:10.13.verse: ‘Level, cleared parkland’ is a term for extinguishment.

sn22.84:10.15.verse: I am here with advice, with support, with instruction.”

sn22.84:11.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn22.84:11.2.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Tissa approved what the Buddha said.

sn22.85:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn22.85:1.2.verse: Now at that time a mendicant named Yamaka had the following harmful misconception:

sn22.85:1.3.verse: “As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death.”

sn22.85:2.3.verse: They went to Yamaka and exchanged greetings with him.

sn22.85:2.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him,

sn22.85:3.1.verse: “Is it really true, Reverend Yamaka, that you have such a harmful misconception:

sn22.85:3.2.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

sn22.85:3.3.verse: “Yes, reverends, that’s how I understand the Buddha’s teaching.”

sn22.85:4.1.verse: “Don’t say that, Yamaka! Don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for misrepresentation of the Buddha is not good. And the Buddha would not say that.”

sn22.85:4.3.verse: But even though admonished by those mendicants, Yamaka obstinately stuck to that misconception and insisted on stating it.

sn22.85:5.1.verse: When those mendicants were unable to dissuade Yamaka from that misconception, they rose from their seats and went to see Venerable Sāriputta. They told him what had happened, and said,

sn22.85:5.4.verse: “May Venerable Sāriputta please go to the mendicant Yamaka out of sympathy.”

sn22.85:5.6.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Yamaka and exchanged greetings with him. Seated to one side he said to Yamaka:

sn22.85:6.1.verse: “Is it really true, Reverend Yamaka, that you have such a harmful misconception:

sn22.85:6.2.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

sn22.85:6.3.verse: “Yes, reverend, that’s how I understand the Buddha’s teaching.”

sn22.85:7.11.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.85:8.1.verse: What do you think, Reverend Yamaka?

sn22.85:8.2.verse: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to form?”

sn22.85:8.4.verse: “Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to feeling?” …

sn22.85:9.2.verse: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to form?”

sn22.85:9.4.verse: “Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies apart from form?”

sn22.85:9.6.verse: “Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to feeling?” …

sn22.85:10.2.verse: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to one who has form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”

sn22.85:11.2.verse: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to that one who is without form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”

sn22.85:11.4.verse: “In that case, Reverend Yamaka, since a realized one is not found by you as a genuine fact in this very life, is it cogent for you to declare:

sn22.85:11.5.verse: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

sn22.85:12.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, in my ignorance, I used to have that misconception.

sn22.85:12.2.verse: But now that I’ve heard the teaching from Venerable Sāriputta, I’ve given up that misconception, and I’ve comprehended the teaching.”

sn22.85:13.1.verse: “Reverend Yamaka, suppose they were to ask you:

sn22.85:13.2.verse: ‘When their body breaks up, after death, what happens to a perfected one, who has ended the defilements?’

sn22.85:13.4.verse: “Reverend, if they were to ask this,

sn22.85:13.9.verse: What’s suffering has ceased and disappeared.

sn22.85:13.15.verse: What’s suffering has ceased and disappeared.’

sn22.85:13.16.verse: That’s how I’d answer such a question.”

sn22.85:14.2.verse: Well then, I shall give you a simile to make the meaning even clearer.

sn22.85:14.3.verse: Suppose there was a householder or householder’s son who was rich, with a lot of money and great wealth,

sn22.85:14.5.verse: Then along comes a person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten him, and take his life.

sn22.85:14.7.verse: ‘This householder or householder’s son is rich, with a lot of money and great wealth,

sn22.85:14.9.verse: It won’t be easy to take his life by force.

sn22.85:14.10.verse: Why don’t I get close to him, then take his life?’

sn22.85:14.11.verse: So he goes up to that householder or householder’s son and says:

sn22.85:14.13.verse: They would serve that householder or householder’s son.

sn22.85:14.14.verse: They’d get up before him and go to bed after him, and be obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.

sn22.85:14.15.verse: The householder or householder’s son would consider them as a friend

sn22.85:14.18.verse: But when that person realizes that

sn22.85:14.19.verse: they’ve gained the trust of the householder or householder’s son, then, when they know he’s alone, they’d take his life with a sharp knife.

sn22.85:15.2.verse: When that person went to the householder or householder’s son and offered to

sn22.85:15.3.verse: serve him, weren’t they a killer then,

sn22.85:15.6.verse: And when they got up before him and went to bed after him, being obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely, weren’t they a killer then,

sn22.85:15.9.verse: And when, knowing he was alone, they took his life with a sharp knife, weren’t they a killer then,

sn22.85:15.13.verse: “In the same way, an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.85:15.14.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.85:15.18.verse: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.85:16.1.verse: They don’t truly understand form—which is impermanent—as impermanent.

sn22.85:17.1.verse: They don’t truly understand form—which is suffering—as suffering.

sn22.85:18.1.verse: They don’t truly understand form—which is not-self—as not-self.

sn22.85:19.1.verse: They don’t truly understand form—which is conditioned—as conditioned.

sn22.85:20.1.verse: They don’t truly understand form—which is a killer—as a killer.

sn22.85:20.5.verse: consciousness—which is a killer—as a killer.

sn22.85:21.1.verse: They’re attracted to form, grasp it, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

sn22.85:21.5.verse: consciousness, grasp it, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

sn22.85:21.6.verse: And when you’ve gotten involved with and grasped these five grasping aggregates, they lead to your lasting harm and suffering.

sn22.85:22.1.verse: A learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.85:22.2.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.85:22.6.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness,

sn22.85:22.7.verse: consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.85:23.1.verse: They truly understand form—which is impermanent—as impermanent.

sn22.85:24.1.verse: They truly understand form—which is suffering—as suffering.

sn22.85:25.1.verse: They truly understand form—which is not-self—as not-self.

sn22.85:26.1.verse: They truly understand form—which is conditioned—as conditioned.

sn22.85:27.1.verse: They truly understand form—which is a killer—as a killer.

sn22.85:27.5.verse: consciousness—which is a killer—as a killer.

sn22.85:28.1.verse: When it comes to form, they are not attracted, do not grasp, and do not fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

sn22.85:28.5.verse: When it comes to consciousness, they are not attracted, do not grasp, and do not fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

sn22.85:28.6.verse: And when you’re not attracted to and don’t grasp these five grasping aggregates, they lead to your lasting welfare and happiness.”

sn22.85:28.7.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, this is how it is when you have such venerables as spiritual companions to advise and instruct you out of kindness and sympathy.

sn22.85:28.8.verse: And after hearing this teaching by Venerable Sāriputta, my mind is freed from the defilements by not grasping.”

sn22.86:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

sn22.86:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Buddha in a wilderness hut.

sn22.86:1.3.verse: Then several wanderers of other religions went up to Venerable Anurādha and exchanged greetings with him.

sn22.86:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him:

sn22.86:1.5.verse: “Reverend Anurādha, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them in these four ways:

sn22.86:1.6.verse: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.”

sn22.86:2.1.verse: When they said this, Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers:

sn22.86:2.2.verse: “Reverends, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them other than these four ways:

sn22.86:2.3.verse: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.”

sn22.86:2.4.verse: When he said this, the wanderers said to him:

sn22.86:2.5.verse: “This mendicant must be junior, recently gone forth, or else a foolish, incompetent senior mendicant.”

sn22.86:2.6.verse: Then, after rebuking Venerable Anurādha by calling him “junior” and “foolish”, the wanderers rose from their seats and left.

sn22.86:3.1.verse: Soon after they had left, Anurādha thought:

sn22.86:3.2.verse: “If those wanderers were to inquire further,

sn22.86:3.3.verse: how should I answer them so as to repeat what the Buddha has said, and not misrepresent him with an untruth? How should I explain in line with his teaching, so that there would be no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

sn22.86:4.1.verse: Then Venerable Anurādha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him all that had happened.

sn22.86:7.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.86:7.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.86:7.16.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’
