sn22.86:12.2.verse: ‘Reverends, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them other than these four ways:

sn22.86:12.3.verse: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists’?”

sn22.86:13.2.verse: In the past, as today, what I describe is suffering and the cessation of suffering.”

sn22.87:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn22.87:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Vakkali was staying in a potter’s shed, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn22.87:1.4.verse: “Please, reverends, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

sn22.87:1.5.verse: ‘Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is sick, suffering, gravely ill. He bows with his head to your feet.’

sn22.87:1.7.verse: ‘Sir, please go to the mendicant Vakkali out of sympathy.’”

sn22.87:1.8.verse: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied. They did as he asked.

sn22.87:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robes, went to Venerable Vakkali.

sn22.87:2.2.verse: Venerable Vakkali saw the Buddha coming off in the distance and stirred in his cot.

sn22.87:2.3.verse: But the Buddha said to him,

sn22.87:2.4.verse: “It’s all right, Vakkali, don’t get up.

sn22.87:2.5.verse: There are some seats spread out, I will sit there.”

sn22.87:2.6.verse: He sat down on the seat spread out and said to Vakkali,

sn22.87:2.7.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Vakkali; I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn22.87:2.8.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

sn22.87:2.9.verse: “I hope you don’t have any remorse or regret?”

sn22.87:2.10.verse: “Indeed, sir, I have no little remorse and regret.”

sn22.87:2.11.verse: “I hope you have no reason to blame yourself when it comes to ethical conduct?”

sn22.87:2.12.verse: “No sir, I have no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct.”

sn22.87:2.13.verse: “In that case, Vakkali, why do you have remorse and regret?”

sn22.87:2.14.verse: “For a long time I’ve wanted to go and see the Buddha, but I was physically too weak.”

sn22.87:3.1.verse: “Enough, Vakkali! Why would you want to see this rotting body?

sn22.87:3.2.verse: One who sees the teaching sees me.

sn22.87:3.3.verse: One who sees me sees the teaching.

sn22.87:3.4.verse: Seeing the teaching, you see me.

sn22.87:3.5.verse: Seeing me, you see the teaching.

sn22.87:4.4.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn22.87:4.6.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn22.87:4.7.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn22.87:4.18.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.87:5.1.verse: And then, after giving Venerable Vakkali this advice, the Buddha rose from his seat and went to the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

sn22.87:5.2.verse: Then Venerable Vakkali addressed his carers,

sn22.87:5.3.verse: “Come on, reverends, lift my cot and take me to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili.

sn22.87:5.4.verse: For how on earth could one such as I imagine dying in an inhabited area!”

sn22.87:5.5.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants, and did as he asked.

sn22.87:5.6.verse: Meanwhile, the Buddha spent the rest of that night and day on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

sn22.87:5.7.verse: Then, late at night, two glorious deities, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side.

sn22.87:5.9.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is intent on liberation!”

sn22.87:5.10.verse: And another deity said to him,

sn22.87:5.12.verse: This is what those deities said.

sn22.87:5.13.verse: Then they bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, before vanishing right there.

sn22.87:6.1.verse: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn22.87:6.2.verse: “Come, mendicants, go to the mendicant Vakkali and tell him:

sn22.87:7.1.verse: ‘Vakkali, hear the word of the Buddha and two deities.

sn22.87:7.2.verse: Late last night, two glorious deities, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side.

sn22.87:7.4.verse: “Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is intent on liberation!”

sn22.87:7.5.verse: The other deity said to him,

sn22.87:7.10.verse: Your death will not be a bad one; your passing will not be a bad one.”’”

sn22.87:7.11.verse: “Yes, sir,” those monks replied. They went to Vakkali and said to him:

sn22.87:7.12.verse: “Vakkali, hear the word of the Buddha and two deities.”

sn22.87:8.2.verse: “Please, reverends, help me off my cot.

sn22.87:8.3.verse: For how on earth could one such as I presume to listen to the Buddha’s instructions sitting on a high seat?”

sn22.87:8.4.verse: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants, and helped him off his cot.

sn22.87:8.5.verse: They repeated what the Buddha had said.

sn22.87:8.14.verse: Vakkali said, “Well then, reverends, in my name bow with your head to the Buddha’s feet. Say to him:

sn22.87:8.15.verse: ‘Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn22.87:8.16.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’

sn22.87:8.19.verse: I have no doubt of that.

sn22.87:8.20.verse: I’m certain that what is impermanent is suffering.

sn22.87:8.21.verse: And I’m certain that I have no desire or greed or fondness for what is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

sn22.87:8.32.verse: I have no doubt of that.

sn22.87:8.33.verse: I’m certain that what is impermanent is suffering.

sn22.87:8.34.verse: And I’m certain that I have no desire or greed or fondness for what is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.’”

sn22.87:8.35.verse: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied, and left.

sn22.87:8.36.verse: And then, not long after those mendicants had left, Venerable Vakkali committed suicide.

sn22.87:9.1.verse: Then those mendicants went up to the Buddha and told him Vakkali’s message.

sn22.87:10.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

sn22.87:10.2.verse: “Come, mendicants, let’s go to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili,

sn22.87:10.3.verse: where Vakkali, the gentleman, committed suicide.”

sn22.87:10.5.verse: Then the Buddha together with several mendicants went to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili.

sn22.87:10.6.verse: The Buddha saw Vakkali off in the distance on his cot, lying with aggregates cast off.

sn22.87:11.1.verse: Now at that time a cloud of black smoke was moving east, west, north, south, above, below, and in-between.

sn22.87:11.2.verse: The Buddha said to the mendicants,

sn22.87:11.3.verse: “Mendicants, do you see that cloud of black smoke moving east, west, north, south, above, below, and in-between?”

sn22.87:11.5.verse: “That’s Māra the Wicked searching for Vakkali’s consciousness, wondering:

sn22.87:11.7.verse: But since his consciousness is not established, Vakkali is quenched.”

sn22.88:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn22.88:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Assaji was staying in a monastery built by a Kassapa, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn22.88:1.4.verse: “Please, reverends, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

sn22.88:1.5.verse: ‘Sir, the mendicant Assaji is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn22.88:1.6.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’

sn22.88:1.8.verse: ‘Sir, please go to the mendicant Assaji out of sympathy.’”

sn22.88:1.9.verse: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied. They did as he asked.

sn22.88:2.1.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to Venerable Assaji.

sn22.88:2.2.verse: Venerable Assaji saw the Buddha coming off in the distance,

sn22.88:2.4.verse: But the Buddha said to him,

sn22.88:2.5.verse: “It’s all right, Assaji, don’t get up.

sn22.88:2.6.verse: There are some seats spread out, I will sit there.”

sn22.88:2.7.verse: He sat down on the seat spread out and said,

sn22.88:2.8.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Assaji; I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn22.88:3.1.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

sn22.88:3.2.verse: “I hope you don’t have any remorse or regret?”

sn22.88:3.3.verse: “Indeed, sir, I have no little remorse and regret.”

sn22.88:3.4.verse: “I hope you have no reason to blame yourself when it comes to ethical conduct?”

sn22.88:3.5.verse: “No sir, I have no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct.”

sn22.88:3.6.verse: “In that case, Assaji, why do you have remorse and regret?”

sn22.88:3.7.verse: “Sir, before my time of illness I meditated having completely stilled the physical process. But now I can’t get immersion.

sn22.88:3.8.verse: Since I can’t get immersion, I think:

sn22.88:3.10.verse: “There are, Assaji, ascetics and brahmins for whom samādhi is the essence, equating immersion with the ascetic life. They think:

sn22.88:4.7.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

sn22.88:4.8.verse: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

sn22.88:4.9.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

sn22.88:4.10.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

sn22.88:4.11.verse: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

sn22.88:4.12.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

sn22.88:4.13.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

sn22.88:4.14.verse: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

sn22.88:4.15.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life is over, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’

sn22.88:5.1.verse: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn.

sn22.88:5.2.verse: As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

sn22.88:5.3.verse: In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

sn22.88:5.4.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life is over, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’”

sn22.89:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

sn22.89:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Khemaka was staying in the Jujube Tree Monastery, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn22.89:1.3.verse: In the late afternoon those senior mendicants came out of retreat and addressed Venerable Dāsaka,

sn22.89:1.4.verse: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:

sn22.89:1.6.verse: hope you’re keeping well; they hope you’re all right. They hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.’”

sn22.89:1.7.verse: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He went to Khemaka and said to him:

sn22.89:1.9.verse: hope you’re keeping well; they hope you’re all right. They hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn22.89:1.10.verse: “Reverend, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

sn22.89:2.1.verse: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said,

sn22.89:2.4.verse: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:

sn22.89:2.6.verse: these five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:

sn22.89:2.7.verse: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.89:2.8.verse: Do you regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self?’”

sn22.89:3.1.verse: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

sn22.89:3.6.verse: “These five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:

sn22.89:3.7.verse: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.89:3.8.verse: I do not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self.”

sn22.89:4.1.verse: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said:

sn22.89:4.6.verse: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:

sn22.89:4.8.verse: these five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:

sn22.89:4.9.verse: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.89:4.10.verse: If, as it seems, Venerable Khemaka does not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self,

sn22.89:4.11.verse: then he is a perfected one, with defilements ended.’”

sn22.89:5.1.verse: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

sn22.89:5.6.verse: “These five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:

sn22.89:5.7.verse: the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.89:5.8.verse: I do not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self, yet I am not a perfected one, with defilements ended.

sn22.89:5.9.verse: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.”

sn22.89:6.1.verse: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said:

sn22.89:7.1.verse: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:

sn22.89:7.3.verse: when you say “I am”, what is it that you’re talking about?

sn22.89:7.4.verse: Is it form or apart from form?

sn22.89:7.9.verse: When you say “I am”, what is it that you’re talking about?”

sn22.89:8.1.verse: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

sn22.89:8.10.verse: “Enough, Reverend Dāsaka! What’s the point in running back and forth?

sn22.89:8.12.verse: I’ll go to see the senior mendicants myself.”

sn22.89:9.1.verse: Then Venerable Khemaka, leaning on a staff, went to those senior mendicants and exchanged greetings with them.

sn22.89:9.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. They said to him:

sn22.89:9.3.verse: “Reverend Khemaka, when you say ‘I am’, what is it that you’re talking about?

sn22.89:9.4.verse: Is it form or apart from form?

sn22.89:9.9.verse: When you say ‘I am’, what is it that you’re talking about?”

sn22.89:9.10.verse: “Reverends, I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to form, or apart from form.

sn22.89:9.11.verse: I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to feeling …

sn22.89:9.15.verse: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.

sn22.89:10.1.verse: It’s like the scent of a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus.

sn22.89:10.2.verse: Would it be right to say that the scent belongs to the petals or the stalk or the pistil?”

sn22.89:10.4.verse: “Then, reverends, how should it be said?”

sn22.89:10.5.verse: “It would be right to say that the scent belongs to the flower.”

sn22.89:10.6.verse: “In the same way, reverends, I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to form, or apart from form.

sn22.89:10.7.verse: I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to feeling …

sn22.89:10.11.verse: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.

sn22.89:11.1.verse: Although a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a lingering residue of the conceit ‘I am’, the desire ‘I am’, and the underlying tendency ‘I am’ which has not been eradicated.

sn22.89:11.2.verse: After some time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.89:11.3.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn22.89:11.7.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn22.89:11.8.verse: As they do so, that lingering residue is eradicated.

sn22.89:12.1.verse: Suppose there was a cloth that was dirty and soiled, so the owners give it to a launderer.

sn22.89:12.2.verse: The launderer kneads it thoroughly with salt, lye, and cow dung, and rinses it in clear water.

sn22.89:12.3.verse: Although that cloth is clean and bright, it still has a lingering scent of salt, lye, or cow dung that had not been eradicated.

sn22.89:12.4.verse: The launderer returns it to its owners, who store it in a fragrant casket.

sn22.89:12.5.verse: And that lingering scent would be eradicated.

sn22.89:12.6.verse: In the same way, although a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a lingering residue of the conceit ‘I am’, the desire ‘I am’, and the underlying tendency ‘I am’ which has not been eradicated.

sn22.89:12.7.verse: After some time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.89:12.8.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn22.89:12.12.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn22.89:12.13.verse: As they do so, that lingering residue is eradicated.”

sn22.89:13.1.verse: When he said this, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Khemaka,

sn22.89:13.2.verse: “We didn’t want to trouble Venerable Khemaka with our questions. But you’re capable of explaining, teaching, asserting, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing the Buddha’s instructions in detail.

sn22.89:13.3.verse: And that’s just what you’ve done.”

sn22.89:14.1.verse: That is what Venerable Khemaka said.

sn22.89:14.2.verse: Satisfied, the senior mendicants approved what Khemaka said.

sn22.89:14.3.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty senior mendicants and of Venerable Khemaka were freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.90:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

sn22.90:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Channa came out of retreat. Taking a latchkey, he went from dwelling to dwelling, going up to the senior mendicants and saying,

sn22.90:1.3.verse: “May the venerable senior mendicants advise me and instruct me! May they give me a Dhamma talk so that I can see the teaching!”

sn22.90:2.1.verse: When he said this, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Channa:

sn22.90:3.12.verse: And yet my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided about the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

sn22.90:3.14.verse: and keeps turning back to the thought:

sn22.90:3.16.verse: But that doesn’t happen for someone who sees the teaching.

sn22.90:3.17.verse: Who can teach me the Dhamma so that I can see the teaching?”

sn22.90:4.2.verse: “Venerable Ānanda is staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery. He’s praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions. He’s quite capable of teaching me the Dhamma so that I can see the teaching.

sn22.90:4.3.verse: Since I have so much trust in Venerable Ānanda,

sn22.90:4.4.verse: why don’t I go to see him?”

sn22.90:4.5.verse: Then Channa set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, set out for Kosambī. He went to see Ānanda in Ghosita’s monastery, exchanged greetings with him, and told him what had happened. Then he said,

sn22.90:7.5.verse: “May Venerable Ānanda advise me and instruct me! May he give me a Dhamma talk so that I can see the teaching!”

sn22.90:8.1.verse: “I’m already delighted with Venerable Channa. Hopefully you’ve opened yourself up and severed your hard-heartedness.

sn22.90:8.3.verse: You are capable of understanding the teaching.”

sn22.90:8.4.verse: Then right away Channa was filled with lofty rapture and joy,

sn22.90:8.5.verse: “It seems I’m capable of understanding the teaching!”

sn22.90:9.1.verse: “Reverend Channa, I heard and learned in the presence of the Buddha his advice to the mendicant Kaccānagotta:

sn22.90:9.2.verse: ‘Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on the duality of existence and non-existence.

sn22.90:9.3.verse: But for one who truly sees the origin of the world with right understanding, the concept of non-existence regarding the world does not occur.

sn22.90:9.4.verse: And for one who truly sees the cessation of the world with right understanding, the concept of existence regarding the world does not occur.

sn22.90:9.5.verse: This world is for the most part shackled by getting involved, grasping, and insisting.

sn22.90:9.6.verse: But if—for all that getting involved and grasping, mental fixation, and insistence and underlying tendency—they do not get attracted, grasp, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’,

sn22.90:9.7.verse: they’ll have no doubt or uncertainty that what arises is just suffering arising, and what ceases is just suffering ceasing.

sn22.90:9.8.verse: Their knowledge of this is independent of others.

sn22.90:9.9.verse: This is how right view is defined.

sn22.90:9.11.verse: “All does not exist”: this is the second extreme.

sn22.90:9.12.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way:

sn22.90:9.14.verse: Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …

sn22.90:9.15.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.

sn22.90:9.16.verse: When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease. …

sn22.90:9.17.verse: That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”’”

sn22.90:10.1.verse: “Reverend Ānanda, this is how it is when you have such venerables as spiritual companions to advise and instruct you out of kindness and sympathy.

sn22.90:10.2.verse: And now that I’ve heard this teaching from Venerable Ānanda, I’ve comprehended the teaching.”

sn22.91:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn22.91:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

sn22.91:2.1.verse: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.91:2.2.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn22.91:2.5.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.91:2.7.verse: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

sn22.92:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, Rāhula said to the Buddha:

sn22.92:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed?”

sn22.92:2.1.verse: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.

sn22.92:2.2.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn22.92:2.5.verse: One truly sees any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.

sn22.92:2.6.verse: That’s how to know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed.”

sn22.93:1.2.verse: “Suppose, mendicants, there was a mountain river that flowed swiftly, going far, carrying all before it. If wild sugarcane, kusa grass, reeds, vetiver, or trees grew on either bank, they’d overhang the river. And if a person who was being swept along by the current grabbed the wild sugarcane, kusa grass, reeds, vetiver, or trees, it’d fall apart, and they’d come to ruin because of that.

sn22.93:1.3.verse: In the same way, an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.93:1.4.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.93:1.6.verse: and they come to ruin because of that.

sn22.93:1.10.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.93:1.12.verse: and they come to ruin because of that.

sn22.93:1.24.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.94:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me.

sn22.94:1.3.verse: When your speech is in line with the teaching you do not dispute with anyone in the world.

sn22.94:1.4.verse: What the astute deem as not existing, I too say does not exist.

sn22.94:1.5.verse: What the astute deem as existing, I too say exists.

sn22.94:2.1.verse: And what do the astute deem as not existing, which I too say does not exist?

sn22.94:2.2.verse: Form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.

sn22.94:2.6.verse: Consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.

sn22.94:2.7.verse: This is what the astute deem as not existing, which I too say does not exist.

sn22.94:3.1.verse: And what do the astute deem as existing, which I too say exists?

sn22.94:3.2.verse: Form that is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

sn22.94:3.4.verse: Consciousness that is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

sn22.94:3.5.verse: This is what the astute deem as existing, which I too say exists.

sn22.94:4.1.verse: There is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

sn22.94:4.2.verse: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

sn22.94:5.1.verse: And what is that worldly phenomenon in the world?

sn22.94:5.2.verse: Form is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

sn22.94:5.3.verse: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

sn22.94:6.1.verse: This being so, what can I do about a foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know or see?

sn22.94:6.5.verse: Consciousness is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

sn22.94:6.6.verse: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

sn22.94:7.1.verse: This being so, what can I do about a foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know or see?

sn22.94:8.1.verse: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Though it sprouted and grew in the water, it would rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to it.

sn22.94:8.2.verse: In the same way, though I was born and grew up in the world, I live having mastered the world, unsullied by the world.”

sn22.95:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Ayodhya on the bank of the Ganges River.

sn22.95:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn22.95:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose this Ganges River was carrying along a big lump of foam. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a lump of foam?

sn22.95:2.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in form?

sn22.95:3.1.verse: Suppose it was autumn, when the heavens rain heavily, and a bubble on the water forms and pops right away. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a water bubble?

sn22.95:3.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of feeling at all … examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in feeling?

sn22.95:4.1.verse: Suppose that in the last month of summer, at noon, a shimmering mirage appears. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a mirage?

sn22.95:4.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of perception at all … examining it carefully. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in perception?

sn22.95:5.1.verse: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. Wandering in search of heartwood, they’d take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There they’d see a big banana trunk, straight and young and grown unskewed. They’d cut it down at the base, cut off the top, and unroll the coiled sheaths. But they wouldn’t even find sapwood, much less heartwood. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a banana trunk?

sn22.95:5.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of choices at all … examining them rationally. And they appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in choices?

sn22.95:6.1.verse: Suppose an illusionist or their apprentice was to demonstrate an illusion at the crossroads. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in an illusion?

sn22.95:6.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in consciousness?

sn22.95:7.1.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.95:7.2.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn22.95:7.3.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.95:8.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn22.95:8.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn22.95:9.1.verse: “Form is like a lump of foam;

sn22.95:9.6.verse: so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.

sn22.95:10.4.verse: when you look at them closely.

sn22.95:11.2.verse: he of vast wisdom has taught

sn22.95:11.3.verse: that when three things are given up,

sn22.95:13.2.verse: this illusion, this lament of fools.

sn22.95:13.3.verse: It’s said to be a killer,

sn22.95:13.4.verse: for no core is found here.

sn22.95:14.2.verse: should examine the aggregates like this,

sn22.95:14.4.verse: whether by day or by night.

sn22.95:15.1.verse: They should give up all fetters,

sn22.95:15.2.verse: and make a refuge for themselves.

sn22.95:15.3.verse: They should live as though their head was on fire,

sn22.95:15.4.verse: aspiring to the state that does not pass.”

sn22.96:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha:

sn22.96:1.3.verse: “Sir, is there any form at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever?

sn22.96:1.7.verse: consciousness at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever?”

sn22.96:1.8.verse: “Mendicant, there is no form at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

sn22.96:1.12.verse: consciousness at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.”

sn22.96:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a lump of cow dung, said to the mendicant:

sn22.96:2.2.verse: “There’s not even this much of any incarnation that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

sn22.96:2.3.verse: If there were, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found.

sn22.96:2.4.verse: But since there isn’t, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

sn22.96:3.1.verse: Once upon a time I was an anointed aristocratic king.

sn22.96:3.2.verse: I had 84,000 cities, with the capital Kusāvatī the foremost.

sn22.96:3.3.verse: I had 84,000 palaces, with the Palace of Principle the foremost.

sn22.96:3.4.verse: I had 84,000 chambers, with the Chamber of the Grand Tower the foremost.

sn22.96:3.5.verse: I had 84,000 couches made of ivory or heartwood or gold or silver, spread with woolen covers—shag-piled or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends.

sn22.96:3.6.verse: I had 84,000 bull elephants with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the royal bull elephant named Sabbath the foremost.

sn22.96:3.7.verse: I had 84,000 horses with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the royal steed named Thundercloud the foremost.

sn22.96:3.8.verse: I had 84,000 chariots with gold adornments and banners, covered with snow gold netting, with the chariot named Triumph the foremost.

sn22.96:3.9.verse: I had 84,000 jewels, with the jewel-treasure the foremost.

sn22.96:3.10.verse: I had 84,000 women, with Queen Subhaddā the foremost.

sn22.96:3.11.verse: I had 84,000 aristocrat vassals, with the commander-treasure the foremost.

sn22.96:3.12.verse: I had 84,000 milk cows with muslin halter and bronze pails.

sn22.96:3.13.verse: I had 8,400,000,000 cloths of delicate linen, cotton, silk, and wool.

sn22.96:3.14.verse: I had 84,000 servings of food, which were presented to me as offerings at daybreak and dusk.

sn22.96:4.1.verse: Of those 84,000 cities, I only stayed in one, the capital Kusāvatī.

sn22.96:4.2.verse: Of those 84,000 palaces, I only dwelt in one, the Palace of Principle.

sn22.96:4.3.verse: Of those 84,000 chambers, I only dwelt in one, the  Chamber of the Grand Tower.

sn22.96:4.4.verse: Of those 84,000 couches, I only used one, made of ivory or heartwood or gold or silver.

sn22.96:4.5.verse: Of those 84,000 bull elephants, I only rode one, the royal bull elephant named Sabbath.

sn22.96:4.6.verse: Of those 84,000 horses, I only rode one, the royal horse named Thundercloud.

sn22.96:4.7.verse: Of those 84,000 chariots, I only rode one, the chariot named Triumph.

sn22.96:4.8.verse: Of those 84,000 women, I was only served by one, an aristocrat maiden or a coquette.

sn22.96:4.9.verse: Of those 8,400,000,000 cloths, I only wore one pair, made of delicate linen, cotton, silk, and wool.

sn22.96:4.10.verse: Of those 84,000 servings of food, I only had one, eating at most a cup of rice with suitable sauce.

sn22.96:4.11.verse: And so all those conditioned phenomena have passed, ceased, and perished.

sn22.96:4.15.verse: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”

sn22.97:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha:

sn22.97:1.3.verse: “Sir, is there any form at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever?

sn22.97:1.7.verse: consciousness at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever?”

sn22.97:1.8.verse: “Mendicant, there is no form at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

sn22.97:1.12.verse: consciousness at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.”

sn22.97:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, said to that mendicant:

sn22.97:2.2.verse: “There’s not even this much of any form that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

sn22.97:2.3.verse: If there were, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found.

sn22.97:2.4.verse: But since there isn’t, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

sn22.97:3.1.verse: There’s not even this much of any feeling …

sn22.97:5.1.verse: consciousness that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.

sn22.97:5.2.verse: If there were, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found.

sn22.97:5.3.verse: But since there isn’t, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

sn22.97:6.11.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.98:1.3.verse: “Sir, is there any form at all that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever?

sn22.99:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

sn22.99:1.3.verse: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

sn22.99:1.4.verse: There comes a time when the ocean dries up and evaporates and is no more.

sn22.99:1.5.verse: But in any case, there is no making an end of suffering for sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving, I say.

sn22.99:1.6.verse: There comes a time when Sineru the king of mountains is burned up and destroyed, and is no more.

sn22.99:1.7.verse: But in any case, there is no making an end of suffering for sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving, I say.

sn22.99:1.8.verse: There comes a time when the great earth is burned up and destroyed, and is no more.

sn22.99:1.9.verse: But in any case, there is no making an end of suffering for sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving, I say.

sn22.99:2.1.verse: Suppose a hound on a leash was tethered to a strong post or pillar. It would just keep running and circling around that post or pillar.

sn22.99:2.2.verse: In the same way, take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in their teaching. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in their teaching.

sn22.99:2.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.99:2.8.verse: They just keep running and circling around form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.99:2.9.verse: Doing so, they’re not freed from form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.99:2.10.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

sn22.99:3.1.verse: A learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.99:3.6.verse: or consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn22.99:3.7.verse: They don’t keep running and circling around form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.99:3.8.verse: By not doing so, they’re freed from form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn22.99:3.9.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.”

sn22.100:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

sn22.100:1.3.verse: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

sn22.100:1.4.verse: Suppose a mutt on a leash was tethered to a strong post or pillar. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it stays right beside that post or pillar.

sn22.100:1.5.verse: In the same way, an unlearned ordinary person regards form like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

sn22.100:1.9.verse: consciousness like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’

sn22.100:1.10.verse: When walking, they walk right beside the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.100:1.13.verse: lying down, they lie down right beside the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.100:1.14.verse: So you should regularly check your own mind:

sn22.100:1.15.verse: ‘For a long time this mind has been corrupted by greed, hate, and delusion.’

sn22.100:1.16.verse: Sentient beings are corrupted because the mind is corrupted.

sn22.100:1.17.verse: Sentient beings are purified because the mind is purified.

sn22.100:2.1.verse: Mendicants, have you seen the painting named ‘Conduct’?”

sn22.100:2.3.verse: “That painting was devised by the mind, but the mind is even more diverse than that.

sn22.100:2.4.verse: So you should regularly check your own mind:

sn22.100:2.5.verse: ‘For a long time this mind has been corrupted by greed, hate, and delusion.’

sn22.100:2.6.verse: Sentient beings are corrupted because the mind is corrupted.

sn22.100:2.7.verse: Sentient beings are purified because the mind is purified.

sn22.100:3.1.verse: I don’t see any other order of beings as elaborate as the animal realm.

sn22.100:3.2.verse: The creatures in the animal realm were devised by the mind, but the mind is even more diverse than that.

sn22.100:3.3.verse: So you should regularly check your own mind:

sn22.100:3.4.verse: ‘For a long time this mind has been corrupted by greed, hate, and delusion.’

sn22.100:3.5.verse: Sentient beings are corrupted because the mind is corrupted.

sn22.100:3.6.verse: Sentient beings are purified because the mind is purified.

sn22.100:4.1.verse: Suppose an artist or painter had some dye, red lac, turmeric, indigo, or rose madder. And on a polished plank or a wall or a canvas they’d create the form of a woman or a man, whole in its major and minor limbs.

sn22.100:4.2.verse: In the same way, when an unlearned ordinary person generates a future life, all they generate is form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.100:4.12.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn22.101:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see.

sn22.101:1.3.verse: For one who knows and sees what?

sn22.101:1.4.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn22.101:1.8.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn22.101:1.9.verse: The ending of the defilements is for one who knows and sees this.

sn22.101:2.1.verse: When a mendicant is not committed to development, they might wish:

sn22.101:2.2.verse: ‘If only my mind were freed from the defilements by not grasping!’ Even so, their mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.101:2.4.verse: You should say: ‘It’s because they’re undeveloped.’

sn22.101:2.6.verse: Undeveloped in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

sn22.101:3.1.verse: Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs.

sn22.101:3.2.verse: But she had not properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

sn22.101:3.4.verse: ‘If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!’

sn22.101:3.5.verse: But they can’t break out and hatch safely.

sn22.101:3.7.verse: Because that chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs

sn22.101:3.8.verse: has not properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

sn22.101:3.9.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant is not committed to development, they might wish:

sn22.101:3.10.verse: ‘If only my mind were freed from the defilements by not grasping!’ Even so, their mind is not freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.101:3.12.verse: You should say: ‘It’s because they’re undeveloped.’

sn22.101:3.14.verse: Undeveloped in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

sn22.101:4.1.verse: When a mendicant is committed to development, they might not wish:

sn22.101:4.2.verse: ‘If only my mind were freed from the defilements by not grasping!’ Even so, their mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.101:4.4.verse: You should say: ‘It’s because they are developed.’

sn22.101:4.6.verse: Developed in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

sn22.101:5.1.verse: Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs.

sn22.101:5.2.verse: And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

sn22.101:5.4.verse: ‘If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!’

sn22.101:5.5.verse: But still they can break out and hatch safely.

sn22.101:5.7.verse: Because that chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs

sn22.101:5.8.verse: properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated.

sn22.101:5.9.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant is committed to development, they might not wish:

sn22.101:5.10.verse: ‘If only my mind were freed from the defilements by not grasping!’ Even so, their mind is freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn22.101:5.12.verse: You should say: ‘It’s because they are developed.’

sn22.101:5.14.verse: Developed in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.

sn22.101:6.1.verse: Suppose a mason or their apprentice sees the marks of his fingers and thumb on the handle of his adze.

sn22.101:6.3.verse: how much of the handle was worn away today, how much yesterday, and how much previously.

sn22.101:6.4.verse: They just know what has been worn away.

sn22.101:6.5.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant is committed to development, they don’t know

sn22.101:6.6.verse: how much of the defilements were worn away today, how much yesterday, and how much previously. They just know what has been worn away.

sn22.101:6.7.verse: Suppose there was a sea-faring ship bound together with ropes. For six months they deteriorated in the water. Then in the cold season it was hauled up on dry land, where the ropes were weathered by wind and sun. When the monsoon clouds soaked it with rain, the ropes would readily collapse and rot away.

sn22.101:6.8.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant is committed to development their fetters readily collapse and rot away.”

sn22.102:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, when the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated it eliminates all desire for sensual pleasures, for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, and for rebirth in a future life. It eliminates all ignorance and eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:2.1.verse: In the autumn, a farmer ploughing with a large plough shears through all the root networks.

sn22.102:2.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:3.1.verse: A reed-cutter, having cut the reeds, grabs them at the top and shakes them down, shakes them about, and flails them about.

sn22.102:3.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:4.1.verse: When the stalk of a bunch of mangoes is cut, all the mangoes attached to the stalk will follow along.

sn22.102:4.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:5.1.verse: The rafters of a bungalow all lean to the peak, slope to the peak, and meet at the peak, so the peak is said to be the topmost of them all.

sn22.102:5.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:6.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant root, spikenard is said to be the best.

sn22.102:6.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:7.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant heartwood, red sandalwood is said to be the best.

sn22.102:7.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:8.1.verse: Of all kinds of fragrant flower, jasmine is said to be the best.

sn22.102:8.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:9.1.verse: All lesser kings are vassals of a wheel-turning monarch, so the wheel-turning monarch is said to be the foremost of them all.

sn22.102:9.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:10.1.verse: The radiance of all the stars is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance, so the moon’s radiance is said to be the best of them all.

sn22.102:10.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:11.1.verse: In the autumn, the heavens are sunny and cloudless. And as the sun is rising to the firmament, having dispelled all the darkness of space, it shines and glows and dazzles.

sn22.102:11.2.verse: In the same way, when the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated it eliminates all desire for sensual pleasures, for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, and for rebirth in a future life. It eliminates all ignorance and eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.

sn22.102:12.1.verse: And how is the perception of impermanence developed and cultivated so that … it eradicates all conceit ‘I am’?

sn22.102:12.2.verse: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.

sn22.102:12.6.verse: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

sn22.102:12.7.verse: That’s how the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated so that it eliminates all desire for sensual pleasures, for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, and for rebirth in a future life. That’s how it eliminates all ignorance and eradicates all conceit ‘I am’.”

sn22.103:1.4.verse: The end that is substantial reality, the end that is the origin of substantial reality, the end that is the cessation of substantial reality, and the end that is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.103:1.5.verse: And what is the end that is substantial reality?

sn22.103:1.6.verse: It should be said: the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.103:1.8.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.103:1.9.verse: This is called the end that is substantial reality.

sn22.103:2.1.verse: And what is the end that is the origin of substantial reality?

sn22.103:2.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

sn22.103:2.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn22.103:2.4.verse: This is called the end that is the origin of substantial reality.

sn22.103:3.1.verse: And what is the end that is the cessation of substantial reality?

sn22.103:3.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn22.103:3.3.verse: This is called the end that is the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.103:4.1.verse: And what is the end that is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality?

sn22.103:4.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn22.103:4.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn22.103:4.4.verse: This is called the end that is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.104:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn22.104:1.5.verse: It should be said: the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.104:1.7.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.104:1.9.verse: And what is the origin of suffering?

sn22.104:1.10.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn22.104:1.11.verse: This is called the origin of suffering.

sn22.104:1.12.verse: And what is the cessation of suffering?

sn22.104:1.13.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving with no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn22.104:1.14.verse: This is called the cessation of suffering.

sn22.104:1.15.verse: And what is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

sn22.104:1.16.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn22.104:1.17.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn22.104:1.18.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.”

sn22.105:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you substantial reality, the origin of substantial reality, the cessation of substantial reality, and the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.105:1.5.verse: It should be said: the five grasping aggregates.

sn22.105:1.7.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.105:1.9.verse: And what is the origin of substantial reality?

sn22.105:1.10.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn22.105:1.11.verse: This is called the origin of substantial reality.

sn22.105:1.12.verse: And what is the cessation of substantial reality?

sn22.105:1.13.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn22.105:1.14.verse: This is called the cessation of substantial reality.

sn22.105:1.15.verse: And what is the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality?

sn22.105:1.16.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn22.105:1.17.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn22.105:1.18.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the cessation of substantial reality.”

sn22.106:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the things that should be completely understood, complete understanding, and the individual who has completely understood.

sn22.106:1.4.verse: And what things should be completely understood?

sn22.106:1.10.verse: These are called the things that should be completely understood.

sn22.106:1.12.verse: The ending of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn22.106:1.14.verse: And who is the individual who has completely understood?

sn22.106:1.15.verse: It should be said: a perfected one,

sn22.106:1.16.verse: the venerable of such name and such clan.

sn22.106:1.17.verse: This is called the individual who has completely understood.”

sn22.107:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five grasping aggregates.

sn22.107:1.4.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.107:1.5.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ gratification, drawback, and escape …

sn22.107:1.6.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand …”

sn22.108:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five grasping aggregates.

sn22.108:1.4.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.108:1.5.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape … Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin …

sn22.108:1.6.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand … Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”

sn22.109:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five grasping aggregates.

sn22.109:1.4.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.109:1.5.verse: A noble disciple comes to truly understand these five grasping aggregates’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

sn22.109:1.6.verse: Such a noble disciple is called a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

sn22.110:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these five grasping aggregates.

sn22.110:1.4.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.110:1.5.verse: A mendicant comes to be freed by not grasping after truly understanding these five grasping aggregates’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

sn22.110:1.6.verse: Such a mendicant is called a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment.”

sn22.111:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, you should give up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for form.

sn22.111:1.3.verse: Thus that form will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

sn22.111:1.4.verse: You should give up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for feeling …

sn22.111:1.8.verse: Thus that consciousness will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.”

sn22.112:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, you should give up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for form; and any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies.

sn22.112:1.3.verse: Thus that form will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

sn22.112:1.4.verse: You should give up any desire, greed, relishing, and craving for feeling …

sn22.112:1.8.verse: consciousness; and any attraction, grasping, mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies.

sn22.112:1.9.verse: Thus that consciousness will be given up, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.”

sn22.113:1.4.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘ignorance’.

sn22.113:1.6.verse: And how is an ignoramus defined?”

sn22.113:1.7.verse: “Mendicant, it’s when an unlearned ordinary person doesn’t understand form, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

sn22.113:1.11.verse: consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

sn22.113:1.13.verse: And this is how an ignoramus is defined.”

sn22.114:1.5.verse: And how is a knowing one defined?”

sn22.114:1.6.verse: “Mendicant, it’s when a learned noble disciple understands form, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation.

sn22.115:1.4.verse: How is a Dhamma speaker defined?”

sn22.115:1.5.verse: “Mendicant, if a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn22.115:1.6.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn22.115:1.7.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.

sn22.115:1.8.verse: If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment with feeling …

sn22.115:1.11.verse: consciousness, for its fading away and cessation, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn22.115:1.12.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn22.115:1.13.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.”

sn22.117:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.117:1.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.117:1.4.verse: They’re called an unlearned ordinary person who is bound to form, inside and out. They see neither the near shore nor the far shore. They’re born in bonds and die in bonds, and in bonds they go from this world to the next.

sn22.117:1.10.verse: They’re called an unlearned ordinary person who is bound to consciousness, inside and out. They see neither the near shore nor the far shore. They’re born in bonds and die in bonds, and in bonds they go from this world to the next.

sn22.117:2.1.verse: A learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn22.117:2.2.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn22.117:2.3.verse: They’re called a learned noble disciple who is not bound to form, inside or out. They see the near shore and the far shore. They’re free from suffering, I say.

sn22.117:2.8.verse: They’re called a learned noble disciple who is not bound to consciousness, inside or out. They see the near shore and the far shore. They’re free from suffering, I say.”

sn22.120:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the things that tighten the fetters, and the fetter.

sn22.120:1.4.verse: What are the things that tighten the fetters? And what is the fetter?

sn22.120:1.5.verse: Form is something that tightens the fetters.

sn22.120:1.6.verse: The desire and greed for it is the fetter.

sn22.120:1.10.verse: Consciousness is something that tightens the fetters.

sn22.120:1.11.verse: The desire and greed for it is the fetter.

sn22.120:1.12.verse: These are called the things that tighten the fetters, and this is the fetter.”

sn22.121:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you the things that fuel grasping, and the grasping.

sn22.121:1.4.verse: What are the things that fuel grasping? And what is the grasping?

sn22.121:1.5.verse: Form is something that fuels grasping.

sn22.121:1.6.verse: The desire and greed for it is the grasping.

sn22.121:1.10.verse: Consciousness is something that fuels grasping.

sn22.121:1.11.verse: The desire and greed for it is the grasping.

sn22.121:1.12.verse: These are called the things that fuel grasping, and this is the grasping.”

sn22.122:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

sn22.122:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita came out of retreat, went to Venerable Sāriputta, and said:

sn22.122:1.3.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, what things should an ethical mendicant rationally apply the mind to?”

sn22.122:1.4.verse: “Reverend Koṭṭhita, an ethical mendicant should rationally apply the mind to the five grasping aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as diseased, as a boil, as a dart, as gloom, as an affliction, as alien, as breaking apart, as empty, as not-self.

sn22.122:1.6.verse: That is, the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn22.122:1.7.verse: An ethical mendicant should rationally apply the mind to these five grasping aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as diseased, as a boil, as a dart, as gloom, as an affliction, as alien, as breaking apart, as empty, as not-self.

sn22.122:1.8.verse: It’s possible that an ethical mendicant who rationally applies the mind to the five grasping aggregates will realize the fruit of stream-entry.”

sn22.122:2.1.verse: “But Reverend Sāriputta, what things should a mendicant stream-enterer rationally apply the mind to?”

sn22.122:2.2.verse: “A mendicant stream-enterer should also rationally apply the mind to these five grasping aggregates as impermanent … as not-self.

sn22.122:2.3.verse: It’s possible that a mendicant stream-enterer who rationally applies the mind to the five grasping aggregates will realize the fruit of once-return.”

sn22.122:3.1.verse: “But Reverend Sāriputta, what things should a mendicant once-returner rationally apply the mind to?”

sn22.122:3.2.verse: “A mendicant once-returner should also rationally apply the mind to these five grasping aggregates as impermanent … as not-self.

sn22.122:3.3.verse: It’s possible that a mendicant once-returner who rationally applies the mind to the five grasping aggregates will realize the fruit of non-return.”

sn22.122:4.1.verse: “But Reverend Sāriputta, what things should a mendicant non-returner rationally apply the mind to?”

sn22.122:4.2.verse: “A mendicant non-returner should also rationally apply the mind to these five grasping aggregates as impermanent … as not-self.

sn22.122:4.3.verse: It’s possible that a mendicant non-returner who rationally applies the mind to the five grasping aggregates will realize perfection.”

sn22.122:5.1.verse: “But Reverend Sāriputta, what things should a perfected one rationally apply the mind to?”

sn22.122:5.2.verse: “Reverend Koṭṭhita, a perfected one should also rationally apply the mind to the five grasping aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as diseased, as a boil, as a dart, as gloom, as an affliction, as alien, as breaking apart, as empty, as not-self.

sn22.122:5.3.verse: A perfected one has nothing more to do, and nothing that needs improvement.

sn22.122:5.4.verse: Still, these things, when developed and cultivated, lead to blissful meditation in this life, and also to mindfulness and situational awareness.”

sn22.124:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Kappa went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn22.124:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

sn22.124:2.1.verse: “Kappa, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.124:2.2.verse: One truly sees any kind of feeling …

sn22.124:2.5.verse: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.124:2.6.verse: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

sn22.125:1.2.verse: Seated to one side, Venerable Kappa said to the Buddha:

sn22.125:1.3.verse: “Sir, how does one know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed?”

sn22.125:2.1.verse: “Kappa, one is freed by not grasping having truly seen any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn22.125:2.6.verse: That’s how to know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed.”
