sn35.64:4.1.verse: And then Venerable Migajāla approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn35.64:4.2.verse: Then Migajāla, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn35.64:4.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn35.64:4.4.verse: And Migajāla became one of the perfected.

sn35.65:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn35.65:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Samiddhi went up to the Buddha …

sn35.65:1.4.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘Māra’.

sn35.65:1.5.verse: How do we define Māra or what is known as Māra?”

sn35.65:2.1.verse: “Samiddhi, where there is the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and things knowable by eye consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:2.2.verse: Where there is the ear, sounds, ear consciousness, and things knowable by ear consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:2.3.verse: Where there is the nose, smells, nose consciousness, and things knowable by nose consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:2.4.verse: Where there is the tongue, tastes, tongue consciousness, and things knowable by tongue consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:2.5.verse: Where there is the body, touches, body consciousness, and things knowable by body consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:2.6.verse: Where there is the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and things knowable by mind consciousness, there is Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:3.1.verse: Where there is no eye, no sights, no eye consciousness, and no things knowable by eye consciousness, there is no Māra or what is known as Māra.

sn35.65:3.6.verse: Where there is no mind, no ideas, no mind consciousness, and no things knowable by mind consciousness, there is no Māra or what is known as Māra.”

sn35.66:0.3.verse: Samiddhi’s Question About a Sentient Being

sn35.66:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called a ‘sentient being’.

sn35.66:1.2.verse: How do we define a sentient being or what is known as a sentient being?” …

sn35.67:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘suffering’.

sn35.67:1.2.verse: How do we define suffering or what is known as suffering?” …

sn35.68:1.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘the world’.

sn35.68:1.2.verse: How do we define the world or what is known as the world?”

sn35.68:1.3.verse: “Samiddhi, where there is the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and things knowable by eye consciousness, there is the world or what is known as the world.

sn35.68:1.4.verse: Where there is the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.68:1.5.verse: Where there is the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and things knowable by mind consciousness, there is the world or what is known as the world.

sn35.68:2.1.verse: Where there is no eye, no sights, no eye consciousness, and no things knowable by eye consciousness, there is no world or what is known as the world.

sn35.68:2.2.verse: Where there is no ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.68:2.3.verse: Where there is no mind, no ideas, no mind consciousness, and no things knowable by mind consciousness, there is no world or what is known as the world.”

sn35.69:1.1.verse: At one time the venerables Sāriputta and Upasena were staying near Rājagaha in the Cool Grove, under the Cobra’s Hood Grotto.

sn35.69:1.2.verse: Now at that time a viper fell on Upasena’s body.

sn35.69:1.4.verse: “Come, reverends, lift this body onto a cot and carry it outside

sn35.69:2.1.verse: When he said this, Sāriputta said to him,

sn35.69:2.2.verse: “But we don’t see any impairment in your body or deterioration of your faculties.

sn35.69:2.4.verse: ‘Come, reverends, lift this body onto a cot and carry it outside

sn35.69:2.7.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, there may be an impairment in body or deterioration of faculties for someone who thinks:

sn35.69:2.8.verse: ‘I am the eye’ or ‘the eye is mine.’

sn35.69:2.9.verse: Or ‘I am the ear … nose … tongue … body …’

sn35.69:2.10.verse: Or ‘I am the mind’ or ‘the mind is mine.’

sn35.69:2.12.verse: But I don’t think like that.

sn35.69:2.16.verse: So why would there be an impairment in my body or deterioration of my faculties?”

sn35.69:3.1.verse: “That must be because Venerable Upasena has long ago totally eradicated I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit.

sn35.69:3.2.verse: That’s why it doesn’t occur to you:

sn35.69:3.3.verse: ‘I am the eye’ or ‘the eye is mine.’ Or ‘I am the ear …

sn35.69:3.5.verse: Or ‘I am the mind’ or ‘the mind is mine.’”

sn35.69:3.6.verse: Then those mendicants lifted Upasena’s body onto a cot and carried it outside.

sn35.69:3.7.verse: And his body was scattered right there

sn35.70:0.3.verse: Upavāṇa on What is Apparent in the Present Life

sn35.70:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Upavāṇa went up to the Buddha …

sn35.70:1.3.verse: “Sir, they speak of ‘a teaching apparent in the present life’.

sn35.70:1.4.verse: In what way is the teaching apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves?”

sn35.70:2.1.verse: “Upavāṇa, take a mendicant who sees a sight with their eyes. They experience both the sight and the desire for the sight.

sn35.70:2.2.verse: There is desire for sights in them, and they understand that.

sn35.70:2.5.verse: this is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

sn35.70:3.1.verse: Next, take a mendicant who hears … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.70:4.1.verse: Next, take a mendicant who knows an idea with their mind. They experience both the idea and the desire for the idea.

sn35.70:4.2.verse: There is desire for ideas in them, and they understand that.

sn35.70:4.5.verse: this is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

sn35.70:5.1.verse: Take a mendicant who sees a sight with their eyes. They experience the sight but no desire for the sight.

sn35.70:5.2.verse: There is no desire for sights in them, and they understand that.

sn35.70:5.5.verse: this is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

sn35.70:6.1.verse: Next, take a mendicant who hears … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.70:7.3.verse: Next, take a mendicant who knows an idea with their mind. They experience the idea but no desire for the idea.

sn35.70:7.4.verse: There is no desire for ideas in them, and they understand that.

sn35.70:7.5.verse: Since this is so, this is how the teaching is apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.”

sn35.71:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, anyone who doesn’t truly understand the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape

sn35.71:1.2.verse: has not completed the spiritual journey and is far from this teaching and training.”

sn35.71:2.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

sn35.71:2.3.verse: For I don’t truly understand the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.”

sn35.71:3.2.verse: Do you regard the eye like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.71:5.1.verse: “Good, mendicant! And regarding the eye, you will truly see clearly with right wisdom that: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn35.71:5.2.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.

sn35.71:5.3.verse: Do you regard the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.71:7.3.verse: Do you regard the mind like this: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.71:9.2.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

sn35.74:1.2.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, and said to him,

sn35.74:1.3.verse: “Sir, in such-and-such monastery there’s a mendicant who is junior and not well-known. He’s sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn35.74:1.4.verse: Please go to him out of sympathy.”

sn35.74:2.1.verse: When the Buddha heard that the mendicant was junior and ill, understanding that he was not well-known, he went to him.

sn35.74:2.2.verse: That mendicant saw the Buddha coming off in the distance

sn35.74:2.4.verse: The Buddha said to that monk,

sn35.74:2.5.verse: “It’s all right, mendicant, don’t get up.

sn35.74:2.6.verse: There are some seats spread out, I will sit there.”

sn35.74:2.7.verse: He sat down on the seat spread out

sn35.74:2.9.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, mendicant, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn35.74:3.1.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

sn35.74:4.1.verse: “I hope you don’t have any remorse or regret?”

sn35.74:5.1.verse: “Indeed, sir, I have no little remorse and regret.”

sn35.74:6.1.verse: “I hope you have no reason to blame yourself when it comes to ethical conduct?”

sn35.74:7.1.verse: “No sir, I have no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct.”

sn35.74:8.1.verse: “In that case, mendicant, why do you have remorse and regret?”

sn35.74:9.1.verse: “Because I understand that the Buddha has not taught the Dhamma merely for the sake of ethical purity.”

sn35.74:10.1.verse: “If that is so, what then do you understand to be the purpose of teaching the Dhamma?”

sn35.74:11.1.verse: “I understand that the Buddha has taught the Dhamma for the purpose of the fading away of greed.”

sn35.74:12.2.verse: It’s good that you understand that I’ve taught the Dhamma for the purpose of the fading away of greed.

sn35.74:12.3.verse: For that is indeed the purpose.

sn35.74:12.5.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.74:20.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

sn35.74:20.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended … there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.74:21.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn35.74:21.2.verse: Satisfied, that mendicant approved what the Buddha said.

sn35.74:21.3.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in that mendicant:

sn35.74:21.4.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

sn35.76:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Rādha went up to the Buddha …

sn35.76:1.15.verse: And the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also impermanent. You should give up desire for it.

sn35.77:1.1.verse: “Rādha, you should give up desire for what is suffering. …”

sn35.79:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha …

sn35.79:1.3.verse: “Sir, is there one thing such that by giving it up a mendicant gives up ignorance and gives rise to knowledge?”

sn35.79:4.1.verse: “Ignorance is one thing such that by giving it up a mendicant gives up ignorance and gives rise to knowledge.”

sn35.79:5.1.verse: “But how does a mendicant know and see so as to give up ignorance and give rise to knowledge?”

sn35.79:6.1.verse: “When a mendicant knows and sees the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact as impermanent, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises.

sn35.79:6.2.verse: And also knowing and seeing the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact as impermanent, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises. …

sn35.79:6.3.verse: Knowing and seeing the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact as impermanent, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises.

sn35.79:6.4.verse: And also knowing and seeing the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact as impermanent, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises.

sn35.79:6.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows and sees so as to give up ignorance and give rise to knowledge.”

sn35.80:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.80:1.2.verse: “Sir, is there one thing such that by giving it up a mendicant gives up ignorance and gives rise to knowledge?”

sn35.80:4.1.verse: “Ignorance is one thing such that by giving it up a mendicant gives up ignorance and gives rise to knowledge.”

sn35.80:5.1.verse: “But how does a mendicant know and see so as to give up ignorance and give rise to knowledge?”

sn35.80:6.3.verse: When a mendicant has heard that

sn35.80:6.5.verse: they directly know all things. Directly knowing all things, they completely understand all things. Completely understanding all things, they see all signs as other. They see the eye, sights,

sn35.80:6.8.verse: And they also see the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact as other. …

sn35.80:6.12.verse: And they also see the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact as other.

sn35.80:6.13.verse: That’s how a mendicant knows and sees so as to give up ignorance and give rise to knowledge.”

sn35.81:1.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.81:1.2.verse: “Sir, sometimes wanderers of other religions ask us:

sn35.81:1.3.verse: ‘Reverends, what’s the goal of leading the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama?’

sn35.81:1.5.verse: ‘The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand suffering.’

sn35.81:1.6.verse: Answering this way, we trust that we repeat what the Buddha has said, and don’t misrepresent him with an untruth. We trust our explanation is in line with the teaching, and that there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.”

sn35.81:2.1.verse: “Indeed, in answering this way you repeat what I’ve said, and don’t misrepresent me with an untruth. Your explanation is in line with the teaching, and there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.

sn35.81:2.2.verse: For the goal of leading the spiritual life under me is to completely understand suffering.

sn35.81:2.3.verse: If wanderers of other religions were to ask you:

sn35.81:2.6.verse: ‘Reverends, the eye is suffering. The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.81:2.8.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also suffering.

sn35.81:2.9.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.81:2.11.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also suffering.

sn35.81:2.12.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.81:2.13.verse: This is that suffering. The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.’

sn35.81:2.14.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.”

sn35.82:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and said to him:

sn35.82:2.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘the world’.

sn35.82:2.3.verse: “It wears away, mendicant, that’s why it’s called ‘the world’.

sn35.82:2.6.verse: Sights … eye consciousness … eye contact is wearing away. The painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also wearing away.

sn35.82:2.8.verse: The mind … ideas … mind consciousness … mind contact is wearing away. The painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also wearing away.

sn35.82:2.9.verse: It wears away, mendicant, that’s why it’s called ‘the world’.”

sn35.83:1.1.verse: And then Venerable Phagguna went up to the Buddha … and said to him:

sn35.83:2.1.verse: “Sir, suppose someone were to describe the Buddhas of the past who have become fully quenched, cut off proliferation, cut off the course, finished off the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering. Does the eye exist by which they could be described?

sn35.83:2.2.verse: Does the ear … nose … tongue … body exist …?

sn35.83:2.3.verse: Does the mind exist by which they could be described?”

sn35.83:3.1.verse: “Phagguna, suppose someone were to describe the Buddhas of the past who have become fully quenched, cut off proliferation, cut off the course, finished off the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering. The eye does not exist by which they could be described.

sn35.83:3.2.verse: The ear … nose … tongue … body does not exist ….

sn35.83:3.3.verse: The mind does not exist by which they could be described.”

sn35.84:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn35.84:2.1.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘the world’.

sn35.84:2.3.verse: “Ānanda, that which is liable to wear out is called the world in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.84:2.4.verse: And what is liable to wear out?

sn35.84:2.5.verse: The eye is liable to wear out. Sights … eye consciousness … eye contact is liable to wear out. The painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also liable to wear out.

sn35.84:2.7.verse: The mind … ideas … mind consciousness … mind contact is liable to wear out. The painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also liable to wear out.

sn35.84:2.8.verse: That which is liable to wear out is called the world in the training of the Noble One.”

sn35.85:1.1.verse: And then Venerable Ānanda … said to the Buddha:

sn35.85:1.2.verse: “Sir, they say that ‘the world is empty’.

sn35.85:1.3.verse: What does the saying ‘the world is empty’ refer to?”

sn35.85:1.4.verse: “Ānanda, they say that ‘the world is empty’ because it’s empty of self or what belongs to self.

sn35.85:1.5.verse: And what is empty of self or what belongs to self?

sn35.85:1.7.verse: sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are empty of self or what belongs to self. …

sn35.85:1.8.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also empty of self or what belongs to self.

sn35.85:1.9.verse: They say that ‘the world is empty’ because it’s empty of self or what belongs to self.”

sn35.86:1.1.verse: Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha:

sn35.86:1.2.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn35.86:2.2.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.86:4.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.86:6.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn35.86:6.2.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.86:10.2.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact: is that permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.86:12.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.86:14.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn35.86:14.2.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.86:16.1.verse: “Is the ear … nose … tongue … body … mind …

sn35.86:18.3.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact: is that permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.86:20.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.86:22.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn35.86:22.2.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.86:24.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact. And they grow disillusioned with the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact.

sn35.86:24.2.verse: They grow disillusioned with the ear … nose … tongue … body … mind … painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact.

sn35.86:24.3.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn35.86:24.4.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.87:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn35.87:1.2.verse: Now at that time the venerables Sāriputta, Mahācunda, and Channa were staying on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

sn35.87:1.3.verse: Now at that time Venerable Channa was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn35.87:1.4.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Mahācunda and said to him,

sn35.87:1.5.verse: “Come, Reverend Cunda, let’s go to see Venerable Channa and ask about his illness.”

sn35.87:2.1.verse: And then Sāriputta and Mahācunda went to see Channa and sat down on the seats spread out. Sāriputta said to Channa:

sn35.87:2.2.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Reverend Channa, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn35.87:3.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.

sn35.87:3.2.verse: The winds piercing my head are so severe, it feels like a strong man drilling into my head with a sharp point.

sn35.87:3.4.verse: The pain in my head is so severe, it feels like a strong man tightening a strong leather strap around my head.

sn35.87:3.6.verse: The winds slicing my belly are so severe, like a deft butcher or their apprentice were slicing open a cow’s belly with a sharp meat cleaver.

sn35.87:3.8.verse: The burning in my body is so severe, it feels like two strong men grabbing a weaker man by the arms to burn and scorch him on a pit of glowing coals.

sn35.87:3.9.verse: I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.

sn35.87:3.10.verse: Reverend Sāriputta, I shall commit suicide. I don’t wish to live.”

sn35.87:4.2.verse: Venerable Channa, keep going! We want you to keep going.

sn35.87:4.3.verse: If you don’t have any suitable food, we’ll find it for you.

sn35.87:4.4.verse: If you don’t have suitable medicine, we’ll find it for you.

sn35.87:4.5.verse: If you don’t have a capable carer, we’ll find one for you.

sn35.87:4.7.verse: Venerable Channa, keep going! We want you to keep going.”

sn35.87:5.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, it’s not that I don’t have suitable food;

sn35.87:5.3.verse: It’s not that I don’t have suitable medicine;

sn35.87:5.5.verse: It’s not that I don’t have a capable carer;

sn35.87:5.6.verse: I do have a capable carer.

sn35.87:5.7.verse: Moreover, for a long time now I have served the Teacher with love, not without love.

sn35.87:5.8.verse: For it is proper for a disciple to serve the Teacher with love, not without love.

sn35.87:5.9.verse: You should remember this: ‘The mendicant Channa will commit suicide blamelessly.’”

sn35.87:6.1.verse: “I’d like to ask Venerable Channa about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

sn35.87:6.2.verse: “Ask, Reverend Sāriputta. When I’ve heard it I’ll know.”

sn35.87:7.1.verse: “Reverend Channa, do you regard the eye, eye consciousness, and things knowable by eye consciousness in this way: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?

sn35.87:7.2.verse: Do you regard the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.87:7.3.verse: mind, mind consciousness, and things knowable by mind consciousness in this way: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.87:8.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, I regard the eye, eye consciousness, and things knowable by eye consciousness in this way: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

sn35.87:8.2.verse: I regard the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.87:8.3.verse: mind, mind consciousness, and things knowable by mind consciousness in this way: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’.”

sn35.87:9.1.verse: “Reverend Channa, what have you seen, what have you directly known in these things that you regard them in this way: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’?”

sn35.87:10.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, after seeing cessation, after directly knowing cessation in these things I regard them in this way: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’.”

sn35.87:11.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Mahācunda said to Venerable Channa,

sn35.87:11.2.verse: “So, Reverend Channa, you should regularly apply your mind well to this instruction of the Buddha:

sn35.87:11.3.verse: ‘For the dependent there is quivering. For the independent there’s no quivering.

sn35.87:11.4.verse: When there’s no quivering, there is tranquility.

sn35.87:11.5.verse: When there is tranquility, there’s no inclination.

sn35.87:11.6.verse: When there’s no inclination, there’s no coming and going.

sn35.87:11.7.verse: When there’s no coming and going, there’s no passing away and reappearing.

sn35.87:11.8.verse: When there’s no passing away and reappearing, there’s no this life or the next or between the two.

sn35.87:11.9.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.’”

sn35.87:12.1.verse: And when the venerables Sāriputta and Mahācunda had given Venerable Channa this advice they rose from their seats and left.

sn35.87:12.2.verse: Not long after those venerables had left, Venerable Channa committed suicide.

sn35.87:13.1.verse: Then Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn35.87:13.3.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

sn35.87:13.4.verse: “Sāriputta, didn’t the mendicant Channa declare his blamelessness to you personally?”

sn35.87:13.5.verse: “Sir, there is a Vajjian village named Pubbajira.

sn35.87:13.6.verse: There Channa had families who were friendly, intimate, and hospitable.”

sn35.87:13.7.verse: “The mendicant Channa did indeed have such families.

sn35.87:13.8.verse: But, Sāriputta, this is not enough for me to call someone ‘blameworthy’.

sn35.87:13.9.verse: When someone lays down this body and takes up another body, I call them ‘blameworthy’.

sn35.87:13.10.verse: But the mendicant Channa did no such thing.

sn35.87:13.11.verse: You should remember this: ‘The mendicant Channa committed suicide blamelessly.’”

sn35.88:1.1.verse: And then Venerable Puṇṇa went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn35.88:1.2.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn35.88:2.1.verse: “Puṇṇa, there are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.88:2.2.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.88:2.4.verse: Relishing is the origin of suffering, I say.

sn35.88:2.5.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.88:2.6.verse: There are ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.88:2.7.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.88:2.9.verse: Relishing is the origin of suffering, I say.

sn35.88:3.1.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.88:3.2.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, relishing ceases.

sn35.88:3.3.verse: When relishing ceases, suffering ceases, I say. …

sn35.88:3.4.verse: There are ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.88:3.5.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, relishing ceases.

sn35.88:3.6.verse: When relishing ceases, suffering ceases, I say.

sn35.88:4.1.verse: Puṇṇa, now that I’ve given you this brief advice, what country will you live in?”

sn35.88:4.2.verse: “Sir, there’s a country named Sunāparanta; I will live there.”

sn35.88:5.1.verse: “The people of Sunāparanta are wild and rough, Puṇṇa.

sn35.88:5.3.verse: If they abuse and insult you, what will you think of them?”

sn35.88:6.1.verse: “If they abuse and insult me, I will think:

sn35.88:6.2.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t hit me with their fists.’

sn35.88:6.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:6.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:7.1.verse: “But if they do hit you with their fists, what will you think of them then?”

sn35.88:8.1.verse: “If they hit me with their fists, I’ll think:

sn35.88:8.2.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t throw stones at me.’

sn35.88:8.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:8.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:9.1.verse: “But if they do throw stones at you, what will you think of them then?”

sn35.88:10.1.verse: “If they throw stones at me, I’ll think:

sn35.88:10.2.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t beat me with a club.’

sn35.88:10.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:10.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:11.1.verse: “But if they do beat you with a club, what will you think of them then?”

sn35.88:12.1.verse: “If they beat me with a club, I’ll think:

sn35.88:12.2.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t stab me with a knife.’

sn35.88:12.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:12.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:13.1.verse: “But if they do stab you with a knife, what will you think of them then?”

sn35.88:14.1.verse: “If they stab me with a knife, I’ll think:

sn35.88:14.2.verse: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are gracious, truly gracious, since they don’t take my life with a sharp knife.’

sn35.88:14.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:14.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:15.1.verse: “But if they do take your life with a sharp knife, what will you think of them then?”

sn35.88:16.1.verse: “If they take my life with a sharp knife, I’ll think:

sn35.88:16.2.verse: ‘There are disciples of the Buddha who looked for a suicide weapon because they were horrified, repelled, and disgusted with the body and with life. And I have found this without looking!’

sn35.88:16.3.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Blessed One.

sn35.88:16.4.verse: That’s what I’ll think, Holy One.”

sn35.88:17.2.verse: Having such self-control and peacefulness, you will be quite capable of living in Sunāparanta.

sn35.88:17.3.verse: Now, Puṇṇa, go at your convenience.”

sn35.88:18.1.verse: And then Puṇṇa welcomed and agreed with the Buddha’s words. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right. Then he set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, set out for Sunāparanta.

sn35.88:18.2.verse: Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Sunāparanta,

sn35.88:18.4.verse: Within that rainy season he confirmed around five hundred male and five hundred female lay followers. And within that same rainy season he realized the three knowledges.

sn35.88:18.7.verse: And within that same rainy season he became fully extinguished.

sn35.88:19.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.88:19.2.verse: “Sir, the gentleman named Puṇṇa, who was advised in brief by the Buddha, has passed away.

sn35.88:19.3.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

sn35.88:20.1.verse: “Mendicants, Puṇṇa was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

sn35.89:1.2.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn35.89:15.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact. And they grow disillusioned with the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact.

sn35.89:15.2.verse: They grow disillusioned with the ear … nose … tongue … body … mind … painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact.

sn35.89:15.3.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn35.89:16.1.verse: And then Venerable Bāhiya approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn35.89:16.2.verse: Then Bāhiya, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn35.89:16.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn35.89:16.4.verse: And Venerable Bāhiya became one of the perfected.

sn35.90:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, turbulence is a disease, a boil, a dart.

sn35.90:1.2.verse: That’s why the Realized One lives unperturbed, with dart drawn out.

sn35.90:1.3.verse: Now, a mendicant might wish: ‘May I live unperturbed, with dart drawn out.’

sn35.90:1.4.verse: So let them not conceive anything to be the eye, let them not conceive it in the eye, let them not conceive it as the eye, let them not conceive that ‘the eye is mine.’

sn35.90:1.8.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact. Let them not conceive it in that, let them not conceive it as that, and let them not conceive that ‘that is mine.’

sn35.90:2.1.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the ear …

sn35.90:3.6.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact. Let them not conceive it in that, let them not conceive it as that, and let them not conceive that ‘that is mine.’

sn35.90:3.7.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be all, let them not conceive it in all, let them not conceive it as all, let them not conceive that ‘all is mine’.

sn35.90:4.1.verse: Not conceiving, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

sn35.90:4.2.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

sn35.90:4.3.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.91:1.3.verse: Now, a mendicant might wish: ‘May I live unperturbed, with dart drawn out.’

sn35.91:1.4.verse: So let them not conceive anything to be the eye, let them not conceive it in the eye, let them not conceive it as the eye, let them not conceive that ‘the eye is mine.’

sn35.91:1.8.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact. Let them not conceive it in that, let them not conceive it as that, and let them not conceive that ‘that is mine.’

sn35.91:1.9.verse: For whatever you conceive it to be, whatever you conceive it in, whatever you conceive it as, and whatever you conceive to be ‘mine’: that becomes something else.

sn35.91:1.10.verse: The world is attached to being, taking pleasure only in being, yet it becomes something else.

sn35.91:2.1.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.91:3.1.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the mind …

sn35.91:3.4.verse: Let them not conceive anything to be the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact. Let them not conceive it in that, let them not conceive it as that, and let them not conceive that ‘that is mine.’

sn35.91:3.5.verse: For whatever you conceive it to be, whatever you conceive it in, whatever you conceive it as, and whatever you conceive to be ‘mine’: that becomes something else.

sn35.91:3.6.verse: The world is attached to being, taking pleasure only in being, yet it becomes something else.

sn35.91:4.1.verse: As far as the aggregates, elements, and sense fields extend, they don’t conceive anything to be that, they don’t conceive it in that, they don’t conceive it as that, and they don’t conceive that ‘that is mine.’

sn35.91:4.2.verse: Not conceiving, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

sn35.91:4.3.verse: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

sn35.91:4.4.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.92:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you a duality.

sn35.92:1.4.verse: It’s just the eye and sights, the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and touches, and the mind and ideas.

sn35.92:2.1.verse: Mendicants, suppose someone was to say:

sn35.92:2.2.verse: ‘I’ll deny this duality and describe another duality.’ They’d have no grounds for that claim,

sn35.92:2.3.verse: they’d be stumped by questions, and, in addition, they’d get frustrated.

sn35.92:2.6.verse: Because they’re out of their element.”

sn35.93:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, consciousness originates dependent on a duality.

sn35.93:1.3.verse: Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights.

sn35.93:1.4.verse: The eye is impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.5.verse: Sights are impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.6.verse: So this duality is tottering and toppling; it’s impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.7.verse: Eye consciousness is impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.8.verse: And the causes and reasons that give rise to eye consciousness are also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.9.verse: But since eye consciousness has arisen dependent on conditions that are impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.93:1.10.verse: The meeting, coming together, and joining together of these three things is called eye contact.

sn35.93:1.11.verse: Eye contact is also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.12.verse: And the causes and reasons that give rise to eye contact are also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:1.13.verse: But since eye contact has arisen dependent on conditions that are impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.93:1.14.verse: Contacted one feels; contacted one intends; contacted one perceives.

sn35.93:1.15.verse: So these things too are tottering and toppling; they’re impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:2.1.verse: Ear consciousness … Nose consciousness … Tongue consciousness … Body consciousness …

sn35.93:3.1.verse: Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and ideas.

sn35.93:3.2.verse: The mind is impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.3.verse: Ideas are impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.4.verse: So this duality is tottering and toppling; it’s impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.5.verse: Mind consciousness is impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.6.verse: And the causes and reasons that give rise to mind consciousness are also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.7.verse: But since mind consciousness has arisen dependent on conditions that are impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.93:3.8.verse: The meeting, coming together, and joining together of these three things is called mind contact.

sn35.93:3.9.verse: Mind contact is also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.10.verse: And the causes and reasons that give rise to mind contact are also impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.11.verse: But since mind contact has arisen dependent on conditions that are impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.93:3.12.verse: Contacted one feels; contacted one intends; contacted one perceives.

sn35.93:3.13.verse: So these things too are tottering and toppling; they’re impermanent, decaying, and perishing.

sn35.93:3.14.verse: This is how consciousness originates dependent on a duality.”

sn35.94:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, these six fields of contact bring suffering when they’re untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained.

sn35.94:1.4.verse: The field of eye contact brings suffering when it’s untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained.

sn35.94:1.5.verse: The field of ear contact … nose contact … tongue contact … body contact …

sn35.94:1.6.verse: The field of mind contact brings suffering when it’s untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained.

sn35.94:1.7.verse: These six fields of contact bring suffering when they’re untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained.

sn35.94:2.1.verse: These six fields of contact bring happiness when they’re well tamed, well guarded, well protected, and well restrained.

sn35.94:2.3.verse: The field of eye contact brings happiness when it’s well tamed, well guarded, well protected, and well restrained.

sn35.94:2.4.verse: The field of ear contact … nose contact … tongue contact … body contact …

sn35.94:2.5.verse: The field of mind contact brings happiness when it’s well tamed, well guarded, well protected, and well restrained.

sn35.94:2.6.verse: These six fields of contact bring happiness when they’re well tamed, well guarded, well protected, and well restrained.”

sn35.94:2.7.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn35.94:2.8.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn35.94:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, it’s just the six fields of contact

sn35.94:3.2.verse: that lead the unrestrained to suffering.

sn35.94:3.3.verse: Those who understand how to restrain them

sn35.94:3.4.verse: live with faith as partner, not festering.

sn35.94:4.3.verse: dispel all manner of desire for the pleasant,

sn35.94:4.4.verse: without hating what you don’t like.

sn35.94:5.1.verse: When you’ve heard sounds both liked and disliked,

sn35.94:5.2.verse: don’t fall under the thrall of sounds you like,

sn35.94:5.4.verse: and don’t hurt your mind by thinking of what you don’t like.

sn35.94:6.1.verse: When you’ve smelled a pleasant, fragrant scent,

sn35.94:6.2.verse: and one that’s foul and unpleasant,

sn35.94:6.4.verse: while not yielding to desire for the pleasant.

sn35.94:7.1.verse: When you’ve enjoyed a sweet, delicious taste,

sn35.94:7.2.verse: and sometimes those that are bitter,

sn35.94:7.3.verse: don’t be attached to enjoying sweet tastes,

sn35.94:8.1.verse: Don’t be intoxicated by a pleasant touch,

sn35.94:8.2.verse: and don’t tremble at a painful touch.

sn35.94:8.3.verse: Look with equanimity at the duality of pleasant and painful contacts,

sn35.94:9.1.verse: People generally let their perceptions proliferate;

sn35.94:9.2.verse: perceiving and proliferating, they are attracted.

sn35.94:9.3.verse: Casting aside all mental constructions of the domestic life,

sn35.94:10.1.verse: When the mind is well developed like this regarding the six,

sn35.94:10.2.verse: it doesn’t waver at contacts at all.

sn35.94:10.3.verse: Mendicants, those who have mastered greed and hate

sn35.95:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Māluṅkyaputta went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.95:1.2.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn35.95:2.1.verse: “Well now, Māluṅkyaputta, what are we to say to the young monks,

sn35.95:2.2.verse: when even an old man like you, elderly and senior, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, asks for brief advice?”

sn35.95:3.1.verse: “Sir, even though I’m an old man, elderly and senior,

sn35.95:3.2.verse: may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief! May the Holy One please teach me in brief! Hopefully I can understand the meaning of what the Buddha says. Hopefully I can be an heir of the Buddha’s teaching!”

sn35.95:4.2.verse: Do you have any desire or greed or fondness for sights known by the eye that are unseen, unseen before, and which you neither see nor think might be seen?”

sn35.95:5.1.verse: “Do you have any desire or greed or affection for sounds known by the ear …

sn35.95:9.1.verse: ideas known by the mind that are unknown, unknown before, and which you neither know nor think might be known?”

sn35.95:10.1.verse: “In that case, when it comes to things that ought be seen, heard, thought, and known: in the seen will be merely the seen; in the heard will be merely the heard; in the thought will be merely the thought; in the known will be merely the known.

sn35.95:10.7.verse: you won’t be in this life or the next or in between the two.

sn35.95:10.8.verse: Just this is the end of suffering.”

sn35.95:24.3.verse: Experiencing it with a mind free of desire,

sn35.95:41.1.verse: “This is how to see the detailed meaning of what I said in brief.”

sn35.95:42.1.verse: And then Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn35.95:42.2.verse: Then Māluṅkyaputta, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn35.95:42.3.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn35.95:42.4.verse: And Venerable Māluṅkyaputta became one of the perfected.

sn35.96:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you who is liable to decline, who is not liable to decline, and the six fields of mastery.

sn35.96:1.3.verse: And how is someone liable to decline?

sn35.96:1.4.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:1.5.verse: Suppose that mendicant tolerates them and doesn’t give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them. They should understand:

sn35.96:1.7.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls decline.’

sn35.96:2.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … encounters a touch …

sn35.96:2.2.verse: knows an idea with their mind, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:2.3.verse: If that mendicant tolerates them and doesn’t give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them, they should understand:

sn35.96:2.5.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls decline.’

sn35.96:2.6.verse: That’s how someone is liable to decline.

sn35.96:3.1.verse: And how is someone not liable to decline?

sn35.96:3.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:3.3.verse: Suppose that mendicant doesn’t tolerate them but gives them up, dispels them, eliminates them, and obliterates them. They should understand:

sn35.96:3.5.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls non-decline.’

sn35.96:4.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … encounters a touch …

sn35.96:4.2.verse: knows an idea with their mind, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:4.3.verse: Suppose that mendicant doesn’t tolerate them but gives them up, dispels them, eliminates them, and obliterates them. They should understand:

sn35.96:4.5.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls non-decline.’

sn35.96:4.6.verse: That’s how someone is not liable to decline.

sn35.96:5.1.verse: And what are the six fields of mastery?

sn35.96:5.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, bad, unskillful phenomena don’t arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:5.5.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls a field of mastery.’ …

sn35.96:5.6.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant knows an idea with their mind, bad, unskillful phenomena don’t arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.96:5.9.verse: For this is what the Buddha calls a field of mastery.’

sn35.96:5.10.verse: These are the six fields of mastery.”

sn35.97:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you who lives negligently and who lives diligently.

sn35.97:1.3.verse: And how does someone live negligently?

sn35.97:1.4.verse: When you live with the eye faculty unrestrained, your mind becomes polluted when it comes to sights known by the eye.

sn35.97:1.5.verse: When the mind is polluted, there’s no joy.

sn35.97:1.6.verse: When there’s no joy, there’s no rapture.

sn35.97:1.7.verse: When there’s no rapture, there’s no tranquility.

sn35.97:1.8.verse: When there’s no tranquility, there’s suffering.

sn35.97:1.9.verse: When one is suffering, the mind does not become immersed in samādhi.

sn35.97:1.10.verse: When the mind is not immersed in samādhi, principles do not become clear.

sn35.97:1.11.verse: Because principles have not become clear, you’re reckoned to live negligently.

sn35.97:1.12.verse: When you live with the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.97:1.15.verse: mind faculty unrestrained, your mind becomes polluted when it comes to ideas known by the mind.

sn35.97:1.16.verse: When the mind is polluted, there’s no joy.

sn35.97:1.17.verse: When there’s no joy, there’s no rapture.

sn35.97:1.18.verse: When there’s no rapture, there’s no tranquility.

sn35.97:1.19.verse: When there’s no tranquility, there’s suffering.

sn35.97:1.20.verse: When one is suffering, the mind does not become immersed in samādhi.

sn35.97:1.21.verse: When the mind is not immersed in samādhi, principles do not become clear.

sn35.97:1.22.verse: Because principles have not become clear, you’re reckoned to live negligently.

sn35.97:2.1.verse: And how does someone live diligently?

sn35.97:2.2.verse: When you live with the eye faculty restrained, your mind doesn’t become polluted when it comes to sights known by the eye.

sn35.97:2.3.verse: When the mind isn’t polluted, joy springs up.

sn35.97:2.5.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.

sn35.97:2.6.verse: When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss.

sn35.97:2.7.verse: And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

sn35.97:2.8.verse: When the mind is immersed in samādhi, principles become clear.

sn35.97:2.9.verse: Because principles have become clear, you’re reckoned to live diligently.

sn35.97:2.10.verse: When you live with the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.97:2.12.verse: mind faculty restrained, your mind doesn’t become polluted when it comes to ideas known by the mind.

sn35.97:2.13.verse: When the mind isn’t polluted, joy springs up.

sn35.97:2.15.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.

sn35.97:2.16.verse: When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss.

sn35.97:2.17.verse: And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

sn35.97:2.18.verse: When the mind is immersed in samādhi, principles become clear.

sn35.97:2.19.verse: Because principles have become clear, you’re reckoned to live diligently.

sn35.103:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, Uddaka son of Rāma used to say:

sn35.103:1.3.verse: Hereupon, ever the conqueror of all!

sn35.103:1.5.verse: boil’s root was dug out by me!’

sn35.103:1.6.verse: Even though Uddaka son of Rāma was no knowledge master, he said ‘I’m a knowledge master.’ Though he was no conqueror of all, he said ‘I’m conqueror of all.’ And though the boil’s root was not dug out, he said ‘I’ve dug out the boil’s root.’

sn35.103:1.7.verse: A mendicant might rightly say here:

sn35.103:1.9.verse: Hereupon, ever the conqueror of all!

sn35.103:2.1.verse: And how is someone a knowledge master?

sn35.103:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant truly understands the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

sn35.103:2.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a knowledge master.

sn35.103:3.1.verse: And how is a mendicant a conqueror of all?

sn35.103:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant comes to be freed by not grasping after truly understanding the six fields of contact’s origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

sn35.103:3.3.verse: That’s how a mendicant is a conqueror of all.

sn35.103:4.1.verse: And how has a mendicant dug out the undug boil’s root?

sn35.103:4.2.verse: ‘Boil’ is a term for this body made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

sn35.103:4.3.verse: ‘Boil’s root’ is a term for craving.

sn35.103:4.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant has given up craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn35.103:4.5.verse: That’s how a mendicant has dug out the undug boil’s root.

sn35.103:5.1.verse: Uddaka son of Rāma used to say:

sn35.103:5.3.verse: Hereupon, ever the conqueror of all!

sn35.103:5.6.verse: Even though Uddaka son of Rāma was no knowledge master, he said ‘I’m a knowledge master.’ Though he was no conqueror of all, he said ‘I’m conqueror of all.’ And though the boil’s root was not dug out, he said ‘I’ve dug out the boil’s root.’

sn35.103:5.9.verse: Hereupon, ever the conqueror of all!

sn35.104:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you an exposition of the teaching, an explanation of one who has found sanctuary from the yoke.

sn35.104:1.4.verse: And what is an exposition of the teaching, an explanation of one who has found sanctuary from the yoke?

sn35.104:1.5.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.104:1.6.verse: The Realized One has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn35.104:1.7.verse: He teaches yoking oneself to meditation for giving them up. That’s why the Realized One is called one who has found sanctuary from the yoke. …

sn35.104:1.8.verse: There are ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.104:1.9.verse: The Realized One has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn35.104:1.10.verse: He teaches yoking oneself to meditation for giving them up. That’s why the Realized One is called one who has found sanctuary from the yoke.

sn35.104:1.11.verse: This is an exposition of the teaching, an explanation of one who has found sanctuary from the yoke.”

sn35.105:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when what exists, because of grasping what, do pleasure and pain arise in oneself?”

sn35.105:2.1.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. …”

sn35.105:3.4.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.105:5.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.116:0.3.verse: Traveling to the End of the World

sn35.116:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling.

sn35.116:1.2.verse: But I also say there’s no making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world.”

sn35.116:1.3.verse: When he had spoken, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

sn35.116:1.4.verse: Soon after the Buddha left, those mendicants considered,

sn35.116:1.5.verse: “The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail. …

sn35.116:1.8.verse: Who can explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha?”

sn35.116:2.2.verse: “This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

sn35.116:2.3.verse: He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

sn35.116:2.4.verse: Let’s go to him, and ask him about this matter.”

sn35.116:3.1.verse: Then those mendicants went to Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.116:3.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. They told him what had happened, and said,

sn35.116:5.1.verse: “Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But he’d pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves.

sn35.116:5.2.verse: Such is the consequence for the venerables. Though you were face to face with the Buddha, you bypassed him, imagining that you should ask me about this matter.

sn35.116:5.3.verse: For he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

sn35.116:5.5.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

sn35.116:5.6.verse: You should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”

sn35.116:6.1.verse: “Certainly he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.

sn35.116:6.3.verse: That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.

sn35.116:6.4.verse: We should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.

sn35.116:6.5.verse: Still, Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.

sn35.116:6.6.verse: You are capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.

sn35.116:6.7.verse: Please explain this, if it’s no trouble.”

sn35.116:7.1.verse: “Then listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn35.116:8.1.verse: “Reverends, the Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail:

sn35.116:8.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, I say it’s not possible to know or see or reach the end of the world by traveling.

sn35.116:8.3.verse: But I also say there’s no making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world.’

sn35.116:8.4.verse: This is how I understand the detailed meaning of this summary recital.

sn35.116:8.5.verse: Whatever in the world through which you perceive the world and conceive the world

sn35.116:8.6.verse: is called the world in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.116:8.7.verse: And through what in the world do you perceive the world and conceive the world?

sn35.116:8.8.verse: Through the eye in the world you perceive the world and conceive the world.

sn35.116:8.13.verse: mind in the world you perceive the world and conceive the world.

sn35.117:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

sn35.117:1.2.verse: ‘My mind might often stray toward the five kinds of sensual stimulation that I formerly experienced—which have passed, ceased, and perished—or to those in the present, or in the future a little.’

sn35.117:1.4.verse: ‘In my own way I should practice diligence, mindfulness, and protecting the mind regarding the five kinds of sensual stimulation that I formerly experienced—which have passed, ceased, and perished.’

sn35.117:1.5.verse: So, mendicants, your minds might also often stray toward the five kinds of sensual stimulation that you formerly experienced—which have passed, ceased, and perished—or to those in the present, or in the future a little.

sn35.117:1.6.verse: So in your own way you should practice diligence, mindfulness, and protecting the mind regarding the five kinds of sensual stimulation that you formerly experienced—which have passed, ceased, and perished.

sn35.117:1.7.verse: So you should understand that dimension where the eye ceases and perception of sights fades away.

sn35.117:1.8.verse: You should understand that dimension where the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.117:1.9.verse: mind ceases and perception of ideas fades away.”

sn35.120:0.2.verse: 12. The World and the Kinds of Sensual Stimulation

sn35.120:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn35.120:1.2.verse: Then a certain mendicant went up to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.120:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn35.120:1.4.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, a mendicant protégé of mine has resigned the training and returned to a lesser life.”

sn35.120:2.1.verse: “That’s how it is, reverend, when someone doesn’t guard the sense doors, eats too much, and is not committed to wakefulness.

sn35.120:2.2.verse: It is quite impossible for such a mendicant to maintain the full and pure spiritual life for the rest of their life.

sn35.120:2.3.verse: But it is quite possible for a mendicant to maintain the full and pure spiritual life for the rest of their life if they guard the sense doors, eat in moderation, and are committed to wakefulness.

sn35.120:3.1.verse: And how does someone guard the sense doors?

sn35.120:3.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with the eyes, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

sn35.120:3.3.verse: If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint.

sn35.120:3.4.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

sn35.120:3.5.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

sn35.120:3.6.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

sn35.120:3.7.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

sn35.120:3.8.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, they don’t get caught up in the features and details.

sn35.120:3.9.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint.

sn35.120:3.10.verse: That’s how someone guards the sense doors.

sn35.120:4.1.verse: And how does someone eat in moderation?

sn35.120:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant reflects rationally on the food that they eat:

sn35.120:4.3.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

sn35.120:4.4.verse: That’s how someone eats in moderation.

sn35.120:5.1.verse: And how is someone committed to wakefulness?

sn35.120:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant practices walking and sitting meditation by day, purifying their mind from obstacles.

sn35.120:5.3.verse: In the first watch of the night, they continue to practice walking and sitting meditation.

sn35.120:5.4.verse: In the middle watch, they lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

sn35.120:5.5.verse: In the last watch, they get up and continue to practice walking and sitting meditation, purifying their mind from obstacles.

sn35.120:5.6.verse: That’s how someone is committed to wakefulness.

sn35.120:5.7.verse: So you should train like this:

sn35.120:5.8.verse: ‘We will guard the sense doors, eat in moderation, and be committed to wakefulness.’

sn35.127:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

sn35.127:1.2.verse: Then King Udena went up to Bhāradvāja the Alms-Gatherer and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.127:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn35.127:1.4.verse: “Worthy Bhāradvāja, there are these young monks who are youthful, with pristine black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life; and they’ve never played around with sensual pleasures. What is the cause, what is the reason why they practice the full and pure spiritual life as long as they live, maintaining it for a long time?”

sn35.127:1.5.verse: “Great king, this has been stated by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha:

sn35.127:1.6.verse: ‘Please, monks, think of women your mother’s age as your mother. Think of women your sister’s age as your sister. And think of women your daughter’s age as your daughter.’

sn35.127:1.7.verse: This is a cause, Great King, this is a reason why these young monks practice the full and pure spiritual life as long as they live, maintaining it for a long time.”

sn35.127:2.1.verse: “But worthy Bhāradvāja, the mind is wanton.

sn35.127:2.2.verse: Sometimes thoughts of desire come up even for women your mother’s age, your sister’s age, or your daughter’s age.

sn35.127:2.3.verse: Is there another cause, another reason why these young monks live the full and pure spiritual life for their entire life?”

sn35.127:3.1.verse: “Great king, this has been stated by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha:

sn35.127:3.2.verse: ‘Please, monks, examine your own body up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

sn35.127:3.3.verse: In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

sn35.127:3.4.verse: This is also a cause, Great King, this is a reason why these young monks live the full and pure spiritual life for their entire life, maintaining it for a long time.”

sn35.127:3.5.verse: “This is easy to do for those mendicants who have developed their physical endurance, ethics, mind, and wisdom.
