sn35.127:4.7.verse: When you taste a flavor with your tongue …

sn35.127:4.8.verse: When you feel a touch with your body …

sn35.127:4.9.verse: When you know an idea with your mind, don’t get caught up in the features and details.

sn35.127:4.10.verse: If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would become overwhelming. For this reason, practice restraint, protect the faculty of mind, and achieve its restraint.’

sn35.127:4.11.verse: This is also a cause, Great King, this is a reason why these young monks practice the full and pure spiritual life as long as they live, maintaining it for a long time.”

sn35.127:5.2.verse: How well this was said by the Buddha!

sn35.127:5.3.verse: This is the real cause, this is the reason why these young monks practice the full and pure spiritual life as long as they live, maintaining it for a long time.

sn35.127:5.4.verse: For sometimes I too enter the harem with unprotected body, speech, mind, mindfulness, and sense faculties. At those times powerful thoughts of desire get the better of me.

sn35.127:5.5.verse: But sometimes I enter the harem with protected body, speech, mind, mindfulness, and sense faculties. At those times such thoughts of desire don’t get the better of me.

sn35.127:5.7.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Bhāradvāja has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn35.127:5.8.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn35.127:5.9.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Bhāradvāja remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn35.128:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn35.128:1.2.verse: Then the householder Soṇa went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn35.128:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why some sentient beings are not fully extinguished in this very life?

sn35.128:1.4.verse: What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why some sentient beings are fully extinguished in this very life?” …

sn35.129:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

sn35.129:1.2.verse: Then the householder Ghosita went up to Venerable Ānanda, and said to him:

sn35.129:1.3.verse: “Honorable Ānanda, they speak of ‘the diversity of elements’.

sn35.129:1.4.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of the diversity of elements?”

sn35.129:1.5.verse: “Householder, the eye element is found, as are agreeable sights, and eye consciousness.

sn35.129:1.6.verse: Pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

sn35.129:1.7.verse: The eye element is found, as are disagreeable sights, and eye consciousness.

sn35.129:1.8.verse: Painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

sn35.129:1.9.verse: The eye element is found, as are sights that are a basis for equanimity, and eye consciousness.

sn35.129:1.10.verse: Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

sn35.129:1.17.verse: mind element is found, as are agreeable ideas, and mind consciousness.

sn35.129:1.18.verse: Pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

sn35.129:1.19.verse: The mind element is found, as are disagreeable ideas, and mind consciousness.

sn35.129:1.20.verse: Painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

sn35.129:1.21.verse: The mind element is found, as are ideas that are a basis for equanimity, and mind consciousness.

sn35.129:1.22.verse: Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

sn35.129:1.23.verse: This is how the Buddha spoke of the diversity of elements.”

sn35.130:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis near Kuraraghara on Steep Mountain.

sn35.130:1.2.verse: Then the householder Hāliddikāni went up to Venerable Mahākaccāna … and asked him,

sn35.130:1.3.verse: “Sir, this was said by the Buddha:

sn35.130:1.4.verse: ‘Diversity of elements gives rise to diversity of contacts, and diversity of contacts gives rise to diversity of feelings.’

sn35.130:1.5.verse: How does diversity of elements give rise to diversity of contacts, and diversity of contacts gives rise to diversity of feelings?”

sn35.130:1.6.verse: “Householder, it’s when a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes and understands it to be agreeable.

sn35.130:1.7.verse: There is eye consciousness; and pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

sn35.130:1.8.verse: Then they see a sight and understand it to be disagreeable.

sn35.130:1.9.verse: There is eye consciousness; and painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

sn35.130:1.10.verse: Then they see a sight and understand it to be a basis for equanimity.

sn35.130:1.11.verse: There is eye consciousness; and neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

sn35.130:2.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant hears a sound with their ears …

sn35.130:2.2.verse: smells an odor with their nose …

sn35.130:2.3.verse: tastes a flavor with their tongue …

sn35.130:2.4.verse: encounters a touch with their body …

sn35.130:2.5.verse: knows an idea with their mind and understands it to be agreeable.

sn35.130:2.6.verse: There is mind consciousness; and pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

sn35.130:2.7.verse: Then they know an idea and understand it to be disagreeable.

sn35.130:2.8.verse: There is mind consciousness; and painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

sn35.130:2.9.verse: Then they know an idea and understand it to be a basis for equanimity.

sn35.130:2.10.verse: Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

sn35.130:2.11.verse: That’s how diversity of elements gives rise to diversity of contacts, and diversity of contacts gives rise to diversity of feelings.”

sn35.131:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

sn35.131:1.2.verse: Then the householder Nakula’s father went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.131:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why some sentient beings are not fully extinguished in this very life?

sn35.131:1.4.verse: What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why some sentient beings are fully extinguished in this very life?”

sn35.131:1.5.verse: “Householder, there are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.131:1.6.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.131:1.7.verse: their consciousness has that as support and fuel for grasping.

sn35.131:1.8.verse: A mendicant with fuel for grasping does not become extinguished.

sn35.131:1.9.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.131:1.10.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.131:1.11.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.131:1.12.verse: their consciousness has that as support and fuel for grasping.

sn35.131:1.13.verse: A mendicant with fuel for grasping does not become extinguished.

sn35.131:1.14.verse: That’s the cause, that’s the reason why some sentient beings are not fully extinguished in this very life.

sn35.131:2.1.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.131:2.2.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them,

sn35.131:2.3.verse: their consciousness doesn’t have that as support and fuel for grasping.

sn35.131:2.4.verse: A mendicant free of grasping becomes extinguished.

sn35.131:2.5.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.131:2.6.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.131:2.7.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them,

sn35.131:2.8.verse: their consciousness doesn’t have that as support and fuel for grasping.

sn35.131:2.9.verse: A mendicant free of grasping becomes extinguished.

sn35.131:2.10.verse: That’s the cause, that’s the reason why some sentient beings are fully extinguished in this very life.”

sn35.132:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis in a wilderness hut near Makkarakaṭa.

sn35.132:1.2.verse: Then several students, pupils of the brahmin Lohicca, approached Mahākaccāna’s wilderness hut while collecting firewood. They walked and wandered all around the hut, making a colossal racket and all kinds of jeers:

sn35.132:1.3.verse: “These shavelings, fake ascetics, primitives, black spawn from the feet of our kinsman, the Lord! They’re honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by so-called inheritors of Vedic culture.”

sn35.132:1.4.verse: Then Mahākaccāna left his dwelling and said to those young students,

sn35.132:1.6.verse: I will speak to you on the teaching.”

sn35.132:1.7.verse: When this was said, the young students fell silent.

sn35.132:1.8.verse: Then Mahākaccāna recited these verses for them:

sn35.132:2.1.verse: “For the brahmins of old, ethics were the highest;

sn35.132:2.3.verse: Their sense doors were guarded, well protected,

sn35.132:3.1.verse: Those brahmins who remembered the ancient legends

sn35.132:4.1.verse: But these have lost their way. Saying, ‘We must pray’,

sn35.132:4.2.verse: they live out of balance, judging by clan.

sn35.132:4.3.verse: Mastered by anger, they take up many arms,

sn35.132:4.4.verse: indifferent to those with craving and without.

sn35.132:5.1.verse: All is vain for someone who doesn’t guard the sense doors,

sn35.132:5.2.verse: like the wealth a person finds in a dream.

sn35.132:5.4.verse: bathing at daybreak, the three Vedas,

sn35.132:6.2.verse: hymns, precepts and observances, and fervent austerities,

sn35.132:6.6.verse: are only used to generate profits.

sn35.132:7.4.verse: that’s the path to attainment of divinity!”

sn35.132:8.1.verse: Then those young students, offended and upset, went to the brahmin Lohicca and said to him,

sn35.132:8.2.verse: “Please, master, you should know this. The ascetic Mahākaccāna condemns and rejects outright the hymns of the brahmins!”

sn35.132:8.3.verse: When they said this, Lohicca was offended and upset.

sn35.132:8.5.verse: “But it wouldn’t be appropriate for me to abuse or insult the ascetic Mahākaccāna solely because of what I’ve heard from these young students.

sn35.132:8.6.verse: Why don’t I go and ask him about it?”

sn35.132:9.1.verse: Then the brahmin Lohicca together with those young students went to Venerable Mahākaccāna and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.132:9.2.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to him,

sn35.132:9.3.verse: “Master Kaccāna, did several young pupils of mine come by here collecting firewood?”

sn35.132:9.5.verse: “But did you have some discussion with them?”

sn35.132:9.7.verse: “But what kind of discussion did you have with them?”

sn35.132:9.8.verse: “This is the discussion I had with these young students.” And he repeated the verses in full.

sn35.132:12.1.verse: “Worthy Kaccāna spoke of someone who doesn’t guard the sense doors.

sn35.132:12.2.verse: How do you define someone who doesn’t guard the sense doors?”

sn35.132:12.3.verse: “Brahmin, take someone who sees a sight with their eyes. If it’s pleasant they hold on to it, but if it’s unpleasant they dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body unestablished and their heart stunted.

sn35.132:12.4.verse: And they don’t truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

sn35.132:12.5.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

sn35.132:12.6.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

sn35.132:12.7.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

sn35.132:12.8.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

sn35.132:12.9.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, if it’s pleasant they hold on to it, but if it’s unpleasant they dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body unestablished and their heart stunted.

sn35.132:12.10.verse: And they don’t truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

sn35.132:12.11.verse: That’s how someone doesn’t guard the sense doors.”

sn35.132:12.13.verse: How accurately you’ve explained someone whose sense doors are unguarded!

sn35.132:13.1.verse: You also spoke of someone who does guard the sense doors.

sn35.132:13.2.verse: How do you define someone who does guard the sense doors?”

sn35.132:13.3.verse: “Brahmin, take a mendicant who sees a sight with their eyes. If it’s pleasant they don’t hold on to it, and if it’s unpleasant they don’t dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body established and a limitless heart.

sn35.132:13.4.verse: And they truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

sn35.132:13.5.verse: When they hear a sound with their ears …

sn35.132:13.6.verse: When they smell an odor with their nose …

sn35.132:13.7.verse: When they taste a flavor with their tongue …

sn35.132:13.8.verse: When they feel a touch with their body …

sn35.132:13.9.verse: When they know an idea with their mind, if it’s pleasant they don’t hold on to it, and if it’s unpleasant they don’t dislike it. They live with mindfulness of the body established and a limitless heart.

sn35.132:13.10.verse: And they truly understand the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where those arisen bad, unskillful qualities cease without remainder.

sn35.132:13.11.verse: That’s how someone guards the sense doors.”

sn35.132:14.2.verse: How accurately you’ve explained someone whose sense doors are guarded!

sn35.132:14.4.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the worthy Kaccāna has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn35.132:14.5.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn35.132:14.6.verse: From this day forth, may the worthy Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.

sn35.132:14.7.verse: Please come to my family just as you go to the families of the lay followers in Makkarakaṭa.

sn35.132:14.8.verse: The brahmin boys and girls there will bow to you, rise in your presence, and give you a seat and water. That will be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

sn35.133:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Udāyī was staying near Kāmaṇḍā in the brahmin Todeyya’s mango grove.

sn35.133:1.2.verse: Then a boy who was a pupil of the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan went up to Udāyī and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.133:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.

sn35.133:1.4.verse: Udāyī educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired that young student with a Dhamma talk.

sn35.133:1.5.verse: Then that young student went to the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan and said to her,

sn35.133:1.7.verse: The ascetic Udāyī teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.”

sn35.133:2.1.verse: “Then, young student, invite him in my name for tomorrow’s meal.”

sn35.133:2.2.verse: “Yes, madam,” he replied. He went to Udāyī and said,

sn35.133:2.3.verse: “Would Worthy Udāyī please accept an offering of tomorrow’s meal from my tutor’s wife, the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan?”

sn35.133:2.5.verse: Then when the night had passed, Udāyī robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the brahmin lady’s home, and sat down on the seat spread out.

sn35.133:2.6.verse: Then the brahmin lady served and satisfied Udāyī with her own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

sn35.133:2.7.verse: When Udāyī had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, she put on a pair of slippers, sat on a high seat, covered her head, and said to him,

sn35.133:2.9.verse: “There will be an occasion for that, sister,” he replied, then rose from his seat and left.

sn35.133:3.1.verse: For a second time that young student went to Venerable Udāyī …

sn35.133:3.4.verse: And for a second time that young student went to the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan …

sn35.133:4.1.verse: She said to him, “You keep praising the ascetic Udāyī like this.

sn35.133:4.2.verse: But when I asked him to preach the Dhamma he just said that there would be an occasion for that, and then he got up and left.”

sn35.133:4.3.verse: “Madam, that’s because you put on a pair of slippers, sat on a high seat, and covered your head before inviting him to teach.

sn35.133:4.5.verse: For the good sirs respect the teaching.”

sn35.133:4.6.verse: “Then, young student, invite him in my name for tomorrow’s meal.”

sn35.133:5.2.verse: Then the brahmin lady served and satisfied Udāyī with her own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

sn35.133:5.3.verse: When Udāyī had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, she took off her slippers, sat on a low seat, uncovered her head, and said to him,

sn35.133:5.4.verse: “Sir, when what exists do the perfected ones assert that there is pleasure and pain? When what doesn’t exist do the perfected ones not declare that there is pleasure and pain?”

sn35.133:6.1.verse: “Sister, when there’s an eye, the perfected ones assert that there is pleasure and pain. When there’s no eye, the perfected ones don’t declare that there is pleasure and pain.

sn35.133:6.2.verse: When there’s an ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.133:6.3.verse: mind, the perfected ones assert that there is pleasure and pain. When there’s no mind, the perfected ones don’t declare that there is pleasure and pain.”

sn35.133:7.1.verse: When he said this, the brahmin lady said to Udāyī,

sn35.133:7.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, Master Udāyī has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn35.133:7.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn35.133:7.5.verse: From this day forth, may Master Udāyī remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn35.134:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near the Sakyan town named Devadaha.

sn35.134:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn35.134:1.3.verse: “When it comes to the six fields of contact, mendicants, I don’t say that all mendicants have work to do with diligence, nor do I say that none of them have work to do with diligence.

sn35.134:1.4.verse: I say that, when it comes to the six fields of contact, mendicants don’t have work to do with diligence if they are perfected, with defilements ended, having completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and become rightly freed through enlightenment.

sn35.134:1.6.verse: They’ve done their work with diligence, and are incapable of negligence.

sn35.134:1.7.verse: I say that, when it comes to the six fields of contact, mendicants do have work to do with diligence if they are trainees, who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.

sn35.134:1.9.verse: There are sights known by the eye that are pleasant and also those that are unpleasant.

sn35.134:1.10.verse: Though experiencing them again and again they don’t occupy the mind.

sn35.134:1.11.verse: Their energy is roused up and unflagging, their mindfulness is established and lucid, their body is tranquil and undisturbed, and their mind is immersed and unified in samādhi.

sn35.134:1.12.verse: Seeing this fruit of diligence, I say that those mendicants have work to do with diligence when it comes to the six fields of contact. …

sn35.134:1.13.verse: There are ideas known by the mind that are pleasant and also those that are unpleasant.

sn35.134:1.14.verse: Though experiencing them again and again they don’t occupy the mind.

sn35.134:1.15.verse: Their energy is roused up and unflagging, their mindfulness is established and lucid, their body is tranquil and undisturbed, and their mind is immersed and unified in samādhi.

sn35.134:1.16.verse: Seeing this fruit of diligence, I say that those mendicants have work to do with diligence when it comes to the six fields of contact.”

sn35.135:1.2.verse: to have the opportunity to lead the spiritual life.

sn35.135:1.3.verse: I’ve seen the hell named ‘Related to the Six Fields of Contact’.

sn35.135:1.4.verse: There, whatever sight you see with your eye is unlikable, not likable; undesirable, not desirable; unpleasant, not pleasant.

sn35.135:1.9.verse: Whatever idea you know with your mind is unlikable, not likable; undesirable, not desirable; unpleasant, not pleasant.

sn35.135:1.10.verse: You’re fortunate, mendicants, so very fortunate,

sn35.135:1.11.verse: to have the opportunity to lead the spiritual life.

sn35.135:1.12.verse: I’ve seen the heaven called ‘Related to the Six Fields of Contact’.

sn35.135:1.13.verse: There, whatever sight you see with your eye is likable, not unlikable; desirable, not undesirable; pleasant, not unpleasant.

sn35.135:1.15.verse: Whatever idea you know with your mind is likable, not unlikable; desirable, not undesirable; pleasant, not unpleasant.

sn35.135:1.16.verse: You’re fortunate, mendicants, so very fortunate,

sn35.135:1.17.verse: to have the opportunity to lead the spiritual life.”

sn35.136:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, gods and humans like sights, they love them and enjoy them.

sn35.136:1.2.verse: But when sights perish, fade away, and cease, gods and humans live in suffering.

sn35.136:1.8.verse: ideas, they love them and enjoy them.

sn35.136:1.9.verse: But when ideas perish, fade away, and cease, gods and humans live in suffering.

sn35.136:1.10.verse: The Realized One has truly understood the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape of sights, so he doesn’t like, love, or enjoy them.

sn35.136:1.11.verse: When sights perish, fade away, and cease, the Realized One lives happily.

sn35.136:1.12.verse: The Realized One has truly understood the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape of sounds …

sn35.136:1.16.verse: ideas, so he doesn’t like, love, or enjoy them.

sn35.136:1.17.verse: When ideas perish, fade away, and cease, the Realized One lives happily.”

sn35.136:1.18.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn35.136:1.19.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn35.136:2.2.verse: touches and ideas, the lot of them—

sn35.136:2.4.verse: as long as you can say that they exist.

sn35.136:3.1.verse: For all the world with its gods,

sn35.136:3.2.verse: this is what they deem happiness.

sn35.136:3.4.verse: is deemed as suffering for them.

sn35.136:4.1.verse: The noble ones have seen that happiness

sn35.136:4.2.verse: is the cessation of substantial reality.

sn35.136:4.3.verse: This insight by those who see

sn35.136:5.2.verse: the noble ones say is suffering.

sn35.136:5.4.verse: the noble ones know as happiness.

sn35.136:6.1.verse: See, this teaching is hard to understand,

sn35.136:6.3.verse: There is darkness for the shrouded;

sn35.136:6.4.verse: blackness for those who don’t see.

sn35.136:7.2.verse: like light for those who see.

sn35.136:7.3.verse: Though close, they do not understand,

sn35.136:7.4.verse: the seekers inexpert in the teaching.

sn35.136:8.1.verse: They’re mired in desire for continued existence,

sn35.136:8.2.verse: flowing along the stream of lives,

sn35.136:8.4.verse: this teaching isn’t easy for them to understand.

sn35.136:9.1.verse: Who, apart from the noble ones,

sn35.136:9.2.verse: is qualified to understand this state?

sn35.137:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, gods and humans like sights, they love them and enjoy them.

sn35.137:1.2.verse: But when sights perish, fade away, and cease, gods and humans live in suffering. …

sn35.137:1.9.verse: The Realized One has truly understood the origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape of sights, so he doesn’t like, love, or enjoy them.

sn35.137:1.10.verse: When sights perish, fade away, and cease, the Realized One lives happily. …”

sn35.138:1.2.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.138:1.4.verse: The eye isn’t yours: give it up.

sn35.138:1.5.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.138:1.8.verse: mind isn’t yours: give it up.

sn35.138:1.9.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.138:1.10.verse: Suppose a person was to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do what they want with them. Would you think:

sn35.138:1.11.verse: ‘This person is carrying us off, burning us, or doing what they want with us’?”

sn35.138:1.14.verse: Because  to us that’s neither self nor belonging to self.”

sn35.138:1.15.verse: “In the same way, the eye isn’t yours: give it up.

sn35.138:1.16.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.138:1.19.verse: mind isn’t yours: give it up.

sn35.138:1.20.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.”

sn35.139:1.2.verse: Giving it up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.139:1.4.verse: Sights aren’t yours: give them up.

sn35.139:1.5.verse: Giving them up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.139:1.10.verse: and ideas aren’t yours: give them up.

sn35.139:1.11.verse: Giving them up will be for your welfare and happiness.

sn35.139:1.12.verse: Suppose a person was to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove …

sn35.139:1.13.verse: In the same way, sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas aren’t yours: give them up.

sn35.139:1.14.verse: Giving them up will be for your welfare and happiness.”

sn35.140:1.2.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to the eye is also impermanent.

sn35.140:1.3.verse: Since the eye is produced by what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.140:1.8.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to the mind is also impermanent.

sn35.140:1.9.verse: Since the mind is produced by what is impermanent, how could it be permanent?

sn35.140:1.10.verse: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

sn35.140:1.11.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn35.140:1.12.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.141:1.2.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to the eye is also suffering.

sn35.141:1.3.verse: Since the eye is produced by what is suffering, how could it be happiness?

sn35.141:1.8.verse: The cause and reason that gives rise to the mind is also suffering.

sn35.141:1.9.verse: Since the mind is produced by what is suffering, how could it be happiness?

sn35.141:1.11.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

sn35.143:1.10.verse: Since ideas are produced by what is impermanent, how could they be permanent?

sn35.145:1.10.verse: Since ideas are produced by what is not-self, how could they be self?

sn35.146:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you old deeds, new deeds, the cessation of deeds, and the practice that leads to the cessation of deeds.

sn35.146:1.2.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak. …

sn35.146:1.4.verse: The eye is old deeds. It should be seen as produced by choices and intentions, as something to be felt.

sn35.146:1.6.verse: mind is old deeds. It should be seen as produced by choices and intentions, as something to be felt.

sn35.146:1.9.verse: The deeds you currently perform by way of body, speech, and mind.

sn35.146:1.11.verse: And what is the cessation of deeds?

sn35.146:1.12.verse: When you experience freedom due to the cessation of deeds by body, speech, and mind.

sn35.146:1.13.verse: This is called the cessation of deeds.

sn35.146:1.14.verse: And what’s the practice that leads to the cessation of deeds?

sn35.146:1.15.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn35.146:1.16.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn35.146:1.17.verse: This is called the practice that leads to the cessation of deeds.

sn35.146:1.18.verse: So, mendicants, I’ve taught you old deeds, new deeds, the cessation of deeds, and the practice that leads to the cessation of deeds.

sn35.146:1.19.verse: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

sn35.146:1.20.verse: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

sn35.147:0.3.verse: The Impermanent as Conducive to Extinguishment

sn35.147:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you a practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.

sn35.147:1.3.verse: And what is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment?

sn35.147:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant sees that the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are impermanent. And they see that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also impermanent.

sn35.147:1.5.verse: They see that the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.147:1.6.verse: mind, ideas, mind-consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent. And they see that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also impermanent.

sn35.147:1.7.verse: This is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.”

sn35.148:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you a practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.

sn35.148:1.3.verse: And what is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment?

sn35.148:1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant sees that the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are suffering. And they see that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also suffering.

sn35.148:1.5.verse: They see that the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.148:1.6.verse: mind, ideas, mind-consciousness, and mind contact are suffering. And they see that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also suffering.

sn35.148:1.7.verse: This is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.”

sn35.150:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I will teach you a practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.

sn35.150:1.3.verse: And what is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment?

sn35.150:1.5.verse: Is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.150:3.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.150:5.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn35.150:5.2.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.150:9.3.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact: is that permanent or impermanent?”

sn35.150:11.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

sn35.150:13.1.verse: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:

sn35.150:13.2.verse: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”

sn35.150:15.1.verse: “Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact. And they grow disillusioned with the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact.

sn35.150:15.2.verse: They grow disillusioned with the ear … nose … tongue … body … mind … painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact.

sn35.150:15.3.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. …

sn35.150:15.4.verse: They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

sn35.150:15.5.verse: This is that practice that’s conducive to extinguishment.”

sn35.151:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, this spiritual life is lived without a resident pupil and without a teaching master.

sn35.151:1.2.verse: A mendicant who lives with a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in suffering and discomfort.

sn35.151:1.3.verse: A mendicant who lives without a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in happiness and comfort.

sn35.151:1.4.verse: And how does a mendicant who lives with a resident pupil and a teaching master live in suffering and discomfort?

sn35.151:1.5.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.151:1.6.verse: Those qualities reside within. Since they have bad unskillful qualities residing within,

sn35.151:1.7.verse: they’re said to have a resident pupil.

sn35.151:1.8.verse: Those qualities master them. Since they’re mastered by bad unskillful qualities,

sn35.151:1.9.verse: they’re said to have a teaching master.

sn35.151:2.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant hears … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.151:3.1.verse: knows an idea with their mind, bad, unskillful phenomena arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.151:3.2.verse: Those qualities reside within. Since they have bad unskillful qualities residing within,

sn35.151:3.3.verse: they’re said to have a resident pupil.

sn35.151:3.4.verse: Those qualities master them. Since they’re mastered by bad unskillful qualities,

sn35.151:3.5.verse: they’re said to have a teaching master.

sn35.151:3.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant who lives with a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in suffering and discomfort.

sn35.151:4.1.verse: And how does a mendicant who lives without a resident pupil and a teaching master live in happiness and comfort?

sn35.151:4.2.verse: When a mendicant sees a sight with their eyes, bad, unskillful phenomena don’t arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.151:4.3.verse: Those qualities don’t reside within. Since they don’t have bad unskillful qualities residing within,

sn35.151:4.4.verse: they’re said to not have a resident pupil.

sn35.151:4.5.verse: Those qualities don’t master them. Since they’re not mastered by bad unskillful qualities,

sn35.151:4.6.verse: they’re said to not have a teaching master.

sn35.151:5.1.verse: Furthermore, when a mendicant hears … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.151:6.1.verse: knows an idea with their mind, bad, unskillful phenomena don’t arise: memories and thoughts that tighten the fetters.

sn35.151:6.2.verse: Those qualities don’t reside within. Since they don’t have bad unskillful qualities residing within,

sn35.151:6.3.verse: they’re said to not have a resident pupil.

sn35.151:6.4.verse: Those qualities don’t master them. Since they’re not mastered by bad unskillful qualities,

sn35.151:6.5.verse: they’re said to not have a teaching master.

sn35.151:6.6.verse: That’s how a mendicant who lives without a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in happiness and comfort.

sn35.151:6.7.verse: This spiritual life is lived without a resident pupil and without a teaching master.

sn35.151:6.8.verse: A mendicant who lives with a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in suffering and discomfort.

sn35.151:6.9.verse: A mendicant who lives without a resident pupil and a teaching master lives in happiness and comfort.”

sn35.152:0.3.verse: What’s the Goal of the Spiritual Life?

sn35.152:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers who follow another religion were to ask you:

sn35.152:1.2.verse: ‘Reverends, what’s the goal of leading the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama?’

sn35.152:1.4.verse: ‘The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand suffering.’

sn35.152:1.5.verse: If wanderers of other religions were to ask you:

sn35.152:2.2.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.152:2.9.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also suffering.

sn35.152:2.10.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.152:2.14.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also suffering.

sn35.152:2.15.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.

sn35.152:2.17.verse: The goal of leading the spiritual life under the Buddha is to completely understand this.’

sn35.152:2.18.verse: When questioned by wanderers of other religions, that’s how you should answer them.”

sn35.153:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, is there a method—apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation—that a mendicant can rely on to declare their enlightenment? That is:

sn35.153:1.2.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’”

sn35.153:1.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

sn35.153:1.4.verse: “Well then, mendicants, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn35.153:1.7.verse: “There is a method—apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation—that a mendicant can rely on to declare their enlightenment. That is:

sn35.153:1.8.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’

sn35.153:2.2.verse: Take a mendicant who sees a sight with their eyes. When they have greed, hate, and delusion in them, they understand ‘I have greed, hate, and delusion in me.’

sn35.153:2.3.verse: When they don’t have greed, hate, and delusion in them, they understand ‘I don’t have greed, hate, and delusion in me.’

sn35.153:2.4.verse: Since this is so, are these things understood by faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation?”

sn35.153:2.6.verse: “Aren’t they understood by seeing them with wisdom?”

sn35.153:2.8.verse: “This is a method—apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation—that a mendicant can rely on to declare their enlightenment. That is:

sn35.153:2.9.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’

sn35.153:3.1.verse: Furthermore, a mendicant hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … encounters a touch …

sn35.153:4.1.verse: knows an idea with their mind. When they have greed, hate, and delusion in them, they understand ‘I have greed, hate, and delusion in me.’

sn35.153:4.2.verse: When they don’t have greed, hate, and delusion in them, they understand ‘I don’t have greed, hate, and delusion in me.’

sn35.153:4.3.verse: Since this is so, are these things understood by faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation?”

sn35.153:4.5.verse: “Aren’t they understood by seeing them with wisdom?”

sn35.153:4.7.verse: “This too is a method—apart from faith, endorsement, oral transmission, reasoned train of thought, or acceptance of a view after deliberation—that a mendicant can rely on to declare their enlightenment. That is:

sn35.153:4.8.verse: ‘I understand: “Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.”’”

sn35.154:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.154:1.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of someone who is ‘accomplished in the faculties’.

sn35.154:1.3.verse: How is someone accomplished in the faculties defined?”

sn35.154:2.1.verse: “Mendicant, if someone meditates observing rise and fall in the eye faculty, they grow disillusioned with the eye faculty.

sn35.154:2.2.verse: If they meditate observing rise and fall in the ear faculty … nose faculty … tongue faculty … body faculty …

sn35.154:2.3.verse: mind faculty, they grow disillusioned with the mind faculty.

sn35.154:2.4.verse: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. … When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

sn35.154:2.5.verse: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

sn35.154:2.6.verse: This is how someone who is accomplished in the faculties is defined.”

sn35.155:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.155:1.3.verse: How is a Dhamma speaker defined?”

sn35.155:2.1.verse: “If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the eye, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn35.155:2.2.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the eye, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn35.155:2.3.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the eye, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.

sn35.155:2.4.verse: If a mendicant teaches Dhamma for disillusionment with the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.155:2.5.verse: mind, for its fading away and cessation, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who speaks on Dhamma’.

sn35.155:2.6.verse: If they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the mind, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who practices in line with the teaching’.

sn35.155:2.7.verse: If they’re freed by not grasping by disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding the mind, they’re qualified to be called ‘a mendicant who has attained extinguishment in this very life’.”

sn35.156:1.3.verse: When relishing ends, greed ends. When greed ends, relishing ends.

sn35.156:1.5.verse: When relishing and greed end, the mind is said to be well freed.

sn35.160:0.3.verse: On Immersion at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

sn35.160:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.

sn35.160:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn35.160:1.5.verse: For a mendicant with immersion, things become truly clear.

sn35.160:1.7.verse: It becomes truly clear that the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are impermanent. And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is impermanent.

sn35.160:1.8.verse: It becomes truly clear that the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.160:1.9.verse: mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent.

sn35.160:1.10.verse: And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is impermanent.

sn35.160:1.12.verse: For a mendicant with immersion, things become truly clear.”

sn35.161:0.3.verse: On Retreat at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

sn35.161:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn35.161:1.4.verse: For a mendicant who meditates in retreat, things become truly clear.

sn35.161:1.6.verse: It becomes truly clear that the eye, sights, eye consciousness, and eye contact are impermanent. And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is impermanent. …

sn35.161:1.7.verse: It becomes truly clear that the mind, ideas, mind consciousness, and mind contact are impermanent.

sn35.161:1.10.verse: And it also becomes truly clear that the painful, pleasant, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is impermanent.

sn35.161:1.12.verse: For a mendicant who meditates in retreat, things become truly clear.”

sn35.162:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn35.162:1.2.verse: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn35.162:2.1.verse: “Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is impermanent.

sn35.162:2.6.verse: and eye contact are impermanent: you should give up desire for them.

sn35.162:2.7.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also impermanent: you should give up desire for it.

sn35.162:2.16.verse: and mind contact are impermanent: you should give up desire for them.

sn35.162:2.17.verse: The pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact is also impermanent: you should give up desire for it.

sn35.162:2.18.verse: Koṭṭhita, you should give up desire for what is impermanent.”

sn35.228:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of the ocean.

sn35.228:1.2.verse: But that’s not the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.228:1.3.verse: That’s just a large body of water, a large sea of water.

sn35.228:1.4.verse: For a person, the eye is an ocean,

sn35.228:1.5.verse: and its currents are made of sights.

sn35.228:2.1.verse: Someone who can prevail over those currents is said to have crossed over the ocean of the eye, with its waves and whirlpools, its saltwater crocodiles and monsters.

sn35.228:2.2.verse: Crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground.

sn35.228:2.3.verse: For a person, the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.228:2.8.verse: and its currents are made of ideas.

sn35.228:2.9.verse: Someone who can prevail over those currents is said to have crossed over the ocean of the mind, with its waves and whirlpools, its saltwater crocodiles and monsters.

sn35.228:2.10.verse: Crossed over, gone to the far shore, the brahmin stands on solid ground.”

sn35.228:2.11.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn35.228:2.12.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn35.228:3.1.verse: “A knowledge master who’s crossed the ocean so hard to cross,

sn35.228:3.2.verse: with its saltwater crocodiles and monsters, its waves, whirlpools, and dangers;

sn35.228:3.3.verse: they’ve completed the spiritual journey and gone to the end of the world,

sn35.228:3.4.verse: they’re called ‘one who has gone beyond’.”

sn35.229:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of the ocean.

sn35.229:1.2.verse: But that’s not the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.229:1.3.verse: That’s just a large body of water, a large sea of water.

sn35.229:1.4.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.229:1.5.verse: This is called the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.229:1.6.verse: And it’s here that this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—is for the most part sunk. It’s become tangled like string, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, and it doesn’t escape the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.

sn35.229:2.1.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches … ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.229:2.2.verse: This is called the ocean in the training of the Noble One.

sn35.229:2.3.verse: And it’s here that this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—is for the most part sunk. It’s become tangled like string, knotted like a ball of thread, and matted like rushes and reeds, and it doesn’t escape the places of loss, the bad places, the underworld, transmigration.

sn35.229:3.1.verse: Those in whom greed, hate, and ignorance

sn35.229:3.3.verse: have crossed the ocean so hard to cross,

sn35.229:3.4.verse: with its saltwater crocodiles and monsters, its waves and dangers.

sn35.229:4.1.verse: They’ve slipped their chains, given up death, and have no attachments.

sn35.229:4.2.verse: They’ve given up suffering, so there are no more future lives.

sn35.229:4.3.verse: They’ve disappeared, and cannot be measured;

sn35.229:4.4.verse: and they’ve confounded the King of Death, I say.”

sn35.230:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose an angler was to cast a baited hook into a deep lake.

sn35.230:1.2.verse: Seeing the bait, a fish would swallow it.

sn35.230:1.3.verse: And so the fish that swallowed the hook would meet with tragedy and disaster, and the angler can do what he wants with it.

sn35.230:2.1.verse: In the same way, there are these six hooks in the world that mean tragedy and slaughter for living creatures.

sn35.230:2.3.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.230:2.4.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.230:2.5.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

sn35.230:2.6.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.230:3.1.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.230:3.2.verse: If a mendicant approves, welcomes, and keeps clinging to them,

sn35.230:3.3.verse: they’re called a mendicant who has swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One can do with them what he wants.

sn35.230:4.1.verse: There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.230:4.2.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, they’re called a mendicant who hasn’t swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve broken the hook, destroyed it. They haven’t met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do with them what he wants.

sn35.230:5.1.verse: There are sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.230:5.2.verse: ideas known by the mind, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.

sn35.230:5.3.verse: If a mendicant doesn’t approve, welcome, and keep clinging to them, they’re called a mendicant who hasn’t swallowed Māra’s hook. They’ve broken the hook, destroyed it. They haven’t met with tragedy and disaster, and the Wicked One cannot do with them what he wants.”

sn35.231:0.3.verse: The Simile of the Latex-Producing Tree

sn35.231:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, still has greed, hate, and delusion, and has not given them up. If even trivial sights come into their range of vision they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.

sn35.231:1.3.verse: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

sn35.231:2.1.verse: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.231:3.1.verse: ideas known by the mind, they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up. If even trivial thoughts come into the range of the mind they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.

sn35.231:3.3.verse: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

sn35.231:4.1.verse: Suppose there was a latex-producing tree—such as a peepal, a banyan, a wavy leaf fig, or a cluster fig—that’s a tender young sapling.

sn35.231:4.2.verse: If a man were to chop it here and there with a sharp axe, would latex come out?”

sn35.231:5.1.verse: “In the same way, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, still has greed, hate, and delusion, and has not given them up. If even trivial sights come into their range of vision they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.

sn35.231:5.3.verse: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

sn35.231:6.1.verse: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.231:7.1.verse: ideas known by the mind, they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up. If even trivial thoughts come into the range of the mind they overcome their mind, let alone those that are compelling.

sn35.231:7.3.verse: Because they still have greed, hate, and delusion, and have not given them up.

sn35.231:8.1.verse: Take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, has no greed, hate, and delusion left, and has given them up. If even compelling sights come into their range of vision they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.

sn35.231:8.3.verse: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

sn35.231:9.1.verse: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches … ideas known by the mind, they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up. If even compelling ideas come into the range of the mind they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.

sn35.231:9.3.verse: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

sn35.231:9.4.verse: Suppose there was a latex-producing tree—such as a peepal, a banyan, a wavy leaf fig, or a cluster fig—that’s dried up, withered, and decrepit.

sn35.231:9.5.verse: If a man were to chop it here and there with a sharp axe, would latex come out?”

sn35.231:9.8.verse: Because it has no latex left.”

sn35.231:10.1.verse: “In the same way, take any monk or nun who, when it comes to sights known by the eye, has no greed, hate, and delusion left, and has given them up. If even compelling sights come into their range of vision they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.

sn35.231:10.3.verse: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.

sn35.231:11.1.verse: When it comes to sounds … smells … tastes … touches …

sn35.231:12.1.verse: ideas known by the mind, they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up. If even compelling thoughts come into the range of the mind they don’t overcome their mind, let alone those that are trivial.

sn35.231:12.3.verse: Because they have no greed, hate, and delusion left, and have given them up.”

sn35.232:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

sn35.232:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita came out of retreat, went to Venerable Sāriputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn35.232:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Sāriputta:

sn35.232:2.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, which is it? Is the eye the fetter of sights, or are sights the fetter of the eye?

sn35.232:2.2.verse: Is the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.232:2.3.verse: mind the fetter of ideas, or are ideas the fetter of the mind?”

sn35.232:3.1.verse: “Reverend Koṭṭhita, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

sn35.232:3.2.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

sn35.232:3.5.verse: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

sn35.232:3.6.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

sn35.232:4.1.verse: Suppose there was a black ox and a white ox yoked by a single harness or yoke.

sn35.232:4.2.verse: Would it be right to say that

sn35.232:4.3.verse: the black ox is the yoke of the white ox, or the white ox is the yoke of the black ox?”

sn35.232:4.5.verse: The black ox is not the yoke of the white ox, nor is the white ox the yoke of the black ox.

sn35.232:4.6.verse: The yoke there is the single harness or yoke that they’re yoked by.”

sn35.232:5.1.verse: “In the same way, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

sn35.232:5.2.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

sn35.232:5.4.verse: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

sn35.232:5.5.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

sn35.232:6.1.verse: If the eye were the fetter of sights, or if sights were the fetter of the eye, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found.

sn35.232:6.2.verse: However, since this is not the case, but

sn35.232:6.3.verse: the fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

sn35.232:7.1.verse: If the ear … nose … tongue … body …

sn35.232:8.1.verse: mind were the fetter of ideas, or if ideas were the fetter of the mind, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be found.

sn35.232:8.2.verse: However, since this is not the case, but

sn35.232:8.3.verse: the fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is found.

sn35.232:9.1.verse: This too is a way to understand how this is so.

sn35.232:10.2.verse: with which he sees a sight.

sn35.232:10.3.verse: But he has no desire and greed,

sn35.232:10.4.verse: for his mind is well freed.

sn35.232:10.23.verse: But he has no desire and greed,
