sn41.1:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.1:1.2.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several senior mendicants sat together in the pavilion and this discussion came up among them:

sn41.1:1.3.verse: “Reverends, the ‘fetter’ and the ‘things that tighten the fetters’: do these things differ in both meaning and phrasing? Or do they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?”

sn41.1:1.4.verse: Some senior mendicants answered like this:

sn41.1:1.5.verse: “Reverends, the ‘fetter’ and the ‘things that tighten the fetters’: these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.”

sn41.1:1.6.verse: But some senior mendicants answered like this:

sn41.1:1.7.verse: “Reverends, the ‘fetter’ and the ‘things that tighten the fetters’ mean the same thing; they differ only in the phrasing.”

sn41.1:2.1.verse: Now at that time the householder Citta had arrived at Migapathaka on some business.

sn41.1:2.2.verse: He heard about what those senior mendicants were discussing.

sn41.1:3.1.verse: So he went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to them,

sn41.1:3.2.verse: “Sirs, I heard that you were discussing whether the ‘fetter’ and the ‘things that tighten the fetters’ differ in both meaning and phrasing, or whether they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.”

sn41.1:4.1.verse: “Sirs, the ‘fetter’ and the ‘things that tighten the fetters’: these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

sn41.1:4.2.verse: Well then, sirs, I shall give you a simile.

sn41.1:4.3.verse: For by means of a simile some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said.

sn41.1:4.4.verse: Suppose there was a black ox and a white ox yoked by a single harness or yoke.

sn41.1:4.5.verse: Would it be right to say that

sn41.1:4.6.verse: the black ox is the yoke of the white ox, or the white ox is the yoke of the black ox?”

sn41.1:4.8.verse: The black ox is not the yoke of the white ox, nor is the white ox the yoke of the black ox.

sn41.1:4.9.verse: The yoke there is the single harness or yoke that they’re yoked by.”

sn41.1:4.10.verse: “In the same way, the eye is not the fetter of sights, nor are sights the fetter of the eye.

sn41.1:4.11.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.

sn41.1:4.17.verse: mind is not the fetter of ideas, nor are ideas the fetter of the mind.

sn41.1:4.18.verse: The fetter there is the desire and greed that arises from the pair of them.”

sn41.1:4.20.verse: to traverse the Buddha’s deep teachings with the eye of wisdom.”

sn41.2:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.2:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to them,

sn41.2:1.3.verse: “Sirs, would the senior monks please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

sn41.2:1.5.verse: Knowing that the senior mendicants had consented, Citta rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled them, keeping them on his right, before leaving.

sn41.2:1.6.verse: Then when the night had passed, the senior mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, went to Citta’s home, and sat down on the seats spread out.

sn41.2:2.1.verse: Then Citta went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and asked the senior venerable,

sn41.2:2.2.verse: “Honorable Senior, they speak of ‘the diversity of elements’.

sn41.2:2.3.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of the diversity of elements?”

sn41.2:2.4.verse: When he said this, the senior venerable kept silent.

sn41.2:2.9.verse: And for a third time, Citta asked him,

sn41.2:2.10.verse: “Honorable Senior, they speak of ‘the diversity of elements’.

sn41.2:2.11.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of the diversity of elements?”

sn41.2:2.12.verse: And a second time and a third time the senior venerable kept silent.

sn41.2:3.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Isidatta was the most junior mendicant in that Saṅgha.

sn41.2:3.2.verse: He said to the senior venerable,

sn41.2:3.3.verse: “Honorable Senior, may I answer Citta’s question?”

sn41.2:3.7.verse: In what way did the Buddha speak of the diversity of elements?’”

sn41.2:3.9.verse: “This is the diversity of elements spoken of by the Buddha.

sn41.2:3.10.verse: The eye element, the sights element, the eye consciousness element …

sn41.2:3.11.verse: The mind element, the idea element, the mind consciousness element.

sn41.2:3.12.verse: This is how the Buddha spoke of the diversity of elements.”

sn41.2:4.1.verse: Then Citta, having approved and agreed with what Isidatta said, served and satisfied the senior mendicants with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

sn41.2:4.2.verse: When the senior mendicants had eaten and washed their hands and bowls, they rose from their seats and left.

sn41.2:4.3.verse: Then the senior venerable said to Venerable Isidatta,

sn41.2:4.4.verse: “Isidatta, it’s good that you felt inspired to answer that question, because I didn’t.

sn41.2:4.5.verse: So when a similar question comes up, you should also answer it as you feel inspired.”

sn41.3:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.3:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to them,

sn41.3:1.3.verse: “Sirs, would the senior monks please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”

sn41.3:1.5.verse: Then, knowing that the senior mendicants had consented, Citta rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled them, keeping them on his right, before leaving.

sn41.3:1.6.verse: Then when the night had passed, the senior mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, went to Citta’s home, and sat down on the seats spread out.

sn41.3:2.1.verse: So he went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to the senior venerable:

sn41.3:2.2.verse: “Honorable Senior, there are many different views that arise in the world. For example:

sn41.3:2.3.verse: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

sn41.3:2.4.verse: And also the sixty-two misconceptions spoken of in ‘The Divine Net’.

sn41.3:2.5.verse: When what exists do these views come to be? When what doesn’t exist do these views not come to be?”

sn41.3:3.1.verse: When he said this, the senior venerable kept silent.

sn41.3:3.3.verse: And for a third time, Citta said to him:

sn41.3:3.4.verse: “Honorable Senior, there are many different views that arise in the world. …

sn41.3:3.7.verse: When what exists do these views come to be? When what doesn’t exist do these views not come to be?”

sn41.3:3.8.verse: And a second time and a third time the senior venerable kept silent.

sn41.3:4.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Isidatta was the most junior mendicant in that Saṅgha.

sn41.3:4.2.verse: He said to the senior venerable,

sn41.3:4.3.verse: “Honorable Senior, may I answer Citta’s question?”

sn41.3:4.6.verse: ‘There are many different views that arise in the world …

sn41.3:4.8.verse: When what exists do these views come to be? When what doesn’t exist do these views not come to be?’”

sn41.3:4.10.verse: “Householder, there are many different views that arise in the world. For example:

sn41.3:4.11.verse: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

sn41.3:4.12.verse: And also the sixty-two misconceptions spoken of in ‘The Divine Net’.

sn41.3:4.13.verse: These views come to be when substantialist view exists. When substantialist view does not exist they do not come to be.”

sn41.3:5.1.verse: “But sir, how does substantialist view come about?”

sn41.3:5.2.verse: “It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn41.3:5.3.verse: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn41.3:5.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn41.3:5.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view comes about.”

sn41.3:6.1.verse: “But sir, how does substantialist view not come about?”

sn41.3:6.2.verse: “It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

sn41.3:6.3.verse: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.

sn41.3:6.7.verse: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

sn41.3:6.8.verse: That’s how substantialist view does not come about.”

sn41.3:7.1.verse: “Sir, where has Master Isidatta come from?”

sn41.3:7.3.verse: “Sir, there’s a friend of mine named Isidatta who I’ve never met. He’s gone forth from a good family in Avanti.

sn41.3:7.6.verse: “Sir, where is that venerable now staying?”

sn41.3:7.7.verse: When he said this, Isidatta kept silent.

sn41.3:7.10.verse: “Sir, I hope Master Isidatta is happy here in Macchikāsaṇḍa,

sn41.3:7.11.verse: for the Wild Mango Grove is lovely.

sn41.3:7.12.verse: I’ll make sure that Master Isidatta is provided with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.”

sn41.3:7.13.verse: “That’s nice of you to say, householder.”

sn41.3:8.1.verse: Then Citta, having approved and agreed with what Isidatta said, served and satisfied the senior mendicants with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

sn41.3:8.2.verse: When the senior mendicants had eaten and washed their hands and bowls, they rose from their seats and left.

sn41.3:8.3.verse: Then the senior venerable said to Venerable Isidatta,

sn41.3:8.4.verse: “Isidatta, it’s good that you felt inspired to answer that question, because I didn’t.

sn41.3:8.6.verse: So when a similar question comes up, you should also answer it as you feel inspired.”

sn41.3:8.7.verse: But Isidatta set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, left Macchikāsaṇḍa,

sn41.4:1.1.verse: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.4:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to them, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to them,

sn41.4:1.3.verse: “Sirs, would the senior monks please accept tomorrow’s meal from me in my milkshed?”

sn41.4:1.5.verse: Then, knowing that the senior mendicants had consented, Citta rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled them, keeping them on his right, before leaving.

sn41.4:1.6.verse: Then when the night had passed, the senior mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, went to Citta’s milkshed, and sat down on the seats spread out.

sn41.4:2.1.verse: Then Citta served and satisfied the senior mendicants with his own hands with delicious milk-rice made with ghee.

sn41.4:2.2.verse: When the senior mendicants had eaten and washed their hands and bowls, they rose from their seats and left.

sn41.4:2.3.verse: Citta instructed that the leftovers of the food be distributed, then followed behind the senior mendicants.

sn41.4:2.4.verse: Now at that time it was boiling hot.

sn41.4:2.5.verse: And those senior mendicants walked along as if their bodies were melting, as happens after a meal.

sn41.4:3.1.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahaka was the most junior mendicant in that Saṅgha.

sn41.4:3.2.verse: Then Venerable Mahaka said to the senior venerable,

sn41.4:3.3.verse: “Wouldn’t it be nice, Honorable Senior, if a cool wind blew, a cloud canopy formed, and a gentle rain drizzled down?”

sn41.4:4.1.verse: “It would indeed be nice, Reverend Mahaka.”

sn41.4:4.2.verse: Then Mahaka used his psychic power to will that a cool wind would blow, a cloud canopy would form, and a gentle rain would drizzle down.

sn41.4:4.4.verse: “The most junior mendicant in this Saṅgha has such psychic power!”

sn41.4:4.5.verse: When they reached the monastery, Mahaka said to the senior venerable,

sn41.4:4.10.verse: Then the senior mendicants entered their dwellings,

sn41.4:4.11.verse: and Mahaka entered his own dwelling.

sn41.4:5.1.verse: Then Citta went up to Mahaka, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn41.4:5.2.verse: “Sir, please show me a superhuman demonstration of psychic power.”

sn41.4:5.3.verse: “Well, then, householder, place your upper robe on the porch and spread a handful of grass on it.”

sn41.4:5.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Citta, and did as he was asked.

sn41.4:5.5.verse: Mahaka entered his dwelling and latched the door. Then he used his psychic power to will that a flame shoot out through the keyhole and the chink in the door-panel, and it burned up the grass but not the upper robe.

sn41.4:5.6.verse: Then Citta shook out his upper robe and stood to one side, shocked and awestruck.

sn41.4:5.7.verse: Mahaka left his dwelling and said to Citta,

sn41.4:6.4.verse: I hope Master Mahaka is happy here in Macchikāsaṇḍa,

sn41.4:6.5.verse: for the Wild Mango Grove is lovely.

sn41.4:6.6.verse: I’ll make sure that Master Mahaka is provided with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.”

sn41.4:6.7.verse: “That’s nice of you to say, householder.”

sn41.4:6.8.verse: But Mahaka set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, left Macchikāsaṇḍa,

sn41.5:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Kāmabhū was staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.5:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to Venerable Kāmabhū, bowed, and sat down to one side. Kāmabhū said to him,

sn41.5:4.1.verse: How should we see the detailed meaning of this brief statement?”

sn41.5:4.2.verse: “Sir, was this spoken by the Buddha?”

sn41.5:4.4.verse: “Well then, sir, please wait a while as I consider the meaning of this.”

sn41.5:4.5.verse: Then after staying silent for a while, Citta said to Kāmabhū:

sn41.5:5.1.verse: “Sir, ‘faultless parts’ is a term for ethics.

sn41.5:5.2.verse: ‘White canopy’ is a term for freedom.

sn41.5:5.3.verse: ‘One spoke’ is a term for mindfulness.

sn41.5:5.4.verse: ‘Rolls on’ is a term for going forward and coming back.

sn41.5:5.5.verse: ‘Chariot’ is a term for this body made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.

sn41.5:5.6.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are troubles.

sn41.5:5.7.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn41.5:5.8.verse: That’s why a mendicant who has ended the defilements is called ‘untroubled’.

sn41.5:5.9.verse: ‘The one who comes’ is a term for the perfected one.

sn41.5:5.11.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given this up, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, and obliterated it, so it’s unable to arise in the future.

sn41.5:5.12.verse: That’s why a mendicant who has ended the defilements is said to have ‘cut the stream’.

sn41.5:5.13.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are bonds.

sn41.5:5.14.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn41.5:5.15.verse: That’s why a mendicant who has ended the defilements is called ‘unbound’.

sn41.5:5.16.verse: So, sir, that’s how I understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha said in brief:

sn41.5:7.3.verse: to traverse the Buddha’s deep teachings with the eye of wisdom.”

sn41.6:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Kāmabhū was staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.6:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to Venerable Kāmabhū, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn41.6:1.5.verse: The physical process, the verbal process, and the mental process.”

sn41.6:1.6.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” Citta approved and agreed with what Kāmabhū said. Then he asked another question:

sn41.6:1.7.verse: “But sir, what is the physical process? What’s the verbal process? What’s the mental process?”

sn41.6:1.8.verse: “Breathing is a physical process. Placing the mind and keeping it connected are a verbal process. Perception and feeling are a mental process.”

sn41.6:2.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:2.2.verse: “But sir, why is breathing a physical process? Why are placing the mind and keeping it connected a verbal process? Why are perception and feeling a mental process?”

sn41.6:2.3.verse: “Breathing is physical. It’s tied up with the body, that’s why breathing is a physical process.

sn41.6:2.4.verse: First you place the mind and keep it connected, then you break into speech. That’s why placing the mind and keeping it connected are a verbal process.

sn41.6:2.5.verse: Perception and feeling are mental. They’re tied up with the mind, that’s why perception and feeling are a mental process.”

sn41.6:3.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:3.2.verse: “But sir, how does someone attain the cessation of perception and feeling?”

sn41.6:3.3.verse: “A mendicant who is entering such an attainment does not think:

sn41.6:3.4.verse: ‘I will enter the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I am entering the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I have entered the cessation of perception and feeling.’

sn41.6:3.5.verse: Rather, their mind has been previously developed so as to lead to such a state.”

sn41.6:4.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:4.2.verse: “But sir, which cease first for a mendicant who is entering the cessation of perception and feeling: the physical, verbal, or mental process?”

sn41.6:4.3.verse: “The verbal process ceases first, then physical, then mental.”

sn41.6:5.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:5.2.verse: “What’s the difference between someone who has passed away and a mendicant who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling?”

sn41.6:5.3.verse: “When someone dies, their physical, verbal, and mental processes have ceased and stilled; their vitality is spent; their warmth is dissipated; and their faculties have disintegrated.

sn41.6:5.4.verse: When a mendicant has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, their physical, verbal, and mental processes have ceased and stilled. But their vitality is not spent; their warmth is not dissipated; and their faculties are very clear.

sn41.6:5.5.verse: That’s the difference between someone who has passed away and a mendicant who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling.”

sn41.6:6.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:6.2.verse: “But sir, how does someone emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling?”

sn41.6:6.3.verse: “A mendicant who is emerging from such an attainment does not think:

sn41.6:6.4.verse: ‘I will emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I am emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling’ or ‘I have emerged from the cessation of perception and feeling.’

sn41.6:6.5.verse: Rather, their mind has been previously developed so as to lead to such a state.”

sn41.6:7.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:7.2.verse: “But sir, which arise first for a mendicant who is emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling: the physical, verbal, or mental process?”

sn41.6:7.3.verse: “The mental process arises first, then physical, then verbal.”

sn41.6:8.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:8.2.verse: “But sir, when a mendicant has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, how many kinds of contact do they experience?”

sn41.6:9.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” he asked another question:

sn41.6:9.2.verse: “But sir, when a mendicant has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, what does their mind slant, slope, and incline to?”

sn41.6:9.3.verse: “Their mind slants, slopes, and inclines to seclusion.”

sn41.6:10.1.verse: Saying “Good, sir,” Citta approved and agreed with what Kāmabhū said. Then he asked another question:

sn41.6:10.2.verse: “But sir, how many things are helpful for attaining the cessation of perception and feeling?”

sn41.6:10.3.verse: “Well, householder, you’ve finally asked what you should have asked first!

sn41.6:10.5.verse: Two things are helpful for attaining the cessation of perception and feeling:

sn41.7:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Godatta was staying near Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Wild Mango Grove.

sn41.7:1.2.verse: Then Citta the householder went up to Venerable Godatta, bowed, and sat down to one side. Godatta said to him:

sn41.7:1.3.verse: “Householder, the limitless release of the heart, and the release of the heart through nothingness, and the release of the heart through emptiness, and the signless release of the heart: do these things differ in both meaning and phrasing? Or do they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?”

sn41.7:1.4.verse: “Sir, there is a way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

sn41.7:1.5.verse: But there’s also a way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.

sn41.7:2.1.verse: And what’s the way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing?

sn41.7:2.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

sn41.7:2.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

sn41.7:2.4.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

sn41.7:2.5.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

sn41.7:2.6.verse: This is called the limitless release of the heart.

sn41.7:3.1.verse: And what is the release of the heart through nothingness?

sn41.7:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing at all’, enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness.

sn41.7:3.3.verse: This is called the release of the heart through nothingness.

sn41.7:4.1.verse: And what is the release of the heart through emptiness?

sn41.7:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

sn41.7:4.3.verse: ‘This is empty of a self or what belongs to a self.’

sn41.7:4.4.verse: This is called the release of the heart through emptiness.

sn41.7:5.1.verse: And what is the signless heart’s release?

sn41.7:5.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant, not focusing on any signs, enters and remains in the signless immersion of the heart.

sn41.7:5.3.verse: This is called the signless release of the heart.

sn41.7:5.4.verse: This is the way in which these things differ in both meaning and phrasing.

sn41.7:6.1.verse: And what’s the way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing?

sn41.7:6.2.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are makers of limits.

sn41.7:6.3.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn41.7:6.4.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of limitless release of the heart.

sn41.7:6.5.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn41.7:6.6.verse: Greed is something, hate is something, and delusion is something.

sn41.7:6.7.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn41.7:6.8.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of release of the heart through nothingness.

sn41.7:6.9.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn41.7:6.10.verse: Greed, hate, and delusion are makers of signs.

sn41.7:6.11.verse: A mendicant who has ended the defilements has given these up, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, and obliterated them, so they are unable to arise in the future.

sn41.7:6.12.verse: The unshakable release of the heart is said to be the best kind of signless release of the heart.

sn41.7:6.13.verse: That unshakable release of the heart is empty of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn41.7:6.14.verse: This is the way in which they mean the same thing, and differ only in the phrasing.”

sn41.7:6.16.verse: to traverse the Buddha’s deep teachings with the eye of wisdom.”

sn41.8:0.3.verse: The Jain Ascetic of the Ñātika Clan

sn41.8:1.1.verse: Now at that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan had arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a large assembly of Jain ascetics.

sn41.8:1.2.verse: Citta the householder heard that they had arrived.

sn41.8:1.3.verse: Together with several lay followers, he went up to the Jain Ñātika and exchanged greetings with him.

sn41.8:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Jain Ñātika said to him,

sn41.8:1.5.verse: “Householder, do you have faith in the ascetic Gotama’s claim that

sn41.8:1.6.verse: there is a state of immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected; that there is the cessation of placing the mind and keeping it connected?”

sn41.8:2.1.verse: “Sir, in this case I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha’s claim that

sn41.8:2.2.verse: there is a state of immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected; that there is the cessation of placing the mind and keeping it connected.”

sn41.8:2.3.verse: When he said this, the Jain Ñātika looked up at his assembly and said,

sn41.8:2.4.verse: “See, good sirs, how straightforward this householder Citta is! He’s not devious or deceitful at all. To imagine that you can stop placing the mind and keeping it connected would be like imagining that you can catch the wind in a net, or dam the Ganges River with your own hand.”

sn41.8:3.3.verse: “Knowledge is definitely better than faith, householder.”

sn41.8:3.4.verse: “Well sir, whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn41.8:3.5.verse: And whenever I want, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled … I enter and remain in the second absorption.

sn41.8:3.6.verse: And whenever I want, with the fading away of rapture … I enter and remain in the third absorption.

sn41.8:3.7.verse: And whenever I want, giving up pleasure and pain … I enter and remain in the fourth absorption.

sn41.8:3.8.verse: And so, sir, since I know and see like this, why should I rely on faith in another ascetic or brahmin who claims that

sn41.8:3.9.verse: there is a state of immersion without placing the mind and keeping it connected; that there is the cessation of placing the mind and keeping it connected?”

sn41.8:4.1.verse: When he said this, the Jain Ñātika looked askance at his own assembly and said,

sn41.8:4.2.verse: “See, good fellows, how crooked this householder Citta is! He’s so devious and deceitful!”

sn41.8:5.1.verse: “Sir, just now I understood you to say:

sn41.8:5.2.verse: ‘See, good fellows, how straightforward this householder Citta is! He’s not devious or deceitful at all.’

sn41.8:5.3.verse: But then I understood you to say:

sn41.8:5.4.verse: ‘See, good fellows, how crooked this householder Citta is! He’s so devious and deceitful!’

sn41.8:5.5.verse: If your first statement is true, the second is wrong.

sn41.8:5.6.verse: If your first statement is wrong, the second is true.

sn41.8:5.7.verse: And also, sir, these ten legitimate questions are relevant.

sn41.8:5.8.verse: When you understand what they mean, then, together with your assembly of Jain ascetics, you can rebut me.

sn41.8:5.18.verse: Ten things: question, summary, and answer.’”

sn41.8:5.19.verse: Then Citta rose from his seat and left without asking the Jain Ñātika these ten legitimate questions.

sn41.9:1.1.verse: Now at that time the naked ascetic Kassapa, an old friend of Citta in the lay life, had arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa.

sn41.9:1.2.verse: Citta the householder heard that he had arrived.

sn41.9:1.3.verse: So he went up to him, and they exchanged greetings.

sn41.9:1.4.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the naked ascetic Kassapa,

sn41.9:1.5.verse: “Honorable Kassapa, how long has it been since you went forth?”

sn41.9:1.7.verse: “But sir, in these thirty years have you achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation?”

sn41.9:1.8.verse: “I have no such achievement, householder, only nudity, baldness, and pokes in the buttocks.”

sn41.9:1.11.verse: how well explained the teaching is. For in thirty years you have achieved no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, no comfortable meditation, only nudity, baldness, and pokes in the buttocks.”

sn41.9:2.1.verse: “But householder, how long have you been a lay follower?”

sn41.9:2.3.verse: “But householder, in these thirty years have you achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation?”

sn41.9:2.5.verse: For whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn41.9:2.6.verse: And whenever I want, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled … I enter and remain in the second absorption.

sn41.9:2.7.verse: And whenever I want, with the fading away of rapture … I enter and remain in the third absorption.

sn41.9:2.8.verse: And whenever I want, giving up pleasure and pain … I enter and remain in the fourth absorption.

sn41.9:2.9.verse: If I pass away before the Buddha, it would be no wonder if the Buddha declares of me:

sn41.9:2.10.verse: ‘The householder Citta is bound by no fetter that might return him to this world.’”

sn41.9:2.11.verse: When this was said, Kassapa said to Citta,

sn41.9:2.13.verse: how well explained the teaching is. For a white-clothed layperson can achieve such a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable meditation.

sn41.9:2.14.verse: Householder, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training?”

sn41.9:3.1.verse: Then Citta the householder took the naked ascetic Kassapa to see the senior mendicants, and said to them:

sn41.9:3.2.verse: “Sirs, this is the naked ascetic Kassapa, who in lay life was an old friend of mine.

sn41.9:3.3.verse: May the senior monks give him the going forth, the ordination.

sn41.9:3.4.verse: I’ll make sure that he’s provided with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.”

sn41.9:3.5.verse: And the naked ascetic Kassapa received the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training.

sn41.9:3.6.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Kassapa, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn41.9:3.7.verse: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn41.9:3.8.verse: And Venerable Kassapa became one of the perfected.

sn41.10:1.1.verse: Now at that time the householder Citta was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn41.10:1.2.verse: Then several deities of the parks, forests, trees, and those who haunt the herbs, grass, and big trees came together and said to Citta,

sn41.10:1.3.verse: “Householder, make a wish to become a wheel-turning monarch in the future!”

sn41.10:2.1.verse: When they said this, Citta said to them,

sn41.10:2.2.verse: “That too is impermanent! That too will pass! That too will be left behind!”

sn41.10:2.3.verse: When he said this, his friends and colleagues, relatives and kin said,

sn41.10:2.5.verse: “What have I said that makes you say that?”

sn41.10:2.8.verse: ‘That too is impermanent! That too will pass! That too will be left behind!’”

sn41.10:2.9.verse: “Oh, well, that’s because the deities of the parks, forests, trees, and those who haunt the herbs, grass, and big trees said to me:

sn41.10:2.10.verse: ‘Householder, make a wish to become a wheel-turning monarch in the future!’

sn41.10:2.12.verse: ‘That too is impermanent! That too will pass! That too will be left behind!’”

sn41.10:2.13.verse: “But what reason do they see for saying that to you?”

sn41.10:2.16.verse: ‘This householder Citta is ethical, of good character.

sn41.10:2.17.verse: If he makes a wish to

sn41.10:2.18.verse: become a wheel-turning monarch in the future, his heart’s wish will succeed because of the purity of his ethics. And then as a proper, principled king he will provide proper spirit-offerings.’

sn41.10:2.19.verse: That’s the reason they see for saying to me:

sn41.10:2.20.verse: ‘Householder, make a wish to become a wheel-turning monarch in the future!’

sn41.10:2.22.verse: ‘That too is impermanent! That too will pass! That too will be left behind!’”

sn41.10:3.3.verse: We will have experiential confidence in the Buddha:

sn41.10:3.4.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

sn41.10:3.5.verse: We will have experiential confidence in the teaching:

sn41.10:3.6.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

sn41.10:3.7.verse: We will have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

sn41.10:3.8.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

sn41.10:3.9.verse: And we will share without reservation all the gifts available to give in our family with those who are ethical and of good character.”

sn41.10:3.10.verse: Then, after Citta had encouraged his friends and colleagues, relatives and kin in the Buddha, the teaching, the Saṅgha, and generosity, he passed away.

sn41.10:4.5.verse: The Linked Discourses on Citta the Householder are complete.

sn42.1:1.2.verse: Then Fury the chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.1:1.3.verse: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why some people are regarded as furious,

sn42.1:1.4.verse: while others are regarded as gentle?”

sn42.1:1.5.verse: “Take someone who hasn’t given up greed.

sn42.1:1.6.verse: So they get annoyed by others, and they show it.

sn42.1:1.9.verse: So they get annoyed by others, and they show it.

sn42.1:1.12.verse: So they get annoyed by others, and they show it.

sn42.1:1.14.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why some people are regarded as furious.

sn42.1:2.1.verse: But take someone who has given up greed.

sn42.1:2.2.verse: So they don’t get annoyed by others, and don’t show it.

sn42.1:2.5.verse: So they don’t get annoyed by others, and don’t show it.

sn42.1:2.8.verse: So they don’t get annoyed by others, and don’t show it.

sn42.1:2.10.verse: This is the cause, this is the reason why some people are regarded as gentle.”

sn42.1:3.1.verse: When he said this, Fury the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.1:3.3.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn42.1:3.4.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn42.1:3.5.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.2:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn42.2:1.2.verse: Then Tālapuṭa the dancing chief came up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.2:1.3.verse: “Sir, I have heard that the dancers of the past who were tutors of tutors said:

sn42.2:1.4.verse: ‘Suppose a dancer entertains and amuses people on a stage or at a festival with mixed truth and lies. When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of laughing gods.’

sn42.2:1.5.verse: What does the Buddha say about this?”

sn42.2:1.6.verse: “Enough, chief, let it be. Don’t ask me that.”

sn42.2:1.12.verse: And for a third time Tālapuṭa said to the Buddha:

sn42.2:1.13.verse: “Sir, I have heard that the dancers of the past who were tutors of tutors said:

sn42.2:1.14.verse: ‘Suppose a dancer entertains and amuses people on a stage or at a festival with mixed truth and lies. When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of laughing gods.’

sn42.2:1.15.verse: What does the Buddha say about this?”

sn42.2:2.1.verse: “Clearly, chief, I’m not getting through to you when I say:

sn42.2:2.5.verse: When sentient beings are still not free of greed, and are still bound by greed,

sn42.2:2.6.verse: a dancer in a stage or festival presents them with even more arousing things.

sn42.2:2.7.verse: When sentient beings are still not free of hate, and are still bound by hate,

sn42.2:2.8.verse: a dancer in a stage or festival presents them with even more hateful things.

sn42.2:2.9.verse: When sentient beings are still not free of delusion, and are still bound by delusion,

sn42.2:2.10.verse: a dancer in a stage or festival presents them with even more delusory things.

sn42.2:2.11.verse: And so, being heedless and negligent themselves, they’ve encouraged others to be heedless and negligent. When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the hell called ‘Laughter’.

sn42.2:2.12.verse: But if you have such a view:

sn42.2:2.13.verse: ‘Suppose a dancer entertains and amuses people on a stage or at a festival with mixed truth and lies. When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of laughing gods.’ This is your wrong view.

sn42.2:2.14.verse: An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say:

sn42.2:3.1.verse: When he said this, Tālapuṭa cried and burst out in tears.

sn42.2:3.2.verse: “This is what I didn’t get through to you when I said:

sn42.2:3.3.verse: ‘Enough, chief, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’”

sn42.2:3.4.verse: “Sir, I’m not crying because of what the Buddha said.

sn42.2:3.5.verse: But sir, for a long time I’ve been cheated, tricked, and deceived by the dancers of the past who were tutors of tutors, who said:

sn42.2:3.6.verse: ‘Suppose a dancer entertains and amuses people on a stage or at a festival with mixed truth and lies. When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in the company of laughing gods.’

sn42.2:3.8.verse: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

sn42.2:3.9.verse: I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha.

sn42.2:3.10.verse: Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”

sn42.2:3.11.verse: And Tālapuṭa the dancing chief received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence.

sn42.2:3.12.verse: Not long after his ordination, Venerable Tālapuṭa

sn42.3:1.1.verse: Then Dustin the warrior chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.3:1.2.verse: “Sir, I have heard that the warriors of the past who were tutors of tutors said:

sn42.3:1.3.verse: ‘Suppose a warrior, while striving and struggling in battle, is killed and finished off by his foes. When his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in the company of the gods of the fallen.’

sn42.3:1.4.verse: What does the Buddha say about this?”

sn42.3:1.5.verse: “Enough, chief, let it be. Don’t ask me that.”

sn42.3:1.7.verse: And for a third time Dustin the warrior chief said to the Buddha:

sn42.3:1.8.verse: “Sir, I have heard that the warriors of the past who were tutors of tutors said:

sn42.3:1.9.verse: ‘Suppose a warrior, while striving and struggling in battle, is killed and finished off by his foes. When his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in the company of the gods of the fallen.’

sn42.3:1.10.verse: What does the Buddha say about this?”

sn42.3:2.1.verse: “Clearly, chief, I’m not getting through to you when I say:

sn42.3:2.2.verse: ‘Enough, chief, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’

sn42.3:2.4.verse: When a warrior strives and struggles in battle, their mind is already low, degraded, and misdirected as they think:

sn42.3:2.5.verse: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, slain, destroyed, or annihilated!’

sn42.3:2.6.verse: His foes kill him and finish him off, and

sn42.3:2.7.verse: when his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in the hell called ‘The Fallen’.

sn42.3:2.8.verse: But if you have such a view:

sn42.3:2.9.verse: ‘Suppose a warrior, while striving and struggling in battle, is killed and finished off by his foes. When his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in the company of the gods of the fallen.’ This is your wrong view.

sn42.3:2.10.verse: An individual with wrong view is reborn in one of two places, I say:

sn42.3:3.1.verse: When he said this, Dustin the warrior chief cried and burst out in tears.

sn42.3:3.2.verse: “This is what I didn’t get through to you when I said:

sn42.3:3.3.verse: ‘Enough, chief, let it be. Don’t ask me that.’”

sn42.3:3.4.verse: “Sir, I’m not crying because of what the Buddha said.

sn42.3:3.5.verse: But sir, for a long time I’ve been cheated, tricked, and deceived by the warriors of the past who were tutors of tutors, who said:

sn42.3:3.6.verse: ‘Suppose a warrior, while striving and struggling in battle, is killed and finished off by his foes. When his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in the company of the gods of the fallen.’

sn42.3:3.8.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.4:1.1.verse: Then an elephant marshal chief went up to the Buddha …

sn42.4:1.2.verse: “From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.5:1.1.verse: Then a cavalry chief went up to the Buddha …

sn42.5:4.8.verse: “From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.6:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

sn42.6:1.2.verse: Then Asibandhaka’s son the chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.6:2.1.verse: “Sir, there are western brahmins garlanded with aquatic flowers who carry pitchers, immerse themselves in water, and serve the sacred flame.

sn42.6:2.2.verse: When someone has passed away, oh! they lift them up, send them well, and convey them to heaven.

sn42.6:2.3.verse: But what about the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha: is he able to ensure that the whole world will be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm when their body breaks up, after death?”

sn42.6:3.1.verse: “Well then, chief, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

sn42.6:4.2.verse: Take a person who kills living creatures, steals, and commits sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, and have wrong view.

sn42.6:4.3.verse: A large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty, circumambulating them with cupped palms and saying:

sn42.6:4.4.verse: ‘When this person’s body breaks up, after death, may they be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm!’

sn42.6:4.6.verse: Would that person be reborn in heaven because of their supplications?”

sn42.6:5.1.verse: “Chief, suppose a person were to throw a broad rock into a deep lake.

sn42.6:5.2.verse: And a large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty, circumambulating it with cupped palms, and saying:

sn42.6:5.3.verse: ‘Rise, good rock! Float, good rock! Float to shore, good rock!’

sn42.6:5.5.verse: Would that broad rock rise up or float because of their supplications?”

sn42.6:5.7.verse: “In the same way, take a person who kills living creatures, steals, and commits sexual misconduct. They use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re covetous, malicious, and have wrong view.

sn42.6:5.8.verse: Even though a large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty …

sn42.6:5.9.verse: when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

sn42.6:6.2.verse: Take a person who doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, or commit sexual misconduct. They don’t use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re contented, kind-hearted, with right view.

sn42.6:6.3.verse: And a large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty, circumambulating them with cupped palms and saying:

sn42.6:6.4.verse: ‘When this person’s body breaks up, after death, may they be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell!’

sn42.6:6.6.verse: Would that person be reborn in hell because of their supplications?”

sn42.6:7.1.verse: “Chief, suppose a person were to sink a pot of ghee or oil into a deep lake and break it open. Its shards and chips would sink down, while the ghee or oil in it would rise up.

sn42.6:7.2.verse: And a large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty, circumambulating it with cupped palms and saying:

sn42.6:7.3.verse: ‘Sink, good ghee or oil! Descend, good ghee or oil! Go down, good ghee or oil!’

sn42.6:7.5.verse: Would that ghee or oil sink and descend because of their supplications?”

sn42.6:8.1.verse: “In the same way, take a person who doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, or commit sexual misconduct. They don’t use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical. And they’re contented, kind-hearted, with right view.

sn42.6:8.2.verse: Even though a large crowd were to come together to offer up supplication and entreaty …

sn42.6:8.3.verse: when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”

sn42.6:8.4.verse: When he said this, Asibandhaka’s son the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.6:8.6.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.7:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

sn42.7:1.2.verse: Then Asibandhaka’s son the chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.7:1.3.verse: “Sir, doesn’t the Buddha live full of sympathy for all living beings?”

sn42.7:1.5.verse: “So why then, sir, do you teach some people thoroughly and others less thoroughly?”

sn42.7:1.6.verse: “Well then, chief, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

sn42.7:1.7.verse: What do you think? Suppose a farmer has three fields: one is good, one is average, and one is poor—bad ground of sand and salt.

sn42.7:1.8.verse: What do you think? When that farmer wants to plant seeds, where would he plant them first: the good field, the average one, or the poor one?”

sn42.7:1.9.verse: “Sir, he’d plant them first in the good field, then the average, then he may or may not plant seed in the poor field.

sn42.7:1.11.verse: Because at least it can be fodder for the cattle.”

sn42.7:2.1.verse: “To me, the monks and nuns are like the good field.

sn42.7:2.2.verse: I teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:2.4.verse: Because they live with me as their island, asylum, shelter, and refuge.

sn42.7:2.5.verse: To me, the laymen and laywomen are like the average field.

sn42.7:2.6.verse: I also teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:2.8.verse: Because they live with me as their island, asylum, shelter, and refuge.

sn42.7:2.9.verse: To me, the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other religions are like the poor field, the bad ground of sand and salt.

sn42.7:2.10.verse: I also teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:2.12.verse: Hopefully they might understand even a single sentence, which would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.

sn42.7:3.1.verse: Suppose a person had three water jars: one that’s uncracked and nonporous; one that’s uncracked but porous; and one that’s cracked and porous.

sn42.7:3.2.verse: What do you think? When that person wants to store water, where would they store it first: in the jar that’s uncracked and nonporous, the one that’s uncracked but porous, or the one that’s cracked and porous?”

sn42.7:3.3.verse: “Sir, they’d store water first in the jar that’s uncracked and nonporous, then the one that’s uncracked but porous, then they may or may not store water in the one that’s cracked and porous.

sn42.7:3.5.verse: Because at least it can be used for washing the dishes.”

sn42.7:4.1.verse: “To me, the monks and nuns are like the water jar that’s uncracked and nonporous.

sn42.7:4.2.verse: I teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:4.4.verse: Because they live with me as their island, asylum, shelter, and refuge.

sn42.7:4.5.verse: To me, the laymen and laywomen are like the water jar that’s uncracked but porous.

sn42.7:4.6.verse: I also teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:4.8.verse: Because they live with me as their island, asylum, shelter, and refuge.

sn42.7:4.9.verse: To me, the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other religions are like the water jar that’s cracked and porous.

sn42.7:4.10.verse: I also teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And I reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

sn42.7:4.12.verse: Hopefully they might understand even a single sentence, which would be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

sn42.7:5.1.verse: When he said this, Asibandhaka’s son the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.7:5.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.8:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

sn42.8:1.2.verse: Then Asibandhaka’s son the chief, who was a disciple of the Jains, went up to the Buddha, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

sn42.8:1.3.verse: “Chief, how does the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan teach his disciples?”

sn42.8:1.4.verse: “Sir, this is how the Jain Ñātika teaches his disciples:

sn42.8:1.5.verse: ‘Everyone who kills a living creature, steals, commits sexual misconduct, or lies goes to a place of loss, to hell.

sn42.8:1.6.verse: You’re led on by what you frequently live by.’

sn42.8:1.7.verse: This is how the Jain Ñātika teaches his disciples.”

sn42.8:1.8.verse: “‘You’re led on by what you usually live by’: if this were true, then, according to what the Jain Ñātika says, no one would go to a place of loss, to hell.

sn42.8:2.2.verse: Take a person who kills living creatures. If we compare periods of time during the day and night, which is more frequent: the occasions when they’re killing or when they’re not killing?”

sn42.8:2.3.verse: “The occasions when they’re killing are less frequent, while the occasions when they’re not killing are more frequent.”

sn42.8:2.4.verse: “‘You’re led on by what you usually live by’: if this were true, then, according to what the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan says, no one would go to a place of loss, to hell.

sn42.8:4.1.verse: Take a person who commits sexual misconduct …

sn42.8:5.1.verse: Take a person who lies. If we compare periods of time during the day and night, which is more frequent: the occasions when they’re lying or when they’re not lying?”

sn42.8:5.2.verse: “The occasions when they’re lying are less frequent, while the occasions when they’re not lying are more frequent.”

sn42.8:5.3.verse: “‘You’re led on by what you usually live by’: if this were true, then, according to what the Jain Ñātika says, no one would go to a place of loss, to hell.

sn42.8:6.1.verse: Take some teacher who has this doctrine and view:

sn42.8:6.2.verse: ‘Everyone who kills a living creature, steals, commits sexual misconduct, or lies goes to a place of loss, to hell.’

sn42.8:6.3.verse: And there’s a disciple who is devoted to that teacher.

sn42.8:6.5.verse: ‘My teacher has this doctrine and view:

sn42.8:6.6.verse: “Everyone who kills a living creature, steals, commits sexual misconduct, or lies goes to a place of loss, to hell.”

sn42.8:6.21.verse: They get the view: ‘I too am going to a place of loss, to hell.’

sn42.8:6.22.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.

sn42.8:7.1.verse: But consider when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.

sn42.8:7.2.verse: In many ways he criticizes and denounces killing living creatures, saying: ‘Stop killing living creatures!’

sn42.8:7.6.verse: And there’s a disciple who is devoted to that teacher.

sn42.8:7.8.verse: ‘In many ways the Buddha criticizes and denounces killing living creatures, saying: “Stop killing living creatures!”

sn42.8:7.9.verse: But I have killed living creatures to a certain extent.

sn42.8:7.10.verse: That’s not right, it’s not good,

sn42.8:7.11.verse: and I feel remorseful because of it.

sn42.8:7.12.verse: But I can’t undo what I have done.’

sn42.8:7.13.verse: Reflecting like this, they give up killing living creatures,

sn42.8:7.14.verse: and in future they don’t kill living creatures.

sn42.8:7.15.verse: That’s how to give up this bad deed

sn42.8:8.1.verse: ‘In many ways the Buddha criticizes and denounces stealing …’

sn42.8:9.1.verse: ‘In many ways the Buddha criticizes and denounces sexual misconduct …’

sn42.8:10.1.verse: ‘In many ways the Buddha criticizes and denounces lying, saying: “Stop lying!”

sn42.8:10.2.verse: But I have lied to a certain extent.

sn42.8:10.3.verse: That’s not right, it’s not good, and I feel remorseful because of it. But I can’t undo what I have done.’

sn42.8:10.4.verse: Reflecting like this, they give up lying, and in future they refrain from lying.

sn42.8:10.5.verse: That’s how to give up this bad deed and get past it.

sn42.8:11.1.verse: They give up killing living creatures.

sn42.8:11.9.verse: They give up ill will and malevolence.

sn42.8:11.10.verse: They give up wrong view and have right view.

sn42.8:12.1.verse: That noble disciple is rid of desire, rid of ill will, unconfused, aware, and mindful. They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

sn42.8:12.2.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

sn42.8:12.3.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by love has been developed and cultivated like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.

sn42.8:13.1.verse: Then that noble disciple is rid of desire, rid of ill will, unconfused, aware, and mindful. They meditate spreading a heart full of compassion …

sn42.8:13.2.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of rejoicing …

sn42.8:13.3.verse: They meditate spreading a heart full of equanimity to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of equanimity to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.

sn42.8:13.4.verse: Suppose there was a powerful horn blower. They’d easily make themselves heard in the four quarters.

sn42.8:13.5.verse: In the same way, when the heart’s release by equanimity has been developed and cultivated like this, any limited deeds they’ve done don’t remain or persist there.”

sn42.8:14.1.verse: When he said this, Asibandhaka’s son the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.8:14.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.9:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at Nāḷandā.

sn42.9:1.2.verse: There he stayed near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

sn42.9:2.1.verse: Now at that time Nāḷandā was undergoing famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw.

sn42.9:2.2.verse: At that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan was residing at Nāḷandā together with a large assembly of Jain ascetics.

sn42.9:2.3.verse: Then Asibandhaka’s son the chief, who was a disciple of the Jains, went up to the Jain Ñātika, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Jain Ñātika said to him:

sn42.9:2.4.verse: “Come, chief, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

sn42.9:2.5.verse: Then you will get a good reputation:

sn42.9:2.6.verse: ‘Asibandhaka’s son the chief refuted the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, so mighty and powerful!’”

sn42.9:3.1.verse: “But sir, how am I to do this?”

sn42.9:3.2.verse: “Here, brahmin, go to the ascetic Gotama and say to him:

sn42.9:3.3.verse: ‘Sir, don’t you in many ways praise kindness, protection, and sympathy for families?’

sn42.9:3.4.verse: When he’s asked this, if he answers:

sn42.9:3.5.verse: ‘Indeed I do, chief,’ say this to him:

sn42.9:3.6.verse: ‘So what then are you doing, wandering together with this large Saṅgha of mendicants during a time of famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw?

sn42.9:3.7.verse: The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!’

sn42.9:3.8.verse: When you put this dilemma to him, the Buddha won’t be able to either spit it out or swallow it down.”

sn42.9:3.9.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Asibandhaka’s son. He rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Jain Ñātika, keeping him on his right. Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.9:4.1.verse: “Sir, don’t you in many ways praise kindness, protection, and sympathy for families?”

sn42.9:4.3.verse: “So what then are you doing, wandering together with this large Saṅgha of mendicants during a time of famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw?

sn42.9:4.4.verse: The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!”

sn42.9:4.5.verse: “Well, chief, I recollect ninety-one eons back but I’m not aware of any family that’s been ruined merely by offering some cooked almsfood.

sn42.9:4.6.verse: Rather, rich, affluent, and wealthy families—with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain—all acquired their wealth because of giving, truth, and restraint.

sn42.9:4.7.verse: Chief, there are eight causes and reasons for the ruin of families.

sn42.9:4.8.verse: Their ruin stems from rulers, bandits, fire, or flood. Or they lose their savings. Or their business fails due to not applying themselves to work. Or a wastrel is born into the family who squanders and fritters away their wealth. And impermanence is the eighth.

sn42.9:4.9.verse: These are the eight causes and reasons for the ruin of families.

sn42.9:4.10.verse: Given that these eight reasons are found, suppose someone says this:

sn42.9:4.11.verse: ‘The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!’

sn42.9:4.12.verse: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.”

sn42.9:5.1.verse: When he said this, Asibandhaka’s son the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.9:5.3.verse: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn42.10:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn42.10:1.2.verse: Now at that time while the king’s retinue was sitting together in the royal compound this discussion came up among them,

sn42.10:1.3.verse: “Gold and currency are proper for ascetics who follow the Sakyan. They accept and receive gold and currency.”

sn42.10:2.1.verse: Now at that time the chief Maṇicūḷaka was sitting in that assembly.

sn42.10:2.4.verse: Gold and currency are not proper for ascetics who follow the Sakyan. They neither accept nor receive gold and currency. They have set aside gems and gold, and quit using gold and currency.”

sn42.10:2.5.verse: He was able to persuade that assembly.

sn42.10:2.6.verse: Then Maṇicūḷaka went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened. He then said,

sn42.10:2.13.verse: “Answering this way, I trust that I repeat what the Buddha has said, and don’t misrepresent him with an untruth. I trust my explanation is in line with the teaching, and that there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.”

sn42.10:3.1.verse: “Indeed, in answering this way you repeat what I’ve said, and don’t misrepresent me with an untruth. Your explanation is in line with the teaching, and there are no legitimate grounds for rebuttal or criticism.

sn42.10:3.2.verse: Gold and currency are not proper for ascetics who follow the Sakyan. They neither accept nor receive gold and currency. They have set aside gems and gold, and quit using gold and currency.

sn42.10:3.3.verse: If gold and currency were proper for them, then the five kinds of sensual stimulation would also be proper.

sn42.10:3.4.verse: And if the five kinds of sensual stimulation are proper for them, you should categorically regard them as not having the qualities of an ascetic or a follower of the Sakyan.

sn42.10:3.6.verse: Straw may be looked for by one needing straw; wood may be looked for by one needing wood; a cart may be looked for by one needing a cart; a workman may be looked for by one needing a workman.

sn42.10:3.7.verse: But in any case, there is no way they can accept or look for gold and currency, I say.”

sn42.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Mallas, near the Mallian town named Uruvelakappa.

sn42.11:1.2.verse: Then Bhadraka the village chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.11:1.3.verse: “Please, sir, let the Blessed One teach me the origin and disappearance of suffering.”

sn42.11:1.4.verse: “Chief, if I were to teach you about the origin and disappearance of suffering in connection with the past, saying

sn42.11:1.5.verse: ‘this is how it was in the past,’ you might have doubts or uncertainties about that.

sn42.11:1.6.verse: If I were to teach you about the origin and disappearance of suffering in connection with the future, saying

sn42.11:1.7.verse: ‘this is how it will be in the future,’ you might have doubts or uncertainties about that.

sn42.11:1.8.verse: Rather, chief, I will teach you about the origin and disappearance of suffering as I am sitting right here and you are sitting right there.

sn42.11:1.9.verse: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn42.11:2.2.verse: Are there any people here in Uruvelakappa who, if they were executed, imprisoned, fined, or condemned, it would cause you sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn42.11:2.4.verse: “But are there any people here in Uruvelakappa who, if they were executed, imprisoned, fined, or condemned, it would not cause you sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn42.11:2.6.verse: “What’s the cause, chief, what’s the reason why, if this was to happen to some people it could cause you sorrow, while if it happens to others it does not?”

sn42.11:2.7.verse: “The people regarding whom this would give rise to sorrow are those I have desire and passion.

sn42.11:2.8.verse: The people regarding whom this would not give rise to sorrow are those I don’t have desire and passion.”

sn42.11:2.9.verse: “With this present phenomenon that you have seen, understood, immediately attained, and fathomed, you can apply the same method to the past and future:

sn42.11:2.10.verse: ‘All the suffering that arose in the past was rooted and sourced in desire.

sn42.11:2.11.verse: For desire is the root of suffering.

sn42.11:2.12.verse: All the suffering that will arise in the future will be rooted and sourced in desire.

sn42.11:2.13.verse: For desire is the root of suffering.’”

sn42.11:2.15.verse: How well said this was by the Buddha!

sn42.11:2.16.verse: ‘All the suffering that arises is rooted and sourced in desire.

sn42.11:2.17.verse: For desire is the root of suffering.’

sn42.11:2.18.verse: I have a boy called Ciravāsi, who resides in a house away from here.

sn42.11:2.19.verse: I rise early and dispatch someone, saying:

sn42.11:2.20.verse: ‘Go, lad, and check on my boy Ciravāsi.’

sn42.11:2.21.verse: Until they get back I worry:

sn42.11:3.2.verse: If Ciravāsi was executed, imprisoned, fined, or condemned, would it cause you sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn42.11:3.4.verse: “This too is a way to understand:

sn42.11:3.5.verse: ‘All the suffering that arises is rooted and sourced in desire.

sn42.11:3.6.verse: For desire is the root of suffering.’

sn42.11:4.2.verse: Before you’d seen or heard of Ciravāsi’s mother, did you have any desire or passion or fondness for her?”

sn42.11:4.4.verse: “Then was it because you saw or heard of her that you had

sn42.11:4.5.verse: desire or passion or fondness for her?”

sn42.11:5.2.verse: If Ciravāsi’s mother was executed, imprisoned, fined, or condemned, would it cause you sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”

sn42.11:5.4.verse: “This too is a way to understand:

sn42.11:5.5.verse: ‘All the suffering that arises is rooted and sourced in desire.

sn42.11:5.6.verse: For desire is the root of suffering.’”

sn42.12:1.1.verse: Then Rāsiya the chief went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.12:1.2.verse: “Sir, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama criticizes all forms of mortification. He categorically condemns and denounces those fervent mortifiers who live rough.’

sn42.12:1.3.verse: I trust those who say this repeat what the Buddha has said, and do not misrepresent him with an untruth? Is their explanation in line with the teaching? Are there any legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

sn42.12:1.4.verse: “Chief, those who say this do not repeat what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false, hollow, and untrue.

sn42.12:2.1.verse: These two extremes should not be cultivated by one gone forth.

sn42.12:2.2.verse: Indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And indulgence in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.

sn42.12:2.3.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn42.12:2.4.verse: And what is that middle way of practice?

sn42.12:2.5.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn42.12:2.6.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn42.12:2.7.verse: This, chief, is the middle way of practice that was understood by the Realized One, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn42.12:3.1.verse: There are these three pleasure seekers in the world.

sn42.12:3.3.verse: Take a pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:3.4.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means.

sn42.12:3.5.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, but don’t share it and make merit.

sn42.12:3.6.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means.

sn42.12:3.7.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

sn42.12:4.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

sn42.12:4.2.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:4.3.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

sn42.12:4.4.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:4.5.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive.

sn42.12:4.6.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

sn42.12:5.1.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

sn42.12:5.2.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:5.3.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

sn42.12:5.4.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, but don’t share it and make merit.

sn42.12:5.5.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

sn42.12:5.6.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

sn42.12:5.7.verse: They enjoy that wealth tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.

sn42.12:5.8.verse: Next, a pleasure seeker seeks wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means.

sn42.12:5.9.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased, and they share it and make merit.

sn42.12:5.10.verse: And they enjoy that wealth untied, uninfatuated, unattached, seeing the drawbacks, and understanding the escape.

sn42.12:6.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:6.2.verse: They may be criticized on three grounds.

sn42.12:6.4.verse: They seek wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

sn42.12:6.5.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for criticism.

sn42.12:6.6.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the third ground for criticism.

sn42.12:6.7.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on these three grounds.

sn42.12:7.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, but doesn’t share it and make merit.

sn42.12:7.2.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on two grounds, and praised on one.

sn42.12:7.3.verse: What are the two grounds for criticism?

sn42.12:7.4.verse: They seek wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

sn42.12:7.5.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the second ground for criticism.

sn42.12:7.6.verse: What is the one ground for praise?

sn42.12:7.7.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the one ground for praise.

sn42.12:7.8.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on these two grounds, and praised on this one.

sn42.12:8.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using illegitimate, coercive means, and who makes themselves happy and pleased, and shares it and makes merit.

sn42.12:8.2.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on one ground, and praised on two.

sn42.12:8.3.verse: What is the one ground for criticism?

sn42.12:8.4.verse: They seek wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the one ground for criticism.

sn42.12:8.5.verse: What are the two grounds for praise?

sn42.12:8.6.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the first ground for praise.

sn42.12:8.7.verse: They share it and make merit. This is the second ground for praise.

sn42.12:8.8.verse: This pleasure seeker may be criticized on this one ground, and praised on these two.

sn42.12:9.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive, and who doesn’t make themselves happy and pleased, or share it and make merit.

sn42.12:9.2.verse: They may be praised on one ground, and criticized on three.

sn42.12:9.3.verse: What is the one ground for praise?

sn42.12:9.4.verse: They seek wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the one ground for praise.

sn42.12:9.5.verse: What are the three grounds for criticism?

sn42.12:9.6.verse: They seek wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

sn42.12:9.7.verse: They don’t make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for criticism.

sn42.12:9.8.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the third ground for criticism.

sn42.12:9.9.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on this one ground, and criticized on these three.

sn42.12:10.1.verse: Now, consider the pleasure seeker who seeks wealth using means both legitimate and illegitimate, and coercive and non-coercive, and makes themselves happy and pleased, but doesn’t share it and make merit.

sn42.12:10.2.verse: They may be praised on two grounds, and criticized on two.

sn42.12:10.3.verse: What are the two grounds for praise?

sn42.12:10.4.verse: They seek wealth using legitimate, non-coercive means. This is the first ground for praise.

sn42.12:10.5.verse: They make themselves happy and pleased. This is the second ground for praise.

sn42.12:10.6.verse: What are the two grounds for criticism?

sn42.12:10.7.verse: They seek wealth using illegitimate, coercive means. This is the first ground for criticism.

sn42.12:10.8.verse: They don’t share it and make merit. This is the second ground for criticism.

sn42.12:10.9.verse: This pleasure seeker may be praised on these two grounds, and criticized on these two.

sn42.12:12.3.verse: What is the one ground for praise?
