sn52.1:1.2.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn52.1:1.3.verse: Then as Anuruddha was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:

sn52.1:1.4.verse: “Whoever has missed out on these four kinds of mindfulness meditation has missed out on the noble path to the complete ending of suffering.

sn52.1:1.5.verse: Whoever has undertaken these four kinds of mindfulness meditation has undertaken the noble path to the complete ending of suffering.”

sn52.1:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna knew what Venerable Anuruddha was thinking. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he reappeared in front of Anuruddha,

sn52.1:2.3.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, how do you define the undertaking of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation by a mendicant?”

sn52.1:3.1.verse: “Reverend, it’s when a mendicant, with respect to the body internally, meditates observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.1:3.2.verse: With respect to the body externally, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.1:3.3.verse: With respect to the body internally and externally, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.1:4.1.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:4.2.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:4.3.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:4.4.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:4.5.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, shunning both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:5.3.verse: internally and externally, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish …

sn52.1:7.1.verse: With respect to the mind internally …

sn52.1:7.3.verse: internally and externally, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish …

sn52.1:9.3.verse: internally and externally, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish …

sn52.1:10.1.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do. …

sn52.1:10.2.verse: If they wish: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, ignoring both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ that’s what they do.

sn52.1:10.3.verse: That’s how to define the undertaking of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation by a mendicant.”

sn52.2:1.2.verse: Then as Anuruddha was in private retreat this thought came to his mind:

sn52.2:1.3.verse: “Whoever has missed out on these four kinds of mindfulness meditation has missed out on the noble path to the complete ending of suffering.

sn52.2:1.4.verse: Whoever has undertaken these four kinds of mindfulness meditation has undertaken the noble path to the complete ending of suffering.”

sn52.2:2.1.verse: Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna knew what Venerable Anuruddha was thinking. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he reappeared in front of Anuruddha and said to him:

sn52.2:3.1.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, how do you define the undertaking of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation by a mendicant?”

sn52.2:4.1.verse: “Reverend, it’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body internally—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.2:4.2.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the body externally …

sn52.2:4.3.verse: internally and externally—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.2:5.1.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings internally …

sn52.2:6.1.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of the mind internally …

sn52.2:7.1.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of principles internally …

sn52.2:7.3.verse: internally and externally—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.2:7.4.verse: That’s how to define the undertaking of the four kinds of mindfulness meditation by a mendicant.”

sn52.3:0.3.verse: On the Bank of the Sutanu

sn52.3:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying near Sāvatthī on the bank of the Sutanu.

sn52.3:1.2.verse: Then several mendicants went up to Venerable Anuruddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn52.3:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn52.3:1.4.verse: “What things has Venerable Anuruddha developed and cultivated to attain great direct knowledge?”

sn52.3:2.1.verse: “Reverends, I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.3:2.3.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.3:2.4.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn52.3:2.6.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.3:2.7.verse: I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.3:2.8.verse: And it was by developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I directly knew the lower principle as lower, the middle principle as middle, and the higher principle as higher.”

sn52.4:1.1.verse: At one time the venerables Anuruddha, Sāriputta, and Mahāmoggallāna were staying near Sāketa in the Thorny Wood.

sn52.4:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna came out of retreat, went to Anuruddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

sn52.4:1.3.verse: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. Sāriputta said to Anuruddha:

sn52.4:1.4.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, what things should a trainee mendicant enter and remain in?”

sn52.4:2.1.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, a trainee mendicant should enter and remain in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.4:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.4:2.4.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn52.4:2.6.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.4:2.7.verse: A trainee mendicant should enter and remain in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

sn52.5:1.3.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, what things should a mendicant who is an adept enter and remain in?”

sn52.5:1.4.verse: “Reverend Sāriputta, a mendicant who is an adept should enter and remain in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.5:1.6.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.5:1.7.verse: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn52.5:1.9.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.5:1.10.verse: A mendicant who is an adept should enter and remain in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

sn52.6:1.3.verse: “What things has Venerable Anuruddha developed and cultivated to attain great direct knowledge?”

sn52.6:1.4.verse: “Reverend, I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.6:1.6.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.6:1.7.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn52.6:1.9.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.6:1.10.verse: I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.6:1.11.verse: And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I directly know the thousandfold galaxy.”

sn52.7:1.2.verse: There Venerable Anuruddha addressed the mendicants:

sn52.7:2.1.verse: “Reverends, when these four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed and cultivated they lead to the ending of craving.

sn52.7:2.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body …

sn52.7:2.6.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.7:2.7.verse: When these four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed and cultivated they lead to the ending of craving.”

sn52.8:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the salaḷa tree hut.

sn52.8:1.2.verse: There Venerable Anuruddha addressed the mendicants:

sn52.8:1.3.verse: “Reverends, suppose that, although the Ganges River slants, slopes, and inclines to the east,

sn52.8:1.4.verse: a large crowd were to come along with a spade and basket, saying:

sn52.8:1.5.verse: ‘We’ll make this Ganges River slant, slope, and incline to the west!’

sn52.8:1.6.verse: What do you think, reverends? Would they succeed?”

sn52.8:1.9.verse: The Ganges River slants, slopes, and inclines to the east.

sn52.8:1.10.verse: It’s not easy to make it slant, slope, and incline to the west.

sn52.8:1.11.verse: That large crowd will eventually get weary and frustrated.”

sn52.8:2.1.verse: “In the same way, while a mendicant develops and cultivates the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, if rulers or their chief ministers, friends or colleagues, relatives or family should invite them to accept wealth, saying:

sn52.8:2.2.verse: ‘Please, my man, why let these ocher robes torment you?

sn52.8:2.3.verse: Why follow the practice of shaving your head and carrying an alms bowl?

sn52.8:2.4.verse: Come, return to a lesser life, enjoy wealth, and make merit!’

sn52.8:3.1.verse: It is quite impossible for a mendicant who is developing and cultivating the four kinds of mindfulness meditation to resign the training and return to a lesser life.

sn52.8:3.3.verse: Because for a long time that mendicant’s mind has slanted, sloped, and inclined to seclusion. So it’s impossible for them to return to a lesser life.

sn52.8:3.4.verse: And how does a mendicant develop and cultivate the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?

sn52.8:3.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body …

sn52.8:3.8.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.8:3.9.verse: That’s how a mendicant develops and cultivates the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

sn52.9:1.1.verse: At one time the venerables Anuruddha and Sāriputta were staying near Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Mango Grove.

sn52.9:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Anuruddha, and said to him:

sn52.9:2.1.verse: “Reverend Anuruddha, your faculties are so very clear, and your complexion is pure and bright.

sn52.9:2.2.verse: What kind of meditation are you usually practicing these days?”

sn52.9:2.3.verse: “These days, reverend, I usually meditate with my mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.9:2.5.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of the body …

sn52.9:2.8.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.9:2.9.verse: These days I usually meditate with my mind firmly established in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.9:2.10.verse: A mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—usually meditates with their mind firmly established in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.”

sn52.9:3.1.verse: “We’re so fortunate, reverend, so very fortunate,

sn52.9:3.2.verse: to have heard such a dramatic statement in the presence of Venerable Anuruddha.”

sn52.10:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the Dark Forest. And he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn52.10:1.2.verse: Then several mendicants went up to Venerable Anuruddha, and said to him:

sn52.10:2.1.verse: “What meditation does Venerable Anuruddha practice so that physical pain doesn’t occupy his mind?”

sn52.10:2.2.verse: “Reverends, I meditate with my mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation so that physical pain doesn’t occupy my mind.

sn52.10:2.4.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of the body …

sn52.10:2.7.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.10:2.8.verse: I meditate with my mind firmly established in these four kinds of mindfulness meditation so that physical pain doesn’t occupy my mind.”

sn52.11:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Anuruddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn52.11:1.2.verse: Then several mendicants went up to Venerable Anuruddha, exchanged greetings with him … and said:

sn52.11:2.1.verse: “What things has Venerable Anuruddha developed and cultivated to attain great direct knowledge?”

sn52.11:2.2.verse: “Reverends, I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.11:2.4.verse: I meditate observing an aspect of the body …

sn52.11:2.7.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn52.11:2.8.verse: I attained great direct knowledge by developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn52.11:2.9.verse: And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I recollect a thousand eons.”

sn52.12:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.”

sn52.13:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that, with clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, I hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.”

sn52.14:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my mind.

sn52.14:1.2.verse: I understand mind with greed as ‘mind with greed’ …

sn52.14:1.3.verse: I understand unfreed mind as ‘unfreed mind’.”

sn52.15:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.”

sn52.16:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand the result of deeds undertaken in the past, future, and present in terms of grounds and causes.”

sn52.17:0.3.verse: Where All Paths of Practice Lead

sn52.17:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand where all paths of practice lead.”

sn52.18:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand the world with its many and diverse elements.”

sn52.19:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand the diverse convictions of sentient beings.”

sn52.20:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand the faculties of other sentient beings and other individuals after encompassing them with my mind.”

sn52.21:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I truly understand corruption, cleansing, and emergence regarding the absorptions, liberations, immersions, and attainments.”

sn52.22:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I recollect my many kinds of past lives, with features and details.”

sn52.23:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, I understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.”

sn52.24:1.1.verse: “… And it’s because of developing and cultivating these four kinds of mindfulness meditation that I realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And I live having realized it with my own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.”

sn52.24:2.5.verse: The Linked Discourses with Anuruddha, the eighth section.

sn53.1-12:1.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn53.1-12:1.6.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn53.1-12:1.7.verse: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

sn53.1-12:1.8.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

sn53.1-12:2.1.verse: The Ganges River slants, slopes, and inclines to the east.

sn53.1-12:2.2.verse: In the same way, a mendicant who develops and cultivates the four absorptions slants, slopes, and inclines to extinguishment.

sn53.1-12:2.3.verse: And how does a mendicant who develops and cultivates the four absorptions slant, slope, and incline to extinguishment?

sn53.1-12:2.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

sn53.1-12:2.5.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption …

sn53.1-12:2.8.verse: That’s how a mendicant who develops and cultivates the four absorptions slants, slopes, and inclines to extinguishment.”

sn53.1-12:3.1.verse: Six on slanting to the east,

sn53.1-12:3.2.verse: and six on slanting to the ocean;

sn53.1-12:3.4.verse: and that’s how this chapter is recited.

sn53.13-22:1.1.verse: (Tell in full as in the chapter on diligence at SN 45.139–148.)

sn53.13-22:2.1.verse: The Realized One, footprint, roof peak,

sn53.23-34:1.1.verse: (Tell in full as in the chapter on hard work at SN 45.149–160.)

sn53.23-34:2.2.verse: a tree, a pot, and a spike,

sn53.23-34:2.3.verse: the atmosphere, and two on clouds,

sn53.23-34:2.4.verse: a ship, a guest house, and a river.

sn53.35-44:1.1.verse: (Tell in full as in the chapter on searches at SN 45.161–170.)

sn53.35-44:2.2.verse: states of existence, three kinds of suffering,

sn53.45-54:1.3.verse: Desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, desire for rebirth in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

sn53.45-54:1.4.verse: These are the five higher fetters.

sn53.45-54:1.5.verse: The four absorptions should be developed for the direct knowledge, complete understanding, finishing, and giving up of these five higher fetters.

sn53.45-54:1.7.verse: It’s when a mendicant enters and remains in the first absorption …

sn53.45-54:1.11.verse: These four absorptions should be developed for the direct knowledge, complete understanding, finishing, and giving up of these five higher fetters.”

sn53.45-54:1.12.verse: (Tell in full as in the Linked Discourses on the Path at SN 45.171–180.)

sn53.45-54:2.4.verse: aggregates, and fetters high and low.

sn53.45-54:2.5.verse: The Linked Discourses on Absorption, the ninth section.

sn54.1:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, when one thing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.1:1.6.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.1:1.7.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.1:1.8.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

sn54.1:2.1.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

sn54.1:2.2.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

sn54.1:2.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

sn54.1:2.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

sn54.1:3.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’

sn54.1:3.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’

sn54.1:3.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mental process.’

sn54.1:3.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

sn54.1:4.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

sn54.1:4.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out gladdening the mind.’

sn54.1:4.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out immersing the mind in samādhi.’

sn54.1:4.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in freeing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out freeing the mind.’

sn54.1:4.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing impermanence.’

sn54.1:5.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing fading away.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing fading away.’

sn54.1:5.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing cessation.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing cessation.’

sn54.1:5.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.1:6.1.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.”

sn54.2:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.2:1.2.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.2:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops mindfulness of breathing together with the awakening factors of mindfulness,

sn54.2:1.4.verse: investigation of principles, energy, rapture, tranquility, immersion,

sn54.2:1.5.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

sn54.2:1.6.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.”

sn54.3:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.3:1.2.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.3:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.3:1.4.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.3:1.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.3:1.6.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.”

sn54.4:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.4:1.2.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.4:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.4:1.4.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.4:1.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.4:1.6.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.4:1.7.verse: When mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way you can expect one of two results:

sn54.4:1.8.verse: enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.”

sn54.5:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.5:1.2.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated to be very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.5:1.3.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.5:1.4.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.5:1.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.5:1.6.verse: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, is very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.5:2.1.verse: When mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way you can expect seven fruits and benefits.

sn54.5:2.3.verse: You attain enlightenment early on in this very life.

sn54.5:2.5.verse: If not, you attain enlightenment at the time of death.

sn54.5:2.7.verse: If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters you’re extinguished in between one life and the next …

sn54.5:2.11.verse: you head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm …

sn54.5:2.12.verse: When mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way you can expect these seven fruits and benefits.”

sn54.6:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, do you develop mindfulness of breathing?”

sn54.6:1.4.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ariṭṭha said to him:

sn54.6:1.6.verse: “But mendicant, how do you develop it?”

sn54.6:1.7.verse: “Sir, I’ve given up desire for sensual pleasures of the past. I’m rid of desire for sensual pleasures of the future. And I have eliminated perception of aversion regarding phenomena internally and externally.

sn54.6:1.8.verse: Just mindful, I will breathe in. Mindful, I will breathe out.

sn54.6:1.9.verse: That’s how I develop mindfulness of breathing.”

sn54.6:2.1.verse: “That is mindfulness of breathing, Ariṭṭha; I don’t deny it.

sn54.6:2.2.verse: But as to how mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail,

sn54.6:2.3.verse: listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn54.6:3.1.verse: “And how is mindfulness of breathing fulfilled in detail?

sn54.6:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.6:3.3.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

sn54.6:3.4.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’ …

sn54.6:3.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.6:3.6.verse: This is how mindfulness of breathing is fulfilled in detail.”

sn54.7:1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākappina was sitting not far from the Buddha, cross-legged, his body set straight, and mindfulness brought to the present.

sn54.7:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you see any perturbation or trembling in that mendicant’s body?”

sn54.7:2.2.verse: “Sir, whenever we see that mendicant meditating—whether in the middle of the Saṅgha or alone in private—we never see any perturbation or trembling in his body.”

sn54.7:3.1.verse: “Mendicants, when an immersion has been developed and cultivated there’s no perturbation or trembling of the body or mind. That mendicant gets such immersion when he wants, without trouble or difficulty.

sn54.7:4.1.verse: When immersion due to mindfulness of breathing has been developed and cultivated there’s no perturbation or trembling of the body or mind.

sn54.7:4.2.verse: And how is immersion due to mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated in such a way?

sn54.7:5.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.7:5.2.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.7:5.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.7:5.4.verse: That’s how immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that there’s no perturbation or trembling of the body or mind.”

sn54.8:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.8:2.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.8:2.2.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

sn54.8:2.3.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’ …

sn54.8:2.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.8:2.5.verse: That’s how immersion due to mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.8:3.1.verse: Before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I too usually practiced this kind of meditation.

sn54.8:3.2.verse: And while I was usually practicing this kind of meditation neither my body nor my eyes became fatigued.

sn54.8:3.3.verse: And my mind was freed from defilements by not grasping.

sn54.8:4.2.verse: ‘May neither my body nor my eyes became fatigued. And may my mind be freed from the defilements by not grasping.’

sn54.8:4.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:5.2.verse: ‘May I give up memories and thoughts tied to domestic life.’

sn54.8:5.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:6.2.verse: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive.’

sn54.8:6.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:7.2.verse: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive.’

sn54.8:7.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:8.2.verse: ‘May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive and the repulsive.’

sn54.8:8.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:9.2.verse: ‘May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive and the unrepulsive.’

sn54.8:9.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:10.2.verse: ‘May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, shunning both the repulsive and the unrepulsive.’

sn54.8:10.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:11.2.verse: ‘Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, may I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.’

sn54.8:11.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:12.2.verse: ‘As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, may I enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.’

sn54.8:12.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:13.2.verse: ‘With the fading away of rapture, may I enter and remain in the third absorption, where I will meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, “Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.”’

sn54.8:13.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:14.2.verse: ‘With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, may I enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.’

sn54.8:14.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:15.2.verse: ‘Going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that “space is infinite”, may I enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space.’

sn54.8:15.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:16.2.verse: ‘Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that “consciousness is infinite”, may I enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness.’

sn54.8:16.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:17.2.verse: ‘Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that “there is nothing at all”, may I enter and remain in the dimension of nothingness.’

sn54.8:17.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:18.2.verse: ‘Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, may I enter and remain in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.’

sn54.8:18.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:19.2.verse: ‘Going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, may I enter and remain in the cessation of perception and feeling.’

sn54.8:19.3.verse: So let them closely focus on this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.8:20.1.verse: When immersion due to mindfulness of breathing has been developed and cultivated in this way, if they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

sn54.8:20.2.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

sn54.8:20.3.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

sn54.8:21.1.verse: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

sn54.8:21.2.verse: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

sn54.8:21.3.verse: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

sn54.8:21.4.verse: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

sn54.8:21.5.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’

sn54.8:22.1.verse: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn.

sn54.8:22.2.verse: As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

sn54.8:22.3.verse: In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

sn54.8:22.4.verse: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’”

sn54.9:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

sn54.9:1.3.verse: Now at that time the Buddha spoke in many ways to the mendicants about the meditation on ugliness. He praised the meditation on ugliness and its development.

sn54.9:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

sn54.9:2.2.verse: “Mendicants, I wish to go on retreat for a fortnight.

sn54.9:2.3.verse: No-one should approach me, except the one who brings my almsfood.”

sn54.9:2.4.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied those mendicants. And no-one approached him, except the one who brought the almsfood.

sn54.9:3.2.verse: “The Buddha spoke in many ways about the meditation on ugliness. He praised the meditation on ugliness and its development.” They committed themselves to developing the many different facets of the meditation on ugliness.

sn54.9:3.3.verse: Becoming horrified, repelled, and disgusted with this body, they looked for a suicide weapon.

sn54.9:3.4.verse: Each day ten, twenty, or thirty mendicants committed suicide.

sn54.9:4.1.verse: Then after a fortnight had passed, the Buddha came out of retreat and addressed Ānanda,

sn54.9:4.2.verse: “Ānanda, why does the mendicant Saṅgha seem so diminished?”

sn54.9:4.3.verse: Ānanda told the Buddha all that had happened, and said,

sn54.9:4.6.verse: “Sir, please explain another way the mendicant Saṅgha might be settled in enlightenment.”

sn54.9:5.1.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, gather all the mendicants staying in the vicinity of Vesālī together in the assembly hall.”

sn54.9:5.2.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied Ānanda. He did what the Buddha asked, went up to him, and said,

sn54.9:5.4.verse: Please, sir, come at your convenience.”

sn54.9:6.1.verse: Then the Buddha went to the assembly hall, sat down on the seat spread out,

sn54.9:6.3.verse: “Mendicants, when this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s peaceful and sublime, a delectable and blissful meditation. And it disperses and settles unskillful qualities on the spot whenever they arise.

sn54.9:7.1.verse: In the last month of summer, when the dust and dirt is stirred up, a large storm out of season disperses and settles it on the spot.

sn54.9:7.2.verse: In the same way, when this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it’s peaceful and sublime, a delectable and blissful meditation. And it disperses and settles unskillful qualities on the spot whenever they arise.

sn54.9:7.3.verse: And how is it so developed and cultivated?

sn54.9:8.1.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.9:8.2.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.9:8.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.9:8.4.verse: That’s how this immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so that it’s peaceful and sublime, a delectable and blissful  meditation. And it disperses and settles unskillful qualities on the spot whenever they arise.”

sn54.10:1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kimbilā in the Freshwater Mangrove Wood.

sn54.10:1.3.verse: Then the Buddha said to Venerable Kimbila,

sn54.10:1.4.verse: “Kimbila, how is immersion due to mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is very fruitful and beneficial?”

sn54.10:2.1.verse: When he said this, Kimbila kept silent.

sn54.10:2.3.verse: And for a third time, the Buddha said to him,

sn54.10:2.4.verse: “How is immersion due to mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is very fruitful and beneficial?”

sn54.10:2.5.verse: And a second time and a third time Kimbila kept silent.

sn54.10:3.1.verse: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha,

sn54.10:3.2.verse: “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

sn54.10:3.3.verse: Let the Buddha speak on immersion due to mindfulness of breathing. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

sn54.10:4.1.verse: “Well then, Ānanda, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

sn54.10:4.4.verse: “Ānanda, how is immersion due to mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is very fruitful and beneficial?

sn54.10:4.5.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.10:4.6.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. …

sn54.10:4.7.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.10:4.8.verse: That’s how immersion due to mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is very fruitful and beneficial.

sn54.10:5.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant is breathing in heavily, and they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

sn54.10:5.2.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

sn54.10:5.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

sn54.10:5.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

sn54.10:5.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:5.7.verse: Because the breath is a certain aspect of the body, I say.

sn54.10:5.8.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:6.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’

sn54.10:6.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’

sn54.10:6.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the the mental process.’

sn54.10:6.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

sn54.10:6.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:6.7.verse: Because careful application of mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths is a certain aspect of feelings, I say.

sn54.10:6.8.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:7.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

sn54.10:7.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out gladdening the mind.’

sn54.10:7.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out immersing the mind in samādhi.’

sn54.10:7.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in freeing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out freeing the mind.’

sn54.10:7.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:7.7.verse: Because there is no development of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing for someone who is unmindful and lacks awareness, I say.

sn54.10:7.8.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:8.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing impermanence.’

sn54.10:8.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing fading away.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing fading away.’

sn54.10:8.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing cessation.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing cessation.’

sn54.10:8.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.10:8.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:8.6.verse: Having seen with wisdom the giving up of covetousness and displeasure, they watch closely over with equanimity.

sn54.10:8.7.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.10:9.1.verse: Suppose there was a large heap of sand at the crossroads.

sn54.10:9.2.verse: And a cart or chariot were to come by from the east,

sn54.10:9.5.verse: or south and destroy that heap of sand.

sn54.10:9.6.verse: In the same way, when a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body,

sn54.10:9.9.verse: or principles, they destroy bad, unskillful qualities.”

sn54.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

sn54.11:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, I wish to go on retreat for three months.

sn54.11:1.4.verse: No-one should approach me, except the one who brings my almsfood.”

sn54.11:1.5.verse: “Yes, sir,” replied those mendicants. And no-one approached him, except the one who brought the almsfood.

sn54.11:2.1.verse: Then after three months had passed, the Buddha came out of retreat and addressed the mendicants:

sn54.11:2.2.verse: “Mendicants, if wanderers who follow another religion were to ask you:

sn54.11:2.3.verse: ‘Reverends, what was the ascetic Gotama’s usual meditation during the rainy season residence?’ You should answer them like this.

sn54.11:2.4.verse: ‘Reverends, the ascetic Gotama’s usual meditation during the rainy season residence was immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.’

sn54.11:2.5.verse: In this regard: mindful, I breathe in. Mindful, I breathe out.

sn54.11:2.6.verse: Breathing in heavily I know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily I know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

sn54.11:2.7.verse: Breathing in lightly I know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly I know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

sn54.11:2.8.verse: I know: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ …

sn54.11:2.9.verse: I know: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ I know: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.11:3.1.verse: For if anything should be rightly called

sn54.11:3.2.verse: ‘a noble meditation’, or else ‘a divine meditation’, or else ‘a realized one’s meditation’,

sn54.11:3.3.verse: it’s immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.11:3.5.verse: For those mendicants who are trainees—who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring to the supreme sanctuary from the yoke—the development and cultivation of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing leads to the ending of defilements.

sn54.11:3.6.verse: For those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—the development and cultivation of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing leads to blissful meditation in this life, and to mindfulness and awareness.

sn54.11:4.1.verse: For if anything should be rightly called

sn54.11:4.2.verse: ‘a noble meditation’, or else ‘a divine meditation’, or else ‘a realized one’s meditation’,

sn54.11:4.3.verse: it’s immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.”

sn54.12:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

sn54.12:1.2.verse: Then Mahānāma the Sakyan went up to Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

sn54.12:1.3.verse: “Sir, is the meditation of a trainee just the same as the meditation of a realized one? Or is the meditation of a trainee different from the meditation of a realized one?”

sn54.12:2.1.verse: “Reverend Mahānāma, the meditation of a trainee and a realized one are not the same;

sn54.12:2.3.verse: Those mendicants who are trainees haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring for the supreme sanctuary from the yoke. They meditate after giving up the five hindrances.

sn54.12:2.5.verse: The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will,

sn54.12:3.1.verse: Those who are trainee mendicants … meditate after giving up the five hindrances.

sn54.12:4.1.verse: Those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—for them, the five hindrances are cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

sn54.12:5.1.verse: Those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements … for them, the five hindrances are cut off at the root … and unable to arise in the future.

sn54.12:5.2.verse: And here’s another way to understand how

sn54.12:5.3.verse: the meditation of a trainee and a realized one are different.

sn54.12:6.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

sn54.12:6.3.verse: ‘Mendicants, I wish to go on retreat for three months.

sn54.12:6.4.verse: No-one should approach me, except the one who brings my almsfood.’

sn54.12:6.5.verse: ‘Yes, sir,’ replied those mendicants. And no-one approached him, except the one who brought the almsfood.

sn54.12:7.1.verse: Then after three months had passed, the Buddha came out of retreat and addressed the mendicants:

sn54.12:7.2.verse: ‘Mendicants, if wanderers who follow another religion were to ask you:

sn54.12:7.3.verse: “Reverends, what was the ascetic Gotama’s usual meditation during the rainy season residence?” You should answer them like this:

sn54.12:7.4.verse: “Reverends, the ascetic Gotama’s usual meditation during the rainy season residence was immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.”

sn54.12:7.5.verse: In this regard: mindful, I breathe in. Mindful, I breathe out.

sn54.12:7.6.verse: Breathing in heavily I know: “I’m breathing in heavily.” Breathing out heavily I know: “I’m breathing out heavily.” …

sn54.12:7.7.verse: I know: “I’ll breathe in observing letting go.” I know: “I’ll breathe out observing letting go.”

sn54.12:8.1.verse: For if anything should be rightly called

sn54.12:8.2.verse: “noble meditation”, or else “divine meditation”, or else “a realized one’s meditation”,

sn54.12:8.3.verse: it’s immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.

sn54.12:9.1.verse: For those mendicants who are trainees—who haven’t achieved their heart’s desire, but live aspiring for the supreme sanctuary from the yoke—the development and cultivation of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing leads to the ending of defilements.

sn54.12:10.1.verse: For those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and are rightly freed through enlightenment—the development and cultivation of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing leads to blissful meditation in this very life, and to mindfulness and awareness.

sn54.12:11.1.verse: For if anything should be rightly called

sn54.12:11.2.verse: “noble meditation”, or else “divine meditation”, or else “a realized one’s meditation”,

sn54.12:11.3.verse: it’s immersion due to mindfulness of breathing.’

sn54.12:11.5.verse: This is another way to understand how

sn54.12:11.6.verse: the meditation of a trainee and a realized one are different.”

sn54.13:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn54.13:1.3.verse: “Sir, is there one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things; and those four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and those seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”

sn54.13:3.2.verse: “Immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. And the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors. And the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.

sn54.13:4.1.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?

sn54.13:4.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

sn54.13:4.3.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

sn54.13:4.4.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’ …

sn54.13:4.5.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.13:5.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant is breathing in heavily, and they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

sn54.13:5.3.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

sn54.13:5.4.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:5.6.verse: Because the breath is a certain aspect of the body, I say.

sn54.13:5.7.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:6.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture …

sn54.13:6.4.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

sn54.13:6.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:6.7.verse: Because careful application of mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths is a certain aspect of feelings, I say.

sn54.13:6.8.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:7.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

sn54.13:7.2.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in gladdening the mind …

sn54.13:7.4.verse: freeing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out freeing the mind.’

sn54.13:7.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:7.7.verse: Because there is no development of immersion due to mindfulness of breathing for someone who is unmindful and lacks awareness, I say.

sn54.13:7.8.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:8.1.verse: There’s a time when a mendicant practices like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing impermanence …

sn54.13:8.4.verse: letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.13:8.5.verse: At such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:8.6.verse: Having seen with wisdom the giving up of covetousness and displeasure, they watch closely over with equanimity.

sn54.13:8.7.verse: Therefore, at such a time a mendicant is meditating by observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn54.13:9.1.verse: That’s how immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.

sn54.13:10.1.verse: And how are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven awakening factors?

sn54.13:10.2.verse: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body,

sn54.13:10.3.verse: their mindfulness is established and lucid.

sn54.13:10.4.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of mindfulness; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:11.1.verse: As they live mindfully in this way they investigate, explore, and inquire into that principle with wisdom.

sn54.13:11.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of investigation of principles; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:12.1.verse: As they investigate principles with wisdom in this way their energy is roused up and unflagging.

sn54.13:12.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of energy; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:13.1.verse: When you’re energetic, rapture not of the flesh arises.

sn54.13:13.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has initiated the awakening factor of rapture; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:14.1.verse: When the mind is full of rapture, the body and mind become tranquil.

sn54.13:14.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of tranquility; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:15.1.verse: When the body is tranquil and one feels bliss, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi.

sn54.13:15.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of immersion; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:16.1.verse: They closely watch over that mind immersed in samādhi.

sn54.13:16.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of equanimity; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:17.1.verse: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of feelings …

sn54.13:17.4.verse: their mindfulness is established and lucid.

sn54.13:17.5.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of mindfulness; they develop it and perfect it. …

sn54.13:17.7.verse: (Tell in full as for the first kind of mindfulness meditation.)

sn54.13:18.1.verse: They closely watch over that mind immersed in samādhi.

sn54.13:18.2.verse: At such a time, a mendicant has activated the awakening factor of equanimity; they develop it and perfect it.

sn54.13:18.4.verse: That’s how the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven awakening factors.

sn54.13:19.1.verse: And how are the seven awakening factors developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom?

sn54.13:19.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness,

sn54.13:19.3.verse: investigation of principles, energy, rapture, tranquility, immersion,

sn54.13:19.4.verse: and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go.

sn54.13:19.5.verse: That’s how the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom.”

sn54.14:1.1.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn54.14:1.2.verse: “Ānanda, is there one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things; and those four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and those seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”

sn54.14:1.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. …”

sn54.14:2.1.verse: And what is that one thing?

sn54.14:2.2.verse: Immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. And the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors. And the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.

sn54.14:2.3.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation? …

sn54.14:2.5.verse: That’s how the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom.”

sn54.15:1.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn54.15:1.2.verse: “Sir, is there one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things; and those four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and those seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”

sn54.15:2.2.verse: “Immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. And the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors. And the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.

sn54.15:3.1.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation? …

sn54.15:3.3.verse: That’s how the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom.”

sn54.16:1.1.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:

sn54.16:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, is there one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills four things; and those four things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven things; and those seven things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill two things?”

sn54.16:1.3.verse: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. …”

sn54.16:2.1.verse: And what is that one thing?

sn54.16:2.2.verse: Immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. And the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors. And the seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.

sn54.16:3.1.verse: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?

sn54.16:3.2.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present. …

sn54.16:18.5.verse: That’s how the seven awakening factors are developed and cultivated so as to fulfill knowledge and freedom.”

sn54.17:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it leads to giving up the fetters …”

sn54.18:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it leads to uprooting the underlying tendencies …”

sn54.19:0.3.verse: Completely Understanding the Course of Time

sn54.19:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it leads to completely understanding the course of time …”

sn54.20:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, when immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated it leads to the ending of defilements.” …

sn54.20:1.2.verse: “And how is immersion due to mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to lead to giving up the fetters,

sn54.20:1.4.verse: completely understanding the course of time,

sn54.20:1.6.verse: It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of them. …

sn54.20:1.7.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

sn54.20:1.8.verse: That’s how immersion due to mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated so as to lead to giving up the fetters,

sn54.20:1.10.verse: completely understanding the course of time,

sn55.1:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a wheel-turning monarch were to rule as sovereign lord over these four continents. And when his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm, in the company of the gods of the thirty-three. There he amuses himself in the Garden of Delight, escorted by a band of nymphs, and supplied and provided with the five kinds of heavenly sensual stimulation. Still, as he’s lacking four things, he’s not exempt from hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. He’s not exempt from places of loss, bad places, the underworld.

sn55.1:1.4.verse: Now suppose a noble disciple wears rags and feeds on scraps of almsfood. Still, as they have four things, they’re exempt from hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. They’re exempt from places of loss, bad places, the underworld.

sn55.1:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha:

sn55.1:2.3.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

sn55.1:2.4.verse: They have experiential confidence in the teaching:

sn55.1:2.5.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

sn55.1:2.6.verse: They have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha:

sn55.1:2.7.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

sn55.1:2.8.verse: Furthermore, a noble disciple’s ethical conduct is loved by the noble ones, unbroken, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

sn55.1:2.9.verse: These are the four qualities that they possess.

sn55.1:2.10.verse: And, mendicants, gaining these four continents is not worth a sixteenth part of gaining these four things.”

sn55.2:0.3.verse: The Objective of the Spiritual Life

sn55.2:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, a noble disciple who has four things is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

sn55.2:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha …

sn55.2:2.6.verse: And they have the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones … leading to immersion.

sn55.2:2.7.verse: A noble disciple who has these four things is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

sn55.2:3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn55.2:3.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn55.2:4.2.verse: confidence, and vision of the truth,

sn55.2:4.4.verse: the objective of the spiritual life.”

sn55.3:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn55.3:1.2.verse: Now at that time the lay follower Dīghāvu was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn55.3:1.3.verse: Then he addressed his father, the householder Jotika,

sn55.3:1.4.verse: “Please, householder, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

sn55.3:1.5.verse: ‘Sir, the lay follower Dīghāvu is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn55.3:1.6.verse: He bows with his head to your feet.’

sn55.3:1.8.verse: ‘Sir, please visit him at his home out of sympathy.’”

sn55.3:1.9.verse: “Yes, dear,” replied Jotika. He did as Dīghāvu asked.

sn55.3:2.1.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the lay follower Dīghāvu, sat down on the seat spread out, and said to him,

sn55.3:2.2.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Dīghāvu, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn55.3:2.3.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

sn55.3:2.4.verse: “So, Dīghāvu, you should train like this:

sn55.3:2.5.verse: ‘I will have experiential confidence in the Buddha …

sn55.3:2.8.verse: And I will have the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones … leading to immersion.’

sn55.3:3.1.verse: “Sir, these four factors of stream-entry that were taught by the Buddha are found in me, and I exhibit them.

sn55.3:3.2.verse: For I have experiential confidence in the Buddha …

sn55.3:3.5.verse: And I have the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones … leading to immersion.”

sn55.3:3.6.verse: “In that case, Dīghāvu, grounded on these four factors of stream-entry you should further develop these six things that play a part in realization.

sn55.3:3.7.verse: You should meditate observing the impermanence of all conditions, perceiving suffering in impermanence, perceiving not-self in suffering, perceiving giving up, perceiving fading away, and perceiving cessation.

sn55.3:4.1.verse: “These six things that play a part in realization that were taught by the Buddha are found in me, and I exhibit them.

sn55.3:4.2.verse: For I meditate observing the impermanence of all conditions, perceiving suffering in impermanence, perceiving not-self in suffering, perceiving giving up, perceiving fading away, and perceiving cessation.

sn55.3:4.4.verse: ‘I hope Jotika doesn’t suffer distress when I’ve gone.’”

sn55.3:4.5.verse: Jotika said, “Dear Dīghāvu, don’t focus on that.

sn55.3:4.6.verse: Come on, dear Dīghāvu, you should closely focus on what the Buddha is saying.”

sn55.3:5.1.verse: When the Buddha had given this advice he rose from his seat and left.

sn55.3:5.2.verse: Not long after the Buddha left, Dīghāvu passed away.

sn55.3:5.3.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn55.3:5.4.verse: “Sir, the lay follower named Dīghāvu, who was advised in brief by the Buddha, has passed away.

sn55.3:5.5.verse: Where has he been reborn in his next life?”

sn55.3:5.6.verse: “Mendicants, the lay follower Dīghāvu was astute. He practiced in line with the teaching, and did not trouble me about the teachings.

sn55.3:5.7.verse: With the ending of the five lower fetters, he’s been reborn spontaneously, and will become extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.”

sn55.4:1.1.verse: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

sn55.4:1.2.verse: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat … and said to Sāriputta:

sn55.4:1.3.verse: “Reverend, how many things do people have to possess in order for the Buddha to declare that they’re a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening?”

sn55.4:1.4.verse: “Reverend, people have to possess four things in order for the Buddha to declare that they’re a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

sn55.4:2.2.verse: It’s when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha …

sn55.4:2.6.verse: And they have the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones … leading to immersion.

sn55.4:2.7.verse: People have to possess these four things in order for the Buddha to declare that they’re a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.”

sn55.5:1.1.verse: Then Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

sn55.5:1.2.verse: “Sāriputta, they speak of a ‘factor for stream-entry’.

sn55.5:1.3.verse: What is a factor for stream-entry?”

sn55.5:1.4.verse: “Sir, the factors for stream-entry are associating with true persons, listening to the true teaching, rational application of mind, and practicing in line with the teaching.”

sn55.5:1.6.verse: For the factors for stream-entry are associating with true persons, listening to the true teaching, rational application of mind, and practicing in line with the teaching.

sn55.5:2.3.verse: “Sir, the stream is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn55.5:2.4.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.”

sn55.5:2.6.verse: For the stream is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn55.5:2.7.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn55.5:3.3.verse: “Sir, anyone who possesses this noble eightfold path is called a stream-enterer, the venerable of such name and such clan.”

sn55.5:3.5.verse: For anyone who possesses this noble eightfold path is called a stream-enterer, the venerable of such name and such clan.”

sn55.6:1.3.verse: when his robe was finished and the three months of the rains residence had passed the Buddha would set out wandering.

sn55.6:1.4.verse: Now at that time the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa were residing in Sādhuka on some business.

sn55.6:2.1.verse: So they posted someone on the road, saying:

sn55.6:2.2.verse: “My man, let us know when you see the Blessed One coming, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.”

sn55.6:2.3.verse: And that person stood there for two or three days before they saw the Buddha coming off in the distance.

sn55.6:2.4.verse: When they saw him, they went to the chamberlains and said:

sn55.6:2.5.verse: “Sirs, the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha is coming.

sn55.6:3.1.verse: Then the chamberlains went up to the Buddha, bowed, and followed behind him.

sn55.6:3.2.verse: And then the Buddha left the road, went to the root of a certain tree, and sat down on the seat spread out.

sn55.6:3.3.verse: The chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa bowed, sat down to one side,

sn55.6:14.1.verse: “Well then, chamberlains, life at home is cramped and dirty, life gone forth is wide open.

sn55.6:14.2.verse: Just this much is enough for diligence.”

sn55.6:14.3.verse: “Sir, for us there is something that’s even more cramped than that, and is considered as such.”

sn55.6:15.1.verse: “Sir, it’s when King Pasenadi of Kosala wants to go and visit a park. We have to harness and prepare his royal elephants. Then we have to seat his dear and beloved wives on the elephants, one in front of us, and one behind.

sn55.6:15.2.verse: Those sisters smell like a freshly opened perfume box; that’s how the royal ladies smell with makeup on.

sn55.6:15.3.verse: The touch of those sisters is like a tuft of cotton-wool or kapok; that’s how pampered the royal ladies are.

sn55.6:15.4.verse: Now at that time we must look after the elephants, the sisters, and ourselves.

sn55.6:15.5.verse: But we don’t recall having a bad thought regarding those sisters.

sn55.6:15.6.verse: This is that thing that’s even more cramped than that, and is considered as such.”

sn55.6:16.2.verse: Just this much is enough for diligence.

sn55.6:16.3.verse: A noble disciple who has four things is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.

sn55.6:17.6.verse: They live at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.

sn55.6:17.7.verse: A noble disciple who has these four things is a stream-enterer, not liable to be reborn in the underworld, assured, destined for awakening.
