sn56.4:2.2.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. …

sn56.4:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.5:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, whatever ascetics and brahmins truly awaken—in the past,

sn56.5:1.3.verse: or present—all of them truly awaken to the four noble truths.

sn56.5:2.2.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. …

sn56.5:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.6:1.3.verse: or present—reveal that they are awakened, all of them reveal that they truly awakened to the four noble truths.

sn56.6:2.2.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. …

sn56.6:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.7:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, don’t think bad, unskillful thoughts, such as

sn56.7:1.4.verse: Because those thoughts aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.7:2.1.verse: When you think, you should think: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.7:2.3.verse: Because those thoughts are beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.7:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.8:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, don’t think up a bad, unskillful idea.

sn56.8:1.2.verse: For example: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

sn56.8:1.4.verse: Because those thoughts aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.8:2.1.verse: When you think something up, you should think: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.8:2.3.verse: Because those thoughts are beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.8:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.9:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, don’t get into arguments, such as:

sn56.9:1.2.verse: ‘You don’t understand this teaching and training. I understand this teaching and training. What, you understand this teaching and training? You’re practicing wrong. I’m practicing right. I stay on topic, you don’t. You said last what you should have said first. You said first what you should have said last. What you’ve thought so much about has been disproved. Your doctrine is refuted. Go on, save your doctrine! You’re trapped; get yourself out of this—if you can!’

sn56.9:1.4.verse: Because those discussions aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.9:2.1.verse: When you discuss, you should discuss: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. …

sn56.9:2.2.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.10:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, don’t engage in all kinds of low talk, such as

sn56.10:1.2.verse: talk about kings, bandits, and chief ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and fragrances; talk about family, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; talk at the street market and the place for water pots; talk about the departed; motley talk; tales of land and sea; and talk about being reborn in this or that place.

sn56.10:1.4.verse: Because those discussions aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.10:2.1.verse: When you discuss, you should discuss: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. …

sn56.10:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.11:1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

sn56.11:1.2.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the group-of-five monks, saying:

sn56.11:2.1.verse: “There are these two extremes, monks, that one who has gone forth ought not to associate with,

sn56.11:2.3.verse: which is this: devotion to the pleasure and happiness in sense pleasures, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected with the goal; and this: devotion to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and not connected with the goal.

sn56.11:2.4.verse: Not having approached either of these two extremes, monks, the middle practice was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

sn56.11:3.1.verse: Now what is this middle practice, monks, that was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna?

sn56.11:3.2.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

sn56.11:3.3.verse: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right endeavour, right mindfulness, right concentration.

sn56.11:3.4.verse: This is the middle practice, monks, that was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

sn56.11:4.1.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering:

sn56.11:4.2.verse: birth is suffering, also old age is suffering, also sickness is suffering, also death is suffering, being joined to what is not dear is suffering, being separated from what is dear is suffering, also not to obtain what one longs for is suffering, in brief, the five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment are suffering.

sn56.11:4.3.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the arising of suffering:

sn56.11:4.4.verse: it is that craving which leads to continuation in existence, which is connected with enjoyment and passion, greatly enjoying this and that, as follows:

sn56.11:4.5.verse: craving for sense pleasures, craving for continuation, craving for discontinuation.

sn56.11:4.6.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering:

sn56.11:4.7.verse: it is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that craving - liberation, letting go, release, and non-adherence.

sn56.11:4.8.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering:

sn56.11:4.9.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

sn56.11:5.1.verse: “This is the noble truth of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:5.3.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of suffering” refers has been fully known - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:6.1.verse: “This is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:6.3.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” refers has been given up, to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:7.1.verse: “This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:7.3.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” refers has been experienced - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:8.1.verse: “This is the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering”- to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:8.3.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering” refers - has been developed - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

sn56.11:9.1.verse: For as long as to me, monks, in regard to these four noble truths - turned like this, in three ways, twelvefold - knowledge and insight as it really is was not quite clear, for that long, monks, I did not declare to the world with its gods, Māra, and Brahma, to this generation, with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men, that I was fully awakened with unsurpassed complete awakening.

sn56.11:10.1.verse: But when to me, monks, in regard to these four noble truths - turned like this, in three ways, twelvefold - knowledge and insight as it really is was quite clear then, monks, I did declare to the world with its gods, Māra, and Brahma, to this generation, with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men, that I was fully awakened with unsurpassed complete awakening.

sn56.11:10.2.verse: To me knowledge and seeing arose:

sn56.11:10.3.verse: “Sure is my freedom of mind this is my last birth now there is no continuation of existence.”

sn56.11:10.5.verse: and the group-of-five monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was said by the Fortunate One.

sn56.11:11.1.verse: Moreover, as this sermon was being given, to venerable Koṇḍañña the dust-free, stainless, Vision-of-the-Dhamma arose:

sn56.11:11.2.verse: Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing.

sn56.11:12.1.verse: Now when the Dhamma Wheel was set rolling by the Fortunate One the Earth gods let loose a cry:

sn56.11:12.2.verse: “The Fortunate One, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.”

sn56.11:12.3.verse: Having heard the cry of the Earth gods the gods called the Four Great Kings let loose a cry:

sn56.11:12.4.verse: “The Fortunate One, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.”

sn56.11:13.1.verse: Thus at that moment, at that second, that cry reached as far as the Brahma worlds,

sn56.11:13.2.verse: and this ten thousand world-element moved, wavered, and shook, and great and measureless light became manifest in the world, transcending the psychic power of the gods.

sn56.11:14.1.verse: Then the Fortunate One uttered this inspired utterance:

sn56.11:14.3.verse: Thus to the venerable Koṇḍañña came the name Aññā Koṇḍañña (Koṇḍañña, he-who-knows).

sn56.11:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.11:0.3.verse: Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.11:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

sn56.11:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the group of five mendicants:

sn56.11:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two extremes should not be cultivated by one gone forth.

sn56.11:2.3.verse: Indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And indulgence in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.

sn56.11:2.4.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.11:3.1.verse: And what is that middle way of practice?

sn56.11:3.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn56.11:3.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn56.11:3.4.verse: This is that middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.11:4.1.verse: Now this is the noble truth of suffering.

sn56.11:4.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

sn56.11:4.3.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

sn56.11:4.4.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

sn56.11:4.5.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn56.11:4.6.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

sn56.11:4.7.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn56.11:4.8.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.11:4.9.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn56.11:4.10.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn56.11:5.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.

sn56.11:5.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of suffering should be completely understood.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:5.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of suffering has been completely understood.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:6.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:6.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be given up.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:6.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been given up.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:7.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:7.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:7.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:8.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:8.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering should be developed.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

sn56.11:8.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering has been developed.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.

sn56.11:9.1.verse: As long as my true knowledge and vision about these four noble truths was not fully purified in these three rounds and twelve aspects, I didn’t announce my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

sn56.11:10.1.verse: But when my true knowledge and vision about these four noble truths was fully purified in these three rounds and twelve aspects, I announced my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

sn56.11:10.2.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

sn56.11:10.3.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

sn56.11:10.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn56.11:10.5.verse: Satisfied, the group of five mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

sn56.11:11.1.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Venerable Koṇḍañña:

sn56.11:11.2.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

sn56.11:12.1.verse: And when the Buddha rolled forth the Wheel of Dhamma, the earth gods raised the cry:

sn56.11:12.2.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Buddha has rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.”

sn56.11:12.3.verse: Hearing the cry of the earth gods, the gods of the four great kings …

sn56.11:12.8.verse: the gods who love to create …

sn56.11:12.9.verse: the gods who control what is created by others …

sn56.11:12.10.verse: the gods of the Divinity’s host raised the cry:

sn56.11:12.11.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Buddha has rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.”

sn56.11:13.1.verse: And so at that moment, that second, that hour, the cry soared up to the realm of divinity.

sn56.11:13.2.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shook and rocked and trembled. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appeared in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.

sn56.11:14.1.verse: Then the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

sn56.11:14.2.verse: “Koṇḍañña has really understood! Koṇḍañña has really understood!”

sn56.11:14.3.verse: And that’s how Venerable Koṇḍañña came to be known as “Koṇḍañña Who Understood”.

sn56.12:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.12:1.1.verse: “‘This is the noble truth of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in the Realized Ones regarding teachings not learned before from another.

sn56.12:1.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of suffering should be completely understood.’ …

sn56.12:1.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of suffering has been completely understood.’ …

sn56.12:2.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.’ …

sn56.12:2.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be given up.’ …

sn56.12:2.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been given up.’ …

sn56.12:3.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.’ …

sn56.12:3.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized.’ …

sn56.12:3.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized.’ …

sn56.12:4.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ …

sn56.12:4.2.verse: ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering should be developed.’ …

sn56.12:4.3.verse: ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering has been developed.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in the Realized Ones regarding teachings not learned before from another.”

sn56.13:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.13:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.13:1.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.13:2.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

sn56.13:2.2.verse: You should say: ‘The five grasping aggregates’.

sn56.13:2.3.verse: That is: form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

sn56.13:2.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

sn56.13:3.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

sn56.13:3.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

sn56.13:3.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for nonexistence.

sn56.13:3.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

sn56.13:4.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

sn56.13:4.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

sn56.13:4.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

sn56.13:5.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

sn56.13:5.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

sn56.13:5.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

sn56.13:5.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.13:5.5.verse: These are the four noble truths.

sn56.13:6.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation to understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.”

sn56.14:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.14:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.14:1.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.14:2.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

sn56.14:2.2.verse: You should say: ‘The six interior sense fields’.

sn56.14:2.4.verse: The sense fields of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

sn56.14:2.5.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

sn56.14:3.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? …

sn56.14:5.1.verse: the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

sn56.14:5.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path …

sn56.14:6.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.15:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.15:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you remember the four noble truths that I taught?”

sn56.15:1.2.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha:

sn56.15:1.5.verse: “Sir, I remember that suffering is the first noble truth you’ve taught;

sn56.15:1.6.verse: the origin of suffering is the second;

sn56.15:1.7.verse: the cessation of suffering is the third;

sn56.15:1.8.verse: and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering is the fourth.

sn56.15:1.9.verse: That’s how I remember the four noble truths as you’ve taught them.”

sn56.15:2.2.verse: It’s good that you remember the four noble truths as I’ve taught them.

sn56.15:2.3.verse: Suffering is the first noble truth I’ve taught, and that’s how you should remember it.

sn56.15:2.4.verse: The origin of suffering is the second;

sn56.15:2.5.verse: the cessation of suffering is the third;

sn56.15:2.6.verse: and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering is the fourth.

sn56.15:2.7.verse: That’s how you should remember the four noble truths as I’ve taught them.

sn56.15:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.16:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.16:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, do you remember the four noble truths that I taught?”

sn56.16:1.2.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha:

sn56.16:2.2.verse: “Sir, I remember that suffering is the first noble truth you’ve taught.

sn56.16:2.3.verse: For if any ascetic or brahmin should say this:

sn56.16:2.4.verse: ‘What the ascetic Gotama teaches is not the first noble truth of suffering.

sn56.16:2.5.verse: I’ll deny this first noble truth of suffering and describe another first noble truth of suffering.’

sn56.16:2.7.verse: The origin of suffering … The cessation of suffering …

sn56.16:2.8.verse: The practice that leads to the cessation of suffering is the fourth noble truth you’ve taught.

sn56.16:2.9.verse: For if any ascetic or brahmin should say this:

sn56.16:2.10.verse: ‘What the ascetic Gotama teaches is not the fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.16:2.11.verse: I’ll deny this fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering and describe another fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

sn56.16:2.13.verse: That’s how I remember the four noble truths as you’ve taught them.”

sn56.16:3.2.verse: It’s good that you remember the four noble truths as I’ve taught them.

sn56.16:3.3.verse: Suffering is the first noble truth I’ve taught, and that’s how you should remember it.

sn56.16:3.4.verse: For if any ascetic or brahmin should say this:

sn56.16:3.5.verse: ‘What the ascetic Gotama teaches is not the first noble truth of suffering.

sn56.16:3.6.verse: I’ll deny this first noble truth of suffering and describe another first noble truth of suffering.’

sn56.16:3.10.verse: The practice that leads to the cessation of suffering is the fourth noble truth I’ve taught, and that’s how you should remember it.

sn56.16:3.11.verse: For if any ascetic or brahmin should say this:

sn56.16:3.12.verse: ‘What the ascetic Gotama teaches is not the fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.16:3.13.verse: I’ll deny this fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering and describe another fourth noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

sn56.16:3.15.verse: That’s how you should remember the four noble truths as I’ve taught them.

sn56.16:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.17:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.17:1.1.verse: Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha:

sn56.17:1.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘ignorance’.

sn56.17:1.4.verse: And how is an ignoramus defined?”

sn56.17:1.5.verse: “Not knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.17:1.7.verse: And this is how an ignoramus is defined.

sn56.17:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.18:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.18:1.1.verse: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn56.18:1.2.verse: “Sir, they speak of this thing called ‘knowledge’.

sn56.18:1.4.verse: And how is a knowing one defined?”

sn56.18:1.5.verse: “Knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.18:1.7.verse: And this is how a knowing one is defined.

sn56.18:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.19:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.19:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I’ve declared: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering.’

sn56.19:1.2.verse: For that there are limitless arrangements, phrasings, and illustrations:

sn56.19:1.3.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that this is the noble truth of suffering.’

sn56.19:1.4.verse: I’ve declared: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.’ …

sn56.19:1.5.verse: I’ve declared: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.’ …

sn56.19:1.6.verse: I’ve declared: ‘This is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

sn56.19:1.7.verse: For that there are limitless arrangements, phrasings, and illustrations:

sn56.19:1.8.verse: ‘This is another way of saying that this is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’

sn56.19:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.20:0.2.verse: 2. Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma

sn56.20:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these four things are real, not unreal, not otherwise.

sn56.20:1.6.verse: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’ …

sn56.20:1.7.verse: These four things are real, not unreal, not otherwise.

sn56.20:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.21:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis at the village of Koṭi.

sn56.21:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn56.21:1.3.verse: “Mendicants, due to not understanding and not penetrating four noble truths, both you and I have wandered and transmigrated for such a very long time.

sn56.21:2.5.verse: and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.21:2.6.verse: These noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path have been understood and comprehended. Craving for continued existence has been cut off; the leash to existence is ended; now there’ll be no more future lives.”

sn56.21:3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn56.21:3.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn56.21:4.3.verse: we have transmigrated for a long time

sn56.21:4.4.verse: from one rebirth to the next.

sn56.21:5.1.verse: But now that these truths have been seen,

sn56.21:5.2.verse: the leash to existence is eradicated.

sn56.21:5.3.verse: The root of suffering is cut off,

sn56.21:5.4.verse: now there’ll be no more future lives.”

sn56.22:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.22:1.2.verse: I don’t deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and don’t live having realized it with their own insight in this very life.

sn56.22:2.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.22:2.2.verse: I deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”

sn56.22:3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn56.22:3.2.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

sn56.22:4.1.verse: “There are those who don’t understand suffering

sn56.22:5.1.verse: And they do not know the path

sn56.22:5.2.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

sn56.22:5.4.verse: as well as the release by wisdom.

sn56.22:5.6.verse: they continue to be reborn and grow old.

sn56.22:6.1.verse: But there are those who understand suffering

sn56.22:7.2.verse: that leads to the stilling of suffering.

sn56.22:7.3.verse: They’re endowed with the heart’s release,

sn56.22:7.4.verse: as well as the release by wisdom.

sn56.22:7.6.verse: they don’t continue to be reborn and grow old.”

sn56.23:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.23:1.4.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.23:1.5.verse: These are the four noble truths.

sn56.23:1.6.verse: It is because he has truly understood these four noble truths that the Realized One is called ‘the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha’.

sn56.23:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.24:1.2.verse: “Mendicants, whatever perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas truly awaken—in the past,

sn56.24:1.4.verse: or present—all of them truly awaken to the four noble truths.

sn56.24:2.2.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.24:2.3.verse: Whatever perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas truly awaken—in the past,

sn56.24:2.5.verse: or present—all of them truly awaken to the four noble truths.

sn56.24:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.25:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see.

sn56.25:1.2.verse: For one who knows and sees what?

sn56.25:1.3.verse: The ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.25:1.4.verse: The ending of the defilements is for one who knows and sees this.

sn56.25:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.26:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, those who you have sympathy for, and those worth listening to—friends and colleagues, relatives and family—should be encouraged, supported, and established by you in the true comprehension of the four noble truths.

sn56.26:2.2.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.26:2.3.verse: Those who you have sympathy for, and those worth listening to—friends and colleagues, relatives and family—should be encouraged, supported, and established by you in the true comprehension of these four noble truths.

sn56.26:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.27:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.27:1.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.27:1.4.verse: These four noble truths are real, not unreal, not otherwise.

sn56.27:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.28:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.28:1.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.28:1.4.verse: In this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, the Realized One is the Noble One.

sn56.28:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.29:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are these four noble truths.

sn56.29:1.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.29:1.4.verse: These are the four noble truths.

sn56.29:1.5.verse: Of these four noble truths, there is one to be completely understood, one to be given up, one to be realized, and one to be developed.

sn56.29:2.1.verse: And which noble truth should be completely understood?

sn56.29:2.2.verse: The noble truth of suffering should be completely understood. The noble truth of the origin of suffering should be given up. The noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized. The noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering should be developed.

sn56.29:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.30:1.1.verse: At one time several mendicants were staying in the land of the Cetīs at Sahajāti.

sn56.30:1.2.verse: Now at that time, after the meal, on return from almsround, several senior mendicants sat together in the pavilion and this discussion came up among them:

sn56.30:1.3.verse: “Reverends, does someone who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?”

sn56.30:2.1.verse: When they said this, Venerable Gavampati said to those senior mendicants:

sn56.30:2.2.verse: “Reverends, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:

sn56.30:2.3.verse: ‘Someone who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.30:2.4.verse: Someone who sees the origin of suffering also sees suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.30:2.5.verse: Someone who sees the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, the origin of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.30:2.6.verse: Someone who sees the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, the origin of suffering, and the cessation of suffering.’”

sn56.31:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in a rosewood grove.

sn56.31:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha picked up a few rosewood leaves in his hand and addressed the mendicants:

sn56.31:1.5.verse: the few leaves in my hand, or those in the grove above?”

sn56.31:1.6.verse: “Sir, the few leaves in your hand are a tiny amount.

sn56.31:1.7.verse: There are far more leaves in the grove above.”

sn56.31:1.8.verse: “In the same way, there is much more that I have directly known but have not explained to you. What I have explained is a tiny amount.

sn56.31:1.9.verse: And why haven’t I explained it?

sn56.31:1.10.verse: Because it’s not beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. It doesn’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.31:1.11.verse: That’s why I haven’t explained it.

sn56.31:2.2.verse: I have explained: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.31:3.1.verse: And why have I explained this?

sn56.31:3.2.verse: Because it’s beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. It leads to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.31:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.32:1.2.verse: ‘Without truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.32:2.1.verse: It’s as if someone were to say:

sn56.32:2.2.verse: ‘I’ll make a basket out of acacia leaves or pine needles or myrobalan leaves, and use it to carry water or ripe palmyra fruit.’

sn56.32:2.4.verse: In the same way, suppose someone were to say:

sn56.32:2.5.verse: ‘Without truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.32:3.1.verse: But suppose someone were to say:

sn56.32:3.2.verse: ‘After truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.32:4.1.verse: It’s as if someone were to say:

sn56.32:4.2.verse: ‘I’ll make a basket out of lotus leaves or flame-of-the-forest leaves or camel’s foot creeper leaves, and use it to carry water or ripe palmyra fruit.’

sn56.32:4.4.verse: In the same way, suppose someone were to say:

sn56.32:4.5.verse: ‘After truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.32:5.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.33:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a stick was tossed up in the air. Sometimes it’d fall on its bottom and sometimes the top.

sn56.33:1.2.verse: It’s the same for sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving. Sometimes they go from this world to the other world, and sometimes they come from the other world to this world.

sn56.33:1.4.verse: It’s because they haven’t seen the four noble truths.

sn56.33:1.6.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.33:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.34:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, if your clothes or head were on fire, what would you do about it?”

sn56.34:1.2.verse: “Sir, if our clothes or head were on fire, we’d apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness in order to extinguish it.”

sn56.34:2.1.verse: “Mendicants, so long as you have not encompassed the four noble truths, regard your burning head or clothes with equanimity, ignore them, and apply extraordinary enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to truly comprehending the four noble truths.

sn56.34:2.3.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.34:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.35:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose there was a man with a lifespan of a hundred years.

sn56.35:1.2.verse: And someone might say to him:

sn56.35:1.3.verse: ‘Come now, my man, they’ll strike you with a hundred spears in the morning, at midday, and in the late afternoon.

sn56.35:1.4.verse: And you’ll live for a hundred years being struck with three hundred spears every day. But when a hundred years have passed, you will comprehend the four noble truths for the first time.’

sn56.35:2.1.verse: For an earnest gentleman this is sufficient reason to submit.

sn56.35:2.3.verse: This transmigration has no known beginning.

sn56.35:2.4.verse: No first point is found of blows by spears, swords, arrows, and axes.

sn56.35:2.6.verse: But the comprehension of the four noble truths doesn’t come with pain or sadness, I say.

sn56.35:2.7.verse: Rather, the comprehension of the four noble truths comes only with pleasure and happiness, I say.

sn56.35:2.9.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.35:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.36:1.1.verse: “Suppose a person was to strip all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in the Black Plum Tree Land, gather them together into one pile,

sn56.36:1.3.verse: Then they’d impale the large creatures in the ocean on large stakes; the medium-sized creatures on medium-sized stakes; and the small creatures on small stakes.

sn56.36:1.4.verse: They wouldn’t run out of sizable creatures in the ocean before

sn56.36:2.1.verse: using up all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in the Black Plum Tree Land.

sn56.36:2.2.verse: There are far more small creatures in the ocean than this, so it wouldn’t be feasible to impale them on stakes.

sn56.36:2.4.verse: Because of the small size of those life-forms.

sn56.36:2.5.verse: That’s how big the plane of loss is.

sn56.36:2.6.verse: An individual accomplished in view, exempt from that vast plane of loss, truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.36:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.37:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the dawn is the forerunner and harbinger of the sunrise.

sn56.37:1.2.verse: In the same way, for a mendicant right view is the forerunner and harbinger of truly comprehending the four noble truths.

sn56.37:1.3.verse: That mendicant can expect to truly understand:

sn56.37:1.4.verse: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.37:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.38:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, as long as the moon and the sun don’t arise in the world, no great light or great radiance appears.

sn56.38:1.3.verse: Day and night aren’t found, nor months and fortnights, nor seasons and years.

sn56.38:2.1.verse: But when the moon and the sun arise in the world, a great light, a great radiance appears.

sn56.38:2.3.verse: Day and night are found, and months and fortnights, and seasons and years.

sn56.38:2.4.verse: In the same way, as long as the Realized One doesn’t arise in the world, no great light or great radiance appears.

sn56.38:2.6.verse: There’s no explanation of the four noble truths, no teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of them.

sn56.38:3.1.verse: But when the Realized One arises in the world, a great light, a great radiance appears.

sn56.38:3.3.verse: Then there’s the explanation of the four noble truths, the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of them.

sn56.38:3.5.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.38:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.39:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.39:1.2.verse: They gaze up at the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking:

sn56.39:1.3.verse: ‘Surely this worthy one knows and sees.’

sn56.39:2.1.verse: Suppose there was a light tuft of cotton-wool or kapok which was taken up by the wind and landed on level ground.

sn56.39:2.2.verse: The east wind wafts it west; the west wind wafts it east; the north wind wafts it south; and the south wind wafts it north.

sn56.39:2.4.verse: It’s because the tuft of cotton-wool is so light.

sn56.39:2.5.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.39:2.6.verse: They gaze up at the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking:

sn56.39:2.7.verse: ‘Surely this worthy one knows and sees.’

sn56.39:2.9.verse: It’s because they haven’t seen the four noble truths.

sn56.39:3.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.39:3.2.verse: They don’t gaze up at the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking:

sn56.39:3.3.verse: ‘Surely this worthy one knows and sees.’

sn56.39:4.1.verse: Suppose there was an iron pillar or an Indra’s pillar with deep foundations, firmly embedded, imperturbable and unshakable.

sn56.39:4.2.verse: Even if violent storms were to blow up out of the east, the west, the north, and the south, they couldn’t make it shake or rock or tremble.

sn56.39:4.4.verse: It’s because that Indra’s pillar is firmly embedded, with deep foundations.

sn56.39:4.5.verse: In the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.39:4.6.verse: They don’t gaze up at the face of another ascetic or brahmin, thinking:

sn56.39:4.7.verse: ‘Surely this worthy one knows and sees.’

sn56.39:4.9.verse: It’s because they have clearly seen the four noble truths.

sn56.39:4.11.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.39:5.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.40:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, take any mendicant who truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.40:1.2.verse: An ascetic or brahmin might come from the east, west, north, or south wanting to debate, seeking a debate, thinking:

sn56.40:1.3.verse: ‘I’ll refute their doctrine!’ It’s simply impossible for them to legitimately make that mendicant shake or rock or tremble.

sn56.40:2.1.verse: Suppose there was a stone post, sixteen feet long.

sn56.40:2.2.verse: Eight feet were buried underground, and eight above ground.

sn56.40:2.3.verse: Even if violent storms were to blow up out of the east, the west, the north, and the south, they couldn’t make it shake or rock or tremble.

sn56.40:2.5.verse: It’s because that stone post is firmly embedded, with deep foundations.

sn56.40:2.6.verse: In the same way, take any mendicant who truly understands: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.40:2.7.verse: An ascetic or brahmin might come from the east, west, north, or south wanting to debate, seeking a debate, thinking: ‘I’ll refute their doctrine!’ It’s simply impossible for them to legitimately make that mendicant shake or rock or tremble.

sn56.40:2.12.verse: It’s because they have clearly seen the four noble truths.

sn56.40:2.14.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.40:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.41:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn56.41:1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn56.41:1.3.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a certain person left Rājagaha, thinking ‘I’ll speculate about the world.’ They went to the Sumāgadhā lotus pond and sat down on the bank speculating about the world.

sn56.41:1.4.verse: Then that person saw an army of four divisions enter a lotus stalk.

sn56.41:1.5.verse: When he saw this he thought,

sn56.41:1.6.verse: ‘I’ve gone mad, really, I’ve lost my mind!

sn56.41:1.7.verse: I’m seeing things that don’t exist in the world.’

sn56.41:2.1.verse: Then that person entered the city and informed a large crowd,

sn56.41:2.2.verse: ‘I’ve gone mad, really, I’ve lost my mind!

sn56.41:2.3.verse: I’m seeing things that don’t exist in the world.’

sn56.41:2.4.verse: ‘But how is it that you’re mad? How have you lost your mind?

sn56.41:2.5.verse: And what have you seen that doesn’t exist in the world?’

sn56.41:2.6.verse: ‘Sirs, I left Rājagaha, thinking “I’ll speculate about the world.” I went to the Sumāgadhā lotus pond and sat down on the bank speculating about the world.

sn56.41:2.7.verse: Then I saw an army of four divisions enter a lotus stalk.

sn56.41:2.8.verse: That’s why I’m mad, that’s why I’ve lost my mind.

sn56.41:2.9.verse: And that’s what I’ve seen that doesn’t exist in the world.’

sn56.41:2.10.verse: ‘Well, my man, you’re definitely mad, you’ve definitely lost your mind.

sn56.41:2.11.verse: And you’re seeing things that don’t exist in the world.’

sn56.41:3.1.verse: But what that person saw was in fact real, not unreal.

sn56.41:3.2.verse: Once upon a time, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

sn56.41:3.3.verse: In that battle the gods won and the titans lost.

sn56.41:3.4.verse: The defeated and terrified titans entered the citadel of the titans through the lotus stalk only to confuse the gods.

sn56.41:4.1.verse: So mendicants, don’t speculate about the world.

sn56.41:4.2.verse: For example: the cosmos is eternal, or not eternal, or finite, or infinite; the soul and the body are one and the same, or the soul is one thing, the body another; after death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.

sn56.41:4.4.verse: Because those thoughts aren’t beneficial or relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They don’t lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.41:5.1.verse: When you think something up, you should think: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.

sn56.41:5.3.verse: Because those thoughts are beneficial and relevant to the fundamentals of the spiritual life. They lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.

sn56.41:6.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.42:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

sn56.42:1.2.verse: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,

sn56.42:1.3.verse: “Come, mendicants, let’s go to Inspiration Peak for the day’s meditation.”

sn56.42:1.5.verse: Then the Buddha together with several mendicants went to Inspiration Peak.

sn56.42:1.6.verse: A certain mendicant saw the big cliff there

sn56.42:1.8.verse: “Sir, that big cliff is really big and scary.

sn56.42:1.9.verse: Is there any other cliff bigger and scarier than this one?”

sn56.42:2.2.verse: “Mendicant, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.42:2.3.verse: They take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:2.4.verse: Since they take pleasure in such choices, they continue to make them.

sn56.42:2.5.verse: Having made choices that lead to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they fall down the cliff of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:2.6.verse: They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:2.7.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.42:3.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.42:3.2.verse: They don’t take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:3.3.verse: Since they don’t take pleasure in such choices, they stop making them.

sn56.42:3.4.verse: Having stopped making choices that lead to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they don’t fall down the cliff of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:3.5.verse: They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.42:3.6.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.42:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.43:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there is a hell called ‘The Great Scorching’.

sn56.43:1.2.verse: There, whatever sight you see with your eye is unlikable, not likable; undesirable, not desirable; unpleasant, not pleasant.

sn56.43:1.3.verse: Whatever sound you hear … Whatever odor you smell … Whatever flavor you taste …

sn56.43:1.5.verse: Whatever idea you know with your mind is unlikable, not likable; undesirable, not desirable; unpleasant, not pleasant.”

sn56.43:2.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

sn56.43:2.2.verse: “Sir, that scorching really is mighty, so very mighty.

sn56.43:2.3.verse: Is there any other scorching more mighty and terrifying than this one?”

sn56.43:3.2.verse: “Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.43:3.3.verse: They take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth …

sn56.43:3.4.verse: They continue to make such choices …

sn56.43:3.5.verse: Having made such choices, they burn with the scorching of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.43:3.6.verse: They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.43:3.7.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.43:4.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.43:4.2.verse: They don’t take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth …

sn56.43:4.4.verse: Having stopped making such choices, they don’t burn with the scorching of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.43:4.5.verse: They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.43:4.6.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.43:5.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.44:1.2.verse: ‘Without truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.44:2.1.verse: It’s as if someone were to say:

sn56.44:2.2.verse: ‘Before the lower story of a bungalow is built, I will hoist up the upper story.’

sn56.44:2.4.verse: In the same way, suppose someone were to say:

sn56.44:2.5.verse: ‘Without truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.44:3.1.verse: But suppose someone were to say:

sn56.44:3.2.verse: ‘After truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.44:4.1.verse: It’s as if someone were to say:

sn56.44:4.2.verse: ‘After the lower story of a bungalow is built, I will hoist up the upper story.’

sn56.44:4.4.verse: In the same way, suppose someone were to say:

sn56.44:4.5.verse: ‘After truly comprehending the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I will completely make an end of suffering.’

sn56.44:5.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.45:1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

sn56.45:1.2.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.

sn56.45:1.3.verse: He saw several Licchavi youths practicing archery near the town hall. They were shooting arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, shaft after shaft without missing.

sn56.45:1.4.verse: When he saw this he thought,

sn56.45:1.5.verse: “These Licchavi youths really are trained, so well trained,

sn56.45:1.6.verse: in that they shoot arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, shaft after shaft without missing.”

sn56.45:2.1.verse: Then Ānanda wandered for alms in Vesālī. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

sn56.45:3.2.verse: Which is harder and more challenging:

sn56.45:3.3.verse: to shoot arrows from a distance through a small keyhole, shaft after shaft without missing? Or to take a horsehair split into seven strands and penetrate one tip with another tip?”

sn56.45:3.4.verse: “It’s more difficult and challenging, sir, to take a horsehair split into seven strands and penetrate one tip with another tip.”

sn56.45:3.5.verse: “Still, Ānanda, those who truly penetrate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path penetrate something tougher than that.

sn56.45:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.46:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, the boundless gloom of interstellar space is so utterly dark that even the luminosity of the moon and the sun, so mighty and powerful, makes no impression.”

sn56.46:2.1.verse: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha,

sn56.46:2.2.verse: “Sir, that darkness really is mighty, so very mighty.

sn56.46:2.3.verse: Is there any other darkness more mighty and terrifying than this one?”

sn56.46:3.2.verse: “There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.46:3.3.verse: They take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth …

sn56.46:3.4.verse: They continue to make such choices …

sn56.46:3.5.verse: Having made such choices, they fall into the darkness of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.46:3.6.verse: They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.46:3.7.verse: They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.46:4.1.verse: There are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.46:4.2.verse: They don’t take pleasure in choices that lead to rebirth …

sn56.46:4.4.verse: Having stopped making such choices, they don’t fall into the darkness of rebirth, old age, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.46:4.5.verse: They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.

sn56.46:4.6.verse: They’re freed from suffering, I say.

sn56.46:5.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.47:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a person were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the ocean. And there was a one-eyed turtle who popped up once every hundred years.

sn56.47:1.3.verse: Would that one-eyed turtle, popping up once every hundred years, still poke its neck through the hole in that yoke?”

sn56.47:1.4.verse: “Only after a very long time, sir, if ever.”

sn56.47:2.1.verse: “That one-eyed turtle might poke its neck through the hole in that yoke, but in any case it’d be sooner than a fool fallen to the underworld is reborn as a human being, I say.

sn56.47:3.2.verse: Because in that place there’s no principled or moral conduct, and no doing what is good and skillful.

sn56.47:3.3.verse: There they just prey on each other, preying on the weak.

sn56.47:3.5.verse: It’s because they haven’t seen the four noble truths.

sn56.47:3.7.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.47:4.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.48:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose the earth was entirely covered with water.

sn56.48:1.2.verse: And a person threw a yoke with a single hole into it.

sn56.48:1.3.verse: The east wind wafts it west; the west wind wafts it east; the north wind wafts it south; and the south wind wafts it north.

sn56.48:1.4.verse: And there was a one-eyed turtle who popped up once every hundred years.

sn56.48:1.6.verse: Would that one-eyed turtle, popping up once every hundred years, still poke its neck through the hole in that yoke?”

sn56.48:2.1.verse: “That’s how anomalous it is to get reborn as a human being.

sn56.48:2.2.verse: And that’s how anomalous it is for a Realized One to arise in the world, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha.

sn56.48:2.3.verse: And that’s how anomalous it is for the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One to shine in the world.

sn56.48:2.4.verse: And now, mendicants, you have been reborn as a human being. A Realized One has arisen in the world, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. And the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One shines in the world.

sn56.48:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.49:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a person was to place on Sineru, the king of mountains, seven pebbles the size of mung beans.

sn56.49:1.3.verse: Which is more: the seven pebbles the size of mung beans? Or Sineru, the king of mountains?”

sn56.49:1.4.verse: “Sir, Sineru, the king of mountains, is certainly more.

sn56.49:1.5.verse: The seven pebbles the size of mung beans are tiny.

sn56.49:1.6.verse: Compared to Sineru, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.49:1.7.verse: “In the same way, for an individual with comprehension, a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering that’s over and done with is more, what’s left is tiny.

sn56.49:1.8.verse: Compared to the mass of suffering in the past that’s over and done with, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction, since there are at most seven more lives.

sn56.49:1.9.verse: Such an individual truly understands about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.49:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.50:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose Sineru, the king of mountains, was worn away and eroded except seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds.

sn56.50:1.3.verse: Which is more: the portion of Sineru, the king of mountains, that has been worn away and eroded? Or the seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds that are left?”

sn56.50:1.4.verse: “Sir, the portion of Sineru, the king of mountains, that has been worn away and eroded is certainly more.

sn56.50:1.5.verse: The seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds are tiny.

sn56.50:1.6.verse: Compared to Sineru, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.50:1.7.verse: “In the same way, for an individual with comprehension, a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering that’s over and done with is more, what’s left is tiny.

sn56.50:1.8.verse: Compared to the mass of suffering in the past that’s over and done with, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction, since there are at most seven more lives.

sn56.50:1.9.verse: Such an individual truly understands about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.50:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.51:1.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, addressed the mendicants:

sn56.51:1.3.verse: Which is more: the little bit of dirt on my fingernail, or this great earth?”

sn56.51:1.4.verse: “Sir, the great earth is certainly more. The little bit of dirt on your fingernail is tiny.

sn56.51:1.5.verse: Compared to the great earth, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.51:1.6.verse: “In the same way, for an individual with comprehension, a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering that’s over and done with is more, what’s left is tiny.

sn56.51:1.7.verse: Compared to the mass of suffering in the past that’s over and done with, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction, since there are at most seven more lives.

sn56.51:1.8.verse: Such an individual truly understands about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.51:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.52:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose there was a lotus pond that was fifty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, and fifty leagues deep, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it.

sn56.52:1.2.verse: Then a person would pick up some water on the tip of a blade of grass.

sn56.52:1.4.verse: Which is more: the water on the tip of the blade of grass, or the water in the lotus pond?”

sn56.52:1.5.verse: “Sir, the water in the lotus pond is certainly more. The water on the tip of a blade of grass is tiny.

sn56.52:1.6.verse: Compared to the water in the lotus pond, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.52:1.7.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.52:1.8.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.53:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are places where the great rivers—the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—join together and converge.

sn56.53:1.2.verse: Suppose a person was to draw two or three drops of water from such a place.

sn56.53:1.4.verse: Which is more: the two or three drops drawn out or the water in the confluence?”

sn56.53:1.5.verse: “Sir, the water in the confluence is certainly more. The two or three drops drawn out are tiny.

sn56.53:1.6.verse: Compared to the water in the confluence, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.53:1.7.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.53:1.8.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.54:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, there are places where the great rivers—the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—join together and converge.

sn56.54:1.2.verse: Suppose that water dried up and evaporated except two or three drops.

sn56.54:1.4.verse: Which is more: the water in the confluence that has dried up and evaporated, or the two or three drops left?”

sn56.54:1.5.verse: “Sir, the water in the confluence that has dried up and evaporated is certainly more. The two or three drops left are tiny.

sn56.54:1.6.verse: Compared to the water in the confluence that has dried up and evaporated, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.54:1.7.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.54:1.8.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.55:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a person was to place seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds on the great earth.

sn56.55:1.3.verse: Which is more: the seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds, or the great earth?”

sn56.55:1.4.verse: “Sir, the great earth is certainly more. The seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds are tiny.

sn56.55:1.5.verse: Compared to the great earth, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.55:1.6.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.55:1.7.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.56:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose the great earth was worn away and eroded except seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds.

sn56.56:1.3.verse: Which is more: the great earth that has been worn away and eroded, or the seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds that are left?”

sn56.56:1.4.verse: “Sir, the great earth that has been worn away and eroded is certainly more. The seven clay balls the size of jujube seeds are tiny.

sn56.56:1.5.verse: Compared to the great earth that has been worn away and eroded, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.56:1.6.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.56:1.7.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.57:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a man was to draw up two or three drops of water from the ocean.

sn56.57:1.3.verse: Which is more: the two or three drops drawn out or the water in the ocean?”

sn56.57:1.4.verse: “Sir, the water in the ocean is certainly more. The two or three drops drawn out are tiny.

sn56.57:1.5.verse: Compared to the water in the ocean, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.57:1.7.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.59:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose a person was to place seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds on the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

sn56.59:1.3.verse: Which is more: the seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds, or the Himalayas, the king of mountains?”

sn56.59:1.4.verse: “Sir, the Himalayas, the king of mountains, is certainly more. The seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds are tiny.

sn56.59:1.5.verse: Compared to the Himalayas, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.59:1.6.verse: “In the same way, for a noble disciple …

sn56.59:1.7.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.60:1.1.verse: “Mendicants, suppose the Himalayas, the king of mountains, was worn away and eroded except seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds.

sn56.60:1.3.verse: Which is more: the portion of the Himalayas, the king of mountains, that has been worn away and eroded, or the seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds that are left?”

sn56.60:1.4.verse: “Sir, the portion of the Himalayas, the king of mountains, that has been worn away and eroded is certainly more. The seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds are tiny.

sn56.60:1.5.verse: Compared to the Himalayas, they don’t count, there’s no comparison, they’re not worth a fraction.”

sn56.60:1.6.verse: “In the same way, for an individual with comprehension, a noble disciple accomplished in view, the suffering that’s over and done with is more, what’s left is tiny.

sn56.60:1.7.verse: Compared to the mass of suffering in the past that’s over and done with, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction, since there are at most seven more lives.

sn56.60:1.8.verse: Such an individual truly understands about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.60:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.61:1.1.verse: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, addressed the mendicants:

sn56.61:1.3.verse: Which is more: the little bit of dirt on my fingernail, or this great earth?”

sn56.61:1.4.verse: “Sir, the great earth is certainly more. The little bit of dirt on your fingernail is tiny.

sn56.61:1.5.verse: Compared to the great earth, it doesn’t count, there’s no comparison, it’s not worth a fraction.”

sn56.61:2.1.verse: “In the same way, the sentient beings reborn as humans are few, while those not reborn as humans are many.

sn56.61:2.3.verse: It’s because they haven’t seen the four noble truths.

sn56.61:2.5.verse: The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

sn56.61:3.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation …”

sn56.131:0.3.verse: Dying as Ghosts and Reborn as Ghosts

sn56.131:1.1.verse: “… the sentient beings who die as ghosts and are reborn as gods are few, while those who die as ghosts and are reborn in the ghost realm are many.

sn56.131:1.3.verse: It’s because they haven’t seen the four noble truths.

sn56.131:1.5.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

sn56.131:2.1.verse: That’s why you should practice meditation to understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.”

sn56.131:3.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

sn56.131:3.2.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.
